# CHARLES the Sixth, by favor of Divine
## Clemency, Elected Emperor of the Romans, forever August, and King of Germany, Spain, Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, Slavonia, etc.; Archduke of Austria; Duke of Burgundy, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and Württemberg; Count of Tyrol, etc.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut decorative initial letter 'C' at the start of the text. The letter is enclosed in a square frame filled with elaborate foliage, vines, and scrolls in a Late Renaissance or Baroque style.</image-desc>

We acknowledge and make known to everyone by the tenor of these present documents, that, whereas our faithful and beloved subject of the Empire, *Joannes Gastel*, has taken care to humbly explain to Us the manner in which he has resolved to commit the *Practical Treasury* <note>original: *Thesaurum Practicum*, a massive legal and political encyclopedia written by the scholar Christoph Besold</note> of *Christoph Besold* to the press; but since he fears that through the envy of rivals, who might imitate this edition, he may be frustrated in the fruit of his expense and labor; and he has therefore humbly petitioned Us that We might most graciously deign to come to his aid against such loss by our Imperial Privilege; We have judged that his equally submissive and fair petition should be granted.

And therefore, by Our Imperial Authority, We firmly inhibit, forbid, and interdict all and singular booksellers, bookbinders, printers, and any others whatsoever exercising the book trade or business, that no one dare or presume to reprint the aforementioned *Besold’s Practical Treasury* under this or any other title for the span of *ten* years, to be calculated from this present day, within the borders of the Holy Roman Empire and Our hereditary Kingdoms and Dominions, or to give it to others to be reprinted, or to bring in, sell, or distribute copies printed elsewhere, without the will and consent of the aforementioned Petitioner, his heirs and successors, obtained in writing.

If anyone, however, by doing otherwise, should presume to violate and treat with contempt this Our Privilege or Interdict, let him know that he is to be deprived of all such copies—wherever they may be found, having been wrongly reprinted or imported—which the said *Joannes Gastel* may claim for himself, either by his own authority or with the help of the local Magistrate; and furthermore, he shall be punished with a fine of *five marks of pure gold* <note>A "mark" was a unit of weight for precious metals; five marks of pure gold represented a very substantial sum, intended to make "pirating" the book financially ruinous</note>, to be paid to Our treasury or fiscal office—

<summary>This page contains an official Imperial Privilege (an early form of copyright) granted by Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI to the printer Joannes Gastel. It grants Gastel exclusive rights to print and sell Christoph Besold’s "Thesaurus Practicus" for ten years, establishing heavy fines for any unauthorized reproductions.</summary>

<keywords>Charles VI, Joannes Gastel, Christoph Besold, Practical Treasury, Imperial Privilege, copyright law, Holy Roman Empire, book trade history, printing monopoly</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>continuity: The fragment "ſtro" at the beginning of this page completes "Aerario Nostro" (Our Treasury), continuing the sentence from the previous page regarding the financial penalties for copyright infringement.</meta>

Our Imperial Treasury, and to the injured party in equal measure, with all hope of pardon removed, We decree [the offender] to be punished, provided that the tenor of this Our Privilege is found printed at the front of the book, and the customary five copies are presented to Our Imperial Aulic Council <note>The *Reichshofrat*, one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire, which handled matters of imperial privileges and feudal law</note>. We therefore command all and singular Our subjects and beloved faithful of the Holy Roman Empire, and of Our hereditary Kingdoms and Dominions, both Ecclesiastical and Secular, of whatever state, grade, dignity, or order they may be; especially those who, established in the Magistracy, administer law and justice either in their own place or in the name of their Superiors, that they should not allow anyone to violate, despise, or transgress this Our Imperial Privilege with impunity; but if they find any stubborn <note>original: *contumaces*, referring to those who willfully defy legal orders</note> offenders, they should ensure they are punished with the fine <term>mulcta: a financial penalty or fine</term> established by Us and restrained by whatever suitable means, insofar as they themselves wish to avoid Our most heavy indignation and the aforementioned penalty. In testimony of these letters, signed by Our hand and secured by the impression of Our Imperial seal, which were given at Laxenburg <note>A market town near Vienna, home to a complex of imperial palaces used as a summer retreat by the Habsburgs</note> on the twenty-second day of June, in the year one thousand seven hundred and thirty-nine; the twenty-eighth year of our Roman reign, the thirty-sixth of our Spanish, and the twenty-ninth of our Hungarian and Bohemian reigns.

# CHARLES.

<image-desc>A circular seal in the center of the page featuring a decorative border enclosing the letters LS (Locus Sigilli), indicating the "Place of the Seal".</image-desc>

->Witnessed by Johann Adam, Count of Metsch.<-

->By the personal command of His Sacred Imperial Majesty,<-
->Johann Joachim Hayek of Waldstätten.<-

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>continuity: This page continues the formal dedication from the previous page. Having established the titles of Emperor Leopold I and Elector Ferdinand Maria, the author now addresses them directly to explain the philosophical reasons for his scholarly retirement and why this specific legal and historical work is dedicated to them. The catchword "stros" from the previous page's metadata matches the end of "Ministros" on this page.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative headband consists of two horizontal rows of repeating ornaments: the top row features stylized starburst or floral patterns, and the bottom row features fleur-de-lis motifs. A large ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' features a floral design within a square frame.</image-desc>

He who has lived well hidden, has lived well, <note>original: *Qui benè latuit, benè vixit* — a famous Ovidian maxim suggesting that a private life away from public turmoil is the most virtuous.</note> the Ancients said. With these words, they meant that an account must be rendered to GOD, the Best and Greatest, <note>original: *DEO T. O. M.* (Deo Ter Optimo Maximo)</note> not just for our business, but for our leisure. And this is most correct, Most August Emperor, Most Serene Elector! For **the art of living well** <note>original: *τὸ benè vivere*</note> is proclaimed of **those who hide well**. Those who deal in works of darkness hide, but they *do not hide well*, because vices that have been concealed for a long time are eventually brought to the light. Those who do nothing hide, and those who do something else hide; but while a great part of life slips away in this manner, it cannot truly be said of them that they *lived well*, because they lived neither for *God*, nor for *themselves*, nor for their *neighbor*, but were born—like useless weights upon the earth—only to consume its fruits.

But he truly seems to me to have *hidden well* who puts these cares before all others: so that, mindful of *Divine worship*, he does not withhold from his soul the food of the divine word; so that he serves all miserable persons in every way; so that he knows himself; and so that he is never less alone than when he is alone. Of such a person it can be said, without the fluttering of flattery, that he *lived well*, because his own conscience does not accuse him, because he knows he has not offended a merciful God, and because he is content with his lot, such as it is. Though enemies themselves may not be lacking, and though adversaries may—at the cost of wasting their own good hours—distort his writings, paintings, and sayings into a wicked sense, or lay traps for his reputation, assets, and *Charitable deeds*, they are all in vain. They scheme in vain and stir up lawsuits in vain; for with *God as Leader* and *Virtue as Companion*, wherever the Pious man moves his steps, he feels a calm sea. Since I believed these things were also said for me, I chose for myself for some years a sedentary life and **active leisure**. <note>original: *otium actuosum* — a concept where one's retirement from public life is spent in productive scholarly or spiritual work.</note> Therefore, when my previous **Historical-Political-Philological-Legal Additions** to the **Practical Treasury** of Christoph Besold <note>original: *Thesaurum Practicum Christophori Besoldi* — a major 17th-century legal reference work</note> (published in honor of the Most Reverend *Bishop of Eichstätt* in the year 1659) were entirely sold out—so much so that "there was no need for hanging ivy for wine that sells itself" <note>An ancient proverb meaning that a good product needs no advertisement.</note>—I decided to enrich this *Treasury* by reading almost countless recent authors.

I did not have to hesitate for long as to whom I should inscribe and dedicate this grand and vast work; YOUR MAJESTY AND SERENITY, as LIGHTS OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE, occurred to me. For if I look to *Besold* himself, his ashes and sacred embers consecrate this work to You. He who was an **Imperial Councilor**, rightly and deservedly owes immortal and greatest thanks to the **House of Austria** even after his death. He who was a **Professor at Ingolstadt** and **Electoral Councilor of Bavaria** owes a grateful kiss to the Patron of the praised **University of Ingolstadt** and to the **Electoral House**. If I look to *Myself* and my family, I recall with gratitude the confirmation of my **Coat of Arms**, the memory of certain **Privileges** mercifully granted to my ancestors by **Rudolph II**, and the continued investiture of **Fiefs** held for 131 years; because Paul Dietherr was among the **Ministers** of the never-sufficiently-praised MAXIMILIAN I...

<vocab>Christoph Besold (1577–1638): A prominent jurist and scholar. Thesaurus Practicus: A massive alphabetical encyclopedia of legal and political terms. Rudolph II: Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1576–1612). Maximilian I: Elector of Bavaria (reigned 1597–1651). Ingolstadt: A key university city in Bavaria.</vocab>

<summary>The author explains his decision to expand Christoph Besold's legal encyclopedia during his scholarly retirement, justifying the work's dedication to the Emperor and the Elector of Bavaria based on Besold's former service to their houses and the author's own ancestral ties to the Imperial court.</summary>
<keywords>leisure, otium actuosum, Christoph Besold, House of Austria, House of Bavaria, legal history, University of Ingolstadt, Imperial privileges, Paul Dietherr</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>continuity: This page concludes the formal dedication addressed to Emperor Leopold I and Elector Ferdinand Maria of Bavaria. The text begins mid-sentence, completing the word "Ministros" (Ministers) from the previous page's final thought about the author's family history and their service to the Austrian throne. The author, Christopher Louis Dietherr, transitions from personal gratitude to a humble request for patronage of his four-year scholarly project.</meta>

...Noble Court Ministers, and was able in every way to enjoy the brotherly friendship of Johann Christoph Fugger <note>Johann Christoph Fugger (1561–1612) was a member of the famous Fugger banking family, known for their immense wealth and influence in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, my family owes these and infinite other things to the *Most August House of Austria*. Indeed, it is now a kind of *religious duty* not to keep silent about the favors of the Divine!

By an equal right, the fact that I obtained a new feudal instrument—and a quite splendid one at that—while the *Empire was Vacant* <term>Imperial Interregnum: the period between the death of one Emperor and the election of the next, during which certain princes acted as administrators</term>, is a benefit of YOUR SERENITY, *Most Clement Elector*. I will not even mention that monks joined to me by blood once lived, and now live in nearby *Freising*, who cannot sufficiently praise your virtues which shine forth so competitively in you. **With a GENEROUS HAND** <note>original: *LARGA MANU* — a Latin idiom meaning to speak or give extensively.</note> I could elaborate on these matters; but it is a matter of conscience for me to distract you from your better cares for even a tiny moment (by "stealing your time") <note>original: *ἀναρέσει τοῦ χρόνου* (anairesei tou chronou)</note>, for which reason I "buckle the clasp" on my desire to speak further. For I know that **BOTH** of you, in the manner of *Gaius Julius Caesar*, are so delighted by studies that you descend even to the *smallest details*.

I ask you at least, again and again, most humbly and most fervently, that you look upon this slight gift with a SERENE COUNTENANCE. Although it is not of such great dignity that your SACRED and MOST ILLUSTRIOUS NAME should be inscribed upon it, nevertheless, among the sincere contests of obedience, a proof of my devotion also had to be shown. Protect me against *biting slander* <note>original: *Adversus Salem nigrum* — literally "against black salt," a Roman metaphor for stinging wit or malicious criticism.</note>, GREATEST HEROES, you who are the SUN and SALT of the world. Thus I will be safe under your shield, just as the house of *Pindar* remained most safe under *Alexander the Great* <note>According to legend, when Alexander the Great destroyed Thebes, he ordered the house of the poet Pindar to be spared out of respect for his genius.</note>.

I hope I shall be permitted to lay this writing at your most clement hands and knees! Look upon it with a kind gaze as I prostrate at YOUR feet, stretch out your right hand, lift me up, and protect me with Imperial and Electoral favor. Thus I shall not regret having spent almost four full years in *your honor*! Thus some *happiness* and joy must be granted *with you*, since a joyful heart does good like medicine, while sadness eats away at the heart of man. May the joy of happy Peace be true throughout the whole Empire and your territory, since there is no truer misery than false joy. May GOD, the Best and Greatest, preserve *you*, along with your *Most August and Serene Houses*, safe and flourishing in the affairs of the Empire for as long as possible amidst these whirlwinds of adversity which have not yet dissipated—you who, by your virtue and merits toward the *Holy Roman Empire*, have already rendered eternity favorable to your name! With this final glance, like a *gem*, I seal these pages. At Nuremberg, February 18th—which is the happy day of *Concord*—in the Year of the Redeemed World 1666.

->Of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty<-
->& Austrian Clemency,<-
->As well as<-
->Of Your Most Serene Electoral Highness,<-
->the most devoted & most subject servant<-

->Sends heartiest greetings.<-
<note>original: "S. D. P." — abbreviation for *Salutem Dicit Plurimam*, a standard formal greeting.</note>

**C**oming to be known some years ago to Mr. Philipp Zorer <note>Philipp Zorer (1585–1637) was a prominent legal official in the Palatinate.</note>, Palatine Councilor and Chancellor of Hilpoltstein, at the very time he published the second part of his *Questions*, he—out of his remarkable affection for me—urged me at a later time to consider and collect some *Additions* to the *Observations* of Wehner <note>Matthias Wehner (1583–1612), author of *Practicarum juris observationum*, a standard legal reference.</note>. When I had almost agreed to this, his printer immediately promised the funds and type for the aforementioned *Questions*, so that he might insert the said *Additions* to Wehner into the Frankfurt catalog, together with a treatise *on House, Hay, Fruit, and Fish Tithes* <note>original: *von Haus-Heu-Obst-und Fisch-Zehenden*</note>, as well as with an "oratorical trefoil" (a trilogy of speeches) on certain rarer subjects. Shortly thereafter, the esteemed printer changed his status and condition and took up a quiet way of life <note>A polite way of saying the printer retired or perhaps passed away.</note>, and the wishes of my friends went in different directions. Some at home asked that I desist from the undertaking, while eminent men from abroad demanded that treatise with reproaches and wished to extort it from me. I set all these things aside from my hands and mind.

Finally, a man born for the public good, greater than any praise and lacking none, Mr. Jacob Speidell, Licentiate of Law <note>original: *U. J. L.* — *Utriusque Juris Licentiatus*, a degree in both Civil and Canon Law.</note>, Chancellor to the most Serene and Reverend Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, and Bishop of Augsburg, asked me by letter to help. He noted that since the *Thesaurus Practicus* <term>Thesaurus Practicus: "A Treasury of Practice," a massive legal encyclopedia by Christoph Besold used by lawyers to find precedents.</term> by Christoph Besold—the most accomplished legal scholar—was to be published anew at the insistence of the printers due to a lack and scarcity of examples, and since his own *Additions* to the *Thesaurus* had already been separated from it to be added to the *Speculo Notabilium* (*Mirror of Notable Things*), he asked that I select certain items from my abundance of "Commonplaces" <term>Commonplaces: notebooks where scholars categorized excerpts, quotes, and legal precedents under topical headings.</term> and enrich Besold’s *Thesaurus* with new *Additions*. I deemed it a sin to refuse or deny anything to such a great patron—the very man whom Mr. Dr. Johann Otto Tabor also suggests should be appropriately imitated in his *Axioms of Barbosa*, in the Preface to the Reader.

With Divine mercy favoring me, I set my hand to the work; under my hands, it grew to such an extent that the *Additions to Wehner* nevertheless remained whole. Thus, the *Additions to Wehner* rest gently; thus, Besold is raised from the ashes. Since in years past, under the incomparable Dr. Ludwell <note>Wilhelm Ludwell (1589–1663), a famous law professor at the University of Altdorf.</note> of blessed memory at Altdorf, I had written and publicly defended a certain legal *Disputation* regarding the "active power to make a will"—or rather, regarding those to whom it is not permitted to make a will—it pleased me to present it under this title or frontispiece: **LEGAL TIDBITS** <note>original: *DELIBATA JURIS* — "delibata" implies things that have been "tasted" or carefully selected from a larger source.</note>. By these words, I was at least mindful of the fact that in preparing and compiling that *Disputation*, I had "sipped from" <note>A play on the word *delibasse*.</note> the manuscripts of my teachers and professors with the greatest care, inspecting them again and again. Thinking of nothing else besides this, I am followed by the charming and utterly more human than humanity itself, the Ludwell-

When in former years I had become known to Mr. Philipp Zorer, Palatine Councilor and Chancellor of Hilpoltstein, at the very time when he published the second part of his *Questions*, he subsequently encouraged me, out of his remarkable affection for me, to contemplate and collect some Additions to Wehner's *Observations* <note>Matthias Wehner (1583–1612) was a noted German jurist whose "Practicae Juris Observationes" was a standard reference.</note>. I set all these things aside from my hands and mind. At last, a man born for the public good, greater than all praise and lacking none, Mr. Jacob Speidel, Licentiate of Both Laws <note>U. J. L. (Utriusque Juris Licentiatus), meaning he was licensed in both Civil and Canon Law.</note> and Chancellor to the Most Serene and Reverend Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, and Bishop of Augsburg, asked me by letter—since the *Thesaurus Practicus* <note>The "Practical Treasury," a massive alphabetical encyclopedia of law.</note> of Christoph Besold, that most accomplished jurist, was to be published anew at the insistence of the printers due to a lack and scarcity of examples—and since his own Additions to the *Thesaurus* had already been separated from it and added to the *Speculum Notabilium* <note>Mirror of Notables.</note>—that I might select certain things from my abundance of Commonplaces <note>Research notebooks where scholars kept organized excerpts and thoughts.</note> and enrich Besold's *Thesaurus* with new Additions. When in former years, under the incomparable Mr. Dr. Ludwell <note>Nicolaus Ludwell (1605–1663), a famous professor of law at Altdorf.</note> of blessed memory at Altdorf, I had written and publicly defended a certain legal Disputation regarding the "active making of a will"—or rather, regarding those to whom it is not permitted to make a will—it pleased me to propose it under this title or frontispiece: *SAMPLINGS OF THE LAW* <note>original: "DELIBATA JURIS."</note>. But why do I write of rarer matters, many as yet "unproclaimed by another's mouth"? For example, the Law of Gardens (*Jus hortorum*). Some say this consists mostly of mere customs. Others say the same of the Law of Tithes. The Law of Tithes is known in general terms and can be dispatched in a few books. The Law of Gardens requires the guidance of a certain practitioner and a voluminous library if it is to be treated according to its dignity. The question of whether one can turn a garden into a meadow, and whether tithes must be paid on those things that grow in gardens, is treated by Caepolla <note>Bartolomeo Caepolla (1420–1475), an Italian jurist famous for his work on rural and urban servitudes.</note> in *On Urban Servitudes, chapter 76.* On tithes from pleasure gardens, Becker writes excellently in *Public Law, book 10, section 28, near the end.* But that single question does not exhaust the whole business. On the Right of a Third Party, Martha of Naples <note>Marcantonio Martha, a 16th-century Neapolitan jurist.</note> has much, but who has dared to write a treatise on this right? An inaugural disputation on "sale by bulk" <note>original: *venditione per aversionem*; a sale where goods are sold as a lot rather than by weight or measure.</note> appeared recently somewhere, but in how many universities is this still unknown? Johannes Monachus <note>Jean Le Moine (c. 1250–1313), a French cardinal and canonist.</note> wrote a whole treatise on clothing and the seizure of garments. But in how few hands is this treatise seen? ...besides those which have been treated by others until now, and as if unspoken by any other mouth, as will appear from this very work. The treatment of a specific law, with a legal opinion added so that the law's practical use becomes clear, is both useful and necessary. <meta>The author is continuing a discussion on the interdisciplinary utility of legal study, arguing that the Law is a "library in itself" for scholars of all kinds. This page follows a discussion on the preservation of academic legal disputations.</meta>

The <term>grammarian</term> <note>Latin: *grammatici*; referring here to scholars of language and literature</note>, long practiced in his art, may draw philological and grammatical points from the Law and demonstrate their use in practice if he consults the practitioners. For example, Rudinger discusses the pronouns **who, which, and that** <note>German: *welcher, welche, welches*</note> in his *Centuria 5, Observation 56*, and the citations therein. On the possessive pronouns **his or its** <note>German: *sein, seines, seine*</note>, see Rudinger *Centuria 4, Observation 56*. Regarding the pronoun "self" <note>Latin: *IPSE*</note>, see Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter, *part 3, consil. 8, num. 76*. The particle **"From"** <note>Latin: *Ex*</note> **is neither exhaustive nor restrictive**, according to the same source. What the adverbs **"until so long" and "all the while"** <note>German: *bis so lang, und alldieweil*</note> signify can be found in Rudinger, *Centuria 1, Observation 66*. Dr. Christoph Philipp Richter also published a *Treatise on the Significance of Adverbs Used in Civil Law*, in quarto, which deserves praise from everyone for its rarity. To this might be joined Albert of Bergamo’s *Treatise on Prepositions*. On the preposition "Of" or "Concerning" <note>Latin: *DE*</note>, see Ludwig’s *Disputations on the Institutes, page 221, letter a*, and the treatises of Antonius Fumeius on Conjunctions and Andreas Ciaffi of Pisa on Gerunds; these works, currently hiding in ancient libraries, deservedly ought to be brought to light once more. On the *Art of Grammar*, see Vossius. 

The **Poet** may find material here regarding the citations of those laws in which poets are praised. The **Logician** <note>Latin: *Dialecticus*</note> can study the law *l. 26. ff. de mun. & hon.*, noting how Herennius Modestinus decreed most things with excellent reason and method through observation and debate. The **Metaphysician** can look to the argument in *l. 1. ff. de haered. vend.*, where the most general consideration of "Being" is addressed, or *l. 5. ff. de precario*, where "privation and habit" are considered, as well as *l. 25. de V.S.* 

The **Mathematician** <note>Latin: *Arithmeticus*</note> can study the division of an inheritance into twelve "ounces" <note>Latin: *uncias*; the Roman *as* (unit) was divided into twelve parts</note>, which are contained under the name of the *as*; the highly complex laws *l. 7. §. 1. ff. solut. matrim.*, *l. 9. ff. de in lit. jur.*, and *l. 110. ff. de R. J.* are relevant here. The **Geometer** will be able to treat the width of a road; the **Geographer**, locations and regions, or the quality of Campanian wine based on the climate of the Campania region. The **Astronomer** can study the hour and the day, and how many paces must be completed in daily travel. The **Physicist** can study rainwater or the description of trees <note>Latin: *dendrographia*</note>; the **Physician's son** can study the fear of contagion and diseases; the **Chemist**, the mixing of gold and bronze, and so on. 

The **Genealogist** finds in this work many illustrious families of Princes and Counts, which he can daily enrich from the books of others. On a journey, if one lacks other books, this work alone can serve as a substitute for a whole library. At the medicinal springs <note>Latin: *Acidulis*; referring to spa towns or mineral baths frequented by the elite</note>, or in any other place where other books are not at hand, one can formulate legal advice from this alone. This very thing happened to a certain great <term>Jurisconsult</term> <note>Latin abbreviation: *Jcto*; a professional legal expert</note> in a grave case. When all the scholars at the springs were destitute of books, and he was meditating on a legal opinion on behalf of the faculty without any literary support, he satisfied the petitioner’s desire excellently using only the **"Golden Books"** <note>Latin: *Aureis*; likely referring to the *Aurei* or "Golden" excerpts of the Digest, though the author may also be punning on gold coins</note> which someone had unexpectedly brought along. 

If anyone enjoys games to pass the time, he will find titles on **Dice**, on **Playing Cards**, and on **Chess**. He who gladly attends to sacred matters will be able to select extensive material on the **Sabbath**, on **Prayers**, and on **Temples**. The **Painter** can find material on colors; the **Printer’s son** can take up the subject of individual letters, using the occasion of the letter "S" (as mentioned below) to write an entire treatise on that one unique little letter. For even if, in a rare subject, the laws and the multitude of authors and objections are not immediately present "in the bag," a single law suffices if its use in practice can be shown. 

The study of <term>excerpting</term> <note>The practice of selecting and transcribing useful passages into a common-place book</note> involves some tedium at the beginning, but later it brings pleasure as your resources grow and you yourself marvel at your own harvest, as Lipsius consoles us somewhere. Thus, when there is a public scarcity of interpreters, you are privately wealthy, as Rupert says in his *Postal Mercury, page 248*. How many laws are there still in the last three books of our Code whose utility is not known to all, or which have not been treated according to their dignity? Many cases that arise today are decided in our *Body of Law* <note>The *Corpus Juris Civilis*</note>, yet we despise the texts and flee to "common opinions." Thus the student clings only to theories, and the practitioner only to practices, when both could usefully join theory and practice together. We often quarrel over things that are established by certain law. Mr. Dr. Tabor treats this at length in *Benedicto 2* and *On the Obligation of Succession in Office, p. 257*. 

In a word, since memory is fleeting, one must excerpt, lest in following years those things which were acquired with great labor slip away and flow past. In this way, with a "short hand," one can be of use to himself and others, make great practitioners his friends, acquire experience in many things, hold a correspondence of letters for delight, and feed both the eyes and the mind without the loss of expense. Our Treasury <note>The book the reader is currently holding</note> abounds with these "eye-bringers"; here, all at once and together, one may look upon **kreuzers, batzens, gnackios, florins, albus-pennies, pfennings, hallers, ternaries, maravedis, and marquet-groats**; that is, a great wealth of things...

...and the abundance, value, and estimation of words. It is helpful to consider and inspect the intrinsic and extrinsic goodness of these words. In this *Thesaurus* <note>original: "Thefauro"; a treasury or storehouse of knowledge, in this context likely a legal dictionary or encyclopedia</note> of ours, new additions have been added to the words of Besoldus <note>Christoph Besold (1577–1638) was a prominent German jurist whose works were foundational in 17th-century law</note>, and entirely new words have joined them. If every single item is not placed in its proper location, it is enough simply to have the ox, even if the stable is not so fit—as the thoroughly learned Drexelius <note>Jeremias Drexel (1581–1638), a Jesuit writer known for his works on Christian devotion and the art of note-taking</note> has well indicated in all things. 

Mr. Rupert writes in his *Epistolary Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurio Epiftolari"</note> on *page 267*: "Regarding commonplaces <term>Commonplaces: A method of organizing knowledge by collecting excerpts, quotes, and observations under general headings for future use</term>, I do not know what I should suggest to you; for myself, I keep my own marginal notes, both for public lectures and for one or two books in which I write down things worthy of memory *without order, without care, and without splendor*, and in the margin of that same book I note the title under which the excerpted passage should be referred." An index, however, is necessary. 

But is it displeasing that I wished to sew my own cloth onto the purple of Besoldus? <note>This is a humility trope: the author compares Besoldus's original work to "purple" (the color of royalty/excellence) and his own additions to a common patch of cloth</note> Yet, in truth, the Besoldian purple shines all the more because of it. But do you wish for some things in these pages to be omitted, or others added, Friend Reader? You shall signify this through letters; no one can think as poorly of these efforts as I myself do. You now have material in abundance for providing better things, correcting some items, informing and teaching, Friend Reader; only favor these attempts. I wanted to provide you the opportunity: "the following day will be the disciple of the previous one," <note>original: "dies pofterior discipulus erit prioris"; a Latin proverb meaning we learn more as time passes</note> and it is not my intention to hold the same opinion forever after receiving better information. I wish for nothing to be detracted from anyone's privileges, immunities, erudition, or dignity; but, hemmed in by the constraints of time, I break off the thread. 

If you favor our attempts now and continue to do so hereafter, Dearest Reader—notwithstanding the Supplement of Wehner <note>Paul Matthias Wehner (1583–1612), a jurist whose work was often updated by later editors</note> published in the year 1661—provided that he at whose expense it is done is present, and if God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "T. O. M." - *Ter Optimus Maximus*</note>, grants life, strength, and health, it will be my pleasure (without violating the Frankfurt Edition) to prepare an entirely separate and singular work, and to take up and complete the Wehnerian additions. But if not, relieve us of that labor, and provide much better things yourselves,

->it is permitted by us.<-

### LORD DIETHERR, THE ENRICHER OF BESOLDUS.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'I' decorated with intricate floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
To add something to things already discovered is easy. So judges the mindless
   crowd, and I agree—but only with reason.
Certainly, where things are known even to the bleary-eyed and to barbers <note>original: "lippis, tonsoribus"; a classical idiom from the Roman poet Horace, meaning something so obvious that even people with poor eyesight or common gossips at the barbershop know it</note>;
   And what boys and girls sing in the crossroads.
But when things are brought forth that are rare, ancient, and buried,
   Scarcely known or read even by learned men of the past,
Then it is right to judge much differently, for that which
   lies open, properly noted, is beyond the grasp of the common crowd.
Such are your works, O DIETHERR, our glory, which your learned
   skill and your ever-watchful study note:
When you bring forth things scarcely known to one in ten,
   and wish to add gems to gold everywhere.
Thus you act so that the glory long owed to BESOLDUS <note>Christoph Besold (1577–1638), the original author of the legal work Dietherr is editing</note>
   now shines more brightly throughout the whole world:
But may a greater grace for such a great deed remain for You
   justly (if indeed grace still remains in this world).
Yet if nothing follows (as Favor is a slippery thing)
   a mind conscious of the right will be able to find solace!

# Encomiastic Poems
## To
## The Noble, Energetic, and Most Learned
## MR. ENRICHER OF BESOLD.
<note>original: "DN. LOCUPLETATOREM BESOLDI" — "Locupletatorem" means one who enriches or expands. This refers to Dietherr’s massive effort in updating and expanding Christoph Besold's legal encyclopedia.</note>

It is easy to add something to things already invented. The mindless crowd
Judges so: and I approve, but within reason.
Namely, when things are known even to the bleary-eyed and to barbers;
And what boys and girls sing in the street corners.
But when things are rare, as well as ancient, buried,
And scarcely known or read before even by learned men,
Then it is right to judge much differently, far beyond
That which lies open to the common understanding.
Such things, DIETHERR, are your honor; it is your learned skill
And your watchful study that marks them:
When you bring forth things scarcely known to every tenth person,
And wish everywhere to add gems to gold.
Thus you act so that the glory long ago due to BESOLD
Now shines more illustriously throughout the whole world:
But a greater gratitude for so great a deed
Should rightfully remain for You, (wherever gratitude perhaps still remains in the world.)
But if no reward follows (as Favor is a slippery thing),
A mind conscious of what is right will be able to find its own solace!

# I. Abbreviations.

<columns>2</columns>

In the preparation of legal **Instruments**, notes or **Ciphers** (called so from the Hebrew *Sepher*, meaning a "letter," and brought to us by the Arabs) and other signs or images by which something can be signified or denoted, are excluded. By "notes," we mean individual letters from which entire words can be gathered. Hence, to "note with notes" means to write concisely, not using full and complete letters. Mæcenas <note>Gaius Maecenas, a Roman advisor to Augustus, often credited with early patronage of the arts and systems of writing.</note> is said to be the author of these, having devised speed in writing (according to Cassius Dio, Book 55). However, they seem much older and were already known in the time of Cicero. Thus, Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist historian who lived in England.</note> (Book 2, Chapter 7) attributes them to **Tiro**, the freedman of Cicero. Tiro's notes are still published by Mr. Gruter and joined to the works of Seneca; they almost imitate the Chinese manner of writing. From these "notes," the name **Notary** is derived.

Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman Law.</note> calls these **Sigla** (as if "single letters" note "single words") and prohibits them in the Code [Law 1, Section 2, *Concerning the Clarification of Ancient Law*]. For, as the Emperor says in another law, one must use full letters, not shorthand. Just as notes and shorthand (concerning which, see Herman Hugo *On the Origin of Writing*, and others), so also **Verbal Abbreviations** must be avoided in legal instruments. These were quite frequent in the Middle Ages, as seen in old editions, and are sometimes called the **Protocol** (discussed later in its proper place), which is essentially an abbreviated draft or "tenor" of a future instrument conceived in few words. This prohibition is clearly confirmed by the Imperial Decree of **Maximilian I** regarding Notaries from the year 1512, in the section "Item":

> Notaries shall also take care to avoid writing their instruments with so many shortened, obscure, or doubtful words, or with ciphers, signs, or notes—especially those not commonly known to all—because these can very easily be altered and forged; instead, they should write with completely common, legible, and recognized letters, in the Latin or German language, etc. <note>original: "die Notarien sollen sich auch hüten..." (translated above from the German).</note>

If someone in a **Will** writes "200" using symbols when they intended to write "100," what is the law? (See the Digest, Book 9, Section 4, *On the Appointment of Heirs*).

There are two purposes for using notes: (1) To take down any speech as it is spoken, so the hand may follow the speed of the tongue, as Seneca mentions in his letters. (2) To hide secret plans, especially in war (see Johann Baptist Besold, Volume 1).

<column-break/>

Giambattista della Porta <note>A polymath known for his work on cryptography and optics.</note> treats this in his work on *Secret Writing*, and I also treat the matter in my dissertation on Legates (Chapter 1, Number 4). But this latter method [encryption] does not aim for speed, since such writing is usually more laborious than the usual style. I say no more, as the famous Bernegger has diligently investigated its antiquity in his notes on Suetonius.

---

### ADDITION.

Only those are promoted to the rank of **Bachelors** who know how to read the abbreviations of the Law. (Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 432).

A legal sentence must be written in full letters or a proper sequence of letters, not rashly described with just a few letters. (Law *ult.*, Code *comminat. Epist.*).

The Romans used "notes" for the sake of brevity; some pertain to the Republic, the Laws, and the Magistrates, and others to private affairs.

**A. P. U. C.** In the year after the founding of the City [Rome].
**A. A. U. C.** In the year from the founding of the City.

**DICT.** Dictator. Many other examples are found in Mr. Dilherr's *Philological Apparatus*. This also concerns **Ciphers**, such as when **C** is placed for one hundred (see Mascardus and others), and secret notes (Höping, *On Legal Instruments*).

If an abbreviation needs to be expanded into full text, the notary's own **Style** must be maintained. (Honthem, *On the Art of the Notary*).

Thus, Cicero in his speech *In Defense of Milo*, calls the letter **A** the "favorable letter." <note>original: "salutarem literam A dicit." In Roman trials, 'A' stood for *Absolvo* (I acquit), while 'C' stood for *Condemno* (I condemn).</note>

<meta>continuity: This page continues the discussion on shorthand and legal abbreviations before moving into specific legal definitions for the words "but," "avocation," and the rights of "appanaged" younger brothers.</meta>

...Cicero says that **A** is the mark of acquittal <note>original: "notam absolvendi"</note>, while the grim **K** is the mark of condemnation. Regarding the writing of a **Will** among children, the Emperor decreed that shorthand symbols <note>original: "notæ"</note> should not be employed, but that everything must be written out in full words. For the ancients were accustomed to write many things in legal **Instruments** and in the **Laws** themselves, not expressing everything in full words through a sequence of letters, but through **Notes**, which they also called **Sigla**—as if they were "single" items, derived from individual letters that denoted entire words as a shorthand for writing. Books of such shorthand symbols by **Valerius Probus**, **Magno** (who lived in the time of **Charlemagne**), and others still exist today, contained in the volumes of the ancient grammarians edited by **Gothofredus** and **Elias Putsch**. The small work of the grammarian **Valerius Probus** on ancient letters is found joined with **Fenestella**; arranged alphabetically, it contains the Names, First Names, and Surnames of **Roman Citizens** and their **Magistrates**, as found described in ancient Codices. It further contains individual letters used in **Civil Law**, regarding **Laws** and **Decrees of the People**, **Actions**, **Perpetual Edicts**, **Weights**, and **Numbers**—a work most worthy of being brought to light again, enriched with new additions for the benefit of studious youth. What **Siglæ** or **Sigla** are is discussed very extensively by **Stökken** in *On the Law of Embassies, question 7, letter C.*

See several other things in **Rittershusius** in *New Novels, page 6, chapter 2, number 8*, as well as 6 and 7, where he says a soldier’s will written in shorthand symbols is valid. However, what are called "letter notes" is excellently and subtly explained by **Viglius** <note>Viglius Aytta, a Dutch statesman and jurist.</note> under the title *concerning military wills, number 3, page 87.* To this point belong those things which **Dr. Bruckmann**, in his *Inaugural [Disputation] on Notaries, chapter 1, position 1*, treated more accurately and fully regarding the first drafts of **Scriveners** and informal **Abbreviations**; see also **Suetonius** (in *Caesar* chapter 56 and *Augustus* chapter 88), who explicitly calls that method of secret writing—which occurs by the substitution of letters (for example, taking D for A, E for B, and F for C)—"writing by notes" <note>This is an early description of the "Caesar Cipher."</note>. **Christian Daum** [writes] on the causes of the loss of certain Latin roots, *page 132*, and the sources cited there.

### 2. **But. However.** <note>original: "Aber. Autem."</note>

The nature of this **adversative particle** is to oppose preceding points in law and in fact; thus it denotes a different case and implies something more. **Bartolus** [discusses this] in the law *hoc amplius*, the section *concerning these however* <note>original: "de his autem"</note> in the Digest *on threatened damage*. Also the Doctors of Law in the law *if so written* in the Digest *on children and posthumous heirs*. This word "**But**" <note>German: "Aber"</note> is equivalent to the conjunctions *and yet, but, truly, however, but rather, but also,* etc. **Rudinger** in his *Observations* on the word *But*, which is explained at length by others; see **Tuschius**, *Practical Conclusions, letter D, conclusion 248*; also **Goldbeck** in the consultation joined to the treatise *on the Gerada* <note>Gerada: a term in Old Saxon law referring to a widow's portion of moveable goods.</note>, *number 101.*

### ->ADDITION.<-

**However** <note>original: "Autem"</note> is also taken to mean "for," "therefore," and is used as a connective. **Forster** in *On the Law of Succession, chapter 26 and the last.*

<column-break/>

### 3. **Recall of a Case. Avocation.** <note>original: "Abforderung. Avocatio."</note>

**Avocation**, **evocation**, **advocation**, and **revocation** are synonyms in current legal terms. **Johann Wames** [discusses this] in chapter *as ours*, 56, under number 1, regarding appeals. **Avocation** is described as the transfer of a lawsuit pending before an inferior judge to a superior one, without an appeal being made. **Gail**, *Observation 2, 41, number 2*; **Graevius**, *Conclusion 1, 41, consideration 1*; see **Rutger Ruland** in the notes to the *Ferrara Process*; **Montanus**, *folio 51 and folio 156*; also **Battista Costa** on *Subsidiary Remedies, remedy 24.*

Although it is a point of very clear law that a superior may "avocate" <note>To "avocate" is to pull a case from a lower court to a higher one before a verdict is reached.</note> a cause pending before an inferior judge to himself, in the state in which it stands before that judge, either by his own motion or at the request of a party (**Berlich**, *Conclusion 1, 6, at the beginning*), and even without a specific cause (**Petrus Antonius Petra**, *On the Power of the Prince, chapter 6, number 69*), sometimes the superior renounces this right by agreement or law. Thus, in **Saxon Law**, the **Elector** does not usually recall cases pending before the **Court Council** <note>original: "Judicio Curiali"</note>; see **Berlich** in the cited place.

Similarly, in **Imperial Chamber Law** <note>original: "Jure Camerali"</note> (part 2, title 35), it is provided that cases subject to the jurisdiction of the Chamber Court should not be recalled by the Emperor's clemency; see **Graevius**, *Conclusion 1, 41.* Although **Berlich** disagrees in *Decision 158*, I would think his opinion should be understood as referring to **extraordinary power** used for a singular reason. See *On the Political Rights of Majesty, chapter 5, number 4*, and **Schrader** on *Fiefs, part 10, section 5, number 183*, etc.

### ->ADDITION.<-

Thus, if **students** voluntarily submit themselves to a jurisdiction other than that of the **Rector**, the Rector can nonetheless recall those cases to himself. **Dr. Bicccius**, *Golden Rules, section 5, thesis 72, letter Q at the end.* This is strictly observed at **Jena**, **Leipzig**, **Wittenberg**, and other neighboring **Academies**. Among these, the university at Leipzig has this privilege above the others: it can recall to itself lawsuits not only moved before the town magistrate, but even those occurring outside the city up to a three days' journey—**21 miles** <note>original: "auf 21. Meilwegs"</note>. **Kirchberg**, *On the Competent Forum, thesis 84*; **Friedrich Besold**, *Additions to the Decisions of Coler, 296*; **Limnäus**, *Public Law, book 8, chapter 9, 59.*

### 4. **Provisioned Lords. Appanaged Princes.** <note>original: "Abgefundene Herren. Appanagiati."</note>

Where the law of **primogeniture** <note>The right of the firstborn son to inherit the entire estate.</note> prevails, the firstborn is bound to assign to his other brothers (who today retain both the dignity and the title of the name) as much as honestly suffices for their sustenance according to the splendor of their birth and the resources of the **Principality**, while still leaving enough for himself to live as a Prince and preside over the Principality with honor. **Riterus**, *On Homage, chapter 3, number 55*; **Keckermann**, *Politics, book 1, folio 115, chapter 25*; **Cothman**, *Response 3, number 26, and following in volume 4.* The French call this exclusion an **Appanage** <note>original: "Appennage"</note>, as if granted for "bread" <note>Latin: "ad panem"</note> and royal support; others call it **Abbannagium**, from the German word *Bann* [ban or decree], as if it were a settlement <note>German: "Abfindung"</note>. This Law, being very ancient...

# Letter A.

<meta>catchword: to be warned.</meta>

Jerome, in his commentary on Genesis chapter 49, suggests that primogeniture was introduced for excellent reasons: first, so that kingdoms, <term>Principalities</term> <note>Latin: "Principatus"</note>, and estates are not destroyed by division, but rather preserved through union. Furthermore, as Lucan testifies in his first book:

> There is no trust among partners in power <note>Latin: "Nulla fides Regni sociis"</note>

This is usually the case. It should also be known that a Prince who has obtained even the smallest part of a Principality through division is nevertheless considered to be and remain a Prince of the entire Principality, according to Hermann Vultejus. In such cases where younger Princes are excluded by the Major or Senior Prince, they receive <term>Fiefs</term> <note>feudal land holdings</note> from him, as can be seen in the <term>Saxon Documents</term> <note>German: "Saxoniſchen Documenten"</note> under letters E, F. 1, and F. 2.

As to whether "Life and Military Service" <note>Latin: "Vita & Militia" – a term for the portion assigned to excluded brothers in some regions</note> is also owed to members of the clergy: see *Ecclesiastical Matters* <note>Latin: "Practicabilia Eccleſiaſtica"</note>, question 66, by Marc. Ant.

Regarding the <term>Appanage</term> <note>a grant of land or money to a younger son of a royal house to provide for his maintenance</note> of the brother of King Louis XIII of France, consult the *French Mercury*, volume 13, page 469.

But there is no need for me to add more on this matter, as I have expressed my thoughts most fully in my *Treatise on Royal Succession, book 1, dissertation 4*, etc.

## ADDITION.

In the past in France, the <term>later-born sons</term> <note>Latin: "ultrageniti"</note> were called by the special name <term>Cadets</term>, as reported from Natalis Comes. Today in Germany, they are called by the special name <term>Separated Lords</term> <note>German: "abgetheilte Herren"</note>, while the firstborn is called the <term>Regent</term> <note>German: "Regierende"</note>. Concerning the later-born Princes of the Empire—the Separated Lords—Nicolaus Myler writes extensively in his *Treatise on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 22*. Regarding the practice in the <term>Electoral House of Brandenburg</term>, Limnaeus teaches in his work on the Golden Bull, chapter 25.

On the Law of Appanage, see Sprenger’s *Axioms of State*, Nicolaus Myler’s specific treatise on the later-born sons of Princes, Springfield on Appanage, and Halbritter on <term>Majorat</term> <note>the right of the eldest son to inherit the entire estate</note>. Larger fiefs that have an attached dignity <note>such as a title or office</note> cannot be divided, though this has been changed by the well-known custom of Germany, as noted by Eberhard Fabricius.

### **5. Separated Children. <note>Latin: "Liberi Separati"</note>**

Under Lubeck Law, <term>separated children</term> <note>Latin: "diſſortes filii"</note> are not only those to whom a certain part of the property is legally assigned before the Senate, but also those who, upon reaching adulthood, are provided for and given in marriage with a specific portion of property as a dowry. The law states: "When a father provides for his son or daughter in marriage with specific assigned goods, with the intention that the child shall be <term>partitioned or separated</term> <note>German: "abgetheilt oder abgeſondert"</note> from him, and the son or daughter, along with their friends and guardians, is satisfied at that time, then such person is considered separated and partitioned, whether the amount be little or much." This is seen as a type of the ancient Roman "Emancipation." Similarly, in the very old customs of Swabia—still not abolished in some places—there were two ways of inheriting when a marriage ended and children remained: the <term>Right of Partition</term> <note>German: "Theil-Recht"</note> and the <term>Right of Possession</term> <note>German: "Verfangenſchafft-Recht"</note>. By virtue of the latter, a certain portion or type of goods, mostly immovable property, was settled upon the children.

Under the former rule, children divided the property man-for-man with the surviving spouse. Thus they were "settled with" <note>German: "abgefertigt"</note> regarding their paternal and maternal inheritance. Consequently, they could not inherit further from the survivor if that person left behind children from a second marriage or another spouse. Mention of this custom is made in the old <term>Wurttemberg Land Law</term>.

Besold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

## ADDITION.

On settled and separated children, see the excellent work of Hahn on the *Law of Things*, and Goeddaeus.

### **6. Renunciation, Letter of Enmity. <note>Latin: "Diffidatio"</note>**

Anyone who decides to wage war against another is necessarily bound to first warn him through <term>Heralds</term> <note>Latin: "Feciales" or "Caduceatores"</note> or through letters, so that he may perform what he owes or return the thing he holds by violence. If the adversary despises and neglects this denunciation and refuses to grant the petition, war is simultaneously declared against him by those same heralds. This act of declaring war is called <term>Defiance</term> <note>Latin: "Diffidatio"</note>. It can be defined as a declaration of hostile intent, by which someone signifies to another that he will pursue him with arms, fire, looting, and robbery. In the past, this was thought sufficient on its own for a war to be considered "just." This custom also flourished in Lombardy and in our Germany, back when <term>Fist-Law</term> <note>German: "Fauſt-Recht" – a period of history where individuals settled disputes through private force rather than courts</note> still prevailed, as seen in the *Speyer Chronicle*. However, after the <term>Public Peace</term> <note>the "Landfrieden," which outlawed private feuds</note> was established, if anyone "renounces" another, writes a letter of enmity, or sets "fire-marks" <note>threatens arson</note>, and threatens to harm him with robbery, fire, or murder, such an act is considered a highly punishable <term>Feud</term> <note>German: "Fehden"</note>.

### ADDITION.

The <term>Fetial Law</term> <note>original: "Feciale Jus"; ancient Roman law concerning the rituals for declaring war and forming treaties</note> was the oldest of all among the Romans, as Fenestella teaches. However, at what time or by whom it was invented is not sufficiently agreed upon among authors; Lord Boecler discusses this extensively in *On Clarigation and Manifests*, chapter 2, where he accurately and fully treats what the Fetial law itself is and from where it originates. On the duty of the <term>Fetials</term> <note>priests who acted as diplomats</note>, see Draco, *On the Patricians*, page 47, number 16. Regarding <term>letters of defiance</term> <note>original: "literis diffidatitiis"; formal declarations of the breaking of a truce or friendship</note>, see the same Boecler in the aforementioned chapter 2 at the end. See also Rittersh. in *Feudal Divisions*, page 568; Barschamp, *On Closed Roots*, page 326.

### 7. Decree. Formal Resolution.
**Decree, Court-Decision** <note>original German: "Abschied, Hof-Bescheid"</note>, Decrees, **Petitionary Process** <note>original: "Supplicatori-Proceß"</note>, do they have the force of a legal sentence? See Beatus in *Saxon Decisions and Sentences*, Volume 5, on judicial matters, part 5, volume 2, folio 189.

### 8. Absolution from an oath taken, etc.
**Absolution from a sworn oath.** <note>original Latin/German: "Absolution von gethanem Eyd &c. Absolutio à Juramento præstito."</note>
In the Archbishop's Court of Naples, the rule is observed that absolution from an oath (or restoration of legal standing) is not granted except solely for the purpose of taking action and testing one's rights before a competent judge, but not for the purpose of raising an objection; see Gallesius, *On Obligations in the Form of the Chamber*, part 2, question 2. And it is granted without summoning the other party, according to the ancient style of the Court, following the counsel of Oldradus, counsel 120. In that same Neapolitan Court, as Marc. Ant. witnesses in *Archiepiscopal Practice*, chapter 4, from the beginning, it is observed that sometimes absolution or restoration from an oath is given after <term>perjury</term> has been committed, provided the other party is summoned. However, he adds that he has often seen this doubted, for in such a case, one must recur to the <term>Pontiff</term> <note>the Pope</note>, as said by Freder. de Senis, counsel 301, and Anchar., counsel 198. For otherwise, it would provide an occasion for perjury, which a Bishop ought to avoid; see Neviz. counsel 23, Cravet. counsel 613, and Bero. counsel 50, number 64, book 1.

But this conclusion discussed by the Doctors admits some limitations, according to which the practice of the Court proceeds. Indeed, (1.) it is limited when the perjurer does not persist in the sin. An example is found in one who sold something out of fear and swore not to contest it: because although he sinned by contesting it and fell into perjury, he can nevertheless seek absolution so that it may be permitted for him to go against the sale. In this case, the persistence in sin ceases, and a penance for the perjury ought to be imposed on him. (2.) It is limited when someone would be a perjurer without <term>malice</term> <note>original: "dolo"</note>—for instance, if a debtor did not pay within the deadline, or if he is otherwise excused from perjury by reason of necessity or difficulty: because the penalty attached to perjury has no place when malice is absent. (3.) It is limited when, within the deadline, a Judge had commanded the swearer not to pay; who, in the event of the deadline passing, does not incur perjury, etc.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.
The right of absolving from a sworn oath is among the <term>Greater Regalia</term> <note>original: "Regalibus majoribus"; rights and privileges belonging exclusively to a sovereign monarch</note>. Bocer, *On the Regalia*, chapter 2, number 135 throughout. It is granted to the political Magistrate for the purpose of taking legal action. Zanger, *On Exceptions*, part 2, chapter 1, number 426; add Lord Doctor Biccius in *Golden Matters*, section 5, treasury 77, letter SS.

### 9. Judgment of Acquittal.
**Acquitting Sentence.** <note>original German/Latin: "Absolutori-Urtheil. Sententia absolutoria."</note>
If a defendant has been summoned based on sufficient evidence and legally examined under oath, or seized for whatever cause or occasion, etc., but it is nevertheless proved and fully established that he in no way committed the crime imputed to him, then he is to be acquitted on the grounds of innocence. Clarus, *In Criminal Practice*, final section, question 57. For whenever a defendant proves his innocence by means other than <term>torture</term> <note>at this time, "proving innocence" often meant surviving judicial torture; Clarus argues for a higher standard of proof</note>, he is definitively acquitted as innocent, regardless of what else occurred in the process. Clarus, in the cited place; Octavius Spatharius in *The Golden Method of Correcting Regulars*, treatise 10, chapter 9, folio 315, where at number 3 he adds: Let <term>Regular Judges</term> <note>judges within religious orders</note> take great care, because they would do no small prejudice to the defendant if they did not acquit him on the ground of innocence when he has firmly proved it, declaring so in the definitive sentence. For as Clarus teaches in the cited place, question 57, number 3: in a case of doubt, an acquitting sentence in a criminal case is deemed to be issued because the charge was not proven, and not on the ground of innocence, unless it is explicitly stated, etc.

### 10. Transcript, Copy.
**Copy.** <note>original German/Latin: "Abschrifft, Copey. Copia."</note>
That which is transcribed from an authentic or original instrument—**from the original or main deed** <note>original German: "aus dem Original oder Haupt-Verschreibung"</note>—is called an *exemplum* <note>a formal copy</note>, commonly a **certified transcript** or **copy** <note>original German: "beglaubte Abschrifft oder Copey"</note>. It must be noted, however, that a copy regularly does not constitute proof unless the Original is produced, according to Law 2 of the Digest *on the faith of Instruments*. For it is not fitting that a suspect writing should have standing in court; see the cited Law 2 and chapter 1 of the Decretals on the same. For it can happen that not everything is faithfully expressed and described; or perhaps he who wrote it did not correctly read the original, or neglected or changed certain things rashly or through wavering effort. Castill., *Daily Controversies*, 16, number 5. And so it ought to be held unjust, even absurd, to wish to prove certain things by uncertain ones. Since that by which another thing is proved ought to be by no means deceptive; Law 5 of the Code *on ignorance of law and fact*; Law 1, section 8 *on dowry pre-legacies*; Laws 33 and 34 of the Digest *on conditions and demonstrations*.
However, a copy provides proof if it is found among the Acts, Mynf. 6, observation 75, number 1, provided it was collated by a Notary of the acts (Mynsing., in the cited place) or placed in an archive (Marta in *Digest of Decisions*, chapter 22; Gabr. conclusion 1 under the title *on proofs*), provided it exists as a full transcription (Mascard. *on proofs*, conclusions 914 and 711, number 61 and following; Cacher. decision 69, number 8; Alex. Trentacinq. book 2, *on the faith of Instruments*, resolution 8, number 8; Gabr. *on witnesses*, conclusion 5, number 16).
Sometimes also a copy provides proof by the authority of its antiquity, which is reputed as law...

Or finally, if a copy was compared with the original by a Notary, as noted by Gail, observation 134, and Mynsinger, observation 79, in the presence of the adversary or in their absence due to contempt <note>original: "contumaciam", a legal term for failing to appear in court</note>, following the authority of the code regarding where crimes must be prosecuted. This pertains to what is commonly called a *Vidimus* <note>original: "Vidimus", literally "we have seen"; a certificate from an authority confirming they have inspected an original document</note>: namely when a Prince or a certain Imperial City attests that they have seen a certain document and found it complete in every part, and thereafter has it transcribed and secured with their seal. It is likewise called a *Transumptum* <note>original: "Tranſumptum", a certified transcript or official copy</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

We do not use duplicates or copies in court, but authentic instruments or the instruments themselves <note>original: "instrumentis ipsis", referring to the original signed and sealed documents</note>. However, if the principal instruments have been lost by fire or perhaps by some other accident, it is permitted to use an index or a copy, provided that the loss is proven, or, if proof is lacking, confirmed by oath. See Busius in his commentary on the Pandects <note>A massive compendium of Roman law</note>.

The cases in which copies and duplicates are trusted can be seen in Omphalius and Gulhusius. Rittershusius shows that even a copy or a set of copies can be called "authentic," and he clarifies the distinction between different types of copies based on Caprus. Add to this the work of Bicc. Most recently, Barbosa covers this in his entire 29th chapter. A copy without the original does not provide proof, as seen in Wesenbeck and the Lindau Acts.

**11. Abbot, Abbeys, Princely Abbots and Abbesses.** Abbot. Abbey.
"Abbot" comes from *Abba*, which means "Father," and is commonly used for the leader of a monastery; hence he is also called a *Prelate* <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy</note>, see Beckmann’s *Latin Origins*. Likewise, Antonio Perez in his *Rule of St. Benedict* notes that Justinian calls them an *Archimandrite* <note>original: "Archimandritam", a Greek term for the head of a monastery</note>. Certain orders, however, especially the Mendicants <note>Friars who live by begging, such as the Franciscans or Dominicans</note>, do not have Abbots, but Priors or Guardians. Abbots also have Priors under them who look after monastic discipline, as Abbots are more occupied with the administration of external goods and property.

Sometimes in histories, Abbots are called Nobles or Lords, which Cujas testifies is still observed in the Pyrenees mountains. Hotman asserts that the famous Hugh Capet, who obtained the Kingdom of France by skill, was called "Abbot Hugh." These were high-ranking nobles, leaders, or secular Barons to whom the King had granted the revenues of abbeys to enjoy for a time. From this perhaps comes the German phrase: *the monasteries are under the protection and shelter of the lords* <note>original: "daß die Clöster in der Herren Schutz und Schirm"</note>. And so Guillaume Paradin in the *Annals of Burgundy* testifies that he has seen many monuments in which the Nobles of France used these names: *Duke and Abbot, Count and Abbot*. Elsewhere: Ab-

<column-break/>

bots and Counts, Abbeys and Counties.

Abbots who are decorated with Princely dignity are commonly called *Princely Abbots* <note>original: "gefürstete Aebbt"</note>, to whom <term>Regalia</term> <note>Royal rights, such as coining money or holding high court, granted by the Emperor</note> also belong. These are included under the term *Princely* <note>original: "Fürstmässige"</note> in the Chamber Court Ordinance. Such Abbots are those of Fulda, Hersfeld, Murbach, Prüm, Kempten, Stavelot, Corvey, St. Emmeram in Regensburg, St. Gall in Switzerland, and formerly Reichenau (which monastery is now incorporated into the Bishopric of Constance, who calls himself the *Lord of Reichenau* <note>original: "Herrn der Reichenau"</note>). Such Abbots use in their letters and titles the phrase "By the Grace of God" <note>original: "Von GOttes Gnaden"</note>. Hundius teaches that *St. Emmeram at Regensburg is a princely monastery*. Likewise, the same author shows that *Tegernsee is a princely abbey*. There are also two Provosts of this rank, namely those of Ellwangen and Berchtesgaden. There are also Abbesses: those of Quedlinburg, Gernrode, Buchau, and Andlau. I mentioned in my treatise on the state of the Republic that Charles IV decorated four wealthy Abbots with the title of Princes.

But this custom appears to be older, based on the records of Charles Stengel in his *Monasteriologium*, where he discusses the monastery of St. Emmeram. That monastery, he says, is immediately subject to the Roman Empire regarding secular matters, from which it holds the "Regalia" in fief. Albert, King of the Romans, granted the Abbot the royal fiefs of the Principality. The same was done by John, King of Bohemia, in the name of his father Emperor Henry (who was then active in Italy) in the year 1313 with these words: *Granting him his principality and royal rights, etc.* <note>original: "Verleihen ihm seine Fürstenthum und Regalien, etc."</note>. Likewise Wenceslaus and Rupert grant in fief the royal and secular fiefs in 1401 and later in 1405: *Feudal lordship and vassalage, etc.* <note>original: "Lehenschafft und Mannschafft, etc."</note>, whereby he is named a Prince of the Empire by those Emperors and Kings.

Emperor Louis IV writes to him thus: "To our beloved Prince, Albert, Abbot of St. Emmeram in Regensburg." In 1332, Louis the Margrave, son of Louis IV, calls him *the honorable and spiritual Prince* <note>original: "den Ehrfamen und Geistlichen Fürsten"</note>. In 1348, the Princes of Bavaria were the Advocates and Defenders of this monastery regarding those goods located in Bavarian jurisdiction; the rest, like the monastery itself, belong to the Roman Empire.

The same Master Stengel says of the Abbot of Kempten: The venerable Abbot obtained for himself and all his successors a notable privilege from Pope Adrian, in which the Pope, calling Kempten "the other or second Rome," established that it be exempt from all episcopal control and perpetually free. To the Abbot, he grants full power to perform sacred rites before noon, and after noon the "power of the sword" <note>The right to exercise capital punishment and high justice</note>, to exercise legal rights, to protect the good, and [to remove...]

### 12. Division of Lordships.
->Separation or Division of Domains.<-

By law, a Kingdom ought not to be divided, although a division was made between the Catholic King <note>of Spain</note> and the Most Christian King <note>of France</note> regarding the Kingdom of Naples; see Francesco Vivius, *Neapolitan Decisions*, decision 130. However, the fiefs <note>term: "feuda", land held from a lord in exchange for service</note> of high dignities, by the notorious custom of Germany, and lower fiefs, by the force of feudal law, can be divided, as per Gail, book 2, observation 153. If one of the partners calls for a division, the others cannot prevent it, Gail, said observation, number 11; Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, book 1, chapter 8, number 36. See what my brother—may he rest in peace <note>original: "p. m." for "piæ memoriæ"</note>—replied in counsel 8, decade 1. When, however, a territory can be divided, the jurisdiction attached to it is usually divided in the same way (whether it be allodial <note>land owned outright</note> or feudal), as Fulvius Pacianus pursues at length in *On Evidence*, book 2, chapter 36, number 78 and following. Since jurisdiction adheres to the territory, it is considered as an accessory and belonging to the whole of the territory and is thus divided or transferred, Law 1, section 1, "In the Beginning," where Bartolus, Baldus, and others comment on the office of the Prefect of the City; Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 6, in note letter A; and Menochius, book 3, presumption 97, numbers 10, 12, and 14. This is also observed in Italy, as Alexander records in counsel 22, number 5, book 4; see me in my treatise *On Successions* and elsewhere. Likewise, Matthäus Wesenbeck, part 1, counsel 32, regarding the division of Royal Rights <note>Regalia</note>.
And it should be noted in such divisions of the Counts and Lordships, etc. <note>original: "Der Graf- und Herrschafften"</note>, that what was previously provided for in an undivided estate with one bailiff, one wood-ward, and other officials at half the cost, must afterwards, in the division of the same, be carried out with double the expense. Therefore, it frequently gives rise to all sorts of confusion and disruption, discord, ill-will, and disunity regarding young timber-cuttings, the impounding of cattle, punishments, the granting of local legal privileges <note>term: "Ehehafften", rights involving local courts or marital/domestic law</note>, high jurisdiction, the appointment of the court, pending legal justifications, and other respects. The subjects are embittered against one another, incited and misled against the neighboring authorities, and—as usually happens in contiguous territories—the door is opened wide to unceasing strife. This is especially true since feudal services are performed in a disorderly manner due to all sorts of misunderstandings; it also falls quite heavily because the fiefs must nonetheless be placed under a single fief-holder <note>Lehenträger</note>, and it is difficult to see how one or the other could be arranged without confusion, etc.
