<meta>This page transitions from discussing the administrative and territorial rights of ecclesiastical princes to the specific civil laws governing physical injury and the calculation of legal damages.</meta>

In a case where someone has been wounded, the law encompasses not only the penalty or monetary fine due to the Judge (<note>original: "die Frevel" - a fine paid to the court for criminal misconduct or "outrage"</note>), but also that which might be owed to the plaintiff for the healing of the wound, or whatever further loss they might suffer from it (unless they themselves provided the occasion by provoking the other). This is noted by Moller in his *Commentary on the Saxon Constitutions*, part 4, constitution 10, number 10. See also Speckhan, century 3, question 6, class 2, number 5, where he states that according to the 10th Elector's Constitution, a provoker owes nothing to the person provoked if they did not kill them, but only mutilated or wounded them. The text there says most expressly <note>original: "daß er einigen Abtrag zu geben nicht schuldig seyn solle"</note> **"that he shall not be obliged to give any compensation."** See Farinaccius, question 119, number 115. He adds that these words are also to be understood regarding the expenses incurred in treating the wound.

In my own deliberations on the Digest (book 9, title 2, question 1), it must be known that in this case, **"an inspection by impartial barbers"** <note>original: "die Besichtigung unpartheyischer Barbierer" — at this time, barbers performed surgeries and medical assessments</note> is absolutely required, according to Lord Bocer, class 8, disputation 2, thesis 34, on the *Lex Aquilia* <note>The Roman law governing wrongful damage to property and persons</note>. There, in the following theses, he adds that no account is taken of deformity caused by scars, nor of the pain or torture—**"of the suffering"** <note>original: "deß Schmerzens"</note>. He says there: the unlearned "forensic brawlers" <note>An insult to poorly trained lawyers</note> err when, in a lawsuit under the *Lex Aquilia*, they **"demand compensation for the pain and damage received."** But what if the lawsuit only mentions the pain (**"of the suffering"**)? Is one deemed to have understood it as "damage"? So they say, and my brother of blessed memory observed such a judgment in February of the year 1614 **"before the High Court here,"** based on the counsel of certain legal experts; similarly **"before the Court of Appeal"** on September 7, 1614.

From this, if maintenance <note>term: "alimenta" — financial support for living expenses</note> is owed for the future because of a crime—for instance, if someone cut off a craftsman's right hand—there is no doubt that the wounded person can seek the value of the work which they will be deprived of, based on the law regarding those who throw or pour things out.

But a distinction must be observed in the method of proof. For interest and damages of this kind, an "oath in litigation" <note>term: "juramentum in litem" — a plaintiff's sworn estimate of the value of their loss</note> can be taken against a willful murderer, according to the text in the Code under the title "whence by force." It is otherwise against one who committed homicide by accident or fault: because then it cannot be proved by an oath in litigation, but by witnesses or other legitimate proofs. See Plotus in his *Treatise on the Oath in Litigation*, section 40; Rolandinus a Valle, counsel 39; Josephus Ludovicus, decision 62 of Lucca.

It should be noted here that a murderer, if condemned to death, is not held **"to a restitution"** <note>original: "zu einem Abtrag"</note>; see Berlichius, volume 4, conclusion 19.

As for what is accepted in Saxon Law, see Martin Coler, *Treatise on Maintenance*, book 3, chapter 12. A plaintiff who cannot swear the oath in litigation under Civil Law—for example, because the damage was brought upon them not by malice, but by fault or accident—will primarily seek their "liquidation" <note>The process of determining the exact monetary value of a debt or loss</note> or proof to inform the Judge's arbitration from the teachings of Coler and Tiberius Decianus.

It must be diligently noted here that a Judge, in estimating damage, ought especially to look at the victim's way of life, namely

<column-break/>

their work and the trade they practice; likewise their age—that is, how much longer they might likely be expected to survive. This is discussed in the glosses on book 3 of the Digest. Thus, once, when a noble soldier was treacherously deprived of both eyes by a wound, the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> awarded many thousands for the military offices he would later be deprived of, as noted by Gail. Also, in the Supreme Court of Württemberg on June 4, 1590, an opponent was condemned to pay 150 florins to a plaintiff whose arm had been made completely useless. Similarly, on September 20, 1586, a defendant was ordered by sentence to give the same amount of florins to a plaintiff because he had weakened the man's arm and some fingers, although these limbs were not rendered entirely useless for his trade.

Similarly, on March 14, 1588, for a female plaintiff whose shoulder the defendant had made so weak that she could hardly use her arm, this damage was estimated at 100 florins.

So too, on May 29, 1594, for a plaintiff who was a blacksmith and whose left hand was made useless for his trade, the defendant was condemned for that damage to 150 florins, as reported by Lord Bocer.

My brother recorded other examples in his private papers: namely, in March 1614, a fifty-year-old man who became useless due to a head wound and could hardly walk without a staff was awarded 723 pounds for the work he lacked and would lack, along with expenses.

But it should be noted **"that he demanded for a four-year loss of time, and 100 florins in expenses."**

In the same year and month, a certain young man of 20 years from Altdorff was awarded 700 florins for a head wound, because of which he could not speak fluently and felt great pain in his limbs; **"included therein were also the expenses (which amounted to 150 florins)."** Add the Franconian counsel of Wehner, 20.

Everything is different if the action is instituted in the name of "real injuries" <note>term: "injuriarum realium" — physical assaults intended to insult or dishonor</note> (which it is altogether advisable to combine with the useful Aquilian action). In such a case, not only the damage but also the injury—**"the disgrace and inequity"** <note>original: "die Schmach und Unbilligkeit"</note>—comes into consideration. Thus, even then, account can rarely be taken **"of the endured pains"** <note>original: "der ausgestandenen Schmerzen"</note>, which are otherwise priceless and cannot be considered as part of the quality of the damage.

Finally, in our practice, it is observed **"that the damage is not immediately valued in the preliminary judgment, but generally a restitution for the inflicted damage, doctor's wages, loss of time, and other incurred expenses is awarded; this, however, is only summarized afterward at the point of valuation, and set in the final judgment: In the matter of N., the previously awarded restitution is taxed and valued for N. florins, which the defendant shall be obliged to repay to the plaintiff in cash (or in installments at the Judge's discretion)."**

However, if anything is awarded in the name of "injuries" <note>meaning insults/dishonor</note>, it is usually determined immediately in the first sentence **"or in the main judgment."** There...

**14. Departure Tax, Deduction, Supplementary Tax.**
->Withdrawal.<- <note>original: "Detractio"</note>

Deduction is twofold: for it is taken either from those departing <note>original: "von Ausziehenden"</note>, who emigrate, or from **inheritances** <note>original: "von den Erbschafften"</note> which are transferred and brought into foreign lands. Most Magistrates claim this right of deduction for themselves in many places by special privilege, municipal law, or custom (*Thomingius, Illustrious Decisions, question 26, number 38*), so that they are accustomed to pluck away sometimes a tenth, sometimes a fourth, and sometimes a third—**the tenth, fourth, or third penny** <note>original: "den zehenden, vierdten oder dritten Pfenning"</note>—or more or less, from foreign heirs (*Andreas Rauchbar, book 1, question 15, in the preface*).

Furthermore, a person admitted into the number of citizens, or having the right of citizenship by birth, is not bound to remain there forever, nor can he be detained against his will by the Magistrate of that place; even if the Magistrate disagrees, it is permitted for him to transfer his domicile elsewhere and emigrate, provided it is not done with malicious intent (*Law: "Order 15," paragraph "penultimate," Digest: "On Municipals"; Law: "In War 12," Digest: "On Captives and Postliminy"; Graevius, book 2, Practical Conclusions, conclusion 36, consideration 2, number 3; Hondedeus, counsel 5, number 13 and following, volume 1; Myself, "On Civil Law," chapter 2, number 11 at the end, and chapter 3, number 10*). In which case, it is accepted in most places in Germany that in this event of transferring domicile and migration, a certain portion or quota of goods—**or perhaps even a double tax** <note>original: "oder etwan auch doppelte Steuer"</note>—can be deducted by the Magistrate (*Berlich, book 3, conclusion 52, number 12; Scheplitz on the Customs of the March, part 3, title 8; Ernest Cothmann, book 1, counsel 19, numbers 1, 2, etc.; Gail, book 2, observation 36, number 9*), where he adds that it is so established in Augsburg, Nuremberg, Speyer, and many other Cities (*Dauth, "On Wills," number 60; Cöppen, "Illustrious Decisions," question 11; Gilmann, volume 3, "Symphorema," folio 143; Dapper, "On Imperial Cities," folio 32*).

But it can hardly be doubted that statutes permitting this deduction are valid. Since they are clearly approved in the **Recess of the Imperial Diet** <note>An official resolution of the assembly of the Holy Roman Empire</note> held in Regensburg in the year 1594 (*Arumaeus on the Golden Bull, chapter 16, number 13, folio 269; Cöppen, decision 11; see Berlich, book 3, conclusion 51 and following*).

However, regarding what some pass down—that the **supplementary tax** <note>original: "die Nachsteuer"</note> is not owed in the case where subjects are forced to emigrate against their will, as was decided in the case of Heilbronn against the City of Schwäbisch Gmünd (reported by Reichwin, "Information," folio 202, number 3)—this can hardly be proven, since the **Religious Peace** <note>The Peace of Augsburg (1555), which allowed subjects to emigrate if they disagreed with their prince's religion</note> of the year 1555, paragraph

<column-break/>

"But where our," etc. <note>original: "Wo aber unsere &c." — a reference to a specific clause in the Peace of Augsburg</note> contradicts this; see Lord Wilhelm Anton *in the annexed Corollaries to the treatise "On Moratory Inducts," folio 13.* But the question is: can such a burden be newly instituted (since it is a **Regalian right** <note>A right belonging exclusively to a sovereign or the Emperor</note>) without prescription <note>Long-standing use that creates a legal right</note> or a privilege from the Emperor? It seems not.

If indeed the Magistrate of any jurisdiction, City, or place has the right of deducting or drawing off a certain portion from inheritances, Legacies, trusts, gifts made in anticipation of death, or household goods and movable property which fall to foreigners, pilgrims, or outsiders—can they use this right or privilege against the children of parents, or parents who are heirs to their children? Our legal experts ask this and say "no" (*Rauchbar, question 15; Schaeffer, "Practical Questions," 10, preface 2*). But usage says "yes." For if a **deduction can be taken** <note>original: "ein Abzug genommen werden"</note> from what one carries out, therefore it is also taken from what one inherits from parents. For it is the **supplementary tax** <note>original: "die Nachsteuer"</note>, and in this place, the inheritance comes out of the tax base (*Myself, "On the Treasury," chapter 4, section 14, number 3; Bornitius, "On the Treasury," chapter 31; Pistoris, 1, question 50, number 15*).

Whether this right of deduction also takes place in the names of debtors <note>i.e., the right to collect on debts owed to the deceased</note>? See altogether *Modestinus Pistoris, part 3, question 124, number 122, etc.* However, regarding a dowry and **festive clothing** <note>original: "vestibusque festivis"</note>, it is hardly likely that anything can be justly deducted (*Cöppen, decision 6*). *Cothmann* also exempts **Academics** from this burden (*Academic Counsels, 19*), and *Arumaeus* followed him (*on the Golden Bull, chapter 16, number 14, folio 249*). In Tübingen, however, only the descending heirs of Professors and Academic Officials are immune here.

But against whom, and in which goods this right has a place, and likewise by what cautions it might be circumvented, consult *Berlich, volume 3, conclusion 53, and see my own treatise "On the Treasury," chapter 4, section 14, verse 3.*

Whether the Magistrate is entitled to the **deduction** <note>original: "der Abzug"</note> in mobile or immobile goods, if the deceased left these behind, or if he who desires to transfer his domicile elsewhere has them in another district or territory? See *Rauchbar, question 17.* And it seems it should be looked at whether **these goods were previously taxed** <note>original: "diese Güter zuvor... versteuret worden"</note> in the place of domicile.

Otherwise, the deduction is regularly not paid for goods situated outside the territory (*Rauchbar, in the place cited; Myself, in the place cited*); for it is paid by virtue of jurisdiction, which does not extend beyond the territory (*Law: Final, Digest: "On Jurisdiction"*), and statutes do not extend to goods situated elsewhere, for example, if they concern the right of succession. But the contrary could be said to hold: because a Citizen is also taxed by reason of goods situated outside the territory; this withdrawal, moreover, is a tax—**a supplementary tax** <note>original: "eine Nachsteuer"</note>, etc. Therefore, etc.

Whether a deduction is to be given from an **Ecclesiastical inheritance**? Since this question was extensively treated and discussed by me in my *Counsels, part 4*, I do not wish to repeat its foundations here. One might also look at the **Settlement of Worms** <note>original: "die Wormbsische Richtung" — a 1521 legal agreement regarding judicial and fiscal boundaries</note>, title 3; likewise *Marta in his treatise "On Jurisdiction," part 4, folio 213.*

But whether a stranger or foreigner, to whom something has been bequeathed, must admit this deduction from the thing bequeathed, or whether the heir must redeem it...

It covers the rights of migration, the authority of local magistrates vs. imperial law, and specific exemptions for family members or academics.</summary>

...and is bound to provide the legacy in full to the legatee? Rauchbar treats this in *Question 16*. Truly, since this burden is imposed on the person and not on the property itself, it is more likely that it does not affect the heir. However, looking at the logic of the law, just as collections <note>general taxes or levies</note> are treated, so too the **Withdrawal Tax** <note>original: "Abzug"; a tax paid when moving property out of a jurisdiction</note> ought to be ascribed to the Royal Rights <note>regalia; rights belonging to the sovereign</note>: and thus it cannot be demanded anew by Nobles without the support of old custom, as already mentioned.

In the Duchy of Württemberg, those foreigners whose lordship has not specifically reached an agreement with His Princely Grace, etc., must pay the **Supplementary Tax** <note>original: "Nachsteuer"</note> on inheritances that have fallen within the land. Otherwise, however, a citizen may move away freely without any payment, and this is by virtue of the named Tübingen Treaty of the year 1514 <note>The "Tübinger Vertrag" is considered one of the most important constitutional documents of Württemberg, often called its Magna Carta, as it granted citizens rights of free movement and due process.</note>.

Neighboring these rights is the **Right of Escheat** <note>original: "Albinagii Jus" or "Droit d'aubaine"; a right formerly held by lords to inherit the property of any foreigner who died within their territory</note>, which in France is counted among the Royal Rights. <margin>Fr. de Clapperiis, decisions on cases 1, single question, part 4, case 2, question 1, page 14. The Noble Lord Mager, treatise on armed advocacy, chapter 15, number 136, etc. I, in "On the Rights of Political Majesty," chapter 7, number 6, and "On Civil Law," chapter 4, number 2.</margin> By virtue of this right, the inheritances of foreigners fall entirely to the treasury. In that case, it is fair that the right of retaliation <note>lex talionis</note> be used against such peoples, and that one also not let their people inherit <note>original: "und daß man auch die Ihrige nicht erben lasse"</note>. Schultes, *Practical Questions 6*; add Hartmann Pistoris, *Observation 43*. Louis Servin, *The Pleadings*, volume 2, page 281 and following, where he provides an elegant decree of the Parliament <note>The Parliament of Paris, which acted as a high court</note> on the question: *whether the children of a Frenchman or Frenchwoman, a servant of the late Lady Margaret of France, Duchess of Savoy, born outside of France, are capable of succession in this Kingdom, and how?* This right truly savors of the older Roman custom by which foreigners were held as enemies. Just as it can be used against Barbarians and infidels, so it is unfair if it burdens Christians living in one Church, among whom there ought to be a closer kinship and a bond of brotherhood.

In the Duchy of Württemberg, citizens—by virtue of the Tübingen Settlement entered into in the year 1514 at Tübingen with Duke Ulrich, and confirmed by Duke Christopher in 1551—are free from the burden of deduction: the **Tübingen Treaty** gives every Württemberg citizen a free departure/and that with his own property <note>original: "einen freyen Zug/& Das mit auch der [hab]"</note>. Provided that the one emigrating: 1. pays all debts; 2. does nothing against the fatherland within a year; 3. acquiesces to the determination of legal cases within a year. Similar privileges are also enjoyed by the citizens of Speyer, Worms, and Kitzingen, as relates Gilman, volume 3, *Symphorema*, page 143; Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 63, page 534.

On the Right of Emigration and Deduction, see the specific booklet by Christoph Schwammann. The customs of France and Italy everywhere observe the right of deduction <margin>Decianus, response 54, number 55; Rauchbar, book 1, question 54.</margin> Question: is he who migrates elsewhere out of necessity, and not by his own fault, bound to pay the right of deduction? Unless one has voluntarily cast himself into the necessity of emigrating,

<column-break/>

namely by committing a crime, it is denied <margin>following the argument of Law 36 at the end, Digest on Judgments; Law 7, section 1, Digest on those compelled to give security.</margin> Köppen, *Decision 11, number 15*; Berlich, volume 5, *Conclusion 52, number 13*. Therefore, it is fair and just that a Magistrate cannot demand an emigration tax from subjects whom he orders to leave his jurisdiction because of **Religion**, as the reporter relates in Gilman. However, the practice of the Empire has taught the opposite until now, according to Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 63, page 532 and following.

**Withdrawal, Departure, and Supplementary Tax** <note>original: "Abzug, Abfahrt, Nachsteuer"</note> are paid by subjects who transfer property outside the territory. Mundius, *On Duties*, chapter 2, number 447, and many following. Bavaria does not know the **Supplementary Tax**; see especially Mundius, chapter 2, number 473. The Counts Palatine were sometimes exempted from the burden of deduction, as it was granted to them to migrate and return where, when, and as often as they wished, without paying even a penny <note>original: "obulo"</note> for it. Mundius, *On the Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 381. Thus the Margrave of Ansbach <note>original: "Onoltzbach"</note> and the Council of Nuremberg reached an agreement that for property located at Fürth or around Cadolzburg, the supplementary tax should go to Nuremberg, but for property around Roth or Schwabach, the supplementary tax should be delivered to the Margrave. Likewise, Johann Conrad, Bishop of Eichstätt <note>original: "Eystätt"</note>, and the Council of Nuremberg reached an agreement on December 12, 1602, regarding subjects in the countryside who did not live in walled cities or market towns, that they should be exempt from the supplementary tax.

If a daughter from Altdorf marries into Nuremberg, the Altdorf authorities take 5 out of 100 florins as a supplementary tax, as seen in the case of the second wife of W. K. Emperor Maximilian II's privilege granted to the city of Frankfurt regarding the supplementary tax and the **tenth penny** <note>a 10% tax</note> before departure is recounted by Limnaeus, book 7, chapter 16, number 31. The tenth penny is also given in cases of inheritance. *Ibid.*

### Augmented Practical Treasury

...there are those who say, see my treatise on *Majesty, page 136.* <note>original: "de Majest. f. 136."</note>
Regarding this matter, the Reverend Father Charles Stengel <note>An 18th-century Benedictine abbot and historian.</note> writes in his *Monasteries, in the Preface to the Reader*: Formerly, he says, schools were attached to monasteries, in which the younger age was shaped in letters suitable for that tender time, and the more mature were shaped for more advanced and rigorous studies. The most learned and proven monks presided over these schools; however, there was a distinction, at least in some places, so that there were two types of schools: some internal, dedicated to the education of the religious <note>i.e., monks and novices</note>; others external, in which secular persons and the children of leaders and nobles were instructed. *See the Antiquities of Fulda, page 35, etc.*

Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous German abbot and polymath.</note> wrote excellently about this same institution in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, and after many points he adds this: A great devotion flourished in them: a zeal for regular discipline burned in their minds which deserved praise, and never allowed them to be idle. For, keeping the divine office <note>The daily cycle of prayers</note> in which all were devotedly engaged, the monks spent the rest of their time in the study of the scriptures, by which they were not only enlightened in understanding but also moved in their affections. Likewise regarding the College of *Liège*, the *Great Belgian Chronicle* records these words: There were at this time (the year 1131) in the Church of *Liège* resident Canons who were the sons of 21 kings, 14 sons of dukes, 29 sons of counts, and 7 sons of knights and barons, among whom were also many distinguished doctors and masters of various nations. Regarding this matter, Aubertus Miraeus also writes in his *Funeral Oration for St. Thomas*, which is attached to the same Miraeus’s *Monastic Origins, page 399*, where he says: We once had very famous schools in our *Benedictine* monasteries: for indeed our ancestors judged from the earliest times of the Church that the care of handing down letters should be entrusted to the <term>Sacred Order</term> <note>The clergy</note>, because they thought it mattered greatly if boys drank in piety along with letters through their ears and eyes, being constantly in the company of churchmen. Thus, in the first centuries, the *Benedictines* labored in that <term>Scholastic Arena</term> <note>original: "Palæstra Scholastica," a metaphor for a place of rigorous training</note> to the great benefit of both themselves and the Republic: from which came the favor of all nations and immense wealth. Afterward, the *Dominican Fathers* devoted the same study and labor to the education of youth, as Ferdinand Castillo and other writers of the deeds of the *Dominicans* record, as well as Pedro de Ribadeneira in the *Life of Blessed Ignatius of Loyola*.

The *Fathers of the Society of Jesus* <note>The Jesuits</note> succeeded or rather joined themselves to these, opening schools throughout the whole world.

Later, Universities were established separately. Thus, according to Peter von Beeck in his *Description of Aachen, page 66*, speaking of *Charlemagne*: For the propagation of the faith, he says, he established sanctuaries of science and Universities, such as the one in *Paris*, in the founding of which he used four most learned disciples of *Bede*, the venerable Priest: *Alcuin, Rabanus, Claudius, and John Scotus*, whom he summoned from England, and from whom *Charlemagne* learned much. Recognizing this benefit piously and

<column-break/>

prudently, Perpinian in his *Oration on Divine and Human Philosophy* says that about eight hundred years ago, in the city of *Paris*, by the authority of the supreme Emperor *Charlemagne*, a seat of human and divine arts was established, and in every age the flower of genius, industry, and erudition has stood forth there. He adds that there are very few well-ordered schools that do not owe their origin and growth to the school of *Paris*. Others say that *Charlemagne* himself at one time visited the school of the *University of Paris* that he had founded, saw the compositions of the poor students and their progress in studies, and praised them with promises of promotion; but to the rich and noble, who relied on the splendor of their families and their wealth, he threatened with an oath that, unless they watched over their studies more diligently, he would deprive them of every degree of honor. He also erected the *University of Bologna*, the *Gymnasium of Ticino* (now *Pavia*), and schools in *Osnabrück*, in one of which the Greek language would be taught, and in the other the Latin language.

The <term>Palatine Vicars</term> <note>Deputies who exercised imperial power during a vacancy in the throne</note> do everything as <term>Provisors</term> <note>original: "Verweser und Verwalter," German terms for administrators or stewards</note>, and their power is in matters which either do not, or cannot without inconvenience, admit delay, as I shall say in its proper place, God willing. But indeed, to erect Universities, to create new Princes, etc., are matters which not only allow for delay but demand it. Therefore, the people of *Strasbourg* did not seek their University from a Vicar, but from the *Emperor*.

Therefore, the right of erecting a University is rightly listed by Afflictus <note>Mattheus de Afflictis, a famous Neapolitan jurist</note> among those things which belong to the Emperor alone. See also Zasius, Seyffel, Matthias Stephanus, and the *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber*. I also discuss this in my *On Majesty, page 185, etc.* Indeed, the creation of Doctors, Licentiates, etc., belongs to the reserved power of the Emperor, and no one has that grace except by the grant of the Emperor; nor has any Bachelor been created by a Vicar thus far, much less a University instituted.

But here it should be noted <note>The following passage was originally in German</note> that against the three *Dutch City Universities*, an exception was raised and argued in a case before the *East Friesland Court of Appeals*, claiming that these schools are not under the Empire or privileged by the *Imperial Majesty*; therefore, legal documents should not be sent there. Although one party pushed for it, claiming that this matter concerned the *repair of dikes* <note>original: "reparationem aggerum"</note>, about which those places have expertise; the other party stood firm, arguing that *East Friesland* is a distinguished member of the *Holy Roman Empire*, and therefore it would not be proper to send records from there to those places, etc.

Nevertheless, there is no doubt that Universities erected and confirmed by the Pope are to be considered true Universities.

Regarding the <term>absolute jurisdiction</term> <note>original: "mero Imperio"; this refers to the high legal authority, including criminal justice, held by a territory or institution</note> of Universities, see the *Criminal Discourse of Hesse* by Hunnium, page 84; and Bockel’s *Disquisitions*, vision 3, number 20. On the question of whether a Rector of a University can be sued for damages after leaving office—<note>original German: "wann er einem unrecht gethan?"</note> "if he has done someone wrong"—the same author on page 98 responds in the affirmative, based on the legal text *nec Magistr.* in the Digest regarding injuries. For a magistrate, having laid down his office, is held to answer for the deeds he committed while in power. This is persuaded by equity itself: since magistrates are also subject to the laws, they are not permitted to act injuriously, and if they exceed their office, they are seen to use illicit force. If it were decided otherwise for an Academic magistrate than for a Municipal magistrate, then this absurdity would follow: that the members of the University would not be free, but under a condition almost like Turkish slavery, as stated in the *Decisions of the Leipzig Jurists*, question 89.

On whether Academics are compared to Clergy, see Lindenim’s *History of Roman Law*, theses 71 and 75.

Indeed, many others have written histories and praises of certain specific Academies: Albericus Gentilis on **Perugia** and **Oxford**; Riccobonus on the **Gymnasium of Padua**; Johann Stephan Strobelberger on **Montpellier**; and regarding the **Academy of Tübingen**, one may consult my own treatise *On Majesty*, folio 168, as well as the treatise *On the Law of Things*, folio 64, etc.
Sweertius also presents a catalog of all Academies in *Athenae Belgicae* [Belgian Athens], folio 59, etc.; Alsted in his *Chronology*, folio 143; the *Chronicle of Chronicles*, folio 1280; add Reusner in his *Introduction*, folio 163.
What an Academy is, however, and where it is, and from whom it was so named, Diogenes Laertius teaches as accurately as he does briefly in Book 2 regarding Plato, of whom he says: "Returning to Athens, he held a school in the Academy." It is, in fact, a suburban gymnasium, wooded, named after a certain hero, **Academus**. And he soon adds that it was originally named **Hecademia** after the same Hecademus, citing the verses of both Eupolis and Timon. These are Timon's verses regarding Plato:
> Among these went that leader Plato, most broad <note>original: "latiſſimus"; a pun on Plato's name, which is derived from the Greek 'platýs,' meaning 'broad' or 'wide.'</note>,
> From whose mouth flowed a melody, such as the cicadas
> Tune with a pleasant voice in the groves of **Hecademus**.
For previously it was called Hecademia with the "He-." Thus far according to Laertius.
You will find the same concerning the origin of the name in the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on classical texts.</note> of Aristophanes on *The Clouds*, and in Suidas's *Lexicon*. Hence, Horace's verse in Book II, Epistle II, should be read thus:
> And to seek the truth among the woods of **Hecademus**.
That is, to seek the truth among the Academics or Platonists; it should not be written "of Academus" <note>original: "Academi"; the author is arguing for the spelling 'Hecademi' to match the hero's name.</note>, since no one was called by that name.
Suidas further says there were three gymnasia in Athens: the **Lyceum**, **Cynosarges**, and the **Academy**. See the Jesuit Peter Halloix's notes on the life of St. Justin, folio 281. Nor was it uncommon to name gymnasia after their location. So also the **Stoics** were named from the place where they disputed, which is called the <term>Painted Porch</term> <note>original Greek: "στοὰ ποικιλὴ" (stoa poikile)</note>, so named from the variety of boards or painted tablets with which it was decorated. Likewise, the **Peripatetics** were named from walking: for in Greek <term>to walk</term> <note>original Greek: "περιπατεῖν" (peripatein)</note> is the word, because Aris-

<column-break/>

-totle, their leader, would philosophize while walking, as Halloix notes in the cited place, folio 282.

### ADDITION.

The Lords Professors at the universities <note>original German: "hohen Schulen"</note> should not be so liberal with **doctoral honors**, lest it reach their ears what that enemy of doctors at Tübingen wrote: "Doctoral honors are nowhere so cheap in Germany as in that place which, by <term>anagram</term>, is called **Labes**" <note>original German: "Labes"; an anagram for the city of **Basel** (Basle). In Latin, 'labes' also means a 'stain' or 'disgrace,' creating a sharp insult against the ease of obtaining degrees there.</note>. When a certain professor at S. asked a student if he knew the law by virtue of which the **B. Doctors** <note>Likely referring to "Bullati" doctors—those created by a papal or imperial bull without the standard rigorous examinations.</note> could be defended, and the student reflected on the matter, the professor told him to look up Law 18 in the introduction of the Digest *on the Aedilitian Edict*. But all these things should be judged in moderation according to <term>equity and the good</term> <note>original: "ex æquo & bono"; a legal principle of fairness.</note>, etc. Their sins are always and continually to be chastised until they repent—those who make a <term>Boundary Stone</term> <note>original: "Terminalem"; referring to Terminus, the god of boundaries.</note> out of any stone, a **Statue of Mercury** <note>original: "Statua Mercurialis"; Mercury was the god of eloquence and commerce; his statues often marked crossroads.</note> out of any wood, and thus make groves out of one or two trees (which, because they have reached the end of their academic studies through diligence, deserve to be decorated with a boundary honor). Thus, by breaking the limits of license, the nation of the learned and unlearned is confused in promiscuous contempt, just as indeed an honor, to which more excellent things ought to be committed, becomes cheapened by its sheer quantity (*Chapter 1 on the privileges and excesses of prelates*). 

If someone praises a small slave at an auction as being endowed with this or that skill, he is ordered by the **Edict of the Aediles** <note>Roman market regulations enforced by officials called aediles.</note> to provide him as such, clearly according to what was said or promised (Law 17, final paragraph, *on the Aedilitian Edict*). Nor will an excuse provide relief—namely, that those things which are brought forward only for the sake of recommendation and in praise of a man are not usually guaranteed (Law 19, *on the Aedilitian Edict*)—since if a seller has promised that he will especially provide something, it is nevertheless not to be bitterly demanded from him, but in moderation according to **equity and the good** (Law 18, at the end of said title). So much so that if someone has promised or said someone is a craftsman, he is not necessarily bound to provide a perfect one, but one skilled to some degree, so that you neither receive one of consummate science, nor again one who is plainly unlearned in the craft. Finally, let it suffice that they are such as—concluding the Jurist in Law 9, paragraph 4 of said title—are commonly called **craftsmen**. 

As if now it were also sufficient here for a craftsman in the **art of Law** to be, at least, slightly skilled; and indeed to be such as those who are commonly promoted, "as they are brought to market" <note>original German: "wie man ſie zu Marckt bringt"</note>. For besides the fact that he who has most greatly admitted the terms of comparison could easily retort and reply (from Law 18, paragraph 1 of the often-praised title), it matters entirely whether one has simply said "a Cook," for example, or truly an "excellent and distinguished" one. So that the former indeed seems to satisfy the requirement even if he provides a mediocre Cook; but he who said he was an "excellent Cook" ought to provide the best craftsmanship in him. And consequently, as in other types of craftsmen, so also in the **art of Law**: since Doctors are not simply praised, but with the eulogy of "Most Illustrious" or "Excellent Consultant," such men must be provided in every respect...

### 17. Done, or these things have been transacted.
<note>original: "Actum, oder geschehen sind diese Ding."</note>

Hondedei says in *consultation 38, number 45 and following, volume 1*, that the effect of this clause is to prove that the legal instrument was read to the parties involved. This clause also denotes the perfection of the instrument and its publication, especially if it is found placed at the beginning, rather than in the middle or at the end. See Marta, *on clauses, part 1, clause 4*, and Anton Hering, *on sureties, chapter 7, number 481.*

### 18. Nobility, Nobleman, Noble Servant, Noble Serf. Noble Ministerial.
<note>original: "Adel, Edelmann, Edle Knecht, Adelschalck. Nobilis Ministerialis."</note>

Concerning nobility and the origin of nobility, see Guillim, *On the Swiss, book 2, chapter 11, folio 240, etc.* and Stumpf in *On the Swiss, book 4, folio 291, etc.* Likewise, Reineccius, *On the Descent of the Nobility; The Silesian Knight-Servant*, where many things are also found concerning the law of the Nobles and the proof of Nobility; add the *Chronicle of Silesian Knights, book 3, chapter 24.* Also see Pontanus, *book 6 of the Origins of the Franks, chapter 15*; Tiraquellus, Stephani, and Peter Frizo in their *individual treatises*; likewise Nolden, Friedenreich in *Politics, part 2, chapter 25*; the *Academic Discourses on the Bull, 4*; Calvin’s Lexicon under the word <term>Ingenuus</term> <note>a person born free</note>; Balthasar Thomas, *folio 13 and following*; Keckermann in *Ethics*; Casman in *Politics, folio 267*, where he discusses what they ought to beware of. See Bisciola, *Various Readings, book 2, chapter 7, chapter 10*, and the two dialogues among the prose works of Tasso, where on *folio 396* he teaches how nobility and dignity differ. Welser, in *History of Augsburg, folio 128*, explains why Nobles are called "Gentiles" by the Italians, French, and English, etc. <note>meaning "of the same clan or gens"</note>. But I do not grasp his meaning, and I think they are rather called Gentiles from "Gens" <note>clan/family</note>, as in <gloss>lineages</gloss>.

The German word **Nobility**, or **the Noble**, <note>original: "Edele, oder der Adel"</note> perhaps descends from the Greek *aithōn* <note>meaning shining or fiery</note>; see Grasser’s *Itinerary, folio 264*, Crusius, *Paralipomena, chapter 22*, and what I have noted in the *Treatise on the Equestrian Order*. This denotes one who is well-deserving or affected by a reward, by which the very origin of Nobility is demonstrated. Stephani, *on nobility, chapter 1, number 10*. The Hebrews also call them *Atfilim*—the elite, the selected magnates—separated from the common crowd and standing out among the people like "armpits" <note>an idiomatic expression for those in high or prominent positions</note>. There are those who derive it from *godal*, as if they were "the great"; see my *treatise on the three types of domestic society, folio 87 and following.* Also Andreas Helvig in *Origins of German Words* under the words **Noble, Eagle, Noble** <note>original: "Adel, Adler, Edel"</note>. Some think it is named after the **Eagle**, <note>original: "vom Adeler"</note> because just as the eagle,

<column-break/>

penetrating more deeply by flying higher, leaves other birds a long distance behind it, so too do the Nobles far excel the other orders of men in the glory of their virtues. But I think the Eagle is rather named after **Noble** <note>original: "Adel"</note> as if it were the "noble bird," rather than the reverse. Or perhaps it comes from *adelon* <note>Greek: αἴδελον</note>, for it was so pleasing because Nobles please everyone on account of their virtues; or from *hedelon* <note>Greek: ἕδηλον</note>, meaning a seat, that is, possession and goods, because Nobles are most often judged by their wealthy possessions.

Thus some incorrectly derive it from Adelo, the son of Friso, the founder of the Frisian race, as in Suffridus Petrus, *Description of Friesland, decade 1, chapter 2, at the end*; Josias Nolden, *on the status of Nobles, chapter 1, number 15 and following*; as well as from the Saxon *Adelingi* or *Edhilingis*, who were leaders of the highest dignity, as in Andreas Knichen, *on territorial law, chapter 1, number 28 and following*. Rather, these groups were named after the **Noble** status <note>original: "vom Adel"</note>. This appears even from Knichen himself, who says in that same place, following others: that the Saxon people consisted of a three-part order. Some were **Adelingi**, namely the more noble; others were **Frilingi**, as if left free <note>freemen</note>; the rest were **Lazzii**, that is, husbandmen or those bound to the soil, called <gloss>their own people</gloss> <note>original: "eigene Leut"; i.e., serfs</note>, as stated by Christian Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle, book 2, chapter 4*; see also the entire Glossary of Lindenbrog under the word *Adelingus*. And concerning the *Adelingi*, see Reineccius, *On the Origin of the Saxons, folio 9 and following*, and the fact that Dukes and Counts were created from them, in the same author's *Annals of Charles, folio 13*.

And although, as the aforementioned Master Nolden says in the cited place, number 29, all subjects or even citizens were once generally called **People**, <note>original: "Leut, sive Leudes, aut etiam Leodes"</note> as in Goldast, *Alamannic Affairs, volume 1, folio 220 and following*, and Lindenbrog in his glossary under the word *Leudes*. Among these, however, certain people serving others were called **Poor People**, <note>original: "Arme Leut"</note> of a servile or rather semi-free condition, not from poverty, but from the hand or arm <note>referring to manual labor</note>. See my *treatise on the three types of domestic society, folio 31*. From this the French speak of **Mainmort** <note>original: "Main mort"; "dead hand," a legal term for inalienable property held by a corporation or church, often associated with feudal burdens</note>. The Nobles, however, were specifically designated as **Man** or **Men** <note>original: "Mann sive Manne"</note>. See my *discourse on Counts and Barons, number 16*. Similarly, among the Hebrews there was a distinction among citizens, such that some were called *Viri* <note>Latin: Men of status/strength</note>, or "sons of the Man," while others were called "sons of the human" <note>distinguishing between elite and commoners</note>. See Piscator in his *Scholia on the Proverbs of Solomon, chapter 8*; Drusius, *Hebrew Questions, book 1, chapter 21, and on passages in Genesis, chapter 31*. We use this in nearly the same sense when we speak of Patricians and Plebeians together. This difference is most clearly observed in *Psalm 49, verse 3*, where the Prophet speaks thus: "Hearken, all you inhabitants of the world; both the sons of the common man and the sons of the great man; the rich and the poor together." And those designated as "sons of the man" are taken to be the Nobles. Similarly, in Saxon feudal law, vassals are simply called **Man**, <note>original: "Mann"</note> as if endowed with virility and a strenuous and upright spirit. Peter Heigius, *part 1, question 2, number 85.*

Why certain families are called "ancient" Nobles and others are not, see Martin, *century 6, disputation 9, question 9*; as to whether one may also be ennobled through the mother, see the same, *disputation 20, question 7*; he also teaches in *question 9* that there are no Nobles under a tyranny. That human society cannot consist of only one class of men was established by **Danaeus, *Politics*, book 2, chapter 6, page 77.** <note>Lambert Danaeus (c. 1530–1595) was a French Reformed theologian and jurist.</note> And it is considered safer and better if nobility of lineage is examined rather than nobility of wealth; for otherwise everyone would seek riches and acquire them through evil arts. Meanwhile, however, the wealth of nobles must be preserved through **fiefs**, **family entails** <term>fideicommissa: legal arrangements where property is held for the benefit of a family line</term>, **renunciations by women** <note>legal agreements where noblewomen gave up inheritance rights to keep estates intact</note>, **rights of primogeniture**, and so on. That there were few nobles in the past under the Franks is reported by **Crusius, book 10, part 1, page 263**, citing **Stumpf in his *Swiss Chronicle*, book 4, chapter 29.** He says there: In those times when the Merovingians ruled France, such a great multitude of nobles was not found as in much later times. For there is not much mention of nobles in chronicles, legal instruments, letters, etc. **Dukes, Princes, Counts, etc.** were only names of **offices**, not titles derived from hereditary lineage.

It should also be noted here that in ancient times, noblemen commonly belonged to the castles and cities, as appears from the **Kitzingen Acts, page 20.**

Regarding the **Origin of the Nobility**, etc. Titles derived from **Villages**, see **Guilliman in *Helvetia*, book 2, page 217**, where he cites a law sounding as follows: Those who have received some favor from the Prince or his relatives should establish and preserve his titles, so that they and their children feel obligated to the King and acknowledge it from that source. Regarding the vices of nobles, consult the **History of Francis II, page 668.** Regarding the nobility of Batavia <note>The Netherlands</note>, see **Junius in *Batavia*, chapter 19.**

Whether a **Count** or **Baron** can or should marry a noblewoman? I have treated this in my **Consilia, part 2**, to which I refer the reader.

In the past, the title of **Noble** was granted only to Dukes, Counts, and Barons, according to **Conrad Rittershusius in his *Introduction to Feudal Commentaries*** and **Christoph Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, book 2, chapter 14, section 19**; indeed, it was even given to Kings. Thus, Charles V was said to affirm himself "by the word of a nobleman," see the **Description of the State of Poland, page 13.** In the year of Christ 1363, the Prioress of Renthy called the Count Palatine Richard "the Noble High-Born."

The rest of the nobility, however, were called **Ministerials** <term>Ministeriales: a class of unfree nobles who served in administrative or military roles</term> or **Feudatories**, commonly known as **Noble Servants** <note>original: "Edle Knechte"</note>, see **Albert Krantz in *Metropolis*, book 3, chapter 11; Crusius, *Swabian Annals*, part 1, book 10**, or **Servants of the Holy Empire**, see the **Imperial Ordinance of the year 1500, title: *Regarding the Tax on Servants and Knights*, Imperial Recess of the year 1500, section "We or the." Joseph Nolden, *On Nobility*, chapter 1, number 58.** And from this, all the Prince's servants were very commonly called **Noble Serfs** <note>original: "Adelschalck"</note>, according to **Lindenbrog in the *Glossary*, under the word *Adelschalck*.** "Noble Serf" is the same as **Noble Servant**. See the **Lindau Acts, page 592 at the beginning, and page 601 after the middle.** This is also testified by Reiner Reineccius in his treatise *On the Original Descent of the Nobility*, pages 24 and following; for he says thus: Noble servants were the others of lower nobility, and they received this name because they were bound to serve their lords in wars and other affairs. Thus, Gregory

And although the Emperor, in the addresses and titles of Counts and Barons, retains this style: "To the Noble, our and the Empire’s dear faithful [Name], Count or Lord of [Place]," unless he grants a title to Princes of a higher rank, they are accustomed to not even open the letters, but to return them without a response, if Nolden does not deceive us in **the cited place, number 61.** The situation is different in France, where the King treats absolutely all nobles and princes (as the comic writer jokes) "with the same comb" <note>an idiom meaning to treat everyone exactly the same, without distinction</note>, with this address: **"To Monsieur, Monsieur, etc." or "To our beloved and loyal [Name], Prince [Name], Gentleman, etc."**

And that in the past, Counts were also commonly called "Noble" by private citizens, but those who were somewhat more prominent were called "Noble and Well-Born," can be proven from many old diplomas <note>official documents or charters</note>. But those of lower rank were called **Noble Servants**, for "man" is a word of dignity.

Certainly, the **Ministerials**, of whom there is frequent mention in German history, are our **Knights**. Among the Saxons, the knighthood are called **honorable and good men**, and because of the service which they owe to Princes by reason of their clientage, they are called **Squires** or **Servants** <note>original: "Knaspen oder Knecht"</note>. In Latin, they are called *servi* (servants), *servientes* (sergeants), and *famuli* (attendants): for this is how the diplomas speak.

They are distinguished from and almost opposed to men of free condition (the **Free Lords** or *Freyherren*) in **Brusch, *On Monasteries*, page 41.** Of these, those who were gifted with a collar <note>a symbol of knighthood</note> were called **Soldiers** or **Knights**; the rest were called attendants or servants. ### ADDITION.

It is more publicly useful for nobility to flourish, according to Cothmann, response 1, number 113, volume 4. "He who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed shall dwell on high," Isaiah 33. This passage is explained by Brentius in his commentary on John, chapter 1, folio 59. The custom of granting nobility through "Patents of Nobility" <note>original: *Adelsbrief*</note> did not begin so recently as some think; for there exists a constitution of Zeno—who held the Empire a thousand years ago—in which he expressly mentions nobility, testifying that it was conferred on some through "honorary letters" <note>original: *Codicillos*</note> without the person holding an administrative office. See law *quoties* 3, section 2, Code *ubi Senatores vel Clarissimi*. Mundius, *On Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 30. There is a noticeable difference between being "Noble" and being a "Nobleman" <note>original: *Edel und Edelmann seyn*</note>. ### 19. Noble Fiefs and Estates.

->Noble Fiefs.<- <note>original: *Feuda Nobilium*</note>

A Noble Fief is properly called that which ennobles its possessor, according to the chapter *quis dicetur Dux*. And it is called "Noble" because it either finds and receives a Noble and displays him as such, or it actually makes a man Noble, according to Baldus.

Commonly, however, they say there is a triple type of Noble fief: Johannes Schneidewein in his *Introduction to Feudal Law*, number 33; Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations* 1, thesis 6, letter b.

<column-break/>

For a certain kind is "Noble," which is otherwise called "Regal," or a "Banner-fief" <note>original: *Fahnlehen*</note>, when the dignity of a Duchy or County is conferred by the Emperor upon a Duke or Marquis, and these are called "Captains of the King."

The second type is *Less Noble*, which a Duke, Marquis, or Count grants to Nobles, who are properly called "Vavassors" <term>Valvassores: vassals who hold land from a great lord rather than directly from the King or Emperor</term>, which is when Princes, Counts, and Lords grant fiefs to those of the nobility.

The third type is *Moderately Noble*, when one holding a fief from a Duke or Marquis grants a sub-fief to other inferiors, who are called "minor Vavassors."

In contrast, an "Ignoble Fief" is one that does not ennoble its possessor, such as those granted by minor Vavassors to the "least Vavassors" (or *Valvafini*). Those who receive these do not acquire any Nobility; these are also called "Burgage Fiefs" or "Peasant-fiefs" <note>original: *Burger- oder Bauren-Lehen*</note>. These almost approach the nature of a long-term lease <term>emphyteuseos: a type of Roman law contract where land is leased for a long period in exchange for a yearly rent</term>, since usually a rent or tax <note>original: *canon vel census*</note> is paid from them rather than military service. Thus I understand what they say: that today even any Peasant <note>original: *Rusticus*</note> can create a fief of his own things, provided he has the legal administration of his property.

The King or Emperor grants nobility through a fief to Vassals of the First Order. To others only if, with the attached burden of military service, the estate has remained in that family from ancient times. For the right of ennobling belongs only to one who holds Majesty (Sovereignty).

In Saxony, only the "Regal Fief" <note>original: *Fahnlehen*</note> has the effect of ennobling. Other noble fiefs (Noble or Knightly Fiefs, <note>original: *Adelich- oder Ritter-Lehen*</note>) are called so not because the Vassal acquires nobility by reason of the fief, but because those who are already truly noble are invested with these fiefs as nobles. (For nobles can, like anyone else, also acquire commoner fiefs for themselves; and conversely, commoners can acquire noble fiefs). See the *Saxon Feudal Law* <note>original: *Lehen-Recht*</note>, chapters 2 and 20:
> Nothing raises a man’s shield, except the Banner-fief.

See also the gloss on chapter 78 and the *Saxon Territorial Law* <note>original: *Landrecht*</note>, book 1, article 27. In this regard, the customs of all Germany seem to agree with Saxon Law. The same custom also flourishes in France. Therefore, in our lands, a certain argument for Nobility cannot be taken simply from the possession of non-regal fiefs.

In Spain, however, every fief for which military service is performed according to the use and custom of that Kingdom is considered noble, according to Intrigliolus.

<summary>This page defines the various ranks of nobility and squires, distinguishing between those who hold titles by office versus lineage, and details the three levels of "noble fiefs" (estates) and how they relate to social status in Saxony, Germany, France, and Spain.</summary>

Thus, even a commoner <note>original: *rusticus*, literally "peasant" or "countryman"</note> who buys a noble fief is not ennobled by that purchase. I discuss this in my work *On the Triple Domestic Society* <note>original: *de trib. domeft. foc.*</note>, page 96. Similarly, certain estates exist in Swabia which are called "free noble estates" <note>original: *freye Adeliche Güter*</note>; these grant certain privileges and exemptions to the possessor—as they also contribute taxes alongside the knightly class <note>original: *sie contribuiren auch mit der Ritterschafft*</note>—but they do not grant actual Nobility. In the same way, one who holds a Duchy is not always a Duke, nor is one who holds a County or Barony always a Count or Baron; rather, they are simply called the "possessors" <note>original: *Inhabere*</note> of those lands.

I add this further point from ancient documents: In the year 1351, the Lordships of Helfenstein and Heidenheim—which previously belonged to independent Barons—were granted by Emperor Charles IV to the Counts of Helfenstein as a noble hereditary fief <note>original: *Edlen Erblehen*</note> to be possessed forever, along with all their appurtenances.

Some believe that a "Noble Fief" <note>original: *Edel Lehen*</note> is a "freed" or "Baronial" fief, because in those times Barons were called "the Nobles."

### 20. The Eagle.

The coat of arms of the Empire features an Eagle <note>original: *Adler*</note> for several reasons: (1) Because Moses prophesied concerning this in Deuteronomy 28:49: "The Lord will bring a nation against you from far away, from the ends of the earth, swooping down like an eagle, whose language you will not understand." Some interpret this as referring to the Romans. (2) Because the Roman Consul <note>original: *Burgermeister*</note> Gaius Marius first carried an eagle on his military standards during the Cimbrian War, and this practice was continued. (3) Because the eagle is the king of all birds and flies the highest.

However, the Roman Eagle has two heads, one looking toward the East <note>original: *Morgen*</note> and the other toward the West <note>original: *Abend*</note>. This serves as a reminder that in ancient times the Roman Empire was divided into two parts, namely by the two co-emperors who ruled simultaneously, as happened frequently after the time of Constantine the Great. See my treatise *On Jurisdiction* <note>original: *de jurisd.*</note>, question 4. The emperors of Constantinople also used a double eagle, as if to show their empire stretched across both Asia and Europe. Furthermore, a double eagle is found on ancient Roman marbles, which is said to denote a "twin legion" <term>legionem gemellam: a military unit formed by the merging of two previous legions</term>, according to Freher's notes on Peter von Andlo, book 2, chapter 14, page 199. Von Andlo writes on this subject in the same place: "Since the eagle was always the most noble heraldic sign of the Empire, it was adopted by the ancient Romans as a symbol for their standards." Valerius reports in book 1 that when Remus and Romulus were observing the omens <note>original: *auspicia*</note> on the sacred Aventine Hill, they saw eagles there. Because the eagle is the queen of all birds, they intended this omen to be a sign of a most prosperous Empire. Nevertheless, Romulus, the father of the Roman Empire,

<column-break/>

did not immediately carry the eagle on his standard from the very beginning. Instead, soldiers even used bundles of hay as their banners. But as wars became more frequent, the leaders of the legions first brought the sign of the eagle onto the standard, as Lucan says:

> When the familiar eagles and Roman standards shone upon the field, etc.

Even today, the crowned eagle remains a consecrated and inviolable emblem in the arms of Emperors, designating the preeminence that the Imperial majesty <note>original: *Cæsarea sublimitas*</note> holds in the world. Thus the Prophet Ezekiel, speaking of Nebuchadnezzar, the monarch of the East, says: "A great eagle with great wings and long limbs, full of feathers, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar," etc. Pierius Valerianus also treats the prerogatives of the eagle extensively in his *Hieroglyphics*, book 19, noting that it carries the lightning bolts of Jove; that it foretold empire and kingship to many; that it is the queen of birds; and that the sight of it indicates happiness. He also notes that the Persians held the eagle sacred before the Romans did, along with other similar facts.

The most learned Drusius also noted in his commentary on the difficult passages of Numbers, chapter 4, that there were four standards in the camps of the Israelites: namely, on the standard of Judah was a Lion; on the standard of Reuben, a Man; on the standard of Ephraim, an Ox; and on the standard of Dan, an Eagle. He adds that the camp of Judah was toward the east, joined by the tribes of Issachar and Zebulun. Reuben's camp was toward the south, joined by the tribes of Simeon and Gad. Ephraim was in the west, with Manasseh and Benjamin. Dan was in the North <note>original: *Aquilone*</note>, joined by the tribes of Asher and Naphtali.

Those who desire to know more concerning these matters should consult Peter von Andlo in his treatise *On the Roman Empire*, book 2, chapter 14, page 123 and following, and the notes of Marquard Freher on the same, page 199. Add also the *History of Insubria* by Puteanus, page 323, and Bisciolus’s *Leisurely Readings*, book 8, chapter 8. To this it may be added that, according to Turinus’s commentary on Psalm 67:14, the emblem of the Chaldeans was the dove.

### 21. Advocates. <note>original: *Advocaten. Advocatus.*</note>

Advocates are those who either lend or lease their labor to litigating parties, or provide a presence that might be silent and passive. The Latins call these men by the general and most broad term *Advocates*; any who provide sedentary labor to litigants (such as those who serve the parties at home by drafting documents or otherwise offering counsel) are so named because they are "called to" <note>original: *advocentur*</note>, summoned, and are present for the parties, as Polletus observes in *History of the Roman Forum, book 2, ch. 1*. They ought to serve the poor for free, according to the traditions of Francesco Vivio, *Neapolitan Decisions, 159*. Advocates, because they instruct their clients, are just as immune <note>meaning exempt from certain taxes or civic burdens</note> in the Universities as Professors, according to Lindenmann, *Theses on Legal History, 48*. They also have this special right: that in all cases they may seek a salary <note>original: *salarium*</note>, which is not owed to others unless specifically agreed upon. Berlich, *Decision 134*.

They are also called Patrons, Pleaders, Legal Experts, Signatories, Technical Assistants, Sub-monitors, Guardians, Praisers, and those who provide an "honorable presence," and even Witnesses. For these are called Advocates by Plautus in the play *The Little Carthaginian* <note>original: *in Pænulo*</note>, where thanks are given to the witnesses, and they are later summoned again in this manner, as the same Polletus observes in the aforementioned place:

> Lycus: *You are wicked; you come to capture me with Witnesses.*
> *None of your people are with me, nor anything of yours.*
> Agorastocles: *Bear that in mind, Advocates.* <note>original Latin: *Mementote illuc Advocati.*</note>

So too in Cicero’s speech *For Quinctius*: Advocates are said to be present for the litigant and the case because, being present on the benches, they protected the case for which they were summoned by their appearance, voice, nod, or otherwise.

Whoever wishes to perform the office of Advocacy must be of unblemished reputation: for one marked by infamy is not admitted, according to the Digest *on requesting, law 1, section 9*. For the duty of an Advocate is a dignity. The gate of dignities ought not to lie open to the infamous, per the Code *on dignities, law 11*. However, the office of Advocacy is indeed a dignity, but one without rank <note>original: *sine gradu*</note>. For dignity is twofold: one without rank, as in the Code *on the Infamous, single law*, there: *for men of unblemished dignity*; the other is with rank, which flows from some honor or Magistracy. Dignity without rank comes not from honor, but from an unblemished reputation. In this kind of dignity, the patrons of the courts excel, and therefore their office is called praise-

Besold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

worthy, in the Code *on advocates of various courts, law 4*. Whence also the Emperor Theodosius in the *New Laws, 31* reports that the Body of Advocates is a nursery of dignities. See Marcilius on the *Institutes, title on exceptions, final section*.

Just as the office of the Judge is necessary so that the wicked may be restrained and the good relieved, so also the duty of the Advocate is considered no less useful. And thus it is said to be a public office, invented for the reason that those who are ignorant of how to protect their own right and plead their case might be succored, Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrariness, case 369, century 4, book 2*; add Giambattista Magoni in *The Advocate's Compass, ch. 6, n. 20 and following*. For this same reason it is written in the Code *on advocates of various courts, law 'Advocati'*: That their office is no less profitable to the human race than if they defended the fatherland with arms.

However, those Advocates are to be detested who burden men with many useless words, following the logic of the Code *on the unravelling of ancient law, law 2*. Aulus Gellius speaks elegantly on this sentiment in *Attic Nights, book 1, ch. 15*: There are those, he says, who are light, frivolous, and troublesome speakers, who, relying on no weight of matter, flow away with wet and slipping words; it is well judged that their speech is born in the mouth, not in the heart, etc. So also Paris de Puteo writes in the *Treatise on Syndicates, on the excesses of Advocates*: The advocates of cases exceed their bounds when they "enlarge their phylacteries" <note>A biblical metaphor for religious hypocrisy used here to mean legal grandstanding</note> by orating so that they may appear as little know-it-alls; the Gospel rebukes them, saying: *they make broad their phylacteries and enlarge the borders of their garments,* etc. And generally, where there is much talking, there is confusion. For while someone boasts in an outpouring of speech, he falls into immediate danger to himself, Code *on the promise of dowry, final law*. And virtue consists in moderate things, as noted in several places, because nothing that is immeasurable exists as a good. Therefore, a Judge imposes an end upon an Advocate who speaks too much, Digest *on those things deleted in a testament, law 'proxima'*, and he can by his office forbid a wordy Advocate, Code *on requesting, law 'quisquis'*; Code *on appeals, law 'ampliorem'*; and the aforementioned law *'tanta'*. See Paris de Puteo in the cited place, where he records the excesses of Advocates; add Arumæus, *Decisions, 11, n. 26*, etc. Likewise, regarding the insolence, audacity, and rashness of Advocates and all those pleading in court in insulting, cavilling, and speaking evil—and how it is to be restrained and punished—Speckhan treats this in *century 2, class 4, q. 40*.

Unlearned forensic brawlers <note>original: *Rabulæ forenses*</note> are called **Entenmeyer** <note>A derogatory term, literally "Duck-Meuer/Mayer"</note> in the local law of Württemberg, *part 1, title 17, section 'Diebes-neben aber', folio 95*, after a notorious instigator of that name who allowed himself to be used in the Peasants' War <note>original: *Baurenkrieg*, 1524–1525</note>.

However, the abundance of unskilled, greedy, and malicious Advocates has caused political thinkers to argue both sides: whether they are useful and should be tolerated in a Republic? See my work *On the Information and Compulsion of Subjects, folio 171 and following*.

Questions concerning Advocates, pertaining to cases of conscience <note>ethical dilemmas or moral theology in law</note>, are discussed by Gutierrez in his *Practical Questions, Book 1*. For instance: Can he take on a truly doubtful case? In an unjust case, ought he to facilitate a settlement? If he provides a legal opinion against someone, may he then properly provide representation for the adversary in that same case? etc. Add my own notes on the section of the Digest <note>original: *ff.*, the standard abbreviation for the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Roman Law</note> regarding "requests." Langlaeus also has much to say on Advocates throughout his *Semestria, Book 1*. One should also see Tuldenus in *On the Corruption of Judges, Chapter 9, Section 16*, etc.; Magonius in his *Singular Treatises*; Hadrianus Pulvaeus in his *Short Works, number 4*; Zamoriensis in the *Mirror, Book 3, Chapter 17, and following*; Gutherius, *Book 3, Chapter 2*; Benius on the *Privileges of Jurisconsults, question 71*, etc.; and Verdier, page 504. Regarding the vices of Advocates, see Hermann Lather in his *Treatise on the Census, Book 2, Chapter 7*.

## ADDITION.

The use of Advocates by those accused of crimes should not be denied because of the potential for abuse, according to Oldekop in *Criminal Observations, page 25*. Regarding the denial of an Advocate, see Justus Oldekop in his *Treatise against Carpzov, page 216*. On the lies of certain Advocates, by which they lie both to themselves and to others, see Zahn in *On Lies, Book 1, Chapter 15, number 2, section 3*. The duty of a good Advocate is first to confirm his own right <note>his client’s legal standing</note> and afterwards to respond to the objections of the adversaries, as noted by Klock, *Volume 1, Consultation 51, number 91*. An Advocate is prohibited from providing representation against his own country, Klock, *Consultation 37, number 391*. Can an Advocate who served the Plaintiff in the first instance serve as the Advocate for the Defendant in the second instance? See Klock, *Volume 1, Consultation 37, number 416*.

The writings of Advocates in the Imperial Chamber <note>the *Reichskammergericht*, the high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> are not valued by the quantity of the pages, but by their quality, according to Walther in *On the Privileges of Doctors, Chapter 18, question 85*. Giovanni Battista Caccialupi wrote an entire treatise on the Office of Advocates organized by questions. To this, join Barbosa's *Axioms, Book 1, Chapter 33*. According to the custom of the renowned Republic of Nuremberg, Advocates are required to swear an oath every year, even if not for every individual case, as witnessed by Ayrer in *On Process, Chapter 11, observation 2, number 12*, and Oldekop in *On Oaths, page 52*. An Advocate sells "just protection," according to Rittershusius in the *Novels, page 541, number 120*. Whether an Advocate can be co-opted from the body of Advocates into the rank of Judges is discussed ibid., *page 530, number 72 and following*. This matter is a point of controversy between Alciatus and Tiberius Decianus, those two "lights of the legal profession."

Draco, in *On the Patricians, Chapter 6, number 28*, explains the origin of the name "Advocate." <margin>Vogtland</margin> The region of Vogtland is called by some the "Land of Advocates" <note>the name *Vogtland* derives from *Vogt*, meaning advocate or bailiff</note>; see my Inaugural Disputation held at Strasbourg regarding the style of the Court in the preface. In the year 1511, there was such a scarcity of Advocates in Nuremberg that Sir Willibald Pirckheimer <note>a famous humanist and advisor to Maximilian I</note> said: *He practiced law because the Council otherwise had a shortage of advocates.* By what means Advocates should seek their salaries, see the late Dr. Biccius in *Golden Rules, section 4, theorem 3, letter ff. at the end*. Whether an Advocate

<column-break/>

can provide representation in a possessory judgment <note>a trial regarding who currently possesses property, regardless of who owns it</note> without sin, if the client does not have the right of ownership in a property case, see Klockius, *Volume 1, Consultation 40, number 19*.

Whether, just as in politics, fallacies may also be permitted to Advocates to win a case? One must distinguish between the skills of Advocates proceeding from mere cleverness and those arts joined with deceit, lies, and similar vices, which are called "deceitful arts," or commonly a *Hilpersgriff* <note>original German: a "helper's trick," implying a legal loophole or sharp practice</note>. See the late Dr. Tabor in the *Collation of Roman and Hungarian Law, part 1, section 1, section 1, E. 5*, where he also speaks of *clever little tricks*. Things acquired from the practice and office of advocacy are treated as "quasi-military property" <note>term: <term>peculium quasicastrense</term> — property that a son or subordinate could hold independently of his father/superior, usually earned through service</note> and are not to be shared, according to Klock, *Volume 2, Consultation 70, numbers 83 and 84*. Others assert the contrary in *number 85*.

If the office of Advocacy were not permitted indiscriminately to everyone in every city, but only to certain and suitable persons, clients would not suffer so many and such great losses. *An advocate should not draft a complaint that is erroneous, obscure, unintelligible, without cause, or without a lawful conclusion and petition. He should not intentionally delay the matter and plunge his client into unnecessary costs. He should not use insulting words in his documents, nor should he contract for a share of the litigation* <note>term: <term>pactum de quota litis</term> — a contingency fee agreement where the lawyer takes a percentage of the winnings, which was often illegal</note>. Rittershusius, *On the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 79*. Obrecht, in *Political Reflections on the Improvement of Land and People*, at length on *pages 57 and 58*. On July 24, 1641, an Advocate who contracted for a share of the litigation was fined 100 Imperial Thalers by the honorable Court of the Land Marshal, and the agreement was previously voided and annulled by the court's authority. Sutting, *Observation 20, number 11*.

From where Advocates get their name, see *The Forum of Protestations, page 470*. Their wordiness in writing, *page 469*; their requirements, *pages 470 and 471*. Regarding Advocates and Proctors <note>legal representatives similar to solicitors</note> who maliciously protract cases for their own benefit and devise various legal maneuvers, see Zorer, *part 1, question 12, number 875*. *Advocates and Proctors cannot contract for a share of the litigation, but they may agree on a certain annual salary with the parties,* *part 2, question 20, number 605, 3, and following*. In conducting cases, that Advocate is best who is skeptical. For it is not enough to have heard a thing once. The client must be forced to say the same things again and again, so that it can be seen whether he says the same thing, according to Barthol. Agricola in the *Treatise on the Qualities and Office of a Good Advocate, chapter 30, page 122*. *Of a blind man and a lame man who could not divide an oyster, the Advocate ate the oyster and gave the blind man and the lame man each a shell,* in Lucidor Schuppius, *letter E. 10*. For the praises and criticisms of Advocates, see the *Supplement of Schwarzenth. to chapter 3, on the preparation of judicial acts*.

### 23. Era.

With the word **Era**, a certain space or number of years is indicated, such as the *Lustrum* among the Romans and the *Olympiad* among the Greeks. One should certainly look at Lælius Bisciola’s *Subsequent Hours*, volume 2, book 12, chapter 10, where he explains at length what an Era is and when they began to be counted, etc.

On this word, see also Grossmann’s *On Civil Time*, thesis 20. The Christian Era, most common throughout all of Europe, has its beginning in the Year of the World 3650 <note>Anno Mundi: a dating system starting from the biblical creation</note>, in that Julian Year which has cycles beginning (if calculated backward) with the second of the Moon and the tenth of the Sun. See Calvisius’s *Introduction*, chapter 17, and in his *Chronological Work* under "Augustus." However, more recent chronologists indubitably assert that there is a common error here of two full years from the true birth of Christ, and that Christ was born in the Year of the World 3947, around the end of September or the beginning of October, in that Julian Year which has the Solar cycle 7 and Lunar cycle 18; see Calvisius in his *Chronological Introduction*, chapters 47 and 48.

### 24. Treasury.

See Theophilus Elychnius’s <note>original: "Bedencken, wie die Gefäll und Einkommen zu verbessern"</note> *Reflections on how to improve taxes and income*. Also see my own separate treatise *On the Treasury*, and the *Strasbourg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 10.

The **Treasury** <note>original: "Ærarium"</note> and the **Fiscal Office** <note>original: "fiscus"</note> differ, as noted by Rittershusius in the *Novels*, page 437, number 1. The Prince’s treasury is likened to the stomach by Aristotle, according to Obrecht in his *War-Political Discourse*, page 12. An empty treasury is like a bell without a clapper, as noted by the same author on page 13. See Klock’s specialized treatise *On the Treasury, More Golden than Gold*, and more recently, Faust’s *On the Treasury*.

### 25. Agents.

Today we call **Agents** those <term>Solicitors</term> or <term>Procurators</term> <note>legal representatives</note> in the Imperial Court and elsewhere: but most of them are "sellers of words" or "procurators for their own profit," in the opinion of Ernest Cothmann in his commentary on the Justinian Code, number 24. Sometimes they are even called spies, according to Besold, Volume 1,

and sowers of doubtful news. In what way they differ from **Legates** <note>ambassadors</note> and when they are usually sent, I have taught in my treatise *On Legates*, chapter 2, number 6 and following.
