### 26. Sub-fief. <note>original: "Afterlehen. Subfeudum."</note>

We call it a **sub-fief** when a **Vassal** <note>a person holding land under a lord</note> likewise grants his own fief to another person as a fief. See the chapter *Beneficium* in the section *If a fief is from a deceased person*; also Andreas Kohl’s specialized treatise *On Sub-fiefs*, chapter 1, number 4.

It is well established that any alienation <note>transfer of ownership</note> of a fief without the Lord’s consent is prohibited, according to the entire title *On the Prohibition of Feudal Alienation* by Emperor Frederick. However, it is considered reserved from ancient law that a Vassal may—even without asking the Lord—grant his own fief to another in the name of a fief, and may "sub-infeudate" him with it. See Montanus *On Fiefs*, book 2, chapter 4; Duarenus, chapter 5, number 6. Hartmann Pistor proves this with many authorities from both the "New Law" and the "Most Recent Law" in book 2, question 44, at the beginning. The French call this benefit an <note>original: "arriere fief"</note> *arrière-fief*. Eguinarius Baro, *On Fiefs* 2, last chapter. The Belgians call one so sub-infeudated an <note>original: "Achterlehemann"</note> *Achterlehemann*. 

Pistor says it is not easy to explain why all alienation is generally prohibited, yet sub-infeudation is nevertheless permitted; but he gives this reason: that the primary right of the fief still resides with the first Vassal, and he remains a Vassal and is bound to provide services to the Lord; but also, through his person, another is bound by the same pacts and conditions regarding that same fief. Therefore, the superior Lord seems to have no just cause for complaint. See Duarenus *On Fiefs*, chapter 12, number 13; Jacobus de Sancto Georgio, number 5. From this, the interpreters teach that a certain lordship remains with the sub-infeudating Vassal by reason of the Right of Vassalage which he has over the person he enfeoffed; see especially Baldus in the chapter *Cæterum*, on judgments; Socinus the Senior, consultation 256, volume 2; and Molinaeus's excellent commentary on the *Customs of Paris*, § 1, gloss 6, number 3 and following; add Kohl, *On Sub-fiefs*, chapter 1.

Lest the Lord suffer any disadvantage because a fief can be granted to another without his consent, three things are chiefly required for the validity of this sub-infeudation: (1.) That the thing be granted to one who is of similar condition and quality for serving the Lord, according to the chapter *Beneficium* and the Law of Corrado. From this it follows that a sub-fief can by no means be granted to the mute, the deaf, or other incapable persons.

### 27. Ancestors. Pedigrees.

It is accepted by the customs of the Germans that eight generations of Nobles on both sides must be proven without any defect of nobility, <note>original: "daß einer vom Vatter und Mutter, und deroselben Groß- und Aelter-Vatter, auch Groß- und Aelter-Mutter, von Alters her ererbten Helm und Schild aufzulegen habe: vel, daß einer seine acht Ahnen zum wenigsten erweisen könne."</note> *meaning that one must be able to display a helm and shield inherited from of old from his father and mother, and their grandfathers and great-grandfathers, as well as grandmothers and great-grandmothers; or, that one can prove at least his eight ancestors.* And how that uncorrupted series of nobility of the Paternal and Maternal lines through eight generations is rightly calculated, my brother (of pious memory) taught in his *Dissertation on Nobility*, joined with my treatise *On the Three Domestic Societies*, folio 124.

This custom of Germany is strictly observed in the **Ecclesiastical Colleges of Capitulars** <note>members of a cathedral or collegiate chapter</note>, especially the higher ones, <note>original: "auf den hohen Stifften"</note> *in the high foundations,* for Princes and Counts as well as for Nobles (*likewise also in the admission to the Knightly Order of Saint John, and the* <term>Knights of Mary</term> <note>The Teutonic Knights</note>), as witnessed by Matthias Stephan in his *Treatise on Nobility*, chapter 5, number 68. This is so that not only is no one admitted unless they are Princes, Counts, or Nobles, but they must also be of the most perfect sort in this manner: <note>original: "Sie müssen vollbürtige Rittersleute seyn, welche ihre Ahnen und Helm beweisen können."</note> *They must be full-blooded knights, who can prove their ancestors and helm.* But according to **Canon Law** <note>the laws of the Catholic Church</note>, no account is taken of nobility in such Colleges, as Stephan says in the cited place. For it is not nobility of birth, but of virtues and honesty of life that make one pleasing to God and a fit servant: to whose governance He called not many noble and powerful according to the flesh, but the ignoble and poor: because there is no respect of persons with Him, as Pietro Ancharano writes in *Counsel* 131, toward the middle; and I in my cited *Treatise on the Three Types of Domestic Society*, folio 97. But others, on the contrary, urge the tenor of the foundation, and that the goods were given to such Colleges on that condition.

Likewise, they are not admitted to the **Knightly Games** <note>tournaments</note> established by Henry I, unless they can prove their nobility from four Paternal and Maternal grandparents, as Stephan says in the cited chapter 5, number 69. For the same reason, in Silesia, the knightly law and judgment, <note>original: "das Ritterrecht"</note> *the Knight’s Law,* requires Nobles who can demonstrate four heraldic insignia, both Maternal and Paternal, as is clear from the treatise on the *Knightly Law and Judgment of Silesia* by Georg Wentzky; Stephan, cited place, number 70.

The Emperor can, however, by the force of his supreme power, grant grace to a **new man** <note>someone recently ennobled without ancient lineage</note>, so as to make him eligible for the Knightly Games or for the Canonical Colleges, as Pruckmann says in his *Treatise on Regalia*, the section on absolute power, chapter 4, member 1, effect 4. Hence in **Privileges of Nobility**, <note>original: "in den Wappenbriefen"</note> *in the letters of arms,* the following words are commonly added: *And because of such integrity of his, Noble good customs, virtue, and as an incentive to others to strive for similar honors, virtue, nobility, and integrity, so we have with good consideration* <note>the text breaks off here</note>

Furthermore, the custom in England is such that those who are today raised from the common people to the dignities of Knights, Barons, Earls, etc., are by everyone’s opinion considered Nobles, Barons, and Earls (Alberico Gentili, *On Marriage*, book 4, chapter 13; Josias Nolden, *On the Status of the Noble*, chapter 6, number 6). Therefore, so that these "recent offspring" of the nobility may protect their new dignity from the malice of others (which follows envy "at its heels") and from insults, it happens that a penal clause is almost always annexed to the Instrument of Nobility (Ludwig Schwartzmair, *Miscellanies*, book 1, chapter 13). Thus, if anyone is offended, they can take action regarding the penalties inserted into the privilege and approach the judgment of the Imperial Chamber Court (Josias Nolden, cited chapter, number 7). For those who are so ennobled cannot be called unworthy; indeed, the Prince, when attesting that he has granted the benefits of nobility because of merits, must be believed (according to law 3 of the *Codex* regarding the crime of sacrilege, and as Menochius records in counsel 1003, number 77 and following, book 11; see Nolden, cited chapter, number 9 and following).

As for the fact that the grandfather and grandmother are included under the name of father or mother, in that case, where the feminine is understood from the masculine and the word "children" is usually extended to "grandchildren," Marcantonio Cravetta discusses and illustrates this in counsel 964 through discourse.

### 28. **Oath, in place of an oath, a learned oath. *Juramentum*.**

Some wish the German word for oath, *Aid*, to be derived from the Hebrew *Ed*, that is, "testimony." For those who swear give testimony to things. Or from *Yoda*, "he knew," because it also requires knowledge. It could also be deduced from the Greek *haidēs*, which signifies the "underworld." For those who swear offer themselves to all the gravest punishments if they deceive. However, that etymology is especially approved by Ebert in his *History of Oaths*, under the title "German Vocabulary," page 18, which Goropius has in book 4 of *Hermathena*, where he makes *Aid* from *Een* or *Ein* [One], and from "one," so that *Aid* is like *Eind* [United]—namely, with Him who alone is truly one, and with whom those who swear assert they agree and consent. Hence, "to swear someone in" <note>original: *einen vereiden*</note> is the same as "to unite someone" <note>original: *einen vereinden*</note>, to compel someone to apply themselves to that one Truth; and to vow themselves to curses if they say anything other than what agrees with that One. Thus Envy <note>original: *Neid*</note>, or hatred, is so called as if it were "not one" <note>original: *nicht Eind*</note>. For those who hate each other are neither united among themselves, nor can they be equally united on both sides with that one Truth; see Speckhan, century 3, question 1, class 4, in the fundamentals, under number 9.

A promise, however, "in place of a rightfully sworn oath," is equated to an oath and is held as a physically performed oath regarding the bond of the contract, so that it can in no way be contravened (chapter *ad aures* and there Panormitanus, number 13, regarding those things which by force or fear; chapter *pervenit* on suretyship; chapter *si Christus* on oaths; Felinus in chapter *praeterea*, number 15, on betrothals; Jason at law 3, section *jurari*, number 3, *Digest* on oaths). In that place, he says it is the same to promise by one's faith as to swear by God. (Zasius in law *ait Praetor*, section *jurati*, *Digest* on oaths; Mynsinger, chapter 1, observation 17; Gail, book 2, observation 59; Borcholt *On Oaths*, chapter 1, number 26; Göden, counsel 108, number 98; Wesenbeck, counsel 10, number 24 and following, and counsel 13, number 102; Thesaurus, decision 47, numbers 2, 9, 11; Francesco *On Suretyship*, chapter 5, number 365; Cothmann, *Academic Responses* 17, number 42; Schürpf, counsel 37, numbers 11 and 21, century 2; and counsel 53, number 19, century 3; add altogether...)

### 29. Oath against Malice. Juramentum Calumniæ.

without abolishing the **oath of calumny** <note>An oath taken by both parties in a lawsuit, swearing they are acting in good faith and not simply to harass the opponent.</note>, *Novels of Justinian 112*. Thus, the "tenth of the litigation" was formerly accepted among the Franks, as is clear from the notes of Bignon on the *Formulas of Marculf, folio 495*. This practice, taken from the Romans, is said to have prevailed so much that for many centuries no other litigation expenses were in use except for a tenth of the matter brought to judgment, and a monetary fine which they called an "amends," as stated by the author Pierre de Fontaines, who flourished under the Blessed King Louis IX <note>Louis IX of France, known as Saint Louis (reigned 1226–1270)</note>, whose ancient constitution on this matter still exists. Finally, King Charles IV decreed that this should be observed everywhere: that the loser should be held liable for the expenses of the winner, not only in the provinces but also outside them, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

The **oath of calumny** <note>original: "Juramentum calumniæ"</note>—which some wish to derive from *calvo* or *calvire*, meaning to deceive or frustrate, according to Alciatus *on the law 'if he is deceived' 233, Digest on the Meaning of Words*; Setser *on oaths, book 3, chapter 1, number 2*—can be defined as a religious assertion by litigants. By this, they promise and maintain that they act (or will act) not maliciously nor with the intent of harassing their opponent, but relying on a sincere confidence in the law and their cause, according to Obrecht *in the treatise on the oath of calumny, chapter 1, number 19*.

# 30. Property, individual goods.
### Proprietas, Bona propria.

This clause is not always to be understood as those goods which belong to us by **full right** <note>original: "pleno jure"</note>. Sometimes "own goods" is also used to call those things which one possesses and from which one perceives the fruits (profits), even if one acknowledges them as being held from another <note>A reference to feudal or leasehold arrangements where one "owns" the use of the land but answers to a higher lord</note>, *Law 1, near the end of the principle, 2, at the words 'our fields', Digest on 'if a field is tax-paying'*; Alexander *consultation 86, beginning 'in the cause given', number 2, at the line 'the word ownership does not stand in the way'*; Schneidewin *on the section 'wild animals', Institutes on the division and acquisition of things, number 5, near the end, at the line 'as if not in their own field'*; Paulus de Castro *consultation 144, beginning 'it seems it should be said', number 1 and following, book 1*. Likewise, it applies if one only has **jurisdiction** <note>The legal right to exercise authority or judge</note> there, see Berlich *decision 151*. These words, **Ownership, and uncontested** <note>original: "Eigenthum, und unansprüchig"</note>, exclude all matter of dispute; likewise, the phrase **that no lawsuit or hindrance shall be raised** <note>original: "daß keine Klag oder Verhinderung eingewendet werden soll"</note> denotes a grant free from all action and legal attack. How **Property** <note>original: "proprietas"</note> differs from **Dominion** <note>original: "Dominio"</note> can be seen in Robert, *Sentences 3, chapter 18*.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding what the word **Property** <note>original: "Eigenthum"</note> specifically denotes, see Klock *volume 2, consultation 39, numbers 20 and 28*. The words **true lords of the property** <note>original: "rechte Eigentumbsherren"</note> imply full ownership without detracting from **direct dominion** <note>original: "dominio directo"</note>, *volume 2, consultation 7, numbers 177, 178, 179*.

That property is a species of dominion is taught at length by Gödd. *on law 25, number 7, on the Meaning of Words*.

Regarding the agreement **with one's own money** <note>original: "mit eigenem Geld"</note>, see *Marburg Consultations, volume 1, consultation 28, numbers 62 and 74*.

# 31. Alchemy. Alchymia.

The word **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchymia"</note> has two "As" <note>The author uses a mnemonic device based on the letters in the German spelling</note>: the first signifies **Medicine** <note>original: "Arzney"</note>, the second signifies **Work** <note>original: "Arbeit"</note>; or, when one misuses it for **Gold-making**, the third signifies **Poverty** <note>original: "Armuth"</note>.

<column-break/>

**Iatrochemistry** <note>original: "Chymiatrica"</note>, which by the benefit of fire separates the pure from the impure, resolves vegetables, animals, and minerals into their principles, and if necessary, coagulates them in turn to create pure medicines: such as **quintessences** <note>The "fifth essence," the most purified form of a substance</note>, spirits, oils, tinctures, magisteries, etc. To this, therefore, belongs the art of distilling waters from herbs, etc., see below at the word **Medicine** <note>original: "Arzney"</note>. Alchemy differs from **Hermetic Medicine**, about which see below, because the latter is a kind of **natural magic** and universal philosophy, of which Alchemy is but a part, see *Ruland’s Lexicon of Alchemy, folio 145 and 149*.

And **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymia"</note> certainly illustrates Theology in many ways, and especially provides certain proofs or examples of the **Resurrection**, as my friend, Mr. Johann Rudolph Camerarius, reports from Quercetanus in his *Collection of Memorable Things, century 1, numbers 92 and 93*. Among other things, he writes: A man of great name, a Pole and a physician among the people of Krakow, knew how to prepare ashes from all parts of any plant so elegantly and philosophically—and that with all the tinctures and impressions of all the plant's parts, and knew how to preserve their spirits so skillfully, the authors of all faculties—that he had more than thirty such plants artificially prepared from ashes. He kept these different plants contained in his glass vessels, sealed with a **Hermetic seal** <note>An airtight seal used in alchemy</note>, which had the name of the plant and its properties inscribed on them. Thus, if someone asked to be shown a Rose or a Marigold, he would then take up the ash of that plant whose likeness he was about to produce. If you desired a Rose to be shown to you, he would exhibit the vessel marked with the title "Rose." When the bottom of the vessel was moved near the fire of a lamp and became slightly warm, that very thin and impalpable ash would emit from itself the likeness of an open Rose. One could watch with open eyes as it gradually grew, became green, and expressed the form of the stem and leaves, and finally the shadow and figure of a genuine blooming Rose, and at last produced a fully unfolded Rose. Nothing was more certain, nothing more elegant, than that from that "shadow-rose" a most manifest Rose could be unraveled and perceived. It was so complete in all its parts that you would plainly call it corporeal, yet it offered itself to be gazed upon as a spiritual idea, though in truth endowed with a spiritual essence. It seemed to consist of nothing else but that it should be entrusted to suitable earth to assume a more solid body. However, when the vessel was removed from the fire, this shadowy figure would slide back again into its ashes, and gradually seek its original **chaos** <note>The unformed, primordial state of matter</note> by vanishing.

The reason for this **secret** <note>original: "arcani"</note> cannot be obscure to one who has at least a taste of **Hermetic Philosophy**; only the process remains hidden. And it certainly seems probable that scarcely anything can be so destroyed that it perishes in every part, or that matter, even when reduced to ash and powder, is entirely stripped of its former form; for always

# Expanded Practical Treasury

<note>original: "semina"; the OCR likely misread "semina" (seeds) as "femina" (woman)</note> certain seeds seem to remain, which are either revived by natural heat or can be brought back to life by the purifying force of fire. The Apostle Saint Paul clearly suggests this in 1 Corinthians 15, where he says: "But someone will say, how do the dead rise? With what kind of body will they come? You foolish man, what you sow does not come to life unless it first dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be: you sow a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or some other kind."

"But God gives it a body as He wills, and to each of the seeds its own body. Not all flesh is the same flesh, but there is one kind for humans, another for beasts, another for birds, and another for fish. It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown a natural body; it will rise a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body, as it is written: The first man Adam was made into a living soul; the last Adam into a life-giving spirit. But the spiritual is not first; rather the natural is first, and then the spiritual."

Certainly, if flowers can be restored, then it is even less likely that a human—the most noble and perfect creature, and a <term>Microcosmus</term> <note>Microcosm: the idea that a human being is a "little world" reflecting the entire universe</note>—would perish so completely that when fire consumes and purges all things, he could not rise again in his spiritual body, be united with his soul, and thus be restored as a perfect human.

Therefore, <term>Alchymia</term> <note>Alchemy: the ancestral science of chemistry and metallurgy</note> should be encouraged for two main reasons: (1) for a deeper knowledge of the <term>Arcanorum</term> <note>Secrets or hidden mysteries of nature</note> of nature, and (2) for the sake of health. With this view, <term>Jacob. Bornitius</term> <note>Jacob Bornitz (c. 1560–1625), a German jurist and political writer</note> in his treatise *On the Sufficiency of Things*, book 2, chapter 19, advises that Princes and Statesmen in this most learned age should take care that they do not allow ordinary <term>Pharmacopœi</term> <note>Pharmacists or apothecaries</note> and physicians to practice medicine in their Republic. Instead, for the sake of human health, they should choose from the ranks of the <term>Chymiatricorum</term> <note>Chymiatrists: physicians who used chemical and mineral-based medicines, often following Paracelsus</note> those known for their integrity and skill, to whom they can entrust themselves and their children in times of sickness.

Yet, the use of Galenic and Arabic physicians should not be condemned. For chemical medicines are not always safe. Those things provided by <term>Chymia</term> <note>Chemistry/Alchemy</note> cure quickly, but they also kill quickly. Furthermore, their cures, which seem miraculous, do not always last. It is as if one were using lime to force the ripening of crops.

But truly (3) <term>Chrysopœia</term> <note>The art of making gold</note>, *making gold and silver*, appears to be a craft full of danger and expense. An anonymous author, in the *Political Discourse on the State of Rome to the Most Christian King* printed in 1626, testifies that it makes even Roman nobles and the Cardinals themselves poorer. On page 14, he writes of the Roman Patricians: <note>original: "Ils font endebtez..." (Middle French)</note> *They are in debt, and the rest of the people too, because each of them, or the greater part, and even the Cardinals and other ecclesiastics, is attached to vanity, to appearances, and to the <term>Pierre Philosophale</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone: a legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note>. And by*

*such occasions, fed by hope, they consume the best of their wealth.*

(German)</note> *He who knows how to make gold does not say so; he who does not know would gladly say so but cannot, and thinks only to deceive me and lie me out of my money.* See <term>Bornit.</term> *On the Sufficiency of Things*, book 2, chapter 41, where he lists examples of some who are said to have made true gold. That is:

> Six things follow from Alchemy:

Mention is also made by <term>le Seigneur de Villamont</term> in book 3, chapter 18 of his *Travels to Jerusalem* regarding a certain Cypriot named <term>Antonio Bragadeno</term>, whom he reports found the <term>Lapidem Philosophicum</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> and praises him with wondrous words. Truly, the Spanish proverb seems to provide the best <term>Alchymiam</term> and method for getting rich: <note>original: "Alquimia provada..." (Spanish)</note> *Proven alchemy: to have a steady income and spend nothing.* That is, consider it "proven alchemy" to have certain revenues and to manage them well.

Not without reason does <term>Hier. Cardan.</term> <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath</note> in his treatise *On Gaining Advantage from Adversity*, book 3, page 202, warn that those things which impoverish a man "sweetly" must be avoided above all. There are five of them: Gambling, Alchemy, Architecture, Criminal Lawsuits, and Luxury. Gambling impoverishes a man in two ways: while money is lost, and while business and skills are neglected. However, not all who gamble lose, but only those who are unskilled, unfortunate, or who play with cheats. Luxury clearly impoverishes a man, whether he pours wealth into lusts or banquets. But <term>Alchymia</term>, always filling the mind with new hope, empties the pockets. # Lit. A.

...suddenly became beggars, I could not easily gather.

*Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant searching for the Hebrew origins of the Bible</note> indeed notes on the passages of *Genesis ch. 38* that **Chemian** is an ancient Egyptian word. For **Ham**, when written with the letter *Heth*, denotes Egypt, which can also be called **Cham**. He argues it is called **Alchemy** if the Arabic article "al" is prefixed, just as in the words *Almanac, Alkermes, Alembic, etc.* Many Spanish words starting with *al* also remain from the Arabic influence.

And alchemy was certainly most ancient: concerning this matter, *Melchior Guilandinus* <note>A Prussian physician and botanist</note> in *On Papyrus, membrane 6, number 5, etc., folio 178*, writes: *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> says that the *diphthera* <note>original: "diphtheram"; a prepared animal skin or parchment</note> which the Argonauts brought back from Colchis was actually a book made of skins which revealed the secrets of that art they call Chemistry—specifically how gold was to be made. He claims that membrane was rightly called "golden" because of the great profit acquired from it. Others interpret the *diphthera* as the skin of the goat that suckled Jupiter, upon which it was believed in antiquity that he wrote everything that happened. From this, things that were neither found in the writings of historians nor preserved in human memory were said to be "sought from the parchment of Jupiter." Although both these explanations profess that writing on skins was practiced long before the Ptolemies (which is enough for me to counter Varro's claim), Suidas's opinion seems to be favored by what the interpreters of Apollonius collect from *Book 3 of the Argonautica* regarding the Golden Fleece, which Mercury supposedly placed there. They use these words: <note>original Greek: "λέγεται τῇ τέχνη̄ ἐπαφῆ, τὸ δέρας τῷ κριῷ γένεσθαι χρυσῶν"</note> "it is said that by the touch of the art <insert>of Mercury</insert>, the fleece of the ram became gold." By these words, it can be seen to signify not that messenger and interpreter of the Gods, distinguished by his winged hat, sandals, and staff, but rather **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyrum"</note>, which chemists use for the smelting of gold. I mean mercury, not the common kind, but that which has been purified seven times from the common sort by fire and white sand. It is privately called the "living silver of the wise," "mercurial water," "matter of metals," "perpetual disposition," the "first matter of the art," "everlasting glass," and "oil of glass." From this kind of liquid, lamps are made that burn perpetually, which would seem utterly incredible if *Hermolaus Barbarus*, a most illustrious man whose faith no one should justly doubt, in his *5th Book of Corollaries*, and *Franciscus Maturantius*, a most learned man, in a *Letter to his friend Alphenus*, had not long ago testified that lamps shining with perpetual brightness are sometimes found in the underground monuments of Italy. Such was the lamp of *Maximus Olybrius* unearthed in the territory of Padua, near the town of Este; *Bernhardinus Scardeonus*, a man of singular learning and admirable integrity, reports in his *1st Book of Paduan Antiquities* that it had burned for over one thousand five hundred years. It is certainly a matter of history that the Emperor Diocletian sought out the ancient writings on the smelting of silver and gold throughout all Egypt and

<margin>Besold, Volume 1</margin>

<column-break/>

burned them, lest the Egyptians, enriched by that art and relying on their wealth, should thereafter rebel against the Romans. Thus I might properly dare to affirm that the study of the chemical art was most ancient among the "barbarian" <note>In the classical sense: non-Greek/non-Roman</note> nations, but derived more slowly to the Romans and Greeks, especially since *Aristotle* also seems to mention it. For in his *23rd Problem, 13*, asking why the sea can emit a flame while drinkable water cannot, he gives the reason that oil can be extracted from salt by art. Indeed, no one will elicit such oil without the chemical art, even if he crushes and binds the salt as tightly as possible with a thousand presses. **On whether alchemists make true and genuine gold**, see *Martinius, century 1, disputation 9, theorem 5; Pererius on Magic, book 1, ch. 12; and Delrio, folio 57.* That alchemists are mostly heretics is evident from the *preface of Gassendi against Fludd*, and the entire book of *Heinrich Khunrath*, where they seem to make Christ into the Philosophers' Stone. **That chemists also have a special and, as it were, "Thieves' Cant" language** <note>original German: "Rotwelsche Sprach"</note>, can be seen in the *Lexicon of Rulandus*. Concerning the frauds of alchemists, see *Simon Maiolus in Dog Days, volume 2, colloquy 5, folio 541 and following*, where he relates the example of Balbinus, and how he was many times deceived by alchemists.

Whoever desires to know more about Alchemy will find it in *Peter Binsfeld on Sorcerers, folio 383; Francisco Torreblanca on Demonology, book 2, ch. 4; Benedict Pererius, book 8 of Physics, ch. 19; Lather, book 3 on Taxes, ch. 11; Me on the Treasury, ch. 3, n. 11.* To which add *Wilhelm Anton in his treatise on the Five-Year Rule, folio 493; and E. Hartmann in various Disputations; Sennert, in the agreement of Chemists, Aristotle, and Galen; Wimpina's New Geography; the Harmonies of Petraeus; the treatises of Matthäus Unzer; Münderer on Vitriol; Pontanus, book 1 of Warfare, folio 211; also Guydius in his treatise on metals, book 1, title 3; and Laelius Bisciola's Leisure Hours, book 18, ch. 1.*

## 35. All, Everything, Everyone. Omnis.

The words "in all other cases" are **universal**, and include all instances, according to the text in the law *Julianus*, *Digest*, on legacies 3; and the law *a Procuratore*, *Code*, on mandates; and to this point, Bartolus says in the law *generaliter*, section *uxor*, *Digest*, on the legacy of a usufruct; and Romanus delivers the same in a similar case, consultation 44.

The word **"all"** <note>original: "omnis, All"</note> includes everything and excludes nothing, according to the said law *Julianus*; and the law *in fraudem*, at the end, *Digest*, on the military testament; with many points added by Decianus in consultation 84, number 13, volume 3; Buratus in consultation 176, number 11, book 2. Indeed, it is even drawn toward improper cases, and by virtue of it, those things are included which otherwise would not be, according to Decianus 69, number 4; Jason in the law *servi electione*, section *cum fundis*, number 24, *Digest*, on legacies 1; Cravetta, consultation 294, number 2, and consultation 447, where he reviews the effects of universal words. Rubeus, consultation 23, number 3; Cephalus, consultation 172, number 9, book 2, and consultation 497, number 20, book 4; Menochius, consultation 26, number 17, book 1, and consultation 123, number 3, book 2. And likewise, universal words encompass those things in which special mention is required, Cravetta, consultation 294, column 3.

### 37. Only. At Least <note>original: "Allein. Duntaxat."</note>.

The word **only** <note>original: "allein"</note> contains a negation for all other cases. Munnoz de Escobar, *on the accounting of administrators*, chapter 7, number 44. Surdus, decision 291, number 19. It prohibits every extension, and excludes everything except what is expressed. Meichsner, *Decisions of the Imperial Chamber*, 9, number 7, book 1. Franciscus Ripa in the final law, question 41, number 136, *Code* *on the revocation of donations*. Bartolus and the Doctors commonly in law 1 of the *Digest* *if anyone does not obey the one administering justice*. Panormitanus in the chapter *Ecclesia* *concerning causes of possession and property*.

Exclusive or limiting <note>term: taxativa - an exhaustive list that allows no exceptions</note> words, such as the words **only, merely, solely, at least, no more, not only**, etc., when placed negatively, affirm what is stated and imply something else about which there was greater doubt and which seemed less likely to be included; see the law *& non tantùm* in the *Digest* *concerning the petition of an inheritance*; the law *& eleganter*, paragraph *non solùm* in the *Digest* *concerning fraud*; the law *non solùm* in the *Digest* *concerning the release of a legacy*; and the law *cum non solùm* in the *Code* *concerning the goods of those who are free*.

When placed affirmatively, however, they affirm that which they state, and exclude or deny every other thing, so much so that they exclude all other persons and all other cases except those expressed. For a limiting word is exclusive of all cases placed outside the statement in which it exists; law 2 of the *Code* *concerning parents who sell their children*; the law *ob æs* in the *Code* *concerning the estates of minors*; the law *contractus* in the *Digest* *concerning rules of law*; and the said chapter *with the Church of Sutri* <note>original: "cum Ecclesia Sutrina"</note> *concerning causes of possession and property*, chapter...

# Expanded Practical Treasury #

<note>original: "Thesauri Practici Adaucti"</note>

concerns the reliability of instruments; see Everhardus in his section on the nature of limiting speech, number 2.

This conclusion—namely, that a restrictive word <note>original: "dictio taxativa"; a word that limits a list to only what is explicitly named</note> excludes all cases located outside the specific order in which it is placed—is limited and restrained in four ways according to the same Everhardus, number 3 and following: (1.) It applies unless something else must be supplied to avoid a contradiction, according to the law *on contracts* in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff. de R. J."; the Pandects of Roman Law</note> *concerning the Rules of Law*, the final law in the *Code* <note>original: "C."; the Code of Justinian</note> *concerning parental power*, and the gloss joined with the text in law 1, at the words "and free" in the *Code* *concerning possession of goods against the will*. (2.) It is limited so that it applies regarding dissimilar cases or persons; however, restrictive words never exclude those having a similar reason, according to the law *on account of money* and the gloss there in the *Code* *concerning the estates of minors*, and the law *so to us* and the gloss on the word "five-year period" in the *Code* *on the Julian law concerning adultery*. For the nature of a restrictive term is to exclude foreign things from itself in such a way that it includes everything pertaining to itself, as seen in the element "exivide Paradiso" at the verse "when however" in the *Digest* *concerning the meaning of words* <note>original: "d. V. S."; de verborum significatione</note>; see Everhardus in the cited place, number 4. (3.) It is limited so that it does not apply to those things which arise from custom. See Ludovicus Romanus, consultation 114, and add Everhardus, number 1. (4.) It is limited so as not to apply to the persons of heirs: because an heir is considered the same person as the deceased, in the *Authentica* <note>original: "auth."; a collection of later laws</note> *concerning an oath provided by a dying person*. Hence, heirs are not excluded by restrictive terms; consult Everhardus throughout the cited location.

Restrictive words, such as **for itself alone**, **for themselves**, etc., create a personal agreement that does not pass to heirs. Hartmann Pistor, observation 154, number 24, where he treats that question: Whether an agreement to buy back <note>original: "pactum de retrovendendo"</note> passes to the heirs.

->ADDITION.<-

See Barbosa under "restrictive words" <note>original: "verba taxativa"</note>, law 18, axiom chapter 5, throughout. On what a restrictive word accomplishes, see Marius Antoninus, book 1, Rule 40, numbers 2 and 6. The word **Alone** <note>original: "Allein"</note> is restrictive, and thus affirms that which it places while simultaneously excluding and denying everything else. Klock, volume 2, consultation 39, number 236.

38. **Everywhere, nothing excluded therefrom.** <note>original: "Allenthalben, nichts darvon ausgeschlossen"</note> Everywhere, Wheresoever.

These words have the broadest possible reach, and thus encompass everything that can be said or thought of, Cravetta, consultation 357, number 27 and consultation 381, number 4. They are even drawn to things unknown or unthought of, since at least in a general sense this is understood to have been intended. Cravetta, consultation 415, number 21 and consultation 680, number 6, following Alexander, consultation 42, column 4, number 8, book 1. Cornelius, consultation 6, book 1. Decianus, consultation 345, number 1. See Andreas Schäfer, *Practical Questions*, part 3, question 44, where he thoroughly discusses this question: Are peasants who are obligated to farm a certain district or a certain collection of fields under the formula: **Everywhere, whatever is contained in such a district, with nothing excluded therefrom**, etc., also bound to farm fields acquired in that district after the contract was made, especially if the Lord, in consideration of this obligation, waived certain other services for them?

<column-break/>

"Everywhere" or "in whatever place" are words that must be restricted to appropriate limits and interpreted civilly regarding a fit and suitable place that grants jurisdiction. Coler, *On Procedure*, part 2, chapter 1, number 57. Since laws always suppose suitable and appropriate limits, as in law 20 *concerning the making of wills* in the *Digest*. Pinellus in law 1 of the *Code* *concerning maternal goods*, part 3, number 85. See Schäfer, part 2, question 35.

->ADDITION.<-

Nothing reserved <note>original: "Nichts ausbescheiden"</note>. Limnaeus in *Public Law* <note>original: "J. P."</note>, book 7, chapter 9, page 145; book 6, chapter 3, page 107 at the end. In several tithe-deeds <note>original: "Zehend-Briefen"</note> the formula is found: **Everything the rain crosses, nothing taken away or given up.** Alexius Haller used the following formula when describing a farm: **My farm, together with its own property and inheritance, and all its other belongings and entries, in village and field, such as houses, wood, stone, shrubs, along with the timber and wood-markers, gardens, meadows, sheepfolds and paths, pastures and grazing, ponds and waysides, also with all its other rights and uses, ground and soil belonging thereto, nothing excepted, nor set aside.**

39. **In every way.** <note>original: "Allermassen"</note> In every manner.

The word **In every way**, which is equivalent to the word "omnimodo" <note>English: in every manner</note> as well as "in all ways," is precise, admitting no exception, restriction, or dispensation whatsoever. Gloss on the law *if with an exception*, the paragraph *but if anyone* on the word "omnimodo" and the paragraph *how far* on the word "omnimodo"; and there Bartolus in the *Digest* *concerning things done through fear*. Tiraquellus in his repetition of the law *if ever* on the word "let it return," number 89, in the *Code* *concerning the revocation of donations*. See especially Barschamp in *Roots of Clauses*, chapter 16, paragraph 1 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

In every way; likewise <term>ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον</term> <note>original: "epi to pleiston"; Greek for "for the most part" or "mostly"</note>, as in law 1, paragraph 2 *concerning the confirmation of guardians*. Vinnius, paragraph 2 of the *Institutes* *concerning guardianships*. The word **In every way** denotes a total similarity. Klock, consultation 13, number 22.

40. **The Commons.** <note>original: "Allmanden"</note> Common goods of the Community.

This is what the common goods of a community are called: regarding which see me in the *Treatise on the Law of Corporate Property*, etc., in the title *concerning the goods of a community*. Add Köppen, part 2, decision question 3.

->ADDITION.<-

In certain places in the Duchy of Württemberg, a person received as a subject is bound to plant a fruit-bearing tree in a certain common place; **he must have a fruitful tree set upon the Commons.** Nicolaus Losaeus wrote an entire treatise *On the Law of Communities*. A community never dies. Barbosa, book 19, chapter 37, axiom 4.

### 41. Alms. <note>original: "Allmosen. Eleemosyna."</note>

Concerning Alms, **on alms**, see the treatise by Sarmiento on Church revenues <note>original: "Sarmienti de reditib. Eccles."</note> throughout, and the joined defense against Navarra. Also see the treatise by Porta **on Church property**. Cardinal Tusch, *Practical Conclusions*, letter E, and Camillo Borelli in his *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 18, where he teaches that Alms and offerings, although they are a commandment, are nonetheless forbidden to be given to the excommunicated and those not in need. He also teaches that they should be given from one's own goods whenever the occasion arises or necessity urges, and that parishioners can be compelled by the Rector of the Church if they refuse to pay the customary alms; however, the poorer among the poor are to be preferred.

That street-begging <note>original: "Gassenbettel"</note> is not to be abolished, see the *Mystical Theology* of Grasser, folio 111 and following, and my own work in the *Synopsis of Politics*, also below under letter B, number 51.

->ADDITION.<-

It is a great alms before God to liberate and defend the poor and the oppressed. Justus Oldekop in his treatise against Carpzov, page 62, number 127.

Alms must not be made from the property of another, according to Barbosa, book 5, chapter 7, axiom 1, and Knipschild *on Fideicommissum* <note>a legal arrangement where property is held for another</note>, chapter 11, number 204. Alms and sacrifice do not please God when they are offered out of crime, axiom 2 in the same work. Cardinal Montalto gave twelve hundred thousand crowns in alms during his life. Zeiller, *Centuries*, epistle 2, page 249.

Lonicer, in his *Turkish Chronicle*, volume 1, book 2, chapter 11, reports from the Turkish Quran (which is as much to them as the Gospel is to us), that whoever truly understands what an excellent and almost divine thing alms-giving is, would cut his own flesh from his arms and share it with the poor if it would serve them. The Turks have inquiries made secretly as to whether there are old, infirm, or sick people in their neighborhood, or poor people, widows, or orphans who need their assistance. To these, they distribute wealth through their servants, but they want no thanks for it and wish it to be kept hidden from whom the alms comes. Alms are the fence that secures all wealth, as the Rabbis say, and Christian mildness can easily erect such a fence.

Regarding "cat and dog alms" <note>likely referring to small, trivial, or indiscriminate charity</note>, see Schweigger in his *Travel Book*, page 193. Zorer, part 2, question 18, number 4095, and the two following, teaches how one should conduct oneself in the giving of alms and what should be considered therein. On pious offerings and alms, see Camillo Borelli in the *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 18; on the alms of St. Martin, see Mr. Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 793. A rich man can become so poor that he must collect alms, according to Richter, *Economic Axioms* 26, page 143.

<column-break/>

### 42. Allodial Land, see below under the words Fief. Feud. <note>original: "Allodium, vide inf. in verb. Lehen. Feudum."</note>

*Alodis* is land held in one's own right, paternal and ancestral. Thus Brissonius in his lexicon says **Alode** or **Alodum, Alodium** or **Allodium** is the name for the personal patrimony <note>inherited estate</note> of every free man, which in the Roman manner they called a "property for assessment" <note>original: "Prædium censui censendo"</note>, or "property by formal ownership" <note>original: "prædium mancipi"</note>: or that which was held by the law of the Roman citizens, or by formal purchase and bond.

Thus in Ado’s *Chronicle*, age 6: "The Saxons having been baptized, the firmness of their faith was strengthened by their free status and their allodial land <note>original: "alodo"</note>; if they should fall back into treachery by abandoning Christianity, they would do so under the penalty of losing their freedom and their patrimony."

From this, the writers of barbarian laws established two kinds of goods: **Allodia**, which were held by full right of patrimony so that no favor, payment, or labor was owed for them; and **Feuda** <note>Fiefs</note>, which were held by the benefit of another so that favor and certain labors were owed for them.

It seems likely to some that the origin of the word first flowed from the fact that the lands of a conquered nation were divided into two parts: the better part was assigned to soldiers as a "benefit" <note>the origin of the word 'benefice' or 'fief'</note> to be enjoyed, and the other part was for the commoners and the rest of the multitude; which even now the Germans call **All Leud** <note>All the people</note>, as if for the entire common people.

See what Pithou noted on this word in his glossary, which he added to the *Capitularies of Charlemagne*; add also Peter Gregory, book 6 of the *Syntagma*, chapter 1. In my own work *On Monarchy*, folio 99, I derive it from the Saxon word *Lot*, which for us is "LOT" <note>original: "LOS"; meaning a share or fate</note>. From which the French still say *Lot* and *Lotir* for "share" and "to allot"; see also my work *On the Nature of Peoples*, folio 102; and Nicod in the *Great Dictionary* under the word *Aleu*, where he says *Alodium* is also called *Alaudium*: because he who holds such land is not bound to "praise" <note>original: "laudare"</note> or name the person from whom he holds it.

Hence an *Alodiarius* is one who has received an *Allodium* from someone, or rather is his bondman. Abbot Geoffrey of Vendôme in an epistle to Gerard: "To Mr. Gerard, Bishop of praiseworthy life, Legate of the Holy Roman See, brother Geoffrey, *alodiarius* and servant of the same see."

The same in an epistle to Canon: "To Canon, Bishop of praiseworthy life, brother Geoffrey, *alodiarius* of the same see, etc."

->ADDITION.<-

Beatus Rhenanus derives *Allodium* from the word *anlöden* <note>to join or solder</note>, according to Rittershusius in *Feudal Divisions*, pages 54, 55.

### 43. As, just as. <note>original: "Als, gleichwie. Prout, Quemadmodum."</note>

The word "as" <note>original: "ut"</note> is sometimes placed for similarity in the sense of "just as" (law *in the snare*, in the *Digest* *concerning the acquisition of ownership of things*), not for explanation, according to Nicolaus Belloni in *Legal Calculations*, chapter 10, at the law *when the Praetor*, section 1, in the *Digest* *concerning Judgments*, number 2.

### 41. Alms. <term>Eleemosyna</term><note>Latin: *Eleemosyna*, derived from Greek *eleemosyne*, meaning pity or mercy, specifically in the form of charitable giving.</note>

On Alms, see the treatise by Sarmiento on Church revenues throughout, as well as the defense against Navarra. Also, see Porta’s treatise on Church Property. Cardinal Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter E; and Camillo Borelli in *The Sum of Decisions*, volume 1, title 18. There, he teaches that although giving alms and offerings are a commandment, it is forbidden to provide them to those who are excommunicated or to those who are not in need. He further states that alms should be given from one’s own goods whenever the occasion arises or necessity urges. Furthermore, a Parish Priest may compel parishioners to pay if they refuse the customary offerings. Finally, the poorest among the poor should be given preference.

Regarding the fact that street begging is not to be abolished, see the *Mystical Theology* of Graffer, folio 111 and following, and my own work in *Synopsis Politica*, as well as below under letter B, number 51.

### ADDITION.

It is a great almsgiving before God to liberate and defend the poor and the oppressed. Justin Oldekop in the treatise against Carpzov, page 62, number 127.

Alms must not be made from the property of another. Barbosa, book 5, chapter 7, axiom 1. Knipschild, *On Fideicommissum*, chapter 11, number 204. Alms and sacrifice do not please God when they are offered from the proceeds of crime (axiom 2, ibid.). <note>original: "Eleemosyna & sacrificium non placent Deo, quæ offeruntur ex scelere"</note> Cardinal Montalto gave twelve hundred thousand crowns in alms during his life. Zeiler, century 2, *Epistles*, page 249.

Lonicer, in the *Turkish Chronicle*, volume 1, book 2, chapter 11, reports from the Turkish Quran (which is as significant to them as the Gospel is to us) that whoever truly understands what a magnificent and almost divine thing almsgiving is would cut the very flesh from his own arms to share it with the poor, if it would serve them. The Turks secretly inquire whether there are elderly, infirm, or poor people, widows or orphans in their neighborhood who need assistance. To these, they distribute generously through their servants, yet they want no thanks for it and wish the source of the alms to remain hidden. Almsgiving is the "fence" that secures all wealth, as the Rabbis say, and Christian gentleness can easily construct such a fence.

On alms given to cats and dogs, see Schweigger in *Travel Book*, page 193. Zorer, part 2, question 18, number 4095 and the two following, teaches how one should behave regarding the reaching out of alms and what should be considered therein. On pious offerings and alms, see Camillo Borelli in *Sum of Decisions*, volume 1, title 18, on the Alms of Martini. Mr. Dilherr, in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 793. A rich man can become so poor that he himself must collect alms. Richter, *Economic Axioms*, 26, page 143.

### 42. Allodium. <note>From the Latin *Allodium*, referring to land held in absolute ownership, rather than a fief held from a lord.</note> See below under the words Fief and Feudalism.

<term>Alodis</term>: one's own land, paternal and ancestral. Thus Brissonius, in his lexicon, says *Alode*, *Alodum*, *Alodium*, or *Allodium* is the private patrimony of any free man, which in the Roman style they called a "property subject to census" or a "manorial estate"—that is, property held by the right of the Roman citizens, or by formal transfer and bond.

Thus in Ado's *Chronicle*, age 6: "Once the Saxons were baptized, the stability of their faith was strengthened by both their free status and their <term>alodo</term> [allodial land]; should they fall back from Christianity into treachery, it would be under the penalty of losing both their liberty and their patrimony."

From this, the writers of the Barbarian Laws established two types of goods: **Allodia**, which were held with full right of patrimony such that no favor, payment, or labor was owed for them; and **Feuda** (Fiefs), which were held by the benefit of another such that certain favors and labor were owed because of them.

It seems likely to some that the origin of the word first flowed from the fact that the estates of a conquered nation were divided into two parts: the better part was attributed to the soldiers to be enjoyed as a "benefit" (fief), and the other part was for the commoners and the rest of the multitude—which even now the Germans call **All Leud** <note>original: *All Leud*, likely a folk etymology for "all the people."</note>, as if for the entire common people.

See the notes on this word by Pithou in his glossary, which he added to the *Capitularies of Charlemagne*; see also Peter Gregory, book 6 of the *Syntagma*, chapter 1. In my own work *On Monarchy*, folio 99, I derive it from *Lot* in Saxon, which for us is *Los* [lot or portion]. From this the French still say *Lot* and *Lotir* for "lot" and "to allot" [to draw lots]. See also my *On the Nature of Peoples*, folio 102, and Nicod's *Great Dictionary* under the word *Aleu*, where he says *Alodium* is also called *Alaudium*: because he who holds such land is "not bound to praise" <note>original: "non tenetur laudare," a pun on *laudare* (to praise/name) and the word *Alaudium*.</note> or name the person from whom he holds it.

From this comes **Alodiarius**, one who has received an *Allodium* from someone, or rather is its master. Abbot Geoffrey of Vendôme, in an epistle to Gerard: "To Mr. Gerard, Bishop of praiseworthy life and Legate of the Holy Roman See, brother Geoffrey, <term>alodiarius</term> and servant of that same see."

The same in an epistle to Canon: "To Canon, Bishop of praiseworthy life, brother Geoffrey, <term>alodiarius</term> of the same see, etc."

### ADDITION.

Beatus Rhenanus derives *Allodium* from the word *anlöden* [to join/solder]. Rittershusius in *Partitions of Fiefs*, pages 54, 55.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of specific phrasing in contracts and statutes. The previous page ended with a discussion on "restrictive words" (taxative terms) and how they limit the scope of a legal document.</meta>

<margin>concerning restrictive terms, number 2.</margin>
This concerns the credibility of legal instruments; see Everhardus in the section "from the nature of the thing" <note>original: "Eberh. in loc. à nat." referring to Nicolaas Everaerts, a famous legal scholar</note>.

This conclusion—namely, that a restrictive term <term>taxativa</term><note>A legal term for a word that provides an exhaustive list, excluding anything not mentioned.</note> excludes all cases outside the order in which it is placed—is limited and restrained in four ways according to the same Everhardus (number 3 and following): (1) It applies unless something else must be added to avoid a contradiction. (2) It is limited in its application regarding dissimilar cases or persons, or those having similar reasoning; restrictive terms never exclude these. For the nature of a restrictive term is to exclude foreign matters from itself in such a way that it includes everything pertaining to it. (3) It is limited so that it does not apply to things arising from custom. (4) It is limited so as not to apply to the persons of heirs, because an heir is considered the same person as the deceased. Thus, they are not excluded by restrictive terms; consult the often-cited Everhardus throughout that section.

Restrictive terms, such as **for itself alone, in and of itself,** etc., create a personal agreement that does not pass to heirs. See Hartmann Pistor, observation 154, number 24, where he treats the question: Whether a direct agreement for repurchase passes to the heirs.

->ADDITION.<-

See Barbosa under "restrictive words" <note>original: "verba taxativa"</note> book 18, chapter 5, throughout. Regarding what a restrictive term accomplishes, see Marius Antoninus, book 1, rule 40. The word **Alone** <note>original: "Allein"</note> is restrictive, and thus affirms what it states while simultaneously excluding and denying everything else (Klock, volume 2, consultation 39).

### 38. Everywhere, nothing excluded therefrom. <note>original: "Allenthalben, nichts davon ausgeschlossen. Ubique, Ubicunque."</note>

These words have the broadest possible meaning and thus include everything that can be said or imagined (Cravetta). They are even extended to things unknown or unthought of, since in a general sense, even the unthought-of is understood to be included (Cravetta, following Alexander and others). See Andreas Schæfer, *Practical Questions*, part 3, question 44, where he examines this question: Are peasants who are obligated to farm a certain district or a certain collection of fields under the formula: **Everywhere, whatever is contained in such district, nothing excluded,** etc., also bound to farm fields acquired in that district after the contract was made? This is especially relevant if the Lord, in consideration of this obligation, had released them from certain other services.

<column-break/>

"Everywhere" or "in whatever place"—these words should be restricted to appropriate limits and interpreted "civilly" <note>interpreted reasonably or according to common sense rather than literal extremes</note> regarding a fit and suitable place that grants jurisdiction (Coler). Since laws always suppose suitable and appropriate limits, see Schæfer.

->ADDITION.<-

**Nothing reserved.** <note>original: "Nichts ausbescheiden."</note> In several tithe-deeds, the following formula is found: **Everything that the rain falls upon, nothing excluded, nor given up.** <note>original: "Alles, was der Regen überschreitet, nichts ausgenommen, noch begeben."</note> Alexius Haller, in describing a farm, used the following formula: **My farm, together with its own property and inheritance, as well as all its other additions and belongings, in village and field, such as houses, tree-trunks, stones, shrubs, along with the woods and timber-marks, gardens, meadows, sheep-folds and paths, pastures and grazing, ponds and pond-sites, also with all its other rights and uses, the ground and soil belonging thereto, nothing excluded, nor set aside.**

### 39. In every way. <note>original: "Allermassen. Omnimodo."</note>

The word **In every way,** which is equivalent to "in every manner" and "by all means," is precise, admitting absolutely no exception, restriction, or dispensation. See Tiraqueau on the revocation of donations. See especially Barschamp on the roots of clauses, chapter 16.

->ADDITION.<-

"By all means," or as the Greek says, <term>ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον</term> <note>meaning "for the most part" or "mostly"</note>. The word **In every way** denotes a complete similarity (Klock).

### 40. Commons. <note>original: "Allmanden. Bona Universitatis communia."</note>

This is the name given to the common property of a community <note>original: "universitas," here referring to a corporate body or town</note>. Concerning these, see my treatise on the law of corporate property, specifically the title on "Goods of the Community." Add Köppen, part 2.

->ADDITION.<-

In certain places in the Duchy of Württemberg, a person received as a subject is bound to plant a fruit-bearing tree in a certain common area: **he must have a fruitful tree set upon the Commons.** <note>original: "muss auf die Allmand ein fruchtbarn Baum setzen lassen."</note> Nicolaus Losæus wrote an entire treatise on the Law of Communities. A community never dies <note>original: "Universitas non moritur," a legal maxim meaning a corporation has perpetual succession</note> (Barbosa).

## 41. Alms. <note>original: "Eleemosyna"</note>

Concerning Alms <note>original: "De Eleemosynis, von Allmosen"</note>, see the treatise of Sarmiento on Church Revenues throughout, and also the defense against Navarrus. See also the treatise by Porta on Church Goods. Also see Cardinal Tuschius, *Practical Conclusions*, under the letter E, and Camillo Borrello in his *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 18. There, he teaches that although almsgiving and offerings are commanded by divine precept, it is nevertheless forbidden to give them to those who are excommunicated or those who are not in need. He further notes that alms should be given from one's own property whenever the occasion arises or necessity urges. Parishioners can be compelled by the Rector of the Church to provide these if they refuse to pay the usual amounts, though the "poorer among the poor" <term>pauperiore inter pauperes</term> should be given preference.

Regarding the fact that street begging <note>original: "Gassenbettel"</note> should not be abolished, see the *Mystical Theology* of Graffer, folio 111 and following, and my own writing in the *Political Synopsis*; also see below under letter B, number 51.

### ADDITION.

It is a great alms before God to free and defend the poor and the oppressed. Justus Oldekop in his treatise against Carpzov, page 62, number 127.

Alms must not be given from the property of another, according to Barbosa, book 5, chapter 7, axiom 1, and Knipschild on *Fideicommissum* <term>fideic.</term><note>A legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of another.</note>, chapter 11, number 204. Alms and sacrifice offered from the proceeds of crime do not please God (axiom 2 in the same work). Cardinal Montalto [Pope Sixtus V] gave twelve hundred thousand crowns in alms during his life, as noted by Zeiller in *Centuria* 2, Letter 249.

Lonicer, in his *Turkish Chronicle*, volume 1, book 2, chapter 11, reports from the Turkish Quran <note>original: "Curaan," which he notes is "equivalent to the Gospel for us"</note> that anyone who truly understood what an excellent and almost divine thing almsgiving is would cut his own flesh from his arms and share it with the poor if it would serve them. The Turks secretly inquire if there are elderly, infirm, sick, or poor people, widows, or orphans in their neighborhood who need their assistance. They distribute aid to them richly through their servants but want no thanks for it, desiring that the source of the alms remain hidden. Almsgiving is the "fence" that secures all wealth, as the Rabbis say, and Christian charity can easily erect such a fence.

On alms given for cats and dogs, see Schweigger in his *Travel Book* <note>original: "Reißb."</note>, page 193. Zorer, in part 2, question 18, number 4095 and the two following, teaches how one should conduct oneself when giving alms and what should be considered therein. Concerning pious offerings and alms, see Camillo Borrello in the *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 18, on the alms of Martini. Mr. Dilherr, in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 793, notes: A rich man may become so poor that he himself must collect alms; see Richter, *Economic Axiom* 26, page 143.

## 42. Allodial Land, see below under the word **Fief**. <note>original: "Lehen"</note>

### Fief. <note>original: "Feudum"</note>

**Allodium** <note>original: "Alodis"</note> refers to one's own land, whether inherited from a father or a grandfather. Thus, Brissonius in his lexicon states that *Alode*, *Alodum*, or *Allodium* is the private patrimony of any free man. In the Roman style, they called this a "census-assessed estate" <term>Prædium censui censendo</term> or "transferable property" <term>prædium mancipi</term>—property held by the law of the Roman citizens, or by formal transfer and bond.

So it is written in Ado’s *Chronicle*, age 6: "Once the Saxons were baptized, the firmness of their faith was strengthened by both their free status <term>ingenuitate</term> and their allodial land <term>alodo</term>." This meant that if they fell back into treachery against Christianity, they would face the penalty of losing both their liberty and their inherited estate.

From this, the writers of the Barbarian Laws established two kinds of property: **Allodia**, which were held by full right of patrimony such that no favor, payment, or labor was owed for them; and **Feuda** (Fiefs), which were held by the benefit of another such that certain favors and labor were owed in their name.

It seems likely to some that the origin of the word came from the fact that when a nation was conquered in war, the estates were divided into two parts: the better part was granted to the soldiers to enjoy as a benefit, and the other part was for the common people and the rest of the multitude. This is what the Germans even now call *All Leud* <note>A folk etymology suggesting "all people" or "common people."</note>, as if for the whole people.

See the notes on this word by Pithou in his glossary, which he added to the *Capitularies of Charlemagne*; see also Peter Gregory, book 6 of the *Syntagma*, chapter 1. In my own work *On Monarchy*, folio 99, I derive it from the Saxon word *Lot*, which for us is *Los* <note>meaning a "lot" or "share" as in a lottery or portion</note>. From this, the French still say *Lot* and *Lotir* for "lot" and "to allot." See also my work *On the Nature of Peoples*, folio 102, and Nicot’s *Great Dictionary* under the word *Aleu*, where he says *Alodium* is also called *Alaudium* because he who holds such land is not bound to "laud" <note>praise or acknowledge</note> or name the person from whom he holds it.

From this comes **Alodiarius**, one who has received an allodium from someone, or rather, is its owner. Abbot Geoffrey of Vendôme in a letter to Gerard: "To Mr. Gerard, Bishop of praiseworthy life and Legate of the Holy Roman See, brother Geoffrey, *alodiarius* and servant of the same See."

The same in a letter to Canon: "To Canon, Bishop of praiseworthy life, brother Geoffrey, *alodiarius* of the same See, etc."

### ADDITION.

Beatus Rhenanus derives *Allodium* from the word *anlöden* <note>meaning to attach or solder</note>, as noted by Rittershusius in *Partitions of Fiefs*, pages 54, 55.

The word "ut" <note>as/so that</note> is sometimes placed comparatively to mean "just as" <term>sicut</term> (as in the law *in laqueo* under the Digest *on acquiring ownership of things*), and not as an explanation, according to Nicolaus Belloni in *Legal Computations*, chapter 10.

...or that it restricts and limits preceding statements, according to Bartolus in his commentary on the law *edita*, note 29, and there also Baldus, the Doctors of Law, and Jason [de Mayno] at note 36; also Francesco Purpurato, note 230; and Decius, note 85, in the section on *producing documents* <note>original: "C. de edend." referring to the Code of Justinian</note>. Schrader says there is no doubt that the term "according as" <note>original: "prout"</note> is equivalent in the German language to the word "how" <note>original: "wie"</note> and the word "as" <note>original: "als"</note>, in Counsel 1, note 301, volume 1.

### ADDITION.

The word "as" <note>original: "ut"</note> is sometimes used for comparison, and sometimes for expressing equality or providing an example, according to Forster in his book of observations, the final chapter.

### 44. Immediately. <note>original: "Alsbald. Illico."</note>

The terms "soon" <note>original: "mox"</note>, "immediately" <note>original: "illicò"</note>, "without delay" <term>in continenti</term>, "at once" <note>original: "statim"</note>, "straightway" <note>original: "gleich"</note>, "immediately" <note>original: "alsbalden"</note>, etc., exclude any interval of time and denote that something is to be done by law or by fact. This is discussed extensively by Matteo Mattesillani in *Singularia* 111, unless the interval is very small; see Baldus on the law regarding *Gallus*, section *ille casus* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de liber. & posthum."</note>. This "small interval" is left to the discretion of the Judge, as noted by Barschamp in his treatise on clauses, chapter 16, section 3, note 33.

### ADDITION.

"At once" <note>original: "statim"</note> is to be understood with a certain tempering of time, according to Forster, book 1, final chapter. "Forthwith" <note>original: "protinus"</note> means "at once" <note>original Greek: "εὐθέως, παραχρῆμα"</note>, as per Vinnius in his section on useless stipulations. "Soon" <note>original: "mox"</note> can mean "afterward," but it also means "immediately." Drawing from Paolo de Castro, Alexander, and others, Viglius Aytta van Zuichem notes this in his commentary on the first law of the Digest regarding *demanding a certain sum*, page 339, notes 85 and 87. "Without delay" <term>in continenti</term> means "from this hour" <note>original: "von stund an"</note>. See Villalobos, note 121, with the additions of Barbosa, book 9, chapter 24, axiom 1 throughout. Regarding what the words "at this hour" <note>original: "zu stund"</note>, "as quickly as," and "at once" import, see Klock, volume 1, counsel 7, note 389.

The particle "and" <note>original: "atque"</note> sometimes means the same as "at once," "immediately," "on the spot" <note>original: "è vestigio"</note>, without any hesitation or delay, or as the ancients elegantly say, "leaving all other things aside" <term>relictis rebus</term>. See Taubmann on Plautus; Gellius; and Rittershusius on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 174. Concerning "suddenly," meaning "very quickly" <note>original: "sehr geschwind"</note>, see Master Rupertus.

### 45. Then. <note>original: "Alsdann. Tunc."</note>

The term "then" <note>original: "alsdann" or "tunc"</note> is an adverb of time <note>citing Digest laws on suspected tutors and conditions</note> and it restricts a legal disposition to that specific time from which it ought to begin. Decius, counsel 63, note 2; Hieronimus Gratus, counsel 106, note 2, part 1. It can also signify the very end of a period of time, and it cannot be verified except in a named case. See Ancharano, counsel 356, note 3; also the Digest on testamentary tutors. Curtio Seniore, counsel 42, note 25; Paciano, counsel 63, note 61 and following; Arumæus, book 2, decision 2, note 33.

Alternatively, the term "then" <note>original: "alsdann"</note> is of such a nature that it requires all preceding actions to be first done and completed before it can dispose of anything. <note>citing the Clementine constitutions on the granting of prebends and rights of patronage</note>. Hartmann Pistor, on feudal questions,

<column-break/>

27, number 26; Bartolus and Socinus, counsel 5, note 7. Hence, before the fulfillment [of the condition], the day has neither come nor passed, nor has the obligation been born. <note>citing Digest law on the meaning of words</note>.

However, this restriction <note>citing Bartolus and others, especially Jason on the Digest regarding children and posthumous heirs</note> does not prevent an extension based on the presumed will of the testator in a similar case to the one expressed. Pietro Surdo, counsel 336, note 46. Regarding the terms "then" and "in that case," and when they restrict a substitution, see Cravetta, counsel 989.

The term "Then" <note>original: "Alsdann" or "Tunc"</note> denotes the first point at which the right of action is born at the end of a timeframe, since it is drawn toward the outcome of a condition. Klock, volume 2, counsel 42, notes 228 and 229; volume 3, counsel 114, note 37 and following.

On what the words "then let it exist" <note>original: "tunc existat"</note> denote, see Klock, counsel 6, note 144. For what the particle "then" imports, see the *Altdorf Counsels*, pages 450, 457, 462. Alemannus on the law of money, page 350. The term "then" <note>original: "alsdann"</note> is restrictive, according to Klock, volume 3, counsel 103, note 45.

See further Symphoremanus Gilman, volume 1, part 2, folio 351, note 16; Marburg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 24, note 131. Regarding "as namely" <note>original: "Als nemlich"</note>, see Marburg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 24, notes 183 and 184.

### 46. So that. <note>original: "Also daß. Ita quòd."</note>

It is said that the clause "so that" <note>original: "ita quòd"</note> stands to augment rather than restrict; however, this does not regularly hold true. Rather, it usually stands as a declarative and taxative <note>meaning it specifies and limits</note> clause, and it restricts the preceding disposition. <note>citing Digest laws on the Trebellian decree and posthumous heirs</note>. Riminaldo, counsel 263, note 40, and counsel 313, note 29, where he says that through these words a <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>a legal trust</note> is restricted to the persons expressed above and does not extend to others. See Master Wilhelm Antonii in the treatise on delays in rescripts, page 313.

Furthermore, the nature of the said clause is that it should be understood according to what was said above. <note>citing the Novels of Justinian on witnesses</note>. Alciatus, counsel 492, note 17; Ruinus, counsel 18, note 11, where he says it is understood in the manner previously stated. Parisius, counsel 70, note 47, volume 2, where he notes it is a relative term, retaining the preceding boundaries. Giovanni Pietro Surdo, book 3, counsel 315, note 29.

### ADDITION.

One should certainly look here at Mundius regarding duties and goods, counsel notes 114, 116, 124, 180. The words "so and in such a manner" <note>original: "ita & taliter"</note> flow from the preceding words and stand as declarations, according to Klock, counsel 6, note 172.

### 47. Altar. <note>original: "Altar. Altare."</note>

Concerning the consecration of Altars, see Petrus Peck in the treatise on the repair of Churches, chapter 36 and following; and Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse in the treatise on Ecclesiastical benefices, chapter 16.
