...or, so that it restricts and limits what came before, according to Bartolus in his commentary on *The Published Law, note 29*, as well as Baldus and other Doctors of Law, including Jason at *number 36*, Franciscus Purpuratus at *number 230*, and Decius at *number 85* in the section *On Producing Documents*. Schrader states there is no doubt that the word "as" <note>original: *prout*</note> is equivalent in the German language to the word **how** <note>original: *wie*</note> and the word **as** <note>original: *als*</note>, in his *Counsel 1, number 301, volume 1*.

->ADDITION.<-

The word "as" is sometimes used for comparison, and sometimes to indicate equality or an example, according to Forster in the final chapter of his *Library of Observations*.

### 44. Immediately. (Latin: *Illico*)

The words "soon," "immediately," "continuously," and "instantly" <note>German: *gleich, alsbalden*</note> exclude any interval of time and denote that something is done by the law itself or by the act itself. This is discussed extensively by Matthaeus Matthesilanus in *Singularia III*, unless the interval is very small; Baldus notes this in his commentary on the *Law of Gallus, section "that case," in the Digest regarding children and posthumous heirs*. This small interval is left to the discretion of the Judge, as noted by Barfschamp in his *Treatise on Clauses, chapter 16, section 3, number 33, folio 385*.

->ADDITION.<-

The word "instantly" <note>Latin: *statim*</note> should be understood with a certain tempering of time, according to Forster's *Library of Observations, Book 1, final chapter*. "Straightway" <note>Latin: *protinus*</note>, meaning instantly, is expressed in Greek as *eutheos* <note>original: εὐθέως</note> or *parachrema* <note>original: παραχρῆμα</note>, as seen in Vinnio's *Section 2 on Ineffectual Stipulations*. The word "soon" <note>Latin: *mox*</note> can mean "afterwards," but it also means "promptly." Drawing from Paulus de Castro, Alexander, and others, Viglius Zuichemus discusses this in his commentary on the first law of the Digest *If a Certain Sum is Sought, page 339, numbers 85 and 87*. "Continuously" <note>Latin: *in continenti*</note> means **from this hour** <note>original: *von stund an*</note>, according to Villalobus at *A. 121 with additions* and Barbosa in *Book 9, chapter 24, axiom 1 throughout*. On the meaning of the words **at this hour** <note>original: *zu stund*</note>, "as quickly as," and "instantly," see Klock in *Volume 1, Counsel 7, number 389*. 
The particle "and" <note>Latin: *atque*</note> sometimes signifies the same as "instantly," "on the spot," "in the footsteps of," or "without any evasion or delay." As the ancients elegantly put it, it means "leaving all other things behind" <note>original: *relictis rebus*</note>, cited by Taubman in his notes on Plautus and Gellius, and Rittershusius in his notes on the *Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 174*. Regarding "suddenly," it means **very fast** <note>original: *sehr geschwind*</note>, according to Lord Rupert.

### 45. Then. (Latin: *Tunc*)

The word "then" <note>German: *alsdann*</note> is an adverb of time, found in the Digest in the sections *On Suspected Tutors*, *On Conditions and Demonstrations*, and *On Force and Armed Force*. It restricts a legal provision to that specific time from which it ought to begin, as noted by Decius in *Counsel 63, number 2* and Hieronymus Gratus in *Counsel 106, number 2, part 1*. Alternatively, it signifies the "extremity of time" <note>the very end or limit of a period</note> and cannot be verified except in the named case, as argued by Ancharano, Decius, Curtius Senior, Pacianus, and Arumaeus.

Or, the word **then** is of such a nature that it requires all preceding things to be first done and completed before it disposes of anything, according to the *Clementines* on the granting of prebends and the law regarding conditions and demonstrations. See also Hartmann Pistor’s *Feudal Questions*.

<column-break/>

*...number 26.* Bartolus Socinus, *Counsel 5, number 7*. Thus, before the fulfillment <note>of the condition</note>, the day has not arrived, the time has not passed, and no obligation has been born, according to the Digest section *On the Meaning of Words*.

However, this restriction—found in the *Law of Titius, section "Lucius," where Bartolus and others, especially Jason, comment—does not prevent an "extension." This extension is made based on the presumed will of the testator in a case similar to the one expressed, according to Petrus Surdus, *Counsel 336, number 46*. On the words **then and in that case**, and when they restrict a substitution <note>a legal arrangement for heirs</note>, see Cravetta, *Counsel 989*.

The word **then** <note>German: *alsdann* or Latin: *tunc*</note> denotes the very end of the time for an action that is first about to arise, since it is drawn toward the outcome of a condition. See Klock, *Volume 3, Counsel 42 and Counsel 114*.

Regarding what the words **then let it exist** denote, see Klock, *Counsel 6, number 144*. For the importance of the particle "then," see the *Altdorf Counsels, pages 450, 457, and 462*, and Alemannus *On the Right of Coinage*. The word **then** is restrictive, according to Klock, *Volume 3, Counsel 103, number 45*.

See also Symphoremus Gilman, *Volume 1, part 2*, and the *Marburg Counsels*. For **then namely** <note>original: *als nemlich*</note>, see the *Marburg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 24*.

### 46. So that. (Latin: *Ita quòd*)

It is said that the clause **so that** <note>original: *also daß*</note> stands as an "augmentative" <note>adding more</note> rather than a "restrictive" <note>limiting</note> term, but this does not usually hold true. Instead, it typically stands as a "declarative" and "taxative" <note>specifically listed</note> term, and it restricts the preceding provision. This is found in the Digest sections *Regarding Children and Posthumous Heirs*. Riminaldus says in his *Counsels* that by these words, a trust <note>original: *fideicommissum*</note> is restricted to the persons expressed above and does not extend to others. See also Lord Wilhelm Antonii in his *Treatise on Delays*.

Furthermore, the nature of said clause is such that it should be understood according to what was said above, as seen in the *Authentics regarding witnesses*. Alciatus, Ruinus, and Parisius all agree that it should be understood in the manner previously stated, and it is a relative term that retains the preceding boundaries, according to Johann Petrus Surdus in *Book 3, Counsel 315*.

->ADDITION.<-

See Mundius *On Duties and Honors* regarding this. The words **in such a way and so** flow from what precedes them and stand as a declaration, according to Klock, *Counsel 6, number 172*.

### 47. Altar. (Latin: *Altare*)

Regarding the consecration of Altars, see Petrus Peck in his *Treatise on the Repair of Churches, chapter 36 and following*, and Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in his *Treatise on Ecclesiastical Benefices, chapter 16*.

### 48. Age. (Latin: *Ætas*)

What age is, and its various distinctions, is treated by Martini in *Century 20, Disputation 4, Question 5*.

Regarding the stages and division of age, see Speckhan in *Question 44, Century 1*, where he states: five stages of age are numbered in the single law of the <term>Theodosian Code regarding those who seek the indulgence of age</term>: childhood, adolescence, established age, perfect age, and old age. At the same time, he discusses those who are said to be "near to infancy" or "near to puberty"—distinctions that must be understood especially in matters of crimes and the imposing of punishments; add to this Cardanus in *Contradictions of Doctors*, book 1, tract 5, contradiction 10.

Astrologers distinguish ages according to the cycles of seven and nine years. From this, they speak of "septenary" years <note>years based on the number seven</note>, <term>climacteric years</term> <note>critical transition years in a person's life, often thought to be multiples of 7 or 9</note>, and "enneadic" years <note>years based on the number nine</note>; see Ranzovius in his *Catalog of Emperors, etc.*, who loved the astrological art, and Bisciola’s *Various Readings*, book 2, chapter 1.

Furthermore, just as these years can have some effect on the human body regarding health and temperament, one may also—not without superstition—ascribe power to them in external matters.

But regarding the age of man, see Guevara in *Epistle 3, 21, folio 116, etc.*, where he also treats the age of the Patriarchs and whether a man is presumed to live up to a hundred years; see also Talentonus, book 1, chapter 17, and book 4, chapter 2; and Bisciola’s *Leisurely Hours*, volume 2, book 13, chapter 3. What is called the "legitimate age"? See Brissonius, book 3 of *Antiquities*, chapter 2. On the change of "complexion" <note>the balance of bodily humors</note> according to age, see Adam Keller in his *Treatise on Successions*, title 5, number 31, folio 70. For the ages have their own changes, as the physicians say, because we change our physical makeup from seven-year period to seven-year period, or from six-year period to six-year period. On the age of diseases, see Talentonus, book 4, chapter 7; on prolonging life and suitable medicines, the same author treats this in book 2, chapter 1 and following. On prolonging life, see Panthius' *Hygiatich*.

<column-break/>

See Deodatus Zacchia in his *Medico-Legal Questions*, book 1, title 1, where he also discusses old age.

And regarding climacteric years, see the treatises by Codruchus and Ranzovius, likewise Puteanus, and also Bisciola in *Leisurely Hours*, book 15, chapter 8. Mr. Harsdörffer, in the *German Secretary*, second part, book 6, epistle 33, speaks of the "Staircase Years" <note>original German: *Stuffens Jahr*, a metaphor for the climacteric stages of life</note>. Regarding the "decisive years" of the physicians, see Cardanus in *Contradictions of Doctors*, book 3, contradiction 2 and following.

On the longevity of certain animals, see Talentonus, book 1, chapter 17, and Neander in his *Gnomology*, folio 396 and following.

->## ADDITION.<-

In Leiden, an eagle lived for over 100 years. Elephants reach 120 years, and thus the age of two men; stags reach nearly 200; camels nearly 100; birds of prey and ravens reach 200. Some trees endure for 900 years or more. Ivy, the grapevine, hyssop, rosemary, and other shrubs exceed the years of humans. See Mr. Harsdörffer in the second part of the *German Secretary*, book 3, letter 34.

A person is presumed to live a hundred years, according to Menochius, *Presumption 6, number 49*. However, the more accepted opinion is that a man is not even presumed to reach the hundred-year mark, according to Antonius Gabriel in *Common Conclusions, title on Presumptions, conclusion 16, number 3*. Corallus, *Miscellany 5, 8, number 2*. Terentia is said to have lived 117 years. Clodia exceeded 150.

Justinian says that Zosimus, at the age of 120, was still strong in the virtues of his mind and the operations of his body, in *Novel 5, chapter 2*. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 48, numbers 27 and 28. The Baron von Lamberg, in his second marriage between his 80th and 90th year, fathered ten sons and four daughters. In a village by Lake Constance <note>original Latin: *Lacu Acronium*</note>, a certain wife born 94 years ago became pregnant by her husband, who was 96 years old, and gave birth to a daughter, though she was stillborn. On <term>longevity</term> <note>original Greek: πολυετία (polyetia)</note> or great age, see Pontanus, *On the Wonders of Wonders*, chapter 17, where Friedrich Forner, the suffragan bishop of Bamberg, found a certain man in 1613 at the edge of the Thuringian forest who had exceeded his 150th year; he had 100 sons, grandsons of 70 years, as well as great-grandsons and great-great-grandsons. Bullæus, in *Consultation 3, number 84*, says that ancient Doctors are far superior to modern ones in weight, number, and measure. Coler, in *On Executive Process*, part 2, chapter 1, number 40, mentions a certain "Veteran Student" of the knightly order who, remaining in the Academy of Leipzig for a full 50 years, kept his rented study in the college; he was equipped with only two books—namely, the Holy Bible and a Latin-German Dictionary—both of which were so covered in dust that any letters could be clearly traced on their surface. The elderly are counted among those in poor health, according to Justus Oldekop in *On Swearing on Another’s Soul*, page 67, number 305. Those in their fifties are considered "Old Men," according to Fabricius in his commentary on Gail.

# Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

Explained on page 33. Chock wrote a treatise *On Old Age*. Also Andreas Laurentius.

There is a certain noble and widespread family, referred to here as "TT," who met in the year 1615. Because **God had blessed their family foundation**, they decided that from that time forward, they would annually give to each member as many Guilders of "Age-Money" as the years they had reached. This was intended as a supplement <note>original German: *Zubuß*</note> to help them save, to better support themselves, to give alms to the poor from those funds, to thank God for His blessing, and to faithfully pray for further grace. A question was recently raised as to whether this money should be placed in a common treasury or if it could be demanded after the death of the parents. Both options were denied.

## 49. Ancient Counts. (Latin: *Comites Imperii antiqui*)

What "Ancient Counts" are, and those who are so designated, I have described in my *Legal Opinions* <note>original: *consiliis*</note>, part 4, final opinion 195, to which I refer the reader.

### ADDITION.

Such families include: 1. The Counts of Salm. 2. The Counts of Ortenburg, treated at length by Limnaeus in volume 1, addition to book 4, chapter 4, page 410. The Counts of Tübingen (who were still numbered among the Estates of the Empire until a few years ago) were present at the destruction of Jerusalem; this is testified by the Senate of Tübingen to the Illustrious Duke Ulrich of Württemberg, on the authority of a diploma from the Emperor Vespasian, which is asserted to still be kept among the archives of the Counts of Tübingen, according to Nicolaus Myler in *On the Princes and Estates of the Empire*, chapter 16, page 146. <note>The claim that a German noble family held a charter from the Roman Emperor Vespasian (1st century AD) was a common way for families to claim immense antiquity, though historians today view such documents as legendary or forged.</note>

How many illustrious families of Heroes and Counts have been left without male offspring within 300 or 400 years is shown in alphabetical order by Klockius in *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 40, number 30; and at number 25 he recounts which Counties the Dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg have brought under their own jurisdiction. He treats the same argument in numbers 26, 27, 28, and 29. The dignity of a Count is older than that of Dukes and Marquises, and in both the Western and Eastern Empires their prerogative was so great that they were ranked above Dukes, according to Knipschildt in *On Entails*, chapter 1, number 155; at number 159 he discusses **those of princely rank**, and at number 160 **the Counts of the Empire**. ## 50. Ancient Customs. (Latin: *Mores antiqui*)

What is said of the Romans:
->**The Roman state stands by its ancient customs and its men.**<-

The same may be said of the Germans; and as Horace implies, all things daily rush toward the worse, when he says:

> The age of our parents, worse than our grandparents, brought
> us forth more wicked; soon to give
> a still more vice-ridden offspring.

> We are not the only ones who consider that morals fall into a worse state every day; it has been the opinion of every age. The canonical books of the Old Testament are as many as there are letters in the Hebrew alphabet, namely 22. The other books, which were not counted in the Canon, were called **Hagiographa** <note>literally "holy writings"; often referring to the third section of the Hebrew Bible or the deuterocanonical books</note>.

# 52. Ancestral Fiefs. (Latin: *Feuda Avita*)

Ancestral or Paternal Fiefs <term>fief: a piece of land held by a person from a lord in exchange for service</term> are those which come to us from ancestors <note>ascending relatives</note> up to the fourth degree, such as from the father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and his father. <note>legal references to the *Books of Fiefs*</note>. Although these should rightly only be called "Paternal," and the other fiefs that come to us from beyond the fourth degree should be called "Old Fiefs," it occasionally happens that one term is used for the other. Thus, old fiefs are called paternal, and vice-versa. However, it is considered good and necessary that one pays careful attention to these words—namely **Old** and **Paternal**—so that they are placed together in the letters of enfeoffment, like this: "We grant the Old or Paternal fief to the said N., etc." This is done so that error and discord might be prevented. <note>References to legal scholars Zasius and Schneidewin</note>. In effect, there is no difference between a paternal and an ancient fief, except that under the "ancient fief" more persons are included than under the "paternal fief."

It should be noted here that a male relative <term>Agnat: a relative whose kinship is traced through the male line</term> who seeks succession to a fief as an "ancient" holder is obliged to prove who the first acquirer was and that he descends from that same person. From this burden of proof, such a relative is not released even if the fief in question has been in his name and family line for many hundreds of years in continuous succession. One scholar even states that not even a span of a thousand years would allow a fief to be called paternal or ancient for distant relatives descending from a different branch; rather, it would always be considered "new" in regard to them. Another writes in these formal words: "nor am I persuaded to believe..." <note>The text cuts off here, leading to the next page</note>.

# Enlarged Practical Treasury

...[it is argued] that for <term>agnates</term> <note>Relatives related through the male line.</note> who are not in possession of a property, because that property was in the family since ancient times, it is presumed to be "ancient" in such a way that those agnates are presumed to descend from the first acquirer. However, this is far from the rule that says if a property has been in a family for a long time, it is presumed ancient. For while that rule is true—and indeed proven by the fact itself—it does not necessarily follow or correctly imply that these specific agnates are descended from the same lineage <note>original Latin: *stipite*</note> that originally acquired the <term>fief</term> <note>Land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service.</note> from which the deceased also sprang. Although I might say this occurs by presumption when they are in possession—that is, it happens by the benefit of possession—it has been decided very often in the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire, based in Speyer and later Wetzlar.</note> that the fact that a fief has been in the same family for a long time does not, by itself, prove that his agnates are eligible to inherit it. Thus says Rosenthal.

And although several legal scholars would like to lend a helping hand to the agnate who seeks the <term>succession</term> <note>The right to inherit the property.</note> of a fief regarding the proof of the first acquirer of the fief and the descent from him, and wish to hold that in case of doubt, a fief should be presumed ancient in respect to the agnate aspiring to the succession; nevertheless, that opinion is rejected by the majority conclusion of legal scholars. This opinion especially cannot hold when the lord of the fief, or another who has a claim from the lord, possesses the fief. In such a case, according to the accepted conclusion, such a fief is not to be presumed ancient in respect to the agnate, but rather "new" <note>original: *novum*</note>. This is both because possession is on behalf of the Lord, and presumption favors the possessor; and because that agnate establishes the foundation of antiquity in that capacity. This is the opinion of Alvarottus, Curtius the Elder, Alexander, Cravetta, and others cited by him, as well as Rosenthal in his work on fiefs.

Furthermore, even in a case where a fief is presumed to be ancient, that presumption for antiquity is not of such great efficacy that a Judge, because of this alone, can definitively pronounce the fief to be ancient.

### ADDITION.

Regarding whether and when an ancient fief that was illegally <term>alienated</term> <note>Transferred or sold to someone outside the family line.</note> may be revoked, see Klock, volume 2. An ancient fief is always established as "new" in the person of an outside buyer. An ancient fief retains its original nature even in the hands of a new buyer if, upon inspecting the original cause, it is found to be ancient; it must be judged as such with the buyer. It is not called "ancient" in the person of the last <term>invested</term> <note>Formally granted the rights to the fief.</note> <term>vassal</term> <note>The person holding the fief from the lord.</note> unless it has come down from the fourth degree of ancestors upward.

Affection toward things that belonged to one's ancestors

is considered a type of loss <note>likely referring to "pretium affectionis" or the sentimental value that complicates legal damages</note>, Klock volume 2. Which fief is called "old" is discussed extensively by Klock in volume 3. One type of old fief is "rectilinear" <note>direct line of descent</note>, another is "collateral" or "extraneous."

Concerning an old fief, an ancestral-paternal, ancient-paternal family- or old-fief: see Obrecht, Gothofredus Antonius, and Knipschildt on family <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>A legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of successive generations of a family.</note>.

**53. Always, All times, Ever, in Eternity,** see below at the words **Ever and always,** and the word **Eternity. Always.** <note>original German: *Allweg, Allzeit, Immer, in Ewigkeit*; original Latin: *Semper*</note>

The word "always" added to a legal disposition signifies a stretch of time, and in every case and time. Similarly, the phrase "in perpetuity" <note>original: *in perpetuum*</note> has a successive stretch into the future, and denotes time "forever and ever" <note>original: *in secula seculorum*</note>, and every case of that time, as Bartolus writes. Many others cite this in the same sense, including Peregrinus, Riminaldus, Castillo, Panciroli, Decianus, and Surdus.

So too the words "at any time" are so universal that they comprehend all time without restriction. And although otherwise infinity is not easily tolerated in law, whenever it is introduced by a clear and transparent agreement of the parties, it must be entirely tolerated.

If, however, a witness says that he saw Titius possess a property "always" for 30 years—even though the word "always" denotes a continuation or perpetuity, and it is impossible that he could have been on the land at every single moment; indeed, even if it is proven that Titius was absent at some time—the witness’s statement is not refuted as false. This is because it could be that the witness saw the tenant pay him the profits every year, or saw that the possessor was always able to use the thing if he wished. Johann Schneidewein on the Institutes.

### ADDITION.

The word "always," when it denotes a continuous act, see Boerius. The word "always" can be verified in 10 or 20 years, and sometimes in three. What the word "eternally" <note>original German: *ewig*</note> or "perpetually" imports, see Klock volume 2. The words "perpetually" and "always" do not alter or extend a fief, and can be verified within a decade. Often great...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the legal interpretation of terms of duration, specifically how the meaning of "perpetual" or "eternal" can shift depending on context, before moving into alphabetical entries for "Amadis" (literature), "Ambacht" (office/guild), and "Ambassador."</meta>

the gravity of matters can turn on the inversion of a single syllable; for example, when the phrase *without any imprisonment* <note>original German: "ohne einige Gefängniß"</note> was changed to *into eternal* <note>original German: "in ewige"</note> [imprisonment]. Sprenger, *On Small Matters*, page 134.

A thing is rightly called "perpetual" even if it lasts only for a certain time, according to Rittershusius in his *Commentary on the New Laws*, page 29, numbers 14, 15, and 16. Thus, in the Old Testament, circumcision and sacrifices are called an "eternal covenant" because they were intended to last as long as it seemed fit to God, the Lawgiver. Due to their long duration, mountains and hills are also called "eternal," as is a possession in Genesis 48:4. However, what constitutes a <term>perpetual fideicommissum</term> <note>A legal arrangement where property is held in trust to be passed down through generations.</note> is taught by Knipschildt in *On Fideicommissa*, chapter 2, number 41 and following. Harpprecht, in *On Obligations Arising from Crimes*, page 56, number 29, establishes a two-fold perpetuity: "periodic" and "absolute." Regarding the clause "that something may remain firm and stable perpetually," and what legal effect it has, see Klock, volume 1, consultation 6, number 14.

## 55. Ambacht, see the words: Office (Amt), Bailiff (Amtsmann), Chief Magistrate (Ammeister). Ambacti.

Regarding this word, Marchantius, in his *Description of Flanders*, book 1, under the heading "Hulst," folio 42, writes as follows: *Ambacht* is composed by our common folk with an aspirated middle; a "fabrication"; from *Amt*, and the contracted *Am*, denoting a public office or the power of commanding, and *Acht*, that is, "I hold in esteem." Thus, an *Ambacht* is a voluntary college of those who deem someone worthy of their obedience, whether in the countryside or the city. For there, almost all "Castellanies" <note>The jurisdiction of a castle or its governor.</note>, and here all bodies of the mechanical arts—and even the crafts themselves practiced publicly outside the law of those fellowships—are distinguished by the name of *Ambachten*.
*Besoldus, Volume I.*

### ADDITION.

In Strasbourg <note>referred to by its Latin name, Argentina</note>, a law was enacted that no one could be elected <term>Ammeister</term>—which is the highest magistrate in the city—unless he could prove he was dedicated to some craft or trade. Draco, *On Patricians*, page 260. Furthermore, he is not permitted to accept any <term>fief</term> <note>Land or rights held from a superior lord.</note> from any Prince or superior.

## 56. Ambassador: see below the words: Envoy (Gesandte). Ambasiator. Legate (Legatus).

"Ambassador" is used for a Legate and descends from the Italian *Ambasciatore* or the French *Ambassadeur*. The Spaniards also call him *Embaxador*, and the modern Greeks *ambasaderon* <note>original Greek: $\alpha\mu\pi\alpha\sigma\alpha\delta\epsilon\rho\omicron\nu$</note>. Meursius, in his *Glossary of the Middle Ages*. The writers of "Barbarous Latin" <note>Medieval or non-Classical Latin.</note>, following their custom, granted this word "citizenship" in Latin. It was common for them to "Latinize" barbaric words—that is, Germanic ones, according to Schottel in *On the Main German Language*, folio 129. Thus, Peter de Vinea, book 2, chapter 8: "The messengers of various prelates, the *Ambasiadores* of the rebellious cities of Lombardy."

*Ambascia* is also used in Latin for a legation or embassy. Salic Law, book 1, section 3: "If he was occupied in a Lord's *Ambascia*, he cannot be summoned <note>original: "manniri"; the author notes this comes "from Mannen", meaning to be cited to court.</note>." However, we Germans did not borrow this word from the Italians and French; rather, they took it from us, and the Germans have reclaimed it. Schottel, folio 129, notes that *Ambacht* was still in use two hundred years ago, as I showed in my *Gleanings on Legates*, folio 11.

There are some, however, who derive it from the Greek *emphadizein* <note>original Greek: $\epsilon\mu\phi\alpha\delta\iota\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$</note>, which means "to send." But it is not probable that the Latin-Barbaric writers took that word from pure Greek; otherwise, the older writers would have used it as well.

The messengers of absolute Princes are called *Botschaften* or *Gesandte* [Envoys]; those of the Estates to the Imperial Diet are called *Deputati* or *Abgesandte* [Deputies]; and those whom a Prince sends to his subjects are called *Commissarii* [Commissioners]. I have noted these and other matters regarding this subject in the aforementioned treatise *On Legates*, folio 15.

An anonymous author, in a political discourse *On the State of Rome*, folio 49, aptly defines a Legate as: *He who is chosen by the Prince to go toward another Prince to represent his person, and there to treat affairs more by the forces of a good understanding and those of fine speaking than by armed force, unless the case requires it; and also to observe the actions and behaviors of him or those to whom he is sent, to worthily play this character on a stage where there are so many clear-sighted eyes.*

But Francesco Guicciardini, in his *Reminiscences*, 1, timely warns: A Prince intending to circumvent another by the labor of his Ambassador must, first of all, deceive the Ambassador himself. For in this way, the Ambassador will execute the business committed to him with greater mental effort—whether he must plead or perform some other task—believing entirely, seriously, and without any simulation, that all these things are being done by his Prince in earnest; whereas he would surely handle them more slackly or timidly if he knew otherwise.

From this, Henry Wotton, formerly the Ambassador of the King of Great Britain to the Republic of Venice, defined the office thus: "An ambassador is an honest man sent to lie abroad for the sake of the Commonwealth." <note>This is a famous pun by Sir Henry Wotton (1568–1639). In English, "to lie" can mean both to reside in a place and to tell a falsehood. Pacian, in book 2, *On Probations*, chapter 33, provides many things worth knowing regarding <term>Legates born at the side</term> <note>original Latin: "Legatis natis à latere"; these are high-ranking papal legates who represent the Pope with his full authority</note>; the <term>Sagmina</term> <note>sacred herbs or tufts of grass carried by Roman heralds</note>, the <term>Cerycia</term> <note>herald's staffs</note>, and the <term>Caduceus</term> <note>the staff of Hermes/Mercury, used as a symbol of peace and diplomatic immunity</note>. Likewise: whether and in which cases they may interpose themselves in their own affairs or the affairs of others; and whether and when the burden of proving the commission of their embassy falls upon the one claiming to be a Legate.

Warsevicius, at folio 104, teaches what kind of Legates should be sent to any given people. <margin>That Legates and envoys should not let too much slip in their speeches, and thereby throw their own proposals into doubt.</margin> <note>original German: "Daß die Legati und Gesandten in ihren Reden sich nicht zuviel heraus lassen..."</note> Michael de Montaigne, in his *Essays*, book 1, chapter 9. Melliet, in his notes on Tacitus at folio 502, advises <margin>that even in great commissions and embassies, for the sake of various considerations, not just one person should be employed</margin>, where at folio 582 he suggests many notable things in favor of Legates. Likewise, Legates should know the language of the place to which they are sent, even if they do not speak it, lest they be deceived by interpreters. Should the expenses and damages inflicted by enemies on the journey be reimbursed to a Legate? Zasius consulted on this in book 1, consultation 20; add also Majolus in *Dog Days*, colloquy 6, folio 779, where he says that although it seems one should conclude that the expenses spent on customary tips <note>original Latin: "honorariis"</note> at an inn ought to be included in the petition—since a Legate bestows these tips to preserve the reputation of his Prince—the contrary is actually truer. Such expenses are considered "luxurious" rather than "necessary" and are generally not recovered, especially since a Legate is paid a set salary from which it will be easy for him to bestow such gifts. However, in this matter, one must look at what is observed in each specific place.

Finally, it should be known that many things are not entrusted to papers which are instead committed to Legates; see Gerbert in his *Epistle*, number 34.

### 58. To Lease Out. Admodiare. <note>This term refers to the practice of tax farming or leasing the revenues of an office to an individual for a fixed fee.</note>

The word is used barbarously as *admodiare* from the French *admodier*, by whom such contractors are called *Admodiateurs*.

**3.** Third, during his lease, he shall undertake <term>renovations</term> of the house's properties where necessity requires and as much as can be done annually, at my and my successors' expense.

**4.** Fourth, the Lessee shall be granted as much firewood as he requires for necessity in the house at Dorlisheim from the forests of the same house, but he shall have no power to sell anything therefrom.

### 59. Office, Stewardship, Steward. *Opificium Ambachtus.*

This denotes the body of a specific head [entity], for instance, of a fortress or a city. <note>original Latin: "Schrad. de feud. part. 3. cap. 4. n. 25. &c."</note> Or **Office** (*Amt*) signifies a community that is governed by a single <term>Prefect</term> <note>original: "Præfecto"; a high-ranking official or administrative governor</note>. Thus, a jurisdiction is undoubtedly attached to an **Office**, because the name **Office**, **Ambactia** <note>a Latinized form of the Germanic word for service or office</note>, **Prefecture**, etc., corresponds with the word **Stewardship** (*Pfleg*). <note>original Latin: "Gilm. Symphor. tom. 1. part. 3. vot. 23. n. 69. vers. alterum caput est."</note> **Stewardship** (*Pfleg*), moreover, designates power or jurisdiction. <note>original Latin: "Gilm. rer. judic. lib. 2. decis. 35 n. 11."</note>

Likewise, in Bavaria, **Steward** (*Pfleger*) is used in place of our **High Bailiff** (*Obervogt*) or **Governor** (*Statthalter*).

The word *Ambactum* or *Ambafcia*, however, is a purely Celtic and thus also Germanic

<column-break/>

word, and denotes a hired servant, as I have just said and also demonstrated from Ennius and Caesar in the *Treatise on the Nature of Peoples*, folio 88. Even now, the Dutch use **Ambachtsmann** for a hired laborer who rents out his services daily to seek his profit; see the entry under the word *Ambacht*.

#### ADDITION.

The word *Ambactus* in the Gallic language signifies a servant, as Festus says in his commentary on Ennius. Among the Gauls, there are two types of liege men: the *Soldurii* <note>devoted retainers</note> and the *Ambacti*. The *Ambacti* of the Gauls are equated with the clients of the Romans according to P. Gregorius in his *System of Universal Law*, book 47, number 17. Once a person is approved in an office, they should not thereafter be rejected, even if they had been unfit before the probation. <note>original Latin: "Klock. tom. 1. cons. 51. n. 337. & seqq."</note> Officials, even if they were appointed for free and voluntarily, cannot be removed from office without just cause. <note>original Latin: "conf. 32. n. 15. & 16."</note>

### 60. Official Books. *Scripturæ & Libri Officialium.*

The writings and books of public officials and others to whom public trust is given deserve public and full credit. For they rest upon public authority and are set over public accounts, revenues, and expenses with public trust. <note>original Latin references: "Beust. in l. admonendi n. 844. Menoch. 2. caf. 91."</note> In ancient times, even bankers (*Argentarii*) were protected by public authority, and therefore their books were considered to have public trust. <note>original Latin: "l. Argentarii. 10. ff. de edend. Bornit. de Instrum. lib. 3. cap. 11."</note>

#### ADDITION.

Certain documents are truly public, such as those written during court proceedings or entered into the records later, such as: census books, **Interest Books** (*Zinsbücher*), or **Interest Registers** (*Zinsregister*), which are kept in public archives, the **Chancery** (*Cantzley*), or the **Town Hall** (*Rath-Haus*); likewise **Manorial Books** (*Saalbücher*), **Land-use Registers** (*Uhrbarregister*), **Tax or Assessment Registers** (*Schatz- oder Steuerregister*), and **Fief Books** (*Lehenbücher*). Some, however, are public in their effect but not truly public in nature: such as those prepared by Notaries.

Writings made by officials appointed for public duty provide legal proof, as discussed at length in the *Altdorf Consultations*, pages 532 and 536, where it is limited to cases where they do not disagree or vary. On the question of how **Official Books** (*Amtsbücher*) provide proof, see Franck, *On the Payment of Fees*, page 36. To what extent **Tax, Assessment, Revenue, Court, Inheritance, or Official Books** provide proof, see Berlich, volume 1, conclusion 36, number 18.

### 61. Official Decrees. *Decreta.*

Official decrees do not carry the weight of a final judgment (*res judicata*); instead, one can always offer to proceed through the ordinary legal process against them, which is a challenge to the merits of the case, etc.

## 62. **Sergeant**, **Court Attendant**. **Provincial Bailiffs**. **Summoner**.

Provincial Bailiffs <note>original: "Cohortales"; historically, these were lower-level staff or soldiers attached to a provincial governor’s office</note> (commonly called **Sergeants** or **Court Attendants**) are the officials and summoners of the Governor in a province. These positions were permanent within the provinces, as noted in the *Law of the Governor* in the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "ff."; the Digest is a massive collection of legal opinions from Roman jurists</note> regarding matters of credit. They are subject to this ministry alone, and are neither chosen at the Governor's whim nor brought into the province by him. See *Dominus Vultejus on the Title of the Code concerning Jurisdiction, title 23, law 1, note 12, etc., page 487.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding the summoners <note>original: "Apparitoribus"</note> of Schönborn in *Politics, book 3, chapter 51*: their office is highly necessary so that, in their absence, more honorable men are not forced to stain themselves with such unpleasant tasks. For example, among the Lithuanians, these tasks are enjoined upon the accuser himself.
There is an extensive discussion on summoners in *Petrus Gregorius’s Comprehensive System of Universal Law in the Index.* A summoner or public messenger is trusted as long as the contrary is not proven by the defendant (*Klock, On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 135, note 11*); see also *Rittershusius in the Novels, page 697.* On <term>Beggar-Judges</term> and <term>Beggar-Reeves</term> <note>original: "Bettelrichtern und Bettelvögten"; officials appointed to manage or expel vagrants and beggars</note>, and what kind of persons should be appointed as sergeants, beadles, and bailiffs, see *Zorer, part 2, question 18, note 4065.*

## 63. **Bailiff**, **Administrative Staff**, **Steward**, **Manager**. **Prefects**. **Officials**.

Magistrates, officials, and the <term>Lay Judges</term> <note>original: "Scabini"; community members who sat in judgment with a presiding officer</note> of the nobility possess no jurisdiction of their own (*Matthaeus Coler, On the Executive Process, part 2, chapter 1, note 121, at the verse "tamen hi" and following*). Instead, they are typically delegated and appointed by Counts and Nobles for only one or two specific cases (*Henning Göden, Consultation 59, note 21*). Thus, they perform and arrange nearly everything according to the command and will of the Nobles or their superiors (*Matthaeus Coler, in the place cited, note 131, near the end*).
Similarly, when a magistrate or another official collects tithes, taxes, and other tributes from the subjects and men of the nobility without imploring the aid of the Nobles, or when he demands the required services from them, he is exercising a "bare ministry of execution," which is not properly a matter of jurisdiction (*Berlichius, Decision 59, number 6*).
If territories are distinct but established under a single Prince and Lord, then one Governor or Prefect can summon the subjects of another Governor without a subsidiary request (*Berlichius, the same Decision 59, note 2*). For example: the Prefect of Tübingen could summon someone living in the Prefecture of Herrenberg, because he is not using his own jurisdiction, but that of the common Prince. However, actual custom observes the opposite, as Berlichius also notes in the same place, note 9.
Furthermore, officials must observe the boundaries committed to them and not step beyond them, nor claim for themselves what has been given to others (*Law "whosoever," 2, Code on Executors and Exactors; Law 1, Code on the Summoners of the Prefect; Law "sent," 6, at the verse "who beyond," Code on the Exacting of Tributes*). See also Baldus on the law *extra*, number 5, at the verse "because every official," etc., in the Digest regarding jurisdiction.

<column-break/>

Conversely, if they act in accordance with their official duties, the Master <note>the superior or employer</note> can be sued for that same act (*Modestinus Pistoris, question 89*).
Likewise, if a <term>Treasurer</term> <note>original: "Quaestor"</note> mismanages the affairs of his Master and converts the income to his own use, which he is later unable to pay back—how should he be punished? This is treated by *Virgilius Pingitzer, Illustrious Questions, 47; Vincentius Hondedeus, Consultation 82, volume 2; Berlichius, final volume, Conclusion 57; Bachov, volume 2, Dispute 30, thesis 1, letter f, page 1066; and myself in the Treatise on the Treasury, chapter 2, final section, number 4, at the end.* Also in several legal consultations; add *Fridericus Mindanus, On the Process, chapter 13, final number.*
There is no doubt that those who behave fraudulently in office—who withhold something from their Masters in the accounting, or otherwise carry it away for their own benefit and to the harm of the Master or the subjects—commit theft <note>original: "furtum"</note> and can be punished as such. And although it seems to many that they should be punished more mildly than other thieves, it is more correct that they deserve to be punished more severely. This is (1) because perjury almost always occurs <note>referring to the violation of their oath of office</note>, (2) because forgery is involved (namely, that the account was falsified), and (3) this crime "tastes of" <term>Embezzlement</term> <note>original: "peculatum"; specifically the theft of public or sacred funds</note>.
However, I do not think those should be punished immediately who do not steal public money, but who are accustomed to apply money entrusted to them to their own use at their own risk—if they are unable to render an account. It is established that these are regularly held liable for the remainder (*Law 2, Law 9, section 1, regarding the Julian Law on Embezzlement*). This applies unless fraud is present and an intent to steal; it does not apply when someone otherwise cannot render an account out of negligence. See *Cöppen, Observation 139, and my second part of Consultations, and also the Treatise on the Treasury.* Thus, the judgment of a prudent Judge must be applied here.
Furthermore, it is one thing to "put everything into the receipts and remain in debt for the balance," and another thing to "falsify the accounts." This distinction should be fairly observed and noted in the punishment of officials. Besides this, it is also deemed advisable to include in their oaths that they shall not use the money, but shall deliver it to the Lordship. See *Petrus Caballus, Criminal Resolutions, 99 and 139.*
And as to how an official or an administrator of provisions—a **Steward** or **Manager**—is held liable if something is stolen from him—when something is carried away from the tithe-barn or the official granary—and how such a theft is proved, see *Johannes Vincentius Hondedeus, Consultation 90, volume 2.*
Finally, almost everything that can be said or known about officials has been compiled with diligent effort by *Paris de Puteo in the Treatise on Syndicates.* To this, you may add *Cavalcanti in the Treatise on the Royal Arm, final part, and Cardinal Tuschus, Practical Conclusions, letter O, under the word "Official."*

This refers to the legal principle that a subordinate's administrative actions are presumed to be known or authorized by their superior.</note> See Cravet, *On Ancient Times*, p. 4, § regarding completed matters, n. 23 and following; Tiraqueau, *On Nobility*, ch. 14, n. 2; Giovanni Battista Costa, *On the Investigation of Fact, Knowledge, and Ignorance*, 72, n. 10 and following; Gratiani, vol. 3, *Forensic Discussions*, ch. 560, n. 31 and 32.

A presumption is made in favor of any Official, as noted by Alciat in *On Presumptions*, rule 3, presumption 15, at the beginning; Menochius, book 2, *On Presumptions*, 85. Regarding those who take away, intercept, and turn public money to their own use, see Dr. Biccius in *Golden Section 4, thesis 178,* where he distinguishes whether the goods were committed to them at their own risk or not—that is, whether they held <term>accountable offices</term> <note>original German: "verrechneten Aemtern," referring to offices where every penny had to be strictly accounted for in ledgers.</note> or not. To specially entrust a matter to someone’s faith signifies, in Common Law, to have a certain "body" or entity to manage. <note>original German: "ein gewiß Corpus zu verwalten haben."</note> Therefore, the man who held an accountable office, even if he made off with many thousands of guilders, was not sentenced to death; yet another, who held an <term>unaccountable office</term> <note>original German: "unverrechnetes Amt," an office without the same strict auditing requirements.</note> and stole only 70 guilders, was punished capitally. <note>original Latin: "capitaliter gestrafft worden." This reflects a legal distinction where the specific nature of the trust violated determined the severity of the sentence.</note> From the mouth of B. Biccius.

### 64. District-Residents. <term>Amtsassen</term>. <note>A class of subjects in Saxony who were under the jurisdiction of a local administrative district (Amt) rather than the high court.</note>

In the Electorate and the other Duchies of Saxony, since the noblemen are <term>Land-residents</term>, <note>original German: "Landsassen," nobles who held estates and were subject to the territorial lord.</note> it is different than among us in Swabia; a distinction between "Mediated" and "Immediate" Nobles has been introduced. The former are called <term>Amtsassen</term>, while the latter are called <term>Schrifftsassen</term> or <term>Cantzleysassen</term>. <note>Residents subject directly to the sovereign's chancery via written summons.</note> See below under the word *Schrifftsassen*.

Furthermore, <term>Amtsassii</term> are and are called those who "sit under the office," who are subject to the local lords and prefects, the <term>district tax-collectors</term>. <note>original German: "Amtschössern," officials responsible for collecting taxes and managing a district.</note> Daniel Moller, *On the New Augustan Constitutions of Saxony*, part 1, const. 5, n. 14; Knich, *On the Investiture of Pacts*, part 2, ch. 5, n. 1 and following; Ritter, *On Homage*, ch. 4, n. 83.

Some argue that this distinction arose because certain nobles acquired rural estates under those Prefects and later subjected them to feudal status—a thing which is undisputed that anyone is free to do. Marta, *On Jurisdiction*, part 1, ch. 29, n. 7 and 8; Cephalus, counsel 168, n. 51, vol. 2; Gail, 2, observation 158, num. 1. Another cause and origin 

<column-break/>

of this matter is derived by Andreas Knich in his *Treatise on Investiture Pacts, book 2, ch. 5, n. 6,* whom you may consult.

Because those estates were "tainted" by mediated jurisdiction from the beginning, and no other change followed in this regard, those Nobles necessarily remained under the mediated jurisdiction of the Prefects by reason of their residence. See Caspar Ziegler, § *Schrifftsassii*, at the beginning, num. 5 and following.

For this reason, <term>Amtsassen</term> receive their <term>first instance</term> <note>The first level of legal hearing or trial.</note> before their own Prefects, and not in the High Courts. <note>original German: "Hofgerichten."</note> The noblemen (just like the citizens and peasants) who reside under the districts must first be sued and held before their officials and tax-collectors. *Electoral High Court Ordinance* under the heading: "Who [should appear] before the High Court," etc.

And although some plaintiff might attempt to sue these <term>Amtsassen</term> in the High Court regarding the first instance, they may nevertheless, through a "plea of the declining forum," <note>original Latin: "exceptionem fori declinatoriam." A legal move to challenge the court's jurisdiction.</note> allege the privilege of the first instance and rightfully petition to be sent back to their own Judge. See Ziegler in § *Schrifftsassii*, conclusion 1, n. 2 and following.

### ADDITION.

Those are called <term>Amtsassen</term> who are subject to local lords, Prefects, or Treasurers—the district tax-collectors—and are summoned before them in the first instance. Daniel Moller, *On the New Augustan Constitutions, part 1, const. 5, num. 14*; Berlich, 1, conclusion 13, num. 5; Reinkingk, 1, class 5, cap. 11, number 47. These <term>Amtsassen</term> are bound to appear and serve not only at the request of the Lord, but also at the request of the Prefect or Treasurer who is over them. Knich, *On the Investiture of Pacts, p. 2, ch. 5, number 7.* The same in *On the Privileges of the Dukes of Saxony*, regarding the word "Dukes," ch. 6, num. 23; see Mundius, *On Offices*, ch. 2, num. 202; Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 4, ch. 4, num. 4.

### 65. District Loss. <term>Amtschaden</term>. Municipal Collection.

<term>Amtschaden</term> is a municipal collection or tax which, in some places, is laid solely upon the villages.

### 66. District Tax. <term>Amtsteuer</term>. Prefectural Collection.

A prefectural collection is that which the Prefect, along with the town senate, imposes on all citizens of the Prefecture, including the towns and the villagers or peasants—the <term>Amtsteuer</term>. Dr. Bocer, *On Collections*, ch. 5, num. 1. A municipal collection is that which the inhabitants of a provincial city provide for the common use of their own municipality. Bocer, in the stated place, number 2.

But truly, since a tax is numbered among the <term>Regalia</term>, <note>Royal rights or prerogatives belonging to the sovereign.</note> a community cannot impose it on its citizens unless a necessity arises regarding those matters which have been committed to their administration. I [discuss this] in my treatise *On the Law of Things*, folio 245.

# 67. Anatomy.
Whether those punished or destined for execution—even while still living—can or should be granted to physicians for **anatomy** is discussed by Everhard Speckhan, century 1, question 7, and Freher, book 1, *Parerga*, chapter 25. Freher argues that the corpses of those condemned to death, <note>original Greek: "τῶν θανατωτῶν"</note> especially those sentenced to the cross, should not be denied to physicians who request them for a righteous and probable use. This is because all such dissection is undertaken for the sake of the public good, and the inspection of mangled bodies is highly necessary for the essential art of medicine. Furthermore, no honor is due to the corpses of those who, before they were killed, were made "slaves of punishment"; <note>original Latin: "servi pœnæ." A legal status where a condemned criminal lost their civil rights and their body became property of the state.</note> therefore, it does not matter what becomes of them, since they could just as well be cast away unburied or left on the hook or the cross.

# ADDITION.
The question is asked: Should a defendant who has been hanged or otherwise punished be handed over to physicians for Anatomy? Bartolus, the "Charioteer of Jurists," touches on this question lightly and leaves it undecided in his commentary on the law regarding the bodies of the punished. However, it is treated most extensively by Harprecht in *On Obligations Arising from Crime*, number 76, and André Laurent in *History of Anatomy*, book 1, chapter 5 and following. Jacopo Berengario da Carpi first brought Anatomy into the light, <note>referring to the first modern anatomical illustrations</note> which Vesalius later perfected as its restorer; see Gabriel Falloppio, *Anatomical Observations*, page 41. If we believe Tertullian, seven hundred human corpses were either skillfully dissected into parts or torn apart like butchers' meat by a single person; see D. Hoffmann, *Disputation on the Liver*, thesis 13. On whether the head of a buried person should be exhumed to perform an Anatomy, see Marius Antoninus, *Various Resolutions*, book 1, case 23, in its entirety.
On this matter, one should consult Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 4, numbers 30, 31, and 32. You will find the marvelous anatomy of an ant in Basil the Great’s 168th letter to Eunomius, page 629. In Basel, in Mr. Plater’s **Cabinet of Curiosities**, <note>original German: "Kunst-Kammer." This refers to the famous collection of Felix Plater, a 16th-century physician.</note> there are two skeletons: one is only as long as a thumb, the other as long as a span; see Zeiller, *German Itinerary*, page 254. The son of Mr. Schoner in Strasbourg once slept in the grass, and a snake crawled into his mouth and stomach, which killed him; but after he was dead, it came out of him again. His body can be found anatomized in this same Cabinet of Curiosities.

# 69. Other, Others, All Others, etc. The Rest.
The word **the rest** <note>original Latin: "cæteri"</note> refers back to similar things, as noted by Jason in his commentary on the law regarding dowry, number 9. Thus, the word **other** <note>original Latin: "alius"</note>, when uttered simply, is repetitive of similar things, according to the gloss on the law concerning fugitive slaves. It establishes the same quality as the preceding words, as noted in the chapter *Sedes* regarding rescripts. See especially Tuschus, letter D, conclusion 245, and Barschamp in *Treatise on Clauses*, folio 377, where he adds that it is not always true that the words "Other, another, or something else" are inclusive. He brings an example from Holy Scripture, which says that Christ was crucified, and **other** thieves; however, Christ is not thereby implied to be a thief.
The phrase **in others** is inclusive of similar things, as per the law on fugitive slaves and the law regarding multiple persons.
The phrase **any others whatsoever** is a universal inclusion; its power and strength are such that it encompasses not only the cases expressed, but also improper cases and those greater than the ones expressed; see Decius, *Counsel* 77; Cravetta, *Counsel* 294 and 308; Tiraqueau, *On the Retraction of Lineage*, section 1, question 7, number 20 and following; Socini, *Counsel* 47, book 4.
Under the word **whosoever**, even the most unusual things can be included, as taught by the same Cravetta, number 7, and Socini, *Counsel* 200, volume 2.
The word **other** or **another** is by its nature relative and representative of the same quality as that which was previously mentioned; see Alexander, *Counsel* 204, number 3 and following, book 2; Ruinus, *Counsel* 130, number 1, book 3; Decius, *Counsel* 182, number 18.

# ADDITION.
In all ancient monuments, the word **the rest** <note>original Latin: "cætera"</note> is written without the diphthong; see also Mr. Dilherr in *Philological Apparatus*, page 47.

# 70. In no other way. Not otherwise.
The phrase **In no other way**, <note>original German: "Anderer Gestalt nicht"</note> or **not otherwise**, or **in no other manner**, has a limiting and restrictive force. Its effect is that a preceding general provision does not take place unless all the qualities expressed afterward are present, and even then, only in the expressed case. See Decius, *Counsel* 61, number 2 and *Counsel* 85, number 4; Parisius, *Counsel* 18, numbers 6 and 7, book 1, and *Counsel* 19, number 15 and following, book 2; Thomas Grammaticus, *Decisions* 49, numbers 3 and 4; Schrader, *Counsel* 36, volume 2, number 1. ### 71. Other Marriage. Second Marriages.

These words designate to the Germans **another**, or a different marriage, and not specifically a "second" marriage. This is because also among the Latins, and in our law, "second marriages" denote not a number, but a difference from past marriages; they include all subsequent marriages without limit. *Law "si quis," section "talem," in the Code on second marriages.* There, a third marriage comes under the name of "second," and the gloss says at *verse 6, "second bed,"* <note>original Latin: "secundo thoro"</note> that every marriage is called "second" which follows the first. *Sichard, in the title of the Code on second marriages, number 9*, says that by the name of "second marriages" come all marriages which are not the first. This is followed by *Menochius, consultation 4, number 38, volume 1; Rollandus a Valle, consultation 72, number 41, volume 1*, where they say that a provision regarding a second marriage also applies to a third, and so on without limit, as *Mantica says in "Conjectures on Last Wills," book 11, title 19, number 9, at the end.*

And it should be noted here that according to the *Edictal Law <note>The "Lex hac Edictali," a law from the Code of Justinian protecting children's inheritance when a parent remarries</note> in the Code on second marriages* (about which see everywhere *Stephanus Durant in his Questions*), a **spouse** <note>original German: "Ehegemächt"</note> **may not leave more to a second spouse than to a child of the first marriage.** But when a child of the first marriage has been provided a dowry by the surviving spouse

<column-break/>

from their own property, or has received something through a gift or otherwise, such things are not counted against the child’s share, and they can still be referred to in the father’s or mother’s will. For such things are counted toward the "legitimate portion" <note>the minimum inheritance guaranteed by law to children</note>.

I am pleased to insert here a legal opinion <note>original Latin: "Consilium"</note> written by me in the name of the illustrious Legal Faculty of Ingolstadt. Since it contains the subject of second marriages and their practice, I hope it will not be unwelcome to the reader.

However, things which seem to pertain to second marriages, and especially to the law concerning them, can be found in the works of *Johannes a Ripa, Johannes de Garron, Stephanus Bertrand, and Johannes Nicolaus of Arles, in special treatises on this matter printed together at Cologne by Gymnicus*, and also in *my own treatise on the three types of domestic society, page 8.*

Accordingly, we, the Dean and Doctors of the Legal Faculty at the Electoral Prince’s University in Ingolstadt, having been duly requested to open our opinion on the "factual scenario" <note>original Latin: "facti speciem"</note> sent to us, and to strengthen it with sufficient reasoning, could in no way refuse this in the service of justice.

Thus, in our assembled College, we have maturely deliberated on this matter, but could find it in no other way than that the inheritance of the late brother, which passed to his mother, rightfully belongs to the two sisters named in the said factual scenario; and that from this, only the **usufruct** <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> or life-long use belongs to their lady mother.

In this matter, we first premise that although under Canon Law <note>Church law</note> the penalties for second marriages are found to be removed, nevertheless those laws which were introduced by Civil Law <note>Roman/secular law</note> in favor of children of a first marriage remain entirely unchanged. The interpreters of both laws confess this with one voice. *Gail, observation 98, book 2; Sarmiento, book 1 of select interpretations, chapter 4; Fachinaeus, book 3, controversy 65; del Castillo Sotomajor, treatise on usufruct, chapter 2, number 16*, where many others are cited. And the famous Cujacius <note>a premiere 16th-century legal scholar</note> elegantly confirms these things already said in his notes *on Novel 22*, where he says the reason for the penalties of second marriages still existing today is that usually the children of the first marriage are affected by injury and loss. If no such children exist, there can be no penalties for second marriages. He says the same *in the summary of the Code on second marriages*: second marriages are restrained by laws so that the children of the first marriage are looked after; by which children, as *Ambrose elegantly says in the 6th book of the Hexameron*, parents are often led astray once the sleeping arrangements have changed.

# Letter A.

custom, the constitution **By this Edictal Law** <note>original Latin: "L. hac Edictali"</note> and similar laws have been abolished, as Virgil Pingizer argues in question 46. For if a custom or "desuetude" <note>the legal principle that a law ceases to have effect through lack of use</note> is contrary to written law, then it must be proved fully and precisely, according to Mynsinger in his 2nd decade, response 13, number 13. But indeed, Fichard proves in his 33rd counsel, number 11 and following, volume 2, that these laws are still observed in many places in Germany. Furthermore, the **Electoral Bavarian Constitutions**, as well as daily practice, do not allow one to doubt this regarding Bavaria and neighboring places, as seen in the **Electoral Bavarian Land Law**, title 14, article 5, chapter 6.

It is further a matter of undisputed law that whatever a mother—who is already entangled in a second marriage <note>original Latin: "funestata," a term implying the legal complications of a second marriage</note>—has obtained through intestate succession <note>inheriting when there is no will</note> or by the will of a son or daughter from the first marriage, she receives only the possession for the duration of her life as her owed portion. She is compelled to leave all of it to those children who survive from the first marriage; nor does she have the power to make a will regarding such resources in favor of any outside person, or to alienate anything. This is found in the law **"Women"** <note>original Latin: "l. fæminæ"</note>, 3, in the Code on second marriages, and the attached authenticating text **"From the Will"** <note>original Latin: "ex testamento"</note>; see Castillo on usufruct <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</note>, chapter 2, number 9, and many following. And indeed, the children not only have ownership of the profits which the mother received from the son's succession when she moved to a second marriage, but they also enjoy a legal mortgage <note>a claim on property as security for a debt</note> granted by the laws on all the mother's other goods, according to the law **"By this edictal law"**, the last paragraph, in the Code on second marriages; Scipio Gentili, treatise on second marriages, chapter 14; and Castillo in the place cited, number 10.

And although it might be granted in excess <note>original Latin: "ex abundanti"</note> that in this case the children expressly consented to their mother’s other marriage, it is nevertheless not in accordance with the laws—especially since it is well-provided in the **Electoral Bavarian Land Ordinance** in the said article 6—that they are nonetheless capable of the aforementioned "benefit" <note>a legal privilege or protection</note> which the laws have granted them. This is because they did not expressly state that, because of such a marriage, the mother should lose nothing of her children's future or already fallen inheritance, neither in regard to ownership <note>original Latin: "proprietas"</note> nor in regard to the use and profit <note>original Latin: "usufructus"</note>.

Indeed, Sarmiensis clearly teaches in his *Select Interpretations*, book 1, chapter 4, that the children of a first marriage who consent to their mother's second marriage cause themselves no prejudice <note>legal disadvantage</note>, and therefore must not be excluded from the benefit of the said law **"Women"** and other laws. Fachin agrees in his *Controversies*, book 3, chapter 65. For first of all, there is no law saying such a thing; secondly, no reason persuades it: for how does a son sin by consenting to his mother embracing a second marriage, which even if he wanted to prevent, he ought not and cannot?

For it is so established by law that he who cannot prevent an act by objecting to it, creates no prejudice for himself by consenting, according to the law **"Caius"** in the Digest on pledge actions, and the law **"Which dowry"** in the Digest on the dissolution of marriage; see Tiraqueau at length on the retraction of agreements, section 1, glossary 9, number 146. And even if the children consenting to the mother's marriage are thought to <meta>catchword: Befoldt Tom. 1.</meta>

<column-break/>

forgive the injury done to them, they are nevertheless not seen to renounce the laws which, by the highest reason and equity, confer benefits and gains upon them when they are so harmed. Similarly, Charles Dumoulin <note>a famous 16th-century French jurist</note> writes in the marginal notes to Filippo Decio's 206th counsel: that Decio advised poorly in that Counsel, and that it does no harm even if the son is present and named in the mother's marriage contract. For it is one thing to honor a mother and her second marriage and to dutifully consent to them; it is quite another to renounce one’s own right. Therefore, a special renunciation is required from a son older than 25 years.

In particular, however, it would have been necessary in every way that the children be sufficiently reminded of the law they hold here, if one wished to hold their consent to the maternal marriage as a renunciation of their right. As Nicolaus Boerius attests in our terms, decision 185, number 23. The laws especially require this for these children, as some are minors and some are women, according to the teachings of Decio, counsel 180, number 8; Gail, book 2, observation 77, number 3; and the Marburg Counsels, 24, number 77 and following.

And although several Doctors go so far as to hold that not only does the children's express consent to the mother's marriage deprive them of their right descending from the above-cited law **"Women"**, but also that it is sufficient if they only consent tacitly—and specifically, if they attend the wedding—as argued by Giovanni Francesco de Ripa in his repetition of the said law **"Women"**, question 14; Decio, counsel 206; Rolando a Valle, counsel 62, number 26, and counsel 95, numbers 2, 3, and following, volume 1; Vivius, *Common Opinions*, 224, at the end; Gabriel, *Common Opinions*, book 3, title on second marriages, conclusion 1, number 37; Gail, book 2, observation 98, number 19 and following; and Forster on intestate succession, book 7, chapter 13.

Yet, this opinion is rejected by others, and indeed with better grounding. For a tacit consent to a marriage cannot be necessarily inferred from presence at the wedding celebration; for many are present at weddings which they do not approve of, but rather, if they were asked, they would blame. But a tacit will resulting from an act is not extended further than what is necessarily inferred from the act itself. See Bartolus on Law 1, the paragraph "If anyone by this interdict" in the Digest on private paths and acts; Cravetta, counsels 292 and 60, number 53. These agree with what the same Bartolus has on the law **"Which dowry"** near the end, where he concludes that in a prejudicial act, a person present and even silent is not seen to consent. Especially because in an act that is hateful, blameworthy, or unpleasant, one who is present and silent is not held to be consenting. Johannes de Garronibus brings these and other foundations to this sense in his treatise on second marriages, part 2, number 7; and Castillo piles up infinite others to the same purpose in his treatise on usufruct, chapter 2, number 100 and number 114, etc. And that bare presence, without other supporting evidence, does no harm to the children here, is proven after Gilken and Antoine Favre by Grævæus, 2, conclusion 98, consideration 1, number 22, etc.

For the consent of guardians does not ensure that a woman marrying a second time avoids the penalties of the law <note>original Latin: "Curatorum enim consensus non efficit, ut mulier secundò nubens evitet pœnas juris"</note>, according to Johannes de Garronibus in the aforementioned part 1, number 9, and indeed through the notes on the law regarding the **contract of guardians** <note>original Latin: "l. pactum Curatorum"</note> in the Code on contracts, and the law on **swearing an oath** <note>original Latin: "l. jurisjurandi"</note> in the Digest, along with similar references. A different opinion proceeds only in that case where the guardians see that it is useful or necessary for the children themselves that the mother marries a second time—for instance, so that the stepfather may support them, or nourish the mother, or for a similar cause.

Even less are we moved to a contrary opinion by what Sichard writes in the often-cited law **"Women"** <note>original Latin: "l. feminæ"</note> at number 5, and what others write: that if a son did not expressly dissent or protest, but died in silence, then that silence ought to be held as approval; so that the remaining children cannot seek the ownership of those goods which the mother had obtained from that deceased brother. According to all of this, and also in view of the reasons sensibly pointed out by the learned advocates of both consulting sisters, we remain of the opinion—saving however the judgment of those who might think more correctly <note>original Latin: "salvo tamen rectius sentientium judicio," a standard legal formula of humility</note>—that the disputed brotherly inheritance belongs in every way to the aforementioned women regarding the ownership <note>original Latin: "quoad proprietatem"</note>, and it cannot be taken from them by any means of law or equity. In witness of this matter, we have caused the Seal of our Faculty to be affixed. Given at Ingolstadt, March 28, in the year 1638.

### 72. Compulsory Services. Posts, Forced Labor. <note>original German: "Angariæ. Posten, Frohnen"</note>

**Angariae** <note>term: "Angariæ" refers to compulsory labor or transport services demanded by the state</note> are, for some, the provision of horses for the public course; among the Persians, there was the **postal run** <note>original Greek: "ἀγγαρείον δρόμημα"</note>, a most rapid course of horsemen, which we call **Posts** <note>original German: "Postas"</note>, as if they were "positions" or relay stations.

*Angaria* is also taken to mean public works imposed because of some business that has arisen which must be provided for quickly, according to law 2 of the Code on the Most Holy Churches. And formerly, by that name were signified the duties of carrying burdens imposed upon provincials.

Furthermore, an *Angarus* is not infrequently understood as a Persian courier, a laborer, a servant, or a messenger of Kings, according to Martinius in his *Philological Lexicon*. And hence they say its origin is Persian, as I noted in the treatise *On Majesty*, folio 182.

But *Angariae* are **forced labor** <note>original German: "Frohndienst"</note>. Hence *Angaria* is used for **Ember fasts** <note>original German: "Frohnfasten, oder Quatember"; likely referring to the quarterly periods when such duties or taxes were collected</note>. And ships were said to be "angariated" <note>original Latin: "Angariari naves"</note> when the necessity of transporting burdens was enjoined upon them. But Arnulphus of Lisieux, on page 79b, uses the word *Angariae* for unjust coercion: "I am often dragged to the royal *angariae* with the rest, and I am troubled by the frequent injuries of those whom I cannot fail." It is also used in this way in Matthew 26 and Luke 15 <note>referring to being "compelled" to carry a burden, like Simon of Cyrene</note>.

However, *Angariae* and *Parangariae* <note>term: "Parangariae" usually refers to extra-ordinary or secondary transport duties beyond the main route</note> differ among legal experts; on which matter, as well as on *Angariae* in general, one may consult Regner Sixtinus, book 2, *On Regalities*, chapter 13, and others writing on royal rights.

The provision of *Angariae* and *Parangariae* is also counted among the "sublime rights" which are called **Regalities** <note>royal prerogatives</note> in book 2 of the *Feuds*, title 56, because these are the proper rights of the King.

### ADDITION.

*Angariae* and *Parangariae* are material burdens consisting of the provision of pack animals, ships, wagons, and labor, which are declared because of some sudden business, according to Gothofredus Antonius in *Feudal Disputations* 3, thesis 8, letter a; Bocer *On Regalities*, chapter 3, page 428, number 238 and following; and most extensively by Mundius *On Duties and Honors* throughout the index. For the Information of the City of **Nuremberg** regarding how the Imperial Postal System is managed there, see Mr. Tabor *On Billets*, pages 89, 90; Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 9, number 133, page 127 and following; and Polydore Vergil, book 5, chapter 13. *Angariare* is a Persian word—
