Even less are we moved to the contrary opinion by what Sichard and others write: that if a son does not expressly dissent or protest, but dies in silence, that silence ought to be taken as approval. This would imply that the remaining children cannot claim the ownership of those goods which the mother had received from that deceased brother. However, it is the most common and true opinion that a predeceased son, even if he did not complain, nevertheless transmits the ownership of his paternal goods to his brothers. This is testified by Ripa and further proven by Johannes de Garronibus in the text "From the Will," number 37 and following.

Following all of this, and also in consideration of the reasons reasonably pointed out by the gentlemen advocates of the two consulting sisters, we remain of the opinion—saving always the judgment of those who might perceive things more correctly—that the disputed fraternal inheritance belongs in every way to the aforementioned women regarding the **ownership** <note>original: "quoad proprietatem"</note>, and it cannot be taken from them in any way according to law and equity. In witness of this matter, we have caused the Seal of our Faculty to be applied. Done at **Ingolstadt** <note>a major university city in Bavaria</note>, March 28, in the year 1638.

Regarding the multitude of wives, see Johannes Drufus on the difficult passages of Deuteronomy, chapter 18. That the Greeks and Romans think differently about **polygamy** <note>original: "Polygamia"</note> can be seen in Baronius in the annals for the year of Christ 921.

->ADDITION.<-

* **Second Marriages** <note>original: "Secundæ Nuptiæ"</note> are all others, whatever they may be, contracted after the first, even if they are not second in order but third, fourth, or even further. An example exists in the Gospel history of the woman who had seven husbands; and in Saint Jerome, an example is recounted of a monstrous multitude and repetition of marriages, of both a man and a woman who had married more than twenty times.

Second Marriages refer to all those after the first, according to the heading and law 6 of the Code on Second Marriages; and

<column-break/>

two parties to a contract are called such even if there are many more, and a "second heir" is what we call the person substituted for the first, even if that substitution occurs at the third or fourth degree. Regarding a woman who died at a great age in 1624, having had and outlived six husbands, see Zeiller, century 4, epistle page 652. Regarding **Margaret of Austria**, and how her three marriages turned out poorly, see the excellent account by Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain in his Historical Relation on Truces and Peace, pages 105 and 106.

### 72. Compulsory Services. Posts, Labor Duties.

**Compulsory services** <note>original: "Angariæ"</note> are, for some, the provision of horses for the public post; among the Persians, there was the **"swift courier-run"** <note>original Greek: "ἀγγαρεῖον δρόμον"</note>, a very rapid course of horsemen, which we call **Posts** <note>original: "Postas"</note>, as if they were "placed positions."

The term is also used for public works imposed because of some business that has arisen which must be provided for quickly. And formerly, by that name were signified the duties of carrying loads imposed upon provincial residents.

Furthermore, a messenger is not infrequently called an "Angarus," referring to a Persian courier, worker, servant, or a messenger of kings, according to Martinius in his Philological Lexicon. Hence they say its origin is Persian, as I noted in the treatise on Majesty, folio 182.

But these services are **statute labor** <note>original German: "Frohndienst," referring to unpaid labor owed by a tenant to a lord</note>. From this, the term is used for **Ember Days** <note>original German: "Frohnfasten, oder Quatember," quarterly periods of prayer and fasting in the church calendar</note>. And ships were said to be "pressed into service" <note>original: "Angariari"</note> when the necessity of transporting loads was enjoined upon them. But for unjust coercion, Arnulphus of Lisieux uses the word on page 79: "I am often drawn with the others to the royal forced labors, and I am troubled by the frequent injuries of those whom I cannot fail." It is also used this way in Matthew 26 and Luke 15.

However, **Angariæ** and **Parangariæ** <note>two levels of transport duty: the former using main roads, the latter using side roads</note> differ among legal scholars; on this matter, and on such services in general, one may consult Regner Sixtin, book 2 on Royal Rights, chapter 13, and others writing on royal prerogatives.

The provision of these transport services is also numbered among the **High Rights** <note>original: "Jura sublimia"</note>, which are called **Regalia** <note>sovereign rights belonging to the crown</note>, in book 2 of the Feudal Law, title 56, because they are the King's own rights.

->ADDITION.<-

**Angariæ** and **Parangariæ** are matrimonial burdens consisting of the provision of beasts of burden, ships, wagons, and labor, which are ordered because of some sudden business. See Gothofredus Antonius, feudal dispute 3, thesis 8; Bocer on Royal Rights, chapter 3; and most extensively Mundius on duties and honors throughout the index. For information from the **City of Nuremberg** regarding how the Imperial Postal system is managed there, see Mr. Tabor on Billets, pages 89–90; Limnäus, book 2, chapter 9; and Polydore Vergil, book 5, chapter 13. "Angariare" is a Persian word...

### 73. Inheritance (Angefall). See below under the words Agreement (Geding), Fief of Grace (Gnadenlehen), or Expectancy (Expectanz).

### Right of inheritance.

The term *Angefall* <note>The German word for "falling to" or inheritance</note> has various meanings. Although it is most commonly understood to refer to **fiefs of grace** <note>original German: "von den Gnadenlehen"</note>, which are owed to someone when the current possessor of a fief dies without male children (as noted by Pruckman), it is not infrequently extended more broadly to denote the same thing as the word "inheritance." In this matter, common usage of speech must be examined, and the true explanation of the term must be sought from it. For since the entire power of words stands or falls based on common usage, as noted by Coler and Pruckman.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the hope of a fief, see Gothofredus, *Antiquarian Disputations on Fiefs*.

### 74. Down Payment (Angeld). A part of the price.

Commonly, contracting parties (when one does not have ready cash <note>original German: "da man nicht baar Geld hat"</note>) are accustomed in sales of estates to pay a part of the agreed price in ready money immediately after the purchase is contracted. The remainder is divided into small sums to be paid annually until the whole price is paid off. The first payment begins in the year following the initial down payment. This immediate portion is commonly called **Down Payment** <note>original German: "Angeld"</note> (as it is given in cash <note>original German: "als welches man baar gibt"</note>), while the part divided into installments is called **Inheritance Money** <note>original German: "Erbgeld"</note> or **Appointed Times** <note>original German: "Tagzeiten"</note>. See Schultes, *Practical Questions*.

->ADDITION.<-

If the price in a sale must be paid in terms or intervals from year to year in installments <note>original German: "auf Tagzeiten"</note>, it is commonly called *Erbgeld*. For the privileges it enjoys, see Berlich.

### 75. Adopted Children (Angewünschte Kinder). Adopted children.

This is the name given to those adopted <note>The German "Angewünschte Kinder" literally means "wished-for children"</note>, concerning whom see the *Institutes* and the *Commentaries of the Jurists*. Add Stobæus, as well as Pythæus in Jan Gruter’s *Critical Treasury*, where among other things he has the following words: "Regarding adoption, I note here those things which our jurists would never say were their own according to the Law of the Citizens <note>original Latin: "ex jure Quiritum"</note>. Therefore, just as the old Roman clerks adopted through the people and the Praetor, so almost all other warlike nations adopted sons for themselves **through arms** <note>original Latin: "per arma"</note>; that is, by the handing over of weapons." The formula for this adoption exists in Cassiodorus, by which Theodoric made the King of the Heruli a son to himself. Likewise, our Justinian adopted the father of Athalaric. In this, it is worthy of notice that this kind of adoption through arms did not grant the same right of being an heir and successor as that which was done by Roman laws. There is an elegant passage on this matter in Procopius’s *Persian War*.

->ADDITION.<-

Adoption **by the hair** <note>original Latin: "per Capillum"</note> was customary for the Franks. Paul the Deacon writes that Charles, King of the Franks, sent his son to Liutprand so that he might take his hair, according to custom; Liutprand, cutting his hair, became his father. The Goths adopted by **touching the beard** <note>original Latin: "barbæ tactum"</note>, or rather by the trimming of the beard. Adoption **by baptism** <note>A form of spiritual kinship</note> was introduced by the early Christians. By our customs, adoption occurs **through marriage** <note>original Latin: "per Matrimonium"</note>, by which children are said to be given into the **morning-gift** <note>original German: "Morgengabam" - a traditional gift from a husband to a wife the morning after the wedding</note>; through a marriage pact, children of different parents become shared.

On adoption, Knipschilt accumulates many points in his work on *Trusts*. On the adoption of a Patrician by a commoner, Draco writes most copiously.

### 76. Legal Entry (Anleitung). Possession by the first decree.

This is nothing other than being put into possession by the first decree. According to common law, it is usually preceded by a citation by edict or public proclamation. This is observed in the Imperial Court at **Rottweil** and the Swabian Provincial Court at **Altdorf**, called **Weingarten**. Indeed, sometimes a declaration of outlawry and a **Letter of Instruction** <note>original German: "Anleitungs-Brief"</note> are also decreed. It is the custom that possession by the first decree—called *Anleit* at Rottweil—encompasses all the goods of the debtor, as in other provincial courts. If no one defends <note>original German: "versprechen wird"</note> against this entry, at the request of the petitioner, the "acquired rights" <note>original Latin: "erlangte Recht"</note> are decreed, which have the force of possession by the second decree. Furthermore, **Letters of Protection** <note>original German: "Schirm-Brief"</note> are issued to the local magistrate, who is bound to carry out the execution. Once that entry (*Anleit*) is signaled to the local magistrate, the possessor can still appear within thirteen weeks and three days to object. If they appear, the case is argued; if not, the petitioner is granted full possession.

## 73. Reversionary Inheritance <note>German: "Angefäll"; also called a "covenant," a "fief of grace," or an "expectancy"</note>.
->*The right of inheritance.*<-

The word **Angefäll** has various meanings. Although it is most often understood as **fiefs of grace** <note>German: "Gnadenlehen"</note>, which are owed to someone upon the death of the current holder of the fief who leaves no male children (*Pruckman, Counsel 31, number 29, volume 1*). However, it is not infrequently extended more broadly to denote the same thing as the word for "inheritance." In this matter, common usage of speech must be examined, and the true explanation of the word must be sought from it. Since all the power of words stands or falls based on the usage of speech (*Coler, On Executory Process, in the preface; Pruckman, cited location, number 30*).

### ADDITION.

Regarding the hope of a fief <note>original Latin: "De spe feudi"</note>, see *Gothofr. Ant. Feudal Disputations 8, thesis 5, letter h.*

## 74. Down Payment <note>German: "Angeld"</note>. A portion of the price.

Commonly, contracting parties (**when one does not have ready cash**) are accustomed in the sale of estates to agree on a portion of the price to be paid in present money immediately after the contract of sale is made; the remainder is divided into small sums to be paid annually until the whole price is paid off. The start of the first payment is made in the year following the initial down payment; and that present portion is commonly called **Angeld** (**as it is given in cash**), while the part divided into installments is called **Erbgeld** <note>literally "inheritance money" or "legacy money"</note> or **Tagzeiten** <note>literally "appointed times" or "due dates"</note>. *Schultes, Practical Questions, book 1, question 23, number 1.*

### ADDITION.

If the price in a sale must be paid through terms or intervals from year to year **in installments** <note>German: "auf Tagzeiten"</note>, it is commonly called **Erbgeld**; for the privileges it enjoys, see *Berlich, 1, conclusion 64, numbers 59, 114, 115, 116.*

## 75. Desired Children <note>German: "Angewünschte Kinder"</note>. Adopted children.

This is the name given to those who are adopted, concerning whom see the *Institutes* <note>a fundamental Roman law textbook</note> and the *Commentaries of the Jurists*. Add Stobaeus, *Sermon 74*, also Pythaeus in Jan Gruter, *Critical Treasury, volume 2, folio 738*, where among other things he has the following words: "Regarding adoption, those things are noted by me here which our legal experts never claimed were their own from the law of the Roman citizens <note>original Latin: "ex jure Quiritum"</note>. Therefore, just as the old Roman formula-makers adopted through the people and the Praetor, so almost all other warlike nations adopted sons for themselves through arms—that is, by the handing over of weapons. The formula for this adoption survives in *Cassiodorus, Variae, book 4*, by which Theodoric made the King of the Heruli a son to himself. So too our Justinian adop-

<column-break/>

ted the father of Athalaric." In this, it is worth noting that this kind of adoption "through arms" did not grant the right of an independent person—that is, of an heir and successor—in the same way as that which was done by Roman laws. On this matter, there is a truly elegant passage in *Procopius, Persian War, book 1.*

### ADDITION.

Adoption by the Hair <note>original Latin: "per Capillum"</note> was customary among the Franks (*Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, book 6, chapter 58*). Charles, King of the Franks, sent his son to Luitprand so that he might take up his hair according to custom; Luitprand, cutting his locks, became a father to him. The Goths adopted through the *touching of the beard*, or even by the *cutting of the beard*. (*Strauchius from Aymon, Dissertation 4, aphorism 14*). Adoption through baptism was introduced by the early Christians, and mention of it is made in *Law 26 of the Code on Marriages*. In our customs, Adoption through *Marriage* <note>original Latin: "per Matrimonium"</note> prevails, by which children are said to be given into the **Morning-Gift** <note>German: "Morgengabam"; the dower traditionally given by a husband to his wife the morning after the wedding</note>, whereby through the marriage contract, the different children become common to both.
Many things regarding adoption are collected by *Knipschilt on Trusts, under the word "Adoption" in the index; Rittershusius in the Novellae, page 396, number 3.* Regarding the adoption of a Patrician by a commoner, most copiously of all, see *Draco on Patricians, page 312, numbers 23, 24, 25.*

## 76. Induction <note>German: "Anleitung"</note>. Possession by the first Decree.

This is nothing other than the induction into possession <note>original Latin: "immissio"</note> by the first Decree, and according to common law, a citation by Edict or public proclamation usually precedes it: **and this is how it is observed in the Imperial Court of Justice at Rottweil, and the Swabian Provincial Court at Altdorf, known as Weingarten.** Indeed, sometimes even a declaration of outlawry and a **Letter of Induction** <note>German: "Anleitungs-Brief"</note> are decreed. It is the custom that possession by the first Decree, the **Anleit at Rottweil**, encompasses all the goods of the debtor, as it does in other Provincial Courts. If no one defends against this induction by the first Decree, **or if it is not contested** <note>German: "oder versprochen wird"</note>, then at the petition of the plaintiff—the **Inductor** <note>German: "deß Anleiters"</note>—the "obtained rights" are decreed, which have the force of induction by a second Decree. Furthermore, executive orders—a **Letter of Protection** <note>German: "Schirm-Brief"</note>—are sent to the local Magistrate under whose jurisdiction the goods are located, who is also bound to carry out the execution. And when that induction, the **Anleit**, has been presented and announced to the Magistrate of the place and the goods, the possessor can nevertheless appear within thirteen weeks and three days (counted from the time the presentation was made) and object to the induction made by the first Decree. If he appears, the case is argued there; if not, at the petition of the person inducted by the secret Decree, he is put into possession. *Paulus Matthias Wehner in his notes on the Reformations of Rottweil, part 2, title 10, folio 143.*

## 110. Annates <term>Annates: a payment to the Church of the first year's revenue from a newly filled ecclesiastical office</term>.

Annates are a form of tax. What kind of tax it is, Platina shows in the life of Pope Boniface IX. He says that Boniface was the first to impose the use of Annates on ecclesiastical benefits <note>church offices providing income</note> under this condition: that whoever obtained a benefit should pay half of the annual revenue to the Apostolic Treasury. This is why they were called "Annates" <note>derived from the Latin "annus" meaning year</note>. For those who desire to know more about Annates, see *Book 7 of the Decretals, title 7, folio 193 and following; Cornelius à Rinthel in The Roman Catholic Jurist, chapter 8,* where he teaches that even the Law of Justinian does not disapprove of the custom of giving something to those ordaining or ministering for the sake of consecration, as if by way of remuneration. For why Annates, both secular and ecclesiastical, are called a "subsidiary remedy," see *Battista Costa in his treatise on subsidiary remedies, chapter 114.*

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the Annates to be paid to the Pope, see *Sprenger in Public Jurisprudence, page 202; Duaren, book 8 on benefits, chapter 3; Gothofredus in his notes on Novel 123, chapter 16.*

<column-break/>

*Molina in his notes on the Edict against small dates <note>original Latin: "contra parvas datas," a specific papal decree regarding the dating of documents for benefices</note>, and the complete treatises of Antonio Massa Gallese, Tommaso Campeggi, and Klock on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 83, number 54, and chapter 149, numbers 43 and 44.*

## 78. Assessment (Anschlag). Estimation, Valuation.

Valuations vary wonderfully according to the circumstances of the times: Thus, in an old letter dated 1462 at Engstladen, in the District of Balingen, the following were assessed:
One Malter <note>a dry measure of volume</note> of Spelt . . . . . **14 Schillings Heller**
One Malter of Oats . . . . **10 Schillings Heller**
A Chicken for . . . . . . . . . . . . **6 Heller**
A Shrove Tuesday Hen for . . **1 Schilling Heller**
A Goose . . . . . . . . . . . . **9 Pfennigs**

Regarding the ancient low prices caused by the poverty of the people, when they did not wish to take up estates even for a small rent, see *Crusius in his Swabian Annals, in the supplement, page 45.* For what it cost to build the ring-walls with the high towers at Lucerne, see *Petermann Etterlin in the Chronicle of the Confederation, page 61.*
But why the prices of things were formerly lower than now will be discussed elsewhere, God willing.

Furthermore, it should be noted that fixed incomes, such as perpetual rents, etc., are often valued at double in the assessments when estates—to which all jurisdiction is attached—are sold; that is, one Guilder is valued per forty units of capital; *see below under the entry "Lordship Rents" (Heren-Gült).*

## ADDITION.

The assessment or appraisal <note>original: "Æstimum sive æstimium"</note>, and how it constitutes proof, see Klock, *consultation 10, numbers 689, 723, 724.* If assessments are found to be faulty or unjust, they must be revised and reformed every four months, Klock, *consultation 28, n. 210.* Regarding appraisers: how high an appraised estate is to be accepted, and whether a new taxation should be undertaken. Whether, where an "enormous loss" <note>original: "enormissima læsio"; a legal concept where a contract is voided if the price is less than half the true value</note> has occurred with the valuation, the law *l. 2. C. de resc. vend.* is to be practiced. See Zorer, *part 1, question 2, numbers 225 to 232.* When appraisers cannot agree on a price, the Judge by virtue of his office establishes a certain value, Suttinger, *observation 126, n. 1,* who usually chooses the middle path, *number 2.*

On the taxation and appraisal of goods, or their adjudication, and when it takes place, see Mr. Zorer, *part 1, q. 2, n. 210; q. 7, n. 520 and following; q. 10, n. 697; q. 12, n. 1049.* To know the price of a thing punctually is impossible. The value of a thing cannot be seen by the eye, but must be considered by the intellect. A modest probability sometimes moves one to value a thing differently than before.

Meadows, even if they are sometimes rendered worse, nevertheless hardly ever fall into disuse. A wasted field can be tilled again. And even if

<column-break/>

a house is burned down, the ground remains. Thus, Horace not undeservedly called these "grounded money" <note>original: "fundatam pecuniam"; capital that is secure because it is tied to land</note>. Moreover, the price of land and similar things is determined by the manner of its fruits and rents, *law "si fundum" 13. pr. ff. de reb. eorum, qui sub tut.* and *law "si fundum" 92. pr. ff. de legat. 1.* And it shall be deemed just if the rent or pension can reach that total amount within a period of 20 years, according to Wehner. However, it is easily apparent to anyone that the prices of castles, towers, and precious houses, which are mostly sterile <note>meaning they do not produce crops or agricultural income</note>, cannot be reduced to the measure of rent; see Mr. Dinner in his singular treatise *On the Just Price of Things, q. 2, art. fin.* where he alleges many points. Mature fruits, even if they have not been harvested, make the land more valuable. The same is not true of an unborn offspring, *law "in Falcidia" 9. ff. ad L. Falcid.* How the "Pound-money" <term>Pfundgeld: a type of land tax or ground rent</term> is taxed, and what is understood by it; namely, that labor-service <term>Robath: forced labor or corvée owed by a tenant to a lord</term> or labor-dues, being an appurtenance to the Pound-money, is not to be appraised further. Suttinger, *observation 125, number 3.* Also, how high to value a manor farm <term>Freyhof: an estate exempt from certain taxes</term>, a nobleman’s seat, a free-allodial or mountain castle, fields, gardens, meadows, breweries, taverns, meat-stalls, vineyards, sheep-service, cheese- and lard-service, brick-kilns, lime-kilns, and stone quarries, see Suttinger, *observation 125, n. 8.*

### List of several items to ask about when one intends to buy or describe an estate in the country.

First, ask the <term>hereditary tenant<note>original: "Erbmann"; the person holding the long-term lease or hereditary right to the land</note></term> on his oath or public word before several neighbors regarding the following items, and afterward inquire about these matters from the shepherds and the former day-laborers of the hereditary tenants.

1. Whether he alone holds this farm, or if there are <term>cottage-houses<note>original: "Kobelhäuser"; small, often humble dwellings or shacks</note></term> within the farm paying rent?
2. What belongs to the village in terms of yard space, houses, barns, granaries, stables, wells, cellars, fences, ovens, and milk pits?
3. What he holds in the fields: gardens, meadows, acres, fields, woods; what kind of wood, ponds, and whether the meadows are mowed twice a year?
4. How many <term>plots<note>original: "Zellen"; units of land or cultivation plots</note></term> are farmed?
5. Whether he has a <term>hereditary deed<note>original: "Erbbrief"; a legal document proving hereditary possession</note></term>?
6. What the inheritance is worth, and what belongs to the estate itself?
7. Whether it requires <term>surveying<note>original: "Vermarckens"; the marking of boundaries with stones or signs</note></term>?
8. In which diocese or lordship the estate lies?
9. To which parish it belongs?
10. What religion?
11. In which regional court district?
12. Whether it is subject to a <term>bailiff’s jurisdiction<note>original: "vogtbar"; under the protection or administration of a Vogt</note></term>, or whether it follows common law?
13. Whether he builds a <term>fief<note>original: "Lehengut"; land held from a lord in return for service</note></term> onto the inheritance?
14. Whether the fiefs are marked off from the estate?
15. Whether it pays rent or <term>endowments for the soul<note>original: "Seelgereth"; payments to the church for prayers for the deceased</note></term>, and to where?
16. Whether it pays <term>tithes<note>original: "Zehenden"; a tenth of produce given as a tax</note></term>, how, and to whom?
17. Whether one pays tithes on the field, or in the barn and house, and whether both <term>great and small tithes<note>Great tithes usually applied to main crops like grain, while small tithes applied to livestock and minor produce</note></term> are given?
18. Whether there is good cattle pasture in the community?
19. Whether it has the right to drive sheep, or if others drive theirs onto it?
20. Whether it has forest rights for construction timber?
21. Whether the community owns wood?
22. At what time of year the <term>ground rent<note>original: "Gült"; the annual interest or rent payment</note></term> falls due?
23. How much it amounts to?
24. By what measure it is weighed or measured?
25. Whether one pays a <term>transfer fee<note>original: "Handlohn"; a fine or fee paid to the lord when a property is sold or inherited</note></term> when the estate is sold?
26. How much that is—out of 15 or 10 guilders?
27. Who holds the right to fines for minor offenses upon it?
28. Whether he must perform <term>labor service<note>original: "Fröhnen"; unpaid labor owed by a tenant to a lord</note></term>? Whether there is an excise tax?
29. To where the <term>high jurisdiction<note>original: "fraisich"; the right to judge capital crimes or "blood justice"</note></term> belongs, and who his neighbors are?
30. Whether it pays taxes, and how much?

### 79. Truce. *Induciæ.*

<margin>Besoldus, Volume 1.</margin>
A truce <note>original: "Induciæ"</note> is when an agreement is made for a short and present

<column-break/>

time so that enemies do not provoke one another; commonly called an *Anstand* <note>a standing-still</note> or a peace that is determined for a certain time, <note>original Latin reference to the Digest on postliminy and truces</note>. According to Varro, a truce is a "Peace of the Camp" for a few days, or a holiday from war; the state of war remains there, but the fighting ceases <note>original: "ibique bellum manet, sed pugna cessat"</note>. *Agellius book 1, chapter 25.* Therefore, it differs from a true peace: because when the truce ends, the parties are at war <note>original: "guerra"</note> again. But concerning the etymology of truce, see *Coler, parerg. chapter 21.*

The barbarians <note>meaning medieval legal writers using non-Classical Latin</note> call a truce *Treuga*, from the German word for "trust" <note>original: "Treu"</note>. Interpreters say, however, that a truce (*Induciæ*) is for a short time, but a *Treuga* is extended for a long time; see the *extraordinary decrees on Truces*. And both peace and truces differ from "Treaties" <note>original: "Fœderibus"</note> in this: a *Treuga* or truce is made between enemies, while Treaties are contracted between allies bringing war.

Moreover, if one party breaks the peace or truce, the other may also legitimately break it, *Gilken on the law "cum proponas" 21. C. de pactis.* Sometimes, however, a pact is added so that the peace is not considered broken by a single injury, but rather the damage must be compensated, *Lehmann in the Speyer Chronicle, folio 762. More gathered in the treatise on Peace.*

->ADDITION.<-

*Kinschot* wrote on the "payment of truces." *Nicolaus Myler* deals extensively with "Letters of Truce" in chapter 5 of *The Princes and States of the Empire.*

A truce is when it is agreed for a short and present time that they should not provoke each other; if these are longer, they are called *Treugæ*; if they pass into peace, they are called treaties (*fœdera*), *Peter Gregory in his System of Universal Law, book 20, chapter 5, number 8.* Add also *Schönborn in Politics, book 6, chapter 38, throughout.*

### 80. Antichrist. *Antichristus.*

Regarding the Antichrist, see *Cardinal Baronius's Index of Annals; Albert of Stade, folio 176 b; Peter of Andlo on the Roman Empire, last book, last chapter, and the notes there by Freher, folio 205 and following.*

Regarding this word, see *volume 1 of various discourses, number 37.* See Mr. Beern’s explanation of whether the Church can err, page 174. Also his refutation of Erbermann, page 647 and following.

### 81. Advocate. *Procurator.*

Advocate <note>original: "Anwald"</note>, as if it were *Præfectus* <note>prefect or overseer</note>, from *walten* or *verwalten* <note>to rule or manage</note>, *R. P. Gretser in his "Divis. Eichstettensibus" folio 160.*

Note that a member of a religious order cannot be an advocate <note>original: "Procurator"</note> according to *Clement 3. de Procur.* if he is cloistered, *gloss there on the word "Clericus."* From this, it follows that the Knights of St. John, Prelates, etc., are not included in this restriction. And that a legal process conducted with a religious person is valid if no exception is raised, as taught by *Cappell. Tholof. question 124 and 131*, which decides that one holding a dignity or administration can appoint an advocate, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding whether the office of an advocate brings infamy, the most elegant discussion of all is by *Draco de Patritiis, page 311.*

221. n. 21. & n. 22. regarding **Procurators of Parliaments** <note>legal representatives or attorneys</note> **and the Imperial Chamber.** Procurators are not truly the owners <note>original: "Domini"</note>, and therefore they cannot establish <term>fiefs<note>land held on condition of feudal service</note></term>, nor alienate <note>sell or transfer</note> the property entrusted to them, nor can they establish a <term>family trust<note>original: "fidei commissæ familiæ"; a legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of a family lineage</note></term>, according to Knipschild *on trusts, chapter 3, note 61.* Regarding whether a lord may be restored to his full original legal standing <note>original: "restituatur in integrum"</note> against the negligence of his Procurators, see Eberh. ### 82. Apothecary. Pharmacist.

Those who prepare and sell medicines are called **Pharmacists** <note>original: "Pharmacopolæ"</note>, according to the *Law 3, section 1, of the Cornelian Law on Assassins and Poisoners.* For it does not seem to diminish the dignity of the medical art if a Physician prepares the medicines himself, or applies his hand to a wound: therefore, certain duties are entrusted to **Pharmacists and Surgeons.**

In well-ordered Republics, these men are bound by a unique oath, the formula of which is recorded by Adam Volckmann *in the Notary Book, part 3, chapter 15,* **regarding the Apothecary’s Oath and his journeymen.** Its principal points are: that he intends to collect <term>simples<note>medicinal herbs or plants used as individual ingredients</note></term> at the proper season and dry them diligently. That he will dispense compounds according to the prescription of the medical art; those which are to be preserved with sugar, not with honey, etc. That he will yield to no one—especially strangers—poisonous substances or those causing abortion. That he will prepare with the greatest diligence those medicines which purge. That he will throw away those which are old or spoiled. That he will sell at a fair price to both the poor and the wealthy. That he will not substitute one thing for another <note>original: "quid pro quo"</note>, but will do everything according to the advice of the Physician. If he does otherwise, and rashly sells poisonous things to either foolish or suspicious people, he is held liable for punishment, according to Menochius *2. cent. 4. case 359.* See especially Jacob Faber *in the treatise on sustenance, leaf 93 and following,* where he has collected many things worth knowing about Pharmacists.

Furthermore, the Pharmacist himself is held responsible if his assistant provides poisons by mistake to someone asking for medicine: on which matter legal responses exist *in the Altdorf Consultations, consultation 31 and following.*

->ADDITION.<-

A <note>original Greek: "παντοπώλην" (pantopōlēn)</note> **general dealer**, or grocer, we call in the vernacular a **Materials-man** <note>original: "Materialisten"; a dealer in raw drugs, spices, and chemical materials</note>, according to Mr. Dilherr, *volume 1, Disputation, leaf 68.*

Pharmacists are indeed numbered among the literate <note>the educated class</note>, but regarding their dignity and precedence, they are categorized among **Merchants**, according to Carpzov *decision 8, part 1.*

Aelian writes *in book 5 of his Various History* that **Aristotle** acted as a Pharmacist; and Theophrastus *in book 9 of the History of Plants, chapter 19* records that Aristophilus of Plataea was a distinguished Pharmacist. In Civil Law, the word <term>Apotheca<note>the root of "Apothecary"</note></term> is used for a wine cellar. A similar passage is found in Salvian, *book 4 against Avarice:* "by you, the wine-cellars <note>original: "Apothecæ"</note> of drunkards are filled with wine." **Regarding Apothecaries,** and in what place they are to be ranked in the competition of creditors, see Zorer, *part 2, question 20, note 6034.* Likewise, whether such priority takes place for previous medical treatments,

<column-break/>

or whether this freedom extends also to **confections and sweets** <note>original: "Schleckerwerck"</note>, *ibid. note 6036.* Pharmacies are laudably furnished, *book 2, chapter 15, note 1 and following,* by Klock *on the treasury,* who in *note 9 and following* also discusses the person and office of the Pharmacist. Against the persons of Pharmacists who claimed payment for things intended more for seasoning food than for curing the sick, the **Strasbourg Constitution on the privilege of creditors** made an exception in *class 1, section 20, there saying:* **But among these, delicacies <note>original: "Schleckerwerck"</note>, which serve more for pleasure than for the patient's cure, and are not properly belonging to the illness, shall not be included.** Compare Beuth, *book 1, chapter 26, on the Right of Preference.*

### 83. Appeal. Appellation.

Whether, outside of a nobleman’s **fief** <note>original: "Lehengut"</note>, the **appeal** should go to and belong to the **Direct Lord** <note>the superior landlord</note> and feudal lord, or to the **Vassal**? See Bidembach, *noble questions, question 9.* Likewise, whether the granting of Jurisdiction also applies to the **Second Instance** <note>the appeals court level</note>, see Camillus Borellus, *on Magistrates, 4, chapter 8.*

In **Feudal cases**, if an appeal is made to the **Emperor**, the judge from whom the appeal is taken must present himself before the Emperor to give an account of the sentence he passed, *chapter 1, final section, at what time the soldier...* where Schenck and Curtius Junior, *part 7, note 33,* comment.

Whether an appeal may be made to the **Court** <note>original: "Aula"; the high imperial court</note>? See my own work *in the treatise on the mixed state, leaf 218 and following.* I have shown *in the singular treatise on appeals* that there is no appeal from the **Electors** <note>the high-ranking princes who elected the Emperor</note>. However, the **Elector of Bavaria** reassumed the Palatine-Imperial privilege with the Emperor's knowledge, and has now instituted a Court of Revision in his own Court. Regarding the **Saxon Privilege of non-appealing** <note>a legal right where a territory's court decisions could not be appealed to the Emperor</note>, see Knichen *in the treatise on Saxon non-provincial law;* add Beatus, *volume 5 on judicial matters, part 5, vol. 1, leaf 324,* who at *leaf 550* reports that in certain places appeals are admitted in criminal cases. Regarding the Privilege of non-appealing, see *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 1, leaf 188.* From which causes an appeal may not be made, see Chockier, *book 2 on exemptions, leaf 71.* Regarding an appeal from a judge whose jurisdiction was extended by consent <note>original: "prorogato Judice"</note>, see *Strasbourg Consultations, vol. 1, consultation 39.* Regarding appeals, especially to a **future Council** <note>an appeal to a General Council of the Church rather than the Pope</note>, see *book 7 of the Decretals, leaf 237.*

Regarding the **challenge to the Tribunal of God** <note>a spiritual appeal to divine justice when earthly justice fails</note>, see the *unique treatise* by Hering; add Camerarius, *Historical Meditations, century 3, chapter 38.* The Old Chronicle of Mainz, *leaf 20,* and Bzovius, *Year 1423, leaf 641.*

Other matters are found **in my own treatise, titled "On Appellatory Aid"** <note>original: "de appellatorio Juvamine"</note>; add Brederodius, Tholosanus, Cletzelius, and others who have written about appeals.

Or at least, according to the common manner of speaking, it does not seem that one should grant a mandate to appeal only for the first act...

cling to an appeal, see Ferrari *in the Form of Appeals from a definitive sentence, number 7.* This fails if it concerns the appellee in the opposite sense, see Contardus *on the single law of the Code, "if concerning momentary possession," question 22, number 7.* What if the appellee does not cling to the appeal? # 84. Archdeacon.

# 86. Archive.

An **Archive** <note>original: "Archiv. Archivum."</note> is a place, or a chest, in which the Acts of a Prince or a city are preserved. Otherwise called a *Tabularium* <note>record-house</note> and *Grammatophylacium* <note>Greek-derived term for a library or archive</note>, or *Archia* and Chancery. From which come the *Archiotæ*, that is, the Keepers of the Archives, *last law, section "if also," of the Digest on duties and honors.* See Bornitius *on Instruments, book 2, chapter 10.*

And that formerly public money and even documents were preserved in Temples and public places is attested by Eberlin *in his treatise on the origin of law, folio 180 and following.* From this, even **Apocryphal books** <note>books of questionable authorship or authority</note> are so named, since they are not in the "sacred crypt" <note>original: "sacra crypta"</note>, says Majer *in Sacred Chaldaism, folio 262.*

It should be noted here, *that the common documents, as well as the family's insignia or coat of arms, are usually kept by those members of the family who are the elders and most worthy, and who have the greater and stronger portion of the Law; such things are not readily entrusted to others who are not of the family,* <note>original German: "daß die Instrumenta communia, nec non insignia domus, seu arma familiæ apud eos, qui sunt de familia, eosque majores natu se digniores, & qui majorem ac fortiorem partem Juris habent, pflegen verwahret, und nicht bald andern, so nicht de familia, anvertrauet werden"</note> Anton Faber *in the Code, book 2, title 1, definition 14, number 2.* Schurff *consultation 50, number 15, century 1, and especially numbers 1, 2, 6, and 7.* Rutger Ruland *on commissions, part 2, book 5, chapter 19, at the end.*

And whoever thus holds the family documents or other common records is bound to produce them for others who have an interest, as often as their necessity requires, *Cöpen decision 7, number 6.*

Full legal weight—referred to as **full faith** <note>original: "plena fides"; a legal term meaning the document is accepted as authentic and sufficient proof on its own</note>—is granted to writings taken from an Archive according to **Common Law** <note>original: "Jure communi"; the Roman-based legal system used across continental Europe at the time</note>, as established in the legal texts *Authentica Adhæc, also Charta de Fide Instrumentorum, Novel 49, chapter 2* and others. This is also the case under Würtemberg Law, as found in the text *title 34, book 1, page 130, section "Item"*: **Rolls, land registers, and other old writings that are preserved in our cities, vaults, and chests. Likewise, interest, tax, and account books kept in our city town halls; all these shall provide good testimony before our courts. However, our courts—especially where an objection is raised—reserve the right to make their own judgment upon them.** See also *Joseph de Sesse, volume 1, decision 21.*

This rule applies especially if the writing is ancient and there is no cause for suspicion. See also Master Rutger Ruland, *On Commissions, part 2, book 5, chapter 3 and following.*

Regarding what else is required for a writing produced from a public Archive to be valid, see extensively *Schrader, volume 1, counsel 5, throughout.*

### ADDITION.

For an Archive to merit "full faith," several requirements must be met, according to Knipschild in *On Imperial Cities, book 2, chapter 12, number 15.* An Archive grants full weight to documents (*number 16*) both within and outside the territory (*number 17*), even if the document lacks formal solemnity, a date, or the name of a consul (*number 18*). It adds legal strength to writings that are not otherwise **authentic** <term>Authentic<note>In this legal context, an "authentic" document is one issued by a public official or notary that carries its own proof of validity.</note></term> (*number 19*). Copies produced from it are trusted (*number 20*), as are private registers (*number 21*). Nicolaus Myler discusses the Law of the Archive in *On the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 47.* Question: Does a writing produced from an Archive provide proof for the one who produced it not only against subjects, but also against third parties? (*same chapter 47*). If someone should craftily steal writings—**such as land registers** <note>original: "als die Lägerbücher"</note>—from a Prince's Archive, or extort them by force from his ministers during wartime, do they provide proof for the one who produces them or for the thief? (*ibid. page 420, chapter 47*).

On the definition of an Archive, see Ruland, *On Commissions, chapter 3.* On who is permitted to maintain an Archive, see the same author extensively in *chapter 4.* Which writings taken from Archives provide full proof is shown by Enno Ummius in *Disputation on Procedure 17, thesis 2, number 9.* Documents found in public archives are trusted; see those cited by Knipschild *On Trusts, chapter 13, number 18, regarding how family records and lineage books provide proof.* If they are kept in a respectable place in the archive of some family and guarded by men above all suspicion, this is taught by Draco in *On Patricians, page 286.* Regarding the writing of a feudal book in an Archive, see Rosenthal, *chapter 14, number 51.*

### 88. Poor Box, God’s Box. <note>original: "Armkast, Gotteskast. Ærarium Sacrum"</note>
The Sacred Treasury is that which contains

<column-break/>

money collected for sacred and pious uses. Its specific method seems to consist of **alms** <note>original: "Eleemosynis"</note>. The use of a sacred treasury or **poor box** <note>original: "deß Gotteskastens"</note> is necessary and has existed in every Republic. For every state consists of the poor as well as the rich and other wretched persons. Public funds for their sustenance must be kept ready, according to Jakob Bornitius, *On Treasury Revenues, book 10, chapter 2, at the beginning.*

The specific method of the sacred treasury, among others, seems to be in the alms which the pious contribute, either at a set time or spontaneously outside the usual order. Various handles and occasions can be offered for this. Alms can be collected every Sunday or Feast Day, **from house to house**. In public inns—**for which reason alms-boxes shall always be set up**—so that travelers may contribute something for the poor. Likewise at solemn banquets, engagements, weddings, baptisms, and funerals—**at betrothals, weddings, christenings, and burial processions.** Add also other ways the sacred treasury can be enriched: from money for the tolling of bells (**bell-money**), and from the price of seats in churches (**pew-money**). Also for graves in public cemeteries or in churches.

Note also the custom in certain cities: as soon as buyers and sellers of real estate have reached an agreement, they are bound to pay some coins for pious uses—for instance, a thaler or a few groschen—and hide it away in the public chest placed in churches for this purpose, attaching a small note as a testimony of the concluded contract; this is commonly called **depositing the God’s-penny** <note>original: "den Gottespfenning einlegen"; a small earnest payment given to charity to seal a bargain.</note>. If this money is not paid, the contract is considered almost null, as Bornitius testifies in the location cited above.

In our customs, there is also a special sacred treasury called **The Saint** <note>original: "der Heilig"</note>. For in the past, certain revenues were almost always destined for the honor of that Saint to whom either the Parish church was dedicated or whom the town or village had chosen as its Patron; these were for sustaining pious burdens, **for the building of churches, or their decoration, and also the maintenance of the poor.**

### ADDITION.
On the collection of alms for the poor and exiles, various methods are recounted by Mundius, *On Offices and Honors, page 403, number 27 and following.* See also Döring in the *Library, under the word "treasury" [ærarium], number 239.*

Poverty holds many privileges and disadvantages in our law, which have been compiled by Speckhan, *1st century, questions 37 and 39*, and Francesco Vivio, *decisions 222 and 268.* The same Speckhan, *question 38*, teaches how poverty is to be proven.

### 90. Arrest, to place under arrest. Arrestum.

**Arrest**, or *Arrestatio*, is a "laying on of hands" <note>original: "injectio manuum"; a formal legal seizure</note>, when a Magistrate forbids someone from leaving the place in which they were found, unless matters have been settled with the person who complained about them before the Judge. Alternatively, it is when the property of someone, for whatever reason and for our security, is detained by public authority so that it cannot be removed from that place against our will while the business is not yet settled (*Petrus Peck, in the treatise On the Law of Halting, chapter 1, number 4; add Matthäus Coler, On Executive Processes, part 1, chapter 2, number 159 and following*). It is also called *Kummer* <note>a German legal term for distress or seizure of goods</note>, as if it were an "impediment" or "hindrance"; see *Becman, Origins, under the word "Gomer."* That a distinction must be made between arrest and execution is clear from the votes of the *Ortenburg Files, especially volume 5*, where it is discussed "whether landed property may also be placed under arrest" <note>original German: "ob auch die liegende Güter zu arrestiren"</note>.

Hence, whoever breaks an **Arrest** is severely punished at the Judge's discretion (*Law 1, Digest, On House-breakers*). Although that law speaks of one who violates a prison, the same applies here (*Oldradus, counsel 65, beginning "here it is treated"*), where he says: breaking an Arrest is equated to breaking out of prison. He is followed by *Mandosius, in the treatise On Monitors, question 8; Petrus Peck, On Arrest, chapter 28, number 1 and following.*

And the word "Arrest" descends from the French *Arrester*, which means to provide a hindrance, to stop one's step, or to stay. Although the French use this word in another, now more common sense, to mean a Sentence, Decree, or Judicial Decision—just as *Jean Papon* titled his observations *Arresta* <note>French: "Arrêts"</note>. And although some derive "Arrest" in this sense from the Greek *aresko* <note>original: "ἀρέσκω"</note>, meaning "I please" [or "I am satisfactory"]; nevertheless, it similarly descends from *Arrester*, from "halting" and "standing." Just as we say: "the sentence stands" <note>original: "stat sententia"</note>, or "it stands in the mind." And likewise, in judged matters, which are held as the truth, one must "stand" by them (*Peter Friedrich Mindanus, On Processes, chapter 46, number 3, book 1*).

But by what law was Arrest introduced, and by what reasoning is it sustained? See *Petrus Peck, in the stated treatise, chapter 2.* Who can halt or arrest the things or goods of another? *Peck* also teaches this in *chapter 3*; and see *Basel Disputations, volume 5, disputation on Arrests, thesis 11 and following.*

However, all Arrests are "odious" <note>original: "odiosa"; a legal term meaning they are restrictive of liberty and should be interpreted strictly/narrowly</note> (*Schultes, in additions to Modestinus Pistoris, question 136, number 15*). It is considered that justice is administered by "oxen" and those ignorant of the law in places where such Arrests and seizures <note>Saxamenta</note> are easily granted (*Coler, On Executive Processes, part 2, chapter 3, number 148*).

They are not granted except for a "liquid" <note>undisputed or clearly calculated</note> debt, or one proven summarily (*Cöpen, question 29, number 16*), to such an extent...

...so that some require only a legal instrument <note>original Latin: "Instrumentum," referring to a formal written document or deed</note>, according to Berlich, *decision 107.*

Regarding who or whose goods may be lawfully **arrested** <note>In this context, "arrest" refers to the legal seizure of property or the detention of a person to secure a debt or court appearance</note>, see Peck, *in the same location, chapter 4*; the Basel Dissertations, *volume 5, dissertation on Arrest, thesis 26 and following*; and Berlich, *volume 1, conclusion 50*, where he teaches how the seizure of things is properly carried out. Likewise, Peck treats who and whose goods or things cannot be seized in *chapter 5*, and the Basel Dissertations in *thesis 40 and following*. Regarding locations where Seizures cannot be made, consult the Basel Dissertations, *thesis 96*. As for what time they may or may not be made, see the often-cited Basel Dissertation, *thesis 96, etc.* And to what extent they may be made during the time of **Fairs** <note>original Latin: "Nundinarum," referring to large periodic markets where special legal protections often applied</note>? Berlich teaches this in *conclusion 53.*

It is doubted whether an **innkeeper** may seize the goods of a **traveler** <note>original Latin: "peregrini," meaning a foreigner or a traveler staying away from home</note> staying with him until satisfaction has been made for food and drink. Those who hold the negative view say that it is not permitted to take a pledge on one's own authority, according to the *Doctors of Law on law 3 of the Code regarding pledges.* For no one, without the intervention of a Judge, ought to be able or allowed to claim for himself another's goods—or even a mortgage—through force and his own deed; for this would be to "render justice to oneself," which is permitted to no one, *by the argument of law 1 of the Code, "that no one should be a judge in his own cause."* But if he should do so, he is compelled both to return the thing to the Master and to restore its price, *according to the Code regarding "where by force."* Indeed, he deservedly loses the right of the debt and the pledge, *according to the law "it stands" in the Digest regarding the Julian law on private violence.* Furthermore, Menochius (*on recovering possession, remedy 5, section 9*) and Coler (*on executive process, part 1, chapter 5, number 106 and following*) record that this specifically applies to the innkeeper.

However, there are others who hold the contrary. For the Innkeeper allows the Traveler to come under his roof, and protects him and his belongings from all fraud and theft; he provides the necessary remedies to refresh his weary strength, silently undertakes the custody of all things brought into the inn, and is even responsible for the deeds of others, *according to the Digest, "Ship-captains and Innkeepers."* Therefore, public utility and equity demand that he be paid as quickly as possible, or that his right be protected through the power of seizure when payment is denied. The innkeeper seems to have, at the very least, a **right of retention**; indeed, in such a case, a **tacit mortgage** <note>An implied legal lien that exists even without a written contract</note> is deemed to be introduced. Thus, a host may, for the price of a single supper <note>original Latin: "cœnæ"</note>, detain as much of the goods as suffices for that payment; so records Baldus *on law 5 of the Code regarding leases.* On this question, see Negusantius *in the treatise on pledges and mortgages, part 1, member 4, numbers 138 and 141*; Coler *on executive process, part 1, chapter 2, number 21*; Cavalcanti, *decision 44*; and Virgil Pingitzer, *question 58.*

Although Seizures are now common throughout all of **Germany**, those Statutes are most reasonable and consistent with equity which prescribe a certain time limit for the person seizing, **within which he must bring a lawsuit regarding the seized goods.** <note>original German: "inner welchem er auf das arrestirte Gut klagen muß"</note> For the understanding of these Statutes, see Moller, *book 4, semestrials, chapter 11.*

A Seizure is released by **security** <note>original Latin: "cautione," usually a financial bond or guarantee</note>, **that the arrested party intends to submit to ordinary law (in an otherwise competent location),** <note>original German: "daß der Arrestatus des ordentlichen Rechtens seyn wolle (in loco alias competenti)"</note> regarding which matter, and 

<column-break/>

how one may release oneself from a seizure, see Cöpen, *decision 35*, and Modestinus Pistoris, *part 3, question 110.*

Seizures are also sometimes granted by **contract** <note>original Latin: "ex pacto"</note>: **Where one signs a written agreement that he may be arrested in all places in case of non-performance.** <note>original German: "Da einer sich verschreibet, daß er aller Orten, im Fall nicht haltens, verarrestirt werden möge."</note> And in that case, the heirs are also bound by it, or a successor in office, according to Hartmann Pistoris, *question 50.* Likewise, Subjects and Ministers can sometimes be bound by seizure for the debts of their Magistrates or Lords, according to Berlich, *conclusion 52.* However, one detained by seizure on account of another, or damaged by some other means, can recover the damage and interest from that person, Cöpen, *decision 36.* Unless that seizure was injurious; in that case, only the one performing the seizure is held liable, since the crime of one person ought not to harm a third party, *by the argument of law 51 of the Digest regarding evictions.*

But see more regarding seizures in Georg Everhard, *counsel 10 and following, volume 1*, and Andreas Gail has treated the Seizures of the Empire in a specific book. See also the individual dissertations in volume 5 of the Basel Dissertations, and regarding the Establishment of seizures, Rosacorb, *chapter 20.*

Regarding the **Saxon Arrest** <note>A specific legal tradition in Saxony that gave creditors who seized property significant priority over others</note>, which grants a priority in the goods of the debtor, see Berlich, *decision 106 and following.* And that point is unknown both in Law and in our customs: **That one creditor's head-start should not harm another,** <note>original German: "Daß eines Creditoris Vorlauff soll dem andern nicht schaden." This refers to the principle that being the first to claim shouldn't necessarily give you total priority, though Saxon law differed.</note> *law "pupillus" where Bartolus comments, Digest, on things done to defraud creditors.* See also Pruckman, *counsel 47, number 167, volume 1*, and the *Princely Württemberg Land Law, part 1, title 75, folio 209.*

### ADDITION.

What is **Seizure and Distress**? <note>original German: "Angriff, Kummer." In old legal German, "Kummer" specifically referred to the seizure of property for debt</note> See Klock, *volume 2, counsel 84, number 15.* Anyone who hinders the release of a seizure after security has been provided is held liable for injuries, Klock, *volume 2, counsel 85, number 14.* A malicious seizer is to be condemned for all damages, expenses, and interest, *said counsel 85, number 14.* If the arrested person flees from the seizure, the penalty he is held to is found in Zahn, *On Lies, book 2, chapter 10, numbers 4 and 5.*

It is well known that by **Saxon Law**, a real right <note>original Latin: "Jus reale," a right attached to property rather than just a person</note> is granted to a seizure, commonly called **a beneficial right** <note>original German: "eine dienliche Gerechtigkeit"</note>, the power of which is so great that the Seizer is preferred over all other Creditors, even those holding any kind of mortgage. Coler, *Executive Process, part 1, chapter 2, number 191.* This applies even against those who obtained a subsequent seizure, Carpzov, *J.R.S. Constitution 28, definition 144.* Moreover, a person is said to have obtained a subsequent seizure not by being the last to receive it from the Judge, but by being slower to approach the judge, even if he obtained it first. Moller, *Semestrial questions, chapter 44, number 16.* In this priority, even moments and points of hours are to be considered and proven, Carpzov, *said definition 144*, since in this single moment the entire safety of the case consists. Schütz, *volume 2, Public Law regarding seizures, number 5, letter B.* Sprenger, *On Modest Matters, page 149, at the end.*

The time prescribed for renewal begins to run not from the day the seizure was requested, but from the day it was obtained. Carpzov, *decision 79, throughout.* It cannot be introduced by custom that the goods of someone sufficiently possessed <note>Meaning someone who has enough assets to cover the debt without needing a sudden seizure</note> may be seized—

## 93. Medicine, and the Doctor of Medicine.

Should Physicians be tolerated in a Republic? See Martinus, *century 9, and the final dispute, final thesis; also century 9, dispute 1, final thesis.* It is true that States can exist without Physicians. For many thousands of nations live without Physicians, and the Roman People existed for more than six hundred years without them, and even condemned the art of Medicine. Pliny, *Natural History, book 29, chapter 1.* Indeed, many ailments must be present where more Physicians are found. Jean de Coras, *on the title "Origin of Law," in the law "Necessarium," section "Post originem" 13,* citing Strabo, *Geography, book 6.*

Cato the Censor, above all others, warned his son to diligently avoid every kind of Physician. Pliny, *in the place cited.* Regarding the Emperor Hadrian, Dio Cassius reports that it was common talk among the people when he died: "A crowd of Physicians killed the King." And of Aurelian Caesar it is read that he never called a Physician to himself when he was sick, but cured himself chiefly through fasting. Vopiscus, *in "Life of Aurelian."* Likewise, Pausanias the Spartan, as Coras reports in the cited place—who maintained his health with no help from a Physician—when asked how he had become so old, replied: "Because I never used a Physician." And to a Physician saying, "You have no illness," he wittily shot back: "That is because I do not use you as a Physician." See Filesacus, *Select Works 1, chapter 17,* and my own treatise *On Life and Death, folio 58 and following.*

<column-break/>

But truly, examples of treatments and medical actions were not only discovered through the constant observation of the first men of the world—who excelled in the integrity of their senses and sharpness of wit—but even the brute animals know them, led by the guidance of wise Nature herself. Thus it is established that wild goats and also stags, when pierced by an arrow, seek out the herb **dittany**. Virgil, *Aeneid, book 12:*

> -- -- That herb is not unknown to wild goats
> When the swift arrows have stuck in their backs.

The Hippopotamus showed the way to the cutting of a vein <note>bloodletting</note>; the Egyptian Ibis was the inventor of clysters <note>enemas</note>. The snake sharpens its sight and casts off old age by using fennel. The lizard eludes the lethal bites of the viper by eating galega <note>Goat's-rue</note>. Dogs purge bile through the upper parts by eating dog-grass. Celandine, the herb of its own name, restores sight to its chicks. Furthermore, those ancient wise men judged that Medicine proceeded from God (though they were ignorant of the true God), and they attributed so much to this art that they scarcely believed it could have been discovered by human wits. And for this reason, they ascribed both the herbs and the demonstration of their powers to the Solar genius <note>Apollo</note>. Ovid, *Metamorphoses, book 1:*

> Medicine is my invention, and I am called
> The Helper throughout the world, and the power of herbs is subject to us.

"The Most High created the Physician," says the son of Sirach <note>from the deuterocanonical Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus</note> in a certain place; "and from God is all healing. The Most High created medicine out of the earth, and a wise man will not abhor it." It seems a part of the piety owed to God to magnify that art in which the most ample and pleasing wisdom of God, and his infinite providence and ineffable foresight, are found scattered everywhere.

It is no wonder, therefore, that Homer—that ocean of all erudition and man most skilled in human affairs—broke out into these words:

Ἱητρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων, which is to say: One man who is a Physician is equal in honor to many others. And finally, that Physician truly reaches out a health-giving hand to the sick who knows how to use remedies in the right place, by right, and appropriately.

And far from these are they who, without accurate study of the Medical art, are accustomed to sell themselves under the false title of Physician; those who, when the mask is pulled away, appear as wicked Jews <note>This reflects the 17th-century legal and social prejudice against non-licensed or non-Christian practitioners</note>, deserters of their profession, unlearned chemists, foolish and common mixers of drugs, meddlers, charlatans, foolish barbers, prying bath-keepers, wandering peddlers, impostors, toothless and babbling old women, executioners, dog-killers, and other such "sons of the earth" <note>low-born individuals of obscure origin</note>.

Among the ancients, Physicians were in the rank of slaves...

Medical Doctors who are actively teaching or registered at a university possess many privileges; notably, they cannot be harassed, as *Johannes Ludovicus* records in his *Lucca Decisions, 6.* For the origin of medical immunity, see *Brisson, Second Selection, chapter 3 and following.*

Indeed, even a statesman <term>Politicus<gloss>a person concerned with the administration and legal order of the state</gloss></term> must know which medicine is superstitious and therefore to be prohibited.

A question debated among the most serious authors must not be overlooked here: whether faith should be placed in amulets, whether they are based on reason, or whether remedies can be found that, by a specific and hidden <term>occult<gloss>at the time, this referred to "hidden" natural properties that were not yet understood by science, rather than "black magic"</gloss></term> virtue, so oppose poisons that they either attract them like a magnet or, by changing them, dull and extinguish them? There are some, among whom is *Thomas Erastus*, a distinguished physician and philosopher, who say that it is false and trifling, fabulous and superstitious—indeed, unworthy of a Christian—to despise natural medicines known by the senses and reason in order to use hidden and unknown drugs that act by a "specific virtue" (that is, a hidden property of the whole substance) to oppose diseases.

Others, conversely, think that amulets are based on natural reason, and therefore all faith should not be withheld from them. They argue that their operation proceeds from the "property of the whole substance," that is, from all the powers of the substance combined. For they say it is not the matter that acts separately, nor the form, nor the elemental mixture <note>original: "crasis elementaria," referring to the balance of the four humors/elements</note>; but rather they act in the union created through the tempering of the coming-together elements. Thus, the whole substance is nothing other than a kind of "conspiracy" or breathing-together of all the powers of the substance to produce the same effect consistent with them. See *Goclenius, Treatise on the Plague, folio 181*; see *Höchstetter, Observation 2, Decade 3*; add *Camerarius, Historical Meditations, Century 3, chapter 30, and Book 2, chapter 76*, where he has much to say regarding amulets and preternatural remedies.

A nearly similar question concerns the magnetic cure of wounds, without the application of a remedy to the body, <note>This refers to the "Weapon Salve" controversy, where the treatment was applied to the weapon that caused the wound rather than the wound itself.</note> <insert>the wound-salve, where one binds the instrument with which one was struck; or wets a splinter in the blood of the wound and places it into the weapon-salve.</insert> See *my own treatise On Life and Death, folio 71.* On this matter there exist the opposing writings of *Rudolph Goclenius* and *Johannes Robertus*, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, whom *Caspar Wenck*, of the same Order, has recently followed.

To me, indeed, remedies of this kind that have no manifest reason seem more suspicious now than they once did. It is true, as *Avenzoar* <note>A famous 12th-century Andalusian physician</note> relates regarding the mind of *Hermes*,

<column-break/>

that there are virtues in vegetables and minerals which, if a man knew them, he would perform that which is performed through the magical art. However, this ointment seems to have foul and necromantic ingredients, namely human skull and blood, moss from the head of a hanged man, and so on.

Furthermore, if anyone uses this ointment and simultaneously employs other medicines, the wound then swells and is seized by a preternatural heat.

A similar cure is that which is done through the "transplantation" of diseases, <insert>when one gives an animal something to eat made from the sick person's blood in a certain manner,</insert> a subject treated at length by *Johann Ernst Burggravius in his Biolychnium*, and *Jacob Lupius in his Treasury of Nature.*

> "Whether you prefer to provide a remedy to the sick through grass,
> or rather through a song: for it is a certain thing for health—"

However, I am inclined to think that natural medicines, by their own natural power, are also useful against the incantations and sorceries of witches and the demon-possessed; see *Bartholomäus Carrichter’s treatise On the Healing of Magical Injuries*, which the *Book of Tobit* also seems to suggest; and add *my own treatise On Life and Death, folio 71.*

It can also be asked here: whether <term>Chymiatria</term> <note>Chemical medicine or iatrochemistry, which used minerals and chemicals rather than just herbs.</note> (which **Angelus Sala of Vicenza** has contained in certain aphorisms and titled *A Synopsis of Chymiatric Aphorisms*) should be tolerated in a well-constituted Republic? See my own treatise *On Life and Death*, page 73.

And certainly, although **Thomas Erastus**, in his treatise on *Potable Gold*, <note>original: "auro potabili"</note> seems hardly willing to concede that healthy medicines can be prepared from minerals; nevertheless, **Quercetanus** <note>The Latinized name of Joseph Duchesne, a famous Paracelsian physician.</note> in his *Tetrad*, chapter 20, page 241, wishes to prove the contrary from the fact that the so-called "dogmatic" physicians <note>Traditional physicians following Galen and Hippocrates.</note> usually send their patients to mineral springs after all their own remedies have been tried in vain—the power of which springs resides in dissolved metallic spirits. But here, caution must be applied, which I mentioned above on page 23.

Furthermore, <term>Hermetic Medicine</term>, <note>A system of medicine based on the works of Hermes Trismegistus and Paracelsus, emphasizing alchemy and spiritual forces.</note> which **Paracelsus** attempted to revive, has other advantages as well, one of which is not to be looked down upon: that it distinguishes the <term>Entia morborum</term> <note>The "Beings" or fundamental origins of diseases.</note> somewhat better. For, (1.) diseases have their origin from the **natural being** <note>original: "ente naturali"</note> or natural essence—that is, from the six unavoidable things without which a person cannot live or move: air, food and drink, rest and movement of the body, fullness and evacuation of the same, sleep and wakefulness, and the movement of the senses and the mind, etc. (2.) The second is the **astral being**, <note>original: "Ens astrale"</note> namely how diseases arise and are caused through the influence and effect of the stars. (3.) The **venomous being**, <note>original: "Ens venenale"</note> in which manner almost all weaknesses may be born from the poison and impurity hidden in food and drink (otherwise called <term>Tartarus</term>). <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to stony or calcified deposits in the body caused by impurities in food.</note> (4.) The fourth is the **Pagoyic being**, <note>original: "Ens Pagoycum" — a term referring to illnesses originating from the human spirit or imagination.</note> how and in what way

<column-break/>

through the spirits of man (namely those which the evil will and desire of man gives birth to from within himself), every kind of disease can be inflicted, and these are for the most part of a magical nature. (5.) The fifth is the **divine being**, <note>original: "Ens deale"</note> where a person is often and many times visited and attacked with all kinds of diseases through the singular secret counsel and will of the All-Knowing God.

**Augustinus Etzlerus** paved the way toward the knowledge of this five-fold disease-producing Being in his treatise *On the Foundation of Eternal Medicine*. Likewise, the second and third beings were explained by **Johann Hayne** in his treatise *On Astral and Tartaric Diseases*.

Furthermore, **Hermetic Medicine** suggests another way of knowing plants, on which matter one may see **Johann Poppen’s** *Herbal*, in which the herbs of the German lands are not only described from the light of nature according to the proper manner of the "Signatures" <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" held that plants resembling parts of the body could treat those parts.</note> of heavenly influence—showing under which planet, under which sign of the **Zodiac**, and in which degree each herb stands—but also how one can recognize from the signatures alone what each herb is to be used for, and how many signatures each herb possesses. Compare also to this the *Herbal* of **Bartholomäus Carrichter**, who indeed took his foundations from **Paracelsus**, but deviated somewhat from him and used a particular method in his writing, and achieved so much with simple herbs that he was thereafter called the "Doctor of Herbs." And as for the claim that **Quercetanus** was illiterate, **Höchstetter** testifies to this in his *Observations*, decade 6, at the end, page 503.

### ADDITION.

**Question:** Is a contract made between a Physician and a sick person valid? Baldus (on Law 13, note 15 of the Code on Transactions) and Jason seem to have admitted this. Others argue to the contrary, whom Busius reconciles in his *Commentary on the Pandects*, folios 112 and 113 in my edition.

Oldekop, in his *Criminal Observations*, page 498, lists four requirements for a Physician so that the death of the infirm is not imputed to him. The School of Salerno teaches: *If doctors fail you, let these three be your doctors: a cheerful mind, rest, and a moderate diet.* <note>original: "mens hilaris, requies, moderata diæta"</note> Under the naming of "nourishment," the expenses of Medicine are included. Jacob Ayrer in his *Historical Process*, part 1, chapter 4, observation 1, number 23. When a witness falls into illness by his own fault, in that case, the person producing him is not bound to provide Medicines (Jacob Ayrer, part 1, chapter 4, observation 1, number 25). If a Professor is a Doctor of Medicine or a public person, but a Doctor of Law holds no public office, the Medical Professor is nonetheless not preferred in seating, standing, or processions (Carpzov, *Illustrious Decisions*, 7, throughout).

For Physicians, March is especially fatal (Richter in *Economic Axioms*, page 71, Axiom 12). Regarding the cure that occurs through the "transplantation" of diseases, see Jacob Lupius’s *Treasury*. For the life of Theophrastus Paracelsus, see Döring, *On Physicians*, part 2, folio 158. In the year 1611, Hippolytus a Collibus became bedridden in Heidelberg, and when the two Physicians employed for him could not agree on one point or another, but rather accused one another in the patient’s personal presence of holding an opinion contrary to the rules of Hippocrates or Galen,

<column-break/>

this Hippolytus a Collibus, in a mix of jest and earnest, made the following sensible speech: *Amidst their bickering, he said he must die according to the Rules of Nature.* <note>original: "Inter ipsorum Altercationem, sibi moriendum esse, secundum Regulas Naturæ"</note> (Lord Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relation of Truces and Peace*, page 27). To the Poles, a Physician is called *Lickarski* <note>Modern Polish: "Lekarski"</note>; we should not experiment without permission (Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 1, number 18). Asclepius is the God of Health (Lord Rupert, dissertation 2, book 1, chapter 8, on Valerius Maximus).

Chrysostom refers us to the workshops of Physicians and bids us seek more examples of "good deceit" from them (*On the Priesthood*, book 1). For a memorable example of a trick played on a feverish man by Physicians, see Rittershusius (on Law 23, page 18 and following) and the observations of Schenck of Freiburg on curing melancholic diseases. On December 30, 1548, Count Maximilian Ecmontanus died of a throat abscess. The shrewd and highly experienced Physician **Andreas Vesalius** <note>A famous 16th-century anatomist who revolutionized the study of the human body.</note> predicted the day and hour of his death to him beforehand, based on mature consideration of the illness. Because of this, on that same day, the Count arranged a meal, invited his good friends to it, distributed gifts among them, took his leave of them, and afterward lay back down in bed and died shortly thereafter without fear, as Thuanus reports in book 5. The outcome of mortality ought not to be imputed to the Physician (Digest, book 6, section 7, *On the Office of the Governor*).

Walther accumulated many questions concerning Physicians in his *Treatise on the Privileges of Doctors*, where he also suggests that Physicians should not reveal the secret vices of the sick—which Hippocrates adds to the Physician’s oath.

The most skillful of Physicians have occasionally heard of some remedy in the form of a lowly animal and have, with great industry, brought it into use. Galen himself did this. It is the mark of an expert to add or take away with judgment, which the common people lack (Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 215; add especially Barbosa, book 11, chapter 17, throughout). Regarding three axioms: one must stand by the assertion of Physicians in the question of a wound (Treutler, volume 1, disputation 18, letter C).
