### Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

**Header:** Lit. A.
**Signature:** Besold Vol. I.

And these are called **Assessors** from "sitting by" (*assidendo*), because they sit beside the judge during the act of judging and make him a participant in their counsel. (Code of Justinian, Book 1, Title 'On Assessors'). Here, "to sit beside" is said to mean "to give counsel." (Digest, Book 9, Section 3). For this reason, they are also called **Counselors**. (Digest, Title 'On the Office of the Assessor'; Justinian's New Constitutions, 17, 60, and 82). See also Donellus, Book 18, Chapter 2, and Bolognetus on the same title.

These differ from the **Assessors of the Imperial Chamber**. For the Assessors of the Chamber are Judges established for the specific purpose of hearing and deciding cases brought before the Imperial Court, according to the Ordinances of the Chamber, Part 1, Book 13. Therefore, they are commonly called <term>Urtheiler</term><note>original: "Urtheiler" — German for "Judges" or "Judgment-givers."</note> in the court ordinances; that is, they are Judges. However, the Assessors discussed in Civil Law are not Judges, but rather the **Counselors of Judges**; they do not judge by their own authority, but sit beside the one judging and suggest counsel to him. Thus, in our law, Assessors are distinguished from Judges. (Eberhard Speckhan, Century 3, Question 10).

The selection of Assessors belongs to the person performing the duty of judging. However, it is safer and more appropriate that they be chosen with the consent of the Litigating parties; for an Assessor accepted by the mutual consent of the parties cannot later be rejected as suspect. (Canon Law, *De Regulis Juris*).

**The Question is asked:** If an Assessor gives bad counsel, is the Judge to be blamed? Regarding this question, Erasmus à Chokier makes a distinction in his treatise on the Lateran Council:

**Civilly**, the Judge will be held responsible if he chose an unskilled Assessor; for then the Judge is at fault. A bad choice constitutes a fault in law. (Digest, 'On the conduct of business'; Caepolla on urban servitudes).

**Criminally**, however, the Judge will not be held responsible unless his own fraud or deceit intervened. (Digest, 'On the office of the Proconsul').

Assessors, on the other hand, will be held responsible in either case without distinction. Indeed, if the Judge decrees something wrongly, the Assessors will be held liable unless they prove their disagreement through a formal protest. For there is a legal presumption that the Judge followed the Assessor's advice in making the decree. (Code, 'On Appeals').

Finally, in the place of these Assessors today, we generally have the **Colleges of Legal Experts** in approved Universities, <term>where one drafts the judgment, or otherwise publishes it upon the advice obtained from legal experts</term><note>original German: "da man die Urtheil abfassen, oder sonst, auf erholten Rath der Rechtsgelehrten, solche publiciren thut."</note>. Our doctors of law also frequently discuss the "sentence delivered based on the counsel of a wise man."

<column-break/>

Regarding its first teachers in Greece, see Vitruvius, Book 9, Chapter 7.

### ADDITION.

At what value it should be held by a Christian, Besold hints in his *Politics*, Book 2, final chapter. On the taxes levied upon Astrologers, see Mundius *On Duties and Honors*, 3, number 193.

### 97. Atheists. Atheist.

In civil law, those men are also condemned as **Atheists** who do not believe there is a God, who deny the resurrection and the immortality of souls; indeed, they are even subjected to the <term>ultimate punishment</term><note>The death penalty.</note>. If any among them, says the <term>Novella 146</term><note>One of the "New Constitutions" of Emperor Justinian regarding the Jews.</note>, presume to introduce the eloquence of vain new voices, or to deny the resurrection, or the Judgment, or that the handiwork of God and the angelic creatures exist, we wish these to be expelled from every place, so that no voice of blasphemy is left remaining. For those presuming to speak anything of this sort shall be subjected to the ultimate punishments, thereby correcting the nation of the Jews by removing this error.

Johannes Corasius opines in his *Miscellanies*, Book 3, that such heretics who deny God himself and take away Divine power should not only be burned alive, but also punished with other exquisite and heavier penalties and tortures, if any harsher ones can be devised. See my own treatise *On Majesty*, folio 102.

And how much **Atheism** harms a Republic, I have shown in my treatise *On Information*, folio 34. For this reason, the Athenians of old also punished those who dared to deny the Gods. On the contrary, Plato divinely says in Book 10 of *The Laws*: If a city and Republic are to be well-ordered, two things especially...

It is most important to remove certain opinions from the minds of citizens: first, that they should not think that God neglects human affairs and actions; second, that they should not rashly persuade themselves that the Heavenly Power is easily appeased. Even Aristotle holily said, "God is the best principle of all things, but the best of virtues is piety." <margin>Plutarch, *Life of Marcellus*.</margin> And consistent with his profession, Philo the Jew says: "The denial of God is the source of all crimes." And even the ancient Romans were once so religious that they preferred to have sacred rites properly administered than to see their enemies conquered.

But a sign of **Atheism** is to attribute all understanding to the senses, as Lucretius says:
<margin>Lucretius.</margin>
> For all things that are believed depend upon the senses.

The Stoics are considered atheists because they hold nature to be God, and they think that even they themselves <margin>Justus Lipsius, *Physiologia Stoica*, Book 2, dissertation 22, page 134.</margin> perish and are resolved into fire, as Lipsius notes in *Physiologia Stoica*, Book 2, dissertation 22, page 134. And as for the belief that the world and nature are God, see the same author in the aforementioned treatise, Book 1, dissertation 4 and following. <margin>Verdier, page 179.</margin> It is certainly better to have a false religion than no religion at all: Verdier, page 179. And the Romans conquered other peoples by religion alone, and because they were not atheists. In Branzius’s *Ciceronian Eulogies*, page 3, <note>Branzius is likely a reference to a legal or rhetorical commentator of the era.</note> it seems that Seneca was an atheist, because almost all his *Consolations* are taken from the position of the desperate—that one must harden oneself and soon run toward any danger, because it is necessary, because it cannot be otherwise, etc., just as the Turks run into battle. And the heretical predestinarians <note>A reference to those who believe in absolute fate or predestination to the exclusion of divine mercy or will.</note> are atheists. And so Seneca very often cites Epicurus. In one thing the Epicureans and Stoics agree, etc.

Clement of Alexandria, in the 5th book of his *Stromata* <margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 5, at the beginning.</margin> near the beginning, established that those who deny Providence must be restrained with punishments. <margin>Laelius Bisciola, *Horae Subsecivae*, Book 6, chapter 1.</margin> But Laelius Bisciola reviews the judgments of the ancients regarding **Providence** in his *Horae Subsecivae*, Book 6, chapter 1.

There are, however, various types of atheists. First, the insane, who say it is vain to serve God, and who proclaim the arrogant to be blessed: "For they who work wickedness are built up," etc. <margin>Malachi, chapter 3, verse 14 and following.</margin> Malachi, chapter 3, verse 14 and following. The leader of these was Cain, who in Genesis 4, verse 4 (if faith is to be given to the Jonathan and Jerusalem paraphrases <note>The author is referring to the Targums, which are ancient Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>) said to his brother Abel: "Come, let us both go outside together." For why was your offering accepted with grace, and my offering was not accepted?" Abel answered and said: "The world was created entirely through Divine Mercy, and it is governed according to the fruit of good works, nor is there any respect of persons in judging. Lit. A.

Plutarch also confirms this in his biography <note>referring to the Roman general Quintus Sertorius, who used a white fawn to claim divine inspiration during his campaigns in Spain</note>. It also benefited Scipio Africanus to be believed to have a divine origin. It has been recorded in literature that this Scipio Africanus used to go frequently to the Capitol <note>The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus in Rome</note> at the end of the night, before dawn, and order the chamber of Jupiter to be opened. He would remain there alone for a long time, as if consulting with Jupiter about the Republic. Plutarch also mentions this in his biography.

Atheists are also frequently those apostates who fall away to Mahometism <term>Mahometism: An early modern term for Islam</term>, as Wenceslaus Budovvetz <note>Václav Budovec z Budova (1551–1621), a Bohemian politician and diplomat</note> testifies in *The Circle of the Clock, leaf 177.* There he writes to an Arabian apostate: if he had any reason, any knowledge (both of which he did not lack), or any spark of conscience, he should weigh those fables, never heard of since the creation of the world, which are most shamelessly fabricated in the *Alkoran* <note>The Quran</note> against his own reason. There the apostate—since he was indeed an atheist and a courtier—responded not so much with anger as with laughter. Indeed, he swore that he had read nothing more absurd in his life than the fables of the Quran; just as he gave no credit to them, neither did he respect or believe the New Testament. Thus, he said, Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist known for mocking religion</note> had rightly mocked all religions, saying they were mere foolishness and the opinions of simple men, or constitutions for the preservation of political order; and that they change with empires, kingdoms, and the inclinations of human emotions. When I heard this from the apostate, I replied: "Behold the fruit of your Mahometism, and of a 'true faith' leading to Heaven, by which you have already seduced several Christians like yourself through such boasting." To which he replied, often laughing: "The world deceives and wishes to be deceived; <note>original: "Mundum decipere, & velle decipi"</note> God gave the earth to be inhabited by men, and reserved Heaven for himself." Therefore, he said, nothing is more advisable than for Christians to leave behind their battles over religion and choose an easier, single religion with the Turks—one in which it is not necessary to unroll so many books, be subject to so many censures of churchmen, and invent 'natural things' as sins—and thus become one. So far Budovvetz.

Even Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> himself, in *Book 1, page 2*, quite shamelessly asserts that the stories of the underworld were fabricated for the purpose of terror and political reasons.

Fourth are the subtle atheists, some of whom are ridiculous and vain, such as Lucian and Martial.

And also Pietro Aretino <note>An Italian author known as the "Scourge of Princes," famous for his biting satire</note>, whose epitaph is reported as follows:

Others are more hidden, such as many of the philosophers who, while wishing to abolish superstition, fell into atheism, as Lucretius testifies in *Book 1*:

Pericles also learned such philosophy from Anaxagoras, as Plutarch says in his biography, where he nonetheless divinely makes a distinction between a natural and a Divine philosopher: he says the former investigates causes, while the latter looks to the purpose of events.

Indeed, the Stoics and Epicureans alike seem to be atheists; and there is little difference in this regard between asserting that everything happens by chance or by fatal necessity. See Theophilus Raynaud <note>A French Jesuit theologian (1583–1663)</note> in *Natural Theology, leaf 528.*

Atheists also do not believe in spirits; see *The Philosophy of Spirits, leaf 2 and following.*

The Sadducees and Samaritans were also atheists, according to Baronius <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Vatican historian</note> in the *Apparatus of the Annals, number 7, etc.*

And in general, philosophy and the study of letters, when piety and Divine grace are removed, seem to tend at a headlong pace toward this atheism.

Pliny was truly an atheist when he writes in *Book 2, chapter 7*: "It is right to believe that the World, and this which we have been pleased to call by another name, the Heaven, by whose curvature all things are covered, is a Divinity—eternal, immense, neither created nor ever to perish. To investigate what is outside it does not interest men, nor can human conjecture grasp it. It is sacred, eternal, immense, all in all, or rather it is itself the whole; finite, yet like the infinite; certain of all things, yet like the uncertain; outside, inside, enfolding all things in itself: it is at once the work of nature and Nature itself." In the same chapter 7, he thinks that God does not care for human affairs; yet there is one God, though humans have established countless ones. See the whole of chapter 7, where he discusses how the belief that the Gods are punishers of crimes exists for the sake of utility, etc.

[Pietro Pomponazzi] <note>The text refers to Pomponazzi (1462–1525), a controversial Italian philosopher who argued that the immortality of the soul could not be proven by reason or Aristotle.</note> stirred up great fame and infamy for himself by publishing a volume in which he strove to prove that souls perish after the death of the body, according to the opinion of Aristotle. He followed the teachings of Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>original: "Aphrodisei"; a 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who denied individual immortality</note>. Nothing more pestilential could be introduced for the corruption of youth and the dissolution of the discipline of Christian life than this dogma, as *Paolo Giovio* testifies in his *Eulogies of Learned Men.*

*Antonio Urceo* (who later took the surname Codrus) of Brescia was also a follower of this same profane opinion for almost his entire life, as Bartholomaeus of Bologna testifies in his biography, saying: "Regarding Christian dogma, he frequently limped in his words, if not in his deeds." When friends asked what he felt about the immortality of the soul, he would answer that he did not know what would happen to him after death—whether the spirit or soul would live on, or perish together with the body. He would say that the things men preached about the underworld were "old wives' tales" used as "fright-masks" <note>original: "anilia... terriculamenta"</note>. Nevertheless, when he was ill at the very end of his life, he requested the Sacraments of the Church. For when he saw the body of Christ <note>the Eucharistic Host</note> being brought to him by the Priest, he beat his breast and face with his hands in the manner of a penitent, professing that he was a miserable man and had never been truly wise, having been led through almost his entire life by such blindness of mind.

So too was *Pomponius Laetus* <note>Julius Pomponius Laetus (1428–1498), a humanist who founded the Roman Academy</note> a despiser of Religion from the beginning. He worshipped above all the "Genius" <note>the protective spirit</note> of the City of Rome and celebrated the city’s birthday every year with a large gathering of learned men. No one ever admired antiquity more; no one spent more effort in understanding it. He loathed his own century and held in contempt whatever our age produced. He would stand still, as if out of his mind, at every encounter with an ancient work, and sometimes even wept profusely at the reminder of what he used to call "better times." *Sabellicus in the life of Pomponius Laetus.*

And so perhaps Pope Paul II deserves an excuse for torturing certain literati—among them Platina, Callimachus, and Pomponius Laetus himself—as if they were impious and wicked men. Elsewhere, *Paolo Giovio* (in his eulogies regarding Pomponius Laetus) censures the Pope on this account as being unskilled in elegant letters and suspicious.

But if anyone wishes to avoid such impiety, let them first cast off the opinion that all things are corporeal and that nothing exists except what can be seen. For in the carnal man, the entire rule of understanding is the habit of seeing, as *St. Augustine* says somewhere. From this, those who deny Demons and judge what is said of Witches <note>original: "Sagis"</note> to be ridiculous—those who doubt everything and make animals rational—seem to be wallowing in this pit.

Truly, regarding Atheism and against Atheists, *Edward Weston* deals with several points and with vigor in *The Theater of Civil and Sacred Life, Book 4.*

### 98. Also, Specially. *Etiam, præsertim.* <note>The text now moves into a legal dictionary format, defining the implications of specific words in statutes.</note>

The word "also" <note>original German: "Auch"</note> implies identity or similarity with preceding things. *Law "etiam," Digest "on the dissolution of marriage." Symphor. Supplic. vol. 1, part 1, decisions and resolutions on the doubt "concerning seizure," number 4. Aretinus, consultation 62, column 2. Decius, consultation 696, number 13. Add Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 32, number 33. Tuschus, under the letter D, conclusion 275, etc.* And by its nature, it implies less doubtful cases, and where there is not as great or equal reason. *The Gloss on the text in Clementine 2, on the word "Church," regarding heretics; and in Law "etiam," Law "final," Code "if a tutor or curator." Alexander, consultation 23, column 2, volume 5.*

Sometimes, however, as *Parisius* notes in *consultation 46, number 30 and following, volume 4*, it is accustomed to imply and include things greater than those expressed, even in strict and exorbitant matters; and that it increases by adding, the *same author* hands down in *number 31.*

Implicative words, such as "also," "mostly," and "especially," <note>original: "etiam, maximè, præsertim"</note> imply, import, or designate that the same thing applies in the contrary case. *Gloss on Law "illud," on the word "to be estimated," Digest "on the Aquilian Law"; Gloss on Law "if a minor," section "restitution," on the word "in sale," Digest "on minors"; and there is a text in Law "if anyone for his wife," in the beginning, Digest "on donations between husband and wife"; and in Law "he who of his father," Code "whence children."* Hence it happens that, when the word "implic-" is found in any law...

<meta>The previous page concluded a philosophical discussion on atheism and the immortality of the soul, transitioning into the "Thesaurus of Practical Knowledge," a legal dictionary. This page continues an entry on the interpretation of inclusive language before moving to terms regarding court sessions, legal advice, and feudal law.</meta>

...inclusive <note>original: "implicativa"</note>, it is not permitted to draw an argument from the contrary sense. *Law 'conventicula', Code on Bishops and Clerics.* For an argument from the contrary sense only proceeds when there is a contrary reason in a contrary case. *Law 'si extraneus', Digest on the condition given for a cause which did not follow.* However, words such as "especially," "particularly," "even," <note>original: "maximè, præsertim, etiam"</note> and the like, imply that the same rule applies in the contrary case. Therefore, where the word "even" or a similar term is placed, an argument cannot be drawn from the contrary sense. See also Nicolaus Everhardus in his section on the nature of inclusive words, throughout.

<note>Latin: "Addition." These sections provide supplemental citations or updated commentary on the preceding entry.</note>

The word "even" <note>original: "etiam"</note> implies a more doubtful case. *Klock, volume 3, consultation 121, number 9.*
The word "Even" is a term of similarity, and it introduces a similar disposition to the preceding one; indeed, it amplifies and extends it. *Mundus on duties and honors, page 449, numbers 110 and 122.*

### 99. Audiens. Audientia.
<note>Latin: "Hearing" or "Audience."</note>

Audience is a judicial term, accepted in the courts, denoting jurisdiction, notice, or judgment. *Wesenbeck in the commentary on the Code regarding the audience of bishops.* From this comes the "Auditors of the Rota" <note>the highest papal court</note>.
In the Imperial Chamber Court <note>the supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, an "Audience" refers to that solemn assembly of the Judge and the Assessors, in which the sworn Procurators are heard as they propose and argue the cases of the parties in writing and by voice. There, the Audiences are regularly held in a public place with open doors every day, except for holidays, in the morning from 7:00 in the summer and 8:00 in the winter until 10:00; in the afternoon, they are held from 1:00 until 3:00. Frequently, however, so many changes are instituted that nothing certain can be handed down here, as can be seen in *title 1, part 3 of the Ordinance of the Chamber.* But add *Schwammann on the Process of the Chamber, book 1, chapter 24.* The same author discusses the holidays on which the Chamber Audiences are vacant in the following *chapter 25.*

### ADDITIO.

"Audience" is granted to Bishops, just as "Jurisdiction" is granted to Magistrates. Audience is less than Jurisdiction: for the civil Magistrate, not the Bishop himself, executes the sentence of a Bishop. *Pacius in his Analysis of the Code on the audience of bishops, number 2; see also Rittershusius in the Novels, question 1, chapter 7, number 47; Calvin on Jurisdiction, chapter 1, theme 6, number 10.*
On what the word Audience designates: *Schwammann, book 1 on Process, chapter 24, number 1.* Description of the Chamber Audience: *number 2.* How and when Audiences are celebrated: *number 3.* What is called the Process of the Audience: *book 1, chapter 23, number 4.* For the sake of modesty, the ancients used the word "Audience" rather than "Jurisdiction," so that they might leave the latter intact for the Political Magistrate. *Rittershusius in the Novels, page 92, number 47; add also page 491, number 7, at the end.*

### 100. Auf alle Weis und Weg. Omnibus modis.
<note>German and Latin: "In every way and manner."</note>

The words "in every way" <note>original: "omnibus modis"</note> include every

<column-break/>

species, every case, and every manner, as the glosses and Doctors write regarding the word "absolute" <note>original: "omnimodo"</note> in the *Law 'cum exceptione', section 'quatenus', Digest on things done through fear.* Cephalus, *consultation 153, number 3*, infers that if a statute exists stating that an Oath provides "absolute proof," <note>original: "omnimodam probationem"</note> such a statute excludes the making of proof to the contrary, if it is against the Law—especially when that word "absolute" is placed with the law by a higher power, an inferior cannot dispense with it or create a law to the contrary. *Decianus, consultation 154, number 12; add Nizolius in 'allegation' 26, numbers 19 and 20.*

### 101. Auf gehabten Rath. Ad Consilium Sapientis.
<note>German and Latin: "Upon advice had" or "Toward the Counsel of the Wise."</note>

In legal sentences, it is customary to express: *on advice had or obtained from legal scholars.* <note>original German: "auf gehabt oder eingeholten Rath der Rechtsgelehrten"</note> It is asked whether the "Counsel of the Wise" must be followed if it is against the Law, especially when the parties wished <insert>for example</insert> *that one should obtain the opinion from this or that Faculty <note>university law department</note>?* See *Paride del Pozzo in the treatise on the Syndicate, section 'Counsel', chapter 3, throughout.* *Pruckman and Cothmann dispute concerning the judgments that one obtains from the Faculties.* The Faculty of Tübingen is accustomed to sign sentences with the clause: *Saving the right of a judgment that perceives [the law] better.* <note>original: "Salvo jure melius sentientis judicii"</note> Someone criticized this because a sentence ought to be certain and should admit no such clause. But it must be known that the Faculty is not the Judge, nor is the Judge compelled to follow such Counsel; therefore, that clause is added out of respect for the Judge, *so that one does not wish to forestall him or give him an order.* Afterward, if the Judge pronounces the sentence and thus accepts the Counsel, that clause ceases, and the sentence is without the condition of "one perceiving more correctly," etc.

### ADDITIO.

Accursius and Bartolus <note>famous medieval legal commentators</note> well note that a Judge ought to give sentences having taken the counsel of Wise Men, and should express this very thing in the sentences. You will find more in Rittershusius in the *Novels, page 648, at the end.* *With well-considered courage, good timely counsel, forethought, and right knowledge.* <note>original German: "mit wolbedachtem Muth, gutem zeitlichen Raht, Vorbetrachtung und rechten Wissen"</note> *Limnäus in the Public Law, book 7, chapter 35.*

### 102. Aufgetragene Lehen. Feuda oblata.
<note>German and Latin: "Offered Fiefs." These were lands originally owned freely that were "offered" to a lord in exchange for protection, then received back as a feudal tenure.</note>

To "offer a fief" <note>original German: "Lehen auftragen"</note> is nothing other than to give oneself into patronage <note>original: "Clientelam"</note>. *Miräus in the Code of Donations, folio 62.* Nor does it imply *the status of a landed subject <note>original German: "Landsasserey"</note>, as is clear from the 'Vindication of Waldeck', part 1, chapter 8.*
And it happens not infrequently that Nobles, and others of more ample condition, freely cede their allodial properties <note>land held in absolute ownership</note>, castles, villages, towns, or districts, or even jurisdiction and other rights alone, to someone more powerful, and afterward recognize them again from him in the name of a Fief: regarding which Fief see *Zasius, part 3, number 8; Wesenbeck, etc.*

Saxon Law <note>Latin: Jus Saxonicum; the legal system of the Saxon regions, widely influential in Northern Germany</note> admits no concession here to the lord, unless he grants the same person free possession for a year and a day: and then the donor is treated no differently than any other person held to be a vassal. *The Land Law* <note>German: Landsrecht</note> article 34. Zobel. part 2. difference 46. Matth. Coler. decisions 80. & 219.

It should be noted here that the words **"freely and uncoerced surrendering, placing out of their power and protection and into the feudal lord's power and protection"** <note>original German: "freywilig, ungezwungenlich aufgebend, ausser ihr Gewalt und Gewehr, in deß Lehenherrn Gewalt und Gewehr setzend"</note> do not necessarily prove that it is a "surrendered fief" <note>term: <term>Aufgetragen Lehen</term> - a fief created when a person gives their own private property to a lord and receives it back as a fief, usually to gain the lord's protection.</note>. For such formulas were very common in the old feudal receptions—especially if the vassal, who is the legitimate successor, had already taken possession of the feudal property before the formal investiture <note>the ceremonial act of transferring a fief</note>, as he is permitted to do—and they were observed as a standard legal style <note>Latin: pro stylo communi</note>.

On this occasion, I have chosen to subjoin the following formula for a **surrendered fief**.

To all those who see this letter or hear it read, we, Ludwig von Bercken, a knight, and Konrad and Mehard, brothers, make it known that Limperg the Castle and all that belongs to it—people, property, wood, field, rights, and jurisdiction—which is our own free allodial property <note>term: <term>ledig eygen</term> - land owned outright without any feudal obligations</note> that Lord Tune von Bercken, our father, bought from the noble Lord Count Rudolf of Habsburg and gave to us, we have surrendered, paternally and freely from our hand into the noble Lord Count Egen of Freiburg's hand, our Lord; and we have received back the same castle and everything belonging to it, as written before, from him as a proper fief; and we have done this with the agreement that the aforementioned Count Egen, our Lord, and all his successors shall be forever bound to us, to shield our property, to advise us and to help us, with body and with goods and with their power, in all those matters where we have the right. We and our descendants who shall ever be possessing or having the castle at Limperg shall also be helpful to the aforementioned our Lord and his successors with the same castle. Thereupon in the land and above, when they have need of it in necessity or otherwise, we shall also be helpful to them with body and with goods, when they have need of it, with good faith and without deceit. And so that this remains firm, unbroken, and eternal, we have both hung our seals to this letter. We have also

<column-break/>

asked the aforementioned Lord Tune von Bercken to hang his seal to this letter as a witness. We, Count Egen of Freiburg, acknowledge that we have bound ourselves to our successors and to the aforementioned brothers, Ludwig, Konrad, and Mehart and their descendants, as is written above: and as a testimony of this, we have hung our seal and the seal of Konrad our son to this letter. I, Konrad, son of the aforementioned Count Egen, have hung my seal to this letter in witness of the described things. I, Tune von Bercken, through my Lord Count Egen and also my two sons, have also hung my seal to this letter for testimony. This was done at Kenzingen in the year when one counted from God's birth thirteen hundred years, on the next Monday after the middle of the Month of Fallow <note>German: Brachmonde; usually refers to June</note>.

And this is done primarily for the sake of protection. And therefore, although by the rigor of the law such fiefs take on the nature of other feudal benefits; nevertheless, it seems unjust that for a minor cause—for example, because investiture was not requested, etc.—they should be considered forfeited: as I advised in decade 2, counsel 7, folio 164.

For when nobles acknowledge their allodial lands <note>privately owned lands</note> from Princes, so that whenever it is necessary they can defend them with a more useful title and a more powerful hand, they are not judged to do so with the intention of creating a prejudice against themselves or their heirs, but rather to provide for themselves with more abundant caution. (Argument from the chapter *post electionem* in the Decretals; see also Abbas and Felinus). Alciatus response 178, n. 2; see also Menochius on presumptions, 91, n. 17.

### 104. Surrender of Fiefs. <note>Latin: Resignatio Feudorum</note>

In our Germany, a custom flourishes that the right of a sold fief must be specifically refunded to the Lord and transferred to the buyer: for before this is done, the buyer is not considered a vassal. On this matter, one should entirely look to Hartmann Pistorius, final observation, throughout; where at number 12 and following he teaches that in this resignation (which they commonly call the *Auflassung* <note>German: surrender or transfer of property</note>), the seller must act diligently and submissively

the fief to the Lord, so that he may grant the investiture <note>the formal ceremony of transferring ownership of a fief</note> to the buyer. Since it is then entirely within the Lord's discretion whether to recognize that new Vassal or not, nothing is lost of the Lord's rights through this alienation <note>the transfer of property ownership</note>. In this way, the strictness of Feudal Law—which dictates that a Vassal loses his fief if he attempts to sell it—is softened. In such cases, it is considered a conditional sale, or rather a contract to sell; it is commonly said that a feudal estate is not seen as truly "alienated" until the formal hand-over, and thus it does not trigger a forfeiture. However, those who seek the Lord’s consent before the sale act more safely, or they protect themselves with other legal cautions, as argued by Heigius in part 2, question 18.

It must not be omitted that if a fief is frequently transferred to outsiders and the Lord always consents to a mere **recording** or **surrender** <note>German: *Auffschreibung* or *Auflassung*; the formal registration or yielding of the property</note>, then the fief (especially if other legal presumptions align) is to be considered hereditary. See my "Counsel on Hereditary Fiefs," which is attached to my treatise "On Royal Succession and Election," page 237 and following.

## ADDITION.

Regarding cession <note>the formal giving up of rights</note>, or the **surrender** <note>German: *Auflassung*</note>, see Christian Lenz in the treatise "On Ceded Names and Actions," chapter 1, number 13.

In the sale of goods, a judicial resignation—the **surrender of the fief** <note>German: *die Aufflassung der Lehen*</note>—is required. If this does not follow, the ownership always remains with the seller, and the buyer gains nothing but bare possession. Berlich, conclusion 82, numbers 49 and 50.

### 105. Uprising. Sedition.

Nothing is more destructive to a Republic than sedition <note>inciting rebellion against authority</note>. Some pursue it with such hatred that they believe the power of the Prince should never even be debated. For there are those who never think themselves eloquent or spirited unless they insolently challenge the excellence of princes, or unless they wound Majesty with the sharp wit of their insane intellects, stripping away that **mystic reverence** which is owed to the throne of God occupied by Princes. Hence, James, King of Great Britain <note>James I of England</note>, in a certain speech delivered in the Star Chamber at London, determined quite relevantly: that the supreme and absolute prerogative of the scepter is not subject to the examination of lawyers and is placed beyond all risk of dispute. So too, Molina argues that even the rule of a Tyrant must be obeyed for the sake of conscience (*On Justice and Law*, treatise 2, dispute 24); add also Filesacum, book 1, chapter 9, regarding whether kings are raised by God sometimes for the purpose of devastation. The hand of God punishes Princes, not the hand of their subjects. Antoine le Pippre, chapter 26, "On Intentions," notes that these questions are dangerous and least of all to be tolerated: Is the rule of a woman legitimate? Is election better than succession? Is the Prince subject to the laws, or are the laws subject to the people? etc. (Besold, Volume 1).

<column-break/>

The same author warns in chapter 207. Grotius, in *On the Law of War and Peace*, book 1, chapter 3, number 8, refutes at length the opinion of those who say that, everywhere and without exception, the supreme power belongs to the people, such that they may punish and restrain Kings whenever they use their power poorly. To this may be added the most excellent Goldastus, "On the Succession of the Bohemian Kingdom," book 1, chapter 5 and following, where he also includes a letter arguing that religion is not a legitimate pretext for rebellion. See also Charron in the treatise *On Wisdom*. But I have dealt with this matter at length in my "Political Preliminaries," page 171 and following.

But however much this matter may be argued plausibly on either side, nevertheless, sedition—even when "just"—is almost always a medicine that is more dangerous than the disease itself. Cinuzo speaks truly and prudently in book 2 of *Military Discipline*, page 245: **"Civil wars, if they are not settled in the beginning, never end except with the extermination of one of the parties or the ruin of the State."** Sedition, which is the daughter of tyranny, may also become the mother of tyranny, whether the Prince, the people, or the state prevails. The so-called defenders of common liberty always act in confusion, as happened in Portugal under Antonio, whom the people favored (Conestagius, book 5, page 294, etc.). Usually, they are seeking their own private advantage while wanting to appear as though they fight for the public good.

And the rule to be held here is this: the old state of affairs must always be favored, and innovators must not be joined. Liberty is always the pretext in a conspiracy, but it is more often a **mask for a worse servitude.** The wise politician Philip Melanchthon <note>a famous Protestant reformer and educator</note> wrote prudently in book 3 of his *Letters*, page 180, to Johann Pfeffinger: "Even if the outcome will eventually show what is being done, nevertheless, until it is proven by such a witness, do not oppose the will of the Emperor."

No Republic lacks the discontented, even those who have a reason for their indignation that is not entirely unjust. Therefore, no Prince would ever be secure if the people were indulged too much. A true note, according to Thucydides, of a seditious time is when those citizens are seen as the most constant who are most eager to kindle hatreds. At such times, Republics are also usually deceived by the hope of foreign aid and bring great calamities upon themselves. It is easier to meet these things at their beginning; if neglected, the discontented rush into their fates through many errors. The confusions are terrible and horrific, whichever side wins. **"When one teaches subjects to go to war, they use it against the authority itself."** <note>original German: *Wann man die Unterthanen lernt kriegen, brauchen sie es wieder die Obrigkeit selbst.*</note> An example is found in Switzerland: **"Where the peasants learned how to break into castles. Likewise, when subjects are allowed to take revenge by their own private authority."**

Regarding the Peasants' War <note>a widespread popular revolt in the German-speaking areas of Central Europe from 1524 to 1525</note>, see the Elegy of Atrocianus; and regarding its confusion, see Gastius in his *Convivial Sermons*, volume 2, page 88. And regarding the rebellion of the Spaniards in the time of Charles V, and how the King of Portugal refused to accept the Kingdom offered to him by the Spanish rebels. Osorius, book 12 of his *History*, page 349; Guevara, book 3 of his *Letters*, letter 1; and...

<summary>This page discusses the legal mechanics of transferring fiefs through "surrender" and transitions into a stern warning against sedition, arguing that rebellion—even for a just cause—usually results in greater ruin than the tyranny it seeks to overthrow.</summary>

And the present calamities of Germany were foreseen by Johann Leuchterus in his treatise *on Alliances*, where among other things he writes the following:

"Since no other government in the Roman Empire is to be hoped for than that which Daniel <note>A reference to the biblical prophecies of the Four Kingdoms in the Book of Daniel</note> indicated, it is not advisable to change it. Instead, let whoever can patch and mend it while we live, punish the abuse, and lay a plaster upon the pox-marks. If one rips open the pox-marks with mercilessness, no one will feel the pain and damage more than those clever barbers who would rather rip open a sore than heal it. Well then, Germany is perhaps ripe, and I fear a heavy punishment; God be merciful to us."

"These are the 'Master Tinklers' <note>German: *Meister Klinglinge*; a derogatory term for pretentious critics who make a lot of noise but have no skill</note> who, out of great wisdom, try to bridle the horse by its tail, and can do nothing more than judge and master other people. When they get the government into their hands, everything goes to ruin with them, just as the saying goes: 'the one who watches the game knows best.' For they think that if they got the ball in their hand, they would hit twelve pins, even though only nine are standing on the green."

"It remains true that where there is an unhealthy body, there will also be pox, pus, and other filth. But government is such a 'beggar’s cloak' <note>German: *Bettler-Belz*; meaning something worn out and patched together</note> and a pox-ridden child that has its blemishes and scars. Therefore, there must be some pious Josephs, Nathans, Zadoks, etc., within it who keep it alive and in being, so that it does not go completely to ruin. The others are pox, sores, the 'French disease' <note>Syphilis</note>, St. Valentine’s sickness <note>Epilepsy</note>, etc.,"

<column-break/>

"who claim to make such a body healthy, like Ziba, Ahithophel, and their kind <note>Biblical figures associated with treachery or self-serving advice</note>."

"Just as women very much dislike being called whores, even if they are so in deed; so truly Kings and Lords do not like to hear, and court-servants even less so, being scolded and punished as the unjust and the wicked, because such things seem to touch their honor too closely. Likewise, such things are done by the most useless 'bumblebees' the earth carries, who can only spit and chatter much, and fill a King's or Prince's ears so that he becomes quite clouded against his faithful servant, etc. Just as the bumblebee—that incompetent, lazy, gluttonous vermin that can make no honey—devours everything the pious little bees make, except that they can buzz, whir, and hum with their wings even more than the right, dear little bees."

But concerning the seditious, see more in Deciani’s *Criminal Treatise*, and also in Gigas *on the crime of Lèse-majesté* <note>treason against the sovereign</note>; and almost the entire *Criminal Process* of Rosbach is occupied with this matter, as is the counsel on this same subject joined to the treatise of Mr. Valentin Volzius. Add Neumair in his individual treatise *on Uprisings* <note>German: *von Aufruhren*</note>.

## ADDITION.

*Reroif*, which is also written *Reroub* <note>Old Germanic/Flemish terms for robbery or commotion</note>, is nothing other than our *Uffruer* [Uprising], commotion, or sedition, still called *Roere* by the Belgians: whence *Roestichter* and *Roervincke* <note>translated as 'Firebrand' or 'Troublemaker'</note>, the author and instigator of disturbances, the torch and inciter of sedition.

Lipsius defines sedition as: "A sudden and violent movement of a multitude against a Prince or Magistrates." Moreover, "Sedition" is said to come from *secedendo* [withdrawing] or going apart, specifically when a disagreeing multitude comes to blows, as Cicero says in book 6 of *The Republic*; Virgil also describes such a thing in *Aeneid* 1, verse 152, in which he excellently depicts the nature of a seditious mob:

> "And just as when sedition has often arisen in a great crowd,
> and the ignoble mob rages in their minds,
> and now torches and stones fly, fury provides the weapons."

Who may be called seditious: see Jacob Ayrer in the *Historical Process*, part 2, chapter 6, observation 1, number 1. With what penalty a seditious person is to be punished: numbers 2 and 3.

Sedition does not immediately end when one seditious person is killed: see Rupert on Florus, book 3, chapter 17, section 2. For the seditious, there is no hope except from the disturbance of the Republic: book 4, chapter 6, section 2, number 2. From what causes seditions arise in a Republic: see Scherbius in *Politics*, page 205 and following.

### 106. Visual Evidence. *Ocularis Inspectio.*

Visual inspection <note>Latin: *Ocularis inspectio*; German: *Augenschein*</note> renders a matter manifest from its own evidence, and therefore it is considered the firmest proof and prevails over every kind of proof. See the law *si irruptione*, where the gloss is found in the Digest *on the boundaries of fields*; Natta, counsel 269, number 9; Matthaeus de Afflictis, decision 23.

...citation 23, number 6. Fulvius Pacianus *on proofs*, book 1, chapter 45, throughout. Domhaud in his *practice on confessions*, number 93. Wesenbeck, *Counsel* 58, volume 2, number 14. Because the eye is a more certain judge than the ear, according to the same author in the cited counsel, number 2, who there brings forward that line from Horace’s *Art of Poetry*:

> Things dropped through the ears stir the mind more slowly,
> Than those which are subjected to faithful eyes.

And ears are more incredulous to men than eyes. For sight is of itself <term>per se: directly or essentially</term>; hearing is by accident <term>per accidens: indirectly or through another medium</term>. Every proof is defeated if a visual appearance testifies to the contrary. Baldus at the law *Deo*, column 3, at the verse "but if we suppose," Code *on Bishops and Clergy*; and the same logic follows from Canon Law, question 27, causa 2, chapter *proposuisti*, and the Doctors of Law there, *on proofs*. Hence Natta, *Counsel* 269, number 6, says that a proof made through the evidence of the fact—that is, through visual inspection—is the best, and those speeches are superlative which agree with the things perceived by the senses. For what the eye sees, no one can faithfully deny. Wesenbeck, *Counsel* 58, number 14. And what is expressly evident does not need to be demonstrated. Baldus, *Counsel* 388, number 6, volume 1. The Holy Scripture agrees in John, chapter 3: "We speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen"; and chapter 1: "I have seen, and I have borne witness." Innocent in the chapter *super hoc* *on renunciations*. Baldus in the law *observare*, section *proficisci*, question 3, Digest *on the office of Proconsul*. On whether visual inspection can be waived, see Bullæus, *Counsel* 6, question 46.

But regarding visual inspection, Lord Rutger Ruland has more in his *treatise on Commissions*, part 2, book 3, chapter 1 and following.

And to this belongs the treatment of experts in an art, <insert>whom one uses for visual inspections</insert> <note>original German: *so man zu den Augenscheinen brauchet*</note>; such as surveyors, boundary markers, master builders, surgeons, and also all kinds of craftsmen, whose information the judge uses at times. Indeed, if they swore from the beginning of their office, <insert>if they are sworn masters</insert> <note>original German: *so sie geschworne Meister seynd*</note>, then a new oath does not seem necessary.

## 107. Augsburg Confession, Adherents of the Augsburg Confession.

Those devoted to the Augsburg Confession.
<note>original: *Augustanæ Confessioni addicti.*</note>

They were thereafter called "Confessionists" because they offered the Confession of their faith, comprised of certain articles, at the Diet of Augsburg to the unconquered Emperor Charles V on June 25, 1530. The Princes who subscribed to this Confession were: John, Elector of Saxony; George, Margrave of Brandenburg; Ernest, Duke of Lüneburg, and Francis his brother; Philip, Landgrave of Hesse; Wolfgang, Prince of Anhalt. The Senate and Magistrate of Nuremberg, and the Senate of Reutlingen. Let the Imperial Recess of that same year be read, at the section <insert>"Thereafter have, &c."</insert> <note>original German: *Demnach haben, &c.*</note>.

The compiler of this Confession was Philipp Melanchthon, a disciple of Martin Luther, <note>The author uses a polemical Catholic tone here</note> an apostate from the Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine. From the very beginning of the nascent novelty, and thereafter until this day, the Confessionists have also been called Lutherans after their author, Luther. The same are also commonly called Protestants. They received this name in the Diet of Speyer in 1529 because, as Surius says, in that same year they refused to subscribe to certain decrees of the supreme Magistrate (see King Ferdinand, who presided over the Diet by the Emperor’s commission). See the *Composition of Peace*, chapter 1, question 1, and chapter 2, question 1.

### ADDITION.

The Augsburg Confession and the Catholic Religion ought to conduct themselves [with mutual respect]. Mundius *on offices*, page 491, number 308.

See the dissertations of Lord Doctor Johann Schmid and Lord Doctor Dorsch; likewise the year 1530, the repeated "Main Defense of the Apple of the Eye of the Holy Roman Empire" <note>original German: *Hauptvertheidigung deß H. R. Reichs Augapffel* - a famous 17th-century pro-Protestant legal defense</note>. Likewise the sermons held by Lord Fabricius on the same. Lord Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, pages 599, 601.

### 109. Leprosy. <note>German: *Ausatz*; Latin: *Lepra*</note>

On Leprosy and Lepers, see the individual treatise by André Laurent, and Guyon, *diverse lessons*, volume 2. Also Pontanus, *History of Amsterdam*, and *Foreign Voices of the New Testament*, folio 94. Also see my own work in the treatise *Considerations on Life and Death*. And regarding Lepers and why they are scarce today, see the Great Almoner of France, Sébastien Roulliard, folio 267 and following; Camerarius, *Leisure Hours*, century 2, chapter 74.

Antonius Bullaeus, in *Individual Decades of Counsels*, response 1, question 7, proves with authorities and reasons that leprosy or any other disease—even contagious and incurable ones, such as the French disease <note>syphilis</note>, the Spanish disease, etc.—does not dissolve a marriage once it has been contracted. See his work. However, it is established from chapter 3 *on the marriage of lepers* that betrothals and promises for the future are dissolved if the disease was unknown; thus a healthy person should not be compelled to proceed with a leper against their will, yet they cannot be rejected if they wish to proceed. See said chapter 1.

->ADDITION.<-

Lepers who are healed are commanded to offer a *Sparrow*, according to the Vulgate translation of Leviticus 4:4 <note>The author likely means Leviticus 14:4</note>. This is because, due to the sharpness of their humors, they are very lustful, just like sparrows, which sometimes mate seven times in an hour. More on this in Dr. Saubert, *on Sacrifices*, page 599.

The question is asked: if a healthy person nevertheless wishes to consummate a marriage with a leper, taking no account of the leprosy, should they be prohibited by the Magistrate? See Cypraeus, *on betrothals*, chapter 13, number 2. On whether leprosy or Elephantiasis is a cause for divorce, see Rittershusius in the *Novels*, page 240, and the authors cited there.

### 110. Breaking Out. <note>German: *Ausbrechen*; Latin: *Effractio*</note>

<column-break/>

->ADDITION.<-

No one ought to leave prison, even if one is able to. Barbosa, book 3, chapter 7, axiom 2. One who flees from prison after an accusation has begun creates a proof for torture against himself. ### 111. Outside. <note>German: *Ausßerhalb*; Latin: *Extra*</note>

The word "Outside" <note>original: *Extra*</note> implies removal and separation, according to the law *absentem* in the Digest *on the meaning of words*. And if it is applied to a City, such as "outside the City," it is not understood as outside the walls of the City, but outside the continuous buildings of the City; under which name the suburbs are included. Archidiaconus in the chapter *statutum*, number 4 and following, *on elections* in the sixth book. It is different if the phrase is "outside the town" <note>original: *extra urbem*</note>, which is specifically contained by walls, as per the same law. Tuschus, letter D, conclusion 280.

->ADDITION.<-

"Beyond" <note>original: *Præterquam*</note>. Tiraquellus, book 1 *on retractions*, section 1, glossary 11, number 73. "Beyond what" <note>original: *Præter quid*</note>. Menochius, book 4, presumption 45, number 3.

### 112. Guaranteeing Indemnity Outside the Law.
->Promise of indemnity.<-

If someone promises that they will defend another "outside the law" or "by deed" <note>German: *Ausßerhalb Rechtens*; Latin: *extra jus, vel de facto*</note>, then those words receive an interpretation based on common law and on what is fair and good. From this it follows that one promising indemnity in such a way is not held liable if the thing is taken by force <note>de facto</note>, according to the final law in the Code *on actions of purchase*. Bartolus at the law *stipulatio ista*, number 5, *on verbal obligations*. Ruinus, counsel 147, number 3, volume 4. This especially holds true when the promising party has not specifically and by name taken a "fortuitous event" <note>an act of God or unpredictable accident</note> upon themselves; and thus they are not held liable even for that under a general obligation of indemnity. Instead, if any such thing happens, it must all be borne by the one to whom the responsibility for all damage and every fortuitous event has belonged without controversy since the time of the loan contract. For the act of a superior <note>a ruler or sovereign</note> is considered a fortuitous event. Bartolus at the law *Lucius* on *contracting a purchase*, and at the law *exceptione*, number 4, *on sureties*, and at the law *impudentiam*, *on evictions*. Baldus at the law *pignus* on *actions of pledge*.

And these things are so true that even if someone promises they wish to be held liable in the event that a thing is recovered through injustice, they are still not held liable for an unjust sentence delivered by a superior. Angelus, counsel 176. Alexander following Bartolus in the said law *exceptione*, number 4. Ernest Cothman, book 1, response 33, number 147 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

A promise of indemnity has no place in crimes <note>original: *maleficiis*</note>. Barbosa, book 9, chapter 38, axiom.

("If you are an honest fellow, and no rogue, then come out and defend yourself," <note>original: *Bist du ein redlicher Kerl, und kein Schelm, ſo komme heraus, und wehre dich dein*</note> or words to that effect). If a challenge is issued with such an offense, must the person challenged to a contest appear for the sake of defending his honor? It is denied, according to the traditions of Jason [Mainus] in law 3, number 34, of the Digest on Justice and Law <note>original: *ff. de Just. & Jur.*; "ff" is a standard abbreviation for the Digest of Roman Law</note>; also Ernest Cothmann, volume 5, response 2; Vasquez, book 1, *Illustrious Controversies*, chapter 18; Pinziger, question 59; and see especially Hunnius in *Criminal Disputations*, chapter 6, thesis 223; and Bulleus in *Academic Discourses*, discourse 1, number 23 and following.

Furthermore, the person challenged can remain with his honor intact in such a case; but if he does come [to fight], he is not usually punished in the ordinary way if he kills the challenger. However, the aforementioned authors discuss this question at greater length, to whom may be added Böckel, inquiry 6, number 12; Knipschildt in the *Treatise on Contracts*, disputation 13; Scheplitz on the *Customs of Brandenburg*; Zeiller on *Tragic Histories*; and the *Strasbourg Consultations*, volume 2, consultation 56.

On the other hand, others consider it ignominious for a Nobleman if he does not appear, and this is according to the custom of Germany, about which Sichardus testifies and discusses at length in consultation 8, among the criminal matters, number 41, page 26. He adds: he who is challenged and does not appear, or "flees Mars"—that is, "on the field" <note>original: *im Feld*</note>—is regarded among Nobles in the same way as a vassal who does not dare to stand with his Lord in the battle line. And he who is challenged regarding the limits of his honor and birthright—"on honor and lineage" <note>original: *auf Ehr und Herkommen*</note>—and does not appear, is regarded as if he has no share in honor. He is barred from the tables and drinking-parties of honorable men, and as a sign of this disgrace, it is customary for the cloth or napkin <note>The author refers to a social "shaming" ritual where a person's place at a communal table was literally cut away.</note> covering the table to be cut away for that portion and width which such a person occupied while sitting. Rudolph Agricola testifies that this type of marking and signal of disgrace was used among the Germans in his letter on the meeting of Emperor Frederick with Charles, Duke of Burgundy. Likewise, by custom, the one not appearing is considered effeminate and unworthy of honorable gatherings. Thus far, Sichardus.

Likewise, if one challenged to a Duel does not kill but only wounds the challenger, he is not held liable by a civil action, nor even for the expenses of medical care, as is hinted in the excerpts on the Title of the *Lex Aquilia* <note>The Lex Aquilia was the primary Roman law governing damages to property and personal injury.</note>, question 2, at the end.

And the person challenged who kills the challenger—even without the "moderation of blameless defense" <note>original: *moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ*; a legal term for proportional self-defense</note>—is not held to the ordinary penalty. See Köppen, observation 11; Berlich, conclusion 16. Nor is he held for damages to the injured party. I have argued this in the *Excerpts of Law* on the *Lex Aquilia*; and hence those challenging each other to a fight are not held to restitution in the "court of heaven" <note>original: *in foro poli*; referring to the court of God or conscience, rather than earthly law</note>, etc.

But Christopher de Capite Fontium <note>Also known as Christophe de Cheffontaines, a 16th-century theologian who wrote against the "point of honor."</note> attacks such challenges at length in his *Confutation of the Point of Honor*, as does the French book titled *The List of Honor* <note>original: *le liſt d' honeur*</note>. And there

<column-break/>

also exist recent and frequently repeated pragmatic sanctions <note>Official royal decrees</note> of Louis XIII, King of the French, by which he detests such challenges and fixes various penalties for them. See especially Zypaeus in his *Analysis of Pontifical Law*, book 5, title on those fighting in a Duel, page 471, where he teaches from Azor that five types of persons are found in duels: (1) Princes, Emperors, Kings, or other Lords who grant a Duel in the lands subject to them; (2) the combatants; (3) their patrons [seconds]; (4) those who advise or sometimes favor them; (5) the spectators who flock to the show.

And it should be noted here that in the Council of Trent, Session 25, chapter 19, the following penalties are contained: (1) All the aforementioned persons are excommunicated by the very fact <note>original: *ipso facto*</note>. (2) Lords who grant permission for a duel in their lands are deprived of jurisdiction over that land where they granted the permission, if they hold it from the Church; if it is a fief <note>original: *feudum*</note>, they are deprived of it so that the fief returns to the Direct Lord. (3) The combatants and their Patrons are marked with infamy <note>original: *infamia*; a legal status involving the loss of certain civil rights and standing.</note>. (4) They incur the confiscation of all goods and the penalty for homicide—that is, they must be punished as if they were murderers, even if death did not follow. (5) Those dying in a Duel are deprived of Christian burial, etc. And of these penalties, excommunication is incurred by the act itself, while the other penalties are incurred through the sentence of a Judge.

->ADDITION.<-

The Republic would never or rarely be peaceful if it were allowed for everyone, as often as an injury arose, to "enter the arena," since the compensation of an injury [by private force] is not only hostile to the law, but also to peace. "For there is a law, a court, and a judge, unless one is ashamed to seek vindication by law," are the words of Quintilian; and for that reason, the sacred reverence of the laws was discovered, so that nothing should be done by hand or by one's own impulse. Cassiodorus, letter 10, book 4. To this point look the texts in the Digest, book 13, § 3: "Why should the praetor allow those to proceed to arms and strife whom he can settle by the power of his jurisdiction?" Also the Code, book 14, *On Jews*: "Therefore the vigor of the courts and the protection of public law are seen to be established in our midst, lest anyone should be able to permit himself vengeance." And law 176 of the Digest *On the Rules of Law*: "What ought to be done through public persons or Magistrates must not be granted to individuals or private citizens, lest there be an occasion for a riot." Therefore, a challenger, even if no damage followed, is punished at the discretion of the Judge, according to the condition of his person. The aforesaid points, however, proceed in that case where a Judge is available and false accusers can be punished through legal channels. It is otherwise if a judge or the slanderer is not available in court. However, it is not permitted for one challenged by insulting words to appear [for a duel], even if the most atrocious words were used. See the Digest, law 15, § 2 and 27, *On Injuries*. But what if the person challenged...

### 114. **By Grace.** <note>original: *Aus Gnaden* / *Ex gratia*</note>

The word "grace" is added for the most part by custom, and Princes are accustomed to use it even in contracts, as reported in Gylman’s *Symphorema*, volume 1, part 1, title on counter-claims, vote 1, number 88, in the case of Erfurt versus Mainz.

->**ADDITION.**<-

Grace granted due to merits is a kind of exchange and a burdensome act <note>original: *actus onerosus*; meaning it involves an obligation or cost rather than being a pure gift</note>, according to Klock, volume 1, consultation 7, number 245; therefore it cannot be revoked (numbers 246 and 248) and it passes into a Contract (number 247). See the contrary in number 342 and following. Graces that exceed justice do not even deserve the name of grace, according to Bulleus in his *Consultations*, page 242. **Letter of Grace** <note>original: *Gnadenbrieff*</note>, or letters of familiarity, in the *Acts of Lindau*, page 604. Grace which has not yet achieved its effect expires upon the death of the one granting it (Klock, volume 1, consultation 7, number 615; see however numbers 696, 697, 701, 702, 705, and 706).

In cases of doubt, acts are not presumed to be permitted by grace <note>that is, as a favor</note>, but rather exercised by right of servitude and for the sake of confirming a right (Bulleus, page 236).

Grace is not presumed (Klock, consultation 10, numbers 444, 445), except among those accustomed to granting graciously (Barboso, book 7, chapter 10, axiom 8). No thanks are owed to one who pays what they owe (argued from the beginning of the *Institutes* on obligations and actions). Regarding that solemn formula, "We, by the Grace of God" <note>original: *Nos Dei gratia*</note>: although Paris de Puteo (in his treatise *On the Duel*, book 7) and Bodin (book 1 of *The Republic*, chapter 10) teach that it belongs to no one except him who recognizes no superior besides God and the sword, nevertheless the Princes of the Empire and other immediate superiors <note>those who report directly to the Emperor</note> similar to them now use this formula (Matthias Stephani on *Jurisdiction*, part 7, book 2, chapter 7, number 41). Serres (in book 1 of his *Inventory*) reports that in France, no one would dare write this without the crime of treason <note>original: *crimine laesae Majestatis*</note>. However, it should not be overlooked that the aforementioned Princes of the Empire do not use this formula when they send letters to the Emperor, but only when they write to their equals or inferiors, or when they command or decree in their own territories. They do this toward equals at the end and in the signatures, and toward inferiors at the beginning of the letters (Reinhold, book 1, class 5, chapter 6, number 202). Add on this formula Besold in his *Politics*, book 1, chapter 2, number 13, where he says that the Princes of Germany use this inscription not by their own right, but by privilege.

<column-break/>

### 115. **Lodging.** <note>original: *Ausspann*; literally "unhitching," referring to a place to rest horses and travelers</note> Dwellings, Right of Hospitality.

**Ausspann** is the common name for dwellings established in antiquity on estates, lands, and Monasteries, as noted by the magnificent Lord Martin Mager in his treatise of incomparable learning *On the Armed Advocate*, chapter 10, numbers 222 and 256. Formerly, these places were called *mansiomatici* or "mansions"—places where one had the right of turning aside and lodging, whether by ownership, some contract, or ancient custom of which no interrupted memory exists among men.

And this right belongs primarily to Great Lords <note>original: *Magnatibus*</note> and Patrons in the Monasteries for which they are Advocates, **for the sake of protection and defense** <note>original: *wegen deß Schutz und Schirms*</note>: specifically, so that they may **lodge their hunting party there, and also that they and their people may unharness their horses while passing through** <note>original: *das Geyägt daselbst einlosieren, auch sie und die Ihrige im Durchziehen ausspannen*</note>, and other similar burdens that exist.

If this is done by a settled agreement, it is rightly observed; but if not, it is wrongly introduced as something new, etc.

->**ADDITION.**<-

A *mansiomaticum* is a place in which one has the right of turning aside by custom, ownership, or some contract (Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 91, number 15). Albergaria <note>Albergary</note> is nothing other than lodging or the provision of hospitality. Hospitality is a "real burden" <note>a legal obligation attached to the land itself</note>. Hostiensis (in the *Summa on Immunity*, number 7, chapter 1) says: Laity ought not to seek or demand *albergum* or lodging from the Church as if it were a debt. The late Lord Doctor Tabor (on *Metata*, page 93) notes that since to the Italians *Albergare* is the same as to lodge or receive into a house, they call hospitality *Albergaria* (lodging and quarters). Regarding **stoppers, horse-drivers, and carters** <note>original: *Ausspannern, Pferdnern, Huffnern*</note>, and whether and to what extent they are bound to provide services or labor for constructing the Lords' buildings, Berlich treats this in conclusion 65 throughout. **Provisions** <note>original: *Atzung*</note> or the Right of Albergary is a sign of superiority, prohibited by Common Law (Klock, volume 2, consultation 98). The Right of Albergary, or **provisions**, otherwise known as **lodging** <note>original: *Ausspann*</note>, which many States of the Empire have in Monasteries, differs from the simple Right of Hospitality (Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 80, at the end).

...they shall have as heirs. *Part 3, title 2, section 17.* However, when these children are still minors, for whom immovable property, livestock, or similar assets in the inheritance are not beneficial, everything is converted into a definite sum of money. This must be paid to them at a set time, or when they reach the age of majority. This sum is commonly called an **Adjudication** <note>original: *Ausspruch*</note> or **Settlement** <note>original: *Ausmahnung*; these terms refer to the legal process of fixing a specific cash value for a child's inheritance instead of giving them physical land or animals</note>, and it serves somewhat as inheritance money, which in Saxon law is commonly called **Inheritance Money** <note>original: *Erbgeld*</note>. Scheplitz, in his work on the *Customs of Brandenburg, part 3, title 2, section 17, number 2*, and Daffelius, in his *Commentary on the Customs of Lüneburg, article 1, number 1*, states: to "make an adjudication" <note>original: *einen Ausspruch thun*</note> is nothing other than to define a certain amount that the children of a first marriage ought to receive from both the maternal and paternal goods, and to make them secure in the name of that defined sum. See Scheplitz in the cited place, number 3, and Cothman, *Consultation 5, volume 1, number 5, at the end.* This term "Adjudication" agrees somewhat with the **Right of Partition** <note>original: *Theilungsrecht*</note> and the **Right of Entanglement** <note>original: *Verfangenrecht*</note>. Regarding what these specific types mean among the Swabians <note>People of Southwestern Germany</note>, one may consult Caspar Wilhelm Scipio in *Decisions of the Imperial Chamber Court at Speyer, book 2, decision 102 and following.*

### ADDITION.

The author says that the **Right of Entanglement** <note>original: *Verfangen-Recht*; a legal restriction where property is "entangled" or reserved for children of a first marriage when a parent remarries</note> agrees with this term. On this law, see Tilemann de Benignis, Rudinger, Scipio, and Keller. This law is observed in Esslingen for both a husband and a wife entering into a second marriage. Knipschild, in *On Entails, chapter 15, number 23*, lists in great detail which assets are called **entangled goods** <note>original: *verfangene Güter*</note>.

### 117. Dowry. <term>Dos</term>.

By this word <note>original: *Aussteuer*</note> is meant not only the Dowry—which is properly called the **Bride’s Treasure** <note>original: *Brautschatz*</note> and not usually the *Aussteuer*—but the term includes all expenses and burdens incurred and contributed for the marriage of daughters. Since the word "to provide a dowry" <note>original: *aussteuern*</note> means nothing other than to marry off, the word *Aussteuer* is therefore nothing other than the expenses made for married daughters. The word *Aussteuer* cannot be taken to mean the Dowry alone, except very improperly and in a very restricted sense. Mr. Ernst Cothmann, *book 1, response 3, numbers 62 and 64.*

### ADDITION.

A dowry of one thousand Ducats is appropriate for a Count. On how large dowries usually are among the Venetians; what kind of dowry is given to Duchesses in the Duchy of Württemberg; and what kind is common among the people of Marseille. These and other matters are found in Knipschild’s *On Entails*. Many points regarding the dowry are collected by Barbosa and by Klock in *On the Treasury*.

<column-break/>

### 118. Uprooting, Forest Sheaf, or Clearing Sheaf. <term>Eradicatio</term>.

The **Uprooting of trees** <note>original: *Ausstocken*</note> is not permitted for the property owner if it is against the will of those who hold the **Forestry Authority** <note>original: *Forstliche Obrigkeit*</note>. This is based on what Cepolla teaches in his *Treatise on Rural Servitudes, chapter 9, number 40*, as well as the Code of Justinian. This, however, is not to be understood as applying to modest clearings, following the reasoning of Bartolus. See also the specific legal opinions on this matter among the various consultations collected and recently published by me in folio, consultation 16 and following.

From this it follows that the **Lords of the Forest** <note>original: *Forstherren*</note> demand the **tenth sheaf** <note>original: *zehende Garb*; a tithe</note> from fields that have been newly cleared, as compensation for the harm done to the Hunt by the uprooting of trees. They call this a **Forest Sheaf** or **Clearing Sheaf** <note>original: *Forst- oder Stockgarb*</note>, and they do not consider it a **New-land Tithe** <note>original: *Noval-Zehenden*; a tithe normally paid to the church on newly farmed land</note>. They also wish to defend themselves with this argument against the tithe-lords and the parish priests <note>who would otherwise claim the tithe for the church</note>.

Concerning a tenant <note>original: *emphyteuta*</note> who uprooted an olive grove and planted a vineyard without the Lord's permission: Valascus, when consulted, responded in favor of the tenant in the proposed case, saying that he should be excused from penalty because he proved the olive grove was already old and used to give little fruit, and some of the trees were almost useless. Therefore, by planting a fruitful vineyard there, he did not deserve the penalty for a breach of contract, based on the reasons alleged there.

### ADDITION.

In the County of **Saarwerden** <note>original: *Saurvvertano*</note> a few years ago, by the advice of the most noble Johann Philipp Streiff von Lauenstein, land covered with forests and brambles was cultivated in such a way that the Counts of Nassau increased their annual income by many thousands of gold coins.

Those whose legal documents retain that ancient clause protect themselves well:
> The right to the tithe on new clearings, new fields, and wherever the rain crosses, remains untouched.

The word **New-land** <note>original: *Novale*</note> is ambiguous and has two meanings. In its broad sense, the jurist Gaius defines it thus: *Novalis* is land that has been cut back and has rested for a year <note>fallow land</note>. In this broad sense, the name *Novale* also applies to a field which is commonly called **Fallow Land** <note>original: *Brackland*</note>. The other meaning is stricter, where *Novale* is land newly brought back to cultivation, of which there is no memory that it was ever cultivated before. **Ground and soil** <note>original: *Gründ und Boden*</note> that is broken for the first time; where one clears brush, shrubs, and twigs, digs out trees or old stumps, stones, roots, and the like, burns them out, clears them, and then breaks and farms such land. This kind of field does not stop being "new-land" if it is cultivated again, but retains its name and the right of new-lands...
