Regarding deserted places and tithes on newly cultivated land <note>Latin: *decimis Novalibus*; a "noval" tithe was a tax on land recently brought under the plow</note>, see Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 70. These "exboscations" <note>Latin: *Exboscationes*; a legal term for clearing woods</note>, as they are crudely called, are the acts of bringing uncultivated places into use by uprooting thickets, stumps, and forests: the clearing of wild hedges, heaths, and shrubs. <note>Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation on Fiefs*, 12, thesis 7, letter D; see also Knipschild on the obligations of a lord toward a vassal, pages 167 and 173.</note>

### 119. Special Arbitration. <note>original: *Austräg*; Latin: *Austregæ*</note>

It is well established that for those subject to the Empire indirectly <note>Latin: *mediate*; meaning they answer to a local lord who then answers to the Emperor</note>, at least three different levels of court <note>Latin: *Instantiæ*</note> are available. Through these, they may press their rights at different times, recovering or bringing forward what was lost through neglect or wrongly rejected.

Therefore, it seemed unworthy that the Estates subject to the Empire directly <note>Latin: *immediatè*; the "Imperial Estates" who answer only to the Emperor</note>—such as Electors, Princes, Prelates, Counts, Barons, and Nobles established in higher dignity—should be in a clearly worse condition, having to entrust themselves, their persons, and their cases to only a single level of court, not without danger. <note>Gail, book 1, observation 1, number 17; Vultejus; Caspar Ziegler.</note> For this reason, it pleased the Great Men of the Empire, with the Emperor's consent, that they should have the Privilege of Arbitration <note>Latin: *Privilegium Austregarum*</note> in place of a first-level court, so they would not be immediately dragged before the Imperial Chamber Court <note>Latin: *Cameræ Tribunal*</note>. Otherwise, they would be compelled to appear directly in the Chamber. <note>Petrus Friderus Mindanus, *On Process*, book 1, chapter 16.</note> Because of this, anyone who usually has their first court appearance in the Chamber Court is proven to be a State of the Empire. <note>Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, chapter 1.</note>

These are called *die Austräg*, from the word *Austragen* <note>meaning to carry out or settle a dispute</note>, because certain members subject to the Holy Roman Empire without a middleman should settle or resolve <note>original German: *austragen oder beylegen*</note> their differences, errors, and disagreements against one another through this means, according to the measure and manner prescribed in the Imperial statutes. <note>Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 10; see Ziegler, who brings 12 expansions on in which cases this privilege applies.</note> Note also Riemer, *On Modern Jurisdiction*.

It should be noted here that there are various types of

<column-break/>

**Arbitrations** <note>original: *Austräg*</note>; some are found in the Chamber Court Ordinances, as is clear from what follows; some are **stipulated arbitrations** <note>original: *bedingte Austräg*</note>, as occurs in contracts or dowry agreements, where people agree on certain persons and methods for how emerging disputes should be resolved. These are also called **voluntary arbitrations** <note>original: *willkührliche Austräg*</note>. There are also **inheritance arbitrations** <note>original: *Erbausträg*</note>, discussed below under that term. And finally, the **Silesian Knightly Right** is a special kind of arbitration.

It must be understood, however, that regarding these privileged levels of court, the *Austräg*, a threefold order of parties is established in the Chamber Court Ordinance <note>part 2, titles 1, 2, and 4</note>.

To the **first order** belong the Electors, Princes, and those endowed with Princely dignity, both Clergy and Laymen. <note>original German: *Churfürsten, Fürsten, und Fürstenmäßige*; Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 2.</note>

In the **second order** are placed the Prelates, Counts, Barons, Nobles, and Cities subject directly to the Empire. <note>original German: *Prälaten, Graffen, Freyen, Herren, die vom Adel und die Städte*; Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 4.</note>

To the **third order** are referred all those subject to the Empire indirectly <note>Latin: *mediate*</note>, who recognize intermediate judges before reaching the Chamber Court. <note>Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 1: "Persons who are not subject to the Empire without a middleman, but to other courts."</note> On the matter of these arbitrations, see Ludovicus Gilhauf, *The Tree of Civil Justice*, and others like Schvvanman and Georg Schubhart.

Rittershusius notes that the **Imperial Cities** also have these arbitrations among themselves. For example, **Strasbourg**, in cases involving the city, obtains judges for the first instance from Worms, Ulm, Basel, Nuremberg, Winsheim, and Weissenburg. **Dinkelsbühl** uses its City Magistrate <note>original German: *Stadt-Ammann*</note>, who takes four assistants, and an equal number from the cities of Nördlingen, Rothenburg ob der Tauber, Schwäbisch Hall, and Donauwörth <note>Latin: *Werda Suevorum*</note>. **Esslingen**, in city cases, allows the ordinary judges, Consuls, and Senates of the cities of Ulm, Reutlingen, and Heilbronn; the choice is up to the plaintiff. **Friedberg** in Wetterau uses the Burgrave and the castle-men <note>Latin: *Burgmannos*</note>. **Regensburg**, in its city business, uses the Council and Senate of Augsburg, Nuremberg, and Ulm; or at the plaintiff’s pleasure, five or seven members from its own Senate. **Reutlingen** uses the Council and Senate of the cities of Ulm, Esslingen, and Schwäbisch Gmünd. **Schweinfurt** has its first instance before its Imperial Bailiff <note>original German: *Reichsvogt*</note>, who takes several Senators...

...joins the judges of Nuremberg and Rothenburg <note>Both were prominent Imperial Cities with significant legal jurisdictions</note>. Schwanmann, *On Chamber Procedure*, book 1, chapter 7. Peter Friedrich, *On Extraordinary Chamber Procedure*, book 1, section 6, at the end.

I do not believe, however, that the judgment of the Special Arbitration Courts <note>original Latin: *Austregarum*; German: *Austräg*—a privileged court where Princes of the Empire settled disputes among themselves</note> can be extended to criminal cases. Reason argues against it, as it is unfitting for criminal accusations to be conducted in such a manner, or for one Imperial State to proceed against another in this way. See my treatise *On the Tribunals of Domestic Society*, leaf 83, where I also add: the privilege of these arbitration courts ceases if a State holds property in another’s territory and is sued in the name of that property; for in that instance, the State is treated as a private citizen. See Wilhelm Anton, *Corollaries to the Treatise on Letters of Moratorium*, leaf 30.

Regarding counter-claims <note>Latin: *Reconventioni*</note>, however, I hardly doubt that there is a place for them in these courts. Giessebert, *On Counter-claims*, chapter 8. Ursinus, in his treatise on the same subject, chapter 27—who compiles Giessebert’s writings everywhere, or rather, placed his own name on Giessebert’s work.

Does the legal principle that "the cohesion of a case should not be divided" <note>Latin: *ne continentia causae dividatur*; a rule preventing a single legal dispute from being split into different courts</note> also apply to these Arbitration Courts—for example, if there are several princes who must be summoned before them? I answer: if there are co-defendants present who do not have the benefit of the Special Arbitration <note>original German: *der Außtråg*</note>, or who have different arbitration rights, then that principle applies. This is noted by Mynsinger, *Observations*, observation 4, century 1. Such a procedure was decreed against Lord Georg Friedrich, Marquis of Brandenburg, and his co-defendants. See Rutger Ruland in his notes on the procedures of Ferrarius Montanus, chapter 10, leaf 68.

But this question is controversial in many ways: can the Aulic Council of His Imperial Majesty <note>The *Reichshofrat*, one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note> be approached immediately, thereby stripping the Imperial States of this benefit of the First Instance? Indeed, legal practice answers in the affirmative. See my treatise *On the Mixed State*, leaf 219, and the treatise *On Jurisdiction*, question 12. One may also see Meichsner, volume 4, discussion 4; Lord Arumaeus, volume 1, discussions 10 and 13, and volume 4, discussion 29; Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, chapter 4, number 124 and following; the *Donauwörth Reminder*, leaf 177 and following. This question is also discussed in the *Hessian Acts* concerning Marburg.

## 120. Absconding. <note>original German: *Austretten*; Latin: *Fuga*</note>

In certain places, when a killer <note>original German: *Todtschläger*</note> takes flight <note>original German: *flüchtigen Fuß setzet*</note> and is later legally accused, his goods fall to the Lord, and his body <note>meaning the compensation for his life</note> to the kin of the deceased. But this is opposed by Article 206 and Article 208 of the *Constitutions of Charles V* <note>The *Carolina*, the unified criminal code of the Empire</note>. Such a custom is certainly irrational and therefore void; consequently, it is only fair that the children of the deceased should have preference in this matter <note>original German: *diß Orts, den Vorzug haben*</note>.

## 121. Meadow-Right. <note>original German: *Au-Recht*; Latin: *Gæa*</note>

Among other things that make the matter of jurisdiction in Silesia obscure and difficult—according to Schifordegker, book 3, treatise 29, chapter 7, at the beginning—there is also that question being debated regarding the *Gæa*, or the Meadow-Right <note>original German: *von dem Au-Recht*</note>. It should be known that the Silesians understand by *Gæa* <note>original German: *unter dem Au-Recht*</note> that place contained in the middle of a hamlet or village which is separated from the huts and barns of the villagers. For in Saxon Law <note>original German: *Jure Saxonico*</note>, a place is called a "village" if it is surrounded by a fence and a ditch. *Landrecht*, book 2, title 55. This is also proven by Civil Law, in which a "villa" is said to be that which is not surrounded by a wall. Wurmser, book 1, title 2, observation 2. Matthaeus Stephani, *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, part 2, chapter 1, number 15. Furthermore, it is established in Civil Law that a village contains within itself jurisdiction, honor, district, the Right of Patronage, and similar things. Rochus de Curte, in the treatise *On the Right of Patronage*, word: *ipse velis*, questions 2 and 3. Baldus... Hence a castle or a village is called a "universal thing." Schrader, *On Fiefs*, part 3, chapter 4, number 25 and following. According to these rules, the Silesians—as the same Schifordegker attests—maintain that the space in the middle of the hamlet or village belongs entirely to the Lord of the village, so that the peasants and rustics have no right in it, and they are completely incapable of holding that right, the Meadow-Right <note>original German: *deß Au-Rechtens*</note>. This is especially true since it is clear that this particular place, called *Gæa* or Meadow-Right <note>original German: *Aue-Recht*</note>, cannot be possessed by private individuals, namely peasants and rustics. For from the beginning, they acquired their goods without this right; while in the original deed of sale, mention is made of this right belonging to the private individual who first acquired the goods, yet the boundaries and borders are usually expressed with great diligence, describing how each peasant estate <note>original German: *Bauer-Gut*</note> is situated along its limits and borders. Therefore, it remains that from the very beginning, the possession and lordship of this particular place...

Schifordegker <note>Likely Caspar Schiffordecker, a 17th-century legal scholar</note> in the cited place elegantly and most solidly treats this question: namely, whether the **Meadow-Right** <note>original: *Gæa*, or *das Aue-Recht*; refers to the right to use fertile floodplain meadows</note> belongs to the Jurisdiction? The peasants in Silesia today, by the grant of their lords, have the convenience of receiving the fruits of the **Meadow**, for which they pay an annual tax <note>original: *censum*</note>. ### 122. Albertiner.

An **Albertiner** <note>A silver coin, likely the Albertusthaler, named after Archduke Albert of Austria</note> is worth 22 and a half **Batzen**, which is 1 and a half Bohemian **Florins**; that is, 22 Batzen plus a half. A double Albertiner is worth 45 Batzen, which is 3 Bohemian Florins. Discussed at length by Alemann in *The Arena of Consultations*, page 538, number 21.

### 123. To Assault.

A vassal is deprived of his fief if he **assaults** <note>original Latin: *assilierit*</note> his Lord, or makes an attack upon his castle or his house, whether the lord is present with his wife or not. See Book 1, Section "Similarly by which modes a fief is lost." An **assault** is an attack against a person or place, whether it is done on foot or on horse, or with siege engines or any other thing. If the vassal knew it was the Lord’s dwelling, whether the Lord was present or absent, and whether the vassal knew of the Lord's presence or was ignorant of it, he is liable. Gemmel, in the *Compendium of Feudal Law*, page 108, interprets the word "**assaulted**" as "besieged" or "attacked." See also Book 2, Title 6, and Rittershusius in *Feudal Partitions*, page 434.

### 124. To Waste. Prodigality.

For what this word denotes, see the Distinguished Doctor Tabor in *Criminal Clusters*, page 97.

### 125. Abecedarian.

Jerome, in the Mosaic discipline, uses the word: **Abecedarians** <note>original: *Abecedarii*</note>, those who learn the A, B, C. Was the Emperor Justinian illiterate? <note>original: *analphabetus*</note> See Rittershusius in the *New Constitutions*, page 665; and at length the Distinguished Doctor Cobius at Section 6 of the *Proemium of the Institutes*, question 8, throughout; and there he cites Balduinus, Hoenonius, Harprecht, Besold, Timaeus Faber, Procopius, Giphanus, Platina, and Ungepauer.

### 126. Old.

The ancient word **Alt** denotes the same as the disjunctive word **oder** <note>meaning "or"</note>. *Acts of Lindau*, leaf 194, in the middle of 805.

### 128. Outflows.

**Ausläuff** is the name given to that part of the Halle saltworks—a cauldron <note>original: *lebetem*</note>—belonging to the Bishop of Magdeburg. Matthias Stephani, *On Jurisdiction*, book 3, part 1, chapter 7, number 15, leaf 83 and following.

### 129. In the Act. Immediately.

See Sprenger, *On the Physician*, page 160. See also Doctor Helden’s *Opinions on Trespass*, where the witnesses held that if the perpetrator is caught **red-handed** <note>original: *auf frischer That*</note> within 24 hours, the punishment does not belong to the local bailiff <term>Vogteyherrn|A local administrative official or protector</term>, but to the High Criminal Authority <term>Malefiz-Obrigkeit|The authority over capital crimes, such as murder or robbery</term>. To this also belongs the settlement between Neuburg and Nuremberg, dated October 21 (31), 1664, number 2.

### 130. Adam, Adamus. See below under the word: Virginity.

Johannes Feron, a lawyer in Paris, reports that **Adam** bore a red shield to remind himself of the red earth from which he was created, and in such a shield a black apple was to be seen, to signify his heavy Fall into sin. Edward Bysshe in the *Notes on Nicholas Upton's Treatise on the Military Office*, leaf 39.

Regarding the name of **Adam**, see Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 11, number 78. Coelius Rhodiginus, book 2 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 21, page 59. Those who attempt to build a case for the excellence of women over men from the fact that woman came forth from a rib—unlike Adam who was made from a clod of earth—toil in vain, as does Cornelius Agrippa in *On the Nobility and Preeminence of the Female Sex*, page 19. They write that **Eve** was created in Paradise, but Adam was created outside of Paradise in the field of Damascus. Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 2, number 19. There are several treatises extant regarding **Pre-adamites** <note>People theorized to have existed before the biblical Adam</note>. Regarding when Adam was created and fell, see Distinguished Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 469. Regarding the **fallen Adam**, see Mr. Harsdörffer’s *Spiritual History-Speeches*, part 1. Thenceforth after the "tunics of skin" <note>Genesis 3:21</note>, that is, after the fall of man. The creation of **Adam and Eve** happened not "in time," but "with time." Augustine, book 2 of *The City of God*, chapter 40, and book 12 of the *Confessions*. Regarding the descendants of Adam and Eve, one may read in Eyring’s *German Proverbs*, leaf 164.

### 131. As. <note>original: *Als. Tanquam.*</note>
An Emperor, when acting as a Roman King, should be understood not just as if he were one, but as truly being one; the word **As** <note>original: *Als*</note> is not to be understood in a doubling sense <note>original: *reduplicativè*; a logic term meaning the word describes the person's specific capacity or office</note>. Limnaeus, *on Public Law, book 3, chapter 9, number 36.*

The word "just as" <note>original: *tanquam*</note> denotes a lack of literal propriety and sometimes expresses the truth of a matter. Mantica *on Conjectures of Last Wills, book 3, title 16, number 6.* See also Boerius, *Decision 44, number 29.*

### 132. Backwater. <note>original: *Altwasser*; literally "old water," referring to an oxbow lake or abandoned river arm</note>
In an old feudal charter, I find these words: "The fishing water, etc., together with its out-flowing and in-flowing backwaters." Such water had been abandoned for many years, and no one had inquired after these backwaters. When the new lord of the fishing water asked about them, one person said they no longer existed in the nature of things <note>original: *in rerum natura*</note>; another believed it could be a lake situated nearby; the third said he had the oldest knowledge of the matter. He claimed one arm was the in-flowing backwater. When this arm overflows and runs out onto the neighboring meadows, it becomes the out-flowing backwater. However, the owner of the meadows uses this little lake himself during the time of the flooding; it is asked whether he does so by legal right?

### 133. Inspection Court. <note>original: *Aischgericht*; a court or official body responsible for the calibration of weights and measures</note>
What this is, is common practice in our court.

### 134. Bloodletting. <note>original: *Aderlaß. Venae Sectio.*</note>
Two days before the Margrave of Beveron died in Paris in the year 1650, he was bled, and from his vein a worm, a span <note>approximately 9 inches</note> long, was drawn out. Zeiller, *Century 4, question 24, page 116.* In which diseases should bloodletting be preferred over purging? Caspar Hoffmann *in the promotion of Caspar Horn, 1626.*

Bloodletting is said to be fatal on the Feast of the Annunciation <note>March 25th</note>. Mr. Dilherr *in Course of Time and the World, page 450.* Emperor Philip was stabbed to death after bloodletting, page 597. The hippopotamus teaches us the cutting of the vein <note>referring to the ancient belief that hippos would bleed themselves by pressing against sharp reeds</note>. Limnaeus *in Public Law, book 8, chapter 4, number 17.* In Spain, the barbers bleed on the left and right, according to the French fashion. Zeiller *in Spanish Journey, page 85.* In Gold City, Guinea, they use no bloodletting at all, except that they sometimes cut a wound or several into the body with a knife so that the blood may run out. Levinus Hulsius. This man knows how to bleed even a gnat. Antenor *in Solomon, chapter 4.* Whether it is necessary for a man to occasionally use bloodletting to preserve his health. Felix Plater *in Medical Questions, question 73.* Regarding bloodletting in hypochondriac melancholy, in the treatment of epilepsy, in malignant fevers, and in kidney disease, see the *Medical Counsels of Balthasar Brunner.*

<margin>Besoldus, Volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

### 135. Field Hay. <note>original: *Ackerheu*</note>
It is called "Field Hay" when it grows on overgrown fields that are not yet being cultivated.

### 136. Ammeister. <note>original: *Ammeisterus*; the chief magistrate of the free city of Strasbourg</note>
Ammeister. He is the highest magistrate in the City of Strasbourg. Draco *on Patricians, page 260.* In the Chamber of the Fifteen Lords <note>original: *Herrn XV. Stuben*; one of the ruling councils of Strasbourg</note> there is a wooden cup upon which all the Ammeisters' coats of arms are painted on parchment around it. The things that Scherb brings forward concerning the Ammeister according to custom are ridiculous. *in Politics, page 111 (in my copy).*

### 137. Crossbow Range. <note>original: *Armbrustrein*</note>
Mornac *on law 7 of the Justinian Code regarding tracks* concerning the pretended privileges of those who practice with bows and cannons on the Field of Mars <note>original: *campo Martio*; a public exercise ground</note>. Strasbourg *Police Ordinance, page 37, section 38.* The late Mr. Dr. Tabor *on Billeting, page 256.*

### 138. Ash, Ash Wednesday. <note>original: *Asch, Aschermittwoch. Cinis Dies cinerum.*</note>
Concerning a man who swore that if the matter were not so, he would suffer his body to turn to ashes. This indeed happened that same night. Zeiller *Century 4, question 24, page 116.* Why barbers were called "ash-men" <note>original: *cinerarii*; likely referring to the use of hot ashes for hair curling in antiquity</note>, Pancirollus *in New Discoveries, page 372 (in my copy).* Concerning hair-curlers and ash-men, Rupert *on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 1, difference 2, section 3.*

Concerning Ash Wednesday or the Day of Ashes, treated extensively by Georg von Hassel *on the Law of the Lenten Season, thesis 34 and following.* Mr. Dilherr *in Course of Time and the World, page 414, section 10.* Mr. Fürer *in Latin Journey, page 90.*

### 139. Arve and Hagab, that is, Locusts. <note>original: *Arve und Hagab, i. e. Heuschrecken. Locusta.*</note>
<note>Translating the Hebrew terms for various species of locusts mentioned in the Bible.</note> Mr. Dilherr *in Contemplations of the World, Field, and Garden, page 514.*

### 140. Suspicion. <note>original: *Argwohn. Suspicio.*</note>
An equal cause of affection excludes suspicion. Hartmann Hartmann *book 2 of miscellaneous practical observations, chapter 1, observation 23, number 1.*

### 141. Air. <note>An obscure unit of currency or tax, possibly related to "Ayr" or a regional variation.</note>
60 Guilders Air. See Limnaeus *volume 2, Additions to book 7, chapter 2, page 84.* 8 Marks Air, *page 85.*

### 142. Provisions, Fodder. <note>original: *Atz, Atzung. Alimentatio.*</note>
This is referred to the Right of Sovereignty and Royal Prerogatives. Klock *Counsel 9, numbers 16, 17, 18, 19.* See however numbers 83, 84, 85, and *Counsel 10, numbers 265 through 272.* Provisions and other burdens deviate from the common law. *Counsel 10, numbers 278 through 285.*

### 143. Ancestor. <note>original: *Anherr. Avus.*</note>
Great-grandparents <note>original: *Ubereltern*</note>. Rudinger *Century 5, Observation 3, in the preface.*

# Practical Treasuries Expanded

<columns>
...specifically belonged to the lord of the village, etc. 
Schifordegker <note>likely the jurist Johann Schifordegker</note> in the cited place, treats this question—whether the <term>Aue-Recht</term> <note>the right to use or profit from riverside meadows and floodplains</note>, also called "Gæa," belongs to the local jurisdiction—at length and with great solidity. In the following chapter, he states: Today in Silesia, peasants have the convenience of harvesting fruits in the floodplains by grant of the lords, for which they pay an annual tax. However, they cannot acquire the legal right itself through "prescription" <note>the legal principle where long-term use creates a right of ownership</note>, nor do the subjects possess anything that belongs to the jurisdiction and ownership of the village. He notes that while they may have "natural possession" of this right at times, it is not sufficient for a legal claim of ownership. This specific area, the <term>Au-Recht</term>, pertains to the public utility of the village as a corporate community, where the rules of prescription do not apply, similar to the laws governing towns and cities.

## ADDITION.

Trithemius, in the *Chronicles of Sponheim* for the year 1325 (page 308), mentions a monastery village called <term>Auen</term> <note>literally "Meadows"</note> and notes that the inhabitants of that village must give twelve measures of oats and twelve chickens every year to the feudal advocate <note>the official representing the monastery's secular interests</note> as part of their feudal duty.

### 122. Albertiner.

An <term>Albertiner</term> <note>a gold or silver coin named after the sovereign who minted it, likely Albert of Saxony</note> is worth 22 1/2 <term>Batzen</term> <note>a common silver coin used in Southern Germany and Switzerland</note>, which is equal to 1 1/2 <term>Bohemian Guilders</term>, or 22 Batzen plus a half. A double Albertiner is worth 45 Batzen, which is 3 <term>Bohemian Guilders</term>. *Discussed at length by Alemann in his "Palestra of Consultations," page 538, number 21.*

### 123. Assaulting a Lord. <note>original: *Assilire*</note>

If a vassal assaults his Lord, or attacks his castle or his house—provided the Lord is present with his wife—he is deprived of his fief <note>the land held in exchange for service</note>. *See Chapter 1, section "similarly," regarding the ways a fief is lost.* An "assault" <note>original: *assultus*</note> is an attack against a person or place, whether carried out on foot, on horseback, with machines, or by any other means. This applies if the vassal knew it was the Lord’s residence, regardless of whether the Lord was actually present or absent, and whether the vassal knew of the Lord's presence or was ignorant of it. Gemmel, in his *Compendium of Feudal Law*, page 108, interprets the word <term>Assilierit</term> <note>to jump upon or assault</note> as meaning to besiege or attack. *See Rittershusius, Feudal Divisions, page 434.*

### 124. To Waste. <note>original: *Antwerden*</note> Prodigality.

Regarding what this word denotes <note>referring to the squandering of property</note>, see Dr. Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings*, page 97.

### 125. Beginner. <note>original: *Abecedarius*</note>

Jerome, in his writings on Mosaic discipline, uses the word <term>Abecedarii</term> for <term>those who are learning their ABCs</term>. There is a question as to whether the Emperor Justinian was illiterate <note>original: *analphabetus*</note>. This is discussed at length by Rittershusius in his *Novels*, page 665, and by Dr. Cobius in his commentary on the *Institutes*, where he cites many authors including Balduinus, Besold, and Procopius.

<column-break/>

### 126. Old Word for "Or". <note>original: *Alt*</note>

This ancient word denotes the same thing as the disjunctive term "or" <note>original: *oder*</note>. *See the Lindau Acts, folio 194, middle of 805.*

### 127. Cut-out Slips. <note>original: *Ausgeſchnittene Zettel*</note>

Regarding these words <note>likely referring to legal or evidentiary scraps of paper</note>, see Matthias Berlich, response conclusion 36, number 113.

### 128. Outflow. <note>original: *Auslauff*</note>

The <term>Auslauff</term> is the name for that part of the salt-pans in Halle that belongs to the Bishop of Magdeburg. *Matthias Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 3, part 1, chapter 7.*

### 129. Red-handed. <note>original: *Auf friſcher That*</note> Immediately.

See Sprenger on *The Physician*, page 160. Also, Dr. Helden’s *Opinions on Trespass*, where witnesses held that if the perpetrator is caught <term>red-handed</term> (defined here as within 24 hours), the punishment belongs not to the local bailiff <note>the *Vogteyherr*</note>, but to the high criminal authority <note>the *Malefiz-Obrigkeit*</note>. This matter is discussed most extensively by Dr. Johann Christoph Oelhafen in a legal opinion on fines for trespassing, which was mentioned above. The settlement between Neuburg and Nuremberg dated October 21 (or 31), 1664, number 2, also belongs here.

### 130. Adam. See also below under the word "Virginity."

Johannes Feron, an advocate in Paris, reports that Adam bore a red shield to remember the red earth from which he was created. On this shield, a black apple was to be seen, marking his heavy fall into sin. *Edward Bysshe in his notes to Nicholas Upton’s treatise on the office of soldiers, folio 39.*

Regarding the name of Adam: see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 11. Some try to build an argument for the excellence of women over men from the fact that woman was made from a rib, while Adam was made from a clod of earth. *See Cornelius Agrippa on the Nobility and Preeminence of the Female Sex, page 19.* Others write that Eve was created in Paradise, while Adam was created outside of Paradise in the field of Damascus—though they labor in vain on this. *Limnaeus, book 2.* There are several treatises extant regarding the "Pre-Adamites" <note>the theory that humans existed before Adam</note>. On when Adam was created and when he fell, see Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 469. Regarding the fallen Adam, see Mr. Harsdörffer’s *Spiritual History-Speeches*, part 1. Since then, we have "tunics of skin," meaning after the fall of man. The creation of Adam and Eve happened not *in* time, but *with* time. *Augustine, The City of God, book 2, chapter 46.* One can read about the descendants of Adam and Eve in Eyring’s *German Proverbs*, folio 164.

### 131. As. <note>original: "Als. Tanquam."</note>

An Emperor, as <note>original: "als"</note> a King of the Romans: here the word "as" is not to be understood in a "reduplicative" sense <note>meaning a separate, doubling role</note>, but rather as "being" or "otherwise." <note>original: "non sicut, sed sive, vox Als non intelligenda est reduplicativè."</note> Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 9, number 36.

The word "as" <note>original: "tanquam"</note> denotes something that is not strictly the thing itself, and yet at times it expresses the truth of a status. Mantica, *On the Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 3, title 16, number 6; see also Boër, decision 44, number 29.

### 132. Backwater. <note>original: "Altwasser"</note>

In an old feudal charter, I find these words: "The fishing water, etc., together with its out-flowing and in-flowing <term>Altwasser</term> <note>literally 'old waters,' referring to abandoned riverbeds or stagnant branches of a river</note>." Such water has been abandoned for many years, and these backwaters were never inquired after. When the new <term>Dominus</term> <note>lord or owner</note> of the fishing rights asked about the backwaters, one person quickly said they were no longer "in the nature of things" <note>original: "in rerum natura"; i.e., they no longer exist</note>. Another thought it might be a lake situated nearby. A third said he had the oldest knowledge of the matter: one branch was the "in-flowing" backwater, and when it overflows and runs out onto the neighboring meadows, that is the "out-flowing" backwater. However, the owner of the meadows uses this small lake himself during the time of the flooding. The question is: does he do so by right?

### 133. Ash-Court. <note>original: "Aschgericht"</note>

What this is, is common practice in our court.

### 134. Bloodletting. <note>original: "Aderlaß. Venæ Sectio."</note>

To the Margrave of Beveron, two days before he died in Paris in the year 1650, a worm a span long <note>the width of an expanded hand</note> was pulled from his vein when he was being bled. Zeiller, century 4, question 24, page 116. On the question of in which diseases bloodletting should be preferred over purging: Caspar Hoffmann, in the promotion of Caspar Horn, 1626.

Bloodletting is said to be fatal on the day of the Feast of the Annunciation <note>March 25th</note>. Mr. Dilherr, in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 450. Emperor Philippus was stabbed to death just after a bloodletting, page 597. The hippopotamus taught us the cutting of veins. <note>original: "Sectionem venæ docet nos Hippopotamus." A common ancient belief that hippos bled themselves on reeds.</note> Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 4, number 17. In Spain, the barbers bleed on the left and right, following the French fashion. Zeiller, in *Spanish Itinerary*, page 58. In the Gold Coast of Guinea, they use no bloodletting at all, except that they occasionally cut a wound or two into their bodies with a knife so that the blood flows out. Levinus Hulsius. This man knows "how to bleed a gnat" <note>a metaphorical expression for being overly meticulous or extracting something from nothing</note>. Antenor in *Salomon*, chapter 4. On whether it is necessary for a person to occasionally use bloodletting to preserve health: Felix Plater in *Medical Questions*, question 73. Regarding bloodletting for hypochondriacal melancholy, in the cure of epilepsy, in malignant fevers, and in kidney disease, see the *Medical Counsels* of Balthasar Brunner.

### 135. Field-hay. <note>original: "Ackerheu"</note>

Field-hay is the name given to hay that grows on eroded or "washed-out" fields which are not yet being cultivated.

### 136. Ammeister. <note>original: "Ammeisterus."</note>

The <term>Ammeister</term> is the highest magistrate in the city of Strasbourg. Draco, *On the Patricians*, page 260. In the "Room of the Fifteen" <note>original: "Herrn XV. Stuben"; referring to the Strasbourg council</note> there is a wooden beaker upon which the coats of arms of all the Ammeisters are painted around the parchment. The things that Scherb brings forth regarding the customs of the Ammeister in his *Politics* (page 111 in my edition) are ridiculous.

### 137. Crossbow Range. <note>original: "Armbrustrein"</note>

Mornac, on law 7 of the Code regarding taxes, discusses the alleged privileges of those who practice with bows and "bombards" <note>early cannons or firearms</note> in the Field of Mars <note>a practice ground</note>. Strasbourg Police Ordinance, pages 37 and 38. The late Mr. Dr. Tabor, *On Billets*, page 256.

### 138. Ash, Ash Wednesday. <note>original: "Asch, Aschermittwoch. Cinis Dies cinerum."</note>

Concerning one who swore that if the matter were not as he said, he would suffer his body to turn to ash—which indeed happened that very same night. Zeiller, century 4, question 24, page 116. Why barbers are called "ash-men" <note>original: "cinerarii"</note>: Pancirollus, in *New Discoveries*, page 372 in my edition. On "ash-stirrers" <note>original: "cinisionibus"</note> and "ash-men," see Rupert on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 1, dissertation 2, section 3.

On the Day of Ashes or the Ash-tide, treated at length by Georg von Dassel, *On the Law of the Lenten Season*, thesis 34 and following. Mr. Dilherr, in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 414, section 10. Mr. Fürer, in *Latin Itinerary*, page 99.

### 139. Arbe and Hagab, that is, Locusts. <note>original: "Locusta."</note>

Mr. Dilherr, in *Contemplations on the World, Field, and Garden*, page 514. <note>The terms "Arbe" and "Hagab" are Hebrew names for different types of locusts.</note>

### 140. Suspicion. <note>original: "Argwohn. Suspicio."</note>

A cause of equal affection excludes suspicion. <note>A legal principle: if you love someone, you are less likely to be suspected of harming them, or vice versa.</note> Hartmann Hartmanni, book 2, *Miscellaneous Practical Observations*, chapter 1, observation 23, number 1.

### 141. Aix.

60 Guilders of Aix <note>referring to the currency of Aachen/Aix-la-Chapelle</note>. See Limnäus, volume 2, *Additions to book 7*, chapter 2, page 84, and the "Mark of Aix," page 85.

### 142. Feeding, Maintenance. <note>original: "Atz, Atzung. Alimentatio."</note>

This pertains to the Right of Sovereignty and Royal Prerogatives. Klock, counsel 9, numbers 16 through 19; see however numbers 83 through 85, and counsel 10, numbers 265 through 272. <term>Atzung</term> <note>the feudal right of a lord to be fed and housed by his subjects</note> and other burdens deviate from common law. Counsel 10, numbers 278 to 285.

### 134. Ancestor. <note>original: "Anherr. Avus."</note>

Great-grandfathers. Rudinger, century 5, observation 3, in the preface.

### 1. Cash, Ready Money, Liquid Assets. <note>original: "Baar, Baargeld, Baarschafft. Pecunia numerata."</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'V' featuring a man in a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

**T**he word "money," when uttered by unlettered men, is understood only as ready cash, or as pence and coins. This is according to the text in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff." refers to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note>, book 30, title 1, law 1, regarding legacies, and in law *sed Julianus* under the section on the giving of a loan in the *Macedonian Decree of the Senate*. These texts expressly state that under the term "money," only ready cash is included. Similarly, the Cardinal in the *Clementines* <note>a collection of Canon Law</note> regarding the significance of words says that money is properly understood as pence. Bartolus, in his commentary on the *Digest*, book 30, title 1, says: if a mention of money is made in the speech of an unlettered man, it is understood as ready cash. Alciatus, in his work *On the Significance of Words*, teaches that the term "money" properly refers to coins or ready cash, citing Pliny’s *Natural History*, book 8, chapter 3. He reports that according to common usage, the word "money" ought to be understood only as ready cash.

As for the expression **Cash**, or **in ready money**, its proper meaning is that the money is held at hand and is prompt or prepared so that it can be counted out immediately. The phrase **in ready money** is considered to be used to the exclusion of merchandise, so that payment cannot be made through goods. Both by common usage and the disposition of the law, only that money is said to be "ready" which is on hand and held at the ready for immediate counting, according to the legal experts cited by Wesenbec in his *Counsels*, 263, number 5—though he adds a limitation in number 30.

Furthermore, Pruckman, in volume 2, counsel 5, number 92, testifies that the word **Liquid Assets** <note>original: "Baarschafft"</note> has nothing in common with immovable property or annual rents, such as **houses, estates, and tenant holdings**. Thus, it is noted in the same place (numbers 132 and 150) that in a <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>a legal trust where property is left to one person to be handed over to another</note> established under the word for "marked money" (**under the word Liquid Assets**), immovable things cannot be included. He denies that the word **Liquid Assets** is the exact Latin equivalent for "money" <note>original: "pecunia"</note>; rather, he says the German word **Money** <note>original: "Geld"</note> is the equivalent of the Latin *pecunia*. This is attested by everyone who has ever learned to speak Latin and German. In number 191, he adds that even if the word **Liquid Assets** were equivalent to "money," the word "money"—even when accepted in its broader sense—contains nothing other than things that consist of weight, number, and measure. He asserts that no one can ever demonstrate that the word **Liquid Assets** in our language has any meaning other than ready money and the names of debtors. Thus, in number 202, Pruckman says it is absurd for anyone to wish to extend a trust so far that a legacy left under the word for "marked

<column-break/>

money" should encompass the entire inheritance of the person making the trust.

## ADDITION.

It is noted in the works of Molinæus <note>the French jurist Charles Dumoulin</note> that in France, no one is compelled to receive "small money" <note>change or low-value coins</note> for debts of a large amount. If someone has handed over money and simply said, "take this money," it is asked: what kind of contract is this? This is discussed at length by Busius in his *Commentaries on the Pandects*, book 12, page 470.

Under the term "money," an exchange <note>original: "functio"</note> with grain or wine is not accepted, as witnessed by Zafius in his commentary on the *Digest* regarding credited things. For a person having money often cannot acquire grain except at great expense. See Köppen, decision 25, numbers 6 and 9; Zorer, part 2, question 8, numbers 650, 651, and 652. **On a hand in the money-till,** <note>original: "Von einem Griff ins Geld"</note> see Limnäus, book 7, chapter 2, on Public Law, volume 2 of the additions.

Under the name of "money," not only ready cash is contained, but all things, both of the soil <note>real estate</note> and movables, and both physical objects and legal rights. See the *Digest*, title *On the Significance of Words*, law 222, where Alciatus and Göddæus comment. This is because **everything can be turned into money.** <note>original: "dann es kan alles zu Geld gemacht werden."</note> Accursius, in his commentary on the *Digest*, says that "money" is the name for everything that men owe on earth and of which they are masters. According to Augustine, "money" is the whole. Therefore, when a quantity is bequeathed simply, no accidental case can grant a release from the debt, even before a delay in payment, since a "genus" <note>a general category of items, like money</note> cannot perish. See more in Zorer, part 2, question 10, number 752 and following. Biccius, in his *Golden Matters*, section 4, number 95, most accurately provides a three-fold meaning of the word money: 1. It signifies all things, both of the soil and movables, which are in our patrimony, including both physical bodies and rights. 2. Sometimes it refers to all and only those things which fall under a loan, i.e., those consisting of weight, number, and measure. 3. Finally, sometimes it refers only to ready cash. Elsewhere, by the naming of "money," the principal sum is usually signified, not the interest, as is held in the *Digest*. Pacius says the word money is accepted broadly for any thing whatsoever. Regarding money in general, see Barbosa, *Axioms*, book 14, chapter 18 throughout. Money is compared to the waves of the sea. See Rittershusius in his *Sacred Readings*. **Consumption-monies,** <note>original: "Consumtion-Gelder"</note> see Schwanman on the *Law of Emigration and Removal*, page 75. **Means of Consumption.** G. T. Oelhaffen, *On the Law of Tolls*, section 176 and 186.

Money without a <term>peculium</term> <note>a small private fund or savings</note> is fragile; that is, a good father of a household ought to set aside some coins for the sake of protection, lest all things in daily...

## 2. The Law of the Bier. Of Cruentation. <note>term: "Baarrecht/Cruentatio." An ancient legal ordeal based on the belief that a victim's corpse would spontaneously bleed in the presence of its murderer.</note>

It has commonly become an established belief that a heavy flow of blood from the corpse of a slain person, occurring when someone suspected of the homicide approaches, provides a sufficient indicator for the use of torture. However, many people reject this opinion, since it could bring any innocent person into mortal danger. They argue that a place for investigation through torture should only be opened for the sake of uncovering the truth when the accused is overwhelmed by likely and probable arguments that arise from some external and known cause. <note>Latin: "l. 3. & l. 8. §. un. C. de quæst." refers to the Code of Justinian regarding interrogations.</note>

Moreover, they assert that this "blood-sign" can by no means be called a reliable indicator, because it arises from causes unknown even to the wisest of men and which are very remote. Indeed, this sign cannot be explained by natural causes, since the bodies of the dead are drained of blood and there is no force within a cold corpse capable of driving out the blood. Therefore, since it is plainly doubtful and uncertain whether that flow of blood is moved by divine will or by the tricks and illusions of some Demon, it ought not to be judged as a suitable indicator for torture. **For it is better for the crime of a guilty person to go unpunished than to condemn an innocent one.** <note>Latin: "Satius enim est, impunitum relinqui facinus nocentis, quàm innocentem damnare." A fundamental principle of Roman and modern law.</note> See also Antonio Tessauro, decision 173.

My own view is that this bleeding—cruentation—ought to be numbered among the indicators for torture, but that it is not sufficient on its own. See my treatise *On Information and Coercion*, leaf 230.

There is also a custom in some places among the Germans that, either at the request of the friends and relatives of the slain or by the duty of the Magistrate, those who were present at the conflict and are suspected of the committed homicide are led to the dead man (they commonly call this **The Law of the Bier**) when the author of the killing is in doubt. They are made to apply their fingers to the wounds, using a set form of words, to see if by chance the true murderer might be revealed, specifically if the touched wound emits blood.

Zieritz notes in his commentary on the *Imperial Criminal Ordinance* (P.G.O. <note>The Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, the 1532 criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>), article 149, that this custom is still used in many provinces of Germany and is not entirely irrational. For historical examples as well as experience itself testify that by this old-fashioned remedy of investigation, many murderers have been convicted and removed by just punishment, not without the evidence of divine vengeance, when combined with other approaching signs and suspicions.

Regarding the reason why a corpse is accustomed to emit blood in the presence of its killer because of preceding contact,

<column-break/>

this is debated variously here and there by Philosophers, Doctors, and Jurists. Many and diverse causes are alleged, as Father Martin Delrio records and praises many opinions and authors on this matter in his *Commentary on Seneca's Octavia*, verse 127. On this question, and also on whether the blood of the slain accuses the killer, see Guillaume Onciacus, question 36; Böckel in his *Criminal Disquisitions*, disq. 6, n. 5; Bisciola’s *Subsequent Hours*, book 15, chapter 1; Kornmann *On the Miracles of the Dead*, letter 10; Joseph Sesse, decision 111; the *Consilia* of Bulla, dec. 1, leaf 22, etc.; and Hering in his treatise *On Homicide*. Most urge the theory of **antipathy**, arising from the vehement hatred of the slain toward the killer, which has impressed a hidden and secret quality upon the body that remains with the corpse. This follows the lines of Lucretius:

> And that body perishes from which the mind is wounded by love,
> For men for the most part fall toward the wound, and the blood
> Spurts out into that part from whence we are struck by the blow;
> And if the enemy is near at hand, a red horror seizes him.
<note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* IV.1048-1051. While the original poem discusses the "wound" of love, the author here applies it to a physical murder.</note>

But Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous physician and occultist.</note> recognizes a double body in man, the visible and the invisible, which he calls the **Evestrum**. He also recognizes a double life; he says it proceeds from this that the blood leaps from the body shortly after death upon meeting the one who brought the violence. See Majolus in *Canicular Days*, on my leaf 18; and Godelmann in his preface to book 3, *On Witches*.

Georg Everhard also writes in volume 1, counsel 35, number 35, that this practice is exercised throughout the Duchy of Bavaria and other provinces.

I also remember a certain case brought from Wertheim in Franconia to the Legal Faculty of Tübingen, where, among other things, the following was found: **"After a diligent investigation, the perpetrator would not be found or confess, and for that reason it was necessary to arrange a Law of the Bier. During this, Nicholas and Balthasar caused no sign on the body—which had already been murdered for 36 hours and had lain partly in a vault and partly, for several hours before the act, under the open sky in rather cold weather with chest and belly uncovered—and both remained quite confident in their first statement."** (Note: four men had waited for the deceased; when the deceased approached with a halberd, the two aforementioned men ran away.)

**"Upon the bringing forward of Jörgen, the body gave forth bloody foam from the mouth."** (Note: this man remained present when the victim was stabbed, but did not lay a hand on him.) But after this, and the bringing forward of Claus the watchman (who had run up by reason of his office and at the demand of others, wanting to make peace, and to the...)

(After the halberd was taken from the slain man) the aforementioned body poured blood from its wounds, and those wounds (which were over the heart) did not behave otherwise than if the heart were still alive.

Despite this, the aforementioned watchman took the prescribed oath <note>Latin: "formulam Jurisjurandi." A specific legal wording used in court.</note> three times. (Note: he placed (1.) two fingers on the mouth of the deceased, (2.) on the stab wound, and (3.) on the navel.) On the following day, the watchman turned himself in as the perpetrator.

From this it appears that the wound and the body of the dead man observed the degrees of guilt. <note>Latin: "Ex hoc apparet, vulnus, corpusque mortui gradus culpæ observasse."</note>

When Jörg was present, naturally red blood foamed from the mouth. (Note: he was essentially the instigator of the business. Therefore, the mouth foamed out of resentment <note>Latin: "ex rancore"</note>, but not the wound, because he was not the actual perpetrator.)

When the watchman was present, nothing happened at the mouth. But when he placed two fingers on the wounds, naturally red blood ran out of them over the sides, so that the surgeon had to wipe it away. When he put two fingers on the navel, the wounds bubbled <note>Latin: "ebullirt"</note> again, opened up, and twitched, just as a pulse-vein beats.

Lorenz had wrestled with the slain man <note>Latin: "occiso"</note>: while repeating the oath, bloody foam ran out of the dead man's mouth, and when he placed his fingers on the wounds, the wounds twitched again and moved. When Lorenz departed, they no longer twitched.

But I know of another very recent example where the slain man, despite almost the same solemnity being observed, gave absolutely no sign: perhaps because the homicide was accidental <note>Latin: "homicidium casuale"</note>, and the blood did not seek vengeance. For it is handed down by many that the spirit passes into the killer, waiting for revenge. <note>Citing Joachim Stephan, *Demonstrationes Politicae*, chapter 19.</note>

Sometimes something happens in this regard miraculously, which does not fall under legal reasoning. Cantipratanus <note>Thomas of Cantimpré, a 13th-century theologian and natural historian.</note> relates an example in Book 1 of *Miracles*, chapter 16, regarding Henry, the Abbot of Blois, who was wickedly killed by his own people, and he writes thus: The venerable Henry, a Canon Regular in the Monastery of St. Mary of Bourge-Moyen in Blois, though he had studied long in Paris, was elected Abbot by everyone against his will. Because he used rigor toward his monks—both by exhorting them to keep the rule and to live honestly, and by maintaining discipline—he was cruelly killed by them through three most wicked scoundrels

<column-break/>

hired for the purpose. While his companion Robert escaped, the body of the slain man was carried to the Monastery and placed in the Church. And see what was done and proven: for immediately, when on the following day those guilty of the crime entered the Church for the burial of the slain man (at the place where the entrails were kept), behold, "the voice of thy brother Abel’s blood" <note>A biblical reference to Genesis 4:10.</note> cried out from the earth as if for vengeance; through the wounds, which had remained dry since the time of the killing, there flowed a most abundant rush of blood in their presence, etc.

The same Cantipratanus relates another example in the aforementioned work, Book 2, chapter 29: In the year of our Lord 1271, it happened in a town called Pforzheim in the German tongue, that a most wicked old woman, having become familiar with the Jews, sold them a seven-year-old girl, orphaned of her parents, to be killed. <note>This refers to a historical "blood libel" narrative, a common but false antisemitic trope of the Middle Ages used to incite persecution.</note> Therefore, in secret, having obstructed her mouth over several layers of linen, they wounded her with incisions in almost every joint of her limbs, expressing the blood with great effort and collecting it most carefully in those same linens. After these torments, the girl having died, the Jews threw her into the flowing water near the town and placed a heap of stones over her. Truly on the third or fourth day, she was found by fishermen by her hand raised toward heaven, and carried into the town, while the people cried out in horror that such a great crime had been committed by the impious Jews. The Margrave of Baden was in the vicinity, who, as soon as he heard of such a great outrage, came to the body; immediately the body itself sat upright and stretched out its hands to the Prince, as if imploring vengeance for its blood or perhaps mercy. After half an hour, it laid itself back down on its back in the manner of the dead.

When the impious Jews were brought to this spectacle, all the wounds of the body immediately burst open, and in testimony of the horrendous death, they poured forth copious blood; they were captured and paid the penalty, etc. So also Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Gloucester, had inflicted the greatest injuries upon Saint Thomas of Hereford, a Bishop in England, because the Bishop protected the rights of the Church while the Earl invaded them. Meanwhile, the Bishop died while away. His relatives took care to bring his bones to his church, the flesh having been entirely removed. As soon as the Earl came to meet them, a great deal of blood flowed from the clean bones, stripped of all flesh and blood. Seeing this, the Earl was struck with terror and, led by penitence, restored all the Ecclesiastical rights he had invaded, as the anonymous author relates in the life of the same Saint Thomas in Surius, volume 7, October 5th. Since, therefore, that blood flowed from dry bones to shake the heart of a wicked and impenitent man—and no bubbling of spirits or infection of the blood could be considered in this case, since Saint Thomas had died without any wound—it necessarily follows that one must believe God works this by a miracle in the body of the slain

I add this: occasionally the bodies of the dead, even those not murdered—namely high-ranking nobles, Princes, etc.—have bled, and many evils followed thereafter. I will include a single example <note>original German: *ausz der Lubeckischen Chronick Joh. And because the bleeding from a dead body was not natural, God without doubt wished to indicate by this—as if by a certain outward sign—the gruesome punishment and bloodshed that followed soon after; for afterward, all manner of misfortune, war, and strife stirred in this place, the land, and in Lübeck, etc.

### ADDITION.

On this matter, see by all means Mr. Boecl. in *The Judge*, pages 21 and 22. Either many light clues concur, such as the flowing of blood either from a wound or from the mouth or nostrils a day or several days after the death of the deceased—in which case experience has certainly taught that this argument has very rarely failed, and thus one can proceed to the first or even second degree of torture—or no other clues appear, and then it would be unjust to torture the accused based on this alone, since we are ignorant of the true causes of that hidden 

<column-break/>

<term>antipathy</term> <note>original: *antipathiae*</note>. See *Marsil. in pract. crim. §. diligently. num. 181. at the end*; *Boër. decision 166. num. 1*; *Menoch. Mascard. and others.* 
Regarding that clue—if the body of a slain person pours blood in the presence of the one suspected of that homicide—Bocer treats it most extensively in *On Questions and Tortures, chapter 3, page 95 and following*, with the citations therein. 
The flowing of blood is either natural or supernatural. If it is natural, its cause will be one and the same, and thus a corpse would always pour blood when the murderer is present. However, that this does not happen is testified by *Thesaur. decision 173. num. 2. at the end; Heig. question 39. num. 96. and following; Setser. on oaths, last chapter, last number.* Therefore, it remains that it is supernatural. Since the cause of this exceeds the understanding of a judge, it clearly appears that it is not of a nature that can inform him with certainty about the murderer; for this reason, he ought to admit no proof unless he can provide a rational explanation for it <note>referencing Digest *law 3. §. 1. regarding witnesses*</note>. 
In some places, people hold that if someone present at a fire finds that the shoes on their feet start to burn, that person is the culprit—a sign similar to the bleeding corpse. **Justus Georgius Schottel in *The German Main Language*, folio 501.**

### 3. Bachelor.

See my work in *Academic Dissertation on Masters, Bachelors, etc.* and in the *Treatise on Academies*; *Lindemann in History of Roman Law, thesis 391 and following, folio 96*; and *Johann Calvin in the treatise on fiefs, folio 194.* 
Bachelors <note>Latin: *Baccalaurei*</note> are also called *Battalarii*. From *Battalo* or *batolo*, which is that strip or list of cloth that priests and doctors wear over the shoulder, and in Venice also the gentlemen, who call it the *beca*, and elsewhere the *cornetta*, the hood, and according to the diversity of places it has a different shape and name. <note>original Italian: *Lexic. Italian.*</note> 
Thus at Ingolstadt, that cloth which candidates for the Master's degree must wear over their shoulders for a period before their graduation is called "Aristotle's Boots" <note>Latin: *Caligae Aristotelis*</note>, etc.

Limn. in J. P. lib. 8. c. 8. n. 26. Camman. disp. on Royalties 3. n. 56.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding this matter, see by all means Mr. Boecler here in *The Judge*, pages 21–22. Either many slight clues concur—such as the outflow of blood either from the wound or from the mouth or nostrils one or more days after the death of the deceased, in which case experience has certainly shown that this argument has very rarely failed, and thus one may proceed to the first or even second degree of torture—or no other clues appear, and then it would be unjust for the accused to be tortured based on this alone, since we are ignorant of the true causes of that hidden antipathy. See Marsilius in *Criminal Practice*, section "diligently," number 181 at the end; Boerius, decision 166, number 1; Menochius, Mascardus, and others. Regarding that sign, if the corpse of a slain man pours forth blood in the presence of one suspected of the murder, Bocerus discusses it most extensively in *On Questions and Tortures*, chapter 3, page 95 and following, and the citations there. The outflow of blood is either natural or supernatural. If natural, its cause will be one and the same, and thus a corpse would always pour out blood when the murderer is present. However, that this does not happen is testified by *Treasury of Decisions* 173, number 2; Heigius, question 39, number 96 and following; Setser, *On Oaths*, last chapter, last number. Therefore, it remains that it is supernatural. Since its cause exceeds the understanding of a judge, it clearly appears that it is not of a nature that can inform him with probability about the murderer, and for this reason he ought to admit no proof except that for which he can provide a reason (Law 3, section 1, *On Witnesses*). In some places, it is held that when someone is present at a fire and the shoes on their feet begin to burn, that person is the perpetrator—a sign much like the bleeding of a corpse. Justus Georgius Schottelius in *The German Main Language*, folio 501.

<column-break/>

### 3. Bachelor.

See my own work in the *Academic Dissertation on Masters, Bachelors, etc.* Also in the *Treatise on Academies*; Lindemann in *History of Roman Law*, thesis 391 and following, folio 96; and Johann Calvin in the *Treatise on Fiefs*, folio 194. Bachelors <note>Latin: Baccalaurei</note> are also called *Battalarii* from *Battalo* or *batolo*, which is that strip or band of cloth that Priests, Doctors, and also in Venice, gentlemen wear upon the shoulder; they call it the *beca*, and elsewhere the *cornetta*, the *cappuccio* <note>hood</note>, and according to the diversity of places, it has different forms and names. *Italian Lexicon*. Thus at Ingolstadt, that cloth which candidates for the Master's degree must wear for a time before their graduation <note>literally "creation"</note> is called *Aristotle’s Boots* <note>Latin: Caligæ Aristotelis</note>, etc.

### ADDITION.

The Bachelor's degree is not a dignity <note>an official rank of honor</note>, but merely a preparation for a dignity, and its granting is not among the Regalia <note>sovereign rights</note> of the Emperor, according to the opinion in *Treatise volume 1, Disputation 1, thesis 7, letter A*. But the contrary opinion is truer, as Saggittarius testifies in *On Counts Palatine*, thesis 30, letter c; Mundius in *On Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 267 and following; Bachov. in *Treatise Limnaeus on Public Law, book 8, chapter 8, number 26*; Camman, *Disputation on Regalia* 3, number 56. At what time the rank of Bachelors was introduced, see Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 90. There are 4 kinds of Bachelors according to Mundius in the cited place, number 268; Becker in *Public Law*, page 251, mentions only three. Albert IV, Duke of Bavaria, was solemnly created a Bachelor of Paris, Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 8, chapter 8*; Wendelin in *Politics*, page 260. Mr. Oelhafen...

in the discourse which is joined to the treatise of Dragonis regarding the <term>Rights of the Patricians</term> <note>original: "Jure Patriciorum"</note>. Sigismund von Herberstein, a writer of Muscovite history (otherwise known as Alessandro Guagnini, a Veronese who also described Muscovy), was a man most distinguished in both letters and arms. Having served three most glorious Emperors—Maximilian I, Charles V, and Ferdinand I—with great distinction, and having skillfully performed many grave and honorable embassies throughout Europe and Asia, he was deservedly decorated with many clear titles of honor and declared the first Baron of his family. Nevertheless, he did not hesitate to extol the glory of his name chiefly because, as a youth of sixteen in the year 1502, he was decorated with his first <term>laurel of philosophy</term> <note>the degree of Bachelor of Arts</note> at the University of Vienna. Hence he is reported to have said: *“This was my first dignity earned from my studies, which some ignorant and foolish people reproached me for under the title of ‘Doctor,’ a rank I was never worthy of, though I often wished to be.”* Among the English, he who wishes to become a Bachelor must remain at a university for three years if he is a nobleman; if he desires to become a Master, seven years; and for the Doctorate, fourteen years. See Zeiller, century 3, letter page 16. On March 29, 1615, 43 Masters of the Liberal Arts were created at Tübingen, and on September 20, 30 Bachelors. But where are those now who, like the aforementioned Herberstein, take care to be depicted in their old age showing the series and dress of their functions on tablets for the sake of a stronger memory, and show that picture to guests, saying with him: *“This form, which represents the title of Bachelor, pleases me above all others; I value this most highly.”* Aemilius Portus is said to have written a singular oration in praise of the Baccalaureate, which Otto cites in J. P. page 690. Older universities, such as Erfurt and Leipzig, create Bachelors of Theology and Law. Walther, on the Privileges of Doctors, page 431. Bachelors are also created in the name of the Emperor, ibid. page 432.

### 4. Margraviate of Baden. Marchionatus Badensis.

No one can doubt the antiquity of the town of Baden. Regarding this matter, Master Johann Kieffer, Doctor of Medicine, writes in his <italic>Description of the Margravial Warm Baths</italic>, folio 65: "To describe the ancient origin and other qualities of this famous city at length is out of place here; we wish to leave such things to the geographers. Concerning its warm baths, it must be noted that one can have no thorough knowledge

<column-break/>

of when the same came into being and began to flourish. However, Philippus Beroaldus, in a letter to the illustrious Jacob, late Margrave of Baden, attributes its building and foundation to the Emperor Antoninus Bassianus Caracalla, who reigned more than fourteen hundred years ago. Therefore, Ricardus Bartholinus of Perugia also speaks thus in the fourth book of his *Austriad*:

> *“You too, Duke of Baden, following no inferior*
> *Auspices, hasten to the Murg, where hoary*
> *Antiquity shows the Antonine gifts to your lands.”*

They wish to prove this from an ancient Roman inscription and heading which is found there in the Cathedral, just as one enters the great door, on the side, carved into a stone on the wall with the following words:

->TO MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS<-
->CAESAR, EMPEROR-ELECT,<-
->SON OF PERTINAX AUGUSTUS,<-
->THE REPUBLIC OF THE WATERS [ESTABLISHED THIS]<-
<note>original Latin: "M. AURELIO ANTONINO CÆS. IMP. DESTINATO PERTINACIS AUG. FILIO RESPUBL. AQUEN." Baden-Baden was known in Roman times as Aquae Aureliae.</note>

From such an inscription, however, nothing else is to be concluded except that our Baden was in great repute and name in the times of the mentioned Emperor, and was not first brought into prosperity by him: as Johannes Langius already indicated in his *Medical Letters*, book 2, letter 49. He, however, is mistaken in that he interprets this inscription as referring to the Emperor Antoninus the Philosopher <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, who began to reign in the year of Christ 162; whereas it is to be understood, as mentioned, as referring to Antoninus Caracalla, who came more than 50 years later. Thus far Master Kieffer.

That the Family of Baden is not different from that of Hachberg, but is one and the same, is testified by Christoph, Margrave of Baden, and Philipp, Margrave of Hachberg, in a reciprocal treaty which they made concerning succeeding one another on St. Bartholomew's Day in the year 1490.

But where these families first draw their origin, and what common trunk or first ancestor of their lineage they have, is not agreed upon among historians and genealogists. See Guiliman, book 5 of *Habsburg*, folio 173; Crusius in his *Annals* under the words Hochburg, Rösteln, etc.; Goldast’s *Constitutional Indices*; Junius on Germany; Gerard de Roo on Austria; Pistor in the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Constance*; Scioppius in the appendix to the *Sacred Class*; and the *Alsatian Chronicle*, part 2, folio 32. Indeed, even the manuscripts themselves, lying hidden in archives, speak in various ways. For some are found who try to derive these families from the ancient Counts of Baden, who formerly lived in the Aargau, in the city of Baden itself, or in the Castle of Ther-

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of the House of Baden, specifically debating whether the Margraves descended from Italian nobility in Verona or from the local Germanic House of Zähringen and Habsburg.</meta>

Lit. B. 81

They lived in the "Place of Baths" <note>original: "Thermarum"</note>, as Rhenanus calls it, or in "Thermopolis" <note>City of Baths</note>, as it is named by Glareanus.

Others summon these most Serene <term>Margraves</term> <note>a title for a military governor of a border province</note> from the city of Rome and fabricate that they arose from the Orsini family; see Franciscus Irenicus in his *Exegesis of Germany*, book 3, chapter 103 and following, and Peter von Andlau, book 1 of *The Roman Empire*, chapter 15.

Certain others wish to trace them back to the ancient kings of the Goths and the Scaligeri, the lords of Verona who descended from them—specifically from Capto, or Anses, the first of the lineage.

Many are commonly persuaded that, without mention of the Orsini or Scaligeri, they arose from the Counts or Margraves of Verona, and that Hermann, Margrave of Verona—having been handed over as a hostage to Emperor Frederick Barbarossa <note>Frederick I, the "Red-Bearded" Emperor</note>—was first placed over these regions and established as a Prince of the Empire. Sebastian Münster, Heinrich Pantaleon, Hieronymus Henninges, Elias Reusner, Albizius, and almost all genealogists and historians have held this view, by which the Margraves of Baden themselves have been deceived, believing their ancestors descended from the Veronese.

But Johann Pistorius of Nidda writes that all these people were hallucinating and were ignorant of the true origin of the Margraves of Baden and Hachberg. He was commissioned to conduct a true investigation and description of the Baden and Hachberg family for a certain and handsome salary. Likewise, Franciscus Guillimannus—a man exceptionally skilled in antiquity—in his *Habsburgica* (or his books on the ancient and true origin of the House of Austria, book 5, chapter 1) and Caspar Scioppius, in the genealogy of the August House of Austria which he added to his *Royal and Classic Council of the Sacred War* in the year 1619, agree. All these men do not fear to assert, from the archives and monuments of the ancients themselves, that the Baden and Hachberg family proceed from the most ancient Counts of Vindonissa, Altenburg, and Habsburg. Therefore, the Habsburg (or modern Austrian), Zähringen, Teck, Baden, and Hachberg families are one and the same. It is therefore not to be doubted that all those who report that the most ancient Princely House of the Margraves of Baden and Hachberg, etc., originated from the Margraves who were in Verona in Italy, are highly mistaken. This is because Hermann III—the grandson of Hermann I, who later became a monk at Cluny (and was the brother of Berthold of Zähringen)—held the Margraviate of Baden long before Frederick Barbarossa came to power or set out for Italy. Guillimannus correctly observes this from a diploma of Emperor Conrad II <note>likely referring to Conrad III, or a specific charter record</note> in which express mention is made of the "Margrave of Baden" <note>original: "Marchionis de Batha"</note>. For the Emperor says in the year of our Lord 1139 that he confirms the privileges of Wicram, Abbot of Pfäfers, in the presence of Albero, Archbishop of Trier; Ortlieb, Bishop of Basel; Duke Frederick; Duke Conrad; Duke Matthew; Hermann, Margrave of Baden; and Adalbert, Margrave of Habsburg.

<note>Besold, Volume I</note>

<column-break/>

Thus it is read in the old Backnang codex <note>a manuscript from the Backnang Abbey</note> that already before, specifically in the time of Pope Paschal II in the year 1116, Hermann, Margrave of Baden, founded a monastery of <term>Augustinian Canons</term> <note>priests living in community under the Rule of St. Augustine</note> in his village of Backnang, for the glory and praise of St. Pancras the Martyr. This foundation was confirmed by Bruno, Bishop of Speyer, at the request of Hermann, on the 13th day before the Calends of March <note>February 17th</note> in the 15th Indiction, in the year 1122. These are the words of the confirmation itself: *“In the name of the Holy and Indivisible Trinity, let it be known to the faithful of Christ, both of the future and present time, that I, Bishop Bruno, assenting to the just petitions, pious vows, and desires conceived by divine inspiration of Margrave Hermann, have granted that he might establish poor Canons of Christ living a communal life according to the Rule of the Blessed Augustine in the church built for St. Pancras the Martyr, which he and his wife Judith and his parents enriched with estates and tithes, etc. In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord 1122, the 15th Indiction, the 13th day before the Calends of March.”*

Indeed, Emperor Frederick I himself confirmed a donation made by the Abbess of Erstein to the same Margrave Hermann for the estate of Besigheim in the second year of his reign, in the year of Christ 1153, the 14th Indiction. At that time, he had not yet entered Italy with an army, and therefore could not have brought Hermann back with him to Germany as a hostage, as is commonly thought.

Therefore, Guillimannus writes it is not without reason that Berthold I "the Bearded," Duke of Zähringen, likely divided the inheritance among his sons, or they among themselves: to Berthold II, the title of Duke and the larger portion; to Hermann, as the younger, the title of Margrave with a dominion not to be regretted. Wolfgang Lazius also trifles here, as in most matters, by saying that the dominion of the Margraves of Hachberg was obtained by Berthold and Conrad of Zähringen and handed over to the Margraves of Verona by Frederick I after he had outlawed both Dukes for rebellion.

But Hermann II married Judith, Countess of Baden; when she brought the Lordship of Baden to him, it gave him cause to write himself as "Margrave of Baden," whereas previously he was called by no other title than "Margrave" alone. This title was later retained by Hermann III, born of Judith, who also adopted his mother's heraldic coats of arms and passed them on to his descendants.

Although it cannot be denied that Hermann IV, son of Hermann III, called himself not only Lord of Baden but also Margrave of Verona under the said Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa, Guillimannus writes that it is proven that this was a title of governance <note>an administrative appointment</note>, not of origin...
