<meta>This page continues the genealogical and historical investigation of the House of Baden, specifically addressing the claim that their "Veronese" title was honorary rather than hereditary, before transitioning into the history of the Duchy of Bavaria and the origins of the Duchy of Austria.</meta>

The same Franciscus Guillimannus <note>a 16th-century Swiss historian known for his work on the Habsburgs</note> argues that after Frederick Barbarossa <note>Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I</note> destroyed Milan and subdued Lombardy—dividing it into several parts—he appointed German nobles to oversee each part, and indeed almost every city, as Italian historians testify. At that time, Hermann, Margrave of Baden, was placed over the already defeated city of Verona as an Imperial Vicar or Governor. Therefore, after he later returned to Germany, he continued to use this "Veronese" title. Few of his successors retained it, and it was used more for the sake of memory than to demonstrate the origin of the lineage or any hereditary possession of the old Veronese Lordship.

Because all of this is so—and since the Dukes of Zähringen, the Counts of Habsburg, as well as the Lords Margraves of Baden and Hachberg, are of one lineage and descent—and since the Lords Margraves of Hachberg years ago held many counties and lordships in the Breisgau, likewise in Swabia, in the Black Forest, and elsewhere (as well as many diverse rights of rule which were gradually brought under the House of Austria): it is therefore not to be doubted that those of Zähringen, Habsburg (or Austria), and the Margraves of Hachberg, as the closest cousins descended from a single trunk <note>original: "stipite," referring to the main line of a family tree</note>, in former times divided their land and people among themselves with equal rights <note>original: "aequali Jure"</note>. No branch would have reserved for itself any territorial sovereignty over the estates of the others, by whatever name such rights might be called.

->ADDITION.<-

<margin>Regarding the Margraves of Baden, see Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 376 and following, and in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 431.</margin>
Sebastian Münster, in his *Cosmography* (book 3, chapter 259, folio 805), reports that the Margraves of Baden and Hachberg descend from one and the same family, which was later divided into the Baden and Hachberg lines. Zasius (in *On Fiefs*, part 5, number 10) and Nolden (in *On the Status of Nobility*, chapter 8, number 170) record that these lords were originally established to stand against the French and to guard the Rhine. Today this family is divided into the Durlach and Baden branches, concerning which see Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 5. Especially add the *Genealogical Tables* of Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain, table 18, published in 1636. On the origin of the Counts, the "Guidones," who were soon after called "of the Bath" <note>original: "de Balneo," referring to the town of Baden</note>, see M. Zeiller, century 4, question 32, page 160.

Regarding this term <note>Verona/Veronese</note>, one should consult Elias Reusner in his *Royal Work* under the Veronese Princes, and Mr. Beer in his *Handbook of Ancient and New Geography*, section 116, 117.

->5. Bavaria.<-

Regarding Bavaria and the Boii <note>the ancient Celtic/Germanic tribe from which Bavaria takes its name</note>, many things are held by the Reverend Father Brunner and Reinerus Reineccius in the *Annals of Charlemagne*, 

<column-break/>

folio 27, verso. Also see Aventinus in the *Bavarian Chronicle* and add Rittershusius in his commentary on Gunther’s *Ligurinus*, folio 95, etc.

In ancient times, Austria "above the Enns" <note>Upper Austria</note> also belonged to Bavaria. Concerning this matter, Mr. Karl Stengel writes in his *Monastery History* (where he discusses Metten): Frederick, surnamed Barbarossa, restored the Duchy of Bavaria and Noricum to Henry the Lion, Duke of the Saxons. Henry was the son of the other Henry <note>Henry the Proud</note> who had been outlawed by King Conrad and ejected from all of Bavaria. The Emperor then transferred and removed his own paternal uncle, Henry <note>Henry Jasomirgott</note>, then the Duke of Bavaria and Margrave of Austria, from that same Duchy. However, because the great nobility and high honor of this Margrave Henry required that he should by no means lose the title of "Duke"—and so that the Dukes of Bavaria might hereafter be less able to cause tumult or rebel against the Empire—the Emperor, by the will and consent of the Princes in the assembly held at Regensburg in the year of our Lord 1156, converted the Margraviate of Austria into a Duchy. He did this by exempting it from the jurisdiction of the Dukes of Bavaria and adding to it certain counties from Bavaria. Thus, this Henry is recorded as having been made and designated the first Duke of Austria.

Bavaria, anciently called Bojoaria or Bojaria, took its name from the Boii, whom the Germans called the "Bojer," hence "Bojerland"—the land, region, or province of the Boii—which is now corruptly called "Bayerland" <note>Bavaria</note>. This designation was also once generally attributed to all of Germany and Gaul because Boian princes ruled in both places. Hence Mainz is called a "city of Bojaria" <note>Bavaria</note> by Saint Eulogius in an epistle cited by Cardinal Baronius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume 10. See also the most noble Mr. Goldast in his work of incomparable learning and diligence, *On the Law of Bohemia*, book 1, chapter 4, near the end.

Is the <term>Electoral dignity</term> <note>the right to vote in the election of the Holy Roman Emperor</note> granted to the Dukes of Bavaria by right of their Duchy? This is a sufficiently intricate question, which I mentioned in my 9th dissertation on *Royal Succession and Election*, folio 215 and following. Mr. Gewold concludes in favor of Bavaria in his *On the Seven-Member Electors*, chapter 10. This opinion is made not improbable by what is found in Lehmann, in the final book of the *Speyer Chronicle*, chapter 29, at the beginning, where he writes:

> Elector Ludwig’s surviving sons, Palatine Rudolph and Ruprecht, in the division of the Palatinate and the Duchy of Bavaria with Emperor Ludwig in the year 1327, received as their own portion for themselves and their heirs the lands along the Rhine river and the Upper Palatinate, which had previously belonged to the Duchy of Bavaria. From that time they established a permanent court at Heidelberg; whereas their ancestors had mostly held court in Bavaria or other places.

And furthermore: Windeck also teaches in *On the Seven-Member Electors* that the <term>Palatine Electorate</term> <note>the office and territory of the Count Palatine of the Rhine</note> belongs to Bavaria. Nor does "prescription" <note>the legal principle of gaining a right through long-term use</note> stand in the way, because of "bad faith" <note>original: "malam fidem," a legal term meaning the possession was known to be wrongful</note>, as the Elector of Saxony has deduced.

### Enlarged Practical Treasury

The same Franciscus Guillimannus writes that after Frederick Barbarossa <note>Frederick I, Holy Roman Emperor</note> overthrew Milan and conquered Lombardy—dividing it into several parts—he placed German nobles over each part, and indeed nearly every city, as the Italian historians testify. ## 5. Ban, Outlawry, Higher Outlawry, Military Ban. <term>Bannum</term>.

The word <term>Bann</term> <note>Ban</note> is equivocal <note>it has multiple meanings</note>. For we say *Baan*, referring to public roads. Hence *Baanen* in *Besold, Volume I*, means

<column-break/>

to make a road level. It is also called **Bannen**, referring to the power of punishing criminals and restraining them (hence <term>Blutbann</term> <note>High Jurisdiction or "Blood Ban," the right to decree capital punishment</note>, <term>Wildbann</term> <note>Forest Ban, the exclusive right to hunt in a territory</note>), as well as the right of casting someone into exile. *Rosenthal, On Fiefs, chapter 7, conclusion 6, number 3.* And <term>bannum</term> is used for that which is proscription and ejection into exile, concerning which we shall say more shortly.

Certainly, <term>Bannum</term>, a word of Frankish origin, is the name for a general mandate issued by the supreme power. Thus are named compulsory mills, <term>Bann-Mühlen</term>, in which one is commanded to grind grain, *see below under the word "Compulsory Mills"* (Zwang-Mühlen). <term>Forbannitus</term> <note>Banished</note>, someone to whom the land is forbidden. *Laws of the Ripuarians, title 89, section 1:*

> If anyone should presume to receive into his house a man who is <term>banished</term>, if he is a Ripuarian, let him pay 60 solidi, etc.

### 5. Ban, Outlawry, Military Ban. *Bannum*.

The word "Ban" (*Bann*) is ambiguous. For we use the word "Baan" to refer to public roads. Hence "Baanen" means

<column-break/>

to make a road flat and passable. The term "Bannen" is also used for the power of punishing criminals and exercising coercion (hence *Blutbann* <note>High justice, involving "blood" or capital punishment</note> and *Wildbann* <note>The right to hunt or exercise jurisdiction over a forest</note>), as well as for the right of casting someone into exile. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 7, conclusion 6, number 3. And "ban" (*bannum*) is taken to mean proscription and ejection into exile, which we will discuss shortly.

Indeed, in the Frankish tongue, "Ban" (*Bannum*) is the name for a general command issued by the supreme power. Thus we speak of "ban-mills" (*Molæ bannales* or *Bann-Mühlen*), in which one is commanded to grind grain; see below under the term "Compulsory Mills." Likewise, there are "ban-ovens" (*furni bannales*), where the entire neighborhood is forced to bring their bread for baking, based on the ban or edict of the superior: communal bake-houses or "Lord's Ovens" (concerning which, see my treatise *On the Treasury*, Schneidewein’s notes folio 276, and Grasser in his *Travels*, folio 345, where he recounts an example of a cruel invention for extorting money by Antonio Leyva). We also say "Coercion and Ban" (*Zwang und Bann*), referring to the extent to which one has the power to compel, command, or forbid. See the magnificent Mr. Mager, in his treatise *On the Armed Advocacy*, chapter 3, number 248 ff., and my own treatise *On the Nature of Peoples*, folio 55 and following.

Estienne Pasquier, in his *Researches*, book 2, chapter 13, folio 208, and book 7, chapter 34, says the "Ban" is public. From this comes "to give to the ban" (*à ban donner*), meaning to treat as abandoned.

The French still use "Ban" today for that proclamation made by a herald. The Italians say "bando" and use it for an edict. See Nicod and Crusca in their dictionaries. Similarly, "Banns" are the announcements of a future marriage (*das Verkünden*).

"Forbannitus" <note>An outlawed or banished person</note> means banished, or "banned outside," to whom the land is forbidden. The Ripuarian Law, title 89, section 1: "If anyone presumes to receive into his home a man who is a *forbannitus*, if he is a Ripuarian, let him pay 60 shillings," etc.

Thus Lazius, in *The Origins of Vienna*, book 2, chapter 3, thinks that Vienna was formerly named *Vendobona* or *Vindebona*, as if it were the "Territory and Ban of the Wends" <note>The Wends were a Slavic people</note>. He thinks Ratisbon [Regensburg] was *Rhætobonna*, the "Praetorium of the Rhaetians."

It is also frequent among writers of the middle ages to use "Ban" (*Bannum*) for a penalty or punishment (*Straff*), as Lehmann says in the *Chronicle of Speyer*, folio 188: specifically, when something is commanded under threat of a penalty.

"Heribannus" (*Heerbann*), or a ban against the enemy, is a summons to the camp or the army, as in Lehmann, folio 189. It also refers to the fine for one not marching in the army; in the Constitutions of Charlemagne: "that Counts should not presume to receive or inquire after the *haribannum*, or any collection for an army cause from free men, except if a messenger comes from our Palace or from our son, who requires that *heribannum*." See Bignon in his notes on the *Formularies of Marculf the Monk*, folio 543; add the Disputation of Hackelmann 11; also the life...

The same Franciscus Guillimannus notes that Barbarossa <note>Frederick I (r. 1155–1190), Holy Roman Emperor</note>, after Milan was overturned and Lombardy subdued and divided into several parts, placed German nobles over individual sections—indeed, nearly every city—as Italian historians testify. At that time, Hermann, Margrave of Baden, was placed over Verona (which had already been defeated) as Imperial Vicar or Governor. Therefore, after he returned to Germany, he subsequently used this Veronese title, which few after him retained, more as a memorial than to demonstrate the origin of the lineage or hereditary possession of the old Veronese domain.

Since all of this is so, and because the Dukes of Zähringen and Counts of Habsburg, as well as the Lords Margraves of Baden and Hachberg, etc., are of one lineage and descent; and also since the Lords Margraves of Hachberg years ago held many counties and lordships, as well as many different jurisdictions and rights, in Breisgau, as well as in Swabia, in the Black Forest, and elsewhere—which were gradually brought under the House of Austria: Thus there is no doubt that those of Zähringen, Habsburg, or Austria, and the Margraves of Hachberg, as the closest kinsmen who sprouted from one trunk <note>original: "stipite," referring to a common ancestor</note>, in former times shared their land and people with one another by equal right <note>original: "æquali Jure"</note>, and no part would have reserved for itself any territorial sovereignty over the other's estates, whatever name that power might have.

### 5. Ban, Outlawry, Higher Outlawry, Army-Ban. The Ban.

The word **Ban** <note>original: "Bann"</note> is equivocal <note>having multiple meanings</note>. For we say *Baan* regarding public roads. Hence *Baanen*, in Besoldus Volume 1, means to make a road level. It is also called **Banning** <note>original: "Bannen"</note> regarding the power of punishing criminals and coercing them (hence the <term>Blood-ban</term> <note>original: "Blutbann," the right of high justice/capital punishment</note> and the <term>Forest-ban</term> <note>original: "Wildbann," hunting rights</note>), and also regarding the right of casting someone into exile. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 7, conclusion 6, number 3. And "ban" is used for that which is proscription and ejection into exile, concerning which we shall say more shortly.

<column-break/>

Indeed, the "Ban," in the Frankish tongue, is called a general mandate proceeding from the supreme power. And thus they are called <term>compulsory mills</term> <note>original: "Molæ bannales" or "Bann-Mühlen"</note>, in which it is commanded to grind grain; see below under the term *Forced-Mills* <note>original: "Zwang-Mühlen"</note>. Likewise <term>compulsory ovens</term>: to which the whole neighborhood is compelled to bring their bread for baking, by the "ban" or edict of a superior: *common baking-ovens or Lord's-ovens*, (concerning which see my treatise *On the Treasury*, Schneidewwin in his notes folio 276, and Grasser in his *Itinerary* folio 345, where he recounts an example of a cruel invention for extorting money by Antonio Leyva.) So also we say *Compulsion and Ban*, as far as one has the right to compel or command, and to forbid. See the Magnificent Lord Mager, in his *Treatise on the Armed Advocacy*, chapter 3, number 248 and following in many places, and my own *Treatise on the Nature of Peoples*, folio 55 and following.

Étienne Pasquier, in *Researches*, book 2, chapter 13, folio 208, and book 7, chapter 34, says the "Ban" is public. And hence *to give to the ban* <note>original: "à ban donner"</note>, as if to give to the ban, means to consider something as abandoned.

The French, even today, use "Ban" for that proclamation which is made by a herald. The Italians say *bando*, and use it for an edict. See Nicod and Crusca in their *Dictionaries*. Thus *Bans* are the denunciations of a future marriage, the *Proclamation* <note>original: "das Verkünden," i.e., banns of marriage</note>.

<term>Forbannitus</term> <note>An outlaw</note>, *banished*, or "bannitus" outwards, *one to whom the land is forbidden*. Ripuarian Law, title 89, section 1: "If anyone should presume to receive into his house a man who is *forbannitus*, if he is a Ripuarian <note>A Frank living on the banks of the Rhine</note>, let him pay 60 shillings," etc.

Thus Lazius, in his *Origins of Vienna*, book 2, chapter 3, thinks that Vienna was once named *Vendobona* or *Vindebona*, as if it were the *territory and ban* of the Vends <note>a Slavic people</note>. *Ratisbon* <note>Regensburg</note>, as if *Rhætobonnam*, the Seat of the Rhaetians.

So also it is frequent among the writers of the middle ages to use "Ban" for a *punishment* <note>original: "Straff"</note>, as in Lehmann in the *Chronicle of Speyer*, folio 188: "Whenever something is commanded under penalty of a punishment."

<term>Heerbann</term> <note>The "Army-Ban"</note>, a ban against the enemy, or a calling to the camp or the army; Lehmann, folio 189, regarding the fine for one not marching in the army; the Constitutions of Charlemagne: "That the Counts should not presume to receive or inquire after the *haribannum*, or any collection for an army cause from free men, except if a messenger comes from our Palace, or from our son, who requires that *heribannum*." See Bignon in his notes on the *Formularies of the Monk Marculphus*, folio 543; add the Disputation of Hackelmann 11, likewise the Life...

...also of St. Hubert, where more is found regarding the ban.

Vitus Amerbachius says that the **Army-Ban** (*Heribannum*) is composed of *bannum* and *Heere*, that is, an army (the Saxons say *Hare*), because that money is specifically contributed to the military, whether as a tribute or as a fine.

**Lombard Laws**, book 3, folio 79: Concerning Army-Bans, we wish that the emissaries <note>original: "missi," the officials sent by the King or Emperor to supervise administration</note> should exact this faithfully, without favor or flattery of any persons, and without terror, according to our command.

**Frankish Laws**, book 4, chapter 71: Whosoever is a free man and has been summoned to the army by ban <note>original: "in hostem bannitus"</note> and has contemptuously failed to come, let him pay the full army-ban, that is, 60 <term>solidi</term> <note>a gold coin or unit of account in the early medieval period</note>. Or if he does not have the means to pay that sum, let him deliver himself as a pledge into the service of the Prince until he is released from the ban through his time served. And he who delivered himself into service because of the army-ban, if he should die, his heirs shall not be held liable for that ban.

Goropio thinks that *Heer* means "common" or "public," hence *Heerstraß*, a public road; indeed, he even thinks Hercules is named as if he were a "common witness" <note>The author likely refers to a folk etymology linking Hercules to 'Heer' (army/common) and 'Kiel' or 'Keile'</note>. And thus the Army-Ban would be a **general summons** <note>original: "ein allgemein Aufbot"</note>. And from there is said *Heer*, an army: a common expedition <note>original: "Heerzug"</note>.

### ADDITION.

The **Ban** and **Army-Ban** are fines paid by those who do not obey the edict by which **Vassals**, equipped with horses and arms, are ordered to be present at the County on a certain day; this edict itself is also not infrequently called the "ban" or "army-ban." Hence some, considering these to be French words, derive them from *ban*, which signifies a fine, and from *Heer*, an army. To this they refer what is decreed in the *Frankish Laws*, book 4, chapter 71: that a Vassal summoned to the army (called out) who stubbornly remains away must pay the full army-ban, that is, 60 solidi, or if he is not able to pay, he must deliver himself as a pledge into the service of his lord until he has paid the ban. I cannot pass over these things which Rittershusius in *Differences between Civil and Canon Law*, page 28, and Cypreus in *On Betrothals*, chapter 11, paragraph 12, bring forward. The proclamation or publication of a new couple made in the assembly of the faithful is also called a **Ban** <note>This refers to the "Banns of Marriage," a public announcement to ensure the legality of a union</note>. He adds that "Ban" is a Gothic word first brought into Italy by the Goths, who also used the Germanic language, and it descends from the word *Band*, as if you were to say *Bandum*, that is, a bond or tie; the word to "banish" (*bannire*) is the same as to bind, to constrain, and to bind with the bond of excommunication. Many excellent things about this word are in Schönborn's *Politics*, book 41, chapter 8. How some have excommunicated or **put under the ban** frogs, forest donkeys, dragons, locusts, rats, flies, hornets, crickets, etc., see Zeiller, century 4, question 46, page 241 <note>This refers to historical ecclesiastical trials against animals or pests that were damaging crops</note>.

# 7. Ban, Imperial Outlawry.
## The Imperial Ban.

The **Imperial Ban** (*Bannum Imperii*) is a judicial censure by which violators of the public peace are interdicted from "water and fire" <note>original: "aqua & igni interdicitur," a Roman legal formula for total exile, depriving one of all social and legal protections</note>, so that they may be received by no one into protection, loyalty, or friendship, and may be harmed with impunity by all, both in their property and their person. See the *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court*, part 2, title 9, a matter which Mr. Gail treats specifically in two books.

The Emperors speak of the Imperial Ban in various ways in their Constitutions:

**Frederick II** in the *Constitution on the status and customs against the liberty of the Church* says: "Under a ban of a thousand marks." From which it appears clearly enough that the Ban can also be understood as a monetary penalty.

The same Frederick, a little further down, speaking of the harsher penalty of the ban: "But if," he says, "contemners of this our constitution are found for a year, we command their goods to be occupied with impunity by all throughout our entire Empire. Saving nonetheless other penalties promulgated against such people in a General Council."

Alciatus in his *Parerga* thinks the Ban is named from the Greeks' "year-long banishment," which was called <term>apepaniautismos</term> <note>original: "ἀπεπανιαυτισμὸς," a term for temporary exile for involuntary homicide</note>, as if it were "ab-annation," that is, a banishment of one year. But certainly that word is far removed from the logic of this term. And it is beyond all doubt that (as was said in the preceding section) the Ban is a purely Germanic word.

After capital punishments were introduced, the interdiction of water and fire ceased, and in its place succeeded deportation. And when deportation was removed as the number of provinces under the Roman Empire was reduced, it came to proscription, which is called the **Ban**, or **Imperial Excommunication**.

And those who are delivered to the ban for a crime—so they are **outlawed and displaced** <note>original: "geächtet und versetzet"</note>—fall from peace into war; their body and life depart into the sacred (meaning they are forfeit), no different than a bird in the air, and they can be killed with impunity by those subject to the jurisdiction of the one issuing the ban, and the killer is considered to have committed no crime. See Andreas Knichen in his *Encyclopedia*, chapter 12, number 4; Coler, decision 108, numbers 2 and 57, where he discusses how one arrives at the "Higher Ban," which is called <term>Aber-Acht</term> <note>The most severe form of the Imperial Ban, often involving a total loss of rights and the destruction of the outlaw's property</note>.

And hence it is asked: whether, with a safe conscience, a banned person can be killed by anyone? And whether he, being attacked, can defend himself? See my commentary on the law of justice and right, question 7; Borell *On Magistrates*, book 3, chapter 6, regarding whether it is permissible to make laws that a banned person be killed. Add on the subject of the Banned, Tuschus under the letter B; and at length Philip Paschalis *On Paternal Power*, part 4, chapter 3; Peregrinus *On the Right of the Treasury*, book 3, title "On the Banned," and book 5, title 2, regarding what those who are restored may recover.

And as to whether those under the ban can enter into contracts, see Knipschild, *Exercises on Contracts*, exercise 1, question 21; add Hermann Stamm in his treatise *On Personal Servitude*, book 1, chapter 3, where he has many things concerning banned persons.

# Letter B.

<margin>
Basel Disputations, volume 2, thesis 4 and following. Also in the same volume, the disputation on security, thesis 116 and following, which discusses whether those under a ban may appeal.
</margin>

When this most recent penalty of proscription was first introduced, a distinction was observed between **Imperial Outlawry** and **The Ban** in this manner: Imperial Outlawry <note>original: "Censura Imperialis," often called "die Kayserliche Acht" in German</note> carried this title within the first year. This is because the Empire "judges" <note>original: "censet"</note> whether a person should be declared under it or not. In our language, "to judge" <note>original: "achten"</note> means to decide, to estimate, or to consider. This penalty stripped the person and their property of all security and peace everywhere. **The Ban** <note>original: "Bannum" or "die Bann"</note>, however, meant that the person could be apprehended by any court, but not killed on sight. After a year, this outlawry and proscription would be repeated and confirmed with even more severe penalties. From this, it is called **The High Ban** <note>original: "die Aberacht"</note>, as if it were an intensification of excommunication and Imperial Outlawry. For just as a minor ecclesiastical excommunication is a "Censure" and the major one is an "Anathema," so civil proscription is either lighter or more severe. Proscription is named "damnation" from the ceremony of "writing down" <note>original: "scribendi"</note>, which Ulpian explains when speaking of private interdiction. From this, we say in Latin "to proscribe" to mean to relegate to exile, or to proscribe for Outlawry, or to make the person and their goods public property. This is because the names of those condemned are usually written in clear letters and displayed in a crowded place to declare them subject to that penalty. Regarding the origin of **Bandits** <note>original: "Banditen"</note> in Venice, see Guillaume Postel, *On the Magistrates of the Athenians*, chapter 10, near the end, folio 485.

Cities that possess **High and Low Jurisdiction** <term>High and Low Jurisdiction: "merum et mixtum Imperium," the legal authority to pass both death sentences and civil rulings</term>, whether by long-standing custom or special privilege, rightly observe the use of both permanent and temporary banishment. For why should they not cast out those whom they see will be useless and harmful to their Republic? Sometimes they even condemn resident citizens not to leave their own houses, following the final law concerning the interdiction of the relegated.

Our German Princes also daily use banishment and interdiction, known as **Legal Restraint** <note>original: "Verfestung"</note> and **Minor Ban** <note>original: "Unteracht"</note>. If a wicked man does not show a subsequent improvement in his ways, a ruler holding High Jurisdiction can banish him directly out of his Province: "He banishes him from the territory and the land" <note>original: "Thut ihm das Gebiet und Lands verweisen"</note>. See Bidembach, question 7, at the verse "non subsequuta."

However, no one can be marked with the **Imperial Ban** by an inferior authority. In many ways, the ban of an inferior differs from that which is imposed by the Supreme Power of all. See Stam, *On Slaves*, book 1, folio 84.

The ban is twofold: for punishment and for **contempt of court** <note>original: "contumaciae," failure to appear or obey a court order</note>.

Nothing is more frequent than for people to be marked with the ban at **Rottweil** <note>a city in Baden-Württemberg famous for its Imperial High Court</note> and in the **Provincial Courts** <note>original: "Landgerichten"</note>, specifically in the Swabian Provincial Court, under this very form:

<column-break/>

> I, N. N., Doctor of Laws, etc., Councillor to the most Serene and Mighty Prince and Lord, Lord N., elected Roman Emperor, at all times Increaser of the Empire, King in Germany, Hungary, and Bohemia, etc., and to the most Reverend and Serene Prince and Lord, N., Archduke of Austria and Prince of Swabia, etc., my most Gracious and Sovereign Lords respectively, and **Judge of the Free Lands** <note>original: "Freylandrichter"</note> in Upper and Lower Swabia, on the Leutkirch Heath, and in the Mountains, etc.: By the power and grace of Your Roman Imperial Majesty and Princely Serenities, I make known to the venerable and spiritual, the well-born, noble, brave, prudent, honorable, and wise—to each and every prelate, count, baron, knight, and member of the nobility, mayors, bailiffs, burgomasters, councillors, judges, and communities who belong to and reside in the district of this Provincial Court: That before this open, proclaimed Provincial Court, held at the appointed time, namely on [Date] in the Holy Imperial City of [Name] on the open, free Imperial Highway, [Plaintiff Name] has so far complained against [Defendant Name] that he has, by judgment and rightful court, brought him into **The Ban** <note>original: "in die Acht"</note>. He remains to this day written in the sworn **Ban-Book** of the Provincial Court as an open outlaw. This I say by the oath I have sworn to my aforementioned most Gracious and Sovereign Lords. Therefore, upon the same [Defendant's Name] insolent contempt of the law, and the further appeal of the plaintiff, and by the power of the aforementioned Roman Imperial Majesty and Princely Serenity, etc., I command you all, and each of you in particular, that you do not shelter, house, or provide for the aforementioned recorded outlaw in your courts, territories, jurisdictions, or bans; nor give him food or drink, nor grind his grain or bake for him, nor generally have any other fellowship with him. If you should do so despite this, and a complaint is brought against you, you shall be judged according to the Law of the Provincial Court. Given with the judgment and sealed with the pressed seal of the Provincial Court on the reverse, etc.

Regarding the ban for contempt of court, see the *Swabian Provincial Court Ordinance*, part 2, title 8, etc. On how to be released from the Rottweil Ban, see the *Rottweil High Court Ordinance*, part 3, title 15, section "After that" <note>original: "Nach dem aber"</note>; however, this is not without the consent of the opposing party, but if one demands too much of another, it is subject to judicial moderation.

A question of great importance is: whether the Emperor, without the common consent of the Princes, can mark a **State of the Empire** <term>State of the Empire: "Statum Imperii," a territory or ruler with a seat in the Imperial Diet</term> with the ban? See Georg Everhard, Volume 2, Counsel 19, and my own treatise *On the Mixed State*, folio 217.

This was disputed—and the controversy does not yet seem to be settled—regarding the proscription of **Frederick the Palatine** <note>original: "Friderici Palatini," referring to Frederick V, the "Winter King," whose outlawry by the Emperor without the consent of the Electors was a major cause of legal friction during the Thirty Years' War</note>,

### 8. Banner, Flag. Standard.

*Fanon* or *Fahn* <note>German for "flag"</note>, referring to a small linen cloth, comes from *panno* <note>Latin for "cloth"</note>, see Lindebrog in his *Glossary* under the word *Fano*. But it is more probable that "Banner" or "Banier" is derived from "Ban" <note>original: "Bannum"</note>. See my work, *On the Nature of Peoples, page 56.* Because one commands <note>original: "gebietet," implying the legal power of the Ban</note> someone to the banners.

*Banus* <note>Ban or Viceroy</note>, a royal presiding officer in the Kingdoms of Hungary joined to the King, who precedes all others with a banner.

Caelius Rhodiginus noted in *Antiquities, book 15, chapter 17*, that a "Bandophoros" <note>Greek: βανδοφόρος</note> is one who carries the leader's sign.

The Modern Greeks also use *bandon* <note>βάνδον</note> for a banner. See the *Glossary*. And even Procopius says that the *Bandum* is a military sign for the Romans. *Banderium*: a cohort of 400 soldiers. In French: *Bandè de gens de guerre* <note>A band of men of war</note>. For us: a small company of mercenary soldiers <note>original: "ein Fähnlein Landsknecht"</note>.

Indeed, in every serious and public matter, the Germanic nations employed the ceremony of the Banner. And among the Germans, just as with the Lombards, banners were used to signify the power of penal judgment and in its execution. Hence the "Banner-Lord" <note>original: "Banerherr"</note>, who possesses criminal jurisdiction, and "Banner-Fiefs" <note>original: "Fahnen-Lehen"</note>, to which the same supreme power is attached.

### 9. Bankrupts, Failures. Ruined Debtors.

"Bank-breakers" <note>original: "Banccæruptores"</note>, the French call them *Banqueroutiers, who make bankruptcy*; who "break the bank," that is, who break the bench <note>original: "rumpunt bancam," referring to the physical breaking of a money-changer's bench after failure</note>. The Italians call them *Falliti* <note>Failures</note>, we call them *Banckherottirer*, as if a breaker of the bench or bank: those who run away on account of debts <note>original: "die Schulden halber ausreissen"</note>. These are also said in the broader volumes of our Law to "withdraw from the market" <note>original: "foro cedere," meaning to cease business or go into hiding</note>, *law 7, section 2, Digest on deposits.* As to whether the surrender of assets <note>term: "cessio bonorum" — a legal process where a debtor gives up all property to creditors to avoid prison</note> marks someone with infamy, see *Concius, Idle Hours, book 2, chapter 18.* Many things concerning this surrender are held by Wilhelm Anton in his *Treatise on Five-Year Letters, etc., page 491*; add *book 7 of the Decretals, page 250.*

But concerning these, see Daniel Sauter’s *Practice of Bankrupts and his Scourge of Failures.* Mr. Arumaeus also has a disputation *On debtors made unable to pay, volume 3, discourse 4, page 145*; and add Latherus *On Surrenders, book 3, chapter 15. Tuschus, letter D, conclusion 105, etc. My own work "On Life and Death," page 24.*

The surrender of assets was formerly called *Chrenechruda* <note>An ancient Frankish legal ritual involving throwing soil and a rod to transfer debt or property</note> through the sod and the rod <note>original: "per durpillum & festucam"</note>. *Limn. volume 2, Additions to book 4, chapter 8, page 311.* Failure <note>original: "Fallimentum"</note> is categorized among fortuitous cases <note>unforeseeable accidents</note>. *Carpzov, Decision 132, number 16.*

Concerning fraudulent and malicious bankrupts and their lies and punishments, see *Zahn on Lies, book 2, chapter 58, number 4.* "Overturners" <note>original: "Eversores"</note>, who have withdrawn from the market with a closed shop, which they used to have in the public forum, *law 7, Digest on deposits; final law, Digest on curators of property*, and have "boiled away" <note>term: "decoctores" — Latin for bankrupts, literally those who have "boiled down" or wasted their substance</note>. On Bankrupt Merchants, see Daniel Sauter’s entire treatise *Failures*. Ruined debtors and the "broken" are infamous—indeed, most notorious, *Klock, volume 2, counsel 50, numbers 23, 24.* They are prone to lying and collusion (number 25); their account books hold a presumption against them (number 26). A bankrupt is presumed to have failed through fraud and fault, and he must prove an accidental cause. *Counsel 50, number 72.* Bertazolus disagrees (ibid., number 28).

Ruined debtors are made by the fault of fortune in three ways. The first rank is derived from fortuitous cases. A fortuitous case is either natural, which a man cannot prevent, such as the force of the sea, ill health, death, etc.; or accidental, which happens by a man's act, such as fires, shipwrecks, or enemy attacks. But a fire is only numbered among fortuitous cases when all fault...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of financial failure and the different classes of legal officials, transitioning from the definition of a debtor's fault to the specific types of bankrupts and the structure of judicial benches.</meta>

...the fault of the debtor is absent. There are, however, three kinds of people who fall into this stain of disgrace through more tragic accidents: 1. by a stormy sea, **through the adversity of fortune at sea**. 2. by robbery, both at sea and on land, **through highway robbery and privateering**. 3. by the fraud of their own debtors, **through the withholding of the debts which their debtors owe them**. These individuals are improperly called Bankrupts <note>original: "Decoctores," literally "those who have boiled away" their assets</note>. A person becomes a bankrupt by their own fault when they waste their goods by dissipating or tearing them apart, or lose their merchandise through gambling, the allurements of prostitutes, or through sumptuous banquets. Besold, in his *700 Witty Sayings, century 1, number 81*, compared the dice of gamblers to the pills of physicians, which, although taken in a tiny dose and quantity, empty a large purse. These people primarily have five ways of deceiving. 1. The visiting of Fairs. These are either minor, such as **weekly markets**, or major and more solemn markets, such as the fairs of Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig, and Naumburg; there, they borrow 1000 florins from one citizen and 1000 from another, and buy goods on the condition that they wish to pay half at the current fair and give the other half at the future fairs. 2. The method of grandiloquence, by which they catch creditors like fish on a hook. 3. Pride in clothing and in feasts. 4. The magnificent and splendid construction of buildings. 5. The sweetness of words. **The deceptions of bankrupts are beyond imagining**, *Zorer part 1, question 10, number 680.* Concerning the ways through which someone becomes a bankrupt—partly by fortune and partly by their own vice—nothing certain can be established, but it must be left to the discretion of the judge. This matter will become clearer through this case: There is a certain Merchant who undertakes large negotiations and promises more in a contract than he has in his own resources; he borrows goods or money, hoping he will profit so much that he can not only satisfy his creditor from whom he borrowed, but also take a profit for himself. Once the contract is completed, he receives the goods, and perhaps because of some accidental chance or other causes, he loses them, or does not sell them for the value at which he acquired them. In such a case, his vice first appears from the fact that the merchant obligated himself to more than he had in his substance and resources. Yet, because his mind, intention, and purpose were to satisfy his creditor, and the goods were lost because of adverse misfortune and unhappiness, it is ascribed to the fault of fortune. How to proceed against bankrupts is shown by *Zorer, part 1, question 10, number 682.* That the surrender of goods <note>original: "cessio bonorum"</note> differs from the disturbance of accounts or bankruptcy is most elegantly taught, according to his custom, by *Rittershusius in the New Works, part 2, chapter 3, number 24.* At the instance of creditors, a general proclamation is sometimes permitted, by which all who know anything regarding the bankrupt's goods are ordered to reveal it under penalty. *Zorer part 1, question 10, number 695.*

<column-break/>

### 10. Bench, Benchers. Judgeship, Judge.

The Judgeship <note>original: "Scabinatus"</note> and the Judges <note>original: "Scabini," often referring to lay judges or assessors</note> are named as if from the bench <note>original: "scamnum"</note>, the **Benchers** <note>German: "Banckhner"</note>; *Winther in his The Assessor, part 1, chapter 3, number 15,* where he says it should not be omitted that in our High Court (that is, **in the Princely Württemberg High Court at Tübingen**) three Benches are held. (1.) **The Noble Bench**, containing the Judges and four Noble Assessors. (2.) **The Learned Bench**, containing five Doctors <note>meaning Doctors of Law</note>. (3.) **The Estates Bench**, containing three persons representing the municipalities; for the Prince chooses the rest: and thus the whole College, together with the Secretary, consists of fourteen persons. See above under *Assessors*.
So also in the Diets <note>the Imperial Diets or "Comitia"</note>, the Imperial Cities occupy two benches, **the Rhenish and the Swabian**.

-> ADDITION. <-

In the Diets, the Imperial and free cities obtain two benches, **the Rhenish and the Swabian Bench**. In what order they sit on these benches is clearly recounted by many, including *Becker in Imperial Law, page 189 at the end and following; Limnäus in Imperial Law, book 9, chapter 1, numbers 146, 147.*

### 11. Confinement to the Tithes. Confinatio.

For the amendment of a past life, Confinement, **the banning into the tithes**, is sometimes applied. **This is when a person is commanded that he may not depart from the territory of his city or village**: which proves mere authority <note>original: "merum imperium," a technical term for the highest level of judicial power, including the power of life and death</note>. *Jacobus de Sancto Georgio on Fiefs; Bidenbach in Noble Questions, question 7, regarding amendment.*
Indeed, it is accepted by our customs **that those who are of no use in the land are banished from it, sometimes even being made to swear an oath to stay across the Rhine or Danube.** See *my work on the law of things, 275, section on the preliminary regarding book 1 of the Digests, question 45.* **But those who have a wife and children, and in whom there is still a good hope of improvement, are banned into the tithes.**

-> ADDITION. <-

Confinement is when someone is not exiled from a place, but a certain place and certain boundaries are assigned to him, from which he may not depart. *Zafius on the law "Imperium" 3, Digest on Jurisdiction.* **As when someone is confined by a judicial sentence to the place where he is a citizen, or to the tithe-district, never to leave it without a pardon.** *Bocer on Jurisdiction, page 212.*

### 12. Field Warden. Camparii.

Among our people, the **Banwarth** is the guardian of the territory. *Mr. Martin Mager on Armed Advocacy, chapter 3, number 268.* Commonly called a **Schütz** <note>a guard or protector of fields and forests</note>.

### 13. Pope.

The name of the Pope (from which our own word is derived, as well as the term *Pfaff* <note>original: "Pfaff"; historically a neutral term for a priest, though it later became derogatory in German</note>) was formerly common to all Bishops; see *Bignon in his notes on Marculf’s Formulas, page 418.* Indeed, among the Greeks, it occasionally happened to be the proper name of a specific man, and the memory of that name is preserved by the famous martyr Lycaon in the *Menologium and Martyrology for March 16th.* Baronius also discusses the name of the Pope at length in his *Annals, Year of Christ 165, number 4, etc.* He says that its true interpretation comes from the Greek *papas* <note>original: "πάπας"</note>, that is, "Father." In this sense, it passed into a title of dignity, so that venerable clerics were addressed this way. Later, it began to be the specific title of Bishops, though it was customarily granted more specifically to the Roman Pontiff, until Gregory VII, in a Council held at Rome in the year 1075, decreed among other things that the name "Pope" should be unique in the entire Christian world, and that no one should be permitted to distinguish themselves or another by that title.

Concerning the election of the Pontiff, see the *Discourse on the State of Rome, page 87 and following, and my own treatise on Royal Succession and Election, page 178.* Formerly, the Emperors <note>original: "Cæsares"</note> claimed this power for themselves. Even the Greek Emperors asserted the right to confirm the Pontifical election; see *Bellarmine, Book 2 on the Pontiff, chapter 17, page 254.* Later, the power passed to the clergy and the people of the Roman Church; see *Bellarmine in the same place, page 253 and the following page.* Even while the pagan Emperors were still ruling, elections were rarely held without disturbances, as *Ammianus and Symmachus note in their Letters, page 305 and following.* But Bellarmine proves that elections are best carried out by the Cardinals in *On the Clergy, Book 1, chapter 9 and following.* There, he investigates: if all the Cardinals were to die, who would succeed to their place? A true and holy election is described by *Suso in the Nine Rocks, page 367,* where he also discusses the Cardinals.

Regarding the etymology <note>the origin of the word</note> of "Pontiff" and "Pope," see also *Speckhan, century 2, class 1, question 19.* On whether he is greater than and ranked above the Emperor, see *Peregrinus on the Law of the Treasury, book 1, title: on those who have Fiscal Rights; and my own work On Majesty, page 18, etc.* See also *Bignon in his notes on Marculf the Monk’s Formulas, page 553,* where he says that <term>Pontifex</term> <note>literally "bridge-builder" in ancient Rome, but used here for the Pope</note> is taken to mean the power of doing, or "acting powerfully." Add to this *Longus’s Chronological Breviary, page 316; Laelius Bisciola’s Leisure Hours, book 8, chapter 10; Martini’s Philological Lexicon under the word "Pope"; Heraldus on Tertullian, 1st digression, chapter 20; Bellarmine, Book 2 on the Pontiff, chapter 31; Lancellotti in the Temple of All Judges, page 532, etc.* On the voice and titles of the Pope, see *Rinthelin in The Roman Catholic Jurist, chapter 20 and following.* Many things concerning the Pontiffs are held by *Zamueriensis in the Mirror, book 2 at the beginning; Chockier, volume 2, on exemptions in the Church, page 4; Gilbert Regius, 2nd century, chapter 28; Rinthelin in the aforementioned treatise, chapter 13 and following.* *M. Antonius Marcellus* wrote on the secular law of the Roman Pontiffs. Can the Pontiff rebuke or excommunicate Kings? See *Longus in the Breviary, page 314.* Can the Pontiff grant a dispensation against divine law? See *Martini in the treatise on Jurisdiction, part 4, century 1, case 64.*

<column-break/>

On why kingdoms were offered to the Pontiffs, see *Baronius, Year of Christ 1075, number 6.* On the origin, rights, etc., of the Pontiffs, see *Matthias Stephanus, book 2 of the Institutes of Canon Law, page 283; Bzovius on the Temporal Monarchy of the Church.* Concerning the controversy between the Emperors and the Pontiffs, especially under Henry IV, see *Serarius on the affairs of Mainz, page 788.* On the jurisdiction of the Pontiff over the Princes of Germany, see the *Marburg Consultations, number 48, volume 4.* Regarding the conclave and the election of the Pontiff, see *Maioli’s Dog Days, 2nd colloquy, 6, at the beginning, page 772.* On the primacy of Constantinople, see *Johann Jakob Gretser in the Defense of Gregory VII, chapter 3,* where you see that it is purely political when the Greeks and the followers of Henry IV insist that **they want to subject the churches to the Empire** <note>original German: "die Kirchen dem Imperio wollen unterwerffen"</note>; which is a characteristic of all heretics.

At this point, one should not overlook that honor—or rather dishonor—which some, especially the "Innovators" <note>a term often used for Protestants by Catholic-leaning writers or vice versa</note>, attribute to Mainz: the story that a "Popess" <note>the legend of Pope Joan</note> once arose from there. This is claimed by almost everyone’s name and enthusiasm, such as *Michael Stifel in his book on the Numbers of Daniel and the Apocalypse.* But it is utterly denied that any such woman ever existed either in Mainz or in Rome; it is a mere and stale fable, as *Serarius clearly demonstrates with infinite arguments in the Affairs of Mainz, book 1, chapter 41 and following,* which you will not regret having seen.

On whether Christ, as a man, is the Lord of the World, see *Molina on Justice and Law, treatise 2, disputation 28,* who in the *following disputation* inquires into the power of the Pontiff in secular matters. As to what his role was in transferring the Empire to the Germans, consult *Gewold on the Seven-Member Council, chapter 8.*

Very many people rail against the Roman Pontiffs quite bitterly. I do not follow them at all; I only add here that they have continually preserved the purity of the Faith regarding the article of the Holy Trinity (see *Baronius, Year of Christ 263, at the end*), and I also noted this in **my own treatise On Majesty, page 24.** They also defended Orthodoxy against the furies of the Arians <note>a 4th-century heresy denying the full divinity of Christ</note>; and Saint Athanasius fled to them for refuge. Likewise, in the cause of Nestorius, the Roman Pontiff defended the truth and Saint Cyril; see *Wegelin of Augsburg in his notes on Cyril, page 192.* Also, the Pontiff converted Germany through his Legates. See the *Composition of Peace, page 138.*

---

### ADDITION.

As for what *Cluverius* reports from *Antonius Sabellicus* and *Johannes Nauclerus* in the *Epitome of History, page 537*: that Pope Alexander III stepped on the neck of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa <note>Frederick I, known as "Red-beard"</note> while reciting the words of the Psalmist from *Psalm 91, verse 13* <note>"You will tread on the lion and the cobra"</note>—this is a most vain fiction. This is confirmed by *Mr. Bernegger in Historico-Political Questions, respondent Robert Königsmann, 1626; and Christoph Adam Rupertus in a letter to Georg Richter, Jurist, December 11, 1643;* and the same *Richter in his Response to Rupertus, December 16, 1643, in Richter’s Selected Letters, page 457 and following; and again Rupertus at great length in Besold’s Historical Synopsis.*

However, Leo Africanus <note>original: "Johanne Leone"</note> says that Iphricus, having been driven out by the Assyrians, consulted an oracle and received the response that he must flee to *Ber*—which in their language means "desert"—and from this the name stuck to the region he occupied. He also notes that because the Africans did not understand the Arabic language, they described the manner of pronunciation as more like a murmur than an articulate voice (which they also call *Barbar*), and so they either gave it the name or kept the name that was given. Also, the cause of this name being so widely spread perhaps came from the Romans, who,

Pacius discusses whether there is trade with barbarians in his *Analysis of the Code*, under the title "Which things cannot be sold," number 3, and the title "On commerce," number 3. **15. Salvage Money. The right of the Treasury over the goods of the shipwrecked.**

The maritime custom that snatches the goods of those afflicted by shipwreck lacks all reason: because it brings lawsuits against one whom God himself has already moved with maritime strife <note>i.e., it is cruel to sue someone who has already been ruined by the sea</note>.

> Profit is sought from shipwreck, and the body
> Cast into the deep is sought just as much as the prize itself.

Parthenius, *On Litigation*, book 1, chapter 13, number 5. Gail, *Observations*, 18, number 1. "Affliction should not be added to the afflicted." <note>original: "Cum afflictis non sit addenda afflictio"</note> Gail, d. obs. n. 5. Whence it has been laudably received in certain provinces that, upon payment of a fee which they call **salvage money** <note>original: "das Bargegeld"</note>, all goods are released freely. Parthenius, *On Litigation*, number 5 at the end. Lather, *On Taxes*, 2, chapter 11, number 39, etc. It is called elsewhere **travel-right** <note>original: "das Fahrrecht"</note>, and by the French **the right of shipwrecks** <note>original: "le droit des naufrages"</note>. See my own work *On Majesty*, page 177. Also **stranding** <note>original: "Stranden"</note> or **ground-stirring** <note>original: "Grundruhr"</note>; see below under the word **Right of ground-stirring** <note>original: "Grundruhrrecht"</note>. Zieritz on the *Criminal Constitution of Charles V*, article 218. And such a custom is found to be prohibited in the law *navigia* and the aforementioned Criminal Ordinance of Charles V. The same is established in the *Practical Supplement* to the observations of Webner, page 10, and by Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Abridged*, pages 8 and 9. And in the Imperial Chamber, mandates are usually decreed against this custom. Gail, book 1, observation 18.

->ADDITION.<-

On **ground-stirring** <note>original: "Von der Grundruhr"</note>, see below under this word; add Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 3, number 36. Lord Doctor Tabor, *Criminal Gleanings*, page 216. What the storm left behind, the Prefect—like a second storm more cruel than the sea itself—snatches from the wretched. The French call it *Varech* (**travel-right**) or **right of shipwrecks**. *Guide to Finance*, page 75. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 114.

### 16. Bastard, Bank-child <note>original: "Banckart"</note>. Illegitimate.

We commonly use this name for all those born illegitimately, of whatever kind, even though *Accursius* in the *Gloss on the rubric: regarding concubines* and the *final law: On natural children in the Code of Justinian*, as well as *Decius* in *Counsel 433, number 14*, seem to have accepted it only for "natural" children <note>In Roman law, "natural" children were those born of a steady concubine, having more rights than "spurious" children born of casual affairs</note>. However, common usage of speech is to the contrary, and in everyday language, we are accustomed to calling everyone born non-legitimately "Bastards." See *Præpositus* on the chapter *venerabili* regarding who are legitimate children, column 7; and *Annæus Robertus* on *Adjudicated Matters*, book 2, chapter 14.

This word seems to some to be derived from the Greek *Bassarid* <note>original: "Βασσαρίς"</note>, which, besides meaning a priestess of Bacchus, is also taken to mean a harlot and a woman of the streets: as if illegitimate children mostly arise from a harlot’s embrace. See *Gabriel Paleotus* on *Spurious Children*, chapter 18, number 3.

Or rather, the word **Bastard** <note>original: "Bastart"</note> descends from the **bark** <note>original: "vom Bast"</note>, as *Schäreus* has it in the *Language School*, folio 168. Just as certain **wines** are also called by this name, according to *Lemnius*, book 2, chapter 34. Namely, when a foreign, unsuitable species comes to another and is stuck and grows in the inner succulent rind or **bark** <note>original: "Bast"</note>, just as if it were in its own trunk and species, much like grafted shoots. **Virgil says in book 2 of the *Georgics*:** <note>original: "2. orig." referring to the Georgics, though the text says "orig."</note>

> They insert a bud from another tree,
> And teach it to grow in the moist bark. <note>original: "Aliena ex arbore Germen / Includunt, udoque docent inolescere libro."</note>

Or, *Bastards* are grafted sprouts that do not grow for themselves, who are "inserted" into a family, but are not blood relations through the male line <term>agnati: relatives through the father's side</term>.

Paternal nobility is not transmitted to these bastards. See *law: non legitima* in the *Digest: on the status of men*, and *law: liberos* in the *Digest: on Senators*; also *Tiraquellus* on *Nobility*, chapter 15, number 20. Since they are not of the house or family of nobles: for those only are contained within a house or family who are of the same paternal lineage <note>original: "agnatione"</note>, according to the *law: pronunciatio*, section *familiæ* in the *Digest: on the Meaning of Words*.

Furthermore, bastards are not of the kindred, as noted by *Ricius* in *Ecclesiastical Decisions* under the title *Right of Patronage*, decision 203, nor do they have paternal lineage. See the *Institutes: on the succession of cognates*, section *vulgò*; see also *Bartolus* on the final law, number 1, in the *Code: on Signatures*; *Guido Papa*, decision 580; and *Paleotus* on *Spurious Children*, chapter 61. There is also a text in the *Decree of Gratian*, distinction 56, chapter *si gens Anglorum*, where it is said that they are not "honorable to men, nor lovable to God," and such illegitimately born persons are considered infamous by the "infamy of fact" <term>infamia facti: a loss of reputation due to one's status or behavior rather than a court's sentence</term>. See *Nicolaus Nolis* in the *Treatise on Transmissions*, chapter 29, numbers 33 and following, although many disagree. See *Hartman Pistor*, volume 1, question 30; *Heigius*, volume 1, question 21; *Thomingius*, decision 48; and *Myself* in *Delibata*, at book 3 of the *Digest*, question 9, folio 273.

Much less do they succeed in Principalities or Kingdoms; see *my treatise on Royal Succession*, folio 115; also *Rœner*, *Practical Observations*, chapter 17; *Florez Diez de Mena*, question 16; and **Char-**

<column-break/>

**lemagne** passed a law that they should not succeed in the Kingdom, as recorded in the *History of Aachen*, folio 35. Indeed, elsewhere the inheritances of deceased illegitimate persons are confiscated, and by custom or singular privilege, they fall to the Treasury <term>Fiscus: the public or royal treasury</term>. See *Hermann Lather* in the *Treatise on Wealth*, book 2, chapter 8, number 17; also *Gosfo* on the *Customs of Arras*, folio 92, namely: if the mother or those joined by the maternal line do not succeed. See *Peregrinus* in the *Treatise on the Law of the Treasury*.

However, whether bastards are held as infamous and can be appointed as heirs? See *Beatus* in the *Saxon Decisions*, volume 3, on *testaments*, part 2, folio 827. Likewise, whether spurious children should be tolerated in a city, *Martini*, century 9, disputation 2, the last thesis; which pertains to the question, **where bank-children are citizens**, concerning which there exists a singular treatise: **whether they are to be tolerated in the Guilds?**

Although bastards or spurious children sometimes turn out well, this happens rarely and almost as if against nature; whence the French say:

-> A good Bastard is a matter of luck, <-
-> A wicked man is so by nature. <-
<note>original: "Bon Bastarde c'est d'aventure, / Maris meschant c'est de nature."</note>

Regarding the nobility of illegitimate children, *Molina* treats this in *On Justice and Law*, treatise 2, disputation 169 and following; *Charles Paschal* on *Paternal Power*, part 4, chapter 2, number 20, etc.; also *Gosfo* on the *Customs of Arras*, the second to last folio. One desiring more on bastards and spurious children should consult *Paleologus* in his singular treatise; *Contius*, book 2 on *Successions*, chapter 11; *Mercer*, book 2, chapter 7 and following; also *Bisciolus*, book 3 of *Leisure Hours*, volume 2, chapter 9.

### ADDITION.

**Slipped by theft** <note>original: "Furto lapsa"</note>) Having slipped from the parent, not in his own stables, or by the right order of procreation—that is, a spurious child. **She fell off the bench** <note>original: "Sie ist von der Banck gefallen"</note>, *Barthius*, *Animadversions on Papinius Statius*, *Thebaid* book 6, page 472.

Spurious children are sometimes distinguished by outstanding virtues. **Hercules** was a "nothus" <term>nothus: a child of a noble father and a common mother</term>, and yet by his own virtue he attained honor equal to the Gods, as *Plutarch* testifies. Likewise, **Theseus, Teucer, Menelaus, Themistocles, and Demosthenes** had the same beginning of birth, according to *Knipschild* on *Trusts*, chapter 8, number 319.

**Timotheus**, the son of Conon, born out of wedlock to a Thracian harlot, said: he gave the greatest thanks to his mother because through her he was the son of Conon, a most famous General, as *Suidas* testifies. The illegitimate sons of **Philip the Good**, Duke of Burgundy, wrote publicly and privately on their family shields: **Anthony, Philip, Bastards of Burgundy.** *Pontus Heuterus*, *Treatise on the Free Birth of Man*, chapter 14. **On the rights over the "wild-catch"** <term>Wildfang: a legal term for jurisdiction over illegitimate children or foreigners</term>, *Klock*, volume 2, counsel 85, numbers 42, 44, 45, and following. The **right of the Wild-catch** granted by means of a feudal contract is granted privately, not cumulatively. *Klock*, volume 2, counsel 85, number 25. **Bastard-dues and the rights over the Wild-catch** are proven by witnesses. *Klock*, volume 1, counsel 29, numbers 840, 841, 842, 843.

Whether a spurious child of a testator can be chosen as if he were a poor person? *Mantica* on *Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 1, title 5, numbers 12 and 13. A dowry can be bequeathed to a spurious daughter. Volume 10, tome 4, number 10.

<header>Letter B.</header>

A **spurious child** <note>original: *Spurius*; in Roman law, a child born from a casual or illicit union, as opposed to a steady concubinage</note> does not exclude a **substitute heir**, unless the substitution was made in favor of the woman. See book 11, title 9, number 23; and clarified in number 24. This applies unless it was specified: "if he should die without legitimate and natural children, or those arriving in any other manner," number 25.

Spurious children are not part of the paternal lineage or the family, as discussed at length by **Knipschild** in the aforementioned chapter 8, number 229. **Harprecht**, in the title regarding injuries (numbers 54 and 55), teaches extensively whether a "Bastard"—calling him such—who has been legitimized by the Prince, may be held liable for injuries. Those legitimized by a **Rescript of the Prince** <note>A formal legal decree from a ruler</note> are in a worse condition than those legitimized by a subsequent marriage, according to **Nicolaus Myler** in *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 54, page 476. **Kinschot** wrote specifically on the subject of legitimation. **Tiraqueau**, in *On Nobility* (chapter 15, number 31), provides a massive catalog of famous men born of unknown fathers who were distinguished in both domestic and military life. See also **Heuter** in *On the Free Birth of Man*, chapter 16. **Paleotus** in the final chapter states: <note>original German: *die Banckart seynd in ein unehrlich Album zu verzeichnen*</note> *Bank-children are to be recorded in a dishonorable register.* **Obrecht**, in *Political Reflections*, page 282, writes: <note>original German: *Bastard kommt nicht von Frantzösischen Bastard... sondern von dem Bast...*</note> *The word "Bastard" does not come from the French "bastard," or the Italian and Spanish "bastardo," but from the **bast** <note>The inner bark of a tree</note>, with which one incorporates, glues, and makes the grafted shoots of the juicy inner bark grow together.* **Lord Harsdörffer** notes that in the ordinances of the **Imperial Chamber Court**, caution is taken so that spurious children are not promoted to the dignity of Assessor. However, at **Tübingen**, the doctoral regalia are not denied to them, as per Harprecht on injuries, section 1, number 240.24, and most extensively by **Walther** in *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 57 and following. Some compare spurious children to children born of a marriage that did not receive a priestly blessing. This controversy is so grave that the **Saxon Courts** cannot agree upon it: see **Strauch**, dissertation 11, aphorism 21.

### 17. Batzen. Batzii.

**Batzen** <note>A type of silver coin</note> come from *Bezen*, which signifies a **little bear**; they were called by this name by the people of **Bern** (who still use that emblem today), and their use was very frequent many years ago. Today, Upper Germany—especially **Franconia**, **Bavaria**, the **Rhine** region, **Swabia**, and **Switzerland**—calculates everything by Batzen: 15 of them make a **florin**, and one is worth 4 **kreuzer**. It is now a type of imaginary currency (like the Guilder or the Pound), <note>original German: *dann wenig gantze Batzen mehr zu finden, auch nirgend mehr gemüntzet werden*</note> *for few whole Batzen are to be found anymore, nor are they minted anywhere else.*

They began to be struck by the Bernese in the year 1500; at first as a large coin, and later named from the sign of the bear which, as just mentioned, they placed upon them. See **Freher** on *Coinage*, and **Tileman Friesen**, book 4, chapter 34.

->ADDITION.<-

The **Batz** is named from the bear—*Bär* or *Bätzen*—imprinted on it, though it later became a common name; see the long and most elegant inaugural lecture of **Auers** held at Basel in 1617, *On the Law of Coinage*, chapter 13, number 71, and there also **Besold**, Volume I.

<column-break/>

As cited: **Money** is divided into "large" and "small"; Batzen are classified among the small. Regarding the Batzen, its value, and its rejection, see **Alemannus** in *The School of Consultations*, page 577.

### 18. Baurenschiedt. The division of disputes by half.

The **Standard Gloss** <note>The authoritative medieval commentary on Roman law</note> on the law *Nefennius* (34, regarding the management of affairs) censures the common opinion of rustics who divide questions down the middle—as if I were to ask for ten, they say they wish to agree and suggest five. **Baldus** reflected on this in the law *When it is necessary* (number 10, Code: *On the goods which are set free*), when he calls a certain decision of **Bartolus** similar to a "Rustic Division." **Jason** reports this more fully (in the law *That*, number 7, Code: *On Collations*), stating that the opinion of Bartolus "proceeded from his own neck" <note>A metaphor for being stubborn or making things up</note> and is "rustic": he acted just like the peasants who divide a question down the middle. From this, the German expression <note>original: *ein Baurenschiedt*</note> **"a peasant's judgment"** <note>Commonly known as "splitting the difference"</note> seems to have been born; it is mentioned by **Keller** in *On the Juridical-Political Office*, book 1, chapter 7, and after him by **Ventura de Valentia** in *The Litigating Virgin*, book 2, chapter 4, number 17.

Furthermore, in the matter of the discovery and acquisition of **treasure**, **Phraortes**, King of the Indians, when about to judge a dispute between a buyer and a seller over found treasure, is written to have said to **Apollonius** (whom he had called into council): that it is not the mark of a wise man if by chance everything is split. **Duarenus** mocks this in his commentary on the title *On Judges*, in the chapter regarding litigants, regarding the judge **Pantagruel** <note>Actually refers to Judge Brindlegoose/Bridoye from Rabelais</note>: <note>original German: *Welcher alle vor ihme kommende lites durch Würffel decidirt...*</note> *Who decided all cases coming before him by dice, yet dared to wager that his judgments were just as good as those of the Parliament of Paris.* See **Rabelais**, *Life of Pantagruel*, book 2.

Nevertheless, such a practice is rightly disapproved and exploded when it is used without necessity or out of ignorance, while justice and equity demand something different. But when necessity demands it—because the matter is perhaps so obscure or ambiguous that even after a diligent and accurate weighing it does not appear which side outweighs the other—there, such a decision is not only free from fault but even deserves the highest praise for wisdom. This is shown by the example of the wisest of kings, **Solomon**, who, in the equally ambiguous controversy of the two women over the infant, ordered the infant to be divided into two parts (though he did this as a pretense to follow the rule of justice) and for one half to be given to one, and the other half to the other. See 1 Kings 3:24 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding division in general, see **Barbosa**, book 4, chapter 41, throughout. **Knipschild**, *On Entails*, passim.

## 19. Building Costs. <term>Impensæ in ædificationem factæ</term>
<note>Expenses incurred for the purpose of construction</note>

See Gilken in the treatise *On Expenses*.

### ADDITIO.
<note>Addition/Supplement</note>

The **refurbishing** of a building is considered more favorable in law than a new construction. Petr. Barbosa in the law regarding divorce, book 8, final section, number 122. The refurbishment of a building is presumed to have been done with money received shortly beforehand, provided it is consistent with the amount and is not excessive. Sprenger, *On the Law of Building*, page 136. Certain people build as if they were going to live forever. Lipsius, book 3 *On Wonders*, chapter 14. Sometimes they even rob the poor to "clothe wood and stones," as Ventura de Valenti complains in book 1, chapter 13, number 14. Martial plays on this in book 9:

->Gellius is always building: now he sets the threshold,<-
->Now he fits keys to the doors and buys bolts;<-
->Now he changes and repairs these windows, then those;<-
->As long as he is building, he does whatever he pleases.<-
->Just so he can say that one word to a friend begging for money:<-
-> "I am building."<-

Sprenger, *On the Law of Building* in the *Prodromus*.

In Strasbourg, if an **Ammeister** <note>A high-ranking municipal magistrate</note> wishes to build, he must do so at his own expense, and not with the city's laborers and equipment.

When someone lends money for the new construction of a house, Zorer demonstrates how he may obtain a priority claim for repayment in part 2, question 20, number 6059. Expenses made for construction must be restored and paid. The same applies to expenses made for the refurbishment and repair of a house, as treated extensively by Knipschild, *On Testamentary Trusts*, chapter 12, numbers 153 and 154, and the citations therein. In former times, one man covered himself with branches, another dug himself a hole or cave, and a third raised a wall for himself out of soft reeds, loam, lime, and clay—having observed such things from swallows' nests—afterward joining wood in between, and finally beginning to build with stones. Such "loam-huts" are still to be seen in the land of the Moors, Libya, and even in some countries in Europe. Pliny, book 7; Strabo, book 17 of his *Geography*.

Murnæus, a distinguished gentleman in France, acquired much money in war, from which he had a beautiful house built and had this written over its door:

->This house, built by Murnæus from much plunder,<-
->Will either collapse, or another robber will possess it.<-

Antenor, in *Solomon*, chapter 7.

<column-break/>

Regarding houses, barns, and stables that are necessary to keep in good repair and to restore: see Obrecht in *Political Reflections*, page 23. Swallows teach us about building. Ludovicus Vives, book 1 *On the Transmission of Disciplines*, volume 1 of his works, page 441. Leone Battista Alberti wrote *On the Art of Building*; in book 1, chapter 10, he mentions walls. Regarding architecture and the art of building, writers include Leone Alberti of Florence, Antonio Labacco, Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, Andrea Palladio, Pietro Cataneo, and Sebastiano Serlio of Bologna. What is required for the convenience of a good building is discussed by Lord Bacon in his *Faithful Sermons* <note>Bacon's *Essays*</note>, chapter 43, page 232. A builder’s skill can be recognized by three things: the stairs, the chimney, and the **Secret** <note>original: *Secret*; a common term for the privy or toilet</note>.

## 20. Both, Both parts. <term>Uterque</term>.

The word "both" (each of two) has this nature: according to the proper and genuine meaning of the vocabulary, it applies only to two things, and it makes a distribution into two equal parts. *Digest*, law regarding creditors, section on two; *Digest*, law regarding if anyone to two; chapter "No one," with the gloss. Schrader, consultation 49, number 10, volume 2. Bartolus on the law "this article," regarding the institution of heirs. See Goldbeck in the collected consultations, treatise *On the Inherited Estate*, number 119.

And although sometimes the word "both" makes a distinction or distribution into several parts (according to the law "and therefore," section 1, regarding stolen goods), this is nonetheless usually done improperly. Schrader, in the same place. Such literal properties of words are to be avoided in other legal dispositions, but especially in wills. Therefore, if it were provided in a certain **Will** <note>original: *Testamento*</note> that the inheritance or left goods should be divided equally among the closer relatives of *both* the male and female testator, it is placed beyond all doubt or risk of interpretation that those goods are to be divided into two equal portions. Schrader, in the same place; see below under **Equal** and **Equally**.

### ADDITIO.
<note>Addition/Supplement</note>

It is doubted what the words "If both should die" and "If they both should die" signify—specifically, whether the condition is fulfilled if only one of them dies. The answer is that it does not seem to be. Indeed, when a testator has used such a word, the condition is nonetheless fulfilled in the person of one for his portion, and the plurality is resolved into singularities, if the testator added other words to which that word "both" or similar refers. This is seen in the specific law "My heirs," book 57, section 1, regarding the Trebellian Decree of the Senate. Pacius provides more and very clear details on this law in his *Analysis of the Code*, title on the substitution of minors, number 26 at the end. When a plurality is resolved into singularities is shown by Everhardus in *Legal Topics*, topic 97, numbers 6 through 10, where he attaches this question: whether, if one of the instituted heirs, for whom a substitution has been made...
