## 21. **Pardon of Criminals.**
->see below under the entry **Granting of Grace.**<-
### The Granting of Grace to Offenders. <term>Aggratiatio delinquentium</term>

The pardon or immunity from punishment for crimes, which the learned doctors call the "granting of grace" to the accused—commonly known as **Pardon** <note>original German: *Begnadigung*</note>—is numbered among the Rights of Majesty and Regalia <note>The "Regalia" are the exclusive rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign or monarch.</note>. On this matter, one should consult Sixtinus, book 1 *On the Regalia*, chapter 2, number 17; Clapmarus, *On the Secrets of Republics*, 17; Bodin, book 1 *On the Republic*, the last section, number 164; Knichen, *On Saxon Privileges*, under the word "Dukes," chapter 5; and my own work *On Majesty*, page 154. From this, he argues that one who possesses "High Jurisdiction" <term>Merum Imperium</term> <note>The legal power to inflict capital punishment or exercise high-level judicial authority.</note> can punish offenders; he proves this by showing that he or his ancestors have released prisoners and pardoned them. See Heigius, question 22, section 24.

However, if a Prince, in his own provincial city, petitions for the pardon of criminals, it is not definitively concluded from this that he lacks jurisdiction. Natta, counsel 636; and the *Illustrious Counsels*, published in folio under my care, counsel 3, number 55; see also **The Vindication of Waldeck**, part 3, chapter 48, page 202.

But grace granted by a Prince does not destroy a civil action <note>A private lawsuit for damages or restitution.</note> belonging to others arising from that crime. Such grace indeed abolishes the crime's punishment, but if the crime is repeated, it aggravates the situation; it is even established that such mercy is sometimes ruinous to the offenders themselves, for they often sin worse afterward, and therefore must be punished more severely. See Nider’s *The Ant-Heap* <note>original: *Formicarius*; a famous 15th-century work on theology and social conduct</note>, page 324. For this reason, a Prince should not be easy in granting grace, nor should he do so for all crimes (see Böckel, final discussion; Hering, *On Homicide*, page 23), nor should he do so without the consent of the injured party. Besoldus, decision 178.

### ADDITION.

The right of granting grace <term>Jus aggratiandi</term> is the public and legitimate power to remit the deserved criminal penalties of the accused or offenders through judicial discretion. The word *aggratiandi* is "barbarous Latin" <note>A term used by Renaissance scholars for medieval Latin words not found in classical Roman texts.</note>, formed from the prefix *Ad* (to) and the noun *Gratia* (grace). A long series of such words and names can be seen in Gerhard Johann Vossius’s treatise *On the Vices of Speech*, books 3 and 4. Furthermore, although this word owes its origin to Latium <note>The region of Rome.</note>, it is found in no suitable author of pure speech and was unknown to the jurists of the ancient age; thus, you might rightly say that while it is Latin by birth, it is not so by usage. Now, however, our usage and the courts have long accepted this word, and it is found everywhere among jurists of no small authority, such as Carpzov and others.

<column-break/>

Petrus Theodoricus in *Criminal College*, dispute 10, thesis 7; Petrus Farinaccius, book 1, counsel 46; Gail, part 2, question 22; Valentin **Winther**, *The Litigating Party*, book 1, chapter 12; Petrus Heigius, part 2; *Saxon Consultations*, part 4. Andreas **Schwartz** treated this entire subject of the Right of Grace very extensively at Tübingen for his license in the year 1647. Regarding the immunity of crimes, see Schönborner in *Politics*, book 7, chapter 2. Such immunity does not delete or remove the shame of the act; rather, those whom indulgence frees, it also marks: it does not take away the infamy of the crime, but merely grants a favor regarding the punishment. Although the punishment is remitted, the blot burned into the soul by the crime will remain forever. Cicero, book 1 *On Laws*; Arnisaeus, *Political Reflections*, section 5. Question: Must faith be kept with criminals to whom immunity has been promised? Farinaccius says this question is much-contested, and distinguishes that faith must be kept if a confession made under hope of immunity was later revoked, but otherwise if it was ratified.

## 22. **Burial of the Dead.**
->see below under the entry **Graves.**<-
### The Law of Burial. <term>Jus Sepulturæ</term>

It cannot be denied that, according to the Canons <note>Church laws.</note>, the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> has the right to grant cemeteries, and their consecration is usually done by Bishops; however, in these times in Germany, where the Reformed Religion flourishes, this is not greatly regarded, but is instead considered a matter of Civil Law <term>Politicum jus</term>.

Ecclesiastical burial is denied to those who kill themselves. For they are cast down through the roof of the house, or dragged out from under the threshold, and carried out upon a rake and burned, or buried in a field by the executioner. Schneidewein, *On the Division of Things*. But should prisoners who die be buried? See Göhausen, *On Witches*, page 405.

However, one who was buried in the earth in an illegitimate manner due to presumed heresy or another crime ought to be dug up and buried according to the Church rite if the suspicion is cleared. Köppen, *Enucleated Questions*, 8, decision 1.

On the law of tombs, and whether they belong to outside heirs, or whether a son retains the tomb of his mother: see Caspar Antonius Thesaurus, book 1, question 11. Also, regarding whether it pertains to the Right of Patronage, see Treutler, counsel 57. And can it be acquired by prescription <note>Gaining a legal right through long-term use.</note>? Nicolaus Everhardus the Elder, counsel 13. That one should not divide common graves <note>original German: *daß man auch gemeine Gräbnissen nicht soll theilen*</note> is found in the *Illustrious Counsels*, Frankfurt edition, part 2, counsel 65.

But I have discussed burial in my treatise *On Life and Death*, page 94 and following, at great length.

Joseph Ludovicus also has many things worth knowing about burials in decision 145, as does the *Archiepiscopal Practice*.

<header>Enlarged Treasury of Practical Knowledge</header>

Marc. Antonio of Naples <note>Marcantonio Gennari, a 17th-century Neapolitan jurist.</note>, in chapter 61, testifies that the Chapter of the Cathedral Church of Naples holds a privilege and has been in the most ancient possession of the right to bury all those dying in the City and Diocese who, though they were able, did not choose a place of burial, unless they possess their own family tomb, etc. Is the "funeral fourth" <note>The *quarta funeralis* was a traditional portion (one-fourth) of funeral fees or offerings due to the parish church or the bishop when a person was buried elsewhere.</note> owed if a distinguished person dies—for example, a Prince, etc.—and after the body is buried in their home country, solemn funeral rites are held in another place? It seems not; according to the notes in the Clementine decree *dubium* regarding burials, "funerals" are defined as those things which are said *with* the funeral procession. However, Calderinus holds the contrary view in his 4th counsel on burials. According to the testimony of Marc. Antonio in the aforementioned place, note 1, this is the practice observed in the City and Diocese of Naples; for the Archbishop of Naples has, from the most ancient times, demanded a fourth part of all the wax candles that are lit around a corpse to be buried in any church, even an exempt one, while the Divine Office is performed. He also demands it when the funeral rites are held for certain Princes who were buried elsewhere.

Regarding persons who ought to be denied ecclesiastical burial, see Medicus in the *Treatise on Burials*, question 11. To deny burial on account of the non-payment of Tithes or any other debt is called impious, based on the argument in chapter *non aestimemus* 13, question 2. Furthermore, creditors who hinder the burial of debtors because of a debt lose that debt, are considered infamous, their goods are confiscated, and they are punished with other penalties (Law *finalis* with the authority *item* Code on the violation of tombs). This applies even more so to a Parish Priest, according to Navarrus, counsel 2 on tithes, where he says it is not permitted for a priest by his own authority to repel parishioners from receiving the Sacraments because they have not paid tithes, nor should Bishops tolerate such scandalous acts, but rather sharply punish those who do them; see Marc. Antonio in the aforementioned place, note 11, and in the annotations.

And note, if anyone asks to be buried among the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>, he should first be carried to the Parish Church, as is the custom to be visited, where the Mass is celebrated and the final "Farewell" is received.

### ADDITION.

A person placed in the moment of death <note>original Latin: *in articulo mortis*</note> is considered as if already dead. Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 602. *How to prove a death* <note>original German: *wie eines Tod zu beweisen*</note>. Zorer, part 2, question 2, number 141 and following: *how to prove the life of an absent person, number 144.*

The Emperor Theophilus showed so much honor to Maria, the deceased daughter of his wife and the Caesar Alexios, that he placed the corpse in a coffin covered in silver, and established her tomb as a Sanctuary <note>Asylum</note> for those accused of any crime; the author is Cedrenus. Some tombs were formerly called "familial," others "hereditary." Those were called familial which someone had established for himself and his family; whereas those were called hereditary which someone had made for himself and his heirs (Law *familiaria* 5, Digest on religious matters and funeral expenses). The right of familial tombs belonged to the agnates <note>Relatives through the male line.</note>, even those not appointed as heirs; it did not belong at all to the affines <note>Relatives by marriage.</note> or the nearest blood relatives who were not appointed as heirs.

<column-break/>

However, the right of a hereditary tomb also looked to outside heirs (Law 4, Law *jus familiarium* 8, section 1, Law *jus sepulchri* 3, Code on religious matters and funeral expenses). See Knipschild, *On Testamentary Trusts*, chapter 10, numbers 118, 119. Add overall the things which Draco most elegantly collected in *On Patrician Right*, page 69, number 7, regarding the ancestral tombs of Patricians. In number 8, regarding the differences between familial and hereditary tombs, and in number 9, he teaches from sacred and other histories that the account of familial tombs was carefully maintained. Let consecrated cemetery land not be sold (Chapter *abolendae* 13, on burials, book 3 of the Decretals). For this reason, King Alfonso of Naples afflicted a certain Priest—who was abusing burials to hunt for money—with a new and almost unheard-of punishment. On which, see more in Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 148, numbers 12 and 13. Hence, in Zorer, part 2, question 20, number 6030, it is asked: *since no place or plot—especially in churches and chapels—is allowed without the payment of a certain amount of money, whether such things may be justly and responsibly reimbursed, and be included in the permissible funeral costs?* Regarding the pride of tombs, Ambrose says well: "They are losses to the living rather than aids to the dead." Johann Gerhard, question 9 on politics, decade 8, question 9: a lowly burial does not harm the good, nor does a grand one benefit the wicked (Chapter *sacris* 12, on burials; chapter *ubicunque sepeliamur* 13, question 2). How the tomb of Archimedes was found, see in Theodor Zwinger’s *Theater of Human Life*, volume 2, book 7, page 575.

*Upon the death of a wife, the funeral expenses and what pertains thereto fall upon the person to whom the dowry falls or remains; and where this is lacking, they fall upon the husband in the same manner.* Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 564.

*On the eulogy of the dead,* see Bonifacius, *On Playful Matters*, book 2, chapter 54, where he also says, quoting Herodotus regarding the Thracians, *that they bury a deceased person with joy and wish him luck, because having been released from the weariness of life, he is now in all happiness.* Zeiller, century 4, question 40, page 214.

*On the Guinea Coast, when a king dies, many others must die with him, and decorate the king’s burial with their heads. For they are stuck all around the grave.* Zeiller, century 4, question 42, page 221. The ancients referred to death through a "closing together" <term>Symphimesis</term> <note>original Greek: <term>ΣυμΦυμι-μον</term>, likely a euphemism for the end of life.</note>. In Inscription VII, page 1060, I find: "He has receded," instead of "he is dead"; in Pliny, book 2, epistle 1: "And he indeed, full of years, has departed." Rupert, in *The Mercury*, page 668.

Dr. David Herlicius has written concerning lightning and other impressions, portents, and fiery miracles: *of lightning, thunder, and all kinds of fire-signs and wonders over the burial of Saint Barnim XI, Prince of Pomerania.*

Cicero, *Philippics* 9: "The sanctity of tombs is in the soil itself, which can be moved by no force, nor destroyed." Cicero, book 2, *On the Laws*: "A tomb [has] many..."

### 23. Beguines, Beghards, and Beguine Sisters.

Lambert le Bègue <note>original: "Lampertus Beguius"</note>, a very pious Priest, preached forcefully in Liège against those living in concubinage. From him were named the **Beguines**, women and girls who propose to live chastely, as Gilles d'Orval, a monk of Val-Benoît, relates in his *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*. 
Others wish them to be named after Saint Begga, an Abbess and the founder of Andenne. 
Religious convents of Beguines are very numerous today among the people of Brabant, Flanders, and Liège, as witnessed by Miraeus in the *Belgian Annals* for the year 1174, page 757 and following. 
Certain virgins under the name of Beguines, living a celibate but free life, came into Brabant from Germany—as some believe, from the Meuse regions. Since they were not at first received into the cities, they settled around the Scheldt River, and there they subjected themselves to the newly built Monastery of Saint Bernard. For a long time afterward, they took their confessors from that Monastery, until, due to frequent abuses, they obtained from the Holy See a secular pastor who would perform divine service for them. These women were brought to Mechelen <note>original: "Mechliniam"</note> and settled for a long time in a street whose name still remains. At last, as their number grew immensely, a portion was sent out as a colony in the year 1249 outside the town walls. There they built a court, workshops, and dwellings for themselves with such success that their habitation looked like a small town, and their number reached several thousand. *History of the City of Mechelen by J. B. Gramaye, book 3, section 7.* 
However, Zypaeus has much to say on the Beguines and their origin in his *Analysis of Pontifical Law*, book 3, under the title *On the Regular Clergy*, page 302 and following. There he says they are neither "regulars" nor "religious" <note>In canon law, "religious" refers to those under formal perpetual vows in an approved order.</note>, because they do not promise obedience to anyone, nor do they renounce their own property, nor do they profess an approved rule, even if they wear the habit they call the Beguine dress. But it is asked whether they are at least "religious" in the sense that pious places and religious congregations are so called. See the same Zypaeus in the cited place, page 304.

The **Beghards**, however, and the Lollards were names infamous for a certain enthusiastic heresy. See Felix Hemmerlin <note>original: "Felicem Malleolum"</note> in his specific treatise written against them. 
The Beghards and Beguines, according to Bognatus (the Beghards were monks and the Beguines were nuns, but without vows), taught that a human being could become impeccable <note>incapable of sinning</note> in this life, and was no longer bound to fasts or

<column-break/>

prayer, and could not grow further in grace, and other things of that kind. Bellarmine <note>A significant Jesuit cardinal and theologian.</note> mentions this in his *Chronology* under the year 1299, which is joined to his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. 
There also exists in the most recent edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, volume 13, page 342, a fragment by Conrad of Megenberg <note>original: "Conradi de Monte puellari"</note>, Canon of Regensburg, against the Beghards and Beguines. 
Regarding the errors of the Beghards and the Beguine women of Germany <note>original: "Alemanniæ"</note>, see also the General Council of Vienne in Carranza, page 343b. Add also the *Chronicle of Chronicles*, book 2, page 436 and following, and below under the word *Libertines*, and likewise the *Catalogue of Heretics* by Petreius under the word *Beguards*.

### 24. Behrnheuter <note>Slacker or Coward; literally "Bear-skinner".</note>.

A *Behrnheuter* comes from those idle, loose people who taught bears to dance and led them around for money, as Schereus says in his *Language School*, page 169. 
Or rather, they are such fellows who lie in no bed, but must make do with a bear-skin.

->ADDITION.<-

Tacitus testifies concerning the Germans that they entered the paths of the camps with their shoulders covered by wild animal skins. For they very frequently took the hides of bears (for this animal was most common among them), so that the skin served them as a bed-covering. From this, it is believable that the name **Bärnhäuter**, which is still hateful to our customs, originated. Limn. *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 6, number 69. Zeiller in the *German Itinerary*, page 25. *Young lords, young bears; old lords, old bears*, as Conrad Heresbach reports in *On the Education of a Prince*, book 1, chapter 15.

### 25. Beicht. Confession.

The Germans call confession *Beicht*, from *bejahen* <note>to affirm or say 'yes'</note>; as if "affirmed," and contracted to **Beicht**. And indeed, as pertains to auricular confession <note>Confession spoken into the ear of a priest.</note> made to a Priest, it is to be recited or revealed to no one. For if a Priest does this, he is deposed, and for all the days of his life he continues as a wanderer in ignominy, according to the Decree of Gregory recorded in the chapter *Sacerdos 2. de poenit. dist. 6.* And Innocent III in the chapter *Omnis utriusque* <note>The famous 1215 decree "Every person of either sex" which mandated annual confession.</note> at the end, says: Let him beware lest by word or sign, or in any other way, he in any measure betray the sin; for whoever presumes to reveal a sin discovered to him in the penitential Judgment, we decree not only that he be deposed from his priestly office, but also that he be thrust into a strict Monastery to perform perpetual penance. With this agrees the Decree of Pope Eugenius in the chapter *si Sacerdos*, and of Honorius III in the chapter *dilectus*, where revealing things entrusted to oneself is pronounced a ruinous act. And Pope Leo in the chapter *quamvis* says: it is not lawful for the conscience of the one confessing to be published to the ears of the people.

And that such a revelation deserves absolutely no trust, nor has any legal effect, and does not even create a "sinister presumption" <note>A legal term meaning a negative inference or a bias against someone's character.</note>, is proven by Mascardus in *On Evidence, volume 1, conclusion 377, numbers 1 and 3*; Menochius in *On Presumptions, book 1, presumption 89, number 26 and following*, and *Counsel 107, number 68, volume 2.*

And concerning the Confession which must not be revealed, a singular treatise was written by Vincentius Carocius; see also the treatise titled *The Splendor of Moral Truth, page 249 and following*; add Villalpando in *Demonology, page 605*; Godelmann in *Treatise on Witches, book 3, chapter 7, number 22*; and Wittum on *Torture, conclusion 98.* Whether it is lawful for a Confessor to betray a future crime was debated in England in the case of Garnet <note>Henry Garnet (1555–1606), a Jesuit executed for his role in the Gunpowder Plot; his defense rested on the Seal of Confession.</note> and Antonius Zimmermann. See the *Flemish Hagiology, page 21*; Paulus Christinaeus also treats this question in *Belgian Decisions, volume 4, decision 196, number 24* and Tiberius Decianus in *Criminal Practice, book 7, chapter 44, number 25*; likewise Florez Diez de Mena, *question 18.* **What is entrusted to the confessor in the confessional box must be kept secret from everyone until death. What a confessor should answer if he were asked about those things entrusted to him in confession, likewise regarding the judgment of the Council of Venice. Lord Dilherr in the *Way to Salvation* <page-num>page 221.</page-num> On the Seal of Confession and the Sacramental Seal. The same author, <page-num>page 711.</page-num>**

Concerning a priest revealing a Confession, or soliciting women to shameful acts <note>original: "tentante mulieres ad turpia"; this refers to the crime of "solicitation," where a priest uses the confessional to make sexual advances.</note> during the act of Confession, Marco Antonio treats this in *Archiepiscopal Practice of Naples, chapter 66*, where he says that the common opinion of the Doctors is (in the chapter *Omnis* <note>Referring to the canon "Omnis utriusque sexus" from the Fourth Lateran Council, 1215.</note> on Penance) that the penitent is to be believed against the Confessor if they say he revealed their Confession, so that he may be punished with an extraordinary penalty. This is because the truth cannot be obtained in any other way. However, the Cardinal there says he can be tortured; and so, as the same Marco Antonio witnesses, a Parish Priest who was investigated in the Archbishop’s Court for soliciting women to shameful acts during the act of Confession—against whom several of them deposed that they had been touched or signaled, and one by words—was tortured but did not confess; he was also suspended from his Office for a year, etc.

Regarding what is said—that according to our Catholic Doctrine, the Seal of Confession cannot be broken to avoid any evil whatsoever—it must be understood that it is not lawful in any way to betray the person of the confessant; for this properly falls under the seal. Otherwise, no one doubts that the sins themselves can be disclosed, either to take advice, or to prevent evils, or for other reasons, provided that from the manifestation of the sin there is no danger that the person who confessed the sin might be identified. Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), an influential Jesuit cardinal.</note> in his *Apology for his response to the book of James, King of Great Britain, the title of which is: A Triple Knot, a Triple Wedge, page 229.*

In other cases, the Seal of Confession has equal force in every crime, even the most enormous, such as the crime of high treason <note>original: "læsæ Majestatis"</note> and heresy as well. The Seal of Confession must likewise be kept even after the defendant has died. See the Reverend Father Martin Delrio, who treats these matters fully and thoroughly in *Disquisitions on Magic, book 6, chapter 1, section 2, volume 3, my page 346, etc.*, where he deals with a crime to be committed and that case where someone revealed something to a Priest, not by way of Confession, but nevertheless under the Seal of Confession.

But regarding Confessions, Confessors, and their office, an Anonymous Theologian has much in *Criminal Cautions, or on Processes against Witches* <note>original: "Caution. Criminal. seu de Processibus contra Sagas"; this is Friedrich Spee’s famous 1631 critique of witch trials.</note>; likewise Filefacus in his *Works, page 667*, and *Treatise on Bishops, 4, chapter 2*; see the *Synodal Statues, page 33.* On the antiquity of Confession, Heraldus on *Tertullian, 2nd digression, chapter 4.* And that it is not lawful to confess by letter or by a messenger to one who is absent is gathered from the declaration of the Congregation of the Council of Trent, *Session 14, chapter 5.*

### ADDITION.

Antonius Fernandes de Moure asks: what can a Confessor do regarding a sin known in Confession concerning the correction of an accomplice? Lord Dilherr treats this extensively in the **Way to Salvation, <page-num>page 711</page-num> and following.**

A Priest cannot be compelled to reveal the Secrets of Confession. Everhardus Fabricius treats this extensively in *Gailius Enucleated, book 1, observation 100, section 2.*

From a confessor’s revelation of secrets, no legal judgment is granted unless the Confessor consents. Höping, *On the Right of the Seal, chapter 14, number 97.* Henry of Hesse wrote *The Secrets of Priests* in Florence in the **Year 1493**, a book which is preserved in the Nuremberg Library. Confession for the discharge of conscience in the forum of penance occurs **when someone confesses or admits something to the confessor.** For example: suppose Titius confessed to a Priest in penance, or in the form of confession, that he had committed homicide, debauchery, adultery, or another crime; this was made known either by the Priest himself or by another who perhaps heard such a confession made before the Priest, or was even the Interpreter of the same Confession. It is asked: does such a Confession harm the one confessing, and does it serve as proof in a secular court, so that he ought to be punished because of it? The negative view is preferred, because that confession is said to God, not to man—or not to him as a man, but as a Priest and vicar of God (chapter *Si Sacerdos* 2, *on the office of the ordinary judge*). Hence, the one revealing it is held liable for damages and can be sued in an action for injuries (*Law 1, paragraph 38, Digest on deposits*). And the Priest incurs a penalty (chapter *Omnis* 12, *on penance and remission*). Furthermore, if he is produced here as a witness, he is not bound to reveal what he heard in confession, and he can boldly say, without the mark of a lie or perjury, that he knows nothing, which they attempt to prove by the word of Christ in *Matthew 24*, where it is said that not even Christ knows the day of judgment for the purpose of revealing it. And regularly, a Priest cannot be forced to disclose those things. Carocius, *On the revelation of confession.* Concerning Secrets, see below under the word **Secret Council.** <note>original: "Geheime Rath"</note>

### **26. Inhabitants.** <note>original: *Beyſaſſen* (German); *Incolæ* (Latin)</note>

These are the residents of a castle, of whatever condition, who are also called *Castle-dwellers* <note>original: *Burgſaſſen*</note>; regarding whom, see *below under the word Burgſaſſen.* Thus Rosenthal, in *On Fiefs, chapter 2, conclusion 78, in the note on the Castle of Friedberg.* He says that many nobles have their homes within the castle itself, yet not all who are registered there are citizens: *Those who are "Castle-men"* <note>original: *Burgmann*</note>. Mention is made of the *Inhabitants of Friedberg Castle from the year 1378, in the section "they shall also," following the verse "also regarding." There it says: also regarding the road-toll, which the Castle-men shall not pay, and regarding their Inhabitants in the Castle, and the gardeners below the Castle, they shall pay no road-toll, etc.* These are the same as *Residents* <note>original: *Beysher*</note>, *those who have residency.* Killinger, *On the Joint Inheritance of Castles, discourse 3, number 183.*

### **27. By Princely Honor, etc.** <note>original: *Bey Fürſtl. Ehren* (German); *Promiſſio ſub data fide* (Latin: A promise under a given pledge of faith)</note>

See *above under the word* Oath <note>original: *Aid*</note>, *in place of an oath,* and Barschamp *in the treatise On Clauses, chapter 29, section "fol," page 661.*

->ADDITION.<-

*By true words, noble and upright, to keep [one] harmless.* These words have the force of an oath between Illustrious and Noble persons. Schurff, *Counsel 17, number 11, century 2.* Mynsinger, *Observation 17, century 1.* Johann Fichard, *Counsel 31, number 14, 15, volume 2.* Bullaeus, *Counsel 10, number 53.* Gail, *Book 2, observation 59.* Hering, *On Suretyship, chapter 27, part 1, number 298.* Coler, *On Execution Process, part 1, chapter 10, number 251.* This is based on the reasoning that in Illustrious persons, good faith <term>bona fides: the legal assumption of honesty and sincere intention</term> ought to abound. However, the essential requirement of an oath—the true and religious invocation of the Divine Power—is lacking in these phrases, nor can it be fulfilled by an equivalent oath.

### **28. To scold as a Scoundrel.** <note>original: *Bey Schelmen ſchelten* (German); *Obligatio ſub infamia* (Latin: An obligation under penalty of infamy)</note>

Regarding the obligation *to scold as a scoundrel,* Gylman responds in *Decision 9, number 36, book 1, Decisions or Judicial Matters in the Chamber,* that while such an addition is firm and valid, it is not valid regarding the pursuit of an action: *that they might thereby be deprived of their honors.* Thus the condition itself is voided, but it does not void the contract; rather, it is treated as if it were not added, like an impossible condition. Scheplitz, *on the Brandenburg Constitutions, part 4, title 3, section 1, number 7.*
Nevertheless, it diminishes one's reputation among grave men if someone does not satisfy such a promise.

->ADDITION.<-

*Scoundrel* <note>original: *Schelm*</note> comes from *taking the shield* <note>original: *Schild nehmen*</note>. Mr. Harsdörffer, in the third part of his *Conversational Games, page 155.* The word becomes an injury when insulting voices are pronounced against someone: as when one calls another a "Good-for-nothing" <note>original: *Nebulo*</note>. See Harprecht, *On Injuries, numbers 52 and 53,* and the authors cited there in a long series. To this point belong the things found in Cypraeus, in Besold's *Volume I,*

<column-break/>

*On Betrothals, chapter 13, page 589, at the end.* "Schelm" is said to be derived from *Schild* (shield), from *scutum*; *Schelmen* as if they were *Schildsmen*, those who have deserted the *Schildmen* <note>i.e., cowards who abandoned their comrades in battle</note>, or *Scholtzmen*, *he who has been scolded.*

### **29. Clause: By the loss of the Lord's Grace.** <note>original: *Bey Verlierung deß Herrn Gnad*</note>

->Clause: Under the indignation of grace.<-

Whenever the Pope threatens the indignation of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, a threat of this kind induces the deprivation of ecclesiastical benefits. Baldus and Alvarotus *on chapter 1, section 2, "likewise he who," and "likewise if an informer," and the gloss there on "what was the first cause for losing a benefit."* See Wilhelm Anton, *On Five-Year Grants and Letters of Delay, page 317.*
The same applies to a Vassal; for if the Lord commands him something under his indignation—*by the loss of the Lord’s grace*—it is understood that in the case of neglected duty, he shall be deprived of his fief. Zasius, *in the Epitome of Feudal Law, part 10, number 40 and following.* Jacob de Saint-George, *on the word "and the promise of the said Vassal," number 37 and following, through the noted text in Law 2, there: "he shall suffer the indignation of our name." Code on the seeking of abolished honors.* This penalty of losing the fief can even be executed by the Lord against the Vassal, according to Johann Hermann Stamm, *On Personal Servitudes, book 3, chapter 36, number 26,* provided that the command was made for a just cause, and one pertaining to the nature of the fief. Otherwise, if the threat of that penalty is deemed more for the purpose of causing fear than for its actual value, the Vassal shall be punished for his disobedience at the Lord’s discretion in a way other than the loss of the fief. Jacob de Saint-George, *in the cited place, numbers 8, 9, and following.*
Zasius seems to disagree, being contrary to himself in this, *on the single law, number 5 and following, Digest: If anyone does not obey the one administering justice,* where he says: The penalty under the indignation of the Lord has today largely withdrawn from the Court, and signifies nothing other than what the words sound like: namely, that the grace of the Lord is lost. See especially Schrader, *Counsel 27, number 102, etc.*
But these two opinions are to be brought into harmony through the distinction just mentioned.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the indignation of the Lord and threats, *Rittershusius in Feudal Parts, page 300.* The custom of *avoiding the Lord’s highest displeasure* is perpetual in the mandates of Princes, as may be observed in the *Letters of Emperor Julian.*

### **30. By loss of the Writing.** <note>original: *Bey Verluſt der Schrifft*</note> Sub pœna præcluſionis <term>Under penalty of preclusion: the loss of a legal right or argument due to a missed deadline</term>.

A deadline established for doing something is a matter of strict law and is exclusive. Cacheran, *Decision 185, number 13.* Surdus, *Decision 203, number 12.* Nor does it admit the clearing of a delay in any way. Blarer *on the law "to be defamed," chapter 8, number 25, Code on free-born manumission.* Surdus, *Counsel 97, number 16, book 1.* Hartmann.

Pistor, question 23, number 55, book 4. Mascardus, *On the Interpretation of Statutes*, conclusion 4, number 18 and following. Since what is permitted for a specific time is considered prohibited after that time, as noted by Modestinus, Pistor, counsel 44, number 5, volume 2, and Pingizer, question 6, number 4 and following. And it is the same whether a right is excluded by the lapse of time or by an express renunciation, as cited in Pistor, question 23, number 54, and Hering, *On Guarantees*, chapter 28, number 4.

Which holds all the more if there is a <term>threatening clause<note>original: *Clausula comminatoria* — a provision in a legal document specifying a penalty or loss of right if a deadline is missed.</note></term> regarding the loss of the document; since that which is specifically enjoined ought to be feared more than that which is understood only by general words, according to the gloss on the chapter *ut vetitus* under the word "without irrational cause" regarding appeals. And once the term has expired, that which no longer exists cannot be extended, according to the Law "But if while remaining" in the Digest *on precarious holdings*, and Law 24 "of goods" in the Digest *on ratifying matters*. Since an extension <note>original: *prorogatio*</note> is nothing other than the stretching out of a delay that is currently slipping away but has not yet lapsed, according to Maranta, part 4, distinction 12, number 2, and Ruland, *On Commissions*, book 2, chapter 12, number 2, part 2. Once the first term has passed, an irrevocable right is said to be immediately acquired by the opposing party, which cannot afterwards be taken away even by the Judge himself against the will and objection of that party.

However, it should be known here that a Judge cannot fine a party with the loss of the entire case due to <term>contumacy<note>The legal term for a stubborn refusal to obey a court order or appear in court.</note></term>, as per the gloss on the single law in the Digest *if anyone says the law*, and Baldus on the law *cunctis* in the Code *on appeals*.

### ADDITION.

A legal deadline <note>original: *Terminus legis*</note> cannot be extended by a person. Giphanius, *On Process*, treatise 2, chapter 8, number 69. Question: whether the day of the deadline is counted within the deadline itself. Regarding this question, Jason and other commentators on Law 1 of the Digest *if anyone provides security*. Fusc discusses this question, as does Giphanius in *On Process*, treatise 1, chapter 10, number 69. When a deadline for acting has been pre-established and has passed, the Plaintiff is still to be heard. For although the deadline for acting is <term>peremptory<note>original: *peremptorius* — final and absolute; a deadline that, if missed, usually bars further action.</note></term>, after which every way to act and bring forth one's right is closed—as noted by Bartolus and the Doctors of law commonly on the Code *regarding those who accuse or not*—indeed, the assignment of a deadline has the force of an interim ruling <note>original: *interlocutoriæ*</note>. Modestinus Pistor, volume 2, counsel 44, regarding the law *if any penalty* in the Digest *on the meaning of words*. And once the deadline assigned for proving a matter has passed, the right is acquired by the opposing party. See Speculator in the title *on delays*, section "now let us see," number 4. For it must be understood in a specific sense that the deadline is peremptory. Bullæus treats this extensively in counsel 4, numbers 9, 10, 11, and 12. The exception of a "narrow deadline" is found in the Authentica *offeratur* in the Code *on the Contestation of Lawsuits*, and Novel 53, chapter 3; the text is in chapter *induciæ* 3, question 3. Menochius, book 2 *on judicial arbitration*, question 5, numbers 6 and 7, where the defendant petitions that a longer term for answering and deliberating be given to him, based on the status of the person, the nature of the case, and the distance of the place.

## 31. Interim Rulings. <note>original: *Beyurtheilen* (German); *Sententia interlocutoria* (Latin)</note>

It is well-settled law that an <term>interlocutory sentence<note>An interim decision made by a judge during the course of a legal case that does not finally decide the entire dispute.</note></term> can be revoked by the Judge who issued it, 

<column-break/>

according to the law *what he ordered* in the Digest *on matters judged*. But whether this can still be done if the ruling has already been put into execution (for example, if a supplemental oath was ordered and has already been sworn) is investigated by Mart. Monterus à Cueva in *Aragonese Decisions*, 3. He concludes in the affirmative: though legal practice does not observe this. Indeed, an Interlocutory sentence can be revised twice, similar to an Appeal. See Vivius, decision 239; Mastrillus, decision 23.

What is called an Interlocutory sentence, and when it has the force of a final <note>original: *definitivæ*</note> sentence, is discussed by Vincent Hondedæus, counsel 27, volume 1; Franciscus Vivius, decision 302; and Mynsinger, century 3, observation 88.

### ADDITION.

Does an "Interlocution of the Prince," specifically so-called and opposed to a Final Sentence, obtain the force of Law? Blessed Lord Cobius reviews the authors for and against this in section 6 of the Institutes *on natural law* and question 7 of the Code.

An Interlocutory ruling having the force of a final one is equated to a final sentence. Jacob Ayrer in *Historical Process*, part 1, chapter 6, observation 4, numbers 24 and 25. An Interlocutory ruling insofar as it contains an irreparable grievance (numbers 19 and 20). An Interlocutory ruling insofar as it is said to have the force of a final one (numbers 26, 27, 28, and following). When an Interlocutory ruling is said to carry its own execution (numbers 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17).

An interlocutory sentence cannot be revoked:
1. If it has been put into execution. 2. If it has been doubled [repeated]. 3. If it has been appealed twice, so that it is strengthened by three conforming sentences. 4. If an "abolition" has been granted. 5. If it was issued by the consent of the parties, it cannot be revoked except by the consent of the parties. 6. If the interlocutory ruling was issued together with the final definition. 7. If it has been confirmed by the Prince. 8. If it ends the office [duty] of the Judge. Ummius, *On Process*, Dispute 19, page 773. Biccius reviews types of interlocutory rulings having the force of a final one in *Golden Rules*, section 5, thesis 144, at the end.

## 32. Siege. <note>original: *Belägerung* (German); *Obsidio* (Latin)</note>

It is said, no less truly than elegantly, that sieges of great cities are the "graves of armies," as can be proven from what Antoine Pippre collected in chapter 100 of *Moral and Military Intentions*, etc.

### ADDITION.

If the principal or metropolitan city is occupied, are the others also considered captured? See Marnix, section 8, resolution 7. Those who leave a besieged place without leave are like traitors, for it is not to be presumed that they desire to return. *Dutch Military Law*, page 99. See also page 85: how to punish one who, in a besieged place, calls out for an agreement [surrender], speaks of it, or incites others to it; he shall die without mercy. *Dutch Military Law*, article 54, pages 111 and 112. Laboring during the time of a siege is a duty of the soldiers...

There are two kinds of sieges, which Schönborn recounts in *Politics*, book 6, chapter 21, page 628. Those fearing a siege ought to rid themselves of the useless crowd <note>original: *inutili turbâ* — referring to non-combatants like the elderly or children who would consume limited food supplies</note>. Rupert in *Observations on Valerius Maximus*, book 7, chapter 4. The besieger besieged; poverty must be hidden. See also chapter 13, and on Valerius Maximus, book 7. The stubbornness of the besieged and their insults against the besiegers, see book 3, chapter 18. What a siege is: It should not be undertaken rashly. It is called the "cemetery of great armies." Things to be observed concerning it: A siege against a city that can send out three thousand men for a breakout is done in vain. How sieges were formerly conducted. Whether the unfit for war should be expelled while it lasts. Besold, book 7, chapter 7, number 38. Whether it is permissible to capture a besieged city while peace is being negotiated. The same, book 2, chapter 7.

### 33. The Granting of a Fief. Investiture.

Investiture, <term>the granting of a fiefdom<note>original: *die Belehnung der Lehenschaft*</note></term>, is so named because, just as a man is clothed with garments, so the Vassal is in a way "clothed" with the Fief through its delivery. This is noted by Afflictus and others in chapter 1, number 2, regarding what investiture is.

And Investiture is twofold: Namely, "Proper" (or real/physical); and "Improper" (abusive or verbal). See chapter 1 on the nature of investiture.

**Proper Investiture** is the taking of physical possession of the fief; specifically, when the Vassal is led into possession of the feudal property by the Lord, or his Messenger or Proxy, **so that he is guided into the feudal estate and consecrated [into it]**. Schneidewin on fiefs, part 4, number 4. Through this real investiture, the "useful ownership" <note>original: *utile dominium* — a legal term meaning the right to use and profit from property, even if the ultimate legal title remains with another</note> and possession of the feudal thing is transferred to the Vassal. Jacobus de Sancto Georgio on the word *investitura*, number 1.

**Improper Investiture**, which is also called verbal, is that which is done with words, with some physical act or sign intervening; such as when the Lord says: *I invest you with such an estate*, while a ring, sword, spear, or other thing is held out, according to the custom of the place. See chapter 1 and Schneidewin, number 4.

In the "Barbarian Laws," the word *Vestitura* is used properly for possession itself, and *vestitus* for "one in possession." In the Frankish Laws, book 4: "That every free man who has four *mansi* <note>a unit of land measurement</note> 'clothed' [possessed] from his own property or from someone’s grant—that is, who has, holds, or possesses four *mansi* either in the name of an allod <note>land owned outright</note> or a fief." Also chapter 21: "If anyone has returned to another our own property, which was in the 'clothing' [possession] of our Father, etc." See Bignon on the formulas of the monk Marculf, page 517. Hence, in certain regions of France, *Vest* and *Devest* [investing and divesting] are legal terms. For even today, the Germans say **Vesten** to mean "to confirm and establish." And from there, per-

<column-break/>

haps, the word "Investiture" descends. I have written on this in *On the Subordinate State of the Republic*, page 90, and *On the Nature of Peoples*, page 105. Just as by the institution of Roman Law, no transfers of property were made by simple agreement alone, but rather by formal hand-over or natural delivery—yet they also added a certain formula of words (which they called a stipulation) for the sake of strengthening and establishing the deal. See the Digest, Law 1, *On Praetorian Stipulations*. So too the Lombards required some rite of a Banner, sword, or spear to be used in addition to the agreement. Calvin in the *Feudal Lexicon* under the word *Investitura*. And although it is not strictly necessary, nor does it matter whether the investing Lord hands over a spear, a sword, or something else physical, it is nevertheless fitting that if a Vassal is being invested with "Absolute Authority" <note>original: *mero Imperio* — the highest form of legal power, including the right to inflict the death penalty</note>, the Lord should do this by the delivery of a sword, since the sign ought to match the thing signified; and the power of the sword is the power over blood. See Law *Imperium* in the Digest, *On the Jurisdiction of All Judges*.

As to what such an "Improper" Investiture effects, consult Schneidewin in his *Epitome of Fiefs*, part 4, and Matthias Wesenbeck, counsel 64. Whether one so invested can take legal action to gain possession is treated by Modestinus Pistor, question 9.

This Investiture, and its rituals, provides a great argument for the very tight bond of obligation by which the Vassal is bound to the Lord.

For what is more abject or humble than simply to approach the Lord, with weapons removed, spurs untied, head bared, sometimes even with knees bent, and with a suppliant hand to receive the banner or sword from him, or from whoever is appointed as his Proxy.

I wish to record the manner of investing used by the Kings of Naples, as described by Pontanus in book 2 of *The Deeds of Ferdinand, Son of Alfonso*. **The King sits** in the middle, on a royal throne placed on a raised floor. The nobles and leaders of the Order sit near him; then stand the crowded ranks of those clad in purple, each in his place. At the King’s feet, kneeling on the right side, is the Master of Letters, who is now called the Secretary; on the left are the Bishops, holding the books of the Gospels spread out in the King's lap. Between these, also kneeling, is the man who is to swear the oath, with both hands placed upon the open books. The Master of Letters leads the words; the man about to swear follows the words. "Therefore, after Ursus had cast himself down at the King’s feet and placed both palms flat on the Code, then the Master began to lead the words, and Ursus followed them: 'I, Ursus Orsini, Count of Nola and Atripalda, of Ascoli, etc.'" When the oath was finished, he lifted his hands from the books. Then the King, taking both of Ursus’s hands by the fingers and thumbs, and inserting his own thumbs within theirs, bound them with his own and placed them upon the Gospels. Here again Ursus, with the Master leading the words, said: "I, with my children and my successors, [commit] myself to Ferdinand my King, my Lord, and to his children and suc-

# ADDITION.

Adam Contzen has much to say regarding the Benedictine order in his *Politics, book 6, chapter 46, number 4*.

### 37. To justify and to punish. <note>original German: "Berechtigen und straffen"</note>
### To execute. <note>original Latin: "Exequi"</note>

Master Petrus Denaisius, in his dispute regarding the Right of Absolute Command <note>original Latin: "Jure meri Imperii," referring to the ultimate power of a sovereign to use force</note> of the Imperial Chamber Court, folio 16, etc., and also in his assertion on folio 92, etc., takes those words **to justify and punish** to refer only to the execution of a sentence, excluding the judicial inquiry. (For in some places it is established that the Absolute Command is taken only for the power of the sword, while the passing of the judgment belongs to another.) Thus, the said words mean nothing other than to impose his right and punishment upon someone <note>original: "als einem sein Recht und Straff anthun"</note>.

In the same way, "to judge" <note>original: "richten"</note> or "to justify" <note>original: "justificiren"</note> is used for execution; and among the Romans, "to act by law" <note>original: "Lege agere"</note> meant to execute a sentence of condemnation.

He adds that it is one thing *to justify* <note>original German: "berechtigen"</note> and another *to vindicate* <note>original German: "rechtfertigen"</note>: the latter denotes the dispute and judicial inquiry, while the former denotes the execution. The latter belongs to the Imperial Chamber Court regarding persons inscribed on the Chamber roll; the former belongs to the City of Speyer.

One should certainly look here at Symphorianus Gylmannus, volume 1, part 2, folio 351, article 4.

### 38. Mine, Ore-pits. <note>original German: "Bergwerck, Ertzgruben"</note>
### Metal mine. <note>original Latin: "Metallifodina"</note>

Metallic veins are found only in mountains, which is why they are called *Mountain-work* <note>original: "Bergwerck"</note>, or mountain operations. Regarding the various types of fossils and metals, gold and silver mines, and Mining Law, many authors discuss this, including Heugius (question 13), Wefenbecker (counsel 60, section 198), Rauchbar (1, question 22), and Giovanni Guidi of Volterra *On Metals*. I myself wrote of it in *On the Treasury*, book 3, chapter 8. Also Matthesius in the *Mountain-Sermons* <note>original: "Berg-Postilla," a famous collection of sermons for miners</note>, and Petrus Albinus in the *Chronicle of Meissen*, where he has many memorable things about mining in general, as does Tileman Fries, book 4, chapter 34.

Because mines, ore-pits, etc., are attached to the high Regalian rights <note>these are rights and privileges belonging exclusively to the sovereign</note>, as per the chapter "which things are regalian," some are of the opinion that they should not be divided. This is especially because they cannot be easily appraised. See part 2 of the *Illustrious Frankfurt Consultations*, consultation 65.

From the Sovereign Right over Metallic Veins, it follows that the authorities—beyond the tithes and other benefits—possess the right of first purchase <note>original German: "Vorkauff"</note> of metals found on the lands of private individuals. This is so that the state may have the necessities of the land which the high sovereign rights are meant to provide, such as coinage, artillery, and the like. It is not so that they should trade with them or raise and inflate the purchase price, but rather to make a beginning. Regarding the wealth of the silver mines of Meissen, Petrus Albinus says this in the *Meissen Mountain-

<column-break/>

Chronicle*, title 4. One finds here and there, not only in old annals but also in the handbooks of the nobility and many citizens, the total amount of the tithe recorded at Schneeberg. From the beginning of the Schneeberg works until the year 1501 (Schneeberg having been discovered 30 years prior), there fell to the Elector of Saxony as tithes 5,199 "tons of gold" <note>original: "Tonnen Golds"; a "ton of gold" was a unit of account representing 100,000 guilders</note>, calculating one ton as one hundred thousand Guilders or Thalers. Just as at that same time a Thaler was minted and issued for no more than one Guilder, the miners still call a Thaler a *Guilder-Groschen* <note>original: "Güldengroschen"</note>.

Furthermore, the same Albinus notes from Melanchthon that from the year of Christ 1471 to 1550, from the Schneeberg veins, more than 123,355 tons of gold were distributed to those who cultivated the veins at their own expense; and more than 20,559 tons of gold were paid to the Princes in place of tithes. Just as much was also paid to them for the marking of silver, known as the *Hammer-tax* <note>original: "Schlegelschatz"</note>. And throughout that entire book by P. Albinus, various and pleasant things regarding metals, miners, and their pits are found collected.

Regarding metal mines and those found at Potosi in the West Indies <note>referring to the Spanish Americas</note>, Bertius has the following in his *Abridged Geographic Tables*, folio 813. The quality of the finest gold is defined by the laws of the Spanish and French at 23 carats and three-quarters of a carat, so that if the mass were 192 parts, three parts of gold would be lacking. For the ratio of silver to gold is nearly twelve-to-one throughout the whole world. Gold is found in three ways: as filings in rivers, in pits and ditches, or by the collapse of mountains and through tunnels driven through long stretches of earth. That which is found in all [these forms] is by far the most perfect and is polished by its own friction; such is found in Spain in the Tagus, the Po in Italy, the Hebrus in Thrace, the Pactolus in Asia, and the Ganges in India. That which is dug from the earth requires much more care. Those who seek it take the *segullum* <note>earth that indicates the presence of gold</note>, wash the sand, and from that which settles, they make a conjecture; thus it is often found on the very surface of the earth by a rare stroke of luck. That which is dug from pits is called *canalitium* or *canaliense* by some. That which is brought out from tunnels they call *arrugia*. Tubalcain is said to have been the first to practice this art, as is clearly related in the Holy Scriptures, Genesis 4:22.

> Statius praises Dalmatian gold:
>
> *When will the Dalmatian mountains*
> *return you to sweet Latium:*
> *where, having seen Dis,* <note>The god of the underworld</note>
> *the pale digger returns,*
> *and is the same color*
> ->*as the unearthed gold.*<-

The nature of silver is nearly similar. The earth is red, other types are ash-colored; silver is found in both by digging pits. It cannot be smelted unless with black lead, or with a vein of lead they call *galena*, which [is found] near the veins of silver...

Elias Montanus wrote a <term>Mining Survey</term> <note>original German: "ein Bergwerck Schau"</note>. On the Law of Metals and Mines, see *J. T. The mining shares and the profits of the shareholders throughout the entire Roman Empire, by a singular privilege and favor toward the mining industry, are not subject to confiscation, no matter how the owners may have committed a crime. *Justus Oldekop, in Criminal Observations, page 385.* Mining shares are commonly called <term>Kukus</term> <note>original: "Kukus" or "Kuxe," a traditional German term for a share in a mine</note>. *Klock, on the Treasury, book 7, chapter 27, number 17.*

<column-break/>

**Question:** Is it permitted to seek metal on another person’s land? This is denied, because gold or silver mines, like the fruits of the fields, belong to those who own the land. For no one can enter another’s field for the sake of hunting or fowling against the will of the owner. Nor can anyone seek treasure on another's property against the owner's will. Much less, therefore, for the sake of digging metal, since wild beasts and birds are counted among common things by the Law of Nations and can therefore be taken by anyone, and treasure is a gift of God (*Law 1, Code on Treasures*) rather than the fruit of the land. Metals, however, are like the fruits of the soil and are in the private ownership of the masters of the land. This is supported by the text in *Law 13, paragraph "if it is established," Digest on common properties*, where Ulpian says: "If there are stone quarries on your land, no one can cut stone there, whether in a private or public name, against your will." These and many other following points are in *Bocerus on Royal Prerogatives, chapter 3, number 167.* If several people wish to seek metal in one and the same field, what is the law? *Ibid. number 168.* Whether the Prince should be preferred in metal mines. *Number 171.* If someone begins to dig metal on his own land, can he follow a continuous metallic vein under a neighbor's land against the neighbor's will? *Number 174.* Mines are counted among immovable property. *Zobel, part 3, difference 10, number 3 and following. Carpzov, Forensive Jurisprudence, part 3, constitution 25, definition 1. Knipschild, on Trusts, chapter 5, number 68; chapter 10, number 96.* However, the proceeds from mines are movable property. *Knipschild, chapter 5, number 68, number 96.* Regarding the height of mountains. *Rupertus in Observations on Florus, book 2, chapter 6, paragraph 9, number 2.* In high mountains, the enemy's gaze is cast down by the rocks, and the mountains disappear into the clouds. *Book 4, chapter 12, paragraph 52.* Whether mountains existed before the flood. *Meyfart in Compendium of Geography, page 16.* In metal mines, it is customary to collect levies, and this contribution is called a <term>Zubuß</term> <note>a mandatory payment or assessment by shareholders to cover operating costs</note>; it is announced four times a year, whenever the account of receipts and expenses is rendered. *Klock, on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 27, number 17.* Some metals are of a middle sort, some of the lowest sort (*ibid. book 2, chapter 33, number 1*), such as Electrum, Bismuth, Antimony, Mercury or quicksilver, orpiment, sulfur, vitriol, alum, and rock salt of nitre and stone. (*Ibid. chapter 33, throughout.*) Cassiodorus most truly said: To seek gold through war is a sin, through the seas is a danger, through falsehoods is a disgrace, but in its own nature, it is a profit. *Drexelius in the Dedication of the "Gold Mine."* Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, around the Christian year 1227, is said to have acquired such a quantity of silver and gold from mines that he could have gilded and purchased all of Bohemia. On the profit of metals, see *Obrecht in Political Reflections, page 101, numbers 38 and 39.*

There is no better mine in all of Germany than in the County of Waldeck, which can be inferred from the gold sand found in the Eder river. *Limn. in Public Law, book 3, chapter 2, numbers 10, 11. Richter, Economic Axioms 36, page 143. Mining Shares, Saxon Consultations, volume 2, part 2, question 16, number 1, folio 61.*

That town is not particularly large, yet the silver mines are extremely rich; for one quintal <note>A unit of weight, roughly 100 pounds</note> yields eighty marks of the purest silver, which is unheard of in other places. The discovery of this mine is credited to the Indians, who, while traveling through those places by chance, discovered the metal. When this became known in Argyropolis, it was immediately decided to distribute the mountain among the citizens, who, through the labor of the Indians, extracted such a force of silver that it might suffice for the whole of Europe.

### ADDITION.

Elias Montanus wrote a **Mining Review** <note>original German: *Bergwercks-Schau*</note>. Regarding the Law of Metals and Mines, see J. T. Sprenger in *Fragments of Public Law*, page 192 and following. The late Master Dilherr, in **Garden Pleasure** <note>original German: *Gartenlust*</note>, chapter 9, page 301 and following.

The mining shares and profits of the practitioners throughout the whole Roman Empire are not subject to confiscation, regardless of the offense committed, due to a unique privilege and favor shown toward the mining industry. Justus Oldekop in *Criminal Observations*, page 385. Mining shares are commonly called *Kukus* <note>A technical term for a share in a mining company</note>. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 7, chapter 27, number 17.

<column-break/>

Question: Is it permitted to search for metal on another's land? This is denied, because gold or silver mines, like the fruits of the land, belong to those who own the property. For no one can enter another's field for the sake of hunting or fowling against the will of the owner. Nor can anyone search for treasure on another's land against the owner's will. Much less, therefore, for the sake of digging metal, since wild beasts and birds are counted among common things by the Law of Nations and thus can be taken by anyone, and treasure is a "gift of God" (according to the law *de thesaur.*) rather than a fruit of the land. Metals, however, are like the fruits of the soil and are in the ownership of private individuals. This is supported by the text in the law *si constat* where Ulpian says: "If there are stone quarries on your land, no one can cut stone there against your will, whether for private or public use." This and many following points are discussed by Bocerus in *On Royalties*, chapter 3, number 167. If more than one person wishes to search for metal in the same field, what is the law? See the same, number 168. Whether a Prince should be preferred in the mines? Number 171. If one begins to dig metal on his own land, can he follow a continuous metal vein under the neighbor's land against the neighbor's will? Number 174. Mines are counted as immovable property. Zobel, part 3, difference 10, number 3 and following; Carpzov, *Forensic Jurisprudence*, part 3, constitution 25, definition 1; Knipschild, *On Trusts*, chapter 5, number 68, and chapter 10, number 96. However, the mining yields are considered movable property. Knipschild, chapter 5, number 68. Regarding the height of mountains: Rupertus in his observations on Florus, book 2, chapter 6. The heights of mountains blind the eyes of enemies with rocks, and the mountains disappear into the clouds. Whether mountains existed before the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>: Meyfart in *Compendium of Geography*, page 16. In the mines, it is customary to demand assessments, which are called a contribution or **Zubusz** <note>An additional payment required from mine-shareholders to cover operating costs</note>, and this is ordered four times a year whenever the account of receipts and expenses is rendered. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 27, number 17. Certain metals are partly of a middle and partly of a lower kind, such as Electrum, Bismuth, Antimony, Mercury (or quicksilver), orpiment, sulfur, vitriol, alum, rock salt, and saltpeter. Cassiodorus says most truly: "To seek gold through war is a crime; through the seas, a danger; through falsehoods, a disgrace; but in its own nature, it is profit." Drexelius in the dedication of *The Gold Mine*. Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, around the Christian year 1227, is said to have acquired such a force of silver and gold from the mines that he could have gilded and purchased all of Bohemia. On the profit of metals, see Obrecht in *Political Reflections*, page 101.

There is no better mine in all of Germany than in the County of Waldeck, which can be seen from the gold-sand found in the Eder river. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 2; Richter, *Economic Axioms*, 36, page 143; *Saxon Consultations*, volume 2, part 2, question 16.

# ADDITION.

Adam Contzen provides many details regarding the Benedictine order in his *Politics, book 6, chapter 46, number 4.*

## 37. To judge and to punish.
### To Execute.

Lord Peter Denaisius, in his disputation on the Right of High Jurisdiction <note>original: "Jure meri Imperii," the sovereign power of life and death</note> of the Imperial Chamber Court, *folio 16, etc.* and also in his assertion on *folio 92, etc.*, takes those words *to judge and to punish* <note>original German: "berechtigen und straffen"</note> to refer solely to the execution of a sentence, excluding the process of legal inquiry. <note>original German: "Because in several places it has become the custom that High Jurisdiction is taken only for the power of the sword, and it is proper for another to pass the judgment."</note> Thus, the said words mean nothing other than "to apply his right and punishment to someone."

In the same way, the terms "to judge" <note>German: "richten"</note> or "to justify" <note>German: "justificiren"</note> are used for execution, just as the Latins used "to act by law" <note>Latin: "Lege agere"</note> to mean the execution of a sentence of condemnation.

He adds that "to judge" <note>German: "berechtigen"</note> is one thing, and "to justify" <note>German: "rechtfertigen"</note> is another: the latter denotes the debate and the legal inquiry, while the former denotes the execution. The inquiry belongs to the Imperial Chamber Court regarding persons inscribed on the Chamber's roll, while the execution belongs to the City of Speyer.

On this, one should certainly consult Symphorianus Gylman, *volume 1, part 2, folio 351, article 4.*

## 38. Mining, Ore-pits.
### Metal Mines.

Metallic veins are found only in mountains, which is why they are called "mountain-work" <note>German: "Bergwerck"</note> or mountain labors. Regarding the various types of fossils and metals, gold and silver mines, and the Law of Mining, Heugius treats these at length in *question 13*, Wesenbec in *consultations 60 and 198*, Rauchbar in *question 22*, and Giovanni Guidi of Volterra in his work *On Metals.* I also discuss this in my work *On the Treasury, book 3, chapter 8.* Furthermore, Matthesius in his *Mining Sermons* <note>German: "Berg-Postilla"</note>, and Peter Albinus in the *Meissen Chronicle*, contain many memorable things regarding mining in general, as does Tileman Fries in *book 4, chapter 34.*

Because mining, ore-pits, etc. <note>original: "2c."</note> are attached to the high regalia <note>sovereign rights</note>, *chapter 1, what things are regalia*, where the Doctors of Law note that some are of the opinion that they should not be divided—especially since they cannot be accurately appraised. See *part 2 of the Frankfurt-edited Illustrious Consultations, consultation 65.*

From the sovereign right over metallic veins, it follows that the government, beyond tithes and other benefits, possesses the "right of pre-emption" <note>German: "Vorkauff"</note> of metals found on the land of private citizens. *Law 1, Code on Metals.* This is so that the state may have the necessities of the land which the high regalia are meant to provide, such as for coinage, artillery, and the like. It is not so that the government should trade with them or raise and inflate the purchase price. *The aforementioned consultation, numbers 21 and 9, to make a beginning.* Regarding the riches of the silver mines of Meissen, Peter Albinus has this to say in the *Meissen Mining*

<column-break/>

*Chronicle, title 4:* One finds here and there, not only in old annals but also in the handbooks of the nobility and many citizens, the sum of the tithes recorded at Schneeberg. From the beginning of the Schneeberg mine until the year 1501 (Schneeberg having been discovered 30 years prior), there fell to the Elector of Saxony as tithes 5,199 "tons of gold" <note>A "ton of gold" was a unit of account, typically 100,000 florins or thalers</note>, calculating one ton for one hundred thousand guilders or thalers. At that same time, a thaler was minted and issued at no higher value than a guilder, which is why the miners still call a thaler a "guilder-groschen."

Also, the same Albinus notes from Melanchthon that from the year 1471 to the year 1550, there was distributed from the Schneeberg veins to those who worked the veins at their own expense more than 123,355 tons of gold; and paid to the Princes in place of tithes, more than 20,559 tons of gold. Just as much was also paid to the same for the stamping of silver, from the "hammer-tax" <note>German: "Schlegelschaß"</note>. Throughout that entire book by P. Albinus, various and pleasant facts about metals, miners, and their pits are found collected.

Regarding metal mines and those found at Potosí in the West Indies, Bertius has the following in his *Abridged Geographic Tables, folio 813:* The quality of the finest gold is defined by Spanish and French laws as 23 and 3/4 carats; so that if a mass were divided into 192 parts, only three parts of gold would be missing <note>i.e., it is nearly pure</note>. For the ratio of silver to gold in almost the whole world is twelve-fold. Gold is found in three ways: as shavings in rivers, in pits and trenches, or through the collapse of mountains and tunnels driven through long spaces of earth. That which is found in rivers is by far the most perfect, being polished by the very attrition of the water; such is found in the Tagus in Spain, the Po in Italy, the Hebrus in Thrace, the Pactolus in Asia, and the Ganges in India. That which is dug from the earth still requires much care. Those who seek it remove the "segullum" <note>a surface indicator of gold</note>, wash the sand, and make a conjecture from what settles; thus it is often found on the surface of the earth by rare good fortune. That which is dug from pits is called "canallitium" by some and "canaliense" by others. That which is brought out of tunnels they call "arrugia." Tubalcain is said to have been the first to practice this art, as is clearly set forth in Holy Scripture, *Genesis chapter 4, 41.*

Statius praises Dalmatian gold:

> When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back
> To sweet Latium: where, having seen Dis <note>The god of the underworld</note>,
> The pale digger returns, and is of the same color
> As the gold he has dug out.

The nature of silver is almost similar. The earth is reddish, or sometimes ashen; silver is found in both by digging pits. It cannot be smelted unless with black lead, or with a vein of lead called "galena," which is usually found near veins of silver...

The limit for digging among the ancients used to be when alum <note>a mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine</note> was found; nothing was sought beyond that. **Question:** Is it lawful to seek metal on another person's land? This is denied, because gold or silver mines, like the fruits of the land, belong to those who own the property. For one cannot enter another's field for the sake of hunting or fowling if the owner is unwilling. Nor can anyone seek treasure on another's land against the owner's will. Much less, therefore, for the sake of digging metal, since wild beasts and birds are counted among common things by the law of nations, and thus can be taken by anyone, and treasure is a gift of God <note>original: "donum Dei"</note>—see the single law in the Code *on treasures*—not a fruit of the land. Metals, however, as fruits of the soil, are in the ownership of private individuals. Meyfart in *Compendium of Geography, page 16.*

In metal mines, a collection is customarily exacted and called a contribution or <term>Zubuß</term> <note>An additional payment required from mine shareholders to cover operating costs</note>, and it is announced four times a year, as often as the account of receipts and expenses is rendered. Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 27, number 17.* Certain metals are partly of the middle and partly of the lowest kind, *said book 2, chapter 33, number 1,* such as Electrum, Bismuth, Antimony, Mercury or quicksilver, orpiment, sulfur, vitriol, alum, and rock salt. *Said chapter 33, throughout.* Cassiodorus <note>a Roman statesman and writer</note> most truly said:

Augmented Treasury of Practice

Regarding what the land of Saxony gained in profit from mines within a few years under the title of "minor royalties" <note>original: "Regalium minorum"; these were smaller sovereign rights over specific minerals</note>, and likewise concerning a plate of solid silver so large that Albert, Duke of Saxony—who held those mines at the time—was able to use it as a princely dining table. In the land of China, although there are rich gold and silver mines which could be worked with great profit, it is nevertheless forbidden by the authorities to dig gold and silver out of the earth because harmful vapors rise from the pits <note>original: "Crufften"</note>. ### 39. **Conclusion. The Closing of a Case.** <note>original: "Beschluß. Conclusio in causa."</note>

When one does not wish to conclude a matter, a judge—having considered the circumstances that ought to be considered <note>original: "consideratis considerandis circumstantiis"</note>—can conclude the case by virtue of his office <note>original: "ex Officio"</note>, or he may accept an "eventual conclusion" as absolute <note>original: "pro pura"</note>. However, when one refers to evidence, the conclusion is made with an offer to provide further proof if any fact remains <note>original: "cum oblatione, si quid facti"</note>. See my own writings in the *Disputations on the Municipal Law of Württemberg*, part 1.

->ADDITION.<-

After the case is concluded, nothing further can be produced as evidence if it concerns the testimony of witnesses or documents. However, the conclusion of a case does not prevent a judge from deciding the matter by an oath <note>This refers to a "decisory oath" where a party swears to the truth of their claim to end the dispute</note>. For this is not a proof provided by the litigant, but rather a provision of the judge for investigating the truth. Fach. 1. contr. 17. Barbosa, book 3, chapter 39, axiom 1, throughout. For the cases in which further proof is admitted after the conclusion, see Lord Doctor Bicci in *Aurea*, section 5, thesis 141, letter Gg. at the beginning. Furthermore, a "conclusion" is the renunciation of further proofs and allegations. According to Common Law, some (citing Mynsinger and Gail) believe this is not a substantial part of the process; however, by the usage and custom of the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, it is so necessary that no sentence may be passed unless the case has been legitimately concluded. If either party refuses to conclude, the judge—against their will and due to their contumacy <note>legal defiance or stubbornness</note>—can accept the case as concluded by virtue of his office and pronounce the main judgment.

### 40. **Burden. Charge. Grievance.** <note>original: "Beschwerung. Onus. Gravamen."</note>

Under this term, both patrimonial <note>burdens on property or inheritance</note> and personal burdens are understood: Law *sine herede* 23, section 9, in the Digest on the administration of guardianship. Cujas on Law *æs quidem* 2, section 1 following, in the Code on provisions and tribute—especially if a universal sign is attached, which does not allow for restriction. Law 28 in the Digest on the institution of heirs. Hence, immunity granted from "every burden"—to be free of all grievances—must be extended universally to all species of immunity. Cravetta, counsel 447.

<column-break/>

5. Roland, Counsel 13, number 32, volume 4. Alexander, counsel 30, number 14 and following, book 5.

->ADDITION.<-

An irreparable grievance <note>original: "gravamen irreparabile"</note> occurs when someone is forced to litigate before a judge who is not their own <note>i.e., a judge lacking proper jurisdiction</note>. Klock, counsel 14, number 148. One may appeal against a future grievance outside of court, but not within a court proceeding. Klock, counsel 15, numbers 2, 3, 4.

### 41. **Besibnen. To prove the defendant's crime by seven sworn witnesses.**

This occurs after a person accused of a capital crime has been fully convicted and found guilty. For greater security, he is released from prison and his bonds and led to a free, public place. There, the magistrate of that place, in the presence of seven witnesses, kindly questions the defendant again, and requests the witnesses to give testimony of his statement in case of need. If the defendant then confesses to his misdeed, he is placed back into prison and bonds, and the Holy Sacrament is thereafter administered to him. Subsequently, after three days, he is led under the open sky or into the usual courthouse, and the "Seven" <note>the seven witnesses</note> are asked to testify, in case of a denial, that the defendant previously confessed publicly to what they report. Upon this declaration and testimony, the defendant is punished as the judgment and law dictate. This is observed in many places in Swabia <note>A region in southwestern Germany</note>; and this act is called *besibnen* from the number of seven witnesses <note>The term comes from "sieben," meaning seven</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the proverb: "one must *besibnen* him" <note>meaning to prove his guilt definitively</note>, and in St. Gallen: "one must show him the seventh book," see the *Acts of Lindau*, folio 654. See especially Adam Keller on *Political Law Offices*, book 2, chapter 17, page 467. Petrus Friedrich on *Mandates*, book 2, chapter 47, number 6.

### 42. **Possession.** <note>original: "Besitzung. Possessio."</note>

When an older possession is preferred over a newer one: Klock, counsel 51, number 180 and following. When a newer one is not considered "clandestine" <note>secretly or illegally obtained</note>: ibid. number 185. When past possession creates a presumption of present possession: ibid. number 184.

He who seizes an already occupied possession achieves nothing. Klock, counsel 7, number 36 and numbers 390, 391; also counsel 28, number 8. Possession that is not quiet or peaceful does not provide legal relief: counsel 10, number 149. One who continues his own possession does not commit an "attempt" <note>an unlawful interference or encroachment</note>: counsel 7, number 101 and following. Proof of possession is not established through "turbid and liquid" <note>unclear or disputed</note> acts: counsel 16, number 226.

The word "possession," as placed in the Religious Constitution <note>likely referring to the Peace of Augsburg or similar treaties regarding church property</note>, cannot be verified by that interpreted and legally subtle understanding of "legal possession," but must be taken—
