<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property and possession rights, specifically addressing how these were defined during the 16th-century religious settlements in the Holy Roman Empire. It transitions from the definition of "possession" to the laws governing "salaries and appointments" (Besoldung).</meta>

Book B. O.

...and it should be understood as true, real, and physical presence upon the thing, or even simple detention <note>The physical act of holding something without necessarily claiming ownership.</note>, so that one does not look at whether a person possesses or detains the property justly, but whether they actually possessed or detained it at the time of the Religious Peace <note>The Peace of Augsburg (1555), which legalised Lutheranism in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. They say that the very words of the Constitution argue for this interpretation. For in the preamble of the section beginning with the word *Since* <note>original German: "Dieweil"</note>, the express words speak of the real and physical presence upon the thing. Shortly thereafter, a limitation is added regarding goods possessed before the Treaty of Passau <note>original: "tractatum Passavinum"; a 1552 agreement that paved the way for the Peace of Augsburg</note>, stating they should not be included under that Constitution—referring me back to the provisions of that same section *Since*.

Therefore, the word "possession," when referred to what precedes it, cannot be understood as anything other than "natural possession," which the previous sections discuss. See Zoanettus in *Explanation of Three Words*, in his works, page 117. For following words are clarified by preceding ones, especially when they are obscure. See Richwein in his *Formulary of Various Petitions*, page 230, and Tilemannus de Benignis, *Vote 2*, page 13. Henry Andrew Cranius agrees in his work *On the Religious Peace*, where he writes: "It is asked whether those words, <term>concerning their possession</term> <note>original German: "um deren Possession"</note>, etc., are to be understood as civil or natural possession?" The latter is more probable, according to Section 19 of the *Religious Peace*, where the word <term>seized</term> <note>original German: "eingezogen"</note> denotes actual detention or physical presence. Nor is it considered here whether one possesses justly or unjustly, as the following words of said Section 19 sufficiently imply. These must be clarified by the preceding words, especially if they are obscure, based on the legal rule "as often as" <note>Latin: "l. quoties 10. C. fam. ercisc."; a citation from the Code of Justinian regarding the division of inheritance</note>. Springer also cites this in *On the Religious Peace*, chapter 9. And although the common rule of law seems to favor "civil possession"—stating that a Legislator's words should be taken according to a legal interpretation, unless they are spoken by a <term>layperson</term> <note>original: "Idiotâ"; in a legal context, this refers to someone without formal legal training rather than a lack of intelligence</note> (in which case they are understood simply as a layperson would use them)—Cranius says this reasoning fails whenever the intent of the legislator is probably established.

### ADDITION.

To hold possessions is not the same as to possess. Lord Doctor Tabor, *On Contracts and Tenant Law*, thesis 49. Maintenance <note>A legal remedy to protect current possession.</note> is not granted to someone who never acquired possession. Klock, *Consultation 28*, number 335.

One is not said to "attempt" <note>In the sense of an illegal act or an "attempt" to change the status quo during a lawsuit.</note> who merely continues their own possession. Vivius, *Opinion 77*, number 34; Joseph Ludovicus, *Perugian Decisions 69*, number 8. So much so, that he who ceases his possession while a lawsuit is pending is said to "withdraw." Roman Rota, *Decision 344*, number 2; Lancellottus, *On Attempts*, part 2, chapter 4, number 3. Rather, he is judged to be "attempting" who prevents another from continuing their possession. Petrus Friderus in *Treatise on the Causes and Matters of Possession*, chapter 9, number 27.

Acts that were contested do not confer possession. Klock, *Consultation 50*, number 320.

<column-break/>

There is no "disturbance" where there is no possession. Bartolus on the law, section 18; Afflictis, *Decision 395*; Menochius, *Remedy 3 for Retaining Possession*, number 24.

No one disagrees that a possessor can continue their possession even while a lawsuit is pending. And this is so true that it even applies when there has been an injunction against continuing possession. Regnerus Sixtinus in his <term>Legal Opinions</term> <note>original German: "im Rechtlichen Bedencken"</note>, question 7.

The phrases <term>To hand over, to place half the village into someone's hands, to hold, to receive and take into one's hands</term> <note>original German: "Eingeben, das halbe Dorff zu Handen setzen, einhaben, zu Handen empfangen und nehmen"</note> designate a true transfer of possession. Klock, volume 2, consultation 61.

No one is to be despoiled of their possession without a prior inquiry into the cause <note>A formal legal hearing.</note>. Even if they were possessing unjustly, they cannot be forcibly removed. Vivius, *Opinion 732*; Menochius, *Remedy 1 for Recovering Possession*, number 109.

Disturbing, violent, and informal acts contribute nothing to the acquisition of legitimate possession. Klock, volume 1, consultation 8.

Barbosa writes most extensively on possession in book 14, chapter 44. Lord Doctor Biccius also wrote a special treatise on the possession of one thing by two or more people. For what possession is, its types, and what is "natural" versus "civil," see Zorer, part 1, question 1. Possession is not acquired through secret acts. Klock, *Consultation 29*, number 218.

## 43. Wages, Appointment.
-> Salary. <-

If those to whom annual salaries are appointed should <term>meet their end</term> <note>original: "diem suum obeant"; they die.</note> before the year is complete, the full stipends for the year in which they died pass to their heirs only if the pay was granted for "liberal service" <note>Work performed by a free person, often of higher status, such as a counselor or professor.</note> or an office of honor/benefit, rather than as compensation for labor. See Rauchbar, part 1, question 25; Peter Aerodius, *Judicial Matters*, book 4; Arumaeus, *Disputations on Principal Laws 5*. Thus, travel money given to a newly appointed Counselor is owed even if the Counselor dies before beginning the journey. See Jacob Schultes, *Practical Questions*, book 1, question 4. Likewise, a full salary must be paid to a lawyer who did nothing in a whole year except write a single letter for a case. The same Schultes, in question 5, discusses <term>whether one must give notice of a termination of appointment half a year in advance?</term> <note>original German: "ob man einem die Bestallung ein halb Jahr zuvor muß auffkünden?"</note>. See also "The Hoopoe of Moller" <note>original: "Upupam Mollerinam"; this likely refers to a specific work by the jurist Moller, perhaps a satirical or distinctive title.</note>, chapter 6.

Although a craftsman should be paid wages in proportion to the time and labor spent, this is sometimes different for others. It is even the case that a soldier who is taken captive—who otherwise deserved well of the State and was privileged—

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of rights and compensation, moving from the possession of property to the regulations governing the "Salarium" (salary or honorarium) for professionals such as professors, advocates, and officials. # Augmented Treasury of Practical Knowledge

If a soldier is taken captive, their stipend must be paid for the duration of their captivity <note>original: "pro tempore captivitatis stipendium fit præstandum"</note>, according to the law as noted by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists</note>. However, in the case of Doctors <note>meaning University Professors</note>, if they should die after they have begun their lectures, they transmit the full salary for that year to their heirs, even those outside the family. This benefit is granted to them by law because of the dignity and integrity of knowledge and the intellect; therefore, the law acts kindly and allows for a broad interpretation. For it is in the interest of the Commonwealth that it be done this way, so that by the hope of rewards, learned and upright men may arise. *Jacobus Benius, On the Privileges of Jurisconsults, part 1, question 22.*

Even though time, labor, and money can usually be divided, the Emperor Severus wrote in a decree that if an Advocate dies, the fee cannot be reclaimed from the heirs. And if the salary has not yet been paid, it is transmitted to the heirs, even those outside the family, for that year. This also applies when the business was not completed through no fault of the Advocate's own. Regarding the salaries of Advocates, I have said more in my *Selections from the 3rd Book of the Pandects, question 5.*

As for the salaries of Officials, Assessors, Judges, Advocates, and likewise Tutors, etc.—concerning when they are due and to what extent they pass to heirs—Johannes Bolognetus discusses this at length. He notes that for "virtuous persons" <note>intellectual professionals like lawyers or doctors</note> who promise their services, it is not considered a standard contract of hire. He reduces the matter to two rules: one applies when the event <note>such as death</note> happens to the employer <term>conductor</term>, and the other when it happens to the employee <term>locator</term>. If the event happens to the employer, the salary for the remaining time is generally owed to all those providing services. But if the event happens to the employee, the total salary is owed to "virtuous" employees, while others are paid proportionately <term>pro rata</term>.

However, regarding the salary for the remaining period of those who have died, this is often judged by local custom. Indeed, in our own University <note>The author likely refers to the University of Tübingen</note>, the salary of a deceased Professor is continued through that <term>angaria</term> <note>original: "angariam"; here referring to the academic quarter or term</note> in which he died, and furthermore for an additional half-year.

It should also be noted that salaries enjoy many legal privileges, so much so that even in the Imperial Chamber <note>The high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, seizures of property have been decreed for debts of salary.

### ADDITION.

See on this word Friedrich Stypmann in his posthumous treatise *On the Salaries of the Clergy.*

<column-break/>

Salaries for the work of Advocates must be calculated fairly and not diminished. Sublime and literate persons should be honored with even greater benefits. Regarding the salaries of Advocates, and the annual salaries or honoraria of any Advocates—not only those provided by the Prince but also those established by private individuals—tutors are said to establish payments for a ward’s teachers not just at any rate, but according to the capacity of the inheritance and the dignity of their birth.

The word "Salary" <note>original: "Salarii"</note> is more honorable than the word "Wages" <note>original: "mercedis"</note>, and it is effectively the same as an "Honorarium" or "Honor." It is received not so much as a wage, but as a <term>gift in return</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀντίδωρον" (antidōron)</note>. If it must be demanded from ungrateful clients, it is not sought through a standard contract of hire, but through an "extraordinary" petition before a Judge or Governor. A general salary or honorarium does not prevent the underlying task from being considered a "gratuitous mandate" <note>a legal service performed out of duty rather than for profit</note>. A salary cannot be demanded from an uncertain promise. A salary is owed to a Doctor <note>Professor</note> even if he could perform no services because he was hindered by plague or the evils of war. It cannot be reduced, nor can he be suspended from office, if he is kept away by illness.

### 44. Special Roll. *Rotulus.*

*It should be noted* <note>original German: "Notandum"</note> that only those witnesses are placed in a **Special Roll** <note>original German: "besonder Rotul"</note> about whom the parties are in dispute, and when the Judge is not immediately available or present. This is done so that later, if such witnesses are rejected by a court sentence, they can be more easily separated from the official Acts. They remain entirely unread, lest the Judge, by scanning them, might develop some bias or inclination in the case.

And it is not the standard "style" <note>court procedure</note> that witnesses are placed in a Special Roll by a decree of the Judge; rather, this is done by the Commissioner himself, or at the request of the parties, so that the Ordinary Judge or the Delegating Authority is not prejudiced, but the matter remains **entirely untouched** <note>original: "omni ex parte integra"</note>.

### 45. To Summon or Agree. *Convenire.*

The word **besprechen** <note>to discuss, summon, or agree</note>, which is equivalent to the Latin word **convenire**, is very broad, encompassing every kind of agreement whatsoever, whether judicial or extra-judicial. See the Legal Acts of the City of Braunschweig <note>Brunswick</note> concerning the Oath of Allegiance.

## 46. Improvement. <term>Melioratio</term>. <note>Latin: *Melioratio*; German: *Besserung*. Refers to the legal right to compensation for value added to a property.</note>

Even if women or males who do not descend directly from the first person granted a fief <note>The "invested" party</note> do not succeed to the estate itself, they are by no means to be barred from compensation for improvements <note>original: "à meliorationibus"</note>, whether the estate is returned to the Lord—according to Book 2 of the *Feudal Laws*, title 28, as noted by Alvarottus, Laudensis, Schenck, and others—or whether the fief passes to the male-line relatives <note>original: "agnatos"</note> by succession. *Wesenbeck, Epitome of Feudal Law, chapter 9; Vultejus, book 1; Schrader, part 9.*

Indeed, this right is so strong that if they are in possession of the property, they have a right of retention over the fief by reason of the improvements and the existing crops <note>original: "fructuum extantium"</note>. *Schrader, Rosenthal, chapter 7.* However, once they have been removed through legal channels or prevented from taking possession, it is difficult for them to obtain a court order for entry based on crops and improvements, according to the legal opinions of Wesenbeck and Cacheranus.

However, Schrader reports that the opposite holds true under **Saxon Law** <note>original: "Jure Saxonico"</note>. Namely, that buildings erected on a fief revert to the Lord, according to the *Saxon Landrecht* <note>The "Land Rights," a foundational code of German law</note> book 2, article 21, and the *New Constitutions* of Augustus. *Zobel, Fachs, Reinkingk, and Coler.* See also Hartm. Pistor and Andreas Scheffer.

### ADDITION.

All heirs succeed to the improvements of a fief, and they may retain the fief until they have been satisfied <note>compensated</note> in their own name. *Klock, volume 2, counsel 32.* When a fief passes to a male-line relative, one might ask whether the vassal or the heir of the private property <note>original: "haeres allodialis," referring to non-feudal land held in absolute ownership</note> may recover the expenses and improvements made for the perpetual benefit of the fief. *Consultation 35.*

A tenant farmer <note>original: "Colonus"</note>, once the price of the improvements has been received, must move out without delay and restore the land to the Lord. See the *Code of Justinian*, law 34, "On Hiring." This law is considered too harsh and is not observed in common practice. *Lord Tabor, On Coloniary Law, thesis 66.*

Improvements take on the nature of the thing for whose sake they were made; see below under the word **Fief** <note>original: **Lehen**</note> in the section "Improvements also." The term "Improvements" is understood in various ways, as discussed extensively by Lord Tabor in *On the Contract and Law of Tenant Farming*, thesis 69.

To whom the improvement of the fief belongs, and how it is to be handled regarding the expenses spent upon it, see Knipschild’s little treatise, *On the Obligations of the Lord Toward the Vassal*, question 6; Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 12*; and Westermann in a rather lengthy inaugural disputation held at Helmstedt in the year 1649, *On Feudal Improvement*. *Besold, Volume 1.*

## 47. Lease. <term>Locatio conductio</term>. <note>Latin: *Locatio conductio*; German: *Bestandt*. The Roman legal contract for hiring or leasing.</note>

Regarding Lease and Hire, see Molinaeus, *On Justice and Law*, volume 2, dispute 485. On the relocation and renewal of a lease, see Franz Pfeil. Whether the "right of first refusal" <note>original: "Juri protimiseos"</note> has a place in a lease is decided by Mastrillus. Also, whether a tenant can raise an exception <note>a legal defense</note> of ownership or debt against the landlord is discussed by Ludovicus Peguera. On when the rent <note>original: "Merces"</note> should be paid by the tenant, see Timaeus Faber.

### ADDITION.

In **Canon Law**, a certain type of lease is called "at farm" <note>original: "ad firmam"; German: "verpachten"</note>. This is derived from the French *ferme*. However, it seems to signify something more than simply "to lease" or "to give or hold a lease." Note the remarks of Cujas on this phrase, who says the Pope uses it in a popular sense. *Finckelt, observation 5; also in his treatise On the Right of Patronage.* More can be found in Lord Tabor’s *On the Provincial Contract and Law of Tenant Farming*, thesis 16.

If a house belonging to another is leased by several owners, one of them alone cannot expel the tenant before the term expires for his own use. *Carpzov, part 2, decision 137.* A tenant does not "possess" the property in a legal sense, yet he is "in possession" because he receives the fruits <note>the harvest or profit</note> for his cultivation and care. *Nicolaus Myler, On the Princes and States of the Empire, page 529.* Unusual and unforeseen cases are excepted in a lease and in any contract. *Klock, volume 2, counsel 72.*

No one can lease what they do not have in their own power and possession. *Code of Justinian, On Farmers and Census, book 11.* A lease made to a more powerful person for a short time is considered an "alienation" <note>a transfer of ownership</note>; thus, anyone prohibited from alienating property is also prohibited from leasing it to a more powerful person even for a short time. *Knipschild, On Entailed Estates, chapter 11.* A lease is said to be for a "moderate" or short time if it is for three, five, or even nine years. *Valascus, On the Law of Emphyteusis, question 29.* A lease is called "long-term" if it is for as long as the tenant wishes, or for the life of the landlord or tenant. *Boerius, Garfias.* Also, if it is for ten years or more, or for three five-year periods, or three nine-year periods with a pact to renew. *Alexander, book 2.*

## 48. Petitions. <term>Preces</term>. <note>German: *Beten*; Latin: *Preces*. Refers to formal requests made to a superior or the court.</note>

Regarding petitions, see Dilherr, book 1, chapter 1, and book 2, chapter 23.

...which is the same as he who [commands]. For the prayers of a superior are regarded as a command and a compulsion. <note>Socin. cons. 263. num. 8; Pacianus cons. 54; Barbosa lib. 14. cap. 75.</note> Public and solemn prayers <note>original: "Preces publicæ ac solennes"</note> are prohibited, but not private and domestic ones, which a person performs alone in their chamber, or with their family, without any priest. <note>Rittersch. in Novell. p. 65.</note> Interrupted days <note>original: "Dies intercisi"</note> are called **half-holidays and prayer days**, likewise days of **penance, prayer, and fasting**, such as those celebrated every four months in the Duchy of Brunswick and Lüneburg, and every month on the day of the "Great Prayers" in Strasbourg.

The Patriarch Isaac went out into the field in the evening to pray, and as the Hebrew word indicates, to have his beautiful devotions and to speak with God. *Genesis chapter 24, verse 21.*

How the Turks pray. *Schweigger in Travelogue, chapter 10, page 34.*

In vain is it asked in Universities: where in the *Institutes* <note>The *Institutes* of Justinian, a foundational Roman legal text.</note> is the **OUR FATHER** found? It appears, however, in the title on donations <note>original: "t. de donat. §. sed primus quidem"</note>, where it says: "Divine Justinian, **OUR FATHER**." <note>This is a legal scholar's joke; the text refers to Justinian as the "father of the law," not the prayer itself.</note> It is fruitlessly told of the Knights of the Holy Sepulchre that they are bound to recite 40 *Pater Nosters* daily, etc. We would do better if we were intent on sacred things, reading Mr. Harsdörffer’s *7 Contemplations on the 7 Petitions of the Our Father*, published in 1651. Devout prayer is a help to the one praying, a sacrifice to God, a punishment to the Devil, a shield against terrors in the night, rest during daily labors, and a protection and solace for the elderly. Philippe de Comines piously writes: A happy outcome of counsel cannot be achieved unless prayers precede, intervene, and follow. When the Turks pray, they turn toward **Midday** <note>South/Mecca</note>, the Jews toward **Evening** <note>West/Jerusalem</note>, and the Christians toward **Morning** <note>East</note>; but no one turns toward **Midnight** <note>North</note>, because it is said that misfortune shall come from there <note>A reference to Jeremiah 1:14: "Out of the north an evil shall break forth."</note>, as can be read in Besold's *On the Nature of Peoples* at the end of chapter 4. Also, in ancient times the Romans performed their prayers toward the morning, and other peoples worshipped the rising sun. *Lipsius in Notes on Tacitus, book 3.* There were different words for the prayers of the Pagans when they slaughtered victims to inspect the entrails—which were called "obtained" <note>original: "impetritum"</note>—and others when they performed a solemn sacrifice to avert omens, which they called "depulsive" <note>original: "depulsorium"</note>; still others when they commended something or someone to the Gods, and others when they fulfilled vows. <note>Rupert. diss. 2. l. 1. cap. 1.</note> The same rites of prayer are found in *Valerius Maximus*. <term>συναγωνίζεσθαι</term> <gloss>to strive together</gloss>, that is, to pour out heroic and very ardent prayers for the Church and the Christian Commonwealth. *In the life of Jakob Andreae.* Regarding what language was used 600 or 700 years ago around the city of Nuremberg, in France, and in Bavaria for the *Our Father* and the *Creed*, see Mr. Leon-

<column-break/>

The Christians in the early Church were accustomed to pray with their faces cast down toward the earth from Easter until Pentecost, to remember the burial and resurrection. *Mr. Harsdörffer.*

Job prayed every day for his children. *Schuppius in "The Afflicted but Patient Job," page 107.* A General once had poor musketeers hanged, but first permitted them to pray one *Our Father*. *Ibid. in the Dedication A. 6.*

### 49. Bed: To step into the bed, to strike the covers. <term>Lectus</term>. <gloss>To ascend the marriage bed.</gloss>

If a groom or bride dies before the wedding, the survivor receives no profit from the statute or the dotal agreement <note>dowry contract</note> unless the marriage was consummated by lying together. This is according to **Saxon Law**, which requires the leading of the bride to the house and **that the bride has stepped into the bed**. *Text of the Landrecht, article 45, book 3.*

Interpreters of Civil Law fall into two opinions. Some follow the affirmative: that even if the bride dies before the wedding, the groom nevertheless gains the dowry. <note>Aretin. in §. fuerat; Socinus Junior.</note> Others assert the contrary. <note>Schurff. cent. 3; Gail. 2. obs. 8; Rol. à Valle; Fr. à Solis.</note> However, the other customs of Germany, and also **Württemberg Law** <note>part 4, title 2</note>, agree with the Saxon Law.

But this phrase, **"to strike the covers,"** <note>German: *die Decken beschlagen*</note> is not to be understood as actual sexual intercourse, but only as the solemn custom **that the couple has been "laid together"** <note>A formal public ceremony where the couple was placed in bed to signify legal marriage.</note>. *Rauchb. 1. q. 31; Moller. 3. semest. c. 23.*

From this the question arises: When two people secretly promise marriage to each other and sleep together, and the man admits to both but then moves away and dies before the public church wedding—is the child born into the world legitimate and able to succeed the father? My brother <note>p. m. conf. 7. decad. 1.</note> advised in the negative. This is for the sake of preserving the vigor of public discipline and honesty. This opinion was approved in the High Court of Württemberg in the appeal case of Calw, between Martin Rotgeb & associates and Christina Maier on June 10, Anno 1618. In that case, a man had promised marriage 30 years prior and had been announced <note>banns of marriage</note> twice, but out of melancholy (because people vexed him, saying he would be raising other men's children), he hanged himself two days before the wedding. Furthermore, the bride was a person of ill-repute and was only supported by one witness...

## ADDITION.

The legacy of the marriage bed <note>original: "Lectus uxorius legatus"</note> and with what ornaments it is owed. See Mantica on the conjecture of last wills, book 6, title 11, number 17, extensively.

According to custom in the lands of Saxony, a husband—who otherwise succeeds his wife in movable goods—is not admitted to the succession before the marriage has been consummated. He must then have "stepped into the bridal bed" <note>original: "das Brautbett beschritten"</note> according to the text in article 45, book 1, and article 31 of the same; also constitution 19, part 3 of Schneidewein. For girls getting married, the nuptial bed was spread (in Greek: *to the nuptial chamber* <note>original: νυμφidίῳ θαλάμῳ</note>), which was called "genial" from the "generating" of children. Servius, in his commentary on the 6th book of the *Aeneid*, says it is as if it were "general" or rather "generable." ## 50. Request-tax, or Bede, Beet, Request-sheaves, Request-grain, Request-wine, etc. Betta.

A "Bede" <note>From the German *beten*, to pray or request.</note> is nowadays nothing other than an ordinary tax, contribution, or assessment <note>original: "Steuer, Schoss und Schatzung"</note> which subjects, primarily peasants, are accustomed to pay and contribute to their territorial lords. Mentioned in the *Symphorema*, volume 2, part 2, vote 15, number 38. Also volume 1, part 2, title 6, vote 2, number 7. Gothofridus Antonius, feudal disputation 1, theorem 6 at the end; Master Goeddaeus in the Friedberg Counsel, folio 8, number 13 and following, point 1.

They are called "Bede" because from the beginning they were demanded mildly and kindly through requests and persuasions. <note>original: "ab initio blandè & benignè per rogationes & suasiones exigebantur"</note> Knichen, on Saxon Law, under the word "Dukes," chapter 5, number 283. Although now they are more like commands in effect than requests. Wesenbeck, counsel 45, number 11, according to the saying: "The request of Dukes is a violent form of praying."

And so, from "requesting" or "praying" <note>original: "Bethen, oder beten"</note> came "commanding" <note>original: "gebieten"</note>, and from "Request" came "Command" <note>original: "Gebot"</note>. Gylman, decision 37, number 27, book 1. Rittershusius on homage, chapter 7, number 161. For truly, Germany was once free from these new impositions. See Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, book 2, chapter 44. As was France, according to Pasquier in his

<column-break/>

*Research*, book 2, chapter 7 and book 7, chapter 40. See my own work on the treasury, folio 68, etc.

However, "Bed" <note>Bede</note> is frequently taken to mean a quota of the harvest, or an annual rent paid in produce, not by virtue of a general tax, but as a real burden on the land.

But "Baet" is taken for a toll or custom duty. See the *Adversaria* of Scriekius, folio 100, from which he says the name "Batavia" <note>The Netherlands</note> descends—as if *Baethave* were the "perceiving of tolls"—and on the following folio, "Batave" refers to everything that pertains to profit and tribute, from "to benefit" or "to be of use" <note>original: "vom batten, nutzen"</note>.

Master Martin Mager, in his treatise on the *Armed Advocate*, chapter 7, number 213, considers "Request-sheaves" <note>original: "Betgarben"</note>, "Request-grain," and "Request-wine" to be certain bundles of grain which were customarily given to magistrates as a favor, in recognition of their lordship. Regarding these "precarious" <note>Meaning granted by favor or request.</note> gifts, and the fact that they are regularly paid only to the ordinary magistrate in Germany, one may see the response of Goeddaeus in the Friedberg case, point 1, number 10 and following.

Thus, someone often pays an annual pension from their estate or land—specifically several bushels of grain—according to the acres and hides <note>original: "jugera & mansos"</note>. This pension is called land-rent <note>original: "terragium"</note>, or by terms like **Lease-grain**, **Hide-grain**, **Debt-grain**, **Seed-oats**, **Bailiff-oats**, or **Dog-oats** <note>original: "Hundshaber," likely a tax for the upkeep of the lord's hunting dogs.</note>, being the third, fourth, tenth, or twentieth sheaf of all fruits. From wine, it may be the fifth or tenth measure. From trees, the fruit of the trees, the third or fourth basket, etc. See Adam Keller on political jurisdictional office, book 2, chapter 10. And today, almost everything is subject to burdens of this kind.

From mines, although the payment of the **Inheritance-tunnel Right** <note>original: "Erbstollen Rechts"</note>—amounting to a ninth or half-ninth—is paid to those at whose expense the water-tunnels were driven (which draw the water away from the other masses), see the Saxon Mining Constitution, articles 51 and 57; Heigius 1, question number 52. Nevertheless, because the power to mine gold and silver must be obtained from the lords of the territory through special concession and renewed every year, besides the **Tithes**, a certain portion of the returns is also assigned to the Territorial Lords. This is commonly called a <term>Free Inheritance-Cuckoo</term> <note>original: "freier Erbkukuß," a mining term for a share in a mine that the lord of the land receives for free, without having to pay into the operating costs.</note>, at the Ground-Lord's own disposal and expense. Heigius, said question 13, number 42. From cows, **Pentecost-cheese** is given; from sheep, **Martinmas lambs** or **March-and-May lambs**. From pigs, either a **Count-pig** <note>original: "Zahlschwein," a lean pig meant for counting or sorting.</note> or a fattened **Milling-pig** <note>original: "Mahlschwein"</note>. From piglets today, they give **St. Anthony's piglets**. From chickens, they give **Jurisdictional hens** (due to the location and the smoke exhaling from the chimney), called **Smoke-hens**. Also **Rental-hens**, **Pentecost-hens**, **Shrovetide-hens**, **Rent-summer and Autumn-hens**, **Capons**, and **Shrovetide-eggs**. From geese, **Martinmas-geese**. Rittershusius, in the cited place, number 162.

### 51. Beggars. <note>original: "Bettler. Mendicans."</note>

Who is considered an "able-bodied beggar," and should he be punished, and with what penalty? See Pegurra, decision 4; Beatus, decisions part 4, volume 4, *On Crimes*, folio 463; Camerarius, century 1, chapter 15 and following, century 2, chapter 74.
How one should deal with such beggars, I have touched upon in my treatise *On the Three Types of Domestic Society*, folio 78 and following.
There are those who think they have performed an excellent service *if they abolish street begging* <note>original: "so sie den Gassen-Bettel abschaffen"</note>, such as Doctor Conrad Dieterich in his *Begging Sermon*. But truly, Christ our Savior willed that the poor always be among us; and we are moved more if we see them and converse with them than if they are banished outside of human society, as it were. See Cardinal Baronius in his *Annals*, Year of Christ 57, number 126, and above under the letter A, number 41. It is certain that in every age there have been beggars. However, they should be provided for in a different way than is commonly done, and the opportunity to work should be offered: which perhaps could be conveniently achieved if some form of servitude were reintroduced, and they were employed in public works, treated liberally, and held in the place of proletarian citizens.
Meanwhile, those who *artfully simulate great injuries and represent them with various cunning* <note>fraudulent beggars</note> are to be detested and severely punished, regarding whom see Schenck in *Medical Observations*, folio 335 and 895.

->ADDITION.<-

Beggars are more prone to lies. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 56, number 1. Examples of these lies are in number 2, and the penalties in number 3.

<column-break/>

How to proceed against *beggars, idlers, loafers*, and those who do not wish to work. Zorer, question 18, number 4085 and following, part 2. It is not enough when *street beggars* are dismissed and sent away, if at the same time an opportunity for work is not created and provided for them, such as requiring them—with or without leg-shackles and irons—to work on public buildings, or to clear and clean the ditches, roads, and streets of a city and community. Number 4089. Thus in the Republic of Strasbourg, there are those who are condemned to public labor, called the *Schellenwerck* <note>literally "Bell-work," referring to a workhouse or penal labor where prisoners wore bells to prevent escape</note>. Biccius, in his *Golden Decisions*. Those who simulate severe illnesses, or falsely pretend to have great bodily injuries and defects when they lack nothing in physical strength and health—and perhaps even use false letters and seals and thereby collect much money, or even commit theft and murder—are to be highly punished upon discovery, and they should be investigated with diligence. Zorer, part 2, question 18, number 4092. On restraining the persistence of beggars, see Schönborner in *Politics*, book 3, chapter 15. Solon willed that an idle man caught three times should be marked with infamy, according to Julius Pollux, book 8 of the *Onomasticon*: Draco, however, even punished them with death, as found in Plutarch’s *Life of Solon*. See the title in the Code *On Able-Bodied Beggars*, and Novel 80, and Cujas there; add Klock, *On the Treasury*, 2, chapter 102, numbers 39 and 49.
A certain man gives all beggars new clothes, takes the old ones in return, and makes a profit. Zeiler, century 4, question 33, page 165.

### 52. Mendicant Orders. <note>original: "Bettel-Orden. Ordo Mendicantium."</note>

We commonly call them "Mendicant Friars," to whom it is permitted to own nothing as their own. For this reason, it can be doubted with good cause whether anything can be bequeathed to them in a will. In this question, Michael Grassus makes a distinction in *Sentences* 1, section "Legatum," question 7. There are some who are Mendicants by their Rule <note>religious law</note>, such as the Friars Minor <note>Franciscans</note>, and nothing can be left to these, even regarding the monetary value—that is, so that it might be sold and spent on their necessary uses. Baldus, in the authority *If any woman*, Code *On the Most Holy Churches*. And Felinus says this is the common opinion in chapter *In praesentiar*, verse *quam*, on proofs. Aretinus on law 1 of the Digest *On Wills*. Signorolus de Homodeis (Consultation 4) and Gabriel Romanus (Common Conclusions, book 4, title on the institution of heirs, conclusion 1, number 1) report it as the more common view. However, libraries and books can be bequeathed to them.
But others are Mendicants more by their constitution than by their order: such as the Preaching Friars <note>Dominicans</note>, and things can be left or bequeathed to these, not so that they retain them themselves or in common, but so that they may sell them and spend the money on necessary uses, according to the authorities cited by Grassus in the said place.
But one should certainly see the *Compendium of Regular Questions* by Emanuel Rodriguez,

### Lit. B.

...Henriques, the Portuguese, under the word **Inheritance**, where the following is held: The **Friars Minor of the Observance** <note>The Observants were a branch of the Franciscans who sought a stricter adherence to the Rule of St. Francis, particularly regarding poverty.</note> are in no way capable of succeeding to inheritances, nor is it permitted for them to have the value of such inheritances—or even a portion of them—bequeathed to them under the guise or form of a legacy (if it can be presumed this was done for their benefit), or to receive them once bequeathed. Rather, Pope Clement V simply forbade such practices by the friars in the decree *Exivi de paradiso* <note>original: "Clem. exivi de verb. signif." — a famous papal constitution from 1312 regarding Franciscan poverty</note>. Thus, if they are appointed as heirs and have no substitute or co-heir, the will is void, and the inheritance will pass to those who inherit in cases of intestacy <note>term: "intestacy" (ab intestato) — the state of dying without a valid legal will.</note>.

Although the **Friars Minor** cannot receive an inheritance, which involves a type of universal right to property, they can nonetheless receive individual gifts or a specific trust <note>term: "fideicommissum" — a legal arrangement where property is left to one person to be handed over to another.</note>, which the **Syndic** <note>The Syndic was a layperson appointed to manage money and property for the Franciscans, since the friars themselves were forbidden from owning anything.</note> may claim in order to provide for the friars' necessities.

If the Friars are not appointed as heirs themselves, but another person is appointed who must sell the inheritance and spend the proceeds on the Friars' needs, this does not seem to be prohibited to the Friars by law in any way; therefore, they may lawfully accept it. Understand, however, that this is provided the amount is not so large that it appears to be done to defraud the rule of poverty, but only to relieve the present or imminent needs of the Friars; otherwise, it would smack of "treasuring up" or hoarding.

Even though the Friars Minor are incapable of receiving bequests in Wills, they are provided for in various ways. First, through the duty of a **Judge**, who by the simple virtue of his office—even if no one brings a case—can compel a person bound by a Will to pay out what was left to the Minors and fulfill the Will. Second, any member of the public has the right to take action, and anyone from the community can sue to ensure that bequests for pious causes (such as for the poor friars, etc.) are fulfilled by the person burdened by the Testator or otherwise held to it. Third, the **Syndic** can claim the aforementioned legacies in the name of the Pope, provided this is done with the other required legal circumstances.

The **Church of the Friars Minor** can be appointed as an heir according to Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note>, since it belongs by right and ownership to the Roman Church; however, Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), another famous jurist and student of Bartolus.</note> thinks otherwise.

**Mendicants** who are able to possess property through special Privileges can succeed in cases of intestacy, unless their own constitutions, confirmed by Apostolic authority, state the contrary—which everyone ought to check.

**Benedictine and Cistercian Monks** succeed in cases of intestacy just as if they were still in the secular world, and they can lawfully claim and keep inheritances, trusts, and legacies by the grant of various Popes.

Regarding the **Origin of the Mendicant Orders**, the following is found in the same question under the word *Order*, page 308, etc.: Although all Religious Orders that live on alms can be called "mendicants" according to the origin of the word, there are four that claimed this name for themselves from the beginning: namely the Orders of

<column-break/>

**Preachers** [Dominicans], **Blessed Francis** [Franciscans], the **Hermits of Saint Augustine**, and the **Carmelites**, who are properly and principally called Mendicants; although some of them may possess stable property in common. To these were added, by Apostolic constitutions, the Order of Minims, the Servants of the Blessed Mary [Servites], the Jesuati of Saint Jerome, and the **Society of Jesus** [Jesuits].

The **Order of Preachers** had its beginning from **Blessed Dominic**, who obtained approval for his Rule around the year of our Lord 1216. Since then, many have flourished in the Church of God in both holiness and knowledge.

The **Order of Friars Minor** is said to be adorned, like the Holy Church of God, with a most beautiful variety of congregations and different practices tending toward one goal. It has as its author and founder the Seraphic Father, **Saint Francis**. He composed two Rules for the Minors, the first of which was approved by Innocent III in the year of our Lord 1212; the second, which the whole Order now holds, by Honorius III around the year 1226. And now the number of Brothers and congregations has grown so large that under one general head—descending in successive order by canonical election from St. Francis—there are four "families": namely, the **Observants** (who branched off from the Conventuals in the year 1414), the **Reformers**, the **Recollects**, and the **Discalced** <note>term: "Discalced" — literally "unshod" or barefoot, referring to those who wore sandals instead of shoes as a sign of austerity.</note>. Under the same Founder's institute are the Conventuals, Capuchins, Amadeans, Clareni, Alcantarians, and Paschalists.

The **Order of Hermits of St. Augustine** was instituted by Augustine himself, as some believe; but when it was nearly destroyed by the ruins of the Vandals, it was restored by a certain Saint William, Duke of Gascony, around the year 1157, from whom they were long called Williamites. But later it was reformed by a certain John, surnamed "the Good," in Italy, and was confirmed by Alexander IV under the name of the Hermits of St. Augustine. There are two congregations within it: the Conventuals and the Observants.

The authors of the **Carmelite Order** were certain devout men on Mount Carmel who worshipped the Blessed Virgin with special honor. John, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, wrote a Rule of life for them, but in the year 1110, Albert, also Patriarch of Jerusalem, composed another more convenient one for them, which Honorius III confirmed; later, Eugenius IV moderated it somewhat, especially regarding abstinence from meat. Today the aforementioned Order is also divided into Conventuals and Observants, from which Observance certain truly zealous men in the year 1558 obtained the first observance of the Rule from Gregory XIII, living under the name of **Discalced Brothers**. At first, they were always under the obedience of the Provincial of the Common Observance, but Clement VIII gave them a General who is independent of all others.

The **Order of the Servants of the Blessed Mary** [Servites] was begun by seven most noble Florentine men on Mount Senario near...

The head and founder of the **Order of Minims** was the illustrious St. Francis of Paola in the year 1450. Because of the great number of both men and women flocking to him, he established three Rules: one for the Brothers, another for the Nuns, and a third for the <term>Tertiaries</term> <note>Lay members of a religious order who do not live in a monastery but follow the order's spirit.</note> or the Cloaked, which were confirmed and approved by Sixtus IV, Innocent VIII, and Alexander V.

The **Order of Jesuits**, or the Society of JESUS, was given its beginning by St. Ignatius of Loyola.

### 54. Clause: "By pledging all my belongings and goods." <note>original: "Clausula sub hypotheca omnium bonorum"</note>

Whether this clause also includes future goods and those acquired by the debtor after the pledge <note>term: "pignus" — a pledge or security for a debt.</note> was contracted, see Mr. Bachovius, *Treatise on Pledges and Mortgages, book 1, chapter 5, number 2.* There, he considers it reasonable that under the name of "goods," only those things which someone possessed at the time the pledge was bound should be included—not future goods, as they are entirely uncertain. This is especially true if the debtor said "his goods." For the word "mine" is in a certain way determinative and restrictive, and signifies that something already belongs to someone, so that under that name, not even what is owed to him is contained. <note>Citations to Roman law: *l. si ita 7* regarding gold and silver legacies; *l. Quintus 27* and *l. scribit 34* under the same title.</note> This is supported by *l. 45 § 1* regarding the recovery of property. Since the property of others is not rightly given as a pledge, a condition should not easily be imagined or implied that "if they become mine in the future," where there is no mention of future things at all. Therefore, we read here and there that in a general <term>mortgage</term> <note>original: "hypotheca" — a legal right over a debtor's property.</note> (*of fixed and movable rights and actions, future and present* <note>original German: "ligend und fahrender jurium & actionum, künfftig und gegenwärtiger"</note>), by which future things would also be held, express mention was made of them and of things to be acquired. <note>Citations to the Code of Justinian and the Digest regarding the priority of creditors.</note> This is also done today, and it is customary to add: "*Present and future.*" <note>original German: "Gegenwärtiger und zukünfftiger"</note> But see Negusantius in his *Treatise on Pledges*.

Since all of a debtor's goods are included under a general mortgage <term>hypotheca</term> <note>A legal claim or mortgage where the debtor retains possession of the property while it serves as security for a debt.</note>, the question arises: are they included with the same legal effect individually, and does this general mortgage affect all items just as if they had been specifically pledged? Furthermore, can these items be recovered through legal action even if they are currently in the possession of a third party? On this question, consult the aforementioned Bachovius in the cited chapter 5, number 3, and throughout the following.

## ADDITION.

A general mortgage does not encompass cash or items intended for daily use. *Barbosa, Axioms, book 8, chapter 15, axiom 3.* Indeed, all goods come under a general mortgage—both present and future—and those acquired by the creditor afterward, even if nothing was expressly agreed upon between the parties regarding them. This includes legal actions, rights, and debts <note>original: "nomina," referring to names in an account book representing debts owed to the debtor</note> of the debtor, as well as merchandise for sale and money; however, it does not include those things which it is likely a person would not specifically pledge, such as furniture, clothing, etc. *Beatus Biccius in his Golden Sections, section 4, thesis 49, letter A.*

We often cannot obtain a loan even from our friends, let alone from others, unless pledges are put forward. Such is the greed, treachery, and distrust of men. Martial alluded to this in this epigram:

> When I ask you for money without a pledge, you say,
> "I have none."
> Yet when my little field stands as security for me, you have it.
> That which you do not trust to me, Telesinus, your old companion,
> You trust to my hills and my trees.

Seneca complains of this matter elsewhere: "There is more security in a thing than in a person." *Rittershufius on Law 23 of the Digest, 'On Rules of Law,' page 108.* Regarding the words by which a mortgage is established, see Cardinal Tuschus under the word "mortgage," and Mantica on ambiguous agreements, book 11, title 10. Also see the final law of the Code, "What things can be given as a pledge," Novel 136, chapter 5; Moller, Semestria 5, 79; Cavalcanti, Decision 2, number 9 and 35. On whether a mortgage is extinguished by assignment, see Surdus, Decision 266.

## 55. Boundary-Letter. Terminal Letters.

The boundaries of a thing—the Boundary-Letter <note>original: "Bezirk-Brieff"</note>—demonstrate possession and ownership. *Sichardus, on Feudal Law, 1, number 87 and following, leaf 142. b.* Such letters are those where the limits and boundaries of a county or territory are specifically designated. For boundaries demonstrate possession and lordship. Hence it is said that a case involving a common boundary has the nature of both a possessory and a proprietary action. *Law 2, final paragraph, Digest, 'On the Regulation of Boundaries'.* Therefore, if by such a writing the boundaries and district of a county, etc., are designated, it is simultaneously implied that ownership and jurisdiction belong to that district. This presumption must be upheld unless the contrary is proven.
Besold, Volume I.

## 56. Bible. Biblia.

Regarding the Vulgate version, see *Filesacus, Select Works 1, chapter 14;* also the individual treatise by *Alberico Gentili.* On the Greek version of the Old and New Testament, see *Cardinal Bellarmine, 'On the Word of God,' book 2, chapters 5, 6, 7, and 14,* and on the Latin version, see the same author extensively in the cited location, chapter 8. Some argue that all interpretations contain something of the Divine, as *Origen* is cited by *Bellarmine, 'On the Word of God,' book 1, chapter 7, leaf 9, column 1.* *Sixtus of Siena* also deals with many translations in the final book of his Library, leaf 649.

## ADDITION.

Regarding all the books of Holy Scripture, see Rittershufius on Amphilochius, pages 99 and 100. The Bible is, as it were, a lenticular crystal <note>original: "Chrystallus lenticularis"</note>—the crystal of the eye, as the physicians say—by means of which the children of God (especially when the true optic nerve, the power of the Holy Spirit, is added) continue the restoration already begun and take heed of what is beneficial for salvation. The Jews are the custodians of the Hebrew Bibles: which Justin Martyr also observed in his *Second Apology for the Christians to the Emperor.* Divine books cannot be exhausted by any amount of preaching; the Bible can never be fully preached out. *Drexelius, 'The Gold Mine,' page 76.* Various versions of the Holy Bible are reviewed in *Rittershufius's Novellae, page 48, number 22.* For those soldiers mentioned in Dinothus, book 2 of the *History of Gaul,* page 152, who threw the Holy Bible into a flowing river while impiously shouting, see *Limnäus, Public Law, book 8, chapter 1, number 65.* Virdungus recounts that a best man, amidst fervent prayers and intent on Bible reading, finally found a Bible that had been suddenly lost on a wedding day and sought for a long time. Francisco Ximenes, the Cardinal and Archbishop of Toledo, spent more than sixty thousand ducats to print the Complutensian Bible. *Zeiller, in his Spanish Itinerary, leaf 80.* You may be surprised to learn that one man gathered all the editions of the Bible into a private library, as witnessed by Master Saubert in his *Nuremberg Library,* page 114. The Bible is also found among the Turks; the teachings of the Holy Prophets and Apostles are found among them in the Arabic language, held by their *Muftis* and doctors. *Schweigger in his Travelogue, page 179.* Theodorus Reincking has published a "Biblical Policy." Bibles written on the finest parchment are mentioned by *Pancirollus in 'New Discoveries,' my page 600.*

### 58. Beer Brewing. *Braxare.*

The entire maritime part of Germany, stretching far and wide along the shores of the German Ocean <note>The North Sea</note> and extending into immense coastal bends, lacks wine entirely unless it is imported by merchants. It is therefore the custom of those regions to brew beer (a type of drink that Diodorus calls <term>Zythum</term> <note>An ancient word for beer made from fermented grain</note>). On this they become intoxicated everywhere, even much worse than the upper Germans do on wine. Whence *Pliny* exclaims in *book 14, final chapter*: *Alas, through a strange ingenuity of vices, a way has been found for even water to intoxicate!*

Mention is also made by *Cardanus, in book 6 on the variety of things, chapter 24*, of a drink called *Hala* used in England and Scotland, which is sweeter than *Zythum* and can be compared to sweet unfermented wine.

Beer otherwise receives various names: in Erfurt it is called *Schlanß*, in Leipzig *Rastrum*, in Magdeburg *Filß*, in Brunswick *Momm* <note>Known as Mumme, a very strong, thick beer</note>, and in Goslar *Guse* <note>Gose, a sour wheat beer</note>, etc. *See the various questions on types of drunkards, corollary 3.* The names themselves have a horrendous sound.

The right of brewing beer—the malting, brewing, and pouring—is generally forbidden to the Nobility, except for necessity and the maintenance of their own household. This is because it causes detriment to the cities, takes away the livelihood of the citizens, and diminishes commerce. *Berlich. decision 31. see Treutler. conference 117.* For those who desire to know more about beer and the right of brewing, see especially *Deodatus in Hygiasticon fol. 154. book 2. Bornit. in the treatise on sufficient things, treatise 2, c. 16. fol. 94. etc. Miscellaneous of Schmetius fol. 611. Coler. in his addition, chapter 10. Goldast in Aleman. vol. 1. fol. 201. The Philosophical Lexicon of Martini and Brower. book 3. chapter 12. fol. 216. Likewise Guyon on various readings, vol. 2, fol. 165. etc.*

<column-break/>

And it is considered a "great invention" <note>This likely refers to a clever but burdensome legal regulation</note> that the villages must buy their beer from the nearest cities. *See the dispute of Clessius on buying and selling.* The same could also be the case with wine.

->**ADDITION.**<-

Regarding the burden of slander: "The beer-carriers have dipped a thief's thumb into the beer." <note>An old expression for cheating or short-changing the customer.</note> *Cothman, 3. response 4. n. 56. & following.* On whether, when a house intended for brewing beer is sold, the tools such as tuns and vessels prepared and intended for that purpose are considered sold along with it: *Thesaur. in individual questions, question 84. Schepliz in the Brandenburg Customs, part 4. title 17. §. 1. n. 4. at the end.*

Gambrivius <note>A mythical Germanic king</note> is held by some to be the seventh of the German kings, and he is said to have been the first to teach the boiling of beer. *Zeiller cent. 4. qu. 45. page 238.* *Micrælius in the preface of part 2. book 3.* says the ancient Germans placed food and drink in the graves of the dead. And a few years ago, sealed glasses filled with beautiful beer—which *Tacitus* calls "a liquid from barley or grain fermented into a certain likeness of wine"—were dug out of the earth where they had been placed many years ago for the benefit of the dead. Such a glass is kept in the house of *Dr. Christopher Albinus, a physician in Stettin.*

*Among the Hebrews, if wine were lacking, they could not offer beer as a libation, because it was unsuitable for sacred use. Code Pesachim: "We had no wine, we brought beer ourselves, and he did not separate [it for sacred use], and therefore he went to sleep without dinner." fol. 107. l. D. Saubert on Sacrifices p. 671. preface.*

*Regarding copper vats made for brewing beer, it is established that if they are fixed to a wall* <gloss>walled-in</gloss>, *they belong to the successors of the fief along with the feudal land, because parts fixed to a wall are seen as members of the building. arg. l. 44. on eviction. For the Right of Brewing, the useful, confessory, and negatory legal actions apply. Hahn on the Law of Things and types of rights in property c. 56. n. 1.*

One who carries out the business of brewing and pouring must bear the tax burdens. *Mundius on offices and honors. c. 2. n. 59.* Question: Do the immediate Nobles and others, who have estates and subjects within the district of some Estate, have the faculty of brewing beer from the grain they receive from annual rents and the cultivation of the land, and thereafter selling it to their subjects and others? This is affirmed. *Extended in Herppffer. in his inaugural dispute, question 16.* In most places in Germany, we see that the **Brew-house**, as well as the **Malt-house**, **Tavern**, and **Right of Pouring** <note>The legal right to sell beer by the glass</note> are sometimes granted to nobles by investiture or privilege. *Knichén. on investiture pacts, part 2. chapter 4. num. 101.* Hence, if they not only brew beer for their own family but also sell it to others, they do no wrong to anyone while exercising their right. *Rauchbar. question 27.* Nor do they bring any stain upon their nobility. *Mynf. decade 15. response 1. q. 3. n. 77. Klock on...*

### 60. Until. <note>German: "Biß"; Latin: "Donec"</note>

The nature of the word *Usque* (until) is to denote the nature or the end of a certain thing, as Cicero taught in his speech against Verres: *Until that limit when the judges were rejected.* And Virgil in the first book of the *Georgics*:

> Even until the end of the intractable winter rain.

And the passage from Paul to the Galatians, chapter 4, corresponds here: *For as long as the heir is a little child, he is under guardians and managers until the time appointed by the Father,* because after such a constituted time, he shall not be under guardians.

The word *Usque* is sometimes placed inclusively and sometimes exclusively. <note>In legal terms, this determines whether the deadline includes the final day or stops just before it.</note> See Tiraqueau on the law of wood, section 1, glossary 11, number 66, page 136; and Cardinal Tuschus, conclusion 171, letter D; and Barbosa on the Meaning of Words under the term *Usque*.

Furthermore, the word "until"—that is, *donec* or *dum*, or *quoad*, or *quousque*—is either a limitation of time or introduces a condition. Bartolus in the law regarding servitudes; Jason in the law regarding heirs; see also the collection by Papien in the form for a wife’s dowry action: "until she has lived her life." See also Angelus and C. Hartman Pistor, *Feudal Questions*, 36, number 6; Moller, *Semestria*, book 1, chapter 42.

<column-break/>

Or it stands in a "suspensive" sense, and introduces only a temporary delay, not a perpetual hindrance. See Schæffer, *Practical Questions*, 33, throughout.

->ADDITION.<-

The words *donec* and *quousque* at least introduce a suspensive and temporary exclusion. Klock, volume 3, consultation 106, number 35.

The word *tamdiu* (so long as) is the same as *quamdiu* (as long as) or *donec* (until). Boër, decision 44, number 30. For what the words *donec*, *usque quo*, *quousque*, *tamdiu*, *quamdiu*, and *quandocunque* (whenever) signify, see Klock, volume 2, consultation 61. In 2 Samuel 6:23, it says: *Michal had no child until the day of her death*—that means: never. <note>This is a classic example of "until" meaning "never," as one cannot have children after death.</note> "You shall not come out until you have paid the last penny." This signifies that one will never leave, because one is always paying the newest farthing while suffering everlasting punishments for earthly sins. The late Mr. Dr. Dannhauer in the *Evangelical Memorial*, page 580.

*Donec* meaning "forever": Scipio Gentilis on alimony, chapter 11, page 41. Valerius Wilhelm Forster, book of various observations, chapter 11. The particle *donec* regularly excludes not forever, but temporarily and in respect to certain persons. Mr. Ludovici in his *Feudal Synopsis*. Vultejus on feuds, page 348. *Donec* is sometimes a purely negative word, not merely suspensive. Tuschus, conclusion 271. It is sometimes used figuratively as an epithet. "Joseph did not know Mary *until* she brought forth." "Noah's dove did not return *until* the waters were dried up"—here it is an "extinctive" term. On the use of this adverb, see Mr. Dr. Gerhard in the *Continuation of the Harmony of the Evangelists*.

*Donec* is not continuative where, in negative statements, it is explained as "never," according to the Rule of Glassius in his *Sacred Philology*. Instead, it should be explained as exclusive (just as in affirmative statements it means "no longer"), or "after," as if you were to say: "After the heavens are no more, man shall rise again." Mr. Dr. Dannhauer in his *Hodosophia*, page 243. On whether the word *Usque* (until) includes or excludes, see Antonius Matthæus on *Crimes*, pages 59, 207, and 712. On what *Usque* signifies, see Villalobos and Tiraqueau.

# Lit. B.

## 62. Bishop. <note>Latin: *Episcopus*; German: *Bischoff*</note>

A Bishop is interpreted as a **Watchman** or **Overseer**. <note>original Latin: *Speculator*</note>. According to the *Decretum Gratiani* (Distinctio 12, canon 1), a Bishop must supervise and correct. Pope Gelasius I, in the decrees (Causa 8, question 1, chapter *qui Episcop.*), states: "He who desires the office of Bishop, desires a good work." He wished to explain what the Episcopacy is: for it is a name of **work**, not of **honor**. It is a Greek term, derived from the fact that he who is placed in charge "super-intends" or looks over them, bearing the care of those beneath him; for *skopos* <note>Greek: σκοπὸς</note> signifies "intent" or "aim." Therefore, Bishops can be called **Superintendents** in Latin: so that he may understand he is not a Bishop if he loves to rule but not to be of use. See Reinhard König, *Politics*, part 1, chapter 35, number 7. Likewise, Rabanus Maurus in book 1 of *On the Institution of Clerics*, chapter 5: The name "Episcopacy" is used because he who is set over others "super-intends," namely by caring for his subordinates. For *skopein* <note>Greek: σκοπεῖν</note> in Latin is said to mean "to intend" or "to look at." *Episkopoi* <note>Greek: Επίσκοποι</note> in Greek is interpreted in Latin as **Watchmen** or **Superintendents**. Hesychius says: *Episkopoi* are "those hitting the mark." <note>Greek: Τυγχάνοντα τὰ σκοπᾶ</note>. Similarly, Clement in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book 2, chapter 25, says that the Bishop is the "Target" <note>original: *Scopum*</note> or focus of everyone among his people.

That term was also used by the ancients in civil matters, as seen in Plutarch’s *Life of Pericles* and Cicero’s *Letters to Atticus* (7.11). For the clarification and explanation of this passage, see Caelius Rhodiginus, book 10 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 3, who says: those whom the Athenians sent to their subject and tributary cities to observe what was happening were called **Bishops** and **Guards**. <note>original: *Phylacas*</note>. This matches the jurist Arcadius, who names those in charge of bread and other goods for sale as "Bishops" in the Digest (law 18, section 7, "likewise also Bishops"), regarding duties and honors. See also François Pollet in *History of the Roman Forum*, book 1; Tholosanus, *On the Republic*, book 15, chapter 2, number 4. Today, the name "Bishop" is understood to refer to those having **Episcopal Jurisdiction**. See Bonacina in the treatise *On Simony*, folio 84.

Regarding the election and power of Bishops, as well as their confirmation and petitioning for office, see the individual treatise by Bartolomeo Ugolini, *On the Office and Power of Bishops*; Paul Laymann, *On Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction*, chapter 4; Joachim Stephan in the treatise *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 2 and following; likewise Matthias Stephan, *Institutes of Canon Law*, book 1, chapter 3 and following, and *On Jurisdiction*, book 3, part 1, chapter 8. See also Bignon’s notes on the *Formulas of Marculf the Monk*, folio 451; Goldast, *Alamanic Works*, volume 3, folio 117; Hackelman, *Disputations on Canon Law*, 11; Mariana, *On the Institution of a King*, book 3, chapter 2; Alzedo in the treatise *On the Dignity of a Bishop*, folio 25; Lancellotti in *The Temple of All Judges*, folio 743, etc. And on the authority of Bishops, see Filefacus in various works; add the treatise *On Episcopal Synods* by Henricus de Bottis and the treatise *On Bishops* by Giovanni Bertachini. The annals of the Franks attest that they undertook nothing of greatness without the counsel and assembly of the Bishops. See Lehmann in the *Chronicle of Speyer*.

Regarding the concordats of the Bishops of Bavaria, see Hund in *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, book 1, folio 98; and on Episcopal law in Silesia, Schickfuss, *Treatise on Law*, book 3. The same author notes that in Silesia

<column-break/>

only the locals <note>German: *Incolæ*</note> are to be promoted to the Bishoprics. See Schickfuss in the *Silesian Chronicle*, book 3, chapter 6.

A record of the Bishoprics of the Christian World may be seen in the *Chronicle of Chronicles*, part 1, folio 14, and many following pages. All spiritual Prelates are subject to the Holy Roman Empire and are members of it by reason of the Empire’s **Regalia** <note>Rights and privileges belonging to the sovereign</note> and temporalities, or worldly authority. See Gail, book 1, observation 30, number 1, and *On Arrests*, book 1, chapter 1, number 12. During the times of Louis the Pious, Bishops were admitted among the **Princes of the Empire**; this was noted in the *Chronicles of the Slavs* by Helmold, and Reiner Reineccius writes in the preface to those annals that it is quite remarkable. See Mr. Gryphiander, *On the Saxon Weichbilds*, chapters 28, 29, and 31; and my own work *On Majesty*, folio 24.

There are four grades and orders of Bishops: they are either **Patriarchs**, **Archbishops**, **Metropolitans**, or **Bishops** simply so called. Tobias Paurmeister, book 2, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 8, number 2; Matthias Stephan, *On Jurisdiction*, book 3, part 1, chapter 7, number 7, who states that all are called by one and the same term, "Bishop." See Lancellotti in *The Temple of All Judges*, book 2, chapter 2, number 2. Indeed, the Pope himself is considered to be within the rank of Bishops, certainly by reason of his holy orders. Pierre Rebuffi in the treatise *On the Concordats*, under the heading "on the approval of conventions," on the word *Episcopus*.

Bishops simply and absolutely so called are also termed **Diocesans**. (For a Bishop has a **Diocese**, while a Metropolitan has a **Province**. Hence it is written: the "Diocese of Constance" and the "Province of Mainz.") They are said to preside over only one city and the villages joined to it, according to Paurmeister, chapter 8, number 3. Whence Panormitanus writes in chapter 1 of *On the Privileges and Excesses of Prelates*, number 1, that it is a received custom in Italy that a place is not considered a "city" unless it has a Bishop. And in the Code (law 36, *On Bishops and Clergy*), it is said: "Let every single city have its own Bishop." See my treatise *On the Law of Things*, folio 222; Ohm, *Disputation on Episcopal Law*, thesis 13; Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, book 2, chapter 18, folio 88; Matthias Stephan, book 3 *On Jurisdiction*, part 1, chapter 8, number 6; Lindeman in *History of Roman Law*, thesis 23.

In **Germany**, however, it is known to everyone that Bishops preside not just over one city, but even over entire Provinces. It is also well known that one Bishop has possessed multiple Bishoprics (although the constitution in the chapter *Dudum* 54, *On Elections*, is to the contrary, in which one having multiple dignities or multiple benefices is forbidden from being elected). An example of this is seen in **Cardinal Albert**, Margrave of Brandenburg, who held the vast Archdioceses of Mainz and Magdeburg together with Halberstadt at the same time, as can be seen from his signature on the Imperial Decree of Speyer in the year 1544. Likewise in **Duke Ernest of Bavaria**, who held not only Cologne and Münster, but also the Dioceses of Liège, Hil—

# Treasury of Augmented Practice
### Page 118

Hildesheim and Freising were subjected to this. Chytraeus <note>David Chytraeus (1530–1600), a Lutheran theologian and historian</note> notes this in his work *Metropolis*. And even now, Philip II, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, presides over two bishoprics: Verden and Osnabrück. König, *cited location, numbers 46 and following.*

Furthermore, according to Canon Law, a Bishop is elected by both priests and laypeople <note>original Latin: *cap. sacrorum. distinct. 36. cap. querelam de elect. Nov. 124.*</note>. However, in the Cathedral Church, this election has been transferred to the **Chapter** <note>the college of clerics who advise a bishop</note> of each diocese. This election refers only to Cathedral Churches, as the nomination of clergy to Parochial churches belongs elsewhere.

Since the Apostle’s authority in 1 Timothy 3 dictates that a Bishop must be **apt to teach, able to convict, and blameless** <note>original Greek: διδασκαλικὸν, ἐλεγκτικὸν καὶ ἀνεπίληπτον</note>, disputes often arose over electing a Bishop from the Chapter when the See became vacant. When there is doubt regarding a candidate’s quality of knowledge or character, the custom of **Postulation** was introduced in the Western Church by the Constitution of the Popes. This concept was entirely unknown to the Greek or Eastern Churches. Namely, "Postulation" occurs when the College or Chapter requests that a specific person be appointed to the Episcopal seat, or when they petition a superior Prelate, Metropolitan, or the Pope to appoint them. The person was then called a "Postulate." Thus, while an **Election** is performed by a Chapter when they choose a person fit for the Episcopacy following the Order of Canons, a **Postulation** belongs to the same Chapter when they recommend or offer a person to the Pope or superior Prelate for promotion to the episcopal office for specific just causes—usually because that person cannot be formally "elected" due to some legal impediment regarding their age, status, or condition.

A consecrated Bishop, after his **Consecration**, possesses the full power of Episcopal Right <note>Latin: *Jus Episcopale*</note> and can ordain and consecrate clerics for ministry. (Before consecration, he only exercises matters of **Jurisdiction**). For this reason, he is also called "Lord." The Greek Canons call him **worthy** or **possessing dignity** <note>original Greek: ἀξιωματικὸν; Phot. lib. 1. c. 36.</note> because he carries all dignity, and indeed the highest, within himself, as he is a pillar of the Holy Church.

Therefore, a Bishop has a **Diocese**, and within it subjects over whom he exercises episcopal right. In this diocese, the Bishop exercises two types of law: **Diocesan Law** <note>Latin: *Lex Dioecesana*</note> and **Jurisdictional Law** <note>Latin: *Lex Jurisdictionalis*</note>. Thus, he exercises voluntary and contentious jurisdiction <note>"Contentious" jurisdiction refers to presiding over legal disputes between parties, while "voluntary" refers to administrative acts like granting permissions</note> over all clerics in this diocese, in civil and criminal as well as spiritual matters. To ensure this exercise remains perpetual and firm, Gregory IX extended this so that clerics cannot move their cases to a secular court without the Bishop's consent.

Similarly, laypeople who live within the Bishop’s diocese are subject to him regarding ecclesiastical censure and other spiritual matters.

<column-break/>

It must be observed, however, that there are two types of Diocese: One exists within the lands of the Church, or within royal ecclesiastical fiefs. In this type of diocese, the Bishop exercises all jurisdiction—contentious and voluntary—in temporal matters (that is, civil and criminal) as well as the spiritual cases of both clerics and laypeople. He holds both clerics and laypeople bound to obedience to him by the right of homage, through an oath of fidelity and subjection.

The other type of diocese exists within the lands of the **Empire**, or the lands of temporal lords. In these lands, although the Bishop does not have dominion or jurisdiction in temporal cases and secular affairs (because jurisdiction over those matters remains with the Lords of the territories), he nevertheless exercises **Diocesan Law** and spiritual jurisdiction over the clerics and laypeople inhabiting those Imperial lands. He also holds and exercises spiritual jurisdiction over sacred, blessed, and religious objects within those Imperial lands. Furthermore, in the temporal and spiritual cases of clerics living and performing the Liturgy in Imperial lands, and in the spiritual cases of laypeople living there, the Bishop exercises not only voluntary but also contentious jurisdiction of Diocesan Law. Thus, the Lords of Imperial lands are excluded from ecclesiastical jurisdiction and Episcopal Right. Hence, Episcopal Right is called **Pastoral Power**, and it contains three elements: **Order**, **Diocesan Law**, and **Jurisdictional Law**.

The first, **Episcopal Right**, consists in **Order**, which is the act of consecration. By this act, through a solemn ritual, certain persons become Clerics and are dedicated to Divine worship. This act impresses a perpetual—or as others call it, **indelible**—character upon the person. This means that those who are received or ordained into the state of the clergy always retain the character once impressed upon them. From this Right of Order also comes the power of **Blessing**, both of persons and things, such as the consecration of Virgins, Temples, Altars, and similar things.

The second, **Episcopal Right**, consists in **Diocesan Law**, which the Bishop exercises in his diocese by the Right of an **Ordinary Judge**. For a Bishop has "ordinary jurisdiction," which he exercises by his own right among his diocesan subjects. Diocesan Law is therefore the right and power of the Bishop to demand in his diocese: ecclesiastical procurement <note>the provision of food and lodging during an official visit</note> or the costs of visitation; the payment of the **Cathedraticum** <note>a small annual fee paid by churches to the bishop as a sign of subjection</note>; the **Synodaticum** <note>payment for the holding of a synod</note>; charitable aid; a fourth part of funeral fees; and taxes and tithes, both regarding persons and property.

The third, **Episcopal Right**, is **Jurisdictional Law**, which is the power of judging controversies...

### 63. Letters of Request.
**Letters of mutual assistance.** <note>original: "Bitt- und Ersuchungs-Brief. Litteræ mutui compassus."</note>

Where it is said that a Judge himself ought to execute his own sentence (Mynfing. *3, Observation 68*), it must be understood to apply if the condemned person is property-owning within his own territory or district. For if the defeated party has no goods there, but the property in which execution must be made is situated in another jurisdiction or territory, in that case the Judge of the sentence requests the other Judge—under whose jurisdiction the defeated party possesses his goods—through subsidiary or rogatory letters, or even **letters of mutual assistance** <note>original: "mutui compassus, durch Bitt- und Ersuchungs-Brief"</note>, so that what he condemned the defeated party to in words, the other may truly and naturally grant to the victor (Mynfing. *cited Observation 68*; Matth. Stephani in *Treatise on the Office of a Judge, book 6, chapter 8, number 4*). For one Judge ought to support and provide aid to another; however, one cannot execute the sentence of another Judge without being requested without it being a nullity, because no one ought to involve themselves in another's process unless requested (Mynfing. *said observation*).

Indeed, a Judge requested by another for execution is altogether bound to carry out the execution upon the goods subject to his jurisdiction, whether he be superior, inferior, or even an equal. For in this situation, respect is held for the prior Judge, who is considered superior regarding that specific case in which he gave judgment, lest the sentence or the decided matter be in vain (following Bartolus; Stephan. *cited location, number 6*). And if the requested Judge refuses to carry out the execution, if he has a superior, he can be compelled to the execution by him (Gail. *1, Observation 113, number 15 and following*). Thus, today Compulsory and Executorial Mandates, including the insertion of a penalty, are usually decreed in the Chamber <note>term: The Imperial Chamber Court (Reichskammergericht) - the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note>; if the requested Judge should despise such a mandate, he is condemned to a penalty, and a stricter Mandate under penalty of the ban <note>term: Imperial Ban (Reichsacht) - a form of outlawry in the Holy Roman Empire</note> can be obtained (Gail. *said location and observation 115*).
