### 76. Making Bridges and Footpaths. The Repair of Bridges and Roads.

This falls under the permission of the Emperor, as is clear from the tenor of the following Privilege.

We, Sigismund, by the Grace of God, Roman King, <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg (reigned 1433–1437) was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Hungary and Bohemia.</note> at all times Increaser of the Empire, and King of Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, etc. We acknowledge and make known publicly with this letter to all those who see it or hear it read, that there have come before us Utel Ulrich Crafft and Hans "the Lions," brothers from Ulm, Our and the Empire’s dear faithful subjects. They have humbly petitioned Us that We might grant them the grace to be allowed to build a footbridge over the Danube at Rieden—which belongs to them, and where they own both banks—so that they may drive their swine across it and also for other necessities; and also that they,

<column-break/>

and their heirs, there at Rieden, where the local jurisdiction and authority <note>original: "Zwinge und Banne"</note> are theirs, may establish and grant a "half and whole court" <note>term: half and whole court (halb und gantz Gericht) - different levels of judicial authority, likely referring to low jurisdiction (minor civil/criminal cases) and high jurisdiction (capital crimes)</note>, as they may best manage with judges, where one may judge matters concerning property, outrages, immorality, and debts, and also other such honest matters, through special grace, graciously judging in the same manner as it is customary to judge at Erbach.

Now, since Our Royal innate goodness always shows itself mercifully to all those who call upon it for grace, and namely to those who have proven and continue to prove themselves with their services and total loyalty, firmly and serviceably, in Our and the Empire’s service. And since We have good confidence in the aforementioned Utel Ulrich Crafft and Hans the Lions, brothers, that they are faithful and serviceable to Us and the Empire, therefore, with well-considered mind, good counsel, and the true knowledge of Our and the Empire’s nobles and faithful subjects, We grant the aforementioned Utel Ulrich Crafft and Hans the Lions, brothers, this grace. We permit and allow them, by Roman Royal power, to strike and make a footbridge over the Danube at Rieden, where both banks are theirs, to drive their swine across and to conduct their other business, according to their best judgment. Additionally, by special grace and by that same Roman Royal power, by virtue of this letter, We give and permit the same Utel Ulrich Crafft and Hans the Lions, brothers, and their heirs, that they may have and establish a half or whole court there in Rieden—however they can best manage with judges who are blameless people—to judge property, outrages, immorality, and debts, and also other such matters. There they may judge, and use, and enjoy the freedoms, graces, rights, customs, and traditions, in every way as the court at Erbach has and uses them. However, regarding any matter on which a verdict is given that they in Rieden cannot determine or recognize, they shall then take the judgment from Erbach for such matters. This grace shall be without prejudice to anyone else's rights. We therefore command all and every Prince, spiritual and secular, Counts, Freemen, Lords, Knights, Squires, Cities, Burgomasters, Officials, and Communities, and also every Land-Judge, judge, verdict-speaker, and all others of Our and the Empire’s subjects and faithful, seriously and firmly with this letter, that they do not hinder the aforementioned Utel Ulrich Crafft and Hans the Lions, brothers, and their heirs, in such Our graces and freedoms, nor speak against them, but rather they...

## 77. Brotherhood. <note>original: "Brüderschafft."</note> Confraternity.

Fellowships, societies, confraternities, which

<column-break/>

were customarily assembled for Divine worship and alms in churches: so that they might pray for one another and hold requiem masses for each other's souls. This practice has a very ancient origin, see Cuspinian *on Monks, f. 169* and Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 1, folio 241.*
Fellowships <note>original: "Fratriæ"</note> are described by Aristotle in the *Politics* as assemblies of men having their own sacred rites and peculiarities; for these men used a common well, which in Greek is called <term>phréar</term> <note>original: "φρέαρ" — meaning a well or cistern; the root for the concept of neighbors or "well-sharers."</note>. In Tertullian, it is commonly accepted for the Colleges of Christians. Tertullian, *book on veiling virgins* and *book to the martyrs.*
Sometimes, however, a Fellowship is used for a conspiracy and a malicious, factious society; as in the *Council of Chalcedon, canon 18.*
Sworn fraternities are proven to be valid by Alexander in *if a father, number 3. Code on the institution of heirs. Tesfaur decision 113.* And they are regarded as a kind of "adoption" that is valid for many things.
Thus it is also a valid agreement by which some promise to treat one another as brothers. Marta, *part 1, clause 185.*

### ADDITION.

Fellowships permitted and approved in religion do not constitute a <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office that provides an income.</note>; therefore, priests of any confraternity or other brothers cannot exchange places; nor can the Bishop demand Episcopal rights from confraternities as if from benefices. Petrus Gregorius in *Syntagma, book 15, chapter 32, n. 12.* How fellowships in France may possess fiefs. *the same, 6. 13. 9.*
He calls you Brother, and she is called Sister. Plautus. See also Lipsius in *Antiquities 3, on the titles of Brother and Sister.* Also that Arabic proverb: *Perhaps he is your brother, but one whom your mother did not bear.* Erpenius, *century 2, proverb 82.* The cause of this proverb was added by the Arabic interpreter in the same place; that one day a certain man saw a man withdrawn with a woman and said to that woman: "Who is he?" She replied: "My brother." He said, "Perhaps he is your brother, but one whom your mother did not bear." And it became a proverb. Rupertus in the *Epistolary Mercury, page 660.*

If someone is present at a fire, and his shoes catch fire or begin to burn, in certain places he is held to be the perpetrator, and this is considered evidence (*pro indicio*)—provided other circumstances align—to justify the use of torture: and I know this was done in a specific case at Oggeltshausen. This phenomenon is treated much like the bleeding of a corpse <note>original: "cruentatio cadaveris" — a medieval legal belief that a murder victim’s wounds would begin to bleed if the killer approached the body.</note>, etc.

See the same work, part 3, chapter 2, number 27 and following. When a fire starts during brewing, must the brewer compensate the neighbors for damages? See the same work, part 2, chapter 3, number 20.

Regarding burned-down houses, the question is asked: if someone has given a house to another person on the condition that they provide him with food and support, can that person still claim maintenance after the house has been burned down by a chance accident? Sebastian de Medicis responds in the affirmative in *On Fortuitous Cases*, part 2, question 7, number 17, citing the text in the law *Necessario*, Digest on the risk and convenience of the thing sold. However, where a burned house was promised, the transaction is considered void: see law 57 on *Contracting a Sale*, and law 1, section 5, Digest on *Obligations and Actions*.

No one can be compelled to extinguish a fire for free: see Matthias Stephan on *Jurisdiction*, book 1, chapter 14, number 73. When it is doubted whose fault caused the fire to break out, one resorts to conjectures: see Thomas Metzger, *Criminal Counsels* 11, number 3. Whether a neighbor may demolish a neighbor's house for the protection of his own house: see *Decisions of Vivius*, 150. Regarding whether compensation should be paid for damage given by fire or not: see *Counsels of Menochius* 54, and *Altdorf Counsels* 96 and 116. On several fires in Constantinople, and how they are handled there: see Schweigger in his *Travel Book*, page 92.

### 79. Guns. Artillery. <note>original: "Büchsen. Bombarda." — referring to early firearms and cannons.</note>

On the invention of cannons, etc., see my own work in *Singular Discourses*, and Camerarius in *Leisure Hours*, century 3, chapter 82 and following. Also Magius, *Miscellanies* 1, chapter 1; Felix Fabri in his *Description of Swabia*, folio 70; Johann de Beka in his *Chronicle*, folio 95, on ancient instruments of war; Fauchet, book 2, *On Knights*; also on the utility of cannons, see Meillet’s notes on Tacitus, folio 702.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

Chronologists place the invention of cannons in the year of Christ 1380, under the reign of Emperor Wenceslaus. There are various species: siege cannons, the "Nightingale," the "Sharp-falconet," culverins, small falconets, field culverins, the "Singer," mortars, "Sharp-bitches" <note>original: "Scharffmetzen" — a type of heavy mortar.</note>, the "Basilisk," and petards. See Schönborn in *Politics*, book 6, chapter 9, throughout.

The inventor of artillery—or the art of guns and cannons—is said to be Berthold Schwarz <note>A legendary German friar often credited with inventing gunpowder and cannons in Europe.</note>, a monk and chemist. See Philippus Camerarius, *Leisure Hours*, century 2, chapter 28, and century 3, chapter 82; Abraham Bucholcer in *Chronological Index* for the year 1380; Seth Calvisius in his *Chronicle* for the year 1342. However, a Spanish historian, Juan de Mariana, in *On the Affairs of Spain*, book 17, chapter 14, reports—no doubt out of envy and ill-will toward the Germans—that they were invented in Lombardy and first used by the Moors in the defense of their city, Algiers, when it was besieged by Christians. (Mariana, book 16, chapter 11). On the other hand, others write that an obscure German, whose name rightly remains unknown because of this godless invention—as Polydore Vergil wishes in *On the Discovery of Things*, book 2, chapter 11—offered this art to the Venetians, who first used guns in the year after Christ’s birth 1380 against the Genoese. See Battista Fregoso, *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*, book 2, chapter 1, under the title "On the first engine of war, which they call a Bombard." See also Polydore Vergil in the same place; compare Johannes Cluver in *Epitome of History* under Emperor Wenceslaus, who dates the invention to 1378. Besold, in *Politics*, book 2, chapter 7, number 13, doubts whether Berthold the Black <note>Berthold "Schwarz" (Black) was so named either for his dark hair or his "black" alchemical arts.</note> actually invented it.

In the armory at Strasbourg in 1649, they showed me the "Pipe-ape" and its mate, the "Twelve Apostles," the "Twelve Heavenly Signs," very large culverins of eighteen feet, and the famous "Mouse-lurer" <note>original: "Maissenlocker" — a legendary massive cannon in the Strasbourg collection.</note>. There are also said to be old wooden pieces there which fire twelve-pound balls and yet still have quite fresh wood. However, according to some reports, they are reinforced with iron on the inside. At the castle in Wolfenbüttel, there is a piece 36 feet long weighing 170 hundredweight, for which 2,299 pieces of iron were forged; it shoots a 100-pound ball, and the cost for the iron and the maker's wages was 1,826 Thalers and 30 Groschen. There are machines which our people call "Storm-gear" <note>original: "Sturmzeug"</note>, but later Latin writers called them *Ingenia* <note>Devices or engines.</note>, and their architects "Engineers" <term>Ingeniarios</term>, naturally from the *ingenium* (ingenuity) that goes into building or moving them. See Lipsius, book 1, *On Siege Engines*, dialogue 1. Thus far Virdungus. Gianello Torriani of Cremona published a distinguished work on machines. Michelangelo, the Roman architect, brought to light a most perfect machine for lifting heavy loads, by whose labor a thousand...

### 81. Love Letter. *Literæ amatoriæ.*

Love letters between lovers prove that a marriage is to be contracted, but not that one has already been contracted, as Franciscus Vivius testifies, decision 241, number 10, page 2.
However, if such love letters, sent by a man to another's wife and written to her, are seen and found in the woman's possession and recognized, do they prove adultery—at least for the purpose of inflicting torture? My teacher, Lord Doctor Bocerus, denies this in Besoldus, Volume I,

<column-break/>

Treatise *On Torture*, chapter 3, number 113.
But Borellus writes regarding this matter in his *Summary of Decisions*, folio 2, title 23, at the end of folio 171: similar letters are sometimes sent to women by those who hate the husband and the like, in order to bring a mark of infamy upon them. I know of a case where a husband found such letters in a woman's pocket <note>original: "posca" — likely a pocket or small bag.</note>, and she, to excuse herself, told the husband that she had indeed received the letters with a heavy heart and kept them only to reveal the sender's wicked intent to him, and had hidden them in her ambiguous silence only to avoid leading her husband into the danger and risk of seeking revenge; the husband believed these things, but many homicides and the destruction of houses and families followed. But God knows how much wicked women can bring about. If this woman were truly free from adultery and did not consent to the solicitor, she could have kept herself at home and committed the letters to the flames, thus preserving her innocence. Therefore, to have kept so many letters seems to have been done out of love for the sender; but nevertheless, so that she herself might avoid death, she brought death upon her lover, and thus love was turned into hatred.

### ADDITION.

Whether love letters sent to a woman are evidence of adultery or debauchery: see Bocer on *Questions and Tortures*, page 271, number 113; Paris, counsel 54, number 64, volume 4; Mascardus *On Evidence*, volume 1, conclusion 64, number 10; Menochius, book 5, presumption 41, final number; Zanger *On Questions*, chapter 2, number 76. If anyone uses love letters or small gifts to assault the chastity of his lord’s wife, the vassal is deprived of his fief. Bocer, class 4, disputation 17, thesis 44. Wooing <term>Beischafft</term>, that is, a matrimonial provocation, is usually a preamble to a matrimonial contract. If someone promises a "matrimonial wooing," and if such a marriage was promised, whether this obliges one to a true marriage: Uranius, counsel 24, decides that words expressing consent to a matrimonial wooing do not bring about the arrangement of a marriage contract. Schottelius in *The German Main Language*, folio 380.

### 82. Fine. See below under the words "Trespass" and "Amends."

The word "fine" <term>büssen</term> is generally understood as an amendment or a pecuniary penalty: to be paid both to the injured party and to the treasury <term>Fiscus</term>, although sometimes it is strictly understood as a penalty to be paid only to the treasury: "Trespass and Fines" <note>original: "Frevel und Büssen"</note>. If it is a simple amendment, it usually refers to the lower jurisdiction. If, however, the fine is large, and of the nature of a penalty that brings about the loss of property, it is numbered among the Sovereign Rights <term>Regalibus</term> in chapter 1, *Which things are regalia*: because it is owed to the treasury and holds the right of the treasury for it; and thus "fining" is sometimes considered among the rights of superiority. And so by this word something is indicated that pertains both to high and low justice <note>original: "meri, quàm mixti Imperii"</note>, and which is as much a Sovereign Right as not, and sometimes regards superiority. See Gœd-

### 83. Bull, Golden Bull. Bulla.

The name "Bulls" is given to letters issued by Emperors, Kings, and great Princes. They take their name from the "Golden Bull" <note>A lead or gold seal used to authenticate important documents</note> which, for the sake of greater dignity and authority, is usually appended. Among the Greeks, this is called a <term>chrysobull</term> <note>original: "χρυσοβέλιον" — literally "golden seal," though the author notes a slight linguistic variation</note>. Luitprand, Bishop of Cremona, in the history of his embassy to Nicephorus Phocas, the Byzantine Emperor, calls it a *chrysobull*, interpreting it as a letter written in gold. This honor was granted to Henry of Brunswick so that he might obtain a Golden Bull, since Nicephorus did not wish to dignify the Roman Pope of his time with that honor; the Emperor judged it sufficient if he sent him letters signed in silver, 

<column-break/>

as the same Luitprand notes. Furthermore, the images of the Caesars were impressed upon the Bulls, even among the Romans. Hence, diplomas are closed with this formula: *For the memory of this matter, and for strength that shall prevail forever, we have ordered this present privilege to be made and to be secured by the Golden Bull, impressed with the stamp of our Majesty.* See Cuspinian in *Austria*, and Knich in *Epops*, regarding the diplomas of Emperor Frederick II, and Meibom on the Golden Bull of Andronicus, folio 14. And regarding the Golden Bull <term>and how it is constituted</term> <note>original: "und wie selbige beschaffen"</note>, many authors discuss it: Coler, *Parerga*, chapter 4; Jacob Pontanus, volume 3 of *Bellaria*, folio 71; Freher on Peter von Andlo, book 2, chapter 5, folio 170; likewise Perionius, *On the Magistrates of the Greeks*, book 1, folio 312, where he discusses the "golden bull" worn by boys among the Romans <note>An ancient Roman amulet worn by children, distinct from the medieval legal seal</note>. Regarding the Golden Bull of Emperor Alexios, see Cardinal Baronius at the end of the year of Christ 1082. The author of *The Mystery of Iniquity*, Plessis, folio 329, attests that Adrian first taught the use of lead in sealing; add also Sethus Calvisius, for the year of Christ 752. Are all the things enacted by the Golden Bull of Charles IV observed today? See Freher’s treatise *On Electoral Guardianship*.

But properly, a *bella* <note>The author uses a variation of *bulla*</note> is a seal; an *abellum* is that which has no seal; see the *Notes on Sidonius Apollinaris*, folio 113. From this come "Bulled Doctors" <note>original: "Bullati Doctores" — those who received their doctorate by a papal or imperial bull/decree rather than through academic examination</note>, who are created by diplomas, not by examination. *Bullare* means to seal or to sign. Marquard Freher on Peter von Andlo, book 2, chapter 7, folio 170; see the barbarian terms in Cantimpré. Add Arumaeus on the Golden Bull, discourse 1, thesis 1. A Golden Bull is a golden seal, usually appended to serious matters and fundamental laws. Thus is the Golden Bull of Charles IV. On this matter, the most learned Meursius in his *Lexicon of Barbarian Greek* at the word *Chrysobullon* says: they were fourfold—Gold, Silver, Wax, and Lead. See Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 3, throughout. The Emperor used all of these; the Patriarchs, however, used only green wax or sometimes lead. The Emperor used gold for constitutions and commands sent to Kings, Sultans, and Governors; see also my own work, *On Elections and Successions*, folio 182.

### 86. Burgau, Margraviate. *Marchionatus Burgoviae.*

This is an ancient patrimony of the Archdukes of Austria. For in the wars which occurred between Louis IV <note>Ludwig the Bavarian (1282–1347), Holy Roman Emperor.</note> and Frederick, Archduke of Austria, in the year 1324, King Louis surrounded the Fortress of Burgau with a harsh siege, which Burkhard Herlbach defended fiercely with his two sons and three hundred knights until the Archdukes Leopold and Albert brought aid to the besieged. Gerhard de Roo, *Austrian History*, book 3, folio 94. And de Roo confirms this same thing where he lists the domains of the illustrious House of Austria, writing thus of the Margraviate of Burgau:
> For more than two hundred years,
> A noble race of Counts cultivated the lands of Burgau.
> When pale death took them (since death dissolves all things),
> The land became subject to the Austrians.
    Lazius also mentions the Margraves of Burgau in *On the Migration of Nations*, book 8, who should certainly be consulted about them. And Bruschius, in *On Monasteries*, records that the last Margrave of Burgau, Henry, died around the year 1282 and was buried in the Wettenhausen Monastery.
    Münster also, in book 3, chapter 279, <gloss>attests that the Margraves of Burgau were in former times a princely lineage, and also that such a Margraviate is 8 miles long and wide.</gloss>
    This Margraviate is called "preeminently" <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν" (kat' exochēn)</note> a Margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire, as is Antwerp. Limn., volume 1, additions to book 4, chapter 4, page 403. Thus the Emperor Maximilian I, in the constitution *On the Privilege of Poets* from the year 1501, in Mr. Goldast's volume 3 of *Constitutions*, folio 482, calls himself the Margrave of the Empire at the Enns and of Burgau; and Goldast notes there in the margin that the Margraviate of Antwerp is called so, but he rather understands it as "the land above the Enns" <note>original: "das Land ob der Enß" — essentially Upper Austria.</note>, which was also a Margraviate.
    Elsewhere, the same Maximilian I, in the *Reformation of the Westphalian Court* from the year 1495, in Goldast, *Constitutions*, volume 2, folio 112, calls himself the Margrave of the Empire and of Burgau.
    In certain diplomas of Charles V, that Emperor calls himself <gloss>Margrave of Burgau, of Oristain, of Gostein, and of the Holy Roman Empire;</gloss> which is to be understood as the Margraviate of Antwerp, as appears <gloss>from the Treaty of the Burgundian Inherited Lands, 1541.</gloss>

Page 131

On the privileges of Doctors, page 47. We know that the Golden Bull of Charles IV, written in the Latin language, is preserved in its original form in Imperial Frankfurt am Main, in the court they call the "Roman Court." It is a quarto-sized manuscript book on parchment, displaying a catalog of sanctions and chapter headings before the main text; it clearly indicates its great age. The Bull itself is made of solid gold, slightly exceeding the size of an Imperial Thaler <note>A large silver coin used throughout the Holy Roman Empire; the "Bull" refers to the seal itself</note>. See more in Höpingk, *On Seals*, page 61. The Golden Bull was a distinguished mark of Patricians and Nobles. See Draco, *On Patricians*, pages 74 and 121.

Can the Golden Bull of Charles IV be repealed? Emperor Charles IV himself intended it to last forever in chapter 1, stating: **we recognize and establish with this Imperial command** <note>original: "wir erkennen und setzen mit diesem Kayserlichen Gebot"</note>, **which shall last eternally.** In chapter 7: **now and for all future times.** In chapter 8: **which shall have force eternally.** In chapter 9, at the beginning: **to be held eternally.** Limnaeus, in his preliminary observations on the Golden Bull, note 8, page 23, goes so far as to say that not even the Emperor himself has the power to repeal it, as he is bound by oath to its observance in the Imperial Capitulation <note>The contract between the Emperor-elect and the Prince-Electors</note>, title 4, section 9, number 2. This is true unless the Electors and the other estates of the Empire consent to its repeal or change for the state and utility of the Republic, as per chapter 12, section 2 of this Golden Bull, where it says: **it shall last at our and their pleasure** <note>original: "auf unser und ihr Wohlgefallen währen soll"</note>. From this, many acts can be upheld—at least by the silent consent of the Arch-Prince Electors and the Estates of the Empire—which were carried out against this sanction and introduced through contrary observance and custom. A very long series of these is recounted by Limnaeus in book 1 of *Public Law*, chapter 11, numbers 101 and 120 and following (where he makes this a two-part question: Has the Golden Bull been continuously observed in all things? and, Can it be changed?). See also Carpzovius, *On the German Royal Laws*, chapter 3, section 3, number 9, and chapter 5, section 8, number 37; and Johann Wurmser, *Exercises in Public Law*, 1, question 6, page 11. More can be found in Stirnius in his treatise *On the Constitutions of Princes*, title 11, section 14, page 322. Regarding the Golden Bull of Sigismund, see the same work, title 12, section 2. Limnaeus recounts the praises and defects of the Golden Bull in his preliminary observations, note 7, page 22; add book 1 of *Public Law*, chapter 11, numbers 98 and 99.

On this word, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 11. Otto in *Public Law*, page 454 and following. The Golden Bull was made at Nuremberg by Charles IV in the year 1356. Carpzovius wrote *Illustrious Questions on the Golden Bull*, feudal dispute 6, question 2.

### 85. Alliances. Treaties.

Regarding treaties and the law of treaties—**on alliances and leagues in times of war** <note>original: "von Bündnuß und Ligen in Kriegszeiten"</note>—**Johann Wilhelm Neumair von Ramsla** has written an elegant and complete treatise. Likewise, Waremund von Erenberg. My own treatise on this specific matter can be added; much regarding treaties is also found throughout Werdenhagen’s *On the Hanseatic Republics*, part 2. See also Menochius, *Counsel* 337, and Calder’s *Discourse* 14.

How an Alliance <note>Latin: *foedus*</note> differs from a League <note>Latin: *liga*</note>, see the *Composition of Peace* in the preface, b. 3.

Every alliance has a sweet beginning, but usually results in a bitter end. It may last for a time as long as it is profitable to us, but when it begins to be a burden, then even a small cause can arise to overturn the letters and seals, the words and obligations; and so it turns to our detriment where we hoped for profit.

A foreign Prince who helps neighbors whose safety is despaired of does the same as a physician called to a dying man: by sustaining his life with restoratives, he merely prolongs his pains.

On the rituals of treaties and the evasion of oaths, see Camerarius, *Historical Meditations*, century 2, chapter 77 and following.

Can the Estates of the Empire enter into alliances? See Arumaeus, *On the Imperial Diets*, chapter 1, number 2, etc. Also, may a Prince **form a league with his subjects? As Charles V did during the Smalkaldic War? As Henry III did in France, and others?** <note>referencing internal alliances against religious or political factions</note> Aubigne resolves this in his *History*, book 1, chapter 4, section 5. Does a vassal who offends his Lord’s ally lose his fief? See Jacobinus de Sancto Georgio *On Fiefs*, page 313. **When do alliances constitute a felony?** <note>original: "Wann die Bündnüſſen ein Feloni machen?"</note> See the *Waldeck Defense of Honor* <note>original: "Waldeckische Ehrenrettung"</note> part 2, chapter 29.

Finally, is it permitted for Catholics to enter into an alliance with Calvinists and Turks? See the opinion of the Cardinals, Archbishops, etc., regarding certain famous pamphlets. See Rigaltius *On Leagues*, and Mattheacius, page 128.

## ADDITION.

In the year 1247, nearly seventy cities entered into certain alliances with the Count of Holland and other Princes and Counts of the Empire for the preservation of public tranquility and justice. Daniel Heider in his *Apology*, chapter 2, page 151. Nicolaus Myler von Ehrenbach in *Archaeology of the Imperial Orders*, chapter 22, number 8.

Regarding the Law of Treaties belonging to the Princes and Estates of the Empire, see Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and Estates of the Empire*, chapter 17, throughout. Certain Estates of the Empire act considerately when they report the causes, scope, and end of alliances (which are permitted in themselves) to the Emperor and seek his confirmation; both to avoid any sinister suspicion and so that what is valid in itself may acquire more strength. Ibid, pages 156, 157. The Estates may also legally enter into treaties with foreigners that do not disturb the affairs and peace of the Empire. Limnaeus, volume 2.

<meta>This page continues the legal and historical survey of the Swabian territories and transitions into a detailed examination of the laws governing guarantors and debt security. Felix Fabri, in the *History of the Swabians*, book 2, chapter 5 (who flourished at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Maximilian I), writes that near Ulm is the noble Marquisate of Burgau, belonging to the House of Austria, in which the citizens of Ulm hold significant camps and villages. Likewise, in chapter 4, he writes: In former years, while the Lordship of Hochberg—<term>the Lordship of Hohenberg</term> <note>original: "die Herrschafft Hohenberg"</note>—was still under the power of the people of Ulm, the Duke of Austria offered them the entire Marquisate of Burgau in exchange for it, which borders the lands of Ulm without any intermediary. But when the people of Ulm refused to make the exchange, the Duke of Austria nevertheless took back the Lordship of Hochberg, paying the Ulm citizens very little, and afterwards pledged the Marquisate of Burgau to the Duke of Bavaria; thus, the people of Ulm now feel their neighbors are their enemies.

From all of this, it appears that this Marquisate is an ancient patrimony of the Austrians.

And although one can hardly guess why Burgau was distinguished with the title of Marquisate, since it was never a borderland <note>original: "limes" — a fortified frontier zone</note> of the Germanic Empire; nevertheless, it should be known that several dominions were distinguished by the title of Marquisate without any regard for borders: as I have already pointed out in my *Dissertation on Counts, number 10.* Or perhaps this was a very ancient Marquisate and a border of the Roman Empire near the Danube. For this reason also, as I have already said, it seems to be called <note>original: "κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν" — Greek for "preeminently" or "by excellence"</note> the "Marquisate of the Empire": just as the Marquisate of Antwerp holds the same honor, namely that it is called the Marquisate of the Empire, which is likewise very ancient and was established against the Danes long before the age of Charlemagne. *Carol Scribanius in Origins of Antwerp, chapter 6.*

### 87. Guarantors. (Fidejussor).

To act as a guarantor <note>original: "Fidejubere"</note> is nothing other than <term>to speak for someone’s credit</term> <note>original: "für einen gutsagen"</note>, to order that something be done upon one's own faith. Thus I consider guarantors to be <term>those who speak for another, promise to make something good, or give their word</term> <note>original: "die für einen gutsprechen, versprechen etwas gut zu machen, die Paroles geben"</note>. *See Hering in the singular treatise on guarantors, chapter 1, section on the word Expromissor.* These words are considered to have the same effect: <term>he shall lose nothing</term> <note>original: "er soll nichts verlieren"</note>. *Paul Christinaeus, Belgian Decisions, vol. 1, decision 111.*

Those words: <term>He shall provide a guarantor, or become a guarantor himself</term> <note>original: "Er solle einen Bürgen stellen, oder selbst Bürg werden"</note>, are found in the *Statutes of Lübeck, book 3, title 1, article 1* in these words: <term>When a complaint is made and proven among citizens and inhabitants regarding borrowed money or a liquidated debt, the defendant shall first be given a period of fourteen days or eight days for payment: If he does not pay then, he must provide guarantors by daylight, or become a guarantor himself.</term> And again in *book 4, title 16, article 4* in these words: <term>If he can have no guarantors, he must become a guarantor himself.</term> For that last part is to be understood not as a provision of a financial guarantee, but as bodily detention,

<column-break/>

or the personal arrest of the debtor: which is necessary so that he may think more maturely about payment. *Mr. Anton Hering, Treatise on Guarantors, chapter 11, number 22.*

The words: <term>that he would allow himself to be persuaded or used as a guarantor</term> <note>original: "daß er sich zu einem Bürgen vermögen oder brauchen lassen wolle"</note>, denote a negotiation rather than a completed contract. *See Pistor, observation 173, number 56 and the following, as well as the additions there.*

The effect of those words, which are often added to guarantee instruments as a clause, is debated: <term>We guarantors wish to be in the wrong, but they, the creditors, shall be simply and alone in the right?</term> <note>original: "Wir Bürgen wollen unrecht, sie aber die Gläubiger sollen schlecht und allein recht haben?"</note> There are those who say it is equivalent to the clause: "We renounce all rights and the help of the laws": regarding which see *Hering on Guarantors, chapter 17, number 34 and following.* But it seemed to others that this clause, as something unusual and ambiguous—indeed, a fuel for many quarrels—should deservedly be banished from the court. For as it is ambiguous and doubtful, it also silently opens a window for fraud and deceit, no less than that other clause:
> <term>This writing shall also be interpreted to the disadvantage of our creditors by no one, whatever guarantor he may be; rather, as the creditor himself, or the holder of the letter with his good provable will, shall interpret, explain, and declare it in all its articles, points, and clauses, to that we shall and will give full satisfaction.</term>
*Hering in the cited place, number 27.* See however *Peter Friederich on Mandates, book 2, chapter 71, numbers 4 and 13; Thoming, Leipzig Decisions, 37, throughout the discourse.*

And it is singularly to be noted that a guarantor of indemnity (who is commonly called a <term>harmlessness-guarantor</term> <note>original: "Schadloß Bürge" — a guarantor who only pays after the primary debtor has been fully pursued</note>), even if he has renounced all help of the laws and rights acting in his favor, still possesses the "benefit of excussion" <note>The right to demand that the creditor first seize the assets of the primary debtor before coming to the guarantor</note>, according to the teachings of *Hering, chapter 27.*

Everything that can be said concerning guarantors has been collected by *Mr. Anton Hering and Valentin Francus in the treatise specifically written on this matter.* Add also *Mr. Wilhelm Anton von Quinquenell, chapter 49, number 38 and following.*

### ADDITION.

<term>Guarantors should be squeezed.</term> <note>original: "Bürgen soll man würgen" — a grim legal proverb suggesting that those who stand as surety often end up being choked by the debt.</note> *Zorer, part 1, question 12, number 918.* Finding a guarantor is not easy for everyone. *Barbosa, book 6, chapter 14, axiom 3.* Standing as a guarantor is regarded as equivalent to payment. *axiom 2.* <term>Much borrowing and lending is a poisoning of your inheritance, and has a stepmother named "sell your goods": she gives birth to a daughter named "sell them cheap": this same daughter has a brother named "out the gate."</term> <note>A metaphorical warning against the cycle of debt leading to poverty and exile.</note> *Hering on Guarantors, chapter 15, number 13.* Today, cautious creditors, as noted by *Treutler, vol. 2, Disputation 28, last thesis, letter G*, usually add a peculiar clause to avoid idle disputes, by which they make the guarantor promise: <term>That he does not wish to be free of the guarantee until the letter and seal are redeemed through honorable payment.</term> And Gomez strongly approves of this opinion.

The city of **Strasbourg** <note>original: "Argentinensis"</note> against the Knights of Alsace in the year 1422 entered into an alliance with the Senate of the Republic of **Basel**, and with **Freiburg**, **Colmar**, **Neuburg**, **Sélestat**, and several other cities for a period of five years; the articles of this alliance were handed down by Herzog in the *Chronicle of Alsace*, book 2, chapter 97. Among the ancients, there were two especially distinguished symbols of alliance and friendship: namely **Bread** and **Salt**, by the use and eating of which they were accustomed to confirm treaties; one serves as nourishment, the other as seasoning, and both truly are a token and sign of <term>philadelphias</term> <note>Greek: "brotherly love"</note> and benevolence. Master Remigius Fesch, a most celebrated Professor at Basel, has treated the subject of alliances professionally.

The Romans were most observant of treaties. Was it not so, even though the Romans were destitute of the true knowledge of the true God? Thus also another exclaims:

> Hear, O nations, do not break the treaties of Peace,
> Nor place your faith behind your kingdoms.

To be sure, they did these things rightly out of fear of either infamy or vengeance. *Aristotle in the Rhetoric to Alexander the Great* says they do not fear to commit perjury because they fear both divine vengeance and human infamy. For no example can be shown in all of history of those who had prosperous fortune for whom it was a pleasure to break faith. Truly, their infamy was always greatest among men, as Caepio, Crassus, Galba, and others pierced by the pens of their own people can abundantly testify. *Rupert, observations on Florus*, book 2, chapter 6, section 5. Treaties were accustomed to be made by the ancients by the **sacrifice of a sow**. Also book 3, chapter 18, section 5.

One sees that in alliances that have been made, those who have jumped away from them without cause and become faithless toward the others have had to pay very dearly for it. *Adam Contzen*, book 3 of *Politics*, chapter 7, number 7, the version on Zeno the faithless. *Lambert Daneau*, *Political Aphorisms from Thucydides*, book 2, number 1, where they recount several examples from Roman histories. The Gods are the avengers of treaties. The punishments of treaty-breakers. *Rupert, observations on book 3, chapter 11, section 6.* The same deities and the same fates are to be expected by the breakers of treaties which Sacrovir once experienced, and which Vindex experienced, concerning whom see *Tacitus*, book 4 of the *Histories*, chapter 57; and which Vladislaus, King of Hungary, experienced in *Bonfinius*, decade 3, book 6, *Chalcocondylas*, book 7, and others. A treaty <note>Latin: "foedus"</note> is named from faith <note>Latin: "fides"</note>; it is a public partnership, whether offensive or defensive. Just as in a partnership of private individuals, one partner sometimes contributes money and the other contributes labor, law 1, Code

### 87. Sureties. Guarantors. <note>original: "Bürgen. Fidejussor."</note>

To act as a surety <note>original: "fidejubere"</note> is nothing other than to "vouch for someone" <note>original German: "für einen gutsagen"</note>, to order that something be done upon someone's word. Thus, I believe sureties are those who "speak well for someone" <note>original German: "die für einen gutsprechen"</note>, promising to make something good, "giving their word" <note>original German: "die Paroles geben"</note>, etc. See Hering in the individual treatise *On Sureties*, chapter 1, section 1. In the index under the word <term>expromissor</term> <note>A legal term for someone who takes over another person's debt as his own.</note>. These words are also considered to have the same effect: "he shall lose nothing," according to Paul Christinaeus, *Belgian Decisions*, volume 1, decision 111.

The words "He should provide a surety, or become a surety himself" are found in the **Statutes of Lübeck**, book 3, title 1, article 1, in these words: "When a lawsuit is brought and proven between citizens and residents regarding borrowed money and liquidated debt, the defendant shall first be given a period of fourteen days or eight days for payment. If he does not pay then, he must provide a surety by daylight, or become a surety himself." And again in book 4, title 16, article 4: "If he can have no sureties, then he must become a surety himself." For that last phrase is to be understood not as a financial guarantee, but as corporal detention or personal arrest of the debtor, which is necessary so that he might think more quickly about payment. Master Anton Hering, *Treatise on Sureties*, chapter 11, number 22.

The words "that he would allow himself to be persuaded or used as a surety" <note>original German: "daß er sich zu einem Bürgen vermögen oder brauchen lassen wolle"</note> denote a negotiation rather than a completed contract. See Pistor, *Observations* 173, number 56, section 4 and following, in many places as well as in the additions there.

The effect of those words is often added as a clause in surety instruments: "We sureties want to be wrong, but they the creditors shall simply and only be right" <note>original German: "Wir Bürgen wollen unrecht, sie aber die Gläubiger sollen schlechts und allein recht haben"</note>. This is debated. There are those who say it is equivalent to the clause: "We renounce all right and aid of the laws." Concerning this, see Hering, *On Sureties*, chapter 17, number 34 and following. But it seemed to others that this clause, being unusual and ambiguous—indeed, a source of many quarrels—should deservedly be banished from the court. For as it is uncertain and doubtful, it also silently opens a window to fraud and deceit, no less than that other clause: "Also, this bond shall not be interpreted to the disadvantage of our creditors by anyone, whatever his burden may be, but as our creditor himself, or the holder of the letter with his good provable will, shall interpret, explain, and declare it in all its articles, points, and clauses, to that we shall and will give full satisfaction." Hering, in the cited place, number 27. See, however, Peter Friedrich, *On Mandates*, book 2, chapter 71, numbers 4 and 13; Thoming, *Leipzig Decisions* 37, throughout the discourse.

And it should be particularly noted that a surety of indemnity, who is commonly called an **Indemnity-Surety** <note>original German: "Schadloß-Bürge"</note>, even if he has renounced all aid of the laws and rights acting in his favor, still has the **benefit of discussion** <term>beneficium excussionis</term> <note>The legal right of a surety to demand that the creditor first try to collect the debt from the primary debtor's assets before turning to the surety.</note>, according to the teachings of Hering, chapter 27.

Everything that can be said about sureties has been collected by Master Anton Hering and Valerius Andreas in a treatise specifically written on this matter. Add Master Wilhelm Anton von Quinquenell, chapter 49, number 38 and following.

### ADDITION.

"A surety should be strangled" <note>original German: "Bürgen soll man würgen." A rhyming proverb warning that acting as a guarantor often leads to financial ruin.</note>. Zorer, part 1, question 12, number 918. It is not easy for everyone to find a surety. Barbosa, book 6, chapter 14, axiom 3. Suretyship is considered as payment, axiom 2. "Much borrowing and lending is a poisoning of your inheritance, and has a stepmother named 'sell your goods'; she gives birth to a daughter named 'give them away cheap'; this same daughter has a brother named 'out the gate'." <note>A metaphorical warning: borrowing leads to selling assets cheaply, which leads to bankruptcy and eviction (being sent "out the gate").</note> Hering, *On Sureties*, chapter 15, number 13. Today, cautious creditors—as Treutler notes in volume 2, Dispute 28, last thesis, letter G—in order to avoid idle disputes, are accustomed to adding a special clause by which they make the surety promise: "That he does not wish to be free from the suretyship until the letter and seal are redeemed through honorable payment." And Gomez strongly approves of this opinion.

Do the words, "moved to be a surety" <note>German: *zum Bürgen vermöcht*</note>, imply perfection of the contract? See Hartman Pistor, 173, number 56. Nowadays, it is incorporated into the duty of subjects not to become a surety for anyone without the consent of their own lord <term>eigenherrlicher Consens</term> <note>This refers to the formal permission required from a feudal lord for a tenant or subject to enter into legal obligations that might affect the lord's interests or the subject's ability to pay their dues.</note>. The question is therefore asked: when such a suretyship is found for a subject, which supposedly occurred 20 or more years ago and was also recorded at a local office, but now the alleged surety excuses himself, saying he did not enter into the suretyship at that time in any other way than upon the following of his lord’s consent? And that he could not obtain it at that time. He therefore did not consider that the suretyship should be effective because the consent was lacking, especially since nothing was demanded of him in 20 or more years. The creditor, however, because he sees that his primary debtor is in bad standing, does not want to release the surety, arguing that in the past one did not look so strictly upon the lord’s consent. It is asked, what is the law? Fiefs should always be "better by a third part" <note>Meaning the value of the fief should exceed the debt by one-third.</note>, then it is acknowledged, i.e., the consent is granted. Regnerus Sixtinus in *Legal Opinions*, in the *Resolution of Question 4, section on the specific facts under letter D*, it seems that a peasant can become a surety without the consent of the lord as far as a personal action <term>actio personalis</term> <note>A legal claim against a specific person based on a contract or debt, rather than a claim against property.</note> is concerned, but otherwise regarding a real or mortgage action <term>actio realis sive hypothecaria</term> <note>A claim against specific property or land.</note>. For the latter is not binding without the lord's consent; the former, however, cannot be forbidden to the heir, because he is not a serf, but is only bound to the lord by reason of his inheritance. It is asked: when two people obligate themselves without the lord’s consent, one with a mortgage and the other without, whether the obligation of both is valid? Answer: both; and he who has the mortgage is preferred when something of the own property remains for the debtor from the sale price of his sold inheritance, because then one returns to Common Law. The clause: "Saving the superior's assent" <note>Latin: *Salvo superioris assensu*</note>. Klock, volume 2, consultation 16, number 69.

### 88. Castle. Fortress.

A "Burg" <note>Latin: *Burgus*</note> or "Castle" <note>Latin: *Castellum*</note>. Thus Freher, *On Lopodunum*, page 13. The Franks call any towns "Burgs," and added them to ancient names, such as **Strasbourg**, **Freiburg**, etc. And a "Burg" was a town, surrounded by a wall and towers and closed with gates. Frequently it also denotes a citadel <term>Arx</term> for Germans. See Cluverius, book 1 of *On Germany*, chapter 13, page 110. Killinger, *On Ganerbia*, chapter 3. Johann Hering, in the *Supplement to the treatise On Mills*, regarding the Law of Burgs. Me, *On the Nature of Peoples*, page 58, and the treatise *On the Law of Things*, page 226. Add Martinitus in the *Philological Lexicon*. Marchant in the *Description of Flanders*, book 1, title *On Towns, Castellanies, Citadels, etc.*, page 32. Coccius in *Dagobert*, page 182, and Goldast in *Alemannia*, volume 1,

<column-break/>

page 183, where [he explains] what a "Bürglén" is. But Luitprand, book 3 of *Deeds Throughout Europe*, chapter 12, says: "And since," he says, "they themselves call a gathering of houses which is not enclosed by a wall a *Burgum*," etc. But a "Burgum" is properly a fortress <term>Castrum</term>, and a "Castellum" is a place next to a fortress where the camp-followers and traders necessary for the soldiers stay. Cluverius, *On the Channels of the Rhine*, chapter 14, page 109. In which sense the French today use their *Bourg* and *Bourgade*; the Italian word *Borgo* also agrees, regarding which the *Vocabolario della Crusca* <note>The famous Italian dictionary established in the 16th century.</note> notes that it is "a street, or collection of several houses without a specific surrounding wall, and properly the additions of houses outside the walls of walled lands." From this also the Burgundians are named, as Orosius reports in his last book, because they live arranged through fortresses <term>Castra</term>.

This word is derived from the Greek <term>pyrgos</term> <note>Greek: πύργος</note>, that is, a tower. Because this word is also sometimes taken for a "City," the word "Citizen" <note>German: *Bürger*</note> seems to show this. But regarding Strabo, book 3, Casaubon poorly notes that those who think this word is German in origin reveal by this very fact their ignorance of these matters, since it is pure Greek. But surely the Teutons have many words in common with the Greeks, and the dispute is still before the judge whether the Greek is older, or rather coeval with our vernacular.

"Burga" is also called a sewer <term>Cloaca</term> by ancient glosses; Martinius derives this word from the German *bergen* <note>To hide, protect, or shelter.</note>, just as the Latin word for sewer is from *latendo* <note>To lie hidden.</note>, and he says that for the English, "Burgk" is a hiding place or a cover. Is perhaps "Burga" taken for a sewer, just as "Castellum" is for a reservoir of spring water, which we call "water-rooms" <note>German: *Wasserstuben*</note>? Vitruvius, book 8, chapter 7, law 1, section "says the Praetor" regarding daily water. Calvin in the *Juridical Lexicon*, under the word "Castellum."

## 89. Citizen, Citizenship, Admitting to Citizenship. *Civis*, *Jus civitatis*.

Under the name of "citizens" <note>Latin: *Civium nomine*</note> come not only those who are within the City itself, but also those who belong to a certain Diocese or County. The Doctors <note>Legal commentators and scholars</note> in the rubric of the Digest on the dissolution of marriage <note>Latin: *solut. matrimon.*</note>; Bartolus on law 3 of the Code regarding the nature of children <note>Latin: *C. de natur. liber.*</note>, who says, following law 1 on municipalities <note>Latin: *ad municip.*</note>, that he who originates from a village <note>Latin: *vicus*</note> derives his origin from the very City to which that village is subject; and those born in a Village or Hamlet <note>Latin: *Villa*</note> are called Citizens of that city to which they pay taxes, according to the authentic text <note>Latin: *auth. quib. mod. nat. eff. sui §. si quis igitur*</note>. See Felenus in the chapter *Rudolphus* on rescripts, note 9, and the express text in the law regarding those born in a village, under the title on municipalities.

People living in the suburbs <note>Latin: *Suburbani homines*</note> also enjoy the privileges of cities: because in favorable legal matters, suburbanites are included under the term "Citizens." See the law regarding buildings in the Digest on the significance of words <note>Latin: *l. ædificia. ff. de V. S.*</note>, which Alciatus, Caepolla, and others explain more broadly both there and in law 2, as well as in the law of Alphenus in the same title.

In certain places, it is accepted that someone who has remained in a city for ten years is made a Citizen. Ludovicus Romanus, singular 676. This applies even if one has not stayed continuously, but for the greater part of that time in the city, based on the argument of law 18 regarding the butcher's shop, the section titled *Sabinus*, in the Digest on instructing a fund <note>Latin: *ff. de fund. instruct.*</note>; and law 156, where it says: one is understood to have possessed for the greater part of a year even if he possessed for only two months. Digest, on the significance of words. See also the text in the chapter *Significatum* on prebends in the sixth book of Decretals <note>Latin: *in 6.*</note>, in the verses "daily" and "how much more frequently," with additions by Romanus in the same place. Furthermore, whether one acquires the status of a burgher <note>Latin: *Burgensiam*</note> of a city from a long-term domicile without official letters? See Boerius, decision 260.

But it must be noted here that although someone may live for a long time in an Imperial City <note>Latin: *Imperiali civitate*</note>—for example, as a Syndic <note>term: Syndicus (a legal representative or advocate for a city government)</note>—he does not thereby become a Citizen, but rather express reception and submission are required. And it is asked: if such a person dies, should he be succeeded according to the local statute? The answer is no, and the place of origin must be looked at: because he is not deemed to have established a domicile there, and primarily because such a person does not recognize the jurisdiction of that City in any other way than by reason of his office; see Schaeffer in his practical questions regarding a certain Noble Widow.

It is a different matter, however, that someone may be subject to a local court <note>Latin: *forum fortiatur*</note> by reason of a crime or a contract in the place where the crime or contract occurred: for this applies to any foreigner if he is found there.

And such a Syndic cannot be sued by reason of inheritances or other obligations in the place of such a domicile. Even contracts regarding Dowry or marriage are not judged according to the statutes of the place or the contract, but according to the husband's court <note>Latin: *forum Mariti*</note>.

But others disagree: since the husband's domicile of residence, not his origin, should be considered. Salicetus on the law *Cunctos populos* in the Code regarding the Supreme Trinity. This is also the reasoning <note>Latin: *ratio*</note> why the wives and 

<column-break/>

widows of Doctors and Professors succeed their husbands according to the Statutes of the city where the Academy is maintained <note>meaning where the university is located</note>, or according to University law <note>German: *Universitätrecht*</note>, even if they were born and married in other places. Matthaeus Coler, *On Executive Processes*, part 1, chapter 3, number 219 and many following; Berlichius, part 3, conclusion 26, number 10.

The law is the same for the wife of one who exercises judgment in some city in the name of a Superior <note>a lord or sovereign</note>, namely that she succeeds her husband according to the Statutes of that city, even if the husband was not a Citizen of that city; this is elegantly explained by Modestinus Pistoris, question 85, number 1 and following.

However, when there are different Statutes and Customs regarding the division of property acquired while the marriage lasted, then the laws of the husband's domicile must be strictly observed. Bocer on the customs of Berry <note>Latin: *Bituricens*</note>, title on the customs of marriage and divorce, section 4, column 4; Covarruvias in the *Epitome on Testaments*, part 2, chapter 7.

Whether someone born in transit through a city is called a Citizen and a native <note>Latin: *naturalis*</note> of that city is investigated by Cevallos, question 158.

Regarding the different classes of Roman Citizens, Gruchius has much in *On the Assemblies* <note>Latin: *de Comitiis*</note>, page 114 and in the Index under the words Citizen, Class, Century, etc. As for who was considered a Citizen in Athens? See Ubbo Emmius in the *Description of the Athenian Republic*, page 97 and following, and in *Ancient Greece*, title on the Athenian Republic, pages 64 and 380.

Citizens of municipalities are bound to perform the Oath of Homage <note>Latin: *Homagii Juramentum*</note>—the Citizen's Oath <note>German: *den Burgers-Eid*</note>—to their own Senate as the Ordinary Magistrate endowed with jurisdiction, and they promise under the religious bond of faith that they will offer due obedience and conduct themselves properly. Knichen, *On Territorial Law*, chapter 3, number 162; Matthaeus Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, part 1, chapter 7, number 212. And this must be performed so necessarily that no one is admitted into the number of Citizens without it, regardless of whether they are a native-born person <note>Latin: *Originarius*</note> or a newcomer <note>Latin: *Advena*</note>. Knichen in the same place; Caspar Ziegler in the section on the State, conclusion 1, number 10.

Regarding this Oath and its formulas, Master Goeddaeus treats it at length in the *Thorough Report on the Imperial City of Friedberg* <note>German: *dem gründlichen Bericht von deß heiligen Reichsstadt Friedberg*</note>, chapters 5 and 6 throughout.

Also, admitted Citizens, together with their children—even those born before—have the same privileges as those born there. See Marius Antoninus, book 2, resolution 42; Sesse, volume 1, decision 90 and decision 167, where he says that the children of residents born outside the Kingdom are not admitted to Offices. Likewise, is a citizen a "natural" of the place where he was born? See the counsel of Francisco de Caldas, which is joined to the tract on restitution to the original state. Surdus, volume 3, counsel 311, regarding whether immunity granted to citizens also pertains to citizens later made by privilege.

The power of creating Citizens belongs to the Senate and other Municipal Magistrates, even without the command, knowledge, or license of the territorial lord <note>Latin: *domini territorialis*</note>. For this is a matter of the law of the Magistrate and of Jurisdiction; it is not among the reserved rights of the Prince, as Peter Anthony de

# 89. Citizen, Citizenship, Admitting to Citizenship (continued)

...see de Petra in the treatise on the power of Princes, chapter 15, number 1. Gylman, volume 5, *Symphorema*, report 10, folio 47, numbers 1, 2, and following. Conrad Lancellot, *On the Time of All Judges*, book 1, chapter 1, section 4, number 3. See my own work on the law of universities, folio 258, and the Würtemberg Provincial Ordinance, folio 4.

At the time of reception as a citizen, the Lord can impose whatever law he wishes; hence it is commonly said that a contract receives its law from the agreement. For instance, if it is agreed that every year, in this or that month, the person shall pay a pair of roosters (which our people call a <term>Rauchhuhn</term> <note>literally "smoke-hen," a tax paid per hearth or household</note>), or a certain measure of grain (which they call <term>Kornpacht</term> <note>grain-rent</note>), or a certain sum of money or shillings (<term>Geldpacht</term> <note>money-rent</note> or <term>Gült</term> <note>interest or debt-payment</note>). Likewise, it may be agreed that he shall work for the Lord as many times as required for plowing, gathering, threshing, or hauling wood to the Lord’s house; see Hufanus on "property-men" <note>serfs or unfree laborers</note>, chapter 6, number 61 and following. However, it is not permitted to experience all these and similar conditions in the cities of Princes and Great Lords; instead, they are mostly introduced by Nobles in their districts and villages, **and by doing so they wish to force a state of serfdom in the meantime** <note>original German: *und wollen sie dardurch mittler Zeit eine Leibeigenschaft erzwingen*</note>, etc. Indeed, the nobility can impose such burdens when they grant someone specific estates; but when they admit someone as a citizen and wish to impose such burdens on him, it is not considered fair, because through this, everyone—contrary to the custom of the region and to the prejudice of the superior Lord—would become serfs.

In Switzerland, citizenship implies a kind of subjection. When a city, village, or land are citizens of Zurich or Bern, those cities wish to claim a sovereign authority over them, or at the very least a "protection and defense" <note>German: *Schutz und Schirm*</note>, etc. See the acts of Bern against Ulenburg; also the acts of Bern against Pruntrut.

**That to make a city great, one must receive foreigners as citizens,** see Meillet on Tacitus, *Political Discourses*, book 6, discourse 5, folio 324 and following.

When someone is received as a citizen who is not a native, he is bound by the custom of almost all places to pay a certain price, **so that he effectively buys his citizenship** <note>German: *damit er das Burgerrecht gleichsam erkaufft*</note>; this is especially customary in the Imperial Cities, and this money is commonly called <term>Burgergeld</term> <note>citizen-money or admission fee</note>.

In certain places, we see it accepted that those who migrate from one place to another for the sake of living and doing business there are not admitted to the right of citizenship (<term>zum Burgerrecht</term>) unless they exhibit letters of testimony from their Magistrate under whom they have lived until now. They must show that they lived in that place honorably and departed in good grace, and at the same time provide sureties that they are legitimately born and free, and are not the "property-men" of any Lord—**that they are rightfully and freely born, and are no one's serf or bondman** <note>German: *daß sie recht und frey geboren, und niemand eigen oder laß seyen*</note>—and that within three years no debts,

<column-break/>

by which the city might be burdened, shall follow them; as Hering speaks in the treatise on sureties, chapter 5, number 333. we commonly call this **Legitimate Birth and the Right of a Freeman** <note>German: *Ehelich Geburt und Mannrecht*</note>. (*Mann* is used for a free person, whereas *Leut* is used for a servant or serf). Würtemberg Provincial Ordinance, folio 4.

One who is found among citizens is, by that very fact, presumed to be a citizen. Hippolytus de Marsiliis on the law regarding minors, section "of many," number 37, in the Digest on questions. And a person is presumed to belong to that city in which he himself is found. Guido Papa in the treatise on presumptions, number 81, near the end. Alciatus on presumptions, rule 2, presumption 15. Schrader, counsel 5, number 65, volume 1.

But now, by our customs, it is permitted to change one's domicile; and by so changing, if he pays the **departure tax** <note>German: *den Abzug*</note> where there is no free migration, he is freed from the burden of the previous city. Rosacorb, chapter 29, number 18. **Yet he must usually settle those matters which were begun during his citizenship.**

This is useful for the decision of a daily question in the Duchy of Würtemberg, where a citizen cannot appeal to the [Imperial] Chamber. If, therefore, someone has a lawsuit while he is still a Würtemberg citizen, but becomes a foreigner while the suit is pending, or has a foreign heir; I do not think he or the heir gains the benefit of a further appeal, because at the time the lawsuit was contested, that right did not belong to him or the deceased.

Regarding the law of citizens, I have dealt with it more extensively in my treatise *On the Law and Orders of Citizens*.

Instead, according to the Regalian rights of the city of Worms, every citizen's or inhabitant’s son—whether of the nobility or not—must, after the death of his father or predecessor, settle with the Honorable Council if he is of single status, first restoring the **tributary law** <note>tax obligations</note>, or if he wishes to establish his own household, apply for citizenship anew and qualify himself according to the proper requirements. Regarding when citizens first began in Germany, see Limnaeus, *On the Public Law*, book 7, chapter 1, number 18. In the Statute of the City of Antwerp, it is expressly contained that anyone born in Antwerp is made a Citizen, whether the parents had a domicile or the right of citizenship there. **Citizen of the Council** <note>original: *Burger deß Raths*</note> concerns the Senate alone; **Citizen of the Council and the City** concerns the whole people, as articulated in the legal case of Nuremberg against Brandenburg, article 324, where the word "and" is well-noted, because if this word "and" is omitted, only the Senate is understood. See also article 332 and following, where the word "commonly" is interpreted in article 329 to mean that not every individual citizen has a share for himself—specifically in the contracts of their Lords and Authorities—but rather all citizens participate in common, and commonly through the hand of the Council: Besold, volume 1.

<column-break/>

Everyone is a part of the City (of the Citizens), as noted by Christian Matthew in *Historical Theater*, under the 4th Monarchy under Emperor Conrad I, folio 523. Conring wrote his *Political Exercises* on the **Citizen and the State**. Thomas Hobbes wrote his *Elements of the Citizen* <note>original: *De Cive*</note>. In Venice, only the **Patricians** <note>the hereditary ruling class</note> are Citizens; see my work *Comparison of the Nuremberg Republic with the Venetian*, book A. 4. Regarding **Honorary Citizens**, see Mr. Speidel in *Mirror of Notables*, page 176. Every Citizen, when they are accepted as a Citizen, must from the very beginning pay a specific sum of money for the right of citizenship. Obrecht, *On the Improvement of Land and People*, page 23. **Citizens, Inhabitants, Residents, Subjects, Dependents, and Relations.** <note>original: *Burger, Innwohner, Hintersassen, Unterthanen, Zugehörige und Verwandte*</note> Limnaeus, *On the Public Law*, book 7, chapter 3, page 99. Besold, *Politics*, book 1, chapter 7, final number. Limnaeus, *On the Public Law*, book 7, chapter 10, number 9. Whether a Prince can force a citizen out of a city? Regarding the **Privilege** that allows one to reside in all Imperial Cities? Besold, *Politics*, book 1, chapter 12, section 69, number 2. Regarding the **Right of Free Departure** <note>original: *Gerechtigkeit deß freyen Zugs*</note>, that one may move away from his citizenship with his goods and property as he pleases, without paying a departure tax. Same author, book 1, chapter 11, section 3, number 2. The name "Citizen" is even given to those who inhabit the fields <note>rural dwellers</note>. Regarding the Counts of Fugger, see Sprenger, *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 402 and following. Limnaeus, volume 1, additions to book 4, chapter 7, page 564.

### 90. Civil War. *Bellum Civile.*

That discipline quickly degenerates in a civil war is taught by Julien Peleus, volume 1, folio 307 and folio 600, where he discusses the cruelty of the **Huguenots** <note>French Protestants</note>, and that a monk predicted an admirable kind of death. Also, that the wars of Christians are unlawful, see in the *Life of Colet*, III. b., in the lives collected by Fichard.

### 91. Civil, Honorable. *Civile.*

That is properly called **Civil** which belongs to the Citizens or the City: hence civil studies and institutions—that is, those pertaining to the society of citizens and the state of the city. In this sense, "civil customs" and doing something "civilly" was spoken of by Cicero. However, since the method of protecting the state of the city demands above all that nothing be done against those things which are for the **public utility**, whatever was of that kind began to be called **Civil**. Conversely, whatever was done against the public utility and would be destructive to civil society was called **Incivil**. See Robert’s *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 11, where he teaches at length what is Civil and what is Incivil, and in the following chapter, what is **Honorable**.

## 92. Mayor and Court. Consul and Senate.

Under Civil Law, jurisdiction and the power to initiate legal actions were also granted to municipal magistrates. Therefore, they have the power to judge smaller financial cases involving up to 300 gold coins <note>original: *aureos*</note> and to hear lighter criminal charges. See the section "to judge" and "they shall also hear" <note>original: *§. judicare. §. audient quoque*</note> in the *Authentica* regarding the defenders of cities. These same officials can proceed according to the law even as far as the seizure of pledges. Law 3, section 1 of the *Digest* regarding the property of others. Cujas, in the summary of the *Code* regarding Municipal Magistrates. Therefore, this power of judgment cannot be taken away from the two-man council <note>original: *Duumviris*</note> and the Senate of the city. Usually, they exercise the law only among those who consent, not among those who are unwilling and who appeal to the Prince's judgment. For even under common law, a municipal magistrate can hear more serious cases if the parties consent. Law *inter*, Digest on Municipalities. Wesenbeck, in the summary regarding Municipal Magistrates, numbers 3 and 6.

But nowadays, municipal cities and their magistrates generally hold jurisdiction even over those who are unwilling. I have discussed this at greater length in my *Treatise on the Law of Things, page 226.*

I wish to add here what my brother of pious memory, Johann Georg Besold, once wrote on this matter in the practical observations he was preparing regarding the municipal law of **Württemberg**.

Here it is appropriate to introduce the investigation of whether the towns of the Duchy of **Württemberg**, or of other Estates of the Empire, enjoy Ordinary Jurisdiction, and High and Low Authority <term>merum & mixtum imperio: 'High' authority refers to criminal justice and capital punishment, while 'Low' or 'Mixed' authority refers to civil and administrative justice</term>? Many authors argue about this in different ways. This is especially true since the decision in such jurisdictional disputes is often provided by custom—which is not always sufficiently clear—rather than by Roman laws, which are often as far removed from our intended purpose as the state of the ancient Roman Republic was from the modern day. Indeed, there are those who defend the position that cities subject to the Princes of the Empire do not even possess simple ordinary jurisdiction unless they have acquired it through a privilege or a formal contract.

They are moved first by the fact that the lords of the lands, or those with territorial jurisdiction, claim all jurisdiction for themselves regarding matters located within their province. Chasseneuz, *On the Customs of Burgundy, title on mortmain, rubric 9, section 4, at the beginning, number 2.* Boerius, *Decision 227.* Francesco Curtius, *Counsel 108, number 5, page 2.* Consequently, the Princes of the Empire are seen to hold all-encompassing jurisdiction in the cities subject to them. Zasius, *on the law regarding Command, number 25 and following, Digest on Jurisdiction.* Just as the Governors of Provinces <note>original: *Præsides Provinciarum*</note> were considered to have the jurisdiction of all Roman magistrates, according to Law 3, section 4 and following, Digest on the office of the Governor. Therefore, our Princes (who rely on a firmer law than the ancient Roman Proconsuls and Governors) possess no less power,

<column-break/>

and consequently, they are considered to hold a well-founded claim regarding the Royalties <term>Regalia: the rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign</term>, High and Low Authority, and the simple jurisdiction of all the cities in their territory (unless an exception is duly shown, following the argument in Law *ab ea parte*, at the beginning, Digest 1, section *cum urbem*, Digest on the office of the Prefect of the City, Law 1, on proofs). See also Law *forma*, section *si verò*, Digest on the census; and Law *pupillus*, section *territorium*, Digest on the meaning of words. Mynsinger, *Decision 13, response 3, number 2 and following.* Cothmann, *Counsel 47, number 112 and following, book 3.*

(2) Furthermore, municipal cities used to exercise jurisdiction only in "other cases" <note>meaning minor civil matters</note>. Law *inter* 28, Digest on Municipalities; Law 1, Code on the defense of the City, section *Novell. 15*. Lord Bocer, *On Jurisdiction, chapter 8, number 92.* So much so, that municipal magistrates could never rightly assert jurisdiction for themselves unless they obtained it from the Prince or the Governor of the province. Law section *quia*, Digest on Jurisdiction; Law *privatorum*, Code on the same. Cothmann, in the cited counsel, number 120.

Thirdly, they add that the territory belongs to the Princes and the cities lack it; therefore, jurisdiction belongs not to the cities, but to the Princes alone. For normally, jurisdiction cannot exist unless it is passively attached to a territory, as argued by Mynsinger in the cited response 3, number 3, and Cothmann, response 47, number 125 and following.

(4) They also wish to demonstrate this by the fact that the Prince’s official, whom they call the Prefect or, in German, the **Bailiff** <note>original: **Vogt**</note>, is found established in these municipalities to act in the Prince’s stead and exercise all jurisdiction in the towns and villages. Thus, the person who presides over a territory is generally called a **Bailiff**, and the terms **Bailiwick** <note>original: **Vogtey**</note> and **Bailiff’s Authority** <note>original: **Vogteyliche Obrigkeit**</note> denote jurisdiction. Wehner, *Practical Observations, under the word "Vogtey"*; Mynsinger, in the said response, numbers 9 and 66.

(5) For this reason, they also say that all jurisdictional acts belong to this Official and Prefect: namely, the right to summon litigants, the right to impose fines, and the right to execute sentences, etc.

Sixthly, those who conduct a dissertation on the towns of this Duchy also use this argument: that in the Cadastres or those books in which the rights of the Prince in every city are recorded—namely, in the **Land Registers** <note>original: **Lägerbüchern**</note>—these words are commonly found inserted:

->That His Princely Grace is entitled to all lordship, power of command and prohibition, as well as high and low authority in such a city, etc.<-

To which, seventhly, they add the text in the first title of the Provincial Law, where at the beginning of the oath formula prescribed for all judges, these words are found:

->I promise and swear to God the Lord, that I shall faithfully and with all diligence attend to the Court of the Illustrious, etc., my Gracious Prince and Lord, etc., here, etc.<-

Lastly, they say that even if the right to appoint guardians <note>original: *tutores*</note> was given to municipal magistrates by the Roman laws (Law 3, Digest on guardians and curators given by these, etc.; Law 2, section *si mater* at the end, Digest on the Senatus Consultum Tertullianum), and that right was part of Mixed Authority <note>original: *mixti Imperii*</note>,

The word *Burgfried* <note>meaning "Castle Peace"</note> is sometimes used for the territory of a castle; sometimes the laws, pacts, and statutes of the co-proprietors <term>German: *Ganerben*, joint heirs who shared ownership of a castle</term> of any fortress or castle are so named: as taken from Modestus Pistoris, *volume 1, of Besold's Council, Tome I.*

page 21, which tend toward the preservation of the Family and prohibit alienation of property to outsiders.

For before the establishment and proclamation of the Public Peace, which we call the *Landfrieden*, travel was generally less safe and secure throughout Germany, and as our people say, the **Law of the Fist** <note>original: *Faustrecht*, where might makes right</note> was in full swing. See Ventura de Valentiis in *The Litigious Virgin, book 1, chapter 1, number 14.* Robbers hid in fortresses among men of their own kind, in the **Robber Castles** <note>original: *Raubschlösser*</note>; see Bodin, *On the Republic, page 887,* and Crusius in the *Swabian Annals.* Noblemen of high birth built fortified strongholds in which they, with their families and more precious belongings, might be safe from the violent invasions of others. Moreover, so that their union might be greater and more constant, and so they could better defend themselves and their property, they entered into fraternities and confederations under certain laws, which they called the *Burgfried* <note>Castle Peace</note>. See Fichardus, *Council 7, number 9.* These laws concerned maintaining peace within the castle and other matters pertaining to the preservation and defense of the co-proprietors <note>original: *Ganerben*</note>: or *Burghut* <note>Castle Guard</note>, as mentioned in the same *Council 7, number 11.* And those so confederated were called *Ganerben*; regarding them, see below under the word *Ganerben*. But because they, degenerating from ancient virtue, began not only to oppress others but also to harbor fellow members who oppressed others, their audacity was restrained by public Imperial Laws, as proven from many Decrees by Cluten in *Sylloge of Daily Matters, thesis 26, under the letter K.*

Sometimes that word is taken more narrowly: namely, for a certain and defined district of a castle and a place of security, in which violations of the peace are restrained with harsher punishments. The penalty for a capital violation is usually the **amputation of the hand**; sometimes it is not capital but carries a heavier monetary fine. See Dr. Killinger in the *Selected Treatise on Co-Proprietors, discourse 3, number 55 and following.* Chassannæus teaches this also regarding the Palaces of Princes in *Catalog of the Glory of the World, part 5, consideration 24, number 125*, where he writes: "We see that the Palaces of Princes (which also holds true in our **Duchy of Württemberg**) carry such security that those attacking someone within them are punished capitally." And he adds that the palace itself enjoys such a privilege, but also the borders of the Palace; Albericus de Rosate holds and proves this by many points in his commentary on the *Code regarding those who flee to the Church.* Add Johannes Hering, *On the Law of Towns, number 726 and following.*

If a place is sanctified—that is, if a Castle Peace sign is posted in a place <note>original: *an einem Ort der Burgfried angeschlagen wird*</note>—then not every person offending there (that is, wounding someone there) can be punished by either death or mutilation of the hand, unless the deed was done with malice.
