## 94 <term>Burgrave</term>. Burggravius.

Burgraves were formerly those to whom the custody of a certain Imperial Castle <term>Reichs-Burg</term> was committed. There were four principal ones among these in Germany, and their judicial seats still survive today, as witnessed by Henning Arnisaeus in his *Treatise on Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, number 15, on the section "But the Burgraves," folio 322. Specifically: the <term>Burgraves of Stromburg, Nuremberg, Magdeburg, and Reicheneck</term>. See Caspar von Lerch, *On the Equestrian Order*, folio 44 and following.

Today there are no longer any Burgraves [in the original sense], since the Emperors hold no private castles in the Imperial Cities. See Nolden, *On the Nobility*, chapter 8, number 172 and following.

Although certain Princes still observe this title: such as the Prince of Saxony, who styles himself the Burgrave of Magdeburg; and the Margrave of Brandenburg, who holds the title of the Burgrave of Nuremberg. See Mr. Killinger, *On Joint-Heirs*, discourse 3, number 148, etc., and also my own *Dissertation on Counts and Barons*, number 11, as well as

## 95. <term>Burgher or Peasant Fief</term>.
->Burgher fief, rustic fief.<-

A Burgher Fief is so called because it is otherwise called an "ignoble" fief, because it does not ennoble the possessor (as happens in a Noble Fief). For it is given by minor vassals <note>original: *valvasoribus*</note> or private persons, to whom this granting is entirely permitted. ### 96. Castle Fief. <term>Feudum castrense</term>.

A Castle Fief, which we call a **Burglehen**, is that which a Lord grants to a Vassal under the agreement that the vassal is obligated to the defense of a specific castle by reason of this grant. <term>Ferrarius</term> on fiefs, book 1, chapter 6. <term>Schrader</term> on fiefs, part 2, chapter 4, number 17. <term>Obrecht</term> on fiefs, book 1, chapter 6, number 14.

<term>Rittershusius</term> confirms nearly the same meaning from Saxon law in chapter 17, book 1 of his feudal partitions, where he writes: <note>original: "Burglehen, heissen solche Lehen..."</note> "Castle fiefs are those fiefs where many noblemen, or joint-heirs <note>original: *Ganerben*; noble co-owners of a single estate or castle</note> as they are called, hold fiefs and feudal rights together in a castle or stronghold from the Princes and Lords to whom the castle belongs." And again in the same place: "Citizens and castle-men <note>original: *Burgmänner*</note> are the names given to the joint-heirs or noblemen who in olden times lived under a Castle-Lord in a castle; they were then called citizens <note>original: *Burger*</note> because of the castle." Add to this Killinger’s highly learned treatise on joint-inheritance, discourse 3, number 131, etc.

<term>Aelurius’s Glatz Chronicle</term>, chapter 2, page 85, discussing the Knight’s Castle of Glatz, writes: <note>original: "daß über solches etliche alte Adeliche Geschlechter..."</note> "that several old noble families in the County of Glatz hold the castle fief over this place due to ancient privileges; today this serves the purpose that, in case of need or in swift and dangerous times of war, the castle community in the town, as well as the people in the countryside, may find safety within it, etc."

### ADDITION.

Regarding the <term>Feudo Castrensi</term> <note>Castle Fief</note>, see <term>Ferrarius</term>, 1. feudal, 6. <term>Schrader</term>, part 2, chapter 4, number 54. The Supplement to <term>Wehner</term>, page 13 and following. A castle fief, in our language a **Burglehen**, is given so that the Vassal may help the Lord in defending a certain castle or fortified town. <term>Rosenthal</term>, chapter 2, question 78, where it should be noted in passing that this type of fief is also considered a male fief in the Courts of Fulda and Hersfeld, as indicated by <term>Knich</term>, part 1, chapter 4, number 40, and <term>Fichard</term>, counsel 18, number 5, in the passage starting "yet I hold it to be so," volume 2. **Castle Fiefs** <note>original: *Feuda Burgensia*</note>, which are located within the castle itself or right next to it, and are commonly called **Burglehen**, are in some places exempt from real estate taxes by special law. <term>Jeremias Reusner</term>, feudal dispute 2, thesis 77 and following. <term>Doctor Tabor</term> on billeting, page 280. <term>Antonius</term>, dispute 1 on fiefs, thesis 7, letter K.

### 97. Castle Slopes. <term>Burghalden</term>.

Wehner thinks that **Burghalden** is the same as the castle itself, and says it is used this way in Switzerland. To me, **Burghalten** seems rather to be the mountains or hills upon which citadels are built: **The Castle Hill** <note>original: *Der Burgberg*</note>. For **Halden** is nothing

<column-break/>

other than a high place in a field, **a hill, etc.** An example is found (to cite one among many) in the City of Kempten; there, a certain mountain or hill, today surrounded by the city walls, is called the **Burghalden**, because many years ago a certain citadel (or castle) was built upon it. <term>Münster</term> in his *Cosmography* on the city of Kempten. <term>Crusius</term> in his *Annals*, book 5, part 3, chapter 5. Similarly, the mountain or hill of the Tübingen Citadel was called **Pfalzhalden**; for that citadel was formerly called the **Pfalz** <note>Palace or Palatinate</note> because of the Counts of Tübingen, who were Counts Palatine. <term>Jacob Werhner</term>. <term>Killinger</term> on Joint-Inheritance of Castles, discourse 3, number 38 and following.

### 98. Castle-man, Administrative Castle-men. <term>Castellanus</term>.

Usually, this is a Vassal of a castle, or one invested with the goods of a certain castle, in Latin called **Castrensis**: **One who holds a castle fief.** <term>Killinger</term>, discourse 3, number 143. For "Man" <note>original: *Mann*</note> in feudal law is properly a Vassal. **Castle-man** <note>original: *Burgmann*</note> is also used for a partner in a joint-inheritance.

But with respect to joint-heirs <note>original: *Ganerben*</note> or co-owners, those who participate in that right are called such.

Thus, **Administrative Castle-men** <note>original: *Regiments-Burgmänner*</note> are the Judges of the Castle, among whom the Burgrave is the supreme authority; the others are considered as Assessors. The rest are called by the common name **Castle-men**.

**The Castle-men or joint-heirs are judged by the Burgrave, according to their castle-peace.** <note>original: *Burgfried*; a legal treaty or status governing the internal peace and jurisdiction of a castle</note> <term>Rittershusius</term> in his *Feudal Partitions*, book 1, chapter 17. See <term>Gylmann</term>, volume 3 of the *Symphorema*, folio 99. Just as a Burgrave cannot be sued in the Imperial Chamber in the first instance, even if he is "immediate" <note>subject only to the Emperor</note>, **but can only be summoned before the twelve Administrative Castle-men**, <term>Schwannmann</term>, *Observations of the Chamber*, 18; much less is he bound to answer before the ordinary Lord of the territory. **This was at first a special privilege for the Castle-men of Gelnhausen by the privilege of Emperor Frederick; later, however, it was also extended to other Imperial castle-fiefs and joint-heirs. Likewise, it applies to the Free Noble Knighthood in Franconia (outside the Duchy of Saxony), as well as Swabia and the Rhineland, which are related to the Empire without an intermediary.** <term>Paurmeister</term> on Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 9, number 74 and following. On **Castellans, or Castle-men**, see the *Acts of Lindau*, folio 600, at the beginning.

### 99. Castle-Residents. <term>Burgsässen</term>.

Those held to be such are people under the jurisdiction of a certain castle or stronghold, just like **Country-Residents** <note>original: *Landsässen*</note>; <term>Killinger</term> discourse 3, number 47; or those who possess a common citadel. From this, **Castle-Seat** <note>original: *Burgsitz*</note> is the right of possessing a castle: and also **a free castle-resident**. <term>Killinger</term>, in the cited place, number 43.

### 100. Castle Site. <term>Burgstall</term>. Ruins of destroyed castles.

Strictly speaking, it is the place where a castle was built—<note>original: *da eine Burg gestanden ist*</note> "where a castle once stood"—a castle site or castle position. By some, it is also called a Small Castle <note>original: *Parvus Burgus*</note> or a little fortress. Killinger, on the discourse of joint-inheritance <note>original: *de Ganerbiis*</note>, discourse 2, number 37.

Most often, it is said of the ruins of a castle: An old castle site <note>original: *Burgstall*</note>, where in former times a castle existed.

->ADDITION.<-

The term "court-site" <note>original: *curtilis*</note> designates a castle site. *Acts of Lindau, folio 731.* A castle site is nothing other than the place where a castle formerly stood, and now only its ruins appear—where a castle once stood. For the word "stall" <note>original: *Stall*</note> descends from the word "to place" <note>original: *stellen*</note>, signifying that a castle had been placed there. *Limnaeus on Public Law, book 4, chapter 4, number 88.*

In Switzerland <note>original: *Helvetia*</note>, where many small castles were leveled to the ground or destroyed, they are accustomed to use the formal Alemannic word *Burghalden* for the ruins, and they call the remains of destroyed castles *Burgstall*, and small, modest castles *Börgle*. *Stumpf, book 6; Goldast on Alemannic Affairs, volume 1, part 1, folio 183.*

### 101. Burgundy. <term>Burgundia</term>.

Regarding Burgundy, and how it was made subject to Germanic Law? *Guiliman, book 4, The Habsburgs, final chapter, folio 148; and on Swiss Affairs, book 2, chapter 7. Lazius in his Austrian Genealogy, book 1, chapter 4,* where he also discusses how that Kingdom was divided into Counties. Add also *Nolden on the status of Nobles, folio 194, etc.; Arumäus on the Imperial Diets, chapter 4, number 85 and following;* and myself in my Politics on the subaltern Empire.

Regarding the Burgundian Treaty <note>original: *Burgundischer Vertrag*</note>, see *Volume 6 of the Legal Consultations of Adrian Gylmann.*

->ADDITION.<-

The Burgundian Circle <note>original: *Burgundischer Kreiß*; one of the administrative districts of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. *Limnaeus on Public Law, book 1, chapter 7, number 30.*

On the Kingdom of Burgundy or Arles, see *Limnaeus, volume 2, Additions to book 1, chapter 9, page 127.*

The Burgundian Transaction <note>legal agreement</note> does not exempt the Duke from the jurisdiction of the Empire, based on the notes by *Br. on the law of enemies, number 4 and following, regarding captives and the right of return. Otto in Public Law, page 711.* The Duke of that Burgundy is summoned to the Imperial Diets: He is not immune from the burdens of the Empire. He is exempt from the judgment of the Imperial Chamber Court, or rather, the Dukes of Burgundy are immune from Imperial contributions and the jurisdiction of the Court; they have the power of distributing the Order of the Golden Fleece <note>a prestigious Catholic order of knighthood</note>, which Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, founded. *Sprenger in his Delineation of the States of the Empire, page 308.* The County of Burgundy, even though it boasts that it recognizes no one as superior except God and the Sword, is nevertheless not only a fief of the Romano-Germanic Empire, but is also bound to observe its

<column-break/>

Majesty by right and merit. *Besold in Politics, book 1, chapter 9, number 9, verse 5.* Note the opinion of Philip II, King of Spain, regarding this: that the Electors and other Princes of the Empire were mistaken if they believed that Flanders and the rest of the provinces subject to him had anything in common with the Empire. See more in *Besold at the cited location.* On the ancient Kingdom of Burgundy, and by what means it came to the Germans. *Ibid. and Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in Historical Reports, part 6, page 215;* add page 141. *Zeiller* first published the description of the Burgundian and Netherlandish Circle in octavo in the year 1649, and afterwards in folio with copper-plate figures.

### 102. Bulk Sale. <term>Venditio per aversionem</term>.

A bulk sale <note>original: *Buschkauff*</note> is so called when one sells something exactly as one possesses it—the disputed with the disputed, the correct with the correct, etc. <note>meaning "as-is," including all potential legal flaws or benefits</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

By bulk <note>original: *Per aversionem*</note>, or "in a heap" <note>original: *en omadi*</note>, in general, in French *en bloc*, and as stated in *Law 58 of the Digest on hiring*, it means the whole for one price. *Pacius, Analysis of the Code, page 395. Wesenbeck on the actions of managers, number 4.* The reason for the name is taken from this: since this sale is made for the body of the goods as a whole, we contract the same as if "turning away" <note>Latin: *aversi*</note> in some manner, the matter not being well-inspected or explored. If things are sold simply by bulk, every risk belongs to the buyer. *The Lord Doctor Ludwig, Disputations on the Institutes, page 253.* To this category also seem to belong "collected sales" <note>original: *Sammethafft*</note>, not "piece-by-piece" <note>original: *Stuckweiß*</note>, when I buy items in their entirety and not by parts or minutely. *The Lord Doctor Rebhan in his Disputation on the wife as a merchant, thesis 58. See Pinellus on Law 2 of the Code on rescinding a sale, part 3, chapter 2, number 3 and following. Neostadius, Decisions of the Court of Holland, 18. Antonius Augustus.* For a long time, I doubted what it meant to sell or lease by "aversion": I finally came to the opinion that since the matter being conducted was not sufficiently explained, it was called "by aversion." But having shared my opinion with our *Laelius*, I believe that when the number, measure, or weight is not stated, or anything else similar to these, the thing is said to be leased or sold by "aversion." *Laelius* continues, thinking that "aversion" is so named because the buyer "turns away" the risk from the seller and takes it upon himself, even if it is not expressed in words; in this, *Accursius* is mistaken. I agree with this reasoning for the name, as I have found nothing better.

Those things are said to be sold by bulk <note>original: *aversione*</note> or through "aversion" by *Ulpian in Law 4, 'if anyone [sells] wine,' sections 1 and 2 of the Digest on the risk and benefit of a sold thing*, which are sold universally for one price, as if in a pile or a heap, however great and however many they may be; which the Greeks call *athroos* <note>in a mass</note>, and the Germans "selling throughout" <note>original: *überhaupt verkauffen*</note>. Thus *Gaius* explains in *Law 35, 'in those things which are pending,' in the following section;* therefore even if it is a flock. *Digest on contracting a sale. Modestinus* also calls a thing bought in bulk in *Law 62, 'he who [is] of the office,' final section, in the same title.* And see concerning this formula—

Formula from Cujacius, *Observations*, book 8, chapter 15. Also in the *Notes on the Institutes*, title on Buying and Selling. Things are said not to be sold in bulk <note>original: *aversione*</note> when they are not sold for a single price, but individually—for example, at a fixed price for each jar <note>original: *amphora*</note> of wine, each measure <note>original: *metreta*</note> of oil, each bushel <note>original: *modius*</note> of grain, or each pound of silver; and finally, for each individual body or head of a flock counted out. Similarly, a lease can be made in two ways: either so that the work to be done is leased for a total sum <note>original: *aversione*</note>, or provided according to feet or measurements. Rittershusius treats this most extensively on *Law 23 regarding the Rules of Law*, pages 100 and 101.

### 103. Beadle. <term>Apparitor</term>.

Lictors, attendants, **beadles, or city-servants** <note>original: *Büttel, Stadt-Knecht*</note>, as they are commonly called, are not considered "infamous" <note>Historically, certain professions like executioners or skinners were "dishonorable" (*infamis*) and excluded from society; this entry clarifies that beadles held honorable status in Württemberg.</note> in Württemberg; *see* the **Princely Württemberg Provincial Law, part 1, folio 53.**

## ADDITION.

The widow of a lictor <note>A beadle or court attendant.</note> should not be denied admission into a guild of craftsmen. Carpzov, *Decisions 18, number 5*. Whether lictors suffer from "infamy of fact," see number 11.

Regarding what kind of persons should be appointed as official servants, **beadles**, and bailiffs, Zorer teaches in part 2, question 18, number 4065. Whether the official servants and their children should be admitted to trades and guilds, see Zorer, question 18, number 4064. In R. in the Margraviate, the judge's maid takes the place of the **beadle**. In A., when the judge commands someone to pay a fine of 5 florins, one neighbor must seize the other who has incurred it and lead him to prison; if anyone insults him for this, he must pay 10 florins. Regarding attendants, see Schönborner, *Politics*, book 3, chapter 51. Lictors and executioners, whose service is most necessary in a Republic, exist so that if they were lacking, more honorable men would not be forced to stain themselves with this mark—just as among the Lithuanians, this duty is enjoined upon the accuser himself. Alexander Ganguinus and Abraham Ortelius in their *Description of Lithuania*; Cromer, book 16. A beadle or other public messenger, such as field-watchmen <note>original: *Marck-feldschützen*</note> and similar informants, is believed when testifying about a matter relating to the execution of his office, until the contrary is proven by the defendant through witnesses. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 135, number 11.

To place the **Beadle's staff** <note>original: *Büttelstab*</note> into the **Beadle's staff**. See the Nuremberg <note>original: *Norica*</note> Statutes from the years 1479 and 1521. Concerning those who hide in the city or the **Beadle's staff** <note>Used here to mean the area of jurisdiction.</note>, title 1, laws 3 and 4. The word perhaps descends from **to summon** <note>original: *Bütten* or *Citando*</note>, and **Beadle's staff** <note>original: *Büttelstab*</note> stands for the jurisdiction which possesses the right of summoning. Questions could be debated here: who possesses the right to have a **beadle**? Does it also belong to mixed power, or "low jurisdiction" <note>original: *Jurisdictioni bassæ*</note>, as they call it—the lower bailiwick? Does the right to fine belong to the territorial lord or the direct lord <note>original: *Eigenherrn*</note> over one who has beaten a **beadle** at a church festival after the beadle has proclaimed an Edict of Peace?

<column-break/>

...after the proclamation of the "Peace-bid" <note>original: *Friedsbott*</note> by said **beadle**. Concerning the judicial staff which a judge is accustomed to hold in his hands: when *Johannes Botzemius*, sitting in judgment, threw it to the ground in a fit of rage, it was seen as an insult to the Imperial Majesty, of which it was a symbol. Therefore, one of the assessors rose and said, "In the name of the Emperor, I lift this scepter from the ground." This zeal for avenging the insult was so pleasing to Sigismund Augustus that he transferred the right of designating the Judge to the Senate. Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 45, number 5. **To abolish the great staffs.** Master Tabor, *On Translocations*, page 61.

### 104. Benefit for the act. <term>Beneficium pro facto</term>.

In law 46 of the Digest, *On Theft*, in the middle: an action for theft is not valued from the time the lawsuit began, but from when the theft was committed; and has anyone ever been "away" from the benefit (that is, the act, by synecdoche, the species being put for the genus, unless we understand "the subtlety of the act" here) of the thief? This text and reasoning can be applied. Master Richter, *Decision 96, number 106*. Master Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings*, page 109. Johan de Selva wrote *On Benefit*.

### 105. Board Games. <term>Alea</term>.

A small English book by James Balmford, *On the Game of Dice*, was published in 1623. The Emperor Claudius wrote a book on the art of dice. Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, chapter 33. Gisbertus Voetius on the game of dice, as well as Leonhard van Ryssen. Charles Leufener of Meissen describes the game of "Lorz" <note>An obscure historical game.</note> excellently.

Law 1 of the Code, *On Dice-players*, according to Odfredus, is not found in the old manuscript codices of Obrecht and many others; by a singular right, a condition is granted to a defeated player to recover what was paid as if it were not owed <note>original: *quasi indebiti*</note>. Cujacius in his commentary on this title. (By the law of Castile, more providently, the very transfer of ownership of the paid money is prevented; see Filiuccius, treatise 37, chapter 6, number 82.) Namely, if the player is vigilant and files a claim in time; for if he fails to do so, the Magistrate himself ought to recover the money and spend it on public works. Law 1, 2, paragraph 3 of the Code on this title. Cujacius and Faber; Farinaccius, question 109, part 5, number 175 and following. Master Tabor, *Benedict*, 7, syllable 1. They played at dice during dinner. Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, chapter 71. "During dinner we played like old men <note>original: *γεροντικῶς*</note> both yesterday and today," where he speaks of the game of dice, which is constant. Hence Cicero in *On Old Age*: "Let him leave to us the knucklebones and the dice." Savaro on Sidonius, book 1, epistle 8: they played with crystal dice. Petronius, page 78, verse 19. **In Strasbourg, in the Cabinet of Curiosities of Master Schoner, there are twenty-four board-pieces made of unicorn** <note>Historically, "unicorn horn" usually referred to narwhal tusks.</note> **weighing forty-seven Loth** <note>A unit of weight; 47 Loth is approximately 730 grams.</note>. **In Munich, in the Cabinet of Curiosities, there are mother-of-pearl board games, likewise of ivory, coral, amber** <note>original: *Agtstein*</note>, **jasper, gold, and silver—the material from which the board is inlaid. # Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

...are **Princely Portraits**. Regarding dice made from cherry pits, see Pancirollus in *Lost Discoveries* <note>original: "Repertis"</note>, folio 560; Drexelius in *The Gold Mine* <note>original: "Aurifodina"</note>, page 336, at the end. Persius in his *Satire 5* says: "this man ruins himself by the die." Great disadvantages follow the game of dice, according to Mr. Rittershusius in *Sacred Readings* <note>original: "Sacr. Lect."</note>, page 579. It is even permitted to disinherit a son due to an obsession with dice (page 588). Custom can establish that the winner of a game is not held to restitution <note>Returning the money won.</note>, as Rain. teaches in *cons. 3. indag. jur. n.* For if fraud is absent, the equal condition of the players and the uncertain outcome of victory seem generally to protect the game itself, following the argument of Law 1 of the Digest *on pacts*. An edict is proposed against those who corrupt men through dice, whether they provide a hiding place for players in their homes or invite others to play. Mr. Dr. Tabor, in the title of the Digest *on Gamblers* in the *Thread of Ariadne*, following the final Law, section 1, of the Digest *on Gamblers*, notes that some—following Lopez, Garcia, and Molina—incorrectly refer to gaming as a contract. Vincent Filliucius (treatise 37, chapter 4, number 49) argues it is a kind of bet <note>original: "sponsio"</note> in which those playing together mutually promise that they will eventually pay if the matter turns out differently than they claim. They were perhaps misled by a false interpretation of our text, where the business conducted seems to imply that an agreement was made between the players so that money would be acquired by the winner; this is how Faber himself interprets that passage in his *Rationalia*, following Cujacius in his notes on Paul. However, the interpretation of the **Gloss** <note>The standard medieval legal commentary.</note> is commonly and deservedly preferred: since, as a rule, all gambling for money—that is, where the goal is winning or losing money—is an illicit act (Law 2, section 1 of this title) and is forbidden to both the Laity and the Clergy (final Law of the Code, same title; chapter *Clerici* 15 *on the life and honesty of the Clergy*; and the Authentica *interdicimus* and the Gloss there).
<margin>Paragraph on Clergy.</margin> It is almost explicitly numbered among crimes in Law 225, *on the Meaning of Words*. This brings to mind the line from Ovid: "This was no light crime to our ancestors." Or at least it is among the extraordinary offenses in Carpzov, part 3 of *Criminal Practice*, question 134, and Farinacius, question 109, number 56 and following. (A few games are excepted, namely those practiced for the sake of skill <note>original: "virtutis"</note> rather than for profit and money, and these are therefore permitted; see Law 2, section 1, and extensively in Farinacius, question 109, part 3, number 106; C. J. Argent. *on gamblers*, thesis 2; Carpzov in the cited place, number 28.) Legal actions are not granted *from* it, but rather *against* it; see Law 1 of the cited title and Damhouder, chapter 28 *on criminal matters*, numbers 6, 9, 20; Antonius Faber on Law 4, section 1 of this title; and see chapter 11 of the *Decretals on the Excesses of Prelates*. Corrupt morals have prevailed to such an extent that playing dice is allowed everywhere by custom. Chilianus König in *Process*, chapter 57, notes that many are not ashamed to determine that a fellow player is not bound by custom to return losses from the game—except for the casuists (whom Clarus calls "holy men" in the passage soon to be cited), such as Molina (Disputation 513), Lessius (book 2, chapter 26, doubt 3), Filliuci (treatise 37, chapter 5, number 67), Clarus (book 5 of *Sentences*, section *ludus*, number 29), and Caccialupi (treatise *on gaming*, number 29). This is despite the objections of the Abbot, Lancellotus, and others in Clud *on the recovery of undue payments*, chapter 6, number 60; Farinacius, question 109, number 175 and following; Heigius 2, question 10, number 32; and others. Saxon Practice is cited by Webner under the phrase **playing on credit** <note>original: "auf Borg spielen"</note>, and various vagabonds <note>original: "agyrtæ"</note> and sycophants are accustomed to rob men with tricks, 
<column-break/>
following the argument of Law 3, in the verse *deinceps*, where it mentions "by fraud and cleverness" in the Code *on gamblers*. Johann Weinrich wrote elegantly in his *Theoretical-Practical Disputation on Dice*, held at Erfurt in 1622. Note 6 of Mr. Dr. Tabor in his *Sylloge*, book 1 of the *Benedicti*, Benedict 7, number 5: A Bishop must not be a gambler, or as the old translator says, "play at the tables" <note>original: "ad tabulas ludere"</note>; see Mr. Rittershusius in the *Novels*, page 39, number 53. In Civil Law, it is held that in minor offenses, prison may sometimes be assigned in place of punishment and chastisement, as in Law 1, the final section of the Digest *on gamblers*. Mr. Dr. Biccius in the *Golden Rules*, section 1, thesis 184, letter hhh; Friedrich Schenck, *Legal Conclusions*, 98. The penalty of prison was sometimes used by the Praetors, as appears from the cited final section; Bartolus writes that this is the unique place where prison is enjoined as a punishment, contrary to Law 8, section 9 of the Digest *on punishments*. It is also said that he who compels another to play should be led to the **stone-quarries** <note>original: "lautumias"</note>. On what is meant by stone-quarries, see Valentin Wilhelm Forster, book 1 of *Observations*, chapter 20. Dice is the fertile mother of vices: Klock, *on the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 101, numbers 4 and 16. It is forbidden under heavy censure and penalties among the Turks and Saracens (number 14). In France, gambling houses <note>original: "alearum Gymnasia"</note> thrive by public permission (number 17). [th]at it is of such an opinion: on a reel, a rope or cord about 150 fathoms <note>A fathom, or Klafter, is roughly 6 feet.</note> long is wound up. At the end of it hangs a long, round lead block, one span long and weighing about 10 pounds. At the bottom, the lead has a small indentation filled with tallow <note>original: "Unschlitt"</note>. When the lead strikes the bottom, the sand or earth sticks to the lead, or in the grease within the lead. Otherwise, one would not know whether the lead had reached the bottom or not. Thus, the sailors can not only know how deep it is in that place—so they do not run aground on the seabed or sand and become stuck—but they can also recognize, roughly, what land they are approaching (whether it be Egypt, Barbary, or Asia) by the color of the earth or clay that has attached itself to the lead, so that they can steer themselves in good time. *Schweigger, the once famous and spirited Preacher <note>original: "Ecclesiates"</note> of Nuremberg, in his Travelogue <note>original: "Hodœporico"</note>* page 244. *On the lead of Limnaeus in the Public Law <note>original: "J. wished to honor with preeminences, he could find nothing grander to grant than to enroll those four Princes, officials of the Empire, with their respective offices and services. ### 110. Banquet. <note>original: "Convivium"</note>

The word is derived from "good rest" <note>original: "bona quiete"</note>, as if it were "bon-quit." See Matthesius’s *Sermons on the Lust for Sin*, 28, folio 134. At banquets, courtly jests often occur, where foxes, wolves, mice, and cats are often brought to the table. Once, beaver tails were served at the table of a great lord. Regarding the confections so often served, see Antenor in *Salomone*, chapter 10; see below under Guest, Host, and also the word Dwarf.

Showing or Demonstration, the *Certification* <note>original: "die Beſcheinigung"</note>, in so far as it differs from proof properly so called, or *Evidence* <note>original: "der Beweiſung"</note>. Berlich, conclusion 38, number 21, folio 226, in the year 1618, in the case of Werner versus Joachim, Schlauerdachen.

See *Forensic Jurisprudence*, part 1, constitution 17, definition 42. More in Melonius, *Treasury of Law*,

### 114. Letters. <note>original: "Litera / Buchſtaben"</note>

A *Letter* <note>original: "Buchſtab"</note> is a staff or branch from a beech tree <note>The author is referencing a traditional etymology connecting "Buchstabe" (letter) to "Buche" (beech wood) upon which runes were carved.</note>. Regarding the invention of German, Greek, and Latin letters, see Lord Harsdörffer in the *German Secretary*, in the preface, pages 8 and 9.

Eastern letters: Bicc. in *Aureis*, in the preface to the reader. On the High Priest's breastplate, there were no images, but rather 12 letters engraved according to the 12 tribes, which they called "Light and Right" <note>original: "Liecht und Recht," referring to the Urim and Thummim</note>. C. Sigonius and Petr. Cunaeus on the *Hebrew Republic*. The Glogau family carries a letter G with a lily in the center; those from Emerking carry a double hook like a reclining Z. The Seybolds carry an S with split and turned-out ends. The Schnelfingens carry a Z turned to the left. A decision made with a single letter: a letter B with a sheath <note>original: "Scheiden"</note> placed next to it. Lord Harsdörffer in the *Great Stage*, in the appendix, number 266. In seals, one should check if nothing in the letters is broken. Höpingk on the *Law of Seals*, chapter 13, number 5. On the office of letters, their properties, and the distinction from hard letters, see Lord Harsdörffer in the first part of his *Poet's Funnel*. The Genoese, once defeated and mixed among the Venetians, were caught while trying to escape the slaughter and were killed to a man by the clue of a single small word. For the Genoese pronounce "Goat" as *Crabe*, while the Venetians say *Cabre*. Hieronymus, in his *Mosaic Philosophical Commentary*, calls those who learn to spell "syllabarians" <note>original: "Syllabarios"</note>. When Suleiman dismissed the ambassadors of Emperor Ferdinand I, he entrusted them with letters in a long and very narrow volume of indented paper, written in Arabic with gold and blue letters, etc. Höpingk on the *Law of Seals*, chapter 3, number 45.

A defect in a letter voids neither a rescript nor an instrument. Sprenger on *The Modicum*, page 99. If notaries write letters that are not legible, they ought to be removed from office: Brinckmann on *Notaries*, position 48. On the origin of writing and letters, see Justus Georgius Schottel in the *German Main Language*, folio 51. A letter is that which is discerned by the eyes, not that which is seen by the intellect alone. Barbosa, book 10, chapter 22, axiom. Letters carved into stone do not constitute proof. Graff, book 1, chapter 4, question 7; Menoch., presumption 59, number 1, and the six following, where a distinction is also made. Angelus says that a rescript is weakened if the first letters are not long, as in the law *bene a Zenone* in the Code regarding four-year prescription.

### 115. Bees. see Virgin. Bees. <note>original: "Bien. vide Jungfrau. Apes."</note>

Bees do not "make" the honey, but rather gather it together. According to Zeiller <note>Zeiller, *Centuriae*, question 33, page 167</note>. Swarms of bees are a bad omen, as Lipsius teaches in his commentary on Tacitus's *Annals*, Book 12, Chapter 4. See also Lindenbrog on Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 18, section 74; add to this Dio, Book 54, page 611. Freinsheim clearly shows the variety of opinions on this in his commentary on Florus, Book 2, Chapter 45.

The industrious little honey-bird, the delicate maiden-folk, the species of golden flies, sets out at the break of day on its floral journey and sucks the sugary sap from the sweetened trees. It frequently chooses the "Masses," <note>likely referring to botanical clusters or perhaps a specific plant type</note> the honeycombs, and the wax to sweeten with sugar. It gathers from the tears of little herbs and hums with gentle tones. The flower remains unharmed, though the bee is equipped with a sting. Much of this is from Mr. Harsdörffer in the third part of the *Poetic Funnel* <note>original: "Poeten-Trichters," a famous 17th-century manual on German poetry</note>, page 148 and following. *From whence are bees named? Their utility is to be judged by their honey and wax.* <note>original: "Apes unde dictæ? Earum utilitas ex melle conjicienda est & cera."</note> Klock, *On the Treasury*, Book 2, Chapter 7, number 5. The care of bees, number 2; their delicate limbs, industry, and generation, number 4. Their King <note>Early modern writers often identified the Queen bee as a King</note> lays aside his sting, number 12. The King of the bees is distinguished by clear marks of nature, number 11. The wisdom of bees, their virginal integrity, diligence, loyalty, and reverence for the King, numbers 7, 8, 9; their learning, number 10; and honey-making in the skull of a lion, page 14 <note>A reference to the biblical story of Samson</note>. Regarding honey tithes, see "Shepherd’s Staff." Every wall can be equipped with bee-baskets <note>beehives</note> so that if someone were to break in and knock the baskets over, he and all those present would be driven back by the enraged bees. Zeiller, *Epistles*, Century 5, page 506. The fertile land of Machakies <note>likely a reference to a region in the Americas or "the Indies"</note> is evidenced by the fact that when an inhabitant goes out into the woods and makes a hole with a hatchet in the first tree he comes to, five or six measures of honey run out, as pure as the mead we have here. Those same bees, however, are quite small and do not sting. Levinus Hulsius. Mr. Harsdörffer treats bees in part 2, XC: their fruit (9), their hearing (12), their form (11), their interpretation and royal government (9), and their voice (13). *Regarding the little bee, see the "Golden Mine" by Drexel, pages 87, 88, 89.* <note>original: "De apicula vide Aurifod. Drexelii"</note> The scent of roses is said to make bees lively and cheerful. Zeiller, Century 2, *Epistles*, page 476. Bees are driven away by an echo. Zeiller, regarding a swarm of bees hidden for three years, Century 4, *Epistles*, page 613. Simon Majolus reports in Volume 2 of *Canicular Days*, Colloquy 2 and 3: When a master or mistress of a house dies, if the bees are not immediately moved to another place, they usually die. Regarding honey-dew on an oak tree, Zeiller, Century 4, *Epistles*, page 609. *Regarding Saxon Law* <note>original: "De Jure Saxonico"</note>: if a swarm of bees flies out of one man’s house or courtyard to his neighbor’s, the neighbor has the right to keep the swarm 

<column-break/>

rather than the one who follows it, because the bee is a "wild worm" <note>term: "wilder Wurm" — in old legal contexts, a "worm" could refer to any small creature or insect; "wild" indicates it is not fully domesticated and thus subject to different property laws</note>. Municipal Law <note>original: "Weichbild," a code of municipal laws</note>, article 120, and the gloss there; see also below. If bees are in a hive in the forest, they belong to the owner of the hive; but if someone encloses them in a tree, they also belong to him, and whoever steals them is a thief. Schneidewein, *On the Institutes of Roman Law*, section on bees, number 6. The bee is a wild worm. Berlich, 5th Conclusion, 50, number 2. How bees are captured and brought under control, ibid. number 10. *A swarm of bees that has flown out of my hive is rightfully seized and enclosed by me, even under Saxon law, if it has settled on the branch of another's tree extending into my garden.* <note>original: "Apum examen, quod ex alveo meo evolavit..."</note> Carpzov, Decision 295.

### 116. Balmond. False Guardian. <note>original: "Balmond. Falsus tutor."</note>

*Thus the ancient Teutons called a false guardian.* <note>original: "Ita falsum tutorem dixere veteres Teutones"</note> Nauclerus, Cujacius, and Crusius. Draco, *On Patricians*, page 244. Wehner, in *Practical Observations*, under the word "Balmond."

### 117. Bottomry. <note>term: "Bodmar, Bodmerey" — A historical maritime contract where a ship's owner borrows money for a voyage, using the ship's hull as collateral. If the ship is lost, the debt is canceled; if it returns, the loan is repaid with high interest.</note>

"Bodmar," or "bodo," says Henisch (f. 415), comes from "Voyt" or "Vogt" <note>steward/overseer</note>, or else from "Boden" <note>bottom/floor</note>, which is to say, "to nourish." *Therefore, a Bodmar is a prefect of provisions or a steward.* <note>original: "Bodmar igitur est præfectus ciborum seu œconomus."</note> The late Mr. Harsdörffer, in *Specimens of German Philology*, page 265.
A singular type of nautical interest <note>loan</note> among merchants is called "Bodemeria," commonly "to take out or pay out on bottomry," *by which, in the hope of greater profit, a certain sum of money is paid to the Ship’s Master on this condition: that if the ship remains safe, the sum is returned with interest, the bottom of the ship having been left as a pledge of mortgage in the meantime; if the ship is lost, the capital also perishes.*

### 118. Pasha. <note>original: "Bassa."</note>

From whence the Turkish officers called "Bashas" derive their name. Berens, *Feudal Disputation 2*, thesis 1, at the end; see also Georgievicz, *On the Customs of the Turks*, folio 41.
*Among the Turks, from the order of the Beylerbeys and the purple-clad Pashas—of whose number four preside over the most serious councils—the eldest possesses the Prince's casket and gem, and is called the Vizier, and dictates decrees to the Scribes and Notaries.* <note>original: "Apud Turcas ex ordine Beglerbegorum..."</note> Paul Jovius, Book 4, *Histories*, page 288. For the current condition of Pashas and Beylerbeys in Turkey, see Aimoin in *History of the Franks*, Book 5; Bizarus, *Genoese History*, Book 3; Limnaeus, *Public Law*, Book 4, Chapter 1, number 8.

Knipschild, *On Imperial Cities*, Book 4, Chapter 1, number 14.
*In Basel, students formerly took part in the election of the Rector.* Limnaeus, *Public Law*, Book 8, Chapter 5, number 10. Christian Wurstisen (or Urstisius)...

...Stisius writes in the Basel Chronicle. *The charm, benevolence, humanity, and hospitality of Basel.* <note>original: "Basileæ amœnitas, benevolentia, humanitas, hospitalitas"</note> Rittershusius in *New Works*, page 723; also Mr. Dr. Leonhard Wurffbein in *Historical Relations*, part 6, page 205. Concerning the bridge there, the Minster <note>The Basel Münster, the city's cathedral</note> and its lead-covered roof, and the great linden tree, which is said to be 316 feet in circumference, and the 42 trees around the church, see Zeiller in *German Itinerary*, page 253.

Basel was afflicted by fire and earthquake, <note>original: "Basilea igne & terræ motu afflicta fuit"</note> and at that time, 46 castles perched upon cliffs in the diocese of Basel alone collapsed, according to the custom of that age. See more in Besold, *Politics*, book 1, last chapter, number 12, volume 1.

In earlier times, the wind blew down the tennis house <note>original: "Ballhaus," a building for ball games popular with the nobility</note> there. From this great earthquake it may have come to pass that near Osterbaden, not far from Basel, dice have been found for uncountably many years. Whether perhaps in Roman times a dice-maker lived there and left behind such a great quantity, which were then scattered by an earthquake so that they are still found under the earth today, is not precisely known. Dr. Remigius Fesch <note>A famous 17th-century Basel lawyer and art collector</note> also showed me an image of Plato in stone and many coins of the Emperors, which he bought up little by little for small sums from peasants who found them in the fields. Just as in the year 1648 in Augst, an hour from Basel, the innkeeper there found two gold rings under the earth and sold them for a pittance, mentioning that he still finds all sorts of coins there. See more regarding these found coins in J. W. Auer, *On the Right of Mintage*, chapter 11, thesis 53. In the "Little Basel" <note>The section of the city on the right bank of the Rhine</note> is the house of Vitus Amerbach and a great treasure of old coins. > ->from which you can see the groves, fields, and little mountains,<-
> ->from which you behold the twin towers and city walls,<-
> ->and hear the harmonies and sweet-sounding melodies.<-

> <note>original Latin: "Julius Ecclesiæ dum præfuit ecce Secundus / dum sceptra Imperii Maximilianus habet / hoc opus excisum, quo Rhenum cernere amœnum / quo nemora & campos monticulosque potes / quo geminas turres & mœnia conspicis urbis / Concentus audis, dulcisonosque modos."</note>

From the great oak that Zeiller mentions, which was formerly by St. Peter’s, tables and plates are now to be found in the marksmen's guild house. In the Town Hall <note>Rathaus</note> there is a panel of the Passion painted so artistically that the Elector of Bavaria wanted to give 4000 Ducats for it; however, the people of Basel did not want money, but desired a piece of land in exchange. Mr.

Remigius Fesch showed me the portraits of many noble painters, such as Raphael of Urbino, Albrecht Dürer (as he is depicted in the Chapel of St. Luke in Rome), Michelangelo, Titian Uccello, and the knight Antonio Tempesta—all the painters in Rome. Also a portrait of Holbein <note>original: "Holzbaum," a variation of Hans Holbein the Younger's name</note> of Basel, who later went to England, and who so skillfully painted the precious and expensive Passion table in the Basel Town Hall. On the Bishop of Basel, see Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 318.

In Basel, the clocks always strike the hour one hour earlier than in the countryside and elsewhere. This is because the city was once to be betrayed at 12 o'clock, and when it should have struck 12, it struck 1 instead, whereby the city was saved; since then, they have let the clock strike thus. <note>This refers to the famous "Basel Time" which persisted until the late 18th century.</note> On the tower of the Rhine Bridge there, a figure sticks out its tongue every minute. <note>The "Lällenkönig," a clockwork head that mocked the "Little Basel" side of the river.</note> The *Danse Macabre* <note>original: "Todten-Tanz"</note> at the Dominican monastery—where sermons are preached in French twice a week—is very long and beautiful, of which the following is written: *In Basel, in the cemetery of the Dominicans, among other things worth seeing, an elegant painting is displayed, commonly called the "Dance of the Dead," representing in a long series the fragile fate of the entire human race struggling with death; by which law death summons persons of every sex, age, and condition, leads them away, drags the willing and unwilling into the shadows, and makes scepters equal to hoes.* <note>original: "Basileæ in cæmeterio Dominicanorum... sceptraque ligonibus æquet."</note> In Basel, 16 students are supported by the legacy of Erasmus of Rotterdam. Students of Philosophy each receive 40 florins and a place at the communal table. Students of other faculties receive 80 florins. In the year 1648, at St. Peter's Square, the *privileges granted to the city by various Emperors* <note>original: "Privilegia Civitati à variis Impp. concessa"</note>—stating that they may not be tried in courts elsewhere, etc.—were read aloud by the City Secretary. This occurs every Sunday before the Feast of St. John, and the Council is appointed the Saturday before. A wreath was then placed upon the head of the City Secretary, and he then read out how all the heads of government and council members were newly appointed. Afterward, a councilman resigned; he presented to the citizens what a blessing it was to have a faithful government. The city servants wear black and white; they wore wreaths on their arms at that time and held yellow staves above them. All officials must wear very high, pointed hats, an ell high, <note>An "ell" (Elle) was a traditional unit of length, roughly 24 inches.</note> and robes of honor. The councilmen, professors, clergy, and the beadle all go about in such habits. If one of the students does not attend the Rector's installation, he is punished; at that time, 24 were punished, each by 3 Batzen. <note>term: <term>Batzen</term> (a silver coin used in Switzerland and Southern Germany)</note>

### 121. Purse. <note>original: "Bursa"</note>

A prince ought to punish the heirs, and not the purse. <note>i.e., fines should not be the primary punishment if it ruins the estate</note> Klock, volume 1, counsel 24, number 22. On the treasury or purse: counsel 29, number 190. Whence the name "purse" comes: Limnæus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 1, number 75, at length. *Bursa* with a diphthong is a money-bag. Thus Peter of Blois uses "Bursa" in Epistle 74. The Greek *byrsa* means a hide or leather. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 43, chapter 20.

## C.

### 1. Calendar, Almanac. <note>original: "Calender, Allmanach"</note>

We call it a *Calendarium* <note>Calendar</note> because the individual *Kalends* are noted in it: and because the *Kalends* are the first day of the Month, and in the distribution of the Month, the greater portion of the days fell under the name of the *Kalends*. Martinius in the *Philological Lexicon* under the word *Calendarium*. Astrologers commonly call it an *Almanac*, which is an Arabic word, as denoted by the article *Al*; some say it is semi-Greek from the word *men*, which denotes a Month; but it seems more probable to me that the word is purely Arabic, which Schindler also favors; and as Martinius proves in the same entry from Porphyry, the word is very ancient and was known to the ancient Egyptians.

Today we have two Calendars: the Old and the New.

The Old Calendar is used in the Imperial Chamber Court at Speyer for issuing legal processes: so decided on July 14, Anno 1583. Decisions or Precedents of the Imperial Chamber, letter C, under the word *Calendarium*.

## 2. Calvinists. *Calvinistæ.*

Regarding Calvinism and Calvinists, see the treatise on what occurred in Marburg regarding the Reformation. Yet they are not to be burdened with unfair hatred because of this, number 33.

# Treasures of Practice, Augmented

**Chimney** <note>original: "Caminus"</note>, a smoke-hole, from the French *chaud*, meaning hot. Quite similar is the Hebrew *chom*, hot. From this comes the Arabic *Chamim*, meaning a bath or a heated room <note>original: "hypocaustum"</note>. Now, it is generally used by us for the structure that receives smoke; regarding this, see Junius in *Nomenclature*. It is a *Caminus* to Cicero; a *spiramentum* <note>vent</note> or *fumarium* <note>smoke-hole</note> to Pliny; an *infumibulum* <note>funnel</note> to Martial and others; and in Greek, $\kappa\alpha\pi\nu\eta$ <note>original: "kapne"; a smoke-vent</note>. In German: smoke-hole, chimney <note>original: "Rauchloch, Schornstein"</note>. In Italian *Camino*, French *Cheminée*, Spanish *Chimenea*, and English *Chimney*. It is also a stone or iron plate, like a wall against the hearth, by which the fire is sustained; hence we call it a **fire-wall** <note>original: "Feuermuare"</note>, or "smoke-prop" <note>original: "Schornstein"</note> from *Schorn*, which means to support or prop up; derived, as I believe, from *securus* <note>secure</note>, so as to make the fire secure or safe. In English, *shore* means to prop up or support, and refers to a fulcrum. On the terms **Schorn** and **Schornstein**, see the extensive notes of Justus Georg Schottel in *The Main Language of the Germans, folio 1408, and folio 512, sections 688 and 689*. To some, **Schoren** is a shovel <note>original: "pala, ein Schauffel"</note>.

Regarding chimneys, which are hollow vents above the fire (from which the Belgians get the word *Kave*), one does not easily find mention in ancient laws. Sprenger treats chimneys extensively in *The Law of Buildings, page 70 and following*. Philander, in his commentary on *Book 7 of Vitruvius, chapter 3*, gathers that the bedrooms and inner chambers of the ancients did not have vents or "throats" <note>original: "gullas"</note> where the smoke might exit—what are commonly called chimneys. However, almost all agree they could be called *infumibula* in Latin. For Cicero, a "bright chimney" <note>original: "Caminus luculentus"</note> meant something else in his *Letters to Friends, book 7*; as did Suetonius in his life of *Aulus Vitellius*, describing a dining room catching fire from the "heat of the chimney." Therefore, I believe the ancients soaked their wood in olive-oil dregs <note>original: "amurca"</note> so that it would burn without the annoyance of smoke, as Cato writes in *On Agriculture, chapter 30*. These were called *akapna* <note>original: "$\alpha\kappa\alpha\pi\nu\alpha$"; smoke-free</note>, for *kapna* signifies smoke. Galen mentions these among others in *Book 1 on Antidotes*.

Furthermore, if anyone investigates Roman fortifications more diligently, they will understand at once how those prudent and well-advised people protected themselves from the cold. Specifically, in a subterranean structure, there was a long arch, and from it, inside the walls, masonry channels were intentionally left running to the upper floors. These had "nostrils" <note>vents</note> opening into all the places where they wished to provide heat, which were covered with removable lids. That arch was partly heated by burning wood (for we find ashes and soot there) and partly filled with boiling water. Thus, through the channels, once the vents were opened, the halls, dining rooms, bedrooms, and similar parts of the building received warm vapor. I believe Placidus the Grammarian understood this when, explaining what a **Zeta** <note>a heated room or suite</note> was, he recorded that the ancients, by letting cold water into a subterranean arch through molds, cooled all the small parts of the house through the emission of a gentle vapor of air. For Galen, in *Book 9, section 10 of The Method of Medicine*, mentions this could be achieved via a channel <note>original: "euripo"</note> when he teaches how to prepare the surrounding air for those with summer fevers—namely, so that a breeze might blow from some channel. See Martinius in *Philological Lexicon* under the word *Caminus*, and Johann Hering in the *Appendix to the Treatise on Mills, regarding Chimneys*.

<column-break/>

In our own age, shrewd tax collectors have devised a toll or tribute to be exacted from the individual hearths and chimneys of houses, commonly called for this reason a **Chimney-tax** <note>original: "Caminarium"</note>, **from every hearth or fire-place**, as witnessed by Hermann Lather in *Treatise on Census, book 1, chapter 2, number 2*. Compare Warnemund ab Ehrenberg in *Book on Subsidies and Burdens of Subjects*. Erasmus of Rotterdam mentions this in *Adages, chiliad 1, century 9, adage 12*. From this, it is called **Hearth-right** <note>original: "Herdrecht"</note> when peasants or subjects pay something to the Lord by reason of their place and hearth; see Gylman, *book 1, decision 12, number 18, folio 174 and 186*. And it is called **Hearth-rent** <note>original: "Herdzinß"</note> which is paid by reason of the ground-area, **because of a hearth-place and site**. Also belonging here are the **Smoke-hens** <note>original: "Rauchhennen"</note>, which one gives from the houses and hearths. Similarly, in ancient times, they called that heavy tribute **Column-tax** <note>original: "Columnarium"</note>, imposed by Roman Generals on the Asiatic and other provinces during the times of the Civil Wars, which they exacted for every column and entrance of the houses; the latter were called **Entrance-taxes** <note>original: "Hostiaria"</note>. See Hering at the cited location, number 67.

->ADDITION.<-

**Shrove Tuesday and Smoke-hens** denote the height of jurisdiction and absolute power <note>original: "merum Imperium"</note>, according to Klock, *volume 2, consultation 7, number 159*; however, see *number 259* and *consultation 98, number 15*.

From the houses and farm-sites, **Smoke-hens** are given, and they are so called because those hens fly up high and there they rest and nest; therefore, they signify the "height" of the Law, and in cases of doubt, all things being equal, they denote absolute jurisdiction. See Tileman de Benign, *Practical Observations, Pentecost 5, observation 1*; Hering on *Mills, question 33*; Hufan on *Serfs, chapter 6, number 64*. See more in Mundius, *On Duties and Honors, chapter 2, number 433*. Zorer, in *part 2, question 5, number 397*, establishes that such **deliveries often signify no jurisdiction or subjection, but merely a recognition of the landlord**, or that it was **simply agreed upon** in a prior contract. See Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 6, chapter 4, number 20*. **Regarding house- and yard-lock, chimney- and smoke-prop money** <note>original: "Haus- und Hofschloß, Camin- und Schornsteingeld"</note>, see Simon Pistor, *consultation 19, book 1*; Schurff, *consultation 23, number 3, chapter 3*; Warems ab Ehrenberg; and Bornit, *On the Treasury, book 5, chapter 7*. In the city of **Segovia**, there is a **chimney made of fine porphyry stone**. See Zeiller, *Itinerary of Spain, page 202*. In **Madrid**, the **chimney in the Audience Chamber is made of jasper**. See the same, *page 228*. Regarding the *Zeta* and whether it was known to the Greeks. For a definition of a chimney, see Sprenger, *On the Law of Buildings, page 83*.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical entries under the letter 'C,' transitioning from the discussion of chimneys and hearths to the legal and etymological definition of a Chamber (Camera), specifically the Imperial Chamber Court of the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

# Lit. C.

**Chamber** <note>original: "Camera"</note> refers to a room, specifically one that is vaulted <note>original: "camerato"</note>. A room of this kind is particularly suitable for the safer keeping of money. Therefore, it signifies a physical location in the Testament of Charlemagne as recorded by Einhard: *The description begins here, as does the list of money found in his Chamber on that day.* Among the Germans, **Chamber** <note>original: "Cammer"</note> signifies a cell, a place in which we store or set something aside, a bedroom, a treasury, a granary, or a dining room; it also refers to a Court, a Hall of Justice, or a Tribunal <note>original: "Dicasterium"</note>. Thus, the **Imperial Chamber** <note>original: "Camera Imperialis"</note> is called the Tribunal of the Roman Empire. See Matthias Martini in his *Philological Lexicon* under the word *Camera*, page 305. On the Imperial Chamber, one may also consult Tobias Paurmeister and Matthias Stephani in their treatises on jurisdiction, as well as Hegius (Book 1, Question 9), Friederich Mindanus in his preface on legal processes, Carpzov in the *Capitulations* (Chapter 9, number 13 and following), Johannes Calvinus <note>Johannes Kahl, a jurist, not the theologian</note> on procedure (folio 152), and myself on appeals (Chapter 2, number 21, etc.). Also see Valentin Riemer in his treatise on jurisdiction (Rule 26), François Hotman in *Franco-Gallia* (Chapter 27, Dispute 18, volume 4), and the Basel Disputations.

Regarding the Jurisdiction of the Senate of Speyer <note>The city where the court was often seated</note> over Chamber officials, see the treatise by Petrus Denaisius and the *Apology of the City*, which is said to have been written by Dominicus Arumaeus <note>original: "D. Albada"</note>.

The Imperial Chamber is often looked upon with contempt because of its long legal processes; for this reason, the Imperial Aulic Council <note>original: "Aula Caesarea"; the Emperor's personal court</note> is today preferred over it. Relevant to this are the traditional accounts in the *Consilia* <note>Legal opinions</note>, part 2, number 271, folio 375, and number 301, folio 362. The author of said counsel says: "Our estimation of that great and supreme Tribunal of the Empire has always been, and rightly is and shall be, most honorable, to such an extent that we consider a man hardly to be regarded as good if his opinion of it differs. Yet the strength of no college, however highly praised, is equal to sustaining such a great burden." Hence, that **Saxon Squire** <note>original: "Sächsische Juncker"</note>, speaking of his wicked and peace-breaking business—which he did not dare to trust to a bribe in court—said: **"He wanted to hang his case on the very same nail,"** <note>original: "Er wolle syne Sache ock an densülven Nagel hangen"</note> because he had conceived a certain hope that if the cause were brought there, it would be settled not in this century, but only in the next.

And regarding the fact that in the Imperial Chamber new precautions are always being taken and lawsuits proceed from rigid formulas, see Lindeman's *History of Law* (thesis 107) and Tennagel on *Process* at the end, where it is noted that the clause **"in every better way"** <note>original: "omni meliori modo"; a legal safety phrase</note> is not observed in the Chamber. On the Parliaments of France, Etienne Pasquier treats the subject extensively in his *Researches* (Chapters 2 and 4, Book 2).

I wish to add here a rather elegant question discussed by a certain anonymous author: **Whether, upon the death of His Imperial Majesty, the jurisdiction of the Imperial Chamber expires or is held in suspense?** Arguments are not lacking for either side; indeed, for the affirmative, they argue:

1. It is persuaded that it is suspended, but does not expire, by the **Golden Bull of Charles IV** (Title 5), where, when the Empire is vacant, the power of exercising judgments in the other Provinces is granted to the **Count Palatine** and the **Duke of Saxony**,

Besoldus Volume I.

<column-break/>

Electors, as **Vicars of the Empire** and Administrators, by virtue of their Privilege. This Right of Vicariate, regarding the administration of justice, has nowhere been abolished.

2. This is known to have been observed after the death of **Maximilian I** in the year 1519. Nor can anyone object that at that time the Chamber's legal inquiry was different than it is today, or that it was established by the Empire alone. For I will reply that it was erected with the consent of the Electors and other Estates of the Empire, as the Preface to the **Chamber Ordinance of the Year 1495** clearly shows. **And although at that time, for the maintenance of the Chamber Court, fees <note>original: "Sportulæ"</note> were placed proportionately on the cases; nevertheless, in the year 1500, it was decreed that the Lord Judge and the Assessors should be paid their salaries from the money falling from the ordained aid <note>taxation</note> of the Holy Empire, and the aforementioned fees should henceforth be discontinued because of the many various complaints that had come in. Afterward, however, and in the year 1507, Emperor Maximilian granted that all and every revenue of the Chamber Court Chancery, including those from fiscal matters and fines then existing or that might occur in the future nine years, should be used for the maintenance of the Chamber Court. But since such fiscal and Chancery revenues for the first year did not reach so high, the Estates offered to pay from their own money for the aforementioned time to make up for the deficiency. The Recesses <note>original: "Abschied"; official decrees of the Imperial Diet</note> clearly demonstrate all of this.** Therefore, both at that time and later, it was the Court of both His Imperial Majesty and the Estates, and sustained by the same, nor was it altered in any way afterward during the life of Maximilian, so that it remained then as it is now: not the peculiar property of His Imperial Majesty alone, but simultaneously the Hall of Justice of the Empire.

3. The Chamber represents the Emperor not only regarding contentious jurisdiction (Gail, Book 1, observation 1, number 7; Mynsinger 4, observation 5), but the processes also emanate in the name of His Imperial Majesty as the **Head**. (Gail 1, observation 14, number 1; Chamber Ordinance, part 3, title 12; see also Petrus Denaisius, Chamber Court, 125, § 4; Augustinus Beroius, question 1). To this Court, the Lord Judge and the Assessors are bound by a peculiar Oath. But what no longer exists cannot be represented; and when the Head is missing, the dignity and jurisdiction—which existed concretely in the deceased Emperor—can hardly remain intact, so that jurisdiction adhering to his person is deemed extinct when the person dies. (Petrus Barbosa on the law *quia tale* 14, number 51, regarding the dissolution of marriage). A Republic can hardly be considered whole; for the Prince, as the Head of the Republic, no less than the head of a man, constitutes one whole and integral unit together with the other members. (Menochius, counsel 1153, number 8). It is also involved in difficulties as to whose name the processes should be decreed and sent out under, since surely a dead Emperor can no longer command anything—unless we reply here that the jurisdiction of the Empire is not extinct, but for the time being transferred to the **Count Palatine** and the **Duke of Saxony**...

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law
### Page 154

...the Electors, who are devoted to filling the roles of the future Emperor in the administration of Justice.

4. This opinion is not lacking in legal reasoning, according to the law <note>original: "l. diem functo. de Off. Assess."</note>, through which text Baldus stated that if a Governor dies before his office is finished, the full salary is still owed. This is supported by Luis de Molina, Juan Parlador, and others. Just as the jurisdiction of Vicars <note>A "vicar" is a representative or deputy of a bishop.</note>, however much it is part of their ordinary power, usually expires upon the death of the Bishop who appointed them, as elegantly explained by Barbosa.

5. Finally, to confirm this opinion with an example, it is also held in the city of Rome that all offices are suspended until the election of a new Pope <note>original: "Pontificis"</note>. This is found in the Clementine decrees <note>original: "Clem. ne Romani"</note>, where only the function of the officials of the Apostolic Chamber <note>The administrative department of the Papal government.</note> is continued after the death of the Pope. This was established so that the temporal revenues belonging to the Roman See—without which spiritual matters cannot long survive—are not neglected in the meantime. It is added that the officials of the Apostolic See seem to remain because the See itself "does not die" <note>original: "Apostolicæ sedis, quæ non moritur"</note>. Specifically, however, the Office of the Auditors of the Rota <note>The highest ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church.</note> is said to expire or fall silent upon the death of the Pope, regardless of whether they had already begun to hear a case. This was the view of Cardinal Zabarella, though some suggest this only applies when the case is "entire" <note>meaning no action has yet been taken</note>. Similarly, the power given to "conservators" regarding business not yet started is extinguished by the death of the Pope.

1. On the negative side <note>The opposing legal argument</note>, it is strongly urged that the Imperial Chamber possesses <term>ordinary jurisdiction</term> <note>Jurisdiction that belongs to an office by law, rather than being a personal favor granted by a ruler.</note>. The Auditors of the Pope or a Prince are considered "Ordinary" judges. Now, ordinary jurisdiction by no means vanishes upon the death of the grantor. It is different for <term>delegated jurisdiction</term> <note>Power "loaned" to an individual for a specific task, which usually ends when the person who loaned it dies.</note>, provided the matter has not yet been started.

2. This holds all the more because His Imperial Majesty and the Empire (or the Estates of the Empire together) conferred jurisdiction upon the Chamber. The Lord Judge and the Chamber Assessors are bound to its protection by a peculiar Oath. Furthermore, it is a legal tradition that the Empire never dies <note>original: "Imperium nunquam mori"</note>; indeed, it endures perpetually even if an Emperor has passed away. It has also become law that judges elected by the people are not dismissed even if the Lord who confirmed them dies.

<column-break/>

3. It is of the greatest interest to the Republic, the Estates of the Empire, and the litigants that the Lord Judge and the Assessors continue their duty in administering justice without any change or suspension. Otherwise, a foul confusion would follow if experienced Assessors, highly trained in Doctrine and Practice, were disturbed and replaced by unskilled and less-informed men. This was also weighed by Pierre Grégoire. Truly, the situation is very different now than in the times of Maximilian I <note>Emperor from 1493–1519; he founded the Imperial Chamber Court.</note>, when this court was not yet burdened with such a multitude of cases; back then, it did not have a fixed seat but was "ambulatory" <note>meaning the court moved from city to city with the Emperor.</note>.

4. If one wishes to look at examples here, the Kingdom of France <note>original: "Regnum Galliæ"</note> comes to mind. In France, the Courts and other magistrates nevertheless retain their command and power when the Prince dies. Thus, when a King has passed, they do not change their expression or even wear mourning clothes <note>A symbolic gesture showing that the Law remains "awake" even if the King sleeps.</note>, although it is customary for the new Prince to confirm their authority with a new decree. Jean Bodin <note>A famous French political philosopher.</note> considers this the firmest foundation of the French state. This is also attested by various legal experts like Chasseneuz and Pierre Barbosa. For this reason, the counselors of the Parliament of Dauphiné are called "perpetual."

5. Furthermore, legal authorities hold that a judge created by a Prince—even if appointed "at the Prince's pleasure" (a will which is otherwise extinguished by death)—does not cease to be a judge upon the death of that Prince, and he should not be revoked by the successor. It is suggested that this was adopted for "public utility." In our current hypothesis, hardly anyone who cares for the Commonwealth would deny that public utility demands that the course of this most praised Tribunal not be interrupted by any innovation or delay.

6. There are many other inconveniences that would arise from a suspension, both for the Lord Archbishop of Mainz, Prince-Elector...

The Imperial Chamber Court cannot be approached by reason of things subject to different jurisdictions, but the action must be instituted in the forum under which the greater part of the assets is located. **Question:** Does the Emperor or the Emperor’s supreme court have concurrent jurisdiction with the **Imperial Chamber Court**? Since, however, from the final cause of the establishment of the Chamber Court (namely, that the Emperor, entangled in deciding the disputes of private citizens, could less attend to the public cares of the Empire, *Chamber Ordinances*, part 2, title 34), it clearly appears that the mind of Emperor Maximilian I, who instituted it in 1495 at the Diet of Worms, was not that it should be in the fullness or extinction of his own power, but that it should take upon itself a portion of his labor. See Becker in *Public Law*, page 74, subsequent sections; and there cited: Stirn *On the Constitution of Princes*, title 12, section 6; likewise Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 2, throughout, who in number 60 determines that the Emperor cannot call to himself lawsuits and cases pending in the Chamber. The judgment of the Chamber is to be preserved by the Estates of the Empire, according to Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, chapter 2, number 90. Chamber decisions ought to be considered and reputed as common law, based on law 1, "On the Constitution of Princes." Gail, 1. *Observations*, 1. number 7 and observation 41, numbers 4 and 5. Strasbourg, 2. counsel 86, number 30. Barbosa, book 16, chapter 44, axiom 3, where it is said that Besold’s view prevails in sentences declaring the Law, but not in sentences deciding the facts, because in this case even the smallest circumstance can change the law.

*Regarding the improvement of the Chamber Court Ordinance, see the "Discourse on what might come up for deliberation at the current Imperial Diet of 1663," letter E. 2. 3. Jacob Blumen wrote the "Newest Chamber Process," as did Johann Beliz.*

Regarding the Imperial Chamber Court, see Otto in *Public Law*, 152; Schmuck’s fourth *Forensic Skirmish*, number 12. Against that august bulwark of revived Justice you may see the bites of serpents: <note>original: "Spirae lites spirant, nunquam expirant, litigantes diu sperant, nunquam aspirant." The Imperial Chamber, according to Baldus, is the "digestive science of laws," without which theory turns out to be largely mutilated, lame, and dangerous.

### §. Chamber Fief, Man-money, Fief of the Chamber.

A **Chamber Fief** <term>Feudum Camerae: A type of fief where the vassal receives an annual payment from the lord's treasury rather than a grant of land.</term> is said to be that which consists in the right to money, to be demanded annually from the Chamber—that is, the treasury of the Lord (or what is the same, from the toll in a certain place or from another pecuniary income, which is usually brought into the Chamber of that Lord). Zasius *On Fiefs*, part 12, number 31. Schrader *On Fiefs*, part 2, chapter 3, number 81. Gottfried Anton, *Feudal Disputations* 1, thesis 4, letter b. Based on chapter 1 at the end, "who is called a Duke," 2. F. 10. and chapter 1 at the beginning, "on the nature of fiefs," 2. F. 68. Rosenthal *On Fiefs*, chapter 2, question 57, number 2. And it is commonly called <note>original: "ein Cammerlehen oder Manngeld"</note> *a Chamber Fief or Man-money.* Gottfried Anton in the cited place.

### 6. Chamber Estates. Demesne Lands. <note>original: "Cammergüter. Bona domanialia."</note>

These goods are otherwise called "Domanialia," from the French *Domaine* <note>meaning "Demesne" or "Domain"</note>: because they were always retained under the Lordship of the ancient Kings or Princes and were never customarily granted to others. See Philip Paschalis, *On Paternal Power*, part 1, chapter 1, number 85; and regarding these, see Zacharias Friedenrich, *Political Books*, chapter 21, page 235, etc. From the beginning, in almost every Republic, there were public goods destined for public use; Princes lived contentedly on the revenues from these and did not burden their subjects with taxes <note>original: "subsidiis"</note>. See my work *On the Treasury*, chapter 1, number 5, volume 1, and number 7, final verse. Likewise, in the same treatise, chapter 1, number 3, regarding the difference and the diverse legal status of the goods which Princes hold, I treat several matters. On this same subject, one may see Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, book 2, chapter 44: *That the Emperors previously had their own estates* <note>original: "Daß die Kayser hievor der Zeit eigne Güter gehabt"</note>, as is gathered from Caspar Lerch, *On the Equestrian Order*, page 25. Concerning the Patrimony of the King of Scotland, see the *Laws of the Kingdom of Scotland* by the Prince.

### ADDITION.

It seems more true that Demesne Lands can be claimed by a subject of the Empire through "immemorial time" <note>a legal concept where a right is held so long that no one remembers the beginning of it</note>. Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 33, page 324. Choppinus wrote regarding the Domain. The "Chamber Estate" <note>original: "Cammergut"</note> is called *Domanium* or *Domaine* by the French; its ownership belongs to the Prince not by hereditary right, but by feudal right, insofar as he is invested with it by the Emperor.

To feudal lawyers, the "Chamber" is the same as the treasury, just as today we also speak of the "Prince’s Chamber" <note>original: "die Fürstliche Cammer"</note>. Likewise, "Chamber Goods" <note>original: "Bona Cameralia, das Cammergut"</note> refers to the Prince's fisc <note>the state or royal treasury</note>. Rittershusius, *Feudal Partitions*, page 463. Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, book 1, page 27, number 13, at the end.

**10. Chancellor.** <note>original: "Canzler. Cancellarius."</note>
The Chancellor is said by some to be named from "canceling" <note>original: "à cancellando"</note>; because he corrects and cancels <note>crosses out</note> royal (or ducal, etc.) decrees and privileges which are to be fortified by the Royal Seal (which is in his keeping) before they are so fortified. Hincmar of Reims, writing to the Bishops of France, says: to which legate <note>original: "apocrisiario"</note> was joined the High Chancellor, who was formerly called "the one in charge of secrets," and subject to him were prudent, intelligent, and faithful men who would write royal commands without the immoderate greed of venality, and would faithfully guard those secrets for them. Chasseneuz in his *Customs of Burgundy*, section "On the Salt Tax," <note>original: "de Gabell."</note> verse "under the seals," <note>original: "soubs. les Seaux"</note> number 1, cites these verses by Poliziano in the Prologue:

> *This is he who cancels the unjust laws of Kings,*
> *And makes the commands of a pious Prince equitable.*
> *If anything harms the people, or is hostile to the laws,*
> *Whatever is harmful ceases to be noxious through him.*

So too Spiegel in his *Lexicon*, under the word "Chancellor," says: It is his duty to inspect the decrees or responses and commands of the Emperor, to cancel those poorly written, and to seal those well-written with his own Signet. Scheplitz in the *Customs of Brandenburg*, part 2, title 2, number 4.
