# Augmented Practical Treasury

...that the Chancellor is the second person of France regarding the administration of justice, so that, as stated in the same place <note>original: "ibid. vers. de potestate"</note> in the section on power, he is greater than the **Constable** <note>The Constable was the highest military officer of the French crown, effectively the commander-in-chief.</note>. However, Philippe de Comines, in his *Commentaries on the Deeds of Louis XI, King of France*, book 2, page 347, testifies that the office of the Constable is the greatest and most ample honor in all of France.

Regarding the precedence of both the Constable and the Chancellor among the French, Jean Bodin likewise discusses this in *The Republic*, book 4, chapter 6, page 502, in these words: "The arbiter and moderator of military discipline and matters of war is he who among us is called the Master of the Soldiers, or the Constable; or he who is considered first in honor among the Marshals or Tribunes of the Soldiers. But the Prince of domestic discipline and of the courts is the **Chancellor**, or the First Secretary. Each is a master of his own discipline, established with supreme power; neither is held under the command of the other, but each is equal everywhere, walking in the same rank and order. Nevertheless, the Master of the Soldiers is superior in dignity and occupies the Prince's right side, while the Chancellor occupies the left. And lest anyone think that this order is granted to the Master of the Soldiers merely because he is held to carry the Prince's sword before him at his right, whenever the narrowness of the path does not allow both to walk together, the Master of the Soldiers goes first, then the Chancellor, followed by the Prefect of the Praetorium. These things are said by me not to define anything regarding honors, but so that it might be understood how far honor differs from command."

In our own courts, it is established that the Office of the Chancellor is the highest as far as the administration of justice is concerned. Hence we also see that, in the Roman Empire, the **Ecclesiastical Electors** <note>The Archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne, who held the right to vote for the Emperor.</note> perform the office of the Chancellorship; for this reason and dignity, they certainly precede the remaining secular Electors, as is clearly gathered from what is handed down by Andreas Knichen in *On the Laws and Privileges of Saxony*, chapter 1, number 74. He says: "Therefore, the Archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne perform the duty of the Election as Imperial Chancellors, just as the secular lords do by reason of their offices; otherwise, it would follow that the Count Palatine would elect in the name of the Palatinate, the Saxon in the name of Saxony, and the Margrave in the name of the Margraviate, which is absurd." *Thus far Knichen.* By these words, he clearly shows that this prerogative in the Roman Empire—namely, that they take part in the election and even precede others—belongs to them by reason of the office of the Chancellorship.

### ADDITION.

The Chancellor is the Mouth, Chest, and Heart of the Prince, the Leader and Governor of all Councils, as taught by the supreme height of legal experts, Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note>, in the *Rubrics of the Code on Inquiries and the Office of Magistrates*, and Carpzov in *Decisions*, 28, number 15.

The dignity of the Chancellor is great, treated at length in Wehner’s *Supplement*, page 15, and Höping in *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 6. Among the Ger-

<column-break/>

mans, the custody of the seals is usually committed to the Arch-Chancellors and the Chancellors of the Imperial Princes and others. See Kirchner, *On the Office of the Chancellor*, chapter 3. For an excellent explanation of the word "Chancellor," see Dr. Tabor’s *On Suffrage*, page 150 and following, where he playfully jokes that the word <term>Canzler</term> <note>Chancellor</note> should not be derived as if he ought to be a "goose-teacher" <term>ganßlehr</term>, but by a contraction <note>original: "synaeresin"</note>, as if it meant "completely learned" <term>Gantz gelehrt</term>. The Chancellors of Universities are mostly Bishops; for example, at the University of Leipzig, the Chancellor is the Bishop of Merseburg; for Greifswald, the Bishop of Cammin; for Rostock, the Bishop of Schwerin. See Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 123; Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 8; and Becker in *Public Law*, page 249. But the Universities of Strasbourg and Altdorf testify that this is not a permanent rule.

Thus, when I was formally seeking doctoral honors at Strasbourg on August 11, 1649, the most generous, energetic, noble, and prudent Lord Johann Christoph von Dragdorff—the Governor of the Republic, a most weighty member of the Council of Thirteen, and the most eminent Chancellor of the University—was a most deserving director of the schools <note>original: "Scholarcha"</note>; he passed away on September 11, 1662. The Chancellors of Universities grant the faculty of announcing Doctors and Masters; these officials are almost always Bishops or other ecclesiastical persons. See Besold, *Politics*, book 1, chapter 12.

## II. Chancellor of the Empress.
## Cancellarius Imperatricis.

This is the **Abbot of Fulda**, who holds the first place among those Abbots distinguished by princely dignity. Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 10. Regner Sixtinus, in *On Regalia*, book 1, chapter 4, says that this Abbot is more powerful than many Bishops, since he contributes twice and sometimes three times more to the Empire than they do. This most powerful Abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict (which is called the "Lady and Queen" of all other German Abbeys by Bruschius in his *Book of German Monasteries*, page 56) was founded and built in the year 744. Its most illustrious prelate is one of the four Abbots of the Empire and the Primate of all Abbots, not only in Germany but also in France, and the **Arch-chancellor of the Roman Empress**. Berthold von Schollisz, who headed the Abbey in the year 1113, added no small amount to this dignity; for as a companion to Emperor Lothar in Italy, he received the regalia from him, with the addition of new privileges for pontifical ornaments. Furthermore, when a controversy arose between him and the Archbishop of Magdeburg, he obtained a judgment that the precedence of seating should be awarded to him, as witnessed by Bruschius, page 60. See also Serrarius, *Matters of Mainz*, book 3, page 519; my own work *On the Precedence of Seating*, page 137; and Brower, *Antiquities of Fulda*, book 1, chapters 15 and 16, where he noted from a diploma of Emperor Charles IV that in the year 1358, the office of Arch-chancellor, with all its privileges, was granted to Abbot Henry, the Emperor's secretary and counselor...

## Chapel, Chaplain. Capella, Capellanus.

Those who think that a Chapel (which we call *ein Capell*) is so named as if it were "capturing the people" <note>original Greek: "capientem λαὸν"</note> are being ridiculous. Regarding the matter itself, it is well established: a Chapel is called a minor church, subject to a larger one, where there is neither a baptistery nor a cemetery; it is like a small shrine <term>Sacellum: a small consecrated space or private oratory</term>. And a Chaplain is the one who is in charge of such a church.

Some assign another explanation to "Chapels," and indeed this is the one: in ancient times, the Kings of France, when proceeding to war, carried the cloak <note>Latin: *Cappa*</note> of St. Martin with them. It was kept under a certain tent, which was called a "Chapel" <note>Latin: *Capella*</note> after the cloak itself, and the clerics in whose custody that Chapel was kept were thereafter called "Chaplains" <note>Latin: *Capellani*</note>. Consequently, that name was transferred in certain regions from them to all priests who are not parish priests <note>German: *Caplonen*</note>.

There are also those who say that anciently, during military expeditions, little huts covered with goat skins <note>Latin: *pellibus caprarum*</note> were made in the tents, in which Masses were celebrated, and the name "Chapel" was drawn from there. Durandus mentions this in *Divine Offices*, book 2, chapter 10; see also Peter von Beeck in *Aquisgranum* <note>Aachen</note>, page 18, and Martinius's *Philological Lexicon* under the word *Capella*.

Some believe that "Chapels" refers to the usual oratories that are not consecrated, as shown by Bernhard, the glossator of Pontifical Law, regarding consecration. The decree there states: "We also grant that if anywhere (which, as our sins demand, has happened very often) churches have been set on fire and burned by Normans, Slavs, Hungarians, or by bad Christians, or in any other way: we permit Masses to be celebrated again in **Chapels**, with a consecrated table, until those churches can be restored."

But for one wishing to know more about Chapels, Chaplains, Arch-Chaplains, and their origin, etc., let them read Riccius in *Ecclesiastical Practice*, page 429; Hospinian on *Temples*, page 88; Le Grand, *The Almoner of France*, and also concerning psalmody, from which comes *Capellmeister* <note>Chapel-master or choir director</note>; Faucher, book 1, *On Origins*, chapter 7; Goldast in *Alemannic Matters*, volume 1, page 183, 197, and 207, where the Arch-Chaplain is taken to be the Chancellor; Marc Antonio in *The Practice of the Archbishop of Naples*, part 1, chapter 91; Choppin on *Ecclesiastical Policy*; and Simonet on the *Reservation of Benefices*, question 37 and following; and concerning Chapels incorporated into monasteries, see the *Dillingen Composition of Peace*, question 63. For what kind of benefice a Chapel is, see Servin's *Pleadings*, volume 2, page 299.

<column-break/>

On whether a Chapel is a church, see the *Toulouse Decisions*, 57.
Who the Deacons are: Borch on *Fiefs*, chapter 5, number 12.
Who the Sub-Deacons are: same place.
Concerning Chaplains: Höpingk on the *Law of Seals*, chapter 64. *Kapel*, whence *Kappellane*. Dr. Saubert on *Sacrifices*, pages 329, 330.

The ancient Alemanni <note>A Germanic tribal confederation</note> used to call the vessels, instruments, and ecclesiastical ornaments of every kind "Chapel" <note>Latin: *Capellam*</note>—whatever was necessary in a Chapel or shrine to perform the sacred rites. Melchior Haiminsfeld Goldast in *Alemannic Matters*, volume 1, part 1, page 180, cites a passage from the cases of Eckehard: "A chest of solid gold, regally distinguished with gems, filled with the highest relics, created in the form of a **Chapel**." And on page 183, he says: The ancient writers called the sacred vessels and ornaments "Chapel," by which, if necessity required, sacred rites could be celebrated in any place on an altar composed of a table or any available material. And it is so called because it was once made from the skins of goats <note>Latin: *caprarum* or *capellarum*</note>, a canopy <note>German: *Himmel*</note>, called *Capelle* by the Alemanni. From there it was transferred to the temple, "a chapel or church" <note>German: *eine Capelle oder Kirch*</note>, and it is known as *Capella* for a shrine among the Italians, and *Chapelle* among the French.

<margin>13.</margin>
## Chapter. Capitulum.

A "Chapter" <note>Latin: *Capitulum*</note> is properly a "little head." However, it is also the place where Monks and Canons assemble, who are therefore usually called "Capitulars," because the heads of the religious order—that is, the ecclesiastical leaders—sit together there. And because in that place the censure of morals used to be carried out, we commonly use the terms *Capitlen* or *Capitel lesen* <note>To read the chapter</note> for "to correct" or "to chastise with sharp words." This word is also used for the place itself, or for the assembled Canons themselves; see Goldast's *Alemannic Matters*, volume 1, page 200. In this view, the "Greater Part" of the Canons constitutes the Chapter; therefore, if there is litigation among the Canons, the Proctor elected by the majority ought to have his expenses paid by the Chapter. See Vivius, *Decisions*, 44.

The Bishop is, as it were, the Head of the Church; his own members, as it were, are the Chapter itself, just as this is literally stated in the chapter *novit* under *those things which are done by Prelates*. For as Cardinals are to the Pope, so Canons are part of the Bishop's body. Panormitanus in the said chapter *novit*.

By the designation "Chapter," otherwise speaking properly and strictly, the Prelate <note>The high-ranking officer, like a Bishop</note> is not included, because although he is the Head, he is not, however, *of* the Chapter; for in the very fact that he is the Head of the Chapter, he ceases to be in the college <note>The collective legal body</note>; and thus the Right of the Prelacy is distinct from the Right of the Chapter. But because the Chapter is nevertheless within the Bishop's jurisdiction, this is almost always understood to include the Bishop in every act, even if it is specifically assigned to the Bishop alone. Nikolaus Reusner, volume 3, consultation 11, number 184 and following.

Concerning the Chapter when the See is vacant <note>Latin: *Sede vacante*, referring to the period between bishops</note>, and its power, see Riccius in *Ecclesiastical Practice*, page 500; Arumaeus in the *Tract on the Imperial Diets*, chapter 4, number 104, etc., especially regarding the changing of religion...

On the various meanings of this word, see Limnaeus, *volume 1, additions to book 1, chapter 12, number 9.*
A **Chapter** <note>Latin: "Capitulum"</note> is the entire assembly or College of Canons of a particular Church. Even if the Bishop is dead, the Church itself is not considered dead or deprived of its head; rather, the Chapter fills his role in the meantime until a new Bishop is elected. Rittershusius in *New Works, page 100, at the end.*
Regarding those who are called "Capitularies," see Lord Tabor on *Quarters, page 261.* On the "Capitular function," see *page 260, at the beginning.*
Just as a chapter is a council or Senate of the Princes and leaders of a Realm, City, or some College—<term>a Chapter</term> <note>German: "ein Capitul"</note>, from which the "Capitol" is also named—so too are the laws called "Capitularies" <note>Latin: "Capitularia"</note>, which are established and ordained in a common Chapter by the consensus of the Nobles and Leaders. Because the wayward were often corrected and delinquents punished in the chapters of monasteries and colleges, the German phrase <term>to 'chapter' someone</term> <note>German: "einen capiteln"</note> or even <term>to read the chapter</term> <note>German: "ein Capitellesen"</note> was born, meaning to rebuke or correct. Melchior Haiminsfeld Goldast, *Alemanic Affairs, volume 1, part 1, folio 200.* In other places, they call this "filching" or <term>giving someone a felting</term> <note>German: "einen Filss geben," a colloquialism for a harsh scolding</note>, derived from the words for "hood" and "head," from which "chapter" also originates.

### 14. Capitulation, Imperial Capitulation. *Capitulatio Caesarea.*

"To capitulate" <note>Latin: "Capitulare"</note> is a new term, and it signifies what is called in this era an "Ordinance" or a "Recess" <note>A "Recess" was a formal decree issued at the end of an Imperial Diet</note>. The ancients called it a Decree, a Decree of the Senate, or Laws. Thus, in the Carolingian Constitutions, it is said: *In the 11th year of the Reign of our Lord Charles, most glorious King, in the month of May, the Capitulary was made.*
Hence the **Imperial Capitulation**: regarding which, and whether it changes the nature of the Sovereign Majesty? See the *dedicatory epistle* of Arumaeus in *volume 4*, who has more on the same subject in the same volume, *discourses 1, 2, 3, and 4.* You will find a dissertation by Lord Carpzov briefly explaining this same Capitulation in the *said volume 4, final discourse, Basel disputes, volume 4, dispute 15.* See also Limnaeus in his *Notes on Otto’s Public Law, folio 16,* and Goldast, *3 Constitutions, folio 424,* where it is noted that Jodocus of Moravia, Father of the August Emperor Wenceslaus, promulgated a sanction regarding resisting the Royal Majesty if he should act against the Ordinances of the Empire, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

It is called a "Capitulation" because it encompasses the main heads <note>Latin: "capita"</note> of the laws of the Empire; perhaps it would be more correctly called by the word "Recapitulation," though that is equally poor Latin, yet no less used elsewhere. See more in Limnaeus, *volume 2, additions to book 1, chapter 12, number 8.*

<column-break/>

For the elected King of the Romans, a **Capitulation**—that is, certain heads, articles, and conditions for the useful administration of the Republic according to the custom of the ancestors and the fundamental laws of the Empire—is proposed by the Electors. Before he is confirmed, he must promise by oath that he will observe these. This is treated extensively by Becker in *Public Law, page 48 and following.* Schönborner makes copious mention of the "Carolingian" Capitulation <note>The contract signed by Emperor Charles V in 1519</note> in his *Politics, page 720,* as does Sleidan in *book 1, page 23.*
Limnaeus expresses the tenor of the Capitulation that **Ferdinand III** swore to in *Public Law, volume 1, book 1, chapter 12, number 35.* He expresses that of **Ferdinand IV** in *volume 2, additions to book 1, chapter 12, number 35,* where he also added annotations on *Why Capitulations were introduced.* See also *volume 2, additions to book 2, chapter 12, number 18.*
Can a Supreme Prince swear to such capitulations while preserving the essence of his Majesty? Although these pacts of capitulation, by which the rights of immense power are narrowed, do not empty or swallow up the majesty of the Prince—for pacts of this kind pertain to the safety of the Empire, upon which the authority, safety, and happiness of the Emperor himself depend—much less is anything taken away from the majesty of the Prince by the oath interposed for the sake of observing these pacts. See Reinckingk, *book 1 on Secular and Ecclesiastical Rule, class 3, chapter 9, numbers 8, 9, 10, 39.* Limnaeus, *book 1 on Public Law, chapter 12, numbers 36, 37, 38,* and his *Annotations on the Imperial Capitulations, prologue, section 2, and section 8, number 22 and following.* See also Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace, book 1, chapter 3, number 16.* Carpzov, *On the German Royal Law, chapter 1, section 10, and chapter 12 throughout.* Nevertheless, the actual Majesty of the Empire rests upon the German Royal Law, or the Imperial Capitulation, as its foundation. Carpzov, in the *said Commentary on the German Royal Law, chapter 1, section 10, number 3, sections 11 and 14, and chapter 13, section 1, number 11 and following.* See also the discussion of the vote of the Seven Electors, specifically Albert, Elector of Mainz, for Charles of Austria, King of Spain, recorded by Johannes Sleidan in *book 1 of his Commentaries, page 12 and following,* among the *Historical-Political Disputes on Dogmatic Law, 4.* Limnaeus, *Annotations on the Imperial Capitulations, prologue, section 8, numbers 1 and the last.* Regarding the Capitulation of Ferdinand IV, Stirn exhibits the warnings of the Estates of the Empire in *On the Constitutions of Princes, title 4, § 7.* For a summary of the Capitulation of **Leopold**, see *title 4, § 8, 9, 10.*

### 16. Carat. Ceratium.

The intrinsic goodness or preciousness of gold, which they call the "alloy" <note>original: "Ligam"</note>, is distributed into twenty-four parts or degrees, which we are accustomed to call *ceratia*—commonly known as "karats." Gold of this highest degree is that which exists purged of all impurity and every foreign metal. Furthermore, these individual karats are divided into 12 grains. From this, the mixture of gold is estimated. See Budelius, *On Currency*, book 1, chapter 16.

The word "karat" <note>original: "Ceratium"</note> is derived metaphorically from the Greek word *keration* <note>original: "κεράτιον", meaning a small horn or the carob bean</note>. Indeed, Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French humanist scholar</note> left this written right at the beginning of book 3 of *On the As and its Parts*: "The *ceratium* is a weight of minute size, named from the grain of the carob <note>original: "siliquae"</note>, which is the fruit of a very sweet Italian tree, about the length of a man’s finger and the width of a thumb. We," he says, "have seen it imported into this city; inside are grains called *ceratia*, sharing the name with the fruit." See the *Strasbourg Disputation on Monetary Law*, thesis 31.

### ADDITION.

<margin>Mr. Speidel, in *Notables*, folio 514. The *ceratium* as used among goldsmiths. Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in *System of Universal Law*, 36. 2. 10.</margin>

### 17. Cardinal. Cardinalis.

Cardinals are named from the word for "hinge" <note>Latin: "cardo"</note>: because just as a door is governed by its hinge, so is the Church governed by their counsel, as noted in the chapter *Sacrosancta*, at the end of the 25th distinction. To them now belongs, by full right, the election of the Roman Pontiff. See my own work *On Succession and Election*, folio 180.

This title of dignity is said to have begun before or around the times of Gregory the Great. See Longus, *Chronological Breviary*, folio 184. In the beginning, they were created from Bishops; later, the Pope chose them from among Bishops, Priests, Deacons, and Sub-deacons, so that he might use them as counselors in ecclesiastical business. They held that place in the Church after the Pope that political Kings hold after the Emperor or the Estates. They were distinguished by the "Red Hat" <note>original: "Rubro galero"</note> by Innocent IV around the year 1205.

By what law the Cardinalate was introduced, and regarding the excellence of Cardinals, Andreas Barbatius <note>A 15th-century jurist</note> treats in his *Treatise on the Excellence of Cardinals*; add also M. Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction*, book 3, part 1, chapter 1, folio 77.

Truly, the Cardinalate is a dignity and an office, not an "order" <note>meaning it is a rank of honor rather than a distinct level of sacramental ordination like the priesthood</note>, which may be recognized from the fact that some are called Cardinal-Bishops, others Cardinal-Priests, and others Deacons: see Servin, volume 1, *Plaidoyez*, folio 238. No one is made a Cardinal who is below the order of Deacons; just as

<column-break/>

no one among the Canons has the right to vote who is not at least a Sub-deacon. Nevertheless, on account of the prerogative of that dignity, Cardinals have Pontifical jurisdiction in the Churches assigned to them as their "Title," and in others subject to them by that Title, even if they have not been co-opted into the order of Bishops. Antonius Cucchus in *Institutes of Canon Law*, book 1, "On the Dignity and Office of Cardinals."

The author of the *Political Discourse on the State of Rome*, folio 15, also mentions that according to the Bull of Sixtus V, there ought to be seventy-two Cardinals (perhaps in imitation of the same number of Christ's disciples; on which see Camillus Borellius in *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 5). About fifty of them reside near the Supreme Pontiff, while the rest are dispersed throughout the Christian world.

A certain author on folio 70 and following says that when the Pope places the red hat on the head of a new Cardinal, he pronounces the following words:

> To the praise of Almighty GOD and the ornament of the Holy Apostolic See, receive this red hat, the singular insignia of the dignity of the Cardinalate: by which it is signified that even unto death and the shedding of blood inclusive, you must show yourself fearless for the exaltation of the Holy Faith, the peace and quiet of the Christian people, and the increase and state of the Holy Roman Church: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

He also adds that the Pope "closes the mouth" of the new Cardinal—that is, he forbids him from speaking in public Consistories as well as secret Councils—and his mouth is not to be "opened" except after a council of the senior Cardinals has been held. There one may also see more regarding the "Cardinal-Nephews" <note>The practice of Popes appointing relatives to the Cardinalate</note> of the Pontiffs.

Furthermore, regarding the "Titles" <note>original: "Titulis"</note> from which some Cardinals take their names, one should consult Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a cardinal and ecclesiastical historian</note> in his *Annals* for the years of Christ 111 and 112. There, at number 4, he says: by "Titles" are understood the houses of the faithful dedicated to Divine worship, in which Christians were accustomed to hold assemblies <note>original: "Synaxes"</note>, which we call Churches. An example of this is found in those brief but truly "golden" letters of Pope Pius to Justus, the Bishop of Vienne. The nomenclature was adopted (so it seems) from fiscal matters: when the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscus"</note> was accustomed to claim something for itself and consecrate it to the Prince, it would place a "Title" upon it. It is established that these were certain veils marked with the images or certainly the names of the Emperors, which Ambrose calls "Royal Curtains." Gregory forbade these from being placed on ecclesiastical property, as he knew that Church "Titles" ought to be far different from fiscal ones. However, we think the difference between the "Veils" and the "Titles" was that on the veils an image of the Emperor was painted, while on the "Titles" his name was inscribed. Moreover, among Christians, the "Title" by which a house was dedicated to Divine worship was the banner of the Cross, as is proved by many constitutions and other ancient monuments. ### 19. Blank Document. Charta blanca, Blancket, vacua Scriptura.

The Spaniards call this *pro cura en blanco* <note>a power of attorney signed in blank</note>, regarding which see Decianus, response 91, throughout the whole of volume 3.
Handwritten notes and seals placed at the bottom of or attached to tablets add much strength to a writing. For he who has set his hand to an instrument as if it pertained to himself—for the sake of authority and faith, not merely for testimony—is considered to confess and approve what is contained therein, and thus is judged to have consented. This prejudices him no differently than if he had drafted the instrument himself, according to the teachings of Franciscus Pfeil, consultation 39, numbers 1 and 2. Nor, he says in number 3, does it matter that the paper was still blank when it was signed. For the one signing is presumed not to have been ignorant of the tenor of the instrument he signs, but to have inspected and known it. Bartolus on the law *How to open wills* <note>original: "l. 1. testam. quemadm. aper."</note>, version 2: "if anyone denies." Therefore, the contrary would have to be shown by legitimate evidence that overturns this legal presumption.
One who signs or applies a seal to a blank tablet, although not immediately obligated when it is written upon (since he did not inspect the tenor of the writing that followed and likely did not yet know it: final law, Code, *Plus valere quod agitur* <note>What is done is more important than what is written</note>; Innocent on chapter 2, *On the faith of instruments*, 6; *Presumptions of Law* in the 6th book of Decretals), nevertheless, he who received a written paper without contradiction and kept it in his possession so that he had the opportunity of inspecting and knowing it, is presumed to have inspected and known it (law 1, section *inspection*, Digest, *How to open wills*; *Authentica* at the words *atqui semel*, there Baldus, section *but it is revoked*, version *add however*, Code, *On proofs*). Thus, he is thought to have consented to and approved what is written. And the allegation of ignorance of that which he ought to have known is rejected, since he had it in his hand so that he could have searched it out for himself or through another. Pfeil, in the cited consultation, final number.
And so, a blank leaf on which a Power of Attorney <note>original: "Procuratorium"</note> is written is valid (Tuscus, letter F, conclusion 409), because it was sent for the purpose that a mandate be written upon it. And in the same way, an instrument for a loan received can be left to the judgment of the Creditor, so that he may add whatever clauses he wishes; see my own work in *Deliberations on Law*, page 2, folio 50. If, however, he should write in a larger sum, there is room for a defense based on "money not paid" <note>original: "non numeratæ pecuniæ"</note> or even a defense of fraud. Similarly, such free mandates are sometimes given to Ambassadors. And Günther even sings of such letters in *Ligurinus*, book 3:

## 20. Carthusians. <note>original: "Cartheisser. Carthusiani."</note>

This Order began in the year of our Lord 1080 according to Polydorus and Genebrardus; however, according to Sigebert, Vincent, Antoninus, and Panvinius, it was in the year 1086. Regarding its beginning, the following is related: A certain Professor in Paris, renowned for his learning, character, and blameless life, rose from his bier during his solemn funeral rites and cried out: *By the just judgment of God, I have been accused.* This happened again on the second and third days. Seeing this, Bruno of Cologne, a Doctor of Laws <term>JC: Juris Consultus</term> and professor at the same school, was terrified by this event and said to those standing by: "You see what a miserable end our life has; there is no place of safety unless we leave the world." Immediately, he withdrew with others to the Diocese of Grenoble, and obtained from Bishop Hugh a completely solitary place located among the cliffs in Celtic Gaul, which was named Chartreuse <note>original: "Cartusiæ"</note>. Francis de Puteo was Prior there, as was Petrus Blomovenne. Among all monks, they have the most rigid Rule. They wear hairshirts <note>original: "veste utuntur cilicinâ"</note>, a black cloak over a white tunic, and a cowl for a head covering. Polydorus. Meat is forbidden to them for their entire lives, even in the most serious illness; otherwise, they are expelled. There is no access for women to them; see Aubert Miraeus, *On the Origins of Monasticism*, folio 209; *The Voice of the Turtledove* <note>original: "Vocem Turturis"</note>, folio 172; and on the Great Chartreuse, Gölnitz in *Gallo-Belgic Itinerary*, folio 413. Regarding the Carthusians, and whether ecclesiastical immunity extends to estates recently acquired by monasteries: see Annuaus Robertus, *On Adjudicated Matters*, book 2, chapter 2.

A **precaution for lawyers** should be carefully noted: when a defendant does not believe the specific sum claimed in the lawsuit, he should respond specifically regarding the amount he *does* believe is owed. This is very helpful; it informs the Judge of the cause and speeds up the process. Schwanmann, in *Chamber Process, book 1, chapter 45, number 21, page 257.* A precaution for maturing (speeding up) a lawsuit: It is free for the defendant, along with the production of specific exceptions, to present the nomination of Commissioners (if he wishes) with a petition for the Commission to be decreed, and to present the first delay. Schwanmann, in *Chamber Process, book 1, chapter 55, number 4, page 213.* 
A **precaution for the defendant**: if a Creditor delays acting on the point of **unpaid money** <note>original: *non numeratæ pecuniæ*; a legal defense used when someone is sued for a debt they claim they never actually received, even if they signed a document for it</note> until a two-year period has passed. He who confessed to having received the money shall appear before the Judge and protest that, although he confessed in the hope of future payment, the payment and delivery were never actually made to him. In this case, the legal exception is made permanent and can be used against the creditor whenever they might sue later. Schwanmann, book 1, chapter 6, numbers 9 and 10, page 33. 
A **precaution for seeking an extension** of a deadline, if the term expires before the order reaches the procurator. Ibid, book 1, chapter 39, number 8, page 212; and a "Recess" <note>A formal decree or stay of proceedings</note> is added in the same chapter. A precaution for accelerating the point regarding attempted actions and inhibitions. Schwanmann, book 1, chapter 38, number 4, page 207. 
A **precaution if legal processes are denied**, book 1, chapter 6, number 6, page 31. 
A **precaution for serving legal papers** through a Notary without risk, book 1, chapter 22, number 16, page 158. 
A **precaution for Creditors**, book 1, chapter 6, number 2, page 32. 
A **precaution for seeking and requesting Imperial Commissioners**, book 1, chapter 3, number 8, page 16. 
A **precaution for one seeking a release**, that he ask for the defendant to be summoned at the same time for the entire principal case. Schwanmann, in *Chamber Process, book 2, chapter 21, number 8, page 227.* 
A **precaution for seeking and calculating the deadline** for filing a formal complaint, book 2, chapter 5, number 16, page 23. 
A **precaution for the appellee** <note>the person against whom an appeal is filed</note>, if the appellant attempts something new, book 2, chapter 9, number 24, page 56. 
A **precaution for appellees** against reckless appellants, book 2, chapter 1, numbers 8, 9, 10, & 11, page 5.

A **precaution in the preparation of Inventories** pertains to the solemnities or the form of the Inventory: the heir who prepares the Inventory should ensure a **Protestation** is added, stating that he has now faithfully indicated and described each and every thing he knows to have belonged to the deceased. And if any things happened to be omitted through ignorance or oversight, which might be found later, he is ready at any time to add them to those already described as soon as they come to his notice. ### 23. Cell. Cella. See below under Kölnhoff.

**Cella** is a place where something is stored away, a storehouse. Festus. It is called *Cella* because those things which we wish to be hidden are concealed <note>original: *celentur*</note> in it. Isidore, *book 15, chapter 3.* It is called a cell because it hides or conceals us. It is also related to the Chaldean word *Celau*, meaning to close or ward off. Furthermore, the private chambers of **Monks** are specifically called **Cells**. Thus, in later Greek, it is *kellion* <note>original: κελλίον</note>, referring to a cleric's room or any small bedroom.

In a broad sense of the name, the word *Cella* includes those areas within a cloister but outside the common dormitory, which an Abbot can grant by dispensation for reasons of illness. Erasmus Chokier, in the *Treatise on Exemptions, part 1, question 43.* Strictly speaking, however, they are only secret and solitary places, separated from the company of men, specially designated for contemplation and for devoting oneself to God; see the text in the chapter *Privilegium* in the *Sext*. In this light, it is often said: **A Monk outside his Cell is like a fish out of water.**

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the little word *Cella*, see Sprenger, *On the Law of Building, pages 63, 64.* Sometimes it is taken for the cloister of a monk; sometimes for a place in which we store things we want to keep hidden; sometimes for a repository in which food and drink are stored—hence the "oil cellar" <note>original: *cella olearia*</note> and "wine cellar" <note>original: *vinaria*</note>. Whether one should say *cella penaria* or *penuaria* <note>both referring to a pantry or provisions-room</note>, we leave that to the critics.

In some Churches, they call the one to whom the distribution of the church's wine and grain is committed the **Cellarer** <note>original: *Cellarium*</note>, of whom mention is made in the law in the chapter *dilecto* regarding prebends in Gregory; because the *cellarium* is the place where necessities for life are stored and from which they are brought out. As St. Jerome interprets in Luke 12: *Consider the ravens, which have no storehouse <note>original: *Cellarium*</note> or barn.* And Plautus mentions the Cellarer in *The Captives*: *take, ask, bring forth what you want, I make you the Cellarer.* Among the Capitular laws of **Charlemagne** held at Aachen in the year 789 on the Kalends of April, chapter 6, it is written of the Monastic Cellarers that greedy men should not be sent, but such as the Rule prescribes. A *Laura* is a small, narrow house of Monks, which we commonly call a cell (*kellion*). Suidas, and from him Cujas. He also observes that "Secretum" <note>a secret or private place</note> is used this way in Law *quidam*, 26 of the Code *on decurions*, book 10, and the last law of the Code *on metals*, book 11. Rittershusius, in *The New Constitutions*, page 79, number 18.

Near the shore of Perugia is a very ancient town, which was once called **Centum Cellae** <note>Hundred Cells</note>, and is now called **Cività Vecchia**, that is, the Old City. Mr. Beer, in the *Handbook of Ancient and Modern Geography, folio 186.* Zeiller, in his *Itinerary of Italy, page 189*, <margin>reports that this place was also called Cincelle, and in ancient times was the homeland of Emperor Trajan. The name comes from the fact that the Romans [built] those houses under...</margin>

### 24. Censure. Censura.

Regarding Ecclesiastical Censures <note>punishments like excommunication used by the Church to enforce discipline</note>, see the treatises of Raphael Rastelli and Johannes of Lignano, from Bologna.

->ADDITION.<-

The Censors among the Romans, according to Lipsius in *On the Roman Magistracy*, book 3, chapter 12 (*O praiseworthy and divine institution!* <note>original: *o laudabile & divinum institutum!*</note>), used to select the Senate; likewise, every five years <note>original: *per singula lustra*; a 'lustrum' was a five-year period ending in a purification ceremony</note> they conducted an examination, and if anyone was unworthy of their position, or if there was anything shameful or tainted in their private life, they noted it and removed them. Concerning the Censors in Venice and Nuremberg, I have spoken in my *Comparison of the Republic of Nuremberg with the Venetian*, which is the twelfth among the Orations of Beatus Rupertus, page 555. On the utility of Censure, see Rupertus on Florus, book 1, chapter 18, number 23, at the words: *As if he were condemning luxury with censorial gravity.* Juvenal refers to this in *Satire 11*:

> When they trembled before the Fabii and the harsh Cato,
> And the Scauri, and the Fabricii, and even the Colleague feared
> the severe manners of the rigid Censor.

The duty of the Censors included the examination of the Knights <note>original: *Equitum*</note>. Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 3. The Emperors once held the office of Censor. See the same author in *Politics*, book 7, chapter 20, section 9. Even the Emperors held the censorial dignity. See also Contzen, book 7, chapter 20, section 7. The Venetian Republic is preserved more by Censure than by war, book 7, chapter 20, section 8. Censure is necessary both now and in the past, book 7, chapter 20, sections 1 and 7. On the shameful disagreement of Censors, book 7, chapter 20, section 6.
Who the Censors were among the Romans and what their duty was: see Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 80, numbers 40 and 41. On their double duty in conducting the census and the supervision of morals <note>original: *praefectura morum*</note>: Schönborner in *Politics*, page 260, at the end; Otto in *Public Finance*.
On the power and necessity of Censors, on Censors as overseers of morals—Censors shall judge the morals of both the husband and the wife—on the severity of Censors, the effects of censorial judgment, the authority of the censorial mark <note>original: *censoriae notae*; a formal mark of ignominy placed next to a name on the census roll</note>, the creation of Censors, and their purification: see Pancirollus in *The Lost Things*. On Ecclesiastical Censure: by which the right to practice religion is taken away from a university or a certain area, and the Clergy are forbidden from administering divine offices there or granting ecclesiastical burial to the dead. See the chapter *si sententia* with those following, and the chapter *is cui* regarding the execution of a sentence, in the 6th book of Decretals. Sprenger in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 281.

### 25. High Jurisdiction, Criminal Court, The Hundred. Centnea. see Blood-ban, Capital Court.

Regions were formerly divided into hundreds <note>original: *centenas*; administrative districts</note>: from this, the term "Zent" has remained for us, signifying a

<column-break/>

smaller district of a village or town; I discuss this in *On Counts and Barons*, number 7; see the entry *Centgraf* <note>the judge of a hundred-court</note>; it is not derived from tithes <note>original: *decimis*</note>.
And now the term **High Jurisdiction** <note>German: *Zentbarliche Oberkeit*</note> is used, almost for absolute power <note>original: *Imperio mero*</note>, though this seems to have no absolute certainty. Thus, in the land of Franconia, only the four cases—murder, robbery, arson, and theft—belong to the jurisdiction of the *Cent*.
Practitioners, especially those of the Imperial Chamber <note>original: *Camerales*</note>, vary and strain themselves strangely regarding the distinction, restriction, and extension of **Zent Justice** <note>German: *Centbarliche Gerechtigkeit*</note>: on which one may see Gylman, *Symphorema*, part 1, title 2, number 58, folio 77; Meischn., title 2, decision 8, book 1, number 4; and volume 2, book 2, decision 2, number 171. Commonly, it is considered in four ways according to custom and received use: the collective and general Cent, the Criminal Cent <note>German: *Fraisch-Cent*</note>, the High Cent, and the middle and low Cent.
Elsewhere, the *Centena* <note>The Hundred</note> encompasses all high criminal cases <note>German: *Fraiß-Malefiß-Fäll*</note>, high and chief indictments, all cases and indictments that concern life and limb, neck and hand <note>original: *Hals und Hand*; referring to capital and corporal punishment</note>, skin and hair, and the like: all high and low commands and prohibitions, within the community, outside it, and on household fiefs, in village and field, alleys and streets, meadows, and squares; all those residing within the land and Cent boundaries (for these are different), also all estates bounded, encircled, included, or situated therein: all taxes and impositions which occur in the Cent as the occasion arises; Cent-duty, which all those of age <note>German: *Müntzige*</note> must actually perform and provide to the Cent. The "Cent-cry" <note>summons to court or pursuit</note>, the "Cent-follow" <note>duty to pursue a criminal</note>, church festivals, protection and patronage—both for those as well as for weddings and baptisms—the protection and peace-commands on the community and bailiwick fiefs; the filling of common offices in villages, dismissals, oaths, the hearing and auditing of their accounts, rectification, departures, entry-rights, storage, fines for craftsmen, master-fees, boundary stones, hearth-money or resident and protection money, the Inquiry-Cent and Bailiff-oats, fodder, meals, and provisions on the estates located in the Cent, camp and fortification money, attendance at the high and common provincial courts, and similar things. See Petrus Leopoldi in Arumaeus, volume 1, discourse 24, thesis 4 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

Originating from causes such as murder, arson, emergency, discipline, and theft, these laws are in no way or path extended or exercised. This is what is called "High-Criminal" <note>original: *Hochfräisliche*; refers to high-ranking criminal jurisdiction involving capital punishment</note> or high Maleficiary <note>original: *Malefitzische*; from the Latin *malefitium*, referring to serious crimes</note> Authority.

In Franconia and its surrounding areas, the "Hundreds" <note>original: *Centen*; a traditional Germanic administrative division of a shire or county</note> have completely shifted, and their civil jurisdiction has transformed entirely into a Maleficiary or Capital Court <note>original: *Halsgericht*; literally a "neck-court" empowered to hand down death sentences</note>. *Acts of Lindau, folio 580.*

## 26. Hundred-Counts. *Centgravii.*

*The Hundred-Counts* <note>original: *Centgravii, die Centgraven*</note> *are those whom the ancient Law of the Alemanni calls "Centenarians." It says of the Assembly: Let it be held in every Hundred according to some custom, in the presence of the Count or his Deputy, and let the plea itself be made before the Centenarian.* <note>original: *Centenario*</note>. Henning Arnisaeus, *On the Right of Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, under number 15, page 322, see "Hundred-Counts." I noted this in my *Dissertation on Counts*, number 7. *For "Grav" means Judge: and therefore "Centgrav" is the Judge of a Hundred.* See the *Nassau Chronicle* by Johann Textor, folio 17, where he has the following: One can observe in the old instruments regarding all sorts of stories, various dealings, and contracts, as well as the histories of the Franks, that as often as they wanted to expressly set down and indicate the location of a place, they used to write in which district <note>original: *pago*</note>, by which water, and in what County, Jurisdiction, and Lordship it was situated. At that time the entire Frankish Empire was divided into Counties, and these Counts and Judges held court and spoke the law through the districts in the name of and on behalf of the King or Emperor. They had their residence and dwelling in a "Burg," that is, a city in which there was a castle and a public assembly <note>original: *mallus publicus*</note>, tribunal, or high court. This can be noted and seen in this County as well as anywhere else in Germany, which in former times was counted as part of Alemannia and ruled by Counts. From this also comes the word *Centenae*, the "Hundreds" <note>original: *Centen*</note> in the common tongue, which has nearly vanished elsewhere, but has remained in this land of Nassau and the County of Nassau-Dillenburg, from the almost ancient custom of the Germans mentioned by Cornelius Tacitus. In the laws of the Alemanni, Franks, and others, frequent mention is made of the *Centenae* and *Centenariorum*, that is, the Hundreds and the Hundred-Counts. *Beatus Rhenanus took good note of this in "German Affairs," book 2, where he says: The regions themselves were divided into Hundreds, from which comes the name of the Centenarian; that magistrate presided over the Hundred, being subject to the Count, etc.*

->ADDITION.<-

"Grav" signifies a Judge, hence "Centgrav" or Hundred-Judge.

<column-break/>

The Centenarian <note>original: *Centenarius*</note>, *concerning whom see, if you please, Knich, "On Territorial Right," chapter 4, number 54 and following.*

In olden times, the Hundred-Count <note>original: *Centgraff*</note> had to decide minor matters, whereas the Land-Judge <note>original: *Landrichter*</note> handled greater causes. *Acts of Lindau, folio 550, after the beginning, and page 570, near the end.* Today, the Hundred-Count is a criminal judge, *ibid. and page 580, at the beginning.* The Hundred-Count has jurisdiction in his Hundred in place of the District-Count <note>original: *Gaugraffens*</note> or Land-Judge in almost all matters, *excepting causes of blood <note>capital crimes</note>, liberty, etc.*, *page 826, after the beginning.* The Hundred-Count was permitted to judge "skin and hair" <note>minor physical punishments</note> but not "neck and band" <note>execution by hanging or decapitation</note>. *page 826, near the end.*

## 27. Hundredweight. *Centupondium.*

Concerning the Hebrew Hundredweight, called a *Ricker*, *see Friesen's "Mirror of Coins," book 2, chapter 4.*

->ADDITION.<-

1. A Hundredweight <note>original: *Centner*</note> is 114 pounds in Braunschweig, 112 pounds in Hamburg, 110 pounds in Hannover and Leipzig, and 100 pounds in Holland and Nuremberg.

The Queen from Arabia <note>the Queen of Sheba</note> presented King Solomon with 120 hundredweights of gold, which amounts to 7 tons of gold. *Antenor in "Solomon," chapter 19; Aleman in "Palæstra Consultat.," page 416.* David took the crown of Melchom from his head, and found in it a talent's weight of gold, beyond the most precious gems, and made a diadem for himself from it, *1 Chronicles chapter 20, verse 2.* In the German version it reads: "a hundredweight of gold in weight." David captured Rabbah and took the King’s diadem, having a talent's weight of gold, and it was placed on David's head, *2 Samuel chapter 12, verse 30.* This is to be understood as the Syrian hundredweight, because Rabbah was located in Syria; it is the fourth part of a Hebrew hundredweight, about 1500 Hungarian Guilders or nearly 12 pounds. *See Adam Berg on "Coins of the Old and New Testament," at the passage for 2 Samuel 12.*

## 28. Chiliasts. *Chiliastæ.*

By this name are designated those who, following the occasion of *Revelation chapter 20*, teach that the Saints will reign for a thousand years before the end of the world. Concerning them and their fanaticism, *see Campanella in "The Golden Political Age," chapter 8, folio 392; Er. Ribera on the "Apocalypse," folio 544; Dieteric in his "Disputation on the Fanaticism of the Schwenkfeldians"; "The Aurora of Wisdom," chapter 21, folio 102; Viterbiensis in his treatise "On the Future Triumphs of Christians"; and the Anonymous author in "Historical-Prophetic Verisimilitudes."*

This error has driven even great and pious men in every age to madness. Among others, even Nicolaus de Clemanges *in his "Description of the Tyrant and the Antichrist," folio 357, where he says:* Between that great judgment of the Lord, which hangs so closely over our necks, and the final judgment (at which point the Lord himself will personally arrive at the end of the ages to judge the living and the dead), it is believed by the learned that a great delay of ti-

...of time to be involved, yet how great that duration shall be, He has forbidden us to discover through curious investigation. However, in that interval of time which we say will pass between the two judgments—and which, because of its tranquility and freedom from the roar of wars and the noise of whirlwinds, Paul himself called a *Sabbath-rest* <note>original: *Sabbathismum*</note>, a rest he more clearly expressed as one to be left for the people of God after immense storms—the Lord will stir up certain Holy Men whom He has preserved for Himself during the storm of this great judgment. Through their ministry, all the sects, tribes, and nations that are currently estranged from the Christian religion and have been changed into wild olives will be grafted back into their original olive tree <note>This refers to the metaphor in Romans 11:17-24 regarding the restoration of Israel and the nations</note>, from which they had long ago been torn away by ruinous error. In quiet tranquility, they shall await the final coming of the Lord and the consummation of the world.

This error was renewed even in the century just past, which was fertile in all kinds of heresy, <margin>See my discussion in the *Treatise on Monarchy*, folio 240 and following; it is also noted in the *Augsburg Confession*.</margin>

Regarding the origin of this opinion, Spondanus (the epitomizer of Baronius) writes as follows under the Year of Christ 118: In the final times of Trajan, the error of the *Millennium* <note>original: *Millenario*</note> crept into some of the Faithful. The author was Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis, who was a listener of John the Elder (not the Apostle John, as some have thought, whom Eusebius refutes). Papias was a man of great name and celebrity. Because of an unwritten tradition (as Eusebius says)—that is, based on a faulty interpretation of the words of others—he thought that what is written in the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> about the faithful reigning with Christ for a thousand years should be understood as an earthly Kingdom to be established here for that number of years after the resurrection of the dead. Eusebius writes more about him and his writings. Because of the high esteem in which the man was held, several other men of great name followed him in this error, including Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, and others. For this error did not progress so far as to pass into heresy, except after it was defended more stubbornly by Apollinaris, at which point it was condemned (as it seems) by Pope Damasus.

Furthermore, the ecclesiastical records provide certain proof that Papias himself, regarded for his holiness, reached the end of his life; his name was entered into those records so that his birthday <note>In early Christian contexts, a 'birthday' (*natalis*) usually refers to the date of a saint's martyrdom or death—their 'birth' into heaven</note> might be continually renewed with an annual celebration. See Sixtus of Siena’s *Library*, book 5, annotation 233, and book 6, annotation 447.

A filth of heretics followed Cerinthus, who from this dogma were called *Chiliasts* <note>term: Chiliast; from the Greek *chilioi*, meaning 'one thousand'</note>. Philastrius calls them *Chilionetitæ*, Augustine calls them *Milliarios*, others commonly call them *Millenarians*, and Damascenus calls them *Pepuzians*, after the city of Pepuza, which they claimed was something divine and Jerusalem itself.

However, while some of the Fathers (as I have already said) moved toward an affirmative view, they did not agree with him regarding the reasoning and the manner. Jerome also, although he attacks this fiction

<column-break/>

frequently, writes in *Book 4 on Jeremiah, Chapter 14*, that he does not dare to condemn it, because many ecclesiastical men and martyrs have said it. Augustine also, in *The City of God, Book 20, Chapter 7*, calls that opinion "tolerable," provided that we understand what Cerinthus said about bodily delights as being instead about spiritual ones; he even writes that he himself once held that opinion. Observe here that Augustine distinguishes the opinion of the Fathers from the heresy of Cerinthus by the name of "spiritual delights." To this also pertains the fact that Irenaeus, although he defends the opinion of the Chiliasts, nevertheless "draws his pen" <note>An idiom meaning to write against or attack with words</note> against Cerinthus in *Against Heresies, Book 1, Chapter 25* because of those dogmas. From this, it follows that celebrated theologians rightly conclude that those pious ancients did not embrace the "Cerinthian monsters" regarding bodily pleasures.

In our own age, the first rank among these curious seekers was held by Augustinus Weber, a furrier <note>term: *pellio*; a person who prepares or sells furs</note>. According to Xystus Betuleius in his *Commentary on Lactantius, Book 3, Chapter 4*, in the Year of Christ 1530, Weber dared to take upon himself the "Chiliarchic" empire of which Cerinthus had predicted, deceiving both himself and others with the delusions of revelations that he boasted of. He had the Anabaptists as his followers <note>original: *Syndromos*</note>, who eagerly seized upon the same error; they are mentioned in the *Augsburg Confession, Article 17*, and by Chytræus in his commentary on *Revelation, Chapter 20*.

This error also pleased certain Photinians. For although Smalcius writes in his *Book on the Divinity of Christ, Chapter 15, page 56*, and Socinus in his *Miscellanea, page 50*, that they do not approve of that sentiment, Socinus nevertheless adds—speaking the mind of his followers, whom he calls "zealous for piety" (*page 50*) and "living a plainly spiritual life, or certainly striving to live so perpetually" (*page 96*)—that this Kingdom of Christ will be a physical one on earth. Specifically, he claims it will be in Judea itself, over the Jewish people in Jerusalem, after that city has been restored by the will and providence of God in that same province and location where it was before (*page 51*).

Johannes Piscator writes in his *Commentary on Revelation, Chapter 20*, that only the martyrs will be resurrected before the universal resurrection of all men, and they will reign with Christ in heaven for a thousand years; only then will the remaining men be called back from death to life.

The more recent Jews also belong here; Buxtorf demonstrates at length in his *Book on the Jewish Synagogue, Chapter 36, pages 511 and following*, that they expect a certain form of a Chiliastic Kingdom in the times of the Messiah, whom they imagine is yet to come.

Altogether to be categorized here are the "New Enthusiasts," who embrace the dreams of Ezekiel Meth (also named Elias of Zion). These "reformers of the world" establish three ages: or the time of the whole world, following the lead of the Anabaptists, about whom Sleidan writes in his *Commentaries, Book 10, page 277*. They divide these ages according to the number of Persons in the Divinity. The first age they attribute to the Father, which they say began...

### 29. Choir. Chorus.

A *Chorus* is a multitude of those singing and dancing together, derived from the Greek word *choros* <note>original: *χορός*</note>. Others derive the name from the fact that, in the beginning, people stood around the altars in the fashion of a crown <note>original: *Coronæ*</note> and sang psalms in that way. Thus, a Choir is called a circle of joined men, or an order of singers. In Greek it is *choros*. Servius says: A choir is properly the song of those with voices joined together. See *Pignorius in the treatise On Slaves, folio 71, citing Seneca's 84th Epistle; book 77 on legacies; and book 34 on the edicts of the aediles.*

The interior area in churches is also called a "choir" because such songs are performed there. From this, the Canons <term>members of a cathedral or collegiate church</term> are commonly called "Choir-Lords" <note>original: *Chorherren*</note>.

### ADDITION.

Suidas <term>a 10th-century Greek lexicographer</term> says the Ecclesiastical Choir is the assembly of those singing in temples. He notes that the Choirs of the churches were divided into two parts under Constantius (the son of Constantine the Great) and Flavian, the Bishop of Antioch. From Antioch, where it began, the custom of singing the Psalms of David back and forth <note>referring to antiphonal singing</note> spread to all parts of the world. *See Peter Gregory in the Compendium of Universal Law, book 15, chapter 22, number 12.*

The Egyptian *Choraules* <note>original: *Choraules* - a flute-player who accompanies a chorus</note>. For the Egyptian flute-players and castanet-dancers <note>original: *Crotalistriæ*</note> were highly prized. *Scaliger on Propertius, book 4; Bernartius on the Silvae of Statius, book 5, at the end; Savaro on Sidonius, book 1, epistle 2.* For the Egyptian boys sang excellently, and for that reason Statius calls them "talkative darlings." The term "Choral" <note>original: *Choral*</note> is used for the choir boys <note>original: *Pueris Choraulis*</note> who are employed among Christians in the ancient Church, concerning whom see *Brouwer on Fortunatus, book 2, epigram 1; Georg Erhard in the Commentary on Petronius, verse 17, my folio 771.* A *Choralistria* is a female jester or entertainer; *ibid, folio 625.*

### 30. Country Bishop. Chorepiscopus.

The *Chorepiscopus* <note>from the Greek *chora* (country/region) and *episkopos* (overseer)</note> was formerly the name for one who performed the care of souls in villages or small towns in place of a Bishop; he was named from *chora*, meaning "place," because he stood in the place of a Bishop. *See Bellarmine, On the Clergy, book 1, chapter 17.* On this point, *Antonio Cuccho in the Institutes of Canon Law, book 1* says: There were formerly certain men called Country Bishops who were indeed inferior to Bishops but superior to Priests. They could be put in charge not only of cities, like Bishops, but also of villages. However, their use is abolished today. *See Laurenz Ohm on Episcopal Law, thesis 13, letter b, volume 2 of the Basel Disputations; and Matthias Stephanus, Part 3 on Jurisdiction, page 1, chapter 8.*

Others derive the name from *chora* taken to mean "the country," as if they were *chorikoi* <note>original: *χωρικοί*</note>, that is, "rustics," or rather

<column-break/>

called "pagan" and "village" Bishops, because they performed the duty and role of a Bishop not in the city, but through the villages and country districts. Their office was held in common with the Bishops, and they were essentially his deputies. However, because they began to claim episcopal honors for themselves under this pretext, and no good reason for their institution remained apparent, they were made obsolete and quashed. *See chapters 4 and 5, distinction 68; Peter Gregory of Toulouse, Compendium of Universal Law, book 15, chapter 12, number 46.*

Nevertheless, we cannot deny that in our own time, Country Bishops <note>original: *Chorepiscopos*</note> still thrive in the primary churches of Germany. Indeed, it is clear from the records of the Imperial Recesses that Philip Christopher von Sötern used this title, "Country Bishop of Trier" <note>original: *Chor-Bischoff zu Trier*</note>, in his signature at the Recess of the Empire at Augsburg in the year 1582, when he was acting as the legate for the Bishops of Worms and Speyer. Likewise, there was a dispute regarding the precedence of the Emperor and the Chamber in the case of Gebhard, the Bishop of Cologne, and the Country Bishop of that same place, as noted from *Gail by Peter Syring in On Religious Peace, chapter 14, my page 142.* The annals of history also teach us that the Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg was the "Country Bishop of Cologne" <note>original: *Chor-Bischoff zu Cölln*</note>. *Christoph Beindorff in Arumäus, volume 3, discourse 9, thesis 6 and following; add Reinhard König in the Political Theater, part 1, chapter 35, number 51.*

### ADDITION.

Cujas explains what Country Bishops are in his *Commentary on the Code, "On Bishops and Clergy."* There were once Country Bishops who received that name from *chora*, that is, a "village," like rustic or rather village-dwelling Bishops. Regarding these, see *Matthias Stephanus, part 1, chapter 8, number 15; and Laurenz Ohm in the treatise On Episcopal Law, thesis 13, letter a.* Country Bishops were assistants to the Bishops. *Adam Contzen, book 6 of Politics, chapter 39, section 7.* Country Bishops were inferior to Archdeacons. *Book 6, chapter 39, section 8.* Country Bishops of the "curveti" <note>possibly referring to a specific administrative district or curved staff</note>, *book 6, chapter 39, section 6.* Country Bishops persist in the territory of Trier. *ibid.* Country Bishops did not dare to lay on hands <term>perform ordinations or confirmations</term>. *book 6, chapter 39, section 9.* Those retaining the name of Country Bishop do not act contrary to the Holy Canons. *book 6, chapter 39, section 10.*

### 31. Christians, Christianity. Christiani.

Regarding Christians, see *Vincent Lupanum, folio 86, etc.* on their progress. *Tertullian in the Apology, chapter 37.* And regarding their most heavy persecutions, see *Camerarius in his "Leisure Hours" or Historical Meditations; also myself in the Historical Synopsis, passim.*

Lælius Bisciola proves in *Leisure Hours, volume 1, book 13, chapter 17, folio 996 and following*, that Christians were once included under the name of "Jews," and that they were called "Christians" as a form of verbal abuse.

### 33. Prince-Electors. Electors.

The Electors are called the Prince-Electors <note>original: *Churfürsten*</note> (who are also called the "Choosers" <note>original: *Wählere*</note> in the native language of the ancient Germans, according to Freher in his commentary on Lupold of Bebenburg’s *Rights of the Kingdom*, chapter 2. Likewise, they are called "Election-Princes" <note>original: *Wahlfürsten*</note> and "Election-Lords" <note>original: *Wahlherren*</note> in the *Saxon Mirror* <term>original: *Sachsen-Spiegel*; a significant medieval German legal code</term> book 1, chapter 6 near the end). They have their name from "Choosing" <note>original: *vom kôren*</note>. See Goldast’s commentary on the *Admonitions*, folio 360. For they hold power when the throne is vacant, "as often as the Holy Empire is empty" <note>original: *so offt das heilig Reich ledig ist*</note>, as is said in the Golden Bull <term>original: *A. B.* or *Aurea Bulla*; the 1356 decree fixing the system for electing the Emperor</term> title 4, paragraph "furthermore," and title 5 at the beginning. This vacancy occurs either by the death or the deposition of the Emperor, whether active or passive: or as is commonly said, either by resignation or degradation (based on the argument in the Clementine decree *ne Romani*, 2, where the gloss on the word "dying" discusses elections and the power of the Electors). It also occurs "as often as the Prince-Electors find it necessary and useful for the assistance of the Emperor, or otherwise for the Holy Roman Empire, even during the lifetime of a Roman Emperor" to elect a King of the Romans <term>the title held by the Emperor-elect before his formal coronation</term>. The dignity of these men is clearly Royal. See Heigius, part 1, question 4, number 51; and Sixtinus, *On Regalities*, chapter 4, number 29, book 1. "Beyond their lineages, no higher or more stately families are to be found." From this it follows "that the Prince-Electors do not address Kings as 'Your Grace,' but as 'Your Dignity' and 'Your Belovedness'; the reason being because they are esteemed as equals to Kings." For they are the Principal Columns of the Empire, the "Noble Pillars of the Realm" <note>original: *Edle Seulen des Reichs*</note>, according to the Golden Bull, chapter 3. "In whom the highness of the Imperial Honor consists," as Emperor Sigismund speaks in the preface of the Golden Bull. Add also Josua Nolden, *On the Status of the Nobility*, chapter 8, number 49 and following. Regarding these men, Gevvoldus and Windeck have published singular treatises most worthy of reading. Add also what I have written concerning succession and election, volume 2, chapter 3. Likewise, Freher on Peter of Andlau, book 2, chapter 1, etc. Furthermore, Caspar von Lerch, in *The German Knightly Order*, folio 40, attempts to prove that formerly "the Nobility of the Empire held the Imperial Right of Election along with the Princes."

There are two Orders of Electors, namely Ecclesiastical and Secular. The first, the Ecclesiastical, consists of three; the Secular, however, consists of four Electors. All of them are encompassed in the following verses:

->Besold, Volume I.<-

<column-break/>

->Mainz, Trier, and Cologne,<-
->Each of these shall be a Chancellor of the Empire.<-
->The Palatine is Steward; the Duke is Sword-<-
->bearer,<-
->The Margrave is set over the Chamber, the Bohemian is Cup-<-
->bearer;<-
->These establish the Supreme Lord for all ages.<-

Among the Ecclesiastical Electors (1.) is numbered the Archbishop of Mainz, who is the Chancellor of Germany and the "face" <note>original: *πρόσωπον* (prosōpon)</note> of the whole College, concerning whom see Serarius, *Matters of Mainz*, book 1, chapter 24, where he also compiles many general facts about the Electors. (2.) The Archbishop of Cologne, Chancellor of Italy, or "across the Alps." (3.) The Archbishop of Trier, Chancellor of Gaul, specifically for that part contained within the Kingdom of Arles <term>a region in SE France that was part of the Empire</term>, which alone acknowledged the Roman Empire. For through the rest of Gaul, there was no need for a Chancellor. Among the Secular Electors, the King of Bohemia claims the first place for himself, whose office is that of the Cup-bearer, or Arch-Cupbearer of the Empire. For he is bound to bring the first drink—not pure wine, but diluted with water, according to the Golden Bull chapter 27, number 5 (perhaps following the precept of Solomon in Proverbs, last chapter, verse 4)—during the celebration of the Imperial Court; however, he is not required to serve while wearing the Royal crown unless he wishes to do so of his own free will. (2.) The Count Palatine of the Rhine <note>original: *Pfaltzgrav beym Rhein*</note> is the Arch-Chef or Arch-Steward of the Empire, "the High Steward of the Holy Roman Empire" <note>original: *der Oberste Truchsaß deß heiligen Römischen Reichs*</note>. See Christoph Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, book 7, chapter 52, paragraph 54. His duty in solemn courts, at the coronation of the King, and other assembly ceremonies, is to carry the apple or golden orb before the Emperor as a sign of universal Empire. See the Golden Bull title 2, and Nolden, cited chapter 8, number 82. See also the *Chronicle of Reichersperg* for the year 1118, concerning the outlawed Duke Leo of Bavaria and Saxony, and how the Palatine then received the Duchy of Bavaria from the Emperor by his own authority, etc.

Regarding the privileges held by the Count Palatine, one should consult the aforementioned Mr. Josua Nolden’s treatise *On the Status of the Nobility*, chapter 8, number 83 and following. (3.) The Duke of Saxony is the Arch-Marshal of the Empire, whose office is to be the Sword-bearer. Just as formerly the Praetorian Prefect carried a sword before the Emperor as a sign of pure command (according to P. Faber, *Semestria*, book 1, chapter 3), so the Saxon carries a naked and drawn sword before the Emperor as a sign of Justice. These two Electors, namely the Palatine and the Saxon, are the Vicars <term>temporary administrators</term> of the Empire when it is vacant: regarding whom see the singular disputation of Michael Schifferer, and the disputation found in volume 5 of the *Basel Disputations*, thesis 18 and following. (4.) The Margrave of Brandenburg, who is the Arch-Chamberlain, guardian of the Royal Bedchamber, and prefect of the treasury. Therefore, his insignia is the Scepter (formerly keys), an instrument of governance, which he carries before the Emperor when he is crowned. Only these men have the right of election, all others being excluded, because they are the Officials of the Kingdom.

Furthermore, the Electors have their own Vicars and Sub-Officers, such as the King of Bohemia having the Hereditary Cup-bearer of Limburg <note>original: *Erbschencken von Limburg*</note>, the Palatine having the Hereditary Marshal of Pappenheim <note>original: *Erbmarschalcken von Pappenheim*</note>, and the Elector of Brandenburg having the Hereditary Chamberlain, the Count of Hohenzollern <note>original: *Erb-Cämmerer Graven von Hohenzollern*</note>. See Nolden, cited location, question 118, and more below under the word "Hereditary Office" <note>original: *Erbamt*</note>.

The Electors may appear for the election even through Proxies, if they are detained by a legitimate hindrance. See the Golden Bull <term>original: *A. B.* or *Aurea Bulla*; the 1356 decree establishing the constitutional structure of the Holy Roman Empire</term>, title 25, the section "whosoever." For the Canons <note>Church laws</note> permit no one to appoint a proxy for electing unless they are entangled by a just impediment and cannot be present themselves. This impediment must even be proven by oath, if necessary. (Chapter *quia propter*, 42, penultimate section, on the Election and Power of the Elected). However, such an oath can hardly be required in our specific case, since the Carolingian sanction <note>The Golden Bull of Charles IV</note> makes no mention of it; see the New Constitutions 18, chapter 5 at the beginning.

Once the Electors have gathered at the appointed time for the Election and the sacred rites have been performed, they swear—by the faith by which they are bound to God and the Holy Roman Empire—that by all their discretion and understanding, with God as their author and helper, they will designate and elect as a temporal head for the Christian people (that is, the King of the Romans to be promoted to Emperor) the one who stands out above others as most suitable, without any price, favor, or promise, or whatever such things might be called. This they confirm by an oath to God, touching the books of the Holy Gospels. The formula for this is as follows:

> I, [Name], Archbishop of Mainz and Arch-chancellor of the Holy Empire throughout Germany, and Prince-Elector, swear upon the Holy Gospels lying here before me, that by the loyalty with which I am bound to God and the Holy Roman Empire, I will, according to all my knowledgeable perception and reason, with God’s help, elect a worldly head for the Christian people and raise a King of the Romans to be Emperor, who is fit for the task, so far as my discernment and reason guide me, and according to my aforementioned loyalty and vote: This my vote and choice I will give without any bargain, reward, gift, promise, or whatever such a thing might be named. So help me God and all the Saints. (Golden Bull, section on the election of a King of the Romans, § 2).

Having performed the prescribed oath, the Election proceeds, where the Archbishop of Mainz has this duty above the others: to ask the gathered Electors for their opinions and votes. He himself, however, is questioned by the Prince of the Saxons. Whomever the majority now elects and appoints is hailed and proclaimed as the most invincible King, later to be declared the Caesar <note>Emperor</note> of the Romans. As to whether someone can elect himself, see Valentin Riemer, *On Jurisdiction*, G. I.

<column-break/>

See Limnäus, in his notes on Daniel Otto’s *Public Law*, page 27.

As to why the Emperors would greet the Ecclesiastical Electors by the name of "Nephews"—"their dear Nephews and Prince-Electors" <note>original: *ihre liebe Neven und Churfürsten*</note>—see Mr. Josua Nolden, *On the Noble*, chapter 8, number 71 and following.

And regarding which Emperor first greeted the Ecclesiastical Electors by this name, the same Nolden should be consulted at the cited location, number 75 and following.

The Electors (whom Albert of Stade in his *Chronicle*, page 215, calls the "Taxers of Princes" <note>original: *Prætaxatores Principum*</note>) are commonly equated to the Praetorian Prefects <term>original: *Præfectis Prætorio*; the highest administrative and judicial officials of the later Roman Empire</term>. Just as there is no appeal from a decision of a Praetorian Prefect (as seen in various laws in the Digest and Code of Justinian), so too Eunapius said that the Praetorian Prefecture was like the Imperial dignity itself, except it lacked the use of the Purple or the ceremonial robe (*trabea*). Thus, even today, there is no appeal from the Electors of Saxony. (New Constitutions of Augustus; Albinus, *History of Meissen*, part 1, title 16). Although this privilege was granted indiscriminately to all Electors in the Golden Bull of Charles IV, title 11, the others lost it through contrary use. (Henning Arnisaeus, book 2, *On the Rights of Majesty*, chapter 2, number 3). Not long ago, however, the Elector of Brandenburg recovered it through an Imperial concession. (Arnold de Reyger, in his *Treasury of Law*, question 4, number 33, book 1; see also my own work, *Treatise on Appeals*, page 72).

Regarding the origin of the Electors, there is a doubtful dispute, which I also mentioned in Dissertation 3, book 2, *On the Elected King*. And indeed, Petrus Cutsenius in *Saxon Catholica*, page 82, proves by induction that neither Pope Gregory nor Emperor Otto was the author of that constitution and sanction; it will not be regretted to have seen his work, and add the *Skirmish on the Seven Electors* by Aemilius Chreggene.

Regarding Electoral Guardianship, see the tract: *What Palatine Richard sought at the Election in Heidelberg*. Likewise, *The Constant Refutation of the Unfounded Heidelberg Report*, etc., printed in Lauingen in the year 1611, as well as the treatise by Gevwoldus.
