### 34. Meeting of the Electors. <note>original: *Churfürstentag; Conventus Electorales*</note>

The Electors are permitted to call and hold assemblies not only for the purpose of electing a King or Roman Emperor, but it is also granted to them to celebrate other gatherings for the safety and well-being of the Empire. *Golden Bull, title 12.* This has been strictly observed until now and preserved by the fraternal union of the Electors, as noted by Goldast in *Political Affairs of the Empire, part 8, chapter 3,* and was confirmed by a solemn agreement contracted between Emperor Ferdinand and the Electors in the year 1558, in these words:

> We also permit that the aforementioned six Electors <note>At the time of this 1558 agreement, there were six active Electors, as the King of Bohemia's role was often restricted to the election itself.</note>, from time to time, according to the power of the Golden Bull and their rights within the Holy Empire, may come together for their own necessity, or when they have burdensome obligations, to consider and deliberate on the same. We shall neither hinder nor interfere with this, nor shall we harbor or conceive any displeasure or ill-will against them collectively or individually; instead, we wish to conduct ourselves graciously and blamelessly toward them in this and other matters, according to the Golden Bull. <note>original German: "Wir lassen auch zu, daß die gedachte sechs Churfürsten..."</note>

In this meeting of the Electors, however, all the most difficult and serious business of the Empire is handled: the alienation and pledging of the Imperial Domain assets, matters of Peace and War, taxes, the maintenance of this College's authority, the defense of Territories, Royalties <term>Regalia: the specific rights, lands, and privileges belonging to a sovereign</term>, and the Rights of the Electors against all force, the removal of seditions, conspiracies, and Leagues against the supreme Head of the Christian World <note>the Emperor</note>, the defense of the sublime honor of the Caesar <note>the Emperor</note>, and the prevention of the Empire's diminishment. In short, all causes looking toward the grace, honor, benefit, and growth of the Empire are treated here, as understood from the cited Fraternal Union of the Electors. Indeed, it is likely from histories that even the removal of an Emperor from the Empire—truly a matter of great weight <note>original Latin: "re mehercle non glandis legendæ"; literally "not a matter of gathering acorns," a Roman legal idiom for a serious matter</note>—was deliberated in this Meeting. Nor do the remaining Princes of the Empire participate in any part of this sublime Right. [References to] Master Doctor Bocer, Bertram.

And the prerogative and dignity of the Electors shines forth all the more greatly, as it is generally less permitted to the other

<column-break/>

States of the Empire to hold any assembly, as noted by Arnold Clapmarius, *book 3, on the Secrets of Republics, chapter 13, at the end.* [Also cited:] Trentacinqu. *book 2, various resolutions, folio 245* and following; an exception is made, however, among others, for that Naumburg Convention, in which the hereditary alliance that exists between the Houses of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Hesse is usually renewed. In that case, lest any sinister suspicion arise from it, they inform the Emperor of the reasons for the gathering. Sleidanus, *Commentaries, book 26, year 1555.* Yet the attendees do not need to seek a special pardon. Finally, Bertram excepts the confederations and meetings of the Hanseatic League; see Carpzov and Reinhard König.

### 35. Cistern. <note>original: *Cistern; Cisterna*</note>

A cistern is a receptacle for rainwater, whose water does not come from the bowels of the earth, but descends through the pipes of the roofs; it is as if it were a chest <note>Latin: *cista*</note> beneath the earth. Thus, it does not have permanent or "living" water <note>spring water</note>, but water gathered from rains. If these are not properly covered and some animal falls in and perishes, the owner of the cistern shall be bound to pay its price, but the dead animal shall belong to the owner of the cistern. A cistern is so attached to a house that if the house is sold, all the cistern's equipment—copper channels, covers, etc.—are included and cannot be removed by the seller; as is also the case in these and similar things:

> Whatever is enclosed by a bond or joint, and is also walled in, the seller may not have broken off or removed, <note>original German: "Was Band und Nied beschleusset..."</note>

as the City of Nuremberg provided in its Statutes. *Volume 6, Basel Disputation on Water Law, thesis 22.*

And such cisterns are found in mountain fortresses, in the mountain-castles <note>original: *Berg-Schlössern*</note>.

-> ADDITION. <-

> At Ruprechtstein, near Sulzbach, at the castle, the brewing and cooking of beer and everything else is performed with cistern water directed from the roofs into the gutters, as I have seen myself with my own eyes. <note>original German: "Zu Ruprechtstein..."</note> Whether an aqueduct can be established from a Castle, and from that receptacle in which water is lifted from a river by a wheel, is discussed at length by Hugo Donellus in his *Commentaries on Civil Law.*

This pertains to that clause, added to the above, which is usually inserted in the instruments of purchase for the sale of houses: with everything that **is joined and nail-fast** <note>original: *Genied und Nagelfest*; a legal term for fixtures that cannot be removed from a property</note>, or **what is earth, joined, and nail-fast**. Agricola, *on Appurtenances, question 11.*

### 37. Citation. Summoning. <note>original: *Manung*</note>

To summon, to warn, to cite, to call into law. Pithou says: *Mannire* <note>An Old Frankish/Latin legal term</note> is to call into law in the presence of three witnesses. *Laws of the Ripuarians*, title 61: If anyone has need of a witness at the *mallum* <note>a public assembly or court</note> before the Centenary <note>a local official</note>, and perhaps the witnesses are unwilling to come to the Assembly, he who needs them must *mannire* (summon) them.

It is also called *Maniare*, which comes a little closer to our [German] word *manen* (to warn/summon); from which comes *Mannita*, a citation or admonition. Thus *Mannitus* means cited or called, from our *manen*, which is elsewhere called *fordern* (to demand) or *häischen* (to ask), perhaps named from *monendo* (warning).

A general citation of those who pretend to have a right is made in many cases if the persons are uncertain. See Blarer on the law *Diffamari*, chapter 2, number 10, etc.; Gail, book 1, observation 57, with Grævus’s notes. Mynsinger, century 2, observation 47: If someone cites his own subject, or someone he can cite outside the territory, he must ask through letters of requisition that the Ordinary <note>the local judge or bishop</note> of the place where the person stays should deliver the citation to him, etc. Concerning an edictal citation [a public notice], see *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 2, counsel 43.

->ADDITION.<-

A person who is cited to appear in the early morning, <term>at the proper early time of day</term>, but only presents himself in court after noon, does not incur the penalty for contumacy <note>legal defiance or failure to appear</note>. Carpzov, part 1, decision 43, throughout. In a citation, the first and last name of the person to be cited must be expressed. Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated*, observation 49, preface. Even if associates are called at the same time, it is not valid [without specific names].

<column-break/>

Only that person needs to be cited to whom the defense principally belongs, nor is a citation required for those who might be harmed as a consequence of that judgment. Knipschild, *On Trusts*, chapter 16, number 195, and those cited there. A citation cannot be removed by Statute or Custom, as Bartolus teaches on the law *omnes populi* in the *Digest: On Justice and Law* and on the law *de quibus* in the *Digest: On Laws*; see also Schurff, counsel 38, century 1, and counsel 9, number 1, century 2.

Should a messenger claiming to cite someone by order of the Judge be believed without previous proof? See Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated*, page 22.

### 38. Clarissines. The Order of the Nuns of Saint Clare.

These are nuns of the Order of Saint Francis. Indeed, Pope Eugenius IV granted to the nuns of the first Rule of Saint Clare—who are otherwise called the *Collectaneae*—that they are not bound to walk with bare feet, but may wear those things which do not come under the name of shoes or are not judged as such, and even shoes when it is opportune. Likewise, that the Generals and Provincials of the Friars Minor of the Observance should have the faculty, with the counsel of the discreet, to dispense the aforementioned nuns from rules regarding food, silence, and any other precepts contained in their Rule. Finally, he willed and declared that the aforementioned nuns do not incur a mortal sin in the transgression of any of the precepts of the first Rule of Saint Clare, except for those four which concern the principal vows: namely, Obedience, Poverty, Chastity, and Enclosure, as well as the election and deposition of the Abbess. *Compendium of Regular Questions*, under the word "Nuns."

On whether the Sisters of Saint Clare are capable of holding property in common and can succeed [to an inheritance] by Will or from one who dies intestate? Vincent Hondedei consulted on this in volume 2, counsel 76, and as I think, he affirms it.

## 41. Codicillary Clause: If this my Testament cannot or should not have stability and force as a legitimate Testament, I nevertheless wish that it be held and valid as a Codicil, or any other disposition and transaction by reason of death.

A <term>Codicillary Clause</term> <note>A safety-net clause in a will stating that if the document fails to meet the strict legal requirements of a "Will," it should still be honored as a "Codicil" (a less formal document)</note> is usually added to a Will in this form; and it then takes place when the Will is not valid due to a defect in the required formalities, according to the text and gloss in the law *Codicillos*, final paragraph, *Digest* on legacies 2. It does not, however, proceed when the Will is invalidated due to a defect of the incomplete will of the Testator, based on the law *ea scriptura*, *Digest* on testaments, and the law *fideicommissa* § 1, *Digest* on legacies 3. Bartolus on law 1, number 7 and following, *Digest* on the law of Codicils; and there is text in the final law of the *Codex* on Codicils, where it is held: that if a testator is unable to fulfill a Testament, and has added a Codicillary Clause in it, that clause shall turn the inheritance into a direct trust <note>original: *fideicommissum*</note>. For that incomplete will of the Testator, in this case, is understood—

<meta>This page continues the legal encyclopedia under the letter "C," moving from the discussion of monasteries and church property to the technical legalities of inheritance law—specifically the "codicillary clause." This clause was a "safety net" used by legal professionals to ensure a person's final wishes were carried out even if their formal Will failed to meet strict legal requirements.</meta>

page 174
The Augmented Treasury of Practice

it is understood that the failure is due to a lack of some formality, not a lack of intent. This is noted by Decius in *Consultation 394* and Laurentius Tenninius in his *Treatise on Clauses, clause 22, number 2.*

Certainly, <term>Codicils</term> <note>informal additions or amendments to a Will that did not require the same strict formalities as the Will itself</note> were invented for the fulfillment of <term>trusts</term> <note>original: *fideicommissa*—a request for an heir to hand over property to another person</note>, as seen in the *Code of Justinian, book 6, title 36 (On Codicils)*. If a testator says in a codicil: "Let Titius be my heir," it cannot be granted strictly according to the rules of Wills; however, the law bends if it is given directly as a trust, as seen in the law *Scævola* regarding the <term>Trebellianic Decree</term>. In such a case, the person appointed as heir by law—namely the person who would inherit if there were no Will <note>original: *ab intestato*</note>—is compelled to accept the inheritance. This legal heir, after keeping their own "fourth" share <note>a legal minimum share known as the *Quarta Falcidia*</note>, is forced to restore the rest of the inheritance to the person named in the trust. This is based on the aforementioned law *Scævola* and Bartolus's commentary on the *Digest*.

If a Will fails because of a defect in the person making it—for example, because they lacked the legal capacity to make a Will—then the aforementioned clause has no effect. For anyone who cannot make a Will likewise cannot create a codicil, according to the *Digest, title on the Law of Codicils*.

When a testator adds a clause to their Will stating they want it to be valid **"in every better way and law possible,"** <note>original: *omni meliori modo & jure, quo possit*</note> it appears they did not wish to bind themselves strictly to a formal written Will, but rather to choose whatever formula or path would allow their will to achieve its power and effect. This clause—*in every better way and law*—has such great force and efficacy that the declaration must be considered valid. This is argued from the *Digest* regarding military Wills. See also Romanus, Bartolus, Castrensis, and Jason. But see also Alexander, *Consultation 176*, and others including Herman Meier on Wills.

Likewise, if a testator inserts a clause into their Will stating: **"If this declaration cannot stand by the law of Wills, let it be valid by the power of any other expression of will, <gloss>that it shall be valid and have force as any other last will</gloss>,"** <note>original German: *daß es gelten und Krafft haben soll, als ein jeder anderer letzter Will*</note> it must be said that the testator did not want their intent to be restricted to a specific legal category, but intended it to be valid in whatever way possible. Baldus advised that a Will of this kind should be upheld with the force of codicils. See Paris, Alexander, and Socinus.

Furthermore, the legal authorities teach that this clause has greater authority than a standard codicillary clause. They explain that while a standard clause might only result in a trust, this broader clause allows for something almost like a direct appointment of an heir. See Meier on Wills, book 3.

When a codicillary clause is added to a Will, it is considered to consist of two distinct arrangements: one testamentary and the other codicillary. Consequently, if the testamentary arrangement fails, the codicillary one retains its power. This is found in the *Code of Justinian* and the *Digest*. See the frequently cited Meier.

<column-break/>

### Should the Codicillary Clause be considered a result of the custom of Notaries rather than the true will of the testator?

The answer is that it is added from the mind of the testator, not merely from the custom of Notaries, because it is customarily included at the testator's direction. Since a Will is read aloud in the presence of the testator, the Notary is understood only to be writing down what the testator willed, what was said, and what was enjoined upon the Notary. This is supported by Cornelius, Decius, and Cagnolus, who notes that even if a scribe makes an error, the intent of the testator prevails. See also Achilles Personalis and others.

The reasoning is that such a clause, when placed in a Will, must perform some function, even if it is customarily used by Notaries as a matter of style. According to Ripa, when a testator hears the clause read and explained in the common tongue, they cannot help but perceive its general force and power. For who would not perceive that they are providing for every eventuality, and that they clearly want what they are doing to be valid, even if they do not understand every specific legal technicality these clauses cover? Indeed, Decius reports that Bartolus was refuted by many legal opinions for suggesting that such a clause does nothing. A Notary may even add the title of "appointment of heir" without fear of being accused of falsifying the document. Since this is the style used everywhere among nations, it carries weight.

On the Codicillary Clause, one may consult Bitsch, a formerly famous Professor at Strasbourg, as well as Vitalis de Cambanis, Tenninius, and Bolognetus. Most recently, see Carpzovius in *Decision 155*.

# ADDITION

Legal scholars <note>original: *Doctores*</note> attribute such force to a Will made between children that, regardless of how it is made, it is always considered to contain a **tacit codicillary clause**—meaning the father is presumed to want his Will to be valid **"in every better way"** possible. This is the view of Sichard and Mynsing. However, this common opinion is contradicted by Giphanius.

This is the primary law relied upon by the Doctors of Law, yet they are often refuted by it. The Codicillary Clause may be placed before, after, or within the Will itself, stating that "if it is not valid by the law of Wills, let it be valid by the law of Codicils." This clause is not assumed to exist unless it is expressly written. This remains true even in a Will made by a parent for their children, even though the Doctors commonly teach that in this case, a Codicillary Clause is silently implied. See Pacius in his *Analysis of the Code*, page 656, and the sources cited there. Regarding when a Codicillary Clause should be understood as implied in a Will between children, see the *Altdorf Consultations*, pages 407 and 410; specifically, it applies if it benefits the children, but not when it brings a disadvantage or creates inequality among them. The Codicillary Clause is silently understood in all Wills, according to Klock, volume 2, consultation 42, number 262.

Regarding whether a Codicillary Clause should have force in the case of a <term>posthumous child</term> <note>a child born after the death of the father/testator</note> who was unknowingly passed over, when the testator did not survive long after the child’s birth, see Bitschius in his *Decade of Cases for a Friend*, Case 10.

### 42. **Collation of Church Property.**
**Collation of Ecclesiastical Benefices.**

->ADDITION.<-

From the <term>collation</term> <note>the formal act of presenting a person to a church office or "benefice"</note> of a church benefit, the person appointed holds a <term>right to the thing</term> <note>original: *jus ad rem* — a personal right to claim the office</note> before they accept it; but once they have accepted, they possess a <term>right in the thing</term> <note>original: *jus in re* — a property right</note>, even without physical possession. For full possession, a formal delivery or "taking hold" is required. See Hahn, *On the Law of Things*, chapter 11, numbers 12 and 14.

### 43. **Collegiate or Foundation Church.** **Collegiate Church.**

In foundation or <term>Collegiate Churches</term> <note>churches where a "college" of clergy (canons) resides, but which is not a monastery</note>, the <term>right of nominating or electing</term> <note>original: *Jus nominandi seu eligendi*</note> belongs to the "College" or the <term>Canons</term> <note>priests who live in a community attached to a cathedral or collegiate church</note>; however, the <term>Patrons</term> <note>wealthy protectors or founders of a church</note> often reserve the right to approve the election once it is canonically performed. This right (namely, providing consent after the election is complete) has this effect: the election is voided if the Patron has a just cause for dissenting. This consent is required for the "well-being" of the institution and out of respect. See the Canon Law in the chapter "As so..." regarding elections. Butrio, in his *Treatise on the Right of Patronage*, chapter 25, number 22.

A church is said to be "Collegiate" when there is a Rector acting as the "Head" and Canons acting as the "members." See Rivianus in his *Rationale* on the chapter "Statute" regarding elections and elective power, number 6. Alternatively, a Collegiate Church is defined as one in which there is a college which holds the governance

<column-break/>

and administration of the church. For a "college" is a certain "fictional body," represented by individuals gathered into one. See Erasmus of Chokier, volume 2, *Treatise on Jurisdiction over Exempt Persons*, part 1, section 2, numbers 9 and 10. A Collegiate Church is proven by legal instruments, especially ancient ones over one hundred years old, and also by the descriptive words in documents which mention "head and members," as confirmed by many, including Cardinal Tuschus in his *Practical Conclusions*, letter C, conclusion 458.

It is a matter of clear law that the reception and election of Canons, and the full disposal of <term>Canonries</term> <note>the office or "seat" of a canon</note>, belongs entirely to the Collegiate Church. See Renatus Choppinus, *On Sacred Policy*, book 1, chapter 32 at the beginning; Aegidius, decision 718; Federicus of Siena, consultation 34 and 61, number 4 at the end; and Tuschus under letters C and E.

Regularly, and by common law, in a Collegiate or <term>Conventual</term> <note>related to a convent or community of monks/canons</note> church, the election belongs to the church or the community; only then is a "vocation" called canonically performed when it was done in this manner, as Hostiensis details in his *Summary*, book 1, on elections. Fachin, volume 1, consultation 55, number 27, notes that election and petition belong to the College.

Hence, the interpreters of both Civil and Canon Law say that a Patron, by making a church "Collegiate," is deprived of his power without any fault of his own, though not without cause. See Antonius de Butrio, *On the Right of Patronage*, chapter 25, at the end; and Henricus de Boich, chapter 12, near the end.

Furthermore, even a secular college regularly holds the right by law to nominate colleagues to be substituted in the place of those who have died, as Professor Cothmann teaches in his *Academic Consultations*, as does Langlaeus, book 7, chapter 10, folio 375.

Regarding the jurisdiction of a Rector of a Collegiate Church, see Father Laymann in his *Canonical Conclusions on Ordinary Jurisdiction*, chapter 7. On Collegiate Churches in general, one may consult Villagut in his *Treatise on Church Goods* throughout, and see above under the word "Canons."

->ADDITION.<-

See Speidel in his *Notables*, folio 700; Menochius, book 3, presumption 90, number 18 and following.

### 47. To Recommend, Letters of Recommendation, Intercessions. *Literæ Commendatitiæ*.

One who falsely recommends someone and affirms they are suitable when they are not, is held liable to the Creditor. Schaeffer, book 1, *Practical Questions*, 46.
However, a simple recommendation of a future debtor obliges no one; Law "if indeed" 12, paragraph "when a certain," there: "he will not be bound, because it was written more for the sake of recommending the man than for the sake of giving a mandate" <note>A legal instruction to act on someone's behalf</note>, *Digest* on *Mandates*, Law "it must be known" 19, where it matters greatly whether he said something for the sake of recommending a servant, or truly promised he would guarantee what he said, on the *Aedile's Edict*. Hence, letters of recommendation are not said to be legally binding. Vitalis de Cambanis, *Treatise on Clauses*, in the clause "enumerated words uttered in letters." Johann Schneidewein in the *Principles of the Institutes* on *Mandates*, number 5. But it is different if fraud <note>original: *dolus*</note> is involved or a false persuasion; Law "but if" 8, Law "servant" 20, *Digest* on *Fraud*. Therefore, a bare recommendation without persuasion is one thing; a cunning and affected persuasion with urging is another, which is entirely binding. See...

### 48. Commander. *Commendator*.

A <term>Commendator</term> <note>An administrator who holds a 'commenda,' a benefice or property held in trust, often receiving its income without being the permanent religious head</note> of any Commandery or Prelacy is not a <term>Prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as an abbot or bishop, with ordinary jurisdiction</note>. Decio, consultation 149, number 5. Christinaeus, volume 1, decision 59.
This fails, however, if it is a perpetual Commandery. Corneus, consultation 66, book 3; Molina in the additions to Alexander, consultation 96, book 4; and consultation 37, where he cites chapter "If many," 21, question 1. If it is not perpetual, he is indeed merely a <term>Procurator</term> <note>A legal agent or proxy</note>: he has legitimate administration, but he does not make the "fruits" <note>The income, crops, or revenues produced by the land</note> his own because he is a guardian; he has no right in the Church, nor in the fruits. Besold, volume 1.

<column-break/>

except for the purpose of collecting, governing, and providing for himself and his ministers, and turning what remains to the benefit of the Church (for "to recommend" is nothing other than "to deposit." Law *Commendare* on the *Signification of Words*; see the Gloss on the law *Nemo* under the word *Commendare* regarding elections). Nevertheless, the opposite happens in practice. Said gloss: <note>original German: *Seynd nicht Commenthureyen, ſondern Abbteyen, welche als Commenden adminiſtrirt werden.*</note> *These are not Commanderies, but Abbeys which are administered as Commends.*
A <term>Commenda</term> is a title regarding administration only, not regarding the acquisition of a right in a benefice. A *Commenda* and a sequestration are considered equal.
Today, Commends are commonly made so that the Commander can turn the fruits not only to the benefit of the Church but also to his own use.
A Commander can lease the property of the Church for several years, can sue and be sued; but he cannot alienate <note>To sell or give away permanent ownership</note> the property.
The Commanders of St. James of the Sword, or of Alcantara and Calatrava, are not bound by a vow of chastity.
The Commanders of St. John of Jerusalem are bound by the same laws, and even stricter ones. Fr. Sarman, *On Ecclesiastical Revenues*, part 2, chapter 5, number 18.
Commanders fight on behalf of the Church. Sarmientus in the treatise *On Ecclesiastical Revenues*, part 4, chapter 1, number 13. Military orders were instituted to defend the Catholic faith with arms, living in chastity, which increases health and strength.
Regarding Commanders, and that they are to be numbered among ecclesiastical persons, and their Commends among ecclesiastical goods; and thus they do not fall under a general mortgage of all goods, even in places where the reformed religion flourishes, my friend Mr. Anton Bullaeus treats this excellently in consultation 10. And regarding Commends and Commendataries, see Camillo Borelli in *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 31.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical legal encyclopedia, specifically focusing on "C" entries. The previous page discussed letters of recommendation and legal advice; this page moves into judicial commissions, the invention of the compass, and the legalities of arbitration agreements.</meta>

<page-num>178</page-num>
<header>Enlarged Treasury of Practice</header>

Ruland <note>Rutger Ruland (1568–1630), a German jurist</note>, my friend; and one should also see Arumæus, volume 4, decision 17.

**Commissions**, for the perpetual memory of a matter <note>Latin: *ad perpetuam rei memoriam*. This is a legal procedure to record witness testimony before a trial begins, often because there is a risk the witness might die or become unavailable</note>, are by law requested from the judge whose tribunal handles the main case. However, among **Persons immediately subject to the Empire** <note>Those who hold their land and titles directly from the Emperor, rather than through a middle-ranking lord</note>, or if at least the person who is to be the defendant in the main case is immediately subject to the Empire: such petitions are not instituted before the Ordinary Judges of the *Austräg* <note>term: *Austräg* — a special system of arbitration for disputes between the estates of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, but in the Tribunal of the Imperial Chamber. Gail <note>Andreas Gail (1526–1587), often called the "Papinian of Germany"</note> records in Book 1, observation 93, number 2, that this is done because when there is danger in delay, the formality of seeking the adversary could not be observed without risk to the party. But that reasoning is not approved by Master Philipp Tennagelius: since such a commission is often decreed when no danger is present. Therefore, he says it should rather be stated that the Imperial Chamber can be approached for this reason; because such a **Commission** proceeds more from Imperial Authority than from ordinary Jurisdiction. On whether a Commissioner of the Emperor is bound to produce copies of the depositions of witnesses for the parties, or rather for the Emperor, see *Strassburg Consultations*, volume 2, consultation 40, paragraph 91. On whether an appeal may be made from the Imperial Commissioners to the Emperor or to the Chamber? See Gail, Book 1, observation 121, and my own work in the treatise *On Appeals*. And if such a Commissioner is given from the "fullness of power" <note>Latin: *plenitudo potestatis*, referring to the supreme sovereign authority of the Emperor</note>, I say no; but if by virtue of the *Austräg*, I affirm it.

### ADDITION.

Commissions are of "strict law" <note>This means they must be interpreted narrowly according to the letter of the law, without broad expansion</note>. See Ummius in *On Process*, pages 420 and 158. Gail, Book 1, observation 35, number 3. The commission for the examination of witnesses is the only one in use in the Imperial Chamber. Ummius in *On Process*, page 158.

### 50. Compass. Navigational Needle.

Gail. The Circle, the **compass** <note>original German: *compasse*</note> well-made together.

Regarding the invention of the **Magnet** in the use of Navigation, see my own work in the discourse *On the New World* <note>Latin: *de novo orbe*</note>, and Gilbert’s treatise *On the Magnet* throughout. Also see Fuller, *Miscellanies*, Book 4, chapter 19.

### ADDITION.

The Magnet is the most delightful miracle of nature. Klock, *On the Treasury*, Book 2, chapter 114, number 49. On where it is born? number 48. Its power? number 47. And whether it was known to Solomon? number 46. On the wondrous works of the Magnet-stone, see Bonifacius in *Historia Ludicra*, Book 13, chapter 16.

### 51. Arbitration. The Compromise.

Regarding **Compromises** <note>term: *Compromissum* — a legal agreement where parties submit their dispute to an arbiter rather than a court</note>, see Lanfrancus de Oriano, Blancus, and Gothofredus Borellus in their individual treatises.

From a compromise, nothing is inferred except insofar as its own words imply by necessity. Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century jurist</note> in the law *Julianus*, column 4, in the section *predicta* on the recovery of undue payments. Nor is it our place to extend the Compromises or agreements of the parties, according to Coler, in his consultations.

<column-break/>

Book 1, number 28 and following. Hence it is specifically handed down that an **arbiter** can only take notice of those things which are expressed in the compromise, and not of others; see the law *non distinguemus*, in the section *on office*, in the Digest *On reaching an arbitration*. Cornelius, consultation 293, number 5, book 3. Blancus, *On Compromise*, question 6, regarding the power of the arbiter, number 5. For otherwise, the **Award** <note>term: *Laudum* — the formal decision or judgment rendered by an arbiter</note> is null by the law itself. Romanus, consultation 115, where he notes the word "validity." Gratianus, *Forensic Disputes*, chapter 162, number 10.

It should be noted furthermore, that a general compromise does not include future matters, even if it were made concerning all disputes. Bartolus in the law *cum Aquiliana*, at the end, in the Digest *On transactions*. Romanus, consultation 115, number 4, last section. Borellus, *On Compromise*, section 2, gloss 1, number 26 and following. Therefore, an award delivered regarding things which were not a dispute at the time of the compromise is not valid. Romanus, consultation 88, number 3, and consultation 108 throughout. This is so even if the compromise speaks of "all disputes pending, turning, and which could turn in the future," yet it is not valid regarding future ones. Romanus, consultation 108. Or if the Clause "from whatever cause" is added: because it is understood to mean the present. Romanus, consultation 88. To such an extent that the Award is null if it is delivered regarding that which was not a dispute between the parties at the time of the compromise, as Tuschus states at length in *Practical Conclusions*, letter C, 447, number 2 and following. Thus, it is not sufficient if the arbiters say that disputes *could* arise in the future, and that for the sake of peace, they wished to "lay their hands" on the discords. Tuschus, cited conclusion 519, number 12.

And regarding the nature of a general compromise, **concerning any and all disputes** <note>original German: *auf all und jede Strittigkeiten*</note>, see Hondedeus, volume 1, consultation 30, number 60, etc.

Whether a compromise admits intervention? Friderich Mindanus, *On Process*, Book 3, chapter 8, number 12. Also, whether and to what extent an appeal may be made from an Arbiter? Rutger Ruland, in the process of Ferrarius Montanus, folio 55 and following.

### ADDITION.

No one is compelled to make a **Compromise**, just as no one is forced to accept an arbitration; but after someone has once made a compromise or accepted an arbitration, they can no longer leap back from it. Rittershusius in the *Novels*, page 510, number 37. One can leave a Judge for an Arbiter. For litigants can renounce the ordinary Process, which they had begun before a Judge, and compromise upon some arbiter, and this is possible both in the first judgment and in the judgment of appeal, because all judgments are meant to be conclusive. Although they cannot be compelled to concord or to compromising against their will, nevertheless that is limited in a long-running lawsuit, in a dissension between distinguished persons, and in a case where there is a fear of armed conflict. What actions are given if the award of the arbiter is not obeyed is excellently taught by the late Master Dr. Biccius in his *Golden Sections*, section 5, thesis 118.

<header>Letter C.</header>

### 52. Letter of Compass, Letter of Petition, see above under letter B, term **Letter of Petition and Request.**

->Letters of mutual compass.<-

Letters of mutual compass—also called Petition Letters and what the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> calls **Letters of Aid**—are used when a judge, lacking jurisdiction over a subject belonging to another's jurisdiction, petitions the Lord of that subject to allow certain actions to be taken against the subject, either by the Lord himself or by the petitioning judge.

Thus, although a magistrate speaking the law outside his own territory is generally not obeyed with impunity <note>original: *l. ult. ff. de Jurisdict.* — referring to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of civil law</note>; nevertheless, a mandate or decree can be obtained from a judge by whose power one may act in a foreign jurisdiction—for instance, to examine witnesses <note>original: *l. 3. in fin. ff. de testib.*</note>, to deliver a citation, or to search for fugitives. For it is recorded that letters are given to magistrates for this purpose in the law <note>original: *l. 1. §. hoc autem ff. de serv. fugit.*</note>. Indeed, the Governors of Provinces where a crime was committed are accustomed to write to their colleagues—the Governors of other provinces where the perpetrators are said to be staying—requesting that they be sent back with their pursuers <note>original: *l. solent. 7 ff. de custod. & exhib. reor.*</note>. This is noted by Fornerius in *Daily Matters*, book 5, chapter 12.

---

->ADDITION.<-

It is in vain to seek by prayer what is already granted by common law. <note>This legal maxim suggests that if the law already allows an action, a formal petition is unnecessary.</note> *Klock, Consultation 7, no. 259...*

Rogatory letters <note>Formal requests from one court to another</note> or letters of judicial subsidy—called a **Letter of Petition**, or in the Imperial Chamber a **Letter of Aid**—are decreed by the magistrate of a location to the magistrate under whose authority a piece of property is situated, in order to carry out an execution of a judgment. *Law 15, § 1 on judged matters.* Lord Tabor, *Special Treatise on the Office of a Judge*; Gail, Book 1, observation 113; Mynsinger, Book 3, observation 68. One jurisdiction must be aided by another <note>original: *una Jurisdictio per aliam adjuvanda est*</note>.

**Letters of Compass** <note>term: *Compasschreiben* — a document defining the "scope" or "compass" of shared legal authority</note> as they are commonly used (Suttinger, observation 138) are only granted upon request. They have been entirely abolished regarding the **seizure of goods** <note>original: *Ansetzung der Güter*</note> in other jurisdictions by the new Execution Ordinance. In these times, when jurisdictions vary so strangely, these "rogatory" or "compass" letters were introduced, by which the magistrate or judge who delivered a sentence asks another to execute that sentence in the other's location. Such letters are mentioned in the *Novels* <note>New laws added to Justinian’s Code</note>. From this, it is understood that the old interpreters are incorrect in thinking that appointed or delegated judges

<column-break/>

have the right of execution. It is well established that they have no Jurisdiction, and much less do they have *Imperium* <note>term: *Imperium* — the high power of state to command and enforce</note>, but they possess only *notion* <note>term: *notio* — the power to hear and investigate a case, but not necessarily to enforce the outcome</note>. This is supported by the law "The Praetor says" <note>original: *l. 5. ait. Prætor. ff. de re judic.*</note>. In fact, the law contradicts them where delegated judges are referred to ordinary judges because they cannot act on their own. Thus, nothing supports them in the law *if against the law* <note>original: *l. 4. C. si contra jus*</note>, where it is said that he who is commanded not to investigate but to execute can nonetheless investigate the truth of a price. For it does not work both ways, as those thinkers believe; execution is a matter of *Imperium* and of the High Magistrate, but investigation is a lesser power which even appointed or delegated judges can perform. Hubert Giphanius, *In the Process of Law*, book 1, page 182.

Letters of mutual compass or Rogatory letters (**Letter of Compass or Petition**) are the documents by which one judge requests another to hear witnesses and to send the testimony of those witnesses back to him in a sealed envelope. *Würtemberg Law, part 1; Wehner’s Supplement, page 17.* The form for a letter of mutual compass or for citing a person in subsidy is provided by Emericus à Rosbach in *Judicial Process*, title 26, number 25.

### § 3. Compulsory Letters.

Regarding the process of Compulsory Letters <note>term: *Compulsoriales* — orders that compel a person to produce documents or evidence</note>: for what are they granted, and what is required? See Battista Costa, *On Subsidiary Remedies*, remedy 18.

Compulsory Letters are considered in a two-fold state. Some are special and "remissory" <note>sending a matter back to a lower court</note> for the production of legal rights, such as confirming the validity of legal instruments. Others are general, which can be decreed even while a lawsuit is pending without being considered an illegal interference <note>original: *attentatorum vitio*</note>. This is because such an act is just and extra-judicial; it does not tend toward the prejudice of the lawsuit, but rather toward assisting the truth. Lancellot, *On Interference*, part 2, chapter 4, unless the judge has been prohibited.

Furthermore, a judge may issue Compulsory Letters to have legal documents relevant to the case produced, and may even examine witnesses after he has obtained jurisdiction over the main matter. Castrensis, consultation 282; Costa, at the end.

---

->ADDITION.<-

Compulsory Letters are to be served by the subject of a lower judge. Carpzov, decision 208, number 16. For the reasons and foundations of this assertion, see numbers 18, 20, and 21. See also the opinion of the Senate of Appeals. Regarding when more restrictive Compulsory Letters are decreed, see Johann Rudinger, observation 92. On Compulsory Letters against a third party, see number 3. Guido Papæ of Dauphiné also wrote on Compulsory Letters.

### 55. Confiscation.

See Peregrinus, *On the Rights of the Treasury*. Stamm, *On Personal Servitudes*, 1, title 2. *Consultations of Strasbourg*, volume 1, question 1, where it asks: whether <term>confiscation</term> <note>original: *Confiscatio* — the seizure of property by the state</note> is also due to a <term>pledge-holder</term>? <note>original: *Pfandherren* — a creditor holding a lien or mortgage on the property</note> Likewise, whether its power extends outside the territory,

volume 2, consultation 81. See also my own *Consultations* throughout.
Concerning the procedure to be observed in the <term>crime of high treason</term> <note>original: *crimine laesae Majestatis* — literally "injured majesty"</note> and the confiscation of goods, and likewise which goods fall under it or not, the following Legal Response treats the matter. It was given by me a few years ago to a certain Nobleman, and it seemed appropriate to include it here now for the benefit of the Reader.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter D featuring scrolls and floral motifs.</image-desc>
Since I, the undersigned, have been requested to open my humble opinion regarding the case summary <note>original: *facti speciem*</note> sent to me and the various attached questions: I have reflected on the matters—as far as possible in a short time given their great importance—and first of all, I wish to remind you of this: because Mr. Martin von R. is to be accused of the crime of High Treason in the first degree, namely <term>rebellion</term> <note>original: *perduellionis*</note> and <term>treason</term> or conspiracy against the supreme and Imperial Majesty, such matters are not always proceeded with according to the Rules of Law, but often according to <term>reason of state</term> <note>original: *secundum Status rationem* — political necessity rather than strict legal procedure</note>. Especially those who are guilty of, or at least suspected of, such a most atrocious crime, are immediately made objects of the utmost hatred, and their deeds and conduct are made unpleasant; no less do those who venture to help them have little hearing or achieve anything fruitful, unless they are in favor elsewhere than with the highest Majesty who feels injured.

For it is not irrelevant that Tacitus <note>Roman historian</note> calls the crime of High Treason a "bond and a necessity of silence": since prosecutions of this kind of crime are undertaken with the goal that no one would dare to speak against the supreme Prince—nay, not even to mutter—much less to attempt anything in fact. Therefore, as an example and to the terror of others, even those who are only suspected can hardly excuse themselves; in which view the same Tacitus calls the judgment of High Treason the "completion of all accusations," and Curtius <note>Roman historian</note> calls it the "despair of safety."

And so hated are those guilty of such a crime, that even the sighs of their relatives are noted and sometimes drawn into the crime; nor is it always permitted for those established in guilt to invoke their "dear ones," as Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, Roman historian</note> says; and that ancient verse pertains to this:

> The crime of High Treason, whomever it touches, <br/>
> <unclear>........</unclear> undermines. <note>The verse implies that treason ruins everyone associated with the accused.</note>

Therefore, the said Mr. Martin von R. should conduct his case quite separately, and it should not be mixed in the slightest with those claims that his children, his brother, and other relatives believe they have upon his property, so that one does not infect, hinder, or make the other loathsome.

Regarding then the person and matter of the frequently mentioned Mr. Martin von R. himself, I state

Lit. C.
Z 3
<meta>catchword: normitan.</meta>

I have no doubt that in the event His Imperial Majesty or his highly esteemed <term>Imperial Aulic Council</term> <note>The *Reichshofrat*, one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire, dealing specifically with matters concerning the Emperor’s direct prerogatives</note> is approached with all obedience and due humility, they will grant Mr. von N. the necessary defense and a regular legal process, as is customary in such matters.

To this end, the zealous and memorable intercessions of distinguished Catholic potentates and princes, or even those of the <term>Evangelical</term> <note>Protestant</note> estates who are in His Imperial Majesty’s favor, could provide significant assistance. It may be that something has already been found in the Heidelberg Chancery from which the <term>notoriety of a permanent fact</term> <note>original: *notorietatem facti permanentis* — a legal term for a fact so obvious it requires no further proof</note> can be established immediately. In such a case, I find no better means than to adopt a state of <term>honest plea for mercy</term> <note>original: *statum deprecationis ingenuè*</note> and not to use many "colors" or pretenses to cover up what clearly shines through. Indeed, this method has been used with success by others who had committed offenses equal to or greater than those imputed to Mr. N.

Undoubtedly, Mr. N. will still have at hand the drafts of the letters sent to Dr. <term>Camerarius</term> <note>Likely Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous physician and humanist</note>, or whatever else was found in Heidelberg of this sort. Through these, or through the impartial opinion of others, he will be able to determine whether and how far such correspondence and writings might be misinterpreted, and whether they may be excused entirely or in part (especially considering the present state of the Empire). This, in my humble opinion, must precede everything and will be the foundation of the deliberation on how Mr. Martin N. should frame his petition to His Imperial Majesty.

For if one were to dispute the process too much, demanding the release of documents and proof of the complaint, requesting space and faculty to defend oneself, and complaining much about being rushed—while on the other hand, one cannot entirely excuse oneself in the main matter—it is to be feared that a bad situation would be made worse. Above all, His Majesty and his Imperial Aulic Council would be exasperated and moved to greater displeasure or severity.

<margin>
For although the necessity of providing or offering a petition, observing holidays introduced for human necessity, hearing the case before a tribunal, or delivering a sentence and contesting a lawsuit may be set aside there, the necessity of not harming justice or truth, or of fully investigating the cause, is not considered set aside. Gigas, in the *Treatise on the Crime of High Treason*, title: *How to proceed in the crime of high treason*, question 2, number at end, folio 149.
</margin>
Otherwise, it is established that even in the case of <term>High Treason</term> <note>original: *crimine Majestatis*</note>, a regular legal process must be maintained.

<column-break/>

And all things introduced by <term>Natural Law</term> <note>original: *Juris naturalis* — the concept of universal right and wrong inherent to human nature</note> and by the Law of Nations through natural reason must be observed, even granted that one proceeds summarily in this crime. Bartolus, in the decree <note>original: *extravag.*</note> *To Repress* <note>original: *ad reprimend.*</note>, under the word "vigor." Only those things which exist by Civil Law can be omitted. Decianus, in *Criminal Practice*, book 7, chapter 42, number 9.

Furthermore, a citation <note>A legal summons to appear in court</note> is required even in the crime of high treason, according to the text in the aforementioned decree *To Repress*, there: "by messenger or letters." Gigas, in the aforementioned chapter, throughout the question, where among other things he writes: "A defect of judgment proceeding from a missed citation, or the nullity of the process, is never cured when the citation was omitted or not lawfully made." Therefore, when the Roman Curia is asked for the healing of nullities made in the process of a case, it heals all other nullities except those arising from a defect of citation, jurisdiction, or the mandate of a procurator. Decianus, in the same work, chapter 24, number 6, teaches that such a citation is required even if one proceeds by way of Inquisition. Likewise, Gigas, in question 8, number 4, says that the same solemnity is required in an inquisition as in an accusation: in that the place and time should be inserted in the inquisition in the same way as in an accusation, for it is not fitting to wander aimlessly in such a great crime. As Peregrinus also writes in *On the Law of the Treasury*, book 4, title 5, number 10: "one cannot arrive at a sentence of confiscation unless the party has been cited; otherwise, the process and sentence would be of no value, since defense is a matter of Natural Law, which cannot be taken away." And the same author in book 5, title 1, number 172, writes that a citation is necessary for the defense of the accused, and one cannot proceed to a sentence of confiscation of goods without a citation, and he attests that this is the common conclusion.

Furthermore, the process must be published to the accused, the subject of inquisition, or the person denounced for such a crime, so that they can prepare their defenses. In favor of this conclusion are the writings of the Provost <note>original: *Præposit.*</note> in the chapter *On Nomination*, section *The Sentence*, at the line *The publication, however*, where he says that the publication of the process is done lest the right of the party be harmed. Question 6 also supports this, along with the text and the <term>gloss</term> <note>a marginal or interlinear commentary</note> in the final chapter of the section *On Heretics* in the sixth book of Decretals, where it is held that even in the crime of heresy, the witnesses are to be made public. To the same point is the text in the chapter *Since Frequently*, in the section *There are also others*, where it is expressly said that in a case of inquisition, the witnesses must be published. Gigas, in the aforementioned chapter, question 19, number 3. Decianus agrees in his treatise, chapter 42, number 11, where he teaches that in this crime the process is to be published and given over so that the accused may defend himself; otherwise, it would be a denial of defense, which would be against Natural Law. He adds that the contrary way of proceeding in certain places is certainly too rigorous.

Likewise, proofs and presumptions in this crime, since it is the most serious and is therefore punished with the most severe penalties, must be more powerful <note>original: *vehementiores* — meaning the evidence must be exceptionally strong</note>. See the chapter *Letters*, where there is a gloss on presumptions, and also the Doctors of Law, especially <term>Panormitanus</term> <note>The influential 15th-century canon lawyer Nicolaus de Tudeschis</note>.

<summary>This page argues that even in cases of high treason, defendants have an inalienable right to a legal defense, formal notification (citation), and access to the evidence against them, based on the principles of Natural Law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a legal discussion on the standards of proof required for the crime of Lese-majesty (high treason). It builds on the principle that the gravity of the accusation demands a higher threshold of evidence than lesser crimes.</meta>

# The Augmented Treasury of Practice

...from Panormitanus <note>original: "normitan." referring to the medieval jurist Nicolaus de Tudeschis</note> in the version starting *note that suspicion.* For as much as the crime is more serious, the proofs there ought to be that much stronger; this is proven in the law regarding famous persons <note>original: "l. famosi"</note> in the Digest under the Julian Law on Treason <note>original: "ff. ad L. Jul. Majest."</note>, and by Gigas under the title *how and by whom it may be proven,* question 29, and Decian in the aforementioned book 7, chapter 45, at the beginning.

And although it is often customary to allege that because of the "enormity" <note>the extreme nature or horror</note> of a crime, it is lawful to deviate from the rules of Law—as cited by Innocent, Baldus, and others mentioned by Hippolytus de Marsiliis in his *Criminal Practice* <note>original: "in pr. crim."</note> section *diligently,* number 159—nonetheless, this is only true in the *punishing* of the crime (specifically when the Defendant has either confessed or been convicted). It is not true in the *proceedings* before it is certain whether the accused or investigated person actually committed the crime, however grave and enormous it may be. Thus, Hippolytus clarifies that statement in the same place at number 175, saying that this is his own new declaration, from which he achieved great honor in the City of Milan. Therefore, it should be diligently noted.

And it is pleasing to report here what Arnoldus Ferronus says in his *Customs of Bordeaux* concerning Jodocus of Louvain <note>original: "Jodoco Lovaringio"</note>, a legal scholar of great name among the French. He says that Jodocus used to laugh at our legal experts and the Pontifical writers <note>Canon lawyers</note> who taught that in the gravest trials of Treason against God or man, one could proceed to torture or condemnation based on lighter indications and arguments, or even on these alone. On the contrary, he believed that the more serious the crime was, the firmer and weightier the evidence and arguments ought to be before we even arrive at the lightest suspicion of such a crime having been committed.

Nor is it enough to prove the act itself; it is also necessary that **malice** <term>dolus: the intentional will to do evil or break the law</term> was involved. Wherever malice is not present, the person accused of Treason is always excused. This is found in the first law of the Digest under the Julian Law on Treason: *if anyone with evil intent* <note>original: "si quis dolo malo"</note>, and in the decree *to be repressed* <note>original: "extravag. ad reprimendam"</note>, at the words: *with a hostile mind.* See also Decian in his *Treatise on Crimes,* book 7, chapter 48, number 14.

And therefore, any cause, even a "colored" <note>plausible or superficial</note> one, provided it is likely, will excuse one from malice, and consequently from the ordinary penalties of this crime, as Decius responds in counsel 905, number 6. Furthermore, a person is excused if he proves that he went over to the enemy with the permission of the Prince, or the Prince’s Vicar, or a Duke.

And so it follows, likewise, if one of the Counselors maintains an innocent correspondence with the enemies of the Prince with the Prince's consent.

Thus, Carolus Ruinus notably teaches that a person does not incur the crime of rebellion and Lese-majesty unless he intends and attempts something with **evil intent** against the prosperity and security of the Prince, and with the purpose of offending him. This is because in crimes, the *will* is examined and not just the *outcome,* according to the Cornelian Law on Assassins <note>original: "l. 7. ad L. Cornel. de sicar."</note>. There, Bartolus says regarding this point at the end, concluding that this is true when the person did not principally intend the crime in question while doing what he was doing. This is best proven in the laws concerning injuries and theft. Cephalus agrees in counsel 75,

<column-break/>

number 7, where he states that the crime of Treason should never be ascribed to one lacking malice, and that not even "gross negligence" <term>culpa lata: extreme carelessness that falls just short of intentional harm</term> is sufficient in this matter. In the same place, at numbers 14 and 23, he teaches that a defect of the will excuses one from malice.

Likewise, since a "bad mind" <note>evil intent</note> is a matter of fact, it is not presumed, but must be proven. See the law on good faith <note>original: "l. bonæ fidei"</note> in the section *to the contrary* regarding the acquisition of ownership.

The rule in the Cornelian Law on Assassins and the law on insults does not stand in the way, because that presumption of guilt could only proceed when there was no other presumption or conjecture in favor of the person under investigation.

Furthermore, Follerus teaches that mere negligence does not make someone guilty of the crime of Treason in his *Criminal Practice,* as does Marsilius and Plotus, who cites several others on this point.

Bursatus also teaches in counsel 152, number 22, that presumed proof is not sufficient in this edict for imposing a direct penalty. Marsilius notes that malice must be proven by the one who alleges it.

And where two presumptions collide—one inclusive of a crime, the other exclusive of it—the exclusive one <note>the one favoring innocence</note> must always outweigh the other. This is supported by Baldus, Brunus, and specifically by Thomas Grammaticus and Ruinus.

Finally, although the law may carry a condemnatory sentence "by the law itself" and "by the act itself" <note>original: "ipso jure & ipso facto"</note> regarding the whole or part of one's goods, or a monetary penalty (so that a human judge's condemnation might not seem necessary), nevertheless, a **declaratory sentence** <term>sententia declaratoria: a formal court ruling that confirms a fact or status, such as a person's guilt, without necessarily issuing a new order</term> of the fact is required. By this, the crime is declared to have been committed, and assets cannot be seized by the **Treasury** <term>Fiscus: the state or royal treasury</term> before this. This is discussed at length by Gabrielius, where he teaches that in the crime of rebellion or Treason, at least a declaratory sentence is required. Cardinalis, Alexander, and others agree, stating that all the laws of the world that impose a penalty "by the law itself" must be understood as requiring a following sentence regarding the facts. This has also been taught in the legal opinions of Curtius Junior, Socinus Junior, Decius, Riminaldus Senior, and Berous, who says that before the declaratory ruling, the penalty has no effect. Bursatus teaches the same regarding the crime of heresy. Therefore, a third party cannot raise an objection regarding the rights of the Treasury before a declaratory sentence is passed. Mynsinger shows with many examples that a declaratory sentence is necessary whenever a penalty is imposed by the law itself, as also suggested by Antonius Faber and Paulus Christina.

<summary>This page argues that the crime of Treason requires absolute proof of "evil intent" (dolus) rather than mere negligence, and emphasizes that the state cannot seize a rebel's property until a formal declaratory judgment of guilt is issued.</summary>
<keywords>treason, Lese-majesty, malice, intent, burden of proof, declaratory sentence, Treasury, property seizure, legal procedure, Roman Law</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of treason cases, moving from the standards of evidence required for conviction to the practical consequences of such a charge, specifically regarding the seizure of property and the rights of the accused's family members.</meta>

# Letter C.

Indeed, that declaratory judgment <note>a formal court ruling that declares a legal status or right</note> is not required for the penalty to be imposed or for the transfer of ownership of goods to the treasury <note>original: "fiscum"</note>. However, it is required regarding the facts of the case and for the legal defense of the possession of those goods. For once the declaration of the committed crime is made, it is then declared retroactively that the property fell under the penalties ordained by the law from that moment, and therefore his goods could be seized. See Panormitanus <note>original: "Abb." referring to the Abbot Nicolaus de Tudeschis</note> in the chapter *it has arrived* under the title *on taxes*; and Berous, Counsel 136, number 95. 

All of this, however, only takes place in a case where the matter is still somewhat doubtful and the presumed Defendant <note>original: "Reo"</note> is entitled to various defenses. But in a case where the matter is so situated that the crime <note>original: "delictum"</note> can be considered notorious <note>obvious or widely known without need for further proof</note>, then the rule specifically applies which Gudelinus records in his *Commentary on the Newest Law*, book 5, chapter 16: namely, that in the crime of high treason <note>original: "crimine majestatis"</note>, the proceedings may move forward as seems expedient to the one presiding over the judgment. For if someone is in notorious rebellion or hostility, then their goods can be occupied even without a declaratory sentence, as Gramaticus teaches in Decision 105 regarding a manifest traitor. See also Gail, book 2, observation 51. For a Prince can condemn a notorious rebel without a summons, confiscate his goods, invade them, and hand them over to another; as Marsilius wrote most fully in his repetition on the law *of each one*, column 2, and Peregrinus in the *Treatise on the Right of the Treasury*, under the title *on Crimes which are not extinguished by death*.

Now, if Mr. Martin N.—as I hope and would gladly wish for him—has such defenses by which he might fully express himself and excuse himself before his Imperial Majesty (as nothing is known to him that would have the appearance of treason, conspiracy, or any other crime that would be irresponsible for an Imperial Councilor in impartial eyes), then in such a case, as understood above, one should apply for a highly respected intercession <note>a formal plea for mercy or intervention by a high-ranking person</note>. This should be done alongside the aforementioned legal rights, yet with great modesty, most humbly requesting an orderly trial to be held before His Imperial Majesty’s Aulic Council <note>term: Reichshofrath; the supreme legal body of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. Following this, one should solicit a prompt and favorable answer through suitable intermediaries in Vienna. Since Count von V. is also said to have had knowledge of the now poorly-regarded correspondences, he might likewise be sought out in this matter and most submissively asked to do his best for the cause.

As for what concerns the second point—the children of Mr. Martin N.—it would be my simple opinion that the best course is not for their father, but rather for their relatives on both the father’s and mother’s lines (who have authority over them either by reason of birth or residence), to take up their cause. They should argue for the children's innocence eventually and

<column-break/>

carry out their other existing legal rights, even if their father—contrary to all hope—had committed some offense. For this purpose, favorable intercessions from well-regarded Catholic potentates and estates would be highly useful. It seems to me that these children could undoubtedly secure: (1.) their maternal property; (2.) the family entails <note>term: fideicommissa avita; property that must stay within a family lineage according to a grandfather's will</note>; and (3.) perhaps the "legitimate portion" <note>the minimum share of an estate that children are legally entitled to</note> of the paternal goods which the father held before the crime was committed.

For although otherwise in the crime of high treason of the first degree <note>original: "crimine laesae Majestatis primi gradus"</note>, the children are punished at the same time and lose their property—according to the law *quisquis* <note>a famous Roman law decreeing that the sons of traitors should be disinherited and live in perpetual poverty</note>—it is nevertheless the judgment of all that it is most harsh for the innocent children of rebels to be punished. No one fails to see that this is contrary to both civil and natural reason. Furthermore, that sanction in the law *quisquis* does not apply to daughters, because in "hateful" matters, an unreasonable hatred toward the male does not include the female. Peregrinus, in *Right of the Treasury*, book 3, says this is the common and truer opinion, adding that writers commonly admit that when paternal goods are confiscated for treason, daughters must still be provided with dowries from the paternal goods. The reasoning for daughters is different from that for sons; for example, King Ferdinand of Naples, having expelled the Prince of Rossano for defection and rebellion, took care that the Prince's daughters were nobly dowried and married.

And even that law *quisquis*, also with respect to sons, has been abolished through the general custom of all Italy as being "hateful and irrational," as witnessed by Angelus, Socinus, and Clarus.

Similarly, in France, these punishments regarding children are not observed, nor in Belgium, as Christianaeus testifies in the *Belgian Decisions*. He says: the "legitimate portion" of the father's goods is preserved for them, or at least maintenance <note>original: "alimenta"</note> is provided to them; they succeed to other relatives and outsiders, and they are not rendered "infamous" <note>losing legal status or reputation</note> by our customs. Binsfeld also asserts in his commentary that the Emperor’s reasoning in that law does not hold.

Daily experience also shows that His Roman Imperial Majesty does not punish the children of known rebels, nor does he take from them what rightfully belongs to them. That maternal goods <note>original: "bona materna"</note> are not included under such confiscation is beyond all doubt, as recorded in the law *quisquis* in the section *wives*: "Wives do not lose their dowries, but recover them." And it should be known that this proceeds and holds true in law even if the wife follows her rebel husband, as Bossius notes in *Criminal Practice*.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the seizure of property following a conviction for high treason. The previous page established that while a formal court ruling is usually needed to seize goods, notorious rebellion allows for immediate occupation of assets. This page shifts focus to the legal protections for the family—specifically the rights of the wife and children to reclaim their portions of the estate from the government Treasury.</meta>

# Enlarged Treasury of Legal Practice
### Page 184

Treatise on the confiscation of goods <note>original: "tr. de publ. bon"</note>, number 73 and following. For this reason, from the confiscation of a husband’s goods, the dowry <note>original: "dos"</note> and all outstanding debts are deducted, as attested by Antonius Faber in his Code, under the title *The Julian Law on High Treason* <note>original: "L. Jul. Majest."</note>, definition 3.

And when a husband’s goods are made public <note>seized by the state</note>, the text in the law *if to the husband* in the section *on the dissolution of marriage* <note>original: "l. si marito. in pr. ff solut matrim."</note> proves that a wife may pre-deduct her dowry and wedding gifts from the <term>Treasury</term> <note>original: "Fiscum"; the state’s financial office</note> just as she would deduct them from her husband’s heirs. This is supported by Socinus the Elder, Counsel 121; Socinus the Younger, Counsel 55, volume 2; Negusantius *on Pledges*, member 1, part 5, number 35; and Rulandus in his work on dowries and wedding gifts, *Treatise on the Profit of the Dowry*, question 59.

This is so true that even a "confessed dowry" <note>original: "dos confessata"; a dowry the husband formally acknowledged receiving, even if a written receipt is missing</note>, which can be deducted against a husband’s heirs and creditors after the expiration of legal deadlines, can also be deducted against the Treasury. See Barbarius in the law *if anyone hereafter* in the Code *on the goods of the proscribed*; Afflictus, Decision 402; Rolandus, Counsel 20, number 16, and Counsel 74, number 10, volume 4, where he cites others.

Furthermore, if the woman is not at fault, she may seek those assets immediately upon her husband being banished. For exile brings about poverty, as noted in the <term>Gloss</term> <note>standard legal commentary</note> on the *Authentica* regarding production of documents, and in the section on guilty men. Indeed, the wife can reclaim her dowry even from the goods of a banished husband that have not yet been made public. And if the husband’s goods have been occupied by the Treasury, the woman can still reclaim her dowry, as stated in Law 1 and the notes there in the Code *on Repudiation*. This was the opinion of Baptista de Sancto Blasio in the *Treatise on the Privilege of the Dowry*, century 2, verse 130, number 46; and Campegis, *on the Dowry*, part 3, question 23, beginning "if the husband be banished."

**Which rights the children, as the mother’s rightful and sole heirs, must now also claim for themselves.**

Secondly, it is also correct that <term>family trusts</term> <note>original: "fideicommissa familiæ"; property meant to stay within a specific lineage</note> must remain with the children or others to whom they were dedicated from the beginning and long before the crime was committed. This holds true notwithstanding the confiscation, and even in the case of the most atrocious crime by the current possessor. This condition also applies to property pre-bequeathed to the eldest son by his maternal grandfather. This is because the rights of children, which are not held in common with the father, do not pass to the Treasury when goods are made public. Since these rights are personal to the children themselves, as Alciatus argues in Counsel 67, book 6, where he cites the writings of Paul de Castro. From this, he decides that conditions placed by a father upon a son’s inheritance—if they have not been rejected by the son—cannot be rejected by the Treasury once the son’s goods are confiscated; for that right is personal to the sons. Bossius held this same view explicitly in the title *on the publicizing of goods*, number 37, where he concludes that the right to revoke a refusal of a father’s inheritance does not pass to the Treasury. This is because it is a special right of the children, not transferable to outside heirs, as taught by Jason and Alexander.

Furthermore, property that a testator has expressly forbidden from being sold <note>original: "alienari"</note> out of favor for the family—so that it remains within the family—does not pass to the Treasury. Instead, once the offender's goods are publicized, it can be

<column-break/>

immediately claimed <note>original: "vendicari"</note> by those members of the family, just as if it had been illegally sold outside the family through a contract or a last will. See Law *The Emperor*, where Bartolus notes this in the Digest *on testamentary trusts of freedom*; Ruinus, Counsel 129, volume 2; and Counsel 23 in volume 5; Decius, Counsel 442, numbers 28 and 32; Gratus, Response 21, last column, volume 2; Berous, Question 41; Rolandus, Counsel 98, volume 2; and Counsel 1, number 44, volume 3; Natta, Counsel 508, number 19.

This is most effective where there is a pure and simple family trust triggered by death, and a prohibition against selling outside the family has been added. Peregrinus, in *on the Right of the Treasury*, book 5, chapter 1, number 98, states that this opinion is the most widely accepted in the world and must not be departed from, even against the Treasury.

He says the strength of this common opinion lies in the fact that not even during the natural life of the offender can the property be confiscated regarding the use of its profits; rather, as soon as the sentence is published, the property must be released to the family. For whenever someone is forbidden from selling a thing to a third party, he cannot "sell" it to the Treasury by committing a crime.

It helps that the Treasury stands in the place of an outside heir. See Law 2 of the Code *on the Julian Law on Violence*; Law 1 of the Code *on the goods of freedmen*; Law 9 of the Digest *on the Julian Law on High Treason*. Therefore, those things which belong by special right to the heirs of a person accused of treason, or to someone else, do not pass to the Treasury. It seems beyond doubt that family trusts are of this nature.

That such trusts belong immediately to the heirs named in them is likewise clear from the fact that a person committing high treason simultaneously loses all rights under <term>Civil Law</term>. He immediately loses the administration of his own goods, even before he is formally accused, according to Gothofredus in his notes on the law *their patrimonies*, number 7, regarding the Right of the Treasury. See also the Code, book 10, law *whoever*, section *emancipations*, where it says: "from the very moment they first thought of entering into the conspiracy."

Furthermore, <term>Civil Death</term> <note>a legal status where a person is treated as deceased for all legal purposes, though still physically alive</note> is regarded the same as natural death, since the same reasoning is found to apply in both cases, according to Afflictus, Follerius, and Mastrillus, Decision 283, number 61 and following.

Thus, if someone burdened with the obligation of a family trust enters a Monastery of Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>—who can own nothing of their own, either in common or individually—then immediately after that monk has made his profession, and without waiting for his natural death, the trust must be restored. Joseph de Rusticis teaches that this opinion should be followed in judging and advising, as it is consistent with the truth and is the common view of both ancient and modern scholars. Most recently, Johannes Mylius in his additions to Augustus Berous, Question 41, defended this conclusion at length, following Baldus and Castrensis.
