<meta>This page continues the legal argument concerning the rights of a family to reclaim portions of an estate after a family member—specifically the head of the household—has been convicted of a crime and their property seized by the state Treasury. It focuses on the legal fiction that a convicted or banished man is "civilly dead," allowing his wife and heirs to claim their legal shares immediately.</meta>

# Lit. C.

Thus, when a husband’s goods are made public <note>original: "publicatis bonis"</note>, and he has been either judged or outlawed—even if the marriage is not actually dissolved—the husband is nevertheless considered truly dead regarding the effect of recovering the dowry, dower rights, and other dotal rights. These are recovered or respectively gained by the wife. This same principle applies even more strongly in cases where the goods of a wealthy husband are confiscated; an undowered and poor wife may immediately take her "fourth" share <note>a legal provision for a widow's support</note> despite the confiscation, even in the crime of high treason <note>original: "laesae Majestatis"</note>. As Mastril explains in decision 283, this ensures that the wife’s condition regarding the property does not worsen due to the husband’s crime.

And although a delinquent <note>a person convicted of a crime</note> may have the **usufruct** <term>usufruct</term> <note>the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note> in a matter subject to restitution, that right is not formal but is joined with ownership, according to the law *from the opposite side* <note>original: "l. ex diverso"</note> in the Digests. See also Peregrinus *on the Law of the Treasury, book 5, number 99*.

Therefore, since the individual loses this ownership, it cannot remain with the Treasury. Ownership of these things devolves immediately to the **agnates** <note>relatives on the father's side</note> upon the "death" of the possessor, because it cannot pass to the Treasury. Thus, neither does the usufruct yield to the Treasury, as it was never separated from the ownership itself; rather, the owner obtains it immediately, as Peregrinus rightly notes. Indeed, in **testamentary trusts** <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>a legal arrangement where property is held by one person to be passed to another, often used to keep estates within a family</note>, the beneficial ownership held by the delinquent cannot remain in suspension, nor can the usufruct be separated from it. From this it follows not only that trusts can be brought into the Treasury due to a crime, but also that because of the crime of the beneficiary, the beneficial ownership immediately passes to the substituted heirs.

Furthermore, a pure and simple trust—where the assets are prohibited from being sold—does not fall under the confiscation of goods, not even during the lifetime of the one prohibited from selling. This is held by Bartolus and commonly followed by other doctors of law. This applies where a person burdened with a trust dies without children or is condemned to the mines; the trust takes effect immediately without waiting for a natural death. Julius Clarus teaches the same regarding any condemned person.

Moreover, following a capital sentence (even if it is not a death sentence) of the burdened heir, the trust is said to be "purified" <note>cleared of the previous holder's interest</note>. The substitute heir is admitted to the inheritance immediately in such a case, as noted by Alexander, Boër, and Bursatus.

That a trust is immediately granted to the next in line after a crime leads to the seizure of goods—even regarding beneficial ownership—is proven by Besold, Volume 1,

<column-break/>

on the law of freedmen, 4, and similar sources.

Furthermore, the fact that the **statutory share** <term>legitima</term> <note>the portion of an estate that the law reserves for immediate family members and cannot be taken away</note> does not fall under confiscation is the more common opinion, as attested by Peregrinus, Farinaccius, and Clarus. Farinaccius asserts that this view is more equitable and favorable. Peregrinus adds that this was settled in a holy and praiseworthy manner in Venice by the exalted and most religious Council of Ten.

This opinion is supported by the fact that the children’s statutory share is said to be owed by **Natural Law** <note>original: "Jure Naturae"</note>. This same point, along with several other reasons, is brought forward by Rolandus à Valle, Sixtinus, and I have treated this matter more extensively myself in part 3, counsel 95.

And although, according to the rigor of **Civil Law**, this might not take place in the crime of high treason—considering that sons are also punished there and must live in poverty—nevertheless, because such severity is relaxed by custom, the **statutory share** shall remain **safe for the children** in the crime of treason as well as in other confiscations.

Regarding, finally, Mr. R., his brother, and other relatives who have claims against him through a trust or by another name: they will also know how to bring forward their individual needs. They should most obediently petition his Imperial Majesty or the **Imperial Aulic Council** <note>the high court of the Holy Roman Empire; original: "Reichs-Hofrath"</note> again to be allowed to present their case and prove their intent. To this end, the intervention and intercession of their superiors or other estates can likely be helpful in many ways. They might perhaps specifically request that His Majesty appoint a **Commissioner** for the separation <note>original: "ad separationem"</note> of their goods from the others.

Because this matter is of no small importance, it would not be unadvisable if a suitable representative were sent expressly to Vienna for this purpose. This person could present the rights of Mr. R.’s agnates and relatives with appropriate demonstrations to the referees and other necessary offices. He could also, quietly and "off the record," explain what might be hoped for, done, or left undone regarding the principal party.

For although almost the same arguments from both the principal party and other interested persons may have already been brought before His Imperial Majesty several times, and no resolution has followed as of yet, one must nonetheless continue with constant reminders, demonstrations, and intercessions.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the confiscation of property following a conviction for high treason. The previous page established that when a man is "civilly dead" due to his crimes, his wife and heirs may claim their legal portions. This page shifts focus to the rights of paternal relatives and creditors against the state Treasury, and introduces a specific legal opinion from the University of Tübingen regarding nobles who served in rebel armies.</meta>

# Expanded Practical Treasury

And because most of the claims of these **agnates** <note>relatives related through the male line</note> arise from the law of entail <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>a legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of a family line, preventing it from being sold or seized for individual debts</note>, one will not easily be able to dispute them.

Regarding other claims that descend from contracts <note>original: "ex contractibus descendentes"</note>, the Treasury <term>Fiscus</term> <note>the state or royal treasury</note> must acknowledge and represent them, since it stands in the place of the heir <note>original: "cùm sit loco hæredis"</note>. In legal actions involving the condemned person, the Treasury exists as the proper successor for both active and passive claims, according to the Code of Justinian <note>original: "l. 2. C. ad L. Jul. de vi publ."</note>. Indeed, it is a "universal successor," as Paul of Castro brilliantly declares in his legal opinions, and is called a successor of law and an "anomalous heir" <note>original: "hæres anomalus"</note>. Therefore, the Treasury is bound to stand by the actions of the condemned person, provided there was no fraud.

Consequently, creditors of those whose goods have been confiscated must appear and briefly explain their claims as much as is sufficient. Once the truth of the debt is known, they must be paid immediately, according to the laws on proscribed goods.

It should be noted that the true debt must be established; otherwise, a mere note of confession <note>a written admission of debt</note> between the alleged creditor and the condemned defendant would not serve as proof. It would be presumed suspicious and feigned unless confirmed by other proofs or legal presumptions.

However, this is always understood to mean that such debts must have been made before the crime was committed <note>original: "ante commissum delictum"</note>. Since property is lost by operation of law once the crime of high treason <note>original: "crimen Majestatis"</note> is committed, a person who has committed such a crime cannot transfer or sell anything from his goods. Nor are debtors who pay the criminal released from their obligations, as is clear from the legal chapters on penalties. This is different from the rules for other, lesser crimes.

But if such debts were used to improve the confiscated goods, or if some benefit from the contract is still present, the Treasury must acknowledge those debts. This is because no one should be made richer through another's loss <note>original: "nemo cum alterius damno locupletior reddi debet"</note>, and the one who enjoys the benefits should also bear the burdens, according to common law.

If, therefore, in this case, the Treasury receives some benefit from such a debt, it must endure the corresponding burden (namely, the repayment of that debt), lest it become wealthier at the expense of a third party (the creditor).

How and in what manner those Lords and nobles who entered military service against the Roman Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire have forfeited their fiefs? Also, whether those who went into the field without deceitful intent <note>original: "absque dolo"</note> have forfeited them? Likewise, if the feudal lord himself recruited them and summoned the vassals under threat of losing their fiefs, should they be held as guilty of high treason? This is made clear from the following legal opinion <term>Consilio</term> written by me in the name of the Faculty of Law at Tübingen. Among other things, it is taught that the Emperor, as the supreme lord over all, must be and is excepted in every oath taken by a vassal to a feudal lord; therefore, arms are not to be taken up against the Emperor under any pretext.

<note>The following section begins with a large, ornamental initial letter 'D' depicting a seated figure in a circular frame, surrounded by vines.</note>

Accordingly, by the command of the Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, various lordships, as well as noble fiefs and private estates, have been seized and confiscated for the reason that various persons have entered military service against Your Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire in a forbidden manner, and thereby are said to have committed the crime of high treason <note>original: "crimen læsæ Majestatis"</note>.

First, it is asked—since most of the nobility, when entering said military service, had no thorough knowledge of where the intended campaign was heading or against whom it was intended—whether those who took the field without deceit <note>original: "absque dolo"</note> have forfeited their goods and fiefs to the Imperial Majesty?

Second, where the feudal lords—as happened in the Electorate of the Palatinate <note>original: "Chur-Pfaltz"</note> and elsewhere—recruited for themselves and summoned the vassals under threat of losing their fiefs: have they fallen into the same crime and forfeited their held fiefdoms on the grounds of high treason?

Now, as we, the Dean and other Doctors of the Faculty of Law at the High School in Tübingen, have been requested to provide our legal opinion on the questions set forth: we have maturely deliberated on this in our assembled college. We have consulted various legal experts who gave their opinions in nearly identical cases after the Schmalkaldic War <note>A mid-16th-century conflict between the Holy Roman Empire and a league of Lutheran princes</note>, and we have looked up other useful authors to further clarify the matter, setting down several evident points.

And first, indeed, although fiefs <term>feuda</term> are usually granted for the purpose of providing service in war, the vassal <term>Vasallus</term> is also bound by his oath and the loyalty performed to provide counsel and help to the Lord against adversaries, so long as he wishes to satisfy his due loyalty and appear worthy of the benefit. Otherwise, it would be a most just cause for losing a fief if the vassal refused the services for which the benefit was primarily granted. To break one's faith is a grave matter. Thus, the command of the Lord seems, in a way, to excuse the vassal.

On the other hand, however, the common and most certain legal principle...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property and rights following a conviction for high treason. Having previously discussed the claims of heirs and creditors against the state treasury, the text now turns to the specific hierarchy of loyalty within the feudal system, specifically how an oath of fealty to a local lord is always secondary to one's duty to the Emperor.</meta>

# Letter C

The rule is that in every **Oath** <note>original: "Juramento"</note>, the authority and person of the Emperor, as the supreme Magistrate, are excepted. This is found in the chapter *Venientes* regarding oaths and the final paragraph on the prohibition of alienating fiefs <term>feudum</term> <note>land or property held by a tenant from a lord in return for service</note> by Frederick. There it is expressly stated that in every oath of loyalty, the Emperor is named as an exception. For this reason, the **Oath of Loyalty** <note>original: "fidelitatis Juramentum"</note> is phrased in these words:

> I, Titius, swear that from this hour forward, and even unto my final breath of life, I will be faithful to you, my Lord, against every man, except for the Emperor and the King.

This is clearly evident from the text of the oath provided in the section on the new form of loyalty. According to this text, the legal experts—and especially **Matthaeus de Afflictis** in note 33—teach that if a Lord is a rebel against the King or Emperor, his **Vassals** <note>persons who have entered into a mutual obligation to a lord or monarch</note> are, by the law itself, freed from their sacred oath of loyalty.

The same is noted in the first chapter, paragraph *nulla*, regarding those through whom investment is made. **Baldus**, in his commentary on the final paragraph, says that according to that text, there are two cases in which a Vassal is not bound to help his Lord in war: namely, against the Emperor and against a prior Lord. This is because the Right of the King must be specifically excepted.

Even if the Emperor is not expressly excepted in the oath of an inferior, because this exception is otherwise inherently and silently present in the oath, it must be considered as if it had been expressed. This is the text in the chapter *Venientes* on Oaths. Hence **Baldus** said that what is virtually contained in a writing should be understood as having been written, even if it does not exist as part of the written word. **Matthaeus de Afflictis** reports and follows this same principle.

Furthermore, **Hartmann Pistor** writes that all interpreters teach with one voice that a Lord of a fief is not to be helped by a Vassal against the Emperor. He adds in the following section that this is so true that if anyone provides aid to his Lord against the Emperor, he loses his fief by that very act, and it reverts to the Emperor. For since in this case he is released by law from the oath given to the Lord of the fief, as warned above, he no longer has any just cause to take up arms against the Emperor. He thus incurs the **crime of high treason** <term>crimen laesae Majestatis</term> <note>literally "the crime of injured majesty," the highest crime against the state or ruler</note> when he takes up arms against the Emperor or the Roman Republic. This brings with it the loss of all goods. This is pursued at length by **Antonio Quetta**, as well as **Hartmann Pistor**, whom **Andreas Kohl** follows and approves, adding this reason: that Vassals and subjects are considered more bound by subjection to the Emperor than to their own immediate Lord. Indeed, a Vassal—

Besold Volume I

<column-break/>

—who refuses to serve against the Emperor is not only to be excused but should be rewarded, as **Ardizon** teaches. This is also illustrated with many citations by **Rosenthal**.

And that he who offends the Lord of his Lord <note>the "overlord" or higher liege</note> loses his fief just as surely as if he had offended his immediate Lord, is also expressly taught in precise terms by **Jacob Thomingius**. He adds this reason: Because just as a thing is affected by a servitude <note>a legal burden on property</note>, so also a fief is affected by the service owed, and it always accompanies it. Furthermore, because the first cause of the benefit <note>the original granting of the land</note> proceeded from the Supreme Lord, the Vassal of a Vassal is bound to love and respect the Lord of his Lord just as much as his immediate Lord. This is confirmed by what Jacob Thomingius writes in the aforementioned legal opinion using these formal words:

> *It also changes nothing that your Graces, as the court servants of the former Elector, wished to go along, since it has already been proven at length above that even a liege-man should not join or provide assistance to his feudal lord—to whom he is nonetheless bound by oath and duty—against the Imperial Majesty.* <note>original German: "So thut auch nichts zur Sach..."</note>

Since in the oath of loyalty, the authority of the Emperor is always understood to be excepted. And a Vassal is released from his oath or sacrament if his Lord shows himself to be a rebel against the Emperor.

Therefore, looking at the authority of the **Common Law** <term>Jus Commune</term> <note>the shared legal system of the Holy Roman Empire based on Roman and Canon law</note>, it cannot be hindered by what is cited by a certain anonymous consultant in **Lundorp**: namely, that a Vassal is more obligated to his immediate Lord than to his mediate Lord <note>a lord higher up the chain with whom he has no direct contract</note>. This person cites the *Speculator* on fiefs, where he teaches: If a King calls the Vassals of a Baron for some business not touching upon public utility, then he would be bound to obey his Baron, his own Lord, rather than the King. **Jacobinus de Sancto Georgio** holds the same, saying this limitation is well worth noting. **Hordleder** refers to this as well.

Nevertheless, that he who offends the Lord of his Lord loses his fief just as if he had offended his immediate Lord is the express text of the law. Therefore, whatever the *Speculator* and others may say—that "the Vassal of my Vassal is not my Vassal"—one must not deviate from the express Text, because the Law must always be certain and defined.

->Thesauri Practici Adaucti<-

...one ought to [be guided by the law], as in Law 2, regarding ignorance of law and fact <note>original: "l. 2. de Juris & fact. ignor."</note>. Therefore, a matter which is otherwise clearly established by manifest texts should not be brought into controversy or investigated through arguments. See the law *ancillæ* regarding theft and the law *non omnes* concerning military affairs. For in certain cases, there is no place for uncertain conjectures; see the law *continuus* at the end, concerning verbal obligations.

And suppose the case that it might be disputable **whether a Vassal is more bound to his immediate Lord than to his mediate Lord** <note>In the feudal hierarchy, an "immediate" lord is the person directly above the vassal, while a "mediate" lord is a higher authority, such as a Duke or the Emperor, who stands above that local lord.</note>; yet such a thing can hardly take place in the case where the **mediate Lord of the fief** <term>Dominus feudi</term> is the Imperial Majesty himself, to whom the German Princes themselves are **Liege Vassals** <note>original: "Vasalli Ligii"; vassals who owe a supreme form of loyalty that outweighs all other obligations</note>. That no one can deny this is attested by Andreas Knichen in his treatise on the Right of Superiority, chapter 6. This is also supported by the traditions of Waremund von Ehrenberg in book 2 on Covenants, chapter 161.

**And also that all Vassals are called "Liege-men" in respect to the Emperor and the King of France, as Guido Papæ writes in decision 309.**

Since also the nobility in Swabia, Franconia, and along the Rhine—even if they are feudal tenants of Electors or other Imperial Estates—nevertheless completely exempt themselves from **true subjection** <note>original: "à verâ subjectione"</note> or provincial status, and wish to depend **directly** <note>original: "immediatè"</note> on the Imperial Majesty as his subordinate noble servants; it follows from this that it is even less becoming for them to allow themselves to be used in any way by their feudal lords against the Imperial Majesty. **For a subject or citizen is more bound to his Lord, or to the Republic in which he lives and to whose full jurisdiction he is subject, than to a Lord of a fief, to whom he is bound only in the name of the fief, and from which bond he can free himself by renouncing that fief.**

This applies all the more for a second reason: because it is publicly known throughout the Empire that the Imperial Majesty, in various mandates, has strictly ordered and forbidden all Electors and Estates of the Empire—under the penalty imposed on those who break the **Public Peace** <term>Landfrieden</term> <note>The legal state of peace within the Holy Roman Empire that prohibited private wars</note> or who strike against the Imperial Majesty—to completely abandon the **Electorate of the Palatinate** <term>Chur-Pfalz</term>, which is the head of the named rebellious Bohemians. They were forbidden to join them under any **pretext** or appearance, and even less to follow or wait upon them with feudal services in such matters against His Imperial Majesty.

**Whoever does a thing prohibited by a Leader (and much more by the Imperial height) or does not observe mandates, is punished by the head <note>This refers to the death penalty</note>, even if he has performed the task well, as Modestinus writes in the law *desertorem* regarding military affairs.**

**From which is built that well-worn legal theory: that the prohibition of a superior binds and constrains, whether it be unjust or not.** Petrus Fridericus, in book 2 on Processes, chapter 26, cites Herculanus: "A prohibition, even if it is notoriously null or obtained by stealth, is not easily to be despised, especially when it proceeds from the powerful; and if one should contravene it without obtaining a remission, there is danger of punishment."

The Palatine or other such feudal tenants should perhaps have excused themselves and invoked the **obligation** with which they are bound as free nobles to the Imperial Majesty. This was faithfully advised in a legal opinion that was published at the time (which now exists in Lundorp’s *Public Acts*, volume 1, book 6, chapter 124) regarding this very question: whether, during the contemporary war-disturbances, feudal services were to be rendered to the Roman Imperial Majesty or to the Electorate of the Palatinate. It was mentioned there that one should first of all rightly distinguish **political counsel** <note>original: "Consilia politica"</note> from **legal counsel** <note>original: "juridicis"</note>. Furthermore, the following very thought-provoking words are found there:

> In these exceedingly high and far-reaching matters, and the doubts arising from them, it is in my opinion safest to remain on the road of the law, as the **Royal Way** <note>original: "viâ Regiâ"</note>. In this way, come what may, one can still find a grounded defense in the law. For when one steps off the legal track, one faces a double danger: that for the sake of the outcome, one might side with those whom fortune has abandoned; and if the leaf turns against one's hope, one would then have no legal excuse to enjoy.

Thirdly, we also fear that the Roman Imperial Majesty will consider himself the **competent Judge** <note>original: "pro Judice competente"</note> in such matters, especially against the nobility, who are not Imperial Estates but the true and immediate subjects of the Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire. **This is because the Emperor regularly—unless some privilege or fundamental Law stands in the way—may judge in his own cause.** (See the laws on testament deletion and on instituting heirs, and Lancellot Conrad in *The Temple of All Judges*).

**Also because the adjudication of controversies of great importance belongs to Majesty alone.** Hence, if an Emperor is slandered, he himself must be consulted (Law 1, Code, *If anyone speaks ill of the Emperor*). And from this, some even say that taking cognizance of the **crime of High Treason** <term>crimen Majestatis</term> is to be numbered among the highest Royal Rights <note>original: "Regalibus"</note>, as otherwise an inferior would be passing judgment on a superior. (See Gigas's treatise on the crime of High Treason and Rudolphin on the Dukes of Italy). A memorable example of this matter is provided by Bernhard Girard, volume 2, book...

<meta>This page continues the legal and political analysis of the consequences following the Bohemian Revolt and the Palatine phase of the Thirty Years' War, specifically addressing the liability of the nobility who sided against Emperor Ferdinand II.</meta>

<page-num>189</page-num>
<header>Lit. C. 189</header>

<margin>
Book 23 on the History of France, folio 14. Discussing the <term>Parricide</term> <note>the assassination</note> of Emperor Albert, concerning whose punishment the High Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> wished to decide nothing, the said Pope saying that it belonged to one Emperor, and not to another, to order the punishment for a murder committed against the person of an Emperor.
</margin>

Having presupposed this, it is to be placed beyond all doubt that His Imperial Majesty and his <term>Aulic Council</term> <note>the Reichshofrat, the Emperor's high judicial body</note> will grant little mercy to those of the nobility who actually served against His Majesty. This remains true even if one wished to bring forward those arguments set forth in the aforementioned considerations in Lundorpius, chapter 125: namely, that all these wars were conducted not against the Holy Roman Empire and the Imperial Majesty in his <term>capacity as Caesar or Emperor</term> <note>original: "qualitate Cæsaris sive Imperatoris"</note>, but rather as an Archduke of Austria. They might also argue that the Electorate of the Palatinate's actions against Spinola's invasion were <term>in terms of defense</term> <note>original: "in terminis defensionis"</note>, and that they had always offered to submit to ordinary legal proceedings, and the like. This is especially true because a grounded reply has already been made to the contrary: that <term>in the person of Ferdinand II</term>, now the most august Roman Emperor, it is difficult to make such an abstraction <term>between the Caesar and the Archduke of Austria</term>, so <term>that by offending the Austrian Archduke, the actual person of the Emperor himself is not harmed</term>. Primarily, the Bohemian affair has been interpreted by His Majesty and many highly esteemed Estates of the Empire in such a way that it affects the honor, good reputation, authority, as well as the legality and standing of His Majesty himself.

To this point, Julius Clarus says in his section on <term>high treason</term> <note>original: "læsæ Majestatis"</note>, number 4, verse 8: it is permitted that someone who harms a Counselor standing at the Prince's side—even out of private enmity—incurs the crime of high treason without distinction. This is because the Prince himself is considered more greatly offended, even if the perpetrator acted because the Counselor represents another persona.

In the same way, His Roman Imperial Majesty (as shown by the documents exchanged on both sides and released in print) in no way concedes that the Electorate of the Palatinate acted <term>in terms of defense</term>. This is because His Majesty was first offended by the taking of the Kingdom of Bohemia, and was allegedly invaded there by military force while his affairs were undefended. Furthermore, the Bohemian Estates did not allow His Majesty's rights in this matter to come before any impartial judge, but instead sat in judgment themselves <term>in a case of unworthiness or crime</term>, after which the Palatine invasion followed <term>under the pretext of turning away harm and in the name of compensatory vengeance</term> <note>original: "sub prætextu aversionis & vindictæ recuperatoriæ nomine"</note>.

And even if the Electorate of the Palatinate might have wished to object with such a distinction, it will likely in no way be permitted to the free Nobility of the Empire, who are the true subjects of the Imperial Majesty and the Empire, and who were not offended or burdened by His Majesty at that time.

<column-break/>

For although defense is permitted by every law, even against an Emperor, a Magistrate, or a Feudal Lord if they use force or exceed their authority—because they are governed by the same rules as others (Fr. Arnisæus on war, n. 44; Schrad. on fiefs, p. 9, c. 3, n. 37; and cap. 4, n. 55 and following; Rosenthal, c. 10, conclusion 11, n. 9; and conclusion 20, n. 26; Bruno, feudal consultations 114, num. 407).

Nevertheless, <term>mediate vassals</term> <note>vassals who hold land from a lord who in turn holds from the Emperor</note> who are also free and of the Knightly Order, and other vassals of no Imperial State but who are <term>immediately</term> <note>directly</note> subject to the Emperor, can hardly allege the <term>right of defense</term> <note>original: "Jus defensionis"</note> for themselves against the Imperial Majesty, their Prince and general Lord. Even if some such right had been available to the Palatine and other Princes against the Emperor (which is by no means established), it would not apply here, because those Nobles were not in the least offended by the Emperor.

Fourthly, it should be noted here what Thomingius writes—and indeed in stronger terms—in the often-cited consultation 12, n. 15 and following, in these formal words: And if one were to say that the two young gentlemen were minors at the time of the war, and that one was only in his 19th year while the other was in his 13th (as was particularly cited in the Regensburg proceedings); yet by their own admission they were already <term>puberes</term> <note>of legal age/pubescent</note> and of age at that time. And sins are imputed not only to adults, but also to minors and those who have reached puberty (chapter "r." on the delicts of children). Indeed, it appears from the law "pupillum" regarding the Rules of Law that not only those of age but even those close to puberty are bound by a crime. And in crimes, no aid is provided to help minors, especially in more atrocious ones (law "auxilium" in the section on crimes, in the Digest on minors). Whence also the Emperors Severus and Antoninus wrote back: In crimes, minors are not helped by the benefit of their age, nor are the characters of the wicked excused by weakness of mind (law 1, Code: if against a delict).

If it were perhaps further argued that the well-mentioned young gentlemen had taken neither oath nor duty for the said campaign; yet this can contribute nothing to their grace, since they were present with the army in their own person, and one was captured in the defeat at Mühlberg. Since the Lord Barons proceeded to the act itself, and in this case even the mere will—let alone the effect of the will—is subject to punishment (law "quisquis" at the beginning, Code: the Julian Law on Majesty).

And therefore, it also matters nothing here that the young gentleman did not remain persistently with the campaign. For since in this case the act itself was proceeded with, and this crime is committed and consumed not only by the deed itself but even by the mere will (said law "quisquis"), consequently that commonly worn rule of law succeeds: <term>once a crime is completed, no one ceases to be guilty through repentance</term> <note>original: "delicto consummato, nemo pœnitentiâ nocens esse desinat"</note> (law "what is a fugitive" at the beginning; and the law "he who with that mind"). Thus far Thomingius.

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the liability of the nobility and subjects during the Bohemian Revolt. # Expanded Practical Treasury
### Page 190

Although all of this is contained in the law as demonstrated above, the aforementioned legal rules also have their exceptions. **First**, it is certain that the <term>crime of treason</term> <note>original: "crimen laesae Maještatis," literally "injured majesty"</note> absolutely requires <term>malicious intent</term> <note>original: "dolum"</note>. This is found in the Pandects <note>the Digest of Roman Law</note> regarding the Julian Law on Treason, which specifies an "enemy mind." Gigas, in his work on the crime of treason, and Carolus Ruina in his fifth volume of legal opinions, both state that a person does not incur the crime of rebellion or treason unless they intend to attempt something with bad intent against the prosperity and security of the Prince, and with the aim to offend him. This is because <term>in crimes, the will is inspected, not the outcome</term> <note>original: "in maleficiis voluntas inspicitur & non exitus"</note>. Bartolus concludes this is true when the action taken did not primarily lead toward the crime in question. Cephalus agrees, teaching that the crime of treason should never be ascribed to one lacking intent, and that even <term>gross negligence</term> <note>original: "culpa lata"</note> is not sufficient in this case, because a defect of the will excuses the intent.

Furthermore, since a "bad mind" is a matter of fact, it is not merely presumed but must be proven. This is not contradicted by the rule in the Code regarding assassins or insults; that presumption of guilt only applies when there is no other presumption or conjecture in favor of the accused. Follerus, Marsilius, and Plotus all pass down the teaching that <term>mere negligence</term> <note>original: "sola culpa"</note> does not make one guilty of the crime of treason.

Similarly, Bursatus teaches that to impose a direct penalty for this crime, "presumed proof" is not enough; intent must be proven by the one who alleges it.

And where two presumptions collide—one suggesting a crime and the other excluding it—the excluding presumption <note>the one favoring the innocence of the accused</note> must always carry more weight. This is supported by Baldus, Brunus, and especially Grammaticus and Ruina.

**Secondly**, we find it taught that if a <term>vassal</term> <note>a person who has entered into a mutual obligation to a lord or monarch</note> or a subject commits something against his Lord or superior out of ignorance or error, it deserves an excuse. This is because knowledge, not ignorance, ought to be punished. Crimes are judged by purpose and will; but one who errs or is ignorant has no "will" to commit a crime.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, where there is no will to offend, there is no place for the penalty of that crime. This ignorance is presumed to exist until the contrary is proven, as Cephalus explains in these very terms.

However, ignorance excuses only if it is "just" <note>meaning reasonable or excusable</note>. For it is certain that one is considered to have acted with intent if they do not do what they know (or ought to know) they are required to do.

It is also certain that a "mistake of law" is considered <term>gross negligence</term>. An unjust cause does not excuse it. Likewise, "affected ignorance" <note>deliberately avoiding the truth</note> is treated as full knowledge, as is "crass and supine ignorance" <note>negligence so extreme it suggests a total lack of care</note>.

**Thirdly**, <term>just fear</term> <note>original: "justus metus," referring to legal duress or acting under threat</note> likewise excuses. We find it taught that a community or city that rebels against its Prince or Lord because of just fear is excused and does not fall under any penalty. This is noted by Joannes de Imola, Decius, and Hieronymus Gigas.

Any "just fear" excuses one from all fault and intent in prohibited acts. This fear is sufficient if a person knows they could easily be compelled to act.

Even the <term>fear of losing one’s honor</term> is called a "just fear," as is the fear of violence being inflicted. Innocentius and Baldus hold that no one is required to commit themselves to danger when it is feared that a situation cannot be escaped without peril. This fear is considered to last as long as the jurisdiction of that Lord lasts. "Just fear" is cited not only when danger is immediate, but even when matters are likely heading in that direction; therefore, it is enough that a just cause for fear exists. Legal experts say just fear exists where there is a "just suspicion," and Angelus says it is the same whether something is done through fear or through a "probable suspicion of fear." The legal glosses teach that just fear suffices as an excuse even if the feared effect does not actually follow.

<summary>This page outlines legal defenses against charges of treason and rebellion, emphasizing that malicious intent (dolus) must be proven and that "just fear" or "excusable ignorance" can mitigate or negate punishment.</summary>

# Treasury of Law, Book C
### Page 191

...judged that it is sufficient to feel fear at least probably, even if not strictly "justly" according to the law.

And in specific terms, Carolus Ruina <note>Carolus Ruina (d. 1530) was a prominent Italian jurist</note>, in volume 1, counsel 23, in the case of the Duke of Gravina under number 7, writes: That even if the Duke had served in person, he would still not have incurred the said crime. For it was demanded and imposed upon him by letters from the Captain of the Enemy League that he must take up arms against the lands of the Empire, under threat of the <term>deprivation of his fief</term> <note>original: "privationis feudi"</note> and his status. Such a penal command induces **just fear**, as is proven by the notes of Bartolus on the law regarding payment; there he concludes that if someone’s debtor was forced by the Republic to pay in order to be freed, he must prove that he was forced by violence. This is said to be proven if a city ordinance is shown to be penal and a grave action is taken regarding it. For it is **just fear** <note>original: "justus metus," a legal standard where a person of "firm character" would be compelled by the threat</note>, according to the final law sections 1 and 2, which deals with the cause of fear. Therefore, given such a penal command and grave action, the said Lord Duke would have been excused from the crime of treason, even if he had served in person and thus against the prohibition made to him. This is because **fear attenuates guilt**, and consequently the punishment, according to the chapter on "Sacred" regarding the cause of fear. The Abbot <note>referring to Panormitanus, a famous canonist</note> introduces that text when a statute warns that whoever does such a thing falls *ipso facto* into such a punishment; he presents a case where someone performed a prohibited act through fear, and asks if they fall under the penalty of the statute? He determines they do not, because fear lessens the fault and the penalty, or at least in execution the punishment must be reduced out of respect for the circumstances. Furthermore, Ruina in that same place thinks that one should avoid the punishment entirely if the fear was "just," as he says was decided in the notes of Alvarez.

For a similar reason, Joannes Cephalus, in counsel 75, through his discourse, frees John Francis Gonzaga from the crime of treason. In numbers 16 and following, he writes: He is to be punished less by the penalty for the crime of treason when he, unwillingly and through fear, destroyed that bridge (which was the question at hand). For, unless he had executed the command of the Prince whose soldier he was, he could have been punished with the death penalty, according to the law in the <term>Digest on military matters</term> <note>original: "ff. de remilit."</note>. In such a case, a person cannot legally be said to have fallen into a crime as a rebel, as Baldus decided in counsel 36 at the end of book 3. And since he was not one of the Prince’s Counselors, he could not inquire whether the command was just or unjust, etc., but was bound to execute it, even if it seemed grave and intolerable to him, as Cravetta says in counsel 233. Terrified by **just fear**, since the danger of death was imminent if he had not obeyed the command of the Prince—to the point that he would have been considered a fool for not fearing—according to Baldus in the counsel on schism, with others through Grammaticus. And most especially, because it suffices to fear at least probably, even if not strictly justly. Thus far Cephalus. Furthermore, one does not incur the crime of treason who does not

<column-break/>

principally intend to harm the Lord, even if a loss to the Lord results as a consequence of the action, following the arguments handed down by Bartolus. This is especially true if he does not persevere; for otherwise, perseverance induces an indication of a preceding intent, according to Baldus and Marsilius.

With this perspective, Albertus Brunus also writes in feudal counsel 69, number 10: Although it is said that someone preparing an army or gathering people without the command of the Prince can fall into the crime of treason (as in the Julian Law on Treason), where the same is said of him who consented... because this proceeds when the act is done **principally to the injury of the state**, and for the effect of harming the Public Majesty. This is the interpretation to be taken: both because it is evident, and because **in matters of punishment, the milder interpretation is to be taken in cases of doubt** <note>original: "in pœnis mitior in dubio eſt ſumenda interpretatio"</note>. This was also the opinion of Angelus regarding the Julian Law on Treason. These are the words of the said Brunus.

To apply these now-established <term>evidences</term> <note>original: "evidentialia"</note> to the present case: whether an <term>Elector Palatine</term> <note>original: "Chur-Pfälziſch"</note> or another Estate's **vassal**, or also a free Imperial Noble, who allowed themselves to be used against the Imperial Majesty’s armies or commanders, has committed the crime of treason according to the guidance of the above deduction—or whether they can excuse themselves by virtue of the following added limitations—will have to be learned from the facts, which are not sufficiently known to us. Presumably, in all places, special and diverse circumstances will be found that can burden, relieve, or excuse one or the other.

To speak of this in general terms, however:
(1) Those will have a hard time extricating themselves who notoriously allowed themselves to be used for the Imperial Majesty’s enemy.
On the other hand, (2) in our humble opinion, those might be excused who initially did not know against whom the campaign was directed, yet afterward could not withdraw without danger, but were forced to hazard their lives alongside others, or endure a greater danger and mockery.
Provided that they (3) subsequently, once it was sufficiently obvious that this campaign was directed against the Imperial Majesty, separated themselves and returned home at the earliest possibility.
Likewise, (4) those **vassals** who served their <term>feudal lord</term> <note>original: "Lehenherrn"</note> upon demand, also because they resided in his land and could not refuse feudal service without danger, nor obey the Imperial **mandates of recall** <note>original: "avocatoriis Mandatis," orders from the Emperor for subjects to leave the service of an enemy</note>—these are not easily to be accused of the crime of treason based on the deductions above. All of which, it is our hope, will find all the more standing with the Roman Imperial Majesty...

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law
### Page 192

...and will move them, according to their innate mercy, to choose a gentler path. For according to commonly held laws, any cause—even a frivolous one—may excuse a person from <term>malice</term> <note>original: "dolo," referring to the intentional "evil intent" required for a crime</note>, as noted by Gabriel in book 7 on crimes, conclusion 8, throughout; where in note 8, he states that even a reckless belief, or even an invalid decree, is thought to relieve one from the charge of malice.

->As was acted in our College on September 14, in the year 1630.<-

To this response, I have chosen to add the following <term>Deduction</term> <note>A formal legal argument or brief</note> exhibited by me a few years ago. In this document, it is asked whether and when <term>fiefs</term> <note>land held from a lord in return for service</note> are subject to confiscation? And if a fief is lost due to the committed crime of <term>treason</term> <note>original: "crimen læsæ Majestatis"</note>, does it pass to the <term>agnates</term> <note>relatives related through the male line</note>, or to the Lord? Furthermore, to which lord does it go—the immediate one or the one above him? And what right does a <term>sub-vassal</term> <note>one who holds a fief from another vassal rather than directly from the sovereign</note> retain in a sub-fief? I hope this will not be unpleasant to the reader, as it is convenient and consistent with the preceding treatment.

### Most Serene, Most Mighty, etc.

Your Imperial Majesty will most graciously remember how I recently most obediently complained that the fiefs held by A. and B. from the Duchy of C., and especially the estate D., were intended to be drawn into the confiscation of property undertaken by Your Imperial Majesty against the current holders.

Although I am very reluctant to trouble Your Imperial Majesty further, it is my duty to take due notice of the strong interest of the <term>wards</term> <note>original: "Pupillen," orphans or minors under legal protection</note> and their guardians involved here. I must also, as much as possible, prevent future worrisome consequences. I am in the most humble hope that Your Imperial Majesty will not harbor any ungracious thoughts regarding this, because several other highly respected <term>Estates of the Empire</term> <note>The princes and authorities who held seats in the Imperial Diet</note> have also submitted similar most humble remonstrances to Your Imperial Majesty and have most obediently requested most gracious moderation.

Therefore, my most humble prayer to Your Imperial Majesty is that you deign to note this in Imperial grace, and most graciously observe that it is not at all doubted here whether Your Imperial Majesty is authorized to carry out confiscation in the matter of the crime of treason against those persons or their property who are convicted of this vice and proven to have committed it with <term>evil intent</term> <note>original: "dolo malo"</note>. For such a right is known to be attached to Your Imperial Majesty’s supreme power,

<column-break/>

especially since it is not unjust that the Majesty himself should undertake the <term>avenging of his own injury</term> <note>original: "injuriæ suæ ultionem"</note>, and therefore enjoy some of the resulting benefits. However, whether such confiscation may be equally extended and drawn to those properties which are not the delinquent's own property, but which he can only have and possess <term>for the days of his life</term> <note>original: "ad dies vitæ," a life-tenancy or usufruct</note>, or as long as he is otherwise legally capable of them—against this, according to my humble judgment, the following grounds and reasons, based both on written law and natural equity, seem to conflict.

Namely, it is first an undisputed point of law that fiefs can never reach persons who are not named or included in the <term>investitures</term> <note>The formal ceremony or document granting the fief</note> against the will of the Lord. Therefore, in respect to the granting of the fief itself, such persons are to be considered <term>stranger heirs</term> <note>original: "extraneis hæredibus"</note>. Rather, in the event that the <term>vassal</term> <note>the person holding the land</note> no longer wishes or is no longer able to possess his held fief, it must fall either to the other relatives capable of holding the fief, or to the <term>Feudal Lord</term> <note>original: "Lehenherrn"</note> himself. Thus, the ownership must be consolidated with the <term>beneficial ownership</term> <note>original: "utili Dominio," the right to use and profit from the land</note> which the vassal previously enjoyed.

Furthermore, it is established that the <term>Treasury</term> <note>original: "Fiscus," the state or royal purse</note> stands in the place of a stranger heir (according to law 2 of the Code on the Julian Law regarding violence, and law 1 of the Code on the property of freedmen). Since, therefore, a fief cannot pass to a stranger heir (as is the text in title 45, whether the agnate or the son of the deceased, with similar passages), it follows from this that it cannot be transferred to the Treasury (as per Gail, book 2 on Public Peace, chapter 14, note 3).

And secondly, although at first glance it might seem—from the law *quisquis* (which says: "to our Treasury with all his goods," etc., in the Code on the Julian Law of Treason)—that in general all the goods of one who is truly guilty of the crime of treason are forfeited to Your Imperial Majesty's Treasury: yet in law 4 of the Digest on the Right of Patronage, and law 3 on interdicts and banishment, those goods are exempted (even in a case of <term>high treason</term> <note>original: "perduellionis"</note>) which belonged to the delinquent by <term>singular right</term> <note>rights held specifically by an individual rather than general inheritance</note> and specifically by reason of his lineage or family. Therefore, it is in no way to be considered that fiefs are included in the confiscation, primarily to the detriment of the Feudal Lord.

Because, naturally, the fief belongs by singular right to the sons or the male relatives (agnates) of the vassal, based on the <term>pact</term> <note>contract</note> of the first acquiring vassal and the granting Lord (title 14, section "if a Captain," where it says: "they succeed into the benefit by the investiture of the father and grandfather"). Hence, once lost, it passes to them; and if they are lacking, or if the fault was committed against the Lord or superior himself, it returns to him (title 24, the final section, and title 37 in the preface, book 2 of the Feudal Laws).

Thirdly, the <term>equity of Canon Law</term> <note>The legal system of the Church, often seen as more flexible or "equitable" than strict Roman civil law</note> entirely agrees with this, and strengthens this opinion with an express text in the chapter *Felicis*, section "if any fiefs," regarding punishments in the <term>Sixth Book</term> <note>The *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law</note>...

<summary>This page argues that if a person is convicted of treason, their feudal lands (fiefs) should not be seized by the Imperial Treasury because the offender does not "own" the land fully; it belongs to their family lineage or must revert to the original Lord. The author cites Roman, Feudal, and Canon law to protect the rights of innocent relatives and superior lords against state confiscation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a legal argument regarding the rights of feudal lords over fiefs when a vassal commits a crime or attempts an unauthorized transfer. It follows the discussion of how feudal property reverts to the lord rather than the state treasury.</meta>

Header: Letter C.

...and specifically sanctions that, when the goods of one guilty of high treason are made public, his fief must pass to the Lord, not to the treasury.

And it appears this text (although it speaks of a Church fief) must be understood generally, because the equity and reasoning of that sanction is general, and thus it may be extended to similar cases. *Law: "for as he says," 13. §. 1. following, Digest: on laws.* Furthermore, specific exceptions are not easily introduced. And a meaning that induces an exception in some case is to be avoided. *Alexander on the law "concerning goods" §. with the trust. at the end. Digest: on the Falcidian Law.* And he who says something is permitted in a specific case must prove it and assign the reason for that exception. *Decius in the chapter "he consulted," note 4, on appeals. Cravetta, counsel 229, note 15. Cephalus, counsel 207, note 15. Borgninus, decision 46, note 13.*

This opinion is further strengthened because, according to general Imperial statutes, even though those who acted against the Public Peace may have their goods seized by anyone, and no one may commit a crime against them; nevertheless, the fiefs are declared <term>reverted</term> <note>heimgesprochen: legally returned to the original owner</note> to the Feudal Lord and are not taken away from him. *Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 9, §. 2. verse: "also the fiefs." Constitution on public peace under the heading: "On Peace-Breakers." Gail, on public peace, book 2, chapter 14, note 6 and following. Rosenthal, on fiefs, chapter 11, conclusion 11, note 16 and following.*

Fourth, it is again undisputed law, and well-established in all feudal courts throughout the whole Roman Empire, that no vassal may change, sell, or in any other way transfer his fief—<note>original: "etiam in æque habilem transferiren"</note> <term>even to an equally capable person</term>—without the express consent of the Feudal Lord; he may not even give it as a pledge, nor perform any act from which an <term>alienation</term> <note>the transfer of ownership to another</note> might follow, even <term>by consequence</term>, without punishment or without it being handled as a crime. *The whole title: on the prohibition of alienating a fief, by Lothar, in the beginning.* Where it is decreed by an edictal law to be valid for all time, that it is permitted to no one to sell the benefits <note>fiefs</note> which they have from their seniors <note>lords</note> without their permission, or to devise any trade by which the utility of the Empire or the Lords might be diminished.

The same is sanctioned in the *title: on the prohibition of alienating a fief, by Frederick*; namely, that it is permitted to no one to sell or pledge the whole fief or any part of it, or to distribute or alienate it in any way, or to judge it <term>for the soul</term> <note>pro anima: a donation to the church for the benefit of one's soul</note>, without the permission of that Lord to whom the fief is known to belong.

And a little after: Meeting the clever machinations of certain people who, having received a price, sell the fief and transfer it to others as if under the color of investiture (which they claim is permitted to them); and so that such a fiction, or anything else devised to defraud the constitutions, may be prohibited in every way, we decree—under the imminent penalty of our authority—that the seller and buyer who are found to have contracted such illicit alienations

<column-break/>

shall lose the fief, and it shall freely revert to the Lord, etc.

And likewise, that a lease for a long period is included under the word "alienation," and also that a vassal is prohibited under penalty of loss from leasing the fief for a long period—for example, ten years or more—as *Rosenthal* proves with many authorities in *chapter 9, member 1, conclusion 7, number 8*. There he also rejects the opinion of Alvarottus and others, and all precautions made to hide a fraudulent alienation, and listens to the reason that in a lease of this kind for a long period, possession and at the same time the <term>useful right of ownership</term> <note>ius utile: the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to the underlying legal title</note> appears to pass to the possessor. But even if it is agreed in a long lease that the useful ownership does not pass to the tenant, he says the vassal is not excused in that case if there is difficulty in recovering the fief from this transfer.

Now, as just humbly mentioned, a feudal tenant can never, through any contract, pact, or agreement, ensure that the fief he holds passes to another person against the Feudal Lord’s will—specifically to one not included in the <term>investiture</term> <note>the formal ceremony of granting a fief</note> nor descended <term>from the first person invested</term>—especially since the Lord cannot be forced to consent to such alienations or transfers, neither to another nor to the vassal himself, <note>original: "in aliam etiam æquè, vel magis idoneam personam"</note> <term>even to another equally or more suitable person</term>. Rather, the Lord is empowered by his <term>bare contract</term> and without showing any cause, to prevent and overturn everything that has occurred in this regard, and even to seize the fief as forfeited. It follows, then, that even less can a feudal tenant cause such a fief to reach another (whoever that may be) through his crime: because crimes and contracts are equated by law in such a way that what cannot be done by way of contract cannot be achieved by committing a crime. *Law: "every," Digest: on judgments; final chapter: on the form of competence; with similar ones: Everhard, "from crimes to contracts."* And what is the law in contracts also holds true in crimes, and vice versa, unless there is a different reason or a contrary decision is expressly found. *Matth. Stephani, in the Dialectic of Law, book 2, place 102.*

Therefore, when someone cannot harm another through a contract, it is entirely most equitable that this cannot happen through a crime, since crimes are more odious than contracts; and it remains eternally true that no one should suffer damage from another's crime, since punishments ought to hold their own authors and not proceed further against those who are far from blame. *Text in the law: "if anyone from his," §. Of the law. Code: on inofficious testaments; the law. Code: on the nature and legitimate children; the law: "on account of husbands." Code: lest a wife for her husband.* And it is not fitting for another third and innocent person to lose their right by the misfortune of another's crime. *the law: "the things of a wife," Code: on donations between [spouses]...*

### Page 194
### Enlarged Practical Treasury

...husband and wife. Law: *If any Priest*. Code: *On Bishops and Clerics*.

It is relevant here that a person who is prohibited from <term>alienating</term> <note>original: "alienare"; the legal act of transferring ownership to another</note> property cannot perform any act through which a transfer of ownership might follow. Law: *Codicils*. Section: *Mother*. Where Bartolus comments on Digest: *On Legacies, book 2*. Tiraquellus, *On Blood Retraction*, Section 1, gloss 2, number 50. Decius, counsel 25, number 2. And thus, one who is prohibited from transferring property is deemed prohibited from entering into a contract regarding a transfer to be made. Bartolus on the Law: *When the law*. Digest: *On Suretyship*, where Castrensis also comments. Consequently, such a person cannot even commit a crime [that leads to seizure]; because by committing a crime, he opens the way for a transfer, especially since a transfer that occurs from a crime is considered voluntary rather than necessary.

Therefore, fifthly, the unanimous conclusion of all legal scholars is that not only under the general <term>designation of goods</term> <note>original: "appellatione bonorum"</note> are fief-estates in no way included, but also specifically, in the case of confiscation or the public seizure of property, the fiefs do not pass to the <term>treasury</term> <note>original: "fiscum"; the state or royal coffers</note>. Instead, they either belong to the <term>agnates</term> <note>original: "Agnatis"; relatives through the male line</note> or fall back to the Feudal Lord.

Indeed, it is a very clear point of Law that in any legal disposition, however general it may be, fiefs are not included under the designation of "goods." Alexander, counsel 2, column 1, volume 4. Decius, counsel 139. Panormitanus, counsel 7, number 3, volume 1, and counsel 12, number 62 in the same volume. And for this reason, Alexander said in counsel 16, column 2, volume 2, that in a general obligation of goods, feudal matters are not included. Guido Papa, counsels 215 and 218, second to last column, verse: *to the eighth*. Afflictis, decision 26, at the beginning. Grammaticus, decision 103, number 130.

Similarly, feudal properties are excluded from a general donation of goods. Afflictis, decision 14. Brunus, counsel 115, number 3. Guido Papa, in the same place as above, as well as in the sale of goods. Chapter 1: *On the Captain who sells a Court*, where all feudal lawyers agree. Cephalus, counsel 29, number 16. Likewise, this holds true in a general <term>trust</term> <note>original: "fideicommisso"; a legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of another</note>. Bartolus and others on the Law: *If the Patrons*. Digest: *On the Trebellian Decree*. Rollandus à Valle, treatise *On the Profit of Dowries*, question 54. And even in the renunciation of goods. Baldus on the authentic: *In succession*, at the end. Code: *On natural and legal heirs*. Socinus, counsel 84, number 5, volume 3.

If, therefore, in these cases a fief is by no means included under the designation of "goods," the same must also be said regarding a sentence of confiscation of property—namely, that the fief is not included in it, nor should it be understood as falling under the laws granting confiscation. This is because the nature of feudal property is separate from other property, and it is not included among them unless specific mention is made of it. Signorolus, counsel 220. Decius, counsel 139, at the end. Afflictis agrees in decision 14, number 9, and most fully Tiraquellus, *On Retraction*, section 1, gloss 5, number 2 and following, book 1, where he concludes from many sources that in any general disposition, feudal goods and rights do not come into play unless they are particularly mentioned.

Thus far the reasoning is clear enough: because certainly a fief is not part of the resources of the vas-

<column-break/>

-sal; rather, only the <term>useful domain</term> <note>original: "utile dominium"; the right to use and profit from the land</note> belongs to him for as long as he lives naturally and civilly. The <term>direct ownership</term> <note>original: "proprietas" / "dominio directo"</note>, however, belongs to the Feudal Lord. And so, a vacant fief is either consolidated with the direct ownership or, by feudal law, passes automatically to the male-line relatives. Likewise, a universal proposition must be understood in such a way that no damage is unjustly inflicted upon a third party. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 11, conclusion 13, letter A.

Sixthly, because anyone who has committed the abominable vice of violating the Majesty of the Emperor or other high potentates is in all ways to be held as <term>civilly dead</term> <note>original: "pro civiliter mortuo"; alive but having lost all legal rights and status</note>. Such a person is undoubtedly in a condition where the Feudal Lord can no longer make use of such a vassal, or as the feudal lawyers say, he can no longer "stand in the Lord's Court." It follows ultimately that his held fief—just as if he had passed away from a natural death—should fall to no one else but the Feudal Lord.

For indeed, if a vassal commits the crime of <term>high treason</term> <note>original: "crimen laesae Majestatis"</note>, he is held as civilly dead. For one committing high treason simultaneously loses all things that belong to Civil Law. Law: *By the loss*. Section: *Those who fail*. Digest: *On the loss of status*. And for this reason, he immediately loses the administration of his goods, even before he is accused. Odofredus on the Law: *Their Patrimonies*, number 7. *On the Law of the Treasury*. Code, book 10, final law. Code: *On the Julian Law of Majesty*, and the Law: *Whoever*. Section: *Emancipations*: there, *from the moment they first thought of entering into a faction or society*. Code, said title.

This is supported by the notes of Baldus on the Chapter: *Imperial*. Section: *By the cunning*. *On the prohibition of alienating a fief*, by Frederick. There he says that a vassal committing the crime of high treason loses his fief by the law itself. Boërius gives his assent in decision 277, number 12.

And that an outlaw is held for dead is also related by Don Garfias Mastrillus, decision 277, number 6. This is even apparent from the fact that no conversation may be held with them, no one may receive or tolerate them under their roof, nor supply them with food and drink; instead, everyone must turn away from them, detest them, and pursue them as enemies. *Chamber Court Ordinance*, part 2, title 10, section: *and where for that reason*, so much so that those who receive them are held to the same punishment and fall under the ban themselves. *Public Peace Ordinance of Worms from the year 1521*, title: *Peace-Breakers and Perpetrators*, section: *which authority however*. Moreover, those committing high treason, if they cannot be seized for worthy punishment, are seen to be noted by the ban by the law itself. And that a person whose goods are made public is likewise held for dead is taught by Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 11, under number 7.

And although "civil death" is not held to be the same as "natural death," and the term "death" is usually understood as natural, not civil (except in cases expressed by law), Chapter: *Received*, verse: *not by death*, *On Rescripts*, in the 6th book. Vincentius Franchus, decision 562, number 8 and following. Hondedei, counsel 62, volume 1, number 3 and following. Yet it seems to be expressed clearly enough in Feudal Law that even civil death stands for natural death. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, conclusion...

<summary>This page argues that feudal lands are distinct from general property and should not be seized by the state treasury in cases of treason or confiscation. It establishes the concept of "civil death," where a criminal is legally treated as deceased, causing their fief to revert to their lord or heirs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument from page 194, asserting that feudal property (fiefs) must return to the original Lord or the rightful heirs rather than being seized by the state treasury when a vassal commits a crime, particularly treason.</meta>

Lit. 195

f. 11. n. 7. or at least for such a cause, it should be held that the <term>fief</term> <note>original: "feudum"; land held from a lord on condition of loyalty and service</note> must return to the Lord: because after the <term>crime of treason</term> <note>original: "crimen Majestatis"; literally "lese-majesty," an offense against the dignity of the sovereign or state</note> has been committed, an enemy can no longer stand in the Lord's Court. Rosenthal, chapter 10, conclusion 36, number 44 and following.

Furthermore, that a <term>Vassal</term> <note>original: "Vasallus"; one who holds land from a lord</note> who has committed such a <term>felony</term> <note>original: "feloniam"; a breach of the feudal contract</note> or such an act that he can no longer stand in the Lord's Court should be deprived of his fief, is a point that the text in chapter 1, *Whether he, as if he killed a brother*, does not allow us to doubt.

And further, it is not only he who is perhaps ejected and repelled by a ban of the Empire, or of the Imperial Majesty, so that he is prevented from coming to the court or the assembly, who is said to be unable to stand in the Court any longer; nor is it only he who comes in body and could be in the Court, but is prohibited from being present in mind or by a magistrate's interdict. Rather, it also includes him who, on account of some <term>infamy</term> <note>original: "infamiam"; a loss of legal standing or reputation</note> or disgrace and dishonesty of person, cannot stand there or be tolerated by the Lord, and cannot move among the Vassals in service or in the acts of the Court (perhaps in judicial proceedings) without dishonor. This is argued from the text in the said chapter 1, there: *or if he has committed such a felony, for example by shaving a man* <note>original: "hominem radendo"; a specific medieval legal example of a humiliating assault</note> *or if he can no longer stand in the Lord's Court, he shall be deprived of the benefit, etc.*

And so, if one burdened with the obligation of a <term>entailment</term> <note>original: "fideicommissi"; a legal arrangement where property is held for another's benefit</note> enters the Monastery of the <term>Friars Minor</term> <note>original: "Fratrum Minorum"; the Franciscans, who take vows of extreme poverty</note>, who can hold nothing of their own in common or in particular, then immediately after the monk has made his profession—without waiting for his natural death—the property must be restored. This opinion should be followed in judging and advising, as it seems very much in harmony with the truth; it is not only the more common view of the old writers, but also the modern ones, as Joseph de Rusticis relates at length in his repetition on the law *When a grandfather*, regarding conditions and demonstrations; and most recently John Mylius in his additions to Augustine Beroius, question 41. This conclusion is defended at length by Jason in counsel 135, number 5, book 1, following Baldus and Castrensis.

Likewise, if a husband’s goods are made public and he is outlawed or banned, even though the marriage is not dissolved thereby, nevertheless, for the purpose of recovering the dowry and dower-rights and other marital rights, the husband is held as truly dead, and the wife recovers or respectively gains those rights.

Furthermore, in an even stronger case, when the goods of a wealthy husband are confiscated, a wife who is without a dowry and in need immediately takes a fourth part, notwithstanding the confiscation—even in the crime of treason. Mastrillus proves this sufficiently after many others in decision 283 through a long discussion; namely, that the wife’s condition regarding his goods should not be made worse by the husband’s crime. And although a dowry regularly only returns to the wife following a natural death, it can happen in many cases that even while the husband is living, the dowry and dower-rights can be reclaimed by the wife. All of these points can be most aptly applied to the case of a fief: for a fief falls to the Lord not only upon the death of those invested, but there are many cases where, while the

<column-break/>

Vassal is still living, the fief is lost and can be reclaimed by the Lord.

Specifically, it is the most common opinion of the Doctors of Law—as Alexander testifies in the law *Finished*, paragraph *here concerning the tax*, number 30—that a fief never comes into confiscation. Instead, even in the case of the crime of treason, it reaches the Lord of the fief. See also Boerius, decision 264, number 7; Curtius Junior, counsel 4, number 20; Rubeus, counsel 134, number 3; Fachinaeus, book 7, chapter 20; and Farinacius in his treatise on crimes and punishments, question 25, number 62, where he cites many authors. Among other things, he reports from Castrensis that if the Treasury seizes such goods, it is said to occupy them <note>original: "de facto"; in practice, rather than by legal right</note> by fact only. He adds that although some Doctors have attempted to argue the contrary, one must not withdraw from the proposed opinion; at number 67, he extends this even to the crime of treason.

Thus, Paul Christinaeus in volume 1, decision 300, number 15, teaches that this opinion rests on very clear texts, and that said texts cannot accept any interpretation other than this: namely, that the fief returns freely and absolutely to the Lord, and this opinion is also the more common one.

Rosenthal agrees in *On Fiefs*, chapter 11, conclusion 11 and 13, where he speaks in terms of a committed crime of treason. Clarus, in the section *On Fiefs*, question 84, adds among other things: "It has always seemed to me unjust and absurd that a Vassal could prejudice the Lord or his <term>agnates</term> <note>original: "agnatis"; relatives through the male line</note> by committing a crime, when he could not prejudice them by <term>alienating</term> <note>original: "alienando"; selling or transferring ownership</note> the land; and since an outside heir is not admitted to a fief of this kind, therefore neither should the treasury be." Marcus Antonius Peregrinus in *On the Law of the Treasury*, book 5, title 1, number 106, infers that fiefs and other things which by their nature cannot be transferred to outside heirs, or transmitted by an act of alienation to a person not included in the investiture or the will, do not pass to the treasury upon the publication of the delinquent Vassal's goods, because they cannot be alienated. Vulteius in *On Fiefs*, book 1, chapter 11, number 140, teaches that in every case where a Vassal commits treason, the fief always devolves to the Lord, whether it be an old or new fief, and whether it is held by contract and foresight or is of a mixed hereditary nature. So much so that while otherwise the goods of one who committed treason are handed over to the treasury, the fief is nonetheless left not to the Treasury, but to the Lord.

Likewise, in the case of a banned Vassal, the fief does not come into the public seizure of goods. If a Vassal of some Baron commits an offense against the King, for which crime his goods are assigned to the Treasury, then in such a case the fief is not applied to the Royal Treasury, but returns to the <term>Direct Lord</term> <note>original: "Dominum directum"; the immediate superior in the feudal hierarchy</note>. Andreas Gail proves this with many arguments in *On Public Peace*, book 2, chapter 12, throughout; and Schrader in *On Fiefs*, part 9, chapter 9, number 16 and following, where he teaches that if a Vassal’s goods are seized for a crime, the Vassal loses the fief, but it is applied not to the treasury, but to either the Lord or the agnate relatives. Antonius Merenda, in book 5 of *Controversies of Law*, chapter 21, where he says in this contro—
