# Augmented Practical Treasury

It is certain within this controversy that the crime of a **Vassal** <note>original: "Vasalli"; a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</note> cannot bring harm to the **Lord**, and therefore, if a case should arise where the **fief** <note>original: "feudum"; land held under the feudal system</note> returns to the Lord—whether according to feudal laws or the specific terms of the agreements made between him and the Vassal—there is nothing that can be discussed regarding **confiscation** <note>original: "confiscatione"; the seizure of property by the state treasury</note>. In such a case, it is clear that the fief belongs rightfully to the Lord.

The same author, in the following chapter, addresses the question of whether an **Emphyteusis** <term>Emphyteusis: a type of perpetual or long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</term> is acquired by the **state treasury** <note>original: "fisco"</note> when someone’s goods are made public. He offers many reasons to support his opinion: all of these are seen even more clearly in a fief, especially one that is a "right" or "masculine military" fief <note>A fief that can only be inherited by male heirs and involves military service</note>. Joannes Petrus Surdus agrees entirely in Decision 284, where he proves through many examples that prohibited goods—those which were granted to someone’s ancestors as an emphyteusis or a fief—cannot be subject to confiscation. This is because the aforementioned emphyteutic property was, by agreement, prohibited from being mortgaged or obligated. Peregrinus discusses this extensively in *The Law of the Treasury*, Book 5, Title 1, Number 98, where he maintains that as soon as goods are confiscated, the **substitute** <note>the person next in line to inherit or hold the right</note> or the one in whose favor the prohibition was made takes the goods immediately, without waiting for the death of the person burdened by the crime. Farinaccius also accumulates infinite examples in Book 1, Question 25, Number 35 and following, where he explains when only alienation <note>selling or transferring property</note> is prohibited, and when there is a **trust** <note>original: "fideicommissum"; a legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of another</note> with an express prohibition, so that in either case, confiscation is prevented. There, Surdus also responds vigorously to opposing arguments.

Seventhly, it is no less important to observe how the **Duchy of E.** <note>Likely referring to a specific territory being used as a case study, possibly the Duchy of Engern or similar</note> is held as a fief from your **Imperial Majesty** and the Holy Roman Empire. Therefore, those estates held by various members of the nobility, or even those of higher standing, which are true fiefs of E., are to be considered **sub-fiefs** <note>original: "Afterlehen"; a fief held from a vassal rather than directly from the sovereign</note> of your Imperial Majesty. Thus, according to the well-known feudal laws, when such **sub-vassals** <note>original: "subvasalli"</note> commit a crime against your Imperial Majesty as the **Supreme Overlord**, all sub-fiefs are opened <note>reverted</note> solely to the **immediate Lord** of the fief. This is the case according to the Law which decides this very question in *Chapter 1, Paragraph 'illud,' on the prohibition of alienating fiefs, by Frederick*. There, **Emperor Frederick** <note>Frederick I Barbarossa, 12th-century Holy Roman Emperor</note> decreed: *We also command that if a Vassal has another Vassal under him, and the Vassal’s Vassal offends the Lord of his own Lord, he shall be deprived of his fief, and it shall revert to his own Lord from whom he held it.* Here, two points are proposed: first, that the Vassal is deprived of the fief when the sub-vassal offends the Overlord; second, it is decided that the fief reverts to his own Lord, that is, the immediate one.

And it should be noted that this text speaks generally about an offense against the **mediated Lord** <note>original: "Domini mediati"; the lord higher up the chain, such as the Emperor</note>, and does not distinguish whether the offense is worthy of confiscation of goods or not. Antonius Guetta proves this with many points in Consultation 6, Number 24. This author was not only a distinguished counselor to your Imperial Majesty’s most highly praised ancestors

<column-break/>

in the Tyrolean government at **Innsbruck**, but also provided legal counsel in matters affecting such most gracious lordships.

The reasons for Emperor Frederick's decree are quite evident. 
(1) Because, strictly speaking, a sub-vassal is not the Vassal of the mediated Lord, but of the **immediate Lord** <note>original: "immediati"</note>. Therefore, although he has committed a crime against the mediated Lord, since he is not bound to him by a Vassal’s obligation, the fief which he loses for the crime is returned—by the best of logic—not to the Overlord, but to the immediate Lord from whom the sub-vassal received and acknowledged it. This is supported by Chapter 1, Paragraph 'finally,' which was the first cause, and Chapter 1, Verse 'but when': *Whether he, who killed the brother of the Lord.*

(2) Otherwise, if the sub-fief were to revolve back to the superior Lord, it would be within the sub-vassal’s power to commit a crime against the superior Lord specifically to take the sub-fief away from the immediate Lord and make his condition worse. In such a case, a grave prejudice would be inflicted upon the lower Lord of the fief, whether the superior Lord wanted to keep the fief for himself or grant it anew to someone else who might not be as pleasing to the immediate Lord. However, the crime of one person ought not to result in the detriment or prejudice of another, nor should anyone be burdened by the hatred felt toward another, as stated in the rule *It ought not* in the *Rules of Law* in the Sixth Book.

(3) Because although the offended superior Lord does not obtain the fief, he still has sufficient vengeance for the injury in that the fief is taken away from the delinquent sub-vassal and applied to the immediate Lord, as noted by Natta in Consultation 119 and Sonsbec on Fiefs, Part 13. The vengeance belonging to the Lord ought to work in such a way that the mediated Lord, who is innocent, is not burdened in any way or suffers a loss of his rights because of another's crime.

Therefore, lest it happen that of two Vassals—one of whom (the sub-vassal) committed a crime, while the other (the first Vassal, who granted the sub-fief) behaved faithfully—both are deprived of the fief, as both would be if the fief were confiscated by the state, it must be said that the fief itself is not to be confiscated. Instead, it is to be transferred to the first Vassal. Jacobus de Belloviso gave primary weight to this very reason, as cited by Baldus in Chapter 1 of the decree by Frederick, where he says: *By this, the true determination is seen, that he who offends the Lord of his Lord is said to offend his own Lord.* And later he adds: *The determination is true; because a Vassal cannot make the condition of his Lord worse: for the felony of the second Vassal against the first Lord cannot harm his own second Lord.*

The more remote Lord, against whom the crime was committed, is therefore satisfied for the injury done to him and the losses suffered by the confiscation of the **allodial lands** <term>Allodial lands: land owned absolutely by an individual, not held as a fief from a superior lord</term> and by the punishment or outlawing of the person of the delinquent himself.

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the rights of lords and vassals, specifically focusing on the legal effects of sub-infeudation—when a vassal grants part of their fief to a lower-tier vassal—and whether the state treasury has a right to seize such lands upon the commission of a crime.</meta>

# Letter C.

<note>Citations to legal authorities: Sonsbec. part. 13. num. 40. & seq. Rosenthal. cap. 11. concl. 18. num. 3. vers. sed si delictum. Guetta cons. 70. n. 22. & seq.</note>

Nor can it be said that a **Vassal**—for instance, a Duke, a Count, or another **State of the Empire**—who grants a portion of his feudal Duchy or territory to a Noble as a **sub-fief** <note>original: "subfeudum"; a fief granted by a vassal to a lower-tier tenant</note>, has transferred all of his **beneficial ownership** <term>beneficial ownership: original "utile dominium"; the right to use and profit from the land, as opposed to "direct ownership" held by the superior lord</term> through this act of sub-infeudation. This is because the transferred right is considered an "inferior" beneficial right, and there remains another "superior" beneficial right beneath it, as Baldus states in *chapter "ceterum" regarding judgments*. This is followed by Alvarottus, who notes that the primary Vassal, even after sub-infeudating, retains rights to services, loyalty, and other matters usually included in the contract. For by reason of these rights, the one who sub-infeudates can rightly be called "Lord." Jacobus de Sancto Georgio weighs this same consideration, asking whether anything remains with the first Vassal who sub-infeudates. He notes that while it might seem nothing remains because he transferred the beneficial interest he held from the Lord, he concludes the opposite: a certain "quasi-beneficial ownership" remains with the Vassal by reason of the **Law of Vassalage** which he holds over the sub-vassal to whom he granted the land.

Therefore, although the first Vassal appears to have transferred the beneficial ownership to the second, because "remnants" remain—and services are owed to him by the second, and the first Vassal is himself the "Lord" in relation to the second—and since recognition and loyalty are equally owed to him, the rights of the one who sub-infeudates are not entirely swallowed up. Consequently, by reason of those remaining rights, the fief is applied to the sub-infeudating lord himself <note>i.e., it reverts to him</note>, and not to the **State Treasury** <note>original: "Fisco"</note> of the Superior Lord.

The writings of Andreas de Isernia and Afflictus support this, stating that it does not matter if the first Vassal is thought to have reserved no ownership when infeudating another. For the "beneficial ownership" remains with the sub-infeudator, while the "exercise of the beneficial interest" is transferred to the second vassal, so that the latter holds a "subordinate beneficial ownership." Afflictus adds that the law expressly states a fief is applied to the sub-infeudating lord because of a fault, and it is "hard to kick against that text." Furthermore, Afflictus teaches that those who say a fief opens to the immediate Lord (not the remote one) are speaking of a transfer by sale with the Lord’s consent; it is different in the case of a crime, when the first Lord is offended by the crime rather than a contract. In that case, the fief is applied to the second Lord, a point which the Feudalists commonly agree cannot be answered without divine inspiration.

<column-break/>

If, therefore, a superior beneficial ownership remained with the first Vassal, then when the fief is applied to the immediate Lord, the beneficial interest is not separated from its cause but is joined to it. It is more fitting that it be joined to the **proximate cause** <note>the immediate lord</note> rather than the **remote cause** <note>the sovereign or high lord</note>, since the proximate cause also holds a superior beneficial interest and only transferred a subordinate one, which can be more easily rejoined to the closer interest. To produce a practical effect, the proximate and immediate cause has more influence than the remote one, as Baldus declares.

Hermann Vultejus approves of this same opinion and strengthens it with many reasons, as do Andreas Kohl, Rosenthal, and Schrader. Hartmann Pistoris testifies that the legal authorities in Leipzig followed this opinion in cases of a fief being alienated without the Lord's consent. Antonius Guetta also defends it extensively as the true and most common view, resolving all arguments that can be brought to the contrary.

<note>The following paragraph is in German</note>
Just as, finally, the opinion of those legal scholars cannot stand who hold that when a Vassal commits the **crime of treason** <note>original: "crimen læsæ Majestatis"</note>, his feudal right—or the beneficial justice due to him from the fief—should be sold to another suitable person of the same condition, and the purchase price should be delivered to the person against whom he committed the offense.

<note>Returning to Latin</note>
For a fief is not confiscated merely in terms of its ownership, but neither is it confiscated in terms of its utility and **usufruct** <term>usufruct: the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property belonging to another</term> during the life of the delinquent vassal. This is taught by Alexander, following Romanus and Imola, who responds that the fruits of a fief belong to the person to whom the fief itself belongs.

And although some disagree and think a Vassal can alienate the utility and usufruct to the treasury for the duration of his life by committing a crime, Farinaccius warns that one should not depart from the superior opinion established above. He notes that after Bossius, this is the common view and is observed in practice. Rosenthal agrees, as does Hartmann Pistoris, all of whom conclude with one voice: when a Vassal’s goods are made public due to a crime, the fief by no means passes to the state treasury, but rather—according to the rules of feudal law discussed thus far—passes to either the **agnate** <note>a relative through the male line</note> or to the Lord, even while the offender is still alive. Nothing else should be said on this part regarding the text of the **Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance** <note>original: "Ordin. Cameral."</note>, where it is held that those who are banned...

<summary>This page argues that in feudal law, if a sub-vassal loses their land due to a crime, the land should revert to their immediate lord (the vassal who granted it) rather than the state treasury, because the immediate lord retains a "superior" beneficial interest. It also asserts that even in cases of treason, the state treasury cannot seize the lifelong profits of a fief away from the rightful feudal heirs or lords.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument concerning the rights of a Lord versus the State Treasury (Fisc) when a Vassal commits a crime. It specifically addresses whether the profits of a fief can be seized by the treasury or if they must revert to the family or the superior Lord.</meta>

...the feudal profits <note>original: "fructus feudales"; the income or produce derived from a feudal estate</note> should be granted to the plaintiff who suffered the loss for the duration of the offender's life, as Rosenthal proves in chapter 11, conclusion 11, number 16 and following. This is supported by the writings of Gail on public peace, chapter 15, number 3 and following, from which it is clear that this occurs because Feudal Law is not considered entirely extinguished due to a ban <note>referring to the "Imperial Ban," a form of outlawry</note>, but is merely held as suspended.

And thus, although offenders may have a certain right to the use and profits of property subject to restitution, that right is not formal but causal, and is joined to the ownership, according to the law *ex diverso*, paragraph 1, in the Digest *on the recovery of property*. See also Peregrinus on the Law of the Treasury, title *on the publication of goods*, book 5, number 99. Therefore, since the offenders lose this ownership, it cannot pass to the treasury; for the ownership of these things devolves immediately upon the death of the possessor to the agnates <term>agnates: male-line relatives who have a right to inherit a fief</term> or respectively to the Lord. Since the right itself cannot reach the Treasury, neither do the profits, as they were not separated from the ownership itself; instead, the profits follow the ownership and are consolidated with it, as Peregrinus rightly notes in the cited title at number 102. Indeed, in fiefs, the beneficial ownership <note>original: "utile dominium"</note> held by the offending Vassal cannot remain in suspense, nor can the profits be separated from it. From this it follows not only that fiefs cannot be surrendered to the Treasury due to a crime (unless they are transferable to outside heirs), but also that, upon the crime of a Vassal and the "opening" of the fief, the beneficial ownership immediately devolves—along with the profits joined to it—either to the Lord or to the Agnates.

Nor is it an obstacle what some say: that a trust <term>fideicommissum: a legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of another, often used to keep estates within a family</term> left in the event of death is understood as natural death, and that in the meantime, goods subject to restitution pass to the treasury with the burden of restoring them after death. For a pure and simple trust, where the goods are prohibited from being sold—which is very similar to a fief—does not fall under the confiscation of goods, even during the life of the person prohibited from selling, as Bartolus holds in the law *Imperator*, number 1, regarding the freedom of trusts. This is commonly followed by the Doctors of Law, as Socinus Junior says in Council 77, number 15, book 2. This opinion is also approved by Rubeus and Cotta. It is supported by the law *ex facto*, paragraph *si quis rogatus*, where if a person burdened with a trust dies without children or is condemned to the mines <note>original: "condemnetur in metallum"; a severe Roman punishment involving forced labor in mines, often equivalent to a death sentence</note>, the trust immediately takes effect without waiting for natural death. Julius Clarus teaches the same regarding anyone condemned to death. Furthermore, following the capital condemnation of the burdened heir, the trust is said to be "purified," and the substitute is immediately admitted to the estate. That a trust is immediately transferred to the next in line when goods are made public due to a crime, even regarding the beneficial ownership, is proved by

<column-break/>

the law *Jure libertorum*, 4, on the Law of Patronage, and Rosenthal in the frequently cited chapter 11, conclusion 9.

Even if it were granted that the profits of a trust could reach the treasury, one could not argue from that to a fief; for a Vassal has less right in a feudal matter than a fiduciary heir <note>the person entrusted with a trust estate</note> does, as Rosenthal observed.

->**[The following is an appeal to the Emperor]**<-

Since the matters mentioned above are so established in law, Most Gracious Emperor and Lord, your Imperial Majesty’s appropriate supreme power and the accompanying power of confiscation in the crime of Majesty <term>crimine Majestatis: high treason against the sovereign or state</term> is not at all contested by me. Rather, my sole intention is that my princely wards <note>children or minors under the author's legal protection</note> be maintained in that which has always belonged to them and their ancestors. They should not be displaced by the crime of another, nor should other Vassals be forced upon them other than those they are bound to recognize by virtue of the ancient feudal investitures. Primarily, however, I trust in Your Imperial Majesty’s most Christian and highly praised spirit—that You would not burden anyone beyond what is proper, but rather, even in cases where Your Imperial Majesty might have more right according to the strict law, You are accustomed to place Your innate mildness and Imperial Clemency before such severity.

Accordingly, I do humbly petition Your Imperial Majesty to most graciously moderate the aforementioned confiscations (should Your Imperial Majesty be minded to continue them). May You command Your commissioners that such execution be carried out without damage to my wards' ducal feudal estates and their appurtenances, and that these be placed in my hands as Administrator. In return, I make the most obedient offer: that I, as Feudal Lord, according to the statutes of the Empire, shall allow none of the income from said feudal estates to reach the criminals for as long as they live or remain in Your Imperial Majesty’s disfavor. Instead, from that which remains annually after necessary provision and maintenance, I shall ensure that those who have legitimate legal claims and demands receive their due. I shall always be diligent to repay such grace to Your Imperial Majesty with most humble obedience, etc.

### 56. Concordats of the German Nation.

Various wars arose from time to time between the Popes and the Roman Emperors, which were primarily moved by the occasion of the election of Bishops. To prevent these from arising further, Emperor Frederick III, through his singular wisdom, provided a remedy by procuring a settlement with Pope Nicholas V in the year of Christ 1447, on the Kalends of April <note>April 1st</note>. This is commonly called the Concordats of the German Nation <term>Concordata: a formal agreement or treaty between the Holy See and a secular government regarding church affairs</term>. On this subject, see Tholosanus *on Ecclesiastical Benefices, chapter 1, number 8, etc., and 24, number 20; the Commentary of Georg Brandenburg on the Concordats; and Simonetta on the reservation of benefices, question 1.*

There are indeed various editions of these concordats; see the *Canonical Trismegistus* by Wolfgang Sigismund von Vorburg, *folio 498.* By virtue of these Concordats, the Emperor ought not to grant secular fiefs to those ecclesiastical persons who have not obtained Papal confirmation.
<margin>Christinæus notes, however, in volume 1, decision 357, number 13, etc., that many churches in Germany did not accept these concordats, but instead boast of broader privileges.</margin>

### 57. Confrontation.

A judge can confront witnesses, as well as accomplices in a crime <note>original: "Socios Criminis"</note>. In such cases, those witnesses should not be brought forward several at a time, but each one individually, face-to-face with the accused himself. Once they have taken an oath of truth in his presence, and the identification of the person has been made, they shall, to the face of the aforementioned accused,

<column-break/>

ratify and confirm all those things which they otherwise deposed. This confirmation is usually done for the purpose of avoiding the repetition of witness testimony and to validate their words and depositions, according to Clarus *in the final section, question 45, number 14.* For witnesses examined solely for the judge's information, without the other party being summoned, prove nothing and provide no evidence unless they are later repeated after the party has been summoned. This confrontation takes the place of that summons and repetition; for confrontation does nothing other than supply a defect in the proof, according to Matthaeus Stephanus *on the Office of the Judge, book 9, chapter 8.* He advises the judge that whenever he can have the witnesses present, he should confront them with the accused rather than arranging for them to be re-examined in his absence. This is because, beyond the fact that such a confrontation presses the accused more heavily, it also greatly opens the mind of the judge, whether by the bold denial and rejection of the matter or the constant assertion of the witness, according to the legal maxim: "You are able to know more" <note>original: "Tu magis scire potes"; a reference to the judge's ability to discern truth by observing demeanor</note>, *law 1, paragraph "and therefore the Divine," in the Digest on witnesses.*

However, a judge will not always allow confrontation. For example, a servant should not be confronted with his Master, a son with his father, or vice versa; nor a timid person with a powerful one, and similar cases. This is because such people find it difficult to dare confirm their word to the faces of those mentioned, at least not without some hesitation.

Similarly, the Judge can confront accomplices with the accused; but since accomplices are unfit to provide testimony due to their complicity (which diminishes their credibility), a simple confrontation done plainly is not enough. Instead, a greater solemnity must be used in the confrontation of accomplices; namely, that they should be tortured in the presence of the examined accused, and thus confirm and ratify their statement under torture, making it valid against the accused. *Stephanus, in the cited treatise and chapter.* This occurs in the confrontation of parties so that they tell each other the truth directly <note>original German: "Geschicht also in Confrontatione partium, daß sie einander selbst die Wahrheit sagen"</note>.

Zanger teaches that confrontation should not be undertaken lightly in his *treatise on torture, chapter 2, number 47 and following.* Julius Clarus also teaches this *in the final section, question 45, number 14*, as does Damhouder *in Criminal Practice, chapter 47, number 1 and following.* Confrontation should not happen unless the truth cannot be brought to light in any other way, and furthermore, when suspicion militates for one side and against the other; only then should it be undertaken with a prior oath <note>original German: "Daß die Confrontation nicht eher geschehen soll, es seye dann, daß die Wahrheit anderer Gestalt nicht mög an Tag gebracht werden, und darzu Vermutung für einen, und wider den andern Theil militiren, und alsdann erst medio & prævio Juramento solche vorgenommen werde"</note>.

Likewise, one cannot, without great cause, confront a person with those who have accused them of witchcraft <note>original German: "so von Unholden angegeben"; "Unholden" here refers to witches or sorcerers</note>. Meanwhile, it is also established that a judge sometimes undertakes a confrontation by virtue of his office, especially in matrimonial cases, where the parties are heard against each other when they stand in contradiction, because these matters are usually done in secret, especially if sexual intercourse is involved, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

It is believed that witnesses worthy of trust should be credited even without a confrontation <note>original: "fine [sine] confrontatione"</note>, according to Lord Tabor in his work *On Confrontation*, page 10. A confrontation is usually decreed as the situation arises or as a second step, before proceeding to the torture <term>tortura: the use of physical pain to elicit a confession from a defendant who denies the charges</term> of a defendant who denies the accusation. Lord Tabor, page 86. A confession elicited through confrontation is seen to have greater force than one given voluntarily. *Legal Collection of Strasbourg on Interrogations in Law*, thesis 22. The confrontation of the defendant with witnesses achieves more than if the witnesses had simply been examined with the party summoned. Matthaeus de Afflictis in *Constitutions of the Kingdom*, book 1, under the section on secret homicide, number 36. Antonio Scappus, book 5, *On Unwritten Law*, chapter 114, number 8, where he further infers and concludes: A defendant is not to be released until he has been confronted with the witnesses, page 106. The learned doctors of law doubt whether a confrontation also makes up for a defect in the written interrogatories; see Lord Tabor’s very extensive treatment of this matter in his treatise *On Confrontation*, page 92. Confrontation alone brings infamy <note>original: "infamiam"; a legal loss of status or reputation</note> with it. Lord Tabor, in the same treatise, page 25.

<margin>Lord Doctor Tabor, *On Confrontation*, page 46.</margin>
Why a confrontation between a witness and a defendant should not be done lightly; in such a meeting, the fear of subornation <note>original: "subornationis"; the act of bribing or inducing someone to give false testimony</note> must be removed. Justus Oldekop in *Criminal Observations*, folio 237, numbers 1 and 2.

<margin>Lord Doctor Tabor in his most elegant treatise *On Confrontation*, page 6, part 1, section 8.</margin>
Many things regarding this matter are to be seen in Scaccia's *On Judgments*, book 1, chapter 86, number 53 and following, and chapter 82, numbers 19 and 26. The word "confrontation" is more accepted by common usage than it is of Latin origin; it is as if you were to say "from face to face" <note>original: "de fronte ad frontem"</note>, a **counter-positioning** or **bringing-together** <note>original: "Gegen- vel Zusammenstellung"</note>. See Wehner’s *Supplement*, page 18.

### 58. Consistory.

A Consistory <note>original: "Consistorium"</note> is a place in which a Prince admits and hears ambassadors and whoever else approaches, and takes notice of legal causes, with the "Consistorians" inquiring into the business and looking into it, as Ammianus Marcellinus says in several places. Thus, among the People of God, there was a supreme Consistory, Council, or Judgment, which was called the *Sanhedrim* <note>original: Hebrew "Sanhedrin"</note> or *synedrion* <note>original: Greek "συνέδριον", meaning "sitting together"</note>; it consisted of 72 Judges, whom he called the 70 Elders. Exodus 24, verse 1; Numbers 11, verse 25. See *Exotic Words of the New Testament*. Cothman in his commentary on the *Code*, number 3. In our law books, it is sometimes called an *Auditorium* <note>a place of hearing</note>, as in *Novel* 23, chapter 1, etc., and the chapter *Romana* under the title *on appeals* in the *Sixth Book of Decretals*. It is likewise called the *Auditorium of the Rota* <note>The Roman Rota, the highest ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church</note>, in which cases are heard, examined, and decided. Sometimes it is called a Chamber <note>original: "Camera"</note>, such as the Imperial Chamber <note>original: "Camera Imperialis"</note>, which is at Speyer.

Today, Consistories is the name given to the Ecclesiastical Courts of almost any judges, in which cases that are purely spiritual and ecclesiastical, or of "mixed jurisdiction"—for instance, matrimonial cases—are handled. Cothman, in the cited place, number 33.

->ADDITION.<-

Our ancestors learned by experience that disputes and cases regarding marriage are frequent and difficult to judge; therefore, they established peculiar courts and hearing rooms to settle them, which 

<column-break/>

are commonly called Consistories. See more in Cypraeus, *On Betrothals*, in the preface, number 13.

### 59. Possessory Agreement.

Regarding a possessory agreement <note>original: "Constituto possessorio"</note>, where one acknowledges that he wishes to possess the purchased or pledged property in the name of the buyer or the creditor <note>original German: "da einer bekennt, er wolle das erkaufte oder verpfändte Gut, nomine emptoris vel creditoris besitzen"</note>. See the individual treatise by Bartholus Romuleus.

->ADDITION.<-

The "Constitutum Clause" transfers all possession and ownership to the person in whose favor it is made <note>original: "constitutarium"</note>. Klock, volume 2, consultation 21, number 1. Possession that has been occupied by another is never transferred through a possessory agreement or other fictional acts. Consultation 21, number 21. Whether one who establishes that he will pay for another enjoys the privilege of discussion <term>privilegio excussionis: the right of a guarantor to demand that the creditor first seek payment from the primary debtor's assets</term>. Consultation 80, numbers 6, 7, and 8.

A possessory agreement is a fictional method of delivery <note>original: "fictus tradendi modus"</note> by which someone who has, for example, sold or donated a thing to another, establishes simply and with bare words that he possesses it in that person’s name, and by this very agreement transfers possession to them. Lord Cobius wrote a most accurate inaugural disputation on this matter in the year 1637 at Altdorf. There also exists a most learned individual treatise on this matter by Andreas Tiraquellus. Add Rittershausen in *The Novels*, page 150. Question: Is the effect of such an agreement extended even to future goods? Tiraquellus and Vitalis de Cambanis affirm this, against Antonio Fabri, in the treatise *On Clauses*.

<margin>Guy Pape. Lord Speidel deals extensively with the possessory agreement in his *Notables*, folio 233.</margin>
Question: Can a Lord seek "laudemia" <term>laudemia: a fee paid by a tenant to a lord upon the transfer of property</term> by virtue of such an agreement before the buyer receives actual physical possession from him? They affirm this against Guy Pape.

It is called a possessory agreement when someone possesses the purchased or pledged property in the name of the buyer or creditor. Law *quod meo*, beginning, in the *Digest* under the title *on acquiring possession*. However, for possession to be transferred through such an agreement, it is required: 1. that the person making the agreement actually has such possession; 2. that the will and intention of the person in whose name the other establishes he is possessing must intervene. Wehner’s *Supplement*, page 8.

### 60. Contract. Contractus.

"Contract" is understood sometimes in a general sense, and sometimes in a specific sense. In the first way, it includes every agreement and whatever is settled between those acting <note>original: "l. 1. §. conventio. ff. de pact."</note>. And it corresponds with the German word **Action/Transaction** <note>original: "Handlung"</note>. In the second way, taking "contract" in a specific sense, it involves a mutual obligation <note>original: "ultrò citróque obligationem"</note>: such as buying and selling, leasing and hiring, or partnership. Law *Labeo*, paragraph *contractum*, in the *Digest* under the title *on the meaning of words*.

A contract <note>original: "Contractus"</note> is so called as if it were a "counter-act" <note>original: "contra seu vicissim actus"</note>, just as "to contract" <note>original: "contrahere"</note> implies to draw together mutually or in turn, descending from a Greek verb. And a contract is properly said to be made when an obligation arises on both sides of the contracting parties, as in the examples placed in the text of the law *Labeo*, paragraph *contractum*; and it is so in a sale. Law *ex consensu*, in the *Digest* under the title *on actions and obligations*. For the buyer is obligated...

...obliged to pay the price to the seller, and the seller is obliged to deliver the thing to the buyer. <note>original: "l. ex empto. in pr. ff. de act. empt."; referring to the Digest of Justinian, Book 19, Title 1</note> For this reason, according to Alciatus in his commentary on the law titled *Labeo*, a contract is so called as if it were a "drawing together" <note>original: "vicissim & mutuò trahere"</note> reciprocally and mutually; or otherwise, as an act done "against" or "in return" for another.

**Improperly**, a Contract occurs when only one party is obligated, as happens in a gift or a formal promise <term>stipulatio: a verbal contract in Roman law consisting of a formal question and answer</term>.

**Most improperly**, it is used when no obligation arises from either side, as in a "naked pact" <term>nudo pacto: an agreement that is not legally binding because it lacks formal requirements</term> made during a settlement, or one made under a condition, as noted by Bartolus and others regarding the Code on settlements.

What falls under the name of a "Contract"? See Mozzius, *On Contracts*, article 6. He argues under number 3 that the term "contract" does not include a "distract" <note>original: "distractum"; the dissolution or undoing of a contract</note>; according to the teachings of Baldus on the final law of the Code, where the text says "to those dissolving and those contracting" <note>original: "distrahentibus & contrahentibus"</note>, thus placing them as different things. This distinction applies more strictly in statutes where words are to be understood in their proper, narrow sense.

But sometimes the name of Contract also includes the dissolution. In the law regarding deserted fields, he who does not pay "contracts," and without doubt, "Contract" is accepted here in a general and broad sense to include even the dissolution of the deal. This is according to the law on every obligation <note>original: "l. omnem obligationem"</note> in the Digest on Judgments; Jason in his commentary on the Institutes; Tiraquell in his treatise on marriage laws; and Petrus Rebuffus.

Thus, a person prohibited from contracting will not be able to release anyone from a debt, because a release of debt is considered a gift <note>original: "donatio"</note>. This is found in the Digest under the section on pacts and gifts, and supported by the legal decisions of Afflictis.

### ADDITION.

A new quality added to a Contract creates a new Contract. Klock, volume 2, consultation 42. How this is to be understood can be seen in number 192. When a contract involves "enormous injury" <term>læsione enormissima: a legal concept where a contract is so unfair—usually involving a price less than half the value—that it is presumed fraudulent</term>, it is presumed to have been made because of fear or some other form of deceit. Klock, volume 2, consultation 34.

A contract is considered new when something is added or taken away. Klock, volume 2, consultation 53. One demands the fulfillment <note>original: "implementum"</note> of a contract from an opponent in vain if they themselves have not satisfied every part of the same agreement. Klock, consultation 39. A contract is not rescinded simply because fulfillment did not follow; rather, one must sue for the observance and fulfillment of the contract or for damages <note>original: "interesse"</note>. Consultation 62. A simulated <note>pretended or fake</note> contract has no substance and is not truly a contract; it is not even made valid by an oath, but is null by the law itself. This is argued against in number 92. A promise to keep a contract pleasing and ratified implies a renunciation of the right to rescind it. Klock, volume 2, consultation 69.

In contracts, the intent <note>original: "mens"</note> of the contracting parties is to be considered rather than their mere words. Knip-
<margin>Besold, Volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

schild, *On Trusts*, chapter 3. Whether trusts <term>fideicommissa: property held by one person for the benefit of another, often established in a will</term> are established more firmly through a contract or through a last will. From contracts, a valid argument can be drawn regarding last wills. On contracts and agreements, see Barbosa, book 3. On the contracts of Monks, see Ritthersh in the *Novels*. On simulated contracts, see Bartholomæus Cæpolla of Verona. On census contracts <note>original: "Censuariis Contractibus"; contracts involving annual payments or ground rents</note>, see Petrus Follerus of Naples. On sworn contracts, see Johannes Guterius.

## 61. Converts.

Those who are called "offered" <note>original: "oblati"</note> to a monastery differ from "converts" <note>original: "Conversis"</note>. The "offered" are those who, without changing their secular clothing, dedicate themselves and their possessions to the monastery. "Converts," however, are those who have changed their clothing, professed their religion, and do not differ from monks except that they are not members of the clergy. See the Fabrian Code and Boerius, Decision 20, where it is added that sometimes a person offers their goods without themselves, sometimes themselves without their goods, and sometimes both themselves and their goods.

## 62. Cuckold. <note>original: "Cornut. Cornutus."</note>

A "horned man" <note>cuckold</note>, according to Johannes Parladorius in *Daily Matters*, book 1, is said to be "naked of heart" <note>original: "corde nudus"</note> who suffers such a disgrace. For as Solomon says in Proverbs, chapter 18: "He who expels a good woman expels a good thing; but he who keeps an adulteress is a fool and senseless."

Indeed, he who calls another man "horned" can be sued in an action for injuries <note>original: "actione injuriarum"; a lawsuit for defamation or insult</note>, and he is bound to provide a formal retraction or "Palinode" to the plaintiff.

The same applies if he calls him a "Cuckoo" <note>original: "Cuculum"</note> or a "Warbler" <note>original: "Currucam"</note> (which is the same as if he had named him "horned"). Such a man is more correctly called a "Warbler." Regarding the cuckoo and the warbler, Aristotle writes in book 6 of *On Animals*, chapter 7: "No one says they have seen the chicks of a cuckoo; yet it lays eggs, but not in a nest it made itself. Instead, it lays them in the nests of smaller birds and eats the eggs it finds there. It especially seeks the nests of wood-pigeons, eating their eggs and leaving its own. The Warbler, in whose nest it lays, then warms and hatches them."

From these words, it is clear that the name "Cuckoo" fits the adulterer, while "Warbler" fits the suffering or "horned" man (as they call him).

The Warbler is a bird not unlike the one commonly called a "Coruxa" <note>likely a screech owl or similar tufted bird</note> in the vernacular, not much different from the Latin word. It is accustomed to raise certain little "horns" of feathers on the back of its head, and from this, the insult "horned" seems more truly to have drawn its origin, according to Parladorius. He says in the following sections that it also pertains to this type of insult if someone, for the sake of insulting, calls a man "a good man" <note>original: "un bon homme"</note> in French; for by that name...

### 66. Letters of Credence. *Literæ Credentiales.*

It is a common saying that one should not believe the messengers or embassies of the Pope or the Emperor without their letters, however much they may otherwise be deemed credible. <note>original: "ut retulit gloss. Landr. lib. 3. art. 63."</note> This is according to the law "If anyone" in the Code on the mandates of princes <note>original: "l. si quis. C. de mand. princip."</note>. However, because a Cardinal does not usually leave the Curia without a legally made commission or delegation, he is therefore believed when he asserts that he is a Legate. Augustinus Barbosa on the law "If anyone" in the Code on the mandates of princes, number 5 and following. Also Speculator under the title "On Legates," section "It remains," verse "What if delegates," whom Joannes Andreas followed in chapter 1 "On the office of the legate" in the *Sext*, and as reported by Antonius de Butrio. Bartolus does not disagree in the law "If for my sake" in the Digest.

Moreover, Letters of Credence <note>original: "lettres de creance, Creditiv-Schreiben"</note> are those which are carried by the person who is said in the letters to be trusted, addressed to the person to whom they are sent. Hippolytus Riminaldus, *Counsel* 9, number 16 in volume 1. See also Vitalis de Cambanis in the treatise on clauses, under the title "enunciative words in epistles." These types of letters were devised for various reasons, and especially so that we might more correctly explain our mind; for it has been found by experience that it is not at all expedient to always commit secrets to writing. For it is possible that either the common people might understand them, or the letters themselves might be intercepted, stolen, or lost. # 67. Cross. <note>original: "Creuß. Crux."</note>

The Cross is also a sign of Judgment. Indeed, a pole or a wooden Cross, if no other mark was present, was erected there, at which the Judge and the Jurors <note>original: "Scabini"; lay judges or assessors in Germanic law</note> were compelled to swear to distribute justice equally.

And certainly, here also something is granted to Religion, in memory of the Cross of Christ. Because of this, that sign was formerly prefixed to legal instruments and diplomas, not only by the Romans, *law 22, paragraph 2, Code on the right of deliberation; Faber, book 3, semester 1, at the end; Novel of Leo 72,* but by the German Emperors themselves. The author of the *Itinerary of Saint Willibald* <note>original: "Hodœporici S. Wilibaldi"</note>, *volume 4, Canon 5*, says: "Thus is the custom of the Saxon people, that on some of the estates of Nobles and good men, they are accustomed to have not a Church, but the sign of the holy Cross dedicated to the Lord, erected on high, for the convenient diligence of daily prayer." Furthermore, it was also used because people had there either suffered punishment or fallen in a duel. Even now, not only in cemeteries but also in those fields where a man was killed, a wooden or stone cross is erected. And it is possible that the Cross, erected for another purpose, also served the use of a sign or a mal-

<column-break/>

-let of Judgment. Such are the crosses that show the way, the "Way-pointers" <note>original: "Wegweiser"</note>. *Thus Robert the Monk, book 2 of the History of Jerusalem, at the beginning: On pilgrimages to the Holy Sepulcher of the Lord,* says that they placed wooden Crosses at the turns of the roads as a testimony, so that it would be known to all that the path was for pilgrims. And specifically in Cities, it was customary for a Cross to be erected, as the author of the *Weichbild* <note>original: "Weichbildi"; referring to the municipal law or jurisdictional area of a German city</note> reports in *article 7*, namely as a sign of Judgment and Jurisdiction. Regarding this, one reads in the ancient vocabulary under the word *Weichbild*: **And it was indicated in ancient times that a large wooden cross was erected in a city or town, on which a hand or sword was placed, as a sign of judgment over neck and hand.** <note>The sword symbolized capital punishment ("neck") and the hand symbolized physical punishment or the power to enforce the law ("hand").</note> *Lord Johann Griphiander in the treatise On Saxon Municipal Law, chapter 66, number 13 and following.*

It is also read in the text of the *gloss on article 7, paragraph 2, and article 9 of the Weichbild*: This is observed even now, where marketplaces and Cities are newly founded, that a cross is fixed as a testimony of Peace, and so that municipal peace may be perceived there; and the Emperor's sign is appended, so that it appears to have been done by his will. *In the same article,* where the Law given to Cities is discussed: **Whereupon the Peace of St. Peter was enacted and given with a cross,** where the gloss says: **by the cross is to be understood the Peace of God for the sake of St. Peter... for to those same places shall belong both spiritual and worldly judgment from the Emperor (that is to be understood by the glove), the spiritual judgment by the cross, and by these two signs is to be understood that there is public law, market privilege, and true peace.** *Lord Griphiander in the said treatise, chapter 76; Georg Rittershusius, On the Law of Asylums, page 47.*

On the subject of the Holy Cross, indeed, *Gretserus* has completed a distinguished work. *See also the notes of Logotheta, page 70 and following; the Questions of Athanasius, page 15 and following; the works of Saint Paulinus, page 711 and following; Heribert Rosweyde, page 86, on the law of Retaliation; the Vindications of Capella, page 48, etc.; Marquardus de Susanis, in the treatise On the Jews, page 38 and following; on the etymology of "Crux" [Cross], Becman in Origins; on the name of the Cross, Nicolaus Fuller, 4 Miscellaneous, chapter 14; on the nails of the Cross, the individual treatise of Curtius; on the form of the cross, Molanus, On Images, book 2, chapter 7 and book 3, chapter 17; on the wood and the diversity of the Wood of the Cross, Pflaumern, page 238; the notes of Logotheta, page 70, etc.; Rinthelin in The Roman Catholic Jurist, chapter 91; on the miracles of the Cross, Osorius, book 4, page 113 and following; Pontanus in his polemics, volume 3, page 93; Fulstin, History of Poland, book 11, chapter 1, where he deals especially with the miracle of the Wood.* That the Cross puts to flight evil spells can be seen in the *Formicarium* of Nider, page 357; and how in exorcisms it puts demons to flight, see the *Treatise on the Power of the Church over Demons* by Raphael de la Torre, page 93. On the Cross of the Good Thief, see the *Spanish Treatise on the Seven Words of Christ, chapter 19, page 244.* In ancient times, places were purified by the sign of the Cross...

...it is established from the final law of the *Theodosian Code* regarding pagans and there: Jacob Gothofredus <note>a prominent 17th-century jurist known for his commentary on the Theodosian Code</note> notes that renegades in Turkey, upon the confirmation of their apostasy, must step and spit three times upon the cross laid before them, as Leonhard Rauwolff <note>a German physician and botanist who traveled the Levant</note> attests in his *Travels in Turkey*, page 404.

Furthermore, regarding the specific title in the *Justinian Code* stating that no one is permitted to carve or paint the sign of our Savior on the ground, or in flint, or in marble: Paul Christinaeus <note>a Belgian legal authority</note> understands this in his *Belgian Decisions*, volume 2, page 53, to refer to the image of our Savior Christ and the Cross together.

But I wish to add, or at least for the sake of interest, a remarkable story related by Thomas of Cantimpré <note>a 13th-century Dominican monk and writer of encyclopedias and miracle stories</note>, who in book 1, chapter 25, page 193, writes thus: I saw with my own eyes a particularly remarkable and devout thing regarding Brother Volvandus, the Prior of the Order of Preachers in Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentina Civitate Teutoniæ"</note>. This man, as the Brothers testified to me with the most proven truth, almost always, whether walking, standing, or sitting, would trace the sign of the cross on his chest with his thumb. It happened that while coming to Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiam"</note>, he fell ill, and as the disease grew worse, he died with a wonderful alacrity of spirit and was buried there among the Friars Minor <note>the Franciscans</note>. (For the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note> did not yet have a house in that city.) Upon hearing this, the Dominican Friars of Strasbourg sent two brothers to Mainz for the body of their deceased Prior, but in vain, as the Franciscans refused to return the buried man. It happened, however, after a few years, when the Franciscans were moving to another location, the Strasbourg Dominicans again dispatched two brothers to Mainz for the body of said Prior. This time, they took up the bones without opposition and returned successfully to Strasbourg. What more? While the brothers were carefully washing the bones, they found the chest bone, to which the ribs are attached at the top on both sides, marked with a most elaborate Cross, serving as a sort of inner shield of the Heart. The cross (which I myself labored to travel forty miles to see, and saw with my own happy eyes) was in the middle of the bone, raised from the bony substance to a very evident thickness, with the three upper arms of equal length and the lower arm most fittingly longer; the ends of the three upper arms were curved back like a blooming lily, and the lower arm was hollowed out as if it were meant to be fixed into a trunk. What then was this sign of a physical Cross in the chest bone, if not the marks of Christ's passion previously held in the mind? And what is designated by the leaves of the blooming lily at the ends of the Cross, if not the badge of most pure chastity, which the body carried firmly fixed in the flesh along with the memory of Christ? Thus far Cantimpré. See also Korman *On the Miracles of the Dead*, book 2 and book 5. On why the Cross is on the Imperial Globe, see Meursius, *Mantissa*, chapter 8. On the punishment of the Cross, see Cardinal Baronius in his 

<column-break/>

*Annals* for the year of Christ 34, number 92. Also Talentoni, *On Hidden Matters*, book 2, chapter 9, where he gives the reason why our most holy Savior was put on the cross with thieves, and why he willed to be affected by such a shameful death; he also demonstrates that not only were thieves usually punished by this kind of death, but also the Carthaginian generals if they used poor judgment even if things succeeded according to their wishes, as well as those among the Hebrews who were to be struck with death for any fault. He shows at the same time that it was customary to break the legs of those crucified while still alive, and for that reason it was rightly said by the Evangelists that the legs of our Lord Savior were not broken, because he was already dead, but the legs of the thieves were, because they were still living; furthermore, all who were lifted onto the Cross were usually fixed to the Cross with nails, and for that reason those two thieves suffered the same; and finally, to the question of whether he who opened the side of the Lord with a spear was named Longinus, as is thought? See his answer, especially in chapter 23.

That the last letter of the Hebrews formerly had the shape of a Cross is taught by Majer in *Sacred Chaldaism*, page 93 and following; and that the sign *Tau* denoted death, see Lucian in *Judgment of the Vowels*, volume 1, near the end, page 83.

### 68. Cross-Sermons [Crusades].

It is well known from history that our ancestors established many great sacred expeditions, which are called <term>Crusades</term> <note>original: *Cruciatæ*</note>, against the Saracens and Heretics in previous centuries, with the highest praise and success. See *Miræus in the Belgian Fasti*, folio 422 and following, where he lists how many there were in order. See also *Reiner Reineccius, Oriental History, volume 1, at the end, folio 83.*

### 69. Critics.

On these, see *The Polymath* by Wouwer, and the *Aristarchus* of Heinsius, folio 3 and folio 206; also the introduction to Nonnus.

### ADDITION.

A "Critic" was once the name for a Doctor or Teacher. Hence, Cicero in his third book *On the Orator* named Isocrates a "singular Teacher." In the first book to Herennius, he said: "our teacher Hermes." More examples were collected by *Walther in On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 15. *Criticism*, when it contains itself within its own boundaries, is the very sun and salt of Literature.

> You boast of being the gainer <note>original Greek: *kerdō*</note> of my writings:
> To be a winner <note>original Greek: *kerdēs*</note> of these, be a craftsman <note>original Greek: *kerdikos*</note> first.
> You can be a craftsman <note>original Greek: *kerdikos*</note> if you have no gainful tool <note>original Greek: *kerdēïon*</note>:
> And lest this be lacking, first let a mind be yours.
<note>This Greek wordplay contrasts the Critic's desire for profit or "gain" with the "skill" required to actually understand a text.</note>

"We shall weed out some thorns with that *Critical* sickle." <note>original: *Lipsius, century 2, epistle 91*</note>. "Would that *Criticism* here did not become a game and an arena for beast-fighters—that is, would that in Philological matters they did not fight merely over useless words." <note>original: *Lipsius, single century, epistle 51*</note>.

### 70. Crowns, Crown-gold.

"Crown gold" <note>original: *Aurum coronarium*</note>.

In the coinage ordinance of Emperor Ferdinand I, as reported by Alemannus in legal consultation 8, question on principles 1, part 32, it is stated: Burgundian or Netherlandish, and French Sun-Crowns shall be taken for 93 kreuzers. Furthermore, all Spanish, Castilian, Valencian, Navarrese, Milanese, Sicilian, Genoese, and Papal crowns are valued at 91 kreuzers. *Tileman Friesen, Mirror of Coinage, book 4, chapter 32.*

And *Budelius, On Numismatics, book 1, chapter 18, number 15*, has the following: *Crowned coins* <note>original: *Coronati*</note> minted in France, if not worn down, clipped, or otherwise diminished in weight—because they weigh 71 moments—therefore one mark of them contains

<column-break/>

68 and a half; they are of twenty-two and a half carats.

The *Shield-coin* <note>original: *Scutatus*</note> or *Solar Crown* <note>original: *Coronatus solaris*</note> is derived not from the Sun, as Jean Bodin claims in his third book *On the Republic*, chapter 6, but from the *solidus* <note>a late Roman gold coin</note>; for the French, following the Romans, held the *solidus* as the standard for a gold coin. *Freher, On Numismatics, chapter 3.* They are called *Scuta* or *Escus* [shields] because of the coat of arms <note>original: *Scutum Insigniorum*</note> stamped upon them.

<term>Crown-gold</term> is what they call the gold from which golden crowns were made. See the single law in the Code *On Crown Gold*, about which *Wolfgang Lazius* writes more in *Commentary on the Roman Republic, book 2, chapter 13*. He errs in saying that crown-gold is a type of tribute, as *Caspar Antonius Thesaurus* notes in his *Treatise on the Appreciation of Money, from the beginning, number 17*.

### 71. Crypt. [Underground Vault].

The word "Grufft" [crypt/grave] is derived from *Crypta*. See *Aubert Miræus, Belgian Fasti, folio 407* and following, where he has many wonderful things to say about subterranean cemeteries and crypts, especially that of Saint Priscilla in Rome.

When dealing with ancient cemeteries in the Roman countryside, which received the bodies of saints in faithful hospitality during the first three centuries, one must not imagine anything similar to modern cemeteries, which lie adjacent to sacred buildings and are out in the open. At that time, temples were not everywhere in plain sight, nor would the continuous storm of persecutions that raged until Constantine the Great have permitted such places. Rather, they were subterranean retreats, like certain vast hollows or cells, which were expanded over time and divided into small chapels, porticos, and walkways. In these, not only were those who had fallen asleep in Christ buried, but also those who were pursued for Christ’s sake could hide; and those who wished to participate in the sacred rites, or perform them, or focus on other exercises of Christian piety, could move about—if not entirely safely, then certainly with less danger. For even the Jews themselves, when sought for death, dug out such hiding places for themselves under the earth, as Dio Cassius testifies regarding the Emperor Hadrian. But in the city of Rome (the seat of the Empire, where the storm against Christians was more fierce), there were many such refuges under the name of "Cemeteries." *Miræus, same location, folio 408.* One can also see *Johann Chilian Neumair, Journey through Italy and Spain, folio 173 and following.*

A citizen of Basel, during an extreme shortage of food, entered the *Crypt of Augst* <note>original: *Augusto Rauracensem*; an ancient Roman site near Basel</note> in the hope of finding treasure; he was seized by such great horror that he died miserably on the third day. These subterranean Roman places, where Christians in the primitive Church used to hide, pray, and bury the deceased during times of persecution, were noted from *Bosio’s Subterranean Rome* by *Doctor Johann Georg Fabricius* in 1653 in his *Lamps of the Ancients*, where he also described the characters, marks, and symbols used by the Christians of the primitive Church when they were in the Roman underground...

### 72. Curmede. Curmedia property.

In the Julich dialect, it is called **Curmede** <term>a form of "heriot" or death duty where a feudal lord claims the best possession of a deceased tenant</term> when, regarding **Curmedia property**—which is to say, quasi-feudal or <term>emphyteutic</term> <note>land held on a long-term lease</note> "Hubegüter" <note>farmsteads</note>—the Lord demands for the <term>investiture</term> <note>the formal handover of the land to the heir</note> the best or second-best item from the livestock (called "living Curmede") or from clothing or other inanimate things (simply so named). Meichsner volume 1, *decision 20*, where there is a full legal opinion **on Curmede property**. Knichen, *On Vesting Pacts*, part 2, chapter 4, at the end. Rosenthal, *On Feuds*, chapter 2, conclusion 64, number 2. Ritter, *On Homage*, chapter 7, number 164, near the end.

->**ADDITION.**<-

**Curmede** in the language of Julich are properties that are quasi-feudal and emphyteutic, which clearly require Investiture. But if the deceased left a son as successor, then that son takes the best of the horses and the best of the oxen, and the Lord takes the second-best for the Investiture. And when the Lord thus takes something from the livestock...

...of the property, for instance the best or second best animal, it is called a **living heriot** <note>original: "lebendige Curmede" - a death tax paid to a lord from the tenant's estate, often the best beast</note>. ### 73. Current Debts. Simple Credit.

**Current** or running debts <note>original: "Current- oder lauffende Schulden"</note> are commonly so called when they are not documented by a formal deed and arise from daily expenses, where no significant capital has been invested, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

In cases of priority <note>legal term: the order in which creditors are paid</note>, almost nothing from the debtor's assets reaches the common and simple current creditors. Zorer, part 2, question 5, number 376. Among priorities, there are three types of personal creditors, and how they are situated is discussed in question 20, number 7059 and following. Current and simple personal creditors are those who have no special exemption nor a pledge/mortgage. Question 20, number 7077 and following.

### 74. Compliment. Complimenta.

Regarding when and how one may use compliments, see Zahn, *On Lies* <note>original: "de Mendaciis"</note>, book 1, chapter 38, number 3.
The thousand-trick Frenchmen call pompous speeches, inventions, and gestures "Compliments"; that is, strictly speaking, to deceive <note>original: "zuteuschen" (modern: zu täuschen)</note>, polite fillers, excuses, and elegant evasions that one knows how to apply and put forward with a turn of the head and shoulders. See *The Taster* <note>original: "Der Schmäckende"</note> in the *Introduction to Courteousness*. Words of courtesy bind one to nothing. Limnaeus in *Public Law* <note>original: "in J. P."</note>, book 4, chapter 6, number 75. The Spanish call them **Words of Compliment** <note>original: "Palabras de Complimento"</note>. Hence Parlodorius writes in *Daily Matters* <note>original: "rerum quot."</note> book 2, chapter 3, number 45: If someone, he says, for the sake of duty or politeness, promises all his goods or mountains of gold, or, as the Italians say, **"my house is yours"** <note>original: "la mia Casa è vostra"</note>, he is not legally bound. Also Ruland, *On Commissions* <note>original: "de Commiss."</note>, book 5, chapter 1. Mager, *On the Armed Advocate*, chapter 18, number 226. To which the Spanish proverb applies: **"Mouth-courtesy is worth much and costs little"** <note>original: "Cortesia de bocamucho vale is poca costa"</note>; and as the Italians say: **"Complimentary words are not sticky"** <note>original: "Parole di complimento, non sono appicicetörie" - meaning they do not create a binding attachment</note>. See Mr. Speidel in *Notables*, folio 225.

### 75. Body of Law. Corpus Juris.

These words are found in the unique law at the preamble of the Code, regarding the action for a wife's property <note>Latin: "l. un. pr. C. de rei ux. act." - referring to Justinian's Code</note>.

### 76. To Lead Around (To Strike Out). Circumducere.

To "lead something around" from the records means to strike it out or delete it. Law "acta" 45, in the Digest on Res Judicata. Hugo Donellus, book 27, *Commentary on Civil Law*, chapter 3.

<column-break/>

Whether there is a place for the "circumduction of a term" <note>legal term: the expiration or annulment of a court deadline</note> in cases of executory mandates and citations for resumption. Schwanmann, in *Chamber Process*, book 1, chapter 38, number 8. In which cases and when does the circumduction of a term occur? Book 1, chapter 31. The term is circumduced in cases of simple grievance. The same at numbers 24 and 63. It is otherwise regarding cases of appeals, chapter 31, number 9, page 184.

### 77. Catherine.

The name Catherine comes from Hecate or Diana, hence "Hecatarina" according to Baronius at the year 307, number 31.

### 78. To Circumscribe (To Deceive). Circumscribere.

### 79. Bankruptcy Process. Crida-Process.

## D.

### 1. Roof and Room. Expenses for the preservation of houses.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'I' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>

**To keep in Roof and Room** <note>original: "In Dach und Fach zu halten" - a German legal idiom for maintaining a building in habitable condition</note> is nothing other than the conservation of buildings: keeping the structures in stoves, doors, windows, clay walls, fences, roofing, and whatever else of this kind may be, just as a diligent father of a household <note>term: *paterfamilias* - the Roman legal standard for a responsible manager</note> should do, repairing them annually and maintaining them as long as they can be preserved. Moller on the Saxon Constitutions, part 2, constitution 32, number 27. Modestinus Pistor, counsel 27, number 123, book 2.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

Regarding this clause, see Berlichius, 2nd conclusion 41, number 42. Gottfried Antonius, *Disputations on Fiefs*, 10, theorem 1, letter b, where he says that modest expenses, such as those pertaining to the conservation of buildings—**to keep the goods in Roof and Room**—are not to be ignored but fall upon the one who has the use of the thing. Law 12, on expenses made on dotal property; law 18, paragraph 2, at the end, on loans: The vassal is obliged to repair dilapidated feudal houses and keep them in **Roof and Room**. argued from the law on usufruct 7, paragraph "since" 2; law "with the usufructuary" 64 and following, Digest on usufruct. Schrader on Fiefs, part 2, section 9, number 23. Goeddaeus, 3rd Marburg Counsel 33, number 61 and following. Knipschild in his short treatise on the obligations of a Lord toward a Vassal, page 181. That which is under the same roof is considered to be included under the term "house"; Sprenger treats the roof at length in *The Law of the Building*, pages 48 to 51. On Reconstruction, see Albertus Brunus of Asti.

### 2. On the other hand. In turn.

The little word **on the other hand** <note>original: "dagegen"</note> introduces a certain antithesis and creates a proportion; final law, Code on gifts before marriage; Authentica "equality," Code on agreed-upon pacts. Göden, counsel 99, at the beginning. Marcus Mantua, counsel 119, number 1, book 2. Bursatus, counsel 179, number 8. See the Legal Lexicon under the word "Vicissim" [In Turn]. It introduces equivalence, satisfaction, and quantitative estimation. Schäffer, *Practical Questions*, 3, number 140.

The phrase "likewise on the other hand" <note>original: "item dagegen"</note> also imports a reciprocal obligation and condition, and is seen to effect a contract of "I do so that you may do" <note>term: *facio ut facias* - a type of contract where one action is performed in exchange for another</note>.

### 3. Dancing. Choruses.

In every age, many pious and grave men have judged that dances should be prohibited. See my treatise *On Education*, folio 17 and following. In this vein, Friar Johann Pauli, of the Barefoot Order <note>the Franciscans</note>, in *Jest and Earnest* <note>original: "Schimpff und Ernst" - a famous 16th-century collection of stories and moral lessons</note>, title "On Dancing," chapter 337, writes gravely:
> No God-fearing man should let his wife or daughter go to a dance; you can be sure she will not return home as good as she went. They desire, or are desired, and they have their hands in an impure hand.

Reinhard Lorich of Hadamar agrees, writing in the *Instruction of a Prince*, folio 206 (in my copy): "This game has been the cause of many disgraces. Often a matron there has lost the honor she kept for a long time. Often an unhappy young girl has learned there what she would have been better off not knowing," and many more things that follow. See also Jacob Martin, *Illustrious Questions*, century 5, disputation 1, theorem 9; and century 7, disputation 4, theorem 10.

### [3. On Dancing]

On Dances and leaping, see Lorinus on chapter 7 of the *Acts of the Apostles*, verse 41. Casaubon on book 1 of *Athenæus*. Scaliger in his *Poetics*. Lucian in his *Dialogues*, volume 4. Bulæus discusses this extensively in his *Panarium*, and others are reviewed by Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 143 and following. King Alphonso was accustomed to say: A dancer and a fool are distinguished only by this: that the latter is a fool for his whole life, while the former is a fool only while he dances. The Sybarites <note>The inhabitants of Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in Italy famous for its luxury and hedonism.</note> taught their horses to dance to the rhythms of flutes at banquets, a practice which led to their destruction <note>Legend says their enemies played flute music, causing the Sybarite horses to dance instead of charge, leading to a total defeat.</note>. Rupertus in his 1st dissertation on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 2, at the end, discusses dances performed with gestures; likewise in book 2, chapter 4, 2nd dissertation. How Emperor Sigismund danced barefoot in Strasbourg with the women through the city is pleasantly recounted in Kirchner in *The Legate*, book 2, chapter 3, number 54 at the end, as well as by Zeiller in *German Travels*, page 603. To this topic belongs what Zeiller brings forth agreeably in the 5th Century of his *Epistles*, pages 296 and 163, on dancing; likewise Mr. Harsdörffer in the 5th part of his *Conversational Games* in the notes on the Riding School regarding "Capriole-leaping" <note>original: "Capriolen-Springen" — a high leap in classical horse riding or dance.</note>. When Hippoclides sought the daughter of Clisthenes to be given to him in marriage, he lost the hope of the nuptials through the foolishness of his dancing, receiving this response: <term>You have danced away your marriage</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπωρχήσαο γεμεν τὸν γάμον". This refers to a famous story from Herodotus where a suitor became so drunk and danced so indecently that his prospective father-in-law called off the wedding.</note>. "You have danced it away," as interpreted by Budé. More on this in Kirchner at the cited place.

### 4. Thereafter. <note>original: "Darnach. Postea."</note>

The particle "thereafter" <note>German: "darnach"</note>, that is, "afterward" <note>Latin: "postea"</note>, entirely separates a legal disposition from those preceding it: for it signifies an interval of time. See chapter *non solum* at the beginning, where Geminianus discusses appeals in the 6th book. Bartolus on the law *fructus* near the end, in the Digest on the dissolution of marriage. Alciatus in the rubric of the Digest on the notification of new works, number 59. Ruinus on the law *Gallus*, number 37, in the Digest on children and posthumous heirs. Zasius advises in the law *certi conditio*, paragraph *deposui apud te*, number 5, in the Digest on seeking a certain thing, and in the law *ait Prætor* 1, number 6, on oaths, that this distinction of "afterward" is not idle or redundant.

The word "then" <note>Latin: "deinde"</note> is significant of the order of degrees; therefore, in matters of succession, this word implies a successive order, so that the closer relative is preferred to the more remote. Baldus, consultation 292, number 2, book 2. Tuschus, practical conclusions, letter D, conclusion 263.

->ADDITION.<-

On how the particle "afterward" <note>Latin: "postea"</note> is to be understood, see Rittershusius in *On Feudal Parts*, page 169.

### 5. Furthermore. <note>original: "Darneben. Præterea."</note>

Johann Forster testifies in *Judicial Processes of the Imperial Chamber*, in the material on nullity, volume 3, folio 761, that the word "furthermore" <note>German: "darneben"</note> is equivalent to the word "besides" <note>Latin: "præterea"</note>, which repeats the preceding qualities.

### 6. That one should have the power to take me up in all places. <note>original: "Daß man mich in allen Enden fürzunehmen Macht haben solle."</note> Renunciation of the privilege of the forum.

<margin>Besoldus Volume 1.</margin>
In order for a renunciation of the privilege of the forum <note>The "privilegium fori" was the legal right to be tried in one's own local or designated court rather than being dragged to a distant jurisdiction.</note> to be enacted, it is not enough to use these words in contracts: *I promise to pay you in any place whatsoever*, or: *I give you the opportunity of convening me in all places*, or: *That you should have the power to take me up in all places.* Or thus: *I give you the opportunity of convening me wherever I may be found.* For this clause is understood to refer only to competent <note>legally appropriate</note> places. Bartolus on the law *si convenerit*, 18, number 4, in the Digest on the jurisdiction of all judges. Mynsinger, century 1, observation 88. Therefore, a special and express renunciation is necessary. Bartolus and Zasius, number 33, in the said law *si convenerit*.

<column-break/>

And these things are to be noted for establishing a Legal Necessity <note>original: "Die Ehehafftin" — a term referring to a legitimate excuse for court absence or a specific required court appearance.</note>, both in the Swabian and the Rottweil Imperial Courts: for in both, the renounced liberty provides a Legal Necessity.

Thus, even if a member of the Imperial Estates has agreed in the most general terms that he wishes to be convened before any judge, he nevertheless enjoys the "Privilege of Austregues" <note>original: "privilegio Austregarum" — a right of the German princes to have their disputes settled by peer arbitration (Austregal courts) rather than standard courts.</note>. For a general renunciation cannot take away this right of a privileged instance; rather, it must be interpreted strictly, so that it harms the person renouncing it as little as possible in a special case. See the law *emptor*, paragraph *Lucius*, in the Digest on pacts. See Hering on *Guarantors*, chapter 23, number 20 and following.

And such unique rights do not fall under such a waiver when they are not expressly mentioned. Cephalus, consultation 427, number 6. Cravetta, consultation 200, number 10. For such words, as said above—that one wishes to be convened before any judge—are to be understood as referring to *competent* judges. Mynsinger noted in century 1, observation 89, that this was the ruling obtained in the Imperial Chamber in the case of Christopher von Knöringen against David the Jew. Caspar Ziegler in *Common Conclusions*, section on the Austregues, column 1, number 29.

->ADDITION.<-

If it is simply promised that payment may be made anywhere, so that the creditor has the power to take up the debtor in all places, then according to the opinion of Gail, book 2, observation 36, final number, and Zanger, book 2 on exceptions, chapter 1, number 154, the claim is rightly made in any place, even one other than where the petition would otherwise have to be instituted. This is contrary to what Mynsinger (century 1, observation 88) and Gilhausen seem to think—that the renunciation of the forum requires a special and specific renunciation. Ummius, dissertation on process 4, thesis 1, number 5 at the end.

### 7. Dovecotes. <note>original: "Daubhäuser. Columbaria."</note>

Regarding Dovecotes, see Costanus, question 17. It is a unique regalian right <note>A "regale" is a right or property belonging exclusively to a sovereign or someone granted royal authority.</note> to be allowed to keep dovecotes. And I myself have seen several Investitures <note>Documents granting a fief or right.</note> where the dovecote is specifically mentioned alongside a castle. Where someone has already slaughtered, killed, and consumed pigeons caught from one another while flying in and out, or if such pigeons have died or been lost, their value can be demanded from the buyer. Zorer, part 2, question 15, number 94. 3.

In France, it is not permitted for everyone to erect dovecotes. Zeiller, century 4 of *Epistles*, page 484. Doves are fruit- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "fruitful" at the bottom of the page.</note>

### 4. Then. <note>German: *Darnach*. Latin: *Postea*.</note>
