### 6. That one shall have the power to proceed against me in all places. <term>Renunciation of the privilege of the forum</term> <note>This refers to a legal clause where a person waives their right to be sued only in their home jurisdiction.</note>.

To establish a "renunciation of the privilege of the forum," it is not enough to use these words in contracts: "I promise to pay you in any place whatsoever," according to Besold, Volume 1,

<column-break/>

or: "I give you the opportunity to summon me in all places" <note>original German: *Daß du mich an allen Enden fürzunehmen Macht haben sollest*</note>. Or thus: "I give you the opportunity to summon me wherever I may be found." For this clause is understood to refer only to competent <note>legally appropriate</note> places. See Bartolus on the law *si convenerit*, 18, number 4, in the Digest on the jurisdiction of all judges; and Mynsinger, century 1, observation 88. Therefore, a special and express renunciation is necessary. Bartolus and Zasius, number 33, in the said law *si convenerit*.

These points should be noted for establishing <term>the legal summons</term> <note>original German: *Die Ehehafftin*. A technical term in Old German law for a legitimate court standing or summons.</note> both in the Swabian and the Rottweil Imperial Courts: for in both places, the waived freedom produces <term>a legal summons</term>.

Thus, although a member of the Imperial Estates might have agreed in the most general terms that he wishes to be summoned before any judge, he nevertheless enjoys the "Privilege of the Austregæ" <note>original Latin: *privilegio Austregarum*. A special right of the high nobility of the Holy Roman Empire to have their disputes settled by peer arbitration rather than ordinary courts.</note>. For a general renunciation cannot take away this right of a privileged instance; rather, it must be interpreted strictly so that it harms the one renouncing it as little as possible in a special case. See the law *emptor*, the section *Lucius*, in the Digest on pacts. See also Hesing on bail, chapter 23, number 20 and following.

And such things involving a unique right do not fall under a general renunciation when they are not expressly mentioned. Cephalus, counsel 427, number 6; Cravetta, counsel 200, number 10. For such words as mentioned above—that he wishes to be summoned before any judge—are to be understood as referring to competent judges. Mynsinger noted in century 1, observation 89, that this was the ruling in the Imperial Chamber in the case of Christopher von Knöringen against David the Jew. See also Caspar Ziegler in his commentary, under the section on *Austregæ*, column 1, number 29.

->ADDITION.<-

If payment is simply promised "anywhere," so that the creditor has the power to proceed against the debtor in all places <note>original German: *also daß Gläubiger Macht habe den Schuldigern an allen Enden vorzunehmen*</note>, it is the opinion of Gail (observation 36, last number) and Zang (book 2 on exceptions, chapter 1, number 154) that the claim is rightly made in any place, even one where the claim could not otherwise be instituted. This is contrary to what Mynsinger and Gilhausen seem to think, on the grounds that a renunciation of the forum requires a special and specific renunciation. Ummius, *Disputations on Procedure* 4, theorem 1, number 5, at the end.

### 7. Dove-houses. <note>German: *Daubhäuser*. Latin: *Columbaria*.</note>

Regarding dove-houses, see Costanus, question 17. It is a unique royal right <note>original Latin: *regale*</note> to be allowed to keep dove-houses. And I myself have seen several investitures <note>legal documents granting land or rights</note> where the "dove-house" is specifically mentioned in connection with a castle. Where someone has already slaughtered, killed, and consumed pigeons that flew in and out and were caught and sold by another, or if such pigeons have died or been lost, their value can be demanded from the buyer. Zorer, part 2, question 15, number 94. 3.

### 9. Denmark and Norway.

#### Dania, Norvvegia.

Krantz testifies that the Dane is subject to the Empire, in book 6 of *Denmark*, chapter 17. See also Arumaeus, *On Assemblies*, chapter 4, number 71. Denmark itself, along with Norway and the North, was conquered by Otto <note>Otto I, Holy Roman Emperor.</note> and added to the Empire, and they always swore an oath of fidelity and subjection. Waldemar received his crown from the Emperor; Peter lived under the same law from Frederick, as did Leo in the Synod. On these matters, consult Cujas, book 1 *On Fiefs*, page 65; Helmold, book 1 of his *History*; and Bodin, book 1 of *The Republic*, chapter 9. Otto of Freising writes thus about this matter in *The Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 5: When that Frederick I, having been made Emperor as quite a young man, learned that there was a grave controversy among the Danes regarding the Kingdom between two kinsmen, Peter and Guoto, he declared a Great Court (I think this was the largest assembly among the Romans) at Merseburg <note>original: *Martinopoli*</note>. He summoned a crowded Senate of all ranks and called the youths from the kingdom to the appointed place and day. They came and explained that they wished to obey his order and command, adding other honors and entreaties. The Emperor sent the Fathers into council. The matter is said to have been decided thus: Guoto, having certain provinces of the kingdom left to him, abdicated the royal name by means of a proferred sword. For it is the custom of the Court that **Kingdoms are handed over or received by the Prince through a sword, and Provinces through a banner.** Peter, however, having received the Kingdom from the Emperor's hand, was bound to him by fidelity and <term>homage</term><note>A formal public acknowledgment of feudal allegiance.</note>. Thus the Crown of the Kingdom was placed upon him by the hand of the Prince; he himself, having been crowned, carried the sword of the King as he walked beneath the crown.

Gradually, however, it fell away from the Empire, as Krantz testifies in book 1, chapter 17; Otto of Freising in the 7th *Chronicle*, chapter 19; Kirchhoff, volume 4 of *Various German Counsels*, counsel 17, number 18; see also Chytraeus, book 20 of *Saxony*.

It is beyond doubt that by reason of Holstein, he is a vassal of the Empire, and therefore a subject. For the legal experts who admit he is a vassal but deny he is a subject do not seem to know what it means to be the vassal of an absolute King. Although the status of vassalage from a non-subject...

The King of Denmark, however, still recognizes the Majesty of the Emperor in the name of **Holstein** <note>original: "Holsatiæ"</note>, and still acknowledges the jurisdiction of that court. See Gail, *On Imperial Arrests*, chapter 6, number 18. In the year 1542, he is described on behalf of the Empire as a "consort member" <gloss>Mitglied</gloss>. If he is a member on that part, it follows that on that part he is under the Head <note>The "Head" refers to the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>.

But is he still a **vassal** by reason of Denmark itself? The Dane defends himself by "prescription" <term>prescription</term><note>A legal principle where a right is gained or a liability ended by the passage of time; here, the claim that because they haven't been treated as subjects for so long, they are no longer legally bound.</note>, and many scholars agree and believe that such a prescription can exist, while others deny it. For prescription is a matter of Roman Law, and applies to those living within the Empire, not those who have withdrawn from it. They deny that prescription can be granted against public law or against the Republic <note>referring to the Empire as a *Respublica* or commonwealth</note>, citing the law "compellit" 6. *Code on 30 or 40-year prescription*. But see my own work in the *Treatise on Appeals*, chapter 2, number 8. Regarding the excursions of the **Normans**, see Carolus Scribanius, *Origins of Antwerp*, page 54, and Justus Lipsius, *Lovanium*, book 1, chapter 3.

There is truly a perpetual hatred between the Danes and the **Swedes**, as I stated in my *Treatise on the Law of Federations*, page 6. Great disputes have arisen from this, primarily because the Danes affected a union of those two kingdoms; see the rebuttal of the deceptions of Petrus Parvus Rosæfontanus, a Danish Knight, written by Janus Minor of Sweden. Concerning this matter, Jacob Ziegler writes in his description of the tyranny of **Christian II**: The Kings of Denmark have often attempted to take the Kingdom of Sweden by arms at other times, their greed fueled by neighboring **Norway**, which they had previously oppressed through factionalism and force. They considered it a most beautiful achievement if they could contract the entire continent, which they call **Scandia**, under one rule. Furthermore, they were invited by the same thing that tempts other mortals—their meager wealth at home. Norway was exhausted by them, while Sweden and **Gothia** <note>The land of the Goths in southern Sweden.</note> were still intact and full of silver and copper. Thus, the happiness of others had injected in them a great desire to seek wealth from what belonged to others.

Regarding Norway, **Botero** <note>Giovanni Botero, an influential Italian thinker and geographer.</note> has this to say: The peoples of Norway were once very powerful; they afflicted England for a long time, harassed France, and obtained dominion in that province which is still called **Normandy**. The Kingdom of Norway, shaken by turmoils, came to the King of Denmark, who, to ensure he remains secure in it, treats the inhabitants harshly and strips them of their resources, so that the wretched men have no hope for a better fortune. And Jacob Ziegler in his *Schonlandia*: Therefore, Norway is at this time under the power of the Danes. These men do not only command legitimate revenues and tolerable taxes, but scraping together every advantage, they transfer it to Denmark, clearly establishing the longevity of their Empire upon the weakness of their subjects. Such is the fortune of Norway. Neither can the very buildings of the cities maintain their old size and dignity, nor is there hope of repairing their status: for Public Assemblies are not permitted for this purpose. No one dares to report or attempt any work by their own judgment, being uncertain of the 

<column-break/>

will of all. See Werdenhagen, *On the Hanseatic Republics*, part 3, page 289.

## 11. Deputation Day. The Convention of Deputations.

When the Imperial Commissioners, Electors, and certain Estates meet, it is called the **Convention of Deputies**, or the Visitation of the Court. This was first instituted by the **Augsburg Decree** of 1555, and consists of the following number of ranks: **Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Palatinate, Saxony, Brandenburg** (all Electors); **Austria, Würzburg, and Münster** (both Bishops); **Bavaria, the Abbots of Weingarten and Ochsenhausen, the Counts of Fürstenberg, Cologne, and Nuremberg**. See the *Recess* <note>The final resolution or summary of an Imperial Diet's decisions.</note> of the year 1555, the section beginning "So sich dann abermals," etc. Here it must be noted well that this office of Deputation was personal from the beginning and did not pass to successors. Later, however, so that the number of Deputies would not be diminished by the death of certain individuals, it was agreed between **Emperor Ferdinand** and the Estates that it should no longer be tied to persons but should become hereditary. See the *Augsburg Recess* of 1559, the section beginning "Nachdem sich darneben," and the following page, with the **Duke of Jülich** further added...

# Augmented Practical Treasury

To the Landgrave of Hesse. Indeed, since it has been observed that "great matters require great helpers" <note>original: "magna negotia magnis indigere adjutoribus"</note> (Velleius, Book 3), and that counsel is sound and complete when it is supported by the harmonious opinions of many (Cacheranus, in the preface to the decisions of Piedmont, no. 7), it was decided that besides those two, others should be added: namely, the Bishop of Constance, the administration of the Burgundian Circle, and the Dukes of Brunswick and Pomerania. See the Recess of Speyer <note>The "Recess" was the official summary of resolutions passed at an Imperial Diet.</note> of the year 1570, section "And so that such important things" <note>original German: "Und damit solche wichtige Ding"</note>. In that addition, the number of Deputies has remained fixed without further increase until now; and in the Assembly of Deputies at Speyer in the year 1600, it was followed to the letter. We know from the Recess of the Assembly of Deputies held at Frankfurt in 1571 that many Estates <note>The "Estates" were the constituent states and authorities of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> converged there. But that must be understood as an extraordinary occurrence, namely for specific causes handled at that time. Otherwise, because of the disturbances of the Empire and internal tumults—to suppress which the forces of one, three, or five Circles <note>The "Circles" (Kreise) were administrative groupings of Imperial states for defense and tax collection.</note> are not sufficient—the Deputies regularly convene. See the section "If then once again" <note>original German: "So sich dann abermals"</note>. Bertram in Arumäus, discourse 9, thesis 12, volume 1.

The Elector of Mainz has the right of summoning this Assembly of Deputies; however, he does not use his own name, but the name of the Emperor. Bertram, in the place cited; add Reinhard König, Political Theater, part 1, chapter 27, number 8 and following.

Concerning the Deputies in the Diets: "When a committee is formed for the advancement of a matter" <note>original German: "Wann man zu Beförderung der Sach einen Ausschuß machet"</note>, see Arumäus on the Diets, chapter 7, number 116 and following, where he writes that usually at the beginning of the Diets, it is asked whether the Estates wish to deliberate "in the full Senate, or before certain Deputies of the same, through a committee" <note>original German: "in pleno Senatu, vel coram certis ejusdem Deputatis, durch einen Ausschuß"</note>. This matter was discussed and concluded in the Diet of Nuremberg in 1431 by Emperor Sigismund and the Estates, "that a committee should be made for the advancement of the matter" <note>original German: "daß zu Beförderung der Sach ein Ausschuß zu machen"</note>. Lehmann, in the *Chronicle of Speyer*, book 7, chapter 80. And this method of consulting was frequently repeated, as in the Diet of 1566 concerning Justice and Peace, and in the Diet of 1594 when the matters of coinage and anticipation were treated. For it is thought that a faster conclusion is provided for settling matters because of the great number of Estates. But others desire to deliberate in the full Senate or Council: because the points of the proposal concern everyone, therefore they ought to be consulted upon by everyone. "So also is there good advice from many heads" <note>original German: "So ist auch aus vielen Köpffen gut rathen"</note>, as a certain Estate said in the mentioned Diet of 1594.

Whether in the Senate of Princes the Deputies ought to be chosen "from the benches" <note>original German: "aus den Bäncken"</note> or "from the Circles" <note>original German: "aus den Kräisen"</note>, see Arumäus in the said treatise, number 122, folio 539 and following.

### 12. Of such a kind. <note>original German: "Dergleichen." Latin: "Hujusmodi."</note>

The word "Dergleichen" is a true mark of similarity, and is verified by relation to another thing. See "It is permitted from the undertaking," in the section on competent courts. Georg Everhard, counsel 47, number 92, volume 1. And it sounds just as if one said "in the same way" or "similarly," which word denotes similarity of fact and manner, as Innocent writes in the chapter "From the rescript," on oaths. Likewise, it signifies equality and identity in all things. See the section "similarly" in the Institutes on the excuse of tutors.

### 13. Therefore, On that account, For that reason. <note>original German: "Derhalben, Derwegen, Deßwegen." Latin: "Igitur."</note>

The word "igitur" (therefore) continues the same discourse (at the beginning of the Institutes on tutelage) and infers from the preceding things to the following things. Albericus on the definition of the word "igitur." Prospero Farinacci, book 1, counsel 9, number 20.

The words "ideò" (for this reason) or "ex hoc" (from this) are placed with respect to all preceding things, so that from the cause of the preceding things a disposition may be made. Therefore it is "illative," because it infers from premises. "And therefore he made etc." denotes the final cause, which is moved by the premises, and therefore it induces a clear demonstration; if these are not true, the release or any contract ceases. Socinus, counsel 159, number 20 and following, book 2. Cravetta, counsel 192, number 21. See Barbosa on definitions, numbers 142 and 144. For what the words "demnach" (accordingly), "quare" (wherefore), "idcircò" (for that reason) signify, see Klock, volume 2, consultation 16, numbers 129, 130.

### 14. Deacons. <note>Latin: "Diaconi."</note>

A Deacon is a Minister, and specifically one who carries out the care of the poor and supplies them with necessities from the collections of the Church. Acts 6.

"Diaconiae" are the hospitals of the poor with their chapels; for the first Deacons were ministers of the poor and widows, who presided over the hospitals of the poor. John the Deacon in the *Life of Saint Gregory*: "Gregory, that most prudent Father of the Family of Christ, deputed suitable men to the individual 'Diaconiae' or 'Xenodochia' <note>Xenodochia: guest-houses or hostels for pilgrims and the poor.</note>; he decreed they were to be protected with privileges so that they might labor more securely, or rather more sagaciously, in the work of piety and mercy." "Because," he said, "we have chosen you, a religious man, to be placed over the tables of the poor for the exhibition of the Diaconate, lest any doubt arise for you from this administration, we have seen fit to support you with this protection, decreeing that concerning that which you have received or shall hereafter receive to be distributed to the tables of the poor or the service of the Diaconate, you shall never be compelled by any man to provide an accounting."

There is also the Deacon in the order of the Clergy, of which these are the grades: Porter <note>original: "Ostiarius"</note>, Psalm-singer <note>original: "Psalmista"</note>—

# ADDITION.

What constitutes "discovered theft" <note>original: "Furtum conceptum"</note>? On "discovered timber" <note>original: "Tignum conceptum," a legal term for stolen building materials incorporated into a structure.</note> see Lord Doctor Rebhan’s *Selected Justinian Questions*, decade 6, question 9, page 35. On the misappropriation of tithed fruit <note>original German: "Von Entfremdung der zehentbaren Frucht"</note>, and those who carry away large quantities of corn-ears, see Werndle’s *On Tithes*, book 2, chapter 1, page 67.

Theft committed out of necessity is excused, according to Knipschild’s *On Trusts*, 11, 316, 453, and 480. Theft is described as Notable, Grand, and Notorious <note>original German: "Tapffer, Groß und Kündlich"</note>.
1. **Notable** <note>original German: "Tapffer"</note>, or remarkable, distinguished, and singular by reason of concurrent circumstances—such as breaking in, or carrying weapons, "when someone by day or night breaks or climbs into our dwelling, or enters to steal with weapons," which type of theft is called "a dangerous theft" <note>original German: "ein gefährlicher Diebstal"</note> in the heading of article 159. In this way, we call a strong and distinguished man a "notable man" <note>original German: "tapffern Mann"</note>. However, the word "Notable" is also used for value, as when we say "a notable fine" <note>original German: "tapffere Geldbuß"</note> for a large and urgent extraordinary penalty. 
2. **Grand**, being worth 5 florins or more, article 160. For that which is below five shillings is called "a minor theft" <note>original German: "ein geringer Diebstal"</note>, article 157, under the heading "The most trivial theft" <note>original German: "Der allerschlechteste Diebstal"</note>. 
3. **Notorious**, manifest, "Public theft" <note>original German: "Offentlicher Diebstal"</note>, for which the thief is decried. See the heading of article 158. 
Lord Doctor Tabor writes most copiously of all regarding theft in his *Criminal Gleanings*. See also Boniface in his specific treatise, and *Dutch Military Law*, which states: "A noble thief should hang on a higher gallows than others." Besold relates a similar example in his *Politics*, book 2, chapter 2, number 22, section 1: "Seven feet higher than another thief." There is a rumor in Klagenfurt of a man suspected of theft who was driven to the gallows, and the next day an inquiry was held regarding the dead man. This is a joke from a banquet. See Megiser in the *Annals of Carinthia*, book 11, chapter 12.

Theft from baths <note>original: "Furtum balneariorum"</note> is mentioned by Casaubon in his notes on Theophrastus; Marquard Freher, book 2 of his *Addenda*; and Philipp Carolus in the *Roman Library*, pages 38 and 39.

The punishment for theft among the Hebrews is discussed by Lord Felwinger in *The Judge*, page 487. The Republic of Danzig sentences thieves and other criminals to carts and the ramparts, ibid. On the punishment of livestock thieves <note>original German: "Von Straff der Viehdieb"</note> who steal sheep, pigs, horses, oxen, cows, chickens, birds, geese, or peacocks, see Pappus in *Dutch Military Law*, page 86. Lord Johann Christoph Oelhafen, in a frequently praised counsel, refers "simple theft" <note>original: "furtum simplex"</note> under 3 Guilders to mixed power or low jurisdiction.

# 16. Servant. <term>Famulus</term>

Hermann Stamm has much to say regarding servants in his treatise *On Personal Servitude*, book 2.

# ADDITION.

To a servant who has contracted his labor for a year, but through ill health could not perform it for a time, the full wage must be paid. See the late Lord Doctor Ludwell’s *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 260, section b. Hippolytus Bonacossa wrote *Questions Regarding Servants*.

# 17. Service. <term>Officium</term>

A lord of jurisdiction can revoke offices at will, unless he gave them for a remunerative or burdensome cause. See the *Faberian Code*, book 8, title 38, definition 18.

# ADDITION.

Fixed salaries are to be established and paid to officials. Gail, observation 44; Mynsinger, observation 7; Lather, *On Taxes*, chapter 16, number 185; Zorer, page 1, 12, number 881. On office, see Barbosa, book 13, chapter 18, throughout the *Axioms*. "Established service" and "measured service" <note>original German: "Gesetzte Dienst, gemessene Dienst"</note>—see Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 4, number 16.

# 18. Domestic Servants. <term>Famuli</term>

Thus are servants called, etc. See Hippolytus Bonacossa’s treatise *On Servitude and Servants*.

### 20. The Same. <note>original: "Dieselbig. Eadem."</note>

The phrase, "That same thing," <note>original: "Eadem illa, Dieselbig"</note> when used simply, does not always denote an absolute similarity in every respect, nor does it exclude different species. [Cites: Glosses on the Digest, Ripa]. It is only considered exclusive when a restrictive particle is added, such as saying "that same thing alone" <note>original: "dieselbig allein, illa tantùm, illa solùm"</note>. Such a phrase, when attached to an affirmative provision, implies a negative—as if all other things were expressly excluded or not considered included. [Cites: Justinian Code, Digest, Aretinus, Decianus].

### 21. Diet, Dit. God. <note>original: "Diet, Dit. Deus."</note>

The ancient word *Dit*, according to Reineccius in his work on the origin of the Mysians, denotes God. From this comes our name *Dieterich*, meaning "rich in God." Aventinus affirms that it also signifies riches, duty, or distinguished services. The word *Dit* is written by others as *Deut*, and by some as *Thioth*. Many compounds of this word are found throughout ancient annals, appearing everywhere; such as *Ditmarus, Ditardus, Ditherus, Dithlindus, Ditbolius, Ditfridus, Ditbertus, Dithelmus, Ditbolfus, Ditardus, Ditburgis, Ditmannus, Ditholdus, Ditgrinus*, and so on.

This name refers entirely to the one whom Plato calls *Theut*, whom he says was the inventor of letters among the Egyptians. He is the same as Hermes, and is elsewhere called *Thoot* or *Thoyt*. Goropius [discusses this in his works on hieroglyphs and the Gauls], where he says this word denotes a "head"—what we call a *Haupt*. I do not doubt that from this, the Teutons—the Germans <note>original: "die Teutschen, vel Ditschen, Teutschen"</note>—derive their name.

->ADDITION.<-

Add the work of Mr. Harsdörffer in his *Specimen of German Philology*, inquiry 11 at the end; and Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in the *Letter* added to the *Comparison of the Nuremberg Republic with the Venetian*; in the explanation of my name; and D. Saubert *On Sacrifices*, page 156.

### 22. Since / Because. <note>original: "Dieweil. Quia."</note>

The word "Because" <note>original: "Quia"</note> is a statement of cause, according to Baldus [legal commentary]. The word "since" <note>original: "weiln, quia"</note> <column-break/> is used causally and for a reason, and denotes the "final cause." <note>In philosophy and law, the "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which something is done.</note> Klock, volume 2, consultation 16, numbers 127 and 128.

### 23. Court, To Appeal, Tuesday. <note>original: "Ding, Dingen, Dienstag. Judicium. Appellare."</note>

*Ding* is usually taken to mean a Court of Justice <note>original: "Judicium"</note>, from which comes *Dinggraven* [Court Counts]. See my entry on Counts, no. 4. From this comes *Dinstag* [Tuesday], meaning the "day of the court," though we now mistakenly call it *Zinstag*. <note>Zinstag implies a "day of interest or rent," which the author argues is a linguistic error.</note> From this also comes *Freyding* [Free Court] and *Vogtding* [Advocate's Court]. Mr. Gryphiander [cites works on municipal laws]. In Bavaria, the word *dingen* is used for "to appeal" <note>original: "appelliren"</note>—see the Judicial Ordinance, title 10, art. 1. Generally, *dingen* means "to litigate" or "seek justice." <note>original: "rechten"</note>

->ADDITION.<-

*Ding* is usually taken to mean a Court. <note>original: "Gericht"</note> Meichsner, book 1, decision 7, page 92. It also means a "Place of Judgment." <note>original: "Gerichtsplatz"</note> Zeiller in his *Travels through Germany*. Caspar von Lerch in his *Discourse on the German Knightly Order* [cites page], from which comes the names of various regional courts: *Gravengeding, Freydeding, Vogtdeding*. In the same sense, "a fenced or summoned court" <note>original: "ein gehegt oder bedingtes Gericht"</note> is used in the *Mirror of the Saxons* <note>original: "Sachsenspiegel," one of the most important legal codes of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, book 3, article 61. Therefore, *Ding* was the term for a judicial forum among the Germans of old, just as it still denotes such for the Swedes and Danes today. Furthermore, from *Ding* meaning "judgment" comes *Dingestag* (mistakenly called *Zinstag* by some), which is Tuesday <note>original: "dies Martis"</note>, the day on which courts were held. Freher *On Secret Judgments*. In Bavaria, *dingen* is called "to appeal." Besold [cites work]. Dr. Dannhauer explains it slightly differently: he says *Ding* is as if one said "Dominical" <note>relating to the Lord</note>, and *Dinstag* is like "The Lord's Day," meaning generally a sacred day. The ancients consecrated the third day of the week to Mars; hence, among some Germans, it is called *Eric* or *Erich*; among others, however, it is called *Thies* or *Ties*, from which the words *Erichtag* or *Tinstag* come. From these, others have made *Dienstag*, others *Ziesstag*, and finally *Zinstag*. Cluverius and Zeiller in *German Travels*. On this word, see Marquard Freher [on Westphalian courts]. *Dienstag* [Tuesday] is the Sabbath of the Moors; see Michael Hemmersam’s *West-Indian Travel Description*, which I edited, pages 56 and 68.

### 24. Manorial Court. <note>original: "Dinghof. Curia dominicalis."</note>

The *Dinghof* is named from the "emphyteutic contract" <note>a type of long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</note>; hence the saying, "Court Law <note>original: "Dingtrecht"</note> breaks Land Law <note>original: "Landrecht"</note>," or it is so called because the stewards <note>original: "Meyer"</note> used to judge there. See the book by Dachtler.

->ADDITION.<-

*Dingstul*, or the "Statues of Roland." <note>Statues of the knight Roland were placed in European cities as symbols of municipal freedom and the right to hold a court.</note> Klock, volume 3. *Dinghof*, see Gothofredus. *Dingstul*: the "highest judgment seat and superior court" <note>original: "der höchste Dingstul und Oberhof"</note>. Limnäus [legal source].

7. c. 31. n. 6. **Manorial Courts** <note>original: "Curiæ dominicales"</note> are rights belonging to Lords over manorial estates. These involve certain modest annual taxes <note>original: "censibus"</note> established as a recognition of the Lord’s ownership, to be paid on fixed days. By law, these rights are held in perpetuity, with the condition that if the taxes are not paid on the due day, they shall double by geometric progression for every day or hour they are late. If the Lords seize property for these unpaid taxes, the estates of the occupants are awarded to the Lord by the knowledge and decree of the tax assessors. In Alsace, both Upper and Lower, these Manorial Courts are accepted and are well known to the inhabitants.

### ADDITION.

In matters introduced only for the sake of public decency, a dispensation can be obtained without wounding the conscience. A favor of dispensation does not allow for expansion beyond its specific terms. Barbosa, book 4, chapter 32, axiom 1, section 2. Bonaguida de Areno wrote a complete treatise on Dispensation, mentioned by Mr. Tabor in his treatise *On Double the Amount*; others call it *On Arrears*. A dispensation is the removal of a legal obligation in a specific case and for a specific person, by which they would otherwise be bound. As Suarez says in book 6, *On Laws*, chapter 10, the term is used in two ways: either properly and strictly, as just defined, or broadly, as signifying the interpretation of the law. On Dispensation in: 1. Matrimonial matters, 2. Wills, 3. Contracts, 4. **27. To Dispute. <note>original: "Disputiren."</note> Disputation.**

On the vanity and abuse of disputations <note>Formal academic debates used to test students and scholars.</note> in the Universities, see Heider, *On Institutions*, 102; Lubinus in his *Satires*; and Thomas of Villanova in his *Sermons*, folio 165.

### ADDITION.

It is a species of crime to dispute about divine matters—something nothing is more common than today—after a decision on the controversies has been made in a legitimate Synod <note>An official assembly of church leaders.</note>. Under Civil Law, such disputations are prohibited without distinction for both Clergy and Laity. However, under Canon Law <note>Church law.</note>, they are forbidden only to the Laity, specifically under penalty of excommunication; they are permitted to the Clergy. Nevertheless, two limitations can be seen in the Civil Law: 1. Unless it is done for the sake of learning in the Schools, for it is not useless to doubt individual points, according to Aristotle. 2. For the sake of convincing a heretic. Rittershusius, *Differences between Civil and Canon Law*, page 469.

From every age, it has been believed most worthy to commit the testing of studies, the skills of the body, and the excellence of voices to trial. [Citing Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*]. There is no one who is not ashamed to be defeated in a dispute. [Citing St. Augustine, *Soliloquies*, chapter 7]. Hence, Johannes Robertus narrates at length that the famous jurist Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a renowned 16th-century legal scholar.</note> stood shamefully during a disputation for the chair at Bourges. He writes: He was reduced to such straits that since he could in no way dilute the objections and arguments pressing upon him, nor did he have anywhere to turn, and could not obtain an end to the dispute from Francisco Duarenus <note>Cujacius's academic rival.</note> (who was presiding as the judge along with his colleagues and argued the custom of the school did not allow it), he feigned illness. He was seen not only turning his back before any signal to retreat was given, but also shamefully rushing away from the speaker's platform barely after the contest had begun. Although Mercator denies this happened, saying: From these points you descend into insults, to which he replies, "sprinkling you with the gold of knowledge," <note>original Greek: "χρυσῷ καταπάτλὸν υμᾶς ἢ γνώσεως"</note> since he considers things coming from you to be an ornament to him. He was also not moved by the fact that you lie in these books, saying he was twice or thrice rejected by the people of Toulouse in his petition for the chair; the Senate and people of Toulouse testify that he was called from Cahors and soon from Bourges and rejected the offer.

# Expanded Practical Treasury

...are by nature inclined, and only honor and glory are sought with deceptive display, rather than with the foundation of truth or concise instruction. For this reason, no people have been found more unfit, or indeed more harmful, for government and giving counsel than those who have been raised and accustomed to such long-winded disputation in schools, yet knew little of the true basis of business. Nevertheless, moderate discussion and a mature consideration of a matter by both sides can often be useful and good.

Because parents have seen such significant expense, time, effort, and labor entirely lost on their children, and have further noted that an unlearned, inexperienced person might speak better on common matters concerning both soul and body—where the true foundation and pure truth are required, not disputation—than a great scholar could, they have grown tired of the expense and have, over time, withdrawn their support.

Today, in the name of the Emperor, legal experts <term>Jureconsulti</term> <note>These were professional legal practitioners and consultants learned in the law.</note> are announced by Universities <note>original: "Academiis"</note> and Counts Palatine. Indeed, by the right of Royal Prerogatives <note>original: "jure Regalium"</note>, this creation of Doctors in any art takes place, and privileges can be granted to them even if no examination has preceded, according to Lord Bachovius’s *Disputation on Justice and Law*, thesis 7. However, since the Doctorate is not a simple dignity but is founded on erudition, lest anyone be able to buy the degree with money, it must be said that the power of creating Doctors is seen to be granted only under the unspoken condition that they be suitable and worthy. Therefore, I believe these "Bullate" Doctors <note>original: "Bullatos istos Doctores"; those granted degrees by a decree or 'bull' rather than university study</note> should be held to the same legal standing as those created in a University, provided they have been examined by those skilled in the art, found suitable, and provided evidence of this through the testimony of good men. See Treutler *on Justice and Law*, thesis 7; and see my own notes on Law 7 regarding Justice and Law, question 4 and following. Clausius teaches in his *Disputation on Squatters' Rights* <note>original: "de usucapion."</note>, chapter 45, that no one becomes a Doctor through prescription <note>A legal term meaning the passage of time or custom alone cannot grant a degree</note>, though it creates a presumption in their favor. But how a Doctorate may be proven, see Pacianus’s treatise *On Proof* in the Index.

Furthermore, should legal experts or Doctors be masters? When was the invention of Doctors? What are their insignia? Should Popes, Cardinals, Bishops, and other Prelates be Doctors? Borellus teaches this in *On Magistrates*, book 1, chapter 8.

And should the children of Doctors of the College be examined for free? Vivius decides this in Decision 159. The same author in Decision 455 states that a Doctor, especially one famous for his writings, should be promoted to public offices ahead of others.

It is pleasing here to attach a controversial question: whether someone who has been examined can be announced as a Doctor in their absence.

And indeed, for the affirmative side, it was brought forward: (1) that many times at Tübingen, the candidates for the Master's degree who have undergone all examinations
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

and received the "good news" <note>original: "bona nova"</note>, as they call it, but subsequently fell ill unexpectedly, were announced in their absence together with the others, and were held without any doubt to be rightly created Masters. In both cases, the same reasoning applies, and no difference is found in this regard between Doctors and Masters. Similarly, (2) the patrons of this opinion brought forward that everything remaining and necessary for the conferring of Doctoral honors regarding this person—namely the taking of the Oath and the administration of the customary solemnities—may be performed and received respectively through a proxy.

Likewise, (3) it carries no little weight that some have referred to the practice of other Universities.

On the other hand, however, others have considered this: that dignity cannot be conferred upon an absent person except by the Emperor. And (2) that the creation of a Doctor, as a certain solemn act, seems to require the presence of the person themselves, just like a coronation or some similar inaugural act.

Item (3), it is safer to follow the ordinary path so that the status of a Doctor created in such a way is not called into question, or a bad reputation created for the University itself. Especially since the contrary practice of certain Universities mentioned was not proven, and among the Masters who were perhaps created in absence as understood above, it does not signify as much, considering they almost always remain within the local territory. See my treatise *On the Law of University Matters and Colleges*, page 213, section 7.

Even less can one be created without any previous examination, even if everyone knows him to be worthy. Since the examination and other things directed toward sufficient exploration are held as the "form" of an Academic Doctor. See the *Additions to the Lectures of Martinus Uranius*, regarding chapter 2 *on witnesses*, number 16, page 115. In this, they differ from "Bullate" Doctors. The Magnificent Lord Melander in his *Commentary on the Process of Noah Meurer*, page 115. It is also to be feared that this would be belittling to a University if such unexamined Doctors were made. And it is an Imperial reserve to create a Doctor with a single word. Ohemius *on the Law of Bishops*, thesis 17, letter T.

But a Licentiate <term>Licentiate</term> <note>A degree ranking below a Doctorate, giving the "license" to teach or practice.</note> who has been solemnly promoted and proclaimed, and who has also already taken the oath, could perhaps be made a Doctor while absent. Since such a person is held as a true Doctor in favorable legal acts. Benius *on the Privileges of Legal Experts*, part 3, at the beginning; Matthaeus Stephanus *on Universities*, chapter 14, number 48; Lord Lansius *on Universities*, page 73; Ritter *on Homage*, chapter 5, number 96, page 73, where he says that those who have only had an inaugural disputation and have legitimately sustained the examination are not called Licentiates, but Candidates...

<meta>This page continues the legal and academic discussion regarding the status of advanced degrees, specifically comparing the Licentiate and the Doctorate, and critiquing the decline in academic standards for these honors.</meta>

...only those who have been given [the degree] should be named, as some think, etc.

For this reason, in my judgment, a Licentiate <term>Licentiatus</term> <note>A degree holder authorized to practice law or teach, positioned just below a Doctor.</note> who has been solemnly inaugurated can more easily be decorated with the title of Doctor while absent than one who has only been permitted to seek and obtain that highest dignity when he wished. This is because the latter requires more ceremonies that demand the physical presence of the person. A comparison is made here between the Licentiate who has been solemnly inaugurated and the Doctor: regarding the examination, the display of customary ceremonies, and other matters during the inauguration, there is absolutely no difference, except that in the inauguration, the title of "Licentiate" is used instead of the word "Doctor." Also, a Licentiate does not provide a banquet <term>prandium</term> <note>original: "prandium"; a customary, expensive celebratory feast paid for by the graduate.</note>, which is why they are jokingly called **sober Doctors** <note>original: "nüchterne Doctores"</note>. And so it is held that when a promoted Licentiate assumes the title of Doctor, absolutely nothing further is required of him regarding ceremonies, nor must he perform anything else, except that he joins other new Doctors in the Act, is publicly proclaimed a Doctor, and helps pay for the banquet. However, for a Licentiate who has only been examined <note>One who has passed the tests but not yet undergone the formal public ceremony.</note>, more is required: namely, the taking of an oath, the performance of ceremonies, the receiving of the Ring and Biretta <note>original: "Bireti"; the doctoral cap.</note>, etc., and a public demonstration of his erudition by debating some legal question.

However, this is handled differently at various Universities, including in this region. The safest course would be to most humbly petition His Imperial Majesty for the extension of privileges, demonstrating the difficulties that arise, and requesting a most gracious grant: that even an absent, solemnly inaugurated Licentiate—or one who has already sustained all examinations—may be inaugurated as a Doctor and receive those honors through a proxy <term>Procuratorem</term>.

Zasius correctly denies this *on law 2 of the Digest "On summoning to court."* The argument is that neither one leading a funeral nor one celebrating a wedding can be summoned to court at that time. For such a summons would be quite untimely and disgraceful. Among the Popes, Limnaeus says he found four Doctors of Law, *in Public Law, book 8, chapter 8, number 8.* Regarding which Archbishops, Bishops, and Electors became Doctors and Licentiates, see Leonhard Wurffbain’s *Historical Relations, part 8, page 241.*

When a certain Italian, prideful of the name of Doctor, sought certain benefits (as they are called) from Gregory XIII—who, previously called Hugo Boncompagnus, was most famous for his learning in both Civil and Canon Law and was a Professor at Bologna—the Pope said to him: "Tell me, are you a *Doctor*, or just *doctorated*? <note>original: "utrùm Doctor ſis, an Doctoratus"</note> For the latter, few things are required; for the former, many things indeed, of which you perhaps have none." This careful distinction of times and merits ought to "tweak the ears" of those who distribute and judge academic honors <term>Diribitoribus ac Brabeutis</term>, lest with a sting of conscience they continue everywhere to mock the doctoral cap <term>tiarâ Doctorali</term> by placing it on unlearned, foolish, and unskilled men. This has become so easy today, especially under "French chimneys" <note>original: "ſub caminis Gallicis"; a contemporary jab at French universities for allegedly granting degrees too easily.</note>, just as in the old days slaves were manumitted by letter or even while the Praetor was going to the baths. Thus the complaint of the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius rightly finds a place here: "that many become veterans by means of certificates sought through fraud, who are not actually so." Neuhusius speaks excellently on this matter in his *Philosophical Sphinx, chapter 25*: "A foolish youth," he says, "comes to the church to receive the insignia of a Doctor. His teachers celebrate him, whether out of love or error. He swells with pride, the common people are amazed, and his kin and friends applaud. Being ordered, he ascends the chair, looking down on everything from on high and murmuring I know not what confusion. Then his elders, as if he had spoken divine words, lift him to the heavens with praises. Meanwhile, the bells ring, trumpets sound, rings fly, kisses are planted, and the round, Masterly Bonnet <term>Bonetus</term> is placed on his head. When these things are finished, he descends as a 'Wise Man,' he who had ascended a fool. A truly marvelous transformation, unknown even to Ovid. Thus are 'Wise Men' made today; a truly wise man is made otherwise."

# Thesaurus of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

...are naturally inclined, and only honor and glory are sought with deceptive pomp, rather than the foundation of truth or concise instruction. For this reason, no people have been found more unfit for government and the giving of counsel—indeed, even more harmful—than those who have been raised and accustomed in schools to such long-winded disputation <note>original: "Disputation"; a formal academic debate used as an examination method.</note>, yet knew little of the true basis of business. Nevertheless, a moderate consideration of a matter is not unhelpful, but can often be useful and good.

Because parents have seen their significant expenses, time, effort, and labor entirely lost on their children, and have further noted that an unlearned, inexperienced person might speak much better on common matters concerning both the soul and the body (where not disputation, but the right foundation and pure truth are required) than a great scholar: they have become tired of the expense and have, over time, withdrawn their support.

Today, in the name of the Emperor, Jurists <term>Jureconsulti</term> <note>Legal experts or consultants learned in the law.</note> are appointed by Universities and Counts Palatine <term>Comitibus Palatinis</term> <note>High-ranking officials with the authority to grant titles and degrees on behalf of the Emperor.</note>. Since the creation of Doctors in any art is done by right of Royal Prerogative, privileges can be granted to them even if no examination has preceded, according to Master Bachov in his *Disputation on Justice and Law, thesis 7, Treutler.* However, since the Doctorate is not a simple dignity but is founded on erudition—lest anyone be able to purchase the degree with money—it must be said that the power of creating Doctors is seen as granted only under the unspoken condition that they be suitable and worthy. Therefore, I believe those **"Bulled" Doctors** <note>original: "Bullatos istos Doctores"; those who received their degree via an official decree or "bull" rather than through the standard university process.</note> should be held in the same legal standing as those created in a University, provided they have been examined by experts in the field, found suitable, and provide proof of this through the testimony of good men. See Treutler on justice and law, thesis 7, and my own notes on law 7 regarding justice and law, question 4 and following. That no one becomes a Doctor through prescription <note>A legal term meaning the acquisition of a right through the passage of time.</note> is taught by Clausius in his *Disputation on Usucaption, chapter 45*, though it does create a presumption in his favor. But how a Doctorate is to be proven, see Pacianus's treatise *On Proofs*, in the Index.

Furthermore, should Jurists or Doctors be considered Masters? When was the title of Doctor invented? What are their insignia? Should Popes, Cardinals, Bishops, and other Prelates be Doctors? Borell teaches this in *On Magistracy, book 1, chapter 8.*

And should the sons of the College Doctors be examined for free? Vivius decides this in *Decision 159.* The same author, in *Decision 455*, states that a Doctor, especially one famous for his writings, should be promoted to public office ahead of others.

It is pleasing here to add a highly controversial question: whether someone who has been examined can be named a Doctor while absent.

Indeed, for the affirmative side, it was brought forward that: (1.) many times at Tübingen, the candidates for the Master's degree who had passed all examinations and received the "good news" <note>original: "bona nova"; a formal notification that a candidate had passed.</note>, but subsequently fell unexpectedly ill, were named together with the others in their absence and were, without any doubt, considered properly created Masters. In both cases, the same reasoning applies, and no difference is found in this regard between Doctors and Masters. Likewise, (2.) the patrons of this opinion argued that everything remaining that is necessary for the conferring of Doctoral honors upon this person (namely the swearing of the Oath and the administration of the customary solemnities) may be performed and received respectively through a proxy.

(3.) It also carries no little weight that some have referred to the practice of other Universities.

On the other hand, others have considered: (1.) that such dignity can only be conferred upon an absent person by the Emperor. And (2.) that the creation of a Doctor, as a certain solemn act, seems to require the presence of the person themselves, just like a coronation or some similar inaugural act.

Item (3.) it would be safer to follow the ordinary path, so that a controversy regarding the status of a Doctor created in such a way is not stirred up, or a bad reputation brought upon the University itself. This is especially true because the practice of certain Universities alleged to the contrary was not proven, and even among the Masters who might be created in absence as mentioned above, it does not mean as much, considering they almost always remain within the local territory. See my treatise *On the Law of Academic Matters and Colleges, folio 213, section 7.*

Even less can one be created without any previous examination, even if everyone knows him to be worthy. This is because the examination and other things directed toward sufficient exploration are held as the "form" of an Academic Doctor, according to the *Annotator on the Lectures of Martinus Uranius.* In this, they differ from the "Bulled" Doctors. The magnificent Master Melander says in his *Commentary on the Process of Noah Meurer, folio 115*, it would also be a cause of concern and a slight to a University if such unexamined Doctors were made. And it is an Imperial reserve to create a Doctor with a single word, according to Ohemius in *On the Law of Bishops, thesis 17, letter T.*

But a Licentiate who has been solemnly promoted and proclaimed, and who has already taken the oath, could perhaps be made a Doctor while absent. Since such a person is considered a true Doctor in favorable legal acts. See Benius *On the Privileges of Jurists, part 3*, at the beginning; Matthaeus Stephanus *On Universities, chapter 14, number 48*; Master Doctor Lansius *On Universities, folio 73*; and Ritter *On Homage, chapter 5, number 96, folio 73*, where he says that those who have only held their inaugural disputation and legitimately sustained the examination are not called Licentiates, but candidates...

...some think that only those [who actually teach] should be called [doctors], etc.

For this reason, in my judgment, a Licentiate who has been formally announced <note>original: "Licentiatus, renunciatus"</note> can more easily be adorned with the title of Doctor even in his absence, compared to someone who is only permitted to seek and obtain the highest literal dignity when he wishes. This is because the latter requires more formalities that demand the person’s physical presence. The situation here <note>The author likely refers to a specific German university context</note> is such that between a Licentiate formally announced and a Doctor, no difference at all is maintained regarding the examination, the display of customary formalities, or otherwise during the announcement, except that in the announcement, instead of the word "Doctor," the title of "Licentiate" is used. Also, a Licentiate does not provide a banquet <term>prandium</term>, which is why they are jokingly called "sober Doctors." It is held that when a promoted Licentiate assumes the title of Doctor, absolutely nothing further is required of him here regarding formalities, nor must he perform further acts, except that he joins other new Doctors in the Ceremony <note>original: "Actum"</note>, is publicly proclaimed a Doctor, and helps pay for the banquet. However, for a Licentiate who has only been examined <note>original: "Licentiato tantum examinato"</note>, more is required: namely, the taking of an oath, the application of formalities like the Ring and the Biretta <note>A square academic hat</note>, etc., and a public demonstration of his learning by disputing some question of Law.

However, this is handled differently at various Universities. The safest course would be to petition his Imperial Majesty for an extension of Privileges, demonstrating the difficulties encountered, and most humbly request that it be explicitly and graciously permitted that even an absent Licentiate, formally announced, or one who has already sustained all examinations, can be announced as a Doctor and receive those honors through a Proxy.

# Expanded Treasury of Practice

...are naturally inclined toward such things, seeking only honor and glory with outward show, rather than the foundation of truth or concise instruction. For this reason, no people have been found more unfit, or even more harmful, for government and counsel than those who have been raised and accustomed in schools to such long-winded disputation, yet know little of the actual basis of business. Nevertheless, moderate discussion and the mature consideration of a matter from both sides can often be useful and good.

Because parents have seen their significant expenses, time, effort, and labor entirely wasted on their children, and have noted that an unlearned, inexperienced man can often speak better on common matters concerning both soul and body (where the true foundation and pure truth are required, not disputation) than a great scholar, they have grown tired of the expense and have, over time, withdrawn their support.

Today, in the name of the Emperor, legal consultants <note>original: "Jureconsulti"</note> are appointed by Universities and by Counts Palatine. Indeed, the creation of Doctors in any art is done by right of royal prerogative <note>original: "jure Regalium"</note>, and privileges can be granted to them even if no examination has preceded, according to Master Bachov in his *Disputation on Justice and Law* <note>original: "disput. de justit. & jur."</note> at thesis 7 of Treutler. However, since the Doctorate is not a simple dignity but is founded upon erudition—lest anyone be able to buy the degree with money—it must be said that the power of creating Doctors is seen to be granted only under the unspoken condition that they are fit and worthy.

<margin>Treutler, *On Justice and Law*, thesis 7. See my notes on law 7, *On Justice and Law*, question 4 and following.</margin>

Therefore, I believe those "Bullate Doctors" <note>Doctors created by a diploma or "bull" from a Count Palatine rather than a university</note> should be held in the same legal standing as those created in a University, provided they have been examined by those skilled in the art, found fit, and provide proof of this through the testimony of good men.

That no one becomes a Doctor through prescription <note>A legal term meaning the acquisition of a right through the passage of time</note> is taught by Clasius in his *Disputation on Usucaption*, chapter 45; however, it does create a presumption in his favor.

...to be called "given" [titles] only, as estimated by some, etc.

For this reason, in my judgment, a **Licentiate** <term>Licentiatus: a degree-holder who has the 'license' to teach but has not yet taken the final ceremonial step to become a Doctor</term> who has been solemnly declared can be more easily decorated with the title of **Doctor** while absent than one who has only been permitted to seek and obtain the highest literal dignity when he wished. ### Enlarged Practical Treasury

23. They should maintain a fineness of 23 carats and 8 grains <note>original: "Carat 8. Grän halten"</note>, and no one, regardless of rank or status, shall exchange, buy, or sell them from the mints, or otherwise accept or issue them in payment for more than 104 kreuzers. However, it is permitted for anyone to accept or issue them at a lower or closer rate. The same is found in the Recess of Spires <note>original: "Comit. Spirens."</note> from the year 1570, in the section "that we also," etc.

It is therefore established that in every individual ducat, 1/72 part is foreign and made of non-gold metal <note>This refers to the "alloy" added to gold to make the coin durable enough for circulation.</note>. Thus, he who has 72 ducats, by refining them to the highest purity, would retain the weight of at least 71 ducats in the purest refined gold <note>original: "obryzato"</note>.

But it must not be overlooked here that, by virtue of the Minting Ordinance, not just any Estate <note>An "Estate" refers to a territory or ruler with political standing in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> privileged with the legal right of the mint may manufacture ducats; but only those who possess gold mines. This is what the Emperor says in the aforementioned section: **Since several Estates of the Empire have high-quality gold deposits <note>original: "hohe Golder fallen haben"</note> in their lands and territories.** And Emperor Maximilian II, in the Imperial Recess at Regensburg in the year 1576, states: **And out of specific, reasonable considerations of the present Estates, Councils, and Embassies, we wish to reiterate here in our Imperial Minting Edict the permit (to mint ducats): namely, that minting ducats is only appropriate for those Estates that have high-quality gold deposits in their lands and territories, etc.** What this phrase (**having high gold or high gold deposits in one's land**) means is clarified by Emperor Charles V in the *Imperial Recess* at Augsburg in the year 1551: **However, others—aside from those who have gold mines—shall henceforth mint no other gold than according to the weight and fineness of Our and the Empire's Electors of the Rhine, as has been minted until now.** The reason for this rule may be the excellence of gold, and that gold currency in general is among the "Reserved Rights" of the supreme Prince, acting as a peculiar mark of supreme Majesty. This is established in the *Lombard Law* and other legal commentaries <note>The author cites several legal scholars, including Zeetschium's "Disputation on the Right of Coinage."</note>.

->### ADDITION.<-

For the Italians, it is *Ducato*, for us Germans **a Ducat** <note>original: "ein Ducat"</note>, used to refer to the currency. This gold coin was first struck by the Venetians and Genoese. But also by the English, as Polydore Vergil writes. What he had in mind, I do not know, as Marquard Freher writes in *On Matters of Money* <note>original: "de re monet."</note> book 1, chapter 3, page 44. In another place, he wrote that the Ducat minted at Rome was named after the Duchy <note>original: "Ducato"</note>, a magistracy first established by Longinus, who was appointed as successor to Narses, the Governor of Italy, by Emperor Justin. In book 2 of *On the Discovery of Things* <note>original: "de invent. rer."</note>, chapter 21. For **Räbleins-Ducats**, see the word **Mint.** A Duke is invested with the golden crown of a Duchy. *Limn.*

<column-break/>

How payment should be made when a loan is granted in specific types of coins, such as Ducats or Thalers, in kind or piece by piece. *Zorer, part 2, question 17, number 2085.* Whether the borrowed ducats must be delivered in the same minting as they were received or not. *Question 17, number 2093. Regarding the Byzantine gold coin, see Draco on the Patricians, page 187.*

A Roman Duke first ordered a gold coin of proper integrity to be struck at Rome, which for that reason was called the Roman Ducat <note>original: "Romanus Ducatus"</note>, using the somewhat barbaric vocabulary of that time. *Girolamo Rossi, History of Ravenna, book 3, page 176 and following.* Tholosan partly disagrees with this narrative in *The Republic*, book 6. However, Giovanni Nicolo Doglioni, in *Venice Triumphant and Always Free*, affirms that this gold currency called the Ducat was first minted in *Venice*, and afterwards struck at *Rome* and elsewhere according to this same form. He adds these words from an ancient Chronicle of the Chancellor: "This Doge Giovanni Dandolo, in the year 1280, caused to be struck with most happy success the most beautiful gold coins called Ducats, which obscured the fame of the gold coins of all other nations, to such an extent that several Christian and Pagan Princes, moved by the fame of the perfection of these same Ducats, caused infinite gold coins to be struck in their image." The name perhaps arose from the inscription or words stamped on this Venetian coin; for on one side the name of the Doge was read, and on the other:

> Let this Duchy, which you rule, O Christ, be given to you.
<note>original: "Sit tibi Christe datus, quem tu regis, iste Ducatus." This is a famous Latin hexameter where the word "Ducatus" refers both to the Duchy of Venice and the coin itself.</note>

*Limnaeus in Public Law, volume 1, additions to book 4, chapter 3, number 32.*

### 34. Duel. See above under letter A, the word "Challenge." Duel <note>original: "Duellum"</note>.

Concerning Duels, see Conrad Lancellot in *The Temple of All Judges*, folio 24 and following. Also Antonio Massani Gallesio on the *Use of the Duel*. Camerarius in *Historical Meditations*, century 2, chapter 19. Louis Guyon in *Diverse Lessons*, volume 2, folio 40. Botero, book 9, folio 59. See my own work in the *Treatise on Punishments*. Böckel, *Criminal Disquisitions*, 6, number 13. Book 7 of the *Decretals*, book 5, title 17. Fabio Albergati. Zeiller in *Sorrowful Histories*, folio 122, 118, and elsewhere, as is established in the Index or the *Treatise on Duels*. Also the *Treatise on the Point of Honor*, and the French treatise *The Bed of Honor* <note>original: "Le Lict d'honneur"</note>. Martin Bonacina's *Compendium* under the word Duel. Caspar von Lerch, on the *Knights of the Teutonic Order*, folio 72. Against Duels, see P. Gretser in *The Saints of Eichstätt*, folio 492. Decrees concerning Duels can be found in Hotoman under *Feudal Words*, folio 600, and many pages following.

When duels were introduced into Italy, see Cardinal Baronius in *Abridged Annals*, folio 63. Whether a person challenged to single combat is bound to allow himself to be killed or rather to surrender himself as conquered, see Jacob Martin, *Illustrious Questions*, century 5, discussion 8, questions 7 and 9. Also Laudensis *On War*, and the commentary there at question 10.

# Letter D.

<margin>Question 10. A memorable example of an execution carried out against duelists <note>original: "Duellatores"</note> is found in the *French Mercury* <note>original: "Mercure François"</note>, volume 13, folio 40.</margin>

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the Duel, there exists an oration by Johann Derrer on the privileges of Altdorf, and a singular treatise by Vischer. See also Schönborn in *Politics*, page 639. A distinguished Count <note>original: "Gray," likely a variant of "Graf" (Count)</note> said publicly at the table to two Barons during the St. Bartholomew’s Market in Linz in the year 1624 that he would not even want to sit in heaven with a coward <note>original: "Verzagten"</note> or one who refused a challenge or a duel. Zeiller, century 1, *Letters*, page 227.

Cajus Rumohr, a Holstein Knight, held a long and accurate dispute regarding the duel in Altdorf in 1658, in which many unique points are alleged, especially that passage by Sebastian Münster in *Cosmography*, book 5, chapter 248, newest edition; Nicolaus Reusner on the Imperial Cities, book 2, chapter 7, concerning Hall in Swabia <note>original: "Hala Suevorum"</note>; Lehmann’s *Chronicle of Speyer*, book 7, chapter 90, and the same in chapter 98 for the year 1440. Zeiller, *Tragic Events*, history 4, near the end.

### 35. Transit of Criminals. <note>original: "Durchfuhr der Maleficanten / Transmissio Delinquentium"</note>

Whether a Prince must allow noblemen to transport their criminals <note>original: "Maleficanten," specifically those accused of capital crimes</note> through his land, or if he can prevent them? In the event that the evildoer appeals to the local Lord for a legal hearing and justice in the place where he is being transported, whether the Lord of the Territory <note>original: "Dominus Territorii"</note> ought to take charge of him, etc. See Bidembach, question 11; Valentin Riemer on jurisdiction, chapter 3; Wehner in *Franconian Counsels*, 92; and my own work on the law of things <note>original: "de jur. rerum"</note>, folio 273.

In the legal records of Ortenburg versus Bavaria, folio 23, a complaint is made on behalf of Bavaria that the Count encroached upon His Princely Highness's authority. He forcibly led a man subject to the provincial court through the Ducal territory, contrary to common and specific provincial laws, and committed other such acts of arrogance, for which the appropriate punishment was reserved.

On whether it is permitted to lead a captured enemy through foreign territory, see Alberico Gentili on advocacy, chapter 6; and regarding a captive led through a Church, see the following chapter.

->ADDITION.<-

Mr. Speidel, in his *Mirror of Notable Things* <note>original: "Speculo Notabilium"</note> under this word: Can a higher judge himself seize a delinquent in a territory where another holds lower jurisdiction <note>original: "bassam Jurisdictionem," referring to minor civil matters rather than capital crimes</note>, without the other’s permission? It is affirmed, because when jurisdiction is granted to someone, those powers without which the jurisdiction cannot be exercised are also deemed granted. Law 2, *Digest* on jurisdiction; chapter "by reason of suspicion," 39, *Decretals* on the office and power of a delegated judge. Moneta on the preservation of judges, chapter 7, numbers 80 and following; and a judge 

<column-break/>

who prepares a case must also be the judge of the preparatory acts. Decianus in his *Treatise on Crimes*, book 4, chapter 30, number 6. Therefore, a superior judge in cases pertaining to criminal jurisdiction may, even without a request, not only verbally cite but also seize and lead away captives who are subjects of a territory in which another holds civil jurisdiction and stewardship <note>original: "Vogtheiam," a form of local administrative guardianship</note>. Franzkius, book 1, *Various Resolutions*, question 18, number 10. Carpzov in *Criminal Practice*, question 109, numbers 80 and 84. Indeed, through the territory of another holder of jurisdiction, an official may lead a delinquent from his own authority through another’s territory until he reaches a place where he again has authority over capital and civil matters. Klock, counsel 53, volume 1.

### 36. Transporting the Deceased. <note>original: "Durchführung der Verstorbenen / Transportare Defunctos per territorium alienum"</note>

There seems to be no doubt that a dead person can be transported through another's territory after a mere notification <note>original: "nudam denunciationem"</note>. For no one should be prevented from using the public road, and transporting a deceased person is different from leading a captive. The latter involves force and seems to reflect a jurisdictional act, whereas the former clearly does not. However, a different practice is observed if, for example, a Lutheran is killed or dies in a Catholic location; in such cases, at the instance of the relatives or the magistrate of their home residence, such persons are usually not released unless a formal written guarantee <note>original: "Revers"</note> is provided.

### 37. Düttich. <note>A type of coin</note>

*Düttich* are nothing other than double silver groschen <note>original: "doppelt Silbergroschen"</note>. They are minted in great quantities and with distinct stamps among the Poles and are common in the Empire. However, they do not match the required standard of quality, and therefore most Imperial Circles <note>Administrative groupings of states within the Holy Roman Empire</note> have sought their rejection or devaluation, even in the Imperial Diets. Hanfman on coinage, among the Basel disputations, volume 2, thesis 5, under the letter f.

### 38. Danube. <note>original: "Donau / Danubius"</note>

->The Danube,<-
->Is the Lady of Grace of all waters,<-
->The Rhine,<-
->May be her husband with honor.<-

Meyfart in the *Compendium of Geography*, page 230. Regarding the Danube as a Count, see Nicolaus Myler on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 3, number 18. The Danube, King of Rivers: Lipsius, book 1, chapter 3, on *Constancy*.

### 39. Gland. <note>original: "Drüß / Glandula"</note>

The word *Drüß* <note>modern German "Drüse," meaning gland or swelling</note> is said to have come from the name *Druso*. Zeiller, *German Itinerary*, page 45. *Deus*, an oak tree <note>referring to a linguistic derivation</note>, comes from a *Drüß*, for if an oak tree fell on someone's head, it would strike a great swelling <note>original: "Drüß"</note>. Schottel in *The German Main Language*, folio 56.

### 40. De.

The particle *De* is equivalent to the particle *pro* <note>original: "pro" (for/on behalf of)</note>, according to *Mr. Dr. Tabor in Synoptic Treatise, page 431, number 18. See Torsellino on the Particles of the Latin Language, chapter 41, sections 4 and 14; Barbosa on frequently used words, word 76, numbers 3, 8, and especially number 18.* *De* is sometimes taken in a negative sense, such as *demens* <note>out of one's mind</note>, *deformis* <note>misshapen</note>, or *degener* <note>degenerate</note>. *Valentin Wilhelm Forster on Pacts, page 15.*

### 41. Diple.

What it means to write a *Diple* <note>A diple is a sideways V-shaped mark (>) used in manuscripts to mark quotations or noteworthy text</note> is explained at length by *Mr. Dr. Tabor in the Elements of Jurisprudence, Corollary 2.*

### 42. Dominicale.

Regarding what a *dominicale* is, see *Dürr on Manorial Courts, thesis 7.* In the Council of Auxerre <note>A 6th-century church council held in France</note>, article 39, these words are found: "A woman cannot receive communion, nor approach the Lord’s Supper, unless she has her *dominicale*, that is, a linen cloth." The host was received by a man not with the mouth, but with the hands, and indeed with washed hands; a woman, however, was compelled to receive it with a linen cloth, not with bare hands. *From the mouth of Mr. Dr. Dorsch.*

### 43. Diets.

Regarding what Diets <note>original: "Diætæ"; political assemblies or parliaments</note> are, see *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 9, chapter 1, numbers 12 and 13.* Any Diet has another within its belly <note>An idiom suggesting that one assembly often spawns sub-committees or further sessions</note>, in the same location, number 27. Articles of the Diet, **Landtags Artickel**, *Mr. Dr. Tabor in the Collation of Roman and Hungarian Law, part 1, section 2, B. 12.*

### 44. Dieta.

A *dieta* <note>dieta here refers to a dwelling or daily room</note> is a place in which the father of the family stays during the day. It is used for a small house prepared for the sake of enjoying its fruits, and likewise for a dining room. *More in Sprenger on the Law of Buildings, page 69.* How a *dieta* <note>here referring to a "day's journey"</note> is calculated, see *Muñoz de Escobar on Accounts, part 2, account 12, where he cites Catellianus Cotta in Memorabilia, under the word Dieta.* What a *dieta* is, see *Boerius, decision 230, numbers 3 and 5.*

### 45. Damit. [With it/So that].

**Damit.** *Compare Marburg Consultations 26, number 233, volume 1.* **Davon.** [Of it/From there]. *ibid, number 195.*

### 46. Devotion. see Love, Faithful.

Devoted, devotion. *Mr. Dr. Tabor on Change of Status, page 230; the same author on Succession of Obligations, page 260.* Devotions are sometimes understood to mean executions of legal orders. *Tiraqueau, book 1 on Retraction, section 1, gloss 9, number 279, at the end.*

### 47. To write with the fingers, To point the finger.

To write with the fingers is to speak with nods and gestures. *Ovid:*
> --- there were no letters on the fingers. <note>A reference to secret signaling or the lack of physical writing on the hands</note>

*Ennius says of a certain unchaste woman:* "She gives letters to others with her finger," which Solomon said in *Proverbs 6*: "He winks with the eye, stamps with the foot, and speaks with the finger." *Hermann Hugo on the First Origin of Writing, page 32.* What "pointing the finger" sometimes implies, see *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 8, chapter 6, number 102.*

<column-break/>

**Schiessfinger** <note>literally "shooting finger"; the index finger</note>, the finger from which one shoots. *Justus Georg Schottel in The German Main Language, folio 46.* If someone cuts off another's finger used for shooting, he shall pay fifteen solidi <note>A gold coin used as a legal unit of compensation</note> in restitution. Pressing the thumb implies favor; turning it is believed to deny it. *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 4, chapter 7, number 39.* A finger is not considered a limb. This rule is approved and distinguished in *Vivant, book 2 on Attempts, section on Homicide, number 5, with the three following; and Claro, final section, question 69, on the word "likewise I ask," there, from this it is inferred.*

### 48. To Destine.

*Destinare* [To destine] stands for *mittere* [to send]. *Law 5, Code of Justinian, on Change of Status.* *Mr. Tabor on Change of Status, page 85, number 15.* This "Destining" contains, however: 1. prior deliberation, and 2. timely notification.

### 49. Depectio. [An Agreement].

*Depectio* is used in a negative sense and as a response in two places in Cicero. *Valentin Wilhelm Forster, Book of Observations, chapter 14, page 24; the same on Pacts, page 14.*

### 50. To Depute.

The word for deputizing <note>original: "Deputandi"</note> is found in *Law 1, Code of Justinian, on the collection of the fiscal estate (11. 73).*

### 51. He Owes.

The word for owing <note>original: "Debendi"</note> has the broadest possible application. *Mr. Dr. Tabor in Elements of Jurisprudence, part 4, section 2, thesis 9, at the end; Limnaeus, book 9, chapter 4, number 30.*

### 52. Delegation.

*Christian Lenz in the treatise on Assigned Names and Actions* deals extensively with delegation. Novation <note>The replacement of an old obligation with a new one</note> is always inherent in delegation. *Zorer, part 1, question 6, number 490.* In delegation, it must be considered when and how it was done. *question 6, number 490 and following.* Whether and how a creditor is bound to accept a delegate from his debtor. *question 6, number 481, and the 3 following; likewise question 9, number 644.* Delegation is understood in various ways. *Mr. Dr. Tabor on the Succession of Obligations in Office, page 277.*

### 53. Donawerd. Donauwerda.

*Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain in Historical Relations, page 201; Limnaeus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 13.*

### 54. That. Datium, Tax.

Regarding **Dazen** <note>A historical term for a local tax or tribute</note>, see the Acts of the Teutonic Knights in the **Nuremberg** Deduction-Script, folio 27.
Regarding the excise tax [**Ungelt**], **Tax/Toll** [**Dass/Zoll**] and all burdens, see *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 9, chapter 2, section 33.*
