**55. Ink. <note>original: "Dinten. Atramentum."</note>**

The tax on ink. *Pacius in the Analysis of the Code, title on taxes, number 6.* Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous Italian jurist</note> holds that the validity of human acts does not depend on a small amount of ink, and the Prince establishes laws not with words, but with substance. *Law 2 at the end, Code on the commonality of laws.*

Regarding the Prefect of Ink, *Rupert in Universal History, book 4, chapter 11.* Those lords who have the power to judge over life and death were permitted to write with red ink. An instrument of obligation <note>a contract or debt bond</note> can be accused of forgery based on a difference in the ink. *Alexander Stiaticus in Practical Observations, chapter 15, number 17.* On this opinion, jurists of great name are cited by *Prospero Farinacci, question 153, part 1, number 15; part 9, number 155.* But although a difference in ink causes someone slight suspicion, *Marra in the Newest Digest, volume 2, title on forgery, chapter 2,* nevertheless, the difference in ink alone does not prove the forgery of a writing, unless a difference in handwriting also concurs. *Giacomo Menochio on Presumptions, book 5, preface 20, number 9; and consultation 221, number 35, book 3.* More can be found in *Bullaeus in Consultations, page 159 and following.* Regarding the diversity of ink, see *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 14, number 7, and those cited there.*

**56. Pentagram. <note>original: "Drudenfuß." Literally "hag's foot," a five-pointed star symbol used in folk magic and protection.</note>**

From where it is named, see *Mr. Saubert on the Sacrifices of the Ancients, page 209.* *Schottelius in the German Main Language, folio 1306.*

**57. People of the Lord. <note>original: "Druhtinsvolck." An archaic German term.</note>**

*Mr. Saubert on Sacrifices, page 154,* used for Christians. Regarding who the *Druden* <note>folk spirits or sorceresses</note> were, and from where this word comes, see *Schottelius in the German Main Language, folio 56.*

**58. Then. <note>original: "Dann. Nam."</note>**

This is not to be understood as causal, but as consequential. *Danhauer in the Evangelical Memorial, folio 890.*

**59. Drillmaster. <note>original: "Drillmeister. Campi Doctores."</note>**

Field Doctors <note>original: "Campi Doctores"; military instructors</note>, *Klock, consultation 20, number 62.* On the bearing of arms and drilling, see *Nicolaus Myler on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 75.*

**60. The. <note>original: "Die. Hæc."</note>**

The word "Die" <note>the feminine or plural "the" in German</note> is not explanatory, but restrictive. *Limnaeus in Public Law, volume 1, additions to book 4, chapter 8, page 611 and following.*

# E.

**1. Noble Servant. <note>original: "Edelknecht. Ministeriales."</note>**

Noble servants <note>original: "Edelknecht"</note> were formerly called warriors <note>original: "Degen"</note>, *Goldast in the Admonitions, folio 364.* The Latins call them *Ministeriales* <note>a class of unfree nobility who served as administrators or knights</note>, regarding whom Bi-

<column-break/>

gnon writes in the notes to *Marculf's Formulas, folio 627 and following.*

->ADDITION.<-

Those have been called "Edlings" or noble servants who were free from their origin and beginning, and whose freedom had lasted from one to another for many years beyond memory, and who were never made into servants or slaves: almost everywhere they are called *Ministeriales*. *Lehmann in the Speyer Chronicle, book 1, chapter 19.*

**2. Gemstone. <note>original: "Edelstein. Gemma."</note>**

See *Johann Guidus in the treatise on Minerals, chapter 6.*

->ADDITION.<-

In Grenoble is the Bishop’s treasury, and among other things, a ring case in which large stones are set into the rings; among others, a large ruby worth 100,000 francs. A small tobacco box made of two rubies is worth 50,000 francs.

> It is set ablaze with gems and gold. This means it flashes with the likeness of a fire. *Barthius, Observations on Papinius Statius, book 9 of the Thebaid, page 974.*

In the case of movable property and goods, one looks at daily purchases and trades, yet precious things <note>original: "res pretiosæ"</note>, such as gemstones and pearls, are excluded from this. *Zorer, part 1, question 2, number 215.* To our ancestors, *Dedt* <note>possibly a dialect variant for "property" or "deed"</note> signifies inheritance, patrimony, goods, or fields: from which the more precious and finer hereditary goods are called *Kleinodia* <note>heirlooms or jewels</note>. *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputes.* A single diamond in Antwerp was sold for 150,000 crowns, which weighed only one ounce. *Mr. Dilherr in Garden Delights, page 340.* The lord of the territory claims the veins of precious stones for himself. *Nicolaus Myler on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 69.* *Volter on Minerals, volume 4.*

*Count Reinhard of Solms in the Description of the Nobility, page 10:* The stones in rings are called gemstones <note>original: "Edelgestein"</note> after the nobility <note>original: "Adel"</note>, because it is said they possess virtues within them. In the crown of the King of France is a stone the size of a walnut, which is presented as a carbuncle and is valued at 30,000 crowns. *Schickfuss in the Silesian Chronicle, book 1, chapter 37,* says the Lords Fugger <note>a powerful German banking family</note> possess the noble adamant <note>diamond</note> of Charles <note>Charles the Bold</note>, which they value as equal to the income of a king.

->Thesauri Practici Adaucti<-
<note>original: "Augmented Practical Treasuries," a common title for legal or encyclopedic reference works of the 17th century.</note>

In the treasury vault at Innsbruck, there is a large diamond said to be worth 50,000 Thalers <note>a silver coin used throughout Europe for centuries</note>. The beautiful golden image of Mary and the knight, which is still in Ingolstadt, is estimated to be worth over one hundred thousand Guilders. Everything is decorated with fine gold and adorned with a great multitude of sapphires, rubies, pearls, and other stones. On the breast of the image of Mary, there is a particular ruby cut like a heart, which is said to be worth 14,000 florins. In Bourges, in the Archbishop’s Church of St. Stephen, there is a chalice of immeasurable value, featuring wonderful and artistic craftsmanship with perfectly round rubies and pearls. It was cast together with its lid in such a way that every little piece is distinct, yet when they are put together, they show no sign of joining; the whole thing is transparent and clearly visible to the eye. **Regarding the Sapphire of Emperor Constantius Augustus** <note>original: "De Sapphiro Constantii Imper. Augusti"</note>, one should see Freher in the pages published in 1602 and recently re-issued. Concerning a jewel kept in an iron box, offered for sale, and **at whose risk it remains** <note>original: "cujus sit periculum," a legal term regarding liability for loss or damage</note>, Mr. Hahn discusses this extensively in the Digest, book 19, title 3, near the end. On the giving of gems for sacrifices, see D. Saubert in *Sacrifices of the Ancients*, page 650. On a person who could split and break a gemstone with his eyes, see Zeiller, century 4, question 40, page 212.

### 3. Edict. Edicta.
<note>Latin: "Edicts" or "Proclamations"</note>

To post public proclamations and edicts <note>original: "Proclamationes & Edicta affigere publica"</note>—to post public mandates and edicts—proves the natural and actual "quasi-possession" of higher jurisdiction, which we now call territorial sovereignty <note>original: "Lands Obrigkeit"</note>. See Natta, counsel 636, number 77; Mascardus on proofs, conclusion 846, number 2; Ruin. counsel 2, number 4, volume 4. To obey these edicts, both in doing something and in refraining from doing something, constitutes a jurisdictional act in itself, although a greater and fuller subjection is thereby established. Knichen in the *Encyclopedia*, chapter 8, citing Baldus on the law *data opera*, number 28, Code on those who cannot accuse: that this cannot occur without the name and right of subjection. The same author at law 2, number 60, Code on services and water: for subjection is possessed through obedience, as Baldus speaks in the rubric on majority and obedience, number 1, by which jurisdiction is both acquired and preserved. Knichen, cited work; Meichsner, decision 6, numbers 26 and 52.

### ADDITIO.
<note>Latin: "Addition" or "Supplement"</note>

Regarding when edictal summons <note>original: "Citationes Edictales"</note> are customary, see Suttinger, observation 8, number 3, where he states: we find summons or notifications "at the doors" <note>original: "ad valvas," referring to the practice of posting a notice on a church or courthouse door</note> in the common law. Gail, book 1, observation 57; Wurmser, book 1, title 6, observation 8. Thus, according to judicial custom, they do not take place unless the defendant cannot be found anywhere and has no residence of his own. Schwarzenth., book 1, act 1, chapter 2, number 8. For this reason, edicts are granted very rarely, or only with an express clause

<column-break/>

granting permission, provided that the execution itself is carried out for those interested parties present in the land. *Ibid.*, on summons issued by the court's office, number 5. Regarding the tearing down of edicts, commands, and mandates, and how this is punished, Melonius treats this in title 49, number 43, where he establishes that whoever removes or tears one down in a malicious manner shall suffer the punishment and penalty for forgery/falsification. To whom the right of posting edicts and proclamations issued by a higher Lord belongs: whether to the one who holds the high sovereign authority <note>original: "Oberbottmäßigkeit"</note> or to the bailiff <note>original: "Vogtherrn"</note>? Since posting proclamations and edicts publicly—and in those matters which concern public utility or even the Prince's own interest—notifying subjects, establishing penalties for transgressors, and exacting them when committed, proves actual "quasi-possession" of higher jurisdiction and is a sign of territorial jurisdiction. Mascardus, conclusion 498, number 2, volume 2; Thomas Michael on Jurisdiction, conclusion 52, letter c; Matth. Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 7, number 350; Klock, consultation 181, number 66, volume 3. It is easy to gather that there is no probable reason why one who holds "mixed power" <note>original: "mixtum Imperium"</note>, meaning lower jurisdiction <note>original: "Untergerichtbarkeit"</note>, could claim this right for himself. Rather, it belongs to the one who enjoys territorial superiority, so that such edicts and proclamations are posted publicly by his authority. Matth. Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 7, number 350. Nor is it necessary to first deliver them to those holding the bailiwick <note>original: "Vogthejam"</note> in that place, by whose command and authority they would later be posted on the church doors or read publicly to the subjects by a minister of the Church. The claim of lower Lords, therefore, that the said right of posting belongs to them, has no basis. H. G. Christoph Gugel the Elder, on February 28, Anno 1571, made a distinction between mandates and their four types: 1. ### 4. Eger. Egra.
<note>Eger, now known as Cheb in the Czech Republic, was a vital border city of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

Eger and the County of Elbogen <note>original: "Elenbogensis," now Loket</note> are situated on German soil and in Upper Bavaria. This city was transformed from a princely city into an Imperial City <note>a city responsible only to the Emperor, not a local lord</note> in the year of Christ 1179. For how it actually came to the Kingdom of Bohemia, see Mr. Goldast, *Bohemia*, chapter 17.

### ADDITION.

The judicial taxes of Eger are noted by D. Mundius, for in his youth he was a counselor and syndic there and observed this laudable custom: that an appellant <note>the person making a legal appeal</note> is forced to deposit a certain sum of money, which they lose if they fail in their case. Schepliz also attests to this regarding the March of Brandenburg in *The State of Brandenburg*, part 2, title 11, page 2, number 1; and Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, chapter 9, number 32. Andernacus notes that certain medicinal waters, even when actually cold, flow out with a certain sound, just as if they were boiling. Such are the acidic springs <note>mineral waters</note> near the Bohemian Forest almost in the very suburb of the town of Eger, and several other springs in the vicinity; because these burst forth boiling with a great sound, like a kind of thunder, they are called "insane and furious." This is witnessed by G. Agricola <note>the famous mineralogist</note> in book 1, *On the Nature of Those Things Which Flow from the Earth*, page 96; and Andernacus in *Dialogue 2 on Baths*, page 124; and Sebizius, *Dissertation on Acidic Springs 5*, section 1, page 160.

Regarding the Eger District, and how the Egerland came to the Bavarian Counts of Vohburg in the year 1120. In the year of Christ 1179, through a marriage, it passed to Frederick I <note>Emperor Frederick Barbarossa</note>, subsequently staying with the Empire through Henry VI, Philip I, until the death of Henry VII in the year of Christ 1313, at which time it came to the Crown of Bohemia. See Leonhard Wurffbain, *Historical Relations*, part 3, page 25. More in part 6, page 134, on how in the year of Christ 915 it was assigned to the Imperial Prefectures <note>original: "Reichsvogteyen"</note> established at Nuremberg by Conrad I.
See Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain, in *Historical Relations*, page 201; and Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 13.

Zeiller in his *Handbook of Memorable Things*, part 1, title "The State of Marriage," reports that in our Germany it is not infrequent for fifty-year spouses <note>those married for 50 years</note> to celebrate a kind of second wedding, repeating the nuptial solemnities. He adds the example of Georg von Pflaumern who, having completed 50 years with the spouse whom in the previous 

<column-break/>

Likewise, Nicolaus Vahrenbühler, a Counselor of Württemberg, celebrated a second solemn wedding in Stuttgart with his wife Regina Walther in the year 1597; and Heinrich von Friesen, Chancellor of the Elector of Saxony, did the same on March 15, 1651, in Dresden.

### 6. Adultery. Adulterium.

Under the most recent Justinian Law <note>the 6th-century Roman legal code that formed the basis of European civil law</note>, the male is punished more severely than the female in this crime (Authority: *But Today*, Code on Adultery), because of the greater constancy of the sex and a lesser propensity for lust. See Tiraquellus in *On Marriage Laws*, number 85 and book 9, number 110; see Jacob Martini, *Illustrious Questions*, century 5, disputation 3, thesis 10. Antonio Monterus in *Decisions of Aragon*, 15, at the beginning, who nevertheless in number 17 reports that even the adulteress is rightly punished with the death penalty according to the laws of the Kingdom of Aragon. In number 21, he disapproves of those who say that—according to general and notorious custom which needs no proof—adulteries should be punished not corporally, but extraordinarily and with fines. Certainly, the Julian Law <note>Lex Julia, an ancient Roman law from the time of Augustus</note> did not punish adulteries with the death penalty. And Saint Augustine, in book 3, chapter 5 of *The City of God*, expressly says: the Romans punished adulterous women with some condemnation, but never with death. See Brisson on the *Julian Law on Adultery*, page 216; and extensively Theodoric in *Criminal College*, Aa. 1. b.; and myself in *On the Three Domestic Societies*, page 12, in the deliberation on book 4 of the *Digest*, question 23. And Richard testifies in his *German Counsels*, counsel 115, number 8: **that he knows of no land of the German nation, outside of the Electorate and Principality of Saxony, in which adultery is punished by the sword.**

See *Counsels of Strasbourg*, volume 2, counsel 63 and counsel 83; *Counsels of Marburg*, volume 4, counsel 43. On whether adultery is punished more severely than homicide, see Jacob Martini, *Illustrious Questions*, century 5, disputation 5, question 10. On the filthiness of adultery, Laelius Bisciola has much in *Subsequent Hours*, book 15, chapter 11.

On whether, if one party confesses to adultery, the one denying it ought to be punished, see Dassel, counsel 21.

So that a woman might lose her dowry and the right to sue for that dowry on account of committed adultery, it is not necessary for the adultery to be proven directly; rather, conjectures and presumptions <note>circumstantial evidence</note> are sufficient. (Chapter: *Since the Cause*, outside of witnesses). See Baldus in chapter 1, column 7, at the verse "I ask whether it is the same to say," and *Under what causes a fief is lost*. See Alexander on Law 2, final paragraph, *On Adultery*, and the glosses and Doctors on Law "Chapter," paragraph "And in the law which says," in the same place. See Marsilius in the title *On Proofs*, number 8. This is also observed in practical courtroom usage, so that when an accusation is brought against an adulteress, one does not have to bind oneself to the strict proof of the act itself: especially...

# Expanded Practical Treasury

one should only set out the circumstances, and subsequently the presumptions <note>legal inferences drawn from known facts</note>, namely: that they have been seen naked with a naked woman <note>original: "nudum cum nudâ"</note>, from which it is presumed that they committed such adultery. If the defendant should deny this, the plaintiff <note>the person bringing the lawsuit</note> intends to prove his case through the indications <note>original: "indicia," or circumstantial evidence</note> imposed upon him by law. He therefore prays to be divorced from her. For the proof must be made in such a way that the marriage can be separated as to the bed <note>legal separation where the couple no longer lives or sleeps together, but may still be technically married</note>, as the commentary decided in the cited chapter "Furthermore," number 35, on the word "by hearsay."

Under the Julian Law <note>The *Lex Julia de Adulteriis Coercendis*, a Roman law passed by Emperor Augustus around 18 BCE</note>, the accusation of adultery against a woman was permitted only to the husband: but for the wife, nothing was available against the husband. See Book 1 of the Code on the Julian Law of Adultery, where the commentaries of Cynus and the Doctors of Law, Wesenbeck in the *Paratitla* on the Digest, number 11; Beust on Matrimony, chapter 23; and Tiraqueau on the Laws of Marriage, book 1, number 42, give these reasons for this matter: first (1) because the wife owes greater reverence and honor to the husband as the head than, conversely, the husband to the wife; and second (2) because adultery in a wife is far more serious due to the uncertainty of offspring and the introduction of a false heir <note>original: "falsi partus suppositionem," the danger of a wife passing off another man's child as her husband's heir</note>. See Speckhan, *Legal Questions*, century 2, class 2, question 7, number 40; and century 3, class 1, question 8.

The sanction of this law agrees with the words of Gellius in *Attic Nights*, who records the old law written from a speech by Marcus Cato: "If you should catch your wife in adultery, you might kill her with impunity without a trial. She, however, if you should commit adultery, would not dare to touch you with a finger, nor is it the law." See Paleottus on Illegitimate Children, chapter 42, number 3.

Whence Syra, in Plautus's play *The Merchant*, complains of the condition of women in the following words:

> By Castor, women live under a hard law.
> And much more unfairly, poor things, than men:
> For if a husband has brought a harlot home secretly from his wife,
> If the wife finds out, it is with impunity for the husband,
> But if the wife has gone out of the house secretly,
> It becomes a cause for the husband: she is driven from the marriage.
> If only the law were the same for the husband as it is for the wife!

These things indeed held true under the old law of the Romans; but today, under Canon Law <note>the ecclesiastical law of the Church</note>, the spouses are judged to have equal rights in this case, by which women are seen to be admitted to accuse the husband of shameful conduct no less than men are to accuse the shameful conduct of their wives. This is based on the teachings of Eberhard Speckhan, cited above. See also my own work in the *Treatise on the Three Types of Society*, page 23. Regarding Jewish jealousy, see Becanus in *Analogy* 22.

**The Punishment of Adultery** belongs to the high jurisdiction <note>original: "merum Imperium," the power of the sovereign to exercise criminal justice and the "power of the sword"</note>: since generally the proceeds of punishments and fines are counted among the Royalties <note>original: "Regalia," the specific rights and incomes belonging to a king or sovereign lord</note>, under the title "What are Royalties" in Book 2 of the Feudal Laws, especially since the crime of adultery is a public one. Nor does it stand in the way that sometimes adulterers are accustomed to be fined in money; for this changes nothing regarding the nature...

<sig>§. 11.</sig>

...of a public trial, since there are many public crimes for which the punishment is a monetary fine.

But indeed, it is accepted by custom elsewhere that acts of adultery are punished by whoever holds the Bailiwick Authority <note>original: "Vogtheyliche Obrigkeit," the local administrative and judicial power granted to a protector or bailiff</note>.

What an adulteress loses according to Civil Law, and also according to Imperial Cities and Statutes, is clear from the two following legal opinions.

And it is also established that such Statutes and Municipal Laws must be observed in judging in that place, and must be held as Common Law. This is the case regarding the statute to be followed, which disposes what a husband should gain from the goods of an adulteress, as Berlich records in part 2, conclusion 29, number 16.

Lit. E.
Ff 3
<meta>catchword: To</meta>

regarding how one should behave in the present case, both according to the guidance of the aforementioned **Disciplinary Ordinance** <note>original: "Zuchtordnung"; a set of local laws governing social and moral conduct</note> and according to **Christian Equity** itself, I shall briefly disclose that I almost entirely agree with the attached opinion of your Honorable and Noble appointed Advocate, Mr. Johann R.

Namely, that **firstly**, the innocent husband should primarily be granted his security, clothes, and what belongs to his body.

Likewise, and **secondly**, all the property he brought into the marriage, and what was inherited from his side or lineage during the standing marriage, by whatever name it may be called, should be returned to him.

Then, **thirdly**, from the property of his departed wife <note>referring here to the "separated" spouse</note>, the same belongs to him, Lenzen <note>likely the name of the husband in this specific case</note>, namely that which the late Hans gave or promised to his daughter—the departed **adulteress** <note>original: "adulteræ"</note>—as a **marriage portion** <note>original: "Heyrathgut"</note>.

**Fourthly**, this departed woman has in every way forfeited all inheritance and expectancy which she might have expected from her husband upon his death, by virtue of the marriage agreement or according to the content of your Honorable and Noble **Statutes and Inheritance Laws**. Likewise, the innocent husband is entitled to whatever was gained or increased during the marriage that they both acquired together; all of which is consistent with and similar to both common law and the aforementioned Disciplinary Ordinance, and is also indisputable to me.

However, I find in the first-mentioned Disciplinary Ordinance, in the section "Likewise also the **Morning Gift**" <note>original: "Morgengab"; a traditional gift given by a husband to his wife the morning after the wedding</note> etc., it is specifically stipulated that the innocent party should be entitled to no less than what they would have inherited from the defaulting party—provided the latter had departed by death—according to your Honorable and Noble **City Law** <note>original: "Stadtrecht"</note>, or according to the evidence of established marriage and contract letters, where such exist.

This point was presumably omitted in the well-considered opinion of the gentleman [Advocate Johann R.] because perhaps your Honorable and Noble City Law and custom dictates that **in the case of no existing children** <note>original: "in casu non existentium liberorum"</note>, one spouse inherits from the other entirely. Thus, according to such an understanding, the guilty party would have lost all their goods and property; on the other hand, it could not be verified what is ordered in the immediately following section "But what beyond such" etc., namely that from what belongs to the defaulting spouse, a certain **portion** should be assigned to the **innocent husband** <note>original: "marito innocenti"</note> **at the discretion of the Magistrate** <note>original: "pro arbitratu Magistratus"</note>.

For if the **innocent husband** inherits the guilty part **as a whole** <note>original: "in solidum"</note>, even while she is still alive, then nothing remains from which anything further could be assigned to the guilty party.

However, this is correct if a marriage letter here contains a provision

<column-break/>

by virtue of which the **husband would have inherited only a certain portion** <note>original: "maritus certam solummodo portionem"</note> from his wife if she had died before him without children; or if, by virtue of city custom, spouses who die without children **do not succeed each other in the whole estate** <note>original: "sibi invicem non in solidum succediren"</note>.

Even if such a custom exists, according to which spouses, when no children are present, inherit from each other entirely, nevertheless, that which is established in the section "Likewise also" etc., as understood above, must have its force and effect.

> **Since it is presumed that nothing in the statutes is placed there in vain** <note>original: "Cum nihil in statutis otiosè positum præsumatur"</note>, and especially such must be interpreted in a way that it is not contrary to the following paragraph: "But what beyond such," etc.

> **Since no one, and especially a law or statute, is presumed to want to correct itself immediately.** <note>original: "Cum nemo, & maximè lex vel statutum, in continenti se corrigere velle præsumatur."</note>

Now, these two paragraphs could not be more appropriately interpreted or brought into **harmony** <note>original: "concordiam"</note> than when one understands the paragraph "But what beyond such," etc. in this way: if the defaulting spouse has anything left over after the innocent party has taken what was due by the preceding disposition, **or by virtue of the paragraph** <note>original: "aut vigore Paragraphi"</note> "Likewise also the Morning Gift," etc.—that is, when by virtue of the marriage agreement, one spouse does not inherit from the other **as a whole** <note>original: "in solidum"</note>.

According to all this, but without prejudice to a better opinion: I conclude that the guilty party may not only in no way inherit anything from the innocent party in the future, but conversely, the innocent party, **after separation on the grounds of adultery** <note>original: "post separationem ex causa adulterii"</note>, should immediately receive exactly what they would have expected **by power of the contract or statute** <note>original: "vi pacti vel statuti"</note> if the guilty party had died before the innocent party. **So that the guilty party appears to be, as it were, civilly dead.** <note>original: "Ita ut nocens pars, quasi civiliter mortua videatur." Civil death is a legal state where a living person loses all civil rights, essentially treated as deceased by the law.</note>

Thus, in such a case, when by virtue of City Law one spouse inherits from the other as a whole or entirely, then the paragraph "But what beyond such," etc. is not to be observed; rather, nothing more shall be granted to the guilty party than their **sustenance** <note>original: "alimenta"</note> and clothes, **out of mercy** <note>original: "ex commiseratione"</note>, according to judicial discretion.

> **And certainly, if it be received by statute or custom that the use or administration of the personal property <note>original: "bonorum Paraphernalium"; property a wife brought into marriage beyond her dowry</note> also belongs to the husband, then the husband also rightly gains those things on account of the wife's adultery. Berlich, conclusion 29, number 19, where he confirms this with several precedents.**

> **For certainly, if we were to say otherwise, it would follow that the woman would obtain a profit from her own crime and adultery, and would acquire free power over her personal property and its use, which otherwise belongs to the husband, which would be absurd. Andreas Rauchbar, part 1, question 47, under number 32 and following.**

**Fifthly**, in the manner already indicated, the guilty party should be provided with—and indeed in any event—their clothes and what belongs to their body; however, for the sake of **equity** <note>original: "Billigkeit"; fairness in legal proceedings</note>, this in no way includes or intends to include anything made of gold or silver, and even less what the **husband** <note>original: "Maritus"</note> has given to the wife as a gift.

Since there is no doubt that even a most perfect gift is tacitly considered revoked on account of the ingratitude of the recipient, or if they have inflicted serious injury upon the Donor, and is therefore revoked by law <note>original Latin: "Cum nemini sit dubium... jure revocetur," citing the Code of Justinian regarding the revocation of donations</note>. It is believed that a wife can hardly inflict a more serious injury upon her husband than if she commits adultery.

**Sixthly**, if beyond what is due to the innocent husband—in the case of the wife dying first—by virtue of the **City Law** or the **Marriage Contract**, there should still be something remaining, that portion belongs to him according to the frequently cited paragraph; but whatever remains beyond that should likewise be given to the innocent party as another portion, at the **discretion of the Magistrate** <note>original: "pro arbitratu Magistratus"</note>.

And I would, according to my humble ability <note>original: "pro mea tenuitate"</note>, agree with the aforementioned Honorable Dr. K. on this point: that from the husband's side, if anything remains, one-third should be assigned to the wife, but two-thirds should remain with the husband. However, it might not be without merit to consider that a distinction should be made between the assets coming from the late Mrs. **Cordula Gäßlerin** and those due to this defaulting wife from elsewhere. This is because the Gäßlerin estate is burdened with a **fideicommissum** <note>a legal trust or entailment where property is held for specific heirs and cannot be sold or easily transferred</note> such that upon the death of Anna, the wife of Caspar Lentzen, these assets can in no way pass to her husband, Caspar Lentzen, with full legal right through succession—and thus much less through a crime <note>original: "nullo modo per successionem: & ita multò minùs per delictum"</note>. Instead, he may only have the **usufruct** <note>the right to use and profit from property belonging to another</note> for the duration of his life. This is because Mrs. Gäßlerin's will expressly ordered that if her sister's daughter Anna, as a co-heir, should pass away before her husband Caspar Lentzen, then he, Lentzen, shall have only the use and enjoyment of the received inheritance for his lifetime, without being able to place any burden or loss upon the substance of the estate through remarriage or any other means.

Which words undoubtedly imply a **fideicommissum**, and perhaps such a trust might be extended so far that, if this Anna should leave no children but only her husband, he should have no more than the possession of such Gäßler assets, while the **ownership** <note>original: "proprietas"</note> must accrue to the other co-heirs. One might then conclude that not the co-heirs, but only—

<column-break/>

—her children and grandchildren were appointed as heirs; thus, in the absence of such, the indicated trust has entirely expired, as it almost appears in the paragraph: "And in the case that my sister Maria, etc." of the Gäßlerin will.

However, because the extent of the Gäßlerin trust cannot be fully determined in the present dispute, one might perhaps use this clause in a future judgment: that nothing is taken away from the Gäßlerin will by this ruling, but rather that those who have a claim in this matter by virtue of that will shall have their understood rights and claims reserved.

For this clause, having reserved the right, grants nothing new, nor does it expand it, but rather preserves what exists, and does no harm even if it is erroneous <note>original Latin quote from Augustinus Barbosa, a famous 17th-century canon lawyer, regarding the use of legal clauses</note>.

And this I have wished to write to your Honors and Excellencies as the requested reply, also offering myself, in case my **intent** <note>original: "mentem"</note> has not been sufficiently understood, to explain further upon request; as I then remain, etc. Dated at **Tübingen**, etc.

->**Christ. Besold.**<-
<note>Christoph Besold (1577–1638) was a prominent German jurist and professor at the University of Tübingen</note>

### Noble, Steadfast, and Highly Learned, also Honorable, Prudent, and Most Wise Gentlemen.

My ready service to your Honors and Excellencies first. Especially Greatly-Favoring and Highly-Honored Gentlemen. What the same have again brought to me regarding **Caspar Lentzen** and his divorced wife was delivered to me by the bearer. Due to other unforeseen business, the requested reply has unfortunately had to be delayed a little longer. I understand from the documents that in the case of existing children, your Honors' **Inheritance Law** <note>original: "Erbrecht"</note> establishes that, in an intestate case, the surviving spouse is the legal and sole heir to the entire estate. Thus, the well-known **Disciplinary Ordinance** <note>original: "Zuchtordnung"</note> in the section "likewise also the morning gift, etc." is made even more obscure, and especially causes the indicated and immediately following paragraph to appear almost irreconcilably opposed to each other.

These two texts also require a distinction between those goods which were brought into the marriage by the guilty party at the start, and those inherited later during the marriage...

worded in such a way that they cannot be reconciled (primarily because no single word is found in this place that would provide such an interpretation), but rather, in my humble opinion, they allow for no other understanding than what was indicated in my previous assessment.

However, I must also confess that such a disposition would be very harsh, even almost **cruel** <note>original Latin: "crudelis"</note>, if one wished to follow it **according to the letter** <note>original Latin: "secundum literam"</note> and in all cases. For instance, if in the present case he, Caspar Lenk, were to die before his former wife, and she were to marry elsewhere—or even if she were permitted to remarry **while the innocent husband is still living** <note>original Latin: "vivente etiam marito innocente"</note>, as sometimes occurs **by means of a special dispensation** <note>original Latin: "mediante dispensatione singulari"</note> from the Lords—and she were to have children, it would be almost contrary to Christian equity if those same children had to be entirely deprived of their biological mother's significant fortune.

Therefore, I likewise consider it very advisable that your Honorable and Noble Lordships' statute be changed in this regard and directed toward a certain portion. In such cases, this portion should remain in the hands of the innocent party from the **personal property** <term>original: "paraphernal"; property belonging to a wife beyond her dowry</term> as well as the marriage gift of the guilty party, serving as a punishment.

And it seems to me, though without wishing to dictate, that it is better to have a certain portion determined **by law or statute** <note>original Latin: "per legem vel Statutum"</note> to be left to the innocent party **from the assets of the guilty party** <note>original Latin: "ex bonis nocentis"</note>, rather than leaving that determination to the **discretion of the Magistrate** <note>original Latin: "arbitrio Magistratus"</note>.

> And indeed, because from the knowledge of the wisest politicians, very few things should be left to the power and discretion of the judge, because he who commands the law to rule, commands God and the law to rule; but he who commands a man to rule, adds a beast, since the desire and anger of both often pervert even the best magistrates; for the law is mind without affection and appetite, as Aristotle elegantly writes in the *Politics*. <note>Besold quotes Aristotle to argue that fixed laws are safer than the personal whims of judges.</note>

It now rests upon the highly intelligent discretion of your Honorable and Noble Lordships whether you wish to set such a forfeited portion at one-third or one-half.

However, so that one does not deviate too far from the old statute—which essentially intends for the innocent party to inherit from the guilty party as if they were already dead—and especially because in such cases, **through the offense** <note>original Latin: "per delictum"</note> of the adulterous party, the innocent party is unjustly deprived of the possession and enjoyment of the guilty party's entire fortune, the future statute might be framed as follows: that the innocent party (1.) shall keep his clothes

<column-break/>

and what belongs to his body, status, and trade, as well as (2.) all property he brought into the marriage and inherited from his own side and lineage during the marriage, especially (3.) the **marital acquisitions** <term>original: "Rungenschafft"; property or wealth gained through the joint efforts of the couple during the marriage</term>, and no less (4.) **half the portion** <note>original Latin: "dimidiam partem"</note> of everything that the **guilty party** <note>original Latin: "pars nocens"</note> brought into the marriage or inherited **while the marriage lasted** <note>original Latin: "constante matrimonio"</note>. Furthermore, the innocent party (5.) shall be required to give the guilty party no more than their necessary clothes, tools, or the like, together with (6.) the remaining half of what they brought in or inherited, and (7.) in the event of future inheritance, neither shall have anything to claim or seek from the other.

It also seems to me further that one should make no distinction between **personal property** and **dowry property** <note>original Latin: "paraphernal- und dotalibus bonis"</note>, but rather conclude indifferently that the guilty party has forfeited **half the portion** <note>original Latin: "dimidiam partem"</note> of all their fortune **through this offense** <note>original Latin: "per hoc delictum"</note>, whether it was brought in at the start of the marriage **as a dowry or by another name** <note>original Latin: "dotis vel alio nomine"</note>, or inherited from their lineage afterward, or otherwise acquired.

Likewise, and because it sometimes happens that a spouse holds property not **with full right** <note>original Latin: "pleno jure"</note>, but solely **by reason of usufruct for life** <note>original Latin: "ratione ususfructus ad dies vitæ"</note>, it could be ordered here that such **right of use** <note>original Latin: "ususfructus"</note> should also remain **at half** <note>original Latin: "pro dimidia"</note>, but only as long as it is due to the **guilty party** <note>original Latin: "nocenti"</note>.

And finally, in the present case, the verdict could be formulated as follows:

### Verdict.

In the dispute that has arisen between Caspar Lenk, a citizen here, on the one part, and Anna N., his divorced wife, on the other part, concerning the separation of their previously commonly held property: An Honorable Court, upon all evidence presented, submissions made, and due consideration, according to the guidance of both this laudable city's **moral code** <term>original: "Zuchtordnung"; a set of local regulations governing social and moral behavior</term> and its own equitable judgment, gives this decision: that you, Anna N., shall be given and delivered your clothes and what belongs to your body, yet excluding anything made of gold and silver, or what he, Caspar Lenk, gave to you as a gift, together with half of everything that she, Anna, inherited during the marriage. The remainder, however, shall all remain with the said Caspar Lenk. Furthermore, all inheritance rights against each other are hereby abolished in all cases; however, this shall in no way prejudice those who, by virtue of the late Mrs. Cordula Gässlerin's will, might consider themselves entitled to make a claim here, but rather their rights shall be reserved in every way.

## ADDITION.

If a married man approaches an unmarried woman, whether adultery is committed, see *Zahn on Lies, book 2, chapter 88, number 1.* Whether an adulterer can be a witness, see Jacob Ayrer, part 1 of his *Historical Process, chapter 7, observation 6, number 3 to 7.* In how many ways adultery is committed, and how it is proven, *ibid. numbers 8 and 17.*

In France, Rebuff writes that it has never been heard of for the punishment of the sword <note>original Latin: "pœnam gladii"; the death penalty by beheading</note> to be inflicted for adultery. Indeed, Antonius Robertus testifies in *Judicial Matters, book 1, chapter 14*, that adultery is even placed in the category of "industrious praise" <note>This suggests a cultural perception of adultery as a clever or gallant feat rather than a crime</note>. Lanf. in his *Oration against France, page 191*, where he also reports from Thuanus's *History, volume 35*, that not only did the Parliament of Paris in the year 1563 take very poorly to the actions of Pigreterius—a man of ancient character and severity appointed over the City of Orléans by Louis de Condé—because he had set a harsher example for Landas Molinus, who had defiled Godarda, the wife of Jean Godin, with adultery. Pigreterius had ordered both Landas and Godarda to be hanged by a noose in a public square in Orléans; truly, even the nobles judged this severity to be unheard of. Schwarz, in *On the Right of Aggravation, page 69*, notes that adultery is unknown among camels and elephants. Klock, in *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 141, number 64*, calls adultery "The Great Game" <note>original Latin: "Adulterium Magnum ludus"</note> at *number 61.* An adulterous woman sins more gravely than a man, *numbers 34 and 37.* *Whether adultery should be punished more harshly than homicide?* <note>original German: "Ob der Ehebruch härter, als der Todschlag zu straffen?"</note> See Zeiller, *century 4, question 9, page 46*, and Gerhard, cited there. Although adultery is a lesser crime than homicide, nevertheless a banished woman, who may be killed, cannot be committed for adultery. See Bonifacius, *On Thefts, page 425*, and those cited there. In Strasbourg <note>original Latin: "Argentorati"</note>, adultery is punished the first time by removal from one's rank or office, the second time by the imposition of the stone <term>original: "impositione lapidis"; a public shaming ritual where the offender carried a heavy "stone of shame" through the streets</term>, and for a third offense, by capital punishment. Furthermore, adultery is twofold: either a man having a spouse lies with a married woman, which the Doctors of Law call **Qualified Adultery** <note>original German: "den Ober Ehebruch"</note>, or a single man mixes with another’s wife, which the Doctors call **Simple Adultery**, as seen in Dr. Bicc., *In the Golden Rules, section 4, thesis 174.* Antonius Matthæi spoke excellently in his *Oration for Constantine the Great on Adulterers*, recited at Utrecht in the year 1644: After security was provided for marriage by the benefit of Constantine the Great, then I believe husbands were inclined to cry out: *Hail,*

<column-break/>

great Prince, victor and triumphator, always Augustus! Now at last it is a joy to take a wife, now a joy to raise sweet heirs. With you as guardian, the house rejoices in security, nor does the marriage bed fear the home-wrecker. But what impelled Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor (r. 527–565)</note> to withdraw the necks of adulterers from the ultimate necessity <note>i.e., the death penalty</note>? See here Stirnius, *On the Constitutions of Princes, title 10, § 9*, and Gaudentius, *On the Morals of the Age of Justinian.* (For he began to act more mildly toward the adulteress, whom he wished to be beaten with rods and thrust into a monastery. Bicc., *In the Golden Rules, page 573.*) Whether this was the fault of his wife, Theodora, who, having exceeded her sex, had nearly subjected the throne of her husband to her own chairs; or whether, as some pious and grave men think, this was the ambition of the Bishops, who, out of a perverse zeal for imitating the Savior, could not bear for adulteresses to be killed—it was done quite wickedly by them. For malice is joined to the infirmity of the sex <note>A common historical prejudice suggesting women were naturally prone to vice</note>, such that unless it is restrained by more atrocious edicts, nothing sane or moderate can be expected from a woman. Although by Civil Law an adulterer is not "infamous" <note>legally barred from certain rights</note> before a sentence is passed, according to *Law 2, § 2* and *Law 14 on witnesses*, and others like Ludovicus Romanus and Freher; nevertheless, he ought to be exiled from tournaments, even if not yet condemned. For "every marriage is left uncertain if people sin in such reverence without any fear," as Cassiodorus writes in *book 5, epistle 32.* Would that in this deplorable century we could proclaim of our Germans that which Tacitus wrote with such truth: *Adulteries are very few in so numerous a people.* Our ancestors, with the sexes mixed, went about naked or for the most part uncovered until puberty and marriageable age, their minds blind toward lust; now, Germany is almost alone among Europeans in covering not only the arms and shoulders, but every part of the breast, and wonders at and abhors nudity in other nations; yet illicit love is not rare, nor are adulteries. Cluver, *book 1, Ancient Germany, chapter 19, page 173: What the mind craves, the garment does not hide.*

> Boniface, the Archbishop of Mainz <note>An 8th-century Anglo-Saxon missionary</note>, writes in his letter to the King in England that even in his time in the old land of the Saxons, there was as yet no knowledge of the Christian religion. Whenever a maiden committed unchastity in her mother’s house, or a wife committed adultery under her husband, the parents themselves would strangle their unmarried daughter with a rope and burn her. As for the adulteress, however, chaste matrons would cut her clothes from the top down to the belt, and having thus bared her, they subsequently whipped her from one village to the next. There, she was received at all times with similar blows by other women appointed for that purpose, and finally was pricked and stabbed with sharp little knives for so long until they had completely killed the adulteress. *Zeiller, German Itinerary, page 42.*

Therefore, the crime of adultery is exceedingly grave and detestable—

### 7. Marriage Vows and Betrothal. <term>Sponsalia</term> <note>Latin term for the formal promise of marriage; the legal status preceding a full marriage.</note>

There is a difference between a *betrothal* or *marriage vow*, and a marriage consummated by physical union. *As it is said in common speech, a man and woman are called husband and wife once they have shared the marriage bed; before that, they are called bridegroom and bride.* Schneidewein on the title *De nuptiis*, part 1, number 4.

But it should be known that occasionally even a betrothal by present consent <note>original: "sponsalia de præsenti"; a vow where the couple says "I take you" (present tense) rather than "I will take you" (future tense).</note> can be rescinded. For only through a consummated marriage do the spouses become "one flesh." <note>original: "una caro"</note> Chapter 2, *on the conversion of spouses*, and chapter *lex* 27, question 2; see also Sanchez, *On Marriage*, book 2, dispute 13, number 1.

And through a betrothal by present consent, a marriage is indeed said to be "perfect in its essence," but not yet "integrally consummated." This is because, even if their souls are united, they have not yet actually become one flesh; for this reason, the marriage is said to be only "initiated." Gloss on the chapter *cum initiatur*, and the chapter *statutum* with those following, 27, question 2; chapter 2, *on the conversion of spouses*.

When, after a betrothal by future promise <note>original: "sponsalia de futuro"; a promise to marry at a later date.</note> has been contracted, some notable inconvenience or a new cause should arise which would have prevented the contract from the beginning, it provides a just cause for dissolving the agreement. The chief reason is the lack of continued intention, and because—since things have notably changed—such a promise no longer seems binding. This is taught by Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a famous canonist.</note> in his *Summa*, under the title *on oaths*, number 3; Gregorio Lopez on law 7, title 1, part 4, gloss *excusation*; Navarrus in his *Latin Manual*, chapter 22, number 27, and in his *Consilia*, book 4, first edition, counsel 34, and the second edition, counsel 9; Cucchus, *Major Institutes*, book 5, title 10 at the end; Pietro Niccolò Mozzi, *On Betrothals*, title *how betrothals are dissolved*, number 17; Angelo in his *Summa*, word "sponsalia," number 21; and there Sylvester, question 10, chapter 17; and more cited by Thomas Sanchez, *On Marriage*, book 1, dispute 62, number 3.

And it is relevant here that the aforementioned rule is said to apply even if the betrothal was confirmed by an oath <note>original: "Juramento"</note>; because an oath follows the nature and conditions of the contract to which it is attached. Law *final*, Code *de non numerata pecunia*, and it is understood to hold while "things remain in the same state" <note>The legal principle of "rebus sic stantibus," where a contract's validity depends on circumstances not changing fundamentally.</note>, as in the chapter *quemadmodum* on oaths; and Thomas Sanchez proves this extensively, where Besold, Volume 1,

<column-break/>

above number 4, holds this same extension in his terms.

And thus Marius Antoninus Maceratensis, Apostolic Protonotary, decided in his *Resolutions*, book 1, number 6, that a betrothal can be rescinded if the groom was unaware that his bride was born of "condemned intercourse" <note>original: "ex damnato coitu"; referring to children born from adultery or incest.</note>. He adds that although a "mistake of quality" <note>original: "error qualitatis"; a mistake regarding a person's attributes rather than their identity.</note> does not nullify a marriage, it is nonetheless no small impediment in the fulfillment of a betrothal, since a mistake excludes true consent.

So too, notable harshness or cruelty, whenever it is newly discovered, is a sufficient cause for dissolving a preceding betrothal by future promise. For such cruelty is sufficient grounds for the separation and divorce of a marriage regarding the bed and mutual cohabitation, as in the chapter *ad literas* on the restoration of stolen property; see also Juan Gutierrez, *Canonical Questions*, book 1, chapter 1, and in his *Treatise on Marriage*, chapter 33.

Likewise, despite the bond of an oath, if a woman should later become leprous, paralyzed, or lose her eyes or nose, or if anything more foul should happen to her, the man is not bound to marry her, even though he could not set her aside if they were already married. This is expressly written in the chapter *quemadmodum* 25, *extra de jurejurando*, and Gutierrez follows this at length in *On Betrothals*, question 32.

And although there is great controversy among the Canonists <note>Scholars of Church law.</note> and those who treat "Cases of Conscience," as to whether a mistake of quality or previous deceit—which was the reason the marriage was entered into—can nullify the marriage, Gutierrez writes on this in *On Marriage*. He asserts, by the authority of many Doctors, that a marriage is not invalidated even by a lie or the trickery used to induce it. However, he limits this not only to such great deceit as would take away consent, but in number 7 he teaches that a "mistake of quality" sometimes overflows into a "mistake of the person" <note>original: "errorem personæ"; a crucial legal distinction where you think you are marrying one person but are actually marrying another (e.g., Jacob marrying Leah instead of Rachel).</note>. In such a case, the person is truly mistaken—that is, the quality so fundamentally defines the person that the marriage is rendered void. Thomas Sanchez treats this most extensively, arguing for and against and establishing rules with his declarations in dispute 18, from number 25 to the end. Finally, in number 38, summarizing it all, he says briefly: this happens when there is a mistake about a quality that designates a specific person, who was not known to the contracting party without that quality, and where it is not clear that the mind of the party was to consent to the person present before them, whoever they might be.

Similarly, a mistake of "servile condition" <note>original: "conditionis servilis"</note>—when a free person contracts with a slave, being ignorant of their status, or a free woman with a male slave—renders the marriage void. Text in chapter 3 and the last, *on the marriage of slaves*; and chapter *si quis ingenuus* 29, question 2, with similar references in Gutierrez, *On Marriage*, chapter 90.

Furthermore, it is often asked: whether this or that phrasing of words implies matrimonial... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the next word is "matrimonialem."</note>

If a girl responds to a youth who is soliciting her, "I do not want you to know me, unless it is done honorably," <note>An idiom for marriage.</note> and the youth accepted that he would do so but then defiled her, should the marriage be seen as contracted? ### 8. Spouses, Wives, and Divorce. <term>Uxor</term> <note>Latin for wife.</note>, <term>Divortium</term> <note>Latin for divorce.</note>.

It is established that in ancient times there were two types of wives: some were called *matresfamilias* <note>Mothers of the household; typically the legal wife of a Roman citizen.</note>, and others simply wives (*uxores*), as seen in Cicero's *Topics* and Callistratus. See especially Robertus, book 1 of *Legal Sentences*, chapter 4. Drusius teaches who the primary and secondary wives were in his notes on Genesis, chapter 65.

Regarding "repudiation" <note>A one-sided dismissal of a spouse.</note> in the Old Testament, see Becanus in his *Analogy*, chapter 23 on divorces; and at what time they were practiced in Rome; and what is the difference between repudiation and divorce? See Bisciola, *Subsequent Hours*, book 12, chapter 16. Master Dilherr, *Elections* 1, chapter 7.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the wife, see Barbosa, book 19, chapter 50, throughout. On the question of whether, at the blessing of an elderly couple, the blessing **"be fruitful and multiply"** <note>original: "seyd fruchtbar und mehret euch."</note> should be spoken? See Zeiller, century 4, question 69, page 356 and following.

### 9. Legal Impediment. <term>Ehehaft</term> <note>An Old German legal term meaning both "marriage" and a "legitimate excuse" or "binding necessity."</note>, <term>Ehehafftin</term>. <term>Legitima impedimenta</term>.

The clause **"with all legal appurtenances"** <note>original: "mit allen Ehehafftin."</note> is interpreted as referring to related properties. And thus in the Allgäu region, *Ehehafftin* are **mills, smithies, bathhouses, and taverns**; <note>original: "Mühlen, Schmieden, Badstuben und Tafernen."</note> certain people contend that these rights belong to the high jurisdiction of a territory, according to experience and Adam Keller. Others refer them to "mixed power" according to Thomas Michael.

In Saxon Law, a legitimate impediment is called **Ehehafft**; that is, **any honest matter or excuse, or sincere hindrance.** <note>original: "ein jegliche redliche Sach oder Entschuldigung, oder auffrichtige Verhinderung."</note> *Saxon Landrecht*, book 2, article 7. Or, an *Ehehafft* is **a weighty and honorable cause which keeps someone bound at home, like a self-evident command, and prevents, holds back, and excuses them from appearing at a certain time and place.** <note>In legal terms, this was a valid reason for failing to appear in court, such as a flood or serious illness.</note> (For in old times, *Ehe* meant a "commandment," as can be read in the *Weichbild* <note>A collection of medieval municipal laws.</note> at the beginning of the chronicle of the creation of the world: "There the Commandment (*Ehen*) was given to the Jews on the 50th day after the departure from Egypt." Likewise, the "Giving of the *Ehe*" signifies the Ten Commandments. Schercus, in the *Secular Language-School*, page 125. Thus, it was formerly called **"the Old Marriage"** <note>original: "die alte Ehe."</note> to mean the Old Testament or Mosaic Law.

Hence, in Saxon Law, before a defendant is condemned for contempt of court as if they were already convicted, they must first be summoned and heard to see whether they can allege any "impediment" as to why they did not appear in court at the appointed time. Therefore, the plaintiff usually asks that the defendant be condemned in *Ehehaft*—that is, to prove a legitimate impediment.

It highlights the intersection of Canon, Civil, and Saxon Law in governing domestic life and court appearances.</summary>

...impediment. And if, after this sentence, the summoned defendant appears and is able to allege and prove just causes for his absence, then his contumacy <note>Contumacy refers to a person's stubborn refusal to obey a court order or appear when summoned.</note> is purged, according to the *Saxon Territorial Law, book 2, article 24.* The interpreters of the Law also commonly agree, handing down the rule: that a contumacious person should not be condemned unless he was first summoned to allege the causes of his absence; otherwise, it would follow that one who was absent due to some just impediment would be condemned. *See Bartolus and Jason on Law 2; Hartmann Pistor, book 1, question 3, number 13.*

But if he does not appear then, or is unable to allege an impediment, the court proceeds to the penalty, and it is pronounced **that the plaintiff has prevailed over the defendant with his claim and award, until [legal] aid has been arisen and obtained**; <note>original: "daß Kläger Beklagten mit seiner Klag und Zuspruch, bis auf die Hülffe erstanden und erlangt hat"; this legal formula indicates the plaintiff has won the right to have the judgment enforced.</note> and soon in the same sentence they are condemned in the main cause, which thereafter is commanded to execution, unless it is suspended by an appeal. See *Hartmann Pistor, at the cited location;* add *Pruckman, volume 2, counsel 4; and Modestinus Pistor, part 2, question 119.*

What, however, are the causes of just excuse which relieve and excuse a summoned person from the penalties of contumacy? One should consult *Speckhan, century 1, question 59,* where at number 41 he enunciates four legitimate causes of excuse, or impediments (**lawful and helpful objections**): <note>original: "ehehafftige und hülffliche Widerreden." In this legal context, "Ehehaft" does not mean marriage, but refers to a "necessary" or "lawful" excuse for missing a court date.</note> namely, the captivity of the defendant, ill health, travel outside the borders of that land (that is, a probable absence due to a journey undertaken for the sake of piety and devotion), and likewise a public expedition <note>Such as military service or a state-mandated mission.</note>. *Based on Law 1 at the end; and the law on absence in the Rules of Law.* And these four impediments, which serve to excuse one absenting himself from judgment, are found in the *Saxon Territorial Law, book 2, article 7.* By these, however, other delays are not excluded—for instance, a lack of safety on the road or at the place of judgment, or others which in any way distract someone from appearing at the judicial term. See *Law 2, paragraph 1, and the following; and Speckhan at number 41.*

### 14. One, A Single. One [masculine], One [neuter]. <note>original: "Einer, Eins. Unus, Unum."</note>

The word *One* <note>original: "unus"</note> has a double meaning in the German language: for sometimes it is a number, but at other times it is a mark of a common name and an indefinite speech. For whenever the word *one* <note>original: "unus"</note> is added in the German language to a noun, it always makes the speech indefinite: thus, *an heir*, *a human*, *an animal*, etc. In German it cannot be said otherwise than *an heir*, *a human*, *an animal* <note>original: "ein Erbe, ein Mensch, ein Thier"</note>. See Layman in the *Defense of the Honoldin Case*, number 455. Moreover, that German particle *Ein* <note>meaning "a," "an," or "one"</note> has precisely the same force and meaning as the distributive particle *Anyone* <note>original: "Quis"</note> holds in the Latin language. Hence, if you wanted to translate those beginnings of laws into German: *If anyone—I will not say should seize...* or *If anyone [reaches] such great audacity of madness...*, [it would be]: *When one does not want to say to rob...* or *When one [reaches] such freedom...* And it is doubtful to no one that such phrases are not exhausted or finished with one single first person, but as often as those things which are stated there happen, so often do such legal dispositions work and take place. For they are explained as *whoever*, as noted in the law *if anyone in so much* [Code: *unde vi*]. See Bolognetus on the law *my heirs* [section: *cum ita*], and Layman in the cited place, number 457; see the following numbers through the law *just as in years* [Digest: *how a usufruct is lost*].

I know that in a certain case of great importance it was doubted whether those words found in an ancient document—*That the subjects are bound to perform one manual service <note>original: "ein Handpienst"</note> for the year*—should be explained so that they owe manual labor once every year, or indeed throughout the year as often as it was requested? And it was judged that they are not held to more than one such service per year, since the word *Year* <note>original: "Jahrs"</note> was specifically added.

### ADDITION.

*One who wants the one thing, wants all things without which that one thing cannot proceed.* Everhard in *Legal Topics*, page 770. *Many masters are not a good thing; let there be one King.* When Procopius, the Martyr of Palestine, had said this, he offered his neck to be struck by the axe. See Eusebius, book 8, chapter 12. And nothing is achieved less effectively than that which is commanded by many. An Empire, says Curtius, which could have stood under one, falls while it is sustained by many. Curtius, book 10. *One sun, one moon, one empyrean heaven, one, as they say, Phoenix.* The Emperor Rudolph II had a bird as white as snow and with the whitest feathers of all, not unlike a duck with a very large beak, which 

<column-break/>

everyone everywhere called "Laughing Hans" <note>original: "den lachenden Hänssel"</note>; for it seemed to laugh—a trait which philosophers attribute only to humans—and it performed all sorts of wonders. But it was bought for a sum of money which, though I noted it, I do not dislike to mention, yet I am almost ashamed to pronounce. If, however, the Emperor could have obtained a match and companion for this one, he would have added as much again to the price. See Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 338. *One indeed, but a lion.* <note>A reference to Aesop's fables where the lioness has only one cub, but that cub is a lion.</note> Ludovico Coelius Rhodiginus, book 29 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 9. One head in a man, *one* soul, one Sheepfold, one Pastor. Ezra the Priest speaks of *one* lily, *one* river, *one* city, *one* dove, *one* sheep, *one* vine, and *one* people. More from the said author on pages 342 and 343. Pererius, in book 4, chapter 7, page 227, celebrates the omnipotence of unity. Scaliger, in *Exercise 365*, notes it is both the beginning and the end of numbers. For *unity* is the formal, material, efficient, and final principle. On the same subject, see also Macrobius in *The Dream of Scipio*, book 1, chapter 6: *The One, which is called monas (that is, unity)*, is both male and female (You will note here from the same author that the odd number is called male, and the even female; and the Arithmeticians venerate the odd by the name of the Father, and the even by the name of the Mother; and the ancients showed the excellence of numbers from surfaces, lines, and all bodies); it is both even and odd. It is not a number itself, but the source and origin of numbers: it refers to God and the soul, and stands over numbers.

> One day had sent all the Fabii to war:
> One day destroyed them all when they had been sent.
-> Ovid, Fasti, Book 2 <-

He who speaks of one seems to deny the other. Law *when the Praetor*, 12 [Digest: *on judgments*]. More in Barbosa, book 19, chapter 38, throughout the axioms. What a single light is, see Tabor in *On the Quarters*, page 285, and Limnaeus, book 9, chapter 1, number 73. Macrobius reports of Pontius that he whispered in the ear of Scipio—that most famous destroyer of Carthage and Numantia and son of Paulus—when Scipio was inviting many friends to share *a single sturgeon* <note>original: "acipenser"</note> (a most noble fish, very sweet to eat, but very rare to catch) which had been given to him: "Watch what you do, Scipio; *that sturgeon is for one man alone*."

In Paris, at the St. Anthony Gate, there is this inscription: *one God, one faith, one King* <note>original: "un dieu, une foy, un Roy"</note>. According to this inscription, the majority of the French Estates, following ancient custom, wish to have only one single King and Lord. See Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relation of Truces and Peace*, page 150.

### 15. One for all, and all for one. One for all, each for the whole. <note>original: "Einer für alle, und alle für einen. Unus pro omnibus, singuli in solidum."</note>

This clause, in cases of suretyship or other obligations of several people, takes away the benefit

benefit of division: well noted by Mr. Hering, *On Suretyship*, chapter 17, number 50, etc.

For although in those words, *one for all* <note>original: "unum pro omnibus, einen für alle"</note>, no mention is made of the <term>benefit of division<gloss>the legal right of a co-guarantor to pay only their proportional share of a debt</gloss></term> according to the sound of the words; in effect, however, that very thing is expressed. For he who establishes by express agreement that he wishes to be held liable <term>in solidum<gloss>for the entire amount of a debt, rather than just a portion</gloss></term> on behalf of the remaining co-guarantors—how does he not renounce the benefit of division? For "the whole" and "the divided" are <note>original Greek: "ἀντιθέσoντα" (antithesonta)</note> opposites in this context. And furthermore, to name a thing, and to demonstrate something by an indubitable sign that is nearly indistinguishable from the name itself, are considered equal in law. *l.9. §. si quis nomen ff. de haeredit. institut. l. certum. ff. si cert. pet.*

And although some dissenting views are cited there; nevertheless, that by these words, *one for all, and all for one* <note>original: "einer für alle, und alle für einen"</note>, the benefit of division is considered renounced, and that this has been observed in judicial rulings so far, is testified by the same Mr. Hering.

Furthermore, all this dispute ceases if to the aforementioned words, "one for all," those words are added (as is customary) *with undivided hand, and that no one should help themselves with the other* <note>original: "mit ungeschiedener Hand, und daß sich keiner mit dem andern behelffen solle"</note>; for no one of sound mind would doubt that by these words a <term>fidejussor<gloss>a guarantor or surety who takes responsibility for another's debt</gloss></term> strips himself of the benefit of division. But meanwhile, let no one think that these phrases—"one for all" and "all for one"—are interchangeable or of equal efficacy. For as the first utterly excludes the benefit of division, so the second properly cannot take place unless one of the guarantors is unable to pay; in which case the remaining solvent guarantors nevertheless retain the benefit of division among themselves. Hering, *cited chapter 17, number 55*. The following clause is also similar in effect and equivalent to the aforementioned clauses: **If also one among us should be summoned for payment, then we all shall and will be considered summoned, and no one shall withdraw with his quota or portion, nor point from one to the other, but each shall be liable for the whole sum.** Hering, *cited location, number 57.*

### ADDITION.

He who has bound himself by contract *in solidum* (for the whole) is not immediately said to have renounced the benefit of division available to him, since even without a contract every person is held liable for the whole by the law itself <note>in certain collective obligations</note>; and the renunciation of a benefit available to someone cannot be introduced tacitly, since no one is presumed to throw away what is theirs. *l. 25. cum de indebito ff. de probat.* Moreover, every renunciation is "odious" (unfavorable) and strictly interpreted, and therefore should not be aided by broad interpretation. *arg. l. 19. cum quidam ff. de lib. & posth. & cap. odia de R. J. in 6.* Such is the force of the contract that, if it is omitted, under the <term>New Law<gloss>The Novellae, or updated laws issued by Emperor Justinian</gloss></term> one of two or more co-debtors is never held for the whole, as they once were under the law of the Pandects and the Code. Rather, the express addition of that clause is necessary for someone to be held for the whole; nor is it sufficient under the New Law, even if

<column-break/>

perhaps this was intended tacitly, since otherwise, in the making of a contract, that which is done should usually be regarded with caution. *l. 3. ff. de reb. cred. Rittersh. in Nov. pag. 165. & 166.* Regarding when the benefit of division ceases, Mr. Dr. Biccius reports briefly and vigorously (as he does everything) in *Aureis section 4. 6. 73. letter M.*, where he recounts 6 modes. On how the little word "all" <note>original: "omne"</note> is restricted, see Barbosa *book 1, chapter 21, axiom* throughout.

### 16. **Unanimously. Concorditer.**

In every legal disposition in which something ought to be done by several people "unanimously" <note>original: "Einhelliglich"</note>, it is understood as being done with no one disagreeing, especially in matters of contract and strict Law. *Alexand. consil. 124. num. 2. & seqq. lib. 2.* Cardinal Tuschus, *pract. concl. lit. D. concl. 252.* Hence, in an act of a <term>universitas<gloss>a legal corporation or collective body, such as a guild or a town council</gloss></term> or College which everyone does together, if it is required that it be done "unanimously," it is understood as with no one disagreeing; and this applies in all cases in which words are to be taken truly and properly. *Alex. cited location.* Clarification: because in those matters in which an act of many is done as if by individuals, or where an act by the majority (see Tuschus *Letter M. conclusion 14.*) is held as a legitimate act as if it were done by all, that occurs through legal fiction and similarity, but not through the literal truth. *Tusch. cited conclusion 253. see me on the law of things f. 239. & seq. fol. also 242. n. 3.*

Indeed, some things belong to individuals as individuals, some to the Collective Body as a body, and some to the Collective Body as if to individuals. Peguera *decision 71.* And thus that common legal maxim—"that which touches all must be approved by all"—has a place only in that which touches all as individuals.

As to whether a majority is required to meet and consent together in those things which are common to several as individuals, or whether individuals (or the majority of them) can consent separately, see Aymon Cravetta, *consil. 63.*

### ADDITION.

Common and low-born people easily disagree, according to the sentiment of the Prince of Poets <note>Virgil</note>:

> The uncertain crowd is split into opposing pursuits.

Men are prone to disagreement. *l. quia poterat. ff. ad SC. Trebell. c. super literis there*: "we have understood that different people feel differently," etc. *extra de Rescriptis.* Hence, because of the difficulty of assembling a <term>universitas<gloss>here meaning the whole population</gloss></term> of the entire people, it is said that a whole population cannot easily consent. *l. 1. §. sin. where also the Gloss. ff. de acquirenda poss. l. un. ff. de libert. univ. The text is most elegant in l. 2. §. deinde quia difficile ff. de Orig. Jur. Civ.* A judge ought to intend nothing else than to bring the litigating parties back to harmony. *l. 1. §. inde quæritur ff. de nov. oper. nunc. nor should he allow...*

Magistrates act rightly who use words first, then deeds <note>original: "verbis, dein erbis" (a play on words: first with words, then with 'herbs' or force)</note> (following the authority of Baldus in the chapter *Formerly*, number 22, in the *Decretals on Rescripts*); they are those who propose and attempt amicable negotiations at the start, and only then apply the remedies of the law, imparting the office and aid of the Judge and instilling it in those eager for litigation. Hence it is very true, as is commonly tossed about: *A lean peace is better than a fat judgment.* <note>original: "Macra concordia melior est pingui fententia." This legal proverb suggests that a modest settlement is preferable to a costly, drawn-out victory in court.</note> And although peace should be urged by a Judge, not commanded; see Menochius, *On Arbitrary Judicial Questions*, case 2, number 8; Ludovicus Molina, *On Justice and Law*. Regarding the Unicorn, Mr. Harsdörffer <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658), a famous German polymath and poet.</note> knew of it in the *German Secretary*, in the second part, book 6, epistle 35 and following.

In Strasbourg, in the beautiful Cabinet of Curiosities belonging to the Gentlemen, there are 24 gaming pieces <note>original: "Brettstein"</note> made of unicorn horn, weighing 47 <term>Loth<gloss>a traditional German unit of weight, roughly 1/32nd of a pound or 15 grams</gloss></term>. The Sieur d'Aubigné writes in his histories that a young nobleman named Süss, in the year 1588, with a small force, captured the city of St. Bertrand in France, located at the bottom of the mountain, and there obtained a unicorn horn valued at 80,000 crowns.
