Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain, *On the Number Seven*, page 368. At the Sorbonne, a unicorn horn hidden under the altar at the Church of St. Denis is shown to foreigners upon request. Its height was so great that even standing on the tips of one's toes, one could not reach its summit with a finger. *In the Life of Jakob Andreae*, page 136.

### 18. Any, any others. <note>original: "Einige, einig andere. Quæcunque quæcunque alia."</note>

The word "any" <note>German: "einige"</note> corresponds to the word "whichever" <note>Latin: "quæcunque"</note>, according to Besoldus, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

which is itself a universal term. *Law 'when anything,' in the Digest on things credited,* so that it ought to be extended infinitely. Johann Goeddaeus, among the *Marburg Counsels*, counsel 28, number 175, volume 1; especially when several other general words concur, for then it cannot even be restricted only to suitable and identical things, but must be accepted infinitely; see Jason in *Law 2, section 'The Praetor,' number 3 and following, in the Digest on those compelled to provide security;* and in *Law 1, section 'announcement,' number 5, at the verse 'I limit,' in the Digest on the announcement of new work.*

The nature of the words "any others" <note>original: "einige andere, quæcunque alia"</note> is such that they refer to things different from those explicitly stated. Socinus the Elder, *Counsel 300, number 2, volume 2.* Socinus the Younger, *Counsel 97, number 5, volume 3.* Hondedei, *Counsel 49, number 13,* from which in the following number he infers that by this word "other" being added to the word "any," all other different and greater things should be understood as included, according to the gloss in *Clementine 1, on the word 'whichever.'* Where Imola, *On judgments and the thing judged.* Socinus the Elder, *Counsel 150, number 12, volume 1.* Riminaldus the Younger, *Counsel 84, number 39, volume 1.* And from the said words, an extension is made even beyond the nature of the act. Curtius the Younger, *Counsel 84, number 39, volume 1.* Goeddaeus, in the cited place, number 117.

### 19. Union of Children. <note>original: "Einkindschaft. Unio prolium."</note>

By the common opinion and assent of the Doctors, it is held that the <term>Union of Children<gloss>a legal arrangement in Germanic law where children from different marriages are treated as a single group of siblings for inheritance purposes</gloss></term>, which was introduced by the modern customs of Germany, is more similar to the subject of <term>adoption<gloss>the legal act of taking another's child as one's own</gloss></term> than to any other matter of Civil Law. It has almost everything in common with it and is ruled and governed by the same rules. For in adoption, fictional children are similarly held as natural and true ones, just as the effects of this kinship and "equalization" <note>original: "parificationis vel exæquationis"</note> are similar, and thirty-three of these are enumerated and recounted by Jacob Rickius in his singular treatise on this matter, chapter 9.

Moreover, Unions of Children of this kind ought to be made before a Magistrate or the Prefect of the place, following an investigation of the case, with Tutors and Curators present, and also after a discussion of the assets or resources of the children in whose name the equalization of children is sought. Rickius, in the cited place, chapter 6. Andreas Gail, *Observations*, book 2, observation 125.

And they also take effect, even if no children were born from the later marriage: see Valentin Forster, volume 1 of the *Marburg Counsels*, counsel 8.

But is <term>paternal power<gloss>Latin: 'patria potestas,' the legal authority held by a male head of household over his children</gloss></term> induced through the union of children, and what are the subsequent effects? See Gilcken, *On Usucaption, part 3, chapter 3, number 64, etc.*

And that the union of children does not take away all power of making a will from the parents is the opinion there at number 221, etc. I have touched upon the rest in the selections for the *Digest, book on questions, 34, page 122.*

Lorenz Catelan, an apothecary at Montpellier, has written about the unicorn, from whom Zeiller (*century 3, Epistle, pages 496–498*) has drawn many memorable things. Charles VIII, King of France, took a unicorn horn <note>original: "cornu Monocerotis"</note> against the will of the Florentines for the price of 7,000 gold pieces. Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain, *on the number seven, page 368*. At the Sorbonne, a unicorn horn hidden under the altar at the Church of St. Denis is shown to foreigners upon request. Its height was so great that standing on the tips of one's toes, a man could not reach its top with a finger. *In the Life of Jakob Andreä*, page 136.

->18. Any, any others.<- <note>original: "Einige, einig andere. Quæcunque quæcunque alia."</note>

The word *any* <note>original German: "einige"</note> corresponds to the word *whichever* <note>original Latin: "quæcunque"</note>, according to Besold, Volume 1,

<column-break/>

which is itself a universal term (*Law 'cum quid', Digest on credited things...*) so that it ought to be extended infinitely (Johann Goeddaeus, among the *Marburg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 28, number 175); especially when many other general words concur, for then it cannot even be restricted only to suitable and identical things, but must be accepted in an infinite sense. See Jason on Law 2, paragraph 'Prætor', number 3 and following...

The nature of the words *any others* <note>original: "einige andere, quæcunque alia"</note> is such that things different from those expressed are referred to (Socinus the Elder, *Consultation 300, number 2, volume 2*). From which the following number infers that by this word 'others' added to the word 'whichever,' all other diverse and greater things should be understood as included, according to the gloss on Clement 1... and from said words an extension is made even beyond the nature of the act.

->19. Union of Offspring.<- <note>original: "Einkindschafft. Unio prolium."</note>

By common opinion and the assent of the Doctors [of Law], it is held that the <term>union of offspring<gloss>a legal arrangement in Germanic law where children from different marriages of the same parents are treated as a single group of siblings for inheritance purposes</gloss></term>, which was introduced by the modern customs of Germany, is similar to no other subject of Civil Law than adoption, and it has almost everything in common with it, and is ruled and governed by the same rules. For in adoption, artificial children are easily held as natural and true, just as the effects of this kinship and 'equalization' or 'leveling' are similar; and thirty-three such effects are enumerated and reviewed by Jacobus Rickius in his singular treatise on this matter, chapter 9.

Furthermore, such Unions of Offspring ought to be made before a Magistrate or the Governor of the place, following an investigation of the case, with Guardians and Curators present, and after a discussion of the goods or assets of the children in whose name the equalization of offspring is sought (Rickius, cited above, chapter 6; Andreas Gail, 2nd observation 125).

And they even have effect although no children were born from the later marriage: see Valentin Forster, *Marburg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 8.

Whether, however, through the union of offspring, parental authority <note>original: "patria potestas"</note> is induced, and the subsequent effects from it? See Gilcken, *on Usucaption, part 3, chapter 3, number 64, etc.*

And that the union of offspring does not take away all power of making a will from the parents, the same author judges there in number 221, etc. Other matters I have touched upon in the excerpts on the Digest, book of questions 34, page 122.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical legal encyclopedia under the letter E. ### ADDITION.

The Union of offspring <note>original: "Unio prolium"</note> is known as "child-unification" <term>Einkindschafft</term>. This occurs when children from a first marriage are legally treated as if they were born of the same parents as the children from a subsequent marriage. After the facts are examined before an ordinary Magistrate, and in the presence of guardians and the children's relatives, they are made equal in status. Master Biccius, in the *Golden Preface*, thesis 46. Works on the union of offspring were written by Mascardus and Rickius, as well as Schöner in his *Inaugural Dissertation* held at Strasbourg in 1642. See also Gail, book 2, observation 125, number 7; Gylman, volume 1, part 3, Chamber Vote 13, number 9; Master Tabor in the *Blessed Collection*, number 1, blessing 5 at the end; Meichsner, volume 4, decision 6, number 33; Musculus, *On Conventional Succession*, class 1, member 3, letter f. According to the Franconian Ordinance, part 3, title 108: a brother united this way does not succeed a united brother. Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 8, number 438, notes: those joined by a union of offspring are considered "fictional and imaginary" children and do not succeed in family entails <note>original: "fideicommissis"</note>. Furthermore, united children are not included in statutes that speak generally of "sons" (chapter 8, number 439). Regarding how such a child-unification <term>Einkindschafft</term> between spouses who already have children takes effect—and how it is not easily revoked once the necessary requirements are met—see Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 483 and the three following. He also discusses whether such an agreement is valid when no children exist from the later marriage (question 7, number 486). A pact for the union of offspring is neither merely dispositive nor conservative, but is acquisitive and irrevocable. Hahn, *On the Law of Things*, chapter 74, numbers 11 and 12.

### 20. Income. <note>original: "Einkommen. Reditus."</note>

By what means may an Estate of the Empire, burdened with great expenses, discharge them and improve its revenues and income? See the *Strasbourg Consultations*, volume 2, consultation 68, and especially volume 1, consultations 9 and 10; see also my own singular discourse on this matter.

### ADDITION.

From where is the word "revenue" <note>original: "Reditus"</note> derived? Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 1, chapter 2, number 19. Revenues are divided into "natural" and "industrial" (number 21); "mutable" and "immutable" (or certain and uncertain, number 22); and "ordinary" and "extraordinary" (numbers 23 and 24). Annual revenues are counted as immovable property. Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 5, number 26. For the formula for an obligation of annual revenue, see chapter 5, number 29. If they involve personal services, to which goods should they be counted? See chapter 5, number 30 and see the entry for **Assessment** <term>Anschlag</term>.

### 21. Wilderness. <note>original: "Einöde. Solitudo."</note>

The word wilderness <term>Einöde</term> is used for a desert or a solitude; it is derived from the ancient word *Oeden*, meaning goods or an estate. Mindanus, book 2, *On Chamber Process*, 42, number 3. By

<column-break/>

this word in Psalm 44, verse 14, it seems that "Islanders" are denoted—those whose proper diet consists of fish. Hence, islanders are called "One-housers" <term>Einhäuser</term> by Noë Meurer. See Gryphiander, *On Islands*, chapter 1, number 18. The word comes not from "One" <note>original: "Ein"</note> but from "Egg/Island" <note>original: "Ey"</note>, which means island; this is from the Hebrew <term>Ai</term>, which signifies the same thing, and is the root of the word island <term>Eyland</term>.

### ADDITION.

In the region of the **Grisons** <term>Graubündten</term>, a place is called **Desertina** <note>Now known as Disentis.</note> because of its wilderness <term>Einöd</term>. Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, volume 1, addition to book 4, chapter 7, number 31. It is called a wilderness <term>Einöd</term> as if it were an uncultivated place, or as if "all were waste" <note>original: "all ödte"</note>, because usually cultivated places were given to soldiers as fiefs, while uncultivated, deserted, and thorn-covered places were left to others. Finckelthaus, *On Illustrious Feudal Controversies*, Dispute 1, Controversy 5, letter B. On Hermits <note>original: "Eremitæ"</note>, see Borch, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, number 20; Boerius, decision 287, number 4. On the life and status of Hermits, see Nicolaus Boerius of Bordeaux, volume 13, part 2, folio 432.

It is of great importance to an authority that lands be diligently farmed and not left lying waste and desolate. Zorer, part 2, number 1, question 83 and following. Elsewhere, it is noted that waste and uninhabited estates were offered for sale and sold (question 1, sections 74 and 93). Concerning the land of Egypt and the wondrous River Nile, by which so many thousands of holy hermits wore out their bodies in "furry tunics" <note>original: "belzenen Juppen"</note>, see Jacob Balde, book 4, *Lyric Odes*, Ode 10, folio 223, and book 3, Ode 47, folio 197.

### 22. Quartering, Soldier-Tax. <note>original: "Einquartirung, Soldaten-Steuer. Præstatio metatorum."</note>

The question is asked: to which authority does the right of quartering <term>Einquartirung</term> belong? In this question, it is commonly held that it follows the territorial sovereignty <note>original: "Landsfürstliche Obrigkeit"</note>. If someone holds the "Power of the Sword" <note>original: "Blutbann" - the right to pass capital sentences</note> but does not simultaneously hold the territorial sovereignty (as can certainly happen), then the one to whom the Power of the Sword belongs may not claim the right of quartering. Furthermore, it can be concluded that if a Lord of a lower court has the right to tax, contribution, and mustering, then he also has the right of quartering; in this case, the Power of the Sword does not carry territorial sovereignty with it. However, where one has only the lower judicial authority and no regalia <note>sovereign rights</note>, he should not rightly claim the quartering of troops. See Rovenstrunck, *On Collections*, folio 108, and the Blessed Master Tabor, *On Quartering*, page 31.

<meta>This page continues the legal and political section under the letter 'E', transitioning from general family and succession law into specific jurisdictional disputes regarding taxation and the quartering of troops. The text focuses on a legal argument for the County of Hohenberg (Austrian territory) against the claims of the local nobility.</meta>

### Letter E.

### A list of those reasons why His Archducal Highness, or his Captain, Council, and Chief Officials of the County of Hohenberg <note>Abbreviated as 'H.' in the text; a reference to the Austrian County of Hohenberg in Swabia</note>, should by no means permit the subjects at Wurmlingen <note>Abbreviated as 'W.'</note> to be burdened with a soldier-tax or the quartering of troops by Junker T.

Firstly, the village of Wurmlingen is indisputably within the territory and district of the County, and is located very close to its capital, Rotenburg <note>Rotenburg am Neckar</note>. Indeed, there is no village in between them; rather, as I believe, their boundary stones touch one another. Therefore, His Archducal Highness has great cause to ensure that no individual member of the nobility, nor the Free Swabian Knighthood <term>Ritterschafft</term> in general, presumes to claim such high rights of sovereignty—such as the quartering of soldiers or demanding a financial contribution in its name—within the villages located in the County of Hohenberg.

Secondly, this is all the more necessary because the aforementioned House of Austria still has many different, unresolved disputes with the Free Knighthood in Swabia. These disputes, as I understand it, have been referred to an arbitration process. In this matter, the House of Austria could suffer a significant legal disadvantage <note>original: "præjudicium"</note> if one were to turn a blind eye to the present case or allow such a strong assertion of authority to proceed.

Thirdly, although Junker T., like those at M., holds a portion of the authority at Wurmlingen as a fief from Austria, this is only to be understood as bailiwick jurisdiction <term>Vogteyliche Botmäßigkeit</term> <note>lower civil and administrative authority</note>. In the meantime, the County of Hohenberg, through its officials at Rotenburg, has exercised and used the high criminal jurisdiction <note>original: "Malefizisch," the right to prosecute capital crimes</note> and other consequences of territorial or high princely sovereignty at all times—not only from ancient times but also to this day—without any hindrance or contradiction.

Fourthly and specifically: whenever a "Turkish Tax" <term>Türckensteuer</term> <note>a tax levied throughout the Holy Roman Empire to fund wars against the Ottoman Empire</note> or other assessment was imposed on the Austrian lands (and thus also on the County of Hohenberg), the people of Wurmlingen always delivered their portion, just like the subjects of other Austrian or Hohenberg towns.

Therefore, it would now be extremely burdensome, indeed intolerable and unjust, if they were simultaneously required to pay extraordinary taxes to the Knighthood or to their bailiff-lord <note>the Junker</note>, and thus be weighed down by a double burden.

Fifthly, it is entirely consistent with the law that the Knighthood may only tax those villages and subjects who belong immediately <note>without an intermediary lord</note> to His Imperial Majesty and the Holy Empire. 

<column-break/>

This does not apply to those situated within the jurisdiction of a Prince or a State of the Empire, who are an inseparable member of that same territory. See my work in the *Treatise on the Treasury*, folio 152.

Seventhly, it is nonetheless true that because Junker T. is a free nobleman and does not reside under Austrian authority, the Imperial Knighthood is authorized to tax his estates and income wherever they may be located (including his revenues from Wurmlingen) with extraordinary levies.

> For it is established that a citizen or subject, or even a member of any body <note>original: "membrum alicujus corporis"</note>—such as the Knighthood—can be taxed even by reason of those goods. For a tax is a mixed duty, which is imposed upon the person because of the property <note>original: "collecta munus mixtum, quod indicitur personæ propter rem"</note>. See my *Decades*, volume 3, counsel 269.

However, this can by no means be extended so far that the said Junker T. can also burden the Wurmlingen subjects (over whom he holds only the bailiwick authority) with such obligations. This is because the residents of Wurmlingen—by reason of the high regalian or princely sovereignty (which carries with it the rights of contribution, quartering, and similar powers)—remain Austrian subjects in every way. These superior rights <note>original: "Jura superiora"</note> have nothing to do with the Knighthood or Junker T. Therefore, T. can by no right <note>original: "nullo jure"</note> derive or shift the taxes he owes for himself and his estates onto these subjects of his lower jurisdiction, according to what I have handed down in the cited *Treatise on the Treasury*, folio 160.

Eighthly, although something to the contrary has been observed to some extent until now—and T. was permitted to tax the Wurmlingen subjects whenever the honorable Knighthood announced a contribution—this nevertheless happened out of error <note>original: "ex errore"</note> and, as indicated above, unlawfully. It is likely that His Archducal Highness or his most noble ancestors knew nothing at all about this. Consequently, no legal right through long-term use <term>præscriptio</term> can take place here, as it lacks good faith <note>original: "bona fide carens"</note> and imposes a burden on subjects that is contrary to natural equity. Furthermore, His Archducal Highness has a well-founded claim <note>original: "intentionem fundatam"</note> regarding the princely sovereignty at Wurmlingen, which supports the things I have taught in the cited treatise, folio 154.

This is especially true because Junker T. cannot show any legal title by virtue of which <note>original: "vigore cujus"</note> this taxation belongs to him. Since this has not been proven, he cannot even claim the legal remedy of maintaining the status quo <note>original: "remedium attentati"</note> against the Lord of the territory while the lawsuit is pending. Concerning territorial law.

And ninthly, even if those of Wurmlingen had to pay the knight-taxes (which, according to the arguments above, they do not), the right of taxation could not be extended to the quartering of troops.

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

...ation, as something separate and diverse, it can in no way be argued or concluded: because the common rule applies here completely, that "only as much is understood to be prescribed as is possessed" <note>original Latin: "tantum præscriptum, quantum possessum"</note>, especially since another (namely the most powerful House of Austria) is in general possession of the jurisdiction. See Wesenbeck in *Paratitla* on the *Digest*, "On Jurisdiction," number 12, at the end.

According to all of this, the subjects at Wurmlingen <note>abbreviated as 'W.'</note> may take comfort in their humble status, for the Lord Captain, Council, and Chief Officials of the County of Hohenberg <note>abbreviated as 'H.'</note> will show them this grace and will in no way permit such burdens to be forced upon them henceforth, etc.

It is also pleasing to add the following legal response <note>original Latin: "Responsum Juris"</note> which is relevant to this discussion.

Between the High-Born Lord, Lord Alwig, Count of Sulz, Landgrave in Klettgau, Hereditary Court Judge of the Holy Roman Empire at Rottweil, Lord in Montecler and Menzberg, Chamberlain to His Roman Imperial Majesty, and appointed Colonel, etc. And then also the High-Born Lord, Lord Maximilian, Landgrave of Stühlingen, Hereditary Marshal of His Roman Imperial Majesty and the Empire, Lord of Höwen, etc. A certain dispute and disagreement has appeared, in that the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen claims against the aforementioned Lord Count of Sulz regarding three villages—named Eschingen, Schwerzen, and Wüllmendigen—which the late High-Born Lord, Lord Karl Ludwig, Count of Sulz, etc., now resting in God, purchased from the said Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen for 35,000 [florins]. In this matter, the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen wishes to reserve and withhold the right to deliver the Imperial and Circle contributions <note>Taxes paid to the Holy Roman Empire and the Swabian Circle</note> into his Landgraviate of Stühlingen; furthermore, he concludes from this that the indicated three villages are obligated to pay and help carry, proportionally, the burdens and war expenses incurred by the Imperial Majesty’s troops quartered in the Landgraviate of Stühlingen.

However, that his Lordship the Count of Stühlingen's Countly Grace has no right to assume any taxation, Imperial, or Circle aid in this place—and even less to demand or seek anything from these villages or their inhabitants regarding the aforementioned quartering—is irrefutably strengthened by the following reasons.

Because, firstly, these three villages at all times—even before they were acquired by the Lords Counts

<column-break/>

of Sulz through purchase—as well as today, are indisputably situated within the territory of the Landgraviate of Klettgau, and have been immediately subject to its high judicial authority, protection, and defense. Thus, they are in no way to be considered an attachment <note>original: "pertinenz"</note> of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen.

Since jurisdiction, especially supreme jurisdiction, creates the distinction of territories; for indeed, "territory" is said to be derived from "frightening" <note>original Latin: "territorium dicitur à terrendo," a traditional legal etymology suggesting territory is defined by the area where a ruler has the power to inspire fear or command obedience</note>. See Law *pupillus* 239, § *territorium* 8, in the *Digest*, "On the Significance of Words." From this, a territory is called a space of land, fortified and armed with jurisdiction; and in this respect, it is also commonly said that jurisdiction is materially and passively inherent to the territory, "like a mist over a swamp" <note>original Latin: "tanquam nebula super paludem"</note>. See Natta, *Consilia* 149, number 19, volume 1.

And also, territory and jurisdiction are held to be the same thing, and he who has jurisdiction is also thought to have territory; for a territory is the district of jurisdiction in which the Lord of the territory has the right of frightening and of command <note>original Latin: "Jus terrendo ac Imperii"</note>. See the final law, where the Doctors of Law discuss "On Jurisdiction"; and Paurmeister, book 1, "On Jurisdiction," chapter 30, number 7.

And although the lower-court authorities <term>Niedergerichtliche Obers</term> <note>Rights of local or "petty" justice, often involving minor disputes and fines</note>, as well as common benefits and dues in these villages, were perhaps possessed and held by the nobility, and subsequently passed to the Lords Counts of Lupfen as holders of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen; yet it cannot be concluded from this at all that the three aforementioned villages became an attachment of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen. In consideration of this, the lower-court authority (which usually belongs to the local residents in their castles, villages, and manors—which are enclosed within a Prince’s territory and also subject to his high territorial sovereignty) does not create a separate territory, nor does it exempt a village from a high sovereign district.

Since a designation is made based on the more powerful part <note>original Latin: "à potiori denominatio fiat"</note>, a certain place can belong to the territory of one Lord even if another holds the lower jurisdiction there, even by right of allodial title <note>land held independently of a superior lord</note>, as common experience attests.

Since the often-mentioned three villages are situated in the Landgraviate of Klettgau by reason of territory and high authority, it follows quite correctly from this that they are in no way to be taxed by the holders of the lower courts, nor are they obligated to help carry their Circle and Imperial levies.

For today, taxes <note>original Latin: "collectæ"</note>, which in the Empire have taken the place of extraordinary contributions for the most successful expedition of the Royal Power, are imposed by virtue of the Regalia <term>Regalia</term> <note>Sovereign rights belonging to the crown or state</note> and high sovereign power <note>original Latin: "meri Imperii"</note>. This is taught by Gail, *Observations* 52, number 22, and the following observation, book 2; Decianus, *Consilia* 41, numbers 41 and 128, volume 2; Wesenbeck, *Consilia* 45, numbers 2, 3, 8, and 20; and Baldus in the title "What are Regalia."

<summary>This page discusses a jurisdictional conflict between the Landgraviates of Klettgau and Stühlingen, arguing that the right to tax and quarter troops belongs to the holder of high jurisdiction (territorial sovereignty) rather than the holder of lower justice or manorial rights.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument concerning the three villages (Eschingen, Schwerzen, and Wüllmendigen) disputed between the Landgraviate of Stühlingen and the County of Sulz (Klettgau). The previous page established the background of the conflict; this page argues that since the villages were sold by Stühlingen to Sulz in 1603, all rights of taxation and jurisdiction were transferred to the buyer.</meta>

Lit. E.

Likewise, the right of collecting taxes <note>original Latin: "Jus collectandi"</note>, according to the truer opinion of the learned Doctors, consists of Sovereign Rights <term>Regalia: rights or privileges belonging exclusively to a sovereign or ruler</term>. This opinion is confirmed by Sixtinus in his work *On Sovereign Rights*, chapter 14, number 17, using many texts and the authorities of a great many Doctors. It appears that this same opinion has also been frequently approved by voting and deciding in the Imperial Chamber Court, as seen in the records found in Meichsner’s *Decisions of the Imperial Chamber*, volume 2, book 1, decision 6, number 129, and volume 3, decision 1, number 13.

It is therefore all the less to be presumed that the often-mentioned three villages, by reason of Imperial or Circle aid <note>taxes paid to the Holy Roman Empire or the Swabian Circle</term>, are to be considered an appurtenance of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen. This is because they were not always part of it, but were first acquired through a purchase from the Lord Count of Lupfen.

Secondly, the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen also has no cause to impose any tax, aid, or other burden on these villages, because His Grafl. Grace <note>a title: "His Countly Grace"</note> sold the same in the year 1603 to the late Lord Carl Ludwig, Count of Sulz, with all rights.

Furthermore, one who sells a thing is considered to sell it free of encumbrance, by his own right, and with a full transfer of ownership <note>original Latin: "cum plena Dominii translatione"</note>. This is supported by the Gloss and Baldus in the code *On Evictions* and proven in the laws of the *Digest* regarding actions of purchase and sale. See also Cæpolus in the treatise *On Rural Estates*, column 4, number 17.

And since jurisdiction today is treated almost as patrimonial <term>patrimonial jurisdiction: a form of authority that can be inherited, bought, or sold like private property</term>, it can therefore be sold and ceded. Consequently, if a place is transferred together with its jurisdiction, no one can doubt that it is considered transferred privately and not cumulatively as far as the seller or transferor is concerned. This is argued from the law on alienation in Alciatus, number 9, and Schrad on fiefs, part 10, section 1, number 132 and following; also Matthaeus Stephanus on jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 38, number 38.

Accordingly, the sales agreement regarding these three villages explicitly provides how the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen promised to yield and grant them—with all their rights and belongings, just as Lupfen and Mösskirch <note>original: "Merßburg"</note> had previously held, used, and enjoyed them—to the late Lord Carl Ludwig, Count of Sulz. Likewise, the Lord Landgrave simultaneously agreed that the Lord Count of Sulz may and shall immediately take the hereditary homage <term>Erbhuldigung: a formal oath of loyalty sworn by subjects to a new ruler</term> from the subjects of these three villages at His Countly Grace’s pleasure, without any entry or contradiction from Pappenheim or Mösskirch. This was established so that the subjects should and would henceforth respect, recognize, and hold the Lord Count as their true, natural hereditary lord. Most importantly, however, this gives the Lord Count of Sulz a strong defense, as it was specifically

<column-break/>

stipulated in the aforementioned sales agreement concerning the outstanding old Imperial Contributions—which fell due before the Diet <note>Reichstag</note> held just before that time—that the same should be reserved for the Lord of Pappenheim to collect. Likewise, property belonging to those three villages that is situated on the other side of the Wutach river in the Landgraviate of Stühlingen is not subject to the Sulz jurisdiction. Thus, only this area, as far as the Wutach flows, shall be subject to the Lord Count of Sulz regarding jurisdiction, where previously it fell under the Klettgau <note>original: "Cleggewisch"</note> high forestry court and sovereign escorts.

From these irrefutable facts, it follows that in the future, the Imperial Contributions ought to be collected by the Lord Count of Sulz as the buyer. Furthermore, whatever is situated across the Wutach—in which the three disputed villages are simultaneously included—belongs absolutely to the Landgraviate of Klettgau. The Lord Seller, by reason of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen, has no jurisdiction or other justice to seek in those parts.

Since the inclusion of one thing is the exclusion of another <note>original Latin: "Cum inclusio unius, alterius exclusio existat"</note>, as found in Thuscus under the letter I, conclusion 71. This applies to every disposition including a certain place, time, thing, or person, because it excludes the rest. See Ruinus, volume 5, and Angelus, number 3. Where something is granted for a specific time, it is seen as denied after that time, because the inclusion of one implies the exclusion of the other. See also Geminianus, number 19, where if power is granted to someone to do something for a certain time, after that time it is considered denied.

Just as an exception confirms the rule in contrary cases <note>original Latin: "exceptio in contrarium regulam firmat"</note>. See the *Digest* on the equipment of a farm, and the Glosses on the *Rules of Law*.

And what was set down in this sales agreement is repeated and strengthened even more thoroughly in the subsequent deed of sale <note>original German: "Kauffbrief"</note>, dated the 18th of the same month and year. Truly, this doubling of the act and the words clearly indicates a greater deliberation and a firm will, especially if it is done after an interval of time. See Augustinus Barbosa in his *Axioms of Law*, axiom 195, number 18: nothing can be added to doubled words.

In particular, it is mentioned in such a deed of sale and acknowledged by the Lord Seller, the current Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen, that these three villages are situated within the district of the Klettgau high sovereignty belonging to Sulz. They were transferred with all rights, among which taxes are mentioned by name—named and unnamed, frequented and unfrequented—with nothing excepted or reserved therefrom,

# Added Practical Treasures #

transferred to the Lord Count of Sulz, and was left to him by sale, along with several other clauses and renunciations which are considered unnecessary to set down here; rather, for the sake of preferred brevity, one should refer only to the literal content of the original bill of sale. And although afterwards, in the year 1610—when the late Lord Carl Ludwig, Count of Sulz, etc., of blessed memory, gave the Lordship of Mettingen to the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen to purchase—the following words were added at the end of the bill of sale drawn up for this purpose, dated February 1st of the aforementioned year: "Finally, it is also clearly stipulated and reserved in this sale negotiation that the holders of the two aforementioned villages, Oeschingen and Schwärzen, now and for all eternity, situated across the Wutach in the Landgraviate of Stühlingen's high jurisdiction, shall have, seek, or claim no lower judicial authority <term>Niedergerichtliche Obrigkeit: jurisdiction over minor civil cases and petty crimes</term> nor anything attached to it, in any way or path; instead, these shall at all times belong to and remain with the specific villages of Horchheim and Leidenschlo. And because the previously mentioned villages are situated in the Muchen valley, belonging to the body <note>original German: "Corpore"</note> of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen, the Lordship of Hewen and Bondorf, for the sake of Imperial and Circle aid <term>Reichs- und Kraishülffen: taxes paid to the Holy Roman Empire and the Swabian Administrative Circle</term>, as they have always belonged, they shall remain so as of old; and both that which has fallen due, as well as that which might fall due in the future, shall be rendered and paid by the subjects there, as is customary in other places, to which the inhabitants of these villages shall give their possible assistance as far as their quota extends at any time—unless it should happen that this quota were taken away from the Landgraviate of Stühlingen and instead applied to the Landgraviate of Klettgau <note>original: "Cleggew"</note>, into which these villages now belong; so let it finally remain. All honorable, upright, faithful, and without trickery."

Yet such words could not support the intention of the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen at all: Because (1) only two villages, Oeschingen and Schwärzen, are mentioned there, while Wüllmendingen is not named at all; therefore it correctly follows that Wüllmendingen can in no way be burdened with any obligation by the highly esteemed Lord Landgrave.

Furthermore, (2) it is no less surprising how this passage came into the Mettingen bill of sale, especially since it is noted there that this passage was clearly stipulated and reserved during the Mettingen sale negotiations, even though in the sale agreement handled shortly before on January 21st, and 

<column-break/>

signed by the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen himself, not a single word of this is mentioned.

But a reference proves nothing if the matter referred to is not established <note>original Latin: "At referens non probat, si de relato non constat"</note>, because there is only as much in the reference as there is in the thing referred to <note>original Latin: "quia tantum est in referente, quantum in relato"</note>. See the Law "from the whole" <note>original Latin: "l. à se toto"</note> in the Digest regarding the institution of heirs; also Peregrinus on Trusts, article 16, number 2, etc. Therefore, if the thing referred to is otherwise, the reference is not to be cared for.

One can also (3) not see how, in the Mettingen sale transaction concerning these two villages and who is entitled to tax them, anything special was negotiated—especially anything that would detract from the older bill of sale drawn up for these villages, or how such a significant burden should have been knowingly and deliberately imposed on these two villages by the Lord Count of Sulz.

Indeed, a change of will is least presumed <note>original Latin: "Mutatio quippe voluntatis minimè præsumitur"</note>, and for a new pact, a new convention and negotiation are necessary, which is not established here.

Therefore (4) it is in every way to be presumed that the Lord Count of Sulz allowed the indicated, very burdensome clause to be placed in the bill of sale out of error <note>original Latin: "ex errore"</note>, primarily because His Countly Grace was not personally present at the preceding sale agreement and could therefore more easily err in the actions of another <note>original Latin: "in facto alieno"</note>.

And a total error is to be presumed because His Countly Grace would have, now and for absolutely no cause <note>original Latin: "sine omni prorsus causa"</note>, let out of his hands and quite thoughtlessly given away that which indisputably belonged to him previously by virtue of the bill of sale received for these three villages, as deduced above.

Moreover, an error is usually presumed rather than a donation <note>original Latin: "Error autem potius, quam donatio præsumi solet"</note>. See the Commentary <note>original: "Gloss."</note> on the Law "Generally," on the word "Cause" <note>original Latin: "in verbo causa"</note> in the Code regarding non-enumerated money; also Mascardus, conclusion 555, number 5 and following, where he extends this even to one's own act.

And that an act should rather be rendered void than a donation presumed <note>original Latin: "Quodque potius debeat reddi actus nullus, quam donatio præsumi"</note> is handed down by Jason, counsel 160, number 3, volume 4, and cited elsewhere by Tiraqueau on the Law "If ever," on the words "bestowed by donation" <note>original Latin: "in verb. donatione largitus"</note>, number 303, at the verse "but also" in the Code on the revocation of donations.

Likewise, the aforementioned error is sufficiently proven because it is stated in the Mettingen bill of sale that both villages, Oeschingen and Schwärzen, have always belonged to the body <note>original: "corpore"</note> of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen, the Lordship of Hewen and Bondorf, because of Imperial and Circle aid; yet this has not been proven at all to this time, nor is it in any way to be presumed from what was deduced above. This is because they are enclaved <note>original German: "inclavirt"</note> in the territory of the Landgraviate of Klettgau, and have not been with the holders of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen since ancient times, but were purchased from a nobleman. Even if the matter were so—namely, if such villages belonged to Stühlingen—the Landgrave of Stühlingen, with the prudence for which he is known, would have included this in the sale

and the letter drawn up concerning it, of the frequently mentioned villages, where it properly belongs, should by no means have been forgotten or omitted.

An error is proved, however, by proving that the matter is otherwise. <note>original: "Probatur autem error, probando rem aliter se habere." referencing laws on age and debt.</note>

Especially if the party in error were striving to avoid a loss, while the other sought profit, or if it concerned the loss of a profit already acquired. <note>original: "Maximè, si errans certaret de damno vitando..."</note>

And although the holders of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen, as long as they simultaneously possessed these three villages, might also have burdened them with Imperial and Circle taxes <term>Reichs- und Craissteuren: taxes paid to the Holy Roman Empire and the Swabian Administrative Circle</term>, which remains to be proven by the opposing side; yet those same villages were to be regarded as an appurtenance of the Landgraviate of Stühlingen solely by the designation of the possessor <note>original: "ex destinatione possessoris"</note>, and not at all by law, or by way of natural inheritance or necessity.

Certainly, such a designation is usually most attended to when it is asked to which territory a place belongs by reason of Imperial Contributions. <note>original: "Qualis certe destinatio..."</note>

The Imperial Recess <term>Reichs-Abschied: the final summary of decisions made at an Imperial Diet</term> of the year 1576 also speaks of various holders and joint heirs of a lordship, where it is indisputable that each possesses a piece of the lordship—which on this side is by no means admitted, but rather the opposing party is still obliged to prove. For he who says something belongs [to him], must prove it. <note>original: "Namque, qui dicit aliquid pertinere, illud probare debet."</note>

Likewise, the usurpation cited by the opposition has no such effect that the intention of His Grace the Count of Stühlingen could prevail, considering that in the year 1603 these three villages, with all cause and right, came to the Lord Count of Sulz, and since then 30 years have not yet passed, which time would be sufficient for the prescription of any kind of jurisdiction. <note>Prescription refers to the legal acquisition of a right or title through long-continued, uninterrupted use.</note>

For jurisdiction without territory, as an incorporeal thing, is not usually prescribed except in 30 years. <note>original: "Etenim Jurisdictio citra territorium..."</note>

Even assuming, though by no means conceding, that some reservation was attached to the sale on the part of the Lord Landgrave of Stühlingen as the seller, or that the common Imperial and Circle aids were stipulated and reserved for the Landgraviate of Stühlingen, one would nevertheless have to interpret this strictly and against the seller, who ought to have stated the law of the contract more clearly. It should not at all be applied to the present unique case, of which the contracting parties by no means thought at that time: for the quartering [of soldiers] is in no way a common Imperial or Circle levy, but was imposed by His Roman Imperial Majesty according to discretion and out of special 

<column-break/>

consideration, whereby one Estate <term>Stand: a territory or person with a seat and vote in the Imperial Diet</term> was burdened more than the other, and the portion of the Imperial levy was not at all taken into account. So that an inference cannot be made from diverse things.

Furthermore, the Landgraviates and subjects of Lord Count Alwig of Sulz are under the protection, shield, or defense of His Imperial Majesty by virtue of the Princely Friedlandish Safe-Conduct <term>Salva Guardia: a formal protection order, here likely referring to one issued by Albrecht von Wallenstein, Duke of Friedland</term>. This was granted because of the loyal devotion that His Grace and his noble ancestors have at all times shown, steadily and uninterruptedly, both to the Holy Roman Empire and to the house of Austria, most blessed by GOD. They were received in such a way that they shall be and remain entirely exempt or free from all military lodging or quartering, as well as from all other war hardships, contributions, money-ransoms, levies, marches, or whatever else such disturbances may be called.

Which privilege, certainly granted for most notable merits, is to be regarded as entirely favorable, and should be interpreted most broadly as a Princely benefit. <note>original: "Quod certè privilegium ob notissima benè merita concessum..."</note>

Likewise, there is no doubt that this is to be applied to the three disputed villages, which are absolutely subject to the Lord Count of Sulz.

It is also not to be heard [i.e., it is unacceptable] that His Grace the Landgrave of Stühlingen objects that such a privilege is not to be understood to the prejudice of a third party, or to the detriment of older pacts; for it is not at all to be presumed, much less has it been shown by proof yet, that the Landgrave of Stühlingen was burdened with quartering higher or lower in regard to these three villages.

In view of all this, it remains once again that His Grace the Landgrave of Stühlingen has absolutely nothing to claim from these three Sulzish villages on account of such quartering. However, it stands, etc.

<meta>This page continues a legal encyclopedia or "Treasury of Practice," specifically discussing the rights and obligations involving the housing of officials, legal objections, and the ceremonial entry of rulers into their territories.</meta>

Jerome Bignon has much to say on this in his notes on the Monk Marculphus’s *Book of Formulas* on page 445 and the two following, where he says that *Mansiones* <term>Mansiones: official lodgings or stations provided for traveling dignitaries</term> and *Paratas* <term>Paratas: preparations, specifically the provision of food and supplies for officials on the road</term> are correctly linked together. In ancient documents from Princes, *Paratas* always follow *Mansiones*, so much so that in certain places one is used for the other, although they are different names and represent different legal rights. Providing a dwelling was called *Mansionaticum*; however, under the name of *Paratas* came those things provided for the journey and for food. This custom is Roman in origin; they called the reception of guests *metatum* <note>original: "metatum"</note>, which is the subject of Title 40 of Book 12 of the Code. Title 12 of the same book, *On Travel Warrants and Stations* <note>original: "de Tractoriis & Stativis"</note>, declares that those who were directed somewhere by the Prince with a *tractoria* <term>Tractoria: a Roman imperial warrant or passport granting the holder the right to use public transport and supplies</term> were to be supported at public expense. Livy reveals the origin at the start of Book 42 regarding the Consul Lucius Posthumius Albinus, who was the first to send letters demanding that the local magistrates come out to meet him, that they prepare a public place where he might stay, and that pack animals be ready when he departed.

Draco also clarifies what Billeting and Lodging are in *On Patricians*, page 158. Omphalius wrote a legal opinion on quartering.

## 23. Objection. *Exceptio*.

The clause "without delay and objection" <note>original: "ohne Verzug und Einred"</note> matches the phrase "immediately, no exception standing in the way" <note>original: "in continenti, nullâ exceptione obftante"</note>, etc. When this is placed in a statute or constitution, a command must first be obeyed, though one's rights are reserved for later. Mynsinger, observation 2, 10. This is the nature of Mandates without a Clause: that one must obey them, despite an illegal act or command, even if the main cause is good; or because of the clauses of the legal instrument, even if objections are present.

### ADDITION.

The clause "saving exceptions" <note>original: "salvis Exceptionibus"</note>. Berlichius 1, conclusion 84, number 98. "Immediately" <note>original: "In continenti"</note>, or "on fresh foot" <note>original: "auf frischem Fuß"</note>. Berlichius 1, conclusion 24. Dr. Tabor, *Elements of Jurisprudence*, part 3, section 3. Dr. Ludwig in the *Feudal Synopsis* and Notes

<column-break/>

on Wesenbeck, page 346: the words **without** any delay and objection <note>original: "**ohn** einigen Verzug und Einred"</note> apply no less to the Statutes on Arrests than to the Statutes on Pledges. Therefore, they can also be understood as referring to the Objection of Property, as Gail notes in observation 14, numbers 7 and 9, on pledges. Schwanmann, decision 10, number 105.

## 24. Formal Entry. *Jus intradæ*.

A token of subjection is held to be the solemn arrival of a Prince, commonly called the "Entry" <note>original: "der Einritt"</note>, where armed subjects devoutly receive their hereditary Lord. Ruland, *On Commerce*, part 3. In the entry, the keys of the city are offered, which metaphorically denotes the recognition of a high rank, as is also taken in sacred scripture: Isaiah chapter 22, Matthew 16, and Luke 11. Therefore, by the handing over of the keys, the transfer of lordship is brought about; as in the law on keys regarding contracts of sale; just as the retention of the keys in a jurisdictional act indicates superiority. See Knichen, number 6 and following.

### ADDITION.

Regarding excessive cavalry, Klock writes excellently in *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 108: "An excessive abundance of horses begets a poverty of revenue." Nor should horses be held in higher value than subjects. Philipp Melanchthon says in his commentary on the Gospel for the 9th Sunday after Trinity, page 466: "See," he says, "what whirlpools, what Charybdises <note>referencing the mythical sea monster that swallowed ships</note> of wealth exist in courts; often a Prince feeds four hundred horses when he barely needs 40 or 50; the rest are fed for show." Lovick, *On the Instruction of Princes*, page 219. Regarding the solemn use of the Prince's Entry (*Einreiten*) received today: Wesenbeck, Council 2, number 78. Adam Keller on the legal-political office, book 2, chapter 12, page 461, on entry-money (*Einzuggeld*). The same, page 361. An entrance with great display touches upon an act of preeminence. Riding out to meet someone is often dangerous, says Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relations*, part 6, page 180. The "Right of Entry" <note>original: "Jus intradæ"</note>, or solemn entrance (*des Eintritts oder Einzugs*), by virtue of which subjects are bound to devoutly receive the territorial Lord with festive display while under arms and to go out to meet him: *Public College of Marburg*, Dispute 6. Compare the law on the office of Proconsul, where subordinate magistrates are plainly forbidden from demanding anything in the name of "entries." The late Dr. Tabor, *On Billeting*, page 36 and following.

## 25. To Pledge. *Oppignorare*.

The word *Einsetzen* <term>Einsetzen: literally "to set in" or "place in," used here for pledging property</term>, according to the common usage of speech in Germany, applies to a pledge, not to a purchase or sale. Schrader, Council 32. Hence a pledge is also called an *Einsatz*.

### 27. Seizure of Evildoers. Imprisonment.

Whether imprisonment <note>original: "incarceratio"</note> pertains to one who holds jurisdiction: and what is the accepted practice regarding the **Nobles of Germany**? Regarding this question, Master Rutger Ruland, in his *Decisions on Controverted Law*, question 14, writes the following: When this question, he says, was alleged in the case of **Hereditary Marshal Pappenheim** against **Ellgau**, it was treated as follows: The appellant, by virtue of purchase, holds simple jurisdiction <term>simple jurisdiction: lower-level legal authority over minor civil matters and local order</term>; one holding such power can seize defendants who commit major crimes, thrust them into prison, and then remand them to the one who holds high jurisdiction <term>high jurisdiction: also known as "merum imperium," the power of life and death or the authority to try capital crimes</term>. *Petrus Jacobus* in his booklet on jurisdiction, number 13; *Alexander* on the law of high jurisdiction, number 22. And it is in these small matters that the jurisdictions of villages, towns, and communities consist. For this reason, the Doctors of Law decide the question of whose authority and jurisdiction imprisonment belongs to in this manner—as *Bartolus* does in the law of high jurisdiction—stating that if it is done for *custody*, until the crime is investigated, it does not belong to high jurisdiction, because it is within the competence of lower magistrates and defenders. It is otherwise if it is for *punishment*: for then it belongs to high jurisdiction, according to *Cagnolus*, who approves the opinion of *Bartolus*. And although a prison may be a sign of high jurisdiction, the contrary argument is made that jurisdiction also includes the power of coercion; otherwise, it would not be called jurisdiction. For all things seem to be granted without which jurisdiction cannot be exercised. Thus, even a judge of civil causes, if a crime should arise during a lawsuit, may punish it. This is supported by the custom of Germany, where Nobles holding simple jurisdiction may imprison people. This must, however, be tempered so that Nobles do not abuse this power or enact anything too harsh. Hence, a Lord may imprison a servant but may not treat him with cruelty. It was therefore concluded there that the Plaintiff indeed has the right of imprisonment, but in his own specific way. But because there has been abuse of this jurisdiction until now, I would prefer, says the Assessor, that this point be entrusted to another and nothing be pronounced, but the defendants simply be acquitted: since jurisdiction can be stripped from a Lord on account of cruelty. However, let him beware lest he act too severely.

To what extent does prison belong to high jurisdiction? See my discussion in the treatise on the treasury, page 144.

### ADDITION.

On Prisons, see *Baldus de Perusio*. On the release of those imprisoned, see *Paulus Grillandus* and *Castellion of Florence*.

<column-break/>

A prison for church ministers in **Stuttgart**, called "The Bible." *Zeiller, century 4, question 51, page 271.*

Whether an imprisoned person can be summoned: see *Ummius* in his work on procedure, page 185. Imprisonment is an irretractable disgrace. *Barbosa*, book 3, chapter 7. For a prisoner, the prison is often a great torture. For this reason, it is called a "bad stay" and a species of torture. The injustice of a prison can always be raised as an objection. One who imprisons another is not held to the penalty for "private imprisonment" if he holds jurisdiction. Subterranean prisons are condemned. *Oldekop, Criminal Observations, page 171.*

### 29. Law of Jealousy.

Since it frequently happened among the Jewish people that certain women—either through hatred or contempt for their husbands, or through pride, rivalry and jealousy, or lust, or some other impudence and boldness—became estranged from their husbands (which happened mostly because of polygamy), they would join themselves to others and hide with them in secret places long enough that they could be polluted and defiled. Even when warned by their husbands and ordered to abstain from such company, they would not obey but nevertheless persisted obstinately in their purpose. It was permitted for husbands, by the Law of Jealousy <note>original: "Lex zelotypiæ" / German: "Eyfergesetz"</note> brought by God through **Moses** in Numbers chapter 5, from verse 11 to the end of the chapter, to charge those suspected of violated modesty and broken marital faith and rights, and to remove them from their presence until the accusation and proof were completed. *Eberhard Speckhan, century 3, Class 4, question 9.*

## 30. Angel. Angelus.

Concerning **Angels**, see the Reverend Father Drexelius’s *Guardian Angel*, and Friedrich Forner in his *Sermons on Angels*. See also Maiolus, *Canicular Days*, colloquy 1 and following, volume 7; Stengelius’s special treatise *On the Creation of Angels*; *Philosophy of Spirits*, folio 266, and throughout the discourse on their Order in the same work, folio 299; and on the battle of the Angels, folio 360. Concerning the **Angels of Empires**, I have treated this in *Politics*, in the treatise *On the Principles and Ends of Politics*; regarding the fact that the Angels of Provinces **pray for their lands**, see the *Roman Catechism*, folio 346, and the aforementioned authors. Regarding **evil Angels** and their fall, see Barth on the Gaul, folio 55 and following.

### ADDITION.

In the **Council of Laodicea**, it is commanded that unknown names of Angels neither be invented nor spoken, as is recorded in the *Capitularies* of the Emperors Charles and Louis, chapter 16. Likewise, that pseudographic <note>falsely attributed</note> and doubtful narratives, or those which are entirely against the Catholic faith (such as that most wicked and false letter which some wandering men, leading others into error, claimed had fallen from heaven), should neither be believed nor read, but burned, lest the people be led into error by such a writing. Chapter 78 of the *Capitularies*. Concerning **imposture**, if anyone should terrify another with an apparition of a Divinity, see Master Doctor Tabor on <term>Stellionatus: a legal term for fraud or deceptive crimes that do not have a specific name</term>. When great changes are impending, new supposed Prophets come forward. There was once such a person at **Tübingen** who was driven into exile. The **Duke of Württemberg** in the year 1648 consulted the College of Legal Scholars at Strasbourg regarding the punishment for an impostor who fabricated Angelic apparitions and claimed that vines dripped blood <note>A common "omen" used to incite religious fervor or panic</note> in order to lead men to repentance. This man was accused of a capital crime, following the example of the citizens of **Cremona** (mentioned by Bossius), who stained their walls with blood to strike terror of the enemy into the citizens. But according to law 3, section 1 on fraud and law 30 on punishments, it was advised that he be punished outside the normal order as an impostor. The citizens of Cremona committed this act

<column-break/>

for the purpose of turning the garrisoned soldiers away from extortions and oppressions. Egidius Bossius, title *On Extraordinary Crimes*, page 362, number 9.

## 31. England. Anglia.

In **England**, there is a "full kingdom" <note>a sovereign monarchy</note>, as I said in the treatise *On Monarchy*, folio 23. But it might seem that **Parliament** shares something of the Majesty <note>sovereign power</note>: see the contents of volume 12 of the *French Mercury*, folio 232. On this matter, Friedrich de Marselaer writes in his *The Ambassador*, folio 130: The authority of Parliament was formerly supreme, greater than that of the King himself; so much so, indeed, that the King was obliged to subscribe to the decrees and statutes of this Supreme Council and could not oppose them. Today, there still exists a certain image of what it once was. The King admits into Parliament whom he wishes, and does not admit those he does not wish; nor is it summoned thereafter except by the consultation and will of the King. It is, however, usually summoned whenever weightier matters are at hand, from which the English Commonwealth might feel urgent loss or benefit. Hence, the King himself sometimes joins that assembly of the Estates, intending to understand the deliberations on both sides, so that he may seem to consult the public good with greater affection; and so that he may simultaneously obtain from his subjects what he cannot command; for although these things may be necessary, he is nevertheless compelled to ask for them. *Reports of Bentivoglio*, folios 212 and 228.

### 32. Decision.

These terms differ: *taking Law* and *taking a Decision*. For a *Decision* <note>original Latin: Entschied</note> is to be understood as referring to a summary process <note>a simplified, faster legal proceeding</note> in cases where one may proceed in such a way. *Law* <note>original: Recht</note>, however, refers to the Ordinary process: for otherwise the words would have no effect.

->ADDITION.<-

Let one thing not diminish another, nor leave another under error: Justinian. For even if he wished there to be some manner of peace, the valuation of it might soon be his own. Neratius. Nevertheless, it is expedient to express openly in words whatever belongs to a binding transaction, so that there is no occasion for a greater tumult—that it does not lead to more or new dealings, or a "Peasant’s Decision" <note>original German: Baurn-Entschied; a derogatory term for a crude settlement that splits the difference rather than following strict law</note>. Paul. Cell. Schmuck, *Legal Disputes*, 6, thesis 47. To divide a question down the middle is the way of rustics, as noted in the Gloss to the law *Nefennius 35* at the end of the digest *on the management of affairs*.

### 33. Deprivation of Honors. Removal from status and dignity.

Although removal from status and dignity—as when one is stripped of his honors—does not fall under the three headings of an action for personal injury <note>original Latin: actionis injuriarum</note> under the Cornelian Law (which lasts 30 years); nevertheless, if it is treated as an action for dispossession <note>original: actione spolii; a claim that one has been "robbed" of their position</note>, it then lasts 30 years, and the action for personal injury can be added to it, provided it is sought within a year. Thus, within the term of one year, both processes were decreed—by reason of dispossession and injury—in the case of *Imlin against Heilbronn*, April 12, 1591. When someone is deposed from an office or dignity, then an action for personal injury is available to him. Otherwise, the office of the Judge is also implored. Furthermore, possessory remedies are available: namely, the *Interdict to keep possession* <note>original: Interdictum uti possidetis</note>. Also, the *Restoration for force* <note>original: Unde vi</note>, if he were in quasi-possession of the honor. This was done in the Chamber in the said case of *Imlin against Heilbronn*, April 20, 1591. See the acquittal in the case of the degradation of Consular dignity, June 5, 1522, in Sailer. And mostly such cases are titled "Dispossession and Injury."
But is one who is thus removed from office said to be affected by a real injury or at least a verbal one? This is the question. And truly it seems to be a real

<margin>Besold, Volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

injury: because it has a permanent effect, and therefore it is called perpetual; or at least it lasts for a minimum of four years, because it was done through force or compelling fear. But if we look at the matter more closely, it seems to last only for a year. Rutger Ruland, book 8 *on remedies against weak things*, chapter 4 *on injuries*, number 10 and following. But the matter is usually tempered so that, regarding the action for injury, that action lasts only one year; but regarding the dispossession, it has 30 years. And this is observed in the Chamber, as the same Ruland testifies in the mentioned place, number 12 at the end.

->ADDITION.<-

Johannes à Sande, in the *Frisian Decisions*, book 5, title 10, definition 2, says that although in the opinion of some, any Magistrate can revoke and depose his officials at his will—provided he revokes them simply with no cause added that smears their reputation—it is otherwise if he removes them for an "infamous" cause; because then this removal cannot be done except for a true and proven cause. Klock, *on the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 130, number 7. Boerius, *decision 150 at the end*. Officials growing rich from public revenues are to be squeezed like sponges. Klock, *on the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 31, throughout. He who can appoint can also remove. There are often various causes through which someone can be removed from office. Barbosa lists these extensively in book 16, chapter 28, axiom 2, at the end.

### 35. Iron Livestock. Perpetual Herds. The Partnership Contract of Socida.

In many provinces, such as Hesse, Thuringia, and elsewhere, it is accepted that subjects are free to leave the soil and migrate to another territory even without a dismissal from their Lords, provided they leave on the farm as many sheep, cows, pigs, horses, geese, chickens, ducks, pigeons, etc., as were originally delivered to them. The Thuringians call these "heads" <note>individual animals</note> *Iron Livestock* <note>German: "Eisern Viehe"</note>, as if they never die, because of the substitution of new animals in place of those that have died. See Law 62 at the end, *On Usufruct*. Others call it *the Guarantee* <note>German: "die Währung"</note> by the same etymology: Friedrich Husanus, *Treatise on Personal Property*, chapter 8, number 10. In this matter, local customs must be observed. For where migrations of this sort are not accepted by custom (as in Mecklenburg,

<column-break/>

where without the permission of the Lords, they cannot move into the cities to learn mechanical arts and manual trades, or to serve citizens or foreign nobles. See the *Mecklenburg Political Ordinance*, title *On Servants*, paragraph *as also occurs*), migrating tenant farmers are rightly reclaimed by the Lord; see the penultimate law in the first section of the Code *On Farmers and Taxpayers*. For those who are bound to provide service to another by reason of subjection, a fief, or another cause, cannot change their location to the prejudice of the Lord, nor move their domicile or their colonies elsewhere against his will. See the text in the law *If anyone a farm*, and the law *If Farmers* in the same title; see also Rauchbar, part 2, question 29.

This applies especially to those registered <note>tax-linked</note> and subjects of a servile condition, known as *Bondservants* <note>German: "Leibeigen Leut"</note>, because they are considered part of the land, such that they cannot be separated from the earth; indeed, they are thought to be so attached to the earth that they cannot be removed from it even by a contract, unless they are alienated <note>sold or transferred</note> together with the farm or the entire estate. See the law *All entirely* in the Code *On Farmers and Taxpayers*. Gail, *Treatise on Arrests*, chapter 8, number 14.

But sometimes a certain number of sheep, cows, etc., are also given as part of a Fief along with the land, which are also designated as *iron sheep or iron livestock*. See Gothofredus Antonii, *Feudal Disputation* 3, thesis 4, title 6. Likewise, *Steel or painted cows* <note>German: "Stählin oder gemalte Kühe"</note> are given in a usurious manner; see the *Württemberg Territorial Ordinance*, folio 119, paragraph *Likewise to one*.

## ADDITION.

The question is asked: does this contract become usurious if livestock are given in partnership <note>Latin: "Socida," a contract where one party provides animals and the other provides labor</note> in such a way that the risk of the loss of the animals is transferred to the shepherd? By such a covenant, the livestock are accustomed to be made and called "iron," such as *iron cows or sheep*, because the ownership never perishes or dies. See Husanus, *On Personal Property*, chapter 8, number 10; Simon Pistor, counsel 11, number 3; Moller, part 3, constitution 33, numbers 1 and 12. Just as in those parts, certain rents are called "steely," as in *Steel-rent* <note>German: "Stähline Gült"</note>; the French proverb alludes to this naming: *A Lord of butter eats a Vassal of steel* <note>original: "Un Seigneur de beurre, mange un Vassal d’acier"</note>. Hotman, volume 2, folio 33 at the end. Some, like Mornacius, affirm simply and without distinction that this is usury. Among the Casuists, Genesius and Minutius Florentinus à Rada (of the Vallombrosan Order), in his compendium of Cardinal Toletanus's *Summa* on the 7th Commandment, chapter 41 at the end, proclaim this partnership to be forced and usurious. The *Württemberg Territorial Ordinance* thunders with the same severity regarding *Usurious Contracts*, page 119, paragraph *likewise to one*, etc., stating there: *Or where the calf dies, that the poor man must pay for the same, or replace it with another good bovine.* See Besold, *Special Disputation on the Same Ordinance*, page 8, thesis 24. However, others respond with distinction and with great preparation, by distinguishing different agreements regarding this monetary matter, as can be seen in Lælius Zechus, *Treatise on Usury*, chapter 7, number 7. They teach that such a partnership is entered into: 1. by way of Lease and hire, 2. by way of a Loan, 3. by way of Custody, or 4. by way of a true Partnership.

### 38. Hereditary Offices.

It is no secret to those who understand anything of the law and traditions of the Holy Roman Empire, how the late Emperor Charles the Fourth—of most glorious memory—with the collective counsel and assistance of the common Estates of the Holy Roman Empire, made special provisions regarding certain offices during the drafting of the Golden Bull <note>The Golden Bull of 1356, a constitutional document that regulated the election of the Emperor.</note>. He gave detailed measures and orders for how things should be conducted at the Imperial Courts (which they call *solemnes Curias*, that is, Imperial Diets and Election Days), both regarding the customary Imperial banquet and processions, and otherwise at all times regarding the preceding princely investitures.

<column-break/>

Namely, in the 29th chapter of the aforementioned Golden Bull, the Prince-Electors <note>The high-ranking princes who elected the Emperor.</note> are not only granted the title and power that they "preside over all offices of the Imperial Court," etc., but there were also appointed for them in such offices their own special substitute officials from certain high and respected families.

At that time, these were: the House of Limburg in the office of Hereditary Cup-bearer; the House of Nortenberg in the office of Steward or Master of the Kitchen; Pappenheim in the office of Marshal; and Falkenstein in the office of Chamberlain. This was done with the public testimony that "even previously they had been given and endowed for this by the Roman Princes" <note>referring to previous Emperors</note>. These families were re-named anew to represent the hereditary offices in certain cases. Because of this, they obtained the names of Substitute Officials, Vice-Cup-bearer, Vice-Marshal, and Sub-Chamberlain—likewise "Under-Cup-bearer," "Under-Marshal," and "Under-Chamberlain"—in the said Golden Bull, chapters 27 and 29.

Furthermore, it is to be understood from history, as well as other Imperial acts and documents, that such hereditary offices subordinate to the four secular Prince-Electors have, through various occasions and opportunities (just as has happened with the Electorates themselves), passed at times to other families. Thus, the office of Hereditary Under-Chamberlain, which the family of Falkenstein held at the time of the Golden Bull, is now held by the princely House of Hohenzollern. Similarly, the office of Hereditary Master of the Kitchen or Hereditary Steward, which was ascribed to the House of Nortenberg in the often-mentioned Golden Bull, passed in the course of time to the House of Selden-Eck.

Likewise, on the Saturday after St. Nicholas in the year of Christ 1538, Prince-Elector Ludwig, Count Palatine of the Rhine—presumably due to the feared extinction of the Selden-Eck line—made provisions for the Hereditary Stewards and Barons of Waldburg. According to history (as notably testified by Sebastian Münster in *Cosmography*, book 3, chapter 274), the Waldburgs had already held this same office many years ago, even in the time of Emperor Frederick I, and had kept the name from it. The Elector arranged it so that after the Selden-Ecks, the Lords Hereditary Stewards should obtain such an office, and according to ancient custom, should hold it as a fief from the Electoral Palatinate. See my own work in *Decades of Consultations*, 2, where I have proven at length that in such offices, seniority <note>original Latin: "Senioratum"</note> takes precedence over the right of primogeniture. This is also customary in other such families. In the will of the Lord Count Charles of Hohenzollern, dated January 24, 1575, which was later confirmed by His Imperial Majesty and is now the Hohenzollern hereditary agreement, these words are to be found:

Regarding the 18th point: our sons and all future Counts of **Hohen-Zollern**, born of legitimate marriage, may also write and use the title, shield, and helmet of **Count of Hohen-Zollern, Sigmaringen, and Vöhringen, Lord of Haigerloch and Wehrstein, Hereditary Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire**, etc. However, only the eldest who is fit for the role shall administer and manage the office of **Hereditary Imperial Chamberlain**, and also enjoy its benefits. He may, however, grant this to another of his name and lineage—whoever is the next eldest after him or is already present at court—which remains at his free will and within his power to do. Thus shall it be maintained as long as it remains with us, our heirs, and our descendants.

But if the holder of the **Hereditary Chamberlain’s Office** is not present at court, or is not available at the Imperial Diet <note>original German: "Reichs-Tag," the general assembly of the estates of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> when his Imperial Majesty grants princely fiefs—whether this happens in the chamber or publicly—and another born Count of **Zollern** is present in those parts (even if he were not a court official), then that same person has the right and power to demand the office fees from the Imperial High Chamberlain or the Court Chancellor, and not to yield them. For we, and our ancestors as well, are in open, guaranteed, and proper <term>Possession vel quasi | possession or its equivalent</term> of this right. As was recently seen seventy years ago, our son **Carl**, being in Prague with His Princely Serenity Archduke **Ferdinand of Austria**, etc., was at the Imperial Court when Duke **Julius of Braunschweig** and the Landgrave of **Lichtenberg** received their fiefs there; the Lord Prothoffy, His Majesty’s Chamberlain, had to surrender and pay both fees to our son **Carl**.

### Most Serene/&c.

Whereas a well-founded Legal Brief <term>Deduction: a formal legal argument or presentation of facts</term> was long ago submitted to Your Electoral Serenity on behalf of Lord **Heinrich**, Hereditary Steward <term>Erb-Truchsäß: a high ceremonial office, originally the overseer of the imperial table</term> of the Holy Roman Empire, Count of **Wolfegg**, Lord of **Waldburg**, as well as the entire Hereditary Imperial Steward lines of **Wolfegg** and **Zeil**, regarding their understood right <term>ratione assertæ prioritatis sive præcedentiæ | by reason of asserted priority or precedence</term> in receiving and stipulating the Imperial Hereditary Master of the Kitchen's Office <note>original: "Erbkuchenmeister-Amt," another high ceremonial office in the Emperor's household.</note> before their kinsmen of the Hereditary Imperial Steward line of **Scheer**; and whereas, in response, the appointed attorney for the aforementioned High-born Lord of the Imperial Hereditary Steward line of **Scheer**

<column-break/>

Indeed, the attorney for the **Scheer** line of the Imperial Hereditary Stewards knew nothing else but that this matter rested for a long time in a <term>tractatu concordiæ | treaty of harmony/peaceful negotiation</term>.

However, because it has now reached the point that this dispute must be decided by Your Electoral Serenity as the Feudal Lord and <term>ita consequenter Ordinario Judice | consequently the Ordinary Judge</term> through a legal sentence, and because it is the duty of the attorney for the **Scheer** line to proceed properly against the previously mentioned Legal Brief of the Counts of **Wolfegg**: therefore, the attorney first repeats and accepts all <term>Acta und Actitata | acts and recorded proceedings</term> in the respective official places. Primarily, however, he refers to and relies upon the detailed <term>Consilium | legal opinion</term> already submitted several years ago on behalf <term>ex parte</term> of his gracious Lords and Principals, which was approved by two faculties of law—namely **Ingolstadt** and **Tübingen**—and of which copies were given to the opposing party, thus making it <term>pars Actorum | part of the records</term>. He refers to this in the most stable form and, for all other contrary points, <term>semel pro semper enixissimè contradicirt | once and for all most earnestly contradicts them</term>. In the event that anything in <term>facto vel jure | fact or law</term> remains unresolved or was passed over as insignificant, he hereby acknowledges or concedes nothing.

Upon this, the attorney for the **Scheer** line of the Imperial Hereditary Stewards very gladly acknowledges—and takes it as an irrevocable confession—that in the opposing Legal Brief itself, right at the beginning, it is found that the Hereditary Stewards of the Holy Roman Empire, Barons of **Waldburg**, etc., of the **Wolfegg** and **Scheer** lines, have for several hundred years now held the <term>Regalia | sovereign rights</term> of the Lordship of **Waldburg** (as their ancient ancestral house) as a common family fief from the Holy Roman Empire in such a way that the eldest of the entire family always received such as a fief, took the resulting feudal letters into his hands, and from there re-granted various sub-fiefs as cases arose.

From this, it is evident <term>ex singulari hujus Familiæ perquam illustris, antiquissimâ, præscriptâ, ac quoque rationi & juri admodum conformi usurpantiâ | from the singular, ancient, prescribed, and also highly reasonable and legally conforming usage of this most illustrious family</term>, that it has been introduced without interruption and has come down to this date in a <term>continuâ serie | continuous series</term>, that those laws which belong <term>ex æquo | by equity</term> to such a prestigious lineage have always been administered and managed by the eldest.
