<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the inheritance of the "Erb-Amt" (Hereditary Office). It specifically addresses whether the title of Imperial Hereditary Steward belongs to a single primary line of the Waldburg family or to the entire house collectively through a system of seniority.</meta>

Since this hereditary office has belonged to the **Barons of Waldburg** for several hundred years—as one is prepared to prove if necessary from histories and other documents <note>original: "ex historiis, aliisque documentis"</note>—and because it gradually passed to other families without sufficient fault of their own, only to return to them collectively in such a way that no single line was favored over another, they generally style themselves as **Imperial Hereditary Stewards** <term>Reichs-Erb-Truchsässen | High-ranking ceremonial officers of the Holy Roman Empire who originally oversaw the imperial table.</term>. They have also been titled, honored, and named as such by his **Roman Imperial Majesty**, the **Prince-Electors**, and the Estates without distinction.

It follows, then, that this dignity belonging to this family <note>original: "huicce Familiæ"</note> cannot be drawn from any right of primogeniture <note>The "Jus primogenituræ" is the right of the firstborn son to inherit the entire estate.</note>, nor can it belong to one individual alone (and subsequently his descendants) to the exclusion of those belonging to other lines. Rather, it must be administered as a right common to the entire family <note>original: "utpote toti Familiæ commune jus"</note> by the eldest, as one who is more worthy by nature <note>original: "tanquam naturâ digniorem"</note>. This is done by reason of seniority, just as the **Regalia** <term>Regalien | Royal or imperial rights and privileges</term> of the **Lordship of Waldburg** and the granting of the same as permanent fiefs are handled. It is certainly nothing new for a lordship to be managed by many, to be received as a fief by many, and for the dependent fiefs to be granted out by many in the same way.

> *For it is not something new that one province is governed by the rule of several, and that jurisdiction and power are possessed and administered equally and as if undivided.* <note>original Latin: "Non enim novum est, unam Provinciam plurium dominatu gubernari, Jurisdictio- nemque & Imperium æqualiter & pro indi- viso quasi possideri & administrari," citing Peguerra, decision 10.</note>

However, in the case of a gathering of many at the **Imperial Courts**, at **Imperial Diets**, and other such assemblies, such a hereditary office can—out of unavoidable necessity <note>original: "ex inevitabili necessitate"</note>—only be administered by one person at a time. Because the Regalia of the **Lordship of Waldburg** remain undivided as common and ancient ancestral property, and because no primogeniture has been introduced there, but rather a **Senioratus** <term>Senioratus | A system where the oldest male member of the entire extended family holds authority, rather than just the eldest son of the last ruler.</term> takes place, the eldest of all the lines of this entire family receives and grants these honors. Even the opposing side must admit there is not the slightest dispute on this point. Therefore, for the reasons of law and equity already suggested above, this hereditary office should not remain with one person alone or be rooted in the firstborn. Instead, like the Regalia and fiefs of the **Lordship of Waldburg**, it should be represented by the eldest among all, without the prerogative of any single line <note>original: "sine ullius Lineæ prærogativâ"</note>. Yet, in his absence <note>original: "in ipsius absentiâ"</note>, others who are present <note>original: "præsentes"</note> should be admitted, likewise according to the prerogative of age <note>original: "secundum ætatis prærogativam"</note>, as is the custom with other similar hereditary offices, specifically the **Hereditary Chamberlain’s Office** currently held by the Princely House of **Ho-**

<column-break/>

**henzollern**. For in the records of the late **Count Karl of Hohenzollern**, dated January 1575 (which was later confirmed by his Imperial Majesty and is now the **Zollern Hereditary Agreement**), the following words are found: "18th. Our sons and all future Counts of **Hohenzollern** born of legitimate marriage may also write and use the title, shield, and helmet of **Count of Zollern, Sigmaringen, and Vöhringen, Lord of Haigerloch and Wehrstein, Hereditary Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire**, etc. However, only the eldest who is fit for it shall manage and administer the **Hereditary Imperial Chamberlain’s Office** and enjoy its benefits, unless he grants it to another of his name and lineage who is the next eldest after him or who is already at Court—which remains at his free will and he has the power to do. This shall be maintained as long as it remains with us and our heirs and descendants."

"But if the holder of the **Hereditary Chamberlain’s Office** is not at Court, or not present at the **Imperial Diet** when His Imperial Majesty grants princely fiefs—whether in the chamber or publicly—and another born **Count of Zollern** is in those parts (even if he were not a court official), then he has the right and power to demand the office fees from the **Imperial High Chamberlain** or the **Court Chancellor**, and not to yield them. For we, and our ancestors as well, are in open, guaranteed, and quiet possession <note>original: "possession vel q. [quasi]"</note> of this."

The same custom exists for **Limpurg** and **Pappenheim**, which can be sufficiently proven if necessary.

From these points briefly deduced here, it appears that the **Lords Imperial Hereditary Stewards of the Scheer line** have a claim founded both by reason of equal offices and by the custom of this family, as well as by other similar rights <note>original: "tam ratione parium officiorum, quàm ex consuetudine hujus familiæ, cæteris consimilibus Juribus fundatam intentionem"</note>. Thus, the Countly opponents lose their case regarding their exception; the burden of proof <note>original: "onus probandi"</note> therefore rests on them by law.

Now, the opponents seek to base their exception in the frequently mentioned Deduction on the undeniable fact that the highly esteemed **Lords Imperial Hereditary Stewards**, in addition to the common ancestral fief, each on the part of his own line, continue to enjoy, receive, possess, use, and benefit from special graces, freedoms, fiefs, and goods from both the **Holy Roman Empire** and the **Electors and Princes**.

With the further suggestion that although it occasionally happens that one or another might acquire even more privileges and goods beyond the ancestral hereditary estates and lordships—perhaps through marriage, inheritance, merit, purchase, or other lawful titles...

The feudal charter <term>Lehenbrief | A legal document recording the granting of a fief</term> is of the same content, and therein Lord Georg and Lord Wilhelm, as well as their male feudal heirs, are called not at all subordinately <note>original: "subalternatim"</note>, but jointly <note>original: "conjunctim"</note>. It is further stated there (which is very important to note) that Lord Wilhelm, Steward (from whom, as already understood, the Scheer line descended), most humbly informed His Electoral Grace that, due to admitted age and weakness, he could no longer carry or fulfill the feudal duties <note>original: "vermannen"</note> of such a fief himself; therefore, with the consent of the high-born liege lord, he transferred his right and grace therein to his son, Wilhelm the Younger,

and handed over: in the same manner as he was enfeoffed in this very feudal charter by way of expectancy <note>original: "per modum expectantiæ"</note>.

Now, if Lord Wilhelm the Elder and his descendants were only included subordinately <note>original: "subalternatim"</note>, or eligible for such dignity only on the condition that they should enjoy it only upon the extinction of the line of Lord Georg, **Imperial Hereditary Steward**, it would not have been necessary for the highly praised Lord Wilhelm to excuse himself on account of his age and, for that reason, leave the carrying of this fief and the fulfillment of feudal duties or the performance of feudal services <note>original: "Servitia feudalia"</note> to his son. Rather, these words—since they are to be understood specifically in light of their practical effect <note>original: "cùm ea maximè cum effectu sint intelligenda"</note>—can allow no other interpretation than that Lord Wilhelm and his feudal descendants, as well as Lord Georg and his sons, were provided for with equal rights and in the present case <note>original: "in præsenti"</note>.

No less do all other feudal charters carry the same weight—especially the one found in the collection of documents of the Counts of the opposing side, which is the first investiture given graciously to all the Lords Imperial Hereditary Stewards after the complete extinction of the **Seideneck line**—namely, that the frequently mentioned Lords Imperial Hereditary Stewards (specifically Lord Heinrich, Frobenius, Georg, Johann, Gebhard, and Jacob, as well as Gebhard, Carl, and Christoph) without distinction, along with their male feudal heirs, shall receive, hold, and carry such Master of the Kitchen office as often as necessity requires, and shall serve, attend, be obedient, and bound to the liege lord with loyalty, vows, and oaths.

And one now lets the whole world judge whether, under such circumstances—and because the feudal charters make no distinction, and because Lord Wilhelm the Elder, for the reason that he could not carry or fulfill the duties as he was bound to do <note>original: "ob-teneatur"</note>, left the same to his son, and because especially Lord Wilhelm and his descendants, as well as others, either swore themselves or had the **oath of fealty** <term>juramentum fidelitatis | A formal oath of loyalty sworn by a vassal to a lord</term> performed in their name—whether, I say, it is to be concluded from this that Lord Wilhelm and his kin were called only secondarily <note>original: "accessorié"</note> and subordinately <note>original: "subalternatim"</note>, or rather with equal right <note>original: "æquo jure"</note>, and that the entire lineage is simultaneously capable of this dignity? As can then be found further detailed in the legal opinion <note>original: "Consilio"</note> submitted most humbly on this side long ago.

And it is established <note>original: "Et constat"</note> that in a fief of this kind, where one possesses it and the rest—who are capable of the same fief in their time and are admitted to it according to the prerogative of rank—such persons capable of the fief are not bound to seek a renewal until they have acquired possession, nor do they have need of a simultaneous investiture...

...mentioned in Chapter 1, at the beginning of the section, and also in the title regarding the succession of brothers or degrees of succession in a fief, Chapter 1, the section on paternal inheritance, and the title on the nature of feudal succession; see Schurff, Consultation 99, numbers 1 and 3, and the Copenhagen Decisions, Question 47, numbers 4 and 5.

Since, therefore, in this case the descendants of Heinrich have always sought the renewal of the Investiture <term>Investituræ | The formal ceremony of granting a fief or office</term>, and since they also performed the feudal oath, it is evident from this that they were not called or burdened as secondary <note>original: "accessorie"</note>, subordinate, or conditional heirs—meaning only upon the failure of Lord Georg’s line. This is especially true because the power of a small word, or rather a conjunctive phrase <note>The Latin refers to the word "and," arguing that it joins the parties together as equals.</note>, designates them as joined together. They are not separated by some successive order of blood, but because of the unity of the language, they are brought together as if into one body, affecting everyone equally and in the same way. See the single law, the section "with these things so defined," in the Code on the removal of lapses, and the laws "if to two" and "if to many" in the Digests on Legacies, Book 2.

Hence, within our own legal terms, there is also the decision of Baldus on the final law of the Code regarding self-inherited and legal heirs (which has also been praised by others): that if a fief is established for a male at the same time or together with a female, then because of these conjunctive words, the female is to be admitted equally and alongside the male—not merely in a successive order where the female follows the male only after he has been removed from this life.

Furthermore, according to the law "now by this right" in the Digests on vulgar and pupillary substitution, as taught by Bartolus and others, a determination in one and the same sentence that receives multiple subjects must be understood in such a way that it determines all of them uniformly and equally.

But also, when several people are called in one and the same legal disposition by their proper names, even without a conjunction placed between them, they are considered joined by words and by the matter itself. Unless shares are specifically established, all arrive equally. See the law "triple" in the Digests on the Significance of Words, and the law "as often as," the section "heirs sometimes," and the law of "Lucius Titius" on Legacies, Book 1.

For this reason, this Hereditary Office is graciously granted or bestowed equally upon all the Lords who are Hereditary Stewards <term>Erb-Truchsässen | A high-ranking court official, originally a "table-setter" or seneschal</term> specifically named in the Investitures, together with their male bodily feudal heirs. Furthermore, regarding the administration—specifically who should take precedence over the other when several are present—this is not expressed in any Investiture. It therefore remains as already most humbly indicated above, and as irrefutably strengthened in the cited Legal Counsel <note>original: "Consilio"</note>, that the eldest among them all shall have precedence.

Against this, it cannot be hindered by the claim made in the opposing side’s legal deduction that the late Lord Jerg, Imperial Hereditary Steward, obtained this office of Hereditary Master of the Kitchen <term>Erb-Küchenmeister-Amt | An honorary court position supervising the royal or electoral kitchens</term> as a reward <note>original: "remuneratorie"</note> for his highly praiseworthy deeds and the knightly service rendered to the Electoral Palatinate <term>Chur-Pfaltz | The territory and dignity of the Count Palatine of the Rhine, one of the electors of the Holy Roman Emperor</term>. Nor does it matter that the same was supposedly granted to Lord Wilhelm subsequently by grace, as an accessory and by way of expectancy. For although the opposing side refers to the Eventual or Expectancy Investiture, yet in Besoldus, Volume I...

...nothing of the sort is to be found therein. Hence it may rightly be said that "The document does not sing" <note>original: "Instrumentum non cantat" — a legal maxim meaning that one should not read into a document what is not explicitly written there</note>, and neither should we "sing." Nothing can be concluded from a presumed intention of the grantors or the recipients against the express words of the document. Considering that, for this time, the dispute is not at all about the occasion, the merits, or the person through whom such dignity again reached the Lords Hereditary Stewards, but rather and solely with what condition, measure, and form they were newly invested or enfeoffed with this dignity.

This can be learned from nowhere else than from the words of the Investiture itself. In those words, as already mentioned above, no such distinction or prerogative of one line over another is to be found; rather, a thorough equality exists. Therefore, when two people compete <note>original: "in concursu duorum"</note> for such an individual office that cannot be served by both at once, the elder is to be preferred according to the Law of Nations, or rather according to Nature itself.

Furthermore, it does not hinder the case that in the first expectancy Lord Georg, who was younger, was placed before his cousin Lord Wilhelm, or that in subsequent Investitures (in which the descendants of the highly esteemed Lord Georg and Lord Wilhelm are always properly named) Lord Georg's successors are constantly placed first.

Because Lord Georg—as is not contradicted by our side—brought about such an expectancy and was in good respect and standing with the Feudal Lord (the Electoral Palatinate) due to useful services rendered which were then in recent memory, he was not unfairly named first; especially since this order was subsequently followed in enumerating the power of both.

However, from this—and because no distinction was made between the two lines either in the first expectancy or in the subsequent investitures—it cannot be concluded that Lord Georg and his descendants were called primarily <note>original: "principaliter"</note>, while Lord Wilhelm and his descendants were considered only secondarily <note>original: "accessoriè"</note> and only in the case of the extinction of the first line.

In further consideration: Lord Wilhelm, as already understood, left this fief to his son, Lord Wilhelm the Younger, because of his advanced age. If Lord Wilhelm's right had consisted only in an eventual succession <note>meaning he only had a right to it if the other line died out</note>, and he did not actually hold the fief himself as his cousin Lord Georg did, then his age could not have been a hindrance to him.

# Expanded Practical Treasury
## (Thesauri Practici Adaucti)

That George was called by equal and par law <note>Latin: "ex æquo & pari jure"</note> is shown by the argument provided by Maranta in the *Mirror*, part 3, number 109, and by Alexander in Counsel 161, after having seen the narratives, book 7, number 3, in the verse beginning "and through this it is clear." This is because the order of the intention should be considered more than the order of the writing <note>Latin: "magis ordo intellectus, quam scripturæ attendi debet"</note>. See also Curt. Jun. counsel 161, number 10; Riminaldus in the decision inserted after the Counsel; Riminaldus Jun. 224, number 49; and Maranta in *Practice*, part 3, number 114.

It is relevant here that the successive order is not observed among those called "copulatively" (jointly) if an outsider arranges the disposition, according to Alexander, counsel 13, number 8, book 4; and counsel 14, number 10, first verse, book 4.

Whatever dispute was raised in the year 1560 by Lord Carl, Hereditary <term>Truchsäß</term> <note>A high-ranking court official, specifically a Lord High Steward or Seneschal</note>, acting as guardian for the children left behind by the late Lord Jacob—of which the document submitted by the opposing side makes mention—cannot be known by this side. However, that dispute must not have conformed at all to the present question, because the <term>fief letter</term> <note>Original: "Lehenbrief"; a formal deed granting land or office under feudal law</note> issued thereafter under letter E proves that the mentioned Lord Jacob, as well as the Scheer line, were invested with exactly the same right as the Wolffegg line.

Furthermore, there is a minor conjecture introduced to strengthen the intention of the opposing Lord: namely, that the fief letters are kept in the Wolffegg archive, while the plaintiff's attorney knows nothing else except that the Scheer branch also possesses several. In this, however, the opposing side is greatly mistaken in claiming that the Lords Truchsäss of the Wolffegg line were always the primary holders <note>Latin: "principaliores"</note> and <term>fief-bearers</term> <note>Original: "Lehenträger"; the person officially responsible for the duties and ceremonies of the fief</note>, and for that reason alone rendered the duty and oath, and that they alone bore all costs and other burdens <note>Latin: "onera"</note> regarding the acceptance of the fief and performance of required services without the help or assistance of the Scheer branch. For even the first Electoral Letter of Expectancy <note>A legal promise of a future fief or office</note> shows that Lord George received such a "life-man-fief" <note>A fief held for the duration of a lifetime</note> not only for himself, but also on behalf of his cousin, Lord Wilhelm. In the other fief letter, it is stated that Lord Wilhelm the Elder, due to his admitted age and weakness, could no longer bear or serve the fief himself, and therefore transferred and handed over his right and grace therein to his son, Lord Wilhelm the Younger. It further states that Lord George, the son of the first Lord George, on behalf of himself and his brother Heinrich, and then Lord Wilhelm the Younger as the head <note>Latin: "Cippus"; used here to mean the foundational member or representative</note> of the Scheer line, received this fief in their own names and persons <note>Latin: "proprio nomine & in personâ"</note>, and also gave their word and oath regarding it.

No less do all other fief letters confirm that, although for the most part only one person performed the actual feudal oath to save on costs, it was nevertheless always done for himself and in the name of all Hereditary Truchsässen (who were also always indicated in the fief letters by their proper baptismal

<column-break/>

names, and none were omitted). Furthermore, no mention is made there of any "fief-bearing" status or any prerogative of rank or line <note>Latin: "gradus-ve aut Lineæ prærogativæ"</note>. As for the letter under label K, it can certainly be seen that the late Lord Christoph, Imperial Hereditary Truchsäß, did not sufficiently understand the nature of this fief, and in this place almost wanted to agree with the current intention of the opposing side. However, such a confession and interpretation, being erroneous <note>Latin: "tanquam erronea"</note> and rebelling against the literal content of the fief letters, cannot be used or interpreted to the prejudice <note>Latin: "in præjudicium"</note> of even the heirs and successors of the one making the confession. For an erroneous confession does not prove, nor does it prejudice the one confessing, even if it had been firmly proven and accepted <note>Latin: "Confessio namque erronea non probat, neque præjudicat confitenti, etiamsi fuisset firmiter probata & acceptata"</note>. See the law regarding "error" in the section on ignorance of law and fact, even if the confession was repeated many times and identically, and even if it was deliberate, or even sworn. And this applies to errors of law as well as fact, as Mascardus proves in his treatise on evidence, conclusion 378. Likewise, Rosenthal in *On Fiefs*, chapter 9, member 1, conclusion 26, number 14, teaches that the extrajudicial and voluntary confession of a vassal harms neither the Lord nor the successors.

Regarding the <term>Acts of Possession</term> <note>Latin: "Actus Possessorios"; formal actions taken to demonstrate legal ownership or the exercise of an office</note>, this was dealt with extensively in the previously cited Tübingen Counsel, but first and foremost it was proven that the late Lord Christoph, of blessed memory, was the first who, after the complete extinction of the Seideneck line, actually served in the disputed office of <term>Hereditary Master of the Kitchen</term> <note>Original: "Erbkuchenmeister"; literally "Hereditary Cake Master," a high ceremonial office at the Imperial court</note>. For this reason, he had a great dispute with His Majesty's court officials. And it is correct that the same occurred in the year 1594 at Regensburg, and later at Prague; likewise in the year 1613. One cannot elude such acts simply because no one from the Wolffegg line was present at the time. For the Scheer branch were always admitted in this place by their own right <note>Latin: "jure proprio"</note> and not as proxies of the firstborn of the Waldeck line. This would otherwise have had to happen if the aforementioned firstborn were the sole fief-bearer and the others of the same lineage or line, if there be any, had merely expectations and no "rooted right" <note>Latin: "Jus radicatum"</note> that was flourishing and active. This is to be seen in the Arch-Offices of the secular Electors, where the one who is uniquely the Elector also uniquely exercises the duties destined for him; the others, although they may be invested simultaneously <note>Latin: "simultaneè"</note> but according to a prerogative of rank, could not interfere at all in such performances even in the absence of the actual Elector without his mandate or authority. From this it can be seen that the right of primogeniture <note>Latin: "Jus primogenituræ"</note> takes place between the Arch-Offices and the Hereditary Offices, as is detailed further in the Tübingen Counsel.

On the other hand, as the opposing counsel himself admits, in the Hereditary Cupbearer-Hereditary Mar-

In the Office of the Hereditary Chamberlain, the eldest always has precedence. Therefore, in cases of doubt <note>Latin: "in dubio"</note>, and because no explicit contrary arrangement <note>Latin: "expressa contraria dispositio"</note> is contained therein, it remains the case that the same must occur for this Office of the Hereditary Master of the Kitchen. It is also presumed that Lord George, by allowing his cousin, Lord William, to be included in the <term>simultaneous investiture</term> <note>A legal act where multiple people are granted a fief at the same time, sharing the rights</note>, had this in view, and desired to introduce nothing new or unusual compared to other offices of the same rank <note>Latin: "ejusdem qualitatis officiis"</note>.

Since it has now been sufficiently proven—both above and especially in the frequently cited Tübingen Legal Opinion, which we here reproduce in its best form and refer to—that both at the first acquisition of this <term>fief</term> <note>Land or office held on condition of feudal service</note> and in the various subsequent investitures, no prerogative or right of priority <note>Latin: "Jus prioritatis"</note> or subordinate investiture was introduced between the Wolfegg and Scheer lines. Nor was one considered before the other in view of rank or lineage <note>Latin: "aut intuitu gradus vel Lineæ"</note>. Much less is there any word to suggest that Lord George and his descendants were invested principally <note>Latin: "principaliter"</note> while Lord William and his descendants were invested only secondarily and by mere expectation <note>Latin: "accessorie & per nudam expectantiam"</note>. Rather, it is as clear as day that at all times, and in all letters of investiture—and thus through an entirely uninterrupted practice—all living Imperial Hereditary <term>Stewards</term> <note>Original: "Truchsässen"; high-ranking court officials</note>, of both the Scheer and Wolfegg lines, were invested with this hereditary office without distinction and with a fully simultaneous right <note>Latin: "simultaneo planè Jure"</note>. Furthermore, as the occasion allowed <note>Latin: "ita ferente occasione"</note>, the Imperial Hereditary Stewards of the Scheer line exercised this right by their own authority <note>Latin: "Jure proprio"</note> and not as representatives of the first-born of the Wolfegg line, and they received the resulting benefits. Especially since the right of the eldest <note>Latin: "Jus Senioratus"</note> is an undisputed tradition in the other hereditary offices, and also among the Imperial Hereditary Stewards in their other common ancestral estates, and the opposing arguments are of no significance. Therefore, the brothers Lord William Henry and Lord Frederick, Imperial Hereditary Stewards, live in the most humble and certain hope that Your Electoral Highness, as the now most gracious feudal lord, will graciously maintain the members of the Scheer line of the Stewards in their obtained simultaneous investiture and its attached well-established rights. Also, so that future disputes may be spared, may you provide a final and proper conclusion to the matter through an Electoral Decree, and graciously direct that the eldest of all simultaneously invested Imperial Stewards shall always serve in this hereditary office when several are gathered <note>Latin: "in concursu plurium"</note>, and shall especially

<column-break/>

collect and receive the customary profits and fees.

This, and whatever else arises from law and equity, or may be appropriate to this matter, the advocate of Lord William Henry, Hereditary Steward, and his associates, humbly submits for a most gracious decision, yet with the usual offer to provide further facts if needed, while all necessity and legal favor remain reserved for his gracious Lord Principal in the best form.

Mention is also made in a deed of sale from the year 1382, *Helfenstein versus Ulm*, of the mentioned Lord Philip the Elder, Lord of Weinsberg, Hereditary Chamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire.

Freher also discusses these officials at length in his notes on Peter von Andlo, book 2, chapter 15, page 206 and following; as does Goldast in his work on Bohemia, book 3, chapter 8, where he says that the **Steward** <term>Trucfessium; a high court official responsible for the table and household</term> is called *Trussatum* or *Trustinum* in ancient documents. Regarding disputes that arise between the Court Offices and the Hereditary Offices, I have appended an anonymous legal opinion at the end of my **treatise on precedence**.

### ADDITION.

->*Lord Speidel, in Notable Matters, page 284.*<-

### 39. Honorable, Steadfast. Noble.

This term **Honorable** <note>Original: "Erbar"</note>, especially in the Saxon courts, is the same as **Noble** <note>Original: "Nobilis"</note>. Hence, in the most ancient style in certain places of Lower Saxony, people speak of the **Honorable and Un-honorable** (that is, the Noble and the Common) countryside or estates; even some Dukes are addressed as nothing other than **Nobles, Honorable, and Steadfast**. For this word **Honorable** and **Steadfast** <note>Original: "Erbar und Ehrnvest"</note> has its root in the Greek word *arete* <note>Original: "αρετὴ"</note>, meaning **Virtue**, which is the primary cause of nobility, for which reason the Emperors are accustomed to grant noble status. *Dauth, in volume 2 of Public Law, page 463.*

And so, in ancient letters, instead of **The Noble and Best**, one more often reads **The Honorable and Best**. *Lord Johann Jacob Draco* in his *treatise on the origin of the patricians, chapter 2, page 224*, reports that the **Honorable Families** <note>Original: "Erbare Geschlechter"</note> is used to mean Patrician and Noble families.

### ADDITION.

Add also *Draco, page 239*, and *Steinberg's disputation on the law, section 43, thesis 9*, where he says: The **Honorable** enjoy a status of natural Nobility. The term **Steadfast** <note>Original: "Ehrnvest"</note> comes from Ariovistus <note>A historic Germanic leader; a common but likely folk etymology of the period</note>. Add also *Gothofr. Anton, Feudal Disputation 4, thesis 1, letter C*, and *Conrad Rittershausen on feudal law, page 105*.

The **Honorable** were once the names for Nobles and Doctors <term>those with advanced academic degrees</term>. The **Honorable** Prince Albert, Bishop of Halberstadt, was so called. *Lord Dillherr, volume 1, disputations, page 77.* **Steadfast** <note>Original: "Ehrnvest"</note> is as much as one who holds fast to his honor. *Harsdörffer in the German Secretary, in the preface.* **Fast** <note>Original: "Vest"</note> signifies firm. Whence it is also customary to place **Steadfast** in titles, as if one who retains and preserves honor. From this comes the verb **to fasten, to make firm, to confirm** <note>Original: "vesten, vestigen, bevestigen"</note>, that is, to confirm or stabilize—or as we say today, to **install**—because through **investiture** <term>the formal ceremony of granting a fief</term> a vassal is confirmed in his fief, introduced, and as it were, installed, as *Giphanius* says. *Finckelthaus in Illustrious Feudal Controversies, Disputation 7, Controversy 2, letter a.*

Freher also deals extensively with these Officials in his commentary on Peter von Andlau, Book 2, Chapter 15, page 206 and following; and Goldast in *On the Kingdom of Bohemia*, Book 3, Chapter 8, where he says that the **Steward** <term>Truchsess; an officer responsible for the household and table of the Emperor</term> is called *Trussatus* or *Trustinus* in ancient documents. I believe it is named as if to say "carried the food" <note>Original: "trug das Essen"; a folk etymology for the German title Truchsess</note>. Regarding the legal disputes that have arisen between the Court Offices and the Hereditary Offices, I have subjoined the legal opinion of an anonymous author at the end of my treatise on precedence.

Lord Speidel in *Notable Matters*, page 284.

### 39. Honorable, Steadfast. Noble.

This particle **Honorable** <term>Erbar</term>, especially in the Saxon courts, is the same as **Noble** <term>Nobilis</term>. Hence, in the most ancient style in certain places of Lower Saxony, one says **Honorable and Non-Honorable** (that is, **Noble and Common**) lands or estates; and even by some Dukes they are addressed as nothing other than Nobles, **Honorable and Steadfast** <term>Ehrnvest</term>. For this word **Honorable and Steadfast** has its root in the Greek word $\alpha'\varrho\epsilon\tau\dot{\eta}$ <note>Original: "aretē"</note>, meaning **Virtue**, which is the primary cause of nobility, for which reason Emperors are accustomed to grant nobility. *Dauth in volume 2 of Public Law, page 463.*

And so in ancient letters, in place of the **Noble and Firm** <term>Edl. und Vesten</term>, one more often reads the **Honorable and Firm**. *Lord Johann Jacob Draco in his most elegant treatise on the origin of patricians, chapter 2, page 224*, who reports the same in *chapter 3, page 138 and following*, that the **Honorable Families** <term>Erbare Geschlechter</term> is used for Patrician and Noble families.

->ADDITION.<-

See also *Draco, page 239; Steinberg's disputation on law 2 of the Digest regarding the origin of law, section 43, thesis 9*, where it is stated: The **Honorable** enjoy a nobility that is simultaneously native/birthright. **Steadfast** <term>Ehrnvest</term> comes from Ariovistus <note>A Germanic leader; likely a traditional or playful etymology connecting the name to 'honor' and 'firmness'</note>. See also *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputation 4, thesis 1, letter C, and Conrad Rittershausen, Feudal Parts, page 105.*

The **Honorable** were formerly called Nobles and Doctors. The **Honorable Prince Albert** was the name given to the Bishop of Halberstadt. *Lord Dillherr, volume 1, disputation page 77.* **Steadfast** is as much as one who holds fast to his honor. *Harsdörffer in the preface of the German Secretary.* **Firm** <term>Vest</term> signifies something solid. Whence even in titles it is customary to place **Steadfast**, as if retaining and preserving honor. From this comes the verb **to strengthen, to make firm, to confirm**, that is, to establish or stabilize—or as we say today, to install—because through **Investiture** <term>the formal ceremony of granting a fief</term> the **Vassal** is confirmed in his fief, introduced, and as it were installed, as *Giphanius* says. *Finckelthaus in Feudal Controversies Illustrated, Disputation 7, Controversy 2, letter a.*

### 40. Inheritance Settlements. Conventional Arbitrations. <note>Original: "Erbausträg. Auftregæ conventionales." These were special legal procedures for settling disputes among the high nobility outside of ordinary courts, often mandated by family law or imperial privilege.</note>

Conventional or special settlements belong to certain immediate estates <note>Those answering directly to the Emperor without an intermediary lord</note>: namely, the conventional judgments of illustrious families, *especially chosen legal settlements* <note>Original German: "sonderlich gewillkührte Rechtliche Austräg"</note>, according to the *Chamber Ordinance, part 2, title 2, at the beginning.* If these exist, they are to be preferred over common ones and must be observed based on those rules (*ibid., Denais on the Law of the Chamber, chapter 156*). And to ensure that no exception regarding incompetence or nullity is raised before these judges, one must act entirely according to the aforementioned title.

And these, in turn, can be of two types: namely, either uncertain or "compromissory" (arbitrary), where the litigants (Princes) directly appoint certain persons to a compromise and promise to obey their settlement. These are frequent among Princes, as can be seen in the historians: for instance, how the Counts of Mansfeld, disputing over borders and inheritance, chose Luther as their arbitrator <note>Martin Luther's final journey in 1546 was to settle this very dispute between the Counts of Mansfeld</note> (*Thuanus, book 2, p. 30*); or regarding the domain of the Celts, where the Palatine, the Duke of Württemberg, and the Duke of Cleves were given as honorary arbitrators (*Thuanus, book 16, page 345*). Or they are "certain," confirmed, and family-based settlements, before whom controversies arising among relatives are settled; such settlements also exist in the most illustrious House of Saxony. For if the Elector and the Dukes of Saxony cannot amicably settle the disputes they have between them through mutual writings, they do not conduct them before common arbitrators according to the *Chamber Ordinance, part 2, title 2*; but rather: (1) they depute grave and learned counselors for an amicable settlement; if these labor in vain: (2) they each depute four noble counselors and two legal experts, who, released from their general oath of office and bound by a specific oath for the case before the agents representing the Princes, hear the cause from the agents and settle it amicably. If they do not succeed in this way: (3) the matter is to be proposed before them orally, so that through three repeated turns of alternating arguments (excluding new evidence at the final turn), a sentence according to Saxon Law must be rendered, as far as possible, on all disputed points. If they cannot agree on this, information must be sought from the Imperial Chamber Court, and thereafter a sentence must be pronounced by the deputies within a year:

> By virtue of the House of Saxony’s *especially chosen legal settlement at Naumburg*, established on February 24, 1554, between the late Elector August, Duke John Frederick the Elder (born Elector), Duke John Frederick the Middle, Duke John William, and Duke John Frederick the Younger of Saxony, their Electoral and Princely Graces, and confirmed by Emperor Charles V, which reads: "Should disputes and failings occur between us or our heirs and descendants in the future, etc., we have agreed with one another in a friendly and fatherly manner to the following settlement, etc."

However, long before this confirmation, the Saxons employed this conventional judgment in their controversies, though with a

<column-break/>

different number of deputies. Thus, in the controversies arising between John the Constant, Elector, and George, Duke of Saxony, it pleased both sides to depute 16 counselors for the decision. Most notably, an arbitration was made at Grimma, thereafter called the "Grimma Verdict" <note>Original: "der Grimmische Machtspruch," a famous 15th-century legal decision in Saxon history</note> (*Quirin. Cubach in vol. 4, at Arumæus, discourse 36, thesis 2. 5. and following; add Rutger Ruland in his notes on Ferrarius Montanus's Process, folio 23 and following*), where he deals fully with Inheritance Settlements and the judges appointed therein. Regarding the Palatine Inheritance Settlements, see the acts of Count Palatine George Hans.

And these special or conventional settlements also exist for other illustrious families, as may be seen in *Beust, on the law of swearing an oath, note 194*. Likewise for confederates, see *Waremund von Erenberg on Confederations, book 2, chapter 2*.

The process in this Saxon Conventional Judgment is clear from the tenor of the Naumburg arbitration or compromise related above (*see Cubach, cited place, thesis 11, etc.*).

Likewise concerning the Judges, by virtue of conventions between a Prince and a certain Senate, and what must be done if certain arbitrators are not given at the request of the Senate, see *Georg Everhard, vol. 2, counsel 54, last question; and the Strasbourg Counsels, vol. 2, counsel 49.*

### 41. Inheritance Union, Inheritance Brotherhood. Family Pacts, Confraternities. <note>Original: "Erbeiniging, Erbverbrüderung. Pacta gentilitia, Confraternitates." These were treaties between noble houses to ensure that if one line went extinct, the other would inherit their lands, keeping the territory within a specific circle of families.</note>

Often, family pacts regarding brotherhood and reciprocal succession in Provinces and Domains (such pacts are called *Inheritance Union* or *Inheritance Brotherhood* among Germans) are entered into between Princes or others holding territories and jurisdiction, should one of the contracting parties die without a male heir:

> that when one of the contracting Lords passes away through death without a male bodily heir, then the survivor, in such a case, shall be empowered to take for himself the named goods and estate by force of the pact and by hereditary right.

And although it is otherwise certain that such pacts regarding future succession are prohibited by law <note>Citing the Roman *Corpus Iuris Civilis*: Digest 45.1 (On verbal obligations) and Code 2.3 (On pacts)</note>. Nor can an inheritance or succession be granted by pact or convention (*Code on conventional inheritances; Code on useless stipulations; Code on natural and legal heirs*). This is true not only when the whole inheritance is concerned, but also when a portion of it was treated (*Code on pacts*).

Nevertheless, it is held as the common and received opinion that these pacts have firm strength, especially in Germany, France, and Italy; as is widely confirmed by *Andreas Gail (book 2, observation 128), Decius (counsel 516), Boerius (decision 355), Zasius (counsel 1), Wesenbeck (counsel 71), Pistor (counsel 8), Hotoman (counsel 1), Gothofredus, and Schæffer.* This is (1) because these pacts concern...

### 40. Inherited Settlements. Conventional Mandates.

**Conventional** or **special settlements** are those belonging to certain "immediate" members <note>The "immediati" were nobles who answered directly to the Emperor, bypasssing intermediate lords.</note>: for instance, the conventional judicial settlements of illustrious families, ->**specially chosen legal settlements**<- (*Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber, part 2, title 2, at the beginning*). If these exist, they are to be preferred over common laws and must be observed (*ibid, part 2, title 2*). Denais, *On the Law of the Chamber*, chapter 156. And so that no objection of incompetence or nullity is raised before them, one must act entirely according to these rules.

And these, in turn, can be of two types: namely, either **uncertain** or **compromissory** (also called **arbitrary**), where the immediate litigants (the Princes) agree to a compromise before certain persons and promise to obey their composition. These are frequent among Princes, as can be seen in the historians: for example, how the Counts of Mansfeld, disputing over borders and property, chose **Luther** as their arbitrator (Thuanus, book 2, page 30). Regarding the jurisdiction of castles, the Palatine, the Duke of Württemberg, and the Duke of Cleves were given as honorary arbitrators (Thuanus 16, page 345).

Or they are **certain**, **confirmed**, and **familial**, before whom controversies arising between relatives are settled; such settlements also exist in the most illustrious **House of Saxony**. For if the Elector and the Dukes of Saxony cannot amicably settle the lawsuits they have between themselves through mutual writings, they do not conduct them before the common *Austräg* <note>Austräg refers to a specialized system of arbitration used by the German nobility to avoid the slow Imperial courts.</note> according to the *Imperial Chamber Ordinance*; instead:
(1) They appoint grave and learned Councilors for an amicable settlement; if these fail:
(2) Each side appoints four Nobles and two Legal Scholars as Councilors who, being released from their general oaths and bound by a specific oath for the case before the representatives of the Princes, hear the case from the agents and settle it amicably. If they do not succeed:
(3) The matter is to be proposed before them orally, so that after three alternating exchanges of arguments (excluding, finally, any new evidence), a sentence is to be handed down according to **Saxon Law**, as far as possible, on all disputed points. If they cannot agree on this, information must be sought from the Imperial Chamber, and afterwards, a sentence must be pronounced by the Deputies within a year.

This is according to the **specially chosen legal settlement of the House of Saxony**, established at Naumburg on February 24, Anno 1554, between the late Elector August, Duke Johann Friedrich the Elder (born Elector), Duke Johann Friedrich the Middle, Duke Johann Wilhelm, and Duke Johann Friedrich the Younger of Saxony, the Electors and Princes, and confirmed by Emperor Charles V, which reads as follows: *Whether in the future between us, or our heirs and descendants, disputes and grievances should occur, etc., we have agreed with one another on the following settlement in a friendly and fatherly manner, etc.*

However, the Saxons employed this conventional judgment in their controversies long before this confirmation, though with a

<column-break/>

different number of Deputies. Thus, when controversies arose between John the Steadfast, Elector, and George, Duke of Saxony, it pleased both sides to appoint 16 Councilors for their decision. Above all, an arbitration was made at **Grimma**, thereafter called the *Grimma Decision* <note>Original: "Grimmische Machtspruch"</note>. Quirin Cubach, volume 4, in Arumaeus, discourse 36, thesis 2, and following sections; add Rutger Ruland in his notes to Ferrarius Montanus, *On Process*, folio 23 and following, where he treats fully **of inherited settlements and the judges constituted therein**. Regarding the Palatine inherited settlements, see the acts of Count Palatine George Hans.

And these special or conventional settlements also exist in other Illustrious Families, as may be seen in Beust, *On the Law of Oaths*. They also exist among Confederates, as in Waremund de Erenberg, *On Federations*, book 2, chapter 2.

What the process is in this **Saxon Conventional Judgment** is clear from the tenor of the Naumburg arbitration or compromise cited above (see Cubach, cited place, thesis 11, etc.).

Likewise, regarding the Judges, by virtue of conventions between a Prince and a certain Senate, and what must be done if certain Arbitrators are not given at the request of the Senate: see Georg Everhard, volume 2, counsel 54, final question; and *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 2, counsel 49.

### 41. Inheritance Union, Inheritance Brotherhood.

-> **Family Pacts, Confraternities.** <-

Often, family pacts concerning brotherhood and reciprocal succession in Provinces and Dominions (called **Inheritance Union** or **Inheritance Brotherhood** by the Germans) are entered into between Princes or others holding territories and jurisdiction, in the event that one of the contracting parties dies without a male heir: *that, when one among the contracting Lords passes away by death without male bodily heirs, then the survivor shall be authorized in such a case to take unto himself the named goods and estate by power of the pact and by hereditary right.*

And although it is otherwise certain that such pacts of future succession are prohibited by law (*Law: Stipulation, Digest on Verbal Obligations; Final Law, Code on Pacts*), nor can an inheritance or succession be given by pact or convention (*Law: Inheritance, Code on Pacts; Law: From that, Code on Useless Stipulations*), not only when it concerns the whole inheritance but also when it concerns a portion of it (*Law: Pact, which concerning dowry, Code on Pacts*).

Nevertheless, the common and received opinion holds that **these pacts have firm strength**, especially in **Germany, France, and Italy**: as is extensively confirmed by Andreas Gail, book 2, observation 128; Decius, counsel 516, volume 3; Boerius, decision 355, number 3; Zasius, counsel 1, number 11 and following, volume 2; Wesenbeck, counsel 71, folio 2; Modestinus Pistoris, counsel 8, question 2, volume 1; Hotman, counsel 1; Gothofredus; Hartmann Pistoris; Schaeffer. This is (1) because these pacts concern only...

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, discussing the scope of inheritance pacts.</note> ...are only established for specific Provinces and Jurisdictions, not for all goods whatsoever, so that the power of free testament remains intact for the contracting parties regarding their other property. Then (2) because these pacts are usually confirmed by the Majesty of the most invincible Emperor himself. Regarding the fact that the Emperor’s confirmation is absolutely necessary, it is taught by Mynsinger <note>Joachim Mynsinger von Frundeck (1514–1588), a renowned jurist of the Imperial Chamber Court</note> in *Counsel 10, no. 39 and following; Counsel 32, no. 21 and following;* Nicolaus Everhardus the Younger, *Counsel 13, no. 2, vol. 2, etc.;* Feschius in the *Basel Disputation on Treaties, thesis 24, letter d, see below.* By this confirmation, the "desire for the death of another" <note>original: "votum captandæ mortis" — a legal concept where a contract regarding a living person's inheritance was traditionally seen as shameful or inciting murder; Imperial approval removed this stigma</note> is entirely excluded. Hotoman, *Counsel 2.* Then, (3) because the Princes of Germany have the power to establish law within their own territories. *Law 2, Code, on the office of the Praetorian Prefect;* Bartolus on *the law of all peoples, no. 8, Digest, on justice and law.* (4) These pacts and statutes are "favorable" <note>In legal terms, "favorable" means they are to be interpreted broadly to achieve their goal</note>, and most of all they look toward the confirmation of the male lineage and ancestry, and toward the peace and tranquility of the Empire (namely, so that subjects are not subjected to a Lord who is either unwilling or unknown, which is usually an occasion for discord and the inversion and ruin of the entire Principality, Gail, *Book 2, Observation 227.*); therefore, they are worthily deserving of favor. Custom is also added to this. But truly, both by Jurists and by Emperors, the foundation of their opinion is frequently taken from nowhere else than common observation. *Law on the emancipated son, regarding the Cornelian Law on forgery; Law 1 at the end, version on the minor, regarding the Silanian Decree of the Senate. See* Faber in *Counsel on Montferrat, part 1, page 140;* Guetta, *final counsel, question 1;* Vincentius Fusarius, *on substitutions and trusts, question 308;* Beati, *decisions, volume 3, on testaments, part 2, page 853; Marpurg Counsels, volume 4, counsel 20, question 1, and counsel 54;* Wilhelm Antonius in the *Corollary to the treatise on the Five-Year Term, page 4;* Limnaeus *on the public law of Otto, page 51;* Peregrinus *on trusts, article 51;* Salycetus *on the final law, Code, on pacts;* all of whom treat this question: whether, when, and to what extent such a pact of mutual succession is valid. Is it permitted, however, to agree <term>that no Catholic shall succeed</term> <note>original German: "daß kein Catholischer succediren solle"</note>, and vice versa? See the *Dillingen Peace Composition, question 48 at the end.* Likewise, is a family pact or long-standing custom valid by which women are excluded from the succession of allodial goods <note>Property held independently, not as a feudal grant</note>? *Strasbourg Counsels, vol. 1, counsel 57.*

Against these family pacts of reciprocal succession, some affirm that a testament can still be made, as does D. Bocer in the *treatise on controversial questions of the right of succeeding in a fief, chapter 2, question 3, my edition, page 89 and following.* But this does not seem probable to me, as I said in the *treatise on Succession and Royal Election, page 148;* add Treutler, *counsel 7.* And the words of the most ingenious Schifordegker pertain here, *book 1, treatise 29, question 2 at the end:* "Our legal school does not allow that a covenant made between living persons should be valid, yet it can nonetheless be revoked by the very person who was once usefully bound by it." Add Reinckingk, *class 1, chapter 4, section 18.* And these "pact-heirs" are like trustees, and this family covenant is like a trust established by pact. Indeed, against

<column-break/>

such pacts, even possession is not transferred, Surdus, *counsel 276, number 14;* and whatever is done against them is null by the law itself, Riminaldus, *counsel 381, no. 47, see the Saxon Acts, page 41.*

In Germany, such a pact was celebrated between the Duke of Saxony and the Landgrave of Hesse, such that whoever of them died without male children, the survivor would be his heir and successor, in the year 1373; this was confirmed by Emperor Charles IV in the public Imperial Diet. Then, in the year 1433, that pact was renewed between their heirs, with the exception and reservation, however, of ten thousand florins, which they could dispose of and bequeath by testament. Similarly, it was confirmed in the Imperial Diet by the authority of Emperor Sigismund. Speckhan, *century 3, question 31, class 1.* Regarding this **Inheritance Brotherhood** <note>original German: "Erbverbrüderung"</note>, one may also see Arumaeus, *on the Diets, chapter 1, no. 21 and following.*

A similar pact is also found celebrated between the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg, and confirmed by Charles V. Concerning which, Decius, having been consulted, affirmed most extensively that it was valid, *counsel 654, page 4.*

On the pact of reciprocal succession between the Kings of Bohemia and the Archdukes of Austria, see Goldast, *on Bohemia, page 718,* and the *counsels* joined to the same treatise.

Likewise, another Pact was celebrated in France between the Illustrious and Noble Brothers, the Lords of Allegres in Auvergne. See Jason, *counsel 5, volume 3.*

An Italian example is also brought forward concerning the Magnificent and Noble Lords of Molza, brothers and citizens of Modena, who made a pact among themselves that the survivor should succeed the one who died first in half of the property, Jason, *counsel 137, volume 4.*

Furthermore, it must be diligently noted that since these covenants are almost always made concerning feudal goods—which cannot even be alienated by testament—the consent, authority, and confirmation of the Feudal Lord is absolutely required in this case. See Gail, *2nd observation, 127, number 7,* and *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 31, question 2.*

It is also useful that a mortgage be added, Peregrinus, *on trusts, article 51, number 71,* so that not only the person but also the things themselves are bound. There are also family pacts prohibiting suretyship, alienation, etc. Hering, *on suretyship, chapter 1, at the end.*

And although these terms **Inheritance Union** <note>original German: "Erbvereinigung"</note> and **Inheritance Brotherhood** <note>original German: "Erbverbrüderung"</note> are used interchangeably and confused by some, nevertheless, if we weigh the matter better, it will not be difficult to recognize that a difference must be established between them. For indeed, **Inheritance Union** denotes a certain and defined manner in which, in every event, both in time of war and peace, one family ought to assist the other, with no mention made of mutual succession, as appears from the letters of the **Inheritance Union** between the Princes of Saxony, Brandenburg, and Hesse, established at Naumburg on July 8, 1587.

**Inheritance brotherhood** <note>original: "Erbverbrüderung"</note> is properly and specifically called that fraternity and pact of mutual succession. Johann Caspar Guttich, *Disputation on Brotherhoods, thesis 1; see also my own work on succession and elections, page 45.*

Here, it must be noted above all else that other pacts are not always reciprocal. For example, the House of Brandenburg succeeds the Pomeranians, and the House of Austria succeeds the House of Württemberg, but not the other way around.

On this subject, there exists a *disputation in volume 1 of the Basel Disputations* by Bartholomaeus Masculus, and in *volume 5* by Johann Caspar Guttich, as well as by Johann Peter Ritter in *volume 1 of the Public Law of Arumaeus, discourse 22.* See also the Magnificent Lord Mager, *on Advocacy, page 646;* Reusner, *Counsel 19 and following, volume 1;* Rosenthal, *chapter 7, conclusion 25 and following;* Reinking, *class 1, 4, chapter 18;* Felchius, *on Treaties, thesis 24;* Barry, *on Successions, book 2, title 3.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding the succession pacts of the Princes of the Empire, see section 25 of Nicolaus Myler’s *Treatise on the Princes and States of the Empire.* By virtue of the Treaty of Kadaň <note>original: "Cadauischen Vertrags"</note>—initiated between Emperor Ferdinand I and Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg, at Kadaň in Bohemia in the year 1534 on the feast of St. John the Baptist, and later declared at Prague in 1599 after the sub-fief was removed—the Archdukes of Austria acquired, through a non-reciprocal pact, a **right of future succession** <note>original: "Expectanz an dem Herzogthum Würtemberg"</note> to the Duchy of Württemberg. See Quett, *Counsel C, number 8;* Limnäus, *book 5 of Public Law, chapter 17, number 3;* Nicolaus Myler, *in the place cited.*

Brotherhoods <note>original: "Confraternitates," often called "Erbverbrüderungen" or "Erbvereinigungen" in German</note> are family pacts entered into between illustrious families so that, if one lineage becomes extinct, their patrimony and Principality may pass to the other according to a fixed law of succession. The Dukes of Saxony entered into such a pact with the Landgraves of Hesse in the year of Christ 1268, with the confirmation of Emperor Rudolf I. The House of Brandenburg later joined this agreement. The Electors of Brandenburg and the Dukes of Pomerania also entered into such a pact in the year 1323; the conditions of this pact were fulfilled in recent years upon the death of the last Duke of Pomerania. See Limnäus *in Public Law, book 4, chapter 8, number 175.* Similarly, the Dukes of Saxony made a pact with the Princes of Henneberg (Limnäus, *book 4, chapter 8, number 173*) so that if the latter failed, the County of Henneberg would pass to the Dukes of Saxony; conversely, the Hennebergs would succeed in the district of Coburg (Year of Christ 1554). The conditions of this pact were likewise fulfilled regarding the Princes of Henneberg in the year 1583. Biccius *in the Golden Bull, prologue, thesis 46, W.* More **examples** are supplied by Schönborn *in Politics, page 162.* The difference between "Inheritance Brotherhood" <note>Erbverbrüderung</note> and "Inheritance Union" <note>Erbvereinigung</note> is noted by Limnäus, *book 4, chapter 8, number 126;* Hahn, *on the Law of Things, chapter 75, final number;* and Becker, *in Public Law, page 104 and following.* These brotherhoods are void without the Emperor's approval. Otto *in Public Law, page 374,* and Knip-

<meta>catchword: Besold's Volume I.</meta>

<column-break/>

schild, *on Trusts, chapter 6, number 246;* Remigius Fesch, *on Treaties, conclusion 24, letter d;* Johann Caspar Guttich, *on Brotherhoods, conclusion 6.* Note why the pact of brotherhood between the Anhalt family and the Elector Palatine regarding the March <note>The March of Brandenburg or similar territory</note> was considered invalid. Knipschild, *on Trusts, chapter 6, number 248.* See on this entire matter Besold, *in Politics, chapter 6, number 41,* and Wurffbain, *in Historical Relations,* who asserts in the *preface, page 42,* that by virtue of a succession pact under Emperor Albert II of Austria, the Kingdom of Bohemia passed to the Archdukes of Austria.

On this term, many authors may be consulted: *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 24, number 44;* Klock, *counsel 6, number 24.*

**42. Heirs, To Inherit, Class for himself and his heirs.** <note>original: "Erben, Erbnehmen, Cl. für sich und seine Erben"</note> Heirs, for himself and his heirs.

The Heir (*Erb*) is so called as if he were the "Master" <note>original: "Heres quasi Herus" — a Latin wordplay suggesting the heir becomes the new owner</note>. Adam Keller, *on Successions, title 1, number 6;* see Killinger, *on Co-inheritance, chapter 1, number 40.* For the ancients called the heir "Lord." Thus Ulpian, in the *Digest on the Aquilian Law* <note>The "Lex Aquilia" was a Roman law concerning compensation for damage to property</note>, responds: "The action of the Aquilian Law belongs to the master <note>original: "hero"</note>," that is, to the Lord. And Pomponius says that even if damage is done to the inherited goods before you formally enter the inheritance, you still have the action of the Aquilian Law for what happened after the death of the one to whom you are heir; for the Aquilian Law calls the heir "Lord." *Law "ob id" 41, Digest.* This is also supported by the *Institutes on the quality of heirs.* For wiser men are accustomed to appoint an heir for themselves in their wills for their posterity, through whom—once the body is dead—the deceased's will may still have some **delight in ruling** <note>original: "delectationem regnandi"</note> over the goods of the departed. *Digest, on usucaption.* Hence, to make someone an heir is to establish a master. Menochius, *on Presumptions, book 4, presumption 133, number 9; see Keller in the place cited.*

Some, however, derive "Heir" <note>Heres</note> from "clinging" <note>haerendo</note>, because in "master" <note>herus</note> the syllable is short, while in "heir" <note>haeres</note> it is lengthened. In this sense, the heir is called one who "clings," being the one closest to the person whose heir he is. Valentinus Forster, *on Successions, book 2, chapter 16, number 2.*

Finally, others derive it from "bronze" <note>aes</note>, as the one who is the successor to the bronze, that is, the money. Whence Cicero in the *Topics* defines inheritance as the money of the deceased. And Varro calls a "Heredium" a field of two acres <note>jugera</note>, which were first divided man by man by Romulus; and because they followed the heir, they were called *Heredia*. Pliny also reports that nowhere in the *Twelve Tables* <note>The foundation of Roman law</note> is a "villa" named, but always a "garden" in that sense; Columella, however, called a small inherited plot of four acres a "little inheritance" <note>haerediolum</note>. And Festus records that the ancients called a small estate a *heredium*, and that the heir Martia cultivated the inheritance she received. Forster, *cited place, number 3.*

Just as an inheritance is nothing other than the succession to the entire legal standing of the deceased; *Digest, on the Signification of Words;* so too is an heir, whether by Will...

<meta>This page continues the legal exploration of inheritance, moving from the broad concepts of "Inheritance Brotherhoods" discussed on the previous page to the specific legal definitions and categories of an "Heir" (Heres). It explores how an heir represents the person of the deceased in both civil and feudal law.</meta>

# Enlarged Treasury of Practical Law
<page-num>266</page-num>

Whether by testament or in the case of intestacy <note>dying without a valid will</note>, the heir is the successor to the entirety of the legal rights held by the deceased. Or, as Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note> defines it: An heir is a master substituted after someone's death into the whole right that the deceased possessed. *Digest 9, title 2, law 1; Digest 47, law 47, on acquiring or omitting inheritance; Digest 59, law 59, on the rules of law.* From this arises the legal maxim: the heir and the deceased represent one and the same person. *Authentica, on the oath by the dying; Code of Justinian, on farmers and tax-payers.* Thus, one type of heir is called "legitimate" <note>by operation of law</note> and another "testamentary" <note>by a will</note>. Both exist by law, but the latter through the law acting by means of a will made according to legal prescription, while the former exists immediately through the law without any human act.

Furthermore, the designation of "heir" refers not only to the immediate heir, but also to those further down the line. For the heir of an heir, and so on, is included under the designation of "heir." *Digest 50, title 16, law 65, on the meaning of words.* For if the heir is the person representing the deceased, even once the inheritance is accepted, that representation will indeed continue through the second and third successor. Indeed, if succession is, as stated in *Digest 50, title 16, law 24*, a succession into the entire right of the deceased to whom we most closely succeed, it follows that the heir's heir also succeeds the first testator, since the right of the first resides in and is attached to the second.

And Paulus says in *Digest 50, title 16, law 70*: It must be understood that "heir" is accepted even through many successions, etc. Modestinus, in *Digest 50, title 17, law 194, on the rules of law*, says: Those who are established as heirs to a deceased person through a succession, however long, are understood as no less heirs than those who exist as primary heirs. And Ulpian, in *Digest 50, title 16, law 170*, says: It is to be believed that by the term "heir," all successors are signified, even if they are not expressly mentioned in words. See generally Fusarius, *on trusts and substitutions, question 339, etc.*; also my own work in the *Montbéliard Counsels, volume 1 of my Counsels*; and Cravetta, *Counsel 38.*

The word <term>Erbnehmen</term> <note>German: inheritance-taking</note> includes not only the heir, but any other successor according to statute or Municipal Law <note>local city or regional laws</note>; Hartmann Pistor, *book 1, question 21, number 30.* Or, it signifies the heir taking the goods of the deceased, whom the Doctors of Law are accustomed to call the "heir of the inheritance." Pistor, *at the cited location, number 9.*

There are, however, three cases, according to Goeddaeus at *law 65 on the meaning of words, number 4 and following*, in which the term "heir" signifies only the immediate heir, which may be seen there.

Likewise, in feudal matters, "outsiders" <note>those outside the bloodline</note> do not come under the designation of *heirs*. For instance, although a fief might be given to a Vassal for himself and his heirs, it is nonetheless understood only to refer to his sons, and not to an outside heir. *See Karl von Kirchberg, on hereditary fiefs, chapter 4, number 39, also numbers 50 and 75*, where he discusses when the expression of "heir" imports a fief; and Hartmann Pistor, *book 2, question 3, chapter 1.*

<column-break/>

likewise the minor client, *on the alienation of fiefs, chapter 1; also if there were, in what way a fief is lost, chapter 1; on feudal succession, chapter 1; with whom, chapter 1; these indeed regarding the degrees of succession, chapter 1; to this and following, in the title "here the law ends," chapter 1; Titius, if a fief was contrary, chapter 1; if a Vassal, chapter 1; similarly on the Laws of Conrad, chapter 1; when indeed regarding those who can give a fief, chapter 1; on two brothers.* Ludovicus Romanus, *Counsel 1, number 5 and Counsel 494, number 2.* Petrus Paulus Parisius, *Counsel 2, number 23 and Counsel 16, number 112, volume 4.* Cornelius, *Counsel 16, number 6 and following, volume 2.* Tiberius Decianus, *Counsel 58, number 12, volume 1.* Henning Goeden, *Counsel 17, number 5, volume 2.* Hardevig von Dassel, *Counsel 45, number 9, book 1.* Menochius, *book 3, presumption 94, at the end.* Zasius, *Counsel 11, number 5 and Counsel 13, number 25, volume 1.* Mynsinger, *century 5, observation 82.* Rudinger, *century 2, singular observation 11, number 4.* And that this is the common opinion is taught by Zabarella, *Counsel 64*; Calderinus, *Counsel 15, on the meaning of words*; Ruinus, *Counsel 16, volume 1*; Socinus, *Counsel 76, column 2*; and Covarruvias, *book 2, various resolutions, chapter 18, number 3.*

The rule handed down above—that namely all heirs to infinity are contained under the term "heirs"—is also limited in that case where mention is made of heirs with the addition "written above" or "written below." In that case, the heirs of heirs do not come forward, but only those who were called and enrolled by name. Bartolus, in *Digest 28, title 2, law 29, on the section "these words."* For those who can be read are called the "under-written" heirs. *Digest 28, title 4, law 1, on those things which are deleted in a will.*

It is also limited in penal matters. For if a testator had burdened the heirs to do something under penalty, the heir of the heir is not included; because in penal matters, which are "odious" <note>legally unfavorable and strictly interpreted</note>, one does not proceed by conjectures, but the matter must be proved most clearly. Jason de Mayno, in *the final law, Code of Justinian, on instituting heirs*; add and see Cagnolus at *Digest 50, title 17, law 194, number 19 and following.*

In obligatory instruments or other contracts, for the sake of greater security, the clause <term>für sich und seine Erben</term> <note>German: for himself and his heirs</note>, etc., is usually added. Regarding its force, consult Bertazolus *in the treatise on clauses of instruments, page 376, etc., and page 420*; and Marta, *on clauses, page 101*, who also records what the clause "for heirs" denotes on *page 354*; "for legitimate heirs" on *page 355, etc.*; likewise "for heirs in perpetuity" on *the following pages.*

Regarding whether and when a penalty passes to the heirs, see Tessaurus, *Decision 144*, and Cacheranus, *Decision 149.*

## ADDITION.

Regarding what the word <term>Erben</term> <note>Heirs</note> means in common usage, see the *Altdorf Counsels, page 589.* For <term>Erben</term> and <term>Erbnehmen</term> <note>Heirs and Inheritance-taking</note>, see Gothofredus, *Antinomies of Feudal Disputations, page 34.* Regarding a fief given for oneself and any heirs whatever, see extensively in the same place. Both sexes are contained under the designation of "heirs," according to Knipschild, *on testamentary trusts, chapter 1, number 92*, unless the subject matter suggests otherwise, *number 93.* In fiefs, only males come under the name of "heirs," *number 94.*

### 43. Hereditary Nobleman. Born Nobles.

See the *Waldeck Defense of Honor*, part 1, chapter 9, sheet 54, where among other things the following is found: And it is further to be noted from the cited letter of fief that the Counts of that time (namely, those of Waldeck) did not simply call and describe themselves as Noble Men, but with the addition of the word "Hereditary," or **Hereditary Nobleman**. This was because they were not ennobled today or yesterday through a Hessian feudal relationship, but had long since been Counts by birth and origin through their ancestral lineage <note>original: "majorum progenie, nativitate & origine"</note>. They are innate Nobles <note>original: "innati Nobiles"</note>, just as the Saxon Law uses the word **Hereditary Nobleman** in such a sense. Saxon Law, book 2, article 2, sections 1–2, and article 42, where the commentary is found.

### 44. Line of Succession. Succession.

To alienate <note>to sell or give away</note>, and to succeed, or **to remain in the line of succession**, are viewed as opposites. Cothman, consultation 40, book 1, number 15. These words seem to encompass every possible reason for succession. Ibid, number 207.

### 45. Inheritance Money. Goods acquired from successions.

It is called **Inheritance Money** <note>original: "Erbgeld"</note>, not because it is paid by just any buyer, but because it is paid by the heir, to whom the hereditary goods were assigned, to a co-heir. <note>This refers to a situation where one sibling keeps the family house and pays the others their share in cash.</note> Coler, on executive process, chapter 3, part 1, number 244. Moller, on the Saxon Electoral Constitutions, 28, number 29, part 1, and constitution 21, part 3. Schultes, on the questions of Modestinus Pistoris, 124, number 32, part 3. Rauchbart, book 1, Saxon questions, question 6, number 8. The same Moller, book 1, semestrial, chapter 26, where he says: There are not a few who believe that every price which must be paid at fixed intervals from the purchase of immovable property <note>real estate</note> is **Inheritance Money**; and these people seem to agree that such a price is commonly and indiscriminately called **Installment Payments and Inheritance Money** <note>original: "Tagzeiten und Erbgeld"</note>. However, it has been accepted both by the High Court and by the Courts of Leipzig and Württemberg, that this right of priority <note>a legal preference in being paid back</note> is granted only to that price (he speaks here of Inheritance Money) which an heir pays to a co-heir for shares of inherited real estate at distinct times. This is the case in Constitution 21, part 3, in the section "But if the woman" <note>original: "DA aber die Frauë"</note>. It does not apply to that which is paid at other times

Besold's Volume 1.

<column-break/>

for immovable goods, namely **on installments** <note>original: "auf Tagzeiten"</note>: which the same Constitution clearly proves in that same place. Nor does it stand in the way that this is commonly called **Inheritance Money** by the public; for the common usage of speaking does not create Law. <note>original: "vulgi namque loquendi usus Jus non facit"</note> Baldus, on a similar point regarding nourishers. Code of Justinian, on common successions.

Regarding the difference between **Inheritance Money**, which is properly so-called, and **Installment Payments**, which are owed for reasons other than inheritance, see the same Moller in the cited place, chapter 41, etc., and add Hartmann Pistoris, observation 142, regarding what money falls under the name of **Inheritance Money**.

### 46. Hereditary Justice. Hereditary Right.

This little word <note>original: "Erbgerechtigkeit"</note> is understood to refer to the entire substance of paternal goods. Br. on the law "if anyone a slave," section "if to someone certain," number 2. Compare the illustrations collected by Johann Baptist Caesar, volume 1, counsel 33, number 25.

->**ADDITION.**<-

**Inheritance Law** or **Hereditary Justice** denotes a hereditary right <note>original: "jus hereditarium"</note>; it can be described as a universal right established in a thing, by which an inheritance is said to belong to us or be ours. Hahn, on the right in a thing, chapter 64.

### 47. Hereditary Court, Hereditary Magistrate. Lower jurisdiction.

**Hereditary Court** <note>original: "Erbgericht"</note> is used for a lower jurisdiction, and is contrasted with supreme hereditary jurisdiction. Commentary on article 28 of the Saxon Law, book 1, under letter b, and in the Latin text at the verse "whatever of such things."

In Silesia <note>A region now mostly in Poland</note>, this term **Hereditary Court** is understood in another sense, as can be seen in Schifordegker, book 3, treatise 29, question 6. He says we must notice here that our legal practitioners err who, in all appointments of village magistrates <note>original: "Investituris Scultetorum"</note>, whenever they find the word **Hereditary Magistrate** or **Hereditary Court**, immediately conclude that the goods of this magistrate are allodial <note>owned outright</note> and not feudal. In this, it is certain beyond doubt that they sin through ignorance of the ancient Law. Thus, it must be held that the word **Hereditary Court** or **Hereditary Magistrate**, when it occurs in old appointments, does not serve to show that the goods of someone...

### 48. Hereditary Estates. Patrimonial property. <note>original: "Erbgüter. Res patrimoniales."</note>

Mr. Cothmann says that patrimonial property (**The Hereditary Estates**), which are prohibited from being sold by statute, are a form of debt <note>original: "æs alienum"; here meaning a legal obligation or "statutory debt" tied to the family line</note>; and he calls it a statutory, customary, and legitimate debt, book 3, response 44, numbers 81, 85, and 97.
