### 50. Hereditary Fief, Male-Hereditary Fief, etc. <note>original: "Erblehen, Erbmann=Lehen &c. Feudum hereditarium."</note>

The Interpreters commonly define a Hereditary Fief as a Fief granted to someone with mention of heirs. *Mynsing, century 4, observation 2, number 1; Gail, 2, observation 154, number 8; Schrad. volume 1, counsel 3, number 77.* See *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 37, question 1.* But the word **Heirs** <note>original: "Erben"</note> does not necessarily imply a hereditary quality, according to what was said above under the entry **Heirs**. However, if the words **to true inheritance, hereditary fief, or hereditary estate** <note>original: "zu rechtem Erbe, Erblehen oder Erbgut"</note> are present in the Investitures, they imply a hereditary fief without controversy, as something granted under a hereditary quality. *Ludovicus de Molina in his treatise on Spanish Primogeniture, volume 1, chapter 8, number 6.* Of the same condition are those words: **to all his heirs and takers-of-inheritance** <note>original: "allen seinen Erben und Erbnemen"</note>, which also cause this fief to

<column-break/>

have the nature of a purely hereditary fief, and indeed generally, as far as the right of succeeding is concerned, and makes it transferable to any successors whatsoever. *Andreas Knichen, on the vesting of pacts, part 2, chapter 5, numbers 14 and following.* It is the same when the words **to all his descendants and heirs** <note>original: "allen seinen Nachkommen und Erben"</note> are added to the phrase *to all Heirs*, as if the word *Whosoever* had been added. *Alexander, counsel 195, number 4, book 6; Gozadinu, counsel 6, number 43; and counsel 27, number 22; Tiberius Decianus, counsel 58, number 32, volume 2; Rolandus à Valle, counsel 60, number 49, volume 1, and volume 2, counsel 79, number 34; Cravetta, counsel 256, throughout; Socinus junior, counsel 114, number 9, volume 2; Julius Clarus in the section on fiefs, question 9, number 2; Hartmann Pistor, book 2, part 1, question 1, number 40.* These words ensure that one can dispose of that fief at will, just like any other allodial property; *Laurentius Sylvanus, counsel 30, number 25 and following; Bursatus, counsel 23, number 170.* (But can one also leave it by will? Although those words, **to all his heirs and descendants**, imply a hereditary fief, this doctrine proceeds "to a certain extent" <note>original: "secundum quid"</note> rather than "simply and absolutely." Mr. Wolff, my kinsman to be brotherly honored, *counsel 1, number 251; Antonius Tessaurus, decision 99, 27,* where he says it was so judged in the Senate. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of how specific phrasing in "investitures" (legal documents granting land) determines the inheritance rights of a family. It specifically examines the "Hereditary Male Fief" and how the inclusion of certain clauses allows for the sale of property or the inclusion of female heirs, which was normally restricted in feudal law.</meta>

Book I.

...sometimes. Law 78. Law on "Power" 215. Law on "Children" 204. Law on "Money" 222. In the Digest "On the Meaning of Words" <note>original: "ff. de V. S."; 'ff' is a standard abbreviation for the Digest, a massive collection of Roman legal rulings</note>, it is stated that words used indefinitely should be adapted to the nature of the fief <note>A fief (feudum) was land held from a lord in exchange for service</note>, according to Menochius, Counsel 1, number 456.

The nature of fiefs, however, is such that they normally reject women, or only admit them to the inheritance if no males survive. Mr. Wolff, in the cited place, number 255.

**Hereditary Male Fiefs** <note>original: "Erb-Mannlehen"</note> differ from purely hereditary fiefs, or **proper fiefs** <note>original: "rechten Lehen"</note>, only in that they must always be formally acknowledged by a male; loyalty must be sworn and services must be performed (even when a woman succeeds to them), perhaps through a husband, son, or another person. Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 14, number 8. Otherwise, a female Vassal <note>A person who holds land from a superior lord</note> in those cases where she is considered capable of holding fiefs, can generally perform the formal acknowledgment herself. Rosenthal, chapter 6, conclusion 31, number 6.

To establish a **Proper Hereditary Fief** <note>original: "ein Recht Erblehen"</note>, it is required that it be granted for the man and any of his heirs, or that it be granted for him, his heirs, and those to whom he might give it. On this matter, Rosenthal treats it more fully in chapter 2, conclusion 36, and Vultejus in chapter 8, number 30. Or, it must be stated that such a piece of land is held as a proper **inheritance, patrimony, or hereditary fief** <note>original: "Erb, Erbgut, Erblehen"</note>, as is the old tradition, law, and custom of such hereditary estates. Knichen, "On the Investiture of Agreements," book 1, chapter 5, number 3. And it should be stated that it was granted for heirs and those receiving by inheritance. Wesenbeck, Counsel 12, number 18. Knichen, cited place, number 12, and Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 15, number 1 and following. Vultejus, "Marburg Counsels," volume 1, response 33, number 43 and following. Regarding the clause placed in the investiture **to have, to hold, to sell,** etc. <note>original: "zu haben, zu halten, zu verkauffen"</note>, and what it implies? See Beatus in "Decisions," tome 5, on judicial matters, part 5, volume 2, folio 248.

And certainly, three opinions are found among the Doctors of Law regarding the effect of this clause. The first is of those who want this clause to be understood according to the nature of the contract to which such an agreement is attached. However, since the nature of a fief is that it cannot be sold without the Lord's consent, they argue that this agreement and clause should be understood such that any sale <note>original: "alienatio"</note> permitted to the Vassal in the letters of Investiture must still be done with the Lord's consent.

But if this interpretation is admitted, there would be no force or efficacy at all in this clause **to have, to sell, to exchange,** etc. <note>original: "zu haben, zu verkauffen, zu verwechslen"</note> and **to deal with it as he pleases** <note>original: "und seines Gefallens damit zu handeln"</note>. It would seem that nothing more was granted to the Vassal than usual; therefore, that opinion should be rightly rejected. For otherwise, words of that kind would be plainly useless. For this reason, other Doctors, such as Belviso, Alvarotto, Isernia, and Laudensis, interpret this clause differently. They say that by its power, the Vassal can not only sell the fief without the Lord's consent but can even transfer its **direct**

<column-break/>

**ownership** <note>original: "dominium directum"</note> to another. In this way, those goods would no longer be fiefs, but would be judged by the same law as other things which one holds with full right, and for which one acknowledges no other superior.

But since, by this interpretation, feudal goods would completely lose their nature and character—and this would undoubtedly be against the will of the direct Lord—a middle path more consistent with equity has been chosen by some Doctors. This interpretation is given: that the clause operates only so that the Vassal, because of it, can sell his feudal goods even without asking the Lord. However, it is under the condition that the sale is made to those who are capable of holding fiefs, and that the direct ownership remains intact, so that the fief returns to the Lord at the proper time and in the proper manner. Beatus, cited place, number 6, where in the following sections he defends this opinion with many arguments.

When, however, the words of the Investiture are not entirely sufficient to prove a purely hereditary quality, then long-standing practice and usage provide the decision. Knichen, cited chapter 5, number 10. For from the followed practice, it is demonstrated whether a fief is purely hereditary or not. Josephus Ludovicus, "Common Conclusions," 38, number 65. And because for a fief to be purely or entirely hereditary is not against the substance of a fief, but only against its typical nature <note>Legal scholars distinguished between the "substance" (the core requirements) and the "nature" (the usual characteristics) of a legal arrangement</note>; Zasius, "Epitome of Fiefs," part 1, at the end, and Fichard, Counsel 19, number 3, volume 2. Therefore, by custom, a fief can easily be changed from a conditional agreement into an absolutely hereditary fief, as noted by Schrader, part 2, chapter 2, number 32 and following. This especially holds true in the case of "immemorial custom," as Schrader discusses extensively in part 1, section 9, number 233 and following.

Such practice is proved from this: when women and other "incapable" persons <note>In this legal context, "incapable" usually refers to those who could not perform military service, such as women or clerics</note> were admitted without controversy, by hereditary right alone, and not merely as feudal successors. For women, distant male relatives, and the wives of Vassals are not admitted except in absolutely hereditary fiefs. Rosenthal, chapter 7, conclusion 60, numbers 1, 5, and 10.

But some also oppose these points: when a fief has been transferred from one person to another not included in the first Investiture, and the reason is not apparent, it should then be presumed that this happened with the Lord's consent rather than because the fief was inherently sellable. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 59, number 7. And they argue it does not seem to be enough to prove that women succeeded, since they could have been invested anew out of grace, by purchase, or for some other reason (and thus the fief became a "feminine fief"), or because of an express agreement (if it had previously reverted to the Lord), or because male relatives could have reclaimed it by right for other reasons, just as... <meta>catchword: ...they were unwilling.</meta>

## Augmented Treasury of Practical Law

...not to have wanted to. <note>original: "noluisse"</note> Rosenthal, chapter 7, conclusion 43, number 12. Therefore, to prove a custom in any single fief, at least two acts are required, and indeed such acts from which it can be gathered that they were done with the intention that they should be observed in that way and done in the future; yet they should feel this tacitly, not expressly. For if they were to pronounce expressly that they always want them to be observed so, it would be a convention <note>A formal agreement or contract</note>, not a custom: and while it would bind the contracting parties themselves, it would not bind other **agnates** <term>Agnates: Relatives related through the male line who have a potential right to inherit the fief</term>, namely those having the right or hope of succession in that fief, whose tacit consent is also required in a custom. See the section "without writing" <note>original: "§. sine scripto"</note> and the commentators there on the Institutes regarding the law of nature, nations, and the city. Rosenthal, chapter 7, conclusion 43, number 10 and following.

To these things add that a **proper fief** <note>original: "feudum rectum"; the standard, traditional type of fief</note>, to which a woman has been admitted once by a privileged grant or a legitimate pact, nonetheless retains its original nature (however much it may be dormant and as if sleeping, until it is revived by a succeeding male), unless it is stated in the **Investiture** <term>Investiture: The formal legal document or ceremony where a Lord grants land to a vassal</term> that it ought to reach further as a feminine fief. Fer. Montan. in the collection of fiefs, book 3, chapter 8, section "you the matter thus" <note>original: "§. tu rem. sic."</note>, followed by Rosenthal, chapter 7, conclusion 69, in note letter K.

Fiefs that are **alienable** <term>Alienable: Capable of being sold or transferred to someone else</term> without the consent of the Lord by force of constitution, statute, or custom, do not degenerate so far—even if they pass to any outsiders whatsoever by intestacy <note>Inheritance when there is no will</note>—as to be considered purely hereditary: but those customs are to be understood strictly and, according to the opinion of many, in such a way that they cause less injury to the **Common Law of Fiefs**, and are not extended further than what has been used and prescribed. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 91, number 11 with following, and conclusion 58, number 22 and following. Since a fief changed in one respect is presumed to have retained its own nature in the rest, it is governed by the law of a proper fief, insofar as it is not demonstrated to have been changed by custom, statute, or convention. Menochius, book 2, presumption 95, number 2. Rosenthal, cited conclusion 58, number 27, and chapter 2, conclusion 54.

Hence it is handed down as a rule that **improper fiefs** <note>Fiefs that deviate from standard feudal rules, such as those allowing female inheritance or sale</note>, which in some respects depart from the common nature of fiefs and are altered, remain under the feudal and simple nature and rule in the other parts that were not altered, and are governed according to it. Jaf. epitome of fiefs, part 12, number 3. Rittersh. book 1, chapter 14, question 2, page 206. But it is replied <note>original: "Sed replicatur"</note>, <insert>that this opinion is not approved by all Doctors [of Law], and moreover is restricted by their own followers to this extent:</insert> that it speaks in those cases where it does not appear that something else has been observed: namely, that fiefs were alienated during the lifetime of the seller without the consent of the Lord and without the penalty of forfeiture or revocation, and this became established by custom. For if 그 custom has also been received by use, so that neither the agnates nor the Lord can ever revoke alienations of this kind, or if it is approved by custom that daughters should succeed in the fief equally with males (excluding more remote males), or even other outside heirs (these others being removed),

<column-break/>

then one must stand by that custom, however harsh. Rosenthal, cited conclusion 58, number 40 and following.

Add that the rule (a fief changed in one respect retains its proper nature in others) does not proceed when it is clear, either expressly or tacitly, from the minds of the contracting parties that they wish to produce an "impropriety" <note>A deviation from standard feudal law</note> of the fief even beyond those things expressed in the Investiture. It also fails regarding those things which follow as a necessary consequence of the impropriety, or are its accessories or attachments. Schrader, part 2, last question, number 76 and following.

However, a fief should not always be considered "hereditary" simply because it was sold once or twice and the Lord provided his consent to this sale. For although the Lord of the fief, by investing the buyers, is considered to have consented to the contract of sale—especially when mention is made of the contract of sale in the letters of Investiture, in which case he seems to have consented by the very fact—nevertheless, that simple consent to alienate does not harm the Lord, nor does it injure his right even in the slightest degree. This is expressly held by Andreas de Isernia in chapter 1, "On the prohibition of alienating a fief," as cited and followed by Alvarottus and the Provost <note>original: "Præpos."</note> there. The same Provost and Alvarottus in chapter 1, section "furthermore by what modes a fief is lost." Zaf. counsel 12, number 5 at the end of book 1. The Doctors of Law are moved by this: because since the Lord, by consenting, was thinking only of the **useful right** <term>Useful right: The right to use and profit from the land (held by the vassal), as opposed to the "direct right" or ultimate ownership held by the Lord</term> of the Vassal, certainly this should not be extended to the rights of the Lordship. They cite the chapters "it is asserted" regarding presumptions. It is not to be presumed that the Lord wished to prejudice himself in his own right, but only that he removed the obstacle (namely, that the Vassal’s right could not be sold without the Lord's consent). Schrader on fiefs, part 8, chapter 4, number 28, and Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 38, number 4 and following. For neither a gift nor a surrender of one's right is presumed unless it is clear from open words. In every act, that interpretation is always to be taken by which the right of the other person is injured as little as possible. Law 3, "On suspected guardians." Hartm. Pistor. book 2, part 2, question 48, number 5 and following. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 1, number 8. And so, from our voluntary acts, nothing should be presumed regarding those things which are not included by necessity. Law at the end, Code, "That a wife for her husband." Zaf. cited counsel 12, number 72, book 1.

<insert>But on the other hand, it could again be considered and noted,</insert> that a contract is understood to have come into consent along with its specific qualities, as Zasius witnesses in the cited conclusion 12, number 7. And that consent granted simply is considered to be applied according to the nature of the contract. Indeed, consent very often receives its declaration from the mind of those requiring it...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property rights, specifically focusing on the implications of a Lord's consent to a vassal's actions and the precise definitions of hereditary possession and vacant estates.</meta>

...if a defender. <note>original: "si defensor"</note> Section: "he who is interrogated" <note>original: "§. qui interrogatur"</note> regarding the action of interrogation. Pistor, book 2, question 12, number 57.

Therefore, the rule—that the simple consent of the Lord does not prejudice his own right—proceeds only in those rights which, belonging to the consenting Lord, have a separate reasoning from the business to which the consent is added; but not in those rights which pertain to the strength and firmness of the act itself. For regarding those matters, a Lord who consents to all his rights—which could have hindered that act in any way—is considered to have renounced them and to have added the strongest validity to that business. This is declared by Andreas de Isernia in chapter 1, at the beginning, column 4, on "who succeeds in a holding"; Camerar. in chapter "Imperialem," pages 339 and 353, regarding the prohibition of alienating a fief by Frederick; Pistor, in the aforementioned question 12, number 56.

So also to the other rule—that a donation or remission of a right is not presumed—the response is that it only applies in a doubtful case. It is otherwise, however, when the renunciation is established from the consent itself; for then, in a clear matter, there is no longer a need for conjectures, and the one consenting is by that very act considered to resign his right.

The words "to heirs and successors," **for himself and his descendants** <note>original German: "für sich und seine Nachkommen"</note>, have this meaning: they include both universal and singular successors. Fichard, counsel 44, number 2. Hence a fief granted for oneself, heirs, and successors (or sold with the consent of the Lord) is transferred even to singular successors, and therefore can be freely **alienated** <term>Alienated: To be sold or transferred to a new owner</term>. Menochius, counsel 216, number 24 and following, with the citations there; Fichard, counsel 51, number 1 and following.

Many authors have written more regarding **hereditary fiefs** <term>Hereditary fiefs: Lands granted to a vassal that automatically pass to his heirs upon death</term>, namely how they are distinguished, by what words they are established, etc.: Lord Kirchberg in a single treatise; Rudinger, book 2, feudal questions; Gothofr. Anton. Feudal dispute 1, thesis 8; Vivius, decision 441; Christinaeus, volume 1, decision 205; myself in the counsel on the subject of succession; and decision 1, counsel 4; Marpurg Counsels, volume 2, counsel 26 and counsel 37; Menochius, counsel 999; Thomas de Martin. in a single treatise on fiefs by agreement and providence, folio 284 and following; and Molinaeus, counsel 50.

## 51. Hereditary or Rent-Fief.

### ADDITION.

Lord Speidel in *Notable Matters*, and below under the word **Rent-fief** <note>original: "Zinßlehen"</note>.

## 52. To hold hereditarily. To have by hereditary right.

To have something by hereditary right is nothing other than to be the master of a thing and to have its ownership. Law "also an outsider," <note>original: "l. item extraneus"</note> Institutes, on the quality of heirs. Although the word **"to Have"** <note>original: "Haben"</note> may be taken in two ways, and both he who simply holds a thing is correctly

<column-break/>

said to "have" it, as well as he who is the Lord of the thing (Law "that stipulation," section "to have," <note>original: "l. stipulatio ista. §. habere"</note> Digest, on verbal obligations), nevertheless in this case, that word must be referred to ownership: since the attached word **"Hereditarily"** <note>original: "Erblich"</note> refers most strongly to ownership. Marpurg Counsel 7, number 3, etc.

### ADDITION.

The little word **Inheritance** <note>original: "Erb schafft"</note> means that the jurisdiction for the people of Nuremberg shall be unhindered regarding the inheritance on their revenue-bearing and rent-paying estates. From the cases of fall, ground, soil, property, and inheritance: Nuremberg vs. Bavaria on the point of Restitution, folio 69. Regarding the phrase **bringing into the inheritance** <note>original: "einbringen in die Erbschafft"</note>: the mixing of brought-in goods with hereditary things. Carpzov, part 2, decision 164, number 17.

The little word **Hereditarily** <note>original: "Erblich"</note> means, according to the well-known and especially Lower Saxon custom, as much as "proprietary" or "owned." It does not come from the masculine noun **the Heir** <note>original: "der Erbe" (heres)</note>, but from the neuter **the Inheritance** <note>original: "das Erbe"</note>, meaning an **allodium** <term>Allodium: Land owned absolutely in one's own right, without any superior lord.</term> or private estate. Lord Doctor Tabor on dowry agreements, page 70.

**To inherit or to fulfill hereditarily** <note>original: "Erben oder erblich füllen"</note> regarding the succession of children and the power of transmitting to them. Dr. Andreas Stöckelius, Nuremberg Advocate, in the Counsel of Christoph Herdesian in the Honoldian Controversy.

**Hereditarily** is the same as **Proprietary**. Wehner. Lord Hahn on the law of things, chapter 35, number 1.

## 53. Heirless Estates. Vacant Goods.

Regarding vacant goods and things treated as abandoned: although under old law anyone was allowed to claim them (Val. Guil. Forster on ownership, chapter 9, number 91), today, however, it is only lawful for those who hold command or jurisdiction to take possession of lost or deserted things after a set time. Bodin, book 1 on the Republic, chapter 10, number 171; however, Sixtinus reprehends him on that name in the treatise on Regalia <term>Regalia: The specific rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign</term>, chapter 9, number 20. See him throughout the entire chapter; he believes that vacant goods belong only to the Emperor and his **fisc** <term>Fisc: The state or royal treasury</term>, through the title of the Code on vacant goods and the final law on the removal of the petition for goods. See absolutely Ziegler, section "Nobles," conclusion 1, number 22, etc., where he reports from Saxon Law: that under the Royal power, one should understand not only the Kings but also all those to whom the sword <note>The power of life and death/high justice</note> has been commanded.

Under customary Saxon Law, vacant goods belong to that judge who has supreme jurisdiction, not to him who has hereditary jurisdiction—**not to the hereditary court, but to the High Court** <note>original: "nicht zum Erbgericht, sondern in die Obergericht"</note>—so that from there he may support the public officials in punishing crimes, and likewise that he may take care that gallows, neck-irons, stocks, shackles, and other such things necessary in the courts for punishing criminals are constructed. *Landrecht* <note>The "Law of the Land," a primary legal code</note>, book 1, article 25. Coler on executive process, part 1, chapter 3, number 258. Goldbec. in the treatise on the degrees of succession, final chapter, number 8 and following.

It also explains that under Saxon law, abandoned or vacant estates fall to the high jurisdiction of the state to fund the machinery of justice rather than to local hereditary lords.</summary>

### ADDITIO. <note>Addition/Supplement</note>

**Vacant goods** <note>original: "Bona vacantia"</note>, which previously belonged to someone, are called vacant when a person dies intestate <note>without a legal will</note> and leaves no legitimate successor from any bloodline or legal title. Today, the benefit of this succession also falls to lower Magistrates who enjoy "mere empire" <note>the highest level of criminal jurisdiction</note>, having acquired it by grant or long-standing custom. See Wehner in *Practical Observations* under the word **King’s People** <note>original German: "Königsleut"</note>.

Regarding what may be called vacant goods, see Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 139, number 2; Obrecht in *Political Reflections*, pages 102 and following. Vacant goods located in different territories are taken by each respective treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note> proportionally according to the territory, per Klock at the cited location, numbers 16 and 17.

### 54. Erbrath. Hereditary Councilors.

These are Councilors who are called hereditary: thus the Counts of Löwenstein and Tübingen are called the **Hereditary Councilors** <note>original German: "Erbrath"</note> of the Dukes of Württemberg.

### 55. Erbregister, Erbbücher. Land-tax Books. <note>original: "Libri censuales"</note>

Regarding the proving of books which are commonly called **Inheritance Registers** <note>original German: "Erbregister"</note> or **Inheritance Books** <note>original German: "Erbbücher"</note>, see Moller, book 4, *semestr.* chapter 37.

### ADDITIO. <note>Addition/Supplement</note>

How the **Inheritance Books** of Nobles and Prefects are proved: see Franzke, *On the Fee for Transfer of Land*, page 36, number 26 and following; Ummius in *On Legal Process*, page 711.

### 56. Erbschuh, Erbkastenvogten. Hereditary Advocacy. <note>original: "Advocatia hereditaria"</note>

It is called a Hereditary Advocacy <note>the right of protecting a religious institution</note> when, in establishing the Right of Patronage, the protection was conceived and directed not only toward the person of the first Patron, but also toward his heirs and successors. See generally Mr. Mager, *Treatise on Armed Advocacy*, chapter 3, number 201, etc.

### ADDITIO. <note>Addition/Supplement</note>

**Hereditary Bailiwick** <note>original German: "Erbvogtey"</note> designates Advocacy and the right of Protection. Klock, volume 1, counsel 37, number 1. **Hereditary Bailiffs** <note>original German: "Erbsvogt"</note> are delegates of the Emperor; compare counsel 37, number 21.

### 57. Erbvertrag, Theilung. Family Compacts. Partition. <note>original: "Pacta gentilitia. Divisio."</note>

The reasoning for this name, or the force of the word itself, indicates that all things have been divided through a settlement <note>original: "transactionem"</note>. Georg Everhard, counsel 32, number 27, volume 1, citing various chapters of the Decretals and the Code of Justinian.

### 58. Erdbidem. Earthquake. <note>original: "Terræmotus"</note>

Regarding earthquakes and their types, see Louis Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 2, chapter 34, folio 677 and following, where he holds many things worth knowing and provides examples for each type.

### ADDITIO. <note>Addition/Supplement</note>

Regarding earthquakes, Schonborn in *Politics*, page 732, establishes that it is a sign of Overturning <note>original: "Eversionis"</note>. Garcæus in *Meteorology*, pages 392 and 411, says it is also an Instrument of the same. One earthquake under Tiberius overturned twelve famous cities of Asia; Tacitus, *Annals*, book 2, chapter 7. Just as many Cam-

<column-break/>

panian towns were overturned by another under Constantine; and a single war of Attila destroyed more than a hundred. Lipsius, *On Constancy*, chapter 16. Furthermore, entire islands have been swallowed up: Helice, Bura, Atlantis, and in parts of Zeeland, two islands with their towns and men. Lipsius, *ibid.* See what was said above under the word **Basel**.

Regarding earthquakes, one may consult Meteren, book 10, folio 328, for the year 1580. Regarding a massive earthquake in Campania, it caused some people to run about like madmen. It did not extend beyond 200 miles. On the cause, effect, and types of earthquakes: a tranquility of the air precedes an earthquake, while pestilence and wind follow it. Seneca, *passim*. Small floor-tiles in a bath were separated and then joined back together by an earthquake. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book 6, chapter 31.

### 59. Erhalten, mit Urtheil und Recht erhalten. To Prevail. <note>original: "Obtinere"</note>

To the Germans, **to prevail by right** <note>original German: "mit Recht erhalten"</note> is the same as saying **to prevail by judgment** <note>original German: "mit Urtheil erhalten"</note>. When they are joined, it is a repetition and an amplification of the same thing, just as is seen in the opposite phrase, **without judgment and right**. Denais in *Assertion of Chamber Jurisdiction*, folio 182 and following.

### 60. Erzbischoff. Archbishop. <note>original: "Archiepiscopus"</note>

Archbishops are called the Princes of Bishops; they are the heads over an entire province containing several episcopal cities. Paurmeister, book 2, chapter 8, number 4, *Treatise on Jurisdiction*.

They are indeed also called Metropolitan Archbishops, in both Canon Law (nearly everywhere in Cause 9, Question 3) and Civil Law (*Novels* 5 and 7), because they were established long ago in a Metropolis—that is, a "mother city." Duaren, book 2, *On the Ministry of the Most Holy Church*, chapter 9. (Regarding his office, see *Compositions of Peace*, page 401 in my copy, and Anton Fabricius, *On Religion*, folio 48 and following.)

In Germany, seven Metropolises or primary seats of Archbishops were established: Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Magdeburg, Salzburg, Bremen, and Riga. Münster, book 1, *Cosmography* in the description of Germany, chapter 25. Onuphrius Panvinius, *On the Imperial Assemblies*, chapters 6 and 13.

Twelve bishops are subject to the Archbishop of **Mainz** <note>original: "Moguntinensis"</note> as suffragans <note>subordinate bishops</note>: those of Strasbourg, Speyer, Worms, Würzburg, Augsburg, Constance (at Lake Constance), Chur (of the Rhaetians), Eichstätt (or Dryopolis on the German river), Halberstadt, Hildesheim, and Verden. Onuphrius, cited chapter 6; Sprenger in *Outline of the States of the Empire*.

The Archbishopric of **Trier** <note>original: "Trevirensis"</note> has three suffragans: Metz, Toul, and Verdun. Onuphrius, cited location; Sprenger in *Outline of the States of the Empire*, page 253.

The Archbishopric of **Cologne** <note>original: "Coloniensis"</note> has five: Münster, Osnabrück, Minden, Utrecht, and Liège. Onuphrius, cited location.

The Archbishopric of **Magdeburg** recognizes four suffragans: Merseburg, Naumburg, Brandenburg, and Havelberg. Onuphrius, cited chapter 6; Sprenger in *Outline of the States of the Empire*, page 309.

Property that previously belonged to someone is called *vacant* <note>original Latin: "vacantia"</note> when a person dies intestate <note>without a valid will</note> and leaves no legitimate successor from any bloodline or legal title. Today, this benefit of succession also belongs to lower magistrates who enjoy "mere empire" <note>original: "mero Imperio" – a legal term referring to high jurisdiction, including the power to punish</note> and who have acquired that right through grant or ancient custom. *Wehner, Practical Observations, under the word "Königsleut" (King’s people).*

Regarding what may be called vacant property, see *Klock, on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 139, number 2; Obrecht in Political Reflections, page 102 and following.* Each local treasury takes a share of vacant property located in different territories in proportion to what lies within its own territory. *Klock, in the same place, numbers 16 & 17.*

### 54. Hereditary Councilors. <note>original German: "Erbräth"</note>

These are Councilors who are called hereditary: Thus, the Counts of Löwenstein and Tübingen are called the Hereditary Councilors <note>original German: "Erb-Räth"</note> of the Dukes of Württemberg.

### 55. Inheritance Registers, Inheritance Books. Tax Books. <note>original Latin: "Libri censuales"</note>

Regarding the proof of books which are commonly called <term>Inheritance Registers</term> <note>original German: "Erbregister"</note> or <term>Inheritance Books</term> <note>original German: "Erbbücher"</note>, see *Moller, book 4, six-month reports, chapter 37.*

->ADDITION.<-

How the inheritance books of Nobles and Prefects are to be proven. *Franzk. on the right of the lord to a fee, page 36, number 26 and following; Ummius on legal process, page 711.*

### 56. Hereditary Protection, Hereditary Chest-Advocacy. <note>original German: "Erbschuz, Erbkastenvogtey"</note> Hereditary Advocacy.

It is called "Hereditary Advocacy" when, in establishing the Right of Patronage <note>the right to appoint a member of the clergy to a specific church</note>, the protection was intended and directed not only toward the person of the first Patron, but also toward his heirs and successors. See especially *Mr. Mager, treatise on Armed Advocacy, chapter 3, number 201, etc.*

->ADDITION.<-

**Hereditary Bailiwick** <note>original German: "Erbvogtey"</note> designates Advocacy and the right of Protection. *Klock, volume 1, counsel 37, number 1.* **Hereditary Bailiffs** <note>original German: "Erb-vögt"</note> are delegates of the Emperor. *counsel 37, number 21.*

### 57. Inheritance Contract, Division. Family Pacts. Division.

The reasoning for this name or the force of the word indicates by itself that all things have been divided through a transaction. *Georg Everhard, counsel 32, number 27, volume 1, citing various chapters from the Decretals and the Code of Justinian regarding prebends, legitimate children, and holidays.*

### 58. Earthquake. <note>original German: "Erdbidem"; Latin: "Terræmotus"</note>

Regarding earthquakes and their types, see *Louis Guyon, Diverse Lessons, volume 2, chapter 34, folio 677 and following*, where he has many things worth knowing and provides examples for each type.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding earthquakes, *Schonborn in Politics, page 732*, establishes that it is a sign of Overturning <note>original: "Eversionis"</note>. It is also an instrument of the same. A single earthquake under the Emperor Tiberius overturned twelve famous cities of Asia. *Tacitus, Annals, book 2, chapter 7.* Just as many

<column-break/>

towns in Campania were overturned by another earthquake under Constantine: and a single war of Attila the Hun overturned more than a hundred. *Lipsius, On Constancy, chapter 16.* Furthermore, entire islands have been swallowed up, such as Helice, Bura, and Atlantis, and in the regions of Zeeland <note>original: "Selandiæ"</note>, two islands with their towns and men. *Lipsius, in the same place; see also what was said above under the word "Basel."*

On the subject of Earthquakes, one may consult *Metteran, book 10, folio 328, year 1580.* Regarding a massive earthquake in Campania, it caused some people to run about like madmen. It did not extend beyond 200 miles. On the cause, effect, and types of earthquakes: a tranquility of the air precedes an earthquake, while pestilence and wind follow it. *Seneca, in various places.* Small tiles, separated from a bath and then joined back together, are moved by an earthquake. *Seneca, Natural Questions, book 6, chapter 31.*

### 59. To Uphold, to uphold by judgment and law. <note>original German: "Erhalten"</note> To Obtain.

For the Germans, **to uphold by law** <note>original German: "mit Recht erhalten"</note> is the same as saying, "to uphold by judgment." And when these terms are joined, it is a repetition and amplification of the same kind seen in the opposite phrase, **without judgment and law** <note>original German: "ohn Urtheil und Recht"</note>. *Denais, on the Jurisdiction of the Imperial Chamber, folio 182 and following.*

### 60. Archbishop. <note>original Latin: "Archiepiscopus"</note>

Archbishops are called the "Princes of Bishops": they are the heads of an entire province that contains several episcopal cities. *Paurmeister, book 2, chapter 8, treatise on Jurisdiction.*

They are certainly also called Metropolitan Archbishops, both in Canon Law <note>the law of the Church</note> and Civil Law <note>secular law based on Roman codes</note>, because they were established long ago in a "Metropolis," that is, a "Mother City." *Duaren, book 2, on the Ministry of the Holy Church, chapter 9.*

In Germany, seven Metropolises or primary seats of Archbishops were established: Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinensis"</note>, Trier <note>original: "Trevirensis"</note>, Cologne <note>original: "Coloniensis"</note>, Magdeburg, Salzburg, Bremen, and Riga. *Münster, book 1, Cosmography, in the description of Germany, chapter 25; Onuphrius Panvinius, on the Imperial Comitia, chapters 6 and 13.*

Subject to the **Archbishop of Mainz** are twelve bishops as "suffragans" <note>assistant bishops of a province</note>: those of Strasbourg, Speyer, Worms, Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipolensis"</note>, Augsburg, Constance (at Lake Constance), Chur (of the Rhaetians), Eichstätt <note>original: "Eichstetensis" or "Dryopolis" on the German river</note>, Halberstadt, Hildesheim, and Verden. *Onuphrius, cited chapter 6; Sprenger, in the Sketch of the States of the Empire.*

The **Archbishopric of Trier** has three suffragans: Metz, Toul <note>original: "Tolanum"</note>, and Verdun. *Onuphrius, in the same place; Sprenger, page 253.*

The **Archbishopric of Cologne** has five: Münster, Osnabrück, Minden, Utrecht <note>original: "Trajectenfem"</note>, and Liège <note>original: "Leodicenfem"</note>. *Onuphrius, in the same place.*

The **Archbishopric of Magdeburg** recognizes four suffragans: Merseburg <note>original: "Merpurgensem"</note>, Naumburg, Brandenburg, and Havelberg. *Onuphrius, chapter 6; Sprenger, page 309.*

### 61. Erz [Ore]. Aes [Copper/Bronze].

**Erz** <note>The German word for ore or metal</note> comes from the Hebrew *Erez* <note>original: "Erez", likely referring to "Eretz" (ארץ), meaning earth or land</note>, which means earth; see Giovanni Guidi in the treatise *On Minerals*, and Talentoni in *Hidden Things*, book 1, chapter 10. There, he demonstrates whether it ought to be called **Aurichalcum** or **Orichalcum** <note>Terms for brass or a golden-colored copper alloy</note>, which is commonly called *Lottone* or *Lattone*, or rather *Ottone* <note>Italian terms for brass</note>, and he provides the reason for each name. Furthermore, he discusses whether it is something native—that is, a metal distinct from others—or rather something manufactured; and if manufactured, whether it consists of gold and copper, or is instead only copper, dyed with an acquired color, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

**Aes** <note>The general Latin term for copper or its alloys, bronze and brass</note> is the name for every kind of money. Tiraqueau, book 1, *Retractions*, section 1, glossary 20, numbers 7 and 10. *As* is said for copper. Tiraqueau, book 1, section 1, glossary 20, number 8 at the end.

Copper [Aes] is more useful than ancient iron, both at home and in military service, and even in medicine. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 30, number 1. The most excellent of all is found in the **County of Tyrol**. Number 2. For how many various works it is suitable, see number 8. Copper was scarcely separable from gold, but now through the industry of the moderns, it is skillfully distinguished. Number 8. In a general sense, the word **Erz** corresponds to **Silver** <note>original: "Argento"</note>; see broadly Aleman in *Palestra Consultationum*, page 523.

<term>Aes</term> and <term>Cuprum</term> [Copper] are <gloss>synonyms</gloss> <note>original Greek: "συνώνυμα"</note>. It is assigned by the Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> to **Venus**. The Germans call it <term>Kupffer</term>; the Greeks call it <gloss>chalkon</gloss> <note>original Greek: "χαλκὸν"</note>. The name *Cuprum*, however, was acquired from **Cyprus**, in which the best and 

<column-break/>

most abundant supply was gathered. It is a bluish metal, participating in a dusky redness, ignitable and fusible; and according to Encelius in book 1, *On Metals*, chapter 13, it is as if a medium between gold and silver. Regarding its differences, see Pliny, book 34, chapter 9; Agricola, book 8, *On the Nature of Fossils*, folio 334; Encelius in the place cited; and Galen throughout his works. Concerning its qualities and temperament, there is, so far as we know, no controversy. For it is established as **hot and dry**; and it is said to have the power of binding, strengthening, thinning, cleansing, and gluing or consolidating. Dioscorides treats "burnt copper" <note>original: "ære usto"</note> in book 5, chapter 42; and how it is prepared is shown at length by Lord Doctor Sebizius in *On Acidic Springs*, Dissertation 1, Section 2, Position 58. Concerning the dross of copper, see Position 59. On the "flower of copper" <note>copper oxide or verdigris</note>, Position 60. On the "scales of copper," Position 61.

**Yellow copper**, or **Aurichalcum**, known as <term>Messing</term> [Brass], has obtained the highest quality and admiration, being much more noble than red copper. Pliny, book 34, chapter 2; Agricola, book 8, *Fossils*, chapter 4. <insert>That which is valued next to gold is not found in the present time, nor is the white kind.</insert> However, modern orichalcum, commonly called <term>Messing</term> [Brass], is manufactured in a far different way; such are the workshops of Vulcan <note>Metaphor for metal-foundries</note> that exist in the **County of Stolberg** or **Wernigerode**, and in the **Duchy of Brunswick** near the very high **Brocken** mountain <note>original: "Bructerum"</note> in Germany, commonly called <term>Messingshändel</term> <note>Brass-works or brass commerce</note>. These are elegantly described by Taubmann.

Different locations supply different types of copper. On copper mines, <term>Kupffer-Bergwerck</term>, ancient and new, see Agricola, book 2, *On Metals*, chapters 10 and 11. Today, those of **Mansfeld** are celebrated. Pure copper is indeed found (Agricola in *Bermannus*, chapter 24, folio 909), but rarely (Georg Fabricius, *Metallic Observations*, chapter 4). The method of **gilding copper** so that it takes on the appearance of gold is handed down by Zasius from Pliny, book 33, chapters 3 and 6. They heat the copper in the fire, he says, until it glows, then extinguish it with vinegar and alum; afterward, they apply gold leaf <note>original: "bracteolas auri"</note>, and the copper thus prepared receives those leaves into itself so that they stick most tightly. If the copper appears pale beneath the leaves, it is then smeared with the liquid of an egg <note>egg white</note>, which removes the color of the copper. Zasius in the cited law *si id quod*, 22, *On Verbal Obligations*.

Regarding **Coronary** and **Corinthian copper**, Guido Panciroli discourses beautifully in *Book of Memorable Things*, in the chapter on *Pyropus* and the chapter on *Corinthian Copper*. There, Salmuth, in his notes from Pliny (book 34, chapter 8) and Isidore (book 16, chapter 19), proves that a certain Cyprian or "Coronary" copper, being ductile, is thinned into plates and, tinted with the gall of bulls, provides the appearance of gold in the **crowns of actors**; and the same, when gold scraps are added, glows with a very thin leaf of **Pyropus** <note>A gold-bronze alloy</note>; whence it is called Pyropus. Concerning which is that line of Ovid: *With Pyropus imitating flames.* With which Propertius agrees in book 4:

> Nor did the painted shield shine with bestowed Pyropus.

The origin of **Corinthian bronze** is derived from this: when Corinth was captured in the year 508 from the founding of the City <note>146 BC</note>, and was burning in a great fire, it happened by chance that gold, silver, and copper melted and were mixed together. And since that mixture found after the fire seemed beautiful, vessels were cast from it and skillfully engraved; because of these vessels, it is reported that Augustus saw to it that certain people were included among the proscribed...

### ADDITIO. <note>Addition/Supplement</note>

Archbishops and Bishops possess not only legal jurisdiction, but also Electoral and Royal Rights <note>original: "Jura Electoralia & Regalia"; referring to the rights of Prince-Electors in the Holy Roman Empire</note>. *Bocer, On Jurisdiction, chapter 8, number 73.*

### 61. <term>Erz</term> <note>Ore or Bronze</note>. Aes.

The word <term>Erz</term> <note>German for ore or bronze</note> comes from the Hebrew *Erez* <note>original: "Erez"</note>, which means "earth." See Johannes Guidius in his *Treatise on Minerals* and Talentoni, *Hidden Things, book 1, chapter 10*, where he demonstrates whether it should be called *Aurichalcum* or *Orichalcum* <note>historical terms for brass or golden-colored copper alloys</note>. In the common tongue, this is called *Lottone* or *Lattone*, or rather *Ottone* <note>Italian terms for brass</note>, and he provides the reason for both names. Furthermore, he discusses whether it is a natural substance (that is, a metal distinct from others) or rather an artificial one; and if artificial, whether it consists of gold and bronze, or is rather just bronze colored with an added tint, etc.

### ADDITIO. <note>Addition/Supplement</note>

All types of coinage are called "Aes" <note>Bronze/Money</note>. Tiraquellus, *book 1, Withdrawal, section 1, gloss 20, numbers 7 and 10.* "As" is also used for bronze. Tiraquellus, *book 1, Withdrawal, section 1, gloss 20, number 8 at the end.*

Bronze is older than iron and more common in both the home and in military service, and even in Medicine. Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 30, number 1.* The most excellent of all is found in the County of Tyrol. *number 2.* Regarding how many various works it is suitable for, see *number 8.* Bronze was once barely separable from gold, but now, through the industry of modern scholars, it is skillfully discerned. *number 8.* In a general sense, the little word "Aes" corresponds to "Silver," as explained broadly by the Germans in Palestine. *Conf. page 523.*

Bronze and copper are <term>synonyms</term> <note>original Greek: "συνωνυμα"</note>. It is assigned by Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> to Venus. The Germans call it <term>Kupffer</term> <note>Copper</note>; the Greeks call it <term>chalkon</term> <note>original: "χαλκὸν"</note>. The name for copper (*Cuprum*) was actually derived from Cyprus, where the best and most 

<column-break/>

abundant supply was collected. See Besold, *Volume 1.* It is a bluish metal, sharing a dark redness, flammable and meltable; according to Encelius, *book 1, On Metals, chapter 13*, it is as if a middle point between gold and silver. Regarding its different varieties, see Pliny, *book 34, chapter 9*; Agricola, *book 8, On the Nature of Fossils, folio 334*; Encelius in the cited place; and Galen throughout his works. Concerning its qualities and temperament, there is, as far as we know, no controversy: it is established as hot and dry. It is said to have the power of binding, strengthening, thinning, wiping away, and gluing or consolidating. Dioscorides treats "burnt bronze" <note>original: "ære usto"</note> in *book 5, chapter 42*, and Dr. Sebezius shows at length how it is prepared in *On Acidic Springs, Dissertation 1, Section 2, Position 58.* On the dross of bronze, see *Position 59.* On the flower of bronze, *Position 60.* On the scale of bronze, *Position 61.*

Yellow bronze, or "aurichalcum"—known as <term>Meßing</term> <note>Brass</note>—attained a particular quality and admiration, being much nobler than red bronze. Pliny, *book 34, chapter 2*; Agricola, *book 8, Fossils, chapter 4.* *This metal, valued next to gold, is not found in the present time, nor is the white variety. Taubmann describes these elegantly. Different locations provide different varieties of bronze. On copper mines, <term>Kupffer-Bergwerck</term>, both ancient and modern, see Agricola, *book 2, On Metals, chapters 10 and 11.* Today, those of Mansfeld are celebrated. Pure copper is indeed found, according to Agricola in *Bermannus, chapter 24, folio 909*, but rarely, as noted by Georg Fabricius, *Metallic Observations, chapter 4.* Zasius, drawing from Pliny (*book 33, chapters 3 and 6*), hands down a method for gilding bronze so that it takes on the appearance of gold. If the bronze appears pale under the gold leaf, it is then smeared with egg white, which removes the color of the bronze. Zasius in *the cited law, If that which, 22, On Verbal Obligations.*

Guido Pancirolli discourses beautifully on "Coronary" and "Corinthian" bronze in *The Book of Memorable Things, titles: On Pyropus and On Corinthian Bronze.* There, Salmuth notes, citing Pliny (*book 34, chapter 8*) and Isidore (*book 16, chapter 19*), that a certain Cyprian or "Coronary" bronze, hammered thin into sheets and tinted with the gall of bulls, provides the appearance of gold in the crowns of actors. The same metal, when adding six scruples of gold per ounce, glows with the very thin leaf of "Pyropus" <note>a gold-bronze alloy</note>; hence it is called Pyropus. Regarding this, Ovid said: "With Pyropus imitating flames." Propertius agrees in *book 4*:

> Nor did the painted shield shine with applied Pyropus.

He derives the origin of Corinthian bronze from this: when Corinth was captured in the year 508 from the founding of the city <note>146 BCE</note> and was consumed by fire, it happened by chance that gold, silver, and bronze melted and mixed together. ### 62. Boundary Zone. <term>Etter</term> / <term>Pomœritium</term>

This is nearly the same as a *pomoerium* <note>The sacred or administrative boundary of a city, traditionally the space left clear on either side of a city wall</note>. The term is used in Swabia to denote a specific space that defines the extent of a village and the limits of the enclosed estates. It stands in contrast to the "woods and fields." Weller, in *Augustan Affairs*, book 4, folio 50, defines *pomoerium* as a space of a fixed measure before the city walls, and sometimes even within the walls.

-> ADDITION. <-

The limits of the <term>Etter</term> <note>A legal term in Southern Germany for a village's jurisdictional fence or boundary</note>. *Etter* denotes that which is within the district. Linden’s *Acts*, folio 96: "in the city, and inside the *Etter*." Folio 98: "the word *Etter* designates a territory." Folio 103.

The little word *Etter* is repeated for the third time in the settlement between Neuburg and Nuremberg on October 31, 1664, there: "from their boundaries, out of their district" <note>original: "Auß ihren Ettern ausser ihrem Geetter"</note>.

High jurisdiction, the right of the ban, and the boundaries <note>original: "Zwingen, bannen, und derselben Etter"</note> of the same: likewise the ban and high jurisdiction, and their boundaries. Limnäus, in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 49, number 2, states it is the same as the fields or plot <note>original: "Flur"</note>. Dr. Hülß in the case of Sippel of Bordorff versus Bayistorff, number 5. Besold, *Consultation 20*. At Hartenstein, a Noble Council of the Palatinate allowed 200 paces—a small distance around the castle starting from the outer walls—to be measured and marked with stones, with the condition that if the boundaries of the garden were not fully included in that area, they should also be incorporated into it. Nuremberg versus Bavaria, *on the point of Restitution*, folio 73.

### 63. Archduke. <term>Archidux</term>

Among the Estates and Princes of the Empire, the Archdukes of Austria shine most brightly. They are called Archdukes for this reason and possess greater privileges than the other Princes of the Empire, which are partly enumerated in Gylman, *Decision 54, number 59, book 2*. Specifically, they are free from all Imperial taxes in perpetuity. Likewise, they owe no service to the Emperor unless they choose to maintain 12 men at the Emperor's expense in Hungary for one month. They are not compelled to appear at the Imperial Diets <note>original: "Comitiis"; the general assembly of the Imperial Estates</note> unless they do so voluntarily: whatever they do or establish in their own lands, the Emperor shall not hinder. Likewise, they may alienate <note>To transfer ownership or sell</note> all their provinces to whomever they wish without the objection of the Empire. Joseph Nolden, *On the Nobility*, chapter 8, number 138 and following. They may also institute new tolls. Beyond this, they shall have all the privileges of other princes; add Münster, *Cosmography*, book 3, chapter 399. There are also Grand Dukes, such as the Grand Duke of Moscow and of Lithuania, but such are not found in Germany; therefore, Marinus Freccia (book 2, *On Fiefs*) and Nicolaus Mozz. (*Treatise on Fiefs*) are in error 

<column-break/>

when they believe that the first-born sons of German Dukes are called Grand Dukes. Nolden, cited above, number 142; see also König, *Politics*, part 1, chapter 36, number 14, etc.

The origin of the Archducal dignity is attributed to Rudolph I of Habsburg. When Austria was left without a legitimate heir and fell open to the Empire, he conferred it upon his son Albert under the title of an Archduchate. Theodor Reink, book 1, *On Secular and Ecclesiastical Government*, class 4, chapter 10, number 4. However, this is not without controversy among historians. Cuspinianus, in his *Life of Emperor Frederick II* and in *Austria*, page 32, writes that the Archducal dignity flourished long ago, before it came to the Habsburg family. He claims it was by the favor of Emperor Frederick II when, having defeated Frederick of Austria in war, he received him back into favor and close friendship, and added to his insignia a golden cross, such as the Emperors wear in their crowns. This happened in the year 1245. Indeed, Arnifaeus, in *On the Right of Majesty*, book 1, chapter 5, at the end, teaches from Münster’s *Geographical Book* that he was even created a King by the said Frederick II. However, because he was summoned several times to the Diet and did not appear, he was stripped of this royal dignity the following year. Natalis Comes, in *History of His Own Time*, book 9, page 199, says that Emperor Frederick III was the first granter of this title—and not without reason. For Emperor Frederick used the title of Duke of Austria, while his son Maximilian used the title of Archduke. This is found in the *Reformation of Emperor Frederick III*, established at Frankfurt am Main in the year 1442, in the beginning, and in the *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court at Worms*, sanctioned in 1495. It is certainly established that the title of Archduke (though not of Austria, but of Lorraine) was first claimed for himself by Bruno, brother of Emperor Otto the Great and Archbishop of Mainz. In the year 953, when he had received the Duchy of Lorraine from his brother the Emperor after Duke Conrad was deposed for rebellion, he deemed it unworthy that, since he was an Archbishop, he should not also be called an Archduke. Mr. Bitschius, in *Annotations on Natalis Comes*, page 200, letter q. And those cited by Paulus Aemilius of Verona, book 3, *On the Deeds of the Franks*; Spangenberg, in *Mirror of Nobility*, part 1, book 10, chapter 4; and in the annotations on Lazius's *Description of Vienna*, folio 139 and following.

Today, this title of dignity is used only in Germany and only by the Most Serene Austrian Family. See my work *On the Subordinate State of the Republic*, folio 97.

-> ADDITION. <-

The Archdukes of Austria are distinguished by royal dignity. Klock, volume 2, consultation 83, number 29. Among the secular princes, the Archdukes—and specifically the Austrian ones—hold the highest dignity in the Holy Roman Empire next to the Electors. Thomas de Haselbach wrote an entire treatise on their privileges, which Cuspinianus cites in his *Life of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa*.

Regarding Archdukes, one may consult, if it pleases, Schönborn in *Politics*, page 566 and following; and Knipsch, *On Entails*, chapter 1, number 112. The Archdukes of Austria...

### 64. Something for something. <term>Aliquid</term>.

The word "something" <note>original: "aliquid vel aliqua"</note> is verified in any thing, even the smallest. Corneus, counsel 158, column 6, book 2. Menochius, counsel 291, number 50, book 3. See Bolognetus on Law 3, number 12, *on requesting a certain thing*. So too the phrase "in some way," when conceived universally and negatively, is verified even in the smallest degree. See the law "if a slave," section "The Praetor says," and Bartolus there, in the Digest *on acquiring inheritance*. Cravetta, counsel 294, number 4. Menochius, counsel 4, number 18, book 1; counsel 273, number 26, book 2; counsel 275, number 15; also counsel 291, number 48 and following.

The Germans say: <term>Ichtwas</term> <note>An archaic German term for "something," similar to "etwas"</note>. The word "some" <note>original: "Aliqua"</note> encompasses everything, as it is a universal term. Marius Antoninus, book 2, resolution 5, number 2. The word "some" effects no reservation <note>In a legal sense, it does not exclude any specific part</note>, Law 2, Resolution 56, number 17.

### 65. Excommunication. <term>Excommunicatio</term>.

Cardinal Baronius, *Annals* at the Year of Christ 57, number 11 and following; and Hakelman, *Canonical Disputations*, 11. Also Villagut’s treatise *On Ecclesiastical Goods and the Interdict*, Book VII of the Decretals, folio 232. Francesco de Platea, volume 14, folio 347, and in the treatise *On Restitution*.

Whether the excommunicated are to be compared to the banished. ->ADDITION.<-

Hardly any will is made according to our customs in which some executors are not appointed—at least two, sometimes even one—to whom the care is entrusted by the testator to ensure that everything they have disposed is fulfilled. ### 67. Exempt Monasteries. <term>Monasteria exemta</term>.

Exempt monasteries are those which are not subject to the local Ordinary or Bishop, but are directly subordinate to the Roman Pontiff. The Roman Emperor, as a Protector <note>original: "Vogt"; a secular legal guardian or advocate</note> of the Roman Church (to which he swears an oath, see *The Composition of Peace*, Dillingen, folio 57), is accustomed to defend them in a singular manner. Thus, Orders that have Generals are almost always exempt. Others who lack Generals are subject to the Bishop or Diocesan authority.
Regarding such exemption—how far it is valid and when it ceases—Erasmus Chokier wrote a singular treatise, *On the Jurisdiction of the Ordinary over Exempt Persons*. However, this power of the exempt was variously restricted in the Council of Trent. See Christinaeus, *Belgic Decisions*, 344, volume 1. But in the year of Christ 1624, a petition was sent to Pope Urban VIII on behalf of the whole Religious State and printed at Ronciglione: where it is argued at length that exempt religious persons should not be subjected to local Ordinaries.
Furthermore, a person exempt by reason of a certain thing or place is not considered exempt by reason of another place or thing. And a monastery that is exempt in its head and as a whole is bound to obey the Bishop in its non-exempt members, according to the express text.

### 71. To become iron <term>Eisern werden; a legal term for a debt moratorium</term>, see above, number 36.

### 72. Et cetera <note>And the rest.</note>.

Whether the diction "&c." covers a matter of special mention or includes a derogatory clause, see Mantica, *On the Conjectures of Ultimate Wills*, book 12, title 8, number 18. What the words "and others" <note>original: "und andern"</note> signify, see Rudinger, century 5, observation 21. And "et cetera" in the same place.

"Et cetera" argues for things similar to those enumerated. Reinkhingk, book 4, 15, 59; they are "amplificative" <note>Words that extend the meaning to include more items.</note>. Ibid. 60. We use the un-German "&c." for "et cetera." It has a threefold use: 1. When I read something and do not finish it, it is the same as "so forth" <note>original: "s. f. a."</note>. 2. When I add it after the title of a person of rank, meaning "and more" <note>original: "u. e. m."</note>. 3. When I cannot name various different things and say "and the like" <note>original: "u. d. g."</note>. Lord Harsdörffer in the 5th part of the *Conversations*, CCXIII, 66, 67, 68. In the Swedish War against Casimir, King of Poland, it was alleged by the Swedish side as a breach of peace, among other things, that contrary to the express pacts of the truce, the word "&c." had been omitted in the royal titles of both parties. Concerning the "Et-ceterated" speech, see my work *On the Style of the Court*, thesis 37. Johann Andreas in the additions to the *Speculum* on instruments; also the section "it is to be seen" <note>original: "§. videndum"</note> and the note that the Notary and Bartolus, counsel 163, page 344.

### 73. Ass. <term>Asinus</term>.

"An ass has no taste for logical modalities" <note>original: "De modalibus non gustavit asinus"; a proverb meaning a fool cannot appreciate nuances of logic.</note>. at the top among the people. Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim, in *On the Vanity of the Sciences*, chapter 102, makes more boast of no animal than of the ass. By this act, they noted the present state of France, because the foreign Guise family treated the sickly boy-king Francis II no differently than those "Ethiopians" treated their mill-ass.

It is well known from Cornelius Agrippa's *Encomium of the Ass* that the ass was a listener to wisdom, but it is nowhere read that he was a teacher. Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 158. Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 4, number 16. Whether an ox and an ass reclined at the manger of Christ, see the late Lord Dilherr, volume 1, disputation 443, 444.

### 83. To catch the fish <term>Der Fisch entpeißen; likely an archaic phrase regarding fishing rights or the loss of a catch</term>.

Acts of the Teutonic Knights in the *Register of Documents*, folio 137. The goods that grew there, they never **seized** <note>original: "entpeißen"</note>, folio 138.

### 84. Contribution of Assets <term>Einwerffen; the legal process of "Collatio bonorum," where heirs return gifts received during the parent's lifetime to the common estate to ensure equal distribution</term>. Real Burden.

When the contribution of assets does not take place, see Klock, volume 3, counsel 104, number 158. The

<column-break/>

matter of contribution is considered odious and unfavorable <note>Legal "odiousness" means the rule is interpreted strictly because it limits someone's rights</note>. The same, numbers 164, 165, and 166. Contributions are made primarily for the sake of maintaining equality. Compare counsel 104, numbers 172 and 473. Only that which someone has received from the person whose succession is being discussed is brought into the contribution. The same, number 170. This is the greatest common maxim in the matter of contribution, number 171. Those who hold a singular title <note>A specific legal grant rather than a general inheritance</note> do not contribute. The same, number 169. Regarding **Contribution**, one should see Vitalis Nemausensis and Johannes Saporta in their specific treatise.

### 85. To Clarify <term>Erklären; a formal legal declaration</term>. Declaratio.

A declaration can always be made, Gerardus, *Singular Matters*, 27. Since it is virtually contained in the thing declared, Vultejus, *Marburg Counsels*, 29, number 12, volume 2. Consequently, it is seen as following the act itself. Lancellotus, *On Attempted Crimes*, part 2, chapter 4, limitation 21, number 8. However, he who admits through a declaration something that was not in the original disposition does not so much "declare" it as "grant" it anew. Rosenthal, *On Feuds*, chapter 7, conclusion 46, number 17, gloss letter S.

### 86. Embarus <note>A figure from Greek mythology associated with a proverb about trickery or sacrifice</note>.

"You are an Embarus," from where does this proverb come? Doctor Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, page 22. Erasmus in his *Adages*. Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in *System of Universal Law*, book 31, chapter 23, number 4. Embarus sacrificed his daughter to Diana. The ancient Pagans believed that hunger was sent by the wrath of a deity due to some grave sin or many sins. For this reason, they often instituted sacred rites to appease the deity. For instance, when the Athenians killed a bear in the temple of Diana of Munychia on the island of Piraeus, they say a famine followed. An oracle was issued saying it would cease if someone sacrificed his daughter to Diana. Embarus did this, having bargained for the perpetual succession of his family as the reward for that sacrifice, as Suidas writes under the entry "I am an Embarus" <note>original Greek: ἔμβαρός εἰμι</note>. And Hesiod in *Works and Days*:

> Neither does famine ever attend men of straight justice,
> Nor disaster; but they share the fruits of their labors in feasts,
> For them the earth bears much sustenance.
<note>original Greek: ἐδὲ ποτ’ ἰθυδίκαισι μετ’ ἀνδράσι λιμὸς ὁπηδεῖ, / ἐδ’ ἄτη, θαλίῃς δὲ μελήλοτα ἔργα νέμονται, / τοῖσε φέρῃ μὴ γαῖα πολὺν βίον.</note>

->that is:<-

> Nor does famine ever dwell among just men,
> Nor harm: for they enjoy their works in feasts,
> For these the earth brings forth much life.

### 87. Family Redemption <term>Erblösung; the right of a family member to buy back ancestral property sold to a stranger</term>. Lineal Retract <note>original: "Retractus gentilitius"</note>.

Lineal Retract. Alphin, *On the Law of Retracts*, conclusion 51.

### 88. Extensions <note>Legal broadenings of a statute's application</note>.

On Extensions, see Petrus Andreae Gammarus of Casale (Bologna), volume 18, folio 247.

### 89. Edged Weapon <term>Eggewapen; likely referring to "Eckewaffen," a blade or drawn weapon used in a crime</term>.

Supplement to Wehner, page 34, under the word "violent act" <note>original: "handhafftige That," meaning a crime where the perpetrator is caught in the act</note>.

<header>Letter F.</header>

## 1. Fabric. Holy. Church Fabric <term>Fabrica Templi; the funds and assets set aside for the maintenance and repair of a church building</term>.

**R**egarding the Church Fabric <term>Kirchen-Fabric</term>, see the *Synodal Statutes of Constance, folio 136.* These are generally laypersons who manage the revenues destined for the foundation <term>Gestift; an endowment or ecclesiastical trust</term>, but under the inspection of the Parish Priest, who is not subject to the secular authority. In these places, it is called the Holy One <term>der Heilig</term>, because every church is consecrated in honor of some Saint. Thus, they are called "Saints' Goods" <term>Heiligen Güter</term>, which are destined for the preservation of the church, not only for the building itself but also for its decoration, etc. <note>In many German-speaking regions, the term "Der Heilig" referred to the legal entity of the local parish church, which could own property independently of the central church hierarchy.</note>

## 2. Factor. Manager <term>Institor; a person appointed to manage a business, shop, or trade on behalf of an owner</term>.

**A** manager is one who is placed in charge of a shop or any other profit-seeking business, with a general mandate under a "free power" clause <note>original: "Clausula cum libera"; a legal provision granting full discretionary power to act</note>, for buying and selling. Because he stands over the business being conducted <note>original: "negotio gerendo instat"</note>, he is called a Manager [*Institor*], and likewise a General Procurator; among us, he is commonly called a Factor <term>Factor; an agent or representative</term>, and also a Name-bearer <term>Namenträger</term> or Bookkeeper <term>Buchhalter</term>. *Book 3, Book 18 of the Digest regarding the Institorian Action.* See *Martinius’s Philological Lexicon under "Institor."*

Therefore, just as such a manager acquires property for his Master by contracting with others through the power of his mandate; so too it seemed equitable to the Praetor <note>The Praetor was a Roman judicial official whose edicts formed the basis of many commercial laws</note> that, just as we feel the benefits from the acts of managers, we should also be bound by their contracts and be able to be sued. See this discussed at length by *Johann Hermann Stam in his very elegant treatise on personal servitude, book 2, chapter 19, following sections; Costa on subsidiary remedies, remedy 91; and Wilhelm Anton in the Corollaries, folio 15; likewise Röner’s practical observations, chapter 31.*

->ADDITION.<-

Even if Factors write themselves down as debtors in a thousand letters, they cannot be sued on that basis <note>Because they act only as agents for their principal, the legal liability typically rests with the employer, not the employee</note>. *Carpzov, decision 10, number 15.*
Whether the appointment of a manager is ended by the death of the one who appointed him, and whether managers are held liable after their appointment for contracts celebrated during the time of their appointment. *Ludwell in the Disputations on the Institutes, page 344, in the Notes to Wesenbeck’s Manuscripts on the title of the Institorian Action.* Regarding the obligation of Factors or Managers, and whether and to what extent they are held liable in their own person and property for contracts celebrated in the name of their Masters, this was treated specifically by *M. Johann Christoph Marci in his Inaugural Address held at Strasbourg in 1644.*
In the years 1659 and 1661, under Doctor Huldericus Eyben at Giessen in Hesse, two legal dissertations were held "On Factors or Managers" <term>von Factorn und Buchhaltern</term>. A "Complementarius" is called a sub-administrator <term>Unterverwalter</term>.

## 3. Banner Fiefs <term>Fahnenlehen</term>. Royal Fiefs <term>Feuda regalia</term>.

**R**oyal Fiefs <term>Feuda regalia; the highest class of fiefs in the Holy Roman Empire, held directly from the Emperor</term> are those granted by the authority of the supreme Prince, with Royal dignity: such as the fief of a Duchy, Margraviate, County, and those of similar or greater

<column-break/>

dignity. These are commonly called "Royal" [*Königische*], and now Banner Fiefs [*Fahnenlehen*], because the Imperial Majesty grants such fiefs to secular princes with banners <note>The banner symbolized the right to lead an army in the Emperor's name</note>, but to ecclesiastical princes with a scepter. *Schneidewin in the Epitome of Fiefs, part 1, number 3; Duarenus on fiefs, chapter 4, number 7; Jacobus de Saint George in his Investitures; Rudinger, 2nd feudal controversy, chapter 58, number 1; Schrader on fiefs, part 2, chapter 3; Vultejus on fiefs, book 2, chapter 8; Pruckmann, counsel 2, book 2.* Examples of this exist in *Otto of Freising, book 2, chapter 5, section 32; Crusius’s Swabian Annals, book 9, part 3, chapter 6,* etc. However, *Knichen* writes that this solemnity of investing with banners fell into disuse a few years ago. The rite by which the Most Serene Elector of Bavaria was invested with the Electorate of the Palatinate is contained in the *Acts of Lundorpius.*

And when a dispute arises concerning such a Royal fief, only the Emperor defines the controversy—that is, he hears that case. However, when the Imperial Chamber <note>The "Reichskammergericht," the highest judicial body of the Empire</note> anticipates the Emperor, then it also takes cognizance of Imperial Fiefs, even if such a fief were a County or Duchy, as *Richwin* hands down. But I will speak of this elsewhere, God willing, under the word "Rights of Princes" <term>Fürstenrecht</term>.

Although the Count Palatine may invest someone with a fief of the Empire while the Empire is vacant <note>The Count Palatine of the Rhine served as Imperial Vicar or regent during an interregnum</note>, the investiture of the Banner Fiefs of the Princes is reserved for the new Emperor and King of the Romans, according to the *Golden Bull, title "On the rights of the Count Palatine,"* where you may see *Buxtorff* and others. Thus Rudolph I, Count of Habsburg, when Austria was deprived of a legitimate heir in his time, reclaimed it for the Empire and granted it to his son Albert. Thence comes the origin of the Dukes of Austria. The Emperor Sigismund also, when the family of the "Bears" <note>The House of Ascania</note> became extinct in Albert, gave the Electorate of Saxony, which had devolved to the Empire, as a fief to Frederick I, Margrave of Meissen. From him, the current Electors of Saxony still descend. *Lord Bocer on Regalia, chapter 2, number 61.*

->ADDITION.<-

Banner Fiefs are commonly so called from the fact that vassals are invested with banners. However, this method of investiture has departed from the Emperor’s Court, and in place of a banner, the Emperor offers a sword—a blade removed from its scabbard—whose hilt the vassal grasps, kissing the tip of its pommel. *Nicolaus Myler on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 19, page 654; Finckelthaus in Illustrious Feudal Controversies, Disputation 2, Controversy 8.*

Only the Emperor confers the greater fiefs, the Banner Fiefs. *Knichen on the Saxon Right of Non-Appeal; Gail, book 1, observation 1; Cluten’s Sylloge, conclusion 20.*

**In Strasbourg, during processions, only the bakers carry a banner; no other craft <note>Handwerck; referring to the city guilds</note> does so.**

The Romans, from the beginning, used bundles of hay tied to poles as banners; thereafter they turned to other signs, namely Wolves, Minotaurs, horses, boars, dragons, etc., which preceded individual ranks, and eventually they began to use the sign of the Eagle.
