### 4. Movable goods and property, see below under the word "immovable property."

->Movable goods.<-
<note>original: "Bona mobilia"</note>

Goods that are fit to be moved and transferred from place to place are called movables, commonly **movable property and goods**, or in a single word, **chattels** <note>original: "Fahrniß"</note>; conversely, immovables are those which by their own nature cannot be moved. *Law 'moventium', Digest on the Significance of Words.* Panormitanus *on the chapter 'nulli', number 9, regarding Church property not to be alienated.* And therefore, under our ownership, there are two principal types of goods: one of movables and the other of immovables. Among movables, I primarily include fruits separated from the soil, according to the *final law of the Digest on requiring defendants*, and Natta says in *Counsel 117, at the end* that this is the proper use of the term, because they can be moved from one place to another. Decianus, *Counsels 44 & 86, book 4.* Mantica, *On Conjectures of Last Wills, book 9, title 3, number 6.* From this, Caspar Antonio Tesauro, in *Forensic Questions, book 1, question 26*, accuses Decius (in *Counsel 482*) and Castrensis (in *Counsel 132, book 1*) of error. They wished to include among movables both hanging fruits <note>standing crops</note> and those separated from the soil which have not yet been counted in the head of the household's granary, led by a certain subtlety regarding the "intended purpose" they imagine the owner holds, rather than the reality of the thing: since hanging fruits are said to be part of the soil. *Law 'fructus', where the Doctors of Law comment, Digest on the recovery of property.* And truly, as to whether the term "movables" in a legacy includes fruits found separated from the soil: see Tesauro *in the stated question, throughout* and Cravetta, *Counsel 329.*

<column-break/>

However, it is doubted whether a ship should be numbered among movable or immovable things. That it is a movable thing is established by the fact that the interdict <note>A legal remedy or injunction</note> *unde vi* <note>"from where by force"; used to restore possession of property taken by force</note> does not pertain to movable things. *Law 1, section 'illud utique' 6, Digest on force and armed force.* But if someone is cast out of a ship by force, there will be no place for this interdict. *Law 1, section 7, same title.*

By the same reasoning, the interdict regarding "force or stealth" <note>original: "vi aut clam"</note> pertains only to those works that are done on the soil. *Law 1, section 'hoc interdictum' 4, Digest on what is done by force or stealth. Law 'if another has done it', 7, section 'we have noted', 5, same title.*

Whatever is done on a ship, or in any other thing—even a very large one, provided it is movable—is not contained in this edict. *Law 'he acts by force' 20, section 'what is on a ship' 4, same title.* And there is no other reason why a ship cannot be given as a fief than that it is a movable thing. *Law 1, sections 6 and 7, Digest on force and armed force.*

Among movable goods are also included granaries that are not fixed to the soil, as Javolenus defines in *Law 'granaries', Digest on actions of purchase.*

Likewise wine vessels, through *Law 'the estate', section 'the jars', Digest on actions of purchase; Law 3, section 'wine', Digest on legacies of wine, wheat, and oil; Law 'even if of ownership', Digest on usufruct.*

No one doubts that money is a movable thing, and therefore the Interpreters commonly teach that it is included under the term "movables" or "moving things." *On the Law 'moventium', 93, Digest on the Significance of Words.* But see Tesauro, *Decision 160*, where he asks whether money is included under the term "movables" such that it is comprehended in a general legacy of movables.

Wild animals, fish, and birds, if they are kept in preserves (**in the ponds**), tanks, or hives for the sake of custody, are then counted among movables. If, however, they are kept so that they may multiply and grow and bring forth fruit <note>profit or offspring</note>, they are considered part of the estate and even pass to the buyer. Antonius Monterus, *Decision 26*, where he also discusses hives.

Joseph Ludovicus has more on movable and immovable things in *Conclusion 48, throughout*; and Mr. Bachov, *On Pledges, book 1, chapter 6, number 3.* Forster, *On Ownership, chapter 7, number 32, etc.*

What should be said regarding Rights and Actions <note>Legal claims or lawsuits</note>? Namely, whether they should be numbered among movables or immovables? See Stephanus Durantus, *Question 22.* Regarding annual rents, the names of debtors <note>accounts receivable</note>, merchandise in shops, war engines, etc. Paul Christinaeus, *Decisions of Belgium, volume 1, decision 213 and decision 112.* *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 2, counsel 11, question 2.* Joseph Sesse, *Decisions of Aragon, 122 and 124.* Beati in *Decisions, volume 3, on Testaments, part 2, folio 414.* Linglois in *50 Decisions, folio 173.*

And this question often arises when movable things are bequeathed to someone: or where, by statute, in **virtue of the Right of Devolution**, <note>original: "Krafft deß Verfangenſchaffts-Rechtens"; a legal custom in parts of the Holy Roman Empire (like Speyer) where property was "entangled" or restricted in favor of a surviving spouse or heirs</note> movables cede to the surviving spouse, which is customary in Speyer and many Imperial Cities. But in that case, actions—especially those pertaining to an immovable thing—as well as annual rents, are counted among immovables: see Tuschus, *letter A, conclusion 342.* And also elsewhere for

**Movable property** <term>Fahrniß</term> <note>original: "Fahrniß"; in early modern law, this refers to personal property that can be moved, as opposed to "immovables" like land or buildings</note> is regarded only as things that are ready for transport, such as household furniture and the like. However, the legal observation is not uniform in all places: thus, items considered movable in one location are sometimes classified as immovable in another.

Regarding the jurisdiction under which immovable things are situated, see especially Schultes, *Practical Questions*, book 1, question 19, throughout.

#### ADDITION.

Movable goods do not constitute something perpetual and durable. Knipschild, *On Entailed Estates* <note>original: "de fideicommiss."</note>, chapter 5, number 2. Movable things destined for the place of immovables are counted as immovables, chapter 5, number 76. Regarding what falls under the name of "movables," see chapter 5, numbers 95 and 100. Money is counted among movables, number 96, unless it is destined for the purchase of immovable property, numbers 72, 97, 99. Movables include gold, silver, precious stones, rings, and jewelry, number 100; as well as plow oxen and horses, number 102.

Are animals contained within the words **movables and household goods** <note>original: "Fahrniß und Hausgeräth"</note>? Klock, volume 3, counsel 125, numbers 2 and 10, and laws 32–35.

### 5. Right of Wreckage. Goods of the shipwrecked.

That the goods of the shipwrecked <note>original: "Bona Naufragorum"</note>, and even the bodies themselves, belonged to the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscei"; the state or royal purse</note> is gathered from the *Chronicle of Albert of Stade*, folio 153 and following.

#### ADDITION.

Do goods lost in the calamity of a shipwreck fall under confiscation? Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 14, numbers 1, 6–17, 28–31, 50. Camman, 8, thesis 32. Friedenreich, *Politics*, 30, folio 25. Guidon, *On Finances*, folio 68. Rosenkrantz, *On Danish Law*, Politics 7.

### 6. Wandering Scholars. Vagabonds.

The wandering scholars <note>original: "die fahrende Schuler"</note> of old were similar to the *Agyrtae* <note>original: "Agyrtis"; in ancient Greece, these were wandering beggar-priests or charlatans</note> whom Plato mentions in the second book of *The Republic*. Saubert, *On Sacrifice*, page 167. Regarding them, Johann Langius writes in his *Medical Symposium*, folio 89: "Indeed, there was once in Greece, and until a few years ago in Germany, a type of men addicted to deceptions and medicine for the sake of profit, whom they called *Agyrtae* and soothsayers. These men wandered from town to town to seek alms at the doors of the wealthy. They claimed to be powerful through divine virtue, incantations, and the mysteries of sacrifices. They asserted that if any crime had been committed by the rich or their ancestors, they could expiate it through the celebration of sacred festivals and the scent of incense; they further claimed they could, at small expense, harm the enemies of the rich—whether guilty or innocent—and take revenge upon them. For they said they held the gods so bound by sorceries, syllogisms, physical bindings of characters, and charms <note>original: "Epodis"</note> that the gods were forced to carry out their commands."

<column-break/>

### 7. Falcons, Falconry. Falcons.

On the use of fowling by means of hooked-claw birds, and how ancient it is, see Lælius Bisciola, *Subsecutive Hours*, book 16, chapter 1, where he also has certain notable remarks on the genus of hawks.

#### ADDITION.

Fowling by means of falcons was an invention of the German Princes, Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 5, number 107. It was also very commonly used by the Kings of the Persians, number 108. The Imperial diadem was offered to Henry I <note>Henry the Fowler, 10th-century King of East Francia</note> while he was fowling, number 106. On the innate hatred between the natures of Falcons and Herons, by which they pursue each other, number 109.

### 8. Counterfeiters. Producers of false money.

If a State of the Empire <note>original: "Status Imperii"; a sovereign territory within the Holy Roman Empire</note> makes false money with the stamp of another, does it commit the crime of high treason <note>original: "Crimen læsæ Majestatis"</note>? I do not believe so. See the Minting Constitutions in the Recesses of the Imperial Diet <note>original: "Reichs-Abschieden"</note>, where it is stated that such persons are merely deprived of their minting right <note>original: "Regali"</note>, and after suspension, if they mint more, they are to be noted under the Imperial Ban.

#### ADDITION.

On secret or illegal minting <note>original: "Hecken müntzen"</note>. On clippers, weighers, extractors, and changers <note>original: "Ripper und Wipper, Auszieher, Auswieger, Aufwechslern"</note> who are equivalent to counterfeiters. Zorer, part 2, question 17, number 1096. Whoever is caught with unclipped money <note>original: "Umbeschröteing"</note>, which is called "Genöste," faces a penalty to the hand with a *Sertine* <note>possibly a specific fine or weight</note>, and to the body with a *Lot* <note>a unit of weight, implying corporal or capital punishment proportional to the theft</note>. Agreement between M. and E.

Falsifying the money of one's own fatherland falls into the crime of high treason, just as he who falsifies the Prince’s money. Gigas, *On the Crime of High Treason*, page 62, number 6. According to the Criminal Ordinance of Charles V <note>The Constitutio Criminalis Carolina of 1532</note>, article 111, money is falsified in three ways: 1. When one fraudulently strikes another's mark upon it. 2. When one adds improper metal to it. 3. If one dangerously removes the proper weight from the money. Hence money is called doubtful, coppered, false, or rejected. In Greek, false coins are called *paratypos* and *paracharagmata*, and those who strike them are called *paracharantai*. These coins are also called *parafeni*, as Lodovico Cælius noted in book 6 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 2. Doctor Bicc has laboriously collected the many ways false money is committed in *Golden Matters*, section 4, thesis 177, letter N.N., where at the end he adds what penalty counterfeiters are afflicted with.

On familiar spirits, see Zeiller’s *Tragic Histories*, folio 46, etc.

#### ADDITION.

Demonic spirits familiar to men and visible. Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in the *Syntagma*.

### 10. Capture and Locking Fees. Expenses on account of incarceration.

A very bad custom prevails almost everywhere that those imprisoned, besides the punishment of the jail itself, are forced to pay money, the **Capture and Locking Fee** <note>original: "Fang- und Schließgeld"; a fee paid by a prisoner to the jailer for the "service" of being arrested and locked up</note>; in certain places, the captives are even required to provide their own food. On account of this, and due to the greed of the guards, innocent people are quite often thrust into prison. Parthenius, *The Litigious*, book 1, chapter 23, number 12.

Regarding the mitigation of the squalor of prisons, I made mention in my treatise *On Punishments and Laws*, page 128. Also, what is the use of a prison, and how many types are there? See Speckhan, part 1, question 19 and following, where he teaches that one type of prison is for penitence, and another for debtors.

Furthermore, by Canon Law, both perpetual and temporary imprisonment is granted for crimes committed by those in the ecclesiastical court, though not for those in the secular court. *Chapter 'Quamvis' 3, on punishments, in the 6th book.* Julius Clarus, *Received Opinions*, final section, question 70, number 4. Ludovicus Romanus, *Singular Opinions*, 711. Since the Church always hopes for the conversion and repentance of delinquents, and does not wish—along with its Prince, God—for the death of a sinner, but rather that he be converted and live <note>referencing Ezekiel 18:23</note>, *Chapter 'Hi qui' 3, question 4*. Since therefore the Church does not inflict the penalty of temporal death, nor brings a judgment of blood <note>original: "judicium sanguinis"; the Church was traditionally forbidden from pronouncing death sentences or participating in executions</note>, *Chapter 'In Archiepiscopatu' on kidnappers; Chapter 'Clericis'; Chapter 'Sententiam'—that Clerics or Monks should not involve themselves in secular business*. Therefore, it punishes a grave crime with life imprisonment, by shutting in the guilty party to perform penance, to be sustained with the bread of sorrow and the water of affliction, so that he may weep for what he has committed, and not commit further things to be wept for: *Chapter 'Novimus' 27, final section, on the meaning of words*. Julius Clarus, said question 70, number 4. Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in the *Syntagma*, book 31, chapter 33, number 24 and following. And certainly there was life imprisonment, of which Seneca makes mention in *Medea*, verse 464:

> -- -- Let him load the hands with chains,
> And overwhelm the one shut in a rock of eternal night.

Furthermore, what the Divine Apostle Paul records in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians—that he was in the depth of the sea by night and day—is understood by the illustrious Baronius in the *Annals*, Year of Christ 58, number 18, to mean the most foul Cyzicene prison: which, because it was very deep and thus pressed downwards, was deservedly called the "Depth of the Sea"; to which, in some part, that most famous prison at Athens was to be compared,

<column-break/>

called the *Barathrum* <note>a deep pit or abyss at Athens into which criminals were thrown</note>; or that at Syracuse named *Latomia* <note>literally "stone-quarries," used as dungeons</note>; or that at Rome called the *Tullianum*; as well as that which is placed by Suidas among the Spartans, called *Ceada*; and another most dark one at Carthage, titled *Ancon*.

### 11. Colors.

What the red, white, and black colors signify, see the annotations of Abermann to Lazius's *Vienna*, page 102 and following.

In Erfurt, certain men are commonly found called **Woad-Gentlemen** <note>original: "Weid-Junckern"; refers to the wealthy merchant class in Erfurt who grew rich from the woad trade</note>, who trade in the herb commonly called **woad** <note>original: "weid"</note> or **red**, with which one dyes. Johannes Baptista Magonus, in *The Right Method of Patronage*, chapter 3, throughout, has collected many things concerning the habit and dress of Advocates, and among other things he also speaks of the color becoming to Advocates; and under numbers 50 and 51, he concludes that the color black is more suitable in clothing, because it is a sign of firmness and perseverance, seeing as it cannot be varied or changed, whereas others can be varied. **Colors are interpreted according to the age of man:** Thus **Silver** marks **Childhood** up to the **7th year.** **Blue** marks **Youth** up to the **15th.** **Gold** marks **Adolescence** up to the **20th.** **Green** marks **Manhood** up to the **30th.** **Red** marks **Mature Age** up to **60.** And **Black** the remaining sad years, until the **End of Life.** Lord Harsdörffer in *Ladies' Conversations*, part 1, conversation 12, number 23. Therefore it has a unique hidden and innate quality in common with poisonous weaknesses, and it draws the decay and harmful humors out of the sick body when it is held near it. The colors of law <note>legal pretexts or "legal fictions" used to justify a position</note> are not always prohibited. Barbosa, book 3, chapter 29, axiom 2, throughout. Steinberg, *On Legal Fiction*, thesis 7, end.

### 12. Ferry Money. Ripaticum.

Thus we call *ripatica* <note>riverbank tolls</note> those taxes which are to be paid for the crossing of riverbanks; this tax is counted among the Regalia <note>royal rights or prerogatives</note>, since it is consistent with natural equity that he who perceives the benefits should also sustain the burdens. And conversely, it is fair that the Prince should apply these taxes toward the restoration and repair of the banks. Otto, *On Public Law*, chapter 11, page 296.

->ADDITION.<-

Whether a winding river may be sought out in order to avoid the payment of *Ripaticum*. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 74, number 7.

### 13. Shrove Tuesday. Bacchanalia.

The author of the Bacchanalia was the one from whom they took their name: Bacchus, previously named Osiris. He was the inventor of the vine and ivy, the first crowned with ivy, the first conqueror, and distinguished with a royal diadem. In his honor, two types of Bacchanalia were customarily celebrated; the first on the 12th

<column-break/>

day of the month of Anthesterion <note>a Greek month</note>, or November, called *Pythoigia* <note>original: "Pythagia"</note>, that is, the opening of the casks; for they would unseal the casks and offer drink to their friends, just as we also do at this time on the day of St. Martin, namely the eleventh of November, differing from the ancients by only one day. The second is around the end of February and the beginning of March, at the end of winter and the beginning of spring, placed primarily in the delight of harmony and ridiculous things. Since Osiris was fond of laughter and was accustomed to being delighted by musicians and dances, he is said for that reason to have had with him a multitude of musicians, and among them nine young maidens, who were accustomed to sing and were instructed by Apollo the Musician in other arts, and were called Muses by the Greeks. Furthermore, he had Satyrs for laughter and the relaxation of the mind, as Diodorus left written in book 1. Even if license gradually grew afterward in the Bacchanalia, and not only buffoons, masked men, actors, dancers, and other persons suited for entertainment were employed, but even certain most shameful things were introduced, as mentioned by Varro in book 16 of *Divine Affairs*, and by St. Augustine in *The City of God*, book 7, and book 18, chapter 13. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 14. These were practiced at the crossroads of Italy and in the town of Lavinium; they are too shameful to be recounted here. However, mystical writers seem to have understood something far different by Bacchus and the Bacchanalia than what is found in common custom. Indeed, that most serious of all authors, Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, regarding the four divine furies, attributes one to Bacchus, which turns the human soul toward the knowledge of mysteries and the worship of God, etc. See Antonio Riccoboni, *On the Gymnasium of Padua*, book 1, chapter 13, folio 136 and following, where he treats at length of "Spiritual Bacchanalia."

->ADDITION.<-

Canon Law has pursued masks <note>original: "Larvas"</note> with such hatred that it called them "monsters of masks" in the chapter *cum decorem*, *On the life and honor of clerics*. Against wicked masked men, there exists a Venetian law from the year 1549, July 18, from the Council of Ten, which imparts to anyone the faculty of killing them with impunity, and commands the village communities to ring their bells against them, to capture and kill them; and it grants their weapons, horses, coins, and whatever is found in their possession to the killers. Losaeus, *On the Law of Universities*, page 79, number 53. Christopher Neander, Philosopher and Jurist, described the history of the Bacchanalia.
Martin Zeiller writes about Shrove Tuesday <note>original: "Fastnacht"</note>, century 1, epistle 16, page 80. The same in century 4, epistle 1, page 5, also pages 234 and 363. Jacob Herrenschmid in his dissertation on the name, origin, and progress of the Bacchanalia. Virdungus in the program added to his orations published together, page 101 and following. Let this word be said against those gravediggers of piety who, enslaved to the annual rites of Bacchus, behave in a detestable man-

## 14. Fasting. <term>Jejunium</term> <note>The Latin term for a religious fast or abstinence from food.</note>

Concerning the various observations of Lent <note>original: "Quadragesimæ" — the 40-day period before Easter</note>, see Filesacus in his various short works, and as to why this number forty is sacred, see Barth on Gallus, folio 82. Regarding long fasting, Paolo Zacchia has many notable things in his *Medico-Legal Questions*, book 4, title 1, throughout the question. Why, however, are fish allowed on Fridays and fast days? This reason is given: that water does not nourish, as Galen wrote in his book *On Water*, following the opinion of Hippocrates, Chrysippus, and Erasistratus. Aristotle in book 5 also believed that fish do not nourish but are immediately resolved back into water. Kornman, in *The Temple of Nature*, counsel 19, where in the preceding consideration he also says that some hold that fish were not destroyed in the Deluge <note>the Great Flood of Noah</note> but were preserved in their own place; thus they were not subject to the curse, just as the water they inhabited was not, etc.

Whether the use of meat existed before the Deluge? Molina, *Introduction to Justice and Law*, treatise 3, disputation 4.

### ADDITION.

On the mountain called Cybele near Naples, there is a monastery upon which—within half a mile's distance—one can neither eat nor bring meat, eggs, or milk-dishes, because worms and maggots grow in them from that hour, whether they be boiled, smoked, or salted.

We read of Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a famous 14th-century legal scholar</note>, that greatest predecessor of the Law, that he ate and drank according to weight and measure so that he might foster the sharpness of his intellect, in order that his genius might always be equally disposed and never altered. The Distinguished Dilherr, volume 1, *Academic Disputations*, page 420. Forster, *On the History of Civil Law*, book 3, chapter 27, number 11. See more extensively Johann Auman, *On the Limit of Human Life*,

<column-break/>

where he writes of Galen, that although he suffered four times from tertian fever and once from a burning fever, he nevertheless lived 140 years (though others prefer 170), and he never ate or drank to satiety, nor did he ever taste anything raw. In Canon Law <note>the law of the Church</note>, regarding the observation of the fast, it is not cared whether one eats little or nothing; hence Gregory, during the fast, granted those fasting permission to eat only "little fish" <note>original: "pisciculis"</note>, not large fish. Chapter *denique*, distinction 4. Sprenger, *On the Modicum*, page 166. How one should observe the weight in food and drink. Zeiller, century 4, question 55, page 287 and following. Regarding moderation/temperance, one should read the beautiful little book by Hygiophilus. Distinguished Harsdörffer, in the *German Secretary*, part 3, title 13. Fasts were instituted in honor of Jupiter according to Horace, *Satires* 2, satire 3; or in honor of Ceres, about which Clement of Alexandria writes in Reinefius, *Various Readings*, book 1, chapter 23; or in honor of the memory of the Muses and Nymphs, about which Josephus Laurentius writes in *Polymathia*, book 2, chapter 26. Rupertus, dissertation 2, book 1, chapter 1. Valerius Maximus. Saint Radbod, Bishop of Utrecht, was so exhausted by fasting that he barely hung to his bones. Always abstaining from meat and wine, he drank water from onyx and gold to hide his holiness. Drexelius, in the *Gold Mine*, page 331. A certain very grave man pronounced differently regarding the Law of Lent than what is decreed by Justinian's Law, not to mention Canon Law: It has never been considered wrong <note>original: "Es sey weder in Geistl. noch Weltlichen Rechten..."</note> in either spiritual or secular laws, nor by their legal scholars, to carry out criminal punishments against evildoers during Lent. This, however, seems less consistent with Law 6 of the Code *On Holidays*. Thus, even things decided by certain law are sometimes called into doubt. Distinguished Doctor Tabor, *On the Obligation of Succession in Office*, page 257, number 8. See also his *Benedictus*, 2. In this time of Lent, no criminal execution or bodily affliction whatsoever ought to take place. Agostino Barbosa on this Law 6. Scaccia, book 2, chapter 6, number 4, *On Judgments*. Nicolaus à Salis on Law 6; since the execution of a blood-sentence is a horrendous and miserable spectacle, from which the soul shrinks—especially at this holy time of repentance and mourning, which was destined by the Church for the holy penitential and passion sermons of our Lord. Sigismund Scaccia, *On Judgments*, book 2, chapter 6, numbers 17 and 18. Carpzov, *Consistorial Jurisprudence*, book 2, theorem 8, definition 151. Nicolaus Mylius, *Repertory*, under the word "holiday days," even those of Easter. Most extensively, Georg von Daffel, my friend, in his very long inaugural theses *On the Law of the Lenten Season*, which it will not be regrettable to have seen. Bishop Albrecht of Strasbourg devised the "Butter-Penny" <note>original: "Butterpfenning" — a tax paid for a dispensation to eat butter during fast days</note> and, for a certain tax during Lent, filled the butter-boxes from such an extorted contribution. The Blessed Doctor Dannhauer in the *Evangelical Memorial*, pages 373 and 381. Eating butter and eggs at this time was granted by indulgence. Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 16, number 47. Concerning Lenten foods, see Mr. Beer in his *Refutation of Ebermann*, page 416.

### 15. Fist Law. <term>Jus manuarium</term> <note>Literally "law of the hand," referring to the practice of settling disputes through private force rather than the courts.</note>

Military law, **the Knightly- or Fist-law**, as some call it, which formerly prevailed in the cases of those contending, has long since been removed, abrogated, and abolished by both Imperial Constitutions and the Statutes of the States of the Empire. Therefore, today no one, under any pretext, can excuse or free themselves from ordinary punishment when they kill a man they have provoked or who has provoked them. Eberh. Speckhan. century 3. question 6. class 2. number 3. See above under *Ausfordern* <note>original: "Ausfordern" — the act of challenging someone to a duel.</note>

->ADDITION.<-

### 16. Bailiff of the Church. <term>Advocatus Ecclesiae</term> <note>A lay official appointed to represent a church or monastery in secular legal matters and to provide military protection.</note>

### 18. Feud. <term>Diffidatio</term> <note>The formal declaration of the end of a peace or friendship, preceding a private war or feud.</note>

I discuss this in *The Art of War* page 80.

Enlarged Practical Treasury

...if his animal kills a man, such as a nobleman, the Master shall pay the composition <note>original: "compositionem"; a legal payment made to settle a grievance</note>, or bear the Feud <note>original: "Faidam"</note>. *Laws of the Lombards, title 5, § 3.* Let him consider it his own fault who presumed to enter upon another's wife, and let no composition be paid to him, nor let a Feud be required.

*Brissonius* shows that a Feud <note>original: "Faidam"</note> is also called "Faida," and is the same as war <note>original: "guerra"</note>.

*Laws of the Lombards, title 30.* That the feud be set aside after the compensation is received. *B. Rhenanus, German Affairs, book 2.* The Franks called "Faida" an open enmity by which one person or several declare war; it was once most notably known among the Germans.

*Faidofus* or *Feidofus*: one who carries out a feud, or to whom enmities have been declared, as in the *Laws of the Frisians*: A man involved in a feud <note>original: "homo faidofus"</note> shall have peace in the Church, in his home, and while going to the Church.

Articles of the assembly between Emperor Lothar, Louis of Germany, and Charles the Bald, Kings of France, in *Miræus, Donation Code, chapter 15*: That the robberies and plunderings, which have been carried out until now as if by legal right, shall cease entirely, and no one should trust that they can presume to commit them with impunity hereafter. There were also frequent declarations of defiance <note>original: "diffidationes"; formal breaks of peace</note> in Germany later, and they were even granted by agreement. *Short Proof in the matter of Sayn against Trier, in document folio 24*, where the following is held:

> And if we should be in breach of this, then Lord Valentine or his heirs may attack the County of Sayn with plundering and fire, until this letter and all points in this letter are fully upheld, without any contradiction from Us or Our Heirs.

And these were valid until the public and perpetual peace was established. Today, therefore, the crime of defiance, because it is against the Public Peace, causes someone by that very fact to fall under the Imperial Ban <note>original: "bannum Imperiale"</note>, which deprives one of their property; as is the text in the *Constitutions of Charles V on the Land-Peace, chapter 3: On the Punishment of Peace-Breakers*, *Modest. Pistor. book 1, question 13, number 3.*

->ADDITIO.<-

Letters of defiance, i.e., those by which war is declared on a lord. *Rittersh. partit. feud. p. 568.* **Letters of Hostility and Renunciation.** *Barschamp. rad. claus. p. 326.* Feud <note>original: "Fehde"</note> signifies hostility or war. *Bodin. book 1 on the Republic, chapter 10. pr. Bocer. cliss. 4. disp. 11. th. 14. fol. 7.* **Feud and Ill-will**, *Limn. J. P. l. 6. cap. 5. p. 125. l. 9. cap. 4. num. 28.* **Without fair and reasonable Feud.** *Limn. lib. 6. cap. 5. p. 123.* Private capital defiances, **Feudings** <note>original: "Befehdungen"</note>. *Heigius part. 2. q. 32. n. 8.*

The word *Fehde* <note>Feud</note> is used by Blessed Luther in the hymn: *To God alone on high be glory*, when he finishes the first stanza with these words: **All feuding has now an end.** The Saxons, whose dialect is the most ancient, say *Feide*, which seems to coincide with the Hebrew *phid* <note>Hebrew: פיד; meaning ruin or destruction</note>, that is, ruin, destruction, whence also the Greek *Phedyo* <note>original: Φηδύω</note>, meaning "I corrupt." *Master Harsdorffer in Philological Specimen.*

*German: Matth. Berlich. 4. conclusion 21. 5. and following.* **Who should be protected in open feuds.** *Dr. Tabor on Change, p. 237.*

## 19. **Vehmic Court. Secret Court.**

Writers also call Secret Courts "Vehmic" <note>original: "Vemica"</note>, because these gradually degenerated into the former. Otherwise, they should be distinguished, as the legitimate and more ancient Vehmic courts were held not only in Westphalia, but in all of Saxony. And so **Fehmengericht** [Vehmic Court], **Fehmenrecht** [Vehmic Law] are found everywhere in Imperial documents: just as the Scabini <note>term: Scabini; lay judges or assessors of a court</note> are called *Feimeri* or *Freimajer* by Trithemius and Johannes of Frankfurt. *Münster*, according to the German version, uses **Judges or Free-Mayors** <note>original: "Scheffen oder Freymayr"</note>. *Freher, in his treatise on secret Courts, derives this word from the German (though unknown to the Saxons) "Fehmen," which means to skim off the foam: because through that judgment the Province is purged of evil men.* *Gryphiander on the Saxon Municipal Law, ch. 59. n. 1. 3. and following. Freher on Secret Courts in Westphalia, page 5.*

->ADDITIO.<-

*Vemedig*, capital censures. *Freher on Secret Courts in Westphalia p. 49.* **Westphalian Vehmic Courts, when they arose.** See the *Lindau Acts fol. 850* where the **Westphalian Free-Chairs** <note>original: "Freystühl"; the specific seats or jurisdictions of the Vehmic judges</note> are mentioned.

**When the Westphalian Vehmic law or blood law, blood court, free-proceeding, or free-chairs were abolished**, see *Schottelius in the German Main Language fol. 504.*

## 20. **Fine, Fine Gold. Refined Gold.**

**Fine gold**, in Latin *obryzum*, *obrisum*, or *obryssum*, whence the color *russus* [reddish-brown], *Pliny book 33, chapter 3.* The test of gold is by fire, so that it glows with a color similar to the fire itself, and they call the gold itself *obryzum*. Some think it is lightly called *aephththon* <note>original: ἄεψυθον; meaning ungrudging or abundant</note>, that is, sincere and thoroughly purified, see *Becman, Origins of the Latin Language, on the word Obryzum f. m. 53. and following. In French "fin," the Italians say "fino".*

->ADDITIO.<-

Pure gold is understood, which is cleansed from foreign metals by art, **Fine gold, pure and well-refined gold.** For chemists today assert that gold, as well as silver, can be reduced to such great purity by art that no heterogeneous metal remains, contrary to the common opinion, which thinks that in a mark of purified gold at least a quarter-carat of foreign metal is left; against whom *Budelius* disputes extensively and elegantly. That gold of 24 carats, and everywhere *obryzum* as if *athyzon* <note>original: ἄθυζον</note>, that is, sincere and delicate: whence also the refined coins... *Pliny book 33, chapter 3. Which Gellius in book 6, night 5, calls "pure, clear gold" <note>original: "aurum purum putum"</note>.*

Book II. Chapter I.

# ADDITION.

Geometry is so useful to the State <note>original: "Republ."</note> that sometimes men can be compelled to learn it, as held by Lucas de Penna in his commentary on the law regarding the excuse of craftsmen. They are called "surveyors" <note>original: "mensores"</note>; these are the boundary officials, field-measurers, and wood-measurers <note>original: "Untergänger, Feld- und Holzmässer"</note>. Adam Keller discusses the legal-political office in book 1, chapter 11, page 87. Joseph Furtenbach treats Geometry extensively on pages 51 to 59. Socrates demonstrated geometric lines to his listeners, as noted by Kirchner in *The Legate*, book 2, chapter 3.

The ancients were accustomed to begin with Geometrics, and those who lacked that science were said to have no "handles" for Philosophy, as Xenocrates used to say:

> The clever man knows how to laugh 
> at the marks carved in the cut dust. 
> — Persius, Satire 1. <note>Persius refers here to a mathematician's diagrams drawn in the sand.</note>

For a most elegant recommendation of Geometry, see Mr. Steinberg in his dissertation on the General Interpretation of Law, thesis 16, 1650. On the 30th of January, about four and a half miles from Roskilde <note>original: "Rosevild"</note> toward Copenhagen, a fortification <note>original: "Schanz"</note> threw itself up from the earth; it was quite ornately laid out with red stones, had two sections, and a ditch filled with water. <note>This likely refers to a contemporary report of a natural phenomenon or a "prodigy" interpreted as a sign.</note>

# 22. Holidays, Feast Days, Festivals.
->Holidays.<-

The exemption for holidays <note>original: "Feriæ"</note> also benefits those who are not themselves occupied in the harvest or the vintage. Although Bartolus denies this in his work on farmers and taxpayers, Eberhard Speckhan adheres to the contrary opinion, citing others to support it. For although the litigants themselves might not be occupied in gathering the fruits of the field, it is possible that their advocates, procurators, or others whose work they use in the case are occupied in the harvest. Thus, because of this probable occupation of all men, or at least most, the holidays ought to be common to all. This is especially true since it is generally provided by the Praetor's Edict that no one should summon an adversary to court during the time of the harvest or the vintage. See also Wesenbeck in his *Paratitla*.

Some things regarding holidays are also contained in my extracts <note>original: "delibatis"</note> on the Digest, book 12.

On feast days, see Cornelius Rinthelis in *The Roman-Catholic Jurist*, chapter 92. Regarding what must be done on holiday days, and whether legal instruments <note>original: "Instrumenta"</note> can be drawn up on them, see Fontanella on prenuptial pacts. There he says that although instruments for contracts and acts of voluntary jurisdiction can be made on holidays for the honor of God, the Abbot notes that Notaries who draw up such instruments sin, unless there is a cause of necessity or piety; this is because they are performing "servile work" <note>original: "opus merè servile"; manual labor or trade work forbidden on religious holidays</note>, which is prohibited. However, an Advocate does not sin by providing counsel, informing a judge, writing, or doing other things that pertain to his profession on a feast day, even for

<column-break/>

money and gain. This is because what can be done lawfully for free on holidays can also be done for money; for the intent of making a profit does not make a task "servile" if the task is not servile by its own nature. On the holidays of Christians and judicial holidays, see Brissonius in his *Ancient Readings* in the chapter on spectacles.

On the Feast days of the Saints, see especially Filefacus, book 1, chapter 6, page 66 and following.

On school holidays, see Tornurup in his commentary on the Satires of Persius. That schools ceased from the month of July until October is gathered from Martial, book 10, epigram 62:

> Schoolmaster, spare the simple crowd:
> So may the long-haired boys listen to you in throngs,
> And the choir of the Muse love you delicately.
> The white days glow with the flaming lion,
> And burning July cooks the parched harvest.
> Let the thongs of the Scythian hide whip,
> And the somber rods—the scepters of teachers—
> Cease, and let them sleep until the Ides of October.
> If children are well in summer, they learn enough.

# ADDITION.

On the harvest, see Tibullus, book 2, chapter 1, verse 47:

> The fields bring harvests, when with the heat of the burning star,
> The annual earth puts down its golden hair.

Ants rest whenever the moon is new. They rest on the 9th day of every month. See Zeiller, book 4, question 48.

Ilico Ummius, in his work on legal process, excellently enumerates what may be performed on holiday days, where he adds that it is also permitted for students to study on those days. Mr. Tabor, in his disputes, notes that on a holiday, subjects are not to be burdened with labor. A statute which allows a judge to proceed in certain cases without the usual solemnities of law means he can also proceed on holidays for the honor of God. The observance of holidays can be limited by local statutes. For what private or family holidays are, see Dracon.

Add to this material the *Victorsschlüssel*, part 10, various discourses, chapters 1 and 2.

And it is well known that even the pagans believed that the edge of a sword could be blunted by a charm, so that it could not pierce the skin with even a light wound. Francisco Torreblanca in...

### 24. Firmly. Constantly.

The word *Firmly* <note>original: "Festiglich"</note> has this effect and implies a disposition to which it is attached: that it cannot be restricted, limited, or plainly removed. For it would be without the power of operation, which is not to be said. Law *si quando*, Digest *on Legacies*, 1.

->ADDITION.<-

A promise regarding *observing constantly and not contravening*, as Martha writes regarding clauses, Part 1, Clause 103, Number 5, brings such force to an agreement that the party can in no way and at no time be permitted to go against the promises; and it ensures that the entire business becomes obligatory by necessity. Compare also Barbosa on clauses, 104, Number 2; and Dr. Tabor in *On Dowry Pacts*, page 64.

### 25. Fortress, Fortification. It stands and Best. Stronghold.

Is it expedient to have fortifications? I have inquired into this in the *Treatise on the Art and Law of War*, folio 71, etc. Truly, it is almost never profitable for a Prince and his subjects for there to be too many fortifications. Citadels are harmful to liberty. And a Prince is not the absolute mas-

<column-break/>

ter where either the magnates hold fortified castles or there are fortified cities in the heart of the territory. And so, under Henry IV, *the Saxons complained against the fortresses*. Lehman, Book 5, Chapter 27, folio 424. *In France, all are being demolished that are not located on the frontiers*. *French Mercury* <note>original: "Merc. Franc."</note>, Volume 12, folio 370.

Thus, in a County, *one is not allowed to build any fortification* without the Count's consent; see the Constitutions of Adolf of the Rhine Islands, folio 52. *Whether a fortress may be built too close to a city*, see the *Records of Speyer against Speyer*. On the utility *of fortresses*, see Meillet on Tacitus, folio 713. And what does it mean to have fortifications? Pippre, *Moral Intentions*, etc., Chapter 108. *Whether such are better than colonies?* Pippre, in the same place, Chapter 128.

The method of fortifying changes by the hour, but that which is without great expense is superior; see the *Discourses* of de la Noue, and such a method is proposed by Claude Flamand and Stevin. *Hornworks* <note>outworks of a fortress shaped like horns</note> *are a new invention, which must however be made in such a way that they can be flanked from the fortress*. See the *Military Discourses* of Praissac, folio 102 and following.

See more on Fortifications in Botero's *Treatise on Fortification*, and *The Justice of the Edomite Construction*, and there the Privilege of Emperor Sigismund, folio 43, in the documents of Johann Jacob Speidel, Licentiate of Both Laws.

### 26. Family Entail <term>Fideicommissum Familiæ: a legal arrangement where a testator forbids the sale of property to keep it within a family line</term>.

This occurs when someone is forbidden from alienating <note>selling or giving away</note> something by the agreement or command of the Testator; see Bartolus Romuleus in his singular treatise, and below under the word **Ancestral Estates** <note>original: "Stammgüter"</note>.

### ADDITION.

Whether a Family Entail can be introduced through Contract or Custom. Klock, volume 2, consultation 33, numbers 3, 4, and 56. Family Entails are established through subtle and far-fetched interpretations of whatever words are used, according to Besold, Volume 1.

...not to be forced. See Gomez, volume 1, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 4, number 6; Donellus, 6th commentary, 25; Vaconius, 4th declaration, 64, number 19 and following, through law 76. A Family Entail is not to be introduced through silent or implied understandings, as it is by its nature "odious" <note>in legal terms, "odious" means a provision that restricts natural liberties, such as the right to sell one's own property, and thus must be interpreted strictly</note>. ### 27. Fishery, Fishing. Right of Fishing <term>Jus piscandi</term>.

The right of fishing belongs to the **Regalian Rights** <note>original: "Regalien"; these are rights and privileges held exclusively by a sovereign or monarch</note>. See the single chapter at the end of *What are Regalian Rights*.

The trapping of beavers and otters is an appendage of hunting and Regalian rights; thus, it also belongs to the lord of the "Wild-ban" <note>jurisdiction over wildlife</note>, forest, and hunt, as a species of hunting <note>original: "Venationis"</note>.

Although by the Law of Nations <note>original: "jure Gentium"</note> the right of fishing in public rivers—in the waters which flow freely as streams—ought to be common to everyone, custom has nonetheless prevailed to the contrary, so that no subject is permitted to fish there without a special grant made for that purpose. For what pertains to the law regarding hunting and fowling, Princes have also taken for themselves regarding fishing; as an argument commonly proceeds from one of these to the other in other cases.

Furthermore, fish are caught in the sea, where the power of fishing is not yet free to everyone (except for sailors, who may catch only for their own use, but truly not to sell), but is restricted by neighbors...

# Treasury of Practice, Augmented

...we see that this is prohibited to the Lords within a range of 100 miles.

Or in rivers, lakes, and marshes. It shall be at the Prince’s discretion, even if the river is private property, to prescribe the manner and the time in which fish ought to be caught or not. For even in those matters which belong to the **Law of Nations** <note>Latin: "Juris gentium," referring to laws held in common by all people, such as the right to use water</note>, the Prince can pass laws aimed at conservation.

Should the **Right of Fishing** <note>Latin: "Juri piscandi"</note> be prescribed annually? As witnessed by Rutger Ruland in his *Discussions on Contested Law*, question 41, this was debated in the case of Pappenheim against Elgawe. It was noted by the Lords, he says, that although the right of fishing in public waters is common—according to the Institutes and the laws on <term>usucaption</term> <note>The acquisition of a title or right to property by uninterrupted and undisputed possession for a prescribed term</note>—to such an extent that a person cannot acquire the right by prescription <note>legal acquisition through long-term use</note> to fish alone in a public stream or its branch. Citing Bruns, Faber, and Angelo, they add the reason: because it belongs to the Law of Nations, and things of that nature cannot be acquired by prescription.

However, this rule fails [has an exception] first: if someone has acquired such a right through **custom**, such as if someone has fished alone for many years and prohibited others from fishing, with the people’s knowledge and without contradiction. (Boër, decision 372; Natta, counsel 522).

Second, it fails in a private lake or river that belongs to another Lord, because then only the owner is permitted to fish there. (Jacobinus de San Georgio).

### ADDITION

The King of Denmark is so rich that, even if the property of the least king in all Europe were sold at the highest price and turned into money, and for such money everything were bought back at the cheapest rate in nothing but wooden bowls, he could still fill and decorate such countless bowls with three types of fresh fish all at once. (Limnäus, volume 2, additions to book 2). From the right of fishing, one cannot correctly argue for the possession or ownership of the water itself. (Klock, counsel 33). The right of fishing is included in a general purchase. A person who has prescribed a right of fishing cumulatively cannot prohibit a co-possessor.

The trade and business of the **Moors** <note>The text likely refers to West or North African coastal peoples</note> is for the most part fishing; they also have certain times of the year and certain instruments with which they always catch different fish.

The Moors catch fish called **sharks** <note>German: "hayen"</note>, which are often longer than a man and quite thick; they have round mouths and five rows of teeth behind one another, with which they are so strong that they often bite off the legs of people who want to bathe, or even devour them entirely.

The Moors caught a large **swordfish**, in which they found 16 living fish. The "sword" from which the fish takes its name is as long as a man, a 

<column-break/>

hand-breadth wide, and has serrations on both sides like a pig's teeth. This sword stands at the front of the fish's head. When the whale notices it, he rises to the surface to catch the swordfish. But the swordfish does not retreat; instead, he goes a little deeper so that he can swim under the whale and cut open its belly with said jagged sword, so that it bleeds out and must finally die, which Michael Hemersam saw many times. The Counts of Wernigerode are the Imperial overseers of fishing. (Limnäus). The right of joint fishing, joint grazing, and joint hunting is supported by the precedents of the Imperial Chamber.

To whom the fish in rivers, weirs, lakes, and ponds belong before a <term>felony</term> <note>In feudal law, a crime that results in the forfeiture of lands</note> is committed or before the death of the vassal. (Knipschild). The people of **China** <note>Latin: "Sinarum populi"</note> raise very large and domestic **crows** <note>The author is describing **cormorant fishing**, mistaking the birds for crows</note> accustomed to catching fish. They constrict their necks with a loose knot so that, while their breathing is in no way blocked, they are unable to swallow or gulp down the food. Thus released from their cages, they dive into the waters with admirable skill; they carry small fish in their mouths and grasp larger ones with their beaks, repeatedly bringing them back to the house from which they left, until, their throats being fully untied, they themselves are also fed to satisfaction. (Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 162). That the fish were not brought by God to Adam on the sixth day of creation to be called by their names, unlike all the creatures of the earth and the birds of the heaven, is discussed at length by Fabricius. A fisherman has the power to strike and stick a pole into the **Pegnitz** <note>A river in Franconia, Germany</note> to bind his nets to it, and the Lord of the meadows may not force him to pull the pole out again or move it elsewhere, or disturb the fishing. Pigs are fattened with fish. (Zeiller, *Travels in Hungary*). The King’s Miller at B. shall give annually 2 eels, or 4 pounds for one. Conversely, he has the power every Friday and every feast day to catch his fish for his house from the waters of the **Rednitz**, regardless of the fact that the water is not his. All those who sell green salmon by the piece at E. must give the E. 3 marks for a back of a salmon, whether he be a citizen or a stranger. Likewise, the 31 overseers at E. give every week to the E. from the waters they have, each one a "service-fish." What fishing is, in what places it is granted, and whether one who has fished alone in a river for a long time can prohibit another. (Biccius). On fishing, see Klock. Crassus mourned a **moray eel** <note>Latin: "Muraenam"</note> that died in his pond as if it were a daughter, and buried it in a tomb. Marcus Cato Uticensis sold 49,000 thousand from his fishponds. Regarding the income from fishing, see the Book of Feuds. When a vassal builds fish-ponds and weirs, the construction costs are to be reimbursed to the heirs of the property.

### 31. Flight. *Fuga*.

Flight is not sufficient evidence <note>Latin: "indicium"</note> to inflict torture on a defendant. For torture to take place, there must be a probable sign of the crime. (Law 8, section "it is necessary," *Code on Investigations*). A sign is called "probable" when it mostly argues for and shows the matter being questioned. However, anyone might flee even if they are innocent and not at all guilty of a crime, for another reason: namely, so they are not seized by force, unjustly thrown into prison, convicted by the false testimonies of men, and punished by death. 

Thus, even if a student flees from his teacher, or a servant from his master, so that they might avoid his anger and cruelty for a time and free themselves from the fear of beatings for a while, it should not be held against them as a fault. (Law "what if a fugitive," 12, section "likewise at 3," and the following section, *Digest on the Ediles' Edicts*). Therefore, simply because someone flees out of fear of prison, torture, or execution—lest they be convicted by false witnesses—it should not be probably concluded that the crime was committed by them. Indeed, that man is called a fool who exposes himself to danger and prefers to argue his case from a prison cell and prove his innocence there. Hippolytus, *On Proofs*, number 279; Boerius, *Decisions* 215, number 29; Gail, book 2, observation 109, number 6 and following.

Furthermore, when it concerns a risk to one's life, it is a matter of more prudent counsel to flee rather than commit oneself to the judgment of an angry judge. (Clementine Decree *Pastoralis*, section "be it therefore," *On Sentencing*). Moreover, although flight is called a sign of a committed crime in the **Criminal Constitution of Charles V** <note>term: Constitutio Criminalis Carolina — the first body of German criminal law, issued in 1532</note>, article 25, last verse; nevertheless, in the following article 27, it is expressly stated that flight is not such a sign that a judge may snatch a caught fugitive away to torture, unless other signs concur with the flight.

Is a person who is attacked bound to flee? For various limitations and distinctions on this question, see Menochius, book 1, *On Presumptions*, question 89, number 36 and following; Mascardus, *On Proofs*, conclusion 819 and following; Zanger, *Treatise on Torture*, chapter 2, number 91; Julius Clarus, book 5, *Sentences*, final section, question 21, number 20 and following.

## 32. Rivers and Common Navigable Waters. <note>Latin: "Flumen navigabile"</note>

A navigable river, by reason of common use and property, is public and belongs to the people; however, in terms of jurisdiction, it pertains to the Sovereign <note>original: "Majestatem"</note>.

Can a Prince prohibit navigation on them? See Rauchbar, first question 23.

Furthermore, Hartmann Hartmanni, book 2, title 46, observation 3, records: An injunction allowing navigation in a public river pertains to private law, but it is otherwise in the case of a superior <note>a higher authority</note>. See also Pfeil, consultations 194 and 196, and what I have recorded in my treatise *On the Law of Things*, folio 10.

Regarding the riverbed, see Milium in his annotations to Augustinus Beroius, question 94; and on the joining of rivers, Camerarius, *Historical Meditations*, century 1, chapter 81; and whether navigation can be hindered by a Prince against ancient custom: *Strasbourg Legal Consultations*, volume 1, folio 266, and volume 2, consultation 62.

Under Roman law, any person could acquire the right of fishing in a public river, number 17. There was a ritual for consecrating rivers among the ancient Germans. For the Rhine was their God and ancestral deity <note>original: "Numen"</note>, as Tacitus testifies in *Histories*, book 5. And a bronze seal of the Rhine was found near Cologne, modeled after the figure of Father Tiber; Freher saw it with the letters: **THE GOD RHINE**. Julius Caesar, according to Suetonius in chapter 81, consecrated horses to the little river Rubicon—located between Rimini and Ravenna, which today is called the Pisciatello—treating it as a God; this is if the reading of the

## 33. Service. <note>German: "Folge"; Latin: "Sequela"</note>

The word <term>Folge</term> <note>meaning "service" or "following" one's lord</note> encompasses several species under it, namely territorial and military service <note>German: "Land und Heerfolge"</note>, court, hunt, and administrative service <note>German: "Gericht- Jagt- Amts- und andere Folg"</note>, to which the power of inspection and command—review and summons <note>German: "Musterung und Aufforderung"</note>—are attached. Andreas Knichen, *On the Rights of Territorial Supremacy*, chapter 3, numbers 351, 359, and following; in these places, he classifies these among the rights of sovereignty, and argues that if these are proven, sovereignty is proven. See also his treatise *On Saxon Law*, folio 151 and following. Sixtin, *On Royal Prerogatives*, chapter 1, number 28.

Military service <note>German: "Heerfolg"</note> occurs when subjects are bound in a time of just war to assist their Lord in person and with their estate; last law, section 1, *On Duties and Honors*; whether the Lord himself initiates the war, or it is initiated against him. This military duty must not be refused by the subjects: through law 4, section 4, *On Military Matters*. Baldus, consultation 483, number 4, part 1, adds this qualification: that they may perform military service through a substitute, based on the argument in the law beginning "no one is," section 6, *On Two Debtors*. See Knichen in his *Encyclopedia*, chapter 11, middle of folio 85.

### 34. Forest and Forestry Authority. Forestry, Forestry Jurisdiction.

A Forest (French: *Forest*) is defined as a broad woodland without an enclosure. *Chaffaneus on the Customs of Burgundy, rubric in the preface, after the gloss on the chapter 'cum dilecti,' where Johannes Andreae discusses donations, as cited by Mynsinger, Counsel 16, number 36.* The same Chaffaneus holds in the said rubric, section 2, on the phrase "Use of wood," that the terms "forest" and "grove" signify the same thing.

A distinction must absolutely be made between the right of hunting (or the law of the chase) and the Forest (or the law of the forest). In the common tongue, hunting is called the *Wildbann* or "Right of the Hunting-Ban" <note>original: "Wildbanns Gerechtigkeit"</note>: in Latin, it is called the "Hunting Ban," or rather the "Ban of the Wild Beasts" instead of the "Woodland Ban," since hunting also occurs in fields. *Thomas Michael on Jurisdiction, thesis 51.* From this, the feminine noun *ein Wildbann* denotes a place where wild animals are kept. *Friedrich on Procedure, chapter 40, number 14.* However, a Forest (*Forst* or *Forstgerechtigkeit*), also called Forestry Authority <note>original: "Forstliche Obrigkeit"</note>, consists of the care and management of the forests and groves. Furthermore, hunting is the right or faculty of tracking, pursuing, and catching wild beasts, and it includes nothing more. But the "Forest," according to the accepted custom of all Germany, includes not only the taking of wild beasts but also other rights of the greatest importance. *See especially Meichsner, book 2, volume 2, decision 2; and Bidembach, Noble Questions, 15.* This hunting, which is performed by the Right of the Forest, is rightly numbered among the Regalian rights <note>Prerogatives belonging exclusively to the sovereign.</note>. *I have written on this in 'On Majesty,' folio 177 and following.*

Moreover, the difference between Forestry Law and the ban on wild animals or woodlands is also seen in this: that in the courts of Princes, the offices of the Master of the Hunt and the Master of the Forest are distinct. The Master of the Forest <note>original: "Forstmeister"</note> is the overseer of the woods and groves, whose duty is primarily to ensure that the woods are not devastated, and that everything is done which pertains to the utility of the forests. Who are called "Hunters"? *Klock, Counsel 29, number 478.* The Master of the Hunt <note>original: "Jägermeister"</note> is placed in charge of the chase, and his duty is to successfully arrange and order all those things that are suitable for hunting. Therefore, the diversity of offices proves the diversity of the matter itself. *Johann Meichsner, volume 2, Imperial Chamber Decisions, book 2, decision 2, number 38.*

<column-break/>

Consequently, one who is granted the Forest has more than one who is granted only the Hunting. Since, therefore, the Right of the Forest and the Right of Hunting differ as "the greater and the lesser" (or rather as "the whole and the part," such that the Right of the Forest is an integral whole consisting of the woodland ban and other parts, *Andreas Knichen, Treatise on Vestitures, chapter 1, number 53*), the grant of the Prince bestowing such a right must be carefully weighed. One must judge from the tenor of the words whether simple hunting was given, or indeed the forest. In the latter case, it is understood that the grant includes not only the right of taking wild beasts, but also of commanding and prohibiting—to impose "Command and Prohibition" <note>original: "Gebot und Verbot"</note>—regarding hunting and matters depending on hunting, but not regarding other matters or causes. *By the argument of the final law, Code on the Jurisdiction of all Judges, where it is noted that jurisdiction granted to one holding a certain administration or business can only be exercised in those cases and questions which pertain to that specific business.*

Furthermore, he to whom not simply Hunting, but also the Right of the Forest is granted, can exercise "High Justice" <note>original: "merum Imperium"</note> regarding hunting matters. Thus, he can criminally punish hunters who hunt against a prohibition—commonly called "Poachers" <note>original: "Wilderer oder Wildpretschützen," discussed below under this word</note>. While one cannot poorly infer High Justice from Forestry Law alone (since they are separate and diverse), nevertheless, when one thing is granted, those things are also granted without which the right cannot be maintained. Thus, in the territory of the citizens of Esslingen, the most Serene Duke of Württemberg holds the Right of the Forest, and by its power, he captures trackers of wild beasts and afterwards punishes them.

Truly, this pertains to the protection or securing of the forest enclosures and the hunting-ban <note>original: "Sicherung der Forstgehäge und Wildbann"</note>, and these are exercised by the right of the Forestry Authority alone. The District Lord or Bailiff <note>original: "Cent- und Vogt-Herr"</note>, by virtue of his general district jurisdiction, his "hundred-court justice" and "hereditary court" <note>original: "Centgerechtigkeit und Erbgericht"</note>, shares nothing of this. Therefore, all offenses occurring on the hunting grounds and within its boundaries belong to the Forestry Authority. *Mynsinger, Counsel 16, numbers 37 and 46; Heig, volume 1, question 15.* Regarding the nobility, and especially the landed vassals <note>original: "Landsassen"</note>, the right "to hunt" does not simultaneously imply the right "to hedge" <note>original: "Jagen... Hagen"</note>; since the latter regularly belongs to the Territorial Sovereign <note>original: "Lands-Obrigkeit"</note>. *Gylman, volume 5, Symphorema, Petition 34, number 18 and following.* And the exercise of hunting granted to them is always understood to be for "small and low game" <note>original: "von dem kleinen und niedern Waidwerck"</note>. *Socini Junior, Counsel 39 and 28, volume 3.* And the superior grantor, or the Territorial Sovereign, is always presumed to reserve for himself the "High and Chief Hunting-Ban" alongside the Forestry Right, *Coburg Territorial Ordinance, title 29,* near the end. They also frequently possess and exercise "Joint Hunting" <note>original: "Koppel-Jagt"</note> with all their landed vassals. *Knichen, on Vestitures, pact 2, number 21, 54; and on Territorial Law, chapter 4, number 297.* Regarding the command to hang clogs/weights on dogs <note>A practice to prevent dogs from chasing game too fast or entering restricted areas.</note>, see *Counsels of Strasbourg, volume 1, folio 52.*

# Augmented Treasury of Practice

However, **Forest Law** or **Forestry Jurisdiction** is not understood to be included under the grant of high sovereignty <note>original: "meri Imperii"; the supreme power of a ruler, including the right of life and death</note>, since they are diverse and separate things, possessing their own distinct and essential differences. Thus, if one is not proven, it does not follow that the other is not proven either. See Mynsinger, *Counsel 16, number 46, section 37*; Noe Meurer’s treatise **On Hunting and Forest Rights,** part 2, under the heading **Whether Forestry Rights belong to the High Authority,** folio 32; and Meichsner, *Decision 4, number 7, volume 2, book 2*; Gylman, *volume 2, Symphony part 5, title 10, volume 2, number 29 and following.*

**The following items are attached and belong to the Forestry Authority:** The power to publish Forest Ordinances and Mandates, and to punish violators of the same; the exercise of high and low hunting <note>High hunting usually referred to big game like stag or boar, while low hunting referred to small game like hares or birds</note>; and the power to punish and forbid the general public from these activities.

**To forbid the improper cutting of trees in the game-ways.** But is a possessor or Lord of a forest, in which another person holds a right or easement <note>A legal right to use another's land for a specific purpose</note>, entitled to cut down many large trees for his own profit? This is considered highly debatable; see *Illustrious Counsels* in folio, edited under my care, counsels 16 and 17. Many deny this: because it would result in fraud and damage to the other person who holds the hunting easement, as the easement would be worsened by that very act. No one ought to worsen a properly established easement by their own authority. <note>The text cites various sections of the Digest (ff.) regarding urban and rural easements to support the idea that an owner cannot ruin the land to the detriment of the person holding usage rights.</note>

**That the clearing of stumps is also not allowed to the owner of the property,** as evidenced by the writings of Cepolla in his *Treatise on Rural Easements, chapter 9, number 40.* However, this is not to be understood as applying to modest clearings, following the arguments written by Bartolus in the law regarding rivers, and Jason at number 79 of the same.

**Wild fruit or acorns <note>original: "Geäcker"; refers to forest mast used for fattening pigs</note> are, in cases of doubt, also subject to Forest Law,** according to Papiensis in his *Forms, book for specific legacies, at the words "before you," number 118;* and Gail, *book 2, observation 68.*

**The power to forbid goats and sheep from being driven into the forest also belongs to Forest Law.** <note>Goats and sheep were often banned because they eat the young shoots and bark of trees, destroying the forest's regrowth.</note>

**The maintenance of dogs and foresters is also an appurtenance of Forest Law and the hunting grounds:** Brunus, *Counsel 127;* Decianus, *Counsel 123, number 27, volume 3,* where he teaches that all things appointed by law or custom are appurtenances, whether they come by right of growth or access. **And therefore this dog-maintenance is also called "hunter's maintenance" <note>original: "Jägerhaber"; a feudal tax or service for the upkeep of hunting dogs</note>.**

**The power to preserve and hunt,** Zasius, *book 2, counsel 6, number 1;* Gail, *book 2, observation 68, number 7,* where he says that a hunting forest can be enclosed with cut wood to capture wild beasts by the person who possesses the right of hunting.

**Windfalls <note>original: "Windfäll"; trees blown down by the wind</note> also belong to the forest.** For it is in the interest of the Lord of the Forest to remove trees that are decayed by age or fallen, so that the hunting

<column-break/>

may be made more productive and convenient. <note>Refers to the Digest on easements, suggesting that keeping the paths clear is necessary for the use of the right.</note>

**To command the cutting of young thickets:** following the arguments noted by Johannes Fabrus on the *Institutes.*

**Also, the removal of sharp fences: as well as the command to "cudgel" the dogs.** <note>original: "die Hund zu prügeln"; this refers to the practice of "knüppling," or hanging a heavy wooden block (a "cudgel") from a dog's collar to prevent it from running fast enough to catch game in protected areas.</note>

**The labor services <note>original: "Frohndienst"; corvée or forced feudal labor</note>, without which hunts cannot be carried out:** such as **the keeping of dogs, the transport of nets, yarn, and dogs, and that the subjects living within the district of the Forestry Authority shall be bound to help and serve in the hunt.** See Mynsinger on *Territorial Superiority, chapter 6, number 78.*

**To erect and build houses for forest-servants.** <note>Refers to rural easements in the Digest.</note> Gail, *book 2, observation 68.*

**To make forest and wood ordinances,** through the doctrine of Bartolus in the law *All Peoples* on *Justice and Law.*

**To punish violators of the Wood, Forest, and Hunting Ordinances.** Choppin, *book 3, title 7;* Jacob de Saint-George, *Treatise on Fiefs, section on hunting.*

**To keep, hire, and dismiss watchmen, foresters, and marksmen,** <note>Refers to laws on the dissolution of marriage and mandates applied by analogy to the hiring of staff.</note> **who are required to keep books for the defense [of the forest].**

### ADDITION I. CERTAIN.

The right of hunting encompasses both fields and forests; hence it is less correctly called a "Forest Ban" <note>original: "bannum Sylvestre"</note> by Gail. The person who presides over this is called the **Master of the Hunt** <note>original: "Jägermeister"</note>. Compare Wehner in *Practical Observations* under the word **Forest Law.**

**Regarding Forestry Authority and Forest Law,** Limn., *book 4, chapter 8, number 188;* **regarding Forest Chambers and the Forest Court,** the same author, *book 7, chapter 35, pages 416, 418.* **What is called a "Forest,"** see Sebastian Medicis *On Hunting, page 4, number 16.* It is a wood or a broad grove without an enclosure. Mynsinger, *Counsel 16, number 36:* **a large wood that is not enclosed by water or otherwise.** For the various forms or titles of hunting, among which is also Forest Law, see Bicc. in *Aureis, page 184.* Regarding Forest Jurisdiction, see Schönborner in *Politics, page 551 and following.*

He who has the right of hunting does not always also have the right of the forest. Rulandus *On Commissions, part 4, book 2, chapter 8, number 43,* **in the case of Schwäbisch Gmünd versus Rechberg.**

He who possesses Forest Law can appoint forest-wardens, **Forest Masters and Forest Servants;** likewise, he can prohibit trees from being cut down, and fine those who cut trees against the prohibition. He may also enclose the wood, **protecting the forest with a hedge, clear stumps, and demand windfalls, fruit, mast, and "forest oats" <note>original: "avenam saltualem"; a tax paid in oats to the forester</note>.** Bocer *On Regalities, page 40;* see Klock *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 2, numbers 21, 23;* Meichsner, *volume 2, book 2, decision 2.*

They call *Barchum* a game park <note>German: *ein Thiergarten*</note>. They call a *Forest* <note>Latin: *Forestum*</note> a place in which wild beasts dwell or are enclosed, and in which one has the right of hunting. Adam Keller.

# 35. Blood-Pledge. The seizure of a pledge for a committed crime.

<note>original: "Fraischpfand. Pignoratio perpetrati criminis." This refers to a specific legal ritual in the Holy Roman Empire where a judge claimed jurisdiction over a murder by taking a token from the scene.</note>

The lord of the territory in which a slain person lies prostrate, according to the most accepted rite of criminal jurisdiction, alone removes the body. From this body, or from a bloodstained part of the slain person's clothing, as testimony of the homicide and a token of criminal jurisdiction—a **Blood-Pledge** <note>German: *ein Fraischpfand*</note>—he cuts something off. This act belongs to high sovereignty <note>Latin: *meri Imperii*; the supreme power of a ruler, including the right of life and death</note> and pertains to the High Judge <note>German: *Centherrn*</note> or the Head Official <note>German: *Schvvanmann*</note>, according to Schvvanmann, part 1, on procedures, chapter 12, number 21 and following; and *Cameral Observations* 86. It also involves measuring the stabs and wounds and taking those measurements for oneself. Schvvanmann, *Cameral Observations* 87.

This also occurs in cases where jurisdiction may belong to several parties: in such a case, the one who arrives first <note>Latin: *præveniens*</note> is not seen to disturb the other. From my own work *On the Right of Territory*, folio 271.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the taking of a "push" or "loop" <note>German: *Schub oder Schlauff*</note> from the **Blood-Pledge**, which is a certain seizure of a pledge for a committed crime as a memorial. Adam Keller, *On the Judicial-Political Office*, book 2, chapter 12, page 405. The granting of safe conduct, or allowing security to delinquents, proves the right of superiority and preserves and protects the quasi-possession of the **High and Blood-Jurisdiction** <note>German: *der hohen und Fraischlichen Obrigkeit*</note>. Cephalus, *Counsel 458*, number 37, book 4. Knichen, *On the Sublime and Regal Rights of Territory*, chapter 3, number 253.

To pick up a **Blood-Pledge**, or to take the measure of stabs and wounds: to whom does this belong? Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 8, number 189. Do the books of quarrels, breaches, and punishments <note>German: *Die Hader- Brüch und Straffbücher*</note> prove high sovereignty or **Blood-Jurisdiction** for the magistrate against a third party? Ruland denies this in *On Commissions*, chapter 6, number 10. Ummius in *Procedures*, page 702. How **Blood-matters and Trespass-matters** <note>German: *Fraisch- und Frevel- Sachen*</note> differ, see G. Herpffer’s *Inaugural Question 12*. One who removes a corpse judicially and, as a sign of criminal jurisdiction, takes a **Blood-Pledge**, is considered to have violated the jurisdiction of another. Besold in *Politics*, book 1, chapter 12, number 78, verse 4. Regarding the "Blood-dispute" <note>German: *Fraisstreit*</note> around Nuremberg, see Zeiller in *German Continuations*, page 59.

In the **Bamberg Penal Ordinance** <note>German: *Bambergischen peinlichen Halsgerichts- Ordnung*</note> of the year 1580, this is called "taking the body-token" <note>German: *Leibzeichen nehmen*</note>, folio 58, articles 229 and 230. It describes what is to be inspected and noted there; likewise regarding the requests for the delivery of the body-token if the slain person falls into another jurisdiction. Likewise regarding outlaws without a body-token. *Ibid.*

# 36. Franciscans. Franciscani.

Saint Francis was born in Assisi, which is a city of the Spoleto Valley. He was the author of this Order; his life was written by Bonaventure and Vincent. Martin the Chaplain, Jacobus de Voragine, and Volateranus relate that he was previously called John; but for certain reasons, which they report, he later wanted to be called Francis. Bonaventure relates that he was led to the monastic life by a certain vision which he recounts. In the said place where he was born, he began his Order. And it is said that when he disputed the Rule with others, he opened the Biblical text after offering prayer and petitions: so that whatever first appeared there should be held as the Rule. Having opened the book, therefore, this passage presented itself: *If you wish to be perfect, sell all you have and give to the poor.* Opening it a second time, they found: *Take nothing for the journey.* A third time this appeared: *Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.* Then Francis said: "These, therefore, shall be our Rule." The Rule written by him and his testament are found in Hospinianus. See *The Voice of the Turtle*, folio 196, and *Regular Questions*, sections on Conventuality, Women, Tertiaries, and elsewhere.

The **Franciscans** are also called by another name, **Minorites** <note>Latin: *Minores*</note> from their humility; and **Barefoot** <note>German: *Barfüsser*</note> because they walk with naked feet; and **Cord-bearers** <note>Latin: *cordigeri*</note> or **Rope-bearers** <note>Latin: *funigeri*</note> from the cord and rope with which they are girded.

This Order is divided into multiple classes: for some are called **Reformed**, others **Capuchins**, others **Conventuals**, etc. See Aubertus Miræus, *On the Origin of Monasteries*, folio 215, etc.

Regarding the antiquity of the Franciscans and other matters relating to this, see the Rule and Testament of Saint Francis, and Bosquier, century 1, chapter 5, folio 9, and through the whole treatise.

The Testament of Saint Francis (which Miræus provides in *Belgian Annals*, folio 576) is reported thus:

> How short life is, how slippery the path, and how 
> Uncertain is death; what rewards for the good, and what 
> Torments are prepared for the evil; these are our meditation. 
> What we do, what we confirm, and what we desire to be 
> An eternal Testament: Greetings and farewell, 
> Dear Father, dear brothers, and dear sisters.

# 37. Frank, Franks. see below under the word Free Franks. Franci.

*Franck* is said as if it were "a free youth" <note>German: *ein freyer Anck*</note>. *Anck* moreover means a youth, whence also come the Latin *anculus* [male servant], *ancillus*, and *ancilla* [maid-servant]. Beckman in *Origins*, under the word *Cyrus*. See Coccius in *Dagobert*, folio 12.

But concerning the Franks, their origin, etc., see Isaac Pontanus’s *Frankish Origins*, Guillimann’s *Helvetian Affairs*, book 2, chapter 9, and Junius in *Batavia*, chapter 9.
