### 38. Frankfurt. Francofurtum.

A fixed location for the Imperial Diets <note>term: Comitia; the general assembly of the estates of the Holy Roman Empire</note> is not defined within the German Empire; nor is it fixed for the Assemblies of the Electors. See Carpzovius on the *Capitulations*, chapter 5, number 11, etc. However, the election of the Emperor is usually not held anywhere else but in Frankfurt. See the *Golden Bull* <note>original Latin: "A. B." for Aurea Bulla; the 1356 decree that fixed the constitutional structure of the Empire</note> chapter 1; Münster, book 3; Daniel Otto, *On Public Law*, chapter 10, page 244; and my own work *On the Succession of Electors*, page 189 and following. There, I also argue that it is a hollow claim, as some say, that one who attains the Empire through a disputed election must besiege Frankfurt, and unless he is driven away within a certain time, the election is confirmed. See also Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, last book, chapter 34; Freher on Peter von Andlo, book 2, chapter 2, page 166; and Arumæus, *On the Imperial Diets*, chapter 5, number 11.

## ADDITION.

Regarding the Patricians of Frankfurt <note>term: Patricii; the elite ruling families of the city</note>, see Draco, *On Patricians*, page 234. There are three orders <note>social classes</note> of that same town; see Draco in detail, page 207; Knipfchild, *On Imperial Cities*, book 3, chapter 14, number 8; and see Limnaeus in *Public Law*. Frankfurt is commended for its equality in the administration of justice for all nations. Besold, *On Politics*, book 1, chapter 11, number 22, section 1. No citizen of Frankfurt is bound to give his daughter in marriage to a court official. Knipfchild, *On Imperial Cities*, book 3, chapter 14, number 22. Emperors cannot mortgage or pawn Frankfurt, number 24, and book 3, chapter 15, number 10. Regarding the hospitality <note>term: Philoxenia; the love of strangers</note> of the inhabitants of this city, see book 3, chapter 14, number 14.

### 39. Franconian Law. Jus Franconicum.

In ancient times, the Roman Empire was governed by two laws: Saxon Law and Frankish Law. From this come the *Swabian Mirror* and the *Saxon Mirror* <note>term: Spiegel; medieval German legal codes</note>. And from that, there were also two Vicars of the Empire <note>deputies who ruled during an interregnum</note>, and defenders of these two laws. Gewold, *On the Electors*, chapter 11; and my own work *On the Succession of Electors*, page 216.

In the foundation of the Richenbach Monastery in the year 1080, it is recorded: Sigeloch was present at this business, along with Henry, Fridehelm, Winchart (a knight of Fridehelm), and Albert and Burchard (knights of the Archbishop). We judged these last ones to be suitable witnesses for this matter because they were **FRANKS**, especially since the aforementioned estate is located in the land of the Franks, and the aforementioned matron with her heirs must be governed and restrained by the law of the Franks.

To this also belongs that distinction handed down by the legal interpreters: that one type of fief is that in

<column-break/>

which one lives by the law of the Franks <note>original Latin: "jure Francorum"</note>—that is, where by local custom or contract the firstborn alone succeeds—and another type in which one lives by the law of the Lombards <note>original Latin: "jure Longobardorum"</note>—that is, where the succession is passed down according to the common rules of feudal law. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 2, question 80; Marta, *On Clauses*, part 2, clause 34; Giovanni Thomas de Marinis, *Treatise on the Types and Qualities of Fiefs*, title 13; and my own *On the Succession of Electors*, page 57. By a similar distinction in Germany, we can call certain fiefs governed by Saxon Law, and others by Lombard or Common Law, because of the peculiar law of "simultaneous investiture"—vulgarly called the **Joint Hand** <note>German: "die gesamte Hand"; a form of collective ownership where several people hold a property together as a single unit</note>—which is used not only in Saxony but also in certain other places in Germany.

### 40. France. Gallia.

Regarding France, see Hotman’s *Franco-Gallia*; on the Kings of the Franks, see Fauchet, *On Origins*, chapter 1 and following; on the comparison of Italy and France, see *Proffas Taffi*, last part, page 171; on the evils that France has suffered, see *The Secret of Finance*.

Arumæus, in *On the Imperial Diets*, chapter 4, number 65, proves that the Roman Empire was never transferred to the Gauls <note>the French</note> either by election or by inheritance, but that France remained joined to the Empire until the time of Hugh Capet <note>the first King of the Franks from the Capetian dynasty, 987 AD</note>, who first transferred its crown into the Capetian family. Nevertheless, there was a very close alliance between the Empire and the Kingdom of France, regarding which see Peter de Vineis, book 1, letters 12 and 18; however, due to a lust for reigning, this alliance was not always maintained as it should have been.

Indeed, within the memory of our fathers, the same Arumæus adds in the cited place, number 68, Henry II, King of France, most wonderfully eluded that alliance by the occupation of three cities: Metz, Toul, and Verdun. One might marvel at the judgment of the Frenchman Thuanus, who in book 10 of his *History* contends that reasons were not lacking why Henry II, having entered into an alliance with the Elector Maurice and other Princes, occupied the Imperial City of Metz. For as is clear from the King's public writing, he professes that he entered the alliance with the Princes for the sake of the public good, and that he sought no private gain or profit in it.

Even if all those arguments of Thuanus were true—by which he contends that by ancient right, namely before the times of Emperor Otto I, the city of Metz belonged to the Kingdom of France—nevertheless, since the King promised by his royal faith that he sought no advantage or profit from that war, what else shall we say but that those arguments were sought as a veil for treachery? Botero wished to hint at this in *On the Illustrious State and Politics*, book 8, chapter 6.

This art of undertaking the "defense" of foreign cities and empires is not unknown to the princes of our century; it was certainly most well known to Henry II, King of France: who, under the pretext of defending the Imperial cities against Emperor Charles V, with marvelous cunning, forti- <note>The text ends mid-word: "muni-"</note>

...joined the most fortified places to himself; which he also attempted at Strasbourg, but with a vain and fruitless effort, etc.

Suppose likewise that the King of France had made no hope of the aforementioned promise to the allies; is it therefore because Metz <note>A city in Northeast France, then a point of contention between the Holy Roman Empire and France.</note> formerly belonged to France, that it could be reclaimed from our Empire by war? The French will not admit this, because one may not argue from what once was to what is presently the case. But specious pretexts, with which they are accustomed to cloak their schemes, are never lacking to cunning minds. When Ahab, King of Samaria, sought Naboth's vineyard, he demanded it be yielded to him under this specious pretext: that it was near and adjacent to his house, and he wished to make it a herb garden <note>See the Bible, 1 Kings 21 (cited here as book 1, chapter 22).</note>. Gnaeus Piso ordered a soldier to be killed because he had returned from a mission without his comrade, as if he had killed him. But as the poor man was already stretching out his neck for the sword, the comrade appeared. The centurion in charge of the execution brought the condemned man back to Piso, who, flying into a rage, ordered the condemned man, the comrade, and the centurion himself to be killed, using this pretext: *“I order you to be led to execution,”* he said, *“because you were condemned; you, because you were the cause of your comrade’s condemnation; and you, because when ordered to kill, you did not obey your commander.”* <note>original: "Te duci inquit jubeo, quia damnatus es: Te, quia causa damnationis Commilitoni fuisti: Te, quia jussus occidere, Imperatori non paruisti." From Seneca's *On Anger*, Book 1, Chapter 16.</note> But wise and prudent judges of affairs detest such pretexts, believing that by such veils—as if by malicious deceits—crime and treachery are made even worse, etc.

Certainly, alas, the same play is being performed today, though the actors are changed. The outcome of which is in the hand of GOD.

### ADDITION.

The world-famous Opitz <note>Martin Opitz, a famous German Baroque poet.</note> says quite deliberately: "That illness which among us is named after France." See Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Poetic Funnel*, page 100.

Johannes Almenar, a Spaniard, wrote specifically on the French disease.

On whether it is called *Syphilis* because it is, as it were, the offspring of "Venereal" <note>Referring here to Venus, the goddess of love, implying sexual transmission.</note> concord and friendship, according to Fallopius' interpretation, and it receives various names. See Pancirolli in *New Discoveries*, page 89 and following. On whether divorce can occur because of the French disease, see Rittershusius in the *Novels*, part 4, chapter 11, number 4, page 240. If a doctor, consulted by someone with a legitimate interest in knowing about the constitution or health of a person named Titius, responds that he is infected with leprosy or the French disease, even if the doctor is mistaken, he cannot be sued for injury/slander; for he is judged to have done it not with the intent to injure, but through a certain lack of skill or for the sake of practicing the art he professes. However, if he affirms it voluntarily and without being consulted—claiming that he has detected by certain signs and indications that Titius is a leper or infected with another disease—it is not doubted that he would be held liable for injury in that case. <note>Harprecht, section 11, on injuries.</note> How common the French disease is in India, see Pancirolli in *New Discoveries*, pages 85, 87; and how it was derived into Europe, page 87. Where this disease came from, see Schupp in *The Afflicted but Patient Job*, page 146. "Honest people are also said to have this disease," page 145.

Regarding the **Daughter’s Tax** <note>German: "Fräuleins-Steuer." A feudal aid where subjects contributed to the dowry of a lord's daughter.</note>, see those cited by Nicolaus Myler in *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 22, page 253.

On whether the subjects of a Prince are bound to establish a dowry for his daughter, see Mundius in *On Duties and Honors*, page 168, number 39 and following, and number 42, and those cited there. It is owed to each individual daughter (number 73) but is given only for the first marriage (number 76). The **Daughter’s Tax** is an extraordinary duty and of a specific kind. Mundius, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 3, number 20.

44. **Misdemeanor.** <note>German: "Frevel."</note> See above under **Penalty** and **Fine.** <note>original: "Buß. Mulcta."</note>

**Peace-Fine** <note>Latin: "Fredum." In early Germanic law, a payment made to the public treasury to buy back the "peace" after a crime.</note>, a judicial fine, a settlement owed to the treasury, a **Misdemeanor.** <note>German: "Frevel."</note> In the Ripuarian Law <note>An early medieval Germanic legal code.</note>, final title. However, one should not pay the Peace-Fine to the judge against whom the fault was committed, but to the one who receives the payment. In the Alemannic Law, title 4, section 1: "If any free man kills another free man within the doors of a Church, let him know he has acted unjustly against God, and the Treasury shall acquire the Peace-Fine." Vitus Amerbach says the Peace-Fine is a punishment proposed for violators of the peace. But on the **Peace-Fine** or **Misdemeanor**, Bignon has much to say in his notes on the *Formularies of the Monk Marculphus*, leaf 444; Coccius in *Dagobert*, leaves 178 and 263; and Goldast in volume 2 of *Alemannic Matters*, leaf 86.

A **Fine** <note>Latin: "Mulcta."</note> is a specific pecuniary punishment for a sin, imposed at the judge's discretion (Law *aliud fraus*, section 1, Digest *on the meaning of words* <note>original: "ff. de V. S."</note>), and it corresponds closely with our local term **Misdemeanor.** <note>German: "Frevel."</note> See Brisson, *Selected Readings*, book 1, chapter 3.

To which level of Power do **Fines** belong? See especially Regner Sixtin, *On Royal Rights* <note>original: "de regal."</note>, book 2, chapter 8; Nizolius, allegation 2, number 20, etc.; *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 1, leaf 443. A certain Assessor, in the case of Lobenberg against Montfort reported on April 20, 1620 <note>original: "A &c. 20."</note>, concluded that they belong to the **High Jurisdiction** <note>Latin: "meri Imperii," the highest level of legal authority, including the power of life and death.</note>, following Jason on the law *Imperium*, number 2, Digest *on Jurisdiction*, who rebukes Baldus for holding the opposite view. The said Assessor added that all criminal cases belong to High Jurisdiction, and fines belong to the person who presides over the community (Bartolus on the said law *Imperium*, number 10, fifth grade).

Yet the contrary seems truer: because the Magistrates of the Roman People, who did not possess High Jurisdiction, were able to impose fines. Master Rutger Ruland, *Decisions on Controverted Law*, question 13. For municipal cities, even under Roman Law, have the power to declare and profit from fines (Law 2, section 1, Digest *if anyone summoned to court does not go*). Cujas in the summary of the Code *on municipal Magistrates*. And this is indeed by virtue of Jurisdiction (Law *more*, section 1 and following, Digest *on Jurisdiction*).

Although it is not so improbable what is commonly said: that formerly Municipal Magistrates were not permitted to declare every fine in every emerging case, but only such a fine as is usually inflicted for the sake of protecting jurisdiction in cases of con-

<column-break/>

-tumacy <note>Refusal to obey a court order.</note> (Law *cui*, Digest *on Jurisdiction*; single law, Code *if anyone does not obey a judge*; chapter *pastor*, section 1, *on the office of a delegate*). See Cothman on the title of the Code *on the manner of fines*, number 7 and following.

And although it is not denied that the profits from fines and punishments were numbered among the **Royal Rights** <note>Latin: "regalia." Sovereign rights belonging to the Emperor or King.</note> by Emperor Frederick (single chapter, *which are regalia*), so that they ought to be brought into the Prince’s treasury (second to last law, Code *on the manner of fines*; Caspar Ziegler in the section *City*, conclusion 1, number 53).

Nevertheless, today this is not observed so strictly; instead, the profits from fines are considered a kind of "fruit" or revenue of Jurisdiction (Bartolus and Baldus on the final law, Digest *on the dissolution of marriage*; Rotenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 63, number 2; Sixtin, *On Royal Rights*, book 2, chapter 8; Borcholt in the single chapter *On Royal Rights*, number 64 and following, where the Doctors of Law commonly agree through the single law, Digest *if anyone should speak the law* <note>referring to a judge's authority</note>).

Moreover, subjects are bound to obey by paying the punishment and fine imposed—to pay the **Misdemeanor** and **Penalty.** <note>German: "**Frevel** und **Buß** zu erlegen."</note> Sixtin, in the place cited. Because no one is bound to pay **Misdemeanor** and **Penalty** except to the one whose lordship he acknowledges (Reinking, *On Ecclesiastical Government*, book 1, class 5, chapter 4, number 68). For these are signs of superiority and subjection (Carlos Tapia on the final law, part 1, chapter 2, number 48, *On the Constitutions of Princes*; Zacharias Vietor, *On Imperial Exemptions*, conclusion 36, fourth verse), and they denote the possession of Jurisdiction (Ritter, *On Homage*, chapter 7, number 175). Here belong: great and high matters, such as **Bloodshed** <note>German: "Blutrunst."</note>; and small and low **Misdemeanors**, such as **Blood-money** <note>German: "Wöhrgeld."</note>, **Assault-settlement** <note>German: "verschlagene Wöhr."</note>, **Insults** <note>German: "Scheltwort."</note>, **Slapping the cheek** <note>German: "Backenschlag."</note>, etc. (Gylman, volume 1, part 1, title 2, volume 1, number 126; Ritter, same place).

If a legacy is left for the **Usufruct** <note>The right to use and profit from property belonging to another.</note> of some Castle that has an attached Jurisdiction, do the punishments and fines imposed for the crimes of subjects go to the one holding the use, or do they belong to the heirs? The hinge of this question turns on whether fines are to be considered as the "fruit" of Jurisdiction. I have just asserted this and proved it with authorities. Therefore, there will be no doubt that these fines and condemnations belong to the person holding the usufruct, and not at all to the heirs; unless it is otherwise established by the intention of the testator. But see also Michael Grass, *Book of Received Opinions*, section *Legacy*, question 32.

### 45. Maliciously and Dangerously. <note>original: "Freventlich und gefährlich. Dolosè."</note>

These words require **malicious intent** <note>term: "dolus" — the legal concept of intentional wrongdoing or fraud</note>, as in the law "in actions" <note>original: "l. in actionibus"</note> in the Digest *on the oath in litigation*. Mynsing, response 20, number 12. However, they do not always require the most transparent proofs of malice; it suffices to prove such an act that induces a presumption of malice because it is against the law; see Wilhelm Anton on *Five-Year Letters*, page 509. For that very thing—that it is against the law—is and is called a **Misdemeanor** <note>original: "Frevel"</note>, as Reichwein states in his *Formulary*, page 101, speaking in terms of the violation of the public Peace.

And from this, it is customary that **one is often seen as liable for a Misdemeanor-Penalty <note>original: "Frevel-Straff"</note>, even if no true malicious intent is present.**

### ADDITION.

To this clause, another is opposed: **gladly and without deceit** <note>original: "freulich und sonder Gefährd"</note>. See Berlich, 2, conclusion 24, number 63. On whether there is a difference between fraud and malice, see extensively Rittershusius on the *Laws of the Twelve Tables*, page 14. There is both "good" and "bad" malice. Whenever "malice" is found by itself, it is understood as "bad malice," page 15. On good deception and fraud, see the same place. Ibid, page 22. **Deceit and cunning are entirely excluded.** Limnaeus, in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 6, page 282.

### 48. Free Hunting. Hunting free to all.

**Free Hunting** <note>German: "Freye Bürsch"</note> is a place where the power of hunting is granted freely to everyone, such as the place on one side of the town of Tübingen. But the question is: if a subject or anyone else begins to track and hunt a deer or some wild beast in such a place, **in the free hunting ground**, can they follow it even into a neighboring forest or another place beyond where the free hunting ground

<column-break/>

ends, and there capture and take possession of it without penalty? It seems more true that they cannot. For this quality of the place—that anyone may hunt in it indiscriminately—exposes the wild beasts to the prey of everyone only as long as they remain in that place, **as long as they stay within the free hunting ground**. But after they have left it, they are no longer subject to the risk of that place: since they are not attached to the soil, nor do they follow the nature or ownership of the soil, but wander freely through fields and forests. It follows, therefore, that by virtue of the quality belonging to that place, they can only be captured in that very place. Diego Covarruvias, book 2, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 20, number 12. Noe Meurer in the treatise *On Hunting and Forest Law*, part 2, title: *How one should hunt wild game*.

Where such a free power of hunting still exists, hunting cannot be prohibited there. See Speckan, volume 1, question 97, and my own work *On Majesty*, folio 178. Since a Prince cannot deprive subjects of their right without cause, which we see belongs to them not only by natural law but also by Civil law (namely, by long-standing use); see Beatus, *Decisions*, volume 5, on judicial matters, page 5, volume 2, folio 714. He can, however, **forbid hunting at unseasonable times**.

->ADDITIO.<-

**Game-driving** <note>German: "Wildfuhr"</note> and **Free Hunting** <note>German: "freye Bürsch"</note>: whether they are opposites. Klock, consultation 29, number 817. On what is understood by "free hunting," number 613.

**Free Hunting on one side of the city of Tübingen.** Zeiller, century 4, question 51, page 271.

Princes ought not to forbid hunting in those places where the faculty of hunting is still free to all: which they call **free hunting ground**. For a legitimate immunity cannot be taken from anyone by right. Those "farsighted guardians of nature" are ridiculous who take away the hunting of wild beasts from the common people just so the species are not lost. More on this in Besold, *Politics*, chapter 4, section 7, numbers 4, 12, page 174, and there Philip Camerarius is cited, *Meditations*, book 2, chapter 69. Hunting of wild beasts in Hungary is permitted to everyone, Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 5, number 51. Whether the prohibition of hunting is in the hand of the Prince is declared in number 26.

### 49. To Marry. To wed.

According to our customs, marriage dissolves the father's power <note>term: "patria potestas" (the legal authority a father held over his children)</note>. I discuss this in *On the Three Types of Domestic Society*, discourse 1, chapter 4, number 6. And hence those about to enter marriage are said in the German idiom **to marry** <note>German: "Freyen"</note>, a word which denotes liberty <note>German: "Freiheit"</note>: because by this bond or link they are freed from the father's power. Vultejus, section 2 of the Institutes, *On Fatherly Power*, number 3. Schneidewin, section 8, number 4 and following, Institutes, *By what modes fatherly power is ended*, folio. Sichard on law 29, Code, *On the law of dowries*, number 15 and following. Barthold Musculus, *On Anomalous Successions*, class 1, member 3, letter 2, number 24. My own work, *On the Three Types*, folio 24. Although others prefer this word to be derived from *Pfreya* or *Freja*, namely the German Venus <note>note: The goddess of love, Freyja</note>; see Moller on the *Saxon Constitutions*, part 2, constitution 10, number 8; and Nonnius in Gruter, volume 1 of the *Critics*, folio 1372; also Goldast on the *Admonitions*, folio 454.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the definition of freedom, specifically examining whether marriage releases a child from the legal control of a father (paternal power) and the etymology of the "Free Franks."</meta>

Lit. F.
Pp 3

However, according to **Civil Law** <note>original: "Jure Civili," referring to Roman Law</note>, marriage is not a means of dissolving **paternal power** <note>original: "patriam potestatem," the absolute authority of a Roman father over his children</note>; indeed, daughters remain under their father's power even if they are married. This is according to various laws in the Digest and the Code regarding the dissolution of marriage and the acknowledgement of children. This seems unjust to **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin, a 16th-century French jurist and political philosopher</note> and contrary to **Natural Law**, specifically that a married daughter should be under the power of her father rather than her husband (Book 1 of *The Republic*, chapter 3). He argues it is also against **Divine Law**, citing Genesis 1: "A man shall leave his father and mother," as well as passages in Ephesians 5, Colossians 3, Titus 2, and 1 Peter 3. The same must be said regarding the **Laws of Moses** in Leviticus 21 and Genesis 24. See also Tiraqueau on marriage laws. This was the same among the **Gauls** (the French), the **Lombards**, and the **Spartans** according to Plutarch. Andreas Gerhard and Stephan Durant also note that in these traditions, married sons or daughters are even able to make their own wills. Among the Romans themselves, as Tiraqueau notes, once a bride had her head covered with the bridal veil <note>original: "flammeo," a flame-colored veil worn by Roman brides</note> and had stepped foot out of her father’s house, she was turned in a circle and thus led into the house of the groom, so that she might not know the way back to her parents’ house. Bodin adds that a wife who remains under her father's power might despise the commands of her husband. However, as Gerhard argues, we should not leave the Civil Law entirely undefended. For these powers are distinct: **Marital power** consists of domestic life and labor; in these matters, the wife is in the power of her husband. But she remains in her **father's power** regarding the legal consequences of her status. The power of a husband over a wife can be maintained without the paternal power being disregarded in the meantime, and vice-versa: by "rendering to the husband what is the husband's, and to the father what is the father's."

->ADDITIO.<-
<note>Latin: "Addition"</note>

By both modern law and custom, and contrary to the law of **Justinian** <note>The 6th-century Roman Emperor whose legal code is the basis for Civil Law</note>, marriages that have been contracted do dissolve paternal power. According to our customs, **emancipation** <note>legal independence</note> is presumed to occur tacitly if a father allows his children to manage their own property or arranges a marriage for them. While this is accepted among the French, Burgundians, and others, it is not a universal rule in our **Germany**, as is clear from the Nuremberg Reformation and **Saxon Law**. Under Saxon Law, although a daughter is freed from her father's power through marriage, it is more accurate to say a son remains under that power, as discussed by Carpzov and others. However, once the right of paternal power over a daughter is extinguished, it does not revive; thus, even if the marriage is dissolved by death, the daughter does not fall back under her father's power but remains her own mistress <note>original: "sui juris," meaning of her own right</note>. <term>From which the words</term> <note>original: "Woher die Wörter"</note>

<column-break/>

**Free**, **To Woo**, and **Matchmaker** <note>original German: "Freyer, Freyen, Freywerber"</note> originate; see Zesi, *Lustinne*, number 69.

### 50. The Free Franks. Ansi. Ansiburi.

Among the **immediate nobles** <note>nobles who answered directly to the Holy Roman Emperor</note>, those of the Franconian region are the most prominent. Hence they are called **the Free Franks** <note>original: "die freye Francken"</note> preeminently <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν"</note>. They derive this name from liberty, for "Frey" and "freyge" mean "free." Some derive the word "Frank" from the French word ***Franc***, meaning free and immune from taxes, and "***Franciscari***" meaning to assert one's liberty. Others, while keeping this meaning, derive it from **Francus** (or Franken), a King of Germany and the founder and father of this nation. **Philipp Melanchthon** <note>A famous 16th-century German reformer and scholar</note> thinks the name "Franck" was formed from the words ***Frey*** (free) and ***Anck***, and that the word ***Anck*** signifies a servant, as if the immediate nobles were the **"free servants of the Holy Roman Empire."** Fabricius rejects this and derives "Frank" from ***Frey*** and ***Inck***. From this come the Saxon terms for nobles, free-born men, or "Iucken," which denotes inhabitants. Thus, "Francken" are nothing other than **"free peoples and inhabitants."**

Hadrianus Junius derives the origin of the Franks from ***Frey*** and ***Ansi***, as if they were **"Free Hanses"** <note>original: "freye Hansen"</note>. In my dissertation on the Imperial Cities, I argued that the **Hanseatic cities** <note>the "Hansestädte," a powerful medieval commercial confederation</note> took their name from the ancient Gothic word ***Ansi***.

This opinion is rejected by Ruland, who says that the word ***Ansi*** is specific to the Gothic language and, by many accounts, denotes those who surpass other men in fortune and wealth, being close to the condition of **Heroes**. Thus, in our native tongue, with an added "h" sound, high-ranking lords were once called ***Hansos***. Even today in **Switzerland** and the **Grisons** <note>original: "Rhaetia"</note>, the nobles and aristocrats who belong to a faction different from the common people are called ***die Hansen***. And in Lower Saxony and Westphalia, those who wish to be esteemed above their station are ironically called ***Hansi***, **"because they want to be big shots"** <note>original German: "dann sie wollen grosse Hansen seyn"</note>. Likewise, **Tacitus** <note>Roman historian</note> mentions the **Ansibarii**, whom some interpret as the ***Ansiburen***, or as we say, **"Free Noble Farmers."**

### 51. Freedom, Sanctuaries, and the Sanctuary Court.

On the specific law of **Asylums** <note>places of sanctuary where a person is protected from legal arrest</note>, a noble treatise was written by the worthy son of the most famous Mr. Rittershusius; see also Becanus *on analogy, chapter 19,* Mr. Dr. Harprecht *book 1 of the Institutes, folio 178 in the new quarto edition,* and Böckel *vision 6, question 1, folio 98.* Add also Peguera *decisions 40, 54, 58, 61 and following,* the *Practice of Archbishop Marcantonio, chapter 17,* Chockier *on Jurisdiction in exemptions, volume 1, part 4, question 65,* Zypaeus *in his analysis of Pontifical Law, folio 281 and following,* Servin *pleadings, volume 3, folio 155 and following,* and Goldast *volume 3 of Alamanic matters, folio 143.*

Can someone who is within a **Sanctuary** <note>original: "Freyheit"</note> be summoned? Valascus, in *treatise 1, consultation 81,* affirms this regarding one fleeing to a Church. However, the privileges of **Reutlingen** <note>a Free Imperial City in Germany</note> have this unique feature: that one may not execute any legal process against a person staying in such places, nor against their goods. See *my work on the Law of Majesty, folio 160.*

Should asylums be established? See Jacob Martin, *illustrious questions, century 7, dispute 1, thesis 10.* On the origin and progress of asylums, see **Hospinian**, *On Temples, book 1, final chapter.* That everyone should enjoy immunity unless they are truly deceitful, or unless they committed a crime *in the place of the crime* specifically in hopes of immunity, is taught by Covarruvias, *2. Variae, chapter 19, number 7;* Gutierrez, *Practical Questions 2, chapter 1, number 13;* and Hunger, *in his orations, part 1, folio 387.* That in **Oppenheim** in ancient times, a sanctuary <note>original: "Freyhung"</note> was established by **Charlemagne** <note>the first Holy Roman Emperor</note> for those who committed unintentional manslaughter, is evident from the *Gleanings of Palatine Antiquities, folio 21.*

According to **Canon Law** <note>Church law</note>, one fleeing to a cemetery enjoys ecclesiastical immunity; therefore, churchyards are also called **Sanctuary Courts** <note>original: "Freyheithöfe"</note>, because there is freedom near and within the churches, and most people flee to the church for safety.

<column-break/>

->ADDITION.<-

Under the name **Free Court** <note>original: "Freyhof"</note>, sometimes places exempt by a Princely veil are understood, and sometimes those which shine forth as sanctioned by the Law of Asylum or security against the death penalty. See Mr. Dr. Tabor, *on Billets, page 249.*

Whether Christians are allowed to retain Asylums: see Klock, *consultation 10, numbers 315–321,* and why they were invented, *number 324.* Regarding the Constitution of Asylums, see Nicolaus Mylerus, *on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 51.* Leibfrid and Peter Sarpi have also written on the Law of Asylums.

There was a grove nearby; this, **Romulus** <note>the legendary founder of Rome</note> made into an asylum. Florus, *book 1, chapter 1, section 9.* Plutarch in *Romulus* says: soon after the foundations of the City were cast, they opened an asylum for fugitives and runaways. Hence, this grove is "infamous" to Lucan and an "infamous asylum" to Juvenal *at the end of Satire 8.* Cyprian calls it a "people gathered from the wicked and guilty." But one must not judge this matter so precipitously. People flee to Asylums either because of **misfortune** or because of **malice**. It is right to receive the former, but the latter should be excluded. Thus in **Divine Law** <note>the Bible</note>, asylums stood open for those from whose hand a weapon had slipped, killing a man. Refuge was also given to slaves. But for one who had deliberately killed an innocent man, or who had disturbed the State of the City, not even the most holy altar of God offered protection, says **Hugo Grotius**—the miracle of our age—in *book 2, On the Law of War and Peace, chapter 21.* Therefore, why do you blame Romulus if he did not return the fugitives? For you cannot call a fugitive "guilty" or "innocent" based solely on the act of fleeing. To put it briefly, Romulus’s asylum finds its own "asylum" (defense) in **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**, who says in *book 2 of Roman Antiquities* that people flocked there from all sides fleeing domestic evils. The Law of Asylums cannot be taken from a single law nor from law alone; it is so widespread that Politicians, Theologians, Lawyers (as they call them), and Canonists all claim it for themselves. See Albericus de Rosate *on the title of the Code regarding those who flee to the Church;* Oldradus *consultation 154;* Petrus Gregorius *in his system of universal law and in book 6 on Government.* There is also a singular book by the jurist **Petri Sarpi** <note>Paolo Sarpi, a Venetian lawyer and polymath</note> *On the Law of Asylums*, translated from Italian by Angerius Frixelburgius. G. Rittershusius explains the etymology of "Asylum" in *On Asylums, page 6.* He enumerates the **Cities of Refuge** throughout Germany on *page 23.* The cautions under which Asylums ought to be tolerated are on *page 115.* Regarding Asylums, see also Otto, *page 211,* Cluten, *question 8,* and Corals, *miscellany 23.* There are also privileged **Free Assembly Courts** <note>original: "freye Dinckhöfe"</note> in **Alsace**, such as in the village of **Ensheim**. This **Assembly Court** has the freedom and the right that no court shall seek anyone therein, whether for manslaughter or for debt. Likewise, if anyone escapes into the court, man or woman, for manslaughter, for debt, or for whatever deed they have done for which they are afraid, they shall be safe in that court. And as long as they remain within it, a Bailiff and a Mayor of the aforementioned...

## 52. Barons or Free Lords.

Latin writers call them **Barones**, a name that is purely Germanic, as I have already demonstrated in the dissertation *On Counts*, etc., which is included in my treatise *On Monarchy*, folio 112. For **Bar** is nothing other than a brave man. **The Book of Heroes** <note>original: "Heldenbuch," a famous collection of medieval German epic poems</note>, part 2:

> Then the heathen woman let
> A mist go forth from her,
> Which smelled most powerfully,
> Near the very bold **Baron**,
> He feared for his honor,
> Lest he must travel with her.

->Likewise:<-

> Has any adventure
> Befallen you here in the forest?
> To him answered quickly,
> The most wretched **Baron**.

*that is, a man most worthy of pity.*

That the word **Baron**, as mentioned in the treatise *On Barons*, is also taken to mean free men or sons, is taught by Pontanus in *Frankish Origins*, folio 595, etc., and is equally evident from the aforementioned **Book of Heroes**, part 2:

> From this may you be protected,
> By the pure Maiden’s **Baron**.

*That is, the son of the Virgin, Christ.*

**Bar**, especially in derived words, increases the meaning, such as *Wonderful, Vicious, Complainable, Marriageable* <note>original: "Wunderbar, Lasterbar, Klagbar, Mannbar"</note>. **Book of Heroes** in the preface, chapter 1. Mr. Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, page 169:

> Also, no one has less honor,
> Than those who are vicious [Lasterbare], etc.

I have read this in ancient monuments: "And if this church should suffer or encounter any hail in the tithes in any year, resulting in **notable damage** <note>original: "bärlicher Schad"</note>, that is, significant loss, the Lordship shall look upon the protection rights and make a reasonable deduction according to the circumstances." Likewise elsewhere in the same place: "so that hail damage occurs which is **notable** [bärlich]," etc. It is also said "to bring no harm nor to **bear** [bären]"—to give birth or to create—and "**arising damage** [bäricher Schad]," *a loss that is coming into being*.

It is also used as **bârig**, that is, in the slightest "a **single** [bârigen] drop," meaning only a drop. Mr. Gryphiander in *The Saxon Weichbild Law*, chapter 46, interprets **Bar** as "capable"; as in *honorable* [erbar] or *notorious* [rugbar].

<column-break/>

**Man** <note>original: "Mann"</note> denotes a powerful vassal. **Book of Heroes**, part 1:

> If you wish, travel with
> Full seventy-two **Men**,
> Each has a hundred knights,
> Should you not attain it.

Likewise, in the same place, the grades of vassals are indicated:

> You Princes and you Lords,
> Counts and Free Men, Servants [Ministeriales],
> Who with great honors,
> Are subject through service.

**Baron**, a free man, a **Free Lord** [Freyherr]. Hincmar, *Letter 1*, chapter 6; see Goldast on the *Exhortations*, folios 414 and 451: "If those good **Barons** after the death of Philip," etc. Here Busæus noted that there is more than one meaning for "Baron." What it meant among the Franks in Hincmar’s century is indicated by Aimoinus, book 6, chapter 52, *On the Deeds of the Franks*: "which ruinous faction, through the zeal and discord of the **Barons**, Counts, and Nobles of the Kingdom, destroyed the land with such great calamity." Sigebert: "He took his **Chief Barons** with him along with a few others; but countless mercenary soldiers (**Soldaten**)." Krantz, book 3 of *Metropolis*, chapter 11, regarding a certain Bishop of Hildesheim: "He equated his **Servants** [Ministeriales]—who alone today wish to be called the Military class—to the city-dwellers drafted for military service; he even led them in ranks, holding them in no less esteem." But later centuries distinguished the orders of the Military and the City-dwellers, so that they no longer allow themselves to be equated. And (what is more arrogant) those who were once called **Servants** or **Vassals** now strive to be called **Nobles**. But the practice of the Princely Scribes and of all who correctly discern the duties of each rank proves their pride wrong. For first, Barons are reckoned among the nobles, then **Free Lords**, then Counts, then Dukes, whom the Pope calls "noble men." Why does a servant suffer himself to be equated with a Duke in this title of nobility?

Boerius, in the *Customs of Berry* in France, thinks those are called **Barons** who have obtained the right of low, middle, and high jurisdiction in some castle by the grant of a Prince. Flavio Biondo, book 5, decade 2: "For the leading men of the city, whom they now call Barons but then called **Captains**, were hostages to the Emperor," etc. Hector Boece, book 2 of the *History of Scotland*, says that among the Germans and Scots they are, as it were, Royal Vassals. See Hotman in the *Feudal Lexicon* and Petrus Gregorius, book 6 of the *System*, chapter 10.

In Spain and elsewhere, those are called **Barons** who are Lords of a territory and have civil jurisdiction; Cancer, *Various Resolutions*, part 3, in the Index under "Baro." See also Fontanella, *On Antenuptial Pacts*, book 1, folio 236. And in the Kingdom of Naples, he is called a **Baron** who holds a "registered fief" <note>original: "feudum quaternatum," a fief recorded in the royal quaternary or register</note> and other vassals. See the *Treasury of Neapolitan Constitutions* and Andreas de Isernia, under the word "Baro."

In ancient documents one also finds "Free Men," "**Banner-Lords**" [Banerherren], and "**Staff-Lords**" [Stabherren], that is, those who possess jurisdiction.

It should be noted here that they are called not only *Baro*, but also *Barus*. For in the Law of the Alemanni, title 96...

### 51. Liberty, Asylums, Sanctuary Court.

On the law of Asylums, the worthy son of the most celebrated Master Rittershusius has written a singular and thorough treatise; see also Becanus on *Analogy*, chapter 19. Master Doctor Harprecht, book 1 of the *Institutes*, folio 178, in the new quarto edition. Also Böckel, *Vision 6*, question 1, folio 98. Add Pegueram, decisions 40, 54, 58, 61, and following. Whether one who is within a **Liberty** <note>a legally exempt area or sanctuary</note> can be summoned? Valascus, treatise 1, counsel 81, affirms this regarding one fleeing to a Church. However, the privileges of Reutlingen have this unique feature: that one may not execute any process against such a person who stays in those places, nor against his goods. According to Canon Law, one fleeing to a **Cemetery** <note>original: "Caemiterium"</note> enjoys ecclesiastical immunity: therefore churchyards are also called **Sanctuary Courts** <note>original: "Freyheitshöfe"</note>, because there is a liberty by and in the church, and most often one flees to the church for refuge.

§. 4. It is said: if the *Baron* <note>original: "Barus"</note> was similar. From this come the terms **Baron-like** <note>original: "Barvo"</note> and **Little Baron** <note>original: "Barunculus"</note>.

There also seems to be a certain difference between *Free Men and Lords.* For the ancient style of address is: *to command all Free Men, Lords, Knights, and Servants.* And around the year 1300, ranks were distinguished as follows: *A man of free condition, a Knight, and the better sort of the Village.*

The status of Barons is indeed ancient; for in the foundation of the Monastery of Saint Gregory at Reichenbach in the year 1080, mention is made of a certain free-born elder named **Bern**, who delivered his small estate located in the Black Forest—in the place called Reichenbach after the stream that flows into the Murg—to William, the Abbot of the Hirsau Monastery. This was given as an eternal inheritance to Saint Aurelius of Hirsau in the presence of suitable witnesses, with the sole request that he should strive to build a monastery there.

In that same record, mention is often made of free men, and likewise of the noble Swabian, Bertold of Spareverrefekke. From this it appears that even then, nobles were distinguished from free men. Mention is also made of Knights (whom I take to be Vassals), and likewise of a free-born woman, even a serving-woman, who had possessed an estate and a <term>benefice</term> <note>a grant of land in exchange for service</note> by hereditary right. However, her <term>allodium</term> <note>land owned outright, without a superior landlord</note> belonged to a certain free-born woman. Mention is made of a certain noble youth, also a knight, a free man, and finally a Captain.

### 53. Free Fiefs. <note>original: "Freylehen. Feudum francum."</note>

A **Free Fief** <note>original: "Feudum francum"</note> is said to be that which is given to a Vassal in such a way that he is immune from all services; see especially Camerarius *on the Imperial law regarding the prohibition of fiefs, folio 258 and following.* It is named from the French word **Franc**, which means "free," as I have already said above. See Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 2, folio 29.* Conversely, a fief is "not free" when the Vassal performs services for the Lord on account of the fief granted to him.

However, a Vassal to whom a Free Fief has been granted is not released from the requirements of fidelity <note>the oath of fealty</note> listed in the law *on the form of fidelity*; rather, the agreement is only that the Vassal shall not perform manual or military service. Although this might seem contrary to the essence of a fief, the nature of the fief remains in other respects. He is therefore bound to keep faith with his Lord, and not only to avoid plotting against the Lord's life, but also to warn him, if possible, so that he does not fall into danger. Schneidewein, *in the introduction to fiefs, number 53,* requires two things for a fief to be "Free." (1.) That it is expressly stated in the grant that it is a Free Fief. (2.) That the person who holds such a fief is not bound to any services or burdens except those expressed in the grant. Therefore, in letters of <term>investiture</term> <note>the formal handover of a fief</note>, such words are usually added: *and they need not perform any services to us for it, just as their parents likewise performed or rendered no service to our ancestors.*

For the effects of a Free Fief, see the same Schneidewein in the cited place, number 55 and following; and add Gothofredus, *Ancient Disputations 1, thesis 7, letter l.*

---

### ADDITION.

In Normandy, in the Kingdom of France, all noble possessions, whether they be feudal or allodial <note>privately owned</note>, are called "free fiefs," because they can only be possessed by "Frankish" men—that is, by Nobles. More on these can be found in Obrecht, *Secrets of Politics, page 45.* A commoner <note>original: "Ignobilis"</note> is bound to pay a certain sum of money to the King for the privilege of holding such land.

On these, see Freher in the *Treatise on the Secret Courts in Westphalia*, where he explains what **Lords of the Chair, Free Counts, Free Jurors, and Vehmic Jurors** <note>original: "Vemeschöpffen," members of the "Fehmic" secret vigilante courts</note> are. ## 52. Barons. *Barones.*

Latin authors call Barons by a name that is surely purely Germanic, which I have already demonstrated in my dissertation on Counts, etc., which is inserted in my treatise *On Monarchy*, folio 112. For a "Bar" is nothing other than **a brave man**. *Book of Heroes* <note>original: "Heldenbuch"; a famous collection of German epic poetry</note>, part 2.

> Then the heathen woman let
> A mist go out before her,
> Which smelled most powerfully,
> By the very bold Baron,
> He feared for his honor,
> He had to travel with her.

->Also:<-

> Has no adventure befallen you
> Here in this forest?
> To him answered quickly,
> The most wretched Baron.

That is, a man most worthy of pity.

The word "Baren" is also taken to mean "children" or "sons," as noted in the mentioned treatise on Barons; Pontanus teaches this in *Frankish Origins*, folio 595, etc., and it is equally clear from the aforementioned *Book of Heroes*, part 2.

> From this may you be protected by
> The pure Maiden’s Son. <note>original: "Der reine Magde Baren"</note>

That is, the son of the Virgin, Christ.

The root "Bar," especially in its derivatives, strengthens the meaning, such as *Wunderbar* (wonderful), *Lasterbar* (vicious/shameful), *Klagbar* (actionable), *Mannbar* (manly/marriageable). *Book of Heroes* in the preface, chapter 1. Doctor Saubert, *On Sacrifice*, page 169.

> Also, no one has less honor,
> Than those who are full of vice [Lasterbare], etc.

Thus I have read in ancient records: "And if some year any damage should occur to the tithes of this church by hail—a **notable loss** [bärlicher Schad] <note>original: "notabile damnum"</note>—then the lordship shall look upon the bailiff-right and, according to the state of affairs, grant a reasonable deduction." Also elsewhere in the same place: "so that hail-damage occurs which is notable [bärlich]," etc. It is also said: "to bring or **bear** [bären/gebären] no harm," and "notable loss" [bärlicher Schad] means a loss that arises or is manifest.

The term "bärig" is also used, meaning "in the slightest," as in "a single drop" [ein bärigen Tropffen]. Master Gryphiander, *On the Saxon Municipal Law* <note>original: "Weichbb." refers to Weichbildrecht</note>, chapter 46. He interprets "Bar" as "capable" [capax]; as in "honorable" [erbar] or "notorious" [rugbar].

<column-break/>

"Man" [Mann] denotes a powerful vassal. *Book of Heroes*, part 1.

> If you wish, then travel with
> Full seventy-two men,
> Each has a hundred knights,
> If you will not allow them this.

The degrees of vassals are also indicated in the same place:

> You Princes and you Lords,
> Counts and Freemen, Servants,
> Who with great honors,
> Are subject through service.

**A Baron is a free man.** <note>original: "Baro, homo liber, Freyherr"</note> Hincmar, *Epistle 1*, chapter 6. See Goldast, *Admonitions*, folios 414 and 451. "If those good Barons after the death of Philip," etc. Here Busæus noted that there is more than one meaning for "Baron." Aimonius indicates what the meaning was among the Franks in Hincmar's century in *Deeds of the Franks*, book 6, chapter 52: "Which ruinous faction, through the zeal and diversity of the Barons, Counts, and Nobles of the Kingdom, extinguished the land with such great calamity." Sigebert wrote: "He took his Chief Barons with him, along with a few others; but of hired soldiers [Soldaten], he took countless numbers." Krantz, in *Metropolis*, book 3, chapter 11, says of a certain Bishop of Hildesheim: "He made his Ministerials <term>Ministeriales; unfree nobles who served in administrative or military roles</term>—who alone wish to be called 'Military Men' today—equal to the city-dwellers drafted for military service, whom he even led in the ranks, holding them as nothing less." But later centuries distinguished the orders of the Military and the City-dwellers, so that now they do not allow themselves to be equalized with them. And (what is more arrogant) those who were once called Ministerials or feudatories now strive to be called "Nobles." But the practice of the Princely Scribes and all who correctly discern the duties of each rank proves their pride wrong. For first, Barons are reckoned among the nobles, then Free Lords, then Counts, and then Dukes, whom the Pope calls "noble men." Why does a Ministerial think he can be made equal to a Duke in this title of nobility?

Boerius, on the customs of Berry in France, thinks those are called Barons who have obtained the right of the lowest, middle, and highest jurisdiction in some fortress by the grant of the Prince. Flavius Blondus, book 5, decision 2: "For the primary men of the city, whom they then called Captains, they now call Barons." Hector Boece, in his *History of Scotland*, book 2, says that among the Germans and Scots they are essentially Royal Vassals. See Hotman in his *Feudal Lexicon* and Petrus Gregorius, book 6 of the *Syntagma*, chapter 10.

In Spain and elsewhere, those are called Barons who are lords of a territory and have civil jurisdiction. Cancer, *Various Resolutions*, part 3, in the index under "Baro." See also Fontanella, *On Antenuptial Pacts*, folio 236. And in the Kingdom of Naples, he is called a Baron who holds a registered fief and other vassals. See the *Neapolitan Treasury of Constitutions* and Andreas de Isernia under "Baro."

In ancient legal instruments, one also finds "Freemen," "Banner-lords," and "Staff-lords," meaning those who possess jurisdiction.

It should be noted here that it is not only called *Baro*, but also *Barus*. For in the *Law of the Alamanni*, title 96, section 4...

### 56. Free Imperial Knighthood. see Knighthood, below under the letter R. Immediate Nobility of the Holy Roman Empire.

It also has the strong appearance that, since the Princes were invested with entire territories and all their honors, they thus also obtained all jurisdiction over the Nobles settled therein. From which it seems further to follow that when Franconia and Swabia still had powerful Dukes, the current free Knighthood were their immediate subjects and had only modest powers of coercion. ### 53. Free Fiefs. *Feudum francum.*

A free fief (**Freylehen**) is so called because it is given to a Vassal in such a way that he is immune from all services. *See especially* **Camerarius** *on the Imperial Law regarding the prohibition of fiefs*, page 258, following sections. It is named from the French word **Franc**, which means "free," as I have already said above. *See* **Guyon**, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 2, page 29. Conversely, a fief is "not free" when the Vassal performs services for the Lord on account of the fief granted to him.

However, a Vassal to whom a Free Fief has been granted is not released from the chapters of loyalty <note>the "formula fidelitatis," a standard oath of allegiance</note>, but it is merely understood that the Vassal shall not perform manual or military service. Although this may seem contrary to the substance of a fief, the nature of a fief remains in other respects. He is therefore bound to keep faith with his Lord, and not only to refrain from plotting against the Lord’s life, but also to warn him, if possible, lest he fall into danger. **Schneidewin**, *in the Preludes on Fiefs*, number 53; who, for a fief to be "Free," requires two things: (1) That it is expressly stated in the grant that it is a Free Fief. (2) That he who holds such a fief is not bound to any services or burdens except those expressed in the grant. Therefore, in letters of Investiture <note>legal documents granting a fief</note>, such words are usually added: *and need not perform any services for us, just as their parents performed no services for our ancestors.*

For the effects of a Free Fief, see the same **Schneidewin**, at the mentioned place, number 55 and following, and add **Gothofredus Antonii**, *Disputation 1, Thesis 7, letter l.*

### ADDITION.

In Normandy, in the Kingdom of France, all Noble possessions—whether they be feudal or allodial—are called "free fiefs," because they can only be possessed by "Frankish" men, that is, Nobles. More on these in **Obrecht**, *Political Secrets*, page 45. A non-noble <note>original: "Ignobilis"</note> is bound to pay a certain sum of money to the King for the "patience" <note>a fee for the king's permission/tolerance for a commoner to hold noble land</note> of the tenure.

### 56. Free Imperial Knighthood. See Knighthood, below under the letter R. Immediate Nobility of the Holy Roman Empire.

That the free **Immediate Nobility** <term>Immediate Nobility; nobles who answered directly to the Emperor rather than a local prince</term> of the Holy Empire is an Estate of the Holy Roman Empire, is proven in a certain treatise printed at Mainz in the year 1626. But for what I once collected on this matter, see my individual treatise *On the Free Equestrian Order*, which is now inserted into my treatise *On Monarchy, etc.*, folio 159. Various privileges for the preservation of the free **Equestrian Status** have emanated from the Emperor: among others, it is to be understood from the Privileges most graciously granted by the current Roman Imperial Majesty and his predecessors of the most glorious memory (from the years 1566, 1578, 1601, and 1620) to the common Knighthood in Swabia, that all Estates, High and Low, Spiritual and Secular, who at the time of the granting of Imperial Freedom already held noble estates or their dependencies for themselves or through their subordinates, or should later obtain them, shall continue to represent those same estates and dependencies within the Knight-

<column-break/>

-hood, even if someone—whoever they may be—wished to put forward another precedent and custom, or any freedom and right, exemption, statute, order, transaction, or compact against this; all of which shall be derogated <note>repealed or annulled</note> by the power and fullness of the Roman Imperial Majesty. It is also such that they may redeem sold estates. See my *Decisions*, decade 3, counsel 1. Likewise, that the **blood justice** <term>blood justice; the power to try capital crimes involving the death penalty</term> is not to be separated from the estates, see my counsel 4, decision 1.

The Knighthood also initially collected taxes <note>original: "collectirt"</note> on the goods of others located in their territories, not because those goods were free, but because the possessors, as Citizens of the Equestrian Order, contributed for the goods located in foreign territories; see me in decade 3, Counsel. Thereafter they also forced these burdens onto other goods located in foreign territories.

And in Swabia, the Nobles formerly held everything and served the Emperor in nothing; see Felix Fabri in *Swabia*, chapter 12, folio 102.

What the power of the Equestrian Order once was appears from the deeds of **Franz von Sickingen**, who defied <note>original: "gepochet"; challenged or intimidated</note> the entire Roman Empire. See the *Sickingen War*. Some wish to believe that after the Roman Empire reached the Germans in former times, and especially after **feudal laws** arose, all Nobles were subject to the Counts or other Higher Estates, both in terms of person and property, regarding Jurisdiction, because **Valvasini** <note>vassals of a lord</note>, according to Feudal Law, are invested by **Valvassores** <note>vassals of a vassal</note>; as Cujacius notes in book 2, title 10, that the true definition of Nobles is included there. From which it further seems to follow that when Franconia and Swabia still had powerful Dukes, the current free Knighthood were their immediate subjects and had only modest powers of coercion. 60. Clause: **Voluntarily, with deliberation and good knowledge, unforced, and unconstrained. Of one’s own accord, and from certain knowledge.** <note>original: "Freywillig, mit Vorbedacht und guter Wissenschafft, ungezwungen, ungedrungen. Sponte, ex certa scientia."</note>

The word *sponte* <note>meaning: "of one's own accord"</note> carries the same weight as the word "voluntarily" (Code of Justinian, *On testamentary guardianship*). It also implies acting "freely," because a person is not considered to act of their own accord if they do so under the compelling power of another's command. When someone promises of their own accord, force and fear are considered excluded (Code, *If against a sale*). Words of this kind argue for a free will, and through the word "freely," every impediment or contradiction is removed. (Natta, *Counsel* 530; Tiraquellus, *On the law of revocation of donations*; Surdus, *Decisions* 265 and 272). This means the act is subject to no necessity. This clause is commonly added to legal instruments: **and this voluntarily, unforced, and unconstrained, as well as with deliberation and good knowledge, etc.** This clause ensures that the contracting parties are not allowed to later claim any ignorance or error. For it is presumed that the parties contracted while led by no ignorance and no error. (Bartolus and the Doctors of Law). Therefore, he who says he contracted knowingly and from certain knowledge is not admitted to the excuse of error. For just as a face appears in a mirror, so does the will reside in words (Baldus, *Counsel* 102). Everything that is expressed in words is considered to have been thought of beforehand. For according to Aristotle, words are the marks and signs of those passions which are in the soul. And for that reason, Baldus says that in clear words, nothing should be added or taken away.

Besoldus Volume I.

<column-break/>

Regarding the Clause: *by no error of law or fact, nor by ignorance,* see Bertazolus, clause 11, glosses 3 and 4.

It must be observed, however, that these clauses are not of such great weight that one is forbidden to speak against them. Firstly, because these clauses are most often added out of the standard habit of Notaries, and therefore they achieve little on their own (according to the teaching of Bartolus and Hering). Furthermore, these clauses only function in cases of doubt, when fear is not established; but when fear is truly justified, they are of no efficacy. This is because the same fear that induces someone to enter a contract also induces them to affirm it in this way. (Hondedeus, *Consultation* 23). For the same reason, those additional clauses usually added suffer from the same defect. <note>The legal logic here is that if someone is being threatened into signing a contract, they are likely also being threatened into saying they are signing it "voluntarily." Therefore, the word "voluntary" shouldn't be taken as absolute proof of freedom if evidence of threats exists.</note>

## ADDITION.
Whether the "vice of fear" is purged by the word *sponte* being placed in an instrument. See Justus Oldekop in *Criminal Observations*, title 4, observation 11, at the end.

To this relates the Clause: *motu proprio* <term>motu proprio; a legal term meaning "by one's own motion" or "on one's own initiative," often used for edicts issued by a Pope or Monarch without a formal request from others</term>, regarding which see Klock, Oldekop, and others. A person who acts "knowingly" is equated with one who renounces or gives up their property and rights of action, from which no retreat is given. The word **voluntarily** <note>original: "freywillig"</note> is understood in two ways (Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 4).

The question is asked: Can a Prince’s "own motion" and "petitions" <note>requests from subjects</note> exist at the same time? Indeed, some believe these can stand together—that the Prince was petitioned, and yet acted by his own motion, as if he were inclined not by the force of the prayers, but by himself (Felinus and Baldus). However, for this to be possible, a certain presumption and suspicion always remains unless the contrary is most clearly established. Enenckel, therefore, denies this question and says that while all those clauses about "certain knowledge" can and usually are added to Rescripts <term>rescript; a written answer from a ruler or religious leader to a query or petition</term> given at a request, it cannot be done with the "own motion" clause, unless we wish to introduce repugnant and contradictory things into the same subject.

# 61. Free Will and Pleasure.
## Free and Full Discretion, Approval.

A judge having free and full discretion to decide, to whom the matter is left to his free and complete will, good judgment, and discretion, cannot—by reason of that free discretion—punish, except in so far as justice would suggest. <note>original: "liberum & plenum arbitrium." In this context, "free will" refers to judicial discretion—the power of a judge to make decisions based on fairness rather than a rigid, pre-set penalty.</note> Baldus notes this in the law *ubi pactum* <note>A reference to Baldus de Ubaldis, a famous 14th-century legal scholar, commenting on the Code of Justinian regarding settlements.</note>. He says that such discretion, since it tends toward the harm of a third party, must be understood as a will that contains equity within itself; he cannot prefer the equal to the unequal. This goes so far that if a judge or magistrate, by reason of this "free discretion," harms a party enormously and unjustly, he ought to be rightfully punished. For an unfair judgment is not considered to have been given to a judge (per the law *creditor* at the end, in the section on mandates); nor by the power of discretion can he condemn someone who should be acquitted, or vice versa. Nor can he condemn unless the crime is established and a full opportunity for defense has been given. <note>original: "copiâ defensionis." This highlights the legal principle of "due process" even when a judge has "free discretion."</note> The scholar Pasif. de Puteo, in his treatise on the <term>Syndic</term> <note>A syndic was a legal representative or official of a corporation or town.</note>, says that one having free discretion cannot condemn against justice or simply use his own whim. Baldus further teaches that discretion given to a Power <note>A high-ranking official or ruler.</note> is understood to apply to the investigation of the case, not the final decision-making: so much so that he can do nothing outside of justice, nor can he, even by the power of general discretion, rush through a whole trial in a single day. For a judgment that is too hurried cannot be considered well-weighed. Indeed, speed that excludes the examination of the cause is seen as excluded by the law itself. A similar point can be seen in the *Legal Response* regarding a case of testamentary succession and a <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>A legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of another, similar to a modern trust.</note> in Strasbourg in the year 1646.

So too, the power of a King, however absolute, is to be understood as the discretion of a "good man." <note>original: "arbitrio boni viri." This is a standard legal benchmark in Roman law, meaning the decision a reasonable, honest, and fair person would make.</note>

### ADDITION.

The clause "at the pleasure of his own will" implies a free and absolute discretion limited by no rules of law. (See the legal experts on the law *Si sic* 75 regarding Legacies). 

Free discretion over one's own affairs ought to be permitted to everyone (Code, *on mandates*). Limit this, however, in those cases where it concerns the Republic; for for the sake of public utility, men are often compelled to sell or retain their own property. <note>This refers to early concepts of "eminent domain," where private rights yield to the common good.</note> Free discretion implies a free faculty or power. Regarding when and by what words free or regulated discretion is said to be granted to a judge by the law or by a person, see Barbosa. It is not enough for someone to have the free and full faculty of making a will, unless he also testifies according to the norm and prescription of the law. <note>original: "secundum Regulas Juris Civ." Even if one is "free" to make a will, they must still follow the legal formalities of Civil Law.</note> For more on this, see the Strasbourg Response in the case of the alleged trust by Leon Burian Bercka.

# 62. Peace, Peace Negotiations.
## Peace, Negotiations of peace.

Regarding Peace, see the goddess *Themis* <note>Themis was the Greek personification of divine law and order.</note>, and Neumair’s individual treatise, and my own work on Politics; also Hugo Grotius’s *On the Law of War and Peace*, and Mantica on silent and ambiguous agreements.

Can the damages inflicted on subjects when making peace be waived by a Prince without their consent? See Schleiff on this question.

### ADDITION.

On not accepting any peace treaty or atonement, see Limnaeus. Peace, Union, and Atonement. The constitution of the **Peace of Westphalia** is to be held as a fundamental law of the Empire. <note>The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the Thirty Years' War and fundamentally reshaped the Holy Roman Empire's legal structure.</note> Boecler and Limnaeus both discuss this. Conring wrote a small book on the "Perpetual Peace to be served between the orders of the German Empire differing in religion." Bernegger wrote the *Trumpet of Peace*.

True peace is the settling of discords; it is the deprivation of war. For the sake of the good of peace, many things are tolerated which otherwise would be prohibited. Peace is not sought so that war may be stirred up, but war is waged so that peace may be acquired. <note>original: "Pax non quæritur, ut bellum excitetur, sed bellum geritur, ut pax acquiratur." This is a classic Augustinian justification for "Just War."</note> For the wars of good men are waged out of a desire for peace, not out of cruelty or greed. **Letter of Peace** (*Friedbrieff*); offenders brought before a magistrate are bound to **vow the peace** (*den Frieden geloben*). Related to this is the *Historical Account of Truces and Peace* between the Austrians and Spanish on one side, and the French on the other, published by Leonard Wurffbain in 1644, covering the years 1477 to 1598 (repeated 22 times). An unjust peace is considered more useful than a most just war (Cicero). Sallust says: "The Republic must be strengthened not only by arms, but—what is much greater and much harsher—by the good arts of peace." Indeed, Tacitus notes that Tiberius was happier because he had strengthened peace through wisdom than if he had finished a war by the sword. War is profitable sometimes; Peace is profitable always. Just as the solitary star of Helen <note>A reference to the "St. Elmo's Fire" or a single star seen by sailors, which in classical mythology (specifically Horace) was seen as a bad omen of storms, whereas the "Gemini" stars brought calm.</note> does not please sailors, so war displeases us.

# Augmented Treasury of Practical Knowledge

### On the term "Frohn" (Lordly Service)

The term is applied to things, for example, **it is a socage estate** <note>original: "es ist ein Frohngut"; a property held in exchange for labor rather than rent</note>, and to persons, as in **he is a socage-laborer or socage-peasant** <note>original: "er ist ein Frohner vel Frohnbauer"</note> according to Meichsner, *Decisions of the Imperial Chamber, volume 5, tome 2, pages 188 and 280.* However, in my *Treatise on the three types of domestic society*, I teach that **Frohn** signifies **common** or **public** <note>original: "gemein"</note>, *page 32, number 5.*

Thus, a **Frohn-prison** <note>original: "Frohnfest"</note> is a public or common jail, which the Italian doctors of law call *Fortezza* <note>meaning a place of "Force" or a "Fortress"</note>, as noted by Peregrinus in *On the Right of the Treasury, book 3, chapter 2, number 10 and following.* In Bavaria, this is called the **Frohn** or **statute labor** <note>original: "Scharwerck"; compulsory labor performed by a tenant for a lord</note>, *Newburg Provincial Liberties, folio 16.*

### On Services (Operae)

**Services** are a daily duty, or **day-service** <note>original: "Tagdienst"</note>, because they are performed by light and during the day: *Law 1, regarding the services of freedmen; Law 2, regarding annual legacies.* That is, from morning until evening, as long as there is light. *Gloss on Law 1 and Law 3 "Services," in the beginning, Digest on the services of freedmen.* This corresponds closely to the words of David in *Psalm 104, verse 23*: **The sun rises, man goes forth to his work, and to his labor until the evening.** These services are divided into **official** and **artificial (or craft-based)**. *Law 26 "If not strong," section 12 "Freedman," on the recovery of undue payments.* **Official services** are those that consist of the duty of the person and relate to the person of the Master, such as being present or accompanying him. *Law 16 "Of that craft," section "Such"; Law 20 "Which unless"; Law "These finally," section 1, on the services of freedmen.* **Craft-based** or **artificial services** are those performed through some skill, such as painting, writing, etc. *Law 65 "Legacies," on legacies, book 3.*

**Peasants**, however, are compelled to provide services by reason and consideration of their lands, which they acknowledge as being held by the grace of their nobles. Matthias Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 2, member 2, number 192.* Husanus in *Treatise on Serfs, question 4, beginning, conclusion 1, number 89.* Indeed, these services are regarded by some as a fruit of Jurisdiction <note>the right of the lord to administer justice over the land</note>. Vultejus, *Marburg Consultations 30, number 208, volume 2.* Andreas Gail, *Book 2 on Arrests, chapter 10, number 2.*

However, one should hardly agree with them: since these services arise more from **agreement**, or from **prescription** <note>long-standing custom having the force of law</note>, Thomas Maul, *On Homage, title 4, number 2 and following*; Caspar Ziegler, *in the section "Nobles," conclusion 1, number 51*; or from the **concession** of the Prince along with the investiture of those services, rather than from the nature of Jurisdiction itself. Moller, *Semestria book 2, chapter 32, number 1.* Knichen, *On Investiture Pacts, part 2, chapter 3, number 30.*

Truly, it is a matter of established Law that Jurisdiction—whether high or low—has nothing in common with the duties and services of peasants (especially of one's own people), unless those services are owed by some other right or are expressly granted in the Investitures. Moller, *Semestria book 2, chapter 32, number 1*; and Knichen, *On Investiture, part 3, number 1.*

The origin of these services began initially from agreement, when the farmer, having received a farmstead <note>original: "mansus"</note>, obligated himself to these or those duties. *Municipal Law, article 3, section "towards a dissolution"* <note>original: "Weichbild. art. 3. §. zu einer Auflösung"</note>. Jacob de Saint-George, *rubric on Rents and Services, number 5.* Coler, *On Executive Process.*

<column-break/>

part 1, chapter 9, number 66 and following; see Ziegler, *in the cited place, number 62 and following.*

It is asked: does a prescription <note>a permanent legal obligation</note> arise from services performed several times? It is answered that one must look at the intent with which it is done. For if it is proven to be done by request <note>original: "precario"; a temporary favor that can be revoked</note>, no servitude can be inferred from it. For possession is not proven through a revocable request. Angelus *on Law "A certain woman," number 1, on the recovery of property.* Aretinus *on Law "Sometimes," at the end of the beginning, number 3, on the acquisition of possession.* Also, no prejudice is caused to the person performing a voluntary act. *Law "Voluntary," on the excuses of tutors.* And things given by revocable request ought not to be turned into a necessity. Albinus *on Law "If a Father," section "If anyone," number 6, on donations.* See Modestinus Pistoris, *part 1, question 38.*

There is a twofold division of these services, according to the aforementioned Ziegler, *at the cited place, number 55*: First, regarding the **manner** of exercise and performance, they are divided into **Wagon-services and Hand-services** <note>original: "Wagendienste & Handdienste"</note>. Those peasants who possess enough land to support plow animals—horses or oxen—**Draft-beasts, horses or oxen** <note>original: "Zugviehe, Pferd oder Ochsen"</note>, perform rural services with their beasts; these are called **smallholders, hitchers, or horse-peasants** <note>original: "Hübner, Anspenner, Pferdner"</note>. For what refers to **Plowing-services**, see *below under the word Plowing-services* <note>original: "Pflugdienste"</note>. The poorer ones, however, who do not have a full farmstead or hide of land, are bound at least to manual services or **Hand-services** <note>original: "Handdienste"</note>. They apply their labor to **manual socage, cutting grain, making hay** <note>original: "Handfrohnen, Getraid abschneiden, Heue machen"</note>, carrying letters, and working with flax, manure, dunging, threshing crops, hunting, and building or repairing structures. Indeed, whatever manual labor exists anywhere, the **cotters** <note>original: "Kottneri"</note> are bound to provide it. Ferrarius Montanus, *book 6 on Fiefs, chapter 3, section "Ordinary."* They are called **cottagers, cotters, cot-settlers, manual-laborers, day-laborers, or gardeners** <note>original: "Hintersiedler, Kötner, Kottsassen, Handfrohner, Söldner, Gärtner"</note>. Husanus *on Personal Servitude, chapter 6, number 66.* Köppen, *Decision 13, number 1.* Ritter, *On Homage, chapter 7, number 14.*

Secondly, regarding quantity, they are distributed into determined, or **fixed and measured services** <note>original: "gesezte und gemessene Dienst"</note>, *Law 24 "As often as," Digest on the services of freedmen.* Specifically, that they ought to serve the Lord and perform services once a month, or once a week, or so many times a year, with a plow or with a wagon—**named socage-days, harvest-, hay-, and May-days** <note>original: "benannte Frohntag, Schnitt- Heu- und Maytag"</note>. Gail, *Observation 62, number 12.* Moreover, services are called "certain" not regarding their substance (for then, because they consist of an act, all are uncertain: *Law 75, section 7, Digest on Verbal Obligations; Law 72, section "Celsus," in the same place*), but regarding their number and quality; for example, when harvest-work or plowing-work is ordered for a certain number of days. For not all of us can do all things. Finally, there are indeterminate services, or **unmeasured, daily services** <note>original: "ungemessene, alltägliche Dienst"</note>, which depend on the will of the lords and must be performed as often as they are demanded. See especially Ritter, *On Homage, chapter 7, number 150 and following.* Gail, *On Arrest, chapter 2, number...*

<margin>
number 2. and book 2, observation 62, number 11. Matthias Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, part 1, chapter 7, member 2, number 163.
