But it must be carefully noted here what Gylman writes in *Decisions of the Imperial Chamber*, book 1, decision 12, number 33, regarding **unmeasured service** <note>original: "ungesehene Frohn"; labor that is not strictly quantified by days or hours</note>. This does not mean that it extends to infinity or that the peasants are held to provide it at all times. Rather, it is sufficient to understand it as applying to specific works and specific labor—not only on a fixed day, but whenever the work is necessary—and it is restricted to customary and usual services, **as it has come down from olden times** <note>original: "wie es von Alters herkommen"</note>. See also and add Ziegler at the cited place, number 56 and following, throughout, where he demonstrates the matter of services copiously. Also see Sixtinus, *On Regalia*, chapter 13, number 49; Zasius in law 26, paragraph 12, *Digest on the recovery of what was not due*; and book 1 of his *Individual Responses*, chapter 2, number 83. In that work, he says that peasants provide these services either according to Court Pacts—which the common people call a **labor contract** <note>original: "Dingnotul"</note>, containing the entire law owed to the Lord and by the peasants themselves—or according to regional custom. He complains that these pacts are strictly observed insofar as they favor the Lords; he wishes they were observed just as strictly in those parts where the rights of the common peasants are described. He also mentions **full regional customary service** <note>original: "völlige Landübliche Dienst"</note>. See Joachim Scheplitz on the *Brandenburg Constitutions*, part 2, title 7, paragraph 52.

And it should be noted here that a lord cannot compel his man to go and perform **transport services** <note>original: "Roydas"; likely related to "Reise" or road-work/hauling</note> outside the territory and jurisdiction of the Lord. Jacobus de Sancto Georgio, *On Transport*, number 7, where he adds the reasoning and the text. See Valentin Forster, *Treatise on Jurisdiction*, part 2, folio 471, and number 173; Rosacorb in *Practica*, chapter 37, number 43; *Precedents of the Imperial Chamber*, under the word "Royde," paragraph "outside territory"; Ziegler in the section "On Nobles," conclusion 1, number 141; Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 71, number 5; Moller, *Semestria*, book 2, chapter 32.

Suppose, however, **it were set down in the labor contract that the subjects must drive and serve the Lord wherever he wishes** <note>original: "es wäre in der Dingnotul gesetzt, daß dem Herrn die Unterthanen, wohin er will, fahren und frohnen müssen"</note>. I do not think this should be understood indefinitely, but should be restricted: **that the subjects must drive even outside the borders, but only for the utility and convenience of the territory itself.** It should **not apply when the Lord has separate and far-distant castles where one does not depend on the other.** This is especially true **since the castle and service in dispute are held as a fief** <note>original: "Lehenbar"</note>, **where it is not presumed that the feudal service is intended for any other purpose than the preservation and improvement of that specific fief.** Therefore, **the inhabitants of a feudal castle are not required to serve in another castle, nor for its benefit. Yet it would be fair, if the Lord does not need the subjects in that specific place, that they provide him a recompense in exchange, or perform service elsewhere provided it is without loss to them.** And in any event, even if these words **"to all places whatsoever"** are noted, the subjects—because of the uncertainty and to avoid being too heavily burdened—could request a determination and specific days, based on the judgment of a good man, as is the law in all matters involving indefinite services, even if one were settled for daily—
<meta>catchword: daily—</meta>

<column-break/>

—service. See my *Treatise on the three types of domestic society*, where I discuss servants.

Regarding peasants obligated to cultivate three or four pieces of land under the formula: **three or four types [of plots], to plow and to plant when and how it is necessary, etc.** <note>original: "drey oder vier Arten, wann und wie es vonnöthen, zu ackern u. zu bestellen, etc."</note>. If for thirty whole years they have cultivated only two pieces, whether they can still be urged to cultivate three or four: see Andreas Schäffer, *Practical Questions*, part 3, question 43.

If a peasant says that he has provided services by request <note>original: "precariò"; out of favor or temporarily</note> for some time, while the Lord conversely claims he demanded them as his right: upon which of them does the burden of proof lie in case of doubt? See Moller, book 4, *Semestria*, chapter 38.

Regarding compulsory transport <note>original: "angariis"; a term for forced postal or hauling service</note>, see Drusius, *Observations*, book 1, chapter 38, *Exotic Words of the New Testament*, folio 85; and Peter Gregory of Toulouse, *On Benefits*, chapter 6, number 10. That the ancient compulsory services of the Jews are still observed in Turkey is testified by Sansovino, folio 70.

## ADDITION.

**On the Public Prison** <note>original: "Frohnvest"</note>, Besold in *Politics*, book 1, chapter 10, number 63. Volume 1, **on the serving and lordly service of subjects** <note>original: "von fröhnen und Frohndienst der Unterthanen"</note>. Gothofredus Antonii, *Disputations on Fiefs*, page 121. Zorer, part 2, question 9, number 674 and following. On the privileges of peasants: Renatus Choppinus. These services or "Frohnen" are either determined or undetermined. They are rural if performed with draft animals. They are either fixed or unfixed; they are called **wagon-service** <note>original: "Wagendienst"</note> when provided for the sake of the estates. All these are discussed at length by Mundius, *On Duties and Honors*, under the letter O.

Services and provisions should be demanded in war rather than money. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 57.

The services of peasants are called **Frohndienst** from the word for "Sacred," as if it were a remuneration for the "sacred liberty" which happened through manumission <note>freeing of a servant</note>. For the ancient word **Frohn** signifies the same thing as the word "Sacred." Thus, a **court messenger** <note>original: "Frohnbott"</note> is so called as if he were a "sacred messenger." Instead of "frommen Boden," one should read **Frohnboten**, the messenger or traveler of the court, who is also simply called **Frohn** in some places. Freher, *On Secret Courts*, page 30. To the ancient Alemanni, **Frohn** was the same as common, public, or popular. Hence the compounds **Frohn-fast** (prison), **Frohn-cross**, **Frohn-enclosure**, **Frohn-tithe**, so that even from this, in many places, "serving" <note>original: "fröhnen"</note> is said of servants when they perform common and owed services for their lords. **Frohn** sometimes signifies a court; thus **Frohnbott**, that is, a **servant of the court** <note>original: "Gerichtsknecht"</note>, and **Frohngewalt**, judicial power. The **court messenger**, who in some places is called the "holy messenger," **that is, the beadle** <note>original: "Büttel"</note>, for a two-fold reason: 1. because according to the custom of the place he swears to his office on holy things, 2. because he is a minister of God. See Besold in *Politics*, under the word "Frohndienst" and the word "Services of Peasants." Indefinite services, **unmeasured statute labor** <note>original: "ohngemessene Scharwerck"</note>, how they are to be understood and reduced to the judgment of a good man: Zorer, part 1, question 11, number 800 and following. What must be considered in the imposition and extraction of services: number 803 and following. **What statute labor the subjects must do during times of war.**

Related to this, see no. 667. Caution regarding omissions and additions, no. 668. Whether the **Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus"</note> is bound to make an inventory when it succeeds to vacant goods, see *Bocerus on Regalia*, chapter 3, no. 34 and following. The possessor of a **testamentary trust** <note>original: "fideicommissum"; a legal arrangement where property is held for another's benefit</note> is bound to draw up an inventory, *Knipsch. on Trusts*, chapter 12, no. 8. He who is bound to render an account is also obligated to create an inventory; likewise in chapter 12, no. 9. When the creation of an inventory is waived by the testator, the description of the goods is nonetheless not considered waived; chapter 12, no. 15, 16, and 33. A son is also bound to provide a description of the goods; chapter 12, no. 43. An inventory is a necessary precursor, the head and foundation of rendering an account, discussed extensively in *Altdorff Consultations*, folio 4, at the end of section 5. Where the ward's goods are meager, an inventory is not necessary; *Sprenger on Modest Means*, folio 101. Regarding the right of sealing and creating inventories, see *Nicolaus Everhardus Junior, Consultation* 47, volume 1. An inventory creates a legal presumption against a Tutor and Curator <note>different types of legal guardians for minors</note>, *Menochius*, book 6, preface 97, no. 1, with no. 8 and following, where a distinction is also made. *Neapolitan Decisions* 13, no. 1. For more on the inventory and to what extent it serves as proof, see *Neapolitan Decisions* 324, no. 13. A more "Latinate" word for inventory is **Repertory** <note>original: "Repertorium"</note>, law 7 of the *Digest on the administration of tutors*. *Dr. Rebhan on Inventories*, section 7, no. 1, notes that its creation is an authority of Public Law, which a private person cannot override; for if this were permitted, as *Lucas de Penna* wittily warns, an inventory might degenerate from "finding" into "lying" <note>original: "inventarium ab inveniendo... fiat inventarium à mentiendo"; a pun on the Latin 'invenire' (to find) vs 'mentiri' (to lie)</note>. At Wolkersdorf, in a criminal case, Brandenburg assumed the right of annotating the goods, which was accepted here as an inventory and guardianship ordinance; regarding which matter Brandenburg desired to make no entry. In the **Inventory of George II, the Rich** in the year 1547, there stands the testator’s command that all his belongings and goods be faithfully described and inventoried, but yet not brought before the authorities, but rather remain in secret only among his guardians; also, his wife's offer of an oath was to be fully believed, and no one, except his children and heirs, should be given a copy at their expense. The creation of an **Inventory** cannot be waived by a testator; *Eberhard Fabricius in Gail Enucleated*, book 2, observation 145, section 2. For the creation of an inventory, the hereditary creditors must be summoned, as well as the legatees and beneficiaries of trusts, whose interest it is to be present at the creation of the inventory if they so wish; *Pacius, Analysis of the Code*, page 641. Regarding how the swearing of inventories before a court should be handled in N., the *Welser Court Ordinance* should be read. Within the three months prescribed by law for completing an inventory, no execution of judgment takes place against the heirs; *Dr. Rebhan, Disputation on the Benefit of Inventory*, part 1, member 1, section 2. *Boerius, Decision* 53, no. 3.

# 72. Foundlings, or Foundling House. Abandoned infants.

Whether infants publicly abandoned, found, and raised (**Foundlings**) <note>original: "Fündling"</note> should be considered and judged as legitimate children, or rather as illegitimate, spurious, and bastards—specifically to the effect of whether they can be legally admitted and promoted to successions, honors, dignities, and ecclesiastical or civil offices? See *Eberhard Speckhan*, century 3, question 14, class 5; *Paleotti on the illegitimate and spurious*, chapter 63.

Regarding such abandoned children and orphanages—**Foundling Houses**—many authors treat them, including *Carranza in his treatise on natural and legitimate birth*, folio 310; also *Zierez, Matthaeus Stephani, and Bullae* in their commentaries on the *Criminal Court Ordinance of Charles V*, article 132. Regarding the method of the Amsterdam Orphanage institution and its decrees and statutes, see *Isaac Pontanus*, book 2 of *Matters of the City of Amsterdam*, chapter 2, folio 68 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

Orphanages <note>original: "Orphanotrophia"</note> have pupils who are minors destitute of parents and means. See the Code of Justinian, *On Bishops and Clergy*. Foundling hospitals <note>original: "Brephotrophia"</note> contain infants, especially those abandoned. *Schönborn in Politics*, page 283. Whichever official <note>original: "Besitzer"</note> stays away without the judge's permission, and arrives before the quarter-hour has run out, shall give two pennies; if he arrives before the second hour of the third part of the hour has passed, one shilling in gold; but he who stays away until the third hour has completely run out, shall give 10 Kreuzer. Such money shall go into the **Foundling Fund**. *Welser Court Ordinance*, page 10.

An orphanage is where boys deprived of both parents are nourished and fed. *Bartolomeo Cartagena of Valencia in his exposition* on the titles of Canon Law, book 3, title 36. In **Strasbourg**, it is called the **Orphanage** <note>original: "Waysenhaus"</note>, wherein is a beautiful garden and four rooms for more than a hundred children; the sick have a special room; they have their own tailor, shoemaker, barber, doctor, and bakery. Each has his own bed, and there is a bed in the middle divided by a board. Each has his own bowl and utensils, etc.

Letters of recommendation. See above under the letter C, word: Letters of Commendation.

# 73. Prince, Territorial Prince, Prince of the Empire, Petty Princes. Sovereign.

A Prince <note>original: "Princeps"</note> is so called as if the "first head," according to *Isidore*, book 9 of *Etymologies*. Or, what is perhaps more correct, it comes from that which "stands before"; and thus our German word **Fürst** takes its name from *vorstehen* (to stand before), and *Princeps* or a *Fürst* is, as it were, a "fore-stander"—that is, one who presides or leads. *Johann Borcholten on Customs*.

However, for someone to be called a Prince of the Empire, an **Imperial Prince**, he must excel in three prerogatives: (1.) He must acknowledge only the Emperor as his Lord. (2.) He must receive his fiefs through a banner or a scepter <note>symbolic items used in the investiture ceremony</note>. (3.) He must possess provinces distinguished by the title of a Principality. See Paurmeister and Ritter as cited above.

**Prince** <note>original: "Fürst"</note> is a general name denoting the Emperor, Dukes, Margraves, etc. When used specifically, it is a particular dignity, such as the Princes of Anhalt, and it commonly attributes a greater dignity to those who are called Dukes <note>original: "Hertzogen"</note>. Rittershusius, Feudal Law, chapter 5; and my own work on Subordinate Power, folio 95. For the Princes of Anhalt, see Sprenger and Limnaeus as cited.

The manner in which the Counts of Hohenzollern were elevated to the Princely Estate on March 19, 1623, at Regensburg—about which Sprenger provides more detail in his *Delineation of the Estates of the Empire*, page 384—appears from the following Imperial Diploma.

However, since through the death of men such high lineages occasionally fall into lack and decline, the more the Imperial Highness—according to their stately origin, benefits, and merits—secures and endows them with higher honors and dignities, the more magnificently the throne of Imperial Majesty is adorned and made visible. Also, the subjects are maintained in the recognition of Imperial dignity and their owed obedience, and are moved and guided toward noble virtues, honorable and knightly deeds, and faithful, steady, and constant services. Beyond this, although We, from such Imperial height and dignity in which Almighty GOD has placed Us according to His Divine Will, and from innate goodness and mildness, are always inclined to consider and promote the honor, dignity, advancement, and welfare of all and each of Our high and low Estates and members associated with the Holy Empire: yet Our Imperial mind is somewhat more inclined and eager to elevate and set into an even higher and greater estate and honor those whose ancestors and they themselves come from an ancient, stately name, stem, and lineage, and who have shown and proven themselves toward Our predecessors in the Empire, Roman Emperors and Kings, and toward Us, the Holy Empire, and Our praiseworthy House of Austria, with special, faithful, and diligent service in times of war and peace, more willingly and steadfastly than others.

Therefore, We have graciously regarded, perceived, and considered the ancient Princely and Countly origin and being of the Counts of Hohenzollern, etc., which sprang from a royal stem. And that already more than three hundred years ago, Our late predecessor in the Empire, Emperor Rudolf the First of this name, [regarded] Count Eitel Friedrich of Zollern, also the first of this name, who with His Majesty’s own legitimate sister—

...had been married to a sister, was elevated to the **Princely Rank**, and was graciously endowed with the **Burgraviate of Nuremberg**. From this line descend the still-living Electors and Princes, the Margraves of Brandenburg, etc., and the Burggraves of Nuremberg, alongside the Counts of Hohenzollern in a direct line. Thus, both the Electoral and Countly houses—Brandenburg and Zollern—are of one blood and origin.

Furthermore, we have brought into credible and thorough experience how, after the death of the aforementioned Count Eytel Friedrich I (who was elevated to the Princely Rank), and the subsequent division between his two surviving sons of the County of Hohenzollern and the Burgraviate of Nuremberg, the ruling possessors of the said County nonetheless used the **Princely Title** and the address **High-born** <note>original: "Hochgebohrn"</note>. They wrote "by the Grace of God" according to the original documents found in the old archives and shown to us through credible transcripts. They also married into and became allied with the most prominent Electoral and Princely families in the Roman Empire. However, the said Counts of Zollern later left behind the aforementioned Princely preeminence and title due to the decline of their counties and lordships, mostly through endured wars and other means, which is how it has remained until now. Additionally, We have no less considered and taken to heart the pleasant, manifold, noble, faithful, knightly, useful, and highly fruitful services which the often-mentioned Counts of Hohenzollern have shown and proven for many ages past to Our highly honored ancestors of the Holy Empire, the Roman Emperors and Kings. In times of war and peace, in many highly important matters and affairs, they spared neither their bodies nor their wealth, remaining upright, honest, steadfast, faithful, and distinguished. We are sufficiently informed of this both from the excellent testimonies granted to the Counts of Hohenzollern through various diplomas by Our highest-named ancestors of the Empire, as well as from other authenticated histories. Accordingly, the High and Well-born Hans Georg, Count of Hohenzollern and Sigmaringen, Our and the Empire’s Hereditary Chamberlain <term>Erb-Cämmerer; a ceremonial office of high rank within the Imperial court</term> and dear faithful subject, Knight of the **Order of the Golden Fleece**, Our Privy Councilor, Chamberlain, and **President of the Imperial Aulic Council** <term>Reichs-Hoffrath; the supreme judicial and administrative body of the Holy Roman Empire</term>, has laudably followed the glorious example of his ancestors to this date. ### ADDITION.

**Territorial Princely Authority** <note>original: "Landsfürstliche Obrigkeit"</note>—what is it? See Klock, consultation 9, number 1. **Princes** and those **of Princely Rank** are joined together and judged as equals regarding the first instance of **Arbitration** <note>original: "Austräg," a specific legal process for settling disputes between estates of the Empire</note> in the Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber. Klock, volume 2, consultation 84, number 32. The ancient **lineage** of the **House of Brunswick and Lüneburg** can be proven to go back more than 1,200 years: on the **paternal** side, from the Roman **C. Actius** through the **Italian Princely House of Este**; on the **maternal** side, however, through the **Welfish Ducal Bavarian lines** from **Widukind the Great** and his ancestors, the ancient **Saxon Kings**, from an even longer time ago.

**The title of Prince** is attributed **to the Emperor**. Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 1, number 117. Some are **Princes of the Empire**, and they enjoy three prerogatives. Chapter 1, number 123. Others are **Territorial Princes**, chapter 1, number 124. Others are **of Princely Rank** and **Princely Counts**, some of whom are listed in chapter 1, number 125. In the Senate of Ferdinand II, newly created Princes are listed, though some are omitted, such as: Hans Ulrich, Prince of Eggenberg, Count of Adelsberg, Baron in Waldenstein, Gösting, Wildau and Straß, Lord in Radkersburg and Pettau, Knight of the Golden Fleece, etc. Regarding recently received Princes, see Sprenger at length in *Delineation of the Estates of the Empire*, page 384 and following. **Princes** envy the neighboring free Cities. Schönborn, in *Politics*, page 93. Barbosa accumulates many points **regarding the Prince** in book 14, chapter 78, throughout the entire axiom. **Question: Does an illustrious Father** have jurisdiction over his children, such that they can be treated as his subjects in court? It is denied. For illustrious sons are equal in dignity with their Father, and are equally **of Princely rank**. "An equal has no authority over an equal" <note>original Latin: "Par autem in parem non habet Imperium"</note>; see Nicolaus Myler at length, *On the Princes and Estates of the Empire*, chapter 53, page 334. To this topic belong the **Masks of Princes** <note>original: "Larvæ Principum," referring to pretenders or impostors.</note>, or the False Philips, False Neros, False Alphonsos, False Fredericks, and False Henrys. Such as Perkin <note>Perkin Warbeck (c. 1474–1499), a pretender to the English throne during the reign of Henry VII.</note>, who carried himself as Richard IV, King of England. See Francis Bacon of Verulam on the affairs of Henry VII under that word.

<column-break/>

See also the entry for Executioner <note>original: "Scharffrichter"</note>, and there the "Mask of the Count," and Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 63, number 2, page 281. More recent examples were collected by Nicolaus Pfretshner, *On Families*, pages 85, 86, 87, and 88.

### 74. Princely Right. Judgment of Princes.

To some, this term <note>original: "Fürstenrecht" or "Judicium Principum"</note> is recent and invented by those said to wish to diminish the power of the Emperor: see the **Donauwörth Remembrances**, page 156 and 166. Reincking, class 1, 4, chapter 19. Meichsner, volume 2, book 2, page 57. To others, this right is said to be approved by long custom and consistent use—namely, that when the Emperor judges fiefs of greater importance, he cannot do so except in the presence of others who are endowed with power equal to the litigants. See my work *On Jurisdiction*, question 13, and the *Treatise on Succession and Election*, book 1, last chapter; add Lehmann, book 2, chapter 9, page 630, and the same at page 176. Caspar Ziegler, section on *Arbitration* <note>original: "Aufträg"</note> at the beginning, page 47. There are those who believe that in the past, the Emperors were not fixed to one location but moved here and there in the Empire; the Princes, Nobles, and nearby Aristocrats always flocked to the Court out of honor and duty, and the Emperor (who then usually spoke the law himself) would, for the sake of greater majesty and indeed at his pleasure, use those he wished as Assessors in the business.

An example is provided to us by the outlawry of Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony, which Krantz describes in *Saxonia*, book 6, chapter 38: The Emperor (Frederick) [Barbarossa], proceeding into the assembly, asked the nobles about the death [sentence], seeking a verdict on what a man deserved who, having been lawfully summoned three times, stubbornly remained absent. It was answered to him, according to the opinion of the Princes, that as justice dictated, he must be stripped of all honor, and being judged by public proscription, he should lose both his Duchy and all benefits held from the Empire, etc.

This opinion is confirmed by what John of Beka writes in the *Chronicle of Utrecht* under the 47th Bishop: Meanwhile, Emperor Louis [IV], having heard of the death of Count William, sitting on the Tribunal in his Imperial regalia, sought the right judgment of equity from many Princes of the Roman Realm. By their delivered sentence, it was decreed that the Principality of Holland should revert to the Roman Empire, because Count William departed from this world without children.

It is also pleasing to place here a copy of the definitive sentence in the **case of Caspar Schlick and Hans von Hohenstein, concerning Limpurg and its dependencies**, delivered by King Sigismund in the year 1431. Its tenor is as follows:

We, Sigismund, by the Grace of God, Roman King, at all times Increaser of the Empire, King of Germany, Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, etc. Acknowledge and make publicly known with this letter to all those...

# Document Letter F.

...to all those who see it, or hear it read: Since We, some time ago, graciously granted the fortress and the toll at Limperg <note>Modern Limburg. This refers to a strategic fortification and its right to collect taxes on passage.</note> to the renowned Caspar Schlick <note>A prominent statesman and Chancellor to Emperor Sigismund in the 15th century.</note>, Our secret and dear faithful servant, as a fief that had reverted to Us and the Empire as a concealed fief <note>A "concealed fief" (verschwiegenes Lehen) was a territory held by a lord without the required formal acknowledgment or investiture from the Emperor.</note>; and since Hans von Hohenstein, who possesses these same goods yet has never acknowledged or received them from Us and the Empire, claimed to have some legal right and title to them; We therefore appointed as a judge in our stead for both parties the high-born Bernhard, sometime Margrave of Baden, Our dear uncle and late Prince, so that he might legally decide between the aforementioned Caspar and Hans. 

And as We, as Elector of Us and the Empire, were recently here, We ordered the case to proceed according to the law. The Margrave informed Us how he had summoned Hans von Hohenstein with his letters three times in succession and commanded him to appear. He also had the aforementioned Hans, who was present, told and requested to answer the complaint of the aforementioned Caspar the following morning. 

And as he [the Margrave] sat in judgment in the Council Chamber at the City Hall of Nuremberg, and with him—at Our command—many Princes, Counts, Barons, Nobles, Knights, and vassals of the Holy Empire, a legal representative appeared for the aforementioned Caspar. He declared through his advocate <note>original: "Fürsprecher," a legal spokesperson who spoke for a party in court.</note> that he was present and wished to pursue the law against Hans von Hohenstein regarding such a fief, as is proper, since the same Hans had been summoned three times and the final day had now passed. 

And although the aforementioned Hans stood there present, he nevertheless refused to answer in legal terms; instead, after making several remarks which he intended to be outside of the formal court proceedings, he willfully walked away from the law and refused to wait for the outcome. Since several Princes and others who were present considered that the summons of Our uncle, the Margrave, had been somewhat truncated <note>A procedural concern that the notice period might have been too short.</note>, they unanimously judged according to the law that since Hans von Hohenstein had been present and refused to submit to the law, but rather walked away, We should summon him twice more before Us and proceed with the case according to the law as is proper. This We have done. 

And as We, on today’s date of this letter, sat in judgment at Our Castle in Nuremberg in Our own person, and with Us were Princes, Barons, Lords, Knights, and vassals of the Empire, the aforementioned Caspar appeared before Us and declared through his advocate—although We 

<column-break/>

had granted him the aforementioned fortress and toll at Limperg as a concealed fief of Us and the Empire, and had also earnestly commanded the aforementioned Hans to vacate such a fief, and had subsequently summoned and called him in succession according to the first judgment made before Our uncle the Margrave—that Hans had paid no heed but had remained absent. Thus, Caspar stood there, waiting for his judgment and legal right, and humbly asked Us to allow the case to proceed. 

We then asked whether such a land-summons had been delivered to his house, his court, and such places as is proper. To this, the aforementioned Caspar answered through his advocate, saying they had been legally announced to him, and he brought forth letters and witnesses to prove this as is required by law. Then We had it loudly proclaimed whether anyone was there on behalf of the aforementioned Hohenstein to answer for him and such a matter. At first, no one came on behalf of the same Hohenstein. 

Thereafter, the aforementioned Caspar again declared through his advocate that he stood there and waited for the third and final day, which had already passed several days ago. He hoped for a legal ruling, since von Hohenstein had still sent no one to answer for him, and requested that the Imperial Ban <note>original: "Reichs Acht," a form of outlawry where a person is stripped of legal rights and their property is forfeited.</note> be declared against the aforementioned von Hohenstein, and that he [Caspar] be legally awarded and endowed with such a fief. 

Upon this, We consulted with our Princes, Lords, Counts, Nobles, Councilors, and faithful subjects, and took before Us the letters of summons and citation by which We had summoned von Hohenstein for the third time. We asked the same Princes and others sitting with Us for the law, and appointed them to recognize the law in this matter. They then took counsel and deliberated, and afterwards all spoke unanimously and with one accord the judgment of the law, through the noble Conrad, Lord of Weinsberg, etc., Our Councilor and dear faithful servant, as follows: 

Since Hans von Hohenstein was finally summoned three times to appear before us for trial regarding the complaint of the aforementioned Caspar Schlick, etc., concerning the fortress and toll at Limperg, and the same Caspar waited for the law for three days and appeared and stood before the court, and the aforementioned von Hohenstein did not attend or wait for such a court day as had been set for him, neither in person nor through his authorized proxies, and thus remained absent in disobedience and insolence, and did not come to answer, and was disobedient to Us and the law...

More on the **Princely Rights** <term>Fürstenrecht: The legal privilege of princes within the Holy Roman Empire to be judged only by their peers (other princes) rather than by common courts or the Emperor's council alone.</term> can be seen in individual discourses and the question: whether the Roman Imperial Majesty, in matters concerning **Princely Duchies, Counties**, etc., which are held as fiefs from the Empire, and which ought to be completely and finally adjudicated against one party, should decide and pronounce judgment alone through his Imperial Court Council, or with the involvement of the Electors and Princes of the Empire? See also *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 1, counsel 110.

No mention is made of **Princely Right** in the **Golden Bull** <note>The Golden Bull of 1356, a fundamental law of the Holy Roman Empire that settled the method of electing the Emperor.</note> or any other Law of the Empire. Reineckinck.

<column-break/>

on government, section 1, chapter 4, chapter 19, number 35. Becker, in *Public Law*, page 67, describes it as a unique privilege of the Princes of Germany in matters concerning a Prince’s body, honor, and feudal tenure, such that the Emperor cannot decide them without the counsel of the Great Men of the Empire as **Peers of the Court**. Reink, in the cited place, number 11.

On **Princely Right**, see Dr. Stirnius on the *Constitutions of Princes*, title 12, § 6, page 343, where he discusses arbitrary judgments. ### 75. Princely Cities. *Municipal Cities*.

Regarding municipal magistrates, and what kind of jurisdiction, etc., they have, see at length Ziegler in *Common Conclusions*, section on 'The City,' conclusion 1, folio 147.

### ADDITION.

Among the Articles of Reformation of Emperor Frederick III, we read that cities are distinguished into **Imperial-Free** <note>German: *Reichs-Frey*. Cities that were subject only to the Emperor and not to local princes.</note> and **Princely Cities**. Limnaeus, book 7, chapter 1, number 29. For the sake of greater clarity, see also number 31 of the same author. Becker, in *Public Law*, page 177, number 4, near the end.

### 76. *Für* and *Vor* [For and Before]. *For*.

*Vor* denotes the estimation of a thing and the price. Klock, volume 2, counsel 40, number 79. *Für* and *Vor* differ. *Vor* signifies succession; *Für* is the same as 'in an instant.' For example, when it says in Luke 24, verse 31: "*Christ vanished from [für] them, not before [vor] them*," it indicates that the body was withdrawn in a moment, which is recounted as a miracle <note>The author is noting a linguistic distinction in German: 'vor' suggests a sequence of events, while 'für' (in this archaic context) suggests a sudden disappearance.</note>. The word **PRO** <note>Latin: "for" or "on behalf of."</note> does not create a condition, but signifies a cause or denotes a manner. Mantica, *On the Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 11, title 22, number 16. On the words: *FOR* a dowry, or by cause of a dowry, number 21. *Ibid*.

### 77. Amicable Act. [Freundstück]. *A case for a friend*.

Elders among relatives can correct juniors. Struvius, *On Private Retribution*, chapter 7, aphorism 1, number 7, page 72. A certain law must be established—see at length Menochius, *On Arbitrary Judgments*, question in the Preface—so that there is less room for favoritism or hatred, law 79, § 1, on judgments. Lord Tabor in the preface of the treatise *On the Government of the Ruling Church*, page 7. Therefore, for one intending to act out of favoritism, that entire series of treatment could generally be defined negatively, as Berlichius seems to have done, part 2, Conclusion 22, number 70, since everything done out of favor is considered to be of no importance.

Regarding questions on behalf of a **Friend**, Aleman deals with this most extensively in his *Palestra of Consultations*, page 714, and those cited there with a full hand. Regarding cases on behalf of a **Friend**, see Tessaur, decisions 86 and 206. Ilicomumius in *Proceedings*, page 621. Should a Judge in the case of a friend take friendship into account? Antoninus, in his *Papinian Jurisprudence*, inference 7, establishes that even the slightest inclination of a Judge in favor of one or the other litigant causes the scales of Justice, deprived of their equilibrium, to tip immediately toward that same side, even with no compelling reason. The Judge easily persuades himself—sometimes even with a clear conscience—that the one he wishes well has a good case, even if he has a bad one. Marcus Tullius <note>The Roman orator Cicero</note> subscribes to this opinion in Book 3 of *On Duties*, number 25: "But a good man will act neither against the Republic, nor against his oath and good faith, for the sake of his friend, not even if he is the Judge over that friend." For he sets aside the persona of the Friend when he puts on the persona of the Judge. He will grant only so much to friendship as to wish that his friend’s cause be the true one. Most worthy of note is what Valerius Maximus relates in Book 6, chapter 4, example 4, concerning Publius Rutilius. When he resisted the unjust request of a certain friend, and that friend said with great indignation: "What need have I then for your friendship, if you do not do what I ask?" he replied: "On the contrary, what need have I for yours, if for your sake I am to do something dishonorable?" Therefore, we shall act much more nobly if we maintain that excellent custom received from our ancestors of asking a Judge: "to do what can be done while preserving one's good faith." Besold, *Political Counsel*, axiom 545. But Bitsch dealt extensively, accurately, and professionally with cases on behalf of a Friend at Strasbourg in the year 1550, in his Inaugural Dissertation titled: *A Decade of Cases for a Friend*; also Schröder in his Dissertation on *Gratification*, thesis 15.

That there is no case given that can be called "for a Friend," but rather "for the devil," since it provides a cause for being thrust down to the underworld. Berlich, part 2, conclusion 22, number 70.

False things are not to be feigned for the sake of friends, nor true things concealed. Limn. in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 4, page 101. On Friends, Barbosa, book 1, chapter 57, axioms 1 to 12. One cannot renounce one's own favor if it also concerns the favor of another. Klock, consultation 11, number 242. Blood relations are in a way part of our own body. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 3, chapter 7, number 70.

### 79 Fiscal Officer, or Criminal Prosecutor.
#### The Fiscal.

Formerly in this City of Nuremberg, this office was held by **the beadle or the executioner's assistant.** <note>original: "der Köb oder des Henckers Knecht"</note> See the **Criminal Records of Nuremberg against Brandenburg**, volume 4, folio 25, verso. The term *Fiscus* <note>The Treasury or the legal department representing the state's financial interests</note> is not inelegantly defined by Andreas Isernia as a "Sack of ill-gotten gains," in the section on the prohibition of alienating fiefs by Frederick. By others, the Fiscal is called the "successor of scoundrels and criminals" <note>meaning the state inherits the property of convicted criminals</note>.

### 80. Window.
#### Fenestra.

Formerly, there was even a tax on windows in Lorraine, but it was most unjust. See Sprenger, *On the Law of Building*, page 55. Regarding what constitutes window-panes, see the same work, pages 55 and 56.
Taxes are imposed on windows. See Mundius, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 3, number 207. Regarding windows, please look at Schröder, *On Incorporeal Rights*, section 18, at great length. See also Personalius, *On Possession*, question 7. **Concerning the obstruction of windows.** <note>original: "Von der Fenster-Störung"</note> Zeiller, century 4, question 9, page 44. Nicolaus Henelius, in *Otto of Breslau*, chapter 10. A tenant is not bound to fit windows or doors at his own expense; this is discussed extensively by Mr. Tabor in *On the Law of Colonate*, thesis 30. Anyone may make windows in their own wall from which they can look into a neighbor's house, according to Carpzov in his *Jurisprudence*, constitution 41, definition 12. See the Nuremberg Statutes, book 3, title 26. Capolla, in his treatise *On Servitudes* <note term="Servitude">A legal right to use another person's property for a specific purpose, such as a right of way or a right to light</note>, in the section on windows, speaks differently than here—namely, according to Common Law. However, this statute stands against the common law. Schröder, section 18, number 17. Yet this law is also approved by the Custom of Lubeck, book 3, title 12, in the article stating: **no new windows.** <note>original: "kein neue Fenster"</note> These words are cited by Ernst Cothmann, volume 2, legal response 93, number 38. See also Cephalus, volume 1, consultation 130, number 11 and following. **In-falling light is not the same as looking-out light.** <note>original: "Einfallende Licht, seynd nicht auffsehende Licht"</note> See the *Orléans Consultations*, folio 73. Whether light from the sides is to be considered, or rather that which is in front of the view of the house. Gratianus, chapter 896. Whether it is permitted by right of liberty to open a window in one's own wall if a servitude has not been established. Köppen, observation 78, number 9. It is not permitted for anyone to make a window in their own property merely to spite another. This is explained by Bargalius, book 6, *On Deceit*, rule 42, numbers 7 and 8. Personalius, *On Possession*, question 7. Regarding windows in a common wall, see Surdus, consultation 387. An agreement of servitude, ensuring that a view is not obstructed, also binds a specific successor of the house. Carpzov, part 2 of his *Jurisprudence*, constitution 41, definition 14. If someone is ordered by a court sentence not to hinder a neighbor opening a window in his own wall, does this mean a servitude has been imposed so that he cannot later obscure that window by building higher? Simon Pistor, consultation 12, throughout. One who has the servitude of building higher, of supporting a load, and of making a window, ought not to place those windows toward the side of a house or monastery of respectable young women and nuns, if he is able to make them in another part of his house's wall. Cavalcanti, book 5, *On Crimes and Quasi-Contracts*, decision 8, number 77. **Concerning slit-windows.** <note>original: "Von Schlitzfenstern"</note> Nuremberg Statutes, book 3, title 26. **Concerning mill-holes, Frankfurt Reformation**, part 8, title 4, section 2. According to common law, no one can be compelled to keep iron grates in their

<column-break/>

windows, nor to replace them, unless it is prescribed by long-standing custom. Gratianus, chapter 752, number 81. At least 100 feet must be left for a view. Cothmann, response 93, number 27, volume 2. He who has made a window in my wall with my consent cannot make another one. Surdus, consultation 387, number 8, book 3. It is a great inconvenience to let light into a neighbor's house by opening a wall and making windows. Cothmann, response 93, number 19, volume 2. Does the rule "to build higher," <note>original: "altius," likely referring to "jus altius tollendi," the right to build higher</note> from the Code on Servitudes, apply if someone acquires part of a house from one who has windows in his remaining part looking into the sold house, so that the buyer cannot obstruct the light by building higher? Tessaur, decision 216.

In our Law it is not new that to behold a thing with the eyes has the same legal effect as touching it with the hand (Law 79, Digest on payments) or with the foot (Law 18, section 2, Digest on acquiring possession). Thus Cujas says in his formal lecture on the law *Those who* (Digest on the services of urban estates): we ought to keep not only our feet but also our eyes off the property of others, for everyone should look only at what is their own. Otherwise, one commits an illicit act. This was the response given by Gyges, son of Dascylus, in Herodotus, to King Candaules, who wanted to show his very beautiful and striking wife to his bodyguard Gyges. He did indeed show her, but to his own terrible destruction, as found in Herodotus, book 1, sections 8-12. <note>The story of Gyges and Candaules is a famous Greek legend where the king's voyeuristic pride leads to his assassination and Gyges taking the throne.</note> And this explanation is also supported by statutes, such as the Lubeck Law, book 3, title 12, article 13: **no new windows**, the words of which Cothmann cites, volume 2, response 93, number 38. It is also in the Nuremberg Reformation, part 2, title 26, book 3, section "There is no one," 1 and argument 8 "unless it were." And so Cephalus advised in these terms, volume 1, consultation 130, number 11 and following, with many others cited there, whom Cothmann alleges in the cited place, number 21. And thus that liberty is limited by the prohibition of "intrusion" <note term="Immission">In property law, the sending of light, smoke, or water onto another's land</note> in Civil Law, making such an act illicit even if one wants to have such "viewing windows" for one's own utility and not to spite another. This is argued from Law 5, section 5, Digest on the claim of servitude, using the example of one who sends smoke or cuts stone there; even if he does it for his own utility and not to spite another, it is nonetheless prohibited. See below under the words **Boundary-mark** <note>original: "Lachen"</note> and **Glassworks.**

### 81. To clench the fist.
#### The boxer's fist.

**To clench the fist, to strike someone with a clenched fist.** Berlich, 5, conclusion 62, number 16. **The whole fist threatens with power.** Mr. Harsdörffer. **Raising both thumbs with a closed fist is a sign of favor and praise.** Speech usually begins with a **hollow fist** <note>original: "boler Faust"</note>—that is, with the middle finger inclined toward the thumb, as can be seen in some of the images and statues of Roman orators. **The closed fist with the thumb hidden signifies memory. The closed fist with the thumb extended signifies science. The closed fist signifies strength and unity.**

### 1. Gallows, Stocks, and Gallows. <note>original: "Galg, Stock und Galg"</note> The Fork. <note>original: "Furca"</note>

**Regarding** the definition of the fork and the gibbet, see Besoldus, *Leisure Hours*, book 19, chapter 9; and that the word *Galg* <note>Gallows</note> comes from *Golgara* <note>likely referring to Golgotha</note>, see *Exotic Words of the New Testament*, page 181.

The punishment of the gallows <note>original: "furca"</note>, as among foreign nations, is also frequently used today in the Roman Empire; ever since Constantine abolished the punishment of the Cross. Sozomen, in chapter 8, at the end.

The erection of the gallows belongs to the degree of High Jurisdiction— <note>Besoldus, Volume 1.</note>

<column-break/>

and it denotes <term>High Jurisdiction</term> <note>Latin: "merum Imperium" — the highest level of legal authority, including the power to impose the death penalty</note> according to Baldus on chapter 2, *What is an Investiture*, and the law *Causa*, Code *On Bishops and Clerics*. Schneidewinus in his *Treatise on Fiefs*, part 2, title *What things may be given in fief*, number 71, who, following Jacobus de Sancto Georgio, adds that if there is a dispute between two cities regarding High Jurisdiction, it shall not be permitted for either of them to erect gallows while the lawsuit is pending. Otherwise, the other party may tear them down by their own authority. This is argued from the law *Quemadmodum*, section 1, at the verse *aliud*, Digest *On the Aquilian Law*, which is usually cited for this purpose: that anyone may, by their own authority and without asking the Lord, destroy that which has been built on their land by another. For, because that which is built on my soil belongs to the soil (according to the Institutes *On the Division of Things*), one should see to it that they destroy what is mine and not another's; hence, I cannot be accused of violence or disturbance. Indeed, he who uses his own right does injury to no one. Anyone may also build and destroy on their own land as they please, even to the detriment of another, according to the law *Proculus*, Digest *On Threatened Damage*. This is elegantly discussed by Alexander de Imola, and Capolla in *On Urban Servitudes*, chapter 30, number 9. See also Costa, Consultation 6, regarding when a gallows may be torn down by one's own authority. Add Schneidewinus in the cited place, number 74, who provides a notable rule regarding the erection of gallows:

> That one may not place a gallows so close to the borders that its shadow touches the foreign jurisdiction, and so that the people may stand within the jurisdiction where the execution is performed, and not on the neighboring foreign jurisdiction, etc.

But today, the erection of gallows is tolerated if they are distant from the neighbor's borders by 24 ells <note>An "ell" (ulna) was a historical unit of measurement roughly the length of an arm</note>, as noted by M. Stephanus at the end of article 215 of the *Constitutio Criminalis*, and also by Zieriz.

By the erection of gallows, the "quasi-possession" of High Jurisdiction is maintained, even if no one has been hanged for 100 years. Angelus on the law *Retinere*, Digest *On Usufruct*, and on the law *Haec autem*, Digest *On Urban Servitudes*. Baldus on the Code *That no one be allowed*. Peguera, Decision 81, number 4, at the end. This is because the sign is sufficient, even if the thing signified <note>the execution</note> is absent. Regarding this, see Matthaeus de Afflictis, chapter 1, number 38, *What is an Investiture*, and Hieronymus Gigante, *On the Crime of Lèse-majesté*, question 41, book 1, folio 102. Cardinal Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter F, conclusion 537, where he has much to say on the erection of gallows.

By the very fact that someone holds High Jurisdiction in a territory, they have the right to erect gallows and keep them standing as a sign of that jurisdiction, for the sake of public utility and to deter others, so that the memory of punishments may be renewed, whether they are newly erected or have long since collapsed. Tuschus, letter F, conclusion 537; Peguera, Decision 81. I follow Bidembach in his *Treatise on Jurisdiction*, folio 103: because since the execution and imposition of punishments are fleeting acts and consequently fade from memory, human industry invented the erection of gallows so that the memory of punishments—

<summary>This page defines various legal and agricultural terms, concluding with an extensive discussion on the "Right of the Gallows" (furca). <meta>This page continues the legal encyclopedia's discussion on symbols of judicial power, specifically focusing on the gallows (furcae) as a physical manifestation of a lord's right to exercise High Justice and the legal disputes surrounding their placement and usage.</meta>

<page-num>324</page-num>
<header>Expanded Treasury of Practical Law</header>

...so that the memory of crimes may be renewed: Thus, monuments were also established for the memory of the human condition, <note>original Latin: "l. quidem in suo. ff. de cond. & demonstr." — referring to the Digest of Roman Law</note>. And so it is clear that in this erection of gallows, a public utility is served: since through this, as if by a kind of continuous lecture—which is even better impressed upon the mind through sight than through hearing alone—men are deterred from evil deeds, <note>original Latin: "arg. instit. de gradib. cogn. in fin."</note> according to Ludovico à Peguera in *Decision 81, number 2.* For this reason, Oldradus <note>Oldradus de Ponte was a famous 14th-century Italian jurist.</note> calls the gallows the "trophies of Justice" in *Consultation 161*; see also Zieritz on *Article 216 of the Criminal Constitution.*

And all these points hold such weight that if no place were found in a territory where gallows could be conveniently placed without causing someone else inconvenience, the lord of the soil could be compelled to sell the land for the sake of public utility: as seen in <note>various citations of Roman law follows regarding the sale of land for public use</note> Peguera in the cited place, number 3.

However, Peguera warns in the same place, *number 3*, that a different rule is observed in Catalonia; there, one possessing **High Justice** <term>merum Imperium: the absolute power of the sword, or the right to inflict capital punishment</term> in a place where another holds all other jurisdiction, cannot keep permanent gallows and other signs there, except when a specific case arises.

That the erection of gallows and signs is an act of **High Justice** is also noted by Gail in *Observation 60, number 5*; and therefore jurisdiction is proven by the mere erection of the gallows. Mascardus, *Conclusion 946, number 10 and following*, as well as the boundaries of jurisdiction, according to Brunus, *Consultation 34, number 6.* Hieronymus de Monte, *On Boundaries, chapter 52, number 4*, because it is not doubted that jurisdiction extends that far, Græven, *Conclusion 60, lib. 2.* Hence it happens that they are not infrequently placed at the borders.

Criminal jurisdiction can also be held and retained without a sign, and therefore one cannot argue: "He has no gallows or post. Therefore, he has no criminal jurisdiction." Likewise, vice versa, just because of a gallows or post, one is not automatically said to have criminal jurisdiction. Meichsner, *Decision 4, number 159.*

For an argument from accidental or accessory signs—such as a gibbet—does not prove necessity: Natta, *Consultation 636, n. 123.* Keller, *On the Judicial-Political Office, book 2, chapter 15.*

Hence it can happen that two judges have equal power of judging in the same place, and yet only one can carry out the execution and erect gallows, according to Decian, *Criminal Treatise, book 4, chapter 41, number 1.* Thus, it is one thing to be able to judge criminally, and another to have the **Blood Ban and Execution.** <note>original German: "den Blutbann und Execution" — the high judicial right to spill blood or carry out capital sentences.</note>

Some have the custom of capturing someone and having them "settled" <note>original German: "berichtigen" — here used as a euphemism for executed</note> in another place, which was formerly practiced among the Nobles in Swabia. But this was done to the detriment of the Counts who held the criminal jurisdiction and the right of execution.

<column-break/>

Regarding which solemnities are to be observed in the erection of gallows, see **in the Imperial Penal Code** <note>original German: "in der peinlichen Halsgerichts-Ordnung" — the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina of 1532</note> **articles 215 and 17**, where it is noted: **"Whether the malefactors should be left hanging on the gallows."** see the Talmud in Sanhedrin <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> *folio 49 and folio 252.*

Hippocrates, in *Aphorism 43*, is the authority for the claim that those suspended and strangled can be restored as long as they do not foam at the mouth. He suggests that this foam differs greatly from the foam of epileptics, who often foam while falling or seized by a paroxysm but without danger to their lives. On the contrary, that foam which appears in the hanged is squeezed from the chest and lungs, where that moisture is characteristic; when it fails, hope for the person's safety is shouted down <note>meaning: they are beyond recovery</note>. See Lotichius in *Petronius Arbiter's Satyricon, book 2, commentary chapter 1*, where he also recounts stories of thieves who, having been hanged and destined for anatomical dissection, revived; he even adds a staggering story of a woman suspended from a cross giving birth.

### ADDITION.

Alciatus says in *Parerga, book 9, chapter 20*: "When I had responded to a question of fact that by the erection of gallows a certain rule of the question and the possession of **High Justice** had been retained, and that upon the sale of the estate, that right did not seem to be separated: behold, a new controversy with my adversary: he denied that the word 'gallows' <note>original: "furca"</note> was ever found in Cicero or the ancient authors in that sense." See more in Barbosa, *Axioms, book 7, chapter 9, throughout.*

Regarding whether **Nobles** are to be hanged for theft or another crime, and whether the gibbet should be erected higher in honor of their nobility, see Gutierez, *book 4, Practical Questions, chapter 15, number 20.* Baldus and Fabius de Arena, *Criminal Decisions 25.* In the University of Paris in the year 1403 (or as others prefer, 1407), the Provost of Merchants had two students hanged on a gibbet, but he was forced to kiss them <note>as a sign of public apology</note> and return them to the School to be buried honorably. Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 8, chapter 9, n. 38.* **Gallows-money** <note>original German: "Galgengeld" — fees for the executioner or maintaining the gallows</note> **Bamberg wishes to attach to the high authorities; it also gained support in the Würzburg Treaty negotiations of 1563.** Laws are called "gallows-like" <note>original: "patibiles"</note>, that is, manifest and apparent, through which the truth, which previously lay hidden in the depths, appears and is brought into the light. Rittershusius, *Feudal Part, page 590.* A gallows <note>original: "furca"</note> differs from a cross <note>original: "crux"</note> not only in name, as Cujacius thought in *Observation 1, 16*, because criminals are said to be "hanged" by the gallows but "fixed" to the cross, but also in form. For even the word "to hang" is referred to the cross. Seneca, *Epistle 7*: "Someone committed a robbery; what did he deserve? To be hanged." That this "hanging" refers to the cross is noted by Petronius in the *Satyricon*: "The Governor of the Province ordered robbers to be fixed to crosses." And Apuleius in *Metamorphoses, book 3*: "I shall fix to a cross that robber, the murderer of my wretched children."

Dr. Tabor, *On Quartering*, page 118.

### 2. **Chaining to the Galleys.** <term>Poena triremium.</term>

The <term>punishment of the triremes</term> <note>refers to sentencing criminals to row in galley ships</note> for life is a penalty we use chiefly against commoners, although there has been variation among the Doctors of Law as to which ancient punishment it succeeded. Among others, Riminaldus in *Counsel 44, number 14*, wished it to be likened to the "banished" of our time; however, Clarus, at the end of *Question 67*, said it is equated to the "deported," although this does not please Borellus in *Counsel 52, number 32* and following; and finally Grassus in *On Wills, Question 28*, equates it to those condemned to perpetual prisons. However, according to the truest and common conclusion of the Doctors, it succeeded the place of "condemnation to the mines" <note>original: "damnationis in metallum"</note> or labor in the mines, since today said punishments are no longer in use, according to authors cited by Grassus and Maestrillo in *Decision 165, number 5*, both regarding condemnation to the galleys for life and for a set time. For the aforementioned punishments have an express similarity: for just as those condemned to the mines were held by the heaviest chains and afflicted with beatings, so too are those condemned to the galleys, as is self-evident. Because of this, they are made "slaves of the penalty," and are equated to the 

<column-break/>

dead. <note>original: "ſervi pœnæ, mortuiſque æquiparantur" — legally, the person is treated as if they have died.</note> The treasury does not acquire property from their person; rather, that which they themselves cannot take is acquired by others who would have held it [as heirs], according to Peregrinus, Farinaccius, and others, as well as Maestrillo in the cited place, number 9 and following; which in number 12 he understands to be true for one condemned to rowing for life, but not for a temporary term.

And because they have lost their citizenship and liberty, they consequently lose the right to make a will or be named in one, as well as the right of intestate succession, and other successors are admitted. Indeed, a will made previously is broken, according to Simon de Praetis in *On the Interpretation of Last Wills*, book 2, interpretation 2, doubt 1, solution 1, number 8, adding that they lose the capacity to be beneficiaries of a will even if they escape or are otherwise removed from prison, citing other authorities and testifying to this as the common opinion. And so, in the case of one condemned to rowing for life, that he be incapable of succession—and with him excluded, those closest in degree succeed—it has been so judged, as Maestrillo testifies in number 17.

->ADDITION.<-

Doctors of Law should not be easily condemned to the galleys. <note>original: "Dd. ad triremes de facili condemnari non debent."</note> Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 340. Today, those condemned to the galleys and to perpetual prison are compared to those condemned to death. And although some think this was changed by *Novel 22, chapter 8*, we nevertheless think that this change—and the fact that those condemned to death today retain the power of making a will—should be ascribed to custom and contrary practice rather than to the said *Novel* which speaks of a different and separate species. J.C.A., book 28, title 1, thesis 7, near the end. Dr. Biccius in *Golden Matters*, page 252, at the end—whom I kiss and embrace like frankincense, like myrrh, as more powerful than any contradiction. From whose tongue I hang as if from a sacred anchor, as from the utterance of a Sibyl, or the oracle of Apollo.

### 3. **Joint-Heirs.** <term>Ganerbii.</term>

Since something was said above under the word *Burgfrieden* regarding the origin of <term>Joint-Heirs</term>: now add who the <term>Joint-Heirs</term> are, or are called. <term>Ganerbii</term>, or <term>Ganerben</term>, are so called as if they were "common heirs" <note>German: "gemeine Erben"</note>, joint owners. And <term>Ganerbschaft</term> <note>joint-inheritance</note> is like a common inheritance where men throw an estate together and do not allow it to be divided. Just as in cases of this kind, it is usually agreed that no one should sell his portion to a stranger, or that the <term>Joint-Heirs</term> are permitted to redeem it.

Truly the word <term>Ganerben</term> is entirely German and a composite, the latter part of which, *Erben*, without doubt denotes "heirs." But the first part of the composition, or the syllable *Gan*, what it means is not clear to everyone. Some derive it from *gehen* (to go, to proceed), as if <term>Ganerben</term> were "going-heirs" <note>German: "Gangerben"</note>, because according to certain of their pacts contrary to Common Law, they pass to a mutual inheritance; for the ancients said *gahn* for *gehn* (to go), just as they said *stehn* for...

# Augmented Practical Treasury
<meta>catchword: with several</meta>

...to stand <note>original: "stehn, stahn"</note>; a dialect still in use in many places today. Others derive it from the word for "sudden" or "hasty" <note>original: "gäh"</note>, which signifies something hurried or quick, as if these Joint Heirs <term>Ganerben; from the German 'gan' (common) and 'erben' (heirs)</term> are those to whom an inheritance passes quickly and hastily through several degrees, as if by a leap. Mr. Killinger discusses this in his elegant treatise *on this matter, discourse 1, number 22.*

Finally, Haenonius *in his 2nd Juridical Disputation, 9, corollary 1* thinks it is derived from the verb "to grant" <note>original: "gönnen"</note>, so that they are "Grant-Heirs" <note>original: "Gönerben"</note>: because they grant peace and unity to their co-heirs; or if this conjecture is pleasing, because they grant the inheritance to one another.

But the more common and accepted opinion is that they are called Joint Heirs <note>original: "Ganerben"</note>, as if to say "common heirs." For the prefix *Gahn* is taken to mean "common" <note>original: "gemein"</note> in compound words, such as "Common Brook" <note>original: "Gahnbach"</note>. This is also indicated in the Imperial Constitutions, such as the *Explanation of the Land Peace* from the year 1500, under the title "Against the Castles of Joint Heirs." Likewise in the *Ordinance of the Land Peace* from the year 1525.

These Joint Heirs are also called Citizens or Castle-men <note>original: "Burger oder Burgmänner"</note>. Rittershusius, in his work on feudal law, book 1, chapter 17, notes from Saxon Law: "Citizens or Castle-men are the names for Joint Heirs or noblemen who anciently lived under a Castle Lord in one castle, where they were then called the Citizens of the castle." The term "Castle-membership" <note>original: "Burgmannschaft"</note> is frequently used for the state of Joint Inheritance <note>original: "Ganerbschaft"</note> in Fichard, *Consilia 1, 13*.

Hence, Joint Inheritance is rightly defined as a certain fraternity initiated among several noblemen of a more generous spirit, governed by specific pacts and laws of mutual succession. It was established so that they might defend themselves and their resources in a common castle against the force and incursions of enemies with joined strength, as I have said under the word *Castle Peace* <note>original: "Burgfrieden"</note>. Which "Castle Peace" is nothing other than a convention or agreement on how one should conduct oneself within the joint inheritance. The word *Ganerbschaft* properly denotes the legal right itself, but sometimes also the Castle in which those confederated Nobles reside.

It must be noted here, however, that the word "Joint Heirs" has one meaning in Saxon Law and another in the regions of Upper Germany. For in Article 17 of the *Saxon Land Law*, Book 1, Joint Heirs refers to collateral heirs who come after brothers and sisters; they are so named from "going" or "hastening" because their succession is easier and more rapid, with no regard for sex, but only for the degree of kinship. Modestinus Pistor, *Consilia 21, number 45*. But in the Acts and Decrees of the Diets, "Joint-Heir Houses or Castles" <note>original: "Ganerben-Häuser oder Schlösser"</note> refers to fortresses held in common by several noble families, as if they were "common heirs of the castles." See especially Killinger in chapter 1; the *Explanation of the Land Peace at Augsburg*, 1500, title: "Against the Castles of Joint Heirs"; the *Ordinance of the Land Peace at Worms*, year 1521; and many other places where mention is made of these joint heirs, as is clear from the cited Recesses. To these, add the *Saxon Mirror*, Book 1 of the Land Law, article 17, and the ancient letters of Fulda

<column-break/>

from the year 1327, which state: "With the will of Frederick his brother, and his other Joint Heirs, who have surrendered and renounced the fief to us." Here, "Joint Heirs" seems to mean those who were invested with the fief simultaneously, who hold it by the "collective hand" <term>gesamte Hand; a legal concept where a group holds property as a single unit rather than as individuals</term>; see the entry for *collective hand*.

There are several such castles in Germany: the Fortress of Rothenberg, situated not far from Nuremberg; the Fortress of Salzburg on the Saale; Friedberg in Wetterau; and Gelnhausen. The privileges of their famous exemptions are recorded in the *Catalog of Privileges*, under the entry "Freedom of Gelnhausen," pages 425 and 430. See also Fesch, *Basle Disputation on Federations*, final thesis, page 5. There are also certain Joint-Heir Cities <note>original: "Civitates Ganerbicæ"</note>: such as Bad Kreuznach, a town located on the Rhine, which has as its co-owners the Elector Palatine and the Margrave of Baden. Likewise Schmalkalden, while the Counts and Princes of Henneberg were still living, belonged half to them and half to the Landgraves of Hesse; today the Landgrave alone possesses it. Mr. Cluten in *Sylloge*, thesis 26, at the end.

Moreover, "Joint-Heir Houses" were nothing other than common houses or castles <note>original: "gemeine Häuser oder Schlösser"</note> for many contracted and united Nobles, into which they would withdraw with their families in times of necessity and war, as if to the safest asylums. It is in this sense that Duke George of Saxony, Landgrave in Thuringia, uses the word in a letter from the year 1526 written to Martin Luther, where the following words are read: "Furthermore, you have established an asylum in Wittenberg, so that all the monks and nuns who rob our churches and monasteries, taking things with them and stealing, have a refuge and stay with you; as if Wittenberg might be politely called a Joint-Heir House <note>original: "Gan-Erben-Haus"</note> for all the apostates of our land, etc." <note>Duke George uses the legal term sarcastically to describe Wittenberg as a 'den of thieves' or a collective refuge for those he considers religious deserters.</note>

Among these Nobles or Joint Heirs, the eldest usually performed the duty of administrator of the property and judge. He was elected for this by the common vote of the more influential Joint Heirs and called a Burgrave <term>Burggrav; from 'Burg' (castle) and 'Graf' (judge/count)</term>. The word *Grav* signified a judge to the ancients; see below under the word *Grav*. For the burden of administration, he kept a specific portion of the profits for himself, while the remaining profits were divided in equal portions among the Joint Heirs. Such Burgraves are still found today among the Joint Heirs of the fortresses of Rothenberg, Friedberg, and Gelnhausen. After they are elected, they are usually invested and confirmed by the Emperors—specifically in those castles which the Joint Heirs hold as fiefs from the Empire. Friedenberg, part 1, chapter 1, number 235. Next to the Burgrave was the Master Builder <term>Baumeister; here meaning a castellan or works-master</term>, to whom a certain administration was likewise committed, specifically that which pertained to the guard and conservation of the castle and the entire joint-heir district. See also my own *Treatise on Monarchy*, page 13, where I discuss Co-owners <note>original: "Condominis, von gemeiner Herrschafft"</note>.

## 4. Auction, Public Sale. <term>Subhastatio; a sale "under the spear"</term>

Regarding the ancient custom of proscribing items for sale, see Barnabé Brisson, *Select Antiquities of Civil Law, book 3, chapter 8.*
Whether a sale made publicly "under the spear" <note>under the authority of an auction</note> can be rescinded on account of an enormous loss <term>læsio enormissima; a legal concept where a contract is voided if the price is less than half the true value</term>, by the benefit of law 2 of the Code *on rescinding sales*? See Berlich, *decision 126.* Likewise, regarding goods auctioned or confiscated, should they be sold according to the Judge’s estimation, or rather according to how they were bid? Modestinus Pistoris discusses this in *question 142.*
Whether the alienation of a minor's property is void due to a lack of a public auction—when the goods are not sold at an open bidding <note>original: "Auffschlag"</note>? Gratianus, *volume 4, forensic disputes, chapter 479.*

## ADDITION.

Pledges are to be sold under the public spear <note>the Roman symbol for an auction</note>. *Law 3 of the Code on the execution of judgments.* Biccius, *in the Golden Rules, section 5, theorem 157, number 2.*
In the ordinance of the City of Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratensis"</note> under the title "The Auction House and the Auctioneer's

<column-break/>

Regulation," <note>original: "Ganthaus und deß Gantkauffers Ordnung"</note> it is announced to all by the voice of the crier that whoever wishes to buy the goods should appear at the designated place within a certain time fixed for this, where they will be given to the highest bidder. Angelus, in his commentary on the *Digest, book 11, on pledges and mortgages, number 7*, thinks these last words must be carefully observed, since by virtue of them the City can be compelled to give that thing, because it has bound itself to do so.
In an auction <note>original: "Vergant"</note>, all sorts of disadvantage and fraud sometimes occur. Zorer, *part 2, question 3, numbers 203, 206.* In such cases, the local custom of each place must be most strictly observed (number 204), as to what effects the legitimate preceding auction should have (number 207 and the two following). As to whether and how a public auction is a form of purchase and sale, see the man beyond all praise and lacking in none, Mr. Frantzkius, *on the transfer fee, pages 294, 409 and following.* It is not a necessary alienation <note>a forced legal transfer rather than a voluntary sale</note>, as discussed at length on pages 390 and 413. Johannes Antonius Mangilius wrote *Questions on Public Auctions*. When ancestral goods are sold under the spear, do the children have the Right of First Refusal <term>Jus Protomiseos; the right of a relative to match the highest bid to keep property in the family</term>? Berlich, *part 2, conclusion 39, number 63.* Carpzov, *part 2, chapter 31, definition 18.*

1. There is the auctioning of contributions and taxes, of which the entire title of the Code *if for public payments* speaks; also of tithes, when the authorities let their income be sold at auction.
2. If property belonging to widows or orphans <note>original: "pupillos"</note> is sold publicly.
3. If the property of burdened debtors is publicly auctioned.
4. If leases are made publicly and "at the spear," as Coelius Rhodiginus notes was customarily done in *book 11, chapter 51.* Gothofredus, *in the summary of the Code on the faith and law of the treasury's spear.* Bachovius, *on the first part of the Pandects, title on the origin of law, section 29, number 2, page 104.*
5. If property that has fallen to the state <note>escheated</note>, committed, or pledged to the treasury is sold duly and solemnly. See the whole title of the Code *on the faith and law of the treasury's spear.* On this argument, see the Inaugural Disputation of Mr. Dr. Tabor *on the faith and law of the treasury's spear* throughout. Postius, *in his additions to the treatise on Public Auctions.*

The word for public auction <note>original: "subhastare"</note> is derived from *sub* (under) and *hasta* (spear), because goods to be sold were placed "under the spear," for a spear placed in the forum was the sign of a saleable thing. Calvinus, *in his Lexicon.* Cujas and Gothofredus, *on the summary of the Code on the faith and law of the treasury's spear.* Bachovius, *on the first part of the Pandects, title on the origin of law, section 29, number 2, page 106,* where he deduces this from various authors. The origin was that Emperors used to sell the spoils they had taken from enemies, especially when towns were captured and stormed—and sometimes they even sold the people themselves—and this was later done with a military spear as a sign, and from there it was transferred into the city for public sales. Alexander ab Alexandro describes the origin of the auction in *Genial Days, book 3, chapter 16:* when cities were captured, the property of the proscribed or the spoils of the enemy were made for sale by placing a spear. Hence, I do not believe the "spear" was a rod given when someone was granted the power to sell some merchandise, as Damhouder thinks in his *compendium on auctions, chapter 1, number 12.* Calvinus, in his *Lexicon*, however, contradicts himself because under the word "spear" <note>original: "hasta"</note> he says the origin of selling began because the spear was a symbol of strength, and by it, Princes protected the authority of their affairs—
