those things which must be done in judgment, by commission of the Judge, they announce to the litigants or others; these are also called *Pedelli* <note>original: "Pedelli", beadles or lower court officials</note>, *Cursores* <note>original: "Cursores", couriers or runners</note>, and *Viatores* <note>original: "Viatores", literally 'travelers', meaning court messengers</note>, as seen in the Law *magis puto* § *ne tamen 13* regarding the property of those under guardianship; the Law *is cui* § *missus 27* in the Digests: *that they be in possession of legacies*; and § *tripli 4* of the Institutes: *on actions*. These are also called court attendants and executors of lawsuits in the said § *tripli*; the final law of the Digests: *what is done out of fear*; Law *omnes 33* § *executorib 5* in the Code: *on Bishops and Clergy*; and Law 1 and Law *omnib 3* in the Code: *on court fees and expenses*.

To what extent should trust be placed in these messengers? Consult Menochius *on judicial arbitration*, book 1, case 112; Tiraquellus *on the retraction of lineage*, § 8, glossary 9, number 2 and following.

Certainly, in the Judgment of the Chamber <note>The Reichskammergericht, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, as in many other well-constituted Courts, it is accepted that if the execution of a Summons is not correctly performed through the fault or lack of skill of the attendant or messenger, he is bound to perform it again from the beginning at his own expense. *Imperial Chamber Ordinance, part 1, title 38, final §; Gail, observation 54; Maranta on the order of judgments, part 6, title on Summons, number 124.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding the messengers (*viatores*), this is dealt with in part 1 of the Chamber Ordinance, titles 34, 35, 36, 37, 47, 55, 82, 84; and Denais, title on Chamber law, 200 and following. The messengers, <term>the court messengers</term> <note>original German: "die Gerichtsboten"</note>, must swear an oath regarding their office. *Socin, article 10, number 5.* Hence they are called Sworn Messengers, <term>sworn Chamber messengers</term> <note>original German: "geschworne Cammerboten"</note>. This was provided for by the law of the Chamber in the said title 84, and well-constituted Courts observe this.

<column-break/>

In the event that the person summoned does not want to accept the complaint, it is customary that the advocate or messenger stick the order or the complaint into the gate or house door, or otherwise lay it down under the door or gate and weigh it down with a stone; this is as valid as if it had actually been accepted. *Suttinger, observation 18, number 7.* If a messenger of the Chamber does not correctly deliver the legal proceedings, he is bound to execute them again at his own expense. *Schvvanmann, Chamber Procedure, book 1, chapter 22, number 6.* The messenger of the Chamber writes the execution performed on the back of the proceedings; a Notary is then required to draw up a formal instrument regarding it. *Book 1, chapter 22, numbers 8 and 9.* Regarding the Office of Couriers in delivering proceedings, see *Roding, Chamber Pandects, book 4, title 13; Johann Andreas Gerhard, Doctor, in the Discourse on the Supreme Judgments in the Roman Empire, pages 51, 52.*

## 42. Court Costs, Expenses. *Judicial Expenses*.

The Clause: *and I pray the defendant be condemned in expenses* <note>original Latin: "& peto reum condemnari in expensis"</note>, and I ask to condemn the defendant to the caused <term>court costs</term> <note>original German: "Gerichts-Ankosten"</note>, as is right, is very useful: because a Judge is not bound to grant his service for private benefit unless requested, etc. *Law 4 § "hoc autem" in the Digests: on threatened damage.*

This clause, therefore, ensures that the Judge is absolutely compelled to pronounce on the expenses and condemn the party who should be condemned, especially if there were no just causes for litigating; otherwise, he would "make the case his own" <note>A legal term meaning the judge becomes liable for damages due to a bad or negligent ruling</note>, and is bound to repay the expenses from his own pocket. *Law "sancimus", Law "properandum" § "sive a." in the Code: on judgments.*

If, however, the Plaintiff does not include this Clause, nor asks for the expenses to be restored to him, no blame can be imputed to the Judge who does not condemn the party to costs, nor is he held liable for the interests of the victor. *Bartolus on Law 4 § "hoc autem" and on Law "properandum" 13 § "sive autem" in the Code: on judgments*, where he says we ought to be cautious to ask in the petition that the defendant be condemned in expenses already made and those to be made until the end of the case. On this Clause, consult also *Oldendorp on exceptions, title on the form of the petition, folio 305, verse "Sixth".*

Expenses are owed, moreover, for various reasons: For (1.) from the victory of the whole case, *per Law "properandum" § "Sin autem alterutra" in the Code: on judgments.* (2) From the "contumacy" <note>legal defiance or failure to appear</note> of the adversary, mention of which is made in Law *sancimus* in the Code: *on Judgments* and in the chapter *dilect.*: *on fraud and contumacy.* (3.) From the fault of the adversary who delays the process of the case, as found established in Law *non ignoretis* in the Code: *on fruits and litigation expenses*, and in the final chapter: *on fraud and contumacy.* (4.) From the "temerity" <note>recklessness or frivolousness</note> of one who drags another into court without a cause of action: as in Law *eum, quem temerè* at the beginning: *on Judgments*, and in chapter 1: *on fraud and contumacy, book 6.* All these types are included under the aforementioned petition.

Regarding expenses in Criminal cases, see *Cardinal Tuschi, letter C, conclusion: expenses in Criminal cases; Berlich, part 4, conclusion 19; Article 104 of the Penal Court Ordinance of Charles V* <note>The "Carolina", the first body of criminal law for the Holy Roman Empire</note>, and the commentators there; and it should be noted that in all crimes, especially where a death penalty or physical punishment is not imposed, the Defendant can be condemned in expenses, damages, and interests. *Berlich, said conclusion 19, number 34 and following.*

And that those under investigation ought to be condemned in expenses even if they are acquitted of the ordinary penalty, if grave evidence exists against them—even in that case where the evidence was cleared through torture—is decided by *Caspar Anton. Thesaur. Forensic, book 1, question 45, number 7 and following.* So also in the Duchy of Württemberg, the defendant is always bound to pay the expenses in criminal matters, even if otherwise acquitted, because the <term>Treasury</term> <note>original: "Fiscus"</note> had cause to complain against him; it is otherwise if he were condemned to corporal punishment under the Cornelia Law.

In that case, moreover, when the Defendant is condemned in expenses according to "the style" <note>customary court practice</note>, it cannot be harmful to him afterwards if he is sued civilly for the same crime, as if he had been involved in "slight fault" <note>negligence vs. intent</note>.

### ADDITION.

The expenses of the lawsuit fall [on the loser] when the Appellant has won in the first Instance. *Gail, 1. Observation 152; and Gylman, 1. decision 10 at the end, and book 2, decision 48.* The loser must be condemned in expenses to the victor, otherwise the Judge is compelled to pay those from his own pocket. *Law "properandum" 13 § "fin autem 6" in the Code: on judgments; Giph. in Treatise on Procedure 2, chapter 9, page 88.* For the extensions and limitations of this rule, as well as the types of expenses, see *Gilken.*

Just as the words **High Court** <note>original: "Hohe Gericht"</note> indicate a superior jurisdiction, involving both pure and mixed authority <note>original: "merum mixtumque Imperium"; in Roman-German law, this refers to the power to inflict capital punishment (pure) and handle civil disputes (mixed)</note>, so too the words **Deep** or **Lowest Court** <note>original: "Tiefe sive Niederste Gericht"</note> indicate a simple and inferior jurisdiction. Thus, the joining of these terms implies a total or all-encompassing authority. See Knich on Saxon Law, regarding the title of the Dukes of Saxony, chapter 5, folio 124 and following; century 2, decade 3. Also see Goeddaeus in the counsel concerning the restitution of the Barons of Vallendar, number 313 and number 471 and following.

The word **Court** <note>original: "Gericht"</note> encompasses all forms of jurisdiction and authority. Klock, counsel 13, number 27. Jurisdiction is tied to the **Court and Command** <note>original: "Gericht und Bottmäßigkeit"</note> and passes to the heirs. Lord Tabor in his questions on Wesenbeck, dispute 2, question 4. From this, it is understood that jurisdiction exists in a territory passively and materially, as if in an inanimate thing, but in the person of the Magistrate, it exists formally and actively, as if in a living subject. ### 40. Court Records. Judicial Acts.

**Judicial Acts** <note>original: "Acta Judicialia"</note> are said to be those things which contain the proceedings between litigants before a judge, and thus include the business inserted into the records, and all things done in court, or in some form of judgment, or done in the presence of the judge and written by the hand of a Scribe <note>or Clerk</note> deputized for this by order of the judge. Law 3, in the Code: *on time and the restoration of appeals*. See Bornitius in the treatise on instruments, book 2, chapter 9. Under judicial acts are understood those things which are entered into public records. Law 1, section 2, in the Code: *on those who are manumitted in the Church*; Law 2, in the Code: *on the production of documents*; and deeds transferred into public monuments. Final law, in the Code: *on the rescinding of a sale*; book 7, section 1, in the Code: *on the Curator of a madman*. See Bornitius in the cited place, under the heading "then," and Bolognetus on Law 2 in the Code: *on the production of documents*.
Judicial Acts deserve **public trust** <note>original: "Publicam fidem"; the legal principle that official records are presumed to be true</note>. Final law, in the Code: *on the matter judged*, there it states: "deeds which are transferred into public monuments, we wish to have perpetual stability." For the public trust should not perish with the death of the investigator <note>the judge</note>. See Gothofredus there, who says: "Acts once promulgated in judgment create perpetual trust, even if the judge who investigated the case is dead or removed."

<column-break/>

See Christinaeus on Belgian decisions, volume 2, decision 88, number 13. Caspar Thesaurus denies that judicial acts come under the name of an "Instrument," book 2, question 17, number 6. Also, a produced document is not "of the acts" itself, but only its production is. Bolognetus, cited place, numbers 10 and 18.

### ADDITION.

Regarding what it means to **lay behind the court** <note>original: "Hinter das Gericht legen"; to file or deposit records officially</note>, see Carpzov, part 2, decision 148, numbers 19, 20, 29. **The records are the vehicle leading to the verdict.** Klock, volume 1, counsel 10, number 548. They establish what is notorious <note>well-known/evident</note>, counsel 14, number 127, and from them the sentence is also declared, counsel 27, numbers 30 and 31. The *Constitutio Carolina* <note>The Holy Roman Empire's unified criminal code of 1532</note>, according to Oldekop, title 1, Criminal Cautions 8, allows and commands fifty-seven times that the Records be transmitted to a College [of Jurists] and a response be sought from there. Lord Tabor in his Criminal Gleanings, on Article 160 of the *Constitutio Carolina*, section 44. To these, I add the Imperial Recess of Regensburg from the year 1654, sections 61, 96, and especially 113. If the records of a previous instance are inept and lacking, the entire process and acts—while preserving the evidence—are usually quashed in the Imperial Chamber <note>the Reichskammergericht</note>. Schvvanman, Chamber Process, book 2, chapter 2, number 9, page 11. When records are lost or were not written down, the plaintiff in the Chamber is ordered to sue anew, and the lower judge is condemned to pay the expenses. Schvvanman, cited chapter 2, number 11, page 51. Regarding when the appealed party is bound to redeem the previous records at the same time, chapter 2, number 7.
It is placed in the Judge's discretion **to send the records away sealed or open**. In the case of J. versus R., the Prince of Neuburg sent the records sealed to Speyer. **Acts** are called whatever is dictated from the mouth to the pen and recorded, or otherwise brought into writing judicially. Lord Dr. Biccius in the Golden Sessions, session 5, thesis 133, describes that "acts" are called all writings made in judgment before a judge, written by the hand of a notary <note>original: "tabellionis"</note> deputized for this. He teaches how acts are to be produced in six conclusions in the cited place. On this entire subject, add Barbosa in his axioms, book 1, chapter 15, throughout two full pages. Judicial acts include within them the **Court Chancellery** and **Recess Books**, and they create unshakeable trust. Ummius in his work on process, page 701. See the **Privilege of Charles over the Court Book of the City of Friedberg** in Limnäus, book 7, number 15. Records are also generally judged to be where something is done by the authority of a Judge in any place, even outside of court. Law *an apud se* section *de manum. vind.* Jason in Law 15, *apud quem 2*, in the Code: *on the production of documents*, number 41.
**Court Books** deserve full trust. Matthias Berlich, 1, conclusion 36, number 18, and those cited there in detail.

## 43. Court Clerk. Actuarius.

We call the Secretaries of the courts Scribes or Notaries (Court Clerks <note>original German: "Gerichts-Schreiber"</note>), who are placed in charge of writing and directing those things which are proposed in judgment—that is, the Judicial Acts. For this reason, they are also sometimes called *Actuarii*.

The duty of these Scribes, according to the memorable chapter *Since against a false assertion, 11. extra. on proofs* <note>A reference to Canon Law (Decretals of Gregory IX)</note>, consists in the recording of all Judicial Acts: such as Extensions, Summons, Recusations of Judges, Exceptions, Replications, Duplications, Petitions, Responses, Interrogations, Confessions, the depositions of Witnesses, the production of Instruments <note>Legal documents or evidence</note>, Interlocutory decrees, Appeals, Renunciations, Conclusions, Sentences, and all other things that occur in either ordinary or extraordinary judgment. Specifically, they must record each and every one of these in the proper order: designating the places, times, and persons, and they must preserve the originals of everything they have written in the Court Registry and Chamber. This is done so that if a dispute should perhaps arise regarding the Process of the judgment, the truth can be declared through these records. Eberhard Speckhan, *century 3, class 3, question 10, under foundation number 6.*

The original copies of the Acts, therefore, ought to remain in the possession of the writer, so that recourse may be had to them if a controversy happens to arise between the litigants regarding the Judge's Process, for the sake of greater trust and the preservation of the truth. Speckhan, *at the cited place.*

However, it is common practice that the Acts, after the copies have been collated and the documents recognized by the adversary, are returned again to the person who produced them. In that case, those copies found in the judicial Archives provide full evidence.

*Clerk of the Trisoley <note>An administrative district or court office</note>, Acts of the Teutonic Order, folio 157, 195, 212, 214. Court or Trisoley Clerk in the Nuremberg Memorial writing, folio 150.*

Freher, *on*

## 44. Rumor, or Common Report. Reputation.

Regarding reputation and its requirements, see Göhauf, *in the treatise on Witches, folio 35 and following.*

Rumor is not sufficient evidence for torture; see Menochius, *on presumptions, book 1, question 89.* Mascardus, *on proofs, book 2, conclusion 754, number 5.* Carrer, *in criminal practice, on evidence, section on the second piece of evidence, number 5, version "however."* Hackelmann, *illustrious disputation 24, thesis 10, under letter A.*

For naked rumor does not even provide semi-full proof. Mascardus, *on proofs, conclusion 754, number 1 and following.* Much less is it sufficient evidence for torture, for the infliction of which not only grave and probable likelihoods are required, but evidence clearer than the midday sun. Rumor, however, is not such a thing, according to that saying of Virgil:

> Rumor is an evil, than which no other is swifter;
> It flourishes by its own activity, and gains strength as it goes:
> Small at first through fear, soon it raises itself into the breezes,
> It walks upon the ground, and hides its head among the clouds.

However, the aforementioned tradition fails in certain cases: (1.) namely, when the accused is already defamed regarding other crimes, and is thus of bad report, condition, and reputation—*when the accused has an ill-repute and is otherwise suspicious* <note>original German: "wann der Beklagte einen bösen Leimut, und sonsten verdächtig ist"</note>. For then, from any slight suspicion touching upon the crime in question, the accused is usually subjected to torments, provided that the rumor concerns the same kind of crime. Hunnius, *in criminal treatise, chapter 3, thesis 155.*

Because one who is once bad is always presumed to be bad (*chapter "once," on the Rules of Law in the 6th book of Decretals*). This is supported by the text of the *Criminal Constitution of Charles V, article 25, section "First"*: *Whether the suspicion falls upon such a bold or reckless person of bad reputation and rumor, that one might expect such a misdeed from them, or whether the same person has previously committed, attempted, or been accused of such a misdeed.* <note>The "Constitutio Criminalis Carolina" (1532) was the first unified criminal law code in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

(2.) There will be a place for torture if the rumor did not begin from spiteful enemies or frivolous men, but from honest and trustworthy persons; according to the said *Criminal Constitution, article 25, version: "yet such bad reputation should not come from enemies or frivolous people, but from impartial, upright people." Chapter "how and when," on accusations.* Zanger, *on torture, chapter 2, number 8 and following.*

But even then, rumor becomes a piece of evidence that must be considered in this case, yet not such a piece that it alone suffices for torture—unless the rumor rests upon reasons and very probable conjectures. *When the common report has a ground and cause.* But see Freher's *treatise on reputation throughout.*

### ADDITION.

To these authors, add Caspar Bragaccia, Hermann Kirchner, Hotoman, Paschal le Vayer, and Rasch. In the year 1657, at Altdorf, Gerard von Stöcken—a native of Rendsburg in Holstein and now a Professor of Law at Strasbourg—conducted his inaugural disputation *On the Law of Embassies* <note>original: "de Jure Legationum"</note> with the highest praise and the applause of all. In that same disputation, he praises others who have written on this subject, such as Matthäus Bortius on Envoys, Gryphiander on Envoys, Jean de Chokier’s treatise on Envoys, Alberico Gentili <note>a foundational figure in the study of international law</note> on Envoys, Melchior Jungker on Embassies, and besides these, at the very end of the disputation, he lists many others from both ancient and modern times.

**48. Statute. Law.** <note>original: "Gesatz. Lex."</note>

To establish Universal Laws <note>original: "**Gesatz und Ordnungen**"; these are statutes and ordinances which bind everyone incorporated into the Roman Empire and must be observed by them</note> belongs to the Emperor alone, by virtue of his supreme power <note>original: "vi Imperii summi"</note>; for the power to make laws is a primary right of Sovereignty <note>original: "jus Majestatis"</note>. See my work *On Sovereignty* <note>original: "de Majest."</note>, folio 145. This is done, however, with the consent and counsel of the Estates of the Empire <note>original: "**mit Hülff und Rath der Ständen deß Reichs**"; the Estates included the Princes, Prelates, and representatives of Imperial Cities</note>. The power to establish a special and local law <note>original: "**Land- und Stadt-Recht**"; provincial and city law</note> generally belongs to the other inferior Princes and Estates of the Empire within their own domains and provinces, with the consent of the leading men <note>original: "**worzu dann der gemeine Ausschuß von der Land schafft, das seynd die Prälaten, die von der Ritterschafft, und die von vornehmen Städten darzu beschrieben werden**"; to which the general committee of the provincial landscape—namely the prelates, the nobility, and those from the prominent cities—are summoned</note>. See Joachim Cloren, *Justinianic Diatribes* 3, thesis 22. For these Princes and other inferiors, distinguished by Princely dignity, represent the Emperor within their own provinces. Therefore, just as the Emperor establishes a universal Law <note>original: "**allgemeine Gesatz und Ordnungen**"</note> by reason of the Empire's universal jurisdiction, so too the other inferior Princes and Estates of the Empire establish law by virtue of their territorial superiority <note>original: "**Krafft Landsfürstlicher hoher Obrigkeit**"</note>. Because they possess only specific, limited territories, and thus their jurisdiction is more specialized, they establish not a universal law but a special one (which binds no one except their subjects). Consequently, they promulgate provincial laws and provincial constitutions <note>original: "**Hof- und Landgerichts-Ordnung**"; court and provincial judicial ordinances</note>, abolish contrary ones, and frequently substitute new ones, to which subjects are bound even without the consent of the Emperor. See Matthäus Coler, *On Executive Process*, part 1, chapter 3, number 5 and following.

And those who are governed by these laws are, by that very fact, considered subject to the territorial jurisdiction of those rulers.

As to whether statutes and laws bind those who have not accepted them through use and custom, see Chokier,

<column-break/>

*On Exemptions*, part 4, question number 66; Magonius, *Decisions of Lucca* 49, number 38; and my own work *On the Right of Sovereignty*, folio 146, etc.

### ADDITION.

In ancient times, Germany sang its laws in the villages <note>original: "vicatim"</note>, when the land was still unformed, the sky harsh, and the culture and appearance grim, as Tacitus states in his booklet *On Germany*. This is the reason why Germans, even today, call the parts of songs or verses a **Statute** <note>original: "**Gesetz**"; playing on the double meaning of 'law' and 'musical strophe'</note>. It is best to proceed by the "Sealed Way," that is, the text of the Laws <note>original: "**welches auch von den Reichs Constitutionen zu sagen, als welche vim Legis obtinent**"; which is also to be said of the Imperial Constitutions, as they obtain the force of law</note>. Zorer, part 2, question 15, number 950. Simon van Groenewegen wrote a treatise *On Abrogated Laws*.

**49. Patrician Families. Patricians.** <note>original: "Geschlechter. Patricii."</note>

Patricians, or **Lineages** <note>original: "**Geschlechter**"</note>, are today called **City-Nobles** <note>original: "**Stadt-Junckern**"</note>. They are the elite of the Imperial Cities and other principal cities capable of aristocratic rule; they are distinguished from **the other nobility who live in the countryside** <note>original: "**der andern vom Adel, so auf dem Land wohnen**"</note> and from those who are vassals of the Princes or the Emperor. In the **Augsburg Book of Families** <note>original: "Augspurgischen Geschlechter-Buch"</note>, published in the year 1582 by Sigmund Feyerabend, a bookseller in Frankfurt am Main, 51 families are recounted who lived there 500 or more years ago and ruled until the beginning of the Guilds, but all of whom have died out except for eight: namely—**Herwart, Welser, Rehlinger, Langenmantel of Sparren, Langenmantel of R. Hofmayer, Ravenspurger, and Ilsung.** Fifty-four more recent ones are named, and 14 who were added on December 29, 1627. See Limnäus, *Public Law*, volume 1, additions to book 7, chapter 4, page 158.

**On the other hand, 39 families are recounted who were accepted and elevated by an honorable Council to replace those that had died out.** Among these families, however, it seems to me that some already enjoyed the right of nobility in other cities, such as **the Imhof, Baumgärtner, and Haller families**, all of whom are numbered among the patricians of the "Greater Houses" of Nuremberg.

**Concerning the families of Worms, see the Worms Chronicle** <note>original: "Wurmsische Khaitung"</note>, book 1. If you look at the origin of the Patricians, they were the sons of the one hundred Senators elected by Romulus, who were called "Fathers" <note>original: "Patres"</note> and were held as a public council (Livy, book 1). And their sons were called Patricians because they could "cite or name their fathers" <note>original: "Patres ciere & nominare possent"</note>, according to Velleius Paterculus.

In Italy, there were formerly Patricians who possessed towers; Merula, book 5 of *Memorable Things*, chapter 4. Likewise in Germany, **the true citizens lived in towers**, such as can still be seen in Esslingen and elsewhere. And the word **Citizen** <note>original: "**Bürger**"</note> is said to derive from the Greek *pyrgos* <note>original: "πύργος"</note>, that is, from "Tower," from which also comes **Burg** for a Castle. For castles formerly had a principal tower. And that the Patricians were formerly Prefects or Governors of provinces can be seen in Guilliman's *Habsburg*, folio 67.

Regarding the lawful number of Senators <note>original: "Patrum," literally "Fathers," the traditional title for Roman Senators</note> required for a session of the Senate at Rome, their dignity, and also the age of Christian Patricians, see Lælius Bisciola’s *Subsequent Hours* <note>original: "horar. subsecivar."</note>, book 3, chapter 17; the same author in book 7, chapter 13, teaches who the "Patricians of the Lesser Houses" <note>original: "Patricii Minorum Gentium"</note> were. These Patricians of the Lesser Houses are distinguished from those of the Greater Houses <note>original: "majorum gentium"</note>, who were Patricians by blood—that is, the descendants of the "Fathers" originally chosen by Romulus. The others, however, were co-opted into the rank of Fathers and later made Patricians. From this, Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his first book of *Tusculan Disputations*, used an elegant metaphor to call some gods those "of the Greater Houses" and others "of the Lesser Houses."

Patricians are also called "Noble at Home" <note>original: "Domi Nobiles"</note> by some, to distinguish them from other types of Nobility. Similarly, Father Rader, in his commentary on Quintus Curtius, book 3, chapter 25, page 106, makes a distinction between those who are noble "simply" <note>original: "ἁπλῶς," meaning absolutely or by birth</note> and those noble "in some respect" <note>original: "κατά τι"</note>. He says the Athenians called Iphicrates, Aristogiton, and Dropides "absolutely" noble because they were famous for their lineage and reputation—that is, they were the most noble. He calls the Spartans only "Noble at Home" in some respect, namely only among their own people at home, not abroad, and not absolutely. All authors have distinguished those "Noble at Home" from the truly Noble. To be "Noble at Home" is a lesser thing than to be "Noble," so the writer of proverbs is rightly noted when he interprets "Noble at Home" as one who is not only famous for wealth and power, but is born noble from nobles. For one who is "Noble at Home" is not commonly considered noble outside his home or his own country; by contrast, he is "Noble" everywhere who is called noble by the laws and customs of all nations, such as those procreated from Kings or some ancient, famous, and noble bloodline, as there is no nation that does not consider these people noble. For "Absolute Nobility" is not moved by location—that is, it is considered illustrious everywhere. Aristotle discusses this in his *Politics*. Authors have looked to this distinction when they called others "Noble at Home," such as Cicero, Sallust, Livy, Apuleius, and others.

*Report on how the families or Patricians in the Imperial Cities, as companions in heraldry, are established against the Imperial Knightly Nobility, and why trade was forbidden to the Knight and Nobleman in ancient times, etc.* See Lerch, *On the Knightly Order* <note>original: "de Ordin. Equestr."</note>, page 11, face 2, *in the section: "when experience now brings."*

But the Honorable Johann Jacob Draco has treated the subject of Patricians fully and elegantly in a separate treatise; add to this Fauchet, *On Origins* <note>original: "des origin."</note>, book 2, chapter 1.

## 50. Siblings. <note>original: "Geschwistrigte. Fratres, Sorores."</note>

In feudal matters, only brothers are called "siblings" <note>original: "Geschwistrigte"</note>, not sisters. Johann Fichard, *Feudal Counsel* 7, number 15, where in number 19 he adds that even according to our custom of speaking, brothers are accustomed to be called "siblings" among themselves.

### ADDITION.

See above under *Brotherhood*. Regarding the naming of brothers and sisters, see Rupert in *The Epistolary Mercury*, page 660 and following. A kinsman in a more remote degree does not come under the name of "brother," nor even a paternal cousin. Klock, counsel 6, number 130. Regarding how the word "Sister" <note>original: "Soror"</note> is to be understood in the law of Bishops and Clerics, see Nicolaus Henelius in *Wratislavisan Leisure*, chapter 33. Blasius Michalorius’s treatise on *Brotherhoods*, from whence they are named. Diego de Covarrubias, *On Wills* <note>original: "de Testam."</note>, chapter on duty 14, number 12, at the verse "but here that." Sisters are not included under the name of "brothers." Covarrubias, *On Wills*, chapter "Your," number 3, last verse. Whether the elder is included under the name of brothers is distinguished in Villal., book 38. Another question on the naming of brothers is proposed in Soares, folio 345. Francesco de Porcellinis and Petrus de Ubaldis discuss two brothers.

Brothers are either joined to one another from both sides <note>sharing both parents</note>, or not from both sides but through only one parent: the former are called *Germani* <note>full siblings</note> by the Latins; *amphithaleis* <note>original: "ἀμφιθαлеῖς"</note> by the Greeks; and *Brothers of full birth* <note>original: "Bruder von voller Geburt"</note> by the Germans.

## 48. Statute. Law.

The power to establish Universal Laws <note>original: "Gesatz und Ordnungen," meaning statutes and ordinances</note>—which bind all who are incorporated into the Roman Empire and must be observed by them—belongs solely to the Emperor by virtue of his supreme Imperial power. Indeed, the power to make laws is the primary right of Sovereignty <note>original: "jus Majestatis"</note>. I discuss this in my work *On Sovereignty* <note>original: "de Majest."</note>, folio 145. This is done, however, with the consent and counsel of the Estates of the Empire <note>original: "mit Hülff und Rath der Stände deß Reichs"</note>. The power to establish special and local law <note>original: "Land- und Stadt-Recht," meaning territorial and municipal law</note> belongs generally to the other lower Princes and Estates of the Empire within their own jurisdictions and provinces, with the consent of the leading men. To this end, the "Common Committee of the Countryside" <note>original: "gemeine Ausschuß von der Landtschafft"</note> is summoned, consisting of the prelates, the knighthood, and representatives from the prominent cities. See Lord Joachim Cluten, *Justinianic Diatribe 3*, thesis 22. For these Princes and other lower officials distinguished by princely dignity represent the Caesar <note>the Emperor</note> within their own provinces. Therefore, just as the Emperor establishes universal Law <note>original: "allgemeine Gesatz und Ordnungen"</note> by reason of the Empire's universal jurisdiction, so too do the other lower Princes and Estates of the Empire—since they possess only specific territories and thus their jurisdiction is also specific—establish not universal law, but special law (which binds no one except their own subjects). They do this by the power of their high authority as territorial lords <note>original: "Krafft Landsfürstlicher hoher Obrigkeit"</note> which belongs to them by reason of their territories. Accordingly, they promulgate provincial laws and constitutions, as well as Court and Territorial Judicial Ordinances <note>original: "Hof- und Landgerichts-Ordnung"</note>; they abolish contrary laws and substitute new ones from time to time, to which their subjects are bound even without the consent of the Emperor. See Matthäus Coler, *On Executive Process*, part 1, chapter 3, number 5 and following.

And those who are governed by these laws are thereby considered to be under the territorial jurisdiction of those lords.

On whether statutes and laws not received by the usage and customs of the citizens are binding: see Chokier,

<column-break/>

*On Exemptions*, part 4, question 66; Magone, *Decisions of Lucca* 49, number 38; and my own work *On the Right of Sovereignty*, folio 146, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

In ancient times, Germany sang its laws in the villages, when the land was still "unformed, harsh in its climate, and gloomy in its culture and appearance," as Tacitus says in his booklet *On Germany*. This is the reason why Germans even today call parts of their songs "Statutes" <note>original: "Gesetz"</note>. It is best to proceed by the "Sealed Way"—that is, the text of the Laws—which can also be said of the Imperial Constitutions, as they obtain the force of law. See Zorer, part 2, question 15, number 950. Simon van Groenewegen wrote a treatise *On Abolished Laws*.

## 49. Lineages. Patricians.

Patricians, or "Lineages" <note>original: "Geschlechter"</note>, are today called "City Squires" <note>original: "Stadt-Junckern"</note>. They are the elite of the Imperial Cities and other principal cities capable of aristocratic rule; this distinguishes them from other members of the Nobility who live in the countryside and from those who are vassals of the Princes or the Emperor. In the *Augsburg Book of Lineages* <note>original: "Augspurgischen Geschlechter-Buch"</note>, published in the year 1580 by Sigmund Feyerabend, a bookseller in Frankfurt am Main, fifty-one lineages are recounted who lived there five hundred or more years ago and ruled until the beginning of the Guilds, but who have all since died out: namely Herwart, Welser, Rehlinger, Langenmantel of Sparren, Langenmantel of R. Hofmayer, Ravenpurger, and Ilsung. Fifty-four more recent families are named, and fourteen who were added on December 29, 1627. See Limnäus in *Public Law* <note>original: "J. Regarding the lineages of Worms, see the *Worms Accounts*, book 1. If you look at the origin of the Patricians, they were the sons of the hundred Senators chosen by Romulus, who were called "Fathers" <note>original: "Patres"</note> and were held as a sort of public council (Livy, book 1). Their sons were called Patricians because they could "summon and name their fathers" <note>original: "Patres ciere & nominare possent"</note>, according to Velleius Paterculus.

## 50. Siblings. Brothers, Sisters.

In feudal law, only brothers are called "siblings" <note>original German: "Geschwistrigte"</note>, not sisters. Johann Fichard, *Feudal Counsel* 7, number 15, where in number 19 he adds that by our custom of speaking, brothers are also accustomed to be called "siblings" among themselves.

### ADDITION.

See "Brotherhood" <note>original German: "Brüderschafft"</note> above. On the terms for Brother and Sister, see Rupert in *Epistolary Mercury*, page 660 and following. An "agnate" <note>a relative through the male line</note> in a more remote degree is not included in the term "brother," nor even a paternal first cousin. Regarding how the word "Sister" <note>original Latin: "Soror"</note> in the law of the Code of Justinian "On Bishops and Clerics" is to be understood, see Nicolaus Henelius in *The Leisure of Breslau*, chapter 33. A treatise by Blasius Michalorius on brothers, including legal decisions, exists [published] in Geneva. From where "Fraternities" get their name, see *On Testaments*. The term "Brothers" does not include "Sisters." Whether the term "Brothers" includes the elder is distinguished in Villalobos, book 38. Another question on the term "Brothers" is proposed in Soares, folio 345. Francesco de Porcellinis and Petrus de Ubaldis write regarding two brothers.

Brothers are either joined to each other on both sides <note>full siblings</note>, or not on both sides, but through only one parent. The former are called by the Latins "Germani"; by the Greeks "amphithaleis" <note>original Greek: "ἀμφιθαλεῖς," meaning blooming on both sides</note>; by the Germans "Brothers of full birth" <note>original German: "Bruder von voller Geburt"</note>.

Likewise, **Siblings** <note>original German: "Geschwisterigt"</note> from both sides (for with this word *geschwistrigt*, the German language designates both brothers and sisters) are called by the Greeks with the single word **half-siblings** <note>original Greek: "ἐτεροθαλεῖς," literally "blooming from another"</note>, and by the Germans as **step-brothers** <note>original German: "Stieffbrüder"</note>, as well as **half-brothers** <note>original German: "Halbbrüder"</note>, or **half-sister** <note>original German: "Halbschwester"</note>, and **step-siblings** <note>original German: "Stieffgeschwistrigt"</note>. See more in Rittershuf, *On the New Constitutions*, page 414.

A brother who alone administers an undivided inheritance acquires no personal possession of it, but possesses it on behalf of the other brothers by right of family intimacy. Klock, volume 2, counsel 61, number 128. A brother administering the goods of his brother and perceiving a profit from them is considered to be acting in bad faith <note>original Latin: "in dolo"</note>, and is bound at the request of the other brother to admit a sharing of the goods. See counsel 70, numbers 71 and 72. A brother does not succeed his brother in a "new fief" <note>A "new fief" (feudum novum) was one recently granted, rather than one inherited through ancient lineage</note>. See counsel 29, numbers 28 and 29. Nor does the "right of accretion" <note>The legal right of a co-heir to take the share of another heir who cannot or will not take it</note> take place in a fief granted to two brothers unless it was expressly agreed upon. Number 30.

## 51. Partnership. *Societas*.

Partnership, commonly called **Society** <note>original German: "Gesell-"</note> or **Trade-Association** <note>original German: "Gewerbschafft"</note>, is defined as an honest agreement contracted between two or more people for more convenient use and more abundant profit. See Azo in the summary of the Code "On Partnership" <note>original Latin: "pro socio"</note> at the beginning; the gloss on the Institutes "On Partnership"; and Capyc. decision 174. And although common ownership sometimes gives birth to discord—as the law says, "with a Father" in the section "sweetest things" in the Digest on legacies—it is nevertheless also accustomed to produce a shortcut to profit. This is because what a man cannot achieve by himself, he seeks through the consideration of a Partner, whose work supplements his own. See the Institutes "On Partnership," section 1. Whence he who is in a Partnership is called a **Partner** <note>original Latin: "Socius"</note> from "consortium," and he is a **Sharer** <note>original Latin: "Consors"</note> to whom a part of the goods belongs; for the Ancients used the word "fate" <note>original Latin: "sors"</note> for "portion," and they are called Partners because of a Partnership of risk or of body, as if bound together into one. Lucas de Penna, in the Code "on the liberality of the Emperor"; Ripa on the chapter "with Matthew" regarding Constitutions.

Whether and when a partnership of public tax-farming <note>the practice of private individuals collecting taxes for the state</note> is considered or presumed to be made, even if the Partners or the Partnership are not explicitly named? Whether and when, and what conditions must meet, for it to pass to the heirs? Whether the benefit and profit after the Partnership is dissolved by the death of one member, while the time of the contract is still running, belongs to the heir of the deceased Partner? Baptista de Hieronymis deals extensively with all these matters in a certain Counsel inserted in the treatise by Peter Nicholas Mozzius on contracts, title "On Partnership," page 516 and many following up to page 542.

Regarding incidental and conventional Partnership, see Ronchegall on the law "the same," section "But if anyone," number 19 and following, regarding "two defendants."

Our doctors of law hand down with one voice that a Partnership <note>Societas</note> differs from "common ownership" <note>Communio</note> or "fellowship" <note>confortoria</note>, as they call it. From this they conclude that if many people hold goods in common, they are said to have common ownership, not a partnership. Thus, if many are bound to one debt, they are not then considered Partners,

<column-break/>

but "fellow-sharers" <note>original Latin: "confortes"</note> of the same obligation, as Tuschus records under the letter S, conclusion 279, at the end, following Alexander, counsel 40, book 2.

And in a case of doubt, common ownership is presumed rather than Partnership, especially if there is an accidental cause (such as the agreement of a common inheritance, or something similar), as the same Tuschus asserts in the said letter S, conclusion 280, number 12. Regarding the partnership of two brothers, see P. de Ubaldis. Regarding what rights a partner has in common goods, see Pfeil, counsel 58. When a payment made to one of the partners creates a release from debt for the others, see Magon, decision 5. Rosacorb treats the matter of Partnership in the context of performing common labor in practical questions, chapter 52.

->ADDITION.<-

A person is known by his associate <note>original Latin: "socius"</note> who is not known by himself. See the law in the Digest "on the office of the urban prefect," and "on inofficious wills." See also Gothofredus Antonius, disputation 11; Hieronymus Reusner on feudal disputations; Obrecht on fiefs, book 4; and Rittershuf on feudal partitions, chapter 5. A Partnership contains within itself a certain right of brotherhood. See Barbosa, *Axioms*, book 17. Whether and how a Partnership is ended by renunciation is covered by Lord Biccius in the *Golden Section* 4, and Locamer in the *Questions on the Institutes*. Whether a partner can alienate his part in common goods to a stranger, and specifically a more powerful person, is in the same, question 12. Those execrable partnerships <note>monopolies</note> by which the price of grain is made dearer are discussed by Klock "On the Treasury," book 2, chapter 82. The Colleges of the East and West India Companies are the chief fortified bulwarks of the Federated Belgian Republic <note>The Dutch Republic</note>. Klock "On the Treasury," book 1, chapter 14, notes by whom and for what purpose they were instituted. Regarding the presumptions that arise against someone from a wicked association, see Borcholt on fiefs. To what degree of "slight fault" <note>original Latin: "levis culpa"</note> a partner is held liable is found in Lord Biccius. Those suffering from the "wicked itch" <note>original Latin: "pravi psora"</note> (which physicians consider the worst kind of scabies) desire to rub it onto those who have dealings with them, so that in a partnership of common filth, their own hidden wickedness may lie obscured. See more in Rittershuf on Amphilochius, page 51. The "greater partnership" <note>original German: "Die mehrere Gesellschafft"</note>, Limn. book 1.

## 52. Sufficiently settled. *To have a sufficiency of immovable goods.*

Possession is called in the German tongue **a holding** <note>original German: "eine Besitzung"</note>, from "sitting" <note>original Latin: "sedendo"</note>. Whence, when we signify that someone has sufficient ownership of things, and indeed of immovable things <note>real estate/land</note>, we are commonly accustomed to say, **he is sufficiently settled** <note>original German: "er ist gnugsam gesessen"</note>. Oldendorp, *On Actions*, class 2, on possession, page 127.

->ADDITION.<-

"Possessors" can be explained simply as the owners of estates, **settled or propertied citizens** <note>original German: "gesessene oder possessionirte Bürger"</note>. See the Code "on censuses" and Lord Tabor in his third corollary to the *Elementary Partitions*.

### 53. **Authority. Mandate.** <note>original German: **Gewalt**. Latin: **Mandatum**.</note>

Various clauses are usually inserted into these. But care must be taken that they are not of such a kind that, through the excessive liberty of the Proxy <note>original Latin: *Procurator*, a legal representative or attorney</note>, they place a burden upon the principals. Such as: **that the attorney has the power to perform everything as fully as if he were himself present** <note>original German: "daß der Anwalt/ alles dieses Macht hat/ bey folle zu verrichten/ als wann er selbst zugegen"</note>. Monterus, in *Decision 38*, notes that such a mandate seems to carry free power, where he also says that the proxy can renounce the lawsuit. For various formulas of Authority, see Cisner.

### ADDITION.

A Proxy Mandate is either general or special. General, which covers all cases, present and future. Special, which is directed only toward a specific case. However, although Special Proxies are in use almost everywhere in the lower courts, they are today eliminated in the supreme assemblies of the Empire—the Aulic Council and the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note>—except for certain cases in which a more specific mandate is usually required in addition to the general one. (*Recess of the Empire of 1654, section "and accordingly," 101.*) In all cases, a Proxy must be furnished with a general mandate according to the said Imperial Recess, which is sufficiently clear both from the formula of the Chamber Proxy, which can be found in Roding (*Book 1, Pandects of the Chamber, title 29, section 6*), and from the formula of the Proxy used in the Aulic Council, which can be seen in the *Ordinances of the Aulic Council of Ferdinand III, at the end, under the words "in each and every."* See also Dr. Johann Andreas Gerhard in his *Discourse on the Supreme Courts in the Roman Empire, page 95 and following.*

Only lawful and honorable matters can be mandated; for a mandate is not contracted for a shameful or dishonorable matter, or anything against good morals (*Institutes, book 3, title 26, section 7*). This is so, however, that he who commits a crime by such a mandate is liable to the person against whom he trespassed, and he who perpetrated it must be punished (*Digest, book 48, title 8, law 15*). See also **Locam.** in the *Notes to the Institutes.*

The boundaries of a mandate must be observed with exact diligence. Acts performed by a Proxy beyond the boundaries of the mandate are binding if the Principal, knowing of them, remained silent. Generally, a Proxy is bound to observe the boundaries not only regarding the instruction itself, but also regarding all its qualities: because even if he exceeds the qualities of the mandate in a small way, he is said to exceed the boundaries. It is considered the same whether something is done against the form of the mandate, or beside it, or beyond it. See **Barbosa** at length, *Axiom 11, chapter 10, axiom 16.*

Regarding the little word **Authority** <note>original German: **Gewalt**</note>, see **Symph. Gylm.** *volume 1, part 2, folio 5.*

<column-break/>

### 54. **Sovereignty. Jurisdiction.** <note>original German: **Gewaltsame**. Latin: **Imperium**.</note>

*Gewaltsame* is used for *Imperium* <note>The supreme power of the state or the right to command</note>, as is clear from its proper meaning.

### ADDITION.

A direct **Heir** <note>original Latin: **Heres**</note> rightly occupies a vacant inheritance by his own authority. **Struvius**, *On Private Redress, chapter 15, aphorism 1, number 1.* So too does a fiduciary heir <note>one who holds an inheritance in trust</note>, if the inheritance itself has been restored by word. **Johann Grake** has written on "one's own authority": redress <note>original Latin: *vindicta*</note> and to "vouch" or "claim" <note>original Latin: *vindicare*</note> denote the repelling of an injury that offends the Commonwealth, life, body, reputation, or our personal and property rights; and this is done either in the matter itself or toward the matter, whether by approaching a Judge or outside of Court. **Struvius**, *On Private Redress, page 10.*

As to when violence against life occurs by presumption, see **Struvius**, *On Private Redress, chapter 4, aphorism 10, number 4, at the end.*

### 55. **Warranty. Guarantee.** <note>original German: **Gewähr**. Latin: **Guaranda**.</note>

The **Saxon Guarantee** <note>original Latin: **Guaranda Saxonica**</note> is thought to benefit a defendant in this way: that he holds the plaintiff bound, as if by a guarantee against eviction, against all who might perhaps afterward wish to sue the defendant for the same cause. (*Saxon Land Law, book 2, article 15; Saxon Municipal Law, article 114.*)

Whether a verbal offering and acceptance of a guarantee suffices, see **Jacob Schultes** in *Forensic Observations, observation 14*, where he says it was certainly not without reason estimated by some of the ancients that it suffices if the plaintiff offers himself by word in the name of a guarantee, and the defendant is content with that offer and accepts it. However, since **Saxon Law** specifically requires this as a matter of form—that the guarantee be promised by the plaintiff in the actual thing, by a physical act, and indeed judicially, with a **clasp of the hand** <note>original Latin: *stipulata manu*</note>, or as is received in some Courts, by the **touch of a staff** <note>original Latin: *contactu baculi*</note> which the Judges hold out in place of their own hand—they say that this same form must be precisely observed.

Whether a plaintiff is bound to provide a guarantee even if it is not requested, see the same **Schultes**. Likewise, whether the provision of a guarantee requires the presence of the adversary.

What, however, is the reason why a **Warranty** <note>Guaranda</note> is provided by the hand, while **Security** <note>original Latin: **Satisdatio**. German: **Vorstand**</note> can be discharged by the pledging of goods? And why, even in criminal cases, only the risk of goods is involved in the case of security, but a warranty draws with it the risk of the hand and even the body? **König** greatly doubts this in *Process, chapter 48*. But this question seems to **Rotchitz** to be free of all difficulty. For it is certain that the warranty was initially invented for "causes of blood" <note>Capital or criminal cases</note>, namely so that for the defendant...

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law #

security should be provided by the paternal relatives <note>original: *agnatis*</note> of the slain or wounded person, whether a settlement has been reached or the defendant was acquitted for just causes, such as legitimate self-defense. <italic>Gloss 1 at the beginning of Book 2, Article 16 of the Landrecht <note>The "Landrecht" was the territorial law of the Saxons</note>; new Gloss on Book 3, Article 14, at the word</italic> **Guarantee** <note>original German: **Gewähr**</note>. <italic>Final gloss in the Weichbild <note>Municipal law for cities</note>, Article 40.</italic> For the criminal prosecution of a homicide or wound belonged to the relatives of the victim. <italic>New gloss on the Landrecht, Book 3, at 14,</italic> **Guarantee.** Consequently, the defendant was in perpetual danger; even if he cleared himself against one accuser, he might later be criminally pursued again by the relatives. However, financial sureties <note>original: *satisdationes*</note> did not address this kind of danger, just as they do not now; rather, they provide security regarding counter-claims and expenses, and in this sense, they provide a benefit rather than removing a personal danger to the defendant. Therefore, a greater penalty was to be established for one who broke a guarantee that concerned a risk to life than for one who merely deprived another of a financial advantage. This is because the law generally favors those who struggle to avoid a loss more than those who strive to obtain a profit. <italic>Law on Error of Fact, section "moreover," Digest on ignorance of law and fact.</italic> Rotschitz, <italic>in the cited place, number 16,</italic> says in the following number: Do not be surprised that even if the case is handled criminally, a guarantee in Saxon Law can be fulfilled by the pledging of goods. For a guarantee is only admitted in those crimes which are not flagrant or notorious, but are "overnight" <note>crimes where some time has passed since the act</note> and doubtful, and in which it is argued (or seems possible to argue) that there was negligence rather than malice—for example, if someone was forced to defend himself and perhaps exceeded the limits of blameless defense. <italic>Gloss in the Weichbild, Article 27, number 2; text of the Landrecht, Book 3, Article 12, at the end.</italic>

### 56. Weight, Ell, Measure. <note>original German: Gewicht, Elen, Maß. Latin: Pondus, Ulna Mensura.</note> ###

Knichen estimates that the right of inspection over measures, weights, and ells <note>an "ell" is an old unit of length, often used for fabric</note>, as well as the inspection of mills, is a public right and belongs to the regalia <note>rights belonging to the sovereign</note> or to territorial sovereignty. <italic>Chapter 4, number 230 and following.</italic> He believes this should be ascribed, at the very least, to "Mixed Justice" <note>original: *mixto Imperio*, a legal term for authority involving both high judicial power and administrative oversight</note>. Thomas Michael, <italic>on Jurisdiction, thesis 103, letter C, with the citations there.</italic>

Provided, however, that such "Mixed Justice" is not subject to the territorial jurisdiction of another. In that case, they are forced to seek the standard <note>original: *archetypum*, the master measurement</note> from the superior capital city. See my work <italic>on Majesty, page 203.</italic>

On false **Weight** and **Measure**, see Benedict <italic>Decisions, volume 2, on Crimes, part 4, page 695.</italic>

->ADDITION.<-

If malice is not proven, it is presumed that an inequity in measurement arose from error or accident, making it unpunishable. Zahn, <italic>on Lies, Book 2, chapter 57, number 4.</italic> If an unjust measure is found with someone who has newly taken up an office or business, it is presumed that they used it out of ignorance. <italic>Ibidem.</italic>

<column-break/>

A Wispel <note>a dry volume measure used for grain</note> in Braunschweig holds 4 Scheffels <note>bushels</note> or 40 Himpten. 1 Scheffel holds 10 Himpten. 1 Himptte holds 4 Viertels. 2 1/2 Wispels in Hamburg and Holland make 1 Last. 1 Fuder <note>a large cartload, usually for wine</note> in Hanover is 12 Malters or 72 Himpten, which are 6 Scheffels in Braunschweig.

The Belgians refused to admit **a common measure and weight.** Klock, <italic>on the Treasury, Book 2, chapter 17, number 4.</italic>

To whom does the inspection of weights, measures, and ells—commonly called **the Calibration of Measures, Ells, and Weights** <note>original German: "die Eich, Maß, Eln und Gewicht"</note>—belong? Guido Papa, <italic>Decision 490, at the end.</italic> Chassan, <italic>in the Customs of Burgundy, on Justices.</italic> Matthias Stephan, <italic>on Jurisdiction, Book 1, chapter 12, number 22.</italic> Merckclbach in Klock, <italic>Counsel 46, volume 1,</italic> refers this to acts of High Justice <note>original: *meri Imperii*, the power of life and death</note>. To the contrary, Knichen, <italic>on Superior Right, chapter 4, number 287;</italic> Besold, <italic>on the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire, page 5, and Counsel 233, number 31;</italic> Bidembach, <italic>Noble Question 7, number 3;</italic> and Tapia, <italic>on the final law, part 1, chapter 2, number 50, Digest on the Constitutions of Princes,</italic> number it among the acts of High Justice. Wehner, in <italic>Practical Observations, at the words</italic> **Hundredweight, Measure, and Weight** <note>original German: **Zent, Maß und Gewicht**</note>, says that in Saxon Law it belongs to the *Zent* <note>high criminal jurisdiction</note>, but in Franconia it refers to the *Vogtheia* <note>advocacy or bailiwick</note>. A distinction should be made between measures already established and those to be established: such that their establishment belongs to sovereignty, but the inspection of established measures is assigned to "Mixed Justice." Besold, <italic>Counsel 211, number 10.</italic> **Unjust measures are to be punished as theft.** **The Turks are very strict regarding measure and weight.** Schweigger, <italic>in Travel Book, page 177.</italic> Half a Steiner peck <note>original: *Metzen*</note> of oil, or 30 pounds for it. **Records of the Teutonic Knights** <note>original German: **Teutschherrische Acta**</note> in the **Roll of Documents**, <italic>page 144.</italic>

Measurements are made according to the customs of neighboring places, for it is in the power of the contracting parties to decide by what measures and prices wine is purchased. Hence, it is regularly permitted for individuals to weigh with any weights that are just. Barbosa, <italic>in Axioms, Book 11, chapter 24, axiom 2.</italic> Public weigh-masters provide full proof. Berlich, <italic>conclusion 36, number 75.</italic> Falsifications of weights, measures, pecks <note>original: *modiorum*</note>, and ells must be punished, following the example of King James of Scotland. Klock, <italic>on the Treasury, Book 2, chapter 36, numbers 1, 9, 10, 13, and 15.</italic> A certain Ecclesiastical Prince acquired a no small increase for his treasury through false measures. <italic>Ibid. number 14.</italic> The right of weights and measures is Royal, <italic>number 2,</italic> yet it is commonly assigned to High or Mixed Justice, <italic>numbers 3 and 4.</italic> **Exemption against and above the road-toll.** Limn, <italic>Book 7, chapter 17, numbers 14 and 17.</italic> Juan de Mariana wrote a singular book <italic>on weights and measures in the year 1611.</italic> On the measures of Holy Scripture, there exists a unique treatise by Heinrich Bindings and Adam Berg from the year 1604. **They weighed it out, that is, they paid.** <italic>Zechariah 11 <note>A reference to the thirty pieces of silver</note>.</italic>

**The weight of a pound** or **the freight weight of three hundredweight stones** <note>original German: "drey Centner Stein"</note> is 11 **pounds** in Braunschweig, and 10 **pounds** in Hamburg and Hanover. Just measures and weights must be used, and he who changes or corrupts weights and measures for the sake of profit is compelled by Canon Law to do penance for 30 days on bread and water.

## 57 Conscience. <note>original: *Gewissen. Conscientia.*</note> ##

Martini has much regarding conscience in his dispute *On the Supreme Good*, 6, throughout.

### ADDITION. ###

In Augsburg, 1492, a writing appeared with the title: *The Lavage of Conscience*. Also, the *Mirror of Conscience* by Blessed John of Capistrano <note>A famous Franciscan friar and theologian known for his preaching</note>.

A pretended conscience does not excuse. Bullæus, counsel 3, page 391. One must not lightly argue against conscience and with God. The same author, page 394. Cothman, volume 1, counsel 1, number 549. The conscience of the Law overcomes the conscience of a man <note>meaning legal requirements take precedence over personal moral feelings in a court</note>. Afflictis, decision 321, number 2. **Dutch Military Law**, article 3, letter f, page 39. Unless one sets aside a scrupulous conscience, they will not escape error. Barbosa, *Axioms*, book 3, chapter 53, axiom 9, throughout. Conscience ought to be informed by the law, and scrupulosity should be set aside. Baldus, counsel 295, number 2, book 1. Francesco Mantica, *On Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 2, chapter 14, number 7. Heig., 2, question 1, number 166. Barbosa, in the cited place, axiom 4: **with a good, pure, and unstained conscience.** <note>original German: *mit gutem, reinen, ungefärbten Gewiſſen*</note> Limn., book 7, chapter 19, page 312. Höpingk calls a religious affirmation "the seal of conscience," in *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 1, number 11. The signs of a bad conscience are blushing, turning pale, and speaking inconsistently; these create a bad presumption <note>in legal terms, a "presumption" is an inference of guilt or liability</note>. Clarus, in question 21, *Criminal Practice*, number 39, the third verse. Hence, from the face, appearance, steadfastness, or trembling—from the evidence of the eyes and speech—the conscience of a delinquent can be observed for what it is. Cited place, axiom 1. ## 58. Gaining. <note>original: *Gewinnen. Lucrari.*</note> ##

Under the word "gaining," one also understands those things which come to us through succession or the totality of an estate, as taught by Modestinus Pistoris, question 164. There he adds that if we look at the proper meaning of the word **gaining** <note>original German: *gewinnen*</note>, it seems to mean the same thing as **to profit** <note>original Latin: *lucrari*</note>. This word applies more to an inherited estate through which we obtain profit than to those things which we acquire by our own industry. See below at the words **earned** and **won** <note>original German: *rungen und gewunnen*</note>, and my dispute on the Princely Württemberg Territorial Law.

What constitutes **Inherited or fallen property** <note>original German: *Erb- oder angefallen Gut*</note>, and how it is distinguished from **well-won, acquired, and purchased goods**, see throughout Cothman, *Counsels*, 40, volume 3.

However, guarantees of this kind involved no such danger, just as they do not now; rather, they concern a caution regarding counterclaims and expenses, and thus represent a benefit to the defendant rather than a risk. Consequently, a greater penalty should be established for one who breaks a guarantee involving the risk of life than for one who merely deprives another of a financial benefit; since in other cases, the law favors those who strive to avoid a loss more than those who strive to secure a profit. ## 56. Weight, Ell, Measure. <note>original: *Gewicht, Elen, Maß, Pondus, Ulna Mensura*</note>

Knichen, in chapter 4, numbers 230 and following, considers the right of inspecting measures, weights, ells <note>a traditional unit of length, often for fabric</note>, as well as millstones, to be a public matter belonging to the "Regalia" <note>sovereign rights of a ruler</note> or to superior authority. Thomas Michael, in *On Jurisdiction*, thesis 103, letter C, and the citations therein, thinks it should be ascribed at the very least to "Mixed Jurisdiction" <note>original: *mixto Imperio*; jurisdiction involving both the power of the sword and lower civil administration</note>.

However, this is only if such Mixed Jurisdiction is not subject to the territorial jurisdiction of another. In that case, they are compelled to seek the standard <note>original: *archetypum*</note> from the capital city of their superior. See my own work *On Majesty*, page 203.

**Regarding false weight and measure**, see Beatus, *Decisions*, volume 2, *On Crimes*, part 4, page 695.

### ADDITION.

If malice is not proven, it is presumed that an inequality of measure arose through error or chance, so that it is not punishable. See Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 57, number 4. Where an unjust measure is found in a newly assumed office or business, it is presumed that it was used out of ignorance. Ibid.

<column-break/>

**A *Wispel* in Braunschweig contains 4 *Scheffels* or 40 *Himps*. 1 *Scheffel* contains 10 *Himps*. 1 *Himp* contains 4 *Viertels*. 2 *Wispels* make 1 *Last* in Hamburg and Holland. 1 *Fuder* in Hanover is 12 *Malters* or 72 *Himps*, which in Braunschweig equals 6 *Scheffels*.** <note>These are specific historical regional units for dry goods like grain</note>

The Belgians refused to admit **a common measure and weight.** Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 17, number 4.

To whom does the inspection of weights, measures, and ells belong—commonly called **the gauging, measure, ell, and weight** <note>original: *die Eich, Maß, Eln und Gewicht*</note>? Guido Papa, decision 490, at the end. Chasseneuz, in *Customs of Burgundy*, on justices. Matthæus Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction*, book 1, chapter 12, number 22. Merckebach, in Klock's *Consultations*, number 46, volume 1, classifies these as acts of "Pure Jurisdiction" <note>original: *meri Imperii*; high sovereign power</note>. Contrary to this, Knichen, *On the Right of Superiority*, chapter 4, number 287; Besold, *On the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire*, page 5, and *Consultation* 233, number 31; Bidembach, *Noble Questions* 7, number 3; and Tapia, at the final law, part 1, chapter 2, number 50, number them among acts of "Pure Jurisdiction." Wehner, in *Practical Observations*, under the words "Zent, Measure, and Weight," says that in Saxon Law it refers to the *Zent* <note>a high court jurisdiction</note>, but in Franconia it refers to the *Vogtei* <note>the office of a reeve or advocate</note>. A distinction must be made between established measures and those yet to be established: such that their establishment belongs to the superior authority, but the inspection of those already established is assigned to "Mixed Jurisdiction." Besold, *Consultation* 211, number 10. **False measures are to be punished as theft. The Turks hold strictly to weights and measures.** Schweigger, in his *Travel Book*, page 177. Half a Steiner-measure of oil, or 30 pounds for it. **Acts of the Teutonic Knights in the Roll of Documents, page 144.**

Measures are made according to the customs of neighboring places, for it is within the power of the contracting parties to decide by which measures and prices wines are purchased. Hence, it is generally permitted for individuals to weigh by any weights that are just. Barbosa, in *Axioms*, book 11, chapter 24, axiom 2. Public weighers provide full proof. Berlichius, part 1, conclusion 36, number 75. Falsifications of weights, measures, bushels, and ells are to be punished, following the example of King James of Scotland. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 36, number 1, and numbers 9, 10, 13, 15. A certain Ecclesiastical Prince acquired no small increase for his treasury from false measures. Ibid, number 14. The right of weights and measures is a Royal right, number 2, though it is commonly assigned to Pure or Mixed Jurisdiction, numbers 3, 4. **Exemption against and above the road-toll.** Limn., book 7, chapter 17, numbers 14 and 17. Juan de Mariana wrote a single book *On Weights and Measures* in the year 1611. Regarding the measures in Holy Scripture, there exists a singular treatise by Heinrich Binding and Adam Berg from the year 1604. **They weighed out—that is, they paid.** Zechariah 11 <note>Specifically Zechariah 11:12: "So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver."</note>

**A pound-weight or carriage-load of three stone hundredweight is 11 pounds in Braunschweig, and 10 pounds in Hamburg and Hanover.** Just measures and weights must be used, and whoever changes or corrupts weights and measures for the sake of profit is compelled by Canon Law to do penance for 30 days on bread and water.

# 58. Winning [Gain]. Lucrari.

Under the word "winning" <note>original: "gewinnen"</note>, it is understood that those things which come to us through succession and the totality of an estate are also included, as **Modestinus Pistoris** relates in question 164. He adds that if we look at the proper meaning of the word "to win" (*gewinnen*), it seems to signify the same as "to profit" (*lucrari*). This word is more suited to an inheritance passed down, through which we obtain profit, than to those things which we acquire through our own industry. See below under the phrase **earned and won** <note>original: "rungen und gewonnen," a legal term for assets acquired through effort during a marriage</note>, and my own dispute on the **State Law of the Principality of Württemberg.**

She surpassed all the women of Italy in her extraordinary beauty and had enticed the Emperor into loving her with the hope of reigning. When she saw him making haste to return to Germany, it is said that she practiced a marvelous skill in crafting a pair of gloves containing poison, which she gave to the Emperor as a gift. Gradually intoxicated and consumed by this, he perished in the 19th year of his reign, as reported by Cuspinian and Caspar Peucer in book 4 of their *Chronicles*, page 600. A similar example of treacherous death is found in Emanuel van Meteren, book 4, chapter 2, page 125. Physicians advise that a Prince should always carry a certain "apple" <note>likely a pomander or scent-ball</note> made of various medicines in his hand, which will be effective against the agonies of poison. In Italy, it is not uncommon for Great Lords sitting at the table to protect themselves with a unicorn's horn <note>original: "unicornis cornu"; actually narwhal tusks, which were believed to "sweat" in the presence of toxins</note> for fear of poisons, as it is said to bead with much sweat and betray the treachery. A Prince must be especially circumspect when reading letters and presented documents; for today, the malice of men is such that they can prepare blotting sand tempered with poison and ink cooked with poison, which can rage against the reader slowly and wastingly by disturbing the eyes, mind, and brain. Therefore, political advisors command that one should not approach the reading of letters unless all sand has been carefully wiped away and one is equipped with reading glasses. Emperor Conrad, the son of Frederick II, was targeted by the treachery of his brother Manfred; he died miserably of poison infused into a medicine he had taken. Charles the Bald breathed his last on the eleventh day after drinking a medicine from the Jewish physician Sedechia, which was actually a powder infected with poison. According to some opinions, Gregory VII had six different Popes executed with poison through Gerhard Brazutus, his mouth-cook <note>a personal chef or taster</note>. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relations*, part 5, page 108. Regarding remedies against poisons, see Rupert on Florus, book 3, chapter 7, section 26.

### 61. Safe Conduct. Safe Conduct to Legal Standing.
->See above under the word: Peace from and to Legal Standing. Salvus Conductus.<-

Where a Prince is to grant safe conduct <note>German: "Glait"</note>: but an Imperial City, or one of the local nobility, otherwise holds all high and low judicial authority: who then may adjudicate a capital crime <note>German: "Malefiz"</note> that occurred on the public way and the open highway? Bidembach, question 17, and Arumaeus, volume 2, folio 35; add the treatise on safe conduct by Maullius and Mr. Becht's dispute on security among the Basel writers.

Although everyone commonly says that any summons from a judge grants security to the person summoned—that it "brings safe conduct with it" <note>original: "bringt Glait mit sich"</note> for coming and going safely—whereby he who must present himself in court at a certain place for the sake of litigation is not to be seized (Digest book 2, final section, *On summoning to court*); nevertheless, those who are summoned to appear in judgment because they are accused of some crime often feel they are not sufficiently protected. They almost always demand that, in addition to the summons, a separate guarantee of security

<column-break/>

be sent to them under the Judge's seal, to have it ready where needed; and only then do they profess that they will obey the summons. Moller, book 2, *Semestria*, chapter 1, from the beginning. This is done to avoid the injury of imprisonment, and so they are not forced to answer while in chains; see above.

The promise of security (called *Franchise*, *sauffconduit*, or *passeport* by the French, and by us *Secure Safe Conduct to Legal Standing* <note>original: "sicher Glait zum Rechten"</note>) is twofold according to our customs: (1) **Tacit**, such as when a Prince's new bride is solemnly led into his court. During the Princely home-bringing of the bride, criminals clinging to the bride's carriage often obtain a pardon for their offenses through the intercession of the new bride. (2) **Express** security is that which is granted so that a criminal may prove his claimed innocence and protection by law: *Safe conduct for the demonstration of claimed innocence*. This, however, is not easily permitted unless it appears probable from a previous inquiry that the delinquent can prove his innocence. Georg Rittershuf, *On the Law of Asylums*, chapter 7, number 14.

And although this granting of security and safe conduct is regularly said to belong to territorial law and sovereignty <note>the right of a ruler over their own land</note> (Digest, *On punishments*; Code, *On shipmasters*; Boerius, decision 179; Meichsner, volume 2, book 2, decision 4, number 172; Knichen, *On Saxon Law*, chapter 5, number 102; and many others);

Yet it is also certain that even Cities invested with jurisdiction by a superior can grant this security. Menochius, *On judicial discretion*, book 1, question 81, number 13; Heigius, part 2, question 21, number 42. And thus they rightly give a person accused of some crime a deadline to appear, and simultaneously the security of coming and going until the end of the case. Caspar Ziegler in the section *The City*, conclusion 1, number 68; Julius Clarus in *Criminal Practice*, final section, question 32, number 14.

This is (1) because otherwise no one summoned would come to the place of judgment without this security. (2) Because no one is bound to present themselves in an unsafe place. (3) Because fear of prison is a "just fear," which can excuse one from being declared in contempt. (4) Because otherwise it would easily happen that an absent person would be condemned without their defenses being properly heard. (5) Because a summons should by its own right grant safe conduct. Moller, *Semestria* 2, chapter 1.

Therefore, the granting of security—*to give safe conduct*—although it is today labeled and claimed as a "regale" <note>a royal prerogative</note>, is nonetheless not numbered among the regalian rights in law (Feudal Law, *Which things are Regalian*). And in truth, it is not a regale; for it does not in any way regard the Treasury or public utility...

...and therefore it is not handled by Pure Power <note>original: "mero Imperio"; the highest form of judicial authority involving criminal punishment</note>, nor indeed by the slightest appearance of it, but by Mixed Power <note>original: "mixto Imperio"; authority involving civil matters and private utility</note>, which pertains to private benefit. And since this "mixed" power is distinguished into three types—great, moderate, and small—the granting of security is attributed to this last type. See Zasius on the law *Imperium* in the Digest *concerning the jurisdiction of all judges*, number 40. And so I think that every Judge competent in that specific crime can grant this security.

Safe conduct is provided either by letters of passage <note>original: "literis tractoriis"</note> or by assigned soldiers who guard and escort those passing through. By letters, which we call a **Safe-Conduct Slip or Letter** <note>original: "Gelaits-Zettel oder Brieff"</note>, and in Saxon Law, the glossary for the *Weichbild* <note>a set of municipal laws</note> article 8, under the words **Tolls and Customs**, calls them **Tickets** <note>original: "Bolleten"</note>: there it says that one should take tickets, which are safe-conduct letters, and the one from whom the tickets were taken should keep the taker harmless within his territory. And this form of conduct is called **written safe conduct** <note>original: "das schrifftliche Geleit"</note>. That which is provided with assigned Soldiers or Horsemen is called **personal or living safe conduct** <note>original: "das persönlich oder lebendig Geleit"</note>. Thus today the phrase **living Safeguard** <note>original: "lebendige Salva Guardia"</note> is frequent; and these conductors today we commonly call **Convoys**, from the French word *Convoyer*, which is the same as "to escort" or "to go with." They are called **Escort-People** <note>original: "Glaits-Leut"</note>, and merchants at fairs are commonly led with a living escort through the escort-territories. Maulius, *On the Right of Conducting*, title 5.

Whether safe conduct can be granted by the Emperor to an outlawed person <note>original: "bannito"; someone placed under an imperial ban</note> without the consent of the offended party? Schrader, *Counsel* 37, number 91 and following.
