### 62. Equally, in like manner. [Equally].

If two spouses testify <note>in a will</note> "that after their death the heirs of both sides should inherit **equally** with each other," then the inheritance is to be divided not by heads <note>original: "in capita"; meaning every individual gets an equal share</note>, but by branches <note>original: "in stirpes"; meaning the inheritance is split into two halves for the two families</note>. It is no small obstacle, indeed, that the Commentators hand down as a rule from the law *interdum* in the Digest *on the institution of heirs*, that this word **equally** <note>original: "æquè"</note> has such force and power that those joined together are admitted equally with those separated; or as Baldus says, it denotes distribution by heads, not by branches. See Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 21, number 7.

But this fails where the particle "equally" is placed between two families: likewise, here there are as if two Wills. And the things handed down by Dynus in the chapter *inspicimus* in the *Rules of Law* (in the 6th book of Decretals) support this, where he prefers that which is more probable over the proper meaning of the words; and he thinks probability is gathered from the affection and necessity of the persons, which here is equal on the part of each spouse: because everyone is believed to have loved their own heirs equally, and consequently also wished to provide for them equally. Ludolph Schrader has an entire legal opinion on this question in volume 2, counsel 49.

> Inequal bullocks do not go well to the plow;
> If you wish to marry aptly, marry an equal.

As for tombs, some are "family tombs," while others are "hereditary tombs." Family tombs are those which someone establishes for himself and his family, to such an extent that out of respect for the right of burial, all heirs and children of any sex or rank fall under this family name—including those who have been emancipated <note>In Roman law, 'emancipated' refers to children legally freed from the father's authority</note>, whether they are heirs or not, according to the records of Pierre François Linglois in his *50 Decisions*, decision 8, question 4, number 5. Sons-in-law and daughters-in-law are also included if other close relatives are lacking, as noted in the same place.

Hereditary tombs are those which someone establishes for himself and his heirs, so that outsiders do not have the right to this tomb unless they have become heirs. See Linglois in the cited place, number 6 and following, where he teaches that this right is granted even to those who have been disinherited, unless the testator specifically forbade it, moved by a "just hatred" <note>original: "justo odio"; a legal term for a legitimate grievance</note>, etc.

## 80. Degree. Degrees.

The knowledge of degrees of kinship is extremely useful and necessary, as the legal expert himself testifies in the *Digest on degrees and affinities*. <note>A reference to the "Corpus Juris Civilis," the foundation of Western civil law.</note> (1.) Because marriage is prohibited within certain degrees. (2.) Because inheritances are passed down through degrees; for a person closer in degree regularly excludes a more remote one from the succession of the deceased (all other things being equal). (3.) Because guardianships are also assigned according to degrees. (4.) For the sake of testimony, since testimony is regularly not admitted between ancestors and descendants. *Schneidewin in the beginning of the title on marriage.* <note>Johann Schneidewin (1519–1568) was a prominent German jurist.</note> A degree, moreover, is the interval by which it is recognized which person is closer to the "trunk" <note>The "stips" or trunk refers to the common ancestor from whom the family line branches out.</note>; or, it is a certain distance of one person from another in the line of blood relation; or, it is the connection of the nearest person to another. And they are called "degrees" by likeness to stairs or sloping places, which we walk upon in such a way that we pass from the next to the next—that is, to the one who is born, as it were, from the other—as stated in the *Digest, section on degrees*. Thus, kinship is the total proximity itself, while the "line" is the separation of proximities, and the "degree" is the transition from one relative to another. *Schneidewin, in the same place, number 9.* There, in the following numbers, he teaches the difference in the calculation of degrees between Canon Law <note>Church law</note> and Civil Law <note>Roman-based secular law</note>.

Regarding the "heresy of the Incestuous" <note>A legal and theological dispute regarding how closely related people could be before marriage was considered incestuous.</note> which several legal experts had stirred up and defended—claiming on the authority of Emperor Justinian that the degrees of blood relation should be counted in the same way for marriage as they are for inheritances—*see the Epitomizer of Baronius, Year of Christ 665.* He testifies that this error flourished greatly in Ravenna, and that the work of Apostolic authority was needed to remove it. Two Councils were summoned in Rome for this purpose; at the first, Pope Alexander threatened excommunication, and at the second, he promulgated it against such incestuous persons.

<margin>The method of counting degrees in Canon Law: Master Biccius in the *Golden Sections*, section 1, thesis 15, number 5. In Civil Law: section 1, thesis 15.</margin>

## ADDITION.

## 81. Count, Counties. Comes, Comitatus.

Many have labored much over the etymology of this name, and in the past, even the god Osiris was not sought after with such diligence. For there are those who derive it from "ditches," which we call *Graben* and the Belgians call *Graven*, as if Counts were those placed in charge of the borders. Others derive it from the Latin *gravis* (serious/heavy), or the French *homme grave* (a serious man), as *Lycklama* suggests. Others from the French *Greffier*, which denotes a notary of the court or a scribe; Lipsius derives it from the Greek *graphein* (to write). Finally, others derive it from the German *Graven*, meaning gray-haired or elders—that is, the chief nobles. *Myself, on Counts and Barons, number 3.*

But it is more certain than certainty itself that the name *Grafve* or *Graph*, as *Aventinus* writes in his *Catalogue of German Names* and *Amerbach* in his *Letters to Zasius*, signifies a "Judge" in the ancient Germanic language, as I also pointed out in my *Special Discourse on Counts*. From this comes the passage in the *Ripuarian Laws*, chapters 55 and 90: "If anyone kills a fiscal Judge, whom they call a Count." For the name of "Count" (*Comes*) was unknown to the earlier Emperors; it began to be given as a title of dignity by Constantine, and shortly thereafter it was taken up for all official power. Thus we have the Count of the Sacred Largesses <note>A high-ranking finance minister</note>, the Count of the Sacred Patrimony, the Count of Private Affairs, the Count of the Orient, the Count of Military Affairs, the Count who rules provinces, and so on. Indeed, even a ship captain was called a Count, as *Cujas* taught from Eustathius, the interpreter of Homer. Generally, the name of "Prefect" turned into the name of "Count," which Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> also defines as *the one alongside the rulers*. <note>original: "ὁ παρ’ ἀρχῶν"</note> Otherwise, the jurist Ulpian defines a "Count" as one who accompanies or follows, or as Labeo says, one who is designated to follow someone for the sake of frequenting their company—such as a Tutor or the companion of a Matron.

As for why the name of "Count" changed its meaning, *Zasius* and *Camden* guess quite aptly that it was done in imitation of the Germans. Tacitus, in his *booklet on the customs of the Germans*, says their *Graphios* (judges) were usually joined to the Princes for the sake of counsel and authority, and he calls them "Counts." He records that the Princes themselves, elected in councils, administered the laws through the districts and villages. Thus, the Counts were the "substitute judges" of the Princes, and Paul the Deacon testifies that such were understood by the Lombards under the name of *Graphios*. Nor does the legal expert mean anything else by "Count" in the *Feudal Laws*, where it says: "If they wish to hide the truth, let them be compelled to swear by the Count or the People." Likewise, the Emperor says: "Let the Count choose for himself seven men of good testimony, and let him arrange things wisely with them." In the Statutes and Agreements of Cologne, "Count and Jurors" <note>original: "Greff und Schöffen"</note> is always put for the Judge and his Assessors—for the Lieutenant and the Judge. Counts were also called the followers of the Court and held administration there. Likewise, for the Imperial Judges...

There are various types of Counts in the Empire. For some are Counts shining with Princely dignity, known as *Princely Counts* <note>original: "Gefürstete Graven"</note>. Formerly there were four "Greater Counts" who, though prominent in their own rank, were considered lesser among the Princes; they were called *the four Counts of the Empire* <note>original: "die vier Graven deß Reichs"</note>. There are, furthermore, Counts who are immediately subject to the Empire and recognize their Counties as a fief from the Empire; the number of these is quite large. There are also those who are immediately under the Empire and have only the Emperor or the Imperial Chamber as their judges, yet they hold their Counties as a fief from some inferior Prince. Finally, there are Municipal Counts, or *Landed Inhabitants* <note>original: "Landfassi"</note>, who, although they are found in the Imperial register, are nonetheless exempted by other Princes of the Empire. Regarding all of these, consult *Jos. Nolden on the Nobility, chapter 8, number 180 and many following.* Furthermore, *Felix Fabri, in his History of Swabian Affairs, book 1, folio 164*, attests that formerly there were Counts who held only a castle, while others also held a territory.

Although in the past, counties and other similar offices were by no means hereditary but were granted at the pleasure of the Emperors, the sons of Counts were nevertheless rarely overlooked. This is attested by the Chapters of Charles the Bald in *Miræus, in the Belgian Annals for the year 877, folio 403.* These records state the following:

> If a Count of the Kingdom should die whose son is with us, let our son appoint from those who were most familiar and closer to that same Count, who, together with the officials <term>Ministeriales; administrative officials often of unfree origin who rose to high status</term> of that same County, and with the Bishop in whose diocese that County is located, shall look after or rule that County until it is reported to us, so that we may honor his son.

> If, however, he should have a young son, that same son, with the officials of the County and the Bishop in whose diocese it sits, shall look after the same County until the death of the aforementioned Count reaches our notice, and the son himself, by our grant, may be honored with his father's honors.

> If indeed he should have no son, our son, with the rest of our faithful subjects, shall appoint those who, with the officials of that County and its own Bishop, shall look after the County until our command is issued regarding it. And for this reason, let him not be angry who looked after the County if we give that same County to another whom we please, rather than to him who looked after it until then. The same must be done regarding our Vassals. See also *Guillim. Habspurg. fol. 122.*

Counts, moreover, were the Judges of an entire District <note>original: "Pagi"</note> (or Province). A Count’s district—that is, a County—called *Contado* by the Italians, *Comitia* by others, and *Pays* or *Conté* in French, was divided into Vicarages, Hundreds, and Decanaries, in which the judges were

<column-break/>

Vicars, and Centenarians <note>original: "Centenarii"</note>—known to us as *hundred-men* <note>original: "hunderste-mann"</note>—and Deans.

That in the age of Charlemagne <note>original: "Caroli M."</note> and his successors, Counts, Marquises, and Dukes were not hereditary and permanent, but were put in charge of governing the Provinces of the Kingdom for a time and could be removed at will, is also clear from *Book 5 of Aimoin, chapter 1*, where he speaks as follows: "Charlemagne ordained throughout the entire land of Aquitaine Counts and Abbots, as well as many others whom they commonly call Vassals, from the Frankish people; it was safe for no one to oppose their prudence and strength with any craftiness or force. To them he committed the care of the Kingdom, as he judged useful: the protection of the borders and the provision for the rural estates." *Miræus, Belgian Annals, under the year 853, folio 347.*

When exactly Counts and Counties were made hereditary is taught by *Guilliman in his Habsburg History, book 4, chapter 2, folio 121 and following.*

According to the custom used by German writers of the Middle Ages, the specific names of Counts were often suppressed because the title was a name of an office, and family surnames were not yet in common use, as *Pasquier* notes in his *Researches*. Rebuking this custom, *Joachim Camerarius in his Nicephorus Chronology* writes: "In our own writers, a certain drowsiness and futility can be criticized; they wrote as if everyone explored and knew the things they were explaining as well as they did, and as if future generations were present then. Thus, they spoke neither clearly nor distinctly about affairs and events, and they are found to have confused persons with names in various ways. Regarding them, what else can we do but wish there had been more diligence, prudence, and learning in them?"

A County <note>original: "Comitatus"</note> is also the Court or hall of a Prince and Emperor, or a Royal judgment, as in the law *milites, section ignominiosa, in the Digest on military affairs*, where the Emperor is present.

The term County, according to Alciatus in his commentary on the law *pupillas 239, section territorium, in the Digest on the meaning of words*, is properly said of the Imperial Court. But because in the time of Charlemagne and the reigns of the Berengars and the Ottos, a Count was sent to rule individual cities, the jurisdiction, territory, and district began to be called a "County" because a Count presided over them. Add *Wesenbec. counsel 295, number 198; Killinger on the Ganerben, chapter 14, folio 158.* The term *Gravia* was also used for a County, and *Gravio* for a Count. See *Bignon in his notes on the Marculf Formulas, folio 59 and following.*

It is well established that the dignity of those we call Counts today had its origin in the fact that Emperors and Kings bestowed that name as a mark of honor upon certain men whom they kept closer and more familiarly by them.

Regarding Counts of this sort and their office, there is an elegant passage among the *Letters of John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres*, which his brother *John Masson* published in Paris from the library of *Papirius Masson. Letter 263.* "Counts," he says, "are so named from their participation in a partnership; whoever does not know this is ignorant..."

The same Bishop <note>Likely referring to a legal authority or author mentioned previously</note> identifies two general types of these Counts: he says those who perform this duty in the Palace are "Palatine" by authority of the Law, while those in the provinces are "Provincial."

And these Counts in France used to be Ordinary Judges. Thus, Gregory of Tours, writing about Saint Nicetius, says that Count Armentarius governed the city of Lyon with judicial power. In the Capitularies of Charlemagne <note>The laws or ordinances of the Frankish emperors</note>, Book 5, Chapter 5, it says: "We will," he says, "that the Counts who are deputized to guard the coast: whichever of them resides in his ministry shall not excuse himself from performing justice because of that guard duty; but he shall have his Assessors <note>original: "Scabinos", lay judges or legal experts who assisted the count</note> with him there, if he holds a Court <note>original: "Placitum", a formal judicial assembly</note> there and administers Justice." See the same Chapter in Book 2, Chapter 1.

It is pleasing to insert here the formula of a **patent of elevation to the rank of Count.**

# We, Frederick, by the Grace of GOD,
### King of the Romans, at all times Increaser of the Empire, Duke of Austria, of Styria, of Carinthia, and of Carniola, Lord of the Windic March and of Portenau, Count of Habsburg, of Tyrol, of Pfirt, and of Kyburg, Margrave of Burgau, and Landgrave in Alsace, etc.

Acknowledge and make known openly with this letter, to all those who see it or hear it read: since the high Imperial Dignity, over which We have been set by the inexpressible and kind favor of God—and from which, in this time, the power, nobility, and office of all the subjects of the Empire originally flow and continue to flow like the light from the sun—takes example from the highest heavenly sphere, which takes pleasure in the many of its chosen ones; and specifically and rightly rejoices when its Imperial Crown is elegantly surrounded and encompassed by many Noble and Faithful men. And the Crown also has honorable certainty that when the number of its Noble and Faithful men is increased, then its praise and honor are greatly increased and recognized. We also hope to achieve more and more when We honor the worthy among Our and the Empire's Noble and Faithful men, and graciously make them higher with Our special and Royal favors.

Now, since the Noble N., Baron of B., Our and the Empire’s dear and faithful 

<column-break/>

ancestor, and he himself, have always honored Our predecessors in the Empire and Us with obedient, faithful, and useful services so willingly and manifoldly at all times, and since they and he have always been found so ready and helpful to the Empire and Us; and since the aforementioned N. and his lawful spouse were also born free and come from a free lineage of Counts: We rightly consider this with Our special Royal favors. To allow the same N. to enjoy this, and to make him and his legitimate physical heirs higher and to graciously dignify and elevate them by Roman Royal power; therefore, with a well-considered mind and the good counsel of several of Our and the Empire’s Electors, Princes, Counts, Barons, Nobles, and Faithful, We have, by Our special Royal favor, dignified, ennobled, and elevated the same N. and his legitimate children, sons and daughters, whom he now has and shall hereafter eternally have, and those who are lawfully born of him and of those same children, and have raised and made them true Counts and Countesses in the name of GOD. 

We dignify, ennoble, elevate, and make them so with certain knowledge, by virtue of this letter and the fullness of Roman Royal power; and We mean, ordain, decree, and will, by Roman Royal authority, that the same N. and his aforementioned children, and all and every person who comes and is born from him and them, as previously stated, shall henceforth be, be called, and be named by everyone as Counts and Countesses of the Holy Roman Empire. They shall also have the true honor and dignity of Counts and Countesses inside and outside of court and in all places, and shall be honored and held as true-born Counts and Countesses, without anyone's interference, trouble, or contradiction. 

And We also command, by Our aforementioned Royal authority, each and every one of Our and the Empire’s subjects and faithful, earnestly and firmly with this letter, that they do not hinder or disturb the aforementioned N., his children, and those who shall come from him and them, as distinguished above, in the aforementioned Our Roman favors in any way, upon Our grace, and as dearly as each one wishes to avoid the heavy displeasure of Us and the Holy Empire. In witness of this letter, sealed with Our Royal Majesty's Seal. Given at Breisach <note>A town in southwest Germany</note>, after the birth of Christ fourteen hundred years, and thereafter in the forty-second year, on the Thursday after St. Augustine's Day <note>August 30, 1442</note>, in the third year of Our Reign.

->By Command of the Lord King.<-
->Wilhelmus Batz.<-

**The Hairy Count.** <note>original: "Comitem pilosum"</note> Guillaume le Breton, the Armorican, in book 10 of his *Philippide*, misunderstood this matter. We understand the term *Raugraven* <note>Rough-Counts</note> not as *Rauchgraven* <note>Hairy-Counts</note>; it refers to a lord of rugged or rough regions, not a man who is himself shaggy or covered in hair. Even now there are nobles called "The Wood-Counts" <note>original: "die Wudgraven"</note> or "The Rough-Counts." However, this could have been a different Hero. In ancient times, there were five distinctions among Counts. Some were simply called Counts; others were Counts of the Palace; others were Centenaries <note>original: "Centgraven", local judges over a "hundred"</note>; others *Gograven* <note>regional or district judges</note>; and finally, others were called *Kuhgraven* <note>literally "Cow-Counts," likely referring to lower rural officials</note>. See Knich, *On the Law of the Land*, chapter 4, number 54 and following. 

In the Empire, there is a threefold order of them. Some are simply called **Counts of the Empire** <note>original: "Comites Imperii" or "Graven deß Reichs"</note>. Others belong to the same order but are more eminent in title and dignity: such as those who, in the Recesses of the Empire <note>The formal resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note>, are usually called **Princely Counts** <note>original: "Gefürstete oder Fürstenmässige Graven"</note>. Examples include the Counts of Habsburg and Tyrol (represented by the Archdukes of Austria), Henneberg, and Arenberg—who were recorded among the Princes of the Empire by Maximilian II. See the Imperial Recess of the year 1594. Also the Counts of Görz, per the Recess of 1576, section: "After which also now..." <note>original: "Nachdem auch jetzo"</note> where it says: "the Princely County of Görz." Also the Counts of Schaumburg, to whom the title of Prince was first conferred upon Ernest by Ferdinand II at Frankfurt in the year 1619. Count Karl von Mansfeld and Karl, Baron of Liechtenstein, were both created Princes by Rudolf II. 

Finally, others are subject to the Empire only "mediately" <note>indirectly; they answer to a superior prince rather than directly to the Emperor</note>, having received their counties as a fief from some lower Prince, to whom they are true landed subjects <note>original: "Landfassii"</note>, and they are not to be numbered among the States of the Empire at all. Hence, they are vassals of Princes and follow their courts in feudal cases. Such are the Counts of Hardegg under the Austrians; under the House of Burgundy, the Counts of Nassau and Breda, the Counts of Bronckhorst, Egmont, and Ijsselstein. Under the Elector of Brandenburg, the Counts of Hohnstein and Schwedt, Lords of Vierraden. Under the Dukes of Pomerania and the Bishop of Cammin, the Counts of Naugard, Eberstein, and Nassau. Under the Archbishop of Cologne, the Lords of Rifferscheid. Under the Duke of Bava-

The Germans use the term **Spanschaft** <note>Countship or fellowship</note> from the word for "Banns" or "Presiding Officers," or rather from "Societies": for among Germans, *Gespann* denotes a companion or one who is yoked together. ->ADDITION:<-

It is a great folly that several of our Princes and Lords wish to claim descent from <term>Troy</term> <note>During the Renaissance, many European dynasties claimed they were descended from Trojan refugees to establish ancient, heroic legitimacy.</note>, especially since the German ancestral kingdom existed before the Trojan kingdom. Troy lasted no longer than 397 years under its six kings, and by the time Troy was destroyed, the German kingdom had already been counted as lasting nearly a thousand years (seven years less, to be precise). From the beginning of the world, it was two thousand eight hundred years (twelve years less). See Aventinus, page 39, column b; Schottel, *On the German Language*, page 137.

Pierre Belon wrote *Observations on Singular and Memorable Things in Greece, Asia, Egypt, etc.*, published by Raphelengius, 1605. Sallust, in *The Jugurthine War*, chapter 85, records that Gaius Marius refused to learn Greek literature, claiming it contributed nothing to the virtue of those who taught it. But let Marius be Marius—that is, a rustic, fierce, and purely military man. Hubert Goltzius wrote the *History of the Cities and Peoples of Greece*. See Limnaeus, volume 1, *Additions to book 7*, chapter 1, section 7, page 113.

Martin Crusius, Professor of Greek and Latin at the University of Tübingen, published eight books of *Turco-Graecia* in Basel in folio. Ubbo Emmius described the *Republics of Greece*; see Felwinger in *The Index*, page 411. Nicetas Choniata wrote *On the Greek Emperors*, Venice, 1569, in quarto.

"It is Greek, therefore it cannot be read." <note>original: *Græca sunt, ergò legi non possunt*. A common medieval proverb used by lawyers who were unable to read the Greek passages in Roman legal texts.</note> For this reason, section 1 of Law 15 in the Cornelian Law on Assassins was completely omitted by the ancients, but restored by Gothofredus. "Here follows Greek, which cannot be understood," says the Gloss on Law 19, under the word "traveler" regarding judgments. Indeed, we cannot resolve many controversies without the Greek text; see an illustrious example in the *Strasbourg Collection of Law* on the Julian Law regarding Extortion, final thesis, Law 7, section 1, regarding exhibits. The Gloss wanders quite a bit in rendering the Greek phrase in Law 29, section 1, regarding those who make wills. However, the Gloss handles Greek well in Law 1, section 3, regarding the word for a "reproach" <note>original: *dicterii*</note> in the section on sailors, innkeepers, and stable-keepers. It interprets the Greek in Law 6, section 1, regarding the word "theater" in the section on religious places and praises the Greek interpreters. See the Gloss on Law 6, final section, regarding religion, on the word "Cenotaph," as to whether Greek texts are authentic. For example, the book of Modestinus, the entire title on the Excuses of Tutors, Law 48 on judgments. Should the Latin version be preferred in that place?

<column-break/>

Barbosa, *Axioms*, book 7, chapter 13, throughout. Spartianus writes of Emperor Hadrian that because he was so deeply imbued with Greek literature, he was called a "Little Greek" <note>original: *Græculum*</note>. Similarly, Julian the Apostate, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, was known for his Greek learning; a more learned Emperor can hardly be found in history, as evidenced by his *Satire on the Roman Emperors*, written in Greek. In that work, he touched upon all the Caesars who previously held the helm of the Roman Empire with wonderful dexterity. Georg Richter, *Oration 11*, page 18. Who is so much a stranger to the world of letters that they do not know the Greeks' concern for speech? It was their solemn custom to demand everything according to the refined standard of Hellenism and to eliminate exotic or flawed elements, so much so that they would not forgive a foreigner for even a syllable pronounced barbarously, as if pure and corrected speech were essential to the height of the Empire. See Mr. Harsdörffer in his *Philological Specimen*, page 89. It is memorable what Suidas writes under the entry for "stranger": that when they were once suffering from poverty and a foreigner promised money, they refused to use his gift because he had said "I lend" with a daringly wrong pronunciation <note>original: *τολμηΐζων δανείω*</note>; but when he had corrected his error and said the word correctly <note>original: *δανείσω*</note>, they allowed him to help the public need with his coins. The Roman Sage himself <note>Seneca</note> explains how flawed and deficient the Latin language is in *Epistle 58*. According to Gellius, the letter is half-Greek; see *Attic Nights*, book 1, chapter 8; Pliny, book 7, chapter 58; Quintilian, book 1, *Institutes*, chapter 6. The Greek language, which boasts of the invention of all arts, is called "half of all erudition" by Scaliger. It is the notary of divine knowledge and the library of all sciences; in it dwell the Graces, festivities, all elegancies, and charms. It is wonderful in the joining of words and a support to the Latin language. In this language, the Emperor decrees laws—those new and final ones. In this, the man of Cos <note>Hippocrates</note> and those who followed him profess medicine. In the same language, Aristotle still has his walkway <note>the Lyceum</note>, Plato his Academy, the Stoics their Porch, and Epicurus his garden. See Heinsius, *Oration 6*. One should see the *Greeko-Barbarous Glossary* of the famous Meursius. "Greekness" <note>original: *Græcitas*</note> appears in the Theodosian Code, the single law in the title *On Liberal Studies*, referring to the study of Greek literature and eloquence. Justinian himself, in the Preface to the Pandects, wishes for the Greek and Latin languages to be eternal, due to the exchange of both in expression. Furthermore, many things in Civil Law are repeated from Greek historians; the sayings of Plato, Demosthenes, Homer, Solon, and Draco are cited. Additionally, the Code of Justinian is scattered with Greek words, and it is even thought to have been written entirely or at least in part in Greek originally. Moreover, certain Greek words are found in use among Latins and were granted, as it were, the right of Roman citizenship; those ignorant of Greek make themselves look ridiculous in explaining them, as seen by the example of Accursius alone. Furthermore, there exists a Greek translation of the *Institutes of Law* by Theophilus, to which interpreters often flee when clearing up obscurities, as is apparent from Gothofredus. What more? Even the Pandects have a Greek interpretation, and the foundations of all jurisprudence...

### ADDITION:

It is a great folly that some of our princes and lords wish to claim descent from Troy, especially since the German hereditary kingdom existed before the Trojan kingdom. The Trojan kingdom lasted no longer than 397 years under its six kings. When Troy was destroyed, one counts nearly a thousand years (seven years less) from the beginning of the German kingdom; and from the beginning of the world, two thousand eight hundred years (twelve years less). Pierre Belon wrote *Observations on Singular and Memorable Things in Greece, Asia, Egypt, etc.*, published by Raphelengius, 1605. "It is Greek, therefore it cannot be read" <note>original: "Græca sunt, ergò legi non possunt"</note>. This phrase explains why section 1, law 15 of the *Cornelian Law on Assassins* was entirely omitted by the old commentators and only restored by Gothofredus. Thus, the *Gloss* wanders aimlessly in rendering the Greek phrase in law 29, section 1, *On Making Wills*. ## ADDITION.

Regarding the <term>Hairy Count</term> <note>original Latin: *Comitem pilosum*</note> mentioned in William the Breton’s *Philippide*, book 10: The matter was poorly understood. We understand the <term>Rough-Count</term> <note>original: *Rauvgraven*</note> not as "Hairy-Counts" <note>original: *Rauchgraven*</note>, meaning a man who is himself shaggy or covered in hair, but rather as a lord of "rough" or rugged regions. Even now, some nobles are called <term>Wood-Counts</term> <note>original: *die Wudgraven*</note> or <term>Rough-Counts</term> <note>original: *Raugraven*</note>. However, this could have been a different hero entirely. For what does the city of Utrecht have to do with our Rough-Counts? See Caspar Barth in his *Observations*.

In the past, there was a five-fold distinction among Counts. Some were simply called Counts; others were Counts of the Palace; others were <term>Centenary Counts</term> <note>original: *Centgraven*; officials presiding over a "hundred," a local administrative division.</note>; others <term>District Counts</term> <note>original: *Gograven*; from the German *Gau*, a regional district.</note>; and finally, others were called <term>Rough-Counts</term> <note>original: *Ruhgraven*</note>. See Knich, *On the Law of the Land*, chapter 4, number 54 and following. In the Empire, there is a three-fold order of them. Some are called simply <term>Counts of the Empire</term> <note>original: *Graven deß Reichs*</note>. Others belong to the same order but are more eminent in title and dignity than the rest; these are the ones usually called <term>Princely Counts</term> <note>original: *Gefürstete oder Fürstenmässige Graven*</note> in the Imperial Decrees. Such are the Counts of Habsburg and Tyrol (whom the Archdukes of Austria represent), Henneberg, and Arenberg—the latter being recorded among the Princes of the Empire by Maximilian II in the Imperial Decree of 1594. Also the Counts of Gorizia (Imperial Decree of 1576, section "Since also now," where it says: "the Princely County of Gorizia"). The Counts of Schaumburg, of whom Ernest was first granted the title of Prince by Ferdinand II at Frankfurt in 1619. Also Count Charles Mansfeld and Baron Charles of Liechtenstein, whom Rudolf II created as Princes. Finally, others are subject to the Empire only "mediately" <note>meaning they report to a local Prince rather than directly to the Emperor</note>; they received their counties as a fief from a lower Prince, of whom they are true <term>landed subjects</term> <note>original: *Landsassii*</note>, and they are not counted among the Estates of the Empire at all. Hence, they are vassals of Princes and follow the jurisdiction of their respective lords in feudal cases. Such are the Counts of Hardegg under the Austrians; and under the House of Burgundy, the Counts of Nassau-Breda, the Counts of Bronckhorst, Egmont, and IJsselstein. Under the Elector of Brandenburg, the Counts of Hohnstein and Schwedt, Lords of Vierraden. Under the Dukes of Pomerania and the Bishop of Cammin, the Counts of Naugard, Everstein, and Nassau. Under the Archbishop of Cologne, the Lords of Reifferscheid. Under the Duke of Bavaria—

<column-break/>

—by reason of particular estates, the Counts of Ortenburg. And so forth. Consult Reinking, book 1, class 4, chapter 14; Liebenthal in his *Political College*, Exercise 9, number 59; and add Bucelin, part 3 of *German Notables*.

The Germans, from their governors or presiding officers, call an administrative district a <term>Spanschafft</term> <note>An old term for a county or administrative district, related to the Hungarian "Ispan."</note>, or rather from "associations" (*Societatibus*). For among Germans, <term>Gespan</term> denotes a companion or "yoke-mate." The Count who presides over any county is called in the Hungarian language an <term>Ispan</term> or <term>Fo Ispan</term> <note>The supreme administrative official of a Hungarian county.</note>. See more in Dr. Tabor’s *Comparison of Roman and Hungarian Law*, part 2, section 1, paragraph 20, regarding what the Counties of the Kingdom are.

<meta>This page continues a legal discussion on the nature of legal instruments, specifically moving into a detailed entry on the "Guaranteed Instrument" (Instrumentum Guarentigiatum), a vital tool in Early Modern European commercial and civil law that allowed for the immediate enforcement of debts.</meta>

Balduin, *on the law ‘etiam’ in the Code on the execution of judged matters.* Cynus & Baldus *on the 1st law of the Digest on Confessions.* Bartolus *on the 2nd law of the Digest on the receipt of arbitrators.*

To **Guaranteed** <note>original: “Guarentigiare”</note> among the Tuscans or Italians is nothing other than to make firm, as appears from the section *If however* in the title *On the Law of Conrad* in the *Uses of Fiefs*, where Baldus says: “To Guarantee” <note>original: “Guarentare”</note> is a Tuscan word. They call a **Guaranteed Instrument** <note>original: “Instrumentum Guarentigiæ”</note> one of firmness and precision, which must be stood by in all respects. Jason, *on the 1st law, the section ‘If anyone thus,’ note 28, in the Digest on Verbal Obligations.* Therefore, a “guaranteed instrument” means the same as one that is firm and ratified. See Parladorius, *Daily Matters, book 2, section 11, on guaranteed instruments, note 3 and following, page 37 and following.*

A public or guaranteed instrument not only has <term>ready execution</term> <note>original: “paratam executionem”; this refers to the legal right to enforce a contract immediately, as if a judge had already ruled on it, without needing a new trial.</note> regarding those things expressly or principally contained within them, but also regarding those things tacitly or indirectly included. Speculator, *on the edition of instruments, the section ‘it remains,’ number 42.* Jason, *on the law ‘since the son,’ number 10, in the Digest on Verbal Obligations.* Baldus, *on the law ‘where still,’ column 4, in the Code on dotal law.* Alexander, *on the law of the nations, the section ‘which almost,’ in the Digest on pacts.* See Alexander, *legal counsel 126, volume 6.* Since that which is gathered tacitly from an Instrument is considered the very tenor of the Instrument itself, it ought to be held as if expressed. *The law ‘with which thing,’ on certain petitions; the law ‘as a whole,’ in the Digest on the institution of heirs; the law of nations, the section ‘which almost,’ in the Digest on pacts.* Boër, *decision 313, number 15.*

Once this execution is carried out, however, one may still pursue their right in court, notwithstanding the judgment brought at the point of execution.

And if it were not for the Guaranteed Instrument, it would not stand out with any prerogative over the others.

Nevertheless, Frederick Martini, *in his treatise on taxes in the Index under the word ‘Public Instruments,’* relates that public instruments—even if they do not have the <term>Guarantee Clause</term> <note>The specific wording that grants the power of summary enforcement.</note>—have ready execution by general custom.

### ADDITION.

Guido de Suzaria of Mantua treats the Guaranteed Instrument in *volume 6, part 2, page 338.* On Guarantees, Benedictus de Barzis, *page 340, book 6, part 2.*

There is a certain distinguished species of Instrument which the <term>Doctors of Law</term> call “Guaranteed,” which they say has “ready execution,” or to use the words of Paul <note>Julius Paulus, a 3rd-century Roman jurist.</note>, is “held as a number” <note>original: “numero habere”; meaning the debt is certain and liquid, requiring no further proof.</note>. It takes its name from *guaranda* or *guardia*, a <term>Lombardic</term> <note>The Lombards were a Germanic people who ruled Italy; many medieval legal terms in Italy have Germanic roots.</note> word denoting security and caution: hence they say “safeguard” <note>original: “salvam guardiam”</note> for custody. For although “caution” is also used elsewhere for a written bond—which our Emperor also used to call “security,” and by the Greek name <term>asphaleian</term> <note>original: ἀσφάλειαν; meaning safety or a physical bond.</note>—the Doctors of Law have adapted this name to this species as if by excellence. This is because the debtor, in order to better provide security to the creditor, takes care to have such a clause written into the instrument—for example, that if he has not returned the loan to the creditor at such and such a time,

<column-break/>

which he received as actually counted out to him, then he gives the creditor the power to pay himself. Rittershufius, *on the New Constitutions, page 627.* Guaranteed Instruments contain within themselves the force of a legal sentence. Joseph de Sesfe, *Aragonese Decisions 40, number 3, and on judged matters.* Riccius, *part 4, Collection 759, the section ‘the reason.’* Hence, a judge may indulge the debtor with that delay which is granted out of mercy to those who have been judged—*through the law ‘if to a debtor,’ 21, in the Digest on judgments*—or a similar delay from the guarantee by his own discretion. For a delay of a modest time is not a significant consideration, *law 31 of the Digest on judged matters; law 21 on judgments.* Nor is an Appeal granted while a guarantee remains in its full strength, because of that conformity regarding the effect which they call “suspensive”; it is otherwise regarding the “devolutive” effect. <note>A "suspensive" appeal pauses the execution of a judgment; a "devolutive" appeal allows the case to move to a higher court but the debt must still be paid in the meantime.</note> Scaccia, *on appeals, book 3, chapter 2, question 17, number 4, and those cited there.* Galganetus, *on the Statutes of the city, chapter 179, book 1, number 4.* Although the disposition of equivalent things is the same, that rule is not perpetual. There is no need to summon the party once the sentence has been brought into execution by the judge. Innocent, *in the chapter ‘by reason’ on appeals.* Bartolus, *on the law ‘from the Divine Pius,’ 15, in the Digest on judged matters.* Galletius, *question 3, part 3*, does not attribute so much authority to the Guarantee that it can be granted abruptly without summoning the party. Zacchia, *decision 154, where the Rota [Court] ruled* that if a summons did not precede, those things which ought to be observed to the letter by law were neglected; since no knowledge of the cause was held, a summons is necessary. *The final section of the Institutes on the penalty for reckless litigation; the law ‘too hastily,’ 1, in the Code on the execution of judged matters.* Indeed, I would not require a summons when, from the cited Decree, a mandate is decreed without a clause; and in general, a public Instrument, if the solemnities are present, does not require formal recognition, but rather inspection and examination, *the final law in the Code on the edict of the Divine Hadrian.* Heigius, *part 2, question 7*, and Bachov, *at number 5*, testify that in these cases one proceeds to execution without summoning the party. See also Wesenbeck on this; Colerius, *part 3, chapter 7, number 10.* It is part of the <term>Statutory Law</term> in certain places that ready execution is granted from Guaranteed Instruments. Carpzov, *part 3, decision 236, numbers 17 and 20.*

These instruments, called by the exotic word “guaranteed” <note>original: “guarentigionata, vel guarentigia aut guarentigiata”</note>, are called in slightly better Latin “confessed” <note>original: “confessionata”</note>. In German they are called **pledged letters and seals** <note>original: “versetzte Brief und Siegel”</note>. Giphanius, *on the law ‘by persecution,’ 24, page 336, in the Code on pledges*, says they **carry or lead their remedy on their back** <note>original: “so die Hülff auf dem Rucken nachtragen oder führen”; implying the document contains its own enforcement mechanism.</note>. Freundberg, *on stays of execution, conclusion 46*, takes the derivation either from *Wardia* and *Wardium*, or *Guardia* and *Guardium* (from which comes *Guaranda*), with the 'W' changed to 'Gu' as is most common among the French, which seems to denote custody or caution; and for the Germans it is the same as **to preserve** <note>original: “wahren”</note>. Or it comes from *warantizare*, which is from the German *wahren*, that is, **to protect, to keep, to hold firm by letter and seal** <note>original: “bewahren, servare, über Brief und Siegel fest halten”</note>, or from *währen* or *bewähren*, meaning **to endure, to prove, to protect, or to defend** <note>original: “währen, seu bewähren, tueri, defensitare”</note>. See William Antonius, *on stays of execution, conclusion 46, number 1.* Tessaurus, *decision 26, number 14.* Vossius, *on the vices of speech and the Glossary of barbarian Latin, book 2, chapter 26, under the word: Warantizare.*

### 85. Groschen. Grossi <note>A silver coin used across Europe, particularly in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>.

**Duttichin** <note>A double silver groschen.</note> or double silver groschen, currently go at 116 pieces to the Cologne Mark <note>A standard unit of weight for precious metals.</note>. They contain 14 *Loth* and 4 *Gran* of fine silver, and are issued at a value of 12 guilders and 9 groschen. See Alemannus in *The Exercise of Consultations*, part 1, question 8, page 43.

A **silver groschen** was anciently considered and valued as equal to a shilling, according to Alemannus in the same work. However, when other explanatory words are added to the term "silver groschen," such as "Princely Coinage," "good money," or the like, then "Imperial Apple" coins or silver groschen are understood. In such a case, a debtor cannot satisfy his obligation by paying in shillings instead of silver groschen. Alemannus, same source.

Twenty Bohemian groschen are to be counted to one Imperial Guilder. Coler in *Executive Process*, part 1, chapter 10, number 13, where he writes among other things: "Since Bohemian groschen (twenty of which make a guilder) had fallen out of use, a Prince of great name—in order to redeem a prefecture pledged by a certain free city for several thousand guilders, which were to be repaid in no other currency than Bohemian groschen—obtained from Emperor Ferdinand a decree that a certain quantity of Bohemian groschen should be newly minted."

->**ADDITION.**<-

1. A **Mariengroschen** <note>A groschen featuring an image of the Virgin Mary.</note> is worth 8 pfennigs in Braunschweig; 1 "good" groschen is worth 12 pfennigs. The city of **Hof** and the land of **Regnitz** were purchased by the Burgraves for 8,100 *Geschock* <note>A "Schock" was a unit of 60 coins.</note> of "broad" Fribourg groschen. See Limnäus in *Public Law*, volume 1, addition to book 5, chapter 7, page 818.

If one speaks simply of "Groschen," should it be understood as the Groschen of the March <note>Brandenburg</note> or those of Meissen? Johann Köppen discusses this in his *Decisions*, 26, at the beginning of this question. They are called **Mariengroschen** from the image of Mary. Alemannus, *On the Right of Coinage*, page 585. The "Three-Kreuzer" pieces first appeared among the Bohemians, which is why they keep the name and are called Prague or Bohemian groschen. Regarding the Groschen of the Empire, see Alemannus, part 1 of his *Consultations*, page 579; on forbidden ones, page 580; old silver groschen, 582; Meissen groschen, ibid.; those calculated to the guilder, 783; old groschen, 583; interest groschen <note>original: *Zinßgroschen*</note>, 583; new groschen, 584; peasant gro-

-schen <note>original: *Bauergroschen*</note>, 582; Bohemian groschen, 584; Guilder-groschen, Thaler-groschen, or silver groschen, 585.

### 86. Lord of the Soil. Dominus Territorii.

Both Wehner and Rudinger take this to mean the "Direct Lord" <note>The superior owner in a feudal hierarchy.</note>; but in my judgment, it is the same as the "Lord of the Territory," who holds supreme and universal jurisdictional Lordship.

And by virtue of this right, it is decreed in Saxon Law (*Landrecht*, part 1, article 35): All ores <note>original Latin gloss: *metallicæ venæ* (metallic veins)</note> that are buried deeper under the earth than a plow can reach belong to the Royal power.

->**ADDITION.**<-

The learned doctors call direct lordship <note>original: *directum dominium*</note> the **territorial right** <note>original: *Grundgerechtigkeit*</note>, or the ownership of the soil—property separated from its use. See Jal. in his law *nihil commun.*, number 11, regarding the acquisition of possession; Ferrari in his *Singular Practice* on the form of a libel for revoking a fief; Donellus, book 9, commentary 14 at the end; Pinellus on the Code regarding maternal goods; Cujas, book 11, observation 35; Eguinarius Baro, book 4 on benefits, chapter 7; and Borcholten on fiefs, who all reject this distinction of lordship. However, it is correctly proved for the sake of familiar tradition by those cited in Gottfried Antonius, *Feudal Disputations* 9, thesis 1; and Lord Hahn in *On the Right of Things*, chapter 43, numbers 1 and 4. He divides "incomplete lordship" into "direct" and "useful." He calls direct lordship the **superior ownership** <note>original: *das mehrer Eigenthum*</note>; and this is threefold: 1. that which the Lord of the fief has, 2. that of the Lord of a long-term lease <note>original: *Emphyteuseos*</note>, 3. that of the Lord of the ground upon which a building stands. "Useful" lordship is the **lesser ownership** <note>original: *das minder Eigenthum*</note>, or the beneficial ownership, also called heritable use; it is likewise threefold: 1. Feudal or Vassal rights, 2. Rights of a long-term lease, 3. Rights to the surface/building.

**Territorial right** <note>original: *Grundgerechtigkeit*</note> has a broader meaning than **ownership of the soil** <note>original: *Grundeigenthum*</note>. Rosenthal on Fiefs, volume 1, chapter 1, conclusion 6, number 7. The Lord of the Soil is obligated to provide justice to anyone complaining against his non-noble servants and people before he himself is summoned to court. Hungarian Territorial Law, part 3, title 26.

### 87. Right of Salvage. Jus circa Bona naufragorum <note>Literally: Law concerning the goods of the shipwrecked.</note>.

By the Rhodian Sea Law, in the law *axiofis* 9 <note>A famous reference in the Roman Digest (14.2.9) regarding maritime law.</note>, it was permitted among other things for the treasury and tax collectors to seize and keep for themselves the property of shipwrecked persons cast up by the waves.

This right of the Rhodian Law, used in ancient times, is still observed today in most maritime places, where things driven to the shore are claimed by the Lords of that territory which the sea washes against. This is called the **Right of Salvage** <note>original: *Grundrühr Recht*</note>. See Speckhan, Century 3, question 45, number 1. Sichard writes that this law is used among those living along the Rhine. And among the French, the Lord of the province and territory takes these goods...

### 90. Golden Fleece. <note>original: "Güldenfluß. Aureum Vellus."</note>

Concerning the Knights of the Golden Fleece, see the *Chronicle of Chronicles* by Gualterius, part 2, folio 30 and folio 134. On whether the dignity of a Knight of the Golden Fleece is greater than that of a Count of the Empire, see Besoldus, part 4, consultation 195, question 9, number 114.

### ADDITION.

It is asked why Philip of Burgundy <note>Philip the Good (1396–1467)</note> gave the name of the "Golden Fleece" to that knightly society? Some refer it to that golden fleece which Jason, having enticed many companions, sought to obtain through arms. But perhaps better (says Jean Bucelin in *Sacred and Profane Gallo-Flandria*, book 2, chapter 13, page 313), Ferreolus Locrius in book 3 of *Maria Augusta*, chapter 7, might have interpreted it as referring to the Virgin Mary, whom the Holy Scriptures foreshadow with the symbol of the Fleece, etc. See Limnaeus, volume 1, addition by J. P. to book 6, chapter 2, number 18.

The Order of the Golden Fleece of 50 Knights was instituted by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, in 1429. See Petrus Calefatus in his *Treatise on Knightly Dignity*, 43 and following; Otto in *Public Law*, chapter 19, page 690; Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 2, number 15. The sign of the same is worn on festive days: book 6, chapter 2, number 21. In the Order of the Golden Fleece, if a Knight of the fellowship dies, then that dignity does not pass to his heirs, to the point that they may not even retain the golden collar <note>The ornate chain worn by members</note>, but are bound to restore it to the Prince of the Order within three months, who then hands it to another who is chosen in the place of the deceased. See Knipfchild, *On Fideicommissum* <term>Fideicommissum</term> <note>A legal arrangement where property is held by one party for the benefit of another, similar to a trust.</note>, chapter 1, number 180, and the authorities cited there, Münster and Noldenius. Regarding what moved Philip the Good to choose the fleece, see Limnaeus in the cited work, book 6, chapter 2, numbers 18 and 19. For the Articles of the Statutes, see book 6, chapter 2, number 24. On whether this fellowship ignores the "law of number" <note>Referring to whether the membership limit is strictly enforced</note>, see Limnaeus, volume 1, additions to book 6, chapter 2, number 21.

### 91. Jülich. <note>original: "Gülich. Juliacum."</note>

Regarding things pertaining to Jülich, see Bentivoglio in *Relations*, folio 353.

### ADDITION.

Whence the family of Jülich, Cleves, and Berg <note>original: "Juliacensium, Clivensium & Montensium"</note> arose: Limnaeus relates a certain fable in *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 10, numbers 1 and 2, but more easily believes the same to be from the Roman Aelian family. Truly, this family became extinct on May 25, 1609, with the death of John William, which gave cause for various disputes. See Knipfchild, *On Fideicommissum*, chapter 1, number 132. In the year 1624, an agreement was reached between the Elector of Brandenburg and the Count Palatine of Neuburg, so that the Elector would have the territories of Cleves, Mark, Ravensberg, and Ravenstein; whereas the Palatine would have Jülich and Berg. Limnaeus, volume 1, addition to *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 10, number 14. The Duke of Jülich is the protector <note>original: "Schußherr"</note> of the city of Aachen. Ibid., number 16.

### 92. Goods. <note>original: "Güter. Bona."</note>

Goods <note>original: "Bona"</note> are so called because they "bless" <note>original: "beant"</note>, that is, they make one blessed. For to bless is to be of benefit,

<column-break/>

according to the law *honor. appellatio*, in the Digest *On the Signification of Words* <note>original: "ff. de U. S."</note>. And they are also called **Goods** <note>original: "Güter"</note> from **Good** <note>original: "Gut"</note>, that is, something good. Whence things which bring more inconvenience do not properly come under the name of "goods," according to the law *propriè bona*, in the same title of the Digest, where Gœddæus comments.

On what properly comes under the name of goods, see Bertazolus in the treatise *On Clauses of Instruments*, clause 12, glossary 2, number 3 and following; add especially Arius Pinellus, in the rubric of the Code *On Maternal Goods*, part 1.

### ADDITION.

Goods are called the sinew of things to be done, the second blood of man, and the guarantor of future necessity. Barbosa, *Axioms*, book 2, chapter 15, axiom 1.

It is in the interest of the Republic that goods be preserved within families. Axiom 3. Divided goods are less useful than united ones. Tiberius Decianus, *Counsel* 73, number 9, volume 2.

Goods are presumed to be <term>allodial</term> <note>Property owned independently, without a feudal superior.</note>, not feudal. Barbosa, in the same place, axiom 6. No one is presumed to be ignorant of the strength of their own goods. Law *quisquis* 15, *On the Rescinding of a Sale*. It is of the greatest interest to us to retain ancestral goods <note>original: "Bona avita"</note>, Digest book 38, law 1, section 15; especially the houses in which perhaps our parents died and we lived as minors, in which it is mournful enough to see the portraits of our ancestors either fixed or torn away. Law 22 of the Code, *On the administration of tutors and curators*; see Barbosa, same place, axiom 9. The diminution of goods leads to the diminution of dignity. Knipfchild, *On Fideicommissum*, chapter 6, number 324.

How the goods of a <term>fideicommissum</term> are to be restored: the same author, chapter 12, number 71 and following.

Goods are so called after the deduction of debt. **Debts are the closest heir.** <note>original: "Die Schulden seynd der nächste Erb." This is a legal maxim: creditors must be paid before heirs can inherit.</note>

By Lübeck Law, goods are either 1.) hereditary or ancestral, **Ancestral Goods** <note>original: "Erbgüter"</note>, or acquired, **Well-won or acquired goods** <note>original: "wohl gewonnene oder erworbene Güter"</note>; 2.) movable, **Traveling Property** <note>original: "fahrende Haabe"</note>, or immovable, which are divided into **Lying Grounds** <note>original: "liegende Gründe"</note> (containing fields, gardens, meadows) and **Standing Inheritances** <note>original: "stehende Erbe"</note> (houses, shops, cellars). Cothmann, *Counsel* 40, number 100, volume 1. Mevius, *On Lübeck Law*, book 1, title 10, article 3, numbers 1, 2, 3. See the Supplement of Wehner.

When the words **Rhenish Guilders** are found in an instrument, they are understood as common guilders, **of guilders in coin, but not in gold**. For commonly and generally, by a Rhenish guilder is meant the currency which is worth fifteen Batzen, or sixty Kreuzers, even if it is called a "good Rhenish guilder." For names must be understood from common and vulgar usage. Law *Labeo* 7, section *servus* 2, in the Digest *On the Legacy of Household Goods*; and we follow that which is frequent in the region in which something was done. Law *semper in stipulat.*, Digest *On the Rules of Law*. Furthermore, in obscure matters we look to that which is most usually done, in the law *ob-*

->Lit. G.<-

To occupy and claim for oneself ownerless things <note>original: "αδέσποτα"</note>, which are wandering and have an uncertain master, is noted by William Benedict... [citations: Speckhan; Gryphiander on Islands].

## ADDITION.

Regarding the goods of the shipwrecked, see Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated*, page 9, **On Ground-stranding and the Law of Ground-stranding** <note>original German: "Von der Grundruhr und dem Grundruhr Recht"</note>; Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, book 2, chapter 7, section 1. See also Lord Tabor... and Limnaeus... whether goods lost in the calamity of a shipwreck fall to the treasury? See Klock *on the treasury*... Schönborn in *Politics*... Selden in his book *On the Dominion of the Sea*... Jacob Gothofredus in his individual dissertation on the Rhodian Law. The **Rhodian Law of the Sea** <term>Lex Rhodia</term> <note>An ancient maritime code from the island of Rhodes that became the basis for Roman and later European sea laws.</note> is dealt with especially in the Digest, book 9... where the Roman Emperor is called "Master of the World" at least by way of a figure of speech <note>original: "Synecdochicè"</note>... see Christoff Tetsch in his *Inaugural Disputation on the Dominion of the World*... also Lord Hönnius... where he cites a gold coin of Emperor Constantine with the inscription: **conqueror of all nations**. Many other excellent points are found there. 

However, in the said passage, instead of "in the age" <note>original Greek: "εν τη ηλικια"</note>, one should read: "in Telia" <note>original Greek: "εν τη τηλικαὺ"</note>—for the ancient Greeks neither added accents nor wrote the subscript "iota"—that is, **on the Island of Telia**, which was one of the Cyclades. But what then is this opposition between the world and the sea, or the Emperor and the law? Certainly, when Antoninus calls himself "Master of the World," he understands not only the land but also the sea; and conversely, the law is mistress not only of the sea but of the land. If you consult the Greek, you will understand without difficulty that instead of "but the law" <note>original Greek: "οδε νόμος"</note>, one should read "but the wind" <note>original Greek: "οδε ανεμος"</note>. Eudæmon was complaining that he had suffered a shipwreck, to which Antoninus replies: that he is indeed the master of the world, but nevertheless the wind holds power over the sea, and the law cannot be imposed upon the wind by him. Therefore, he could not guarantee that Eudæmon would not suffer a shipwreck.

A case involving a shipwreck ought to be handled summarily, even if it is alleged that a theft was committed from the wreck. The **Caroline Constitution** <term>Constitutio Carolina</term> <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, issued by Emperor Charles V in 1532, the first body of criminal law covering the Holy Roman Empire.</note> in article 218 rightly accuses this abuse by which the goods of the shipwrecked are claimed by the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>. This power was formerly thought to be granted to the treasury and to the tax-collectors living on the seacoasts by the Rhodian Law. Although this usurpation is said to persist elsewhere... an injustice is done to Denmark if it is drawn into

<column-break/>

participation in this guilt in Besold’s first volume. This is shown by the following **Constitution from Book 3 of Danish Law**, chapter 63: If those who suffered shipwreck escape onto land alive, all people, whether they are Governors <note>original: "Præfecti"</note> or others, shall abstain from their goods, so long as the shipwrecked persons themselves—either by their own industry or through others they hire—are able to rescue the goods from the greed of the sea. Neither the Governor himself nor a lower magistrate shall dare to prohibit or hinder them from hiring anyone who wishes to offer their labor in saving the goods. But if it is proven by truthful witnesses that the Governor himself, or through his servants, stole anything from them before they abandoned the goods in despair or yielded them to an occupant, or if he blocked the help of hired assistants: he shall be removed from his governorship and restore everything stolen. A determination of other penalties follows, restraining both private and public persons who participate in this injury. See more in Rosenkranz *on Danish Law*, Position 7.

### 88. Guardian. <note>original: "Guardianus"</note>

**Guardians** and other prelates of a convent, such as Rectors, Priors, etc., are truly Prelates holding an ecclesiastical dignity. **Vicars**, however, are only Prelates when they preside over convents which, due to the small number of brothers, are not called by the name of a Guardianship, but the name of Vicar is assigned to them; otherwise (that is, in other cases) they are not Prelates.

The **minor matters** which Guardians can exercise by right are all those pertaining to the observance of **Regular Discipline** <note>The rules governing a religious order.</note> and the ordinary governance of the Convent, for which they can compel their subordinates through censures. The **major matters**, however, are those which strictly pertain to Episcopal jurisdiction: such as licensing subordinates for holy orders, appointing Preachers and Confessors, dispensing and absolving from reserved cases, inflicting heavier punishments, and similar things.

**Abbots**, who are presented by Kings and set in place by the Supreme Pontiff (such as many of the Order of St. Benedict), are in truth **Greater Prelates**, since they possess immediate Episcopal jurisdiction. This is from the *Compendium of Regular Questions* by Father Emmanuel Rodriguez, under the word "Guardians."

### 89. Guaranteed Instrument. <note>original: "Guarentigiatum Instrumentum"</note>

A **Guaranteed Instrument** (which is also called "confessed") is one that has **ready execution** <note>Meaning the debt can be collected immediately without a new trial.</note>, named from *Guardia*, that is, the security which the **guaranty clause** <note>original: "clausula Guarentigii"</note> provides to the creditor. This is commonly drafted as follows: **"that the creditor shall have the power, with or without legal action, without a stay of litigation, without preceding citation or process, to proceed immediately by way of fact; in the case of non-performance, to pay himself from the pledged security by his own hand, as if all legal rights had been fulfilled."** <note>original German/Latin: “daß der Gläubiger Macht haben soll, mit oder ohne Recht, absque litis sufflamine, ohne vorgehende Citation und Process, alsbald per viam facti zu procediren, auf den Fall der Nichthaltung, sich auf dem eingesetzten Unterpfand, selbst de facto eigener Weise bezahlt zu machen, tanquam omni jure peracto.”</note>

# Enlarged Treasure of Practical Law
## Letter G.

Scuris 14. *Digest on the Rules of Law, chapter "we inspect," under the same title in the 6th book.* <note>original: "ff. de R. J. c. inspicimus. tit. eod. in 6." This refers to the Digest of Justinian, a foundational Roman law text.</note>
Furthermore, the provision regarding coins is to be understood as referring to smaller denominations. *Law on coins, Digest on legacies, book 3.* And finally, we interpret an obscure agreement against the Creditor, who could have stated the law more clearly. *It pleases the ancients; 39. Digest on pacts; Law on when it is asked 26. Digest on credited things.* This is agreed upon by the *Silesian Land Ordinance, part 2, Constitution 29, there stating:* In many old contracts, the words "Rhenish Guilders" appear on their own <note>original: "absolute"</note>, and it is not expressed whether it was gold or coin: but because in ancient times the Gold Guilder was struck to the value of one Guilder in coin, it is agreed here that such words as "Rhenish Guilders" are to be understood as one Guilder in coin, as it was valued at that time. *Mynsinger, century 1, observation 65; century 5, observation 83, number 1.* Thoming, *decision 19, number 12.* Likewise, the words "good Guilders" <note>original: "guter Gülden"</note> are understood as silver money; they are applied to coin, and not to gold. *Saxon Land Ordinance, in the cited place, the version beginning "thus also."*

This is limited if other small words are added to the words "Rhenish Guilders," such as "full" or "full-weight" <note>original: "voll, oder vollwichtig"</note>. Alemannus, *Consultation 8, principal question 1, part 9. Mynsinger, century 5, observation 85.* See the *Illustrious Consultations of Baptist Caesar, consultation 16, part 1 & following consultations.* Also the word "weighty" <note>original: "wichtig"</note>. *Consultations on the Saxon Constitution, book 1, part 5, case 18, number 13.* Or "good of gold, and heavy of weight" <note>original: "gut von Gold, und schwer von Gewicht"</note>. *Mynsinger, century 5, observation 83.* For in this case, one must stand by the express agreement, and no other fictional sense should be assumed. Since to raise a question in clear and express matters is to undertake vain labor and to toil in vain. Or even "Rhenish Guilders in Gold." Alemannus, *in the cited work, folio 450.* And it should be noted here that formerly one Rhenish Gold Guilder was not more than 60 <term>Kreuzer</term> <note>original: "Grucif." A small silver/copper coin used in Central Europe.</note>. Likewise also one Guilder Thaler. But today the price of gold has increased because of the low quality of silver, which the Saxon silver mines seem to have brought about.

Rhenish Gold Guilders generally contain 18 <term>karats</term> and 6 or 9 grains in their gold; 72 pieces go into a <term>Cologne Mark</term> <note>A standard unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 233 grams.</note>, and they were formerly worth 75 Kreuzer. Ferdinand’s <note>Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1558–1564)</note> Minting Ordinance at Augsburg on August 18th, in the year 1559, in the section "Hereupon we ordain, set, and will, etc."

The Florin, in German "ein Gülden," had its name and origin from the city of Florence. They are also called Florins because of the flower <note>The lily or fleur-de-lis</note> formerly stamped on that money, as Christopher Ladinus testifies *in his glosses on the Italian poem by Dante.* Plotus also records this *in his additions to the Consultations of Martinus Laudensis, consultation 52.* Just as many coins received their name from the image stamped on them, such as "Caroli," "Cabalotti," "double roses," and "two heads," "golden Suns," "Philippi," "Julii," "Pauli," and similar ones. See *Caspar Antonius Thesaurus in his treatise on the increase of money, part 1, number 24.* Even the word "Guilder" <note>original: "Gülden"</note> among us is still written using the initial letters "fl."

Later, these florins were also minted in Germany, and their use was very frequent. However, it happened that they degenerated in intrinsic fine-

<column-break/>

-ness. Therefore, others were minted by the four Electors of the Rhine, which were called "Rhenish" <note>original: "Rhenenses"</note>. But when the said Rhenish coins, which were minted to the value of one florin or 60 Kreuzer, increased in value (as happens) due to the deterioration of the small silver money according to which they were valued, Tileman Fries states in the *Mirror of Minting* <note>original: "Münzspiegel"</note>, book 4, chapter 15: then custom introduced "imaginary florins" <note>Money of account used for bookkeeping rather than physical circulation</note> which retained the aforementioned name and value; and florins began to be minted in Silver to that value, which in Upper Germany were called "Guilder Thalers" or "Guilder-Groschen," and in Lower Germany "simple Thalers" <note>original: "schlechte Thaler"</note>. Furthermore, even when the value of both gold and silver florins increased again, that legal and imposed value remained; by the benefit of which these imaginary florins of fifteen <term>Batzen</term> or sixty Kreuzer remain with us today. *Bornitius, book 1, chapter 10.*

On what comes under the name of "Guilder" in cases of theft, see *Zieritz on the Criminal Constitution, article 157.*

Otherwise, two or three hundred years ago, a Guilder was a Ducat, just as the Florin is named after the gold coin of the Florentine Republic: see Freher, *On Money*. Thus one also finds in old letters: "N. N. one thousand Guilders, all of good and rightly-weighed Hungarian and Bohemian Guilders, good of gold and heavy in weight." Likewise in other instruments, "Florin-ker Guilders" <note>original: "Florenker Gülden," likely referring to Florentine Guilders</note> are sometimes mentioned.

For one Gold Guilder, the Imperial Chamber Court <note>The highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</note> recognizes five-quarters of a Guilder. Author of the *Decisions or Prejudices of the Imperial Chamber*, section "Gold Guilder." *See also the consultations of Modestinus Pistoris.*

-> ADDITION. <-

The *Solidus*, which is also called a gold piece <note>original: "aureus"</note>, is commonly accepted and calculated for a Hungarian gold piece, and the Chamber has sometimes pronounced it so, as witnessed by *Gylmann, volume 3, Symph., page 111.* Some count it for a Rhenish gold piece or Gold Guilder. *Wurmser, 5, observation 11. Gail, 2, observation 39.* Richard, however, *on the law 'whoever', Code on runaway slaves*, says that according to the opinion of others, the name *Solidi* in Germany includes the Rhenish gold pieces of 15 batzen; see *Master Ludovicus, Disputation on the Institutes, page 301, letter h*, who interprets *solidi* as Hungarian gold pieces.

The Florin, or golden Florentine, or Gold piece (German: "Florenker Gülden" or "Gulden"), was first minted at Florence (named after the lily flower, which it had on one side, as stated by *Freher, On Matters of Minting, book 2, chapter 3; Thesaurus, On the increase of money, part 1, number 24*; hence the word Guilder is written as "fl.", *Tileman, book 4, chapter 15*). Later it was also minted in Germany and other places, where its use was once very frequent (according to Freher), though today it is rarer (*Mynsinger, 4, observation 1, number 6*). It happened, however, that florins degenerated in intrinsic goodness; therefore, others were minted by the 4 Electors of the Rhine (Rhenish, "Rheinische Gulden"), others were Hungarian ("ungarische Gulden"), and others were named differently. *Freher; Lehmann in the Chronicle of Speyer, book 4, chapter 22.*

# Letter G.

When the value of Florins <note>original: "Floreni"</note> increased according to local custom and time, practice introduced "imaginary florins" that retained the original name and value. Since these were of various types, another kind of florin followed, minted in silver to match the value of the aforementioned gold ones, each worth 60 units. The High Germans call these **Gold-thalers** <note>original: "Guldenthaler"</note> or **Gold-groats** <note>original: "Guldengroschen"</note>, while the Low Germans call them **base thalers** <note>original: "schlechte Thaler"</note>. For some time, calculations were made according to these. However, when the value of both the real and these silver coins increased again, a legal and fixed value remained, by which the "imaginary florins" worth 15 Batzen <note>a coin worth 4 kreuzer; original: "Baß"</note> remained in use. Therefore, a gold coin or florin represents 15 Batzen or 60 Kreuzer. This value is observed not only in the Chamber Court Ordinances but also in other contracts and obligations. This rule fails, however, in Chancellery Law, where it is worth 16 Batzen and 1 Kreuzer, which is commonly called **Chancellery Currency** <note>original: "Cantzleywährung"</note>. **Rhenish Guilders** <note>original: "Rheinische Gulden"</note> are accepted as common guilders **in coin**, but not **in gold**. Likewise, the words **good guilders** <note>original: "gute Gülden"</note> are used <note>citing legal scholars Mynsinger and Berlichius</note>. This is restricted, however, if the legal document specifies **full-weight or well-weighted Rhenish guilders**, or terms like **weighted**, **correctly weighed**, **good**, **current**, **Rhenish Guilders**, or **good of gold** and **heavy of weight**, or **Rhenish Guilders in gold**. There is also the solid gold coin, the **Rhenish Gold Guilder**, whose value is **five quarters of a guilder**, which makes 75 Kreuzer, as can be seen in the Chamber Court observations of Tileman, Gylman, and Wilhelm Scipio. In New Cairo, Mr. Fürer first saw that currency of the Republic of Nuremberg at a money-changer's table which we call in our native tongue **Gold-groats** <note>original: "Guldengroschen"</note>, which had begun to be minted by the Nuremberg Senate shortly before, as noted on page 29 of his highly praised *Itinerary*. Regarding the Nuremberg Thalers, commonly called **Gold-thalers** or **Gold-groats**—so called because of their former frequency of being minted in our city—their thinness today is monstrous and they are almost invisible <note>citing Tobias Oelhafen, "On the Goddess of Money," Oration 5</note>. Regarding **Rhenish Gold Guilders**, Zeiller writes <note>in "German Itinerary" and his letters</note> that gold and silver are used for them, and they were first struck by the four Electors on the Rhine, from which they take their name. It is not that they were made solely from gold found in the Rhine (which is not inferior in quality to Hungarian gold), though they were better in the beginning when gold was found there sooner than elsewhere.

In the Nuremberg Statutes, one finds the **Guilder of City Currency** which today is worth 20 Batzen and 20 Pfennigs; however, the **Guilder of Country Currency** makes 20 Batzen, most extensively from all sorts of **Alemannic Guilders**, as seen in the *Palæstra Consultationum*.

<column-break/>

A Hungarian Guilder is worth 100 Pfennigs <note>citing Augustinus Wagner in his work on the laws and customs of the Kingdom of Hungary</note>.

### 94. Golden Number. <note>original: "Güldenzahl. Aureus Numerus."</note>

When the date of Easter was discussed at the Council of Nicaea, the so-called "Golden Number" was established for the purpose of more easily finding the Paschal day of any given year; it contains a cycle of nineteen years, as St. Ambrose testifies in his *Epistle to the Ephesians* <note>see Baronius, Year of Christ 325</note>.

The **Golden Number**, which is also called the **Lunar Cycle** <note>original: "Monden-Circul" or "Cyclus Lunaris"</note>, as well as the **Nineteen-Year Cycle** <note>original: "Decemnovalis"</note>, is a period of nineteen years. After this time has passed, all new and full moons with their quarters return again to their previous old positions in the Zodiac, and after every nineteen years, the "interval"—that is, the time between Christmas and Shrove Tuesday <note>Lent</note>—begins anew <note>citing Barth. Scheræus in the "German Language School," page 203</note>.

See Mr. Speidel in his *Notable Matters*.

### ADDITION.

The situation with the **Estate-share** <note>the right to a deceased serf's goods; original: "Budtheil"</note> was such that when serfs married each other and the wife died before the husband, the best bed or another piece of her household furniture, of which he had the choice, fell to the Bishop. If, however, the male serf died, the best livestock, horse, and the best clothing of his estate were due and granted to the Bishop or the Foundation Bailiff; this was called the **Head-right** <note>original: "Hauptrecht"</note>. Regarding this Head-right or Estate-share, the same author recounts <note>in book 7, chapter 56</note> that the **Death-tax** <note>original: "Mortuarium"</note> is commonly called **Inheritance-right**, **Wine-meal**, **Head-fall**, **Head-right**, or **Death-fall**. In some places, the lords take the best horse; in others, if they lack horses, the best head of cattle; in others, the best garment; in others, a certain quantity of money—a piece of gold, or 2 or 3 guilders. Elsewhere, they take a certain quantity of wine, one or...
