## 96. Guelphs and Ghibellines; Guelfi & Gibellini.

When in the year of Christ 1125, the Emperor Henry V died without children at Utrecht on the 15th day before the Calends of June, and the Princes held an Imperial Diet at Worms, most of them named Lothair as King of the Romans. Lothair was the son of Count Gebhard of Supplinburg and Arnsberg, descended from the Counts of Querfurt, and had been appointed Duke of Saxony by Henry V. They arranged for him to be crowned at Aachen on the Ides of September. From that point, he numbered the first year of his reign, though he had competitors: Conrad, Duke of Franconia (the nephew of the late Emperor Henry by his sister), Leopold, Margrave of Austria, and Charles, Count of Flanders. The others were soon brought to order, but there was a more serious struggle against Conrad and his brother Frederick, Duke of Swabia. However, through his great authority and the intervention of St. Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, at the assembly of Bamberg, Lothair often received them back into favor after they had been defeated.

By this Emperor Lothair, Conrad—who is surnamed the Great, Margrave of Landsberg and Lusatia—was the first of his line to be invested as Margrave of Meissen in the year 1126. He had as his wife Luitgard (not Lucia, as Father Felix and Bruschius wrongly have it), the sister of Conrad, who was elected Emperor after Lothair in the year of Christ 1139. This Conrad faced opposition from the Guelph faction, which had already begun in the time of Henry IV. He prepared an expedition to Jerusalem <note>The Second Crusade</note> at the urging of St. Bernard of Clairvaux. In this expedition at Frankfurt, he himself, along with many Princes of Germany and even his adversary Duke Welf, was marked with the sign of the Cross. But that expedition had an unhappy end, with their army largely destroyed partly by hunger, partly by the harsh weather, partly by the weapons of the Saracens, and by the trickery and fraud of the Greeks. The business was left unfinished, and because of

<column-break/>

<margin>Welf, the son of Azo, Margrave of the Italians, took up the Duchy of Bavaria. He had previously married the daughter of Otto, Duke of the Bavarians. From the Welfs, the family of the Dukes of Brunswick, who reign today, traces its origin. (Miræus in the Annals of Belgium, for the year 1071, page 621 in my edition).</margin>

the massive slaughter of his men, the Emperor was forced to return with a heavy heart. After his return, when the war between him and Welf was renewed, it is said that the names of "Guelphs" and "Ghibellines" were first heard. These names came from two families, Weiblingen and Welf. From the first, the Emperors arose; from the second, very powerful Dukes arose; and for many years they fought one another for supremacy. Many believe that the Guelph and Ghibelline factions later arose in Italy, where they first began to be heard of under Emperor Frederick II. For a long time, they afflicted the Christian world due to the discord between the Roman Popes and the Emperors. (Stengel, on the Monasteries of the Order of St. Benedict, where he discusses Elchingen; and myself on Education and Literary Studies, page 4, at the end).

In the time of the Ghibellines, the "plagues" of the Guelphs arose and began to rage far and wide, spreading everywhere with sword, fire, and devastation. In most cities and towns, dissensions and riots broke out between the clergy and the laity—the former adhering to the Pope, the latter to the Emperor. From this it happened that in the year of Christ 1246, the Emperor Conrad, who governed Germany during the absence of his father Frederick II, burned the Church of Neresheim out of hatred for the Counts Hartmann and Albert of Dillingen, who had remained loyal to the Pope. The following year, when he again set up camp there, he set fire to everything in the vicinity. And when the same King, in the year 1249, placed his camp in the territory of Neresheim for a third time, Henry, Margrave of Burgau, set fire to the Cloister and the Church of Saints Andrew and Blaise. (Stengel, where he discusses Neresheim; see also my work, the Historical Synopsis).

### ADDITION.

The Guelphs and Ghibellines arose under Frederick II, according to Megiser (see "Privileges of Altdorf"). In past centuries, some in Italy were Guelphs and others Ghibellines; the former adhered to the Pope, while the latter adhered to the Emperor. Reincking (on the Governance of the State and Church, Book 1, Class 2, Chapter 7, number 13) thinks the Ghibellines were so named because they followed the Lord of Gebello <note>likely a Latinization of Waiblingen</note>. The origin of Frederick Barbarossa’s family was from the Weiblingens, from which they were called "Guiblingi," a name the Italians changed to "Gibellini." The Guelphs, on the other hand, were so called as if they were "Zealots of the Faith," according to the reasoning given by Bartolus in his treatise on the Ghibellines, number 1. More on this matter can be found in Limnäus (on Public Law, Book 1, Chapter 7, number 63), whose reading has always been a "beehive" <note>original: "apiaria," meaning a source of sweet or useful information</note> for me, as Rittershusius says in his work on Amphilochius, page 45. ## 97. The Rooster. <term>Gallus</term>.

Why the image of a rooster is placed upon church steeples. Saubertus, *On Sacrifices*, page 54. In the head of a poultry-cock, within the brain when deboned without fracturing (which happens easily when it is boiled for a long time), a lily is observed. *The Roman Tapestries, which my dear Mr. Harsdörffer published, page 43.* <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658) was a famous Nuremberg polymath and poet.</note> From this, Limnaeus in *Public Law*, Book 6, chapter 6, number 36 notes: The restless genius of the Gauls <note>A pun on *Gallus*, which means both "rooster" and "a person from Gaul/France"</note> progressed so far that they even observed the insignia of their King marked in the head of a rooster, and they drew from this a great argument for Royal power. For in the head of a poultry-cock, in the brain entirely deboned without fracture, a toad is found on one side, which, when turned onto its back, is expressed as a lily on the other side. <note>This refers to a legend that the French fleur-de-lis was a transformed version of the older heraldic toads of the Franks.</note> In many places, in the event of a death, the village magistrate takes an ox, the local shepherd takes a poultry-cock (the house-cock), and the sexton takes a bratwurst. Stuckius, *Justinian Exercises*, part 1, decade 8, assertion 6, letter E, page 331. At the end: The noble nature of the poultry-cock is excellently suited for many lessons of virtue. He is the index of time; the monitor of vigilance; the master of that choir whose song—

<meta>This is Besold's Volume 1.</meta>

<column-break/>

—is God: the very image of fortitude. He provides the indication of time to mortals by the "cock-crow" <note>original: "gallicinio"</note>. However, this is not at a fixed moment or a strictly set point, as the "Master of Subtleties" <note>Referring to the scholar Julius Caesar Scaliger</note> refutes by his own experiment in Exercise 239. He says: There have been those who dared to ascribe fixed hours for singing to the rooster; I have found them to be speaking falsely, both in my former night-watches and later in my nocturnal studies. Nevertheless, more frequently and as if by an order of nature, he distinguishes two nocturnal times with his song: the beginning of the third military watch in the very middle of the night, when the inclination happens from midnight toward the coming day and light; and the fourth watch, about three hours before sunrise. Pliny says in Book 10, 21: With the sun, roosters go to sleep, and at the fourth military watch they are recalled to their cares and labors; they do not allow the sunrise to creep up on the unwary, but announce the coming day with song. "The hunters of truth" <note>original: "οἱ τῆς ἀληθείας θηρευταὶ" (Greek)</note> have hunted for the causes of this cock-crow, but many have not even found its tracks. There is a fable which the poets have handed down concerning *Alectryon*, the attendant of Mars, who was changed into a rooster so that he might pay for his crime at that point in time when he committed it. They say that while he was placed on guard when Mars was in Heaven with Venus (just as Dido and the Trojan Leader were in the same cave), he succumbed to sleep and failed to announce the sunrise, thereby allowing Vulcan to trap them in his nets; and he expiated that crime through his metamorphosis and his perpetual song. <note>In mythology, Alectryon was a youth Mars stationed outside his door to warn of the sun-god Helios's arrival during his affair with Aphrodite/Venus. He fell asleep, the lovers were caught, and Mars turned him into a rooster to always announce the sun's arrival.</note> An opinion regarding the rooster's desire for the hen carries a shadow of truth but not the reality; it was refuted by the same Scaliger in these words: It is manifest that he does not sing from a desire for the hen, since he sings after mating; he sings when she is present, he sings when he is full, and other things that are "rather like old wives' tales" <note>original: "αἰγερολογικώτερα" (Greek)</note>. Those who suggest a certain magnetic harmony between the returning sun (as it nears our horizon) and the crested bird are closer to the truth. In this game of the Sages, it seems to me those who attribute it to joy and a certain sense of perceived rest have "thrown a Venus" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "to have a stroke of luck" or "hit the mark," based on a winning roll of dice.</note>; the weight of vapors has been unburdened and the food digested. For because the warm and thin blood of the rooster has excited breaths and vapors in the muscles due to the nocturnal constitution of the air, he seeks to dissipate those vapors, along with the phlegm collected by the cold of the night, by clapping his wings and singing from his throat—not unlike how other animals dispel gases by stretching or yawning. Gerhard Johann Vossius has these latter points in Book 3, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chapter 88. From wherever the reason for the cock-crow is sought, the purpose is nonetheless clearly established: it is the natural distinction of hours and intervals, which is to be directed more carefully and certainly by human art. It is an argument of superstitious ignorance that clocks are not admitted among the Turks; for if they were held publicly, it would seem that something of the authority of the sextons and the ancient rite would be diminished. Hence they have "Talismans" <note>Presumably referring to Muezzins or religious officials</note>, a class of men dedicated to the ministry of the temples; these men use measures made of water, by which, after they have recognized that the dawn is approaching, they raise a cry—

# Enlarged Practical Treasury

...they raise their voices from a high tower built for that purpose, by which they exhort and summon men to worship God. They do the same in the time between sunrise and noon; and again between noon and sunset; and finally at sunset, they use a very sharp voice, vibrating it with a modulation that is not unpleasant, which can be heard further away than one might believe. Thus, the entire day for the Turks is divided into four spaces, longer or shorter as the season of the year dictates; however, all time during the night remains uncertain. This is the account of *A. Ghiselin de Busbecq* in his first epistle. <note>Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq (1522–1592) was a 16th-century diplomat who wrote famous letters about his travels in the Ottoman Empire.</note>

There is also another purpose for the cock-crow: the waking of mortals from sleep and a reminder of vigilance. For the night-watchman summons not only the farmer, the craftsman, and the steward to their domestic works, but he also urges the traveler on his journey and rouses the lawyer to the late-night study of his case, as *Horace* suggests in his *Satires, Book 1, Satire 1*: *The man skilled in justice and the laws praises the farmer when a client knocks at his door at the cock's crow.* See *Walther, on the privileges of Doctors, page 363*. *Cicero*, in his speech *For Murena*, said to Servius regarding the legal expert—whom he compares to a soldier—that the crowing of cocks rouses the lawyer just as the sound of trumpets rouses the soldier. Furthermore, the cock is the catalyst for schoolwork. *Martial* certainly treats the schoolmaster harshly because he opens the school of letters before the cock's crow—that is, before the lawful and seasonable time.

> The crested cocks have not yet broken the silence:
> Already you resound with cruel murmuring and lashes.

The cock is said to "crow" <note>original: *cucurire*</note>, just as the thrush "warbles," the starling "chatters," the partridge "clucks," the goose "cackles," the duck "quacks," the swan "trumpets," the vulture "screams," the bee-eater "chirps," the owl "hoots," and the bee "hums." That famous command of the Lord ought to resound in everyone's ears, which appears in *Mark 13:35*: *Watch therefore, for you do not know when the master of the house will come—in the evening, or at midnight, or at the cock-crow, or in the morning.* The cock is a good housemate (<term>meletē</term> <note>original: *μελέτη* — meaning 'practice' or 'exercise'</note> according to *Ambrose* in Book 5 of the *Hexaemeron*); he rouses the sleeper, admonishes the worried, and comforts the traveler, testifying to the progress of the night with his melodic signal. When he crows, the bandit leaves his ambush; when he crows, the fearful sailor sets aside his sorrow. *These are the words of Ambrose.* 

The most excellent goal of the cock-crow is the "stage-management" of divine praises; for all songbirds, as soon as they wake from sleep, sing their little tunes—the musical forest cries out, and the air, full of winged singers, makes it known. Yet the cock leads the choir, being the first to sing; having raised a loud signal for nearly a thousand paces, he begins the melody. Thus, Man, the Prince of Creatures, is provoked to similar pursuits and morning hymns, nor can he excuse his own laziness when surpassed by the industry of the music in the air. A certain learned man recalls an answer given to him by a rather talkative servant when he tried to wake him using the example of the birds. The servant replied rather coldly: "By your leave, my master, for these little birds we now hear singing in the gardens of this house are not of the same temperament as men, but are of a hotter nature, and they do not have large heads, but very tiny little brains, so that in a very short space of time their vapors are consumed and their sleep is dissolved."

<column-break/>

To the high-spirited bravery of the cock belongs also the terror it strikes into the lion, which is caused by its crowing. *Pliny*, in the place cited, says: *Alone among birds, it looks frequently at the sky*, raising its sickle-shaped tail on high. Therefore, they are a terror even to lions, the most noble of wild beasts. This is followed by many "elevated" authors <note>original: *ἀναείρμοι* — writers of high standing</note>, although there is no lack of examples of degenerate cocks being devoured by lions. Their praised pugnacity, kindled by a desire for glory, was set forth as an example and an omen by the Athenians. According to *Aelian* (Book 2, Chapter 28), they had a law that cocks should fight in the theater one day every year. Nevertheless, when the cock feels himself unequal in the conflict, he cowers and pleads in a wondrously dejected way, leaving the spectators with a laugh and the Greeks with a proverb: <term>ptēssei hōs tis alektōr</term> <note>original: *πτήσσει ὡς τίς ἀλέκτωρ* — "he cowers like a cock"</note>. 

These and many other matters are held in a long series in a *Program* by the Excellent Lord Dr. Dannhauer, who through diligent reading and daily meditation made his breast a library of Christ. This was publicly set forth at Strasbourg on November 1, 1647. Partly because of its admirable elegance, and partly because it is in the hands of so few, I have judged it worthy to be transcribed more freely so that it might see the light again. 

Regarding the crime of Parricide, various doctors give reasons why a rooster was added to the leather sack <note>The *Poena Cullei* was an ancient Roman punishment for killing a parent, where the murderer was sewn into a sack with a dog, a rooster, a viper, and a monkey, and thrown into the water.</note>, which *Harpprecht* reviews in his notes on the Institutes, on public judgments, number 25, and those cited there. *Titus Livius*, in Book 2 of his third decade, writes of a hen turning into a male and a cock into a female, and that this was held to be a prodigy. *Goedd.* on the *Signification of Words*, number 5. Now, since by God's favor I have recovered my health, I owe a cock to your Aesculapius. <note>original: "gallum debeo Aesculapio tuo." A reference to Socrates' famous last words, indicating a debt of gratitude for healing.</note> See *Lipsius, Century 1, Epistle 2*. Regarding the *Cock of Aesculapius*, see *Philippus Carolus*, Book 1, *Various Readings*, chapter 12, at the end. 

Roosters are highly esteemed, especially in villages, in place of clocks because of their vigilance, as they certainly begin their song at midnight. Also, when they are provided with juniper berries—which grow so abundantly in the cold northern lands—they make a good dish for the table. *Zeiller, Century 5, Epistles, page 171.* Regarding the "Hahnrey" (cuckold), see *Limnaeus in Public Law, Book 6, observation 95*, also the terms *cucurbita* (gourd) and *beccus* (beak). *Berlich, part 5, conclusion 59, number 43.* Lucius Marineus Siculus, an otherwise famous historian, writes in Book 5 of *Spanish Matters* toward the end, that in the very old Spanish city of *Santo Domingo de la Calzada*, he saw a cock and a hen which, after they had been strangled and roasted, became alive again and jumped around on the table. The cock also immediately crowed. They lived for seven years afterward and left behind young ones from which others have descended. Pilgrims take feathers from these, and yet they never run out. *Zeiller, Century 2, Epistles, page 3.* Five feet of a cock announce the "flight of the capon," that is, the flight of the poultry-cock. *Mindan. chapter 20, number 41 on the continuation of a case.* The lion cannot hear the cock cry out without rage because the hearing canals in his ears are much too large, and such a...

...a sharp and subtle voice to be endured without bitterness. *Zeiller, Century 3, Epistle page 663.* For St. Anthony's Fire <note>original: "Erysipelas," a skin infection</note>, they recommend cherry wood cut on the day of St. Gall <note>October 16th</note> in the month of October. The three sons of the great Emperor Charles—Pippin, Charles, and Louis—were made to fight before him, by order of their mother, Empress Hildegard. They let three roosters loose together (which is also said to have happened in Paris around the time of the Battle of Prague in 1620) so that they might know which son should succeed the father. As it happened, the rooster of Louis overcame the others, and he indeed later became Emperor. *Zeiller, Century 2, Epistle page 419.* Phidias <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE</note> formed a statue of Pallas Athena for the people of Elis, upon whose helmet he placed a cock: a fierce and bold animal that fights for honor and glory rather than prey, a herald of light and vigilance, and a symbol of military service most fitting for a leader. *Limnaeus, Book 6, chapter 6, number 78.* In the court of a Baron, there is a rooster belonging to Lord A, a white hen belonging to Lord B (which laid an egg), and a black hen belonging to Lord C (which hatched and brooded said egg). Later, in the courtyard of Lord D, a chick is born. The question is asked: does said chick belong to all the aforementioned, or to the Baron, or to Lord D, or to the owner of the rooster, or the owner of the white hen, or the owner of the black hen? See the "Disputation on the Egg and the Chick" below in the form of a legal counsel, under the words *Hüner* (chickens) and *Hennen* (hens), and *Lord Biccius in the Golden Sections, section 3, thesis 22*, where we judge that the offspring follows the mother rather than the father.

Regarding the Swiss, in the sacred chapel of St. Gall, this peerless eulogy is found: *Just as you hated no one, so too no one hates you, Gallus.*

On the death of a rooster, John Steuccius of Meissen wrote excellently, among other things:

> If any faith is put in the Turks, a giant cock stands in the heavens,
> And with its fierce throat, it rouses its bird-kin.
> As soon as it crows "cock-a-doodle-doo" from the dark axis of the sky,
> Immediately, I was crowing "cock-a-doodle-doo" upon the earth.

## 98. Roaming the Alleys. Nightly wanderings.

Nightly wanderings <note>original: "Nocturnæ discurſationes," often called "Gaſſaten gehen" in German</note>, or roaming the alleys, are for the most part harmful, especially if they are done with shouting, the clashing of weapons, attacking houses, breaking windows, and injury to others. Students who frequently roam at night are like stars that rise at sunset <note>achronic</note> and set at sunrise <note>cosmic</note>. They go to bed in the morning when the sun rises and "rise" at night. *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 8, chapter 6, number 108.* They treat day as night, like the Antipodes <note>people on the opposite side of the earth</note>; that is, as Tacitus speaks in *Annals 16, chapter 18, number 1*, they spend the day in sleep and the night in duties and delights.

## 99. Guilds, Street-Masters. Guilds.

Guild or "Gaſſeln." Street-lords or commissioners for the guilds. *Limnaeus, book 7, chapter 10, number 15.* The word "Gildae" is read as "Guild" in the life of Fi-

<column-break/>

chard, and in *Draco on Patricians, page 207.* See "Guild-master" <note>original: "Gildenmeiſter"</note>.

## 100. Gravel, Arena-Warden. Arena.

"Grieß" is the arena <note>the sandy floor of a tournament or combat area</note>, and "Wärtel" (whom we today call "Wärter," a warden or attendant) is one who serves another by his observation. There is much on this word in *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, number 118 throughout; book 1, Additions to book 5, chapter 7, page 752.* Warden, Lurker, Arena-Warden: *Limnaeus, volume 1, Additions to book 5, chapter 7, page 750, 757.* The word "Warner" <note>Warden/Warner</note> is also mentioned on pages 758 and 759.

## 101. To Pay, Debts, Money-Rent.
->Payment Rule<-

"Gelden" stands for paying <note>original: "Bezahlen"</note>. "That which I have become indebted for and ought to pay." "Gelder" is used for creditors. The little words "Geldpacht" (money-rent) and "Kornpacht" (grain-rent) are found in *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 4, number 19.*

## 102. Granges.

"Grangiæ," that is, small villas or farmsteads. *Moneta on Tithes, chapter 9, question 2; Klock on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 92, number 6.*

## 103. Certainty. Certain.

"What is more certain is safer," says the *Speculator* regarding the plaintiff. From this arose that common proverb: "Hold to the certain, but let go of the uncertain." *Canon: "if anyone however..." 4, at the end, on Penance, distinction 7; Meichsner, volume 3, decision 6, number 69; Dr. Tabor in Criminal Clusters, page 272.*

## 104. Cloth of Gold. Garments rustling with woven gold.

No one should wear "Guldene Stück" <note>cloth of gold</note>, lace, pearls, and the like, unless they have first paid the excise tax on them. *Bornitius on the Treasury, book 4, chapter 2, regarding Belgium.* What if, as the Ephesians once did, a law were placed throughout the whole Empire that men and women should not wear gold for ten years; but whatever they currently possessed, they should lend to the Empire. *Obrecht in Political Reflections, page 49.* Women and maidens who watch and are related to those in the Tournament should have no more than 3 or 4 decorated gowns, among which there shall be no cloth of gold or gown made entirely of pearls. A member of a tournament shall wear no cloth of gold or silver except for their doublets. *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, page 124.*

## 105. Grass, Aftermath, Hay. Hay, Grasses.

No one shall mow on the common ground or other meadows and in the woods with scythes or scythe-sharpening hammers <note>original: "Dengelſtumpffen"</note> under penalty of one guilder; however, grazing is not forbidden, which grass shall remain in the community for the benefit of their own livestock. ### 108. Grammar.

Grammatical Canons are the rules of grammarians. See *Ausonius, Epigram 128. Rittershausen on Amphilochius, page 101.*

->A Grammarian is not happy, nor was he ever,<-
->Nor is anyone happy who bears the name Grammarian.<-
->But if anyone ever existed who was happy beyond fate,<-
->He, at last, has exceeded the Grammatical Canons.<-

You can distinguish students of law who think it a sin to touch any books other than law books from those who love more elegant speech as easily as you can tell the goat-like and unwashed from the perfumed and polished. *Budé, Annotations on the Pandects, at the law "but he is present." Locati, page 668.* Hence Athalaric, King of the Goths, spoke well to the Senate of the City of Rome

<column-break/>

in *Cassiodorus, book 9 of the Variae, chapter 21:* "The first school of the grammarians is a most beautiful foundation." And wisely Albericus Gentilis says in his *readings of Virgil, chapter 19:* "Grammar does not disgrace the highest men." It was not a source of shame for the great Emperor Caesar, the great Physician Galen, the great Theologian Augustine, the great Jurist Labeo, or the great scholar Varro; they even wrote private treatises on the subject. However, it was the common fate of these most excellent men to be called "Grammarians" out of contempt, which happened to Erasmus, Lipsius, Drusius, and Scaliger. Yet, it is clear from *Alciatus, book 9, part c, 24,* and *Barbosa's Axioms, book 7, chapter 9 throughout,* that such subtle knowledge is not strictly required in a legal practitioner. Dr. Tabor, in his work on *alienation regarding loans, page 360, number 6,* believes someone read the grammarians diligently. Grammarians are confident and headlong in judging, *ibid. page 442, number 11.* Seneca, in *Epistle 88,* describes the grammarian: "The grammarian is occupied with the care of speech; if he wishes to wander further, he deals with histories; and at the furthest extent of his borders, with poems." In *Epistle 95,* he calls them the "guardians of the Latin language." From these passages, it appears that this title was once honored, although in later times it fell into such contempt along with literature that no petty schoolmaster <note>original: "Magistellorum," a diminutive, mocking term for teachers</note> today greatly enjoys this praise; see the preface to the *Grammar by Gießen. Dr. Tabor on billeting, page 204.* Does false grammar void a sentence? See the *Gloss and Bartolus on Law 2, Code regarding the recitation of dangerous sentences.* A grammarian was once called a Doctor. *Walther on the Privileges of Doctors, page 15.* It is harder to earn the title of a good grammarian once than to earn the name of Doctor in three faculties; *ibid. page 183.* Masters of Arts are not content with the title of grammarian; *ibid. page 235.* No trust should be placed in letters that contain a manifest error in construction; *Chapter 11, outside "on rescripts."* Bartolus teaches in *Law 8, number 5, Digest on gold and silver legacies,* that a Prince's rescript <note>a formal written reply or decree</note> is voided by an evident grammatical flaw. See also *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 12, section 11, number 98 and following.* In the 3rd disputation on *Public Law, thesis 14,* added to Clapmarius and held under Rittershausen: although Servius Sulpitius surpassed everyone of his rank in skill and was significantly touched by humanistic literature, he did not hesitate to submit his rods of office <note>original: "fasces," symbols of Roman magisterial power</note> to the grammarians' switches, and to most diligently ask M. Varro through letters about more obscure words. *Antonius Matthaeus in his Oration on the Modesty of the Ancient Jurists.* Although Caius Aquilius Gallus was not unlearned in speaking, since Marcus Tullius [Cicero] held first place in that field, if any question of fact was referred to him, because it had nothing to do with law, he would say "one must go to Cicero," as stated in that place. ### 109. Learned Servants. <note>original: "Gelehrte Diener" / "Ministri eruditi"</note>

Learned servants—in which matters they have the first voice before Princes, Counts, Lords, and Knights. Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, book 9, chapter 4, page 141. **Learned servants, people, and bees must be well looked after so that they remain.** Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 107. A supply of learned men is not common or easily obtained. Ummius, *On Legal Process*, page 45.

### 110. The Thick-Witted and Dull. <note>original: "Grossi & Grossolani"</note>

"Grossi" are unripe figs. Posthumius Albinus in his first *Annals* regarding Brutus: "For this reason, he made himself out to be a stupid brute, eating little green figs [grossulos] with honey." Caspar Barth, *Adversaria*, book 43, chapter 12.

Not all fools lack intellect, even if their minds are sometimes more obtuse and stupid. These are the ones the Interpreters of law call the *Grossi* and *Grossolani*. Rittershusius, *On the New Constitutions*, part 9, chapter 6, page 536, number 101. They are clearly midway between the prudent and the insane; that is, those who are neither endowed with a full mind nor entirely deprived of it, but who possess some measure of prudence. Thus, "fools" is sometimes used for those who are not very wise, since the laws themselves recognize degrees of human wisdom. Law 4, section 3: "if he is so foolish." *Digest, On the Ediles' Edict*. If these people have some sense and understanding, though it be simpler, more obtuse, and duller, you may—along with Bocerus (class 3, disputation 1, thesis 19) and the *Argentine Collection*—grant them the right to make a will. Mantica, *On Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 2, title 5, number 14, where he calls them "Grossolani." Mr. Rebhan, *Introduction to Justinian*, disputation 7; Dauth, *On Wills*, page 178, number 220.

### 111. Groats. <note>original: "Grütz" / "Puls"</note>

### 131. Canon Law. [Jus Canonicum].

On the differences between Civil <note>Roman secular law</note> and Canon Law <note>Church law</note>, Conrad Rittershusius, who deserved well of the entire literary republic, wrote excellently. Most recently in 1661, at Jena, there appeared the *Idea of Imperial, Private, Public, CANON, and Feudal Law*, by Christoph Hain of Löwenthal, Count Palatine of the Emperor.

In Venice, 1491, the *Concordance of Discordant Canons* <note>The "Decretum Gratiani," the foundation of Canon Law</note> was published by Andreas of Calabria. In the same place in 1496, Aegidius de Mandelbertis wrote *Questions of Pontifical Law*. These authors are preserved in the Nuremberg Library. Giovanni Battista Viviani wrote the *Rationale of Canon Law*, divided into five books, published at Cologne in 1628. How Canon Law should be read and how places from it should be cited is taught by Vultejus in his *Prolegomena to Roman Jurisprudence*, page 57 and following, and Pacius in his *Introduction to the Analysis of the Institutes*, page 11. ### 133. The Sheaf-Game. [Garbenspiel].

On the "Sheaf-Game," see Sprenger in *The Practice of Exchange*, page 24. **Stockfish [cod] are caught in January at Bergen in Norway; there is a special established society for this. In the past, whoever wanted to enter it had to endure the "Sheaf-Game."** The members would place the initiate in a basket, hang him in smoke for several hours, throw him into the water, and drag him under the ship. If one endured this, he made himself eligible for the Stockfish Company. It is a form of <term>academic deposition</term> <note>a traditional, often violent hazing ritual for new students or guild members</note>, although it is abolished nowadays.

# H.

The H is not actually a letter, but a breathing <note>original: "anhauchen," a phonetic aspiration</note>, with these added words: *if I may be added to the others* <note>original: "si cæteris addar"</note>. The full symbol can be found on page 12, part 2, of the *Discourses* of Mr. Harsdörffer. Drexelius, in his *Golden Mine* <note>original: "Aurifodina"</note>, calls this letter H a "breathable letter" on page 178, and a "breathing element" on page 180.

The ancients used H very sparingly, even in vowels, as when they said *ædos* and *ircos* <note>without the H, where we would expect "haedos" (goats) or "hircos" (he-goats)</note>. More on this from Mr. Dilherr in *Philological Apparatus*, page 63.

## 1. Goods and Estate. *Bona mobilia & immobilia*.

According to the common and established use of the mother tongue (which must be observed, and according to which words are to be understood), the term *Haab* <note>translated here as "Goods"</note> denotes "movable goods," while *Gut* <note>translated as "Estate"</note> denotes "the underlying ground" <note>immovable property or land</note>. Matthæus Wesenbec, part 5, counsel 209, number 75 and following.

### ADDITION.

All goods, even down to a hairpin <note>original: "aciculam capitis," a legal metaphor for total seizure of assets</note>. Rittershufius in *The New Constitutions*, page 233.

Thus, as a rule, the full amount can be sought and demanded from debtors. Carpzov, part 1, chapter 32, decision 15. Georg Acacius Enenkel in the *Treatise on Military Privileges*, book 1, privilege 19, number 1. A debtor may be shaken out down to the very last farthing <note>original: "quadrantem"</note>. Wesenbec on the Digest, *On the Ceding of Goods*, number 4; and there Mr. Ludwell speaks at length, as they say, "down to the pouch and the little bag." Hilling in *Donellus Unfolded*, chapter 27, letter P. Bachovius on the Institutes, book 4, title 6, and on the *Tractates*, volume 2, page 554, "to the last penny" <note>original: "obulum"</note>. Mevius on the *Laws of Lubeck*, book 1, title 3, article 1, number 24; nor should anything be left to him except his daily clothing with which he covers his body. Berlich, part 1, conclusion 80, number 50. The Laws of Lubeck agree with this, as reported and explained by Mevius, book 3, title 1, article 10. When a debtor dies who is notoriously insolvent, his remaining goods are inventoried by the creditors within six weeks of their knowledge of the death, and if it seems appropriate, they are sealed. If his widow has surviving children by him, she must afterwards ensure that guardians are appointed for them, and within six months she must vacate the house and the estate, retaining at least a modest tunic and cloak. And she must thus vacate the house, inheritance, and goods with a coat and a cloak <note>original: "Heucken," a traditional hooded cloak worn in the 16th and 17th centuries</note>, not the best, but not the worst. Besold, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

The word "has" or "to have" denotes **Ownership** <note>original: "Dominium"</note>. For a person is properly said to "have" that thing of which he has ownership. See the law *habere*, and the doctors of law there, in the Digest *On the Signification of Words*. This word is therefore to be understood with full effect. See the law *nomen filiarum*, at the end, in the Digest *On the Signification of Words*. Bertachinus in the *Repertory* under the word *habere*, number 16. Therefore it is handed down that one is properly said to "have" that thing over which he has both ownership and possession, but not that thing in respect to which he has only a legal action or even a rooted hope. Bartolus on the law *nemo vi dicitur*, Digest *On Restitution*. Cagnolus on the law *qui actionem*, Digest *On Rules of Law*.

Although the word "is held to be" <note>original: "habeatur"</note> may denote a fiction and not the truth; nevertheless, if the words "in all things and through all things" <note>original: "in omnibus & per omnia"</note> precede it, that word "shall be held" <note>German: "werde gehalten"</note> denotes the truth. This is a unique text in law 2, section *furiosus*, under the words "in all things," Digest *On the Law of Codicils*. Angelus on the law *in negotiis*, Digest *On Res Judicata*.

And so that a foreigner might enjoy the privilege of true citizens in court, the precaution is to use mixed words, namely: "he shall be held as and shall be" <note>German: "daß er Burger sey, und dafür gehalten werde"</note>. Bartolus on the law *is qui pro*, Digest *On Usucapion*, where he said: that those words, "held as a citizen," make a true citizen. However, regarding his original city, that is not called a true citizenship, but a fictional one. Corsetus in his singulars, letter H, under the word *habeatur*.

It must therefore be noted that for the word "shall be held" to imply the truth, it is necessary to add another phrase that denotes the truth, namely "in all things and through all things." This doubling of words induces a more effective result. Baldus in the *Authentica* "but when the testator," Code *On the Falcidian Law*, and in the law "neither births," Code *On Probations*. Johannes de Imola on the chapter "and if Christ," *On Oaths*, where he says: "Speech that is doubled is considered to be uttered with greater and more mature deliberation." See the gloss on the Clementines, *On Appeals*, and the text in the law "since we know," Code *On Farmers and Tax-Payers*. Also, those words "in all things and through all things" are exceedingly general, very pregnant with meaning, and exclude nothing. From the argument noted in the law *balista*, Digest *On the Trebellian Decree*, and the law "if a stranger," *On Dotal Law*.

### ADDITION.

The word "to have" <note>original: "habere"</note>, joined with the word "to possess," implies both civil and natural possession. Klock, volume 2, counsel 61, number 34.

One is not so much said to "have" who simply holds a thing, as is he who is the owner of the thing. Law *stipulatio ista* 38, section *habere* 9, Digest *On Verbal Obligations*. Regner Sixtinus, 3rd Marburg Counsel 7, number 3. To hold something in all parts, entirely unbroken and irrevocable <note>German: "In allen Stücken ganz unverbrochen, unwiderrufflich etwas halten"</note>. Limnaeus, book 4, chapter 8, page 178, on the words: "shall be held."

### 3. Hoers, Day Laborers, Sickle-Service, and Hand-Labor. *Operarii, Operæ manuariæ*.

Those who do not own a plow are bound to perform these types of manual labor <term>manual labor: services performed by hand rather than with oxen or horses</term>. Usually, a person who maintains a plow is considered to have more property and is therefore bound to double the obligation. Baptista Caesareus, in *Illustrious Counsels of the Juriconsults*, part 1, counsel 85, number 1. There, the question is asked whether nobles are bound to contribute equally with their peasant neighbors living in the village toward burdens in times of necessity, and specifically in the case of **the paying of the cavalry.** <note>original: "bey Erlägerung der Reuter," referring to the costs of quartering or funding mounted soldiers</note>

### ADDITION.

**Hand-labor** <note>original: "Handfrohnen," a form of feudal corvée labor</note> includes tasks such as **cutting grain, making hay, running messages,** or standing guard at the lord’s camp. Berlichius, *Conclusion 64*, number 4 and following. These tasks, which are carried out by hand, are called **Hand-labor** or **Hand-service,** and elsewhere **Day-work** or **Corvée-work.** Those who perform them are called **Hand-laborers, Cottagers, Wage-earners, Smallholders, or Cottars.** <note>original: "Handfröhner, Hintersiedler, Sölner, Krötener, Kotsassen," various historical terms for lower-class rural tenants with little to no land</note> Limnäus, book 6, chapter 4, number 15; Mundius, *On Burdens and Honors*, chapter 4, number 87.

### 4. Earnest Money, Engagement Gifts, and Hand-Pledges. *Arrha*.

Earnest money <note>original: "Arrha" or "Arrabo"; for this word see "Exotic Words of the New Testament," 414</note> is a gift given by the Groom and Bride to each other as a testimony and a kind of pledge of the future marriage promised between them. This earnest money is given and received not for the sake of simple generosity, but as a sign of good faith. Mozzius, in the *Treatise on Marriage*, section on accidents of marriage, number 1; Beust, *On Matrimonial Law*, part 1, chapter 6; Speckhan, *Century 3, question 10, class 1*; see also Wilhelm Anton, *On the Five-Year Period*, in the small corollary, leaf 15. Hence the common proverb: **"If the finger is ringed, the maiden is promised,"** etc. This has nothing in common with a dowry or a gift made specifically because of the wedding. When earnest money has been exchanged, a betrothal is presumed to exist. However, when a ring is given by a Priest or in his presence, then marriage itself is presumed. See the gloss on the chapter *Feminae*, 30th question, 5th section, under the word *annulus* (ring). Nevertheless, because the giving of earnest money can be interpreted in different ways, it proves nothing for certain unless the specific words spoken are known or the local custom is understood. Nonetheless, the legal presumption will favor a betrothal—not just because the law favors marriage, but because between such persons, a gift is not presumed to be a free and clear donation without further obligation. Albertus Gentilis discusses this extensively in *On Marriage*, book 2, chapter 26.

<column-break/>

This ring is usually placed on the finger next to the smallest on the left hand <note>the ring finger</note>, for the reasons passed down by Gellius in book 10, chapter 10, and Macrobius in *Saturnalia*, book 7. <note>Ancient authors believed a nerve or vein ran directly from this finger to the heart</note>

When this earnest money has been exchanged, if the one who gave it breaks the engagement, they lose the money. If, however, the one who received it breaks the engagement, they are forced not only to lose what they received but to return an equal amount from their own property; thus, they are held to a "double earnest" when they are over 25 years old. If they are a minor, they are only held to the amount they received, as the Emperor declares more fully in the Code, *On Betrothals*, law 5. **Earnest money** <note>original: "Hafftgeld"</note> is otherwise distinguished from a down payment on a price, because earnest money is not given after an interval of time.

Regarding when the penalty for losing earnest money ceases, see Beust, leaf 9.

It is the nature of earnest money that once a contract is fulfilled, it is turned into part of the payment; in the meantime, it serves as evidence that a contract was celebrated. See law *Fin.* under *De Lege Commissoria*. See also Hartwig Dassel, *Counsel 28*, book 1. Nor does giving these tokens mean the matter is no longer "entire" <note>meaning the contract can still be modified</note>, except when it is clear they were given as part of the price, in which case one cannot withdraw from the contract. Jalius, on the law *Ab Emptionem*, number 4, in the Digest *On Pacts*; add Martinus *On Clauses*, page 269. In the Digest *On the Contract of Purchase*, the jurist Gaius says: "What is often given as earnest money for a purchase does not mean that the agreement would be void without it, but rather that it can be more clearly proven that a price was agreed upon." See also Ludovicus Molina in the *Treatise on Justice and Law*, volume 2, treatise 2, dispute 338, number 2.

### ADDITION.

Earnest money proves a contract at least by a "good presumption" <term>good presumption: a legal assumption that holds true unless proven otherwise</term>. This is why a "sub-betrothal" <note>giving a ring as a secondary pledge</note> through an engagement ring does not itself create a betrothal, yet it proves that a contract was truly made. And the act of allowing a ring on a woman's finger is said to presume a marriage contracted by "words of the present" <term>words of the present: a binding vow of "I take you," rather than "I will take you"</term>, unless the contrary is proven. Matthew Coler, part 2, decision 30; Carpzov, part 4, constitution 4, definition 8; Barbosa, *Axioms*, book 1, chapter 80. On what earnest money is, see Cypraeus *On Betrothals*, page 400; it does not matter what material it is made of (page 404). On why rings are given in place of earnest money, see page 402; among the ancients, earnest money was never given in great value (page 407). Rings are more correctly given under the name of earnest money (page 404). For more on rings, see Eggebert Schaum of Frankfurt on the Oder in the *Treatise on Rings, their Law and Use*, published in 1620 by Georg Rittershusius.

Earnest money is not required for the substance of a purchase and sale. Mr. Biccius, in *Golden Selections*, section 4, thesis 86; on when it is permitted to withdraw under the loss of earnest money, see thesis 87; on what must be done with the earnest money once a contract is fulfilled, see thesis 88. The giving of earnest money...

### 5. Lifelong Bachelors. *Cœlibes*.

That bachelors were once treated with ignominy, and indeed with insult, can be seen in Gæddus, regarding the Law of Eunuchs, 128, in the Digest regarding the Meaning of Words; also in Plutarch’s *Life of Lycurgus*; and Johann Crug’s *Political College*, discourse 2, thesis 22. The Roman Censors Camillus and Posthumius ordered those who had reached old age as bachelors to pay a sum of money into the public treasury as a penalty. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 4. Furthermore, they could not inherit anything from the wills of fellow citizens, according to Sozomenus, book 1, chapter 9. This practice is even maintained in a certain district of the Palatinate called the **Odenwald**: there, those who have passed their 25th year and profess a life of celibacy are called **Hagestölzen** <note>original: "Hagestölzen," a term for confirmed bachelors with specific legal disadvantages</note>. Their property after death is surrendered to the treasury because they spent their years "empty of the names of husband and father," as reported from Schönborner’s *Politics*, book 1, chapter 6, by Mr. Hartmann Lather in *On Taxes*, book 3, chapter 3, number 38. However, Wehner understands this term differently here.

> How and in what manner the **Alberspach Monastery**, located in the Duchy of Württemberg, may inherit from the bachelors after their death, is made clear from the following.
> 
> Those persons are called **Hagestölz** who, whether they be men or maidens, remain in an unmarried state until the fiftieth year of their age; likewise a widower or widow who remains unchanged in the state of widowhood for thirty years.
> 
> And when such aforementioned men or maidens pass away unmarried after the expiration of fifty years, or likewise a widower or widow after the passing of thirty years in the state of widowhood, and leave no bodily heirs behind them, the Lordship of Alberspach inherits their **movable goods**, but not their **real estate**, unless it be their own property <note>i.e., allodial land</note>; for the fiefdoms belong to the feudal lord by right of ownership.
> 
> Even if such deceased persons left behind a father, mother, siblings, or other blood relatives in an ascending or descending line, they shall inherit nothing from the estate.

->ADDITION.<-

The right of succeeding to those who have spent their years "empty of the names of husband and father"—commonly called **Hagestölzen**—is well-documented in historical records. Because they neglected the duty of raising offspring, they were forced to pay penalties into the treasury and could take nothing from the wills of citizens; indeed, they were frequently marked with ignominy.

In the Landgraviate of Nellenburg, the treasury takes the property of the sons of priests and other illegitimate children, such as those born out of wedlock or bastards; in ancient times, these were also called **die Hagstölzen**. Adam Keller, *On Juridical-Political Office*, book 2, chapter 13, page 431.

Besold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

Regarding celibacy and men without children, Mr. G. Richter writes most beautifully in his *Letters*, page 410.

A **Hagenstölker** is so called because he "props up a cave" <note>original: "suffulciat antrum," likely a folk etymology or a reference to living in a small, solitary enclosure</note>. In the Odenwald, those over the age of 25 who are not in a marriage are called by this name. A **celibate** is one who does not have a wife, or a woman who does not have a husband, even if they do not live chastely. Hence Martial, in book 12, epigram 64, comparing a bad poet who recites his verses for free to a "bachelor adulterer," says:

> *The bachelor corrupts without fear of retaliation.* <note>original: "Corrumpit sine talione cœlebs."</note>

This is to say: just as a bachelor adulterer who seduces other men's wives cannot suffer the same injury in return from the husbands he has wronged (since he has no wife of his own), so I cannot pay back in kind the bad poet who ruins my verses by reciting them.

A person is also called "celibate" who remains in widowhood after losing a wife. Suetonius says of Galba in chapter 5: "Having lost his wife Lepida and two children by her, he remained in celibacy." And shortly after: "He had solicited Galba while he was still a husband, let alone when he was a bachelor." See more in Pacius, *Analysis of the Code*, page 974 and following. The Censors in the Roman Republic expressly forbade celibacy. Cicero, in his book *On the Laws*, notes that the Censors Camillus and Posthumius ordered elderly bachelors to pay a specific fine into the treasury; nor could bachelors receive anything from Roman wills. See Knipschild, *On Testamentary Trusts*, chapter 1, number 2. The Corinthians deprived bachelors of the honor of burial. The Spartans <note>original: "Lacones"</note> ordered them, by edict, to be stripped of their clothes in the middle of winter and walk through the marketplace. The Argives would not promote them to any offices. Among the Athenians, they were dragged around the altar on feast days and beaten with whips. Wendelinus, *Politics*, page 12. On whether one should marry, see Lipsius, *Selected Letters*, century 1, letter 31. In that part of the Odenwald belonging to the Palatinate, those over 25 and still single are called **Hagestölzen**, and their goods are confiscated after death for the reason that they "spent their years empty of the names of husband and father." See Mr. Dilherr, volume 1, *Disputations*, folio 526; Knipschild, *On Testamentary Trusts*, chapter 8, number 93; Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 4, number 82.

One should not listen to those who sing that line of Plautus: "He who can avoid women, let him avoid them, so that he daily takes care beforehand not to do what he might regret the day after." See my notes on that passage of Luther: **To rise early and to marry early, no one shall regret,** in the pamphlets titled *Early Love*. Among the ancients, the single state was held in such contempt that among the Greeks and Romans, bachelors were burdened with a certain annual tax, and no one could easily attain city offices unless he was married. Indeed, if all men were without wives, the whole world would die out in a hundred years. Mr. Harsdörffer, part 3 of his *Conversations*, pages 48, 59. The Legislator of the Spartans not only imposed a penalty on him who did not take a wife, but also...

In Egyptian law, it was established that every brave man should wear a "cantharon"—that is, a scarab engraved on a ring—because that animal was considered a <term>ἄθηλυ ζῶον</term> <note>original Greek: "athēly zōon," meaning an animal without females; ancient naturalists believed scarabs were all male and reproduced by rolling dung</note>, that is, a creature without females. Thus, it often happens that before the age of twelve, a child may have three or four marriages already arranged, hoping by this haste to prevent the King's tyranny. All these things may be read, proven by many witnesses and testimonies, in Arnisæus, *Political Lectures*, pages 623 to 635, and in *Political Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 9, page 194.

### 6. Holy. Sacred.

Xiphilinus calls the titles of Caesar, Emperor, and Augustus <term>ἱερὰ ὀνόματα</term> <note>original Greek: "hiera onomata," meaning holy or sacred names</note>. > The Fathers call things "Holy" (Sancta) and "August";
> We call the temples "August" when they are duly consecrated by the hand of Priests.

The origin of this word "August" descends from "augury," and refers to whatever Jupiter increases by his power.

### 10. Capital Jurisdiction. Pure Authority.

Whether there is a difference between the "Halsgericht" <term>Halsgericht: literally 'neck court,' the right to try capital crimes</term> and the "Blutbann" <term>Blutbann: the 'blood ban' or right of high justice</term>? Also, whether a nobleman who possesses all authority but lacks the outward signs/symbols may set them up for himself? See Bidembach, *On Noble Questions*, 14; Ludovicus Peguera, *Decision 81*; and my own work in the consultation joined to the end of the *Treatise on Jurisdiction*.

The word **Halsgericht** encompasses the entire "merum imperium" <term>merum imperium: the absolute legal power to command and punish, specifically regarding the death penalty</term>. Indeed, it includes both "merum" and "mixtum imperium" together, as Schneidewein teaches and testifies in *On Fiefs*, part 2, question 6, number 85. He says there: He who possesses the High and Capital Jurisdiction (Halsgericht) has the power of the Sword and the right to punish wicked men, so that he can investigate and judge all crimes, both public and private. These include the crimes of murder, adultery, forgery, incest, rape, arson, and theft. Regularly, he has the right to judge misconduct and evildoers that concern "skin and hair, body and life." From this, it follows that the investigation of "atrocious real injuries" also belongs to him: such as fighting wounds that are as deep as the middle finger and as long as its longest joint. Likewise, flesh wounds, wounds that chip the bone, or wounds through the skull or bones. Likewise "marks of shame," which include all...

Wounds below the face that hair can cover. <note>original German: "Wunden unter dem Angesicht, sodas Haar bedecken kan"</note> For when such wounds are inflicted with malice and on purpose, one can act both criminally and civilly. And this holds true even if the attachment in the investitures <note>legal documents granting land or rights to a vassal</note>—regarding the jurisdiction over blood <note>original: "Bann über das Blut zu richten," the power to pronounce death sentences</note> and the command of such a jurisdiction to a suitable official—were not present, which clause nonetheless thoroughly removes all doubts.

Furthermore, whoever has the **execution of criminal causes and sentences** usually also possesses the **cognition** <term>cognitio</term> <note>the formal legal examination or trial of a case</note> of the same, and vice versa: even if, in the grant of the jurisdiction over blood, it was not specifically mentioned. According to the rule in Law 2 of *On Jurisdiction* and Law 3, paragraph "what it has," of the Digest *On Rural Estates*. For to whomever the consequence was granted, every necessary antecedent must also be considered granted, and vice versa. Since one cannot reach the execution of a penalty unless a criminal trial has first been held and the criminal sentence pronounced. For **High Jurisdiction** <term>merum Imperium</term> <note>the total power of the sword; the authority to inflict capital punishment</note> is something whole and integral, of which **Criminal Jurisdiction** is a part. Therefore, because of this part, the whole itself will be judged to be of the same nature as the part. (Law 3, paragraph "in certain," Digest *On Acquiring Possession* and the Law "place" with the notes there). Baldus shows that this is to be noted in fiefs (in chapter 1, column 3, *On Agreements between Lords and Vassals*). But these rules fail by custom, as in Cologne, and likewise in the Imperial Chamber Court, where some have the trial and others the execution. Thus also in the past, **noblemen** in their villages captured criminals and sometimes tortured them, and thereafter brought them to other places where they or others held the high court, and there they were judged.

Longovallus also reports that **High Jurisdiction** encompasses every more serious coercion whatsoever, and all degrees of High Jurisdiction designated by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential 14th-century jurist</note>. He teaches that all cases concerning corporal punishment belong to High Jurisdiction. For whatever cases tend toward the punishment of criminals shall be judged under the name of High Jurisdiction.

Thus, all **Capital Crimes** <note>original: "Maleficia," crimes carrying penalties of life or limb</note> belong to **High Jurisdiction**, such as: all parricides, all homicides, all poisonings, all seditious persons, all who force women to abort a fetus already quickened <note>meaning a fetus that has begun to move in the womb</note>, all who lay hands on themselves <note>suicide</note> because of a guilty conscience, all sacrileges, all rapes of nuns or those having carnal knowledge of them, all incest (especially when joined with adultery), kidnappers of virgins, those harming divine and human majesty <note>treason or blasphemy</note>, public and notorious robbers and thieves, those manufacturing or knowingly spending counterfeit money, arsonists, raiders, assassins,

<column-break/>

all adulteries and sodomitical crimes, all who harbor robbers, embezzlers of public funds, pimping, those breaking a "false guard" <note>likely referring to the breach of a protective legal status or custody</note>, those publishing a defamatory libel to another's infamy, those preparing or administering harmful poisons, prison-breakers, those walking with a weapon for the purpose of killing a man, those giving false testimony, those administering a love potion, or those striking pregnant women to cause an abortion, those ordering, ratifying, or providing aid to homicide or the aforementioned crimes. (Chassanaeus, *On the Customs of Burgundy*, rubric 1).

Likewise, **condemnation to the mines**, the cutting off or mutilation of a limb—such as a hand, finger, or ear—and the deprivation of liberty. (Bolognetus on the law *Imperium*, numbers 39, 40, 60 and following).

For the **ultimate punishment** <note>the death penalty</note> and the mutilation or truncation of a limb are of the same degree. (Zasius on the law *Imperium*, number 12).

Likewise, **condemnation to perpetual imprisonment** belongs to High Jurisdiction. (Bolognetus and Cagnolus). Cagnolus says that those punished in this way lose the active and passive capacity to make a will. For perpetual imprisonment is compared to slavery, and perpetual imprisonment is an ultimate punishment. (Valascus). Indeed, even imprisonment for a time for the purpose of punishment belongs to High Jurisdiction, though of a lesser degree, because it is dispatched by the noble office of the judge for public utility and tends toward punishing. The same applies if it is done for the purpose of fining due to disobedience. (Bolognetus).

**Deportation** and **relegation to the galleys** <note>original: "triremes"</note> or into exile also pertain to High Jurisdiction, as Bolognetus maintains following the Doctors of Law. For he who cannot deport likewise cannot relegate, and a deported person is considered dead. (Cagnolus). For deportation is **civil death**. (Valascus). And to relegate is of the same power as to deport.

**Flogging** <note>original: "Fustigatio"</note> and all corporal coercion belong to High Jurisdiction, according to Bolognetus and Cagnolus, who says that flogging in noble persons is compared to capital punishment. For every punishment by which the body is sharply worn down or afflicted pertains to High Jurisdiction.

**Torture** likewise, whether imposed for punishment or for investigating and expressing the truth, belongs to High Jurisdiction. (Bolognetus, Cagnolus, Caccialupus, and Valascus).

Even **moderate coercion** of the body—such as when someone carries a stone (for instance, to places of scandal) <note>a common shaming punishment for slander or minor offenses</note> or is exposed to the crowd on a column <note>a pillory</note>—belongs to High Jurisdiction. (Zasius and Bolognetus).

Thus, the permanent removal from dignity, an ignominious discharge, and every cause imposing a mark of infamous punishment are counted under High Jurisdiction...

Valasc. n. 176. Zaf. num. 11. Bolognetus through l. licet. 103. ff. de V. S.*

To these, add excommunication, according to *Bolognetus, num. 79.* and in the same way, under the name of capital punishment, excommunication is also included. *Caccialup. num. 27.* where he says that, unless it is applied because of defiance <note>original: "contumaciam," legal stubbornness or failure to appear in court</note>, excommunication is of the same nature as the case in which it occurs. *Valasc. num. 179.* where he limits this statement, saying it does not apply if the excommunication is requested by a private party. *Bolognetus, n. 82.* holds that a monetary fine, even a light one, belongs to **High Jurisdiction** <term>merum Imperium</term> <note>The supreme power of the state to punish crimes with the sword or other penalties</note>, because it concerns legal punishment and is carried out by a noble office for the public benefit. Bolognetus thinks this is most true when the penalty is paid to the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>: because in that case, the cause is criminal, and a monetary fine is then equated to corporal punishment, according to the *gloss on law Lex Cornelia at the beginning, ff. on injuries.* and those things noted in *law venia. C. on summoning to court. Bartolus in the final law. ff. on private crimes.* which are supported by *Zaf. at the said law Imperium. n. 17.* saying that any fine, however light, which is imposed for the public good on account of crimes—even if it were only two gold pieces—belongs to High Jurisdiction.

Hence, the confiscation of goods also belongs only to him who has High Jurisdiction and the **Power of the Sword** <term>Gladii potestas</term>. *Bolognetus in l. Imperium num. 83. and Valascus, who says it belongs to the highest command, num 181.*

And since banished persons are equated to deported persons, according to *Valasc. n. 178.*, therefore the act of banishing belongs to him who has High Jurisdiction.

*Valascus, num. 138.* also refers the accusation of a suspicious and ungrateful man to High Jurisdiction. And since it belongs to the same person to absolve as it does to condemn: therefore, the absolution of those who are accused of crimes or have been captured belongs to no one else but the Lord of High Jurisdiction. *Bolognetus n. 149. Caccialup. n. 30. Valascus n. 64.*

Moreover, the laws and the Doctors of Law <note>original German: "Recht und Dd." referring to established legal scholars</note> hold that whoever has the power to exercise high authority in one degree also has the power and authority to exercise it in all other degrees belonging to high authority: because the substance of all degrees of High Jurisdiction is not different, but only the quality is different. And therefore, *Sapia* teaches at *l. Imperium, n. 55. & seq. ff. de Jurisd.* that all degrees belong at once to him who has exercised only one degree.

To have **High Criminal Jurisdiction** <note>original German/Latin: "Die Hohe Fraischliche Obrigkeit," 'Fraisch' refers to the terror of the high court or capital punishment</note> normally signifies nothing regarding religion: for it is a matter of clear law that he who has jurisdiction in criminal matters cannot be said to have absolute jurisdiction in all things, unless—God forbid—one were to proceed with fire and sword here in the Empire and other lands. Since, therefore, those over whom one has only the power of the sword cannot truly be called 

<column-break/>

subjects, he cannot use the benefit of the constitution toward them, since it is expressly provided therein that he who can use that benefit is "he to whom the subjects belong." <note>This refers to the "Cuius regio, eius religio" principle—the right of a ruler to determine the religion of his subjects.</note> *clause:* "No estate shall force another, nor the subjects of the same, to his religion." *see Richvvin. in form. mihi f. 211. n. 2.*

In some places, high authority regarding superior matters is restricted to certain cases: such as homicide, murder, arson, also robbery and theft where the thief (male or female) has stolen more than the value of ten guilders. The legal examination <term>cognitio</term> of other crimes, as well as the power of pardon, remains with the Vassal, excluding the execution where one is to be judged from life to death.

## ADDITION.

Jurisdiction is commonly divided into high or superior and low or inferior, so that **High Jurisdiction** <note>original German: "die hohe Obrigkeit, hohe Gericht, Blutban, Peinliche Gericht"</note>, including the Court of Blood and Criminal Courts, is considered to contain both pure and mixed power; and he who has this type of jurisdiction is judged to have both pure and mixed power at once. *Befold. de Jurisd. Imp. Rom. cap. 21. § part. 5. conf. 233. n. 34. Obrecht. de Jurisd. cap. 3. num. 27.* **Low or Inferior Jurisdiction** <note>original German: "die Nieder= oder Unter= Gerichtbarkeit"</note>. *Befold. de cap. 21. Knipschild. de fideic. cap. 10. n. 105.* In Nordhausen, the Council has the authority to exercise all command over the citizens, and all acts of High and Mixed Jurisdiction as well as simple jurisdiction; they maintain their own law and court servants, the jailer <note>original: "Stockmeister"</note> and the executioner <note>original: "Scharffrichter"</note>; they have the right of arrest, the stocks, and the tower; and when a punishable person is caught, they have him accused, answer, and argue before them, the Council; they also order judgments for torture, obtain and speak the verdict, and have the torture carried out by their military officers through the executioner. In that place, the Bailiff <term>Vogt</term>, the Count of Hohenstein, has nothing to do with it until the accused reaches the stage of execution. Then a letter is sent to the said Imperial Bailiff, and he is asked to send his judges from Clattenberg and let the **Neck-Court** <note>original: "Halsgericht," a court with the power to sentence to beheading</note> be hung. Before this, the Counts and the City were in dispute, because the Counts wanted to judge over "neck and hand" in the fields and countryside, etc. *Limn. in J. P. l. 7. cap. 38. n. 5.* Regarding the freedom of the city of Nuremberg over homicides, concerning hand and neck. *Limn. l. 7. c. 35. p 418.* What a **Criminal Complaint** <note>original: "Peinliche Klag"</note> is, *see Mr. Bicc. in Aur. p. 792.* The High Criminal Neck-Court. *Justus Oldekop, in two treatises against Carpzov. fol. 197. 198. 200.* Regarding the word "Criminal" <note>original: "Peinlich," related to 'pain' or 'penalty'</note>, should it refer only to afflictive bodily punishments, or is it truly extended to similar and lighter ones?

### 11. Hanseatic Cities. <term>Civitates Hanseaticæ</term>
<note>The Hanseatic League was a powerful medieval commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in Central and Northern Europe.</note>

I have discussed the Hanseatic Cities in my treatise *On Treaties*, and likewise in the treatise *On Ambassadors*, and also in the dissertation *On Imperial Cities* at the end. It is not my wish to repeat or transcribe those points here. One may also consult Werdenhagen in his individual treatise; Arumæus, *On the Assemblies*, Chapter 4, Number 130; the *Chronicle of Chronicles* by Gualtherus, Part 3, folio 494; and Pontanus, *Frankish Origins*, Book 2, Chapter 8. But as for what pertains to the etymology of this word, it should not be investigated too anxiously now: Since in Ratisbon <note>Regensburg</note> there is a magistrate who is called the **Hanse-Grave** <term>Hansgrav</term>, and who hears disputes concerning trade, etc. In this sense, "Hanse-Cities" would be nothing other than "Trading-Cities." For "Hansa" denotes a "Society" <note>original: "Societatem"</note>, such as merchants are frequently accustomed to enter. Marchant, *Description of Flanders*, Book 1, folio 23.

Indeed, some say **Henstætte**, as if cities of this kind took their name from "hens" <note>The author is likely dismissing a folk etymology linking the word to "Hennen" (chickens/hens).</note>.

And Lindemann, *On the Origins of Civil Law*, Thesis 3, thinks they are called "Anseatic Cities" as if they were "on the Sea" <note>German: "an d' See"</note> or "Hanse," as if belonging to the "Great Ones," as the Saxons used to call them, or **Prestigious Cities** <term>Ansehnliche Städte</term>. In the same way, the Princes of the Goths were called **Anses**, as if they were semi-gods. See the *Genealogy* by Scalichius.

Regarding the Hanseatic Cities, it is also pleasing to add what Hans Regkmann has in the *Lübeck Chronicle*, folio 35: In the year 1381, the entire German Hanse was gathered together at Lübeck and held a meeting. It happened, however, that the people of Braunschweig <note>Brunswick</note> had rebelled against their authorities, and had killed some of their Council, and banished others from the city; for this reason, they had been banished from the Hanse for eight years, so that they were not allowed to trade in any society of the Hanseatic Cities. They therefore sought grace and forgiveness before the delegates of the common Hanse-City at Lübeck. And that same event proceeded with a public confession, such that the delegates from Braunschweig had to go with bare heads

<column-break/>

and barefoot from St. Mary’s Church to the Town Hall, carrying burning candles in their hands, and fell on their knees before the Hanse-City, seeking forgiveness for their disobedience. And they were thus let back into the community of the Hanse, so that they might be equal to the other cities, and might have and use all privileges and jurisdictions in the four **Cantons** <term>Cantonen</term>: namely at Bruges in Flanders, at Bergen in Norway, at London in England, and at Novgorod in Russia.

From this history and example, it is to be noted that the alliance of the common Hanseatic Cities was undertaken not only for the sake of trade, but also to maintain common peace and unity, and good government, and obedience in all cities; for this reason, they also held such powers of punishment among themselves.

The same author, at folio 59, concerning the year 1447, reports a decree <note>original: "Abschied," a formal resolution of a diet</note> of the Hanseatic Cities regarding rebels, with the following content:
> Furthermore, the Cities have fully agreed that, whenever it is necessary and beneficial to renew the Hanse: if it should happen that in any Hanseatic City the Council is rendered powerless by its citizens, the new Council of that city shall be unworthy to sit in the Council of the other cities of the Hanse until such time as they have gained power over their citizens. The city shall be "un-hansed" <note>Original: "verhenset," meaning excluded or stripped of Hanseatic rights</note>, and their goods and their citizens shall be taken and judged according to Hanseatic Law. And the four cities lying nearest to that city shall announce this to the common cities, and also to the merchants wherever they are, so that they shall pursue and hold to this as prescribed, under the same penalty.

Regarding the justice of the Hanseatic Cities, see the *Jurisprudence of Republics*, Chapter 5.

...use a seal. Caspar Lerch of and in Dürnstein, part 1, *The Origin of the Imperial Knightly Nobility*, Principle 124, page 238. Höpingk, *On the Right of Seals*, chapter 4, section 5, number 119. The Hanseatic League <note>original: "Corpus Hanseaticum"</note> at one time consisted of 80 cities, indeed 108. In the year 1660, that vast Society was contracted to a few cities. In the beginning, it coalesced with no public authority; later, however, it was approved by the Princes under whom they were situated and confirmed by the Empire. Stökken, *On the Right of Embassies*, thesis 2, letter d.

### 12. Ham, Hamburg. <term>Hamburgum</term>.

*Ham* is an old Saxon word meaning a grove or a woods. Thus, in Dithmarschen, you will find two groves, one called *Suderham* <note>South-grove</note> and the other *Norderham* <note>North-grove</note>.

To the Frisians, a *Ham* is a pasture field or a meadow surrounded by a small ditch. And from this, the most flourishing city of Hamburg drew its name—not from the "Gambrivii" <note>An ancient Germanic tribe</note> as certain learned men suppose, nor from Hammon Jupiter, nor from Hama the fighter, as Cranzius asserts; nor even from salted hams <note>original: "pernis salitis"</note>, as Goropius Becanus dreams, but from the forest *Ham*, near which the city began to be built. See Werdenhagen, *On the Hanseatic Republic*, part 3, folio 78.

That the City of Hamburg is a State of the Empire, and that it is considered a State in the decrees of the Imperial Chamber Court, is attested by Richvvin in his *Forms*, folio 129, number 1. See Cranzius regarding the judgment of Charles IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1346–1378</note>, stating it is of a "mixed status."

->ADDITION.<-

On the word *Ham*, the origin of the City of Hamburg, and the noble family "von Hamme," see Saubertus, *On Sacrifices*, page 328 and following. In Hamburg, there is the Guest House <note>Hospital</note>, the Orphanage, the House of Correction, the Plague House, and the Smallpox House.

The word *Ham* signifies a forest or grove, a **Forest** <note>original: "Forst"</note>, because formerly a forest between the Alster and Bille rivers, called Ham, was located there. Other places are also called by this name, such as *Ham* in Holland, *Ham* in Westphalia, and *Ham* in Frisia. The people of Dithmarschen call a willow-plot or a meadow a *Ham*. Others trace the origin to Hama, a distinguished and vigorous soldier. Münster, Book 3 of his *Cosmography*, chapter 444, page 1008. Johannes Georgius Becanus, who rejects both Hammon and Hama in Book 6 of *Antwerp Antiquities*, page 661, derives it from *Ham*, that is, from salted hams. For he says there was once a very famous market here for salted goods and smoked pork. Limnäus, in *Public Law*, Book 7, chapter 23, numbers 2 and 3. The City of Hamburg, together with the University of the Duchy to which it is attached, was always accustomed to be granted in fief to the Duke of Holstein, to whom it performed homage in former times and even continues to do so today. Hotman proves the same from Cranzius in *Feudal Disputes*, chapter 24. However, since the Princes of Holstein attempted many years ago to appropriate that city for themselves as if it were simply subject and purely provincial, and tried to exercise sovereignty there, Charles IV settled this dispute in Lübeck, as Cranzius in Book 10, chapter 2 re-

<column-break/>

counts: he ordered Hamburg to obey the Counts (for such they were then, who today are Dukes of Holstein), saving the liberties which they merited from the Imperial height. This is nothing other than if he had said that the City, regarding its immunities, liberties, and privileges, is immediately subject to the Empire <note>This refers to "Imperial Immediacy," meaning the city answered directly to the Emperor rather than a local prince</note>: and in respect to these, the Prince can command nothing from them. Hence, it truly ought not to be called fully subject to him. Besold, *On Politics*, Book 2, chapter 12, number 70, volume 2.

### 13. Merchant Ledgers. <term>Libri mercatorum</term>.

Since accountings are made by merchants by reason of their office (and he is called a Merchant who carries on trade by buying and selling, according to the laws), it is not unfittingly asked whether full credit is regularly given to their books and accounts in favor of the one writing them? See Nicolaus Janua, *On Private Writings*, Book 4, folio 845 and following; and Bolognetus on Law 1 of the Code *On Producing Documents*.

And whether the merchants of our time are bound to produce their books of accounts to establish the intention of another party, namely the plaintiff: see by all means Janua at the cited place, folio 865 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

The **Merchant Ledgers** <note>original: "Handelsbücher"</note> of merchants provide "half-full proof" <note>original: "semiplenam probationem"; a legal term meaning the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive on its own</note>, and the full proof can be completed with a "supplementary oath" <note>An oath taken by a party to "top up" incomplete evidence</note>. Suttinger, Observation 73, throughout. On what is required for a merchant’s book to provide half-full proof, see number 4. Schvvarzenthaler, in the treatise *On Stipulations*, number 38, attests that the aforementioned custom flourishes in Austria.

Regarding the Registers of Merchants, commonly called *Handelsbücher*, and whether and to what extent they provide evidence for the writer, see Gail, Book 2, Observation 20. Treutler, volume 2, dispute 5, thesis 1, letter f. Furthermore, the Doctors of Law have introduced many unique rules regarding merchants, about which almost nothing exists in our Roman law. Rittershusius, in the *Novels*, page 627. Giphanius, at folio 347, equates merchant ledgers to public writings. The books of merchants, even if they are bankrupt, prove a fact between other persons. *Decisions of the Rota of Genoa*, decision 10, number 6. Credit is not given to a book of sketches or memos <note>original: "rachetæ sive memorialium"</note>, even if some entries are verified. Ludovicus, *Decisions of Lucca*, 42, number 35. A book of relative entries ought not to be believed. Ludovicus, *Decisions of Lucca*, 42, number 38. The statute that merchant books should be believed is restricted only to those things which pertain to a mercantile cause. Cravetta, *On Antiquity*, part 1, section 9, number 8. One stands by the merchant’s book if the question is only about the quantity. Cravetta, same section, number 9. On the proof of books and registers of merchants and craftsmen, see König, *On Procedure*, part 3, chapter 28. Wesenbeck, Counsel 36, numbers 8 and 23. Vivius, Opinion 806. Diaz, Rule 138. If the sum is small, the books of merchants deserve full credit. Cothm.
