### 14. To remove hand and foot. <term>Restitution of the thing and possession</term>.

To remove hand and foot <note>original: "Hand und Fuß abthun"</note> is the same as to make restitution of a thing and its possession, according to Kulando in *On Emphyteusis* <note>a type of long-term land lease</note>, folio 75.

->ADDITION.<-

Chiromancy <note>palm reading</note> and Chiroscopy <note>observation of the hand</note> are not proven by the Book of Job. Mr. Dilherr, volume 1, Disputation, folio 762 and following. **Regarding the interpretation of the hand**, John Bulwer, an Englishman, has written an entire book <note>referring to *Chirologia: or the Natural Language of the Hand*, 1644</note>. **Ulna** means the arms. **To sleep in the arm of the Father** <note>original: "In ulna Patris dormire"</note> means to be carried in maternal arms. The **Ulna** <note>an ell</note> is a measurement of the extension of both hands or the forearm, as noted by Servius. Caspar Barth, *Observations on Papinius Statius's 10th Thebaid*, page 1201. The words **to step away** <note>original: "abtretten"</note> and **to remove the hand** <note>original: "Hand abthun"</note> presuppose a previous possession, which no one can give up unless they once held it. Klock, volume 2, counsel 39, number 150. These words, **to remove hand and foot**, specifically from lands or estates that do not belong to oneself, include not only the restitution of the object itself but also the possession of it, and even more so. ### 16. Hand-peace. <term>Manual peace</term>.

Manual peace, or *handfried*, is so called because it is immune from violence, just like a "hand-taken deed" <note>original: "handhafte That," referring to a person caught "red-handed" in a flagrant crime</note>, because the hand denotes violence. ### 17. Hand-kissing. <term>The kissing of the hand</term>.

Plutarch records that when Cato was departing from his Province, the soldiers reverently kissed his hand. This kind of honor, he says, was granted only to Commanders, and to very few at that time. It is clear from this that the ceremony of kissing is very ancient. Manutius writes further on this in book 10 of *Various Readings*, chapter 1: "Since it is common practice today when greeting powerful people or showing them honor that we move our own hand to our mouth, I have asked whether this was also practiced by the ancients, or if, like most other things, this foolish kind of flattery was devised by the servile minds of modern courtiers?" I responded that this custom seems to have been derived and propagated from that very ridiculous superstition of the ancients who worshipped many gods. For they were accustomed, when they passed a temple or saw some wood or stone in which they thought there was something divine, to bring their hand to their mouth and with a thin murmur pray to those wooden and stony gods to favor them.

Others derive this custom from elsewhere, namely from the Turks. For when Turkish princes treat each other with mutual reverence, they are accustomed to press their lip three times with a finger; from them, these common kissings of the hands spread to the Spaniards, Italians, and French, and now even to the Germans—as it is easier to imitate these follies than virtues. Martin, *Ethical Disputations* 10, question 12, at the end.

->ADDITION.<-

Soldiers kissed the hands of the Emperors. Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book 4, chapter 3, page 118. Others touched the hand of a Prince as a sign of security: *It shall be my part of peace to have touched the right hand of the tyrant.*

Angelus, as a witness for himself on the law regarding greetings in the Code on sentences, says he was always admitted by the Supreme Pontiff not to the kissing of the feet, but to the kissing of the hand. Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, book 8, chapter 8, number 117. **Osculology** <note>the study of kisses</note> was written by Jacob Herrnschmid, Chief Priest of the Church of Nördlingen, and by Georg Rittershusius in a discourse on kisses published in Frankfurt an der Oder in the year 1621.

On the custom of kissing the hands of Emperors and Great Men, see among others Gothofredus on law 16 regarding gifts before marriage; law 12 and 17 on domestics and protectors. Salmasius in his *Notes on Vopiscus*, page 440, where he wrongly criticizes Lipsius for writing that those worshipping were accustomed to first extend the hand and then immediately bring it to the mouth; for it was done the opposite way, since in different times and in different acts, different things were pleasing. Lipsius, *Electra*, book 2, chapter 6. Muretus, *Various Readings*, book 10, chapter 1. *The Prince's Clock*, book 1, chapter 38. Olearius in his *New Oriental Travel Description*—

# Treasuries of Practical Knowledge, Augmented.

...renounced the right, but he still retains the right to demand the full **transfer fee** <note>original: "Laudemium"; a fee paid by a tenant to a lord when a lease is transferred</note>, unless he has expressly gifted it. Surdus *decision 200, number 6.* Knichen, *On Clothed Pacts, part 2, chapter 4, number 195.* Bursat, *counsel 137, number 24, etc.* Consult Ziegler in the *previously cited place, number 247 and following,* where at number 284 he says that those who believe that a transfer fee not yet collected should be counted among the "pending fruits" <note>unharvested profits of the land</note> are correct. Surdus, *counsel 84, number 4, volume 1,* and after him Johann Baptist Costa, *On Retraction, chapter 8, case 11, number 5.* And so, if the **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis: a heritable lease where the tenant improves the land</term> belongs <term>to a parish</term> <note>original German: "zu einer Pfarr"</note>, that uncollected fee is not passed on to the heirs, but goes to the person who succeeds to the [church] office.

The burden of the transfer fee also applies in acquisitions by will, such as if a stranger (one not arriving from the descending family line) is appointed as heir and acquires the leased land, or if the leased property falls to him by title of a legacy or a trust. Saliceto on *the final law, number 11, Code on the law of emphyteusis.* Amadeus de Ponte, *On the Transfer Fee, question 31.*

For if the lease has passed by succession to the children, the payment of the transfer fee cannot be demanded from them, because they are said to be included in the first **investiture** <note>the formal act of granting the lease</note>: as Jason held on *the final law, number 41, where* Saliceto, *Code on the law of emphyteusis.* Amadeus de Ponte, *On the Transfer Fee, question 19.* Coler, *decision 33, number 31.* This is because they do not acquire the lease anew, but continue what was previously acquired; namely, they already held the same **beneficial ownership** <note>dominium utile: the right to use and profit from the land</note> as their father. *Law "in suis" 11, Digest on children and posthumous heirs; the last law, Code on the disenfranchised, and others following.* Knichen, *On Clothed Pacts, part 2, chapter 4, number 58.* Matthäus Wesenbeck, *counsel 16, number 13, volume 1.* However, this fails in the case of those who were not included in the first investiture, or who are "stranger" heirs, in whom the ownership is not continued by law through succession. Saliceto and Jason in the *cited places.* And this must be particularly noted, even though in many places custom dictates that even children are compelled to pay the transfer fee anew.

Likewise, if a lease is given by a father to a daughter as a **dowry**, whether estimated or unestimated in value, the Lord cannot demand a transfer fee, because it is a "necessary alienation" <note>a transfer required by social or legal duty</note>: for a father is required to provide a dowry for his daughter. *Law "qui liberos" 19, Digest on the rite of marriages.* Jason on *the final law, number 49, Code on the law of emphyteusis.* Cravetta supports this decision in *counsel 213,* adding another reason: the transfer fee is not to be paid when the new tenant was included in the first investiture; and a daughter is included in that case when the lease was given to the father and his children as heirs.

When a **corporation** <term>univerisitas: a legal body or community</term> is once invested with a lease and pays the transfer fee once, since it is not said to "die," its successors are not compelled to pay the transfer fee. Albertus Brunus, *counsel 44, number 12.*

A transfer fee is not owed to a new successor when the Lord of the lease dies, or if he, while alive, sells the tenants. This 

<column-break/>

was established for that case when a new *tenant* is introduced. *Final law, Code on the law of emphyteusis.* And that is for the reception or investiture, which is not broken when the one granting it dies or is changed. *Argued from chapter 1, those who hold succession, and chapter 1, if invested with another's property.*

But concerning the transfer fee, see the individual treatises of Georg Franzke, Amadeus de Ponte, and Laudensis; add Acacius Antonio Ripoli, *Various Legal Resolutions, chapter 7.*

->ADDITION.<-

**Transfer fee** <note>original: "Laudemium"</note> is a barbarous word and unknown to Latin writers.

*Laudemia* in the feminine gender appears in Wesenbeck, *counsel 16, part 1.* The verb *Laudare* [to praise/name] enjoys many meanings, such that it is the same as to extol with words, as in Virgil, *Book 2 of the Georgics*: "praise the vast fields" <note>original: "laudato ingentia rura"</note>, meaning to name them. Likewise in the same work: "who does not know the altars of the unpraised Busiris," <note>original: "illaudati... Busiridis"</note> that is, one who should not even be named. *Law 6, section 5, Digest on the action of purchase.* Plautus, *in The Captives, act 2, scene 3.* What it means to "praise" or name an Author is explained by Mr. Biccius in the *Golden Sections, section 5, thesis 102.* Usually, however, it means to approve by word, writing, or by the deed itself. Hence Cicero in his *Oration for Sextius*: "Pompey approved and praised the opinion of Cotta." Amadeus de Ponte of Lombriasco, *Questions on the Transfer Fee, 2.* To "praise" among the **Feudalists** <note>scholars of feudal law</note> is to arbitrate or judge. Rittershusius in *Feudal Divisions, pages 467, 538.* To "praise" can mean to establish by common counsel and consent. Franzke, *On the Transfer Fee, chapter 1, numbers 12, 13, 14.* Alciatus prefers it to be called *Laudativum* in his *Parerga*, because it is more Latin, just as *donativum* comes from *donando* [giving]. Giphanius, *Introduction to Feudal Law, chapter 2, final number,* thinks it can be called an *arbitrium* [judgment] in Latin, moved by Cicero’s *Oration against Piso*, with whom Calvin agrees in his *Lexicon of Feudal Words*, using the word *lauda* in place of a passage in Justin, *Book 11, chapter 12, number 4*: "Alexander wrote back that his things should be given to him, and ordered the suppliant to come and permit the judgments [arbitria] of the kingdom to the victor." *The same, Book 22, chapter 2, number 5.* More elegantly and truly it can be called an **Entrance Fee** <note>original: "Introitus"</note>, as it is in Pliny, *Book 10, Epistle 113*: "all who are thereafter chosen as <term>admitted members</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐιλευτοι" (eileutoi)</note> must give a certain amount as an entrance fee." *Second to last law, section "alumno," Digest on legacies, 3.* Suetonius, *in Claudius.* It is also called a **relief** <term>relevium</term>, Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 8, thesis 8, letter C,* because by being provided it "relieves" the one to whom it is paid, and it is paid to one in need; but this word is almost exclusively used in feudal matters. Rosenthal, *On Feuds, chapter 6, conclusion 66, number 1.* The Swabians call the transfer fee <term>Handlohn</term> <note>German: "hand-wage"</note>; it is perhaps named from the act of signing <term>Weglösin</term> <note>German: "redemption/clearance"</note>; others call it <term>Lehnwahr</term> <note>German: "fief-protection"</note>, <term>Lehengeld</term> <note>German: "fief-money"</note>; in Alsace <term>Ehrischaß</term> <note>German: "honor-tax"</note>; in Bavaria <term>Anleuth</term> <note>German: "admission"</note>, <term>Ergöhung</term> <note>German: "gratification"</note>, <term>Ehrschaß</term>. The Emperor Leo in *Novel 13* calls it an <term>entry fee</term> <note>original Greek: "εισδευτικον" (eisdeutikon)</note>, see Pacius in *Analysis of the Code, page 429.* Franciscus Solsona in *The Lamp of the Transfer Fee* uses barbarous terms: <term>Foriscapium</term>, <term>adduamenta</term>, <term>adhoa</term>, <term>capsoldi</term>, <term>Anata</term>, <term>Servitium bursale</term> (Jacob de Ayellis wrote a *Treatise on the Adhoa*), <term>Acapita</term>, <term>Vassatium</term>, and **the golden pen** <term>penna aurea</term>. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of property transfer fees (laudemia), specifically focusing on whether these rights can be lost over time through neglect or legal prescription. # Letter H

*Franzkius on transfer fees, chapter 1, number 21. Master Doctor Tabor on Emphasis, thesis 60.* Things that are customarily given for the sake of honor or recognition—such as **transfer fees** <term>laudemia: fees paid by a tenant to a lord when a lease is transferred to a new person</term> and **sales taxes** <note>original: "ventæ"</note>, as they are called—belong to the person entitled to the profits of the land. *Guido Papa, decision 477.* The **small transfer fee** <note>original German: "kleinen Handlohn"</note>, which amounts to only a quarter, is mentioned in the settlement between *Eichstätt* and *Nuremberg* in the year 1613. For example, the **provost** <note>original: "P. V." likely Praepositus Vicedominus</note> took 20 florins for a penalty and transfer fee because a mother in *V.* had transferred her small estate to her son. In the same year, when a widow there remarried, he took 7 florins. Thus, some take transfer fees for death or marriage, whether the hand [the person holding the property] is dead, purchased, gifted, or bound. Whether a widow is bound to give a new **relief fee** <note>original: "relevium"; a payment to a lord to "take up" a deceased relative's lease</note> upon the death of her husband? See *Molinæus on the Customs of Paris, folio 222.* At *Q.* there are three estates held as fiefs from the Cathedral Provostry of *Bamberg* that pay no transfer fees, because it is a **bailiwick tax** <note>original German: "Vogtey Gült"; a specific type of administrative tax rather than a feudal lease fee</note>. Freedom from paying a transfer fee is recognized through the **prescription of time** <note>the legal principle where a right is gained or lost due to the passage of time</note>. However, jurists hold that this prescription occurs if the Lord has invested a new **long-term tenant** <term>emphyteuta: a tenant under a heritable lease who must improve the land</term> without any reservation of the transfer fee, and thereafter has received the **annual rent** <note>original: "canon"</note> from the same person for 30 continuous years, never making mention of the debt for the transfer fee. *Johann Baptist Costa on Retraction, chapter 8, case 11, numbers 11 & 13.* *Papon* testifies in *book 12, title 3* that this opinion has even prevailed against the Church. *A. Faber in his Code on the Law of Emphyteusis, definition 53. Guido Papa, decision 161, number 2.* But in truth, no one is judged to have surrendered their right, since a gift is not presumed (*Law 25, On Proofs*), and because **investiture** <note>the formal ceremony of granting a lease</note> is not the kind of act that cancels a claim or is contrary to it. (*Law 6, Law 7, On the Commisory Clause*). See *Suevius on transfer fees, chapter 2.* And they wish for this to hold much more strongly in the case of **immemorial prescription** <note>a period of time so long that no living person remembers its beginning</note>, which on account of its age obtains the force of law (*Laws 1 & final, Digest on keeping off rainwater*) and stands in place of a statute (*Law on this right, section on conducting water, Digest on daily and summer water*) and serves as the truth, as *Baldus* teaches (*on Law 1, in the 3rd note, Code on services and water*), *Innocent* (*on chapter 2, On total restitution*), and *Felinus* (*on chapter "Accedentes," column 2, On prescription*). It supplies every defect and makes firm and valid that which is otherwise void, null, and invalid. *Baldus on Law 1, Code on the status of the deceased. Balbus on prescription, part 1, question 6, number 8.* For then, if the **direct lords** <term>domini directi: the ultimate owners of the property title</term> have many times registered new tenants without a request for any transfer fee, and have accepted simple rents from them, issuing **receipts** <note>original: "apochas"</note> in the best form, the Doctors of Law say they have lost their acquired right. And they extend this not only to past rewards (that is, **transfer fees on expired honors** <note>original German: "Laudemia auf die verfallene Ehrschäß"</note>) but they also stretch it to future ones, or toward the extinction of the right in its entirety, according to the common legal proverb: *The negligence of those who came before excludes the claim of those who follow,* which *Bartolus* with his citations emphasizes (*on Law on the ward, section "if in many places," 16, On notification of a new work, number 2, version "if negligence"*); *Tuscus* does somewhat the same (*conclusion 11, number 34, at the end*). And this is much 

<column-break/>

more the case if a frequency and plurality of acts or sales has intervened. (When an **estate subject to transfer fees** <note>original German: "Ehrschäßig Gut"</note> has already passed through five or six hands) beyond the just interval of time, within which, though the thing was alienated several times, nothing was paid to the Lord. *Panormitanus on the chapter "To the audience" on prescription, number 17,* whom *Franzkius* cites and does not reject (*on transfer fees, last chapter, number 17*). Those who deny that the right to a transfer fee can be lost by prescription bring forward this reason: that the matter is one of **mere faculty** <note>a discretionary power or optional right that doesn't expire just because it isn't used</note>, which in any case can be demanded or not (*Law 2, Digest on public roads*). *Francesco Balbus on prescription, part 4, part 5, first question, begins "I take a fourth part," number 1 and following. Wesenbeck on the title On Usurpations, number 10. Also Consultation 2, number 47. Gail, book 2, observation 18.* This is because it is a matter of free choice or will, against which prescription does not run, and because possession (or quasi-possession) cannot be acquired from acts of mere will. (*Law of Proculus, Digest on threatened damage; Law 1; and finally Law "if in mine," Digest on keeping off rainwater.*)

They take a second reason from *Law 2, Code on the prescription of 30 or 40 years.* They urge a third reason because it is an established law that whenever a long-term tenant reaches the point where he wishes to call the ownership of his direct Lord into question, he loses that right entirely. *Julius Clarus in the section on Emphyteusis, question 25. Amadeus à Ponte, question 50. Corbus, book on the Law of Emphyteusis, chapter 1, number 2.* One must distinguish between the transfer fee taken **materially** (that is, the profit or price that could be demanded from each individual act of sale) and the transfer fee accepted **formally**, for the Right itself of demanding that one-fiftieth part. In this way, the transfer fees themselves (that is, the money to be paid on each occasion) are indeed lost by prescription after 30 years, and thus the past benefit is lost; however, the **right to the transfer fee** <note>original: "jus Laudemiale"</note> is not—that is, the power to demand a transfer fee in the future when a case of sale arises. This is because that right is one of mere faculty, and therefore cannot be lost by prescription. This is especially true when claimed by the possessor against the Lord (*Law 2, Code on the prescription of 30 or 40 years*), and because nothing more can be lost by prescription than what was actually possessed (*Law 1, section "if anyone in service," Digest on private paths and drives*). Finally, since the laws of prescription are **odious** <note>in legal terms, "odious" means they restrict rights or are unfavorable, and thus should be interpreted narrowly</note>, they are not to be rashly extended. (*Chapter "lest some," On privileges, in the Sixth Book of Decretals.*) It is otherwise regarding the actual collection and profit of this right, the neglect of which is surely lost by a prescription of 30 years, like other rights. Nor does that axiom—which is frequently on the lips and pens of the practicing lawyers—overturn this distinction: namely, that "the negligence of those who came before excludes the claim of those who follow." For this rule applies when that preceding act stands as a cause to the following ones, not when it has another and different cause, as *Bartolus* himself and his commentator *Alexander* noted in the same place. Hence, a sale that was celebrated within 30 years (even if others preceded it) is not excluded, but the transfer fee for it can be demanded even in the 20th year. When I agreed with this opinion in previous years, specifically regarding a certain garden with houses attached to it,

### Treasury of Practical Law, Augmented

situated outside the walls of this city, which annually **pays two florins in coarse coin as ownership rent** <note>original German: "in grober Münz zu Eigenzinß zinset"</note>, from a new and indeed most noble **hereditary leaseholder** <term>emphyteuta: a tenant who holds a long-term or perpetual lease of land, often requiring improvement of the property</term>. As the **direct lord** <term>dominus directus: the legal owner of the land who retains ultimate title while another has the right of use</term>, I would demand the **transfer fee** <term>laudemium: a fee paid to a lord when a leasehold property changes hands</term> by the highest legal right, following the division made among co-heirs regarding the portions received, according to the Nuremberg Reformation, title 23, law 13, final paragraph. **If an ancestral estate in the country is transferred through purchase, inheritance, etc., the portion taken up** <note>original German: "So ein Erbgut auf dem Land durch Kauff, Erbfall, &c. soll der angenommen Theil"</note> should be subject to the fee. 

In part, the **prescription of a long period of time** <note>a legal claim that a right is lost or gained due to the passage of time</note> and a plurality of acts (though not yet proven) was alleged against me as a reason for no fee being paid; in part, it was argued that this contract is rent-based, and consequently without a transfer fee (see Master Bicc. in *Golden Section 2, thesis 45*). But the small word **"ownership rent"** <note>original German: "Eigenzinß"</note> argued against this, which the opposing party claimed in vain was placed there improperly. 

Further opposition came from Berlichius (2, conclusion 47) and Zorer (part 1, question 11, number 793), regarding what some assert: **"the hen carries the transfer fee on its tail"** <note>original German: "die Hennen trägt das Handlohn auf dem Schwanz"; a legal proverb suggesting that the payment of a small annual tribute, like a chicken, implies a larger transfer fee is owed upon sale</note>. That rule indeed holds true generally, yet it suffers many exceptions, as there are certain estates for which a hen must be given annually, yet no transfer fee is to be paid. 

Furthermore, I myself possess a meadow for which the leaseholder pays annually **a measure of oats** <note>original German: "ein Summer Habern"</note> and a transfer fee in cases of alienation, yet he does not give a hen. Moreover, because hens in former times cost only a few coins or small pennies, easy and credulous antiquity sometimes waived them, and sometimes sought them as a reminder of the transfer fee. Concerning this, I will speak at another time. 

What if, after a contract of purchase and sale is completed—and thus the matter is no longer "untouched"—the parties soon regret it and withdraw from the contract? Nevertheless, the transfer fee must be provided, as Hartmann Pistor teaches (question 50, number 13). He declares in the following number 14 when a matter is said to be no longer "untouched." In this case, according to the customary law of various places, the amount of the transfer fees varies considerably; and therefore it must be sought from the customs of each nation, as Argentræus advises (concerning transfer fees, chapter 5). 

This quantity is different under the law of **Saxony, Thuringia, and Franconia**—namely, the 20th part of the price (Klock, *On the Treasury*, 2, chapter 42). Another rate is observed in Mantua, Ferrara, and in certain places in the Duchy of **Prussia**, where the amount of the transfer fee is the 10th part of the price. By the customs and statutes of **Nuremberg**, it is the 15th part—6 florins and 40 cruciferi for every hundred—**Ownership lord and so the** <note>original German: "Eigen Herr und so der"; citing Nuremberg Statute title 23, law 13</note>. I myself have seen that for one and the same field, the transfer fee was not paid uniformly; sometimes it was by agreement (very cheap), sometimes a 10th part, and sometimes a 15th part. There is even a case where, in place of a transfer fee for a meadow, **a sugar loaf** <note>original German: "ein Zuckerhut"</note> was offered. **What must be observed regarding such deformity, see** Berlichius, decision 74. There is no concealment or delay for transfer fees that are not owed. Although free heirs may be bound by custom to perform the transfer fee for succession, it is not permitted to seek it from individuals after a division, nor when the person of the Lord has changed, unless this is specifically proven to be

<column-break/>

introduced by custom (Carpzov, book 1, title 9, response 88). If heirs divide the property among themselves and attribute the leasehold property entirely to one person, they are bound to notify the lord and pay him the transfer fee for the portion that belonged to the others. In respect to those others, this division constitutes an **alienation** <note>the legal transfer of property to another</note> for their parts, just like a sale, to which this division is compared. 

A buyer who lies to the Lord about the true price in order to pay less of a transfer fee, or to subvert the Lord's right to retain the property by **right of first refusal** <term>prælatio: the right of a lord to buy back the leasehold himself if the tenant intends to sell it</term>, loses the estate (see Jean Papon in *Customs of Bourbon*, folio 352; Zorer, part 1, question 11, number 768). Whether transfer fees are owed on the total price if movable items are sold together with a house or land, see the elegant decision of Boërius (229). **How seeds or standing fruit are to be valued, and whether they are also subject to transfer fees, see** Nuremberg Statute (book 4, title 11, section **"The Grain"** <note>original German: "das Getraid"</note>). 

If a leasehold estate is among the goods of a **fideicommissum** <term>fideicommissum: property held in trust for another, often to keep it within a family</term>, and it is alienated, the **usufructuary** <term>usufructuary: someone who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it</term> gains the transfer fee. More on transfer fees can be found in Zorer, Hartmann Pistor, Jacobus de Ayello, and Henry von Miltitz, a Knight of Meissen, in a dispute held at Strasbourg in 1643. Whether in sudden changes within a year one or multiple **relief fees** <note>original: "relevium"</note> are owed, see Zorer (part 1, question 11, number 784). See also below under the word **"Fief-warantee"** <note>original German: "Lehenwahr"</note>.

### 19. Handmal. Judicial site or mark.

In the glosses to article 33 of the **Municipal Code** <note>original: "Weichbild"; a collection of medieval German laws</note>, it is held that **Handmal** is nothing other than **the place of the court where one is a juror; it is called Handmal because he or his parents have sworn with their hand upon the holy relics, and because he still has his hand-sign on the judge's chair** <note>original German: "dann die Statt des Gerichts, da einer ein Schöpff zu ist, und heißt darum Handmal, daß er oder seine Eltern mit der Hand auf den Heiligen geschworen haben, und daß er noch sein Handzeichen hab an dem Schöpffenstuhl"</note>. Gryphia notes that **Handmahl** is a convenient and proper place of judgment, as if one had sworn with his own hand in that place to obey the law. Hence the phrase **"to prove Handmahl"** is used for **"to prove one's origin or descent."**

Book H.
Catchword: 4. C.

...are considered; however, private letters of this sort possess greater authority) than what a person has written by their own hand as a private citizen and signed with their customary manual seal, or which they have sealed with their own signet: commonly called **a manuscript that someone has written with their own hands and impressed with their usual seal.** <note>original German: "ein Handschrifft, die einer mit eignen Handen geschrieben, und sein gewöhnlich Pettschafft vorgedruckt hat."</note>

There are four species of private writing. (1.) **Receipt** <term>Apocha: a formal written acknowledgment that a debt has been paid or property received</term>, which is nothing other than a document made by a creditor and given to a debtor, in which the creditor declares that payment has been made by the debtor himself; in Latin it is called a **Reception** <note>Latin: *Receptio*</note> (see *The Digest, final law, regarding the recovery of undue payments; and the law concerning shops, section on receipts, under the title on theft; and the Code, regarding many receipts in the title on the evidence of instruments*). **Bornitius** in *On Instruments, book 2, chapter 40,* notes it is commonly called **a Quittance or Receipt** <note>original German: "Quittantz, Quittung"</note> because it renders the debtor quiet and secure.

2. **Counter-Receipt** <term>Antapocha: a document given by the debtor to the creditor, serving as an acknowledgment of a debt or a record of a specific transaction</term>, which is made by the debtor and given to the creditor, containing the payment of the money itself; this is properly called a **note** or **handwritten bond** <term>Chirographum: a document written and signed by the party to be bound</term>, by which the debtor confesses that he owes the creditor, or by which the debtor binds himself, **a manuscript in which the debtor makes himself liable to the creditor and acknowledges having received a certain sum of money or something else.** <note>original German: "ein Handschrifft, da der Schuldner dem Gläubiger sich pflichtig macht, und ein gewisse Summa Gelds oder anders empfangen zu haben, bekennet."</note>

3. **Account Book** <term>Liber rationum: a ledger or book of accounts maintained by an individual or merchant</term>, **a calculation book** <note>original German: "ein Rechenbuch"</note>, which anyone creates for themselves of their own accord.

4. **Letter**, which is sent to someone, **an epistle or missive.** <note>original German: "ein Epistel oder Sendschreiben."</note>

On whether and when private writing constitutes proof, see at length **Nicolaus Januam** in *Treatise on Private Writing, question 4.*

# ADDITION.

Writings, although written by a private hand, if sealed with the seal of any **Ordinary** <term>Ordinarius: a judge or official with regular jurisdiction, such as a bishop or magistrate</term>, provide full proof for and against a third party in matters pertaining to the office of the sealer, even if no witnesses are signed below. The text for this is in *chapter 2, on the evidence of instruments.* The reason is that just as a signature is said to authorize letters written by a private hand, so too does a sealing. **Höpingk** in *On the Law of Seals, chapter 11, section 11, number 190 and following.* Private writing gains strength from the fact that an authentic seal has been applied to it. *Same author, chapter 10, section 1, number 88.* There are four species of private writing. 1. **Receipt** <note>Latin: *Apocha*</note>, which the **Emperor** in the *Code, law 18, under the title on witnesses* calls **"security"** <note>Latin: *securitatem*</note>, wishing to express the Greek term **assurance** <note>original Greek: ἀσφάλειαν</note>, by which a creditor confesses to have received the money owed. **Pacius** in *Analysis of the Code, page 342.* He who falsely denies that he wrote a receipt must be punished (see *The Digest, law 16, penultimate and last section, on the evidence of instruments*); if he is proven wrong by a comparison of letters, he pays 24 **shillings** <note>Latin: *solidos*</note>; if he is convicted by legitimate proof, besides the said penalty of 24 shillings, he can no longer deny that payment was made to him, but is absolutely compelled to stand by the writing. **Pacius** in *Analysis of the Code, page 341*; or, as **Rittershuf.** says in *On the New Constitutions, page 636, number 6*: he who denies the confession of payment made to him deservedly suffers that penalty, so that the sum

<column-break/>

contained in the receipt is forced to be credited against the debt, and he must provide as much again. Receipts in the **New Constitutions 72** <note>referring to the *Novellae* of Justinian</note> are called **proofs of debts** <note>original Greek: ἀποδείξις τῶν χρεῶν</note>, as also in *New Constitutions 46 and 49*, declarations of paid money. **Rittershuf.** in *On the New Constitutions, page 457.*

After 30 days, a creditor cannot prove that payment was not made against a receipt given by himself, according to the *sufficiently clear text of the Code, law 14, section 2, regarding money not paid.* **Zanger** in *On Exceptions, part 3, chapter 14, number 32.* **Zorer**, *part 2, question 17, number 2014.* Thus it is testified to be pronounced in the Electoral Saxon Courts by **Carpzov** in *Forensic Jurisprudence, part 2, constitution 29, definition 19, and response 90, book 2.* Although in the **Court of Conscience** <term>forum conscientiae: a religious or moral tribunal rather than a civil court</term> they say it is otherwise, **Trentacinq.** *Various Resolutions, book 3, resolution 20, number 33, at the end.* **Mantica** *On Tacit and Ambiguous Agreements, book 18, chapter 6, number 5,* and on that account an **Evangelical denunciation** <term>denunciatio Evangelica: a procedure in canon law where a person is warned of a sin to bring them to repentance</term> is applicable. **Mantica** *book 3, title 1, number 13,* that is, the office of the Judge, **Mantica** *book 24, title 5, number 23.*

Just as it is the same thing for something not to be done as for it to be done less than legitimately; so too it is the same thing not to keep an account book as to keep one, but not **formally** <note>Latin: *solenniter*</note>. **Cavalcan.** *part 1, section 2, decision 39, number 45.*

The **entry** of accounts ought to be shown before the **exit** <note>meaning income should be listed before expenses</note>. **Barbosa** *book 16, chapter 7, axiom 3.*

Therefore, an account book must contain things given and received, and indeed fully and in **good faith**, according to the *Digest, law 111, on conditions and demonstrations.* **Baldus** on *the Code, law 6, number 17, regarding conditions*, infers: not in a heap, according to *The Digest, law 82, on conditions and demonstrations*, nor in a sack, according to *The Digest, law 3, section 6, on the status of freemen*, nor **under a cloud** <note>meaning vaguely or obscurely</note>. **Bartholomew Socinus**, *volume 1, consultation 73, number 6, and volume 2, consultation 213, number 4.* Instead, it should include everything that has been received and spent, **individually**. **Gylm.** *volume 4, part 1, vote 27.* And specifically described with items placed next to each other, according to *The Digest, law 2, section 2, on the administration of matters pertaining to the city.* **Berojus**, *volume 1, consultation 192, number 18, second point,* requires that accounts described in the ledger contain the **cause**, namely, from what cause the income was brought in and from what cause the expense was sent out. So **Stracha** in *On Merchants, part 2, number 60.* And indeed, the accounts must contain enough so that if they contained something uncertain and obscure, it would be the same as if they did not contain it at all; because it is the same thing if a cause is not expressed, or if it is expressed but not clearly, with certainty, and intelligibly, according to **Alexander**, *book 2, consultation 182, number 5.* Whence an account not sufficiently rendered can always be requested again and again to be rendered correctly. **Barbosa** *book 16, chapter 7, axiom 6, third point.* In an account book, there must necessarily be the addition of the day and time **we have found...**

### 21. Hand-Stroke. Betrothal.
<term>Handstreich: literally a "hand-stroke," referring to a formal handshake or manual gesture used in some regions to legally seal a betrothal agreement.</term> <term>Sponsalia: the formal Latin term for betrothal or the ceremony of promising to marry.</term>

In certain places, betrothals are called by this name, concerning which see *Book 7 of the Decretals, book 4, title 1; Paulus Zypaeus in the Analysis of Pontifical Law, book 4, folio 398 and many following.* A betrothal is one thing, and a wedding is another; although in Holy Scripture "betrothed" is sometimes used for "married," as in *Deuteronomy 22.*

->ADDITION.<-

In a Betrothal, consent is indeed involved, but it concerns the future rather than the present. However, interpreters of Canon Law have also identified certain betrothals that function "of the present" <note>Latin: *de præsenti*. This refers to a promise that creates an immediate legal marriage bond rather than a promise to marry later.</note>. *Rittershusius in the New Works, page 192.*

### 22. Hand-Signature. Subscription.
<term>Subscriptio: the act of signing a document at the bottom, which carries specific legal weight.</term>

A signature is regularly made below the notation of the name of the person who writes it or arranges for it to be written. Or it is made by those who were present at the business for the sake of testimony—that is, the Witnesses. It is made either by one's own hand, commonly called **with one’s own hand-signature** <note>original German: "mit eigener Hand-Unterschrifft"</note>, which the person writes himself; or by another's hand, which someone else has penned in the name of a person who is unable to write.

From this, the signature derives its greatest force and energy. For the signer is deemed to approve everything contained in the writing; therefore, it prejudices him <note>legally binds or disadvantages him</note> as if he had written the entire thing himself. Text in *law so, 8, section it does not seem, 15, on the modes of...*

<column-break/>

...ping. and *law 1, on the word 'subscription,' regarding the constitutions of Princes*, where the text says that the signature of a Prince alone does the same thing as if he had written the entire Letter. Add *Jason on law 'if so stipulated,' 126, section Chrysogonus, on Verbal Obligations; and Baldus in the Authentica 'against' in the Code on money not counted.* This is certainly true if someone signs as a principal party, but it is otherwise if they sign as a witness. For in that case, such a signature does not prejudice the witness, according to *Brunnus in the said section Chrysogonus; and the text is in law 'if a Father,' 6, in the Code on suretyship; Schneidewin on buying and selling, in the beginning, number 9.*

However, as to whether and when someone prejudices themselves by their presence or signature in any act or instrument, see *Socin, rule 385; Mascardus, conclusion 1341; Negusantius on pledges, part 3, member 1, number 6.*

Hence, witnesses commonly tend to add this clause:

> Which I acknowledge to have occurred as a witness requested for this purpose, and do hereby sign myself as testimony to it, yet without harm to myself and my heirs. <note>original German: "Welches ich als dazu erbetener Zeuge geschehen zu seyn, bekenne, und mich dessen zu Gezeugnuß hiemit unterschreibenthue, doch mir und meinen Erben ohne Schaden."</note>

Hering, however, in *On Suretyship, chapter 17, number 7*, says that this clause is not strictly necessary but is an act of "abundant caution." By the law itself, the signer and his heirs remain unharmed by the simple act of Signing and Sealing. *Moller on the Saxon Constitutions, 52, number 17 and following, part 2; Coler on executive process, part 3, chapter 1, number 127; Hering in the place cited.*

Secondly, the above conclusion <note>that a signature binds the signer to the whole text</note> does not apply when the signer has not read nor understood the contents of the writing they signed. In that case, it does not prejudice them. *Final law, and there Baldus, in the Code 'more to be valued'; Oldradus, counsel 329, number 10; Bartolus on law 'which of the dowry,' number 26, and there Bolognetus, number 139, on the dissolution of marriage; Felinus in the chapter 'since,' number 48, on proofs; Angelus in the law 'if so stipulated,' section Chrysogonus, column 1; Alexander in the said law 'which of the dowry,' penultimate column.* This should be carefully noted, according to *Jason in the said section Chrysogonus and Modestinus Pistoris, counsel 37, volume 1, number 1*, regarding Lords and Princes who are accustomed to signing blank sheets—commonly called **blank checks or signed blanks** <note>original German: "Chartenbiancken"</note>. They are not understood to have confirmed those things that are written afterward, unless they had notice of them; ratification is not presumed to have been made except for those things which were read, known, and correctly understood by the ratifier himself. *Oldradus, counsel 329, final column; Cravetta, counsel 179, number 14.*

In case of doubt, however, the signer is presumed to have had knowledge of the contents of the writing, such that the one alleging ignorance is bound to prove it. *Jason in the said section Chrysogonus.*

It should further be noted that the omission of a signature, where it is otherwise necessarily required, voids the Instrument. For it is established that a Testament not signed nor sealed by witnesses is held to be imperfect, *according to the law 'this most consulted,' 21, in the Code on testaments.* The same is observed in contracts according to the *law 'contracts,' in the Code on the evidence of instruments.*

Letter H.

However, in a Father's Will <note>original: "Testamento Patris"; a specific category of testament in Roman law with relaxed formalities intended for distributing property among one's children</note>, it is not necessary for the Father to sign. *according to law 22, Code on Testaments.*

Also, if anyone has written an entire Will or Codicil <note>A supplement to a will used to modify or add provisions without rewriting the entire document</note> with their own hand, and has specifically stated in the writing that they composed it with their own hand, the handwriting of the entire testament is sufficient, and no other signature is required. For writing and signing are considered equivalent. *law 28, Code on Testaments; Novels on the Trustworthiness of Instruments, final section; gloss on law "fidejussor," section "pater," Digest on Pledges; and on law "si ita stipulatus," section "Chrysogonus," Digest on Verbal Obligations.* This applies unless the person stated they signed for the sake of trust <note>original: "fidei causa"; usually implying a signature was intended as a final act of verification</note>: for then, if that was not done, the writing is considered imperfect.

Whether a signature is sufficient in Wills where a Statute mentions "that someone wrote the testament" <note>original German: "daß einer das Testament geschrieben"</note>? See my discussion in *Disputations on the Municipal Law of Württemberg, part 3.*

A private Letter also provides proof even without a signature or seal, provided its form is consistent—that is, it contains the name of the sender, the name of the recipient, a narrative, and a conclusion. *Nicolò de Passeribus* at length in *Treatise on Private Writing, book 1, question 1, number 18, etc.; Menochius, chapter 94; Mascardus, conclusion 626, number 20, 42, and following.*

---

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the clause "harmless to me and my heirs" <note>original German: "mir und meinen Erben ohnschädlich"</note> *Zorer, part 2, question 5, number 352.*

The writing of a signer proves a mandate <note>A legal authorization or command to act on another's behalf</note> *law 1, section 4, regarding orders; also law 3, regarding those with him,* where *Gothofredus on the word "subscribere" [to sign]. Barbosa, book 17, chapter 13, axiom 18.* A signature performs the same function as a holograph <note>original: "holographum"; a document written entirely in the handwriting of the person whose name it bears</note>. *section 1, version "instrum." law on Verbal Obligations; law "si ita stipulatus," 126, section 2, and there Jason on Verbal Obligations; Reusner, volume 2, on testaments, part 1, chapter 4, numbers 14 and 15.* For a signer is deemed to have virtually written everything that they signed. *Julius Clarus, section "testamentum," question 14, number 1, and the annotator there; at length Dauth on law 21, section "ex imperf." number 28, Code on Testaments, page 444; see however Everhardus, book 1, counsel 13, number 49 and following.*

Without a signature, even a public seal does not establish authenticity. *Barbosa, book 17, chapter 60, axiom 2.* A signer is deemed to consent to the things signed: discussed copiously by *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 15, number 153 and following.* For a signature is made to confirm those things found in the writing; see the highly notable remarks of *Felinus on chapter 2, number 2, on the trust of instruments,* where regarding this reasoning he says it is the same to sign a private document written by another as it is to write it with one's own hand, or to assert that it is from one's own hand: since it makes no difference whether one writes the instrument with their own hand or simply signs it. Discussed most extensively by *Barbosa, book 17, chapter 60, axiom 1.*

Strictly speaking, a Signature is the under-noting of a name by one's own hand to a text already reduced to writing. *Honthem, book 2, on the Art of the Notary, chapter 51, number 3.* A signature is an act, *Besold, Volume 1,*

<column-break/>

of which the issue and conclusion are questioned. *Baldus, counsel 175, number 2, book 1; Montero, Decisions of Aragon 12, number 24.* The signature of a Notary is one of the essential parts of a legal instrument. And this Signature is only said to be "made" when the proper name is added at the bottom, either alone without any mark, or with a mark by one's own hand or another's, with the word "signed" or "has signed." *Kirchner, book 2, on the Law of Legates, chapter 8, number 84; Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 15, section number 11.* A Notary is also accustomed to add a signature of their own hand, known as an idiograph <note>A unique personal mark or signature</note>, and to press their sign or signet; or an emblem with a symbol, which either the person who created the Notary gave to them, or the Notary chose for themselves. If by chance the instrument was written by someone else, such as a substitute or an assistant to the Notary, the Notary usually adds this fact to his signature. *Rittershusius in the Novels, page 633, at the end.* One who writes above, signs, or describes something is presumed to have knowledge of the contents. *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 15, number 205 and following.* This is expanded and limited: in an Imperial Recess <note>original: "Recessus imperii"; the final resolutions or decrees of the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire</note> sometimes only the Emperor signs, as we see done at the Imperial Recess at Worms, Year 1545; the Imperial Recess at Regensburg, Year 1546; and the Imperial Recess, Year 1555. Today, as is the custom, they express nothing but the Emperor's own name, for example, "Charles I" <note>original: "Carolus Primus"</note> they signed. The Kings of Portugal, when they signed diplomas, were always accustomed to add five dots .·.·. which they called "wounds," in memory of the wounds of our Savior. *Conestagio, book 6, folio 331.* The King of Spain sometimes does not sign his own name, but connects only these words: "I, the King" <note>original Spanish: "yo el Rey"</note>. *Baudius on the Truce of the Belgian War, book 2, page 36.* Sometimes the Archchancellor of the Empire signs with the Emperor, as was done at the Imperial Recess at Augsburg in the Year 1548; the Imperial Land-Peace established at Augsburg in the same year; the Imperial Recess at Augsburg, Year 1551; and the Imperial Recess at Augsburg, Year 1559. More on this in *Limnaeus on Public Law, book 9, chapter 1, page 47.* In the Court Ordinance of Weser <note>original German: "Weserischen Gerichts-Ordnung"</note> it is found that the presiding assessors here should accept no product [legal filing] unless it be signed by the hand of the Advocate and the Procurator. But if one party does not believe that the same person wrote the document, then it shall be required of the opposing party to promise in place of an oath and maintain that he who signed the document composed it, and no one else helped him with it, so it should remain; but if he cannot do that, he shall be obliged by that same promise to have the true Advocate or maker of the document sign it, and therefore use no deception. If a seal is lost, the signature must be relied upon. *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 15, section 1, number 209.* A signature on another's writing regularly confirms it and provides proof against the signer. *numbers 211, 212.*

## 23. Tradesman. *Artisan.*

According to the manner of speaking in Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratensi"; refers to the city of Strasbourg</note>, the "Trades" <note>original German: "die Handwerck"</note> are called Tribes <note>original: "Tribus"; the local term for guilds that held political power</note>, into which both Patricians and commoners are enrolled, excluding the Nobles, who have their own separate assemblies. Thus, that word is used in opposition to the Nobility; an ignoble person endowed with virtue is said to be "of the Trades" <note>original German: "von den Handwercken"</note>, as noted by Mr. Bernegger in his *Supplement to Tacitus, century question 2, at the end.*

That statute which some Colleges of Workers <note>original: "Collegia Opificum"; early term for guilds or professional associations</note> have—namely, that what one person has begun or cut out, another may not finish—is invalid. This means it is not permitted for one to finish what another started. On the contrary, it is expressly decreed in the law *on monopolies* <note>original: "l. un. C. de monopol."; referring to the Code of Justinian</note> that anyone is allowed to finish, without fear of any loss, what was begun and left behind by another. For it is not permitted to make statutes against those things prohibited by Common Law, such as Monopolies, among which the Emperor includes these conspiracies of workers. Therefore, in France as well, such statutes are rejected, as testified by Pierre Rebuff in his *Constitutions of the Kingdom of France, treatise on the master of artisans, book 2, article 4, glossary 2, number 18.* See also Moller in his *Semestria, chapter 15*, and my own *Treatise on Colleges.*

However, is that statute or custom valid which is accepted in the Colleges of Tailors and Shoemakers in some places, namely that no one should marry a wife from outside the trade—meaning "one must marry into the office" <note>original German: "da einer ins Amt freyen muß"</note>? Speckhan affirms this in *century 3, question 5, class 1*, provided there is someone available with whom he can lawfully contract. This seems to have been established for the purpose of better preserving the integrity of the trades. This does not contradict the freedom of marriage, since there is a choice of which woman among many he may love or wish to take as a wife. Where there is choice, there is liberty and free will, which is absolutely required in marriages as a substantial foundation. It would be otherwise, however, if a statute or custom tried to force someone to marry a specific person, such as the daughter or widow of a certain man (for example, "if one were forced to marry the daughter or widow of a preacher" <note>original German: "da einer eines Prädicanten Tochter oder Wittib freyen müste"</note>). In that case, the freedom of marriage and free will would be hindered, since there is no choice there, and thus liberty is restricted to a specific individual. See Speckhan at the cited location, number 15 and following, and Stephan on *Jurisdiction, book 2, part 2, chapter 7, folio 383, etc.*

The trades must not be confused, and "no trade should encroach upon another" <note>original German: "und soll kein Handwerck dem Brandern eingreiffen"</note>, such as Joiners and Carpenters, or Saddlers and Strap-makers, etc. Regarding the law of the Egyptians, which set limits and boundaries for talents, and by which no artisan was allowed to practice any art except his father's, see Cunaeus on *The Hebrew Republic, book 1, chapter 5.*

## ADDITION.

The law and ordinance of the Sworn Cloth-makers <note>original German: "Geschwornen Zeugmacher"</note> extend only to the four

<column-break/>

capital cities: Bayreuth, Kulmbach, Hof, and Wunsiedel, which for this reason also have their regular inspections.

"Every trade has a golden floor" <note>original German: "Ein jedes Handwerck hat einen guldenen Boden"; a proverb meaning a trade is a secure source of wealth</note>, but one must search for it up to the elbows <note>A metaphor for hard, physical labor</note>. More people live by their art than by other sources of income, of whatever kind they may be. For from just those two trades, wool and silk, many thousands of people seek their livelihood in Milan, Venice, Florence, and Genoa. Obrecht mentions this in his *Political Reflections on the Improvement of Land and People, page 125.* Selim I, Sultan of the Turks, when he wished to enlarge Constantinople in both inhabitants and wealth, summoned several thousand highly skilled artisans of all mechanical arts from those two very famous cities, Belgrade and Cairo, to Constantinople. The Poles, who sought Duke Henry of Anjou as their King, wanted the same: that he should bring a hundred families of craftsmen with him to Poland. *ibid.* It is fitting for Princes to strive diligently toward this, to make their cities famous with distinguished masters. Barbosa, *Axioms, book 1, chapter 82, axiom 3.* Every regent and sovereign should not permit tradesmen to unite with one another in their trades so that one shall not sell, contract, or make his finished work cheaper or for less than the other; rather, they should strictly forbid this under a high monetary penalty. For through this, harmful price hikes and inflation can be prevented in these dealings. Thus we see in the law *on monopolies* <note>referring again to the Code of Justinian</note> that it is heavily prohibited for merchants to conspire and bargain among themselves not to sell goods for less than they themselves have determined, or for Artisans and Contractors <note>original: "Ergolabi"; those who take on work for a price</note> to agree among themselves that what work one begins, another shall not finish. Hence, Dr. Hippolytus de Collibus says to Magistrates: "care must be taken that works and crafts are completed solidly, without any fraud, deceit, or pretense, according to the laws of each trade, and that factions or conspiracies are not hidden under the pretext of trades," in his *booklet on the growth of the city, chapter 15, at the end.* Regarding the Guilds of tradesmen <note>original German: "Innungen der Handwercksleut"</note>, see *Saxon Consisterial Matters*, page 34, following 45. Regarding the privilege that someone alone may sell certain goods, see Pacius in his *Analysis of the Code, page 412.* See Felwinger on *Monopolies, thesis 2*, regarding the illicit agreements of merchants so that goods are not sold for less than they have determined among themselves. See Zorer, *part 2, question 18, number 4060*; Pacius at the cited location; and Felwinger, *thesis 15.* Regarding the pact of artisans and contractors (that is, redeemers who undertake work to be done) that work begun by one shall not be finished by another, or that no one should take over the care of something that had been committed to another's care: Zorer, *part 2, question 18, number 4059*; Pacius also at the cited location; Felwinger, *thesis 18.* "A mind intent on many things is less focused on individual ones" <note>A legal maxim suggesting that specializing in one trade leads to better quality</note> from the law *on Assessors*. Barbosa, *The Rich Treasury, book 14, chapter 39, axioms 4 & 5.* No trade should infringe upon another, but each should remain solely and uniquely with its own. Where there is an elegant case regarding *Saddlers and Bridle-makers* <note>original: "Ephippiariis & Franariis"</note> from Berlichius.

24. Hans, Hanse, Hansiburii, Ansiburii, Hanse-Town, etc.

See the mirror <note>original Latin: "speculum"</note> of the most excellent and learned Johann Jacob Speidel.

### ADDITION.

Our ancestors called the Huns "the Hayne," and "Great Haynen" those who equaled the Huns in stature. The sons of Anakim were giants not in stature, but in authority; hence the Greek terms <note>original Greek: "ἀναξ" (anax), "ἄναντες" (anantes)</note> meaning **"Lord"** or **"King,"** applied to the sons and brothers of Kings—the **"Great Hanses."** <note>original German: "Grosse Hansen"; a colloquial term for powerful or boastful men</note> Salius in XVII says: these are the strongest names. Plutarch calls them "great names" <note>original Greek: "μεγάλα ὀνόματα"</note>. Statius in the *Achilleid* II: "There the immense names compete." Persius calls them the "huge Tituses." We Germans say **"Great Hanses"** and **"Free Hanses"**, just as the maritime cities were called by their immunities, which once united in Germany against the incursions of barbarians and for the convenience of trade; and because no cities were received into that society unless they had the right of closing and opening their own gates: the name of the **"Free Hanses"** <note>original German: "der freyen Hansen"</note> was claimed for them. From this, a conjecture regarding the notation of the "Hanse" itself is at hand. Philippus, *Various Readings of Charles II*, chapter 15, at the end.

25. Head-right, Death-case, Dead-hand, Pasture-mark, Garment-fall, Fee-release, Dead-hand. <note>original terms: Hauptrecht, Todfall, tode Hand, Waidmal, Gewandfall, Frehnlösen, morte main</note>. The right of escheat, or death duties <note>original Latin: "Jus caduci, mortuaria"</note>.

In certain places, especially in parts of Montferrat, Savoy, and Piedmont, it is received by stat-

<column-break/>

ute or the custom of the place, **that a serf, when he dies without biological children, must leave to his lord a third part of his goods and property (whether this is done by Will or without a Will).** Menoch. *Arbitrary Judges*, question 230. See Adam Keller, *On Intestate Succession*, title 27, number 3 and following. Add Mr. Wager, *On Armed Advocates*, chapter 7, number 755 and following. And Stuck. in *Exercises on Justice*, part 1, decade 8, assertion 6, under letters e. m. f. 331, writes at the end: Certain cities have this by special custom, that when the head of a family dies, the wife is bound to give the Magistrate the husband's middle-tier clothing (which is called **"Garment-fall"** <note>original German: "Gewand-Fall"</note>) which he used, as well as a prepared bed. In this Duchy (that is, of **Brunswick**), he says, and in most other places, the secular Magistrate takes an ox, the local pastor takes a rooster—the **"house-rooster"**—and the sexton <note>original Latin: "Edituus"</note> takes a **bratwurst**.

So also in Hesse and surrounding places, as witnessed by Johann Hermann Stamm in his treatise *On Bondmen*, chapter 22, number 7. The Lords do not take a third part of the goods, but upon the death of a bonded woman, the most precious garment belongs to the Lord; and upon the death of a bonded man, the best horse or ox is owed to the Lord. **If a serf woman dies, the best dress commonly falls to the Lord, and from the man, the best horse or ox.** Crusius, *Swabian Annals*, part 3, book 10, chapter 11, folio 575. In a Charter for the Monastery of St. Michael, or the Monks outside Bamberg, by Emperor Henry II, it is held: "We ordain that the final tax—by which services omitted or neglected are supplied—namely the **Head-right** <note>original Latin: "jus capitale"</note> from deceased men, which is the best horse, or if they lack a horse, the best head of cattle; and from women, the inner and outer garments, shall be transmitted to the Church." Brusch, *On Monasteries*, folio 87. b. Andreas Knichen, *On Vestiary Pacts*, book 2, chapter 3, number 25. But because this right seemed too harsh to the Lords, it has been accepted and observed that the Lords receive a sum of money from the heirs of the deceased serf, based on the value of the deceased's inheritance. Zal. book 1, *Singular Responses*, chapter 3, number 79.

This right is called by us the Right of Escheat, also "mortuaries," **Death-case, Head-right, Pasture-mark,** and from the pact which the heirs of the deceased enter into with the Lord or his officials regarding the better beast left by the bondman, they are accustomed to call it **"the negotiation of the best head"** <note>original German: "die Thädigung des besten Haupts"</note>, that is, the settlement for the best animal. Sichard. on law *libert. 11. n. 4. C. de test.* Stamm. ibid. number 7.

Caspar Klock, in *On Contributions*, conclusion 3, calls this Right of Escheat the **"Mourning-right"** <note>original German: "Traurrecht"</note>. Stamm. in the cited chapter, number 8, notes that because it was considered beyond measure unjust, the rebellious Peasants in the year 1525 demanded that the Princes of Germany abolish and remove it entirely, as reported by Sleidan in his *History*, book 5.

We also call it **Death-case** or **Dead-hand** <note>original Latin: "morte main"</note> specifically from this: when a serf man has died and left no property or nourishment from which the Bishop could be paid,

### 26. House. <note>original: "Hauß. Domus."</note>

Although a "House," according to Bertazolium in his treatise on *Instructions*, is understood in various ways in law, nevertheless, when a "House" is mentioned in legal instruments, it is mostly understood as a building constructed for habitation. According to the Logicians <note>original: "Dialecticos"</note>, this consists of three things: namely, the ground, the wall, and the roof. See the gloss on the law <note>original: "gl. in l. solum. ff. de rei vind."; a reference to the Roman Digest regarding the recovery of property</note>. According to the Jurists, however, it consists of the ground and the "surface," which seems to be the same thing, since the roof exists upon the surface. See Fusarius in his treatise on *Substitutions*. A difference is established between a "house" <note>original: "domum"</note> and a "dwelling" <note>original: "ædes"</note>, namely that "dwelling" has a broader meaning than "house," which encompasses every single building. However, Bertazolium does not entirely admit this distinction.

When a house is granted, sold, or bequeathed, the contiguous garden is also included as an accessory to the house, or as part of the house's appurtenances <note>original Latin: "tanquàm accessorium ad domum... de pertinentiis domus"</note>. See the law regarding estates in the *Digest*. For this reason, when a house or castle is granted as a fief, the contiguous garden will also be seen as granted. For the accessory follows the principal thing. See Cagnolus on the law of principals.

Whether a small attached cottage is also included when a "house" is bequeathed? See the *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 1. Likewise, if a house is bequeathed simply, whether the entire house is considered bequeathed.

Under the name of "house" is included the doorway and all other things which are fixed to the building. Just as a person cannot be seized <note>arrested</note> within a Church, so too they cannot be seized at its doorway; and if a statute punishes someone for attacking another in their house, they shall be punished with the same penalty if they attack them in the doorway, or before the door, or in the porch. This is the opinion of Mastrillus and many others.

Regarding the other meaning of "house," namely when it is used to mean a "family," such as the House of Bavaria, Saxony, etc., see my work on families.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

The ways and means by which the owner of a ruinous house or building may be compelled to make repairs: Klock, volume 2. What is contained under the name of "Buildings": Dr. Rebhan, *Selected Justinian Questions*. Even a single clod of earth can be called "land," and the cheapest material can be called a "house." See Zorer, part 2. What falls under the word <term>Wohnung</term> <note>dwelling</note> and the word <term>Wohnhaus</term> <note>dwelling-house</note>: see Agricola on *Appurtenances*. Regarding a bequeathed house: if it has been destroyed and rebuilt, is it still owed to the heir? See Mantica. A statute speaking of someone wounding another "in a house" does not take place in a shop <note>original: "Apotheca"</note>. When a house is bequeathed with everything existing therein, it is understood to mean at the time the will was made.

The name "Oswald" is more correctly <term>Hauswalt</term>, meaning "governor of the house." The name <term>Heinrich</term> <note>Henry</note> is the same as <term>Heimreich</term>, meaning "rich at home" or "rich in families." Regarding "Bender-houses" <note>original German: "Von Benderhäusern"; likely referring to cooperages or specific guild houses</note>, see the *Frankfurt Reformation*. One's own house ought to be the safest refuge for everyone <note>original Latin: "Domus sua tutissimum cuique debet esse refugium"; a fundamental maxim of privacy and property rights</note>. No one can be dragged out of their house against their will, or physically seized; this applies in civil cases, but not in criminal ones. However, a debtor suspected of fleeing can be dragged from the house even on a feast day or solemn day. A house should not be valued by the cost of the building, but by its income. What is done in a house or building is presumed to have been done by the inhabitants. The word "house" is used for "family" in the Code and the Digest. The term "house" encompasses the family and also the court. It includes those said to be of the same "House" <note>original: "Casata"</note> and "Stock" <note>original: "Cippo"</note>, and all who are joined by blood or bear the same arms and insignia. Regarding whether a small attached cottage or a contiguous garden is included in a house bequest, or whether rights and legal actions are included when a house is bequeathed with "all things stored therein": for all these, see Agricola on *Appurtenances*. By the grant of a house or building, those things which are there for the purpose of perpetual use are also considered granted, such as keys, ironwork, and lock... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "clau-" for "claudere" or "claustra" (locks/bolts)</note>

### 27. House-poor People. <note>original: "Hausarme Leut. Pauperes."</note>

Those who elsewhere are called the "house-seated poor" <note>original German: "Haussis-send Arme"</note> are those who are not vagrants or those who beg from house to house, but rather those who are ashamed to beg and yet suffer poverty in their own households.

->**ADDITION.**<-

Poor, oppressed people who are destitute of their goods and possessions not by their own fault or action, but by the harshness of fortune, or the actions or injuries of others, or by the bad condition of the times, and are thus suddenly precipitated and thrust into decline. Limn. *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 19, page 312, at the end. "Poor people" used as a term for "subjects." <note>This notes a linguistic shift where "poor people" became a legal synonym for a lord's subjects.</note> See the Bill of Sale for the Castle of Eschenbach, Anno 1583: "With our bodies, belongings, goods, and poor people." Gylm. in *Symph.* volume 1, part 1, title 4, folio 300.

Augustine denied that thefts should be committed with the intention of feeding the holy poor. As the saying goes: "To steal the leather and give the shoes for God's sake." See canon 10, cause 34, question 4; add canon 8, cause 14, question 5. Master Tabor in *Crim. Clusters*, page 109.

### 28. Vagabonds. <note>original: "Hausheblich, vagabundi, Landstreiffer."</note>

Peguera reminds us in decision 3, from the beginning, that the Holy Scripture teaches the rejection of vagabonds and idle men began at the very creation of man.

And a vagabond, according to Clarus in *Criminal Practice*, question 3, at the verse "But here I ask," is one who wanders through the world and does not have a fixed domicile anywhere in which he lives.

And hence also in our law, vagabonds suffer under great hatred. Specifically, those who have no fixed seat of habitation in the Provinces; and who daily wander through various cities, nor have a firm domicile or residence anywhere. Peguera, in the same place, numbers 9 and 14. And also, in whatever place and wherever they are found, they can be summoned and punished. Plot. counsel 133, number 14. Grammat. decision 26, number 9. Clar. in *Criminal Practice*, question 3, at the verse "Furthermore." Cæpoll. *Criminal Counsel* 58, number 23. Boss. title *On the Form of Composition*, number 70. Ruin. counsel 18, number 3, book 4. And for that reason, Bartolus said in law *the absent heretic* § *accordingly*, number 4, Digest *on judges*, whom Duen. refers to and follows in rule

<column-break/>

378, limit 4: that many <term>Ribalds</term> <note>scoundrels or low-life vagrants</note> are hanged in cities or castles wherever they are found, since they have no legal forum anywhere. A wife is bound to follow such a man; likewise, these men are not admitted as fit witnesses in either civil or criminal cases. Peguera, in said decision, number 10, etc., and also number 16 and following.

Indeed, it is not permitted for a vagabond to contract a Marriage, unless the requirements are observed which are held in the *Summa* of Silvester de Prierio under the word "Marriage," number 7, verse 4, and better in the Council of Trent, Session 24, chapter 7, where the following words are found:

> *There are many who wander and have uncertain homes, and as they are of wicked character, having abandoned their first wife, they marry another and often several others in different places while the first is still living. Wishing to meet this disease, the holy Synod paternally warns all whom it concerns not to easily receive this class of wandering men into marriage; it also exhorts secular magistrates to restrain them severely; and it commands parish priests not to be present at their marriages unless they have made a diligent inquiry; and, the matter having been reported to the Ordinary <note>the local Bishop</note>, they have obtained permission from him to do so.*

Petr. Nicol. Mozz. *On Contracts*, title *On Marriage*, question "who can contract marriage," number 23.

Furthermore, Peguera in said decision, number 12 and following, testifies that in the Province of Catalonia, the punishment of flogging <note>original Latin: "fustigatio"</note> or of serving five years in the royal galleys <note>original Latin: "triremibus"</note> is imposed on vagabonds.

There is, however, great dispute among the Doctors of Law as to whether those who are "banned"—that is, those whom one has banished from the land—are called vagabonds, and whether the rules set for vagabonds are also considered set for the banned? See Peguera, in the same place, number 14.

And although it might seem at first glance that it is so, because they seem to be without a city or domicile (Law 17, § 1, Digest *on punishments*; Law 1, § 2 and 3, *on legacies 3*), nevertheless the contrary opinion is truer: namely, that someone is not made a vagabond by the ban alone, because he can have a domicile in another city. Otherwise, if he were to wander through the world without a certain habitation, then he should certainly be held as a vagabond. Clarus, question 39, at the verse "I was asked." Alberic. in *Treatise on Statutes*, part 4, question 80, at the verse "likewise I ask."

->**ADDITION.**<-

On who is a vagabond, see Jul. Clar. § final, question 39, at the verse "but here I ask," with the following verse. Soar. B. 5. and V. 2. Pap. decision 202, number 2.

Wandering, "gardening," <note>original German: "gartende"; a term for mercenary soldiers who wandered and lived off the land through begging or plunder</note> and masterless soldiers, and other such servants, are not to be tolerated to the harm and detriment of the poor subjects. Law *generally*, § 2, *them*, Code *on Bishops and Clergy*. Imperial Recess of the year 1555, § *and therewith prompted Police Ordinance* Anno 1577, title 7, regarding the masterless and "gardeners." Gerh. *on testimonies*, last difference, thesis 20. Boc. book 1 *on war*, chapter 26, number 7. Denais. in *Chamber Law*.

### 30. House Search. <note>original: "Haussuchung. Visitatio domestica."</note>

A search in the homes of others, commonly called "house-searching" <note>original German: "die Haussuchung"</note>, on account of a stolen thing, for the owner of the thing

<column-break/>

is regularly not legal; indeed, it seems to be prohibited. For under this pretext, our homes would serve the curiosity of everyone—homes which ought to provide us with a safe and free dwelling. Law "Plerique" 18, *Code on Summoning to Law*. For the laws have judged it harsh and unjust for anyone to enter another's home against the owner's will, so much so that an action for damages <note>original: "actio injuriarum"</note> is given on this account. Law "Qui in domum" 23, *Digest on Injuries*; law 18, *On Summoning to Law*. It is also dangerous to peer into the secrets of a house against the owner's will and resistance, since it is beneficial to the head of the family that the secrets of his estate not be laid open. For it is a heavy thing either to uncover the lowliness of one's domestic affairs or to subject one's riches to envy. Law 2, in the beginning, *Code on when and to whom the fourth part*. Johann Schneidewin on paragraph "Conceptum" 9, number 2, *Institutes on Obligations arising from Crimes*.

However, if some evidence appears against the person whom I suspect has stolen my property, the Judge, having been approached, can grant me a search in the other person's home. Argument from laws 101 and 105, *Digest on the Rules of Law*, and law 1, in the beginning, *On Inquiry*. Cujas on Paul's *Sentences*, 2, 31. Boër, decision 174. Clarus, *Sentences*, section on theft, 3. For this is done for the sake of public utility, to which private utility is not preferred; for then it is granted for the purpose of restraining delinquents and deterring others from these crimes.

It should be noted that although a search in the homes of others is granted, especially where public utility is involved (Law "Quosdam," *Code on Metals*; Law "Omnis," at the end, *Code on Aqueducts*), nevertheless the Magistrate today does not usually grant the license to search to the owners themselves from whom the thefts were committed, lest scandals follow. Instead, they send their own officers <note>original: "executores"</note> to search, sometimes even while the owners are present. Boërius, decision 174. Jean Papon in *French Arrests*, 23, Arrest 6, number 3. Alciat, consultation 462. Add Schneidewin on the said paragraph "Conceptum" and Andreas Gerhard on the *Institutes*, decade 17, question 4.

Furthermore, although it is of undisputed law that an inquiry is a species of high jurisdiction <note>original: "meri Imperii," referring to the power of the sword or supreme sovereign authority</note>, and no one can inquire unless he holds high jurisdiction (especially in crimes and criminal causes: *Speculum*, book 3, part 1, title on inquiry, section 1, number 4), yet this "inquiry" properly so called cannot be held here. Paolo di Castro, consultation 349, beginning "It should be noted that adultery," number 1, near the middle, section "For it was done," book 1, where he says in these formal words that a preparatory information of this kind, made for a solemn inquiry, cannot be called an "inquiry." Since it is done only to inform the mind of the judge, and the form of an inquiry is not observed in it, it may be done even without the preceding formal procedure, and without providing a copy of the defense and articles, etc. Or it is only called a "most general inquiry." Berlich, decision 170, number 3. For it is done only for investigating delinquents, not for punishing them, on account of light offenses; hence it belongs to the lower jurisdiction, as the jurists of Leipzig also answered. Berlich, in the cited place, number 5. But concerning...
