### ADDITION.

Concerning the investigation of thefts according to ancient custom, one may look to *Gellius, Book 11, Number 7*, at the end, and the observations therein by *Philippus Carolus*; also *Alexander ab Alexander, Genial Days, Book 6, Chapter 10*; *Turnebus, Adversaria, Book 30, Chapter 23*; and *Hotoman, Bachov, and Borcholt* in their commentaries on the Institutes regarding obligations arising from crime. The true reasoning for the ancient custom seems to be this: in former times, a person searching for stolen property in another's house would enter wearing only a simple flaxen loincloth <note>original: "licio & lino cinctus." This refers to the ancient Roman legal ritual of "searching with platter and loincloth" (lance et licio), intended to prevent the searcher from hiding stolen goods in their clothes to plant them in the house.</note> and would hold a platter—that is, a wide, round dish—before their eyes. This was done out of respect for the presence of mothers or virgins <note>original: "propter matrum f. aut virginum præsentiam." The platter served as a modest visual barrier while the searcher was nearly naked.</note>, as *Bachovius* teaches from *Festus, Book 10*. In other respects, even today, if urgent evidence exists, a search for stolen property is usually conducted by the authority of a Magistrate, even in someone else's home. See *Schneidewin, Borcholt, and Niellius* on the same section of the Institutes; *Cujacius* on Paulus; *Cagnolus*; and *Georg Rittershuf on the Law of Asylums, page 116*. This solemn search for stolen goods was also practiced among the Greeks, as *Plutarch* indicates in his *Life of Demosthenes, page 20*. He writes that the citizens of Athens, fearing that the account of the money Harpalus <note>Harpalus was a Macedonian nobleman and treasurer to Alexander the Great who fled to Athens with a massive hoard of stolen wealth.</note> had distributed to the orators would be discovered, instituted a sharp investigation, searching every single house. Only the house of Callicles, son of Arrhenidas, was immune from that search, because he had just been married and had his bride inside.

### 31. Hebrew, The Hebrew Language.

On the Hebrew language, see the *Orations of Gedinus and Avianus*; *Bartholomew Majer on Sacred Chaldaism*; *Widmanstadt's* preface to the New Testament in Syriac; the anonymous treatise on Hebrew vowel points; the prefaces to the Chaldean <note>Often referring to Aramaic in this period.</note> Grammars by *Münster* and *Buxtorf*; the orations of *Thomas Erpenius*; *Scriekius's* Adversaria and Origins; the preface to *Marianus's* Noah’s Ark; the Masoretic commentary of *Buxtorf*; and *Selden* on the Syrian Gods and Rabbinic books. On the utility of the Hebrew language, see the *Pontifical Constitution of Martin*, and the *Golden Apples*. *Fuller* and the *Swiss writers on Chaldean paraphrases* teach that the Hebrew language is closely related to Syriac. As to whether it has changed in regards to its language or script, see the *Talmud, Tractate Sanhedrin, folio 186 and following*.

### ADDITION.

Robert Stephanus wrote a most useful work on Hebrew phrases. Johannes Clajus

<column-break/>

of Herzberg, in *Book 3 of his Prosody*, wrote on the method of composing verse among the Hebrews.

*Jerome of Stridon* <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Vulgate Latin.</note> possessed such a memory, according to the testimony of *Augustine*, that he mastered the languages and scripts of the Hebrews, Greeks, Chaldeans, Persians, Medes, Arabs, and almost all nations. Hence, the Bishop of Hippo <note>Saint Augustine</note> wrote this eulogy for him: *No man knew what Jerome did not know.* *Drexel, in The Gold Mine, pages 10–11.*

The Hebrew language is the original mother and source of all languages, as affirmed by *Jerome*, *Galatinus*, and *Isidore of Seville in Book 9 of his Etymologies*. All other languages are branches of it, and Hebrew surpasses them all in its regularity. This language was born justly with the first just man; it had God as its Author and Adam as its Interpreter. *Casaubon* notes that it encompasses the greatest mysteries, as do *Cornelius Agrippa* and *Causin*. Therefore, it is called the "vernacular of God" and the "holy tongue" <note>original: "lingua sancta"</note>, not merely because the holy books were written in it (for if that were the only reason, Greek or Syriac—which *Theodoret* prefers over Hebrew—would also deserve the name), but because it is not a human invention. *Mr. Harsdörffer in Specimen of Philology, disputation 12.* Philipp Cluverius argues <note>original German: "beweist"</note> that Hebrew is not the very oldest language; he maintains that the language of our first parents is no longer to be found anywhere, and will not be heard until the Last Day, when all the elect shall speak it together. See more in *Zeiler, Letter Collection 1, page 404*. Theodore Beza, even in his old age, could recite entire Psalms in Hebrew and any chapter requested from St. Paul's Epistles perfectly in Greek. *Thuanus, History, Book 134.* From the lands of the Narisci <note>An ancient tribe in the area of the Upper Palatinate, Germany.</note>, there was a peasant who was not uninitiated <note>original Greek: "αμυηϑης"</note> in the Hebrew language and its dialects; despite working at the plow and among the labors of a farm steward, he learned it from the foundations so that he could read, write, and understand Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldean. More on this in *Mr. Saubert's 2nd Oration on Libraries, page 94*. Johannes Christianus Keckius of Strasbourg, whom I knew in Basel at the house of Buxtorf, was a seven-year-old boy who responded promptly regarding the Hebrew language, explained sacred texts, and spoke in Hebrew whatever he was commanded. The Hebrew language is holy, first, and eternal. So judge the Masters of the Hebrews. *Rabbi Asaria in Me'or Enayim, chapter 57, from the Talmud, Sanhedrin:* in their opinion, it is called the Holy Tongue because it will endure forever <note>original Hebrew: "קיימ: מה צדיקים לעולם קיומם כחקיהם לעולם" — translating to "it stands: just as the righteous endure forever, so their laws endure forever."</note>. *Dr. Dannhauer* mentions this in the program for the funeral of the "Professor of the Holy Lip" <note>A poetic title for a Professor of Hebrew.</note>. For more on the Hebrew language, see the judgment of Johannes Weitzius in a letter to Mr. Dilherr. Muleaffes, the King in Africa <note>Mulai Hassan, the Hafsid King of Tunis, 16th century.</note>, wept for nothing more during the conquest of Tunis than the fact that the ancient Arabic books were left behind to be destroyed.

<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on the ancient Roman practice of searching for stolen goods using a ritual involving a loincloth and a platter. ### 32. Heerbann. The Summons.

In the Lombard Laws, a *Bannum* <note>A term for a proclamation or the penalty for violating one.</note> signifies a penalty of 60 shillings and an equal number of lashes. However, in these same laws, *Bannum* is also used with the exact same meaning as it was among the Franks. This is indicated in the *Ripuarian Laws (Chapter 1, Title 67)*, the *Frisian Laws (Title 17)*, and the *Laws of the Franks (Title 4, Book 4)*. In these passages, those called to war by the Prince are said to be *Banniti* <note>summoned or "banned" into service</note>. Furthermore, the *Heribannum* is a tax or fine exacted from those who have neglected to obey the *Heribanno*—that is, the "summons of the Lord" (as they used to say) or the summons of the Prince. See *Lord Mager, On Armed Advocacy, Chapter 3, Number 256*, where more details are given, as well as *Lindenbrog in the Glossary*.

### ADDITION.

*Travel-money, Army-shield, Heerbann.* See *Limnaeus, Public Law, Book 2, Chapter 4, Number 11* and the authorities cited there.

On the *Heribannum*, see *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputation 7, Thesis 6, Letter E, at length*. The word *Heribannum* is taken to mean a "citation for recruitment" by *Cujacius in his Commentary on Feuds*, who is cited by *Cypraeus in his work On Betrothals, Chapter 11, Section 12, Number 6*. The word *Heribannum* is composed of the German word *Heer*, meaning an army, so that when a recruitment is proclaimed for the army, all vassals are said to be called to the army so that they may come, send a substitute, or bring a certain sum of money to the treasury. Or, if you prefer to link it to a Greek word, you might say *ban* comes from <term>pan</term> <note>original: πᾶν</term>, meaning "all," because the whole army is called. From this we also derive the terms *pistrinum bannarium* <note>a "ban-mill" where all inhabitants were legally required to grind their grain</note> and *libanum bannarium* <note>a "ban-oven"</note>, which serve all the people of a certain place in common. This is also the origin of the French word *Arrierban* <note>the arrière-ban, or general summons to all vassals</note>. *Petrus Gregorius.*

### 33. Heergewette. Military Inheritance, or expeditionary things.

In Saxony and neighboring regions, there are certain specific types of property to which the closest male relative <note>original: "der nächste Schwertmagen," literally the "sword-kin," referring to agnatic relatives through the male line</note> succeeds. They call this *Heergewette* <note>German for "army-gear"</note> or "expeditionary things" (on which see *Berlichius, Part 3, Conclusion 24*). Among other items, the best horse with its saddle belongs to this inheritance. *Berlichius, in the cited Conclusion 24, Number 6.* If, therefore, such a horse is not present, but only a young male foal <note>original: "ein Hengst-Füllen"</note>, the question arises whether it belongs to the *Heergewette* and is owed to the closest male relative. See *Berlichius, Decision 24*, where he reports that the Court of Lay Judges in Leipzig ruled in the negative.

*Heergewette* refers to the equipment that belongs to a man's person for a military expedition <note>original: "Heerfarth"</note>, as stated in the *Gloss on Saxon Feudal Law, Chapter 65, Number 8*; there, and also in the *Gloss on Land Law, Book 1, Article 22, at the words "so shall the woman"* and *Article 27, at the words "which man," version "Heergewette however"*; and the *Gloss on Town Law, Article 25, at the beginning, Number 2*. Relevant are the *Law of Arms 41, Digest on the Meaning of Words* and the *Law "No one," Code on Things which must not be exported*. *Rotschitz, Introduction on the Division of Goods, Heergewette, Article 22, Number 1.* To this belong, according to the *Gloss on Feudal Law*, two basins, a tablecloth, a cushion, and an army-bolster <note>original: "Heerpful," a military-grade mattress or bolster</note>, according to *Besoldus, Volume 1*.

<column-break/>

Also, the man's armor, in its entirety and the best available for a man's body; the best horse, saddled and bridled; the man's sword and his knife; plus his personal belt-set <note>original: "Gewette"</note>, that is, his belt and garments. Furthermore, the man's bed shall be prepared and arranged for him by those who take the *Gerade* <note>The "Gerade" was the female equivalent of the Heergewette—a woman's personal effects inherited by female relatives</note>, just as it stood during his wife's lifetime: his table with a tablecloth, his bench with a bolster, and the chair with a cushion. But add and see especially the aforementioned *Rotschitz* throughout that section. In *Article 23, on expeditionary things which are counted under Town Law*, he also has several other noteworthy points on these matters.

As to whether *Heergewette* is owed from each individual estate left by the deceased in different locations and territories, see *Modestinus Pistoris, Part 2, Question 54*.

### ADDITION.

*On Heergewette and the Army-bolster, see Rudinger, Century 2, Observation 93, in full.* To the expeditionary things belong the deceased man's sword, his best horse with saddle and bridle, his shield and best armor, his daily clothing, his military mattress—that is, the second-best bed—along with a pillow and two sheets, one tablecloth, one hand-towel, two plates, a copper kettle for cooking fish, and a ladder <note>original: "climacter," likely a field ladder or tool for an army wagon</note>. *Matthaeus Coler, Decision 203, beginning "By Civil Law a nobleman," Number 8*, where he lists these items; see also *Part 1, Schneidewin on the Title of the Institutes regarding intestate succession, Title on succession between husband and wife, Number 53*.

Regarding this word, one may consult the *Saxon Consultations, Volume 2*, and the *Annexed Resolutions, Question 5, Number 13, folio 53*; *Berlichius, Part 3, Conclusion 24, Number 6*, and *Part 1, Conclusion 65, Number 31 and following*.

### 34. Heerischliß. Army-Splitting.

*Herislitium* <note>Latinized form of the German *Heerischliß*</note> is the penalty for deserting or avoiding military service. Indeed, among the Franks, the crime of deserting the army was called *Heerischliß* (as if to say a "splitting of the army"). This is reported from *Beatus Rhenanus and Knichen* by *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputation 7, Thesis 6, under Letter E, at the end*. To the above, it is useful to add *Schottelius in The German Main Language, page 484*, where he also discusses what is meant by *Heerritt, Herireita, Hariraida* <note>Terms for a military expedition or raid</note>.

### ADDITION.

The Law of Lothair, King of the Lombards: "If anyone, while fighting against the enemy, abandons his comrade or acts out of malice, if he deceives him and does not fight alongside him, let him suffer the loss of his life." Among the Franks, it was a capital offense to desert the army, which they called in their own language *Herischlitz*. *Beatus Rhenanus, Book on German Affairs.* The Emperors Marcus and Antoninus decreed that the goods of those who died in desertion should be confiscated. *Book 4 on Military Matters, Book 12; Petrus Gregorius in the System of Universal Law, Book 19, Chapter 10, Number 21.*

### 35. **Heathen, Heathen Religion. Gentiles, Gentile Religion.**

See Otto Heurnius’s *On Barbarian Philosophy*, and Nemesius’s *On the Worship of the Stars*. In the latter, at folio 108, he notes that the power of the stars may be repelled through prayers directed toward them. Add to this the *Themis* of Pighius, Volume II; the *Magic World*; Selden’s *On the Gods of the Nations*; and Natalis Comes’s *Mythology*. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy and alchemy</note> attributes oracles to the constellations, a claim denied in the *Philosophy of Spirits* at folio 5. However, that denial is misplaced, for such a constellation "binds" the Demon or Spirit of the Statue—which seems to be the nature of all the ancient statues of the Heathens. Hence, St. Paulinus says: *The Gods of the Heathens are demons.* <note>original: "Dii Gentium Dæmonia sunt"</note>

Astrology is also a part of heathen theology: for it seeks to appease the "intelligences" or demons of the stars through hymns, sacrifices, and so forth. In contrast, Christian Theology alone achieves this by renouncing the World and all created things, clinging to God alone, sighing for Him, and reaching Him through the means prescribed and practiced in the Church.

Regarding the origin of Idolatry, see Barth’s notes on *The Gaul*, folios 67 and 70; and on mortal Gods, see Bisciolus’s *Hours of Leisure*, volume 2, book 3, chapter 13.

->ADDITION.<-

Pagans are contrasted first with "city-dwellers" (*urbani*), in which case the term signifies those who live in villages (*pagi*) outside the city, as in Cicero’s *Pro Domo Sua*: *There is no College in this city, no villagers [pagani].* Secondly, they are contrasted with "soldiers" in the final law of the Code *On Inofficious Wills*. From this comes the term *paganicum* for a marketplace or public forum. See Rittershusius in *New Constitutions*, page 559. Regarding the "pagan judgment," see the same author, page 490. Thirdly, they are contrasted with Christians and Jews; in the Title *On Pagans and Sacrifices*, they are also called "Ethnics" <note>From the Greek *ethnikos*, meaning "of the nations"</note>. In the Theodosian Code they are called "Greeks." Pacius, in his *Analysis of the Code*, teaches who the Pagans are and what the penalties for Paganism are.

The superstition of the Ethnics went so far that it was considered a ritual crime to drive away birds that had built nests in temples. When the fugitive Pactyas entered the temple at Cyme as a suppliant, and Aristidicus, a nobleman of the Cymaeans, went around the temple removing sparrows and other small birds nesting there, a voice was heard from the inner shrine addressing Aristidicus: "Most wicked of men, what madness has possessed you, that you dare to tear away my suppliants?" See Rittershusius, *On the Law of Asylum*, page 28. Various superstitions of the Gentiles are recounted by the famous Rupertus, who spent entire days in his study without eating, as if buried among his books. See his first dissertation on Valerius Maximus. On whether the books of the Gentiles should be read, see Rittershusius’s notes on Amphilochius, page 82.

The "Three Good Heathens" are Hector of Troy, Alexander the Great, and Julius Caesar. Heathens <note>German: *Heyden*</note> are so named because they dwelt in the fields, in the forests, and on the heaths <note>German: *Heyden*</note>, and performed their idol-worship there.

<column-break/>

As noted by Mr. Dilherr in *Selected Works*, book 2, chapter 6, folio 202. At Ottmarsen near Breisach, a round temple of Mars is clearly visible. On the Pagans, their sacrifices, and their temples, see Paul Christinaeus’s *Belgian Decisions*, volume 2, decision 45. When Wittekind <note>Widukind, the leader of the Saxons who fought Charlemagne</note> turned from a Heathen into a Christian, he began to bear a white stallion in his coat of arms instead of a black one.

### 36. **Holy, Sacred.**

The Roman Empire is called "Holy," *the Holy Roman Empire* <note>German: "das heilige Römisch Reich"</note>. Thus, in ancient times, the Emperors were called *Divi*, meaning "Divine" or "Heavenly." See my work *On Majesty*, chapter 2. For that name is an adjective. Perottus in *Cornucopia*, Corasius, and Prateius in his *Lexicon* discuss this. Those who claim the Emperors were called *Divi* as if they were literally Gods (*Dei*) are in error. Thus Festus says a "Divine Hero" is one whose lineage comes from the supreme Jove. Some believe the Roman Empire is called "Holy" because it transitioned from heathen rulers and has now been handed over to Christ.

The German word for "Holy" (*heilig*) is derived from *Heil* (salvation or health), or from the Hebrew *Chail* <note>Hebrew: חיל</note>, meaning "strength" or "power."

->ADDITION.<-

On the "Holy Empire," see Reinking, book 2. Our Empire is called "Sacred" (*das Heilige*) and sometimes "Sacrosanct." (Indeed, antiquity itself confused these terms: see Festus on the word *Sacer*, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* 3, citing Trebatius). For the reasons behind this, see Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 7.

See also Friedrich Balduin’s sermon on the Nativity of Christ; add Chasseneuz, *Customs of Burgundy*, where he argues that the Kingdom of France, rather than the Roman Empire, ought to be called "Holy," because kingdoms are approved by God, whereas empires are not. There is an old proverb: *Let him be a Saint, provided he is not alive.* <note>original: "Sit Divus, dummodo non sit Vivus." A cynical remark suggesting people are only called holy or deified once they are no longer around to interfere.</note> See Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relations*, part 5, page 92.

### 37. **Home, Dwelling.**

*Magum* <note>A Latinized Celtic root for a field or market, often found in place names like Nijmegen</note> is a domicile, a seat, and a very convenient and steady station of the Romans. For what is commonly called *Heim* <note>Home</note> in so many German names today seems to have been called *magum* in the past. Hence *Neomagum* is like "Neuheim" or "Neuhaus" <note>New-home or New-house; today Nijmegen</note>. And so it is with others. From *mago*, the terms *magar*, *magaria*, and *magalia* were used, and eventually Virgil’s *mapalia* <note>huts or cottages</note> arose, as Varro, Festus, and Isidore teach. Truly, anyone who knows the Punic and Hebrew languages (of which St. Jerome and others speak) is led to believe that *magar* and *magum* are the Hebrew *magor* <note>dwelling place/sojourn</note> and *mahum* or *magon*, since they are essentially the same nation. To this same point, Münster often says that *Neumeg* refers to "new kin" or "new neighbors" who move to a...

### 40. Helten, Helden. Heroes.

To the ancients, it was *Cheld*, or with a doubled breath, *Hheld*, which is now our *Held* (Hero). Goldast, in his *Ancient Admonitions*, page 366. I believe, says the same author, that the *Helvetians* <note>the Swiss</note> were so named as if they were kinsmen of the Celts. Thus we have names like *Hildebrand*, as if "Celt-Brennus," and likewise *Hiltibold*, *Hiltiman*, and *Hiltiwin*. Indeed, *Chilt* is a name used for both sexes, for which we have examples in *Hildegard*, *Hiltrut*, *Hildegund*, *Adelheid*, *Ragnhild*, and so on. The reason for this is found in legends. The Celts say there was a Queen whom Hercules met, fathering a son named *Celtus*, from whom the tribe took its name. Female names are derived from her, and masculine names from him. And I believe this "Celt" is the *Hilte* <note>a "bogeyman" figure</note> with whom nurses threaten wailing infants. Berosus, however, names him as a King, and Appian records that *Celtus* was the son of Polyphemus, not Hercules. Let the reader decide which author to trust.

### 41. Heller, Farthing.

The *Heller* <note>a small German coin</note> is named after the mint at Hall <note>Schwäbisch Hall</note>, from which these coins were produced in great quantity. Matthias Cleiss, *On the Genuine Essence of Loans and Money*, section 57. Others believe they are called *Haller* as if they were a "half-penny" (*halber Pfenning*), *Helbling*, or *Halbling*.

In ancient legal instruments, three Hellers "good and valid" are paid for one Pfennig. Sain, against *Trier*, in the documents on page 24. Since they are unequal, he says, it may well happen that a Heller in one place is as good as, or better than, a Pfennig in another.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the title "Dominus" (Lord or Master), moving from the previous page's discussion on the legal distinction between an owner and one who holds the right to use property. It examines the term's evolution from a domestic title to an imperial honorific, and finally its social application across Europe, particularly in Germany and Austria.</meta>

...is of the Law of Nations <note>original: "Jurisgentium"</note>. *Law 'From this law' 3, Digests on Justice and Law.* Furthermore, the usufructuary <note>one who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note>, although not the Owner of the thing, is nevertheless called the Master of the Right of Usufruct; and therefore, according to the subject matter, he can be called a Master. **Alexander**, *Counsel 129, number 3, book 2.* See **Chard.** **Tusch.** *Practical Conclusions, letter D, conclusion 614, number 7 and following.*

### ADDITION.

At first, those were called "Masters" <note>Latin: "Domini"</note> who presided over a house or held some domestic mastery; later, however, the meaning of this word was extended even to the power of commanding. Thus, **Virgil** calls the Romans *Masters of the world*, and the **Jurist** calls **Antoninus** *Lord* in *the penultimate law, Digests on those things which are deleted in a will.* **Pliny** calls **Trajan** "Lord" in his Epistles and in his Panegyric to Trajan. Augustus, however, preferred to be called *Emperor* <note>Imperator</note> rather than Lord. Eventually, not only Princes but all were called "Lords" by those who wished to show them dutiful honor. Thus **Nefennius** calls **Paul** *Lord* in *Law Nefennius 22, Digests on the Falcidian Law.* **Seneca** also reports that even in the time of Nero, it was customary to call those encountered on the road "Lords" if their names did not come to mind. **Elbertus Leoninus**, *On Usufruct, chapter 5, number 23.* He who was first after the Emperor was greeted with the general title *Despotes*, that is, *Lord*, just as the first Brother of the King is called *Monsieur* <note>My Lord</note> today among the French. **Julius Caesar Bulenger**, *Treatise on the Roman Empire, book 8, chapter 1.*

The Latin title of *Dominus*, which was humble in the beginning, gradually ascended to the highest peak, and though it remained there for some time, it also began to be shared with others whose fortune had not yet reached those higher summits. To the ancients, a *Dominus* was one who provided a banquet, and "dominia" were banquets—not just any, but those celebrated at home. **Lucilius** in his *Satires, book 13*, says: "First, let all 'dominia' and 'sodalitia' be abolished," understanding by *sodalitia* those feasts provided by Magistrates or fellowships in public places rather than in one's own home. **Connan**, *3. commentary 3. number 1. and 10. commentary 5. number 7.* **Cujas**, *11. observations 12.*

In the following age, the title of Lord was considered so grand and proud by the Romans that some Emperors refused it, the name "Lord" being fitting for God; this is treated extensively by **Limn.** in *Public Law, book 4, chapter 6, number 61.* Some, however, approved the word, *numbers 62, 63.* Some of the Popes followed this in their letters to the Emperors, *number 64.* According to some political authors, *Digest 41 on Legacies 3, Law 13, section 1 on Annual Legacies*, and **Tacitus** in *Annals 3*, Civil Law grants much reverence to women, as it calls them Mistresses <note>Dominas</note>, and indeed Most Holy Mistresses. **Limn.** in *Public Law, book 2, chapter 14, number 3.*

Whether a husband is compelled to greet his wife as Mistress is discussed in *numbers 65 and 66*, and extensively by **Walther** in *Privileges of Doctors, page 291.* A Doctor <note>an academic title-holder</note> is to be 

<column-break/>

I also remember that **Starenberg** indignantly returned a sealed letter to someone because the writer had used the word **Baron** and not **Lord** on the address. See **Petrus Gregorius**, *Syntagma 15, number 2.*

### 44. Lord’s Rent, to be valued according to the Lord’s Rent. Manorial Tributes <note>original: "Census dominici"</note>.

In the valuation of estates, it is not customary to estimate the guilder <note>Gulden</note> as 20 florins of capital, but the settled money-guilder is reckoned at thirty guilders, and the unsettled at twenty-five guilders; and the *malter* of grain (sixty *viertel* counted as one *malter*) at one guilder; annually the *fuder* of wine at fifteen

<column-break/>

guilders. However, the prices of wine and grain vary in our time, and are reckoned significantly higher.

->ADDITION.<-

That the most correct way is to make the valuation of the division according to the Lord’s Rents <note>German: "Herrengülten"; a fixed ground rent paid to a feudal lord</note>. See **Meichsner**, *volume 2, decision 5, folio 179, 188, 229, 452.* And from the common custom and observance of Germany, there is a certain and prescribed estimation of how high one should value the buildings and Lord's rents, likewise the grain. **Gail**, *On Imperial Pledges, chapter 18, number 12.* Hence those who give grain as a loan ought to value it in no other way than by the "Lord’s valuation." **Wehner**.

### 45. Sovereignty. Royalties see below under the word Royalties <note>original: "Regalia"</note>.

Through the word *Herrlichkeit* <note>translated as 'Sovereignty' or 'Lordship'</note>, today in Germany "Royalties" are designated, and it carries the same meaning as the word *Regalia*; **Schrader** confirms this with many points and says it is beyond all doubt. *Borch. counsels, part 2, counsel 18, verse 'similarly also'.* **Regner Sixtin**, *On Royalties, book 1, chapter 1, number 19, and chapter 5, number 105.*

The word *Herrlichkeit* also includes criminal judgments, the High Court <note>German: "das Halsgericht", literally the 'Neck-Court', referring to jurisdiction over crimes punishable by death</note>. **Tileman**, *Decisions of the Imperial Chamber, volume 3, number 60.* Therefore, it must be understood according to the subject matter and the circumstances of the persons. **Cothman**, *Academic Counsels 39, number 8.*

->ADDITION.<-

In the Recesses of the Empire <note>resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note> and the Imperial Capitulation, by which the Royalties are confirmed to the States of the Empire, and in the *Political Reform* under the title *Of Craftsmen's Sons*, they are called: Royalties, Sovereignties, Lordships <note>Regalien, Hoheiten, Herrlichkeiten</note>. Strictly speaking, "Royal Rights" <note>Regalia jura</note> are called the supreme rights of those who shine forth with more illustrious or other dignity in the Republic.

What "With all high sovereignty and lordship" <note>Mit aller Hoch- und Herrlichkeit</note> signifies. **Limn.**, *On Public Law, book 7, chapter 1, number 50, page 34.* The most noble aristocratic lordships. **Dr. Tabor**, *On Votes, page 227.* Therefore, nowadays the following words are inserted into feudal letters: *Yet to us and ours etc. in our feudal holdings, lordships, superiorities, rights, and customs, and otherwise to everyone in his rights without harm.* In 1652, such letters were sent back because of the novelty of a single little word being inserted. ### 46. Lordship. Barony.

**Lordship** <note>German: *Herrschafft*</note> means the same thing as a Barony <note>Latin: *Baronia*</note>, and has since the most ancient times. There is no difference between a "Free-Lord" <note>Baron</note> and a "Lord," nor between a "Free-Lordship" and a "Lordship," as discussed at length by **Paurmeister** in *On Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 10, number 31 to the end.* And because "Lordship," just like "County" <note>Latin: *Graffschafft*</note>, is a collective name for an entire community—denoting and containing Cities, Villages, fields, Territory, and all similar things subject to a Baron (the Lord)—as taught by **Sichard** in *Feudal Consultations 1, number 22.* From the fact that a Lordship is granted under the name of "universal Domain" of that land with full jurisdiction, **Henricus Rosenthal** in *On Fiefs, chapter 2, conclusion 1, number 4* concludes that it must be understood to carry royal dignity and power. It claims for itself everything that other royal fiefs or allodial lands <note>land owned outright rather than held from a superior lord</note> claim: and thus also the right of territorial superiority. **Freccia** agrees in *On Fiefs, book 2, title 'Who is called a Chamberlain', number 47; see also Gaeddaeus in the consultation on the restitution of the Barony of Vallendar throughout, especially number 151 and following, and number 311 and following.*

**Lordship** signifies nothing other than a territory possessing simple Jurisdiction and "Mixed Command" <note>Latin: *mixtum Imperium*; the power to enforce the law and manage civil administration</note>, according to **Gylman**, *book 1, decision 1, number 41*; **Wehner** in *Practical Observations, under the word 'Herrschafft'*; and *Acts of Lindau, folio 846 near the end.* Indeed, sometimes "Pure Command" <note>Latin: *merum Imperium*; the highest legal power, including the right of execution</note> is inherent to it. **Gylman** notes in the same place (number 165) that such a naming also contributes to the proof of a territory's status. **Cravetta**, *Consultation 673, number 12 near the end.* For indeed, the quality of a thing is recognized by its name. *Law 1, Code on the office of the Prefect of the city; Law 'Defenders', Code on the defenders of Cities; Jason, Consultation 16, number 42, book 2, with the citations therein.*

**Lordship**, however, not infrequently differs from a Barony. For one who possesses "Regalia" <note>term: *Regalia* refers to royal rights such as minting coins, collecting tolls, or high justice</note> is not necessarily said to have royal dignity. Not every grant made by an Emperor or King bestows royal dignity, but only that through which a fief is granted that has royal dignity attached to it. **Paciano**, *On Proofs, book 2, chapter 36, number 215.* For Regalia are rights, whereas goods having royal dignity attached are not rights but physical things to which the dignity clings. **Sixtinus**, *On Regalia, book 1, chapter 3, number 9.* Therefore, those who have Regalia do not obtain the name of royal dignity or any other peculiar name from them; but those who possess goods with royal dignity attached are designated as Dukes, Marquises, Counts, or Barons. **Sixtinus**, *chapter 3, numbers 12 and 18.*

Ownership of lands, people, and estates without inherent Jurisdiction cannot be called a **Lordship**, territory, or district. **Gylman**, *Judicial Matters, book 1, decision 1, number 42.*

## ADDITION.

What the word **Lordship** <note>German: *Herrschafft*</note> imports. **Klock**, *Consultation 50, number 195.* What the words **Lordship and Court** <note>German: *Herrschafft und Gerichte*</note> denote. **Klock**, *volume 3, consultation 181, number 105.*

Someone once prepared a list of lands from such places as can be found nowhere in the world except in the titles of new Lords, which often serves only for poor reputation. Concerning the praise for Mr. **Harsdörffer** <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer, a famous Baroque poet and scholar</note>, see **Schupp** in *A Friend in Need, page 123.* It is a wonder of the world that he discusses everything knowable. Nothing can be imagined more vain than titles and the boasting of names and coats of arms that signify no actual thing. **Tolosa**, *On the Republic, book 6, chapter 11, number 13.* For a title without the reality is like faith without works. **Riminaldus**, *Consultation 602, number 66.* Some, like the soldier in Plautus <note>a reference to the 'braggart soldier' archetype in Roman comedy</note>, mock themselves with grand titles of "Gurgustidonian" fields and other foot-and-a-half-long titles, for which there is scarcely room in Utopia or any land of shadows. **Victor**, *On the Causes of Exemptions, conclusion 31.* 

When **Charles V** wrote to **Francis I**, King of France—with whom he had business—according to the requirements of his Majesty, the Imperial titles and the provinces and dominions of the illustrious House of Austria filled a large space on the paper. The biting Frenchman, in his response, took up just as much space by repeating "France" in this manner: **"Francis I, King of France, of France, of France,"** etc., adding that his single kingdom of France was sufficient to dominate all the provinces of the Empire. **Piccart**, *Decade 4, Historical-Political Observations, chapter 10, page 228.* If anyone stuffs the smallest matters into titles, they imitate the King of Morocco, who some years ago is said to have sent a letter to the United Provinces of the Netherlands with a long title thirty rhythmic verses long, followed by only three or four lines explaining the actual matter for which the letter was written. **Limnaeus**, *On Public Law, book 4, chapter 6, number 39.* 

Beneath the image of the most warlike hero **Johann de Werth** <note>a famous general in the Thirty Years' War</note>, only these words were inscribed: **"This is Johann de Werth, who deserves all titles, and seeks none."** **Zeiller**, *Century 3, Epistle, page 503.* **"After all, one pays no money for titles"** <note>German: *Man giebt ja kein Geld für die Titul*</note>, as **Draco** says in *On Patricians, page 229.* Therefore one can well measure them out with a **Brabantine ell** <note>original: *Brabantischen Elen*; a unit of length used for measuring cloth, implying the titles are as long as fabric</note>, as **Schupp** says in *The Inept Orator, page 16.* **"Many a man has a title without a calf"** <note>original: *Titul sine vitulo*; a pun on 'title' and 'cattle' (vitulus/calf), meaning a title without any property or wealth to back it up</note>, just as Pope Paul III in 1546 made **Olaus Magnus** Archbishop of Uppsala in Sweden, and **Robert Venantius** Archbishop of Armagh in Ireland <note>at a time when these areas were Protestant and the Catholic appointees could not actually go there</note>, so that they had only the bare title, as can be read in **Sleidanus**. 

**Heliogabalus** <note>Roman Emperor known for eccentricity</note> commanded his servants to collect **spiderwebs**. When they brought together about ten thousand pounds of them, the Emperor said that from this one could understand how great the city of Rome was, as **Lampridius** testifies in *Life of Heliogabalus, chapter 26, folio 334.* **Zeiller**, *Century 2, Epistle, page 506.* Regarding what use vain titles are, see **Zeiller**, *Century 4.*

### 46. Lordship. Barony.

**Lordship** <note>original: "Herrschafft"</note> means the same as **Barony**, and has since the most ancient times. There is no difference between a **Free Lord** <note>original: "Freyherrn"</note> and a **Lord**, or between a **Free Lordship** and a **Lordship**. This is discussed at length by *Paurmeister, On Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 10, number 31 to the end.* Furthermore, that **Lordship**, just like a **County** <note>original: "Graffschafft"</note>, is a collective noun for a corporate body, denoting and containing Cities, Villages, fields, Territory, and all such things subject to a Baron, **the Lord**, as recorded by *Sichard in Feudal Consultations, 1, number 22.* Because **Lordship** is granted under the name of "universal Dominion" of that land with all kinds of Jurisdiction, *Henricus Rosenthal, On Fiefs, chapter 2, conclusion 1, number 4* concludes that it must be understood to coincide with royal dignity and power. It claims for itself all things that other royal fiefs or allodial <note>land held independently of a superior lord</note> lands claim: and thus also the right of territorial superiority. *Freccia, On Fiefs, book 2, title 'Who is called a Chamberlain', number 47* agrees; see also *Goeddæus in the consultation on the restitution of the Barony of Vallendar, throughout, especially number 151 and following, and number 311 and following.*

**Lordship** signifies nothing other than a territory to which simple Jurisdiction and 'mixed empire' <note>Latin: "mixtum Imperium"; power over civil matters and minor crimes</note>—*Gylman, book 1, decision 1, number 41; Wehner in Practical Observations under the word 'Herrschafft'; Acts of Lindau, folio 846 at the end and following*—or indeed sometimes 'pure empire' <note>Latin: "merum Imperium"; the power of life and death</note> is attached. *Gylman, same location, number 165.* This naming also contributes to the proof of [possession of] a territory. *Cravetta, consultation 673, number 12, near the end.* For quality is recognized by the name. *Law 1, Code of the office of the Prefect of the city; the law 'defenders', Code of the defense of the City; Jason, consultation 16, number 42, book 2, with those cited there.*

**Lordship**, however, not infrequently differs from a **Barony**. For one possessing royalties <note>Latin: "regalia"; specific rights or privileges of a king</note> is not said to have royal dignity, nor does every grant made by an Emperor or King bestow royal dignity. Only that grant through which a fief is bestowed having royal dignity attached to it does so. *Pacianus, On Proofs, book 2, chapter 36, number 215.* **Royalties** are indeed rights, but goods having royal dignity attached to them are not rights, but physical things to which dignity adheres. *Sixtinus, On Royalties, book 1, chapter 3, number 9.* Therefore, those who have **Royalties** do not obtain the name of royal dignity or any other peculiar name from them; but those who possess goods with royal dignity attached are called **Dukes, Marquises, Counts, and Barons**. *Sixtinus, same chapter, numbers 12 and 18.*

**Dominion over lands**, men, and estates without inherent Jurisdiction cannot be called **a Lordship** <note>original: "ein Herrschafft"</note>, a territory, or a district. *Gylman, Judged Matters, book 1, decision 1, number 42.*

In *Novel 70* <note>a decree by Emperor Justinian</note>, **Hönnius** speaks best of all in his most absolute dissertation *On Dignities, thesis 6, throughout*. Concerning those greedy for honor, **Drexelius** says in *The Gold Mine, page 310*: Let those greedy for any kind of glory be judged, who, being destitute of praise, have gathered sprigs of laurel with a hurried hand from deserted mountains and the piratical prows of fly-boats <note>small, fast pirate ships</note>. And on page 312, concerning the most vain titles: The King of Bisnagar <note>original: *Rex Bisnagensis*; the Vijayanagara Empire in India</note>, Spouse of good fortune, God of the most powerful Kings of great provinces, King of all cavalries, Lord, Master and Teacher of those who do not know how to speak, Emperor of three Emperors, Conqueror of all he sees, Preserver of the conquered, whom the eight parts of the world fear and dread, Destroyer of Muhammadan armies, Lord of all provinces he has subdued, Knight to whom no one is equal, and vanquisher of the strongest, etc. There is need of a torch <note>to see the way through</note> for a title this long. In rebuking the vanity of titles, I could easily bury a whole day: but I do not wish to pollute this virgin paper with such things. I shall add at least one more thing. The word **Dominion** <gloss>German: *Herrschafft*</gloss> is most general; it even contains places recently acquired. **Mindanus** *On the Continuance of Cases, book 3, chapter 21, number 26.*

### 47. Estate of Lords, Estate of Knights. The Equestrian Order.

**Schrader** teaches in *volume 2, consultation 23, number 10*, that there is a supreme distinction between the order of Illustrious Men and those who belong to the **Equestrian Order** <note>the knightly class</note>, known as the **Estate of Lords and Knights** <gloss>German: *Herrn- und Ritterstand*</gloss>. This is apparent both from the difference in name, from which a difference in the thing or meaning is gathered, and also because there are many grades of Nobility: for some are Simple Nobles, others More Noble, and others indeed Most Noble. *Law "ut gradatim", at the beginning, Digest, on duties and honors; chapter 1, on children born of a marriage to a Morganatic wife, Besold, Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

*Law "quæro", Digest, on the restoration of birth; Law "tradimentis", Code, on the Episcopal court; Schrader in the cited place, number 13.*

In some places, such as in Austria, the **Estate of Lords and Knights** are separated from one another: as they also are in the German-Roman Empire. In other places, however, they are compressed into a single class.

The word **Baron** <term>Baron: originally a "man" or "vassal," it became a specific rank of nobility</term> is sometimes taken generally for any noble, as can be seen in **Matthæus de Afflictis** *chapter 1, number 1, on those who can grant fiefs*. **Schrader** *On Fiefs, part 10, section 1, number 25*. **Surdus** *consultation 453, number 56, book 3*. When it is used specifically, it is distinguished from the other grades of nobility, as in **Limnäus**, *Public Law, book 4, chapter 5, number 7.*

### 48. Duke. Leader.

**Duke** <term>Duke: from the Latin *Dux*, a military leader</term> seems to be named from "leading an army," according to **Isidore**, *Etymologies, book 9, title "On kingdoms and military terms."* **Zasius** in *Epitome of Fiefs, part 5, number 6*. **Oldendorp**, *class 5, on beneficial actions*. Hence the German word **Duke** <gloss>German: *Herzog*</gloss> is as if he were a **Lord of the March** <gloss>German: *Herr des Zugs*</gloss>, that is, the Lord of the army. **Borncholt** *On Fiefs, chapter 6, number 31*: that is, that he marches before the army, or makes a march with the army. **Ulrich Zasius** agrees in *On Fiefs, chapter 5*. See my own *Treatise on Subordinate Commands, page 96*; and at length **Rudolph**, *Treatise on the Dukes of Italy*. **Hotman** in the *Feudal Lexicon* under the word *Duces*. **Meursius** in the *Gallo-Greek Lexicon* under the word Δὺξ <note>Greek: *Dux*</note>, where he discusses the Grand Duke <gloss>Italian: *Gran Duca*</gloss>, or **Grand or Arch-Duke** <gloss>German: *Groß- oder Erz-Herzog*</gloss>.

And **Marculphus**, an ancient writer, shows that Dukes, Margraves, and other Magistrates once depended on the will of the supreme Prince. He says, "It is not easy to commit a **judicial dignity** <note>original: *judiciariam dignitatem*; an office combining administrative and legal power</note> to just anyone, unless their loyalty and vigor are first seen to be proven; therefore, since we seem to have found both your loyalty and your usefulness, we have committed to you the action of the County, Duchy, or Patriciate in that district which your predecessor was seen to have managed until now, for the purpose of acting and ruling." He calls it a "judicial dignity" and says it was granted not for possessing, but for ruling. **Henning Arnisaeus**, *On the Law of Majesty, book 2, chapter 4, number 15*. **Paulus Aemilius** says more clearly in *Chilperic, book 1*: "In the beginning, Dukes and Counts were set over tribes and cities by Kings, and when it seemed fit, they were dismissed. Later, a custom grew strong that they would not be forced to leave their command unless convicted of a crime, and finally, it was provided by the oath of Kings as each was gifted with that office." In what year and how **Reinold**, the second of this name, Count of Guelders, was created a Duke by **Louis IV the Bavarian**, is clear from the following:

> Louis IV, to all who shall see these letters, greetings. Since Rudolph, Count of Guelders, born of royal stock, has performed many services for the Empire and is still able to perform them, along with Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, and Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, and King John...

### 47. The Estate of Lords and Knights. The Knightly Order.

Schrader teaches in volume 2, consultation 23, number 10, that there is a supreme distinction between the order of "Illustrious Men" and those who belong to the knightly order—that is, between the **Lords' Estate** and the **Knights' Estate**. This is apparent from the difference in their names, from which a difference in the reality or meaning is gathered. It is also because there are several grades of Nobility: for some are Simple Nobles, others are Nobler, and some are indeed Most Noble. (See *On Offices and Honors*, and chapter 1 regarding children born of a morganatic marriage).
*Besoldus, Volume 1.*

(See the law beginning *I ask* in the *Digest* on the restoration of birth, and the law *By deliveries* in the *Code* on the Episcopal court. Schrader, in the place cited above, number 13.)

In some places, such as in Austria, the **Lords' Estate** and **Knights' Estate** are separated from one another; this is also the case in the German-Roman Empire. In other places, however, they are grouped into a single class.

The word **Baron** is sometimes used generally for any noble, as can be seen in Matthaeus de Afflictis (chapter 1, number 1, on those who can grant fiefs). ### 48. Duke.

The word "Duke" <note>Latin: *Dux*</note> seems to come from "leading an army" <note>Latin: *ducendo*</note>. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book 9, title on the names of kingdoms and the military. Zasius in *Epitome of Fiefs*, part 5, number 6. Oldendorp, class 5, on beneficiary actions. From this comes the German **Herzog**, as if it were "a Lord of the March" <note>German: *ein Herr des Zugs*</note>, that is, the Lord of the army. Borcholt, *On Fiefs*, chapter 6, number 31: **"that is, he who goes before the army, or makes a march with the army."** Ulrich Zasius agrees with this in *On Fiefs*, chapter 5. See also my own treatise *On Subordinate Powers*, folio 96; and at length Rudolph in his treatise *On the Dukes of Italy*. Hotman in his *Feudal Lexicon* under the word *Duces*. Meursius in his *Greco-Barbarian Lexicon* under the word *Dex*, where he discusses the "Mega-duke" <note>Greek: *Megas Doux*</note>, the **Grand Duke**, the **Great Duke**, or **Archduke**.

Marculphus, an ancient writer, shows that Dukes, Margraves, and other magistrates formerly depended upon the will of the supreme Prince. "It is not easy," he says, "to commit judicial dignity to just anyone, unless their loyalty and vigor have first been proven. Therefore, since we have found your loyalty and usefulness to be certain, we have committed to you the action of the County, the Duchy, and the Patriciate in that district which your predecessor was seen to have managed until now, for you to act and rule." He calls it a "judicial dignity" and says it was granted not for possession, but for ruling. Henning Arnisaeus, *On the Right of Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, number 15. More clearly, Paulus Aemilius says in *Chilperic*, book 1: "Initially, Dukes and Counts were placed over peoples and cities by Kings, and were dismissed when it seemed fit. Later, the custom became established that they were not forced to leave their command unless convicted of a crime; and finally, when anyone was gifted with that office, it was secured by the oath of the Kings." In what year and in what manner Reinold II, Count of Guelders, was created a Duke by Louis IV the Bavarian, is clear from what follows:

"Louis the Fourth, to all who shall see these letters, greetings. Since Rudolph, Count of Guelders, born of royal lineage, has performed many services for the Empire and may yet perform more, [and with the witness of] Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, and Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, and King John..."

With the King of Bohemia, Rudolph Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, Rudolph Duke of Saxony, and Louis Margrave of Brandenburg, our firstborn son, in attendance, we create the said Reinold, formerly a Count, the Duke of Guelders <note>Original: "Geldriæ." Reinold II "the Learned" was elevated to Duke by Emperor Louis the Bavarian in 1339, though this text dates the charter to 1309, likely referring to an earlier confirmation or a transcription error in the source.</note>, along with his legitimate descendants, granting this privilege: whenever we or our successors shall hold Parliaments, or when any new Princes are created, or similar public acts are celebrated, he shall then personally clothe us in the Imperial robes.

Furthermore, when our successors, the Kings of the Romans, are crowned at Aachen, Milan, and Rome, he or his heirs shall place the Royal Crown upon the heads of said Kings, shall carry it, and bear it in their hands. Moreover, for the greater splendor of the said Duchy and Principality, we assign to him, according to the custom of the Empire, four officials named below and their heirs: namely, *Jacob van Myxlaer* as Steward <term>Oeconomus: a high-ranking official overseeing the household or estate</term>; *Everhard van Vuillp* as Marshal; *Theodoric van Tiendem* as Cupbearer or Pourer; and *Guilielm van Brouchuüsen* as Chamberlain. Likewise, we grant him the right of minting gold coins, according to the value of the currency of the Archbishop of Cologne, the Duke of Brabant, and the Counts of Hainaut and Holland. In testimony of the truth of this, we have ordered these letters to be written and confirmed with our Seal. Given at Frankfurt on the 19th day of March, in the year of our Lord one thousand three hundred and nine.

### 49. Marriage Gift. Dowry.

It is well established from Bignon, *in notes on the Formulas of Marculphus, page 561 and following*, that in ancient times husbands endowed wives, and not wives husbands. Tacitus says somewhere, regarding those Germanic tribes: the wife does not offer a dowry to the husband, but the husband to the wife, etc.
On whether marriage gifts <note>Original: "Heyrath-Güther"</note> must be equal? See *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 2, consultation 10.* Concerning a father endowing a daughter, from whose assets it is reckoned to be made? See Carocius’s *singular treatise.*

### ADDITION.

In the most illustrious Hessian family, by virtue of a fraternal arrangement, we see that a just dowry there is 24,000 Rhenish florins; and if no male heirs are left and only one daughter remains, the dowry is increased by 4,000 Rhenish florins. Car. von Hagen, *Public Law, book 2, chapter 7, number 2*, stating there, "it is also..." 
In the Duchy of Württemberg, it is 20,000 gold pieces, and the maximum dowry for the Nobility in Swabia does not exceed four thousand florins. By the law of the Venetians, it was not permitted to give more than six thousand gold ducats as a dowry to a Patrician. And if a Patrician married a commoner, they fixed the sum at two thousand gold pieces. Sprenger, *On Modesty, pages 89, 90.* That a dowry is sometimes established from public funds, I have shown in several places *in the Comparison of the Republic of Nuremberg with the Venetian Republic, which is among Rupert's Orations, 12, page 560.*
For what a father among the Moors gives to a son as a marriage gift, see Michael Hemmersam’s *Description of a West-Indian Journey, which I edited, page 31.*
If a dowry is given by a father in another’s name (as because he is perhaps the administrator for the daughter, or her debtor), then if he pays it, he does not act as a father, but as any administrator or debtor would; and it will deserve the name of an "adventitious" dowry <term>dos adventitia: a dowry coming from a source other than the father</term> rather than a "profectitious" one <term>dos profectitia: a dowry provided directly from the father’s own property</term>, *book 5, sections 6 and 11, under this title.* In cases of doubt, however, he is presumed to have given as a parent, not as a stranger, *book 7, Code on promised dowries*, even if the daughter has her own property and is wealthy in her own right, so that she could be endowed from her own means. Barbosa, *book 4, chapter 51, axiom 7*; Zorer, *part 2, question 7, number 533*; Knipschild, *On Trusts, chapter 6, number 235*; Sichard, *on said law 7, number 4.* The reason for this presumption lies in the paternal duty, as a father is bound to endow his daughter *said law 7, law 19, on the Duty of Parents, law 43, on Legacies 3*, so that having been endowed, she may marry better and find a husband more easily, *said law 19, law 2, under this title.* From this source comes the Imperial decree *in said law 19*, that a father who refuses to give a dowry to his daughter can be compelled to endow her according to the extent of his means and the dignity of his lineage, *said law 19, said law 7*—not indeed by right of action <note>i.e., a standard lawsuit</note>, but by the office of the Judge, Gail, *book 2, observation 95, at the beginning.* According to Alexander, *consultation 7, number 10, volume 1*, and Socinus, *consultation 101, number 3, book 3*, it is a famous and celebrated question whether a father, who had bequeathed 4,000 for his daughter's dowry in his will, but while surviving and seeing her married, gave only 2,000 as a dowry...

<header>Letter H.</header>

If someone has established a dowry: should he be considered to have reduced a legacy <note>A "legacy" here refers to a specific gift left in a will.</note> because of this? No. Campez, in his work *On the Establishment of Dowries and Their Privileges*, part 1, question 36, reports that this was debated by Johannes de Ysolanis of Bologna and Johannes Friedrich Sol in his treatise *On the Dowry*, question 8. On the subject of the dowry and its privileges, see also Novellus Baldus, Jacobus Butrigarius, Odofredus, Phanucius de Phanuciis, Johannes Friedrich Sol, Antonius Guibertus Costanus, and Johannes Campez, in the folio edition printed at Lyon, and in the Nuremberg Library, the Venice edition of 1499. Also see Constantinus Rogers and Martinus Pegius on the law of dowry privileges.

A father bequeaths to his son a <term>gift on account of marriage</term> <note>original: "donationem propter nuptias" — a gift from the groom's side to the bride, often matching the dowry</note>; the mother records 825 florins of interest from it, which are then disputed by the son after the mother's death. The question is whether this gift on account of marriage must necessarily bear interest? Regarding this case, see the "Response" mentioned below under the word <term>Counter-dower</term> <note>original: "Widerlag" — a German legal term for property settled on a wife by a husband in exchange for her dowry</note>. If the husband did not seek the interest on the dowry while alive, he is seen to have gifted it; it remains at the husband's risk and is confirmed upon death. Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 547.

The gift on account of marriage—the counter-gift—is transferred from the deceased's widow to the heirs; it does not fall to the <term>agnates</term> <note>Male-line relatives</note> who are simultaneously invested in the fief, as a dotal estate might. Carpzov, part 2, decision 168. How the payment of a dowry is proven is taught by Mascardus, volume 1, *On Evidence*, conclusion 362.

## 50. Marriage Contracts. Dotal Pacts.

On these, see Fichard, volume 1, counsel 15, and the materials I have transposed from the notes of my brother, Johann Georg Besold (of pious memory), in the 3rd dispute on the Municipal Law of Württemberg, thesis 61, etc.

### ADDITION.

A treatise on prenuptial agreements exists by Neostadius. Kohl also wrote on dotal pacts. Johannes Petrus Fontanella published a vast work on marriage contracts.

When a marriage gift is promised to someone at the time of their betrothal, and a formal marriage contract is drawn up regarding that gift as well as the counter-dower and other matters, but the marriage gift is neither brought into the marriage nor has interest paid on it: the question arises whether the husband is bound by such a marriage agreement in such a way that he cannot ordain or dispose of something else. Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 462 and following; also numbers 530 and 587. If a wife does not fulfill the marriage contracts, the husband is likewise not bound to them. Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 586 and following. The husband, when drawing up the marriage contract, presumably looked toward the payment of the marriage gift. In the same question 7, number 598.

Agreements are rightly added to the promise or giving of a dowry, not only at the time of the contract but even after an interval. <note>Citing various sections of the Code and Digest of Roman Law regarding pacts and dowries.</note> For this reason they are called "dotal pacts," and the writings made about them are "dotal instruments"—not because it is strictly necessary to put them in writing, but because they are usually written and documented for the sake of greater proof and reliability. Vultejus, book 1, *Civil Law*.

Besold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

c. 20. Everhard Speckhan in his *Synopsis of the Law*. Bornitius on instruments, book 2, member 2, chapter 37. Therefore, if these agreements are lawful and honorable, they provide the law for the case, so that the legal action for the dowry must be shaped according to those conventions. However, if they contain anything contrary to the law or good morals, or things which oppose the very nature of a dowry—for instance, if it is agreed that the husband shall not enjoy the fruits <note>The income or produce generated by the dowry property.</note>, or that the dowry should be taken away from a surviving wife, etc., and her condition is thereby made worse—they are considered as if they were never added. The most recent law rejects inequality in pacts, requiring equal conditions on both sides for the dowry and the gift on account of marriage, following the principle of equality in the Code. Sometimes, however, by local custom, the gift on account of marriage is not only larger than the dowry but even double its size, especially in Saxony. Schneidewin on the Institutes, number 4. Beust on dowries, chapter 7. Rittershusius writes the same regarding the regions of Nuremberg, Swabia, Bavaria, and the Palatinate. Conversely, sometimes the dowry is larger than the marriage gift; see Coler, decision 192, and Hartmann Pistor, book 1, questions 4 and 5. That modern court practice has relaxed this requirement for equality in quantity is taught by Master Biccius, following Gail and others. Even if under Civil Law dotal pacts regarding universal succession <note>Inheriting the entire estate.</note> are not valid even as a "gift in anticipation of death" <note>original: "donationis mortis causa"</note>, a different rule has been received from the well-known customs of Germany, and especially the Republic of Nördlingen. Hartmann Pistor, Heigius, Gail, and Antonius Faber. These are valid with the force of a last will if five or seven witnesses are present. Carpzov, *Forensic Jurisprudence*, 2, constitution 43, definition 2, number 1.

Widows, by virtue of marriage contracts, gain all the husband's goods; even that which the husband reserved for himself to give to his blood relatives or whomever he wished is owed to her if he dies without making such a disposition. This is how Johannes Petrus Fontanella defines it in *Marriage Contracts*. Modestinus Pistor treats this matter more extensively in question 168, where he cites many legal precedents; and there his commentator, Jacob Schultes, testifies that today judgment is undoubtedly pronounced according to this opinion. Besold recently followed and praised these authors. See also Rauchbar, Bursatus, Cephalus, and others cited by them. Thus Dr. Taber reviews it in *On Dotal Pacts*, page 84. But on page 92 of the same work, he explains his own mind more freely: we do not dwell on Besold's authority here, since he speaks not only without the Law, but even the authorities cited by him, such as Modestinus Pistor and Fontanella, clearly establish the contrary and support our sen-

In the Frankfurt Reformation <note>The *Reformatio Francofurtensis*, a local legal code of Frankfurt am Main</note>, page 3, title 2, sections 4 and 5, it is decreed: first, indeed, that dowry pacts which treat of succession are useless (as per said section 4); and yet, the same section adds that they shall be valid if they have been confirmed by death. This is as if to say: those pacts shall not have the effect of contracts, but shall have the force of a last will if they are confirmed by death and not revoked, following the argument in *Book 32, section 2, of the Digests regarding donations between husband and wife.*

### §. 51. Witches, Fiends, Sorceresses. *Sagæ*. <note>The Latin term *Saga* originally meant a fortune-teller or wise woman, but in this period refers specifically to a witch.</note>

These are those who have dealings and pacts established with Devils. And they are called **Fiends** <note>original: "Unholden"</note>, as if "without grace" <note>original: "ohne Huld"</note>, those to whom no one is gracious.

They are also called in certain places **Trutten** <note>A South German/Austrian term for a witch or nightmare-spirit</note>, also **Wichherssen**, from the Saxon **Wicken**, which is the same as **soothsaying**. There are some who think **Witches** <note>original: "Heren" / "Hexen"</note> are named after a certain Queen of the Amazons, as noted by Aventinus in book 1, and Zeiller in his *Historical Tragedies*, folio 85. They are likewise called **Striges** <note>originally referring to mythical screech-owls that sucked the blood of infants</note>; see Becman in *On Origins* under the word *Strix*. See also Gregory of Toulouse in his *Syntagma*, book 34, chapter 20, number 3, where he identifies two species of witches. And Bisciola teaches in his *Subsequent Hours*, book 13, chapter 21, that <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "veneficium" — literally "poisoning," but legally used for harmful magic</note> is common among women.

And if these women have simultaneously harmed humans, they are usually burned. If they have harmed no one, it seems argued in *Article 109 of the Imperial Criminal Constitution* <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* of 1532</note> that they ought to be punished outside the ordinary rules according to the quality of the crime, where it says: **"but where someone has used sorcery, and had done no harm to anyone with it, etc."** Truly, I think that "using **sorcery**" is predicated of Magi and men of similar grain: not of her who is truly a witch; **"Who has renounced God and His saints, and has explicitly bound herself to the enemy of the human race."** And that they are to be condemned for the pact and renunciation alone (which is the primary consideration), is taught by Delrio in book 5, section 16; Lord Friedrich Martin in his *Treatise on Taxes* at the aforementioned Article 109; and Torreblanca in book 3, chapter 13. Especially since that pact exists as something so horrendous and execrable: just as recently in a certain Imperial City a certain witch voluntarily gave herself up and confessed **"that the evil spirit wrote her name in a black book, and to that end made two tears in the thumb of her right hand, and let out as much blood as was necessary for such an entry."**

Among those, however, who think that witches <note>original: "Lamias" — a term for child-devouring demons, used here for witches</note> should not be punished with the extreme penalty, there is also **Antonius Praetorius** in the aforementioned **Thorough Report on Sorcery and Sorcerers**, as well as **Theodorus Thummius** in his *Individual Disputations*, and there is the **Weyerian** view <note>Referring to Johann Weyer (Wierus), who argued that "witches" were actually mentally ill</note>, which is a species of heresy and atheism; for Weyer wrote about delusions and witches in a very dangerous manner and against the mind of the ancients, whom Bodin also refuted in a special booklet added to his *Demonomania*.

<sig>H</sig>

<column-break/>

And regarding the fact that witches must be burned, see **Georg Pictorius of Villingen** in his *Table Talk*, part 2, folio 85.

**From the Carolina Constitution, Article 44**, it appears what the principal indications of incantation and sorcery are, namely, if (1.) someone seriously intends to teach the magic art to another.

(2.) If anyone has threatened to inflict a <term>maleficium</term> <note>harmful magic or "evil doing"</note> upon someone, and the effect followed. *Julius Clarus, book 5, opinions, section "final," question 21, number 37; Bruno on Indications and Torture, part 1, question 3; Menochius, book 1, on Presumptions, question 89, number 60.* And although threats do not prove the deed, they nevertheless prove capital enmities. *Through the law "licet," Digest on Arbitrators; Baldus on the first law of the Code "If anyone has cursed the Emperor," whom see in the Speculator, title on Presumptions, section 1, verse "depone."*

In these cases, however, because of the fallibility of the signs and through what has been seen in such matters, the Judge ought to be extremely prudent and cautious, according to Paris de Puteo in his *Treatise on Syndics*, at the word "Torture," where he relates a story worthy of note on that matter.

(3.) If a defamed sorceress was born of parents who were sorcerers and magi. For if the Mother is a witch, the daughter is usually one as well, according to the well-worn and daily proverb: **"The apple falls not far from the tree."** To which that other one harmonizes: **"The beer often tastes of the barrel."**
Thus Catullus:
> For a Magus must be born of a Mother and her Son. <note>original: "Nam Magus ex Matre & Gnato gignatur oportet" — Catullus 90, referring to the belief that Persian Magi were the product of incest.</note>

Therefore, even incestuous couplings produce such offspring.

(4.) If witches are equipped with toads, sacrificial victims, human limbs, wax images, or pierced needles: this is a probable indication of sorcery; as is this: if a woman who is commonly held to be a witch is seen to touch her enemy, and he suddenly falls down dead, or is seized by leprosy, distortion of the limbs, apoplexy, or a sudden disease. Bodin, *On the Demonomania of Sorcerers*, book 4, chapter 2.

(5.) If a witch invokes a demon, speaks with a demon, and he responds, even though he is not seen. Bodin, *On the Demonomania*, book 4, chapter 3.

(6.) If a certain woman, who was held to be a sorceress, lay down in her bed in the evening, but in the night, with the doors locked, she began to be absent for a moment, and afterwards, with the door still closed, she is proven to have returned to her bedroom. Bodin, *On the Demonomania*, book 4, chapter 1; see Fachin, *Counsel 93, volume 1.*

(7.) If in the chest of a certain woman suspected of sorcery there is found an instrument of mutual obligation, a contract entered into between the witch and the Devil. Bodin, *in the same place.* Likewise **Witch Ointments and the like**. See Merula, *book 1 of Memorable Things, chapter 13 and chapter 4*, where he speaks of the Gnostics (so named from knowledge), as well as witches (named from "presaging"), and in the following chapter.

8.) If a woman, standing in water, throws water from the earth into the air, or if a **witch** <note>original: "saga"</note> is seen pouring a potion into an animal which is later found dead, it is considered evident proof of the **magical arts**. <note>See Peter Binsfeld in his commentary on the final law 'concerning the crime of sorcery' (*de Crim. malef.*), specifically regarding indicators.</note>

9.) If a **witch** <note>original: "Saga"</note> promises a suspicious cure to an afflicted person: <gloss>When they claim that they can drive away the troubling **elves**. <note>original: "Elben." In Germanic folklore, "elves" were often blamed for sudden illnesses or seizures.</note> Or when they have caused harm, they fall under suspicion.</gloss> See Berlichius, conclusion 4; Torreblanca in *On Demonology*, page 386 and following; Binsfeld, folio 465 and 602 in his treatise on sorcery. However, should one turn to **soothsayers** <note>original: "sortilegos"</note> to recover health, specifically when someone has been attacked by one of them? See the *Treasury of Exorcisms*, folio 442 and 633, for much discussion on the difference between one who is **possessed** <note>original: "Dæmoniaci"</note> and one who is **bewitched** <note>original: "maleficiati"</note>.

It must be noted, however, that no one can be condemned to death based on these signs alone, unless a confession by the witch is added. This follows the law *qui sententiam 16* under the title 'on punishments,' and with this text agrees the **Imperial Criminal Code of Emperor Charles V** <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* of 1532, the first uniform body of criminal law in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, Article 22, where it reads: *It is also to be noted that no one shall be finally sentenced to corporal punishment based on any report, sign, or suspicion; rather, one may only be questioned under torture if the report, as it is later found, is sufficient. For if someone is to be finally sentenced to corporal punishment, it must happen through their own confession or proof, as is clearly found in other places in this Code, and not based on presumption or reports.* See my own collections of legal decisions at the end.

In the year 734, the Emperor Leo ordered the execution of Georgius—who held the rank of Patrician and at that time served as the Urban Prefect of Constantinople, a man most devoted to equity—because he had acquitted certain poor women who had been accused of being harmful. It was alleged they were accustomed to slaughtering nursing infants by attacking them unexpectedly, entering through cracks or crevices in houses not large enough for their bodies, or even coming in while the gates were closed. Ignatius the Monk records this event more fully in the *Life of Tarasius*, rebuking those who believe such **illusions** <note>original: "præstigias"</note> can actually occur. But regarding this narrative of Ignatius, see Delrio’s *Magical Disquisitions*, book 2, question 27, section 2; and the most illustrious Baronius, regarding the year of Christ 734.

Whether **vampires** or **night-witches** exist <note>original: "lamiæ seu striges." *Lamiae* were child-devouring demons; *striges* were owl-like spirits that sucked blood.</note> is no small dispute among learned men, concerning which see Cardanus in *On the Variety of Things*, book 15. Those who rely strictly on the principles of nature mock such things as fables. Thus, great doubt has arisen concerning them, with some judging that they exist and others denying it. Those who affirm their existence bring forward experiments; but then they show such contempt for religion and its mysteries that they do not even think it lawful to recite such things. They worship the **Master of the Games** <note>original: "ludi Dominum," likely a reference to the Devil at the Witches' Sabbath.</note> and offer him libations as if to a God. The death of infants often follows after they have touched them;

<column-break/>

in others, as they themselves reported, only **sorcery** <note>original: "veneficium"</note> was the cause of harm. And they confess these things under torture, even though they know such a confession will be their destruction.

Nor does the outcome differ from the confession, since many little boys, otherwise of good health, have wasted away unto death without a manifest cause. And just as an art itself is established from many experiments, so with so many people agreeing on one thing—namely, deaths and deeds of the same nature—this history seems to be a matter of actual art rather than the mere outcome of some **evildoing**.

These same women confess that they lead dances, leap, joke, feast, and lie together at most splendid banquets; they become drunk, grow weary, and suffer such things according to their own estimation. Therefore, they either dream, or imagine, or lie, or tell the absolute truth. To lie on the **rack** <note>original: "eculeo"</note>, and at such evident peril to their lives, is absurd.

To dream is no less unlikely: for those who dream, dream of different things, and not always; but these women always dream the same things on a set day, and they are nearly identical, with little difference between them.

To imagine the same things borders on madness; yet they are otherwise prudent, and they see these things while awake, not through sleep. They even lead their daughters and teach others: for which reason these **profane rites** <note>original: "profana sacra"</note>, full of pleasure, must be true. See Thomas Erastus's treatise on witches, where he proves this same point with many arguments, as does **Bodin** against **Weyer**. <note>Jean Bodin was a famous proponent of witch-hunting, while Johann Weyer was a physician who argued that "witches" were actually suffering from mental illness (melancholy).</note>

But that same Cardanus <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath.</note>, just as he speaks ambiguously in other matters concerning Divine providence, the immortality of souls, and invisible spirits—leaning toward the camp of the **Atheists**—so he does in this part. In the aforementioned place, folio 977, he writes thus: *It is established that these women are often rightly punished because they are sorceresses, or even for impiety; however, for the most part, they are merely foolish, and a full confession and judgment (as could be established for robbers, thieves, and other wicked men) cannot be completed for the death penalty. Instead, everything is full of vanities, lies, contradictions, and inconsistency: for that which is said about them meeting and bearing witness against those who were absent is entirely false; they only meet regarding the day of the gathering when it has been made public. That argument, if examined correctly and diligently, shows that this art is entirely false, and they do not truly gather together as one: for one woman could expose a hundred or even more, since so many are present by their testimony.*

And a little later: *No one, therefore, will judge these women—heretics, worshippers of demons, impious, and homicides—unworthy of death. If, however, the deed itself is absent and they suffer only from a delusion, they are of the sort of fools; yet this kind of folly is also dangerous. Because of this, unless they repent, they are usually condemned to death. For besides this superstition, women have been found who killed boys, seasoning their flesh with salt—for what purpose I know not. One woman, while I was watching, paid the penalty for such unusual cruelty.*
