->### Expanded Practical Treasury<-

Furthermore, they offer no cures for health except those known from herbs through long experience or the advice of a Physician. Nor do they cause deaths except through poisons given among food; certain wicked prostitutes know more types of these poisons than **witches** <note>original: "lamiæ," a term for a female witch often associated with child-stealing or vampiric behavior in folklore.</note> do. Yet their insanity often proceeds so far that they make themselves out to be the authors of diseases and misfortunes that have happened to their enemies, for the sake of boasting, even though these things happened to them by chance.

So too, many deny the sexual union of such wretched females with the Devil, which is nevertheless confirmed by the very consistent confessions of everyone. See Guillaume Bouchet, *The Evenings, chapter 8, folio 241*; join those treating witches in general such as Delrio, Francisco Torreblanca, Nicolas Rémy, etc.; Maiolus, *volume 2, Dog Days, colloquy 3*; Hatron, *On Piety and the Kingdom, folio 107, etc.*; Zeiller’s *Additions to Rosset's Tragic Histories*; Jonston, *On the Constancy of Nature, folio 60*; Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 2, folio 54*; Carranza, *On Natural Birth, etc., folio 711*; Tornielli, *In the Annals, folio 78*; Martin, *century 6, disputation 2, question 7*; Rueff, *On Conception, book 5, chapter 6.*

And it is clear from confessions that sometimes wives have been compressed by the Devil under the appearance of their husbands, so that women cannot be secure. Therefore, there is a need for prayer and sobriety, and marriage must also be used chastely; in the marital bed, one must not engage in intercourse with a wife everywhere, nor out of bestial pleasure, nor likewise should the wife satisfy the husband in such a way, etc.

Regarding **incubi** and **succubi** <note>Incubi were male demons and succubi were female demons believed to have sexual relations with humans during sleep.</note>, Cantipratensis has certain things in *book 2, chapter 57.* Add also Guillaume Böckel's recently published *Visions, inquiry 6, number 2, etc.* and *my own work On Majesty.* Thyræus, *On the Appearance of Spirits, folio 30, etc. on transportation and other things*; Binsfeld, *On the Confessions of Sorcerers.* What things can the Devil not achieve even through mages? See Martin, *disputation 9, century 9, question 4, and century 10, disputation 9, question 5,* where he discusses the carrying away of mages outside of their bodies.

On the Demonic sleep of Witches, see Sennert, *Medical Institutions, folio 314 and folio 404.*

That the goods of witches should fall to the **State Treasury** <note>original: "Fisco"</note> is proved by Lord Friedrich Martini, a most excellent Jurist and Professor at Freiburg, in his *singular dissertation on the treatise of taxes, annexed.* But Lord Adam Keller fights for the contrary opinion in his *Treatise on Intestate Succession, folio 275.* Whatever the law may be: it is harsh to deprive children and a husband of the benefit of succession, which is owed to them either by statute or by law. See Berlichius, *part 4, conclusion 5, number 27*; see *Book 7 of the Decretals, folio 485*; Farinacci, *On Heresy, question 181*; and the same Keller in his *Treatise on the Juridico-Political Office, folio 432.*

And the rigor of Confiscation (where it is observed and carried out) could be tempered by Christian charity in this way: that first, all expenses should be fully required from the goods of the executed person, so that the Magistrate does not bear the cost for the destitute; (2) that nothing be taken from the descendants; (3) that the hope of succession not be withdrawn from the husband; (4) that the ancestors be allowed to reclaim what came from them; and (5) that the Treasury be preferred over collateral relatives, especially remote ones. Although these things are not in harmony with written law, a Magistrate having full jurisdiction and the power to establish statutes could do this, since they are not against the law, but alongside it.

It was decided to join the following two Legal Responses.

> We, the undersigned, have read through the set of facts sent to us, and have weighed all the circumstances found therein with proper diligence; however, for our part, we cannot judge that the female prisoner should be subjected to **torture** <note>original: "Tortur"</note> at this time. Rather, she should be set at liberty upon providing a guarantee or an oath to appear again at any time at the request of the Authorities, along with payment for her sustenance and other expenses incurred on her behalf. In the meantime, however, diligent watch should be kept over her life and conduct.

For although otherwise in the **crime of treason against divine majesty** <note>original: "crimine læsæ Majestatis divinæ," which refers to witchcraft as a crime against God.</note>, and specifically if an inquiry is made into the crime of sorcery or soothsaying—as a hidden matter, exceedingly outrageous and detestable—even the accomplices or associates of the crime, and their confession persisted in during torture even unto death, is held as a sufficient indicator for torture; according to Prospero Farinacci, *question 43, number 58, 67, and following.*

Which specifically takes place in the case when two or more accuse other associates of the same crime, as Georg Everhard teaches in *volume 1, counsel 2, number 40*, following the text in the *Decretals*, and Binsfeld in his *Discourse on the Confessions of Sorcerers.*

However, it is concluded almost commonly by legal scholars on the other hand that while this accusation made by other witches is to be regarded as an urgent indicator <note>See Binsfeld, *On the Confessions of Sorcerers, folio 228 and following, in many places.*</note>, yet in and of itself, unless other indicators concur, it is not enough for torture. See Farinacci, *said question 43, number 147, etc.*; Lord Bocer, *On Inquiries, chapter 3, number 98.* And in these terms, Cothman writes that little should be deferred to this indicator regarding Torture, *response 12, number 267 and following*; with whom Fichard agrees, *counsel 108, volume 2, also counsel 3, number 4.* Where he says in these formal words: we know from experience that often such evil women have also falsely accused innocent, pious, and noble persons, primarily out of hatred and envy, because they would gladly see, when they themselves must burn, that the whole world should burn as well. Nor does the Law permit that he who has confessed regarding himself be tortured against the head of others. *Law 16, section 1, of the Digest on Inquiries.* The Jurist Paul gives a most elegant reason for this in *Sentences, book 1, title 17, section 7*, in these words: he who has confessed about himself cannot be tortured against another, lest he bring the safety of another into doubt when he has despaired of his own.

Furthermore, that this indicator is not suitable for torture is also proved by the fact that no mention is made of it in the **Criminal Ordinance of Emperor Charles V** <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* of 1532.</note>, Article 44, among those indicators...

...circumstances which are said to likely prove poisoning or witchcraft <note>original: "veneficium sive maleficium"</note>: Fichard uses this argument in these very terms in his *Consultation 108, verse:* "that also the mere..."

To this is further added what Alciatus writes in his commentary on the chapter *Perniciosa*, number 66, *On the Office and Power of the Ordinary*, in these words: "Although credit is given to accomplices of a crime in such an offense, nevertheless this must not be extended to those things which do not appear certain and true, but can occur through the illusion of demons."

Now it is known, and could be proven from proven Catholic writers, that the wretched enemy of the human race often takes on the form of another, pious person, in order to strengthen his subordinates in their malice, or also to create danger for the innocent.

It is indeed true that witches <note>original: "Sagas"</note> are transported from place to place by demons; yet on the contrary, it must be conceded that sometimes only specters of women are seen in such games and dances. For trustworthy histories testify that at one and the same time, women were seen in places very distant from each other, which cannot happen by the nature of things; therefore, no faith should be placed in this evidence full of fraud. (According to the argument in Book 3 and Book 8, single paragraph, of the *Code on Questioning*).

And we find from the above statement of facts <note>original: "facti specie"</note> no other evidence; therefore the prisoner—as Article 31 of the Criminal Constitution of Charles V <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the unified criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1532.</note>, section "Fourthly," etc., requires in these our terms—cannot be held so suspicious that one may undoubtedly expect the said misdeed from her; or as Martin Delrio speaks in his *Magical Disquisitions*, book 5, section 3, page 42, "so that it can certainly be believed that those naming her are not lying."

Considering that the prisoner would not shed a single tear, this is held by the aforementioned Delrio (book 5, section 4, page 77) to be a "vain and frivolous sign." Also, from the frequently mentioned facts of the case, it appears only that the prisoner has become suspect and under scrutiny for this vice only since various witches were executed from her village and surrounding places.

No other causes for such suspicion are indicated; therefore, it is quite probable that the aforementioned suspicion arose solely through the "inculpation" or denunciation by those others who were executed.

Finally, we are moved to such a decision also by this: that the prisoner has already been flogged with rods—thus somewhat terrified or "painfully questioned" <note>A legal euphemism for torture.</note>—and yet she would confess nothing.

Therefore, we hold that one should not proceed beyond such a degree of torture based on the circumstances of this single piece of evidence (the denunciation), and we do not doubt that, in the event the prisoner is truly guilty and diligent watch is kept over her in the manner understood above, she will soon reveal herself, nor will she easily be able to withdraw

<column-break/>

from her deserved punishment. This agrees with the decision of the Faculty of Law at Tübingen, which Dr. Thummius inserted into his *Disputation on Magicians*, as did Dr. Helfrich Ulrich Hunnius in his *Criminal Discourse*, thesis 41.

### Christophorus Besoldus, Doctor.

The enclosed criminal court records—produced between N.N., the Lord Prosecutor as the accuser on one side, and Agnes N. of N., the defendant on the other, up to the announcement of the final judgment—we have read with all diligence to draft the requested legal opinion. We have found that the primary doubt in this place is in what manner the defendant should be punished for her committed and confessed witchcraft.

Now, she has indeed confessed that at the suggestion of the evil spirit, she renounced Almighty God and committed other such loathsome acts several times; yet in her judicial answer, it is constantly denied that she has ever, to this time, inflicted harm upon any person, livestock, or people. In which case, both several legal scholars and especially many theologians are of the opinion that one cannot arrive at the death penalty. Ludovicus Gilhausen, in his *Tree of Criminal Judgment*, chapter 2, title 17, number 17, in the middle at the verse "furthermore, if witches confess," where he says that in this case, magicians and witches should be punished either by flogging, banishment, or a monetary fine.

To which, secondly, is added that the defendant is only 19 years old; here again, the legal teachers almost unanimously conclude that one cannot arrive at the ordinary death penalty even in high crimes. For Josephus Ludovicus Decius confirms with many authorities that minors cannot be punished with the penalty of natural death, but with another discretionary punishment near death; he says that the Doctors conclude thus by common consensus in every kind of crime, not only in crimes consisting of omission, but also in commission, and even in grave crimes.

Thirdly, it might quite clearly be held that the criminal defendant should be looked upon with a somewhat lighter punishment, considering she was shamefully seduced and, according to her claim, fell into this vice as if unknowingly, and is now very well suited for repentance—especially since she was taken in for another misdeed and voluntarily confessed the witchcraft herself.

And that the punishment ought to be mitigated for one who is not convicted but voluntarily confesses and repents before proof is offered, and identifies accomplices in the crime, is taught by Prosper Farinaccius in his *Criminal Practice*, part 3, title "On the Confessed and Convicted Defendant," question 81, chapter 5, number 147.

# Treasury of Augmented Practice

...the competent and resulting [legal remedy] from the facts narrated. Hence, he adds a word there that should be perpetually noted. When you are ignorant, he says, of which action or which remedy is available to you, or how you ought to conclude in your petition <note>original: "libello"</note>—perhaps because of a tangled set of facts or a multitude of factors, or because of a doubt in the law—then you should narrate the facts diligently and congruently. In the conclusion, do not ask for anything specific, nor conclude anything specific, but in place of a specific conclusion, simply say at the end of the petition:

*On all and singular counts, I ask that Law and Justice be administered to me, both collectively and separately, cumulatively and alternatively, referring each point to each part, in every other better and more effective mode and form in which this can and should be done by Law—in the most steadfast form and measure, as such should, can, or may most powerfully occur in Law.* <note>The final phrase was originally in German: "in der allerbeständigsten Form und Maß, wie solches in Rechten am kräftigsten geschehen soll, kan oder mag."</note>

This clause acts as an appendix to what came before, and it is so powerful that in a doubtful case, the petition may be accepted in whatever way best supports the intention of the Plaintiff <note>original: "Actoris"</note>. It is therefore very useful for sustaining a doubtful petition, as noted by Jason in the aforementioned section on all [actions]. See also Hartsoft on the law, number 81.

Jason also reviews three effects of this clause in his commentary on the law regarding petitioners, number 5, in the *Code on Pacts*; Antonius Gabriel lists nine in his title on concluding clauses, through the whole of folio 612. Add also Oldendorp on exceptions, the title on the form of petitions, folio 306 and following; and Calam on the method of articles and proofs, folio 66, number 24. See also Decio on the law regarding petitioners, number 4, at the verse "wherefore I ask" in the *Code on Pacts*; Vantius in the treatise on the nullity of Processes, the title on nullity and defects of process, number 25, at the verse "furthermore this nullity"; Capycius, decision 10, number 22, at the verse "which was in the petition"; Giovanni Battista Afinius in civil practice, section 4, chapter 4, number 5, at the verse "likewise they are accustomed"; and Nicolaus Everhardus in *Legal Topics*, the topic "from their effect," number 7. In that place, among other things, Everhardus says: "Regarding this, I want you to know that the said Clause has another maximum and singular effect; for if in a Petition concluding a narrative made regarding both Possession <note>original: "possessorio"</note> and Ownership <note>original: "petitorio"</note>, the aforementioned Clause is added, then if Ownership is proven but not Possession, a sentence can be rendered on the Ownership by virtue of said Clause." Panormitanus says this singularly in the chapter *Since the beloved*, on the order of cognitions; as do Giovanni da Imola on the laws *If with none* and *In sum* in the *Digest on Res Judicata*; Baldus on the law *of uncertain things* near the end of the *Code on Interdicts*; Felinus in the chapter *It is permitted*; and De Simonis, Angelo, and Jason in the section on all [actions] in the *Institutes on Actions*. See especially Hartmann Pistor, book 1, question 45, number 24 and following. However, if the plaintiff had clearly asserted that he would act at least on the ownership <note>petitory action</note>, then to avoid contradiction, the petition is not extended to possession <note>possessory action</note>, according to Alexander, counsel 99, volume 5, and counsel 110, number 2, volume 5; and Hartmann Pistor in the same place at the final number. Add Socinus, counsel 128, beginning "Most Just Judge" at the principle.

"Be therefore cautious," says the same Everhardus, "that you never omit placing it in the Petition to be drafted by you: because I have seen many fail because of the omission of this Clause, having taken up an inept conclusion, who would not have failed if they had placed the said Clause in the conclusion;

<column-break/>

and be all the more cautious because he who is ignorant of the nature of an action easily errs in forming a conclusion well and aptly, which causes many to fail." See the first law, with the notes there by the singular gloss, on the manner of speaking, and the chapter "Examined" on judgments.

It must be noted, however, that the often-mentioned Clause, however useful it may be, does not produce its effect when a specific exception is found against the generality of the Petition in which this Clause was added, and a specification is demanded. This is according to Alessandro da Imola, following Baldus, Angelo, and others cited by him in counsel 1215, volume 1, and Everhardus in the cited place, number 8.

And this Clause also ought to achieve its effect only when it would result in an advantage for the Plaintiff. It is otherwise if it would redound to his detriment, for then one must stand by the specific conclusion rather than extending the petition by the often-mentioned general Clause against the Plaintiff's intention. Alexander, counsel 200, number 7, volume 2, where he teaches that the effect of this Clause is that the remedy which is most favorable to the plaintiff is seen as the one intended. Jason, in the section on all [actions], number 15, *Institutes on Actions*; Nevizanus, counsel 79, number 5. For he says, "this Clause is added in favor of the plaintiff, therefore it must not be twisted to his hatred." See the law *Because in favor* in the *Code on Laws*. For even otherwise, it is regularly in the power of the plaintiff to interpret the petition as he wishes, since it must always be understood according to the mind and interpretation of the plaintiff. See the law *If anyone* on judgments; Hartmann Pistor, book 1, question 45, number 26.

->ADDITION.<-

On the effects of the Clause, *I ask that law and justice be administered to me*. Klock, counsel 29, number 35. It encompasses both possessory and petitory matters. The same author, volume 2, counsel 2, number 6.

A Judge is seen to be implored regarding expenses if the saving clause <note>original: "clausula salutaris"</note>, *I ask law and justice to be administered*, or another similar one, is added to the petition. See especially Rittershusius in the *Novels*, page 490; "to be pronounced just and equitable." Mynsinger, observation 22 at the end; Gail, book 1, observation 151, number 22; Wesenbeck in the *Commentary on law 15*, number 12, *Code on Judgments*. Also Ummius in *Process*, pages 897 and 265, at the end of page 266 at the beginning. Regarding the clause by which the noble office of the judge is invoked: see Ummius, pages 265 and 177. Regarding the clause: *in every better form of Law and Statutes, in which it can, is accustomed, and ought to be done*: Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated*, page 24. Also Ummius, page 264; Schwannmann on the process of the Imperial Chamber, book 1, chapter 1, number 12 at the end; Marcantonio, *Various Resolutions*, book 2, resolution 49, number 8. Regarding the Clause *not in the manner of a solemn petition, but as any request whatsoever*: the same author, page 262.

Saving clauses <note>original: "clausulæ salutares"</note> are compared to the **herb Betony**, because they are accustomed to heal all defects of petitions, and by their virtue, a Judge can not infrequently bestow his office toward supplying a defect in the petition. Gail; Rosbach; Lord Ludwig in *Process*, chapter 8; see me in my inaugural disputation on the *Style of the Court*, thesis 55; Carpzov in *Forensic Jurisprudence*.

<margin>Saxon Part 1, Constitution 2, Definition 16. Eberhard Fabricius in his *Enucleated Gail*, page 24.</margin>
On the clauses of both laws <note>referring to Civil and Canon law</note> and on conclusions, see Vitalis Cambanus and Hugo Celsus in the 4th book, *Venice, 1570*. Barschamp *on the root of clauses*. Barbosa *on frequently used clauses*.

The clause or protestation: **concerning all of this, and calling upon law and justice for each one in particular in the best form.** <note>original German: "über diesem allen, und einen jeden insonderheit Recht und Gerechtigkeit bester Form anruffend"</note> **Seeking that law and justice regarding all and singular these matters be administered to him in every better way.** <note>original Latin: "Super quibus omnibus & singulis jus & justitiam petens omni meliori modo sibi administrari"</note> The words "regarding all and singular" have this effect: in criminal cases, a conviction can be made based only on what has been proven, even if many things were charged and not all were proven. Hugo Celsus handily explains this in his *Clauses of Petitions*, and he asserts the same regarding the words "collectively and separately," as he suggests in the same place. The remaining words compel the office of the Judge to admit a general petition, so that he may draw out whatever conclusion is most appropriate for the plaintiff based on the facts narrated, such as awarding expenses even if not requested, or allowing oaths to be administered that were not asked for. On all these matters, see *The Forum of Protestations, page 313*, and *On Clauses not in the Solemn Form of a Petition, page 308*.

## 53. Hereunder. Below. <note>original: "Hieunden. Infra."</note>

The word "below" <note>Latin: "infra"</note> refers only to the contents and descriptions within the legal instrument itself. Bartolus on the law *Concerning children*, section *these words*, where others [discuss] *vulgarian and pupillary [substitution]*. Paris, *Counsel 113, number 24, volume 1*. It has the same effect as if everything named and described there had been listed right here, as Bartolus notes in the aforementioned section. Aretinus and others [note this] in the law *If anyone [substitutes] a son*, final section, *on acquiring inheritance*. Curtius Junior, *Counsel 115, number 27*.

->ADDITION.<-

On the word "Below," see Tiraqueau, *book 1, on Retractions, section 1, gloss 11, number 76*. The phrase "as above" <note>Latin: "ut supra"</note> refers to preceding matters along with their specific qualities. Marius Antonius, *Various Resolutions, book 1, resolution 4, number 6*. The words "as was said" refer to the present part of the document. *Resolutions, book 1, folio 110, number 7*. The word "aforementioned" is in *Resolution 2, book 1, number 21*. Preceding words clarify subsequent ones and carry more influence. *Resolution 3, book 1, number 60*. The nature of the word "aforementioned" <note>Latin: "praedictum"</note> is to repeat preceding things with all their qualities, according to Klock, *Counsel 37, numbers 77 and 78*. The nature of the German word for "aforementioned" <note>German: "Vorgesetzter"</note> is to repeat preceding things with all their qualities. Klock, *volume 3, counsel 165, numbers 8 and 9*.

"Named here below," *Marburg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 25, number 43*.

## 54. In turn, conversely. Reciprocally. <note>original: "Hinwiederum, hingegen. Vicissim."</note>

The words "In turn" or "conversely" imply a condition, and a reciprocal, hypothetical, or conditional obligation.

## 55. Shepherds. Guards, Herdsmen.

Guards are condemned for damage done to grass by animals, according to Vivius, *Decision 280*, where

<column-break/>

he extends this even to the animals of the Church and of ecclesiastical persons. He also explains how damage caused by animals to crops that are currently in the blade <note>that is, young green shoots</note> should be appraised.

->ADDITION.<-

The overseer of forests or pastures is the one who has care over them. Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 2, number 24*. Forest guards are called "banderii." *number 33*. If someone, in the process of expelling and driving away an animal that does not belong on their land, harms it more harshly or differently than they should—for instance, if a mare miscarries because she was driven away—that person is held liable for the damage. *Digest, book 5 and 39, regarding the Aquilian Law; and the law on preserving [property] 14, final section, on prescriptive words, number 27*. On who the "Shepherd of Apollo" is, see P. Gregory, *Syntagma 18, chapter 24*. Under the term "livestock" <note>Latin: "pecudum"</note> in the Aquilian Law <note>A Roman law providing compensation for damage to property</note> come four-legged animals that graze in herds; this does not exclude beasts of burden, but it does exclude wild beasts and also dogs. Dr. Tabor, *On the Law of Livestock-Partnerships, page 11*. A swineherd is also called a *porculator*. Guards of geese are called *Anserarii* or <note>original Greek: χηνοβόσκοι—goose-feeders</note>. *Digest, book 66, on legacies 3*. Dr. Tabor, *ibid, page 12*. A shepherd who, when an army is approaching, offers the livestock entrusted to him to his master in a timely manner, is freed from all risk or liability. Dr. Tabor, *On the Law of Livestock-Partnerships, page 50, number 8*.

To whom the right of pasturing belongs: see Marius Antoninus of Macerata, *book 3, resolution 42, number 1, sections 6 and 7*. Regarding the right of pasturing at the time when crops have been harvested, **during open times, and not in enclosed fields.** <note>Refers to the "open field system" where land was shared for grazing after harvest.</note> Schneidewin, *On Rural and Urban Servitudes, number 33*. **Whoever has three hides of land <note>original: "Huffen"—a measure of land roughly 30 acres</note> or more may keep his own shepherd, unless another custom has been introduced. Provided that he remains with his sheep and cattle on his own hides of land and does not trouble others. Whatever the shepherd loses while under his guard, he shall pay for it. When one animal lames another before the eyes of the shepherd, the shepherd must name the animal that did the damage and must swear to it; then the owner of the animal that caused the damage is obliged to take the wounded animal into his care as long as it can still follow and walk to the field. But if it dies, he shall pay for it according to its established value.** <note>original: "Wehr Gelde"—compensation money, similar to blood-money for animals.</note> *Ibid, numbers 38 and 40*. **On the great misunderstanding between high potentates regarding the borders of cattle-drives.** Leonhard Wurffbain, *Historical Accounts, part 6, page 187*. **Between the blowing of the two horns, that is, while the cattle are kept indoors.** <note>A phrase referring to the winter season or the period when livestock are not permitted on the commons.</note>

However, the **shepherd’s staff** <note>original: "Hirtenstab"</note> pertains only to a certain modest municipal power: namely, the authority to build roads, to arrange and manage the clearing of livestock, to punish when damage is caused by livestock, to impound stray animals, and similar matters. See the *Confessions of Strasbourg, volume 1, confession 2*, concerning the granting of the shepherd’s staff, page 69 and following.

->ADDITIO.<-

**Feeding with the staff** <note>original: "Mit dem Stab füttern"</note> refers to the holding of a court assembly, or specifically the tax for fodder and meals that usually followed such an assembly. *Acts of Lindau, page 806.*
In Hackl, the shepherd’s staff changes hands, and the shepherd gives 7 pfennigs to the one who holds the promise. **Grazing money** <note>original: "Weidegeld"</note> is considered insofar as it concerns the profits of jurisdiction. Indeed, this money is paid so that damage to the fields may be avoided, and that pastures remain intact, protected, and uninjured, being opened or closed at the proper time. Gregory of Toulouse explains this beautifully in his *Syntagma, book 3, chapter 15, number 10*. Otherwise, a fine is imposed on transgressors. For this purpose, **forest and field guards** <note>original: "Custodes saltuarii banderii"</note> are appointed, who are regarded as part of the jurisdiction, and consequently, the benefits go to the Lord. Furthermore, under the general clause "and other vogt-like authority" <note>referring to the *Vogt*, a medieval administrative official</note>, the pastoral right is also included, along with the right of conferring the staff or rod, commonly called the **shepherd's staff**. See Knichen *on the law of territory, chapter 4, number 502*, and Klock *on the treasury, book 2, chapter 2, number 32*. Regarding **enclosed grazing fields**, see the same at number 22, where he also discusses grazing money, cow-tax, and driving-tax. Anyone putting animals into the pastures, woods, or groves of the Prince without having the right of pasturage loses those animals, and they are given to the treasury. See number 24 and 28. The right of pasturage is counted among immovable property. Knipschild *on entails, chapter 4, number 36*.
According to **Saxon Law**, everything is considered "wild by nature" that cannot be guarded with shepherds. Such are bees, peacocks, pigeons, wild hens, partridges, quails, and geese (though regarding these, see Tabor *on the Law of Society, page 12*). Biccius in his *Golden Rules, section 3, thesis 19*. Damage is caused to pastures and grounds by buildings. Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 46, number 24*. Estates in the country are sold with **rights of use and pasture** <note>original: "Wun und Waid"</note>. In the assessment of the noble estate at Widerspach, the grazing money is listed, which for many years was leased to Ramersdorf over the winter for 8 florins. Thus, tithes <note>a tenth part of produce or income paid as a tax</note> are owed from animals in the place where they live, where they receive their food, and where they are guarded or pastured by persons. See the chapters *Ad Apostolica* and *Pastoralis* regarding tithes. Concerning **Blood Tithes or Living Tithes**: these are taken from everything that goes under the shepherd's rod, such as cattle, calves, sheep, goats, lambs, and geese. Werndtle *on tithes, page 53 and 67*. Those who pluck geese beforehand cheat the tithe-lord. Werndtle page 75: one goose out of ten, and if someone 

<column-break/>

buys and resells geese, one out of ten is also owed; tithes are also owed from pigs, two pfennigs from a calf, two pfennigs from a foal, one pfennig from a lamb, tithes from bees, a hen from every hide of land <note>original: "Hueb," a traditional unit of land</note> for the hay tithe, and a **smoke-hen** <note>original: "Rauchhun," a hen given as a hearth tax</note> from every house. *Arnhöchstät Records, 1473.* But in the year 1517, the matter was settled differently: from every occupied farmstead, one smoke-hen annually, or three pfennigs instead; for a foal, one pfennig; for a calf, one heller; for sows and geese, a tenth; and a tenth of the bees. Werndcle *on tithes, pages 54 and 68*.

## § 8. History.

Credibility is granted to historians and chroniclers even in legal judgments, at least where the contrary is not shown. <note>Legal authorities like Bartolus and Jason are cited here to show that historical records can serve as evidence in court.</note> They shift the **burden of proof** <note>original: "onus probandi"</note> onto the person asserting the opposite. Full credit is especially given to chronicles and histories when they are supported by common report or opinion, or if they are aided by other evidence—for instance, if they are drawn from **public archives** and have been considered authentic for a very long time. In such cases, they deserve credit regarding ancient matters. One must also believe in paintings, writings, sculpted columns, stones, walls, or other monuments found in churches or other public or private places; this is even supported by the judgment of the Imperial Chamber.

In the **Municipal Law of Würtemberg**, it is provided **that town clerks should create a History Book and daily record unique occurrences.** <note>original German: "das die Stadtschreiber sollen ein HistoriBuch machen, & quotidie excurrentia singularia annotiren"</note> **But this is neglected, just as many good ordinances in such a Duchy are poorly kept. And now daily matters are forgotten; and in 200 years (if the world stands that long), our descendants will know as little as we do now about what happened before such a time.**

Regarding what should be thought of the genealogists Münster, Herold, Stumpf, etc., see Georg Everhard, volume 1, consultation 27, from the beginning.

### ADDITION.

It is sometimes helpful to present the contrary view; indeed, this is the duty of a faithful historian: to recount from the mouths of those telling the story not only the bare names of persons but the facts themselves as they are. This should be done in such a way that it remains uncertain whether the historian adds his own vote of approval to their words or not. See the *30 Philological and Historical Epistles on the Testimony of Flavius Josephus*, which Master Christoph Arnold reviewed. Credit must be given to historians. The genealogies of the descendants of any family serve as proof.

<column-break/>

**Christ comes from a spotted and stained lineage, etc.; no one should reproach another for their lineage.** <note>original German: "Christus ist aus einem maculirten und befleckten Geschlecht..." This refers to the inclusion of "sinners" in the biblical genealogy of Jesus to emphasize humility.</note> **That young nobleman wanted to prove that the Totte family was the oldest lineage of the Swedes and Danes, for Peer Totte had already lived in the time of Virgil. For it stands in Virgil: "Through various disasters, THROUGH SO MANY [PER TOT] crises of things."** <note>This is a linguistic joke; the nobleman is punning on the Latin words "per tot" (through so many) to claim his ancestor "Totte" was mentioned in the Aeneid.</note>

Historical works flourish if they possess the three requirements of history: **truth** <note>Greek: αλήθεια / alētheia</note>, **freedom of speech** <note>Greek: παρρησία / parrhēsia</note>, and **impartiality** <note>Greek: απάθεια / apatheia</note>, or freedom from affections and passions. According to the Father of Roman Eloquence <note>Cicero</note> in book 2 of *On the Orator*: History is the **witness of times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the mistress of life, and the messenger of antiquity.**

It is the **witness of times** because it is a commemoration of things done and an exposition of those things which happened in each age, both ancient and modern, in the Ecclesiastical and Political state.

It is the **light of truth** because, without **partiality** <note>Greek: προσωποληψίας / prosōpolēpsias; literally "respect of persons"</note>, it narrates candidly and sincerely those things which were said, deliberated, concluded, and acted upon, and what the outcome of each was, for no one's favor or hatred, and for no one's benefit or detriment.

It is the **life of memory** because those things which happened in ancient and recent centuries tend to fall easily from the memory. Therefore, memory draws from history a healthy remedy, as it were, for its own weakness and inconstancy. Memory revives when it contemplates the acts of past times within history as if in a great theater or a most polished mirror. Hence they say Plato derived "History" from the phrase "to stop the flow of memory" <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τὲ ἴσασθαι τὴν τῆς μνήμης ῥύσιν</note>, because it stays the failing and wavering memory like a perennial river.

It is the **mistress of life** because it offers us various types of patterns <note>paradigms</note> which can deter the wicked from vice and crimes through the fear of those punishments and unhappy outcomes that befell men of the same sort. Conversely, it can inflame the good toward the exercise of piety, the study of virtue, love of Fatherland, the desire for immortality, and a longing for honor, glory, and rewards. They are moved and incited by the example of those who served the Republic and the whole Fatherland excellently and laudably, and therefore received the greatest rewards for their good deeds. Hence, not undeservedly, History is called by venerable Antiquity the **beginning of wisdom** <note>Greek: ἀρχὴ τῆς φρονήσεως</note>...

...wisdom: a <note>original: "ἀκινδυνος διδασκαλία"</note> safe instruction, a kind of doctrine and training that is free from all danger; an inestimable treasury of civil wisdom; and it has been called a most fertile theater of examples, inciting us to the exercise of virtue and honesty and calling us away from vice. It is, finally, the **Messenger of Antiquity**, because it allows us, within a short span of time and without great labor, to know those things that happened many centuries before we or our parents were even born. This is undoubtedly the reason that drove various nations—even the uncivilized and those most distant from refined literature—to write **Annals, Ephemerides** (or daily logs), **Cosmographies, Chronologies, and Genealogies** in various languages.

At the University of Strasbourg, the following men explained history: *Nicolaus Gerbelius, Michael Beutherus, Johannes Pappus, Philippus Glaserus, Philippus Rihelius, Casparus Bitschius, Matthias Berneggerus, Johannes Henricus Bœclerus, and Johann Sebastian Gambsius*. To these, one should add the world-famous historian *Johannes Sleidanus*, who, although he never taught history there, wrote and published almost all of his historical monuments in that city. Regarding him, **Emperor Charles V** passed this judgment: *“Either Sleidan was my Chancellor, or my Chancellors were my traitors.”* <note>The Emperor was amazed at Sleidan's accurate insider knowledge of imperial affairs.</note> For more, see *Bernegger, in the Demolition of the Laurentian Idol, page 77.* It was pleasing to inspect the house in Strasbourg that the praised Sleidan inhabited. It was also pleasing to view the historian’s portrait with admiration in the Strasbourg Library. 

*Casparus Brülovius*, so that no one is defrauded of their honor, had indeed undertaken the profession of History and had inaugurated it with a solemn oration, as is the custom; but having been cut down by <note>original: "φθίσει & hydrope"</note> consumption and dropsy, this excellent man, most worthy of a longer life, was unable to complete what he had in mind. *Thus far, Master Melchior Sebizius, most excellent physician at the University of Strasbourg.* 

Those who do not join examples to their precepts are considered not unlike those who are content with the sweet smell of rich dishes but do not actually touch the food itself. Historical and chronological books prove this; see *Thoming. conf. 26. n. 22. vol. 1.* and *Cardinal Tusch. Practical Legal Conclusions, vol. 4, letter H, conclusion 139.* When do historians not take account of time? Master Arnold, *in the cited place, pages 379, 380.* They sometimes use repetitions, pages 109, 110. Which historians the Jews do not believe, *page 33.* 

**Histories are a book of the living, and a trumpet by which the dead are awakened, as if made living and brought to the light. They are the seal of omnipotence, the mirror of judgments, and a theater of God's justice.** Zeiller, *century 4, letter page 495.* On the utility of Roman history, see *Cl. Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 7, dissertation 1.* If there is any kind of study anywhere upon which either the inept curiosity of men, or their monstrous pride, or their poisonous envy tries to impose severe laws, it is this study of ours which we commonly call **History**. For unless one knows everything that others imagine in their dreams, as *Juvenal* says:

<column-break/>

> That the rule of words be firm for the Teacher,
> That he read Histories, and know all authors,
> As well as his own nails and fingers, so that if by chance he is asked,
> While heading to the baths or the pools of Phoebus, he might say
> Who was the nurse of Anchises, the name and homeland of the stepmother
> Of Archemorus; let him say how many years Acestes lived,
> How many jars of wine the Sicilian gave to the Phrygians,

As the Satirist of Aquino <note>Juvenal</note> sang at the end of *Satire 7*; unless, I say, he responds to the indulgence of their wishes, you will immediately hear the barking of Cerberus: "Behold the grand name of an Historian!" *Cl. Rupertus in the Prologue to Pomponius.* That profane matters do not entirely lead one away from sacred thoughts, see *Cl. Rupertus, dissertation 2 on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 6.* Regarding what kind of credibility historians deserve in Law, see *Gilken. on law 15, Code on Pacts, number 87.*

**Jovius** <note>Paolo Giovio</note> reaped this fruit of lying: even when he writes the truth, he is held in suspicion. No writer, as far as history is concerned, has not lied about something. *Limn. vol. 2, additions to book 5, chapter 2, page 337.* 

Three historians were named **Martial**: 
1. Martial the most noble Poet, a Spaniard by birth. 
2. Cornelius Martialis, a Tribune and chief centurion in the time of Emperor Flavius Vespasian. 
3. Julius Martialis, likewise a Tribune, in the time of Otho. 
There exists yet a fourth in *law 20, Code on Pacts*, of whom it is entirely unknown who he was. See the Legal Disputation held at Strasbourg in 1663 under Master Dr. Friedrich Deckher, *On Delivery by which Ownership is Transferred, §. 5.* 

In 1651, Zeiller wrote a catalog of the most distinguished and best-known historians, chronologers, and geographers in two parts, to which a third part in octavo was added in 1657. In 1661, an addition to the Catalog of Historians was published.

### 59. Wedding Gifts. Munera Nuptialia.

**Xenia**, or wedding gifts, which friends offer to the newlyweds at the wedding celebration—**the gifts which, according to moral custom, are presented by the invited guests at the bridal table on the honorable wedding day**—the question is: do they belong to the Bride or the Groom? Or should they be shared in common, or divided according to the friendship? See *Speckhan. century 3, question 16, class 1.* It is more likely that they should be divided equally; no regard should be had for "from which side" (as they say) they come. Since the friends and relatives of both betrothed parties are presumed to give to both equally; see *my 3rd Disputation on Municipal Law...*

### 60. Court. <note>original: "Hof. Curia."</note>

It is called a **Court** <note>original: "Curia oder Hof"</note> because parliaments and legal judgments were formerly conducted "under the open sky" <note>original: "sub dio"</note>, that is, in an open courtyard. This is seen in *The Great Almoner of France* <note>original: "Le grand Aumoisnier de France"</note>, folio 6. Even today, the District and Rottweil Courts, as well as the **Hundred Courts** <term>Centgericht: An ancient form of local jurisdiction held in the open air, typically presiding over a "hundred" or subdivision of a county.</term>, are held under the open sky. See Goldast, *Alemannia*, volume 1, folio 191 and 206.

It is sometimes used to mean a **Diet** <note>original: "Diæta"</note>, signifying an appointed assembly or congregation. In the *Glossaries of Junianus Maius*: a **Diet** is a place in the home where we simply spend time with no specific business or use. For the Greek word <note>original: "διαιτάομαι"</note> means "I reside" or "I live." Latin writers of later antiquity call this a **Court** <note>original: "Curia"</note>; and this word is also used in the **Golden Bull** <note>The Golden Bull of 1356 was a decree that fixed the constitutional structure of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. Albert of Stade, folio 163, page b: "there he went to the Emperor's Court and sought a judgment." From this also comes the term **Palace Court** <note>original: "Hofgericht"</note>, because formerly, as mentioned, judgments were carried out in the Hall or Court even by the King or Emperor himself, and they were not stationary. See Pontanus, *Frankish Origins*, book 6, chapter 16. **Court** <note>original: "Hof"</note> is also used to mean a manor or estate <note>original: "Curte"</note>; see Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation* 1, thesis 4, letter f.

### ADDITION.

1. See my own work in the *Inaugural Disputation on the Style of the Court*, thesis 2. Barbosa, in *On the Signification of Legal Terms*, definition 67: a Court is sometimes understood as a place in which matters are "cared for" <note>a wordplay on "Curia" and "curare" (to care for)</note>, and sometimes for the order of men who do the caring. Dr. Agricola on law 10, paragraph 3 of the Code regarding proscribed goods. 
2. **Court** signifies an area surrounded by a wall or otherwise enclosed. 
3. A **Hall**, i.e., the house of a Prince: a **Princely Court** <note>original: "Fürstlichen Hof"</note>. 
4. A city house: the **Town Hall** <note>original: "das Rathhaus"</note>. 
5. **Jurisdiction**, as when we say a cleric is to be "handed over to the secular Court." 
6. **Judicial bodies**, in which sense we speak of the Provincial Courts of Leipzig, Jena, and the **Palace Court** <note>original: "Hofgericht"</note> of Tübingen. 
7. A **Palace** <note>original: "die Pfaltz"</note>, an Imperial Court, or buildings consecrated to the Emperor, according to the single law in the Code on Palaces. Thus, the Emperor is said to celebrate his first Court at Nuremberg in the Golden Bull, title 25. **Peers of the Court** <note>original: "Pares Curiæ"</note> or of the manor; see the single chapter on "if there is a controversy over a feudal investiture," paragraph 3. These are the fellow-vassals of the same Senior or Lord in the same territory. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation* 4, 6, chapter. Who the **Courtiers** <note>original: "Curiales"</note> were is stated by Dr. Tabor in *On the Obligation of Succession in Office*, page 261. What it means "to give a name to the Court" is found on page 262. Words of **courtesy** <note>original: "Curialitatis"</note> do not create a binding obligation. Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 6, number 75. Regarding the Court, these verses ought to hold true:

> This place hates wickedness, loves peace, punishes crimes,
> preserves the laws, and honors the upright.
Besold, Volume 1.

There is a common proverb that says: he who cannot swallow a bowl full of mustard at once and laugh at the same time is not fit to be a courtier. The Spaniards say: "Many words, few deeds." Zeiller, century 4, question 49, page 261.

### 61. Manor Farm, Peasant-Fief, Hereditary Rent. Also Hearth-Estates, etc. Hereditary Lease. <note>original: "Hofgut, Bauren-Lehen, Erb-zinß. item Herdgüter, &c. Emphyteusis."</note>

In our customs, these are called **Hereditary Leases** <term>Emphyteusis: A type of contract where a person is given the use of land forever or for a long term in exchange for an annual rent and an agreement to improve the land.</term>. An **Hereditary Lease** <note>original: "Emphyteusis"</note> is defined as the leasing of immovable property made in perpetuity for an annual payment (hence they are also called **Hereditary Rent Estates** <note>original: "Erbzinßgüter"</note>), under this law: that as long as the payment is made, the property cannot be taken away from the tenant. Law 1, Digest, on tax-paying or leased land. 

**Emphyteusis** is a Greek name from the word <note>original: "ἐμφυτεύω"</note>, that is, "to implant" or "to graft." Just as in grafting, one tree is inserted into another so that it clings to it and retains its nature according to its portion; similarly, by this contract, a thing is transferred from the Lord to the tenant in perpetuity in such a way that it always acknowledges the original and direct Lord and provides him with benefit. In Latin, **emphyteusis** is nothing other than **improvement** <note>original: "melioratio"</note>. For in the beginning, only sterile fields were granted to farmers so that they might cultivate them and make them better and fertile, and from there pay an annual pension. But today, not only sterile lands are given, but also fertile goods. Azo in his *Summary of the Code on the Law of Hereditary Leases*. Johann Schneidewin on the title of the Institutes concerning leasing, paragraph "furthermore," number 2. Except in the Church, which gives only those things that seem appropriate to the steward and other governors of the Church. Law "or perpetual also," Code on the Holy Church. Accursius on the said paragraph, on the word "of hereditary lease."

**Manor Farms** <note>original: "Hofgüter"</note> are elsewhere also called **Hearth-Estates** <note>original: "Herdgüter"</note>; for a "hearth" <note>original: "Herd"</note> or fireplace is used to mean a House, to which a barn, a yard, and certain lands usually belong.

However, we must see what the difference is between an **Hereditary Lease** <note>original: "Emphyteusis"</note> and a **Fief** <note>original: "Feudum"</note>. First, they differ in that a fief is granted freely and graciously, as I explained under the word **Fief** <note>original: "Lehen"</note>, as a reward for some debt of service. It is of the inherent nature of a fief that only **personal service** is owed and performed for it: that the vassal must earn the fief through knightly service and with his own body. Hence, in Letters of Investiture, this clause is usually added: *For which he shall be our faithful liegeman, as he has promised us in loyalty and done his feudal duty, to warn us of harm, to promote our best interests, to faithfully earn the fiefs, and also to follow us whenever the need arises, and to conduct himself according to the law and custom of such man-fief estates.* See *The Marburg Consultations*, volume 2, consultation 11.

An **Hereditary Lease**, however, is granted for a certain annual payment of a "Canon" or pension, as stated above. 
2. A vassal is only required to provide services when requested, and is not bound to provide them annually. Chapter "it is permitted," in the section on feudal controversies of the deceased.

<meta>This page continues the legal lexicon of the "Thesaurus Practicus," focusing on the specific rights and obligations associated with property law, particularly the "Emphyteusis" (a long-term or hereditary ground lease) and how it differs from feudal tenure.</meta>

The ground tenant <term>Emphyteuta: A person who holds land under a long-term, often hereditary, lease known as an emphyteusis, requiring them to improve the land and pay an annual rent.</term> is indeed bound to offer the rent <note>original: "canonem"</note> every year. For otherwise, if it is an Ecclesiastical Ground Lease, and the ground tenant does not pay the rent within two years, he loses it, according to the chapter *potuit* under the title *on leases* <note>original: "c. potuit extra locati"</note>. If, however, it is a private ground lease, and the tenant ceases to pay the pension for three years, he can be expelled according to Law 2 of the Code *concerning the Right of Ground Leases* <note>original: "l. 2. C. de J. emphyteu."</note>. Nor shall the ground tenant "purge the delay" <note>An attempt to settle a debt after the deadline to avoid penalty.</note> once the three-year period has passed. For the aforementioned Law 2 says expressly that he who does not pay for three years can be rejected "in every way" (which phrasing altogether excludes the precise purgation of delay, according to Jason on the said Law 2, number 73); indeed, the law imposes this penalty upon him by the law itself <note>original: "ipso jure"</note>. Moreover, where a penalty is imposed by the law itself, the delay cannot be purged. This is based on the principle: if a certain day has been added by law or by a person under the condition of a penalty, within which something ought to be done or given, and it was not done or given, the penalty is said to be incurred by the law itself; so much so, that no purgation of delay can find a place. This is supported by Law *magnam* of the Code *concerning contracts* and various other legal citations.

3. A fief <note>original: "Feudum"</note> is regularly only transferable to males—to **male bodily heirs** <note>original: "auf die Mannliche Leibs-Erben"</note>—and not to females. Whence, by the naming of an "heir" in feudal matters, only males are included, according to the section *etsi Clientulus* on the *alienation of fiefs*. A ground lease <note>original: "Emphyteusis"</note>, however, also passes to daughters and external heirs, as we have noted on Law 3 of the Code *concerning the right of ground leases*.

It should be noted here in passing that although an argument from the force of a name is considered valid in our Law (whereby a thing is presumed to be as it is named), such that when the word **Hereditary Rent** <note>original: "Erbzinß"</note> is found in a legal document—a term that denotes a Ground Lease—the grant would necessarily seem to be called a ground lease.

However, that is only true insofar as the name is free of all doubt and has only one meaning. If it is equivocal and ambiguous, then the argument from the force of the name ceases. Hence, Alexander Raudensis says that a grant made under the name and title of a ground lease does not immediately imply a ground lease unless it is clearly, transparently, and specifically proved from elsewhere. This is for one reason: because the word "Emphyteusis" is equivocal. Therefore, the argument does not hold that "a hereditary rent <note>original: "ein Erbzinß"</note> is paid for this property, therefore this property or estate is a ground-lease property."

<column-break/>

<margin>Because that payment of pension can also be made from a fief, especially if the subject matter allows for it.</margin>
When is a ground-lease right proven from a uniform payment? See the *Saxon Consultations, part 1*. Whether ground leases are forfeited if they are not demanded? See *Marburg Counsel, 56, volume 4*. Regarding a ground tenant failing in the payment of a single penny, see *Valasco, Consultation 86*. Regarding the rent to be paid where it is not established that the goods are ground-lease property, and concerning the right of retraction and the producing of the title, see *Strasbourg Counsel, volume 2, consultation 8*. Whether a rent-payer can yield the property and free himself from pensions, see *Grivellus, decision 99*. On the **forfeiture of estate farms** <note>original: "Von Verlustigung der Hofgüter"</note>, see *Altdorf Counsel, volume 1, counsel 33*. Whether it is permitted to change the face of a rent-bearing estate? *Grivellus, decision 15*.

It is also asked here: After various forfeitures <note>original: "caducitates"</note> have been incurred by the ground tenant for various reasons, are all of them, however many there are, considered abolished and remitted by the reception of the Rent? This is affirmed by Antonio Monterus à Cueva, decision 5. For by the reception of the Rent, a certain "reintegration of status" is considered to be introduced: and one who was not a ground tenant is judged to be a ground tenant. This reintegration of status, however, can only occur in regard to all matters unless an express protest regarding the reservation of the forfeiture is proven to have intervened. But see the already cited Monterus, who distinguishes this in various ways.

Likewise, a forfeiture incurred during the time of a predecessor who knew of it and remained silent cannot be raised against the successor of the ground tenant. It is more probable, however, that it can be ceded among the living. *Monterus, decision 35*.

->ADDITION<-

A ground lease <note>original: "Emphyteusis"</note> is understood to be contracted if it is said that a certain annual quantity is given for Rent <note>original: "pro Canone"</note>. **A hereditary tenant <note>original: "Ein Erbrechter"</note> is deprived of his hereditary right when he does not deliver the owed rent and every burden lying upon the estate at the proper time, or lets the estate fall into decay.** *Zorer, part 2, question 1, number 88*. Whether this also takes place when a hereditary tenant performs the owed duty only in part? *Question 1, number 88*. Likewise, where several hereditary tenants hold an estate, one of whom does not perform his duty, though it has been done by the other. *Question 1, number 88*. Question: As in sales, should the consent of the Lord be required in other transfers of ground-lease rights, for example, donations or exchanges? To which the answer is affirmative, but with a distinction: that in sales, consent is required both from the beginning of the contract and at the entry of the new ground tenant; but in other transfers, it is required only at the entry into possession. This distinction is supported by Meier and Locamerus.

## 62. Court-Fief. *Feudum aulicum.*

It is called a Court-Fief when an Emperor, Duke, or Count invests someone with a fief on the condition that they perform a duty in his Court, such as the office of Steward <note>original: "Dapiferi"</note>, Cupbearer <note>original: "Pincernæ"</note>, Court Marshal <note>original: "Præfecti aulæ"</note>, etc. Schrader *on fiefs*, part 2, chapter 4, number 54; add Gothofredus Antonius, disputation 1, thesis 7, letter K.

### ADDITION.

See Rosenthal, chapter 2, question 76, number 3. Vultejus, volume 1, fief 8, number 49.

## 63. Manorial District, Manorial Jurisdiction. *Hoffmarchia.*

Noble estates in Bavaria are named thus, or a *Hofmarck* is the jurisdiction of a nobleman. Hence *Hofmarcks Herren* (Lords of the Manor), as in other places they are called *Erbsassen* (hereditary residents), elsewhere Barons, and elsewhere also *Land-Herren* (Lords of the Land). Wherefore in the deeds of sale concerning such things, it is customary to state: our castle, market town, and lordship N. N., as it is surrounded with gates, moats, and other buildings, together with the court and manorial district <note>original: "Hofmarck"</note>, including all and each of its attachments and belongings, courts, markets, legal privileges <term>Ehehaftten: Ancient legal rights or local customs pertaining to a specific jurisdiction, often involving mandatory services or monopolies.</term>, compulsions <note>original: "Zwingen"</note>, bans, stewardships <term>Vogteyen: The office or jurisdiction of a protector or advocate who exercised secular authority over an area.</term>, farm buildings, mills, and all other legal rights, also farmsteads, hides of land <note>original: "Huben"</note>, estates, smallholdings <note>original: "Sölden"</note>, building sites, gardens, meadows, pastures, visits, drives, paths, fields, fallow lands, mosses, fisheries, fishing waters, ponds, together with the high and low hunting rights for red deer, and whatever else it might be named. See the Altdorf Consultations 111, in the preface, pages 724, 725. *Newburg Land-Freedom*, folio 9 and folio 13b, and everywhere also at the end.

### ADDITION.

*Hofmarck* among the Bavarians designates a territory: a Court-March or Court-Boundary <note>original: "Curtimarchia, vel Curtimarca"</note>. *Acts of Lindau*, folio 629.

## 64. High Authority, Royal Power. *Merum Imperium. Potestas regia.*

High Authority <note>original: "Hohe Obrigkeit"</note> is not always taken for the power of the sword <term>Gladii potestas: The legal authority to impose the death penalty.</term>, but mostly for superior jurisdiction and the highest degree of "pure command" <term>Merum Imperium: The supreme power of a magistrate, including the right to exercise criminal jurisdiction and capital punishment.</term>, to which confiscation and other rights are inherent. Andreas Goldeck *on the Right of Inheritance* <note>original: "de Jure Gerada"</note>, chapter 5, near the end, number 8, folio 170; where he says: supreme jurisdiction is called in the *Weichbild* <note>A traditional code of municipal and regional law in German cities.</note> Article 59, "Royal Power," where the gloss says: by "Royal Power" one should understand not only the King, but also all those to whom the sword is entrusted. Schneidewin, *Institutes on inheritance from the intestate*, under the rubric *on the succession of the treasury*, number 17. See Bidembach, *Nobility Questions* 1.

Where it must be noted that the Nobles formerly held only the hereditary court <note>original: "Erbgericht"</note> in their villages, which is why they were also called *Vogtsherren* (Lords Protectors) in Swabia; however, the High Authority belonged to the Counts, even in a subject territory, though we might wish to say that the Nobles themselves were immediately under the Empire.

Regarding what pertains to High Authority: see above under the word *Halsgericht* (Capital Court), also Bidembach, *Nobility Questions* 7. Riemer, *on modern jurisdiction*, volume 3, and K. 1b. Ripol, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 1, number 320, etc. Schickfus in the *Silesian Chronicle*, part 3, folio 319. The *Palatine Resolution of the Knighthood* given in the Upper Palatinate, folio 14, where it lists what are felony cases <note>original: "Malefitz-Fäll"</note>; likewise folio 16, what are lower-court cases, etc. Crafts, taverns, etc., to where they belong. Likewise folio 20.

That "pure command" <note>original: "merum Imperium"</note> does not make the inhabitants absolutely subjects can be seen in the *Peace of Dillingen*, question 32, number 13.

### ADDITION.

On the definition of "pure command," see Biccius in the *Golden Works*, section 5, thesis 54, and here regarding its division into full and less than full. The division of "pure command" by Jean de Clapiers into 6 degrees is to be seen in Bocer *on Jurisdiction*, 5, chapter 9. It is not unusual, says Limnäus in book 4, chapter 8, number 188, that to one belongs the territorial princely authority <note>original: "landsfürstl. Obrigkeit"</note>, to another the sovereignty and majesty of the land, to a third the hunting rights <note>original: "Wildbahn"</note>, to a fourth the forest rights, to a fifth the criminal jurisdiction and high court <note>original: "Fraiß und Cent"</note>, and to a sixth the stewardship and hereditary court.

## 65. Hide, Huob. *Prædium.*

*Huff*, to the Germans, is a property <note>original: "prædium"</note>, a plot of land as much as is almost enough for one farmer for his family's affairs; later Latin authors call it a *Huba*. Hence *Hubgüter* (Hide-estates). Rosenthal, chapter 2, conclusion 64. See Goldast on *Ancient Precepts*, folio 437, where he says this word is very ancient. Brouwer, *Antiquities of Fulda*, folio 260. *Hobgetta* was the tax and revenue which the colonists paid. Whether *Hoba* indeed [is the same as] a Court- [fief]...

->ADDITION.<-

What "A Hide of Land" <note>original: "Ein Hube Lands"</note> is, is discussed at length by Lord Doctor Tabor in *On the Contract and Provincial Law of Tenants*, section 39.

*Houba* or *Hufa*, or *Hiufa*, or *Guifa*, according to the Lombard Laws, and according to *Frisius*, is a part of a plot of land or an estate divided among several heirs. *Aventinus* calls "hubas" those fields usually plowed by two oxen, and *Vadianus* calls it a part of an estate that is mostly pasture. *Spigelius* says it is too wide a term to be so strictly confined, and that it embraces all land suitable either for harvest or haymaking, in which there are several huts. However, Coccius, in his notes on Dagobert, chapter 29, page 117, observed that a Hide is not a fixed measure of land but an indefinite one, based on the convenience and opportunity of each place, and includes roughly as much land as is sufficient for a Peasant to maintain his household.

In Alsace, Hides comprise thirty fields, as can be seen from the Court Covenants <note>original: "pactis Curialibus"</note>, such as the Court-Registers <note>original: "Dinck-Rodel"</note> of Niederhausbergen, Sachsenheim, Leimersheim, Dingsheim near Krießheim, Geispolzheim, Ongenharst, Eckboltsheim, and elsewhere. See **Wehner under the word *Huob, Hubgüter*.** Dürrdeum in *On Manorial Courts*, thesis 19 at the end. In certain places, all these lands are held by ground lease <term>emphyteusis</term> or are subject to rent; in some places, they are numbered among fiefs because of the loyalty owed, although they may be called "degenerate and improper fiefs." **Lasius on degenerate fiefs; Zal. on fiefs, part 11,** number 2.

**Hubgüter,** that is, peasant fiefs. **Rosenthal,** chapter 2, question 64.

### 66. Hünerfaut. **An official pressing for the annual payment of death-taxes.**

A Lord can appoint certain Officials, commonly called **Aus-Hoer** <note>literally "listeners" or registrars</note> or **Hünerfaut** <note>literally "poultry-advocate," as death-taxes were often paid in poultry</note>, who are to have all the "own-people" <note>serfs or subjects</note> and their descendants specifically listed in a register. They are to strike the dead from the roll, add those who arrive annually, and faithfully remind them of the payment of death-taxes <note>original: "mortuariorum"</note> and other things to which the own-people are bound to their Lords according to the custom of the region. They should defend them against unjust force so that they do not transfer their domicile elsewhere without the consent of their Lord, and they must diligently provide that no prejudice is created against the Lord in his right of cultivation, but rather that his Right should grow. *Stamm on own-people, chapter 25, number 11,* citing the *Palatine Provincial Ordinance, title 8,* which the reader should consult. And this is extended so that even a Prince or another, who has own-people living in the territory of another Lord, can ordain an Official,

<column-break/>

an *Aus- und Hünerfaut*, for the protection of his own Right in that place.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding this word, one should see Sprenger in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 204.

### 67. Hur, Hurenhäuser, Hurerey.

->Prostitute. Brothels.<-

**Hur** <note>Whore</note> is foolishly derived from "hora" <note>hour</note> by **Scherzius** in his *Domestic Language School, page 164.* More correctly, Lord Martinius in his *Philological Lexicon* under the word *Meretrix* <note>Prostitute</note>, derives it from "heuren," that is, to hire for a wage or to lease; whence "Heurath," that is, marriage, a universal lease. Furthermore, that a virgin who, captured by the force of love, has allowed her virginal modesty to be shaken by a lover, is not to be considered a prostitute, and thus a base and infamous person, is proved by **Lord Dr. Harpprecht on section "non autem" 1 of the Institutes *on inofficious wills*, number 31 and following.** Cephalus, *counsel 140, volume 1.*

**Brothels** <note>original: "Lupanaria"</note>, whether, and why they should be tolerated. See **Langlaeus, *Semestria*, book 8, chapter 8, etc., and Metr. *on information*. Kizel *on marriage*, chapter 8, theorem 2. Nicolaus à Salis in *Siciliment.* at the authentic collection 3,** page 869.

Regarding prostitutes and fornication, various points are held by **Coler in his *Parerga*, chapter 8. Marquardus de Susanis, *Treatise on the Celibacy of Priests*, chapter 18, and on the vileness of Prostitutes, Freher, 2 *Parerga*, chapter 14.**

->ADDITION.<-

### 69. To wear a hat, to take off a hat. The Cap. <note>original: "Hut tragen, Hut abziehen. Pileus."</note>

->**ADDITION.**<-

A messenger bringing a hat from the sender is not always to be believed. Heino von Hachten, *On the Messenger*, chapter 9, paragraph 47. In some places, those who have surrendered their assets to creditors <note>original: "cesserunt bonis"; a form of bankruptcy</note> are required to wear a hat or a hood <note>original: "capitium"</note> of a yellow or green color as a sign of the surrender; this itself carries a certain degree of infamy. A green hat signifies one who surrendered his assets having been made poor by his own foolishness. Limnaeus, volume 2, addition J. P. to book 4, chapter 8, page 313. Regarding the gifting and exchange of a hat, see Zahn, *On Deceit*, book 1, chapter 44, number 2.

Slaves who were manumitted <note>legally freed</note> and made free citizens would shave their heads and take up the *pileus* <note>a felt cap</note>, and this was the badge of liberty. Plautus in *Amphitruo*, act 1, scene 1, last verse: "So that I here today, bald with a shaved head, may take up the cap." Slaves were said to be "called to the cap" when they were called to freedom. Pacius, *Analysis of the Code*, page 747. Therefore, they walked in the funeral procession with their heads covered and wearing caps, before the body of the one who had freed them. Persius, *Satire 5*:

> This is mere liberty, which these caps grant us.
> From here comes the trumpet, the candles: and at last the "blessed" man,
> Laid out on a high bed, and smeared with thick balsams,

<column-break/>

> Extends his stiff heels toward the door: but he,
> Made a citizen only yesterday, is carried by men with covered heads.
<note>This passage describes a slave who was freed by his master's will, now participating as a free citizen (Quirite) in the master's funeral.</note>

Those manumitted by a will also appeared in public wearing the cap. Pacius, *Analysis of the Code*, pages 747 and 755. Those who received direct liberty from the master’s will preceded the bed on which the master’s corpse was carried, wearing their caps; they followed other beds that displayed the images of the deceased’s ancestors.

A "cap" <note>original: "pileum"</note> is also the name given to that membrane or skin in which a fetus is wrapped <note>the amniotic sac or caul</note>. Salmasius on Solinus, page 939.

The hat was once a sign of liberty. Volaterranus, book 30, *Philology*, page 329. Johannes Goropius Becanus, book 3, *On the Franks*, page 87: while our people are called to the "cap," a manifold liberty is given to them: students are called from the servitude of being disciples to the liberty of leading, and they are promoted from the company of those who remain silent to the class of those who respond. Formerly, those who escaped a storm were accustomed to take up a hat. Stuckius, book 2, *Antiquities of Banquets*, chapter 28, page 230. The same is granted to Doctoral candidates. For they, too, sailing through the stormy sea of the sciences, driven about on all sides by the burning assaults of a bristling Jupiter and a bilious Neptune, have finally reached the port of Erudition. To appear in the presence of others with the head covered is a sign of the greatest honor. And we know of the excellent Duke of Charles V, who sought that privilege of the Spanish nobles—to be with a covered head around the King—with a clever response. For when he was troubled by gout and advised by Charles to sit rather than stand, he replied that the ailment was not in his feet, but in his head. In the act of Graduation itself, the same honor is held for the Candidates, so that even if they have their Patrons, Princes, and Superiors at their side and in their sight, they may nevertheless keep their heads covered without any note of rudeness. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 8, number 91.

Citizens restored from captivity to liberty followed the chariot of their triumphant benefactor while wearing caps. The hat was formerly held as a badge of absolute liberty and the highest nobility; its ancient shape was hemispherical, similar to the shell of a larger egg cut into equal parts. Lucian relates that the Garamantes <note>an ancient Saharan people</note> once preferred to wear such head coverings made from the larger eggs of ostriches. Now, however, craftsmen ignorant of these mysteries form them with a flatter top, about which Pighius writes in *Hercules Prodicius*, pages 301 and 302. On the coins of Brutus—who, after Caesar was killed, seemed to himself to have recovered the liberty of the Roman people—we see on one side his image with the inscription: *Brutus, Imperator, Lucius Plaetorius Cestianus*. On the other side, a cap between two daggers with the title *EID. MAR.* <note>The Ides of March</note>, because Caesar was killed by Brutus and other conspirators with that kind of weapon on the Ides of March. And from this example, Henry II, King of the French, ordered certain coins to be struck when he undertook an expedition into Germany in the year of Christ 1552. For just as he wished to indicate that the end of his war was so that the Princes...

It is a just honor to uncover the head in the presence of honorable men; nor is this custom merely some servile flattery that our own age has devised. Curtius writes that *Canus, a leader of Alexander’s forces*, when about to speak before the King, removed the helmet from his head according to the custom of his people. The same custom belonged to the Romans. Hear Seneca: "If I see a consul or a Teacher, I shall perform all those acts by which honor is customarily shown: I shall dismount from my horse and I shall uncover my head." Thus, when Lucius Sulla wished to show the greatest honors to the young *Gnaeus Pompey* because of his supreme virtue and the way he had strenuously aided Sulla’s faction, it is recorded in memory that Sulla was accustomed to descend from his horse, rise from his seat, and uncover his head—honoring ancient dignity in the manner of the ancients. How does this square with what other authors write, that not only the Romans of old, but also the Germans, Italians, and Gauls, went with heads open and without covering? Certainly, among all the ancients, this was the case; in all their styles and dress, they are represented promiscuously without head coverings. There is a clear passage in *Suetonius*, who says that of all the honors decreed to him, *Julius Caesar* used none more gladly or frequently than the right to perpetually wear a laurel crown—and this was *to hide his baldness*. (*Regarding why "Baldy" was a term used at banquets among many nations, see Saubert, "On Sacrifices," page 234. On baldness, see Limnaeus in "Public Law," book 2, chapter 1, number 13. The bald are excused. They are praised by Rango in "On Wigs," page 54: "Laurel branches cover a bald head." <note>original German: "Lorbeerzweig bedecken ein Kaahlkopff"</note> Martin Mylius in "Pleasure Garden of Graceful Wisdom," page 573.*) Yet Caesar would have hidden it more fully with a cap, if such had been in common use among the Romans. It should be noted in passing that the ancients walked with heads uncovered, but covered them at certain times and for specific reasons, such as for sacred rites or some uncertain peril. Those about to worship God prayed with covered heads, as in *Plautus’s Amphitryon*. He invokes the immortal gods with clean hands and an uncovered head; but the Priests <note>term: "flamines"</note>, Augurs, and Heralds <note>term: "feciales"</note> were veiled of head for their duties, as *Varro* writes, as were Emperors about to devote themselves for the Republic. Yet the Tribunes of the People were not to be covered when performing consecrations, nor were those condemned for some good cause, as *Cicero* and *Lipsius* demonstrate. Also, in the games, during travel, and in military service, they wore head coverings; thus it must be understood that it was the *uncovering* of the head by which Great Men were honored. *Plutarch* states clearly: The Romans, if they met anyone to whom honor was due and

<column-break/>

happened to have their heads covered by their garments, would reveal them. I see this also questioned among the learned: whether the ancients practiced what is customary today—that in saluting the powerful and showing them honor, we move our hand to our mouth. More on this elsewhere. Doctors <note>meaning those holding the highest academic degree</note> are to be heard with their heads covered by all Magistrates. Limnaeus, *in "Public Law," book 8, chapter 8, number 117.* On the doctoral cap or tiara, see Walther, *on the privileges of Doctors, page 448 and following.* The term "Silk Cape" <note>original: "Cappa de serico"</note> is found in Ludovicus Romanus, *singular 260*. On whether a hood is a garment, see *Tholosaeus, decision 248*. Basil, the King of the Moscovites, ordered a cap to be fixed to the head of a certain Ambassador with a nail because he had covered his head in a rustic <note>meaning rude or disrespectful</note> manner. See *Sigismund, Baron von Herberstein, in "History of Moscovy." On the bare head and the uncovering of the head, see Saubert, "On Sacrifices," page 277.*

Discussed at length by Lauterbach, *on the Messenger, question 37.* "To bring glasses under one hat." <note>original German: "Gläser unter einen Hut bringen"; a German idiom meaning to bring different parties into agreement or to reconcile conflicting views</note> Harsdörffer, *in "The Great Stage," volume 125, number 9.
