### 70. Homage, Hereditary and Territorial Homage. <note>original: "Huldigung, Erb- und Lands-Huldigung. Homagium."</note>

Homage <note>term: "Homagium"; derived from the French *homme*, meaning to become the "man" or vassal of a lord</note> is defined as the Oath of Fidelity which subjects living in a certain territory perform for their Lord, in accordance with his jurisdiction and their subjection, for as long as they remain in that territory. Andreas Knichen, *on Territorial Law, chapter 3, number 155.* And this is performed not because of property possessed, but with respect to the person, and it is this which truly makes one a subject. Coler, *on the process of execution, part 2, chapter 1, number 23.* Geil, *on pledges, chapter 15, number 7, and book 2, observation 35, number 2. And it is taught that the first recognition and proof of subjection is made through this oath.* Thomas Michael, *on Jurisdiction, conclusion 57. Meichsner, volume 2, book 2, decision 4, number 122. Cothman, counsel 47, number 38, volume 1. See Knichen in the "Encyclopedia," chapter 3, throughout.*

Homage or Hereditary Homage <note>original: "Homagium oder die Erbhuldigung"</note> is considered a Universal Act of Jurisdiction, under which every other act is necessarily contained. For when a Prince ensures that his subjects swear obedience, he is then in "quasi-possession" of Jurisdiction and its consequences; because the nerve of obedience encompasses all other acts of Jurisdiction. Anyone refusing to perform such Homage can be coerced, either by the imposition of a fine, the seizure of their castles or possessions, the taking of pledges, or other such remedies provided in the law. *Ortenburg Acts, folio 32.*

<meta>This page continues the legal and symbolic discussion from page 448 regarding the transition of power and the rituals of status. While the previous page focused on the "cap of liberty" and gestures of respect like uncovering the head, this page defines the formal legal bond between a ruler and those under their authority, specifically the concept of "Homage" (Homagium).</meta>

Lit. H.

And "Homage" <note>original: *Homagium*</note> is so named as if it were "man-ship" <note>original: *Hominium*</note>, because he who performs this oath is said to become the "man" <note>original: *homo*</note> of the Lord, or as if he becomes mine; or he conducts himself as a man—that is, he professes himself a subject. We call this *Hereditary Duty*, *Homage*, or *Loyalty*, as if it were a *Covenant* to be *loyal and true*. <note>original German: *Erbpflicht*, *Huldigung*, *Holdung*, *Geding*, *hold und treu*</note>

"Man-ship," Homage, Acknowledgment <note>original Greek-derived: *Homologia*</note>, and Fealty are *Synonyms*. Most frequently, Homage is understood in two ways: either as carefully weighed regarding a beneficial matter granted by feudal law (called "Vassalage" for that reason), or in consideration of subjection, which can be called "subject-homage." Within this second meaning, an ambiguity occurs: for it is taken either for the loyalty of subjection itself, or for the act of swearing by which that loyalty is confirmed. *Raudensis, response 1, number 366, book 2.* Not unlike in feudal law-making, "fealty" sometimes denotes the very form of the fief by which it is established, and sometimes the formula of the oath. *Chapter 1, section "in fin. quæ fuit prim. caus.", etc.*

There are many species of Homage: for one is performed by *Vassals*, another by *household servants*, another by *confederates*, or others according to the nature of the contracts and obligations. *Rosenthal on Fiefs, chapter 6, conclusion 85, and following; Fachin. cons. 58.*

This type of Oath was unknown to Civil Law <note>Roman law</note> and was later introduced by almost universal custom on the occasion of the feudal system. *Bruning on various universal species, conclusion 33; Caspar Ziegler in the section "City" in limitations, number 27.* Therefore, it must always be performed according to received custom, and no innovation is to be tolerated there. *chapter "dilecti" on majority and obedience.* Hence, if a Prince wishes to change it, it is rightfully denied by the subjects. *Specul. title on fiefs, section "quoniam".* For a Prince is bound to preserve the City in that state in which he found it. *Law "nomine", Code on Decurions.* And a City subjected to any Lord ought to be regulated by the Laws, Statutes, and Customs of that City itself, and not those of a newly arriving Lord, according to *Bartolus, Baldus, and Salicetus, and after them Goeden, cons. 31, number 7.*

Nor does it always imply subjection. Thus Cologne, Speyer, Worms, etc., perform Homage to Bishops. Sometimes it implies a "mixed subjection." Thus Hamburg swears to the Duke of Holstein, and likewise Brunswick to its Prince.

This Oath is correlative, or often reciprocal. For just as subjects swear obedience and subjection to their Lords: *To be humble, obedient, loyal, true, and ready.* Also: *What a faithful inhabitant and subject is bound to do for his rightful hereditary Lord and Prince of the land.* <note>original German: *Unterthänig, gehorsam, hold, treu und gewärtig zu seyn... Was ein getreuer Landsaß und Unterthan seinem rechten Erbherrn und Landsfürsten zu thun schuldig ist.*</note> *Gylm. book 2, decisions in the case of M. against the Bishop of W., number 8, page 725.*

So the Lords, in turn, also swear that they will be faithful to their subjects, and whatever Privilege or

<column-break/>

Custom they possess shall remain safe and undiminished for them. Hence the proverb: *Faithful Lord, faithful servant.* *Valentin Forster on jurisdiction, part 2, page 462, number 147.* And this condition is seen to be tacitly inherent in the obligation of Homage, even if it is not explicitly stated, or even if the Prince binds himself to it by oath. *See also Lord Bocer, treatise on regalia, page 484, number 44.*

The Oath of Subjection, however, differs from the Oath of Fealty (which Vassals perform to their Lords for the benefits or fiefs received from them, *that they wish to be true and loyal to their Lord.* <note>original: *daß sie wollen ihrem Herrn treu und hold seyn*</note>). This is because [Fealty] is performed for those things which the Vassals received from the Lord in the name of a fief. The former—namely *Homage*—is performed to a Lord even if one holds no goods from that Lord. Fealty is for military service; Homage is for subjection. When the benefit of the fief ends, Fealty also ends; Homage is performed by reason of subjection and retains its force as long as the subject remains in the Territory. *Forster, as cited, number 148.*

Likewise, one is bound to perform the Oath of Subjection in person <note>original: *ipse per se*</note>, not through a proxy <note>original: *per Procuratorem*</note>, as a Vassal might. Just as a citizen must resign his Right of Citizenship <note>original German: *das Burgerrecht*</note> in person. *argument from law 35, Digest on Rules of Law.*

Although Homage implies subjection, it does not induce a kind of servitude upon a free person <note>literally "a free head"; *in capite libero*</note>. For ownership <note>original: *dominium*</note> is one thing, and sovereignty <note>original: *Imperium*</note> is another. *Myself in "Political Preliminaries," page 74.*

Homage must be performed by subjects whenever the person of the Lord is changed, by death or any other way; likewise whenever someone is a subject of another: *as often as a hereditary Lord departs by death or in another way, the subjects are bound to perform the hereditary duty upon request.* <note>original German: *so offt ein Erbherr mit Tod oder in ander Weg abkommt, seynd die Unterthanen die Erbpflicht... zu leisten schuldig.*</note> For those living in a place where someone has high and low jurisdiction <note>original: *Merum & Mixtum Imperium*; referring to the power to command and punish in both criminal and civil matters</note> are bound to perform the Oath of Fealty to him. *Surd. cons. 87.* ... where some attempt to prove, by an argument from the contrary sense, that even Clergy possessing temporal goods from Laymen are bound to perform such an Oath. Hence the penalty for a subject refusing to perform this Oath to the Lord without just cause is the loss of property. *Schrader, cons. 23.* Because this oath—the *sworn Homage* <note>original German: *die eydliche Huldigung*</note>—is required from subjects for the purpose of maintaining peace and tranquility, and so that the suspicion of sedition may be purged and removed, and the Lord may be made secure. *Chapter 1, "qual. jur. deb. Vas."* He who refuses to perform the Oath regarding the public peace is punished by the forfeiture of goods. And a subject who refuses to do what he is bound to do by Law is said to live rebelliously. A rebel, moreover, is liable to lose all feudal and allodial goods...

It must be noted here that if any City performs this Oath or Homage to any Prince, when it was previously immune <note>free from such obligations</note>, it loses its Privilege and becomes subject. Hence, a confession made against one's own liberty is not valid, because it is made against nature—that is, against the natural state of man. Much less is it valid when someone has been compelled to give their word in writing that they are not free. *See the law "not even if willing" and the Glosses and Baldus there, in the Code on liberty cases.* And in the said law, Baldus concludes that if a Lord makes a transaction with a man [to enslave him], it is not valid, as it is against the natural state. He also records in the same place that if the Emperor, the Pope, or the King of the French should make any City swear fealty to him when it was not his own, it would not be valid: because he would then be acting in the manner of a Tyrant. And from this, it was concluded in the Imperial Chamber Court, in the case of **the small town of Wangen against all the Lords of Laibs**, etc., that such an oath is null by the law itself. Rutger Ruland, *decisions on controverted law, question 21.*

Indeed, this violent occupation of a City, and the illegitimate compulsion of Citizens to swear, does not work to create subjection; even the Vice [legal flaw] is not purged even if the Prince’s Confirmation follows. *Law on authority, 3, in the Code on "where by force."* Gail, *book 2, observation 54, number 8,* through the sources cited there.

It is very well known, and daily experience testifies, that Castles, Villages, and other such things are usually granted to Nobles by Princes, along with their attachments, appurtenances, Jurisdiction, and other benefits; and indeed with various Clauses, which often imply Higher or Lower Jurisdiction. I pose this case: **Several citizens in an Imperial City have a dispute or legal proceeding at Speyer <note>The seat of the Imperial Chamber Court</note>; it is asked whether, in the meantime, they must take the annual Citizen's Oath?** I answer that they must. (1) They are nonetheless still subjects. (2) Even an appeal made from a Judge does not prevent him from remaining the Judge in other causes; and if they refuse this Oath, they can be punished with arrests, imprisonment, etc. This is argued from the writings of Gail, *on arrests, chapter 10, number 1.* They can, however, perform the homage with a **protestation** <note>A legal reservation of rights so the oath doesn't undermine their court case</note>.

But is a City situated within a territory to be forced into homage? *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 2, consultation 41.*

Therefore, in the *Ortenburg Records* <note>original: "Actis Ortenburgicis"</note>, on page 24, the Ortenburg legal representative <term>Procurator</term> <note>A legal representative or agent acting on behalf of a noble in court.</note> complains that, concerning his person, he is neither subject to the grace and favor of the Bavarian administration, nor to any of their Princely Governments; otherwise, he would not know what his Countly preeminence should offer him. Likewise, he states that he will not submit himself to the subjection of the Territorial Prince, nor to the authority of their government.

And *it is held on page 39* <note>original: "habetur"</note> that it is an established custom where such a potentate—who holds various kingdoms, principalities, border-lands, counties, and lordships, many and more—uses each according to the local custom, quality, and freedom of each land specifically and respectively in his titles, administration, and decrees, as has been traditional from of old for this or that kingdom, principality, land, or lordship. We have examples of this in many Roman Emperors of most noble memory, and still within the Empire, and no less among other kings, princes, and lords who are members of the Holy Roman Empire. All of these were not ashamed, though they held Imperial and Royal dignities, to nonetheless sign themselves as princes, counts, and lords of those specific places, to govern there, to pass judgment, to take and to give, according to the lesser dignity, land, and tradition. Thus, they bore not one or two, but many persona <note>In a legal sense, a "persona" refers to the different legal roles or capacities one individual might hold simultaneously.</note>. Just as a subject can be employed in two, three, or more offices, and thus can be summoned in both personal and property matters. This is provided for by Law, and additionally in the Imperial Recesses <note>The official resolutions of the Imperial Diet (Reichstag).</note>, especially that of the year 1548, which specifies that neither counts nor lords are to withdraw themselves from the authority of the princes, etc., in matters where they are subject to them through their person, or by reason of their land and people.

On page 112, the Count says that he is not the only Imperial Estate <term>Reichs-Stand</term> <note>A member of the Holy Roman Empire with the right to vote in the Imperial Diet, holding territory directly under the Emperor.</note> who possesses estates located within the land of Bavaria, but that there are many more among the bishops and prelates. However, it can never be proven in eternity that these individuals, because of their landed estates, acknowledged or obligated their persons to Bavarian subjection, or in personal matters made themselves *liege men* <note>original: "pro hominibus ligiis"</note> of the Duke of Bavaria because of their Bavarian properties, or regarded and recognized him as their natural hereditary lord or territorial prince.

And it is added on *page 113: Whenever a King, Prince, or Count has and possesses property outside his Kingdom, Province, or County, in the territory of another King or Prince, by reason of which property he is accustomed to perform an Oath of Fidelity, he is not by this made a subordinate or subject by reason of his person or by personal obligation; nor does he fall under that jurisdiction regarding his person, except in his own Kingdom, Principality, or County. In which, by reason of property situated elsewhere, he cannot be immediately cited by the Lord of the place or territory, nor can anything be commanded of him that binds his person—*

<column-break/>

—all these things are proven in *the chapter "ex parte" concerning competent jurisdiction and in the Clementine decree "Pastoralis" in the section "denique & rursus" where Cardinals and Giovanni da Imola write on judgments and matters decided. Because no one is truly and properly a subject by reason of property alone.* <note>original Latin legal citations omitted for brevity in note: refers to standard Canon and Civil law texts used in the 17th century.</note> The same was felt and advised by Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist.</note> regarding the person of the Prince of Württemberg, legal opinion 451, number 30. Natta holds the same in opinion 445. *Hence an obligation of this kind, which is made because of a thing and on the occasion of a thing, is more real (relating to property) than personal.*

Otherwise, if every Imperial Estate who has property in a principality had to be a landed resident <term>Landsäß</term> <note>A resident subject who owes taxes and service to a territorial prince.</note> of that prince, even in personal matters, then two most absurd inconveniences would follow.

**The first**, that his Imperial Majesty would keep very few princes, counts, lords, and estates in his immediate subjection <note>The status of being "Imperial Immediate" (unmittelbar) meant answering only to the Emperor, not to a middle-man like a Duke.</note>, because those with property in the lands of other estates would be landed residents by reason of subjection.

**The second**, however, is that such Imperial Estates would have more lords and authorities in personal matters simultaneously, at the same time, and in full. While yet a true and Liege Homage <note>A "liege" homage was an absolute personal bond of loyalty, usually reserved for one's primary sovereign.</note> includes within itself personal subjection. And because the Count, in this quality of his person, is bound by homage to the Emperor, he cannot be thus bound and subject to the Duke of Bavaria; because nature itself teaches that no one can be the liege man of two lords in full at the same time. In other "common" and non-liege homage, the Oath of Fidelity does not grant jurisdiction and the right of subjection over the person, except only by reason of the property, in as far as the property extends. Therefore, if something were committed by reason of the property for which one would act to punish the person, he could not be summoned in the territory where the property is located. And thus has it been the custom in all parts of the Empire.

It is argued on *page 88 on the part of Bavaria*, that because it is the Law that where one has the majority of his property, there he also has the *Right of Domicile* <note>original: "Jus domicilii"</note>. The Count also occasionally occupies Mattighofen and other properties in rotation, possessing them himself, and at the very least has his household family and "bread-servants" <note>original: "gebröttte Diener" - servants who receive food and board from the master.</note> (as he calls them in the Third Mandate of the Religious Peace) residing there. Thus, neither the Count himself nor his bread-servants could be subject to anyone else by reason of habitation and domicile than to him to whom the territory of those parts belongs.

It is also not strange, but happens often, that one has *two habitations and two domiciles* <note>original: "duas habitationes und duo domicilia"</note> at once: residing in one personally, and living in the other at another time. He can also have...

The execution money, the **Enforcement Fee** <term>Hülffgeld</term> <note>German: *Hülffgeld*; a fee paid to the court or official to carry out a judgment.</note>, must not be paid out if all the acts—namely of execution, handing over of property, and appraisal—have not preceded and been actually performed. This fee is to be estimated from the price of the auction, **Carpzov, part 3, Decision 176, number 2.** Execution cannot be carried out against him or those against whom no sentence was issued. **Following Bartolus and Borcholt; Johannes Melonius in the Index of Forensic Matters, under the word "Execution."** The new **Execution Ordinance** <note>original: *Executions Ordnung*</note> is mentioned by **Sutting, observation 112, number 5; observation 117, numbers 4 and 5.** Execution regarding feudal property <note>original: *in bonis feudalia*</note> according to Common Law applies only to the usage and profits <note>usufruct</note> as long as the Debtor lives, but now it applies also to the feudal goods themselves. **Sutting, observation 109, throughout.**

"Execution" is called **the Aid** <term>Hülff</term> or **letting the aid proceed** <term>die Hülff ergehen lassen</term> by the Germans, because it is the "extreme aid" of the bidder, by which the winner is consulted so that he is not forced to contend in court any longer, **Coler on Executory Process, in the preface, number 26.** It is the **Execution or fulfillment of the judgment** <term>Vollstreckung oder Vollziehung der Urtheil</term>. **Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court, part 2, title 48.** To dispossess someone of his goods in a legal manner. **Gloss on the Landrecht, book 3, article 43, number 4.**

A contumacious person <note>one who defies a court order</note> in our Law is condemned just as one who has confessed, *law 53, regarding the matter judged*, since contumacy induces a "fictional confession," *final law, paragraph 7, Code on the oath regarding malice; law 1, paragraph 2 at the end, Code on the removal of assertions; chapter 2, on confessions in the sixth book of Decretals.* Why, therefore, should the judge not be able to accept a handwritten bond <note>original: *chirographum*</note>—which a contumacious debtor refuses to acknowledge—as if it were confessed, and order execution? As was pronounced in the case of **P. against Q., Gail, book 1, observation 15, number 15 and book 1, observation 80, number 6**; and in the case of **Johann Volfstadtes against the heirs of Ulrich Reslings at Leipzig, in the month of May, the year 1632. Carpzov, Forensic Jurisprudence, part 1, constitution 10, definition 10.** However, in this case it is required that the creditor accuses the debtor's contumacy and requests the writing be held as recognized, *law 13, paragraph 2, Code on judgments; Authentica "he who once," Code on how and when the judge...* and afterward, at the requester's petition, the Judge should declare the defendant contumacious and that he holds the bond as recognized, *said law 13, paragraph 3*, because otherwise it depends on the judge's discretion whether he wishes to compel him to recognize it, **Gloss on law 6, paragraph 1, on the word "let him confess," regarding confessions.** Thus in the case of **Münster against Bentheim**

Causes of **Legally Justified Excuses** <term>Ehehafften</term> are the same as those that are privileged and revocable <note>can be called back to a higher court</note>, **Limnaeus in Public Law, book 9, chapter 3, number 9.** Concerning the condemnation of a defendant—unless he comes to defend himself at the third term, with the excuse of a just impediment reserved—he is condemned as convicted **subject to a Legally Justified Excuse** <note>original: *bis auf Ehehafft*</note>, **Wesenbeck on the Pandects, regarding accusations, number 8.** The necessity of a most important business, *last chapter, XI, question 3.* An external burden of necessity, *law "it pleases," paragraph C, Code on the Holy Churches; chapter "generally" 40, XVI, question 1.* A moment of inevitable necessity, *chapter "having been asked" 13, outside of rescripts.* A pressing moment of necessity, *chapter "Yours in the Lord" 10, outside of age; chapter "on marriages" 3, XXXI, question 2; chapter "letters" 13, outside of the time of orders.* Inevitable and urgent trouble, *if none 15, XXIII, question 8.* The ultimate weapon of necessity, **Reinkingk, on the Secular State, 162, class 3, chapter 3, number 68** at the end. In German: **Legally Justified Necessity** <term>Ehehaffte Noth</term>. *Text of the Landrecht, book 2, article 7.* **True Necessity.** **Eberhard Spech, century 1, question 59, number 41.** **Legally justified and unavoidable need** <term>Ehehaffte unvermeidliche Nothdurfft</term>. **Francis Pfeil, Counsel 174, numbers 4 and 9.** and then a "highly pressing **Necessity**," **Pfeil, Counsel 146, number 7 at the end.** An "obvious **Necessity**." **Imperial Recess at Augsburg, 1566, paragraph "therefore the utmost necessity."** **Rightful Necessity. When these legitimate impediments are contested, the contumacious person is said to have "risen and obtained up to the half": on which matter he explains diligently. **Hartmann Pistor, book 1, question 4; Andreas Rauchbar, book 1, question 1.** **Barbosa deals at length with impediments in book 9, axioms, chapter 11, throughout.** A person accused of a capital crime who is absent is publicly sought and called by public denunciations and Edicts, with letters also sent to the judge of the province where the delinquent person stays. Concerning the search for defendants <note>Latin: *de requirendis reis*</note>, the final law of the Code on this subject states that if a person comes forward to defend themselves after a year, they are admitted. If found guilty, they are punished more severely; if innocent, however, they are acquitted. They recover their reputation <note>Latin: *existimatio*; legal standing or honor</note>, but not their goods, which remain with the state treasury <note>Latin: *fiscus*</note>, according to the second law of the Code on the search for defendants. For what the treasury has once occupied in the name of a penalty, it never returns. The restoration of rights <note>Latin: *restitutio in integrum*</note> returns only citizenship and reputation to the condemned, not the penalty already paid (according to the Law of Julius on Bribery), unless the Prince specifically restores the goods as well. Today, by the general custom of Germany, murderers and those guilty of other notorious crimes for which death was to be inflicted are condemned in their absence after a formal summons. Sichard, in his commentary on the law "not always" (number 14) regarding how and when a judge should proceed, writes that there is a similar custom among the people of Bruges in Flanders, as noted by Damhouder in *Criminal Practice*, chapter 75, number 7. Regarding one who wishes to be helped by the pretext of a hindrance, and what they must prove: see Zorer, part 2, question 7. One cannot be said to be hindered if they can easily remove the hindrance, according to Knipschild in *On Entailed Estates*, chapter 16, number 99.

**Expenses of Execution.** **Enforcement Fee** <term>Hülffgeld</term> <note>German: *Hülffgeld*; a fee paid to court officials to carry out a judgment.</note>. See Matthias Berlich, conclusion 81; Daniel Moller, book 2, chapter 40; and Giovanni Baptista Asinius’s treatise on execution, chapter 84.

### 72. *Hunds. Tag.* Dog Days.

Regarding the stars and the Dog Days <note>Latin: *dies caniculares*; the hot, midsummer period associated with the star Sirius, the "Dog Star."</note>, see Talentonus, book 2, chapter 9, and Bisciola, volume 2, chapter 2, where he discusses the power of the star and why it is called Sirius.

---

## ADDITION.

Simon Majolus wrote specifically about the Dog Days. Upon the rising of the Dog Star, the sun’s vapors are intensified, the seas boil, wines in the cellars fluctuate, ponds are stirred, and throughout that period, dogs are most driven to madness <note>rabies</note>. From this, Persius writes in his third Satire:

> The mad Dog-star has long been ripening 
> the parched harvests.

Concerning the heat of the Dog Star and its origin, see the very accurate and pleasant notes of Philippus Carolus on Gellius. In the Imperial Chamber <note>Latin: *Camera Imperialis*; the high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, the Dog Days are made non-working days <note>Latin: *nefasti*; days when legal business was suspended</note>, calculated from July 8th to August 14th, according to the Chamber Ordinances. This is perhaps so that the summer heats may be mitigated by the leisure of those holidays. Ummius discusses this in his *Process*, as does Doctor Biccius, who distinguishes holidays into "solemn" and "sudden." Solemn holidays are either divine (Sunday or feasts, both fixed and movable) or human. Human holidays are those for the harvests and the vintages. Sudden holidays are declared out of the ordinary for successful events. And these holidays in the

<column-break/>

Imperial Chamber are clearly defined.

From the 8th day of July until the 14th day of August inclusive, the Imperial Chamber shall be on holiday; these are called the Dog Days or the "Great Holidays." During these Great Holidays, the Assessors <note>judges</note> nevertheless meet on certain days of the week—Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—to decree or deny processes of all kinds as the situation arises. The reason, perhaps, is because petitions for lawsuits and other extrajudicial causes can hardly admit or endure a delay of so many weeks. However, no formal audiences, neither in the morning nor the afternoon, are celebrated, even though the Decree of 1654 seems to argue against this; experience teaches otherwise. Furthermore, whenever the clause "Excluding holidays" is inserted into legal Processes, it is understood to mean these Great Holidays. Under this said clause, they correctly include not only these Great Dog Day holidays, but also those of the Birth of the Lord <note>Christmas</note>, Easter, and Pentecost. Finally, although certain feasts of Saints are not celebrated by the members of the Chamber belonging to the Augsburg Confession <note>Protestants</note> for religious reasons, nevertheless, on the days they fall, they are holidays in the Chamber because the legal style dictates it. The "harmful Dog-star" is also mentioned in relation to dice games:

> *For it was his highest desire to know what the lucky six would bring,*
> *and how much the ruinous Dog-star would strip away...*

Persius, Satire 3. <note>original: "Es war um die Würffel und das Damriegel-Spiel zu thun."</note> *It was a matter of the dice and the game of backgammon.*

### 73. *Hund tragen.* Carrying the Dog.

**Dog-Carrying** <term>Κυνοφορία</term> <note>Greek: *Kynophoria*; literally "carrying a dog."</note> was a military punishment, as Arnold of Lübeck and Otto of Freising write concerning the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa: An old custom grew into law among the Franks and Swabians, that if any Noble, Court Official, or Peasant was found guilty of such excesses before his Judge, before he was punished by a death sentence, he was compelled to carry a symbolic object from one county to the next for his ignominy: a Noble carried a **dog**, an Official a **saddle**, and a Peasant a **plow wheel**.

> —— He split the wood with the pitiless bronze. <note>Greek: κέασε ξύλα νήλεϊ χαλκῶ; referring to the preparation of a sacrifice.</note>

He split the wood with unyielding iron, in the description of a swine sacrifice. For this purpose, the Hebrews also had their <term>lignisecas</term> <note>Latin: "wood-cutters"</note>: such were the Gibeonites, whom *Joshua* assigned to the service of the temple (*Joshua 9:27*). Regarding Wood-cutters and Wood-splitters, see *Saubertus on Sacrifices, page 263.* Regarding the festival of <term>Xylophoria</term> <note>Greek: "carrying of wood"; a Jewish festival where wood was brought to the Temple for the altar fire</note> instituted for bringing wood for the sacred fire, see *Saubertus, page 361.* Regarding wood for sacrifices, see *page 360.* Concerning the types of wood used in the rites of Bacchus, Venus, Jupiter, Mars, and Hercules, see *pages 360–361.* In the sacrifice of expiation, there were four rows of wood (*page 361*). The right of wood-gathering is proved by reputation alone. On this, see *Ummius on Procedure, page 749.* *Horace* writes:

> A puppet moved by another's strings. <note>Latin: *Ducitur ut nervis alienis mobile lignum*; literally "wood moved by foreign nerves." Here cited to illustrate the legal use of the word "lignum" for an object.</note>

The <term>lignandi jus</term> <note>Latin: "right of gathering wood"</note> is acquired by immemorial prescription <note>A legal claim based on "time out of mind," where a practice has existed so long its beginning is forgotten.</note>, according to *Klock, consultation 37, number 334.* In the right of wood-gathering, the lord against whom the prescription is made is preferred (*Klock, consultation 21, number 139*). By what legal remedies can the possession (or quasi-possession) of wood-gathering rights be defended? (*Consultation 37, numbers 373–376*). The right of gathering wood is acquired over such a length of time that no memory of its beginning exists to the contrary (*Bellon, Consultation 49, resolution number 5*).

Irish wood is said to tolerate no poisonous animal. *Zeiller, in Travels through Great Britain, page 224.* In the written travels of Lord Augustin, Baron of Mörsperg of the Order of Malta, it is stated that Newcastle in Northumbria is a pleasant place and city, but it suffers from a lack of wood; therefore, they mine <term>Steinkohlen</term> <note>German: "stone-coal"; mineral coal</note> from a mountain for burning, which is transported far and wide by water and land; and a beggar would rather take a piece of coal than a piece of bread (*Zeiller, century 3, Epistle, page 30*). Regarding the scarcity of wood, see the *Travels of Pureri, page 34; Limnaeus on Public Law, book 3, chapter 2, number 30; and Zeiller, century 2, Epistle, pages 47 and 427.* Regarding the right of cutting wood, see *Dürr on Manorial Courts, thesis 28, concerning woodpiles; Klock on the Treasury, book 2, 15, numbers 30 to 40; and above under the word "floating."*

According to regional custom, thorns, small herbs, stubble, briars, and other things of that kind may fall under the name of "wood," though in other places they would by no means be included under that term (*Law 55 of the Digest on Legacies 3, under the term "wood"*). *Livy, in book 38,* reports that Manlius, moving his camp against the Gallogrecians, passed through a land called <term>AXYLON</term> <note>Greek: "woodless"</note>; he notes the land has this name because it bears not only no timber, but not even thorns or any other fuel for fire; the inhabitants instead use cow dung for wood. They say the same is used in many parts of Flanders and other neighboring places (*Goeddaeus on the Meaning of Words, law 167, number 10*). There is also that dug-up earth which they call <term>Torff</term> <note>German/Dutch: "peat"</note>, with which the people of Lower Germany fuel their fires. This and similar materials are included under the name of "wood" in these places. Furthermore, although certain woody things are burned—and for that reason are kept to be consumed by fire—

<column-break/>

they do not fall under the legal name of "wood" if another more principal purpose exists. Examples of this include charcoal, acorns, olive pits, sulfur-matches, etc. "Cooked wood" refers to wood that has been toasted by fire or sun, dried out, and rendered arid with specific care so that no sap remains to create smoke, especially if it is sprinkled with *amurca* <note>Latin: the bitter, watery sediment of olive oil</note>; this is asserted from *Pliny and Cato* by *Franciscus Marius, On the Parts of Buildings, chapter 4, book 2.* These are also called <term>acapna</term> <note>Greek: "smokeless"</note> because the Greek word for smoke is *kapnos*. <term>Sulphurata</term> <note>Latin: "sulfurated things"</note> are kindlings for catching fire, coated on the tip with sulfur. *Martial* writes:

> ->Like the peddler from across the Tiber,<-
> ->Who trades pale sulfur-matches<-
> ->For broken glass.<-

Papinius also mentions glass:
> ->Everyone trades common sulfur<-
> ->For crushed glass.<-

The <term>Eichenbaum</term> <note>German: "oak tree"</note> lasts up to three hundred years; it grows for a hundred years, stands still for the next hundred, and in the third or final hundred years, it declines again. *More on this in Martin Mylius’s "Pleasant Garden of Wisdom," chapter 31, page 489.* See also "Shrubs," regarding the durability of juniper wood. If the rights of hunting, wood-gathering, or even the right of patronage or jurisdiction are sequestered <note>Legally set aside or confiscated temporarily</note>, it is rightly asked of the Sequestrators who shall have the right of presenting and conferring, hunting, cutting wood, and exercising jurisdiction, if such rights cannot be omitted without loss (*Bocer, class 2, disputation 11, theses 13 and 14*).

On what is contained under the name of wood, see *Viglius in Method of Civil Law, book 13, chapter 5, rule 27.* Add also *Boerius, decision 177.* In privately owned forests, one may indeed cut and enjoy the necessary fuel and building wood, provided it is done without poisoning <note>Possibly "damage" or "spoiling"</note> or prejudice to the wildlife. Agreement between Neuburg and Nuremberg, October 21/31, 1664, number 3.

We know that wood is consumed with immense prodigality in workshops <note>Latin: *ergasteriis*; specifically referring here to mints or industrial works</note> which rise up daily in almost every corner with marvelous multiplication, contrary to the express laws of the Empire (see *Goldast on Catholic Coinage, title 13, page 58 and following*). Indeed, we find wood so depleted that today the Magistrate has barely enough even for those "avenging flames" which the Imperial Constitution (*Book 2 of the Code on Counterfeit Money*) assigned to those adulterators of the coinage (*Limnaeus in Public Law, book 3, chapter 2, number 66*).

To whomever maintenance <note>Latin: *alimenta*; support or alimony</note> is owed, wood must also be provided, which is necessary both for the kitchen and for the heating of the stoves and other needs (*Law "He who provisions," section "wood" of the Digest on Legacies of Provisions; Jacobus Faber on Maintenance, page 13*). ### 79. That is. <note>original: "Hoc est."</note>

*That is*, these words have the force and nature of a restriction in legal documents. *Response of the Faculty of Law at Strasbourg in a case of testamentary succession, letter b. 4.* And, it sometimes signifies "that is," for example: *Abraham and his seed, that is, his seed after him. Lord Johann Fabricius in his explanation of Psalm 105.*

### 80. Tenant Resident. <term>Hintersaß: A resident who lived on a lord's land and paid rent but did not have the full status of a citizen or a full subject.</term> Precarious inhabitants.

*Hintersaß* differs from a *Subject* <note>original: "Unterthan"</note>. *Limnæus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 35, pages 408, 409.* The nobility delight themselves with this distinction, and the commoners <note>original: "N." possibly referring to neighbors or commoners</note> are made only *tenants*, and not *subjects*.
*Back-settlers, grain-laborers, cottagers, and manual laborers.* <note>original: "Hintersiedler, Körner, Kotsassen, Handfrohner"</note> *Mundius on Duties, chapter 4, number 47. Limnæus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 4, number 15.* In what way does a *Tenant Resident* <note>Hintersaß</note> differ from a *Lower Resident* <note>Untersäß</note>? The little word *Lower-resident* is found in Limnæus in *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 16, pages 374, 376, 377; book 4, chapter 8, page 147; and volume 1, additions to book 5, chapter 7, page 843, twice.

### 81. Helmet. <note>original: "Helm. Galea."</note>

*To surrender a fief with hand and with helmet.* 1432. *Wöhrdt.* Others place it "with hand, mouth, and stalk," <note>original: "mit Hand, Mund und Halm"</note> using a straw, a small rod, or a reed. *Gemmel in the Compendium of Feudal Law, pages 29 and 34.* Distinctions of Helmets: *Draco on Patricians, pages 296, 297.* On the origin of the word and name for helmet, see *Limnæus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 6, number 68.* The helmet is twofold: the *Tilting Helmet* <note>Stechhelm: a closed helmet used in jousting</note> and the *Tournament Helmet* <note>Thurnierhelm</note>, number 71; closed and open or perforated. *Ibid.* Legal scholars enjoy the same privileges and immunities as nobles; for they may use noble insignia—namely the open helmet and military crest <note>original: "tymbróque militari"</note>—decorated with an open shield and helmet, provided they refrain from the insignia of a specific family. *Chassaneus in the Catalog of the Glory of the World, part 1, consideration 38. Jos. Nolden on the Status of Noble Citizens and their privileges, chapter 5, number 38.*
Of old, the helmet, shield, and arms of the Emperor glittered with gold. *Nazarius, Panegyric to Constantine:* the noble helmet shines, and with the flashing light of gems, it shows the divine head; the shield gleams with gold, and the arms shine with gold. *Bulenger on the Roman Empire, book 2, chapter 3, page 92.* The Imperial and Royal helmets are most distinct from others. *Limnæus in Public Law, book 2, chapter 7, number 46.* When the last of a name and lineage dies, the seal, shield, and helmet are sometimes broken or smashed at the grave, and sometimes laid aside and buried. *Rudinger, 5th observation, 46.* Diodorus writes thus of the adornment of the Gauls: They place bronze helmets on their heads which have large protrusions and crests, presenting a magnificent appearance to those watching. *Limnæus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 6, numbers 78, 79, etc.*

<column-break/>

### 82. Hens. <note>original: "Hennen. Gallinæ."</note>

If an animal eats the dung of a hen: *Vegetius on the Veterinary Art, book 3, chapter 85.* Regarding "leprosy chickens" <note>original: "Aussatzhühnern"</note>: *Mundius on Duties and Honors, chapter 2, number 45, and the full citations there.*
*The black Hen of Henneberg on seals.* *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 8, number 2. Limnæus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 6, number 18. Zeiller in the Continuation of Germany, page 214.* Whether *Shrove Tuesday hens* or chickens carry with them a jurisdiction and legal right. *Zorer, part 2, question 5, number 396 and the following two.* Mundius specifically on *Smoke Hens* <note>Rauchhüner: a tax paid in poultry per household or "hearth"</note>, which are paid as a sign of subjection, jurisdiction, and lordship; *On Duties and Honors, chapter 2, number 433.* There are *Garden hens, Shrove Tuesday hens, Pentecost hens, Harvest hens, Rent hens, Summer hens, Shepherd hens, Arbor hens, Life hens, and Head hens.* <note>These represent various feudal taxes paid in poultry at different seasons or for different rights</note> *Limnæus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 4, number 20.* There are also *Forest hens*, or *45 Pennies* in their place. *Half hens, two-and-a-half Harvest hens, a third part, two-thirds of a hen, one-fourth.* *Mundius, same location.* There are *Honor hens*. Also. There are *Promise hens*; for example: when a son keeps his mother with him as a tenant for the duration of her life. At Gleißhorn, all six must annually give 11 pennies for one "smoke hen" because of the forest right to the Lord at Z. The right of retraction <note>The legal right to buy back family property</note> does not apply to geese, hens, or calves. *Reinking on the Retraction of Kinship, question 3, number 121.* John III, Bishop of Strasbourg, gave no one an audience early in the morning until he had consumed a boiled hen for breakfast. *Lord Doctor Dannhauer in the Evangelical Memorial, page 380.* Philip II, King of the Spains, by the persuasion of *Valesius the Physician*, most famous after Galen, was sustained for 20 years by the eating of hens alone. For the Spaniards imitate the Egyptians, who put hens into an oven so that they might embrace and cherish the hatched eggs, and thus more often conceive offspring. From *Nicephorus Gregoras, book 2*, it is established that in the Eastern Empire the Empress's crown was called the *Oval*. For when those who were in charge of the flocks of hens there collected all the eggs that the hens had laid each year and sold them for gold, in a short time, from that money, a crown was fashioned for Empress Irene, distinguished with gems and small stones, which the King called "the Oval" because it had been purchased from sold eggs. *Limnæus in Public Law, book 2, chapter 14.* It is unusual to us that they do not, as we are accustomed, place eggs under hens to be incubated in Cairo, but through certain men in the months of March, April, and May, with much dung and manure piled up, they construct a huge structure like an oven. Into this they bring so many eggs that at each turn (which is always finished in the space of twenty-one days), they animate and produce up to four hundred thousand chicks by the vapor of the sun and the putrefying manure alone. Cairo has five or six such ovens, but other cities and villages have many more. *Lord Führer in his Itinerary, page 30. Johann Helffrich.*

### 79. "That is" (Hoc est).

"That is" (*Hoc est*), or in German *das ist*; these words have the force and nature of a restriction. See the *Responses of the Strasbourg Faculty of Law* in the case of testamentary succession, book 6, page 4. And "And" (*Und*) sometimes signifies "that is" (*hoc est*); for example, "Abraham and his seed" means "Abraham, that is, his seed after him." Master Johann Fabricius in his explanation of Psalm 105.

### 80. Cottager (Hintersaß). Precarious residents.

A "Cottager" (*Hintersaß*) differs from a "Subject" (*Unterthan*). Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 35, pages 408–409. By this distinction, some lords delight in granting others only the status of cottagers and not full subjects.
Other terms for these classes include "Rear-settlers" (*Hintersiedler*), "Smallholders" (*Kötner*), "Cottagers" (*Kossassen*), and "Manual Laborers" (*Handfrohner*). Mundius, *On Duties*, chapter 4, number 47. Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 4, number 15. How do a *Hintersaß* and an *Untersaß* <note>Two technical terms for types of lower-tier residents or tenants with varying levels of legal rights</note> differ? The term *Untersaß* is found in Limnäus's *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 16, pages 374, 376, 377; book 4, chapter 8, page 147; and volume 1 of the *Additions*, book 5, chapter 7, page 843, twice.

### 81. Helmet (Helm). Galea.

To surrender a fief "with hand and with helmet." 1432, Wöhrdt. The helmet is twofold: the *Stechhelm* <note>A heavy, closed jousting helmet used in tilting</note> and the *Thurnierhelm* <note>A more open, barred helmet used in general tournaments</note>. Number 71: closed and open or perforated. In the same place, it is noted that Legal Consultants <note>Doctors of Law or high-ranking jurists</note> enjoy the same privileges and immunities as Nobles; they may use noble insignia—specifically the open helmet and military crest—with "open shield and helmet" <note>original: "mit offenem Schild und Helm"</note>, provided they abstain from the specific insignia of certain families. Chassaneuz, *Catalogue of the Glory of the World*, part 1, consideration 38. Joseph Nolden, *On the Status of Civil Nobility*, chapter 5, number 38.
In ancient times, the helmet, shield, and arms of the Emperor glittered with gold. Nazarius in his *Panegyric to Constantine* says: "the noble helmet shines, and with the flickering light of gems reveals the divine head; the shield and arms glow with gold." Bulenger, *On the Roman Empire*, book 2, chapter 3, page 92. The Imperial helmet, like the Royal one, is highly distinct from others. Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 7, number 46. Diodorus writes thus of the Gallic finery: "They place bronze helmets on their heads, which have great protrusions and crests, presenting a magnificent appearance to onlookers." ### 82. Hens (Hennen). Gallinæ.

If an animal eats chicken dung, see Vegetius, *The Art of Veterinary Medicine*, book 3, chapter 85. Concerning "Leprosy Chickens" (*Aussatzhühnern*). Mundius, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 2, number 45, and the full citations therein.

The right of retraction <note>The legal right to buy back family property</note> does not apply to geese, hens, or calves. Reinking, *On the Retraction of Blood Relations*, question 3, number 121. Johannes III, Bishop of Strasbourg, gave no audience to anyone early in the morning before he had consumed a boiled hen for breakfast. Master Dannhauer in the *Lutheran Memorial*, page 380. Philip II, King of Spain, by the advice of the physician Valesius (the most famous after Galen), was sustained for 20 years solely by the offspring of hens. For the Spaniards imitate the Egyptians, who put chickens into an oven so that they might embrace and cherish the hatched eggs, and thus conceive offspring more often. It is clear from Nicephorus Gregoras, book 2, that in the Eastern Empire the Empress's crown was called the *Oval*. For there, those who were in charge of the flocks of chickens collected all the eggs the hens laid each year and sold them for gold; in a short time, from that money, a crown distinct with gems and stones was fashioned for Empress Irene, which the King called "Oval" because it was acquired from the sale of eggs (*ova*). Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 14. It is unusual to us that they do not, as we are accustomed, set eggs under hens to be incubated in Cairo, but through certain men in the months of March, April, and May, they pile up much dung and manure to build a great structure like an oven, into which they bring so many eggs that in each turn (which always ends in a space of twenty-one days), they animate and bring forth up to four hundred thousand chicks by the heat of the sun and the putrefying manure alone. Cairo has five or six such ovens, while other cities and villages have many more. Master Führer in his *Travel Diary*, page 30. Johann Helff-

Concerning the Egg and the Chick, there exists a complete Disputation in the form of a legal opinion, most worthy of public light. These matters were placed by me in this way in the first edition in two volumes in quarto. Later, however, in the year 1661 at Breslau <note>original: "Uratislaviæ"</note>, this Disputation emerged from the library <note>original: "Museo"</note> of Andreas Senftlebius. Andreas Dinnerus, a Doctor of Civil Law, communicated this playful bit of festive wit to Andreas Senftlebius for public reading thirty-five years ago and more, as the formal words of the published Disputation teach us.

# DISPUTATION
## Concerning the Egg and the Chick in the form of a legal opinion.

## THE CASE.

In the courtyard of Baranus, there is a Rooster belonging to Lord A. and a white hen belonging to Lord B. which laid an egg, and a black hen belonging to Lord C. which "egged" <note>An archaic or technical term for the act of nesting or adopting the egg</note> and brooded said egg. Thereafter, in the said courtyard, a chick was born. It is asked: does the said chick belong to all of the aforementioned, or to the said Baranus, or to the Lord of the Rooster, or to the Lord of the white hen, or to the Lord of the black hen?

<column-break/>

# PARTITION OF THE OPINION.

In this question, I shall maintain the following order: as gathered from the theme, I will make the six parts written below, in the first of which it is argued that the chick belongs to all the aforementioned.

## HANDLING OF PART I.

And first, thus: when many things concur in the production of some effect, the effect ought not to be judged to proceed from one more than from the other. <note>Citing Roman Law: Digest 3.4; Code 20; etc.</note> And what is noted (a) in the law regarding procurators and the common law of legacies. But such is the case in this proposal, as gathered from the theme. Therefore [it belongs to all].
<gloss>(a) Everywhere the Author mentions "noted," he understands the Accursian Gloss.</gloss> <note>The Glossa Ordinaria of Accursius was the standard medieval commentary on Roman law.</note>

Second, thus: The effect is to be attributed to none of the extremes when none of them is sufficient by itself. But the effect must be granted to the community of all when they are of the same kind, according to the saying: "Those things which do not help individually, help when many." <note>original: "Et quæ non prosunt singula, multa juvant"</note> See the laws on proof and testimonies. It would be otherwise if they were of different legal status, because then it is granted to none. But such is the case in this proposal, as appears from the words of the presumed theme. Therefore.

Third, thus: the effect, or benefit, ought to be assigned in proportion to those laboring or deserving—in the manuscript it stood as "merchants," <note>original: "Mercantium," likely a scribal error for "Merentium" (deserving)</note> as in the laws regarding annual legacies and the duties of the Consular office.

Fourth, thus: between the cause introducing something anew and the cause fostering that which is introduced, there is no difference. <note>Citing the Code of Justinian</note> But such is the case in the proposal: because the white hen introduced it anew [laid the egg], and the black hen "egged" and brooded that which was introduced. If therefore there is no difference in reason, then a diversity of law ought not to arise.

Fifth, thus: the reasoning for joined things is the same, as in the laws regarding legacies and the abolition of caduca <note>Term for lapsed or unclaimed inheritances</note>. But all the aforementioned animals are joined in the production of the effect itself. Therefore, they ought to be judged as joined and not separate. Which is declared: those things of which one always requires the help of the other are not judged to be separate from it. But they are judged to have one harmony. Therefore, the same harmony and same reason of all these is judged, not separated. Therefore, it does not follow in law that they are separate—

Sed & his ff. de procur.* From all of which it seems to be concluded that the said chick ought to be awarded to all the aforementioned together.

# PART II.
## THE DISCUSSION.

Now let us arrive at the other part in which it is concluded that the chick belongs to no one. And first, thus: An argument from a list of sufficiently enumerated parts is valid in Law, as in law *8. patre ff. de his, qui sui vel alien. J. sunt*, and law *obligationum fere 44. §. 1. placet de obl. & act.*, law *7. ex stipul. C. de sentent. & interloc. omnium jud.* and law *maritus 8. cum quaeritur ff. de procur.* But things are acquired by men either by the Law of Nations <term>Jus Gentium: laws supposedly common to all humanity</term> or by Civil Law <term>Jus Civile: the specific laws of a city or state, like Rome</term>, as in law *1. with those following ff. de acquir. rer. dom.* and the *Institutes, section 11, de R. D.* But by neither of those methods can this chick be acquired by any of the aforementioned parties, as I shall declare below. Which I declare thus: Acquisition does not happen by the Law of Nations, because sometimes this acquisition is obtained through occupation (when a thing was in the property of no one), as in law *3. ff. de A.R.D.* and the section *ferae 12* with those following in the *Institutes de R. D.* Sometimes this happens through distinct accession <note>original: "accessionem distinctam" — when one thing is added to another but both remain identifiable</note>, such as those things born from our animals, as in the *Institutes, same section, item ea 19* and law *itemque 6. ff. de A.R.D.* But a "newborn" cannot be called that which was not part of the internal organs <note>original: "pars viscerum"</note>, as in law *1. §. 1. ff. de vent. insp.*, which was not the case with this chick. Sometimes this happens through concrete accession <note>where two things are fused together</note>, which is not the case here, as in law *7. adeo §. 2. praeterea* and the *Institutes, same section, praeterea 20.* Sometimes this happens through specification <term>Specification: creating a new type of object from someone else's material, like making wine from another's grapes</term>, as in the said section *adeo 7. §. cum quis 7. ff. de acquir. rer. dom.* and law *si frumentum 5. §. 1. idem Pomponius. ff. de rei vind.* and law *si ex meis 26. ff. de acquir. rer. dom.* And it is not our case, as noted in the said section *cum quis 7* and the section *cum aliena 25. J. de R. D.* Sometimes this happens through the confusion of one material with another, which similarly is not our case, as in the said law *7. §. 8. voluntas* and the *Institutes, same section, si duorum 27* and law *Marcellus 3. §. final* with the following law *ff. de rei vind.* Sometimes this happens through planting (that is, the method of grafting), as in section *Titius I. de R. D.* and in law *qua ratione 9. ff. eod.* Sometimes through delivery made from a contract by the Law of Nations, as in the said law *9. qua ratione §. 5. hac qq.* and the *Institutes, same section, in §. per traditionem 40.* But by none of these methods can the said chick be acquired by any of the aforementioned, as appears from the premises. Therefore, acquisition by the Law of Nations fails; it also fails by Civil Law, as in the *Institutes de usucap.* <meta>catchword: E.</meta>

<column-break/>

Secondly, it is thus shown from the sufficiently enumerated parts that it belongs to none of the aforementioned. And first, it is shown that it does not belong to the Baron <note>The landowner or lord on whose property the event occurred</note>. For chicks do not follow the Master's land, as in law *non magis 16. ff. de act. empt.* and law *si apes 26. ff. de furt.* and the *Institutes de R. D. in §. apium 14.* And the reason is because they have no physical connection to the soil. Therefore, they do not follow the soil, as in law *granaria 18. ff. de act. emt.* and law *Titius 60. ff. de acquir. rerum dominio* and law *21. cum fundus ff. de instruct. & instrum. leg.* and the final law *ff. de supellect. leg.* Likewise, that which is hosted does not follow the ownership of the host: and law *nemini 24. C. de episc. aud.* and the final law *C. in quibus causis cess. long. temp. praescr.* Likewise, it does not follow the ownership of the master of the Rooster itself, because an addition <note>accessio</note> does not follow the "active cause" from itself; nor again does it follow an animal of the male sex, as noted in the *Institutes* in the said section *Item ea quae 19. Inst. de R. D.* and in law *si frumentum s. §. 2.* It is likewise written in the Digest *de R. V.* Furthermore, although perhaps the rooster contributed something by arranging the egg, and thus the material to receive such a form: nevertheless, he does not pull the formed thing to himself, as argued in law *liberorum 52. §. 14. quod tamen Cassius* and law *si cui lana 70. in pr. ff. de legat. 3.* Likewise, it cannot be said to belong to the owner of the white hen <note>The hen that actually laid the egg</note>. For an egg, in passing into a chick, ceases to be an egg, nor is it reducible to its original material. Law *Seja 6. §. final ff. de auro & arg. legat.* and law *quaesitum 78. §. 4. illud* and law *lana 88. ff. de legat. 3.* and law *si convenerit. 18. §. penultimate ff. de pign act.* and the said law *adeo 7. §. 3. in flumine ff. de Adquir. R. D.* Therefore, the owner of the white hen ceases to have ownership of the egg once the thing is destroyed, as in law *§. sicut in pr. ff. quib. mod. pign. vel hypoth. solv.* and law *inter stipulantem 83. ff. de V. O.* Likewise, from the moment the egg is extinct, it is not to be argued from it, as in law *qui res 98. §. 8. aream ff. de solut.* and law *cui 3. §. 1. de postul.* Likewise, it cannot be said to belong to the owner of the black hen <note>The hen that sat on the egg and brooded it</note>: because if it belonged to the black hen, it would be by that reasoning because she had "specified" it <note>created a new thing from material</note>. But here those things do not intervene through which a thing is acquired by the one performing "specification": namely, good faith, acting in one's own name, or in the name of another who ratifies it, and that the material is not reducible to its original state, as in the said section *cum quis 7* and the said section *cum ex aliena 25. Inst. de R. D.* and the said section *2. item l. s. ff. de rei vind.* For two things are lacking in the black hen, because the egg lacks action [of her own], as in law *1. in pr. ff. si quadr. paup. fec. dic.* Furthermore, since the black hen herself brooded the egg, and from it the chick itself emerged, the effect ought not be attributed to the first cause: otherwise (it is understood, ownership would be acquired, or the effect would be attributed) to the first cause that brooded and which disposed it, as if to the nearest cause, as in law *legitima 6. ff. de pact.* and law *ex placito 3. C. de rer. permut.* Likewise, the one disposing and the thing qualitatively disposed are not considered to be of the same kind, as in the final law *ff. de fund. instr. & instr. leg.* Likewise, even if the chick is said to be produced from the hen, it is not a new thing that the producer and the produced are judged by different laws, law *si aliena 10. §. 2. Scaevola ff. de Usucap.* and law *qui vas. 48. §. 2. si ancilla ff. de furt.* <meta>catchword: Tertiò</meta>

Thirdly, as follows: No acquisition of property occurs through an animal that lacks the capacity for legal action, as stated in the law *r. §. 9. per cum* in the Digest <note>The Digest (abbreviated as "ff.") is a massive compendium of Roman legal jurists' writings compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> regarding the acquisition of possession. This is exactly the case in the matter at hand. Therefore [it belongs to no one].

Fourthly, as follows: Since each of the owners of these animals claims to have full ownership (*pro solido*), and it does not appear that the chick belongs to one more than the other—since all these animals contributed (for there could be no chick without the rooster, nor without the white hen, nor without the black hen)—they therefore hinder one another. This follows the law *quotiens 34. ff. de usufr.* and the law *si quis servum 8. §. si inter ff. de legat. 2.* According to this, by reason of doubt, no acquisition of property is made, as per the law *si fuerit 10. ff. de reb. dub.* and the law *5. si frumentum §. fin. ff. de rei vind.* and in the law *cum duo 17. ff. de in diem add.* and the law *in tempus 62. §. 1. quotiens ff. de hered. inst.* and the law *duo sunt Titii 30. ff. de test am. tut.* From these citations, it seems to be concluded that the chick should be awarded to none of the aforementioned parties.

### TREATMENT OF PART III.

Furthermore, let us arrive at the third part, namely, the side of the Landlord <note>original: "Barani" — likely referring to a "Baron" or specific landowner in this legal hypothetical</note>. First, as follows: An animal draws its legal subjection and status from the whole [the land] in which it drew its origin, as per the law *1. ff. de censib.* and law *x. C. de municip. lib. 10.* and law *7. cives C. de incol. lib. 10.* and law *provinciales 190. ff. de V. S.* This is the case in the matter at hand. Therefore [it belongs to the Landlord].

Secondly: Those things that are produced on an estate, so that they might exist there, follow the estate, as per the law *debitor 32. ff. de pignor.* and law *cum ita 32. ff. de leg. 2.* and law *qui saltem 67.* and law *si ita 85. ff. de legat. 3.* This is the case here. For this animal was brought into being on the estate of the Landlord; hence it seems to have a continuous cause there, from which it had its natural production, based on the argument in law *foramen 28. ff. de serv. urb. prad.* These points suffice for the Landlord.

### TREATMENT OF PART IV.

Now let us arrive at the fourth part, namely, that the chick should be awarded to the Owner of the Rooster. The cause in the "agent" (the active party) is stronger than in the "patient" (the passive party), as in law *2. & fin. ad SC. Tertul.* and law *2. §. objicitur 15. ff. eod.* But this domestic rooster, loving hens just as a masculine man loves women, behaves by way of the agent, as noted in law *1. C. ad L. Pomp. de parricid.* This is further strengthened because every thing is named more by its agent than by its patient, as in law *1. ff. de S. R. P.* and law *si quis minas 32. ff. de usufruct.* Such is the case with this rooster. Therefore [the chick is his].

Secondly: He who makes a subject ready to receive its "form" <note>In Aristotelian legal logic, "form" is the life or soul of the thing, while "matter" is the physical body</note> draws the formed thing to himself, as in law *3. accepisse ff. de pollic.* and law *et si non sint 20. §. i i. quid ergo ff. de auro & arg. leg.* and law *si cui lana 70. §. minor 1. l. item leg. 49.* and law *qui filiam 64. in f. ff. de leg. 3.* Such is the case with the rooster, who prepared the egg itself to receive its "form," that is, the development of the chick. Therefore.

Thirdly: The right of the masculine sex, as it is more perfect and noble, ought to be preferred to the right of the feminine sex, as in law *1. ff. de Senat.* and in

<column-break/>

many sections of the Digest concerning the status of men (*ff. de Stat. hom.*), law *si fuerit 10. §. fin. ff. de reb. dub.* and the final law in the Digest on the equipment of an estate (*ff. de fundo instruct.*). This is strengthened because every "accession" <note>Term: <term>accession</term> (Latin: *accessio*). A legal principle where the owner of a primary object becomes the owner of everything that is added to it or produced by it.</note> comes from the more powerful and noble source, as per law *quicquid 27. §. 2. cum partes ff. de A. R. D.* and law *si non sint 20. §. 13. perveniamus ff. de aur. & arg. leg.* and law *sancimus 34. C. de donat.* and law *quærit. 10. ff. de stat. hom.* and law *8. majorem ff. de pact.*

Fourthly: The right is stronger in the commanding cause (otherwise known as the initiating cause) than in the perfecting cause, as per law *1. ff. de O. J.* and law *si filius 78. ff. de V. O.*, law *Pomponius 15. ff. de neg. gest.*, law *i. §. 11. si interrogvero §. si servus 30. ff. depositi* and law *3. §. 20. scio ff. de minor.*, law *ubi judicium 30. ff. de Judic.*, law *1. ff. de pœn.*, law *3. si filius C. ad SC. Maced.* But the said Rooster can be called the commanding or initiating cause. Therefore. From these points, it is concluded that the chick should be awarded to the Owner of the Rooster.

### TREATMENT OF PART V.

Next, let us arrive at the Owner of the White Hen. First, it is argued thus: It is now plain that the egg follows the white hen, for she produced it. Therefore, just as offspring, it follows the white hen herself, as in the section on hens (*§. Gallinarum*) and in the section *item ea 19. J. de R. D.* <note>The Institutes (J.) of Justinian, an introductory law textbook.</note> and law *in bona fidei 40. in f. ff. de A. R. D.* and the single law *§. 9. sexus C. de rei uxor. act.* and law *sed etsi 25. §. fin. ff. de hered. pet.* With this established, it is inferred: that which remains from the property of the owner of the white hen ought to be his, as per law *solum 49. ff. de rei vind.* and law *de eo 12. §. 3. si quis ff. ad exhib.* and law *si servus 14. §. 2. bove ff. de condict. furt.* Nor do I care whether it is an immediate accession of the white hen (as the egg was) or an accession of one thing by means of another (as the chick was), as per law *quod si oves 26. ff. de petit. hered.* If it were said otherwise, it would be absurd: regarding the acquisition of ownership of the accession itself, one would not look at how the accession was caused, but only at how it was perceived—which is against law *divortio 9. §. 9. non solum ff. solut. matrim.* and the argument in law *3. §. 1. ff. de minor.*

Secondly, as follows: A "specification" <note>Term: <term>specification</term> (Latin: *specificatio*). A legal concept where a new object is created from someone else's materials. The question is whether the owner of the material or the creator owns the result.</note> yields to the maker only when three things concur: namely, that the maker acts in their own name, in good faith, and that the finished product cannot be reduced back to its original raw material, as per the Digest and Institutes citations. Otherwise, the "specification" remains in the ownership of the person who owned the raw material. But these three conditions could not have occurred together in the black hen who performed the "specification" [by brooding]. For good faith cannot exist where consent is lacking, as per law *ejus qui 21. ff. si cert. pet.* and what is noted in law *1. C. de adquir. poss.* Therefore, the chick will remain in the ownership of the person who owned the raw material—namely, the original egg.

Thirdly: An argument by the reduction to an "inconvenience" <note>A legal argument showing that a particular interpretation leads to an impractical or absurd result.</note> is valid in Law, as per law *3. in hac §. 11. si mecum ff. ad exhib.* and law *in 77 ff. de contrab. emt.* and law *divortio 7. §. 5. ff. solut. matr.* But if the said chick were granted to the Owner of the Black Hen and not the White Hen, then...

V. P.* and the final law of the Digest regarding pledges, and the law *mortuo 60. ff. de judic.* and law *1. §. 10. hac actio ff. si quis testam. lib. juss. esse fuer.* But the chick is substituted for the egg: For substitution is the putting of a later thing in the place of a prior removed thing, as in the law *vetus 68. ff. de usufr.* and law *1. ff. de novat.* <note>Regarding novation, or the replacement of an old obligation with a new one.</note> Therefore [the chick belongs to the owner of the egg].

Fifthly: This chick does not belong to the Master of the black hen. Therefore, it ought to be in the ownership of the master of the white hen, which produced the egg. Proof of the premise: For the offspring is born from the one who fosters it only when the fosterer acts as the immediate cause and not just as the means of the effect. For then the effect arises from that immediate cause so defined, as in law *legitima 6. ff. de pactis* and law *3. ex placito* of the Code regarding the exchange of things. Likewise, since the black hen acted only as a filler [of the incubation process]: the effect does not follow from the filler, as in law *7. quod enim ff. de novat.*

Sixthly: More attention should be paid to the original cause, and the effect attributed to it, as in a novation; see the final law of the Digest regarding the petition of inheritance, and the law *interveniunt. 20. §. cum prædiximus 4. ff. de petit. haered.* and what is noted in the law *certi condictio 9. at the beginning, ff. si cert. pet.* and law *tut. 69. ff. de fide instr.* and law *clam. 5. ff. de adqu. poss.* But the white hen was the original cause of those things which followed afterward. Therefore.

Seventhly: That which is in dispute, in case of doubt, is to be attributed to the older cause. Law *11. at the end* of the Digest regarding the regulation of boundaries, and proved in law *7. emancipatum ff. de Senator.*

Eighthly: Whatever is the cause of the cause is also the cause of the result, as in said law *certi condictio at the beginning, ff. si cert. pet.* and law *manumissiones 4. ff. de l.* and law *1. ff. de pact.* But the white hen was the cause of the egg, and that preceded it, even though the chick is born from the egg by the work of the black hen. Therefore, it ought to be attributed to the first white hen as the preceding cause, as in *inter eos 19. ff. de re jud.* and law *3. in duob. ff. de duobus reis* and law *pluribus 32. ff. de Proc.* From these points, it seems to be concluded in favor of the Master of the white hen.

### TREATMENT OF PART VI.
### AND THE LAST.

Now let us arrive at the sixth part, namely, that the said chick is attributed to the Master of the black hen. And first, as follows: When a species <insert>*Besoldus Volume I.*</insert> <note>Besoldus (1577–1638) was a prominent German jurist whose works are being cited here.</note>

<column-break/>

passes into a "specification" <note>In Roman law, *specificatio* occurs when someone creates a new thing (a *nova species*) from another person's material.</note>, it ceases to be that species, and the whole is attributed to the one who "specified" it, as in law *Seja 6. at the end* of the Digest regarding gold and silver legacies, and the said section *cum quis 7.* and said section *cum ex aliena materia 25.* of the Institutes regarding the division of things, and law *lana 88. ff. de legat. 3.* and law *sed si ex meis 26. ff. de A. R. D.* And thus the material passes into the finished object, and ceases to be the material, and follows the finished object, if it cannot be reduced to its first form, as in law *si convenerit 18. the second to last paragraph, si quis ff. de pign. action.* and the said law *quæsitum 78. the second to last paragraph, si quis ff. de leg. 3.* Nor should anyone say that the species yields to the specifier only when the three conditions mentioned in said section *cum quis 7.* and section *cum ex aliena 25.* are found to occur together; for that applies to a specifier who has an intellect. Those words should be understood in the context in which they can apply, as in law *post accusare 12. §. omnibus ff. de accus.* and law *1. §. 12. non autem omne ff. de fluminibus.* Now, in the case of a specifier lacking intellect <note>the hen</note>, I do not say that it is acquired by the specifier, i.e., the hen, but is acquired by the Master of the specifier. Just as in a case where active acquisition is sought, the good faith of the person is considered, as in law *in hujusm. 12. ff. de cont. emt.* and law *cum mancipium 51. ff. de adil. edict.* Hence it can be said, since it proceeded naturally from the black hen itself, that this should be accepted calmly, whether the condition of the other person becomes better or worse; and for that reason, it is useless to ask about good or bad faith, as in law *2. §. 6. ap. man. ff. de aq. & aq. pluvia arcenda* and law *flumine 24. §. 2. vitium ff. de damn. infect.* and law *si servus 29. §. 9. si fornicarius ff. ad l. Aquil.* Or it could be said that insofar as that specified thing is clinging to the object, it yields to the specifier as a part, as in the final law *si fraudator §. fructus 6. ff. quæ in fraud. cred.* But if it is not clinging, but separate and segregated, then it is sought as an accession <note>a legal addition to property</note>, as in law *qui scit 25. §. alieno ff. de usur.* and law *qui fundum 40. §. 3. fundi ff. de contrah. emtion.* And according to this, we follow the Right of the body from which it is perceived—such as from the sweat, heat, and warmth of the hen itself—rather than the power of the seed from which it originates, such as the egg itself, as in said law *qui scit. §. 11. ff. de usur.*

Secondly, as follows: The right is stronger in the cause that impresses the form than in the material cause; because it is the form that gives being to a thing, as in law *9. Julianus §. 1. si quis ff. ad exhib.* and law *non sunt liberi 14. ff. de stat. hom.* and law *si is, qui 80. §. 1. quædam ff. ad L. F. alcid.* But the black hen impressed the form upon this material, which is the egg itself. Nor should anyone say that the white hen was the cause of the egg, and the egg the cause of the chick, to conclude that whatever is the cause of the cause is also the cause of the result. Here it must be noted that while whatever is the efficient cause of the efficient cause is the cause of the result (as in law *liberos 10.* and law *7. mancipatum ff. de Senat.* and law *sed si hac lege 10. §. 9. liberos ff. de in jus. voc. l. liberorum 215. ff. de V. S.*), whatever is the efficient cause of the *material* cause is not the efficient cause of the result, as in law *ex hoc 5. ff. de J. & J.* For the Law of Nations (*Jus Gentium*) is the efficient cause, but the obligation is the material cause of an action, as in law *licet 42. §. 2.*
