# Enlarged Practical Treasury

in the section *on Attorneys* <note>original: "ff. de Procurat." refers to the Digest of Justinian</note>; and yet it does not follow that the Civil Law produced the action itself, as noted in *the law "from this" § and law 2. § 6. from these* in the section *on Obligations and Actions*. So in the present case: the white hen was the efficient cause (of the material cause) of the chick. Just as in a similar case: an acorn joined to the earth produces a tree; from the tree, as if from material, a ship is made; yet it does not follow from this that the ship belongs to the soil or the Master of the soil, as noted in *the law "but if from mine" 26* in the section *on Acquiring Ownership of Things*. Sometimes, however, the material cause is the mediated and not the immediate cause of the natural cause, as in *the law "the action for a certain thing" 9* in the section *if a certain thing is sought*. But in this case, the black hen itself was the formal cause. Likewise, looking at it from a different perspective, the said black hen was the efficient cause of the chick itself; therefore, the chick should naturally be named after her, as the one impressing the form, as in *law 2 at the beginning and in § 2 later* in the section *on Obligations and Actions* and *law 1 § 6*.

Thirdly: when something is added to or taken away from a fact, the thing itself is transformed, a new species is created, and such a new species would be named after the one who made it, as in *law "in conventional matters" 52* and *law 1 § 3 "when it is added"* in the section *on Verbal Obligations* and *law 1 at the end* in the section *on Praetorian Stipulations* and *law 6 "civil law"* in the section *on Justice and Law*. But such is the case here, that the black hen transformed the egg into the species of a chick. Therefore [the black hen's owner prevails].

Fourthly: Art imitates nature <note>Latin: "Ars imitatur naturam"</note>, as in *law "adoption" 16* in the section *on Adoptions*. But it is thus in nature: the hen that brooded the egg treats the chicks as her own, and they treat her as theirs. Therefore [she is the mother]. And the *Gloss on law 1* in the section *on Total Restitution* supports this. Therefore.

Fifthly: The fruit should be attributed more to the one who labors, following the argument in *law "Seja" 6* in the section *on Gold and Silver* and the argument in *the final law* of the Code *on Alluvion and Marshes* and *the final law* of the Code *on Deserted Fields* and in the *section "but lest"* in the *Authentica on Judges* and *said law 2 "in the name of the Lord" near the middle* and in *§ 9 "each one"* in the Code *on the office of the Praetorian Prefect of Africa*. But the final black hen labored more in bringing the chick into existence, as we see naturally.

Sixthly: An effect is attributed to the one who breathes in the spirit <note>Latin: "instanti spiritum," referring to the spark of life</note>, as in *law "posthumous" 12* in the section *on Unjustly Broken Wills* and *law 11 "who to children" § 2 "who of a Will"* in the section *on Possession of Goods according to the Tablets* and in *§ 4 "otherwise"* in the Institutes *by what means a will is weakened*; which is noted in *title "from enemies" 15 § "but that" 3* in the section *on what causes manumissions do not occur*. But this black hen, by her own sweat and heat, breathed in the spirit, bringing the egg forth into an animal. Therefore.

Seventhly: this chick had its being from the warmth and brooding of the black hen; for by her heat and sweat and the covering of her wings, it was brought into being. Therefore, it follows her: as is said of a tree, which took root by the nourishment of another's earth, as the same Pomponius writes in *law 5 (§ elsewhere begins: "if grain") § 3 on the tree* in the section *on Lawful Reclamation* and *law 7 "so much" the final §* and *law "by what reason" 8 at the beginning* in the section *on Acquiring Ownership of Things*. We can therefore say, it is credible that the tree was made foreign to its original owner by the nourishment of the earth, and thus the chick belongs to the Master of the black hen, as in *said law "but if from mine" 26 § 2 on the tree* in the section *on Acquiring Ownership of Things*.

<column-break/>

Eighthly: what is acquired from the labor of my property is considered as if acquired from my property itself, as in *law "which goods" 23 after the beginning* in the section *on Acquiring Ownership of Things*. But from this egg, an animal was brought into being by the labor of the black hen. Therefore, it is acquired for the Master of the hen, as if acquired from his own property.

Ninthly: An animal that does not touch another, either at the time of conception or birth, does not follow it, nor does it have anything in common with it, as in *law "Paulus" 29 § 1* in the section *on Private Property* and *law "if it shall be agreed" 10 § 2 "if a field"* in the section *on Actions for Pledge* and what is noted in *law 1* in the section *on the Salvian Interdict* and *law 6 "Titius"* in the section *on Direct and Legal Heirs*. But the chick, according to the time of conception and also its extraction from the shell <note>Latin: "extra guffum" — the author notes "guffum" is an Italian word meaning "eggshell"</note> when it ceases to be an egg, touches the Master of the egg at none of the said times. Therefore.

Tenthly: A thing is named after that which confers the more noble part, as in *law 4 "to order," and what is noted there, on the Jurisdiction of all Judges*. But such is the case with the black hen. Therefore.

From all these points, it is concluded that the said chick falls to the Master of the said black hen: And I think this side is truer, being strengthened by stronger reasons, consonant with natural law, and conforming to the common sense of men: notwithstanding the arguments alleged to the contrary, to which the solution appears from what has been sent before.

What Dr. Tabor thinks of this problem *in his treatise on Confrontation* is clear from page 2 of the Preface, where: "Corydon's rooster is constantly in Amyntas's granary; he brings welcome assistance to Damon's white hen to produce an egg; but Lycidas's black hen, haphazardly sitting and brooding on this egg, hatches a chick. It is asked, who of these four is the Master of the hatched chick?" This subtlety is intended if you labor to show that the chick belongs to no one according to the Law and its interpreters, perhaps because neither can discern what is his own and what is another's: although Plutarch seems to conclude, according to Grotius *on the Law of War and Peace, book 8 § 18*, that it belongs to both parents; see what follows there, as well as on *page 3*.

## On Living Hedges
See the *Frankfurt Reformation <note>The "Reformation" refers to the revised city laws of Frankfurt.</note>, part 9, title 4, sections 4 and 5, where it states:* Regarding the planting of hedges, which are prepared to ensure a living and lasting peace, it shall be held that because they expand over time, they must be set one and a half quarters of a rod <note>A "rod" or *Ruthe* was a traditional unit of length, roughly 12 to 16 feet; a quarter rod would be about 3 to 4 feet.</note> away from the boundary stones or furrows. No trees of any kind should be planted within them. Furthermore, the height of such hedges (when they are bundled/trimmed) shall not exceed one and a half quarters of a rod. Such planting of living hedges shall only be permitted (according to the aforementioned measurement) in fields and meadows, but shall not be allowed at all in cabbage patches and vineyards, etc. All the above-mentioned regulations for the planting of trees, hedges, and fences shall be understood to apply only between neighbors and their properties; however, facing a public road, anyone may build, plant, or make hedges and fences within their own boundary stones and secure their property as best they can. Any parts of the hedges hanging over the public road, as well as bushes in front of properties growing into the path, must be cleared away at the latest 14 days before St. Martin’s Day <note>November 11th, a common deadline in the agricultural calendar for settling debts and finishing seasonal work.</note> of each year.

On how to value thorn bushes, brush, and shrubbery, see *The Tripartite Law of the Land of the Kingdom of Hungary, part 1, title 133, folio 77.* On forcing a neighbor to remove parts of hedges, fences, or trees, see *Frankfurt Reformation, part 9, title 2, section 1.* On who may be called "Hedge-riders" <note>original: "Heckenreuter," referring to vagabonds or perhaps border patrols</note>, see *Speidelius in his Mirror of Notable Things under this word.*

## Hops. *Lupulus.* <note>The OCR reads "Supulus," but the Latin term for hops is *Lupulus*.</note>
Hops generally yield a harvest for more than 3 or 4 years. On how to prepare hop gardens, see *Johann Colerius in Oeconomia, book 5, chapter 81. If someone cuts down a field of hops, see Berlichius, 5, chapter 52, number 40.* If the hops wind themselves around a fence, whoever has the root in their yard shall grab the fence and pull the hops; whatever follows him is his, but whatever remains on the other side belongs to his neighbor. Similarly, the branches of his trees should not hang over to his neighbor's detriment. *Schneidewein, title on the Division of Things, page 176.* On the etymology of the word *Lupulus* (hops), see *Klock on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 3, number 4.* On the picking of hops. The term "trees" includes hops. *Berlichius, 5, conclusion 52, number 28. The right of buying and selling hops (the Hop-Trade), the Senate of Breslau in Silesia claims for itself alone, see Knipschild on Imperial Cities, book 5, chapter 22, number 21.*

## 84. Hair-pulling.
Country folk, due to a lack of gifts <note>Meaning they lacked gifts or money to give to witnesses to ensure they remembered an event.</note>, lead nearby boys by the hair and show them the established boundaries. *Lenz on Boundaries, thesis 37.* On what the shaving of hair indicates, see *Lord Tabor on Confrontation, D. 1, question 4, and Besoldus, Volume 1.* <note>In many European legal traditions, children were taken to property boundaries and had their hair pulled or were even slapped so that the physical pain would make them remember the location of the boundary markers for decades to come.</note>

## 85. Salt-worker. *Salis coctores.*
Salt-workers (those who boil salt). *Lord Tabor on Changes, page 253,* where he discusses the small houses of the salt-workers built within the salt-works themselves. Shortly after: These barns and coverings are designated for the boiling and preparation of salt. The word "Hall" <note>A Germanic root specifically associated with salt-production sites, such as Halle or Hallstatt.</note> is frequently repeated there, such as: "This salt-work is divided into 14 Halls." Shortly after: "According to the size of the Hall-portion held." Then: "mentioning such 14 Halls." *And on page 251 regarding Changes,* the salt-halls are mentioned.

Army Herald or Senator of the Army. *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, number 122.*

From where the name "Hidalgos" is derived for Spanish nobles. *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 1, number 7 throughout; see above under the word Fidalgi.*

Regarding long points or double-axes (halberds). *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputation 1, theta 1, letter E. Finckelthaus, in Illustrious Feudal Controversies, Disputation 1, Controversy 5, letter B at the end. Lord Tabor on Arms, page 39.*

*Antonius Matthaeus in his Oration for the Law of Constantine the Great regarding Adulterers, page 6. Besoldus, book 1, chapter 11, number 10,* there it says: Citizens are born either from both parents being citizens, or from only one, who in some places are called "Hybrids." *Kirchner, Disputation 15, Corollary 1.*

## 90. Court Messenger. *Præco juratus.*
A public messenger or sworn herald. *Matthaeus Berlichius, 1, conclusion 36, number 70.* He provides full proof in citations and other cases pertaining to his office. *Colerius on Executive Process, part 1, chapter 7, number 16 and following; and part 3, chapter 9, number 103 and following. Tiraquellus on Family Retraction, section 8, glossary 9, number 10 and following. Menochius, book 2, on Judicial Arbitrations, century 2, case 112, number 1 and following.* Some disagree without distinction, stating that a public messenger or sworn herald is not to be believed. Others think differently, leaving it to the judge's discretion whether he wishes to believe the public messenger in matters regarding his office or not. Regarding sworn messengers—the sworn Chamber Messengers—through whom Chamber Processes must be served, see *Dr. Johann Andreas Gerhardi in his Discourses on the Supreme Courts in the Roman Empire, the Aulic and the Chamber, page 51.*

## 91. Executioner or Execution Fee. *Sumtus executionis criminalis.*
Regarding the costs in criminal executions. *Matthaeus Berlichius, 1, conclusion 64, number 109.* The agreement between Neuburg and Nuremberg, October 21/31, 1664, number 7 at the end.

### 92. Home-Disturbance. <note>original: *Heimsucht*</note> The breach of domestic peace. <note>original: *Fractio pacis domesticæ*</note>
Regarding this term, see Symphorianus Guyllonius, volume 1, part 1, folio 124, number 175.

### 93. Half-Share. <note>original: *Halbscheid*</note> The half. <note>original: *Dimidium*</note>
Limnäus, in his *Additions to the Public Peace, volume 2, book 7, chapter 25, page 246*, mentions this word twice. It is used when reprisals <note>Legal seizures of property to satisfy a debt.</note> are applied to one half of a debt, while the other half is reserved under arrest with a warning for a certain time, to see if the principal debtor might perhaps comply. This word appears in the mandate of reprisals for Millendonck, President of the Imperial Chamber, against Joyese, in the month of April, 1642. The "Half-share of the purchase price" <note>original: *Die Halbscheid an Kauffschilling*</note> refers to the repayment of one half.

### 94. Lord’s Favor. <note>original: *Herrgunst*</note> Precarious Tenure. <note>original: *Precaria*</note>
The rights of "free-hold" <note>original: *Freystifte*</note> or the justice of the Lord's favor. <note>A legal term for land held at the will of the lord, rather than by permanent right.</note>

### 95. Secretly. <note>original: *Heimlich*</note> Covertly. <note>original: *Occulte*</note>
An action is considered to be done deceitfully when someone acts in secret; he acts "in secret" who has not notified the person whom he feared, or could have feared, would object. Justus Oldekop, *on oaths, page 97.*

### 96. Hedge-Inspection. <note>original: *Hagenschau*</note>
*Acts of Lindau, folio 813, folio 10, at the beginning:* the inspection of defective fences, as well as overgrown hedges and trees that obstruct the road. The "Path-Inspection" <note>original: *Pfadenschau*</note> is distinct from the "Hedge-Inspection"; the former is conducted annually regarding the fences and enclosures of properties, while the latter, regarding the opening and clearing of roads from overgrown hedges, brushwood, and trees, is undertaken only every third year. *Ibid, folio 813.*

### 97. Hope. <note>original: *Hoffnung*</note> Hope. <note>original: *Spes*</note>
Porcelain pieces can be symbols of great and long-lasting hope. For they are made of a certain mass composed of gypsum, ground egg, the shell of a sea lobster, and other substances; if this mass is properly compressed and thickened, it is buried deep underground in some secret place which a father designates for his children. And there it remains hidden for eighty years. <note>This reflects a common 17th-century European myth that porcelain was made by burying a mixture of ingredients for decades before it could be harvested and fired.</note> Pancirollus, in *The History of Memorable Things Lost and Found, page 141 and following.* See Mr. Fürer’s *Travels in Egypt, Arabia, etc., page 42.* Even "hope alone" is understood as something that can be bequeathed in a will. Mantica, *on the Conjectures of Last Wills, book 9, title 1, number 17.* A probable hope and a thing or an acquired right are judged as equal. Klock, *consultation 103, number 8, and consultation 114, numbers 12, 213, 214; and consultation 123, number 76.* The hope of succeeding in a fief <note>An estate of land held on condition of feudal service.</note> is both probable and significant. Klock, *consultation 69, number 41.* A deceptive hope of succeeding is customarily called a "waking man's dream." Klock, *consultation 7, number 321.* Regarding the legal clause: "if the plaintiff shows that he has hitherto appealed to the defendant in a friendly manner, and has obtained nothing but hope," and its effect, see Ummius in *Disputations on Legal Process, 6, number 56.* Hope and fear drive life. In the 

<column-break/>

Selected Letters of Mr. Georg Richter, *page 113.* Impatience for hope eventually destroys. *Ibid, page 5.* The hope of getting away with it <note>original: *impunitatis*</note> is an enticement to sin. Cicero, *For Milo.* Klock, *on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 142, number 9.* A healthy severity overcomes a vain hope for mercy. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus and Brutus, 2.* The hope of a thing, or of a person, makes a stipulation valid. Boerius, *decision 172, number 7.* The hope of a "pupillary substitution" <note>A Roman law concept where a father appoints an heir for his child in case the child dies before reaching adulthood.</note> is not transmitted. *Decision 38, number 22.* It is a sign of a great nature to always hope. Those who least lose heart in adversity, but insist on deeds and strength—whether in public or private life—are rightly judged as the most excellent, says Pericles in Thucydides, *book 11.* See more in Rupertus’s commentary on Florus, *book 4, chapter 8, section 3:* "The spirit was increased by misfortunes." *And on book 3, chapter 7, section 20:* "The fortune of the Roman people always rose greater in times of trouble." *And on book 1, chapter 10, section 2:* Hope that depends on the will of another cannot truly be called hope. *Altdorf Consultations, page 244.* The hope of a paternal inheritance can be given as a dowry by a woman with her father's consent; and if that woman dies before both her husband and her father, and the husband subsequently dies before the father-in-law, that hope can be transmitted even to outside heirs (such as the sons-in-law's children from a second marriage) by virtue of the dowry contract. *Altdorf Consultations, page 241.* Any hope of succession can be brought into a contract. *Ibid, page 244.* "Hope upon which no account can be settled." <note>original: *Hoffnung, darauf kein Rechnung zu machen*</note> Zorer, *part 2, question 5, number 368.*

## I.

### 1. **Hunting, Hunting-Rights, Grace-Hunts, etc.** <note>original: *Iagen, Iagrecht, Gnaden-Jagten*</note> Hunting. The right of hunting. <note>original: *Venatio. Jus venandi.*</note>

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'V' at the start of the word 'Venationis', decorated with swirling vines and flowers.</image-desc> The exercise of hunting, especially for large beasts—to fell the "high game" <note>original: *das hohe Wildpräth*; usually refers to deer, boar, or other large antlered animals reserved for the nobility.</note>—is considered manly, warlike, and heroic. Lyclama, *last book, Eclogue 12.* This belongs specifically to nobles and other magnates and cannot be taken from them except by lawful prescription. <note>A legal claim based on long-term use.</note> *Chapter 1, section 'nemo retia', on keeping the peace; Law 12 'officium' on military affairs; Chapter 1, 2, and the whole title on the hunting of the clergy.* And that the most ancient kings and princes were devoted to hunting is clear from Neander, *in his collection of maxims, folio 132; added to by Meiller at...*

# Enlarged Practical Treasury
### 92. Home-invasion. Breach of domestic peace.
<note>original: "Heimsucht. Fractio pacis domesticæ."</note>
Regarding this term, consult Symphorianus Guyllon, volume 1, part 1, folio 124, number 175.

### 93. Half-share. Half.
<note>original: "Halbscheid. Dimidium."</note>
Limnäus, in *Public Law* <note>original: "J. P." for Jus Publicum</note>, volume 2, addition to book 7, chapter 25, page 246, mentions this word twice. It refers to when reprisals are used for one half, and the other half is reserved under seizure <note>original: "in arresto"</note> with a threat for a certain time, in case the principal debtor <note>original: "principalis debitor"</note> might comply. This term is used in the mandate of reprisals of Millendonck, President of the Imperial Chamber, against Joyese in April 1642. The "half-share of the purchase price" <note>original: "Die Halbscheid an Kauffschilling"</note> means the half-share in Eichstätt.

### 94. Lord’s Favor. At Will.
<note>original: "Herrengunst. Precaria."</note>
The right of free-tenancy <note>original: "Freystifft"</note> or tenure at the lord’s favor.

### 95. Secretly. Hidden.
<note>original: "Heimlich. Occulte."</note>
What one does secretly is judged to be done deceitfully <note>original: "Dolosè fieri censetur, quod quis clàm agit"</note>. A person acts "secretly" who has not notified the one whom he feared, or could have feared would object. Justus Oldekop, *On Oaths*, page 97.

### 96. Hedge Inspection.
<note>original: "Hagenschau."</note>
Lindau Records <note>original: "Lindauische Acta"</note>, folio 813 and folio 10 at the beginning. This refers to the inspection of faulty fences, as well as overgrown hedges and trees that obstruct the road. The "Path Inspection" <note>original: "Pfadenschau"</note> is distinguished from the "Hedge Inspection"; the former is carried out annually regarding the fences and enclosures of properties, but the latter—regarding the opening and clearing of roads from overgrown hedges, shrubs, and trees—is performed only every third year. (Ibid, folio 813).

### 97. Hope.
<note>original: "Spes."</note>
Symbols of great and long-lasting hope can be compared to porcelain. For porcelain is a certain mass composed of gypsum, crushed egg, the shells of marine locusts <note>The author is repeating a common early-modern European myth that Chinese porcelain was made from a mixture buried underground for decades.</note>, and other materials; if this mass is properly packed and thickened, it is hidden underground in a more secret place, which a father designates for his children. And there it remains hidden for eighty years. Pancirollus, *On Newly Discovered Things*, page 141 and following. See also Mr. Fürer’s *Travels through Egypt, Arabia, etc.*, page 42. Hope alone is also understood to be able to be bequeathed. Mantica, *On the Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 9, title 1, number 17. A "probable hope" and a "thing" or an "acquired right" are judged as equals. Klock, *Consultations* 103, number 8 [and others]. The hope of succeeding in fiefs <note>term: "feudis" - estates held under the feudal system</note> is probable and considerable. Klock, *Consultation* 69, number 41. A false hope of succession is customarily called "a waking dream." Klock, *Consultation* 7, number 321. Regarding the legal clause—"if the plaintiff shows that he has hitherto appealed to the defendant in a friendly manner and obtained nothing but hope"—and its effect, see Ummius, *On Legal Process*, Disputation 6, number 56. Hope and fear stir up life. In the *Selected Letters*

<column-break/>

of Mr. Georg Richter, page 113. Impatience for hope eventually leads to ruin (ibid, page 5). The hope of impunity is an enticement to sin. Cicero, *In Defense of Milo*. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 142, number 9. Wholesome severity overcomes the empty hope of mercy <note>original: "Salutaris severitas vincit inanem spem clementiæ"</note>. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus and Brutus*, letter 2. The hope of a thing, or of a person, makes a formal agreement <note>term: "stipulationem" - a verbal contract in Roman law</note> valid. Boër, *Decisions* 172, number 7. The hope of a "pupillary substitution" <note>term: "Substitutionis pupillariis" - a legal arrangement where a father appoints an heir for his underage child in case the child dies before reaching adulthood</note> is not transmitted. Decision 38, number 22. It is a sign of a great nature to always hope. Those who least lose heart in adversity, but instead persist in deeds and strength—whether this is done publicly or privately—are rightly judged to be most excellent, as Pericles says in Thucydides, book 11. See more in Rupertus's commentary on Florus, book 4, chapter 8, section 3: "The spirit was increased by evils." And on book 3, chapter 7, section 20: "The fortune of the Roman people always rose up greater in times of trouble." And on book 1, chapter 10, section 2: Hope that depends on the will of another cannot be called hope. *Altdorf Consultations*, page 244. The hope of paternal succession can be given as a dowry by a woman with her father's consent; if that woman dies before both her husband and her father, and the husband subsequently dies before the father-in-law, that hope can be transmitted to outside heirs—such as sons from a second marriage—by virtue of the dotal pact <note>original: "pactum dotale" - a prenuptial agreement regarding dowry</note>. *Altdorf Consultations*, page 241. Any hope of succession can be drawn into a contract (ibid, page 244). "Hope upon which no account can be made" <note>original: "Hoffnung, darauf kein Rechnung zu machen"</note>. Zorer, part 2, question 5, number 368.

### 98. Bound-by-Force.
<note>original: "Hropant."</note>
In the Bavarian Laws <note>original: "Leg. Bojor."</note>, title 3, chapter 1, section 8: "if one has entangled another by force but not tied them," which they call *Hropant*. *Band* refers to a binding or ligament, but what *Hropit* means is not clear.

### 99. Enclosures.
<note>original: "Heeger."</note>
Assessments and enclosures on the Elbe River. *Saxon Revenue Matters*, page 60.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical legal encyclopedia, moving from the letter 'H' (concluding with 'Heimlich' or Secretly) to the letter 'I'. This section focuses on the legal rights, classifications, and regulations of hunting (Ius Venandi), a significant aspect of feudal law and land management in the 17th century.</meta>

<page-num>469</page-num>
<header>Letter I.</header>

<margin>See Tacitus folio 69. Martinus century 6, disputation 5, questions 9 & 10.</margin>
Those who hunt, however, must take care that they apply themselves to hunting at the proper time regarding the protection of the fields, without damage to the fertile lands and estates <note>original: "ohne Schaden der fruchtbaren Länder und Güter"</note>. Furthermore, Tiraquellus, in his work *On Nobility* <note>original: "de nobil."</note> chapter 37, number 149, warns that they should not incur immoderate expenses regarding hunting. For Cicero, in book 2 of *On Duties* <note>original: "offic."</note>, calls such people "prodigals" who pour out their money on hunting equipment.

Hunting is called either High <note>original: "Superior"</note> or Low <note>original: "Inferior"</note>. We call High hunting the pursuit of stags and wild boars; the High Hunt <note>original: "die Hohe-Jagt"</note>, for black and red game <note>original: "schwarz und roth Wildpräth"</note>, and this hunting is classified among the Royalties <note>term: "Regalia" - rights and privileges reserved specifically for a sovereign or monarch</note>. (For a broader discussion of this question, see Pruckmann in his section on hunting, question 1, and Sebastian Medicus *On Hunting* <note>original: "de venat."</note>, question 27.) This is because it is usually expressly reserved in the granting of a Fief <note>A legal grant of land in exchange for service or loyalty.</note>; "yet we reserve for ourselves the High Hunt, and the black and red game" <note>original: "doch behalten wir uns bevor, die Hohe-Jagt, schwarz und roth Wildpräth"</note>. Low hunting refers to animals of a smaller or lesser type: the hunting rights for hares, foxes, and small woodcraft <note>original: "Jagtsgerechtigkeit an Haasen, Füchsen und klein Waidwerck"</note>. For just as in a general grant of jurisdiction, only the lowest or smallest degree is conveyed, so also only the low hunt is considered permitted in a general grant. See Hegius, part 1, question 15, number 62.

Regarding what specifically belongs to "small woodcraft," etc., see the *Declaration of the Upper-Palatinate Privileges*, folio 24, and whether the hunting of hares and foxes should also include roe deer. See *Strasbourg Consilia*, volume 1, consultation 88, question 3.

Grace-hunts <note>original: "Gnaden-Jagten" - hunting rights granted by the favor of a ruler rather than by permanent legal right</note> cannot be transferred or ceded to another. First, because privileges granted to someone out of singular grace cannot be yielded. See Tiraquellus *On Lineal Retraction*, section 26, gloss 1, number 61; Bartolus on the law *etiam* in the Digest *on oaths*; and the law *non solum*, section *si puella* in the Digest *on marriage rites*. Second, because grace-hunts of this kind do not pass to the heir of the person to whom the grant was made, but vanish with the person. See the law *cum precario* 12, section 1, *on precarious grants*. For it is a personal privilege, which does not go beyond the person. Those things which do not pass to heirs cannot be ceded. See law 42 and Bartolus’s commentary there, in the Digest *on the administration and risk of tutors*.

Grace-hunts can be freely revoked by the grantor or his heir whenever it pleases him; they can and may be revoked and demanded back at the pleasure of the Lord or his heirs <note>original: "können und mögen nach Belieben des Herrn, oder seiner Erben widerruffen und abgefordert"</note>, and then granted to another without hindrance from the person to whom they were previously allowed by petition. For a "precarious grant" <note>term: "precarium" - a legal arrangement where property is held at the will of the grantor, who can take it back at any time.</note> is that which is granted for use by a petitioner for as long as the grantor allows. See laws 1 and 2 of the Digest *on precarious grants*. Lord Harprecht, in his treatise *on R. D.*, number 222, says: This is so true that even if hunting is granted precariously by a Prince for a certain time, it can be revoked even before the time has expired, according to the text in the law *precario* 12.

<column-break/>

For even if a tacit agreement not to revoke before the time expires is included in a hunt granted for a certain period, such an agreement is repugnant to the nature and substance of a precarious grant. It is rightly rejected as useless and of no value. Indeed, it is a general rule that all agreements, whether tacit or express, which are against the nature and substance of a contract, are of no importance. See law *precario* and law *ubi donatus* 27 in the Digest *on donations in case of death*.

I wish to insert here the formula for a Lease and Grace-Hunt <note>original: "Bestand und Gnaden-Jagens"</note>, as such was granted by Lord Ludwig Friedrich, Duke of Württemberg, etc., to the princely favor of Adam von Au.

> By the Grace of God, We, Ludwig Friedrich, Duke of Württemberg and Teck, Count of Mömpelgard, Lord of Heidenheim, etc., Guardian and Administrator: We acknowledge publicly and make known with this letter to everyone, that We have graciously granted and allowed to Our guardian-vassal and dear faithful Adam von Au, upon his submitted humble request and petition, as well as the proceedings held, in the following district of the Tübingen Forest and Genninger ward: which begins at the brook in Eschingen, and goes up the brook to Genneckingen into the village, from there to the valley-mill, and down the valley to Genningen into the village, and from there by the nearest path back up to Eschingen to his previous hunting grounds, and nothing further than what is recently mentioned; and conditionally, to direct, hunt, and stalk <note>term: "bürschen" - to hunt or stalk game, often specifically referring to the use of a firearm or hunting in a quiet, stealthy manner.</note> after hares, foxes, roe deer, as well as red and black game. Namely, the black game through the whole year; however, in early migrations, and where the red game can do immediate damage to the grass <note>original: "Grues Schaden"</note>, it shall be permitted for him to begin the hunting more timely, and for such purpose to seek dispensation. This shall always be conducted in woods and fields according to the manner and custom of a woodsman, and for this purpose only his trusted and sworn servants shall be used alongside him. In this, however, We have expressly reserved for ourselves that whenever We have need of roe deer or hares, We may at any time have our own men stalk or catch what is necessary in those parts. Also, if someone in this place is proven and known to have traditionally exercised the low woodcraft, nothing shall be taken from him by this grant.

It shall also be permitted to Our guardian-subjects, by virtue of the granted concession, to stalk the red and black game on their cultivated fields located around and between the woods in this district. However, for the red game, this shall last only as long as the crops are in the field, but for the black game, the lease shall last through the whole year. Those who hunt, however, ought to take care that they apply themselves to the hunt at the proper time regarding the protection of fields from wildlife, **without damage to the fertile lands and estates.** <note>original German: *ohne Schaden der fruchtbaren Länder und Güter*</note> And lest they incur immoderate expenses regarding hunts, Tiraquellus warns in *On Nobility, chapter 37, number 149.* For Cicero, in *On Duties, book 2,* calls such people "prodigals" who pour out their money on hunting equipment.

Hunting is called "Superior" <note>The "High Hunt"</note> in some cases, and "Inferior" <note>The "Low Hunt"</note> in others. We call the hunting of stags and wild boars **High Hunting, black and red game,** <note>original German: *die Hohe-Jagt, schwartß und roth Wildpräth*; "red game" refers to deer, while "black game" refers to wild boar</note> and this type of hunting is classified among the <term>Regalia</term> <note>Royal rights or prerogatives belonging to the sovereign</note> (on which question see more extensively in Pruckman, *in section "hunting," question 1,* and Sebastian Medicus, *on hunting, question 27.*) This is because it is usually expressly reserved in the granting of a <term>Fief</term>: <note>Land held on condition of feudal service</note> **"yet we reserve for ourselves the High Hunting, and the black and red game."** <note>original German: *doch behalten wir uns bevor, die Hohe-Jagt, schwartß und roth Wildpräth*</note> Inferior hunting is for smaller beasts or those of a lower status, **the hunting rights for hares, foxes, and small game.** <note>original German: *Jagtsgerechtigkeit an Haasen, Füchsen und klein Waidwerck*</note> For just as in a general grant of jurisdiction, only the smallest or least hunting rights are included: so also only the inferior hunt is thought to be permitted. Hegius, *part 1, question 15, number 62.*

Regarding what specifically belongs to "small game," etc., see the *Declaration of the Upper Palatinate Privileges, folio 24,* and whether hare and fox hunting also extends to roe deer. *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 1, Consultation 88, question 3.*

**Precarious hunts** <note>original Latin/German: *Venationes præcariæ, Gnaden-Jagten*; these are hunting rights granted as a personal favor or "grace" rather than a permanent legal transfer</note> cannot be transferred or ceded to another. Firstly, because privileges granted to someone out of singular grace cannot be ceded. Tiraquellus, *on the retraction of lineage, section 26, gloss 1, number 61.* Bartolus, *on the law of oaths,* via the laws *if from many* and *not only* regarding the rites of marriage. Secondly, because precarious hunts of this kind do not pass to the heir of the person to whom the grant was made, but vanish with the person. *Law regarding precarium 12, section 1.* For it is a personal privilege, which does not go beyond the person. Moreover, those things which do not pass to heirs cannot be ceded. *Law 42 and there Bartolus, on the administration and danger of tutors.*

Precarious hunts can be freely revoked by the grantor or his heir whenever it pleases them; **they can and may be revoked and demanded back at the pleasure of the Lord or his heirs, and then be granted to another without hindrance from the one to whom they were previously granted by request.** <note>original German: *können und mögen nach Belieben des Herrn, oder seiner Erben widerruffen und abgefordert, und alsdann einem andern ohne Verhinderung der jenigen, welchem sie bishero Bittweiß gestattet, verliehen werden*</note> For a <term>precarium</term> <note>A legal grant held by prayer or request</note> is that which is granted for use to one asking by prayers for as long as he who granted it suffers it to be so. *Laws 1 and 2, on the precarium.* Lord Harprecht, *treatise on R.D., number 222,* says in the following number: And this is so true that even a hunt granted precariously by a Prince up to a certain time can be revoked even before that time has elapsed.

<column-break/>

For even if a silent agreement not to revoke the hunt before the time has elapsed is inherent in a hunt granted for a fixed time: because such an agreement is repugnant to the nature and substance of a precarious grant, it is rightly rejected as useless and of no value. Indeed, it is a general rule that all agreements, whether silent or express, which are against the nature and substance of a contract, are of no significance. *Law on precarium; Law where donated 27, on donations in cause of death.*

It is pleasing to insert here the formula for **a lease and gracious hunt,** <note>original German: *eines Bestand und Gnaden-Jagens*</note> such as was granted to the noble Adam von Au by Lord Ludwig Friedrich, Duke of Württemberg, etc.

<meta>This page continues from page 469, which began discussing the legal definitions of hunting (Ius Venandi) and the distinction between "High" and "Low" hunting rights. This page provides a specific legal example of a hunting contract from the Duchy of Württemberg and then transitions into a scholarly legal debate regarding the scope of such grants.</meta>

# 470
# Augmented Practical Treasury

...be obligated to allow the pursuit of the hunt for [Name]. Within such a district, he shall remain the leaseholder <note>original: "Beständner"</note> and shall not infringe upon another in his hunting. However, when he has shot an animal in his hunt, or given it a wound from which it did not immediately fall, he may follow it according to hunting custom as long as he tracks the blood trail <note>original: "Schweiß," literally "sweat," but a technical term for a wounded animal's blood</note>. If he kills it in another district, or if it falls of its own accord, it shall follow to him without refusal, provided no deception is used, under the penalty which We have reserved for Ourselves according to the nature of the case.

In return, he, Adam von Au, shall pay to Our Forest Warden <note>term: "Waldvogt" - a high-ranking official overseeing a princely forest</note> at Tübingen a yearly lease payment of one hundred Guilders, and seventy-five Guilders for three horses which he is to keep for Us on account of the old hunts; specifically, half the amount on Michaelmas <note>September 29</note> and the other half on Candlemas <note>February 2</note>, and for the first time following at such time, in good, acceptable currency, and deliver it into his secure hands.

The lease shall extend for six years, and the leaseholder is obligated to maintain it for such time; his submitted bond <note>original: "Revers"</note> must also be expressly directed to this end, even if the game should somewhat diminish and no longer be present in such quantity as at the beginning.

In addition, it shall be free and open to Us at any time to cancel such lease and concession, to take the hunts back to Ourselves, and to terminate them entirely. Furthermore, the leaseholder shall also be obligated to maintain the Princely Rights <note>original: "Fürstliche Jura"</note> of this conceded district, to keep the boundaries <note>original: "Lauhen"</note> and boundary stones in good condition, and shall not cite this concession sooner or later as a permanent right <note>original: "Gerechtigkeit"</note>, nor allow others to do so on his behalf, nor permit any other infringement in such a district. If he should notice such things, he shall pursue the perpetrators and poachers and help to catch them, or report them to Us and identify them by name, so that We may then carry out the reserved punishment according to another's crime; the transgressor shall then also be obligated to compensate the leaseholder for the damage caused to him in such a manner, according to fair estimation.

Finally, We wish to reserve for Ourselves all Princely Authority, laws and jurisdictions, punishments and fines in this hunting district, as We have exercised them until now, and that nothing be diminished by this concession.

For greater witness of this, We have publicly printed Our Princely Guardian's Seal hereupon. Given at Stuttgart, the 13th of the month of August, in the year 1629.

->Ludwig Friedrich, &c.<-
->L. S.<- <note>Locus Sigilli: Place of the Seal</note>

<column-break/>

When one grants the power of pursuing and capturing larger wild animals, such as stags and boars (commonly called <term>the high or black coarse game</term> <note>original: "das hohe oder schwarze grobe Wildpräth"</note>), it is understood that the power to capture smaller wild animals—<term>the small game</term> <note>original: "das kleine Wilpräth"</note> such as foxes, hares, and the like—is also granted. This is because to whom the greater thing is granted, the lesser thing also seems to be granted. The favors <note>original: "beneficia"</note> of Princes are to be interpreted most broadly. *Law: l. fin. ff. de constit. Princip. c. cùm dilecti. de donat. c. cùm olim tibi. de verb. signif.*

However, to some, the negative view seems more probable. For just as with a servitude <note>a legal burden on property</note>, the manner added to a hunting concession must be observed most strictly, and one is not permitted to exceed it. *Laws: l. servitutes 4. §. modum 1. ff. de servit. l. certo generi 13. ff. de S. P. R. etc.* This is because the writing of the concession has its own limits and proves those limits, and no further. Therefore, what the writing does not say, we also must not say. *Baldus in c. Rudolphus on rescripts, etc.* Since in this type of concession a limit <note>original: "modus"</note> is applied—namely, that it is permitted to take larger game—he to whom the concession was made cannot cross this limit to take animals of a smaller kind. *Reasoning from Law: l. diligenter 5. ff. mand.*

I believe it should be distinguished thus: whoever possesses <term>high hunting jurisdiction</term> <note>original: "die hohe Jagbarkeit"</note> by virtue of their authority <note>original: "vi jurisdictionis"</note>, by power of the Forestry and Territorial Sovereignty <note>original: "in Krafft der Forstlichen und Lands Obrigkeit"</note>, that person also has the right of taking smaller game. This is not the case if he has prescribed it, or holds the right to hunt <term>high game</term> <note>original: "das hohe Wildpräth"</note> by some other specific private law.

He who has the right of hunting in a forest also has the right of enclosing the forest for the capture of animals, commonly called <term>the right of the hedge</term> <note>original: "die Gerechtigkeit deß Hagens"</note>, meaning he may strike a hedge into the wood. *Bidemback. qu. nobil. 12. Gail. lib. 2. obs. 68. etc.* Lord Harpprecht in his *Treatise on the Division of Things* says: However, I do not wish this to be taken as if he who has the power of hedging and surrounding a forest with wooden barriers <note>original: "ligneis plagis"</note> could also cut wood in that forest for the use of the enclosure <note>original: "deß Hagens"</note>. Rather, if he wishes to enclose the grove or forest with wooden barriers, or to erect a <term>hedge</term> <note>original: "ein Hag"</note>, he must do so with his own wood and without prejudice to another. This is because these barriers—<term>the hedges</term> <note>original: "die Hagen"</note>—are like nets and snares. He who desires to use the hunt is bound to carry it out with his own nets and dogs; since servitudes are strictly interpreted by law and neither should be extended beyond its case. *Laws: d. l. certo generi. 13 ff. de serv. R. P. etc.*

Whether hunting is considered the "fruit" or profit of the land? See *Modestinus Pistor. part. 1. q. 15.*

Here fits the question: does a Prince, by reason of his Forestry Sovereignty, have the right to hunt alongside the nobility settled in his land? Hunting is sometimes restricted to a certain genus of animals. Hunting is counted among recreations, but not that which is called the "most wicked art"—the arena-hunt <note>original: "arenaria," i.e., gladiatorial or staged beast-fights</note>, whose spectators also sin mortally—but rather that which is done without noise by placing nets or snares, which is permitted to Laymen and Clergy. *Barbosa, book 19, chapter 4, axiom 3.* We read that hunting was a form of recreation for Alexander the Great, Pompey, Trajan, Antoninus Pius, Hadrian, Maximilian I, and today for most Princes; just as fishing was for Augustus, ball-games for Alexander, painting for Hadrian, and instrumental music for Nero. ## 2. Year. *Annus.*

A year is understood in law in two ways: firstly, **naturally**, as a year is understood to consist of 365 days. *Law "When the heir," section "Stichus," Digest on the status of freemen.* Secondly, according to Bartolus in the said section "Stichus," a year is understood **artificially**, as we take it from the Nativity of the Lord to the next Nativity. See Arumaeus, *Decisions*, book 2; Arnold Rayger in the *Treasury*, section "Year." But the Archdeacon in chapter "If because of," column 2, verse "January," *On Rescripts in the Sext*, says that there is a **natural** year, a **usual** year, a **ceremonial** year, and finally an **emergent** year. See Sylvanus *On Feudal Recognition*, question 9 and following; Alberico Gentili *On the Appeal of Diverse Times*, chapter 3; Robertus, *Sentences*, book 1, chapter 2. A **natural** year is that which I mentioned above, beginning from any given day until the end of the same, counting 365 days and 6 hours. Chapter "Quadragesima," *On Consecration*, distinction 5. The **usual** year begins <insert>†</insert> in January, lasting until the following January, according to the Latins, and therefore *January* is named from the "door" <note>Latin: *janua*</note> of the year, chapter "Fasting," 76, distinction. But the **legal** year begins from April unto the next April, according to the Moons. And this is among the Greeks and Hebrews, as in the said chapter "Fasting." The **ceremonial** year, however, is from feast to feast, and this is among all nations, through chapter 1, *On Consecration*, distinction 1. An **emergent** and final year is that in which something great occurs, such as from the departure from Egypt, when the Israelite people were freed from Egyptian servitude; it is called "emergent" according to Thomas de Marinis, *Treatise on the Types and Quality of Fiefs*, title 2, folio 166, because something new "emerges." The Jews and Greeks compute the year from the first Olympiad: but the Romans from the Founding of the City. We Christians, however, compute from the Incarnation of Christ or from His Nativity, according to various customs, chapter 1, at the beginning, distinction 23. Others call it an "Era." Regarding the computation of the Year of the Lord, Bartholomaeus Bartazolius in his *Treatise on Clauses*, 1, gloss 2, has the following: It must be seen at what time the Years of the Lord are to be computed, because they are computed in different ways; in which it should be known that even before the coming of Christ, years were begun in different ways,

<header>Letter I.</header>

For the Romans calculated their years from the Indiction <term>Indictio: a fifteen-year cycle used for taxation and dating in the Roman Empire</term>, the Hebrews from the Flood, and the Greeks from the Herculean Games <note>The Olympic Games</note>, which were held every five years on Mount Olympus. Today, however, we calculate from the years of the Incarnation of our Lord and the Emperor, as stated in the glosses of the legal codes <note>referencing various sections of the *Corpus Juris Civilis* regarding the naming of the Emperor</note>. But indeed, that years should be calculated from the Nativity of Christ is a decision of the Rota <note>The Roman Rota, a high ecclesiastical court</note>, which is the standard rule according to the jurist Brunus. This is also held as more correct by the Abbot <note>Panormitanus, a famous canon lawyer</note> in his commentary on the faith of instruments. One gloss says that some begin the year from the Nativity, others from the Incarnation; Johannes Andreae adds that some start from the Circumcision <note>January 1st</note>, and others on the eighth day before the Kalends of October <note>September 24th</note>, as was done before the coming of Christ. Regarding this, he refers to specific legal notes which hold that the custom of the locality must be observed, and the years should begin according to that custom; this is the truest view according to Bartolus. Add to this what Oldendorp writes concerning statutes of the City: whether a statute is valid which says that unless someone pursues their right within a year and a day <term>inner Jahr und Tag</term>, they are thereafter not admitted. He concludes, with Bartolus, that such a statute is valid, as it serves to settle the disputes of men who live their lives in the same city—or as the saying goes, "in the same ship"—among whom discord is particularly destructive.

Whether the beginning of the New Year should be calculated from the day of Christ’s Nativity (December 25th) or from the Kalends of January (January 1st) is investigated by Schäffer. See also Carranza in his treatise on natural and legitimate birth, where he discusses the division of the year. On whether the year, day, and month must necessarily be placed in legal documents, see Fontanella on prenuptial agreements.

"After certain hymns," that is, after several years. Horace, *Odes*, book 1, ode 15. Regarding the Island of the GOOD YEAR, see Bertius in his *Brief Account of the World*, page 46.

This festival of Anna Perenna was carried out with great celebrity and a ritual pomp more than "Attalic" <note>extremely luxurious</note>. For not far from the Tiber, the Roman people crowded together, each according to their station, and indulged their spirits. Some were under tents made of green branches, or under cloaks stretched over lush reeds; others, under the open sky, invited one another to drink cups flowing with the flower of nectar. They would drain as many cups as the years they wished to live, extending their hopes to the years of the Sibyls or the "three-ages-of-men" <note>long-lived figures of myth</note>. The City Master of Strasbourg wishes a "Happy New Year" to the citizenry; see Limnäus. Regarding New Year's gifts <term>Strenis</term>, see the disputation held under Rauscher at Tübingen in 1641. A "continuous year" consists of 365 consecutive days; a "useful year" <term>Annus utilis: a legal term for a year where only the days on which a person is legally able to act are counted</term> consists of the same number of "useful" days, even if collected from a series of several years. On the Astronomical and Civil year, many things are handed down by Charles Annibal Fabrot and Carranza.

**terms regarding this can be found: Hunting Ground <note>Wildbahn</note>, Bird Pasture <note>Vogelweid</note>.** See *Symphoremata Gylmanni, volume 1, book 2, folio 129, and following up to number 144.* Regarding the proof of Hunting Rights, *Symphoremata Gylmanni, volume 2, folio 33.* The clause: "With Huntings": **With forests, hunting grounds, hunts, and wolf pits.** *Mundius, on Offices and Honors, chapter 2, number 259, and those cited there.* **Lower game**, fowling, the capture of hares, and sometimes the pursuit of wild boars with dogs, which is commonly called **from the leash** <note>original: "vom Strick aus"</note>, and only at stated times when neighboring Princes have finished hunting. *Ibid, number 260.*

To free a region from noxious wild beasts is considered not just a release, but truly a useful labor and worthy of a Prince. *Marquard Freher, in his exposition on the Sapphire of Emperor Constantius Augustus, says this significantly.*

## 2. Year. <note>original: "Annus"</note>

A *Year* is understood in law in two ways: in one way *naturally*, as a year of 365 days is understood. *Law "cum hares," section "Stichus," Digest on the status of freemen.* Secondly, according to *Bartolus in the said section "Stichus,"* a year is understood *artificially*, as we take it from the Nativity of the Lord to the next Nativity. *See Arumaeus, Decisions, book 2, in the "coron. à Princ." Arnold Rayger in the Treasury, section "Year."* But the Archdeacon in *Chapter "si propter," 2nd column, verse "Januarius," on Rescripts in the 6th book of Decretals,* says that there is a *natural, usual, ceremonial* year, and finally an *emerging* year. See *Sylvanus, on Feudal Recognition, question 9 and following; Alberico Gentili, on the names of different times, chapter 3; Robert, 1st Sentences, chapter 2.* A *natural* year is that which I mentioned above, beginning from any day until the end of that same day, counting 365 days and 6 hours. *Chapter "quadragesima," on Consecration, distinction 5.* The *usual* year begins in January and goes until the following January, according to the Latins; therefore *January* is named from the *Janua* <note>Latin: door or gate</note> of the year. *Chapter "jejunium," 76th distinction.* But the *legal* year begins from April to the next April, according to the Moons. And this is among the Greeks and Hebrews, as in the *said chapter "Jejunium."* The *ceremonial* year, however, is from feast to feast, and this is among all nations. *Through chapter 1, on Consecration, distinction 1.* The *emerging* and final year is that in which something great happens, such as from the exit from Egypt, when the Israelite people were liberated from the slavery of Egypt; and it is called "emerging," according to Tommaso de Marinis, *Treatise on the Types and Quality of Feuds, title 2, page 166,* because something new emerges. The Jews and Greeks calculate the year from the first Olympiad, but the Romans from the founding of the City <note>A.U.C. - Ab Urbe Condita</note>. We Christians, however, calculate from the Incarnation of Christ or from His Nativity, according to various customs. *Chapter 1, in the beginning, distinction 23.* Others call it the *Era*. Regarding the calculation of the Year of our Lord, Bartholomew Bartazolous has the following in *Treatise on Clauses 1, gloss 2,* where he writes: It must be seen at what time the Years of our Lord are to be calculated, because they are calculated in different ways; in which it should be known that even before the coming of Christ, years were begun in different ways,

For the Romans calculated years from the **Indiction** <note>original: "Indictione"; a 15-year cycle used for tax and legal dating</note>, the Hebrews from the **Flood**, and the Greeks from the **Herculean Games** <note>the Olympic Games</note>, which were held every five years on Mount Olympus; but today, years are calculated from the **Incarnation of the Lord** and from the **Emperor**: as stated in the *gloss on the rubric of the Code regarding indictions; the gloss on the Authentic 'that the name of the Emperor should be placed first'; and the text beginning 'in the name of the Lord,' distinction 23.* However, that years should indeed be calculated from the Nativity of Christ is a *decision of the Rota <note>The Roman Rota, the highest papal court</note> regarding the Nativity, which is the regular rule according to Bartolus in his commentary on the Digest... and the Code regarding accusations*, which is more correct according to the Abbot <note>Panormitanus, a famous canon lawyer</note> *in the chapter 'among the beloved,' number 13, on the faith of Instruments.* And the *gloss on the Clementines 1, on the word 'from the time,' concerning the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith* says that some begin the years from the Nativity and others from the Incarnation; *Johannes Andreae* adds that still others begin from the Circumcision <note>January 1st</note>, and others on the eighth day before the Kalends of October <note>September 24th</note>, as was done before the Advent of Christ. On this matter, he refers to the *notes on the Speculum regarding the editing of Instruments, section 2, in the following verse*, where he holds that the custom of the place must be observed, and the years should be started according to that custom; this is most true, as *Bartolus* notes. Add what *Oldendorp* writes regarding exceptions in the title on usucapion <note>acquiring ownership through long use</note>, page 459 and following. He asks whether a city statute is valid which states: unless someone pursues their right **within a year and a day** <note>original: "inner Jahr und Tag"</note>, they shall not be admitted thereafter. Here, along with *Bartolus on the Digest and the Code regarding 30-year prescription*, he concludes that such a statute is valid, since it brings people closer to settling their disputes—especially those living in the same city and, as the saying goes, "living their lives on the same ship," among whom discord is particularly destructive.

Should the beginning of the **New Year** be calculated from the day of the Nativity of Christ (December 25th) or from the Kalends of January? *Schæffer* investigates this in *part 3, question 1*; see also *Carranza in his treatise on natural and legitimate birth, page 517, where he discusses the division of the year.* Regarding whether the Year, Day, and Month must necessarily be added to legal Instruments, see *Fontanella on prenuptial agreements.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding the Year of Grace: *Lord Doctor Tabor on Transfers, page 197.*

"After certain winters," that is, after several years. *Horace, Book 1, Odes, Ode 15.* Regarding the Island of the GOOD YEAR. *Bertius in his Summary of the World, page 46.*

The Romans numbered the years by the Consuls, about which see *Johannes Rosinus in Roman Antiquities and Salvian of Marseille, Book 6, on the Government of God.* Although there were two Consuls every year for a long time in the Roman Republic—and sometimes "substitute" Consuls <note>original: "suffecti"</note> as well as "ordinary" ones—under the later Emperors, it became the custom to create only a single Consul, as the Emperors themselves wished to be considered in the place of the second Consul. *Rittershusius on the New Constitutions, page 632.*

*Besold, Volume I.*

The people of **Hameln** count the years from the **departure of the children** <note>original: "ab exitu liberorum"; a reference to the legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, which the town used as a chronological marker</note>. *Rittershusius on the New Constitutions, page 633.* What an Indiction is: *Didacus, Book 1, resolution 12, number 4.*

The **Indiction** is the **Romans' tax-counting number** <note>original: "der Römer Zinszahl"</note>; regarding its origin, see *Covarrubias, Book 1, Varied Resolutions, chapter 12.* Each one encompasses three Olympiads, that is, fifteen years. *Rittershusius, same page.* The custom of using Indictions in numbering years began in the times of Constantine the Great and Licinius, according to the *Consulate. Klock on the Treasury.* Scribes should begin legal Instruments with the name of the Emperor and express the year of his reign. *Rittershusius, page 632.* Instruments are regularly to be issued without the day and the Consul. *Ummius on Procedure, page 730.*

Legal acts must be issued in their entirety, with the day and the Consul. *Lord Doctor Biccius in Golden Sections 5, thesis 133, at the end.* In practice, there is never any doubt that Instruments are declared null if the years of Christ are omitted. *Covarrubias, Practical Questions, chapter 20, number 2.* See also *Scaccia, Book 2, chapter 11, number 1186 and following.*

Different years yield different harvests of grain; while some years are sterile, others are fertile, about which there is an elegant passage in Aristotle at the end of the second book of *Rhetoric*.

How the year in which an heir is bound to execute the will of a testator is calculated: *Rittershusius, page 331, number 9.*

On the Kalends of January, as the month enters, sacrifices are made both publicly and privately to **Anna Peranna** <note>an ancient Roman goddess of the year and renewal</note>, so that one might "year" and "pass through the year" <note>original: "annare, perannareque"</note> favorably. The **Festival of Anna Peranna** was conducted with great celebration and a ritual pomp more than Attalic <note>meaning extremely luxurious or magnificent</note>. For not far from the Tiber, crowds of Romans gathered, and each with their companions indulged their "Genius" <note>the individual spirit of enjoyment</note>: some under tents made of green branches, or under togas stretched over luxuriant reeds; others under the cold vault of the sky. There they perhaps invited each other quite liberally to cups flowing with the flower of nectar, and according to the health and years of life of others, they drained as many cups as they had years, extending their toasts to the years of the Sibyls or to three centuries. **A New Year's wish is offered by the City Master of Strasbourg to the citizens.** *Limnäus in Public Law, Book 7, chapter 3, page 72.* Regarding New Year's gifts <note>original: "Strenis"</note>, see the *disputation held under Rancher at Tübingen in the year 1641.* A "continuous year" consists of 365 consecutive days; a "useful year" <note>term: "Annus utilis"; a legal term for a year where only days on which legal action was possible are counted</note> consists of as many "useful" days, even if collected from a series of several years. *Cujas notes three things required for a useful year. Lord Biccius in Golden Sections 5, thesis 162.* Regarding the Astronomical and Civil Year, much is handed down by *Charles Annibal Fabrot and Carranza.*

### 3. Year and Day. Annus & Dies.
In **Saxon Law**, "a year and a day" <note>original: "Jahr und Tag"</note> consists of six weeks and one year. *Gloss on the Saxon Mirror, article 38, book 1; Town Law (Weichbild), article 21; Fief Law, chapter 16, at the end.*

the phrase *a year and six weeks* <note>original German: "ein Jahr und sechs Wochen"</note>. ## ADDITION.

The space of one year never runs against someone who is unaware of it, *Barbosa, book 1, chapter 63, axiom 1.* Under feudal law, a soldierly Vassal is given a year and a month, but a peasant <note>original: "pagano"</note> is given a year and a day to seek **Investiture** <note>The formal ceremony where a tenant receives land from a lord</note>; this is treated extensively by *Gothofredus Antonii, feudal dispute 8, thesis 3, letters a and b.* Regarding how this time should be calculated, see *Sylvanus, question 9 and following.* Question: Can the Lord extend this time against the Vassal's will? It is affirmed by *Gothofredus Antonii in the same place.* "A year and a day" is a matter of the form and solemnity of custom and the law of **retraction** <note>The right to buy back property</note>. *Berlich, 2, conclusion 40, number 13.* If tenant farmers <note>original: "Hubarii"</note>, having been summoned by their Lords or bailiffs, do not pay the required rent within a year and a day, *when a year and a day has passed* <note>original: "wann es Jahr und Tag gestehet"</note>, then the estate is forfeit <note>original: "zyher"</note>, and one shall seize that same estate with a free hand; this is then called a *death-knell* <note>original: "Seelaut"</note>, and it then belongs solely to the Lord. *D. Dürr, on Manorial Courts, thesis 37.*

4. **Jauchart. A Yoke.**

A yoke or an acre <note>original: "Jugum vel jugerum"</note>, a *Jauchart*, is the space of a field that an ox, or *a yoke of oxen* <note>original: "ein Joch Ochsen"</note>, can plow in one day. See *Pliny, book 18 of the Natural History, chapter 3, page 709; Mr. D. Tabor, on Contracts and Tenant Law, thesis 40.* Today in the Netherlands and many other French regions, they call this same unit a *Jornatam*: *a journal* or *a day's worth of land* <note>original French: "un journal, ou journee de terre"</note>.

## ADDITION.

See below under the word *buying* <note>original: "kauffen"</note>, number 9. *Besold.*
A tax based on the acres of land was imposed by King Henry I of England. *Klock, on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 53, number 53.* One *Morgen* <note>a German unit of land, literally a "morning"</note> is 320 city-feet long and 160 city-feet wide. In Braunschweig, 1 *Morgen* or field contains 120 rods <note>original: "Ruthen"</note>. 1 rod contains 16 feet. 1 foot is 11 inches, squared. A donation of a plot of "three acres," even if there are more acres present, includes them all. This rule is approved and distinguished in *Villal. D. 142 and Soarez D. 231 and following.* A common or arable field, extending to one *plow* <note>original: "aratrum"</note> or team of His Royal Majesty. *Tripartite Work of the Hungarian Land Laws, part 1, title 133, folio 77.*

5. **Always and at all times, when and at whatever time he pleases, sooner or later. Always whenever.**

The words *always, whenever, as often as*, and *always and at all times* <note>original: "semper, quandocunque, toties quoties, je und allwegen"</note> designate an in-

<column-break/>

-finity of time. According to the law *sita stipulatus 55* of the Digest regarding guarantors; *Baptista* on the law *qui bona, final paragraph* of the Digest on threatened damage; where also see *Johannes de Imola*. *The Speculum, title on arbitrators, final paragraph, at the line "what if it is said." Alexander, counsel 144, at the line "but the man not willing," volume 2.*

Hence, if in a contract for **repurchase** <note>original: "pacto de retrovendendo"; an agreement allowing a seller to buy back property later</note> this clause is added: *so that whenever the seller or his heirs wish to offer the price, etc., they can receive the land back*, <gloss>meaning that at any time, when it pleases the seller or his heirs to repay the purchase price <note>original: "Kauffschillings"</note>, they shall be unimpeded in redeeming the sold property and taking it back for themselves, but shall be entitled and authorized to do so,</gloss> it results in the seller or his heirs always and forever having the right to redeem, notwithstanding the thirty-year **prescription** <note>A legal time limit after which a right is lost</note>. See *Caspar Thesaurus, forensic questions, book 2, question 72; Gratian, volume 1, chapter 2, part 1; the text in the law "what if he is unwilling," paragraph "if anything was so sold,"* in the Digest on the edict of the aediles; where *Bl. and Angelus* note that where the word *whenever* is placed in a promise, the statutory or legal prescription does not run. *Ruinus, counsel 111, number 7, volume 1; Christoph Besold, notable questions of Public Law, part 2, counsel 85, number 69 and following; Melonius in the Treasury of Feudal, Civil, and Criminal Law, in the Index of forensic matters.* The words *as often as* <note>original: "toties quoties"</note> designate the same; regarding these, see the entry *so often and much*, unless he has possessed it as his own, or has spoken against the redemption; for from that time, prescription begins.

The same is also judged regarding the word *wishing* <note>original: "volendi"</note>, which grants to everyone the natural faculty of doing what he pleases, as singularly handed down by *Oldradus, counsel 187, number 4.*

Nor is it any contradiction that these words, signifying perpetual time, are to be restricted to a space of 30 years, *following the reasoning of the law "rebus" 20, paragraph 1* of the Code on dowry rights; where an action for a dowry is said to be limited by a thirty-year boundary: although it is expressed elsewhere that the cause of a dowry is always and everywhere paramount, *law 1 of the Digest on the dissolution of marriage; following the law "minor" 39, paragraph "he who decided" 4* of the Digest on the edict; where it is handed down that someone is bound in the name of eviction perpetually: and yet it is certain that this action is prescribed in 30 years. Indeed, actions that are prescribed in 30 or 40 years are called "perpetual." *Following the reasoning of the law "The Praetor says" 20, paragraph "this interdict" 6* of the Digest on the reporting of new work. That argument, I say, moves nothing, because it is true and takes place in the disposition of the law, but not in the disposition of a man. For when one law says that an action is perpetual, or a right is held forever, but another law says that every action is extinguished by a space of 30 years: lest a clash and contradiction of laws follow, it is necessary to interpret "perpetual time" in this way, so that it does not exceed thirty years. This reasoning completely ceases in a disposition made by a man <note>i.e., a private contract</note>. See *Cynus on the final law of the Code on Judges; Imola, counsel 25, at the beginning*, where he says that infinity is tolerated when it proceeds from the agreement of the parties.

<margin>Mr. Harprecht on **usucapion** <note>The acquisition of a title or right to property by uninterrupted and undisputed possession for a prescribed term</note> at the beginning, number 167.</margin>
I also add this: in contracts, no word should be considered to have been added uselessly, and the intention of the contracting parties should not be restricted against their will. Now, these words "always and forever" <note>original German: *je und allwegen*</note>, when added to a pact of sale, would be entirely useless if they did not have a legal effect. *Wesenbec, counsel 2, number 52.* And if a certain time had been expressed in the pact—for instance, 50 years—no **prescription** <note>The loss of a right because of the passage of time</note> would run before that time had passed. Why, then, if an infinite time is expressed, should it not be the case that it never runs out? *Laws: "quod si nolit," Digest on the Aedilian Edict; law 7, section 4, Code on 30-year prescription.* The seller would be frustrated in his expectation and deceived—persuading himself that he could redeem the land without any time limit—and such deception is condemned by the laws. *Law 3, section "Magistrum," on the action against a shipowner; see Gerhard on the Institutes, decade 6, question 3, throughout.*

This opinion—namely, that a seller can redeem property whenever he pleases—is also supported by *Barbat, counsel 51, column 8, volume 1; Paris, counsel 92; Johannes Igneus on the law "in cognitione," number 76, Digest on the Silanian Senate-Consult; Alciat on the law "petens," in gloss 1, Code on pacts; Chasseneuz on the Customs of Burgundy, title on redeemable rents, section 1, gloss 1, column 2, verse "limita," and counsel 11, verse "vigesimo."* There, he cites many others who held the same view. And *Hieronymus Laurentius, decision 129, number 2 and following*, records that no prescription can be alleged, not even of the longest duration.

It must be noted here, however, that although the word "whenever" <note>original Latin: *quandocunque*</note> by its nature encompasses an infinite permanence of time, it must nevertheless be restricted according to a declaration following afterward. *Menochius, counsel 151, number 33 and 50; add Jacob Schultes, practical questions, book 1, question 55, number 69.*

->ADDITION.<-

If a Buyer responds to a close relative who is boasting that they want to take back the sold item by saying, "come as often as you wish, I will gladly admit you," then if a year passes, they are no longer admitted. *Berlich, 2, conclusion 40, number 15.* This is because these words should be understood to mean "provided that one comes within the legitimate time." Furthermore, such words do not seem to renounce the prescription of time. The word "whenever," etc., is understood to refer to the legitimate time. *Berlich, 2, conclusion 2, number 88, and those cited there.* The word "whenever" includes all time. *Marius Antoninus, V. R. book 2, reference 40, number 20.*

### 6. To each and everyone. *Cuilibet.*

The word "each" <note>original Latin: *Singulis*</note> distributes things separately and assigns them **in solidum** <note>meaning each person is responsible for or entitled to the whole, rather than just a share</note>. *Law "hujusmodi" 84, section 12, verse "singulos," Digest on legacies 1; law 37, Digest on vulgar and pupillary substitution, under "singulis"; Digest on the Falcidian law.* And the distributive "To anyone" <note>original Latin: *Cuilibet*</note> by its nature assigns a thing to each individual
<insert>Besold, Volume I.</insert>

<column-break/>

**in solidum**. *Law 22, section 1, "unicuique," Digest on the division of a family estate; law "hoc articulo" 29, verse "quisque," Digest on the institution of heirs; Paris, counsel 16, number 15 and 17; counsel 13, number 9, verse "in solidum."*

The distributive "Anyone" <note>original Latin: *Quilibet*</note> has the same power, granting an act **in solidum**: *Law 32, section 13, Digest on the reception of arbitrators; law 13, verse "æquè," Digest on the institution of heirs; see Roland à Valle, counsel 70, number 44, volume 3.* It works distributively so that individuals are considered as named and expressed; *the Doctors on the final law, at the word "una," where Jason, number 9, Code on pupillary and other substitutions; Farinacci in Criminal Practice, book 1, question 22, number 15*, noting that this word applies integrally and separately through all predicates: and signifies or attributes an act **in solidum**; add *Jacob Aleman on simultaneous investment, manual page 22.*

->ADDITION.<-

To anyone (*Cuilibet*). A disjunctive statement is satisfied by the truth of a single part. *Law 5, on the condition of institutions; law 129, on verbal obligations; chapter "in alternativis," on the rules of law in the 6th book of the Decretals.* Cujas reads it as *cui libet*, with the words separated, meaning "to whom it pleases." *Vinnius, section 11, on the institution of heirs.*

"Together" <note>original German: *Sammathaft*</note>, for "jointly." *Strasbourg Constitution, issued 1532.* The phrase "To all and singular" suffers no restriction. *Reinkingk, on the Roman-German Empire, 1. 2. 2. 72.*

### 7. However. *Tamen.*

This little word is adversative and restrictive, and consequently exclusive of all cases outside of the statement in which it is found. *See throughout Meichsner, decision 2, volume 2, book 1.*

->ADDITION.<-

"However" <note>original Latin: *Tamen*</note> is a limiting and restrictive word. *Marius Antoninus, 1. Resolution 27, number 6; Reference 102, number 11.* It introduces a manner and a condition. *Law 1, Reference 51, number 4.*

9. **Now, now as then, and then as now.** <note>original: *Jezt, jezt alsdann, und dann als jezt*</note> Now as if from then <note>original: *Nunc pro ut ex tunc*</note>.

This Clause is of such importance that even if something contrary exists, it is not only considered pure and referring to the present time; but it is even referred to the future time. *Gloss on Clement 1, on the granting of prebends & on the chapter "how it may be" & on the chapter "desiring," on elections, book 6.* Baldus *in the single chapter, number 16 & following, on the Military Vassal who is defiant.* Philippus Corneus *counsel 278, number 14, volume 3.* Alexander *counsel 111, number 27, volume 6.* Cothman *counsel 17, number 101 & following, volume 1.* Negusantius *on pledges & mortgages, member 2, part 2, number 5.* See Tuschus *letter D, conclusion 279.* Thomingius *volume 1, counsel 2, number 26, etc.* See Fontanella *on antenuptial pacts, part 1, folio 82.*

The word *now* <note>original: *nunc*</note>, is of the present time, Baldus *in the authentic "contra," number 1, Code on the Trebellianic Decree* & denotes the present beginning of an obligation. Alexander *in the law "of this kind," law 2, number 3, Digest on verbal obligations.* Felinus *in the chapter "although the cause," in note 6 on evidence.*

### ADDITION.

The effect of the Clause *From now as if from then.* Klock *counsel 7, number 281 following.* The effect of the Clause *from now as if from then* in a possessory agreement. Klock *volume 2, counsel 28, number 2, 3.* The Clause *While matters remain the same* <note>original: *Rebus sic stantibus*—a principle that a contract is only binding as long as the circumstances remain essentially the same.</note> is believed to be inherent in all acts & dispositions. Carpzov *decision 294, number 21.* The Clause *While matters stand so* is limited in two ways. *Acts of Lindau page 27 at the end.* The Clause *While matters remain the same* is understood in all Dispositions. Klock *volume 3, counsel 109, number 53.* even in testaments *number 54, & counsel 110, number 19, & counsel 138, number 6, & counsel 142, number 32.* Betrothals of the present are considered contracted through the words: **Now, herewith.** <note>original: *Jezt, hiermit*</note> Lord Christoph Philipp Richter *part 2, counsel 8, number 19, folio 37.* Sotus *4, distinction 17, question 2, article 1.* **As they now wish to have promised their daughter to you herewith, so that you and no other shall have her.** <note>original: *Als wollen sie euch nun jezt hiermit ihre Tochter zugesagt haben, daß ihr und kein ander sie haben sollet*</note> Concerning the Clause *while things remain in the same state.* Carpzov *Decision 123, number 25.* Nicolaus Myler *on the Princes & States of the Empire, chapter 49, page 437.*
