10. **To him. To him.** <note>original German: *Ihme*; original Latin: *Ipsi*</note>

For a full understanding of the question: Whether an act, in which the word *to him* <note>original: *ipsi*</note> is applied, is personal, so that it passes to the heirs: Noalis sets out several cases *on transmission, case 28, folio 355.* The first is in contracts, and then the word *to him* does not stand restrictively, but only descriptively, and therefore it does not hinder transmission; but contracts, notwithstanding the word *to him*, pass to the heirs. *Law "that stipulation," section "But just as," at the end, Digest on verbal obligations; law "if necessary," section "on selling," Digest on actions regarding pledges.* Mantica *on tacit & ambiguous agreements, book 3, title 1, number 40.* Because everyone is presumed to look out and provide for his heir as for himself, which presumption is not removed by the word *to himself* <note>original: *sibi*</note>, because it is a strong presumption proceeding from natural feelings, not admitting contrary proof, Menochius *on presumptions, book 1, question 3, number 5.* Baldus *in the rubric of the Code on evidence, number 6, verse "example."*

The second case is in another disposition, and then it is either a simple grant or a prohibition: If a simple grant, the word *to himself* does not stand restrictively, but descriptively; and it passes to the heirs: Because the addition of a person in a grant naturally transmissible to heirs does not make the grant itself personal and non-transmissible, Jason *in the law "so stipulated," number 15, Digest on verbal obligations.* Thus we see that these words: *I will give you the keys to the kingdom of heaven*, do not exclude the successors of Peter, see Baldus *in the chapter "per," number 3, on the office of a delegate.* Jason *in law 1, number 30, Digest on the office of his [the delegate].* Ruland *counsel 55, number 54 & following, book 3.*

It is declared (1.) because just as this word *to himself*, applied in a grant transmissible to heirs, does not make the grant itself persona-

<summary>This page discusses the legal privileges and origins of the Jesuits and the Knights of Jesus Christ, followed by a detailed legal analysis of timing clauses like "now as then" and the transmissibility of rights to heirs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of specific phrasing in grants and prohibitions, moving from the definition of personal rights to the social and legal implications of modes of address and the etymology of regional place names.</meta>

...personal, and not transmissible, and thus it does not alter the nature of the principal act: so it would work much less in the reverse if it were applied in a non-transitory grant—for instance, where the specific skill of a person was chosen, or in an act inherent to a person, or otherwise not transferable to heirs.

It is declared (2) to proceed in the pure terms of the word **to him** <note>original: *ipsi*; the Latin dative pronoun used to specify a particular recipient</note>; it is otherwise if it should appear from elsewhere that the grant is personal, which can appear through conjectures, some of which Menochius <note>Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), a prominent Italian jurist known for his work on legal presumptions</note> recites in *Presumptions*, Book 3, presumption 103.

It is declared (3) in a prohibitory disposition; and then if the prohibition itself is made concerning those things which are of a permitted kind, the word **to him** added in the prohibition stands restrictively and is personal, so that the prohibition does not pass to others. See Curtius Senior, Counsel 50; Menochius, Counsel 82, number 158; Tiraquellus <note>André Tiraqueau (1488–1558), a French jurist specializing in customary law</note> in *On Contractual Retraction*, section 1, glossary 6, number 25. To these add Jason in the law *filius f. § Divi*, number 151, *Digest: On Legacies 1*; and in the law *qui filium § in omni*, number 17, *Digest: On Acquiring Inheritance*; Baldus, Counsel 304, number 1, book 5. The reason is: because since in the category of permitted things all are understood to be permitted which are not specifically found to be prohibited, as per the law *mutus § cum quaeritur*, *Digest: On Procurators*, therefore a prohibition is not extended beyond the prohibited person. See the law *si vero § de viro*, *Digest: On the Dissolution of Marriage*.

The fourth case is in a prohibition made concerning those things which are of a prohibited kind, such as in the prohibition of alienating <note>To "alienate" in a legal sense means to transfer ownership of property to another.</note> trusts, fiefs, Church goods, and similar non-alienable things. In such a case, the word **to him**, contained in the final prohibition by a person, is not judged to revoke the primary prohibition of the law, which therefore remains in its strength and passes to others: because where a double prohibition exists, if one is removed, the other does not cease. See the law *si domus*, *Digest: On Urban Servitudes*; *Institutes: On Marriages*, section on affinity; Menochius, Counsel 36, number 36; Oldradus, Counsel 268, number 2.

The word **TO HIM** <note>original: *IPSI*</note> used in place of "his." Chapter 3, *Decretals: On Testaments*.

## 12. In.

The preposition **In** denotes "insideness," *Digest: On Rivers*, section *in flumine*; *Institutes: On the Division of Things*, section *cum in sua*; and in the very place itself, the text is express in law 1, section *ne quid*, *Digest: Lest anything be done in a public place*, where it is said that what is done on the bank is not said to be done "in the river," especially when it is joined to the ablative case; then it signifies place, seat, and situation. Baldus in the rubric *On the Dissolution of Marriage*, number 3. Riminaldi Junior, Counsel 388, number 32. Nizolius, *Allegations* 16, number 12.

And it should be noted that "at" <note>original: *am*</note> is one thing, and "in" is another; for example, if we say: **at this city**, or **in this city**. "At" or "near" can also extend itself to neighboring places.

# ADDITION.

**Before or upon reaching the legal years.** Here the opposition is not between the words "before" and "in the attainment of puberty": which denote movement toward a limit and the proximity of the limit, as if one said, while he properly reaches that age. For the word **While** <note>original: *Dum*</note> denotes an act while it is in the very process of being done and perfected. A text and example of a clearly similar form is contained in law *si quis* 7, section 2, *Digest: On the Jurisdiction of All Judges*, where it says, "but if while it is proposed, or before the proposal." Therefore the meaning is: if before the civilly determined puberty, or very near to puberty. See section 9, where it says: "that he who is near puberty should have the same status in law." *Institutes: On Useless Stipulations*.

**In, within, to sit in and under the authority of a Prince.** Master Speidel in *Notables*. The word **in** implies a condition. Marius Antoninus, *Roman Questions*, book 2, reform 31, number 3. To be "in" a territory and "of" a territory are different things. Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, chapter 2, number 241 and following.

### 14. Clause: In the best form and measure.

-> Clause: In every better way <note>original: *omni meliori modo*</note>. <-

This clause, **in every better way**, when found in legal instruments or elsewhere, is usually of great significance. For it ensures that the act is upheld in whatever way it can be. Baldus and Imola <note>Famous medieval commentators on Roman law</note> in the law *cum pater*, section *filius* <note>Digest 31.1.77.25</note>, say that if it is placed in a will, it has the same power as a "Codicillary Clause" <note>A provision that allows a document to remain valid as a codicil even if it fails to meet the stricter requirements of a formal will</note>, and it makes the will valid in whatever way possible. See Alexander, counsel 112, volume 3; Socinus, counsel 66, number 7 and following, volume 3; Decius, counsel 14, number 3, and counsel 77, number 4; Gozadinus, counsel 46, number 26, and counsel 78, number 5; Durandus on *Testamentary Acts*, title 11, caution 1, number 2; Menochius, *Arbitrary Judgments*, book 1, question 47.

-> ADDITION. <-

Regarding the clause **in every better way**, see Barbosa on *Clauses*, 95; Berlich, part 3, conclusion 15, number 59; Marius Antoninus, 2nd *Various Resolutions*, 49, number 8; and the Lord Ludwig on *Last Wills*, page 474 at the end; Schwanman, *Processes*, book 1, chapter 1, number 12 at the end; Klock, volume 2, counsel 2, number 16.

For a thorough examination of these words, consult the *Marburg Counsels*, volume 3, counsel 28, number 61, and the *Forum of Protestations*, page 307 at the end and following.

### 15. Informative Process. <note>original: *Processus informativus*</note>

In an **Informative Process**, justice is administered by the "Royal Hand" <note>the sovereign's direct authority</note>, as it was before formal legal actions were invented; the technicalities of Civil Law actions are not scrutinized. See Antonio Petra on the *Power of the Prince*, chapter 25, limitation 6, number 23.

---

### 16. Within. <note>original: *Intra*</note>

The word **Within** <note>original: *Intra*</note> includes only its endpoints and excludes those things that are outside, according to Socinus, counsel 211, at the beginning of book 2. If a deadline is assigned for doing something "within ten days," that act can be performed on any day of those said ten days, but not afterward; thus, it includes the endpoints and excludes those outside. Geminianus, counsel 121, number 3; add Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, title D, conclusion 299, where at number 3 he says that wherever the word **Within** signifies time, such a word includes all the designated time, according to the chapter *frequens* in the *Sixth Book of Decretals*.

-> ADDITION. <-

**Within** is an inclusive word, Berlich, 2nd conclusion 49, number 43. How the voice **Within** is to be understood, see Berlich.

### 17. Holder of this Letter. <note>original: "Innhaber diß Briefs"; Latin: "Possessor instrumenti"</note>

By these words, any third-party possessor is understood, or anyone holding these letters or writings, whether by title of purchase, exchange, pledge, or gift, or held by permission <note>The legal term "precario" refers to something held by the favor or permission of another, revocable at will</note> or in any other way obtained, possessed, or held from the heirs and the heirs of the heirs. This is according to the law *habere 188* where the Doctors of Law comment on the *Digest* regarding the significance of words, and the law regarding stipulations where Duarenus comments on the *Digest* regarding verbal obligations. This is especially true since the word *Innhabern* <note>German: "Holder"</note> corresponds to the words *detentator* <note>One who physically holds an object</note> and *detinere* <note>To detain or hold back</note>. To detain, moreover, is to possess, or to be in possession, or even to occupy, to hold by permission, or simply to be present upon the property. See Johannes Goddaeus among the *Marburg Consultations*, volume 1, number 110; Zasius on the law of possession in the *Digest*; and the various imperial constitutions regarding maternal goods and the law of dowries.

---

->ADDITION.<-

<margin>Lord Tabor, to whom this matter pertains. See the law on credited things, i.e., to the heir or the possessor of goods; or generally "to any faithful holder of the letter" <note>original: "getreuen Briefs Innhaber"</note>. Add Zorer, part 2, question 20, number 7073, and those cited there.</margin>

*Detentator* <note>The Detainer</note>. *Detentio* <note>Detention</note> is taken in two ways in the Laws. 1. Generally, such that it includes both possession properly so-called and its opposite form, which lacks a specific name and is called "naked detention" <note>Physical holding without legal claim</note>; hence it happens that "to hold" sometimes means "to possess." 2. Specifically, for that type of detention alone which is not considered possession in the eyes of the law. See Lord Biccius in his *Golden Rules*, section 3, thesis 150, letter EE. Even if a debtor in a bond <note>A formal legal promise to pay</note> promises that he will pay "to any good-faith possessor and detainer" <note>original: "b. f. possessori & detentatori"</note>—that is, "to any faithful holder of the letter"—he is nevertheless not bound to do so if the transfer <note>The assignment of the debt</note> is suspicious. See Thomas Trivisanus, *Venetian Decisions*, 42, number 17; Guido Papa, decision 567; and Berlichius, part 1, decision 32.

Regarding these words, see the *Marburg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 28, number 109.

### 18. Holder of the Principality or County. <note>original: "Innhavern des Fürstenthums oder Grafschafft"</note>

<margin>The power to ennoble is not sufficient unless the will to ennoble is also present. Charles Molinaeis on the law regarding verbal obligations. Alexander of Lodi on the treatise of analogy. Fiefs can be given by such lords even without nobility, and nobility can be granted without fiefs. Vultejus, on fiefs, chapter 8. From this it is thought to happen that sometimes someone is invested by the Emperor with a Duchy or County,</margin>

<column-break/>

as the **Holder of the Principality or County**, and yet he is not a Duke or a Count. See Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 2, question 2, number 9, and the *Subscriptions of the Imperial Recesses* <note>The official resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

The words produced so far and those following are by Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, 1, thesis 6, letter b. According to the dictates of our feudal law, if the Emperor or another endowed with the power of ennobling grants someone a fief that is noble by custom—such as a Duchy, County, or Barony—in case of doubt, he is also judged to have had the will to confer nobility. See the book on who is called a Duke; Mascardus *On Evidence*; Vultejus; Rosenthal; and Gail *On Imperial Arrests*.

### 19. Inquisition. <note>Investigation or Inquiry</note>

<margin>Lord Speidel in his *Notables*.</margin>

Regarding the "most general investigation" <note>Latin: "inquisitione generalissima"</note> used in villages or other places, commonly called a **House-search** <note>original: "Haus-suchung"</note>, to which species of jurisdiction they belong. See Berlichius, *Decision 20*.

An investigation properly so-called cannot be said to exist when it is only a certain preparatory information leading toward a formal inquisition. Berlichius, number 20. Or at least it is called a "most general investigation" (number 3), for it is done at least to track down delinquents, not to punish them (number 5).

---

->ADDITION.<-

Bonincontrus of Bologna, son of Lord Johannes Andreas, wrote the *Treatise on Accusations and Inquisitions* (Venice, 1496), which is kept in the Nuremberg Library <note>original: "Bibliotheca Norica"</note>. Regarding an Inquisitor who lies, see Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 42. Regarding the **Spanish Inquisition**, see the same chapter 42, number 3. Regarding a suspect who lies, see chapter 43. On "What are called Inquisitors," see the *Tripartite Work of Hungarian National Law*, part 3, title 27. An uncertain investigation is not to be admitted at all but regarded as void: Barbosa, book 9, chapter 67. A true confession does not supply a defect in the investigation (Axiom 3). A denunciation <note>A formal report of a crime</note> does not substitute for an investigation (Axiom 4). A copy of the evidence with a delay for clearing oneself must be given to the suspect before torture. See Christoph Philipp Richter, part 6, consultation 31.

For an investigation to be legitimate, four things are required: (1) that the crime be great and damaging; (2) that it be preceded by ill-repute, public rumor, and that evidence be present (Barbosa); (3) that the circumstances be well-weighed; (4) that the judge investigates crimes committed within the last twenty years. See Lord Biccius in his *Golden Rules*, section 5, thesis 178. Investigation takes the place of an accusation. For the same solemnity is required in an investigation as in an accusation.

### 20. Filing the Records. <note>original: "Inrotulation. Inrotulatio actorum."</note>

The person under inquiry must be summoned for the **filing of the records** <note>The "Inrotulatio" refers to the official gathering, binding, and indexing of legal documents into a "roll" or file for the court’s review</note>. Oldekop in the treatise against Carpzov, question 7, page 128 and following. For the reasoning behind the filing of records, see pages 132 and following. The filing of records in criminal cases requires the trust of the judge. See the same author in *Criminal Observations*, page 35, and what sorts of precautions lawyers should take on page 36.
See the **1654 Renewed Imperial Court Council Ordinance**, title 3, paragraph beginning with "whenever also" <note>original: "wann auch"</note>.
The parties must be present and assist in the filing of the records, lest a lawyer who is alone with the judge might suggest something to the judge, or slip some writing into the records that was not previously exhibited in the court. Berlichius, conclusion 48, number 31, and the citations there from the *Speculator* <note>A common nickname for the legal scholar Guillaume Durand</note>.
Much depends on the filing, collation <note>The process of comparing copies against original documents to ensure accuracy</note>, and arrangement of the records; therefore, it is well worth the effort for the party or the lawyer to be present themselves and not trust this to a common, inexperienced **clerk** <term>sollicitatori</term>. For an incorrect or biased collation can easily harm someone in the main case or their legal rights. Suttinger in observation 77, number 1. Much time is often lost through incorrect collation (number 2). What must be observed during collation is found in numbers 3, 4, 5, and 6. If a party has introduced unauthorized innovations, they can be properly punished (numbers 7 and 8). The process of collation must be submitted to the chancery sealed by both parties or their lawyers (number 9). What is to be brought to the collation by virtue of the office <note>Latin: "ex officio"</note> is in number 10. A caution for the lawyer, so that he may request the authentic publications at the right time (number 11). Once the collated process is taken up by the **dispatcher** <term>expeditore</term>, the opposing party is no longer admitted to further action without a **restoration to the original state** <note>Latin: "restitutio in integrum"; a legal remedy to restore a party to their position before a specific legal event occurred</note> (number 12). The Protonotary of the Imperial Court Council shall record with special diligence in the protocol what happened during the registration of the acts, and after the filing is completed, take the records and deliver them to the registry. So that the **refererees** <note>The officials who report on the case to the higher judges</note> are not identified through such filing of writings or in any other way, nothing should be noted in the records in their handwriting, nor should any letters be marked in the margins. Imperial Court Council Ordinance, title 3, paragraph "whenever also" and following.

### 21. Closing a Matter. <note>original: "In Sachen beschliessen."</note>

When a matter is set for a decision—specifically regarding an **interlocutory** <note>A temporary or provisional decision made during a trial before the final judgment</note> point—the word "submitted" is used; but in **definitive** <note>The final judgment that ends the case</note> matters, it is "concluded" <note>German: "beschlossen"</note>.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

Lord Doctor Biccius repeats the same words in *Aureis*, section 5, thesis 141, at the end. Although the word "Definitive" is not used in the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Justinian's Roman Law</note>, it occurs quite often in the *Code*: law 3 and 11, *regarding sentences and interlocutory matters*; law 16, *regarding judgments and titles*; and *as long as the lawsuit is pending or after a challenge*. Lord Biccius in *Aureis*, section 5, thesis 143, at the end.

### 22. Instance. <note>original: "Instantia."</note>

**Instance** <note>In legal terms, this refers to the ongoing status or "life" of a lawsuit while it is active in court</note> is properly nothing other than the connection and continuation of the process brought before the court, and by that very fact it differs from the **Action** <note>The legal right to sue</note> as a matter of legal pursuit: or it is the exercise of the trial from the **joinder of issue** <note>original: "litis contestatio"; the point where the parties formally agree on the matter to be decided</note> until the sentence. Sichard on the law *properandum*, number 3, in the Code *regarding Judgments*, and in law 4, number 4, *regarding pacts*. This stands in direct opposition to the lawsuit or the principal cause itself. Law *post edictum* 73, paragraph *circumducto*, in the Digest *regarding Judgments*. But see Ziegler in *Common Conclusions on Golden Practice*, in the prelude *regarding instance*, number 2 and following.
And here it must be noted that an instance begun with any litigant passes to the heirs of that same litigant both **actively** <note>The right to sue</note> and **passively** <note>The liability to be sued</note>: thus the instance itself must be pursued in the same state in which it was found with the deceased. That it passes to them actively, we have the text in the law *si operarum* (Digest *on the works of freedmen*) and the law *si petitor* (Digest *on judgments*); and that it passes against them passively is likewise provided for in the law *si cum hoc* (Digest *on bail*), where Bartolus (number 2), Angelus, and Paulus de Castro (number 3) comment on the law *servus* (Digest *regarding those marked with infamy*).
Moreover, an instance is said to have begun for this purpose not only through the joinder of issue, but also through the provision of security for the payment of the judgment. Law *si defunctus* (Digest *on procurators*), and by that text Paulus de Castro in the said law *si cum Homine*, number 3, *on bail*; and even by the summons alone. Baldus on law 1, number 2, in the Code *on death while an appeal is pending*; and there is text in the chapter *gratum* (*on the office of legates*) and the chapter *proposuisti* (*on competent forums*). Nicolaus Noalis in the treatise *on transmissions*, chapter 55, number 2, where in the following sections he provides several expansions and restrictions of this conclusion.
Whether the instance perishes when the judge is changed, see Modestinus Pistoris, part 2, question 96. Likewise, whether an instance started by the possessor of an **entailed estate** <note>original: "Majoratus"; an estate that must be passed whole to the eldest son</note> passes to the successor? Castillo, *Controversies*, book 2, chapter 9.

Lord Christoph Philipp Richter, part 1, chapter 48, number 25 and following, page 308. After an instance has been established, it cannot be renounced unless the opposing party consents (part 1, chapter 54, number 17, page 371). Instance in civil cases is continued in the heirs. Carpzov, decision 29, number 12. Instance is transmitted by operation of law to the heirs; see the same author, decision 36, number 12. Under common law, an instance begins from the **care/guardianship** <note>original: "Curatione"</note>. Klock, consultation 41, number 72. A **creditor** <note>the person to whom money is owed</note> does not immediately lose the right to an **obligation** <note>a legal debt or duty</note> due to the loss of a **Legal Instrument** or **Contract** <note>original: *Syngraphæ*; a signed written agreement</note>. ### 24. Insul. Island.

Lord Gryphiander wrote a most absolute treatise on **Islands**. And there, in chapter 2, he defines an **Island** as land enclosed on all sides by water. Historians and poets, whom he cites there, use this description. Furthermore, I derive the origin of the word *Eyland* <note>German for island</note>, that is, Island, from the Hebrew *Ai*, which means Island.

Indeed, all islands are produced either by **nature** or by **human work**. The former are either perpetual, created together with the beginning of the World, or they arose afterward, which Baldus (a future Jurist) calls "accidental" in law 17, regarding legacies 3. And these are born either slowly and successively, or by some sudden force. Bartolus attributes the former to Divine power and the latter to fortuitous chance. It is simpler for us to say that Islands are either **native** (natural), **fortuitous** (accidental), or **man-made**. Concerning all of these, see Gryphiander in the cited place, chapter 5 and following. A **Native Island** or natural island is one which nature has produced in its accustomed way of acting, or whose generation is from nature. Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, book 7, chapter 7. Whether islands have existed since they were created at the beginning of the world is taught by Gryphiander in the aforementioned treatise, chapter 5, number 4 and following. Concerning the islands of the **Rhine**, see the Constitution of Emperor Adolph with Freher’s Commentary.

**Fortuitous islands**, which are produced by the impulse of another and indeed more violent cause, also proceed from nature, but from a nature "angry and as if disturbed." Law 15, *On Inofficious Wills*. Thus, Aristotle in *Rhetoric*, book 1, chapter 10, says those things happen by nature whose cause is in themselves or follows an order. For they happen in the same way either always or for the most part. But those things which are "beyond nature," their cause seems to be fortuitous. Gryphiander, chapter 7, from the beginning. Hence the Romans called "fortuitous" those things which had no cause, nor any sign as to why they would happen. Cicero, *On Divination*, book 2, argument § 39. *Institutes, On the Division of Things*. One ought to seek the outcomes of these things rather than their causes. Cicero, *On Divination*, book 1. And although native and fortuitous islands are distinguished from one another subtly; nevertheless, in a broad sense <note>original: *ἐν πλάτει* (en platei); Greek for "broadly speaking"</note> they are encompassed under one common name, and are opposed to **artificial** or man-made ones. Law 20, *On Rural Servitudes*; law 28, *On Urban Servitudes*; law 1, § 10 and 15, *On Rainwater*. Thus nature and art are opposites. Aristotle, in the beginning of *Mechanical Questions*: nature and culture.

To whom newly formed islands <note>original: *Insulæ de novo natæ*</note> belong is a matter of great doubt among legal scholars. Even in the body of the law itself <note>referring to the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the collection of Roman laws</note>, one finds almost contradictory and conflicting texts. Generally, it is concluded that when an island forms in a navigable and strong flowing river, the high authority or Lord of the River possesses only the **jurisdiction** <note>legal authority</note> or command over it, while the **utility**—such as grass, pasture, and the like—belongs to those private individuals who own estates or rights on both banks. This is clearly taught by Peregrinus, *On the Rights of the Treasury*, Book 8, Number 61 and following; Andreas Schæffer, Question 17, Part 2; Heigius, Part 2, final question; Hartmann Pistor, Book 4, Question 17; and Tuschus under the word *Insula*.

Others hold a contrary opinion, as seen especially in Johann Gryphiander’s excellent treatise *On Islands*, Chapters 11, 17, and following. These scholars argue that such islands or river-islands <note>original: *Werder*</note> do not belong to those who have estates or rights on the banks, but rather belong entirely and by full right <note>original: *pleno jure*</note> to the high authority or **Lord of the Territory** who has all-encompassing jurisdiction on both banks and in the river, as a **regal** <note>a royal or sovereign right</note> and fluvial benefit. The precedents of the Imperial Chamber Court <note>original: *Cameralia Præjudicia*</note> also lean this way, as cited in Johann Thileman of Benignus, *Collection*, Part 2, Decision 2, Volume 7; and Johann Forster, *On Judicial Procedure*, Chapter 15; Sixtinus, *On Regalia*, Book 2, Chapter 3, Number 27.

Regarding this, I hold the first view to be closer to the truth of **Written Law**, but the second opinion to be closer to the **customs and traditions of Germany**. See Noë Meurer, *On Water Law*, Part 1, Number 8, and throughout Part 2. However, one must take careful note of: (1) Whether the island emerged on its own or was caused by a man-made structure. (2) Whether it arose gradually or appeared suddenly after a great flood. (3) Whether the bank on one or both sides was eaten away by the water and pushed back, so that the island formed to the detriment of those who had estates and pastures there. Primarily and fourthly (4), one must diligently look to the established tradition on the **Danube** and other local circumstances.

### 25. Summoning to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. <note>An appeal to the Final Judgment of God when earthly justice is denied.</note> *Appeal to Judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.*

### ADDITION.

Death does not always follow such a summons. <note>original: "Auf ſolche Ladung erfolgt nicht allzeit der Tod."</note> Zeiller, century 4, question 18, page 81.

One who is unjustly oppressed can appeal to the tribunal of God, and examples prove that such an appeal has, as it were, been accepted by God. Regarding Ferdinand IV, King of Spain, Fulgosus reports in book 1, chapter 6, that when he was summoned to the tribunal of God by two knights (whom he had condemned as guilty of high treason based on false accusations and envy, ordering them to be thrown headlong from a very high tower), he died on that very day, just when he was thought to be sleeping. The same Fulgosus in the cited place tells of a certain Neapolitan Templar in Bordeaux who was condemned to the fire. Seeing Pope Clement and the King of France, Philip the Fair, in a window, he broke out in a loud voice with these words: *“Most cruel, most merciful tyrant <note>referring ironically to the Pope</note>, since there is no longer anyone left among mortals to whom I can appeal for the heavy burden with which you unjustly afflict me, I appeal to the just Judge, Christ my Redeemer. I call you before His tribunal, together with King Philip, so that within a year and a day you both appear there, where I shall set forth my case and justice shall be administered without wicked favor.”* And within that time, *Clement* was suddenly seized by death, and not long after *Philip* also perished. Besold, *On Appeals, chapter 2, section 1, 3.* A similar example from Olaus Magnus regarding Johann Turson is reported by Doctor Dannhauer in the *Evangelical Memorial*, folio 880. What the Valley of Jehoshaphat is otherwise called, where it is located, and what kind of graveyard was there is discussed by Doctor Dannhauer in the cited treatise, page 879.

This expression is discussed in *Joel, chapter 3, at the beginning*, where Osiander and Camerarius comment in *Leisure Hours, part 3, chapter 38*, where they cite Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrariness, question case 388*; Julius Clarus, *5th Sentences, question 83, number 7*; *Parties in Litigation, book 1, chapter 1, number 38*; Besold in *Politics, book 2, final chapter, number 55*, and *On Punishments, folio 131*; Conrad Dieterich *on the Wisdom of Solomon, volume 1, sermon 2, folio 26*; Doctor Rümelin *on the Golden Bull, part 2, dissertation 2, corollary 2*; Besold, *On Caring for the Republic, final chapter, section 10 at the end*. Regarding the summons to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, see the extensive account by Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Great Theatre of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, iii. 197. page 357, and the three following pages.

### 26. Interdict.
<term>Interdictum: A legal decree or prohibition issued by a court, often to stop an action or protect a status quo.</term>

Mr. Speidel in his *Notable Matters* under this word.

### ADDITION.

Interdicts are subject to the court in the place where the property is located. <note>original: "in loco rei ſitæ"</note> Thus Ummius in *On Legal Process*, page 113; whether they are also in the place of residence <note>domicile</note> is discussed there and on the following pages.

Cicero was condemned to exile by Crassus, Caesar, and Pompey. However, his property was confiscated, his houses were razed to the ground as if he were an enemy, and the area where they stood was consecrated as a temple to Liberty. He was ordered to be 468 miles away from Rome. Furthermore, an edict was issued that if he came within those boundaries, both he and those who received 

<column-break/>

him could be killed by anyone with impunity. Dio Cassius, book 38 of *Roman History*. Petrus Gregorius in the *System of Universal Law*, book 31, chapter 6, number 16. Saint Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, treats the Interdict at folio 14, folio 338. Regarding the Ecclesiastical Interdict <note>a censure excluding the faithful from certain spiritual goods</note>, see Johannes Galderinus of Bologna, folio 14, folio 225; Johannes de Lignano of Milan, folio 14, folio 335; Nicolaus Pulvæus the Frenchman, volume 14, folio 333. On the interdict "as you possess" <note>original: "uti poſſidetis"—a decree to protect current possession of property</note>, see Virginius de Boccatiis of Cingulo, volume 3, part 2, folio 100. Regarding the Interdict of a City, castle, or other place, and concerning those things which ought to be observed within it, see Johannes Andreae of Bologna, volume 14, folio 344.

A person may be barred <note>interdicted</note> from the practice of law <note>original: "Advocatione"</note> either for a time or forever, although no one can be perpetually prohibited from using their own skill. Pacius, *Analysis of the Code, page 161, number 10.* If a judge simply forbids someone from pleading cases, and neither expresses that he prohibits it forever nor defines a certain time for the prohibition, the prohibition is understood to be made for a "long time," that is, ten years. *Number 11.* An interdiction sometimes includes a command that one should not leave a certain place or one's own house—as in the final law under the title *On Interdicts and Religious Matters*—or the house of another, when we say, "to grant house arrest" <note>original German/French: "bailler Pareſtenſa maiſon, ou ailleurs"</note>. Petrus Gregorius in *System of Universal Law, book 31, chapter 6, number 16.*

### 27. Interest.
<term>Interesse: In this context, it refers to "legal interest" or "damages"—the compensation for loss or the profit one failed to make due to another's breach of contract or delay.</term>

See Bolognetus on title 3, *On Fruits and Interest*. How interest may be sought and proven due to delay <note>original: "ex mora"</note>, see Pfeil, *Counsel 60*; Rosacorb, *Practical Observations, chapter 55.* Interest for delay cannot be sought if the creditor has accepted the principal amount without protest. <note>original: "ohne Proteſtation, das Hauptgut angenommen"</note> Schæffer, 1st section, question 40. Regarding interest for lost profit <note>term: "lucri ceſſantis"</note> and actual loss sustained <note>term: "damni emergentis"</note>, when it can be sought and when it is called "certain," see Castillo, book 2, chapter 1. Regarding interest, for which the seller's mere words should be believed, see Barschamp, *On Clauses, chapter 3, section 3*. On Interest and the difference between simple usury and Interest, its just and allowed petition, as well as its proof, see below in a certain "Counsel" inserted under the word *Usury* <note>original: "Wucher"</note>, where it is taught in many places when it is permitted to take more than 5 up to 12 or 15 out of 100 florins.

### ADDITION.

Interest can be defined as the just utility centered on the thing itself which is being discussed, which we would have had if the adversary had not caused damage or had not cut off our profit. *Law 13, Digest: That a matter is held as ratified.* Add Zorer, *part 1, question 5, number 451.* However, although the extent of someone's interest consists more in fact than in law, and is uncertain and difficult to prove (*ibid. number 454*; Barbosa, *book 8, chapter 76, axiom 4*), Justinian nevertheless, in the *Unique Law, Code: Concerning that which is of interest*, set a certain limit <note>taxation</note>, separating "certain" cases from "uncertain" ones—that is, those which have a fixed quantity or nature, or those which do not. In certain cases, he forbids this "interest" from exceeding double the amount <note>of the original value</note>; that is, that it be no more than as much again as the principal matter...

In uncertain cases, he left it to the discretion of the judge to estimate how much it truly matters to the plaintiff, because only that which is of interest enters into the obligation; and therefore, there is no "single" amount here by which a "double" amount could be established. See the accurate discussion by Doctor Biccius in *Golden Sections, Section 5, Thesis 149, KK.* Pacius explains at length which cases are certain or uncertain in *Analysis of the Code, on the sentence which for that, number 3.* Interest, regarding the nature of things, is certain, according to Barbosa, *book 9, chapter 76, axiom 3.* Interest is sometimes called a penalty, as in Pacius, *On Locations, number 8.* It is called a penalty in relation to the matter or the opponent, whose action is punished by this payment; however, in relation to the plaintiff, it is not a penalty but the pursuit of the thing and indemnity <note>Compensation for loss or damage</note>. Thus, it is not surprising that "that which is of interest" is sometimes called a penalty, and sometimes a penalty is contrasted with it. See Doctor Cob. on *law 24, regarding Rules of Law.*

Interest is lawfully demanded and has been substituted in the place of usury <note>The practice of lending money at high interest; here, "interesse" is a legal way to compensate for loss without violating anti-usury laws</note>, Zorer, *part 1, question 12, number 1002.* Whether and when interest ought to be remitted, see *question 1, number 107 and following. Also question 8, number 601 and 3 following. Also question 14, number 1221.* On what constitutes extrinsic interest and intrinsic interest, see Petrus Gregorius in *System of Universal Law, book 21, chapter 10, number 10.* If the interest ceases, the plaintiff is not heard, Barbosa *book 9, chapter 76, axiom 8.* Caspar Gaballinus of Cingulo wrote a singular treatise on "that which is of interest" <note>original: "De eo quod interest"</note>.

On interest regarding lost profit <note>original: "lucri cessantis"</note> and emerging damage <note>original: "damni emergentis"</note>, see Johann de Castillo, *part 2, Legal Controversies, chapter 1.* Doctor Speidel in *Collection of Legal Questions, under this word.*

### 29. Interim-Measures. Provisional remedy.

These are so named when it is asked what must be done in the meantime (*interim*) while the principal case (which is said to require a deeper investigation) is being expedited. These are judged based on the nature of a quasi-momentary possessory or provisional decree, by which the principal business or lawsuit is not prejudiced <note>The provisional ruling does not decide the final outcome of the main case</note>.

<column-break/>

Thus Gailius also writes in *book 1, observation 5, number 3* that the Spanish call the process of litigious possession an *Interim*, the French call it *Recre-dentiam* <note>Recredence</note>, the Belgians call it a *Provisional Remedy*, and others call it an *Informative Process*. Budæus, in his *Pandects on the final law of the origin of law*, calls it a "Vindicatory Lawsuit."

However, although an Arbiter may not grant a provision, but requires the service of a Judge, as per *the Law: "The Praetor says," paragraph 1, Digest on the right of deliberating.* Rebuffus, *Treatise on Provisional Sentences, in the preface, number 17.*

There is no doubt, however, that it can be expressly agreed in an Arbitration that the arbiter may pronounce and bring sentence upon this matter.

Likewise, a debtor is condemned by way of provision to the payment of a pension which he seeks to delay because of a lawsuit, Rebuffus, *in the same place, number 125.*

And when the case concerns the rescission of a contract, in the meantime a party is condemned by provision—the one seeking the contract to be rescinded—to maintain the contract, provided security is given for what is received in the meantime while the suit over the rescission is pending, Rebuffus, *ibid, number 132.* He also teaches at *number 134* that a provision should not be granted through which the entire principal matter would be decided.

Similarly, in the matter of litigious possession, any possessor is to be maintained in their possession or quasi-possession, Grævus, *conclusion 5, number 6.*

### 30. Intervention. Interventio.

**Regarding Intervention**, see Ruland in his commentary on Ferrarius Montanus, *Process, folio 3 and following.*

### ADDITION.

The case of a third party intervening, whose interest is asserted, is summary <note>A simplified, faster legal procedure</note>, and serves to impede the execution of a judged matter, Gailius, *book 1, observation 69, number 4 and observation 67, number 9.* Mynsinger, *century 2, observation 1.* Rittershufius in *Novels, page 493.* A woman can intervene for a stranger, but not for her husband, Rittershufius, *cited place, page 155, number 9.* Whether and to what extent intervention has a place, see Berlichius, *book 1, conclusion 25, throughout.* No one can intervene except the one whose interest is at stake, Ilico Ummius in *Process, page 444 (my edition).* What intervention signifies, see the same author, *pages 442–443*, and who is able to intervene, *page 442.* In which cases intervention has a place, *page 446.*

A third party intervening hinders the Execution, Zahn, *On Lies, book 2, chapter 45, number 2.* If the intervening party lies, what penalty they deserve, *ibid, number 3, and those cited there:* Francesco Marci, Surdus, Hond., Boër, Grævus, and others.

On intervention in the matter of a pledge <note>original: "causa pignorationis"</note>, Symph. Gylman, *volume 2, folio 119.* When a third party intervening is to be admitted to the case, Gailius, *book 1, observation 71.* Symph. Gylman, *volume 2, part 1, page 1.*

An intervening third party, if they knew the case was being argued and allowed another to act, prejudices themselves <note>They lose the right to complain later if they stayed silent</note>, Eberhard Fabricius in *Gailius Enucleated, book 1, observation 70, and those cited there.* Question: Does Intervention have a place before a Commissioner? Eberhard.

### 31. The Order of Saint John. <note>original: "Johanniter Orden. Ordo Equitum S. Johannis."</note>

Regarding this Order, Heinrich Pantaleon wrote a singular history. See also Marc. Anton. in *Ecclesiastical Matters for Practice, question 20,* on whether the Knights of Jerusalem may be admitted to the succession of fiefs <note>land or rights granted by a lord in exchange for service</note>; add also the Bulls, *final Counsel.* See the *Chronicle of Chronicles, part 2, folio 2 and following.* On whether they are truly "Religious" <note>members of a monastic order</note> and cannot be summoned except in an Ecclesiastical court, see Costa, *Counsel 42,* Riccius, *Decisions of the Court of Naples, decision 321,* and Stephan Durant, *question 6, folio 40.*

For a praise of the Maltese <note>the Knights of Malta</note>, see *Delights of the Italian Poets, part 2, folio 14 and following.*

Can they make a will? Ludovicus, *decisions 87 and 109.* Can they be legal proxies <note>Procuratores</note>? This is affirmed by the gloss in *Clement 3, on the word "Religious" regarding Proxies.*

It is pleasing to add the Bull of the Supreme Pontiff Urban VIII, by which he confirms all privileges to this Order, directed to the Grand Prior or Master, and the other brother knights of the Priory of Germany <note>original: "Alemanniae"</note> of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem.

By which all and each of them, in virtue of holy obedience and under the penalty of automatic excommunication <note>original: "excommunicationis latae sententiae"</note>, are commanded not to neglect, or permit to be neglected, anything that would be appropriate for the conservation, increase, and defense of the goods and other rights of the Order, etc., in the following tenor:

->URBAN VIII, POPE<-

To our beloved sons, Frederick Hundt, Prior, and the other brother Knights of the Priory of Germany of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem.

Beloved sons, greetings and Apostolic Blessing. The Roman Pontiffs, who held the most well-known merits of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, have always held it in high regard among the other Military Orders and have embraced it with peculiar charity and zeal. All of this has received a great increase in us from your devotion and observance toward Us and the Apostolic See. Thus it is that we greatly desire that the goods and other rights of your Order not only grow daily for the glory of God and the confusion of the enemies of the faith, but we are also most concerned about those things that can in any way hinder, diminish, or delay such progress. Therefore, although we do not doubt that you, out of your piety and zeal for the Catholic Religion, will apply the care you owe to the conservation and increase of such goods and rights, the Apostolic office which we unworthily hold does not cease to demand of us that we do not neglect to oversee these goods and rights as much as we are able with the Lord's help.

<column-break/>

Therefore, by our own motion <note>original: "Motu proprio," a decree issued by the Pope personally</note> and from our certain knowledge, we charge and command you, all and each, in virtue of holy obedience and under penalty of automatic excommunication, that you—nor any of you—at the instance, sight, or contemplation of anyone of any dignity or prominence (even if worthy of special note and needing to be expressed), for any cause or any sought-after color or pretext, publicly or secretly, directly or indirectly, neglect or permit to be neglected anything appropriate for the conservation, increase, and defense of the goods and other rights of your Order. Nor shall you harm or violate the Ecclesiastical jurisdiction, nor permit it to be harmed, violated, or usurped in any way. If it should happen that the validity of the privileges granted to you or your order by Us or our predecessors, the Roman Pontiffs, or their interpretation, is acted upon or discussed, you must remit that entire matter to the knowledge and declaration of the Apostolic See. For from this moment, we decree as null and void whatever else may be attempted regarding these matters by anyone of any authority, knowingly or ignorantly, acting to the contrary, notwithstanding any other factors. Given at Rome at Saint Peter’s, under the Ring of the Fisherman, the 6th day of June, 1624, in the first year of Our Pontificate.

### ADDITION.

What is Irregularity? See the Doctors on the chapter *Furiosus*, part 1, in the preface, number 1. This is said to be a matter of human law, according to the Doctors in the same preface, number 2.

A dispensation for Irregularity must be made expressly. Marius Antoninus, book 1, final reference, chapter 73. A person is "irregular" if they minister in an order they do not hold: hence, a Deacon is irregular

<column-break/>

if he administers extreme unction <note>the anointing of the sick</note>, performs a solemn baptism, or solemnly blesses water. Ibid, number 22.

A dispensation for irregularity must be made expressly, ibid. Irregularity is incurred if someone handed over to a secular court is punished by a penalty of blood <note>capital punishment or mutilation</note>. A protestation does not help, book 3, reference 2, number 15. When irregularity is incurred through fault, book 3, reference 16, numbers 13, 14, 17. One does not incur irregularity while performing a lawful act, ibid, numbers 14 and 15. One does not incur irregularity by killing an attacker in necessary self-defense, ibid, number 16. Irregularity is not incurred without deceit <note>original: "dolo," implying criminal intent</note>, ibid, number 17. A judge ought not to judge someone as irregular in a case of doubt, number 18. Whether irregularity is incurred only in cases expressed by law, whether an extension is permitted, and whether it is permitted to argue from a similar case, ibid, number 20.

### 33. Is. <note>original: "Ist. Est."</note>

The word "Is," by its own nature and property, properly signifies the present time, not the future. Hence, it ought not to be referred to the future, according to the points handed down by Bartolus on the law *If Alimony*, number 2, in the Digest *On Alimony Legacies*. Castrensis on the law *Because a Building*, number 2, in the Digest *On Urban Servitudes*. Especially because words are to be understood as referring to the present rather than the future, Cephalus, counsel 253, number 21, book 1.

The word "Is" also, by its own nature, signifies property and truth. Bartolus on the law *If a Husband*, paragraph *of the law* regarding the Julian Law on Adultery. Baldus on the law *Those things which by chance*, Code *on the action of pledge*. Decius on the law *That which is more*, Digest *on Rules of Law*. Hondedei, counsel 57, number 29, volume 1. It signifies substance and existence more than likeness; indeed, in the world there is no word so expressive of real existence and truth. As Jason writes on the law *In the choice of a slave*, paragraph 1, *on Legacies I*. Menochius, counsel 106, number 223. And see Castillo, *On Usufruct*, chapter 32, number 14 and following.

And from this, the ineffable name of the Most High God, **IHUH** <note>The Tetragrammaton, Yahweh/Jehovah</note>, is derived from "to be," and most excellently expresses the essence of the All-Highest Monarch. Since He alone truly exists, and all things depend upon Him, much like an image in a mirror depends upon the thing itself which it represents.

### ADDITION.

that as the *law of names and causes*, the verb BE <note>original: "SIT"</note> is in itself a signifier of substance and truth, according to Marcus Aurelius <note>original: "Marius Antoninus," the Roman Emperor and philosopher</note> in *Book 2, Resolution 42, number 8.*

## 34. Likewise. Likewise. <note>original: "Item. Item."</note>

The word *Likewise* <note>original: "Item"</note> sometimes stands as a connective, and sometimes otherwise. Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century Italian law professor</note> discusses this in his commentary on the *Digest* <note>original: "ff.", the primary collection of Roman law</note>. However, when an incomplete or imperfect clause—lacking a subject or a verb—is added to a preceding statement using this word, as in a case where the verb "sold" is missing, the verb is supplied from the preceding statement along with all its specific qualities. In this way, a repetition is implied. See the law "From the sentence" in the *Digest* regarding appeals. See also Tuschus, *Conclusion 303, letter d.*

### ADDITION.

The word *Likewise* and when it induces the repetition of a condition is explained with many examples by Mantica in *Conjectures on Last Wills, Book 10.* Likewise, it is a connective word. See Jacobus Alvarottus in his *Lectures on Feudal Customs, page 13.*
The word *Likewise* repeats the qualities of the preceding items, according to Marcus Aurelius. Regarding particles that are repeated twice, such as *and, and* <note>original German: "und, und"</note>, see Lord Carpzov and Dr. Tabor. In Frankfurt, the court clerk must be paid three hellers <note>A small copper coin</note> for every "Item" listed in an inventory. Regarding how much value is required to constitute a single "Item," see the city of Frankfurt's renewed Reformation <note>The city's updated legal code</note> *part 6, title 3.*

## 35. Jubilee Year. Jubilee year. <note>original: "Jubel-Jahr. Jubilæus annus."</note>

Justus Ricquius, a Canon of Ghent, wrote a treatise on the Jubilee Year; one may also consult Fuller, Guyon, and Cunæus's *The Republic of the Hebrews, book 1.*
Regarding the Lutheran Jubilee Year, see *Jubilee upon Jubilee* by P. Adam Conzen; likewise the *Pseudo-Jubilee*, published at Molsheim.

### ADDITION.

The reason the Jubilee Year was introduced is discussed by Petrus Gregorius in his *System of Universal Law*, concerning the Jubilee of the Hebrews. He also discusses the utility of the Hebrew Jubilee and the comparison between the Jewish and Christian Jubilee. Regarding the Papal Jubilee, see Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2.* The first Jubilee of the Protestants <note>original: "Evangelicorum"</note>, marking the Reformation begun by Luther in the year 1517, commenced at Wittenberg on the first of November in the year 1617 with a public debate, as noted in Helvicus's *Chronology*. A similar Jubilee was held at Wittenberg in the year 1602 in memory

<column-break/>

of the birth of the University, which had then stood for one hundred years, having been established by Frederick, Elector of Saxony, in the year 1502 on Saint Luke's Day. Just as such a Jubilee was held in Rome in the year 1650, so it is held more frequently based on the institution of Boniface VIII, who set it at every 100th year (such as the year 1300); this interval was reduced to 50 years by Clement V, and Gregory XI reduced it to 33 years. Finally, Paul II and after him Sixtus IV restricted it to every 25 years. See Sleidan's *History, book 21*, Platina in the *Life of Boniface VIII*, and Zwinger in his *Theater, volume 27, under the word Jubilee.* The Jubilee of the University of Tübingen was in the year 1617.

## 36. Jeweler. Gem-seller. <note>original: "Jubilirer. Gemmarius."</note>

Regarding the punishment of swindlers <note>original: "Zuntarorum"</note>, in German called *Jubilirer* <note>From the French *joyallier* or Italian *gioielliere*</note>. For those who sell false gemstones, see Hippolytus de Marsiliis, where he states they are to be punished as thieves, or even more severely on account of the fraud. Under Saxon Law, they are punished by flogging and banishment, though the penalty is moderated or increased according to the nature of the crime and the status of the person.

### ADDITION.

Hippolytus de Marsiliis calls those who sell false gems as if they were precious "Juntatores," and says they should be punished more severely than thieves.
A jeweler who sells false gemstones is punished as a thief, according to the *Digest* regarding extraordinary crimes. 
We read that imposters were sometimes restrained more lightly, as in the writings of Trebellius Pollio regarding Emperor Gallienus. When a certain imposter sold glass gems to the Prince's own wife as if they were real, and she, having discovered the ruse, wanted him punished, the Emperor ordered the seller to be thrown to a lion. However, he then released a capon <note>A rooster</note> from the cage, and ordered it to be announced by a herald: "He practiced a fraud, and now he has suffered one." And thus he sent the merchant away. The earth contains in its womb a certain brood of gems to satisfy human pride and avarice. Is there a great difference between gems, precious stones, and pearls? See Klock, *On the Treasury*, where he discusses the word PEARL <note>original: "PERLA"</note>, and why it is called a "Union" <note>term: <gloss>Unio</gloss> - A Latin term for a large, unique pearl, so named because no two were thought to be exactly alike</note>. On the wondrous value of various gems and the taxes upon them, see number 4.

## 37. Jews. Judæi. <note>original: "Juden. Judæi."</note>

Regarding the Synagogues of the Jews, see the specialized treatise by Buxtorf. On their Messiah, see Schickard's *On Royal Law*. On the Talmud, see the section on the Sanhedrin. Regarding the Jewish faith <note>original German: "vom Jüdischen Glauben"</note>, see Antonius Margarita. On why the Jews were formerly idolaters and are now heretics, see Cunæus, *The Republic of the Hebrews.*

# Letter J

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 17.</margin>
What their condition was after the destruction of the City <note>Jerusalem, destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD</note>; <margin>Ibid. chapter 23.</margin> Why it was said they worshiped the head of an ass? <margin>Fuller, *Miscellanea*, book 3, chapter 8.</margin> Fuller brings forward a far-fetched reason for this. Perhaps this rumor was attributed to the Christians, who were also called Jews, <margin>Baronius, in the Index.</margin> and this arose because the "little ox and the little ass" <note>original German: "das Oechslein sin das Eselein"</note> were placed at the Nativity of Christ; see <margin>Cunaeus, in the said treatise, book 3, chapter 4.</margin> **Whether Jews should be hanged by their feet?** <note>This refers to the "Jewish Execution" (*Judenstrafe*), a humiliating form of capital punishment where the condemned was hung upside down, often between two dogs.</note> Remus, in his paraphrase of the final article of the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* <note>The criminal code of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, issued in 1532</note>, reports that certain judges rely on a mere custom—though a highly irrational one—of hanging Jews upside down by their toes. <margin>Remus, *Paraphrase of the Carolina*.</margin> He argues that the law does not distinguish between thieves, whether they be Jews or Christians; and to inflict such a monstrous punishment only causes the Jews to hate us.

Nor is it reasonable to think that Jews can be forced to join the Christian faith by such means. There are other ways by which the path to conversion would be better and more secure. See <margin>in the *Analysis of Canon Law*, page 461.</margin> where it is suggested that wealth acquired through usury <note>lending money at interest</note> should be left to the Jews as if for "pious uses," provided it helps them convert more easily. To the same end, <margin>The Council of Basel, Session 19.</margin> decreed that in the place where converted Jews are baptized, they should acquire all the rights and privileges of citizens. However, as long as they do not convert, Pope Paul IV forbade them from owning immovable property <note>real estate</note> on March 23, 1556. <margin>Pope Paul IV, 1556.</margin>

It is asked: Are the Jews slaves of the Christians? For the negative view, it is argued: (1) Slaves are considered as nobodies—indeed, as if they were dead—in the eyes of the law, <margin>Digest, *On the Rules of Law*, law 209.</margin> they own nothing of their own, and consequently have no power to make contracts, write wills, or alienate property in any other way. Since a non-entity has no legal qualities, and yet Jews do possess ownership of things and can make wills regarding their goods; and since they freely engage in commerce with Christians, <margin>Arguments from the Decretals, chapters *miserabilem* and *quanto magis*, on usury.</margin> and no Christian, except the Governor of a Province, can set the price of their goods for them. <margin>Code of Justinian, *On Jews*, law 9.</margin>

(2) Slaves do not have the legal standing to appear in court. Yet Jews litigate in the courts and take legal actions in the solemn manner. <margin>Code of Justinian, *On Jews*, law 8.</margin>

(3) Among slaves, there is no legal marriage nor "just nuptials," since just nuptials belong to Civil Law, and slaves are compared to the dead under Civil Law. Even if they have children through cohabitation, those children are not under the "parental power" of the parents, since one who is under another's power cannot hold others under his own. Jews, on the contrary, contract legal marriages, and thus hold their children under their parental power. <margin>Panormitanus, note 3, on the conversion of infidels; Afflictis, decision 151.</margin>

The contrary view (namely, that Jews living in the Empire and elsewhere are slaves of the Emperor and the Princes in whose territory they reside) is held by <margin>Felidius; Cagnolus; Zasius; and Besold, volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

In favor of this opinion is an express text <margin>in the Decretals, chapter *etsi Judaeis*</margin> which says: that their own guilt submitted the Jews to the perpetual servitude of the Christians. Hence, it is said they are fostered by Christians out of human kindness and mere piety, grace, and compassion, <margin>Decretals, chapter *Judaei*, on witnesses.</margin> and *in the chapter etsi Judaeos.* They are also called slaves of the Treasury <note>Fiscus</note> or the Imperial Chamber. <gloss>Thus, the Jews owe a "Coronation Tax" and a "Sacrificial Penny" <note>original German: "Crönensteur und Opfferpfenning"</note> to a Roman Emperor when he takes office.</gloss>

Against the Jews, see <margin>The Council of Vienne in Lazius, *On Vienna*, book 2, page 65 and following.</margin> Boverius also wrote against them, <margin>Boverius, page 179.</margin> recounting many miracles that were performed regarding the Jews.

Regarding the Jews living in Turkey and their status, see <margin>Bellonius, *On the Turks*, page 176; and *The Turkish Court*, part 1, page 49.</margin> That the Jews are and remain exiles, and why? See <margin>Filefacus, *Select Matters*, chapter 12,</margin> where he has many things worth knowing about the Jews, <margin>pages 186 to 204.</margin>

On the Privileges of the Jews, one should see <margin>Julius Benedictus Crescentius, in *Consultations on the Privileges of the Jews*, volume 6; Symphorema, pages 238 and 268.</margin>

If someone offends a Jew <gloss>who has a sovereign safe-conduct <note>original German: "Landfürstl. Glait"</note>, then this case belongs to the Sovereign Prince to decide, and he is the competent judge, and not the one who otherwise holds high and low jurisdiction <note>original: "merum & mixtum imperium"</note>, etc.</gloss> See <margin>Zypaeus, *Analysis of Canon Law*, book 3, page 460.</margin>

The things that Julius Conradus Otto <note>A Jewish convert to Christianity and professor of Hebrew</note> writes in the *Preface to Gali Razia* <note>Hebrew for "The Secrets Revealed," a 1605 work intended to prove Christian doctrines from Jewish sources</note> regarding modern Jews are noteworthy: Very few Hebrews understand the Hebrew language, let alone the Talmud or other books of the Rabbis, but live for the day like brute animals. Although they pray, scarcely a few notice what they are praying; thus the greatest part of them does not know what they believe, or in what state they might die and seek eternal life. The world also cares little for their salvation or perdition. There is no doubt that many Jews would uniquely desire conversion, if only they were certain of some of the Articles of Faith, and if they were not persuaded that the reading of the Old Testament—in which they place their greatest trust—is completely neglected in the churches of Christians. This false persuasion is no small cause for why they adhere so firmly to their own religion.

But if kings, princes, and others who provide homes for this nation in their territories would, with a singular zeal for piety, compel them to attend sacred gatherings and sermons, there is no doubt that many, having cast away this false opinion, would be led to Christianity. This has been found to happen in Rome and other places, where not only has a special College <note>The Collegium Neophytorum</note> been built—in which Jews, Turks, and others who desire to take the name of Christ are instructed by teachers—but they are also supported at public expense until they are [ready].

On the comments regarding the origin of the Jews, see at length Boecler, in his annotations to Tacitus's *Histories*, book 5, chapters 2 and 3, page 165 and following. Whether the Jews, as well as the Christians, are included under the section "on investigation" <note>original: "§. de indaganda"</note> in the drafted Imperial Recess, and are therefore bound to perform it, see most recently Johann Wolfgang Hiller in *Juridical Demonstration* on this very matter, letter D. 2. For a Jew to remain obstinate in his faith is a sin against God, yet this crime is not to be punished in an external court, Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 62, number 42.

### 38. Juncker. Country-Juncker, City-Juncker. Noble, Junior Lords.

A noble is commonly called "Juncker" by the Germans, by a contraction <note>original: "Synæresin"</note> as if he were a "new man" <note>original: "novus homo"</note>, a new lord, a "young master" <note>original: "junger Herr"</note>, as if he were a hero or lord flourishing in youthful age and strength, more fit for bearing arms and conducting affairs. Matthäus Stephani *on Nobility, book 1, chapter 1, number 11*. But it is more likely that we say this title was given to the second-born sons; see Calvin's *Legal Lexicon under the word "Infans"*. Master Dracon *on Patricians, chapter 2, book 3, folio 215, etc.* He is also called "Jungherr" (Young Lord), not by reason of age, but by reason of dignity. In Ulm, the "Elder Lords" are called Seniors. From this, all nobles who descend from the ruling elite are called "Junckern." The seniors were Knights. And although we call the juniors "Junckern," as if young masters, we do not call the seniors "Senckherren" <note>The author is making a play on words: "Jung-" (young) vs. "Sen-" (from senior, but sounding like "sinken," to sink or lower).</note>. See Goldast, *volume 1, part 2, of Alamannic Matters, folio 392*.

The name <term>Juncker</term> <note>A title for minor nobility or young lords, from the German "Jung Herr" or "Young Lord."</note> was also formerly given to the younger sons of Dukes, Princes, and Counts who had not yet attained a position of rule, as noted by Johann Stumpff in the *Swiss Chronicle*, chapter 19; I also discussed this in my *Treatise on the Equestrian Order, number 3.* Thus, it was provided for by the Statute of the Counts of Hanau that the firstborn should claim the territory for himself by customary law and be distinguished as Lord <term>Herr</term>, while the younger brothers should be named <term>Junckherren</term> <note>original: "Junckherren"</note>. See Knichen in the *Encyclopedia*, chapter 1. In a similar manner, within the noble family of Elß—as attested by Lord Joseph Nolden in *On the Nobility, chapter 1, number 25*—it is accepted that those who are still under paternal power, and whose father is still living, are called: *Sons of Elß* <note>original: "Söhne zu Elß"</note>. However, the father, and those who have been released from paternal power (even if they remain under some form of guardianship or care), are called *Lords of Elß* <note>original: "Herren zu Elß"</note>. Indeed, even the sons of Kings were greeted with this title, as Cyriacus Spangenberg writes in the *Chronicle of Henneberg, chapter 5, book 5*. There, Otto, the son of the King of Denmark, is called <term>Juncker</term> <note>original: "Juncker Otto von Dännemarck"</note> Otto of Denmark; likewise, Nolden affirms, citing Lord Goldast, that Cathedral Canons were formerly called "God’s Junckers" <note>original: "Gottes Junckern"</note>. This name was later adopted by the lower nobility (for as virtue declines, the arrogance of titles usually grows), and yet some in certain places are now beginning to shrink away from it. Nolden, in the cited place, number 27, says that a <term>Juncker</term> was considered a "Little Lord" <note>original: "Dominiculus"</note>, whereas the elder was a <term>Master</term> <note>original: "Herus"</note>.

## ADDITION.

It is not uncommon among our people to call nobles <term>Junckherren</term>, as if they were "young lords" <note>original: "junge Herren"</note>; I interpret this based on the context not as "younger" lords in age, but as "lesser" lords in respect to the "greater" lords or Princes. For "young" <note>original: "jung"</note> and "small" <note>original: "klein"</note> not infrequently have a single and consistent meaning among our people. In the diplomas of the Dukes of Brunswick from the year 1374, this little word is seen used in illustrious families. See Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 6, chapter 1, number 15*. From a certain epitaph, Reinerus Reineccius, in his *Treatise on the Original Descent of the Nobility*, records: *The Noble, Well-Born Juncker, Juncker Bernhard, Noble Lord of Lippe*. See also Johann Norderman, *On the Right of the Principate, conclusion 88*. Henningus Jurgens treats this matter at length in his *Disputation on Appanage, thesis 31*.

### 40. Jurisdiction, Court, Authority. Jurisdictio.

Whether and when matters of jurisdiction are presumed to be feudal or not? This is discussed at length below under the word <term>Fief</term> <note>original: "Lehen"</note>, in the Consular Questions, question 1, where it is also taught at length what is comprised by the word <term>Court</term> <note>original: "Gericht"</note>, especially when joined with these words: <term>Stocks and Gallows</term> <note>original: "Stock und Galgen"</note>, together with the <term>Ban to judge over blood</term> <note>original: "Bann über das Blut zu richten," referring to High Justice or the power of capital punishment</note>, etc. See also above under the word <term>Court</term> <note>original: "Gericht"</note>, with the <term>Courts</term>.

->ADDITION.<-

Jurisdiction is numbered among immovable things and is attached to the soil. *Knipschild* on *Trusts*, chapter 5, number 18. Which things pertain to simple jurisdiction. *Chapter 10, number 104.*

When a vassal obtains jurisdiction and authority over a fief or a feudal castle from another source, the same does not accrue to the fief itself, but falls as personal property to the vassal's own heirs. *Schrader* on *Fiefs*, part 2, section 9, number 11 and following; *Molinaeus* on the *Customs of Paris*, title 1, section 1, glossary 5, number 44 and following; *Knipschild* on the *Obligation of the Lord toward the Vassal*, page 157. So much so, that even if the feudal lord had granted only the castle or other estate as a fief and reserved the jurisdiction or authority over it for himself, but subsequently sold that jurisdiction to the vassal, it still does not accrue to the fief or become feudal, but belongs to the vassal's personal heirs. *Rosenthal*, chapter 10, conclusion 43, number 19. An inherited court <note>original: "Erbgericht"</note> gives no jurisdiction or justice, and to whom such regularly belongs. *Zorer*, part 2, question 5, number 398.

Furthermore, Viglius Zuichemus, otherwise a most learned Jurist, fostered many monstrous opinions, such as his claim that women possess only half of human reason. On the truth and excellence of legal science, see Petrus Andreas Gammarus of Casale, Bologna, volume 1, folio 132; and Gundisalinus Villadiego, volume 13, part 2, folio 258. Jurists have not been ashamed to learn even from peasants, following the argument of Law 79, section 1, *On Legacies*, book 3, there: "Proculus heard the old peasants saying." Jurists are bound to respond even when asked about the Law against their will. Klock, *Consultations*, 14, number 1. Those who flatter the profits of the powerful are not Jurists, but ministers of iniquity. Klock, *Consultations*, 29, number 268, and *Consultations*, 28, number 105. Catellianus Cotta of Milan deals with the legal expert in volume 1, folio 137. Antonius Massa Gallesius of Rome deals with the training of legal experts in volume 1, folio 168. Johannes Monachus deals with the defenders of the law in volume 3, part 2, folio 122.

The Order of Jurists is spoken of and slandered most poorly among people born with malevolent dispositions; but if we wish to speak the truth, not a few are found who, without any discrimination, as long as the hope of deceitful money shines, undertake to plead causes. And truly, as Nilus the Bishop and Martyr says: those who provide patronage to the wicked are not only helpers in crimes, but are also defiled by the communion of sin. That divine Plato, in the first book of *The Laws* at the end, so execrates this kind of man that, by a proposed law, he thinks a citizen in a well-ordered Republic should be punished with death if he is convicted of having, through greed, turned the strength of justice in the minds of the judges to the contrary, and moved many lawsuits beyond opportunity, or assisted those moving them.

The principal end of the student of Jurisprudence should not be the hope of obtaining gain and honor. The Jurist Sabinus did not have great wealth, but was sustained by his students.

So Ulpian, Scaevola, Papinian, and Modestinus, although they were very wealthy and conspicuous with the highest honors, nevertheless those heights provided for some of them the occasion of the greatest calamities. For Gaius Cassius was driven into exile by Caesar. Ulpian was rejected from his dignity with ignominy by Elagabalus. Papinian, who is called the "Asylum of Law," was exposed to the swords of the soldiers by Antoninus Caracalla and died most miserably, struck by the axe.

Since at no time has the nourishing <term>Themis</term> <note>The Greek goddess of divine law and personification of Justice</note> and her noble clients been without their accusers and detractors—who, like that monster of the human race, Gaius Caligula, either plotted or wished for the destruction of the Law and its Consultants—so in this particular age, most fertile in slanders and all impiety, some attack with such an atrocious pen and defile the glory, prerogative, and axiom of Justinian's Law and its cultivators, that they do not blush to attribute the cause of all <term>disorder</term> <note>original Greek: ἀταξίας (ataxias)</note>, sedition, and war to the order of the Doctors of Law. And lest without color...
