# The Expanded Treasury of Practice

...they are immediately caught in their madness, slandering under the color and cloak of falsehood; they construct and stuff their insults with fabricated reasons.

They seek authority for their claims partly from the Pope and partly from the Emperor. From the decrees of the Popes, they especially honor the rescript of Honorius III in the chapter *On the Watchtower* <note>original: "super specula"; a 1219 papal decree</note> [28. *concerning the privileges and excesses of Prelates*]. But the Popes, having pushed aside the Laws of the Emperors, thrust their own decrees upon an unwary people. (Mejer *on heretics*, p. 340; Flacius, Gerhard, Conring *on the origin of German Law*, chapter 25, p. 106 and following). Even the Roman Catholic writers call the Law of Justinian <note>the Roman legal code compiled under Emperor Justinian I, which forms the basis of Civil Law</note> a "treasure of all doctrine and erudition." (Duaren, P. Faber, Baronius, Matthaeacius). Valla, though otherwise somewhat unfair to the interpreters of Law, says the same in the preface to his third book of *Elegantiae*. Honorius can also be excused, since he does not exclude the study of Civil Law entirely, but only in the district or region of Paris (Lutetia), where it happened to be offensive to the Royal Majesty. This was because the French King seemed to have already departed from and been freed from the power of the Roman Empire; thus, it was seen as inappropriate to publicly admit the interpretation of Imperial Law in the royal city itself. This is similar to how, in Spain, it was forbidden under penalty of death for anyone to receive Imperial Law (Oldradus, *Counsel 69, number 6*). But our enemies desire to see the entire "Choir of Doctors" <note>the community of legal scholars and professors</note> driven out not only from France and Spain, but from the Roman-German Empire itself. They falsely claim that in the year 1441, it pleased Frederick III:
> that all Doctors of Law in the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation shall no longer be tolerated under any laws at the Imperial Chamber Court <note>original: "Cammer-Gericht"; the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, nor in the councils of any Prince or others, but shall be completely abolished.

That counterfeit <term>Hippolytus à Lapide</term> <note>a pseudonym for Bogislaus Philipp von Chemnitz, a famous critic of the Hapsburgs</note> (for so this "Virbius" <note>a mythological figure reborn; here implying a man hiding behind a new name</note> corrupts his own name) names this "Sibylline leaf" <note>a mysterious or prophetic document</note>—concerning the exclusion of legal experts from both private judgments and public councils—a Law of the Empire in the preface of his dissertation on the *Law of the State*. With a wicked sort of religious devotion, he prays to God that it be carried out. But Frederick III was not the author of this fictional constitution, as the Emperor's name appears nowhere, neither in the heading nor the signature; it also lacks the Imperial seal or wax stamp. Frederick III showed the opposite sentiment through his actions when he founded the Universities of Mainz and Greifswald, endowed them with privileges, and wished for legal experts to be honored with the Doctoral cap and other prerogatives, holding the Doctors of Law in the highest esteem. (Christoph von Hagen *on Usury*, preface p. 12). Furthermore, Goldast himself admits (in his *Index of where the Imperial Statutes are taken from*, p. 312) that this famous paper was spread by an unknown author under the title *The Necessity of the German Nation*. He adds:
> It appears from all indications that this reformation was made neither by the Emperor nor by His Majesty's command, but was created by the Cities of the Empire at a "City-Day" gathering; and afterwards, at the general Imperial Diet, based on their advice, it was 

<column-break/>

humbly presented to His Imperial Majesty for his consideration and counsel.

In this matter, while we completely accept the compiler's opinion insofar as it is a denial [of the Emperor's authorship], we rightly reject the added assertion, as it rests on mere conjecture (and perhaps on the argument that in certain Imperial Cities, Doctors of Law are not admitted into the Senatorial order). For it cannot be proven by any inscription, signature, or other characteristic that this was the opinion of all or most cities—cities which are, after all, primarily guided by the advice of Doctors of Law. This was rightly noted against Goldast by Dr. Conring (in his *History of German Law*, ch. 32, p. 149). See also Walther, Limnäus, and especially the very accurate program of Lord Tabor, proposed at Strasbourg on May 15, 1648, where he discusses this extensively and solidly. There is a truly excellent epitaph of Broncus, written for "Hippolytus à Lapide" and other haters of Doctors, of which Johann Steuercirus is the author:

->The Jurist Broncus, the glory of shysters,<-
->Was made a head shorter just yesterday.<-
->How? While death was bending the fatal Jurist,<-
->It struck out three little letters from his name.<-
<note>A Latin wordplay: "Jurist" (JCtus) minus three letters (J, C, T) leaves "us," implying he was stripped of his professional identity. It also jokes that being "shorter" (brevior) means he was decapitated or diminished by death.</note>

Regarding what a Jurist is, Limnäus (in *Public Law*, book 8, ch. 4) runs through all the sciences. He asks whether a knowledge of Grammar is necessary for him. He discusses the supreme utility of Jurisprudence and Jurists, who were once held in great esteem and glory among the Romans. The ancestors of Emperors were Jurists. For Didius Julianus, who obtained the Empire after Pertinax, the great-grandfather was Salvius Julianus, twice Consul, Prefect of the City, and a Jurist, which made him even more noble. (Mundius, *on Offices and Honors*). In France, legal experts made into Senators and Royal Councilors transmit their nobility to their descendants. (Marquard Freher in notes on Peter von Andlo). [They speak] of "in-laws, tongue-leapers, quarrel-heads, spectacle-breakers, and snake-eaters" (from Vigelius Felw, *on the Judge*, p. 471).

Finally, "cease your hissing, viper!" This is what they used to call a <term>shyster</term> <note>original: "causidicum, sive rabulam"; a noisy or deceptive lawyer</note> or a forensic brawler, and not without reason. For Apuleius says of such shysters in his *Apology*: "Now there is a certain custom allowed to shysters of that sort, whose wild tongues are used to planting their venom in another's pain." "Wild," meaning "vipers," as Scipio Gentilis explains in the same place. So below: "in the manner of a viper, to breathe black poison from a snowy tooth." Ammianus Marcellinus has more on these "vipers" (book 30). Others call them "dogs," as Horace does to Cassius Severus, and call their words "dog-like" or "canine eloquence." Ovid says in *The Ibis*:

->He hurls his dog-like words throughout the forum.<-

Sallust calls it "canine eloquence" in his *Fragments*, and Columella in his preface calls it "the canine pursuit of barking."

### 42. Infant.

The name "Infant" <note>original: 'Infans'</note> includes every son and daughter of whatever age, as argued in the law *uxorem 41* in the *Digest on legacies*. This meaning was in use in Rome in the age of Jerome, as he himself testifies in his *Questions on Genesis*. From there, it was brought into Spain and today refers to a title of dignity, both for the children of Kings, who are greeted as "Infantes" (see Otto in *Public Law*, page 159; Draco on *Patricians*, page 217; Molina, volume 3, *On Faith and Justice*, page 1), and for those lords who are called "Infancones" more for the antiquity and splendor of their lineage than for their power and wealth (Cabedo, *book 2, decision 107*). Children of seven years are called "infants" in the law of Ulpian. An infant is excused by "innocence of intent" <note>original: 'innocentia consilii'; meaning a child lacks the capacity for criminal intent</note> (Law *infans 12* in the *Digest on the Cornelian Law concerning Assassins*). Barbosa treats this at length in *book 9, chapter 50*. Infants can be elected as Kings (Knipschild, *On Fideicommissum, chapter 8*). Among the Spanish, that son of a Prince is called an "infant" whose father and elder brother are living, because he does not have the "faculty of speaking" <note>A wordplay on 'infans' (not speaking)</note> in the administration of the Principality (Bonifacius *on thefts*, page 436).

Furthermore, in Spain he is called an *Infant* because he does not have the faculty of speaking in the Republic (Matthaeus Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 7*; Draco on *Patricians*; Besold in *Politics, book 1*).

### 43. By the Law Itself.

By the Law itself <note>original: 'Ipso Jure'</note>, that is, by Civil Law. Otherwise, "by the law itself" has the same value as "by law alone" (Vinnus on the *Institutes*). What "by the law itself" means is defined in Fichard's additions to Villalobos, page 300; Vasquez, chapter 28; and Vigelius in *Method of Disputed Law, book 15, chapter 14*.

### 44. Intact.

When a matter is still said to be "intact" <note>original: 'Integra res'; a legal state where no action has yet been taken to change a situation</note>. See Master Tabor, *Elements of Jurisprudence, part 3, section 3, thesis 39*, near the end; Zorer, part 1, question 8; Sturm *on Legal Repentance, chapter 3*. The word "entirely" <note>original: 'integre'</note> signifies a perfected thing (Marius Antoninus).

### 45. To judge for the soul.

To judge for the soul <note>original: 'Judicare pro anima'</note>, that is, to bequeath a fief for pious causes (Rittershusius, *Feudal Partitions, page 156*; Giphanius in his *Treatise on Feudal Law, chapter 2*). See also the *Books of Feuds 55*, where the same phrase appears.

### 46. Indult, Indulgence.

An **Indult** <note>a specific privilege or exemption granted by a high authority</note> or **Indulgence** <note>in this legal sense, the remission of punishment for crimes</note> falls within the competence of the Prince and is recorded among the "Reserved Rights" <note>prerogatives held exclusively by the sovereign</note>. See Klock, *volume 1, counsel 37, numbers 63 and 64.* However, such a right can be acquired through long-standing custom (*ibid. number 65*). An Indult can also refer to a document of requisition, according to Gothofredus Antonius in his *Feudal Disputes, page 146.* For more on Indulgences, see Antonius Rosellus of Padua and Ludovicus Bologninus. On "Plenary Indulgence" <note>the full remission of temporal punishment</note>, see Felinus Sandaeus of Ferrara. Acts performed through special indulgence do not carry the force of Law, nor can they create a binding precedent <note>original: "praejudicium"</note>. See *Law 1 on the Constitutions of Princes* and Arnisaeus, *Political Re-readings, chapter 6, section 3, number 6.* See also Barbosa, *Book 9, chapter 46, axiom*; consult "Connivance" in the same place, and *Axiom book 19, chapter 48, axiom 1*, which states: one must deviate from the prescription of the laws only when the law itself permits; the Courts overlook small matters <note>original: "Curiae in modicis connivent"</note>. Also Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Dispute 4, thesis 8.*

### 47. To go toward denial.

The phrase "To go toward denial" <note>original: "Ad inficias ire"</note> is considered a barbarism <note>a non-standard or corrupt use of Latin</note> in *Law 44, section 4 on the Division of Inheritances*. Classical Latin writers instead say "to go denial" <note>original: "ire inficias"</note>. This specific law was altered by Tribonian <note>the Byzantine jurist responsible for the Justinian Code</note>, who added certain words to the writings of the ancient Jurists. See Rittershusius in *New Works, part 9, chapter 19, number 6.*

### 48. To be inherent in a contract.

On what it means "to be inherent in a contract" <note>original: "Inesse contractui"</note>, see Master Tabor, *Elements of Jurisprudence, part 3, section 3, thesis 39.* Pacts added to "good faith" contracts are said to be inherent—that is, they inform the contracts themselves and increase the rights of the plaintiff. See *Law 7, sections 5 and 6; Law 27 on Pacts*, where C. F. A. notes more in *thesis 93*. Pacts added immediately during the transaction are said to be inherent to the business itself. See Barbosa, *Book 14, chapter 1, axiom 19*, and Master Paulus Gambs' *Inaugural Dispute on Added Pacts.*

### 49. I will. I want.

**"I want to buy it thus; I want to accept it thus; I want to sell it to you thus; I want to leave it to you thus."** <note>original German: "Ich will es alſo kauffen, ich will es alſo annehmen..."</note> Through the word "I will" <note>Latin: "volo"</note>, parties are seen to have consented to a present contract. See the *Strasbourg Collection of Laws, on the contract of buying, thesis 31.* On the clause "If he shall have willed it," see Master Ludwig, *Disputes on the Institutes, page 171, G.*

### 50. Valuables.

Regarding what things are called **Valuables** <note>original: "Jocalia"</note>, and whether this includes **bridal wagons or bridal chests** <note>original German: "die Brautwagen oder Braut-Käſten"</note>, see Cothmann, *counsel 3, number 42* and Pruckmann, *counsel 34, number 48.* It also includes things given to children to help build a household, such as **help and house-taxes [dowries] that a father gives his child.** <note>original German: "Hülff und Hausſteuer, ſo ein Vatter ſeinem Kind thut"</note> See Master Carpzov, *Jurisprudence, constitution 11, definitions 15 and 16*; *Leipzig Decisions 476 and 735, volume 2*; Pfeil, *counsel 131*; and Gail, *Book 2, observation 91, number 5.* See also Scipio, *Book 2 on donations between husband and wife, chapter 29.* If "valuables" are bequeathed in a will, there is a question of whether festive and precious garments

<column-break/>

are owed. See Mantica, *On Conjectures of Last Wills, book 9, title 3, number 23.*

### 51. Injury.

A word or writing that is slightly harsh is not immediately considered injurious <note>libelous or insulting</note>. Ummius, *On Procedure, page 262.* In Lower Saxony, a person who has committed an injury sometimes strikes himself on the cheek with these words: **"Mouth, you spoke it, therefore you lied."** <note>original German: "Maulda du ſagteſt, da lögeſt du"</note>
Regarding "mediated injury" <note>insults delivered through a third party</note> through Counselors, Ministers, or Subjects, see Master Stirnius's *Five Titles of Public Law, thesis 3, section 6.* On injuries committed against a State of the Empire, see *title 3, sections 7 and 8.* On when injuries should or should not be avenged by war, see Adam Contzen, *Politics, book 10, chapter 9, sections 2, 3, and 4.* An injury committed against chastity or life is restored with great difficulty, whereas those against fortune or honor are restored most easily (*ibid., book 10, chapter 9, section 2*). On the diversity of injuries, see the same source. Satisfaction for injuries between different Republics should be handled moderately according to the Law of Nations (*ibid.*). Harsh insults do not always damage a reputation. Georg Adam Struvius, *On Private Vengeance, chapter 10, aphorism 6, number 20, page 93.* A person is believed to have acted with the intent to insult <note>original: "conviciandi animo"</note> if, moved by anger, they accuse someone of a crime, even if the crime is true (*ibid. number 3, page 108*). Regarding the **Fine for the Tongue** <note>original German: "Emenda Linguae"</note>, which is **"imposed by a judge because of an unjust or false complaint brought before His Majesty or another ordinary judge, or often because of shameful and dishonorable words poured out against an honorable man; it can be settled and paid with twenty-five marks, totaling one hundred gold guilders."** <note>original German: "welche wegen unbillich und falſchen fürgebrachtter Klag... durch den Richter aufgelegt wird..."</note> More can be found in the **Hungarian Land Law**, *part 2, title 72, throughout.* However, Sylla was immediately impatient of injury. See Rupert on Florus, *book 3, chapter 21, section 6.* For mortals are accustomed to this: injuries move in a circle; they are ignited by mutual turns and balanced out, as Brunn says in *Annals book 15, page 958.* But this is usually contrary to humanity and good morals. For in this way, anger leaves nothing behind, and "deep ash buries the entombed nations," as the Tragic judge says in *Hercules Furens, verse 361.* A noble person does not remember an injury. Rupert on Florus, *book 3, chapter 21, section 19.* Recommendation can arise from injury (*Law 4, title 4, section 4. 2*). The memory of injuries lasts longer than the memory of benefits (*Book 4, chapter 2, section 92*).
For the definition of injury, see Master Biccius in *Golden Rules, section 4, thesis 154.* For its primary divisions, see the same. Whether the truth of an insult excuses one from an action for injury, see *ibid., letter Aa* and Master Ludwig, *Disputes on the Institutes, page 311, end.* Regarding a "libelous painting" <note>original: "pictura famosa"</note>, see the *Strasbourg Legal Collection, book 47, title 10, theses 38, 39, and 40.* **"As Master Biccius once told me: In Leipzig, a tailor asked a painter to paint an angel on his shop sign. The painter promised and did so. But when rainy weather arrived, the tailor's neighbors asked him why he had a billy-goat painted on his sign? Then the trick came to light: the painter had painted a goat with oil colors underneath, and an angel over it with water colors."** <note>The rain washed away the water-colored angel, leaving the oily goat—a common visual insult to the tailor's status.</note> On the subject of jokes, much is collected by Zahn, *On Lies, book 1, chapter 45, throughout.* In cases that concern...

<meta>This page continues the legal lexicon under the letter "I," specifically focusing on the legal definitions, penalties, and procedures surrounding "Injuria" (Injury/Insult). It moves from theoretical definitions of physical versus verbal insults to specific local laws and ends with a formal imperial summons.</meta>

<page-num>499</page-num>
<header>Letter I.</header>

...concern acts, injuries, and marks of disgrace. Nuremberg against Bavaria regarding the matter of Restitution, based on the chapter on Amnesty and Grievances, pages 80 and 81.

A **physical injury** <note>original Latin: *injuria realis*</note> occurs when someone proceeds to an act, which however terminates outside of that person’s physical body <note>meaning the insult is directed at their property or dignity rather than a physical strike to their person</note>. Properly speaking, an injury is either **verbal** or **physical**: verbal is either words spoken by mouth, or written, or properly written, or those having a likeness to writing. Physical is either committed properly outside the body. **Personal**, which terminates in the person. It is customary for Legal Scholars <note>original: *JCtis*, an abbreviation for *Jurisconsultis*</note> to reduce a three-part division to a two-part division, following the example of Law 5, Digest on Pacts.

Those who have suffered an injury estimate its value. Thus, when there were many indications of theft against a woman in Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentinae*</note>, and an inquiry was made with the knowledge of the Magistrate, the woman, later found innocent, estimated this injury at 2,000 florins; however, she obtained nothing because of the Magistrate's order. **The execution of Law does not constitute an injury** <note>original: *Juris Executio non habet injuriam*; a legal maxim meaning that a person acting under legal authority cannot be sued for doing their duty</note>. See Book 13, section 1, book 33 of the Digest on this title. Master Doctor Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 311. One who inflicts a verbal injury on a man and immediately revokes it is not held liable for injuries. Through revocation, the action for injuries ceases. Justus Oldekop in *Criminal Observations*, title 5, observation 27. In some places, the injurer is held to pay a certain price for his infamy for the insult, which is called **Lie-money** or **Mouth-money** <note>original German: *Lügen oder Mundgeld*</note>. See the *Supplement to the Observations of Wehner*, page 43. According to that saying of Lyra: Those not knowing how to respond aptly and reasonably turn themselves to insults and retaliations of injuries; yet on the contrary it remains true that the little **Aesopic lamb** standing further down the stream must make the water murky for the **wolf** residing in a higher place. <note>A reference to Aesop's fable where the wolf makes a false accusation against the lamb to justify eating it; the author suggests the powerful often blame the weak for impossible things.</note> A **hedgehog** cannot avenge itself better than when it sticks its head between its legs and lets the dogs bite at it. For thereby the dogs get bloody mouths, and no harm happens to the hedgehog. Even so shall you be invincible if you ask nothing after all the disgrace and contempt. Schupp in *Lucidor*, letter G. A petition for injuries must contain the year and month, even if pursued civilly. Eberhardus Fabricius in *Gailius Enucleated*, page 25. He who affects a virgin or matron—that is, frequently follows her silently against good morals—is held liable for injury; for constant following creates, as it were, some infamy. Law 15, section 22, 23, Digest on injuries. If someone who suffered an injury remained silent, let his silence remain forever. Law 10, at the end, Code on the revocation of gifts. Rebhan in *Hodegata*, page 658. **Hamburg City Law**, part 4, article 58. Can an injury done to a Judge be punished by himself? Eberhard Fabricius in *Gailius Enucleated*, book 1, observation 39. He who, being falsely accused of a crime, hurls the lie back at the injurer with a certain exaggeration—as if he had brought it forth like a robber and adulterer—has no reason to fear an action for injuries. Master Carpzov, part 3, Decision 247, number 25. Spoken words, accusations, or injuries <note>original German: *Ausgegossene Reden, Inziche oder Injurien*</note>. Master Suttinger, observation 15, number 3. Question from Besold, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

...within what time an action for injuries is prescribed <note>expires</note>, and it is said that it does not last beyond a year. Law 5, Code on this title. The question is, which year is understood here, and it is said to be the **"useful year"** <note>original Latin: *annus utilis*; a legal term for a year consisting only of days on which legal business could actually be conducted</note>. Law 14, section 2, on the grounds of fear. The reason is because the Jurisdiction of the Praetor was included in a year; for what if his Jurisdiction had been established in the later months? But he whose Jurisdiction does not extend beyond a year ought not to delay and prolong this action further. A useful year is twofold: 1. By reason of the beginning, so that the beginning is "useful," and thereafter the days are continuous; 2. By reason of all days. A year is useful if: 1. The plaintiff has the power of acting. 2. The defendant has the power of responding. 3. There are judicial days, according to Law 1, Digest on various and temporary prescriptions. If, therefore, the year were "useful" in every single day, the time would be too long. An injury, whether verbal or physical, inflicted upon a **Doctor** <note>referring to a University Professor or high scholar</note> is called **atrocious**, and must be punished more severely than if it were done to a commoner. Walther on the *Privileges of Doctors*, page 323. For an injury done to a Doctor, one can act under the Julian Law, page 324. The injuries of friends are the gravest. Master Rittershusius, *Sacred Readings*, page 564. An injury can even be done by **omission**, argued from Law 2, Digest on the Pompeian Law on parricide, and Law 5, penultimate section, on the Julian Law of Majesty. Master Doctor Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 311. Question: Whether figurative "bites" or "stakes" <note>original German: *Stangen*; likely symbolic marks or public shaming devices</note>, by which one thinks they are being silently noted, should be disregarded in silence rather than immediately avenged? Affirmed first by Law 7, section 4, Digest on injuries. Marquard Freher, book 2 on Existence, chapter 8, number 8. **He who cannot take a joke should not go among people.** <note>original German: *Wer nicht kan Schimpff verstehen, soll nicht zu Leuten gehen.*</note>

...concerning deeds, injuries, and slanderous labels. Nuremberg against Bavaria regarding the matter of restitution, from the chapter on Amnesty and Grievances, pages 80 and 81.

A **real injury** <note>original: "injuria realis"; a physical act of aggression or insult rather than spoken words</note> is where someone proceeds to an act, which nevertheless ends outside of that person’s body. Properly speaking, an injury is either **verbal** or **real**: verbal injury occurs either through spoken words, or in writing, or through things bearing a resemblance to writing. Real injury is committed either outside the body properly, or is **personal**, which ends upon the person. It is customary for jurists to reduce a three-part division to a two-part one, following the example of *Law 5 of the Digest on Pacts.*

Those who have suffered an injury estimate its value. Thus, in Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentinæ"</note>, many signs of theft were present against a woman, and an inquiry was made with the knowledge of the Magistrate; the woman, later found innocent, estimated this injury at 2,000 florins, yet she obtained nothing because it was done by the Magistrate's order. **The execution of the law does not constitute an injury** <note>original: "Juris Executio non habet injuriam"</note>, *Book 13, Section 1, and Book 33 of the Digest on this title.* Master Doctor Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes, page 311.* He who inflicts a verbal injury on a man and immediately revokes it is not held liable for injuries. Through revocation, the action for injuries ceases. Justus Oldekop, in *Criminal Observations, title 5, observation 27.* In some places, the injurer is held to pay a certain price for his infamy as a fine for the insult, which is called **Lie-money or Mouth-money** <term>Lugen- oder Mundgeld: A traditional German legal fine paid as compensation for slander or verbal insults</term>. See the *Supplement to Wehner’s Observations, page 43.* According to the words of Lyra: those who do not know how to respond aptly and reasonably turn themselves to insults and retorts of injuries; yet, on the contrary, it remains true that the little Aesopic sheep standing downstream must be the one who "muddies the water" for the wolf dwelling in the higher place <note>A reference to Aesop's fable where the wolf finds a false excuse to eat the lamb</note.

> A hedgehog can take no better revenge than when he puts his head between his legs and lets the dogs bite at him. For by this, the dogs get bloody mouths, and the hedgehog suffers no harm. Just so shall you be invincible, when you care nothing for all mockery and contempt. Schupp in *Lucidor*, letter G.

A legal brief for injuries must contain the year and the month, even if it is a civil proceeding. Eberhardus Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated, page 25.* He who "affects" a virgin or a matron—that is, who frequently follows her silently against good morals—is held liable for injuries; for constant following provides, as it were, a certain infamy. *Law 15, sections 22 and 23 of the Digest on injuries.* If anyone who has suffered an injury remains silent, his silence shall remain forever <note>meaning he loses the right to sue later</note> *Law 10 at the end, Code on the revocation of donations.* Rebhan in *The Guide, page 658.* Hamburg City Law, *part 4, article 58.* Can an injury done to a Judge be punished by that same Judge? Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated, book 1, observation 39.* One who is falsely accused of a crime does not have to fear an action for injuries if he retorts the lie upon the injurer with some exaggeration, as if he had brought it forth as a robber and adulterer. Master Carpzov, *part 3, Decision 247, number 25.* Outspoken speeches, accusations, or injuries. Master Suttinger, *observation 15, number 3, Question.*

<column-break/>

The question is at what time an action for injuries is prescribed <note>expires due to the statute of limitations</note>, and it is said that it does not last beyond a year. *Law 5, Code on this title.* It is asked which "year" is understood here, and it is said to be a **useful year** <term>Annus Utilis: A legal term referring to a year made up only of days on which the court is in session and the plaintiff is legally able to act</term>. *Law 14, section 2, on things done through fear.* The reason is that the Praetor’s jurisdiction was enclosed within a year; for what if the action had been instituted in the later months of that jurisdiction? But he whose jurisdiction is not beyond a year ought not to delay and prolong this action any further. A "useful year" is twofold: 1. By reason of the beginning, so that the beginning is useful, and thereafter the days are continuous; 2. By reason of all days. A year is useful: 1. So that the plaintiff has the power of acting. 2. The defendant has the power of responding. 3. So that there are judicial days according to *Law 1, Digest on various and temporary prescriptions.* If, therefore, in every single day the year were "useful," the time would be too long. An injury, whether verbal or real, inflicted upon a **Doctor** <note>A scholar or university professor</note> is called **atrocious** <note>original: "atrox"; a legal category for especially heinous or severe insults</note>, and is to be punished more heavily than if it were done to a commoner, Walther *on the privileges of Doctors, page 323.* For an injury done to a Doctor, one can act under the Julian Law. *page 324.* Injuries from friends are the most serious. Master Rittershusius, *Sacred Readings, page 564.* An injury can even be done by omission. Master Doctor Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes, page 11, Question.* Regarding **symbolic bites** <note>original: "anmorsus figuratos"</note>, such as "pokes" or "stings" <note>original: "Stangen"</note>, if anyone thinks he is being silently noted, should he rather pretend silence than immediately seek vengeance? Marquer, *book 2 on Existence, chapter 8, number 8.* **He who cannot understand a jab should not go among people.** <note>original German: "Wer nicht kan imppf verstehen, soll nicht zu Leuten gehen."</note>

### 46. Pardon, Indulgence.
**Pardon** <note>original: "Indultum"</note>, **Indulgence**, and the Remission of crimes belong to the Prince, and are counted among the **Reserved Rights** <term>Reservata: powers held exclusively by the sovereign</term>. Klock, *volume 1, counsel 37, numbers 63, 64.* However, such rights can be acquired through custom. *Number 65, ibid.* A pardon is, in essence, a document of formal request, according to Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation on Fiefs, page 146.* On Indulgences, see Antonius Rosellus of Padua and Ludovicus Bologninus. F. A. thesis 93* provides more. Pacts added immediately are said to be inherent in the business itself. *Barbosa book 14, axiom chapter 1, axiom 19.* Master Paulus Gambs, *Inaugural Disputation on Added Pacts.*

### 49. I will. *Volo.*

A word harshly spoken or written is not immediately an **injury** <note>original: "injuriosa"; meaning a legal insult or slander</note>. Rupertus, *on Florus, book 3, chapter 21, section 6.* For so mortals are accustomed. Injuries go in a circle; they are kindled by mutual turns and compensated, as Brunn speaks, *book 15 of the Annals, page 958.* But mostly this is against humanity and good morals. For in this way, anger leaves nothing behind, and "deep ashes bury the entombed nations," as the Tragic judge says in *Hercules Furens, verse 361.* A noble man does not remember an injury. Rupertus, *on Florus, book 3, chapter 21, section 19.* From an injury comes a recommendation, *book 4, chapter 4, section 4, 2.* The memory of injuries lasts longer than that of benefits. *Book 4, chapter 2, section 92.*

For what constitutes an "injury," see Master Doctor Biccius in his *Golden Titles, section 4, thesis 154.* Its principal divisions are there as well. Whether the truth of a reproach excuses one from an action for injury. *Ibid, letter Aa.* Master Doctor Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes, page 311, end.* On the **defamatory picture** <note>original: "pictura famosa"; a visual libel</note>, see the *Strasbourg Juridical College, book 47, title 10, theses 38, 39, 40.* As once in Leipzig, a tailor (as Doctor Biccius told me) asked a painter to paint an angel on his shop sign. The painter promised and did so. But when rainy weather arrived, the tailor's neighbors asked him why he had a billy-goat painted on his sign? Then the fraud came out: the painter had painted a goat underneath with oil colors, and an angel over it with water colors. On jests, many things are collected in Zahn, *On Lies, book 1, chapter 45, throughout.* In cases that

# Letter I.

These concern deeds, injuries, and slanderous descriptions. Nuremberg *against* Bavaria regarding the point of Restitution, from the chapter on Amnesty and Grievances, *folios 80 and 81.*

A **real injury** <term>injuria realis: an injury through an action, such as a physical assault or a tangible deed</term> exists where someone proceeds to an act, though it is limited to something outside the victim's person. Properly speaking, an injury is either **verbal** or **real**. A verbal injury is committed through spoken words, or through writing—either formal documents or things bearing a resemblance to writing. A real injury is properly committed outside the body. A **personal injury** is one that terminates on the person. It is customary for legal experts <term>JCtis: Jurisconsultis, or legal scholars</term> to reduce a three-part division to a two-part one, following the example of *Law 2 of the Digest on Pacts.*

Those who have suffered an injury estimate its value. For example, when many signs of theft were present against a woman in Strasbourg, and an investigation was conducted with the Magistrate's prior knowledge, the woman was later found innocent. She estimated the injury at 2,000 florins, yet she obtained nothing because the search was done by the Magistrate's order. **The execution of the Law does not constitute an injury** <note>original: "Juris Executio non habet injuriam"</note> *Book 13, section 1; Book 33 of the Digest on this title; Mr. Dr. Ludwig, Disputation on the Institutes, page 311.* A person who inflicts a verbal injury on someone but immediately recants it is not held liable for injuries. Through revocation, the legal action for injuries ceases. Justus Oldekop, in *Criminal Observations, title 5, observation 27.* In some places, the injurer is required to pay a certain price for the infamy caused by the insult, which is called **Lie-money or Mouth-money** <note>original: "Lugen oder Mundgeld"</note>. See the Supplement to the observations of Wehner, *page 43.* According to that saying of Lyra: Those who do not know how to respond aptly and reasonably turn themselves to insults and the throwing back of injuries; <note>The following is a German proverb based on Aesop</note> yet on the other hand, it remains true that the little Aesopic lamb standing down by the brook must be the one making the water muddy for the wolf situated in the higher place. A hedgehog cannot avenge itself better than when it puts its head between its legs and lets the dogs bite at it. For by doing so, the dogs get bloody mouths, and no harm comes to the hedgehog. Just so, you shall be invincible if you care nothing for all mockery and contempt. Schupp in *Lucidor, letter G.*

A **libel of injuries** <term>Libellus injuriarum: the formal written complaint in an injury case</term> must contain the year and the month, even if the case is handled as a civil matter. Eberhardus Fabricius in *Gailius Enucleatus, page 25.*

Anyone who harasses a virgin or a matron—that is, follows her frequently and silently against good morals—is held liable for injuries; for such constant following creates a certain infamy. *Law 15, sections 22 and 23 of the Digest on injuries; Section 1 of the Institutes on the same.*

If someone who has suffered an injury remains silent, his silence shall remain forever <note>meaning he waives the right to sue later</note>. *Law 10 at the end of the Code on revoking donations.* Rebhan in *Hodegeta, page 658.* Hamburg City Law, *part 4, article 58.*

Can an injury done to a Judge be punished by that same Judge? Eberhard Fabricius in *Gailius Enucleatus, book 1, observation 39.*

One who, having been falsely accused of a crime, flings the lie back at the injurer with a certain exaggeration—as if the other had brought it forth like a robber or adulterer—has no reason to fear a legal action for injuries. Mr. Carpzov, *part 3, Decision 247, number 25.*

Poured-out speeches, accusations, or injuries. Mr. Suttinger, *observation 15, number 3; Quistorp in Besold, Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

Regarding how much time must pass before an action for injuries is barred by the statute of limitations: it is said that it does not last beyond a year. *Law 5 of the Code on this title.* The question is asked, what kind of year is understood here? It is said to be a **useful year** <term>annus utilis: a legal year consisting only of days when the court is in session and the plaintiff is able to act</term>. *Law 14, section 2, regarding cause of fear.* The reason is that the Praetor's jurisdiction was included within a year; for what if the action had been instituted in the final months of that jurisdiction? But he whose jurisdiction does not extend beyond a year ought not to delay and prolong this action any longer. A "useful year" is twofold: 1. By reason of the beginning, so that the start is a "useful" day, and thereafter the days are continuous. 2. By reason of all the days. A year is "useful" when: 1. The plaintiff has the power to act. 2. The defendant has the power to respond. 3. There are judicial days, according to *Law 1 of the Digest on various and temporary prescriptions.* If, therefore, the year were "useful" only in regards to individual days, the time would be too long.

An injury, whether verbal or real, inflicted upon a **Doctor** <term>Doctor: here meaning a Doctor of Laws or a high-ranking scholar</term>, is called "atrocious" and is to be punished more severely than if it were done to a commoner. Walther, *on the privileges of Doctors, page 323.* For an injury done to a Doctor, one can sue under the Julian Law. *Page 324.* Injuries from friends are the most grievous. Mr. Rittershusius, *Sacred Readings, page 564.* An injury can also be committed by **omission** <note>failing to do something one is obligated to do</note>. *Argument from Law 2 of the Digest on the Pompeian Law on parricide; Law 5, second to last section, on the Julian Law of Majesty.* Mr. Dr. Ludwig, *Disputation on the Institutes, page 311.*

Question: Whether "figurative bites" or "poles" <note>likely referring to symbolic insults or satirical signs</note>, by which someone thinks they are being silently marked, should be ignored in silence rather than immediately avenged? The former is affirmed through *Law 7, section 4 of the Digest on injuries.* Marquard Freher, *book 2 on Existence, chapter 8, number 8.* **He who cannot take a joke should not go among people.** <note>original: "Wer nicht kan Schimpff verstehen, soll nicht zu Leuten gehen."</note>

### COPY of the Summons regarding injuries: H. against I. & Associates.

We, **Ferdinand the Third**, by the Grace of God, elected Roman Emperor, etc. send Our and the Empire's dear, faithful, and devout Hans Adam and Susanna I., currently residents of the city of R., then Hans Wilhelm F. of L. V. W., and Georg Wilhelm of B., Our Grace, Love, Faithful, and Devout.

To Our Imperial Chamber Court <term>Cammergericht: the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</term>, Our and the Empire's also dear and faithful I. H. has most humbly given us to understand that, although in the known laws, general Imperial statutes, and other ordinances it is healthfully and well-provided, and also earnestly commanded and ordered under high penalties, that no one—whoever they may be—should touch another’s well-established honor, disparagingly traduce them, or burden them with all kinds of injuries, much less to order them to be poorly treated by secretly hired servants, to feign a feud, and to threaten all sorts of self-assumed impropriety; nor should anyone allow themselves to be hired for this purpose to injuriously attack other honorable people and to overrun them in their own houses in an improper manner, to feud with them, and to threaten all kinds of inconvenience, but rather each person, if they have a claim or demand against another—

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

If anyone believes they have a claim, they should use the honest paths of the law and be satisfied with that; however, you, S. and H. A., have observed this in the least, but rather acted entirely against it in a punishable manner. When, on the 27th of February / 8th of March last, at a wedding held at an inn, the Plaintiff entered into a conversation with you, Susanna, toward evening during the dance, and mentioned—with quite mild words—that he had previously been treated scornfully by you, you quite immodestly called him and other honest people liars. Furthermore, without any cause, you brought the Plaintiff's noble status or lineage into dispute; when he said nothing more than that he would not let himself be despised by you, and was as good as you and yours, you immediately burst out most **insultingly** <note>original: "injuriosè"</note>. When he said he was as good as you, you told him he lied like a frivolous rogue and a thief, and in such a manner that he was compelled to answer again **in defense of his honor** <note>original: "pro defensione honoris"</note>. And although people parted from one another that evening over this, you, S. and H. A., were not satisfied, but on the following Wednesday, the 28th of February / 9th of March, you hired and appointed two noblemen—namely H. W. of [etc.] and you, G. W. of [etc.], both landed subjects of Palatinate-Neuburg—to further insult the Petitioner. You went to harass him improperly in his own dwelling, which **should be every man’s safest refuge** <note>original: "cuivis tutissimum receptaculum"</note>. You two noblemen willingly and joyfully allowed yourselves to be used for this purpose, and that same morning came to the Plaintiff, addressed him immodestly, and in the name of the woman, Susanna, demanded a formal apology and sought **satisfaction** <term>satisfaction: a formal legal or social redress for an insult to one's honor</term> for what had happened the previous evening at the dance. When he answered mildly—stating that since he was the one insulted by you, Susanna, and not you by him, he should be the one given satisfaction for his honor’s sake—you two, hired and appointed **to commit insult** <note>original: "ad injuriandum"</note>, went back to report to your principals. But before a quarter-hour had passed, you returned, and in the name of Susanna, you not only verbally suggested a supposed **counter-insult** <term>retorsion: a legal defense where one claims their insult was a justified response to a previous insult</term> (though no insults had occurred on his part), but beyond this, you attacked him in a most punishable way with many heaped-up insults. You declared that you would hold him for a frivolous rogue and a thief, and would proclaim him as such to everyone, as well as a scoundrel, a dog, etc., as long as you lived; that whenever you saw him or heard of him, you would spit at him, and further, you intended to have him mistreated by secretly hired servants. You said he should be safe from you neither on the open streets nor roads, with the further meaning that you, Susanna, confessed that you had called the Petitioner a rogue and a thief the previous day at the dance, and you had this told to him once more: that if he said he was as good as you or your lineage, then he was a frivolous

<column-break/>

rogue and a thief. And although after this had been repeated several times, you hired and appointed noblemen—having carried out this inglorious execution and task—each departed, yet you returned about an hour later, and thus for the third time, to his dwelling. You, Susanna, accompanied them to the house yourself, and being thus escorted, repeated the aforementioned abusive words, insults, and threats with even greater immodesty, **heaping injury upon injury** <note>original: "injurias injuriis cumuliret"</note>. You made it as gruesome as you possibly could, and along with many threats (as all of this shall be brought forward in detail and **point by point** <note>original: "articulatim"</note> in the **bill of complaint** <term>klag-libell: the formal written statement of a plaintiff's case</term>, proven, and executed in the **presentation of the case** <note>original: "deductione causæ"</note>), you again took your leave.

Since these are the kind of insults that the Plaintiff could never sit through, and which he could not let pass unnoticed **while keeping his honor intact** <note>original: "salvo suo honore"</note>—especially as they were reiterated so many times that there is no room to doubt your **purpose and intent to insult** <note>original: "de proposito & animo injuriandi"</note>—these things went to his heart all the more painfully because you insulters (both Susanna and her associates, as well as you two hired noblemen) are of full age, reason, and experience. You should and could have well known that such things are punishable and forbidden. Nonetheless, you would not agree to a friendly satisfaction for the Petitioner, but both on the very next day (when you were sent for by him) you repeated such insults, and have persisted in them until this hour, continuing your threats and seeking all means and opportunities to bring him into misfortune. Therefore, to place himself in safety and because of such heaped-up, highly punishable injuries inflicted **out of premeditation and after a lapse of time** <note>original: "ex proæresi & intervallo"</note>, it was necessary for him to make use of the legal means and remedies available. Indeed, he would rather not have 20,000 Thalers—and would rather lose more from his own—than to let such **most atrocious injuries** <note>original: "injurias atrocissimas"</note> pass by unpunished and in silence. And because the interested parties and insulters here are **from different legal jurisdictions** <note>original: "diversi fori"</note>—you, S. and W. A., being at the time subject to the authority of the City of R., but you other two co-defendants of the nobility, H. W. and G. W., being landed subjects in Palatinate-Neuburg and therefore subject to the **jurisdiction** of Wolfgang Wilhelm, Count Palatine of the Rhine—and because this matter is sought **based on the same grounds and for the same end** against all of you together, We are petitioned to issue this Our Imperial Summons. This is done **because of the cohesion of the case and so that he is not forced to litigate the same matter or business before different judges** <note>original: "ob causæ continentiam & ne ejusdem rei vel negotii causam coram diversis judicibus litigare cogatur"</note>. The collective jurisdiction is founded upon the well-known laws and judicial ordinances, and the matter appropriately belongs there. Accordingly, he has humbly called upon Us to grant this Our Imperial Summons to you, so that

### 52. Tallow. <note>original: Inschlicht. Sebum.</note>

Others write it as *Unschlit*, meaning tallow or animal fat. Concerning the tax and inspection of tallow, as well as the prohibition of its export from the country. *Bavarian Provincial Ordinance, book 5, folio 24.* See also the word **Soap**.

### 53. Inventory. <note>original: Inventarium.</note>

See **Found-book** <note>original: Fundbuch; a register of assets.</note>. Regarding what things ought to be recorded in an inventory, see *Supplement to Wehner, folio 38.* Several authors have written specialized treatises on inventories, including *Francesco de Porcellini, Sebastian Monticulus, and Rolando à Valle*, whom *Lord Rebhan* praises. To these should be added *Angelo Petrus, Johannes Corrasius, Guido Papæ, and Zorer, part 1, question 9, number 950.* By the drawing up of an **Inventory**, the acceptance of an inheritance <note>original: "Aditio hereditatis"</note> is not presumed (number 651). *Phannucius de Phannuciis* wrote about the inventory. Regarding the acceptance of an inheritance with the benefit of an inventory, see *Baldus de Perusio*. For the proper form of drafting an inventory, see the aforementioned *Guido Papæ*.

One is deprived of the "benefit of inventory" <note>A legal protection allowing an heir to limit their liability for the deceased's debts to the value of the assets in the inventory.</note> if they request time for deliberation. *Fr. Marci, decision 28, part 1.* On whether a son loses his "legal portion" <note>The minimum inheritance guaranteed by law.</note> for failing to complete an inventory, see *Johannes de Castillo, part 3, chapter 5.* Children of a first marriage are held liable to their stepmother for a failure to complete an inventory, even if the estate is insolvent. *Fr. Marci, decision 57, part 1.*

<column-break/>

### 54. In the Original State. <note>original: Integro Statu.</note>

On what the term "in the original state" implies. Discussed at length in the *Acts of Lindau, folios 877 and 878.*

### 55. Janissaries among the Turks. <note>original: Janitſeri apud Turcas.</note>

Who the Janissaries are <note>The elite infantry units that formed the Ottoman Sultan's household troops and bodyguards.</note>. *Klock, On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 5, numbers 42 and 45.* The army of the Janissaries is rightly called the "terror of the world." *Besold, On Politics, book 1, chapter 10, number 12. Busbequius* <note>Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, a 16th-century diplomat who wrote extensively about the Ottoman Empire.</note> in his *Advice on organizing military affairs against the **Turks***.

### 56. Suspending Justice. <note>original: Justiren. Justetium.</note>

The intermission or suspension of jurisdiction. *Draco, On the Fatherland, page 78.*

### 57. Accusation / Exoneration Court. <note>original: Inzucht.</note>

The praiseworthy **Inzucht** or **Exoneration Court** <note>original: Purgations-Gericht; a court specifically for clearing one's name against slander or formal accusations.</note> at Nuremberg. *Acts of the Teutonic Knights, folio 129.* Accuser <note>original: Inzüchter</note>, folio 201. Accuser and exonerated party. *Ibid.* Add *Felwinger, On the Judge, page 391.* "Inzucht" used in place of "Injuries" <note>Meaning formal insults or slanders.</note>. *Dr. Suttinger, Observation 15, number 3.*

### 58. Enclaved Rights. Incorporated Rights. <note>original: Inclavirte Jura. Incorporata Jura.</note>

See the word **Fief**, section "So they are for the eighth," page 551, and the word **Borders**, page 335. They are also called incorporated rights.

### 59. Coercion. <note>original: Impressio.</note>

Coercion and compulsion. *Klock, volume 1, consultation 51, numbers 42 and 44.* Coercion and compulsion are presumed in cases of extraordinary usurpations introduced against common law. Coercion is deemed to have occurred if there is a just fear of future coercion, even if no physical force follows.

### 60. To Administer Justice. <note>original: Justiciern. Exequi.</note>

To administer justice, or to execute a legal sentence. *Denaisius, On the Law of Absolute Power.*

### 61. Jubilee / Horn. <note>original: Jobel. Cornu.</note>

*Jobel* means horn, and *Jobelin* means horns in Hebrew. See *Limnäus, volume 1, Additions to book 6, chapter 8, number 95.*

### 62. Fulfillment. <note>original: Implementum.</note>

Regarding the failure of fulfillment. *Regnerus Sixtinus* in *Legal Opinions, in Resolution of Question 5, in the preface.* One who does not satisfy their part of a contract cannot benefit from that same contract, nor can they compel the other contracting party to fulfill the pact or contract. *See the law "I seek," section "between the lessor," in the Digest on leasing; Baldus on the law "seeking," number 46, in the Code on pacts; Jason on the law "since you propose," 2, numbers 4 and 5, in the Code on the same; Mascardus, On Proofs, conclusion 387, number 9, and throughout; Cravetta, consultation 246, number 3; Alciatus, consultation 7, number 5, book 8; Decianus, consultation 60, number 44, volume 2; Bursatus, consultation 101, number 16, volume 1; Modestinus Pistoris, consultation 2, number 30, and consultation 45, number 3, volume 1.* The **Defense of non-fulfillment** <note>original: Exceptio implementi non secuti</note>, or of faith not kept, cannot be raised, however, if one has by their own act—and indeed not by one, but by many—done that which...

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical legal and historical dictionary from the previous section. ...what is intended to be called failure of performance <note>original Latin/German: "non secutum implementum"</note> is approved and strengthened. That rule—stating that one may withdraw from a contract due to failure of performance, and that it is permitted to break faith with one who has broken faith—only applies regarding the same chapter of the agreement, or at least a connected one, but not in separate or diverse matters. The legal defense <term>exception: a formal plea used to delay or defeat a claim</term> of non-performance rescinds the entire contract. *Berlichius, part 2, decision 174, number 9.* This defense has a place in connected matters and in reciprocal acts, even those celebrated by different persons. *Decision 175, numbers 6 and 7.* It is not the defendant who uses this defense who must prove it, but the adversary against whom it is opposed. *Decision 174, from numbers 1 to 7.* A judge can supply this defense by virtue of his office <note>Latin: "ex officio"; meaning the judge acts on his own authority without a request from the parties</note>. *Decision 174, number 8.* On whether a third party can allege this defense, see *Decision 175 throughout.* The observance of performance in accidental pacts is not so strictly required. *Decision 174, number 13.* He who has not fulfilled the agreement himself ought not to complain about a pact not being kept toward him. *Barbosa, Axioms, book 9, chapter 19, Axiom 1.* From a failure of performance, the deceit <note>Latin: "dolus"</note> of him who was bound to perform but did not is argued. *Axiom 2.* He who was bound to perform must prove that he has performed. *Axiom 3.* No one is permitted to withdraw from a settlement <note>Latin: "transactio"</note> due to a failure of performance; rather, action must be taken, and the path of the law used, so that it may be fulfilled. *Cravetta, counsel 854, number 1.*

Regarding the word "Jässen" <note>An archaic German term for fermenting or yeasting</note>. *Master Harsdörffer in the German Secretary, in the second part, book 6, letter 32.* It is taken to mean "to digest." Also "to separate." Also "fermentation."

# K.

On the doubling of the letter "tt." See *Claius, "To the German-loving Reader," in the Descent into Hell and Ascent into Heaven, page 24.*

### 1. Emperor. <note>German: "Kayser"; Latin: "Imperator"</note>

To us, this is the same as the Latin *Cæsar*. According to the testimony of *Justus Lipsius* in his work on pronunciation, the ancient Latins pronounced the word *Cæsar* just as the Germans now enunciate *Kayser*. But regarding the status of the Romano-Germanic Empire, see *Thuanus, book 2, at the beginning, and my own treatise on the Mixed State and in the booklet on the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire.* Regarding the name of the Emperor, see *Dionysius, book 52, page 493, page 508, and page 515 in my copy.*

On the Emperor being a Monarch, see the *Preface to the Religious Peace of Dillingen.* He does indeed establish laws with the advice of the Estates <note>The Imperial Estates: the princes, prelates, and cities that held a vote in the Reichstag</note>; however, this does not diminish his Majesty. *Günther in the*

<column-break/>

*Ligurinus, book 8, verse:* "Though he himself indeed," etc. Therefore, in the time of Frederick I, it was an absolute Monarchy, but in terms of its administration, it was an Aristocratic mixture.

Charles V defended the liberty of Germany while defending certain Estates against others. *Composition of the Peace, chapter 3, question 16.* The Emperor <note>Latin: "Cæsar"</note> even condemned the Elector of Saxony to death. *Sleidanus, book 19, year 1547.*

And that the authority of the Emperor must not be diminished was proved by the author of the *Donauwörth Reminder* <note>original: "Donawertischen Erinnerung"; a legal-political text regarding the 1606 religious troubles in that city</note>, page 143. Heinrich Bebel also observed and warned of this many years ago in his short works (which are subjoined to his *Oration in Praise of Germany*):

> Why do you recount the decrees of the Fathers? Why the words of the Senate,
> Who have always looked out for their own private goods?
> If they would also respect the advantages of the King and the Kingdom,
> And if that which the Emperor ought to have were given:
> Then the unconquered eagle would penetrate to the Chinese and the Indians.
> Thus can the decrees of the Fathers rightly be of help.
> But while all procure their own advantages; and all
> Are accustomed to hold their own will in place of the Law,
> And they cherish plunderers and thieves in their breast,
> Having shaken off the laws and the yoke of the Emperor,
> And while they despise the unfeathered Eagle; while each one labors
> To pluck the feathers from this thin bird and despoil it:
> Let it be no wonder to you (for you, not the King alone,
> accomplish all things)
> If the entire Empire should collapse.

On whether an Emperor can be deposed? See *Master Goldastus in Bohemia, book 1, chapter 5.*

That the Roman Emperor precedes the Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> was acknowledged even by Bethlem Gabor <note>Prince of Transylvania and a leader of anti-Habsburg forces</note>. See *Volume 12 of the French Mercury, page 124.*

On whether the Imperial Majesty gives the deciding vote when the Estates disagree? See *Paurmeister on Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 2, number 62.*

But regarding the power of the Emperor or the Majesty of the Emperor, see *Dietrich on the Supreme Power of the Highest Empire and the Individual Disputation on Imperial Jurisdiction, volume 4 of the Basel Disputations; The Donauwörth Reminder; Arumäus on the Comitia, chapter 3, number 9 and following; Lancellotti in the Temple of All Judges, page 5 and page 270 and following; Riemer on Jurisdiction, M. 2; Academic Discourse on the Bulls, 5; and Pflug in his Oration.*

->**ADDITION.**<-

The Emperor cannot exercise jurisdiction within the territories of the Estates. *Klock, counsel 22, numbers 91, 92, and 93.*

The Emperor has universal jurisdiction only regarding protection, not regarding ownership <note>Latin: "dominium"</note>. *Klock, counsel 7, number 83.*

# Letter K.

Tertullian—and one greater than all Majesty—says in his fourth book *On the Trinity* that "nothing is greater than his Majesty on earth" <note>original Latin: "omni Majestate major... cujus in terra Majestate nihil majus"</note> (referencing book 12 of the Code of Laws). For this reason, he can boast by a better right of a fourfold "B" <note>original: "quadruplici β"</note> and be called "King of Kings, King of Kings, he shall reign," <note>original Greek/Latin: "βασιλεύς, βασιλέων, βασιλέων, βασιλεύσει" (Basileus basileōn...)</note> as Bodin says regarding the Turkish Emperor in chapter 9, book 1146. In his Empire exists absolute power <note>original Greek: "αὐτοκρατεία" (autokrateia)</note>—called *Signoria* by the Italians and *Souveraineté* by the French. No empire is more sublime, as the Emperors Louis IV and Frederick the Fair testified of themselves using the words "over all the world" <note>original German: "über alle Welt"</note>. Cuspinian treats this at great length in *On Austria*; see also Barbosa, book 9, chapter 14, axiom 1. The Emperor alone is the Master of Roman Citizens (Law 3 of the Code *On the Supreme Trinity*). As the "Husband of the Republic," <note>original Latin: "Reip[ublicae] Maritus"</note> he stands out like the morning star among all Kings in the midst of the southern mist. By his word alone he creates a City; by his word alone he creates Doctors <term>Doctor: here meaning a high-ranking academic or legal authority</term>; by mere nomination he appoints Dukes, Marquises, Counts, and Nobles. (Barbosa, same location, axiom 2). The Emperor must always be consulted in doubtful matters (Symmachus, book 1, epistle 33); hence he is called a "living law on earth" <note>original Latin: "animata lex in terris"</note>. (Novella 110; Barbosa, axiom 3). The Emperor is to be chosen only from among the Germans. (Barbosa, axiom 4; Limnaeus on Public Law, book 2, chapter 2, number 82; see also Becher on Public Law, page 34). Arnold Engelbrecht, in his 1640 inaugural address on the Roman-German Empire and the States of the Empire (thesis 6 and following), demonstrated from a continuous series of histories that the Imperial dignity has not been hereditary but elective from the very beginnings of the Empire. The Emperor cannot make the Empire hereditary (Knipschild *On Testamentary Trusts*, chapter 1, number 173). The Emperor cannot be rejected as a biased judge (Ausurer in the treatise *On Rejection*, number 5; Menochius, counsel 194, number 12; Deciani, book 1, counsel 26, number 1; Graevius, conclusion 33, number 5; based on the text in Law 1 regarding the Julian Law on Bribery). Furthermore, Ummius in *On Proceedings*, page 32, discusses how an Emperor differs from a "King of the Romans." On page 130, he notes that an Emperor may be sued before the Elector Palatine in civil cases; but regarding criminal matters, it is questioned. On page 131, the Emperor, if summoned as a Duke, can be called to an *Austreg* judgment <term>Austreg: a traditional legal arbitration process between states of the Holy Roman Empire</term>. On the names "Emperor," "Caesar," "Augustus," "King," and "Prince," see Limnaeus at great length in his *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 1. On the definition of the Emperor, see the whole of chapter 2. On the election of the Emperor, see chapter 3. To dispute the power of the Emperor is considered sacrilege (Rittershusius in *The New Constitutions*, page 62, number 12).

Regarding the Emperor's Aulic Council <term>Aulic Council: one of the two supreme courts of the Holy Roman Empire, dealing with matters of imperial feudal law</term>, see Stirn *On the Constitutions of Princes*, volume 4, sections 9 and 10, and title 12, sections 6 and 7. On whether and to what extent the administration of Imperial business belongs to the Emperor, see title 2, section 1; title 3, sections 9 and 10; and title 4, sections 9 and 10. On whether it is permitted to appeal from a "Caesar poorly informed" to one "to be better informed," see Eberhard Fabricius at length in *Gailius Enucleated*, page 61. On the power and jurisdiction of the Emperor, see Mr. Georg Christian Mansisch. On the difference between *Caesares* <note>the Emperors</note> and *Caesones* <note>those cut from the womb, i.e., C-sections</note>, see Limnaeus, book 1, chapter 1, number 19. On those called "Innates" <note>original German: "Ingeniti, Ausschindling"</note>, see number 20, and Wehner in *Practical Observations* under the word *Usschindling*.

On the power of the King of the Romans, and whether and to what extent he can confer benefices in the absence of the Emperor, see Symphoreus Gylmann, volume 1, part 3, folio 55.

<column-break/>

On the Power of the Emperor, see Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, counsel 1; Besold in the treatise *On Majesty*, chapter 4, folio 28; Gilhausen in *Civil Judicial Practice*, chapter 1, part 1, section 1. No one can style himself "Emperor" in an absolute sense unless he has been crowned by the Roman Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>; otherwise, he is only "King of the Romans" or "Emperor-Elect." See Caspar Ens in the *Political Treasury*, book 1, chapter 6, folio 129. Regarding the phrase "Under the Emperor's indignation," or "to plead for the Emperor's peace," <note>original German: "bey dem Kayser Fried bitten"</note> see *The Forum of Protestations*, page 268. Regarding "Portraits of the Imperial Virtues," <note>original German: "Von der Kayser Tugend Bildnüssen"</note> see our own Betulius’s *East-Land Laurel Grove*.

### 2. Empress. *Imperatrix*.

Regarding the *Augusta* <note>title of the Empress</note>, see my writings scattered throughout *Politics and Jurisprudence*, and on whether she possesses "Majesty," see Limnaeus on Daniel Otto’s *Public Law*, folio 12 and folio 40. The Emperor Otto, in a certain charter displayed by Faber in the *Montferrat Counsels*, folio 1, calls his spouse a "partner in the Empire" <note>original Latin: "Imperii participem"</note>.

### ADDITION.

*Augusta* means "venerable and reverend." Thus, Justinian calls his Theodora "venerable" (in the last section of the Institutes *On Usucaption*) and his "most reverend Spouse" (number 8, chapter 1). For this reason, Bodin unfairly condemns him; Justinian calls her this not on his own behalf, but on behalf of his subjects. See Hilliger on Donellus, commentary 23, chapter 2, letter Y. Regarding the ancient privileges of the *Augusta*, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 14, numbers 7, 8, and 9. On where an Empress is anointed, see number 19. On whether the crime of "lese-majesty" <term>lese-majesty: treason or an offense against the dignity of the sovereign</term> can be committed against the *Augusta*, see numbers 25 through 28 and following. The *Augusta* has almost the same privileges as the Emperor (Otto in *Public Law*, page 188). The *Augusta* is also permitted to make a will and to change one already made (Pacius, *Analysis of the Code*, page 591).

Regarding the phrase "if it shall so please," see Mr. Speidelius in the *Mirror of Notable Things*, page 679, at the beginning.

### 3. Imperial Prerogatives and Reserved Rights. *Reservata Imperatoris*.

"Regalia" are so named from the word for King (*Rex*). In our language, these royal and sovereign rights are indicated as "Imperial Prerogatives and Reserved Rights" <note>original German: "Kayserl[iche] Hochheiten und Reservaten"</note>. They are defined as rights that belong to the Emperor (or to another with his consent) for the sake of preserving the Republic. (Borcholt in the repetition of the unique chapter *What things are regal*, number 2; Vultejus, book 1, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, number 6 and following; see also my own work in the special Disputation under the word *Regalien*).

### ADDITION.

Stamler wrote a treatise *On Imperial Reserved Rights*, and Schöffer an inaugural conclusion *On Caesar’s Reserved Rights*.

A "reservation" presupposes that a reserved right existed beforehand (Barbosa, book 16, chapter 43, axiom 2). "Regalia" are so called as if they were "strongly Kingly" <note>original Latin: "valdè Regia"</note>. (Gothofredus Antonii, *Feudal Disputations*, 3, thesis 6, letter b). Whence Günther, in book 7, most appropriately calls them "Royal Rights." Baldus in the *Proem to Fiefs* and Everhard in *Topics*, location 129, number 9, call them "the most sacred of sacred things." Cicero calls them "the rights of Majesty."

The Germans call these: **Imperial Highnesses and Reserved Rights** <note>original German: "Kays. Hochheiten und Reservaten"</note>. See Clapharius, *On the Secrets of the State*, book 1, chapter 10. Also the Imperial Recess of Regensburg from the year 1576, in the section beginning "thereby then" <note>original German: "§. dardurch dann"</note>. Otto in *Public Law*, page 307. These rights of the Roman Emperor are his own, as the text argues in Law F. 14, in the Preface of the Constitution of Emperor Frederick regarding the Peace of Constance, in the section "we will," regarding the **Regalia** <term>Regalia: the specific rights, powers, and privileges held exclusively by a sovereign</term>, where it says: "Those things which specifically belong to our Excellence." Indeed, they belong to the Emperor either by possession or by grant, as they are granted to others only by the Emperor. See the Imperial Recess of 1530 at the end of page 235, where it says: *Whoever holds Royal Rights from Us or the Holy Roman Empire.* <note>original German: "So Regalien von Uns oder dem H. Röm. Reich hat."</note> Bocer, in *On the Regalia*, page 8, states: "The Emperor is judged to take others into a **share of the responsibility**, but not into the **fullness of power**" <note>original Latin: "in partem sollicitudinis, non verò in plenitudinem potestatis"</note>; for that power rejects all division and is like a **Holy of Holies**, into which no one is admitted except the Prince. Becker, in *F. P.*, page 60, says: "The Greater Regalia are said to be joined to the Emperor’s very bones, so that they cannot be torn from him." Bartolus Camerarius, in his repetition on the chapter *Imperialem* regarding the prohibition of alienating a fief by Frederick, notes that they cannot be separated from the Prince any more than the rays of the sun can be separated from the sun itself. Barbosa, book 16, chapter 20, axiom 1.

See **Regalia** below under the letter R; regarding what is required for Regalia to be seen as granted, Lord Doctor Ludwig lists them in his *Feudal Synopsis*, chapter 13, page 77.

### 4. Imperial Government. *Regimentum Imperii*.

Emperor Maximilian I, alongside the Imperial Chamber Court <term>Cammergericht: the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</term>, also established a **Governing Council** <note>original German: "Regiments-Rath"</note>. Because he was away from the Empire on account of the Turks and the King of France, he could not conveniently exercise his Imperial Highness and Office in the meantime. However (according to the Government Ordinance of 1500, in the preface), so that peace and justice would not be hindered despite his many travels and wars, he ordained, outside of the Chamber Court, another **Imperial or Royal Government** of 16 persons. This body, in the absence of his Royal Majesty, was to handle all Imperial business (except for high matters, etc.) in his stead, and among other things, keep an oversight of the Imperial Chamber Court, so that it remained orderly and that the judgments delivered were executed. Nevertheless, the Emperor reserved for himself the right of revocation. Emperor Charles V also did this later; see the *Donauwörth Memorial*, folio 149, etc.

### 5. Imperial or Royal Ornaments. *Insignia Regalia*.

Regarding the **Royal Ornaments**, commonly called the **Royal Finery** <note>original German: "Königl. Zierd"</note>, see Godfrey of Viterbo, part 19 of his *Chronicles*; Peter von Andlau, *On the Roman Empire*, book 2, chapter 6; and in the notes of Freher, folio 188 and following.

<margin>
See section "likewise if anyone" 44, on the division of things; Law "with keys" 47, on contracting a sale; chapter 1 in the preface 2. F. 2. Otto in *Public Law*, page 280. For what and how many they are, see Crusius, *Swabian Annals*, part 2, book 5, chapter 7, near the end. Onuphrius Panvinius, *On the Imperial Assemblies*, chapter 8 at the end. Gustavus Selenus, *On Chess*, book 1, chapter 5, near the end. Peter von Andlau and Marquard Freher, *Notes on the Roman Empire*, book 2, chapters 6 and 8.
</margin>
**Royal treasures, ornaments, insignia, and symbols** <note>original Greek: "Βασιλικὰ κειμήλια, κόσμια, ἐπίσημα & σύμβολα"</note>, by which the Emperor is placed, as it were, into possession of the kingdom, like the jewels of the Royal Treasury.

### 6. Chamber Fief. *Feudum Cameræ*.

**Chamber Fiefs**, called *Feudum Cameræ* or *Cavenæ*, are so named when a Lord invests a vassal with certain annual rents, payments, or income from his **Chamber** <term>Chamber: the state treasury or private exchequer of a ruler</term>, from his customs duties or other income, which are paid to the vassal annually. These are called **improper fiefs** because the heirs of the vassal (though there is a difference between the law and the custom) are often not burdened with them. They are also not paid to the vassal if the Chamber's income were so diminished that it would suffer want and necessity, or if it were burdened with significant debts. Zasius, *On Fiefs*, chapter 12, conclusion 8.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the Fief of the Chamber and the Cellar <note>original: "Cameræ & Cavenæ"</note>. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations* 1, question 4, letter f. To feudal lawyers, the "Chamber" is the same as the **Treasury**, just as today we also speak of the "Prince's Chamber" <note>original German: "die Fürstl. Kammer"</note>; likewise, "Chamber goods" <note>original German: "das Kammergut"</note> refers to the treasury of the Prince. Rittershusius, *Feudal Partitions*, page 463. Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, page 221, number 13: "A fief of the Chamber is a stipend granted to a vassal by a Lord from his treasury." A **Fief of the Cellar** <note>original Latin: "Feudum de Cavena"</note> is a stipend granted to a vassal from the storehouse. Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, folio 271. Pensions from the Chamber and the Cellar are counted among **immovable property**, and for that reason, a fief is usually established in them. Knipshild, *On Trusts*, chapter 5, number 25. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 4, conclusion 6, number 5, and in the note at letter a. As far as the Chamber Fiefs or **Personal Stipends** <note>original German: "Manngelder"</note> are concerned—as when a vassal is given a certain amount of money, wine, or grain annually as a fief—it is held in such a way that even if the vassal dies at the beginning of the year, his heirs are nonetheless followed and provided with the full year's money, wine, or grain. Berlich, 3, Conclusion 43, number 39. Knipshild, *On the Obligations of a Lord to a Vassal*, page 147, and those cited there.

Regarding the Fief of the Chamber and the Cellar (or *Canepha*, as some read from the Italian idiom), see Lord Doctor Ludwig, *Feudal Law*, chapter 4, in the Manuscript, page 22. Incorporeal things and Rights are counted among immovables, such as when a fief is given from the Chamber or Cellar; in which case the substance and the place of the thing is that **right of ownership** by whose force the lord grants this fief. The "usufruct" <term>Usufruct: the right to enjoy the use and advantages of another's property short of destroying it</term> is the act of receiving what results from the Right of ownership. Lord Doctor Ludwig, in the cited treatise, chapter 12, my page 69. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, page 56, letter A.
