### 7. Combat Wounds. *Wounds the length of a fingernail.* <note>original Latin: "Vulnera longitudine unguis."</note>

**Combat wounds** <note>original German: "Kampffwunden"</note> according to **Saxon Law** <note>original Latin: "Jure Saxon."</note> are those which are as deep as the nail of the middle finger and as long as the longest joint of that same finger. *Rotshitz in Criminal Judicial Process, article 2, number 2* and as I reported above under the word **Capital Jurisdiction** <note>original German: "Halsgericht"</note>. More can be found under the word **Surgeon** <note>original German: "Wundartzt"</note>.

### 8. Coffer-Steward, Stewardship Authority. <note>original German: "Kastenvogt, Vogteylich Obrigkeit"</note>

-> *Church Advocate, The Right of Advocacy.* <- <note>original Latin: "Advocatus Ecclesiæ, Jus advocatiæ."</note>

**Coffer-Steward** <term>Kastenvogt: an official who managed the treasury or "chest" (Kasten) of a church or monastery</term> refers to the **Defender** of a monastery, whom the common people call an **Advocate**. Or it may refer to the **Patron or Founder**; see *Speckhan, century 3, class 1, question 35, folio 434 and following.*

And so an **Advocate** is a **Defender** who speaks on behalf of another, a **Patron**. The word **Steward** <note>original German: "Vogt"</note> is shortened from **Advocate**, meaning a **Guardian** <note>original German: "ein Pfleger"</note>: one who defends a minor <note>original German: "einen Unmündigen"</note>, who has no "mouth" <note>original Latin: "os"</note> to speak for himself. **Legally Capable** <note>original German: "Mundbar"</note> means "without a mouth," for *bar* means "free" or "without"; hence a **Defenseless Place** <note>original German: "Mundbarer Fleck"</note> is one which has no defender. From this, in the old days, Nobles were **Lords of Stewardship** <note>original German: "Vogtsherren"</note> who defended a village in the name of the Emperor. Eventually, from this defense, a jurisdiction was created, the **Stewardship Authority** <note>original German: "die Vogteylich Obrigkeit"</note>, and **Steward** <note>Vogt</note> came to stand for "Lord," as in **Steward of Bern**, **Steward of the World**, etc. It is possible that *Vogtey* <note>Stewardship</note> is a German word, and **Fief of Stewardship** <note>original Latin/German: "Fœdum ein Vogtthum"</note> comes from *vochden, voget*, etc.

In the past, monasteries were like minors, to whom either the Emperor or the founders gave **Advocates, Guardians, or Stewards** <note>original German: "Pfleger, Vögt"</note> who defended them and exercised judgments, both civil and criminal. These men also inspected the accounts and administered all civil matters, but they did so in the **name of the Monastery**, not by their own right. For this, they were given rewards, the **Steward’s Right** <note>original German: "das Vogtrecht"</note>, which included a third part of the **fines** <note>original German: "Freveln"</note>, lodging, hunting rights, and **provisions** <note>original German: "Atz"</note>, etc.

Later, as that defense transformed into a legal right and various extortions arose from it, the defense of the **Advocate** became hated because of the abuse, and that right was the subject of various disputes.

The **Full Right of Advocacy** belongs to the Roman Church and to all Imperial Churches, and to absolute Kings by their own right, as they are the **Nourishers of the Church** <note>original Latin: "Nutritii Ecclesiæ"</note>.

It also belongs to the lords of territories where monasteries are located within that territory, specifically (1) to those who were formerly Kings, such as the **Bavarians, Saxons, Swabians, Austrians**, etc. Later also to those who were invested with a closed territory, to whom **secular authority over the monasteries** is also specifically granted in their investitures. (2) It also sometimes belongs by the reservation of the founders, although they often renounce this right.

What the duty of a **Defender** was, *Pelagius writes in a rescript to Antonina Patritia*, who asked for a monk to be made a Defender; in this, he shows that the duties of a monk and a **Defender** cannot be reconciled. For the monks, he says, there is quiet, prayer, and the labor of their hands; but for these defenders, there is the hearing of cases, contracts, acts of
<meta>Translator note: The text at the bottom "Befoldi Tom. I." refers to the first volume of Christopher Befold's Thesaurus Practicus.</meta>

<column-break/>

public litigation, and whatever either ecclesiastical institutions or the necessity of petitioners requires.

In the past, a monastery was free to take whichever Advocate it wished, according to *Martin Crusius, part 3, folio 273.* Sometimes that right was extended only to the descendants of the **Endowment** <note>original German: "des Stiffts"</note>; see *Stengel, in his Monastery-Logos*, where he writes regarding the **Monastery of the Holy Cross in Werden**:
> However, in the name of our Apostolic See, your parent made this same offering: that while he lives, he shall have the Stewardship of that place; likewise, after his death, his son whom he has now. If that son has an heir, he too shall be the Steward. But if no son remains as an heir to either Manegold or his little son, then it shall be permitted to the Abbess and the Congregation itself to choose a Steward for themselves, according to God, though he must be requested from the Apostolic See.

An example of a free Stewardship, containing nothing but defense, is recorded by Bruschius concerning the **Monastery of Ebrach**: where he writes that a privilege was given to it by the Emperor Louis the Bavarian at Nuremberg in the year of our Lord 1319. In this, it is written that Otto von Wolfskehl, Bishop of Würzburg, confessed that he had no other right of Stewardship over the Ebrach monastery except in the name of the Holy Roman Empire. In the same letters, this Stewardship is commended by Imperial Authority to the aforementioned Bishop Otto, to be exercised only so long, and no longer, as the Abbot of Ebrach has need of it or wishes to use it. Furthermore, a caution was added that if the Abbot no longer wishes to have the Bishop as a Tutor or Advocate, he is free to request another from the Roman Emperor. This very privilege was later confirmed by the succeeding Emperors Charles IV in 1352 and Wenceslaus in 1387.

And on the preceding folio, the same Bruschius records a diploma of Conrad Augustus, son of Emperor Frederick, which among other things contains this: that at the request of Alhard, the venerable Abbot of Ebrach, and his convent of the Cistercian Order, our faithful subjects, we have taken that same church of Ebrach into the protection of our and the Empire's defense, along with its persons and all its goods, and specifically with the estate of Schwabach and its attached parish and belongings, in healthy imitation of our ancestors. By the special paternal authority which we exercise and our own, we firmly decree: that just as the Cistercian Order has always been free and immune from every kind of Advocate according to its primary institution, so henceforth the same church (except for the Roman Emperor alone) shall be subject to no Advocates at all (unless it has voluntarily submitted itself to one, in such a way that it may later change its will) regarding its estates and possessions. But later, these Stewardships became almost hereditary and degenerated into territorial jurisdiction.

But concerning Stewardship, Advocates, and the rights—

### ADDITION.

Regarding civil and criminal matters, certain **Advocates** were formerly appointed by the Emperors, as shown by examples from the Bishoprics of Worms and Würzburg, and the monasteries of Fulda, Kempten, and Weissenburg. ### 9. To buy and to sell: Death-purchase, selling to ruin. <term>Emtio venditio: the legal contract of purchase and sale</term>

The clauses included in instruments of purchase and

<column-break/>

sale are explained by Bertazolios in his *Treatise on Clauses*. But for what it means to buy **by the Bulk** <note>original Latin: "ad Corpus"</note> or **by Measure** <note>original Latin: "ad Mensuram"</note>, see Bertazolios in the said treatise, folio 504; Mozzius *On Contracts*, title *On Purchase*, folio 302; and Lord Bozer, class 2, disputation 3, thesis 19; and see below at the end.

Is only the specific contract of purchase and sale contained and understood by the term "purchase and sale," or are other contracts included under that term? According to Mozzius, *On Contracts*, title *On Purchase and Sale*, folio 300, number 26, there are two opinions of the Doctors of Law. Indeed, some say that no other contract comes under the name of purchase and sale, because the contract of purchase must be considered such that it differs from other contracts of exchange, donation, and the like. This opinion is supported by the text in chapter 1, *On those things done by prelates*, where the contract of purchase and sale is placed as distinct from other contracts.

Those holding the contrary view, however, bring forward the Law *Statu liberi*, section 1, near the middle, in the Digest *On the status of free men*, where the Jurist responds that the word "purchase" comprehends every act by which ownership is transferred. Petrus Costallus, *Adversaria*, part 4, title *On pledges and mortgages*, on law 24, says that when alienation or sale is prohibited, the giving of a pledge is also prohibited. For through pledging, one arrives at a sale, even against the will of the debtor. It is certain that when an act is prohibited or granted, the preparations for it are also prohibited or granted.

However, if someone is prohibited from buying, he is not necessarily considered prohibited from receiving a pledge. Thus, although **deported persons** <note>those banished or stripped of rights</note> cannot buy and sell, they can still pursue actions that descend from those contracts, because that is a "lesser right." But of this last assertion, five limitations are brought forward by Petrus Mozzius:

(1) It fails—meaning this interpretation does not proceed—when mention is made of a **price**, because then it must be understood solely as a purchase.

(2) It fails in **penal or restrictive matters**: because under the name of "purchase," only the contract of purchase would come, as it differs from others. And from this, according to the same Mozzius, it is inferred that if a purchase and sale is prohibited in a sentence or Decree of a Judge, it is understood as purchase in the strict sense, and thus not as any other contract. For the words of a sentence or decree must be strictly accepted and interpreted. This, however, should be understood unless the Law or Statute, by prohibiting sale...

### 11. Purchase Price. Price.

The quantity of the price (whether it be large or small, Surdus, *Consultation 151, number 32*) provides no small conjecture for knowing what is contained in a sale. For when the quantity of the thing is agreed upon, that thing is considered to be fitted to the price. Menochius, *book 3, presumption 73, number 1.* And above all, the quantity of the price argues that the contracting parties did not intend for jurisdiction <note>the legal authority or lordship over land</note> to be included. Barbatius in *the chapter "Rudolphus," number 83, on rescripts*, and Menochius, *book 3, presumption 67, number 47 and presumption 73, number 1.* Namely, when by the inclusion of jurisdiction, the valuation would be rendered unjust and inequitable: because in doubt, it is to be presumed that the price is just and such as it ought to be by law. Surdus, *Consultation 151, number 32*; and thus, regularly, the valuation is according to the return or yield of the thing. Surdus, *in the same place, number 6.*

### 12. Scarcely, with difficulty. Scarcely <note>Latin: "Vix"</note>.

The nature of the word "vix" <note>scarcely</note> is such that it admits no limit, *argued from Law "Vix certis" 53, Digest on judgments; Law "Tutor" 19, at the verse "quando vix," Digest on the Velleian Senate-Consult*; or if it does admit a limit, it nonetheless happens barely and with difficulty, <term>mogis</term> <note>Greek: μόγις; with difficulty</note> or <term>schole</term> <note>Greek: σχολῇ; hardly or at leisure</note>, and thus improperly. *Law "Alienationis" 28, section "vix est," Digest on the Meaning of Words.*

### 13. Tenant Farm. Hide of Land <note>Latin: "Mansus"</note>.

"Keelnhof" was an old word among the Alemanni <note>a Germanic tribal confederation</note> for the same thing as a "mansus" <note>a hide of land, enough to support a family</note>. A *mansus* is said to be as much as one can work with one pair of oxen in a year: *as noted in chapter 1, extra, on censuses, and in the customs of fiefs, if concerning a controversy over investiture of a fief, chapter 1, penultimate section.* Barclay *on the law "if so" regarding the legacy of gold and silver.*

The ancients, in instituting and donating to churches, formerly attributed hides of land almost entirely for the maintenance of the Priest who was placed over the Church. Thus they also formerly had "Curtes" <note>courts or manor houses</note>, that is, a "Keelnhof" or "Renthoff" <note>rent-farm</note>, in the villages, to which the census and returns were given to be carried to the Monasteries.

So also Master Goldastus in his *Observations on the German Warnings of Tyrol, King of the Scots, page 411*, extensively deduces that the "Cölenhof," the "Colonus's hide" <note>original: "Coloni hobam"</note>, and the cultivators of the hides were called "Coloni" <note>tenant farmers</note>, and adds: the word of our countrymen "Keller" <note>cellarer or steward</note> retains its force, which has been corrupted by the common people, since in antiquity it was "Cölner" or "Colonarius," one who exacts the returns from the tenants, whom the Archdukes of Austria in the parts of Upper Alemannia call a "Huobmeister" or Master of the Hide. Just as the overseers or "Villici" <note>bailiffs</note> are sometimes called "Curtiles," so those tenants are always called "Casati," "Casales," or "Hofluth" <note>court-people</note>: who just as today, so formerly, were either freedmen or mostly slaves.

And afterward he adds: in the old book of Hirsau concerning the donation of the Knight Dietmar in the year 1103. There (in Franconia) sixty "jugera" <note>acres</note> made one hide—

...they did; but six hides there made twelve hides for the people of Hirsau <note>Hirsau was a major Benedictine Abbey in the Black Forest</note>. This is found in Crusius, *Part 2 of the Swabian Annals*. However, my own view, which I have observed among writers, is that a **hide** <note>original: "hoba"; a unit of land deemed sufficient to support a family</note> is not a fixed measure of land, but an indefinite one, according to the convenience and opportunity of each location. You can see this disparity even now in the **Rent-farm** <note>original: "Zinshof"</note>, the **Tax-farm** <note>original: "Gülthof"</note>, and the **Tenant-farm** <note>original: "Cölnhof"</note>, whether they be for census, tribute, or service. The word *hoba* migrated from the Germans into the word **Farm** <note>original: "Hof"</note>, with the distinction of names being removed. *Thus far that author.*

Therefore, a **Tenant-farm** <note>original: "Cölnhof"</note> is taken to mean a dwelling and a colonary hide <note>original: "hoba Colonaria"</note>, for a hide or farm-estate where a **Cellarer** <note>original: "Keller"</note> or **Bailiff** <note>original: "Mayer"</note> resides; hence, in this region, the terms **Tenant-farm** and **Bailiff-farm** are taken as synonyms. The clergy in other territories also commonly possess such estates and place a bailiff upon them, who at times participates in some of their jurisdiction in their name.

Thus, the venerable House of God at **Reichenau** <note>A famous island monastery on Lake Constance</note>, in the city of Tuttlingen (which is now incorporated into the Duchy of Württemberg), has a tenant-farm which the possessor holds as a heritable fief; he pays a yearly **fixed rent** <note>original: "Canonem"</note> to the said House of God, and a portion of the tithes belongs to such a farm, as do other goods. No less does the venerable Foundation at **Lindau** possess a **Tenant-farm** <note>original: "Keelnhof"</note> in a village that once belonged to the lords of Bodman and later came to the Imperial City of Überlingen. By virtue of this, a portion of the fines is owed to the high Foundation. And this very thing, which is called a *Keelnhof* in Swabian lands, is denominated as **Cells** <note>original: "Cellas"</note> in other places. By this name one does not mean those Cells within the Cloisters of Monks—namely, secret, solitary places separated from human company, specifically deputed for contemplating and being free for God—as in *chapter "privilegium" regarding the Meaning of Words, in the 6th book of Decretals; Erasmus Chokier, in the treatise on exemptions, part 1, question 43.* In this regard it is often said: *A monk outside his Cell is like a fish out of water.* But besides these, there are other **Monastic Cells**, about which Christopher Brower, in *book 1 of Fulda Antiquities, chapter 7*, writes as follows: Since many estates, lands, and villages had already been added to the wealth of the monastery through the liberality of kings and the prompt zeal of faithful Christians to do good for the cultivators of the piety born here, it was provided by the authority and counsel of the elders that, in order for the administration of these to be more fruitful and faithful, they should put priests and monks in charge of the more cultivated and fertile places; and they built churches there to keep the servants in their duty and to rightly govern the tenants. Indeed, they called these priests **Provosts** <note>original: "Praepositos"</note>. Their duty was, like the parish priests of old, to administer the expenses for the community at Fulda, to provide the necessities for food and worship, to refresh the servants, and to receive pilgrims traveling back and forth. Therefore, just as among the ancients and those speaking Latin, **Cell** <note>original: "Cella"</note> is rarely used for a *private bedroom*, but most often and very frequently for a **pantry** and **storehouse** <column-break/> in which food and drink are stored, and from which provisions are brought forth: so the ancestors of the people of Fulda called that place a **Cell** in which they kept the pantry, grain, and provisions set aside for the use of both the brothers and the guests. These cells, inhabited by frugal fathers of the family and equally religious men, were the nourishers and nurses of the monastic assembly. See also Coccius in *Dagobert, chapter 16, page 151 and following*, where he has much to say about the dual meaning of Cells.

Thus Rudolph, in the *Acts of Rabanus*, first testifies that the estates scattered through various provinces were so administered by him that he committed some to be managed by laymen, but others—especially those equipped with churches—to be managed and disposed of by priests. This is supported by the privilege of Alexander III, recorded by Freher in the *Chronicle of Lorsch, page 96*, by which he decreed that the provostships of cells and the "obediences" of the monastery of Lorsch should only be committed to the monks of the chapter. *Acts of Lindau, page 842.* And the same author in another place reveals the use of Cells in the case of the priest Anthadus: whom he writes was the Provost of the places subject to the Monastery, and that his duty was to supply the necessary items to the brothers from there at stated times.

It seems, therefore, that for the provision of such **Cells**, certain hides or farmsteads were designated. These clearly correspond with our estates which are called **Tenant-farms** <note>original: "Cölnhof"</note>. Add the *notes to Cantipratensis, page 168, and Bignon in his notes, page 630.* Concerning the **Cellarer**, see Alciat, *in his Diversions, book 2, chapter 20.*

1. In name. 3. In the matter: tenant-farms concern Church goods; manorial courts concern secular goods as well as Church ones.
4. In form. Possessors of tenant-farms pay a yearly **fixed rent** <note>original: "canonem"</note>, which is properly what long-term tenants provide (*final law, Code on the Right of Emphyteusis*). Hide-holders pay a yearly census, a <term>Dinckhofszins</term> <note>a rent specific to a manorial court farm</note>.
5. In the purpose. Those fixed rents are collected for the maintenance of the priests who are placed over the Church; the census of the manorial courts is for another purpose. Namely, principally for the sake of preserving mutual concord and friendship contracted between neighbors. Less principally, as can be gathered from the court agreements...

## 14. By no means, not at all. *Nullatenus.*

The expression **by no means** <note>original: "nullatenus" or "nullo modo"; in German "Keineswegs" or "gar nicht"</note> implies the legal nullity of an act, according to the singular gloss on the authority *si qua mulier* regarding the Velleianum decree. When the word *nullatenus* is placed in a law or canon, it carries as much weight as an annulling clause of a decree: and thus it removes the power of granting a dispensation <note>a legal exemption from a rule</note>, as noted by Imola regarding the Clementines on sequestered possession and fruit, specifically on that text's use of the word *nullatenus*. See also Jason on the law regarding pecuniary matters.

But regarding the phrase **in no way, by no means** <note>original: "nullo modo, nullatenus, Keineswegs"</note>, see also Cephalus, counsel 53, number 23, book 1. Castillo on usufruct, chapter 26, number 4 and following. Marsilius, singular 675. Felinus in the chapter *cum accessissent*, number 8, on constitutions. Simon de Pratis on the interpretation of wills, book 2, interpretation 3, doubt 2, number 12 and following. Tiraquellus on the law *si unquam* under the gloss *revertatur*, number 95, on the revocation of donations. Volcmar Heiss on testaments, century 2, conclusion 99, number 2.

Furthermore, the word **in any way** <note>original: "ullatenus"</note>, when preceded by a negation, is universally exclusive, just like the word *nullatenus* in chapter 1 regarding married clergy in the sixth book of Decretals. See also Decius in the chapter on letters, number 13, on rescripts; and chapter *eam te*, number 33, on judged matters. Gigas on pensions, final question, number 10. Jacobus Antonius Martha on the exercise of jurisdiction between the Ecclesiastical and Secular, century 2, case 153. It has the force of a Sentence and an invalidating Decree, and it strips away the ability to act to the contrary. See the gloss on the aforementioned authority *si qua mulier*. Tiraquellus on the law *si unquam*, at the word *revertatur*, number 92, on the revocation of donations.

### ADDITION.

The words **in no way** <note>original: "nullo modo"</note> contain an annulling clause. Klock, counsel 6, number 184. The words **in no manner** <note>original: "in keine Weise"</note>, that is, *nullo modo* or *nullatenus*, when uttered negatively, include everything. Klock, counsel 8, number 76, 77. On the force and efficacy of the words **not at all, thoroughly** <note>original: "nullatenus penitus"</note>, see Klock, counsel 6, numbers 185, 186, 187.

Nothing is understood to be permitted even with a dispensation. Cavallus in his common and contrary commentaries, question 808, number 59. For this expression has such great power that it prevents even every dispensation. Tiraquellus on the law *si unquam* under the gloss *revertatur*, number 93, on the revocation of donations, who in the following numbers attributes the same power to the words **Not at all** and **Thoroughly** <note>original: "Nullatenus & penitus"</note>, treating them as absolute terms that receive neither limitation nor modification. Raudensis, response 20, number 32, book 2. Barbosa on the frequent use of the word *nullatenus*, 226, number 13, and the word *nullo modo*, 228, number 4.

## 15. Tally sticks. *Bacilli fissi.*

**Split sticks** <note>original: "Bacilli fissi"</note>, commonly called **Tally sticks** <note>original: "Kerbhölzer"</note>, are categorized among "improper" instruments or "quasi-instruments." This is because they do not have the true form and quality of a proper legal document, but have been accepted as proof due to their similarity to one. And although they consist of neither letters nor other properties of a formal Document, they nevertheless provide proof as if they were written records and have the same effect as proper documents, following the argument in the law of the Julian Code. See Bornicius on *Instruments*, book 2, chapter 46. Lord Ruland on *Commissions*, part 2, book 5, chapter 12, number 6; Moller, 4th semester, chapter 37; and Boerius, decision 105.

> Regarding **Württemberg Law**, part 1, title 34, *On Tally sticks and Slips*, we read it provided thus: Since at times our subjects satisfy and content themselves with poorly made tally slips or sticks against one another, if someone brings any tally stick or slip into court to prove his debts, and the matching slip or stick is also shown by the other party and found to be identical, then credit shall be given to them, and our court shall rule accordingly. But how one should proceed when the other party has none? See there.

### ADDITION.

A wooden token <note>commonly called **Tally sticks**</note> allows for immediate execution of a judgment. Parladorius, *Daily Questions*, part 1, section 5, number 15. Ummius on *Process*, page 928. Berlich, 1, conclusion 36, number 113. Sticks notched across with grooves, or **Tally sticks**, provide semi-full proof, since by long-standing custom these are very frequent both in the countryside among peasants and in the towns among Citizens. *Speculum*, book 2, part 2, title on documents, section "it now remains to be said," 7, number 4. Sticks notched across with grooves have great power of proof, so much so that a person denying that he received such letters or sticks must take an oath, following the argument in laws regarding deposits and proofs. Wehner, *Practical Observations*, page 438. Those papers which the French call **divided** <note>original: "partitas"</note> and the Germans call **cut slips** <note>original: "ausgeschnittene Zettel"</note>, as well as split sticks used in both country and town, commonly called **Tally sticks**, provide proof because the carved notches demonstrate how much was given or paid, or how much ought to be given, paid, or performed. Boerius, decision 105, numbers 7 and 8, where he advises that the same applies to the **notching of cloth** <note>original: "incissura panni"</note> that has been given for dyeing; a small portion is cut off and given to the Owner for the purpose of identifying it. However, in all these things, as in other proofs, both the local custom and the wisdom and integrity of the judge carry the most weight, as Moller rightly advises in his 4th semester, 37.

### § 6. Candle, selling by the candle.
->Sale by the candle.<-

Sometimes, things are not only sold but also leased and hired out by the water-clock <note>original: "Clepsydra"; an ancient Greek timing device</note> or by the **candle** (which they commonly call **by the candle** <note>original: "bey der Kertzen"</note>). This is done so that if the sand runs out or the candle is extinguished after the **last bid** <note>original: "nach dem letstern Bott"</note>, and before any more spirited bidder can surpass the previous one, the property is awarded to this final bidder, provided they are otherwise suitable. See Hering on Sureties, chapter 6, number 19.

We commonly call this **selling by estimate** <note>original: "auf ein Anschlag verskauffen"</note>; and this is how the **tithes** <note>a tax of one-tenth of agricultural produce</note> are usually given out annually. Namely, the tithe, as it still stands in the field, is estimated at a certain quantity of fruit; then those present "strike" <note>bid</note> upon it with a certain quantity of fruit, and every **strike** <note>bid</note> is recorded.

However, the seller reserves the **last strike** for himself; so that he may either let the tithe go for that amount or keep it for himself.

### § 7. Coppersmith’s Protection. Protection of workers in
->copper.<-

To the class of Protections and their related matters belong those singular **Safeguards** <note>original: "Tuitiones"</note> which are sometimes owed and provided to an entire guild of certain craftsmen by Princes, based on ancient custom or a specific grant from the Emperors. For instance, the **Elector Counts Palatine** <note>high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire</note> have, from time immemorial, held all copper-smiths (called **Keßler** by us) living in the Rhine region and certain parts of Eastern Franconia under their peculiar protection. They hold the **Advocacy** <note>legal guardianship and representation</note> over them as a fief from the Empire, and the most noble **Zobel** family holds it as a sub-fief. This comes with this notable privilege: that the smiths are bound to supply the family with enough copper household utensils for the entire domestic use of the household for free. See Mr. Mager on Armed Advocacy, chapter 15, number 120 and following. And, as I believe, the **Counts of Hohenloe** also have a similar shield <note>protection</note> over the coppersmiths.

Likewise, the protection of the **Potter’s Guild** <note>original: "Hafner-Handwerck"</note>. (In Faenza there live very many potters, and the vessels they make are considered the best in Italy. Zeiller in his *Travels of Italy*, page 209, number 27. See also page 208, where he says: the walls are made of mirror-work and pottery-work, having many colors.) This protection was

<column-break/>

formerly committed to the most noble **Offenburg** family. Its dignity is still diligently defended by Mr. **Henry of Offenburg**, etc., who communicated the Imperial diploma <note>official charter</note> itself to me, which reads as follows:

Thus, the same potters have represented to us that they cannot fulfill such freedom, order, and custom unless they had a **pious man as a Head-Lord**, who would represent and speak for them before Princes, Lords, or Cities, or in other places where it shall be necessary. Also, as they are accustomed to come together every year on account of such ordinances, that he might be present on such days and help them, to see if any among them should act or wish to act against such freedom, order, and custom, and to punish them, and in whatever other matters they would need him—whether with his castles or protection—to be the best help and counsel to them. ### 19. Children. <note>Latin: "Liberi"</note>

Under the term "Children," according to Law 220 in the Digest *On the Signification of Words*, are included grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and all others who descend from them. The **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>the foundational code of Roman law</note> includes all these under the name of "one's own heirs" <note>original: "suorum"</note>. Frequently, the laws find it necessary to use the names of specific relations—such as sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons—when they do not intend for a benefit to be provided to all who come after them, but only to those they list by name. But where it is not provided to specific persons or certain degrees, but to all who are born of the same stock, it falls under the term "children."

### On the Definition and Rights of Children

are included in the term. Hence, in Section 2 of the said law, it is held that a person is not considered to have died without children if they left their grandchild as an heir. Clarus, in his commentary on *law 56, section 1, "cognoscere"*, states: Under the term "children" are included not only those under parental power, but all who are independent (*sui juris*), whether of the male or female sex, or descending from the female line. See Layman in the *Honoldina Case*, number 31 and following; and Modestinus Pistor, part 3, question 118.

Moreover, they are called "children" (*liberi*) because they are given by the generosity of the Gods, or because they are born from us in a free condition and are free by nature. Therefore, this is the natural name for those who descend from us. Tiraquellus, on *the law "si unquam"*, verse "suscepit," number 16, *Code on the revocation of donations*. Since by nature all men are born free, see *Section "The Law of Nations," Institutes on the Law of Nature, Nations, and Civil Law*, and *Section "Institutes on Liberty"*.

If mention is made of "children" in any legal instrument, the question is asked whether "natural" <note>meaning illegitimate children</note> are also included, or whether only "legitimate" children come under this name? See Paleotti, *On Illegitimate Children*, chapter 30.

Likewise, grandchildren are included under the term "sons" (*filii*). See *the laws "liberorum" and "filii" in the Digest on the Significance of Words*, which applies most strongly in last wills and in the arrangements made by ancestors. Bartolus on *law "liberorum"*, column 1; Decius, *Counsel 391*; Curtius Junior, *Counsel 22, Counsel 75, num. 5, Counsel 113, and Counsel 116*. This proceeds most especially when some absurdity would otherwise follow. Curtius Junior, *Counsel 111, num. 8*; Alexander, *Counsel 9, num. 2, vol. 1*.

This is especially true if it appears that the testator, in his arrangement, took into account his agnatic lineage <note>family relations through the male line</note> or his family; in that case, grandchildren are always included under the term "sons" and are considered to have been called to the inheritance. Socinus Junior, *Counsel 19, vol. 1*; Paul de Castro, *Counsel 40, vol. 2*; Curtius Junior, *said Counsel 111, num. 10*; Paris, *Counsel 89, num. 7, vol. 2*. See Hartmann Pistor, *book 4, question 9, num. 36 and following*, where he discusses when "sons" are *not* included under the term "grandchildren." See also Cephalus, *Counsel 72, num. 9*; Sesse, *Decision 53, vol. 1*; Fusarius, *On Substitutions, questions 311, 314, 319, and following*, where he also discusses if and when natural children, posterity, descendants, etc., come under the term "sons." And whether the substitution of "the children" <note>original German: "der Kinder"</note> extends to infinity, see Molinaeus, *Counsel 51*.

The clause or condition "if he should die without children" <note>Latin: "si sine liberis decesserit"</note> fails to take effect if even one surviving son, or a grandchild born of a son or daughter, or a great-grandchild, or even a posthumous child is left behind, as can be seen from *law 2* and the commentary there by Baldus, *Code on conditions inserted*; *law 6, section 2, Code on the Trebellian Decree of the Senate*; and *the law "cum avus", Digest on conditions and demonstrations*. Since a person is not seen to have died "without children" who has even one son or one daughter, they are not "without children." *Digest on the Significance of Words*. For here, following common usage, the plural phrasing is resolved into the singular, or has the force of the singular number, and is verified in a single individual. *Said law "non est sine liberis", law 3, section 2, Digest on the management of affairs*. See Reusner, *On Wills, vol. 2, ch. 7, part 1*.

The condition "if [he dies] without children" is understood to be implied in any fiduciary arrangement <note>fideicommissum, a legal trust where property is held for another</note>. Klock, *vol. 2, counsel 33, num. 58*. Whether the word "Children" <note>original German: "Kinder"</note> designates only sons and daughters according to the mind of Zasius, see Klock, *vol. 3, counsel 104, num. 135 and 146*; see the following *num. 156, 157*. A ward <note>pupillus</note> is also said to die "without children" in *the law "credendum" in the verse "if indeed," Digest on who seeks a guardian or curator*. Bartolus, Imola, Alexander, Alciatus, Zasius, and most others in *law "Centurio" on vulgar and pupillary substitution*, "without bodily heirs" <note>original German: "sine Leibs Erben"</note>, *Altdorf Counsels, fol. 548, 549*. "There is nothing dearer than a grandchild" <note>original German: "Es ist nichts liebers dann Kindskind"</note>, Cypraeus, *On Betrothals, p. 30*. Females do not come under the name of "children" if a statute or legal disposition excludes them. Knipschild, *On Fiduciary Trusts, ch. 1, n. 96, 98*. The name of "children" is common to both sexes. *Ibid. n. 98*. And the determination for "descendants" is one and the same. *Ibid. & ch. 11, n. 297*. Nothing is sweeter than one's own children. *ch. 8, n. 181*. Children born of a noble father and an ignoble mother are noble. *ch. 7, n. 52*. While the parent is still living, children are regarded as quasi-owners of paternal property, as Barbosa explains at great length in *book 10, ch. 17, axiom 1*. It is naturally equitable that children obey their parents. *Axiom 2*. Equality among children is founded on natural law. *Axiom 3*. Children are not permitted to challenge the actions of their father. *Axiom 4*. When a dispute arises regarding the upbringing and maintenance of children, as well as the management of their property, what must be observed in their decision. <note>original German: "Wann Streit wegen der Kinder Erzieh- und Unterhaltung, wie auch Verwaltung deren Güter sich ereignet, was bey deren Entscheidung zu beobachten."</note> Zorer, *part 2, q. 12, n. 844*. <meta>This page continues the philological and legal exploration of the term "children" (liberi/filii), moving from literal definitions to metaphorical usage in various languages, followed by a transition into the criminal laws regarding infanticide and abortion.</meta>

It is a specific observation of philologists <note>scholars of language and literature</note> that the term "children" can also refer to a single offspring. One should consult Augustine, *The City of God*, book 16, chapter 40, and Aulus Gellius, book 2, chapter 16. There is a most delightful *catachresis* <note>the metaphorical use of a word in a way that departs from its literal meaning</note> used by the Hebrews regarding the word **Son**, whenever they apply it to animals and inanimate things. For example, in Psalm 114, <margin>4.</margin> "the mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like the sons of the flock." In Proverbs 30:17, "The eye of a defiant son shall be eaten by the sons of the eagle." Scaliger very wittily used this same trope when he spoke of the *heirs of the Storks*. In Lamentations 3:13, "he has shot into my kidneys the *sons of his quiver*," meaning his arrows. This same elegance is found in the Greek idiom. Pindar describes rain through a roundabout phrase as <note>original Greek: παῖδας νεφέλης</note> *the children of the clouds*. Anacreon the lyricist calls <note>original Greek: γόνον ἀμπέλου τὸν οἶνον</note> *wine the offspring of the vine*; which vine, in turn, is hailed by Euripides as the *mother of wine*. Plautus referred to this in his play *Amphitruo*, making the character Sosia speak of a vessel full of wine: "I drew it out, just as it was born from its mother, as pure wine." *Varro, as cited by Nonius, says that Regret <note>original Greek: μετά μέλον / metamelon</note> is the son of inconstancy.* He also calls the North Winds "frenzied sons of the Seven Stars" <note>the Septentriones or Big Dipper constellation</note>, and calls Truth the "foster-child of Attic Philosophy." Horace, in Book 1, Ode <margin>13.</margin> 14: "Although you are a Pontic pine, the daughter of a noble forest." <margin>Philip Caroli, Book 1, Introduction to New Readings.</margin> When a certain man had diligently planted his wife's garden but had produced no children, he consulted an oracle on how he might obtain offspring. The oracle responded that he should travel abroad and stay away for a long time. It hinted that he was too lustful, and therefore his seed was too watery and fluid, and consequently less fit for procreating children. It thus advised him to travel and stay away from his spouse long enough so that he might return home "well-moneyed" or provided with good thalers <note>coins</note>. A man ought to forge children when the body flourishes, which happens around age 36 or 37; but he ought to bring forth books or the works of the mind when the soul flourishes, which occurs when the number seven is multiplied by itself—that is, in the 49th year. Scherbius, in his *Politics*, pages 358–359. On the Law of Children, see Marcus Vertranius Maurus Gallus. On the number of children exempting parents from public duties, see Ferdinandus Paez of Lisbon.

On the word *Children* <note>German: Kinder</note>, if you please, see the *Saxon Consultations* and Didacus Januarius 2 at the end, annexed to Resolution question 41, number 3 and following, folio 85. In Strasbourg, a person is honored with three shillings if they raise a child for eight years; if they raise two, they receive six shillings, specifically eight days after the Oath Day <note>Schwertag, a local civic ceremony</note>.

### 20. Infanticide, Forcing Miscarriage. *Infanticidium. Abortus.*

In France, a woman who gives birth in secret is executed. In Germany, she is tortured so that it may be known whether she killed the offspring, and thus the very act of secrecy is considered evidence <note>referring to the *Peinliche Halsgerichts-Ordnung*, the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina</note>, article 34 and following. Zanger, *On Torture*, chapter 2, number 171. But concerning infanticide and its signs, see especially Grivell, decision 19, and Berlich, part

<column-break/>

4, conclusion 7, and the *Criminal Ordinance* of Charles V, article 131, and the commentary there by Bodin, *On Demonomania*, book 4, chapter 5. Regarding the draft of abortion <note>the potion used to induce it</note>, see Freher, *Parerga*, book 1, chapter 17; and regarding abortive birth, see Carranza in his treatise *On Natural and Legitimate Birth*, folio 598; and concerning procured abortion and its penalties, Carranza in the same place, folio 606. Is it lawful for physicians to give a draft for abortion? Rhumelius, *On Human Birth*, chapter 6.

->ADDITION.<-

See **Exposing Children**. Is a person worthy of the ordinary penalty for homicide if they have killed a human fetus not yet brought forth—which doctors call an **Embryo**—and forced the birth, or was the cause of a woman miscarrying a conceived fetus? Harpprecht discusses this most extensively in *On Public Law*, section 5, numbers 33, 34, 35. See also Mr. Ludwell's *Disputation on the Institutes*, page 368, where he determines that if a quickened <note>living/animated</note> fetus is driven out, there is room for the ordinary penalty; but if it is unquickened, the extraordinary penalty applies. Finally, he adds that although this opinion is accepted in practice, it does not seem consistent with Civil Law, because even a quickened fetus is not yet a human being, but is only said to have been the *hope* of a human being. Law 9, section 1, *Digest on the Falcidian Law*; Law 14, *Code on the freedom of trusts*. See also Ludwell in his notes on Wesenbeck, title *On Extraordinary Crimes*, Law 38, section 5, *On Penalties*: he who gives a draft for abortion or a love potion is not punished with the capital penalty by reason of the fetus, but because the death followed either of the woman herself to whom the abortion draft was given, or of the person to whom the love potion was administered. Philippus Matthaeus on Law 187, *On Rules of Law*. On the penalties of those procuring abortion and those taking a potion for sterility, see Vivius, decision 92, and *Thesaurus*, decision 12. From what circumstances abortion may be proven and how witnesses are to be admitted, see Vivius, decision 458. On the signs of infanticide, see Metzger *On Torture*, conclusion 140; Bocer *On Torture*, chapter 3, number 121, folio 280 and following; Gilhausen in *The Tree of Crimes*, chapter 6, part 7, on the section of questioning 2, number 82 and following. How infanticide is punished: *Thesaurus*, decision 13; Metzger, *Criminal Consultation* 6; Wittum, *Criminal Consultation* 4. How is a mother who kills an infant in the womb punished? *Thesaurus*, decision 12. For the formula of the sentence in a case of infanticide, see Metzger, *Criminal Consultation* 6 at the end. In the year 1656, in the month of September, Catharina Dörfferin in Leipzig laid hands upon her child; she made a band or rope out of grass, placed it around the child's neck, and intentionally strangled it so that her shame might not be made public. After being held for six weeks, on account of the confessed murder committed against her child, she was placed in a sack together with a dog, a rooster, a snake, and a cat (instead of a monkey) and was thrown into the water and drowned. <note>This refers to the *Poena Cullei*, an ancient Roman punishment for parricide, adapted here for infanticide.</note> Johann Philippi, in *Practical Use of the Institutes*, book 4, title 18, section 5, Eclogue 88, number 8.

## 21. Throwing away or abandoning children. *The exposure of infants.*

Mr. Speidel, in his *Notable Observations* under this word: If an infant is abandoned in a place where one person holds superior jurisdiction and another holds inferior jurisdiction, and it is unknown who abandoned the child, which of them is responsible for the care and education? Response: The one who holds the superior jurisdiction. Berlich, *conclusion 1, number 14.*

### ADDITION.

The abandonment of newborn infants—or "bloody infants," as they are called in the title of the <term>Code of Justinian</term> <note>original: "tit. C. de infant. expof." refers to the legal section on abandoned children</note>—is no light crime. The poet Juvenal calls them "still red from their mother." Famous on this subject are the *Letters of Pliny and Trajan*, book 10, letters 64 and 65. Not without merit does Justinian exaggerate this deed with many words in his <term>Novels</term> <note>new laws issued after the main Code</note> 153, calling it a crime alien to human sense, and something that would be unbelievable even among barbarians—as if to say it surpasses all the monstrous cruelty of barbarism. See more in Rittershusius on the *Novels*, page 695 and following; Pacius, *Analysis of the Code on abandoned infants*; and Wesenbeck on the *Digest* regarding the Cornelian Law on Assassins, and the manuscript notes of Mr. Ludwig there. By the act of abandonment, the <term>paternal power</term> <note>original: "Patria potestas"; the legal authority a father held over his children</note> is dissolved. Mr. Biccius in his *Golden Sections* notes that no one can reclaim their offspring from a person who took them in out of mercy when they were perishing. How a woman who abandons her infant or her birth is to be punished can be seen in Berlich. Under Civil Law, it is at the judge's discretion, but if the children die, she faces the penalty of the Cornelian Law <note>usually death</note>. In <margin>Saxony</margin> however, she is punished by flogging, but if death follows, she faces the penalty for <term>parricide</term> <note>the murder of a close relative</note>. Add Harpprecht on *Public Judgments*. Formerly, parents held the power of life and death over delinquent children, though grandfathers did not. However, this right fell into disuse because paternal power ought to consist of piety, not cruelty. Hence, parents who kill their children are punished with the penalty for parricide—even for illegitimate children, whom Nature does not distinguish from others, as well as those born of incest or adultery. Johannes Philippi, a legal consultant, writes on this in his *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*. The Leipzig Jurists wrote to the Magistrate of Torgau in May 1617:
> He should, on account of the murder committed and confessed upon his child, which he fathered in adultery with N. N., be sewn into a sack along with a dog, a rooster, a snake, and a cat, instead of a monkey, and be thrown into the water and drowned. <note>This refers to the "Poena Cullei," an ancient punishment for parricide where the killer was drowned with specific symbolic animals.</note>

Regarding who should nourish an abandoned infant and who should inherit from them, see Tessaurus, *Pedemontan Decisions*. Whether infants abandoned in public, found and raised—<term>Foundlings</term>—are to be considered as just and legitimate children, or rather as unjust, illegitimate, and base-born; and specifically, whether they can be admitted and promoted to successions, honors, dignities, and ecclesiastical or civil offices. See Speckhan, *century 3, class 1, question 14.*

## 22. Impregnation and child-related matters.

->Defloration <note>the loss of virginity</note>. See below under the letter S.<-

Martin Uranius gave several legal opinions on the point of defloration, which exist in his *Consultations*, volume 3. Can a settlement of this kind be valid in such cases? Uranius affirms it in his 20th consultation, but I doubt it because of the favor owed to the offspring.

A woman who opens her house at night and admits those entering is presumed to be a prostitute, according to Farinaccius, *volume 3, question 136.*

### ADDITION.

On the subject of defloration, much is held above under the word **Maiden**. For the <term>defilers</term> <note>original: "Stupratoribus"; those who commit "stuprum," or illicit sexual acts with a respectable woman</note> of virgins and widows living honorably, the Julian Law imposes a penalty of the loss of half their goods for those of higher status; and corporal punishment, such as flogging with perpetual banishment, for those of lower or more humble condition. Johannes Philippi writes on this in his *Practical Use*. By Divine and Canon Law, the defiler must either marry the woman he has violated or provide her with a dowry. The choice belongs to the defiler. The dowry must be provided according to the social status of the woman. The defiler is bound to provide nourishment for the child if pregnancy follows. If she has mixed herself with many men, she cannot seek support; why? Because of her own conduct. Depending on the quality of the person defiled, the punishment can be made more severe. Can someone be removed from the order or College of Senators because of this crime? Mr. Carpzov affirms this in his *Decisions*. The crime of defilement is considered scandalous. Is the penalty for defilement a capital one? The penalty for defilement does not absorb the interest of the offended party. Regarding the punishment of those who attempt to defile and corrupt girls not yet of age, see Christoph Philipp Richter. Defilement and the loss of virginity can best be proven by an inspection of the body, for example, by midwives. The praised Richter notes: "Whether this is urgent proof, when the maids often pick bed-feathers off the cloak, indicating that a male has been in Julia's chamber, from which carnal union is proven." Besold cites various authors on this in his *Collection of Legal Questions* under the words "carnal union," "defloration," and "defilement."

<meta>This page continues the legal and ecclesiastical lexicon, specifically focusing on "Seduction" (Stuprum) under the letter S and "Churches" (Kirchen) under the letter K.</meta>

<page-num>519</page-num>
<header>Letter K.</header>

One who boasts of <term>seduction</term> <note>original: "Stuprum"; in this legal context, it refers to illicit sexual intercourse with a respectable unmarried woman</note> or glories in it, as if he had carnally known a certain person, can be forced to revoke the injury done to the harmed person’s reputation and be punished by flogging. Christoph Philipp Richter, *part 5, chapter 21, number 3, folio 80.* The property of a fleeing seducer ought to be granted to his closest paternal relatives to manage, provided that a dowry for the seduced woman is first established from it, and alimony for the illegitimate child is decreed thereafter: Richter, *part 5, consultation 16, number 6, folio 58.* A seducer is bound to provide for the child's nourishment only after three years have passed. *Part 5, chapter 16, number 2, folio 58.* This rule fails <note>i.e., is an exception</note> if the mother is so poor that she cannot manage to nurse the child herself. *Ibid, number 3.*

Seduction committed in such a way that it does not constitute <term>incest</term> <note>sexual relations between close relatives</note> according to Divine Law is usually punished by perpetual banishment. *Ibid, number 4.* The ordinary penalty for seduction according to the <term>Julian Law</term> <note>Lex Julia; an ancient Roman law governing marriage and morals</note> is not a capital crime; however, an extraordinary penalty (as nearly all punishments have begun to be today) is applied otherwise. Klock, *Consultation 194, numbers 100, 101, 102.*

The <term>deflowering</term> <note>loss of virginity</note> of a bride on her wedding night was, by the Law of the Scots, owed to the King. That law was abolished by Malcolm, and a gold coin was substituted for the redemption of her modesty. Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in *Syntagma of Universal Law.* King Malcolm, at the urging of his most holy wife Margaret, abolished this most shameful custom in human history and decreed in the Year of Human Salvation 1090 that a bride should pay a gold coin to the lord of the place for the sake of redeeming her modesty. *In the same place.* A case of seduction committed by a certain person was investigated by the Council of Altdorf, *35, throughout folio 141 and following.* Seduction was categorized among "atrocious crimes" by the Romans. Terence says:

> Does it seem like a small thing to you to corrupt a girl
> ->who is a citizen? Also:<-
> You have corrupted a girl whom you had no
> ->right to touch:<-
> Now that is first a great sin, yet
> ->it is still a human one:<-
> Others, even good men, have often done it.

Cypræus, *On the Law of Marriage, chapter 10, section 11, number 3.*

On whether a man who deflowers a virgin is bound to take her as his wife, see Marius Antonius, *book 1, reference 28, number 1.* The punishment for a seducer who lies, claiming to be single when he is not. Zahn, *On Lies, book 2, chapter 88, number 3.*

In a case of deflowering, see the *Consultations*, where a man was condemned to a fine of 50 gold coins for the deflowering of a virgin related to him in the second degree of consanguinity—though he could have been punished more severely for committing incest—and was ordered to pay three florins for the expenses of the childbirth. Uran, *volume 3, on deflowering, consultation 1.* Regarding the methods and acts by which carnal union is rightly proven or not, see Uran, *on deflowering 3, consultation 7 and consultation 14.*

### 23. Churches. Temple.

From the Greek <note>original: "κύριος κυριακός" (kyrios, kyriakos)</note> *Lord* and *belonging to the Lord*, our word *Kirch* (Church) is derived, and in the Saxon dialect, *Kersche*, namely "the house of the Lord," as Becman records in *Origins, under the word Cyrus, folio 203.* In what way the ancient Christians also called them *Houses of God, Sunday Houses*

<column-break/>

or houses dedicated to God (from which we still have *Dom* and *Domkirche* <note>Cathedral</note>), and from what the words *Domb* and *Dombherrn* <note>Cathedral and Canons/Lords of the Cathedral</note> are said to be derived. Klock, *Consultation 35, number 254.* Likewise they were called *Basilicas, Churches, etc.* as can be seen in the works of Origen, Tertullian, Jerome, Eusebius, and others. But they used the names *Temple* and *Shrine* more rarely, as those names smacked of paganism. Yet today we use them more frequently and interchangeably. Nor is it wrong to do so simply because they come from the Heathens. Otherwise, what Greek and Latin words have not been contaminated by their spit? Should they therefore be trampled underfoot? But the ancients had other reasons for what they maintained. For they often lived in the midst of Heathens, or in their neighborhood; and so that they might separate themselves from their idolatry even by external symbols, they used other words which immediately proclaimed Christ the Lord, and thus more effectively stung the enemies of the Lord.

And it should be noted here that the name *Temple* is a general one. For the ancients called any large places *Temples*, as if they were "ample roofs" <note>original: "tecta ampla"</note>. Varro, in *book 6, On the Laws*, takes it to mean an elevated place from which one may gaze out: for properly, a place either in the Sky or on the earth marked out by an Augur is designated; it was called a Temple from "protecting" or "viewing" <note>original: "à tuendo"</note>, because from every part, or from it, every part could be seen; from this also the word *contemplate* is derived. Thus Cicero in *book 2, On the Laws* said: "Let the Augurs have the temples declared and free." It is taken specifically for the Heaven and the primary world. Hence that Vestal Virgin in Ennius, *book 1*, cited in Cicero’s *On Divination*:

> Although I was stretching my many hands toward the blue
> ->Temples of the Sky<-
> weeping, and calling out with a coaxing voice.

The same Ennius in *book 6*:

> Neither the sea nor the earth, nor the bright Temples
> ->of the Sky.<-

A Temple was also taken for enclosed places, whether sacred and dedicated to a Divinity, or not sacred; and also sometimes for a tomb; see Lælius Bisciolus, *Subsecutive Hours, volume 2, chapter 7, book 14; and Fuller, Miscellany 2, 9.*

When did churches begin to be built? See Bernegger, regarding the *Image of Loreto, folio 260, etc.* The reason why it was forbidden in Greece to build new churches and only to preserve the old ones was the eruption of the Barbarians. Joachim Stephani, *on Novel 67, number 4.*

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the words: Temple, Shrine, see Saubert, *On Sacrifices, page 324.* The pews in temples pertain to "immovable property." Mevius, *On the Law of Lübeck, book 1, title 10, article 1, number 6, 75.*

A Bishop spent 41 years building the beautiful church at Merseburg; in the same building there are as many windows as there are days in the year, as many marble pillars as there are hours in the year, and as many portals as there are months in the year. Zeiller, *century 4, question 43, page 233.* Kirchmeyer, *on the greater Church.* The steward <note>original: "Schaffner"</note> who manages and accounts for the church revenues. *Acts of Lindau, page 842.*

### 21. Abandoning or Exposing Children. <note>original: "Kinder hinwerffen, aussetzen, &c. Expositio infantum."</note>

Master **Speidel**, in his *Notable Remarks* under this word: If an infant is exposed in a location where a superior and an inferior jurisdiction overlap, and it is unknown who abandoned the child, which of them is responsible for the child's care and education? Answer: The one who holds the superior jurisdiction. **Berlich**, Book 1, *Conclusion* 1, *number* 14.

### ADDITION.

The exposure of newborn infants—or "blood-stained" infants, as they are called in the heading of the <term>Code of Justinian</term> <note>a collection of Roman laws compiled under Emperor Justinian I</note> regarding the exposure of infants—is no light crime. **Juvenal** <note>a Roman poet known for his satires</note> calls them "still red from their mother." Famous on this subject are the **Letters of Pliny and Trajan**, Book 10, *Letters* 64 and 65. Not without reason does **Justinian** exaggerate this crime with many words in <term>Novel 153</term> <note>the "Novels" were new laws issued after the Code</note>, calling it a crime "alien to human sense," and one that would not be believable even among any barbarians—as if to say it surpasses all the cruelty of barbarism. See more in **Rittershufius** on the *Novels, page* 695 and following; **Pacius**, *Analysis of the Code* on the heading "concerning exposed infants"; **Wesenbeck** on the <term>Cornelian Law regarding Assassins</term> <note>Lex Cornelia de Sicariis; a Roman law against murder and poisoning</note>, and there the notes of **Master Doctor Ludwig** in his *Manuscript Notes.*

By the act of abandonment, <term>paternal power</term> <note>original: "Patria potestas"; the legal authority a head of household held over his children</note> is dissolved. **Master Doctor Biccius** in *Golden Sections* 1, *thesis* 27, *number* 10; for no one can reclaim their offspring from the person who, out of mercy, took in the child when they were perishing. See the final law of the *Code on Exposed Infants* and the <term>Decretals of Gregory IX</term> <note>the standard collection of Canon Law</note>. On how a woman who exposes her infant or her delivery should be punished, see **Berlich**, 4, *conclusion* 7. Under Civil Law, the punishment is at the judge's discretion, and if the children die, the penalty of the Cornelian Law applies. In <term>Saxony</term> <note>a powerful state within the Holy Roman Empire with its own legal tradition</note>, however, it is punished by flogging, but if death follows, it is the penalty for <term>parricide</term> <note>the murder of a close relative</note>. Add **Harprecht** on *Public Judgments*, § 5, *number* 99.

In ancient times, parents held the "Right of Life and Death" over delinquent children. Grandfathers did not. However, this right eventually fell into disuse due to its atrocity, since Paternal Power should consist of <term>piety</term> <note>affection and duty</note>, not cruelty. Hence, parents who kill their children are struck with the penalty for parricide. This even applies to children born out of wedlock, whom Nature does not distinguish from others, as well as those born of incest or adultery. **Johannes Philippi**, Jurist, in *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*, book 1, *selection* 55, title 9. The <term>Lay Judges of Leipzig</term> <note>Scabini; experts in local law who advised on court cases</note> wrote to the Bailiff of Torgau in May 1617: "Because of the murderous deed committed and confessed against his child, whom he fathered in adultery with [Name], he shall be sewn into a sack along with a dog, a rooster, a snake, and a cat, instead of a monkey, thrown into the water, and drowned." <note>This describes the "Poena Cullei," an ancient Roman punishment for parricide where the criminal was drowned with specific animals</note> B. R. W.

Regarding who must nourish an exposed infant and who shall inherit from them, see **Tessaurus**, *Piedmontese Decisions* 118. Whether infants publicly exposed,

<column-break/>

found, and raised—<term>Foundlings</term> <note>original: "Fündling"</note>—should be considered legitimate children or rather illegitimate and "spurious," and whether they can be admitted to successions, honors, and ecclesiastical or civil offices by law, see **Speckhan**, *century 3, class 1, question 14.*

### 22. Impregnation of a Maiden, Seduction. <note>original: "Kindsschwängerung, Kindshändel, Defloratio"; see below under the letter S.</note>

Several legal opinions on the point of <term>deflowering</term> <note>the loss of virginity</note> were given by **Martin Uranius**, which are found in his *Consultations*, volume 3. Can a settlement of this kind be valid in such cases? **Uranius** affirms this in *Consultation 20*, but I doubt it because of the favor owed to the child.

A woman who opens her house at night and admits those entering is presumed to be a prostitute. **Farinaccius**, *volume 3, question 136, number 95.*

### ADDITION.

Concerning deflowering, much is found above under the word *Virgin*. For the seducers of Virgins and of widows living honorably, the <term>Julian Law</term> <note>Lex Julia; Roman law regarding marriage and adultery</note> imposes a penalty of the loss of half their goods for those of higher status; and physical punishment—namely flogging with perpetual banishment—for those of lower status or humble condition. **Johannes Philippi**, Jurist, in *Practical Use*, book 4, *selection* 84. By Divine and <term>Canon Law</term> <note>Church law</note>, the seducer must either marry the woman he has dishonored or provide her with a dowry. The choice lies with the seducer. The dowry must be provided according to the social status of the woman. The seducer is bound to provide for the child if pregnancy follows. One who sleeps with many men cannot seek maintenance, and why? Because the paternity is uncertain. Based on the quality of the person seduced, the penalty can be made more severe. Can someone be removed from the rank of the Senate or the College of Senators because of seduction? **Master Carpzov**, *Decision 17*, affirms this. Seduction is a scandalous crime. Is the penalty for seduction a capital crime? Decision 17 says the penalty does not absorb the interest of the offended party <note>meaning the victim can still sue for damages</note>. Penalty for those who attempt to seduce and corrupt girls not yet of marriageable age: **Christoph Philipp Richter**, *part 6, consultation 15.* Seduction and deflowering can best be proven by an inspection of the body, for example, by midwives. The praised **Richter**, *part 5, consultation 21.* Whether there is "urgent proof" when the maids often pick bed-feathers off a man's cloak after he has been in a woman's chamber, from which carnal union is proven? **Besold**, *Consultations*, part 3; **Mascardus**, volume 1, *On Proof*; and **Besold** in *Collection of Legal Questions* under the words "carnal union," "deflowering," and "seduction," where he cites various authors.

One who boasts or brags about illicit intercourse <note>original: "Stuprum"</note>, as if he had physically known a certain person, can be compelled to retract the injury done to the person’s reputation and be punished by flogging. Christoph Philipp Richter *part 5, chapter 21, number 3, folio 80.* The property of a seducer who flees should be granted to his closest male relatives to manage, provided that a dowry for the seduced woman is first established from those assets, and maintenance for the illegitimate child <note>original: "spurio"</note> is decreed from them thereafter: Richter *part 5, counsel 16, number 5; chapter 16, number 2, folio 58.* This fails to apply if the mother is so poor that she cannot afford to nurse the infant. *ibid. number 3.* Seduction committed in such a way that it does not constitute incest according to Divine Law is usually punished by permanent banishment. *ibid. number 4.* The ordinary penalty for seduction under the <term>Julian Law</term> <note>Lex Julia; a Roman law concerning adultery and moral conduct</note> is not a capital offense, yet it is not uncommon for extraordinary penalties (which nearly all penalties have begun to be today) to be applied otherwise. According to the Law of the Scots, the deflowering of a bride on her wedding night was once owed to the King. > Does it seem a small thing to you to violate a citizen virgin?
> Also:

In a case of deflowering, see the *Counsel* where a man, for deflowering a virgin related to him in the second degree of consanguinity, was condemned to a penalty of 50 gold pieces (though he could have been punished more severely for committing incest) and three florins for the expenses of the childbirth. Uran. *volume 3, on deflowering, counsel 1.* On the methods and acts by which physical union is rightly proved or not, Uran. *on deflowering 3, counsel 7 and counsel 14.*

### 23. Churches. Temple. <note>original: "Kirchen. Templum."</note>

Becman reports in *Origins, under the word 'Cyrus,' folio 203,* that our word *Kirch*—and in the Saxon dialect, *Kercke*—flows from the Greek *kyrios* <note>original: "κύριος"</note> and *kyriakos* <note>original: "κυριακός"</note>, meaning "of the Lord," specifically a house of the Lord. In the same way, the ancient Christians called the houses of God "Dominical Houses" <note>original: "Domos Dominicas"</note> or "Houses Dedicated to God" (from which we still get the terms *Dom* and *Domkirche* <note>Cathedral</note>), from the word *Domb* or *Domb-herrn* <note>Canons of a cathedral</note>, as explained in Klock, *counsel 35, number 254.* They also called them Basilicas, Churches, etc., as can be seen in the works of Origen, Tertullian, Jerome, Eusebius, and others.

But they used the names "Temple" and "Shrine" <note>original: "Templi ac Delubri"</note> more rarely, as these smacked of paganism. Yet we today use them more frequently and interchangeably. Nor is it necessarily wrong to do so just because they came from the pagans. Otherwise, which Greek and Latin words have not been contaminated by their influence? Should they therefore be trampled underfoot? But the reasons the ancients protected themselves were different. For they often lived in the midst of pagans or in their neighborhood; so that they might separate themselves from pagan idolatry even by external symbols,

<column-break/>

they used different words here—words that would immediately proclaim Christ the Lord and thus irritate the enemies of the Lord more effectively.

And it should be noted here that the name "Temple" is a general one. For the ancients called any large places "Temples," as if they were "ample roofs" <note>original: "tecta ampla"</note>. Varro, in *book 6 on Laws*, takes it to mean an elevated place from which one may look out: for properly, it designates a place either in the Heavens or on earth marked out by an Augur <note>a Roman religious official who interpreted omens</note>. It was called a "Temple" from *tuendo* <note>protecting or watching</note>, because it could be seen from every side, or every part could be seen from it; from this, the word *contemplor* <note>I contemplate/gaze</note> is derived. Thus Cicero said in *book 2 on Laws*: "Let the Augurs have the Temples declared and freed." It was first used specifically for the Heavens and the world. Hence that Vestal Virgin in Ennius, *book 1*, quoted in Cicero's *on Divination*:

> Although I stretched my hands toward the blue Temples of the Sky,
> Weeping, and called out with a coaxing voice.

The same author in Ennius, *book 6*:

> Neither sea nor earth, nor the shining Temples of the Sky.

"Temple" was also used for enclosed places, whether sacred and dedicated to a Divinity or not sacred; and even sometimes for a tomb, see Læl. Bisciol. *Substitutory Hours, volume 2, chapter 7, book 14,* and Fuller, *Miscellaneous 2, 9.*
When did churches begin to be built? See Bernegger *on the Image of Loreto, folio 260, etc.* The reason why it was forbidden to build new churches in Greece, allowing only the preservation of old ones, was the eruption of the Barbarians, Joach. Stephani *on Novel 67, number 4.*

-> ADDITION. <-
---

Regarding the words: Temple, Shrine. Saubertus *on Sacrifices, page 324.* Benches in churches pertain to "immovable property," Mevius in *Lübeck Law, book 1, title 10, article 1, number 75.*

A bishop spent 41 years building the beautiful church at Merseburg; in that same church, there are as many windows as there are days in the year, as many marble columns as there are hours in the year, and as many portals as there are months in the year. Zeiller, *century 4, question 43, page 233.* *Kirchmeyer* <note>a church administrator</note>, that is, the supervisor of a major church. The *Schaffner* <note>steward</note> is the one who manages and accounts for the church's revenues, *Acts of Lindau, page 842.*

### 24. Church Penance. <note>original: "Poenitentia Ecclesiastica"</note>

An Ecclesiastical Judge (even in crimes of common jurisdiction, such as adultery, debauchery, usury, blasphemy, and other similar ones) by imposing <term>Church Penance</term> <note>original: "Kirchbuß"</note>, or by absolving the public criminal from it, does not prejudice the secular judge regarding the political penalty (though the secular penalty may sometimes be milder). Since the jurisdiction of both magistrates has been violated and offended, the offender must give satisfaction to both according to the quality and mode of each jurisdiction. A prior action in one court does not prevent the defendant from being sent to or hauled before the other for punishment afterward. Caspar Leipold, *On Concurrent Jurisdictions in the German Empire, final question.* And although Andreas Gail, in *On Public Peace, observation 11, number 26*, distinguishes regarding the removal of the political penalty whether the priestly penance was public or private—suggesting that the former might remove the political penalty while the latter does not—legal practice nonetheless observes the contrary without distinction. Panormitanus... Leipold... for ecclesiastical penalties tend primarily toward the correction of morals, the abolition of scandal, and the expiation of the church's guilt; but secular penalties are for satisfying the Commonwealth, which was offended, and political justice, which was violated. Gail, *cited location, number 25.*

In the Duchy of Württemberg, those guilty of adultery were formerly punished by being forced to sit on a small stool in the church <note>a "stool of repentance"</note>. But this punishment, in the most recent ordinance <note>original: "neuen Lands-Ordnung"</note>, was changed to a prison sentence.

->ADDITION.<-

Very many crimes are of <term>mixed jurisdiction</term> <note>original: "mixti fori"; cases that can be heard in either church or secular courts</note>. For concerning perjury, sacrilege, adultery, and many other crimes (about which Marta, *book 2 on Jurisdiction*, writes throughout, and others elsewhere), both the secular and ecclesiastical judge can decide. They are called "mixed jurisdiction" because an accusation is rightly instituted in either court. See Ummius in *On Processes, page 148.* Lehmann, in the *Chronicle of Speyer, book 2, chapter 35*, writes: Whoever shows himself to be slow, negligent, or disobedient in paying tithes has not only brought church penance upon himself so that he is excluded from the community, etc. Public apology in the temple (church penance), where such a thing is established, is to be ordered with the knowledge and approval of the Superintendent, and shall by no means be converted into a fine <note>literally "converted into money"</note>. Johann Philippi, *Legal Consultant, in Practical Use of the Institutes, book 4, title 18, section 4, Eclogue 84, number 17.*

The common people, accustomed to liberty and once freed from the righteous yoke of the Bishops, with difficulty allow those old laws to be imposed on them again, and they especially hate...
