### 25. Church Attendance. Parish Usage.
Even if the usage of a parish <note>original: "Kirchgang"</note> and the place of burial <note>original: "wann die Leut lebendig oder todt an ein Ort gehören"; when people belong to a place whether living or dead</note> are established, the jurisdiction of the territory is not conclusively proven if the division of spiritual jurisdiction differs from the temporal one. See Luchinus de Curte in his treatise *For Saint Salvator*, number 34, folio seven; Menochius, *Counsel* 21, number 28 and following; Michael Teuber, *On Jurisdiction*, thesis 5, letter E. However, it is otherwise (following the argument from a ceasing cause and from the contrary) when the right of the Parish and the City is concluded within the same boundaries, based on the arguments noted by Hieronymus de Monte, *On Boundary Regulations*, chapter 12, number 6, and chapter 13, number 3.

->ADDITIO.<-
<note>Addition</note>

One type of church is a "mother church" <term>matrix</term> <note>literally "womb" or "source"</note>, and another is a "parish church." The term "mother church" is used in two ways: 1. For a Cathedral or Episcopal church; 2. For a parish or principal church which has a limited parish and other small shrines or chapels under it, in respect to which it is called the "mother." Nicolaus de Milis, in his *Golden Repertory*, letter E, number 8. Although either of these might be understood by the name "mother" depending on the subject matter and the nature of the business, in cases of doubt, it refers to the Cathedral. A parish church is also called "baptismal," because the baptismal fonts are located there and the parishioners are baptized there. *Gloss* and Panormitanus on the chapter *When it happens*, 29, *On Tithes*.

### 26. Church Property, Church Assets. See above, *Ecclesiastical Goods*.
Regarding church property, see Filefacus in his short work *On Lay Sacrilege*; Stephanus, *Canon Law*, book 2, chapter 5.

On church ornaments <note>original: "Kirchen-Ornat"</note>, Stephanus, in the same work, chapter 2, teaches that one should in no way seize them, <note>original: "soit pour la guerre, soit pour autres affaires, à cause que c’ est chose illicite de metre la main à l’ argenterie des Eglises"</note> "whether for war or for other affairs, because it is an illicit thing to lay hands on the silver of the churches." See also Meillet, *On Tacitus*, book 8, political and military discourse 10, page 537 and following.

->ADDITIO.<-
<note>Addition</note>

Heinrich Petraeus, in his treatise *On Monasteries*, pages 3 and 4, records those curses full of evil inserted into the instruments of even small donations: **"Whoever takes these goods, his lungs and liver shall be consumed within his body."** <note>original: "Wer die Güter nimmt, demselben soll Lungen und Leber im Leib verzehren."</note> See the word *Ecclesiastical Goods*. Regarding the triple distinction of these ecclesiastical items, see Alemanus in *The Palace of Consultations*, page 258.

A legacy left to a "pious cause"—or what was then thought to be pious, such as the celebration of masses, the invocation of saints, or the use of monasteries—which has ceased among true Christians <note>a reference to the Reformation</note> because that use is discovered to be impious, is not revoked. It does not revert to the heirs of the testator, but must be converted to other pious uses. Carpzov, in *Forensic Jurisprudence*, part 3, chapter 13, decision 27, number 3 and following; Hieronymus Schurff, century 1, counsel 47, number 11 to 14, and in the same century, counsel 90; Wesenbeck, counsel 37, number 6, 7, and following. Sacred things <term>Res sacrae</term> consist of: 1. All places and buildings destined for pious uses, such as for gathering, feeding, refreshing, and caring for the poor, orphans, the elderly, the sick, the weak, the maimed, and the infirm. 2. Offerings or votive gifts: such as sacred vessels and vestments used in performing divine service, or those necessary for divine religion, as the Emperor says in law 21, "We decree to no one," in the Code *On the Most Holy Churches*. Indeed, this includes even those things which pertain only to the decoration of sacred buildings and divine worship. Here may be included images and sacred tables (altars), which we know in many churches or monasteries are made of gold and silver and adorned with precious gems. 3. Also to be aggregated with sacred things are estates, fields, vineyards, meadows, etc., which belong to churches or monasteries or other pious, religious, or venerable places, whether they be in the city or the countryside. This includes the tenant farmers and rural servants by whom those estates are worked and cultivated; which Justinian, in his *Epitome of the Novels*, elegantly calls "members of immovable things" <note>original: "membrarum rerum immobilium"</note>. Also included are the "civil grain supplies" <term>annonae</term>, or "civil breads" as they are called. Rittershusius, *The Novels*, page 109, numbers 9, 10, and 11. Some sacred things are movable, others are immovable (number 12). Some belong directly and principally to divine worship, others by consequence (number 14). The more the Church began to abound in these external riches and vast estates, the more it began to degenerate. **"Religion gave birth to riches, and the daughter devoured the mother."** <note>original: "Religio peperit divitias, & filia devoravit matrem."</note> On church property, see Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 83; Pacius, *Analysis of the Code*, page 466. On "civil breads," see law 3 in the Code *On Quadrennial Prescription*; Rittershusius, *Feudal Partitions*, page 94; Cujas, *Observations*, book 26, chapter 17, where he also teaches what "stepped bread" <term>panis gradilis</term> <note>bread distributed to the public on the steps of buildings in Rome</note> is. On whether sacred things should be transferred to secular use, see Caspar Ziegler, book 1, dissertation 2; Valerius Maximus; Bernegger, *Discourse on Tacitus*, question 180; *The Work of Temples*, Lipsius, century of miscellaneous letters, 27. On costly Mass vestments, see Zeiller in his *Travels through France*, in the city of Bourges.

### 27. Churchyard. Cemetery.
A cemetery is judged in the same manner as a church; see Mastrillus, *Decisions*, 22, number 5; and it enjoys ecclesiastical immunity. Borellus, title 1, number 41.

A tomb was even placed for a crow <note>original: "Cornici sepulchrum positum"</note>, as noted in Lipsius, Century 3, Letter 59, at the end. ### 28. Parish Village. Parochia.

This is a locality to which others are "parished" <note>meaning they are legally and ecclesiastically attached to that specific church</note>. The entire territory where this village and its associated subsidiary churches are located is called a *Kirchspiel* or parish. See Gebhard, *On Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction*, section 15, folio 310, number 324.

### 29. Church Patronage. Jus Patronatus.

The **Right of Patronage** is that which is acquired by someone in the Church because they themselves, or their ancestors, established the church, built it, or increased it with their own wealth, with the consent of the Bishop. From this right, both honor and burden result, along with certain benefits.

And that the Right of Patronage is acquired from the beginning in one of three ways—namely, by the assignment of land, by building, or by endowment—is noted by the gloss on the chapter *Piamentis* 16, question 7, and by Hostiensis in his summary on the title *On the Right of Patronage*, section 2, as well as by Innocent, Panormitanus, and other Doctors of the Law on the same rubric.

Furthermore, the Right of Patronage is transferred in one of four ways: namely, by hereditary succession, by exchange, by gift, and by the sale of the entire estate to which it belongs <note>original: "Universitatis bonorum"</note>, by reason of which it is granted, as held by Innocent in the aforementioned place and the Doctors in the chapter *Cum seculum* on the Right of Patronage.

Hence, the Right of Patronage belongs to no one unless they themselves acquired it in one of the three primary ways, or if they hold it from another through one of the four modes of transfer. As to whether it may be acquired by prescription <note>long-term possession or custom</note>, see Gilken, *On Usucaption*, part 3, chapter 9, folio 723; and Bonacina, *On Restitution*, dispute 1, last question, section 2, number 11, where it is stated that the Right of Patronage is never acquired by prescription when it is established that the Church was once "free" <note>meaning independent of a lay patron</note>.

On whether a usufructuary <note>someone with the right to use and enjoy the profits of a property they do not own</note> holds the Right of Patronage, see Grivellus, decision 37. Regarding the four-month period given to laypeople to present a candidate for office: does it run from the day they knew of the vacancy or from the day it became vacant? See Florez Diez de Mena, question 3. Does the Right of Patronage pass to the treasury through confiscation? Besold, Volume 1.

Baronius records in his annals for the Year of Christ 752 that the Kings in France hold the Right of Patronage over Bishops. Regarding who elected the High Priest of the Jews, see Cunaeus, *On the Republic of the Jews*, book 2, chapter 1.

It must be noted here that the possession of the right of presentation (or Patronage) does not itself prove the actual Right of Patronage: since they are separate things, and possession has nothing in common with the legal right or ownership <note>original: "nec quicquam commune habeat possessio cum jure seu proprietate"</note>, as the text states in the law *Naturaliter*, section 1, regarding the acquisition of inheritance. From one separate thing, one cannot rightly infer the other; see the law *Papinianus* and the commentary by Bartolus. And it often happens every day that the right of presentation belongs to one person while the possession stays with another. See Martin Uranius, counsel 18, number 4.

And this must be known: once a church has been founded, constructed, and endowed—after its foundation, construction, or even after its consecration—the Right of Patronage cannot be newly acquired in it. Because once it is "free," it cannot receive "servitudes" <note>legal burdens or obligations to an external owner</note>. See the gloss on the chapter *Piamentis*, where it says that anyone giving something to a Church after its consecration is not called a Patron, but a benefactor. See Petrus Duennas, rule 229.

If a Baron erects a church in a castle, does it become feudal? See Marc. Antoninus Genuensis, *Ecclesiastical Practice*, question 351. The Church remains free when the Right of Patronage passes to the Treasury. See the same, question 393.

He states at the end: "The Right of Patronage which we use today in the Reformed Evangelical Churches differs greatly from that right which the Canons disposed by the ordinance of the Popes." Regarding the origin of the Right of Patronage, see Klock, *Consultation* 51, number 105, 106. The reason for introducing the Right of Patronage, number 108 and 110. Just as he who manumits <note>frees</note> a slave becomes the Patron of that now-freed person, and acquires the right of Patronage over him, which encompasses many things (see *Law 1 of the Digest, On the Right of Patronage*), so too he who builds a Church or an Oratory house (which is also called a <term>Proseucha</term> <note>original: "Proseucha," from the Greek word for a place of prayer</note> by Juvenal and other Latin authors) and endows it—that is, assigns certain revenues or other goods to it—acquires the Right of Patronage over that same Church. By the force of this Right, not only he himself but also his heirs may nominate or present someone to the Bishop to perform the sacred duties in that Church. This Right of Patronage, introduced in later times, is not indeed Spiritual, but nevertheless clings to Spiritual causes; see *Title 2 of the Decretals, book 3, On the Right of Patronage*, and Cujacius in his *Recitations on the Decretals*, at chapter 3, *on judgments*, and at chapter 18, *with Bertoldus, on sentences and res judicata*. One may also consult the more famous German practitioners, Martin Uranius, *Consultation* 18, volume 2. Likewise, two long and beautiful consultations following the *Consultations* of Johann Borcholt, numbers 3 and 20, the first of which was written by Nicolaus Everhard, and the other by Ludolph Schrader.

### 30. Church Fairs, Protection of Church Fairs.

#### Encaenia. Protection of the Encaenia.

*Encaenia* <note>original: ἐγκαίνια</note> signifies to the Greeks: (1) Feast days of dedication, as in John 5 and Luke 4. For in ancient times, Sacred houses, Libraries, statues, and even public works were dedicated. Whence Quintilian, book 7, chapter 2, says: "There is no one who has not at some time begun to sin, nor was it first through the crime of the Encaeniads." See Turnebus on this passage, book 12, chapter 11.

(2) Sometimes this word is taken for a certain new kind of games, and a new sort of processions, indicating that he who is honored by them has performed some great deed. Trebellius Pollio. And thus *Encaenia* is used generically for the Feast of dedication, or for a time when something new has been made or renewed. Matthaeus Martinius in his *Philological Lexicon*.

Hence *encaeniare* means to introduce something new, as in the *Onomasticon* of Petrus Danielis: "Encaenia are games of honors and trophies."

The word *Encomium* <note>a speech or song of high praise</note> is not far removed from this, which was a song issued in praise of a Victor for his immortality, in which his magnificent deeds were sung with illustrious proclamation.

The protection of the Church Fairs, which they call <term>Kirchweyhuſchug</term> <note>original German: "Kirchweih-Schutz," meaning the protection or legal oversight of the church dedication festival</note>, shares in the right of defense. For when the initial feast days—namely the Dedication of the Temple (concerning the origin of which Polydore Vergil discusses in *On the Invention of Things*, book 5, chapters 7 and 13)—are celebrated in villages and towns, it is customary in parts of Franconia and Saxony, and other neighboring places, for the Lords of the territories who hold Lower Jurisdiction to not only sell wine by measure through their deputies, but also to protect those fair-like gatherings through certain officials, to <term>vertretten</term> <note>represent or advocate for</note> the <term>Kirchweyhuſchug</term>. Nevertheless, in many places, it has become established by ancient custom that not only the Lords of the territory—who hold the <term>Bogtey</term> <note>Vogtei; bailiwick or advocacy</note> on the streets—but others holding jurisdiction only in certain estates, have the right on the initial days of dedication to draw and distribute wine, to <term>fürzulegen</term> <note>lay out</note> and <term>auszuſchencken</term> <note>pour out/retail</note> the <term>Bannwein</term> <note>Bann-wine; wine sold under a local lord's monopoly</note>. See Mr. Mager, *On Armed Advocacy*, chapter 15, number 107 and following, where at number 113 he says it should be noted concerning the protection of the *Encaenia* that <term>Kirchweyhuſchug</term> is one thing, and <term>Kirchenſchug</term> <note>Kirchenschutz; general church protection</note> is another. For the former is annual and exercised only once a year; the latter, however, is continuous, and can belong even to one who has no jurisdiction over the Church; and it is derived from the words <term>Kirch</term> <note>Church</note> and <term>Schug</term> <note>Schutz/Protection</note>.

Church-Mass, Church-Fair, Kermesse <note>original German: Kirchmeß, Kirmeß, Kermeß</note>; see Fritsch *On Fairs, chapter 1, numbers 21 and 25.* Today, dedication festivals are generally celebrated in all villages and hamlets; we commonly call them "Church-dedications" <note>original: Kirchweyhungten</note>, that is, feast days marking the initial dedication of a temple. When these are finished, the Peasants make offerings to Bacchus <note>a classical reference to getting drunk</note> and pay their dues, not only emptying whole barrels by drinking, but sometimes clashing with one another with fists and weapons. Therefore, by virtue of the lower village magistracy and ancient usage and tradition, the noble Teutonic Order holds the church-dedication protection in Ober- and Unter-Reimlingen. The dedication festivals of the Jews are far different from these of our people. Klock, in the same place. ### 31. Can, to be able. <term>Potest. Posse</term>

The word *potest* <note>he, she, or it can</note> has four meanings in law.
(1.) **By Law** <note>original: de Jure</note>: since we "can" do that which we are legally able to do, as in the law *filius* at the end... and there Paulus de Castro... Therefore, not even the Supreme Emperor "can" do that which is not permitted by Law. Baldus... Just as no other Judge is understood to "be able" to do anything except what he can do by the law's grant... For the power, force, and proper notion of the word *potestatis* <note>power or authority</note> is to be able *legitimately*: so that we are by no means said to "be able" to do what we can do with unfairness or injury to another: since that power is not so much "potency" as it is "impotency" and weakness. By this reasoning, even the Best and Greatest Lord <note>God</note>, although He can indeed do all things, nevertheless cannot sin: as Baldus elegantly writes, adapting this to the Roman Prince... And this pertains to what I have said in the *Treatise on Majesty*, folio 64 and following, also folio 69, etc.
(2.) **According to Good Morals** <note>original: secundùm bonos mores</note>, as in the law *nepos Proculo*... the reason is: because those things which are done against good morals are considered impossible... and there is no "ability" for impossible things.
(3.) A meaning of this word *potest* is **According to Nature** <note>original: secundùm naturam</note>. For of that thing which has an impediment according to the natural course of nature, there is no power, and no "ability" is reckoned...
(4.) This word *potest* has a meaning **In Fact** <note>original: de facto</note>, because where an act is included, there also is power, or vice versa... The word "can" <note>potest</note> does not induce necessity, but rather will...
The words "it is not allowed" <note>non licet</note>, or "it shall not be allowed" <note>non licebit</note>, imply a precise necessity, they deny power, they resist the act, and they invalidate what is done otherwise. Nizolius, *Allegation 26, number 15.*

### ADDITION.

One is believed to "be able" to do that which one can do against the will of an adversary; and no one is said to "be able" to do that which he can be prohibited from doing by another. Donellus... more extensively, Barbosa, *book 14, chapter 47, axiom 5.*

<header>Expanded Practical Treasury</header>

A person is considered "able" if they have the capacity to fulfill a condition <note>original: "Posse quis videtur, qui potest facere, ut conditioni pareat"</note>, according to the Digest, Book 50, Title 17, Law 174. Barbosa, *Axiom 4*. However, a person is not said to be "able" to do that which is against the Law, because legal language must always be understood in accordance with the Law <note>original: "secundùm Jus"</note>. See the Digest on letting and hiring, and the title on the significance of words. Barbosa, *Axiom 7*. Furthermore, a person is not said to be "able" to do things that cannot be done honorably <note>original: "honestè"</note>. *Axiom 8*. We say we "can" do something when we can do it conveniently or suitably. *Axiom 9*. The word **"Can"** or **"Is Able"** <note>original: Potest</note> when used in an affirmative law implies a necessity, according to Marius Antoninus, Book 3, Response 25. On the meaning of the word **"Permitted"** <note>original: Licere</note>, see Marius Antoninus, Book 1, Response 95.

For what may be called "possible," see Zorer, part 1, question 11, number 838 and following; also question 14, number 1231. On what the German term **"Could"** <note>original: Könnten</note> denotes, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 58.

### 32. To come and to fall. <term>Pervenire</term> <note>A legal term describing how property or rights "devolve" or pass from one person to another.</note>

The proper use of these words does not necessarily require that something "comes" to someone only through legal succession. Rather, even that which is obtained through a contract is said to "come" to someone, especially when dealing with a specific object. <note>Citing various laws from the Digest on the "significance of words" and "sale of inheritance."</note> See also Hartmann Pistor, book 3, question 8.

To say something "comes" or "has come" to someone refers only to that which truly, actually, and effectively reaches them. <note>original: "verè, realiter & cum effectu"</note>. See Socinus on the "acquisition of possession" and Bertachinus in the *Repertory* under the word "perveniat."

## ADDITION.

Regarding the meaning of the German phrase **"to come rightly and honestly"** <note>original: recht und redlich kommen</note>, see Klock, volume 3, consultation 182, number 83. On the terms **"To inherit, to fall, to come"** <note>original: Erben, fallen, kommen</note>, see Klock and the authorities cited there. On what the terms **"to transfer, to hold, and to fall back"** <note>original: transferre, tenere & recidere</note> denote, see Klock, volume 2. The phrase **"To come and grow by inheritance"** <note>original: Erblich kommen und erwachsen</note> means it happens through the right of succession, and not through a new grant or concession.

To what type of succession the phrase **"to fall by inheritance"** <note>original: Erblich fallen</note> refers, see the *Strasbourg Consultations*, volume 1. The words **"to reach, to devolve or slip, to be competent, to be due to"** <note>original: pervenire, devolvere sive labi, competere, zustehen</note> are used when they designate the completion of an acquisition. It is not presumed that a thing has "come" to someone <note>meaning the burden of proof is on the claimant</note>, according to Menochius, book 6. The exception is this: if it is certain that the thing came to the deceased, it is presumed to have also "come" to the heir.

### 33. King. <term>Rex</term>

The German word **"König"** <note>King</note> seems to be derived from the word for power, **"können"** <note>to be able</note>, **that is, to have the ability and to be strong**, or perhaps even from **"wissen"** <note>to know</note>. Or it may come from **"Kunneÿn"**, which means to hunt. In this sense, a **"König"** would be like a

<column-break/>

"Hunter" <note>original Greek: Κυνηγός (Kynegos)</note>, which is how Nimrod is described in the Holy Scriptures. The Burgundians of old called their Kings by the general name **"Hendinos"**, as Ammianus Marcellinus notes in book 28; this seems to be our word **"König"**. The Greeks very aptly called a King *Basileus* <note>original: βασιλέα</note>, as if he were the "base of the people" <note>original: βάσιν τᾶ λαᾶ</note>, that is, the foundation of the People. For the term *Ciningi* <note>an old Germanic form</note>, meaning Kings, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*.

Isidore, in *Origins*, book 9, says: Kings are called *Basileis* among the Greeks because, like bases, they support the people. Pope Nicholas I wrote to King Charles:
> Unless you, who are placed in Royal sublimity, had supported the world with your sweat like the bases of a massive building, you would by no means have been allotted the Greek name of *Basileōn* <note>Kings</note>.

The title is also used for a Judge, as noted by Caelius Rhodiginus. There were also "Kings of the Banquet" <note>original: Basilei Conviviorum</note>, for a custom grew among the Greeks to choose by lot a leader who, presiding over the feast, would dictate the rules to the guests.

So too the Hebrew *Adonai* means "Lord Sustainer." This Greek derivation is more pleasing than the conjecture of Fuller, who derives *Basileus* from the Hebrew *Moschal* <note>to rule</note>. Monarchs are also sometimes called "Dominions" in an absolute sense. The word "Lord" <note>original: Dominus</note> properly denotes the power of life and death, as Curtius notes in book 4: "When you sit upon the Royal Throne, you are the Lord of the life and death of all citizens." This is why the French today reserve their title **"Sire"** for the King alone; Fuller derives this from the Hebrew, but it accords more with the Greek *Kyrios* <note>Lord</note> or our German **"Herr"**. See more on the names of rulers in my treatise *On Monarchy*, chapter 3.

In former times, according to Nolden, those designated for the Empire were called "Princes of Youth." Later, the Germans called them the "King of the Romans" <note>original: Römische König</note>, so that even while the right of voting was being exercised, the successor would be certain. This followed the Roman custom where the Emperors were called *Augusti* while those designated as heirs during the Emperor's life were called *Caesars*. Similarly, in France, the successors to the Kings are called the "Dauphins of the Kingdom" <note>original: Dauphin de France</note>. This is because Humbert, Prince of the Dauphiné, ceded his principality to Philip of Valois on the condition that the next heir to the Kingdom be called the Dauphin, holding that territory as a fief of the Empire. In Spain, the male heirs are called *Infantes*, and the daughters of the King are called **Infanta**. Isabella is a witness to this...

The Duchess of Brabant, the widow left by Archduke Albert of Austria, is greeted by the common name the **Infanta** <note>original: "Infanztin"</note>. However, he who is sworn in as King while his father is still living is called today the **Sworn Prince** <note>original: "Principe Jurato"</note>. In England, the Princes of Wales are called *The Prince of Wales*. Cujacius *on chapter "ex parte" 47, regarding appeals and refusals.* In Scotland, they are called the Dukes of *Rothesay* and the *Prefects of Cumbria*; in Greece, the *Despot*, according to Tholosanus *book 18, "Syntagma Juris," chapter 2, number 20.* In Tartary, the title is *Galiba*, Broniovius *on Tartar affairs*; in Denmark, the *Heir of Norway*, a title which the Dukes of Holstein also use today. But concerning Kings and their origin, power, and rights, Conrad Lancellot deals with these at greater length in his *Temple of All Judges, book 1, chapter 2, from page 463 to page 500,* which you may consult. Regarding the **King of the Romans** <note>original: "De Rege Romanorum, vom Römischen König"</note>, see below under the **letter R, at the entry "King of the Romans."**

->ADDITION.<-

This distinguished honor is added to the dignity of the Roman Emperor: just as in ancient times the Roman Empire gave Kings to the Jews and other peoples, so too, after the Empire devolved to the Germans, the same reverence remained. Thus, our Emperors have adorned the **Princes of Bohemia**, **Poland**, **Denmark**, and **Sweden** with Royal dignities. For example, *Frederick I gave the royal insignia to Canute, Duke of Denmark.* Trithemius *chapter 17.* Otto III attributed this dignity to the Pole, Sleidanus *book 3, "On Monarchy."* Frederick I *in the year 1164 created the King of Sardinia.* However, Frederick IV refused such great insignia of royal honor to *Charles of Burgundy* when he sought them. Crusius *Swabian Annals, part 3, book 7, chapter 9.* And although other Kings may possess the same power in their own Kingdom as the Emperor does in the Empire, they cannot nonetheless create Kings, as they cannot make others equal to themselves. Therefore, Kings rightly look up to and venerate the Emperor as the creator of Kings, as if they were his own creations, according to Becker in *Public Law, page 28,* and the same author *on the King of the Romans, ibid. page 84 and following.*

The right of a King is to be supported by the Kingdom, and indeed with Royal pomp: also, that the Kingdom should supply him with everything necessary both for waging war and for preserving peace. These subsidies are owed to the King by the people, and are necessarily paid by a faithful people, Dominicus Soto *book 3, on Justice and Law, question 6, article 7.* Thomas Stapleton *in "Promptuarium Morale," 32nd Sunday after Pentecost, page 383.*

34. **Queen. <term>Regina</term>.**
Mr. Speidel *in "Notabilia" under this word.*

->ADDITION.<-

Not only the King of the Romans, but the Queen,

<column-break/>

if she is present, comes a little later to be anointed and crowned, Bortius *part 1, Public Jurisprudence, chapter 2, thesis 48.* Petrus de Andlo *book 2, chapter 7.* Otto in *Public Law, page 298.*

**Royal Power. <term>Potestas regia</term>.** See above under **letter H, at the entry "High Authority" <note>original: "Hohe Obrigkeit"</note>.**

35. **Right of Common Pasture. <term>Koppelwaid</term>. <term>Jus compascendi</term>.**
This is the right of common grazing, which however does not mean that the pastures become common property as if they were owned by all, Meichsner *book 1, decision 36, number 10.* Gylman *in "Symphorema," part 1, volume 2, title 17, volume 7, number 10.*

->ADDITION.<-

What are common pastures? Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter *part 1, consultation 36, number 24.* How far the right of common pastures extends, *number 25, page 238.* In the law of grazing, if there is sufficient space elsewhere for the livestock of a particular community, the owner of the pastures is preferred. *ibid. number 28.*
Anyone can have as many livestock in the common pasture as they wish, Berlich *2, conclusion 49, numbers 14, 15.* However, it very often happens that among those who simultaneously hold the right of grazing, discords arise in certain places, *Genesis 13, verses 7, 8, 9 <note>A biblical reference to the strife between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot.</note>,* especially if two or more communities have the common right of grazing in neighboring fields, and one has more livestock than the other. Here the question is asked whether the right of grazing can be divided, and whether it should be divided according to the number of acres, or rather according to the number of heads of cattle and "smoking houses" <note>A "smoking house" refers to an inhabited household with a hearth, used as a unit for taxation or rights.</note>, Berlich *ibid. numbers 16, 17, 18 and following.*
Although the three villages, Leinburg, Diepersdorff, and Haimendorff, are one community, each has its own guard <note>original: "Hut"</note> for the cattle, livestock, and pigs; however, when there are acorns, it is all one guard for the pigs, back and forth across boundaries. On April 26, 1561, a judgment was issued in the Court of the Peasants regarding the horse-pasture <note>original: "Rosshur"</note> of these three villages, deciding that each village among the three could seek horse-pasture in the paddocks <note>original: "Espannen"</note>, regardless of how or in what manner that might occur between one village and another. Thus, regarding such horse-grazing, there is no more dispute; likewise, on May 13, 1565, with the advice of the "10 Men" together with several elders from the three communities, it was so declared, requested, and stipulated to seek horse-grazing back and forth.

How the rights of common pasture—commonly called **Koppelwaid**—and the servitudes of grazing differ from each other, Cöppen *decision 12.* Whether the use of the pasture or the division of the pasture itself can be requested and carried out, Tessaur *decision 71.* Whether pastures ought to be divided, Cravetta *counsel 154.* Tessaur *Decisions of Piedmont, 72.* Regarding an attempted possessory action concerning a grazing right, Besold *counsel 9, decade 2.*

These words, due to the arrangement of the doubling <note>Refers to the legal habit of using two synonymous words (hendiadys) for emphasis.</note>

## 37. Imperial Circle. <note>original: "Kräiß-Circulus"</note>

See the **Swabian Circle Constitution.** Concerning the Constitution of the Imperial Circles and their Captains, see Mr. Stirnius, *On the Constitution of Princes, title 12, paragraph 6 and following.*

**It should be noted** that when one **Estate** <term>Stand: a member of the Empire with the right to vote in the Diet</term> sues another from outside his own Circle, then, without regarding the arbitration courts <note>original: "non attentis Auftregis"</note>, the matter can be handled in the Imperial Chamber Court, as Ziegler relates in *Common Conclusions, paragraph "Auftrega," conclusion 1, number 44.*

## 38. Circle Tax. <note>original: "Kräißsteuer. Circulares Collectæ."</note>

Circle Taxes are those collections imposed upon the Circles of the Empire. For the Roman Empire is distributed into Circles, or *Kräiß*, and originally there were only six of them: namely, the Franconian, Bavarian, Swabian, Rhenish, and Saxon Circles. *Imperial Recess of Augsburg, Year 1500, title: "How twenty persons were taken into the government," final paragraph.* Afterward, four others were added: the Austrian, Burgundian, Electoral Rhenish, and Upper Saxon Circles. *Imperial Recess of Nuremberg, Year 1522.* Each Circle has certain Prefects, or Circle Colonels <note>original: "Kräiß-Obriste"</note>, to whom the power to call an assembly is given—those who have the power to announce a Circle Diet <note>original: "Kräißtag"</note>. Mr. Bocer, *On Collections, chapter 3, number 3.*

->ADDITION.<-

*Maximilian I* in the year 1500 distributed the Empire into six Circles, to which 4 others were later added due to urgent necessity. Otto in *Public Law, page 513.* Mundius, *On Offices and Honors, chapter 2, number 122 and following.* Jacques Auguste de Thou, *History, book 2, at the beginning.* Wehner in *Practical Observations, under the word: Estate of the Empire. Concerning the 10 Circles and what rights they have.* Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and Estates of the Empire, chapter 12, page 86 and following. Concerning the Imperial Circle-Aid against the Turks*, see the legal counsel of Johann Baptist Eisen, Doctor of Laws, printed in 1663.

Circle Taxes, which concern the utility of the Roman world, are imposed on the Imperial Circles; they are commonly called *Kräißsteuer*. Mundius, *On Offices and Honors, chapter 2, number 121.*

## 39. Circle Diet. <note>original: "Kräiß-Tag. Conventus circulares."</note>

The assemblies of the Circles, the *Kräiß-Tage*, are either Universal or Particular. They are Universal when all Circles meet; they are Particular when only certain Circles, or the Estates of only one Circle, convene. They are called Universal insofar as they regard one another; otherwise, they are referred to as particular meetings in view of and with respect to the Universal Diets of the whole Empire. See by all means Aru-

<column-break/>

mæus, *in the treatise On the Diets of the Empire, chapter 2, number 32 and following*, where he provides much information worth knowing about the institution of the Circles and the assemblies of multiple Circles.

Each Circle elects its own Leaders, Envoys, and Counselors according to its own judgment: Circle Colonels, Associates, and Counselors <note>original: "Kräiß-Obriste, Zugeordnete und Räthe"</note>. If a Leader should neglect his duty or otherwise be hindered, then the office of Envoy is transferred to one of the associates in each Circle, who is commonly called a "Subordinate" <note>original: "Nachgeordneter"</note>, while the rest are called "Associates." Mr. König, *in Political Theater, chapter 27, part 1, numbers 11 and 12*, where he relates other matters pertaining to this. Add Bertram in Arumæus, *On Diets, volume 1, thesis 14 and following.*

->ADDITION.<-

In the Circle Diets, business is conducted regarding contributions, the approval or rejection of coinage, the presentation of Assessors for the Imperial Chamber Court, the execution of Imperial sentences and mandates, and the preservation of the public peace. Mundius, *On Offices and Honors, page 90.* Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 2, number 128.* Matthias Stephani, *On Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 4, number 48.* However, sometimes things are done outside the normal order <note>original: "extra ordinem"</note>, specifically when the Emperor demands a "charitable subsidy," as they call it, from the circles due to imminent danger; in such cases, the Emperor usually sends his own Commissioners and explains the reasons for the extraordinary convocation. Arumæus, *On Diets, chapter 2, number 44.*

Leaders, Envoys, and Counselors are elected. P. Denais, *in book 1 of the Chamber, title 212, under the phrase: "preservation of the public peace."* Mundius, *On Offices, chapter 2, number 124.* On whether the Circles have any jurisdiction in the matters they handle, see Bertram. Their power is restricted to the Constitutions of the Empire. Mundius, *On Offices, chapter 2, numbers 129, 131.* Explanatory councils or assemblies are called **Coinage Inspection and Valuation Days** <note>original: "Probation- und Valvation-Tag"</note>. *Code of Justinian, book 2, title "On the weight and gold brought in."* Ferdinand’s **Assay Ordinance** <note>original: "Probier-Ordnung"</note>, published at Augsburg in the year 1559, *in the preface, where it says:* "So that our coinage may be upright and handled as is proper and more magnificently executed, and so that all fraud in coinage may be prevented as much as is humanly possible, we have, etc." Budelius and Molinæus mention this. *Thus Marcus Gratidianus, as Pliny testifies in book 33, chapter 9, established a "ludum"—that is, a school or system for testing coinage—so that the frauds of counterfeiters could be met more expeditiously and promptly.* Furthermore, two days are to be held every year in Germany, specifically in each circle: *namely, the Calends [1st] of May and the Calends of October.* Regarding the security and safe conduct of those who travel to these assemblies, see the *Coinage Edict, paragraph "so that also."* In what way, first and before all else, both the mint-masters and the general and special **Public Weighers** <term>Zygo-statæ: officials responsible for the public scales to ensure the weight of gold and coins was accurate</term> are bound by the pledge of all their goods to do nothing that could in any way contradict their office, and that they will not leave the circle to which they have sworn an oath without the permission of the circle and the Lord, is explained in the *Coinage Ordinance.*

### 42. War. Bellum.

On War and the Law of War, see my work in *Special Political Discourses* and *Martinus Laudensis in his individual treatise* and his commentator, Conrad Schleiff. On whether it is lawful to wage war, see Cardinal Baronius in his *Annals for the Year of Christ 1053, number 3.*
On the war of any German Prince, see the *Marburg Consultations, volume 4, consultation 48.* On unjust war, see the *Consultations of the Duchy of Mantua, article 1.*

->ADDITION.<-

On whether the Germans have fallen away from their ancient military virtue, see Mr. Stirn, *On the Constitutions of Princes, volume 8, section 5.* Whether the Romans or the Germans were superior in war, *volume 8, section 5.*
The right to wage war belongs to the Emperor alone. Becker in *Public Law, folio 83.* Lancellot in *On the Royal Law, thesis 103.* In time of war, all laws, legal actions, and rights lie dormant. Zorer, *part 1, question 14, number 1234 and following, and part 2, question 1, number 87; question 3, number 379; question 6, number 450, and the two following.*
The gentleness of peace ought to soothe what the calamity of war brought about. Zorer, *part 1, question 12, number 950.* What does the fear of war produce? Zorer, *part 1, question 7, number 543; question 8, number 578; and question 14, number 1242.*
War is numbered among fortuitous events and matters of necessity. Zorer, *part 1, question 1, number 47; question 7, number 542; and part 2, question 3, number 223.* Barbosa, *book 5, chapter 2, axiom 3.* War does not grant a remission from the performance and payment of debt. Zorer, *part 1, question 1, numbers 44, 47, and 176.*
From civil wars, both the names and the substance of various burdens arise, *Law 1, in the preface, Code on the removal of lapsed inheritances.* <note>original: "C. de cad. toll." refers to the Codex Justinianus</note> Barbosa, *book 2, chapter 1, axiom 1.* Something is said to be done "in time of war" even if it happened a little before or after. *Axiom 4.* What things are said to be "acquired in war"? Klock, *On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 87, numbers 20 and 21.*
When subjects may take action for the restoration of things taken during wartime, Gail, *book 2, observation 57, number 6.* To whom do movable goods captured in war belong? Merenda, *book 2, controversies, chapter 22.* War must not be undertaken rashly, especially by Christians, to whom war is not permitted unless it is just and legitimate; discussed at length by Barbosa, *book 2, chapter 2, axiom 2.*

### 43. War-Chamber. Aerarium militare.

The military treasury <term>Aerarium militare</term><note>The fund specifically designated for military expenses and veteran pensions in Roman and later law</note> is that which serves the military, or the military administration. See Jacob Bornitius, *On the Revenues of the Treasury, book 1, chapter 4.*

->ADDITION.<-

The military treasury was established by Augustus with new taxes. Klock, *On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 3, number 18.*

### 44. Military Discipline. Disciplina militaris.

On whether it is right to make soldiers in Italy? See Calderinus, *discourse 22.*

->ADDITION.<-

On ancient and modern military discipline, and that the ancient form should be recalled: Zorer, *part 1, question 12, number 686 and following; also number 913.* Georg Obrecht of Strasbourg, Jurist, in his *Special Disputation on Military Discipline*; Cinuzzi, *On Military Discipline*; Dominicus Cyllenius, *On Military Discipline*. Hans Wilhelm Kirchhoff also wrote on the same subject.
The main points of military discipline are: to live honorably, to harm no one, and to help every man. Pappus in *Body of Military Law, page 4.* The disorder of military discipline is a sign before the Last Day, *page 2.*
The military was once a school of prudence; today it is a school of wickedness. It stands as far from ancient discipline as virtue does from vice. Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 149, numbers 81 and 82.* The vices of soldiers despoil their own Fatherland, not the enemy, *numbers 83 and 84.* They consider all goods to be their prey, *number 85.* A leader should restrain the first impulse of the soldiers. Schönborn in *Politics, page 643.* Otherwise, they act plainly like Nero, who sang <note>original Greek: "ὤειδεν"</note> the fall of Troy while Rome was burning; having perpetrated their crimes, they sing a solemn song to the citizens: "Joseph, my dear Joseph." <note>A reference to a traditional German carol, used here to illustrate the soldiers' mockery or hypocritical piety after committing atrocities</note> Tabor, *On Billeting, part 1, chapter 6, thesis 15.*

### 45. Military Law. Jus militare.

Mr. Speidel in his *Notable Observations.*

Military Counselors or Paymasters <term>Diribitores</term> are either ordinary and fixed, or extraordinary and uncertain. The *Ordinary* ones are the Master of the Horse, the Master of the Armory, and the Master or Prefect of the Infantry. For these, together with the Leader of the war, always carry the general care of the whole army and consult on its advantages and disadvantages. Reinhard König in *Political Theater, part 3, chapter 10, number 4.* The *Extraordinary* Counselors—

## 40. Illness. <note>original: "Krankheit. Morbus."</note>

Regarding infirmity and its legal privileges, see Thomas Actius *in his individual treatise.* On the faking of diseases: which diseases are most commonly faked, which are easier and which are more difficult to imitate? And by what method are those who feign illness detected? See Paolo Zacchia *in Medico-Legal Questions, book 3, title 2, question 1 and following.*

### ADDITION.

Illnesses that are difficult to fake, see Justus Oldekop *in Criminal Observations, title 3, observation 22.* On those typically faked by prisoners, *same author, title 3, observation 21; and how they do it, see the same and page 181.* On the governors of the sick, see Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire, page 330.* When a tenant farmer <term>Huber: a farmer holding a specific measure of land called a 'Hube'</term> allows a property to become so "sick" <note>deteriorated</note> that it cannot bear the rent, Dürr *speaks of deterioration in his work on Manorial Courts, theorem 38.*

Illness or ill health is not an impediment to a contract or a settlement, *Law "Fanum" 26, Code on Settlements.* However, it grants an exemption from guardianship if it is permanent, *Law 10, final paragraph, Digest on Excuses from Guardianship.*

In the proof of illnesses that are usually stirred up by excessive overindulgence, one must yield to the opinions of physicians. Barbosa *book 11, chapter 49, axiom 1.* Even those whom we care for as sick are understood to serve us, if they desire to serve but are hindered by ill health. *Law "Cum Heres" 4, paragraph "Stichus" 5, at the end, on the status of freedmen.*

Whether marriage is dissolved due to an incurable disease, see Rittershusius *in the New Works, folio 240, number 4.* Regarding a major, bed-binding illness <term>Morbus fonticus: a legal term for an illness so severe it prevents a person from attending court</term>, *folio 520, number 39.* On miraculous cures using rings, see Höpingk *on the Law of Seals, chapter 2, number 160,* and Kitsch *on Gold Rings, number 159 and following.*

A sick or otherwise honorably injured soldier shall nonetheless receive his pay, according to Emperor Maximilian II’s *Articles of War, article 63.*

Contagious diseases are an obstacle to a marriage being contracted, but not to one already contracted. Schönborner *in Politics, page 49.*

<margin>Besoldus, Volume 1.</margin> Those weakened by illness, widows, and orphans are entitled to a singular legal forum <note>jurisdiction</note>, based on the *Constitution of Emperor Constantine in the single law of the Code "When the Emperor [intervenes] for orphans."* There, this law is held: that the aforementioned persons should not be summoned except to their own local court, and so strictly that they cannot be dragged elsewhere even by a decree of the Prince. *Final law of the Code "If against Law or utility."* Conversely, they may bypass the lower judge and appeal to the Emperor's judge, especially when they dread the power of their adversaries. *Said single law of the Code "When the Emperor [intervenes]."* For in this case, they are seen to need the Emperor's help, as appears from the things held

<column-break/>

by Obrecht *on Jurisdiction, book 3, chapter 18, number 12.* For what constitutes a major bed-binding illness, see above. Add also Ummius *in Legal Process, page 783.* A sick person is not bound to send a proxy. *Ibid.* Girolamo Capivacci gained over eighteen thousand crowns from the cure for the "French disease" <note>Syphilis</note>. *Zeiller, French Itinerary, page 100.*

On infirmity, see Chasseneuz *on the Customs of Burgundy, in the preface under the word 'Maladie', folio 46.* Regarding the word "sick," see Mr. Harsdörffer *The Poetical Judge, part 3, page 297.* On sleepiness and fever, see Mr. Harsdörffer *in the Great Theater of Joyful and Instructive History, volume 195, page 355 and following.* Regarding the nature of Job’s illness, there are 17 different opinions on it, see Schuppius *in The Afflicted but Patient Job, page 141 and following.*

## 41. Kreutzer. <note>Latin: Crucigerus.</note>

They are named this way because a cross is commonly stamped upon them.

Four Kreutzers make one standard Batz <note>a common south German silver coin</note>, Mynsinger *century 1, observation 65.* Sixty Kreutzers are worth one Imperial Guilder; 243 and a half pieces are made from a Cologne Mark <note>a standard unit of weight for precious metals</note>, containing 6 Loth and 4 Grains of fine silver, of which the Mark is worth 10 Guilders, 26 Kreutzers, and one-seventh of a Kreutzer. *Ferdinand I's Minting Ordinance at Augsburg, August 19, 1559, paragraph 7.* Alemannus *in the Gymnasium of Consultations, 8, principle 1, part 41.*

### ADDITION.

For coins under five Kreutzers, no one is bound to accept such coins for a payment or value exceeding 25 Guilders. *Ferdinand I’s Minting Ordinance, August 19, 1559, paragraph "the now-mentioned common Imperial Coin."* Alemannus *in the Gymnasium of Consultations, page 520.* Similar municipal laws are cited by Alincus *on Executions, paragraph 7, chapter 178, at the end.* Georg Fabricius proves in *book 7 of the Origins of Saxony, folio 790, that smaller coins were struck so that in paying for services and labor, and likewise in purchasing necessities, there would be a low-value currency and the prices of things could be increased less easily.* This agrees with what is cited from Molinæus *treatise on usury, 99, number 748,* in the *Saxon Consultations, book 1, question 921, number 28:* namely, that tiny coinage was not made for conducting trade and paying large debts, but only for changing larger coins or supplying what remains over when something must be added to or subtracted from a sum or price. Kluck *on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 84, number 71.* Expenses incurred may be paid in any currency, even the smallest, as Grævius strongly argues in *1, conclusion 152, final number,* which can be seen in Ummius *in Legal Process, page 901.* Various terms for small coins are recounted by Leuber *on Monetary Reduction, and in his Inaugural Dissertation on various payments of monetary names and debts, thesis 19:* Kreutzers, Batzis, Gnackis, Albus, etc. *Binger-heller, Old-heller, Young-heller.*

Advisors are chosen from the whole army, specifically Veteran Soldiers, who possess exceptional experience in military matters. <note>original: "Veterani Milites, qui singulari experientiâ rei militaris pollent"</note> See Obrecht, *Disputation on the Constitution of War, thesis 151.*

### 47. Military Guardian, Military Bailiff. <note>original: "Kriegischer Vormund, Kriegsvogt"</note>

->Guardian for a lawsuit.<- <note>original: "Curator ad litem"</note>

We commonly call guardians for lawsuits "Military Bailiffs" <note>original: "Kriegsvogt"</note> or military guardians. Their duty ends when the case is finished (for a limited cause produces a limited effect, and when the cause ceases, the effect ceases, as per the canon law regarding appeals) unless they are appointed for all cases. See Gail, *Observations, book 2, number 108,* and Mynsing, *Centuria 1, observation 87.* Furthermore, a minor himself asks the judge to grant him such a guardian, according to the Digest on tutelage. If he does not wish to ask, the judge will compel him by virtue of his office to nominate a guardian; if he still does not nominate one, the judge himself will appoint someone for him. See Schneidewin, *Institutes on Guardians, number 10.* On guardians for lawsuits, see especially Gratianus, *Forensic Discussions, volume 2, chapter 225.*

Whether a minor who already has a general legal representative <term>Procuratorem generalem: an agent with broad power of attorney</term> can be forced to choose a specific guardian for a lawsuit is decided by Don Garf. Mastrillius, *book 1, decision 54.*

Under Lombard Law, women are under perpetual guardianship. <note>original: "in perpetuâ Tutela"</note> See my own work, *Treatise on Tutelage, chapter 14.* The Saxons still use this law, and the Statutes of Württemberg also approve of it, *part 2, title 29.*

<margin>Besoldus, Volume 1.</margin>
It is established, however, that those guardians who are appointed today for adult women—either by statute or by custom (and who are commonly called *Kriegsvögte*)—are very different from those who are given under Common Law to wards, minors, spendthrifts, or the insane. Therefore, they should not be judged by the same laws. For while true Tutors and Curators <term>Tutor/Curator: categories of legal guardians for those unable to manage their own affairs</term> are ordained under Imperial Law to govern the persons of wards or others, and at the same time to manage their goods freely as if they were the owners <note>original: "tanquam Domini"</note>...

<column-break/>

...they are therefore required to provide security <term>Satisdatio: a legal bond or financial guarantee to protect the ward's assets</term>. They must create an inventory, keep a Book of Accounts, and render an account of their administration at the end of their service. Indeed, they must even take an oath to execute their office faithfully, a practice derived from the *Novels* <note>The "Novellae Constitutiones" were laws issued by Emperor Justinian</note> and which many other laws and doctors require as solemn formalities. This is noted by Bartolus, Maranta, and Paul Montr. in his *Treatise on the Law of Tutelage, chapter 32*, along with countless others.

The Guardians of Women <note>the "Kriegsvögte" mentioned previously</note> perform none of these duties, because they do not take any administration upon themselves. Instead, they only assist women in their contracts and litigation with their authority and advice; as current practice testifies throughout almost all of Europe, and especially in our own domains. And because they lack administrative power, they are not required to give accounts to the women, nor can they be sued in a tutelage trial. Nor are their goods subject to a "silent mortgage" <term>Tacit Hypothec: a legal claim on a guardian's property that exists automatically to ensure they don't defraud a ward</term> as the assets of other guardians are. This is testified to with one voice by the distinguished legal practitioners near us, such as Daniel Moller and the *Augustan Constitutions*. There, it is taught that a guardian of this kind is not obligated to a woman further than to advise her faithfully and to the best of his understanding. For such are usually the words of the Letter of Guardianship. 

When he has done this (Moller continues), even if the outcome does not match the advice—which is not rare—or even if he did not give the very best advice, there is nothing for which he can be blamed. Rather, the woman ought to blame herself for not choosing another guardian who was more capable in counsel, since it is in her power to choose whom she wants. The reason for this decision is clear and evident: because there is no legal obligation arising from advice that was not fraudulent. And since an outcome cannot be guaranteed, it is enough that good faith was provided. The same is held by Berlichius and others, such as Rauchbar, who writes expressly on this controversy: A woman...

<meta>This page continues a legal discussion regarding the duties and liabilities of guardians, specifically transitioning from general illness-related excuses to the specific legal status of adult women under guardianship in the Brandenburg and Saxon legal traditions.</meta>

<page-num>532</page-num>
<header>Augmented Practical Treasury</header>
<meta>catchword: no. 6.</meta>

In Saxon law, adult women are not equal to minors <note>original: "minoribus"</note> in all respects. Among other differences, if a woman is harmed in a contract made with the authority of her Curator, she is not granted "restitution to her original state" <note>original: "restituatur in integrum"; a legal remedy where a person is released from a contract that unfairly harmed them</note>, according to *Wesenbeck, Counsel 11, n. 27 and Counsel 74, n. 7 and following; Moller on the Augustinian Constitutions 15, part 2, n. 98 and following; Berlich, Chapter 18, n. 41 and following.* However, this benefit of restitution is not denied to Minors harmed by the authority of their Curators under Common Law <note>original: "jure Communi"; referring to the Roman-based legal system used across Europe</note>, as seen in *Law "If Titius" 48, Digest on Sureties; Law "The Praetor says" 7, § "Not only," Digest on Minors; and the whole title on the intervention of a Tutor or Curator.*

Nor is it an objection that the aforementioned Doctors <note>legal scholars</note> speak only of Saxon Law and courts. For since the Brandenburg March <note>the region around Berlin</note> used Saxon law and customs before the publication of Elector Joachim I’s Provincial Constitution in 1527, the custom of appointing Tutors for adult women has remained to this day. Consequently, these Tutors are to be judged according to Saxon Law. A most reliable witness to this is Friedrich Pruckman, Councilor to the Elector, in *Counsel 48, number 192 and following, book 1,* and after him, Scheplitz in *Customs of the March, part 3, title 6, number 5, and part 3, title 2, § 23, number 7.*

Furthermore, it is also true under Civil Law <note>Roman law</note> that one cannot always argue by analogy from a Minor to a Woman, as Alciatus elegantly confirms in *Presumptions, rule 1, preface 42, sub-number 3; Socinus, Counsel 50, number 4, book 3; Abel Strasburg, Conference 4, number 44 and following.* This is also the text in *the final law at the end of the beginning, Digest on the Velleian Decree of the Senate* <note>original: "SC. Vell."; a Roman law that prohibited women from taking on the debts of others</note>, where Pomponius expressly says: a woman should be regarded in all respects as a cheated Minor, *compare the final Law, Code on Ignorance of Law and Fact; Law "Although" 11, same; Law "If with a Minor" 12, at the end, Digest on Minors.*

It does not hinder the argument that these texts do not speak specifically of women established under Tutelage. Since the Velleian Decree, which proceeded from the providence of that most distinguished Order <note>the Roman Senate</note>, *Law 2, Digest on the Velleian Decree,* provides as much, or rather more, protection for women than any tutor could, as is clear from *the whole title of the Digest and Code on the Velleian Decree.*

Finally, even if we were to grant that through this custom of the Brandenburg March there has been a return to the most ancient Roman law—in which women were in perpetual tutelage <note>Citing Cicero, Boethius, and Ulpian</note>—we still cannot conclude there is a total equality between the Tutors we are discussing now and other types of guardians. Even under that Old Law, there was a vast difference between a Tutor of orphans <note>original: "Pupillorum"</note> and a Tutor of adult women. This difference was most significant in the management of assets <note>original: "bonorum administratio"</note>. Tutors of women did not have this management, just as they do not have it now. For Ulpian explicitly writes in *the cited title 11, § 24* in these words: "Tutors of male and female orphans both conduct business and provide authority; tutors of women, however, only provide authority." <note>original: "auctoritatem duntaxat interponunt"</note>.

What could be said more clearly? And this is exactly what was said above: that Tutors of women today are only employed for advice and assistance

<column-break/>

and to complete the legal personhood of women, especially in court proceedings; they do not act as administrators of the assets, which the women themselves hold with full right. Scipio Gentilis further teaches this elegantly in *Commentary on the Apology of Apuleius, note 10. 21,* where he has these words: "Although he (speaking of the Tutor of an adult woman) should not be thought of as a Tutor in the proper sense. For even in those times when they were under the tutelage of their husbands, that Tutelage was not the same as that of orphans, as the same Boethius shows. He was rather a certain consultant and <term>parasates</term> <note>original: "παρασάτης"; a Greek term for one who stands beside, a supporter or assistant</note> than a Tutor."

These words agree excellently with our Curatory <note>the legal document appointing a curator</note>, in the words: **In which she, as a woman, did not know how to advise herself,** and then: **to the best true understanding for her benefit, or to be legally assisting.**

Such a Tutor today is therefore, as in the past, an <term>Einrather</term> <note>German: advisor</note> and <term>Beystand</term> <note>German: legal assistant or supporter</note>, a Consultant and <term>parasates</term>. Consequently, he cannot be sued based on the advice he faithfully shared, even if the outcome did not exactly correspond to it, *per the cited law on counsel.* Where Decio and the Doctors note *on the rule: "No one is bound by advice"* in *Rules of Law in the 6th book.* An elegant reason is given in *Law 2, final §, Digest on Mandates,* where the Jurist says: "A mandate of this kind (namely, one given only for the sake of the recipient) is advice rather than a mandate, and for that reason it is not binding: because no one is bound by their advice, even if it does not benefit the person to whom it was given, because everyone is free to investigate for themselves whether the advice is beneficial." *Compare chapter "Whoever" 14, question 1, with "Formerly" at the end, and the gloss there, Decretals on Arbitrators.*

Nor is it an objection that the final words of the Curatory are cited: **thereto the laws bind you.** For these general words do not have the power to make Tutors of women liable for everything that Tutors of orphans or Curators of Minors are liable for; there is no trace of that there. Instead, the words must be adapted to the subject matter and understood according to it: namely, that the Tutors given to the female Plaintiff provide all those things that are incumbent upon Tutors of women by Law and Custom, *Law "If stipulated" 4, Digest on Usury; Law "But if" 11, § "Likewise if" and Jason there, Digest on Oaths; and most broadly Everhard in Topics: "From the subject matter."*

Moreover, it is established from the preceding points that these men are bound to women for nothing other than faithful advice and assistance.

It is no objection that a Consultant is bound even by advice alone if the person would not have contracted without that advice, as per the text in *Law "If of remunerating" 6, § "Clearly," Digest on Mandate.* For that text does not speak of a Consultant, but of a Mandator <note>one who gives a legal order or commission</note>, not of advice, but of a mandate. And although a Mandate given for the sake of the recipient alone is called advice rather than a mandate, *cited law 2, near the end, Digest on Mandates,* no necessity forces us to take this text in § "Clearly" as referring to such a mandate given for the sake of the recipient. Certainly, François Connan, *book 7, Commentaries on Civil Law, chapter 14, number 6.*

No. 6. He provides an example in that Mandate which is given for the sake of the person receiving the mandate and another, so that it is not merely Advice; and he adds notably: that if we interpret this as broadly as we are permitted by the words themselves <note>original: "scilicet dict. §. plane"</note>, there would be almost no one who would not be bound by Advice. For everyone would say that they did by someone's advice what they would not have done unless they had been warned and persuaded by them.

<margin>Letter L.</margin>
Gothofredus, however, in the mentioned section, letter L, expressly notes that he who gave a mandate to someone who otherwise would not have acted is not held liable unless he had simultaneously guaranteed that he would provide for any loss, following *Law "If an inheritance" 32, at the beginning, Digest on Mandates.* Therefore, Decius rightly infers in the mentioned law *on Advice*, under number 1, in the section "from that reasoning": that the rule "Advice does not bind" holds place even when someone would not have acted otherwise; because the same reasoning applies, namely that Advice does not impose necessity. Petrus Peckius teaches the same in the mentioned chapter *No one from advice*, number 7, *on the Rules of Law in the Sixth Book of Decretals*, where he extends that rule to say it applies whether the person to whom Advice is given would have acted otherwise or not: because the same reason applies in both cases, namely, that the person who is consulted could decide for themselves whether it was expedient to follow this Advice or not; and there he rejects the opinion of Dynus, who decided the opposite. This was also the mind of Accursius in the mentioned Law 2, at the end, at the word "because no one," *Digest on Mandates*; Johannes Andreae in the mentioned chapter *No one*; Perusius in the same place, where he expressly says: that in contracts or quasi-contracts, one is not held liable for Advice, whether the person to whom the advice is provided would have done it otherwise or not. The same is said by Decius and Ludovicus Romanus and Cuchalon in their additions to Decius.

And certainly, if we subjected such Curators of Women to so many and such great burdens and dangers—under which other true Tutors for the most part succumb—there would finally be no one who would take the protection of that sex upon themselves.

### ->ADDITION<-

Regarding the Curator for litigation <term>vom kriegischen Vormund; literally: the "war-like" or "combat" guardian</term>, who is given to women under Saxon Law, it is noted by Setler in chapter 4 *on Oaths*, number 34 and following: that without a special mandate from the woman, he cannot demand an oath from the defendant. This is also found in Ummius *on Procedure*, page 558 of my copy, and Carpzov, part 3, decision 229. Regarding whether a woman can establish a testament without the assistance of a "combat guardian," see Lord Christoph Philipp Richter, part 4, counsel 16.

### 48. Fortification of the War. Joinder of Issue.

We commonly call the Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis Contestatio"; the formal start of a trial where the issues are defined</note> <term>ein Kriegsbevestigung; the fortification or securing of the war</term>. For a forensic trial has the appearance of a military battle. The "summons to court," and those things which are preparatory today, take the place of the declaration and notification of war. This is, as it were, the first clash of the combatants; whence of old there was a certain solemnity of the Joinder of Issue

<column-break/>

the joining of hands <note>original: "manuum consertio"</note>. Then, in place of truces, there are delays, which are also called truces <note>original: "induciae"</note>. Hence Cicero, in his speech *For Caecina*, speaks of "clashing in action," and "clashing for the defendants." See also the laws in the Code *on Forgery* and the historical works of Polletus and others.

### ->ADDITION<-

The response of a defendant using the words <term>er stelle es dahin; "he leaves it as it is" or "no comment"</term> does not constitute a true and legitimate joinder of issue, according to Carpzov, part 1, decision 40. It is a matter of recklessness if, after the joinder of issue, one or the other of the litigants allows the case to lie dormant for many years, as noted by Carpzov, part 3.

The joinder of issue is the cornerstone, the base, and the foundation of the entire judgment, upon which all acts rest; these acts are the vehicle to the sentence. In Common Law, it is one of the substantial parts of a judgment, so much so that if it is omitted, it vitiates the entire process, as Barbosa explains at length. He who allows the issue to be joined contracts a legal obligation through the judgment. An issue joined under a condition is considered as not yet joined. The term Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis contestatio"</note> is named from the "Lawsuit" <note>Lis</note> and the "Witnessing/Contesting" <note>Contestatio</note>. <term>In German: the fortification of the war</term>; the metaphor is taken from the battle line of war: which, while it is being drawn up, the battle is said to be prepared and strengthened. The judgment begins from the joinder of issue, and before the joinder of issue, there is no judgment, as Donellus and Pruckmann note. Those things which precede the joinder of issue do not deserve to be called acts of the court, but rather preparations for it. In Canon Law, the judgment also begins from the delivered citation, specifically so that nothing new may be introduced. In Saxon Law, however, a judgment in criminal matters begins with the judicial outcry <note>original: "clamore judiciario"</note>, according to the *Landrecht* <note>the territorial law code</note>, book 1, article 62. "If a man raises the hue and cry" <term>Schreyet ein Mann das Geruffte</term>, that is, one who says a crime is flagrant, he begins the judgment with that solemn cry, and he must carry it through by law, for the hue and cry is the beginning of the complaint. As to whether a joinder of issue is necessary in the remedy of "restitution to the original state," in the remedy of nullity, or in public trials, see Giphanius. Ummius is very prolix on this matter in his *Process*. Once the issue is joined, the "instance" <note>the active stage of the trial</note> begins to run, because it is not called an instance unless the judgment has commenced through the joinder of issue.

### Augmented Practical Treasury

After the edict 37, *Digest on Judgments*, law 15 "more," on ratification.

The clause and protestation of "not contesting the lawsuit" <note>original: "de non contestanda lite"</note>, which is common in practice, is not taken into account when the defendant nevertheless argues his necessary points in the main case, according to the writings of <margin>Gail, observation 73, numbers 6 and 7; Schwarzenth, book 2, action 1, chapter 3, number 11.</margin> Gail. The Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis Contestatio"; the formal start of a trial when the parties agree on the matter to be judged</note> has this effect, according to both Common Law and the procedural Style of the Court: that all guarantees <note>original: "cautiones"</note> and dilatory exceptions <note>original: "exceptiones dilatoriæ"; legal tactics used to delay a case rather than settle the merits</note> that do not concern the main case are cut off, <margin>Gail, observation 47, number 13.</margin> so that the defendant <note>original: "Reus"</note> will not be heard regarding them further. <margin>Mynsinger, 1st observation 74.</margin> Regarding other effects of the Joinder of Issue—that it prevents the changing of the legal Complaint <note>original: "Libelli"</note>, creates a "quasi-contract" and a pending suit, makes the legal representative the "master of the suit," removes the oath of malice <note>an oath that the parties are acting in good faith</note>, interrupts the statute of limitations, and so forth—see <margin>Gail, mentioned observation 74, number 4 and following; Rosbach in practice, title 49, number 27.</margin> Gail. Whether it is permitted in the "court of the soul" <note>original: "foro animæ"; a religious or moral context</note> to deny the Plaintiff's intention and, in that event, to submit an exception, is discussed by <margin>Franzkius, book 2, resolution 19.</margin> Franzkius, who distinguishes between one who knowingly and intentionally supports a bad cause, and one who either has a defense for himself or believes he has one, yet being somewhat fearful, sometimes does not believe it safe to simply oppose it; in the former case he says it is not permitted, in the latter he allows it—see his work. <margin>Suttinger, observation 41, almost throughout.</margin> It is clear and undisputed law that when the "strengthening of the strife" <note>original: "Kriegsbevestigung"; the German term for Joinder of Issue, marking the foundation and bedrock of the entire legal justification, Gail, 1st observation 75</note> is omitted or skipped in a case, then the rest of the process shall certainly be held as null and informal, as is extensively taught by <margin>Vantius on nullities from procedural defects, number 28 throughout; Gail, 2nd observation 25, number 1; Mynsinger, observation 74, century 3; Wurmser, title 3, continuous observations 2 throughout; Melonius in the index of forensic matters.</margin> Vantius on nullities from procedural defects, number 28 throughout. On the Joinder of Issue, there exists a small book by Nicolaus Vigelius, which is joined to his *Logic of Law*. For affirmative and negative, general and special Joinder of Issue, see <margin>Christoph Philipp Richter in counsel, part 1, chapter 2, number 53, folio 16.</margin> Christoph Philipp Richter. The Joinder of Issue is understood to have been made if it was not made due to the delay of the adversary, <margin>part 1, counsel 18, number 40, folio 119.</margin> How the Joinder of Issue is performed, <margin>part 3, counsel 31, number 108, folio 208.</margin> A person prevailing in a possessory action <note>a lawsuit over who currently holds property</note> is excused from the restitution of fruits <note>original: "fructuum"; profits, crops, or rents</note> gathered by him up until the Joinder of Issue in a petitory action <note>a lawsuit over who actually owns the legal title</note>. But from the time the issue is joined on the ownership claim, he will indeed be held to the restitution of the fruits. The reason is that a sentence passed on ownership absorbs the sentence passed on possession and renders it void. If the sentence, in contemplation of which the possessor held the thing, is rendered void, then the thing itself must be restored along with its fruits. However, the Jurors of Leipzig <margin>Scabini Lipsienses</margin> responded to the contrary: that one is excused from the restitution of fruits without distinction, even those gathered after the Joinder of Issue.

<column-break/>

If G. R. has initiated a legal action in a possessory case <note>original: "in Possessorio"</note> against you regarding a meadow, in which you have obtained a legal victory, and therefore the mentioned G. R. has attempted to sue you in a petitory case <note>original: "in Petitorio"</note>; although you may have lost the law in such a dispute, since you had previously prevailed in the possessory case and thus had a significant reason to involve yourself with your opponent in the ownership claim, you may not be sentenced to the restitution of fruits gathered or to be gathered. <note>original: "V. R. W." - likely a legal abbreviation for a ruling or "Under Rightful Law"</note> Firstly, because he who prevailed in the possessory action is deemed to have a just cause for litigating and for being provoked into a petitory judgment. He who justly provokes a judgment and has a just cause for litigating is not made a "possessor in bad faith" <note>original: "malæ fidei possessor"</note> after the Joinder of Issue, nor is he held to the restitution of fruits gathered or to be gathered. Secondly, because one having possession for himself, even if it is less than "Canonical" <note>fully compliant with church/legal standards</note>, is excused from being condemned to pay expenses. Thirdly, because a possessor in good faith <note>original: "b. f. [bonæ fidei] possessor"</note> who has a title is excused from the restitution of gathered fruits even after the issue is joined. Therefore, he shall be much more excused if a sentence passed in a possessory action is added to his title. Finally, although a possessor in good faith becomes a possessor in bad faith from the time of the Joinder of Issue and is held to the restitution of gathered fruits, this is true for those who are truly placed in bad faith by the Joinder of Issue—for example, if a feudal property, or a long-term lease <note>original: "Emphyteutica"</note>, or a rented thing, or something belonging entirely to another is sought, or is claimed due to a felony or a crime committed, or because the lease time has passed, and the cause of the claim is true and known to the possessor, tenant, or vassal, but he nevertheless wishes to contend obstinately; then a condemnation of fruits is deservedly made. It is otherwise if I buy a thing from someone I thought was the owner, but you say it belongs to you and bring nothing forward besides the claim and notification; then because I truly have good faith, the notification or Joinder of Issue makes me a possessor in bad faith not truly, but by a legal fiction, and for that reason I am deservedly excused from gathered fruits until a final sentence is issued and passes into a judged matter <note>original: "rem judicatam"</note>, as is beautifully and elegantly taught by <margin>Johann Garl, treatise on expenses and improvements, chapter 23, beginning almost at the last number 44.</margin> Johann Garl there; which having been premised, he rises at number 45 and the following numbers. <margin>Berlich, part 1, decision 7, throughout.</margin> Berlich. Likewise, when on October 31, 1663, this sentence was published in Nuremberg in the Peasant Court <note>original: "Judicio Rusticorum"</note> in the case of DD. against F.: that the defendant must surrender the mentioned three acres of wood to the plaintiffs, and also must make proper restitution for what he gathered in usage from the mentioned wood from the time of the claim made by the plaintiff's side; but as far as the disputed little patch of meadow is concerned...
