<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the liability of advisors and guardians. It specifically examines whether a guardian appointed for an adult woman under Saxon and Brandenburg law carries the same legal responsibilities and liabilities as a guardian for a minor child.</meta>

### Added Practical Treasury ###

In Saxon law <note>original: "jure Saxonico"</note>, adult women are not considered equal to minors in all respects. Among other differences, if a woman is harmed in a contract even with the authority of her Curator <term>Curator: a legal guardian appointed to assist an adult, whereas a 'Tutor' usually managed a child's affairs</term>, she is not granted "restitution to her original state" <note>original: "restituatur in integrum"; a legal remedy that cancels a contract to prevent unfair loss</note>. This is noted by *Wesenbeck, Counsel 11, n. 27* and others. However, this benefit of restitution is not denied under Common Law to Minors who have been harmed while under the authority of their Curators, as seen in the *Digest on guarantees* and the *Digest on minors*.

Nor is it an obstacle that the aforementioned doctors of law speak only of Saxon Law and courts. For since the Margraviate of Brandenburg used Saxon laws and customs before the publication of the Provincial Constitution by Elector Joachim I in the year 1527, the custom of appointing Guardians for adult women has remained to this very day. These guardians are therefore to be judged according to Saxon Laws. A most wealthy witness to this fact is *Friedrich Pruckman, Electoral Councilor, in counsel 48* and after him *Schepliz in the Customs of the March, part 3*.

Furthermore, it is also true in Civil Law <note>Roman Law</note> that one cannot always argue from the case of a Minor to that of a Woman, as *Alciatus* elegantly confirms. This is found in the text of the *Digest on the Velleian Decree of the Senate* <note>original: "Senatus Consultum Velleianum"; a Roman law that prohibited women from acting as a guarantor for others' debts</note>, where Pomponius expressly says: a woman should be regarded in the place of a cheated Minor in all things <note>meaning they both deserve protection from being misled, but are not legally identical</note>.

It does not hinder this argument that these texts do not speak of women placed under Guardianship; since the Velleian Decree, which proceeded from the providence of the most distinguished Order <note>the Roman Senate</note>, provides as much—indeed more—for women than any guardian could.

Finally, even if we were to grant that through this Brandenburg Custom we have returned to the most ancient Roman Law, in which women were in perpetual guardianship <note>original: "in perpetua tutela"</note> as mentioned by *Cicero in his Oration for Flaccus* and *Ulpian in his fragments*, we should still not conclude that there is a total equalization between the Guardians we are discussing and others. Even in that Ancient Law, there was a very great difference between the Guardian of orphans <note>original: "Pupillorum"</note> and the Guardian of adult women. This difference lies in the most important part of Guardianship: the administration of property. The Guardians of women did not have this, just as they do not have it now. Ulpian writes this expressly: "The Guardians of male and female orphans both manage affairs and interpose their authority; however, the Guardians of women only interpose their authority."

What could be said more clearly? And this is exactly what was said above: that Guardians of women today are employed only for Counsel and assistance

<column-break/>

and to complete the legal standing of the women, especially in court proceedings <note>original: "in Judicialibus"</note>; they are not acting as Administrators of property, which the women themselves hold with full right. *Scipio Gentilis* further teaches this elegantly in his *Commentary on the Apology of Apuleius*, where he has these words: "Although one should not think that he was properly and truly a Guardian" (speaking of the Guardian of an adult woman). For even in those times when they were under the guardianship of husbands, that Guardianship was not the same as that of Orphans. He was a certain Counselor rather, and a supporter <note>original: "παρασάτης" (parastates)</note>, rather than a Guardian.

These words agree excellently with our Guardianship Decree <note>original: "Curatorio"</note> in the phrasing: **"In which she, as a female, would not know how to advise herself,"** and then: **"to be helpful or legally standing according to the highest true understanding."**

Therefore, such a Guardian today is, as in the past, an **Advisor and Assistant** <note>original: "ein Einrather, und Beystand"</note>, a Counselor and a supporter. Consequently, because of that Advice which he faithfully imparts, he cannot be sued even if the outcome does not precisely correspond to the advice, as per the *Law on Advice*. An elegant reason is given in the *Digest on mandates*: a mandate of this kind (namely, one given only for the sake of the person being advised) is more Advice than a mandate, and for that reason, it is not binding. No one is bound by Advice, even if it does not turn out well for the person to whom it was given, because everyone is free to investigate for themselves whether the advice is expedient for them.

Nor is it an obstacle that the final words of the Guardianship Decree are cited: **"to which the laws bind you."** For these general words do not have the force of making Guardians of women bound to all the same things as Guardians of Orphans or Curators of Minors, etc. There is no trace of that there; rather, the words must be adapted to the subject matter and understood according to it: namely, that the Guardians given to the female Plaintiff perform all those things which are incumbent upon Guardians of women by Law and Custom.

It is clear from the preceding points that these men are bound to the women for nothing other than faithful Advice and assistance.

It is no objection that a Counselor might be bound even by advice alone if the person would not have entered a contract without that advice <note>referencing the Digest on mandates</note>. For that text does not speak of a person giving Advice, but of a Mandator (one giving a command); not of Advice, but of a Mandate. And although a Mandate given solely for the sake of the person receiving it is called Advice rather than a mandate, no necessity forces us to take that text as referring to such a mandate. Certainly *François Connan* in his *Commentaries on Civil Law*...

<summary>This page argues that under Saxon and Brandenburg law, guardians for adult women act only as advisors (Einrather) and assistants (Beystand), rather than property managers. Consequently, they cannot be held liable for the outcome of their advice, as women retain full rights over their property and the freedom to choose whether to follow such counsel.</summary>

### Expanded Practical Treasury
<page-num>532</page-num>

Under Saxon law, adult women are not equal to minors in all respects. Among other things, if a woman is harmed in a contract entered into with the authority of her Guardian, she is not granted "restitution to her original state" <note>original: "restituatur in integrum"; a legal remedy that cancels a contract to restore a party to their previous position</note>, according to *Wesenbeck, Counsel 11, n. 27 and Counsel 74, n. 7 and following; Moller on the Augustinian Constitution 15, part 2, n. 98 and following; Berlich, chapter 18, n. 41 and following.* However, this benefit is not denied to Minors under Common Law when they are harmed by the authority of their Guardians, according to *Law "If Titius" 48, Digest on Sureties; Law "The Praetor says" 7, § "not only," Digest on Minors; and the entire title on when a tutor or guardian intervenes.*

Nor does it matter that the previously cited doctors of law speak only of Saxon law and courts. For since the Margraviate of Brandenburg used Saxon laws and customs before the publication of the Provincial Constitution of Elector Joachim I in the year 1527, the custom of appointing Guardians for adult women has remained to this very day. These guardians are therefore to be judged according to Saxon Laws. The most abundant witness to this is *Friedrich Pruckmann, Electoral Councilor, in Counsel 48, number 192 and following, book 1;* and after him *Scheplitz, in the Customs of the March, part 3, title 6, number 5; and part 3, title 2, § 23, number 7.*

Furthermore, it is also true under Civil Law that one cannot always argue from a Minor to a Woman, as *Alciatus elegantly confirms in "On Presumptions," rule 1, preface 42, under number 3; Socinus, Counsel 50, number 4, book 3; Abel Strasburg, Counsel 4, number 44 and following.* This is also the text in the *final Law, at the end of the beginning, Digest on the Velleian Senate Decree,* where Pomponius expressly says: a woman should be held in the place of a defrauded Minor in all things <note>This refers to the Roman legal protection for women, treating them as needing similar protections to children against being cheated</note>, *supported by the final Law, Code on ignorance of law and fact; Law "Although" 11 of the same; and Law "If among Minors" 12, at the end, Digest on Minors.*

It is no obstacle that these texts do not speak of women placed under Guardianship; since the Velleian Senate Decree <note>original: "S. C. Vellejanum"; a Roman decree that prohibited women from undertaking liability for the debts of others</note>, which proceeded from the providence of that most distinguished Order, *Law 2, Digest on the Velleian Senate Decree*, provides as much—indeed more—protection for women than any guardian could, as is clear *from the entire title of the Digest and Code on the Velleian Senate Decree.*

Finally, even if we were to grant that through this Brandenburg Custom there has been a return to the most ancient Law of the Romans, by which women were in perpetual guardianship, *Cicero in his Oration for Flaccus; Boëtius on Cicero's Topics, book 2; Ulpian in the Fragments, title 11.* Nevertheless, we should not conclude that there is a total equality between the Guardians we are now discussing and others. Even under that Old Law, there was a very great difference between a Guardian of Orphans <note>original: "Pupillorum"</note> and a Guardian of adult women. This is especially true in the most important part of Guardianship, which is the administration of assets. Guardians of women did not have this, just as they do not have it now. For *Ulpian* expressly writes in the *cited title 11, § 24* in these words: "The Guardians of male and female orphans both manage affairs and interpose their authority; however, the Guardians of women only interpose their authority."

What could be said more clearly? And this is exactly what was said above: that Guardians of women today are only employed for counsel and assistance

<column-break/>

and to complete the legal persona of the women, especially in court proceedings; they are not managers of the assets, which the women themselves hold with full right. *Scipio Gentilis* elegantly teaches this further in his *Commentary on the Apology of Apuleius, note 10, 21,* where he has these words: "Although he should not be considered a Guardian in the proper sense (speaking of the Guardian of an adult woman). For even in those times when they were under the guardianship of husbands, that Guardianship was not the same as that of Orphans, as the same Boëtius shows. He was rather a certain Consultant and <term>assistant</term> <note>original Greek: παραστάτης (parastates); a legal supporter or advocate</note> than a Guardian."

These words agree excellently with our Curatory <note>the document of appointment</note> in the words: <insert>wherein she, as a woman, would not know how to advise herself</insert>, and then: <insert>to be helpful or legally assisting according to the highest true understanding.</insert>

Therefore, such a Guardian today, as in the past, is an <term>advisor</term> <note>original German: "Einrather"</note> and <term>assistant</term> <note>original German: "Beystand"</note>, a Consultant and an advocate. Consequently, he cannot be sued because of that advice which he faithfully shared, even if the outcome did not exactly correspond to it, *according to the cited law "on advice." Where Decius and the Doctors of Law on the cited chapter "No one from advice"* with the notes there *on the Rules of Law in the Sixth Book.* An elegant reason is given in *Law 2, final §, Digest on Mandates,* where the Jurist says: "A mandate of this kind (namely, one given solely for the sake of the person receiving the mandate) is more advice than a mandate, and for 그 reason it is not binding: because no one is bound by Advice, even if it is not beneficial to the person to whom it was given, because everyone is free to investigate for themselves whether the advice is beneficial for them," *supported by chapter "Whoever" 14, question 1, with "Once" at the end, and the gloss there, extra, on arbitrators.*

Nor does it matter that the final words are cited from the Curatory: <insert>to which the laws bind you.</insert> For these general words do not have the force of making guardians of women liable for all those things for which Guardians of Orphans and Curators of Minors are liable, etc., of which there is no trace there. Rather, they must be adapted to the subject matter at hand and understood according to it: namely, that the Guardians given to the female Plaintiff provide all those things which are required of Guardians of women by Law and Custom, *Law "If stipulated" 4, Digest on interest; Law "But if" 11, § "likewise if" and the commentary by Jason there, Digest on oaths; and most extensively Everhard in "Legal Topics," the section on subject matter.*

Moreover, it is established from the preceding arguments that these men are bound to women for nothing other than faithful advice and assistance.

It is no objection that a Consultant may be held liable from advice alone if a person would not have contracted without that advice, according to the text in *Law "If for the sake of remunerating" 6, § "clearly," Digest on Mandates.* For that text does not speak of an Advisor, but of a Mandator <note>one who gives a legal command or instruction</note>; not of Advice, but of a Mandate. And although a Mandate given only for the sake of the Mandatary is called advice rather than a mandate, *cited Law 2, near the end, Digest on Mandates,* yet no necessity forces us to take this text, *the cited § "clearly,"* as referring to such a mandate which is made only for the sake of the Mandatary. Certainly, *François Connan, book 7, Commentaries on Civil Law, chapter 14...*

The question was raised: what is understood by the little word *Anspruch* <note>German for "Claim" or "Title"</note>? Does it refer to the time when the lawsuit was set in motion in court, or the Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis Contestatio"; the formal start of a trial</note>, or a claim made outside of court and a mere contradiction, since the lawsuit was being aired before the Senate regarding possession? It is asked: what is understood to be denied by the general words of the Joinder of Issue, "I deny the facts as narrated, according as..." <note>original: "nego narrata, prout &c."</note>? Christian Lenzius, *On Names and Assigned Actions*, chapter 7, member 1, number 95. A Joinder of Issue made with the general words "I deny the facts as narrated, according as..." is neither simply affirmative nor negative, but is implicit, *number 96.* One who contests a lawsuit with said general words is to be considered neither as one who denies nor as one who confesses, *number 97,* because of the nature of the word "PROUT" <note>Latin for "according as" or "just as"</note>, which denotes that some contents of the legal complaint are true, while others are false, even though it may not appear which are which, *ibid., according to the cited Doctors of Law.* This general and overly deceptive Joinder of Issue—"I deny the facts as narrated, according as they are narrated"—was invented to avoid the penalty dictated for liars, *number 98.* In the Electorate of Saxony, the Joinder of Issue must be made specifically and regarding all and individual chapters and contents of the published complaint, as is decreed in the *Electoral Constitutions, part 1, Constitution 10, and in the Ordinance of Judgments and Process, title 16,* *ibid. number 99.* If a summoned guarantor denies expressly and specifically that they provided a guarantee, but is later convicted after evidence is produced, I believe they should deservedly be punished with the penalty for liars and not be admitted to the benefits otherwise available to guarantors, specifically the "assignment of actions" <note>the right of a guarantor to take over the creditor's claims against the main debtor</note>. For on account of a lie committed regarding that which is the cause of a benefit, one loses the benefit itself. Thus, Andreas Scheffer reports that a guarantor was excluded from the "exception of discussion" <note>the right to demand the creditor sue the main debtor first</note> due to a denial made during the Joinder of Issue, *part 1, question 38.* The Joinder of Issue is twofold: Affirmative on the part of the plaintiff, and Negative on the part of the defendant. Others explain these types differently; see Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated, book 1, observation 73.* Is the Joinder of Issue and the order of Law required in mandates and for releasing captives? *said book 1, observation 78, throughout.* The Joinder of Issue is necessary in both interlocutory and definitive matters brought to the Chamber <note>the Imperial Chamber Court</note> through appeal, *observation 76.* An oath has the force of a Joinder of Issue, Zahn, *On Lies, book 3, chapter 6, number 90.* This is properly to be said of a judicial oath, which one party offers to the other in court with the Judge's approval, *ibid. He gives an example in that Mandate <note>original: "Mandato"; a legal commission or instruction</note> which is given for the sake of both the person instructed and another, so that it is not considered mere Advice <note>original: "merum Consilium"</note>; and he adds a notable point: that if we were to interpret this as broadly as the words themselves allow (specifically in the section *plainly* <note>original: "§ plane"</note>), almost no one would escape being obligated by their advice. ### 48. War-Fortification. Joinder of Issue. <note>original: "Kriegsbevestigung. Litis Contestatio."</note>

We commonly call the Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis Contestationem"; the formal moment a lawsuit is officially begun</note> a *war-fortification* <note>original: "ein Kriegsbevestigung"</note>. For a legal proceeding has the appearance of a military battle. The summons to court, and the preparatory steps today, take the place of the declaration of war and denunciation. This is, as it were, the first clash of the combatants. Hence, in ancient times, a certain solemnity of the Joinder of Issue [was marked by]

<column-break/>

the joining of hands <note>original: "manuum consertio"</note>. Then, in place of truces, come the delays, which are also called "truces" <note>original: "induciæ"</note>. Hence *Cicero* in *For Caecina* speaks of "clashing in action," and those clashing on behalf of defendants, in the penultimate law of the *Codex* on the *Cornelian Law concerning Forgery* <note>original: "l. pen. C. ad l. Corn. de fals."</note>. See *Polletus*, Book 1 of *History*, chapter 4, number 4; *Theodorus Marcilius* in the collection on the *Laws of the 12 Tables*, chapter 18; *Forcatulus* in the *Legal Sphere*, chapter 1, number 38 and following; *Hilliger* on *Donellus*, book 24, chapter 1, letter B, in the notes; add *Parladorius*, book 1 of *Daily Matters*, chapter 14, where he also discusses why it is called "Joinder of Issue."

### ADDITION.

The response of a defendant using the words: "he leaves it to the court" <note>original: "er stelle es dahin"</note> does not constitute a true and legitimate joinder of issue, according to *Carpzov*, part 1, decision 40. It is a matter of recklessness if, after the joinder of issue, one or the other of the litigants allows the case to lie dormant for many years, *Carpzov*, part 3, decision 219, number 11.

The joinder of issue is the cornerstone, the basis and foundation of the entire judgment, upon which all acts rest; these acts are the vehicle to the sentence. In Common Law, it is one of the substantial elements of a judgment, so much so that if it is omitted, the entire process is voided, as discussed extensively by *Barbosa*, book 10, chapter 24, axiom 1. He who allows the issue to be joined contracts a judgment <note>original: "judicio contrahit"; i.e., enters into a binding legal relationship to abide by the court's decision</note>, law 3, section 11 of the *Digest on Private Property* <note>original: "ff. de pecul."</note>; law 57 of the *Digest on Payments*; law 20 of the *Digest on the Claim of Inheritance*, axiom 2. An issue joined under a condition is considered not yet joined, law *if anyone* 8 of the *Digest on those who omit the cause of a will*, axiom 3. Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis contestatio"</note> is named from the "Lawsuit" (*Lite*) and the "Joinder" (*Contestatione*). In German, it is *war-fortification* <note>original: "die Kriegsbevestigung"</note>; the metaphor is taken from the battle line of war, which, while it is being drawn up, is said to be prepared and "fortified" for battle. A judgment begins from the joinder of issue, and before the joinder of issue, there is no judgment, *Donellus*, *Commentaries*, book 23, chapter 1, page 2, and book 24, chapter 1 at the beginning; *Pruckmann*, counsel 15, number 117, volume 1. And those things which precede the joinder of issue do not deserve to be called acts of judgment, but rather its preliminaries, *Baldus* on the *Authentica* "clergyman," number 8 of the *Codex on Bishops and Clergy*; *Alexander*, counsel 182, number 6, volume 6. In Canon Law, a judgment even begins from the delivery of the citation, specifically so that nothing may be altered, *Pruckmann*, said volume 1, counsel 15, number 73; *Cardinal Zabarella*, counsel 10, number 4; *Abbas Panormitanus*, counsel 98 at the beginning, book 1. In Saxon Law, however, a judgment in criminal matters begins with the "judicial cry" <note>original: "clamore judiciario"</note>, *Saxon Territorial Law* <note>original: "Landrecht"</note>, book 1, article 62. *A man shouts the Hue and Cry* <note>original: "Schreyet ein Mann das Geruffte"</note>, that is, one who says a crime is flagrant, and with that solemn cry initiates the judgment, *which he must complete according to the law, for the Hue and Cry is the beginning of the complaint* <note>original: "das muß er vollführen mit Recht, dann das Geruffte ist der Klagen Anfang"</note>. Is a joinder of issue necessary in the remedy of "restoration to original state" <note>original: "restitutionis in integrum"</note>, in the remedy of nullity, and in public trials? See *Giphanius* in *Process*, book 1, chapter 15, page 126 and following. *Ummius* is very lengthy on this matter in his *Process*: he discusses on page 488 whether it is required in every cause, and on page 489 in which cases it fails. Once the issue is joined, the "instance" <note>original: "instantia"; the active period of a lawsuit</note> begins to run. *Romanus*, counsel 174, number 4, and 147, number 10, book 6; *Cardinal Tuschius*, volume 5, conclusion 397, number 12; law *to be hurried* 13, section 1 of the *Codex on Judgments*; because it is not called an "instance" unless the judgment has started, and it is initiated through the joinder of issue, law *and*...

He provides an example regarding a Mandate <note>A legal commission or contract where one person acts for another</note> that is given for the sake of the agent and another person as well, so that it is not considered mere Advice; and he notably adds: that if we interpret this so broadly as the words themselves allow us (namely, in the stated paragraph *plane*), there would be almost no one who would not be bound by Advice. This was also the view of Accursius in the mentioned *law 2, final paragraph, at the word "because no one," in the Digest on Mandates*; John Andreae in the mentioned *chapter "No one"*; and Petrulus in the same place, where he expressly says: that in contracts or "quasi-contracts," one is not held liable for advice, whether the person to whom the advice is given would have done it otherwise or not. The same is held by Decius in the *final chapter, "on the office of a legate," at the twelfth line*; Ludovicus Romanus in *Singularia 769*; and Cuchalon in his *additions to Decius on the mentioned law on advice, at letter B.*

And certainly, if we were to subject such Guardians of Women <note>original: "Mulierum Curatores"</note> to so many and such great burdens and dangers—under which other "true guardians" <note>original: "Tutores"</note> for the most part succumb—there would eventually be no one willing to take up the protection of that sex.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the Guardian for a lawsuit <note>original: "Curatore ad litem"; in German "vom kriegischen Vormund" or "the warlike guardian"</note>, who is given to women under Saxon Law, it is noted by Setser in *chapter 4 on Oaths, number 34 and following*, that he cannot defer an oath to a defendant without a special mandate from the woman. See also Ummius in his *Process, page 558 in my edition*; Carpzov, *part 3, decision 229, numbers 25 to 35, on the question: Whether a woman can establish a Will without the assistance of a legal guardian*; and Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter, *part 4, counsel 16, number 14 at the end, and numbers 12 to 15.*

### 48. Fortification of the War. Joinder of Issue.

We commonly call the Joinder of Issue <note>original: "Litis Contestatio"</note> a *Fortification of the War* <note>original: "Kriegsbevestigung"</note>. For the courtroom has the appearance of a military battle. The summons to court, and the preparatory steps taken today, take the place of the formal declaration and denunciation of war. This is, as it were, the first clash of the combatants. Hence, in ancient times, the Joinder of Issue involved a certain solemn

<column-break/>

clasping of hands <note>original: "manuum consertio"; an ancient Roman ritual symbolizing a struggle for property</note>. Then, in place of a truce, come the delays, which are also called "truces" <note>original: "induciæ"</note>. Hence Cicero, in *For Caecina*, speaks of "clashing" in an action, and those "clashing" on behalf of defendants, in the *penultimate law of the Code on the Cornelian Law regarding forgeries*. See also Polletus, *History of Fortitude, book 1, chapter 4, number 4*; Theodorus Marcilius in his *Collection on the Laws of the 12 Tables, chapter 18*; Forcatulus in the *Legal Sphere, chapter 1, number 38 and following*; Hilliger's notes on Donellus, *book 24, chapter 1, letter B*; add Parladorius, *Daily Matters, book 1, chapter 14*, where he also explains why it is called a "Joinder of Issue."

### ADDITION.

The response of a defendant using the words: "he leaves it to the court" <note>original: "er stelle es dahin"</note> does not constitute a true and legitimate joinder of issue, according to Carpzov, *part 1, decision 40*. It is an act of recklessness if, after the joinder of issue, one or the other of the litigants allows the case to lie dormant, often for many years, as noted in Carpzov, *part 3, decision 219, number 11.*

The joinder of issue is the cornerstone, the basis and foundation of the entire judgment, upon which all acts are supported; these acts are the vehicle toward the sentence. According to Common Law, it is one of the substantial elements of a judgment, so much so that if it is omitted, it vitiates the entire process, as argued extensively by Barbosa, *book 10, chapter 24, axiom 1*. He who allows the issue to be joined contracts a legal obligation through the judgment, according to the *Digest on the private fund, law 3, paragraph 11*; *Digest on payments, law 57*; and *Digest on the petition for inheritance, law 20, axiom 2*. An issue joined under a condition is considered as not yet joined, according to the *Digest on those who omit the cause of a will, law "if anyone," paragraph 1, axiom 3*. The "Joinder of Issue" <note>original: "Litis contestatio"</note> is named from the "Lawsuit" (*Lis*) and the "Joinder/Witnessing" (*Contestatio*). In German, it is the *Fortification of the War* <note>original: "die Kriegsbevestigung"</note>: a metaphor taken from a battle line; while it is being drawn up, the battle is said to be prepared and strengthened. A trial begins from the joinder of issue, and before the joinder of issue, there is no trial, according to Donellus, *Commentaries 23, chapter 1, page 2 and book 24, chapter 1, at the beginning*; Pruckmann, *Counsel 15, number 117, volume 1*. Those things which precede the joinder of issue do not deserve to be called acts of the trial, but rather its preliminaries, according to Baldus in *the Authentica "clericus," number 8, Code on Bishops and Clerics*; and Alexander, *Counsel 182, number 6, volume 6*. By Canon Law, a trial also begins from the delivery of the citation, specifically so that nothing may be changed thereafter, as noted by Pruckmann in the *stated volume 1, counsel 15, number 73*; Cardinal Zabarella, *Counsel 10, number 4*; and Abbot Panormitanus, *Counsel 98, at the beginning, book 1*. In Saxon Law, however, a trial in criminal matters begins with the "judicial cry," according to the *Land Law [Landrecht], book 1, article 62: "A man cries out the Shout"* <note>original: "Schreyet ein Mann das Geruffte"</note>, that is, he who says a crime is flagrant and begins the trial with that solemn cry, "must complete it by law, for the Shout is the beginning of the accusation." On whether the Joinder of Issue is necessary in the remedy of "restoration to the original state" <note>original: "restitutio in integrum"</note>, in the remedy of nullity, and in public trials, see Giphanius in *Process, book 1, chapter 15, page 126 and following*. Ilico Ummius is very detailed on this matter in his *Process*: on whether it is required in every case, he discusses on *page 488 of my edition*, and in which cases it fails, on *page 489*. Once the issue is joined, the "instance" <note>the ongoing legal proceeding</note> begins to run, according to Romanus, *Counsel 174, number 4 and 147, number 10, book 6*; Cardinal Tuschi, *volume 5, conclusion 397, number 12*; and the *Code on judgments, law "it must be hastened" 13, paragraph 1*, because it is not called an "instance" unless the trial has started, and it is entered into through the joinder of issue...

Ecclesiastical fiefs <note>property or offices held under the church</note> are conferred by a kiss. <note>original: "Geistlichen Lehen werden durch einen Kuß verliehen."</note> As noted by Piccart in his *Political Observations*, decade 6, ridiculous narration 4 at the end; and Arnisaeus, *On the Subject and Exemption of Clergy*, chapter 7, number 21, page 240.

### 58. Art Cabinets. Techniothecæ.
Art Cabinets <note>original: "Kunst-Kammern"; these were the precursors to modern museums, collections of curiosities, art, and mechanical wonders</note> or "Techniothecæ" of Princes, as discussed by Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 35, number 37. The Saxon collection at Dresden, the Württemberg collection at Stuttgart, and the Bavarian collection at Munich exhibit, in a single glance, a treasury <note>original: "Ceimiliarchium"</note> and compendium of the hand-crafted arts of German ingenuity. 

Consider the wooden flying dove of Prince Archytas of Tarentum <note>a Greek philosopher and mathematician credited with inventing the first autonomous flying machine</note>; or the Eagle which flew out to meet the August Emperor Maximilian for a quarter of a mile outside the city of Nuremberg, where it hung suspended above the Emperor’s head and accompanied him as he entered the city. Likewise, the ingenious mechanical Rooster of Augsburg and Strasbourg, as mentioned by G. Rittershusius, *On the Right of Asylum*, page 173.

Regarding artistic objects, masterpieces, and Art Cabinets, see Zeiller in his *Itinerary of Italy*, pages 60, 61, 63, etc. Myrmecides of Miletus and Callicrates of Lacedaemon fashioned four-horse chariots together with their drivers so small that a fly could hide them with its wings. They also built a ship that a tiny bee could cover with its wings; the same men inscribed an elegiac couplet in golden letters upon a tiny sesame seed. Callicrates even made ants out of ivory, and other animals so small that their parts could scarcely be distinguished from one another. See Aelian, *Various History*, book 1, chapter 17, page 14; and Pliny, *Natural History*, book 7, chapter 21, and book 36, chapter 5. 

Cicero, in his *Academic Questions*, recorded that Homer’s poem, the *Iliad*, was written on parchment and enclosed within a nutshell. Adrianus Junius testifies that he saw a cherry stone carved into the shape of a tiny basket, which contained fifteen pairs of dice with their pips skillfully distinguished. He also asserts that Franciscus Alumnus wrote out the Apostles' Creed and the beginning of the Gospel of Saint John upon a small medal <note>original: "denariolo symbolo"</note> without shorthand notes. There is also the eternal monument in Antwerp of a painted fly, mentioned by Philippe Bosquier, part 4, *The Academy*, sermon 1, chapter 2, folio 14; and Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, folio 336 and following. An "Exoticomathium" is a building in which ancient things and items brought from the foreign world are preserved; in German, *ein Kunst-Kammer*. Liebenthal, *Political Collections*, exercise 5, thesis 25. See also the entry for "Minuta" <note>small things</note> for more pertaining to this.

### 59. Combat. Pugna.
Combat and "to fight" <note>original: "Kampff & kämpffen"</note> are truly derived by some from the word for "field" <note>original: "campo"</note>. Indeed, Sidonius somewhere uses the phrase "to obtain the field" to mean "to achieve victory," which our people say word-for-word as "to keep the field" <note>original: "das Feld behalten"</note>. Virdung, *On Agriculture*. A "Champion" <note>original: "Campio"</note> is a proxy for a fight. Rittershusius, *On Feudal Law*, page 582, at the end; from *Kampff*, which is a struggle or contest, comes *campio*, page 27. 

Regarding "Combat," see the *Sachsenspiegel* <note>The "Saxon Mirror," the most important code of German customary law</note>, articles 62 and 63, book 1. Also *Parth. Litig.*, book 2, chapter 2, at the beginning; and Farinaccius, book 1, counsel 9, number 4. On the law of combat <note>original: "von dem Kampff-

<column-break/>

recht"</note>, see especially the *Sachsenspiegel*, book 1, article 63, page 156.

### 60. Cherry Thief.
If someone steals ripe edible fruits <note>original: "essende Früchte"</note>, such as grapes, apples, pears, cherries, and the like—and if they pluck them to eat them immediately in the vineyard, field, or on the road itself, but do not carry them away elsewhere for the sake of profit—they are not held liable for theft, nor punished with any other penalty. Berlich, 5, conclusion 53, number 10. 

However, if someone collects and plucks such fruits not to eat them immediately, but to carry them away with him to make a profit, then he is indeed held liable for theft. He is not, however, punished with the ordinary penalty of the noose <note>original: "laquei"; i.e., hanging</note>, but with another extraordinary penalty, according to the status of the person and the deed, following local custom and statute. In Saxony, this is punished with a fine of 30 shillings. In addition to this fine, he is required to make restitution for the damage. 

As the Leipzig Jurists <note>original: "Scabini Lipsienses"</note> have pronounced: If several people have climbed into a fenced-off orchard at night and torn cherries from the trees, and have chopped off the tops or branches with the cherries from several fruitful growing cherry trees, or otherwise torn them apart, they are obligated by civil law to pay for the damage, and to give the owner of the garden thirty shillings in pence as a fine. However, if the matter is pursued as a criminal case, you may punish them with temporary imprisonment, or with banishment for a year, or with a substantial fine. 

See Berlich, 5, conclusion 53, number 16. Where a great abundance and noble quality of cherries may be found is designated by Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 3, number 2. On the island of Neera <note>Banda Neira, Indonesia</note>, if anyone wished to take some field or tree fruits from the neighboring places near Fort Nassau for their own better physical sustenance, it was absolutely forbidden under penalty of being publicly whipped and branded. Johann Sigismund Wurffbain, in his *Account of the East Indian Voyage*, page 20. In Strasbourg, a special kind of "Welsh cherry" grows; they are sour like morellos, yet look in color like "Hiessen" <note>a local variety</note>; they have small stems and are not ripe for a long time while they hang on the tree—one must let them all fall off before they can be eaten.

### 61. Chalk. Creta.
See Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, book 1, chapter 7, number 53. Chalk <note>original: "Creta"</note> is a tenacious earth; there are caves of chalk-bearing earth and merchants of the chalk-making art. Dr. Tabor, *Gleanings of Crimes*, page 237. Who is permitted to use white chalk? Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 79; and the same in book 1, chapter 11, Addition, page 120. Horace, in *Epodes*, ode 12:

> Now the damp chalk remains.

Between the wrinkles of the cheeks there was so much chalk that you would think a broken wall was suffering in a rainstorm. Petronius, page 69: rivers of sweating acacia <note>gum arabic used in cosmetics</note> flowed through the fountain.

*Vinegar on the chalk. The whitened ox. Whitened ambition.* <note>original: "Essig auf der Kreiden. Cretatus bos. Cretata ambitio." *Chalk is a tenacious earth,* Columella, *On Agriculture*, book 3, chapter 11. A person who digs with the intent to steal is held liable for theft, even if they have not carried it away, because by digging they move the chalk from one place to another, according to Doctor Tabor. Among rural servitudes <note>legal rights over another's land</note> is included the right of extracting chalk, Doctor Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 87, at the end of letter G. Chalk is also included under the legal name of "metal," Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrations*, book 2, century 6, case 530, number 14.

Women with heavy feet <note>a common historical euphemism for pregnancy</note> often crave chalk, lime, sometimes coal, or even wagon grease. *Harsdörffer, in the Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories, number 67, section 5.* Regarding yellow chalk, see Limn., *On Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 79.

A few years ago, a citizen of Nuremberg <note>original: "Civis Noricus"</note> fell ill in Munich during the fair <note>original: "Meß oder Dult"</note>. As the illness suddenly overwhelmed him, he signaled for someone to bring him a piece of chalk. This was done, and with it, he wrote his last will and testament on the bottom or lid of a shipping barrel, and then he passed away.

## 62. Lime Kiln. Calcaria fornax.

In the year 1565, a new lime kiln was built by the community in L. in the Au, costing 36 guilders. It was decreed that anyone burning lime therein should pay 6 pounds in rent.

On February 24, 1607, the community resolved that henceforth, when a foreigner burns lime in the communal kiln alongside a community member, the foreigner shall pay 6 pounds and 9 pennies to the community, and the community member shall pay one "ort" <note>a quarter-coin</note>. However, if a foreigner burns lime alone, he shall pay 1 guilder, 4 pounds, and 6 pennies for use of the communal kiln; a community member burning alone shall pay 4 pounds and 6 pennies. This rule shall be upheld whether a citizen burns with a foreigner or with a tenant; the citizen must pay, whether he provides the wood or the stone. Should it happen that one or more persons have stone at the kiln, and another has already set stone inside but refuses to burn it, the next person in line—whoever they may be—shall have the power to burn out the set stones, provided they immediately reset the kiln for the previous owner.

<column-break/>

*The servitude of burning lime* <note>original: "Servitus calcis coquendæ"</note> *is a right by which someone may burn lime on another’s land for the use of their own estate. This is likewise a rural servitude,* as is clear from the law. It provides the convenience that as much lime may be burned as is necessary for the estate, such as for building or repairing houses and huts where crops are gathered. It becomes an "urban" servitude when established for a city property. If, however, it is established so that a profit can be made from the lime, it is called a personal rather than a real servitude. Caepolla, *On Rural Estate Servitudes*, chapter 10. The right of burning lime is also numbered among rural servitudes by Doctor Ludwig and Fomann. On the legal rights of lime kilns, see Klock, volume 3, consultation 149, number 38. The "Overseer of Lime" <note>original: "Calcis Præpositura"</note> was a position of dignity among the Romans, Adam Contzen, *Politics*, book 7, chapter 30. Cassiodorus, *Epistles*, book 7: *Cooked lime, matching the color of snow and lighter than sponges. Our authority appoints you to the cooking and distribution of lime.*

*Regarding workshops for cooking lime, they pay taxes,* Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, chapter 6, number 154.

What "calcination" <note>heating a substance to high temperatures to change its properties</note> is among smelters and chemists is well known. "The joining of a building with hardened, coarse sand ensures its permanence," says Harsdörffer. In many hearts, stones of lime have been found as large as a hazelnut. *Harsdörffer, in the Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories, volume 131, section 11.* A room recently plastered with lime has been a cause of death. <note>likely referring to carbon monoxide or lime fumes in unventilated spaces</note> Rupertus, *On Valerius Maximus*, book 9, chapter 12. On calcining lime to make statues: Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 35, number 5.

## 63. Klingen. Strepitus.

*Klingen*, as a noun, signifies a valley; as a verb, it signifies to clang or sound. Limn., *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 15, number 1.

## 64. Supplementing a Claim. Editio actionis.

Supplementing a claim: Vultejus, *Scholarly Disputations*, chapter 6, page 63. If the plaintiff, in the formal presentation of their case, mentions opponents or documents, these must be presented and produced along with the claim itself. This allows the defendant to better understand whether they should yield or contest the case. For that production of documents is not primarily for the sake of the documents themselves or the effect for which they are usually brought forward—namely, to prove what is being brought in the action—but rather to make the action itself and its presentation clear, or...

...or, as we say in court today, **to complete the complaint**: <note>original: "die Klage damit zu ergånßen"</note> From which it follows that, once a legal process has reached the stage of producing evidence, the documents themselves prove nothing at all unless they are formally re-submitted as proof. ### 65. Retail Shops and Stalls.
<note>original Latin: "Kram. Tabernaculum." *Kram* refers to a small shop or retail trade, while *tabernaculum* is a tent or booth.</note>

**Pack-carriers**, **vagrants**, and **peddlers** <note>original: "Rumichkerer, Landfahrer, Hausierer"</note> are the names given to those who carry their retail goods on their backs. This is further explained in the *Bavarian Provincial Ordinance*, book 5, folio 20, at the end.

The word **Kram** (retail shop) is derived from the word **Marck** (market) through a transposition of letters. <note>A common early modern etymological theory, suggesting the words share the same roots by rearranging the letters.</note>

If a woman conducts business with her husband, in that case, one spouse is compelled to pay for the other; see the title in our *Nuremberg Reformation*, title 28, book 6. She may indeed obligate herself for others even without her husband's consent, provided that the husband’s portion, which he has or expects from the common business, is not prejudiced or diminished by this. Lord Hieronymus Wurffbein discusses this in *Differences between Civil Law and the Nuremberg Reformation*, Class 1, Member 2, section 2, thesis 66. To this, you may add what the praised author has added through his own private industry to the newest edition (currently still damp from the press, in octavo format) at this location under numbers 106 and 107; it suffices to have pointed these out as if with a finger.

Regarding a **wife appointed to trade**, see Francisco de Caldas. Note in the *Nuremberg Reformation* that **"sitting in an open shop or market"** <note>original: "so, zu offnen Kram und Marck sißen"</note> is a specific situation that occurs with retailers. However, **"conducting common trade"** <note>original: "gemeine Gewerb aber treiben"</note> is a general category that includes **Innkeepers** <note>original: "Caupones"</note> alongside merchants. Hence, these words contain the general reason why **retailer-wives and innkeeper-wives** <note>original: "Krämer und Wirthsweiber"</note> are held liable, as confirmed by Gail, book 2, observation 90, number 5. There, these two are placed distinctively: **those who sit in an open shop, or those who keep an inn with their husbands.** It is added that in both cases, the wife is held liable as if by the law of partnership. Likewise, examples clarify the rule. The examples attached here show that the words **"open shop"** denote **drapers**, **money-changers**, **retailers**, and the like. Through the words **"conducting common business in another way,"** it refers to **innkeeping**. What is the law if the husband is mostly away at the market? The answer is that in case of doubt, **retailer-wives** are held liable even in this case, because it is not required that the wife be physically sitting at the shop at all times to be held liable; it suffices that both spouses share equally in loss and profit. For the retailer's trade is nonetheless a common one, even if they do not sit at the shop themselves, but rather through their male and female servants. Therefore, it applies even more so when one of them sits there alone.

But where one or the other spouse openly conducts a **separate retail business**, then the other spouse is not held liable. Thus Gail, book 2, observation 90, number 6, regarding the case where the wife has her own separate business. The title of

<column-break/>

**Merchant** <note>original: "Mercatoris"</note> is to be denied to those who only sell items in small amounts by the yard, measure, number, or weight. For those are properly called **Merchants** who trade in bulk—that is, with a large supply. However, those who only sell goods in small pieces (the **retail-sellers** <note>original: "die quåmessen"</note>) are called **vendors**, or in German, **Krämer**. These people usually sell what they buy at a higher price and above its value; they are known for being remarkably good at lying, swearing false oaths, cheating, and deceiving, and they praise the goods they want to push onto others more than is fair, according to Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 29, number 56.

The question of who properly is she who trades with her husband—that is, who may truly and properly be called a **merchant-wife** or a **market-woman** <note>original: "ein Kram- oder Marckfrau"</note>—is excellently taught by Lord Dr. Rebhan in his *Summary Delineation* of that question, proposed at the renowned Academy of Strasbourg. On what should be done regarding **retailers who overcharge for everything**, see Zorer, part 2, question 18, number 4057. How to handle debts from **retail goods, craftwork, victuals, domestic servants**, and where things are borrowed on registers and accounts in a **meeting of creditors** <note>original: "concursu Creditorum"</note>, see Zorer, part 2, question 17, number 3044 and following. A wife practicing common trade or innkeeping with her husband can be sued for the husband's debts, if she **"sits in open retail shops and markets."** This pertains to the Strasbourg constitution regarding those who have lost their inheritance. The **Benefit of the Velleian Decree of the Senate** <note>A Roman law (SC Velleianum) that prohibited women from standing as a surety or taking on another person's debt. This protection was stripped from women engaged in trade so they could be held accountable in business.</note> is unavailable to a **Merchant-wife**, when she is a **market- or shop-woman**, and it cannot be alleged as a legal defense. A woman is called a **merchant** who buys and sells, keeps open shops and windows, and weighs and measures out with weights, scales, measures, and yards, according to Lenz. This custom is attested by Simon Pistoris, Hering, Gail, and the Marburg consultations. See also the **Statutes** and **Reformations** of the most famous German Republics: Saxony, the Hessian Provincial Ordinance, Strasbourg, the **Nuremberg Reformation** (book 6, title 28), the Reformation of Frankfurt am Main, and the Statutes of Lübeck, Lüneburg, Colmar, and Cologne (as attested by Mynsinger). Likewise, if anyone from abroad wishes to consult the statutes, they should look to the Constitution of Emperor Charles V given at Brussels on October 7, 1531, and repeated on October 4, 1540.

...or, as we say in court today, to supplement the complaint <note>original German: "die Klage damit zu ergänzen"</note>. From this it follows that once a trial has reached the stage of proof, the documents themselves prove nothing at all—unless they are reintroduced as evidence—and are regarded (at least regarding their effectiveness as proof) as if they had never been brought forward, according to Vultejus in the cited place.

### 65. Shop. Stall. <note>original: "Kram. Tabernaculum."</note>

Those who carry their wares <note>original: "Kramen"</note> on their backs are called peddlers, vagrants, or hawkers <note>original: "Kümichkerer, Landfahrer, Hauſierer"</note>. This is further explained in the Bavarian Territorial Ordinance, book 5, folio 20, at the end.

The word "Kram" [shop/stall] is derived from the word "Markt" [market] through a transposition of letters.

If a wife conducts business with her husband, in that case one spouse is compelled to pay for the other; see Title 28, book 6 in our Nuremberg Reformation <note>The "Nuremberg Reformation" refers to the city's updated legal code.</note>. Indeed, she can bind herself for others even without her husband's consent, provided that the husband's portion—which he holds or expects from the common business—is not prejudiced or diminished by this. Lord Hieronymus Wurffbain discusses this in *Differences between Civil Law and the Nuremberg Reformation*, Class 1, Member 2, section 2, thesis 66. To this, add what the praised author added through his own private industry to the newest edition (which is currently wet from the press in octavo format), under numbers 106 and 107; it suffices to have pointed these out as if with a finger.

Regarding a wife put in charge of trade, see Francesco de Caldas. Note that in the Nuremberg Reformation, book 6, title 28, the phrase "to sit at an open stall and market" <note>original: "ſo, zu offnen Kram und Marck ſißen"</note> is a specific type of trade seen among shopkeepers. However, "conducting general trade" <note>original: "gemeine Gewerb aber treiben"</note> is the general category, which includes innkeepers in addition to merchants. Hence, these words contain the general reasoning for why shopkeepers' wives and innkeepers' wives are held liable; this is confirmed by the writings of Gail, book 2, observation 90, number 5, where these two are placed distinctively: "those who sit at an open stall, or keep an inn with their husbands." It is added that in both cases the wife is held liable as if by the law of partnership. Likewise, examples clarify the rule. The examples attached here show that the words "at an open stall" denote drapers, money-changers, shopkeepers, and the like. However, through the words "conducting common trade in another way," innkeepers are included. What is the law if the husband is mostly away sitting at a market? The answer is that in doubt, the shopkeepers' wives are held liable even in this case: because it is not required that the wife actually "sit at the stall" at all times in order to be liable, but it suffices that both spouses share the same loss and profit. For the shopkeeper's trade is nonetheless common, even if they do not sit at the stall themselves but do so through their menservants and maidservants. Therefore, it is even more so when one of them sits there alone.

But where one or the other spouse openly kept a private retail stall <note>original: "Einſhandkram"</note>, then the other spouse is not held liable. So says Gail, book 2, observation 90, number 6, regarding the case where the wife has her own separate business. The title

<column-break/>

of "Merchant" <term>Mercator</term> is to be denied to those who only sell piecemeal by the yard, measure, number, or weight. For those are properly called Merchants who trade "in the lump" <term>cum aversione</term>—that is, with a great abundance of goods. Those who only sell merchandise piecemeal are called retailers <note>original: "die quõmeſſen"</note> or, in German, *Krämer* [shopkeepers]. These people usually sell what they buy at a higher price and above its value; they are remarkably skilled at lying, swearing false oaths, defrauding, and cheating, and they praise the goods they want to push off more than is fair. See Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 29, number 56.

Lord Doctor Rebhan, Professor at the illustrious Academy of Strasbourg, teaches excellently in his *Summary Delineation* of the same question (proposed 1639), regarding who specifically is the one who trades with her husband—that is, who is truly and properly called a trading wife, a shop-woman or market-woman <note>original: "ein Kram- oder Marckfrau"</note>. Regarding what should be done about shopkeepers who overcharge for everything, see Zorer, part 2, question 18, numbers 40 and 57. How to handle debts for shop goods, artisan work, food, and servants in a bankruptcy <term>concursu Creditorum</term>, and where goods were borrowed on registers and accounts, see Zorer, part 2, question 17, number 3044 and following. A wife who exercises a common trade or innkeeping with her husband and "sits at open shop-stalls and markets" can be sued for the husband's debt; see the Digest, "On the action against a shipowner," and "On partnerships." To this pertains the Strasbourg Constitution regarding disinherited heirs, the section "where it happens." Add also Chasseneuz in *Customs of Burgundy*, David Mevius on *Lübeck Law*, and Stracha *On Trade*. The benefit of the *Senatus Consultum Velleianum* <note>A Roman law that protected women by making it illegal for them to guarantee the debts of others.</note> is unavailable to a "Trading Wife" <note>original: "uxore Mercatrice"</note>, when she is a market-woman or shop-woman, and it cannot be alleged as a legal exception. A woman is called a trader if she buys and sells, keeps open stalls and windows, and weighs and measures out and in with weights, scales, measures, and yards. 

Many authors testify to this custom, including Simon Pistoris, Hering, Gail, and the Marburg Consultations. One may also see the Statutes in the Constitutions of the Elector of Saxony, the Provincial Ordinances of Hesse, and the Reformations and Statutes of the most celebrated Republics of Germany: Strasbourg, Nuremberg, Frankfurt am Main, the Laws of Lübeck, Lüneburg, Colmar, and Cologne (as Mynsinger testifies). Likewise, if anyone wishes to consult the statutes of foreign lands, look to the Constitution of Emperor Charles V given at Brussels, October 7, 1531, and repeated October 4, 1540.

See also *Lord Rebhan*, in the same dissertation, theses 13 and 14. **Workshops** <note>original Latin: *Ergasteria*</note> are those places assigned to trade (*Code of Justinian*, book 2, regarding billeting), such as **retail stalls, workshops, and offices** <note>original German: *die Kramläden, Handwerkstäden und Officinen*</note>, in which formerly bondmen, and today servants and attendants, perform their labor (*Code of Justinian*, book 10, section "if any," and book 21, regarding public works). ### 66. Chains. <term>Catena</term>.

If a husband gives his wife clothing and precious items—such as jeweled rings, bracelets, and **golden chains**—pertaining only to the decoration of her body, and if there is no evidence of an express gift <note>i.e., a formal deed of gift</note>, is he presumed to have donated them in case of doubt? If so, such a gift would be confirmed upon the husband's death, and the heirs would have no right to reclaim those items. *Gail* (in *Observations*, book 2, observation 91, numbers 1 and 2) makes a **distinction** between necessary daily use and finery. In the first case, a gift is presumed; in the latter, it is not, and the husband’s heirs may reclaim such precious things. The more precious ornaments of a woman remain under the **ownership of the husband** (*Gail*, here at number 5). However, according to **Saxon Law**, the *Gerada* <note>A traditional legal term for a woman's personal property, including jewelry and household linens</note> or female ornaments are properly part of the wife’s own estate (*Matthias Berlich*, part 2, *Practical Conclusions*, 15, number 36). Whether female ornaments given to a wife by her husband belong to her upon his death can also be seen in *Arnold Reyper*’s additions to *Mynsinger*, century 5, observation 24; *Eberhard Fabricius* in *Gail Enucleated*, book 2, observation 91; and other legal authorities such as *Menochius*.

**Chains made of fire-irons and flints** <note>original German: *Feuereisen und Feuersteinen*. This refers to the collar of the Order of the Golden Fleece, which features these symbols.</note>, see *Limnäus* in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 2, number 17. 

Regarding **Chains of the Golden Fleece** <note>original: *güldenen Flusses*, likely a variant or error for *Vlies* (Fleece)</note>, and when one is permitted to wear them, see *Limnäus* in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 2, page 24.

Regarding the **chain as the "biting vinegar of satire"** <note>a metaphorical reference to the constraints or 'shackles' of social criticism</note>, see *Limnäus*, book 6, chapter 6, page 201.

**Chains** and gold or silver ornaments are **not taxed**; for the reason why, see *Mundius on Duties and Honors*, chapter 6, numbers 310 and 312. The golden chains of **Doctors** <note>referring to those with doctoral degrees</note> should not exceed the value of two hundred florins (*Walther on the Privileges of Doctors*, page 284). See also the *Saxon Police and Clothing Ordinance* of the year 1612, page 14. **Small thieves are hung from iron chains, but great ones from golden chains** <note>A cynical proverb suggesting that wealthy or high-ranking criminals escape the harsh punishments of the poor, or are "bound" only by their wealth. Original: *Kleine Diebe hängt man an eiserne, grosse an güldene Ketten*.</note>, *Lord Doctor Tabor in Criminal Gleanings*, page 115.

**Clement of Alexandria** writes that women in ancient times had to wear the image of a serpent around their necks to constantly remind themselves of the cunning seduction of their Mother of Sin <note>Eve</note>. However, they later transformed such an image into golden chains and necklaces set with precious stones (*Lord Harsdörffer in The German Secretary*, part 2, book 3, epistle 50).

The **linked band**, the **round-braided chain**, and the **rings heavy as fetters**, see *Lord Harsdörffer in The Poetical Funnel*, part 3, page 288. For a **song of thanks** for a received golden chain, see *Besold*, volume 1.

<column-break/>

See *Betulius's East-Country Laurel Grove*, page 352 and following. Concerning a **golden chain so heavy that 48 men had to carry it**, see *Lord Dilherr in Garden Pleasure*, page 303.

### 67. Clothing. <term>Vestes</term>.

**Striped clothing** <note>original Latin: *Virgata vestis*</note>. The surface of the garment is made in a striped manner. For what "striped" entails, see *Lord Doctor Rebhan*, *Selected Justinian Questions*, decade 6, question 8. If a husband dies before his wife, the **widow retains even the appraised clothing** which was later worn out by her (*Scipio Gentilis on the Valuation of Dowry Goods*, folio 170). On the contrary, *Coler* (Decision 286, number 35) teaches that it is sufficient to return such items in whatever condition they are found; the heir receives a garment worn out without the fault of the user (*Elbert Leoninus on Usufruct*, chapter 12, number 12).

Regarding the common proverb about what gives wings and spirit: **"Clothes off, clothes on"** <note>original German: *Kleider aus, Kleider an*. Likely referring to the transformative power of status through dress.</note>, *Limnäus*, book 2, chapter 2, number 59.

In the year 1560, a **Clothing Ordinance** <term>sumptuariae leges</term> was written in **Nuremberg**. Such **vestiary and sumptuary laws** <note>Laws intended to restrain luxury and reinforce social hierarchy</note> must be observed (*Limnäus*, book 6, chapter 5, folio 152; *Mundius*, question 9, number 36). Clothing was created not for the sake of ornament, but for **governing the body** <note>i.e., for modesty and protection</note>, see the law *quamvis 26* regarding legacies of gold, and *Wesenbeck*, number 3; *Barbosa*, book 19, chapter 12.

Regarding **distinctions in dress**, see *Draco on Patricians and their Luxury*, page 275. On the clothing of **Louis XI**, page 276. Clothes, although cold themselves, receive heat from us and then preserve and cherish our body with that heat we gave them (page 157). The statutes of the **Illustrious Republic of Venice** set certain limits on finery and ornaments, which not even those matrons who have married men of the **Equestrian order** <note>the knightly class</note> are permitted to exceed. Following *Matthias Bossus on the Immoderate Finery of Women* (folio 314), see my own work in the *Comparison of the Nuremberg Republic with the Venetian*. 

Such **sumptuary and vestiary laws**, where certain things are allowed to specific ranks, are also strictly required by the **Political Constitutions of the Empire**. These are observed not only by the Venetians—as witnessed by *Bembo* in his *History of Venice* (book 1) and *Klock on the Treasury* (book 2, chapter 94, number 33)—but also by the people of **Nuremberg**. See *Celtis in Nuremberg*, chapter 15, at the beginning, where he discusses sumptuary laws regarding banquets for betrothals, weddings, baptisms, and funerals (*Klock*, ibid, number 35). 

Indeed, the most honorable **Nuremberg Senate** requested and obtained the Venetian law-giving code from their ambassadors for their own use. See *Georg Rittershusius on the Right of Rings*, who says: "This code of laws is even now preserved in the **Nuremberg Town Hall, bound in red leather**; I remember having the opportunity to inspect it three years ago." The Venetians defend these sumptuary laws fiercely; when they noticed they were being gradually undermined, they ensured they were renewed under heavy penalty on January 18, 1651. **Lazarus Bayfius** wrote specifically on the subject of clothing, and most recently **Octavius Ferrarius** in Padua, 1654. Join this with *Limnäus*, book 6, chapter 5, page 152. Christians are bound by Christian vestiary laws to arbitrary punishment or other penalties published in the statutes in well-ordered...

### 66. Chains. Catena.

If a husband gives his wife clothing and precious items—such as gem-set rings, bracelets, and **gold chains**—intended solely for bodily ornament, and there is no clear evidence of an express gift, is it assumed in case of doubt that he has given them to her? A woman’s more valuable ornaments remain under the ownership of the husband, according to Gail (number 5). ### 67. Clothing. Vestes.

**Striped clothing** <note>original Latin: "Virgata vestis"</note>. This refers to the surface of a garment decorated with stripes. What constitutes a "striped" item? See Lord Doctor Rebhan, *Selected Justinian Questions*, decade 6, question 8. ### 68. Monasteries. <term>Coenobia</term>.

Monasteries brought to a better state by the Evangelicals <note>Protestants</note>, see *Carpzov*, decision 114, number 5. These are similar to the ancient monasteries, number 6.

For what purpose monasteries were formerly erected, see *Lather*, book 3, chapter 18, folio 917 and following; and *Heinrich Petræus’s Treatise on Monasteries*, which is worthy for all Princes to read, as *Lather on the Census*, book 3, chapter 18, folio 929, reminds us. *Hospinian on the Origin and Progress of Monks*. *Karl Stengel in Monasteriology*. *G. Bruschius on the Monasteries of Germany*. For what name every foundation has, see *Zeiller’s German Itinerary*, folio 212.

Regarding what noble persons of the estate of Lords were in Salzburg, Passau, Freising, and Seckau, as Archbishops, Bishops, and Provosts, see *Zeiller in the Theater of Tragedy*, page 205, 208, regarding monasteries...

See Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 5, number 44. Vadianus wrote on Monasteries. Conrad of Pfäfers wrote on the *History of the Monastery* <note>original Latin: *Casus Monasterii*</note>. ### 69. Kunigund. Cunigundis.
Kunigund, whom the King favors, from the German *Gunst* <note>favor</note>: King’s Favor. Regarding St. Cunigunde’s red silk thread, see above under the word "Bamberg."

### 70. Cold. Frigus.
The French word *chault* <note>hot</note>, meaning warm, was once pronounced "Kalt" <note>German for cold</note>; today they say "Scho" <note>modern French: chaud</note>, according to Besold in *Politics*, page 348.
Regarding "Kalt" from the French word *chault*, Tacitus in book 12 of the *Annals*, chapter 43, spoke of the "mildness of winter" <note>original Latin: *modestiam hyemis*</note>, by which grain could be brought in by ships; it was established that no more than fifteen days' worth of food remained for the city, but by the great kindness of the Gods and the mildness of the winter, they were rescued from extreme danger. See Rupert on Florus, book 4, chapter 2, section 28. All bodies are more enduring of cold, see the same author, book 2, chapter 6, section 12. The Swedes can endure the cold so well that one finds Swedish soldiers were able to endure 18 hours on sentry duty in the cold winter, as noted by Zeiller in *German Travels*, page 422. One reads in Bonfinius, decade 3, book 1, on *Hungarian Affairs*, folio 690; also in Meiger’s *Core of History*, about very hard, unnatural winters and cold spells, in which people, livestock, and trees were harmed, the sea froze for many miles out, and birds fell to the earth from the frost so that one could catch them, and they were often found dead over their eggs. Horses' hooves froze off, as happened in the years 763, 786, 832, 1310, and 1608, when there was such a great cold in Germany, the Netherlands, France, and England that the Thames at London in England froze so that one could drive and ride over it for six weeks. See more in Zeiller, century 4 of the *Letters*, pages 504 and 515. Remedies for frostbite, Zeiller, century 2 of the *Letters*, pages 302 and 303. Why death caused by cold is considered peaceful? Zeiller, century 5 of the *Letters*, page 378. Why cellars and deep wells are warm in winter but cold in summer? Zeiller, century 5 of the *Letters*, page 379.

### 71. Grain Lease. Locatio.
Grain lease, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 4, number 19. Lease <note>original: *Pacht*</note> and Leasing is said of those who have received the use of a field for a certain portion of the crops, see Hahn on the Digest *on leasing and hiring*, page 653.

### 72. Cottagers, Smallholders. Incolae precaria.
Cottagers and smallholders <note>original German: *Kotener, Kotsassen*</note>, Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 4, number 15. Also called "house-dwellers," "wage-threshers," or "earth-threshers," see Johann Philippi in the *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*, book 1, title 5, section 4 and following, *Eclogue* 38, number 5.

### 73. Kilitsch.
Kilitsch, a slightly curved sword <note>a scimitar or kilij</note>, according to Lord Doctor Tabor, *On Arms*, chapter 2, number 7.
Besold, Volume 1.

### 74. Dung. Stercus. see Manure Heap.
Short straw, that is, dung, Lord Doctor Tabor *On Tenant Law*, thesis 67. How much significance manuring <note>original Latin: *Stercoratio*</note> contributes to the profits of the estate, ibid. thesis 44. If an estate is sold or bequeathed, the dung-heap and the straw remain for the buyer and the heir, d. thesis 44. If a tenant farmer is forced to move, he must leave all straw or manure prepared on the estate at the property, by the reasoning in the law regarding the sale of a farm, section 2. It should be noted, however, that the word for improvements, *Besserung*, is understood in various ways: sometimes more strictly, as in this place, for manuring, because the fields grow fat and are enriched by it, see Berger *On the Law of the Spade*, thesis 5; Tabor, thesis 69.
Saturn was called "Stercusius" because he was the first of all to fertilize the earth with the joy of dung. The Frisians use dried dung in place of wood for fuel, Klock *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 4, number 21. Marl <note>original Latin: *Marga*</note> is the marrow or fat of the earth and a dug-up soil serving to manure fields; in German, it is *Mergel*, as if *Marghel*, because it makes the earth more fatty <note>original Latin: *pinguem*</note>, or from *Mürr* <note>soft/tender</note> and *Geil* <note>fertile/lush</note>, because marl is soft and fertile. For to the Germans, "Geil" means fat, fertile, abundant: whence Pliny in book 17, chapter 6, *on marl*: "A thicker abundance is gathered from it," that is, more abundant crops are gathered in that place which was manured by it. Martinius prefers to derive *marga* from "to wither" <note>original Latin: *mareo*</note>. For it is withered and "rotten" earth, that is, soluble. For "rotten" is not always corrupt and useless. In some things, a moderate rot is loved for certain ends, as in dung and cheese. Thus, we cannot eat medlars <note>a type of fruit</note> before their pulp softens and begins to tend toward rot, Klock *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 1, number 76.
That the dung should not be sold out of the community unless no buyer is available within the community. Megeld. *Community Ordinance*.
Coal dust manurers very well and makes the soil fruitful, Olearius in the *Persian Travel Description*, folio 101. Question: if a rural estate is sold, is the dung-heap considered sold at the same time? Agricola *On Pertinences*, question 14; Sprenger *On Moderate Things*, page 135. A tenant farmer should apply the required improvements, he shall put the manure yearly upon the goods, that is, manuring <note>original Latin: *stercorationem*</note>, law 7, Code *on the public post*.
Praise of dung see under *Majoragio*, but especially in Zeiller, century 3 of the *Letters*, folio 558 and following. Lorent Catelan on the Unicorn, chapter 4, folio 147 and following.

### 75. Cards. Lusus chartarum.
The ancients did not put the four suits <note>literally: "pieces"</note> into the cards in vain: 1. The **Acorn**, to indicate that those who fall too much in love with it are swinish. 2. The **Green Leaf**, to indicate that those who play for profit are rustling <note>fickle</note> and thoughtless. 3. The **Heart**, to indicate that those who fall in love with greedy gambling have a hardened heart. 4. The **Bells** <note>original German: *Schelten*</note>, to indicate that those are foolish who [play] for...

Playing for money, since one is ultimately not helped by the authorities to recover the property won <note>original: "zu dem gewonnenen Gut bey der Obrigkeit nicht hilft"</note>, according to the *Nuremberg Reformation, title 13, law 5.* Both the one who plays and the one who watches the game, or lends money for the game, is punished with an equal penalty as those playing. *Baldus, in the introduction to the interdiction concerning Bishops and Clerics,* where he teaches the same should apply to the one who teaches someone how to play, as noted in *Maranta on judicial order, part 6, number 35, folio 470.* Worthy readings regarding card games can be found in the *Saxon Police Ordinance of 1612, page 72.*

*A certain merchant, by a special privilege which allowed him to be the sole distributor of playing cards in Spain for ten years, amassed immense wealth, according to Klock on the treasury, book 2, chapter 101, number 21.*

The playing card tax <note>original: "Kartenspiel-Zoll"</note> was introduced in Naples in the year 1578. For every new deck of cards, one must give the King 1 Carlin <note>a Neapolitan silver coin</note>. This tax is now leased or sold annually for 20,000 Ducats, according to *Mesiger in Neapolitan Delights, page 234.* If someone plays with another on credit <note>original: "auf Borg"</note> with cards, dice, or in other ways, he or his heirs are not obligated to pay the amount borrowed; and even if guarantors were provided for this, the guarantee shall not be valid, see *Wehner’s Supplement, page 8.* *Gisbertus Voetius discusses card games in his Disputation on Games of Chance, pages 60, 71, 72, 192, and Leonhard à Ryßen in his work on the same, pages 89 and 119.*

Cards are the "passport to the poorhouse" <note>original: "Paßbrief zum Spital"; "Spital" here refers to a charitable hospital or almshouse for the destitute</note>, says *Master Harsdörffer* in the *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive History, volume 51, number 8.* The current King of France was instructed in various sciences through all sorts of card games <note>This refers to educational card games designed for the young Louis XIV</note>.

### 76. Coal. Carbones. <note>See also "Stone-coal"</note>

*Coals, burning coals, and firebrands made from cooked wood, Klock on the treasury, book 2, chapter 4, number 16. Fossil coals [stone-coal], number 17.* Stone-coal <note>original: "Steinkohlen"</note> measured by the charcoal-measure, *number 18.* Here also should be included *combustible turf*, which the Belgians call *Peat* <note>original: "Torff"</note>, which is a natural, marshy, fat, and thick sod of earth, *number 19. Fossil earth, Rudinger, century 2, observation 98, number 3.* Which I myself saw in a long series in previous years at Ulm. Cut from dry marshes. He describes earth cut into squares and dried, which provides for the hearths of the Belgians, having in mind a similarity to figs that have been crushed and reduced into masses. But he spoke rather of "marescas," which are marshes dried or parched by the sun, from whose depths that earth is extracted. Combustible earth was called *Turb* by the Germans, as noted by Barthius in *William the Breton, book 2 of the Philippide. Regarding the provision of coal, Master Tabor in 'On Arms,' chapter 1, number 16.* Should stone-coal be numbered among the Royal Rights <note>original: "Regalibus"; these are rights or resources reserved for the sovereign</note>? *Wehner's Frankfurt Consultations 88. Besold in Politics, book 1, chapter 4, number 39, section 1.* On the difference between coal-earth <note>original: "Kohlerd"</note> and stone-coal, *Libavius in Singularities, book 3, chapter 2, part 3, pages 1000 and 1001. On bituminous earth [ampelite], the whole of chapter 2.*

*On soft coal* <note>original: "De carbone molli"</note>, also called velvet-coal <note>original: "Sammetkohlen"</note>, the same author, *part 3, book 8, chapter 11. I. E.* the coal-measure is leased to citizens for interest, and one is registered for it.

*The material of coal*, since it is held principally for another use, is not understood to be wood <note>a legal distinction meaning timber laws might not apply to coal</note>, *Rudinger, century 2, observation 93, number 4.* A modest, honest man may well punish someone with an unextinguished firebrand <note>original: "unbeschüttten Brand"</note>, *Schneidewin, title on injuries, page 614, number 5.
