### 77. Crab. Cancer.

*On terrestrial crabs, Pancirollus in 'New Findings,' page 55.* Regarding crabs weighing two pounds, *Zeiller in 'Itinerary of Italy,' page 104.* In the Electorate of Saxony, the Jurors of Leipzig responded to Johann von Plößen in July 1628 in a case of crab-theft: Since B. T., when he was handed over to the executioner for a certain measure according to our pronounced judgment, stood and confessed that he had poached crabs <note>original: "gekrebset"</note> for three years in the Count's and your preserved fishing streams along with his companions; it might have happened about 13 times in total, and they caught without risk 10 or 11 shocks <note>a "shock" was a unit of 60</note> in your stream, and in the Lord Count's stream about a shock of crabs or 6 together; therefore the subject of the inquiry, because of his crime, shall be punished with the *Fratto di Corda* <note>a form of torture/punishment where the hands are tied behind the back and the person is hoisted up; here defined as "extension of the hands"</note> with two drops <note>original: "zwo Spring"</note>, and thereafter be eternally banished from the land. *B. R. W. Johannes Philippi, Legal Consultant, in 'Practical Use of Justinian's Institutes,' book 1, title 1, section 2, number 11, Eclogue 1.*

*River crayfish, Klock on the treasury, book 2, chapter 5, number 92.* In Jacob Führer von Haimendorff's *Travel to Constantinople*, on page 375, it says that when he came to Selymbria, otherwise Silivri, they were presented with crabs that were three large man-spans long. On the island of Celebes there are crabs from which four men can be satisfied. Crabs are very healthy for people with consumption <note>tuberculosis</note>. When someone applies crabs boiled with honey, they draw out thorns and other things that have been stuck into the flesh. *Johann Colerus in 'Oeconomy,' book 16, chapter 72.* In the Gold Coast of Guinea, many crabs are caught of a kind like the crabs in Norway that live in the rocks: they are quite good to eat, yet better at one time than another, which comes from the waxing and waning of the moon. Regarding the "pocket-crab" <note>likely a crab that hides in crevices</note> in high stone cracks on a very high mountain, *Adam Olearius in the 'Persian Travel Description,' book 4, chapter 12, page 450.*

->I am sometimes black, sometimes red,<-

->I am eaten, and I also eat away<-

<note>This riddle refers to the word "Cancer," which means a crab (black when raw, red when cooked), the zodiac constellation (in the heavens), and the disease of cancer (which "eats" limbs and brings one to the grave).</note>

### 78. Cheese. <note>Latin: Caseus</note>

See Zeiller, *Travels in Germany*, folio 435, 656, century 4, epistle 400, page 712, 102; century 1, epistle, page 221; century 2, epistle, page 103; century 5, epistle, page 161; in *Travels in Italy*, pages 91, 118, 120. In the year 1531, at the suggestion of John Francis, Count of Somaglia, four cheeses were made in the Milanese city of Lodi, each of which weighed 500 small pounds (one pound being 24 lot <note>a historical unit of weight, approx. 15-16 grams</note>). In the city of Parma, much cheese is made because of the good pasture, which is held in higher value than others; they are of such a size that some measure 6 spans in diameter <note>a "span" is the distance between the thumb and little finger, roughly 9 inches</note>, and it takes two men to lift such a cheese from the ground. In the court records of Geypolzheim, it is written that whoever receives property should give a cheese that is so wide that if one places a thumb in the center of the cheese and stretches the other fingers around it, the bailiff and two or three farmers <note>original: "Huber," meaning owners of a hide of land</note> have enough to eat from the edges of the cheese that stand outside the reach of the spanned or stretched fingers, and the remainder falls to the farmers. The tithe of cheese is given to the pastor in whose parish the cheese is made. Werndle on tithes, page 71, at the end. Cheeses also belong among the "Bent" goods <note>likely referring to specific feudal duties or types of land tenure</note>, *Statutes of Cologne*, folio 127.

### 82. Cat-Knights, Cats. <note>Latin: Feles</note>

Those who have not yet eaten should guard themselves against the breath of cats, as their meat is very harmful and they spread pestilence, Zeiller, century 4, question 46, page 244 and following.

"Casius" <note>bluish-gray</note> is the proper color of the eyes, which some have also called "feline" after the eyes of cats. Hence, among the Chinese, it is a mark of bad character; when they seek to insult someone, they call them "cat-eyed," which is the greatest of all insults among them with which they can attack a person of good reputation. Limn. volume 1, Additions to book 2, chapter 1, page 195. Soliman had

<column-break/>

a cat nailed to a cross, according to Dr. Dannhauer in the *Evangelical Memorial*, page 197. Female apparitions are known to take the form of cats to blind the children of God; as happened when a supposed cat jumped into an honorable man's bed, but soon after became a woman once he attacked her, held her, and cried out, and she resumed her previous form. Bock in the *Oettingen Brack*, folio 10 and 61. The epitaph of someone who died from a cat bite, Zeiller in *Travels in Italy*, folio 147, column 2.

The Arabs made images of cats from gold and, like the Egyptians, honored them as a god, Bock in the *Oettingen Brack*, folio 11. This was because they observed that this animal has a great affinity with the moon: it sees at night, and its eyes tend to become large or small according to the moon's waxing and waning. The cat is a symbol of freedom. The word *Galea* <note>helmet</note> comes from the Greek *gale* <note>original: γαλη</note>, which means a cat, because ancient warriors covered their heads with cat skins to make themselves look terrifying to the enemy. Christian Becmann on *Origins*, folio 373, 374. "Cavaliers," "Knights," or "Cats" <note>military fortifications or siege engines</note>, Schwarz on *Fortifications*, thesis 46. Cat-knights <note>original: "Katzenritter"</note>.

This is the name given to those who practice the art of wrestling <note>original: "artem Palæstricam"</note> for the sake of profit, *Saxon Law*, exercise 37, book 1. Not everyone can tolerate cats, Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, volume 142, number 2.

### **87. Changeling.** <note>German: *Kielkropff*; Latin: *Infans subditus*</note>
Consult, if you please, Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, page 138, number 9, regarding this word. <note>A *Kielkropff* was a folkloric term for a deformed child or a "changeling" believed to have been left by supernatural beings.</note>

### **88. Clover.** <note>Latin: *Trifolium*</note>
Clover-master <note>German: *Kleemeister*</note>, Rudinger, century 2, observation 42, number 5. The three-leaf clover drives away snakes. (Farnef. book 3...). ### **89. Strategic Ruse.** <note>Latin: *Strategemata*</note>
Regarding stratagems <note>clever maneuvers used in war</note>, one may consult Sextus Julius Frontinus, Zeiller... Andreas Brunner in the second part of the *Bavarian Chronicle*, page 713, and Mr. Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in *On Truce and Peace*, page 147. Also in his *Historical Accounts*, part 6, page 153.

### **90. Orphan’s Money.** <note>Latin: *Pecunia pupillaris*</note>
A common and widespread opinion creeps about that everything owed to wards <note>minors under guardianship</note>, even if it does not originate from parents or ancestors, has a right of priority <note>a legal preference to be paid first</note>—it is called "children's money" <note>German: *Kindergeld*</note>—yet this actually only applies to the assets of guardians regarding property bought with the ward's money.

### **91. Kitchen Wagon.** <note>German: *Kuchenwagen*</note>
A whole or half one for a certain taxable or hereditary leasehold estate <note>original Latin: *pro prædio quodam Censitico vel Emphyteutico*</note>. That this once existed in the Palatinate is evident in several places from the Breitenstein fief records.

### **92. Mangers.** <note>German: *Kripffen*</note>
A dry stable and dry mangers. From Dinckhoff’s Registry <note>German: *Rodel*</note> at Sachsenheim: when an Abbess of the Convent of St. Stephen comes to the prescribed court or village, one must place her horses in the farmsteads <note>German: *Hubhöffe*</note> in the village, and she shall have dry stables and dry mangers from those farmsteads. One must give fodder from the farm to those horses, and the stable shall be so sturdy and good that no harm comes to the Abbess or her horses from behind or beside them. If, however, the Abbess suffers harm thereby, the steward <note>German: *Meyer*</note> who resides on the farm must compensate for it. More in Dürr, *On Manorial Courts* <note>original Latin: *de Curtis Dominicalibus*</note>, thesis 22.

### **93. Garlic.** <note>Latin: *Ophio scorodon*</note>
See "Onion" <note>German: *Zwiffel*</note>. Hermann or Heinrich of Luxembourg was jokingly and seriously called "Hermann Garlic" <note>German: *Knuffloch*</note> by the Onions or Garlicks. Mr. Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Accounts*, page 92.

### **94. Bestowing Gifts on Children.** <note>Latin: *Donatio in Festo Nativitatis Christi*</note>
If spouses give gifts to each other—according to the custom received throughout the Christian world on the Feast of Christ’s Birth—under the name of Christ, "letting the Holy Christ bestow gifts" <note>German: *lassen den heiligen Christ bescheren*</note>, such a gift can be valid in this case, as it proceeds not from mere impulse, but rather from pious celebration for the birth of Christ. (Berlichius, part 2, conclusion 15, number 29).

### **95. Copper Smoke.** <note>German: *Kupfferauch*</note>
Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 19, page 306. Gray and white. <note>This refers to zinc oxide or "furnace calamine," a byproduct of smelting copper or brass.</note>

### **96. The Pillory.** <note>German: *Kaack*</note>
Judging with the *Kaack*. Limnäus, volume 2, additions to book 7, chapter 2, page 83. With a clear distinction between citizens and foreigners, the Honorable Council also judges with the *Kaack*. <note>The *Kaack* was a public platform or pillory used for shaming and punishing criminals in North German cities.</note>

### **97. Innkeeper.** <note>German: *Kretzschmar*; Latin: *Caupona*</note>
Inn-garden <note>German: *Kretzgarten*</note>, Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2... *Kretzschmar*, that is, a "serving town" <note>German: *Schenckstadt*</note>. Hereditary innkeeper <note>German: *Erbkretzschmar*</note>. Beatus in *Definitive Saxon Sentences*... The word *Kretzschmar* is also used by Carpzov... Five groschen fine for drawing a knife <note>German: *Messerzuge*</note> in the administrative villages where there are no hereditary innkeepers. In the Electoral Saxon Tax and Moderation of 1612, page 32: that no one shall establish new taverns <note>German: *Kretzscham*</note>. Christian Philipp Richter... Lower tavern <note>German: *Niederkretzscham*</note>.

### **98. Bondsmen.** <note>Latin/Polish: *Kmethones*</note>
This is what bondsmen <note>serfs or subjects</note> are called in Poland. (Rudinger, century 3, observation 45, number 4; Treutler... Johannes Philippi in *Practical Use of the Institutes*...).

### **99. Mining Shares.** <note>German: *Kukus*; Latin: *Partes metallicæ*</note>
Regarding hereditary shares <note>German: *Erbkukus*</note>, see above under the word *Bethe* <note>a type of tax</note> and under the word "Mining," page 92.

### **100. Restricted Inheritance Lands.** <note>German: *Kaphangüter*</note>
Those goods in Thuringia and neighboring places, which are commonly called *Kaphangüter*, can be classified and numbered among improper feudal holdings, but not among taxable lands, since they have this characteristic: that they shall fall to and be inherited only by male persons and not female persons. (Leipzig Sentence... Finckelthaus...).

# L.

There is an entire sermon in existence that does not use the letter L, intended to show that it is not strictly necessary in the alphabet. (Leonhard Wurffbain, *Historical Relations*, part 6, page 166). The custom of carrying the letter Lambda <note>the Greek 'L'</note> on shields was practiced among the Spartans, as described at length by Gregor Richter in his *Epistles*, page 825.

### 1. Land-Heirs. <note>Latin: *Hæredes vulgares* (Ordinary Heirs)</note>

The personal heirs <note>German: *allodiale Erben*; those who inherit property owned outright rather than held in feudal service</note> of deceased vassals, who are not themselves eligible to inherit the fief <note>the feudal estate</note>, are called **Land-Heirs**. (See Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 3, number 66). Can such heirs be sued if the feudal property was legally pledged to creditors? Or are the creditors instead required to demand payment of such debts from the feudal successors <note>those who take over the fief</note>? (See Andreas Rauchbar, book 1, *Saxon Questions*, question 44).

->ADDITION.<-

The personal heirs of a vassal are the daughter (Rosenthal, chapter 7, conclusion 54, number 1; and chapter 10, conclusion 10, conclusion 43, number 36) or another heir. To these, one might add the creditor (see Gothofridus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, 12, thesis 7, letter f). Regarding whether a vassal can grant a fief as a pledge or mortgage, see the same author (9, thesis 5, letters h and i). A feudal successor who is not simultaneously the personal heir is not liable for debts beyond what was contracted for the improvement of the fief. (Gothofridus Antonius, as above, thesis 9, letters d and e). A successor does not pay the debts contracted by the previous possessor of a family trust <note>Latin: *fideicommissum*</note>. (Knipschild, *On Family Trusts*, chapter 11, number 230).

On these words, see the *Saxon Consultations*, volume 2, and the additional resolutions at the end, question 10, number 4, folio 55.

### 2. Provincial and Municipal Law. <note>Latin: *Jus provinciale & municipale*</note>

In the *Ordinance of Civil Order* <note>German: *Policey-Ordnung*; "Police" here refers to general administrative governance</note> of the late Emperor Rudolph II from the year 1567, title 10, it is granted that in every place and among all estates, the **Municipal Statutes, Decrees, and Edicts**, etc., should be sought out, improved, organized, and brought into a clear, understandable harmony—especially regarding judicial processes and cases standing in law and custom.

Thus, not only Princes and Lords, but also many prominent cities in the Empire—such as Freiburg, Worms, Nuremberg, Frankfurt, etc.—have their own **Municipal Laws**.

Municipal Laws are found everywhere, relating not only to legal processes and contracts;

### ADDITION.

Concerning Statutes and Provincial Laws and their interpretation, see Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 39, throughout. Individual States of the Empire can introduce new law in their territories, not only alongside but even against the common law <note>the general legal system, often based on Roman law</note>. Formerly, provincial or municipal magistrates were hardly allowed to attempt such a thing. But after the rights of Territorial Sovereignty were granted to the States, they extended their Autonomy <note>self-governance</note> so far that they began to grant Statutes not only different from but contrary to common law (*Knipschild, On the Rights of Cities, book 2, chapter 10, number 33*). This happens with the Emperor always consenting, or at least looking the other way. (*Political Ordinance of 1577, title "On Jews," last paragraph*). This is supported by the *Chamber Ordinance, part 1, titles 13 and 57*; and discussed at length by Dr. Tabor in *On Contracts and Colonary Law, thesis 22*.

For the administration of justice, the territorial lord also issues edicts and Provincial Constitutions <term>common provincial laws and ordinances</term>, through which he can abolish common laws without consulting the Emperor and substitute new ones in their place (*Knichen, On Territorial Law, chapter 1, number 180*). And according to these, the Chamber Court is bound to pronounce judgment. (*Chamber Ordinance, part 1, title 56; Becker in Forensic Practice, page 118*). Thus, the territory of the Elector Palatine has its own Statutes; so do the Duke of Bavaria, the Duke of Württemberg, and other Princes. Similarly, the Republic of Nuremberg has its own Reformation <note>a comprehensive legal code</note>; so do the Republics of Lübeck and Lüneburg; and other places have their own Statutes. Especially those living in Saxon lands, or where Saxon Law is observed, must pay particular attention to what is established by Saxon Law.

Question: Are the Provincial Statutes and Constitutions (<term>land-ordinances</term>) of Dukes, Marquises, Counts, etc., a portion of Civil Law or rather of Praetorian Law? That is, are they permanent or temporary? The former must be affirmed according to the law (*Law 9 and Institutes on Law*), where the law which each people constitutes for itself is called "Civil Law" by Gaius, and in the same place by Bartolus it is called the "law of the people" (*Jason on the Law of Stipulations, section 9, in the Digest on Verbal Obligations*), where he says: since Bartolus, everyone generally agrees. See more in *Musculus, On Agreed Successions, member 1, class 1, conclusion 1; and following.*

## 3. Land-Peace. Public Peace.

Since after the Constitution of the Divine and happily remembered Maximilian I for the holding of Public Peace in the Empire—promulgated at Worms in the year 1495 and at Augsburg in the year 1500—it often happened among the States of the Empire that a cause of

<column-break/>

protecting and defending one's possession led individuals to claim the right to seize subjects at will in another’s territory or land. This led the States of the Empire to take up arms. Therefore, so that one does not interrupt or overturn the possession of another, and the inferior is not suppressed by the superior, but public tranquility is preserved in the Empire—and since it is fitting for no one more than the Emperor to protect the welfare of the Republic (*text in Law "For the Welfare" regarding the Office of the Prefect of the Watch*), in which tranquility the welfare of the entire Roman Imperial world rests (*Section 1, How to proceed in crimes of Treason, in the Extravagantes*)—the subsequent Emperors, namely Charles V at Worms in 1521, at Nuremberg in 1522, and at Augsburg in 1548 and 1551; Ferdinand at Augsburg in 1555 and Ratisbon <note>Regensburg</note> in 1557 and at Augsburg in 1559; and Maximilian II at Augsburg in 1566, Spires <note>Speyer</note> in 1570, and finally Ratisbon in 1576, with paternal concern and the consenting votes of the States and Estates of the Empire, brought the most healthy and necessary Constitution concerning the Public Peace (<term>the Landfriede</term>) back to the anvil <note>original: "sub incudem"; meaning they revised and refined it</note> and have kept it sound and protected until now.

Andreas Gail wrote a singular and elegant treatise on this subject, and Laurentius Reichwein collected certain noteworthy points pertaining to it in his *Formulary, folio 86 and following*, as did the compiler of *Chamber Court Precedents* under the word "Landfried," and others treating the Law and Process of the Chamber Court. See also Rosacorbus, *Forensic Practice, chapter 34*.

### ADDITION.

The <term>Public and Religious Peace</term> are constantly treated as equal (*Klock, volume 1, counsel 51, number 248*). The Royal Public Peace was established at Worms in 1495. The Imperial Recess at Nuremberg in 1522, under the title <term>Clarification of the Public Peace</term>. Public peace and quiet are so highly favored that, for the sake of retaining and preserving them, one may depart entirely from all rules of common law, and that which is otherwise prohibited is permitted (*Zorer, part 2, question 17, numbers 20 and 26*); see there for the praise and benefits of peace (*question 8, number 579, and question 12, numbers 877 and 882*). The restoration of peace is to be sought anxiously (*question 12, numbers 877 and 882*). The peace of the peoples is the protection of the Fatherland, the unity of the common people, and the fertility of the land, as Lucas de Penna says (*in his commentary on the Code, on public joy*). He who does not have Christ's peace, left in his testament, is not called his heir (*Gloss on the chapter "Apostolicam," on the word "peace," in the Sext*). Shortage and poverty often extorted peace from both warring parties (*Klock, On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 4, number 20*).

A land-sheaf <note>original: *Landgarbe*; a portion of the harvest paid as rent</note> is either a fixed annual rent—a certain measure of fruit or wine from the land—or a half, third, fourth, or fifth part of the fruits. Thus, the tenant is called a sharecropper <note>original: *colonus partiarius*</note>, and such properties are called half, third, fourth, or fifth-part estates <note>original: *halb, drey, vier oder fünff theilige Güter*</note>; see the Supplement to Wehner under this word.

### §. Territorial Sovereignty, Princely Territorial Authority. Territorial Right. See shortly below under Territorial Supremacy.

Territorial sovereignty <note>original: *Lands-Obrigkeit*</note>, or high authority <note>original: *hohe Obrigkeit*</note>, is defined as the power, protection, and defense exercised by reason of territorial jurisdiction. It is indeed universal, according to Thomas Michael in *On Jurisdiction*, conclusion 44, letter D, involving every kind of command and the right to inspire fear <note>original: *terrendi jure*; the power to enforce laws through punishment</note>. See Andreas Knichen, *On Territorial Right*, chapter 1, number 26; Caspar Ziegler, *Comments and Conclusions*, section on "Land-holders," conclusion 1, number 8; and Lord Goeddaeus in his *Counsel concerning the Lordship of Vallendar*, number 103 and page 159. Bidembach, in *Noble Questions*, question 1, makes this a twofold power, as does Hering in his *Treatise on Mills*, question 11, number 22, relating it specifically to jurisdiction and lordly power.

And it is usually granted by the law of supreme and universal jurisdiction. However, it is not always granted under the name and quality of "Princely Territorial Authority" <note>original: *Landsfürstliche Obrigkeit*</note>, as Knichen argued in the cited location and in *On Saxon Law*, chapter 4, number 60. For what if a foreigner is co-opted into the number of the Estates of the Empire? In that case, through the co-option itself, he also tacitly receives the Territorial Right—the Territorial Sovereignty and Lordship—together with the Royal Prerogatives <note>original: *Regalia*</note>, according to the text in the section "We of the Romans" in the *Peace of Constance*.

Even if he does not have the name and right of a Prince, for otherwise the title of "Estate" would be empty. Ziegler, in the same place at number 10, thinks an exact distinction must be made between the Right of Princes—the

<column-break/>

Princely Territorial Authority—which adheres only to the persons of Princes themselves, and the Right of Territorial Sovereignty and Lordship, which is granted along with the territory even without a special title. See Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction*, book 1, chapter 26, number 13; Bruning, *On Universal Right*, conclusion 19; and Bidembach, *Noble Questions*, 1, number 10. Furthermore, when the Emperor grants a territory to someone, then that person has full jurisdiction over the subjects; see Uranius on the chapter "Of One" concerning oaths, number 10.

This right is denoted in the old feudal charters <note>original: *Lehenbriefen*</note> from the time of Emperor Sigismund and before by this clause: "with his princely lordships, honors, and dignities, together with their customs, districts, rights, courts, vassals, properties, towns, castles, lands, people, estates, game-preserves, spring-works, salt-works, and all their appurtenances." Therefore, principalities are also granted as proper princely fiefs.

This eminence seems to be nothing other than the highest grade of power within the Empire, assigned to it by Bartolus; it presupposes all inferior grades and indeed all other jurisdiction that is said to belong to a Prince, such as the power to establish law, etc.

There is a difference between being "within a Prince's land and sovereignty" and "sitting under a Prince's land and sovereignty"; see Ziegler, page 104. For it is one thing to be *in* a territory, and another to be *of* the territory.

Under Princely Territorial Authority fall: the oath of hereditary homage, the mustering of troops, the selection of soldiers, prohibitions, the duty to follow the lord, the publication of mandates, the right of subjects to seek recourse or appeal, the summoning of subjects to provincial diets <note>original: *Landtägen*</note>, fines, confiscations, the pardoning of criminals, safe-conduct, the filling of offices, the improvement of police and statutes, the accounts for cities, villages, orphans, hospitals, and guardianships, tax contributions, weights, measures, coinage, etc. Add to this especially Caspar Leipold in Dominicus Arumaeus, discourse 13, question 12.

Princely Territorial Authority is also proven when the judicial acts of lower courts are requested by, deposited with, or reserved elsewhere by the Superior; or if contracts are confirmed and protected by the application of the Superior’s seals. Likewise, it is shown if subjects must request permission when they wish to take out loans, etc.

What constitutes Princely Territorial Authority? Whether a Prince or Lord, by virtue of the same, has the right to use superiority or authority over those of the nobility settled in his land? See Bidembach, *Noble Questions*, 1.

Whether a Prince, regarding major rivers—the Rhine, Danube, Neckar, etc.—that flow through the authority and estates of the nobility, has the right to exercise Princely Territorial Authority? See Bidembach, question 13.

But regarding Territorial Jurisdiction, so much has been written by so many that to add more here would be superfluous. Nevertheless, see what I have written in the treatise *On the Subordinate State of the Republic*, page 189, and also my treatise on juris-

# ADDITION.

Limnaeus, in *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 8, number 188, states that the Estates of the Empire <note>The various princes, bishops, and cities with a vote in the Imperial Diet</note> possess territorial princely authority <note>original: *die Landsfürstliche Obrigkeit*</note> within their own territories. For after the provincial governors and military leaders began to be invested with hereditary and patrimonial rights over the provinces they previously governed by mere title of office or temporary appointment, not only was the utility and jurisdiction transferred to them, but also the superiority and the royal dignity annexed to it. This authority, because of the territory to which it was granted and annexed, earned the name "territorial": <margin>commonly called territorial princely authority,</margin> in the case of Princes; but in the case of other magistrates, it is called "territorial or high authority" <note>original: *die Lands- oder hohe Obrigkeit*</note>, as per Reinkingk. Although this right of territorial superiority is "active" in the person of a Prince, Count, or Baron, as noted by Nicolas Boerius, it is "materially and passively" bound to the territory and the district, much like a fog clings to a marsh, according to Natta and Manticus. Becker notes in *Public Law* that if homage is demanded by the Lord of the territory as a Territorial Prince <note>original: *als Landsfürsten*</note>, it implies subjection; however, if it is received for another purpose, it will have a different legal effect.

Territorial princely authority is inherent to the entire territory. The Territorial Prince <note>original: *Landsfürst*</note> and the Territorial Subject <note>original: *Landsas*</note> are correlates; the prince possesses a special "Territorial Law" and a "Court of Justice" <note>original: *Landrecht, Hoffgericht*</note>. This authority is typically called "Princely" in a Prince, "Countly" in a Count, and "Noble Territorial Authority" <note>original: *Adeliche Lands- Obrigkeit*</note> among the immediate nobility, according to Meichsner in the case of Hirnheim against the Electoral Palatinate. There is a distinction between being located "in a Prince’s land and jurisdiction" and "sitting under a Prince’s authority." Territorial jurisdiction is also called "Territorial Highness and Lordship" <note>original: *die Lands Hoheit und Herrlichkeit*</note>. This specific form of territorial princely authority was once unknown in the Empire, as noted by Nicolaus Bellus in his work on the disturbances of the Roman Empire.

## 6. Provincial Court in Swabia <note>original: *Landgericht im Schwaben, Judicium Provinciale Sueviæ*</note>.

The district of the Provincial Court in Swabia

<column-break/>

was perhaps originally the boundaries of that ancient Duchy, because this court is older than the last Duke of Swabia. This Provincial Court in Swabia is an example of territorial subjection <note>original: *Landsässerey*</note>, although many were granted exemptions from it during the time of the Dukes. It seems to be a particular sign of territorial subjection that jurisdiction is also established in "compulsory court sessions" <note>original: *Ehehafftinnen*; these were legally mandated gatherings for local governance or specific feudal obligations</note>.

Regarding the Imperial Provincial Court’s freedom from nullification, see page 44. The Provincial Court has concurrent jurisdiction only with those Estates settled within its district, which is nonetheless extended by the Provincial Court Ordinance, part 1 and part 2.

That the Provincial Court is also established in criminal matters <note>original: *peinlichen Sachen*</note> can be proven from the section "In Matters However" in the first part, and elsewhere in the second part. Therefore, those who are absent or fleeing can be summoned there for criminal proceedings; if they are found guilty, the actual punishment remains the responsibility of the ordinary local authority.

The description of the ancient district of the Swabian Provincial Court, and how far its jurisdiction and concurrent judicial power extend, is set down in the Provincial Court Ordinance in the following manner. First, the Provincial Court judges across the Danube, up to the land of Württemberg, and as far as the Lech river up toward Reitte at the bridges; thereafter over to Dachheim, to the Grisons at the beginning of Switzerland, then toward Constance, and also over to Stockach, and from there as far as the district of the Swabian land extends. The Provincial Judge has a concurrent judicial power and jurisdiction; by virtue of this, he may issue commands and prohibitions to the settled Estates, as is the custom and usage in other Imperial Provincial Courts.

In the matter of our Provincial Court’s ordinary concurrent judicial power and authority just described, it shall remain so once again, as it has come down from olden times. However, small and insignificant claims, which do not amount to the value of one Guilder in principal assets, shall not be accepted at this Provincial Court—unless it happens that the plaintiff was denied justice by the other nearest authorities, or delayed, or if the plaintiff would have to pursue his claim before such authority at greater cost than at the Provincial Court. Cases concerning the Provincial Court's compulsory sessions <note>original: *Ehehafftinnin*</note>, superior rent-lordship <note>original: *Ober-Zins-Herrlichkeit*</note>, servitudes <note>original: *Dienstbarkeit*</note>, and similar rights are also exceptions; in those cases, even if they are below the named sum of one Guilder, this Provincial Court shall henceforth have and keep its concurrent judicial power, as has been customary since antiquity. But for the sake of greater accuracy in these matters, the claim of every plaintiff shall be investigated and explicitly stated in the summons, and whoever provides his claim and right for the purpose of obtaining a citation shall do so voluntarily...

The Provincial Courts shall be held as they have been from ancient tradition and as they have been in use during this time, in the following three Imperial Cities: Ravensburg, Wangen, and Isny, and then in the market town of Altdorf, called Weingarten. The Mayors and Councils of each of the three Imperial Cities <note>Cities that were self-governing and held their authority directly from the Holy Roman Emperor</note>, and especially the Magistrate <note>original: *Amman*</note> and Council of the town of Altdorf, shall—as has happened until now—appoint as many Verdict-speakers <note>original: *Urtheilsprecher*; these were lay judges or assessors who determined the verdict</note> as are necessary so that each Provincial Court may be staffed with twelve Verdict-speakers. These Verdict-speakers shall swear the following oath regarding the Provincial Court to the Mayor and Council of each city by which they are appointed, and also to the Magistrate and Council of the frequently mentioned town of Altdorf.

Although from ancient times, far beyond human memory, it has been customary at the Provincial Court that whoever—of high or low standing—wished to claim themselves or their people away from the Provincial Court <note>A legal maneuver to move a case to one's own local jurisdiction</note> had to present their Imperial or Royal privileges <note>Documents granting exemptions or special rights</note> in the original or as a credible certified copy <note>original: *Vidimus*</note>, along with the most recent Imperial and Royal confirmation, through a Verdict-speaker of the Provincial Court. This was accompanied by a written request for removal before the court. The referral <note>original: *Remission*</note> would then legally follow, except in cases of "legal impediments" <note>original: *Ehehafftinn*; specific legal excuses like illness, flood, or war</note> defined hereafter. This included the condition and ruling that the plaintiff, his attorney, or whomever he brings or sends, be sent a free, secure safe-conduct <note>original: *Glait*</note> within fourteen days following such a referral to his house or court. Furthermore, upon his request, free, unconditional, and unprolonged justice should be granted and occur within six weeks and three days following his demand before the judge to whom he was referred. Nevertheless, for the grace and benefit of all high and low estates, the nobility, cities, and communities—so that they do not have to send their original privileges across the land so frequently—We graciously grant, as far as it concerns Us, that henceforth the mentioned estates, nobility, cities, and communities who possess privileges may present such privileges with the most recent confirmation, either in the original or a credible transcript <note>original: *Transsumpt*</note>, together with the last confirmation of a Roman Emperor or King. This may be done either through proven, matriculated Imperial Notaries and two witnesses, or through the sworn Provincial Court Procurators <note>Legal representatives</note> before the sitting Provincial Court. This needs to be done publicly and solemnly only once at all four of the jurisdictional sites <note>original: *Malstätten*</note> of the Provincial Court (alongside a written request for removal, should they or any of their subjects be cited to said court). Upon this presentation <note>original: *Insinuation*</note>, a Provincial Judge—with the proviso that the rights and justices of this laudable Provincial Court regarding its exempt legal impediments, privileges, ancient traditions, and customs, as well as primarily those of His Roman Imperial Majesty and the most noble House of Aust-

*Besoldus, Volume I.*

<column-break/>

ria, and otherwise everyone else’s authority, shall remain unprejudiced and unharmed—shall ensure such privileges and latest confirmations are properly inscribed by the court clerks into a dedicated book kept for that purpose at the four jurisdictional sites of the Provincial Court, at the parties' expense, and shall be diligently compared against the originals by the Provincial Judge.

Thereafter, at every Provincial Court session, as often as they or their people are cited, they may simply bring forward their written requests for removal through permitted advocates or attorneys. In these, they shall refer to and request the showing of their privileges and confirmations previously brought before the Provincial Court and recorded in the protocol. Upon such written request, the referral (excepting the Provincial Court’s legal impediments) shall take place with the condition and ruling as previously mentioned. And if a plaintiff should again complain before the Provincial Court that the safe-conduct did not reach him at the appointed time, or that justice was denied, delayed, or not kept unconditional according to the referral, and if such is found to be true, then the matter shall no longer be referred elsewhere but shall be retained before the Provincial Court.

We also will that henceforth all Our holders of fiefs and pledges <note>Lands held in exchange for service or as collateral for a debt</note> of the Austrian subjects and estates, of whatever standing or nature they may be—of which Our Provincial Judge in Swabia has an orderly, specified list at hand—shall primarily claim those same Austrian fiefs and Our own subjects' estates and lordships by virtue of the Austrian privileges and request the referrals. In such cases, where no Provincial Court legal impediment occurs, the referral shall be granted; otherwise, the request for removal shall be denied.

Otherwise, and in all other matters concerning themselves, their own subjects, and estates, they may make the requests for removal by virtue of their own privileges of exemption, though these shall be left with a permanent distinction and exception for the legal impediments.

From the Provincial Court, can one appeal to the Chamber Court? <note>original: *adpelleter ad Cameram?*</note> See Rosac. last chapter; and I have said certain things on this matter in my treatise on the aid of appeals <note>original: *de appellat. juvamine*</note>. Add this under "Imperial Chamber Precedents" <note>original: *Præjudicia Cameralia*</note> at the word *Landgericht*. Such courts are found throughout Germany; there are many. And those in Swabia seem to be remnants of the Territorial Law <note>original: *Juris Territorialis*</note> which the Dukes of Swabia once held.

### ADDITION.

The Provincial Courts <note>original: *Judicia Provincialia*</note>, once belonging to the Dukes of Swabia, were later transferred to the Empire, and by the Empire pledged to the Austrians; they seem to smack of that ancient subjection from the father <note>meaning inherited from ancestral lineage</note>. See Limnaeus in *Public Law* <note>original: *J. P.* or *Jure Publico*</note>, book 6, chapter 3, number 56, near the end.

## 7. Land-ditches. Moats. Territorial Boundaries.

Regarding the legality of making land-ditches <note>original: *Landgräben machen*</note>, see Rœner, chapter 20, where he discusses a case involving the Duke of Württemberg.

### ADDITION.

Regarding whether the establishing, cutting, and maintaining of land-ditches <note>original: *Landgraben, richten, schrotten und führen*</note> is a sign of Jurisdiction and Sovereignty, see Klockius, volume 1, counsel 27, numbers 23, 24, 25, 26, 28.

Marcus, the Governor of Syria, when Agrippa was fortifying Jerusalem, took care to denounce the new work to him in the name of Claudius Caesar, as recorded by Josephus in *Antiquities*, book 19, chapter 7. Frederick I ordered the Genoese to cease their fortification as if they were fortifying a city, as sung by Günther in the *Ligurinus*:

> —— Lest the people proceed to enclose the city,
> Having been ordered to desist from the wall they began.

A decree and report from Dr. Matthias noted that even in the year 1417, by Emperor Sigismund at the Council then held at Constance—with the advice and assistance of the present Electors and Estates of the Empire—the ditches, walls, oriels, fortified precincts <note>original: *Burgkfrieden*</note>, and other bulwarks thrown up at that time at M. and M. were, with full knowledge of the case, struck down by judgment and law, and such a judgment was also brought to actual execution; see Anton Coler, *On the Law of the Empire*, section 26, number 5; joined with law 9, *sacra* in paragraph 4, *muros* of the Digest *On the Division of Things*; see also Bl. Cunæus, *On the Hebrew Republic*, book 1, chapter 7, page 58. However, these things concern those who do so without Investiture <note>The formal ceremony of being granted land or office by a superior</note>. The Estates of the Empire can fortify castles and build and maintain strongholds; see Knichen, *On Territorial Law*, chapter 3, number 238; Sixtin, *On Regalia*, book 2, chapter 1, number 15; Ming, *On Territorial Sovereignty*, chapter 5.

## 8. Provincial Judicial Authority. *Jurisdictio provincialis*.

Provincial judicial authority <note>original: *Landgerichtliche Obrigkeit*</note> is taken to mean the jurisdiction of any Imperial Prefecture, a provincial bailiwick <note>original: *Landvogtey*</note>: which for the most part has a jurisdiction concurrent with other courts, and therefore "prevention" <note>A legal principle where the first court to take up a case gains the right to finish it</note> has a place in it, as noted by Keller, *On the Office of Jurisdiction*, book 2, chapter 12, page 402 in my copy; judging in civil and criminal cases, just as the Imperial Chamber Court has concurrent jurisdiction with the Emperor, as noted by Gail, book 1, observation 29, number 33. In this court, however, criminal cases are not received except by reason of a nullity in the process; Gail, book 1, observation 1, number 27. Provincial judicial authority (although it sometimes seems to drag landed subjects <note>original: *Landsassen*</note> with it) does not imply Territorial Subjection: since even the Immediate Estates <note>High-ranking nobles or cities that answer only to the Emperor</note> are subject to it in certain matters.

### ADDITION.

Immediate Nobles are not subject to any provincial court, as noted by Besold in the *Discourse on the Equestrian Order*; Cluten in *Sylloge of Daily Matters*, thesis 26; and Wehner under the word *Landsassen* [landed subjects]. For although

<column-break/>

Princes—under the pretext of provincial and princely authority <note>original: *der Land & Fürstlichen Obrigkeit*</note>, forestry, feudal matters, and a thousand other ways—have often attempted and continue to attempt to this day to drag them as subjects to the Provincial Courts <note>original: *für die Landgericht*</note>, nevertheless the nobles themselves, bearing this stain with difficulty, have always opposed it. Sometimes, overflowing with a just grief, they have presented letters to the Emperor, stating that under the appearance of Provincial-Princely Authority, forestry rights, and feudal justice, people wish to deprive them of their freedom and turn them into landed subjects <note>original: *zu Landsassen machen*</note>. Hence in the year 1592, a mandate was issued by the Emperor Rudolph II, that the Chamber Court should not pronounce against their liberty under the pretext of high authority <note>original: *der hohen Obrigkeit*</note>.

On whether Provincial Judicial Authority implies Jurisdiction, see G. Herpffer in *Noble Questions*, question 2; and Besold, counsel 211, number 17.

## 9. Landgrave. *Landgravius*.

Landgraves or Provincial Counts <note>original: *die Landgraven*</note> were formerly judges of an entire Province, and judges of the interior (to distinguish them from Margraves <note>original: *Marchionum*; counts of the borderlands</note>) who were judges of a land that lies between the borders of the Empire, according to Petrus de Andlo, book 2, *On the Roman Empire*, chapter 12; Henning Arnifæus, *On the Law of Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, under number 15, page 322 in my copy, at the verse beginning *Landgravii verò*; and myself in the treatise *On Counts*, number 9.

### ADDITION.

Landgraves are also called Princes, or Princes of the Empire <note>original: *Fürsten des Reichs*</note>. And although Landgraves and Margraves are from the class of Counts, today they are superior to them and are placed in the rank of Princes; see Heig, *Illustrious Questions*, 2, number 55, part 1; Ruland, *On Commissions*, part 2, book 5, chapter 4, number 26. Properly speaking, those are called Landgraves today who are enfeoffed with a Principality called a Landgraviate, and who possess the same under a princely quality; Reink, class 1, 4, chapter 13, number 27. Such in the Empire are the Landgrave of Thuringia, of Hesse, and of Alsace, to which Schönborn in his *Politics*, page 569, adds the Landgrave of Leuchtenberg. The Landgraves of Leuchtenberg are counted from an ancient Princely family among the four Landgraves of the Holy Roman Empire; the eldest was Gebhard I in the year 1180. More can be found in the *Genealogy of the High Counts of Windischgrätz and Oettingen*, book 4, at the beginning. However, those who by reason of certain domains hold the title of Landgrave, but do not hold them under the quality of a Principality, are not called Princes, but Counts or Barons. Thus the Counts of Pappenheim write themselves as Landgraves of Stüllingen; the Counts of Sultzen as Landgraves in Gletkau; and the Counts of Fürstenberg as Landgraves in Baar, as noted by Becker in *Public Law*, page 167. Regarding the origin of the Landgraves of Thuringia and Hesse, consult Peucer, *Chronicle*, book 5, page 998 and following. The dignity of Landgraves was formerly temporary, but today it is hereditary.

## 10. Land-servant. Soldier. <note>original: *Lands-knecht. Miles.*</note>

->See Mr. Speidel in his Noteworthy Remarks on this word.<-

### ADDITION.

On whether the soldiers of our own time enjoy the same privilege that soldiers once enjoyed, see Bocer on torture and interrogations, page 335 and following. Among the Romans, one could rise by degrees from a Soldier to honors: first becoming a Tribune, then a Leader <note>original: *Dux*</note>, and finally a Lieutenant <note>original: *Legatus*</note>, see Carpzov, decision 24, number 19. During the time of a public expedition, the statute of limitations is suspended <note>literally "sleeps"</note> for soldiers, decision 116, number 10.

Up until my own age, those who carried pikes <note>original: *sarissas*</note>, battle-axes, and swords were called *Swiss* <note>original: *Helvetii*</note>, even if they were born in the middle of Germany; this continued until finally, due to hatred of the Swiss, the name for provincial soldiers—that is, *Landsknecht*—began to emerge and become famous; see Pirckheimer’s histories, page 73. Besold in Politics, book 2, chapter 7, number 6, volume 2. Regarding ancient military pay, see Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 250. On the marriage of the *Landsknecht*, and the privilege that was once granted to soldiers to contract marriage without any solemnity, see Besold in Politics, book 1, chapter 11, number 68. 

In our Law, a "militia" <note>This term refers to any organized service to the state, not just combat</note> is given as two types: the armed service <note>original: *militia armata*</note>, discussed in the Code and the Digest [various citations provided], which was ended by a triple discharge: honorable, for health reasons <note>original: *causaria*</note>, or ignominious. See Gudelin on the newest law, book 5, final chapter. 

The other type is the unarmed or civil service <note>original: *inermis sive civilis*</note>; such were the offices of those who were enrolled in some school or order among the Statutes to assist in the public business of the rulers. From these offices, they obtained certain annual revenues and payments from the ruler’s generosity. [Citations from Gothofredus, Gudelin, Perez, and Cujas follow]. 

The service of the *silentiarii* <note>Palace guards or ushers who maintained order and silence</note> seems to be of this kind: see especially Pappus in *Dutch Military Law*, page 93, at the beginning, and those cited there. They kept watch in the Palace of the Prince and commanded silence there, especially while the Prince was sleeping;

<column-break/>

concerning them, see the whole title of the Code *On the silentaries and their decurions*, book 12, title 16. There, Cujas notes that the Emperor Anastasius decreed that whatever was given to obtain this service—whether by the silentaries themselves, their parents, or any outsider—was not subject to contribution <note>a legal requirement to share assets</note>, and this was confirmed by Justinian. 

Such also appears to be the service of the twenty-six *assistants* or helpers of the Quæstor, whom Gothofredus interprets as the Chancellor. This office could be sold for one hundred gold coins <note>original: *solidis*</note> and could pass to heirs, provided the money was paid and the Quæstor consented; indeed, it could pass to children even if they were not the heirs. This is taught in the *Novels of Justinian*, number 35, which is by Julian, and was omitted in the Scrimger edition but inserted by Contius with others into our Latin versions. 

Similarly, mention is made of the service of the *apparitors* <note>court attendants or bailiffs</note>, the service of the *numerarii* <note>accountants</note>, and the *scriniarii* <note>clerks or archivists</note>. To ensure that no one, while counted in any service, should take on the worries of an accountant, or aspire to service after resigning, it was decreed by the Emperors Leo the Younger and Zeno. And so that they might be admitted to the privileges of the more splendid services after completing their prior duties with steady labor—specifically those who sought honor through devotion, not those who sought it out of greed—a notable statement was made by the Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian. 

Regarding the "service" of Advocates, see the Code *On the advocates of various judges*. Some of these services were alienable <note>able to be sold</note> and could pass to heirs in a certain way, while others were not. See Gudelin and the Digest regarding the legacy of a service or a service that has been purchased. Regarding such services, it must be understood that Justinian established that anyone who lent money for the purchase of a service, and solemnly agreed on a mortgage of it with a right of preference in a witnessed document, shall be preferred regarding that service over all creditors who have an earlier mortgage—even over a wife seeking the return of her dowry. See Cöper on the preference of creditors in competition, part 1, section 1.

To harden the skin against the blow of a sword is a diabolical art. However, another person who clashes with such men can rightly mix glass with the bullets, or grains of wheat without any superstition, provided it is established by experience that the devil is fought in this way. For since he is the enemy of the whole human race, he can and should be fought through all lawful natural things. The devil deceives all with whom he makes a pact; and to whom he promises immunity from the strike of a bullet, he exposes to the clubs of peasants, so that he perishes by a worse death than he otherwise would. See Velsten in *Ethical Questions*, decade 5, question 4. Jacob Martin.

# LEGAL OPINION

## On the risk to be borne in a Contract of Hire and Lease.

->Prepared by the Lord Doctor Gregor Biccius, in the name of the most honorable faculty, in the month of January, 1641.<-

->Invoking Divine Protection!<-

When the court records and collected testimonies were sent to us—the appointed Senior Dean and the other Doctors of the Law College at the University of the Free Imperial City of Strasbourg—regarding the concluded but still undecided lawsuit between Master Johann and Jacob Brucker, carters and citizens of Basel, and Mr. Johann Georg König, as the authorized advocate and representative of the other interested carters as plaintiffs on one side; and then Mr. J. F. B., member of the local city court <note>original: *L. St. Gerichts*</note>, as defendant on the other side, with the request to briefly provide our legal opinion on the same: We have found, after diligent reading of the submitted writings and mature consideration of all involved circumstances, as well as after a collegiate consultation, that although the main dispute rests on this single question: namely, whether the defendant Mr. B. is obliged and bound to compensate the plaintiff carters for all sustained loss and damage regarding the seized horses, along with the costs of settlement? Nevertheless, for the complete clarification of the matter, four other special questions must necessarily be set forth and decided beforehand: 

First, what kind of contract was actually negotiated between the defendant Mr. B. and the plaintiffs here, and consequently, what kind of legal action was initiated by the plaintiff carters?

Second, how far and how much is the defendant Mr. B. bound or not bound to the plaintiffs by the nature of the contract made?

Third, whether the plaintiffs have proven the facts to a legal satisfaction: that the defendant, at the closing of the contract, used various words from which it could be inferred that he obligated himself to something further and beyond the nature of the contract?

And then fourth and finally, in the event that the words attributed to Mr. B. are proven, whether according to the law <note>original: *in jure*</note> it can be concluded that the defendant guaranteed the carters against all danger, especially regarding the horses, and is therefore obligated to compensate them for the subsequent loss of the robbed horses?

<column-break/>

Of which four special questions, according to the request, we shall treat briefly, yet with the added reasons for doubt and decision <note>original: *rationibus dubitandi & decidendi*</note>, by the granting of Divine Grace.

### Regarding the First Question.

As far as the first question is concerned—namely, what kind of contract was actually negotiated between the defendant Mr. B. and the carters here, and consequently what kind of action was initiated by them? We answer briefly that it is a Contract of Hire and Lease <note>original: *Contractus Locationis und Conductionis*</note>, and the plaintiffs, although they never explicitly used the name, have seized upon and filed an "action of the hirer" <note>original: *actionem conducti*</note>.

For since both parties agree on this: that on the 4th of October they came to an agreement that the plaintiffs, with their horses, wagons, and gear, should collect about 108 loads <term>Saum; a traditional unit of weight for wine, roughly 150 liters, representing what a single pack animal could carry</term> of wine—which the defendant had lying in various places in the Margraviate—and bring it to Basel; while the defendant Mr. B. should pay them 39 Batzen <note>a South German silver coin</note> in freight charges for each load. It appears that all the essential elements of Hire and Lease are present, and thus this reached agreement can be labeled with no other name.

> For Hire and Lease <note>original: *Locatio conductio*</note> is defined as a contract entered into by consent between those parties, of whom one party provides a thing to be enjoyed or used, or their labor in the matter or person of another; the other party, however, promises a certain, immediately defined payment for the fruit or use of the thing or for the labor. <note>original: *pr. & §§. seqq. J. de Loc. Cond. l. consensu 2. pr. & §. 1. ff. de O. & A. l. naturalis 5. §. 2. l. 22. ff. de præsc. verb.* — These are citations to the Institutes and the Digest of Roman Law.</note>

Because the submitted records also clearly indicate that Mr. B. initially sought an opportunity to collect his wine from the Margraviate, and for that reason, through his servant M. L. B., had the butcher approached, who not only declared himself ready to drive in person but also afterward brought the current plaintiffs to him for that purpose.

As can be seen from the deposition of the aforementioned M. B. regarding article 1: there he, the witness, said to the carters they should go with him to Mr. B., who expected him to drive to Böllingen and collect wine, etc. And in the response to the 1st article of the 2nd interrogation: the witness says Mr. B. had asked him several times for it. Likewise, from the plaintiffs' complaint, page 1, face 2: in the Spalen suburb, M. L. B. came to him, mentioning that Mr. J. F. B. had already been to him several times and desired that he would do him the favor of finding carters for him. Also from the defendant’s exceptions, page 6, face 2, in the middle: it is true that Mr. Defendant sought an opportunity to collect the previously mentioned wine.

So... <note>catchword at bottom of page</note>

Lit. L. <note>Letter L</note>

Thus, it is to be established beyond doubt that in the present contract, Mr. B. is to be held as the Lessor <note>original: *Locatorem*; the person who hires a service or leases out property</note>, and he may use the legal action of the lessor <note>original: *actione Locati*</note>, while the carters <note>original: *die Fr.*, likely an abbreviation for *Fuhrleute*</note> are the Hirers <note>original: *Conductoren*; those who take on the work</note>, and they have also legally instituted the action of the hirer <note>original: *actionem conducti*</note> against him.

*For although in the case where a contract of hire and lease for performing work is said to be celebrated, there is no agreement among everyone as to who is the lessor and who is the hirer, as the various opinions are reported by Henricus Bocerus in his Commentary on the Law 23 of the Digest concerning the Rules of Law, number 94, page 175 and following. <note>original: *Henr. Bocero in Comment. ad L. 23. ff. de R. J.*</note> It seems more correct, however, that he should be held as the lessor who first offered himself, and as the hirer he who accepts the offer’s terms, whether he performs the work for the other, or the work is performed for him by the other. Bocerus, ibid. page 178. This is supported by examples brought by Cujas, book 2, chapter 28; also law 11, paragraph 7: "he who had hired [conduxisset] the transport of wine from Campania"; law 13, paragraph 1: "If a shipowner has hired [conduxerit] a cargo to be carried to Minturnae"; and law 25, paragraph 7: "he who hired [conduxit] a column to be transported." Digest on hiring.* <note>original: *ff. locati*</note>

And nothing here is hindered by the claim made by the plaintiffs in their replies on page 24, second side, middle, alleging that behind this contract lies a deceitful persuasion and coaxing which gave cause and occasion for it, whereby the contract would be completely null and void, so that it could produce no legal action, but only a "pretorian action of fraud" <note>original: *actio doli prætoria*; a secondary legal remedy used when no other action is available</note> could be instituted as a last resort.

For it is easy to answer to that: (1.) that the plaintiffs have not yet proven that they would not have undertaken similar agreements to fetch other people's goods at that time if they had not been deceitfully coaxed and persuaded by the defendant. Especially since, because of their trade, they allow themselves to be used for such tasks at any time, even during the dangerous times then occurring. Furthermore, by their own admission in the complaint on page 1, they had celebrated this very same contract the day before, and therefore had intended to drive into the Sundgau to fetch wine for the steward of the Cathedral Provostry in Basel—and they would undoubtedly have actually driven there, had they not found the provided convoy to be too weak.

*Furthermore, fraud is properly said to give cause to a contract when he who is deceived by fraud would not have entered into the contract otherwise, unless he had been induced to enter it by fraud. Joachim Mynsinger and others in the section on intentions [animorum] 28, Digest on actions; Hermann Vultejus, book 2, Roman Jurisprudence, chapter 4, number 88 and following.*

(2.) Much less have the plaintiffs legally demonstrated that any fraud <note>original: *dolus*</note> was involved on the part of the defendant Mr. B., or that he concealed anything from the plaintiffs of which he had good knowledge, or on the contrary, that he presented as certain that which he did not actually know, from which a fraud could be presumed, as they aim to suggest in their replies on page 25 at the beginning. Because to

<column-break/>

leave aside that normally a fraud—especially by persons of such unblemished reputation who have been called to court and other positions of honor—is not presumed, but must be proven against them according to what has already been alleged by the defendant in his rejoinders on page 33; such a presumption is powerfully refuted. Firstly, because the defendant Mr. B. sent various victuals, barrels, and even his own son and son-in-law along with these contracted wagons. He certainly would not have placed them, or the wine itself, in danger if he had possessed certain knowledge of it, or even suspected it with probability. Secondly, by the deposition of M. L. B. on the 4th Article, who states under a bodily oath that after the defendant Mr. B. spoke these words—that he wanted to assure the carters that there was no Imperial soldier in the Margraviate—he immediately added that they should just keep quiet and not make a fuss, because the plan for the two aforementioned colonels was also made here. The defendant would likely have omitted these words if his intention had been merely to coax the plaintiffs into this contract in a deceitful and malicious way and thereby plunge them into the resulting danger.

Furthermore, nothing else prevents this: that the defendant Mr. B. writes in his exceptions on page 6, side 2, near the end, that the carters had offered him their transport services, from which it would follow that they were the initiators and authors of this contract. Therefore, according to the rule cited above, they should have instituted the "action of the lessor" <note>original: *actionem locati*</note> as the lessors [locatores] in this situation. For while it may well be that during the negotiation in Mr. B.'s house, the carters might have presented their services in response to Mr. B.'s question about where they came from (page 1, side 2), it has already been explained above that previously—and as L. B. determined the time in the response to article 6, paragraph 5, as about eight days prior—the said L. B. had been approached several times by Mr. B. to procure carters for him. L. B. willingly took this upon himself and, at Mr. B.'s request, brought the plaintiffs to him. Thus, it is just as if Mr. B. had first approached them himself and offered himself first.

*For what one does through another, he himself is to be thought to have done. Law "not only" [non solus] 22, paragraph "to buy" [emere] 1, Digest on the cause of liberty; law 1, paragraph "to have cast down" [dejecisse] 12, Digest on force and armed force.*

The first question therefore has its decision: that in the present case, both parties concluded a hiring and leasing agreement <note>original: *locationem und conductionem*</note>, in which Mr. B. is the lessor [locator] and all the carters together are the hirers [conductores], who also have instituted no other than the "action of the hirer" <note>original: *conducti actionem*</note> against the defendant.

### Concerning the second question.

Regarding the second question, namely: how far and how much the defendant Mr. B. is bound to the plaintiffs by the nature of the contract made,

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

Whether he is liable or not, it is unnecessary to lose many words on the matter, especially since even those who have only briefly looked at law books know that because the **Contract of Hiring and Leasing** <note>original: *Contractus Locationis conductionis*</note> is of such a nature that both parties expect to derive a benefit from it, they are therefore always obligated to answer for any **deceit** <note>original: *doli*; intentional wrongdoing</note> or even **gross and slight negligence** <note>original: *latæ & levis culpæ*</note>. If one party causes damage to the other through such faults, they must make it good and provide compensation.

*This rule is proposed in law 5, paragraph 2, which states: "where the utility of both parties is involved, as in a lease, both deceit and negligence are held to account." This is agreed upon in law 23 of the Digest on the Rules of Law, law 9, paragraph 5, law 11, law 25, paragraph 4, and law 60, paragraph 7 of the Digest on hiring.* <note>The author is citing various sections of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of civil law, to prove that in a standard business contract, both parties must act with reasonable care.</note>

However, where damage or disadvantage is caused to the other party by an unfortunate accident—by whatever name it may be called—without any deceit or the aforementioned negligence of the contracting parties, he must bear that loss himself. He cannot legally compel his fellow contracting party to restore or compensate for it. This is established and ordained not only in this type of contract but in other "good faith" contracts as well.

*For the death of animals, and things which happen without fault—such as the flight of slaves who are not usually guarded, robberies, riots, fires, floods, and the attacks of bandits—compensation is provided by no one. See law 23 and especially law 6 of the Code on the action of pledge: "Those things which happen by fortuitous events, since they could not be foreseen (among which is the attack of robbers), are not compensated in any good faith judgment."*

Since the complaining carters, in their long presentations so far, have never alleged—and presumably cannot allege with any basis in truth—that the cited robbery and abduction of their horses was caused by the defendant Mr. B’s **deceit, gross negligence, or slight negligence**, but must instead view and hold such an accident as a mere **fortuitous event** <note>original: *casum fortuitum*; an unavoidable accident</note>, it follows of its own accord that they must take such an abduction upon themselves by the **nature of the contract** performed. They cannot expect the defendant Mr. B. to provide compensation, unless they had altered this **ordinary nature of the contract** through a special **Agreement** <note>original: *Convention*</note> or treaty, thereby increasing the defendant's obligation. This will be discussed in the following questions.

### Concerning the Third Question.

The third question—whether the plaintiffs have proven **in fact** <note>original: *in facto*</note> that the defendant used certain words during the closing of the contract from which it could be inferred that he obligated himself to something further and beyond the nature of the contract—should rightly be weighed and discussed with special diligence. This is because, without a detailed understanding of the **facts**, it is not possible to decide or determine anything substantial in law.

<column-break/>

*For the law is situated in the fact and the cause. Digest law 52, paragraph 2. And the whole weight of the matter consists in the fact, as Baldus says in law 27 of the Code on pacts; for by a very slight change in the facts, the whole law is often changed. See law 31 of the Digest on the excuse of tutors, law 45 on legacies; add Oldekop on the Oath, page 26, and in the treatise against Carpzov, page 48; as well as Diether in his inaugural disputation on the Style of the Court, submitted for public examination at Strasbourg in 1649, thesis 64, and the authorities cited there.*

This is especially to be observed in disputes arising from negotiated and settled contracts.

*For in contracts, one primarily considers that which was acted upon between the contracting parties. Digest law 34 on the Rules of Law; law 6, paragraph 1 on the contracting of a sale; Decius in counsel 552.*

In this case, there are primarily three types of statements that the plaintiffs undertake to prove: 1. That the defendant, Mr. B., supposedly said at the time the contract was made that it was as safe in the **Margraviate** <note>original: *Marggrafschafft*; the territory of a Margrave, likely Baden-Durlach in this context</note> as in his own house. 2. That the defendant supposedly added that there was no "Imperial man" <note>an Imperial soldier</note> in the Margraviate. 3. That he promised the carters sufficient **Convoy** <note>armed escort</note> and security.

The plaintiffs attempt to show that these words were truly uttered by the defendant using the following reasons and grounds: 1. Because the defendant, Mr. B., admitted and confessed to having spoken such words during a voluntary negotiation. For regarding the fourth article—which was drafted to ask whether it is not true that when Mr. B. was asked if he must confess to saying it was as safe in the Margraviate as there (meaning in his house), and that there was no Imperial man in the Margraviate, and finally that he promised sufficient convoy both from the city and the Hunninger Sconce <note>a military fortification</note>, he answered, "Yes, I confess this, and I will also confess it to you before the court"—Mr. F. Lützelmann answered the Council that this was entirely true, and Mr. N. G. answered the Council consistently that this was true. This round and voluntary confession not only constitutes a legitimate proof in itself but also entirely frees the plaintiffs from any further burden of proof.

*For there is no better proof in the world than a party’s own confession. Canon Law, chapter "quoniam" 21; and more weight is given to the confession of a principal party than to many witnesses testifying to the contrary. Johannes de Anania, counsel 8, number 65. And by a confession, one is relieved of the further burden of proving. Mynsinger, century 5, observation 88.*

And although the cited confession of the defendant occurred during a granted attempt at an amicable settlement and thus occurred outside of court—and such **out-of-court confessions** <note>original: *confessiones extrajudiciales*</note> usually do not immediately prejudice the confessor and can easily be revoked...

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

<margin>A singular interpretation in Law 41 "We command" and in Law 24 "Questioned," Code on the cause of liberty; confirmed by the author of the Strasbourg Consultations, volume 1, consultation 35, number 20.</margin>

However, because he made this confession in the presence of the plaintiffs, it can also be alleged and cited in court as a perfect **proof** <note>original: *Probation*; legal evidence required to prove a fact</note> against him.

> For a confession made outside of court in the presence of the other party is damaging, and serves as proof in court for the person to whom it was made. <note>original: "Nam confessio extra judicium parte præsente facta, nocet, & probat in judicio pro eo, pro quo facta est." Cited from Johannes Andreae's additions to the *Speculum Juris*, under the section "Now it must be seen," and other legal authorities like Alexander and Bertachini.</note>

2. Because the defendant, Mr. B., presumed to entice one or another of the hired carters with "offered drinks" <note>an attempt to bribe or loosen tongues with alcohol</note> to release him from their existing claim—specifically, he is alleged to have made such a request to H. Vogelwaid. For on the other point of the indictment, which read among other things: "except for H., who said Mr. B. urged him to do it, and for that reason had wine brought to him, under the pretext that P. K. had also released him, so what did he want to start?" Mr. J. P. drafted his answer as follows: When J. B. asked H. Vogelwaid whether Mr. B. had previously urged him, while they were alone, to release him from the claim and had brought him drink for that purpose, Vogelwaid answered me "yes," mentioning that he had been served the best wine with the intention of making him drunk. This matches Mr. R. G.'s answer to the second article. Now, it is easy to draw the presumption that Mr. B. would not have sought and desired the release so diligently if he had not been certain that he had spoken words that made him obligated and liable to the carters.

> For no one is presumed to seek a release except he who feels himself bound and tied, since a "deprivation" implies the existence of a "position." <note>original: "Nec enim liberationem quis quærere præsumendus, nisi qui se constrictum & ligatum esse sentiat..." A philosophical legal principle: you don't ask to be freed from a knot unless you are actually tied up. Citing Law 4, Digest on Actions and Obligations.</note> And there is no deprivation where there was no possession. <note>original: "privatio non est, ubi non fuit habitus." Citing Law 43, paragraph 9, Digest on the Edict.</note> For it presupposes a possession; Mevius is not released if he was not even held liable. <note>Citing Law 116 of the Digest and other codes regarding "unjustly broken" contracts.</note>

3. Because M. L. B. the butcher, who was present in person when Mr. B. came to an agreement with the plaintiff carters regarding their wages in his house, testified under a legally administered oath: that the defendant Mr. B. not only let slip the words alleged above but indeed used even stronger and more binding language, as is clear as day from the fourth point of the indictment directed at his person. For when L. B. was asked therein: whether it was not true that Mr. B. further said there was no "Imperial man" <note>a soldier of the Holy Roman Emperor</note> in the Margraviate <note>the territory of a Margrave, a high-ranking nobleman</note>, as they all had plenty of work to do elsewhere.

<column-break/>

> These words contain in themselves only a simple report. <note>original: "Quæ verba nudam relationem tantùm in se continent."</note>

His answer is found recorded in the following words: On the fourth point, the witness testified that Mr. B. said he wanted to "assure" the carters (the producers) that no Imperial man was in the Margraviate.

> These words seem to contain something more than a simple report—namely, a certain verbal guarantee. <note>original: "cautionem quandam verbalem." Referring to Besold's *Practical Treasury* under the entry "assure."</note>

Although the reasons introduced now give a fine appearance, as if the plaintiffs had proven the aforementioned speeches to legal satisfaction: however, when the matter is weighed more closely, and each point is handled distinctly and separately, and L. B.'s testimony is distinguished from the **deposition** <note>original: *Deposition*; a formal statement given by a witness</note> of the two gentlemen requested as assistants for an out-of-court settlement—as such distinctions and divisions are very prudent and useful for finding the truth.

> For as Quintilian witnesses in the 4th book of his *Institutes of Oratory*, chapter 5: through division the case becomes clearer and the mind of the questioner more receptive. <note>original: "Nam teste Quint. lib 4. Instit. Orat. cap. 5. in pr. per partitionem fit causa lucidior..." This is a classic rhetorical principle applied to law: breaking an argument into parts makes it easier to understand.</note> And things that are delivered distinctly and separately are more easily understood. <note>Citing further legal authorities like Bonacossa de Curtili and the Strasbourg Consultations.</note>

It will be found quite otherwise; namely, that the plaintiffs have not proven almost a single point as it should be by law.

Regarding the testimony given initially by M. L. B. alone on the first point, he was questioned in the third article of the indictment with these words: "Did not the said Mr. B. say, 'Drive for me into the Margraviate where there is only one kind of people, for it is as safe there as here,' meaning in his house?" But he formalized his answer in this way: Regarding the third point, he, the witness, knew nothing else than that they should drive to Böllingen in the Margraviate, and Mr. B. said that there was only one kind of people there. But he could not remember those words—namely, that Mr. B. said it was as safe in the Margraviate as in his own house. Therefore, this witness's testimony does not serve the plaintiffs at all in verifying this first point.

What the witness was asked regarding the second point, and in what manner he answered it, has already been told in detail above in the 3rd reason for doubt; to which this should be added: Although the witness affirmed this point, and even testified as if Mr. B. had used these words—that he wanted to "assure" the carters that no Imperial man was in the Margraviate—nevertheless, he, the witness, testifies in that very same response to the 4th Article, that Mr. B. immediately added the following questionable words: they should just keep quiet and not make much of a fuss, because...
