### Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

...then the plot against the two aforementioned colonels was also hatched here, through which he sufficiently explained his speeches. He wanted to give the carters <note>original: *Fuhrleute*; independent contractors who transported goods by wagon</note> to understand that even if no Imperial troops were stationed in the Margraviate <note>original: *M.*, referring to the Margraviate of Baden-Durlach</note>, they were nonetheless so close to the frontiers that, if the matter were not kept secret, a plot could easily be carried out, as has happened several times before.

> *For words must be understood and interpreted alongside their accompanying circumstances.* <note>original Latin: "Verba enim cum modo annexo accipienda & interpretanda sunt." Citing legal authorities Bartolus and Decius regarding military wills and treason laws.</note>

Regarding the third point, the complaining carters almost admit themselves that their case is not entirely correct. For where they were supposed to prove that the defendant, Mr. B., promised a sufficient convoy <term>convoy|an armed escort provided for protection during travel</term> and security—as they boastfully claimed in their complaint on page 3—stating that "he finally convinced them by promising sufficient convoy, passage, and security," they actually narrowed the questioning <note>original: *Interrogatorium*; a formal list of questions for a witness</note> much more strictly, asking M. B. (witness number 5) only this:

->Whether it is not true that he further promised to give a sufficient convoy, both from the city and from the Huningue fortification?<-

In this question, the previously mentioned "passage and security" were completely passed over in silence, and only the "sufficient convoy" was mentioned. Regarding this, the witness N. N. who was heard knows absolutely nothing. For he answered the fifth point of the indictment thus: The witness knows nothing else to say except that Mr. B. spoke of a "strong convoy" from the City of Basel <note>original: *St. B.*</note> and Mr. Sch.; but the witness did not hear the little word "sufficient" convoy and cannot remember it in the slightest. This witness also confirmed this repeatedly in other parts of his deposition <term>deposition|a witness's out-of-court testimony reduced to writing for use in court</term>. In the answer to the preceding fourth point, he used these words: as far as the Swedes were concerned, he would provide the carters with a strong convoy from both this city and from Mr. Sch.

Regarding the fifth question of this fifth point directed at him alone, he gave his statement thus: he heard Mr. B. say he wanted to give the carters a strong convoy from both this city and from Mr. Sch.

From this it is publicly evident that the plaintiffs, in verifying this third point, have failed as far as this witness's deposition is concerned. Ultimately, M. L. B.—who was the only one present at the aforementioned contract and thus the only witness questioned on it—attested to hearing only these words from the defendant B.: that he wanted to assure the carters that no Imperial soldier was in the Margraviate, and that he would give them a strong convoy from the city of Basel and H. Sch.

<column-break/>

As for the testimonies of Mr. Johann Lüß and Mr. R. G., both Councilors, regarding what happened during the out-of-court settlement negotiations: they were not questioned separately and distinctly on the three points mentioned above, as would have been proper for a full inquiry into the truth. Furthermore, the "security" so grandly promised was not included at all in the fourth point of the indictment directed at them, which according to its literal words reads:

Whether it is not true that when Mr. B. was asked if he must not admit saying it was as safe in the Margraviate as in one's own house; likewise, that there was no Imperial soldier in the Margraviate; and lastly, that he promised a sufficient convoy from both the city and H. Sch., he answered: "Yes, I admit this, and I will also admit it before the court."

Now, although both these honorable gentlemen witnesses confirm this article to be true, as seen in their answers—which is why the complaining carters rely so heavily on this disposition in their third round of legal replies <note>original: *triplicis*; a stage in written legal proceedings</note> and trust it almost alone to win the case—one must nevertheless take careful note of the exceptions <note>original: *Exceptiones*; legal objections to the validity of evidence or witnesses</note> introduced by the defendant's side against both the persons and the statements of the witnesses (which in our opinion are not entirely to be rejected). These show that the confession made by the defendant was not "pure and simple" <note>unconditional</note>, but was made with a certain "quality" <note>specific context or condition</note> and attachment, as stated by the witnesses. For Mr. J. L.'s own words on the 4th interrogation regarding the attachment to the fourth point read:

And Mr. G., when everything contained therein was presented to him, answered that he admitted it and wanted to admit everything he had previously admitted before the court.

These words comprise a qualified confession <note>original: *qualicatam Confessionem*</note> and refer expressly to what the defendant Mr. B. previously said and admitted at the conclusion of the contract in his house. No one else can give testimony about that except M. L. B., who was physically present, and who, as heard above, has already testified. Thus, according to the law, this confession by the defendant cannot be accepted by the plaintiffs in any way other than with the attached "quality" or context; without it, the confession cannot be prejudicial to the person who made it.

> *For in civil cases, as is the case here (for it is different in criminal cases), the response and confession of a defendant must be accepted by the plaintiff along with its specific quality [condition].* <note>original Latin: "Nam in causis Civilibus... responsio & confessio rei cum sua qualitate ab actore acceptanda est." Citing various Roman Law codes and commentaries by Bartolus, Baldus, and Alexander. A "qualified confession" is viewed as more of a denial than an affirmation if the attached condition is not met.</note>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of a 1641 case involving Mr. B (the defendant) and several carters (plaintiffs). The previous page established that the carters were seeking compensation for stolen horses based on verbal assurances of safety given by Mr. B. This page scrutinizes the legal weight of those verbal statements and whether they constitute a binding guarantee of security.</meta>

# Lit. L.

*If the fact were denied in all respects, it cannot prejudice the one confessing, according to the arguments by Gail in "On Public Peace," book 1, chapter 17, numbers 2 and 7; see also book 2, observation 106, number 7.* <note>original Latin: "factum per omnia negatum foret, ideò confitenti non præjudicare potest..." These citations refer to Andreas Gail, a prominent 16th-century jurist specializing in imperial law.</note>

This should apply all the more in the present case, since not only do both witnesses testify unanimously that Mr. B. protested in the most polite manner right at the beginning of the settlement negotiations, stating that he owed the present carters <term>carters|independent transport contractors who moved goods by wagon</term> nothing, nor did he intend to involve himself with them in the slightest outside of a legal ruling. Indeed, he solemnly swore—**Note Well**—that he had not promised them as much as they claim.

*See their response to the 1st Article of the 1st Interrogation.* <note>original Latin: "Vide eorum Respons. ad 1. Articul. Interrog. 1."</note>

Thus, it is not well to be presumed that the defendant, Mr. B., would have so completely forgotten himself as to have confessed *purely* and *simply* at one time and *in a single breath*, as it were, that which he had so solemnly contradicted and rejected in the *same act*.

*For such a contradiction is by no means to be presumed in law. See "Among the beloved," from the Decretals on the faith of instruments; Burfatus, counsel 5, number 15. Since all leases and dispositions are to be understood in such a way that no repugnancy [contradiction] is found in them. See the Digest, law 188, on the Rules of Law, where Decius comments; as well as in counsel 517, number 4; Socinus the Younger, counsel 125, number 16, volume 1; Alciatus, "On Presumptions," 31.* <note>The author is citing a vast array of medieval and Renaissance legal authorities (Decius, Socinus, Alciatus) to prove that legal statements must be interpreted to be consistent, not self-contradictory.</note>

Furthermore, Mr. R. G. attested to such a confession by the defendant only in general and *in excessively general words*, but by no means mentions in *species* [specifically] or in particular what and how much the defendant actually confessed later regarding the points presented to him, which he had initially so solemnly contradicted. See the *response to the aforementioned 1st interrogation, article 1*, where he afterwards—**Note Well**—confessed himself.

*Such generalities, however, are said to be obscure (Digest, law 40, on the Law of the Fisc); moreover, in obscure matters, that which is minimal is to be chosen, and a favorable interpretation must be made (Digest, laws 9, 114, 168, preface and paragraph 4, on the Rules of Law).* <note>original Latin: "Talia autem generalia dicuntur esse obscura..." This is a fundamental legal principle: if a statement is vague, the court should choose the interpretation that imposes the least burden or penalty.</note>

And by means of this evidence, those objections mentioned above in the *reasons for doubt* <term>reasons for doubt|rationibus dubitandi; a standard part of a legal brief where the author anticipates and addresses opposing arguments</term> can be very easily countered.

For regarding the first objection, the *effects of confession* cited there are to be *restricted* only to those *made purely and simply*, but by no means *extended* to those that are *qualified and made under a certain manner and restriction*, such as the present case.

The dismissal requested in the second objection—because it rests solely and uniquely on the *deposition* of Hans Vogelweid, the co-plaintiff, but is otherwise not demonstrated by any legally valid *probation* [proof]—can be rejected as easily as it was alleged. This is because it is a clear matter of law that no one can be both plaintiff and witness in the same case.

Just as in the third *reason for doubt*, the testimony given by the often-mentioned M. L. B. by means of a physical oath does not at all provide the three *specified* points:

*Besoldus, Volume I.* <note>This refers to Christoph Besold, a famous German jurist of the early 17th century.</note>

<column-break/>

rather, it only testifies that the defendant, Mr. B., spoke these words to the carters at the conclusion of the contract: He wanted to assure them that no "Imperial man" <note>This refers to soldiers of the Holy Roman Emperor during the Thirty Years' War.</note> was in the Margraviate <note>original: "M.", referring to the Margraviate of Baden-Durlach</note>. Also, that he wanted to give them a strong *convoy* <term>convoy|an armed military escort</term> at St. B. and H. Sch. <note>likely referring to the fortifications at Stein and Huningue</note>, and that the word "assure" [versichern] in this *phrase* does not necessarily carry a *guarantee* [cautionem] with it, as will be reminded with more detail in the fourth question during the *refutation of the 1st reason for doubt*. With this, the third question also reaches its sufficient decision.

### Concerning the Fourth Question.

In the fourth and final question—which is set solely on the instance of the speeches used, as both witnesses L. M. G. attested—it is asked whether it can be concluded in *Law* that the defendant, by virtue of these speeches, spoke for [guaranteed] all danger to the carters, especially regarding the horses, and is therefore obligated to reimburse them for the encountered loss of the stolen horses? Initially, there appear several significant *foundations* [legal grounds] in view of which it could be concluded that the defendant, Mr. B., through such speeches, took the danger upon himself *beyond the nature of the contract*, and had placed the carters outside of said danger.

For firstly, the defendant's words—"It is as safe in the Margraviate as in his house"; also, "There is no Imperial man therein," or as M. Bienz testified, "He wanted to assure them there was no Imperial man therein"—cannot well be interpreted otherwise than that the *conductors* [the carters] should have to fear no danger (as danger cannot coexist with safety), but rather that if any danger should appear, it should concern the *locator* [the employer/Mr. B.].

*For security and danger are opposites: he who posits one of the opposites—as here the Lord defendant posits security in the Margraviate of Baden—necessarily seems to remove the other, namely danger, from the carters (Digest, law 15, on the exception of a matter judged; law 124, preface: "one of which being posited, it is necessary for the other to be removed," on the Significance of Words; law 40, on Proctors). Moreover, under the term "danger," accidental occurrence is included as a species under its genus, as shown in the Digest, law 5, on maritime interest, and other sources cited by Hieronymus Pantfchmann, Practical Questions, book 1, question 10, number 25, and question 6, number 3. Just as the attack of robbers and bandits is counted among accidental occurrences (Code of Justinian, law 6, on the action of a pledge).* <note>original Latin: "Sunt enim securitas & periculum contraria..." The argument is that by promising "security," Mr. B. legally assumed the "risk" of "accidental occurrences" like banditry, which usually the carters would bear.</note>

It is, however, a known and manifest law that one can take upon oneself the danger of a thing—which otherwise does not fall to him *by the nature of the contract*—through a special promise.

*For the risk of a thing can be undertaken by agreement (Digest, law 7, paragraph 15; also law 13, paragraph 5, on hiring).* <note>original Latin: "Nam periculum rei pacto suscipi potest..."</note>

Secondly, the laws permit that all those words used by both parties at the negotiation and conclusion of a contract...

...been [the words], should be interpreted in such a way that they are not seen as superfluous, without effect, or, as it were, idle and **unproductive**. Rather, they should be understood to have their own certain and singular effect, even if such an interpretation does not entirely agree with the <term>Common Law|Jus Commune, the subsidiary Roman legal system used in the Holy Roman Empire</term>.

> For the words of contracts are to be interpreted in such a way that they achieve something, and are not superfluous or idle. *Baldus, on the Heading 'On contracting a sale,' question 11.* <note>original Latin: "Verba enim contractuum ita interpretanda sunt, ut aliquid operentur, & ne sint superflua & otiosa."</note> Where he maintains that in contracts, not even the smallest word (and not even a syllable) should be considered superfluous. *The same Baldus and the Gloss on Law 1 of the Digest, 'That which is done out of fear.'* In order that the words do not appear superfluous, a departure from the Common Law shall be judged appropriate. *Felinus on chapter 1 of the Decretals, 'On rescripts'; Jason de Mayno on Law 1 of the Digest, 'Whatever the Law'; Decius on chapter 'Pastoralis' 53 of the Decretals, 'On appeals'; Alexander, counsel 158, volume 2.*

Now, all force and effect would be stripped from the aforementioned words if they were not understood to mean that the carters were placed in the boasted security and were freed from all danger stemming from the Imperial soldiery.

Indeed, thirdly, even if the aforementioned speeches of Mr. B. were to be cited as doubtful, obscure, or unclear, it would first follow that they must be interpreted *against* him. A meaning must be forced from them that serves against him rather than for him, considering that Mr. B. represents the person of the <term>lessor|locatris</term> in this contract. He must therefore blame himself for why he did not express the <term>law of the contract|Lex contractus</term> with clearer and more distinct words, and why he did not explicitly assign the risk to the <term>lessees|conductores; here, the carters</term>.

> For an obscure and ambiguous agreement harms the one who leased the property, in whose power it was to write the law of the contract more clearly. *As Papinian wrote in Law 40 of the Digest, 'On agreements.'* <note>original Latin: "Obscuram enim pactionem & ambiguam ei, qui locavit, nocere, in cujus fuit potestate legem apertius conscribere."</note>

Fourthly, this is all the more true because the defendant, Mr. B., as witnesses have shown during the negotiation of the contract, was the one who personally spoke those frequently mentioned words. Thus, in this case, he is the <term>proponent|proferens; the party who offers the wording</term>, against whom any obscurity or doubtfulness that might arise must be interpreted and the explanation framed.

> For doubtful and obscure words are to be interpreted against the proponent. *As shown by Pantschmann, in the said book 1 of 'Practical Questions,' question 6, number 9, after the middle of page 53, column 2.* <note>original Latin: "Verba enim dubia & obscura, contra proferentem esse interpretanda."</note>

This is especially true because this contract was not negotiated among legal scholars and experienced persons, but was established between the often-named Mr. B., as a merchant, and the carters named in the records, who are <term>unlearned laypeople|idiotas; in a legal context, this refers to those without formal training in law</term> and people uninstructed in the law. In such cases, the exchanged words and speeches are to be explained in the sense that they are commonly understood and used by such persons ignorant of the law.

<column-break/>

> For words uttered by legal experts are to be understood according to a legal interpretation; but words uttered among the unlearned and those ignorant of the laws are to be accepted in that sense which applies to laypeople. *Baldus on chapter 1, 'On the succession of Feuds'; Imola on chapter 'Since to you' 13, 'On testaments'; Alexander, counsel 9, which begins: 'Having seen the words of the testament,' number 4, volume 1, where Charles Dumoulin [Molinæus] adds notes; and the same Alexander, counsel 44, which begins 'it would seem,' number 7, volume 5.* <note>original Latin: "Verba enim à Jurisperitis prolata... Prolata verò inter imperitos & LL. ignaros accipienda sunt eo in sensu, prout in Idiotas cadunt."</note>

Now, however, when Mr. B. was asked in the second interrogation regarding the fifth point directed at him—namely, what was understood by a "sufficient convoy"—he formalized his answer thus: he understood by the word "sufficient convoy," in his limited understanding, as much as if one were to vouch for someone. A similar understanding and interpretation might likewise have been found among the other carters.

But despite these and other reasons, we hold unanimously that it is similar to and consistent with the laws that the defendant, Mr. B., by virtue of the many cited speeches, **did not take any risk upon himself**, much less did he obligate himself to the compensation of the occurring damage; and for this we have substantial and well-founded motives and reasons.

And initially, indeed, it is a well-known point of law that not every single word exchanged by both parties during the negotiation of a contract obligates and binds the parties without distinction. For commonly, before they truly agree on the matter, many vain words are used, and much looking-on, yielding, changing, and improving is brought onto the path.

> A notable example is in Law 'If by will' 8, there: 'and hardly after long contentions, etc.' *Code, 'On the rescission of a sale.'* <note>original Latin: "Exemplo notabili in l. si voluntate... C. de resc. vend."</note>

Rather, the **promises** must be most precisely separated and distinguished from the <term>mere statements|nuda dicta</term>, reports, boastings, commendations, and other incidental talk.

> The express text in Law 19 of the Digest, 'On the Edict of the Curule Aediles,' where Ulpian speaks thus: "It should be known, however, that even if he [the seller] has said certain things, he ought not to guarantee them—specifically those things which pertain to the mere praise of a slave." And there: "It matters much what he said for the sake of commending the slave (**Note Well**) or whether he promised that he would guarantee what he said." Join this with paragraph 2: "A statement is thus discerned from a promise, etc." and paragraph 3: "Those statements or promises alone are to be admitted (**Note Well**) which are spoken in such a way that they are guaranteed." For boastful, commendatory, invitational, and similar words of this kind dispose of nothing. *Argued from Law 'If truly' 12, paragraph 12, Digest, 'On mandates'; Bartolus and Baldus and the Doctors [of law] commonly; Hippolytus de Marsiliis, 'Singularities' 57.* <note>original Latin: "sciendum tamen est, quædam, etsi dixerit, præstare eum non debere... ad nudam laudem servi pertinent... dictum à promisso sic discernitur... verba jactatoria, commendatitica, invitatoria..."</note>

If then the so-often mentioned words of the defendant Mr. B.—namely, that "it is as safe in the [military] March as in his house," or "there is no Imperial soldier in it"—consist, according to their proper meaning, in the terms of a **mere statement** and a report, but in no way like the following...

...decided to remain strictly within the <term>natural elements of the contract|naturalibus contractus</term>. For this reason, the terms must necessarily be interpreted and understood in such a way that they do not exceed the limits set in the laws for such a contract.

> For wherever it is not inferred through the suitable nature of the words brought forth by a contracting party that they deviate from the nature of the contract—as is the case here—then they must always be referred to the nature of that same contract and must not exceed its limits. <note>original Latin: "Nam ubicunque per aptam naturam verborum... nec ejus limites excedere debent"</note> For example, see the **Digest, Book 19, Title 2 (on Hiring and Leasing), Law 29; Book 39, Title 2, Law 43; and especially Book 22, Title 1, Law 4, where it says: "because it is not probable that the seller promised more than he would be compelled to provide by a legal judgment of purchase."** <note>original Latin citations: "l. 29. ff. Loc. Cond. l. 43. pr. vers. & quod in stipulatione. ff. de damn. infect. & inprimis l. 4. pr. ... ff. de usur. & fruct. Pantschm. d. q. 6. n. 27. & seqq. p. 41."</note>

And sixthly, this opinion is strengthened not a little by the fact that the laws generally conclude that, in cases of doubt and when the words do not obviously imply something else, the contracting parties intend to change and alter the nature of the contract they intend to conclude as little as possible, but rather are inclined to remain entirely within it.

> For it is less possible that contracting parties, seeing the nature of the contract, would wish to alter anything. <note>original Latin: "Contrahentes enim videntes contractus naturam velle alterare quidpiam minus sit possibile"</note> This is argued in **Digest 39.2.24.2; Digest 43.26.21; and the Feudal Laws.** <note>original Latin citations: "arg. l. 24. §. 2. vers. vitium ff. de damn. inf. l. 21. ff. de precario c. unic. de feud. non hab. prop. feud. nat. 2. Seventhly, it also serves the defendant Mr. B. significantly that at the time he negotiated with the plaintiff carters regarding the collection of the wine, such <term>plundering|Blackereyen</term>, robberies, and the unhitching of horses on the open roads around St. B. <note>likely referring to a specific locality, possibly St. Bernhard</note> were very common. > For a <term>lessor|locator</term> <note>In this context, the merchant hiring the service</note> is not held liable for that event which the <term>lessee|conductor</term> <note>The carters performing the service</note> could have easily foreseen, and which was customary to happen at that time. <note>original Latin: "Nec enim tenetur locator ad eum casum, quem potuit conductor facilè prævidere, & qui solitus erat eo tempore evenire"</note> See **Digest 26.7.13; Digest 19.2.9.1, where it says: "because he ought to have foreseen that this could happen"; and Digest 39.2.13.6, which says: "they have only themselves to blame."** <note>original Latin citations: "fac. l. si fundus. 13. pr. ff. de rebus eorum, qui sub tut. l. si quis domum 9. §. 1... l. 27. pr. ff. loc. cond. l. qui bona. 13. §. 6... > For when the slightest negligence is required by the nature of the contract, if "risk" is added by a pact, that should indeed be understood as covering an accidental event. Therefore, it would be incumbent upon the plaintiff carters, if they wish to legally maintain their intended action, to properly prove that the seizing of the horses occurred through the fault of the defendant Mr. B. Now, so that the previously cited opposing arguments might be properly refuted as necessity requires, one need not dwell long on the first argument, since it yields no necessary conclusion or consequence. This argument recounts that during the negotiation of a contract, it is stated that there are no troops in this or that place. Likewise, it adds that he wishes to "assure" him that there are no troops there. Furthermore, he promises the other party safety and claims he will be responsible for any occurring misfortune.

> But proofs must be certain and conclusive <note>original Latin: "Probationes autem certæ & concludentes esse debent"</note> **according to the Decretals and the Code, so that they conclude by necessity.** <note>Legal citations: c. 8. extra de probat. l. 20. C. eod. Alex. conf. 118... Pantschm. d. lib. 1. q. 1. n. 26. p. 9.</note> **Moreover, the little word "assure" in common and out-of-court usage sounds more like the warmth of someone inviting another to contract rather than providing a formal guarantee; it is borrowed, of course, from the French formula: "I assure you" (*Je vous asseure*), which carries absolutely no insurance, much less an assumption of risk.**

Regarding the second point, the cited legal passages are to be understood as referring to those words used during the final closing of a contract <term>with the intent of permitting|animo permittendi</term>, and which are incorporated into the contract as a substantial part of it. They can, however, in no way be extended to those speeches exchanged by the parties before they have reached a formal agreement, or those told simply to facilitate the contract or uttered <term>with the intent of boasting|animo jactandi</term>.

> According to the third distinction brought forward in the first reasoning for the decision.

To which other class of speech the words of Mr. B. in this dispute undoubtedly belong.

The third argument is left in its place, remaining valid only in cases involving an <term>obscure pact or agreement|pacto und conventione obscura</term>. However, it cannot be applied to our present case, in which it has not yet been proven that such a pact or agreement was established by the parties, as has already been demonstrated from the lack of essential elements in the second reason for the decision above.

The fourth reason is not <term>perpetual|perpetua</term> (universally applicable), considering that the words of a contract are not always interpreted against the speaker, but sometimes also against the one who bases his intention upon such words—just as the complaining carters in our case place the sole foundation of their alleged claim upon Mr. B’s words.

> Doubtful and uncertain words of a contract are to be interpreted against the one who bases his claim on the words of the contract. <note>original Latin: "Verba autem contractus dubia & incerta interpretanda sunt contra eum, qui se fundat in verbis contractus"</note> **This is all the more true in this specific type of case, since the Lord Owner has his intention grounded in common law.** <note>Citing Digest 38. §. 18. and various legal commentaries.</note>

Furthermore, the fifth and final objection is easily countered by the fact that the true and proper understanding of the words "a sufficient escort" should be taken not from the self-imagined opinion and understanding of Mr. B or anyone else, but rather from <term>common usage|ex usu communi</term>, and what is generally considered a sufficient escort according to the circumstances.

> Since names and terms must be understood not from the opinions of individuals, but from common usage, according to the clear and open text of the law. <note>original Latin: "Cum non ex opinionibus singulorum, sed ex communi usu nomina exaudiri debeant..." citing Digest 7. §. 2.</note>

For otherwise, such opinions and self-conceived interpretations of common people are far too weak and insignificant to serve as legal proof.

> For proof through the opinion of the common crowd is doubtful and uncertain. <note>original Latin: "Probationem enim per opinionem vulgi dubiam atque incertam esse docet..."</note>

Therefore, in conclusion, according to all this and as far as the submitted records entail: (for if the complaining carters could demonstrate through legal order that a binding promise was made to them by the defendant Mr. B. through other and more significant speeches regarding the feared danger and insecurity, the decision would have to be drafted differently, which we here attest), the presented main question is to be resolved and answered in this manner: that the defendant Mr. B. is in no way guilty or obligated by law to reimburse the carters named in the records for the loss and damage suffered due to the seized horses, nor for the legal costs expended therein.

->Saving the judgment of those who are better informed of the facts.<-

->By Lord Andreas Dinnerus, Great Jurist of Würzburg.<-

<meta>This page continues the transition from the legal case involving the carters into a formal academic oration by Andreas Dinnerus, as noted at the end of the previous page. ### The Augmented Practical Treasury
# 568

Everyone knows the position of this matter, and I hope I might bring something to you and to the Nuremberg Republic that is pleasing, fortunate, and beneficial. Indeed, my affairs had been so reduced by the "benefit" of illnesses that I thought I would never again undergo this kind of service in all my life. I thought it better to finish than to fail <note>original: "satius esse definere, quàm deficere"</note>. Whether I had pleased this audience in a similar duty before, I had been seen enough; or if I had displeased them, it would be better to depart with a sense of longing rather than with a sense of surfeit. 

But because it is not permitted for us little mortals to declare what each will or will not do tomorrow—since many things happen in life that force you to do what you never intended—I have allowed myself to be woken from sleep, as if resting in a harbor with folded sails. I have changed my plan to once again launch the ship that had been hauled ashore and commit its sails to the winds. I ask you, in your great favor, authority, and benevolence, to deign to assist its progress. 

Regarding the subject, listeners, do not be surprised if I was especially anxious about what I should choose and what I should approve for you. For who could hope to satisfy so many, so refined, and so demanding ears, which require such variety? Therefore, since I saw that I could not gain your attention through the natural pleasantness of my voice or the brilliance of my delivery, *I have attempted to achieve it through the novelty of the subject. Regarding this, I boldly and with all assurance confirm to you that nothing of this kind has been said or heard in this Academy since its very origin.* 

*This, however, should not be taken as an insult to the most eloquent men, as if this subject had escaped their diligence, but rather should be attributed to the happiness of former times, in which nothing at all was heard concerning the transit of armies through these places and similar movements and offenses of war.* 

But so that I do not keep you in suspense any longer, I will first tell you what incident led me to this present undertaking. The matter is this: When, near the end of the sixth month of the past year, 1631, I observed from the tower of this town several banners of infantry and cavalry crossing through the common fields near our town and through the territory of the illustrious Senate of Nuremberg: *A friend who stood next to me, trembling, asked me who I thought these approaching men were—friends or enemies? I replied with what <term>Pomponius the Jurisconsult|ICtus</term> suggested to me then: "Those are not to be held as enemies against whom we, or against whom our Magistrate, has not publicly decreed or declared war."* <note>Legal citations: l. 118. ff. de V. S. & l. 24. ff. de captiv. & post l. revers.</note> *"But what," he asked, "if they do not refrain from injury? If they rob those they meet, slaughter the innocent, and strike at the walls—do you still not count them among the number of enemies?" "No," I said, "since war was not declared by either side—"*

<column-break/>

*—but I hold them in the same place that Pomponius held them, namely, as bandits and robbers.* 

"This is where I was going," he replied, "namely, that it is permitted to intercept them as bandits, to overwhelm them while they wander, and to kill them when they are violent. *Just as," he said, "you would say the same is permitted against those who are not enemies in the present moment, but who are nevertheless about to serve our enemies and are crossing through our fields. It is clear they have undertaken their journey to the enemy with that intention, and have already sworn an oath to them and received wages, so that once joined with them, they might hang over us in a flood.* Either it will be unjust to harm any enemy, or it is lawful and permitted to punish with loss and destruction those who prepare for themselves a path to the enemy through another’s land." 

So he spoke. From his speech, I began to understand that I had entered into a dispute that would be much more difficult to explain than to provoke. I realized that such a noble question would not be satisfied by the foundations I had laid, unless I went to the books and learned what I should build upon those foundations to complete the consideration of this matter, much like the character in *Plautus*. 

And now indeed my *dialogue partner* is not present, which means I cannot guess what he might have wished, or even been able, to bring forward against soldiers continuing their way toward our enemies while *wearing out or terrorizing* <note>A wordplay on "terentes" (treading/wearing out) and "terrentes" (frightening).</note> a foreign territory. Yet it is credible that if he were present, as far as I can grasp in thought, he would speak to you in almost this manner: 

*"Do you not see, men of Germany, that these soldiers who cross through your borders with the intention of joining your enemies—to whom they have already given their names—are indeed enemies, whatever they might pretend? They are enemies, as the Greeks would say,* by anticipation <note>original: κατά πρόληψιν</note>, *that is, as I interpret it, by preoccupation or according to a presumed will. They do not lack the intent or the plan to bring violence upon you and lay snares for you; they only lack the strength and their allies."*

The word <term>Territory|Territorium</term>, which the <term>Jurisconsult|ICtus</term> says is derived from "frightening" (*terrendo*) <note>Legal citation: l. 239. §. territorium. ff. de V. S.</note>, is so called because the Magistrate of that place has the right of "frightening" within those borders—that is, the Right of Removal. Do you not believe this is violated by these masked guests? Or do you believe no reverence is owed to a territory, which even sailors—the lowliest class of men—understand, so that they believe they can only do in ports what does not injure the territory and Jurisdiction of others? No other reason can be given for this, except that when the territory changes, the power changes; yet that change does not provide security. But to whom? The Doctors of Law say even to an enemy, whom it is not permitted to hunt in a foreign jurisdiction! Even to one who is captured for a crime in a foreign land, so that he may be released, and the change of ownership profits his liberation. Who can doubt that since in such cases a violated prohibition is avenged and the hand of the territory is defended by the Lord, it could be much more avenged against those who cross through our fields to join themselves to our enemies?

He distinguishes between formal enemies of the state and "bandits" (soldiers without a declared war), and discusses the legal protections and rights associated with sovereign territory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the academic oration of Andreas Dinnerus. Having introduced his topic—the legal and moral status of troops passing through a territory to join an enemy—he now lays out the arguments for a "preemptive strike" policy before transitioning to his own, more lenient perspective.</meta>

# Letter L. 569

And why should you excuse those who, having previously struck a social treaty with our enemies or accepted pay from them, are led through our borders? Should you excuse them because they are not enemies *at this present moment*, rather than fearing them because they are *about to become* enemies in the very near future? True is the **saying of Jason** <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a famous Italian legal commentator.</note>, who says that it is the same for something to exist in the present as it is for it to be expected in the near future. From him also comes another tradition: just as a **proscribed enemy** (whom he calls "banned") can be killed with impunity, so too can one who is *about to be* proscribed. Furthermore, what could be clearer than what everyone has learned from **Papinian** <note>A celebrated Roman jurist; the citation refers to the Digest of Justinian regarding military wills.</note>: *A soldier ordered to be girded for battle is immediately considered as already girded*? For a gladiator prepared for a fight, once the battle is set, the lot is cast: either to kill, if he strikes first, or to fall, if he hesitates. You may find this same sentiment in the writings of **Aulus Gellius**. You may also see it frequently emphasized by the Emperors: *It is better for rights to be preserved intact than to seek a remedy after the cause has been wounded.* It is better to intervene in time than to seek vengeance after the end result, as stated in the **Code of Justinian** <note>original: "l. ult. C. quando licet unicuique sine jud. se vind." – a law regarding the right of self-defense without a judge's intervention.</note>. From this arose the rule of the legal Interpreters: *It is permitted to prevent. No one is bound to expose themselves to danger. No one except a fool or a madman waits for the first blow.* All these points follow the same logic that everyone admits in natural matters: that a potentiality near to an act is considered as the act itself. *No one spares a snake lurking in the grass the moment it comes into sight; one does not wait for it to strike first or raise its head in threat.* And here the words of **Ovid** <note>referred to here by his family name, Naso.</note> apply:

->To be able to harm is enough.<-
->To which we also recognize this:<-
->Destroy first that which has the power to destroy others.<-

Then kill the enemy while his spirit is small (as **Saint Jerome** says in his *Epistles*), lest the weeds of wickedness grow; let it be crushed in the seed. Thus far his view. Nor does the logician **Everhardus** disagree in his "Topic from Neighbors," saying that the beginning must be considered when the end necessarily follows the beginning. A municipal law once forbade anyone from exporting grain to neighbors under a set penalty. A man was found on the road who intended to export it outside the territory. **Julius Clarus** <note>A 16th-century Italian jurist.</note> judged that this man should also be punished. If you accept the historian **Livy** as a fit judge of this controversy—indeed, if you accept the Romans, the Masters of the World—it can be obscure to no one what they thought should be decided in a similar case. The Romans were waging war with the Latins. The people of **Lanuvium** <note>An ancient city in Latium, near Rome.</note> had decreed to come to the aid of the Latins against the Romans. Their first standards and auxiliary forces had barely exited the gates when news arrived of the Roman victory. Upon receiving this news, the Lanuvinians, moved by repentance, turned their standards back into the city. Did they get away with an attempt so brief, consisting of only a few steps from the forum to the gate? Not at all! For they were forced to hear the haughty voice of the Roman Praetor declaring that for such

<column-break/>

a tiny journey, a great price must be paid to the Romans. See also the legal text <note>original: "l. 13. §. 6. de jurej."</note>: "He swore petulantly; do not swear" <note>original: "ὤμοσεν ἰῶς μὴ ὄμνυε"</note>. These most wise men were not ignorant of what was recorded by the same Livy in another place: *There is more spirit in the one inflicting danger than in the one repelling it, and greater hope in the one bringing force than in the one parrying it.* Therefore, thinking there should be no delay in such a matter, they moved for war against **Philip of Macedon**, lest, having likewise subdued Greece, he move against them first, as recorded in **Zonaras** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine historian.</note>. **Julius Caesar** also had no other reason to attack **Ariovistus**, King of the Germans, than his claim that he must be punished before he became more powerful and brought some evil—and even because he *intended* to bring evil. To be brief, it seems to me that the actions of those who thought it wise to prevent dangers already meditated and prepared against them by others are in no way to be blamed. Regarding our question: they believed it right to strip of life and goods those troops passing through to join our enemy, caught on the road through our territory. For if they had once escaped the borders of those who allowed them passage, it would be too late to seek punishment. 

You have here, Gentlemen, the summary of those things which, in our opinion, can be disputed against those travelers by the one to whom we assigned that role; we are persuaded that this opinion has pervaded many minds. However, if I perceive that it pleases you, I will hereafter disclose why I have **withdrawn my support** from that view. At the same time, I trust that you will not be so addicted to the opinion just brought forward, nor to your own predetermined views, that you will not willingly allow me to relieve you of these harsh judgments, and that you will bear with equanimity the freedom of a man who is independent in his judgment and opinion. It is not new for a principle that was considered valid by advocates in the pleading of cases to be seen as a flaw by Judges—whose place in defining this controversy you hold today by your great merit. To begin from here, Gentlemen, I seem to see (and I wish for you to consider more attentively) what drove the patron of the contrary opinion to such a cruel and more-than-Catonian <note>Referencing Cato the Younger, known for his unyielding and harsh moral rigor.</note> sentence, as to strip of both life and goods those caught in our jurisdiction who were passing to our enemy. Three points seem to me to be the main ones, containing all the other arguments brought for the defense of that cause: 

*   **First**, he indicated that for someone to be considered an enemy, it was sufficient if he *could* have offended the lord of the territory at a future time, and he thought nothing else necessary for the name and reality of a soldier. 
*   **Second**, he judged that there was no difference between an actual loss and a mere inconvenience. 
*   **Third**, he treated and valued the initial stages of a hostile act and its end or consummation as equal. 

When I have demonstrated that all these points rest on no law and are far removed from the sides of leniency and mercy—which nature has taught me—I hope I shall easily lead you to my own judgment.

<sig>Cccc</sig> <meta>Besold, Volume I. Catchword: First</meta>

# Page 570
### Augmented Treasury of Practice
<meta>catchword: hostem (enemy)</meta>

First, therefore, I wish to ask my opponent this: by what things does he believe a soldier is made, or what does he wish me to think in this case? Did you think this one thing was sufficient—that he gave his name to the enemy, that pay was promised to him by the enemy’s commander, and that he made a journey through another’s land at the expense of that same commander? Why do you keep silent or mutter? The **legal expert Ulpian** <note>original: "Ulpianus Jurisconsultus"</note>, speaking of soldiers, does not allow us to doubt: *Those who are not yet in the ranks, even if they have been chosen and are traveling at public expense, are not yet soldiers: for they must be enrolled in the ranks.* <note>original: "l. 42. ff. de test. mil." — Digest 29.1.42, regarding military wills.</note> What could be said more clearly? You, however, being mistaken in your mind, thought that a soldier was authorized simply by **the swearing of the oath** <note>original: "sacramento dicto"</note> and being received into the military ranks or catalogs. Yet this latter cannot happen except for a lawful soldier who has already performed the military oath. You believed soldiers were gathered in such a confused and disorderly way that in their selection there was no second or third step. But the matter is otherwise. *For besides the oath, the ranks are required, and the distribution into those ranks.* <note>original: "l. 42 ff. de test. mil. Limn. in J. P. lib. 4. c. 8 n. 140."</note> Others add the **tattoos or marks** <note>original: "stigmata seu notas"</note> with which recruits and factory workers are usually pricked, as noted by **Cujacius** <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a prominent French legal humanist.</note>. In all things (says the legal expert **Gaius**) I notice that a thing is perfect only when it consists of all its parts. Listen to **Cino da Pistoia** <note>original: "Cinum Pistoriensom"; a famous 14th-century Italian jurist.</note>, a legal expert of established authority, who says there is no recruitment so disorderly that these three things ought not to come together: **Selection, confirmation, and the entering of the office**; if these happen to be torn apart, the **full right** <note>original: "Jus plenum"</note> is not acquired by the one elected. He proves there that this order is observed by nature itself, because even in the constitution of a human being, these three follow one another: **generation** (which happens through conception), **formation**, and **birth**; otherwise, we are not all made complete:

> who, by the union and marriage
> of body and soul, consist as one 
> joined together.

As **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, Roman poet and philosopher.</note> most elegantly expresses it. He shows in the same place by the example of an heir that no fewer things are required for the constitution of a **civil persona** <note>A "legal person" or status in society.</note>, and that the law imitates nature in this. *When an heir is written down by the testator, that is "generation,"* he says; *when the testator dies, "formation" occurs; but the day of birth is the same as the day of entering the inheritance.* Behold a double origin of man: one natural, and the other civil. In a similar way, **Cino** denies that a recruit is a soldier unless he has these three: 1. that he has been entered into the ranks, 2. that he is **girded** <note>original: "cinctus"; referring to the ceremonial sword-belt.</note>, and 3. marked with the brand, even if he had perhaps given his name to the enemy. In this dispute, Cino, who compares this military selection with civil election, seems to me to look back to **Plato**, who in the *Protagoras* declared that the military art is a part of the civil art. But I leave this aside. Certainly, it is established that a man cannot be called a **just soldier**

<column-break/>

who is not perfect in every part. In the same way, for instance, we speak of a **just war** <note>original: "bellun justum"; a war meeting specific legal and moral criteria.</note> as being opposed to banditry, and in the same sense we distinguish "just enemies" and "just forces" and a "just army" from sudden and extraordinary raids or pillaging. Thus, nothing can be called complete unless it has absolute perfection, so that nothing at all remains; nor is anything "full" that requires an addition. <note>Citing various legal authorities including Tiberius Decianus and the Digest.</note> I think you understand, listeners, that if the name of "soldier" is taken away from the one who passes through foreign territory, nothing remains that ought to be punished by the loss of either goods or life. For if I ask the advocate of the opposing side why he thinks a trap should be set for one passing through his land who has not yet provoked him with injury, or why death should be offered: it is certain he will respond with nothing else than because "he is going to serve my enemy," and because "it is permitted to kill all those serving in the military who cross over to the enemy." But if they perhaps wage war **in their minds or with words**, would you immediately call that "military service," which is not outside the context of public armed conflict? *Is your Mars in your windy tongue and those fleeting feet?* <note>original: "An tibi Mavors ventosa in Lingua..."; quoting Virgil's Aeneid 11.390, mocking a boastful but cowardly warrior.</note> For although many services are performed without weapons, we cannot even imagine military service without the preparation of arms. In this, there is nothing that does not lurk under the protection of arms, or where present force and damage do not reside; only when we drive these from our necks are we judged to have put on **just arms** for our safety. *For no omens of arms can be good, except those which we take up for the sake of protecting faith and safety.* You notice, surely, that those who were heading toward the enemy through our land without harm were not rightly called "militants" (from the word for "strife" <note>A wordplay on *militantes* (soldiers/serving) and *lis* (strife/lawsuit).</note>). Yet you, confident in your mind, responded that the same law should be established for those about to serve the enemy immediately as for those already serving. I believe indeed that it seems so to you, as if the penalty of the law would hold both the future soldier and the present one alike: just as present time itself is joined with the future. However, there is a very close conjunction of both times, from which it can be understood that the present time is brief and always changeable in both directions, since it is left behind by the past and passes into the future—as the author of the **Panegyric to Constantine** once discussed on behalf of the people of Autun <note>original: "pro Flaviensibus"; referring to the citizens of Augustodunum (Autun).</note>. *For there are and always have been those who said the present time is so tiny and incomprehensible that it accepts no length, because it is nothing other than the junction of the past and the future, and whatever runs through it plucks from the future.* Since you furthermore doubted whether any present time were given, it is no wonder that you [dragged] the future soldier toward the enemy...

<summary>Dinnerus argues that a recruit is not legally a soldier until they have completed specific rites (oath, enrollment, and branding). Consequently, travelers passing through territory to join an enemy cannot be legally killed as "soldiers" because they lack the "perfect" status required by law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the oration of Andreas Dinnerus regarding the legal status of individuals moving to join an enemy force. He is currently arguing against the "indiscriminate interpretation" that would treat a recruit as a full enemy soldier before they have been formally integrated into the ranks.</meta>

# Page 571
### Letter L. 571
### Cccc 2
<meta>catchword: genus; reference: Besoldus, Volume I.</meta>

to wish to take vengeance on an enemy as if he were a present enemy through a **promiscuous interpretation** <note>Meaning an interpretation that fails to distinguish between different categories or times.</note>. What should be said, Listeners? I do not think you side with the patron of the opposing view in this matter, nor that you are delayed by that confusion of times which took its origin from the diversity of Sects between the **Platonists and Peripatetics** <note>The Platonists (followers of Plato) and Peripatetics (followers of Aristotle) debated the nature of time and the universe's origin.</note>: of whom the former argue that there is a beginning of the world and of motion, but an end to neither; while the latter acknowledge the infinity of both. Certainly, those who take away the difference between the two times—the present and the future—from the common life of men and the most simple **General Law** <note>original: "G. jure" referring to Jus Gentium or General Law.</note> are to be thought no wiser than those who strive to remove spring from the year. For time itself is nothing unless it is adapted to the uses of men and serves their necessities and actions. From these alone is it nearly discerned what the present and what the past time carries. My dear poet **Titus Lucretius** does not allow us to be ignorant of this in Book 1, before the middle, with these verses most suited to our purpose:

> Time likewise exists not by itself, but from things
> themselves
> Follows the sense of what has passed in an age;
> Then what thing presses on, and what follows thereafter:
> Nor must it be confessed that anyone perceives time by itself,
> Removed from the motion of things and their calm rest.
> <note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book 1, lines 459–463. The poet argues that time is an accident of objects and events, not an independent substance.</note>

Indeed, the **Founders of Law**, **Papinian and Mavianus** <note>Papinian was a celebrated Roman jurist; 'Mavianus' likely refers to Maevianus or a similar legal authority.</note> (I believe), would have been most unskillful in all things and business conducted among men, when they defined that it matters much whether a **condition** <note>A legal requirement in a contract or will.</note> was conceived for the present, the future, or the past, as when a testator speaks thus: *Let Sempronius be the heir, if Titius is consul;* or thus: *I bequeath one hundred to Titia if she marries me; if she comes to the funeral.* 
<margin>Law 16, Digest on conditions and demonstrations.</margin> 
But these men, if they had possessed even a tiny bit of judgment, and if their minds had not been clouded by the subtleties of philosophers, would have believed that whatever ought to be given, done, or performed in the present was impossible, because in these obligations of the dying, no present time would be established for their wills. O what sharp wit! O what charming trifles, yet not unlearned! But now, putting play aside, let us handle serious matters. They cannot be led to pronounce such a cruel sentence without an example—a sentence I believe they have pronounced against those who would one day serve the enemy—because a heavier sentence could not be dictated even for those who are actually serving or for defeated enemies. From where shall we say this imitation of an example was handed down to you, if not from **Trajan, the best of Emperors**? What did he do? Others answer for you in this manner: *Epistle 38 and following, Book 10.* When **Pliny**, the author of the Epistles, who then held the Proconsular command of **Bithynia** <note>A Roman province in modern-day Turkey.</note>, reported to that master of his that one or two slaves had been discovered among the recruits who had given their names for military service, and to use Pliny’s words, had already spoken the **military oath** <note>original: "Sacramento militari"</note>, yet had not yet been recorded in the

<column-break/>

ranks; this ought not to have gone unpunished for them. Trajan, consulted on the manner of punishment, wrote back in this opinion: *If indeed the slaves offered themselves for military service of their own accord, they must be punished: Nor does it matter much that they were not yet distributed through the ranks.* 
<margin>Law 2, paragraph 1; Law 8; and Law 11, Digest on military matters.</margin> 
By this response, they say it is established that since it is a crime to offer oneself as a soldier, it suffices that the military service has begun for there to be a place for execution and punishment. I hear Trajan’s law, yet how it favors the contrary opinion is not sufficiently clear. The Emperor there pronounces regarding **slaves**, who were barred from military service by Roman laws. By these men, if their servile condition was concealed and perhaps in fraud of their masters, so that they might withdraw themselves from their power, they had affected military service, a grave crime to be expiated by death was contracted; **Arrius Menander and Martianus**, the legal experts, also judged this besides Trajan. Therefore, although such men were not yet placed in the ranks, but only bound by the military oath: the Emperor shows this does not help them avoid punishment, bringing forth the reason that the day on which those fugitives first spoke the military oath and were approved, required the truth of their origin from them. It is not, Listeners, it is not in those slaves a crime merely started and begun—which would receive perfection from the distribution into ranks, as was thought—but it is a **consummated crime** <term>crimen consummatum</term> <note>A crime that is legally complete.</note> on that very day when, being admitted to the oath, they were bound to prove themselves free men, and lied about their condition so that they might strip themselves of slavery as if by this perjury. We find nothing similar in our case. There are no slaves here, no lie, no reward for a lie, no flight from workhouses, no theft of liberty. What then? A **future enemy**; an **imperfect and unjust soldier**; a meditated danger; an **uncertain offense**; a passage through another's field that is so far harmless; a **damage not yet done** <note>original: "damnum infectum" — a legal term for potential damage that has not yet occurred.</note>. Indeed, I am not unaware that those who pass through in this way can become enemies: which **potential** <note>original: "potentiam"</note> the Patron Opponent says stands for the **act** <note>original: "actu"</note>, and this is held in everyone's mouth: that it suffices that the potential is enough, especially that which is near to the act. We said above that this is the other strongest foundation of the contrary opinion. In which matter, what the **Speculator** <note>Likely referring to the legal writer Durantis, known as 'Speculator'.</note> and the "ventilators of nature" <note>A disparaging term for those who debate abstract natural philosophy.</note> might decree, there is no time now to investigate. However, we have received that the divine interpreters of the law—among whom it is certain that **Jason** <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a famous Italian jurist.</note> was included—diligently considered what kind of argument this question turned upon: whether it was capable of favor and leniency, or full of hatred and envy. It will now be yours to estimate to which class you wish to refer this dispute of ours concerning quasi-warlike injuries, concerning the harm and damage threatening a peaceful province from poorly-received enemies and the punishments of the same. Or because the laws have consented to the sins of mortals, so that the offense of war began to be permitted if it becomes public, nor is the most mild...

<summary>Dinnerus argues that potential future threats or incomplete military recruitment cannot be punished as completed crimes, distinguishing between the intent to join an enemy and the legal fraud committed by slaves who illegally joined the Roman army.</summary>

### Page 572

...kind of men who rejoice in treachery, malice, and blood on either side: Therefore, should this interpretation be applied to those who spurn all humanity from themselves? Perhaps you will be more captivated by an example. Suppose someone entered the house of Titius with the intent of stealing. He was suddenly caught before he had handled any item in the house <note>original: "contrectavit." In Roman law, the physical handling or moving of an object, known as *contrectatio*, was essential to define the crime of theft.</note>. Nevertheless, Titius demands that he be condemned for theft, even though his effort was in vain. Titius argues that the power to punish exists even for an act that caused no harm. However, that man I mentioned, Jason <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a celebrated Italian jurist.</note>, in his commentary *on Law 3 of the Digest regarding the acquisition of possession*, teaches that such a defendant need not fear the stones of condemnation <note>Referring to the "calculi," or pebbles used by ancient judges to cast a vote for guilt or innocence.</note>. The reasoning of the Law proves this, for it denies that there is a theft where there is no physical handling of the property. For the Wise, out of a hatred for punishments, do not allow what the Law has established regarding a completed theft to be extended to a *mere* thought of theft; they are always more inclined toward mercy and the mitigation of punishment. Now, how great do you think this difference is—if any can exist—between one who is caught in a foreign territory before he has begun to serve our enemy as a soldier, and one found in another's house before the handling of the desired object?

*In both cases, a crime has been conceived, but it is not yet born, nor is it ripe for punishment; and since our entire dispute concerns the harming of those whom we once feared might harm us: we think no one is so remote from the knowledge of the Law that they would believe the Interpreters of the Laws favor the harming of men more than the punishments to be imposed for theft or private injury. In the case of a thief, there is a penalty; in the case of one passing over to the enemy, there is vengeance. We seek nothing in a penalty that gives delight, and nothing in vengeance that is merely for profit.* <note>The author distinguishes between *poena* (legal penalty) and *vindicta* (vengeance or redress), arguing that neither should be pursued for cruel satisfaction.</note> Nor should anything in either case be encouraged, according to Tiberius Decianus <note>A 16th-century jurist known for his work on criminal law.</note> in *Consultation 19, Book 3*. Furthermore, concerning the infliction of harm, these same men have handed down what the law would be in a certain other question not unlike our own. A man proscribed or banished by a sentence had appealed from the City: in which proscription no one doubts that the condemned man is made an enemy of that place from which he was ordered to go into exile, so that he might be harmed with impunity by anyone from that community. The question was asked: even if the sentence of proscription is suspended by an appeal—or as we say, *while the appeal is pending*—can the condemned man still be harmed with impunity? Those most grave and proven men saw the power of doing harm, which was *extended to the Citizens like a sword* by the very law of the municipality; yet they did not wish to consent too closely to the killing of the condemned man in such an attack. For they thought it could happen that in the cause of the appeal, the judge might pronounce that the appeal was made rightly and in order, and that the previous judge had judged neither by Right nor by the Laws. Certainly, if it were discovered that there had been no valid sentence from the previous judge, they did not doubt that both the matter previously judged and the appeal itself ought to be set aside and annulled, and thus the defendant would escape the crisis. Therefore, as long as any hope remained for that condemned man, and as long as any just element was lacking for the full force of the proscription sentence, for so long did they maintain he was safe from danger and

<column-break/>

hostile harm. This was upheld by Raphael Cumanus, Petrus Anchoranus, Johann Baptista, Philologus Hispanus, and Julius Clarus in his *Practice of Criminal Law*, in the section on homicide, verse "successively," that is, numbers 63 and following. These men truly attributed the same Right to one so condemned, even if he had not yet appealed from the sentence brought against him, provided the time within which he could appeal had not yet elapsed. For I clearly understood, along with the ancient founders of the laws, that this deadline must be awaited, and whatever time remained was in his favor; for they wished themselves to be considered most distant from the desire to do harm (*Digest 70 on payments; Law 38, § 16; and Law 41, § 1 on the Obligations of Words; Law 17 on the Rules of Law*). And Bartholomaeus Socinus <note>An influential 15th-century Italian jurist.</note> is much occupied in demonstrating this in his commentary *on Law 3, § 10 of the Digest on the Acquisition of Possession*, as reported by others. Let us also put it to the test in other cases, to see if we can track down this limit and goal of time, which punishment ought to follow and not precede. For in this way, by the same effort, we will demonstrate the falsehood of what is commonly tossed about in our controversy: that it matters nothing whether something is of the present, or is expected in the near future. It is cautioned by the law of the province that he who inflicts a lethal and death-bringing wound upon a citizen should be put to death. *Sempronius has been wounded lethally in the judgment of the Doctors: the Defendant is snatched away to his execution, without waiting for the death of the wounded man.* Indeed, at first glance, it seemed that the very letter of the law demanded that defendant for immediate punishment and rejected all delay. To be sure, a law can act in such a way that what it wishes and commands is done faster than said, and it may not allow a *moment of time* to intervene: which is different in legal actions, which can only operate in time, or at least so that no natural moment intervenes (*Canon "Ponderet," 14, Distinction 50: We need time, so that we may do something more maturely*). But this opinion is far from the truth: for the law did not speak in such a way that the one wounding should undergo capital punishment instantly or immediately, on the spot, and that all space of time before the death of the wounded man should be excluded. Therefore our doctors (among whom is *Jason* and others) responded that here, too, the day of death must be awaited, even though it were certain that Sempronius would die from the wound. Because (*as Jason says on Law 8, number 11 on the Obligations of Words*) the Statute speaks of one "killing," and thus of one "dead": it is therefore necessary that death has followed. Behold the injury, behold the vengeance, which the law itself granted as if on the present day, yet delayed to a future time. Since these things are certain, I cannot wonder enough why, in the case of those setting out toward the enemy, who are not yet enemies, you accept a different law: for you affirm that while they are still in preparation, they can be harmed and slaughtered with impunity. This haste and readiness to inflict injuries is too much—forgive me, I pray. For these angers and offenses which you cook up against those travelers are nothing other than injuries, even by the testimony of *Marcus Tullius Cicero*, who, writing in *Book 1 of On Duties*, rightly called them such.

For he shows *in that same place* that those injuries, which are inflicted intentionally for the sake of doing harm, often proceed from fear: when he who thinks to harm another fears that, unless he does so, he himself may be affected by some inconvenience. But you, indeed, remove fear, and there will be nothing at all that can incite you to harm those men, *according to the Digest, on the grounds of fear* <note>original: "l. ff. quod met. caus." refers to Digest 4.2, *Quod metus causa gestum erit*.</note>. Nothing can be law that fear has dictated, nor does the praetor <note>A Roman judicial officer.</note> hold as valid what was done out of fear. Indeed, fear is contrary to law, as is violence, *according to Law 116 of the Digest, on the Rules of Law*. It is the weakness of your own mind, not right reason, which commands you to offend those by whom you have not yet been provoked, and to count as enemies those who are not yet so. A weak mind is much shaken before it is overwhelmed; nor is it a wonder, because more things usually terrify such a mind than actually weigh upon it: it suffers more often from opinion than from reality. *Before the time, that same man chooses to be miserable, even though those things which he dreaded as imminent have not yet come, and perhaps will never come. O blind minds of men, which are sometimes tormented by certain things more than they ought to be, or tormented before they ought to be, or tormented by things that ought not to torment them at all—as is found in the Roman Sage, Seneca, in Epistle 13.* But it is enough for me to have touched upon these things as if in passing: for a long time now, the learned eyes of those Law Students whom I behold have been calling me back to the responses of the experts. My own eyes dwell upon their faces, and for their sake, following the lead of the *Poet from Venusia* <note>Horace, who was born in Venusia.</note>, this whole "war" will be willingly fought. Therefore, if I were to ask them whether it is true what *Angelus* <note>Angelus de Ubaldis (1328–1400), a famous jurist.</note>, as reported by *Jason* <note>Jason de Mayno.</note> *on Law 2 of the Code regarding inofficious testaments*, wrote: that he who offends a Scholar who had been ordered to be enrolled in the register <note>The *matricula*, or official university roll.</note> should be struck with the same penalty as one who has already been enrolled and placed, as it were, among the Academic ranks? Do you not think they would first answer that, because it concerns an offense and a penalty, the punishment should not be sharpened by interpretation, but rather softened? And that *Angelus* was deceived by certain rules of Law and wandered from the path? Among these rules would be the one reported above: *that power near to the act is regarded as the act itself, and the beginning is what is considered*—and similar maxims, which can have no place in such an odious argument. And to proceed to speak to you of words accepted for the assumption of other degrees and honors in the Academy: *Andreas Barbasia* taught that a *Licentiate*, that is, a *Doctor-designate* (whom *Guillaume Budé* <note>A famous French humanist (1467–1540).</note> in his *Additions to Baldus on Law 3 of the Code regarding theft* called by the Greek word *methodidaskalon* <note>original: "μεθοδιδάσκαλον," meaning a teacher of method or an instructor.</note>), is not included under the name of "Doctor" in matters of penalties, so that in those cases also, hatreds <note>In legal terms, "odious" matters refer to those involving punishments or burdens, which jurists argued should be interpreted narrowly.</note> might be restricted. Let no one think this was determined by him without reason: for it is not certain that he will become a Doctor, or that he will not suffer a rejection, since he knows he must first be examined and approved. *Baldus* also, when a certain city was said to have killed a man elected as Bishop, replied that a "Bishop" did not seem to have been killed, so that there was no place for the penalty

<column-break/>

which is established against the killer of a Bishop. Note (says *Baldus*) that a thing does not receive its name from what it will be, but from what it is. To what that points, you understand with no trouble: that soldiers who have not yet been approved, nor are currently serving, ought not to be named enemies, even though it is clear they have been chosen, *according to Law 42 of the Digest, on military wills*. This matter, regarding these Candidates for military service, does not require a longer Speech, because they have not been so chosen that they, or those through whose lands they pass, can know whether the enemy toward whom they are heading will receive them or use their labor. And who shall compel him to enroll into the ranks those not yet approved? For he is free, by the widely accepted custom—according to that *Eclogue* <note>A selection or muster.</note> of the *Greeks* which we call the levy, the purification of arms, and the parade of the Cavalry—to reject those bound by any stipend. Our *Students*, the *hope and flower of this university*, would add—I say they would add—if one must lean toward either side, there is less danger if the ship leans a little toward Scylla rather than toward Charybdis <note>Two mythological sea monsters; choosing the "lesser of two evils."</note>, as the *Homeric Circe* advised, *Homer, Odyssey, Book 12*. For thus, where it concerns the punishment of men, there is less evil in clemency and kindness than in cruelty and bitterness. Nor indeed did the *Jurist Arrianus* think otherwise, who wished us to be more prone and ready to liberate than to bind, *according to Law 47 of the Digest, on Obligations and Actions*. I myself cannot help but defend their side by another reasoning not so well known to interpreters of the Law, and I too shall turn my sails toward Scylla. And since many will easily concede that the passage of these enemies has the appearance of an injury, I shall—with your permission, I hope—philosophize briefly in the Socratic manner against whoever feels this way. Either you think those passers-by are wicked and worthy of vengeance, or you simply think it is wicked to inflict an injury. But does it seem just to you to compete with such people by injury? I think not. For if he is wicked who first affects another undeserving person with an injury, he who returns the injury is certainly equal to him in wickedness. And if he who returns an injury does wrong, he who compensates evil with evil does no less wrong, even though he is avenging an evil. For we see it arranged in the same way regarding benefits: he who returns a benefit nevertheless does a good deed, even though he would have been naturally obligated to repay the benefit, *according to Law 25, section 11 of the Digest, on claiming an inheritance*. Just so, he who repays an evil—as the proverb says, *he drives out one nail with another* <note>original: "clavum clavo extundit."</note>—does no less evil, even though he was first badly treated. *Is anything more absurd than to establish Law out of injuries?* The Emperor *Theodosius* says the occasion for injuries ought not to arise from the same place where laws arise, *Law 6 of the Code, on whence violence*. Just as *Africa* always brings something new, so this *Euripus* <note>A strait with violent, shifting currents; here a metaphor for a volatile situation.</note> of retaliatory injuries always brings some danger...

For as those who, for the sake of profit, commit themselves to the dangers of the sea and are about to set out on Plautus’s "wooden horse" <note>original: "equo ligneo Plauti"; a poetic metaphor for a ship.</note>, they usually bind themselves with great interest on their loans: so too those who indulge too much in anger while seeking to avenge a loss involve themselves in the greatest interest-payment of calamities. Where an athlete competes with another athlete on equal terms <note>original: "æquo Marte," literally "with equal Mars," meaning a fair fight</note>, we see that happen which Horace says:
