<margin>Law 6, last section, Digest on the risk and benefit of a sold thing; Law 13, last section, Digest on threatened damage; Last law, last section, on the faith of instruments; Last law, section 13, at the verse "but because certain," Code on the law of children; Last law, Code on the sentence for that which is of interest; Law 23, Code on the Most Holy Churches.</margin>

For that is an infinity <note>Dinnerus refers to an "infinite" cycle of litigation and revenge</note>, unfriendly not only to law and human actions, but also to the lives of mortals: *for the swift flower of our narrow and miserable life's briefest portion hastens to run its course,* as Juvenal says in Satire 9. For if the one who has been affected by injury or loss perpetually compensates evil with evil, it is necessary that one evil sprout from another, litigation from litigation, and injury be propagated from injury. For by whatever right you grant to him who first received an injury the power to return it, the vengeance returns to the other excused by that same right; by which reasoning there will clearly be no end to offenses and losses. *This, however, is not to move the "Camarina"* <note>The text reads "Canarinam," likely a typo for "Camarinam." To "move Camarina" was a proverb meaning to stir up a settled evil or a "hornets' nest."</note> *but to move the very springs of wickedness, which they do, as many as hold out a previous injury as an excuse for a present one.* Maximus Tyrius <note>A 2nd-century Greek Platonist philosopher</note> in Dissertation 2. *Nor are there other things that destroyed Greece than the over-valuation of one's own injury, which erupted into infinite forms; than implacable fury, immortal anger, the desire for revenge, and ignorance of the law. For if both the Greeks and all those whom injury first attacked could have persuaded themselves of this: that injury itself is the greatest evil to those who inflict it, and that it is a punishment more severe than war, or the overturning of walls, or the devastation of lands, fires, or any tyranny—they would never have succumbed to so many and such great calamities in the past.* Plato, in Book 5 of the *Laws*, judges the cause of such great disasters to be none other than that men are ignorant of how the wicked are punished, and in that they are greatly deceived while they think this is the punishment: whenever they feel the injury they inflicted is being

<column-break/>

inflicted back on them in turn, when their greatest punishment is wickedness itself. Nor was the mind of Marcus Tullius Cicero any different in the *Second Philippic*, in which place he laments the cruelty of Publius Dolabella against Gaius Trebonius in mournful ways, so that even if some rhetorician were to exhaust all modes of pity, he could hardly represent it as Cicero did; in that place, Arnoldus Ferronius <note>Arnauld de Ferron (1515–1563), a French jurist and historian</note>, a supreme legal expert and most upright Senator, judged him an ornament of his Gaul in his *Commentary on the Customs of Bordeaux, Book 2, Title 12, page 325.* Cicero, therefore, in the stated place, says: *But Dolabella indeed was so unmindful of humanity, as if he had never been a participant in it, that he exercised his insatiable cruelty not only on the living, but even on the dead.* O much more miserable Dolabella, than he whom you wished to be most miserable! And a little later: *More miserable, therefore, is he who has taken the crime upon himself, than he who is forced to undergo the wickedness of another.* Wherefore also he whom I praised above, Plato in *Gorgias* (on Rhetoric): *For I think thus, he says, that both I and you and other men are of this opinion, that we consider doing injury to be worse than receiving it. And not to pay the penalty is worse than to pay it.* This was inserted into his collections or commonplaces by the Blessed Maximus the Philosopher <note>Likely Maximus the Confessor, a 7th-century theologian</note> concerning the Martyrdom of Christ. And again elsewhere, Plato (in the *Apology for Socrates*) under the persona of Socrates:

> For hold this well, O Athenians: if you kill me, you will not harm me more than yourselves. For neither Meletus nor Anytus (Socrates’ accusers) have harmed me in any way, nor indeed could they. For I do not think it is right, or divinely permitted, for a better man to be harmed by a worse. Perhaps he could kill me, or drive me from the city, or mark me with a note of infamy. These things, indeed, he and perhaps someone else considers great evils: but I do not think so; rather, I hold it much more among evils to do the things which this man is now doing, and what follows.

Philosophy also, in Severinus Boethius, *On the Consolation of Philosophy, Book 4, Chapter 4*, disputing with the same person: *Do you deny, she says, that every wicked person is worthy of punishment? By no means. But that those who are wicked are unhappy is clear in many ways. It is so, I said. If, therefore, you were presiding as a judge, she said, upon whom would you think the punishment should be inflicted: upon him who had done the injury, or him who had suffered it? I have no doubt, I said, that I would satisfy the sufferer through the pain of the doer. The inflictor of the injury, therefore, would seem more lowly to himself than the receiver? It follows, I said. From this, therefore, and other causes, it appears from that root in the texts—that baseness by its own nature makes men miserable—that an injury inflicted on anyone is the misery not of the receiver, but of the inflicter.* Thus far Boethius. To pursue more things of this kind would be not so much difficult for me as it would be tedious for you to hear. Therefore I return to the interpreters of the law, and I see I must take care lest these students of mine get stuck on some other scruple. For I did not hide from the very beginning of this Disputation...

<meta>This page continues the legal and philosophical analysis of self-defense and preemptive strikes. Having previously discussed the psychological toll of vengeance, the author now turns to specific legal precedents regarding "outlaws" (banniti) and the dangerous doctrine that one might kill a person who is merely *about* to be proscribed. He contrasts the "Golden Doctor" Castrensis with other jurists like Socinus, arguing that the law should never be used to encourage preemptive violence.</meta>

### Lit. L. 575 ###

A certain saying of the great **Jason** <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a famous Italian jurist.</note> is commonly celebrated concerning one who was very close to proscription and destruction: Jason conceded that such a person, as an enemy already proscribed (an "outlaw" [**bannitum**], as he says), could be killed with impunity. This is found in his commentary on the *Code of Justinian*, book 2, title "On Inofficious Testaments." While **Paulo de Capro** and others approved of this doctrine, many claim that few or none have followed it, as **Catellianus Cotta** notes in his *Memorabilia*, page 430. This refers to **Castrensis** <note>Paulus de Castrensis (d. 1441), a highly influential legal scholar.</note>, whom they once called the "Golden Doctor." And who does not know how great the authority of both men is in the Law? However, **Aretinus** and **Alexander**, as well as **Bartholomaeus Socinus** in his commentary on the *Digest*, book 3, section 10, have attacked this doctrine of his. They deny that a person should be considered an outlaw simply because a sentence of banishment or proscription could be passed against them in the near future. They judged that Castrensis had been plunged into that error by a flawed deduction which was born from a combination of things utterly fighting against each other. For because he had learned from **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most famous medieval jurist.</note> that someone who is very close to being acquitted and freed by a Judge’s sentence should be treated as if already freed, he thought it followed that someone who is very close to being proscribed should, before the sentence is even issued, be treated as an outlaw or proscribed person.

In this reasoning, I wonder which I should marvel at more: that he saw no difference between sentences, one of which would bring destruction to the condemned, and the other of which would bring aid against the false accusations <term>calumnia: a malicious or false accusation</term> to the innocent; or truly, that he wished to ignite the license for offenses "before the day" and add a spur to vengeance, as if to an unbridled horse? But it would be worthwhile to know how the adversaries try to snatch from our hands this club of the most equitable distinction between favors and hatreds—with which we have beaten them thus far—or at least try to render it useless. Why not? For they act as if they were mimes behind a curtain, whose hidden differences hold us in vain and mock us. 

Therefore, they show that it greatly pleases them that we have said more than once that in punishments, hatreds (penalties) are to be restricted, but favors are to be expanded <note>original: "c. odia de R. I. in 6"; refers to the legal maxim *Odia restringi, et favores convenit ampliari* found in the *Liber Sextus* of the Canon Law.</note>. They cry out that this is nowhere more clearly seen than in this very dispute of ours concerning a soldier found passing through another's land. For if the lords of the soil through which he makes his way had attacked him, or perhaps killed him, they argue that by that very act and the harm completed, they seem to have earned a "favor," the use of which the laws intended to be greatest in acquitting and freeing defendants. And so, since those men did not dare to deny that an offense had occurred, they thought that the Lords of the territory should be treated with favor for no other reason than because they thought acquittal was necessary for them. But who can longer endure such a slanderous twisting of the Laws to a sense most foreign to them? By the judgment of these men, as I see it, the favor of the laws is sought through injuries and crime—a favor which it was right for us to purchase through probity, peace, and charity. For these men, a completed felony makes them "favorable," though before the crime was perpetrated and the loss inflicted on the innocent, they would have been 

<column-break/>

judged worthy of no grace or benefit of the laws. 

It is a wonder, indeed, that they did not also judge those offenders worthy of a reward! On the contrary, patience and compassion toward guests would have rendered them less dear to the Laws. By your faith, listeners, could any painter with his artistic brush have more expressly signaled the true form of a sophism? You know that such a thing must be avoided in legal responses more cautiously than viper’s blood. I think not. Yet there exists in **Lucan**, Book 4 of the *Pharsalia*, the speech of **Photinus** <note>Photinus was the eunuch advisor to Ptolemy XIII who famously argued for the murder of Pompey the Great.</note> persuading the King of Egypt to the same:

> ->*Right and divine law make many people guilty, Ptolemy;*<-
> ->*praised loyalty pays the penalty (he says), while it*<-
> ->*supports those whom fortune crushes.*<-

By this "noble" sentiment, **Pompey** (who had earned the name "the Great") was then condemned to death. It was a sentiment worthy of that author, who complained that the whole power of scepters perishes if one begins to weigh what is just. He argues in the same place that respect for honesty overthrows battle lines, and therefore should be kept far away in similar consultations about war and peace, bringing forward this reason: that

->*as the stars are distant from the earth,*<-
->*and flame from the sea, so is the useful from the right:*<-
->*He who says there is a liberty for crimes:*<-
->*—— which protects hated kingdoms*<-
->*and the removal of limit from swords.*<-

Always fear, Photinus adds, the man whom cruel things will make ashamed. But I myself am first ashamed and weary, listeners, to have been troublesome to you with the recitation of these things. Now, what kind of thing is it, or in what place should it be held, that in the mockery of this "wisdom" <note>original: "fannientis sapientiæ"; wisdom that acts like a *fannio* or jester.</note> they have devised—that the "favor" of these offenders is to be treated as often as their acquittal is sought? *What kind of monster is this?* Is an acquittal to be held as "favorable" even when it is certain that there can be no place for it? Or when the committed felony and the loss inflicted by injury is fully established? *To harm no one is a law not so much of all Nations, as of God himself.* 

Yet, if we follow these Masters, avoiding His punishment will be the business of the delinquent, if—the thought of some inconvenience occurring to his mind which he might suffer from the one approaching—he leaps forward to cause injury before he has been provoked. For by that very act he will both become "gracious" and hope for pardon, because he ensured by a hurried offense that no one else besides himself should first commit a crime against the law. As if, therefore, the law invited a man to commit a crime, or aided the proclivity for harming others that exists in man, they have commanded him to hope well for liberation from punishment because an offense followed. Oh, what wonderful foolishness, how deep are the roots of folly! Where are the old Jurists now, whose sayings are these: *Great reason persuades that punishments be paid for felonies; the vigor of public discipline demands it. Acts committed against the Laws ought not to go unpunished; the malice of men must not be indulged, nor should his own cunning benefit anyone. No one [should profit] from his own...* <note>The catchword "suo" suggests the famous maxim "Nemo ex delicto suo conditionem suam meliorem facere potest" — No one can make his condition better through his own crime.</note>

The author argues that law should promote peace and probity rather than providing excuses for early retaliation, citing classical literature and the "Golden Doctor" Castrensis.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral argument regarding the dangers of private vengeance. The catchword from the previous page was "cele-", suggesting a word like "celebrated" or "accustomed," leading into the discussion of the risks involved in pursuing revenge.</meta>

### Page 574 ###
### Treasury of Practical Law, Augmented ###

...is accustomed. For just as those who, for the sake of profit, commit themselves to the danger of the sea and are about to set out on the "wooden horse" of Plautus <note>original: "equo ligneo Plauti"; a metaphor for a ship from the Roman playwright Plautus.</note>, usually bind themselves with great interest; so too those who indulge too much in anger when seeking to avenge a loss involve themselves in a very great "usury" of calamities. When one athlete competes with another in a fair match, we see that happen which Horace says:

> *We are struck, and with as many blows we consume the enemy,* <note>original: "Cadimur & totidem plagis consumimus hostem," from Horace, *Epistles* 2.2.97.</note>

because both have been trained in a similar sport, and an equal desire for glory is seen in both—though in such a way that it is sometimes a matter of very little danger, and often even of great praise. We find nothing similar in the meeting of good men with the wicked. For because neither was trained by the same <term>Lanista</term> <note>A manager or trainer of gladiators.</note> nor in the same wrestling school for the same sword-fighting, nor are they competitors for the same crown and palm of victory, what is to stop the honest men from usually leaving the contest as the inferiors, forced to surrender to the arrogant victors? But we must also now see what fruit or what utility follows this pursuit of avenging and returning injuries.

<margin>Law 6, last section, Digest, regarding the risk and benefit of a sold thing; Law 13, last section, Digest, regarding threatened damage; final Law, last section, regarding the trust of instruments; final Law, section 13, at the verse "But because certain," Code, regarding the law of children; final Law, Code, regarding the sentence for that which is of interest; Law 23, Code, regarding the Most Holy Churches.</margin>
This pursuit is an infinity that is not only hostile to the law and human actions, but also to the life of mortals: *for the swift little flower, the shortest portion of our narrow and wretched life, hastens to pass away,* <note>original: "festinat enim decurrere velox flosculus angustæ miseræque brevissima vitæ portio," from Juvenal, *Satires* 9.126.</note> as Juvenal says. For if the one who has been affected by injury or loss perpetually compensates evil with evil, it is necessary for one evil to spring from another, for a lawsuit to be born from a lawsuit, and for injury to be propagated from injury. For by whatever right you grant to him who first received the injury the power to return it, he is excused by that same right when the vengeance returns to him; by which reasoning there will plainly be no end to offenses and losses. This is not just "stirring up the dog-like" (as the proverb says), but moving the very fountains of wickedness, which is what all those do who hold up a prior injury to justify a present one. Maximus Tyrius, in his second Dissertation, argues that nothing else destroyed Greece but the over-valuation of one's own injuries—which erupted into infinite retaliations—as well as implacable fury, immortal anger, the lust for revenge, and ignorance of the Law. For if both the Greeks and all those whom injury first attacked could have persuaded themselves of this: that injury itself is the greatest evil to those who inflict it, and that it is a heavier punishment than war, the overturning of walls, the plundering of lands, fires, or any tyranny, they would never have succumbed to so many and such great calamities in the past. Indeed, Plato, in the 5th book of the *Laws*, judges that the cause of such great slaughters is nothing other than that men are ignorant of the way in which the wicked are punished; and in this they are most deceived, while they think that the punishment consists of having the injury they inflicted

<column-break/>

inflicted back upon them in turn, whereas their greatest punishment is their own wickedness. Nor was the mind of Marcus Tullius Cicero any different in his *Second Philippic*, in that place where he laments the cruelty of *Publius Dolabella* toward *Gaius Trebonius* in mournful tones. Even if one of the teachers of Rhetoric were to employ all the methods of evoking pity, he could hardly represent it as Cicero did; in that passage, Arnoldus Ferronius <note>A 16th-century French jurist and historian.</note>, a supreme legal expert and most upright Senator, considered it an ornament of his native Gaul in his *Customs of Bordeaux, Book 2, title 12, page 325.* Therefore, Cicero says in the mentioned place: *But Dolabella indeed, was so unmindful of humanity, as if he had never been a partaker of it, that he exercised his insatiable cruelty not only on the living, but even on the dead.* O, Dolabella is much more miserable than he whom you wished to be the most miserable! And a little later: *He is therefore more miserable who takes the crime upon himself, than he who is forced to undergo the villainy of another.* For this reason, that Plato whom I praised above says in the *Gorgias* (or the 5th book on Rhetoric): *For I think thus, that both I and you and other men are of the opinion that doing an injury is worse than receiving one. And not to pay the penalty is worse than paying it.* Blessed Maximus the Philosopher <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), a Christian theologian.</note> inserted this into his collections, or commonplaces, concerning the Martyrs of Christ. And again elsewhere, Plato (in the *Apology for Socrates*) speaks in the person of Socrates: *For hold this well, O Athenians: if you kill me, you will not hurt me more than you hurt yourselves. For neither Meletus nor Anytus (the accusers of Socrates) have harmed me at all, nor indeed could they. For I do not think it is right, or divinely permitted, for a better man to be harmed by a worse one. Perhaps he could kill me, or drive me from the city, or mark me with the brand of infamy.* These very things, and perhaps someone else, he considers great evils; but I do not think so, but I consider it a much greater evil to do the things that this man is now doing, and what follows. Philosophy also, in the works of Severinus Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy, Book 4, prose 4*, disputing with the same: *Do you deny,* she says, *that every wicked man is worthy of punishment? Not at all. But it is clear in many ways that those who are wicked are unhappy. It is so, I said. If, therefore, you were sitting as a judge, upon whom would you think the punishment should be inflicted: upon him who had done the injury, or him who had endured it? I do not doubt, I said, that I would satisfy the one who suffered through the pain of the one who did it. The inflictor of the injury, therefore, would seem more wretched to himself than the receiver. It follows, I said. From this, therefore, and for other reasons rooted in the texts—because baseness by its own nature makes men miserable—it appears that an injury inflicted on anyone is the misery not of the receiver, but of the inflictor.* Thus far Boethius. It would not be so difficult for me to pursue more such examples as it would be tedious for you to hear them. Therefore, I return to the Interpreters of the law, and I see that I must take care lest these students of mine get stuck on a certain other scruple. For I did not hide from the very beginning of this Disputation...

<meta>This page continues a legal and moral debate regarding whether a person who is "about to be outlawed" can be killed with impunity. This page introduces the opinions of famous legal scholars on the status of the "proscribed" individual.</meta>

### Page 575 ###
### Letter L ###

A certain saying of the great **Jason** <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a highly influential Italian jurist.</note> is commonly cited concerning a man who was on the verge of proscription and ruin: he argued that such a person could be killed with impunity, just as if he were already proscribed (or "banned," as he puts it). **Catellianus Cotta**, in his *Memorabilia* (page 430), approved of this doctrine, which originated with **Paulus de Castro**. This is the same **Castrensis** whom they once called the "Golden Doctor"; and who does not know how much authority both these men hold in the Law? However, **Aretinus** and **Alexander** attacked this doctrine, as did **Bartholomaeus Socinus** in his commentary on the Digest <note>original: "ad l. 3. §. 10. ff. de A. vel O. poss."; referring to Book 41, Title 2 of the Digest of Justinian.</note>. They deny that a man should be considered "banned" simply because a sentence of banishment or proscription could soon be brought against him. They also judged that **Castrensis** was hurried into this error by a faulty collection of arguments, born from joining things that are completely at odds with one another. Because he had learned from **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most famous medieval jurist.</note> that someone who is on the verge of being acquitted and freed by a judge's sentence should be treated as if they were already free, he thought it followed that someone about to be proscribed should be treated as already banned or proscribed before the sentence was even issued. 

In this reasoning, I wonder which is more amazing: that he saw no difference between sentences where one brings destruction to the condemned, while the other brings help to the innocent against the false accusations of a prosecutor? Or that he wanted to light the fuse of license for offenses before the day of judgment, adding a spur to vengeance like a rider to an unbridled horse? But it will be worthwhile to understand how our adversaries try to wrest from our hands this "club" of most equitable distinction between favors and hatreds, with which we have struck them down until now. Why wouldn't they? They act like actors behind a curtain, using hidden distinctions to frustrate and mock us. They show themselves to be greatly pleased that we have said more than once that in punishments, hatreds [or penalties] must be restricted, while favors [or benefits] must not be extended <note>original: "c. odia de R. I. in 6."; a legal maxim from the *Regulae Iuris* meaning "Penalties should be narrowed and favors broadened."</note>. They shout that this is nowhere more clearly seen than in this very dispute of ours concerning a soldier found passing through someone else's land. They argue that if the lords of the soil through which he travels had attacked or perhaps killed him, they should be seen as having earned "favor" by the very act of the crime, since the laws intended for such favor to be used extensively in acquitting and freeing defendants. And so, while these men did not dare to deny that an offense had occurred, they thought the Lords of the territory should be treated with favor for no other reason than that they believed an acquittal was necessary for them. 

But who can longer endure such a malicious twisting of the Laws to a completely foreign meaning? By the logic of these judges, as I see it, the favor of the laws is sought through injuries and crime—a favor which we ought to earn through integrity, peace, and charity. To these men, a completed crime makes the perpetrators "favorable," though before the crime was committed and damage inflicted on the innocent, they would have been held 

<column-break/>

worthy of no grace or benefit of the laws. It is a wonder, truly, that they did not also judge those who commit the offense to be worthy of a reward, while those who displayed patience and compassion toward strangers were rendered less dear to the Laws. By your faith, listeners, could any painter with his skilled brush have more clearly marked the true form of a sophism? You know that in legal responding, such things must be avoided more cautiously than viper's blood. I think not. Yet there exists in **Lucan's** fourth book of the *Pharsalia*, the speech of **Photinus** to the King of Egypt, persuading him of the same:

> *Justice and right make many people guilty, Ptolemy,*
> -> *he says.* <-
> *Praised loyalty pays the penalty while it supports*
> -> *those whom fortune oppresses.* <note>original: "Jus & fas multos faciunt, Ptolemæa, nocentes: / Dat pœnas laudata fides, dum sustinet / quos fortuna premit." From Lucan, *Pharsalia* 8.484–486. Photinus is advising the murder of Pompey.</note>

By this "noble" sentiment, **Pompey** (who had earned the name "the Great") was then condemned to death. It was a sentiment worthy of its author, who complained that the entire power of scepters perishes if one begins to weigh what is just. He argues in the same place that respect for honesty overthrows battle lines, and therefore should be kept far away in similar consultations about war and peace, bringing forth this reason: 

-> *as the stars are distant from the earth,* <-
-> *and fire from the sea, so is the useful from the right.* <note>original: "fidera terrâ ut diſtant, & flamma mari, ſic utile recto."</note>
-> *He who says there is a liberty for crimes,* <-
-> *—which protects hated kingdoms* <-
-> *and the removal of restraint from swords.* <-

Always fear, **Photinus** adds, the man who is ashamed of cruel things. But truly, listeners, I myself have long been ashamed and weary of troubling you with the recitation of these things. Now, what kind of thing is this, or where should it be ranked, that these practitioners of a "maddening wisdom" have devised: that the "favor" of these offenders is discussed as often as their acquittal is sought? *What kind of monster is this?* Should an acquittal be considered "favorable" when it is certain that there is no place for it? Or when the crime committed and the damage done by the injury are fully established? *To harm no one is a law* <note>original: "neminem lædere lex eſt"</note> *not so much of all Nations, but of God Himself.* Yet if we follow these Masters, avoiding His punishment will be the business of the delinquent, if—the thought of some inconvenience he might receive from the one coming toward him having entered his mind—he leaps forward to cause injury before he has been provoked. For by this very act, he will both become "favored" and hope for pardon, because by hurrying the offense, he ensured that no one else would commit a crime against the law before him. As if, therefore, the law invited a man to commit a crime, or aided the inclination toward harming others that exists in man, they have commanded him to hope well for liberation from punishment once the offense has followed. Oh, what wondrous folly, for deep are the roots of stupidity! Where are the <term>Jurisconsults</term> <note>Legal experts or orators who provided legal opinions in ancient Rome.</note> of old now, whose sayings were these: *Great reason persuades that penalties be paid for crimes; the vigor of public discipline demands it. Things committed against the Laws ought not to go unpunished; the malice of men must not be indulged, nor should his own cunning profit anyone: No one [should benefit] from his own crime...*

<meta>This page continues the legal debate regarding whether a person can be treated as an enemy or an outlaw (proscribed) based on their intent or a future status, rather than a completed action. The previous page established that famous jurists like Bartolus and Castrensis disagreed on whether someone "about to be proscribed" should be treated as already banned.</meta>

### Augmented Practical Treasury ###

One ought to experience the gain from one's own position <note>Original: "Suo lucrum sentire debet." A legal principle that benefits and burdens should follow the same party. Citations follow: Digest 9.2.5; 46.1.70; 46.3.95; 9.2.51; 6.1.35; 10.4.11; Code 4.2.14.</note>. But it is believable that those who barely remember they are men have long since forgotten all these principles; yet they have not forgotten how to quickly seize and firmly hold a granted opportunity to do harm even before the appointed day, if any hope of prey or deceitful gain shines forth. However, malice requires an occasion or—as the Prince of Philosophers <note>Aristotle.</note> puts it—a **purpose** <note>original: "προθέσει" (prothesei)</note>. Once malice has found this, it will rejoice in offending all men and even Jove himself, walking upon the heads of men, just like that **Homeric Ate** <note>In Homer’s Iliad, Ate is the goddess of folly and ruin who treads on the heads of men to lead them astray. Citation: Homer, Iliad 19, line 91 (referenced here as Iliad 4 in the Giphanius edition).</note>. For thus did the father of all virtue describe that most destructive goddess, from whom all evils were soon to be derived onto the human race. Therefore, it stands, and shall always stand for the defense of the wretched, that there is a distinction between a future enemy (if indeed he is to be one) and one whom a present attack and force declares as such; between a soldier merely chosen and one already proven; between damage actually inflicted on provincials and that which is only slightly or even fruitlessly feared—as in the words of **Lucretius** <note>Roman poet and philosopher.</note> (Book 5): *for that which was feared too much before is now eagerly trampled underfoot*—and between that interpretation of the law which applies to a doubtful crime and that which applies to a certain and manifest one. Indeed, if we wish to disturb and mix together all these things that are so far removed from one another, we shall render all of life dangerous, treacherous, and infested.

But if the Patron of the opposing opinion <note>The scholar arguing the other side of this legal case.</note> cannot be led to cross over to our camp in this way, nor yet feels himself defeated (as usually happens to those defeated in an argument), let him know that it is very easy for us to bring into the battle line other "auxiliary cohorts" of distinctions besides those with which we have fought so far—on the condition, however, that *if the battle is renewed and he is overthrown, he must confess himself twice defeated*. 

Therefore, you say that military service <note>term: "militia" — here meaning the legal status of being a soldier for a foreign power.</note> must be considered and even punished by death in these "guests" who travel through our territory toward enemy lands. I ask you: since this is not "pure" military service, what do you consider it to be? For you could have learned from those points we have so often hammered home that we have not taken up the defense of assassins, nor of bandits, nor of active soldiers who were caught red-handed with bloodied hands or a still-warm intent to do harm. Regarding such people, **reason has taught the learned, necessity the barbarians, custom the nations, and nature the beasts** <note>A famous rhetorical flourish often attributed to Cicero.</note> that it is impossible for an injustice to be done to them. Therefore, there must be another type of "military service" that you pursue with such great hatred. Come now, I pray, of what kind is it, or what is it called? I will answer for you, if you permit. And I prove it is of the kind that contains a **condition** <note>term: "conditio" — a legal qualification that suspends the effect of an act until a future event occurs.</note>, or a quality that is accustomed to suspend the acts of men and defer them to a future event or the judgment of another. For it is well known that a "condition" is so named because it is "established" like a law—that is, the thing done depends on a future outcome.

<column-break/>

Do you ask for the formula of this condition? Here it is: *If he shall have been with our enemies, or if he who has given his name to military service is received by the enemies: even if the enemy wished to use his labor*, as noted by **Alciatus** <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist.</note> and **Albericus Gentilis** <note>Alberico Gentili (1552–1608), a founder of the science of international law.</note>. However, since a deed is nothing before it is done, and because that which is pending is not the same as that which is completed, it would be entirely just, O Listeners, for you to consider someone traveling toward enemies (whose soldier he has not yet become) as being within the "time of the condition" so long as he refrains from injury and wrongdoing, and you should guarantee him safety from all danger. For why should we think this military "condition" has any less weight than a sentence of proscription <note>term: "proscriptio" — the act of being declared an outlaw who can be killed by anyone.</note>? For in such a condition, it is the constant opinion of all Interpreters (such as **Julius Clarus** in his *Criminal Practice*) that it is implied *unless there was an unjust provocation*, so that before the matter is determined in a second judgment, the sentence of proscription does not hold, nor can the condemned man be harmed. But I have no mind to **re-cook the cabbage** <note>note: "cramben recoquere" — a Latin idiom (from Juvenal) meaning to repeat a stale or boring argument.</note> already served above. 

Furthermore, to pave the way for another distinction, I should like to ask my Antagonist whether he wishes those who go to a neighboring enemy by private choice to be judged by the same law as the enemy itself. Does he interpret this as "military service" in which there is neither any unjust harm, nor the authority and struggle of public arms? No one, I think, would assign the judgment and power of declaring and waging war to these **ragged fellows**, whom no solemn oath, nor conspiracy, nor summons (such as existed in the old days) had made soldiers for the necessity and utility of the Republic, but rather the narrowness of their family estate and private poverty. **Eric, King of the Swedes**, was not ignorant of this; when war was declared against him by the people of Lübeck, he replied, maintaining his majesty, that **"kings ought to declare war on kings, and peasants on peasants,"** as found in **Jacques Auguste de Thou** <note>French historian (1553–1617).</note>. He was hinting, evidently, that war can only be undertaken and waged by those endowed with supreme power who claim the rights of majesty for themselves. 

Yet my adversary, a harsh man, judged to the contrary: he even sought "military service" in those who, chosen by no public authority, fearfully crossed the cloddy fields of their neighbors, doing nearly the same thing as **dogs in Egypt, who, while lapping water from the Nile, dash away and run across in a most perilous flight** <note>An ancient legend (told by Pliny and others) that dogs lap the Nile while running to avoid being seized by crocodiles.</note>. It is ignorance not to know the difference between a public plan and the private thought of any individual; it is to be unaware that *some things are useful publicly, others privately*. It is cruelty to propose death as a punishment for a private plan by which no one has yet been harmed—as if punishing the "dream" of one who might wish to be a soldier. Indeed, his ignorance will appear more manifest from the very things the Antagonist himself brought forward earlier from **Livy** (Book 8)...

<meta>This page continues the legal argument from page 576 regarding whether a person can be punished for an intended crime that has not yet been completed. The previous page discussed the distinction between a future enemy and a present one, using legal precedents to argue that mere intent or "about to be" status should not carry the same weight as a finished act.</meta>

## Letter L. ##

He mentions the people of Lanuvium <note>Lanuvium was an ancient city of Latium, south of Rome. They often fluctuated between being Roman allies and enemies.</note>, who had decreed to come to the aid of the Latins against the Romans, in order to show that they were rightfully punished by the Roman Praetor. He handled the cause of the Romans in such a way as to respond that merely marching outside the City of the Lanuvinians was sufficient for punishment. This is true: for it ought not to have benefited them that, upon learning of the Roman victory, they had recalled their standards into the city and departed from the war alliance and fellowship of the Latins as if the matter were still untouched. This, therefore, was correct regarding the punishment. But that other point was less correct and less subtle: that he did not see that a public plan, the consensus of the whole community, and a decree of the magistrates concerning the bringing of aid to the Latin people constituted a war against the Romans—even if the allies and the Fetial <note>The Fetials were a college of priests in Rome who oversaw the rituals of declaring war and making treaties.</note> engines of war were only brought out after the conflict. "Enemies are those," says **Ulpian** <note>original: "Hostes sunt... Ulpianus l. 24. de captiv. & postlim. revers." Ulpian was one of the most influential Roman jurists. The citation refers to Digest 49.15.24.</note>, "against whom the Roman people have publicly decreed war, or who have decreed it against the Roman people." Therefore, it is the public decree that made the Lanuvinians enemies and made them liable to punishment—not a bare plan, nor a hidden meditation of aid in the mind which is separated from every act. *It remains now that we attack the adversary on that side where it is likely he has placed his chief hope of victory.* He had heard that in **Italy** there are certain Statutes by which townspeople are forbidden from exporting grain <note>original: "frumentum"</note> to neighbors outside the municipality under penalty of death or other proposed penalties, as noted by Aegidius Bossius in various tracts. He had also received the work of Julius Clarus <note>A prominent 16th-century Italian jurist.</note>, but what a man, with what authority, with what praises! He interprets these statutes so that even one caught on the journey, having exited the boundaries of the municipality with grain, would be compelled to undergo the same penalty. Our opponent contends that this Law should not only be held onto with "all his nails" <note>An idiom meaning to hold onto something very tightly or tenaciously.</note>, but should also be transferred to any cases in which the punishment of a "crime not yet formed" is sought. I am truly not far from pronouncing that proverbial saying: *I ask for sickles, and am answered about a hoe* <note>original: "mihi falces postulanti de ligone responderi." A Latin proverb used when someone gives an irrelevant or off-topic answer.</note>. For when I ask what penalty is established by Civil or Common Law for those passing through our territory to the enemy, the adversary responds concerning a custom which perhaps exists in **Milan** or elsewhere in **Italy**. I do not mention this as if those intercepted on the road were too clumsily compared—one of whom goes to serve the enemy as a soldier, while the other exports provisions elsewhere, yet neither reaches the destination. Nor do I say this as if the Duumviri <note>Local municipal magistrates.</note> and other municipal officials or prefects of the grain supply in Italy did not have suitable reasons for their legislation. But it is because we have found that those very Authors whom the Antagonist so greatly admires, when consulted on Common Law, responded differently and relaxed much of the rigor of such punishments. See Raphael Fulgosius <note>original: "Raph. Fulgos. ad l. 4. ff. de usufr."</note> and others.
Besoldus, *Volume I.*

<column-break/>

Giovanni Francesco à Ripa <note>A 16th-century Italian jurist.</note> writes concerning the plague, whom Clarus alleges and follows in the place mentioned above. They did not wish for Statutes, which had been established in some small corner, to be allowed so much power that they might extend their wings, as it were, beyond their own nest—extending to other provinces, to other types of acts, and to other persons besides those expressed in those same Statutes. Finally, they could not endure that a law so narrow in its municipal authority should overcome and, as it were, bury not only all Civil Laws, but also the Law of Nations. *For the Law of Nations <note>original: "Jus Gentium." This refers to the customary laws shared by all humanity, often contrasted with the "Civil Law" of a specific city or state.</note> does not punish crimes unless they are completed.* And **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis, a famous medieval jurist.</note> provides this reason, not without subtlety: that when a crime not yet completed is held as completed, this is not done according to nature (which holds the opposite), nor properly, but through a legal fiction. Agreeing with him, Alexander of Imola <note>Alexander Tartagnus, a famous legal commentator.</note> did not fear to call such a fiction an "insult to the Law of Nations" in a clearly identical case. He defines in that same place that Natural Law does not allow the death penalty to be imposed for a wound from which death does not follow. Concerning the prohibited exportation of wheat or other things to barbarians and others outside the borders, we must see how the Civil Law speaks. *If anyone,* says the Emperor Marcian <note>original: "Marcianus Imp." Referring to a law in the Code of Justinian 4.41.2.</note>, *shall have sold any kind of arms to barbarians of any nation, contrary to the interdicts of our piety, anywhere: we decree that all his goods be claimed by the treasury, and that he himself undergo the capital penalty.* What does the Adversary think those words, *if anyone shall have sold*, mean? Can an act not be considered completed such that while the prohibited goods are within the borders and still on the road, the penalty cannot be demanded? In this same way, the municipal law ought to have been interpreted, especially if it had been conceived thus: *if anyone shall have exported, if anyone shall have extracted.* See Suarez <note>Rodrigo Suárez, a Spanish jurist.</note>, which those great men, the Interpreters of the Laws, did not hide—unless they considered the force of Custom in those places where they lived to be stronger than the Emperor (whom no one obeyed there) and feared this "tyranny" of custom. You know these commonly tossed-about sayings: *The Emperor does not rule elsewhere, but is a private man. Custom received elsewhere rules.* Custom is introduced without the Prince knowing; he disdains to confirm it. What if I also mindfully warn that, through that arrangement of precepts, it does not seem quite rightly composed, so that nothing deviates from the ruler's square and all corners meet for equality of punishment? The act is "pure" <note>In this context, "pure" means a simple, direct act without conditions.</note> in the one who exports wheat against the prohibition of the law; nothing that depends on that act or the mind of the exporter can be considered. But in the one who risks passage to our enemy on our land, *it is not a pure act, but one suspended by various conditions*, which, if they fail, he knows he must return to his former stalls and the lot of a civilian.

<meta>This page continues the legal argument concerning whether a person—specifically a traveler or a "soldier" in transit—should be punished for an intended crime or mere presence in a territory before any harm has been done. The author continues to dismantle the "Antagonist's" (the opposing lawyer's) arguments.</meta>

# Treasuries of Practical Knowledge, Augmented #

The mind of the one departing is itself doubtful, unaware of present circumstances, uncertain of the future, and ignorant of the will of those toward whom he is traveling. Looking at this diversity of minds, it seems to me not at all surprising that the interpreters of customs and Statutes have proceeded with such severity. They have judged that a person exporting grain, caught on the road, should be immediately condemned, so that they might not export it at all until they have left the territory of those prohibiting it. They judged it as if it had already been extracted, even though it was still found within the territory; they considered the mere intent of transporting the grain as equivalent to the completed act of exportation. Indeed, we praise these men for their prudence and caution, as they deserve. However, lest anyone think that such a punishment for an exporter was approved by Common Law <note>original: "Jure communi" — the body of law based on Roman legal principles common to Europe at the time.</note>, they signified by adding the phrases *according to Custom* and *among us* that the reality of the facts in their own country is one thing (*for every custom is a matter of fact*), while the law that is widely known or commonly observed by all is another. <note>Citations refer to legal commentaries by Baldus de Ubaldis and Giulio Claro on maritime and criminal practice.</note> For I believe you, my listeners, expect me to inquire more accurately now into those "corollaries" of my Antagonist, which he added with a generous hand to his other reasons, so that we may skillfully return those arguments to him like a ball he has struck. One such argument was regarding the violation of territory by mere transit; another was about a gladiator prepared for a fight; another about a Serpent, whom no one spares even if it is still hiding; and another regarding Kings *Philip and Ariovistus* <note>Philip V of Macedon and Ariovistus, a Germanic king; both were preemptively attacked by Romans who feared their potential for harm.</note>, who were intercepted by the Romans and Caesar before they could cause harm. But what kind of crime is this, if a "son of the earth" <note>original: "terra filius" — a person of obscure or humble origin, or simply a common man.</note> travels through the earth—the *Mother of all*—as if having received safe-passage <gloss>original: "salvo conductu"</gloss> to join other "little brothers of the Giants"? What if he believed the use of the earth to be common by Natural Law, no less than the use of air, flowing water, the sea, and the shores? Aelius writes that the earth (*terra*) was named from "treading" (*terendo*), because it is trodden by feet. Just as in the books of the Augurs, the earth was written with a harsher gap to be "terra," which is the earth to us. This earth is trodden not only by men, nor only by the fierce race of lions or herds of oxen, but as Lucretius says in *Book 5*:

> *And the light-sleeping hearts of dogs with faithful breasts,*
> *And every race that is born from the seed of beasts of burden,*
> *And the wool-bearing sheep alike were meant to tread [it].*

Clearly, you found it difficult to endure that this soldier of ours pressed upon foreign soil—not a soldier, yet not keeping himself within his own oak groves, despising the precept of Theocritus. For that poet of Syracuse warns in his *Wayfarers* <note>original: "hodœporis, in Idilio" — referring to Theocritus's Idylls.</note>:

->Keep your lizard in the oak trees.<- <note>A proverbial way of saying "stay in your own place" or "mind your own business."</note>

But this is a minor point. What should I say came into my adversary's mind, when he dares to compare the soldier—whom he imagines as having been born in a single night like a *fungus*—

<column-break/>

—with a Gladiator or a *Lanista* <note>A trainer or manager of gladiators.</note> prepared for a fight? He dares to compare this mild and gentle man of ours—the kind of man whom the ancient age (which thought military fortitude consisted of a hand doing everything) called by the Greek word *prean* <note>original: "πεᾶαν" (πρᾶον) — meaning mild or meek.</note>, or in Latin, *a distorted kind of insult* <note>The author is likely playing on the word "pravus" (distorted/bad) and its phonetic similarity to the Greek term for mildness.</note>—to such a fighter. You have compared this distorted and "fungus-like" soldier to some prize-fighter, as if he had as much spirit for winning as he actually has for fleeing, should some sudden danger or fear force him to stay his foot and turn back his steps. Then, with an easy metamorphosis, you turned the same man from a gladiator into a serpent, to whom a landowner owes no more mercy than to wolves if found in his field. Finally, since you judged the nature of this "false soldier" to be suited to all shapes—this man whom you just transformed from a human into a light-shunning beast that lives in hiding—you did not hesitate to suddenly lift him from his lowly rank and place him upon the throne of fearsome Kings.

> *He has no beast of burden, no servant, no companion,*
> *His knapsack <gloss>German: Ranzen</gloss> and whatever coins he has, he carries all with him,*
> *He dines with his knapsack, sleeps with it, and washes with it:*

With these words, the author of the Latin Satires, *Lucilius*, graphically depicted this man of ours heading into enemy territory. You wished to make the "false fires" <note>Campfires used by travelers to simulate a larger force or for warmth.</note> of those traveling through another's estate—which they are accustomed to light for night-time illumination or for the sake of the cold, and which the Greeks call *pseudopyra* <gloss>German: Wachfeuer (Watch-fires)</gloss>—appear no less terrifying to onlookers than the legitimate armies of Kings *Philip* or *Ariovistus* <gloss>German: Ehrenvest (Honorable)</gloss>, from whom the Romans once feared the fire of war within their borders. A man commits no sin if he decides that a person of known wickedness or reckless audacity is no different from a goring ox or a kicking donkey. Yet, there is no small difference between an animal that can cause damage <note>term: "pauperiem" — a technical legal term for damage caused by a four-footed animal without the owner's fault.</note> but cannot commit a legal injury, and a rational animal—a human—who is capable of both law and injury. But what has this traveler deserved, who prepared to harm no one, plotted the destruction of no one, and perhaps was even thinking of fleeing somewhere just so he would not have to fight? What does he have in common with a *serpent*, this man whom I can place neither among the *mice* nor the *birds*? It is easier to say what he is *not* than what he is. Perhaps you will say I am mocking you; but I am not laughing. I only note that when you turned this guest (not yet a soldier) into so many miraculous things, like some *Proteus* <note>A sea-god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape.</note>, you forgot to call him a *bat*. For as it says in the fables, that animal persuaded the *rooster* that it was a *mouse*, but told the *cat* it was a *bird*, so that it might escape danger. It showed *fur and teeth to the rooster*, which the bird-kind does not have, and *wings to the cat*, with which it could fly up at night and be carried into the heights even without the rowing of feathers.

<page-num>579</page-num>
<header>Letter L.</header>

<margin>Befoldus, Volume 1</margin>
...which nature denied to the mouse-kind, and was given only to Daedalus among men (if it is worthy of belief); so too for him on whose account you stirred up the Tyrian seas <note>A poetic reference to a long or stormy journey.</note>, whether you call him a guest or by any other name, you should know that many things are present by which he sells himself now to the soldier class, now to the civilian <term>paganorum</term> <note>In Roman law, a "paganus" was a civilian or non-soldier, rather than a religious "pagan."</note> class, or flatters both; yet he himself either doubted his own status and condition or is lying, and like a bat, he does not sufficiently distinguish where to turn safely in the dark. Furthermore, he displays a confidence—which ignorance of things usually produces—and other provocations of "bravery" that suggest a soldier, yet in the face of true dangers, he is second to no civilian in fear and hesitation: a **helmeted hare** <note>original: "lepus galeatus" — a proverbial expression for a coward dressed as a soldier.</note>, as they say, otherwise harmless and exposed as prey to everyone.

You have here, excellent Listeners, the sum of the Defense which I undertook for a soldier who is not yet a soldier. I did this so that, above all, I might show to our most flourishing and learned youth that for those devoted to the study of Law, the path is not entirely blocked to reviving for modern use the ancient custom of declaiming. This was a practice which the Rhetoricians once claimed for themselves by their own right in those controversies which have now begun to belong properly to the Jurists. And this method of treatment is not only suited to acquiring the faculty of speaking, but is also extremely useful to the Jurists themselves. This was the view of many, especially of him who ought to be worth a multitude to us, **Andreas Alciatus, the most eloquent of the legal experts** and the **most legally expert of the eloquent**, who judged this matter excellently, as he did all things. See the complete letter of Alciatus, from which this passage is taken, at the end of this oration. He used to say that the legal opinions of experts like Alexander, Corneus, Socinus, and others who are still held in high value, would be nothing other than declamations if you took away their "nomenclature"—that is, the list of authors they cite in great numbers.

If this is not enough to earn your vote and approval, I hope you will at least not blame me for this: that although I could expect no protection from the texts of Civil Law or its interpreters, I have followed Equity by every footprint, right to its very lair, in this argument. The power of Equity, because it is stirred by nature itself, is eternal and immutable among all nations. For what comes from nature always has the same power everywhere: just as fire, which burns here among us, burns likewise among the Chinese <note>original: "Sinas"</note>.

Furthermore, I confess (as I declared at the beginning) that anyone would seek in vain for talent, judgment, or the brilliance and rhythm of words in this argument. If such things had ever been in me, and had not been rendered dull by the diseases of body and mind, I would have taken my chances in legal lectures rather than bringing my case into a foreign forum. The mind of a mortal man, Listeners, cannot suddenly lay aside a defect it has conceived from the shocks of disturbances, or bodily illnesses, and the injuries of men. Indeed, **rivers, once storms have arisen, do not—even when the serenity of the sky returns—immediately regain their former clear appearance so that their banks flow with a silent and calm march of waters.** You will find no other reason for this than that both require tranquility after a disturbance—something that hardly happens in a short interval after a recent flood, and without which the study of literature cannot stand.

And **let me add only this regarding bodily diseases: how much it is to be wished that the remnants of them could be removed as quickly as some believed the danger of a scorpion's sting could be avoided?** Although I do not doubt this will seem ridiculous to you, I will nevertheless report it from the authors. **Apuleius**, in his book on rural matters, recorded that the cure for that evil is **that the one struck by the scorpion should sit upon a donkey facing the tail; the result being that the donkey is tormented instead of the man, and takes all the pain into itself.** **Democritus** (I know not which one) is also the author of the idea that **one struck by a scorpion will feel no more pain if he immediately approaches a donkey and whispers familiarly into its ear: "A scorpion struck me," and with that word, transfers the pain to this new possessor.** <note>Citing Pierius Valerianus, *Hieroglyphica*, book 12, folio 91.</note>

If, in this manner, the corruption of parts and the spoiled instruments of the soul could produce the depravity of the body, or the crookedness, distortion, and weakness of the limbs, it would indeed be very easy to instruct even someone lying in illness or at death's door in this way: **"It is permitted to be sick, it is permitted to die, provided you neglect none of those things which the healthy manage correctly."** I now dismiss those who act thus, and I reverently refer them to the judgment of the Son of God, the holy and just prince of life, who says in **Matthew chapter 23, verse 4** and **Luke chapter 11, verses 42 and 40**: <note>original: "ὅτι δεσμέυσι φορτία βαρέα καὶ δυσβάστακτα, καὶ ἐπιτιθέασιν ἐπὶ τὰς ὤμας τῶν ἀνθρὼπων, τῷ δὲ δακτύλῳ αὐτῶν οὐ θέλεσι κινῆσαι αὐτά."</note> **"For they bind heavy burdens and hard to bear, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers."** And in another place: <note>original: "ὅτι παρέρχεσθε τὴν κρίσιν καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ Θεοῦ."</note> **"that you pass over judgment and the love of God."** For since He had clearly testified that **"He preferred mercy over sacrifice"** (Matthew 9:13)—that mercy, I say, which **Gregory of Nyssa** calls the mother of benevolence, the pledge of love, and the bond of all friendly affection—it is clear that He, in His goodness with which He embraces His worshippers, wished to damn such inhuman commands. To Him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise and glory for eternal ages.

***

You open the blocked path of controversies among the Rhetoricians and make it very easy. This matter pertains not only to acquiring the skill of speaking but is also extremely useful to us Jurists <term>JCtis</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Jurisconsultis," legal experts learned in the law.</note>. For the legal opinions of the learned—think of *Alexander*, *Corneus*, and *Socinus* <note>Famous medieval and Renaissance legal commentators: Alessandro Tartagni, Mariano Socini, and others.</note>, who are now so highly valued—what are they other than declamations, if you take away the technical names of the laws? Indeed, very few of the Professors of the humanities can provide this. And if any were able, they preferred to move on to Jurisprudence, which produces richer fruits, rather than grow old among a few fictional themes. Thus it happened that the practice of this most beautiful teaching perished. I truly rejoice that it is being revived by you and brought back into public use with such glory, and I confess that I owe you much on this account. Nor do I think this in any way opposes the *Ciceronian* authority, which ought to be sacred to everyone, since he himself used to voluntarily introduce the characters of those who would oppose him. For in this way, the truth shines out more clearly in the Socratic manner. *Domitius the Client* used to say, if I am not mistaken: *Speak against me, so that we may seem like two people* <note>original Latin: "Dic contra, ut duo videamur." A witty request for a lawyer to argue the opposing side to help the client prepare.</note>. Therefore, there is nothing for you to fear, my dear *Aonius*, that those who attribute everything to *Cicero* will be hostile to you. For I am one of them, yet I love you greatly for this very reason; far be it from me to think that you have diminished or even slightly harmed the *Ciceronian* majesty. On the contrary, I would dare to affirm under oath that *Cicero* himself would have agreed with your opinion, unless the argument of the case he was supporting demanded otherwise. For outside of that specific context, it is clear enough from all his works how much he always attributed to *Civil Law*. Success to you, then, excellent man, who represents ancient eloquence to us, restores the custom of declaiming lost by the neglect of our ancestors, and asserts the dignity of *Civil Law*. You not only take nothing away from the reputation of *Marcus Cicero*, which is already judged favorably by all, but it seems *Alciatus* <note>Andrea Alciatus, a famous humanist jurist.</note> looked back to the law *if a tree, 17, section 2, "sometimes"* in the Pandects <note>original citation: "l. si arborem 17. §. secundo interdum ff. de S. V. P." — a reference to the Digest of Roman Law.</note>. In which, however, *Ulpian* wrote *by reflection* <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ἀντανάκλασιν"; the author explains this as "per refractionem" or "per repercussionem luminis" — the bouncing back of light or sun rays</note>, so that you make it shine out more and more. For these many virtues of yours, I, as one of the crowd of students, profess to owe you as much as I can scarcely testify in words.

### 11. Territorial Defense. Vassal Defense. Services of war and peace.

What "Territorial Defense" <term>LandS-Rettung</term> <note>The obligation of a subject or vassal to defend the territory of their lord.</note> entails in letters of enfeoffment. Whether it is to be understood as service within or outside the borders of the land, or as personal service, and at whose expense the Knighthood shall be provided. See Bidembach, *Question 21.*

And authors who have written about the services to be performed in times of peace and war, and the "Cavalcade" <term>Cavalcaris</term> <note>A military service performed on horseback.</note> of the Vassals, such as Antonius Borrinus, contribute to this topic.

How far the term "Territorial Defense" <term>LandSrettung</term> extends. Rudinger, *Century 3, Observation 29.*

### 12. Landed Subject, Subject Status. Landed Residents, Residency.

The term "Subject Status" <term>LandSaSSerey</term> is newly devised; it is either a matter of fact, and is used for the persistence or possession of an estate which someone has in another’s Domain or territory; or it is a matter of law, and is used for all the due obedience which someone promises to his Lord. Gylman, *Decision 40, Number 32, Book 1.* Hence a "Landed Subject" <term>LandSaS</term> is nothing other than a man under jurisdiction, who can be commanded and ordered in all things. Schwanmann, *Decision 10, Number 31.* However, see also in the same *Decision, Number 115, at the beginning.* Gylman, *Book 1, Chamber Decisions 46, Number 32.* Hence the Noble Landed Subjects are called "mediated" <term>gemittelte von Adel</term> <note>Nobles who do not hold their land directly from the Emperor, but from an intermediate Prince.</note>, who are subject to the territory of some Prince. Meichsner, *Volume 2, Book 1, Decision 8, Folio 389.* Caspar Ziegler, *in the section on Landed Subjects, Conclusion 1, Number 14*, who says in the following number that although it cannot be denied that the definition of "Subject Status" is dangerous, as it was sought carefully and curiously at many Imperial Diets but never found. Waremund de Erenberg, *Treatise on Federations, Book 2, Chapter 1, Number 40.* It should be noted that what Spanish and Italian authors—especially Fontanella in his *Treatise on Antenuptial Pacts, Part 1, Folios 234, 261, and 278*—write about Barons can be applied to the Nobles and Landed Subjects who have subjects and villages.

And Princes or other Estates who possess "High Territorial and Supreme Sovereignty" <term>hohe Lands- und Ober-Herrlichkeit</term>, have their Landed Subjects and inferiors, or a territory, district, and domain, or a space of land armed with Jurisdiction and supreme command, where the power to coerce <term>terrendi potestas</term> belongs to them. Beër, *Decision 227, Number 7 and following.*

For "Landed Subjects" and "Subject Status" are related to the Right of the territory and to "Territorial Authority" <term>Lands-Obrigkeit</term>, and take their derivation from "sitting on the land" <term>LandSiSSen</term>. Meichsner, *Volume 2, Part 2, Chamber Decision 8, Number 4.* Indeed, "Landed Subject" and "Territorial Authority" regard each other like active and passive roles. But see altogether Ziegler in the cited place, *Number 13 and many following.*

And although Landed Subjects are mediated, they usually possess not only dignity but also some power; Nevizan says this belongs to them by the right of ancient Nobility in *Forest of Nuptials, Book 4, Number 134.* For they very often possess villages, hamlets, castles, and that kind of land granted by Princes with their attachments, appurtenances, jurisdiction, and other modes. Rosenthal, *on Fiefs, Chapter 8, Conclusion 8.* Schrader, *on Fiefs, Part 3, Chapter 4.* So much so that peasants are forced to provide an oath of fidelity and subjection to their Nobles, as people living under their Jurisdiction and maintaining a household there. Husan.

But indeed, landed subjection <term>Landsasserey</term> <note>A legal condition where a person or estate is subject to a local territorial prince rather than being directly under the Emperor.</note> is said to be in force in those places where no one can possess anything without the burden of even personal subjection. Thus, the Pappenheim family held lordships <term>Herrschafften</term> in Saxony and was summoned there, even for debts that were made in Swabia. Another type is where the villages, which free nobles possess, are subject to landed subjection, but not the persons themselves. It is proven in the Peace Treaties that by reason of some castle or town belonging to the territorial jurisdiction of a Duke, a subject—and thus a landed vassal—cannot have the exercise of a different religion even in his own citadel, even if he is "immediate" <term>immediatus</term> <note>Holding status directly under the Emperor, without an intermediate lord.</note> by reason of his person.

In the provinces of Swabia, Franconia, the Rhineland, and Wetteravia, landed subjection <term>Landsasserey</term> does not prevail. There, the immediate Nobles never acknowledge a Prince as their magistrate, but only the Emperor or the Imperial Chamber <note>The high court of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> as their superior. However, in Bavaria, Saxony, and Hesse, it does prevail. In those former places, if an "immediate" person or a State of the Empire has a home or goods, he is nevertheless not bound to swear subjection to the Prince, since residing in the territory of another Prince where landed subjection does not prevail does not immediately imply subjection.

### 13. Territorial Sovereignty and Lordship. <term>Superioritas territorialis</term>.

<margin>See Vorburg in the Summary of All Canon Law, page 35 and following. Layman, book 1, treatise 4, chapter 7, section 2, number 5; and chapter 8, only section. Marburg Counsel, volume 4, counsel 25.</margin>
The Princes of Germany and its States hold Imperial rights in their territories, called "Territorial Sovereignty and Lordship" <term>Landes-Hoch- und Herrlichkeit</term>. Master Wilhelm Anton in his treatise on *Rescripts of Delay*, page 85. But how is it understood when it is said that a Bishop in his Diocese can do as much as the Pope in the whole Church? Likewise, that a Prince or State of the Empire can do as much in his territory as the Emperor in the Empire?

When Territorial Authority over a monastery is to be proven, see the Treatise of the Reverend Bishop of Augsburg against the Monastery of St. Ulrich in Augsburg.

<margin>Imperial Decrees of the years 1548 and 1577. Bernhard Wurmser, Practical Observations, title 28, observation 28, number 9. Caspar Leipold on Concurrent Jurisdiction in the Romano-German Empire, question 12, page 277. See Knichen on Territorial Law and in the Encyclopedia. And it is nothing other than Princely Territorial Authority, mentioned above. Regarding the sovereignty of the Count of Flanders, see Marchantius in the Description of Flanders, book 2, page 177 and following.</margin>
Furthermore, the consequences of Territorial Sovereignty are the Regalia <note>Royal prerogatives or rights.</note>: customs/tolls <term>Zoll</term>, safe-conduct for the dead and the living <term>todt und lebendig Glait</term>, the right of receiving Jews, and granting five-year moratoria and letters of stay for debts <term>Inducias moratorias, Quinquennales und Anstandsbrieff</term>, and other such things. Imperial Recess of the years 1548 and 1577.

Johann Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 8, number 188.

In most principalities, there is a special "Provincial Assembly" <term>Landschafft</term>: consisting mostly of Prelates or Clergy, Nobles, and Deputies of the towns, who are called Provincial Estates <term>Land-Ständ</term>, and their meetings are called Diets <term>Landtäg</term>, regarding which more below. There are, however, principalities where such Orders do not exist,

### 15. Territorial Defense. Defense and Guarding of the territory.

Territorial defense <note>German: *Landschuß*</note> is nothing other than the general defense and guarding of territories, in both law and fact: it is attached to the higher jurisdictions and rights of sovereignty. *Zakus, counsel 14, number 8.* And this belongs to the Prince alone, or to one who holds the rights of a Prince, as well as to universal lords who possess all jurisdiction and sovereignty; following others, see *Master Mager, "On Armed Advocacy," chapter 8, number 422 and following.*

Hence, in defiance of this defense, subjects cannot commit themselves to the protection of another, except in certain specific cases.

->ADDITIO.<-

Protection is also numbered among the higher rights of sovereignty. *Chasseneuz, in "Catalog of the Glory of the World," part 5, number 195.* For by law, such protection belongs only to the Prince or to him who holds the rights of a Prince, to protect, shield, and maintain the subjects in their ancient traditions, freedoms, rights, and justices. *Gail, "On Arrests," chapter 8, number 12; Meichsner, volume 2, book 2, decision 3, number 5,* where he says this was considered at length in the case of Mainz against Erfurt. *More in Becker, "On Public Law," page 115.*

### 16. Taking Land-tenancy Rights. Tenant Right <note>Latin: *Jus colonarium*</note>.

On what the hereditary lease, the land-tenancy lease, and the hereditary land-tenancy lease <note>German: *Erbleihe, Landsiedel Leihe, Landsiedel Erbleih*</note> consist of, see *Master Doctor Tabor, "On Contracts and Provincial Tenant Right," thesis 20.* A "land-settlement" <note>German: *Landsiedel*</note> is a country seat or a landed estate. Hence those words "to have taken and arisen from land-tenancy rights," "to take and to hold," are commonly understood as a perpetual lease <term>emphyteutic contract</term> <note>A long-term lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a low rent and the right to treat the land as their own.</note>. *Johann Fichard, Latin Counsel 23, number 1.* Thus also those words "to take and to hold" <note>German: *entnehmen und bestehen*</note> cannot be understood or interpreted as anything other than a lease. *Fichard, in the same place, number 5.*

<column-break/>

->ADDITIO.<-

*Wehner, in "Practical Observations" under the name "Landsiedelei,"* is in error when he thinks that word—even in the Constitution of Solms itself—is accepted as being the same thing as a perpetual lease <term>emphyteusis</term>. Tenant Right <note>Latin: *Jus Colonarium*</note> is the "Land-tenancy right." The contract is the "Land-tenancy lease." A tenant <note>Latin: *Colonus*</note> is a land-tenant or "Landsiedel."

The possessions of sub-vassals, on account of their small size, are called "sub-settlements" <note>German: *Afftersiedeln*</note>, otherwise "sub-fiefs" <note>German: *Affterlehn*</note>. *Gemmel, in "Compendium of Feudal Law," page 41.* Thus it is pleasing to hunt for a little grape from the thicket, or a small cluster from the briar patch. In some places, rustic benches are called "Siedeln" or "Siedelbänck."

### 17. Provincial Towns. Municipal Cities.

Regarding Municipal Cities <note>Latin: *Civitates Municipales*</note>, see *Poncetus; also Guillaume Fornerius, "Selected Works," book 1, chapter 13,* where he discusses what a Municipal Law is.

On how it may be proven that a city is a provincial town <note>German: *Land-Stadt*</note>, see *The Waldeck Defense of Honor, part 3, chapter 38 and following.* Likewise, is Rostock a provincial town? *Cothmann, Academic Counsel 47, number 22, etc.*

That in provincial towns the Lord may pass judgment if his own household is mistreated is established from the Constitution of Adolph, section 4.

->ADDITIO.<-

Provincial towns are addressed by their Lords with the title "dear faithful" <note>German: *liebe Getreue*</note>. *Acts of Lindau, page 38, at the beginning.* Provincial towns, under the German Emperors, were able to hold capital jurisdiction <note>German: *peinlich Halsgericht*</note> and display their emblems, *page 615, at the end.* Municipal cities only have a private archive or chest, *page 99, in the middle.*

*Mynsinger, observation 5,* reports that a provincial city <note>German: *Land-Stadt*</note> is summoned by the Lords of the Province in the Imperial Chamber. And generally, the commentator *Hartmann Hartmann, book 1, observation 1, number 7,* reports it has been decided that the Princes of the Empire must sue their subjects in the Chamber. *Immediately see Ummius, "On Procedure," my page 135.*

### 18. Provincial Tax, Land-petition. Provincial Collections.

Provincial collections <note>Latin: *Collectae provinciales*</note> are commonly "Land-taxes" <note>German: *Landsteuer*</note>, which the Estates and Orders of the Empire impose upon their subjects for the utility of their territory, by virtue of the regalian rights <term>regalia</term> <note>Rights and powers belonging to a sovereign.</note> granted to them by the Emperor, or obtained by the right of long-standing custom. *Mynsinger, response 64, decade 7; and response 1, at the beginning, decade 15. Rosenthal, "Treatise on Fiefs," chapter 5, conclusion 34.* These collections, the "Land-taxes," are for the cares and labors which the Estates of the Empire sustain; and also in compensation for the expenses which the Lords must make and suffer for the maintenance of peace and quiet among the subjects, and for the preservation of their own dignity; and for the salaries of officials for the administration of justice—provided, however, that the consent of the subjects is obtained, or of those who represent the subjects, such as the Territorial Estates <note>German: *Landstände*</note>.

Some believe that the "Land-request" <note>Latin: *Landbede*</note> is one thing—namely, those taxes which are granted precariously, that is, at the request of the Princes and with the consenting votes of the subjects—and that the "Land-tax" <note>Latin: *Landsteuer*</note> is another, which can be and usually is imposed even upon those who are unwilling. However, Coler rightfully disagrees with this in *Counsel 1, number 231,* where he says: just as the term "extraction" <note>Latin: *exactio*; a legal term for a tax or levy</note>—as seen in the chapters *si quis Romipetas* and the title *on the extraction of tribute*—is a general term, so too the term *Landbethe* is general and encompasses every collection, whether it is requested or commanded. For it is a matter of certain and indubitable law that no collection can be commanded of the unwilling; rather, for a tax to be imposed, it is required that the subjects upon whom it is laid be summoned for this purpose, and thus it is imposed with the consent of all.

The *Landsteuer*, or provincial collection, is a patrimonial duty <term>munus patrimoniale</term> <note>A duty attached to the possession of property rather than to the person.</note> and can be indexed against outsiders <note>Latin: *Forensibus*; those living outside the immediate jurisdiction but owning property within it.</note>. Collections are divided into ordinary ones—commonly called *Landsteuer*, *Schoß* <note>A traditional German hearth or property tax.</note>, or *Schätzungen* <note>Assessments or appraisals.</note>—which have a certain annual, regular, always uniform, and perpetual payment; see William de Cuneo and Cynus. They are also divided into extraordinary ones, such as the *Landbeth* or Contributions, which are not declared except for public utility and demanding necessity, outside the normal order.
