### 19. Public Roads. *Viæ publicæ*.

Public roads (*Landstraßen*) are sometimes understood to be Royal, Imperial, Free, or belonging to the Holy Roman Empire; likewise they are designated as *Heer* (from "army") <note>German: *Heerstraße*; a military or main highway.</note> and in certain places *Haydenstraßen* <note>Heathen-roads.</note>, after the heathens or pagans by whom the common people believed military roads were paved before the birth of Christ, as Miraeus testifies in the *Code of Donations, folio 87.* These are not only the roads where the public commonly goes (since people commonly go through private roads as well), but those whose soil alone is left public and directed within certain limits of width by one who had the right of making it public, so that it might be traveled and passed through publicly. Therefore, village roads <note>Latin: *Vicinales*</note> are distinguished from these, and are not public unless they were established from the contributions of private individuals. See Henning Arnisaeus, *on the Right of Majesty, book 3, chapter 5, number 1*; see also Schneidewin on the *Institutes*, and my own work *on the Law of Things, folio 15 and following.*

In ancient times, such great account was taken of these roads that in the Roman Republic, certain "Overseers of Public Roads" <term>Curatores Viarum Publicarum</term> were appointed by the Emperors.

Indeed, it was also the function of the Aediles and Censors to manage the care of public roads, and to contract for them to be paved with flint within the city, and to be leveled and bordered outside the city, as Sixtinus notes from Livy. So today in France, there is a great Overseer of the roads of the whole Kingdom, who is called the "Master of bridges, passages, and paths" <note>French: *Maistre de ponts, passages & chemins*</note>. Tholosanus, *Syntagma, book 3, chapter 13, number 5.*

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion of sovereign rights (Regalia) within the Holy Roman Empire, moving from the topic of provincial taxes (Landsteuren) to the legal status, maintenance, and security of public roads.</meta>

# Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

Public **roads** are categorized among the Sovereign Rights <note>Latin: *Regalia*; rights belonging to the monarch or high-ranking lords</note>, according to the chapter *which things are royal*. This is because the protection and defense of these roads belong to the Prince, as stated in the *Code on the office of the proconsul* and the *office of the praetorian prefect*. See also Schneidewin on the *Institutes*, who notes that even if a Noble is granted a Castle with its territory, and even if they are granted both high and low jurisdiction <note>Latin: *mixtum & merum Imperium*; the authority to preside over civil and criminal cases, including the power of capital punishment</note>, this does not mean the Public Road is granted to them. These rights include not only jurisdiction over the roads or their repair (which is often a burden rather than a financial benefit to the Treasury), but the entire right and all revenues that depend on public roads, just as Radewicus explains regarding the sovereign right of rivers. Therefore, Accursius is mistaken when he says that public roads belong to whichever city they are in, and when he interprets "granted by law" as meaning local municipal law. For in the chapter *which things are royal*, public roads are assigned to those who hold Sovereign Rights, whether by temporary grant or by formal concession; Sixtinus testifies that this is observed by custom in his work *On Sovereign Rights*.

Furthermore, in Roman law, those roads are properly called "public" which belong to the Roman people. Others are regarded as similar to private property, as noted by Caepolla in *On Rural Servitudes* and Arnisaeus.

This right of Public Roads is so much a part of the Emperor’s Reserved Rights <note>Latin: *Reservata Imperatoris*; rights that only the Emperor can exercise or specifically grant</note> that even those who have been granted high and low jurisdiction, or a Castle with its Territory, do not possess the Sovereign Right over a Public Road without a special concession, as I just cited from Schneidewin. However, it cannot be denied that Princes, Dukes, Counts, Barons, and others to whom such high and low jurisdiction has been granted by the Emperor can exercise jurisdiction on Public Roads: thus, the investigation and punishment of a crime, such as robbery or murder committed on a public road, belongs to them. This is because Jurisdiction has nothing in common with Sovereign Rights, but they differ entirely in their nature.

Since those who travel and carry merchandise on such Public Roads must pay tolls, taxes, and passage fees <note>Latin: *vectigalia, gabellæ ac pedagia*</note> to the Princes who hold the roads, it follows that the security of the roads also belongs to those Princes, so that safety is provided to those traveling. Indeed, if this safety is not provided as it should be, the travelers can legally seek to have the damages they suffered reimbursed by the Prince. This is supported by Mynsinger, Schurff, Gail, Rosenthal, Sixtinus, and Köpen.

<column-break/>

decision 37, number 4. Saxon Law <note>Latin: *Jus Saxonicum*; one of the most important legal codes of the Holy Roman Empire</note> agrees in *Book 2, Article 27*, where it says: "To whomsoever he gives safe-conduct, he shall protect from harm, or compensate him for the loss." <note>Original German: *Wem er Geleit giebt, den soll er vor Schaden bewahren, oder ihme den Schaden gelten.*</note>

Indeed, it is also decreed in the Constitutions of the Empire that the local magistrates must keep all roads under their authority safe at their own expense, prohibit violence and robbery, and pursue highwaymen. The Imperial Circles <note>Administrative groupings of states within the Holy Roman Empire</note> should have their bandit-hunters ready to pacify and scout the roads whenever necessary, according to the *Imperial Recess of 1548* and *1555*. See also Freher’s notes on Peter von Andlo, where he discusses bandit-hunters and warns them not to be corrupted—a point on which Ausonius mocks Theon in his *5th Epistle*:

->Or while performing greater deeds, do you pursue the thieves<-
->Wandering through the whole region? They who, fearing the worst from you,<-
->Might call you to share in the loot. You, mild and an eater<-
->Of human blood, forgive crimes for coins.<-
->You call it an error, and set a price for the driven-off<-
->Cattle, and from a Judge, you cross over to a partner in crime.<-

John of Salisbury testifies in *Book 5, chapter 15* that this type of justice is called "errant" <note>Latin: *errantes*; traveling or wandering judges</note> among the English.

However, this is not observed as strictly as it should be, except when "Safe-conduct Money" <note>German: *Geleit-Geld*</note> is specifically paid to the Lord for protection, as those flocking to or departing from fairs <note>Latin: *Nundinarum*</note> usually do.

If a murder is committed on a public road—on a common, open highway <note>German: *an einer gemeinen offenen Landstraßen*</note>—who has the right to investigate and punish? Is it the Lord who owns the public road by virtue of Sovereign Rights, or the one who possesses the fief or castle there with high and low jurisdiction? On this, see Speckhan.

It cannot be occupied by any individual, even through long-term use <note>Latin: *praescriptio*; a legal claim based on long-standing possession</note>; otherwise, a restorative or reintegrating injunction is granted against the occupant. *Book 2, final reference, chapter 16.* Roads and territories must be kept secure by the communities; otherwise, they are held liable for damages. *Book 3, reference 24, throughout.* Public roads, called <term>common army and country roads</term> <note>German: *gemeine Heer- und Landstrassen*</note>, are in our law also called royal, military, praetorian, and consular roads (*Law 2, § 22, regarding things in public places*), because it pertains primarily to the Prince, or to the one to whom he has granted this right, to repair, fortify, and keep the public roads in good condition. <term>Mr. Doctor Ludwig in *Synopsis of Fiefs*, chapter 13.</term> <term>Gothofredus Antonii, *Disputation on Fiefs* 3, thesis 7, letter c.</term> refers to public roads among the "lesser" Sovereign Rights; for although public roads serve the prominence of the Empire more than the profit of the treasury, <term>Gothofredus Antonii</term> does not mean the physical body of the road itself—which belongs to the people—but rather the proceeds from tolls; not the territory or jurisdiction, but those fees collected from travelers. <term>G. But how do we reconcile <term>Pomponius</term> with <term>Suetonius</term>? For <term>Pomponius</term> says this happened at the same time, that is, in that ancient period of the free Republic? Yet <term>Suetonius</term> says <term>Augustus</term> devised this as a new duty in *chapter 37*: "He devised new offices: the care of public works, of roads, and of waters." The learned <term>Lipsius</term>, in his notes on <term>Tacitus's *Annals*, Book 3</term>, explains that the "Overseers" must be distinguished from the "Board of Four." For when those ancient four men (whom <term>Pomponius</term> mentions here, or whom <term>Varro</term> calls the *Viocuri* <note>Road-curators</note>) were not enough, two more were added to make a "Board of Six," as <term>Dio</term> indicates. Later, "Extraordinary Overseers" were found, whom they assigned to individual roads. Thus <term>Plutarch</term> says <term>Caesar</term> was the Overseer of the Appian Way, and <term>Cicero</term> says <term>Thermus</term> was Overseer of the Flaminian Way. Therefore, <term>Augustus</term> made the duty of these Overseers—which was previously neither permanent nor fixed—into a certain and permanent office. These are the people our ancestors left behind when they conquered the lands, according to the legal decision <note>original: *Bescheid*</note> *item and German gloss on the word.* There they left the peasants <note>Latin: *Bauren*; referring to the agricultural class</note> *see article 44, book 3; see also* Herman Stamm, *On Bondmen <note>original: "de hominib. propriis"</note>, chapter 1, number 2.* Also my own work *On the Types of Domestic Tribal Societies, leaf 31.* They have a certain affinity with the ancient "surrendered freedmen" <note>Latin: *Libertinis dedititiis*; a class of former slaves who had surrendered in war and were freed but lacked full citizenship</note>, according to Friedrich Husanus in his *Treatise on Bondmen, chapter 2, number 29.* 

Histories teach us that in those times when the Saxons waged war against the <term>Obotrites</term> <note>A confederation of West Slavic tribes in modern-day Northern Germany</note> and neighboring peoples to compel those unwilling to embrace the Christian religion, they used the same law against the conquered that victors were anciently accustomed to: namely, they held them in the place of <term>chattel slaves</term> <note>Latin: *mancipiorum*</note>. Nevertheless, in the same manner that the Spaniards treated the subjugated Saracens, they left the lands to be cultivated by them, so that the province would not be reduced to a wilderness and become fruitless to the victors themselves. Whatever they left to such "surrendered" people, the <term>Right of Ownership</term> <note>Latin: *Jure Dominii*</note> nonetheless remained with the lords, so much so that the nobles and prefects are able to expel them and take the land back for themselves. *See* Pontanus, *Origins of the Franks, book 6, chapter 15.*

Or they are called *Lazzi*, because they were released from slaughter <note>German: *lassen*</note>; from which also *Lassafare*—"to let go"—crept into the Italian language as a trace of the old Gothic-Germanic tongue, which Lazius enumerates in *On the Migration of Nations, book 9, at the end of page 552*. Thus, those enslaved to service in exchange for the sparing of their lives were called <term>Ministerials</term> <note>Low-born officials or knights who served a lord</note> and <term>bondmen</term> <note>German: *Dienst und Eigenleut*</note>. Knichen, *in the Encyclopedia, chapter 1, near the end.*

Today, under <term>Saxon Law</term> <note>The *Sachsenspiegel*, the most important legal code of the German Middle Ages</note>, the *Lassen* are equated with freedmen. Whence, as Köpen testifies in *book 1, observation 171, number 2*, in many places it is the custom that the lords and noblemen, after the death of their subjects whom they call the *Lassen*, if no heir is born of their body, take their goods entirely, or a half, or a third part, or a specific portion thereof, according to the local opportunity and tradition.

### 23. The Latin Language. Lingua Latina.

On the origin of the Latin language, *see* Becman, *in the Manual, chapters 5 and 9, and in Origins, leaf 136.* Selden records that it was once very obscure, *On the Syrian Gods, page 59*, just like the Germanic tongue; *see my own work, Treatise on the Nature of Peoples.*

Leonhardus Aretinus believes that even in the time of Cicero, the common people spoke differently than they wrote, *book 6, letter leaf 273.* But Floridus Sabinus refutes this in Gruter's *Lampade, volume 1, page 1084; see also* Poggio, *Convivial Histories, 3.*

However, I have said before that the dialect of the rustics was different, *in my Treatise on the Growth of Empires, leaf 63.* From this, the Latins themselves (as the Italians do today, according to Bembo in *Prose in the Italian Tongue*) learned their language. Julius Bellus, *in the Political Hermes on Travel, leaf 59 and following*, where he has more on the Latin language. This language was later changed, and ancient, upright words were abolished: Seneca, *Letter 59*, while it was being spread too widely; namely into Africa, Gaul, Spain, etc. Even Germany was not ignorant of it, but later it was completely abolished by barbarian incursions. Thus Sidonius Apollinaris says in *Letter 17 of Book 4, to Arbogastes*: "The pomp of the Roman speech, if any still exists anywhere, though long since abolished in the lands of the Belgians or the Rhine, resides in you alone." It remained for a time in the Gauls, but shortened and corrupted, whence it is called <term>Rustic Roman</term> <note>The vernacular "vulgar" Latin that evolved into the Romance languages</note>. Pasquier, *7, Research, chapter 1.* Finally, in Italy as well, it was changed into the common idiom: roughly around the time of Gregory the Great, a truly holy Pope. Fauchet, *volume 1 of Antiquities, book 5, chapter 2.* The same happened in the Gauls and Spain, as well as Britain. It receded further from Latin where there was a greater abundance of those who flooded those regions; *see my treatise, On the Nature of Peoples and the Mutation of Languages.* And how the Latin language was changed is taught in the *Explanation of the Heliacal Table.*

Did the Romans speak in Latin? *See* Verdier, *Diverse Lessons, leaf 89 and* Barthius, *Adversaria, book 12, chapter 2, and also book 52, chapter 19.*

### 24. Lay Brothers. <note>Latin: *Fratres Laici*</note>

Lay brothers, or converts, when they solemnly promise the three essential vows <note>poverty, chastity, and obedience</note> according to a Rule approved by the Apostolic See, into the hand of a Prelate capable of incorporating them, are truly "Religious" <note>in the legal sense of belonging to a monastic order</note> and ecclesiastical persons. However, if they are promoted to Holy Orders without the license of their Prelate, they are to be punished with the heaviest penalty and deprived of their clerical tonsure. Furthermore, they should be deprived of any use of the Orders and the recitation of the Divine Office, and be reduced back to the mere lay state. *Compendium of Regular Questions by Manuel Rodriguez, under the word "Laici."*

->ADDITION<-

### 26. Land Registers. <note>Latin: *Catastri*; German: *Lagerbücher*</note>

See my work in the *Disputations on the Municipal Law of Württemberg, part 1, theorem 69.*

Regarding the "location book" <note>original: *Lagenbuch*</note>, see those cited by Wehner in *Practical Observations, pages 58 and 61.* The Lord's or the City's location book, tax book, rolls, or registers. Regarding tax registers, *Rudinger, Century 4, observation 41.* There is one book in which only non-feudal goods are described, and another in which nothing other than feudal matters are found. The feudal lord is obliged to hand over to his vassal <note>original: *Lehenmann*</note> and his feudal agnates <note>blood relatives on the father's side</note> the documents belonging to the fief, and those concerning the fief's parts, appurtenances, and boundaries, such as bills of sale, feudal books, land registers, records, and evidence. *Rosenthal, On Fiefs, chapter 8, conclusion 33, number 1 and following.* This takes place not only in new fiefs but also in old ones. *Rosenthal, conclusion 33, numbers 1 and 4 in the note to letter b; Knipschild, On the Obligations of the Lord toward the Vassal, question 1, number 44.* **Land Registers** are books in which estates and manors, fields, vineyards, meadows, gardens, and houses are circumscribed—how they lie, where, and against whom they border—with their boundaries, ends, locations, and neighbors noted down, as is usually done in the Renewals <note>official surveys or updates of land rights</note> of the Lords,

It is customary to re-describe fiefs or rent-paying estates and to renovate the land registers <note>original: *Lagerbücher*</note> every 10 or 11 years, on account of the changed names of the owners <note>original: *propter mutata nomina possessorum*</note>. Wehner discusses this in his *Practical Observations, page 61.* A wise and sensible lord once complained that he had often followed Wehner’s advice and re-described one of his tithe-lands because of the changed names of the owners, securing it at great expense. However, this frequently renewed tithe-description caused him more legal disputes than his other tithe-land, which had not been described for over a hundred years. Therefore, one should proceed with caution regarding new descriptions.

### 27. Fiefs. *Feuda.*

To some, the word for fief <note>original: *Lehen*</note> seems to derive its origin from *Leudis* or *Leodibus*. By this name, vassals are called—that is, the "Faithful"—from the French word *Leaux* or *Loyaux*, or perhaps more likely from the German *Leut* <note>meaning "people"</note>. Cujacius discusses this in his *prolegomena on feudal matters*. However, it seems more correct to me that it comes from the verb "to lend" <note>original: *leihen*; in the Saxon language *lehnen*</note>, by which we signify the granting of a thing for some use, whether it be a loan for use <term>commodatum</term>, a permissive occupancy <term>precarium</term>, or a loan for consumption <term>mutuum</term>. One may gather how much difference there is between these from the *Institutes of Justinian*. For a Fief <term>feudum</term> is granted to a vassal for a certain use, although that use is much fuller and better than a simple servitude, use, or usufruct. *Rittershusius, in Partibus Feudalibus, chapter 1, book 1, number 14.*

Opposed to fiefs or feudal estates <note>original: *Lehengütern*</note> are allodial lands <note>original: *Allodia*</note>, which are free hereditary estates <note>original: *Frey-Erbgüter*</note>. An allod is each person’s own free patrimony or property, which someone holds from no one and recognizes no superior for, except God. *Molinaeus, on the Customs of Paris; Decianus, responses.* It is called an allod <note>original: *Allodium*</note>—see Lindenbrog under the word *Alode*—as if it were "not recognized from elsewhere" <note>original: *quasi aliunde non recognitum*</note>, according to Albericus de Rosate, though this is not entirely pleasing. Rather, *Allodium* would seem to be called *alaudium*, from the fact that those who hold estates by that right have no author or superior Lord whom they are able or bound to "praise" <note>original: *laudare*, a play on the word *alaudium*</note>. *Budaeus on the Customs of Paris; see above under the word Allodium.*

And Hotoman, in his *Feudal Lexicon, page 632*, thinks *Allodium* is named from the German word *an-löden*, which means to solder or glue together. This is because allodial goods are so joined and coherent to a family that they cannot be torn away from it, being as it were inseparable. In contrast, fiefs are easily lost for various reasons. Add to this Rittershusius, where he cites the *Commentary on the laws of Charlemagne*.

The German word *Lehen*, however, we express through the word *Feudum* <note>Fief</note>, about which word one may

<column-break/>

consult Goldast’s *Alamannic Affairs, volume 1, page 210.* In the old days, it was called *Veoden*. And what is that among the Scots? See the *Laws of Scotland, folio 3, verso.*

Regarding the origin of fiefs, my brother of blessed memory, Johannes Georgius Besold, delivered a singular Oration, which is joined to the *Tubingen disputations printed by Eberhard Wildius.* I have also seen a Diploma given to the Monastery of Lindau by the Emperor Louis in the year 866, where mention is already made of Fiefs. And Fauchet reports that Emperor Louis the Pious gave small fiefs to his soldiers; he treats the origin of fiefs at length in *On Dignities* and Pasquier in *Researches*. See also the notes on the *Formulas of Marculphus*, Pilo Soacius in his *Feudal Preludes*, and Caspar à Lerch on the *German Knightly Order*.

But the opinion of Lord Rittershusius seems most true: that the institution of fiefs is Germanic, introduced not only by the Lombards (who, having set out from Germany, entered Italy and occupied that part which is today called Lombardy), but also already by other peoples of Germany, such as the Alemanni, Franks, Bavarians, Swabians, and Saxons, and even the Goths, as Hotoman wishes. For all these peoples contributed eagerly to the adornment of this "Pandora’s box" <note>an allusion to Hesiod’s myth, suggesting many sources contributed to the final form of feudal law</note>. I, however, would exclude the Goths, since today there are no fiefs in Spain and Portugal. *Ludovicus Molina, treatise on Justice and Law.*

Arguments for this are that historians of German affairs are almost the only ones who make mention of fiefs. For, although the Italians and French are also found to have used fiefs, you should know they received them from the Germans when the Lombards occupied part of Italy and the Franks occupied part of Gaul. For the useful and praiseworthy institutions of any nation are easily drawn into example and adopted into the customs of other peoples. You have an example in the *emphyteusis* <term>emphyteusis: a long-term Roman land lease</term>, or tax-paying fields. The Romans seem to have borrowed this kind of contract from the Byzantines.

Furthermore, the Germanic origin of Fiefs is sufficiently proven by the feudal names themselves and the formulas, which are for the most part Germanic; although certain words today are scarcely understood by the Germans themselves. See my work *On the Nature of Peoples, page 102* (where I reduced them to their true, that is, Germanic origin). This is less to be wondered at here on account of their antiquity; since the same happened to the later Romans regarding the language in which the Royal laws and the Twelve Tables had been written. This difficulty and obscurity of words also happens to us because they are often wonderfully corrupted when they are poured into another language, and when they are accommodated to Latin custom and endings.

It argues that the feudal system is fundamentally Germanic in origin, distinguishing it from allodial (freehold) property and tracing its spread through Europe via the Lombards and Franks.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins and nature of fiefs (feuda), specifically focusing on their military origins and their evolution into hereditary titles within the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

Letter L.
Eeee 3
<page-num>589</page-num>

The first and most ancient cause of this institution seems to have been that Princes might attach to themselves beneficiaries whose military service they could use in expeditions whenever the need arose. In this way, they would have what was effectively a permanent army, and the reward and incentive for this service were certain estates granted to them, from which the **Vassals** <note>original: *Vasalli*</note> could honorably support and maintain themselves. It is for this reason that vassals are so often called **Soldiers** <note>original: *Milites*</note> in the *Books of Fiefs* <note>The *Libri Feudorum*, a 12th-century collection of feudal laws.</note>.

This is also the best method for preserving newly acquired territories, as my brother explained in the aforementioned speech, and as I discuss in my treatise *On the Increases of the Empire* near the end. These are similar to the **Timars** <term>Timariæ; land grants given by the Ottoman Sultans in exchange for military service</term> of the Turks. Even the Japanese are not ignorant of this institution, according to Molina in *On Justice and Law*, volume 2, dispute 485. Moreover, it is probable that the German Princes who occupied either Gaul or Italy granted the lordships of the conquered nations to illustrious men of their own race to strengthen the rule for themselves, their descendants, and their people. On this, see Vincentius Cabotius, *Legal Disputes*, book 2, final chapter. 

Indeed, from the historians of German affairs, as well as from the constitutions of certain Emperors and German Kings, it is quite clear that among other reasons, fiefs were also given to both Bishops and laymen so that the ruler would have many **Companions** <note>original: *Comites*, the root of the word "Counts"</note> and associates for expeditions. This was especially true for the **Roman Expedition** <note>original: *Romana expeditio*</note>, which they undertook to seek the **Golden Crown** from the Roman Pontiff, after they had already received the **Iron Crown** at Aachen and the **Silver Crown** at Milan. For in ancient times, they were crowned in these three places. 

After crossing the Alps, before proceeding directly to Rome, they used to gather at **Roncaglia** <note>original: *Romaliis*; the Roncaglian fields near Piacenza</note> and pitch camp. There they would hold assemblies for several days and deliberate and decide with the Princes of the Empire regarding law and legislation, peace and war, and the entire Commonwealth. Any who held benefits from the Emperor were required to be present in those fields and camps. If, when summoned by the voice of the herald to the muster, they did not respond or perform their sentry duties around the Emperor, they were deprived of their fiefs for **contumacy** <term>legal term for stubborn disobedience or failure to appear in court</term>, whether they were clergy or laymen—unless, by chance, they had obtained permission to remain at home. See on this matter Otto of Freising, book 2, chapter 12, and Gunther at the start of book 2. This is commonly called the **Roman Expedition** <note>original: *Römerzug*</note>. This, I say, appears to have been the first occasion and cause for instituting fiefs: that there might be certain military benefits and "sinews" by which the German Empire might be held together and flourish. But afterward (as usually happens), the practice began to spread more widely; fiefs were granted not only for military duties but also for other honorable offices to be performed in peace.

Furthermore, this pertains to the origin of Fiefs: just as in the past **testamentary trusts** <term>fideicommissa; property held by one person for the benefit of another</term> were very weak in their early days—their first cradles depending only on the "faith" or honesty of the heirs—they were later more and more confirmed and reduced to the necessity of Law, as the Emperor witnesses in the *Institutes*, "On testamentary trusts."

<column-break/>

So too, the beginnings of Fiefs were very thin and weak, but gradually the institution grew from a meager start. The Feudalist elegantly declares this in the first book of the *Books of Fiefs*.

Furthermore, regarding the birth and growth of Fiefs, there is a memorable passage in **Nicholas of Cusa**, the Cardinal (who lived at the time of the Council of Basel), in chapter 28, book 3 of *On Catholic Concord* <note>original: *De Concordia Catholica*</note>. I will recite it here, as it illustrates the aforementioned point quite well. He says: 

"Even then, the appointed Princes, Dukes, and Counts were ordained to hold their positions as public offices by Imperial command, removable at the Emperor's will, and were required to give an account of their ministry to the Public Treasury. After this—because the sons of Senators, though they were initially only of the Equestrian rank, eventually reached the Senate—it was introduced that if the parents conducted themselves properly in office, the sons would not be deprived of that same office. This was done so that fathers would be less inclined toward greed, having certainty of their succession in office, and also so that their subjects would be less burdened by the father when they knew his own descendants were to rule over them. 

However, so that no disadvantages harmful to the Emperor's domains would arise for the Imperial Majesty from the future growing power of these officials, **Feudal Statutes** were introduced, along with the strictest oaths of maintaining loyalty. These had to be sworn by every person being established as a Vassal and kept inviolably under penalty of losing the Fief. Finally, another law was issued: that no one could succeed to multiple great fiefs cumulatively. This was to prevent the power of subjects from growing so great through such accumulation that they might—in a tyrannical rage and unmindful of their oaths—seek the summit of ruling (the appetite for which grows by acquisition), thereby cheapening the power of the Empire through schismatic turmoil. 

Moreover, it was the custom of the Emperors to admit accusations of broken faith and perjury, so that loyalty—through which alone the Empire persists—should never be undervalued through negligence. The penalty for one who did not keep their faith was deprivation of the fief. And then, lest envy perhaps incite a nobleman of the same blood against the person to whom these confiscated goods were given, the sacred Emperors frequently granted those lapsed estates to the Churches, etc."

Fiefs, especially those with an attached title of dignity, were not at all hereditary from the beginning; rather, this was introduced later by custom. Master Rittershusius assigns the reasons for this in *Feudal Divisions*, book 1, chapter 12. However, **Hotman** <note>François Hotman (1524–1590), a famous French legal scholar</note>, in his *Feudal Disputations*, chapter 18, rebukes this custom so severely that he exclaims nothing more absurd could be said. And indeed, the authority of the Emperors is lesser because of it. Emperor **Frederick I** <note>Frederick Barbarossa</note>, in the section "Furthermore concerning Duchies," book 2, title 55, prohibits the feudal dignities of the Empire from being divided among several co-heirs, and thus he seems to approve the custom that they should pass to a single successor, for example...

There is an excellent passage on this matter by Nicholas of Cusa in *On Catholic Concordance, book 8, chapter 28.* From this observation, we learn that the condition of **Prefectures** <term>Præfecturarum; high-ranking administrative or military offices</term> and Public Offices in the German Empire was once not unlike that which exists today among the **Pashas and Beys in Turkey** <note>original: *Bassarum & Begorum in Turcia*</note>, and in the Polish Kingdom among the **Palatines and Castellans** <note>High-ranking regional governors and military commanders</note>. Today, says Hotman in his notes *on title 1, book 1*, in our France, all Magistrates are commissioned by the King with this formula: **"as long as it shall please us."** <note>original: *quamdiu nobis placebit*</note>

Regarding **allodial** <term>allodialibus; land owned outright by an individual, rather than held as a fief from a lord</term> goods mixed with **feudal** ones, and the proof thereof, see *Surdus, counsel 180, throughout*; and are all goods within the district of a Feudal territory considered Feudal? See *Schwanman, counsel 4.* "How and in what manner are Fiefs and Private Property to be separated from one another?" <note>original German: *Wie und was gestalten Lehens und Eigens von einander zu separiren?*</note> This is demonstrated most extensively in the *Marburg Counsels, volume 4, counsel 37; add Graeven, book 2, conclusion 62.*

In France, although commoners of the people are considered no less capable than Nobles of holding feudal goods that come to them through **lawful succession** <note>original: *successione legitima*</note>; however, regarding a new acquisition of a fief by any title other than lawful succession, it is attested by Grivellus in *Decisions of Dole, 32, number 2*, that something else has always been observed in Burgundy. For he adds that no commoner was ever permitted to acquire or possess a fief unless this was granted to him by the indulgence and liberality of the Prince.

### Your Serene Highness, etc.

Whereas Your Princely Grace sent me a copy a few days ago of a **Petition** <note>original: *Supplication*</note> by which the family of M., through a mere concealment and misrepresentation of facts, has presumed to obtain from His Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, a **Mandate to restore and no longer disturb** <note>original: *Mandatum de restituendo & non amplius turbando*</note> without a clause against Your Princely Grace regarding the entire matter of the claimed loss of possession of the Castle and Village of N.; along with a letter from the aforementioned most high Imperial Majesty to Your Princely Grace graciously requesting better information and a report, you have graciously

<column-break/>

passed these to me, and thereby commanded that within a set time, I—as the rightful holder of the indicated castle and village and because of my interest in this place—should submissively send my necessary professional opinion to Your Princely Grace’s Chancery.

Regarding such gracious communication, I first offer my most obedient thanks and submissively report how, first of all, I have heard with great wonder that the family of M. (who claim to be Your Princely Grace's **Vassals** <note>original: *Lehenleut*</note>) have slandered Your Princely Grace quite unkindly and with great disparagement, not only in previous extrajudicial claims but also before Electors and Princes (where they obtained strong intercessions through inaccurate accounts), accusing you of doing them the highest injustice—an accusation clearly without foundation. Yet they have in no way found themselves satisfied with this, but have furthermore presumed to persist in such clearly inaccurate insinuations in their aforementioned petition to His Roman Imperial Majesty, as the highest Justice and most eminent authority in all of Christendom.

Yet they should rightly take to heart that toward Your Princely Grace, whom they acknowledge as their **feudal Lord** <note>original: *Lehenherrn*</note>, they ought to use greater modesty, as **Rosenthal warns in *On Fiefs, chapter 12, conclusion 11, number 43*** <note>original: *monente Rosenthalio de feud. cap. 12. conclus. 11. num. 43.*</note>, and they should rightly remember **that for atrocious or dishonorable verbal injuries by a Vassal against a Patron, the fief is lost, and it can be reclaimed by the Lord, and thus can much more easily be retained by him** <note>original: *quod ob atroces vel inhonestas injurias verbales Vasalli in Patronum, feudum amittatur...* citing Schrader and Vultejus</note>.

And this likewise holds true, even if the insult which the Vassal charges against the Lord of the fief were true: since even he who defames someone with a true insult is held liable for injuries. <note>original: *Cum & is, qui vero convitio aliquem infamat, injuriarum teneatur...* citing Covarruvias and Cravetta</note>.

In view of this, it is also commonly taught that a **Vassal** <note>original: *Vasallum*</note> cannot call his Lord into court without prior permission. <note>original: *sine prævia venia Dominum in jus vocare non posse...* citing Everhard, Jason, and others</note>.

Indeed, His Roman Imperial Majesty found the highly offensive accusations to be of such importance and so weighty that His Majesty could in no way believe Your Princely Grace capable of such injustice as the family of M. have complained of; rather, he most graciously and laudably deemed it a necessity to write to Your Princely Grace for the submission of proper information and a report before His Imperial Majesty's final resolution and declaration.

Secondly, I find this petition of M. so composed that it is framed with particular advantage to themselves—namely, to make Your Princely Grace’s actions and this whole matter all the more odious—suggesting that the family of M. once held possession of this feudal castle and village...

<meta>This page continues the legal defense of a territorial lord’s right to reclaim a fief (a land grant) after the death of the last occupant, Hans Melchior von M., arguing against the claims of distant relatives who seek to recover the property through a simplified legal mandate.</meta>

<page-num>591</page-num>
<header>Lit. L. 591</header>

<column-break/>

They claim to have obtained the property, but were supposedly removed and driven out from it; for this reason, they seek a "mandate for restitution and against further offense." <note>original: *mandat de restituendo, & non amplius offendendo*</note> **This presupposes a possessory action for recovery and a complaint regarding "spoliation"** <note>original: *possessorium recuperandæ & quærelam de spolio*; "spoliation" refers to the wrongful deprivation of possession</note>. Yet it can never be proven that the petitioners, after the death of their cousin Hans Melchior von M. (the last possessor), ever attained actual possession (or even the appearance of possession) of these fiefs. Rather, it can be demonstrated immediately and *in the present moment* <note>original: *in continenti*</note> that Your Princely Grace had the aforementioned goods seized as an "opened fief" <note>A fief that has reverted to the lord because the line of succession ended or was forfeited</note>, and thus obtained possession of them **without any fault—namely, not by force, not secretly, and not by request.** <note>original: *sine omni vitio, ac nempe nec vi, nec clam, nec precario*; these are the standard Roman law requirements for valid possession</note>

**It is, moreover, the right of the Lord that when he finds no one else in possession, he may, on his own authority, seize the property as vacant.** <note>Citing legal authorities: Baldus, Decius, and Menochius</note> **And regarding the Lord of a fief: that he can occupy a fief opened to him on his own authority when no one else is in possession,** as taught by Tiraquellus <note>original: *tract. de morte...*</note>, Ferrari <note>original: *in form. libelli...*</note>, and it is the common doctrine of those repeating the law on how possession is acquired. <note>original: *Menoch. remed. adipiscend.*</note>

From which, thirdly, it follows quite clearly that even if the opponents wished to interpret their request as an "action to obtain possession" <note>original: *Possessorium adipiscendæ*</note>, they could in no way succeed with it—much less come into possession of these goods **by way of a summary order and without a prior ordinary trial**, nor could they even initiate an ordinary possessory remedy or turn this into a case for a mandate.

**For the common opinion is that the legal remedies for obtaining possession do not apply against a Lord who possesses a fief without fault,** according to the interpreters of feudal law <note>original: *in cap. 1. si de feud. defunct.*</note> and Rosenthal.

Fourthly, the von M. family could not succeed with the mandate process for this reason as well: they must sue in the proper and ordinary manner because they have not proven that they undoubtedly descend **from the "First Acquirer"** <note>original: *à primo Acquirente*</note>—that is, from those von M. ancestors who were granted this castle and the village of N. as a fief 300 years ago. They must first prove this clearly; otherwise, they can achieve nothing in either a **"Petitory" action** <note>a lawsuit based on the right of ownership</note> or a **"Possessory" action** <note>a lawsuit based on the fact of possession</note>.

An ordinary trial is undoubtedly required for such proof, and as the von M. family failed to provide this in their extra-judicial submission to Your Princely Grace—despite how hard they tried—it will be equally difficult for them to perform this in the future, **especially since we are dealing with a very ancient matter.**

Furthermore, fifthly, it is correct that the current von M. claimants—even according to their own family tree—are related to the last deceased possessor of the

<column-break/>

disputed fief much further than the **seventh degree, according to the calculation of Civil Law.** In such a case, feudal laws do not allow for succession. **For whether a fief passes immediately to collateral relatives, or was first passed down to descendants (after whose removal it is transferred to the agnates), in the past, agnates and collateral relatives only succeeded up to the fourth degree; later, a new law was introduced so that a fief could reach the seventh degree.** <note>original: *c. un. §. hoc quoque sciendum...*; "agnates" are relatives related through the male line</note>

Sixthly, the von M. family themselves admit in the petition they submitted to His Imperial Majesty that the late Friedrich von M. was deprived of this fief due to an accused **felony** <term>Feloni; in feudal law, a crime or breach of contract by a vassal that results in the forfeiture of their land</term>. Subsequently, through a specially obtained pardon, it was granted to his son Hans Melchior as a **"New Fief"** <note>original: *Feudum Novum*; a new grant that starts a new line of succession, often cutting off distant relatives of the previous holder</note>. And because such a felony constituted **contempt for the Lord**, the aforementioned fief (according to the more frequent opinion of feudal legal experts) reverted to the Lord of the fief. Even if the **agnates** <note>male-line relatives</note> would have had a right at that time in the event of succession, that right was completely cut off and taken from them **through this crime of the possessor.**

**When a vassal commits a fault against the person of the Lord, the Fief reverts freely to the Lord,** as the most recent authorities, such as Antonius Merenda, prove with many arguments while answering opposing views.

And although the petitioners, in the wording of their submission, raise various claims of "unequal circumstances" that supposedly occurred during this deprivation of Johann Friedrich von M., the von M. family does not deny that the oft-mentioned Hans Melchior possessed this fief as a **"New Fief."** Your Princely Grace was **in possession (or quasi-possession) of that right** for many years. By virtue of this, after Hans Melchior died without bodily heirs to the fief, Your Princely Grace could seize the much-mentioned fief **as a New and Open fief in the person of the last possessor**, and could lawfully grant it to me again out of special grace.

It is particularly important to note here that, despite all this—which happened long ago with both Hans Friedrich and his son Hans Melchior, and which was undoubtedly well known to the opponents as a widely publicized fact—they have not yet protested or challenged it in any way. Therefore, it can be even less cancelled now **abruptly** and through a quick mandate process, nor can the petitioners attain possession of this feudal estate, as such a matter requires at the very least **a deeper investigation and a full hearing of the case.**

## 592 Thesauri Practici Adaucti

...knowledge, and thus requires an ordinary Legal Process.

For when the question arises whether a paternal kinsman <note>original: *agnatus*</note> of a deceased Vassal, claiming an ancient fief <note>original: *feudum antiquum*; a fief inherited through a family line</note>, should be placed into possession of it, our Doctors of Law usually teach that the kinsmen claiming the fief is ancient and seeking entry <note>original: *immissio*</note> must be put into possession after the death of the Vassal, even if the Lord objects. However, this rule suffers various limitations; for instance, it is different if the Lord wishes to prove immediately <note>original: *in continenti*</note> and without deep investigation that the fief is actually a "New Fief" <note>original: *feudum novum*; a fief granted specifically to the individual, not his ancestors</note>; in that case, the entry into possession is blocked. *Alvarott. num. 5. Laudens, num. 2. Præposit. num. 2. Afflict. num. 5. Schenck. num. 3. & Ravenn. in cap. 1. regarding the fief of a deceased.*

In this case, however, not only can it be proven immediately that the fief is a New Fief from the most recent Investiture <note>The formal ceremony or document granting the land</note>, but the opposing parties themselves admit that the last Vassal possessed the fief as a New Fief. In such a case, the right to be put into possession entirely ceases. *Isern. in cap. 1. in c. pr. Laudens. num. 5. Præposit. num. 2. Afflict. num. 1. regarding the fief of a deceased.* Here, all authorities assign the reason for this entry to be the possession of the deceased, which descends as if joined to the kinsmen; they argue the Lord should not be heard if he does not deny the fief exists, unless the last deceased held it specifically as a New Fief. This is supported by the writings of *Rosenthal. cap. 11. conclus. 11. n. 34.* where he writes: A petition for possession is based on the fact that the deceased held the Tusculan estate in his possession as an ancient fief at the time of death, and that the claimant is his nearest capable kinsman, etc.

If, therefore, in a case where neither party is in possession, the Lord must be put into possession when the last Vassal held the fief as a New Fief, this should hold even more strongly in the present case. His Serene Highness, the Lord of the Fief, and those who derive their rights from him, must be protected in their possession. This is especially true where not only did the last deceased Vassal possess this village solely by the title of a fief (and thus the adversaries do not claim a title from the most recent Vassal, but from much older ancestors, which they have not yet proven), but also because His Serene Highness took possession of the vacant property without any legal fault many years ago.

For it is also commonly said that a fief is not presumed to be ancient if the Lord, or someone else asserting it is new, is already in possession. Indeed, possession suggests whether a fief is new or ancient depending on what is more useful to the one possessing it, and the burden of proving the contrary is transferred to the opponent, unless the possession was obtained wrongfully. *Jacob de Bellovis. in cap. 1. on the succession of brothers.* This distinction is followed by *Isern. in d. §. si verò num. 5. Afflict. num. 6. Alvarott. num. 3. Alciat. presumption rule 3. num. 2. Menoch. presumption 93. num. 10. book 2. & on judicial arbitration.*

<column-break/>

191. num. 2. and following. And Rosenthal *chapter 2. conclusion 31. num. 4.* rightly warns that some people mistakenly believe that the law allows possession to be taken away from a Lord who already holds it, or that possession should be granted to a Vassal until the end of the full legal trial.

**Seventhly**, it is without doubt that this fief does not depend upon Your Princely Grace’s Duchy of S., nor your Princely County of T., but rather depends upon the County of B. This county, as is again undeniable, is located right in the middle of Alsace, situated between the Lower-Austrian lands belonging to His Imperial Majesty and the noble House of Austria, and the Bishopric of Strasbourg.

Now, however, in these surrounding places, and in both Lower and Upper Alsace, there is a well-known and uninterrupted custom that has been maintained at all times since years immemorial: that **Joint Investiture** <note>original: *Simultanea Investitura*, or *gesamte Hand*; a legal arrangement where multiple family members are formally recognized in a single deed to ensure they can inherit from one another</note> is the practice. Therefore, even if a vassal can prove that he descends from the original recipient <note>original: *à primo acquirente*</note> of the land, he still cannot succeed or follow a relative from a side-branch <note>original: *ex latere*; a cousin or uncle rather than a direct descendant</note> unless he, or at the very least his father, was specifically included or named in the letters of investiture <note>original: *Lehenbriefen*</note>.

And this Custom, although contrary to Common Feudal Law, is nevertheless valid (since all Feudal Law consists of nothing but customs) and is considered to conform to the most ancient customs of the Germans. *Rauchbar. book 2. question 21. Gothofred. Anton. feudal dispute 1. thesis 17. at the end.* It is also considered sufficiently proven—at least by presumption—that such a custom exists in a specific Court if it follows the general custom of the Region and the observations of neighboring places; thus, the burden of proving the contrary is thrown back upon the one who denies it. For the custom of one Province is also applied to a neighboring one. *Raudens. decision part 1. Pisan decision 5. num. 74. & decision 21. num. 4.* where he cites others. And the custom of a neighboring region, especially among those joined in family, is extended to another, *law 'venditor' 13. section 'si constat' of the Digest on common estates. Cravett. counsel 94. num. 5. & counsel 118. num. 3.* Since we must proceed from similar cases to similar cases. *Castrens. counsel 164. num. 2. vol. 7. Purpurat. counsel 326. num. 8. book 1. Raudens, response 1. num. 54. book 2.*

**Eighthly**, I also trust that I can immediately <note>original: *in continenti*</note> provide enough evidence that, specifically within Your Princely Grace’s Lordship of B., various different noble fiefs possess this nature, type, and quality of the aforementioned Joint Investiture. Indeed, many years ago, rulings were issued on this basis, and those who attempted to claim the succession of the fief were at times rejected because they were not named in the letters of investiture.

It is a certain and indubitable rule of Law that in deciding feudal controversies, the **Custom of the Court** <note>original: *Consuetudo Curtis*; the specific rules of the Lord’s own local administration</note> must generally be given more weight than general Feudal Law. *Schrader. part 10.*

### Lit. L.

*Section 7, numbers 17 and following. Chassanaeus confirms this common view in his commentary on the customs of Burgundy, under the section on fiefs, § 7, glossary 2, on the nature of felony <note>original: "felon. naturâ d' iceluy"</note>. See also Molinaeus on the Customs of Paris, title 1, § 7, number 34; Modestinus Pistoris, Consultation 59, number 48 at the end.*

*It is likewise established that a judicial custom is established by two similar acts, and thereafter it is said to be customary and usual to judge in that manner. Citing Bartolus on the law regarding alimony; Vincentius de Franchis, Decision 238, number 3; Rugerius, Consultation 38, number 30; Fabius de Anania, Consultation 61, number 70.*

**Ninthly**, the four ancient fief-letters <note>Documents proving the grant of a fief and its conditions</note>, which the opponents attached as copies to their most humble petition submitted to your Imperial Majesty, clearly show that this specific fief was governed by **Simultaneous Investiture** <note>original: "Simultaneam Investituram"; a legal arrangement where multiple family members or branches are invested with a fief together to ensure mutual succession rights</note>. For this purpose, it is expressly stated in these fief-letters—not only in the first one but also in each subsequent one—and the names are listed of those who should be eligible to receive the fief in any future vacancy.

But it is especially important to observe in two of the fief-letters that this fief was granted each time according to the custom and tradition of the Lordship of V., from which the fief originates. These words, *and this special and clear provision must be interpreted and understood in such a way that it requires something singular and different from common Feudal Law, as this was introduced and agreed upon regarding this Fief.*

Now, however, regarding the noble fiefs of the County of V., one would know of nothing else to name *that would deserve such a singular, special, and carefully considered provision* other than precisely this **Simultaneous Investiture**.

Furthermore, it is a fact, and the opponents themselves cannot deny it, that even if they should descend *from the first ancestor* <note>original: "à primo stipite"</note>, the line from which Hans Friederich and Hans Melchior descended was separated from the line of the current petitioners many years ago, *both in terms of persons and property*. This separation was such that Friederich and Melchior's ancestors completely omitted and passed over the others in the aforementioned fief-letters.

*But truly, even if one holds a Simultaneous Investiture in the highest degree, if he nevertheless wishes to retain it and eventually enjoy the right of succession, it is necessary that—as often as the possession of the fief is interrupted, either by the death of the Lord or the death of the Vassal and possessor—he must petition for the Investiture to be renewed for himself within a year and a day from the time he learns of the vacancy.* This means that he "petitions for the fief" <note>original: "die Lehen muetet"</note> and seeks investiture again. *Pruckmann, Consultation 39, number 120; Zanger, on exceptions, part 3, chapter 26, number 252 and 327 (where he testifies that this was the response given by the Lay Judges of Leipzig and also by the Faculty of Law at the University of Tübingen on May 11, 1603); Hartmann Pistoris, book 2, question 20, number 32; Schurff, Consultation 16, number 1 and following, century 1; Besold, Volume I.*

<column-break/>

*This renewal of Investiture is so strictly required from the person jointly invested that the objection of "failure to renew" can be raised against him not only by the Lord of the fief himself and other kin jointly invested, but even by any third party to whom the fief might have been sold or transferred. In such a case, the claimant cannot reclaim the fief from the possessor through a legal action to revoke the transfer. Hartmann Pistoris, cited question 20, number 33 and following; Zanger, cited part 3, chapter 26, number 247 and following.*

*Therefore, Simultaneous Investiture expires through division. For if several people possessing one and the same fief later divide that fief, they lose the right of Simultaneous Investiture through such a division, and they no longer have the expectation of succeeding one another unless they have taken care to be jointly invested with that new fief. Zanger, cited chapter 26, number 253 and following; Vultejus, book 1 on fiefs, chapter 9, number 106; Schrader, on fiefs, part 7, chapter 1, number 38.*

*Indeed, the right of Simultaneous Investiture is lost through division not only in a "New Fief" but also in an "Ancient Fief." Köpen, Decision 44, number 9, and Decision 47 under number 8; Schneidewin, on fiefs, part 6, number 22.*

*And thus, in feudal matters, "once excluded, is said to be always and perpetually excluded." Chapter 1, paragraph "Because also the Bishop or Abbot"; Cephalus, Consultation 133, number 12; Angelus, Consultation 110, column 3.*

Since it is now, Gracious Prince and Lord, of great importance to Your Princely Grace—not only for the sake of my fief, so that your own dealings may be justified and maintained, and saved from the disrespectful and unkind complaints of the von M. family—but also because it is highly necessary for the County of V. fiefs in general (in my humble estimation) that this practice of **Simultaneous Investiture** be upheld and preserved: therefore, I live in the humble and certain hope that Your Princely Grace will take up this matter with earnestness in all places and be graciously minded to maintain me in such a fief. Especially since no judge, and least of all the Roman Imperial Majesty (since this matter would stand to be settled before his most noble **Imperial Aulic Council** <note>original: "Reichs-Hofrath"; the supreme judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</note>), could find the von M. family's "impetition" <note>A legal challenge or claim</note> and demand to be in accordance with legal equity, for the reasons just heard and many others which shall be further strengthened and introduced by me in due time.

**Tenthly**, however, such a fief does not depend *immediately* <note>Meaning directly, without an intermediary lord</note> upon Your Imperial Majesty, such that it would belong before him and no other judge. Rather, this is a matter to be decided and examined *purely and simply according to Feudal Law and Customs*. In this regard, it belongs neither *in a claim of ownership* <note>original: "in petitorio"</note> nor *in a claim of possession* <note>original: "possessorio"</note> before an Ordinary Judge, but rather before the **Peers of the Court** <note>original: "ad Pares Curiæ"; the equals of the vassal who traditionally judged feudal disputes</note> and before a proper Feudal or Manorial Court, *since in effect the dispute is between a Lord and an alleged Vassal.*

Accordingly, I am submitting to Your Princely Grace the attached humble petition for the opening of such a...

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding which court has jurisdiction over a feudal dispute. The previous page discussed "Simultaneous Investiture" and the specific customs of the Lordship of V. The text transitions from a German explanation of why a specific legal action was taken into a formal Latin legal treatise on the authority of the "Peers of the Court."</meta>

...of such a Feudal Court <note>German: *Lehengerichts*</note>, which I had drawn up quite some time ago, even before I ever knew that the Roman Imperial Majesty might be importuned and approached regarding these matters. Because it was hidden from me then whether they wished to sue or remain silent longer to their own advantage, I wanted to act based on the law *diffamari* <note>original: *ex L. diffamari*; a legal procedure used to force a person who is spreading rumors about a legal claim to either bring the case to court immediately or remain silent thereafter</note>.

For even before the Peers of the Court <note>original: *Paribus Curiæ*; a jury of social equals, typically other vassals of the same lord, who judged feudal disputes</note>, a claim based on that well-known law *diffamari* can be initiated, as noted by Schrader, *part 10, section 5, number 146.*

Nor is there any doubt that if a dispute exists between a Lord and a Vassal, it must be aired before the Peers of the Court, excluding the Ordinary Judge. This applies whether the dispute between Lord and Vassal is a real action, a personal action, a mixed action, an action against a thing, a good-faith action, a strict law action, a Praetorian or Civil action, a property-recovery action, or an action by the Office of the Judge. In all these cases, a dispute moved between a Lord and a Vassal by reason of a fief belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court, as handed down by Antonio de Butrio in his commentary on *c. cæterum, number 8*, and as is the opinion of Hostiensis, Imola, and Egidio Bellamera in the same place.

Nor should it be decided otherwise, even if the dispute is between a Lord and the male-line relatives <note>original: *Agnatos*</note> of a deceased Vassal concerning the succession of a fief. For instance, if the relatives of the deceased Vassal claim that the contested fief is "Ancient" <note>inherited from ancestors</note> and therefore acquired by them by right of succession, while the Lord asserts that the fief is "New" <note>newly granted to the last holder</note> and thus returned to him upon the Vassal's death. This dispute belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court, according to Zasius, *consil. 13, num. 36*, and is sufficiently proven by the text in *c. 1. an apud Judic. vel Cur. Dom.*

And they even extend this to the case where the litigation moved between the Lord and the Vassal is possessory <note>original: *Possessorium*; a legal action concerning who currently holds the land, rather than who has the ultimate legal title</note>. This controversy regarding possession belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court, whether the Vassal acts against the Lord, or conversely, the Lord against the Vassal in a possessory matter. Citing *c. 1. §. si verò Vasallus*, and the doctors on *de milit. Vasall. qui contum.*, Zasius on fiefs, and Menochius on the remedies for retaining possession.

Many of our most excellent German jurists have followed this same opinion: Schurff, Nicolaus Everhardus, Borcholt, and Sixtinus in his work *On Regalities*. Fachinaeus also considers it the common and true view in *7. controvers. 10.*

The jurisdiction belongs to the Ordinary Judge only if the possession is in dispute between two vassals, or between a Lord and a Vassal, and they are debating not through an ordinary possessory judgment, but through what they call a "most summary possessory judgment" <note>original: *judicium possessorium summariissimum*; an expedited legal process for immediate, temporary possession</note>, or "momentary possession," as per Vultejus on fiefs,

<column-break/>

book 2, chapter 2, number 41—a case in which we are clearly not involved.

And this expansion of jurisdiction holds place whether the possessory judgment involves a question of ownership <note>original: *causa proprietatis*</note> or not. In either case, the matter belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court.

Indeed, Rosenthal states in *c. 12. conclus. 12* that everyone agrees: if a feudal possessory case involves a question of ownership or a Petitory question <note>original: *Petitorii*; a legal action to establish a permanent right of ownership</note>, it must be referred to the feudal judge and his court.

But here the Opponents conclude regarding the fief itself; they bring up the fief not incidentally or descriptively, but as their principal argument. Likewise, the exceptions already brought forward and those to be brought forward below precisely concern the fief. Therefore, this present case cannot be handled without a ruling on feudal law, and thus it involves an intertwined question of ownership, which is established as happening always, or at least mostly, in feudal possessory cases. Citing Rosenthal, *d. concl. 12. n. 76. and following.*

All of this also applies whether the remedy is for acquiring, retaining, or even preserving or confirming possession; whether the possessory action is plenary or summary, or whether it is ordinary or extraordinary. Citing Schrader on fiefs, *part 10, sect. 5, num. 143. and following.*

Furthermore, when an action instituted by reason of a fief—either by a Lord against a Vassal or by a Vassal against a Lord—descends from Feudal Laws or Customs, then the dispute without doubt belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court, and indeed **generally and without distinction**. Citing Innocent on *c. cæterum. num. 5.* and Hostiensis, Antonio de Butrio, and Bellamera.

They say this also applies even if the action regarding the fief does not descend from feudal laws or customs, but from Common Law <note>original: *Jure Communi*; the body of Roman-canonical law used across Europe</note>, provided that the matter is handled as a fief. In that case, the controversy belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court, as Innocent, Butrio, Imola, Bellamera, and others judge.

Nothing stands in the way, even if the Vassal says he is a Vassal and the Lord denies this. Nevertheless, the dispute moved between this Vassal and the Lord belongs to the jurisdiction of the Peers of the Court. Citing *cap. 1. de controvers. inter Episcop. & Vasall*, Wurmser, Zasius, and Johannes Blancus.

And certainly, in cases occurring between a Lord and a Vassal, the Peers of the Court possess a jurisdiction that excludes other judges; in the eyes of the law, the jurisdiction of all other judges is considered set aside. Citing Schrader.

on feudal law, section 5, numbers 173 and 177. From this, they conclude that even superior Judges or Magistrates are not permitted to call away <note>Latin: *avocare*; the legal act of a higher court taking a case from a lower court</note> cases belonging to the knowledge of the Peers of the Court and drag them to their own forum.

They say this conclusion is so true that it even applies to the Roman Emperor or another Prince who acknowledges no superior. For it is not customary for him to call away feudal cases belonging to the knowledge or forum of the Peers of the Court: for this reason, that they do not wish those cases or lawsuits—the knowledge of which an inferior acquired through a contract—to be called away and dragged to their own forum, neither for the Roman Emperor nor for other Princes acknowledging no superior. This is supported by Martino da Lodi, chapter 1, number 14; and the Provost near the end regarding the controversy between the Bishop and the Vassal; and Schrader in the said section 5, number 180 and many following.

And although the Imperial power is great, and it is established that the Prince is released from the laws <note>Latin: *legibus solutam*; the doctrine that the sovereign is not bound by civil law</note> (*Law "Princeps" 31, Paragraph "ff. de leg."*), he nevertheless is not accustomed to using this absolute and extraordinary power without a great and rational cause.

And indeed, the Prince is released from the Laws conditionally—namely, for a certain cause and for the sake of public safety. Therefore, things given conditionally ought to cease when the condition does not occur—that is, when public safety does not demand it (Raudensis, *On Analogy*, chapter 37, number 4).

And specifically in our case, the often-praised Schrader teaches in section 5, number 279, that even cases or lawsuits moved between the Lord of a fief and the Vassals by reason of a simultaneous investiture <note>original: *simultaneæ Investituræ*; a legal arrangement where several people are invested with a fief at once, often ensuring the right of succession for secondary heirs</note> belong entirely to the knowledge of the Peers of the Court.

### Statement of Facts

Be it known that when Lord Ferdinand von E., etc., passed away on January 6th, 1610, without legitimate bodily heirs, his two surviving sisters—Lady Maria, widowed Countess of R., and Lady Eleonora, both born von E., etc.—inherited their brother's personal estate *ab intestato* <note>Latin: "from the intestate"; inheriting from someone who died without a will</note> (which included half of the Lordship of S.). They then most humbly petitioned Emperor Rudolph, of most Christian memory, for the granting of the feudal Imperial Fiefs of said Lordship, namely the Market Rights, the Court, the Stocks and Gallows, together with the Ban to judge over blood in the village of T. They based this on the foundation that such Imperial Fief pieces are specifically attached to the property, both by virtue of ancient tradition and by the Imperial Privilege granted to the Knighthood in Swabia in 1610, and are thus hereditary and alienable to qualified outsiders.

However, they encountered strong resistance from the then Imperial Prosecutor <note>original: *Reichs-Fiscal*; the official responsible for protecting the financial and feudal interests of the Emperor</note> (whose arguments and evidence they could never see or receive via copies). The Prosecutor pretended—as was only learned a year and a half ago from fragmented communication of his writings—that the family von E. had been newly invested with such fief pieces as a "Right Fief" <note>original: *feudo Recto*; a standard military fief with strict rules of succession, rather than an inherited property right</note> due to a previous grant, and that these rights had therefore escheated <note>returned to the Emperor's ownership</note> upon the unannounced death of the purchaser from the von E. family. Nevertheless, the investiture was granted to the two sisters von E., as in olden times, but only in the year 1616 by Emperor Matthias, of most noble and blessed memory, specifically based on these accounts (expressly inserted into the Letter of Investiture):

Namely, that these fief pieces were founded on being hereditary and having come to them by virtue of the privileges given to the Free Imperial Knighthood in Swabia in 1609 regarding High Jurisdiction (that the same should not be taken away from the estates).

These two foundations were then next considered (after Lady Eleonora passed away) by the now-reigning Roman Imperial Majesty, regarding the well-mentioned Lady Countess as the successor in...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding jurisdictional disputes and imperial fiefs. While the previous page established general principles of feudal law—specifically that cases should be heard by "Peers of the Court"—this page provides a specific case study involving a dispute over the Lordship of S. between Hans Christoph von B. and a Countess of R. (from the house of E.). It details the legal maneuvers used to claim rights to a fief and the resulting imperial decrees.</meta>

# Enlarged Compendium of Legal Practice

In the years 1620 and 1623, the feudal letters <note>documents granting a person possession of land or rights in exchange for service</note> pursued as a whole were allowed to be re-entered and recovered word-for-word.

Regardless of this, Hans Christoph von B.—as the holder of the other half of the Lordship of S.—obtained in the year 1624, through influential intercessions <note>appeals made by powerful intermediaries on someone's behalf</note> to the aforementioned imperial fiefs of the other party, an "expectancy" and "eventual investiture" <note>a legal promise from the Emperor that he would receive the fief once the current holder died</note> from the most high Imperial Majesty. Soon after, based on the same presuppositions, he sought and obtained letters of eventual obedience and homage <note>formal oaths of loyalty from the subjects</note> directed to the subjects of the house of E., which were acquired secretly and through deceit and the suppression of truth <note>Latin: *sub- & obreptitiè*; a legal term for obtaining a grant by lying about facts or hiding relevant information</note>.

All of this was done under a false pretense, as if: 1. the specific Lordship along with its regalian rights <note>term: <term>Regalien</term> (royal or imperial prerogatives such as the right to collect taxes, mint coins, or administer high justice)</note> had only been divided for a short time, specifically for eighty years; 2. this had been permitted by his ancestors through extreme negligence and connivance <note>Latin: *per summam incuriam atque conniventiam*; essentially "looking the other way"</note>; 3. because of this, peace and unity in the Lordship had been extinguished; 4. therefore, no further contracts with the Countess would help, no matter how good they seemed; 5. especially since through the unexpected continuation of such halved imperial rights, many crimes <note>Latin: *delicta*</note> were not punished at all, or only poorly, and justice <note>Latin: *Justitia*</note> was not being properly administered; 6. in doing so, he also exaggerated the merits of his ancestors and finally established as the main foundation of his claim that the consent granted by the Holy Empire to the family of E. regarding this fief was a special grace that would expire upon the death of the Countess, causing the fief to revert to the Empire or be extinguished.

Although the said Countess of R., upon first hearing of this clandestine acquisition, complained most highly to the Imperial Court and proved thoroughly—both through her own embassies and well-founded writings—that the Lordship of S. had been divided multiple times among the family of B. themselves for two hundred years; that more than a hundred years ago, one half had been sold by its owners to outside families with the full knowledge and advice of the holders of the other half; and that there had not been as much conflict then as there was now being stirred up by the house of B. itself. She specifically noted that peace and contracts had been so well observed by the Lords of E. and the Countess that both parties had shared the same advocate <note>lawyer</note> for fourteen years.

Furthermore, crimes had been jointly adjudicated by both holders with the advice of legal scholars, and justice had not been neglected in the least. She attached a comparison of the merits of the families of E. and B., along with a stately execution of the case supported by twenty documents, showing that the imperial rights of S. had been inseparably attached to the property for ages and were heritable and transferable to any outside heirs.

<column-break/>

Yet, such a legal deduction and clarification by the Countess did not sufficiently result in the annulment <note>Latin: *cassation*; the striking down of a legal ruling</note> of the deceitfully obtained eventual feudal and homage letters (primarily for the reason that such an annulment would be unbefitting of the Emperor’s reputation and majesty). Instead, it only achieved this much: that on October 13 of the past year, 1625, a copy of the rejection was granted to von B., along with a two-month deadline for a counter-argument. He was also ordered that, until the matter was decided, he should not presume to interfere with or take over the Countess’s possession of her half of the imperial rights, even if she were to die in the meantime, without His Imperial Majesty’s express permission.

Nevertheless, von B. never made a formal legal response, either within or after the expiration of those two months, up to this hour (because he found his cited reasons for the grant to be shaky and the Countess’s rejection insurmountable). On the contrary, the Imperial Fiscal <note>the state prosecutor or financial officer of the Empire</note>, acting on behalf of von B., submitted an extensive request on November 27 for the granting of an "eventual sequestration" <note>the temporary seizure of property by the state until a dispute is settled</note> of the imperial fief to the Lord Abbot of Z., and obtained it within four days, once again without the Countess being heard.

Upon this, the Countess requested that this sequestration be annulled again for the significant reasons cited, or at least lifted under a guarantee (which she offered at the same time).

However, nothing more was achieved than that von B., once again without her knowledge and through two other intercessions, extracted a decree that merely set aside the previous suspension (as if it had been granted based on a mere unproven claim, thereby depriving him of his assigned eventual possession until the ownership case <note>term: <term>Petitorio</term> (the legal action concerning the ultimate right of ownership, as opposed to "Possessorio" which concerns who currently holds the property)</note> was resolved). Immediately after, without hearing the other side <note>Latin: *inauditâ alterâ parte*</note>—treating her as the plaintiff against the order of law—a decree was issued on June 25 in place of a sentence regarding possession <note>Latin: *Decretum loco Sententiae in Possessorio*</note>, delivered unilaterally, with the following summary:

That the investiture and letter of obedience granted by His Imperial Majesty to the aforementioned von B. for the future event shall remain in place, notwithstanding what the Countess has applied against it so far; and both the decree of October 23 and the subsequently ordered commission are again canceled and revoked. Furthermore, the said Countess shall not be prevented from, but rather reserved the right to, pursue her legal rights regarding ownership <note>in the "Petitorio"</note>, should she believe she has any.

Before this possessory judgment was issued, and as early as May 30, this Countess—out of various considerations (which are detailed in a letter to His Imperial Majesty cited below)—directed all her subjects of the Lordship of S. to swear an actual eventual oath of homage to Lord Frederick, Lord of W.
