Lit. L.

Which the Imperial Prosecutor <note>German: *Reichs-Fiscal*; the official responsible for representing the Emperor's financial and feudal interests</note> soon learned of through von V., and subsequently petitioned a venerable Imperial Aulic Council <note>the high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> for the release of said Homage Instrument <note>the document recording the subjects' oath of loyalty</note>; it was granted that the Countess's steward—who arrived in Vienna somewhat late because of the then-beginning Upper Austrian Peasants' Uprising—had to submit it on the following July 18th. He also submitted an urgent defense of such homage, including the aforementioned considerations.

On the other hand, copies of this issued decree were not only obtained and sent to the Countess by the next post: but it was also mentioned at the beginning that copies of the writings submitted by the previous Imperial Prosecutor regarding the imperial fiefs from the years 1610 to 1616 had been received. However, the most important main attachment, marked *sub N. 2. a.* (to which all others refer), could not be found among them, nor has it been found since despite further inquiries.

While this was transpiring in Vienna, here in the local territory, von V. likewise had the judgment he received (which had already reached the Countess by post long before) delivered to the Countess via Bartholome Q. on July 18th, along with the eventual fief and letters of obedience produced in the year 1624. Her Grace accepted these for her person willingly; however, for significant reasons, she warned the Notary against the intended similar delivery <note>legal term: *Insinuation*; the formal service of a legal document</note> to her subjects in S. When he nevertheless proceeded with it and, that very evening, posted the said three documents on two of the Countess's taverns in S., and on the following evening attempted to bring the same three pieces to the peasants in the tavern at H.: those posted pieces at S. were respectfully taken down again, while the Notary at H. was prevented from the forthcoming delivery by a servant of Lord Friedrich of W. with a regiment or soldier’s staff <note>a symbolic or literal staff of authority/force</note>.

As the often-mentioned Countess of R. could easily conclude from the above events and other concurrent circumstances that she would not be able to proceed or reach a peaceful conclusion for her advanced, frail age without further assistance and interest against von V.’s powerful promoters and lords—especially because a rumor had broken out among the subjects that Lord von V. had obtained something against the aforementioned assignment and homage, and intended to trouble them further with it.

Thus, she (and certainly not out of malice or a premeditated intent to oppress her opponent, but rather to save herself from ruin and

<column-break/>

the nearly total loss of her Lordship of S., as well as to escape further intrigue and the entire matter) not only revoked and canceled the said assignment and homage again on November 10th, 1626, despite her heir and her husband being named; but furthermore, she resigned and assigned the ownership of her Lordship of S. to His Princely Highness Archduke Leopold of Austria <note>Leopold V, Archduke of Further Austria</note>. This was done as to her most gracious protector, who—by virtue of his Princely status and its dependencies—is more powerful than Lord von V., yet in terms of judicial power or other office and command, he is not formidable or superior to him, as he can neither command nor forbid him. This ownership was resigned and assigned freely <note>Latin: *liberè*</note> (as it had already been assigned once before to His Princely Highness for a half share <note>Latin: *pro parte dimidiâ*</note> in exchange for promised protection; also, insofar as it was allodial land <note>term: <term>Allodium</term> (land owned outright, not held as a fief from a lord)</note>, it had never been litigious or disputed), though with a reserved life-long usufruct <note>the right to enjoy the use and profits of the land for the rest of her life</note>. At the same time, the hereditary and alienable imperial fief-pieces inseparably attached to the lordship were handed over in the state and essence they were then in, and under the condition <note>Latin: *sub conditione*</note> of prior settlement, followed by hereditary and sub-enfeoffment <note>term: <term>Afterbelehnung</term> (the process where a tenant-in-chief grants a portion of their fief to a sub-tenant)</note>. This was based on the motives and causes clarified in the aforementioned letter to His Imperial Majesty, as well as those shining forth from this very set of facts or representation of the case <note>Latin: *ex hâc ipsâ Specie Facti oder Figuratione Casus*</note>.

This resignation was solemnly accepted <note>Latin: *solenniter acceptiren*</note> on the said November 10th by the appointed officials of the Bailiwick of Swabia on behalf of His Princely Highness. They took the homage of the subjects and, at that very moment <note>Latin: *eodem instanti*</note>, had the well-mentioned Lord Friedrich take the oath in his own name and as his wife's legal guardian <note>term: <term>Ehevogt</term> (a male legal representative for a married woman)</note>, as the incoming liegeman, since the half-lordship had been granted back to him and his wife as a sub-fief <note>Latin: *Afterlehensweis*</note> under the conditions heard.

Lord von V. did indeed have a thresher deliver a sealed letter to the Notary required for this release and homage before the official act <note>Latin: *actu*</note> began, and had the messenger run away immediately. However, since the preparations for the act were already in full swing, the petitioners and the officials of the Bailiwick reminded the Notary to first perform the official act for which he was present, and only then to attend to other side-business and open this letter (on which von V.'s coat of arms was recognized). Thus, only after the act was completed did he break open the letter and find within it a requisition, along with two copies of the below-named Imperial mandates, besides silver and gold. All of this he sent back to von V. through his son, offering his services in all due propriety should he be requested in the proper manner <note>Latin: *debito modo*</note>.

# Increased Practical Treasury

In the years 1620 and 1623, the enfeoffment letters <note>documents granting the right to a fief</note> were further pursued **in their entirety** <note>original Latin: *in solidum*</note> and, word for word, were allowed to be re-entered and recovered.

Despite this, Hans Christoph von B., as the holder of the other half of S., in the year 1624, through penetrating **intercessions** <note>requests for mediation or favor</note> with N. N., and through the same with the aforementioned Imperial Majesty, sought and obtained an **expectancy** <note>a legal right to future possession</note> and eventual **investiture** <note>the formal handover of a fief</note> regarding the imperial fiefs of the other party. Soon thereafter, based on the same presuppositions, he secretly and deceitfully <note>original Latin: *clam, sub- & obreptitiè*</note> obtained eventual letters of obedience and homage addressed to the subjects of E. S.

All of this was done under a false pretext, claiming: 1. that the actual lordship and its feudal **regalia** <note>royal or imperial rights and privileges, such as minting or high justice</note> had only been divided for a short time, specifically for eighty years; 2. that such a division had been permitted by his ancestors **through extreme negligence and connivance** <note>original Latin: *per summam incuriam atque conniventiam*</note>; 3. that peace and unity in said lordship had consequently been extinguished; 4. so much so that no contracts with the Countess, however good they seemed, would help any longer; 5. especially since through the unexpected continuation of such halved Imperial Regalia, many **crimes** <note>original Latin: *delicta*</note> were not punished at all, or only poorly, and **justice** <note>original Latin: *Justicia*</note> could not be properly administered; 6. wherein he also highlighted the **merits** <note>original Latin: *Merita*</note> of his ancestors and finally established as the main foundation of his presumption that the **consent** <note>original Latin: *Consens*</note> granted by the Holy Empire to the House of E. regarding this fiefdom would **expire** <note>original Latin: *exspirir*</note> upon the death of the Countess, and thereby such a fiefdom would definitely lapse or revert to the crown.

Although the said Countess of N., upon first hearing of this behind-the-scenes acquisition, complained most strongly to the Imperial Court and, both through her own embassies and through well-founded writings, thoroughly demonstrated that the Lordship of S. had been divided multiple times among those of von B. themselves for two hundred years; furthermore, that one half had been sold by its owners more than a hundred years ago to foreign families with the full knowledge and counsel of the holders of the other part; and that no more disputes had arisen from this than had previously existed among those of von B. themselves; but especially that peace and contracts had been so well observed by the Lords of E. and the Countess that both parties were able to make use of a single **advocate** <note>legal counsel</note> for fourteen years.

Just as the **crimes** <note>original Latin: *Delicta*</note> were jointly adjudicated by both holders with the advice of legal scholars, and **justice** <note>original Latin: *Justicia*</note> was by no means neglected in this regard; this was accompanied by a **comparison** <note>original Latin: *Collation*</note> of the **merits** <note>original Latin: *Meriten*</note> of E. and B.; as well as a stately presentation, well-supported by 20 **documents** <note>original Latin: *Documentis*</note>, showing that the S. Imperial Regalia had long been **inseparably** <note>original Latin: *inseparabiliter*</note> attached to the ownership and were heritable and alienable **to any outside heirs** <note>original Latin: *ad quoscunque extraneos hæredes*</note>.

<column-break/>

Yet, such Countly **deduction** <note>legal argument</note> and clarification were not sufficient to bring about the requested **annulment** <note>original Latin: *Cassation*</note> of the eventual fief and homage letters obtained **secretly and deceitfully** <note>original Latin: *sub- & obreptitiè*</note> (primarily for the reason that such an annulment would be unbefitting to Imperial **reputation** <note>original Latin: *Reputation*</note> and sovereignty); rather, it only achieved so much that von B., on the 13th of **October** of the recently passed year 1625, was granted a copy of the rejection along with a two-month deadline for a counter-argument; and he was thereby ordered that, until the matter was decided, he should not presume to take **possession** <note>original Latin: *Possess*</note> of the half-share of the Imperial Regalia belonging to the Countess, even if she were to pass away in the meantime, without His Imperial Majesty’s express permission, nor should he take them over of his own will.

Nevertheless, von B. did not proceed with the main case either within or after the expiration of those two months, up to this very hour (because he found the reasons for his **attainment of the writ** <note>original Latin: *Impetrations*-Ursa-chen</note> to be shaky and the Countess's rejection to be insurmountable). Instead, the Imperial **Prosecutor** <note>original Latin: *Reichs-Fiscal*</note>, for the benefit of von B., applied to the Lord Abbot of Z. on the 27th of **November** following with a broad request for the granting of an **eventual sequestration** <note>a legal seizure or setting aside of property</note> of the Imperial fief, and obtained the same within four days, once again without the Countess being heard.

Whereupon the Countess requested to **annul** <note>original Latin: *cassiren*</note> this again for the significant reasons cited, or at least to lift it **under bond** <note>original Latin: *sub cautione*</note> (which she offered at the same time).

However, nothing more or further was accomplished by this than that von B., again without her knowledge, came forward with two other **intercessory letters** <note>original Latin: *Intercessionalibus*</note> against the **suspensive** <note>halting the effects of a previous ruling</note> decree that had been set aside (as if it had been granted on mere unproven claims, and he was thereby **deprived** <note>original Latin: *destituirt*</note> of his assigned **eventual possession** until the investigation of the **ownership rights** <note>original Latin: *Petitorii*</note>). And immediately thereafter, **without hearing the other side** <note>original Latin: *inauditâ alterâ parte*</note> (who had been made the plaintiff **contrary to the order of law** <note>original Latin: *contra Juris ordinem*</note>), a **decree in place of a judgment on possession** <note>original Latin: *Decretum loco Sententiæ in Possessorio*</note> was delivered to him unilaterally on the 25th of **June** last, of the following summary content:

That the **investiture** and letter of obedience granted **in the event** <note>original Latin: *in eventum*</note> by His Imperial Majesty to the aforementioned von B. shall remain in effect, notwithstanding everything the Countess has applied against it so far; and both the **decree** of October 23rd and the subsequently ordered **commission** are again lifted and **revoked** <note>original Latin: *revocirt*</note>. Furthermore, however, the said Countess's rights to carry out her **ownership claims** <note>original Latin: *jura in Petitorio*</note>, should she believe she has any, shall not be hindered but rather shall be reserved.

But before such a **possessory** judgment was issued, and as early as May 30th, this Countess, out of all sorts of **considerations** (which are carried out in considerable detail in a letter to His Imperial Majesty cited shortly below), directed all her subjects of the Lordship of S. to perform actual eventual homage to Lord Frederick, Lord of W.

<header>Letter L.</header>

Which the Imperial Prosecutor <note>original German: *Reichs-Fiscal*; the high-ranking official responsible for representing the Emperor's financial and legal interests</note> immediately learned through von B., and subsequently requested the production of the **instrument of homage** <note>the formal legal document recording the subjects' oath of loyalty</note> from the honorable Imperial Aulic Council <note>original: *Reichs-Hofrath*; one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note>. It was granted that the Countess’s steward—who arrived in Vienna somewhat late due to the then-erupting **Upper Austrian Peasants' Revolt**—had to present the document on the following July 18th. He also submitted a hurried defense of this homage, including the previously mentioned considerations.

However, a copy of the resulting decree was not obtained, nor was it sent to the Countess by the next post. Instead, as mentioned at the beginning, copies were obtained of the documents submitted between 1610 and 1616 by the previous Imperial Prosecutor regarding the **Imperial Fiefs** <note>original: *Reichs-Lehen*; land held directly from the Emperor</note>. Nevertheless, the most important primary exhibit, labeled N. 2. a. (to which all others refer), could not be found among them, nor has it been located despite further requests.

While these matters were proceeding in Vienna, here in the local lands, von B. likewise had his judgment (which the Countess had already received by post long before) delivered to her on July 18th by Bartholome Q., along with the **contingent fiefs** and letters of obedience obtained in 1624. Her Grace personally accepted these; however, she warned the Notary, for significant reasons, against his intended delivery of the same documents to her subjects in S. When he nevertheless proceeded and, that same evening, posted the three documents on two of the Countess's taverns in S., the papers were modestly removed the following day. When the Notary tried to present the same three items to the peasants at the tavern in H. toward evening, he was prevented from delivering them by the servant of Lord Friedrich of W., who brandished a weapon and used a regimental or soldier's staff.

Since the frequently mentioned Countess of R. could easily conclude from this course of events and other incoming circumstances that she would not be able to proceed or reach a peaceful conclusion in her advanced and frail age without greater assistance and interest against von B.'s powerful promoters and masters: especially because a rumor had broken out among the subjects that Lord von B. had extracted something contrary to the aforementioned assignments and homage, and intended to trouble them further with it.

Thus she has (not out of any danger or intent to oppress her opponent, but rather to save herself from ruin and 

<column-break/>

the nearly total loss of her Lordship of S., and to escape further intrigue and the entire affair) not only once again revoked and abolished the aforementioned assignment and homage on November 10, 1626, despite her heir and her heir's husband being named therein: but she has also **resigned and assigned** the ownership of her Lordship of S. to His Serene Highness Archduke Leopold of Austria—as her most gracious protector—who, by virtue of his Archducal rank and its dependencies, is more powerful than Lord von B. (otherwise, regarding judicial power or other office and command, he is not formidable or superior to von B., as he can neither command nor forbid him). 

This lordship had already been signed over once before to His Archducal Highness **for half the part** <note>original Latin: *pro parte dimidiâ*</note> in exchange for promised protection; and as far as the **allodium** <note>original: *Allodium*; land owned outright rather than held as a fief</note> was concerned, it had never been in dispute. She resigned this **freely** <note>original Latin: *liberè*</note>, yet reserved for herself the **usufruct** <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of the property</note> for the duration of her life. At the same time, she also handed over the hereditary and alienable Imperial Fiefs inseparably attached to the lordship, in the condition they were then in, and under the condition of prior settlement and subsequent **sub-fief investiture** <note>original: *Afterbelehnung*; the granting of a fief by someone who is himself a vassal</note>. This was done based on the motives and causes deduced in the letter to His Imperial Majesty (and as shines forth **from this very type of fact** <note>original Latin: *ex hac ipsâ Specie Facti*</note>).

His Archducal Highness, having heard of this resignation, had his appointed officials from the **Bailiwick of Swabia** <note>original: *Landvogtey Schwaben*</note> solemnly accept it on the said November 10th. They took the homage of the subjects and, at that same instant, had the well-mentioned Lord Friedrich (to whom and his wife half the lordship was granted as a hereditary fief and the feudal parts as a **sub-fief** <note>original: *Afterlehensweis*</note>) sworn in as the incoming liegeman in his own name and as his wife's legal guardian.

Before this act of relaxation and homage began, von B. had a thresher deliver a sealed letter to the Notary required for the work, and then immediately had the man run away. However, since they were already in full preparation for the ceremony, the petitioners and the officials of the Bailiwick reminded the Notary to first perform the act for which he was present, and only afterward to attend to side business and open this letter (on which von B.'s coat of arms was recognized). Therefore, he only broke open the writing after the act was completed, finding within it a requisition along with two copies of the Imperial mandates named below, besides silver and gold. He sent all of this back to von B. via his son, offering to perform all duties should he be requested in the proper manner.

# Expanded Practical Treasury #

Following this, on Monday, November 23rd, a Secretary of Prince Z., in the presence of a notary and two witnesses, served the Countess—and the following day, also Lord Friederich of B.—the originals of the two previously mentioned mandates. These were, namely, a **Quashing Mandate** <note>original: *Cassatorium*; a legal order nullifying a previous act</note>, *with an annexed summons to show proof of the division*, and a **Mandate of Non-Offense** <note>original: *de non offendendo*; an order to refrain from hostile or violent actions against another party</note>.

In the first of these, the homage performed by the honorable subjects on the previous May 30th was **quashed** <note>original: *cassiret*; declared null and void</note>. Furthermore, the well-mentioned Countess, Lord Friederich, and his wife were ordered, under penalty of 20 Gold Marks, not only to immediately release the said subjects from their forced duties and oaths but also to provide proof *regarding the division* <note>original: *de partitione*; likely referring to the division of the inheritance or estate</note> within two months, etc. The other mandate (which was extracted by the party from B.) summarily states that—based on the highly exaggerated *narrative* <note>original: *narrata*; the version of events presented to the court</note> stemming from Notary H.—the Countess and Lord Friederich of B. were commanded, under penalty of breaching the Public Peace and other legal punishments, to take no hostile action themselves, nor permit their people to do so, against the said party from B., his servants, subjects, or notaries. This applied to all their persons, property, and goods, wherever located, without first obtaining a legal judgment. Instead, they were to use the standard legal channels for disputes.

Despite this, the well-named Countess sought a **Restoration to the Original State** <note>original: *Restitutio in integrum*; a legal remedy to reverse the effects of a court decision</note> through an extensive deduction and petition directed to the Elector N., as well as through a letter of intercession dated November 26, 1626, against the aforementioned *possessory* decree <note>original: *possessori Decret*; a ruling concerning the right of possession</note>. She most humbly requested at least a better, more impartial investigation into the fiefs, along with an unobjectionable suspension of the "Letter of Obedience" extracted by the party from B., which almost entirely swallowed up the allodial land <note>original: *Allodium*; land held in absolute ownership, rather than as a fief from a lord</note> of the Lordship of S. Furthermore, the Archduchess <note>likely a reference to the wife of Archduke Leopold</note> and Archduke Leopold of Austria, etc., intervened once more on behalf of the Countess through an extensive informational letter dated January 19, 1627, written in a similar vein.

Meanwhile, the Countess sent a letter (dated December 19, 1626) to the Court, in which she substantively defended or excused the assignment and homage performed for her desired daughter and son-in-law, *against the stated facts of the alleged quashing mandate* <note>original: *contra narrata allegati s. mandati cassatorii*</note>. Nevertheless, she credibly demonstrated the (previously occurred) release of such homage. She also sufficiently indicated the resignation made to the Archduke as the most gracious Protector. Although she most humbly prayed for further support from the Imperial Aulic Prosecutor, nothing certain was granted. Instead, the opposite occurred on March 23, 1627: an Imperial command was served to Notary Schwartz, the city clerk at

<column-break/>

A. etc., by a deputy of Prince Z. in the presence of a notary and witnesses. In this command, he was not only ordered—under threat of inevitable punishment and the loss of his notarial office—to *immediately and on the spot produce copies* <note>original: *copialiche in continenti*</note> of the instrument drawn up regarding the aforementioned act of homage performed for Archduke Leopold of Austria; he was also further commanded, by his notarial oaths and duties and to avoid other relentless, serious punishments, to provide a detailed and thorough written report:

Whether the aforementioned letter of requisition from the party from B. was opened before the homage was completed; whether he had read it, along with the included certified copies, or allowed the aforementioned Countess and her assistants and advisors to read it; and whether he had delivered a copy of it, or had heard, noticed, and perceived from them that the Countess, Lord Friederich of B., and the said assistants, advocates, advisors, and officials had knowledge of the existing Mandate of Annulment, etc.

But the matter did not end there. The said deputy of Z. subsequently, on March 24th and the following days, served an Imperial summons—obtained by the aforementioned Notary and the Imperial Aulic Prosecutor *concerning injuries and the violation of notarial privileges, witnessed* <note>original: *super injuriis & violatione Privilegiorum Notariatus, testatò*</note>—to the Countess, Lord Friederich, as well as an advocate, an administrative clerk, three servants, and two subjects. By virtue of this, they were all, and each one individually, charged with the penalty of 50 Gold Marks incorporated into the *notarial instrument*. The three servants were charged because they had detained and beaten the Notary at H.

The Countess and Lord Friederich, however, were charged because the procedure presumably happened on their Graces' orders.

**Also**, Dr. Heider and the administrative clerk Schönheinz were charged because the former delivered the first, and the latter the second, written threat <note>original: *Commination*</note> to the Notary.

Furthermore, Georg Rogg, a farmer at S., was charged because he had driven the three servants to H.; and Michael Steub, an innkeeper there at H., because he had helped to seize the Notary. Moreover, the alleged verbal and physical *injuries* were valued at 4,000 Guilders.

Regarding this incident and the *summons*, a **statement of facts** <note>original: *species facti*</note> was drawn up without delay and sent to the honorable Faculty of Law at **Tübingen** for legal advice. From there, a counsel was sent back in haste, which was immediately brought to the Imperial Court on May 3rd as a precaution. Following this, on the 10th of the *same month*, a main proceeding took place (under the heading: *Petition for the presentation of the instruments of service and notarization* <note>original: *Petitio exhibitionis Instrumentorum Insinuationis & Notariatus*</note>).

The case was sent to the law faculty at Tübingen for expert legal counsel as both sides battled in the Imperial courts.</summary>

### Lit. L. ###

<note>original: "junctis, in subsidium, non competentis Actionis & aliis litis finitæ seu intentionis Exceptionibus, &c. annexâ etiam eventuali Litis contestatione"</note> joined as a backup against an incompetent legal action, along with other exceptions regarding a finished lawsuit or the plaintiff's intent, and including an eventual joining of the issue <note>This refers to a standard legal defense strategy where the defendant raises multiple procedural objections at once</note>, was sent thereafter; just as a supplementary writing was directed there shortly after on August 2nd; all of which was properly delivered by the Count's agent.

In the meantime, on May 6th, the Lord of B. <note>Hans Christoph von Berg</note> again had a certified copy of an **Imperial Order of Possession** <note>original: *Immissions-Befehl*; a court order to put someone in legal possession of property</note> served. This had actually been issued on the previous January 22nd and essentially stipulated that, in the event of the Countess’s death, his representative, Lord Z., should immediately put the Lord of B.—in the name of his Imperial Majesty—into the **possession or its equivalent** <note>original: *possessionem vel quasi*</note> of the Imperial fiefs and regalia <note>Crown rights and privileges</note> at S. E. He was to gather the subjects and, in the best legal form, release and discharge them from their duties and oaths which they might have been bound to at that time to anyone else. Furthermore, he was to declare everything that contradicted the rights obtained by B. as **null and void by the law itself** <note>original: *ipso jure null- und nichtig*</note>. He was to show the subjects the B. investiture, the letter of obedience, the judgment, and its confirmation, directing them to the Lord of B. and having them swear actual fealty to him. Should they resist, or should anyone try to prevent them or turn them away, he was authorized by the full power of the Emperor to strictly compel them to their duty under penalty of fines and other punishments, and to avoid Imperial displeasure. He was to maintain, protect, and handle the Lord of B. in this matter against anyone, regarding everything attached to such Imperial fiefs and regalia by law, land, and custom. Those who claimed to have any existing rights were to be referred to his Imperial Majesty. Nothing was to be omitted that might be required **in any way** <note>original: *ullo modo*</note> for the complete seizure and delivery of the aforementioned Imperial fiefs and regalia, as well as their maintenance.

But it did not stop there: although the Countess, through letters of intercession from the Electors and hereditary Princes, strongly sought a **restoration to the original state** <note>original: *Restitutionem in integrum*; a legal remedy to cancel the effects of a prior judgment</note> against the possession decree.

During this time, she also filed persistent **objections regarding deceit and concealment** <note>original: *Exceptiones sub- & obreptionis*; a claim that the opponent obtained a legal order by hiding facts or lying</note> at Court against the obtained Mandate of Non-Offense. Nevertheless, on the following September 13th, 14th, and 15th, an Imperial envoy, in the presence of Notary B. and witnesses, delivered a **Quashing and Injunction Mandate** <note>original: *Cassatori- und Inhibitorial-Mandat*</note> to her Grace and her son-in-law, Lord Friederich, as well as to Daniel Heider and Wolff Sattler (both Doctors of Law), and also to Thomas Scheitenberger, the administrator at St. Jacob Behlen and manager of the Lordship of B., to each individually.

<column-break/>

According to this mandate, and under penalty of twenty Gold Marks, the Countess was ordered—while **reserving the right to sue for ownership** <note>original: *reservato tamen petitorio*</note>—to revoke, quash, and stop the **transfer** <note>original: *Cession*</note> made to the Archduchy of Austria, as well as the instruction and homage of her S. Lordship and subjects.

Lord Friederich of W. and his wife were commanded not to interfere, either themselves or through others, with the Imperial Treasury or the Lord of B. regarding the **seizure of possession or its equivalent** <note>original: *Apprehension possessionis vel quasi*</note>, or the use and exercise of the Imperial fiefs and regalia, in the event of the Countess's future death.

Furthermore, the two aforementioned advocates and officials, as well as all other consultants, lawyers, and servants employed by the Countess in this matter, were forbidden and restrained from providing further legal counsel in the ongoing cases regarding the Imperial judgment issued in the possession matter. Remarkably, this mandate had been dated and issued on May 21st, nearly four full months before it was actually served.

However, since these various mandate proceedings—according to all presumptions and circumstances—flowed and originated from a single source, namely from biased and poorly founded information **in law and in fact** <note>original: *in Jure & facto*</note>, the Countess's party was forced and compelled to draft a well-founded Counter-Information against it. This was humbly presented to his Serene Highness Archduke Leopold, as the protector and now also the feudal lord of half the Lordship of S., requesting his representation. In return, his Princely Highness graciously shared with the Countess an Imperial reply dated April 30, 1627, along with an enclosed report and narrative (detailing the actual nature of the disputes) that had recently been delivered. His Highness's consultants had drawn a summary counter-report from **the records and proceedings** <note>original: *aus den Actis und Actitatis*</note>, identifying the defects and flaws of the legal process.

Because of all this, and because his Serene Highness had fully taken over the representation of the Countess, Lord Friederich of W., and their servants and lawyers, a further delay was obtained. Nothing further was submitted to the Imperial Court on the Countess's side, except that Dr. Heider, on October 21st, declared his conditional compliance with the recent Injunction Mandate. Additionally, on October 23rd, the Countess and Lord Friederich—to facilitate their remaining court cases, **to be free of harassment** <note>original: *pro redimenda vexâ*</note>, and to reduce legal costs—reached a settlement with Notary O. They granted him forty Guilders in compensation for his alleged pain, damages, and lost time (in exchange for his renunciation of his claims, though saving the interests of the Imperial Court Prosecutor).

<meta>This page continues the legal dispute concerning the Lordship of S., specifically detailing nine points of legal inquiry (informationes juris) submitted for expert opinion regarding the division of property between feudal and private holdings.</meta>

# The Expanded Treasury of Practical Law #

As all the above-mentioned matters, and whatever else pertains to the case, may be found credibly documented in the accompanying acts and writings; and in view of this, a steady and well-grounded legal opinion is now requested concerning the following points:

First, whether the Countess who is ceding her rights, or now her assignee <note>original: "Cessionarius"</note>, His Princely Highness Archduke Leopold of Austria, is in the right and sufficiently grounded in the **legal claim regarding the quantity of feudal matters** <note>original: "in Petitorio, ratione quantitatis rerum Feudalium"</note>? Specifically, is it correct that in the Lordship of S., only four—or rather only three—pieces (namely the right to hold a market, the High Court of Justice or "Blood Ban" <note>The power to pass death sentences</note>, and the **symbols of execution** <note>original: "Signa executiva"</note>, which are the stocks and the gallows) originate as fiefs from the Holy Roman Empire, while everything else is allodial <note>Private property held in absolute ownership, not as a gift from a lord</note> or personal property?

Thereafter and second, how the aforementioned assignee or the aforementioned Countess stands (or does not stand) **in the same legal claim** regarding the declared quality of such feudal pieces? Specifically, are they inseparably attached to the private ownership and of a completely hereditary and saleable nature? <note>original: "hoc est, feuda merè hæreditaria, alienabilia, & ad quoscunque hæredes transitoria & inseparabiles pertinentiæ allodialis Dominii S."</note> <note>This asks if the fiefs are "purely hereditary and transferable to any heirs" and part of the private estate's belongings</note>.

Thirdly, how one is equipped regarding both points—that is, **with regard to the feudal quantity and quality**—furthermore also in the **matter of possession** <note>original: "in Possessorio"</note>; or what one may use for help and comfort in this regard?

Fourthly, is this side at least so well-grounded in the above three points that the Countess should and may be **fully restored** <note>original: "wider in integrum restituirt"</note> to her previous status, contrary to the decree of possession issued on June 23, 1626? And in this case, regarding the **future seizure** <note>original: "futuræ apprehensionis"</note> of the private and feudal properties, should it be left to the express regulation of feudal law, or at least to the suspensive decree issued before it on October 23, 1625, until the matter is further clarified?

Likewise, and fifthly, whether the first act of assignment and homage performed **in the event of death** <note>original: "in eventum"</note> toward Lord Frederick of B. and his wife was a punishable and **legally void** <note>original: "ipso jure nichtiges"</note> attempt (as the Imperial Treasury Attorney <note>original: "Reichs-Hof-Fiscal"</note> has complained)? Or whether it can be justified and excused—and to what extent—despite the obtained Mandate of Cancellation, given the previously mentioned urgency, defense, and the letter written by the Countess on December 26, 1626?

## First Question.

Regarding this, we can conclude nothing other than that in the present case there are not only three, but in every way four general or main pieces: (1.) the market right, (2.) the bailiwick jurisdiction, (3.) the symbols of execution or stocks and gallows, and finally (4.) the **criminal jurisdiction** <note>original: "Jurisdictio Criminalis"</note>, or the "Ban" to judge over blood. These all stem from the Roman Empire as fiefs. Consequently—which is the primary dispute in this question and seems somewhat doubtful—wherever the word "Court" is placed and found in all investitures, it does not at all mean the criminal jurisdiction, but necessarily the lower civil authority. Therefore, the same may in no way be considered **allodial** <note>Private property held in absolute ownership</note> or personal, but must be recognized and received as an Imperial fief, just like the Blood Ban or the exercise of criminal justice.

<margin>Alex. consil. 87. n. 17. lib. 5. Göden. cons. 36. num. 4. Alciat. cons. 12. num. 11. vol. 3. Abb. cons. 82. num. 6. vol. 1. Rol. à Vall. cons. 89. num. 1. & seq. vol. 2. Anton. Gabriel. tit. de præsumpt. concl. 9. n. 1. lib. 1. **Everyone admits that jurisdiction was introduced by Public Law and flows from the Emperor as the sole source.** <note>original Latin: "Jurisdictiónemque de Jure Publico introductam esse, & ab Imperatore tanquam unicâ scaturigine fluere, fatentur omnes."</note> Rosenthal. de feud. cap. 5. quæst. 4. num. 2. & 7.</margin>
To this conclusion we are first moved because the Roman Imperial Majesty, with respect to all types of jurisdiction in the whole Empire and against all those possessing jurisdiction, has a **well-founded intention** <note>original: "fundatam intentionem"</note>. And that jurisdiction is complete within the Prince, and flows entirely from him, **just as streams from a spring, rays from the Sun, and branches from a tree** <note>original Latin: "pariter atque de fonte rivuli, à Sole radii, & ab arbore rami"</note>, as Cravetta records after Anchora and others.

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

Enfeoffment <note>original: "Infeudationem"</note>, *Knichen, On the Rights of Territory, chapter 1, number 86.*

And although it is otherwise correct **that jurisdiction, especially low jurisdiction <note>original: "Jurisdictio bassa"; this refers to minor civil and criminal cases not involving the death penalty</note>, sometimes exists by another reason in the hands of the owners of the territory, villages, and castles, and especially that the Nobility in Swabia—by right of allodial property <note>land held absolutely, rather than from a superior lord</note>—usurp that form of jurisdiction which is commonly designated as advocatory authority <note>original: "die Vogtepliche Obrigkeit"</note>.** Therefore, they are also commonly called "Bailiffs" <note>original: "Vogtsherrn"</note>, and by virtue of such jurisdiction, they are empowered to establish statutes or "Bailiff-books." This could be said with some plausibility regarding the Lordship of S. (as it is titled and named), even where one has brought about such low-court authority through long-term usage <note>original: "per diuturnam usurpantiam"</note>.

However, these and many other conjectures—and whatever else of the same kind one might bring up—all fall to the ground when specific and undeniable letters of enfeoffment <note>original: "Lehenbrieffen"</note> are found, according to the correct understanding of which even the low-court authority, **and thus the jurisdiction <note>original: "& ita Jurisdictio"</note>,** stems from a fief.

**For it cannot be doubted that a fief is proven through acts of Investiture <note>the formal ceremony or document granting a fief</note>, and those things found included in the Investitures are considered feudal.** *Oldradus, counsel 272, beginning "Reverend Father."* **And that a fief is proven from the Investiture alone—even to the detriment of the one invested—is taught by Hostiensis** *in the summary, title "on fiefs," section "in what ways," at the phrase "what if a Vassal." Oldradus, counsel 159, column 2. Albericus on the law "Titius 2" at the end, Digest "on the action of purchase" and on the law "if for certain years," Code "on pacts." Jason, counsel 235, at the end of book 2. Curtius Junior, counsel 21, column 2, after the middle, and counsel 140, column 2, at the end, and counsel 184, and in the treatise "on fiefs," part 2, question 6, treatise 6.* **And that the proof of a fief becomes most clear from Investitures and Acknowledgments alone, was advised by** *Cravetta, in his responses for the Son-in-Law throughout, but especially at number 425.*

Now, to prove for the second point, as previously indicated, from the letters of enfeoffment themselves that both the low and high authority in the village of V. is feudal and must be recognized as such: it is nonetheless provided for in the law **that the first Investiture must be regarded as the root, and as it were the base and foundation of all subsequent ones; and to its tenor, as if to a guiding star <note>original: "cynosuram"</note>, one must perpetually recur, setting others aside; nor can it be changed or revoked even by the supreme Prince without the consent of either party.** *Section "notandum," title "on those who can give a fief." Law "cum satis," second to last, section 1, at the phrase "let them beware," Code "on farmers and censuses." Last law, Code "on the arbiter of guardianship." Law "sicut," section Code "on Obligations and Actions." Law "contractus 23," Digest "on the Rules of Law." Curtius on fiefs, question 7, number 43. Sylvanus, questions 34 and 38. Duarenus, chapter 7, number 20. Sonsbec, part 9, number 29. Zasius, part 6, number 23. Borcholten, chapter 1, number 25. Schrader, part 5, chapter 2, number 28 and following. Rosenthal, chapter 6, conclusion 29, number 1, conclusion 69.*

Because, however—as God willing shall be mentioned shortly hereafter—these same rights, which are currently being disputed, were likely private property <note>original: "eigen"</note> before that time, **and depended on the Holy Roman Empire solely by right of Privilege <note>original: "& solummodò jure Privilegii"</note>,** and also

<column-break/>

only **after the deposition of Emperor Wenceslaus <note>Wenceslaus IV was deposed as King of the Romans in 1400</note>,** were they granted as a fief to the most high Holy Roman Empire—either to those of V. as the holders of the entire Lordship of S. (in which the mentioned village is situated) for many years, **or by some other means <note>original: "vel aliâ ratione"</note>—becoming subject to feudal law.** Since the first Investiture or letter of enfeoffment drawn up regarding this is not present, but the oldest among those one may have stems only from the late Emperor Maximilian I, of most glorious memory, dated 1494, then this same document (which is not contradicted by any party) must be carefully considered according to its literal content and right understanding.

**For fiefs are matters of strict law <note>original: "stricti Juris"; meaning they are interpreted narrowly according to the text</note>, and therefore their words or those of the Investitures are to be interpreted strictly, and in such a way that nothing is assumed from the outside.** *Wesenbeck, part 2, counsel 60, number 11. Knichen, "on the vestment of pacts," part 2, chapter 1, number 61, etc. Rosenthal, chapter 6, conclusion 28, number 1.*

**And when one or another Investiture is perhaps present (even if it is not the first), especially if it makes mention of preceding ones, then one stands by that one or those, and the other earlier ones are presumed to agree with them.** *Boerius, decision 24, number 64. Menochius, counsel 1, number 83. Cravetta, counsel 92, number 8 and following. Rosenthal, chapter 6, conclusion 69, number 9.* **Because a reference, if it is authentic or certain in itself, provides proof even without the document it refers to.** *Boerius, decision 281, number 92. Mascardus, "on proofs," volume 2, conclusion 923, number 6.* **Both of whom testify that this doctrine is commonly accepted.** *Rosenthal, chapter 6, conclusion 69, number 10.* **Just as a Confirmation in special form otherwise proves the thing confirmed,** *Molinaeus on the Customs of Paris, section 1, number 71 and following, and Rosenthal in the cited place.* **And hence, if the first Investiture has perished either by fire or some other accident, and only the last one exists: it is nonetheless presumed to have been made according to the first Investiture in all its clauses, pacts, and points.** *Zasius in the epitome of fiefs, part 6, number 23, and Schrader on fiefs, part 5, chapter 2, number 44.*

Now, in the above-cited Investiture of the most highly mentioned late Lord Maximilian I, His Imperial Majesty, it is related how two brothers <note>original: "zween Gebetter"; archaic German for kinsmen or brothers</note> of R., then living, most humbly petitioned that he graciously grant them as a fief the market rights <note>original: "Marckrecht"</note>, the court, the stock and gallows <note>original: "Stock und Galgen"; symbols of high jurisdiction or the power to punish</note>, together with the ban to judge over blood <note>original: "Bann daselbst über das Blut zu richten"; high jurisdiction involving capital punishment</note> in the village of V. situated in their Lordship of S., which had been granted to them by His Imperial Majesty’s ancestors in the Empire and which they had held and used until now.

in all letters of enfeoffment <note>original: "Lehenbrieffen"</note>, even those where half the lordship of S. had already passed from the noble lineage of B. to other foreign families—specifically to the Barons of E.—this has been repeated and included in the letters of enfeoffment most graciously granted at all times.

That many different general or main articles were granted in such investitures <note>the formal ceremony or document granting a fief</note>, as has already been suggested above, is evident in our opinion. This is shown both by its own nature and because the fourfold enumeration <note>original: "quadripartita enumeratio"</note> is clearly and distinctly found within them. Therefore, opposing assumptions and arguments in a contradictory judgment will likely have little effect: *since in clear matters there is no room for conjecture, and even presumptions are weakened by other stronger ones.* <note>original: "cùm in claris non habeant locum conjecturæ, & etiam præsumptiones per alias firmiores enerventur"</note>

For firstly, the market right <note>original: "Marcktrechts"</note> is mentioned, which we, for our part, understand as the **Right of Fairs** <note>original: "pro Jure Nundinarum"</note>. This is because for its exercise, either a singular privilege or an imperial investiture is considered necessary. Indeed, it is not lawful for anyone to establish fairs even on private estates at their own will, but it is necessary that they be obtained from the Prince. <note>original: "per l. 1. ff. de nundin." referencing Roman law on fairs</note> For it is established that the right of solemn and public fairs belongs to the **major regalia** <note>high sovereign rights belonging to the Emperor or a supreme prince</note>, as stated in the law where Sichardus notes that lower princes do not have it within their own sovereign rights to be able to grant this privilege even in their own provinces. <note>Citing Gail, Bodin, and Sixtin, prominent legal scholars of the era.</note>

Common fairs, however, which we commonly call **weekly markets** <note>original: "Wochenmarckt"</note>, can be established and celebrated without such a privilege. <note>Sichard. ad rubr. C. de nund. n. 13.</note> For they involve a matter of fact rather than a matter of law, since they lack the immunities and other prerogatives ascribed to solemn annual fairs. <note>Tesaur. decis. 364. n. 4.</note> Therefore, in this context, the "market right" is to be understood in its more powerful and legally proven sense—namely, concerning the **annual market**, which is among the sovereign rights and requires the grant of the Supreme Prince. <note>Græven. 2. concl. 60. conf. 1. n. 2. & 3.</note>

Since the village of T. is also a market town <note>original: "Marcktfleck"</note> and presumably has its specific annual fairs, and such a thing cannot happen without a special Imperial favor, and since no other documents are found here except the mentioned letters of enfeoffment and the privilege of the late Emperor Wenceslaus—in which the market right is mentioned in almost the same wording—it is reasonable to conclude that the said term "market right" is to be understood as the **Right of Fairs** <note>original: "de jure Nundinarum"</note>.

For the subsequent quality of possession declares what the intention of the parties was from the beginning. <note>Jos. Ludov. comm. concl. 38. n. 12.</note> It is presumed that the Lord and Vassal

<column-break/>

bound themselves to that which the subsequent practice represents. <note>Idem ibid. n. 50.</note> This is because subsequent practice <note>original: "observantia"</note> is said to be the best interpreter of any act, and especially of feudal investitures. <note>Menoch. cons. 32. num. 45.</note> Hence, where a doubt exists as to whether jurisdiction is included in the sale of a castle, one examines what has been observed in practice: because a later deed clarifies the prior act, and the understanding must be adopted which the effect and outcome of the matter prove to be true. <note>Jos. Ludov. d. l. n. 6.</note>

One might, however, interpret this word "market right" as the **rights of a market town** <note>original: "Marckfleckens Gerechtsame"</note>, for that right also appears to require a special Imperial grant. In the Roman Empire, the power to confer upon a place "spirit and life," or **Town Right** <note>original: "Jus Civitatis / Stadtrecht"</note>, belongs to the Emperor alone as a major sovereign right. <note>Citing Obrecht and Clapmar.</note> An illustrious example of this is recorded regarding Emperor Maximilian I, who in 1514 forbade Count Albert of Mansfeld from presuming to grant the status of a town to a certain village with these words:
> Since it is not fitting for you or anyone else to establish town rights or other matters belonging to the high sovereign authority without special permission, we command, etc.
<note>Bruning. de var. Univers. Spec. Cluten. rer. quot. concl. 22. lit. d.</note>

This is so true that if someone were to establish a city without the Emperor's consent (at least a silent one), it would neither truly be a city nor could it usurp the rights of a city. <note>Natta. consil. 636. n. 100.</note>

However, we for our part cannot believe that this is what is meant here, because the letter of enfeoffment reads: "That in the village of T. the **market right** be granted as a fief." By contrast, if His Imperial Majesty had intended to grant the right that the said village of T. should be a market town, he presumably would not have placed the market right *in* the village of T. For it is one thing to grant a right *within* a certain place, and another to grant the right *of* the place itself.

Likewise, the "Town Right" or the justice of a market town is not usually granted by right of a fief, but by virtue of a **Privilege**, which is given only once; it is not customary to renew it as those rights granted in feudal investitures are.

Otherwise, this little word "Marcktrecht" <note>Market Right</note> might be interpreted in several other ways, namely (1) as the **Right of the Territory** <note>original: "pro jure Territorii"</note>, especially if it is written as "Marckrecht" <note>Boundary Right</note> (as we find in some copies of the letters and privileges); and also (2) as the **Right to establish Statutes**. Regarding this latter meaning, Johann Gryphiander writes the following: "Market Right" <note>original: "Marcktrecht"</note> is this: that the market people...

And although it is otherwise correct *that jurisdiction—especially low jurisdiction—sometimes belongs to the possessors of the territory, villages, and castles for other reasons, and particularly the nobles in Swabia claim that form of jurisdiction by allodial right* <note>right of absolute ownership, independent of a feudal lord</note> *which is commonly designated as* **the Bailiwick Authority** <note>original: "die Vogteylische Obrigkeit"; the administrative and judicial power held by a local protector or 'Vogt'</note>. Now, to demonstrate from the letters of enfeoffment themselves—as previously indicated—that both the low and high jurisdiction in the village of T. are **feudal** <note>original: "feudalis"</note> and must be recognized as such, it is nevertheless provided for in the law: *that the first investiture must be regarded as the root, and as it were the basis and foundation of all subsequent ones. One must perpetually return to its terms as if to a guiding star* <note>original: "cynosuram"; literally the constellation of the Little Bear used for navigation</note>, *setting others aside; nor can it be changed or revoked even by the supreme Prince against the will of either party. (Citing various legal authorities including Duaren, Rosenthal, and Zasius).*

However, as it will please God to show shortly hereafter, these same rights <note>original: "jura"</note> currently under dispute were presumably owned outright in former times, *and depended solely on the Holy Roman Empire by right of privilege*. Also,

Therefore, this document (which is not contested by either party) must be carefully observed according to its literal content and correct understanding.

*For fiefs are matters of strict law, and therefore the words of the fiefs or their investitures are to be interpreted strictly, such that nothing is assumed from outside the text. (Citing Wesenbeck and Rosenthal).*

*And when one or another investiture is present (even if it is not the first), especially if it mentions those preceding it, then one stands by that document, and the others are presumed to agree with it. (Citing Menochius and Mascardus). This is because a reference, if it is authentic or certain in itself, provides proof even without the document it refers to. Furthermore, a confirmation in a specific form proves the thing confirmed... Hence, if the first investiture has perished by fire or other accident, and only the most recent exists, it is nonetheless presumed to have been made according to the first investiture in all its clauses, pacts, and points. (Citing Zasius and Schrader).*

Now, in the above-cited investiture of the most high and late Lord, Emperor Maximilian I, it is **recorded** <note>original: "referirt"</note> how at that time two living cousins "von R." most humbly requested that the Emperor graciously grant them as a fief the **Market Right, Court, Stocks and Gallows** <note>original: "Marcktrecht, Gericht, Stock und Galgen"</note>, together with the "ban" to judge blood <note>original: "Bann daselbst über das Blut zu richten"; the authority to impose capital punishment</note> in the village of T., situated in their Lordship of S. These rights had been granted to them by his late Imperial Majesty's ancestors in the Empire and had been held and used by them until then.

Whereupon His Imperial Majesty further determines <note>original: "dispositive"</note> that, having considered their humble and appropriate request, and with deliberate mind and good counsel, he graciously grants as a fief to the same "von V." <note>the scribe likely means "von R." or a related lineage</note> in the mentioned village of T., the Market Right, Court, Stocks and Gallows, together with the authority to judge blood, just as these were formerly granted to them by the aforementioned ancestors of His Imperial Majesty, etc. These words are potent for us, *and changing only what needs to be changed* <note>original: "mutatis solummodo mutandis"</note>...

<summary>This page analyzes the legal status of jurisdictions in the village of T., concluding that they are feudal rights (fiefs) rather than private property, based on a 1494 investiture by Emperor Maximilian I. It establishes the legal principle that later feudal documents are presumed to follow the terms of the original grant, even if the first document is lost.</summary>

# Lit. L.
### Gggg 2
->Besoldus, Volume I.<-

in all **letters of enfeoffment** <note>original: "Lehenbriefen"; formal documents granting a fief</note>, even where half of the **Lordship of S.** has already passed from the noble families of B. to other foreign lineages—specifically to the **Barons of E.**—these rights have been repeated and included in every most graciously granted letter of enfeoffment.

That many different general or main articles were granted in such **investitures** <note>original: "Investituren"; the formal ceremony or document of transfer</note>, as already suggested above, is evident in our opinion. This is clear because a four-part enumeration is visibly and distinctly found therein, so that any contrary assumption or argument in a **contradictory judgment** <note>original: "contradictorio Judicio"; a legal dispute with opposing parties</note> would hardly prevail: **for when things are clear, there is no room for conjecture, and even presumptions are weakened by other stronger ones.** <note>original: "cùm in claris non habeant locum conjecturæ, & etiam præsumptiones per alias firmiores enerventur."</note>

For firstly, the **market right** <note>original: "Marcktrechts"</note> is mentioned, which we, for our part, understand as the **right of fairs** <note>original: "pro jure Nundinarum"</note>, for the exercise of which either a singular **privilege** or an **investiture** from the Emperor is considered necessary. Indeed, it is not permitted for anyone to establish **fairs** <note>original: "Nundinas"</note> even on private estates at their own will; rather, it is necessary that they be obtained from the Prince <note>original: "l. 1. ff. de nundin."</note>. For it is well-established that the **right of solemn and public fairs** belongs to the **major regalia** <note>original: "Regalia majora"; sovereign rights held exclusively by the monarch</note>, according to the law <note>original: "l. un. ubi Sichard. C. de nund."</note>, which says that inferior princes do not have this in their own **regalia** <note>original: "Regalibus"</note> such that they could grant this privilege even in their own provinces <note>citing Gail, Bodin, Sixtin, and the Author of the Counter-Report of the Lordship of Wertheim</note>.

Common fairs, however, which we commonly call **weekly markets** <note>original: "Wochenmarckt"</note>, can be established and celebrated without such a privilege <note>original: "Sichard. ad rubr. C. de nund. n. 13."</note>. For they involve a matter of fact rather than a matter of law, since they lack the immunities and other prerogatives ascribed to solemn fairs <note>original: "Tessaur. decis. 364. n. 4."</note>. Therefore, in this context, the **market right** <note>original: "jus mercatus"</note> must be understood in its more powerful and legally proven sense—namely, as an **annual market** <note>original: "anniversario mercatu"</note>, which is among the **regalia** and requires the grant of the Supreme Prince. <note>original: "Græven. 2. concl. 60. cons. 1. n. 2. & 3."</note>

Because the **village of T.** is also a **market town** <note>original: "Marcktfleck"</note> and presumably has its own fixed annual fairs—which could not happen without a special Imperial favor—and since no other such rights are mentioned here except for the cited letters of enfeoffment and the privilege of the late **Emperor Wenceslaus** (which mentions the market right in almost the same wording), it is quite proper to conclude that the aforementioned word **market right** is to be understood as the **right of fairs** <note>original: "de jure Nundinarum"</note>.

Indeed, the **subsequent quality of possession** declares what the intention of the parties was from the beginning <note>original: "Posterior quippe qualitas possessionis declarat, quid à principio fuerit partium intentionis."</note>, and it is presumed that the Lord and the Vassal bound themselves to

<column-break/>

that which the following practice represents. <note>original: "Idem ibid. n. 50."</note> This is because subsequent practice is said to be the best interpreter of any act, and especially of feudal investitures. <note>original: "Menoch. cons. 32. num. 45."</note> Hence, when a doubt exists as to whether **jurisdiction** is included in the sale of a castle, one looks at what has been practiced: because a later act declares a prior deed, and the understanding should be taken as that which the effect and outcome of matters proves to be true. <note>original: "Jos. Lud. d. l. n. 6."</note>

One might nonetheless interpret this word **market right** as the **rights of a market town** <note>original: "Marckfleckens Gerechtsame"</note>, for that right also seems to require a singular Imperial grant. In the **Roman Empire**, the power to confer the spirit and life, or the **City Law** <note>original: "Stadtrecht" / "Jus Civitatis"</note>, upon a place belongs to the Emperor alone as a **major regale**. <note>original: "Obrecht. de Regal. c. 8. concl. 188."</note> On this matter, an illustrative example is cited of **Emperor Maximilian I**, who in the year 1514 prohibited **Count Albrecht of Mansfeld**—who presumed to grant city rights to a certain village—with these words:
> Since it is not fitting for you or
> anyone else to establish city rights or anything
> else that belongs to the high authority without
> special permission, we command, etc.
<note>original: "Bruning. de var. Univers. spec. Cluten. rer. quot. concl. 22. lit. d."</note>

This is so true that if anyone were to establish a city without the Emperor's consent (at least a tacit one), it would not truly be a city, nor could it usurp the rights of a city. <note>original: "Natta. consil. 636. n. 100."</note>

However, for our part, we cannot maintain that this is what is meant here, because the letter of enfeoffment reads: "That in the **village of T.** the **market right** is granted as a fief." Whereas, if His Imperial Majesty had intended to grant the entire right by which the said village of T. should be a market town, he presumably would not have placed the **market right of the village of T.** "in the village," etc. For it is one thing to grant a right **in** a certain place, and quite another to grant the right **of** the place itself. <note>original: "Aliud est enim, concedere jus in aliquo loco, aliud item est jus ipsius loci."</note>

Furthermore, the **city law** or the **rights of a market town** are not usually granted as a fief <note>original: "jure feudi"</note>, but by virtue of a **privilege**, which is given only once; it is not customary for it to be renewed like those things granted in feudal investitures.

Otherwise, this little word **market right** could be interpreted in several other ways, namely: (1) for **territorial right** <note>original: "pro jure Territorii"</note>, especially if *Marckt-recht* (as we find in some copies of the letters of enfeoffment and privileges) is written as something else <note>original: "non Marcktrecht scri-batur"</note>. And also (2) as the **right to establish statutes**. Regarding this latter meaning, **Johann Gryphiander** writes in *On the Saxon Municipal Law* <note>original: "de Weich-bild. Sax."</note> that the **market right** is this: that the market people...

# Thesauri Practici Adaucti.

In former times, people established laws among themselves by their own will, according to the Law of the Franks <note>original: "Carols-Recht"; referencing Carolingian law or the laws of Charlemagne</note>, such as those from Cologne across the Rhine, Magdeburg, and other significant cities. *And later, from a certain gloss on Saxon Law, he adds:* It is called city right <note>original: "Stadtrecht"</note> because each city chooses it for itself by divine instruction according to its own judgment, and such law is called a voluntary law <note>original: "willkore Recht"</note>. *From these examples, it likewise follows that Market Right, City Right, Voluntary Ordinance <note>original: "Willkühr"</note>, and Municipal Law <note>original: "Weichbild"</note> are synonymous.*

*However, this latter meaning appears to refer to Saxon customs, whereas the former meaning—found in the Scripture's phrasing of legal cases where "Market-Right" [Marcktrecht] rather than "Boundary-Right" [Marckrecht] is used—seems to conflict. Both definitions, however, should be rejected here because subsequent practice (namely that, as already mentioned, the village of T. possesses the privilege of a yearly fair) clearly determines what was actually granted.*

Similarly, the third and fourth parts of the fief, namely **Stock and Gallows** and the **Ban to judge over the blood** <note>original: "Stock und Galgen, auch Bann über das Blut zu richten"; these are traditional symbols and legal terms for high jurisdiction, including the power of capital punishment</note>, are clear in themselves. By this, it is undoubtedly understood that the **Vassals** <note>original: "Vasalli"</note>, by virtue of such **investiture** <note>formal grant of a fief</note>, shall have the power not only to pass judgment over blood but also to execute such sentences and to erect the usual **Signs of Execution** <note>original: "Signa"; such as gallows or pillars</note>. Otherwise, there might be some doubt whether a nobleman, even if he holds all authority but lacks these **Executive Signs** <note>original: "Signa executiva"</note>, may erect them himself. *Bidembach. quæst. nob. 14. Peguera decif. 81.* Thus, there are many *who restrict **Criminal Jurisdiction** only to the investigation of crimes and misdeeds, and separate it entirely from the execution of lawful punishments, which they call **High Jurisdiction** <note>original: "merum Imperium"; the supreme power of the sword</note>. Obrech. de Jurisd. cap. 3. num. 8. following, & cap. 7. num. 1.*

*And that **Execution**, which is a matter of physical action, is sometimes separated from **High Jurisdiction**, which consists in the investigation, the legal process, and the condemnation, as Denais also teaches at length in his dispute on the law of High Jurisdiction.*

*Hence, Criminal Jurisdiction can be held or retained even without the physical Sign [the gallows]; and thus the argument is invalid: "He does not have the gallows or the post; therefore, he lacks Criminal Jurisdiction." Just as, conversely, one is not said to have Criminal Jurisdiction simply because they possess a gallows or post. Meichsner. decis. 4. n. 159. vol. 2. book 1. For an argument based on accidental or accessory signs, such as the gallows, does not prove necessity. Natta cons. 636. num. 123. Keller. de offic. Jurisdict. Politic. book 2. chap. 15. And so it indeed usually happens that two judges in the same place have equal power in judging, and yet only one of them can carry out the execution and erect the gallows. Decian. in tract. Crim. book 4. chap. 41. num. 1. Græven. 2. conclus. d. 6. cons. 2. num. 16. There are places in the **Holy Roman Empire** <note>original: "Imperio Romano Germanico"</note> where one Estate has the investigation*

<column-break/>

*of criminal cases, while another has the sole power of execution.*

But the other part set down in this letter of enfeoffment (namely, the Court) we could not perceive otherwise than as referring to **Lower Jurisdiction** <note>original: "pro bassa Jurisdictione"; referring to civil matters and minor crimes as opposed to "high" or capital jurisdiction</note>, insofar as it is opposed to superior or high jurisdiction. *Which indeed includes not only those things commonly referred to as simple Jurisdiction, but also some of those considered to be of **Mixed Jurisdiction** <note>original: "mixti Imperii"; a middle ground of judicial authority</note>. Eberh. Speckh. cent. 1. quæst. 90. Coler. de process. executiv. p. 2. c. 1. n. 105. Matth. Steph. book 1. de Jurisd. c. 3. n. 70. Wehner under the words:* Court, High Court.

Thus, through these words—Court, Stock and Gallows, along with the Ban therein to judge over the blood—it is our indubitable assessment that not only the full **High Jurisdiction** <note>original: "Imperium"; consisting of both the investigation and execution of criminal cases</note>, but rather **all-encompassing Jurisdiction** <note>original: "omnimoda Jurisdictio"</note>, covering both high and low authority, is granted as a fief.

*For those things contained under separate designations cannot be considered the same thing. And this is the nature of separation and of things placed separately: that they induce a diversity of the matter, and one cannot be inferred from the other, according to common legal theory.* If one also intended, by this entire phrasing (Court, Stock and Gallows, along with the Ban to judge over the blood), to grant only **High Jurisdiction** and not also the **Lower Jurisdiction**, one could have easily omitted that little word "Court" <note>original: "Gericht"</note>, as the other terms would have been sufficient.

*Moreover, it is established that all words found in legal instruments, especially in **investitures**, are to be interpreted in such a way that they perform some function, so that none of them may be said to have been added idly or redundantly. Claud. Pratejus. de Reg. Jur. book 7. tit. 7. c. 2. pag. 895. Cravett. cons. 135. num. 24. Rol. à Valle cons. 54. num. 21. vol. 4. And that in the contracts or dispositions of men, not even the smallest word [should be ignored]. Gail. 2. observ. 28. Schrader. de feud. pag. 2. part 9. Sect. 3. num. 166. Gabriel Roman. book 3. title on buying and selling, conclusion 1. num. 54. Rol. à Vall. cons. 1. num. 123. & cons. 55. n. 45. vol. 3. Dec. cons. 626. num. 7. Indeed, not even a single syllable should be deprived of its legal weight, as Ulpian answers in the law "item veniunt 20.": there, a congruent interpretation must be adapted to each individual word of the Senate decree. Bald. ad rub. quæst. 9. ff. de contr. empt. Tiraq. de Retract. Convent. §. 1. gl. 2. num. 23.*

Similarly, if His Imperial Majesty had intended to interpret the preceding little word "Court" solely through the words "Stock and Gallows, along with the Ban to judge over the blood," and not rather to grant something further and more extensive than what was meant by the word "Court," he would have added another word, *to wit*,

<meta>catchword: namely (nemlich)</meta>

It emphasizes the legal principle that every word in a formal document must have a distinct, non-redundant meaning.</summary>

# Letter L.

namely, as etc. and not said: Court, Stock, and Gallows; Low Jurisdiction, that is, as, namely, etc. Stock and Gallows.

In particular, it would be quite strange if His Imperial Majesty intended the word **Court** <note>original: "Gericht"</note> to signify the high authority, <note>original: "sive potestatem in criminalibus causis"; meaning: "or the power in criminal cases"</note> the right to pass judgment, and only afterward chose to place these words together with the **Blood Ban** <note>original: "Bann über das Blut"; the legal authority to impose capital punishment</note>.

*Since indeed that expression "including" [samt] demonstrates that the former is something different from the latter (Deciani, Consultation 123). And the small word "including" joins and increases rather than explains what precedes it (Bartolus on the law "Gallus", where Jason confirms this).*

Most importantly, however, our opinion is strengthened by the fact that, although that little word **Court** has many and varied meanings, it is nevertheless commonly understood—especially in **Investitures** <note>the formal ceremony or document where a lord grants a fief to a vassal</note>—to refer to **Low Jurisdiction** <note>original: "niedere Gerichtbarkeit"; legal authority over minor crimes and civil disputes, excluding the power of execution</note>.

*For in cases of doubt, words ought to be understood according to the common custom of speaking (Cravetta, Consultation 9).*

*And even in a grant from the Prince, one must not depart from the proper meaning of the words (Romanus, Consultation 89; Cravetta, Consultation 29).*

*Indeed, there is no doubt that many legal doctors intend for the word "Court" to denote only simple jurisdiction or even "mixed power" [mixtum Imperium], and this is supported by legal reason (Meichsner, Decision 23; Menochio, Presumption 97).*

And although it is highly disputed whether the word **Court** in letters of **fief** <note>original: "Lehenbrieffen"; documents granting land and rights in exchange for service</note> is meant to include both High and Low Jurisdiction—as can be seen in the works of Schurff, Wesenbeck, Vultejus, and Rosenthal—it is rarely the case that the word "Court" alone is taken to mean High Jurisdiction to the exclusion of Low. More commonly, it is taken to mean **Low Jurisdiction** alone.

And although the following words are found in the Imperial letters: that they (the **Vassals**) should be impartial judges when exercising the Blood Ban, acting toward the rich as the poor, and the poor as the rich, without regard for courage, gifts, favor, fear, friendship, nor enmity, nor any other thing except just judgment and law as is proper, and in such a manner as they would wish to answer for it before Almighty God at the Last Judgment, etc.

<column-break/>

Yet it cannot be concluded from this that the Imperial Investiture is to be understood as referring solely to the **Criminal Court**, and specifically on the grounds that the aforementioned rule—regarding how the Vassals should exercise their feudal authority—is only noted in the context of the *exercise* of Criminal Courts. For such a **careful provision** <note>original: "solicite Provisio"</note> was added solely regarding **Criminal Jurisdiction** and its execution for this reason: **because where the danger is greater, one must act more cautiously.** A readier aid is needed where the opportunity for sinning is easier and more prone to harm, as the dictates of right reason themselves suggest.

Therefore, experience shows that where only Low Jurisdiction is granted, it is never customary to incorporate into the letters of fief instructions on how the Vassals should behave in the **administration** of such lower courts.

On the other hand, when the **Blood Ban** is given by His Imperial Majesty, or by Princes and other such high estates, **in the name of a fief** <note>original: "feudi nomine"</note>, such a reminder is always attached, and almost in the same words as in the present Investitures.

Indeed, even in those letters of fief where it is indisputable that both High and Low Authority are feudal, such a necessary **admonition** is nonetheless added only regarding the exercise of criminal jurisdiction. Nothing more is added for the Low Courts than what was mentioned at the beginning; such a form with all its content is inserted in the Ortenburg records against Bavaria. And the reason for this difference is obvious: because a loss caused by a sentence in **civil matters** can be repaired through appeal and recourse to a Superior; but in **criminal matters**, where by custom no appeal is granted, every loss burdens the accused permanently.

Thus, we also do not let ourselves be misled by what might be brought forward from King **Wenceslaus's** <note>Wenceslas IV (1361–1419), King of Bohemia and King of the Romans</note> diploma of the year 1394, which might seem to oppose our decision. In that document, the said King Wenceslaus graciously granted to the three brothers of B. (who were then living) as holders of the Lordship of S., that they may and shall have **Market Rights** and **Courts, Stock and Gallows** in their village of T.

Since the territory of S. was a lordship even before Wenceslaus and from ancient times, and as King Wenceslaus himself states, S. was already a fortress and had its own office at that time, a necessary conclusion must be made: that such a territory was graced by **allodial right** <note>original: "jure allodii"; land ownership that is absolute and not subject to a superior landlord</note> with some dignity, honor, and jurisdiction—at least Low Jurisdiction—just like other even lesser noble castles and villages in the land of **Swabia**, and specifically in the **Allgäu**, where S. is located.
