# Expanded Treasury of Practice

From this, it might further be inferred that—because King Wenceslaus first gave the **court** <note>original: "Gericht"</note> to the family of B. out of special grace—this should be understood as referring to high authority and the type of court which noble estates in those parts usually do not possess by their own right, but must obtain from the Roman King or Emperor through a singular concession or privilege. It would follow that this is not the same as the jurisdiction or court authority which the Lordship of S. presumably already held from ancient times by its own right as a lordship.

However, this can be answered in several ways: (1) It is to be presumed that the Lordship of S. was at all times adorned with every kind of jurisdiction; however, all of these together, both high and low authority (as happens with many principalities, counties, and lordships), must be recognized either by right of a **fief** <note>an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</note> or at least as a privilege from the Holy Roman Empire, and such privileges must be confirmed by every subsequent Roman Emperor.

Furthermore, it cannot be demonstratively concluded from this **diploma** <note>an official charter or document</note> that the market court and the **signs of execution** <note>original: "signa executiva"; physical symbols like gallows that represented the power to carry out the death penalty</note> were first given to the Lordship of S. or its associated market town T. by King Wenceslaus, and that they did not possess them before. Rather, it may well be that the family of B. had only then first come into possession of the aforementioned lordship, and therefore had their existing imperial privileges confirmed, or otherwise sought confirmation from Wenceslaus.

And although this does not appear expressly in the said concession of Wenceslaus, we know nevertheless that because of ancient simplicity, not everything was traditionally written with as much detail as is done now—especially by that Emperor, who, because of his laziness and reckless administration of the Empire, not only tarnished his own reputation but was also deposed from the Empire. Regarding this Emperor, <term>Rosacorb</term> <note>refers to a legal authority or author</note> writes in *Forensic Practice, chapter 83, number 13* that Wenceslaus sent out blank pieces of parchment, allowing anyone to write whatever they pleased upon them. He thus conducted such an intolerable reign that he was legitimately deposed by a sentence of the Estates of the Empire, and in his place, Rupert of the Palatinate was assumed into the government. This Rupert, on the advice of the princes, revoked and annulled all privileges and scripts of Wenceslaus while Wenceslaus was still living; therefore, no one can make use of those same privileges either in or out of court.

Secondly, nothing binding or useful to the present case can be deduced from this diploma of Wenceslaus because it is not a **Letter of Enfeoffment** <note>original: "Lehenbrief"; a document formally granting a fief</note>, but rather a privilege. By means of such privileges, Imperial Cities and even independent counties and lordships commonly hold and receive their **regalia** <note>rights or powers traditionally reserved for the sovereign</note>, high and low justice, and the 

<column-break/>

**Blood Ban** <note>original: "Blutbänn"; the legal authority to pass judgment resulting in bloodshed or execution</note> from the Holy Roman Empire.

On the other hand, the often-cited **Investiture** <note>the formal legal act of granting a fief</note> of the late Emperor Maximilian I is a true Letter of Enfeoffment, and it is much more detailed than Wenceslaus's diploma. Note that King Wenceslaus mentions only the market right and the court, stock, and gallows; however, in Emperor Maximilian’s Letter of Enfeoffment, these words are added: "along with the ban to judge over blood." This extension and addition, based on what was argued above, is of very great importance to the present question. It provides such clarification that the word **Court** <note>original: "Gericht"</note>—to avoid redundancy and the distasteful repetition of synonyms, and for other weighty reasons—must necessarily be interpreted as **Low Jurisdiction** <note>original: "bassa Jurisdictione"; authority over minor offenses and civil matters not involving the death penalty</note>.

Suppose, then (but not conceding), that the word "Court" in Wenceslaus's diploma was intended to mean criminal jurisdiction: it is still no necessary consequence that it must mean the same in the investiture of Maximilian I, which is much more extensive and clear. One cannot draw a sound inference between things that are different both in words and in legal fact. In the hundred years that passed between Wenceslaus's diploma and Emperor Maximilian I's investiture, many changes must have occurred regarding the Lordship of S. and the rights now in dispute. Consider that those very rights which Wenceslaus gave to the family of B. through a privilege and gift, without any mention of feudal recognition, were later received as a fief from Maximilian I by the family of B. Thus, in the meantime, these rights must have been converted into a fief or matured into a feudal state by some other means. Therefore, one should not look at what Wenceslaus gave by privilege, but at what subsequently became a fief. In the absence of the first investiture, this must be learned from the oldest available one, as argued above, without regard for what was contained in Wenceslaus's privilege. For even if the **bailiwick authority** <note>original: "Vogteylich Obrigkeit"</note> had been owned outright in Wenceslaus's time, it could well be that it later became an Imperial fief; it was common for noble neighbors, princes, and other Estates of the Empire to sometimes turn their castles, villages, or even just one or two specific types of jurisdiction into a fief.

Let it suffice that it has been shown that in the investiture of Maximilian I, the word "Court" is to be understood as Low Jurisdiction according to a more sound interpretation of the words. Therefore, there is no longer any room for the conjectures (of which many different ones were suggested in the Information at number 123, primarily derived from Wenceslaus's diploma).

And to touch upon this further: although the word "Court," when spoken in the singular number, refers to a...

<meta>This page continues the legal argument from page 606, further analyzing whether the term "Court" in historical grants refers specifically to criminal jurisdiction or encompasses civil authority as well.</meta>

Lit. L.

A regular jury-court <note>original: "Schöpffenstuhl"; a traditional panel of lay judges or "scabini" who declared the law</note> or a formal, closed assembly and convention of a magistrate, governor, or judge, along with his associated assessors, assistants, and sworn court officials—as is understood and learned from the terms: Land, Court, City, Market, Village, Forest, Cent <note>original: "Cent"; a regional court with jurisdiction over capital crimes</note>, Penalty, Honor, Guest, Damage, Man, Bailiff, or Mayoral court, etc. However, it does not follow from this that the aforementioned word "Court" should be interpreted as a criminal court, but rather as a civil court. Specifically, because civil matters are also decided by such a court, and the faculty to arrange a criminal court is already sufficiently—indeed, redundantly—indicated by the following words: "the ban to judge over blood" <note>original: "Bann über das Blut zu richten"; the legal authority to impose the death penalty</note>. Therefore, if the word "Court" were meant only as the power to hold a criminal trial <note>original: "pro facultate Criminale judicium"</note> or a capital court <note>original: "Halsgericht"</note>, it would have been unnecessary. For this reason, it must signify something other than the power to judge over blood: *namely, jurisdiction over civil causes, and the power of judging within them* <note>original: "Civilium nempe caufarum Jurisdictionem, in iisque judicandi potestatem"</note>.

In the same way, it is no error that the Lord of S. transferred his half-share of the Lordship of S. to the Lords of E. by sale in the year 1582—in a sense contrary to our decision—stating that all authority was his own property, and only the market rights, court, and the ban to judge over blood, along with the stocks and gallows, etc., were Imperial Fiefs <note>original: "Reichs-Lehen"; land or rights held directly from the Emperor</note>. Likewise, the great-uncle <note>original: "Patruus magnus"</note> and grandfather <note>original: "Avus"</note> of V., namely Hans Ulrich and Dionysius von V., held their own half, along with their feudal regalia <note>royal rights or privileges</note>, in the same regard.

For all of this—*being matters conducted between other parties, and indeed prohibited to the vassal under penalty of forfeiture* <note>original: "tanquam res inter alios actæ, imò sub pœna Caducitatis Vasallo prohibite"; "caducitas" refers to the loss of a fief if the vassal violates feudal law</note> (specifically when a feudal matter *is either sold or possessed as if it were personal property* <note>original: "pro allodiali"</note>)—can in no way be harmful or a hindrance to a third party, *and especially not to the Imperial Treasury or the Lord of the Fief*.

In this regard, it must also be carefully noted that the aforementioned deed of sale cites the *words of investiture* <note>the formal language used when granting a fief</note> somewhat inconsistently, claiming that only the market rights, court, and the ban to judge over blood, along with the stocks and gallows, are Imperial Fiefs. It is reported in the instrument of sale *as if* "Court" and "Ban to judge" were *explicitly placed together and synonymously* <note>original: "tanquam disertè conjunctim, und συνωνύμως posita essent"</note>. However, this does not occur at all in the letter of fief from Emperor Maximilian (which is cited as the source); rather, a far different *arrangement of words* <note>original: "politus verborum"</note> is observed. Specifically, it says there: "Court, Stocks, and Gallows, together with the ban to judge over blood." *In that phrasing*, "Court" is not *joined by any conjunction* with the "ban to judge over blood," but is instead separated and distinguished *by the insertion* of the words "Stocks and Gallows." Furthermore, the little word "together with" is added not to "Stocks and Gallows," but to the phrase "ban to judge over blood."

<column-break/>

Now, since it follows from what has just been deduced that at T., all jurisdiction—both high and low court—are Imperial Fiefs: it further follows that all rights there *which savor of the nature of jurisdiction or command, and cannot be exercised by a private person by their own authority and right of ownership, but are considered to require the grant of a superior, and especially an Imperial concession (such as are all those rights commonly called Regalia)* <note>sovereign rights like minting coins or collecting tolls</note>, or those which have been raised, established, and introduced *anew* by the possessors of the Lordship of S. *by the power and pretext of all-encompassing jurisdiction*, are indisputably and in every way feudal. *This is especially so since the increase of a thing is governed by the nature of the principal thing, and is deemed to be one with the principal, particularly when no different reasoning exists. (Citing Menochius, legal counsel 26, number 35; and counsel 201, number 145, etc.)*

*This is also supported by the text in the law regarding legacies* <note>original: "l. cum fundus de legat. 2."</note>, where an addition made to a bequeathed estate yields to the benefit of that estate, even if the addition was made while the testator was still living. *From this it is usually gathered that an addition becomes the property of whoever owns the principal thing; and following this text, Angelus taught in the laws regarding customs and dowries.* If a Prince granted jurisdiction in a Castle, so that it might later be expanded, the jurisdiction is extended even to the addition. *Angelus* was followed by *Jason (book 1, number 15, on the jurisdiction of all judges)* and also by *Brunus (treatise on additions, conclusions 9 and 17).* And so, where a title of personal acquisition <note>original: "allodialis"</note> does not appear, an addition united to a fief is considered feudal. *Baldus (in his work on the fiefs of the deceased, against Schrader) cites to this effect William Benedict (regarding testaments)*, and the same is concluded by *Ludovicus à Molina (treatise on primogeniture, book 1, chapter 26, number 6)* regarding *Majoratu* <note>an inheritance that stays with the eldest son to keep the estate intact</note>.

*Improvements as well, and those things which were established for the perpetual use of a feudal property, take on the nature of that for whose sake they were made. (Tiraquellus, on the right of proximity, section 36; Pistor, book 2, question 42).*

*All these things rest on the reasoning that the more worthy thing draws the less worthy thing to itself. (Wesenbeck, legal counsel 4, number 69, book 1).* And what a *Vassal* prescribes by reason of a fief, when the fief is opened <note>vacant</note>, all of that likewise returns to the Lord. *(Molina, on the Customs of Paris, section 7, number 30).*

Therefore, we cannot conclude otherwise than that the toll and the forest, insofar as these rights are exercised in the village of T. or its boundaries, are simultaneously held as fiefs.

*For although under a general grant of all-encompassing jurisdiction, the other Regalia <note>royal rights</note> are not contained (because they are only granted specifically by the Prince), (Zasius on Fiefs, page 5; Obrecht on Jurisdiction, chapter 1).*

Thom.

# Augmented Treasury of Practical Law

### Thomas Michael, Disputation on Jurisdiction, Thesis 68.
Likewise, although the law of the forest <note>original: "jus forestae"</note> or forest jurisdiction is not understood to be included under a grant of "mere empire" <note>original: "merum imperium"; the highest level of criminal jurisdiction, including the power of capital punishment</note>—since these are diverse and separate things with their own distinct and essential differences—see Joachim Mynsinger, Response 16, numbers 46 and 47; Noë Meurer, *On Hunting and Forest Rights* <note>original: "von Jag- und Forstrechten"</note>, part 2, rubric: "whether the forest pertains to the high authority," folio 32; Meichsner, Decision 4, number 7, volume 2, book 2; Gylman, *Symphorema*, volume 2, part 3, title 10, volume 2, numbers 29, 30, and 31.

However, it does not follow to the contrary that when a vassal <note>original: "Lehenmann"</note> makes use of a toll or a forest while the jurisdiction is held in feudal tenure, that in such a case the tax and forest law should be considered allodial <note>original: "allodiale"; property held in absolute ownership, independent of a feudal superior</note> and not feudal. Just as one cannot conclude: "This man has a convenient jurisdiction, therefore he may also seize the Regalia" <note>original: "Regalia"; the crown's exclusive rights or prerogatives, such as minting coins or collecting certain taxes</note>, so it seems correctly concluded that if an all-encompassing feudal jurisdiction exists, the lord also obtains the Royal Rights that are seen to belong to it. For an even greater reason, the duty and hereditary homage <note>original: "Pflicht und Erbhuldigung"</note> in this our case can be said to be feudal. For it is established in the legal texts that those living in a place where someone holds high and low criminal jurisdiction <note>original: "merum & mixtum Imperium"</note> are bound to provide an oath of fidelity. To this pertains what Barthélemy de Chasseneuz says: he who holds "high justice" <note>original: "haut justice"</note> can say that the people are his, and that he is the Lord of that land.

Similarly, although jurisdiction—whether superior or inferior—has nothing in common with the services and labor of peasants <note>original: "servitiis & operis Rusticanorum"</note>, especially those of serfs <note>original: "hominum propriorum"</note>, unless those services are owed by some other law or are expressly granted in the Investitures <note>original: "Investituris"; the formal legal documents granting a fief</note>. See Daniel Moller, *Semestrium*, book 2, chapter 32, number 1; Knichen, *On Enfeoffment*, pact 3, number 1.

Nevertheless, those services which are demanded by power of jurisdiction, rather than by the right of serfdom <note>original: "Leibeigenschaft"</note>, can be said without error to pertain to the feudal grant of jurisdiction. In that case, they are included under the name of "forced labor" and "extraordinary labor" <note>original: "Angariarum & Parangariarum"; terms derived from Roman law for compulsory transport or labor services</note>. Sixtin, *On Royal Rights*, book 2, chapter 13; Tuschus, letter A, folio 330.

Entirely different from these are the labors that descend not from jurisdiction, but from manumission, contract, or long-standing custom <note>original: "praescriptione"</note>, and these are not thought to make a person a subject. Forster, *On Roman Jurisdiction*, part 2, annotation to the law, number 162 and following; Sichard, on the Code, title "On the labor of freedmen"; Knichen, *On Investiture*, book 2, chapter 3; Petrus Friderus, *On Mandates*, book 2, chapter 46, number 5.

However, it must be especially well-noted here that these rights now being discussed are not feudal throughout the entire Lordship of S., nor in its other towns, but are feudal solely and exclusively in the Village of T. This is exactly what the literal content of the oldest letter of enfeoffment <note>original: "Lehenbrieff"</note> that

<column-break/>

one may find brings with it quite clearly and expressly, where it is set down: "In the village of T., situated in the Lordship of S., market rights, court, etc."

Now, a Lordship <note>original: "Herrschafft"</note> is one thing, and a Village <note>original: "Dorff"</note> situated within such a Lordship is another. For they differ entirely, as a part differs from a whole. And what is stated about a part individually must not be extended to the whole, especially regarding the extent of territory. Matthias Stephanus, *Legal Dialectics*, book 2, location 14, numbers 10, 13, and following.

This is especially true if the entities are separate, each of which constitutes a whole by itself—as in our case, every village and hamlet has its own specific boundaries <note>original: "Marcken"</note> and is distinguished from others. In such a case, an argument from the part to the whole, or from one part to another part, is not valid. The argument that applying a feudal quality to the whole would contain a rigor repugnant to equity is taught by Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 15, number 4; he says this rigor is contrary to natural liberty and equity, and proves it with many authorities.

Furthermore, since the feudal rights <note>original: "Lehenbare Jura"</note> are specifically restricted and confined by the words "to the Village of T. situated in the Lordship of S.," it follows undeniably from this that such rights are not to be drawn further, or applied to the entire Lordship. Rather, the other places within the lordship are excluded; consequently, all rights that have been exercised and used outside of T. until now are allodial <note>original: "allodial und eigen"</note> and owned outright.

For the inclusion of one thing is the exclusion of the other, and vice versa.

And every legal provision including a certain place or thing excludes the remaining ones, as Ruinus fully teaches in counsel 112, number 3, book 5.

Added to this is that it is not permitted to restrict nor to extend the tenor of an Investiture, but one must accept and interpret its words exactly as they sound. Baldus, on chapter 1, number 1; Rolandus, counsel 67, number 1, volume 1; Schürpf, counsel 98, century 1; Wesenbeck, counsel 60, number 11, part 2; Pistor, question 1, part 1, number 4; Knichen, *On Enfeoffment*, part 2, chapter 1, number 61, etc.

For an Investiture itself is a matter of "strict law" <note>original: "stricti Juris"; meaning it must be interpreted narrowly according to the letter of the text</note>, as Wesenbeck notes in the cited location, and a fief must be interpreted strictly. The words are to be taken as they lie, and nothing external is to be understood or assumed. Rosenthal, chapter 1, conclusion 5. In cases of doubt, the words of investitures receive an interpretation more in favor of the Vassal and against the Lord, as noted by the interpreters of the law on agreements <note>original: "de pactis"</note>.

# Letter L.

Hence, although whenever the greater part of an estate is feudal, and the remainder is part of that same whole, it is presumed—provided no other title appears—to be of the same feudal nature; nevertheless, this presumption is considered overturned by stronger proof when specific feudal parts are listed in the grant <note>original: "concessione"</note>. For in that case, it is understood that the others are not feudal, according to Rosenthal, chapter 10, conclusion 43, number 26. He adds: this is also the case when the investiture <note>original: "Investitura"; the formal ceremony or document granting a fief</note> or recognition states: "The Count of B. has received the feudal pieces and the high jurisdiction <note>original: "Blutbann"; literally the 'blood ban,' the power of capital punishment</note> in the aforementioned County of B. as a fief." Certainly, the entire County, nor even a large or major part of it, can be presumed to be feudal. But if a declaration is made regarding two or more things existing in that County, stating they are feudal, or if the vassal <note>original: "Vasallus"</note> or his heir asserts that two things located there are feudal and says he is unsure about the others but believes them to be allodial <note>original: "allodiales"; property owned outright without a feudal lord</note>, the burden of proof falls upon the Lord of the Fief <note>original: "Domino feudi"</note> if he seeks other things as feudal beyond those demonstrated and confessed. This is because things are presumed to be allodial rather than feudal, even if they are Counties or jurisdictions.

It is also correct that the jurisdiction <note>original: "Jurisdictio"</note> in a lordship, town, village, fortress, etc.—especially that which is called <term>bailiwick authority</term> <note>original: "Vogteylich Bottmässigkeit"; the legal power of a protector or bailiff over a territory</note>, and in case of doubt is held to be allodial—can be transferred to another person by many titles other than a feudal one. See Tiraquellus on the law *if ever* <note>original: "l. si unquam"</note>, under the word "bestowed by donation," number 338; Menochius, Counsel 191, number 24, volume 2; Bursatus, Counsel 46, number 10, volume 1.

So too are the noble estates in Swabia commonly situated so that they have the aforementioned low jurisdiction <note>original: "bassam Jurisdictionem"; legal authority over minor civil and criminal matters, excluding capital crimes</note>. It is also nothing new that in a district or lordship only a certain spot, or several particular estates, or certain specific rights are granted as a fief, or otherwise become feudal, while everything else (estates as well as jurisdictional and similar rights) remains true allodial property.

And since it is factually correct that a lordship existed long ago—many years even before specific feudal rights were defined in the Imperial feudal letter <note>original: "Lehenbrieff"</note> of Maximilian I (as the mention of the fief itself indicates)—it follows quite conclusively that the same lordship held the rights, high authorities, and sovereignties belonging to a lordship in all places of its associated territory, and thus in each and every village and hamlet. These rights, as well as the lordship itself, are to be considered allodial and one's own, except for those rights mentioned in Emperor Maximilian I’s feudal letter concerning the village of T.

And it does not lead us astray that in the new investitures—especially after the lordship of S. was separated into two parts—it is commonly stated that the market rights, court, stocks and gallows, together with the authority to judge blood <note>original: "Marcktrecht, Gericht, Stock und Galgen, mit samt dem Bann über das Blut zu richten"</note> in the village of T., located in

<meta>Besold, Volume I.</meta>

<column-break/>

the whole lordship of S., are held as a fief from the Roman Empire. For such words do not imply at all that the entire lordship of S., or the jurisdiction within it, is feudal; rather, they signify that the often-mentioned village of T. is situated within the whole lordship of S., and the jurisdiction therein is granted as a fief to each co-owner according to their due portion and as much as belongs to them.

Firstly, the grammatical sense <note>original: "Grammaticus sensus"</note> even of that formula found in the most recent Imperial investitures (as just indicated) does not allow the feudal rights expressed in the feudal letters to be extended further than to the village of T., because the words "In the village of T." sufficiently provide the restriction we are arguing for here.

Moreover, the words "situated in the whole lordship of S.," etc., may not be interpreted in a sound sense <note>original: "sano sensu"</note> to mean that the indicated village of T. extends through the entire lordship; for this is contrary to the very notoriety of the facts.

Accordingly, the words "in the whole lordship of S." are to be understood in no other way than that the often-mentioned village of T. is located within the entire lordship of S., and thus belongs equally to both holders of such a lordship, and the said rights are feudal in that entire village.

Even if this should unexpectedly be understood differently, one should look not to the younger, but rather to the older investitures, as in them no mention is made of the whole lordship alone, but the feudal jurisdictional rights are predicated only of the village of T. But in feuds, the first investiture is always to be regarded as the root of everything <note>original: "At in feudis semper prima Investitura tanquam radix omnium est attendenda"</note>, as Baldus says in chapter 1, volume 2; Alexander, Counsel 9, number 12, volume 1; Decius, Counsel 53. And the first investiture must be so strictly observed that this holds true even if it is contrary to the nature of the fief, as taught by Baldus and others.

And hence all following investitures are said to have a relation to the first, and are deemed to be made for confirmation, not for the derogation <note>original: "derogationem"; the partial repeal or weakening of a law or grant</note> of the first preceding one. Therefore, they cannot produce a contrary effect or a derogation. See the law on legacies uselessly given <note>original: "l. legata inutiliter"</note>, Digest, *on legacies*, 1.

And although the very first investiture concerning this fief is not present, nonetheless one stands by the oldest of those that can be had, and the earlier ones are presumed to agree with it, according to Boërius, Decision 24, number 62; Menochius, Counsel 1, number 83; and others. And one must, with this oldest...

<meta>This page continues the legal assessment of whether the jurisdiction over the village of T. and the lordship of S. is feudal or allodial (owned outright). The previous page established that if a grant specifically lists certain feudal parts, other parts of the same estate are presumed to be allodial.</meta>

The investiture <note>original: "Investitur"; the formal ceremony or document by which a lord granted a fief to a vassal</note> shall remain in effect until it is demonstrated on the part of the Feudal Lord that a contrary agreement was reached through a specific convention, entered into with the intent of renewing or changing the original investiture.

According to all of this, we remain of the final opinion regarding this **Question** that, although there are some specific feudal rights <note>original: "Jura feudalia"</note> named in the feudal letters within the village of T., this fief cannot and should not be extended or drawn beyond T. into the remaining market towns and the entire territory of the Lordship of S. in any way.

## Question Two.

Regarding the second question, which is otherwise quite doubtful in its own right, we—omitting the reasons for doubt, as they may be more conveniently refuted while strengthening our own opinion—conclude decisively and unanimously that the above-mentioned feudal rights are inseparably attached to the ownership, and are of a certain kind: that is, they are **purely hereditary fiefs**, alienable <note>original: "alienabilia"; able to be sold or transferred</note>, and transmissible to any heirs.

To be sure, we cannot, in this instance, rely so strongly upon the privilege most graciously granted by the late Emperor Rudolph II (of most glorious memory) to the Noble Free Knighthood of the Swabian lands in the year 1609. By virtue of that privilege, the sovereignty and the Blood Ban <note>original: "Blutbann"; the right of a lord to exercise capital punishment, often symbolized by a sword</note>, which are held as a fief from the Holy Empire, shall not be separated from such estates; it also states that the market town of T., along with all its appurtenances, is a Noble estate and incorporated into the Free Imperial Knighthood. However, the aforementioned privilege was drafted for a different type of case, as the specific wording implies: one where it is not "every kind of jurisdiction" <note>original: "non omnimoda Jurisdictio"</note> that is held, but only the Blood Ban and the High Court or its symbols held as a fief from the Holy Roman Empire.

<margin>Knichen, *On the Law of Territory*, chapter 1, number 254 and many following; and *On Investiture Agreements*, chapter 1, number 67, part 2. Moditius, § Privilege, questions 23 and 34.</margin>
It is well-established, however, that the favors granted by Princes are to be interpreted broadly, provided they do not concern matters of jurisdiction or similar powers.

But nonetheless, we are of the opinion that this feudal right <note>original: "Lehenbare Gerechtigkeit"</note> is hereditary and transmissible to any heirs, and is at the same time an inseparable appurtenance of the allodial <note>original: "allodial"; property held in absolute ownership, without a feudal superior</note> domain or territory of S.

<margin>Zafius, *On Fiefs*, part 4, number 6. Everhard, *On Fiefs and Emphyteusis*, column 3, and elsewhere. Mynsinger testifies to the common opinion in century 4, observation 2. Fichard in his additions to Villa, letter f.</margin>
We are moved to this conclusion first because legal scholars commonly hold that, in cases of doubt, a fief is presumed to be hereditary—that is, transmissible to any heirs.

<column-break/>

[...number 15.] Thomas Marinus, in the treatise *On the Nature and Quality of Fiefs*, preface, number 52. Bursatus, consultation 3, number 4, where he also notes this is the more common opinion. All the aforementioned authors say this holds true especially when there are clues present that strengthen this presumption and make it more probable; many such clues are found in our present case, as will appear clearly in the following, God willing.

Secondly, it is especially important to note that it was not the territory itself—namely, the Lordship of S. or a share of it—nor the village of T. that was granted as a fief, but only the jurisdiction within them. Conversely, it is correct and indeed beyond dispute that the territory, both of the entire Lordship of S. and of the village of T. situated within it, along with the people living there, is held allodially <note>owned outright</note> and is not feudal at all. As a piece of property, it has not only been sold several times but was also acquired and brought into possession by the Barons of E. under that very same title of purchase.

Therefore, it follows that whoever lawfully acquires the indicated land and soil also necessarily possesses the full jurisdiction and the Regalia <note>original: "Regalia"; the royal rights or prerogatives of a sovereign, such as minting coins or high justice</note> by right of an inseparable accessory—though with the burden that they must recognize it from the Empire as a fief and perform the usual services in that name. For these rights by their nature inseparably adhere to the territory, and can neither belong to nor be due to a person without the territory.

<margin>Menochius, book 3, *On Presumptions*, number 6. Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 6, number 7. Hart. Pistor, book 2, question 42, number 44. Petr. Frideric. Mindanus, book 3, chapter 20, numbers 24 and 26.</margin>
For although jurisdiction is something distinct from the territory itself, that difference is nevertheless only conceptual <note>original: "rationalis"</note>, and by no means a physical <note>original: "realis"</note> reality, especially according to our customs. Here, jurisdiction is not granted by the Right of Magistracy but resides in the lands themselves and cannot be separated from them—just as a service is attached to the soil, or as a seal is part of the wax. <margin>Baldus, consultation 322. Jurisdiction is above the territory as a mist is above a marsh through active power. Baldus, title *On the Peace of the Realm*. Socinus, consultation 34. Jason, book 1. Cravetta, consultation 411. Tuschus, letter I, conclusion 543.</margin> And therefore, if the territory is divided, the jurisdiction is by no means separated but is instead broken into pieces along with the parts, as Castrensis notes. Hence, Bartolus teaches that jurisdiction alone cannot be sold without the castle or place to which it clings.

Nor is it a contradiction that legal commentators everywhere teach that allodial jurisdiction is united to a feudal castle as if to a body. This principle only serves to ensure that, in a case of doubt, this union does not take anything away <note>original catchword: "detra-" (detractum)</note> from either feudal or allodial law.

It establishes that such jurisdiction is hereditary and cannot be separated from the physical land.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the lordship of S. and the village of T., specifically focusing on the legal principle that jurisdiction (the right to administer justice) is naturally and legally tied to the land itself (the territory), rather than being a separate, detachable right.</meta>

# Lit. L.
### H h h h 2

...it should be considered that the rights of both the **Vassal** and the **Lord** remain secure. Just as the direct ownership <note>original: "directum Dominium"</note> of these jurisdictional matters by the Holy Roman Empire remains intact and preserved <note>original: "sartum tectum"</note>, even if these rights follow the allodial territory <note>land owned outright, not held from a lord</note> as inseparable accessories.

Furthermore, although one might argue from "possibility" to "reality"—that is, that Jurisdiction *could* be added to a territory separately, and therefore *must* have been added separately—this argument does not hold. For this reason, **Capicius** in *Decision 27, number 36* specifically teaches that just because it is possible for one person to be the Lord regarding Jurisdiction and its revenues while another is Lord regarding the territory and its produce, it does not immediately follow that Jurisdiction does not naturally cling to the territory, or that the matter stands that way in every case. This is especially true here, where many factors coincide to imply a hereditary and inseparable union of the Jurisdiction with the territory.

As a general rule, where a difference is not expressly apparent, Jurisdiction is considered to be inherent in the Territory, as noted by **Boerius** in *Decision 227, number 7*. It is reputed to be annexed to any territory, at least by custom, as taught by **Anchoranus** in *Consultation 42, number 3*, and **Gylman** in *Judicial Matters, book 1, decision 1, number 174 and following*. In this view, a territory is defined as a space of land fortified by jurisdiction, according to **Baldus** in the section on royal rights, **Meichsner** in *Decision 6*, and **Petrus Friderus** in *Contested Cases, chapter 20, number 31*.

Although a Territory can occasionally exist without Jurisdiction, Jurisdiction cannot be exercised without a Territory, because it is bounded by that Territory. This is argued by **Bartolus**, **Baldus**, and the doctors of law in their commentaries on Jurisdiction. **Sapia**, at number 63, states that the common legal resolution is that jurisdiction is "passively and materially" present within the Territory.

Indeed, Jurisdiction is considered to regard the Territory to such an extent that if the Jurisdiction ceases, the Territory is also said to cease to exist in a legal sense, according to **Baldus** in *Consultation 202, book 2*.

Therefore, in cases of doubt, Jurisdiction is presumed to have been granted by the Prince along with the Territory, as noted by **Bartolus** and followed by **Alexander** in *Consultation 7, number 10, book 5*.

It is also a point of certain Law that whoever acquires a Territory—whether by a universal or a singular title—also acquires the Jurisdiction clinging to that Territory. This is supported by **Boerius**, **Natta**, **Covarrubias**, and **Faber de Monte** in his treatise on *Buying and Selling*.

And this is so true that for the person to whom a Territory is transferred by any title, not only is

<column-break/>

simple Jurisdiction acquired, but also **High and Low Justice** <note>original: "Merum & Mixtum Imperium"; the 'Merum' or 'Pure' empire refers to the power of the sword and capital punishment, while 'Mixtum' or 'Mixed' refers to civil and minor criminal authority</note> clinging to the Territory. **Natta**, **Paulus de Castro**, and **Molinaeus** attest that this is the commonly received opinion. Furthermore, royal rights <note>original: "Regalia"</note> clinging to the Territory—such as public rivers and the like—also pass to the person who acquires the Territory by any title, as taught by **Caepolla**, **Jacobus de Sancto Georgio**, and **Alciatus**. The same applies to taxes already imposed or established, as well as the right to collect road tolls <note>original: "pedagium"</note> already in effect, and the right to confiscate the goods of condemned criminals.

**Thirdly**, this inseparability should take hold all the more so that both the Sovereign Rights <note>original: "Regalia"</note> and other jurisdictional matters are not separated in such a way that one person holds the Territory and another holds the Jurisdictional rights. There are countless territories and noble estates to be found that are otherwise owned outright <note>original: "eigen"</note>, but where only the Jurisdiction is held as a fief <note>original: "Lehenbar"</note>. In such cases, over time—to the great loss of the nobility, the lineages, and the subjects themselves—the estates and the authority would be torn away from each other in the manner of Pentheus <note>A reference to the Greek King Pentheus, who was torn limb from limb; used here to describe the destructive fragmentation of a lordship</note>. This would necessarily lead to and spring forth into innumerable disputes, misunderstandings, and discord.

Furthermore, the reasoning and methods so highly boasted of by **V.**—with which he, as the holder of the other half of the **Lordship of S.**, sought the consolidation of the entire Jurisdiction from **His Imperial Majesty** as the Feudal Lord—would also not hold up. He has already obtained an "expectancy" <note>original: "Expectanz"; a legal claim to future possession or succession</note> in the event of the future death of the **Countess of R.** (though, as is fair and cannot be otherwise by law, this is without prejudice to the better rights held by the aforementioned Countess). Instead, countless new disputes would arise immediately after the Countess’s death, particularly regarding the separation of what is held as a fief and what is owned outright. In that case (even assuming the pieces named in the feudal letters are held as a "feud by agreement and providence"), there would be a very difficult struggle over what belongs to the feudal rights and what should remain with the heirs of the allodial property.

Even more difficulties will arise in the future, day by day, and also for the Imperial...

# Augmented Practical Treasury
### H h h h 2

...His Majesty, under his most noble Imperial Aulic Council <note>The *Reichshofrat*, one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, would be constantly approached and troubled if every person involved were to administer and keep what is theirs (as is to be expected), and if no one were willing to yield to another or sell their right or share.

A true matter of litigation, however, would primarily be this: that the Jurisdiction <term>Jurisdiction: the legal power to administer justice and govern</term> does not apply to the entire Lordship, but is held as a fief <note>original: "Lehenbar"</note> only in the village of T., while in the remaining estates it is allodial <note>land owned outright, not held from a superior lord</note> or owned as one's own. Indeed, countless disputes of this kind, with almost identical circumstances, were experienced with the Lordship of Mündelheim, <note>original: "quæ sanè controversia non solùm summa Imperii Tribunalia, ipsámque S. S. Cæsaream Majestatem, aliósque Imperii Summantes diutinè divexavit, sed & Præclarissimorum Ingenia exercuit mirè."</note> which controversy surely troubled the highest Tribunals of the Empire, the Sacred Imperial Majesty himself, and other leaders of the Empire for a long time, and remarkably exercised the minds of the most illustrious thinkers.

And likewise, examples of litigation are encountered everywhere where the forms of the Empire are confused rather than properly mixed—namely, where types of jurisdiction, or rights reflecting jurisdiction and superiority, are torn apart and separated by privilege or custom. <note>original: "Ac item ubivis exempla litium obvia sunt, ubi confuse potiùs quàm ritè mixtæ sunt Imperii formæ, puta, ubi distractæ & separatæ ex Privilegio vel consuetudine sunt vel species jurisdictionis, vel Jurisdictionem & superioritatem redolentia Jura."</note> This was sufficiently experienced between the noble Imperial Chamber Court <note>The *Reichskammergericht*</note> and the city of Speyer, as well as in the affairs of the city of Friedberg against its Burgrave, etc. Yet, if the Territory remains separated into two equal parts as it has been until now and shall be hereafter, all these disputes can be avoided. This is because the long-established observance and <note>original: "consuetudo, quæ in alteram quasi transit naturam"</note> custom, which passes as it were into a second nature, facilitates and makes easier the administration of this shared Lordship in many ways. Many territories can be found that are such "joint lordships" <note>original: "gesamte Herrschafften," referring to *Ganerbschaft* or shared inheritance</note> and are governed without special conflict. This is because among our learned doctors of law <note>original: "apud Dd. [Doctores] nostros"</note>, almost all disputes and doubts that arise in such common lordships are already found to be reasonably decided, <note>original: "ut videre est apud Borell. de Magistrat... Covarruv... Modest. Pistor... Jacob. Werner. Killinger. de Ganerb... Pacian. de probat..."</note> as can be seen in the works of Borellus, Covarruvias, Modestinus Pistoris, Jacob Werner Killinger on Shared Inheritances, Pacianus, and others.

Fourth, it is an unquestionable legal doctrine <note>original: "quod in judicatione, an feudum aliquod proprium aut hæreditarium sit, tunc inprimis inspici debeat mos & consuetudo Regionis."</note> that in judging whether a certain fief is "proper" [feudal] or hereditary, the habit and custom of the region should be inspected first. <note>original: "Natura enim feudorum confiderari dupliciter potest, nempe secundum Jus Feudale scriptum, & secundum mores ac consuetudines Regionum"</note> For the nature of fiefs can be considered in two ways: according to the written Feudal Law, and according to the habits and customs of the regions, as noted by Thomas Marinus in his treatise on fiefs.

And indeed, this nature of the Fief according to the custom of the Region ought to be attended to more than that which follows the written Law, as decided by Guido Papæ following Hostiensis. <note>original: "Et hæc quidem natura Feudi, secundum morem Regionis attendi magis debet, quàm illa, quæ est secundum Jus scriptum..."</note>

Now, however, in the Holy Roman Empire, it is a nearly universal custom regarding both Earldoms and Lordships, as well as free noble estates, that when only the Regal Rights <term>Regalia: royal rights or prerogatives granted by the sovereign</term>, the Blood-ban <term>Blood-ban: "Blutbann," the right to exercise high jurisdiction involving capital punishment</term>, and other

<column-break/>

jurisdictional matters are held as fiefs, but the territory itself is not conceded or granted as a fief under a collective name (such as Land, Castle, Town, Village, County, or Lordship), then whoever acquires the territory by another specific title (such as purchase, exchange, etc.) is invested <note>Investiture: the formal ceremony of being granted a fief</note> or enfeoffed without contradiction and upon the mere written notice of the previous Vassal. Consequently, this "request for investiture" <note>original: "requisitio Investituræ"</note> is regarded as nothing other than a mere request <note>original: "pro nudâ requisitione"</note> to hold and use such rights by the favor of the Emperor or another Superior. Indeed, it has happened frequently and without number that Counties, Lordships, or free noble estates have been sold to persons of higher or lower rank—even to clergy or cities—and these buyers were immediately enfeoffed with the jurisdictional rights, even without requesting any consent from the agnates <note>male-line relatives who would typically have a say in feudal transfers</note>. This fact is notorious in all places and could be proven with many examples.

Fifth, regarding these fiefs, it must also be considered that only the persons currently possessing the territory are ever invested, and no mention is made of descendants or feudal heirs. From this, it is again to be noted that these feudal jurisdictional rights are of such a nature <note>original: "ut non hæredes feudales, sed quoscunque Territorii possessores vel Dominos subsequantur."</note> that they follow not the feudal heirs, but whoever the possessors or Lords of the Territory may be. For if by chance no mention was made of the heirs or sons in the investiture, the doctors of law—cited in a long catalog by Vultejus—maintain that this is a hereditary fief. <note>original: "Etenim si fortè in Investitura hæredum filiorum nulla mentio sit facta, hoc feudum hæreditarium esse... Dd. affertant, longo Catalogo relati à Vultejo..."</note> Jason also testifies that this is the common opinion.

And although some legal teachers have separated themselves from this opinion, it is nevertheless not to be rejected when other supports concur, as even the dissenting parties hold. For this is precisely why no successor, feudal heir, or other person is expressed in these cases: to indicate that the right follows whoever is the possessor of the territory, and not just the males or other descendants of the Vassal as his feudal heirs. <note>original: "quod Possessorem Territorii quem-cunque, non verò masculos, aut alios Vasalli descendentes, tanquam ejus feudales hæredes sequatur."</note>

This reasoning is also strongly emphasized in the previously cited Privilege of the Knighthood <note>The *Ritterschaft*</note>, and it is therefore concluded that the Blood-ban belongs inseparably to the estates, because in the letters of enfeoffment, generally only the possessor or holder is named, and not the heirs, as is done in other investitures.

Sixth, it also follows that this is a purely hereditary fief <note>original: "Feudum merè Hæreditarium"</note> and clearly deviates from the common nature of a fief (where only male descendants from the first invested person succeed), because, as the legal records and the attached documents show—and as will be touched upon further below—it has been so for time immemorial, both before and after these...

# Letter L. 613

The Lordship came from the fifth relative at any time, and **without any contradiction** <note>original: "sine omni contradictione"</note>, those of both male and female sex—even widows and other strangers who would otherwise be ineligible heirs by **Feudal Law** <term>Feudal Law: the body of legal customs governing the relationship between lords and vassals, often restricting inheritance to male soldiers</term>—were admitted or enfeoffed without any objection or hesitation, provided they simply applied for the **investiture** <term>Investiture: the formal ceremony or legal act of handing over a fief to a tenant</term>, in whole or in part, and **in what proportion** <note>original: "qua proportione"</note> the territory was granted to them.

From this otherwise inadmissible succession, as well as the investitures that followed it, it appears that both the one granting and the one receiving took into account **hardly at all the succession of blood and the right of agnation** <term>Agnation: inheritance strictly through the male line</term>, **but entirely and solely the hereditary quality, or at least the possession of the territory.** Since a stranger cannot succeed in a fief unless it is purely hereditary or transferable to all possessors, etc. For indeed, in a Hereditary Fief, one succeeds by hereditary proportions. Natta *counsel 159. n. 20.* Baldus *on the law "sibi decem" § "si partus" ff. de pact.*

**Furthermore, a fief once made hereditary never thereafter ceases to be hereditary**, as Knichen left written from Mindanao and Zuchardus. *Treatise on invested pacts, chapter 1, number 179.*

Seventhly, it is particularly important to note that when Lord Friedrich von E. ended his earthly life in the year 1610 without heirs of his body, and thereupon his noble sisters (among whom was the now-widowed Countess of R.)—as the closest property-heirs left **without a will** <note>original: "ab intestato"</note>—humbly and properly petitioned for the granting of these Imperial fiefs belonging to the half-lordship of S. (even though they otherwise could not succeed in a Fief by Agreement and Providence for many reasons), Lord Hans Heinrich von M. and Lord Zacharias N., etc., both Imperial Councilors and commissioned for the seizing of E. and other vacant Imperial fiefs, considered the aforementioned **regalia** <term>Regalia: the sovereign rights or properties belonging to the Crown or Emperor</term> to be **escheated** <term>Escheat: the return of land to the lord or state when there are no qualified heirs</term>. Especially since the **Imperial Fiscal** <term>Imperial Fiscal: the legal officer representing the Emperor’s financial interests or treasury</term> wished to open, claim, and seize everything for Your Majesty’s Chamber.

However, when the highly esteemed Countess and her noble sisters interjected such constant refusals at every turn, and their **right of succession** <note>original: "jus successionis"</note> was clearly illuminated at the court of the Imperial Majesty, finally six years later—preceded by sufficient examination of the case and notwithstanding the laborious contradiction made by the Lord Fiscal—the requested enfeoffment was most graciously granted. Thus, it was judged *by the very fact* against the Imperial Fiscal, and therefore the Countess’s **exception of a judged matter** <term>Exceptio rei judicatæ: a legal defense stating that the matter has already been settled by a final judgment and cannot be litigated again</term> was established. Since at that time there was a dispute concerning the same matter and the same right or cause of seeking (namely, whether this fief is transferable to any heirs not included in the Investiture nor descending from the first acquirer) and also between the same persons (namely, the Imperial Fiscal,

<column-break/>

pretending and anxiously insisting that this Fief was open [for seizure], and the Lady Countess, most constantly denying this), all of which are considered sufficient to generate the "exception of a judged matter." Zanger, *on exceptions, part 3, chapter 15.* And indeed, whenever a subsequent judgment infringes upon that which was debated in a prior judgment, then the exception of a judged matter stands in the way. Zasius, *on the law "when it is asked" § "he who with a part" ff. de except. rei judic.*

And even if no formal sentence had been issued in this place, it is nevertheless correct and entirely undeniable that the then-reigning Imperial Majesty commanded by **Decree** <note>original: "per Decretum"</note> that the Lady Countess be enfeoffed, and such enfeoffment was repeated in the very same form as the Lady Countess now seeks—namely, that such fief-related rights be hereditary.

It is well established, moreover, that whatever the Emperor has pronounced, even informally, is so firm that it ought even to be held as law, *law 1, on the constitution of Princes*, where Antonius Faber [writes] in his reasoning: "Hence a sentence brought against the Prince's will is by that very law just as if it were brought against the Law." Moditius, *§ "The will of Princes," number 2.* And not only the Sentence of the Prince, but also his **Contract has the force of Law**. Baldus, *on law 1, in the preface, ff. de Const. Princ. through the penultimate law, C. de don. inter vir. & uxor.*

And this is to be understood primarily regarding observance, not that they have the force of Universal Law, as per Bartolus *on the law "Cesar" ff. de publican.* On the contrary, they commonly say that a contract is **intensively more powerful than a Law**: because it binds the successor, which a law does not do. *Final chapter "on rescripts" in the 6th book; chapter "it became known" on elections.* It is otherwise "extensively," because Law binds all Contracts.

And also the acts of the Supreme Princes are held as law. Thus, when King Philip of Spain commanded Count Egmond—who was discussing weightier matters with him—to cover his head by putting on his hat, by the evidence of that honor, he was judged by the sentence to have received the dignity of a Prince. Kirchner, *2, on legates, chapter 5, folio 234.*

And it also seems fitting that a royal successor by law should uphold the act of a preceding Prince performed in the Princely name, even if he is not his [private] heir (provided it does not greatly harm the Crown or go against the Laws or the Majesty of the Empire). Because this is not only general for all Guardians who enjoy free administration, but otherwise, no one would be able to contract with Princes, no one could have faith in their promises and words, and at the same time, **public trust** <note>original: "publica fides"</note>, dignity, and Princely honor would collapse. Lord Georg Acacius Enenckel, *3, on Privileges, chapter 11.* Chokier, *on Jurisdiction in exemptions, part 3, question 2.* Daniel Otto, *dissertation on Public Law, chapter 8, folio 202.*

Likewise, if a Prince were to annihilate the contracts of his predecessor, he would choose a path through which

likewise, its acts would sometimes be overturned. *Cluten in Syllog. rer. quot. thes. 18. at the end.*

And because such an **investiture** <term>Investiture: the formal legal act of putting someone in possession of land or a title</term> followed for the consulting Countess after the Lord’s objection and the filing of legal claims on both sides, it is by no means to be considered a mere **favorable concession** <note>original: "gratioſâ aliqua conceſſione"</note>. Similarly, the clause in the **feudal charter** <term>Feudal charter: a legal document recording the granting of a fief</term> mentioning "also by grace" cannot imply a **revocable investiture** <note>original: "precariam Inveſtituram"</note>. This is because the same wording is found in older charters, such as from the year 1535 and many others. Moreover, the word **"Grace"** <note>original: "Gratia"</note> is mostly added out of custom, and Princes are even accustomed to using it in **contracts** <term>Contract: here referring to the mutual legal agreement between a lord and a vassal</term>. As cited in Gylmann, *Symph. vol. 1. p. 1. title on counterclaims, vol. 1. num. 88. in the case of Erfurt vs. Mainz.*

Furthermore, the words of **fairness** <note>German: "Billigkeit"</note> are placed alongside or before the clause "also by grace," through which the most earnest will to grant the **fief** <term>Fief: an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term> in every better and more valid way is sufficiently testified—and not at all that such enfeoffment occurred out of **pure and mere grace** <note>original: "ex purâ & merâ gratiâ"</note>.

Likewise, the feudal charter directed to the Countess of R. is not drafted as if a **New Fief** <note>original: "Feudum Novum"</note> were being established in her person, but rather the content specifies that Her Grace succeeds to such feudal rights by **hereditary right** <note>original: "hæreditario jure"</note> or through inheritance.

These words—namely, that such feudal rights are hereditary—even if they seem to be stated as a mere narrative, nevertheless prove the point fully for many reasons: (1.) because they are repeated in this way in two investitures. For indeed, **doubled narrative words** <note>original: "verba enuncia- tiva geminata"</note> have the same effect as if they were **dispositive words** <term>Dispositive words: language in a document that actually creates or transfers a right, rather than just describing it</term>. *Mynsinger, decade 2. response 18. n. 43.* with the citations there. (2.) Because they were set down not only upon the preceding most humble petition of the Countess, but also after the completed legal process between the Imperial Prosecutor and the Countess, where the question was specifically debated whether all these rights were to be judged based on the nature of a hereditary fief or not. But **Rescripts** <term>Rescript: an official written answer or decree by the Emperor</term> are explained not only by preceding events, *chapter 'inter dilectos' where Felinus num. 14. on the reliability of instruments. Menochius, book 4. presump. 190. num. 4.* And in case of doubt, an investiture is considered to have been made according to the preceding petition (and here, in even stronger terms, according to the decision of the often-mentioned fiscal litigation made by His Imperial Majesty). *Law 1. and there Jason. Code on diverse rescripts. Schrader on fiefs, part 2. section 2. question 5. n. 14. near the end.* But also narrative words in contracts (of which kind an investiture is one), when uttered between the same parties, provide full proof. *Law 'optimam'. Code on contracts and committed stipulations.*

And this holds true especially when those narrative words are found to be uttered as a statement of the cause or reason. *Rosenthal, chapter 6. conclusion 24. num. 11. Mascardus on evidence, vol. 2. conclusion 621. num. 39. & 44.*

Hence, it is specifically taught that the Lord—

<column-break/>

believing the assertion of the **Vassal** <term>Vassal: a person who holds land from a superior lord in exchange for loyalty and service</term> and silently conceding by saying: **"Wherefore we grant him this fief, etc."** <note>original: "Quare nos illi hoc Feudum concedimus, &c."</note>—is seen to prejudice himself and his successors. *Mynsinger, dec. 4. resp. 43. num. 15. Rosenthal as cited, num. 14.*

Likewise, it is of no significance here that His Imperial Majesty allowed the clause **"yet to Us and the Holy Empire our rights remain untouched"** <note>original: "doch Uns und dem Heiligen Reich an Unſern Rechten unvergriffen"</note> to be added or followed. *Regarding what the Reservation Clause 'Saving the Right of the Empire' effects, see Klock, vol. 1. cons. 15. num. 92. & 111.*

For although it may appear that such a **Reservation Clause** <term>Reservation Clause: a legal provision that keeps certain rights for the grantor despite the transfer of property</term> keeps all lordly rights safe in every way, as *Zasius, counsel 12. n. 36. l. 1.* believes;

Nevertheless, the mentioned clause has this meaning: **that it does not refer to those things about which express mention was made in the preceding words of the investiture**, lest the Lord should seem to contradict himself, or to correct himself immediately, and thus seem to want to take away with one hand what he gave with the other. Therefore, this clause must not be dragged into things already granted and specified, nor should it refer to the main points which would be destroyed if such a reference were allowed.

Therefore, it must not work this effect of opposing the preceding specific details, which Schrader explains at length. *on fiefs, part 6. c. 6. n. 36. and following; also p. 8. c. 4. n. 31. Hartmann Pistor, book 2. qu. 48. n. 32. & Peter Heige, qu. 20. part 2.*

And that this clause, if it is placed at the end and in the executive words, has absolutely no effect, is taught by *Menochius, counsel 2. n. 58. through chapter 1. at the end, on prebends.*

Furthermore, it can be said that such a reservation, being uncertain and general, does not help the grantor nor harm the invested feudal tenant. *Law 'intrandi'. Digest on common estates.* Where a reservation of servitudes made through the sale of a fief in general terms is of no use unless the servitudes themselves are otherwise specified. *Corn. counsel 146. col. 2. near the end, l. 4.*

Thus, a **reservation** of exceptions in general does not help because it is uncertain and obscure. *Gloss and Doctors on the chapter 'pastoralis' on exceptions.* Through that text, *Jason on the law 'scire oportet'. section 'scire'. Digest on the excuse of tutors.* The same *Jason on the law 'act.' in the 3rd note. Code on transactions.* For a foundation cannot be sought from what is uncertain and obscure. *Law 'duo sunt Titii'. Digest on testamentary tutors.*

And furthermore, such a reservation of the rights of the Roman Empire must be understood according to the nature of the act to which it is attached. *Law 'si stipulatus' verse 'verum'. Digest on interest. Law 'damni' verse 'and that'. Digest on damage not yet done. Law 'filiusfam'. Digest on donations.* So that, namely in this case, the Vassal loses nothing of what was granted. Indeed, the words are restricted to those things which are of the **nature of the contract**. *Innocent on the chapter 'ex literis'. on the right of Patronage. Baldus on the law 'from the Procurator'. Code on mandates. The same Baldus, counsel 434. book 1.*

This also proceeds in universal words, which are restricted to those things which are of the **nature**...

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the Countess's feudal rights. The previous page established that the term "grace" in her investiture did not negate her legal right. This page focuses on the interpretation of the word "hereditary" and argues that even if one legal basis for her claim (the 1609 Knightly privileges) were found inapplicable, the investiture remains valid based on other sufficient grounds and the historical practice of the fief's transfer.</meta>

# 615 Letter L.

...the nature of the act. <note>original Latin: "tura actus." Completing the citation from the previous page.</note> *Baldus, Counsel 67, column 2, after the middle, book 3.*

Indeed, words are interpreted in an improper sense so that they may be understood according to the nature of the act. *Law 'si tibi pecuniam', Digest 'si certum petatur'; Law 'si unoff.', 'locat.'; Romanus, Counsel 509, volume 2.* This also applies in a sworn act, in which words are likewise interpreted improperly <note>In legal terms, "improperly" means interpreting words beyond their literal or strict dictionary definition to fit the specific legal context.</note> so they are understood according to the nature of the act. *Cornelius, Counsel 129, number 2, at the end of book 3; through the text in Law 'fin.', Digest 'qui satisdare cogantur'.*

Since the Imperial Fiscal <term>Imperial Fiscal: the state prosecutor or legal representative of the Holy Roman Emperor's financial and sovereign interests</term> has now, as often mentioned, very strongly contested that these **feudal rights** could in no way reach the Lady Countess of R., and yet Her Grace was nonetheless **invested** or enfeoffed with them as hereditary: it follows undeniably from this that at that time, this fief was held to be a true **hereditary fief** <term>Hereditary fief: a 'Feudum haereditarium,' which can be passed down to heirs rather than reverting to the lord upon the vassal's death</term> by the Decree and irrevocable Judgment of His Imperial Majesty. For although the word **heirs** <note>German: "Erben"</note> or **hereditary** <note>German: "erblich"</note> does not always imply an absolutely hereditary fief <note>original Latin: "Feudum absolutè hereditarium"</note>, *Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 12, number 9*, so much so that such a fief is not even inferred from the words "by means of hereditary succession," if we believe *Philipp Matthaeus, Marburg Counsel, volume 2, response 26, number 147*. This, however, only holds true in the matter of a **proper fief** <term>Proper fief: a standard military fief that usually follows strict rules of male-only succession</term>; but in **improper fiefs** <term>Improper fief: a 'Feudum improprium,' which deviates from standard feudal rules, often allowing for female or collateral succession</term>, this wording includes all women. *Tesaurus, Decision 146, numbers 8 & 12.* Indeed, it includes all outside successors: namely when subsequent observance, or even the preceding wording, declares them an heir, according to the notes of *Josephus Ludovicus, Common Conclusions, conclusion 38, number 64.* Moreover, it was already stated above that these feudal rights had already passed to whichever possessors of the territory since antiquity.

Furthermore, it is proven that the word **hereditary** <note>German: "erblich"</note> (which is found in later investitures) is to be understood not as standard feudal succession, but as that which is similar to **allodial** <term>Allodial: 'allodialis,' referring to land held in absolute ownership, independent of a superior lord</term> succession; otherwise, it would be useless and superfluous here, whereas words in feudal contracts should not be without the power to operate. *Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 40, number 3.*

And hence, in a similar case, it is handed down that when the consent of the Lord would accomplish nothing because it was superfluous (perhaps because the fief is alienable without his consent by pact or custom), it is then understood to prejudice his own **direct right** <term>Direct right: 'jus directum,' the superior ownership right held by the lord over a fief</term>. *Schrader on Fiefs, part 8, chapter 4, number 28, section 'this second conclusion fails,' etc.; and Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 38, number 13.*

And although it might be held that the investitures most graciously directed to the consulting Lady Countess—because such feudal pieces came to Her Grace as hereditary and by virtue of the privileges given to the **Free Imperial Knighthood** <term>Free Imperial Knighthood: 'Freye Reichs-Ritterschafft,' noblemen who held their land directly from the Emperor</term> in the year 1609 (regarding high sovereignty and that the same should not be taken from the estates)—and although mention was made above at the very beginning of this second question that such a privilege might not be perfectly applicable to the present case, it might therefore be held that this investiture, as if

<column-break/>

**obtained by trickery** <note>original Latin: "subreptitia"</note> and emanating from a **false cause**, would be of no benefit to the Lady Countess. *Menochius, Counsel 103, number 61; and the same, Counsel 439, number 19.* For which reason an investiture granted as if to a legitimized person, when the legitimization is actually invalid, is otherwise regarded as null. *Menochius, Counsel 799, number 34.*

However, it must be well noted here that such an investiture, as already frequently mentioned, followed after a sufficient investigation of the case <note>original Latin: "post sufficientem causae cognitionem"</note>, and the consulting Lady Countess brought forward not only the Knighthood's privilege but several other and various reasons for her aid. She also won the hereditary feudal succession through legal contest. Furthermore, in the indicated **feudal charters** <note>German: "Lehenbrieffen"</note>, the aforementioned privileges of the Knighthood were not merely introduced as the sole reason <note>original Latin: "loco causae"</note> why the Lady Countess should succeed, but it is specifically set down and mentioned that such feudal rights are hereditary, and thus belong to the consulting Lady Countess. Thus, we are now in those terms of which our Doctors of Law are accustomed to declare: if something is granted for several reasons, if one fails, the grant nonetheless usually retains its force, and should not be regarded as being of no importance. And so in a legal petition, if one cause is sufficient for victory, even if several are expressed, only that which is relevant matters, and the others do not need to be justified. *Tuschus, Letter L, conclusion 310.*

And likewise, if several reasons are expressed in a **Sentence** <term>Sentence: 'Sententia,' a formal judicial decision or judgment</term>, for instance one which is unfit and another which is fit, then the sentence is upheld. *Romanus, Counsel 235, regarding the first part, under number 3*, where the marginal note on the word "Defense" etc. brings forward many concurring authors. And similarly, if something is disposed for several reasons, when one ceases, the disposition does not cease. *Bellonius, Counsel 74, number 15 and following.* Thus *Castrensis* also declares, *Counsel 342, at the end, section 5, book 2*: if someone was moved to do something for several reasons—for example, at the request of friends, and also because of a promise made regarding liberation, and for other reasons—each cause operates, and the promise of liberation nonetheless produces the exception of liberation just as if it were the sole reason. It suffices that it was also for that reason, as *Bartolus* declares more fully in the *Extravagantes* <note>The 'Extravagantes' refers to certain collections of canon law or legal commentaries</note> *'ad reprimendum', 'nec eorum absentia', number 14 and following, section 'nunc a.'*, where he says: when several final causes are expressed in the law, if each or any one of them is sufficient by itself, it is enough for one to be present: because a conjunction is placed for a disjunction. *Law 'saepè', Digest 'de Usuris'.*

Eighth, these feudal rights are also to be held as a **purely hereditary fief** <note>original Latin: "pro Feudo merè haereditario"</note> because the Lordship of S., the village of T., and the feudal rights enclosed within it have come to completely foreign lineages several different times—not only in the hereditary manner just mentioned but also by **way of purchase**. This occurred not secretly but publicly, with no one impeding or contradicting it, and with the knowledge and consent, or at least the connivance, of both the Lord of the Fief and those of

After the aforementioned Ferdinand von Freyberg likewise ended his earthly life, and thereby the said half of the noble Lordship of S., along with its associated feudal rights, devolved or fell to his surviving widow and daughter. These two women were most graciously enfeoffed by the aforementioned Emperor Charles in the year 1550, though through Hans Jacob von S. as their appointed **feudal proxy** <term>Feudal proxy: "Lehenträger," a male representative who formally held the fief on behalf of women or minors who could not perform military service</term>. 

Because some time later the mentioned widow passed away, her daughter requested and received these feudal rights through her husband, Count Gabriel of N., from the subsequent Roman Emperors Ferdinand and Maximilian (both of most glorious memory) in the years 1562 and 1566 respectively. Furthermore, after her husband's death, she received them again from the most high Emperor Maximilian II through her guardian Hans Sigmund von Freyberg in 1573. Finally, she requested and bore them as a fief from Emperor Rudolph II, of most blessed memory, in 1577.

Beyond this, it further happened that the mentioned Freyberg daughter eventually died without any legitimate bodily heirs. [Schönau], Erolzheim, Essendorff, and Rietheim, numbering twenty-two persons in total. Of these two, the said Lord Ferdinand most faithfully and obediently requested and easily received the aforementioned Imperial feudal pieces from the most high Emperor Rudolph II in that same year—both for himself and as a proxy for his brother Hans Ernst. Later, in 1604, when Hans Ernst died without bodily heirs and the half-part of the Lordship of S. fell entirely to Lord Ferdinand, he received the investiture again.

It is especially important to note that in these **alienations** <term>Alienation: the legal transfer of ownership to another person</term> of the Lordship of S., according to the contents of the purchase deeds, the feudal rights were always handed over through honest and fair purchases **without any mention of the feudal lord's consent** <note>original Latin: "sine omni mentione consensus Domini feudalis"</note>. Nevertheless, the new possessors were invested with them upon mere application. Consequently, the **most free faculty of selling** was hereby approved, as is most clearly evidenced by the documents in the records, especially those added under Number 13.

But the **Consent of the Lord** declared through a subsequent **Investiture** <note>original: "At Consensus Domini per subsequentem Investituram declaratus"</note> works in such a way that it is seen to encompass everything arising from the contract. And consent regularly takes on the nature of the act upon which it is found to be interposed. *Camerarius, in chapter "Imperialem", page 342.*

And just as a **Stipulation** (which is a matter of strict law) takes on the nature of **good faith** if it is interposed upon a contract of good faith—*Jason in the rubric "of verbal obligations"; Bartolus in law "videamus", paragraph "if actions", on usury*—so also an assent given after the act is perfected will be regulated by the contract. *The same Camerarius, page 410.*

Furthermore, it is a settled point of law that the **alienation of a hereditary fief** <note>original: "alienation hæreditarii feudi"</note> is considered a distinguishing mark. *Natta, Counsel 501, number 3, book 3; Menochius, Counsel 218, number 5, book 9, and Counsel 606, number 1, volume 4.* And that it is then judged just like any other hereditary matter. *Sylvanus, Counsel 30, number 26; Vivius, Decision 443, number 12, book 3; Cacheranus, Counsel 57, number 3, citing many others.*
