### Letters: L. 617

<column-break/>

...can be alienated due to the pressure of hunger <note>original Latin: "famis alienari queat"</note>, as is well-proven by Curtius Senior in Council 50, number 24. Likewise, the transfers of this our present Fief have remained in effect because, after these sales, the buyers always enjoyed the rights to it; thus, it remained perpetually transferable <term>alienable: able to be sold or transferred to new owners</term> and can even be transferred by a will, as is extensively argued by Surdus in Council 105, numbers 11 and 12. And so this fief (namely those jurisdictional rights that are feudal in the Village of T.), since it has often been transferred to strangers and various different families, one must admit that it has been made transferable, and can now pass to anyone. Cephalus says in Council 307, number 40, that this is especially true when there are actual instruments of transfer (as in our case), because these prove the local custom. In this same sense, Curtius Junior in Council 171, number 9, teaches that an ancient fief that can be transferred to the detriment of the paternal relatives <term>agnates: male-line relatives who would usually inherit a fief</term> is said not to have the "proper nature" of a fief; rather, the person to whom it was given holds it only according to the specific terms by which it was granted.

Furthermore, a Fief which is transferred to a complete stranger with the consent of the Lord and the paternal relatives becomes, from that point on, a entirely **New Fief** in the person of that stranger. Thus, for the paternal relatives of the original seller (in our specific case), all hope of succeeding to the property appears to be cut off, according to the notes of Schrader, part 8, chapter 5, number 25 and following.

Therefore, although the words of the Investiture <note>Investiture: the formal ceremony and document granting a fief</note> might be somewhat doubtful, and one might not clearly learn from them that the frequently mentioned feudal rights are transferable to any heirs whatsoever and are inseparably attached to the territory; nevertheless, through so many successions and transfers that are clearly contrary to regular Feudal Law, all doubt is removed.

For when the words of the Investiture are not entirely sufficient to establish a purely hereditary quality, then *observance* and long-standing use provide the decision. Knichen, *On the Clothing of Pacts*, part 1, chapter 5, number 10. Indeed, it is demonstrated by the resulting observance whether a fief is purely hereditary or not. And because for a fief to be purely or entirely hereditary is not against the core substance of a fief, but only against its typical nature, it can be changed without great difficulty by custom from a restricted pact into an absolutely hereditary fief, as noted by Schrader, part 2, chapter 2, number 42 and following. This is especially true in the case of immemorial custom <note>immemorial custom: a practice so old that no one remembers its beginning</note>.

To this should also be added what His Electoral Serenity in Bavaria <note>The Elector of Bavaria, a high-ranking prince of the Holy Roman Empire</note> had written in a clearly similar sense in the formal legal report concerning the **Fronsberg Succession Matter**, part 1, folio 39, with the following words: "Regarding the Imperial Fiefs, it should be noted that Lord Georg

<margin>Besold, Volume 1</margin>

<column-break/>

Fronsberg, alongside his other lordships and estates, also held the Lordship of Mündelheim located in the Swabian Circle during his lifetime and left it behind after his earthly passing. This lordship, in land and people, together with all belonging estates, superiorities, and rights, appears to have always been possessed and held as private property <term>allodial: property owned outright, not as a fief</term> by his parents and ancestors. From the Holy Empire, nothing more was received or held as a fief than a certain specific customs-tax, forestry right, and the 'Blood-Bann' or High Court <term>Halsgericht: the right to exercise capital punishment</term> belonging to the Lordship. These fiefs were indeed not originally 'Free Fiefs of Grace,' but only over the last two hundred or more years were they gradually offered as fiefs by the holders of said lordship from their free property at various times. This was done not to diminish the free ownership of the lordship, but for greater prestige, and to obtain protection and defense from the Holy Roman Empire. Furthermore, these same fiefs, together with the free lordship, have been successively and freely transferred, changed, and inherited within the mentioned time among six different families of Princes, Counts, Lords, and Nobility—such as those of Mündelberg, Hochschlißen, the Dukes of Teck, the Counts of Wertheim, and those of Rechberg and Freundsberg—including both men and women, and members of the clergy and laity, both between living persons <note>Latin: "inter vivos"</note> and by reason of death <note>Latin: "mortis causa"</note>, as free, continuous hereditary fiefs and inseparable appendages of the free lordship."

Therefore, the Lord of Freundsberg, being the last of his line and name, had all the more reason not only to dispose of such fiefs in his will but also to grant them to his universal heirs, instituted with certain measures and order, namely Wolff Veit von Märlein and Maria, the daughter of the Count of Schwarzenberg.

This opinion is clearly in agreement with our own, and having been issued by such a great Prince, whose wisdom and experience in affairs is most celebrated by all, and in the very same terms we are currently using, it ought deservedly to be of the greatest weight. And no hindrance should be brought against this by what feudal lawyers commonly teach: that fiefs which are transferable without the lord's consent by virtue of a statute or custom do not degenerate so far that they pass to any strangers or are considered purely hereditary. They argue those customs should be strictly interpreted so as to harm Common Feudal Law as little as possible. For it is presumed that a fief changed in one respect retains its proper nature in others and is governed by the law of a 'right fief' unless it is demonstrated to have been changed by custom, statute, or agreement.

### Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

presumption 95, number 2; and Rosenthal, on conclusions 58, number 27; and chapter 2, conclusion 54.

Hence, it is handed down as a Rule, that **improper fiefs** <note>original: "Feuda impropria"; these are fiefs that do not follow the standard rules of feudal law, such as those allowing inheritance by women or the sale of the land</note>, which in some ways depart from the common nature of Fiefs and are altered, shall remain under feudal nature and rules in all other chapters or points that were not specifically altered, and shall be governed according to them. *Zasius, epitome of fiefs, part 12, number 3. Rittershusius, partitions of fiefs, book 1, chapter 14, question 2, page 206, verse: improper fiefs.*

Since this opinion is not approved by all **Doctors** <note>original: "Doctorn"; referring to learned legal scholars</note> (for many dissenting from *Rosenthal in said conclusion 41, number 12 and conclusion 58, number 24* are cited), and is further restricted by their own **followers** <note>original: "Asseclis"</note> to those cases where it is not apparent that a long-standing custom has been observed. For if it has been so received by use, and neither the paternal relatives <term>agnates: male-line relatives</term> nor the Lord ever revoked such sales, or if it is approved by custom that daughters should succeed in the fief equally with males (even when more distant relatives are excluded), or even other outside heirs when these relatives are removed (as obtained in our specific case), then that custom, however harsh, must be upheld, as *Rosenthal in said conclusion 58, number 40 and following* teaches.

Likewise, the above argument should not be pushed back, where it might be said that the old, highly esteemed Roman Emperors—even if they later explicitly or tacitly approved, through subsequent **investitures** <note>original: "Investituras"; the formal ceremony of granting a fief</note>, the simple sale of a fief made without their prior or reserved consent—did not thereby prejudice themselves or give up anything of their feudal rights.

Indeed, although the Lord of the Fief, by investing the buyers, is deemed to have consented to the contract of sale—especially when the contract of sale is mentioned in the letters of Investiture, in which case he seems to have consented sufficiently by the act itself, *arguing from the law 'Paulus' in the Digest on 'ratification'; and law 'if however' 48, section 'To him who' in the Digest on 'edicts'*—nevertheless, that simple consent to the transfer does not harm the Lord, nor does it damage his right even in the slightest, as *Andreas de Isernia* expressly holds in *chapter 1 on the 'prohibition of fiefs' by Frederick*, as cited and followed by *Jacobus Alvarottus in the same place, after preface 4, column 4, verse 'I ask whether by license'; and the Provost in the same place, column 5; the same Provost after Alvarottus in said chapter 1, section 'furthermore, by what modes a fief is lost'; Zasius, counsel 12, number 5 at the end of book 1.*

Nor is it to be presumed that the Lord wished to prejudice himself in his own right, but only that he removed the obstacle (namely, that the Vassal’s right could not be sold without the Lord's consent), *Schrader on fiefs, part 8, chapter 8, number 28; and Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 38, numbers 4 and 5.* Just as in other cases, the donation or giving up of one’s right is not presumed unless it is established by clear words, *law 'if one', section 'before all' on 'pacts'; law 'if the Lord' on 'urban servitudes'*; and in any act, that interpretation is always to be taken by which the right of another is harmed as little as possible, *book 3 on 'suspected guardians'; chapter 'with beloved' etc.; 'with to the hearing' on*

<column-break/>

*non-resident clergy; Craverta, counsel 33, number 24; Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 18, number 8, and in note 'c'.* And thus, from our voluntary acts, one should not presume things that are not necessarily included. *final law in the Code: 'that a wife for her husband'; Zasius, counsel 12, number 72, book 1.*

But on the other hand, it shall again be considered and noted, that a contract (as also warned above) is understood to have come into the grant with all its qualities, as witnessed by *Zasius in counsel 12, number 7, through the final law at the end regarding 'freedom of trusts'; arguing from law 'when the father', section 'from the institution' on 'legacies 2'; and law 'legacy' on 'legacies 1'.* And that consent simply granted is deemed to be applied according to the nature of the contract, *through law 'if a stipulation', section 'truth' on 'usury'; law 'if truly' in the Digest on 'hiring'; law 'if afterwards' in the Digest on 'ratification'; Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 19, number 8, and in note 'h'.* Indeed, consent very often receives its clarification from the mind of those requiring it, *law 'if concerning', section 'he who interrogates' on 'interrogatory actions'; H. Pistor, book 2, question 12, number 57.* Therefore the rule (that the simple consent of the Lord does nothing against his own right) proceeds only in those rights which, belonging to the consenting Lord, have a separate reason from the business to which the consent is added, but not in those things that pertain to the strength and stability of the act. For as far as those are concerned, the consenting Lord is deemed to have renounced all his right by which he could have hindered that act in any way, and to have added the most valid strength to that business with all its qualities (and so in the present case, to the past and truly hereditary purchases of the half-part of the **Lordship of S.** with all its appurtenances), as *Andreas de Isernia* declares in *chapter 1, preface, column 4, 'who can hold succession'; Camerer in chapter 'Imperial', pages 339 and 353; Martinus Freccia, book 2 on 'authority and power of barons over sub-vassals', section 29, number 8, verse 'it also fails'; H. Pistor, said question 12, number 56, book 2.*

So also to the other rule (that the donation or giving up of one’s right is not presumed), it is answered that it applies only in a doubtful case; but it is otherwise when the **Renunciation** is clear from the consent itself: for then, in a clear matter, there is no longer a need for conjectures, *law 'continuous', section 'when thus' on 'verbal obligations'.* For he who consents is deemed by that very act to resign his right. *law 'if a common slave' on 'donations between husband and wife'; law 'at Celsus', section 'it is sought' on 'the exception of fraud'; law 'guarantor', section 'father' on 'pledges'.*

According to all of which (especially when all the reasons cited so far are weighed together and joined, one of which clarifies and strengthens the other), we can once more not otherwise judge, find, or conclude, than that these feudal rights are truly hereditary, and especially inseparably fixed <note>original: "inseparabiliter suffigirt"</note> to the territory; thus they are transferred and divided with the same to whichever possessors it falls by ancient title, though they must be recognized and properly served as fiefs of the **Imperial Majesty** <note>original: "Kayserl. Maj."</note> and the **Roman Empire**.

## Third and Fourth Question.

Regarding these questions, we rightly and with all due respect honor the decision granted by the most noble Imperial Aulic Council <note>original: "Kayserlichen Reichs-Hofrath"; one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note> on June 25th of the long-past year; much less do we have cause to doubt in any way that such a decision was composed and issued based on highly significant reasons and grounds. Nevertheless, there are such considerable remedies in the "Possessorio" <term>Possessorio: the legal stage focusing solely on who currently holds the property, regardless of who truly owns it</term> for the Lady Countess that, if the matter were still entirely fresh <note>original: "si res adhuc planè integra esset"</note>, we for our part—and quite impartially—would hold that not only the Lady Countess, but also her heirs by law or by Testament <note>original: "ab intestato sive ex Testamento"</note> coming after her blessed passing, should be left and maintained in the possession and occupation of this half-lordship of S., until in the "Petitorio" <term>Petitorio: the legal stage where the actual ownership and nature of the title is determined</term> it might be properly settled and clarified according to the law, both regarding the quality and nature of this Fief <note>original: "Feudi"</note>—namely whether it is hereditary and inseparably attached to the Territory or not—as well as regarding the quantity, meaning what and how much belongs within it.

For there is simply no remedy for obtaining possession <note>original: "remedium adipiscendæ possessionis"</note> to be seen or found by which the Imperial Fiscal <note>the state's financial/legal officer</note> or the Lord of V. could obtain the occupation of the disputed fiefs and make the Lady Countess a plaintiff in the Petitory stage, considering that the Expectancy <note>original: "Expectantz"; a legal promise of a future grant of a fief once the current holder dies</note> obtained by the Lord of V. can in no way deteriorate the right and authority of the Lady Countess or her heirs, nor be harmful to them in any way.

For although a promise or Expectancy, which is made to another in the event of a Vassal's death—whether the Vassal himself knows of it or is ignorant—can be made, it nevertheless must not be made to the detriment of that Vassal or in fraud of his successors, according to the text in chapter 1, there: "provided that while he is living no detriment to his fief occurs to him." Likewise in the section: "this however must be said of that soldier, who has no successors to the fief." See *Schurff, century 1, counsel 53, number 6.* Just as even the Prince, the supreme Lord of all, cannot do this, nor is he presumed to wish it, through the rule "in granting" 7, on water and rainwater. Therefore, a benefit from the Prince must always be interpreted in such a way that it does not prejudice a third party in their own right, *law 'neither Augustus', Code on emancipated children*, as after *Alvarus*, *Ludovicus Fachs* hands down in the counsel found in *H. Pistor, book 2, part 2, question 20, number 22.*

<margin>Besoldi Volume I.</margin>
Therefore, in that grant, the Right of Successors is understood to be excepted, which they can claim by Law or custom. *Modestinus Pistor in Leipzig Counsel number 41*, which is found in the same place in the said question 20. And thus this Investiture <note>the formal ceremony of granting a fief</note> always has this condition attached: if the possessor dies without an heir, the fief shall have reverted to the Lord, so that only then

<column-break/>

does it take effect, when the fief has been "opened" <note>reverted due to lack of heirs</note> to the Lord or his heir, according to the text in the chapter "on customs, if concerning the fief of the deceased," *H. Pistor, said book 2, question 28, number 6.* But when a successor exists (whether universal or particular), especially for a fief that is asserted to be hereditary, it is by no means "opened," and thus this condition fails; when it fails, the disposition granted upon it also entirely expires. *Law 'to reach the day', on the Meaning of Words; H. Pistor, question 28, number 11.*

That even an allodial heir <term>allodial heir: an heir to private, non-feudal property</term> in a presumed hereditary fief must be protected, and even less should the possession, use, and enjoyment of those rights or goods be withdrawn from such an heir when they are claimed probably and in good faith as private property: "Since he has for himself the firmest presumption of Law, that in case of doubt, a thing is judged to be allodial." This is maintained here and there by the legal scholars as an established principle, so that we do not consider it necessary to mention it at great length here.

Indeed, the unanimous traditions of the Doctors <note>learned legal authorities</note> go so far as to say that a daughter or another heir, even if they have been cast out from possession or do not have it, should nevertheless prevail in a possessory judgment. Thus *Rosenthal, chapter 7, conclusion 48, number 2*, establishes a firm rule: "If a daughter is the heir instituted by the Father in a testament, she should be placed in possession of the feudal goods which the Father possessed at the time of death, no less than the allodial ones," notwithstanding the contradiction of sons or paternal relatives <term>agnates: male-line relatives</term>, or even of the Lord himself—saving for them in the meantime those other remedies which concern the Petitory stage. Thus it was clearly decided in the Imperial Chamber <note>original: "Camera Imp."; the highest court of the Empire</note> in the difficult case of *Virmond against Virmondt*, and the daughter was specifically placed in possession by the remedy of "obtaining" <note>a specific legal action to gain possession</note> even into the fiefs, notwithstanding the contradiction of the agnates, with the Petitory stage alone reserved for the agnates. And that sentence was published on April 15, Anno 1577, and "restitution to the original state" was sought against it, but denied on June 16, Anno 1580; a revision was also sought, but finally in Anno 1587 it was of no use at the point of execution. It is established, therefore, that this proceeds more indubitably if this woman or daughter is already in possession. For then she is all the more to be preserved and maintained in that possession until she is evicted by another remedy. This was obtained in the Imperial Chamber in the case of *Calenberg against Catenberg*, and the sentence was delivered in Anno 1572 in a case of convention, where the sisters were sued by the agnates, who used various combined remedies for recovery as if those agnates had been ejected from certain fiefs by the deceased's sisters, but the sisters obtained an acquittal. To these Chamber Precedents enumerated by Rosenthal, that which is most well-known in the Imperial Court can be added: namely *Wolckenstain*, where the women, as heirs of the deceased possessor and partners against *Eberstein*, were allodial heirs, notwithstanding the contradiction of the agnates,

# Enlarged Practical Treasury

And regarding feudal goods and rights, depending both on the Empire and other Princes, and also regarding the claim of a family trust <term>fideicommissum: a legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of a family lineage</term>, these were admitted indifferently into all goods, with the right of the male relatives <term>agnati: relatives through the male line</term> reserved to be brought forward in the "Petitorio" <term>Petitorio: the legal stage where actual ownership and the nature of the title is determined</term>. And this sentence (as it was issued in the Imperial Chamber <note>original: "als in Camera Imperiali ausgefallen"; the Imperial Chamber Court was one of the highest judicial bodies in the Holy Roman Empire</note>), though suspended for some years due to a revision, was nevertheless put into execution a few years ago by order of His Imperial Majesty, and was judged most equitable by the renowned Aulic Court.

In the same place, Rosenthal further teaches that clearly no difference should be made between the Lord and the male relatives, and he attests that all interpreters feel this way without exception; he adds that no urgent reason for a difference exists here. For although this could be argued in a case where it is clear that fiefs <term>feuda: land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal</term> exist—especially if the Lord anticipates the women by seizing possession, because he previously held "Civil possession" <note>legal possession as recognized by law</note> of the thing granted as a Fief, and therefore the "Natural possession" <note>actual physical control</note> might seem consolidated with the Civil immediately upon the death of the Vassal. But it is said that here we are dealing not with the possession of the thing itself, but with the natural and civil possession of the *fief*, while only natural possession of the *thing* itself; regarding such possessions, no such effective consolidation seems to occur. And even assuming it does occur, the difficulty remains that a deeper investigation into the Lordship or its status is required where the heir or woman either denies it is a fief or claims she is capable of holding it, and thus claims the "useful ownership" <term>dominium utile: the right to use and profit from land, as opposed to "direct ownership" held by the lord</term> has been transferred to her. Therefore, the Lord's assertion of ownership remains doubtful until the examination in the Petitorio; and for that reason, that naked presumed resistance by which the Lord is protected where it is clear the matter is feudal does not seem to suffice against the favor of the heir in the "Possessorio" <term>Possessorio: the legal stage focusing on who currently holds the property, regardless of final ownership</term>, even if the matter might stand differently in the Petitorio. Surely, if the Lord wishes to enter into natural possession by reason of his Civil possession, and the Vassal resists, he hardly disturbs the Lord in his Civil possession. And also, when the successor of the Vassal calls the Lord's right into question—for example, if he contends that the right of the fief is not yet ended—he in no way disturbs the Lord's Civil possession (since he acknowledges him as the direct Lord), much less intends to despoil him. Nor can the Lord, under the pretext of being despoiled and to continue his own possession, eject the successor. Rosenthal, chapter 10, conclusion 41, number 50, with cited reference m.m.

Also contributing here are the things which the already often-praised Rosenthal teaches in said chapter 7, conclusion 50 and following: that among the hereditary remedies available to heirs, those also apply which the deceased merely held; and therefore, if an heir claims some right in fiefs not without probability, he should prevail in the Possessory remedies, with the Petitorio remaining safe. And that sisters or cousins and heirs of the deceased Vassal, provided they claim a right in the fiefs—for example, that they are either purely hereditary or "feminine" <note>fiefs that could be inherited by women</note>—ought to be put into possession, even against the Lord or others holding them, as

<column-break/>

the same Rosenthal proves elsewhere, namely in conclusion 12, number 83, chapter 12. Nor is there any doubt that a daughter and heirs appointed in a will should be put into possession according to the final law of the Code on the Edict of Divine Hadrian <note>original: "l. fin. C. de edict. D. Had. toll."</note>; the same Rosenthal teaches this in chapter 7, conclusion 48 through his discourse, especially if it is shown at least summarily that the matter is hereditary. Marius Freccia, book 3 on the difference between fiefs and pacts, difference 17. Petrus de Gregorius in the treatise on the granting of fiefs, part 4, question 11, at the verse "even if it be said" etc., column 22. Natta, counsel 679, number 17, folio 4. Afflictis, Neapolitan Decisions 119, number 3 and following. Intrigliolo in the Century of Fiefs, question 51, number 14 and following.

But that the consulting Lady Countess has great, indeed lawful reasons <note>original German: "Daß aber die consulirende Frau Gräfin grosse, ja rechtmäßige Ursachen hab"</note> to claim the feudal rights as legal and hereditary has been sufficiently detailed above in the other question; there, this specifically benefits the highly esteemed Lady Countess: that she has several different Imperial Letters of Investiture <note>original German: "Kayserliche Lehenbrief"; formal documents granting a fief</note> to present. By virtue of these, Her Grace—after the opposition of the Lord Fiscal—was invested while claiming and indeed expressly with hereditary quality, which is the very thing being done today by her Lord successor.

In which case, where someone holds a title from a Prince's predecessor, the disposition of the Law of Zeno does not apply <note>original: "L. benè à Zenone C. de quadr. præscr."; a law concerning four-year prescriptions on property claims against the treasury</note>. Albericus on judged matters, in 6. Ludovicus Romanus, counsel 298, "Almighty God." Delrio on the title of the Law of Zeno.

It is furthermore established that an Investiture proves the case against the one who grants it, and that if anyone contends something else should be introduced beyond the later Investiture, this requires a deeper investigation and seems to belong to the Petitorio. And likewise, when an heir wishes to obtain the vacant possession of an inheritance by his own authority, it must be said, according to all the Doctors of Law, that this is permitted to him, as Menochius pursues at length in remedy 6 on obtaining possession, numbers 412 and 414. Thus also, if the succession of a fief is passed to anyone (as in our case, where a hereditary Fief is asserted, passed to any heirs of the Lord Count), they may enter and seize its vacant possession by their own authority without any other delivery or new Investiture. Thus, they are to be defended in that possession as true possessors against all men, even against the Lord himself. Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 56, number 6 and following. Moreover, Meichsner teaches in Decision of the Chamber 13, number 58, in the section "But neither in the interdict," volume 3, that a woman or another heir, especially from a will, should be put into possession of feudal goods which the deceased possessed at the time of death by the office of the Judge, no less than allodial <term>allodial: land held in absolute ownership, not subject to a feudal lord</term> goods, notwithstanding the contradiction of the male relatives or the Lord, while preserving their other remedies in the meantime.

Citing various legal authorities, it asserts that "possession" (Possessorio) is a protected status that cannot be overturned by a Lord or male relatives until the "ownership" (Petitorio) is fully proven.</summary>

# Letter L.

And from these points, the same Meichsner infers that since a female heir can revoke and acquire possession of feudal property—which she never previously held—even from the male relatives <term>agnati: relatives related through the male line</term> (or those holding a legal expectation of the land) who currently possess it and object to her claim, she is even more entitled to take and hold those goods that were never in the possession of the male relatives or claimants. *Decision 9, number 152, section beginning "from which to infer," volume 3.*

On the other hand, Feudal Law <term>Jus Feudale: the body of law governing the relationship between lords and vassals</term> nowhere teaches that a Lord, upon the end of a fief, can occupy the property on his own authority. Rather, the opposite is established in the text of the *Chapter 1, at the beginning, and Paragraph 1, regarding the fief of the deceased.* Insofar as those opposing the claim assert that they are vassals (specifically in our case, the future allodial <term>allodial: land owned outright, not held from a lord</term> heirs in what is claimed to be a hereditary fief), the feudal texts certainly never permit the Lord to proceed by force <note>original: "de facto"</note>, even if he holds total jurisdiction in the place where the fief is located. Therefore, the opinion of those who wrote that such a Lord could, upon the end of a lineage, send in his Treasury <term>Fiscus: the Emperor's private or state treasury</term> or seize the fief on his own authority appears false, as Rosenthal explains at length in *Chapter 10, conclusion 4, number 72 and following, and number 8*, where he even extends this rule to the Emperor, provided the Emperor is proceeding by ordinary power rather than his absolute "fullness of power" <note>original: "plenitudine potestatis," a legal concept where a monarch acts above common law</note>.

In this matter, it must also be considered that the Imperial Treasury, because of its "mighty arm," can always regain possession (if it is later granted to them) much more easily than a weak estate or a simple vassal could in the opposite case. Moreover, in the meantime, the Treasury can protect itself from loss through various legal remedies—often better than others can—according to *Rosenthal, cited chapter 10, conclusion 41, number 73, section "likewise if another."* Relevant here is the principle that in cases of doubt, one should not favor the Treasury. Pliny the Younger says in his *Panegyric to Trajan* that the Treasury’s case is never a bad one unless it is under a good Prince <note>This implies that a good ruler does not allow his tax collectors to bully his subjects or take advantage of legal grey areas</note>. Hence, it is recorded of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius the Philosopher that he never favored the Treasury, as Covarrubias compiles here and in many other places in *Varied Resolutions, Book 1, Chapter 16, at the beginning.* The same is noted in the law *non puto* regarding the right of the Treasury, which permits one to always judge against the Treasury in doubtful questions—that is, in those cases where full proof has not yet been established. Peregrinus, *On the Right of the Treasury, Book 6, Title 6, Number 23.* This applies most especially to cases of seizing possession. In other matters, the Treasury’s unique privileges do not apply here; beyond those, it is established that the Treasury uses the same law as a private citizen, unless it is found to be specifically privileged. *Law "likewise on compensation,"* with similar citations. This privilege is not presumed in cases of doubt, *according to the cited law "non puto," Decius on the law "in ambiguous matters," and Peregrinus, cited book 6, title 1, number 1 and following.*

Regarding what remedy might be undertaken to thwart the judgment already rendered against the consulting Countess in the possessory case <note>a legal action to determine who has the right to physical possession, regardless of who "owns" the land</note>, it is very difficult to decide. In this instance, a "Nullity" <note>an argument that the judgment is legally void from the start</note> does not apply, and even if such were contained within it, we could in no way consider it advisable to pursue such a path.

<column-break/>

Likewise, an Appeal <term>Appellation: a formal request to a higher court to change a decision</term> will find no place here. For as it is not permitted to appeal from the Prince <note>the Emperor</note> (*Law 1, on those from whom appeals are not allowed*), since he is the very one to whom one would appeal; it follows that since an appeal transfers a case to a higher Judge, not to an equal or a lower one (*Law 2, paragraph "if anyone" on appeals; Maranta, part 6, same title, number 357; Speculator in the section "now let us treat," at the beginning*), the Prince, having no superior, cannot be the subject of an appeal.

There are also other persons from whom, due to a special privilege, it is not permitted to appeal, even though they recognize the Prince as their superior. This was true in the past of the Roman Senate (*Book 1, at the beginning, section "it should be known" on those from whom appeals are not allowed*), and the same applies to a Judge appointed by the Emperor with the clause "with appeal removed" <note>original: "remota appellatione"</note> (*cited Law 1, final paragraph*). The Praetorian Prefect is also counted among these (*Single law, Code on the sentences of the Praetorian Prefects*). For the Lawgiver considers these officials to be too excellent to wish to burden anyone by judging either unjustly or contrary to the law's prescription. The Prince believed that those who, because of their singular industry (as the Jurist says in *Law 1 on the office of the Praetorian Prefect*), and their proven loyalty and gravity, are called to the magnitude of this office, would judge according to their wisdom and the light of their dignity, just as he himself would judge. And just as in the most high Imperial Chamber Court—which (in our century) exists as the supreme consistory and tribunal not only of the Emperor but of the Empire itself (*by Title 35, part 2 of the Chamber Ordinances*) and holds concurrent jurisdiction with the Emperor in cases committed to it (*according to Gail, observation 11, at the end*), indeed representing the Emperor himself in the administration of justice (*Gail, observation 29, number 2*)—there is absolutely no place for an appeal from a sentence delivered there (*cited Title 35, part 2 and Title 5, part 3*). Thus, for almost the same reasons, the same must be said of the Imperial Aulic Council <term>Aulico Cæsareo Judicio: the Emperor's personal high court</term>. Thus, no other means remains in this place than to undertake the benefit of Supplication <term>Supplicationis beneficium: a formal petition for mercy or a review of a case, usually addressed to the monarch's sense of equity</term> to the Most Sacred Imperial Majesty himself. For indeed it sometimes happens that those who profess themselves to be the Priests of Justice, and who are its strenuous and constant cultivators, sometimes wander from the true mark (for to err is human). This happens while they are too intent on the technicalities of the law <note>original: "Juris apicibus," the "peaks" or fine points of law</note>, or while they do not always know how to judge skillfully between the various or differing opinions of the Doctors <note>legal scholars</note>, sometimes accepting a false opinion for a true one. That this very often happened to the Jurists themselves, from whose responses our law is fashioned, is more than sufficiently testified by a reading of our entire body of law. Frequently, they are also deceived by an error not of law, but of fact, and they decree something other than they ought...

It concludes that because the Emperor and his high courts have no superiors, the only remaining legal path is a formal petition for mercy or "Supplication."</summary>

### Augmented Treasury of Practical Law

...are accustomed to maintain, so that no one could complain about the law of such a supreme Judge, or feel themselves unfairly burdened or affected by any injury through a sentence, and find no path open to them to demonstrate the justice of their cause.

And since it is Divine rather than human to be equally wise at all hours—to discern the honorable from the dishonorable, the just from the unjust, and never to swerve to the right or to the left—it was not right that a presumed confidence in the administration of the Republic's scales and Rule of Justice should result in any loss, or that the weight of the high estimation held for any Judge should be preferred over the injury of another. It was therefore wisely established that, although it is not permitted to appeal from the sentence of certain Judges due to their excellence, a license for <term>supplication: a formal petition to a sovereign or high official to review a case</term> is nonetheless granted to those who claim they have been harmed. For it is not in the public interest for the protections of the law to be denied to individuals, as the Divine Emperors Diocletian and Maximian prudently wrote back <note>original: "rescripserunt"</note> in the Code, under the title on the sentences of the Praetorian Prefects.

And it seems beyond controversy that this **Supplication** can be offered under common law at any time within a two-year period, according to the express text of the law. Since, to our knowledge, no public law of the Empire has removed this right, we believe it also applies to sentences issued by the **Most Illustrious Aulic Council** <note>The Aulic Council (Reichshofrat) was one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire, based in Vienna and personally overseen by the Emperor.</note>.

Therefore, a most humble Supplication should be submitted to Your Imperial Majesty, because the two years have not yet passed since the troublesome decree regarding possession <note>original: "in possessorio"</note> was issued. In this petition, the grievances of that decree should be laid out, yet it should be submitted in every way with the most gracious advice and support of Your Princely Serenity to deflect ill-will <note>original: "ad invidiam"</note> from the Lady Countess. In such a Supplication, one could then also most obediently request <term>restitution to the original state: a legal remedy (restitutio in integrum) that cancels the effects of a legal act or judgment to restore someone to their previous position</term>.

For it is the common opinion of the **Canonists** <note>Scholars of Church law, whose opinions often influenced civil and imperial law.</note> that restoration to the original state is granted against a sentence on the pretext that it was rendered against the right of the litigant. This is the view of Hostiensis, whom others generally follow. This view should be embraced as the more equitable and kind in cases of doubt. This especially holds true if investiture <note>The formal ceremony of granting a fief.</note> is sought from the Prince. Because of his supreme power, and because he can grant or take away authority from judgments, he ought to grant it if the unfairness of a sentence is discovered and it seems equitable to him. And even if

<column-break/>

this could not be done by way of a legal restoration <note>original: "ex Justitia"</note>, it could nevertheless be sought through a Supplication by way of grace <note>original: "ex gratia"</note>, as argued by Bodin and others.

However, in the case of **Fugger versus Mäxelrein** <note>A famous 16th-century legal battle over the Lordship of Mindelheim.</note> right there in the Imperial Court many years ago, a similar judgment was issued under almost identical terms as this one. Even when the matter was brought to the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>The Reichskammergericht, the other supreme court of the Empire, often in competition with the Aulic Council.</note> and citations were issued, they were in turn quashed by a Sentence. Rosenthal reports the summary of this lawsuit in these words:

"Many have written specifically that the Emperor shall be the Judge between two vassals contending over a fief, such that one is held to the other for <term>eviction: the legal recovery of property from a person by a superior claim</term>. This was greatly disputed in the case of Lord Johann Fugger against the Lord Baron of Mäxelrein, concerning the Baronate or Imperial fiefs of Mindelheim. The Emperor had promised these to the said Fugger in the event that the last male vassal of the Frönsberg family should die without male children. When that condition occurred, Mäxelrein and his associates contended that those fiefs were of such a nature that female relatives could succeed in them. Having occupied possession, they presented the deduction of their right, the ancient investitures, and the Will of the last vassal (in which he was named heir) to the Emperor's court, seeking to be granted investiture and confirmed in possession. This was refuted by Lord Fugger’s side, who argued the fief was a male fief and sought to be put in possession. After legal opinions <note>original: "Consilia"</note> were presented, the Emperor, through a sentence drafted by the Imperial Aulic Councilors in the year 1587, decreed that Fugger should be put in possession and appointed two Princes of the Empire as commissioners to carry this out. Mäxelrein opposed this the following year and obtained a citation from the Imperial Chamber Court, attempting to block the possession through this pending lawsuit. Mäxelrein argued the Emperor could not be the Judge because he was personally liable to Fugger for the eviction. Nevertheless, he labored in vain, etc."

Additionally, Your Imperial Majesty or his **Treasury** <note>original: "Fiscus"</note> will not likely want to get involved in a lawsuit to dispossess the consulting Lady Countess. On the other hand, the law provides that in this case, a claim for ownership <note>original: "Petitorium"</note> and a claim for possession <note>original: "Possessorium"</note> usually do not prejudice each other, as taught by Schrader.

Therefore, it might perhaps be more advisable for the consulting Lady Countess that Her Grace either...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the Countess's inheritance dispute, specifically focusing on whether her claims should proceed through the ownership trial (Petitorium) or the possession trial (Possessorium). The previous page discussed the right of "Supplication" (appealing to a sovereign for a case review), and here the counsel debates the risks of pursuing both legal paths simultaneously.</meta>

...to vigorously pursue the <term>Petitorium: a legal action regarding the right of ownership or title</term>, omitting the <term>Possessorium: a legal action regarding the right of physical possession</term>, or at least not to neglect the Petitorium. He should prosecute both legal actions at the same time in such a way that the Possessorium—which has been made very doubtful due to the sentence already passed—does not also make the Petitorium more <note>original: "magis odiosum"</note> unfavorable or hold it up longer. We, for our part, reasonably leave this to those more knowledgeable and experienced in the court’s procedures.

## Question Five.

Diese Frag <note>The text begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'D'.</note> This question depends entirely on the resolution of the points set forth above. In the event that the disputed feudal rights are absolutely hereditary, they can be transferred to any heirs whatsoever, and even to an adopted son, as specifically judged by Curtius Junior <note>consil. 138. num. 9. & 15.</note> because an adopted son is also called an heir and a legitimate successor <note>original: "hæres, legitimusque successor"; see the Institutes of Justinian, On Adoption</note>. And it is established that in a fief that is purely, absolutely, or entirely hereditary, judgments regarding succession and <term>alienation: the transfer of property rights to another</term> are made no differently than for any other inherited property. According to Vultejus <note>on fiefs, book 1, chapter 8</note> and Rosenthal, such a fief can be transferred to any outside successor, to women, to any legatee through contracts, and by Will as well as through <term>intestacy: dying without a will</term>, even without the consent of the Lord and the <term>agnates: male-line relatives</term> intervening <note>Cravett. cons. 713; Schrader p. 8; Rosenthal cap. 9</note>. However, the rights of the Feudal Lord remain preserved <note>Knichen. de vestitur. pact.</note>.

If the judgment in the possession case is to be pushed back, then this omission discussed in the present question is justified in itself. Considering that if the Lord of B. or the Imperial Prosecutor were directed to the ownership trial (Petitorium), then while the lawsuit is pending <note>original: "lite pendente"</note>, no action could be taken even against the Countess's <term>Allodial heirs: heirs to property held in absolute ownership, not subject to a feudal lord</term>. For the possession of an <term>agnate</term> or any other opponent is usually called "vicious" <note>original: "possessio vitiosa," meaning legally flawed or illegal</note> when he seizes it by his own authority <note>Cravett. consil 134; Achil. Personal.</note>. This is true even if the possession were vacant and not yet seized by the heir, provided the inheritance has been entered into <note>Bartolus on the Code</note>. This is expanded so that it proceeds even if the heir only entered the inheritance while the controversy was pending, for the law creates a fiction that the inheritance was entered from the day of the deceased's death. Conversely, the possession of another is considered violent and flawed, as Meichsner collects and proves,

<column-break/>

decis: 13. num. 46. 49. 60. & 350. where he further writes: that just as the intent to acquire is presumed, so also is the intent to possess.

Thus, as reported and as can be seen in Document number 49, this <term>Huldigung: a formal ceremony of homage or oath of fealty to a sovereign</term> was performed out of the most humble respect for His Imperial Majesty with such a protective caution: that while things remain in this state <note>original: "rebus in hoc statu durantibus"</note>, the homage should apply only to the ownership of the Lordship of S. and not simultaneously to the imperial feudal rights. This was by no means forbidden to the Lady Countess even while the lawsuit was pending, seeing as Her Grace's ownership was never challenged or made a matter of dispute. Moreover, in any event <note>original: "in omnem eventum"</note>, everything that occurred here was done without malice <note>original: "sine dolo"</note>. Malice is not presumed in cases of doubt, nor has it been proven; even slight causes can excuse a person from it, thus it happened without any punishable reproach.

Indeed, to perform an "attentatum" <note>an illegal act or innovation during a pending lawsuit</note> is entirely a crime, and matters concerning such acts are considered under penal law. Therefore, it requires <term>dolus: intentional wrongdoing or malice</term>, just as in other crimes <note>Rob. Lancellotus, treatise on attentates</note>.

On acts performed while an Appeal is pending <note>original: "De Attentatis Appellatione pendente"</note>, see Hieronymus Manfredus, Franciscus Herculanus, and Robertus Lancellotus. A person is not said to perform an "attentatum" if they are simply continuing their own possession; indeed, someone who stops their possession while a lawsuit is pending might be said to be acting foolishly. Rather, he who hinders someone from continuing their possession is the one considered to be performing an "attentatum" <note>Petrus Fridericus</note>.

In this case, the consulting Lady Countess is not only cleared of all malice, but this act of Homage—which some wish to portray as a forbidden act performed during a pending trial—is sufficiently justified. This is because the flaw of "attentatum" does not apply to a universal heir who takes possession of inherited goods over which a lawsuit was pending between the deceased and another. Such possession, although taken while the suit is pending, is not called an illegal "attentatum" but rather a "continuation." The continuation of possession is not considered prohibited, even if it were against the law being argued in court, and even after a formal prohibition <note>original: "post inhibitionem"</note>. This applies not only when the same person continues possession, but also when there is a change of person, provided the new person represents the one whose possession is being continued. Hence we see that a universal heir can seize the goods of the deceased without the flaw of "attentatum."

# Thesauri Practici Adaucti
### [The Treasury of Practical Law, Expanded]

...they are accustomed to protect, so that no one might complain about the legal right of such a supreme Judge, or feel themselves unfairly burdened or affected by some injury through a sentence, with no path open to them to demonstrate the justice of their cause.

And since it is Divine rather than human to be equally wise at all hours—to discern the honorable from the dishonorable, the just from the unjust, and never to turn to the right or to the left—it was not fitting for that presumed confidence in the State’s administration of the balance and Rule of Justice to be a detriment to anyone. Nor should the weight of reputation held by any Judge be preferred over the injury of another. It was therefore wisely established that although it is not permitted to <term>provoke: to formally appeal to a higher court</term> against the Sentence of certain Judges due to their excellence, a license for <term>supplication: a humble petition for a grievance to be heard by the sovereign</term> is nonetheless granted to those who claim they have been harmed. For it is not in the public interest for the protections of the laws to be denied to individuals, as the Divine Emperors Diocletian and Maximian prudently wrote in their response <note>original: "l. un. C. de sent. Praefect. Prator." — referring to the Code of Justinian regarding the sentences of Praetorian Prefects</note>.

And it seems to be beyond controversy that this Supplication can be offered according to common law at any time within a two-year period, according to the express text <note>original: "per text. expressum..."</note>. Since this right has not been taken away by any public law of the Empire that we know of, we believe it also applies to sentences issued by the Most Illustrious <term>Aulic Council: the Reichshofrat, one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</term>.

Therefore, a Supplication should be most submissively presented to Your Imperial Majesty, because the two-year limit since the burdensome decree issued in the <term>possessory: a legal action regarding the right of physical possession</term> has not yet passed. In this petition, the grievances against said decree should be detailed, yet it should be submitted in every way with the most gracious advice and support of Your Princely Highness, so as to avoid <note>original: "ad invidiam"</note> ill-will or resentment toward the Lady Countess. Furthermore, one could also most obediently request <term>restitution in integrum: a legal remedy that restores the parties to their original condition before a contract or judgment</term> as a secondary option within the same Supplication.

For it is the common opinion of the <term>Canonists: experts in Church law</term> that restitution to the original state is granted against a sentence on the pretext that it was delivered against the right of the litigant. This is the view of Hostiensis <note>in cap. 2. de purg. vulg.</note>, whom others commonly follow. This view should be embraced as the fairer and more merciful one in cases of doubt. This especially applies if <term>investiture: the formal act of giving someone legal possession of a fief</term> is sought from the Prince. By reason of his supreme power, and because he can give or take away authority from judgments, the Prince must grant it if the unfairness of a sentence is discovered and it seems just to him.

<column-break/>

Even if this could not be done through the path of legal restitution by Justice, it could nonetheless be sought through a Supplication out of grace <note>original: "ex gratia"</note>, as argued by Bodin and others.

However, in the case of **Fugger versus Mäxelrein**, a similar judgment was issued in the Imperial Court many years ago under almost identical terms as this one. Even when they tried to bring the matter to the <term>Imperial Chamber Court: the Reichskammergericht, the other highest court of the Empire</term> and had issued <term>citations: formal court summons</term>, those were again quashed by a Sentence. The legal scholar Rosenthal records the summary of this lawsuit in these words:

*Many have written specifically that the Emperor shall be the Judge between two <term>vassals: individuals holding land in exchange for service</term> contending over a <term>fief: a feudal estate</term>, so that one is held liable to the other for <term>eviction: the loss of property due to a superior legal claim</term>. This was greatly disputed in the case of Lord Johann Fugger against the Lord Baron of Mäxelrein, concerning the Barony or Imperial fief of Mindelheim.*

*The Emperor had promised this to said Fugger in the event that the last male vassal of the Frönsberg family died without male children. When this condition was met, Mäxelrein and his partners contended that those fiefs were of such a nature that female relatives could succeed to them. Having taken possession, they presented their legal arguments, ancient investitures, and the will of the last vassal (in which he was named heir) to the Emperor’s court, requesting that the investiture be conferred and possession confirmed. However, this was refuted on Lord Fugger’s behalf, who argued it was a male-only fief and requested to be put in possession. After legal counsel was presented, the Emperor, through a sentence issued by the Imperial Aulic Councilors in 1587, decreed that Fugger should be put in possession and appointed two Princes of the Empire as commissioners to carry this out. Mäxelrein opposed this the following year and obtained a citation from the Imperial Chamber Court, attempting to block the possession through this pending litigation. Mäxelrein argued the Emperor could not be the Judge because he was liable for the eviction. Nevertheless, he labored in vain, etc.*

Besides this, His Imperial Majesty or his <term>Fiscus: the Imperial treasury or state legal office</term> will not likely wish to involve themselves in a dispute over possession with the consulting Lady Countess, since it is established in law that in such a case, the ownership trial (*Petitorium*) and the possession trial (*Possessorium*) do not usually prejudice each other.

Therefore, it might be more advisable for the consulting Lady Countess that Her Grace either...

...to vigorously pursue the <term>Petitorium: a legal action based on the right of ownership</term>, while omitting the <term>Possessorium: a legal action based on the right of mere possession</term>, or at least not to neglect the ownership claim. One should prosecute both legal actions at the same time and in such a way that the possession claim—which has been made very doubtful due to a sentence already passed—does not also make the ownership claim more "odious" <note>meaning: legally unfavorable or prejudiced</note> or cause further delay. ### Question Five.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' featuring floral motifs.</image-desc>
**D**eciding this question depends entirely on the resolution of the matters set out above. For in the event that the disputed feudal rights are absolutely hereditary, they can be transferred to any heirs whatsoever, and even to an adopted son. This was specifically the opinion of Curtius Junior <note>original: "consil. 138. num. 9. & 15."</note>, because even an adopted son is called an heir and a legitimate successor <note>original Latin: "quia etiam ipse dicitur hæres, legitimusque successor." §. Sed hodie Inst. de Adopt.</note>. It is well established that in a fief that is purely, absolutely, or entirely hereditary, judgments regarding succession and alienation <note>the transfer of property</note> are made no differently than for any other hereditary property. Vultejus writes <note>original: "de feud. lib. 1. cap. 8. num. 30."</note>, as does Rosenthal <note>original: "cap. 2. conclus. 35. num. 2."</note>, that such a fief can be transferred to any outside successor, to women, or to any legatees through contracts—both by Will and by <term>intestacy: dying without a will</term>—even without the consent of the Lord or the <term>agnates: relatives related through the male line</term> intervening. This is supported by Cravetta, Schrader, and Rosenthal <note>original: "Cravett. cons. 713. numero 4. Schrader. p. 8. cap. 8. num. 9. Rosenthal. cap. 9. conclus. 58. num. 23."</note>, provided that the rights of the Feudal Lord remain intact.

If the judgment regarding possession is also to be pushed back, then this omission discussed in the current question is justified in itself. This is because if the Lord of B. or the Imperial Prosecutor were directed toward the ownership claim, then <term>lite pendente: while the lawsuit is pending</term>, no attempt could be made to take action against the Countess’s <term>allodial heirs: those who inherit property held in absolute ownership, not subject to a feudal lord</term>. For the possession of a kinsman or another challenger is usually called "vicious" or defective when they seize it by their own authority <note>original: "Quia Agnati vel alterius Contradictoris possessio vitiosa dici solet, quando eam propria authoritate adprehendit"</note>. This is true even if the possession were vacant and not yet taken up by the heir, provided the inheritance has been accepted. For the law creates a fiction that the inheritance was accepted from the day of the deceased’s death. Conversely, another's possession is considered violent and defective, as Meichsner collects and proves all these points,

<column-break/>

in decision 13, numbers 46, 49, 60, and 350, where he further writes: that just as the intention to acquire is presumed, so also is the intention to possess.

Furthermore, as reported and as can be seen in Document number 49, this act of <term>homage: a formal oath of loyalty by a vassal to a lord</term> was performed out of the most humble respect for His Imperial Majesty, but with such a protective caution that, while current conditions persist, it should be understood to apply only to the ownership of the Lordship of S. and not simultaneously to the imperial <term>regalia: royal rights or privileges</term> held in fief. This was certainly not forbidden to the Countess even while the lawsuit was pending, considering that Her Grace's ownership was never challenged or made a matter of dispute. Moreover, in any event, everything that has transpired in this place was done <term>sine dolo: without malice or deceit</term>. Such deceit is not presumed in cases of doubt, nor has it been proven; even the slightest causes may excuse one from it, and thus these actions were done without punishable reproach.

Indeed, to make an unlawful attempt <note>original: "attentare"</note> is entirely a crime, and the subject of such attempts is considered a penal matter. Therefore, it requires malice, just as in other crimes.

Regarding "Interferences committed while an Appeal is pending" <note>original: "De Attentatis Appellatione pendente"</note>, Hieronymus Manfredus, Franciscus Herculanus, and Rubertus Lancellotus write: He is not said to commit an interference who continues his own possession; so much so that he who ceases his possession while a suit is pending is said to be "foolish" <note>original: "desipere"</note>. Rather, he is thought to commit an interference who hinders someone from continuing their possession.

In this case, however, the Countess seeking counsel is not only cleared of all malice, but this act of homage—which some wish to characterize as a forbidden interference committed while the suit was pending—is sufficiently justified. This is because the defect of an "interference" does not apply to a <term>universal heir: one who succeeds to all the rights and assets of the deceased</term> who takes possession of hereditary goods about which a lawsuit was pending between the deceased and another. Such possession, although taken while the suit is pending, is not called an interference, but rather a "continuation." The continuation of possession—even if it were against the law brought into court, and even after a prohibition—is not considered forbidden. This is supported by various legal authorities including Gabriel, Paris, Ruinus, Decius, and Nevizanus. This rule applies not only when such continuation is done by the same person, but also when it occurs with a change of person, provided that person represents the one whose possession is being continued. Hence we see that a universal heir can take up possession of the deceased's goods without the defect of an "unlawful interference."

...now if he is the heir. And there, see Balbus <note>original: "Bald. col. 1. vers. nota istam. C. de litig."</note> and Lancellottus on the matter of innovations while a lawsuit is pending <note>original: "de attent. lite pendente limit. 1. n. 17."</note>.

Up to this point, the Lady Countess has always successfully maintained the "continuation" <note>the ongoing legal status of holding the property</note> discussed in the present question, particularly before the judgment in the <term>Possessorium: a legal proceeding focused on who currently holds or occupies property, rather than who owns the ultimate title</term> was issued. This was done especially by virtue of the <term>investitures: formal legal acts of installing someone in a fief or office</term> granted to her person. These disputed rights, being hereditary, were possessed in such a way that they could pass to any heirs whatsoever, and thus she was able to transfer this continued possession to his Grace V. This is primarily because the act of <term>homage: a formal acknowledgment of loyalty by a tenant to a lord</term> was performed as something secondary to something else—namely, it was done principally to maintain ownership. In such a case, a claim regarding "attempted innovations" <note>illegal changes made to a property's status while a lawsuit is ongoing</note> cannot be pursued. This is supported by Parisius <note>original: "cons. 172. in causa num. 12. lib. 4."</note>. Furthermore, ownership held "undivided" <note>original: "pro indiviso"</note>, and particularly ownership of feudal rights, cannot easily be possessed in a physical sense, according to Bartolus. Jason also teaches that in such a case, claims of "attempted innovations" are excluded.

## Question Six.

Regarding the <term>Petitorium: a legal action where the plaintiff seeks to establish their actual ownership or title to a property</term>, it is correct in and of itself that the consulting Lady Countess may continue to use both her old advocates and servants, or seek new ones, even without further petition. Since her Ladyship has been granted the freedom—and indeed was fully permitted—to initiate the Petitorium and to pursue the legal arguments she deems sufficient in this matter, and since explicit mention of this was made in the Decree concerning the <term>Possessory Judgment: the court's decision on the right of possession</term>, it follows conclusively from this: that her Ladyship is allowed and permitted to use all kinds of necessary means by the highest legal right <note>original Latin: "jure optimo maximo"</note>. For indeed, to whomever something is found to have been granted, then surely all those things must also be considered permitted without which that thing cannot be conveniently accomplished, according to commonly known laws.

In our understanding, almost the same opinion holds for the Petitorium. As set out above, her Ladyship is not prohibited from most humbly petitioning against the decision issued in that judgment, nor from seeking <term>Restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy that restores a person to their original position or cancels a legal disadvantage</term>. Furthermore, the <term>remedies: legal ways to correct a wrong or enforce a right</term> prescribed in law, both ordinary and extraordinary, are granted and permitted to everyone. No one who uses them with modesty should be drawn into unfair suspicion or be prevented from using them, especially since no one should be condemned before a sufficient examination of the case <note>original Latin: "ante sufficientem causæ cognitionem"</note>, or before he has been sufficiently heard regarding such remedies. For all these things contain something of the "natural defense," which ought not to be taken away from anyone, nor restricted or narrowed. This is noted by Tuschus. Likewise, an advocate may provide his patronage in a doubtful case, as Magonius signifies in his *Cynosura Advocatorum*, and as the *Summa Sylvestrina* also notes under the word:

<column-break/>

Advocate. Likewise, in cases involving the <term>patrimony: the inherited estate or wealth</term> of the Prince and the <term>Fiscus: the public or imperial treasury</term>, although Balbus advises advocates to abstain from deciding cases against the Treasury, he nevertheless adds that they must and can refer the parties to the Justice of the Prince. This should certainly not be done crudely, but with a modest and humble deduction of reasons.

Because the consulting Lady Countess, in this extensive and very important matter, might not easily appoint new advocates or other servants—nor would anyone else likely want to involve themselves in this matter, or if they did, no one could sufficiently inform themselves in a short time—her Ladyship has all the more reason to most humbly solicit her old advocates and servants.

Indeed, for one who cannot find an advocate, one is given by the court's office, especially to women and others who, through fear of a more powerful adversary, cannot find an advocate <note>original Latin: "l. 1. §. 4. ff. de postul. l. 9. §. 5. ff. de offic. Procons."</note>. Finally, the elegant law of the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus also pertains here, where they wrote: "With our authority, you may also provide patronage for private citizens against the Treasury, provided that you decline to take up a case which you perhaps handled when you were an Advocate of the Treasury."

## Question Seven.

The resolution of this present question can likewise be easily drawn from what has been deduced above. For even if the often-cited Decree, which was issued to the disadvantage of the Lady Countess in the possessory case, were not retracted; and even if it were correct in both the Petitorium and Possessorium that those rights which are <term>Imperial Fiefs: lands or rights held directly from the Emperor</term> would revert to the Imperial Majesty and the Holy Empire after the death of the aforementioned Lady Countess, it would still remain entirely free for her Ladyship, during her lifetime, to petition for the fiefs and property in the proper manner. Where necessary, she could also file a complaint against V. based on the law <note>original: "ex L. Diffamari," referring to a law allowing a person to force someone else to bring a lawsuit or remain silent about a claim</note>. Furthermore, her Ladyship’s future <term>allodial heirs: those who inherit property held in absolute ownership, rather than as a fief</term> would be entitled to keep these items or rights that are not notoriously feudal in their hands until such time as a legal decision is made, and after a sufficient examination of the case, it is declared what is a fief and what is private property, as has already been set out above.

Truly, there is a very firm presumption of Law that any matter in doubt is "allodial" <note>held privately rather than feudally</note>. Those who base their claim on an <term>investiture: the formal grant of a fief</term> ought rightly to blame themselves if they did not state the contract more clearly, or if they did not take care to have a catalog or description of the feudal goods written down, according to Rosenthal. Nor is anything understood to be granted that the words of the investiture do not expressly state.

Rosenthal, *chapter 8, conclusion 28.* and first the granting must be proved, and thus the delivery and the concession into a <term>fief: land held from a lord in return for service</term>, before a restoration is to be made by the <term>allodial: property owned independently, without a feudal superior</term> heirs of the <term>Vassal: a person who owes loyalty and service to a lord in exchange for land</term>, Rosenthal *chapter 8, conclusion 32, number 12.* And indeed, the allodial heirs, when they deny that they are Vassals, cannot be urged to produce a Catalog or description of the feudal properties, Rolandus à Valle, *counsel 66, number 15, volume 3.* Molina, *on the Customs of Paris, title 1, section 31, number 2.* Capycius, *on investitures, chapter on the 5th edition of feudal lords, column 2, section 'limit as aforesaid,' section 'he indeed who denies,' page 181.*

### Question Eight.

Regarding this question, it is quite correct that the Imperial <term>Fiscal: the public prosecutor or state attorney</term>, regardless of the Notary’s settlement <note>original: "Transaction"</note>, is entitled to pursue the alleged public interest in one way or another, and his position has not been prejudiced in the slightest by such a settlement.

For the public Law is not derogated by the agreements of private persons <note>original: "Pactis enim privatorum Juri Publico non derogatur"</note>. And this is also the nature of a settlement, and of any other agreement, that it does not prejudice others, but only those who are party to the agreement, *law 3 in the preamble, Digest on settlements, title 5, Code on matters between others.* Farinacci, *question 4, number 31, etc.* Tuschus, *letter T, conclusion 347.* which Gailius also teaches in almost our very terms, *book 1, on the Public Peace, chapter 11, number 20,* where he adds that a settlement is valid in the violation of public peace, but for the Instance to perish, it is necessary to settle similarly with the Proctor of the Fiscal, Besoldus, *Volume I.*

<column-break/>

and that by reason of public vengeance, which he also repeated, *book 2, on the Public Peace, chapter 6, number 5.*

And although he who settles seems to confess the crime, *law 'not condemned,' where the gloss is on the Code 'on those who are marked with infamy,' law 'since' of the Digest on the same.* Hence it is that settlements in the Chamber <note>The Imperial Chamber Court</note> regarding injuries are not confirmed, although otherwise the confirmation of contracts can be sought from a Judge, and indeed ought to be done, Gail, *book 2, observation 102, number 15.*

Yet, in cases of <term>injuries: legal wrongs or insults to one's honor</term> especially, and those concerning a certain private crime, it is entirely un-forbidden to pacify and to unite oneself. Indeed, Paulus the Jurist counts among lawful agreements those made in cases of theft and injuries, by which the action is considered removed by the law itself, *law 17, section 1, on agreements.* And it contributes here that *law 18 of the Code on settlements* expressly makes mention of public Crimes, because it is prohibited in public Crimes that do not bring the penalty of blood, and by that it seems to hint, by an argument drawn from the opposite, that in private matters another rule is received. And furthermore, the reason is different in each case: in private matters the private interest is principally looked at, in public matters the public interest. Nor does it stand in the way that *in law 1 of the Digest on those who are marked with infamy,* he is pronounced infamous who has settled in his own name regarding goods seized by force, theft, etc., because he who settles is indeed considered to confess the Crime, *law 6 of the said title.* For such a rule is in no way to be drawn to the present settlement made with the Notary, because he did not act criminally, but only pursued his own interest.

Moreover, it is established that if one acts civilly, a settlement is permitted, *law 'sometimes,' section 'whoever guardianship,' Digest on theft; law 'after the decision,' Code on the same; law 'if for a thief,' Digest on the recovery of stolen goods.* Fachinaeus, *book 1, chapter 9.*

### Question Nine.

Conversely, it is correct regarding this question that, for the very reasons just indicated, the Lord Advocate and the Clerk mentioned in this Question may still properly vindicate the Injury inflicted upon them by the Notary, regardless of the fact that the principal interested parties have reached a friendly settlement with the Notary. Likewise, we do not doubt that, at least on this name, the Notary may be sued for injuries, because he sharply accused the said Lord Advocate and Clerk before his Imperial Majesty without foundation, and also worked out heavy processes and mandates against them by his false suggestions, not to mention the extra-judicial defamation.

For it is established that an accuser or plaintiff who does not prove his case is held liable for injuries, even if he has rumor on his side, since the presumption of Law militates against him. Cravetta, *counsel 796, number 10.* Menochius, *case 32, in the preamble, where at number 33* he teaches that certain causes may indeed excuse one from <term>calumny: the making of false and defamatory statements</term>, so that the calumniator is not held by the likeness of the punishment, or another which has been substituted in its place, but not...
