...now if the heir. <note>original Latin: "nunc si hæres"</note> and there Baldus, column 1, at the verse "note that one." Code, on litigious matters. Lancellotus, on attempts while a suit is pending, limitation 1, number 17, etc.

Now, the Countess here, especially before the judgment in the <term>possessory action: a legal proceeding regarding who currently holds physical control of property</term> was issued, has at all times also achieved the <note>original: "Continuation, de quâ in præsenti quæstione agitur"</note> continuation of possession which is at issue in the present question. This is especially true by virtue of the investitures directed to her Grace's person, having possessed the disputed <note>original: "Jura"</note> rights as inheritable, <note>original: "& ita ad quoscunque hæredes transitoriè"</note> and thus passed on to any heirs whatsoever; therefore, by <note>original: "continuando suam possessionem"</note> continuing her possession, she was well able to transfer such rights to the Lord V.'s Grace. This is primarily because the act of homage was performed <note>original: "accessoriè ad aliquid aliud, imò principaliter"</note> as an accessory to something else—indeed, principally for the maintenance of ownership. <note>original: "quo etiam casu via attentatorum, agi non potest"</note> In which case also, one cannot proceed by way of legal challenges to maneuvers made during a pending suit, as per Parisius, counsel 172, in the case number 12, book 4. Considering that ownership <note>original: "pro indiviso"</note> in an undivided state, and especially <note>original: "Jurium feudalium"</note> feudal rights, cannot be easily possessed, as noted by Bartolus on the law regarding the ejection of a slave, at the section "Labeo." And there Jason, number 17, Digest on legacies 1, where he teaches that in such a case, challenges to maneuvers during a pending suit are excluded.

## Sixth Question.

As far as the <term>petitory action: a legal proceeding regarding the actual legal title or ownership of property, rather than just possession</term> is concerned, it is in and of itself correct that the consulting Countess may, even without further petitioning, continue to use both her old advocates and servants, or apply for new ones. For since her Grace has been permitted to initiate the petitory action and to carry out the legal arguments she believes she has in this matter—and this was indeed permitted and express mention of it was made in the <note>original: "Decreto, Possessorium Judicium"</note> Decree concerning the Possessory Judgment—it follows conclusively from this that her Grace is granted and allowed <note>original: "jure optimo maximo"</note> by the highest and best right to use all kinds of necessary means. <note>original: "Etenim cui aliquid concessum invenitur, tunc sanè facilè simul omnia etiam ea permissa censeri debent, sine quibus illud commodè expediri non potest, per Jura vulgata."</note> For to whomsoever something is found to be granted, then surely all those things must also be considered permitted at the same time, without which the matter cannot be conveniently carried out, according to common laws.

According to our understanding, the same opinion holds in the petitory action. For as argued above, her Grace is not prohibited from most humbly petitioning against the decision issued in <note>original: "illo Judicio"</note> that judgment, or simultaneously seeking <term>Restitutionem in integrum: a legal remedy that restores the parties to their original position before a contract or judgment</term>. Furthermore, the <note>original: "Remedia in jure præscripta, tàm ordinaria quàm extraordinaria"</note> remedies prescribed in law, both ordinary and extraordinary, are granted and permitted to everyone; nor should anyone who uses them with modesty be drawn into suspicion or be prevented from doing so. This is especially true since no one should be <note>original: "condemnirt"</note> condemned <note>original: "ante sufficientem causæ cognitionem"</note> before a sufficient examination of the case, or before he has been sufficiently heard regarding such remedies. <note>original: "Continent enim ea cuncta aliquid de defensione naturali, quæ nemini adimi, vel restringi, coarctativè debet."</note> For all these things contain something of natural defense, which ought not to be taken away from anyone, nor restricted in a limiting way. Tuschus, conclusion 130, letter D. And likewise, an advocate may provide his patronage in a doubtful case. Magonius, in the *Cynosura of Advocates*, chapter 43, number 13, which is also noted in the *Summa Sylvestrina* under the word:

<column-break/>

Advocate. Likewise, in cases involving the patrimony of the Prince and the <term>Fiscus: the public treasury or state's financial interests</term>, Baldus advises in counsel 253, "the illustrious Lord," at the end of book 1, that advocates should abstain from deciding cases against the Treasury; however, he adds that they should and can refer the parties to the Justice of the Prince: which, indeed, should not be done nakedly, but with a modest and humble deduction of reasons.

Furthermore, because the consulting Countess cannot easily appoint new advocates or other servants in this extensive and very important matter, nor would anyone else likely want to involve themselves in this case—or even if such were to happen, no one could sufficiently inform themselves in a short time—her Grace has all the more reason to most humbly solicit for her old advocates and servants.

<note>original Latin: "Quin & ei, qui non invenire potest Advocatum, ex officio aliquis datur, fœminis præfertim & aliis, qui metu potentioris Adversarii non inveniunt Advocatum..."</note> Furthermore, for one who cannot find an advocate, one is provided by the court's office, especially for women and others who, through fear of a more powerful adversary, cannot find an advocate. Digest, on requesting, law 1, section 4; Digest, on the office of the Proconsul, law 9, section 5; Digest, on the affairs of those under guardianship, law 5, section 11. Finally, the elegant law 3, Code on the Advocates of the Treasury, also pertains here, where the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus wrote: "With our authority, you may provide patronage to private individuals even against the Treasury, provided that you decline to take up that case which you perhaps handled when you were an advocate for the Treasury."

## Seventh Question.

The resolution of this present question can likewise be easily taken from what has been deduced above. For even if the often-cited Decree, which was issued to the disadvantage of the Countess in the possessory action, should not be retracted—and even if it were correct in both the petitory and possessory actions that those rights here which are an <term>imperial fief: land held directly from the Holy Roman Emperor</term> would fall to His Imperial Majesty and the Holy Empire upon the death of the aforementioned Countess—nevertheless, it would not only remain free to her Grace during her lifetime to petition for the fief and the <term>allodial property: land owned independently without any feudal obligations</term> in a proper manner, and where necessary, to sue against Lord V. <note>original: "ex L. Diffamari"</note> according to the law *Diffamari*, but her Grace's future allodial heirs would also be entitled to hold these pieces or rights that are not notoriously <note>original: "feudalia"</note> feudal in their hands until such time as a legal ruling is made on this matter, <note>original: "ac post sufficientem causæ cognitionem"</note> and after a sufficient examination of the case, it is declared what is a fief or private property, as has already been argued above.

<note>original Latin: "Quippe firmissima Juris præsumtio est, rem quamlibet in dubio esse allodialem..."</note> Indeed, it is a very firm presumption of the Law that any matter in doubt is allodial, and those who base their claim on an investiture must rightfully blame themselves for why they did not state the contract more clearly, or why they did not see to it that a catalog or description of the feudal goods was written down. Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 15, number 70. Nor is that understood to be granted which is not expressly stated in the words of the investiture. Rosen-

First, the giving must be proved, and thus the delivery and the granting of the <term>fief: land or rights held from a lord in exchange for service</term>, before the <term>allodial heirs: those inheriting private property not subject to feudal service</term> of the Vassal are required to make restitution. For if he is ready to affirm by the sanctity of an Oath that he is ignorant of the feudal properties, he shall be excused, and cannot be further compelled. Rosenthal, chapter 8, conclusion 32, number 15.

Baldus in the chapter "A Vassal if a fief," number 9; and there Laudensis, number 11; Alvarus, number 10; Praepositus, number 3; Afflictis, number 19, on the fiefs of the deceased; and in chapter 1, numbers 13, 18, and following, on the controversy between males and females, after Pileus, question 119. And then the burden of proof lies with the Lord, as the plaintiff, and the defendant is not to be deprived of his possession by common laws; <note>original German: "man wolte dann, wider Verhoffen, ex plenitudine potestatis procediren, und diese Eminenz gebrauchen, deren sich der König in Franckreich und andere Absoluti Reges anmassen"</note> unless one would, contrary to expectations, proceed from the <term>fullness of power: absolute sovereign authority</term> and employ that "eminence" which the King of France and other absolute Kings claim for themselves, inasmuch as they never litigate while out of possession. Choppin on the domain of France, book 3, title 10, at the end; Papon, book 5 of arrests, title 1, arrest 9, where he gives as a rule <note>original French: "que le Roy doit plaider saisi"</note> that the King must plead while in possession.

### Question Eight.

Regarding this question, it is quite correct that the Imperial <term>Fiscal: the state's legal representative or prosecutor</term>, regardless of the Notary O.’s settlement, is entitled to pursue the claimed public interest in one way or another; nor has anything been prejudiced against him in the slightest by such a settlement.

<note>original Latin: "Pactis enim privatorum Juri Publico non derogatur"</note> For the private agreements of individuals do not override Public Law. And this is also the nature of a settlement, and of any other convention: that it does not prejudice any except the contracting parties. Law 3, in the beginning, Digest on settlements; title on matters between others in the Code; Farinacci, question 4, number 31; and Tusch, letter T, conclusion 347. Gailius teaches this in almost our exact terms, book 1, on Public Peace, chapter 11, number 20, where he adds that a settlement is valid in a violation of public peace, but for the legal instance to perish, it is necessary to similarly settle with the Procurator of the Fiscal,

<column-break/>

and this is by reason of public vengeance, which he also repeated in book 2, on Public Peace, chapter 6, number 5.

And although <note>original: "is, qui transigit, delictum fateri videatur"</note> he who settles may seem to confess to a crime (Law "not condemned," where the gloss is, Code on those marked with infamy; Law "since," Digest, same title), and hence it is that settlements in the Chamber regarding injuries are not confirmed, even though otherwise the confirmation of contracts can be requested from a Judge, and indeed ought to be done (Gailius, book 2, observation 102, number 15).

Nevertheless, in cases of <term>injuries: legal claims regarding personal affronts or defamation</term> especially, and those concerning similar private crimes, it is entirely permitted to pacify and reach an agreement. Indeed, the jurist Paulus counts among lawful pacts those made in cases of theft and injuries, by which the action is considered removed by the law itself (Law 17, § 1, on pacts). And it contributes to this that Law 18, Code on settlements, expressly makes mention of public crimes, stating that settlement is prohibited in public crimes involving capital punishment; by which it seems to imply that in private crimes, the rule is different, reasoning from the contrary. And furthermore, the reasoning is different in both: in private matters, the private interest is primarily looked at; in public matters, the public interest. Nor does it stand in the way that in Law 1, Digest on those marked with infamy, he is pronounced <term>infamous: a legal status involving the loss of certain civil rights</term> who has settled in his own name regarding goods taken by force, or theft, etc., because he who settles is indeed considered to confess the crime (Law 6, same title). However, such a thing is in no way to be applied to the present settlement made with the Notary, because he is not acting criminally, but only pursuing his own interest.

Moreover, it is established that if a case is handled civilly, a settlement is permitted. Law "sometimes," § "who the guardianship," Digest on theft; Law "after the decision," Code, same title; Law "if for a thief," Digest on the recovery of stolen goods; Fachinae, book 1, chapter 9.

For it is established that an accuser or plaintiff who does not prove his case is held liable for injuries, even if he has rumor on his side, since the presumption of Law fights against him. Cravetta, counsel 796, number 10; Menochius, case 32, at the beginning, where at number 33 he teaches that certain causes may indeed excuse one from <term>calumny: the making of false and malicious statements to damage someone's reputation</term>, so that the slanderer is not held to the "likeness of punishment" or another penalty substituted in its place, but...

However, we are of the opinion that this must be brought before His Imperial Majesty, as the matter is already present there; otherwise, the aforementioned two gentlemen might face the <term>Exceptio litis pendentiæ: a legal objection that the same case is already being tried in another court</term>. <note>original: "Quia ubi cœptum judicium est, ibi finiri debet"</note> Because where a trial has begun, there it ought to be finished, according to the law [Digest, *de judic.*], so that the continuity of the case is not divided, and so that one is not questioned twice for the same offense against good faith [contrary to the text in law *licet*]. Based on the same foundation, Gail [book 1, chapter 11, number 25] teaches that in the Imperial Chamber, in cases involving a breach of the Peace, the objection of a pending lawsuit is admitted, with which Mindanus [chapter 5, number 24] agrees.

Likewise, an action for injuries arising from a pending lawsuit cannot be initiated until that lawsuit is finished [Hartmann, observation 26]. And this is especially true so that no prejudice is done to the pending case, as noted by Angelus and Jason in the Institutes, and by Chassaneuz in the *Customs of Burgundy*. However, on this side, one will provide oneself with a formal protestation before His Imperial Majesty or the highly esteemed <term>Reichs-Hofrath: the Imperial Aulic Council</term>, indicating that these two gentlemen do not release the Notary from the law, but rather intend to vindicate such high injuries in the proper manner, reserving the right to undertake this in the best form at the proper time.

Nonetheless, it is also to be feared that if one were to legally challenge this Notary, he might show enough through various <term>Conjecturas: circumstantial evidence or inferences</term> that a <term>Juramentum purgationis: an "oath of purgation" where a defendant clears their name of a crime by swearing their innocence</term> could be imposed upon him.

## Tenth Question.

Although we have found in our reading of these entire records that the Lord of V. has occasionally used harsh language and was accused of a reprehensible appetite for others' property, and likewise, the process conducted here before the Imperial Aulic Council was charged with various accountable defects.

Yet we are of the certain opinion that all of this is to be excused <note>original: "à prætensâ injuriâ"</note> from the charge of alleged injury, and should in no way be considered punishable or highly reprehensible, 

<column-break/>

since indeed all these things happened <note>original: "necessitate factorum, causáque defensionis licitæ"</note> out of the necessity of the facts and for the purpose of a lawful defense.

<note>original: "Constat autem, quod injuria absque animo injuriandi non fiat..."</note> It is well established, however, that an injury does not occur without the <term>animo injuriandi: the specific intent to insult or harm someone’s honor</term>. Here, malice, intent, will, or the purpose of injuring and inflicting an insult are required [citing the Institutes and various legal experts like Wesenbeck, Menochius, and Cravetta]. For it is the intent and the state of mind that creates the injury, not the act itself or the effect. And no penalty can take place where fraud and malice are absent [Digest, *de V. S.*].

Especially since all of this occurred in <term>Judicio: in a court of law</term> and out of strong necessity for the defense of the Lord of V. It is <note>original: "Recepti Juris"</note> accepted law that even a shameful objection brought during a trial—such as claiming witnesses produced against oneself are forgers, wicked, or criminal, or if one claims the opponent has acted against their sworn word—should not be considered an injury in case of doubt, even if these claims are not proven. Instead, it must be left to the judge's discretion whether the cause and probability of saying them excuse the speaker [citing multiple legal authorities including Mynsinger and Fachinaeus].

It also helps that the <term>Dn. Comitissa: the Lady Countess</term> is the interpreter of her own words, and in doubt, the better presumption should be accepted [Digest, *pro soc.*]. To make this interpretation, presumptions should also be drawn from the timing and the writings of the opponent. Therefore, since neither a likelihood of intent nor precise and necessary proof can be brought, it is clear that in this doubt, nothing can be imputed to the Lady Countess, especially because in the submitted writings on behalf of Her Grace, it has been solemnly and repeatedly protested that there is no intention to dispute the highness and full power of His Imperial Majesty, nor to doubt or deny the Imperial Fiefs out of malice, but only to introduce the available legal defenses.

Likewise, the process conducted by the highly esteemed Imperial Aulic Council is not in itself charged with any fault or defect; rather, what occurred was entirely and intentionally directed toward establishing and strengthening the <term>Remedia & beneficia juris: the legal remedies and benefits</term> sought by the Lady Countess. This is permissible for all parties and, <note>original: "tanquam ad defensionem tendens"</note> as it tends toward defense, should never be forbidden, especially since no judge should take this poorly...

### Eleventh and Final Question.

Because it has already been established above that the <term>Feudal Rights: rights held as a fief from a lord, rather than owned outright</term> in the Lordship of S. extend only to the village of T. and not beyond or outside its boundaries; and because the remaining territory of such a Lordship—including the hamlets located therein and the jurisdiction belonging to them—is <term>allodial: land owned independently, free of any superior lord</term> and private; and furthermore, since we cannot find that the places or villages named in this question are subject to the T. <term>High Court: "Halsgericht," literally "Neck Court," referring to the jurisdiction over capital crimes</term> in such a way that the one who holds the T. High Court by feudal right can consequently use such authority outside the T. boundaries, nor must the separate owners permit this to him—considering that the feudal T. High Court is expressly restricted to the village of T. and no <term>appendages: "Pertinentiarum," meaning lands or rights that belong to a main property</term> were mentioned there; and because the fact that criminals in the entire Lordship were judged and executed at T. happened by the designation and free will of those who held the entire Lordship, and not by some necessary legal dependency—therefore, the criminal jurisdiction or other authorities in the Lordship of S. cannot be regarded as an appendage of the feudal rights.

For it is an accepted rule of law that "appendages" are a matter of fact, and therefore whenever it is denied that one thing belongs to another, it must be proven. <note>Citing various legal authorities like Alexander Tartagnus, Boerius, and Oldradus to support that legal dependencies aren't assumed but must be evidenced.</note> And that when a castle is granted with its rights and appendages, jurisdiction is only included in that specific place, not in neighboring estates, which are presumed to be allodial, as held by Rimini the Younger, Afflictis, Menochius, and others.

Likewise, proximity and bordering alone, without other proofs, do little to argue that a village or neighboring places are among the appendages of a Castle, as proven with good resolutions satisfying this entire business by many cited for and against—

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

—as proven by Antonio Gabriele Romano, Vultejus, Afflictis, Mozzius, and others. And it is well established that even where mention of appendages is made in the <term>investitures: the formal ceremony or document granting a fief</term>, nevertheless, remote appendages are not considered feudal; indeed, it is not enough if "appendages" are expressed by the grantor with a general word, but specific mention of this or that one must be made.

And even more strongly: the proof of appendages on the part of the asserted direct Lordship is not fulfilled by the fact that a <term>Vassal: a person holding land under the feudal system</term> during the time of his possession administered these or those villages or referred them to the feudal Castle; this is proven with evident arguments by Rosenthal and others.

Since the total jurisdiction—which the consulting Countess and her ancestors possess in their half-share of the Lordship of S., except for the village of T.—is entirely their own property, it follows quite correctly from this that we fall within the terms of the Imperial Privilege most graciously granted to the <term>Knighthood: "Ritterschafft," the Imperial Knights who held their land directly from the Emperor</term>. Furthermore, His Imperial Majesty, upon most humble and sufficient demonstration, will in no way burden the Countess’s own share of the Lordship of S. (where neither the jurisdiction nor anything else is feudal) with the subreptitiously <note>"Subreptitious" refers to obtaining a legal grant by concealing the truth.</note> obtained investiture of the <term>Power of the Blood: "Blutbann," the right to pass death sentences</term> held by V. Rather, the Countess, by virtue of the mentioned privilege, was most graciously granted such Power of the Blood and <term>signs of execution: "Signa executiva," such as gallows, marking a territory's high jurisdiction</term> in those parts at the same time as V. For the Countess, by reason of such estates as well as those of V., is undoubtedly a member of the Knighthood; and Her Grace exercises all authority in these villages by her own right and in her own name, just like other nobles in neighboring places capable of holding the said Privilege, and she allowed crimes committed outside of T. to be judged and punished at the feudal T. High Court only for the sake of greater convenience.

# Thesauri Practici Adaucti

Regarding the Imperial Fiefs, they have provided their excellent opinion. However, the resolution of the first question—concerning both the previously disputed opinion of the consultants and the concept formulated by the Archducal Austrian Privy, Court, and Regimental Councilors—appears somewhat inconsistent. Therefore, absolute necessity requires that the motives presented here and there be further explained and additional legal instruction sought.

For although the aforementioned Faculty of Law established as the first reason for the decision that <note>original Latin: "quod Jurisdictio competens inferiori, in dubio, juxta omnes ferè Juris interpretes feudalis reputetur"</note> jurisdiction belonging to a lower lord should, in case of doubt, be considered feudal according to almost all interpreters of the law.

Yet, following this (near the end of the first question, in the section "It is also correct, etc."), it is accepted as correct that jurisdiction in a lordship, fortress, etc.—especially that which is called <term>Vogteylische Botmässigkeit: administrative or protective authority held by a 'Vogt' or advocate</term>—should, in case of doubt, be held as <term>Allodial: land or rights owned absolutely by an individual, without being subject to a feudal lord or duties</term>; since it can be transferred to another under many titles other than feudal ones.

Regarding the second reason for the decision: it must first be repeated from the thorough counter-information marked No. 123 that the Lordship of S. possessed high and low authority even before the grant by King Wenceslaus. This can be concluded not only by conjecture but quite clearly from the 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th, and 16th foundations found there. This is especially true given these two additional supporting points that Lord Gail <note>Andreas von Gail (1526–1587), a leading legal scholar of the Holy Roman Empire's supreme courts.</note> and Knichen <note>Andreas von Knichen (1560–1621), an influential jurist specializing in territorial law.</note> assert: <note>original Latin: "Communi Francorum & Suevorum sensu, Castra immediatorum nobilium, subditos & territorium habere."</note> In the common understanding of the Franks and Swabians, the castles of the <term>Immediate Nobility: nobles who answered directly to the Emperor, rather than an intermediate territorial prince</term> possess both subjects and territory.

Likewise, the freedom issued to von B. in the year 1621, registered under Letter W, itself demonstrates how the estate B. (located within the district of the Lordship of S., of which it is a part) has always possessed all high and low authority, needing only a <term>Halsgericht: a 'neck-court' with the power to impose capital punishment</term> and the right of execution. Consequently, the current Roman Imperial Majesty granted that estate the <term>Blutbann: the 'blood-ban' or criminal jurisdiction over crimes punishable by death</term> and the right to erect signs of execution as a new fief. From this grant, as well as many other documents that could be presented, it is especially evident that high and low courts belong to noble and manorial estates not only by feudal law or privilege (which must be confirmed by every Emperor) but often by ancient custom, <term>Immemorial Prescription: a legal right established by having existed for so long that its origin is beyond human memory</term>, or free donation. In these cases, one did not specifically seek confirmations from a newly elected Roman Emperor, but only the granting of the feudal Blood-ban usually obtained for that purpose. For one.

Furthermore, it can hopefully be clearly demonstrated from the diploma of King Wenceslaus <note>Wenceslaus IV (1361–1419), King of Bohemia and King of the Romans.</note> (if one considers the words as they are written and observes the common style used by Emperors and Kings in granting new or confirming old favors) 

<column-break/>

that the aforementioned Wenceslaus gave the market rights, stocks, and gallows to the von B. family for the first time. This was done out of special grace, with deliberate intent, good counsel, and proper knowledge, for the sake of their past and future service; no mention is made of any predecessors or previous favors or their confirmation. Besides, it is impossible that the von B. family only then acquired the often-mentioned lordship, as they had already married into it 100 years earlier through the only daughter of the last Lord von B., according to W.’s register and other reliable reports.

At that time, it was neither customary nor common for noblemen to seek confirmations for their allodial and private estates or their jurisdictions (as is common for the Estates regarding their privileges). Furthermore, all those familiar with the Empire know well that the <term>Cassatio Privilegiorum: the annulment of privileges</term> by Wenceslaus never took full effect. Instead, many of those privileges were knowingly confirmed by later Emperors (when they were certain of the matter), both generally and specifically, just like other Imperial liberties. More often, they were tacitly accepted, and the Estates were gradually left in possession of them, and were often upheld in the Imperial Court and Chamber—otherwise, many would not have sat quite so comfortably.

This diploma undoubtedly holds the same status, and one cannot sufficiently understand why—since it is not a "fief letter" but a privilege (or more correctly a <note>original Latin: "Concessio vel beneficium per notata Menoch. cas. arbit. 336. n. 24. & seqq." referring to Giacomo Menochio’s legal work on judicial discretion.</note> concession or benefit which operates just as much as, or even more abundantly than, an investiture) and is similar to other Imperial ranks and liberties—nothing binding or legally useful can be deduced from it.

Finally, from the enclosed <term>Vidimus: an authenticated copy of a legal document</term> (which the city of W. issued in 1502 at the request of the two joint owners of the Lordship of S. regarding Wenceslaus’s grant and Emperor Maximilian I’s first fief letter), it can easily be inferred that Heinrich and Balthasar von B., as owners of the now-divided Lordship of S., possessed no other common documents regarding market rights, courts, stocks, and gallows than that very grant from Wenceslaus and Maximilian I’s fief letter, and they considered them valid. Otherwise, they would have placed such older confirmations or investitures in common hands and taken transcripts of them; especially since it is narrated in the said fief letter from the year 1494 that these items were granted to them by the ancestors of the late Emperor Maximilian I, the Roman Emperors and...

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis regarding whether the jurisdictional rights held by the Lordship of S. are feudal (held from a superior) or allodial (privately owned). It specifically examines the historical charters granted by King Wenceslaus and Emperor Maximilian I.</meta>

and were bestowed to kings of the most praiseworthy memory.

Thus, the fief charter <note>original: "Lehenbrief"</note> of the aforementioned Emperor Maximilian I is not only held by the city of W. within the entire verified copy <note>original: "Vidimus," a certified legal copy of a document</note> as a confirmation of the grant from Wenceslaus <note>Wenceslaus IV (1361–1419), King of Bohemia and Germany</note>, and stated twice: but the previously cited claims of those seeking the charter must also be understood as referring specifically to Wenceslaus's concession. Since no other concession exists, the common legal rule applies: <note>original Latin: "Paria sunt autem non esse vel non apparere per vul." — things which do not exist are considered the same as those which do not appear.</note> Furthermore, a plural number is often verified by a single instance according to well-known laws.

In particular, such a fief charter itself must be interpreted according to that concession and held as the first formal investment of the fief; because it expresses the concessions of the previous Emperors and Kings only through the simple word of "granting." *However, in cases of doubt, every grant is presumed to be allodial <note>privately owned without feudal obligation</note> rather than feudal.* <note>original Latin: "Omnis autem concessio in dubio præsumitur potiùs allodialis, quàm feudalis." citing Vultejus on fiefs.</note> This is especially true in matters of jurisdiction granted by a Prince, as explained at length by Menochius. And yet, it grants them to be held as a fief from then on and forevermore in the manner of a fief. *The word "henceforth," however, refers to future time.* <note>original Latin: "Verbum autem hinfürter, est futuri temporis."</note>

From this, it follows further that because the named stakeholders and the first to offer the fief recognized the four items established in the first concession of Wenceslaus—namely market rights, the court, the stocks, and the gallows—and the subsequent observance known best to them <note>original Latin: "quæ etiam optima dispositionum interpres" — which is also the best interpreter of arrangements</note>, they themselves explained this, including the clause regarding the "blood ban" <note>the authority to sentence someone to death</note>. They surrendered and received these rights as a fief exactly as they had held and used them until then. Therefore, the resulting investment of the fief includes nothing more or further than those four items: namely Market Rights (which is understood here, according to the customary and immemorial practice observed so far, as both the right to hold fairs and the legal status of a market town; *notwithstanding that subtle legal distinction between the "right of a place" and "right in a place"*); because it was not the village, but the owners of the village who were granted market rights and more—even a gallows, which one usually sets up outside the village—as well as the High Court <note>original: "Halsgericht," the court of life and limb</note>, or the blood ban, stocks, and gallows.

*For a confirmation gives nothing new.* <note>original Latin: "Confirmatio enim nihil novi dat." citing Gail.</note> *A confirmation gives nothing new, but corroborates existing rights.* <note>citing Graevius and others.</note> This is seen in the Strasbourg legal response in a case of testamentary succession in 1646. And the clause, "just as the ancestors possessed it," refers to the fief itself as it was once possessed in fact, and to its substantial parts

<column-break/>

*which have existed until now, according to the doctrine of Zasius and Andreas Gylmann. And thus it excludes every feudal addition, and indeed every presumption of a feudal addition. For nobles are accustomed to recognize their allodial <note>absolute/private</note> property from Princes for this reason: so that, whenever necessary, they can protect themselves with a more useful title; not because they wish to generate prejudice against themselves.* <note>citing Alciatus and Menochius.</note> *Hence, in case of doubt, an interpretation must be made based on what is good and fair in favor of the Vassal and against the Lord.* <note>citing Rosenthal on feudal commentary.</note>

Against this, the argument concerning the "separate determination of words," which mentions "together with the ban," etc., has no special significance. It is well known that such legal maxims <note>original: "Brocardica"</note> have their exceptions; the argument from the placement of words follows the custom and intention of the parties, and the common rule of law itself admits *that often joined things are taken as separate, separate things as joined, and sometimes loose things as distinct.* <note>citing the Digest on the significance of words.</note> Thus, it is of no importance that the word "Court" could have been left out (if it were only meant to signify a criminal high court), as the other words—stocks, gallows, together with the ban—would have been sufficient. *Since all words found in legal instruments, especially in those of investment, should be understood in a way that they are not idle or redundant, but achieve something.*

Because, on the contrary, it was already indicated above that Emperor Maximilian proceeded based on the applicants' report (as they recounted and stated the concession of Wenceslaus and the observance that followed it), the attached explanatory clause, "together with the ban," etc., was inserted for the sake of greater clarity, just like the preceding words of the first investment.

*But the unnecessary multiplication of words does not change the substance of the matter.* <note>original Latin: "Atqui multiplicatio verborum non necessaria, substantiam rei non mutat."</note> *And John Andreae and others speak a beautiful word: That those things which are to be brought forward in contracts, letters, instruments, and privileges cannot be repeated frequently enough, in order to remove the sophistical and malicious interpretation of certain people; lest it happen to us and be objected against us, as is said in the law: "you should blame yourself for not stating the law of the agreement more clearly." Thus it is not strange that superfluous words are sometimes written, and those stand without effect.*

It emphasizes that legal confirmations do not grant new rights but reinforce existing ones, and that redundant legal language is often used simply for clarity.</summary>

# Expanded Practical Treasury
### Page 630

For this happens in many other cases and words; as noted by Jason de Mayno in Law *petens* number 8, Code on Pacts, and in Law *cum propon.* number 3, Code on Transactions, where he says the word "immediately" <note>original: "statim"</note> may stand without any operational effect. Barbarius says something similar in Counsel 1, column 17 at the end of Book 3, responding similarly regarding the word "almost" <note>original: "ferè"</note>. And Jason responded excellently in Counsel 12, last column of Book 1, that in contracts many words stand without any operational effect. Furthermore, words achieve nothing when the contrary intent of the contracting and disposing parties is clear, and also when the subject matter suggests otherwise. Thus both points are proven by Socinus the Younger in Counsel 45, number 25, Book 1, and Decius in Counsel 473, number 11, as Menochius considers all these points in Counsel 179, number 20. Add to this that a word cannot be called superfluous if it performs some merely declaratory effects <note>it clarifies something already implied</note>, according to Law 2, paragraph *quod si in tanta* 13, Code on the Clarification of Ancient Law; Law *stipulat. commodiss.* 53 on Verbal Obligations; and Law *quae dubitationis* on Rules of Law. And it does not immediately follow that if a provision is not necessary, it is therefore superfluous, as Marius Salomon declares most elegantly in Law *Gallus* section *quidam* under number 9 and following, regarding children and posthumous heirs; this is referenced and followed by Camillus Gallini in *On the Signification of Words*, Book 10, chapter 23, number 30. Indeed, words are said to operate sufficiently when they remove a doubt that might have existed. Hartmann Pistor, Book 2, question 3, number 69. Finally, a redundancy of words is tolerated rather than allowing some absurdity to be introduced, Cravetta, Counsel 70, number 30, or rather than the intent of the disposer being harmed. The same Cravetta, Counsel 808, number 17.

In the same vein, it is argued in opposition: If His Imperial Majesty, through the words "Stock and Gallows" <note>symbols of high jurisdiction involving capital punishment</note> together with the "Jurisdiction" <note>original: "Bann," referring here to the right to command and punish</note>, etc., intended only to interpret the preceding term "Court" <note>original: "Gericht"</note>, and did not intend to grant something further through an extensive interpretation, then he would have added a word such as "that is" or "namely," etc. He would not have said "Court, Stock, and Gallows," but rather "Court, that is, namely Stock and Gallows."

Against this, it must be considered that His Imperial Majesty did not intend to interpret the word "Court" through the following words "Stock and Gallows," but rather intended to interpret both these and those words together solely with the clause "together with the jurisdiction," etc. Therefore, he did not need to use the terms "namely" or "as"; especially because he endeavored, as is right, not to deviate from the narratives <note>the formal descriptions provided in the petition</note> of those applying for the fief, or to change anything therein. Thus, he did not even seek to remove or improve the tautology <note>redundant repetition</note> which those receiving the fief committed through the words "together with" <note>original: "mit sammt," where both words mean nearly the same thing</note> (where either one would have been enough). Furthermore, this fief charter was not drafted with any particular precision (being issued outside the usual seat of the Imperial court, perhaps while traveling, at Füssen), nor was elegance and orderly final connectivity highly observed; in which, for example, the section beginning "and therefore with well-

<column-break/>

considered," etc., was concluded with the words "to graciously grant as a fief" instead of "granted."

With this, the argument drawn from the terms "together with the jurisdiction" <note>original: "mit sammt dem Bann"</note> etc., is also addressed (specifically whether they demonstrate something different from what follows, and rather augment rather than explain the preceding). Here it is also reminded that the word "and," or "together with," or "with" (about which Decian and Jason speak) does not always correspond to the German clause "together with" <note>original: "mit sammt"</note> but also to "with one another" <note>original: "mit einander"</note>, according to Meichsner, Decision 9, number 197. (On what the words "by-" and "with one another" import, see Klock, volume 3, counsel 118, number 4). Furthermore, the conjunction "with" <note>Latin: "cum"</note> joins only accessorily, not principally, like the conjunction "and" <note>Latin: "Et"</note>, Everhard in *Topica* on the nature of conjunctions, number 3. Indeed, when a conjunction is placed between words sounding the same (as here between "Court" and "Jurisdiction to judge over blood"), then, because this is against the nature of a conjunction, the conjunction is removed and those two are mostly resolved into one, with one being an adjective of the other: Law 1 in the preamble, on Pacts, where Bartolus and Everhard speak at the cited location, number 11.

Furthermore, there is no obstructive significance in what was reported regarding the meaning of the term "Court" <note>original: "Gericht"</note> (that it signifies only simple and mixed power <note>terms for lower levels of judicial authority</note>). For the opinion that "all-encompassing jurisdiction" <note>original: "omnimoda jurisdictio"</note> is meant by it is held as the more accepted view, as can be seen in Wesembeck, Rosenthal, and others cited by the opposition, as well as Thomas Michael, *On Jurisdiction*, conclusion 70. Therefore, in law it is considered correct that if someone proves a village belongs to him "with territory" (as is evident here from the Charter of Wenceslaus, that the fortress of S. together with its office, in which the village of T. is located, belonged to those of B.), then he also has a well-founded intent under common law that jurisdiction—and thus high justice <note>original: "merum Imperium," the power of life and death</note>—in said village and its territory belongs to him, by an argument taken from the general to the specific. Meichsner, Decision 4, number 115, volume 2, book 2, adding: for where the Lordship, superiority, and jurisdiction are established, the quality and quantity are very easily presumed. Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrariness*, Book 1, question 76, number 14. Following from this, if it is absolutely necessary that only a specific type be denoted by that word, it should be drawn toward the more powerful rather than the weaker meaning (if the subject matter suggests it). This is especially true because the renowned faculty itself, following Castianzo, presupposes that he who has high justice can say the men are his and he is the Lord of that land. Not to mention now that this entire consideration applies to "Courts" <note>original: "Gerichten," plural</note> (that is, when the word is used in the plural number) and not to "Court" <note>original: "Gericht," singular</note> (when it is uttered in the singular number and denotes a judgment), and thus is not applicable here; as this distinction is sufficiently explained in the Counter-Information under Number 123, section "Secondly," etc., and thereafter also in the section "Once it is known to the Empire," etc.

# Letter L.

The separation or the distinction of the **Power of capital punishment** <note>original: "Blutbann," the legal authority to shed blood or impose the death penalty</note> and **Capital Court** <note>original: "Halsgericht," literally "Neck Court," a court with jurisdiction over crimes punishable by death or corporal punishment</note> from the high and low courts (as they have been explicitly expressed in the Imperial letters of enfeoffment, especially from the times of Emperor Maximilian I—who zealously opened the Blood Ban to the Empire—and in the further appendix: that before, around, and after the times of Wenceslaus <note>original: "antè, circà, & post Wenceslai tempora"</note>, the word "Court" <note>original: "Gericht"</note> was used in privileges, transactions, and confirmations—which could therefore be cited by name and in great number—not for a civil judgment, but solely for a criminal judgment <note>original: "non pro civili, sondern allein pro criminali judicio"</note>; frequently, especially according to the subject matter <note>original: "pro subjectâ materiâ," meaning the legal context determines the definition</note> (according to which the words of any disposition, and especially of investitures, are to be understood <note>original: "juxta quam cujusvis dispositionis, cumpri- mis verò investiturarum, verba accipienda"</note>, according to Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 1, number 102; even if it were necessary for the words to be used improperly <note>original: "etiamsi verba impropriari necesse esset"</note>, Mynsinger, decade 11, response 6, number 25. Indeed, words are always to be understood according to the quality and condition of the matter to which they are directed <note>original: "Siquidem verba semper intelligenda sunt secundum qualitatem & conditionem rei, ad quam diriguntur"</note>. The same Mynsinger, decade 8, response 73, number 30). This is also how it was sometimes set down in Charles V's *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* <note>The 1532 criminal law code of the Holy Roman Empire</note>.

Likewise, it does nothing to impede or hinder the introduction by an honorable Faculty <note>Referring to a university law faculty acting as legal consultants</note> that, even if the word "Court" was set for a criminal judgment in the charter of Wenceslaus <note>original: "in Diplomate Wenceslai, pro criminali judicio"</note>, there was no necessary consequence here whether the same must have occurred in a more extensive and clearer investiture <note>original: "investiturâ extensiori magisque clarâ"</note>; since an inference is poorly made from those things which are diverse both in words and in the matter itself and in law <note>original: "Cùm ab iis, quæ tàm verbis, quam re ipsâ & jure diversa sunt, malè illatio fiat"</note>.

For because it was already mentioned above, and the Maximilianic investiture clearly brings with it that His Majesty confers as a fief to the kinsmen of B. only that which was previously granted to them by their ancestors, and which they have held and used until then: so such an investiture, as to the essence or the thing itself granted <note>original: "quoad quidditatem sive rem ipsam concessam"</note> (for there is no talk here of the quality of the grant <note>original: "de qualitate enim concessionis hîc sermo non est"</note>), cannot be different in matter or law <note>original: "re ipsâ & jure"</note> from that original or root grant <note>original: "originali sive radicali illâ concessione"</note> of Wenceslaus. Rather, by necessary consequence <note>original: "necessariâ consequentiâ"</note>, the word "Court" must be used in one and the same meaning in both places.

<margin>
For a referring privilege can contain no more than that which is referred to <note>original: "Referens enim Privilegium non plus con- tinere potest, quàm relatum"</note>, Gylman, *Symphorema*, volume 2, part 2, vote 15, number 4. Because the referred is believed to be within the referrer <note>original: "Quia rela- tum referenti inesse creditur"</note>. Gail, Observation 82, number 25.
</margin>

And accordingly, what the Maximilianic investiture contains in more detail regarding the form and manner of judging over blood <note>capital crimes</note> is meant and to be taken only as an explanation of the word "Court" used in the Wenceslaus grant, and the clause placed after it (and to judge and risk therewith, as is law and custom <note>original: "und damit richten und gefahren, als Recht und Gewohnheit ist"</note>: where the word "to judge" <note>original: "Richten, judicare"</note> can be appropriately applied to none of the aforementioned preceding pieces other than to the Court); primarily because the change of their rights <note>original: "Mutation jurium ipsorum"</note> and the introduction of a feudal title <note>original: "inductio tituli feudalis"</note> suspected by the honorable Faculty between the times of Wenceslaus and Maximilian I <note>original: "intra tempora Wenceslai & Maximiliani I."</note> is sufficiently refuted by the tenor of the Maximilianic investiture and the inspection placed above; especially since it has also been sufficiently demonstrated before this that not only that first investiture, but also that root grant must be considered <note>original: "quod non solùm illa pri- ma investitura, sed etiam concessio illa ra- dicalis attendenda sit"</note>.

<column-break/>

Against this, however, it does not constrain or mislead that the <term>advocacy jurisdiction</term> <note>original: "vogteylische Obrigkeit," the authority held by a 'Vogt' or protector over a territory</note>, which was one's own <note>allodial/privately owned</note> in the time of Wenceslaus <note>original: "tempore Wenceslai"</note>, could well have afterwards become an Imperial fief; just as sometimes the neighboring princes of the nobility and other Estates of the Empire might surrender their castles and villages, or perhaps only one or another type of jurisdiction <note>original: "unam atque alteram tantummodo speciem jurisdictionis"</note> as a fief, etc. Since an inference from the possible to the actual <note>original: "à pof- se ad esse"</note> is not strong; much less is it admitted that the word "Court" (placed in the singular number and attached to the words **Stock and Gallows** <note>symbols of high jurisdiction/capital punishment</note>, etc.) should be held, from a sounder understanding of the words <note>original: "ex saniori verborum intellectu"</note>, for a low jurisdiction <note>original: "pro bassa jurisdictione"</note>; primarily because the honorable Faculty itself acknowledges the meaning of "judgment" <note>original: "significatum judicii"</note> not without difficulty; and only finds difficulty in the fact that such a judgment should not be taken for a civil rather than a criminal court (which is sufficiently and redundantly indicated by the following words, "together with the ban to judge over blood"): but this has already been sufficiently answered above.

This, in turn, is as good as nothing <note>it does not detract</note> or brings no defect, that the understanding <note>original: "Intellectus"</note> of those from S. and the old family of B., which they drew from ancient observance <note>original: "ex antiquâ obfervantiâ"</note> concerning the pieces of the fief and brought to light in their treatises, is regarded by the honorable Faculty as a matter done between others <note>original: "res inter alios acta," a legal principle that a contract or judgment cannot harm those who were not parties to it</note>, prohibited under penalty of forfeiture <note>original: "sub pœna caducitatis prohibita"</note>, and not at all prejudicial to the Imperial treasury <note>original: "fisco Imperiali minimè præjudicialis"</note>; and thereby even the placement of the words <note>original: "Positus verborum"</note> is demanded rigidly, exactly as it stands in the letters of enfeoffment: since from this it at least appears in what sense the feudal Imperial fiefs were used and documented by the holders (who, as honest and already deceased members of the nobility, are not to be suspected of any intentional misappropriation of the fief <note>original: "fürsetzliche Interverfio feudi"</note>, according to the cited works of Wesenbeck, part 1, counsel 2, number 78 near the end and following), and were even reported to the feudal lord himself (since S. could not hide his sale during the dispatch); therefore, to remove all unequal understanding, one should look more to the observance than to the site or order of words <note>original: "Situm oder Ordinem verborum"</note>.

[Zell]: and therefore exclude the entire remaining half of the Lordship from it. **Consequently** <note>original: "consequenter"</note>, they declare all the rights belonging to the consulting Countess outside the village of T. (among which even the customs and hunting rights can be preserved) to be allodial: For the reason that only the rights belonging to the village of Zell were granted as a fief to the Roman Empire, or to Maximilian I.

However, because it has already been argued above that Emperor Maximilian only granted as a fief that which his ancestors, **and specifically** <note>original: "& sic nominatim"</note> Wenceslaus, had previously conferred upon those of B. **by allodial right** <note>original: "jure allodii"</note>: the previous difficulty arises once more, and this dilemma emerges: that at the time of the highly mentioned Lord Wenceslaus, the fortress and the entire district of Kißlegg (in which the village of S. is situated) either already had a jurisdiction (whether it be low, or high, or both at once), or must have had none at all.

If it already had a jurisdiction (as has been strongly illustrated from the **Privilege** of the Knightly Order and other **demonstrations**), it would not have first acquired it specifically for the village of T., but rather sought and obtained that which the entire Lordship had lacked until then—namely, what does not belong to **territories** that already possess **high and low jurisdiction** <note>original: "merum & mixtum Imperium"</note> to exercise without a special Imperial **concession** <note>note: citing Thomas Michael on jurisdiction, conclusions 68, 69, 70</note>. Specifically, these are the **Regalia** <note>term: "Regalia" are high sovereign rights belonging exclusively to a monarch, such as coining money or high justice</note> of market rights, the **Capital Court** <note>original: "Halsgericht," the right to trial for crimes involving the death penalty</note> (which is also a lordship, according to the records in Gylm. Symph. vol. 1. part 3. vote 23. n. 60. & 78.) and the signs of punishment <note>original: "maleficischen Zeichen," such as gallows or pillories</note>. (For just as the criminal judgment itself—the Capital Court or **Blood Ban** <note>original: "Blutbann"</note>—is among the Royal Rights [Regalia]: so too is the erection of execution signs, according to German practice, which the Privilege of Rudolph II granted to the Nobles of Swabia sufficiently proves, considered equivalent to Royal Rights; nor does it inherently belong to criminal jurisdiction (whatever Bidenbach may argue to the contrary from theoretical reasons in *Noble Questions* 14, n. 3. and following). Rather, it belongs to him who has the criminal judgment or the power of execution, as established by the writings of Oldradus, Decianus in *Criminal Treatises*, Zasius, and Gail, Observation 60, n. 6.) Just as the Stewards of Höfingen did for the first time under Emperor Maximilian with their market town of Theinhausen (which was already held as a fief), where they requested and obtained the Blood Ban through 

<column-break/>

a special grace or freedom, in addition to the high and low courts they already possessed there: As can be clearly understood from the attached **copy** of the first fief-letter concerning the said Theinhausen. And furthermore (for a greater explanation of what was discussed above **concerning the meaning and acceptance** <note>original: "de significatu & acceptione"</note> of the clause regarding the authority to judge with the Blood Ban), it is to be noted that in later times, namely on February 20, 1580, Emperor Rudolph II, in a **decree** issued between Von Picken (as the then-holder of the market town of Theinhausen) and the community there, referred to the **contents** of the fief-letter in this manner and **in these formal words** <note>original: "his formalibus"</note>:

That it belongs to His Imperial Majesty and the Empire, and in its stead, to the recently mentioned Von Picken, by virtue of his fief-letter, all high and low jurisdiction, with all lordship and justice, together with the power to judge with the Blood Ban at Theinhausen.

This **resumption** <note>original: "Reassumptio"</note> now appears not unlike the Maximillian **investiture** over the **Royal Rights** at S., and almost as tautological (unless that which is stated **for the sake of greater clarification** <note>original: "majoris declarationis gratiâ"</note> is considered **superfluous**: though it is **not in truth**, as per the **above-cited arguments**).

But if the Lordship of S. (**to return to the path**) had no jurisdiction at that time (**which is neither likely nor credible**), but first **obtained it from Wenceslaus**: then this **inconvenience** must follow: that a jurisdiction was brought about through this only for the village of T. (as a **part** of the district or **body**), but the **head** <note>original: "Caput"</note> or the fortress, and **the rest of the body itself** <note>original: "ipsum reliquum corpus"</note> or the district (outside of the heart or the village of T.) remained or was left without any **jurisdiction** or sovereign power. This, however, is by no means to be established (based on the counter-information and its arguments, especially the first), and is also **diametrically** opposed to well-known historical practice.

It is also not untimely to consider that, if the **jurisdiction** of the town alone were held as a fief, and the other half of the Lordship were entirely private property: it would nevertheless be a **nearly intolerable burden** <note>original: "onus propè intolerabile"</note> for the owner of the private property, in the **event** of the fief reverting to the lord, either to live as a subject under the jurisdiction of Von B. in his previous residence in the village of T. (since the old fortress has entirely decayed, and the holder of the other half has it in common), or to establish and seek **anew** another seat and parish church (outside of such a market town, which is now called S. and has become the **head** of the entire Lordship).

In accordance with all this, a commendable Faculty of Jurists is most diligently requested to take these further motives and doubts into mature deliberation, and where possible, **preserving justice and equity**, to [render a] decision...

# Letter L.

The decision on the first question is to be explained such that the **Imperial Fiefdom** <note>original: "Reichslehenschaft"</note>, by reason of the word "Court," should not be determined as a criminal or capital court and the **High Jurisdiction** <note>term: "Blutbann" or Blood Ban; the right to pass death sentences</note>; yet it should also not be extended to the civil jurisdiction itself. Instead, it should at least be restricted and drawn to the **Civil Judgment** <note>original: "Civile Judicium"</note>, or the establishment, maintenance, and ban of an ordinary civil court alone. To this end, a venerable Faculty of Jurists, by all appearances (in the section "And although in Imperial Fief-letters," <term>etc.</term> joined with the section "and further regarding this," <term>etc.</term>), is itself somewhat inclined.

And this opinion is assisted and helped significantly by the fact that years ago, even those who previously held **Compulsion and Ban** <note>term: "Zwing und Bänn"; the right to command and punish within a territory</note> in a village, nevertheless sought and obtained the establishment of an ordinary court there from the Roman Emperors. This is seen in the attached copy of such an **Imperial Privilege** (granted by Emperor Sigismund in the year 1418) to Ytel, Ulrich, Krafft, and Hans the Lion of Ulm, granting them that they may build a bridge over the Danube at Rieden, which is theirs, and where both banks are theirs.

Likewise, that they may have and establish a half or whole court in Rieden, where they hold "Compulsion and Ban," as they may best manage with judges who are **impartial people** <note>original: "ohnversprochen Leut"</note>, to judge matters of property, trespass, misconduct, and debt, and other such things. There they may judge, enjoy, and use the court with the freedoms, graces, rights, customs, and traditions, and in every measure, as the court at Erbach has and has traditionally held, <term>etc.</term> More such examples will surely be found. Especially because years ago, special concessions and graces were issued and granted for even lesser matters belonging to a civil court: Such as when Emperor Charles IV in the year 1365 gave this special grace to the **Magistrates** <note>term: "Schöpffen"; lay judges or elders of a city court</note> of the city of Friedberg, that whatever judgments they shall henceforth speak and share at the court in Friedberg: they may have described in a book by their scribe, <term>etc.</term>

Likewise, that the most highly esteemed Emperor Charles, in 1368, further granted the grace to the citizens, magistrates, the council, and the residents of the aforementioned city of Friedberg, that they may build a house upon the street in their city of Friedberg, wherever it seems most convenient to them and the city, in which they shall and may hold court, <term>etc.</term>

Beyond which, an ultimate decision is now duly expected on behalf of the consulting Countess.

---

Years ago, Emperor Maximilian the First of this name, then living, granted to two cousins of S., as holders of the Lordship of S., upon their most

Besoldus, Volume I.

<column-break/>

humble request and prayer, with deliberate courage and good counsel, the **Market Right, Court, Pillory, and Gallows** <note>These were physical symbols of "High Jurisdiction" or the power over life and death</note>, together with the "Ban to judge over blood," as a gracious Imperial Fief in the village of T., located in their Lordship of S. from B. This is shown and carried out more fully in the Imperial Fief-letter drawn up regarding this.

However, because the mentioned Lordship of S. has even more villages, hamlets, and other appurtenances, and currently, through several highly respected Lord Commissioners most graciously appointed by Your Imperial Majesty for this purpose, the **fief is to be separated from the private property** <note>original: "das Lehen von dem Eigenthum abgesondert werden solle"</note> in those places: the question is asked: Whether the fief-rights expressed in the most highly mentioned Emperor Maximilian I's Fief-letter are by law to be understood as applying to the entire Lordship of S., or are to be restricted solely to the village of T., and the remaining Lordship is to be considered **private property** <note>term: "Eigenthum" or "Allod"; land held outright without feudal obligations</note>?

Accordingly, we, the Dean and other Doctors of the Faculty of Jurists at the University of Tübingen, were graciously requested to provide our lawful and entirely impartial opinion on the question set forth above. Thus, in our assembled College, we have diligently read the Imperial Fief-letter of the most illustrious late Emperor Maximilian I and other relevant documents sent to us, maturely weighed all circumstances, and can find and judge nothing other than that, firstly, the territory of both the entire Lordship of S. and the village of T. situated therein, with all their appurtenances (except for the special rights indicated in the aforementioned Imperial Fief-letter), are **allodial** <note>private</note>, owned, and not at all subject to a fief.

For it is an unquestionable **Legal Axiom** <note>original: "Axioma Juris"</note> that **in case of doubt, all property is considered private and free, and is never presumed to be bound by a feudal connection.** <note>original: "quod in dubio omnia bona allodialia & libera reputentur, nec unquam feudali nexu innodata præsumantur"</note>. And this is also usually extended to Baronies, Counties, and other similar territories.

> Just as experience equally shows, it is not uncommon in Swabia, and indeed in all of Germany, that Counties, Baronies, and likewise the estates of Free Nobles, even those decorated with jurisdiction, exist as purely allodial, and they recognize the Imperial Majesty by reason of sovereignty, but not as the Lord of a Fief.

Furthermore, the Lordship of S. has been sold as private property, not only publicly and at various times, but also half of the same has passed to the Barons of E. under that title, **not without the knowledge of His Most Holy Imperial Majesty.** <note>original: "non insciâ SS. Cæsareâ Majestate"</note>.

> These certainly frequent alienations <note>sales/transfers</note>, made openly and in the sight of the entire Empire, seem most firmly to strengthen the said legal presumption—which militates in favor of private property and against a fief—also regarding this territory and as much as concerns this Lordship with its appurtenances.

Secondly, we are also of this firm opinion: that the rights named in the Imperial Fief-letter <note>original: "Lehenbrief"</note> are not feudal <note>original: "lehenbar"; meaning held under a lord rather than owned outright</note> in the entire Lordship of S. or its other towns, but should be held as feudal solely and exclusively within the village of T.

### ADDITION.

A "half-fief" <note>original: "Ein halb Lehen"</note>, according to long-standing custom in Lower Alsace, is a lease for a short term of nine years; a "full-fief" <note>original: "ein gantz Lehen"</note> is for a long term of eighteen years. Note: The fact that the fief should be accounted for nowhere else than before the fief-courts implies nothing other than that the Lord of the Fief <note>original: "Dominus Feudi"</note> possesses feudal jurisdiction. <term>Schrader on Fiefs, page 10, section 3, no. 19; Nicolaus Everhard, counsel 15, vol. 1, throughout; Pruckmann, counsel 16, no. 9 and following, book 1.</term> A fief is called "new" <note>original: "Feudum novum"</note> when it was acquired for a new reason. <term>Counsel 18, number 65.</term> In cases of doubt, a fief is presumed to be "ancient" <note>original: "feudum antiquum"</note> rather than new. <term>Counsel 12, numbers 1, 2, 3, 4.</term> The contrary is asserted in <term>number 42; see also counsel 29, numbers 7 and 40.</term> A fief can be considered ancient or new from different perspectives. <term>Counsel 12, number 43.</term> A fief transferred from one family to another is always considered new. <term>Counsel 29, numbers 26 and 27. Regarding what are called "Quaternate fiefs," see Neapolitan Decisions 282, 60, number 1, with ten following.</term>

**28. Note: In rightful fiefdom, for rightful fiefs, as a fief, in the manner of a fiefdom, or as is the nature and quality of fief law.** <note>These are standard legal formulas used in documents to define the type of land tenure.</note>

Regarding which fiefs these phrases refer to, see <term>Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, counsel 41, numbers 137 and 153; and counsel 45, number 2, vol. 8; Fichard, counsel 10, number 4, at the section "And although," vol. 2; Gothofredus Antonius, feudal disputation 1, thesis 7, and preface letter e near the end; Imperial Counsels of Baptista Caesar 84, number 21, etc., part 1.</term>

### ADDITION.

Note: What the phrase "to rightful fiefs" <note>original: "Zu rechten Lehen"</note> denotes. <term>Klock, vol. 3, counsel 182, no. 95, and the citations there; Gemmel in the Compendium of Feudal Law, pages 149 and 143.</term>

<column-break/>

Some wish to extend this wording to a "female fief" <note>a fief that could be inherited by women</note>, which is, however, as much a departure from the nature of a fief as it is absurd. See <term>Zasius, counsel 13, p. 1.</term> The Lord always consents, saving the right of his direct ownership—"yet without harm to our rights and fiefdoms" <note>original: "doch uns an unsern Rechten und Lehenschafften unschädlich"</note>—as is practiced in the Courts. <term>Based on the law "if a debtor," section 1, Digest on how a pledge is released, there, page 95.</term> The phrase "as a free fief" <note>original: "zu einem freyen Lehen"</note> exempts one not only from burdens but from other conditions not expressed in the investiture. The phrase "this free estate as a fief" <note>original: "Diesen freyen Hof zu lehen"</note> frees one from services only; in other respects, it remains a true fief. <term>Ibid., page 18.</term>

**29. Fief-letter. Letters of investiture.**

Although under Feudal Law a public instrument or "Witnessed Brief" is not strictly required for the substance of an Investiture <note>the formal act of granting a fief</note>—<term>per the text in the section "for if," where it says: "If an instrument should be lacking because it was not made," and the section "if however," title "what is investiture"; Alvarotus in chapter 1, number 4, and after him the Provost, ibid., number 5, said title</term>—nevertheless, today by custom, letters of investiture (or Fief-letters) are regularly produced. This occurs not only for a new fief but also in the renewal <note>original: "renovatio"</note> of an ancient fief, where the instruments of investiture are renewed—"that the fief-letters be renewed" <note>original: "daß man die Lehenbrief vernêuert"</note>. And because the tenor <note>the specific wording and intent</note> of the Investiture takes precedence even over general Feudal Law—"as one daily directs and conducts oneself according to the fief-letters"—one must ensure that such letters are drafted diligently and cautiously. <term>Johann Schneidewin in the Epitome of Fiefs, part 4, number 30; see him at the following numbers, where in number 35 he asks:</term> If the first Investiture says one thing, and the second is found to be altered, which one should be followed? And according to <term>Curtius on Fiefs, part 2, number 42,</term> the answer is that the tenor of the first and ancient investiture—"the oldest fief-letter" <note>original: "der ältessen Lehenbrief"</note>—must be observed. For when a fief is ancient, the original status must not be changed, <term>per the text in chapter 1 on the "Decrepit Age of a Vassal," where Alvarottus, number 2.</term> Furthermore, that which is substituted should reflect the nature of that for which it is substituted. <term>Law "if him," section "who of injuries," Digest "if anyone should caution."</term> For a renewal is a confirmation of an ancient right; and thus, by consequence, this Renewal ought not to introduce anything to the contrary—namely, a certain correction of the ancient letters of investiture, "the old fief-letters."

Hence, in case of doubt, when an ancient Investiture is established, the subsequent one is presumed to have been made according to the conditions placed in the first. <term>Final chapter, at the end, on him who made an end of recognizing.</term> Therefore, this clause is usually added to Instruments and Renewals: "and we grant him such goods with all their honors, dignities, uses, freedoms, and rights, nothing excluded, but in every measure as his ancestors held them as a fief from us and our predecessors, honorably brought down, possessed, and obtained." See <term>Strasbourg Counsels, counsel 60, vol. 2; and vol. 1, counsel 36, question 1, extensively by Karl Kirchberg.</term>
