### ADDITION.

Investiture is a term with many meanings <note>original Greek: "πολύσημον"</note>. Sometimes it refers to the actual possession of the fief, which is a consequence of the contract rather than something folded into it. At other times, it refers to the legal instrument recorded for the sake of memory regarding the act of investiture, called the **fief-letter** <note>original: "der Lehenbrief"</note>. Now, and more properly, it denotes the act of investing itself, in German: **the enfeoffment** <note>original: "die Belehnung"</note>, as noted by Gothofredus Antonius in *Feudal Disputations 4, thesis 1, letter c.* The "first investiture" is called the root, and as it were, the basis and foundation of all subsequent ones. According to its terms, as if to a guiding star <note>original: "Cynosura"</note>, one must perpetually return, setting all other things aside. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations 8, thesis 9, letter C; Disputation 6, thesis 3, letter a.* Above all, the oldest and first investiture must be inspected. Rosenthal, *on fiefs, chapter 9, conclusion 40, number 1.* Richard, *volume 1, counsel 10, number 2.* So that against this same document, neither the Vassal can impose any burden or prejudice against the blood-relations <note>male relatives entitled to succession</note>, nor can the Lord of the fief (or the direct Lord) impose such against the Vassals and **emphyteutic tenants** <note>tenants with long-term leases who improve the land</note> contrary to the prior condition. Rather, the Lord of the fief or the direct Lord is precisely bound to invest the Vassal and the tenant without innovation <note>unauthorized changes</note>, and to grant him either the fief or the lease. Menochius, *counsels 400 and 474, number 3.* Gravetta, *counsel 241.* Natta, *counsel 502, number 32, and 554.* Zasius, *on fiefs, chapter on feudal succession.* Gail, *book 2, observation 49, number 4, and book 7, observation 142, and 159, number 3.* Indeed, not even the Emperor or a Prince, out of the fullness of his power, by his own motion or certain knowledge, can decree otherwise or change the conditions of the fief for the worse. Menochius, *Presumption 2, 13.* Decius, *counsel 148.* Socinus, *counsel 164, column 4.* Gabriel, *on not taking away acquired rights, conclusion 5.* Parisius, *book 1, counsel 23, number 68, and Mynsinger 4, observation 88.* Regarding letters of reversal, see Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations 8, thesis 9, letter e.* <gloss>A feudal lord is bound, when a vassal dies, to grant the next feudal kinsman and successor, or heir to the fief, a fief-letter in the customary written form.</gloss> Baldus, *on the law regarding multiple receipts in the Code on the credibility of instruments.* Wesenbeck, *on fiefs, chapter 8, numbers 15 and 31.* Vultejus, *on fiefs, book 1, chapter 7, number 42, at the verse "and this instrument."* Rosenthal, *on fiefs, chapter 6, conclusion 67, number 1, and in the note there at letter C.* Knipschild, *on the obligation of the Lord toward the Vassal, question 1, number 28.* <gloss>In the resolution of feudal disputes, one must first look to the fief-letter, and based on its content, formulate the decision and responses; according to the law "always in stipulations," 34, Digest on the Rules of Law.</gloss> Gail, *book 2, observation 50, number 15. Mynsinger, book 5, observation 76, number 1.* Vultejus, *on fiefs, book 2, chapter 3, number 22. Knipschild, on the obligation of the lord toward the Vassal, question 1, number 1.*

### 30. Feudal Service, Knightly Service. Services of Vassals.

Fiefs are granted chiefly for this purpose:

<column-break/>

that Vassals, in exchange for the benefits granted to them, should perform certain Services for the Lord, which are commonly called **feudal services** <note>original: "die lehendienst"</note>. This is by virtue of the oath, the wording of which may be seen under the entry **Vassal** <note>original: "Lehenmann"</note>. These services are required especially in Expeditions and during times of war. For fiefs were granted for perpetual military service, much like the **Timars** <note>original: "Timaria"; Ottoman land grants for military service</note> among the Turks. In ancient times, wars were waged by Vassals alone, and they consisted mostly of the multitude of Vassals. Now, since various limitations have been introduced, and the Vassals of the Empire have become absolute Lords, few such fiefs are given, etc. And that feudal services, **the feudal services** <note>original: "die Lehendienst"</note>, are to be performed most especially in time of war, is clear from the chapter *The Lord making war* in the title *here the law ends* and the title *if the vassal has not lost.* And just as the duty of Soldiers is said to be established and constituted for the handling of arms and the necessity of wars (*law on soldiers, Code on hiring; final law, Code on the right of deliberation*); so also the service and chief duty of Vassals is spent in war and the handling of arms (*the said chapter, The Lord making war*). Fiefs are regularly granted only to someone who can perform military service (*title on whether a fief can be changed or another imperfect fief retained; and the title on the law of Conrad, section "similarly"*). Because of this, it is read indiscriminately in those same Books of Fiefs that Vassals are properly called **Soldiers** <note>original: "Milites"</note> (*title on various soldiers who laid down their war arms; title on the Soldier-Vassal who is contumacious*). Antonius Borrinius, *on the military service of subjects, chapter 1, from the beginning, page 2.* And although no mention of Services was made between the Lord and the Vassal in the granting of the fief, they must nevertheless be performed; since it is of the nature of a fief that Services be performed (*title 23, at the end, book 2; and in title 55 of the said book*).

The Lord shall summon the Vassal either in person or through his Proxy, or even by letters, which shall contain the notice that the Vassal must come to aid the Lord. *Gloss on the final section of "on the firm law of peace" regarding the word "legitimate."* And it is held there under the title **allodial** <note>land held in absolute ownership rather than feudal tenure</note>, by Jacobinus de Sancto Georgio under the word "and they promised," number 33, that in some places this requisition is made by an Edict posted in public. All the Doctors of Law on the said final section "regarding custom," as witnessed by Schneidewin in *Epitome of Fiefs, part 5, number 99:* <gloss>a specific letter of summons is sent to each vassal, or when it occurs so urgently, it is sent in an open form from one nobleman to another, who must give the messenger an acknowledgment that such a summons-letter has been correctly received and delivered.</gloss>

However, it is often asked whether the Vassal is bound to be present in person to assist the Lord and perform Services for him, or whether he can send a substitute?

And certainly, in that case when the specific industriousness of the person was not chosen, the Services can be completed and administered through a suitable person of **equal social standing** <note>original: "Ebenbürtigen"</note>, similar and equal to the Vassal himself. *Text where the gloss is found in the section "firmly" on the prohibition of alienating a fief by Frederick.* On this question, see Schneidewin in *Epitome of Fiefs, part 5, number 112.*

Additionally, see Guyon, *Diverse Consultations, volume 2, chapter 7*, regarding the origin of the **arrière-ban** <note>original: *ban ariere ban*; a royal proclamation calling all vassals to military service</note> and those who are obliged to serve.

### ADDITION.

At whose expense, and how a vassal is bound to perform **feudal service** <note>original: *Lehendienst*</note> upon demand, whether inside or outside the territory, and how to handle matters if the vassal suffers any damage as a result. Zorer, *part 2, question 9, number 727 and following.* A vassal must bring aid to his Lord against all men (*Chapter "Est & alia," 2. Feudal 7*), even against his own brother, son, and parent (*Chapter "Domino," 2. Feudal 28*). However, these points are not without doubt among the legal interpreters. For regarding the **Parent**, it seems quite harsh and inhuman to many that a vassal should be required to aid his Lord against him; since nothing is more contrary to nature and divine precepts than to attack the father from whom we have our life, and to deprive him of that life. Zafius, Fornerius, Bocer, and Cujacius warn that those words, "and the father," are absent from the ancient Code and should therefore be deleted. Hotoman distinguishes between whether the father is plotting something against the Fatherland, or against another private Senior or Lord. Lord Rittershusius, in *Feudal Partitions, page 276.* Conversely, the **Feudists** <note>legal scholars specializing in feudal law</note> commonly defend the affirmative view based on the express text of *2. Feudal 28*, from which they argue one should not depart. Nor does the fact that reverence is owed to the father by Divine and natural law stand in the way. For he invokes the laws in vain who commits acts against them. Therefore, against a father who unjustly harms his Lord, scorning divine and human law, a son may justly take up arms. Add Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 7, thesis 5, letter f.* Furthermore, some teach that the Lord should not be aided against a son, both from the nature of reciprocal relationships and by the logic of the **Pompeian Law on Parricide** <note>original: *l. 1. ff. ad L. Pomp. de parricid.*</note>. But the first argument presupposes that a vassal should not defend his Lord against his father, which was just demonstrated to be false. The latter argument only holds if the son has not offended the Lord against justice and equity. Finally, some contend that a vassal ought not to aid his Lord against a brother, because the reasoning of religion and humanity does not permit a brother to lay snares for a brother’s life. Truly, it is one thing to plot against a brother's life without just cause, and another to oppose him in a **just war** when he is offending the Lord against right and law. The former is wicked and illicit, while the latter is permitted. Add Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation 7, thesis 5, letter G.* From this rule, the following are excepted: 1. The Emperor, King, or Prince (Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation 7, thesis 5, letter d*), which is commonly extended even to the Pope. 2. An **older Lord** <note>original: *Dominus antiquior*</note>. An older Lord is not only the one to whom a prior oath was given, but also the one whom the first person to acquire the fief held as Lord.

<column-break/>

3. The **Fatherland** <note>original: *Patria*</note> of the vassal is excepted. 4. The person of the vassal himself. Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation 7, thesis 5, letter c.* Services are usually appraised according to the size of the fief. If, therefore, the Lord wishes to undertake an overseas war and demands more than what was agreed in the contracts, the judgment should be in favor of the vassal; if the services are defined, they are owed; if nothing is defined, the response should be in favor of the defendant <note>the vassal</note> to relieve him of the burden. On this whole subject, see the very accurate Dr. Ludovicus in *Synopsis of Fiefs, chapter 14.*

Services can also be **playful and unusual** <note>original: *ludicra & insolita*</note>, such as the vassal being required to sing a song on a certain day, carry a green branch, or escort the Lord's wife to church on festive days. Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation 7, thesis 1, letter D.* Or to run the **quintain** <note>a medieval sporting target used for jousting practice</note>, or that a new vassal must offer a lark, carried and bound in a cart drawn by oxen. Choppinus, *On the Laws of Anjou, book 1, chapter 31, number 8.* Borellus, *Counsel 1, number 147.* Or to impose silence upon the frogs <note>a traditional duty to keep frogs quiet so the Lord could sleep</note>. Menochius, Knichen, Limnäus in *Public Law, book 1, chapter 11, number 97.* Thus in a district of **Franconia**, a certain nobleman is bound to offer the Lord every year around St. Martin's Day a **wren** <note>original: *regulum*, German: *ein Zaunschlüpfferlein*</note>, that smallest of birds, in recognition of the fief. That pact is shameful and illicit which gave the Canons and Counts of Lyon a certain license, in recognition of fiefs, to sleep with the brides of vassals on the first night. This pact they called the **right of the loosened hip** <note>original: *jus laxandae coxae*</note> or the right of **connagium**. Camillus Borellus, *Counsel 1, number 158.* Choppinus, *chapter 31, number 8.*

A vassal is bound to protect the Lord of the fief against anyone, even against his own brother, and biological father and son, when they wish to fight against the Fatherland and Religion. *According to the law "minime" 35, on religion and funeral expenses; the law "if anyone from children," paragraph "Parent," on acknowledging children.* Bocer, *On the Law of Lords, book 1, chapter 4, number 76.* Rosenthal, *On Fiefs, chapter 8, conclusion 14, number 5.* Bocer, *said chapter 4, number 78 and following.* Schrader, *On Fiefs, part 6, chapter 5, numbers 1 and 12.* Knipfchild, *On the obligation of the Lord toward the Vassal, question 1, numbers 13 and 14.*

### 31. Feudal Expectancies. <term>Expectantia feudi</term> <note>A legal grant giving someone the right to a fief that is not yet vacant, but will be in the future.</note>

On giving **expectancies** <note>original: *Expectanzen*</note> on a fief which was previously sold, see Schrader, *Counsel 43.* Plebst, *Feudal Disputation 2, thesis 5, etc.* Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 8, thesis 5, letter a.* Semonet, *On the reservation of benefices.* *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 2, counsel 8.* On an expectancy granted to two people, Valascus, *Consultation 72.*

### ADDITION.

**Investiture** can be performed not only for a fief that is already "open" <note>vacant</note>, but also for one that is expected to become open. When this hope is fulfilled, the time of the death of the possessing vassal is joined with the time the investiture was granted, as if it were happening for the first time, so that the Lord must absolutely place him in vacant possession.

Letter L.

But what happens if, in the meantime, while the possessor of the fief is still living, the Lord should pass away? Even if the heirs are not specifically mentioned, they shall nonetheless be bound <note>original: *l. veteris. l. sin. C. de contrah. & committ. stip.*</note>. If a man is the last of his name and lineage, his **fief** <note>original: *Lehen*</note> can be requested from the Feudal Lord, and the **expectancy** <note>original: *Anwartung*; a legal right to a property that will be granted in the future, usually after the current holder dies</note> may be announced to another. Schurff, *consil. 59, no. 1, cent. 2*; Hartman Pistor, *2, quest. 27, no. 15*. Concerning **investiture in the event of death**, also known as an expectancy or **reversionary grant** <note>original: *Anwartung*</note>, see Berlichius, *2, concl. 54, throughout*. If two or more people are invested with the same fief in the event of the possessor's death, who is to be preferred? *no. 63.*

### 32. Feudal Court. Judgment of Peers.
<note>original: *Lehengericht. Judicium parium*</note>
Regarding the Courts, see below under Letter M, at the word **Court of Vassals** <note>original: *Mann-gericht*</note>.

The Peers of France are the Peers of the Court <note>original: *Pares Curiae*</note>; see Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, vol. 2, chap. 30, fol. 640 and following*.

### ADDITION.
Even if the cause for the loss of a fief is obvious, the Feudal Lord is not thereby deprived of his property **by the law itself** <note>original: *ipso jure*</note> or by the act alone; rather, an ordinary legal process is required, and the cause of the forfeiture and removal must be carried out in the legal proceedings and before the Feudal Court. Mynsinger, *decad. 11, respons. 7, no. 16 and following*, regarding how the vassal's affairs are disposed. Knipschild, *On the Obligations of the Lord toward the Vassal, quest. 2, no. 54*. Even in those cases where ownership is forfeited by the law itself, a knightly judgment and declaration must still precede it, stating that the Feudal Lord has forfeited the ownership and is bound to surrender it to the vassal. *number 55.* The **Peers of the Court** <note>original: *Pares Curiae*</note> are the fellow vassals of the same Senior or Lord within the same territory. Different territories belonging to one Lord create different Courts, and the vassals are not peers even if they all received their benefit from the same hand. They are so named because, with respect to each other and the benefit flowing from the same lordly source, they are equals <note>original: *pares*</note> to one another, though they are unequal and inferior in the eyes of the Lord himself. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 4, thesis 6, letter C.* The feudal forum is that in which feudal controversies are handled between the Lord, the Vassal, and the Peers of the Court. *Chapter "Ex transmiss." and Chapter "Verum extra. de foro compet."* Rittershusius in *Novell. page 559, no. 11.*

The Peers of the Court ought to be chosen by the Lord and the Vassal together. Klock, *vol. 2, cons. 5, no. 9.* This is expanded in *no. 10.* For a judicial precedent from the Imperial Chamber, see *no. 11*; however, see *no. 56.* Peers must be from the same territory or province in which the asserted vassal has his domicile. *cons. 5, no. 15.*

<column-break/>

### 33. Feudal Lord. Lord of the Fief.
<note>original: *Lehenherr. Dominus feudi.*</note>
He is not called "Lord" because he retains absolute ownership and property of the feudal estates and merely yields the use and profit to another; rather, it is either following the example of the ancients, who used to address someone as **Lord** <note>original: *Dominus*</note> as a title of honor (just as patrons of old commanded such a greeting from their clients as a mark of submission, according to Franciscus Polletus in *History of the Roman Forum, book 2, chapter 10*), or because the Feudalists wished to substitute this Latin word for the vernacular **Signore** <note>the Italian term for Lord</note> (which is what the Lombards called the feudal patron out of reverence). You will also frequently find him called the **Senior** in common usage. See Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 2, th. 1, letter b.* Etienne Pasquier, *7, chap. 7, f. 969*, and Lord Goldast in his work *Senior*.

### ADDITION.
The Feudal Lord is bound to loyalty not only out of **courtesy** <note>original: *ex urbanitate*</note> or goodwill. Knipschild, *On the Obligations of the Lord, question 1, no. 50.* The Feudal Lord should not show himself too rough or harsh toward his vassal. Knipschild, *On the Obligations of the Lord toward the Vassal, quest. 1, no. 66, end.* A faithful Lord makes a faithful servant; a gracious Lord makes a gracious servant. Mynsinger, *decad. 11, resp. 7, no. 2 and following.* Wesenbeck, *cons. 9, no. 3.* Vultejus, *chap. 10, no. 37.* Knipschild, *cited quest. 1, no. 8.* The Feudal Lord is bound to be faithful to his vassal, *dist. quest. 1, no. 6*, and a Feudal Lord should regard and hold his vassal as if he were his own son. *no. 9.*

2. The **duty** <note>original: *Officium*</note> of the Feudal Lord consists in **security and safety**, such that a Feudal Lord keeps the secrets of his vassal, which have been entrusted to him, confidential. *no. 2.* 
3. In **honor**, that the Feudal Lord ensures that law and justice are administered to a vassal, and that no hindrance happens to him in that regard. *no. 3.* 
4. In **utility**, that the Feudal Lord seeks and promotes the benefit of the vassal, and warns of and averts any harm to him. *no. 4.* 
5. In **ease**, that the Feudal Lord does not make his vassal’s affairs and business difficult or obstructive. *no. 5.* 
6. In **possibility**, that the Feudal Lord does not make his vassal’s business and affairs—which are possible—impossible. *no. 6.*

### 34. Vassal, Feudal Duty.
<note>original: *Lehenmann, Lehenpflicht. Vasallus. Vasallagium.*</note>
Whether a vassal or **steward** <note>original: *Provisor*</note>, by virtue of his letter of investiture, must serve against everyone, with no one excepted. See Bidenbach, *quest. 20.*

And there exist recent legal opinions in the Acts of Londorpius, both for and against the Nobility, who served the Count Palatine as their Feudal Lord against His Imperial Majesty.

<meta>catchword: vermuth- [likely referring to 'presumption' or 'presumed']</meta>

And it appears that the strict obligation existing between a Lord and a Vassal descends from the ancient law of the **Soldurii** <note>original: *Solduriorum*; these were a class of devoted retainers or bodyguards among the Gauls</note>, which Caesar mentions in the third book of *The Gallic War*.

The name **Vassal** <note>original: *Vasallus*</note> among the Lombards or Germans seems to correspond to the German word *Gesell* <note>original: *Gesell*; meaning a companion, associate, or journeyman</note>, which signifies a "Comrade" or "Count" <note>original: *Comitem*</note>, according to Jacob Cujacius in his *Introduction to Feudal Law*. Cornelius Tacitus also seems to confirm this in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*. He calls Vassals "Companions" <note>original: *Comites*</note>, saying that the Germans always had many Companions—that is, Vassals. They were called Companions or Vassals because they accompany the Lord when he goes to war.

For this reason, Vassals are called **Peers** <note>original: *Pares*</note> among themselves, as if they were "equal companions" <note>original: *gleiche Gesellen*</note>; see Hotoman in *Feudal Disputes, chapter 2* and in his lexicon under the word *Vasallus*; see also Heigius, *1, question 2, number 26, etc.*

However, I believe that "Vassal" or "Vassus" is derived from the words "to fasten" or "to grasp" <note>original: *festen, vel fassen*</note>, as I stated in my *Treatise on the Nature of Peoples, folio 106*, and *On Subordinate Empires, folio 89*.

A Vassal is also called a **Beneficiary** <note>original: *Beneficiarius*</note>, undoubtedly from the "benefit" <note>original: *beneficii*</note> or property granted to him as a fief; see Hermann Vultejus, *On Feudal Law, book 1, chapter 4, number 13*.

Likewise, he is called **Faithful** <note>original: *Fidelis*</note> <note>original citations: *cap. 1. in princ. an. remov. deb. test. cap. 1. §. & quia de his, qui feud. dare poss. c. 1. si de inv. feud. contr. fuerit.*</note> because of the "faith" or loyalty he owes to his Lord. This is the origin of the German phrase "dear faithful one" <note>original: *lieber Getreuer*</note>. Nevertheless, it is not only Vassals who are called "faithful" and "dear faithful ones," but also those who are subject to someone's jurisdiction or bound to someone by an oath. See Eguinarius Baro in his *Commentary on Feudal Customs, book 2, title 5*; Vultejus in the place cited; and see Schrader, *Counsel 17, volume 1*, regarding the penalty for one who refuses to provide the Oath of Fealty.

Although the status of being a Vassal does not, in itself, turn a non-subject into a subject <note>original citations: Mynsinger, *century 3, observation 30*; Rosenthal, *On Feudal Law, chapter 11, conclusion 14*; Andreas Gail, *On Pledges, chapter 15, number 3*</note>. I also noted this in *On Subordinate Empires, folio 72, etc.* The granting of a fief never makes a person a subject by itself, nor is the Vassal necessarily a subject of the Lord of the fief, nor can the fief itself impose subjection. See Matthaeus Wesenbeck, *Counsel 1, number 57*; Paurmaister, *On Jurisdiction, chapter 8, number 42*; Marta, *On Jurisdiction, part 4, chapter 133, number 13*. Although there is a great distance—many "parasangs" <note>an ancient Persian unit of distance, here used metaphorically to mean a great gap</note>—between the Oath of Subjection and the Feudal Oath, as I explained above under the word **Homage** <note>original: *Huldigung*</note>, see nevertheless Ludolph Schrader, *On Feudal Law, part 6, chapter [blank], number 6, etc.*, Gail, *On Arrests, chapter 7, number 9 and following*, and Matthias Stephani, *book 2 On Jurisdiction, part [blank], chapter 7, number 22 and following*, where one may see the reasons for this distinction, which he pursues at length.

Furthermore, the Oath of Subjection binds more strongly than the Oath of Fealty or the Cliental Oath. See Caspar Ziegler, *Section on Landed Subjects, conclusion 1, number 15*, citing Andreas Knichen, *On the Law of the Land, chapter 3, number 163*; Cravetta, *Counsel 517, number 3*; Rolandus a Valle, *Counsel 1, number 30, volume 3*.

And although, according to the same Ziegler in the cited place, number 65, a vassal is sometimes called a subject of his Lord in common usage, as noted by Cravetta, *Counsel 29, number 17*.

<column-break/>

See Paurmaister, *On Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 8 and chapter 9, number 49*; see also Rosenthal, *On Feudal Law, chapter 5, conclusion 78*; and the *Defense of Philibert de Conte di Verv* in the *Treatise on the Peace of Savoy*. This usage, however, is not to be understood as strictly true or fully effective, but rather as an improper or abusive use of the term. See Mynsinger, *Counsel 77, number 8, decade 1*. For this "misuse of words" <note>original: *catachresis*</note> crept in by way of feudal recognition, services, and loyalty, rather than by reason of true subjection. See Paurmaister, *cited book 2, chapter 8, number 40*; Petrus Friedrich Mindanus, *book 1 on Procedure, chapter 32, number 2*. And it is not a new thing for someone to be called "Lord" who is not actually the Lord of the territory, but is so called only in a certain respect. See Capicius, *Decision 26, number 31*; Ziegler, *cited place, number 70 and following*.

Likewise, a Lord must return the favor to his Faithful One or Vassal in all things; if he does not, he is judged "faithless" <note>original: *malefidus*</note>. See *Book 2 of Feudal Law, title 6, final section*. And because, as Seneca says in the sixth book of *On Benefits*, a benefit is a common bond that ties two people together: there is a reciprocal faith between us. Or, as it is put elsewhere, a Vassal and a Lord are like "spouses" to each other—that is, joined by a common bond of faith. See *Feudal Law, final title*; Rittershusius, *Feudal Divisions, book 2, chapter 10*.

From this, the proverb arose: **Faithful Lord, faithful servant.** <note>original: *Getreuer Herr, getreuer Knecht.*</note>

Whether a Vassal is bound to produce his title deed <note>original: *editionem tituli*</note>, and if he does not, whether and when he can be deprived of his fief due to the denial of his feudal status, is made clear by the following legal response.

---

**H**igh-born Gracious Count, regarding what Your Gracious Lordship wrote to me on July 5th concerning the small town of **Ulenbach**, and your command to provide my thoughts as soon as possible on the matter of producing the title deed, I have not wished to neglect putting such a task into action for Your Lordship.

Since I find from the records that the indicated town of Ulenbach, along with its dependencies, is held against Person A as a **mortgage-fief** <note>original: *Pfand-Lehen*; a fief held as security for a debt</note>: it follows that one can hardly refuse the production of the title deed. There is also the danger to be expected that if one refuses such production—and thus by necessary consequence denies the feudal status—then Person A could bring a charge of **felony** <note>original: *Feloniam*; in feudal law, a breach of duty leading to forfeiture</note> based on this denial, and seize such a fief entirely without compensation. One might perhaps try to bring this up under the pretext that, during the current Count’s **guardianship** <note>original: *Vormundschafft*</note>, nothing can be yielded by the **wards** <note>original: *Pupillen*; minor children under legal protection</note>. Their side of the guardianship was informed that such a town was a true **allodial property** <note>original: *Eigenthum*; property owned outright, not as a fief</note> and an unquestionable **dependency** <note>original: *Pertinenz*</note> of Person C, and has been used as such from time immemorial and possessed without any feudal recognition. Therefore, even if someone from ancient times had some right there, such a right...

# Enhanced Practical Treasury

And it seems that the strict obligation that exists between a Lord and a **Vassal** <note>term: *Vasallus*; a person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service</note> descends from the ancient law of the **Devoted Followers** <note>original: *Soldurii*; a class of loyal retainers mentioned by Caesar</note>, of which Caesar writes in book 3 of the *Gallic Wars*.

The name "Vassal" among the Lombards or Germans seems to correspond to the German word **Companion** <note>original: *Gesell*</note>, which signifies a "Comrade," according to Jacobus Cujacius in his *prolegomena on feuds*. Cornelius Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, seems to confirm this. He calls Vassals "Companions": saying that the Germans always had many **Companions** <note>original: *Comites*</note>, which is to say, Vassals. They were called Companions or Vassals because they accompany the Lord when he goes to war.

->Hence, Vassals are called **Peers** among themselves, as if they were **equal companions** <note>original: *gleiche Gesellen*</note>; see Hotoman in *disputations on feuds, chapter 2*, and in his *lexicon* under the word *Vasallus*, as well as Heigius, *question 2, number 26, etc.*<-

But I truly think that "Vassal" or "Vassus" is derived from the words **to bind** <note>original: *fesslen*</note> or **to seize** <note>original: *fassen*</note>, as I stated in my *treatise on the nature of people, folio 106*, and *on subordinate empires, folio 89*.

A Vassal is also called a **Beneficiary**, naturally from the thing which is granted to him as a **benefit** <note>original: *beneficium*; the land or right granted</note> in the form of a fief, according to Hermann Vultejus, *on feuds, book 1, chapter 4, number 13*.

Likewise, he is called **The Faithful One**, from the **faith** <note>original: *fides*; loyalty</note> which he owes to the Lord, from which comes that German expression: **dear loyal one** <note>original: *lieber Getreuer*</note>. However, it is not only Vassals who are called "faithful" and "dear loyal ones," but also those who are subject to someone's jurisdiction or bound to someone by an oath. See Eguinarius Baro in his *commentary on feudal customs, book 2, title 5*; Vultejus in the place cited; and see Schrader, *legal opinion 17, volume 1*, concerning the punishment of one who refuses to swear the oath of fidelity.

Although the status of "Vassalage" does not turn a non-subject into a subject, as noted by Mynsinger, *century 3, observation 30*; Rosenthal, *on feuds, chapter 11, conclusion 14*; and Andreas Gail, *on pledges, chapter 15, number 3*. I also address this in *on subordinate empires, folio 72, etc.* The granting of a fief never, by itself, makes one a subject; a Vassal is not a subject of the Lord of the fief, nor can a fief impose subjection. See Matthäus Wesenbeck, *legal opinion 1, number 57*; Paurmeister, *on jurisdiction, chapter 8, number 42*; and Marta, *on jurisdiction, part 4, chapter 133, number 13*. And even if the **Oath of Subjection** <note>original: *Huldigung*; a general oath of allegiance to a sovereign</note> and the **Feudal Oath** <note>the specific oath of a vassal to a lord</note> are as far apart as many miles <note>original: *parasangis*; an ancient Persian unit of distance</note>, as I gave above under the word **Homage**, number 1; see nevertheless Ludolph Schrader, *on feuds, part 6, chapter 1, number 6, etc.*; Gail, *on arrests, chapter 7, number 9 and following*; and Matthäus Stephani, *book 2, on jurisdiction, part 1, chapter 7, number 22 and following*, where one may see the reasons for this diversity, which he pursues at length.

Likewise, the oath of subjection binds more strongly than the oath of Fidelity or the **Client's oath**. Caspar Ziegler, under the section *Land-dwellers, conclusion 1, number 15*, citing Andreas Knichen, *on the law of the land, chapter 3, number 163*; Cravetta, *legal opinion 517, number 3*; and Rolando à Valle, *legal opinion 1, number 30, volume 3*.

And although sometimes, according to the same Ziegler in the cited place, number 65, and by a common way of speaking accepted by some, a Vassal is called a "subject" of his Lord, as in Cravetta, *legal opinion 29, number 17*.

<column-break/>

Paurmeister, *on jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 8 and chapter 9, number 49*; see Rosenthal, *on feuds, chapter 5, conclusion 78*; and the *Defense of Philibert, Count of Verrua, in the treatise on the Peace of Savoy*. This, however, is not to be understood truly or with full legal effect, but rather as an **improper usage** <note>original: *abusive*</note>. See Mynsinger, *legal opinion 77, number 8, decade 1*. For this **misuse of terms** <note>original: *catachresis*</note> crept in by reason of feudal recognition, services, and fidelity, and not by reason of true subjection. Paurmeister, *cited book 2, chapter 8, number 40*; Petrus Friedrich Mindanus, *book 1 of Procedures, chapter 32, number 2*. And it is not new for someone to be called **Lord** who is nevertheless not the Lord of the territory, but only so in a certain respect. See Capicius, *decision 26, number 31*; Ziegler, *cited place, number 70 and following*.

Likewise, a Lord must return the favor to his **Faithful One** or Vassal in all things; if he does not, he is judged to be **bad-faith** <note>original: *malefidus*</note>, *book 2 of feuds, title 6, final section*. And since, as Seneca says in *book 6 on benefits*, a benefit is a common bond and binds two people together: there is a reciprocal faith between us; thus the Vassal and the Lord are like **spouses** to one another—that is, joined by a common bond of faith. *Book 1 of feuds, final title*; Rittershusius, *on feudal divisions, book 2, chapter 10*.

->From this the proverb arose: **Loyal Lord, loyal servant** <note>original: *Getreuer Herr, getreuer Knecht*</note>.<-

Whether a Vassal is bound to **produce his title** <note>term: *editionem tituli*; showing the legal document proving his right to the land</note>, and if he does not do so, whether and when he can be deprived of the fief due to the denial of its feudal nature, is made clear from the following legal response.

***

**High-born Gracious Count**, regarding what Your Grace wrote to me on July 5th concerning the little town of **Ullenbach**, and commanded me to open my thoughts on what might be handled regarding the **production of the title**, I have not wanted to neglect setting such things into motion for Your Grace's benefit.

Because I now find from the records that the indicated little town of Ullenbach, together with its appurtenances, is held as a **pledged fief** <note>original: *Pfand-Lehen*; a fief used as collateral for a debt</note> against Person A: it follows that one will hardly be able to refuse the **production of the title**. Furthermore, one must expect this danger: that if one should refuse such production, and thus by necessary consequence deny the **feudal status** <note>original: *qualitatem feudalem*</note>, then Person A could bring forth a charge of **Felony** <note>term: *Feloniam*; in feudal law, a breach of contract by the vassal that results in the total loss of the land</note> based on this denial, and would seize such a fief entirely without compensation. One might perhaps bring this up specifically under the pretext of the ongoing **Countly Guardianship** <note>original: *Gräfl. Vormundschafft*</note>, arguing that nothing could be surrendered by the wards <note>original: *Pupillen*; minors under guardianship</note>. It could be argued that the Guardians, for their part, were not otherwise informed than that such a town was a **rightful property** <note>original: *rechtes Eigenthum*; allodial land, not a fief</note> and an unquestionable dependency of Person C, and had been used as such for time immemorial and possessed without any recognition of it being a fief. Therefore, even if someone from ancient times had some right there, such a right was...

# Letter L.

...presumably discharged, and indeed certainly extinguished through lawful prescription <note>term: *Præscription*; a legal method where a right is gained or an obligation is ended because a specific amount of time has passed, similar to a statute of limitations</note> and the passage of time.

Therefore, to the detriment of the Count's wards <note>original: *Gräfl. Pupillen*; children under legal guardianship, likely the heirs of a deceased nobleman</note>, especially after the prescription has been legally completed, one could not enter into any dispute in this matter. This completed prescription should be put forward as a defense in the event that the opponent could produce an old right or title.

*Since the defense of the passage of time is among those prescriptions by which defendants are protected by the law itself, it can be raised not only as a peremptory plea <note>original: *peremptoriæ*; a defense that completely destroys the plaintiff's claim</note> against the merits and justice of the case (according to the law of the buyer, Code on long-term prescription), but even to prevent the formal opening of the suit or the entry into litigation (according to the law on all 30 or 40-year prescriptions; see the legal counsels of Schurff, Wesenbec, Modelynus, and Pistor).*

*And a thing acquired through usucapion <note>term: *usucapion*; the acquisition of ownership by long-term possession</note> is one's own, not another's (as noted by Angelus on the Code regarding judges, and before him Gothofredus in the summary on the prescription of immovable things, and Balbus on prescription).*

**When it now comes into dispute whether this small town is a fief <note>term: *Lehen/feudum*; land held from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty</note>, or whether Party A has a right to seek there, the defense of prescription is raised first, before one enters into the main substance of the case. It follows that Party A cannot in any way demand that the Count's guardianship produce a title of ownership. Instead, this entire dispute belongs in another place—namely before the Ordinary Judge <note>original: *Judicem Ordinarium*; a regular civil judge rather than a specialized feudal official</note>—and cannot be pulled into any court belonging to Party A. This is because the noble wards are not at all subject to Party A, but are notoriously a distinguished estate of the Holy Empire. Furthermore, the matter itself under dispute, along with its appendages, is not located in the territory of Party A or under its command or jurisdiction, but is situated in the Holy Roman Empire. Thus, the jurisdiction of the court can in no way be established outside the Roman Empire, regardless of whether Party A wishes to initiate an action to recover property, a pledge action, or any other action whatsoever.**

And although the often-mentioned Party A wants to turn this matter into a feudal holding and bring it to the Feudal Court, nevertheless, according to the nature of the circumstances, the matter belongs to the ordinary court, *since the question is: is the matter feudal, or if it was, has that right been extinguished by prescription?*

*For if a legal petition seeks a judgment based on a fief, the jurisdiction of the feudal judges is only established if the feudal nature of the land is admitted by both sides (Rosenthal, On Feuds, chapter 12).*

*And when both sides do not agree it is a fief, or where the defendant flatly denies the thing is feudal, then one must go to the Ordinary Judge (Rosenthal, as cited).*

Just as one could also offer to seek a legal judgment before the ordinary judge in such an event.

<column-break/>

And for my part, I do not believe that even if this town were to be estimated as belonging to Party A, one could force a charge of felony <note>term: *Felonie*; in feudal law, a breach of duty by a vassal—such as denying the lord's rights—that could result in the loss of their land</note> by claiming that the denial of the feudal status (namely by raising the defense of prescription) was a mere pretext. *For he who exercises his own right does injury to no one. Lawful prescription grants the right entirely to the possessor; and since the possessor was ignorant without deceit or gross negligence and probably believed the thing was not feudal—or, what is the same thing, that it had been changed from feudal to allodial <note>term: *allodial*; land owned absolutely, without any feudal duties to a lord</note> through lawful prescription—he seems to deserve excuse (according to the tradition of Rosenthal, chapter 12).*

*And a vassal is only deprived of a fief if he denies it while knowing it is a fief (Zahn, On Falsehood, book 2), not if he lacks deceit or gross negligence (Rosenthal, chapter 10); to the extent that some say the burden of proof lies on the Lord to show that the vassal denied the fief through deceit or fault.*

*It is also found recorded that if the Lord wishes to demand the legal documents, he must first ask the vassal whether it is the vassal who denies the Lord's right (so the Lord may act upon the offense); or if the vassal affirms the Lord's right, the Lord can order him to show the documents (Rosenthal, chapter 8). However, the same author adds that if the vassal offers a probable cause for his denial, then the judgment belongs to the Peers <note>original: *Pares*; the vassal's social equals</note>, not to the Lord.*

*If, however, the defense of prescription is raised, and it is said that the feudal quality has been extinguished by it, then the knowledge of the Ordinary Judge seems necessary. Rosenthal (chapter 10) records that it is a wise precaution for a doubting vassal to respond tentatively or with doubt, and then he cannot be deprived of the fief; just as he is safe if he responds obscurely without deceit or gross negligence.*

Therefore, even if one wished to respond in this matter and in this event, it could be done in a doubtful way without prejudice to one's rights.

*Rosenthal also adds that a negative response can be revoked before the contestation of the suit <note>original: *litem contestatam*; the point where the legal issues are officially defined</note>, and also under the pretext of the defendant being a minor.*

But besides this, it will be well to consider whether one's position on the point of prescription is firm enough to exclude gross negligence regarding the denial of the feudal status, and whether one can prove the known requirements of prescription? *Some indeed doubt whether a vassal can gain freedom for a feudal estate against the Lord in the space of 30 years (Bocer, Treatise on Feudal Prescription; Vultejus, On Feuds).*

*But the legal scholars commonly embrace the affirmative opinion (Rosenthal, chapter 6), where he proves and confirms with several reasons that if the vassal has entirely denied the fief, or refused to perform services when requested, or in any way overturned the Lord's possession, and from that time...*

### Letter L.

...presumably discharged, and indeed certainly extinguished through lawful **prescription** <note>original: *Præſcription*; a legal principle where a right or obligation is lost or gained due to the passage of time, similar to a statute of limitations</note> and expiration.

Thus, to the prejudice of the Count's **wards** <note>original: *Pupillen*; minors under the care of a guardian</note>, especially after the prescription period has been legally completed (which, in the event that the opposing party could produce an old right or title, should be effectively protected by raising an objection), one cannot enter into any dispute in this matter. Since among the number of those prescriptions by which parties are protected by the law itself is the "objection of the prescription of time," which can be raised not only as a final defense against the merits and justice of the case <note>original: *l. emptor. 9. C. de præſcript. longi tempor.*; referring to the Code of Justinian regarding long-term prescription</note>, but also to prevent the contestation of the lawsuit or the entry into trial <note>original: *l. omnes 4. C. de præſcript. 30. vel 40. ann.*; laws regarding 30 or 40-year limits</note>. *Schurff, counsel 52, number 16, century 1. Wesenbeck, counsel 14, number 67. Modestinus Pistor, counsel 10, numbers 6 and 8, volume 1, and counsel 24, number 15 and following, volume 2.*

And a thing acquired through **usucapion** <note>original: *uſucapionem*; gaining ownership by long-term possession</note> is one's own, not another's, *Angelo in law 1, number 59, on judges*, and before him Gothofredus *in the summary of the title on the prescription of immovable things, section "verum," verse "quid si jam completa." Balbus on prescription, part 2, section 3, preface, question 9, number 2.*

When it now comes into dispute whether this small town is a **fief** <note>original: *Lehen*</note>, or whether "A." has a right to seek therein—but first and foremost, before one involves oneself in any primary way, the objection of prescription is raised—it follows that "A." cannot in any way demand the "showing of the title" <note>original: *Editionem tituli*</note> from the Count’s guardianship. Instead, this entire dispute belongs in another place, namely before the **Ordinary Judge** <note>the standard civil judge, rather than a specialized feudal court</note>, and cannot be drawn into any Court of "A." at all. Considering that the Lords who are wards are not subject to "A." at all, but are notoriously a distinguished **Estate of the Holy Empire** <note>the high-ranking political entities of the Holy Roman Empire</note>; also the matter itself under dispute, with its appendages, is situated simply within the Holy Roman Empire and not in the territory of "A." under his rule or jurisdiction. Thus, by no reasoning can the competence of the forum be established outside the Roman Empire, regardless of whether "A." wished to bring a claim for recovery of property, a pledge action, or any other action whatsoever.

And although the oft-mentioned "A." would wish to make a feudal matter out of this business and bring it to the **Feudal Court** <note>original: *Curia feudalem*</note>, nevertheless, according to the circumstances of the case, such a matter belongs to the ordinary judge, since it is specifically asked: is the matter feudal, or if it was, has that right been extinguished through prescription?

For if it is petitioned and concluded in the legal brief as a fief, the jurisdiction of the feudal judges is not established unless the feudal quality is admitted by both sides. *Rosenthal, on fiefs, chapter 12, conclusion 2, number 10.*

And when both parties do not agree it is a fief, or where the defendant flatly denies the matter is feudal, then one must go to the Ordinary Judge. *Rosenthal, in the same place, number 17 and following.*

As one could then, in such an event, offer to submit to a legal decision before the ordinary judge.

<column-break/>

And for my part, I do not hold that even if this small town were to be valued for an "A.," one could (namely by raising the objection of prescription) force a **felony** <note>original: *Feloni*; in feudal law, a "felony" was a breach of contract by a vassal, such as denying the lord's rights, which could lead to the loss of the land</note> under the pretext of denying the feudal quality. Since he who uses his own right does injury to no one. Furthermore, a lawful prescription grants a right entirely to the possessor; and since the possessor was ignorant of the status without malice or gross negligence, and likely believed the thing was not feudal—and what is more, that through lawful prescription it had been turned from a fief into **allodial** <note>original: *allodialem*; land owned independently, without a feudal lord</note> property—he seems to deserve an excuse. *Based on the arguments provided by Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 4, number 28.*

And only then is a vassal deprived of a fief if he has denied the fief while *knowing* it was a fief, *Zahn, on Deceit, book 2, chapter 96, number 1*, and not if he lacks malice or gross negligence. *Rosenthal, chapter 10, conclusion 32, from the beginning*; so much so that some say the burden of proof lies with the Lord to show that the vassal denied the fief through malice or fault.

So it is also found recorded that if the Lord wishes to demand the legal documents, he must first of all be asked by the vassal whether it is the vassal who denies the Lord's right, or if the Lord is acting upon a committed offense; or if the vassal affirms the right, the Lord can order him to produce the documents. *The frequently cited Rosenthal, chapter 8, conclusion 33, number 12 and following*, who nevertheless adds in *number 15* that if the vassal offers a probable cause for denial, then the judgment belongs to the **Peers** <note>the vassal's social equals</note>, and not to the Lord.

However, if the objection of prescription is raised, and it is said that the feudal quality was extinguished by it, then by the arguments derived above, the knowledge and judgment of an Ordinary Judge seems necessary. *Rosenthal, chapter 10, conclusion 32, who in number 12* records that it is a safeguard for a doubting vassal to respond "under doubt" or "tentatively," and then he cannot be deprived of the fief, as is also the case if he should respond obscurely without malice or gross negligence.

Therefore, if one wished to respond in this place and in this event, such a response could perhaps be made tentatively and without being seized upon.

Rosenthal also adds in the same place that a negative response can be revoked before the trial begins, and under the pretext of being a **Minor** <note>referring to the legal protections afforded to the young Count's wards</note>.

But besides this, it will be well to consider whether one is grounded in this place on the point of prescription (at least to exclude gross negligence regarding the denial of the feudal quality), and whether one can prove the well-known requirements of prescription? Some indeed doubt this: whether a vassal can prescribe the freedom of a feudal estate against a Lord in the space of 30 years? *Bocer, treatise on feudal prescription, chapter 2, number 46 and following. Vultejus, on fiefs, book 1, chapter 9, number 19.*

Truly, the Doctors of Law commonly embrace the affirming opinion, *Rosenthal, chapter 6, conclusion 82*, where he records, proves, and confirms with several reasons that if the vassal has entirely denied the fief, or when requested has refused to perform services, or in any way has interrupted the Lord's possession, and from that time...

...at the time when something of this kind was done; [if] the Lord allowed 30 years to pass, then at last the freedom of the thing possessed by the Vassal—provided he was not acting in bad faith—is considered to be established by prescription <note>term: *Præscriptio*; a legal rule where a right is gained or an obligation ended after a certain period of time has passed</note>.

And regarding the specific terms of our case, Giovanni Pietro Surdo <note>original: *Joann. Petrus Surdus*; a 16th-century Italian jurist known for his legal "Decisions"</note> in *Decision 3* teaches that prescription applies even in the case of a pledged fief. He says this holds even more strongly if an oath was added to the agreement to sell back <note>term: *pacto retrovendendi*; a contract clause allowing the original owner to buy back property within a set time</note>, especially if a span of 40 years has passed. As he also teaches in *Decision 2*, prescription is not understood to be removed by the words "always and whenever" added to a buy-back agreement.

Whether and in what manner it can be proven in this place that "in this regard the possession of A. has been inverted" <note>original: *possessio A. interversa fuerit*; a legal term for when someone holding property on behalf of another begins to hold it as their own</note>, such that the Counts also held and possessed the small town of Ullenbach and its appurtenances as free, unencumbered, and without claim from A., and that nothing was conceded to A., but rather every request was purely refused, will be learned from the Acts and Documents of the Countly Chancery. For my part, I believe nothing else than that, beyond human memory, nothing was ever conceded to A., nor was any feudal service ever performed, but the requests made at various times were always refused. One should remain upon this point, repeat such refusals, and offer to settle in the proper legal venues; in the event that it is deemed advisable, one could simultaneously assert immemorial prescription <note>term: *immemorialem præscriptionem*; a claim that a right exists because "the memory of man runneth not to the contrary"</note>.

->Which [is submitted to] Your Countly Grace, etc.<-

->Given on September 21, 1630.<-
->C. B.<-

### Oath of the Noble Vassals of the Duchy of Württemberg.

In the place and name of the Illustrious, High-born Prince and Lord, Lord Johann Friedrich, Duke of Württemberg and Teck, Count of Mömpelgard, Lord of Heidenheim, our Gracious Prince and Lord, the deputy of the Lord High Steward <note>original: *Land-Hofmeister*; the highest administrative official in the princely court</note> grants to you what he should grant on behalf of His Princely Grace, though excepting the rights of His Princely Grace, his heirs, and the feudal law of men. And you shall vow and swear an oath to God Almighty, to promote and work for the welfare and best interests of His Princely Grace, to warn of and prevent damage to him, to be faithful to His Princely Grace, and to do what a vassal <note>term: *Lehenmann/Vasallus*; a person who held land from a lord and owed him loyalty and service</note> is bound and obligated to do for his rightful feudal lord, to give judgment with the men of His Princely Grace when you are exhorted and required to do so. To make known concealed fiefs <note>original: *Verschwiegene Lehen*; lands that should be registered as fiefs but have been kept secret from the lord</note>, if you should know or learn of them, and to give a written description of your fiefs, whatever their names, and to give and take

<column-break/>

letters regarding them within the next four weeks. All faithfully and without deceit, etc.

On whether the Vassal's oath can be changed and enforced so that the Vassal is bound to help the Lord against the fatherland, see Schäffer, *3. question 48.* Compare the Marburg collection, *volume 4, counsel 55.*

On whether the Emperor, concerning a Duchy he held before attaining the Empire, must still provide a pledge of loyalty after attaining the Empire. Or whether a Vassal who attains a higher rank than his Lord is freed from his homage <note>original: *hominio*; the formal acknowledgment of allegiance to a lord</note>, see Hotman, *Illustrious Questions, question 35.*

## ADDITION.

The vassal should not behave too delicately or sensitively toward his feudal lord. Knipschild <note>original: *Knipschild*; Philipp Knipschild, a famous 17th-century jurist of feudal law</note> in *On the Obligations of the Lord toward the Vassal, question 1, number 66.* When the vassal does not have actual and thorough information on what belongs to the fief, the lord is bound, at the vassal's request, to name the fief, the individual pieces, and their appurtenances, boundaries, and what is actually included and belongs therein, and to hand over a special inventory of the feudal properties and pieces, *number 43.* In those cases where a forfeited fief falls back to the lord, it falls to the lord only for as long as the delinquent vassal and his male descendants are living; then it goes to the nearest agnates <note>term: *Agnaten*; relatives related through the male line</note>, *question 4, number 10 and many following.* Regarding what expenses for improvements the heirs of a deceased vassal may demand, see Knipschild, *ibidem, question 8, number 41 and following;* and which they may not demand, *number 58 and following.*

### 35. Feudal Claim or Renewal.
->Renewal of Investiture<-

A vassal who does not request investiture <note>term: *Investitura*; the formal ceremony of being put in possession of a fief</note> within a year and a day loses the fief. Klock, *volume 2, counsel 4, number 174.* This is expanded in *number 175* and limited in *numbers 176, 178, 179, 182;* see also *counsel 13, numbers 2 and 3, and numbers 11, 15, and 16.* A fief can exist without investiture. Klock, *volume 2, counsel 6, number 53;* the contrary is decided in *numbers 54, 55, 56.*

See the individual treatise of Laurentius Silvanus, and the *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 26, question 2.*

When a vassal does not acknowledge the fief, it prejudices the agnates <note>original: *Agnatis*; the male relatives who stand to inherit the land</note>, therefore they must be careful. Silvanus, *On the Acknowledgment of Fiefs, question 87.*

Whether the fiefs must be requested whenever the administration of a prince who is a minor changes? I think it is safer that it be done.

If investiture is denied to a vassal due to the alienation <note>term: *alienation*; the transfer of property to another person</note> of certain things, how may he be helped? Beatus, *volume 2, On Miscellaneous Contracts, folio 23, etc.*

Letter L.

Compare section 48. Whether a fief lost because investiture <note>original: *Investituram*; the formal ceremony or act of granting a fief</note> was not requested should return to the Lord or to the children and agnates <note>term: *Agnates*; relatives related through the male line</note>. Klock, volume 2, consultation 6, number 157. An old fief is not made new by a new form of investiture. Klock, volume 2, counsel 29, numbers 1, 2, 3, 4. Declared at number 36. The renewal of a fief remains valid in the strength of the old right, consultation 29, number 6.

### ADDITIO.

Without distinction of the type of fief, the fief falls back to the Feudal Lord when the renewal of investiture—the granting and renewal of the feudal letters—has not been sought at the time of change within the certain and customary period. ### 36. Provost of the Fief. <note>original: *Lehenprobst*</note> Overseer of feudal matters.

### 37. Feudal Succession. <note>original: *Lehen Succession*</note>

### ADDITIO.

See Knipschild, *On Trusts*, under the word: *feudi successio* [feudal succession], extensively. In a hereditary fief, the successor must be the heir of the last person to die. Klock, volume 2, consultation 1, number 100 and following. In fiefs, succession looks back to the trunk <note>term: *Stipitem*; the original ancestor from whom the family line descends</note>, and it is always understood that the succession of the first acquirer is being treated. Counsel 6, numbers 2, 3, and 120. A fief cannot be called "open" <note>note: "open" here means vacant and reverted to the Lord</note> when there is a certain successor based on the agreement of the first acquirer. Consultation 21, number 52.

There are various cases where, even if the vassal <note>note: the person holding the land in exchange for service</note> has sinned and committed a grievance against the Feudal Lord, the fief does not fall to the Lord, but rather to the feudal heirs, and they are not prejudiced by the vassal's crime. Such as when: 1. The vassal offends with intent and the Lord's will against the same, so that the fief might be taken from the feudal heirs. Knipschild, *On the Obligations of the Lord*, question 3, number 11. 2. When the vassal commits a wrong through the Lord's own fault and provocation. Number 12. 3. When the fief was granted to a family, and it falls from one agnate to another. Number 13. 4. When the fief was granted to the father and son by name and at once, and the son possesses and enjoys his share during the father's lifetime. Number 14. 5. Likewise, when the fief was granted to other agnates and feudal heirs jointly and primarily. Number 16. 6. When the content of the feudal letters implies that the fief should pass from one vassal to another. Number 16. 7. When the Feudal Lord and vassal harm each other. Number 18. When the Feudal Lord has forgiven and pardoned the crime of the vassal. Number 19.
Besoldus, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

Case where, because of the father's crime, nothing is taken from the sons. Number 31 and following.

### 38. Feudal Proxies. <note>original: *Lehenträger*</note> Feudal representatives.

If a vassal leaves several heirs and the fief remains undivided, then not all are accustomed to receive investiture and swear the oath; instead, they choose someone from their number who may receive investiture and swear in the common name of all. This person we commonly call the "Fief-bearer" <note>original: *den Lehenträger*</note>, who is usually the eldest among the brothers or agnates. See section: "All sons" and there Accursius, *Books of Fiefs*, book 2, title 26, joined with the paragraph *firmit.*, book 2, title 55. Rittershusius, *Feudal Divisions*, book 1, chapter 8, number 25. However, he does not have a special privilege by that reason, since he is only a Proxy <note>original: *Procurator*</note>, not the Lord or the first or principal among the partners.

Women also provide a "Fief-bearer." And he is sometimes an outsider. And the fief is not renewed as long as such a Proxy lives. And it is considered an innovation <note>note: in this context, an unfair or illegal change in custom</note> if one wants to force the vassals to request the fief as often as anyone who has a share in it dies.

But when all those in whose name a Fief-bearer has power die, the heirs must request it and appoint a Fief-bearer anew. For a mandate <note>note: a legal authorization</note> expires with the death of those giving the mandate.

Upon the death of a long-term tenant <note>original: *Emphyteuta*</note>, whether his heirs can choose one from among themselves to seek the renewal of investiture, or appoint a guardian (commonly a Fief-bearer <note>original: *Lehenträger*</note>). See Berlich, *Decisions*, 20.

Also, whether a long-term tenant buying a tenancy from one who was invested in it through a proxy (through a Fief-bearer <note>original: *einen Lehenträger*</note>) is bound to seek investiture again while the previous proxy is alive: and whether, if he does not do so, he loses the tenancy. Modestinus Pistor, *Questions*, 133.

Furthermore, when service must be performed by one in the name of all (a "bearer" <note>original: *einen Träger*</note>), the question is who ought to choose him, the Lord or the Vassals. And the feudal legal experts attribute this to the vassals in this case, provided they take care that they are not anticipated by the Lord due to being in discord over the choosing. See Gottfried Anton, *Feudal Disputation* 7, thesis 3, letter f.

### ADDITIO.

In a word, a "carrier" <note>original: *portitor*</note>. Rittershusius, *Feudal Divisions*, page 124. Who and what a Fief-bearer <note>original: *Lehenträger*</note> is, and whether he is only from a community. Mr. Franzkius, *On Transfer Fees*, page 150, number 138 following. Whether also on the part of multiple heirs. Page 151, number 137. He is like a feudal holder, and the right of seeking investiture, as well as every transfer fee <note>original: *laudemii*; a fee paid to a lord when a fief changed hands</note>, is estimated from his person. In the same place. If a fief belongs to a multitude, such as a Church, it is handled through a Prelate or another suitable person destined for it, whom they call a substitute, a Fief-bearer <note>original: *ein Lehenträger*</note>.

### 39. Sale of a Fief, Alienation.
->Alienation of a fief.<-

Regarding the alienation <note>the legal transfer of ownership or rights to another</note> of a fief, see the cases in the *Altdorf Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 32; *Marburg Consultations*, volume 4, consultation 14; Schwanmann, consultation 3 and 11: where, if, and when the alienation or sale of a fief can occur? Likewise, whether the alienation of a fief to a stranger is valid if the agnates <note>term: *Agnates*; relatives related through the male line who usually have a right of first refusal</note> do not wish to redeem it, and whether a fief can be sold at the start or during the long absence of an agnate? Schwanmann, consultation 12. Whether a paternal fief surrendered to creditors can be revoked by the agnates? Beatus, in *Miscellaneous Decisions*, volume 2, on contracts, page 462, etc.

Whoever consents to the alienation of property which might have come to him by some chance, completely prejudices his own rights. Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 48, number 31. Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 9, conclusion 39, in note letter b. And when a vassal, with the consent of the agnates, has alienated a fief absolutely to a complete stranger with no condition or pact added, then both the vassal and the consenting agnates completely lose every right they had in this alienated fief; so much so that if the buyer dies without heirs capable of holding the fief, they themselves are not restored to the succession of this fief, nor do they have any way to reclaim it. Chapter 1, paragraph "furthermore" on how a fief is lost, and paragraph "Titius" if sons [dispute] regarding a deceased's fief. Schrader, *On Fiefs*, part 8, chapter 5, number 25. Moreover, it is the same whether this consent of the agnates precedes or follows the alienation, Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 77, number 3. Since a ratification coming after the fact is considered equal to consent, text in chapter 1, on the alienation of a paternal fief, and there the gloss on the word "not having," through the final law in the Code on the Macedonian Decree of the Senate; and Göden agrees, *Feudal Consultations* 19, number 9.

Rosenthal, said conclusion 77, number 3, and chapter 7, conclusion 5, number 5. And here, not only express consent but also tacit consent is sufficient. Alvarus and the Doctors on chapter 1, paragraph "furthermore" on how a fief is lost. Zasius, consultation 13, number 112, book 2. Fichard, consultation 23, number 8, volume 2. Schrader, part 8, chapter 5, number 4. Rosenthal, said chapter 77, number 5. Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, book 1, chapter 10, number 64. Indeed, agnates are judged to have tacitly approved an alienation when, being present, they did not contradict the act which they could have prevented by contradicting it. Schrader, part 8, chapter 4, number 7. Hartmann Pistor, book 2, chapter 7, number 4. Rosenthal, said chapter 77, number 15. This is true even if they do not proceed further or to other external acts. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 29, number 2. Or when those who were absent allowed an entire year to pass from the time the alienation to a stranger was made and was probably known to them. Fichard, consultation 23, number 9 and following. And especially if they knowingly allowed 30 years to slip away. Schenck in his *Greenery*, conclusion 95. Wesenbeck, *On Fiefs*, chapter 8, number 11; and Vultejus, chapter 10, number 64, verse "if however at the time."

Furthermore, when the hope or right to a fief has been lost through the consent or ratification of the agnates, it seems that all recourse must also be denied to their heirs and descendants. For one ought to observe the deeds of one's ancestors, nor should one be heard requesting the contrary, according to laws 1 and 2 of the Code "if against a sale." See also the law "from the beginning" in the Code on actions and obligations. But if he attacks those deeds, he ought not to have the benefit from them which he appears to renounce, and nonetheless he is held to their observance, through the text in the chapter "when once" on cessations, etc., and from that with the agreement there in the gloss on the Rules of Law in the 6th [Book of Decretals]. Göden, *Feudal Consultations* 21, number 13. And an heir is bound to hold the deed of the deceased as entirely valid and to approve it. Decianus, response 56, number 99 and following, volume 3. This has a place not only in allodial <note>privately owned property not subject to a lord</note> lands, but also in fiefs alienated by a vassal, according to the teaching of Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, book 1, chapter 11, number 93 and following. It obtains not only for the immediate heir, but also for the mediate heir—that is, the heir of an heir—and so on, through law 65 where the gloss and Doctors [comment] in the Digest on the Signification of Words. Boerius, decision 23, number 20. Add that regularly, anyone who consents to an act performed by another is regarded just as if he himself had performed that contract. Schrader, *On Fiefs*, part 10, section 8, number 103. Whence his heir is also deservedly bound by it, so that he cannot further revive rights once surrendered and extinguished. Göden at length, *Feudal Consultations* 20, numbers 13 and 23. Especially because a fief which is alienated to a complete stranger with the consent of the Lord and the agnates becomes entirely "new" in the person of that stranger, by the argument of law 20 in the Digest on judging payments. And thus all hope of succeeding is seen to be cut off from the agnates of the alienator, as noted by Schrader, *Feudal Treatise*, part 8, chapter 5, number 25 and following. See Kohl in the treatise on sub-fiefs, last chapter, number 5 and following. Thomingius, 1, consultation 8.

...he is understood to have wished to renounce or repudiate the right sought by others from the grant of the original Lord and the stipulation of the first acquirer, but only the right belonging to his own person, or that which would fall to him upon the death of the Vassal. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 79, number 3; Schrader, part 8, chapter 8, numbers 2 and 11. For the right of the Agnate <note>a relative through the male line</note> is separate from the right of the one who had consented, and in an ancient fief, as many grants are understood to exist as there are persons succeeding to the fief. Rosenthal, said conclusion 79, number 12, and chapter 11, conclusion 7, number 5. This goes so far that one succeeding to a fief is said to obtain it by his own right and from the agreement placed in the first grant. Rosenthal, said conclusion 79, in note letter c.

From this common opinion of the legal interpreters, Rosenthal (in the often-cited conclusion 79, number 6) argues that heirs who oppose such an alienation are by no means acting against the deed of the deceased: because he consented only regarding his own right, not that of another; and thus his obligation, as Schrader (chapter 8, number 8) teaches, does not pass to the heirs so as to extend beyond the life of the alienator <note>the person transferring the property</note> himself. There is therefore a difference between alienating and consenting to alienation. Rosenthal, in the same place. Just as it is generally one thing to sell, and another to consent to the one selling. Law "Aliud," 116, *Digest on the Rules of Law*; and therefore, one prohibited from alienating is not understood to be prohibited from consenting to another who is alienating. Schrader, part 8, chapter 4, number 35 at the end. Thus, the children of consenting Agnates are not always bound to uphold the alienation of a fief, Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 15, number 4, unless those parents obligated themselves beyond simple consent, or even promised for the actions of the heir. Rosenthal, said conclusion 79, number 10. From this it follows that one and the same fief can sometimes become "New" with respect to those consenting or alienating, but remain "Ancient" with respect to others. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 80, number 4.

But this consideration does not hold in a fief that is absolutely hereditary, or otherwise alienable by custom without the consent of the agnates; for according to the more accepted opinion, neither an agnate nor a son can revoke it in any way, regardless of the title under which it was alienated. Schrader, chapter 8, number 9, part 8; Vultejus, book 1, chapter 11, number 95.

Furthermore, that decision only takes place in a doubtful case, namely when it is not clearly established whether those alienating, or consenting to alienation, wished to prejudice the rights of their Agnates. It is otherwise if it is established from the agreed-upon acts or from elsewhere that they wished to derogate <note>detract from or take away</note> from even the future right of the sons or agnates; for then the sons or Agnates, as heirs of the one alienating or consenting, are bound to acquiesce to this obligation and uphold the consent, nor can they recover fiefs alienated in this way. Schrader, chapter 8, number 2 at the end, and number 11 near the end; Rosenthal, conclusion 79, number 10. Furthermore, the rule (that he who consents

Besold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

to an alienation is seen to alienate it himself) seems intended to be understood according to the subject matter and the thing being disposed of, or the alienation being discussed. Rosenthal, chapter 9, conclusion 41, number 24. Therefore, alienating and consenting to alienation are different to the extent that a different and separate reason for them is found. However, they ought to be considered equal when the same reasoning applies to both, according to the Law "Cum quis," 125, *On the Rules of Law*; see the disputation of Gottfried Anton, theses 6 and 10, letter B.

But regarding the right of revoking an alienated fief, and how much time passes before this right is lost to prescription? See Kirchberg, *On Fiefs by Agreement and Provision*, chapter 5, number 54, and following at length.
