# 40. Pledging of Fiefs. <note>original: "Lehensverpfändung. Oppignoratio ratio feudi"</note>

Regarding the pledging of a fief, see the *Strasbourg Legal Opinions*, volume 1, opinion 45; Baptista Costamala in his *Treatise on Subsidiary Remedies*, folio 97, etc.; and my own *Choice Legal Matters*. In the Bishopric of Würzburg, permission must be granted to pledge fief-estates up to two-thirds of their value, or to assign them to daughters.

### ADDITION.

A fief given as a pledge or mortgage with the Lord’s consent returns to that same Lord with the financial burden still attached if the family line fails <note>The "line" refers to the male bloodline required to inherit the fief</note>. Klock, volume 2, opinion 16, number 158.

If the Liege-Lord pledges the feudal dues <note>income derived from the fief</note>, he thereby forfeits his ownership. Knipschild, *On the Obligations of the Lord toward the Vassal*, question 2, number 45. According to German custom, a pledged fief passes to female heirs. Klock, volume 2, opinion 16, number 70. Johann Fichard asserts the contrary in *German Opinions* 7, numbers 4 and 5, page 14.

# 41. Forfeiture of Fiefs. <note>original: "Lehensverwürkung. Felonia"</note>

Regarding "felony" <term>felony: in feudal law, this refers to a breach of faith or violation of the contract between Lord and Vassal</term>, its causes, and the legal process, much is contained throughout the second part of the *Waldeck Defense of Honor*; see also *Strasbourg Legal Opinions*, volume 2, opinion 58.

To whom does a fief lost through felony return? See Kirchberg, *On Hereditary Fiefs*, chapter 5, number 97 and following. Can the Lord, on his own authority, revoke a fief lost by the Vassal’s fault? *Strasbourg Legal Opinions*, volume 1, opinion 26, question 4, and opinion 27. Is a fief lost because parricide <note>the murder of a parent or close relative</note> was committed? *Strasbourg Legal Opinions*, volume 1, opinion 42. When is the Lord himself deprived of the fief? See Schwanmann, opinions 5 and 7.

### ADDITION.

Forfeiture <term>caducitas: the lapsing of a right or property to the superior Lord</term> through the breaking or recovery of a fief once effectively transferred does not expire. Klock, volume 2, opinion 30, number 20. A forfeiture incurred due to some neglect is considered forgiven by the Lord's acceptance of the feudal fees. Opinion 48, number 169. Unless the Lord is unaware of the forfeiture. Number 170. In cases of doubt, such ignorance regarding the offense is presumed. Number 171. The right to claim forfeiture is limited by a 30-year statute of limitations. Opinion 30, number 20, and opinion 48, number 172. A declaration of forfeiture against an heir has no standing if the predecessor's status was already declared while they were alive. Klock, volume 2, opinion 30, number 19. Those who are stubborn or defiant in the accounting of feudal properties incur the penalty of felony. Klock, volume 2, opinion 30, number 3. The claim of felony belongs to a higher level of ownership dispute and investigation, which does not hinder the initial formal granting of the fief. Opinion 19, numbers 26 and 27. The Lord is deprived of the ownership of the fief if he denies the formal grant <note>investiture</note> within a year and a day. This opinion is common-

<column-break/>

ly held. Regnerus Sixtinus in *Legal Considerations*, resolution 7.

Presumptive evidence is not sufficient to prove a felony. Klock, volume 2, opinion 4, numbers 189 and 190.

The Liege-Lord forfeits his ownership:
1. When the Vassal is engaged in an open field battle or great danger, and the Lord deserts him. Knipschild, *On the Obligations of the Lord*, question 2, number 3.
2. When the Lord secretly stalks or plots against his Vassal. Number 4.
3. When the Lord attacks the Vassal with insulting words and shames him. Number 5.
4. When he attacks the Vassal with force or trickery. Number 6.
5. When he actually kills the Vassal. Number 7.
6. When he accuses the Vassal of a crime or misconduct. Number 9.
7. When he provides testimony against the Vassal in criminal matters. Number 11.
8. When he starts a defamatory legal action against him. Number 12.
9. When he reveals his Vassal's secrets to cause him harm. Numbers 14 and 15.
10. When he does not provide what he is bound to by the terms of the feudal charter. Number 17.
11. When he refuses to grant the Vassal the formal investiture and the usual feudal letters, or delays the investiture beyond a year and a day. Number 18.
12. When the Lord denies the Vassal justice or delays it too long. Number 19.
13. When the Lord's son commits an offense against the Vassal, and the Lord does not remove him. Numbers 21 and 22.
14. When he makes an alliance with the Vassal's enemies to his disadvantage. Number 13.
15. When he allows the Vassal's enemies passage through his lands. Number 24.
16. When he commits immorality with the Vassal's wife, fiancée, daughter, or sister. Number 25.
17. When he attacks the honor of the Vassal's wife, son, father, mother, or members of his household. Number 28.
18. When the Lord commits parricide. Numbers 31 and 32.
19. When the Lord commits the crime of Treason <note>Lèse-majesté</note>. Number 33.
20. When the Lord breaks the public peace of the land. Number 34.
21. When he commits an act of treachery. Number 35.
22. When he has been condemned in a criminal case. Number 36.
23. When the Lord can no longer stand with honor among others. Numbers 37 and 38.
24. When he besieges the Vassal’s city, castles, or houses. Number 39.
25. When he dispossesses the Vassal. Number 40.
26. When he does not warn him of danger. Number 42.
27. When he causes damage to the Vassal’s property. Number 43.
28. When he does not set him free <note>likely from debt or captivity</note>. Number 44. See more in that little treatise, which is more golden than gold.

# ADDITION.

A prince should exercise great care for his subjects and treat them as if they were his own children and grandchildren. <note>original: "tanquam filios & nepotes tractet"</note> *Law 'si quis filium' 34, where Jason discusses the start of the Code on inofficious wills.* Great consideration must be given to subjects so that they are not burdened by their Lords or suffer losses, but rather that the Lords consult for the subjects' interests as much as for their own. *Barbosa, book 17, chapter 55, axiom 1.*

## Feudal Rent. <note>original: "Lehenreich"</note>

To pay the feudal rent, the old feudal rent; that is, feudal money in Sulzburg and Parsberg. This is a commonly used term.

## 43. Feudal Entry Fine. <term>laudemium: a fee paid by a vassal to a lord when a fief was transferred to a new owner or heir</term>

They call the *laudemium* the "Lehenwahr." *Klock, On the Treasury, volume 2, title 42, numbers 3, 31, 52. Also volume 2, chapter 65, number 4. Berlich, Decisions 74, number 14; Decision 22, number 3. Rudinger, century 3, singular observation 92, numbers 1, 3. Franck, On Entry Fines, pages 31, 59, 88, 123, 124, 145, 148, 168, 317, 438, 453, 475, 492.* In a feudal deed <note>original: "Lehenbrief"</note> it is written: "A small estate <note>original: "Gütlein"</note> together with a garden." Now, this estate has only a very small garden attached to it, while there is a large garden located some distance away. The hereditary tenant <note>original: "Erbmann"</note> wishes to keep this large garden free from the "Handlohn" <note>another term for the entry fine</note> for two reasons: 1. Because it is not a legal accessory of the small estate, but was purchased separately, and a third party once held a "hen-rent" <note>original: "Hennen," a small symbolic tax</note> upon it which he has since paid off. 2. Because this large garden was previously a field and only later obtained the status of a garden through a settlement with the community. It is true that the feudal lord wants to adhere strictly to his deed, which says "a garden" rather than "a little garden." However, where no other large garden exists, the little garden may well be called "the garden." Thus, only one garden is mentioned, not two; therefore, the large garden should not be newly burdened with an entry fine, as is sometimes pointlessly contested.

An extract from the Harrish Treaty of the year 1495: Likewise, since disputes have arisen regarding the fiefs and entry fines which the citizens of Nuremberg and their subjects hold as fiefs from my gracious Lord, Margrave Frederick: it is agreed that henceforth, from these citizens and their settled subjects, for purchased fiefs—or fiefs where the contract was made equivalent to a sale—an entry fine of 1 florin for every 10 florins of value shall be given for the fine, the deed, and the writing fee. But regarding fiefs that have come to and fallen upon the citizens by inheritance, those who receive such hereditary fiefs shall give 1 florin for every 50 florins of the feudal valuation for the fine, the deed, and the writing fee.

Whether an entry fine is owed again in the case of a repeated "retraction" <term>retractus: the right of a family member or lord to step into a sale and buy back property sold to a stranger</term>, the negative view is more equitable. For the fine is owed only by reason of a sale. A retraction is not so much a new sale as it is a transfer of the same purchase to another buyer out of the necessity of the

<column-break/>

contract. *Zoesius on Law 18 of the Digest, regarding retraction, Gent. number 127.* If the entry fine has been exacted in various ways, one should ask whether to return to the disposition of Common Law. *Berlich, Decision 74, number 1.* There is a safeguard for Lords so that a certain quantity can be sought in this case. *See number 4 and the response of the Leipzig Jurists, number 5,* as well as the reasoning of the Leipzig Faculty of Law, *number 6 and following.* For the contrary opinion, there is a response from the Wittenberg Jurists, *number 14,* based on the reasons cited in *numbers 15, 16, and following.*

Even though Lucas von Zwemern—from whom you held several fields as fiefs—has passed away and his estates have passed and fallen to his sons: you still cannot be consistently forced to pay any entry fine to them. This would only be the case if a different practice had been established by a legally standing local custom, and if it had been held inviolably over a period exceeding legal memory <note>original: "über Rechts vermehrte Zeit"</note> that every time the Feudal Lord died, the feudal tenants must pay an entry fine; in such a case, you would be obliged to pay it now. *See the Imperial Decisions. Most recently, Johann Philippi, Jurist, in the Practical Use of Justinian's Institutes, book 1, title 2, section 9, number 6, at the end of Selection 27.*

To establish a "prescription" <term>prescription: a legal right acquired by long-continued usage</term> so that a greater entry fine must be paid than is owed by law or ancient custom, a span of 30 years is required. *Christoph Philipp Richter, part 6, counsel 6, number 9, folio 122.* When a Lord boasts that he has a greater or larger right—for example, that his tenants are obliged to give 8 pence or 3 kreuzers in entry fines from their estates and vineyards instead of 6 Würzburg pence or one shilling—the judge, at the instance of the person whose reputation is harmed by this claim, can set a deadline for the boasting Lord to prove his right. Once this deadline has passed, he is no longer to be heard. *Same counsel 6, numbers 15 and 16.*

## 44. Apprenticeship Year, Apprentice. <note>original: "Lehr-Jahr, Lehr-Jung"</note> *Tyrocinium. Tiro.*

If someone gives themselves to another to be instructed in some craft, with a pact that they shall remain with them for a certain number of years—that he completes the fixed "Lehr-Jahr"—and he runs away: is he bound to the full time anew, or only for as many days as he was absent? That is, whether he should start learning again from the beginning or merely complete the set years. I think indeed *following the argument of Law 4 and Law 14 at the end, Digest on the status of free men,* that it suffices if he remains with the craftsman for as many days as he was absent, for in this way he seems to have cleared his delay. However, the custom of certain craftsmen observes the contrary. *See my treatise On the Law of Guilds, folio 59.*

### 45. Bonded People. <note>original: "Leibeigne Leut"</note> Bonded men. <note>original: "Homines proprii"</note>

Concerning bonded men, serfs, servants, etc., see the individual treatises by Hermann Stamm and Friedrich Husanus. Add Werdenhagen, *on Hanseatic Republics, part 1, page 220* and many following, and here and there in Mager, *on armed advocacy, chapter 6, number 730* and following. Uranus, *counsel 50, volume 2.* Hering, *on suretyship, chapter 7, number 317,* etc. My own discourse, *on types of domestic society, chapter 6.* Reineccius, *on the Poet of Charlemagne, page 59* and following. Caelius Rhodiginus, *in the Index.* Pignorius, *on servants and family.* Bodin, *on the Republic.* Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 1, page 36 and page 46.* Reineccius, *on Saxon Origins, page 10.* Pontanus, *Frankish Origins, book 6, chapter 15.* Goldast, *Alemannic Matters, volume 2, page 3* and following, and *volume 3, page 75* and following. Coler, *Additions, last chapter.* Bisciolus, *Leisure Hours, book 7, chapter 8,* where he relates which nations have always lived in servitude and what the origin of servitude was. The same author teaches in *the cited location, volume 2, book 13, chapter 8 and following* how servants are to be treated, what the burdens of servitude once were, how servants were pressed and oppressed among various nations, and what the types of servants are. Regarding whom it is permitted to hold as servants, see Martin, *College 1, dispute 10, question 5.*

Furthermore, men, or bonded peasants <note>original: "Rustici proprii"</note>, serfs <note>original: "Leibeigne Leut"</note>, are bound to the labors <note>original: "operas"</note> owed to their Lords. See Hering, *on suretyship, page 16, number 317.* For services are not to be extended or expanded, but rather confined within specific limits. *Chapter 'dilect.' on the office of the Archdeacon.* Wherefore, if any undue labors are performed, they are presumed to have been extorted through force and fear. *Law 'Si per impressionem' 11. Code on those things which occur through force and fear; law 'cum satis' 23. §. 1. toward the end. Code on farmers.* And just as a freedman does not owe labors to his Patron unless they were promised, for instance by an oath or a formal agreement; *law 'ut jurisjurand' 7. on the labors of freedmen; law 44 at the end, on causes of freedom.* So too a bonded man, a serf <note>original: "ein Leibeigener"</note>, does not owe other labors or payments to a Lord than those to which he bound himself, either in the contract itself, or by tacitly accepting a farmstead to which this or that burden was attached, or expressly, that is, by making a new agreement. Friedrich Husanus, *on bonded men, chapter 6, number 60 and following.*

For a Lord, at the time of the transfer of a farmstead (which our people call an "inheritance" <note>original: "ein Erbe"</note> or "farm" <note>original: "Hof"</note>, and among the poorer sort, a "cottage" <note>original: "Katen"</note>), can impose whatever law he wishes. *Law 6. Code on the exchange of things; law 1. §. 'si conven.' 6. on deposits.* For example, if he agrees that every year, in this or that month, the tenant shall pay a pair of roosters, which our people call the "smoke-hen" <note>original: "das Rauchhun"; a tribute traditionally paid per chimney or hearth</note>. (For, because those hens fly high and nest there, or rest at night, they also signify the "height" of the law, and in case of doubt, "pure sovereignty" <term>merum Imperium: the highest level of legal authority and criminal jurisdiction</term>) or a certain measure of grain, "grain-rent" <note>original: "Kornpechte"</note>, or a certain sum of pennies or shillings, which we call "money-rent" <note>original: "Geldpacht"</note> and "interest" <note>original: "Gülte"</note>. Likewise, that he shall work for the Lord so many times by plowing, gathering, threshing, or carrying wood into the Lord's house. And indeed, these labors are chiefly performed by those who are granted enough land by the Lords that they can maintain horses or plow-oxen; our people call these "team-drivers" <note>original: "Anspanner"</note> or "helpers" <note>original: "Hülffner"</note>, and the labors themselves "plowing services" <note>original: "Pflugdienste"</note>. Husanus, *cited treatise, chapter 6, number 66.* 

Conversely, the poorer cultivators or their own men, who do not have enough land or resources to maintain their own horses or fulfill the duties of transport and plowing, are called "cottagers" <note>original: "Kötenner, Köter, Kotsassen"</note>, or "hand-servants" <note>original: "Handfroner"</note>, and they call the labors themselves "hand-service" <note>original: "Handdienst"</note>. These people, no less than the others, perform labors for their Lord and pay something annually according to the measure of their resources and the land granted to them. Husanus, *cited location.* But to acquire such bonded men for oneself anew does not pertain to any others than those who hold all-encompassing jurisdiction.

The condition of bonded men, the serfs <note>original: "Leibeignen Leuten"</note>, is not the same everywhere. In Westphalia, they are held under a harsher law, since those to whom they belong succeed them in a half-share of their property, and they cannot marry off their children outside the community of bonded people unless they have sought permission from those whose interests they serve—they must first seek the consent of their Lords <note>original: "müssen zuvor um Bewilligung ihrer Herren ersuchen"</note>. (See Arnisaeus, *on the Republic, page 115, number 4, etc.*) Bonded men of this kind are found in Swabia and elsewhere. These come very close to the condition of slaves. In Poland, bonded men are called *Kmethones* <note>original: "Kmethones"; likely the Polish 'kmiecie'</note>; they are indeed in a harsh condition, yet they are not slaves in the way the ancients were. René Choppin, *book 3, on Domains, at the end, under the title of Patrimonial Finances.* 

In some places, on the other hand (especially in the Duchy of Württemberg), bonded men <note>original: "Leibeigene"</note> are in a better condition; no differently than those who are not bonded, they have the freest administration of their goods. Thus, while they may appear to have been bonded when they die, while living they were free—that is, free in reality, bonded only in name. This freedom of theirs even after death is sufficiently apparent from the fact that they have successors by will and by intestacy, just like those who are not bonded (except for the death-tax <note>original: "Hauptfall"; a tax or best-asset forfeiture due to the lord upon a serf's death</note>). But these matters are better observed through local custom than learned in schools, as Vultejus says, *on §. 2, last number, Institutes on the law of persons.* In Livonia, the rural people, if they do not pay the enjoined tax, are flogged most miserably by their nobles.

*Aldions, Treasury Servants, Aldiones, Liti, Ministerials, Household Servants:* In the Constitutions of Charlemagne, edited by Veit Amerbach, it is written thus: Concerning Public Aldions belonging to public law, let the *Aldiones* or *Aldianes* live in Italy under the same law of servitude to their masters by which the *Fiscalini* or *Liddi* live in France. See *Goldast, volume 3, leaf 80.*

The word *Liddi* <note>A class of semi-free people among the Franks.</note>, however, seems to be the same which is still used among us in the common term *Liedlohn* <note>original German: "servant's wages"</note>, that is, the wages of male and female servants; thus both words (*Aldii* and *Liddi*) are Germanic, and differ in nothing except that one was then in use in Italy and the other in Gaul.

*Aldius, a ministerial servant,* see the *Laws of the Lombards, book 1, leaf 11, in the Law of Lothair.* If anyone, in a suddenly arising quarrel, pulls a free man by the beard or hair, let him pay 6 solidi <note>A gold coin used as a unit of legal compensation.</note>. If he does so to a ministerial servant, or an *aldius*, or another's rural servant, let him pay as if for a forbidden grape, one solidus. *Likewise on the following leaf:* If anyone knocks out the eye of a one-eyed free man, let him pay two-thirds of the value at which he would have been appraised had he killed him. If, however, he knocks out the eye of a one-eyed *Aldio* or servant, let him pay for him as if he were dead.

*A "Penny-man" <note>original: "Denarialis homo"</note>, a man set free by the tossing of a penny before the King.* Pithou in the *Glossary of Lombard Law, book 2, part 70.* A "Penny-man" can now acquire an inheritance into his own recognition until he reaches the third generation. Here an old commentator noted in the margin: Note that a "Penny-man" is not under power, because he was made free by the hand of the King, with a penny. <note>This refers to a Frankish ritual of manumission where the King struck a penny out of the person's hand to symbolize their freedom.</note>

*Ripuarian Law, title 59, § 4.* If, however, a "Penny-man" dies without children, let him leave no heir other than our royal treasury.

*Fiscalinus, a Royal man.* Thus Charlemagne himself explains in his Constitutions. A royal man: that is, a treasury servant <note>original: "fiscalinus"</note>, and whether an Ecclesiastic or a Layman, if killed, let him be compensated with 100 solidi.

*On the origin of bonded men,* I treated in *the said chapter 6, on the three types of domestic society.* In the year 409, the Germans, mad with envy, turned their weapons against their own throats. For the Alemanni, begrudging the fact that they had to obey the Franks because of the cities across the Rhine, brought bloody wars upon their King Clovis, at first with happy success. They took possession of the aforementioned cities, the yoke of the Franks having been cast off by them, and First Germany was reclaimed as far as Cologne. Clovis, having moved again in a war of recovery, was so hemmed in by the Alemanni that no hope appeared for any remaining safety. There, remembering that his wife (a companion in the Christian faith) had often preached the powerful help of the omnipotent Christ—whom he otherwise cared nothing for—driven by necessity, he prayed fervently. Just as He excludes no one, so He graciously heard Clovis; so much so that, with His help, he inflicted a great slaughter on the enemies and gained a glorious victory. While he pursued them after crossing the Rhine, he conquered Alemannia, which was trembling with fear. For the sake of cutting off future uprisings, their weapons were taken away, and their wives and children were delivered into perpetual servitude after the manner of the Romans, utterly extinguishing their original liberty.

Afterward, when lords, led by true religion and conscience, realized that this device of the heathens ought to be far removed from Christians—who were set free by the blood of Christ—some, out of compassion, voluntarily released the yoke of servitude; some granted liberty to obtain eternal salvation; and some finally abdicated their lordly power upon receiving money, etc. More on this in *Franz Guilliman, on Swiss Matters, book 2, chapter 10 and following*, where he writes of the despoiling of ancient liberty and dignity, and the servitude that followed the Battle of Tolbiac, etc. See also *Welser, Augsburg Matters, book 8, leaf 136 and following*, where he thinks not all the Alemanni were conquered then.

When a high magistrate reserves the bondage, such a bonded person, even if he lives in a city, must nonetheless pay his "body-hen" <note>original: "Leibhenn"; a symbolic annual tribute, often a chicken, paid to acknowledge the lord's ownership of the person</note> and other rights to his high-lord: not by virtue of jurisdiction (from which he is now freed), but by virtue of Servitude, and those things which arise from it by custom. For the common rule—"No hen flies over the walls"—is no longer accepted today. *Zorer, part 2, question 2, number 159.* Indeed, in the Duchy of Württemberg, a **General Order** was issued against this rule only a few years ago.

However, when a territory has dual-lordship <note>original: "Zweyherrig"</note>, and one lord wants to declare the departing person free, but the other does not; then such a right, because it is indivisible and does not allow for separation in one person, means the condition of the one prohibiting the move is stronger, or perhaps the matter must be decided by a judge.

### 46. Dower, Widow’s Estate, Purchase of Dower. Dotal Dowry.

In the Saxon Territory, it has been received by very long use among the Nobles that, by reason of the dowry brought in, a gift on account of marriage—which they commonly call **Dotalitum**, or **Dower** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note>—is established in a specific way, separate from the disposition of Common Law. Thus, there, **Widow’s Estate** <note>original: "Leibzucht"</note> or **Dower** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note> is a gift that a husband makes or gives to his wife, in fruits or in interest, which he must give with the leave and permission of the heirs (*unless it were movable goods*) and confirm with the Lord's will. *So says the gloss in Feudal Law, chapter 31, column 2, number 2, there: 'You should know what a dower is.' citing there §. "but we most fully," Institutes: 'on donations.' Beust, on matrimonial law, part 3, chapter 9.* More expressively, a gift on account of marriage or a dower seems able to be defined from the gloss in the **Territorial Law <note>original: "Landrecht"; specifically the Sachsenspiegel</note>, book 1, article 21, on the word "Leibzucht"**, which, joined with the said *gloss in Feudal Law, chapter 31, and the gloss in the Municipal Law <note>original: "Weichbild"</note>, article 22, number 1. Georgius Rotschitz, treatise on Dower, article 1, number 19.* Thus, if a woman brings a dowry to her husband, an equal amount should legally be made for her dower in return. And the dower should be equal to the dowry, and whatever is lacking in the dowry shall also be lacking in the dower. **Territorial Law, book 1, article 20, there gloss on the word "The Possession," section "The third gift," and article 21, there new gloss, letter d. Rotschitz, same place, number 3.** See him throughout the whole article and treatise. *Hartmann Pistor, book 1, question 4, number 1,* where he writes: When a husband dies first, there is owed to the widow, in place of the gift on account of marriage, as much from his goods as she brought to the husband in the name of a dowry; and both the dowry and the gift on account of marriage, being calculated into one sum, for every hundred (or for each hundred), ten must be paid annually. For example, if the woman had brought five hundred florins as a dowry, then five hundred would likewise be owed to her from his goods; and for this combined sum of dowry and gift on account of marriage, one hundred florins should be paid annually (namely ten for every hundred), as long as the widow survives. For when she dies, the dower—since it is customary to grant it only for life, just like a usufruct—is ended by the death of the beneficiary. See, however, *Pistor on this question and the following question*, where it is discussed: Whether a dower is owed to a widow who did not pay the dowry while her husband was living, but only offers it after his death. **Also question 14.** Whether, by reason of a dower which she obtained from her first husband for life, a second husband is bound to establish a dower again.

Whether a noble wife has a privilege in her dower by which she is preferred over her husband's creditors while he is still living. See *Modestinus Pistor, part 2, question 26.*

It is also called a **life-annuity** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note> or a **prebend-purchase** <note>original: "Pfrund-kauff"</note>, when someone purchases a yearly income for the duration of their life <note>original: "ad dies vitæ"</note>, consisting of money, produce, wine or food, housing, etc., for a specific sum of money. This often occurs in hospitals and monasteries. From this, a question arises: If someone has purchased a life income from the Church for 100 gold coins based on the revenue of a farm, and they live an exceptionally long life, are they required to restore anything to the Church? Cavallos, question 850, denies this because the outcome was uncertain <note>meaning it was a legal gamble on life expectancy</note>. It is with this same perspective that higher interest rates are allowed for maritime loans <note>original: "usuræ nauticæ"; high-risk loans for sea voyages</note>.

### ADDITION.

What a **life-annuity** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note> or **widow’s support** <note>original: "Leibzucht"</note> is, see Conrad Rittershul in *Feudal Law, part 339.* A fief <note>original: "Feudum"</note> is by no means obligated as a mortgage for a dowry or a widow’s provision without the consent of the feudal lord and the subsequent ratification of the agnates <note>paternal male relatives</note>. For this reason, Saxon law warns that it is safest to establish widow’s provisions with the consent of the feudal heirs, according to *Feudal Law, chapter 31,* which says: *with the sons' leave* <note>original: "mit der Söhne Laub"</note>. See also the text of the *Landrecht* <note>Territorial Law</note>, *book 3, article 75:* *the right of gift and widow’s support for wives exists in allodial property <note>privately owned land</note>, but not in fiefs.* Gothofridus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations, 6, thesis 8, letter b.*

What is meant by **dower** <note>original: "Dotalitium"</note>, **widow’s settlement** <note>original: "Wittumsverschreibung"</note>, **life-annuity** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note>, and **widow’s support** <note>original: "Leibzucht"</note>. See Zorer, *part 1, question 3, number 278 and following.* When a man provides his wife with a yearly allowance <note>original: "Deputat"</note> of money, grain, etc., for the duration of her life or her widowhood, this explains how it should be managed and when such things may be demanded. Zorer, *part 2, question 8, number 647.* A dower and a gift are established for women by the husband; commonly called **widow’s support** <note>original: "Leibzucht"</note> or **life-annuity** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note> (and it is a sort of usufruct <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note>). On this, one may consult Joachim von Beust in his *Treatise on Dowries, chapters 9, 10, and 11.* Also regarding the **morning-gift** <note>original: "Morgengaba"; a gift given by the husband to the wife the morning after the wedding</note>, explained by Scipio after Cujas in *Feudal Law, book 2, chapter 9.*

Are the agnates and feudal successors bound to establish the widow’s **life-annuity** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note> before it is proven that the dowry was actually brought into the marriage and used for the benefit of the fief? See Lord Christoph Philipp Richter, *part 3, counsel 29.* Are the agnates and feudal heirs who did not consent to the dower bound to provide what the deceased vassal promised his wife beyond the legitimate and customary limit? *Ibid.* In determining the quantity of the dower, that which the custom and usage of each province requires ought to prevail. *Ibid. number 9.* A dower can be established even if a dowry was not brought in. The praised Richter, *part 1, counsel 46, number 12.* The dower, like a usufruct, is extinguished by the death of the widow.

<column-break/>

The dower absorbs the dowry <note>meaning the widow cannot claim both the return of her dowry and the full dower payment if they overlap</note>. Richter, *part 1, counsel 64, number 7.* In the March <note>the Margraviate of Brandenburg</note>, dowers are valid even if the agnates did not consent. *Counsel 64, number 10.* The dower is substituted in place of the dowry. Carpzov, *decision 59.* It is at the widow's discretion whether to demand the dower or to reclaim the dowry. However, in either case, the bringing in of the dowry and its conversion to the benefit of the fief must be proven. The dower and the "gift on account of marriage" <note>original: "donatio propter Nuptias"</note> are sometimes confused, though they differ in certain respects. The dower is established for the life of the wife. Upon the widow's death, the dower reverts to the husband's feudal heirs, but not the "gift on account of marriage." The dower rests on the same law of proof as the dowry itself. What is the difference between a dower and a wedding gift regarding a "silent pledge" <note>a legal lien or security</note>? Once a widow accepts the dower, the claim to the dowry expires. What is the annual pension in a dower? According to the notorious custom and observance of the Princes of Germany, the dower relates to the burdens of the fief itself, not just the personal burdens of the Vassal. Klock, *counsel 155.* The gift which nobles make to their wives in compensation for a dowry is called by various names. The French call it *doerum* or *doarium*, the Flemish *duariam*, those of the Dauphiné *supervitam*, the Savoyards and Neapolitans *dotarium*, the Canonists *dotalitium*, others *victilitium*, and the Germans **widow’s support** <note>original: "Leibzucht"</note>, **life-annuity** <note>original: "Leibgeding"</note>, or **life-estate** <note>original: "Leibgut"</note>, as if it were a profit that clings to the person and body and is extinguished with it. Others call it **widow’s-settlement** <note>original: "Wieddumb"</note>, because it is established for the widow and expires at her death, or **life-interest** <note>original: "Leibzins" or "Leibgüldten"</note> when it consists of yearly revenues. See Wehner’s *Supplement* under the word **Leibzucht**.

This term is discussed in the *Saxon Consultations, volume 2, part 1, question 12.* Regarding the dower or "Doarium," in German **widow’s support**, also **life-annuity**, and the **morning-gift** <note>original: "Morganatica"</note>. See Rittershusius and Michael Teuberus.

### 47. Life-hens. A yearly poultry tribute.

According to the custom of certain places, **women in childbed** <note>original: "Kindbetterinn"; women recovering from childbirth</note> are exempted from the **life-hen** tribute for that year. See above under the word **Bethe** <note>a type of tax or petitionary aid</note>.

### 48. Bodily feudal heirs. Feudal successors.

The term **bodily feudal heirs** <note>original: "Leibs lehenbare Erben"</note>, found in letters of investiture, is to be understood only as referring to males (even if the word **sons** was not added). Schneidewin, in *Summary of Feudal Law, part 6, member 2, on feudal succession without a will, number 15.*

Regarding Saxon Law, it is said that **fief-heirs** <note>original: "Lehen-Erben"</note> are understood only as **male bodily heirs** <note>original: "männlichen Leibs-Erben"</note>. It is presumed that both the person granting the fief and the one receiving it were looking more toward the right of male-lineage <term>agnatio: kinship traced through the father's side</term> and the succession of blood, rather than the literal dictionary definition of "heirs" <note>original: "heredibus"</note> or the general quality of inheritance usually gathered from that word. Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 3, number 3; see also Fichard, consultation 82, number 9, volume 2. And not only sons, but also grandsons are included. Molin, consultation 50.

The word **fief-heirs** <note>original: "Lehen-Erben"</note> implies that a fief of this kind exists by "pact and providence" <term>ex pacto & providentia: a fief created by a specific contract or arrangement rather than ancient custom</term>. For when these words—**to him and his fief-heirs**—are placed in the documents of investiture <note>the formal ceremony of granting a fief</note>, then the fief is not considered a simple hereditary one, but one acquired by contract and specific arrangement. Johann Köppen, book 1, decision 54, number 13. And even if it were not clear that the fief was acquired by contract, in cases of doubt it should be presumed as such, according to those cited by Octavius Cacheranus, consultation 12, number 11, and Schrader, *On Fiefs*, part 2, chapter 9, number 31. This is despite others concluding it should be treated as hereditary, such as Alciatus, response 160, number 9; Natta, consultation 501, number 20; and Cephalus, consultation 152, number 55, book 2.

Indeed, the first opinion is truer, as Schrader attests in the cited place, and it is more common according to Thomas de Marinis in *On Fiefs*, under the section on pacts and providence, number 24. This is also the view accepted in the Imperial Chamber <note>the supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, as reported by Joachim Mynsinger, century 4, observation 2, number 5, where he states it was so judged in his time.

## ADDITION.

Fiefs are thought to be established by "pact and providence" using the following formulas most common in Germany: **for himself and his male bodily fief-heirs**; likewise: **his rightful bodily fief-heirs**; or: **fief-heirs of the same rightful male-lineage, of the shield and helmet** <note>referring to noble status</note>; likewise: **only their male bodily fief-heirs, of the name, helmet, shield, and family, for himself and his heirs capable of holding a male-fief.** Zasius, *On Fiefs*, part 8, number 16; Wesenbeck, chapter 6, number 9; Schrader, part 2, chapter 3, number 27. Hartmann Pistor disagrees most broadly in question 3, book 2. Rosenthal seems to agree with him in chapter 2, question 45, number 3, though see the same author in chapter 2, question 78. They also want a fief to belong to this class if it is given to someone for himself and his male heirs, or legitimate heirs: **to him and his legitimately born male bodily heirs**; see those cited by Gothofredus Antonii, *Feudal Disputations* 1, thesis 8, letter K. The words **no male**

<column-break/>

**bodily heirs** <note>original: "keine mannliche Leibs-Erben"</note>, how they are to be understood. Klock, volume 1, consultation 7, number 477. The word **bodily heirs** <note>original: "Leibserben"</note> denotes **male heirs** <note>original: "Manns-Erben"</note> depending on the subject matter. Number 925, 926, and following. The word **fief-heirs** <note>original: "Lehens-Erben"</note> is regularly understood to mean males. Klock, volume 3, consultation 182, number 85, though depending on the subject matter, it can also mean females. The words **legitimate heirs** <note>original: "Eheliche Erben"</note> and **bodily heirs** differ. Words like **legitimate heirs of the male sex** are strictly understood to mean descendants. In a broad sense, they also pertain to heirs of the blood.

### 49. Body and Life Punishment. Corporal Punishment. <note>original: "Leib- und Lebensstraff. Pœna corporalis."</note>

If we take the word **body-punishment** <note>original: "Leibstraff"</note> generally, it includes both **punishment of the body and of life** <note>meaning both physical discipline and the death penalty</note>. However, if used specifically, it can be contrasted with **life-punishment** <note>capital punishment</note>. By similar logic, the term "coercion" taken broadly includes death; taken specifically, it is distinguished from the penalty of natural death. See Matthew Stephanus in the introduction to the *Criminal Constitutions*, number 13. This must be noted in statutes where words are to be interpreted strictly. Decius, in law 6, and Mr. Cothmann, *Academic Responses*, 1, number 206.

## ADDITION.

Under penalty of death, **by the highest free [punishment]** <note>original: "bey dem freyen höchsten"</note>, *Wehner’s Supplement*, page 27. Peter Friedrich Mindanus, in *On Process*, book 2, chapter 9, number 22, calls a penal action where bodily punishment is sought a **criminal complaint** <note>original: "peinliche Klag"</note>; where a fine is paid to the treasury, a **civil fine-complaint** <note>original: "bürgerliche Busſklag"</note>; and where a fine is applied to the injured party, a **civil damage-complaint** <note>original: "bürgerliche Schadensklag"</note>. The word **criminal/painful** <note>original: "peinlich"</note>, whenever used in the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* <note>the criminal code of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V</note>, refers to the coercion of the body according to the opinion of Mindanus. Yet it must often be counted among non-corporal punishments: for in unnamed punishments, it refers the judges back to common law. *Article 105: Of unknown criminal cases and punishments.* It is well known in that law that crimes are many times punished by monetary loss, where loss combined with infamy is contrasted with the bodily coercion mentioned previously. It may be permitted to appeal a fine, yet this does not apply if the fine was substituted in place of a capital punishment, as discussed extensively by Mr. Rebhan, *On Fines*, thesis 28.
In the *Laws of the Bavarians*, title 3, chapter 1, paragraph 21, the term **Lidolaip** is used for the day of death; **laib** means body, but what **Lido** might be is not clear, says Lindenbrog in the Glossary. Schottelius, **in the German Main Language, page 688.**

### 51. Performance, Notice of Performance, Entry. Debt-Hostage Contract <term>Obstagium: a legal arrangement where a debtor or their guarantors stayed at a specific inn at their own expense as a penalty until a debt was paid</term>.

A Debt-Hostage Contract is one by which guarantors, in the name of the principal debtor, in the event that payment is not made at the agreed and appointed time, bind themselves to the creditor. They agree that when requested by the creditor, his heirs, or another in his name, they will go to a public inn <note>original: "hospitium publicum"</note> named for the hostage-hosting. There, all and each of them, with as many servants and horses as are listed in the caution-bond, shall enter and not leave until the creditor is satisfied regarding the principal debt, the interest, and all damages and expenses. In common speech, this is called **Entry and Performance**, or **Notice of Performance** <note>original: "Eintritt und Leistung, oder Leistmanung"</note>. It was a kind of "quasi-capture," for the debtors presented themselves as if to a prison.

These Hostage-contracts were introduced for the eventuality that debtors, out of fear of this practice (which acted as a penalty added to the contract), would provide payment more quickly and conveniently. Being thus detained, they would think more diligently about ways to satisfy the debt and would more frequently seek out—and more easily find—relatives and others to pay for them or otherwise secure the creditor. This was done so that those detained might return to their former liberty, which they might not have bothered to do if they enjoyed full natural freedom. For it is well known that such debtors, who gladly take out loans, are often "sleepy" <note>sluggish or indifferent to their obligations</note> and seek only to delay from day to day, until they see that extreme remedies are applied to extreme diseases.

However, both the debtors and the guarantors were so burdened by these practices and exhausted by the heaviest expenses that they were frequently reduced to extreme poverty.

And it is established that many had to promise to present themselves at a certain place for "Performance," and to stay there and maintain public and customary company, eating twice a day at the market price, without bargaining, according to the custom and Law of Performance <note>original: "Leistungsrecht"</note>. This meant he should not bargain for a set price for his meals—or as they say, "take the penny's worth"—but must take the free meal with other guests and not leave nor be released until it was finished. He even had to replace horses or servants who

<column-break/>

departed from the "Performance" <note>the stay at the inn</note>, always sending other suitable ones to the Performance in place of those who had left, etc.

It is well known (as Lord Meibomius says in *Origins of the Mark, page 39*) that this custom was used in Saxony 300 years ago. This is clear from the letters of Baldwin of Wenden the Younger, where it is written: "For more abundant caution, the honorable men Borchard the Elder and Borchard the Younger, called 'of Bertensteve,' Henry and Ludolf (Knights), and George the Servant (Squire) <note>original: "Famulus (Edelknecht)"</note> of Wenden, have agreed with us. If our aforementioned sons and daughters, due to some intervening obstacle, do not resign or consent to the said property after being requested, then the said Knights and Squire together with us, and we with them, shall enter the City of Brunswick. We shall remain there and not exit without the permission of the buyer." These letters were given in the year 1318.

Because of the foul abuse of this practice, which Daniel Moller describes, these contracts were first eliminated from the Electorate of Saxony, and then from the entire Empire.

Brother Johannes Pauli, in the treatise *Jest and Earnest, title 'On Lovers,' chapter 161*, says: "Costly meals are called 'Hostage-meals' <note>original: "Gieselmahl"</note>. When someone performs at a city or at a nobleman’s house with a knightly stallion, they eat costly meals so that the great expenses will rise, causing them to be paid and settled all the more quickly. That is why one 'performs.' This law was devised and found, to the sorrow of the nobility, by Duke Berchtold of Zähringen, after the nobility killed and poisoned his two sons; they lie in a coffin in Solothurn, at St. Ursula, as Felix Hemmerlein writes of it."

This is a different kind of "Performance," where the creditor consumes the debtor's resources to bring him to payment all the sooner.

### ADDITION.

On whether and in what manner contracts in which a person binds himself to prison for a civil debt are to be considered valid or not, see *Mynsinger, observation 57; Gail, book 2, observation 45; and in 'On the Public Peace,' chapter 2; Moller, book 3, semester 30; Berlichius, conclusion 28.* These "Performances" and Hostage-contracts in debt matters—which are nothing other than mere gluttony and carousing <note>original: "meræ crapulæ und heluationes"</note>—were abolished in the Police Ordinance of 1577, title 17, under the rubric "On Usurious Contracts." This was done throughout the Holy Empire. See *Colerus on Executive Process, part 1, chapter 8; Berlichius, observation 28, number 106; Wesenbeck on Sureties, number 5; Köppen, decision 3; Zorer, part 1, question 10, number 702; Carpzov, Jurisprudence of the Consistory of Saxony, part 2, constitution 22, definition 30.* A monk can be given as a hostage, or placed in a Hostage-contract by his Abbot for the debt of the monastery. *Chapter 9, from the rescript on oaths.* However, this was also removed by the Imperial Constitution, by which hostage-contracts of this kind are prohibited. *Rittershufius in the Novels, pages 74 and 152.*

<page-num>652</page-num>
<header>Augmented Practical Treasury</header>

A **debt-hostage** <term>Obstagiatus: someone placed in a state of legal confinement due to debt</term> is someone who, at the warning of a legal party or a judge, has entered into a debt-hostage arrangement. *Martin Coler, Part 1, On Executive Process, chapter 6, number 57.* For the evacuation of the garrisons at Heilbronn and Frankenthal, hostages were given on the condition that as soon as it was established that these garrisons had been withdrawn from both sides, each of these hostages would be permitted to return to their own people without loss or harm. *March 4, 1652.*

The use of the **debt-hostage arrangement** <term>Obstagium</term> is not uncommon in Germany among the Nobility; it is commonly called **the performance** <note>original: "die Leistung"</note>. For if, in a civil case, the agreed pacts under the obligation of the debt-hostage arrangement are not kept, the debtors or their guarantors are **summoned to performance** <note>original: "werden in die Leistung gefordert"</note>. That is, they are warned by a letter from the creditor to present themselves according to the formula of the obligation at the agreed place and time, not to depart until the promises are fulfilled. From this, it is clear that these types of arrangements are a species of imprisonment. <term>See Law: "succurritur etiam," section "vinculis," with the following law, and law "nec non 28," section "item si quis" in the Digest: "On what grounds those of age..."</term> Legal doctors commonly conclude that these debt-hostages and obligations toward imprisonment are valid in civil cases, since it is a grave matter to break one’s word. <term>See Law: "de constituta pecunia" (On promised money) in the Digest.</term> However, these do not apply to a debtor surrendering their goods, because through a legitimate surrender of assets, one is freed from the debt-hostage obligation; for the surrender of assets frees a debtor from prison. <term>See Institutes, final section, "On actions"; and Law 15 in the Digest, "On the surrender of goods."</term> These types of debt-hostage arrangements are even tolerated by the Imperial Constitutions, as appears in the Political Ordinance of the year 1548, under the title "On usurious contracts," final section. However, because of abuse and public scandals, this was changed by the newest Imperial Law of the year 1577, under title 17, as witnessed by Gail, book 2, observation 45, after number 6. See especially here Lord Doctor Ludwig’s *Disputations on the Institutes, page 242*, at the end, and the citations there by Lord Carpzov, *Forensic Jurisprudence, part 2, constitution 22, definitions 11 and the last.* Coler, in *Executive Process, part 1, chapter 8, number 23*, testifies that debt-hostages first came from military practice; they were introduced primarily so that debtors, out of fear of them—as a kind of penalty added to the contract—would provide payment more quickly and conveniently. In the past, in Germany, this was also widely extended and practiced among the nobility for guarantees. The reason for the prohibition in the cited Recess of the year 1577 expressly adds: "because it has since been experienced many times..." To which can be added from Beust’s commentary on the law "admonendi," number 344, *On Oaths*, that debt-hostage arrangements degenerated into drunkenness and gluttony. As Hering says in *On Guarantees, chapter 17, number 75*: "Our Germans, once sent into the debt-hostage stay, lived like Antipodes, treating day as night." That is, as Tacitus writes in *Annals, book 16, chapter 18, number 1*: "they passed the day in sleep, and the night in duties and pleasures." Corthmann, in *Counsel 26, number 9*, notes that these arrangements were: 1. Ruinous to the state. 2. Scandalous. 3. Expensive and harmful to the guarantors. 4. Fatal and damaging to the principal debtors, whose "skin is in the game." 5.

<column-break/>

Wearisome and tedious for magistrates. 6. Burdensome for creditors. 7. Contrary to the art of the good and the equitable. 8. Finally, they were sad and mournful, since they bring the appearance of a prison. These points were extracted and repeated by Lord Johann Otto Tabor in his *1644 Disputation at Strasbourg regarding the Law of the Debt-Hostage* in the Provincial Constitution of Holstein, where he asserts they are still in use. They are also most elegantly explained and deduced by Lord Wesenbeck in *On Contributions, pages 156-158*. Add also Lord Doctor Ludwig in the *Notes on Wesenbeck*, under the title "On guarantees," number 5, where this agreement is held to be licit in certain parts of the Empire, such as among the nobility of Holstein. See the *Instrument of Peace between the Emperor and Sweden, article 8*, at the end. The form of the old debt-hostage contract is as follows:

> For greater security, we have appointed as legal guarantors four of our citizens from our Council, whom they shall then select and choose. Thus, if we do not pay them for the aforementioned improprieties named by them, they shall have full power and legal right to summon those four citizens of our Council, or a portion of them as is convenient for them, to perform. And whoever is thus summoned by them shall, upon his good faith, within the next eight days without any delay, enter into the performance at a public guesthouse here in Nuremberg, to which he is summoned. He shall perform according to the law and custom of guests, and shall not leave the performance until we have entirely and completely settled and paid the interest due, along with the honest and harmless damages, as if they had received them, without deceit. But if one or more of such citizens of our Council who were thus summoned to perform were not at home, or could not perform themselves, each may send a servant in his place to perform in the manner prescribed above. And to whichever citizen of our Council who would thus be summoned and perform, we also promise to release them graciously without any harm to them. 1548. Dieterich’s Submission.

The nobility in Holstein have adopted a similar "riding-in" <note>original: "Einreiten," the act of traveling to the place of confinement</note> among themselves. Thus, if a debtor does not keep up with payment at the *Umschlag* <note>A major annual financial settlement and fair</note>, which is held as a fair in the city of Kiel every year in the month of January, he must keep himself in the **pledge-stay** <note>original: "Inlager"</note> assigned to him in a certain house, as if in prison, until he satisfies his creditor. This ordinance still remains in effect in Holstein, and it was further confirmed by a general Imperial decree, both in the past peace negotiations of Münster and Osnabrück <term>Instrument of Peace between the Emperor and Sweden, article 8, section "on investigation," at the end</term>, and in the Imperial Recess at Regensburg that followed in 1654, in the section "consequently they establish the same." Concerning the abuse in performances, and how those who have been summoned to performance...

# 53. Clarification, Higher Clarification. First and second Refinement.

First and second refinements <note>Latin: "Leuterationes"</note>, commonly called **Clarification** <note>German: "Leuterung"</note> and **Higher Clarification** <note>German: "Oberleuterung"</note>, are usually ascribed to the remedies of Saxon Law. These are more like clearer deductions of a case—almost in the manner of a revision—than declarations of a sentence. Properly, they tend toward this: that whatever was written obscurely in the sentence may be declared and explained by further deduction, although sometimes by this method prior sentences are reformed by the same judge. See Wesenbec in the commentary on the Digest, title *On the matter judged*, number 10. However, Ernest Cothmann proves in his *Response* 39, number 473, that this happens in practice rather than by strict law. Daniel Moller agrees with him in *Saxon Constitutions*, constitution 19, verse 25, part 1. Indeed, in second clarifications (**Higher Clarification**), prior sentences can be reformed because in those cases there is a different judge, who rightly improves the sentence of the prior judge. Moller, in the place cited; Cothmann on the Code, title 19, book 1, number 31. But regarding Clarification and Higher Clarification, see by all means Pruckmann, *Counsel* 33, folio 1; and Cöppen, *Observations* 2, observation 103.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding Clarification, see Rudinger, Century 3, observation 47, throughout.

Clarification is not unlike an Appeal. See the Gloss in *Feudal Law*, article 30, at the beginning. It is called a common benefit, similar to an appeal, in the *Elector of Saxony’s Constitutions*, part 1, chapter 19, verse:

<column-break/>

which also, no less than appeals, should be common to both parties. Moller, *Four Semesters* 35, and *Commentary on the Saxon Constitution*, chapter 19. Rauchbar, question 1, number 12. In the courts of the Dukes of Saxony, where an Appeal is not permitted, Clarification succeeds in its place. Likewise, a Higher Clarification of a prior sentence takes place before the same judge (in which matter an appeal differs, as it does not take place before the same judge, unlike a revision or clarification). See Rittershusius in *The Novels*, page 653, number 5, and page 661, number 2, and the authors cited there. Clarification was introduced for this primary purpose: so that a sentence which is obscure or doubtful in some point may be declared, which is what the word itself implies. See the anonymous author in the consultation *On the Improvement of the Justice System*, paragraph "and even when the judgment." Wesenbec, *On the matter judged*, at the end. Thus, grievances caused by chance error, negligence, or even the lack of skill of the litigating parties or the judge—which otherwise could hardly be removed even with great effort through an appeal—may be repaired and revoked by this "short hand" and with little expense. Gilhausen in *The Tree of Judgment*, chapter 8, part 7. Rosbach in *Civil Process*, title 77, number 2. But the abuse of this matter is clear, because they use this benefit at least to delay the process, and under the pretext of clarification, they seek the annulment and reformation of the sentence, as Wesenbec testifies in the place cited. From this, a new process is instituted, the same as in an Appeal, and thus it is plainly stripped of the purpose for which it was introduced, a matter about which the aforementioned anonymous author complains at the end of that paragraph. Clarification is an extraordinary method of reforming an unjust sentence. See also Ummius in *On Process*, page 795; Pruckmann, *Counsel* 1, number 33.

# 54. People. Subjects, Men.

*Leudi*, *Leudes*, *Leodes*, **People** <note>German: "Leut"</note>, are called "men" <note>Latin: "homines"</note> everywhere among German and French historians; they are commonly called subjects. As in Gregory of Tours, book 9: in the pact between Childebert and Guntram, it was agreed that those *Leudes* (subjects) who provided an oath to Lord Guntram, etc. See Hotoman, *Feudal Lexicon*, under the word *Leodes*. Meitner *On Counts*, number 15; and Goldast, *Alemannic Matters*, volume 1, folio 216.

**With service-people, people** <note>original: "Mit Dienstleuten, Leuten"</note>; by these words are described both the other subjects as well as the fruits of Jurisdiction and Sovereignty, or forced labor and postal duties <note>Latin: "angariæ & parangariæ"</note>. These are undoubtedly counted among the regalian rights <note>rights belonging to the sovereign</note>. See the chapter *Which are regalia*, and Lord Goeddaeus in the *Valendar Case*, number 316. And although this word in our vernacular signifies any kind of service, and **service-people** are also those who, either by agreement or custom (even to those of lower status), are bound to service—as our bondservants and tenant farmers usually are—yet when it is joined with the phrase **Lordship and Court, High and Low** <note>original: "Herrschafft und Gericht, Hohe und Tieffe"</note>, it is part of the description of those rights which a certain territory possesses...

<summary>This page defines the military role of a Lieutenant and explores the specific Saxon legal remedy of 'Leuterung' (clarification), while also beginning an etymological and legal study of 'Leut' (subjects and bondservants).</summary>

...it is scarcely possible that it should not also be understood as referring to **forced labor and transport services** <note>Latin: *angariis & parangariis*</note>, or to **Jurisdictional Services**: owed not only for lower jurisdiction, but also for higher jurisdiction. According to Chapter 1, Rosenthal *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 70 and following.

### ADDITION.

The term **People** <note>German: *Leuten*</note> does not denote ordinary subjects, but either **bondservants** <note>German: *Leibeigene*</note> or **protected people** <note>German: *Vogtleut*</note>: *Acts of Lindau*, folio 930, near the middle. Limit this as stated there. The word **Vassalage** <note>German: *Mannschaft*</note> admits various meanings. *Acts of Lindau*, page 132, in the middle, and the following page at the end.

**Fief** <note>German: *Lehen*</note> is not derived from the word for "people" <note>German: *Leut*, or Latin *Leudis*</note>, as Cujas thinks in *On Fiefs*, book 1, at the beginning, followed by Borcholt in chapter 2, number 13, and Jacob Kleist in his *Prolegomena on Feudal Conclusions*, page 10; rather, it comes from the verb **to lend** <note>German: *Leyhen*</note>. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations* 1, thesis 2, letter a. **Question:** If a castle is granted with its appurtenances, are the people—the **Vassalage** <note>German: *die Mannschaft*</note>—included? And if credit is to be given to Baldus, *Consilia* 97, number 2, volume 3, they also follow as a consequence of the territory, to whose soil they are attached as possessors. See Br. on law 2 of the Code *On vacant goods*, book 10. Merckelbach in Klock, *Consilia* 54, number 7, volume 1, treats them no differently than **serfs tied to the land** <note>Latin: *servi adscriptitii*, literally "enrolled slaves"</note> who follow the estate, according to law 7 of the Code *On fields and census*, book 11; although Surdus in *Consilia* 323, number 35, and others cited by him, seem to think otherwise. Hence it is that in the **Common Tongue** <note>Latin: *Lingua Vernacula*, here referring to German</note> we say that a Duchy or Marquisate is nothing other than the people and the estates: **Land and People** <note>German: *Land und Leut*</note>. Tuschus, letter R, conclusion 87, number 7. Regarding serfs tied to the land, it is otherwise doubted whether they are properly "slaves." This is asserted by the late Master Cobius on the Institutes, *On the law of persons*, question 5.

To this belongs the **People’s Court** <note>German: *Leutgericht*</note> in Franconia. See Matthias Stephani, book 1, *On the office of a Judge*, chapter 5; and Master Felwinger in *The Judge*, page 410.

### 55. The Law "If anyone slanders" (Lex Diffamari).

On the law **If anyone slanders** <note>Latin: *Lex Diffamari*; a Roman law principle used when someone publicly claims to have a legal right against you but refuses to sue. This law allows the target to force the slanderer to "put up or shut up" by bringing the case to court within a set time.</note> see the specific treatises by Blarer and Mundius. Add also Gail, book 1, observation 9; Ruland on the *Ferrar Process*; Montanus, folio 182; and Rosacorb, *Forensic Practice*, chapter 24; Meichsner, volume 1, decision 5; Joseph Sesse, decision 115, regarding the process and practice of that Law. In the law *If anyone slanders*, an out-of-court boast and a single final summons are sufficient, as taught by Joseph Ludovicus, *Lucca Decisions*, 32. Whether a pending lawsuit is established by this, see Zanger, *On Exceptions*, part 2, chapter 13.

In this Law, for its constitution to take place, practitioners require a **malicious defamation**. The summons in it must also be made with the insertion of a threat of **perpetual silence** <note>meaning if they do not sue now, they can never sue on this matter again</note>. It can also be joined with an action for injuries <note>slander/libel</note>.

In a criminal case arising from the law *If anyone slanders*: See the *Strasbourg Consilia*, volume 2, consilium 59, where it is asked who is the competent judge, and how the summons against the defamer should be made? And whether a single summons is sufficient.

<column-break/>

Since the following Legal Response contains several elegant questions regarding the matter of the law *If anyone slanders*, it was decided to append it here.

Noble, Valiant, and especially highly favored Sir, offering my always ready service: I must first apologize that the requested legal opinion regarding your **Feudal Castle and village of M.** has been delayed. This happened partly due to illness, partly due to other business which I could neither set aside nor postpone, and partly because the matter is very extensive and important.

Otherwise, however, I have since then not only read through the documents sent to me—which I am still holding until you request them back—with all diligence, but have also found that since you do not currently seek a final verdict on the main issue, but only require my humble opinion on how this matter might proceed without delay to a lawful, impartial trial, the following questions might perhaps be briefly discussed.

Namely and first: whether you could sue the people of M. under the law **If anyone slanders** <note>Latin: *ex L. diffamari*</note>, and specifically in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>Latin: *Camera Imperialis*; the highest court in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, and by means of such a remedy force them to bring their alleged claim against you before a **competent judge** <note>Latin: *coram Judice competente*</note> within a certain time?

Secondly: if such a summons based on the law *If anyone slanders* is obtained from the highly praised Imperial Chamber Court against those from M. upon your humble request, whether they would then be obliged to sue you before the said Imperial Chamber Court, or whether it remains free and open to the people of M. to seek you out before the **Imperial Aulic Council** <note>German: *Reichs-Hof-Rath*; the Emperor's personal court</note> or elsewhere regarding this matter?

Thirdly: if you either would not or could not sue the aforementioned people of M. in Speyer <note>the seat of the Chamber Court</note> under the law *If anyone slanders*, or if it were otherwise problematic to do so: whether one could not conveniently initiate this same process before the **Feudal Judge** <note>German: *Lehensrichter*</note> (considering this whole matter consists of a **feudal controversy** <note>Latin: *controversia feudali*</note>)? And whether this must happen before His Princely Grace as **Feudal Lord**, or before the **Peers of the Court** <note>Latin: *Paribus Curiae*; a jury of one's social equals in a feudal court</note>?

Fourthly: whether this matter can, by any means <note>Latin: *ullâ ratione*</note>, be brought immediately by the people of M. to the **Imperial Court** <note>Latin: *Aula Caesarea*</note>, or whether an appeal may be made there from a judgment issued in the Feudal Court, bypassing the Imperial Chamber Court?

# The First Question.

As to what concerns the first question, it seems to some extent doubtful. For although otherwise under common law <note>Latin: *de jure communi*</note> it is held that the **Law regarding Defamation** <note>Latin: *L. Diffamari*; a Roman law principle allowing a person to force someone "boasting" of a legal claim against them to either sue immediately or remain silent forever</note> has a place in every kind of case, civil and criminal (Gail, book 1, observation 9, number 2). And not only in personal actions, but also in real actions, likewise in matters of ownership <note>Latin: *petitorio*</note> and possession <note>Latin: *possefforio*</note>, and also in crimes (Magenhorst in *Commentary on the Ordinances of the Chamber*, part 2, title 25). And thus, it applies generally against all defamation, according to the common, received, and approved tradition of the Doctors of Law <note>Latin: *Dd.*</note> (Blarer on the *Law regarding Defamation*... number 1; Cesare Contardi... chapter 3, number 24 and following; Otto Melander, part 2, on the *Constitution regarding the Law of Defamation*, on the words "in all civil matters," folio 369). Many more are cited by Graeve, book 1, conclusion 9.

However, it might be held that **Your Lordship** <note>German: *E. Str.*, an abbreviation for *Euer Strenge*, a formal title for a person of legal or noble standing</note> could not draw a process from the **Law regarding Defamation** in the Imperial Chamber <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> in the present matter: seeing as you have been defamed and accused by those of M. in such a way that Your Lordship holds their **Ancestral Fief** <note>German: *Altväterlich Lehen*</note> against the law. Whereas, to establish a process based on the *Law regarding Defamation* in the Imperial Chamber, according to the Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance (part 2, title 23), it is necessary—and the aforementioned law may not be understood or used there otherwise—that it be in matters of **Breach of the Peace** <note>German: *Friedbrüchigen*; a violation of the Public Peace or *Landfrieden*</note>, **Insult** <note>German: *Schmach*</note>, and other similar things, in which such defamation occurred in a dangerous, fraudulent way, or in some other way to the disadvantage and grievance of the other party.

Hence, it is also usually required here that the defamation be "grave" (Graeve, book 1, conclusion 10, consideration 1, number 1). And such that it could disturb the public peace and cause a scandal. From this, they very commonly say that this Constitution of the Chamber establishes jurisdiction not in just any defamation, but only in more **atrocious injuries** which are done craftily, with malicious intent, or in another way to the prejudice and grievance of another, and tend toward that end; as Graeve also warns (conclusion 9, number 9), and Schwanmann notes (observation 161, number 2) that there is no small difference between **Civil Law** and **Chamber Law** <note>Latin: *Jus Civile & Camerale*</note>.

Nevertheless, regardless of all this, I for my part incline more toward the view that Your Lordship can extract a process against those of M. in the Imperial Chamber: especially because the most important requirement is met, namely—in my certain opinion—that both Your Lordship and the disputed property are **immediately subject** <note>Latin: *sine Mittel*; "without middleman," meaning they answer directly to the Emperor rather than a local prince</note> to the Imperial Majesty and the Roman Empire. In that case, notwithstanding any local arbitration rights <note>Latin: *Austregis*; special courts for disputes between estates of the Empire</note>, the Chamber is the competent judge regarding the judgment of defamation, after...

<column-break/>

<margin>162, number 4.</margin>
...So too is the other requirement regarding the **quality of the defamation itself** to be considered; although the Ordinance expresses only two causes in which it may apply, it nevertheless admits other similar ones with the words: "In **breach of the peace**, **insult**, and other such things, in which such defamation occurred in a dangerous, fraudulent way, or in another way to the disadvantage and grievance of the other party" (*Ordinances of the Chamber*, book 2, title 1). Here, although some understand "similar causes" to mean only those from which public scandal may arise and the tranquility of the Empire may be disturbed by the public slander, it is more correct to say that those causes are implied which offend the **reputation and standing** <note>Latin: *famam & existimationem*</note> of a person in any way, as Magenhorst reports (at title 25... part 2). There he adds that this requirement is not to be disputed so anxiously, since the defamed person can sue under the *Law regarding Defamation* in almost every kind of case according to the discussions of Common Law. So much so that even one who is disturbed in his possession by defamation can sue from this law (Wesenbeck, *Legal Opinions* 96, number 7; Magenhorst, in the cited place, who refers to a summons decreed from this in the Chamber in the case of **Mainz against Saxony**).

If one also looks through the complaints and petitions made by those of M. against Your Lordship before various **Electors** <note>The high-ranking princes who elected the Emperor</note>, one will find therein very harsh, provocative, and quite shameful words; moreover, a **public scandal** is also involved here, seeing as this matter has resounded very widely, has already been brought before many potentates, and the Duke of E., as the **Feudal Lord** <note>German: *Lehenherr*</note> who also invested Your Lordship and refused the disputed fief to the opponents, is accused of a notable impropriety.

As in a letter to the Duke of H., dated October 5, 15--, Your Lordship is accused of acting with a **"bad conscience"** in declaring that you would cling to your (unlawful) possession until you are removed from it by the ordinary courts. With this added: that Your Lordship undoubtedly believes yourself well-secured by the current state of **endless legal delays** and the ways of the world. And in that same place, it is requested that His Princely Grace should not allow Your Lordship to "jump around" those of M. so intentionally and wantonly, and to de facto withhold this M. **ancestral family fief** from them any longer against obvious and tangible equity—likewise "making water run against the stream"—and that such a thing would otherwise, in truth, look strange to the honorable **Knighthood in Alsace**, to whom the basis of the matter is known. Item, that Your Lordship should not rightly desire "to warm yourself further at another's property."

Almost identical defamatory and far-reaching words were presented by those of M. to the **Elector of Mainz**...
