...brought forward, both of which result in no small disgrace to the Princely Grace <note>The Feudal Lord</note> and also to Your Lordship <note>German: *E. Str.*, for *Euer Strenge*, a formal address for a person of legal or noble standing</note>. This is clearly seen in His Electoral Grace’s letter of intercession to the Landgrave in Hesse. These and more highly provocative words, which are to be gathered from various parts of the letters, should also be included with some elaboration in the **Petition for Citation** under the **Law regarding Defamation** <note>Latin: *L. Diffamari*; a legal tool to stop someone from publicly claiming rights over your property without actually filing a lawsuit</note>. In every way, these words are injurious and scandalous, and are to be tolerated neither by His Princely Grace nor Your Lordship. For to withhold someone's property *de facto* against manifest law, with a **bad conscience** <note>Latin: *malâ conscientiâ*</note>, to attempt something, to enrich oneself with another's goods, and the like—especially when a highly distinguished Prince, surrounded by so many counselors, ignores it and supports such an **unjust alleged detainer** <note>Latin: *iniquum assertum detentatorem*</note>—this has a very broad significance and is an intolerable accusation.

Thus, the **third requirement** is also met, namely the proof of defamation in this place, specifically the **defamatory letters** <note>Latin: *litteræ diffamantis*</note> and other documents to demonstrate the defamation, which must be presented together with the petition in the Senate of the Chamber. (Chamber Ordinance, title 25; Mynsinger, century 5, observation 81, number 4; Gail, observation 10, number 7).

This is because the copies of the opposing party's letters, which I find among the records, could undoubtedly be supported by the originals immediately.

## The Second Question.

Regarding the second question, it might not seem implausible to say that even if a Citation under the **Law regarding Defamation** is recognized against those of M., the case might not necessarily be heard in the Chamber Court, but Your Lordship might be ordered to bring the complaint **before any competent judge** <note>Latin: *coram quocunque Judice competenti*</note>. Indeed, this is sanctioned in the previously cited Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, title 25, with these words: "But where the defamed person is not immediately subject to the Empire, or is not subject to the Chamber Court in the first instance, then a specific time shall be set for him to bring his complaint before the judge to whom the matter properly belongs." With the addition that if he did not do so, eternal silence should be imposed upon him, and otherwise, the matter should be handled and proceeded with according to the common laws and ordinances of the Imperial Majesty and the Empire. (Gail, book 1, observation 11).

Now, it could be said with good reason that the present matter, in the **first instance** <note>Latin: *quoad primam Instantiam*</note>, could have a different judge, **both by its own nature and by reason of the persons litigating** <note>Latin: *tam ex sui natura, quam ex personarum litigantium ratione*</note>.

For firstly, it has now come to the point that His Imperial Majesty’s **Aulic Council** <note>The *Reichshofrath*, a competing high court to the Imperial Chamber</note> exercises **concurrent jurisdiction** with the Chamber in all cases, and even those with immediate status, regardless of arbitration rights <note>The *Austräg*; a system of noble arbitration</note>, are accustomed to being sued there. Therefore, it appears as though Your Lordship, even after obtaining a

<column-break/>

**Citation** under the **Law regarding Defamation**, might be sued by those of M. before His Imperial Majesty.

Secondly, those of M., by virtue of the Chamber Court Ordinance (part 2, title 5), could avail themselves of the **Arbitration process** <note>German: *Austräg*; a privileged legal procedure for high-ranking members of the Empire to settle disputes through noble peers rather than standard courts</note> and compel Your Lordship to name three Electors, Princes, or persons of princely rank who are impartial, from whom they would choose one as judge. They of M. might also most humbly request an impartial **Commissioner** from His Imperial Majesty: or otherwise use the arbitration process against the Princely Grace of the Feudal Lord, according to the contents of the Chamber Ordinance (part 2, title 4).

Or thirdly, because this is a **Feudal Case** <note>Latin: *Causa feudalis*</note>, they could complain against Your Lordship before the Feudal Judge. In which case, because the matter touches His Princely Grace himself as the Feudal Lord, that same law must be claimed for Your Lordship in this place, and an impartial **Feudal Court** must be arranged by His Princely Grace.

**For if a controversy arises between a Lord and a Vassal concerning Investiture, the loss of a fief, its recovery, or a similar cause, then the Peers of the Court judge** <note>Latin: *Quippe si controversia agitur inter Dominum & Vassallum... tunc Pares Curiæ judicant*. This refers to the principle that a vassal should be judged by his equals—other vassals of the same lord</note>. (Chapter 3, de prohib. feud. alien. by Frederick; Nicolaus Mozz, title on the nature of fiefs, number 13, folio 241; Rutger Ruland on Commissioners, part 4, book 8, chapter 1, number 2, folio 484; Rosenthal, part 2, chapter 12, conclusion 3, number 1 and following. And also where the Lord has invested one with a fief which another says belongs to him: Georg Everhard, volume 1, counsel 28; Keus, counsel 25, volume 1; Schwanmann, observation 11).

But notwithstanding this, in my humble opinion, the present matter could perhaps be kept in the Chamber Court even **regarding the main business** <note>Latin: *quoad principale negotium*</note>. Primarily if Your Lordship requests this in the petition, and if His Princely Grace, as the Feudal Lord (who is otherwise the judge between vassals), would remit this matter to the Chamber through a special letter and indicate that His Princely Grace, being an interested party himself, cannot well take on this judicial office. This is especially true since the **Peers of the Court** <note>Latin: *Pares Curiæ*</note>—namely other vassals dependent on the County of F.—could not well be tolerated as judges by His Princely Grace. Considering that in the present case, this question must be principally disputed: whether the F. fiefs generally have the nature of **Simultaneous Investiture** <note>Latin: *Simultaneæ Investituræ*; a legal arrangement where several people are invested with the same fief at the same time, giving them collective rights</note>, with which the aforementioned F. vassals would be indiscriminately interested.

If this were to happen, and His Princely Grace could be persuaded to make such an application, I would be of the opinion, for what it's worth, that this matter should be kept in the Chamber.

**For although if the defamed person is immediately subject to the Empire, but cannot be drawn to the Chamber in the first instance, either because of arbitration rights or for another reason, then the Imperial Chamber remains the judge regarding the setting of the deadline and the imposition of silence, but refers the main case to...** <note>Latin: *Quamvis enim si diffamatus quidem Imperio immediatè subsit...*</note>

<margin>Gail, Book 1, Observation 12, numbers 1 and 3.</margin> He may refer the case to the ordinary judge, <note>Latin: *Gail. lib. 1. obs. 12. n. 1. & 3.* refers to Andreas Gail, a prominent jurist of the 16th century</note>. There is, however, a limitation: if the ordinary judge is suspected of bias, or if he himself refers the case, or is unwilling or unable to administer justice, as noted by the Assessor of the Chamber in the *Prejudices* under the heading *Law regarding Defamation, folio 1* <note>Latin: *præjudiciis verb. L. Diffamari. f. 1.*</note>. In such instances, the principal cause is retained within the Chamber Court. Schwanmann <note>Another legal authority</note> notes (after citing others) that if a case is referred from the ordinary judge to the Chamber, then the **Citation** under the **Law regarding Defamation** <note>Latin: *L. Diffamari*</note> is not decreed based on specific requirements or the benefits of the Chamber’s Ordinance, but proceeds according to **Common Law** <note>Latin: *Jure Communi*</note>. In Observation 15, he also teaches that the jurisdiction of the Chamber regarding the first instance can be extended either tacitly or expressly.

### Third Question.

Regarding this question, we must repeat what has already been suggested above: that His Princely Grace, as the **Feudal Lord** <note>German: *Lehenherr*</note>, who would otherwise have the right to pass judgment between **Vassals** <note>Latin: *inter Vasallos*</note>, cannot be the judge in this matter. This is because the M. family (as they themselves mention in their petition) have nothing to do with Your Lordship, nor were they in any way dispossessed by Your Lordship; rather, they complain solely because His Princely Grace took the disputed fief from them and granted it to another. From this it follows that the dispute is between the M. family as plaintiffs and His Princely Grace as the defendant. To speak plainly, even though His Princely Grace did not initiate this matter himself but maintains that Your Lordship was granted this fief **at the risk of litigation** <note>Latin: *cum periculo litis*</note>, the **nature of the case itself** <note>Latin: *ipsa natura causæ*</note> is not changed. Nevertheless, Your Lordship must urge the **Right** <note>Latin: *Jus*</note> of His Princely Grace and make use of it in the **course of the case** <note>Latin: *processu causæ*</note>. Therefore, it remains necessary that an impartial **Feudal Court** <note>German: *Lehengericht*</note>, composed of the vassals who depend on the County of F., be established by His Princely Grace. One might then (as already suggested) consider them biased **on account of common prejudice** <note>Latin: *propter commune præjudicium*</note>. However, it rests upon the discretion of His Princely Grace and Your Lordship whether you wish to litigate **before such a suspected judge** <note>Latin: *coram tali Judice suspecto*</note>. For the **rejection of a judge is introduced for the benefit of the party** <note>Latin: *Recusatio enim Judicis in favorem partis est introducta*</note>, and he who could raise such an exception is not prohibited from renouncing it.

If His Princely Grace or Your Lordship should wish to resolve this matter before these **Peers of the Court** <note>Latin: *Parib. Curiæ*</note>, one could also sue there under the **Law regarding Defamation** <note>Latin: *L. Diffamari*</note> and compel the opposing party **to act** <note>Latin: *ad agendum*, meaning to file their lawsuit or be silent</note>. In this way, this matter would likewise reach the **Ordinary Process**.

<meta>signature: Besoldi Tom. L</meta>

<column-break/>

For, as has already been said above, according to the Law and the common tradition of legal interpreters, that **Remedy** <note>The *L. Diffamari*</note> has a place in all cases indifferently, and thus also in feudal matters.

### Fourth Question.

Although it has already been noted above that all complaints against **immediate subjects**—whether they be Nobles or Estates—take place before His Imperial Majesty's **Imperial Aulic Council** <note>German: *Reichs-Hofrath*; the Emperor's personal court</note>, I, for my part, cannot see how the present matter could be accepted there to the **prejudice** of the feudal judge, or against his will (especially if one or the other party objects). Even if Your Lordship or His Princely Grace, the Feudal Lord, were sued regarding this matter in the **Imperial Court** <note>Latin: *aula Cæsarea*</note>, I am of the opinion that His Princely Grace should properly object and submit to the **Judgment of the Peers of the Court** <note>Latin: *Judicio Parium Curiæ*</note>, yet **saving the right of appeal** <note>Latin: *salvo Jure appellandi*</note>.

For it is undoubtedly the law **that controversies concerning mediate fiefs** <note>Fiefs held through an intermediary lord rather than directly from the Emperor</note>, **and where no Imperial Fief is being disputed, cannot be dragged before the Emperor or another Ordinary Judge against the will of the parties—and especially if the Lord of the fief dissents—but must be aired before the judge competent by reason of the fief.**

And what is now indicated does not run contrary to what was argued above in the **Second Question**. For although it was mentioned there that this matter could be withdrawn from the feudal judgment and brought to the Chamber in the **first instance** <note>Latin: *primâ instantiâ*</note>, and even the Peers themselves could be rejected as suspected: this would only take place if His Princely Grace or Your Lordship voluntarily submitted to the Chamber's judgment and wished to set aside the available exceptions regarding the feudal judgment. But if one party should implore the **Imperial Aulic Judgment** <note>Latin: *Judicium Aulico-Cæsareum*</note> and Your Lordship wished to decline it, one must not only remain silent regarding all exceptions against the feudal judgment, but rather provoke that judgment and appeal to it.

Regarding the **Second Instance** <note>The appeal</note>, I harbor the concern that if this matter reaches the **Peers of the Court**, an appeal could be made from them either to the Chamber or to the Imperial Aulic Judgment, especially given the conditions of these times.

**For it is not a matter of doubt that one can appeal from the Peers to the Chamber, provided that no higher Lord of the fief exists, as Rosenthal teaches most fully (final chapter, final conclusion) and as I also taught in the treatise on appeals (chapter 4, number 16).**

But the **Common Practice** <note>Latin: *Praxis Communis*</note> now suggests that an appeal could also be made to the Imperial Court.

However, if the present matter should reach the Feudal Court and Your Lordship should lose, you could then [appeal] to the Imperial...

### ADDITION.

Who is the plaintiff and who is the defendant in a trial for defamation? Also concerning the penalty for defamation. Zahn treats this at length in *On Lies, book 2, chapter 28, throughout.* <note>Reference to Balthasar Zahn, a legal scholar</note>

The law regarding defamation <note>Latin: *L. diffamari*, a specific Roman law from the Code of Justinian</note> under the title "concerning the manumission of the free-born" <note>Latin: *de ingen. manumiss.*</note> was truly used only in **cases of legal status**, as indicated not only by the text of the law itself but also by the reasoning for the decision. This reasoning is specialized, stemming from the greatest favor shown to the very grave issue of one’s status—which can easily be harmed by the words of men <note>Latin: *arg. l. 9. C. de Nupt. l. 29. ff. de manum. test.*</note>—so that one might even voluntarily bring forward proof of one's own status. Giphanius <note>Hubert Giphanius (1534–1604), a legal scholar</note> notes this on the aforementioned law. The use of this law today, even though slavery has been abolished, can be great in cases of a **nobleman**, a **serf**, a **tenant farmer**, a **taxpayer**, a **vassal**, and so on, when it is publicly rumored that someone is or is not of such a status. 

However, they clearly abuse this practice, wanting it to have a place not only in status cases but also in every other case, whether civil or criminal, and in actions against property as well as against persons. Gail <note>Andreas Gail (1526–1587), an influential judge of the Imperial Chamber Court</note> and others testify to this, as does Giphanius, who notes that this abuse even began to be somewhat restricted in the Imperial Diets of 1530, 1532, and 1548. That unnecessary extension often clashes with the principles of law, as Giphanius proves. Antonius Faber <note>Antoine Favre (1557–1624), a famous Savoyard jurist</note> and Sarmiento also argue that by setting aside legitimate actions and making trouble for good people—harassing them daily with lawsuits and their expenses—it nurtures litigation and breeds great confusion in the State. Therefore, the aforementioned expansion is rightly rejected by Antonius Faber and Giphanius, who praises Sarmiento. In a trial for defamation, the defamed party brings the charge before his own judge, not before the judge of the slanderer. The late Doctor Biccius <note>Gregor Bickers</note> notes this in his *Golden Theses*. Regarding the condition under the Law of Defamation, see the *Observations of the Chamber Court* and various legal collections by Gail and Marquard Freher. Freher, following the example of Cicero—who called the action for fraud a "dragnet" <note>Latin: *everriculum*, literally a fishing net that sweeps the bottom</note> for all malice—and Tertullian—who called the Julian Law the "ax" for all lusts—does not hesitate to call the action from the Law of Defamation a **dragnet for all lies and injuries**.

<column-break/>

But Antonius Faber denies this in his *Pragmatic Errors*, showing that nothing is more unfair than forcing a person to immediately go to trial—perhaps unprepared with evidence and resources—just because they hastily or foolishly threatened someone with a lawsuit. He argues that if this way of acting is permitted, lawsuits are not decreased but provoked and multiplied. Francisco Sarmiento wants the same, warning that under the shield of this law, paths are provided not so much for justice as for **false accusations** <note>Latin: *calumniandi*</note> and infinite lawsuits are stirred up. For this reason, he says it should be exploded <note>i.e., rejected or driven out</note> from the State; he even asked a certain Cardinal who was Prefect of the Signature in the Roman Rota <note>The highest appellate tribunal of the Catholic Church</note> not to sign commissions for defamation cases, so as to completely remove the abuse of this law. Salicedus, Conradus, Cagnolus, Doctor Dinner, and others have written on this law. See also Antonius Oliban. We hate false accusations <note>Latin: *Calumniam odimus*</note> and we turn away from all evasion. A false accuser sins more seriously than a murderer, a thief, or a blasphemer, according to Menochius. One is said to commit a false accusation who objects or acts against his own legal documents, as noted by Klock.

### § 6. Libertines.

The heresy of these people is very ancient and was well enough known in the times of Ruusbroec <note>Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381), a Flemish mystic</note>. I also made mention of them in my *Introduction to Politics*. 

The **Anabaptists** renewed that heresy in the Netherlands, as reported by Miræus in the *Annals of Belgium* for the year 1525, where he writes: Quintin the Tailor of Picardy, with his companion Coppin, spreads the dogma of the **Libertines**, for which crime (and others) he was executed at Tournai, though he first abjured the heresy. 

Likewise, David George <note>David Joris (c. 1501–1556), a major Anabaptist leader</note> scattered his heresies through Frisia and Holland. This false **Liberty** is the foundation of heresies and atheism. Similar to these Libertines are the **Autonomists** or **the Free-staters** <note>German: *die Freysteller*</note>; see the treatise by Faber on religion and the *German Theology* <note>Latin: *Theologia Germanica*, a mystical text from the 14th century</note>, which frequently attacks these spirits. 

And in effect, all **heretics** are **Libertines**, because they do not believe the Church, but themselves. 

Those ancient ones called themselves "Free Spirits" <note>German: *freye Geister*</note>; they were also called **Lollards** <note>Latin: *Nolhardi*</note> and **Beguines**; see above under the word *Beguines*. Their followers today are mostly the Menists, the Stifelians, etc., and in Spain the **Alumbrados** <note>A mystical sect in 16th-century Spain, often translated as "The Illuminated"</note>, mentioned in the *French Mercury* for the year 1623. Regarding them, see Suso, Ruusbroec, and Tauler in the Index, and Nider in *The Book of the Ants*, where he writes the following about a person of this sort, or a heretical priest: I once knew a wealthy virgin of no small status...

...by the judgment of all her neighbors and my own, she was very devoted and chaste. She had a certain religious Confessor who possessed great prudence and integrity, whom she obeyed for a long time. Finally, she was called to the small house of certain women who were "devout" in name, where a secular priest—who seemed very honorable but was actually corrupt in matters of the true faith—used to visit. Then he began to take some of them aside and deliver special teachings on patience, obedience, and the most difficult arts of contemplation. 

The wretched man feigned that he saw them as more disposed toward the Divine, and in this way he further deceived that sex, which is most desirous of empty glory <note>A common medieval and early modern trope regarding the supposed vanity of women</note>; the aforementioned Virgin was the primary among them. Finally, the priest began to soothe them—or rather, to act maliciously—until he persuaded them that women must renounce all modesty, just as Christ did, he claimed, by hanging naked on the cross for us. He asserted that unless this was done, no one could reach the peak of perfection. 

From then on, some of that fragile sex fell into such folly that they would strip themselves naked in various places before the clergy who were their accomplices, though without carnal intercourse. Finally, he persuaded them that the most divine Sacrament of the Eucharist—which a priest is barely worthy to receive once a day, just as Christ offered Himself once to the Father on the altar of the Cross—should be taken by the women many times a day. He claimed that sacramental grace was increased by every communion (as he said), not noticing that this was against the general custom of the entire Church. 

Thus it happened that sometimes in a secret place, three women, totally naked, kneeling before the aforementioned traitor, would receive the Sacrament of the Eucharist more than fifty times in the same hour and day. Meanwhile, men who were accomplices—namely secular clergy—lay with the women, and sometimes many lay with many in one bed. They did not proceed to "carnal fall" <note>Sexual intercourse</note>, as they confessed, but rather they restrained themselves from each other to utterly renounce the passions of Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, here representing sexual desire</note>—though in truth they infected themselves even more. 

Among them, this "continent" priest was said to be of the highest perfection. Other famous and good women were also brought secretly from distant religious houses to this filthy and piggish workshop; they acquired "indulgences of demons" just like the household members. For the principal actors of this wickedness, by God's arrangement, were finally captured and forced to publicly revoke their heresy. And so this nest was dispersed in one place—I know not if in others—with extreme confusion. Thus far **Nider** <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438), a German Dominican theologian famous for his work on witchcraft and heresy, *Formicarius*</note>, who has other similar accounts throughout the cited location.

### 17. The Licentiate. <term>Licentiatus</term>

According to the custom of certain Academies (for example, *Perugia*, *Benius on the Privileges of Jurists*, in the *prologue to part 3, number 14*), those are called **Licentiates** <note>A "Licentiate" is an academic degree between a Bachelor's and a Doctorate, granting the "license" to teach or practice</note> who, having undergone a test of their abilities before certain individuals, are judged fit to commit themselves to a public

<margin>Besoldus, Volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

examination before the College and the Bishop. These cannot be said to have earned the Degree or the dignity of the Doctorate, since they can still be rejected in the public Examination. (*Abbot on the chapter 'cum secundum', number 14, concerning prebends*; see also *Gratius, counsel 116, book 2*; see *Master Friedrich Mockel, dissertation on rewards, thesis 84, page 45*, which is included among the Tübingen disputations.)

**Licentiates** are also those who, after their learning has been privately approved by the judgment of the College, are commended as worthy of the laurel, and having received permission from a superior to proceed to the doctorate, merely omit or defer the insignia <note>The formal robes, ring, and hat of a Doctor</note> for some reason. Since they have earned the right to be made Doctors, even though the insignia (which represent an external quality rather than the essence of the status) have not been conferred, they nevertheless enjoy the immunities and privileges of Doctors. This is taught by *Angelus in section 'quædam', number 19, Institutes on actions; Bolognetus in the law 'cum quid', number 31; Benius in the cited place; based on the law 'penult' on military wills; and the law 'qui pœnæ' 7, section 'Divus', on manumission.* Add also *Gabriel in common conclusions, title on seniority and obedience, single conclusion.*

Finally, **Licensure**, as a peculiar degree next to the Doctorate, is conferred separately by a certain public act, in which all those solemnities used in the promotion of a Doctor are employed, except for the Doctoral insignia. It is very well known from general custom that one honored with this degree is considered a Doctor in all favorable matters and is included under that name. (*Mattheus Stephanus on jurisdiction, book 3, part 2, chapter 14, number 98; Guido Papa, decision 390; Ruland on commissioners, book 1, chapter 14, final number.*)

And it follows that, according to the public law of the Empire, the non-noble Assessors in the Imperial Chamber <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> must be jurists adorned with a title; it is held that not only Doctors, but also Licentiates who have been publicly inaugurated in a University with the customary ceremonies and rites, as stated, are considered fit.

Whether a **Licentiate** is considered a Doctor is also discussed in the *Ecclesiastical Practices of Marcus Antonius Genuensis, question 611*. See what I have written *on the title of Doctor and Christian, volume 1, decision 104 and following, and decision 212.*

Those who have not yet received the insignia, but have been elected and authorized, are considered Doctors in favorable matters. (*Alciatus on law 57, on the meaning of words.*)

A **Licentiate** is not admitted where the quality of the Doctorate is specifically required (*Riccius in his practice of various resolutions, 467*). But he says there that **Licentiates** are those who are examined only once, and are explored by means of a preliminary examination to see if they are worthy; therefore, they acquire there not a dignity, but a presumption of ability. Otherwise, it is established that one who has been rigorously examined is considered a Doctor (see *Faber on alimony, page 76*). And on the question of whether one who has been rigorously examined *can pass* <note>original: *ju passiren?*, likely a typo for the German *zu passiren*, meaning 'to pass' or 'be accepted'</note> as a Doctor, I think a distinction must be made: either the solemnity is required and is a matter of formality—in which case the formal conferral of the title must be present...

# Treasuries of Practical Knowledge, Enlarged

...either it is not required, or the question is simply one of sufficiency; in that case, it is entirely sufficient and nothing further is required. Since the ultimate goal—that is, the **status of a Doctor**—is already well and sufficiently established through examinations, the actual learning cannot be bestowed afterward by the ceremony of **placing the hat**, or the granting of the **ring** or the **opened book**. <note>In the early modern period, a Doctor's graduation involved specific symbolic objects: a hat (pileus), a gold ring, and an "opened book" to signify the right to teach.</note>

<margin>Peter Friderus, Book 3, Chapter 5, Number 30.</margin>
Furthermore, a person who has been examined in one place and has obtained a **Licentiate** <note>A degree ranking between a Master and a Doctor, granting the "license" to teach.</note> cannot receive the **Doctoral Degree** elsewhere. This is, as it were, due to the continuity of the legal cause.

### ADDITION.

Do those who have endured a rigorous examination without a solemn graduation ceremony enjoy **Doctoral Privileges**? *Sprenger in Public Jurisprudence, page 43* and *Matthaeus Stephani, Book 3 on Jurisdiction, Part 2, Chapter 14, Number 106* write as follows: This last point must be added regarding Licentiates: to obtain the title and degree of Licentiate, it is not enough for someone to have been examined and to have disputed publicly in order to enjoy all the privileges belonging to Doctors, unless it is otherwise accepted and maintained by custom in a particular University. Yet this very limitation seems to be taken **with a grain of salt** <note>original: "cum mica salis"</note>; for such a custom will scarcely be alleged that has been confirmed by a contradictory judgment. See also *Pierre Grégoire, on the Art of Law, Chapter 34, Number 23; Limnäus, Book 8 on Public Law, Chapter 8, Number 43;* and *Ritter, Treatise on Homage, Chapter 5, Number 96,* where he says: those who have only held an **Inaugural Disputation** and have lawfully sustained the examination should not be called Licentiates, but only **Candidates**. *Lord Walther on the Status and Law of Doctors, Chapter 20, Section 146, Question 97. Add also Christinaeus, Book 1, Decision 104 and following; Cothmann, Academic Consultations 44, Number 33; Fabricius on Alimony, folio 76; Lord Doctor Tabor on Transfers, page 202. The Program proposed on March 25, 1644, at the graduation of three Most Learned Jurists at Strasbourg; Menochius on Arbitrary Judgments, Case 379, Number 18; Lansius on Universities, page 73.* Licentiates are also called **Pro-Doctors**. *Egidio Thomato, Treatise on Patrimonial Offices, Section on Physicians 9, Number 9, at the verse "therefore," page 432.* Regarding that rule: that Licentiates are equated to Doctors in favorable matters and may use and enjoy their honors, Law, Privileges, and immunities—namely those who have attained the name of Doctor, even if the **Insignia** <note>The physical symbols of the office like the gown or ring.</note> (which represent an outward quality rather than the essence or substance of the thing) have not been solemnly conferred upon them. These are cited at length by *Alemannus in the Arena of Consultations, page 213.* Indeed, even if a Doctor, at the time of his doctorate, does not provide the **banquet** to which he is bound by the form of the Statute, *Baldus* left it written in his notes on the law *if a donation, 22, through this text in the Code on Marriage* that nothing is taken away from his dignity by this omission. This is reported, and seems to be followed by,

<column-break/>

Johann de Annania in the *rubric of the Clementines on masters, column 2.* However, he seems instead to silently rebuke *Baldus* for requiring a banquet according to the form of the Statute, the omission of which ought to invalidate the act; this was the opinion of *Jason in "What might be expressly," 1, column 6, page 31, number 27, in the Digest on children and posthumous heirs.* This much is certainly placed beyond the risk of doubt: some establish a certain difference between Doctors and lawfully promoted Licentiates in the very preparation of the **Banquet**. Regarding the **University of Tübingen**, *Besold* testifies in the *Practical Treasury, in the older edition under rubric 29, letter D, page 218, section,* that for this reason—because there, between a solemnly announced Licentiate and a Doctor, there is no difference in the act of announcement regarding the Examination, the application of customary ceremonies, and everything else, except that in the announcement the title of **Licentiate** is used instead of the word **Doctor**, and because the Licentiate pays for no meal—it is therefore customary there to jokingly call Licentiates **Sober Doctors** <note>original: "nüchtere Doctores." A pun suggesting they are "sober" because they haven't paid for the wine for a graduation feast.</note>. And it is the custom that if a promoted Licentiate assumes the title of Doctor, nothing further is done toward him regarding ceremonies, except that he joins himself with the other new Doctors, is publicly proclaimed a **Doctor**, and at the same time pays for the banquet. On the other hand, in a person who is at least an examined **Licentiate**, there is required the **taking of the oath, the application of ceremonies, and a public specimen of his Erudition** by disputing on some question of Law. To this *Walther on Doctors, Chapter 20, Section 147, page 424 and following* adds his support. Notwithstanding these things, at Tübingen, *Marcus Imelin Schwarz*, *Christophorus Welling*, and other Licentiates have instituted banquets. Similarly at Altdorf, *Gerhard de Stökken*, having been promoted as a Licentiate, paid for a meal and instituted a solemn banquet; but when he changed his mind and thought it equally in his interest to seek Doctoral titles, he was announced as a Doctor in his absence in a second act, and he paid for this final banquet for the fulfillment of the title.

### § 8. Love Potion. Philtrum.

A **Philtrum** <note>A love potion or charm.</note> or a cup given to a person to induce love is called by the French **poisons to make one love** <note>original: "poisons pour faire aimer"</note>. From the drinking of this, the **Poet Lucretius** is said to have died. See *Guillaume Bockel, Disquisition 6, number 23, etc.,* where, according to his custom, he argues on both sides: whether one providing such a potion should be punished with the ultimate **capital punishment**, if death or a disturbance of the mind (as usually happens) follows from it. I believe that an **arbitrary penalty** <note>A penalty left to the judge's discretion rather than fixed by law.</note> has a place here; however, it can be more severe, taking the circumstances into account. Indeed, it ought even to be capital if anyone has used **sorcery**. Love is indeed sometimes procured by this means; see *Binsfeld on Sorcery, folio 427, etc.,* but that love is a **madness**, and it almost never results in a good outcome, nor does a harmonious marriage arise from it...

## ADDITION.

**Love cannot be forced.** <note>original: "Lieb mag nicht gezwungen werden."</note> You shall not extort being loved. Harpprecht shows what a love potion is made from in *Paragraph 5 of the Institutes on public judgments,* namely from poisonous herbs and other illicit things, which for the sake of love incite a great madness, and finally death. *Juvenal, Satire 6:*

<margin>Satire 6.</margin>
> This one brings magic chants, that one sells Thessalian
> love potions, with which they might vex the mind of a husband
> and strike his buttocks: that you are foolish comes from this;
> from this comes the darkness of the mind, and a great forgetfulness of things
> you just did: yet this is tolerable, if you do not
> also begin to go mad, like that uncle of Nero’s,
> into whose whole forehead Caesonia poured the brains 
> of a shivering foal. — — <note>Juvenal is describing the madness of the Emperor Caligula, allegedly caused by his wife Caesonia's love potion made from *hippomanes*, a substance supposedly found on the foreheads of newborn foals.</note>

Those who offer such things are punished with the ultimate penalty <note>the death penalty</note> if death follows, since they could have easily foreseen the danger, and the matter sets a bad example. *Paolo Ghirlandus in the treatise on sorcery, question 12, number 3 and following; Tiraqueau, On Marriage Laws 14, throughout, and law 38, paragraph 5 of the Digest on punishments.* He who gives a potion for abortion or a love potion is punished with capital punishment, not because of the fetus, but because death followed either for the woman to whom the abortion potion was given, or the person to whom the love potion was offered. *Lord Ludwig’s* explanation of *paragraph 5* should be interpreted *from chapter 5 on homicide and law 3, paragraph 2 of the Cornelian Law,* which extended the penalty to him who, though he had not committed homicide with a dagger, had provided an abortion potion. This penalty takes place,

<column-break/>

if anyone kills an infant; the same penalty remains through emphatic reasoning, whether the woman herself or the person (that is, the animated fetus) should perish. *Lord Doctor Tabor.* Those who refer these words only to the abortion potion and explain <term>the term "person"</term> <note>original: "τὸ homo"</note> as the animated infant, prove the same thing by the same thing. And Freherus was elegantly mocked by a certain Celsus for this reason, because he dragged these words only to the abortion potion, arguing that one swallowed by a love potion does not usually die, but is driven to madness. *Book 1 of the Parerga, chapter 17.* For this paradox of his is refuted by the catalog of those killed by love potions in *Zwinger’s Theater of Human Life, volume 2, book 7,* and by daily experience. *Decianus, book 9, treatise on crimes, chapter 23, number 8.* The genuine exposition of this paragraph is supplied to us by the *Basilica, book 60, title 51, chapter 38,* <note>The *Basilica* was a 9th-century collection of Byzantine laws.</note> which renders its final words thus: "but if he who drinks dies, he who gave the potion is punished with the ultimate penalty." From this it becomes manifest that the <term>legal text</term> <note>original: "Ictum"</note> speaks of the death not of the one in the womb, but of the person to whom either the abortion or the love <term>drink</term> <note>original: "πόμα"</note> was given. Therefore, the word "woman" refers to the abortion potion, for it is not usually offered to anyone but a woman; but the word "person" <note>homo</note> refers to the love potion, for it is accustomed to be offered equally to a man as to a woman. And so also feels *Thesaurus, Piedmontese Decision 12, numbers 2 and 4. Lucullus* ended his life after taking a love potion. <note>Lucius Licinius Lucullus, a Roman general, allegedly died from a potion given by his freedman.</note> *Lucretius* the poet, drawn into madness by his wife Lucilia through the offering of a love potion, brought about death by his own hand. *Pancirolli in Things Lost, page 448.* Lovers live in another’s body, according to *Seneca*, and are compared to madmen in *Novel 78; Schneidewin, final paragraph on abolished successions, at the end.* Upon this foundation leaned that young man in *Terence*, who, having falsely claimed to be a eunuch, when he had done a little something, begged for pardon: saying he had done it not for the sake of insult, but for love. Immediately he receives both pardon and favor from the mistress *Thais*. "And by Pollux," she says, "for 그 reason I now forgive you more. I am not of such an inhuman nature, Chaerea, nor so inexperienced, that I do not know what power love has." Let those who mix love potions be terrified. *See Carpzov, Criminal Practice, part 21, number 2.*
Concerning the love potion, consult *Rodrigo de Castro in The Political Physician, book 4, chapter 2; Bernhard Zieritz on the Caroline Constitutions, article 130; Speckhan, century 3, question 5, class 2; Tiraqueau.*

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of titles and relationships between lords and those who serve them, specifically focusing on the terminology of fidelity and the reciprocal duties within the feudal system.</meta>

<header>Treasury of Practical Law, Enlarged</header>

In the absence of more pressing or concurrent proofs, subjection is not necessarily inferred, as I stated above under the entry **Gracious Lords.** <note>original: "Gnädige Herren"</note> For the word *Dominion* <note>original: "Dominii," meaning lordship or ownership</note> is to be understood according to the subject matter; it is sometimes taken to mean eminence and dignity, sometimes direct or useful ownership, or even mere protection. Thus, even though "faithful vassals" are named as such in the feudal laws <note>referencing *c. 1. §. 1. 8. 1. & cap. un. 1. F. 10.*</note>, they are not considered "subjects" or "landed residents" outside of specific feudal circumstances. This is supported by Natta, Cacheranus, and Gail in his observations on pledges and arrests, where he testifies that it is an accepted style of address for vassals to be called **Dear Faithful ones.** <note>original: "Liebe Getreuen"</note> Cothmann asserts that this title specifically concerns them, and Bruning notes that in the record offices <term>Grammatophylaciis; a Greek-derived term for a treasury of documents or archives</term> of Princes, letters to both subjects and vassals are inscribed in this manner: **to our dear faithful ones.** <note>original: "unsern lieben Getreuen"</note> The same applies to clients; because they are the "faithful" of their protector and must remain so, this title is granted to them. This has been observed in the way the Saxon Court writes to the cities of Mühlhausen, Nordhausen, and Erfurt, which are client cities of the Electors and Dukes of Saxony, as noted by Waremund ab Ehrenberg.

### ADDITION.

The words **dear faithful** <note>original: "liebe Getreue"</note> do argue for subjection, according to Klock, though he elsewhere presents a counter-argument. The term "devoted" implies a subject, or an obedient subordinate; "most devoted soldiers" implies devotion, while "indevotion" stands for disobedience, according to Doctor Tabor and his work on obligations of succession.

If it is expressly agreed that "fidelity" shall not be offered, one must distinguish between the meanings of the word: when it is taken to mean the "oath of fidelity," the matter is clear and the agreement is valid; but when it refers to the actual affection and faith of the vassal, such an agreement is void. According to Antonius Gothofredus, the oath of fidelity must be provided whether the fief is small or large. There is no fief from which fidelity is not owed; indeed, when a fief is granted, it is always understood to be granted under the condition that the vassal will be faithful, **that the feudal tenant be loyal, faithful, and obedient to his feudal lord.** <note>original: "daß der Lehenmann seinem Lehenherrn hold, getreu und gewärtig sey"</note> Conversely, the Lord owes an equal fidelity to the Vassal. Hence that famous <note>original: "πολυθρύλητον" (polythryleton), a Greek word meaning much-celebrated or notorious</note> German saying, **faithful lord, faithful servant**, <note>original: "getreuer Herr, getreuer Knecht"</note> and also **Loyal Lord, Loyal Servant.** <note>original: "Holdherr, Holdknecht"</note> Indeed, they are joined together by such a tight bond that the Lord seems to have the Vassal as a spouse. The letters of both subjects and vassals are inscribed with the same style: "To our beloved and faithful," or **our dear faithful ones.** See Liebenthal.

<column-break/>

In the *Political College*, Exercise 15, question 3, it is noted that a Prince writes to both subjects and landed residents as **our dear faithful ones, but to others as our dear special ones.** <note>original: "unsern lieben Getreuen... unsern lieben Besondern"</note> This is echoed in the Marburg Counsel and by Bruning. **Everything that a vassal and feudal tenant is obligated to perform for his feudal lord, a feudal lord is also duty-bound to do for his vassal.** <note>original: "Alles was ein Vasall und Lehenmann seinem Lehenherrn zu leisten verpflichtet, das ist auch ein Lehenherr seinem Lehenmann zu thun schuldig."</note> Wehner calls this a "sacred ordinance" of feudal law. According to Schenck, this may seem terrifying or displeasing to a lord, yet it must be carefully observed. Knipschild, writing on the obligation of the Lord toward the Vassal, argues that this is not merely out of "urbanity" <note>refined courtesy</note> or goodwill—as some like Abbas have claimed—but rather the Lord is bound to it by the strength and obligation of the feudal contract struck between them. Furthermore, even without the Lord performing a specific feudal duty or oath, he is bound to his vassal in all the same ways the vassal is bound to him by his sworn oath. This is because it is only for the sake of honor that the Lord does not swear a feudal oath to the vassal; his fidelity and faith are beyond doubt because he loved his vassal enough to grant and honor him with the estate as a fief. Therefore, although the Lord does not swear the oath as the vassal does, the Lord is just as highly obligated by his acceptance of the vassal’s oath as if he had sworn it himself. This principle is supported by Mynsing and Knipschild.

The Senate of the Empire swears fidelity and obedience to the Emperor: **To be faithful, loyal, and obedient to the Roman Emperor and the Empire.** <note>original: "Dem Röm. Kayser und dem Reich treu, hold und gehorsam zu seyn."</note> See Waremund ab Ehrenberg and Limnäus for more detail.

See Master Speidelius in his *Notables*.

### ADDITION.

In Venice, there is a mechanical device <note>original: "Kunststück von einem Feuerzeug"</note> which, when operated, can light 400 fuses that can be used immediately. Likewise, there is a lantern in which—as some say—a light was maintained for 500 or even 800 years within the tomb of Antenor. <note>Antenor was the legendary Trojan founder of Padua; "eternal lamps" were a common fascination in early modern science and archaeology.</note>

### 62. Alloy, Minting. <note>original: *Liga, Legieren.*</note> The Alloy:

Alloy <note>original: *Liga*</note> is the grade and quality of metals, and I think it is that which the French call *alloy*. And it is called so from the Law <note>original: *à Lege*</note> because the addition of foreign metal must be done according to the law of the Empire. See Marcellus Donatus, folio 1042.

### ADDITION.

The addition of copper they commonly call <term>the Red</term> <note>original: *das Roth*</note>, but of silver, <term>the White</term> <note>original: *das Weiß*</note>. The mixing ought to be done moderately and justly. Truly, that mixture is moderate and most equal which is closer to the purity of the metal, such as in gold, if a mark <term>mark; a traditional unit of weight for precious metals</term> consists of 23 parts of gold and a twenty-fourth of foreign metal, since pure gold is contained in 24 parts. Budé and Bodin assert that gold coins of this quality were struck in France. In silver, the mixing is equitable if a mark contains 11 "denarii" <note>here used as a unit of fineness</note> of silver and a 12th part of copper, since pure silver consists of 12 denarii. This law of mixing, the species of mixture, or the grade of metal, is commonly called <term>Liga Aloy</term>, the <term>Pagament</term> <note>bullion or base metal</note>, the <term>Zusatz</term> <note>additive</note>, <term>Weight and Fineness</term> <note>original: *Schrott und Korn*</note>, and the <term>Gehalt</term> <note>content or value</note>. There is much straying from this Law. But one should not look at what was done at Rome or elsewhere, but what ought to be done for the public safety and the utility of individuals. Law 12 regarding the office of the procurator of Italy. The word Alloy <note>original: *Liga*</note> also signifies <term>an alliance</term> <note>original: *ein Bündniß*</note>, from "binding" <note>original: *à ligando*</note>. Rittershusius, part on feuds, page 71. See Vossius book 3 on the corruption of speech, chapter 20, page 478. Krantz, book on the Northmen 4, chapter 7. Hence the League of Peace, the Holy League. <meta>This page continues the alphabetical legal encyclopedia under the letter L. Having previously discussed labor wages (Liedlohn), the text now shifts to the legal classification of property, specifically focusing on "Immovable Goods" (Real Estate) versus "Movable Goods" (Personal Property).</meta>

Letter L.

**Immovable Goods** <note>original: *Immobilia Bona*</note> are properly those things which, by their own nature, cannot be moved. <note>See Digest 50.16.93 "on the meaning of words"; Panormitanus on the chapter "to none" regarding Church property; and others.</note>

Some argue that shares or interests in metal mines, commonly called *mine-shares* <note>original: *Bergetheil*</note>, should be counted among immovables. <note>See the glosses on the Code 5.13.1 and Digest 24.3.7.</note> Although the profits gathered from them are not strictly classified as "recurring fruits" <term>fructuum renascentium; natural products like crops that grow back annually</term>, the practical use of this question is very significant in Saxon law. According to that law, a husband gains ownership of a dowry consisting of movable goods. Therefore, mine-shares do not fall to him as owner; however, he does receive the profits <note>original: *fructus*</note> which he collects from them while his wife is alive. This was established in the Electoral Constitution 25, part 3.

By the same reasoning, a father who holds a "usufruct" <term>usufruct; the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it</term> over the "acquired assets" <term>adventitiis bonis; property a child receives from sources other than the father, such as an inheritance from a mother</term> of children under his power, does not receive the actual ownership of the mine-shares, but only the interest or the benefits derived from them. <note>See Baldus on Digest 24.3.7.</note> But see Jacob Thoming, question 12, where he debates this matter from both sides.

But what should be said regarding **Debts** <note>original: *Nominibus*; literally "names," referring to entries in a ledger</note> and **Legal Actions** <note>original: *Actionibus*</note>? Certainly, these can be referred to neither as movables nor immovables, but as a third species of goods: "incorporeal things" <term>incorporeales; intangible rights that exist only in law, like a debt or a copyright</term>. <note>See Digest 42.1.15 and Code 7.37.2.</note> Hartmann Pistor asks whether the "names" (debts) of debtors are included in a gift of "movable goods and everything contained in the house, with nothing excepted."

However, if necessity forces these debts to be classified into one category—either movable or immovable—then they belong to either the movable or immovable category based on the nature of the thing to which they are attached. For example, a legal guarantee for a gifted estate is considered an immovable thing, because he who has an action to recover a thing is seen as possessing the thing itself. <note>See Digest 50.17.15.</note>

So also "servitudes" <term>servitutes; rights to use another's land, such as a right-of-way</term> considered by themselves are rights and incorporeal things, and "bonded serfs" <note>original: *servi adscriptitii*; peasants legally bound to the land</note> are immovable things. Relatively speaking, in relation to the land, both the rights and the serfs are judged by the law of immovables.

<column-break/>

It is not a new concept for legal actions and obligations to be judged according to the nature of the thing they concern. Indeed, they are "divisible" or "indivisible" depending on whether the thing described in the obligation is divisible or indivisible. <note>See Digest 45.1.2 and 45.1.4.</note> This is true even though, as incorporeal things, they do not naturally admit to being physically divided. They are also considered "certain" or "uncertain" with respect to what is contained in the obligation. <note>Citing Alciatus and Gail.</note>

Regarding **annual rents** <note>original: *annuis reditibus*</note>, whether they are added to the category of movables or immovables, see Modestin Pistor, question 124, and Cravetta.

Do "merchandise" existing in shops follow the nature of movables or immovables? On this, consult Wilhelm Forster *On Ownership*, chapter 7.

**Beds** <note>original: *Lecti*</note> that we have in inns for public use are counted among immovable things. For such beds are judged to be "appurtenances" and "attachments" <term>pertinentiis & cohærentiis; things belonging to or structurally joined to a property</term> of the inn, and are numbered with the immovables. This is because they were acquired for the purpose of remaining there perpetually. For without these, the "right of hospitality" <note>the business of running an inn</note> could not be conveniently managed. Heigius testifies that this has been decided more than once. This decision is supported by Article 23 of the *Municipal Law* <note>original: *Weichbild*; the traditional law code for German cities</note> and the judicial opinions following it regarding "Inheritance of Goods" <note>original: *von Gerade*</note>.

It must be noted here that "things of the soil" (immovable goods) are under the territory and **Jurisdiction** of the place in which they lie. <note>See Code 3.19.3.</note> This is true even if their owner lives in another territory. For the statutes of a territory, by reason of the goods located within it, bind even those who are not subjects of that ruler. They affect the things themselves, whether possessed by a citizen or a foreigner. Therefore, where there is a legal dispute about being "put into possession" of a plot of land, the order must be carried out where the land lies. Also, the tax on a field must be raised in the city where it is located.

Whether **mills** <note>original: *molendina*</note> should be counted as movable or immovable things, see Johann Hering in his *Treatise on Mills*, question 8.

### ADDITION.

Above, we spoke regarding movable goods, furniture, and pearls. As Peregrinus says, immovable goods do not follow the legal status of the person, as movables do.

### Enlarged Treasury of Practical Law

1. <note>References to legal authorities: Gylman, Barbosa (Book 9, Chapter 9), and Tuschus.</note> **Immovable property** is defined as those things which do not move from their place but are confined by certain boundaries. <note>Tuschus, Conclusion 104, no. 1.</note> Furthermore, things are considered immovable or "clinging to the soil" when they are so attached to an immovable object or the ground that they either form a part of it, or cannot be separated from it at all—or at least not usefully and in good faith. <note>References to scholars: Ferrar. Montan. and Schrader on feudal law.</note> Whatever is added to, clings to, or is destined for use with immovables is regarded as **Immovable**. <note>Legal principle: so that one and the same thing, with its rights and attachments, is not judged by different legal standards.</note> All things from which "fruits" <term>fructus; recurring profits or harvests</term> are gathered are counted among immovables. <note>Knipschild, Chapter 5.</note> Rights are also classified as immovables, as are:
*   **Regalian rights** <term>Regalia; sovereign rights belonging to a monarch</term>
*   **Jurisdiction** <note>The right to administer justice</note>
*   **Tolls, passage fees, and taxes** <note>original: *vectigalia, pedagia, gabellæ*</note>
*   **The Right of Retraction** <term>Jus Retractus; the legal right to buy back property sold to a third party</term>
*   **Fines and penalties** not yet collected
*   **Confiscation of goods**
*   **Tithes** <note>original: *decimæ*; a tenth of produce given to the church/state</note>
*   **Chamber and cellar pensions**
*   **Annual rents**, if they are owed from immovables and are perpetual.
*   **Legal actions and claims** <note>original: *Actiones & nomina*</note>, if they relate to immovable property.
*   **Servitudes** <term>servitudes; legal rights to use someone else's land, such as easements</term>
*   **Grazing rights** for cattle
*   **Peasant services** <note>Labor owed by feudal tenants</note>
*   **Hunting and fishing rights**
*   **Fish in a pond** or pool kept for the purpose of breeding. <note>See Chassan. on Burgundian custom, folio 597.</note>
*   **Mills** built on land or riverbanks.
*   **Windmills** <note>original: *Windmühl*</note>, which are driven by the winds.
*   **Islands**
*   **Castles or fortresses**, and the fortifications considered along with the castle.
*   **Cannons and weapons of war**
*   **Timber forests, olive groves, and vineyards.**
*   **Quarries** and other metal mines.
*   **Wine presses** or oil presses.
*   **Serfs** "bound to the soil." <note>original: *homines glebæ adscripti*</note>
*   **"Iron cattle"** <note>original: *eisern Vieh*; a legal arrangement where livestock provided with a farm must be returned in equal number/value at the end of a lease</note>
*   **Money** set aside for the purchase of immovable property.
*   **Beds and furniture in inns**, which were acquired with the intent and purpose of remaining permanently in those lodgings.
*   If a testator <note>the person making a will</note> has ordered **precious items** to be kept in the family.
*   **Seals, armor, weapons** <note>original: *Pettschafft, Harnisch, Waffen*</note>, even a portion of the animals, as well as supplies of **wood, stone**, and the like, are sometimes considered immovable. <note>Petr. Wes. consil. 61.</note>

## 64. Liege Feud, Liege Man. <note>original: *Ligisch Lehen, lidig Mann. Feudum ligium.*</note>

A **Liege Feud** is one for which an Oath of Fidelity is performed against all men in the world, without exception. This applies to the Supreme Prince or Emperor, and other Lords who do not recognize a superior. <note>Goth. Anton., feudal dispute 1.</note> Thus, the person swearing such an oath is called a **Liege Man**, as if he were "bound" and "tied" to the one to whom he swears. <note>original: *ligatus*; bound</note> <note>See Specul. and Baldus, vol. 2.</note>

For this reason, the Estates of the Empire exist as the **Liege Vassals** of the Emperor, as is also proved by the Oath they are accustomed to perform. <note>See Knich. on Territorial Law, and my own work on the State of the Subordinate Republic, p. 93.</note>

A **Liege Vassal** (one who is immediately and totally subject) is also called a "homologus." <note>original: *homologus*; a Greek-derived term for someone in total agreement or submission</note> This same concept is understood by the ancient German term, **Lidius Mann** <note>likely related to "ledig" or "leute," referring to a man bound by feudal service</note>, which is mentioned in certain older Investitures. However, according to Albert Crantzius in his *Chronicle*, Book 4, the word "Liege" <note>original: *Ligium*</note> is an Italian word and signifies a **confederation** <note>or "league"</note> rather than total subjection. Among writers of a less refined age, the term is not always taken so strictly. Jean Bodin <note>a famous political philosopher</note> noted this in Book 4 of *The Republic*, Chapter 9, where he presents the Oath of the Duke of Guelders: "I become the Liege Vassal of Charles, King of the French, in consideration of fifty gold crowns to be paid to me before the feast of St. Remigius." Yet it is clear they only made a treaty between them; the Archbishop of Trier understood this correctly when he called himself an "Ally and Confederate" of the King, rather than a "Vassal" like the others. <note>See also Henning Arnisaeus on the Rights of Majesty.</note> For more on Liege status and the ritual by which a "liege man" is made, see Camerarius and Hotoman.

Albert of Strasbourg <note>original: *Albert. Argent.*</note> mentions in his *Chronicle* a "society" or "treaty" between a Prince and a Frank: oaths were exchanged and letters drafted, and a **perpetual league** <note>original: *liga perpetua*</note> was confirmed. The Marquis contracted a "League" with Mastino of Verona and betrothed his daughter to Mastino's son.

# 667
### Lit. L.
#### Pppp 2

<note>References to commentaries on the Second Book of Fiefs, Title 52; Gothofredus; and Antonius’s feudal Disputations.</note> In terms of its form, a **fief** <term>feudum; a landed estate held on condition of feudal service</term> is divided into **Liege** and **non-Liege**. This is discussed at length by Gothofredus Antonius and Dr. Tabor. **Liege** status is determined **according to the letter** <note>original Greek: κατὰ ῥητὸν</note> of the law in the *Clementines* <note>a collection of canon law</note> and the *Second Book of Fiefs*, and **according to the spirit** <note>original Greek: κατὰ διὰνοιαν</note> of the law because some vassals are bound more strictly than others. Formally, the effect is evident not only in common legal disputes but also in "Major" or **Regalian fiefs** <term>feudis Regalibus; those involving sovereign rights</term>, as seen in the Kingdom of Sicily. <note>Scholars cited: Giphanius, Cujas, Obrecht, Setfer, Gudelinus, Melander, and Rosenhane.</note>

The difference in utility for the person granting the fief is that they should not recognize any superior lord. Hence, some doubt whether the King of France holds a Liege fief, as he recognizes the Pope as a superior at least in matters of conscience. On the part of the recipient, he must recognize no other superior. There is also a difference in effect: in a **Liege fief**, there is no room for withdrawal or "repentance," as it binds the parties irrevocably. 

The distinguishing features are debated: 
1. That the fief must be explicitly stated as "Liege" (though one should not cling strictly to formal words if equivalent terms are used).
2. That the vassal subjects all his goods to the superior (though the oath of vassalage and the oath of subjection differ). 
3. In such a fief, the Prince alone may judge, rather than the "Peers of the Court." <note>Refuted by Finckelthal and Carpzov.</note> 

A **Liege** vassal provides the strictest loyalty, whereas in a non-Liege fief, one swears loyalty "in a certain respect." <note>Conrad Rittershusius, Chapters 71–73.</note> No one can be a Liege Vassal to two lords at once. In a non-Liege fief, if a man is a vassal to two lords, it must be determined whom he should assist in war. Dr. Ludwell, Chapter 3. **Philip of Austria**, the son of **Maximilian I**, received the Counties of Flanders and Artois as a **Liege Fief** from the King of France, **Louis XII**, without any hesitation. <note>Leonhard Wurffbain, *On Truces and Peace*, pp. 88, 99.</note> The most extensive discussion of Liege Fiefs is by Mauritius Wilhelm von Gulchen in his 1656 inaugural disputation at Strasbourg.

### 65. Lindau. Lindavia.

This city bought itself free from **Count Hugo of Bregenz** for 24 marks—half gold, half silver—(which was permitted to them, according to Peter Heigius, Part 1, Question 19) and subsequently surrendered itself to the **Holy Roman Empire**. <note>See Sebastian Münster's *Cosmographia*, Book 3, and my funeral oration for Valentin Neuffer.</note>

In the chronicle of **Thomas Leyrer** of Rankweil (first transcribed in the year 1133 and first printed in Ulm in 1486), it says that Hugo (son of the Lord of Bregenz) had a castle in Lindau which

<column-break/>

at that time was not in the lake. A man from Ems had a daughter named Eva, who was very beautiful; Hugo took her and made her pregnant. There was a man living in the city named **Schönstein**, who advised the people of Lindau to speak with their lord, Hugo, suggesting that he take a large sum of money from them to set them free. In return, they would help him build a fortress and residence for his "dear lady" <note>his mistress or beloved</note> so she would be safe and his enemies could not harm her. They negotiated until he agreed on a price of 42 marks, half gold and half silver. With this, he built a fortress called **Bodmann**. When his father died, he took Eva in marriage and had three sons with her. The Lords of Rosenfan did not want them to be heirs, as Hugo was quite simple-minded, and the Lord of Rosenfan took the inheritance with him. He gave Hugo his brother’s estate of Melchingen from the blessed **Reichenau** <note>a famous Benedictine monastery on Lake Constance</note> as a "refuge house," and gave the Abbot 21 marks of silver for it, taking over Bregenz with all its land and belongings. Hugo’s sons were called the "Lords of Bodmann." The Lord of Bregenz carries a coat of arms featuring a horned cushion with a yellow stripe through the middle and three black perches <note>fish</note> within it.

A certain anonymous author in a manuscript collection has the following: Hugo, son of Count Hugo of Bregenz, flourished under **Emperor Henry III**. At that time, the citizens of Lindau, afflicted by the continuous flooding of the Lake, freed themselves from the power of the Count for 42 marks of silver. Leaving their houses, they retreated to the **Island of Lindau**, where there was a monastery of **Free Canonesses** <term>Canonicarum Liberarum; a convent for noblewomen who did not take full monastic vows</term> built by Count Adalbert of Buchhorn after surviving a shipwreck. By joining their small houses to this monastery, and with many people flocking there from other places, they soon created a town which is today an Imperial City and is called Lindavia. Others suggest the occasion for the city of Lindau was that Hugo had seduced a noblewoman from Bodman and, fleeing his father’s wrath, freed the Lindauers upon receiving money in the year 1166.

From similar private manuscript fragments: At that same time (the year 1066), there was a town situated in front of the island, built down by the lake, called **Eschach**. It belonged to the Count of Bregenz and was completely burned down. A citizen there named N. Schönstein advised that they should buy themselves free from the Count. This was done, and they gave the Ladies <note>the nuns</note> 42 marks, half silver and half gold. Count Hugo of Bregenz took this and built or fortified **Bodmann** so that he would be safe from the Lords of Ems, who were feuding with him over a marriage. Once this happened, the citizens moved from the burnt castle of Eschach onto the island to the **Abbess** and became her **emphyteutic tenants** <term>Emphyteuten; tenants on a long-term lease</term>. This is why the **ground rent** <term>Bodenzins; a tax or rent paid for the use of land</term> still exists for the houses they have not bought free from the Lady Abbess. To help the new city grow further, the monastery was also made a "sanctuary" or tax-free zone.

The price was 52 marks, half in silver and half in gold. From this money, the castle of Bodmann was later built.

### 66. Line. Lineage.

A **Line** is a collection of persons descending from the same root <term>stipes; the ancestor from whom a family branch originates</term>, containing degrees of relationship and distinguishing kinships. That person from whom the others—whose connection is being investigated—descend and draw their origin is called the **Root**. Just as Philip, King of Spain, is the root of the Emperors Charles and Ferdinand, and of all those descending from them. The word "Line" includes not only males but also females descending from them. Tiraquellus, *On Lineal Retraction, section 1, glossary 9, number 224.* When is it otherwise? See Paschal, *Treatise on Paternal Power, part 4, chapter 9, number 53, etc.*

And it is threefold: one is the **Ascending** line, which is called the superior line, in which are contained the persons from whom we draw our origin: such as a father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and all other persons ascending to infinity.

The second is the **Descending** line, which is called the inferior line, in which are contained the persons who draw their origin from us: such as sons, grandsons, etc.

The third is the **Transverse Line**, which is called **Collateral**, and it encompasses those who are joined to us from the side, from whom we did not draw our origin, nor they from us, and yet we are propagated from one stock and blood: such as brothers and their children, paternal uncles, paternal aunts, and the rest of the transversals. And this

<column-break/>

collateral line is divided into an equal line and an unequal line. An **Equal line** is spoken of when the degrees of those whose kinship is being questioned are equally and evenly distant from the common root: for example, two brothers are in an equal line, for each is equally distant from the root—namely, the father—by one degree. An **Unequal line** is spoken of when one person precedes another in degree, and the persons whose kinship is being questioned are not equally distant from the common root: as is the case with a brother and a brother’s son. For the brother, as has been said, is distant from the root—namely the father—by one degree, while the brother’s son is joined to the root in the second degree; thus they are in an unequal line. Schneidewin, *at the preface of the Institutes on Marriage, number 4 and following.*

A line is also divided into masculine and feminine, as Cumanus notes in *Counsel 2, number 6.* For although a woman is of her father's line, her children begin to belong to the mother’s line; because the paternal line is broken through the woman, and the origin of kinship takes its beginning from her after she passes into another family. Curtius the Younger, *Counsel 1, number 24 and following.* Hence, a granddaughter by a son is said to be of the masculine line, because she is under her father’s line; but those descending from her are of the feminine line. See Paschal, *cited chapter 9, number 67, etc.*

The Germans also make a distinction between **House and Lines** <note>original: "unter Haus und Linien"</note>. Thus, for example, the Electoral House of Saxony is divided into various lines, as I noted in the *Treatise on Family Law, at the end.*

### ADDITION.

**What a line is.** Didacus, *On Marriage, chapter 6, section 6, number 4 with the following;* Menochius, *book 4, presumption 88, number 11.* Under the designation of "Line," both sexes are included, unless a specific law or a person's legal disposition excludes females. Knipschild, *On Entails, chapter 1, number 85 and following.* Properly speaking, descendants—not collaterals—are included, *chapter 1, number 87,* unless a general sense and the preservation of the agnation <term>agnatio; kinship through the male line</term> is implied, *chapter 1, number 88.* To admit a kinsman from a more remote line where there would be no place for the author of the line himself is like a monstrosity, *chapter 9, number 75.* The line of a second-born son excludes by its own calling, *ibid.* A line differs from a family, *chapter 1, numbers 79, 85, and 106.* The transition from line to line, *chapter 9, number 70.* **To cast a line:** Used by Plautus in *The Haunted House* <note>original title: "Mostellaria"</note> to mean fishing for or exploring someone's mind. "I will not show my meaning by example; I will cast a line." **Lines** is sometimes taken to mean a day, as in: "within the seventh line." Zenodotus. There was an edict at Athens that they should lead out the army before the seventh day of the month. **To be moved to the lines** is a phrase from the Circus <note>referring to the starting lines of a race</note>, and Seneca speaks of it in *Letter 49:* "I feel myself being moved to the lines." Lipsius interprets this phrase more extensively. Rupertus, *book 1, chapters 6, 7, 8, difference 2, section 11, on Valerius Maximus.* **Line** signifies a small cord or thread, since it is made from flax <note>original: "lino"</note>. Isidore, *Etymologies, book 19, chapter 18; law 26 on the Falcidian Law; the last law, the last section, on gold and silver.*
