# 669
## Letter L.
### Pppp 3
<meta>catchword: 12. ff.</meta>

In law, a string of pearls <note>original: "linea margaritarum"</note> is called *a cord of pearls* <note>original: "eine Schnur Perlen"</note>. Pearls that are counted are called *numbered pearls* <note>original: "Zahlperlen"</note>. Limnaeus, in *Additions to Public Law, volume 1, book 6, chapter 6, page 106.* Pearls are typically perforated so that women may wear them on a string as an ornament. *Law 27, section 'if with the husband,' on the Aquilian Law.* If a string of pearls is stolen, the number of pearls must be stated. *Law 52, section 25 of the Digest on Theft.* Dr. Tabor, in *Clusters of Crimes, page 229.* A long line signified condemnation, while a short line signified absolution. Hermann Hugo, *On the First Origin of Writing, page 155,* citing Suidas. In a transverse line <term>linea transversa; a side-branch of a family tree, such as cousins</term> there is also an order of descendants and ancestors, not only in the direct line <term>linea recta; parents, children, and grandparents</term>: although we are more accustomed to using these terms for the latter than the former. Rittershusius, *On the New Constitutions, page 417.* The word "verse" <note>original: "Versus"</note> is used for a line of text <note>original: "Zeil"</note>. Drexel, *In the Gold Mine, page 163.* In Civil Law, the **Bloodline** <note>original: "Linea Sanguinis"</note> refers to the ascending, descending, and transverse lines: because every heir of blood, race, and kinship is contained within these three lines. However, a **Legal Title** <note>original: "titulus Juris"</note> is the term used in the same law when the bloodline fails—that is, where succession is granted by a right other than blood, such as the succession of a spouse, a partner, or a freedman. This is because when the *bloodline* is absent, a spouse succeeds a spouse, a partner succeeds a partner, or a freedman succeeds a patron. If both the bloodline and the legal title are missing, the property is considered vacant and is claimed by the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>. Mr. Obrecht, in *Five Different Political Secrets, page 28.* Interlinear writings or additions made between one line and another suggest the falsity of a legal instrument and may completely nullify it. However, this is limited to cases where the changes are in a substantial or suspicious place within an authentic document, and where the sense of the words cannot otherwise be gathered from what precedes or follows. *Farinacius, part 6, question 153, page 2.*

### 67. Liquidated Debt. *Debitum liquidum.*

Just as a "liquid" matter is the sole subject and object of legal execution <term>execution; the enforcement of a court judgment</term>, and the reason why one may proceed directly to enforcement by mandate or command; so among other requirements that make a debt "liquid" is a **certain cause of debt**. Peter Friedrich, *On Mandates, chapter 59, numbers 1 and 7, book 2.* For without a cause, there is no obligation, and without an obligation, there is no legal action. Hence, if the cause of the debt is missing or unclear <note>original: "illiquidam"</note>, the debt itself and the document confirming it are invalidated, or at least the alleged notoriety of the debt is obscured. See Magonius, *Decisions of Lucca, 79.* A document is not called "liquid" before its conditions are cleared. Wesenbec, *Consultation 188, under number 25.*

Thus, a debt is not liquid if the cause of the debt is disputed. Similarly, it is often said that although documents regarding a deposit have "ready execution" even under Common Law <note>original: "paratam executionem"</note>, *Law 'if anyone' where the Doctors discuss the Code on deposits,* this should only apply to a 

<column-break/>

true and real deposit, which is established by the actual counting of money; it does not apply to a "confessed" deposit <note>a deposit that exists only on paper because the parties agreed to say it was made, even if no money changed hands</note>. Bartolus, *Consultation 332;* Baldus, *Consultation 384, number 1, book 1;* Kirchhoff, *In Common Opinions, century 2, conclusion 67.*

A debt becomes liquid either by the confession of the opponent, by the nature of its constitution, or by the ease and speed of proving it. Hilliger, *on Donellus, book 16, chapter 15, letter CC.*

However, a **fictitious confession** <note>original: "Confessio ficta"</note> does not deserve "ready execution." Antonius de Butrio, *In the Repetition of Civil Law, on the word 'guarentigia' <note>guarentigia; a clause in a contract where the parties agree to immediate enforcement without a trial</note>.* Baldus, *In Additions to the Speculator, title on appeals, section 'likewise it is asked,' and in Law 'we command,' section 'surely,' Code on Sacred Churches.* In this regard, a true confession differs from a fictitious one. Natta, *Consultation 32, number 18, book 1.*

This applies most strongly where it is clear that the reality of the situation is different from what is contained in the documents. In such cases, one thing was done while another was simulated; this defense <note>original: "exceptio"</note> is never considered signed away by an agreement or even by a Statute. Corbulus, *In the Treatise on Causes for Loss of Emphyteusis <term>emphyteusis; a long-term land lease</term>, title on causes of private alienation, limit 23, number 2;* Tiraquell, *On the Right of Redemption, section 1, glossary 2, number 13 and following.*

Furthermore, even when a document is public and notarized with a guarantee <note>original: "guarentigiatum"</note> or contains **Execution Clauses**, a person is not prevented from raising an exception <note>a legal defense</note> against the contract contained within it. Based on the teachings of Bartolus, *Law 1, section 2, and Law 'small,' Digest on things done by force or stealth;* Antonius de Canari, *In the Treatise on Execution of Instruments, number 25.*

Similarly, a Statute that rejects all exceptions is not thought to exclude those defenses which arise from the very nature of the act or business upon which the document was made, even if they are not expressed in the document. Felinus, *In the chapter 'from the part,' 2, number 2, where Decius number 57 discusses delegated office;* Menochius, *On Presumptions, book 2, presumption 48, number 14;* Carocius, *On Excussion, 1, question 14, numbers 11 and 18,* where he says this exception can be raised even if the document promised to pay "freely and without any controversy." This is supported by the text *in Law 'I ask,' section 'between the lessor,' Digest on leasing.* The reason is that words—no matter how earnest, general, or repetitive—never refer to or remove that which arises from the intrinsic nature of the act. Bartolus, *above cited;* Barladorus, *Everyday Matters, final chapter, part 5, section 11, number 26.*

Thus, the **Defense of money not paid** <note>original: "Exceptio pecuniæ non numeratæ"</note> is never considered rejected. Cynus, *In Law 'in contracts,' Code on non-counted money;* Jason, *In Law 'he who money,' number 7, Digest on certain claims;* Fachin, *Book 2, Controversies, chapter 84.*

The same must be said for the defense of property not delivered, or the failure to fulfill the contract. Carolus de Grassls, *In the Treatise on Exceptions, 13.* It is the nature of this defense that it is sufficient for it to be alleged within the legal exceptions and arguments. Bartolus, *In Law 'him who so,' section 'who so to you,' where Jason number 12 discusses the Digest.*

The same must be ruled regarding the exception of **most enormous loss** <term>enormissimæ læsionis; a legal doctrine where a contract can be rescinded if the price is extremely unfair, usually more than two-thirds or three-quarters off the true value</term>. For even if a Statute prohibited "restitution to the original state" in a case of "enormous loss" <note>loss exceeding half the value</note>, it is not deemed to also prohibit it in a case of "most enormous loss." Oddo, *On Restitution to the Original State*, question 15, title 8, number 77.

### ADDITION.

A matter is **liquid** <term>liquidum; a debt or claim that is certain, evident, and undisputed in its amount</term> when it is immediately clear through a legal instrument or the confession of the opposing party, as shown extensively by Coler, *On Executive Process*, number 69 and following.

A "liquidation after the fact" <note>original: "Liquidatio ex postfacto"</note> achieves the same effect as that which was clear from the beginning. See Law 4 of the Code on Testamentary Manumission, and there Baldus; Law 30, final section, on the Action of Pledges; Law 22 of the Digest on Mandates. **A clear claim should not be delayed because of an unclear one** <note>original: "Liquidum non debet retardari propter illiquidum"</note>. Law 'statu liber rationem' in the Digest on Enfranchised Slaves. Curtius Junior, Counsel 122, number 3. Cavalcanti, *On Tutors*, number 215. Munoz de Escobar, *On the Accounting of Administrators*, chapter 21, throughout. For no place for compensation <note>offsetting a debt</note> is to be hoped for when comparing a clear debt to an unclear one. Law 'fin.', Code on Compensation, section 30 of the Digest on Actions; nor for a debt deferred to a future date. Lord Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, 14, Thesis 7, letter K. Indeed, execution <note>the enforcement of a court order</note> for clear debts can rightly be carried out even while litigation remains pending over unclear ones. Lancellotti, *On Attempts*, part 2, number 4, limitation 28; and an unclear matter in a defense should not delay a clear matter in an action, which is true when the defense requires a deeper investigation. Mævius in *Commentary on the Law of Lübeck*, book 5, title 6, article 2, number 1. Berlich, volume 1, final conclusion, number 86. That which can be clarified promptly must be considered "liquid," as Antonius Faber elegantly teaches in the Code, book 4, title 23, definition 2, number 3. However, a matter is called "liquid" in three ways: either what is evident from a party's confession, or from the nature of the question of fact or law (which is always certain), or finally, from the speed of proof. It must be clear *what*, *what kind*, and *how much* is owed. Barbosa, book 10, chapter 21, axiom 2, at the end. That which is certain, defined, ready, and clear should not be confused with the uncertain. Peregrinus, Counsel 8, number 12, book 2. It should not be further clarified through a long process and the "clatter of the court" <note>original: "strepitúmque judicii"; referring to noisy, complex litigation</note>, but rather, that which is most ready should be ordered for execution. This does not mean proceeding "really" <note>physically</note> at once by invading possessions or seizing property—for this is the process of enemies, who are not undeservedly called the "scum of men" and "candidates for fierce swords"—but by first commanding and warning, with a competent deadline fixed for satisfaction, according to Law 31 and Law 56 of the Digest on Judged Matters, and the single Law of the Code on Confessions. A "liquid" matter is a declaration against which nothing can be opposed. Johann Baptista Costa, *On Retraction*, chapter 8, case 9, number 11. Carolus de Grassi, *On Exceptions*, from chapter 36, final number. Or,

<column-break/>

where the quantity and cause of the obligation are clear. Köppen, question 34; or regarding the justice, cause, and truth. Donellus at section 30, Institutes on Actions; as well as the ease of proof. Donellus, 16, commentary 15, and there Hilliger at letter CC. **But in this day and age, no written contract is so pure; people are found who torture the law, stretching it, narrowing it, coloring it, and casting shadows upon it.** <note>original German: "Aber heutigs Tags ist keine Verschreibung so lauter, es finden sich Leut, welche das Recht foltern, und strecken, auch engern, färben und schattiren."</note> Scipio, book 3, Decisions of the Imperial Chamber, 85. Gail, *On Arrests*, chapter 9, number 17. On what "liquidly" denotes, see Vultejus, *Scholarly Disputations*, chapter 7, page 75 and following. Baldus, in Law 2 of the Code on Execution of Judged Matters, number 9, says that an "unliquidated" instrument contains a "veiled obligation." Although an uncertain sentence can sometimes be made, especially in universal matters (Ludovicus Romanus, Counsel 211, number 5), it cannot be sent for execution unless a **liquidation** <note>the process of determining the exact amount</note> is first performed. Lord Doctor Ludwig on Wesenbeck, Digest on Judged Matters, number 7. Execution for unliquidated expenses, even if included in a sentence, cannot be carried out before liquidation. Execution does not happen unless the matter is clear in its root and substance. Jason at Law 1 of the Digest on Producing Documents, number 31. Cravetta, Counsel 164, number 2. Add Cardinal Tuschi, *Practical Conclusions*, 210, letter A. In matters needing liquidation, no "default" <note>mora; legal delay</note> is contracted until it has been declared by a Judge. Law 2 of the Code on Interest and Fruits. The article of liquidation acts as an incident to the execution of a sentence, which takes on the nature of the principal matter. Clementine, *Dispendiosam*, 2, on Judgments. Thus, a sum liquidated by a calculator will be ordered for execution no differently than if the liquidation were expressly and virtually contained in the sentence itself; it is understood as truly and properly known when it is held by reference to something else. Law 5, section 1 of the Digest on Judged Matters; Law 6 where Jason comments on the Digest on Things Credited. A matter can be called "liquid enough" if it is very close to being liquidated. Johann Baptista Costa and Marta. That which is certain, defined, and clear should not be further clarified through the "clatter of the court," but that which is most ready should be ordered for execution. See Zorer at length, part 1, question 2, number 182 and following.

### 68. Letter of Release. Affrancamenta. See above: Serfdom.

Unfree people <note>original: "Homines proprii"</note> obtain the freedom enjoyed by others in various ways; and as a testimony of this matter—namely, of **manumission** <note>the act of freeing a slave or serf</note>—they are given **Instruments of Manumission**, called a **Letter of Release** <note>original German: "Laßbrief"</note>, or elsewhere called **Man's Right** <note>original German: "Mannrecht"</note>. For serfs were not called "Men," but were designated as **"poor folk"** <note>original German: "arme Leut"</note>: either because of their poverty, or because they do not have an "arm" <note>original: "brachium"</note>—that is, power and liberty. In this view, they are also called **"dead hands"** <note>original French: "des mains morts"</note> by the French. For "hand" <note>original: "manu"</note> is used to mean power or authority.

It is commonly held almost everywhere that **Manumissions** <term>manumissio; the formal act of releasing a slave or serf from the power of their master</term> are performed by Lords under this express protest: that if it happens that the freed person dwells again in the territory of the manumitting Lord, he must again be subjected to agricultural service. Law 'final', section 'reverentia' of the Code on the Goods of Freedmen.

### 69. Redemption. Retraction.

The word **Losung** <note>A German term for redemption or drawing lots; here used for the legal right to buy back property</note> applies not only to payment, but also to redemption. Baptista Caesar in *Illustrious Counsels of Jurists*, part 2, counsel 67, number 55. Here I take it for **Retraction** <term>retractus; the legal right of a family member or co-owner to step into a sale and buy property at the same price offered by an outside buyer</term>, concerning which various questions arise, which I have brought forth from the notes of my Brother, on part 2 of the *Württemberg Territorial Law*. See the *Collection* of Johann Jacob Speidel under the word "Retractus." ### ADDITION.

It is reckless and dangerous to commit a matter to fortune. Fichardus, volume 1, counsel 12, number 23. The Venetians distribute their offices by lot. Hence it is said: **The lot settles the strife** <note>original: "Das Loß stillet den Hader"</note>. Among the Venetians, magistrates are chosen by lot from an urn. Contarenus, book 1, *On the Republic of Venice*. On how the Venetians effect the drawing of lots if something is to be done, see Pancirollus, *On Lost Things*, book 1, page 351. Coteræus, *On the Right of Soldiers*, book 3, chapter 8. **A lot is not something evil, but is a thing indicating the divine will in human doubt.** Canon 'sors', 26, question 2. Whence we see that in doubtful cases, a matter is often committed to fortune. Law 14 of the Digest on Judgments; Law 24, section 17 of the Digest on Fideicommissary Liberties; Law 's.' of the Digest on the Partition of Inheritance; Law 3 of the Code on Legacies. Treated extensively by Barbosa, book 17, chapter 42, axiom 1. **Lots are not to be easily believed.** Canon 'non statim', canon 'non exemplo', 26, question 2. Barbosa in the same place, axiom 2. Everyone is subjected to the lot for his own admission, nor is he made the successor of another's crime. Canon 'crimin.', 1, question 4. **Sorcery is prohibited by law.** Barbosa in the same place, axiom 4. Reinking limits this regarding retraction, question 2, number 94 and following. He is seen as the plaintiff who first called for judgment, or if both called, it is customary to discern by lot. Law 13 and Law 14 of the Digest on Judgments. Mr. Riccius in *Golden Matters*, section 5, Treasury 14. Petrus Gregorius in the *Syntagma of Universal Law*, book 34, chapter 5, number 2. If a thing cannot be conveniently divided, let it be committed to lot, especially if everyone is seeking the same thing, so that it belongs to him whom the lot prefers. Final law of the Code on Legacies. When heirs appointed in equal parts cannot agree among themselves with whom the hereditary cautions (which the common folk call "inheritance documents") should remain, they ought to draw lots regarding that matter, or by consent and vote choose a friend with whom they may be deposited. Law 'if there are any cautions' in the Digest on the Partition of Inheritance. Marcus Valerius, captured by Ariovistus <note>A leader of the Suebi in the 1st century BC</note>, was liberated by the benefit of lots, because in his presence it was consulted three times by lot whether he should be killed immediately by fire or reserved for another time. From this we can gather that among the Gentiles, judgments were also sometimes decided by lot. P. Victorius explains in book 25, *Various Readings*, chapter 15, the custom of drawing lots and the ancient use of the urn, when small buckets or water-jars were cast in with water and "lots"—that is, certain tablets of various materials which had a fixed meaning—and then that which was taken out first established the judgment. As Plautus indicates in *Casina*, where he introduces that old man, a lover of a young girl, after he could not obtain what he desired from his servant, speaking thus and committing the whole matter to lot:

> *Go inside, and call out your wife immediately,*
> *Come here quickly,*
> *And bring a bucket here with water and the lots.*

Pausanias also teaches in *Messenia* that lots were once made from the earth, when he discusses the division of the Messenian land coveted by Cresphontes against Aristodemus, the son of his brother.

The Emperor Probus <note>Roman Emperor from 276 to 282 AD</note>, while he was still a General, according to the testimony of Flavius Vopiscus in his biography, once ordered a magnificent horse—capable of traveling a hundred miles in a day and captured from the *Alans* <note>An Iranian nomadic people of antiquity</note>—to be placed in an urn to be given to whichever soldier the lot fell upon. Regarding the judges chosen by lot, and those chosen as substitutes: *Petrus Gregorius in his Comprehensive Treatise on Law, book 34, chapter 5, number 14.* On when it is permissible to use lots, see extensively *Pancirollus, On Lost Things, page 348, and the citations therein.* Why an appeal may be made from a judgment by lot: *page 349.* Not even by a party injured by more than half: *ibid.* In Ecclesiastical matters, drawing lots is not permitted: *page 350.* The lot is not evil in itself: *page 351.* The drawing of lots among Athletes: *ibid.* To the French, *Lot* is used for a lot or even a portion, which to the Germans is *Los*, and figuratively an Inheritance <note>original: "einès Erbtheil"</note>; it is used by the Greeks as *kleros* <note>original: "κλῆρος"</note> for both a lot and an inheritance. *And so "Allot" signifies coming from one's assigned inheritance. Isaac Pontanus, Origins of the Franks, folio 514.* The lot is threefold: *Divine, Political, and Curious* <note>In this context, "curious" refers to superstitious or occult practices</note>: *see Bernegger, Questions on Tacitus’s Germania, 2. 49.* A lot only has a place when there is such necessity that neither reason nor counsel can be applied. If two candidates for a kingdom run in an election who are equal in virtue and other requirements, a lot must be used so that neither appears to be rejected out of contempt. *Lord Doctor Ludwig, On Aristocracy, Thesis 12, letter a.* How should the lot be admitted? *Extensively, Lord Felwinger, On Aristocracy, Thesis 12.* On the nature of the lot, its division, the providence of God in a fair lot, whether Dice constitutes a lot, and on Games of Chance: *Leonardus à Ryssen and Hermannus à Spreckelsen, 1664, in an Inaugural Dissertation held at Strasbourg regarding the Drawing of Lots.*

### 71. **Standard Gold. Pure Gold.** <note>original: "Lötig Gold. Aurum purum."</note>

Those words, *by several Marks of standard gold* <note>original: "bey etlicher Marck lötiges Golds"</note>, inserted into sentencing judgments or Mandates, are to be understood as referring to pure gold, not to a baser sort. *See Budelius, On Coinage, book 1, chapter 23, number 14.*

And it is called pure or *lötig* <term>lötig; a term used to describe the purity of silver or gold, indicating it meets a specific weight standard</term> because it is heavier than that which has other metals mixed in.

For *lötig* means "weighty," just as it is generally called weighty after the specific type of weight <note>the "Lot" was a traditional unit of weight</note>.

### **ADDITION.**

*One Mark of standard gold equals 72 gold guilders. Schwanmann, book 2, chapter 18, number 19.* The words *standard gold* <note>original: "lötigs Golds"</note>, when inserted into Imperial mandates, as well as arrests or sentencing judgments, are to be understood as pure gold. *Gail, 2. On the Public Peace, 6 & 9; Wurmser, title 7, on the Significance of Words; J. W. Auer, On the Law of Coinage, chapter 8, number 40.* It is also called *fine standard silver* <note>original: "fein lötig Silber"</note>, *number 41.*

### 72. **Lorraine. Lotharingia.**

Regarding Lorraine, see *Justus Lipsius, On Louvain, book 1, chapter 9; and Arumaeus, On the Imperial Diets, chapter 3, number 122, etc.*

<column-break/>

In the year 855, the Emperor Lothair I distributed his kingdom among his three sons: to *Louis* he assigned Italy with the Empire; to *Lothair II* he gave that part of Gaul which from then on was called Lothair’s Kingdom—*Lothryck* and *Lotharingia*. To *Charles*, the youngest, he assigned Provence. He himself entered the Monastery of *Prüm*, located not far from Trier, where on September 27th he piously fell asleep in the Lord, providing a rare example of worldy glory being held in contempt.

It should be noted here that *Lotharingia* was named not after Lothair the Elder, as Sigebert, Divaeus, and others have written, but after Lothair the Younger. Regino of Prüm expressly testifies to this in his deeds of this year, as do other ancients; logic itself confirms it. For Lothair the Elder held not only Lorraine, but also Italy and the Empire. *Aubertus Miraeus, in the Belgian Annals, under the aforementioned year 855, page 353.* The same author writes regarding the *year 959, folio 499*: *Lotharingia* further obeyed first Kings, and later Dukes; as its boundaries were often changed, so it is difficult to describe them. The first King of Lorraine was Lothair the Younger, who died without legitimate offspring at Piacenza, in Italy, in the month of June, 869. The inheritance was due by right to his brother, Emperor Louis II, then acting in Italy; a decree of Pope Hadrian II exists in his favor. However, his uncles, Louis the German and Charles the Bald, opposed it. For as soon as Charles heard that Lothair had died, he immediately flew to Metz, and there in that same year was consecrated King by several Bishops of both kingdoms. Louis, as was natural, was annoyed that the kingdom of his nephew Lothair—of which he himself had set aside a part—was being entirely usurped by Charles. Finally, a pact was entered into: the two brothers met in a defense post <note>original: "Procaspide"</note> on the Meuse, between Herstal and Meerssen, in the district of Liège, and divided that kingdom between them in equal portions. From this division, it is established that the part of Lorraine across the Meuse fell to Louis, and the part on this side of the Meuse fell to Charles.

For a long time, it remained uncertain whether Lorraine would adhere to France or to the German Empire; concerning this matter, the same *Miraeus, page 504*, relates the following: Giselbert first adhered to Charles the Simple, and governed the Lorrainers in his name. After the death of King Charles, as the Lorrainers wished to be subject to Henry (*the Fowler*), King of Germany, a certain Lorrainer named Christian, feigning illness, captured Duke Giselbert by trickery when he was summoned, and sent him to the King so that he might subjugate Lorraine through him. But having observed the industry and power of Giselbert, the King betrothed his daughter Gerberga to him and placed him in charge of Lorraine again, as Sigebert says in his *Chronicle*. Widukind relates these same events in almost the same words in *book 1*.

For the origin of the Dukes of Lorraine, see Franciscus de Rosieres, a French nobleman and Archdeacon of Toul, in his book printed in Paris in folio in the year 1580 under the title *Stemmatum Lotharingiæ & Barri Ducum* <note>original: "Lineage of the Dukes of Lorraine and Bar"</note>; likewise, Master Doctor Leonhard Wurffbain in his *Genealogical Tables, 24.* There are three grades of Dukes: 1. ### 73. Handing over of Malefactors. <term>Remissio delinquentium</term> <note>The formal process of "remitting" or sending a criminal back to the jurisdiction where the crime was committed; similar to modern extradition</note>.

By a certain general custom, the law of *Remissions* has been departed from. See Wesenbeck in his *Summary of the Digest, on trials.* Covarruvias, *Practical Questions, chapter 11, number 10.* Julius Clarus declares that this is the common opinion of the Doctors of both Laws <note>Civil and Canon law</note> and is observed every day, *book 5, final section, question 39, verse "but whatever the law," and at the end.* Caeppolla says this custom stands and is valid even if crimes remain unpunished, *Criminal Consultations 29, column 3.* Johannes Damhouder in *Criminal Practice, chapter 35, at the end,* and most recently after them, Gail, *book 1, on Public Peace, chapter 16, numbers 30 and 31.* This was introduced for this reason, according to Besoldus, *Volume I,*

<column-break/>

because jurisdictions have now become <term>patrimonial</term> <note>meaning legal authority was treated as private property or an inheritance belonging to a lord</note>, and the States of Germany are more "jealous" regarding them than the Italians are regarding their wives. It could easily happen that if remissions were frequent, the great Magnates would acquire a right of superiority over their less powerful neighbors. Nevertheless, in Germany and other Provinces, in the case of more atrocious crimes, a remission is usually made for the sake of example to the place of the crime as a favor <note>original: "precario"</note> and by the right of friendship, neighborhood, and goodwill. This is done under an *antigraph* or "Reversal letters" <note>original: "Reversalibus"</note>—on a *Revers* or formal acknowledgment—from the Magistrate or Lord who requests the remission, stating that such a remission will not harm the jurisdiction of the one sending the prisoner, but is done without prejudice to their rights. See Gail in the *cited place.* Matthias Stephanus, *On the Office of the Judge, book 1, chapter 8, number 58.* These remissions are more frequent between equals, or from a lesser lord to a greater one, but not the other way around: and Princes do not quickly hand over a criminal to a member of the nobility.

# ADDITION.

The Governors of Provinces in which a crime has been committed are accustomed to write to their colleagues—that is, the governors of other provinces where the accused is said to be—and request from them that they transmit the accused to them along with the prosecutors. *Digest, law 7, on the custody and exhibition of defendants; Novel 134, chapter 5.* Sometimes the governor of the other province in which the accused was found writes to the Magistrate under whom the accused committed the crime, and refers the merit of the case and the quality of the person to him. *Code, law 1, on exhibiting or transmitting defendants.* Today, according to the custom of Germany, one captured in a foreign territory is not remitted to the place of the crime, but receives his forum and judgment in the place of captivity, and undergoes punishment there. The "sending over" of prisoners does not take place. Igneus witnesses that the practice of France is also observed such that no such remission occurs, in *Law on Trusts, number 232:* and the same is observed concerning the custom of the Kingdom of France. See Theodorik in *Criminal College, dispute 4, Thesis 3, throughout.* However, it is common in Germany and other provinces for more atrocious crimes, for the sake of setting an example, that a remission is made to the place of the crime as a favor and by right of friendship, neighborhood, and goodwill; and this under an antigraph or reversal letters, as they call them, of the Magistrate or Lord requesting the remission, stating that such a remission will not be a detriment to the jurisdiction of the one remitting, but will be without prejudice—upon a *Revers* and counter-acknowledgment. Matthias Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 30, number 17.* Gail, *On Public Peace, book 1, chapter 16, number 31.* Theodorik, *cited place, letter D.* In the Electorate of Saxony, it is testified that remission is necessarily made by the *Electoral Constitution, title:* that one should allow the evildoers who have committed crimes in administrative districts and fled to be followed back into those districts. The accused is to be transmitted along with the prosecutors. *Digest, law 7, on the custody of defendants.*

### 74. **Lübeck Law.** *Jus Lubecense.*

Lübeck Law extends even outside its home territory, reaching into places where the illustrious Republic of Lübeck has no jurisdiction. Thus, the people of Rostock use the same law, as Master Cothmann proves with many examples. Likewise, the Poles and Silesians use Saxon Law freely and without coercion; so too do many Vandalic and Hanseatic <note>The Hanseatic League was a powerful medieval commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in Central and Northern Europe.</note> cities use the laws of Lübeck, fearing no loss of sovereignty by doing so. Furthermore, in Livonia <note>Modern-day Estonia and Latvia</note>, the citizens of Reval <note>Modern Tallinn</note> hold to Lübeck Law. It is not a new thing for laws to be adopted by other peoples outside their original territory. For example, the Rhodian Law <note>The ancient maritime law of the island of Rhodes</note> was observed across the neighboring seas in antiquity. Similarly, Visby on the island of Gotland was once the most celebrated marketplace in all of Europe, and there sailors took their laws; in that place, just as among the Rhodians, maritime laws were established.

->ADDITION.<-

Johann Sibrandus edited the Lübeck Law. One may not appeal "from Lübeck" <note>i.e., appeal against a ruling based on this law</note> against one's own signed document or confession in debts that are clear, liquidated, and confessed. This same rule is observed in Holstein, Frankfurt am Main, Hamburg, Venice, Padua, Genoa, Florence, and throughout all of Italy. The Society of the Holy Trinity among the people of Lübeck—otherwise known as the <term>Circle Brothers</term>, and today as the <term>Noble Youths’ Company</term>—has for many years not only worn insignia consisting of a ring, open at the bottom and decorated with a half-extended circle, but has also obtained a new privilege. Regarding the Bishop of Lübeck, Sprenger treats this in his *Delineation of the States of the Empire, page 332.*

### 75. **Vacant Fiefs.** <term>Ledige Fäll</term>

<note>This term refers to "escheated" or "vacant" fiefs—estates that return to the feudal lord because the tenant died without heirs or committed a crime.</note> See Jacobus de Ardiz in his *Summary, chapter 27*, and other legal authorities such as Rosenthal and Schneidewin.

<column-break/>

The term <term>vacant fiefs</term> is accepted in Feudal Law for when someone dies without children. According to the Treaty of Harry, in Bayreuth and Ansbach <note>original: "Onolzbach"</note>, these vacant fiefs are not subject to fines. On March 1, 1639, it was indicated to the Chancery Taxator at the Imperial Court that he should not burden the Nuremberg feudal tenants regarding vacant fiefs; however, the Nuremberg vassals should, as often as a vacancy occurs, formally report to the Protocol of the Imperial Aulic Council and receive a recognition of the matter. But what were "vacant falls" <note>original: "ledige fäll"</note> in tournaments, when in their descriptions it is often narrated that someone "had so many vacant falls"? See the later volume under this entry.

### 76. **Wood-Rights.** <term>Laub</term>

<note>Literally "foliage," this refers to the communal rights to harvest timber or graze livestock in a forest.</note> A full farmstead has a "whole wood-right," a small cottage has a "half wood-right" regarding timber, communal pastures, and the number of cattle allowed to be kept, which is to be researched from the old communal charters, etc. Sometimes a "whole wood-right" consists of 5 or 6 cords <note>original: "Klaffter"</note> of wood when one harvests. In some places, a small cottage that has few appendages has only a quarter wood-right.

### 77. **Lying.** *Mendacium.*

On whether lying and speaking falsehoods are the same thing, see Martin, *Centenary Questions, 5, dispute 6, thesis 8.*

If someone commits an injury by saying "You lie!" but adds a "protestation of honor"—such as saying "Saving your honor," "Without harm to your honor," or "That is not true, but a lie"—does he deserve to be excused? Those who deny this base their reasoning on the fact that the crime of lying is most foul <note>See Acts 5:3, regarding Ananias lying to the Holy Spirit</note>, more serious than theft <note>See Ecclesiasticus 20:26</note>, a certain plague of the mind, and the most effective poison of the soul. Thus Epænetus used to say: Liars are the authors of all crimes and injuries. This vice, which is a crime in itself and brings infamy upon the one committing it, makes whoever charges another with it liable for injury. The word "you lie" is insulting because it reproaches a person with a wicked act. This holds true even if the person uses the aforementioned disclaimer ("Saving your honor"). For whenever a disclaimer is contrary to the act itself, it achieves nothing and cannot relieve the one causing the injury. Legal experts say that in a matter of fact, the arts of words or simulated disclaimers are of no use, and when the act is more powerful than the words, the disclaimer provides no relief. However, when someone speaks to defend their own innocence and preserve their honor against someone who has unjustly accused them of a crime (for example, if one is accused by another...

...of theft, adultery, etc.) and says in return: *You are lying*, he is not held liable for a legal action for injuries <note>original: "actione injuriarum"; a Roman law concept where a person could sue for damages to their reputation or person</note> according to Bartolus on Law 25, Section 1 of the Digest regarding procurators. Likewise, if a person is provoked and responds in such a manner, he is to be pardoned, as seen in Law 14, Section "if a freedman," for he is believed to have "retorted" <note>original: "retorsisse"; the legal principle of returning an insult in immediate self-defense</note> the injury in defense of his own innocence. For whatever a provoked person does is presumed to be done for his own defense. The doctors of law <note>original: "Dd."; refers to the "Doctores," or established legal commentators</note> agree on the Law regarding force and justice, and Law 25 regarding procurators. Gail, in book 2, observation 101, number 4, notes: Just as a physical attack creates the right to repel force with force, so a verbal attack may be retorted with words. And wherever an attack is unlawful, the defense is lawful; consequently, an action for injuries has no place. **For he who exercises his own right does injury to no one.** It is further certain that no one is held liable for an injury unless his deceit and intent to injure are established, as per the Cornelia Law, Section 9, and the Code of Justinian. Hence, the **intent to injure** <term>animus injuriandi: the specific malicious intent required to prove a person committed a verbal or physical insult</term> is called the foundation and substance of the injury. Cites include Gaeden, Mynsinger, and others. The will and the purpose also distinguish the acts. It is not the deed itself that is questioned, nor is the outcome of the deed regarded, but rather the will and the cause of the person doing it. Indeed, the primary cause and intention must be looked upon and considered.

Since, therefore, the intent to injure is absent in one who is provoked—and thus the primary cause—so that there is no place for a legal action for injuries, its effect also rightly ceases. For when the principal cause does not stand, the accessory consequence vanishes.

->ADDITION.<-

The law punishing a lie must be understood to apply only if the lie was told with deceit <note>original: "dolo"</note>, gross negligence, and full knowledge. It is otherwise if it was not done with deceit, gross negligence, nor knowingly. In a case of doubt, it is presumed to have been said with deceit and knowledge when it is said for the benefit of the liar himself. Wurmser, *Miscellaneous Observations*, 10.

An enemy is believed to lie. An enemy is not believed even if he is at the point of death. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 1. A **fiction** <note>original: "fictio juris"</note> is against the truth, but it is held as the truth for legal purposes. Bartolus writes on this regarding usurpation. Everyone is presumed to be endowed with the character of their native land. No lie is so impudent that it lacks a witness. Pancirollus in *The Lost Things*, page 587. One should not care what others have said, but rather what can be said based on the truth. Zasius, book 2. For nothing is so excellent that the lust for slander does not dare to attack it; no infant is so tender and beautiful that some foul-smelling old crone <note>A reference to folk superstitions regarding the "evil eye" or bad luck being "blown" onto the fortunate</note> has not breathed upon it; no maiden is of such skilled beauty or rare modesty that some "critic of sandals" <note>An allusion to the story of Apelles the painter, where a cobbler critiqued more than just the sandals in a painting</note> does not find fault; no tree is so straight that the forces of Aeolus <note>The god of the winds</note> do not sometimes rush against it.

### 80. Ludwig. Ludovicus.

Our ancient Germans gave their princes and lords exceedingly beautiful names, such as *Ludewig* in the Saxon language, meaning a protection or fortress of the people <note>original: "praesidium, arx populi"</note>. For *Wig* signifies a castle or stronghold where one finds refuge and can retreat in times of need. Thus, a prince ought to be a "Ludwig": a comfort and refuge for the people. See Luther in the 5th Jena volume, page 154, at the end.

Master Stirn provides the chronology, legislation, and statecraft of Louis the Pious in the *Treatise on the Constitutions of Princes*, title 1, sections 1–3; of Louis II, title 11, sections 1–3; of Louis the Stammerer <note>original: "Ludovici Balbi"</note>, title 11, sections 1–3; of Louis IV, sections 11 and 13–15; and of Louis the Bavarian, title 11, sections 13–15. Regarding Louis the Pious, besides this surname, Lipsius remarks in book 1, chapter 5 of *Louvain* that there were "not many beautiful things" to be found in him. Master Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain, in his *Historical Relation*, part 5, page 84, and Wormius in book 5 of *Danish Monuments*, monument 7, present two coins unearthed in Denmark near Lejre. On one, a cross is seen, surrounded by this inscription: **HLUDWICUS IMP.** <note>Emperor Louis</note>; on the reverse is the figure of a temple, around which is written **XPISTIANA RELIGIO** <note>The Christian Religion</note>. The other coin similarly has **HLUDWICUS IMP.** around a cross, while the other side features larger characters, not surrounding any image, reading **VENECIAS** <note>Venice</note>. Master Georg Richter, in his *Select Letters*, page 815 of my copy, discusses why in various histories Louis is called "the German" <note>original: "Germanicus"</note>. See also Master Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain on *Truces and Peace*, page 175 of my copy.

Ludwig, as if *Leutwick*, means "defender of the people." See Besold in *Politics*, book 1, chapter 17, number 52, volume 3. Ludwig is the "refuge of the people" or "asylum of the afflicted," *Luitwig*, according to Aventinus; it is said to be, as it were, the path or asylum of the people, to which folks retreat <note>original: "weichen"</note> from misfortune. See Master Harsdörffer in *Specimen of Philological Disquisitions*, XI, section 37, where: *Wick* is called an asylum, to which one retreats. *Ludwig*, to which the people retreat. Saint Louis <note>Louis IX of France</note> was enrolled among the saints by Boniface, according to Petrus Gregorius in the *System of Universal Law*, book 15, chapter 38, number 10. Louis the Severe in the year 1245. Louis II, nicknamed "the Virtuous," entered the Palatinate in 1437. Louis III in 1508. Louis IV in 1576. Among the Roman Emperors, Louis I, surnamed the Pious, was born in 776, elected in 814, and died in 840. Louis II was born and elected in 855 and died in 875. Louis III, surnamed the Stammerer, was born in 8 <note>the text is missing digits</note>, elected in 877, and died in 879. Louis IV was born in 8 <note>missing digits</note>, elected in 900, and died in 912. Louis the Bavarian was born in 1284, elected in 1314, and died in 1347. *Luz* and *Lute* are derived from the word *Luitweg*. This is treated extensively by

<column-break/>

Master Speidelius in his *Notables*, page 886. It is also written as **HludoWicus** in the epitaph of Louis II. The *Life of Louis the Pious* is found in the *History of the Franks* by the Twelve Writers, page 336 and following.

### 81. To Praise. Loben. <note>See also Handlohn (transfer fee) and Laudemium (landlord's fee)</note>

To praise <note>original: "Laudare"</note> among the Feudalists is to arbitrate or to judge. See Conrad Rittershusius in his *Feudal Divisions*, pages 467 and 538. For what it signifies in Civil Law, see Master Dr. Biccius in *Golden*, page 696, at the end; and on the difference between "laudation" <note>commendation</note> and "nomination," see page 698. "Praise in one's own mouth stinks" <note>original: "Proprio laus fordet in ore"</note>; this is limited whenever it is not attributed to vain boasting, but to defense or as an example. Barbosa, book 10, chapter 5, axiom 1. "One ought not to increase the malice of another by praising him." Axiom 2.

The ancients used to say *Præficini* or *Præfiscine* <note>meaning "without the evil eye" or "no offense intended"</note>. Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book 10, chapter 24. Scaliger notes that *præfiscine* is said regarding the present, and *præfiscini* regarding the future. Plautus says: "Now let me say this *præfiscini*." Elsewhere: "Add to the praise, *præfiscini*." See Steuechius in book 3 of the *Florides* of Apuleius of Madaura.

A seller is permitted to say many things for the commendation and praise of his own property which he desires to sell, and indeed at as high a price as he can. See the Code on rescinding sales, and the Digest on contracting purchases, on fraud, and on the aedile’s edict, according to that common saying:

"He praises the wares who wishes to push them off on a buyer." <note>original: "Laudat venales qui vult extrudere merces"</note>. However, the buyer is free to believe these things or not. Therefore, if he is harmed by that praise, he ought not to complain about the seller—who did what the Laws allow him to do and what agrees with his own desire to sell the item at the highest price—but about himself, since that proverbial saying can be thrown back at him: "Learn to shop more cautiously." <note>original: "Disce cautius mercari"</note>. Conrad Rittershusius should be consulted on law 23 regarding the Rules of Law, page 207 of my copy. One who is sued in a real action <note>a lawsuit over property</note> can "praise" <note>name/cite</note> his own "author" <note>the person from whom he acquired the title/warranty</note>. Christoph Philipp Richter in his *Counsels*, part 1, chapter 14, number 26, folio 68. When the "exception of praise" <note>a legal defense naming the source of title</note> takes place, see ibid., number 25. The effect of such praise, see ibid., number 28 and following. Namely, this exception is raised by naming the author and requesting that the lawsuit be denounced <note>formally announced</note> to them. Part 3, chapter 31, number 139, folio 216. In encouraging and sharpening the mind, it is most effective if you praise the one you are exhorting, if we believe Cicero. But Pliny the Younger, in book 5, letter 17, declares it the sharpest stimulus for one giving advice if you incite them with praises. For, as the Poet sings, "It holds a great spur for glory"; or as another says, "Praised virtue grows." Conversely, Agathias affirms that the sharpness of the most excellent minds is blunted when they are not praised. This is confirmed by that passage of Pliny in his *Panegyric*: "For hitherto, however sincere and upright minds were, even if it did not distort them, a wretched but true reputation still dulled them: for you see, if I do anything well, Caesar will not know, or if he knows, he will not give testimony..."

### 82. To Labor. <note>original: "Laborare"</note>

Conrad Rittershusius indicates what "to labor" <note>original: "laborare"</note> means to feudal lawyers in his *Feudal Divisions, page 379.* Master Doctor Ludwig also discusses this in his *Feudal Synopsis, chapter 16, page 90 of my manuscript.* Why is the word "labor" used to describe being in the grip of a disease, when the sick do not actually work—and are indeed forbidden from working by their doctors? This precept is discussed at length in Pliny the Elder, *Book 1, chapter 22.* It is an imitation of the Greeks, for whom the words <term>ponein</term> and <term>poneisthai</term> <note>original Greek: πονειν & πονεισθαι</note> signify both "to labor" and "to be sick." See Hippocrates, Galen, and others. For this reason, the Latins express both the burden of work and physical pain with one and the same word.

Lucretius writes in Book 2 of *On the Nature of Things*:
> It is pleasant, when the winds ruffle the water on the great sea,
> To behold from the land another's great labor. <note>original: "Suave mari magno..."</note>

Florus writes: "The credibility of the Annals labors <note>meaning "struggles" or "is strained"</note> for us to believe it."

### 83. It is Permitted. <note>original: "Licet"</note>

The term *it is permitted* <note>original: "Licet"</note> signifies a fact of action, not necessarily a legal right. <note>Citations: Institutes on Actions 4.6.5; Digest on Peculium 15.1.9.7.</note> "Licet" is often a mark of an exception rather than a statement of opposition. Master Doctor Biccius in his *Golden Works, page 204.*

### 84. Lützel. <note>Old German for "little"</note>

*Lützel* or much. *Lützel* means "little." Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 35, page 388.* "Any and all appeals of the same persons, whether they be few <note>original German: "Lützel"</note> or many." *Weser Court Ordinances, page 46.*

### 85. Leyr. A second drink pressed from the toasted remains of squeezed grapes.

The *Leyr* is a "second drink" <note>original: "potus secundus"</note>. Master Doctor Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings, page 226.* Elsewhere it is called *Laur* or "after-wine" <note>original German: "Nachwein"</note>, made from the toasted remains of pressed grapes—that is, from the seeds and skins. *Discussed extensively in the same source.*

### 86. Love. <note>original: "Lieb. Amor."</note>

It is not only the sons of Atreus who love their wives, as Sextus Caecilius said proverbially from Homer, and as Ulpian repeated in the Digest <note>Law 13, section 1, regarding the Julian Law on Adultery</note>. See Conrad Rittershusius on Law 23 *Concerning Rules of Law, page 143*, and in his commentary on Salvian, Bartholomew Bellencinus, and Remigius de Gonny.
The Prince-Electors write to Kings using the title: "Your Love" <note>original German: "Euer Lieb"</note>, and not: "Your Grace" <note>original German: "Euer Gnaden"</note>, because they are considered equal to Kings. Moller, *Semestria, book 1, chapter 40.* Waremund ab Ehrenberg, *On Confederations, book 1, chapter 2, number 147.* *Minne* also means love. *Minnen* means to be touched by the love of women. *Minnehülff* means helping through love. Schottelius in *The German Main Language, page 1074.* "To love in the Greek fashion." Rittershusius in *Novels, part 12, chapter 9, number 2.*

<column-break/>

### 87. Love-children. <note>original German: "Liebkinder"; Latin: "Parthenii"</note>

This is what the Constitution of the Elector Palatine calls them in *part 4, title 2.* Elsewhere they are called "Virgin-children" <note>original German: "Jungfrau Kinder"</note>. See Conrad Rittershusius in *Novels, part 7, chapter 5, number 2.* Referring to Craig in *On the Lacedaemonian Republic, chapter 6; Zarius Sturcius, Disputation 2, Thesis 46.* The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> required a legitimate union for one to be a citizen; those who were born of virgins before marriage were called *Parthenii* <note>Greek: "children of maidens"</note>, or "Stichling" <note>likely "thistles" or "prickles"</note>, or "Love-children," and were ordered to be excluded.

### 88. Legality. <note>original: "Legalitas"</note> See Notary.

Legality <note>original: "Legalitas"</note> here means fitness or suitability. Conrad Rittershusius in *Novels, page 608, number 7.* "Legal books of proven faith." Guido Papa, *Decision 441.* Gail, *Observations 2.20.* Menochius, *Counsel 214, number 3, at the end.*

### 89. Lobotrophi. <note>Managers of hospitals for the infirm</note>

*Lobotrophi*, or the overseers of *Lobotrophia*—those houses in which the maimed, the mutilated, the lame, and others deprived of the use of their limbs and who are weak or unfit for labor are supported. Master Conrad Rittershusius in *Novels, page 107.* Cujas in his commentary on *Novels 7* and in the *Paratitla on the Code concerning Bishops and Clerics.*

### 90. Lug ins Land. <note>German: "Look into the Land"</note>

This is the common name for a certain tower in Nuremberg, because from there one has a view far and wide. *Lugen* means to watch or spy. *Lugdunum* <note>the city of Lyon</note> is nothing other than a watchtower, from *Lugen* (to watch) and *dún*, which means a hill. Virdungus in his commentary on *Agricola, page 74, recent edition.*

### 91. Gingerbread. <note>original: "Lebkuchen. Libum."</note>

It is written that a certain *Count of Werdemberg* swallowed up the *County of Albeck* through the sweet cakes <note>original: "libis dulciariis"</note> he received from the people of *Ulm*. Lanf. in his *Orations, page 918.* See "Mead" <note>original: "Meth"</note> in the same place, and the *Bavarian Land Ordinance, book 4, folio 9*, where it is noted that the gingerbread bakers <note>original German: "Lebzelter"</note> now also brew good Mead. On the same folio and on folio 12, it states that an innkeeper should not serve confections or gingerbread to a guest without the guest's request. Among the "arts of pleasure," Klockius, in *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 37, number 15*, also counts the arts of fine dining and gourmet cooking. See Bornit, *Treatise on the Sufficiency of Things, book 2, chapter 81, and following.*

### 92. Litany. <note>original: "Litany. Litania."</note>

Regarding Litanies, see *Novels on the Most Holy Bishops, 123.* The law forbids laypeople from performing litanies—that is, rogations or public and solemn prayers—without the presence of Bishops and Clergy. It also mandates that the holy crosses carried at the front of Litanies must not be stored anywhere except in the place of sacrifice or a sacred location. Even the Emperors use the word *Litania* in the *Code concerning Heretics, law 3.* Litanies are also called rogations or public processions. Cujas also observed this, citing *Novel 67, chapter 1.* Concerning Litanies, see Conrad Rittershusius in *Novels, part 1, chapter 5, throughout.*

### 93. Lautern. <note>original: Luthra</note>

In the town of Imperial Lautern <note>original: Luthra Cæsarea; modern Kaiserslautern</note>, a chapel is visited where Frederick Barbarossa <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1155–1190</note> was accustomed to pray. In Royal Lautern <note>original: Luthra Regia; modern Königslutter</note> there is a monastery of monks and an Imperial Tomb, located three stones' distance from Brunswick. See *Master Doctor Leonhard Wurffbain, part 1 of his Historical Reports,* in the index listing where all the Emperors from Charlemagne onward lie buried.

Lautern with the surname "Imperial" is Kaisers-Luther or Kaiserslautern. *Master Doctor Leonhard Wurffbain in Historical Reports, part 7, page 235.* Royal Lautern is Königslutter. See *Conrad Rittershusius's notes on Günther, page 125.* "Lauther"—or in the Saxon dialect, "Luther"—is an old name; there have been many kings and even Emperors in Germany by this name.

### 94. Leather. <note>original: Leder; Corium</note> See also: Money. <note>original: Münz; Moneta</note>

Concerning gold and silver leather. *Klock, On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 35, number 6.* The crafts involving animal pelts and the hides of horses, cattle, calves, deer, sheep, and goats for clothing, footwear, and domestic or farm equipment; hence the tanners and curriers—specifically red-tanners <note>bark-tanners</note>, white-tanners, and makers of Cordovan leather. Likewise, those who prepare Russian leather <note>a fragrant, durable leather</note>, crimped chamois leather, and gilded or silvered leather <note>known as "Gold-leather"</note>. Tanners generally prepare skins with the powder of oak bark: which the Germans call "tanning" <note>original: deha-nen</note>, as it dyes them a chestnut color and binds the fibers. *Klock, On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 35, numbers 4 and 11,* discusses harness makers, saddlers, holster makers, and sheath makers. A fine legal case regarding saddlers and bridle-makers was decided by *Matthias Berlich, decision 26, number 1, 2, and following*, where a case regarding the pouch-makers of Brunswick is also related by the jurist *Dauthius*. *Klock, book 2, chapter 35, numbers 46 and 47,* discusses saddlers, harness makers, and coach-builders. *Master Doctor Christoph Philipp Richter, part 2, counsel 39, throughout.* Regarding that proverb, "Stealing the leather and giving the shoes as alms," because alms should not be made from another's property. *Barbosa, book 5, chapter 7, axiom 1: Alms that are offered from a crime do not please God. Ibid.* In Suidas, regarding the phrase <term>epi busēs theseōs</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ βύσης θέσεως</note>, that is, "to sit on a hide," it is recorded that it was a custom among the Scythians that if someone was wronged by another and felt themselves unable to match their adversary for revenge, they would sacrifice an ox, boil the meat cut into pieces, and sit upon the stretched-out hide of the shoulder with their hands behind their back. Among the Scythians, there was no greater form of supplication. Anyone who wished to help would take a piece of the meat, place their right foot on the hide, and promise to bring aid to the best of their ability; this was considered the most sacred of oaths. *Petrus Gregorius Tholofanus in his Compendium of Universal Law, book 50, chapter 8, number 18.* Removing the skin with the hair as a punishment. *The same, book 37, chapter 2, number 17.* To be flayed with rods and pincers. *Ibid., number 12.*

<column-break/>

Among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, leather was struck with an official stamp to serve as a substitute for minted money. *Seneca, On Benefits, book 5, chapter 14.* In Saxon Law, as a mark of contempt for an unrighteous sect, Jews were ordered to stand barefoot upon a pigskin when swearing oaths. *D. Kastelius in his Inaugural Disputation on the Jews, thesis 132.* Discussed at length by *Limnäus, volume 1, Additions to Public Law, book 3, chapter 2, number 40, page 298 and following.* A man is said to have a debt whether he owes gold coins or leather struck with a public stamp (such as was used by the Lacedaemonians to serve as currency), which Isidore also seems to affirm in *chapter 17 of Etymologies, book 16.* According to Seneca, as cited by *Cujas, Observations, book 7, chapter 33,* when Sense asks, "Will you die?" Reason responds: "I know my debt; I contracted this with my creditor, and I cannot go bankrupt." *Göddäus on the Meaning of Words, at law 159, number 3.* Regarding ox hides: although it seems like a minor trade, it is actually one of the best, and many thousands of them are brought annually from Mexico in the West Indies and from Hungary. *J. T. Sprenger in his Practice of Exchange, page 30 in my copy.* In the Margraviate of Brandenburg-Ansbach <note>Onoldino</note>, the red-tanners' guild must prepare four types of leather in one vat: horse-leather, cattle-leather, buck-leather, and calfskin. Above, under the word "Cuirass" <note>original: Küriss</note>, we heard that "Cuirassiers" are so named from "leather" <note>original: Corio</note> with which they were armed, hence the French still today say *Cuirassiers*, from *Cuir* <note>leather</note>. *As Biterolf says of the Prince of Henneberg:* "Then he stepped before the Thuringian lords in a dragon's hide" <note>original: Kür</note>, that is, leather. *Ulpian in the Digest 25.3* regarding legacies of gold and silver says that blankets and Babylonian fabrics, which are usually spread over horses, are not considered clothing. *Martian*, among the items subject to tax, lists "Babylonian skins" and "Parthian skins." *Digest, final law, § 7, on Tax Collectors.* Most understand "skins" to mean those painted with Babylonian skill, relying on the testimony of Pliny, who says in *Book 8* that Babylon was most famous for weaving various colors into painted garments and gave its name to Babylonian tapestries. *Tertullian writes the same in On Female Dress.* St. Jerome also mentions Babylonian skins in his *Letter to Laeta.* Indeed, dappled tapestries are spread over horses by Eastern peoples; however, because the Jurist specifically calls them "skins," the conjecture of *Busbequius* <note>Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, 16th-century diplomat</note> seems most probable to me. He writes that Assyria, of which Babylon is the capital, produces the most elegant lynxes, whose skins sell for 15 or 16 gold crowns. He acquired such a lynx as a gift for the Emperor because of the beauty of its hide, which was so great that when compared to common lynxes, it seemed a different animal entirely. He did not doubt that these were the "Babylonian skins" once so highly valued, mentioned in the law *Interdum* in the *Digest on Tax Collectors.* *Philippus Carolus, Various Readings, book 2, chapter 2, near the end.* In Apuleius it is said: "You are playing with someone else's hide" <note>meaning to take risks at someone else's expense</note>. *In Plautus:* "The skin is being stripped from my own back." Regarding one who wears a deerskin in which he dressed himself,

### 95. Marking. Boundary Walk. Boundary Tree. <note>original: Lochen; Lochreise; Lochbaum</note> Boundary trees. <note>original: Arbores terminales</note>

Boundary trees, called "Antemissæ" by others, are customarily marked with signs and holes <note>original: "foraminibus"</note> so they may be distinguished from other trees growing on the border; and lest these holes be overgrown by bark, they are renewed after some years have passed. *Johann Friedrich Lentz, on Boundaries, Thesis 23.* However, *Montanus, on Boundaries, chapter 19, number 4*, says that such signs are deceptive, since peasants can easily make such holes at their pleasure when the other party is absent.

<column-break/>

### 96. A summons brings safe conduct with it.

->A summons provides security.<- <note>original: Citatio securitatem præstat</note>

Everyone commonly says that a summons provides security, or "brings the safe conduct <note>original: "Glait"</note> with it." *Heigius, volume 2, question 22, number 40.* See however *Icon Ummis, Disputation on Procedure 5, in the corollary. At length.* To summon and challenge to combat. *Limnäus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 16, number 40.* To summon, to demand, to complain. *Limnäus, ibid.*

### 97. Territorial Defense. <note>original: Landwehr</note> Territory.

Concerning the destruction of the territorial defense. *Symphorema Gylmanni, volume 2, part 1, book 1, folio 39.* Territorial defense, watchtowers, toll-gates, ditches, enclosures, and fortifications. *Limnäus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 16, page 224.* From the common city hedgerows and territorial defenses. *Limnäus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 19, page 309.*

### 98. The Stone of Shame. <note>original: Lasterstein</note> The stone of scandal. <note>original: Lapis scandali</note>

The imposition of the stone of scandal or the "infamous stone" <note>a public punishment where a convict, often for bankruptcy or adultery, was forced to carry a heavy stone through town</note> is a punishment belonging to the High Jurisdiction <note>original: "meri Imperii"; the power of life and death/high criminal justice</note>. *Bocer on Jurisdiction, chapter 5, number 43.* It pertains to the lesser High Jurisdiction. *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 1, consultation 2, number 175.* See above under the <term>word Adultery</term> regarding the imposition of the stone. Regarding the stone of reproach <note>original: "lapide vituperii"</note> in Padua. *Limnäus in Public Law, volume 2, additions to book 4, chapter 8, page 310.*

### 99. Lilies. <note>original: Lilien; Lilia</note>

Lilies are ornaments for tombs. *Limnäus, book 8, chapter 8, number 46.* *Lord Harsdörffer* treats the lily very beautifully in the *German Secretary*, in the second part, *book 5, epistle 3.*
The Rabbis write that on the two great main columns in the Temple of Solomon, called Boaz and Jachin <note>meaning Strength and Stability</note>, a decorative wreath of lilies was to be seen, as well as on the seven-branched lampstand; and there our Savior says, when He speaks of the flowers in the field: "Consider the lilies," *Matthew 6:26.* And *Esdras*: "Out of all the flowers you (GOD) have chosen for yourself the lilies," *2 Esdras 5:24.* Gregory Nazianzen calls it a royal flower <note>original: βασιλικὸν ἄνθος</note>, either because its shape resembles a scepter, or because snakes flee from it, and it gives off a heart-quickening scent. The coat of arms of the King of France is said to have been given to the first Christian King, Clovis, from heaven by an angel, and from that time they carry three golden lilies floating in a sky-blue shield. *Add Limnäus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 6, numbers 33, 34, 36. Claude d'Espence wrote a treatise on the three French Lilies.*

### 100. Laughter. <note>original: Lachen; Risus</note>

The Roman Republic was transformed from an Aristocracy into a Democracy by the well-timed laughter of a single little woman. *Livy, book 6.* *Job 29:24*: "If I laughed with my children, they did not become too bold because of it." Regarding this, *Gregory says in Moralia, book 20, chapter 2*: "He who presides over others should be feared even with a laughing mouth, and loved even in his anger, so that joy does not make him contemptible, nor does sever-

It is not to be wondered at that our Savior never laughed, because nothing new ever happened to Him <note>The idea that Christ never laughed was a common medieval and early modern theological trope, based on his perfect foreknowledge and the weight of human sin.</note>, and one also reads of several serious pagans that they never laughed, such as Phocion, Cato, and Crassus. Why God was angry over Sarah’s laughter, and not over Abraham’s, when the angel announced to them in their high age that they should beget children? This is treated at length by Lord Harsdörffer in the *German Secretary*, part 1, book 10, page 28. The most weighty writer Tertullian says: "There are many things worthy of being refuted by laughter, lest they be honored by gravity: But care must be taken that the laughter itself is not later laughed at, if it were unworthy: Otherwise, wherever laughter is worthy, it is a duty." <note>original Latin: "Sunt multa risu digna revinci... officium est."</note>

*Nerva is read to have been ridiculed. Limnäus in Public Law, book 8, chapter 8, number 69.* Antonius Matthaeus on the modesty of the ancient *Jurists, page 8.* Precocious and very swift laughter is given to no one before the fortieth day <note>This refers to the ancient belief that infants do not truly smile or laugh until they are forty days old.</note>. *Ridiculous things. Lipsius’s Commentary on Tacitus.* "Give me a laurel to bite, so much do my vitals leap for laughter." You may seek an explanation from Xiphilinus’s *Commodus*: Petronius: *He moved his sides with no indecent laughter.* Bisselius, in *Icaria*, describes such laughter quite gracefully elsewhere: "He seemed to laugh lightly with his lips turned inward, showing the whiteness of his teeth. He pressed it into himself within his breast-band, lest the drink he had just taken should flow back through his nose from immoderate laughing." This was a thing he had guarded against as a lifelong rule, having noted it more than once at other banquets. For what is more foolish than those "trumpets" of people laughing effusively? What is more uncivil than the dripping of immoderate saliva? When solids and liquids run together into one and the same foulness, hanging down like infamous icicles onto the dinner-square. Another author: "To raise a loud laugh worthy of Democritus." <note>Democritus was known as the 'laughing philosopher' because he mocked the follies of mankind.</note> On excessive laughter, Petronius says: *Gyton stood among these things and was dissolving his very vitals with laughter.* Juvenal:
> The nation is a comedy: Do you laugh? He is shaken

Whereupon this melancholic person became even more dismayed, and soon after, "the rose" <note>An old term for Erysipelas, a skin infection, often used proverbially for a sudden ill turn of fate.</note> came over him, as they say in the proverb. Thus this artist was quite accurate with his prophecy. When Socrates had long endured Xanthippe brawling in the house, and at last, exhausted, had sat down before the door, she, further irritated by the man’s quiet, poured dishwater <note>original Latin: "lotio," referring to wash-water or urine.</note> over him from the window. ### 1. Machiavellians. Defenders of Machiavelli.

Regarding *Machiavelli* and his defenders, the Reverend Father Drexel <note>Jeremias Drexel (1581–1638) was a Jesuit devotional writer and preacher to the court of the Elector of Bavaria.</note> writes the following in *Phaethont*, part 1, chapter 22, section 3, page 466: "Machiavelli's defenders should know that we are not unaware of certain learned warnings from this author; nevertheless, if his doctrine is approved as a whole, it must necessarily follow that a great ruin of religion and morals will occur. For that great master of fallacies, Niccolò Machiavelli, in book 2 of his *Discourses on the Republic*, chapter 13, dared to offer this plague to the world and did not blush to commit these words to paper: *'This, it seems to me, is what Xenophon means: that a certain art of deceiving is necessary if you wish to ascend to a high pinnacle and make any remarkable progress.'* By this art, Gian Galeazzo <note>Gian Galeazzo Visconti (1351–1402), the first Duke of Milan.</note> snatched the Principality of Milan from his uncle Bernhard. Machiavelli adds: *'We consider fraud necessary for everyone who attempts to grow from small beginnings and climb to a certain great height; which is all the less shameful the more one can hide it and cover it with some honorable veil.'*"

Who would not be indignant at such a shameful pen? (Father Drexel continues). A learned and religious man, Philippe Bosquier <note>A Flemish Franciscan preacher (1562–1636).</note>, rightly condemning this writer, says: *"Machiavelli, from a Florentine scribe, was suddenly made a Master of Kings and Monarchs: O head worthy of a hundred thunderbolts!"* And yet there are states that claim for themselves the Christian and Catholic name where Machiavelli is read to boys almost in their cradles. What is there to wonder at now, that from such a Master such disciples are formed, most skilled in feigning, deceiving, and dissembling?

->ADDITION.<-

There exist Hermann Conring's <note>A polymath and advisor to royalty, Conring was a pioneer in German legal history.</note> *Political Observations on Machiavelli’s Prince*. I cannot pass over here the judgment of a most accurate jurist and most worthy censor—I, who am accustomed to hate preconceived opinions about authors worse than a dog or a snake. In *On Embassies*, book 3, chapter 9, where he instructs his Ambassador from Philosophy, he says: "In this business of words, it is not truly the case that one should say the most excellent and propose for imitation Machiavelli and his clearly golden observations on Livy. For as to those who wish him to be a most unlearned and wicked man, that is nothing to me; I praise his singular prudence, and I do not defend his impiety or wickedness, if there be any. Although, if I consider the book published against him, if I respect Machiavelli’s condition, and if I rightly judge his purpose in writing—if I also wish to assist his sayings with a better interpretation—I do not indeed see

<column-break/>

why the reputation of the dead man cannot be freed from those accusations. He who wrote against him (understand this to be Innocent Gentillet <note>A French Huguenot lawyer whose 'Anti-Machiavel' (1576) popularized the negative view of Machiavelli.</note>, a jurist of Dauphiné) neither understood him nor failed to slander him in many things; and such a man is altogether one who is most worthy of pity. *Machiavelli* was a most sharp praiser and advocate of Democracy: born, educated, and honored in that state of the Republic; a supreme enemy of Tyranny. Therefore, he does not favor the Tyrant, nor is it his purpose to instruct a tyrant, but rather, by making his secrets public, to exhibit him naked and conspicuous to the wretched people. For are we ignorant that many Princes were such as he describes? And why is it troublesome to such Princes that the man's works live and are kept in the light? This was the counsel of a most prudent man: that under the guise of princely instruction, he might educate the people." Thus speaks Alberico Gentili <note>An Italian jurist and one of the founders of the science of international law.</note>. Yet there also exists Caspar Barlaeus’s <note>A Dutch polymath and theologian (1584–1648).</note> dissertation *On the Good Prince* against the persuasions of the Florentine writer N. Machiavelli, which he scattered in his books on the Prince, the Republic, and others, where among other things he speaks thus: "*Niccolò Machiavelli* of Florence, a man of perceptive intellect but a most perverse judge of what is honorable, is believed to have earned some stage-applause among posterity for being ingenious rather than pious. In his books on the Prince and the Republic, he shapes for us a Ruler of the State whom a truly remarkable prudence (as he calls it) may commend, but whom virtue and integrity leave in a most wretched divorce. You would say a monster of a Prince is being adorned, not a Prince; an impostor, not a Father of the Fatherland; instead of a shepherd of the people, a crafty layer of snares, a shrewd broker of his own advantages, and a wolf clothed in purple, for whom every crime, provided it is prosperous and happy, stands for virtue, and religion itself is merely a trade for profit—that one thing which he thinks useful to himself and the Republic. Indeed, that most famous writer lived in that Court in which I am doubtful whether the writer rubbed his political mange onto his Princes, or the Princes onto the writer." More can be found in the said dissertation, published in folio at Amsterdam, 1633. Justus Lipsius <note>A famous humanist scholar who attempted to reconcile Machiavellian 'reason of state' with Christian morality.</note> in his *Politics*, book 4, chapter 13, seems to defend the "Pseudo-Politicians." He says: "Is it lawful that some small amount of fraud be lightly mixed in? I think so: whatever certain Zenos <note>Referring to the Stoic philosopher Zeno, known for rigid moral standards.</note> may deny me, who approve only that one path to praise directed by virtue." He adds: "Wine does not cease to be wine if it is lightly tempered with water; nor is prudence not prudence if there is a little drop of fraud in it," which he defines as "shrewd counsel, deviating from virtue and the Laws, for the good of the King and the Kingdom." But let those Politicians see to it, lest while they defend the earth, they lose heaven!
