### 3. Master. <note>original: "Magister"</note>

Those to whom the primary care of matters is entrusted, and who show greater diligence and solicitude for the things they oversee than others, and who are able to instruct others and show the way—these are called **Masters**. *Law 57, regarding the Significance of Words*. Furthermore, even the **Magistrates** themselves are named by derivation from "Masters." This term, being quite broad, was eventually transferred from economic and civil matters to scholastic ones. Today, indeed, it is specifically used for those skilled in Philosophy. Yet, for no other reason is that name held in contempt and cast down by some, except that we must often return to the tradition of Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciati (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist.</note>, who writes on *Law 57* that some are called "Masters" based on what they *ought* to be, even if they are not. In the meantime, an ignorant Master becomes a shameful fable, and empty Masterships are not undeservedly mocked.

This happens when a foolish youth, about to receive the insignia of the Mastership, ascends the Chair <note>The "cathedra" or professor's seat.</note>, looking down on everything as if from on high, and murmuring I-know-not-what confused or prescribed nonsense, while his teachers celebrate him either out of love or out of error. He swells with pride, the common folk are stunned, relatives and friends applaud, bells ring, trumpets sound, rings fly about, and the Master’s cap is placed upon his head. When these things are finished, he descends as a "wise man," though he had ascended as a fool—a transformation so truly marvelous that even Ovid <note>The Roman poet famous for his *Metamorphoses*.</note> did not know of it.

Truly, Philosophy is the study of wisdom and an action worthy of a philosopher; it is the knowledge of things divine and human, acquired through study, and the university of all disciplines as far as can be gathered from nature and the experience of nature. This is that **polymathy** <note>Universal learning across many fields.</note> which some (lacking either talent or industry) have condemned as plainly useless. Having overturned the accepted and rigorous Law of learning, they have, as if through a broken door, rushed into the Royal disciplines <note>Law, Medicine, and Theology</note> while still base and unpolished. Regarding Orators, Cicero says in his third book *On the Orator*: "Those ancients, right up to Isocrates, joined the cognition and science of all things pertaining to human morals, life, virtue, and the Republic with the method of speaking." Similarly, Plato in the *Protagoras* reports of the Sophists: that they were accustomed to teach Arithmetic, Astronomy, Geometry, Music, and also Civil science and Economics. They disputed about virtues, vices, and the nature of the immortal Gods, as Maximus of Tyre suggests in his 8th dissertation. Nor did they despise Grammar or other minor matters. They took no less care for History, which they cultivated as a part of their duty.

<column-break/>

He who approaches **Theology** while neglecting this all-encompassing erudition does so, as the saying goes, "with unwashed hands" <note>original: "illotis manibus" — a metaphor for being unprepared or irreverent.</note>, like one approaching the table of a great Prince. The great Scheckius <note>Jakob Schegk (1511–1587), a Lutheran physician and philosopher at Tübingen.</note> judged otherwise when he wrote in his first book *On Demonstration*: *"I indeed judge that the Churches will only then be quiet and blessed, if either true philosophers apply themselves to Theology, or if theologians philosophize piously."*

Those who lack this foundation and yet handle the **Law** will not escape the common Italian saying, which calls *"a mere lawyer, a mere ass."* <note>original: "merum Legistam, merum Asinum"</note>

Furthermore, the name of "Master" was formerly given also to Doctors, especially in Theology; hence our "Masters of Theology." Even in the privileges of the **University of Tübingen**, mention is rarely made of "Doctors," but only of *"the Master and the Students."*

Decius <note>Filippo Decio (1454–1535), an Italian jurist.</note> suggests that a Master of Arts who subsequently obtains the degree of Doctor should be preferred over another Doctor, in his commentary on the chapter *Clerici*, number 12 and following, *On Judgments*.

In praise of the Philosophical Mastership, Master Albert Hungerus <note>A 16th-century theologian and philosopher.</note> has a speech in his *Partitions*, book 4, oration 23.

I add no more here, but see my specific *Dissertation on Masters, Bachelors, etc.*

## 4. Magnet. <note>original: "Magnet. Magnes."</note>

Regarding the weighed power and nature of the **Magnet**, proven by examples, see Laelius Bisciolus, *Subcessive Hours*, volume 2, book 1, chapter 3; Keckerman in *Nautical Problems*, folio 601; and myself in the *Discourse on the New World*, and on the *Declination of the Magnet*; also Hulsius in the *Guidebook*, chapter 11.

### ADDITION.

The first magnet is said to have been found on Mount Ida by a herdsman named Magnes. He noticed an attraction because of the nails in his shoes or slippers and the spike of his staff, which stuck to the ground <note>original: "clavis crepidarum & baculi cuspide hærentibus"</note>; thus it takes its name from him. See Zeiller, *Letters*, century 1, page 416; Pancirollus, book 2, title 11, page 578; and Pliny, book 36, chapter 16. Pliny calls the magnet "the most pleasant miracle of nature." <note>original: "Magnes jucundissimum naturæ miraculum."</note> Klock, in *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 114, number 49, discusses where it is born; at number 48, its virtue; and at number 46, whether it was known to Solomon. Martin Zeiller, in his *Itinerary of Italy*, page 116, mentions a magnet stone that is a half-ell long and a half-ell thick, which attracts an iron chain weighing 45 pounds (Münster says 50) and does not let it fall, as Master Furtenbach also testifies.

Bodin, in *The Entirety of Nature*, stated that nothing is more admirable than the magnet and called its use "plainly divine" in *Method of History*, chapter 7. The great Scaliger gives no other exact reason for this thing than that he does not know it. More can be found in Pancirollus at the cited place. Dr. Hyppolitus à Collibus says that though the **Magnetic Mountains** are unknown to most, they nevertheless turn the edge of steel, when rubbed with a magnet, toward their own regions. See also Georg Obrecht in *Political Reflections on the Improvement of Land and People*, page 122.

## 5. Court, Court-man. <note>original: "Mahl, Mahlmann. Mallus."</note>

**Mallus** <note>An ancient Germanic term for a judicial assembly or court.</note> and **Placitum** <note>A Latin term for a public assembly or a judicial decision.</note> are accepted indifferently as the same thing. This is even known to Canon Law <note>Church law</note> in chapter 33, distinction 65, and chapter 2 of the extra-decretals regarding the fighting of Clerics; likewise in Feudal Law, in the section "if

<column-break/>

any rustic," *Feudal Laws*, book 2, title 27, where Hotoman correctly reads "placitum" for "palatium" <note>This marks a scholarly debate: did the law mean a "palace" or a "public assembly"?</note>. Lord Goldast, in his notes to volume 1 of *Alemannic Matters*, folio 177, establishes this distinction between the words: that a **Placitum** denotes a public assembly of the nobles, an **Imperial Diet** <note>original: "einen Reichstag"</note>; while a **Mallus** denotes a general judgment <note>A local court</note>. Whether this distinction always holds is doubted by Lord Gryphiander in his treatise on *Municipal Law*, chapter 65, number 9. He adds that both vocabulary words seem to be Germanic, received into the Latin language by use like many others. The former is derived from *Plan* or *Plaz* <note>Place/Square</note>, and the latter from **Mahl**, that is, a "sign" or "mark." From this come the compounds: **Boundary-mark** <note>original: "Mahlzeichen"</note>; **Engagement-gift** <note>original: "Mahlschatz", used as a pledge or earnest money</note>; **Boundary-stone** <note>original: "Mahlstein"</note>; **Jurisdictional limit** <note>original: "Mahlbann"</note>; **Judicial sign** <note>original: "Handmahl"</note>; and **Rights of citizenship** <note>original: "Bauermahl"</note>. And from here seems to have arisen **Mahlmann**, that is, a person bound to the court <note>original: "Dingpflichtig"</note>, used for a subject. See the citations in Gryphiander, chapter 65, number 10 and following.

### ADDITION.

To "manire ad mallum" means to challenge in law or to summon/demand before the court or the "Mahl-place." <note>original: "für Gericht oder für die Mahlstatt mahnen oder fordern."</note> See Schottel in *The German Main Language*, folio 129.

On the word **Mallum**, see Dr. Tabor, *On the Legitimate Use of Arms*, page 162.

**Mallus** or **Mallum**, like **Placitum**, denotes the tribunal where judgment is held. The *Lorsch Chronicle*, folio 79, mentions in a diploma three principal "malli," which are commonly called **Unbidden Things** <note>original: "ungebetene Dinge." In medieval law, these were regular court sessions held at fixed times, which people had to attend without receiving a specific summons.</note>. Knichen, in his treatise *On the Law of Territory*, chapter 4, number 91, interprets "Unbidden Things" as a "summoned court" <note>original: "Curia indictam"</note>, that is, sessions that are ordinarily carried out on a certain and designated day. **Curtis** <note>Court</note> is also used for a palace. See Antonius, *Feudal Differences*, 1, theorem 4; Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 9, number 72. There are also "Palaces" for the right of holding and inhabiting royal residences, a right granted to no one except the King or those to whom he has granted it. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, 3, theorem 8. Interpreters vary on what is to be understood by **Palatia** <note>Palaces</note>. Hotoman thinks "Palaces and Assemblies" should be read as the Germanic *Plaz* <note>Place/Square</note>, by which names he wishes to signify the right of markets or the forum, since the Emperors took for themselves alone the right of establishing markets, whereas formerly it belonged to the Senate. But this is rightly displeasing to Lord Scipio Gentilis, *Disputations on Regalian Rights*, thesis 175, and Sixtinus, book 2, chapter 17. Others, therefore, understand "Palaces" as the Royal or Imperial seats, concerning which see the Code *On Palaces and Houses*, book 11; Aegidius Bossius, *On Regalian Rights*, number 38; Sixtinus, number 2; Vultejus, chapter 5, number 17; and Bocer, chapter 10, number 162. But even this is disapproved by Lord Scipio Gentilis, who understands "Palaces" here to mean **Praetoria** <note>Administrative halls</note>, in which the Governors of Provinces and other Magistrates live and deliver the law. This explanation is also held by Hotoman and Dr. Ludwig in his *Feudal Synopsis*, chapter 13.

### 6. Steward. <note>original: "Majer. Major."</note>

### ADDITION.

For the various ways the term "Major" <note>a steward, bailiff, or farm manager</note> is used, see *Felinus on the chapter 'Super eo.' & 2. col. pen. regarding witnesses* and extensively in *Barbosa, book 11, chapter 4, axiom 1.* On **Manorial Farms, Vassal Farms, and Steward-Farms,** <note>original: "Dinckhof, Mannhof, Majerhöfen"</note> see *Gothofr. Anton. Feudal Disputations 1, thesis 4, letter f.* Regarding what bailiffs and tenant farmers owe to the Lords of the estate, see *Petrus Gregorius in the System of Universal Law, book 18, chapter 23, number 15.* Some bailiffs hold the "first cut" <note>original: "Vorschnitt"</note> during the harvest season, as can be seen in certain records: "when every steward who wishes to reap is ready, no one else shall reap that day nor hire reapers." Some are exempt from all collective taxes: "the steward of said farm shall reside there without any taxation." Some enjoy the right to cut wood in the forests, whether they need it for fuel or for building farmsteads. "That every steward residing on the farm shall take from the woods all the timber he needs for building on that same manorial farm, and for burning, without any opposition." Some have the right to appoint field-guards and forest wardens, <note>original: "Bannwarthen"</note> who are also known as field-protectors, meadow-wardens, or foresters. See the entry for the word **Bannwarthen**.

In the Court Records <note>original: "Dinckrodel"</note> of Leymersheim, in the section "and he who receives the view of the estate," it says: "he gives the steward a supplement of 6 Pfennigs for a hat, and to the farm-hands two quarters, and again for four Pfennigs cheese and bread, and to the messenger a quarter of wine." Likewise, the Court Records of Geypoltzheim state: "Item, whoever receives goods from the steward, he gives for every *Sester* <note>a dry measure</note> one Pfennig as a supplement to the steward and the farm-hands who are with him, of whom there should be at least two or three, and a 'monastery-measure' <note>original: "Closterohmen"</note> of wine, and a Simmel-bread that shall be so long from the earth that it reaches above the knee, etc." Court Records of Ittelnheim near Schnersheim, in the fourth section, state: "and if he was not previously a farm-hand, he is obliged to pay a measurement-fee for the oath and for the residency, and to put down 1 Shilling Pfennig." Court Records of Ittelnheim: "The Lord of the manorial farm shall come riding into the steward's farm with 1½ horses and 1½ men, <note>This likely refers to a specific feudal entitlement for fodder and lodging for a set number of attendants.</note> and the steward's wife shall give him a bundle of hay, and the steward shall put the horses in the stable and lock the stable well, etc., and the steward's wife shall lay the Lord of the manorial farm upon a scoured bed with rustling sheets."

### 7. Majesty. <note>original: "Majestät. Majestas."</note>

The title **Majesty** belongs solely to the Emperor, see *Arumæus on the Imperial Diets, chapter 3, number 44 and following.* But if we wish to speak politically, all those who recognize no superior can be said to possess *Majesty*. To some, the title "Royal Dignity" <note>original: "Königl. Würde"</note> is given, and this pertains to Courtly Law. Meanwhile, the Kings of Denmark and Bohemia do not use this title of **Majesty** in the Imperial Diets; because they are present there as members of the Empire,

<column-break/>

On Sovereignty and the signs it consists of, see *Guyon, Various Lessons, volume 3, chapters 24 and 25,* where there is a continuation of the marks of sovereignty with several histories contained on this subject.

Regarding Majesty and the Rights of Majesty, I have treated this in a *separate discourse*, to which I refer the reader.

And it should be noted that the solemn ceremony <note>original: "apparatus ille folennis"</note> performed when Imperial Fiefs are granted is called **Majesty**, for example: **"We, Sigismund, by the grace of God Roman King,"** etc., **"as we sat in our Royal Majesty, adorned with such dignity and beauty as is fitting by right."**

### ADDITION.

There is a threefold meaning to the Law of Majesty. **1.** There are those who place Majesty in the gravity of the person, which is venerable to the sight and hearing. See *Tacitus, Annals, book 2; Hermann Kirchner on the Republic, disputation 2, thesis 2; Althusius, Politics, book 19; Lipsius, Politics, book 2, chapter 16; Matthias Bortius in Arumæus, Academic Discourses, volume 1, discourse 30, chapter 1.* By this [presence], it is said that a certain Italian—who had intended to throw the most invincible Emperor Charles V out of a window from the top of the *Parheium* <note>a splendid building in Rome</note> while the Emperor was inside contemplating it—was deterred from his wicked purpose. See Philipp Camerarius, *Operæ Subcisivæ, century 1, chapter 30, at the beginning.* We read that others were likewise deterred and recalled from the nefarious purpose of killing Princes by this same quality, see *Camerarius, in the same place; Michael Piccart, Observations, decade 6, chapter 1.* **2.** There are those who take the word Majesty as a term of honor separate from power, and thus place Majesty solely in the preeminence of external dignity, as do *Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus, On the Republic, book 8, chapter 3; Suetonius in 'Tiberius,' chapter 30; Arnifæus, On the Right of Majesty, book 1, chapter 1, throughout.* In this respect, the Kings of the Lacedæmonians <note>Spartans</note>, the Doges of the Venetians, and others enjoying Royal dignity but exercising no actual royal power, can be said to have Majesty. **3.** Finally, there are those who use the word Majesty insofar as it consists of supreme power, in which sense Majesty is accepted by the Interpreters of Law <note>e.g., in the Digest and Code of Justinian</note> and commonly by political writers. *Arnifæus, On the Right of Majesty, book 1, chapter 1; Joachim Stephanus, On Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 7, number 8; Matthias Bortius in Arumæus, volume 1, Academic Discourse 30, on the Nature of the Right of Majesty, chapter 1, number 1.* Majesty is a divine power, descended from heaven. *Camman, On the Right of Majesty, Disputation 1, thesis 18.* Majesty is taken either for power or for preeminence. In the latter meaning, it is established that only the Emperor has Majesty, because he towers over all, *Chapter 6 on Res Judicata; Novell 30; Law 'Cum multa,' Code on Property,* whence he is also called **Most Serene** <note>original: "Allerdurchläuchtigst"</note>. Daniel Otto in Arumæus, volume 2, *Academic Discourse 15, thesis 2.* And all Princes willingly yield the first place to him...

### 9. Master-song. <note>original: "Maistergesang. Cantio Magistralis."</note>

The ancients, namely the Greeks and Latins, expressed the deeds of early heroes in rhythms and introduced many fictional and false elements into them. These were imitated by the ancient Germans in the **Book of Heroes**, **Teurdanck**, etc. To this also belong the *Master-songs*, commonly called *Maistergesang* <note>The tradition of German lyric poetry and song practiced by guilds of artisans and middle-class poets in the 14th–16th centuries</note>, see Draconius *on the origin of Patricians, chapter 11, number 6.*
However, it often happens that poetry of this kind degenerates either into lewdness or into scurrility. See Taubmann *in the preface to Virgil's Gnat.*

Regarding Master-songs, the Italian writer Christopher Milaeus says in *Universal Historical Counsel, chapter 6, final section*. Thuanus *book 127 of his histories, at the end.* Poets and ham-hocks <note>original: "Schuncken"</note> are crowned with laurel leaves because both are well-suited for drinking. Mr. Harsdörffer in the fifth part of his *Conversations, CCXIX, number 8.*

### 10. Criminal Matters. <note>original: "Malefitzsachen. Maleficium."</note>

Under the name of "maleficium" (Criminal Matters) come all criminal causes that can be prosecuted criminally and whose punishment belongs to the high jurisdiction <note>original: "meri est imperii" — the power of life and death held by a sovereign or high magistrate</note>, *law 3 on Jurisdiction, law 6, penultimate section on the office of the President, law 70 on the Rules of Law.* This includes both capital and non-capital cases, *law 2, law 28, principle on punishments; Obrecht on Jurisdiction, chapter 7; Ruland on Commissions, book 2, part 1, chapter 3, number 8 and following.* And these may either deserve a punishment to be inflicted on the body, **bearing corporal punishment**, (as almost all crimes are, for one hardly finds any for which corporal punishment is not either established by law or imposed extraordinarily by the judge's discretion. *final law on private delicts, final law on theft, final law on injuries, law 11, section 1 on house-breaking, law 8 on public trials.* In which case it is always possible to arrive at the torture of the body if the Judge so decides, *said final law on injuries, final law on house-breaking.* If, however, the Judge has imposed a fine instead of corporal punishment, it is considered in the same category, so that Appeals—which are prohibited in the Imperial Chamber <note>original: "Camera Imperiali"</note> in criminal cases only for those **bearing corporal punishment**, *Imperial Recess of the Year 1530, section "Item als sich"; Ordinance of the Chamber, book 2, title 28, section "Item nach"; Gail book 1 on Peace of the Public, final chapter, number 36*—are received there even from such fines substituted in place of corporal punishment. *Mynsinger, century 3, observation 43; Ruland on Commissions, book 2, chapter 3, number 8 and following,* which matter I have discussed in my treatise on Appeals.) or the punishment may be monetary, as in the example of the *sole law in the Code on the Julian law on bribery, final law in the Code on the Julian law on extortion, law 3 in the Code on Assessors.* And by the almost common consensus of the Doctors of Law (*although not always consistent with the Civil Law of Justinian*), sometimes the action is for a monetary penalty to be applied to the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>, *law 9, 22, and 25 on the Silanian Senate Decree, law 9 and 15, section 2 on the law of the treasury.* This is imposed no less than by one who has criminal jurisdiction and high power. *law 6 on the office of the Proconsul, law 70 on the Rules of Law, arguing from law 6 on accusations.* Although an appeal from it to the Imperial Chamber is permitted, etc.

## ADDITION.

The words "where the matter required corporal punishment" are explained by Denaisius *in his Dispute on the Right of High Jurisdiction*.
*Maleficium* contains every crime, wickedness, and foul deed, *law 1, if a household is said to have committed theft.* In Greek it is *kakērgēma* <note>original: "κακέργημα"</note> meaning a "badly done act": and also *by excellence* <note>specifically/preeminently</note> it is sometimes used for the notable crime of poisoning and sorcery.

...be accepted as a crime <note>original: "maleficium"</note>, as in the title on wrongdoers and mathematicians <note>A reference to a specific section of Roman Law, "De maleficis et mathematicis," which dealt with sorcery and forbidden arts</note>. See Peter Gregory in *Syntagma Juris Universi*, book 30, chapter 1, number 5.

Doing evil deeds is wrong also because of the example it sets for others. <note>original: "propter exemplum aliorum"</note> See Digest book 5, *On the Cornelian Law regarding Assassins*; discussed extensively by Barbosa, book 11, chapter 7, axiom 1. A crime requires the payment of a penalty. Master Bicc. in *Aureis*, section 5, thesis 192. All punishments are either capital—**painful life-punishments** <note>original German: "peinliche Lebensstraffen"</note>—or non-capital, such as **corporal punishment, penance, and fines.** <note>original German: "Leibstraff, Buß und Geldstraffen"</note> Digest book 28, on punishments; book 2, on public judgments. Capital punishments are those by which the condemned suffers either natural death (the loss of the soul/life), or civil death (the loss of citizenship), or slavery. Digest book 2, on punishments. Non-capital punishments are those where there is no danger to the "head" <note>In Roman law, "caput" or head referred to one's legal status or life</note>, some of which involve physical restraint of the body, and others involve injury to one's reputation. Digest book 28, section 1; book 6, section 2, on punishments. Master Bicc., in the cited location.

According to our customs, only those punishments are properly called "criminal"—**painful** <note>original German: "peinlich," related to the word for "pain" or "torture"</note>—which afflict the body, such as the death penalty, flogging, or the amputation of a hand; **those that go to skin and hair.** <note>original German: "die zu Haut und Haar gehen," an idiom meaning punishments affecting the physical person directly</note> Carpzov, *Criminal Treatise*, part 3, question 102, number 31 and following. However, in Civil Law, all punishments, whether corporal (inflicted on the body of the offender) or pecuniary (paid to the treasury), come under the name of "criminal," as shown by Peter Theodor in *Collegium Criminale*, dispute 10, thesis 2, letter d; Hunn, *Collegium Criminale*, dispute 6, thesis 5; Master Carpzov, cited question 102, number 27; Master Ludwell in *On Procedure*, chapter 1.

### 11. Court Location. <note>original: "Mahlstatt. Locus judicii."</note>

*Mallus* or *Mallum* <note>An ancient Latinized Germanic word for a legal assembly</note> means "Judgment" from the old German *Mahl*, from which the place for executing judgment is called a **Mahlstatt**. Hincmar in *Epistle 4*: "Provision must be made that no one is forced to come to the *mallum* or the *placitum* <note>A formal court hearing</note> against the decree of the Lord Emperor Charles, except for the Judges <note>original: "Scabini"</note> and the one seeking a legal cause." Vitus Amerbach, in his annotations to the Constitutions of Charles, says: In Lombard Laws, *mallum* and *placitum* are very often joined together for the sake of explanation, and *mallum* is a word of German origin. For we call a proclaimed or designated place **a Mahl** or **Mahlstatt**, which is why fowlers in some places say **to mark** <note>original German: "malen"</note>, that is, to note a spot. Indeed, because of this connection, he suspects that even the name *placitum* is German, derived from **Platz**, which signifies a place or area. Generally, however, *Placita* are judgments or assemblies established for the debate of causes. From this, *mallare* means to summon someone to court before a judge. Guilliman, *The Habsburgs*, book 3, chapter 1, page 66, where he says: They call the assembly or the Diet <note>original: "Comitia"</note> a *Placitum*, not only the ancient writers of former times but also the diplomas of Kings, using a German word bent and forced into a Latin form.

<column-break/>

->ADDITION.<-

Charles V promised in the Imperial Decree <note>original: "R. A." for Recessus Imperii</note> regarding the government at Worms in the year 1521, section "and shall be mentioned," *that he would not and should not hold the **Mahlstatt** [location] of the Imperial Diet further [South] than Augsburg or further [North] than Cologne.* The **judgment seats** <note>original German: "Die Dingstul"</note> are also called *Mahlstatt* or **unbidden matters**, <note>original German: "ungebeten Ding"</note> as witnessed by Dauth in *Hypothesibus*, section 8. *Mahlstatt* signifies a station, and a station is a place where either men or beasts of burden stand still. Hornigk, *On the Royal Right of Posts*, page 3.

### 12. Of Age / Puberty. <note>original: "Mannbar. Pubes."</note>

Should puberty be judged by the physical condition of the body? See Lycklama, last chapter, law 13. On the word *Bar*, see above under the word **Baron** <note>original: "Freyherr"</note>, where *Bar* sometimes increases the meaning.

->ADDITION.<-

A person under the age of puberty <note>original: "impubes"</note> is understood to have completed their years when they reach the final day, and the day begun is considered as completed. This is the same as in the *Aelian Sentian Law* via Digest book 1, on manumissions; however, Borcholt warns that this only applies to males. For in females, according to the same author, the day must be fully completed (per Digest book 5, on those not permitted), so that although they obtain the right to make a will sooner than men, they are also more strictly confined by the boundary of time. Fornerius in law *anniculus* 143, on the meaning of words. Whether this fits our Law can perhaps be doubted with good reason. When asked why females reach puberty faster than males, the Doctors <note>Legal scholars</note> answer: because they are weaker, colder, and moister than males. Small apples ripen faster; sturdy ones later. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* book 7, chapter 7: moist and loose things grow faster. For willows grow faster than oaks. See Forster, book 1, on the Institutes, number 17, and those cited there. Those "proximate to puberty" are those who are only six months away from it. Discussed at length by Barbosa, book 11, chapter 7, axiom 3. **Underage** <note>original German: "unmündig"</note> means one who has not reached puberty. Draco, *On Patricians*, page 186.

**These are taken to mean Feudal Books.** <note>original German: "Lehenbücher"</note> For "Man" <note>original: "Mann"</note> is used to mean a Vassal.

<meta>This page continues a legal discussion regarding court procedures, specifically transitioning from the nature of crimes and punishments into the procedural mechanics of judicial mandates and the rights of defendants to contest them.</meta>

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Knowledge
### Page 688

Nothing changes concerning the nature of a mandate, and the Chamber <note>The Reichskammergericht or Imperial Chamber Court, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> can also decree a **Mandate with a Clause** <note>original Latin: "Mandatum cum Clausula"; a court order that gives the defendant an alternative, such as "do this or show cause why it shouldn't be done"</note> by virtue of its office, even if a **Mandate without a Clause** <note>original Latin: "Mandatum sine Clausula"; a peremptory order requiring immediate compliance without an initial hearing</note> is requested. Reichwin, *in form. fol.* 203. *num.* 4. *& seqq. Also fol.* 226.

The same Reichwin has collected very many examples of Mandates without a Clause in the *cited location, fol.* 525. *& seqq.*; see also the individual treatise by Peter Friderich.

According to the Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance <note>original German: "Kayserlichen Cammergerichts-Ordnung"</note> and praiseworthy observation, in cases prohibited by law <note>original Latin: "in causis jure prohibitis"</note>, Mandates without a Clause are granted without a prior citation of the party. However, this occurs only in those cases of such a nature that the committed act cannot be excused from penalty in any way. For otherwise, where the deed is so arranged that it might be excused for some reason, then such a mandate ought not be decreed without a citation of the party. For even where a penalty is said to be incurred by the law itself, a citation is required. *Law: ejus qui delatorem, and Bartolus there, on the Law of the Fisc; and in the chapter 'cùm secundum Leges' in the section on confiscation, and the Doctors there in book 6.* Tiraquellus *in his repetition of the law 'si unquam' on the word 'revertatur,' num.* 400, where he confirms this with many authorities. Gabriel Romanus, *book 7, common opinions, conclusion 12, num. 1 and following.*

Likewise, in any declaration of a penalty, even where it does not concern the loss of possession, a citation is required. *The Gloss on the section 'præsenti de conf.' on the word 'constiterit,' and in section 2 'de poen.' on the word 'constiterit.'* Angelus Romanus and Imola *on the law 'is cui bonis' regarding verbal obligations.* Ruinus, *counsel 50, vol. 1, and counsel 154, vol. 1.* Therefore, no act ought to be annulled through mandates without a Clause. Granted, it is said that the annulment of a contract is not a penalty where someone desires to obtain nothing for themselves through a void contract that they did not have before. Baldus and Castrensis *on the law 'nemo Martyres' regarding the Holy Churches.* For that is to be understood regarding the annulment of an act from which no prejudice is brought against a party.

How is a judge's precept resolved into the force of a citation? Johannes Robertus, book 3, *chapter 17*; this occurs in Mandates with a Clause.

Mandates without a Clause are not given to an assignee <note>original Latin: "cessionario"; someone to whom a right or property has been transferred</note> unless he proves the assignment. Berlichius, vol. 1, *conclusion 55, num. 45.*

When a contract is void, a person is heard even if there is a pact not to oppose it, or even an oath; it is otherwise in a rescission, because he ought to pay first. Maestrillus, *decision 14, num. 16, toward the end and following.*

Regarding which exceptions executive mandates admit, and that execution may nonetheless be enjoined while the case remains preserved: see Colerus, *part 4, chapter 2, throughout the discussion, especially num. 28.* Chamber Court Ordinance, *book 2, title 23, at the beginning.*

The things that can be opposed in a process of Mandates are almost the same as those in a summary process; concerning these, see Marcellus Calamus and Carolus de Graffis *on statutes repelling all exceptions.*

And it should be noted that in each and every mandate matter—even if the execution was mandated and ordered—nevertheless the **exceptions of incompetence** <note>challenging the court's jurisdiction</note>, likewise **lack of permission**

<column-break/>

**to summon to court** <note>original Latin: "venia in jus vocandi"</note> in cases where the laws require it, as well as **subreption and obreption** <note>original Latin: "sub- & obreptionis"; subreption is obtaining something by concealing the truth, obreption is by stating a falsehood</note>—namely, that the petitions and mandates brought forward by the complaining side do not rest on the ground of truth, etc.—must always and in all cases be used and permitted, as Gail teaches in *observation 14.*

Furthermore, it is established that in an executive process, only **notorious exceptions** <note>obvious or self-evident defenses</note> are admitted, the proof of which can be easily obtained at present, or which can be proven immediately. Panormitanus *on the chapter 'literis,' num. 30, on the restitution of spoils.* Wesenbeck, *counsel 6, part 1, num. 66.*

From this, all exceptions are repelled that tend to delay or retard the process in any way. For this reason, so that a judge does not interpose his role regarding a "ready execution" <note>original Latin: "parata executione"; a fast-tracked enforcement of a debt</note> which is urged by a creditor by force of a pact or statute, it is necessary for the truth of the opposed exception to be established for him, specifically through **instruments** <note>legal documents or deeds</note> and not through live vocal testimony, which requires a broader investigation. Rebuffus, *on executive sentences, art. 9, gloss 3, num. 49.* Menochius, *arbitrary cases, case 17, num. 7.*

And thus, notwithstanding the exceptions of the defendant, the "ready execution" proceeds, though the defendant’s right is reserved to prove the opposed exception in another instance after the execution has been carried out. Berlichius, *vol. 1, final conclusion, num. 83* (where he says that only after the execution is done can the debtor recover what he paid unduly). Colerus, *on executive process, part 4, chapter 2, throughout the discourse, especially num. 28*, where he adds that he remembers for 30 years now that sensible judges have for the most part judged this way in practice. See Tuschus, *practical conclusions, letter E, conclusion 408*, regarding which exceptions are admitted against **Guarentigiated Instruments** <note>original Latin: "Instrumenta Guarentigiata"; notarized documents that include a clause allowing for immediate execution without a full trial</note>. Add Cofta, *counsel 73*, and Cancer, *various resolutions, tom. 2, chap. 3*, where they have much concerning Guarentigiated Instruments.

And because in **Mandates without a Clause**, no exceptions are granted regarding the merits of the case—and these must be discussed fully, separately, and individually in their own place in an ordinary trial regarding ownership or possession—the person obtaining such a mandate should, in his replies, establish a difference between the outrageousness, the enormity, and the injustice of the act, and the merits of the principal case, and not allow these to be mixed. Peter Friderich Mindanus also advises this in *book 2 on mandates, chapter 15, throughout the discourse.*

If this were not done—namely, if one were to take notice of exceptions tending not against the Guarentigiated Instrument itself but against the action or the cause of the obligation—then everything handed down by the interpreters of our law regarding the difference between the ordinary executive process and the force and efficacy of Guarentigiated Instruments would be entirely in vain and useless.

<summary>This page discusses the legal procedures for court mandates in the Holy Roman Empire, specifically the differences between mandates with and without clauses, and the limited circumstances under which a defendant can delay execution through legal exceptions.</summary>
<keywords>Mandate with a Clause, Mandate without a Clause, Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, executive process, Guarentigiated Instruments, judicial citation, legal exceptions, subreption, obreption</keywords>

### Enlarged Practical Treasury

...nothing changes concerning the nature of the mandate, and the Court <note>The *Camera*, or Imperial Chamber Court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> can also decree a **Mandate with a Clause** <note>original Latin: "Mandatum cum Clausula"; a court order that provides an alternative, such as "do this or show cause why not"</note> by its own office, even if a **Mandate without a Clause** <note>original Latin: "Mandatum sine Clausula"; a direct, peremptory order</note> is requested. See Reichwin, *in forms, folio 203, number 4 and following, as well as folio 226.*

The same Reichwin has collected very many examples of mandates without a clause in the *cited location, folio 525 and following; and see the individual treatise* by Peter Friedrich.

According to the Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance <note>original German: "Kaiserlichen Cammergerichts-Ordnung"</note> and praiseworthy observance, in cases prohibited by law, **Mandates without a Clause** are granted without a previous **Citation** <note>A formal summons or notice to appear in court</note> of the party. However, this only happens in those cases of such a nature that the committed act cannot be excused from punishment in any way. Otherwise, where the fact is of such a kind that it might be excused for some reason, then such a mandate ought not to be decreed without a Citation of the party. For even where a penalty is said to be incurred by the law itself, a citation is required. See *the law concerning him who is an informer* <note>original Latin: "l. ejus qui delatorem"</note> and Bartolus's commentary there in the Digest *on the Law of the Treasury*; and in the chapter *since according to the Laws*, the section *on confiscated goods*, and the doctors' commentary there in the sixth book of Decretals. Tiraquellus in his *repetition on the law 'if ever' under the word 'he shall return', number 400*, where he confirms this with many authorities. Gabriel Romanus, *book 7, common opinions, conclusion 12, number 1 and following.*

Likewise, in any declaration of punishment, even where the loss of possession is not at stake, a Citation is required. See the *Gloss on the present Clementine Decree regarding confession, under the word 'it shall be established', and in the second Clementine Decree regarding penalties, under the word 'it shall be established'.* Angelo de Ubaldis, Romanus, and Imola on the law *he to whom the goods*, in the Digest *on Verbal Obligations*. Ruinus, *counsel 50, volume 1, and counsel 154, volume 1.* Therefore, an act should not be annulled through mandates without a clause. It may be said that the annulment of a contract is not a penalty where someone seeks to gain nothing for themselves through a null contract that they did not have before. Baldus and Castrensis on the law *no one [shall honor] Martyrs*, in the Code *on the Most Holy Churches*. For that is to be understood regarding the annulment of an act from which no prejudice is brought against a party.

How is a Judge’s precept resolved into the force of a citation? Joannes Robertus, *book 3, chapter 17*, which occurs in Mandates with a Clause.

Mandates without a Clause are not given to a transferee <note>original Latin: "cessionario"; one to whom a right or property is transferred</note> unless he proves the transfer. Berlichius, *1st conclusion 55, number 45.*

When a contract is null, a person is heard even if there is a pact not to oppose it, even under oath; it is otherwise in a rescission, because he must pay first. Mastrillus, *decision 14, number 16 at the end and following.*

What exceptions do **executive mandates** <note>Orders intended to enforce a judgment or undisputed debt</note> admit, and that execution should nonetheless be enjoined while the case remains preserved? See Coler, *part 4, chapter 2, through the discussion, especially number 28.* Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, *book 2, title 23, at the beginning.*

The things that can be opposed in the process of Mandates are almost the same as those in a summary process, concerning which see Marcello Calam and Carlo de Graffis *on statutes repelling all exceptions.*

And it should be noted that in each and every mandate matter, even when execution has been mandated and commanded, nevertheless the exceptions of lack of jurisdiction <note>original Latin: "incompetentiæ"</note>, and likewise the failure to seek

<column-break/>

permission to sue <note>original Latin: "venia in jus vocandi"; a requirement in some legal systems to ask the court's permission before suing certain people, like parents or patrons</note>—in cases where the laws require it—as well as exceptions of **stealth and deception** <note>original Latin: "sub- & obreptitiis"; referring to obtaining a legal favor by concealing the truth or stating a falsehood</note>, namely that the petitions and mandates brought by the complaining side do not rest on the ground of truth, etc., must always be used and admitted. Gail, *1st observation, 14.*

Furthermore, it is established that in an **Executive Process** <note>A fast-track legal procedure to enforce a debt or obligation</note> only **notorious** <note>Obvious, well-known, or indisputable</note> exceptions are admitted, specifically those for which proof can be easily had at present, or which can be proven immediately. Panormitanus in the chapter *letters, number 30, outside the topic of Restitution for Spoliation.* Wesenbeck, *counsel 6, part 1, number 66.*

From this, all exceptions are rejected which tend to delay or retard the process in any way. For this purpose, it is necessary for the Judge to interpose his parts concerning the ready execution which is urged by the creditor by virtue of a pact or Statute; he must be certain of the truth of the opposed exception, and the same must be proven through **Instruments** <note>Written legal documents/deeds</note>, not through the testimony of living voices, which require a broader investigation. Rebuffus, *on executive sentences, article 9, gloss 3, number 49.* Menochius, *on arbitrary cases, case 83, number 7.*

And so, notwithstanding the exceptions of the defendant, the court proceeds to the ready execution, yet with the defendant’s right reserved to prove the opposed exception in another instance after the execution has been carried out. Berlichius, *volume 1, final conclusion, number 83* (where he says that only after the execution is done can the person recover what he paid unduly). Coler, *on the executive process, part 4, chapter 2, throughout the discussion*, especially number 28, where he adds that he remembers for 30 years now that sensible judges have, for the most part, judged this way in practice. See Tuschus, *practical conclusions, letter E, conclusion 408*, regarding which exceptions are admitted against **Guaranteed Instruments** <note>original Latin: "Instrumenta Guarentigiata"; notarized documents that allow for immediate enforcement without a trial</note>. Add Costa, *counsel 73*, and Cancer, *various resolutions, volume 2, chapter 3*, which contain much regarding Guaranteed Instruments.

And that in Mandates without a Clause, no exceptions are granted regarding the merits of the case, and these must be fully, separately, and individually discussed in their own place in an **Ordinary Judgment** <note>A full, standard trial</note>, whether seeking ownership or possession. The person obtaining such a mandate must, in his replies, establish a difference between the outrageousness, the enormity, and the injustice of the deed, and the merits of the principal case, and not allow these to be mixed with those. Peter Friedrich Mindanus also advises this in *book 2, on mandates, chapter 15, throughout the discussion.*

If this were not to happen, and one were recently to take notice of exceptions not against the **Guaranteed Instrument**, but tending against the action itself or the cause of the obligation, then everything that is handed down in our law and by its interpreters regarding the difference between the ordinary executive process and the force and efficacy of Guaranteed Instruments would be entirely in vain and for nothing.

### ADDITION.

**Mandates** regarding the four cases <note>original Latin: "Mandata auf die vier Fälle"; referring to specific legal circumstances where the Imperial Chamber Court could issue an immediate order</note> according to Title 23 of the Chamber Ordinances, part 2, concerning when they may be extracted: see Klock, volume 1, consultation 37, numbers 369, 371, and 372; and consultation 48, numbers 13 through 20. **Mandates without a clause** <note>A peremptory court order requiring immediate action without an initial hearing</note> allow for excuses regarding the non-commission of a penalty, but not for reasons regarding the non-partition of assets. See Klock, volume 1, consultation 2, number 2. For when mandates can be decreed in the Chamber without a clause, see consultation 2, number 5.

A mandate, a command, or an order excuses the person who is under a necessity to obey. <note>original Latin: "Mandatum, jussus & imperium"; a legal principle that one is not liable for an act done under the legal compulsion of a superior</note> See the law *in fraudem 10* at the final paragraph in the Digest *concerning those who are unworthy*; also the law *si tantum 13* in the Digest *on the Falcidian Law*. This is treated extensively by Barbossa in book 11, chapter 10, axiom 1. Even when a mandate without a clause is obtained, there is still room for claims of "subreption" or "obreption" <note>Legal terms for obtaining a court order through either the concealment of truth (subreption) or the statement of a falsehood (obreption)</note>. See Ummius in *On Procedures*, my page 353, and the authorities cited there. Regarding whether a mandate without a clause should be decreed for a debtor’s sealed writings—as if for a liquid and confessed debt—see Hopingk *On the Right of Seals*, chapter 11, numbers 33 and following. On how a seal, among other things, creates a basis for a mandate without a clause, see chapter 10, number 90. Schwanmann provides the differences between mandates with and without a clause.

### 15. Manngeld. Money that is given to the heirs of the slain.

This is what the ancient Germans called the pecuniary penalties for murderers <note>original Latin: "homicidarum pœnas pecuniarias"; this refers to "Wergild," the "price of a man" paid to a family to prevent a blood feud</note>. See Heigius, book 1, question 8, number 81. For under the laws of the Lombards and others, homicides and almost all crimes were punished with a monetary fine. In the Saxon tradition, this is called *Wehrgeld* <note>original German: "Wehrgeld"; the protective or defense money paid as restitution</note>.

This money, known as **man-money** or **atonement-money** <note>original German: "das Mann- oder Sühngeld"</note>, belongs not only to the agnates and male relatives—the **sword-kin** <note>original German: "die Schwertmagen"; relatives linked through the male line who were entitled to carry weapons</note>—but also to the female relatives, the **spindle-kin** <note>original German: "die Spillmagen"; relatives linked through the female line, associated with domestic labor like spinning</note>. It should be noted that under Lombard and Saxon law, it was once observed and ruled differently: namely, that the "vengeance of the blood" and consequently the monetary penalty (commonly called *Manngeld*) pertained to the agnates alone. See Hering *On Sureties*, chapter 10, number 352, etc., and Pistor, observation 203.

### ADDITION.

On **Manngeld**, see Gottfried Antonius, page 17, *Disputations on Fiefs*, 1, theorem 4, letter b, where the term signifies the same as a **Chamber-fief** <note>original German: "Cammerlehen"; a fief held directly from the treasury or chamber of a lord</note>. But according to Treutler, volume 1, disputation 5, theorem 5, letter d, **man-money** or **atonement-money** is the name for that money given to the sons or male relatives of the slain. See more at that location and the authors cited there.

### 16. Mann. A Man or Husband.

The term is sometimes used to mean **Husband** <note>original Latin: "Marito"</note>. From this, a question arises: Is a marriage proved if a woman says, "He is my **man**" <note>original German: "Er ist mein Mann"</note>? See Uranius, volume 3, consultation 21, folio 137, number 9. In ancient times, **Man** was used to mean **Vassal** <note>original Latin: "Vasallo"</note>, as I mentioned above under the word **Baron** <note>original Latin: "Freyherr"</note> and in the treatise *On Barons*. Similarly, the Spaniards and today Varro use it for a "brave man" and "husband." A legacy left to a boy "when he becomes a

<column-break/>

**man**" must be paid even to an unmarried man once he reaches 25 years of age. See Pfeil, consultation 69.

### ADDITION.

Rodornius Scrickkius says in book 3 of his *Adversaria*, chapter 6: "Modern critics labor in vain over the origins of the gods Tuifco and Mannus <note>Legendary ancestors of the Germanic people mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus</note> while they think it must be referred back to our word **Mann**, which signifies a male person." For Caesar, in book 6 of the *Gallic Wars*, speaks of the Germans thus: "They count in the number of the gods only those whom they can see and by whose power they are openly helped: the Sun, Vulcan (Fire), and the Moon; of the others, they have not even heard by report." "Behold," says Rodornius, "Caesar recognized the God of the Germans, *Tiefcon* or *Tiefonn*, as **The Sun** <note>original German: "die Sonn"</note>, for nothing is more beautiful than the Sun; just as he recognized **Mann** or *Maan* as the **Moon** <note>original German: "Maan" or "Mond"</note>." For more on this, see Justus Georgius Schottel in *The German Main Language*, folio 70.

Husbands, that is, Spouses. See the law *si vir 52*, paragraph 1, at the end, *on donations between husband and wife*.

### 17. Mann- or Fief-Court Men. A Feudal Court.

If there is a controversy between a Lord and a Vassal concerning a fief, it is not the Lord who judges, but the **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Pares Curiæ"; other vassals of the same rank who ensure an impartial trial</note>, as they are called. This is according to the texts in the *Books of Fiefs*, title 10, book 1; titles 39, 20, 22; the paragraph "Ownership is ended" in title 29; and title 55, book 2. Schwanmann treats this question more extensively in consultation 7, as does Eberhard Speckhan in century 2, question 35, class 4, whom you should see. To this, compare what Güntherus says in the *Ligurinus* <note>An epic poem by Gunther of Pairis about the deeds of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa</note>, when he writes:

> ->*If a lawsuit arises for a fief, which you admit was*<-
> ->*received through his grant, but you now deny it;*<-
> ->*If the Vassal moves the case, not you, but the Court*<-
> ->*shall hear as Judge, and determine the cause in a set order.*<-

Now this is called the **Award of the Peers** <note>original Latin: "Laudamentum Parium"</note> according to book 2 of the *Books of Fiefs*, title 21. Sometimes it is called the **Praise of the Peers** <note>original Latin: "Laudatio Parium"</note>, as in the Constitutions of Emperor Henry II. "To praise" (*laudare*) in place of "rendering an award" (*ferre Laudum*) is nothing other than to judge. To the Germans, this judgment is called the **Man-Court** <note>original German: "das Manngericht"</note>. The reason why the Lord is not the Judge in this case is given as follows: because no one can be a judge in his own cause. See Rittershusius, *Feudal Partitions*, book 2, chapter 9, number 6. However, it must be noted here that if a Lord has many vassals, whether all, or which ones and how many of them, are to be chosen for the decision of the case. See Schrader, volume 1, consultation 1, numbers 707 and 717; Schwanmann, observation 11, number 17; and Schneidewin in the *Epitome of Feudal Law*, part 9, number 25.

But what if the Lord has no peers at all who have acknowledged a fief from him? See Schneidewin at the cited location, number 24. Or what if they are not suitable? See Speckhan, century 1, question 35, class 4, numbers 15 and following.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding judicial mandates, specifically focusing on the procedural differences between mandates issued with or without a "clause" (a provision allowing the defendant to explain themselves before execution) within the context of the Imperial Chamber Court.</meta>

-># Treasuries of Practical [Legal] Knowledge, Augmented<-

...nothing changes concerning the nature of the mandate, and the Chamber may also, by virtue of its office, decree a **Mandate with a Clause** <note>original Latin: "Mandatum cum Clausula"; a court order that requires the defendant to either comply or appear in court to explain why they have not</note>, even if a **Mandate without a Clause** <note>original Latin: "Mandatum sine Clausula"; a peremptory order for immediate action without an initial hearing</note> is requested. *Reichwin, in forms, folio 203, number 4 and following; also folio 226.*

The same Reichwin collected many examples of Mandates without a Clause in the *cited location, folio 525 and following; see also the individual treatise* of Peter Friderus.

By virtue of the **Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance** <note>original German: "Kaiserlichen Cammergerichts-Ordnung"; the foundational procedural law of the highest court in the Holy Roman Empire</note> and laudable practice, in cases prohibited by law, Mandates without a Clause are granted without a prior **citation of the party** <note>A formal summons to appear in court</note>. However, this occurs only in those cases of such a nature that the act committed can in no way be excused from penalty. Otherwise, where the facts are such that they might be excused for some reason, then such a mandate ought not to be decreed without a citation of the party. For even where a penalty is said to be incurred by the law itself, a summons is required. *Law: "ejus qui delatorem" and the commentary by Bartolus there, Digest on the Law of the Fisc; and in the chapter "cum secundum Leges," section on confiscation, and the Doctors of Law there, in the 6th book.* Tiraquellus *in the repetition of the law "si unquam" on the word "revertatur," number 400,* where he confirms this with many authorities. Gabriel Romanus, *book 7, Common Opinions, conclusion 12, number 1 and following.*

Likewise, in any declaration of penalty, even where it does not involve the loss of possession, a summons is required. *Gloss on the Clementines "praesenti" concerning confirmation, on the word "constiterit"; and in the 2nd Clementine concerning penalties, on the word "constiterit."* Angelus de Ubaldis, Romanus, and Imola *on the law "is cui bonis," Digest on Verbal Obligations.* Ruinus, *council 50, volume 1, and council 154, volume 1.* Therefore, no act ought to be annulled through mandates without a clause. It may be said that the annulment of a contract is not a penalty when someone seeks to gain nothing for themselves through a void contract that they did not have before. *Baldus and Castrensis on the law "nemo Martyres," Code on the Most Holy Churches.* This is to be understood regarding the annulment of an act from which no prejudice is caused to the party.

How is a judge's precept resolved into the force of a citation? Johannes Robertus, *book 3, chapter 17*; this occurs in Mandates with a Clause.

Mandates without a Clause are not given to an assignee <note>original Latin: "cessionario"; someone to whom a right or property has been transferred</note> unless he proves the assignment. *Berlichius, part 1, conclusion 55, number 45.*

When a contract is void, a person is heard even if there is a pact not to oppose it, or even an oath; it is otherwise in a rescission, because one must first pay. *Maestrillius, decision 14, number 16 at the end, and following.*

Regarding what exceptions executive mandates admit, and that execution may nevertheless be enjoined while the case remains preserved, see *Colerus, part 4, chapter 2, through the discussion, especially number 28; and the Chamber Court Ordinance, book 2, title 23, at the beginning.*

The things that can be opposed in the process of Mandates are almost the same as those in a summary process, concerning which see Marcellus Calamus and Carolus de Graffis *on the statutes repelling all exceptions.*

And it should be noted that in all and every Mandate-matter, even when the execution has been ordered and commanded, nevertheless the exceptions of incompetence, and likewise the failure to seek

<column-break/>

leave to sue <note>original Latin: "venia in jus vocandi"; a formal permission required in some legal systems to bring a lawsuit against certain parties, such as parents or patrons</note> in cases where the laws require it—no less than the claims of **subreption and obreption** <note>legal terms for obtaining a court order by concealing the truth (subreption) or stating a falsehood (obreption)</note>, namely that the petitions and mandates brought forward by the complaining side do not rest on the ground of truth, etc.—must always be used and admitted, as Gail teaches in *observation 1, 14.*

Furthermore, it is well established that in the **Executive Process** <note>A streamlined legal procedure used to quickly enforce a clear debt or obligation</note> only "notorious" exceptions are admitted—those, namely, for which proof can be easily obtained at present, or which can be proven immediately. *Panormitanus in the chapter "literis," number 30, De Restitutione Spoliatorum.* Wesenbeck, *council 6, part 1, number 66.*

From this, all exceptions are rejected which tend to delay or retard the process in any way. For this reason, so that the Judge does not withhold his hand from the "ready execution" <note>original Latin: "parata executio"; an execution of judgment that is ready to proceed without further trial</note> which is urged by the creditor by virtue of a pact or statute, it is necessary for the truth of the opposed exception to be clear to him, and indeed through written documents <note>original Latin: "Instrumenta"</note>, not through oral testimony <note>original Latin: "testimonia vivae vocis"</note>, which requires a wider investigation. *Rebuffus on executive sentences, article 9, gloss 3, number 49.* Menochius, *Arbitrary Cases, case 17, number 7.*

Thus, notwithstanding the defendant's exceptions, one proceeds to the ready execution, while the defendant's right is reserved for another instance for the proof of the opposed exception, after the execution has been carried out. *Berlichius, volume 1, final conclusion, number 83* (where he says that only after the execution is done can the debtor recover what he paid unduly). *Colerus on the executive process, part 4, chapter 2, throughout the discussion, especially number 28,* where he adds that he remembers for 30 years now that sensible judges have, for the most part, judged this way in practice. See *Tuschus, Practical Conclusions, letter E, conclusion 408,* regarding which exceptions are admitted against **Guaranteed Instruments** <note>original Latin: "Instrumenta Guarentigiata"; notarized documents containing a clause that allows for immediate execution of the debt without a trial</note>. Add *Costa, council 73, and Cancer, Various Resolutions, volume 2, chapter 3,* where they have much to say about Guaranteed Instruments.

And because in **Mandates without a Clause**, no exceptions are granted regarding the merits of the case, these must be fully, separately, and individually discussed in their own place in an ordinary judgment (whether petitory or possessory). The one requesting such a mandate must, in his replies, establish a difference between the "exorbitance," the "enormity," and the "injustice of the act" on one hand, and the "merits of the principal case" on the other, and not allow these to be mixed. *Peter Fridericus Mindanus also advises this in book 2 on mandates, chapter 15, throughout the discussion.*

If this were not to happen—namely, if one were to take notice of exceptions tending not against the Guaranteed Instrument itself, but against the action or the cause of the obligation—then everything handed down in our law and by its interpreters regarding the difference between the ordinary executive process and the force and efficacy of Guaranteed Instruments would be entirely in vain and useless.

<summary>This page discusses the strict procedural rules for "Mandates without a Clause" in the Imperial Chamber Court, emphasizing that immediate execution is standard and that most defenses (exceptions) can only be heard after the execution has occurred to prevent legal delays.</summary>

<header>Letter M.</header>

### ADDITION.

**Mandates** <note>original Latin: "Mandata"; formal judicial orders or injunctions issued by a court</note> for the four cases according to *title 23 of the Chamber Ordinance, part 2, regarding when they may be extracted. Klock, volume 1, consultation 37, numbers 369, 371, and 372; and consultation 48, numbers 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20.* Mandates without a clause <note>original Latin: "Mandata sine clausula"; a peremptory order for immediate action without allowing the defendant an initial chance to explain themselves</note> allow for reasons of non-commission of a penalty, but do not allow for reasons of non-partition. *Klock, volume 1, consultation 2, number 2.* Regarding when mandates may be decreed in the Chamber without a clause, see *consultation 2, number 5.*

A mandate, a command, and an exercise of authority excuse the person who is under a necessity to obey. <note>Under Roman law, a subordinate generally could not be held liable for an act done under the direct order of a superior</note> *Digest, law: "in fraudem" 10, final section, on those who are unworthy; law: "si tantum" 13, on the Falcidian Law.* Discussed extensively by *Barbosa, book 11, chapter 10, axiom 1.* Even when a mandate without a clause is obtained, there is still a place for **stealthy or deceitful acquisition** <note>original Latin: "sub & obreptioni"; legal terms for obtaining a writ by concealing the truth or stating a falsehood</note>. See *Ummius on procedure, page (in my copy) 353,* and the authors cited there. On whether a mandate without a clause should be decreed for the sealed writings of a debtor, as if for a liquid and confessed debt: *Hopingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 11, number 33 and following.* How a seal creates a place for a mandate without a clause among other things: *chapter 10, number 90.* The differences between mandates with and without a clause are provided by *Schwanmann.*

## 15. Manngeld. Money given to the heirs of a slain person.

This is what the ancient Germans called pecuniary penalties for homicide. *Heigius, book 1, question 8, number 81.* For under the laws of the Lombards, etc., homicides and almost all crimes were punished with a monetary fine. Which in Saxony is called **Wehrgeld** <note>original German: "Wehrgeld"; the value placed on a person's life, paid as compensation to prevent a blood feud</note>.

This money—the **Man-gold** or **Atonement-gold** <note>original German: "Mann- oder Sühngeld"</note>—belongs not only to the paternal relatives and males, the **sword-kin** <note>original German: "Schwertmagen"</note>, but also to the females, the **spindle-kin** <note>original German: "Spillmagen"</note>. Although under Lombard and Saxon law it was once observed and pronounced otherwise—namely, that the vengeance of blood, and consequently the monetary penalty commonly called *Manngeld*, pertained only to the paternal male relatives. *See Hering on suretyship, chapter 10, number 352, etc.; and Pistor, observation 203.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding *Manngeld*, see *Gothofredus Antonius, page 17, Feudal Disputation 1, thesis 4, letter b,* where it signifies the same as a **Chamber Fief** <note>original German: "Cammerlehen"; a fief consisting of a regular cash payment from a treasury rather than land</note>. But in *Treutler, volume 1, Disputation 5, thesis 5, letter d,* "Mann- or Sühnegeld" is the name given to that money which is paid to the sons or paternal relatives of the slain. More can be found in the *cited place and the authors mentioned there.*

## 16. Mann. A Man.

This is sometimes taken to mean a **Husband**. Whence it is asked: Is a marriage proven if someone says, "He is my man" <note>original German: "Er ist mein Mann"</note>? *Uranius, volume 3, consultation 21, folio 137, number 9.* In old times, "Man" (*Mann*) was used for a **Vassal**, as I said above under the *word Baron and in the treatise on Barons.* Similarly, the Spanish today use *Varon* for a brave man and a husband. A legacy left to someone "when he becomes a

<column-break/>

man" <note>original German: "wann er zu einem Mann wird"</note> must also be provided to a bachelor who has reached 25 years of age. *Pfeil, consultation 69.*

### ADDITION.

Rodornius Scrickkius in *book 3 of his Adversaria, chapter 6,* says: Modern critics labor in vain regarding the origin of **Tuifco and Mannus** <note>mythical ancestors of the Germanic peoples mentioned by Tacitus</note>, thinking it should be referred to our word *Mann*, which signifies a male human. Because *Caesar in book 6 of the Gallic Wars* speaks of the Germans thus: "They count in the number of the gods only those whom they see and by whose power they are openly helped: the Sun, Vulcan, and the Moon; the rest they have not even heard of by report." Behold, says Rodornius, Caesar recognized the God of the Germans, *Tiescon* or *Tiesonn*, the Sun (*die Sonn*), for nothing is more beautiful than the Sun; as well as *Mann*, the Moon (*Maan*). More on this in *Justus Georgius Schottel, on the German Main Language, folio 70.*

"Husbands" (*Mariti*), that is, Spouses. *Digest, law: "si vir" 52, section 1, at the end, on donations between husband and wife.*

## 17. Mann- or Feudal Court-Men. Feudal Judgment.

If there is a controversy between a Lord and a Vassal concerning a fief, it is not the Lord who judges, but the **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Pares Curiae"; other vassals of the same rank holding fiefs from the same lord</note>, as they are called. *According to the text in title 10, book 1 of the Feudal Laws; titles 39, 20, 22; and the section "finitur Dominium," title 29; and the section "per" title 55, book 2.* But *Schwanmann, consultation 7,* and *Eberhard Speckhan, century 2, question 35, class 4,* treat this question more broadly; see them. To this, compare what Güntherus says in the *Ligurinus* <note>A 12th-century epic poem about Frederick Barbarossa</note>, when he says:

> If a lawsuit is moved regarding a fief, which the vassal
> Admits was received from you, but you deny it;
> Let not you, but the **Court** sit as Judge
> To hear and determine the cause in the established order.

This is now called the **Award of the Peers** <note>original Latin: "Laudamentum Parium"</note>. *According to title 21 of the Feudal Laws.* Sometimes it is called the **Praise of the Peers** <note>original Latin: "Laudatio Parium"</note>, as in the *Constitutions of Emperor Henry II, in Ardizonus and Alvarottus.* To "praise" (*laudare*), in the sense of bringing forth an award (*laudum*), is nothing other than to judge. To the Germans, this judgment is called the **Man-court** <note>original German: "Manngericht"</note>. The reason why the Lord is not the Judge in this case is given as follows: because no one can be a Judge in his own cause. *See Rittershusius, Feudal Partitions, book 2, chapter 9, number 6.* But it must be noted here: if the Lord has many vassals, whether all of them, or which and how many among them, are to be chosen for the decision of the case. *Schrader, volume 1, consultation 1, numbers 707 and 717; Schwanman, observation 11, number 17; Schneidewin, in the Epitome of Feudal Law, part 9, number 25.*

What if the Lord has no Peers at all who have acknowledged a fief from him? *See Schneidewin, in the cited place, number 24.* Or if they are not suitable? *Speckhan, century 1, question 35, class 4, number 15 and following.*

<header>Augmented Practical Treasury</header>

Regarding the **Judge between Vassals** <note>original Latin: "De Judice inter Vasallos"; a vassal is a person who holds land in exchange for allegiance and service</note>, see *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 1, consultation 31, question 1, and consultation 46*. On the Judge between a true and an asserted vassal, see *Strasbourg Consultations, volume 2, consultation 56*. A vassal is not required to provide an **Oath of Calumny** <note>original Latin: "Juramentum Calumniæ"; a formal oath that a party is not bringing a lawsuit out of malice or deception</note>, as noted in *volume 1, consultation 43*; nor is he deprived of his fief for obtaining a mandate against his Lord, according to the records of *Schwanmann, consultation 9*.

Regarding the **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Pares Curiæ"; these were other vassals of the same rank who sat in judgment of their fellow vassals to ensure fairness</note>, and whether they may pass judgment against clergy, see *Costa, consultation 2, folio 42*.

If the Lord granting a sub-fief or the vassal holding that sub-fief must be summoned, it must be done before the nearest Peers. *Schrader on Feuds, part 10, section 5, number 211; Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 7, number 19.* Who should choose the **Substitute Governor** <note>original German: "Statthalter"</note> in such a case? I believe this should be done by the Peers themselves, who may choose one from among them by lot or another method.

->The following legal response is relevant here:<-

**Highly and Nobly Born Gracious Lord**, your Grace recently commanded me to draft a legal opinion regarding the princely fiefs or estate lands, and for this purpose, you sent me the enclosed case, memorial, and report. Following your humble command (as soon as my health and other inconveniences permitted), I have reflected on these matters with diligence. First, I found it very proper, as your Grace yourself highly and wisely maintains—since these lands originate from the **Cathedral of G.** <note>original German: "Gottshaus G."; likely an abbey or cathedral referred to by its initial</note> and the occupant holds a **sub-fief** <note>original German: "Afterlehen"</note>—that the Lord Bishop of H., in his Grace as the Lord and owner of said Cathedral, be first informed of these matters in detail, and that everything be undertaken with his good knowledge and gracious approval. Perhaps the following deduction might provide guidance on how to slightly expand the memorial already drafted for this end.

Otherwise, and secondly, concerning the **Judge**, it is correct that according to feudal law such matters belong to the Peers of the Court, and specifically those of the **immediate Lord** <note>original Latin: "Domini immediati"</note> (such as your Grace) and not to the Lord Bishop as the **Superior Lord** <note>original Latin: "Domini superioris"</note>, according to the teachings of *Schrader, part 1, section 5, number 11; Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 7, number 19.*

Thirdly, in the arrangement of a **Feudal Court** <note>original German: "Lehengericht"</note>, it is required—as appears in *Berlichius, part 1, conclusion 62, new edition*—that the Lord, if he is the plaintiff, should summon all and every Peer living in the same court and territory, and seek a proxy appointed by him, so that they may cite one or more vassals (against whom the Lord wishes to bring action) to a certain day, so that the vassals, together with the Lord, may constitute the Feudal Court.

Furthermore, regarding common feudal law, the Lord alone cannot choose the Peers of the Court and appoint them to constitute the feudal judgment,

<column-break/>

but the Lord and the defendant vassal must do this jointly. Thus, if the Lord chooses one, the vassal chooses the second; if the Lord chooses the third, the vassal chooses the fourth, and so on, alternating. In this way, they continue to choose one after another to form the feudal judgment until they reach the number approved by the Lord.

However, if the defendant vassal does not appear on the appointed day, or if he appears but refuses to choose Peers to constitute the Feudal Court, then the Lord alone may choose the Peers and constitute the court.

These chosen vassals, under the **oath of fealty** <note>original Latin: "Juramento fidelitatis"</note> they provided at the time they were invested with their lands, are to resolve the controversy between the Lord and the vassal; it is not necessary for them to swear a new oath.

Furthermore, the proceedings before the Peers, as in other courts, may be presented in writing or orally at the discretion of the parties.

Just as it is within the Lord’s discretion to name how many Peers are to be chosen by each side, the Peers chosen by the Lord or the vassal have equal power.

From this, in my opinion, it follows that neither the Feudal Lord nor the defendant vassal should appoint a **Substitute Governor** <note>original German: "Statthalter"</note>, but rather the chosen lay-judges <note>original German: "Mann-Richter"</note> should elect one from among themselves, by lot or some other fashion, for this purpose.

Fourthly, it is correct that one must appeal from the Feudal Judge to the **Immediate Superior**. Namely, if there is a next-highest superior (that is, an intermediate Lord), then the appeal must be made to him by both the Peers and the Lord; but if there is no immediate superior, then the appeal must be made to the Lord of the Tribunal, namely the **Ordinary Judge** <note>the regular judge with jurisdiction over the territory</note> to whom the matter is subject. *Mynsinger, century 5, observation 5.*

As for why the aforementioned *Mynsinger* seems to doubt whether one must appeal step-by-step in feudal cases, that does not apply to the case of a sub-fief, or when a sub-fief is being disputed. Therefore, in the present case, the appeal from the appointed Lay or Feudal Court must be made to the **Palace Court** <note>original German: "Pfalz"</note> of the Cathedral G., from which one could otherwise regularly appeal.

I fear, however, that because the Most Noble **House of Austria** <note>the Habsburgs</note> claims jurisdiction over certain sovereign cases—especially the right of appeal in the place where the property is located—new complaints will once again reach **Innsbruck** <note>the seat of the regional Habsburg administration</note> regarding this matter.

Therefore, it might be wise to deliberate maturely with the Lord Bishop of H. on how to approach the matter, and whether to draft a joint letter to Innsbruck. In this letter, it should first be notified how things stand here and what we intend to argue, as the Bishop, through consequence and by reason of his jurisdiction, is likewise strongly interested.

It also addresses the complexities of appellate jurisdiction, specifically the potential for legal conflict with the Habsburg administration in Innsbruck.</summary>
