<meta>This page continues the legal advice of Christopher Besold regarding feudal disputes. The previous page introduced the concept of Peers of the Court and the specific legal question regarding peasant sub-vassals holding princely fiefs.</meta>

### Letter M.

I, for my humble part, would consider it best if Your Princely Grace in H. were to negotiate with these **sub-vassals** <term>Subvasallis: lower-tier tenants who hold land from a vassal rather than directly from the sovereign</term> through a **commissioner** <term>Commissarium: a representative appointed to handle a specific task</term> or by other means, so that the **vassals** <term>Vasalli: those who hold land under a lord in exchange for loyalty</term> would agree to a **compromise settlement** <term>Compromiß</term>, or that **in place of their peers** <term>loco Parium: usually, a vassal had the right to be judged by others of their own rank</term> they would agree to air this **controversy** <term>Controversiam</term> before Your Grace’s High Court. From there, they might afterwards appeal to Innsbruck, Reichenau, or wherever the matter properly belongs. I suggest this because, to my knowledge, it is not common for a **Court of Peers** <note>German: "Manngericht"; a formal feudal court where noble vassals judged one another</note> to be established in the **cases of such sub-vassals** <term>causis talium Subvasallorum</term> who are simple peasant folk. In their case, it is suspected that their tenures are more likely **hereditary leases** <term>emphyteuses: a type of long-term lease where the tenant improves the land</term> and farmsteads or manorial estates rather than **true noble fiefs** <term>vera feuda</term>.

It would, moreover, not be fitting for Your Grace to involve yourself in a formal legal dispute with such vassals and peasant folk. Furthermore, if Your Grace were to require other vassals of higher social standing to serve as judges, I do not know if they could be persuaded to do so.

Fifthly, I cannot see by what right one could cut off these tenants' right of **appeal** <term>Appellation</term> against their will, or force them to become the plaintiffs. For if one wished to evict them from these estates without a legal ruling, they would immediately complain **concerning the seizure** <term>super spolio: a legal claim regarding the wrongful deprivation of possession</term> and bring this matter to the regional court as a formal grievance—or at the very least to Innsbruck—causing Your Grace the greatest inconvenience.

> <note>original Latin: "Feuda enim regulariter per culpas non ipso Jure, sed mediante sententia privante, committuntur..."</note> For fiefs are usually forfeited through faults not by the operation of the law itself, but by means of a judicial sentence of deprivation; even if the vassal's offense is notorious. Indeed, even when a fief is forfeited by the law itself, a declaratory sentence is nonetheless required. For it is said that a sentence is required even regarding the "notorious" nature of the act, if it is called into doubt.
>
> And all laws by which something is said to be forfeited by the law itself require a declaratory judgment to revoke possession and to establish that the forfeiture has occurred. Thus, if it is done otherwise, mandates can be obtained from the Imperial Chamber or another superior even without a specific clause. See Rosenthal, chapter 10, conclusion 41, throughout the discussion.

And sixthly, it is correct that when **sub-vassals** <term>Affterlehenleut</term> commit a **felony** <term>feloniam: in feudal law, a "felony" was a breach of the duty of loyalty to the lord</term>, <note>original Latin: "etiam contra Dominum mediatum Superiorem..."</note> even against the superior overlord, the fief nevertheless falls to the immediate grantor <note>in this case, Your Grace</note> and not to the Church of C., <note>original Latin: "per text. expressum..."</note> according to the express text in the Imperial Chapter, section "illud," on the prohibition of alienation by Frederick; Rosenthal, chapter 11, conclusion 18, at the beginning; Andreas Kohl, treatise on sub-fiefs, chapter 4, number 52, and following.

As for the seventh point, whether these vassals have committed a felony and should therefore be **deprived** <term>priviren</term> of all their rights, I cannot yet correctly **judge** <term>judiciren</term> at this time. This is because I have not seen the "fief-letters" (deeds) and therefore cannot certainly determine **the nature and type of this fief** <term>quale & cujus naturæ hocce sit feudum</term>. It will also be necessary to know in what manner these feudal estates were **transferred** <term>alienirt</term>, and what some of the **possessors** <term>Possessores</term>

<column-break/>

hold as their own property; whether those who **committed the felony** <term>feloniam committirt</term> are still alive; and whether the current possessors or their heirs might **defend themselves by prescription** <term>præscriptione tuiren: a legal defense based on the passage of time/long-term possession</term>, or otherwise argue that this felony was at least **tacitly forgiven** <term>tacitè remittirt</term>. Such forgiveness would be assumed if they were **invested** <term>investirt: formally granted the land again</term> or if the **annual dues** <term>Canones</term> and fees were accepted from them without protest, and so forth. Since the **loss of a fief** <term>amissio feudi</term> is quite **harsh** <term>odiosa: literally "hateful," referring to a penalty that the law seeks to avoid if possible</term>, it requires **true malice** <term>verus dolus</term> or at the very least **gross negligence** <term>lata culpa</term>. Thus, the **doctors of feudal law** <term>Feudisticis Doctorib.</term> bring forward many and almost innumerable **excuses** <term>Excusationes</term> by which such vassals might protect themselves.

It is also to be noted from the **facts of the case** <term>Figuration casus</term> that these sub-vassals are permitted to use, enjoy, possess, sell, and mortgage these farmsteads. This **implies** <term>importirt</term> a **hereditary fief** <term>feudum hæreditarium</term>, in which the tenants have a much greater right than they would in **standard** <term>propriis</term> or "true" fiefs.

Primary attention must be paid to **what agreements** <term>ad quæ pacta</term> these sub-vassals are **bound** <term>adstringirt</term> in the fief-letters. Likewise, because several others possess these lands as their own property, those possessors could not be brought before a **feudal judge** <term>ad Judicem feudalem</term> because they do not recognize themselves as vassals.

It must also be considered whether proper land-registry books or renewals exist, by means of which one could **immediately** <term>in continenti</term> prove **specifically** <term>speciatim</term> which pieces of land belong to such a fief.

At the same time, it sometimes happens in cases such as this that the forfeiture is not strictly enforced. Instead, the lords of the fief accept a fine or monetary penalty and thereafter create a new order for how such fiefs are to be held in all ways in the future.

Therefore, in conclusion, I maintain once more that one should investigate all matters thoroughly according to the guidance of this brief and simple **deduction** <term>Deduction: a formal legal reasoning</term>. Afterward, the matter should be brought in detail to the Princely Episcopal Chancellery in H. There, one should mediate the matter so that His Princely Grace either summons the sub-vassals to Merseburg or delegates a member of the distinguished council to a nearby location. Subsequently, as the suzerain—**not indeed by force of jurisdiction** <term>non quidem vi Jurisdictionis</term> but solely to prevent a long and complicated dispute—they should **attempt** <term>tentiren</term> to see if the matter might be settled entirely through goodwill, or at least directed toward a swift legal process.

I submit this to Your Grace without any presumption, and in all ways **subject to the judgment of those more prudent** <term>salvo calculo prudentiorum</term>. I remain obediently ready to further explain my opinion upon receiving further reports and to strengthen it with more legal grounds. Executed on March 6th, the year 1631.

-> **Christopher Besold.** <-

# Enlarged Practical Treasury

Concerning **Peers of the Court** <note>original: "Pares Curiæ"</note>, and to whom an appeal should be made. See *Schrader, book 1, number 718, etc.*

**Peers of the Court** are so named from the "equality of fiefs," because they hold equal fiefs. For example, if a case involves Counts, other Counts should serve as the judges, concerning which see *chapter 1, if concerning a fief a Vassal is interrupted by someone.* Others, however, hold that **Peers** refers to **co-vassals** <note>original: "Convasalli"</note> who hold their fiefs from the same Lord. Concerning this, see *Alvarotus in the title: if regarding an investiture between a Lord and a Vassal.* But *Panormitanus, in chapter 'cæterum mihi' in the 6th column, regarding judges,* says that regarding who are considered Peers for a feudal judgment, the custom of the Lord’s Court is the best interpreter. *Henning Göden, counsel 29, volume 2,* where one may see the German process against rebel Vassals; add *Schrader, counsel 15, volume 1.*

*Eberhard Speckhan, century 2, question 35, class 4, number 15,* calls those **Peers of the Court** who, in the same Court, courtyard, house, or territory in which the disputed fief or **benefice** <term>beneficium: a grant of land or income in exchange for service</term> is located, acknowledge their dependent fiefs from one and the same universal Lord. The House, Court, or Courtyard <note>original: "Domus, Curia seu Curtis"</note> is, as it were, the "dominant benefice" from which the fiefs depend, and where the rents are collected and the feudal judgments are usually carried out; these are sometimes called *Dinchhöfe* <note>German: manorial or assembly courts</note>, and sometimes *Mannhäuser* <note>German: vassal-houses</note>. But see *Speckhan in the cited place.*

However, this must be added: although according to feudal customs **Peers of the Court** are not held to judge against their will, today by the customs of Germany they are bound to do so, etc. *Schwanman, observation 11, number 9, etc.,* and therefore this is sometimes inserted into the **Letters of Enfeoffment** <note>German: "Lehenbrieffen"; the formal documents granting a fief</note>.

Whether the Emperor alone, without the intervention of the **Peers of the Court**, can take notice of the greater fiefs of the Empire, see *Arumæus, volume 1, discourse 11.* I have also dealt with this matter myself in my *Treatise on Jurisdiction, chapter 13, and on Succession and Election, book of dissertations 14.*

Regarding Feudal Judgment and the Feudal Judge, see *Rosenthal and Schrader;* likewise *Speidel in his Collection, parts 1 and 2,* under the heading *Feudal Judge.*

->ADDITIO.<-
<note>Latin: "Addition"</note>

Feudal or **Vassal Courts** <note>German: "Lehen oder Manngericht"</note> are treated in *chapter 'ex transmissa' and chapter 'verum' regarding competent forums. Vultejus on fiefs; Lord Doctor Rittershusius, book 2, Divisions of Feudal Law; Finckelthaus in Illustrious Feudal Controversies, Controversy 23, at the end.*

### 18. Men, Castle-men. Vassals.

A common clause in **Investitures** <term>Investiturarum: the formal legal transfer of a fief</term> is "with Men and Castle-men" <note>German: "mit Mannen und Burgmannen"</note>. Although these words by themselves do not prove **superiority** <term>superioritatem: sovereign authority over a territory</term>, they signify the **direct ownership** <note>original: "directum Dominium"</note> that one has in those things for which others are **sub-enfeoffed** <term>subinfeudati: when a vassal grants part of their land to another lower vassal</term>. While the words "Men" and "Castle-men," when used simply, are usually interpreted as **Vassals** <note>original: "Vasallis"</note>, when joined with other terms they describe a "totality of things" <note>original: "universitatem rerum"</note> that has a certain right of superiority and dignity annexed to it. This is because Vassals and Castle-men,

<column-break/>

or **Men of the Garrison** <note>original: "Castrenses Viri"</note>, also belong to this "totality," which is sometimes expressed in the Investitures of Princes and Counts with these words: "With people, fief-holdings, etc." <note>German: "Mit Leuten, Lehenschafften, &c."</note> as found in *Knichen on the Law of the Duchy of Saxony, page 120.*

### 19. Male-Fief. A masculine fief.

Regarding the clause, "as a proper **Male-Fief**" <note>German: "zu einem rechten Mann-Lehen"</note>, see *Schrader, counsel 14, volume 1.*

### 20. Male Line. The masculine line.

Whether the **Male Line** <note>original: "Linea Masculina"</note>, when mentioned by a **Testator** <term>Testatore: a person who has made a will</term>, begins from the person of the testator himself or from his descendants. See *Gravina, counsel 556.*

->ADDITIO.<-
<note>Latin: "Addition"</note>

Masculinity expressed in one case is considered repeated in another; treated extensively by *Barbosa, book 11, chapter 13, axiom 3, and cited there in a long series.* In fiefs, the masculine does not include the feminine (axiom 1, near the end). That a girl is signified by the term "boy" <note>original: "puer"</note> is stated by *Ulpian, law 163, on the Meaning of Words, dispute 1;* women in childbirth are called "those recently from labor" <note>original: "puerperas"</note>. 2. In Greek, the word **child** <term>παιδίον (paidion)</term> is used commonly for both. Against these, *Alciatus* grumbles in two ways: 1. A woman in childbirth <note>original: "puerpera"</note> is not named from "boy" <note>original: "puer"</note>, but from "girl" <note>original: "puera"</note>. 2. The example of the Greeks means nothing, since among them **child** <term>παῖς (pais)</term> is a common noun, but no Latin speaker would use "boy" <note>original: "puer"</note> in the feminine gender. But the first argument either fosters an **absurdity** <term>ἄτοπον (atopon)</term>—that males are also contained in a feminine word (contrary to law 45, at the end, regarding Legacies 2), which *Alciatus* himself confirms from antiquity is a terrible example (*book 2, Miscellanies, chapter 48*)—or it implies that a woman who has given birth to a boy is not a "puerpera." The second argument misses the point: the Jurist does not intend to look at common grammatical gender, but sought the promiscuous use of speech and the meaning of the Latin word in the Greek, as is often done (*laws 236, 239 on the Meaning of Words*). Therefore, there is no need to translate it as **child** <term>παιδίον (paidion)</term>, as *Brecheus* did, religiously following his master *Alciatus*. See also *Gœddæus* in his commentary on the repeated lecture on the title *Concerning the Meaning of Words*, in the explanation of law 163, section 1, numbers 1 and 2. The masculine does not conceive the feminine in "different matter" (*Philipp Knipschild on Trusts, chapters 1, 48, and 85*) when a different reason underlies it (*law 49*); when the person disposing the property wanted to preserve the **agnation** <term>agnationem: relationship through the male line</term> (*law 50, chapters 8, 133*); or when he specifically expressed the quality of being male (*law 51*).

### 21. Male Heirs.

"From **male heir** to male heir" <note>German: "Von Mannserben zu Mannserben"</note>. See *Castillo, Daily Controversies, book 2, chapter 2.*

When is the calling of males in a person's will considered to be for the sake of preserving the male lineage, or for the sake of introducing a preference, and when is the quality of masculinity considered repeated? *Castillo, in the cited place, chapter 4.*

->ADDITION.<-

**Fiefs** <term>feuda: land held on condition of service and loyalty to a lord</term> established by contract and foresight are considered to be created using the following formulas, which are very common in Germany: *for himself and his male heirs of the body. Likewise: his rightful heirs of the body: the shield- and helmet-fief heirs of the same rightful male line. Likewise: all their male heirs of the body: of the name, helmet, shield, and lineage, for himself and his male-fief-capable heirs.* <note>German original: "für sich und seine männliche Leibslehens-Erben. Item seinen rechten Leibslehens Erben: desselben rechten Mannstammes Schild- und Helmslehen-Erben. Item allen ihren Männlichen Leibslehens-Erben: des Nahmens, Helms, Schild und Geschlechts, für sich und seine Mannlehenbare Erben." These phrases ensure the land stays within the male noble bloodline.</note> In this same class is the fief given to someone for himself and his male heirs, or his legitimate heirs, *to him and his male heirs born of a legitimate marriage.* <note>original: "ihme und seinen Eheleibgebohrnen Mannlichen Leib-Erben"</note> See more extensively Gothofredus Antonius, *Disputation on Fiefs, 1, theorem 8, letter K.*

### 22. Male-Hereditary Possession. <note>original: "Mannserbliche Inhabung"</note>

This is used for an eternal pledge <note>original: "ewige Pfandschafft"; a form of mortgage where the property is held indefinitely</note>. *Thus the Lords who are Imperial Hereditary Stewards and Barons of Waldburg, etc.* hold several towns, such as *Riedlingen, Munderkingen, Mengen, etc.* in possession under this same title from the highly noble House of Austria.

### 23. A Man’s Mow. A Manor. <note>original: "Mannsmad. Mansus."</note>

The Latins call it *Mansum*, as if it were a *man’s mow* <note>original: "Mannsmad"</note>, that is, as much as one man can mow in a single day. Just as this applies to meadows, so *Manngrab* <note>a man's dig</note> is used in vineyards, *Mannwerck* <note>a man's work</note> in fields, and *Mannstoffel* in the Alps. See Schottel in *The German Main Language, page 498.* However, *Mansus* is a common word from the middle ages derived from *Mansio* <note>a dwelling or staying</note>, from which the French word *Maison* also descends; it is used *for a peasant farm* <note>original: "für einen Baurenhof"</note>, or for a plot of land with a certain measure of field. See my own *Treatise on the Nature of Peoples, page 105 and following.* From this also comes the term *manentes* <note>those staying; tenant farmers</note>, see Cujacius *on law 8, Code on the grain supply and tribute, book 10.*

There were three kinds of *Manors*: *Lordly, Free-born,* and *Servile*. <note>original: "Dominicatus, ingenuilis & Servilis."</note>
They called the *Lordly Manor* <note>original: "Mansum Dominicatum"</note> the Lord's own particular manor, which the Lord himself cultivated and whose fruits he took; while the fruits of the *Free-born* <note>original: "ingenuilis"</note> and *Servile* manors were collected by the *manor-tenants* <note>original: "mansuarii"</note> to whom they were granted, with only a tax reserved for the Lord, and other conditions which were lighter on the free-born manor and heavier on the servile one.
In a similar way, one reads of "lordly fields," that is, personal lands, and likewise "lordly lands, courts, and vineyards." See Aubertus Miraeus, *in the Annals of Belgium for the year 877, page 3988.*
A *Manor* is properly said to be as much land as one person can work with a pair of oxen in a year, as noted by Bartholomäus Schobinger in *Goldast, volume 3 of Alemannic Matters, in the additions to Joachim Vadianus, page 134, and Vadianus himself in volume 2, page 83.*
Aventinus, *book 3*, explains a *huba* <note>a hide of land</note> and a *mansus* as what is plowed by a two-horse team; and a *Curtis* or *hosa* as what is plowed by a four-horse team. Amerbachius thinks it is a *jugerum* <note>an acre or "yoke" of land</note>, and that the word *mansum* is named as if from "measure"; Hotomannus follows him, influenced by the similarity to the word *Mansmat*. Cujacius and Pithoeus say it is an estate, a farm, or an inheritance from which a farmer can comfortably support himself and his family, and moreover pay tax and tribute to the Lord. See *Cluten in the Roman Expedition, page 19.*

<column-break/>

Add Calvinus *on Fiefs, book 1, page 46.* Borellus *on the Edict of Magistrates, book 4, chapter 9, number 32 and following.*
**Mansionaticus** <term>the right of lodging</term>, also called hospitality or reception. In the Constitution of Charlemagne: "It has reached the ears of our clemency that certain Dukes and their junior officials, hunters, and others living in and traveling through the territories, are taking 'lodging-rights' and small carts."
From this, Vitus Amerbach says: "What if the 'lodging-tenants' were those who create wealth in the countryside, or on estates, which they still call *mansi* in Italy." From this, he who holds a manor from a Lord becomes his "man," etc. See Ritter *on Homage, page 39, number 59.*
*Mansum* means a house; see Hincmar, *Letter 7.* There are Priests among us who do not have as many parishioners as those who hold manors. Add Cantipratanus *on foreign words, under the word 'Mansionarius'.* Truly, in the past, one whole manor was assigned to every Church, free from any service. See Tholossanus *on Benefices, chapter 15, number 1 and 4.*
**Mansuarius** is one who cultivates one manor. To Cassiodorus and Gregory, *Mansus* or *mansum* is neither a house, nor a courtyard, nor a garden, but a field of a certain mode and measure. For this reason it was called *metatus* <note>measured out</note> by the ancients, because in the divisions and assignments of fields, surveyors were employed.
But Baldus defines a *Mansus* as an estate in which men dwell.
Others say that a *Manor* is a specific estate or a measured field containing twelve *jugera* <note>acres</note>, so that whenever we name a Manor, we understand 12 Acres.

->ADDITION.<-

*Mansmadt*, or *Mannemadt*, or *Mansus*, that is, a large piece of land, as much as can be cultivated in one day with two oxen. See Werndle *on Tithe Law, book 3, chapter 3, my page 181.*
*Kölnhöff* was an old word among the Alemanni <note>a Germanic tribal confederation</note> for the same thing as a *mansus*. A manor is said to be as much as one can work with one pair of oxen in a year, as noted *in chapter 1 of the Decretals on taxes, and in the Uses of Fiefs...* Truly, the ancients, when establishing and donating to Churches, almost always assigned *manors* for the maintenance of the Priest who was placed in the Church. According to Saxon Law, no one is allowed to graze their cattle separately (which would reduce the fee for the common Shepherd) unless he has three *manors*, or *three 'hufen' of land.* See Berlich, *conclusion 49, number 36.*

### 24. Sutlers. <note>original: "Marckhedanter. Lixa."</note>

Military merchants, who have food, drink, and other such things prepared for the sake of the army, we call *Sutlers* <note>original: "Marckhedanter"</note>.

They shall tap no beer or wine one hour after sunset or one hour before sunrise. ibid. No violence shall be done to the sutlers. Imperial Articles of War of Maximilian II, article 43. Sutler.*

Pliny, in *Book 7, Chapter 43*, suggests they were called "fuffarranei" <note>original Latin: "fuffarranei," likely referring to those wearing coarse garments or hidden soldiers</note>; no one shall plunder or rob them. *Dutch War Ordinance, Article 20, in the annotations of Pappus, letter b.*

## 25. **The Mark**. Marca.

The name "Mark" can be applied not only to raw material <note>physical weight of metal</note> but also to its valuation. For just as a *Pound of gold* is rightly said to be paid out whether it is the physical mass itself or seventy-two gold coins <note>original: "Goldgülden"</note> paid in place of the pound, according to the law *quotiessunque* <note>Code of Justinian, on the collection of taxes</note>; so a *Pound of silver* (specifically pure silver) is rightly said to be paid not only in physical material but also if it is paid in ten gold pieces or coins. *Single law, joined with the gloss on "qui nos" in the Code on the price of silver.* The reasoning is the same whether a Mark of silver is paid in raw material or its value is paid out as eight thalers. *Albertus Brunus on the increase of money, preface number 7; Jacob Thoming, Decision 19, number 11.*

Thus, according to common usage, the names "pounds" or "marks" of gold and silver usually refer not to pure silver or gold, but rather to the common alloyed metal. Just as the name "Rhenish gold pieces" or "Rhenish florins" is to be understood as Rhenish florins in actual coinage, rather than their weight in gold. From this it follows that in the constitutions or decrees of the German Emperors, as well as in private contracts, pure or unmixed gold and silver are usually distinguished from the mixed alloy by adding the terms: "pure gold" or "fine silver." <note>original German: "lödig Gold, oder fein Silber"</note> See *Thoming, cited decision, number 13 and following; add also Budelius on Money, book 1, chapter 13.*

### ADDITION.

**Mark of Silver** <note>original: "Marck Silber"</note> was worth no more than 3 florins and 60 kreutzers 300 years ago. *Acts of Lindau, fully on page 486 and following, and at the end of page 345.*

What a Mark is. What a *Ferto* or *Farto* <note>a fourth of a Mark</note> is. *Limnäus in Public Law, book 4, chapter 7, Addition page 433 at the end.* A Mark of Ducats according to the Monetary Edict contains 23 parts in the alloy and 10 grains in weight, and produces 67 Ducats or parts. *Section "furthermore because" of the Monetary Edict; Imperial Recess of the year 1570, section "that also."* Gold of 18 carats and 6 grains equals 72 parts or gold coins. *Said Monetary Edict, section "furthermore the guilders"; Imperial Recess of the year 1576, section "and from special."* In the time of Frederick III, the alloy was better, namely 19 carats. *Reformation of Frederick, Year 1442, section "Also when also."* In thalers, the Mark receives 14 lots and 4 grains. From a mark of silver containing 14 lots and 16 grains, nine and a half florins must be minted. On the mark of gold and silver, see most extensively *Johann Wolfgang Auer, numbers 64 and 65, on the law of Money; Schwannmann in the Processes of the Imperial Chamber.*

## 26. **Market Town**. Marckfleck. See above **Fleck** under the letter F. **Pagus**.

In Germany, those places are commonly called **Market Towns** <note>original: "Marckflecken"</note> which have their own Capital Jurisdiction <note>original: "Halsgericht," literally "Neck-Court," a court with the power of life and death</note>,

<column-break/>

stocks, and gallows. This is because it is neither traditional nor permitted for everyone in every place to exercise such criminal authority under their High Lordship.

Although today there is a great difference between *Cities* and *Markets*: nevertheless, when they were first founded and the towns were small beginnings, these terms were used interchangeably in Saxony. Hence they are sometimes called *Municipia* from their "munitions" or fortifications, according to *Article 6 of the Municipal Law* <note>original: "Weichbild"</note>, and sometimes *Foralia* because they have a "forum" or market, *Article 7, section 2 of the Municipal Law and Fief Law, chapter 31, section 11*, where the vernacular text interprets "fortified places and market sites" as **Mountain and City**, or commonly **Market Towns**. Thus, the gloss on *Article 66, book 3 of the Territorial Law* <note>original: "Landrecht"</note> interprets "forum" as a **Market**, consisting of all kinds of civic trades which belong to the cities. Likewise, Lübeck is everywhere called a "forum" by *Helmold, Book 1 of the Slavic Chronicle, 77.* See especially *Lord Gryphiander's tract on the Saxon Municipal Law, chapter 74.*

### ADDITION.

From Gryphiander, see especially here *Limnäus in Public Law, book 4, chapter 8, Addition volume 1, page 644.* According to German customs, a **Market Town** must necessarily have a civil and criminal court. *Acts of Lindau, page 62 after the beginning and page 211 after the middle.*

## 27. **Mark, Boundary Stone, Land Borders**. Marck, Marckstein, Landgränzen. Marca. Termini Limites.

*Marca* signifies a limit or a shared border, from the German **Marck**, which in the vernacular denotes the limit of a territory or of fields. Mention of "marks" is frequent in many charters of later Kings, especially those of Charlemagne and his successor, Louis the Pious. And Rudolph von Ems, in his *paraphrase of the Old Testament* (which, according to Bibliander, he wrote five hundred years ago), mentions Marks when he says:

> The borderland Vahitan,
> To the mountains of Caucasus,
> Your other separate Mark was
> The Red Sea, there goes its line,
> And divides itself in the Mark.

They are also called "the Markets" or "the Borders," and today in many places the **Land-defense** <note>original: "Landwehr"; a defensive earthwork or boundary ditch</note>. For *Marca*, the word *mardus* is also found, *Jodocus Coccius in Dagobert, chapter 19, page 179; Goldast, Alemannic Matters, volume 1, page 393*, from which word the title of **Margrave** <note>original: "Marchionum"</note> descends; see the *next entry*.

*Limits*, however, are the signs or marks that demonstrate the boundaries of an inherent jurisdiction, depending either on nature or on human art—commonly called **Land Borders**. From nature depend rivers, streams, ditches, mounds, mountains, and valleys. From art, however, are established inscribed stones fixed in the ground, columns, marked trees, etc. *Hönnon, Political Disputations 2, thesis 42, letter b at the end; see my own work on the Law of Territory, chapter 2.*

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical legal dictionary under the entry for 'Mark' (boundary), following the previous page's discussion on 'Mark' as a unit of weight and currency. # Letter M.

After the Roman Empire was devastated by the invasions of the Goths and Lombards, and the Empire was transferred to the Germans, the divisions of the Provinces were made by **Marks** <note>original: *Marchas*, or *Marckstein* (boundary stones)</note>. Thus, in the East, the **Eastern Mark** <note>original: *Ostenreiche Marck*, the root of the name 'Austria'</note> reached the Avars and the Hunns in Pannonia, serving as the limit of the Eastern Realm. The **Western Mark** <note>original: *Westenreiche Marck*, or *Neustria*</note>, however, separated the Franks from the neighboring Saxons, Alemanni, and Burgundians—that is, the western limit of the Kingdom. From these, the names **Austria** and **Neustria** arose, over which Counts once presided as "Dukes of the Frontiers" <note>original Latin: *Ducem Limitaneorum*</note> while that distinction remained, and they began to be called **Margraves** <note>original: *Marggravii*</note> by the soldiers. Therefore, as many limits as there were from the beginning, there were just as many Margraves: namely, the Avar, the Garentan, the Friulian, the Saxon, the Spanish, and the Norman. Later, many more began to exist. *Valentin Forster, on Jurisdiction, part 2, page 309, number 12 and following.*

In our times, public terms and limits distinguish Kingdoms, Principalities, Duchies, Counties, Territories, Jurisdictions, etc.

Regarding Heathen Boundary Stones or border-marks, see *Marx Welser’s Augsburg Chronicle*, part 1, page 25 and following, where he discusses the **Augsburg boundary signs**, and at the end of page 24, he writes among other things:

> In the territory of Augsburg, near certain villages along the road, one finds small mountains or little hills. It is easily seen that they were piled up by human hands, packed together in a round shape as if they had been turned on a lathe, and I hold that these served in place of boundary stones. Beneath these, the ancients used to place charcoal, ashes, crushed shells, and lime, some of which might perhaps still be found if one were to dig deep. From this, several vagabonds and **swindlers** <note>original German: *Landbescheisser*, a vulgar term for charlatans</note> emerged, who "spun a yarn" <note>original German: *eine Nasen gedrehet*</note> for the inquisitive and simple folk, claiming that wherever such hills are found, a treasure lies buried there. They claimed these treasures must be lifted with certain ceremonies and devilish incantations, and were placed there as a sign by those who buried the money. Many people were talked into this and led into ruin, but now it is better understood, etc.

**Marked rocks** <note>original: *Petræ notatæ*, or *gezeichnete Stein*</note> are used as markers in border areas. There were also **marked trees**, about which see Forster, cited above, number 15. In Swabia, these are called *Lochen* <note>meaning 'holes'</note> because they mark or designate such trees with carved holes.

A boundary stone is not subject to prescription <note>a legal principle where a right is gained or lost over time</note>, see *Jacobus de Puteo in the allegations for the community of the land of Valencia, number 41, cited in Hieronymus de Monte’s treatise on defining boundaries.* But regarding boundaries, see *Beroius, question 48, and the annotations there, and Speidel in the Sylloge, parts 1 and 2.*

## ADDITION.

There are also **Shoulder-marks** <note>original: *Achselmarckung*</note>, such as

<column-break/>

those found at Clarspach in the disputed meadows. Also **Seat-marks** <note>original: *Sesselmarckung*</note>. These properties must be designated before they are leased; the lord must first have them surveyed, staked, and marked with stones. *Dr. Tabor, on contracts and the law of tenant farmers, theses 26, 29, at the end.* That is, he must distinguish the borders with barriers, stakes, or stones. If a boundary stone on a communal land is accidentally cast out, torn down, or if it falls over and is lost, and the neighboring communal member does not report it to the lordship as soon as they learn of it, they shall be liable to pay a fine of 2 pounds for every stone. *Measuring fees. General Ordinance.* Regarding dangerous "over-plowing," "over-mowing," or "over-fencing"—that is, the **movement of limits**. *Adam Keller, on the Judicial-Political office, book 2, chapter 15, page 452.* Regarding over-plowing or over-mowing that occurs without damaging the boundary stone: see *Nuremberg against Bavaria regarding the point of Restitution, page 68.* **Schied** <note>a boundary or decision</note> is an act of the administrative authority. *Klock, volume 1, consultation 10, numbers 489 and 490.* **Schied**, the inspection walk <note>original: *Untergang*</note>, and the marking of estates with stones. Also, specific private boundaries and field boundaries. Regarding land-dividers or boundary-inspectors, see *Ruding, century 3, observation 30.* On punishments, legal justifications, and fines regarding the Mark and boundary stones, see *Limnäus, on Public Law, book 7, chapter 35, page 418.* "Goals" <note>original: *Metæ*</note> are named from measuring, likewise "Frontier" from the Italian, whence the Germans get *Frontier*, or *Grängen* <note>borders</note>, similar to a *Kranz* <note>wreath or crown</note>. For boundaries encircle fields like a crown. **Divisions** <note>original: *Scheidungen*</note> come from "to divide" <note>original: *scheiden*</note>; **Markings** <note>original: *Marckungen*</note> from "to mark" <note>original: *märcken*</note>, and from this come the boundaries of the Empire, the **Imperial Marks**. See more in *Oettinger’s special treatise on boundaries, book 1, chapter 2.* Ancient boundaries were named after the winds, according to *Montanus in his treatise on boundaries, chapter 16, number 2.* Not only lands and possessions, but also rights—such as pastures, hunting, and tithes—are circumscribed by their own limits. From this, the terminal stones showing these borders receive their names: **Pasture-stone** <note>original: *Weidstein*</note>, **Hunting-stone** <note>original: *Jagdstein*</note>, **Tithe-stone** <note>original: *Zehendstein*</note>. There are also **Construction or Authority stones**, **Escort stones** <note>original: *Gleitsstein*, for toll/escort limits</note>, **Asylum stones** <note>original: *Freyungstein*</note>, **Forest stones**, **Marking stones**, **Estate stones**, **Road stones**, **Water stones**, and **Parish/Corpse stones** <note>original: *Leichstein*</note>. *Oettinger, cited above, book 1, chapter 17, number 1.* Likewise, jurisdiction is included within certain limits which no one is permitted to step beyond. For the most part, jurisdiction is tied to the territory; thus, the limits of the territory are regularly held to be the limits of the jurisdiction. And whatever is included within the limits of a territory is presumed, in case of doubt, to be under the jurisdiction of the one to whom the territory belongs. *Reink, on Secular and Ecclesiastical Rule, book 1, class 5, chapter 1, number 24.* For what it means to be "without eggs or signs," see *Wehner*. The stones and boundaries of fields receive their power and validity from the placement of small pebbles underneath, which are commonly called **Indices** <note>original Latin: *Indices*, 'witnesses'</note>. *Hieronymus de Monte, on regulating boundaries, chapter 16, number 3*, because they "indicate" the meaning. They are also called witnesses, and *Beleg* <note>proof</note>, and *Eyer* <note>eggs</note>, and marks. Likewise *Beylagen* <note>additions</note>; these pebbles, tokens, and signs are added and buried under the stones through a solemn ritual by designated and sworn **Stone-setters** <note>original: *Steinsetzer*</note>, and they are usually bricks or charcoal. And from this it is asked, if the large stones are removed, and the surveyors...

...if no signs are found under them or near them—or as they say in German, if they are *without eggs* <note>original: *ohne Eyer seyn*; this refers to the practice of burying charcoal, pottery shards, or coins ("eggs") under a boundary stone to prove its original placement if it were ever moved</note>—should they be returned to their former place? See *Rul. de comm. part 2, book 6, chapter 1, folio 259.*

**Question:** Can boundaries also be established on the high sea? It can hardly be denied that parts of the sea are limited in some way, either by a certain number of miles and furlongs, or by the adjacent land. Properly speaking, however, boundaries can in no way be established in the sea. Hence **Saint Ambrose** says, "We have heard of the Geometer (the earth-measurer), but never of the *Thalassometra* (the sea-measurer)" <note>original Latin: *l. 5. Hexaëmer. c. 10.*</note>.

The use of these stones is very ancient, originating with the second King of the Romans, **Numa Pompilius**, who lived in the year of the world 3236. <note>References: Halicarnassus, Pliny, Plutarch</note>. Certain parts of boundary stones are marked with peculiar characters at the discretion of the surveyors; in the past, the sign of the cross was incised, but today a *boundary-mark* <note>original: *Schleusse*</note> is used, which sometimes represents a straight line, sometimes a triangle, and occasionally a semicircle, depending on whether the boundaries they designate are straight or transverse. The upper part of the stone is usually called the **head**, the lower and thicker part placed into the trench (the **bed**, or *das Lager*) is called the **foot**, and the remaining parts are called the **sides**.

There are also **boundary trees**, called *Antemissæ* by some, and in German called *Locheisse*, *Lochen*, or *Lochbaum* <note>Trees marked with notches or holes to serve as permanent landmarks</note>. See *Mont. c. 19. n. 4.* and **Ausonius** in his *Epigrams*:

> *We wonder that men perish, yet monuments crumble,*
> *Death comes even to stones and to names.*

And **Owen**, Book 1 of his *Epigrams*:
> *As if the graves themselves could not die.*

In the Digest <note>original: *l. 3. §. 2. de termino moto*</note> under the title "Concerning the Moving of a Boundary Mark," the founders of the Law teach that boundary questions are obscured in many ways. For just as the ancients divided the boundaries of fields among themselves by various signs—namely, man-made ditches, trees sent before (perhaps meaning "by art"), the course of intervening rivers, or the ridges of mountains, as **Aggenus Urbicus** writes in his *Commentary on Julius Frontinus*—so too were crimes variously committed regarding these things.

It is doubted how the act of one who turns a single tree into a thicket <note>original: *arbustum*</note> should be reckoned as a crime. For should this not rather be considered praiseworthy and rewarded, if many trees are generated from one, since a plantation or multiplication made even on another's soil is primarily useful and fruitful for the owner? However, **Cujacius** <note>Jacques Cujas, a famous 16th-century French legal scholar</note> considers that a tree becomes a "thicket" and this crime is committed when shoots <note>original: *stolones*</note> are repeatedly cut back from a tree. Indeed, **Saxon Law** also binds with this crime anyone who cuts back fruit trees placed for the sake of establishing boundaries. <note>References: Landrecht lib. 2. art. 26; P. Theodor. Disp. Crim. 3.</note>

Whether the law speaks of this same specific case is doubted. For, leaving aside for a moment that "cutting shoots" and "making a thicket" are hardly used as equivalents anywhere else, the resection of shoots—

<column-break/>

especially when done not in a single impulsive moment but repeatedly—does not so completely invert the shape of the tree that it cannot be recognized. It certainly does not change the face of the landscape. Even if one wishes to excuse Cujacius by suggesting he implies not just the cutting, but the propagation of the cut growth, this cannot be applied to "shoots" properly so called. Their sprouting, bushy growth, and subsequent planting is clearly useless and without hope of future offspring, as **Pliny** <note>Book 17, chapter 1</note> testifies.

**Antonius Matthaeus** <note>A noted jurist</note> advises that by *arbustum* (thicket), one should not understand a stunted tree, but a "vine-supporting tree" or a vineyard "married" to trees. However, since the word *arbustum* is not used here as an adjective (as in "vine-supporting trees" planted in groves), but as a noun: We prefer to retain the proper meaning of the word—by which *arbustum* indicates a **shrub** <note>Greek: *ὁ θάμνος*</note> or a **grove** <note>Greek: *δένδρον*</note>—and accept the legal opinion thus: that the crime of "moving a boundary" also applies to him who plants shrubs next to a single boundary tree, so that as they grow, the face of the landscape is transformed.

To this we can bring the examples related by **Hieronymus de Monte**: peasants confusedly plant a tree of a different genus or nature when establishing a border between estates. For instance, if there is a grove of poplars, they might plant an oak or an elm; or conversely, if it is a grove of oaks, they plant a poplar or a chestnut. If someone then plants more trees of that same genus, the characteristic use of the original tree will perish, or certainly be made doubtful, as the appearance of the place has been changed.

**Dr. Tabor**, in a program for two candidates in the year 1640, discusses the **five-foot prescription** <note>original: *præscriptione... quinque pedali*</note>, arguing it should not be alleged whether the dispute concerns boundaries or a specific place. However, the Code of Justinian stands in the way. For if only the "long-term prescription" is removed, then not all are.

The common response distinguishes between the establishment of the **five feet** and anything further. In the first case, if the dispute concerns that space which the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The ancient foundation of Roman Law</note> ordered to be left between neighboring fields—so that both owners could walk, act, and turn a plow—then no prescription applies. In the second case, if a lawsuit is moved concerning land boundaries beyond five feet, it is terminated by a **30-year prescription**, provided the neighbor has possessed the limits of the field quietly for that long. **Cujacius** follows this view, as do most others. **Pacius** alone denies that the law says anything about a five-foot prescription. **Dr. Wisenbach**, in a specific disputation held at Franeker in 1644, approves only the opinion of Cujacius, setting aside others like Peter Crinitus and Nicolaus Valla. He reports from the laws on usucapion <note>acquiring ownership through long use</note> regarding the space within five feet...

(which lie between neighboring fields) there is no acquisition through long-term use <note>original Latin: *usucapio*</note> of their width; (as was long ago provided for in the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE) were the foundation of Roman Law</note>) nor is there prescription—that is, acquisition through long-term use (according to the constitutions of these Emperors). Regarding new boundary stones, or the realignment of half-lost boundary stones that have been plowed out or moved; likewise, no one other than the field-sworn officials <note>original German: *Feldgeschwornen*; local men sworn to honestly oversee land boundaries</note> shall undertake such stone-setting. Those who dig up, throw out, or intentionally cover the set stones—be they young or old—with sod, earth, or otherwise, shall pay 10 florins to the field court and have the thrown-out stones reset at their own expense. *As cited.*

Boundaries are expressed by tree branches and by trees, by columns, by statues, by stone mounds, by mountains, by valleys, by rivers, by royal roads, and by stones. *Boniface, regarding thefts from various places.* Concerning the marking and distinction of boundaries <note>original German: *Hotter*; a term for a jurisdictional or communal boundary</note>, as well as the setting up and rectification of the same, see the *Decree* or *Tripartite Work* of the Hungarian Land-Law, *Part 1, Title 84.* It states that no prescription <note>legal expiration of a right</note> is allowed in the rectification of boundaries. *Part 1, Title 85.* Which boundary charters are valid or not. *Part 1, Title 86.* On the preparation of the boundary. *Part 2, Title 18.* On the completion of the boundary marking. *Part 2, Title 19.* Boundary marking celebrated through an amicable agreement and declaration. *Part 1, Title 86.*

### 28. Margrave. *Marchio.*

Margraves (those invested with a March <note>a border territory</note>, *chapter on who can be called a Duke*)—*Marckgraven*—were prefects of the Empire’s borders and judges of the limits; without doubt, they were similar to the "border prefects" <note>original Latin: *Præfectis limitaneis*</note> mentioned in the law *Spectable Men* <note>original: *l. viros spectabiles. C. de divers. off. lib. 12.*</note>. They were *Border Judges* or *Border Princes* who are judges over such a land that lies on the borders of the *German Empire*. *Menochius, Counsel 302, number 19, volume 4.* For "Mark" signifies a boundary, like a *Border-limit*. Indeed, the ancient Gauls, and even our Germans, called a military horse a *March*. From this, they had the *Marshall* <note>original: *Marckschall*</note>, a dismounting from a horse, and *Märmorphin*, a fall from a horse. *Lindenbrog in the glossary under the word "Marach."* Even now, the Westphalians interpret a horse as a *Mähre* <note>mare</note>, and likewise the Swabians are accustomed to call a mare a *Märr* or *Mesrich*. But it is not at all pleasing that some conclude from this that a Margrave means

<column-break/>

a Prefect of the Cavalry. *Alciatus, Book on the Single Combat, Chapter 32. Cujas, on the chapter regarding those who can grant a fief; whom we commonly call "Count of the Stable"* (because he is the Count or Prefect of the stable), or also a *Marshall*, from *March* or *Märe* (Horse) and *Schalck* (which denotes a servant), as I said in the *Treatise on Counts and Barons, number 10.* Add *Josias Nolden, on Nobles, Chapter 8, number 167 and following.* See *Reinhard König in the Political Theater, Part 1, Chapter 36, number 36 and following, folio 542 and following. Gothofridus Antonius, feudal dispute 2, thesis 4, letter d.*

Lampridius, in his life of *Alexander Severus*, describes the offices and domains of Margraves (as some believe) when he says: "Only those things captured from enemies were granted to the Border Leaders <note>original: *Limitaneis Ducibus*</note> and soldiers, so that they would belong to them if their heirs performed military service, and they would never belong to private citizens; saying that they would serve more attentively if they were also defending their own things." He certainly added animals and slaves to these, so that they could cultivate the fields they had received, and so that the lands neighboring the barbarians would not be deserted through a lack of men or the old age of the owners, which he thought was the safest course. Although Constantine did not remove the border legions without detriment to the Republic. *Zosimus, Book 2. Stephanus Vinandus Pighius in Hercules Prodicius, in the introduction to the 6th book of the Annals of Belgium.* Nevertheless, necessity taught Princes that borders cannot safely lack guardians. See *Arnisaeus on Majesty, folio 322, at the end.*

But whoever desires to know more about Margraves should see *Fauchet, on Origins, 2, Chapter 3. Albinus in the Meissen Land Chronicle, Title 9*, where he discusses the little word *Mark* and how the *Margraviates* arose one after another, and specifically treats the *Margraviate of Meissen* at length; among other Margraviates, he lists the *Mark of Antwerp, the Mark of Austria, Styria, the Mark of Bavaria* (which latter, according to *Lazius on the migration of nations, Book 7*, is said to have been Austria above the Enns before Frederick Barbarossa), *the Mark of the Sorbs, the Mark of Landsberg in the East-land, the Mark of Brandenburg, the Mark of Saxony or Brunswick, the Mark of Schleswig, the Mark of Meissen, the Mark of Lusatia, etc.* The same author, in the *following title*, treats the first growth of the *New Mark of Meissen*. Add *Reineccius on the Meissen Lineage, folio 98.*

On the Austrian Margraves, see *Lazius on Vienna, Book 3, Chapter 2.*

->ADDITION.<-

Margraves were formerly called *Liminarchæ* <note>literally "Rulers of the Threshold" or borders</note>. *Gothofridus Antonius, Fiefs 2, thesis 4, letter d.* But they were guardians of the greatest ports. See *Book 2 of Fiefs, 10, verse:* "it is said, however," where *Antonius* wrongly taxes the Feudalists in the cited place. See *Argentreus in the advice on the partitions of nobles, question 14, number 15, page 2246. See Lord Doctor Tabor in the Clusters of Crimes, page 225, and on arms, chapter 1, number 18.*

Both the dignity and the office of Margraves was previously unheard of in Germany; it first appeared in the times of *Charlemagne and the following Emperors*...

### 35. Slap. Alapa.

He who is struck with a slap <note>original Latin: *alapa*; original German: *Maultasch*</note> does not suffer a loss <note>term: *damnum*; physical or financial loss</note>, but an injury <note>term: *injuria*; an affront to one's legal personhood or honor</note>. *Maranta in Proceedings, Part 4, Distinction 1, Number 9.*

<column-break/>

But it is considered a grave injury. *Vivius, Decision 46*, where he discusses how the person inflicting it should be punished.

Hence, some say that it is permitted to repel a slap with a sword, and if the striker falls wounded by that blow, the defender is not held liable for the killing. *Following Bartolus and Angelus; Marius Salomo in his commentary on the law 'ut vim', number 8, section 'hence of all', Digest on Justice and Law.* However, this is to be understood in such a way that he is not punished with the ordinary penalty, not that he is entirely immune from blame.

Whether it is permitted to strike a slap against someone who is said to have told a lie, see *Köpen, 2. Observation 82, Number 8*, according to that common proverb: "A slap belongs on a lie" <note>original German: *auf eine Lügen gehört eine Maultaschen*</note>.

### ADDITION.

It is not permitted to strike a blow <note>original: *colaphum*</note> against one who inflicts injury with words, unless he has inflicted it upon a person of high standing. *Struvius on Private Revenge, Chapter 10, Aphorism 10, Number 90, Page 118; Berlich, Part 5, Conclusion 64, Number 30.*

It is shameful and dangerous to beat wives with strikes. *Harprecht on the Institutes, § 11, regarding injuries.* For those verses are condemned:

> ->A nut, a donkey, and a woman are bound by a similar law:<-
> ->These three do nothing right if the beatings cease.<-

"A slap belongs on a lie." Phavorinus the Philosopher mentions this law in *Gellius, Book 20, Chapter 1*, where he argues against this penalty as being too meager and therefore inciting men to crimes. "For who will there be," he says, "so poor that twenty-five asses <note>a small Roman coin</note> would deter him from doing an injury?" He also indicates that the same penalty was disapproved of by Labeo, who wrote a commentary on the Twelve Tables and recounted the example of the wicked and insolent man Lucius Neratius. He took it as a delight to strike the face of a free man with the palm of his hand as each person came his way, immediately counting out those 25 asses so that no one could complain further. *See Rittershusius on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, Class 3, Page 2, Chapter 36; Lord Doctor Ludwig, Commentary on the Institutes, § 7 on injuries; and in Disputations on the Institutes, page 312, at the end; Balduin in his Annotations on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, Laws 53, 61, 62; Hotman on § 7 of the Institutes, under this title.* He who gives someone a slap in the mouth shall receive one in return and be banished from the company; a wound does not hurt an honorable man as much as a slap on the cheek. *Dutch Military Law, Article 34, and there Pappus in his annotations.* Whether...

### 36. **Further more.** <note>original: *Mehr weiters / Hoc amplius*</note>.

<margin>On the phrasing of "further more," see Tusch, volume under the letter D, conclusion 286.</margin>
->ADDITION.<-

The phrase "further more" <note>original Latin: *hoc amplius*</note> introduces a repetition of everything that can be agreed upon. See Mantica on *Conjectures of the Last Will*, book 7, title 5, number 8. Especially Capyt, decision 6, number 7, and decision 163, number 1 and following.

The particle "more" <note>original Latin: *magis*</note> is sometimes taken comparatively <note>original Greek: *συγκριτικῶς* (synkritikōs)</note>, but at other times positively <note>original Greek: *θετικῶς* (thetikōs)</note> or absolutely. See Bocer on *Jurisdiction*, chapter 4, number 19. "More" is sometimes placed not comparatively, but plainly and simply. Wilhelm Forster, book of observations, last chapter. "Further" <note>original Latin: *amplius*</note> occurs as a substitute for "more" among legal experts just as it is used by good authors. Master Tabor in *Elements of Jurisprudence*, part 3, section 4, in the appendix, thesis 5, on "insertion."

### 37. **Increaser of the Realm.** <note>original German: *Mehrer des Reichs*; Latin: *Augustus*</note>.

Emperors are called *Augusti*, a title derived from "augury" <note>original: *augurio*</note>, and at the same time from "increasing" <note>original: *augendo*</note> the Empire. Indeed, the Emperor was chosen by observing the omens; hence he was named *Augustus*, as if consecrated by divine signs—blessed with a divine name, preeminently to be venerated, as if it were a name for something divine. See Cothman on the titles of the Code, number 6. Tiberius used this name rarely; see Marcello Donato, *folio 573.* Hence Ovid writes in the first book of the *Fasti*:

> The Fathers call sacred things *Augusta*; we call 
> the temples *Augusta*, duly consecrated by the hand of priests. 
> The augury of this word also depends on its origin: 
> and whatever Jupiter increases <note>original: *auget*</note> with his help.

Add Suetonius on *Augustus*, Dio book 53, Hotoman, Wesenbec, and the Doctors on the Proem of the *Institutes*. See Coras, book 2, and then Cornelius, number 16 and following, on the origin of law. Also Robbigium, book 6 of *Critica*, chapter 2; myself on the *Growth of Empires*, chapter 1; and Meursius in the *Mantissa*, chapter 29.

But *Augustus*, being derived from "increasing," matches our common phrase: **Always an Increaser of the Realm.** <note>original German: *allezeit Mehrer des Reichs*</note>.

For every Emperor ought to have this purpose: that he should increase the realm, even if this does not always happen. Thus, the Count Palatine of the Rhine says during the Coronation of the Emperor: **"Receive the spherical globe, so that you may subject all the nations of the earth to the Roman Empire, and may deserve to be called the glorious Augustus,"** as seen in Simon Schard on the *Origin of Elections*, folio 42. See Afflictus on the titles, chapter 1, on what constitutes regalian rights; and law 3 of the Digest on the office of the Prefect of the Night Watch.

<column-break/>

->ADDITION.<-

The Emperor is called *Augustus* not so much after Augustus Octavian, the nephew of Julius Caesar, but rather as an allusion to the word for "increasing" <note>original: *augendo*</note>, because the Prince ought to increase his Empire, not diminish it. On the occasion of this name, it has been asked: is it lawful for the Emperor to alienate <note>sell or give away</note> those things that belong to the Empire? We deny this, along with Paurmeister in book 2 of *Jurisdiction*, chapter 4, number 61; Hotoman, *Illustrious Questions*, question 1; Bronchorst, century 4 of *Apparent Contradictions*, assertion 87; Hönnonius, disputation 6, controversy 20; and Conrad Rittershusius in the Proem to the *Institutes*, page 6, who tries to resolve the difficulty with a distinction. See Harprecht, number 55, who responds to most contrary arguments, and Master Cobius on the *Inscription of the Proem of the Institutes*, question 4. See the text of the Election Agreement <note>original Latin: *Capitulationis*</note> of Emperor Charles V in Sleidan, book 1 of the *Commentaries*, and that of Ferdinand III, article 9, which begins: **"To this and especially."** Hence Baldus writes in chapter *intellecto* 33 on the *Law of Oaths*, and Antonio Peregrinus in *On the Law of the Treasury*, book 1, page 97, number 71, that the Empire is not in the "purse" of the Prince—meaning he cannot destroy its rights and throw them out the window like money. See Wendelin in *Politics*, page 109.

### 38. **Perjury.** <note>original German: *Meinaid*; Latin: *Perjurium*</note>.

Concerning perjury, see the individual treatise by Herdefiani; add Farinacius on *Simulation and Forgery*, question 160; Barschamp in the treatise on *Clauses*, chapter 30, paragraph 8, chapter 2, number 2; and Speidel in the *Sylloge*, parts 1 and 2, under the word "perjury."

->ADDITION.<-

He who makes someone swear an oath when he knows that person will likely commit perjury or break the bonds of the oath is worse than a murderer. This is according to Felinus and Afinius on *Executions*, paragraph 8, chapter 2, number 22. An oath is often compared to the planet Mercury: just as Mercury is good in the house of a good planet but bad in the house of a bad planet, so an oath's character depends on its context. See Zafius on law 1, number 4, on the *Law of Oaths*; Beut on the title of the *Law of Oaths*, number 35; Cothman, volume 4, response 5, number 17. One who does not satisfy local statutes does not necessarily become a perjurer, according to Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 6, numbers 37 and 38. Indeed, one becomes a perjurer if they have sworn to observe those laws and then do not fulfill the oath by their actions (number 39). Perjury is the violation of a lawful oath, according to Barbosa, book 14, chapter 23, axiom 1. Perjury is generally not committed without malicious intent <note>original: *dolus*</note>, axiom 2. Whatever excuses a delay also excuses one from perjury, axiom 3. No one is believed to want to commit perjury to the destruction of their own salvation, axiom 4. It is a sin to swear falsely, but not simply to swear, axiom 5. Perjury has God as its avenger. Law 2 of the Code on *Credited Matters* (in Ummius on *Proceedings*, page 571 of my copy) should be understood as referring to perjury committed not by deliberate and planned counsel of the mind, but in the heat of love or anger, without prejudice to any third party—though even then, it is not immune from all punishment. See Tetsch, *Inaugural Disputation at Basel*. Ruland treats this law at length in *On the Purgation of Oaths*, chapter 7, aphorism 3 and following. See also Pacius in the *Analysis of the Code* on this title. In law 2 of the Code on *Credited Matters*, a perjurer...

### 39. Majority of Votes. <note>original German: *Meiste Stimmen*; Latin: *Majora vota*</note>

What the majority concludes, the remainder are also bound to consent to, even in matters where some right is already deemed to have been acquired by the minority party, according to the records of Berlich, *decision 125*. However, in explaining this rule, he says in *number 4* that the majority can only prejudice the minority in matters regarding them as a collective <note>original: *universos*</note>—not by their own individual right, but as Tutors, Curators, Senators, and the like. It is otherwise if the matter concerns them by their own right as individuals. See Surdus, *counsel 65*; Moditius on the section *Concerning the Decree of the People, question 53, etc.*; and myself, *On Aristocracy, folio 31*. See especially the two detailed legal opinions <note>original German: *zween ausführliche Rathschlag*</note> concerning the session, standing, and vote of the Honorable, Free, and Imperial Cities of the Holy Roman Empire, printed throughout in Frankfurt in 4to. Indeed, long ago the Protestants fought against the plurality of votes. Hortleder, *volume 1, folio 50*. And they revived this dispute again in the year 1613; see myself, *On the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire, question 15*.

->ADDITION.<-

The majority part draws the minority to itself. Klock, *volume 1, counsel 27, number 49*, even if it is of a different quality. *counsel 50, number 158*. On whether the majority prejudices the minority, see Klock, *counsel 20, numbers 197 through 200, and 204 through 206; and counsel 35, number 287, 339, 340, 341, and following*. The consensus of the majority is not sufficient in voluntary acts, *ibid. number 203*. This is restricted in *number 250*; see *questionable counsel 35, numbers 329, 330, and numbers 346, 352, 353*. The majority does not prejudice an exempt minority party, *number 207*. This is explained in *number 251 and counsel 31, number 85*. In cases of necessity and public utility, the majority compels the minority to contribute. Klock, *volume 1, counsel 20, numbers 241, 242*. This is extended in *number 243*. When majority rules should not be admitted. Limnaeus, *On Public Law, book 9, chapter 1, number 189*. observation 23, number 5 and following. In a time of plague, in order to banish melancholic thoughts, any kind of game or play is permitted. <note>Cited from Ripa’s *Treatise on the Plague*, chapter 4, number 157.</note>

One reads of a man from the noble family of Zuhmen (or Zaumen) in Pomerania, that in the year 1314 he fell into a wondrous melancholy and believed himself to be dead. He was, however, restored to his senses through a clever trick—which often works best for such persons—wherein several people dressed themselves as corpses and had food and drink brought to them. By this means, they led the gloomy man back to consuming food, which he had previously refused. <note>Cited from Zeiller’s *Centuries of Letters*, page 620.</note> Melancholy and pain are also driven away through good conversation, although other remedies are better suited to different nations: for the French, singing; for the Spaniards, wailing and howling; for the Italians, sleep; and for the Germans, drinking. In China <note>original: *Sina*</note> there was a nobleman who refused to urinate because he believed he would drown the entire city with it. A wise doctor cured him in this way: he had an old barn on the nobleman's estate set on fire and ordered all the servants to cry out that there was no water available to quench such a fire. If the master did not wish to see his property lie in ashes, he must release the supply of water he had gathered for many days. When this delusional nobleman saw the fire, he relieved his bladder to quench it and was thus restored to health. <note>Cited from Harsdörffer’s *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, page 272.</note> See also Schonlin on *Melancholy*. Another man imagined himself to be made of glass and therefore begged that no one touch or break him; when they wished to satisfy him, they had to bind him in straw and, instead of solid food, pour nourishing juices into him under the pretext of preserving them in glass vessels. <note>original: *d. loc.*, referring to the same source.</note> Regarding the property of those who commit suicide out of the disease of melancholy or madness, rather than out of a guilty conscience for a crime committed—should such goods be subject to confiscation? Whether not having an organized memory is a sign of stupidity. <note>Cited from Mantica, *On Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 2.</note> On when forgetfulness is presumed, see Menochius, book 6, presumption 32.

It cannot be said how much memory is strengthened by that time which is otherwise usually the cause of forgetfulness <note>i.e., the night/sleep</note>. Therefore, the Owl was sacred to Pallas Athena among the Athenians, because "counsel comes in the night." <note>original Greek: *ἐν νυκτὶ ἡ βολη*</note> See Dannhauer in his *Treatise on Memory*, page 43. Thuanus, in book 23, year 1559, relates that Amarus Ranconetus also kept such a habit: after taking a light meal, he would give himself to rest at nightfall; having finished his first sleep, he would rise, and shortly after compose himself for rest again. What he had ingeniously begun in his first meditation, he would most successfully complete immediately upon waking from his second sleep. Memory naturally ascends, it does not descend. <note>Dannhauer, page 50.</note>

The manner of preserving and increasing memory is explained at length by Ruland in *On Commissions*, book 1, chapter 9 and following. Ludovicus Romanus Pontanus, an excellent legal scholar, is praised for having such a great memory that he was thought to yield to none of the ancients. Concerning him, Aeneas Sylvius <note>Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II.</note> broke out into these words: "He was mindful of everything he had ever either read or heard, nor had he forgotten anything he had seen. Nor did he, like other jurists, merely cite the beginnings of laws in debate, but as if he were reading the Code itself, he would recite the text from memory." Socrates used to say that a person only knows as much as they keep in their memory. One can pull everything from memory like a thread from a cloth. <note>Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 41.</note> Muretus writes that he knew a man in Padua, originally from Corsica, who could recite 36,000 words by the sole benefit of local memory, in any order, even backwards. # Enlarged Treasury of Practical Knowledge

For what is read in our Vulgate Bible at **Deuteronomy 16** as a "free-will offering" is called *Missah* in Hebrew and Chaldean. This was what they offered to God in thanksgiving for the fruits of the earth, which they also ate in the Temple in remembrance of their past servitude and their liberation from it. Since all these things align perfectly with the Sacrifice instituted by Christ, our ancestors preferred to use this name rather than that of any other sacrifice. This is because that first offering made by our Lord Jesus Christ of himself—of which Isaiah says in **chapter 53**, <note>original Latin: *oblatus est, quia ipse voluit*</note> "he was offered because he himself willed it"—is recollected as a voluntary act. Indeed, it is believed that this name was handed down to the Romans from Hebrew sources by the Apostles Peter and Paul themselves; the Apostle James, Bishop of Jerusalem and "brother of the Lord," also passed this on to his followers in the Mass he left to posterity. That the Roman Church used this term from its very beginning is proven by the fact that Pope Pius, who was close to the time of the Apostles, called this same sacrifice the "Mass" <note>original: *Missam*</note> in his *Letter to Justus of Vienne* (found in the first volume of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*). Cornelius and other Roman Pontiffs did the same, as did the Council of Rome under Sylvester, the second Council of Carthage <note>Council 2, chapter 3</note>, the Council of Agde <note>Chapter 47</note>, and others. Likewise, Ambrose mentions it in his *Letter 33 to Marcellina*, Augustine in his *Sermon on Time 251*, Victor of Vita in his *History of the Vandal Persecution*, book 2, and finally all other more recent authors. So says the aforementioned writer.

More regarding the Mass, its antiquity, and its celebration can be found in Filefacus's *Treatise on Parishes*, page 6 and following; Alzedo in his *Treatise on Episcopal Dignity*, folio 142; J. Deculeo in his *Letters*, folios 198 and 114; Polydore Vergil in *On the Discovery of Things*, chapter 12; Ritius on the Kings of the Franks under Capet; and Cornelius à Rinthelin in *The Roman Catholic Jurist*, chapter 100. In the latter, he discusses how the holy sacrifice of the Altar should be exceedingly honored and should not be celebrated in private places, but only in those consecrated to God by Bishops. See also Longus’s *Chronological Breviary*, folio 118 and following.

That a single person cannot celebrate multiple Masses on the same day—and that anyone doing otherwise should be severely punished—is taught by Marc. Antonius in *The Practice of the Archbishop’s Court*, chapter 64.

Regarding whether the little word *Meß* <note>Mass</note> signifies a tribute or a labor service <term>Frondienst: a form of feudal socage or forced labor</term>, see the *Evangelical Weather-cock* <note>original German: *Evangelischen Wetterhanen*</note>, printed in octavo at Ingolstadt, page 231, where it is stated: "The little word *Meß*, taken from the Apostles, means in Hebrew as much as a tribute or labor service. Just as a peasant or a feudal tenant brings his *Meß*—that is, his due tribute or service—to his lord, or performs labor for his prince so that he may acknowledge him as his lord and fulfill his obedience, so too have they spoken: 'I will go to Mass,' or 'hear Mass.' It is as if they were saying: 'I will give God his due tribute, or perform my service,

<column-break/>

and offer it in the highest and most pleasing ministry.'"

### 43. Mass, Yearly Fair, Weekly Market. <note>original: *Meß, Jahrmarckt, Wochenmarckt. Nundinæ.*</note>

It is not permitted for anyone to establish fairs <term>Nundinæ: traditional Roman term for market days or fairs</term> according to their own will, not even on private estates. Instead, it is necessary that they be obtained from the Prince who holds the right to grant fairs, according to law 1 of the *Digest: on fairs*. For it is established that the right to hold solemn and public fairs belongs to the "Greater Regalia" <term>Regalia majora: the high sovereign rights and prerogatives of a monarch</term>, according to the single law... <meta>catchword: where</meta>

<meta>This page transitions from the theological discussion of the "Mass" to the legal and economic definition of fairs and markets (which in Latin and some Germanic contexts shared related terminology or were categorized under the same alphabetical entries). It examines the legal rights required to establish markets and the protections afforded to those who attend them.</meta>

<page-num>705</page-num>
<header>Letter M.</header>

...where Sichard, in his commentary on the *Code concerning Fairs* <note>original Latin: *Cod. de nund.*</note>, says that even lower Princes, within their Royal Prerogatives <note>original: *Regalibus*</note>, do not have the power to grant this Privilege within their own Provinces. See Gail, book 2, observation 69; Bodin on the *Republic*, book 1; and Sixtinus on *Regalia*, book 1. See also the author of the **well-founded counter-report** <term>wohlgegründten Gegenberichts — a common title for legal rebuttals in the Holy Roman Empire</term>, written against the **Councillors of the Bishop of Würzburg, etc.** <term>Bischöffliche Würzburgische Räthe, 2c.</term> in chapter 13. However, the Emperor has never been accustomed to granting a Privilege for Fairs to anyone without first hearing from the adjacent and neighboring Cities that might have an interest in the matter. See Gail and Schönborner.

That this Right was also obtained from the Senate in ancient times is testified by Barnabas Brisson, citing Pliny’s *Letters to Valerian*, where he says: "A skillful man of Praetorian rank petitioned the Senate for permission to establish fairs on his lands." The envoys of the people of Vicenza opposed it. Thus it is established that even the Emperor Claudius, subjecting himself to public laws, petitioned the Consuls for the right of Fairs on his own estates.

Fairs are of three kinds: **weekly markets** <term>Wochenmärckt</term>, **annual fairs** <term>Jahrmärckt</term>, and **large trade fairs** <term>Messen</term>. **Large trade fairs** <note>original: *Messen*, referring to major international fairs like those in Frankfurt or Leipzig</note> belong to the Emperor; **annual fairs** likewise, as they are a consequence of founding a city or making a **market town** <term>Marckflecken — a settlement with market rights but not full city status</term>. But today, Princes take this right for themselves. Something else must be said regarding **weekly markets**, as will follow below.

Fairs, according to Cujas, are markets held for the sake of the country folk, who bring their goods in a crowded gathering. The ancients intended these to be "feast days" <note>original: *feriatum diem*</note>, meaning a vacation from legal business. However, later by the Hortensian Law, it was decided they should not be holidays, so that the peasants coming to the City to sell their goods could simultaneously settle their legal disputes. They are called *Nundinae*, as if "nine-day-fairs" <note>original: *novendinae*</note>, because they were celebrated every ninth day. These weekly fairs, being introduced by custom more for the sake of the food supply than for general trade, are not part of the Royal Prerogatives <note>original: *Regalibus*</note>; therefore, they can be established without a Privilege or grant from a superior.

The legal favor shown to fairs is great, which is evident from the fact that during their time, neither the goods nor the person of anyone should be detained or arrested.

For by granting the right of such fairs, public security is understood to be granted to those who assemble at the Fairs for the sake of trade. Thus, within the days of the Fair (which were several, as can be gathered from the law), that is, before the signal is given by the bell that they have ended, they cannot be summoned, imprisoned, or arrested under the pretext of a civil or private debt—

Besold's Works, Volume I.

<column-break/>

—not only by those who obtained the Privilege of the Fairs, but also by other merchants. (It is otherwise in smaller markets, because markets are not "safe" regarding debts and taxes in the way Fairs are. See François Mignon.) It does not matter whether those Fairs are weekly, monthly, annual, held every five years, every seven years, or are "Appearance" fairs <note>original: *Apparitionis*</note>—that is, those celebrated around the time of the Birth of the Lord, when the Star appeared to the Magi. Nor does it matter if they are Fairs of Easter, All Saints, or the month of August, all of which are mentioned by Socinus Junior. The reason is so that goods, which are undoubtedly necessary for the preservation of this life, may be imported and exported more freely and in greater abundance. Regarding this matter, many writings exist by Alexander, Baldus, and others. However, I would wish this to be understood—as Peter Peckius says in his *Treatise on Arrests*—unless the debt has been sworn by oath. For just as a decree removing another general sworn decree does not apply to a specific sworn decree, and just as a Safe Conduct granted to someone does not extend to sworn debts, it seems that for the same reason a person can be detained and arrested for a sworn debt. Therefore, Creditors are advised to have the promise of payment confirmed by the bond of religion and a formal oath.

Just as it is not permitted to arrest someone during the time of the Fairs in the place where they are held, so too is it prohibited in the place without which merchants cannot come to the Fairs <note>meaning the access roads or neighboring jurisdictions necessary for travel</note>.

Can a debtor renounce the immunity of this time or place? Peckius discusses this, saying: Regarding the time, there is no doubt that the immunity of the Fairs can be renounced. For although Fairs enjoy public favor (namely, so that goods needed by the state or City may be brought in), they primarily concern the convenience of private individuals. Thus, one must stand by the common Rule: whenever a Law introduces something primarily for private favor—even if it has a secondary public cause attached—that favor can be renounced.
