*regarding the penultimate law of the Code on agreements; see also Brisson on the universal law, number 2, regarding legacies.* But see *Moller, book 1, six-month term, chapter 12.* This is provided, however, that such a renunciation is specific and express. *Law 1 and the commentary there by Romanus and others in the Digest on 'if anyone is called to court'; see Peckius in the cited chapter 12, numbers 3 and following.*

However, these Fairs, which a People—acknowledging some Superior Prince—usurps for themselves without any Privilege from their Prince, without prescription from time immemorial, and without the Prince’s knowing consent, do not possess that legal Privilege. *See Law 1, under the section 'by the grant of the ancients or our authority,' and the commentaries by Baldus and Salicetus on the Code concerning fairs; see also Peckius on the same law, numbers 5 and following.*

It should further be noted here that this right of Fairs, and the exercise of them, can be taken away by a Prince for a just cause, notwithstanding a very long duration of time exceeding the memory of man. This is *according to Law 1 of the Digest on fairs and the single law of the Code on the same.* As a legal expert consulted on the facts, *Natta* responded at length in *counsel 511 and following* regarding a market case; his opinion in judging was followed by the Senate of Piedmont, as reported by *Tessaurus in decision 264.* Similarly, Charles IV took that right away from the people of Frankfurt and transferred it to Mainz; however, after the death of Günther, he restored it to them through the intervention of Rudolf of the Palatinate and the Margrave of Brandenburg. *See Peucer, book 5 of the Chronicles, page 805; Arnisaeus, book 2 on Sovereignty, chapter 2, number 18.*

Common fairs, which we call **weekly markets** <term>Wochenmarckt</term>, can be established and celebrated without any Privilege. *Sichard on the title of the Code regarding fairs, number 3.* And although in many places they are recorded as being granted, they can nevertheless be held even without the Prince’s license, and they constitute a matter of fact rather than a matter of law. This is because they lack the Privileges and other immunities that are usually granted to solemn fairs. *Tessaurus, decision 364, number 4.* Therefore, in this context, the "right of market" is to be understood in its more powerful and commonly accepted sense: namely, of the anniversary market, which is among the **royal prerogatives** <term>regalia — rights belonging exclusively to the sovereign</term>. *Graeven, book 2, conclusion 60, consideration 1, numbers 1 and 3.*

Municipal Cities, if they possess jurisdiction granted to them by a just title, are permitted to establish weekly trade centers or common Fairs—**weekly markets** <term>Wochenmarckte</term>—even without the prior knowledge of the Superior Lord. *Matthias Stephanus on jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 1, section 2, number 104.* Nor is there a need for Privileges and other immunities to grant them, which otherwise tend to be attached to solemn Fairs. And they were introduced by a certain custom not so much for the sake of trade as for the sake of the **food supply** <term>annonae gratia — ensuring the local population has access to grain and bread</term>. *Matthias Wesenbeck in his summary of the Digest, under the title 'On Fairs,' number 1.*

A **Market** <term>Marckt</term> is a forum, a place in a City where things of every kind are put up for sale. From this, **hamlets or small market towns** <term>die Flecken, oder kleine Städtlein Marckt</term> are so named, because it is permitted to **hold a market, and craftsmen may earn a living there.** <note>original German: *Marckt halten, und sich allda Handwercker ernähren mögen.*</note> Since ancient times, when our ancestors were converted to the faith, there were not yet as many Churches as there are in this age;

<column-break/>

rather, those living further away were forced to travel several miles to the Parish on Sundays. For that reason, some shepherds, innkeepers, cooks, peddlers, and various craftsmen would station themselves there to provide necessities to those arriving.

Regarding Fairs and the law of Fairs, one may also consult *Marcellus Donatus, page 644,* and *Brisson on the ancient Jurisdictions, book 1, chapter 15.* A catalog of Fairs is held in the *Chronicle of Chronicles, page 308.*

On the Right of the Vienna Trade Center and its most ancient Privileges, see *Lazius on Vienna, book 2, chapter 8.*

### ADDITION

Whether sworn debts enjoy the privilege of Fairs is discussed very extensively by *Fritsch on Fairs, chapter 7, numbers 40 to 62.* Can someone effectively renounce the privilege of Fairs? *Chapter 7, number 63.* Can the Emperor or a Prince transfer the right of Fairs perhaps granted to a City to others without cause? *Chapter 12, number 2 and following.* Regarding the **payment weeks** <term>Zahlwochen — specific weeks at a trade fair designated for settling debts</term>, see *Carpzov, part 2, decision 133, numbers 3 and 19,* where he discusses the clause: **at the usual time of payment.** <note>original German: *zur gewöhnlichen Zahlungs-Zeit.*</note>

Regarding **crimes at the Frankfurt Fair** <term>Freveln auf der Franckf. Meß</term>, see the *Frankfurt Reformation, part 10, title 2, at the end.*

"Fairs" <note>original Latin: *Nundinae*</note> are named as if they were "nine-day-ers" <note>original Latin: *novendinae*</note> because they recurred every ninth day. *Plautus in the Aulularia* teaches: "That man is a 'Fair-day cook'; he is accustomed to go to cook on the ninth day." Feasts were celebrated at fairs, which is why "Fairs" sometimes stands for the Feasts themselves. When a partnership was formed to buy and meet together, so that one would provide the "fairs"—that is, the feasts—for the rest, and release them from business: if he did not pay for them, he must be sued both as a partner and for the sale. Regarding this law, see *Jacques Cujas, Observations, book 4, chapters 17 and 25, page 174.* More on this material was collected by *Dr. Dorsch in the funeral program for Johann Philipp Mogesser, 1646.*

The institutions or customs of later times have added many things to Fairs beyond the mere transport and exchange of various goods—things which might sometimes make sensible people feel either nauseated or amused. Regarding the **Zurzach fairs** <note>original Latin: *Zurzacensibus nundinis* — a major trading site in Switzerland</note>, *Theodor Zwinger* has this in *volume 24 of the Theater, book 2, page 4042*: "The Zurzach fairs," he says, "which are very famous, are held twice a year on the eighth day after Pentecost and on the Calends of September. At these, there is a singular custom: the Swiss Prefect publicly 'leads the rope'—if I may put it that way—in a dance of public prostitutes, and he gives a dinner with an honorarium to whichever prostitute danced most skillfully. This is perhaps in memory of a pious service which a prostitute performed for Emperor Albert II, who was killed near Windisch by the treachery of his nephew Rudolf (for he breathed his last in her lap at the spot where the high altar in the Königsfelden monastery was later placed). It was established by Queen Elizabeth of Hungary to honor [the memory] of her **Father**..." <note>The text cuts off at the catchword 'Patris' (Father).</note>

In the **Greater Fairs** (such as those in Leipzig and Frankfurt), which are granted to cities by the Emperor as a privilege for the purpose of conducting trade (Law 1, *On Fairs*), no one can be barred under the pretext of a private debt (Single Law, Code, *On Fairs*). Hence also the Saxon Electoral Constitution 30.1: <note>original German: "Wir wollen absonderlich, daß in allen Fällen innerhalb der offentlichen Märckt..."</note> **"We specifically desire that in all cases within the public markets, for the sake of trade and business, freedom shall be maintained; no arrest shall take place, nor shall anyone be detained on account of civil matters or obligations."** However, regarding debts contracted within the fairs themselves, they may rightly be summoned to judgment there. Matth. Stephani, book 1, chapter 29, number 52. Just as in certain places specific judges are appointed to hear these cases: for example, in Strasbourg they are summoned **before the appointed Fair Masters.** <note>original German: "vor dem verordneten Meßherrn"</note> But this is only true if the creditor sold in expectation of immediate cash and did not rely on the buyer's credit. The power to grant fairs or a public market belongs to the Imperial Majesty. Bocer *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 1, number 43, page 42. Also *On Regalian Rights*, chapter 2, number 238. Menochius, counsel 302, number 31. Brisson, *Selected Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 15. Tesaurus; Besold, Volume 1.

decision 264, number 2. During a Fair, neither the goods nor the person of a debtor can be detained by arrest before the signal is given by the bell that the fair has ended. Bocer, chapter 2, *On Regalian Rights*, number 240, and those cited there.

# 46. Mile. <term>Milliare</term> <note>A mile, derived from "mille passuum" or a thousand paces</note>.

There are two kinds of miles, according to Henning Göden, *Counsel* 12, who writes the following: "One is measured by law, so that a thousand paces or steps shall make one mile—five feet making a pace, and the foot being 15 fingers wide—and 20 of these miles are calculated for a day's journey; these are also called the *Legal Day's Journey* and the *Legal Mile*, as is commonly determined." <note>This defines a standardized Roman-style mile for legal calculations of travel time</note>

The other mile is a common mile, or called a <term>Milliare vulgare</term>: This is estimated from the custom of each specific land where miles are used. Therefore, these regional miles are of unequal length and measure. Thus, in Westphalia and Switzerland, the miles are longer than in Thuringia and other good lands. See also Schäffer, 1, question 24.

The <term>Milliare</term>, which is also called a <term>Milliarium</term>, according to Antonius Augustinus in his *Emendations*, book 14, was a golden column <note>The *Milliarium Aureum*</note> placed at the head of the Roman Forum, from which all the roads of Italy took their beginning and end, as gathered from the words of Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) and Tacitus (*Annals* 17), the latter saying: "Otho, leaning on his freedman, proceeded through the Tiberian house into the Velabrum, and from there to the golden milestone below the Temple of Saturn." And as the former writes, Rome is divided into fourteen regions, with 265 crossroads: the measurement of this space running from the milestone at the head of the Roman Forum to the individual gates. The word "mile" is derived from a "thousand paces," as per Antonius Augustinus, book 4. Since the miles used to be marked by stones, Martianus said: "Senators are not required to exercise guardianship beyond 

<column-break/>

the hundredth stone <note>the 100th mile-marker</note> from the city." (Law: *propter*, § *fin*, Digest *on the excuse of tutors*). Furthermore, the Emperors Valentinian and Valens wrote back in a decree: "Soldiers are ordered to gather stakes for themselves no further than the twentieth stone." (Law 2, *on the delivery of military provisions*). In the Capitoline Forum, one can now see a restored marble column having a bronze ball placed upon it, taken from the Vatican obelisk when it was moved from its ancient site and placed before the doors of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles <note>St. Peter's Basilica</note> by the care of Pope Sixtus V.

On miles, see also Barthius on Rutilius, folio 195 and following.

## ADDITION.

Of the Persian miles or <term>Farsang</term> <note>A parasang, roughly 3.5 miles</note>, one can travel 12 or even 14 in a day. Miles must be measured according to the custom of each place. Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter, part 1, counsel 65, number 5. Miles are usually measured by the benefit of a wheel <note>An early odometer</note>. (Ibid, last number). Where no custom exists, the measurement should be made from the city gate to the hedges of the village (numbers 6 and 7).

An Italian mile has eight stadia <note>Greek units of distance</note>, but a German mile has thirty-two. Meisner in his *Compendium of Geography*, page 132. The Romans measured the intervals of places by thousands of paces, which were called miles, and they marked each mile with stones or pillars; hence we read everywhere "at the first, second, or third stone" from the city (page 134). The question is asked: how far can a ship travel in a day? A cargo ship <note>original: "Lastschiff"</note> or vessel with a moderate wind can travel eight Italian miles in one hour; with a good wind, 12; with a "fortune" or strong wind, 20 miles. Thus, with a moderate wind in 24 hours (a day and night), 48 German miles may be completed in sailing; with a good wind in a day and night, 70 German miles; but with a "fortune," nearly 126 miles. Herodotus in *Melpomene* writes that a ship may go 70,000 steps in a day; now, 4,000 steps make one German mile, which equals no more than 17 miles. However, 2,000 years ago, people were not so experienced in navigation. One kind of mile is legal, another is common. Schneidewin, title *on actions*, § *rursus*, number 42.

How miles are to be computed and according to which road they are to be measured (number 40). If miles are to be measured, the custom of each place must be observed (number 41). Twenty miles are prescribed for each day for those absent to return (number 39). See also Dr. Nicolaus Rittershusius, *On Absence*, thesis 187. If a horseman were to cover 15 German miles each day, he would be able to reach the Moon from the surface of the Earth in no less than 5 years, 2 months, and a bit more.

Petrus de Bella Pertica <note>a 13th-century French jurist known for his work on Roman law</note> explains this in question 236: Either a thing is common to everyone—such as the common property of a University—in which case that which is common is not *mine* (according to the section on the division of things in the *Institutes* <note>a foundational Roman law textbook</note>). Or a thing is common as it belongs to individuals—specifically two or more—and in that case, what is common is also *mine* (by the law on marriage rites), though it is called "mine" improperly (as in the laws on the significance of words).

### ADDITION.

Those pronouns "Mine" and "Thine," which some find so ominous, are quite consistent within themselves. They did not provide an opportunity for evil on their own, but could—and certainly should—have been introduced for the preservation of things and the nourishment of peace and harmony. Therefore, they are said to have begun by the Law of Nations <term>Jus Gentium</term> <note>a legal concept of "natural law" common to all peoples</note> in the *Hungarian Customary Law*, Prologue, title 4. Add Bernegger’s questions on Tacitus’s *Agricola*, 138.

"Mine" and "thine" are synonyms for ownership <term>dominium</term>.

The terms "mine" and "thine" are sometimes understood more broadly, so that the voice encompasses not only the "right in a thing" <note>original: "jus in re," referring to direct ownership</note> but also the "right to a thing" <note>original: "jus ad rem," referring to a claim or credit</note>. See laws 91 and 143 on the significance of words, and laws 71 and 73 on legacies. Hence we even say "my debt" <note>original: "æs alienum meum," literally "my foreign bronze"</note> meaning what I owe to another, and "your debt" meaning what you owe to another. Cicero uses this in *For Roscius* and the *Verrine Orations*. Seneca is very clear in *On Remedies for Fortuitous Events*: "I recognize my debt; I indeed contracted this with the creditor." Mr. Tabor, in *Elements of Jurisprudence*, part 3, section 4, thesis 25, note 5. What cannot be reclaimed <note>vindicated</note> is not "mine." Mr. Tabor, on alienation in the context of loans, page 485, number 23. "Mine, thine, his" designates everything that belongs to someone by right of ownership or quasi-ownership, or by right of possession, even if it is common to others, or has been given as a pledge or mortgage. On the contrary, Ulpian denies in law 27, paragraph 2 on the legacy of gold and silver, that a debt is the property of the creditor. More in Mr. Tabor on alienation, page 401 and following. "Mine" is spoken of in various ways; see the same location, pages 409 and 444.

Another person's business becomes "mine" through ratification. In my own property, I am allowed to do anything for my own benefit and utility. What is mine cannot become "more mine" (legal axiom 2). *Cl. Mir und den Meinen unschädlich* <note>German: "Harmless to me and mine"</note>. Minden is a Hanseatic Episcopal City; its name is derived from *Min* and *din* <note>Low German for "mine" and "thine"</note>. For when Widukind, King of the Saxons, had accepted the Christian faith and was baptized by the first Bishop, Herimbert, he allowed Charlemagne to give the Bishop a certain place on the Weser river; and thus the King said, *das Schloß soll mein und dein seyn* <note>German: "the castle shall be mine and thine"</note>. More on this in Sprenger’s *Outline of the States of the Empire*, page 334.

### 48. Metals. <term>Metallum</term>.

Regarding Metals and Metallic things, see Caesalpinus. Thurneisser on *Metallic Waters*. Vidius in his individual legal treatise.

Metal is a type of non-living mixture that is dug out of the earth. It contains seven forms or species under it: *Gold, Silver, Copper, Electrum <note>a natural alloy of gold and silver</note>, Tin, Lead, and Iron.* (Isidore, book 16, chapter 16). Galeottus Martius (in book 14 of *On Promiscuous Learning*) relates these, following the Astrologers, to the powers of the seven Planets in this order: He attributes *Gold* to the Sun because of its color and value; *Silver* to the Moon because of its color; Tin to *Jupiter* because of its color and similarity of nature; *Copper* <note>original: "Æs"</note> to Venus because of its color and inflexible nature; *Lead* to Saturn because of its coldness and weight; *Iron* or *Steel* to Mars because of its dryness. He adds *Quicksilver* <note>Mercury</note> in place of electrum to Mercury because of its mobility. But see Bificiolus, *Leisure Hours*, book 5, chapter 11, and more in volume 2, book 17, chapter 14, where he refutes the opinion of those who think metals should be referred to the planets.

As to how gold, silver, and other metals are born, Georgius Agricola <note>the "father of mineralogy"</note> and other miners have recorded the traditions.

### ADDITION.

On Metals: J. T. Sprenger in *Fragments of Public Law*, page 192 and following. The Lord of a territory adjudges mines of alum and vitriol <note>sulfate minerals</note> to himself. (Goedd. counsel 1 on gold mines; Afflictus, decision 321). Johannes Guiddit. Volter. wrote *On Minerals* and *On Iron Workshops*. Mr. Tabor on "Metals," page 248. Encelius wrote *On Metallic Matters*.

Other metals are partly of a middle and partly of a lower kind, such as Electrum, Bismuth, Antimony, Mercury (or quicksilver), Orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide, used as a pigment</note>, Sulfur, Vitriol, Alum, Rock Salt, Nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, and Stone. (Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 33, throughout). The confusion of metals is most ruinous to the State. The weights of metals belong to the Count of Sacred Largesses <note>a late Roman financial official</note>. On the doctrine of metals, see Albertus Magnus and Andreas Caesalpinus. Albinus, in part 4 of the *Meissen Mining Chronicle*, asserts that the Dukes of Saxony collected 41,118 "tons of gold" <note>a unit of value, often representing 100,000 thalers, rather than literal weight</note> from the Schneeberg veins within 79 years, from the tithes and the marking of silver. Obrecht in *Political Reflections*, page 101.

Of the German springs (among which is also Griesbach, located not far from Strasbourg), it is said that while they were not permitted to be used freely by all who wished, but only upon payment of a steep price, they completely dried up. ### 50. Misdeed, Maltreatment, Offense. <note>original: "Missethat, Mißhandlung, Delictum"</note>

Cothmann says in his *Academic Responses*, 1, number 198, that the terms "Misdeed" and "Maltreatment" <note>original: "Missethat und Mißhandlung"</note> properly denote a most atrocious offense <term>delictum</term>.

In the Law Faculty of Tübingen, this distinction <term>discrimen</term> is observed between "Maltreatment" and "Excess": the former word is used in sentencing if the act was illegal and unjustifiable <note>original: "unverantwortlich"</note> from the very beginning. "Excess" <term>Exceß</term>, however, is used if, for example, someone defended himself justly at the start, but afterward, out of heat or passion, did not observe the limits of blameless self-defense.

### § I. Crop Failure, or a Poor Harvest Year.
### Sterility.

Sterility, according to some, is said to occur when the seed that was cast is not taken up <note>i.e., fails to germinate</note>. Covarruvias, however, in *Various Questions*, chapter 30, number 1, teaches that it can be called sterility when only two parts are collected out of the usual three.

Others called it sterility when the doubled seed was not recovered <note>meaning the harvest did not yield even twice the amount of seed originally planted</note>; this opinion seems fairer than the former, according to Mozzius in *On Contracts*, title on leasing and hiring, my folio 416, number 12. But it is more likely that this should be left to the judgment of the judge. Menochius, *Arbitrary Judgments*, case 76.

However, when and in which cases may a tenant farmer <term>Colonus</term> <note>a tenant who works the land for a landlord</note>, due to the sterility of the crops, legally seek a reduction of his rent, or not? See Speckhan, century 3, question 22, class 1, where he lists nine cases in which the payment of rent may cease. These are: (1.) Unusual swarms and flocks of starlings, jackdaws, sparrows, cranes, mice, and locusts, which are very harmful and infest the crops. (2.) Infestation by worms. (3.) Blight or mildew. (4.) Excessive and unusual hail, snow, and rain, which beat down the standing corn, break the stalks, shake out the grains, occupy and flood the fields, and wash away or rot the seeds and fruits. (5.) Floods, and the immoderate, unusual, and almost miraculous rushing and surging of rivers and waters. (6.) Immoderate drought and unusual heat of the sun. (7.) Storms, landslides, and earthquakes. (8.) Incursions by pirates, robbers, bandits, and enemies, by which the tenant is driven from his farm. (9.) Vicious and harmful weeds, such as darnel in oats and similar tares, by which the crops are often corrupted, choked, and sometimes transformed. The foundations of these cases are handed down by Everhard Speckhan in the aforementioned question 6, and add Pantshmann, volume 1, question 1, etc.

### §2. With. [Latin] *Cum*.

The word *With* implies a gathering together, and also a conjunction. Final law, and the commentators there, *Code: on the substitution of minors and others*. It joins things as being equally principal, according to the commentators on the law *si ancilla*, *On Legacies*, book 1; and it couples things more strongly than a simple conjunction. Ruinus, counsel 190, number 7, book 1; Riminaldi Junior, counsel 128, numbers 39 and 40; Nizolius, in allegation 18, number 45. It also has an accessory meaning when the thing itself is usually accessory to another. Law 1, where Bartolus comments on the *Digest: on the legacy of a peculium*. And thus it joins by way of an accessory, but not by way of a principal disposition. Therefore, a disposition concerning any right of patronage or legal right *with a tomb* or other adjunct works so that the adjunct is always an accessory: thus, if the principal disposition is void, the accessory will also be void by necessary consequence; see extensively on this word, Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter D, conclusion 258.

### §3. Dowry or Marriage-Money. [Latin] *Dos*.

What is *Marriage-Tax* <note>original: "Ehesteuer"</note> to the Germans, is *Dowry* <note>original: "Mitgifft"</note> or *Marriage-Money* <note>original: "Ehegeld"</note> to the Saxons, and *dos* to the Latins: from "giving along" <note>original: "vom Mitgeben" - explaining the etymology of the German word *Mitgift*.</note>.

### §4. With or Without Law. [Latin] *Via juris, vel sine ea*.

A prominent legal question is whether, if the ordinary path <note>a full trial</note> is first attempted, it prejudices the executive path <note>a faster, direct enforcement</note> for the same qualified person? This is commonly denied, and they teach that once a plaintiff has chosen the path of judgment, they cannot return to the path of fact. Law *de pupillo*, section *meminisse*, *On the reporting of new work*; Antonio Monterus, decision 22. For in an Ordinary Judgment, from the very contesting of the lawsuit <term>litis contestatio</term>, the right is sought by both the Judge and the Party. Thereafter, to their prejudice, the party itself cannot vary in its manner of proceeding. It is different, therefore, if one proceeds executively, where a pending lawsuit is not recognized; thus several competent executive paths can be attempted simultaneously or successively. Monterus, decision 23.

Whether, because of this clause, *with or without law* <note>original: "mit oder ohne Recht"</note>, inserted into an obligation, a Mandate without a Clause can be decreed in the Imperial Chamber? See Schwanman in *Observations of the Chamber*, observation 131; Hering on *Suretyships*, chapter 25, number 115, etc.; and Mindanus on *Extrajudicial Processes*. See Wilhelm Antonius in the *Corollaries*, my folio 30.

<note>Addition</note>

Exception: unless it was so agreed by a special pact, perhaps through an executive clause *with or without law*. ### 55. **Mediate Estates.** *Status mediati.*

This is the name given to those who are not immediately subject to the Emperor, but are subject to other Estates—such as Electors, Princes, etc.—subjecting them *mediately*, or *without mediation* <note>original: "ohne Mittel." In this context, it means they are directly under a local lord rather than the supreme Emperor.</note> as we commonly say.

## ADDITION.

Landed gentry or landed subjects <note>original: "Gemittelte von Adel oder Landsassen"</note> are those who are bound to appear before their territorial prince <note>original: "für ihrem Landfürsten"</note> indifferently in all cases, even those not involving feudal matters. <note>Cluten in *Sylloge of Daily Treasures*, 26.</note> They provide a double oath to the lord of the territory: one regarding the feudal property, and the other regarding their subjection. The oath given for the sake of the benefit—that is, the fief—ceases when the benefit ends; however, the other oath, given for the sake of subjection, retains its force as long as one remains in the territory. <note>Johann Ferrar Montanus, *On the Use of Fiefs*, book 6, chapter 1.</note>

### 56. **Mixed Authority.** *Mixtum imperium.*

Mixed Authority is called **Middle Authority** <note>original: "Mittel Obrigkeit"</note> in which jurisdiction is also present. <note>referencing Law 3 of the *Digest: on jurisdiction*.</note> Sometimes jurisdiction is inherent within it, and sometimes it is merely attached to it. It is inherent when the right of command is exercised principally in a matter: for instance, when a Judge grants "total restitution" <note>A legal remedy returning a party to their original status.</note>, or when he appoints judges for litigants, or if he assigns possession of goods, or orders security to be given for "threatened damage." <note>original: "damni infecti." A Roman law term for potential damage to property.</note> Truly, mixed authority is attached to jurisdiction when it serves a lawsuit that has already been initiated: for it is then exercised not for its own sake, but for the sake of explaining that jurisdiction and bringing it to its desired end. Since this mixed authority is so attached to that jurisdiction, it passes along with it when delegated, because without it, jurisdiction could easily be evaded.

The greatest power of this Authority, however, consists in deciding, pursuing, and ordering.

And it is called "Mixed Authority" because it takes something from "Pure Authority" <note>original: "mero Imperio." This usually refers to high justice, including the power to impose capital punishment.</note>—namely that which is carried out by the high office of the Judge—and something from ju-

<column-break/>

risdiction specifically, in that it looks toward private utility. <note>Schneidewin, *On Fiefs*, part 2, number 78.</note> In that work, the author describes six degrees of mixed authority in the following numbers.

Mixed authority belongs only to those who possess pure/high authority, and not to others. <note>Bartolus on the law *Imperium*, number 16 in the *Digest*.</note> Since it is the power of hearing, defining, and executing in civil lawsuits, which cannot be dispatched without such authority, it therefore belongs to all to whom pure authority is granted. From this, two rules are drawn. One is that mixed authority belongs only to the higher magistrates who possess Pure Authority. The other is that those to whom pure authority is not granted cannot possess mixed authority either. Zasius <note>A famous 16th-century German jurist.</note> taught the same, asserting that "Great" and "Moderate" mixed authority belongs only to the higher magistrates, such as Governors, and not to the lower ones; and that they could not have delegated these to lower officials except because of their many preoccupations. Great mixed authority, indeed, requires a full examination of the case, yet it consists in the high office of the judge and contains either real or personal coercion.

Regarding which cases pertain to mixed authority? See Counsel 3 (which is by Dradelius, a Jurist of Augsburg) among the *Illustrious Counsels* published by me, chapter 2; and also Ripoli's *Various Resolutions of Law*, chapter 1, number 279 and following.

But all these things have this variation in our modern customs: according to them, there are only two species of jurisdiction, **High and Low Authority**. <note>original: "hohe und niedre Obrigkeit." Referring to the author's own works *On Magistrates* and *On Jurisdiction*.</note>

## ADDITION.

Can mixed authority be delegated? This is discussed at length by Ilico Ummius in *On Process*, page 155, and Bocer in *On Jurisdiction*, page 251. Mixed authority is said to be that in which jurisdiction is present, and which belongs to a Magistrate by his own inherent right. On this, see Meier in *Endoxis*, decade 1, chapter 6. There are two degrees of mixed authority. The first contains those things that are more of jurisdiction than of authority—that is, things that consist more in hearing a case than in commanding—such as when someone who has delegated jurisdiction hears a minor matter outside the normal order, or grants possession to heirs of a person who died with or without a will. The second degree encompasses those things that are more of authority than of jurisdiction—that is, things that consist more in commanding than in hearing—such as if one who has delegated jurisdiction orders someone to provide suitable security,

### 57. With legal exercise. <note>German: *Mit rechtlicher Ausübung*</note>

### 58. Clause: With certain knowledge, and from the fullness of power. <note>Latin: *Ex certa scientia & plenitudine potestatis*</note>

The force and power of these clauses are so great that in those cases where the Prince employs them, nothing can be opposed that might restrict the grace and benefit of the Prince. <note>Cited from Baldus in the prologue to the *Decretals*.</note> Furthermore, it cannot even be said to the Prince: "Why do you do this?" Indeed, against that which the Prince does from **certain knowledge**, no one is to be heard at all; rather, anyone presuming to call it into doubt must be rejected entirely, with a perpetual silence imposed upon them. See especially Jacob Thoming, volume 1, counsel 5, number 92 and following.

### ADDITION.

**Knowingly, with good knowledge, will, and pleasure.** <note>German: *Wissentlich, mit gutem Wissen, Willen und Belieben*</note> See Höpingk, *On the Right of Seals*, chapter 12, number 19, and more fully in chapter 10, number 55. When the clause "from certain knowledge" is added, all defects in a legal dispensation are considered discarded. <note>Coller, counsel 1, number 186.</note> Wehner in his *Practical Observations* under the word "knowingly" <note>German: *wissentlich*</note> notes that it excludes all error. Cothmann, response 4, number 351, volume 4, states that an act done from certain knowledge cannot be revoked. Nor should those things done by the Prince from certain knowledge be disputed. <note>Schurff, counsel 53, number 10.</note> On what the clause "from certain knowledge" imports, see Marius Antoninus, book 1, resolution 46, numbers 7 and 11.

### 59. With and at the same time. <note>Latin: *Unacum*; German: *Mit und zugleich*</note>

The word *una* (together) is an adverb of gathering, and imports the same meaning as the word *simul* (at the same time). Its nature is to gather the predicate with its subject. <note>Found in the Code of Justinian regarding the substitution of minors.</note> It requires the concurrence of all those things which are to be joined. <note>Bartolus, counsel 4, number 4.</note> Baldus, in his commentary on the Code regarding the removal of lapses, says that "informality" <note>Irregularity or lack of proper legal form</note> is to be avoided in things that are coupled together uniformly. Hartmann Pistor, book 2, question 21, number 26.
*Tonsius, Resolution 1.*

<column-break/>

The word *With* <note>Latin: *Cum*</note> has greater efficacy than the simple conjunction *And* <note>Latin: *Et*</note>; it induces a tighter connection. <note>From the Digest on the legacy of instruments.</note> It makes one thing out of diverse parts. <note>Ruini, counsel 164, volume 5.</note> The word *with* also excludes the order of succession <note>i.e., it implies simultaneous rather than sequential rights</note>, according to Mantica on *Conjectures of Last Wills*.

### ADDITION.

When a vassal is invested for himself and his male heirs **together with** <note>Latin: *simul cum*</note> females, the females also succeed. This is true even if the little word "together" <note>Latin: *simul*</note> is omitted. Regarding the efficacy of the word "with," see Carpzov, decision 171.
**Alongside and with** <note>German: *Neben und mit*; Latin: *unà, cum*</note> join things as "equally principal." They couple things more strongly than a simple conjunction. <note>Calvin in the *Lexicon of Law* under the words *cum* and *una*.</note> Dr. Rebhan in *On the Wife of a Merchant*, thesis 26. "With" holds every prerogative of rank and is used in an augmentative sense. The word *unà* implies a simultaneous conjunction. <note>Marius Antoninus, book 2, resolution 35; see above at number 52.</note>

### 60. Clause: With protestation and precondition, that he does not intend this to be shameful to the defendant, or to injure his honor: but only wants to mention or bring it in for the execution and demonstration of his fairness. <note>German: *Mit Protestation und Vorbedingung, daß er hierdurch Beklagten nicht schmählich gemeinet, oder an seinen Ehren verlezet...*</note>

Since it often happens that to recount a fact, one must use words that at first glance appear insulting, it seems relevant to the matter that the Plaintiff <note>Latin: *Actor*</note> protest that he acts not for the sake of mockery or injury, but according to his own right and the truth of the matter in all things said in the Legal Brief <note>Latin: *Libello*</note> and Articles. In this case, the plaintiff is not held liable for **injury** <note>Latin: *injuriarum*; here meaning slander or defamation</note>. For he who uses his own right does no injury.
If, however, the Plaintiff or Defendant objects with something shameful or insulting against the adversary which is neither true nor probable, there will be grounds for an action of injuries. For a "calumnious excuse" does not remove the injury. Nor will this protestation help him if it is contrary to the facts. See my own dispute *On Injuries*, volume 2 of the *Tübingen Disputations*. Regarding an injury reproached during a trial, and whether an action can be instituted on that name before the main case is finished, see Meichsner, decision 4. Thus, it is permitted to object to a crime in a witness if they are burdened by ill-repute.

And so, this protestation <note>A formal legal declaration made to preserve a right or prevent an implication of consent.</note> has a place in deeds or words that do not necessarily imply an injury, but are ambiguous and can be understood in either sense. Likewise, in such cases, if malicious intent <note>Latin: *calumnia*; referring to "calumny" or the bringing of false or vexatious legal charges</note> is apparent, a protestation of this kind does not save the party.

### ADDITION.

Litigants often protest that they will say nothing for the sake of insult or injury, but will speak everything according to the law and the truth of the matter. The Doctors of Law believe that by this clause, litigants free themselves from the vice of Calumny. However, Obrecht rightly teaches in *On Forms of Petitions*, chapter 16, number 9, that such a protestation achieves nothing whenever malicious intent is evident. <note>Citing the Code of Justinian and the Decretals.</note> Truly, a protestation contrary to the fact cannot and should not achieve anything. Since calumny descends from a deceitful mind, it will easily appear where the malice seems contracted. For not every word spoken or written somewhat harshly is insulting. And Oldendorp (whom he calls the "Sulpitius of Germany") notably says in his *Treatise on Petitions*, page 304, that those words, "it is false," or "he speaks falsely," which Advocates frequently use, do not constitute an injury. See also Ummius in *On Process*, page 262 and following.

#### 61. Clause: With the pledging of all my property and goods, etc. <note>German: *Mit Verpfändung aller meiner Haab und Güter*; Latin: *Clausula sub hypotheca omnium bonorum*</note>

The clause for the pledging of goods <note>A "hypotheca" is a mortgage or pledge where the debtor keeps possession of the property but the creditor has a legal claim to it.</note> is therefore necessarily added to an instrument of obligation (especially a loan), so that the property is affected by a "real burden." By reason of this, the entry into the land—subsequently following from the agreement of the contracting parties—grants a "real right" <note>A right tied to the physical property itself, rather than just a personal promise from the debtor.</note> and thus possession with the profit of the fruits. Without this hypothecation, entry by force of the convention or statute does not acquire possession, but only a personal right and the bare holding of the occupied land. See Coler, *On Executive Process*, part 3, chapter 12, extensively.

### ADDITION.

I call it a "general mortgage" when it affects all the goods of the debtor, including those acquired after the mortgage was made. However, this does not include things which, because of affection or daily use, it is unlikely anyone would have specifically pledged—such as furniture, clothing, a concubine, natural children, and other things mentioned in the Digest and Code. <note>Citing the Digest, book 13, title 7, and the Code of Justinian.</note> This applies even if they were already among the debtor's goods at the time of the obligation. Add the Lord Dr. Biccius in *Golden Sections*, section 4, paragraph 49, letter A; Bachov on *Pledges*, book 1, chapters 5–7; Zoesius’s *Commentary on the Digest*, title on pledges, number 12; and Hermann Meyrer, *On the Preference of Creditors*, book 1, title 5, number 3.

<column-break/>

#### 62. Clause: With the reservation of each person's rights. <note>German: *Mit Vorbehalt eines jeden Rechtens*; Latin: *Clausula Salvo jure quorumcunque*</note>

That clause—*saving the rights of any others whatsoever*—attached to a confirmation, is of very little or clearly no importance. <note>Arguing from the Digest regarding public places.</note> See Zasius, counsel 6, number 25; Rosenthal, *On Feuds*, chapter 6, conclusion 61; and Schrader, part 6, chapter 3.

### ADDITION.

On the effect of the clause *Saving the rights of whomever* and similar ones, see Klock, volume 3, counsel 155, number 54. Note, however, numbers 171 and 173. A third party must prove their own interest. Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated*, book 1, observation 69. For the clause "Saving our rights and those of the Empire," see the *Acts of Lindau*, page 444. "Saving the rights of a third party" is understood in all investitures <note>The formal act of granting a fief or office.</note>. Its omission creates a presumption of a fraudulent grant. An erroneous assertion does not diminish the right of a third party.

A Lord is safe from the danger of "eviction" <note>The legal recovery of property from a person by someone who has a better title; here, it means the Lord isn't liable if the recipient loses the property to a third party.</note> if he grants property as a fief with the clause "saving the rights of others," translated as: *we grant him the estate, as much as we have the right to grant therein.* Borcholten and Schneidewin disagree with Zasius and Molina. See Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, 7, thesis 10, letter E. On that clause "Saving the rights of any others whatsoever," see the same author, *Disputation* 8, thesis 9, letter S. This clause is regularly and silently inherent in privileges: *saving the right of a third party*, so they are not extended to the damage of another. It frees the Lord from liability for eviction, even more so if this was agreed upon by express pact.

#### 62. Clause: With the reservation and condition of not entangling oneself in any excessive proof; but only to clarify and carry out that which is useful and advantageous to the Plaintiff for the preservation of his hoped-for justice and victory. <note>German: *Mit Vorbehalt und Bedingung, sich zu keiner überflüssigen Beweisung zu verstricken...*</note>

The clause, *not binding himself to prove unnecessary things, but only those which suffice to obtain victory in the case*, pertains to the fact that a plaintiff <note>Latin: *actor*</note> is not held to prove everything proposed in the petition. This is contrary to Baldus, who says this protestation is useless since the necessity of proving is imposed on the plaintiff by law. Otherwise, the plaintiff is held to prove everything if they omit this clause. See the Canonists on the chapter *Dilecti*.

Lit. M.

regarding deceit and contempt <note>Latin: *de dolo & contum.*</note>. See Bartolus on the law *Divus*, in the Digest *on the matter of judgments* <note>Latin: *ff. de re judic.*</note>; Jason at paragraph *omnium*, note 161, Institutes *on actions*; Paul de Castro on the law *habebat*, 13, at the end, Digest *on the institutory action*; Johann Schneidewein at the said paragraph *omnium*, note 121; and Haersolte, *on actions* in the introduction, note 82.

Furthermore, in those matters which are required for proof by legal necessity, this Protestation is of no use, but only in "adventitious" matters <note>Non-essential or secondary points added to a case.</note>: that is, those which, even if not proven, the action may nonetheless take place. See Bartolus on the law *denuntiaffe*, paragraph *quid tamen*, Digest *on the Julian law regarding adultery*; and on the law *non solum*, paragraph *sed ut probari*, Digest *on the reporting of new works*.

## ADDITION.

The party filing a petition <note>The "Libellans" or plaintiff.</note> reserves all privileges for themselves as if untouched. In particular, they reserve the right of not being bound to prove more than what is necessary for the victory of the case. They claim the power of this clause is such that it frees one from the proof of those things which, though brought forward in the petition, do not concern the merits of the case itself. And following Bartolus, Zasius entirely believes (at the beginning of his notes on the Digest *on actions*) that without this clause, the plaintiff must prove every single thing brought forward, even if they do not strictly touch upon the cause itself. However, Baldus rightly denies (on law 5, note 1, Code *on the freedom of causes*) that this clause is of any significance. Although Obrecht (in *Forms of Petitions*, chapter 16, number 5 and following) disapproves of this, it nonetheless seems most true. For nothing else ought to be proven except what serves the lawsuit itself. See Illicon Ummius in *On Process*, page 262, and more extensively on page 620; the Lord Doctor Ludwig, *Notes on Wesenbeck regarding proofs*, number 7; and Maurus Antonius, book 1, resolution 83, number 8.

### 64. Clause: With the reservation and consent of the Liege Lord. <note>German: *Mit Vorbehalt und Bewilligung des Lehenherrn*; Latin: *Clausula Salvo consensu Domini directi*</note>

If a vassal <note>A person holding land (a fief) from a superior lord in exchange for service.</note> alienates <note>Transfers or sells ownership of property.</note> a fief without the consent of the Lord, but inserts into the instrument of sale this Clause, *saving and reserving the consent of the Lord* <note>German: *mit Vorbehalt und Bewilligung des Herrn*</note>, should he be deprived of the fief despite the included Clause? For the clarification and decision of this question, it is customary to distinguish as follows: Either the vassal hands over possession, or he does not. In the first case, a vassal who alienates a fief but does not hand over physical possession does not lose the fief, because of the added words *saving and reserving the Lord's consent*. Andreas in chapter *imperialem*, paragraph *scriba*, note 23, and in the paragraph *callidis*, note 21, *on the prohibition of alienating fiefs* by Frederick, where he says that the delivery of possession causes the loss of the fief. Therefore, by the opposite sense, as long as he does not truly and actually alienate the fief, the vassal does not lose his ownership. Baldus agrees in chapter 1, paragraph *donare*, *how one was formerly able to alienate a fief*; and on the word *bellaria*, title *on the Peace of Constance*; Curtius in part 4, question 21, number 122.

In the second case, however, when the vassal sells

<column-break/>

and transfers physical possession to the buyer, even if he adds the Clause *saving and reserving the Lord's consent*; nevertheless, it must be said that the fief is lost, because he transferred possession to another. Baldus in chapter 1, paragraph 1, final column, *what was the first cause for losing a benefit*; Curtius in part 4, question 21, number 212; Felinus in chapter *quae Ecclesiae*, *on Constitutions*. Because even by alienating and transferring possession to another, he did everything he could in contempt of the Lord. Hence, he is not excused when he says, *saving the Lord's consent*. For in an act already done, the artifice of words is of no use. Bartolus in the law *if any stranger*, Digest *on acquiring inheritance*. And a protestation contrary to the act itself does not relieve nor profit the party. Law *non solum*, paragraph *morte*, Digest *on the reporting of new works*; and this Clause is rightly judged as if it had not been added, and thus can produce no effect.

When a pledge of a fief <note>A mortgage or security on the property.</note> has been made by a vassal to his creditor with the consent of the Lord—*since the liege lord has given his favor for it* <note>German: *da der Lehenherr die Gunst darüber geben hat*</note>—if the fief later reverts to the Lord—*when the fief falls back to the liege lord again* <note>German: *da dem Lehenherrn das Lehen wiederum heimfällt*</note>—it is asked whether the Lord is then bound, on account of the consent provided, to pay the debt from the feudal goods? See Schneidewin in *Treatise on Fiefs*, part 4, number 44, where at number 46 he decides that such consent profits the creditor, and in this case, just as in an alienation made with the Lord’s consent, the Lord himself is prejudiced. Chapter 1, paragraph *if indeed*, *on alienating fiefs*, etc. Imperial [decree] *on the prohibition of alienating fiefs* by Frederick, paragraph *profecto*, *what is the law if afterwards another fief*, and chapter 1, paragraph *if indeed*, *on alienating fiefs*. For by the consent of the Lord, that obligation is confirmed as if the Lord himself had pledged it, according to the text in the law *obvenire*, Digest *on verbal obligations*. Hence, he cannot go against his own deed. Hartmann Pistor, question 48, number 14 and following; Fachin, book 7, *Controversies*, chapter 56.

This conclusion, however, according to the same Schneidewin in the cited place, number 47, is notably limited: it does not apply when the Lord consented to the pledge with the added Clause, *saving his feudal right* <note>Latin: *salvo suo jure feudali*</note>. For then, if the fief reverts to the Lord, the Lord is not bound to pay the debts of the vassal from it, following the argument in the law *if a debtor*, paragraph 1, Digest *on how a pledge is dissolved*. And so it is observed by Custom, according to Zasius. Let the Lords therefore be cautious when they consent to an obligation on a fief, that they add that Clause, *saving our feudal right*, *just as these words are commonly attached and added in letters of favor: "We give our favor and consent to this, yet without prejudice to our princely authority, regalia, knightly services, feudal rights, or other jurisdictions which we have inherited over such estates, but rather we hereby reserve the same for ourselves without harm."* See especially Afflictus in the paragraph *what therefore*, number 5, *on investment of another's property*.

## ADDITION.

Even silent consent given in person is sufficient. Gothofredus Antonii, *Feudal Disputations*, 9.

### 65. May. To be Able. <note>German: *Mögen*; Latin: *Possunt*</note>
The word "may" is equivalent to the word "can," which denotes not a strict necessity, but either a free will or a causative necessity, according to Lancellot, Cumanus, and others. Ludolph Schrader, *On Fiefs, part 10, section 19, number 194.*

However, this word "can" may also imply a precise necessity due to the subject matter or the nature of the thing being discussed. This can be sufficiently proven from the writings of Baldus and Raphael Cumanus... followed by Schrader in the same location, number 197.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding what the word "Could" <note>German: *Könnten*</note> denotes, see Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 9, chapter 1, number 58.* On what the word "May" <note>German: *Mögen*</note> imports, see the *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 79, number 36.* Symphorematus Gylmann, *volume 1, part 2, page 351, number 13*, notes that this word refers to both what follows and what precedes it. "May" is a word of permission, not of command. Denail, *On the Right of Absolute Power.*

### 67. Monarchs. Monarchy.
I have discussed Monarchy and Monarchs in a specific political discourse. On the Roman Monarchy, see Stapleton, *On the Great Roman Church, book 4, chapter 1.* On the advantages of Monarchy, the Reverend Father Contzen in the *History of the Abyssinians, folio 3.* Regarding the Four Monarchies, see Tornielli in the *Annals, Year of the World 2016, page 152 and following, where on page 152, column 2, he writes as follows:*

> Only four of these Monarchies are mentioned in the Sacred Books, not because others were not to be established after them until the end of the world (for we see that the Empire of the Turks later succeeded the Roman, and it is probable others will rise after it), but because those four alone were meant to precede the Kingdom of Christ, which was to last in this world until the final Day of Judgment, and thereafter eternally in Heaven. This Kingdom is none other than the Kingdom of Christ and His Holy Church.

Furthermore, regarding the four Monarchies (namely the Assyrians, the Persians and Medes, the Greeks, and the Romans), it should be known that they are called by the name of "Monarchies" not because they always used a monarchical government, or because each one always had only a single Head; but because certain great Monarchs existed within them.

These Kingdoms also did not always remain in the same state of power, but as happens in human affairs, they frequently suffered much, not only from foreigners but even from their own subjects; and they were often divided, weakened, and torn apart. Yet they are not said to have ceased for that reason, until they finally fell in such a way that they could no longer rise again.

It should also be known that one should not believe these Kingdoms succeeded each other in such a way that the Second did not exist at all until the First entirely ceased, nor the Third until the Second was utterly destroyed, nor the Fourth until the Third was completely abolished. For it is clear that the Kingdom of the Medes and Persians existed before the Kingdom of the Assyrians was extinct. Likewise, the Kingdom of the Greeks began long before the destruction of the Persian Kingdom.

And likewise, the *Roman Empire* was sufficiently powerful before the Greek Kingdom was entirely subdued. But these Kingdoms are said to have succeeded one another because the beginning of the second was much later than the start of the first, and similarly for the others. Furthermore, as time progressed, the later ones successively prevailed over the earlier ones, and finally, with the earlier one extinguished, the later was magnified to such an extent that, by the consensus of all, it was certain that the supreme power on earth remained with it.

Since, however, of these Kingdoms, the Third—namely that of the Greeks—was not always under one Prince <note>original: "sub uno semper Principe"</note> like the two prior ones, but after the death of Alexander the Great was divided among several Lords and Kings, and nonetheless each one seems to have belonged to the Greek Kingdom. Therefore, this Kingdom, unlike the two previous ones, was not extinguished all at once, but gradually and by parts subdued by the Romans, with its diverse Kings and their Kingdoms being subjugated at different times. Thus it happens that it cannot be said to be entirely extinguished until the last of its Kings was overcome and brought into their power. The end of this Kingdom is reported to be around the year of the Battle of Actium <note>31 BCE, where Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra</note>, since Egypt, which had been no small part of the Greeks, was only then taken from its own Kings by Augustus Caesar and added to the Roman Empire. *Torniel. f. 153. from the beginning.*

### 68. Month. <note>German: *Monat*; Latin: *Menfis*</note>

Months constitute the division of the year, just as hours do for the day.

For how many days a month is understood to be, see Rauchbar, book 2, question 24. And according to Thomas de Marinis in his treatise *On the Kinds and Qualities of Fiefs, title 2, folio 165, number 57*, two Glosses <note>marginal or interlinear explanations of law</note> are cited: one by Johannes Andreae on the chapter "If on account of" regarding rescripts in the *Sixth Book of Decretals*, and another on the chapter "How dangerous it is" regarding elections in the same book. These held that a month is understood to be as many days as the month has in which the "arising month" begins: for example, if it begins on the sixth day of February—which has twenty-eight days, except in a leap year <term>bissextus: the leap day added to the calendar</term> when it has twenty-nine (according to the law *cum bissextus* in the Digest *On the Signification of Words*)—the arising month ends on the sixth day of March. (I have discussed what an "arising year" <note>Latin: *annus emergens*</note> is under the word "Year" <note>German: *Jahr*</note>). This opinion is 

<column-break/>

commonly followed by the Doctors of Law in the law *divisione* in the Digest *On the dissolution of marriage*; by Johannes Andreae, author of the gloss on the *Sixth Book of Decretals*, chapter *quàm sit*, under the word "month"; by Bartolus in the law *cùm bissextus*, number 1, in the Digest *On the Signification of Words*; the same in the law 1, number 5, regarding the standing of judicial causes; the same in the law *de divisionon*, number 1, regarding the dissolution of marriage; and in law 1, at the beginning, in the Code *On the time of appeals*. It is also followed by Angelo in his report on law 22, number 6, in the Code *On the right of deliberation* in the Florentine lectures; by Alexander in the said law *de divisione*, number 4; and in his *Counsel 114*, number 6; by Socinus on the failures of rules, rule 260; by Rochus de Curte on the right of Patronage under the word "honorable," number 85; by Alciatus on the law *cùm bissextus*; by Wurmser in *Practical Observations*, title 50; by Menochius on *Judicial Arbitrations*, case 50; by Thomas de Marinis in his *Treatise on Fiefs*; by Alberico Gentili in his *Treatise on the Designations of Different Times*, chapter 4; by Schwannmann in *Cameral Procedure*, book 1, chapter 27; by Tuschus in *Practical Conclusions*, letter M, conclusion 197; by Thomas Sanchez in his *Treatise on Marriage*, book 2; by Sigismondo Scaccia in his *Treatise on Judgments*, book 2; and by Oldendorp on *Exceptions*, under the word "Month." Decius, however, in the law *Where the law* in the Digest *On the Rules of Law*, concludes that if "Month" is stated simply, it should be understood as the twelfth part of a year, which is declared to be 30 days; and thus it consists of thirty days according to the text in the Code *On the Right of Deliberation*. There it says: "where the law makes mention of two months, he who comes on the sixty-first day is to be heard." Here, however, one day is added out of kindness <note>original: "ex benignitate"; a legal grace period</note>, which is to be understood in a favorable cause. Cagnolus on the same law, number 1. Thus, by the designation of "month," when uttered simply and absolutely, 30 days are understood (chapter *illicita*, question 3), unless mention was made of some month in particular and specifically: because then we determine the Month according to the number of days of that month. Imola and Alexander in the law *divisione*; Socinus in *Counsel 99*, volume 3. See also Lorenzo Sylvano in his *Treatise on Fiefs*, question 11; Caranza on *Natural and Legitimate Birth*, page 517; and Alberico Gentili on the *Designation of Different Times*, chapter 4.

Some months are Lunar, others Solar. A Lunar Month is called the space that intervenes from one joining of the Moon with the Sun until the next. This is threefold: one is called the *month of wandering* <note>original: "Menfis peragrationis"; the sidereal month of ~27.3 days</note>, another the *month of following* <note>original: "consecutionis"; the synodic month of ~29.5 days</note>, and the third the *month of illumination*. The month of wandering is the time in which the Moon completes one entire circuit from some point until it returns to the same point, and it consists of 27 days, 8 hours, and a third part of an hour. The month called *of conjunction* or *following* encompasses as much time as the Moon spends traveling from one conjunction to another; that is, when the Moon, joining with the Sun and having completed its course, follows the Sun again. This is 29 days and 12 hours, with 44 minutes and some seconds.

### Expanded Treasury of Practice

The month of **illumination** <note>original: "illuminationis"</note> is the name given to the period when the Moon, casting its light upon the earth, is visible to us and is not yet, as they say, "combust" <note>a term in astrology/astronomy meaning the moon is too close to the sun to be seen</note> or obscured by the brilliance of the Sun. This period is said to last 26 days and 6 hours. Arumaeus states this in Book 2, *Decisions on the Crown, number 24.*

<margin>Augustine, chapter 7, book 1, on the parts of man.</margin>
The **Solar** month, however, is what Galen calls a **full** month, and it consists of thirty days.

Among the Greeks, the Moon is called *mēn* <note>Greek: μήν</note>, from which their term for months, *mēnes* <note>Greek: μήνες</note>, is derived; the Latin word *menses* comes from this, according to Varro in Book 5 of *On the Latin Language*, because the months are clearly defined by the motion of the Moon. This motion of the Moon is considered either by itself, or in relation to the Sun. From this, astronomers identify two types of months: the **Periodic** and the **Synodic**. The former is the space of time in which the Moon travels from a fixed point in the circle of latitude on the Ecliptic back to that same point; this lasts twenty-seven days, seven hours, and some small fractions. This measurement is rarely used except by astronomers and physicians. **Synodic** months, which are defined by the Moon's departure from and return to the Sun, are quite unequal due to the inconsistent speed of both celestial bodies. For when the **Sun is at its perigee** <note>closest point to Earth</note> and the **Moon is at its apogee** <note>farthest point from Earth</note>, the month lasts nearly thirty solid days; conversely, when the Sun is at its apogee and the Moon at its perigee, the month lasts less than twenty-nine days and seven hours. On average, the time of a synodic month is determined to be twenty-nine days, twelve hours, and nearly three-quarters of an hour, as taught by Johannes Kepler in Book 6 of *Copernican Astronomy, part 4, page 789.*

In ancient times, these months were adapted for common use by taking the whole number closest to those fractions of hours and minutes—namely, thirty solid days. These months, used by the Greeks and other nations even before the Romans, were called Political, **Civil**, or **popular** months, because they were observed in political regulations and civil business. However, since twelve such months made a year of no more than three hundred and sixty days—which falls short of the Solar Year by five full days and a quarter—it became necessary to intercalate <note>insert</note> new months called **Mercedonii** <note>intercalary months intended to realign the calendar</note> after a cycle of a few years. This gave the Pontiffs <note>high-ranking Roman priests</note>, who were responsible for this care, constant opportunities for confusion. Whether through bad faith or negligence, they abused this power of intercalation so much that the calendar was thrown into chaos: the Harvest festivals did not fall in summer, nor the Vintage festivals in autumn. Finally, Julius Caesar, having taken control of the Republic and turned his attention to its organization, adjusted the year to the course of the Sun, so that it would consist of three hundred and sixty-

<column-break/>

five days. He abolished the intercalary month and ordered one day to be intercalated every four years. See Plutarch and Suetonius *in the Life of Caesar*, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia, Book 1, chapter 14.*

In the Julian Year, the 365 days were distributed into twelve months in such a way that, starting from March—the first months, during which the Sun moves at its slowest, were assigned 184 days, while the remaining months were given only 181. Thus, some were given 31 days, others 30, and only February, being the last, received the remaining 28 days.

By this method, the Solar Year was described in a civil manner, and these months took the place of the earlier ones (which were all thirty days long <note>original Greek: τριημ-ήμερον</note>). These became the Political and popular months we still use today. See Joseph Scaliger, *Chronological Canons, Book 3*, and Kepler’s previously cited work.

In the law *Lecta* (40) regarding *credited things* <note>Latin: "de rebus creditis"</note>: where interest—referred to as "monthly"—or a penalty is expressly promised for thirty days, it is certain that it should be understood according to the months shown in the **Calendars** <note>original: "Kalendaria"</note>; that is, months that usually exceed thirty days by one day. For it is well known that moneylenders used to operate according to the ancient **Kalends** <note>the first day of the Roman month, when debts were due</note>, as Hieronymus Groslotius and Barnabé Brisson have explained at length. The very name "Calendar" is evidence of this. Hence Ovid writes in Book 2 of *The Art of Love*:

> He who fears the Puteal <note>a spot in the Roman Forum where creditors gathered</note>, and Janus, and the swift Kalends,
> Let the borrowed sum of his money torment him.

He calls the Kalends "swift" because they seem to return too quickly for the desires of debtors, bringing with them the accumulation of interest. See also what Hornigk adds in *On the Royal Right of Posts*, page 122. Otherwise, the calculation of **one-percent interest** <note>original: "usurae centesimae"</note> could not be consistent, yielding twelve coins annually—one for each month. Hermolaus Barbarus, then Budé, and others have corrected the error of Accursius (who fell into a mistake through ignorance of antiquity), proving this so clearly that it can no longer be doubted. If all months were set at no more than thirty days, it would be necessary to add a sixth part of a coin (or a fifth in a leap year) on top of the twelve, or to end the year at only three hundred and sixty days. This would contradict the form of Public Law and the rulings of Julian and Paulus, who everywhere attribute no fewer than 365 days to the year.

Indeed, as Menander says, all things are done and judged by time. Therefore, the care of distributing years, months, and days should hold a primary place in every Republic. What need was there to correct the Calendar...

# ADDITION.

**Question:** Is the inclusion of the month in a legal instrument to be considered a necessary solemnity <note>a formal requirement for legal validity</note>? A distinction must be made: either the day cannot otherwise be established, in which case it cannot be omitted without the document being nullified—indeed, one who omits the month can even be punished for forgery (Tægius in *Criminal Treatise*, part 14, number 39). Alternatively, the day is certain of itself, such as if it is written: "On the Feast of St. John the Evangelist," or "The Nativity of the Lord," and then the inclusion of the month is not necessarily required (Bartolus and others on the law *si quis* 6, paragraph *si initium* 6, number 23; Felinus on chapter 1 of the extra-decretals *On the Faith of Instruments*). The month in the Roman Republic can be divided into the **Julian** month, which runs from Calends to Calends <note>the first day of the month</note>, and is completed in 31, 30, 29, or 28 days depending on the various determination of feasts (according to the common verse: "April has thirty," etc.), and the **Common** month, which is taken for 30 days in common law. This can be gathered from law 31, paragraph 22, and the final law, paragraph 1, where 3 months and 90 days are taken for the same thing (Novels 115, chapter 2; Cujas *On Usucaption*, chapter 10, number 14). From this, the doctors of law form a rule: when mention of months is made indefinitely in our law, it is regularly to be understood as periods of thirty days (Caranza *On Natural and Legal Parturition*, chapter 12, paragraph 5, numbers 41–42). 

However, they limit this in the case of months granted for the **Prosecution of an Appeal**, which are 31 days (Law 2 and the last law on the time of appeals; Cujas and Caranza as cited above). Law 101 *On the Rules of Law* does not stand in the way, because, as the title suggests, it has a singular reason for deciding; there, the matter is decided not by ordinary law, but by the Law of Cognition <note>a more flexible legal procedure where the judge has more discretion</note> alone. That is, where petitions are heard without a formal legal complaint, and something beyond the disposition of ordinary law is indulged, such as vacation from duties or the extension of legal time (see the final law on the *Excusation of Tutors*; law 5 on *Veterans*; law 15 on *Summoning to Court*). Suetonius also confirms this difference between ordinary law and "cognition" in his life of Claudius, chapter 15, saying: "When another man was called upon by his adversary concerning his own lawsuit, and he denied it was a matter of 'cognition' but belonged to 'ordinary law,' Claudius forced him to argue the case immediately before him." See Rævardus on said law 101, unless you prefer, with Cujas, to strike out those words "and on the first day," which are not read in the books of the **Basilika** <note>original Greek: βσιλικών; a 9th-century collection of Byzantine laws</note>. **Emperor Charlemagne** <note>original German: Kaiser Carl der Grosse</note> gave names to the months, as Eginhard writes of him in his yearbook. Master Harsdörffer in the *Poetic Funnel*, page 95. Master Rupertus in *Universal History*, book 4, chapter 9. Numa Pompilius divided the year into 12 months. Likewise in book 4 of the *Prolegomena*.

# 70. Mordacht. Outlawry. <note>original Latin: "Forjudicatio"</note>

Throughout Germany it everywhere prevails and practice observes that against homicides and those guilty of other notorious capital crimes—who, having committed the offense, either flee to avoid capital punishment or come to **outlawry** <note>original: "forjudicationem"</note>—they proceed to the **Mordacht** <note>A Germanic legal process of proscription or "murder-ban" for those who flee justice</note>. This follows the process touched upon by Rosbach in *Criminal Process*, title 1, chapter 5, number 11, where he gives the formulas for accusing contumacy <note>defiance of court authority</note>; number 12 for summoning; and number 13 for sentencing.
Regarding this custom, see by all means Hermann Stamm in the treatise *On Personal Servitude*, book 1, chapter 5, throughout.

The plaintiff may cry out over the perpetrator three times, "Woe! Murder!" <note>original: *Wassnach Jo, oder Mörder Jo*; traditional legal cries used to initiate a public pursuit or "hue and cry"</note>, as is the custom and tradition in this matter in every region. *Ibid.* Regarding the pronouncement of the Ban:
> Just as you have been sentenced to the Murder-Ban by judgment and law, so I take your body and property out of the Peace and place them into the Un-peace; I declare you honorless and lawless, and I declare you free to the birds in the air, the beasts in the forest, and the fish in the water. You shall have no peace nor safe-conduct on any street, nor in any **Immunity** <note>original: *Mundat*; a geographically defined area of legal privilege or sanctuary</note>, that is, privileged places that Emperors or Kings have granted. I declare all your fiefs that you hold to be vacant and released from their lords, etc.

## 71. Morning Gift. *Morgengaba*.

The term *Morganatica* is of Lombard origin; it is found in Title 29, Book 2 of the *Books of Fiefs* regarding children born from a **Morganatic marriage**. However, among the Doctors of Law, there is not total agreement on what *Morganatica* is. Some say it is that which is taken upon the death of the husband (Andreas de Isernia, Martino da Lodi, and Jacopo di San Giorgio in his work on fiefs). It is not ineptly called *Morganatica* as a gift which, among the Lombards, the groom gave to the bride on the day of the nuptials while greeting her in the presence of relatives and friends before the wedding feast. Thus, *Morganatica* is the same as the **Morning Gift** <note>German: *Morgengab*</note> according to the text of **Saxon Law** <note>The *Sachsenspiegel*, a major German legal code</note>, Book 1, Article 20, and the glosses on the Feudal Law and the *Weichbild* <note>municipal law</note>. It is a gift that every man of knightly rank gives to his wife in the morning when he goes to the table with her. A man may also give this morning gift to his wife whenever he wishes. The word *Morgengabica* is composed from the German idiom: *Morgen*, which means "morning," and *Gab*, which signifies "gift." See Hartmann Pistor, Book 1, Question 44. Therefore, *Morgengabicum* may be interpreted as a "morning gift," by which a donation made on account of marriage is signified. In Civil Law, it is called "betrothal bounty" (*sponsalitia largitas*), and in Canon Law, it is called a "dower" (*dotalitium*).

In our customs, the **Morning Gift** differs from the **Widow’s Jointure** <note>German: *Widum*; property settled on a bride for her use after her husband's death</note>, and it is taken as the "price of virginity" which the groom gives to the bride after the marriage bed has been shared, in the form of money, chains, or jewelry. This is also given to young widows. In Spain, these are called *Arrhæ* <note>earnest money or bride-price</note>.

In what things the betrothal bounty con-

<column-break/>

-sists, or what belongs to the Morning Gift, see Georg Rotfchitz in the treatise *On Dowry, Personal Property, etc.*, Article 17 throughout. Moller, Book 2, Chapter 43, asks: Under Saxon Law, is a noble widow owed mares as part of her Morning Gift, if the head of the household, out of necessity, once or twice hitched them to a carriage or plow, even though he did not otherwise use them for such work?

If a wife dies before her husband, does she transmit to her next of kin those things which the groom usually gives as a gift on the first day of the wedding, namely the Morning Gift? See Hartmann Pistor. I believe that the *Morganatica*, or **Morning Gift**, belongs to the wife and she may do with it as she wishes, both during the marriage and after; for it is considered part of the wife’s brought-in property.

**Marriages contracted "at the Morganatic"** <note>This is the origin of the term "Morganatic marriage," often called a "left-handed marriage," where the spouse and children have no claim on the husband's titles or main estate</note> are those where a man marries a woman on the condition that his children shall not inherit from him, but must be satisfied with a certain fixed settlement.

This is often done in favor of children from a prior marriage or for the benefit of agnates <note>relatives on the father's side</note>. This is especially the case if someone marries a woman who is not his equal in nobility. See my work *On Succession and Elections*, Chapter 9.

Regarding the Morganatic gift, see Berlich and Cypreus on the *Law of Marriages*.

## ADDITION.

To "take at the Morganatic" <note>Latin: *Ad Morganaticam accipere*</note> is, as the Milanese said, a case where it is expressly provided in the dowry agreements that children born from a later marriage ought not to be capable of holding the dignity of the parents; that is, the children produced from such a marriage shall inherit nothing from the father, nor carry his title, but shall be obliged to let themselves be settled with a certain sum. Cujacius explains what these words mean: "not wishing to exist in sin," he means the father does not wish to do injury to a son of a first marriage, nor to harm the memory of a first spouse by bringing in a stepmother who is a commoner, when the first wife was noble. See more in Rittershusius and Besold. Such an agreement ensures the fief is left to the children of the first marriage and does not belong to the children of the second marriage, who are forced to be content with the **Morning Gift** or the donation made on account of the wedding.

**Wedding generosity** <note>original: *Sponsalitia largitas*</note> is that which a nobleman regularly gives to his wife in the morning before he sits down for the wedding feast. It is the custom of the nobility, in the morning after they have lain together, to give and bequeath to the bride a gold chain, or otherwise a piece of jewelry, or even money as a **Morning Gift** <note>original: *Morgengab*</note>. By the disposition of Saxon Law, these are owed to the wife after the husband's death and are counted toward the wedding generosity: all field-livestock, cows, goats, pigs, and unbridled horses. What the Morning Gift is, why it is given, to whom it belongs, and whether it applies to others besides virgins. Question 7, number 510 and the three following. This Morning Gift is something different from "wedding generosity" or "gifts on account of marriage" <note>original: *donatio propter nuptias*</note>. Question 7, number 514.

### 72. Arsonists. *Incendiarii*.

He who maliciously, deceitfully, and deliberately sets fire to another’s house in a city, and moreover for the sake of plunder, is to be punished by the law of retaliation <note>original: *pœna talionis*; an eye-for-an-eye punishment</note> and by vengeful flames. This is based on the Digest, *On fire, ruin, and shipwreck*, and the Digest, *On punishments*. According to the Imperial Constitution of Charles V, Article 125: Malicious arsonists who have been convicted shall be punished from life to death with fire. See also the Constitution of the Elector Augustus, section 17, part 4. This punishment is still observed today in the Holy Roman Empire. See, however, Böckel, inquiry 6, number 33; add also Lord Bocer’s treatise *On Arson*, number 66, etc.

->ADDITION.<-
