# Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

The Scholastics, however, contend that these Laws are divine in no other way than that in which Demosthenes said "The laws are a gift of the Gods." <note>original: *Leges donum Deorum esse dixit*</note> Joachim Stephani, in *On the Jurisdiction of the Jews and Greeks, book 1, chapter 10, number 45.* It should also be noted that one and the same Mosaic Law can be partly judicial <note>civil or court-related</note> and partly truly moral. Punishment generally descends from the Law of Nature, but the specific determination of the penalty is judicial and thus has been abrogated <note>repealed or voided under the New Covenant</note>. Besold, *Counsel 52, number 8 and following. Question: Are the judicial or forensic laws of Moses abrogated?* One must distinguish between the *Mosaic* forensic laws that retain the character of moral and natural law, or the reason of common law; and between those that have a singular and particular respect to the Jewish Polity and people. Laws of the former kind, as perpetual and immutable, bind not only the Jews, but all and every mortal perpetually; just as all positive laws, to be just, must conform to the natural and moral Law. Laws of the latter kind, however, since they were mutable by their origin and nature, and adapted only to the Jewish state, do not necessarily bind the consciences of Christians to their observation. Speckh. *century 3, class 4, question 12, § middle opinion of those who distinguish.*

The most learned man Johann Drusius, in his *Unique Book on Questions Asked by Letter, Epistle 13 to the Most Ample President Jacques Auguste de Thou:* The name Moses is declined by the Latins as *Mosis* and *Moseos*; *Moyses, Moyseos*; *Moses, Mosæ* and *Mosi*. This last form is from the ancients, who used the dative case for the genitive <note>possessive</note>, as in "to Achilles" or "to Ulysses." Thus "the flight to Themistocles" or "a fellow-student to Aristotle." You may find *Moyseos* in Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 8.* You find *Moseos* in the same author's books *Against Faustus the Manichean, book 14, chapter 1.* In the language of the Egyptians, *MOS* is said to mean water. Amphilochius with the notes of Rittershusius, *page 81.* Painters depict Moses with horns <note>original: *cornua appingunt*</note>, perhaps led by the passage in *Exodus chapter 34, verse 29.* <note>The Hebrew word for "radiant" or "sending out rays" is similar to the word for "horns," leading to a famous mistranslation in the Latin Vulgate.</note> But they do many things without reason; they satisfy the rules of art but do an injury to the truth of the matter. ### 74. Mußtheil. Food Provisions.

**Mußtheil** <term>Mußtheil: A legal provision in Saxon Law referring to the foodstuffs a widow is entitled to from her deceased husband's estate</term> (that is, Food Provisions) <note>original: *Cibaria*</note> comprises all the food that remains after the thirtieth day in every house of the husband; thus the text of Saxon Law seems to define it, *book 1, article 22, § after this the woman must.* It is defined in another way in the *Gloss on the Land Law, book 1, article 24, on the word 'fattened', verse 'then Mußtheil is.'* Where it says: **Mußtheil** is all kinds of food which a man has stored and procured for his own necessity, and the wife takes such **Mußtheil** after her husband’s death, half from the thirtieth day, and the other half remains for the heirs. See Rotschitz, *Treatise on Dowry, Personal Property, Mußtheil, etc., article 18.*

Regarding what things consist of Food Provisions, or what belongs to the **Mußtheil** according to the Land Law, see the same Rotschitz, *at the cited place, article 19, throughout.* What belongs to it according to Feudal Law, the same author teaches in *article 20, throughout.*

By Saxon Law, a noble widow is owed, as **Mußtheil**, even half of that grain which the husband had stored in order to sell, but which was not sold during his lifetime, as Moller teaches, *book 3, semestria, chapter 24*, whom you should see, *throughout.*

## 75. Mother Church. Cathedral Church.

*Matrix* <note>Latin: "Matrix," literally meaning womb or source</note>, the Cathedral Church. Even cities are called this, which by the Greeks are named *metropolises* <note>original: "μητροπόλεις"</note>, mother cities, from which many other cities were born and led forth; see Robbigius, book 8, chapter 15, and my own work *On the Law of Universities*, folio 231. And from this comes the Cathedral Church, from which others depend.

Thus according to Tranquillus <note>Suetonius</note>, we understand the "matrix tree" to be the one from which a great many offspring of shoots sprout forth. The Head Church <note>German: "Hauptkirche"</note>, where the pastor lives, is called the *Mater* or *Matrix* <note>Mother</note>, but where no pastor lives, or which church is incorporated into a parish, is called the *Filia* <note>Daughter</note>, so that she should direct herself according to the parish church, as the daughter follows the mother. Schæreus in the *Spiritual Language-School*, letter M, folio 25.

->ADDITION.<-

See above under the word *Church*. A Cathedral Church of the Pope <note>referring to major basilicas</note> is not exempt from the jurisdiction of its Bishop. Marius Antoninus, *Roman Validations*, book 1, refinement 107, number 6. The Church is called the Bride and Wife of the Prelate, and is widowed by his death. Barbosa, book 5, chapter 2, axiom 6. A church is presumed to have been built by the inhabitants of that place. From a legal presumption, the Lord of the territory has a founded claim in this regard even in Cathedral Churches, Abbeys, and other Colleges situated under him. Axiom 23. Which are Cathedral Churches? Petrus Gregorius in *The System of Universal Law*, book 17, chapter 3, number 15.

*Matrix*: Johann Forster in his *Hebrew Dictionary*, page 789, calls it the "pious mother." For just as that thinner membrane <note>the pia mater</note> which strengthens and covers the brain provides a motherly guardianship to it so that it is not harmed, and has therefore attained the name of "pious mother," so too the membrane of the womb <note>matrix</note>, because it is similar to the other in both material and function, is also called "pious mother" by the Hebrews. And from this, since the womb protects the fetus most diligently and is easily affected when something harsh happens to it, for that same

<column-break/>

For there we see this word used: "Because her heart yearned <note>original: "adusta sunt viscera ejus"; literally "her bowels were burned"</note> for her son." It is taken: 1. for a Cathedral or Episcopal church. Chapter *venerabili* 22, *Concerning the Signification of Words*. 2. for a Parish or Principal church, which has a limited parish and other small buildings or chapels under it, in respect to which it is called the "mother." ## 76. Mills. Molendinæ.

Regarding Mills, see especially Hering in his specialized, copious, and elegant treatise; Tuschum under letter M; and my own work *On the Law of Things*, folio 11.

Many today refer Mills to the Superiority of the Territory <note>territorial sovereignty</note> (see especially Hering *On Mills*, question 9), which has its origin from this: because on a public navigable river it is not permitted to build without the license of the Prince, or the one holding royal rights <note>term: "regalia"; sovereign rights belonging to a monarch</note> in that place. Law *quò minùs*, where the Doctors of Law commonly comment, in the *Digest on Rivers*. Rosenthal *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 28, numbers 5, 6, and 7, where he indicates the reason for this is that the rivers themselves are royal rights, according to chapter 1 of *What are Royal Rights*. See Goeddæus, *On the Restitution of Baron Vallendar*, number 318.

Whether millers are to be admitted to honors, see Hering, same work, question 1, number 5 and following.

Whether one who has ground grain for free for a long time acquires a right therefrom? See Bullæus, consultation 5, question 5. On prohibiting the building of a mill in the upper or lower part of the river, see Costaman, consultation 74; *Marburg Consultations*, volume 4, consultation 38.

Whether the inspection or visitation of mills belongs to the High Criminal Court <note>original: "Malefitzischen"</note> or rather to the Bailiff and the lower court authority is a very doubtful and common question, etc. as appears from those things which, after Knichen, Scheplitz, and others, Johann Hering most recently reported in his *Complete Treatise on Mills*, question 45, number 36 and following. But I am of the opinion that it is first necessary to know whether the High Judge claims for himself the princely sovereignty, or only the criminal jurisdiction? Item: who in those parts is entitled to establish regulations over weight, measure, and grain-tax <note>term: "Mäß"; a fee taken in kind by the miller</note>? Likewise, whether the nobleman who holds the lower court authority is, by reason of the estate, immediately subject to the Holy Roman Empire and contributes to the Knightly Chests <note>term: "Ritter-Truhen"; a tax fund for the imperial knights</note>? For when the High Judge has only the criminal jurisdiction and is not the Sovereign Prince of the area, he has no business burdening himself with the mills, except in a case of crime, when either the millers or others

### ADDITION.

A new mill <note>Latin: "Mola nova"</note> must be built in such a way that the usual course of the water is not diverted by back-flooding or otherwise, lest damage be caused to the neighbors. Klock, volume 1, consultation 33, number 35. No right is acquired by a miller even from a uniform usage of a thousand years. Klock, volume 1, consultation 18, number 35.

If someone has ground grain or baked in a mill or oven for 20 or 30 years without paying any fees or money: whether a certain right of servitude <note>Latin: "jus servitutis"; a legal right to use another's property</note> is thereby introduced? Bullæus, *Consultations*, page 236; letting the corn be ground freely without fees. Bullæus, page 237. Mills belong to the inspection of the civil authority, not the high authority. *Acts of Lindau*, page 355, after the middle.

Mills built on land or on riverbanks are immovable things, as are the wheels and other instruments of the mill. Knipschild, *On Trusts*, chapter 5, number 42. It is otherwise in the case of **Ship-mills** <note>German: "Schiffmühlen"; mills built on floating platforms in rivers</note>, number 43. Master Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 81, letter C. And **Hand-mills**, as well as **Horse-mills**, which are driven by horses. Andreas Scheffer, *Practical Questions* 39, number 8, part 3; Knipschild, number 45. **Windmills** are air-driven <note>Greek: "πνευματικὰ"; literally "pneumatic" or "wind-powered"</note> or moved by the wind, and are considered immovable things, number 44. Concerning the versatile character of millers—how "pious" the miller is who has hair on his tongue and in his hand <note>A proverbial expression suggesting millers were untrustworthy or "rough" characters</note>—see Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 8, numbers 33 and 34, at great length. At least the hand-mills, pushing-mills, and turning-mills, or those driven by beasts of burden, were known to the ancients, numbers 1 and 2. On **water-mills**, number 3; on **ship-mills**, number 4; on **water-mills**, number 5; on **wood-cutting and saw-mills**, number 12; on **oil-mills**, number 14; on **powder-mills**, number 15; on **paper-mills**, number 16, and there regarding the **rag-merchants** <note>German: "Lumpen-Jubilirer"; literally "rag-celebrators," a sarcastic term for those who collected rags for paper-making</note>; on **fulling-mills**, number 17; on **boring-mills**, **ore-mills**, **stamping-mills** or **crushing-works**, **copper-mills**, **iron-hammers**, **brass-hammers**, **wire-mills**, **salt-stone**, **woad-mills**, **grit**, **millet**, **mustard-mills**, **tanning-bark**, **lime-mills**, **coal-mills**, **calamine**, **gold-mills**, **pepper-mills**, number 18; on **polishing and grinding mills**, number 19; mills for draining and drying entire lakes and ponds, number 21; on **compulsory mills** <note>German: "Zwangmühlen"; mills where local residents were legally forced to grind their grain</note> and **communal ovens**, number 29. **Mülhausen**, an old city of Thuringia, named as if "house of mills." Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 34. On **milling fees**, the same author, book 7, chapter 16, number 44; book 7, chapter 17, numbers 10 and 11.

<column-break/>

Whether mills can be given as a **fief**? <note>Latin: "in feudum"; land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal</note> Some float on the waters, such as **ship-mills**; some are wind-powered, such as **windmills**, which one can move to another place without great effort; some are attached to the soil. Some wish for those which float on the waters, as well as those moved by the wind, to be categorized among movable things and therefore cannot be granted as a fief; but because those mills that travel upon rivers like ships are usually tied with ropes, and wind-powered ones are also not easily moved from their place, they are considered as things attached to the soil and part of the land, especially when the lord has a certain right there, such as the fact that the neighbors are perhaps necessarily forced to come to that mill, which is commonly called a **ban-mill** <note>Latin: "molendinum bannale"</note>, or a **compulsory mill** <note>German: "Zwangmühl"</note>. Jacobinus de Sancto Georgio in the *Gloss* on the word "mills." Schneidewin, part 2, number 54, with Rosenthal, chapter 4, conclusion 4. Vultejus, book 1, chapter 5. Knichen, *On the Vesting of Pacts*, part 2, chapter 4, numbers 49 through 56 inclusive. Rudinger, *Observations* 66, century 5. And with others, I think that mills of this kind may rightly be enfeoffed under this law and recognized as fiefs.

Regarding **mill inspection**, see the opinion of Doctor Helden. The mill-viewing and ordinance are to be held as an appurtenance of the high authority, and also of the general territorial and police ordinance; just as in the year 1559, a Noble Council of the City of **Nuremberg** renewed such an ordinance for the millers settled under the Nuremberg high jurisdictions, regardless of whose subjects they remained. So too is an opinion from the year 1568 available: since a Noble Council at Hohenst. holds the high authority, they therefore also have the power to establish measures, weights, gauges, and the like. No one can, by virtue of private property rights, establish a mill or territorial ordinance that extends into another high jurisdiction.

> None behave more maliciously and negligently in the things entrusted to them than **millers**: it is a kind of quasi-legal theft. Andreas Knichen, *On the Supreme Territory*, chapter 4, number 251.

The question is asked, whether millers and their children should be excluded from the **guilds**, offices, and trades? Zorer, part 2, question 18, numbers 40, 63. **Unjust measures** are to be punished as theft. For this reason, the master millers at H. and O. were required to have their small measures poured out at **Herspruck**; the master allowed it to remain so, and undertook the same at the N. mills, since other places also maintained this, and the violators are punished as criminals <note>Latin: "Malefitz"</note>. A mill-race, whether it be under-shot or over-shot, and which does not lack water in the summer, is valued at 10,000 Marks. More on this in Augustinus Wagner’s *Hungarian Land Law*, part 1, title 133.

Whether one having a mill in part of a river can prohibit another from building a new one in the vicinity? Doctor Biccius in *Golden Questions*, section 3, thesis 175, letter S. C. F. A. title 13, book 43, thesis 7. Master N. states that the number of mills in **Cairo**, which are turned by horses and donkeys, amounts to three thousand and forty.

### 77. Monk.

Regarding monks and the types of monks, as well as the monastic state, etc., see Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year 228 AD. Antonio Perez in his *Commentary on the Rules of St. Benedict*, throughout the index, especially folio 64. Filesacus, *On Bishops*, chapter 17. Zamuriensis in his *Mirror*, book 2, chapter 21 and following to the end. Johann Nicolaus in his *Handbook on Benefices*, folio 7 and following at length. Rinthelir in *The Roman Catholic Jurist*, chapter 49, chapter 55 and following. Coccius in *Dagobert*, chapter 6, folio 40. Fabricius, *On Religion*, where he notes that St. Jerome mentioned them. Stammen, *On Personal Servitude*, book 1, title 4, chapter 1. Stephanus Duranti also discusses various points regarding the law of monks, their vows, and inheritance in his *Questions* throughout. Regarding the religious of the Old Testament, see Becanus, *Analogy*, chapter 9, and regarding the Essenes, see Foller, *Miscellany 1*, chapter 3.

Regarding the reform of religious orders, see the Carmelite Johann Baptista de Lezana, in volume 4, and on the method of correcting regulars <note>Latin: "Regularium"; members of religious orders living under a specific rule, such as monks or friars</note>. See also Octavius Spatharius, *Criminal Practice*, especially from the beginning.

When monks first appeared in the West, namely in the year 340 AD: see the Reverend Father Laymann, *Just Defense*, folio 449. Monks were formerly called "Pallium-wearers" <note>Latin: "Palliati"; from the 'pallium,' a simple cloak associated with philosophers</note> and were the philosophers of the Christians: see *The Exiled Cloak*, folio 142 and following. Bignon shows that in ancient times monks were not clerics in his notes to *Marculf's Formulas*, folio 427, where among others he cites St. Jerome in praise of the solitary life; he demonstrates in several ways that the cause of monks is one thing, and that of clerics another—the latter are meant to feed the flock, while the former are meant to be fed <note>original: "hoſce paſcere, illos paſci"; a play on words suggesting clerics perform active ministry while monks receive spiritual or physical support in seclusion</note>, etc.

How strictly are the religious subject to the Pope? Laymann in *Just Defense*, folio 50 and following.

That the monastic state is a serious matter, see *The Imitation of Christ*, book 3, chapters 10 and 56, also book 1, last chapter; and Molanus, *On Images*, book 4, chapter 21.

Regarding the Order of St. Basil, see Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 3, folio 614 and following.

<column-break/>

Whether a monk, after his profession <note>The formal taking of monastic vows</note>, can revoke a will that he made before entering? It is generally denied: Cavallus, question 806; Covarruvias, *On Wills*, chapter 2. Rodriguez (see "Will") says he can, however, clarify or interpret the will.

Does a will become void simply by entry into a religious order? *Ecclesiastical Practice*, Marcus Antonius, question 333.

A monastery is capable of holding property; it generally succeeds in place of a son to the goods of its professed members' parents <note>A legal concept where the monastery inherits what the monk would have inherited if he had not entered the order</note>. See the title *On Proofs*; Nicolaus Everhardus, consultation 26, number 19. *Blessed Places*, volume 3, *On Wills*, part 2, folio 269. Regarding the legal argument comparing a slave to a monk, and how far it proceeds: see the same Everhardus in *Legal Topics*.

Under what intervening conditions may one transfer from one religious order to another? Bonacina, *On Enclosure*, folio 71 and following.

Regarding those who protest or reclaim against their profession of vows: Bonacina, ibid, folio 224, etc. To whom do the goods belong that a monk acquires after being ejected from his order? Bonacina, in the said treatise, folio 164.

Eunapius, Rutilius, etc., have much to say against monks, on which see Barthius, folio 151 and 171, and throughout. But those authors were Pagans <note>Latin: "Gentiles"</note>.

Who may properly be called "Monks": Mr. Dr. Biccius in his *Golden Decisions*, section 1, thesis 27, letter Z. Monks have nothing of their own, but acquire everything for the monastery, so much so that monks found holding private property ought to be buried in a dunghill <note>Latin: "in ſterquilinio ſepeliri debeant"; a severe traditional monastic penalty for violating the vow of poverty</note>. Others say that a monk indeed dies to the world regarding his works and its vanity, but not regarding his rights and inheritances: axiom 2. Monks ought to have neither a "will" nor a "won't" <note>meaning they should have no personal desires or will separate from their superior</note>: axiom 3. The habit does not make the monk, but the profession of vows does: axiom 4. A monk cannot be in several monasteries at once. If a monk entering a monastery protested that his goods should be retained, can he make a will after entry? Mr. Dr. Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 128.

## 76. Protection, Guardianship, Minor, Protector, Client, etc. The Law of Clientage. <note>The original terms Mundbar, Mundburt, etc., derive from the Old Germanic "Mund," meaning "hand," symbolizing the power or protection one person holds over another.</note>

The Law of Clientage is also called by the common name *Mundburt*, a word signifying **free protection and defense**, <note>original German: "freyen Schutz und Schirm"</note> that is, advocacy, defense, guardianship, and the state of being a client. 

In the *Laws of the Lombards* <note>A Germanic people who ruled parts of Italy</note> the word *Mundium* often occurs, and it usually signifies tutelage or guardianship. Hence they called Guardians *Mundwaltos*, from the administration of lordship; these are the people we today call *Vormunder* <note>German for guardians</note>, as if they were prefects of a lordship. *Mündlein, Unmündig, Mundbare* <note>Terms for minors or those under legal protection</note> are Old Frankish words for **one who has no legal guardian**, <note>original German: "der keinen Vogt hat"</note> one who lacks a tutor, and who, being unable to defend himself because of age, is subject to the power of a Guardian. **A Baron is free and unencumbered.** <note>original German: "Baron est frey ledig"</note> From this also comes "a protected plot," <note>original German: "ein Mundbarer Fleck"</note> which has no guardian. See generally Mr. Mager, *On Advocacy*, chapter 2, number 245 and following; add Dracon, *On the Origin and Law of Patricians*, chapter 6, page 185 and following; and my own work, *On Treaties*, folio 57; and the *Acts of Lindau*, folio 879.

### ADDITION.

The Lombards call a *Mundualdus* a curator who must be appointed for a woman. Marant., part 9, number 85 and following; Conrad Rittershusius, *On the New Constitutions*, part 9, chapter 3, number 17, page 494. On whoever makes himself a *Mundmann* <note>a client or protected person</note> of another: Limnaeus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 35, number 16. Women were in perpetual tutelage, and could do nothing without the authority of a *Mundualdus* (that is, a guardian), for *Mund* is the same as power and authority. Goldast, *In the Discourse on the Law of Representation in Primogeniture*, page 367; they could alienate <note>sell or give away</note> nothing. Finckelthauf, *On Illustrious Feudal Controversies*, Dispute 5, controversy 14, at the end.

## 79. Minster. Collegiate Church. <note>The term "Münster" (Minster) originally referred to a monastery but came to describe large, significant churches or cathedrals.</note>

Episcopal churches are almost always called by this name, such as those at **Strasbourg, Speyer**, etc. Sometimes, pre-eminently, <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν"</note> even more notable temples built with rare craftsmanship are distinguished by this name as if they were wonders, such as **The Minster at Ulm**, etc. 

Likewise, the Latin word *Monasterium* is used for a **Cloister**. <note>original German: "für ein Closter"</note> This is because formerly the Canons <note>clergy members belonging to a cathedral or large church</note> in episcopal cities **where there is a Minster** differed very little from monks. History everywhere confirms that those we today call Collegiate Chapters of Canons were once essentially monasteries: that is, the Canons led a common life together, lived together, and ate together.

<column-break/>

A house of Canons is called a "Monastery" because at that time—before discipline had slackened and the institutions of a holier age had become obsolete—the Canons lived under one roof and in a single building, content with one baker and a shared steward. This is also the origin of their title "Brothers," although they were not bound by any Monastic Rule. See Krantz, *On the Metropolis*, book 3, chapter 15.

Hence also Beeck, *In Aachen*, folio 19, etc.: The name "Monastery of St. Mary" was given to the High Church, commonly called the **Minster** <note>original German: "Münster"</note>, because the clergy and servants of God previously professed a stricter observance of their Rule, living in a Cloister, using one dormitory and one refectory <note>dining hall</note>. This was so they could more easily assemble to celebrate the Canonical Hours and mutually admonish one another regarding their life and conversation. They were called Canons (that is, "Regulars") following the example and imitation of the Greeks; their superior was an Abbot. And this type of order of Canons Regular, which originally flourished in this Monastery, was first instituted by the Apostles themselves and later reduced to a specific Rule by St. Augustine. Because of this, it retained the name "Canon," as if observing the "Canon" (Rule) of the Apostles and the ministers of the early Church. Indeed, they were those who had "one heart and one soul," who continued daily with one accord in the temple and, breaking bread in their houses, took their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people. <note>A paraphrase of Acts 2:46</note> 

Possidonius, Bishop of Calama and a disciple of St. Augustine, says in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter 5: "Having been made a priest, he soon established a monastery within the church and began to live with the servants of God according to the manner and rule established under the Holy Apostles; most importantly, no one in that society was to have anything of his own, but all things were to be held in common, and distributed to each as they had need." 

The same Order began to flourish again in the Church of St. Quentin at Beauvais under the venerable and Saint Ivo, provost of that church and later Bishop of Chartres. From this, many writers conclude that the Order of Canons holds primacy among all ecclesiastical orders in antiquity, doctrine, governance, nobility, and the number of saints. Their discourse, however, concerns the order of Canons Regular. Under such an excellent institute, the Brothers in Aachen anciently served God worthily. Even today in this Basilica, there exist the formulas of prayers poured out to God, the author and giver of all good things—namely the Psalms, Verses, and Collects which the Abbot used in the reception of Brothers, as well as similar prayers used when giving a travel pouch and staff to brothers setting out on a journey. These indicate clearly enough the regular discipline, which has preserved names into our own age such as the Dormitory (in common speech **the Dormiter** <note>original German: "der Dormiter"</note>), in whose arched and ancient wooden vaulting no spiders or cobwebs have ever been seen; and the Brothers' Mill (the **Brüder Mohlen**). Added to these is the custom of the Cloister...

# Letter M. Page 729 ADDITION.

The rule has come down even to this age that no one of the <term>Canonical profession</term><note>Canons were clergy who lived in a community attached to a cathedral or large church, often following a specific rule of life.</note> is permitted at this time to depart from the City of Aachen to go elsewhere, unless power has first been requested and granted by the Dean or a colleague from another place; punishments are decreed for those who show contempt. The rest of the "regular" <note>Living according to a *regula* or monastic rule.</note> institute was full of wisdom: for instance, pardon for a fault had to be sought with the body prostrate on the ground and arms outstretched; a forty-day imprisonment was mandated for the guilt of a crime or for disobedience; and absolutions from penance were granted through solemn prayers. I say that such punishments and expiations once imposed to break the bonds of sin have now entirely vanished and been purely suppressed. 

Just as many Canons of other churches had long ago abandoned these monastic rules—namely in Trier, as witnessed by Trithemius, the Abbot of Sponheim; the religious members of the Great Temple of St. Peter and St. Paul under the leadership of Bishop Theodoric around the year 966 AD. The Canons of Speyer under Bishop Balderic of Mainz and Worms likewise cast off the community of the "Regular" life. So, by the example of these and others, under Emperor Otto III and Notger, Bishop of Liège, the Brothers of Aachen became more relaxed and abandoned their monastic profession, longing for the <term>ownership of temporal goods</term><note>In earlier times, these clergy lived communally and owned nothing personally; "proprietary" canons were allowed to own private property and live in their own houses.</note>. Indeed, even earlier under Emperor Otto I, they had begun to change their names; instead of "Religious" or "Monk," they were called simply "Canons" without any addition, and their superior, having changed the title of "Abbot," began to be called the "Provost." 

Regarding this, Molanus writes: "The church was called the Monastery of St. Mary by our ancestors because twenty Clerics established by Charlemagne lived there regularly and according to canon law in obedience, eating and sleeping together in common within the Cloister, according to the statutes of the Council of Mainz held under Charlemagne. But they shook off this 'sweet yoke' for themselves, as did those of Mainz and many others under Otto III and their Bishop Notger, who converted the twenty regular Clerics into twenty-eight proprietary Canons, because they judged that the malice of the times required it."

Georg Fabricius, in Book 1 of the *Annals of the City of Meissen* under the year 972, writes the following about Bishop Volschuld (or Volrad, according to Lambert), a close associate of Bishop Willigis of Mainz: "He distributed the times for readings, prayer, and ecclesiastical duties; he took his food with the Canons, who in better times in these lands did not manage their own private households, but were the household of the Bishop; nor did they use substitute vicars, but were themselves the ministers of the Church. For the first institution of these colleges was very similar to monastic discipline, and this Church is called a 'Monastery' in Papal letters."

Likewise, Bruschius affirms in *On the Bishopric of Eger* (folio 4. A.) that it is certain all colleges of Canons were once Monasteries.

Besold, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

The high Cathedral of Speyer, constructed by the Emperor Conrad the Salic, is famous and conspicuous for its Mount of Olives and the tombs of several Swabian Emperors—such as Conrad II, Henry II, Henry IV, Henry V, and their August spouses. A distich <note>A two-line poem.</note> is read there, inscribed on their tombs:

> The son lies here, the father here, the grandfather here, the great-grandfather there,
> Here lies the great-grandfather’s wife, and here those of Henry the Elder.

Limnæus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 46, number 5.

Schradæus discusses the high cathedral of Strasbourg very thoroughly in an entire book; it is most worthy for its structure and elegance, holding a place among the wonders of the world that is by no means the lowest.

The height of the Strasbourg tower exceeds 515 cubits. In the year 1275, the church—which is now called the *Münster*—was finally finished, and thus was fully built over 260 years, even though the work initially proceeded so well that they reached the roof in 13 years. They spent 10 years on the foundation of the tower until it was level with the ground, even though several hundred men worked on it. In height it has 574 "work-feet" and is transparent <note>Referring to the open-work Gothic spire</note>. Above the chapel or middle tower of the Minster, it is written with beautiful, raised, Old-Frankish letters:

->IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1277, ON THE DAY OF BLESSED URBAN, MASTER ERWIN OF STEINBACH BEGAN THIS GLORIOUS WORK.<-

We have seen, printed in 1665 in the so-called *Report regarding the House, Lordship, and County of Delmenhorst*, a catalog of all the Bishops of Münster from 300 years ago, starting from Ludwig, Landgrave of Hesse, Bishop of Münster in 1365, down to the current Christoph Bernhard von Galen—a man of ancient landed nobility and high qualities.

A legal-political and historical discourse on the question: Whether one should remain committed to the places where the Thaler is valued at the old rate of 24 Groschen according to the Imperial Coinage Ordinance of the Year 1559, or follow those who have increased its value. Legal opinions of Philipp Baumgartner. A discourse on monetary change by Ulrich Volrat; and a treatise on the same matter by Johann von Fuchte. Lindemann’s Synoptic explanation of the Contract of Loan. The responses of the jurist Wolff Hiller. The responses of Lustricus; and my own in the *Consilia*, and many others.

**Money** <note>original: *Moneta*</note> is derived from "warning" <note>original: *monendo*</note>, surely because of its office, purpose, and use: because by the impression of a seal and the inscription of a certain authority, it warns us of the time, weight, and value. Jacob Alemannus in his *Consultations*, part 18. Furthermore, the word **Coin** <note>original: *Münz*</note> embraces every kind of numismatic item, and indeed in contracts it is mostly understood as silver and is distinguished from gold. See the Police Ordinance of the Year 1648, in the section "On Usurious Contracts." It is also very frequently understood as referring only to small silver change. It is also called **Money** <note>original: *Geld*</note>, hence **Building-money** <note>original: *Baugeld*</note>, **Watch-money** <note>original: *Wachtgeld*</note>, etc. In these cases, it either stands for all currency, as the ancient Germans called the pecuniary fines for homicide **Man-money** <note>original: *Mangeld*; this refers to Wergild, the value placed on a person's life paid as compensation</note>, or it is distinguished from gold, as in the Chamber Court Ordinance: "Gold or Money."

Money must not be shaped or published in any form other than what is customary to be struck, under penalty of 50 marks of pure gold. Ferdinand’s Coinage Ordinance, August 19, Anno 1559, in the section "Therefore we decree": that henceforth in the Empire of the German Nation, no mint-lord of high or low station shall mint, strike, or issue as payment any other coin than what is expressly presented in this Edict, upon avoidance of Our and the Empire's heavy displeasure and a penalty of 50 marks of pure gold, etc.

There are three substantial requirements of any money which constitute its **essence** <note>original: *τὸ εἶναι*</note>. First, that the Coin be of legitimate weight. Leviticus ch. 19 v. 35; Proverbs ch. 20 v. 10; Jeremiah ch. 32 v. 9; 1 Chronicles ch. 21 v. 25. Also in the Code of Justinian regarding ancient coinage: "of the required weight" and "with an even balance." Second, that the coin be of good quality, or of a proven type; it must certainly not be false. The law regarding "false money" in the Digest; also terms like "rejected," "adulterated," or "sacrilegious" are used for coins that are counterfeit or tampered with.

Third, a **Public Form** is required. This is the official stamp or image that grants the coin its status.

<column-break/>

See especially Freher, who treats extensively the definition and requirements of money or coins, and also discusses money-changers. Guyon teaches that Tartar money is made from the bark of the Mulberry tree. Regarding the money of the Greeks, see Camerarius in his treatise on *The Knightly Matter*. On the various valuations of money, see Bisciolus, volume 2.

The Right of Minting money is counted among the **Regalia** <term>Regalia</term><note>Rights or privileges belonging exclusively to a sovereign or monarch.</note>, called **the Minting or the Right of Coinage** <note>original: *das Müntzen oder Münz-Gerechtigkeit*</note>. I discuss this in my work *On Majesty*. It is said in the *Saxon Mirror* <note>The *Sachsenspiegel*, the most important record of customary law in medieval Germany.</note> that the King of the Romans, in whatever city he entered, had the right to the coinage no less than the taxes. Nicolaus Myler and Johann Kizel also state that an inferior cannot make money unless it is granted by the King or Emperor, or unless they have prescribed a right from a time beyond memory. Thus, the right of minting in Germany is a Regalian right, not a mark of inherent majesty; it is reserved and does not belong to the States of the Empire by right of their territory, but by a singular privilege from the Emperor. This is also why the **Eagle** is stamped especially on the heavy and Imperial coins.

The impression on coins from a public die was invented so that its value would not be corrupted by the material, and so that one type might be distinguished from another in its kind, both by Province and by Value. Also, so that the image or figure of the Prince stamped on the coin might, through a certain reverence, deter wicked men from adulterating it. Hence, those who imitate the die of another prince, or even their own Prince's die to strike unauthorized money, are punished as counterfeiters. Nor should those minor rulers <note>original: *Reguli*</note> escape punishment who, abusing the right of minting acquired through investiture, cause the image or character of other Princes to be stamped, and thereby strike and spend false and rejected coins, introducing them into the territory of those Princes whose coins they wished to imitate. For these men, by reason of this crime, could be punished by the very Prince in whose dominion they distribute such money.

This impression of an image also makes it so that subjects may more easily believe—or foreigners spending it may trust—that the material so stamped contains the real substance and is not adulterated, and that the just weight is present, without the extra labor of the scale or balance. This impression is of such strength and power that money so stamped cannot be refused by a creditor; indeed, such refusal is punished as a capital offense. This is not, however...

a creditor should not be forced against his will to accept the currency of another Prince, even if it is in common use, especially if it has once been banned. <note>original: *Mart. Laudenl. de monet. num. 3.*</note> For a rejected penny is not a penny. <note>original: *Reprobus enim denarius non est denarius*</note> This is discussed at length by Tiraquellus. <note>original: *Tiraquel. de retract. lignag. §. 1. gl. 20. num. 11.*</note> But see also Tessaurus on this point.

It is well established that the Kings of Bohemia are permitted to strike coins in any form. But are they also allowed to invent new ones? A distinction is usually made between **Provincial Money** <note>original: *Landmüntz*</note> and **Public or General Money** <note>original: *Reichs-Müntz*</note>. For the use and necessity of the Kingdom and Provinces, the King is not prohibited from inventing any new common forms; but for Imperial currency, it is not so, unless he wishes to risk being prohibited by the Emperor and the Estates of the Empire. <note>See Lord Goldast in *Bohemia*, book 4, chapter 2, page 425.</note>

Long ago, in the time of Pope Boniface VIII around the year 1302, money was quite worthless, as historians report. Regarding the money of Tours <note>original: *Moneta Turonensi*</note>, Nellus de San Geminiano says it was diminished out of the greed of the Prince so that he might profit more. Signorolus de Homodeis discusses the changed money of Pisa. <note>original: *de Pisana moneta mutata*</note>

Whether a creditor, against his will, is allowed to return the estimated value if the currency has changed after a castle was pledged as security. <note>See Roener in *Observations on Legal Practice*, chapter 35.</note>

On the change of money, see Curtius, *Conjectures*, book 3, chapter 15. Also, how coins have risen in value at all times, especially from the year 1518 until 1565 in Cologne. <note>original: *Statuta Coloniens. part. ult. f. 84.*</note> Likewise on page 87, where it discusses the **Payment Masters** <note>original: *Payements Herren*</note> and their office. Those who manufacture false money are handed over to be burned in the flames, according to the decree of the Emperor Constantine. <note>original: *ex Imp. Constantini Sanctione l. 2. C. de fals. monet.*</note> This was confirmed by Charles V in the Criminal Constitution, article 11. This is commonly understood to apply to one who mints false money under the form and image of the Emperor. However, regarding one who mints false money under the image of a lesser Prince who has the right of coinage, some say he should be punished with capital punishment—that is, by exile or deportation. <note>original: *Clarus in §. falsum. n. 22.*</note>

In truth, this distinction between the money of a High Prince and a Lesser Prince can hardly be gathered from the said law. Indeed, during the reign of Constantine, no one except the High Prince himself was allowed to mint money, and no lesser Prince, as Covarruvias testifies. But reasons for mitigating punishments should be sought from wherever possible. Regarding **money clippers** <note>those who shave the edges of coins to steal precious metal</note>, see the seventh book of the Decretals.

*Besold, Volume I.*

<column-break/>

The use of coinage was invented for the purpose of being a convenient medium of **exchange justice** <note>original: *Justitiæ commutativæ*, the justice of fair trade</note>, or as Aristotle says in the first book of his *Politics*, a "common sponsor" and the price of saleable goods. For this reason, it ought to be struck and fashioned not from base metal, but from precious metal, according to Nicolas de Clemangis in his treatise *On the Fall and Restoration of Justice*. He says there: "Therefore, that which is the price ought to be made from some precious metal; otherwise, how can it be a price if it contains nothing precious in itself?" Furthermore, it must be made of such a material that is considered dear and precious not only among the natives of the Fatherland, but also equally among foreigners: so that through it, one may participate with them in the exchange of merchandise through buying and selling. Hence, the goodness of a coin descends from the **Law of Nations** <note>original: *jure Gentium*</note>. What is it, therefore, to make coins from such a material that contains no preciousness in itself, except to alienate other regions from the use of trade? Without this, no state can endure for long or remain inviolate.

According to the Constitutions of the Emperors, no path to high dignities was formerly open to **Minters** <note>original: *den Müntzern*</note>. <note>Johann Hering, *Treatise on Mills*, question 1, number 13.</note> Yet today they are of better condition, and are considered no less free-born <note>original: *ingenuis*</note> than other men. <note>Sixtinus, *Treatise on Regalian Rights*, chapter 9.</note> Budelius proves they can ascend to some grade of honor.

On the corrupt state of monetary affairs, see Arumæus.

**Ceremonies:** when they sing the Mass, they use strange instruments, such as two drums, like kettledrums, which they beat while singing; one has a little rattle <note>original: *Schlötterlein*</note> which is covered in bells, which he strikes with his other hand so that it rings; another has an instrument like those used by the Moors, similar to a half-drum, also hung with bells. They stand together, hopping and dancing with one another, singing many "Hallelujahs." In *Furer’s German Travelog, page 194*: <note>original Latin: *Murænas & serpentes compertum est...*</note> *It has been discovered that eels and snakes are stunned by musical harmony and thus captured; the asp, however, wraps its ears with its tail so that it is not enticed by the sweetness of the melody, losing its venom and wasting away, and it can be of great use in making medicine.* On this point, the most keen Kepler says: <note>original: *vilis merx est...*</note> *It is a cheap ware that Codrus does not buy to feed his belly, but Cleopatra buys to adorn her ears.* Lord Abdias Trew, *Disputation on Music 1, thesis 6.* Prætorius wrote the *Musical Compendium* <note>original: *Syntagma Musicum*</note>. At the end of *Trew’s 1st Disputation on Music*, he posed a corollary: Was the music of the ancients more perfect or less perfect than our modern music? First, regarding the Hebrew Republic, it seems to have been similar to a concert of trumpeters or buglers <note>original: *der Trompeter*</note>, and thus a middle ground between the variety of modern artistry and the common simplicity of singing. It is better to hear a horse neighing than a lewd musician, because, as Saint Augustine testifies: <note>original: *plus placet Deo latratus canum...*</note> *The barking of dogs, the lowing of cattle, and the grunting of pigs please God more than the singing and prayer of indulgent clerics.* Ferdinand Prætorius could not die in London until the musicians before his bed, through a lovely song, had delivered his departing soul to the angels: a story also told of Dr. David Rungius. Zeiller, *1st Century of Letters, page 529; see also page 528.* Sigmund Schack, in the 103rd year of his age, wanted to learn the lute. Zeiller, *4th Century of Letters, page 618.* <note>original Latin: *Ex jussu Sauberti nostri...*</note> *By the order of our Saubert, while he was still strong, those standing by the dying man sang that little song mixed with tears and groans,* "When my little hour comes" <note>original German: *wann mein Stündlein*, a famous funeral hymn</note>, *and they did not want him to approach the heavenly sweets and luxuries without music. See my work in the "Living Library of Nuremberg," in my five Orations published together.*

Regarding the songs of the Bards and the masters of melodies, see Saubert, *On Ancient Sacrifices, pages 163, 164.* A Hessian nobleman, a Schezel by family, did not know whether the jaw harp <note>original: *Maultrummel*</note> belonged among the stringed instruments. Johannes à Muris and Nicolaus Vincentius wrote about music. Regarding the musicians called "Siticines" <note>funeral horn blowers in ancient Rome</note>, see Rittershusius *on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 24 at the end.*

### 82. Military Muster. <term>Lustratio</term> <note>a formal inspection or purification of troops</note>.

Soldiers are reviewed and approved by those who have the right of approval. *Law 1, Code: Who can serve in the military.* The Emperor can approve. *Law 17, Code: On military affairs; Law 9, Code: On various offices.* Sometimes also the Masters of the Soldiers and illustrious Generals. *Second to last law, Code: On military affairs.* Today, this act, which they call the military probationary <note>original: *militum probatorium*</note> or the **muster** <note>original: *die Musterung*</note>, is carried out by military commissioners, whom it behooves to know everything beforehand according to their wisdom and dignity, and to admit the fit into military service but reject the unfit. Schönborn, *Politics, book 6, chapter 13.* But that power descends from the law of the territory: Muster, march, and following <note>original: *Musterung, Reiß, Folg*—the obligation of subjects to follow their lord to war</note>.

Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 7, thesis 2, letter f.* They are also called "Bulletins" <note>original: *Balleten*</note>: for the French *bullea* or *bulletin* (a small slip or ticket/token of lodging) seems to be formed from *bulla*. ## 82. Muster. [Lustratio]

Soldiers are reviewed and approved by those who have the right of approval. *Law 1 of the Code, "Who may serve in the military."* The Emperor can approve them. *Law 17 of the Code, "On military affairs," and Law 9 of the Code, "On various offices."* Sometimes even the Masters of the Soldiers and the illustrious Generals can do so. *Second to last law of the Code, "On military affairs."* Today, this act, which they call the military probation or the Muster <note>original: "die Musterung"</note>, is carried out by military commissioners, who must investigate everything according to their wisdom and dignity, adopting those suitable for military service and rejecting those who are unfit. *Schönborn, Politics, book 6, chapter 13.*
But this power descends from the law of the territory: Muster, march, and follow <note>original: "Musterung, Reiß, Folg," referring to the right to call up and review troops</note>.

# 83. Shared Administration <note>original: *Mutschirung, Mutschârung*</note>. A fraternal agreement regarding inheritance through rotating governance.

Where the law of primogeniture <note>The legal right of the firstborn child, usually the eldest son, to inherit the entire estate</note> prevails, the firstborn excludes the others, and the supreme power of the whole kingdom remains with him; the legitimacy of his portion is called "the whole kingdom" by legal interpreters. Sometimes, however, the administration is committed to two brothers at the same time, while the others are excluded by means of an assignment of certain revenues; this is called rotating governance <note>original: *vicissitudinaria gubernatio*</note>, commonly called *Mutschierung* in German, or by others *Mutschärung*. Lord Goldast, *On Majorities*, final chapter, number 21. See also my own work, *On Succession and Election*, page 95.

->ADDITION.<-

A family trust <note>original: *Fideicommissum* — a legal arrangement where property is held for the benefit of a family lineage over generations</note> is sometimes established so that the use of the territory is divided among noble brothers, but the exercise of jurisdiction is transferred to the elder with a certain benefit. Besold, *Nomico-Political*, book 1, discourse 6, number 12. Or, brothers may administer the provinces for one year or three years, as Johann Lauterbach writes in *The Christian Prince*, final chapter, number 131. This kind of rotating governance is usually called *Mutschierung* or *Mutschasrung* in German. Besold, cited above, number 12. Knipschild, *On Family Trusts*, chapter 6, number 316 and following. Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 7, page 76. Additions, volume 1. Sprenger, *On Public Jurisprudence*, page 425 and page 431.

# 84. Mummies. <note>original: *Mummien, Mummiæ*</note>.

Regarding the mummies in Egypt, the dried dead human bodies. Salomon Schweigger in his *Description of the Journey to Constantinople*.

<column-break/>

...Constantinople, book 3, chapter 20, throughout; where at the end he deals with the question of whether the number of mummies always remains the same. Lord Fürer in his *Travels*, page 25, reports that the inhabitants call both the place and the corpses themselves "mummies." Johann Helffrich, in his *Description of the Journey to Jerusalem, Egypt, Mount Sinai, Cairo, and Alexandria*, recounts that on the 11th of December he came to a place which was called "the Mummies." There he found mummies, the dead bodies of several deceased heathens who had their burial in the aforementioned place. These bodies remain uncorrupted. However, they are entirely coal-black, because every limb, small and large, is very diligently wrapped in small, narrow cloths dipped in precious balsam, and afterwards the whole body is enveloped and tied in a broad cloth, just as one wraps small children. These bodies are found in holes, thus buried in the sand. In some of these, when they are unwrapped, one finds inside their body, instead of intestines, carved little men or animals, and similar fantasies. The Moors who live nearby search for these with all diligence, for they sell them to the merchants in Cairo, by whom they are further transported. Some of the Moors also eat them out of curiosity. Cited location. Plato, long ago in the *Phaedo*, celebrated these medicated corpses in Egypt from nearly three thousand years ago, which endure uncorrupted to this day, not without the great amazement of those inspecting them; the common people call them mummies. However, Melchior Guilandinus, in his excellent treatise *On Papyrus*, section 24, proves from Dioscorides and Galen that these corpses used to be preserved or medicated with cedar juice <note>original: *cedri succo*</note>: they report that "cedar-juice" <note>original: *cedrium*</note> is called by some the "guardian of dead bodies" or of dead parts. More in Pancirolli, *On Lost Things*, page 282.

# Enlarged Treasury of Practical Knowledge

The gnawing of strings by mice, especially if it is total so that not even a thread remains, ruins the instrument. *The same author, page 322, number 92.* Mice are thieves. Vultures, hawks, goatsuckers, crows, and octopuses are indeed thieving animals, but the mouse does not yield much to them. For in gold-refining workshops, mice steal <note>original: *furantur mures*</note> (such is the sweetness of stealing), but because of this, their bellies are cut open to recover the stolen goods. At Lavinium, mice gnawed silver shields; at Antium, they gnawed a golden crown. Livy, *Book 30, preface.* Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his vast knowledge of the natural world</note> writes that he saw a mouse that held a candle at a banquet. Zeiller, *Epistles, century 2, page 156.* Regarding mice, see Guido Pancirolli, *volume 2, title 1, in the Notes on Pliny, book 8, chapter 57.* Drexelius, in *The Gold Mine, page 165,* relates that among the Swiss, a parish priest had four daily dinner companions: a mouse, a cat, a dog, and a small bird. He made them so familiar through gentle discipline and habit that, whenever he wished, they would eat breakfast, lunch, and dinner from the same small dish. This was recounted by one who saw it with his own eyes. In Dresden, there is an "Indian mouse" <note>likely a guinea pig or a similar exotic rodent</note> as large as an otter. Zeiller, *Epistles, century 3, page 500.* And for six examples of high-ranking persons who were eaten by mice, see the treatise called "The Mouse Tower," <note>original: *Mäusthurn* — a reference to the legend of Bishop Hatto of Mainz, who was allegedly eaten by mice as divine punishment</note> written extensively in the year 1618. In chapter 16, he treats the legal proceedings against mice <note>referring to historical animal trials where pests were legally excommunicated or ordered to leave a territory</note> and how they were defended by Bartholomé de Chasseneuz in France. It is suggested that one should shove crayfish into mouse holes. Michael Knab in *The Prayer Book, folio 42.*

Justinus writes in *Book 2* regarding the Scythians: "The use of wool and clothing is unknown to them; and although they are burned by continuous cold, they are nonetheless clothed in the skins of wild beasts or mice." Even today, as even schoolboys know, the most luxurious skins of *mice* <note>original: *Murium* — likely referring to ermine or sable, which were sometimes called 'Pontic mice'</note> are brought from Scythia and the coldest regions for the winter attire of *grandees* <note>original: *Megistanum* — high-ranking officials or nobles</note>. Adrien Turnèbe mentions this in *Book 15, Adversaria, chapter 13.* Furthermore, the use of these skins is also common among the *Chinese*. Giovanni Pietro Maffei, *History of the Indies, book 6.* More can be found in Pancirolli, *On Lost Things, pages 62–63, regarding forest mice and their skins.* On the docility of the mouse, he writes elegantly on *page 62*, so that we may now believe that an ape once learned to play board games <note>original: *latrunculis* — an ancient Roman strategy game similar to chess</note>, as Castiglione claimed in *The Courtier*, and that an elephant used to write the strokes of Greek letters in the dust; for the Egyptians even thought a certain genus of baboons <note>original: *Cynocephalorum* — 'dog-headed' monkeys</note> were skilled in letters and that they themselves were related to them because of this knowledge. Whether the foreign mouse is the same as the civet <note>original: *Zibetho*</note>, see Pancirolli, *page 67.* Plautus always introduces hungry and voracious parasites who gnaw another's food just like mice. See Philipp Carolus in the *Roman Library on Annona* <note>The Roman grain supply</note>, citing Virgil from *Book 1 of the Georgics* regarding another's field:

> —often the tiny mouse
> has set up his home and built his granaries 
> under the earth; or the blind moles 
> have dug out their chambers, and the toad is found 
> in hollows, and all the many monsters 
> that the earth brings forth.

<column-break/>

The "God-beloved mouse," <note>original: *Götterliebe Maus*</note> the mongoose <note>original: *Ichneumone*</note>, is spoken of at length by Clajus in *verse 531, on the Resurrection.* In Augsburg <note>original: *Augustæ Vindelicorum*</note>, a crypt is shown in the Church of St. Ulrich, into which St. Ulrich miraculously gathered all the mice and dormice of the city.

### 86. Flies. <note>original: *Mucken* (German), *Musca* (Latin)</note>

A pilgrimage church was erected to Beelzebub <note>Literally "Lord of the Flies"</note>: as Lazarus Soranzo writes in his *Ottoman, chapter 64,* that Murad III died in the year 1595 and was buried in the Church of the Fly-King, which he had built during his life. Zeiller, *century 4, question 1, page 3.*

It is well known from Suetonius, Dio Cassius, Aurelius Victor, and others, about the private hour of Domitian <note>Roman Emperor known for his cruelty</note>, in which he did nothing more than stab flies; hence, when someone asked if anyone was inside with the Caesar, it was not absurdly answered by Vibius Crispus: "Not even a fly," as Suetonius reports. For Sextus Aurelius Victor, in Andreas Schott’s edition, presents this answer thus: "Not even a fly, unless perhaps in the wrestling ring <note>original: *Palæstra*</note>." Here the joke arises from the ambiguity between the foul wrestling of Domitian and the *gymnastic* <note>original: *γυμναστικην*</note> wrestling ring, as Joseph Scaliger teaches at length in his *Observations on the Chronicle of Jerome.* Virdung in his commentary on *Tacitus’s Agricola, pages 210–211.* Mr. Speidel in his *Mirror of Notables, page 786 (my edition)*, reports that he once heard in a discussion from someone that there is a certain nobleman in Austria who, in recognition of his fief, must offer two bushels full of flies to his Lord. Themistocles persuaded the Athenians not to change their magistrates by telling a fable about a fox and flies; see the *Political Observations on Florus* which are annexed to Rupert's edition of Florus, *book 1, chapter 23, at the end.*

Regarding the impudence of the *fly*, see Pancirolli in Rupert’s edition, *page 375.* Hence, in Cicero’s *On the Orator, book 2*, it was ridiculously said of a most troublesome youth: "Drive away the flies, boy." I pray that *Myiagrus*, that *God of Flies* <note>A hero or god invoked to drive away flies</note>, to whom we read the people of Elis sacrificed to avert a plague in Pliny’s *book 10, chapter 28*, is always angry with them. Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas and Petrus Ramus in the *preface to book 2 of the Mathematical Schools, page 62*, mention the *mechanical iron fly* that could fly. Myrmecides of Miletus became famous for other monuments of praised industry in the same genre: for he is read to have fashioned a four-horse chariot from ivory, which a fly could cover with its wings. See Drexelius in *The Gold Mine, page 336.* Through the industry of Aldrovandi <note>A celebrated 16th-century naturalist</note>, over *seventy* different kinds of flies were observed, distinct in their limbs, color, and shape. Maximilian Sandæus in *Symbolic Theology, folio 279.* Mr. Leonhard Wulffbain in *On the Number Seven, page 360.* Plautus in *The Merchant, Act 2, Scene 3, verse 26:* "My father is a fly; nothing can be kept secret from him, nor is anything so sacred or profane that he is not immediately present there." See Philipp Carolus in the *Roman Library.* A painted fly is an eternal monument in Antwerp <note>Referring to the anecdote of the painter Quentin Matsys, who painted a realistic fly on a masterpiece to fool his master</note>. Philippe Bosquier, *part 4, Academic Conclusions, chapter 2, page 14.* Concerning the *iron fly*...

### 87. Manna.

Whether the Manna of the children of Israel was the same as the Manna we have today? See Zeiller, century 5, epistle, page 358. The same author, century 4, question 30, page 151 and following. ### 88. Myrrh.

Dubravius writes that in Moravia they also dig frankincense and myrrh out of the earth, and reports that in his time, Lord Wenceslaus of Berka and Daub found an entire human body on his estate of Sternberg that was made of pure myrrh, and could be used for incense. Zeiller, page 189, *Travels in Germany*. On Myrrh, Pancirollus in *Things Lost*, my page 49, 51.

### 89. Mastic.

From the island of Chios is brought the most precious tree resin, Mastic or Mastix; it grows from the Lentisk tree <note>Lentisco</note>. Salomon Besold, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

### 90. Matza.

It is the custom in Sion <note>Latin: Seduni, the capital of the Swiss canton of Valais</note> that when they wish to proscribe <note>to outlaw or condemn</note> someone, they carve a certain image of a most shameful man into the root of a tree and place it before the door of the one to be proscribed. They call this "the Matz" <note>original: "die Matz"</note>, where individuals gather and consume the crops of the proscribed person. Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 344. In Valais, it savors of ostracism, "to bring someone the Matz" <note>original: "einem die Matzen bringen"</note>. Simler on Valais, book 1, folio 6. Sebastian Münster, book 3 of the *Cosmography*, chapter 34.

The "Matza" is a wood of conspiracy, woven from tree roots which they twisted together so artfully that it represented a certain image of a human face to those looking from a distance. Christoph Rupert on Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 1.

### 91. Almonds [Sheaves].

Leaving grain in "almonds" <note>original: *Mandeln* — here referring to a specific way of stacking grain sheaves in the field, likely named for the shape or a quantity of 15</note> in the field. Berlichius, conclusion 3, number 47, end. To stack grain in sheaves, ibid.

### 92. Malt.

Malt. See Berlichius, conclusion 3, number 48, number 38 and following. The malt-house. Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 5, number 79. The barbaric word *bravium* denotes *polenta* or malt. Vossius, *On Vices of Speech*, book 2, chapter 3, page 184. The right of roasting or soaking barley, the "Malt-Right" <note>original: *Maltzrecht*</note>, is not necessarily tied to either high or low jurisdiction (which the Doctors call superior or inferior), neither to the High nor the Hereditary Courts. Thus, if the right of roasting and brewing was historically exercised on a feudal estate, it is rather presumed that this was also granted among the appurtenances or accessory rights. Mr. Tabor on *Beer Law*, chapter 2, section 6; add chapter 3, section 8, and chapter 5, section 3.

From what *polenta* <note>malt or grist</note> is made. Zythander à Bude in his treatise *On Brewing and its Annexed Rights*, part 1, chapter 3, number 1. Who is the owner of the malt made from another’s barley and wheat, ibid. number 3. Selling malt to nobles is forbidden, ibid. number 14. Who shall be the owner of the beer brewed from another’s malt, book 3, 15. Whether malt should be numbered among edible things, book 3, 16. Whoever enjoys the right of brewing may also prepare malt, and vice-versa, number 17. The preparation of barley water <note>original: *ptisana* — a medicinal drink made from pearled barley</note>, expressed with these words "to make the malt" <note>original: "das Maltz machen"</note>, is described by Knipschild in *On Imperial Cities*, book 2, chapter 26, number 82. Zythander à Bude on the *Rights of Brewing*, part 1, chapter 3, number 32. Spelt, commonly called malt <note>original: *Maltz*</note>, in Greek *byne*. Klock on the *Treasury*, book 2, chapter 11, number 1. Drying houses for the preparation of barley water, from "making malt," number 13.

### 94. Painter.

**Raphael of Urbino** once painted a sick man so accurately that a physician was able to recognize from the painting how the man was afflicted with a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever spikes every four days</note>. **Sultan Selim created the painter Gentile Bellini a Knight.** Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 1, number 57. *Painters and miniaturists who deceive with counterfeit colors are held liable to the Lord for damages as a punishment for their lie; indeed, they are liable for the crime of fraud* <term>stellionatus</term> <note>A Roman law term for "swindling" or fraudulent dealing that doesn't fit a specific category like theft</note>. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 97, number 4. **Luke** is called a **Physician** by Paul, not a **Painter**, in *Colossians 4, verse 14.* And, if he was a Jew, as indeed he was, and from the number of the seventy disciples, it is not likely that he was a painter, since among the Jews these arts were not in use, *as is understood from book 4 of Origen's Against Celsus.* **Bernegger** in *The Demolition of the Loretto Idol, page 38.* *On Professors of Painting*, **Mr. Tabor** on *Metathesis*, page 206. Limnäus in *Public Law, book 9, chapter 1, number 68.* Painting was once numbered among the liberal arts, so much so that slaves were forbidden from practicing it. See Pliny, book 35 of the *Natural History*, chapter 10. **Vitruvius** requires in his *Architect* that an architect ought not and cannot be a Grammarian like Aristarchus, but he should not be "unlettered" <note>original Greek: ἀγράμματον</note>; nor a Musician like Aristoxenus, but he should not be "unmusical" <note>original Greek: ἄμουσον</note>; nor a Painter like Apelles, but he should not be unskilled with the "stylus" <note>original Greek: γραφίδος</note>. Painting is a "mode of acquisition" <note>A legal concept where one gains ownership of the materials by the act of creating art upon them</note>, and the painting draws the tablet to itself <note>meaning the art is more valuable than the wood it is on</note>, according to Dr. Biccius in *Golden Rules, section 3, thesis 36, preface*; how it is a mode of acquisition under the law of nations, *section 3, thesis 6.* On what legal actions are available regarding a painting, *section 3, thesis 36*, middle. On defamatory paintings, *section 4, thesis 155.* Regarding **Albrecht Dürer**, the world-famous Nuremberg painter, **Balde** writes:

->Albert’s circle, drawn with only charcoal,<-
->is a ring for your fingers, O maiden of Nuremberg.<-

And **Jean-Jacques Boissard of Besançon**:

> Because things are painted by you on breathing tablets,
> we believe those things live and speak with open mouths.

**He painted** *things that could not be painted: light in the shadows, lightning, thunder, and winds.* At **Stuttgart** in the Pleasure House <note>The *Lusthaus*, a Renaissance festival building</note>, there is a painting of a hawk in full flight striking the head off a heron, and the heron continues to fly even without its head. King **Attalus** valued a single tablet by the painter Aristides of Thebes at 60,000 crowns. Drexel in *The Gold Mine, page 249.* **Julius Caesar**, intending to dedicate two paintings, *Medea* and *Ajax* by Timomachus, in the temple of Venus Genetrix, bought them for eighty talents, or 48,000 crowns.

<column-break/>

The Italians begrudged Germany and the city of Nuremberg that Albrecht Dürer was born among them and not in Italy. The famous Italian painter of that time, named **Michelangelo**, gathered as much of Dürer's work as he could and, out of pure envy toward the German nation and toward the Nuremberg painter Dürer himself, he tore them to pieces, burned them, and destroyed them.

**John of Burgundy**, nicknamed "the Fearless," was very deeply offended when he noticed the portrait or likeness of his wife Margaret in the chamber of Louis of Orléans. Treated at length by Leonhard Wurffbain in *On Truces and Peace, pages 95, 96.* The Young Lords of Prague were excellent painters, from whom the painters received their red and white coat of arms. Wolfgang Lazius, book 8, *Migration of Nations*, page 408. **On the most precious painting of Apelles**, see Zahn, *On Lies*, book 1, chapter 44, at the end. At Basel, Messerius had the following likenesses of the Doctors who were promoted there, which Dr. Remigius Fesch had copied: these include **Alciati, Baron, Duaren, Contius, Hotman, Doneau, Baudouin, Cujas, and Mercerius** <note>These are all famous 16th-century legal scholars</note>. The esteemed Mr. Fesch also has portraits of distinguished painters, such as **Raphael of Urbino, Albrecht Dürer** (as he appears in the Chapel of St. Luke in Rome), **Michelangelo, Titian, Uccello, Ritter, Antonio Tempesta**, all the painters of Rome, and **Holbein** of Basel, who later went to England and painted the precious table in the Town Hall at Basel. On "tried" or "experienced" painters, see Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Great Theatre of Delightful and Instructive Stories*, volume 199. It is told that a Venetian once asked a German: *“In which country does the eagle have two heads?”* The German replied aptly: *“Right next to the country where the lions have two wings, as your Evangelist Mark is painted.”* On the art of painting, the following have written: *Michelangelo Buonarroti, Raphael of Urbino, Titian, Federico Barocci, Zuccaro, and Bassano.*

### 95. Table.

On the order of arranging the tables of the Emperor, the Empress, and the Electors. **Sprenger, *On the Modest Amount***, page 176. Even where several people sit at round tables, the more excellent place of sitting can be determined from the position of the hall, the door, the hearth, the windows, and also the cupboard. Marselaer in *The Ambassador*, book 2, dissertation 12. "You set a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it," treated extensively by **Saubert** in *On Sacrifices*, page 699. Tables in Scripture. Dr. Biccius in *Golden Rules, section 5, thesis 128.* Money-changers <note>original: *Mensarii*</note>, Alemannus in *On Money*, page 871. Table-setters and coin-minters, page 870. The table is seven steps higher than all others. Limnäus.

### 96. To Clean Up a Draft. To bring into the world. <note>original: "Mundiren. In mundum redigere." In legal terms, "mundum" refers to a clean, final copy of a document</note>

Instruments received into the "world" <note>the final draft</note>, according to the *Code* regarding the faith of instruments. To "bring instruments into the world" means to write them out on another clean sheet of paper. Ritterschul. in *Novels*, page 631, number 34.

### 97. The Mount of Piety. <note>original: "Mons Pietatis"; a charitable pawnbroker run as a non-profit to provide low-interest loans to the poor</note>

Paul Laymann in *Moral Theology*, book 3, chapter 16, number 11. Schottelius **on the Main Language of the Germans**, folio 491. Klock **on the Treasury**, book 2, chapter 20, numbers 5 and 25. Fl. Fortunatus, Venice, 1498. Cardinal Thomas de Vio Cajetanus, volume 6, part 1, folio 419. Those houses in Italy where money is lent to the needy against a pledge, provided that they return it at the proper time, are described by Zeiller in his 4th century of *Epistles*, page 281. Zeiller in the **Itinerary of Italy**, folio 7, 75, and 81. Bernhardus Scardon, book 2 of the *History of Padua*, class 5. The Republic of Nuremberg received its laws for the Mount of Piety in the year 1618 from Venice and Augsburg; see my own work in the **Comparison of the Republic of Nuremberg with that of Venice**. Bornitius, in **On the Treasury**, chapter 7, reviews various reasons why a Mount of Piety might be erected for the sake of accumulating public money. Regarding the Old, New, and Newest Mounts of the Venetians, one may read Johann Ruremund in **The Key to Wealth**, octavo edition, 1623, Strasbourg, chapter 40, pages 152 and following.

On the Mount of Piety, see by all means Mr. Harsdörffer in the **Great Stage of Pleasant and Instructive History**, volume 174, number 7. Join to this the *Inaugural Disputation on Interest Accruing to Loans* by Paul Schermar, a Patrician of Ulm, 1629.
<sig>Besoldus, Volume 1.</sig>

<column-break/>

Held at Tübingen under the presidency of Besoldus, chapter 2, theses 18 and 19. It would indeed be holier if such "mounts" were established for free, as Leo X suggested in the Lateran Council in a bull issued on this matter. However, it is not forbidden to demand something in the name of interest for expenses and for "emergent loss" <note>original: "intereſſe damni emergentis"; a legal term for the actual loss a lender suffers by not having their money available</note>, according to the canon law regarding precarious holdings. It is only just that those who are found to provide their service for a time should receive a wage. Johann Ruremund, in the aforementioned **Key to Wealth**, chapter 22, discusses these mounts at length, as does Thomas de Vio. The renowned Senate of Ulm established a similar "mount of piety" in the year 1619, which it called **"the Loan Office"** <note>original: "das Anlehen Amt"</note>, to assist the poverty of the indigent through such loans, so they would not be swallowed by the abyss of heavy usury. However, due to the subsequent confusion of the currency and the misery of the times, it was not much used and is today entirely abolished.

### 98. The Margin.

Writing in the margin is held suspect. See Ummius **on Procedure**, page 731, at the end. Related to this are "Apostilles" or additions, about which Farinaccius writes in part 6, question 153. One also speaks of the **margin of a riverbank** or the **margin of walls**. There is also the "marginalized" instrument of appeal, as they call it; see Schwanmann **in Chamber Procedure, book 1, chapter 12, number 4.**

### 99. Monopoly.

Lauber, in *On the Saxon Staple*, translates **monopolium** into German as **"sole trade"** or **"sole trade-constraint."** Also **"sole purchase"** and **"sole sale."** Necessity sometimes extorts monopolies when the treasury is utterly exhausted. Fritsch **on Fairs**, chapter 11, number 15.

No one has the power to buy before a thing has been brought to the public market. Cinuzzi, book 1, chapter 51, number 55. Otherwise, a monopoly would be practiced, which is forbidden in the single law of the *Code* regarding monopolies. Johann Berber also wrote on this in the **Traveler's Guide to Law, part 1**, rubric 28; Egidio Bossio in the **Criminal Treatise, under the rubric on unions and conspiracies**; and Damhouder in **Criminal Practice, chapter 134, on Monopoly.** France practices monopolies in salt, and Spain in the gold mines of the Indies. The magistrates of Breslau claim for themselves the right of buying and selling hops, which is forbidden to others under heavy penalty. In Bohemia, the Lords arrogate to themselves the right of brewing beer, from whom the subjects must buy it. Thus, in most places in Germany, you will find **"common beer houses, common bathhouses, and forced mills"** <note>original: "gemeine Bierhäuſer, gemeine Badstuben & Zwangmühlen"; facilities where local residents were legally required to use only the lord's establishment</note>. That trade was seen as cruel which Antonio de Leyva, Governor of Milan for Charles V, practiced when he enjoined by strict law that everyone buy bread from public shops, and that no one should make it for themselves. Sabellicus in the *Supplement*. Sprenger in **Axioms of State, axiom 20, pages 120 and 121.** It pertains immediately to the Imperial Chamber, and the first instance is not considered...
