### 100. Scattered Gifts.

<term>Missilia</term> <note>original Latin: "Missilia," things thrown</note> are gifts that are thrown to the common people, also called "scatterings." Seneca, in *Natural Questions* book 2, quoting Gaius, book 9, penultimate section, *On the Division of Things*. See also Suetonius in *Augustus* chapter 98, *Caligula* 18, and *Nero* 11. Also the *Code on Consuls*, book 12, and the *New Constitutions* <note>original: "Novellae"</note> 105, chapter 2. It is an argument of folly to scatter coins and drag one’s robes. The ritual of scattering money in later times is described at length by Master Rupertus, book 7, chapter 8, section 2, on Valerius Maximus. Those from Aachen assert <margin>that it has been a custom from olden times that a reigning Mayor is allowed a "hand-grab" into the money thrown among the common folk at the time of a Coronation, and whatever he manages to grab, he may keep.</margin> Limnäus, book 2 of the *Additions*, page 82.

### 101. The Right of Reprisal.

We exercise the <term>Right of Reprisal</term> <note>original: "Marduæ jus," or Law of the Marches/Reprisal</note> not against our own countrymen, but against foreigners, and only with the permission of the Prince. For example, if Spaniards plunder the goods of a French merchant, and that merchant encounters a Spaniard, he may plunder him by equal right; this is practiced most especially on the borders. Cujas on the *Code*, book 11. See more under the word <term>Pledge-seizure</term> <note>original German: "Pfandung"</note>.

### 102. Minutiae (see also: Chamber of Wonders, Artists).

Joseph Scaliger says: Small things must not be neglected, because without them, greater things can hardly be understood.

<column-break/>

What is smaller than a mathematical point? Delrius has a praise of it in his third *Panegyric on the Mother of the Lord Assumed into Heaven*: "Nature is nowhere more entire than in her smallest things." See Pliny, *Natural History*, book 11, chapters 2, 5, and 24. You will find the admirable anatomy of an ant in Basil the Great, in his 168th epistle to Eunomius, page 629. To the Emperor Augustus, his procurator sent from Africa (scarcely credible to say) nearly four hundred shoots from a single grain of wheat; others say 400 grains. Similarly, one sent to Nero three hundred and forty stalks from a single grain. More on this matter can be found in Drexelius, *The Gold Mine*, pages 335–337. In the <term>Chamber of Wonders</term> <note>original: "Kunstkammer," a collection of curiosities and art</note> in Munich, there is a cherry stone with 107 faces carved on it. In Dresden, on one cherry pit, more than 100 faces or heads can be counted distinctly, among which the head of a Pope with his triple crown can be recognized. Furthermore, on a penny from Mainz, there are 24 spinning wheels, and upon it a carriage with a maiden turned from ivory. Master Georg Älurius, in his *Chronicle of Glatz* published in 1625, says that the little town of Lewin in the County of Glatz is very famous for the good spoons made there, and that he four times saw 12 dozen spoons worked into a single cherry pit. Because of a nail, the horse loses a shoe; because of the shoe, the horse is lamed; because of the horse, the rider falls; because of the rider, his companions fall; because of them, the whole army—and with it the land and people—is set into irrecoverable ruin. Such disaster can stem from a lowly nail. It is wise and profitable for a traveler to seek out small things. Seneca, in his 49th Epistle, speaks of the lovers of useless questions. Oswald Nördelinger, the famous master-turner, was able to fit 1,500 ivory cups into a natural peppercorn. Someone in Mechelen, in Brabant, hollowed out a cherry stone like a spindle-basket and placed 15 pairs of dice inside, with their eyes [pips] clearly distinguished. An Italian was able to write the Apostles' Creed on a penny without abbreviations. Someone in Prague wrote the Lord's Prayer in a circle so small it could be covered with a <term>Heller</term> <note>a tiny copper coin of very low value</note>. In ancient times, someone wrote Homer’s *Iliad* so finely on parchment that it could be enclosed in a nutshell. Leo Brunner, here in Nuremberg, previously had a list printed of several small pieces of art he prepared, which are a wonder to read about, but will be seen with even greater delight.

### 104. Mulberry. *Morum*.

Regarding the name of the **Mulberry tree**, and why it is called *Moros* and *Morus* by the Greeks and Latins—meaning the <term>foolish or unwise tree</term> <note>original: "thöricht oder unweise Baum," playing on the Greek word "môros" for fool</note>—though it is meant in a contrary sense. Whether *Morus* comes from *Mauris* or Moors, which signifies black. Whether *Morus* is derived from *Moror* and *Mora* <note>meaning "to delay"</note>. See Martin Mylius, Rector at Görlitz, in his translated *Pleasant Garden of Wisdom*, pages 214–215. From this comes the proverb: "He is earlier than a mulberry tree," ibid. page 216 & following. Although one find entirely white mulberries in some places, according to Hieronymus Bock's report, Benedict Curtius maintains that such are not fit for eating but are reserved solely for the use of <term>silkworms</term>. Athenæus writes that Hegesander testifies how, during his lifetime, the mulberry trees bore no fruit for twenty years in a row. Following this, such a sudden "gouty plague" <note>original: "Podagramische Pest," a disease resembling gout</note> occurred that not only men, but also women, maidens, boys, and girls were commonly afflicted by it. Indeed, it eventually reached the herds of sheep and goats, ruling so strongly among the livestock that barely a third remained alive. Ibid. p. 218. The famous jurist and orator Pasienus Crispus loved a mulberry tree so much that he often rested under its shade, hugged and kissed it, and even "honored" the tree with wine by pouring it over the roots. Ibid. page 221. Regarding the **Fig-mulberry tree** <note>the Sycamore</note>, page 221 following. The poets imagine how, in a certain age of the world, many people grew on trees in the forests and

<column-break/>

were later turned back into oaks, laurels, or mulberry trees. Balde, book 8, *Silvae*, Ode 14, folio 279.

Regarding the **silk-tree** and **silkworms**, see Adam Olearius in the *Persian Travelogue*, folio 579 following. The King of Spain receives 30,000 crowns in tax every year in Granada alone from the mulberry leaves used to sustain the silkworms. Zeiller, *Itinerary of Spain*, page 340. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 6, number 2. A branch of a mulberry tree broken off during a new moon and kept, then tied to an arm, is said to stop the bleeding of wounds, the nose, the mouth, and the <term>golden vein</term> <note>a historical term for hemorrhoids</note>. Dry wood from the mulberry and laurel tree bound together is said to produce fire. Michael Knab in the *Book of Delights*, folio 86. See below under "Shrubs." Regarding Mahomet Bassa's seal, depicting a silkworm on a mulberry leaf, see the excellent work of Höpingk, *On the Form of Seals*, chapter 5, § 26. On the mulberry tree and silkworm, see Master Dilherr in *Garden Pleasure*, p. 499. All of Syria, and especially Tripoli, abounds in silkworms, which weave webs in the manner of spiders for the clothing and luxury of women; as found in Pliny, a Pamphylian woman named Pamphila, daughter of Latois, first discovered how to unweave and re-weave these on the island of Cos. Fürer in his *Itinerary*, p. 101.

In the courts of Württemberg and other Princes, *Moreta*, or mulberry groves, are planted. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 6, number 7.

**Ludovicus Morus** <note>Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, known as "Il Moro"</note> brought a birthmark into the world from his mother's womb in the shape of a mulberry <note>original: "Maulbeers & Mori"</note>. Others say that just as the mulberry tree is the last of all trees to bud and turn green, yet brings its fruit along with it immediately, so too this Ludovicus Morus was not over-hasty in his counsels. Rather, he proceeded slowly and deliberately, but what he finally decided upon, he put into action without delay. To this end, "from the delay of counsels" <note>original Latin: "à mora consiliorum"</note>, he carried a mulberry tree with its fruit in his personal emblem. More can be found in Master Leonhard Wurffbain, *On Truces and Peace*, page 64. For more on the mulberry tree, see Master Harsdörffer’s *Poetic Funnel*, part 3, page 339. The mulberry tree does not bud until the cold has passed. Earthly plants have a natural sensitivity. Master Harsdörffer in the *Great Theatre of Joyful and Instructive Stories*, volume 182, number 2. On the mulberry tree, see Michael Knab in *Orchard Management*, page 85.

### 105. Mephitis.

**Mephitis** is properly the stench of the earth coming from sulfurous and putrid waters; in the groves, it is heavier due to the density of the woods. Virgil:

> —and the dark [woods] exhale a cruel stench <note>original: "mephitim"</note>.

Persius, in *Satire 3*, understands it as the most foul gases resulting from indigestion of the stomach:

> From the throat slowly exhaling sulfurous stenches <note>original: "mephites"</note>.

### 106. **Milk. *Lac.***

The tithe-collector <note>The official responsible for collecting the "tithe," a 10% tax on agricultural produce</note> should allow young cattle to remain at home with their mother's milk for a time. *Master Johann Werndtle on Tithes, book 2, chapter 3, pages 78–79.* Why milk that has been corrupted by sorcery <note>original: "veneficio"</note> may be restored to its good quality within a few hours if it is mixed with human dung. *Hornigk on Postal Law, page 563.* Regarding the making of libations <note>Ritual pouring of a liquid as an offering to a deity</note> of milk, honey, and wine. *Saubertus on Sacrifices, page 675 and following, page 664.* *Horace:* "They appeased the Earth with a pig, and Sylvanus with milk" <note>original: "Tellurem porco, Sylvanum lacte piabant," from Horace's Epistles book 2, epistle 1</note>. *Prudentius, book 1 against Symmachus:* "He receives a bowl of milk and these sacrificial cakes of vows every year" <note>original: "Sinum lactis & haec votorum liba quotannis accipit"</note>. In the sacred rites of the Good Goddess <note>Bona Dea, a Roman deity associated with chastity and fertility</note>, when they performed a wine libation, they did not call it wine, but said it was milk; however, in the rites of Rumia <note>A Roman goddess of nursing mothers</note>, wine was never present, only milk, and even the sacrificial victims were sprinkled with milk. *Saubertus, page 665.*

**Milk, hair, and wool are <term>industrial fruits</term>** <note>A legal term for products derived from animals or land through human labor</note>. Permission to eat milk and dairy products was granted by Pope Sixtus. *Limnaeus, book 7, chapter 16, number 37.* When a certain highly intelligent man titled his book "Catechism Milk," another person remarked that this title was not appropriate; because of the deep and precious subject matter, such a book should be called "Catechism Rhine-wine" or "Malvasia" <note>A prestigious sweet wine</note>. On whether a woman having milk in her breasts is necessarily a virgin. *Ilico Ummius in Processu, page 630.* Regarding milk and calves obtained from distrained cows <note>Cows seized to satisfy a debt</note>: must these be restored in legal cases of pledging? *Schwann, observation 75, numbers 1–2.* Poppaea Sabina, the wife of Emperor Nero, always traveled with five hundred she-asses and often bathed in donkey milk so that her body would not become wrinkled. *Zeiller, century 1, Letters, page 143.* Regarding the donkey milk with which ancient Roman women washed their faces so they would not have to look so hideously into the mirror, see *Jakob Balde, book of Epodes, ode 12, folio 303.* *Neander, in the History of the Bacchanalia, page 133,* tells of the *Cobali*, who are malicious and deceitful demons, harsh and pitiless. *Coelius Rhodiginus, Ancient Readings, book 2, chapter 7.* Unlike these are the **Kobolds**, whom people believe live in the hidden parts of houses or in woodpiles; in Sarmatia <note>An ancient region covering parts of modern Poland, Ukraine, and Russia</note> they feed them sumptuously with all kinds of food because they are said to bring grain to their providers by stealing it from others' barns. When these spirits wish to live and be fed somewhere, they declare their intention to the masters of the house in this way: at night they pile up scraps of wood in the house and place various animal droppings into milk pails full of milk. If the master of the house notices this and does not scatter the wood or throw the dung out of the pails, but instead eats the soiled milk with his whole family, the spirits are said to appear and remain there; as Johannes Meletius writes in *Delrio, book 2, Disquisitions on Magic, question 27, section 2.*

What the "land flowing with milk and honey" signifies. *Master Dilherr, volume 1, Disputations, folios 760–761.* Milk is bad for those with aching heads; likewise, milk is not at all suitable for those with fevers. It fills a cold stomach with gas, relaxes it with excessive moisture, greases it as if with oil, 

<column-break/>

and renders it weaker. Furthermore, it easily increases or curdles within the stomach, becoming cheese-like. In a warm stomach, it quickly spoils, so that for slight reasons it is perverted into the nature of a poisonous humor, or the form of yellow or greenish bile. *Felix Plater in Medical Questions, question 77.*

The early Romans sometimes lived on milk. *Rittershusius on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 208.* To be weaned is to be "driven from the milk." *The same author on the Digest, book 23, page 19.* To a <term>usufructuary</term> <note>someone with the legal right to use and profit from property they do not own</note> to whom the use of a herd is bequeathed, all fruits belong by full right: both the offspring and the milk and wool. *Schneidewin on Use and Habitation, page 213.* For more on milk, see Mr. *Harsdörffer in The Poetical Funnel, part 3, page 345.* On "Devil's Milk." *Master Dilherr, Time and World Affairs, page 519, section 16.* Also **Wolf's Milk** <note>original: "Wolfsmilch," the plant Euphorbia, known for its milky sap</note>. In Switzerland, there are many people who live solely on milk without bread, and grow old and grey in good health. *Zwinger.* It is suspected by some that the Franks and Gauls are so named from their "milky" <note>pale</note> color. *Isidore, book 9, Etymologies.* For milk in Greek is *gala*. *Crusius in Lectures on Feudal Constitutions, page 8.* The Court Records of Ensisheim: The bailiff of the court shall come annually on the third day after St. Martin’s Day, and travel to the court for the assembly with six horses and one mule, and he shall be well-served with good **milk-mash** <note>A traditional thick porridge made with milk</note>, and a stable, and hay. *Homogalaktas* <note>Greek: "Same-milk"</note> is the name for children and their children's children who have enjoyed the same mother's milk. To "dumpel" butter <note>original: "Butter ausdumpeln"</note> means to make butter by the agitation of milk; "Dumpel-milk" is buttermilk. *Schottel in the German Main Language, folio 1306.* What one should feed cows so that they give much milk. *Zeiller, century 4, question 46, page 246.* It is written of the Church: "You shall suck the milk of the nations, and you shall be nursed at the breasts of kings." *Isaiah, chapter 60.*

### 107. **Mercury. *Mercurius.***

Mercury, the overseer of profit. The god of thieves and merchants, and the presiding deity of dreams. *Saubertus on Sacrifices, page 40 and following.*

The "good" and "bad" Mercury. *Limnaeus on Public Law, book 8, chapter 6, number 36.* What kind of god Mercury was among the pagans, and what his sacrifice was. *Master Dilherr, volume 1, Disputations, folios 216–217.*

Solomon undoubtedly had beautiful stables, for he kept some fifty-seven thousand six hundred horses, as Lorinus has calculated.

# 109. Manuscripts. Letter M.

**Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> related this story about **Ptolemy** <note>Specifically Ptolemy III Euergetes of Egypt</note>: when the Athenians were suffering from a shortage of grain and struggling with the high cost of food, he would not grant them grain (as Egypt was then the granary of Greece) until they allowed him the opportunity to copy the original works of the Princes of Tragedy—**Aeschylus**, **Sophocles**, and **Euripides**. In this matter, he acted with such integrity <note>The author likely uses "integrity" ironically here, as the story continues to show Ptolemy kept the originals</note> that, besides granting them an exemption from taxes, he gave them 15 talents as a security deposit; however, once the copies were made and the originals sent back—which he was not supposed to do—he kept the originals and donated the deposit money instead.

**Mr. Dr. Georg König** in his brief speech <note>original: "Oratiuncula"</note> regarding the efforts of Illustrious Men in Founding Libraries, delivered at **Altdorf** on June 30, Anno 1644.

The **Library of Cluny**, described in a specific book by **Peter of Cluny**, was lost in the year 1562 during the storming of that monastery. To the great sorrow of scholars and the incredible detriment of the **Republic of Letters** <note>A term for the international community of intellectuals</note>, it perished through military lawlessness or fire, as the illustrious **Thuanus** <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou, a French historian</note> writes; he called it a most copious library, furnished with every kind of manuscript equipment.

The **Library of Leiden** in the Netherlands is very well-stocked with Arabic manuscript codices. Mentioned by **Mr. Dr. König** in the aforementioned place.

Precious Manuscript Books. **Adam Conzen**, *Politics*, book 6, chapter 13, section 7. On the most famous libraries, book 4, chapter 16, section 20.

**XII. Library Laws** certainly deserve to be added here: 
1. Let no one enter without the librarian's permission. 
2. Let no one be admitted except those of proven trust and integrity. 
3. Books of all faculties are to be arranged in good order. 
4. All books shall show the subject matter and the name of the author on an external title. 
5. Let there be another book that contains a catalog of all books in alphabetical order. 
6. In that catalog, the name of the author, the subject of the book, the size, and the color should be described. 
7. No one, not even the librarian himself or a Consul, shall be allowed to take a book out unless a signed receipt <note>original: "Chirographo"</note> is given. 
8. If anyone takes one out, let him return it after a month. 
9. They shall take care of the cleanliness of the library and the books. 
10. Twice every year, the librarian shall advise the Senate regarding the purchase of new books. 
11. Forbidden books shall be banished. 
12. No one shall leave a mark on the books, either with ink or by folding the paper <note>dog-earing pages</note>.

In the **Library of Strasbourg** <note>original: "Argentinensi"</note>, printed forms of this kind are used: "Therefore, I the undersigned confess that I have accepted on loan from the Library of the Illustrious and Renowned Academy of Strasbourg, under the law that I shall restore it within the space of a month; if by chance the book should receive any damage or staining, I shall pay the price of the loss, as determined and prescribed by the Academy Overseers <note>original: "Ephori"</note> and the Librarian. Executed on the — day of the Year of our Salvation restored through Christ —." I signed several forms of this kind in the year 1649, when I was successfully composing my inaugural dissertation on the style of the Court, by carefully collecting choice excerpts and searching here and there.

<column-break/>

**Marcus Welser**, the magistrate of Augsburg, could not obtain the Letter of **Isidore** from the manuscripts of the **Duke of Bavaria** in any other way than under a bond of one thousand florins, which he provided and shared with **Mr. Conrad Rittershusius** without the latter's knowledge. See the life of C. Rittershusius. Regarding the broad reliability of manuscripts, see the 30 *Philological and Historical Letters* concerning the testimony of **Flavius Josephus**, reviewed by **Mr. Christoph Arnold**, pages 139–140.

**Bologna** has a magnificent library full of handwritten books, which **Angelus Roccha** is said to name in his book on extant libraries. *Zeiller in his Travels in Italy, page 124.*

Manuscripts lie hidden and do not make a profit like prisoners. The celebrated **Mr. Rupert** mentions this in his work on **Pomponius**. The very well-equipped library of **Augustus, Duke of Lüneburg**, is adorned with various inscriptions here and there. A chest filled with manuscripts bore this concluding sentiment <note>original: "Epiphonema"</note>:

> Behold the food of genius; to know is nothing sweeter than 
> ->art:<-

Yet **Tantalus** <note>A figure from Greek mythology punished with eternal thirst and hunger</note> himself endures a similar thirst. Perhaps this follows the opinion of **Cicero** <note>original: "Tullii"</note>, who affirms that nothing is sweeter than to know everything. *Book 4, Letters to Atticus, letter 10.*

At the **Escorial** <note>The historic residence of the King of Spain</note>, a book is shown bound in gold, which is valued at four thousand ducats: in it, the life of Christ was painted by one of the order's monks, and the corresponding psalms and responses were written by another monk with his own hand. *Zeiller, Travels in Spain, page 215.*

At **Basel**, there is a manuscript of **Thucydides** in the library, which **Mr. Buxtorf** showed to me. **Turnebus** <note>original: "Turbenus"</note>, in book 28 of his *Adversaria*, chapter 22, says that **Demosthenes**, a most diligent imitator of Thucydides, copied Thucydides ten times; **Robertus Titius** says seven times; and **Lucian**, from whom those others took their information, says eight times. *Mr. Dilherr, volume 1, Dissertations, page 731.*

In the **Nuremberg Library** <note>original: "Bibliotheca Norica"</note> is preserved an almost enviable treasure of hand-written books: many Bible codices; a Greek Liturgy written in a time very close to the Apostles (as our ancestors indicated); the works of **St. Jerome**; the works of **Augustine** comprised in twelve volumes; an unpublished paraphrase of the Psalms by **Athanasius**; various homilies of **Chrysostom**, especially on Matthew, of which **Thomas Aquinas** is said to have remarked that he would rather possess them than the city of Paris; many works of **Bernard**, **Gregory**, **Dionysius**, and **Origen**; most of the works of **John of Damascus**; and some of **Prosper**. Also, **Nicholas of Lyra** on the Old and New Testaments. The works of the aforementioned **Thomas**, divided into fifteen volumes; the *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>A standard collection of biblical glosses or interpretations</note> in sixteen volumes; the *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History* in many volumes; the writings of **Nicholas of Cusa**; various works by **Gerson**; the works of **Cardinal Hugh**, **Hugh of Prato**, and **Hugh of Siena**; **Haimo** on the minor prophets; **Innocent** on *The Contempt of the World*; the notes of **Abbot Joachim** on the Apocalypse in two volumes; the *Clock of Wisdom* by **Henry Suso** <note>original: "Johannis à Seus"</note>, not yet printed by type; **Alanus** on the *Six Wings of the Cherubim*; a volume by **Peter of Blois**

### 110. Momus.
<note>Momus was the Greek personification of mockery and harsh criticism.</note>

Let the Wit <note>original: "Sal Mercurii" / Salt of Mercury</note> be retained, and let Mockery <note>original: "Sal Momi" / Salt of Momus</note> be avoided. The former is bright, the latter is black. The former is generous and learned, the latter is impious and profane. The former proposes sharp warnings with a certain beauty of expression. The latter flutters here and there scurrilously, wandering wider than is proper. The former pours a becoming cheerfulness into the souls of the listeners. The latter bites and gnaws at those present with a hateful bitterness. *Neander in his History of the Bacchanalia*, page 9.

I do not invent enemies in the manner of those who, with an effort more than ridiculous, try to frighten away the Zoili <note>harsh, envious critics</note> on the frontispieces of their papers. For others know and complain enough—and it has very often been barked at me—that these letters are "fruitless." This is because they believe Mammon and Ambition are the "Greater Gods." As for me, far from being moved by common judgments, I feel a stimulus added to me to walk more intently in this racecourse. It happens to such critics as it did to Ajax, who, when he thought he was dealing out a hollow slaughter among the Greeks, sat alone among the cattle <note>In Greek myth, Ajax was struck with madness and slaughtered a flock of sheep, thinking they were his enemies</note>. Why then should I provoke the sordid, who care for nothing if the fields of talent grow wild and are overgrown with ferns and briers? Why the ungrateful, who pursue with hatred all the elegant, hardworking, faithful, and distinguished defenders and guardians of literature? Why the unhealthy, who labor under a perpetual fever for plucking at what they do not understand and despair of achieving? Why the jaundiced and the bleary-eyed, to whom everything looks filthy that is not filthy? Why the impure, who like Harpies touch everything on Phineus's table and foul everything with their touch? More on this in *Mr. Rupert's Prologue to Pomponius*.

Regarding unskilled Censors, see *The Illustrious Rupert on Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapters 10, 11, 12, section 5 and following*. Our urban Jesters, though they know nothing, know everything; men born with the Graces angry at them, and always most occupied in doing nothing. Such a person does as much in that business as a camel does in a painting <note>A proverb for a person attempting a task for which they are entirely unsuited</note>. In delivering a judgment on such a matter, he is a total blank <note>original: "alba linea" / a white line, meaning a neutral or ignorant judge</note>. This "itch" for judging and censoring is as great now as the giddiness and blindness <term>giddiness and blindness <note>original: "μετεωρία καὶ ἀβλεψία"</note></term> of those who

<column-break/>

are so busy in doing nothing. See *Philip Carolus in the Taste of Philology*, page 4, near the end. Therefore, someone has rightly written:

> Without art, without toil, without diligence I compose,
> Therefore, do not judge me by your own head,
> Until you know, sweat, sharpen, and carve in your mind,
> I have started and I'm sailing on:
> Until you peek, bow, dress up, and press in your head,
> My pot is already emptied:
> Until you patch, lard, pinch, and knit in your brain,
> My thread is already wound off the reel.

Just as beetles <note>original: "Cantharides"</note> are often born even on blooming roses, so too is innocence sometimes exposed to the bites of slanderers. If the pleasure of speaking ill stimulates others, I will not delay, but like the dog from Albania once given as a gift to *Alexander the Great*, I will avenge myself with contempt alone; I shall value their barking as much as a fierce elephant values the buzzing of a fly. *Baldus, consultation 44, book 4.* Today, Pygmies are blinded by the boots of Maximinus <note>Maximinus Thrax was a giant Roman Emperor; the phrase implies small people trying to fill shoes too large for them</note>! Just as I rejoice to be stirred by good, honest men who mind their own business first—indeed, I always revere their pointing finger—so I am accustomed to laugh at the "pepper" of a busybody <term>busybody <note>original: "πολυπράγμονος"</note></term>, and I turn no other shield toward them than that most gentle one of the most gentle Emperor *Marcus Antoninus*: "How much leisure he gains who does not see what his neighbor says, does, or thinks, but only what he himself does, and ensures that this is just and right." More in *Rupert's Prologue to Pomponius*.

### 111. Marble.

In Rome, at St. Pancras, there are the most beautiful transparent marble stones that one can find in Rome. From *The Building of the City of Rome, 1447*, printed in Rome by Stefan Planck of Passau.

In Mr. *Plater’s* cabinet of curiosities in Basel, I was shown marble from the countryside near Florence. How a wild fig tree might split a marble stone is described most extensively by *Martin Mylius in the Pleasure Garden of Pleasant Wisdom*, pages 212, 213, etc. *Camerarius* in his "flowery images," taken from the books of *Jovius*, is cited in the same place. Marble, sculptures, and paintings are expensive things. Regarding marble, *Pliny’s* complaint is not in vain in *book 36, chapter 1*: "We cut down mountains and drag them away for no other reason than for luxury—mountains which it was once a wonder even to have crossed. To our ancestors, it was almost a portent that the Alps were surmounted by *Hannibal* and later by the Cimbri; now they themselves are cut into a thousand types of marble. Promontories are opened to the sea, and the nature of things is leveled. We carry away those things which were established as boundaries for separating nations, and ships are built for the sake of marble; and through the waves, the most savage part of nature, the ridges of mountains are carried here and there with a madness even greater than when a vessel is sought for cold drinks. Cloudless cliffs close to heaven are hollowed out so that people may drink from ice <note>Pliny is critiquing the use of mountain stone for luxury cooling or vessels to hold ice</note>."

Let each person think for themselves what prices one hears for these things, and what massive weights one sees being carried and dragged. Scaurus brought three hundred and sixty marble columns to his temporary theater <note>referring to Marcus Aemilius Scaurus's lavish theater built in 58 BC</note>, but these were from the paternal plundering of provinces and the proscription lists of Sulla. Lucullus gave his name to a type of marble as a memorial to his vanity, and these columns were thirty-eight feet tall. We see the swift triumph of vices. Lucius Crassus the Orator was the first to have columns of foreign marble, but they were from Mount Hymettus and only six in number, nor were they longer than twelve feet; yet this was not without reproach, for because of this, Brutus used to call him the "Palatine Venus." <term>Adam Contzen, Politics, book 8, chapter 14, section 9</term>. See also how <term>Jacobus Balde</term> <note>a famous Jesuit Neo-Latin poet</note> at Schleißheim near Munich viewed the white marble statue of Marcus Tullius Cicero and what he spoke there. *Lyric Poetry, book 2, Ode 25, verse 93.*

The most excellent marble quarry lies near the sea, by the river called the Magra <note>the Magra river flows through the Carrara region, famous for its marble</note>, from where it is afterwards transported in ships to many other lands. *Joseph Fürtenbach in the Mirror of Art, folio 106.* On the art of cutting and polishing marble, see *Pancirollus in "The Lost Things," pages 67, 68.* The Lord of the territory adjudicates the veins of marble to himself. *Nicolaus Myler on the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 69.*

Regarding letters inscribed in marble, see *Decianus, Counsel 135, number 2* and *Klock, volume 3, counsel 6, number 103.* Is it permitted to enter a field and search for marble against the owner's will? Under the legal designation of "stones" <note>original: "Appellatione saxorum"</note>, marble is included. *Johannes de Plate, title on miners and metals, book 10 of the Code.* If someone makes a statue from another person's marble, does he become the owner of that statue? This is discussed at length by *Mr. Rebhan, Selected Justinian Questions, Decade 6, question 6.* For a father to profit from the fruits of the stone-quarries, it is required that the metals and stones—if they are marble—renew themselves <note>original: "renascantur" / regrow</note>, as is customary in Gaul and Asia. *Beor, decision 51, number 2* and *Modestinus Pistoris, part 3, question 129, number 99.*

"Now the chin, now the neck, now the hands, now the whiteness of the feet placed within a slender bond of gold, had surpassed the Parian marble." <note>Parian marble from the island of Paros was the gold standard for whiteness in antiquity.</note> *Horace:* "The beauty of Glycera burns me, purer than shining Parian marble." Regarding the sale of marble and other things attached to buildings, see *Zahn on Falsehoods, book 3, chapter 8, number 36.*

### 112. Mansfeld, Mansfelda.

At Angers, on the rampart, these words stand upon a piece of artillery:

> The Wotsack <note>A "Wotsack" or "Wadsack" was a large decorative drinking vessel, often sent as a ceremonial gift</note> am I named,
> Count Hoyer of Mansfeld and Count
> William of Dillenburg sent me as a
> welcome-gift.

*Zeiller, Itinerary of France, page 307.* In the year 1512, Emperor Maximilian granted the grace to Count Hoyer of Mansfeld that all Counts of Mansfeld might and should henceforth style themselves as "Well-born" <note>original: "wohlgebohrne"</note> and seal with red wax, whereas until that time they had only used

<column-break/>

green wax. *Spangenberger in the Mansfeld Chronicle, chapter 348, page 404.* In Saxony, the most famous of all is the County of Mansfeld, named after the town of Mansfeld, which includes four other counties within itself. *Cluverius.* All the current Counts of Mansfeld are descended from those of Querfurt. The first Count styled himself: Burckhard by the Grace of God, Noble Lord of Querfurt, Count of Mansfeld and Hardeck, Burgrave of Magdeburg. More in *Zeiller, continuation on Germany, page 472.* Regarding the alienation and exchange of goods in the County of Mansfeld, see *Heigius, part 1, question 19, number 28 and following.* *Zeiller, continuation on Germany, page 84.* Some claim that the German Lords and Counts of Mansfeld had an ancestor in their lineage who sat at King Arthur's Round Table in England. *Zeiller, Itinerary of Great Britain, page 46, and Itinerary of Germany, folio 142.* For more on this, see *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 4, chapter 4, number 92; in the Particular State of Ferdinand II, pages 140, 144; and Sprenger in the Delineation of the States of the Empire, page 396.*

The Counts of Mansfeld may seal with white wax. *Limnaeus, Public Law, book 1, chapter 11, number 32.* The mines of the County of Mansfeld were formerly recognized as belonging to private persons, until they were taken by the Counts in the year 1535 and brought into the treasury. In 1484, the Counts of Mansfeld received Heldrungen from the Counts of Hohnstein. In 1487, the said Counts became vassals of the Elector of Saxony by reason of the mines. *Sprenger in Public Jurisprudence, page 439 and following.*

### 113. Manifesto. <note>original: "Manifestum"</note>

A manifesto is commonly defined as a public or formal notification or proclamation, which is communal, originating from certain knowledge and specific authors. *Farinaccius, Criminal Questions, 21, number 6.* On what it means to manifest a belief, see *Gothofredus, Ancient Feudal Disputations, page 180, letter f.*

### 114. Munition-Money. <note>original: "Munition-Geld"</note>

Munition-money: that which should be given quarterly to the watching Endymions <note>a poetic term for sentries or night-watchmen, referencing the mythical sleeper Endymion</note> for powder and lead <note>original: "Kraut und Loth"</note>, even from the tax-exempt houses. For more, see *Mundius on Counts Palatine, chapter 3, number 357.*

### 115. Mead. <note>original: "Meth. Mulsum."</note>

Regarding mead-brewing in Russia, see *Olearius in the Persian Travelogue, folio 205.* They brew magnificent mead from raspberries, blackberries, cherries, and others. *Ibid.* Regarding the boiling of mead, its inspection and tax; also the abolition of "Bock-mead" <note>a strong variety of mead</note>. *Bavarian Provincial Ordinances, book 4, folio 9.* In the year 1614, the city of Greifswald gave the Duke of Pomerania annually no more than one tun of mead and the same amount of wine, and was otherwise exempt from all ordinary taxes. *Zeiller, Itinerary of Germany, page 376.*

Drinking honeyed wine <note>original: "Mulsum sumere"</note>. Among the ancients, cups were not handed to guests but were placed upon the tables. *François Pithou in his Collections on Petronius, page 156.*

### 116. Knife. <term>Culter</term> <note>Latin for knife, specifically associated with sacrificial or kitchen tools</note>

Ovid writes: *And he stains the knives, struck with blood.* And shortly after: *That sacrificial victim warms the knives plunged into it.* *Metamorphoses, book 15.* *Saubertus in "On Sacrifices," page 47.*

On July 28, 1638, in Strasbourg, it was decreed that it had not been proper until now for the masters of the cooper’s trade <note>original: "Küblerhandwercks," makers of tubs and buckets</note> and their servants to carry vintner-knives and hoop-knives <note>original: "Kieffer und Bandmesser"</note>. Rather, they had done too much and acted wrongly in this; therefore, they should henceforth abstain and refrain from such things. In this matter, they should not infringe upon the vintner-coopers <note>original: "Kieffern," specifically the makers of wine barrels</note> or otherwise interfere with their trade regarding the drawing of wine, under penalty of 5 pound-pennies for every violation. Later, upon the protest of those condemned, this decree was mitigated and clarified on July 8, 1648, stating that the masters of the cooper's trade and their servants should once again be permitted and allowed to carry vintner-knives. *Lord Tabor, "On the Carrying of Weapons," chapter 2, section 7.* Under the name of "offensive weapons," some include swords intended for sharpening pens or those prepared for the table—penknives and bread knives <note>original: "Feder- und Brod-Messer"</note>—following the singular gloss in the *Authentica de armis* and *Felinius on the chapter "Ita quorundam" regarding the Jews.* The annotator to *Ludovicus Romanus* (Note 267) writes foolishly; for in this matter, when we speak of the naturally lawful use of arms—such as carrying them (for it is another thing if we are treating their abuse; see *Wehner* under the word *Messer* <note>Knife</note>)—common and smaller knives with which we cut bread, or penknives <note>original: "Federmeſſerlein"</note>, do not fall under the definition of "arms." However, they are included in the prohibition and punishment of unlawful use: for then even a knife is reckoned among illegal weapons. *Reusner, book 2, decision 21*, says there: *The knife is a deadly murder-weapon, and whoever causes harm with it, it goes to his neck.* <note>meaning they face the death penalty</note> Add *Coler, Wehner, and Carpzov, part 2, criminal question 3, numbers 8 and 10.* The bread knife is a thievish, murderous weapon. *Rudinger, century 3, observation 58.* *Bulleus, legal response 5, number 48.* Therefore, in the public peace-decrees <note>original: "Friedbot"</note>, some of the nobility even include pocket knives. If penknives or common knives for cutting bread do not properly fall under the 

<column-break/>

name of "arms," it follows that the carrying of them does not fall under either legal or statutory prohibition. *Novel 85 on Arms, chapter 4*, says: *We permit smaller knives, which no one uses in battles.* This is supported by the text in *2 Feud. 21* regarding a vassal soldier who has laid down his war-arms. However, we understand this to apply only to the knives just defined. For regarding the knives that the Italians call "olive leaf" <note>original: "fronde d' Oliva"</note>, it was decided in the Archbishop's Court of Naples that an Edict imposing penalties on those carrying daggers and stilettos also applies to someone carrying such a knife of two palms in length. *J. Alois Riccius, decision 122 of said Court.* To this may be referred the Papal Bulls which prohibit the carrying of certain knives, found in *Arnisæus, book 2, "On the Law of Majesty," chapter 5, section 5, page 337.* Those who supply knives to defendants in prison so they may lay violent hands upon themselves <note>commit suicide</note> to avoid ignominy are, by common opinion, held liable under the *Cornelian Law on Assassins*. *Adam Keller, "On Juridico-Political Office," book 2, chapter 12, page 419.* The Greenlanders have knives made from the molars of a sea-fish, which they call *Ekulugsua* <note>likely the Greenland shark, "Eqalussuaq" in Greenlandic</note>, but which *Piso* in his *Natural History of Brazil* and *Jonston* call *Piratia Pua* in the Brazilian language. *Olearius in his "Travel Description of Persia," folio 174.* In Strasbourg, in the Baker's Guild Book, page 47, there exists an article regarding knives and long weapons. Among the ancient Germans, if something was so hard that it could not be properly torn apart or mastered with the teeth, they had a common knife for that purpose, which hung in a certain place nearby in its sheath. Similarly, in some places in France, almost an entire table of people often makes use of a single knife, one borrowing it from the other. *Zeiller in the "Travel Description of Germany," folio 25.* We Germans say: "A traveler should leave his hat-string at home, but not his knife," for he cannot do without it. In the Cabinet of Curiosities at Munich, there are two plain knives on a table in a single sheath, through which the lightning <note>original: "Wetter," here meaning a thunderbolt</note> struck a hole, leaving the sides of the sheath uninjured. *Zeiller, same work, page 88.* The thunderbolt <note>original: "Donner-Keil"</note> is of three kinds: some set things on fire, some shatter things, and some are of such subtle nature that they penetrate other bodies and injure the internal parts. Many times, a child in the mother's womb, a sword in its sheath, wine in a barrel, or money in a purse has been shattered and destroyed by thunder/lightning, while the mother remained alive, the sheath whole, the barrel intact, and the purse undamaged. See *Lord Sebizius "On Acidic Springs," pages 84, 85.* Such wondrous stones are thrown by the storm. *Zeiller, century 4, question 52, page 277.* *Huitha, huuiotha, aura*—from these comes our word *Wetter* <note>Weather/Storm</note>. *Lord G. Richter in his Epistles, page 510.* In the East Indies, one gives an ox, a cow, or a sheep for a knife or a small piece of iron. *Levinus Hulsius.* In the year 1635, a young servant boy of 12 years, born in the village of Grünwalde, located 7 miles from Königsberg, [named...]

Letter M.

One named Andreas Grünhaide, on May 29, swallowed a knife of considerable length, which was later removed from his stomach through an incision in Königsberg on July 9, and he was restored to his health; Georgius Lothus <note>a prominent 17th-century physician and professor</note>, Physician to the Elector of Brandenburg and Professor there, has published the history, operation, and cure of this case. Concerning a knife in Venice, which is valued at 6,000 crowns. *Zeiller, Travels in France, page 63.* At Strasbourg, in the district of Ensisheim, *as is evident from the Public Roll*, this court has the liberty that no court of justice shall seek anyone therein, whether for homicide or for debt. If someone escapes into the court, he shall be and remain safe, and a bailiff and a mayor of the aforementioned court shall give him water and bread. An "armed hand" simply means a sword in the hand, or a harmful knife, or a bow, or a crossbow. *Petrus Pappus in Dutch Military Law, page 47.*

### 117. Middle Beer. <term>Cerevisia mediocris</term> <note>A beer of medium strength, often used in religious or legal contexts as a middle ground between water and strong wine</note>.

In the Roman Penitential, among other restrictions imposed upon a murderer, it is also prescribed that he abstain from drinking wine and use only "middle beer" (*Mittelbier*) temperately. *Chapter "interfecisti" 2, regarding Homicide. Lord Tabor, On the Law of Beer, first part, chapter 1, section 10, and in the Corollary on Dizythum (barley beer), page 105.*

### 118. Idleness. <term>Otium</term>.

The use and meaning of the word *maleferiati* <note>meaning those who celebrate holidays in an evil or idle way</note> and where it originated is discussed extensively by *Lord Rupert in Universal History, book 4, chapter 10.* A mind vainly vacant produces nothing good. *Barbosa, book 13, chapter 33, axiom 1; Zorer, part 1, question 12, number 894*, where he explains "vainly vacant" as "abounding in idleness." How to proceed against an idle person who does not increase his property but only consumes it. *The same, part 2, question 18, number 5006 and following; Hippolytus de Collibus, On the Increase of Cities, chapter 23.* He says that in Antwerp, censors are appointed to watch over idle people and compel them to some trade or expel them from the city. The Athenians and Lucanians handled the causes of idleness such that if anyone was convicted of lending anything to a luxurious <note>profligate or idle</note> man, he lost the loan, according to Stobaeus. The Emperor Antoninus Pius withdrew salaries from many whom he saw were idle and useless, saying: "Nothing is more foolish, indeed nothing more cruel, than if the Republic were gnawed at by those

<column-break/>

who contribute nothing to it by their labor." Solon wanted a man caught three times in idleness to be marked with infamy, according to *Julius Pollux, Onomasticon, book 8.* Draco, however, even punished them with death, as found in *Plutarch's Life of Solon. See Rittershufius, Novellae, page 698.* The extermination of the idle is illustrated by the noble example of the bees, cited by Hugo of Brandenburg against the idle, *number 16.* Idleness is most sweet when it is spent in literature.

### 119. Knights of Saint Mark.

The Venetian Duke <note>the Doge</note> was accustomed to create Knights of Saint Mark. For the Republic of Venice has Saint Mark as its patron. *See Limnäus, On Public Law, book 6, chapter 2, number 51.* Concerning the Treasury of the Venetians, which the Procurators of Saint Mark guard, see my funeral oration for Lord Cornelius Marci, publicly delivered in 1646.

### 120. Knights of Saint Maurice.

Amadeus VIII, Duke of Savoy, established the Order of Saint Maurice in the year 1434. After this had lasted for several years, it finally fell almost into disuse, until it was joined to the Order of Saint Lazarus by Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, in 1573, with the consent of Pope Gregory XIII. *Limnäus, On Public Law, book 6, chapter 2, number 64.*

### 121. Martinmas. <note>The feast of St. Martin, November 11</note>

The citizens of Ysen must pay 100 *hellers* <note>small copper coins</note> annually to His Imperial Majesty on St. Martin’s Day. Concerning St. Martin’s Monastery, St. Martin’s House of God, St. Martin’s Mountain, Castle, and Fortification. *Zeiller in Travels through Hungary.* There are also St. Martin’s Pears. Around Martinmas, the subject is at his most prosperous <note>meaning he has harvested his crops and is best able to pay taxes</note>. *Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 646.*

### 122. Millrosen. <note>A type of gold coin, likely the Milreis</note>

A *Millrosen* with the broad cross contains 22 carats and 9 grains of fine gold, which amounts to 31 *batzen* <note>a silver coin used in southern Germany and Switzerland</note>. *See Alemannus, On the Law of Money, consultation 29, principal question 1, part 30, page 539, number 3.*

### 123. Moon. <term>Luna</term>.

Witnesses testifying that they saw something by the light of the moon are not of entirely sound faith <note>meaning their testimony is legally unreliable</note>. *Justus Oldekop, in Criminal Observations, title 4, observation 28, number 3.*
Concerning the sacrifices and offerings to the moon among the pagans, which were repeated at the new moon, see *Saubertus, On Sacrifices, page 92.* The moon is the mistress of the waters and the mother of frogs according to Paracelsus. Concerning the mountains of the moon, see Libavius in *Singularia*. Dr. Herlicius has written a special treatise on the spots of the moon. It may be known that it was held as sacred by the ancients that he who thought the moon should be named with a feminine name and sex would be fated to always serve women; but he who believed it to be a male god would dominate his wife and suffer no feminine snares. *Philipp Carolus, at the end of his Philological Taste. It is debated whether the moon was Venus, or a female, etc. <note>original: "nummas Venus esset" - likely an OCR error for "num Luna Venus esset"</note>. Nicholas Fuller writes of this in his *Theological Miscellanies, book 1, chapters 13, pages 86 and 87*. They write the same regarding the Moon, and sometimes call it "Lunum" <note>the masculine form of the Latin 'Luna'</note>. However, there is a festive observation by certain authors that it was ordained by the ancients that whoever thought the Moon should be called a woman would see an "emperor" at home <note>meaning a wife who rules over him</note>; but he who believed it to be a Male God would dominate his wife and impose silence upon his "hen" who wished to crow. Furthermore, I think that hesitation arose from the fact that Semiramis <note>the legendary Queen of Babylon</note> disguised her sex as a wife, and as the son of Ninus, she pretended to be a boy, as found in Justin’s *History, book 2, chapter 2*. More on this in Rupertus, *at the cited location*. The sign of the Moon is expressed on the banners of the Turks, which the Ottonian Emperors brought over from the defeated Byzantines. Busbequius discusses this matter in his *Letters*, as does Lipsius in his *Questions*. The Moon is the *Counselor of Love*. Philipp Caroli treats this at length in his *Roman Library, page 12 of my edition*. Petronius says: "Delighted, she laughed so charmingly that she seemed to me to put forth a full face like the Moon from behind a cloud." On this passage, note in passing that the most celebrated beauties are compared to the Moon in Hesiod, Musaeus, Oppian, Smyrnaeus, and others. Regarding the eclipses of the lights <note>the sun and moon</note>, it is amazing how much the ancients raved, believing the Moon, stirred by a magic incantation, was suffused with a red glow as if blushing, or even seeing the deeds of sorceresses at night. For this reason, they thought the laboring Moon should be assisted by the clanging of brass <note>to drown out the witches' spells</note>; see Fuller in *Theological Miscellanies, book 1, chapter 13, page 86*; Phil. Caroli on Aulus Gellius, *book 2, chapter 28*; and most fully Mr. Fürer in his *Travelogue, pages 35, 36*. What is not common that nature made best? The Sun shines for everyone. The Moon, accompanied by innumerable stars, even leads wild beasts to their pasture. Petronius, *page 117*. Plautus says in *The Ass-Dealer*: "Daylight, water, Sun, Moon, night—these things I do not buy with silver."

The Moon rules the sea, money rules the world, and hope rules the pious. The Moon is the symbol for the number one hundred, because in the beginning there were one hundred Patricians. Draco, *On the Patricians, page 71*. ### 124. Walls. <term>Murus</term>.

To what extent those living outside the walls are called peasants. Carpzov, *decisions 2, number 21*. Inhabitants of the suburbs are citizens just as much as if they lived within the walls. *Ibid.*

To trust in walls and fortifications alone is unworthy of men. Cl. Rupertus, *discourse 1 on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 7*. Whether walls are also considered sacred in municipalities. Mr. Dr. Biccius, *in Golden Matters, section 2, thesis 14, letter G.*

### 125. Butcher. <term>Laniator</term>.

In Swabia they are called *Chehaffin*, referring to the inspection of grazing and the slaughterhouse. *Acts of Lindau, folio 858.* Among the Russians, should a shortage of executioners occur, the butchers must provide several from among their own ranks. Olearius in the *Travel Description of Persia, page 275.* Regarding ox markets, see Sprenger in *The Practice of Exchange, folio 18.* Regarding trade in ox hides, *ibid., folio 30.* Regarding the ordinance that cattle and slaughter animals must first be offered to the butchers of the cathedral chapter before being brought into the city. Klock, *volume 3, counsel 149, number 323.* In the *Nuremberg Reformation, title 21, book 5, etc.*, it is arranged that if a certain sum of money is granted by the Magnificent Magistrate (or his officials in his name) to the butchers—that is, the butchers' guild—to buy a number of oxen or cattle on credit, whether for the poor or the rich, then the current and future property (both movable and immovable) of every butcher who buys such cattle on credit is bound by a tacit mortgage. This mortgage has priority over all other creditors who do not have a specific or general express or tacit mortgage on the debtor's property. This remains in effect so that if there is a delay in payment at any time, the said officials have the power—even without a formal trial and outside the usual court procedures, as the words of the *Reformation title 21* state—to seize the pledged goods and property for the overdue debts and installments, to sell them, and to help themselves to the full amount of the debt and damages, just as if they had sued for all of this in court and won. Mr. Johann Hieronymus Wurffbain, *Differences between Civil Law and the Nuremberg Reformation, page 254 in the recent octavo edition.*

In the year 1558, the butchers in Königsberg carried a sausage—one should read Emperor Leo's *Novel 58* <note>a "Novel" is a new law added to a legal code</note> against sausages and the heavy penalties he placed on them. But he meant blood sausages, and not those made of ham, with which the butchers will excuse themselves. It was a strange prohibition—they carried it around, and it was 198 cubits long. ### 126. The Middleman (Mediarius).

Who is a middleman? Dr. Tabor, *On the Law of Society, page 14*. They are sharecropping farmers <note>original: "Partiarii coloni"</note> who give a portion of the harvest to the lord and reserve a portion for themselves.

### 127. Monosyllables.

Monosyllabic names were often assigned to slaves. Draco, *On Patricians, pages 232 and 2170*. On the total number of monosyllables, see Martin Zeiller in the *Dedication of the 1st Century of Letters*.

### 128. Michael.

Regarding the founder of the Order of Saint Michael, see Mr. Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 6, chapter 2, number 30*. On this order, see Zeiller, *4th Century, question 23, page 197*. That order was instituted on August 1, 1469, by King Louis XI of France. He recognized Saint Michael as the protector of France and therefore honored him with the highest devotion. The document containing the institution of the order and its statutes is presented at great length from Megiser by the aforementioned Limnaeus. Usually, only 36 nobles and princes are admitted to this order. Chasseneuz, *On the Glory of the World, part 9, consideration 19*. Otto, in *Public Law, page 690*.

### 129. Mahomet (Muhammad).

What was the seal of Muhammad, the Turkish Emperor, and what inscription made it famous? The seal of Muhammad Pasha was quite pleasant; both are shown by Höpingk in *On the Law of Seals, chapter 5, numbers 25 and 26*. Regarding the wickedness of Muhammad, see Rupertus, *Political Dissertations on Valerius Maximus, chapter 2*. Muhammad, out of excessive lust, consorted with the female donkey he rode. Zeiller, *4th Century, question 32, page 160*.

Muhammad ordered the flowers from his garden to be sold to raise money. Klock, *On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 5, numbers 16 and 17*. He was just or generous to no one, unless he was being liberal toward his mistresses. *Ibid, numbers 18 and 19*. The origin of the Mohammadans is found in *book 1, chapter 5, number 1*. Muhammad II was the conqueror of two empires, 12 kingdoms, and 200 cities. *Book 2, chapter 47, number 98*. Muhammad had 16 or 17 wives, and he attributed all his adulteries, fornications, and lusts to God. *Volume 2, chapter 141, numbers 59 and 60*.

The Miracles of Muhammad. Mr. Harsdörffer, in the *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories, volume 154, numbers 10 and 11*.

### 130. Mother (Mater).

In the procreation of a daughter, the mother is called the "root," while the child is the "flower and fruit." If she is the root, she is said to bear the entire weight of the union and marriage, which revolves around the procreation of offspring. For women are "split open" to give birth, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies in the *9th Ethics*, saying that the generation of mothers is more laborious, and that they know better who their children are than fathers do. Barbosa, *book 11, chapter 14, axiom 1*. Whether a Prince born of a commoner mother should be called to the assembly or have the right to vote. Limnaeus, *Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, number 64*. The mother of King Sigismund I of Poland was the daughter of an Emperor, the granddaughter of an Emperor, the sister of a King, the wife of a King, the mother of four Kings, and the grandmother of two Kings; she thus far surpassed that Lacedaemonian woman <note>referring to Gorgo of Sparta or a similar historical figure</note> who was merely a King's daughter, a King's wife, and a King's mother. Zeiller, *Travels in Germany, page 533*. Nature points to the mother, while Civil Law points to the father. Barbosa, *at the cited location, axiom 4*.

A sailor from Sardinia had very realistically formed on his arm <note>a tattoo</note> the image of a Pope, who had a dragon beneath him and an angel with a crown above him. More on birthmarks <note>original: "Muttermahl"</note> can be found in Mr. Harsdörffer’s *German Secretary, part 10, title 12*.

If a mother confesses that her son is illegitimate <note>original: "spurium"</note>, she is presumed to be lying, out of favor for the marriage <note>a legal protection to keep the child legitimate</note>. Following Vázquez, Cynus, Panormitanus, Alexander, Decius, and others; see Gail, *Observation 97, number 8*. Zahn, *On Lies, book 3, chapter 7, number 6, at the end*. Regarding a mother confessing she is an adulteress: the same Zahn, *book 1, chapter 28, number 4*, says: A mother confessing her son is the product of adultery, though she certainly prejudices herself regarding the stain on her honor and modesty, in no way harms the son, because she is presumed to lie in this matter out of favor for him and in honor of the marriage...

## 138. Mutzettel, Investiture Certificate. *Attestatum investituræ petitiæ.*

*Through which brief entry the request for investiture is proven. See Crusius, 'Feudal Lessons', page 67 in my copy, and the supplement to Wehner, page 53 under this word. Schneidewin, 'Treatise on Fiefs', part 5, chapter 2, number 128.*

When someone is specifically enfeoffed <note>granted legal right to land</note> with certain specific feudal estates by an investiture certificate <note>original: "Mutzettel"</note>, this does not extend to other feudal estates that are neither named nor included therein. Therefore, when Rutger von Rakenburg was enfeoffed with Kostenheim in 1611, and on behalf of his fellow-enfeoffed cousins with Kospa, Dürrenstein, and Schein, the claimant was not entitled to include the fief of Ruckersbangk—which is not a pertinent part belonging to any of the aforementioned estates. He could not excuse himself by claiming it was an error by the feudal secretary that the Ruckersbangk fief and other houses of the von Rakenburgs were omitted in the certificates. Instead, since von Rakenburg accepted those certificates and kept them until now without requesting the most gracious enfeoffment as his cousins did, he cannot enjoy the right of redemption based on the shared enfeoffment he claimed.

### 142. Mainz (*Moguntia*).

The harsh words of Sprenger: Mainz was built by a leader of the Magi, who in the year 1362 before the birth of Christ was banished from Trier with his followers and settled in Mainz; hence they say that the name Mainz <note>original: "Moguntia"</note> comes from ancient times. N. Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 250, and in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 374. Mainz was anciently a free and Imperial City; in the year 1462, it was captured by force during an incursion by its own Archbishop. Limnäus, volume 2, additions to book 1, chapter 9, page 153. 

Dr. Leonhard Wurffbain, in a table on November 6th of that same year, demonstrated extensively which Archbishops and Electors were in Mainz from the year 1000 to 1650. Regarding the threat of Gerhard von Eppenstein, Elector of Mainz: Wurffbain in *Historical Reports*, part 5, page 113 at the end, and page 114. Having the Electors of Mainz and Trier together: Wurffbain part 4, page 82. What Mainz brought together in terms of land and people: the same author, part 5, page 106. Concerning the seven Archdioceses: part 4, page 47. On the Elector of Mainz: Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 4, throughout. Zeiller wrote a *Topography of the Archbishopric of Mainz* in 1646, and an appendix to that same Archbishopric in 1654.

### 143. Medicine (*Medicina*).

Boschius wrote a disputation on the "Harmony of Physicians and Physicists." Regarding a doctor who lies about being able to cure himself: Zahn in the treatise *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 75, throughout. Physicians sometimes lie to themselves. The same author, in the same place, chapter 17, number 3. They lie to others for the sake of a little profit,

<column-break/>

number 4. We lie to ourselves regarding the hand of the physician, number 5. The judgments of physicians are suspect in Law, number 6.

Idle and malicious men vomit their venom even against skilled physicians: they call medicine a poisonous plague, a kitchen of demons, a drainer of purses, an art resting on no solid foundations, the most inconstant of all disciplines, and mere guesswork. For these reasons, they do not hesitate to shamelessly babble that it was once proscribed by the Romans and utterly eliminated from their Republic. They insult physicians as <term>skatophagas</term> <note>original Greek: "σκατοφάγας" – dung-eaters</note>, and with other mockers and scoffers call them <term>skopotas</term> <note>original Greek: "σχοπότας" – watchers/drinkers of urine</note>. With the foul-mouthed crowd of Paracelsus, they label them as bath-attendants, heaters, cleaners of filth, purse-suckers, harpies, and vultures who insult the corpses of men. They foully accuse them of being ring-wearing, gold-chained, and purple-clad braggarts, apes of pagan philosophy, confessors of lies, and walking elemental, material, and trivial things. Those who are followers of Spagyric <note>alchemical</note> and Hermetic medicine, they ignominiously call "creatures of darkness," "secret-keepers," "charcoal-burners," "ash-stainers," "gold-melters," "impostors," and "robbers." Nor do they think they do an injustice to the order of physicians, because even in ancient centuries, physicians always had a bad reputation. The Emperor Hadrian, when he was close to death, is said to have cried out that "a crowd of doctors killed the Emperor," and he wanted this dirge and lamentation inscribed on his tomb. Pliny did not hesitate to make it known that "physicians learn through the dangers of the sick, and conduct experiments through deaths," and that "only a physician has the highest impunity for killing." Philemon added his own opinion to this judgment, being accustomed to say that "only a physician and a lawyer are permitted to kill without punishment." The same Pliny recorded in literary monuments that "no one is given greater trust than one professing to be a physician, even though in no other lie is the danger greater." He also adds this: that "the plague of morals flows from nowhere more greatly than from medicine." "Only physicians command Emperors." Seneca writes that they are so disposed that "it goes badly for a sick man if he has made his physician his heir." It is commonly spread about that "to live medically is to live most miserably" <note>original: "Medicè vivere, esse pessimè vivere"</note>. They say that physicians prescribe in their rigid diets things that can be observed by no one; that they would not buy for a farthing the very things they prescribe to others; and that if their commands were followed, men would eventually perish from hunger and thirst. For they say there is nothing in the gardens, nor in the fields and lands, nor in the mountains, hills, forests, and waters, that is safe from their censorial rod—for in all kinds of foodstuffs, they have something to criticize. The mere counting of these slanders is, among the learned and wise, a refutation in itself. As that scholar joked about a physician: "Sirach nonetheless calls doctors only patchers" <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus, though here used satirically to suggest doctors merely "patch up" people poorly.</note>.

"Yes," said the Physician, "if no rag were ever torn, the old cobbler would have nothing to patch." <note>This German proverb suggests that doctors, like cobblers, rely on the "wear and tear" of the human body for their livelihood.</note> Should there be specialists for each individual disease? See *Johannes Talentonus, Varied Readings, book 2, chapter 6.* Should a Physician himself be healthy? See *the same author, book 3, chapter 6.* In Muscovy <note>The Grand Duchy of Moscow, or early modern Russia.</note>, only the Prince has Physicians, according to the *French Mercury, folio 35.* Among the French, there is a proverb: *It is a bad thing to be "Red" when dying* <note>original: "quil faisoit man vais estre Rous pour morir" – a reference to the historical prejudice against red-haired people or perhaps the "flushed" look of the dying; here it refers to the chaos caused by too many doctors.</note>; this is because of the disputes and the great number of Physicians who attend to sick Princes. And I know not whether men who live without a Physician, content with surgeons and certain experiments (which almost no nation has lacked), live more unhappily or die sooner. See *Celsus, book 1, chapter 1* and *Stanihurst on Irish Affairs, folio 43.* Certainly, frugality and sobriety are a man’s best medicine, according to the aphorism of Pyrrhiniculus the Gascon; see *Lycosthenes' Aphorisms, folio 4.* Hence, *Owen, book 3, epigram 123*:

->*If mortals loved to live according to nature,*<-
->*There would be no need for medical help.*<-
->*If men were wise, they would lack for brawls*<-
->*And greedy lawsuits, and the chatter of the complaining court.*<-
->*Thus Bartolus would go behind the bookshelves in disarray,*<-
->*And the mouse would gnaw on an unread Hippocrates.*<-
<note>Bartolus of Saxoferrato was a famous medieval jurist representing Law; Hippocrates represents Medicine. The poem suggests that a simple, natural life would make both lawyers and doctors obsolete.</note>

Our own *Besoldus* says more on this in *Politics, book 2, chapter 4, section 8, number 82, page 697 and following.* Military law provides relief for Physicians, as seen in the section *Physicians of Soldiers* <note>original Latin: "l. inter eos §. Militum Medici ff. ex quib. caus. maj." – a citation from the Roman Digest.</note>. Furthermore, the *Emperor Antoninus* decreed <note>original: "l. 1. C. de Profess. & Med." – Code of Justinian</note> that Physicians of the Legions, as long as they are absent on behalf of the Republic, are not compelled to take up civil duties, so that they do not even have to receive a guest. Menecrates the Physician desired nothing as praise for his medicine. See *Dannhauer in the Evangelical Memorial, page 656.*
A Physician who takes on a hopeless case is excused <note>from liability</note>, whereas it is otherwise for an Advocate. See *Boerius, Decision 323, number 25.* On when a single Physician is to be believed: *the same decision, number 23.* Praises of medicine, and how many Physicians each city ought to have: *the same decision 323, numbers 22 and 24.*

### 144. Metaphysics.
Dr. Jacob Hacker said that in the very entrance of his lectures, he would candidly exhort his listeners that whoever was not a *Metaphysician* should not enter his lecture hall. *Adam Keller, on the Office of Juridical Politics, page 82 and page 78*, writes that among <term>Jurisconsults</term> <note>Legal experts or jurists.</note> he knew of no one who was a *Metaphysician* except for *Dr. Johannes Streidacher*. He considers that true Logic is more useful to jurists than the many theoretical and sterile theorems of the *Metaphysicians* are to practice. On who the *Metaphysicians* are, see *Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, book 8, chapter 9 of Universal Law, number 1.*

### 145. Mulise. Abandoned property.
That is, belonging to no one, vacant or abandoned. *Adam Keller, on the Office of Juridical Politics, book 2, chapter 13, page 430; Wehner under the letter M, same entry.*

<column-break/>

### 146. Mir. To me.
The word "To me" <note>original: "Mihi"</note> does not impede a pupillary substitution <note>A legal arrangement where a father appoints an heir for his child in case the child dies before reaching puberty.</note> if other conditions are met. *Mantica on Conjectures of Last Wills, book 5, title 7, number 5.*

### 147. Fair-goods (*Meßgüter*).
*Limnaeus, book 2, Additions to book 2, chapter 9, number 132.* The "Fair-goods" <note>Goods intended for sale at the Great Fairs, such as those in Frankfurt or Leipzig.</note> are distinguished from "Step-goods" (*Staffelgütern*). Also, with Fair-goods for which one is authorized, one may sail past without unloading. Ibid.

### 148. Territorial Retraction (*Marcklosung*).
The right of territorial retraction <note>The legal right of a local authority or neighbor to reclaim land or goods before they are sold to an outsider.</note>. *Ayhin on the Law of Retraction, thesis 21 to 44.*

### 149. Mirpa.
->To Apollo Grannus<-
->A Statue with<-
->The Base "Mirpa."<-

Where the word "Mirpa" comes from, no one can easily say. Velser himself, who first made this inscription public, says it is unknown unless it is a proper name, in *Augsburg Affairs, page 276.* Scaliger the younger, in *epistle 145*, derives it from a primitive Greek word *mirphios* <note>original: "μίρφιος"</note>. We say that the word consists of sigla <note>Abbreviations or coded letters.</note>. Unless these are properly explained, nothing is achieved. We are dealing here with a very obscure and complex matter; even if a suitable meaning is assigned to these single-lettered expressions <note>original: "μονογράμματοις"</note>, no one can be certain that it is the exact same meaning intended by the person who set the stone. However, lest I seem to have said nothing and left the matter untouched, I interpret "MIRPA" to mean: *Hasten quickly to the matter, depart* <note>original: "Maturè In Rem Propera, Abi."</note>. This "averting speech" <note>original: "ῥήσις ἀποσεφικὴ"</note> is found elsewhere in almost the same words. Although, if we wish to speak the truth, those sigla are nothing other than a "play on marble" by the stonemason who, as that class of men is wont to do, was too generous with his own ideas here. He thought that a formula usually reserved for funeral inscriptions could also have a place in this dedication made to Apollo Grannus. *Mr. Johann Michael Dilherr, volume 1, Academic Disputations, pages 70 and 71.*

### 150. Monstrance (*Hierotheca*).
Regarding the law of the Monstrance <note>The vessel used in the Catholic Church to display the consecrated Eucharistic host.</note>, in which the Pope believes the Lord's Eucharist is contained; if someone steals a Monstrance while the Holy Sacrament of the Altar is within it, see *Article 172 of the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* <note>The penal code of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1532.</note>.

### 151. With all Diligence (*Summa cum diligentia*).
These words require the most exact diligence from the person promising it, just as the words "any fault" include even the slightest negligence. *Christoph Philipp Richter, part 3, Counsel 8, number 102.*
