# N.

## 1. After. <note>original: "Nach. Post."</note>

The word *After* <note>original: "Post"</note> is used in various ways. Sometimes it is uttered to mean "immediately" and denotes a time following right away; for example, when we say, "one after another they came to him," and so on. Many ancient writers used this meaning, and legal experts <note>original: "JCC" for Jurisconsulti</note> have sometimes taken this word to mean an immediate time with no interval between. See *Tessaurus, Piedmontese Decisions, 30, number 1,* among others.

For this reason, Albertus Pergamensis writes in his *Treatise on Prepositions, number 85,* that this word does not always denote a gap in time. For just as the word *Before* <note>original: "ante"</note> signifies a time that precedes, so too *After* will denote its opposite: the time that follows.

At other times, however, this word is taken to mean an interval of time, and indeed this is its more common use. *Corfeti* notes in his *Singularities, letter P, under the word "postea"* <note>afterwards</note> that this is the word’s proper and natural sense. Since this word has been used in various ways by writers, some have argued that it denotes an uncertain time, making the term ambiguous and used indiscriminately. From this arises a question among legal interpreters regarding a witness testifying that "Titius possessed the property after Caius"—whether this testimony is conclusive and constitutes proof. See *Tessaurus, decision 30,* as cited above.

The word *After* refers to the outermost limit and the end. <note>The author cites various sections of the Digest, the primary collection of Roman law: Book 31 (De legatis 2), Book 40 (De manumissione testamento), and Book 35 (De conditionibus et demonstrationibus).</note> *Bartolus on Law 2; and Viglius there, number 110; Hering on Sureties, chapter 22, number 75, etc.*

### ADDITION.

On what the word *After* imports, see *Viglius Zuichemus on Wills, page 381, number 110.* On how the little word *Afterwards* <note>original: "Postea"</note> is understood, see *Rittershusius on Feudal Partitions, page 169.* The famous Rupertus, in his *On the Origins of Law, chapter 4, section 17,* confirms the usage of the Roman jurist Pomponius that *After* means *Then* <note>original: "Post, deinde"</note>, using the example of the Prologue written for Trogus Pompeius <note>An ancient Roman historian</note> at the 27th mark: *Then, afterwards* <note>original: "Dein, postea"</note> under the guard of Stryponius, etc., so that no one might disturb the ancient reading from its place or substitute a new one.

*After* and *Then*. This doubling of two little words that mean the same thing is frequent among good authors, and vice versa: *Then, afterwards.* See *Rittershusius on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 202.* Therefore, it sometimes signifies the same thing as the works of Besoldus, Volume I.

<column-break/>

Then, as is very often seen in the works of *Plautus* <note>A Roman playwright known for his comedies</note> and other ancient writers. Just as "therefore" <note>original: "igitur"</note> is used for "only then" <note>original: "tunc demum"</note>; as in the play *The Haunted House* <note>original: "Mostellaria"</note>: "It is a wretched business, *only then* to dig a well when thirst already grips the throat."

## 2. Successor-Heir. <note>original: "Nach-Erbsatzung, Affter-Erb. Substitutio." These German terms refer to the legal practice of naming a backup or secondary heir.</note>

To "substitute" in a general sense means to put someone in the place of another, as if sub-leasing or submitting, or to act as a surrogate. <note>Citing the Institutes of Justinian (on the division of things) and the Digest (on usufruct and the rights of the treasury).</note>

But in this legal case, the verb "to substitute" is used more strictly for the substitution of an heir only, or for that surrogacy which is customarily done in a last will and testament; specifically, when a testator appoints someone in his will as a backup to the primary heir.

And "substitution" <note>original: "substitutio"</note> seems to be so named because it was written "underneath" <note>original: "subtus"</note>—that is, not on the first wax tablet (where the name of the primary heir was placed), but on the lowest or second wax tablet which was positioned below the first. Thus, substitution is spoken of as a "sub-institution," or an appointment made underneath. From this, we call it the *Successor-Heir* <note>original: "Nach- oder Affter-Erbsatzung"</note>.

But it is unnecessary to add more on this matter for this reason: the subject is vast. By providing legal counsel on this topic alone, the great jurist Baldus earned more than 5,000 Ducats! Many significant treatises exist on this, such as those by Nicolaus Intrigliolus, Vincentius Fusarius, and others.

### ADDITION.

Can a "trust-based substitution" <note>original: "Fideicommissaria substitutio" — an arrangement where an heir is bound to pass the inheritance to another person.</note> be made in contracts? See *Klock, volume 2, Counsel 17, number 7.* Regarding the noble and famous "Honoldian Controversy," whether a tacit condition is implied in a substitution made among the children of brothers (specifically: "if they die without children"), a legal Opinion or Response was published by the legal scholar Christoph Herdesianus at Nuremberg in 1567, printed by Ulrich Neuber and Theodoric Gerlatzen, featuring endorsements from several universities and most learned men. Does a "Compendious Substitution" <note>A simplified form of naming a backup heir</note> made by a commoner after the inheritance has been entered and the ward has reached maturity expire, or is it valid by the law of trusts? See *Christoph Philipp Richter, part 4, counsel 9, number 2, folio 40,* where it is explained more extensively in the following numbers.

A "common substitution" <note>original: "Substitutio vulgaris"</note> is not to be extended from one case to another. *Part 4, counsel 15, number 39.* One case is for express substitution, another for tacit substitution. *Ibid, next number.*

Substitution is considered more powerful and effective than the "right of accretion" <note>original: "jus accrescendi" — the right of surviving heirs to receive the shares of those who cannot or will not inherit.</note>. See *Barbosa, book 17, chapter 62, axiom 1.* A substitution conceived for only one case cannot be extended to another. *Axiom 2.* An express "pupillary substitution" <note>naming an heir for one's child who might die before reaching adulthood</note> contains within it a tacit common substitution. *Axiom 3.* One cannot perform a substitution for oneself. *Axiom 4.* Reciprocal substitution...

how it is introduced. *Knipschild on Fideicommissum, chapter 2, number 46.*

Substitution can also occur in contracts. *chapter 6, number 30.* It is understood to be of the same nature as the original appointment. *chapter 6, number 115.* In direct substitution, an extension is made from case to case. *chapter 7, number 105.* But not from person to person, even if the same reasoning applies. *chapter 7, number 107.* When several people are substituted under a collective name, if only one survives, he alone is admitted. *chapter 9, number 16.* Those originally instituted as heirs are considered more favored than those substituted. *chapter 16, number 159.*

On the subject of Substitutions, the following have written: *Antonius Fumejus of Paris, Baldus de Ubaldis of Perugia, Bartolus of Saxoferrato, Johann Dilectus Duran of Gualdo, Lancellottus Politus, Paulus Leonius, and Ulrich Zasius.* Of all these, *Vincentius Fusarius* wrote best on Substitution.

Regarding this matter of Substitutions, *Johannes Kreiffelmann of Nuremberg* disputed for his degree at Altdorf in the year 1640. The subject of Substitutions is vast and profitable; *Baldus* often boasted that he earned over 15,000 florins from it. *Raphael Cumanus on the title of the Digest regarding common and pupillary substitution; Schneidewin on the title regarding common substitution, number 1.* A mother or grandmother cannot create a <term>pupillary substitution</term> <note>A legal provision where a parent names a backup heir for a child in case the child dies before reaching the age of puberty.</note>, yet such a substitution can sometimes be valid as a <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>A trust-like arrangement where a person is entrusted to hand over property to another.</note>. *Lord Christoph Philipp Richter, part 2, counsel 15, numbers 37 and 30.*

But are those persons excluded by a tacit pupillary substitution? See *part 4, chapter 17, folio 105.* <term>Cardinal Francesco Mantica</term> treats Substitution at great length in *On Conjectures of Last Wills*, where he accumulates various questions in the index. *Lord Doctor Ludwell*, of blessed memory, treats Substitutions methodically, accurately, and most extensively in his treatise on last wills, Part 2, chapter 2, where he also provides several rules. Should a fideicommissary substitution made for grandsons be extended to the sons and daughters of the testator? *Carpzov, decision 22, number 1.* The reasons for the affirmative view are found in *numbers 2, 3, 4, and 6*; but the negative view is truer, *number 7*. The reasons for the decision are in *numbers 8, 10, 12, and 13*; the arguments for the affirmative are refuted in *numbers 14, 15, 17, and 19.* See the *Opinion of the Leipzig Judges, number 20.*

Fideicommissary substitution is not included in a statute that mentions substitution generally. *Vivius, opinion 846, number 7.* Regarding <term>common substitution</term> <note>original: "vulgari Substitutione." This is the simplest form of substitution: "If A is not my heir, let B be my heir."</note>, see the *Nuremberg Statutes, title 30, law 1, section 1.* In these words, three cases of common substitution are specifically expressed. *Obrecht, Dispute 21, thesis 191.* And *Sfortia Oddo* says in his *Treatise on Substitution, part 2, question 4, folio 42*: common substitution with respect to the appointee is always made with negative words (namely, "if he will not be the heir") or at least privative words (namely, "if he should die before entering the inheritance"). Regarding pupillary substitution, see the *Nuremberg Statutes, book 30, law 2; Berlich, decision 111; Thomas Maul in his treatise on last wills, title 21, on pupillary substitution, folio 665; Spino à Carceres in the Mirror of Testaments, glossary 23, number 11.* See also *Intrigliolus on Substitutions, opinion 1, question 66.*

<column-break/>

Although a woman cannot make a pupillary substitution for her son—since she does not have legal power over him—nevertheless, if a pupillary substitution is made by a mother, it is resolved into a trust <note>original: "fideicommissum"</note> until the age of puberty. *Gratianus, chapter 583, numbers 17 and 18; Valascus, consultation 54, number 5, volume 1.*

Even though the *Gloss and the common opinion of the Doctors* <note>The "Doctors" refers to the established legal scholars of the time.</note> hold that a mother can encumber the "legitimate portion" owed to a son so that the father does not have the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another.</note> of it, because the text does not expressly provide for this, the contrary has been pronounced in the Imperial Chamber. *Scipio, decision 35, book 2.*

Can a daughter-in-law be excluded from the succession of a daughter in the father-in-law's will, and must the causes for exclusion be proved by the heirs substituted for the daughter? *Coler, decision 251.*

Regarding <term>exemplary substitution</term> <note>A substitution made for a person who is mentally incapacitated, modeled after pupillary substitution.</note>, see the *manuscript will of the noble Lady von Rabenstein.* But what should be thought of exemplary, reciprocal, military, and fideicommissary substitution, and how these species can be reduced to the common and pupillary types—either by similarity or by resolution—so that they derive their essence from them, was taught after *Vultrejus (book 13 of Jurisprudence)* by *Lord Doctor Tabor* in his *Elementary Jurisprudence, part 2, thesis 34, throughout.*

In a substitution made "without children" <note>original: "sine liberis"</note>, if the substitute dies leaving a son, and the substitute also dies some time after entering the inheritance, the right to be substituted has already expired (even if the condition of the substitution did not persist). This is so certain that even if the son refuses to succeed his father, a substitute claiming his own right will not be heard because a male heir existed. *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Dispute 6, thesis 6, letter a.*

Regarding substitution under the condition "if he dies without children," the so-called *Response* printed in Strasbourg in 1646 deals with this at length, in the case of the testamentary succession and claimed trust left by the most illustrious Leo Burianus Berkha, etc.

### 3. Hot Pursuit. <note>original: "Nacheil. Persecutio."</note>

It is established that under Common Law, a magistrate outside his own province and territory is regularly considered a private citizen, and he is not obeyed with impunity. *Final law, Digest on jurisdiction.*

Hence, a summons cannot be made in another's territory, as daily experience testifies; rather, it is done through subsidiary and requisitory letters. Therefore, a person who follows a fleeing person and captures them without the permission of the Lord of that territory may be held liable for injury; the captured person must be released immediately before anything else. *Final law on the office of the city prefect; law 3, Digest on the office of the Proconsul.*

However, this same thing is not to be said if someone committing a crime immediately flees into another's territory; for then he can be apprehended and captured there. Because an act already begun in one territory is continued in another. And if it is done immediately and on the spot <note>original: "in continenti"</note>, the act is considered continuous. *Steinberg, volume 5, Basel Disputes, dispute on territory, thesis 8*; and see my own work *on Territory, folio 272.* Nevertheless, it is better if he is presented to the magistrate of that territory.

### ADDITION.

The question is asked: whether a delinquent, or a disturber of the public peace—such as vagabonds and those idle soldiers, <note>original: "Gart- und Herrnloſe Knecht und Landläuffer"</note> masterless servants and wanderers who roam everywhere in the villages and streets, or who stealthily "fine" the peasants of their geese and chickens, <note>A sarcastic way of saying they steal livestock under the guise of authority.</note> omitting no crime, and even rising at night to plunder, and who are ordered to be driven from the borders of the Empire as disturbers of the Public Peace—whether it is permitted to pursue such a person from one territory into another and apprehend him there, which we commonly call <term>Nacheil</term> <note>Hot pursuit; the immediate chase of a suspect across jurisdictional boundaries.</note>? 

This is affirmed by *Law 1 of the Codex regarding the condition of members of the municipal or governor's court, section "if the Judge" 2; Title on maintaining the peace and its violation, book 2 of the Feudal Laws; and the Julian Law on adultery.* This is expressly stated in the text of the *Imperial Recess of Augsburg from the year 1555* <note>An "Imperial Recess" was the official summary of the decisions made at a meeting of the estates of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> where it says, "one shall pursue after the same," and so forth. Likewise, the *Imperial Recess of Augsburg of 1559* states at the end that they may "pursue and strike them down without compensation" to the authorities and the Circles <note>The "Imperial Circles" were administrative groupings of states within the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. 

The question follows: Is it permitted to immediately apprehend a delinquent fleeing into another's territory? This is what is commonly called <term>Nacheil</term>. This is affirmed by the said *Imperial Recesses*. However, *Zasius (on the last law, number 10, regarding Jurisdiction)*, *Hackelmann (dispute 4, thesis 14)*, *Petreus (Criminal Conclusions 20)*, *Gail (book 1 on Public Peace, chapter 16, number 25)*, and *Mynsinger (Observation 28)* disagree.

For although a person found elsewhere should be sent back with a security guarantee at the request of the Judge of the place where the crime was committed, this does not prevent me from being able to catch a delinquent immediately and capture them in a foreign territory. It is only when he has escaped the pursuit once that one must then petition the Judge of that place to capture the fugitive and present him at the place of the crime. *Based on Law 18, section 11 on damage caused.*

Nor does it stand in the way that I cannot perform an act concerning Sovereignty or <term>Jurisdiction</term> <note>The legal power to act or make judgments.</note> in another's territory. Hence, a summons cannot be executed in a foreign territory, as *Ummius teaches (Dispute on Procedure 5, number 60)*.

For we are dealing with a case where an act was begun in one territory and only completed in a foreign one; because of the "right of neighborhood," no one can or should deny this. Such an act is also granted by the law of indivisibility. It is a different matter when an act of Jurisdiction begins in a foreign territory; that cannot happen except by one who holds Jurisdiction there. Regarding whether a Magistrate can lead delinquents out of a foreign territory or through a foreign territory to his own court, see *Lord Christoph Philipp Richter (part 6, Consultation 25), Besold (book 1 of Politics, chapter 12), Gail (on Public Peace), Mynsinger, and Wehner (in Practical Observations under this word).*

<column-break/>

### 4. Descendants. Cl. For himself and his descendants. <term>Deſcendentes</term>.

The words <term>Deſcendentes</term> and *haredes*—Descendants and Heirs—are by their own nature fit to include both males and females. *Alexander (on Law "but if this", section "children", regarding summoning to court); Cornelius (Consultation 190, book 3); Jason (on Law "if anyone", number 25, regarding the jurisdiction of all judges).* Such a general phrasing is to be understood generally, and thus, consequently, no exclusion—namely of women—should be established. Since women descend from a parent just as much as males do. *Cornelius (Consultation 263, book 1)* says that the word "Descendants" causes women to be included, even if "sons" was mentioned earlier, since the word "descendants" is general. And for who comes under the name of "Successors," see *Cravetta (Consultation 251)*; also whether successors in dignity are held liable, see *Knipschild (on Contracts, dispute 1, question 20).*

But the question is asked: If an <term>Emphyteuſis</term> <note>A long-term or perpetual lease of land where the tenant is treated almost as the owner, provided they pay rent and maintain the land.</note> was granted to Titius for himself, his sons, and his descendants, do women then also come under the name of descendants? At first glance, based on what was argued above, it seems so. For that grant for oneself and descendants ought to be understood for both sons and daughters, just as in last wills and testaments, where the masculine term includes the feminine, according to *Law "so written" (on Legacies 2) and Law "if anyone thus" (on Testamentary Guardians).*

However, the contrary negative opinion is more common: that this grant is only to be understood and interpreted as referring to males, not females. *Rolandus à Valle (Consultation 93, book 2), Natta (Consultation 576, book 4), Clarus (on the section regarding Emphyteusis, question 32), and Antonius Gabriel (book 5, title on the meaning of words, number 95).* For in contracts, the masculine does not include the feminine, except improperly and through extension. *Law "in the case of adoptees" (on Adoptions); Cephalus (Consultation 306, number 33, and more fully in Consultation 312, book 3).*

Nor does it matter that the word "Descendants," being common and general, can refer to both males and females. According to *Joseph Ludovicus (Decision 29, number 20)*, this holds true when the word stands alone, but not when it is joined to the word "sons." Because the participle "descendants" is then clarified to mean males, as the general word "Descendants" must be defined by the specific word "Sons." *Law 1 (where Socinus Senior comments); Cephalus (Consultation 11); Curtius Junior (Consultation 321, book 3).*

But for a greater explanation of this question, add *Ludovicus (said Decision 29), Lord Ulricus Wolff (Consultation 1, number 256), and Marta (on Clauses, part 2, clause 45).*

<summary>This page discusses the legality of 'hot pursuit' (Nacheil) across territorial borders to apprehend criminals and analyzes whether the term 'descendants' in legal contracts includes both men and women.</summary>

**Descendants** are said to include everyone down to infinity, whether they are male or female. <note>Cited from Mantica, *On Conjectures of Final Wills*, book 8, title 18, number 13.</note>

When descendants are understood to be called **successively** (one after the other). <note>Ibid, number 56.</note>

Descendants beyond the **fourth degree** <note>The degree of kinship, usually counting generations from a common ancestor.</note> do not seem to be burdened by a prohibition against selling or transferring property, even if it was expressly stated that the goods should not remain in the family forever. However, what if it was said that he wanted the property to reach descendants perpetually? <note>See book 8, title 2, number 21.</note>

Descendants are described down to infinity as both males and females, and those who are born from them. <note>Book 8, title 11, number 1.</note>

Those "descended from the body" of someone are also called **Grandchildren** and **Great-grandchildren**, whether born from the male or female lines. <note>Ibid, number 3.</note>

Under the term "descendants" are also included those who have not yet been conceived. <note>Ibid, number 4.</note>

Whether females descended from males are admitted when descendants are substituted through the male line or the "virile" (masculine) sex. <note>Ibid, number 9.</note>

The word **Descendants** embraces both males and females. <note>Cited from Knipschild, *On Testamentary Trusts (fideicommissum)*, chapter 1, number 89.</note> See which cases are excepted. By **Feudal Law**, females do not come under the name of "descendants." <note>Chapter 1, number 90. Feudal law often restricted inheritance to males to ensure military service could be provided to the lord.</note> This applies even if a trust is left to male descendants from the paternal line. <note>Chapter 1, number 91.</note> Or if by a local statute females are excluded when males exist. <note>Chapter 1, numbers 91 and 96.</note> Or if the testator wished to preserve the property within the <term>agnation</term> <note>The male line of descent.</note>.

Under the name of **Descendants** and **Family**, posterity comes down to infinity. <note>Chapter 9, number 111.</note> The German words *Kinder* (children), *Erben* (heirs), and *Nachkommen* (successors) include only males in feudal matters. <note>Cited from Klock, volume 3, consultation 182, number 409.</note> However, the doubled phrasing, "Heirs and Successors" <note>original: "Erben und Nachkommen"</note>, includes both males and females. The words "Children and Successors" are highly personal and are to be restricted to the closest descendants of the testator's male relatives. <note>Consultation 103, numbers 36 and 37.</note> Regarding when the term "Descendants and Heirs" refers to both male and female. <note>Klock, volume 2, consultation 2, numbers 93 and 94.</note>

An old Magistrate and Elder in Strasbourg, **Wolfgang Schötterlein**, saw with his own eyes 17 children, 108 grandchildren, 111 great-grandchildren, and 2 great-great-grandchildren. <note>Cited from Mr. Dannhauer in the *Evangelical Memorial*, folio 884.</note> The widow of **Bartholomäus Viatis**, born Schlüsselfelder, outlived 117 grandchildren and great-grandchildren, 70 of whom were still living at her funeral.

**Magdalena Forster**, who died in 1644 in her 90th year at Hersbruck as an exile, lived to see 56 grandchildren, 64 great-grandchildren, and 2 great-great-grandchildren. #### 6. According to his understanding, good judgment, or discretion.
*Secundum ejus prudentiam.* <note>original: "According to his prudence."</note>

This clause is usually added in settlements by parties when they say the **Arbitrators** should act "according to their prudence." This implies the **judgment of a good man** <note>original: "arbitrium boni viri" - a legal standard of reasonableness and fairness.</note>. <note>Fesinus following Imola and Panormitanus in the chapter "Do not lean" (ne innitaris) under the title "On Constitutions"; the same Panormitanus in chapter 1, column 4, "On the sequestration of possessions."</note> This does not mean one's own naked or arbitrary will. <note>Cited from laws on testamentary trusts.</note> Nor can it be understood as "bad prudence" that is not informed by the law. <note>Camillus Borellus, *On Settlements*, section 2, glossary 6, number 30.</note> This is because it must always be understood as prudence submitted to **reason**; otherwise, it would not be called "prudence" but "folly." For Prudence, as Macrobius taught, insofar as it is a political virtue, is the act of directing everything to the norm of reason, which considers whatever it does, and wills or does nothing except what is right. <note>See especially Menochius, *On Arbitrary Judgments*, book 1, questions 7 and 8.</note>

### ADDITION.

Let all things be done with **discretion**, which is the mother of all virtues. <note>Chapter 1, "On the office of the custodian."</note>

"Lean not on your own prudence" <note>original: "Prudentiæ tuæ ne innitaris" - a reference to Proverbs 3:5, used here in a legal context.</note>, but let each person set a limit to his own prudence. <note>Common Extravagants, 2, in the preface, "On heretics."</note> Regarding the clause "saving the good pleasure of the Lord," see Gothofredus Antonii, *Feudal Disputation* 11, thesis 6, letter b.

**Scaliger** says: "I love subtle minds, but I hate those that are too subtle." Or as they attribute to **Scipio Africanus**: "He who is great in small things is always small in great things." Prudence born from danger and misery is a wretched thing. <note>Pliny in the *Panegyric*; Mr. Rupert, *Political Dissertations* in the prologue to Valerius Maximus.</note>

### 7. The Nearest. <note>original: "Nächste. Proximior."</note>

Concerning the **nearest** person in the male line and bearing the surname of the testator, if such a person has been named as a substitute heir: how is this proximity to be calculated? Specifically, should we look at the time of the testator's death, or the time when the <term>fideicommissum</term> <note>A legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of another, similar to a modern trust.</note> comes into effect? This is discussed by Cravetta *in legal opinion 831.*

->ADDITION.<-

The person **nearest** in degree of kinship is preferred over one more remote. *Berlich, conclusion 24, number 47.* Whether those who are "near" <note>In the sense of neighbors or close relatives.</note> are preferred in a purchase. *Pacius, in his Analysis of the Code on contracting sales, number 10.* The **nearest** <note>original: "der Nächste"</note> differs from the **eldest** <note>original: "dem Ältesten"</note>. *Knipschild, on testamentary trusts, chapter 6, number 269.* Whether proximity should be measured in relation to the person who established the trust, or the last person to possess the property. *Chapter 6, number 269; chapter 9, number 76 and following.* If "the nearest" has been called to inherit, and there are several people in the same degree of kinship, is only one admitted? *Chapter 6, number 269; chapter 9, number 14.* If a testator has appointed or substituted "the nearest" <note>original: "den Nächsten"</note>, and there are several in the same degree, they are all admitted. *Chapter 9, numbers 14 and 15.*

What is defined as proximity in Law. *Conrad Rittershusius, in the New Laws, page 388, sections 4 and 5.* Greater proximity is demonstrated by the priority of the degree of kinship. *Discussed extensively by Barbosa, chapter 106.* Anyone is permitted to give aid to a neighbor <note>original: "proximo"</note> against the use of force. *Ibid, chapter 115, rule 4.*

### 8. Exit Tax. <note>original: "Nachsteuer. Jus detractus."</note>

The **Exit Tax** <note>original: "Nachsteuer"</note> is the deduction taken from the property of citizens when it is moved away. See *above* under the word **Deduction** <note>original: "Abzug"</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

The migration and deduction tax is taken even from **Maintenance payments** <note>original: "Alimentis"</note>. *Christoph Schwannmann in his Compendium on the Law of Emigration, page 19.* Johann Baptista von Baumsdorff, his wife, and their legitimate bodily heirs and their heirs' heirs, have obtained Imperial Grace <note>A special exemption or privilege granted by the Emperor.</note> to not be burdened with any land, city, village, or feudal taxes, nor any **exit tax**, redemption fees, levies, assessments, war taxes, or other aid and investment money, etc. *See the Privileges granted to the Baumsdorff family.* Citizenship and the exit tax sometimes do not bind Counts. *Mundius, on Counts Palatine, chapter 3, number 381.* Regarding exit taxes on property sold for religious reasons, or when something is bequeathed to a **Minister** <note>A clergyman or church official.</note>, even if the legacy remained within the same jurisdiction. *Limnaeus, in Public Law, book 4, chapter 8, page 159.* Not only in **Wittenberg**, **Rostock**, and **Tübingen**, but also in certain other cities, nothing at all is deducted from those emigrating; in these places they take no exit tax from those moving out or departing, such as at **Kitzingen** in Franconia, etc. *Wehner; Mundius on duties, chapter 2, number 471 and following.* To this belongs the **Right of Escheat** <note>original: "Albinagii Jus"</note> used among the French, which they call in their own language **the right of the foreigner** <note>original: "le droict d'aubaine"</note>, by which the goods of foreigners dying

<column-break/>

there fall to the Royal Treasury. The **effect of this law** is that the foreign heirs of such a resident do not succeed to the estate, but the Treasury intercepts them. The **Republic of Strasbourg** <note>original: "Respublica Argentoratensis"</note> exercised this same right in 1639 regarding the property of the deceased **Golschen**, a **pastry baker**, who was indeed a citizen of Strasbourg; however, since his heirs were not citizens of Strasbourg, but rather a nephew by his brother who was a foreigner, the Treasury excluded them by the **right of retaliation** <note>The legal principle of "tit for tat," where one state treats the citizens of another state the same way its own citizens are treated there.</note>, since the French also exercise this law against the people of Strasbourg, as Dr. Rebhan well noted *in his remarks on Speidelius's Notable Matters.* See *Limnaeus, in Public Law, book 8, chapter 9, number 68.* The "Law of the Albinati" <note>Referring to those "from the Elbe."</note> concerns the goods of those born across the **Elbe**—that is, outside the ancient borders of the Frankish Empire. When the Trans-Elbian Saxons or **Holsteiners** were conquered and subdued, **Charlemagne** <note>Charles the Great, King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor.</note> forced a huge number of them into Gaul and Flanders so they would not start further rebellions; he also stripped them of the right to make a will and the right of intestate succession, except among close paternal relatives. This is where the practice began of their goods revolving to the Treasury as "fallen property." *Nicolaus Burgundus, treatise 14 on the Customs of Flanders.* The safeguards by which this deduction can be avoided are provided by *Berlich, conclusion 52, number 88 and following to the end.*

Who must pay the **Exit Tax**. *Besold, in Politics, book 2, chapter 4, number 22, volume 1 and citations there; Jacob Curtius, volume 1, conjectures, book 1, chapter 51; Rauchbar, questions 15, 16, 17; Schaeffer, legal questions, part 2, question 10; Köppen, decision 11; Berlich, part 3, final question.* Whether an **Increase** <note>A surcharge or adjustment for inflation/currency value.</note> is owed when paying these taxes (known in German as *Nachsteuer, Abzug, Abfarth, Auslösung*, etc.)? Should one look at the time of the Edict or municipal law for this increase, or rather the time of payment? *Auer, on the Law of Coinage, chapter 15, thesis 120.*

The **Legatee** <note>The person receiving a specific gift in a will.</note> is held responsible for the deduction tax, not the heir. *Carpzov, Jurisprudence, part 3, Constitution 38, definition 20; Matthäus Stephanus, on Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 7, member 1, number 29, folio 250 and following; Matthias Berlich, conclusion 52; Johann Köppen, decision 11, throughout.* Whether the exit tax concerns only full **Citizens** or also **Residents** <note>original: "Incolas, Schutzverwandte"</note>? Whether the **right of retaliation** <note>lex talionis</note> has a place in the migration tax is debated. Some affirm it, but it is opposed by the Constitutions of the Empire. *Discussed at length by Christoph Schwannmann in his Compendium on the Law of Emigration, chapter 7, numbers 1, 2, and 3.*

### 9. Names / Surnames. <note>original: "Nahmen/Zunahmen. Nomen, Cognomen."</note>

In Rome, after the overthrow of the Republic and in the Provinces, a custom first prevailed where the Nobility used many names, yet each had a personal Name <note>original: "Nomen"</note> which they always placed last. For a later age always placed the personal Name after all the others. In this, they certainly turned away from the use and custom of the ancient Romans. For among the Romans, while the Republic stood, the personal name was that which came first, that is, the **first name** <note>original: "prænomen"</note>: by which indeed brothers themselves, when...

<meta>This page continues the legal and historical lexicon, moving from the definition of kinship to a detailed exploration of "Names" (Nomina), their historical evolution in Rome, their significance in Christian tradition, and legal axioms regarding identity.</meta>

# Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Enlarged

While they shared other common names, they were distinguished among themselves by first names: for example, *P. Cornelius Scipio* and *L. Cornelius Scipio* were brothers <note>original: "P. Cornelius Scipio, & L. Cornelius Scipio fratres." The 'P.' stands for Publius and 'L.' for Lucius.</note>. Likewise, *M. Tullius Cicero* and *Q. Tullius Cicero* were brothers. Later, however, they began to use and be distinguished by their last names as proper names rather than their first, such as the brothers *Salvius Otho* and *Salvius Titianus*, and similarly *Flavius Vespasianus* and *Flavius Sabinus*. See *Jacques Sirmond in his notes on C. Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius in the preface*, where he discusses the proper names of the Middle Ages, teaching where they were usually derived from and how they differ from the ancient Roman usage. On page 8, he records that in later centuries, the custom of assigning names was such that both a person's proper name and the added names—whether surnames or first names (all of which varied in almost every instance)—were for the most part borrowed from parents and relatives: fathers, paternal uncles, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and other loved ones. For example, the names of Bishop *Fulgentius* were: *Fabius Claudius Gordianus Fulgentius*, of which *Claudius* had been his father's proper name and *Gordianus* his grandfather's. And the names of the son of the orator *Symmachus* were *Q. Flavianus, Memmius, Symmachus*, from which he obtained the surname *Flavianus* from his paternal uncle, and *Memmius* from his paternal grandfather, *Memmius Orfitus*; and so it was with the others. No other rule should be sought for names of the later age. For fixed and established names of the clan and family were no longer in use as they once were—names which were common to brothers and passed down to descendants: such as when all were called *Cornelii* or *Julii* who were born from the *Cornelian* or *Julian* clan <term>gens</term><note>A 'gens' was a Roman clan or group of families sharing a common name and claiming descent from a common ancestor.</note>, and likewise *Scipiones* or *Cicerones* who were in the house and family of the *Scipios* or *Ciceros*.

But all things began to gradually change and decline with the fall of the Republic. Although initially some traces of the ancient custom remained in the *Clan Names* <note>original: "Gentilitiis Nominibus"</note> which were retained by some families, such as in the *Salvii* and *Flavii*, as the examples show. Afterward, however, even this was neglected, to the point that there was finally no certain name for the family or the clan; sons often differed from their fathers, and brothers from each other, by all or nearly all their names, as the same *Sirmond* teaches in the cited place, page 9 and following. See also *Pasquier's Researches in the Index*.

Regarding the change of names, see *Hayton, chapter 33*, and *Reineccius* there, and also *P. Contzen in his Commentary on Romans in the preface, question 4*. Where he discusses Paul and why he changed the name *Saul* to *Paul*, he relates from *Augustine* as follows: he says *Paul* chose this name not by his own mind's whim, but by God's command. For this pattern of the Saints is found in Holy Scripture: that they changed names not by their own will, but by God's nod, as Scripture teaches. Not that the change of a name is not otherwise a matter of choice, but that in Scripture no one is found to have changed a name except by Divine command, and because there was a unique reason in Paul’s case: for it was expedient for the whole Church to know that he was *Saul*, who had previously been the persecutor; in *Acts 9*, he is called *Saul* by Christ.

<column-break/>

Therefore, people often ask: if the name was changed at his conversion, why was he not immediately called *Paul*? The answer is easy. In the beginning, the name *Paul* was known only to a few, and therefore he was called *Saul*; but after he departed from Antioch and converted Sergius <note>Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of Cyprus.</note>, the name was then so well-known that almost no one was ignorant of it.

We also read that Christians sometimes changed their names, but for a different reason, as *Eusebius* writes in *Book 8, chapter 21* regarding five martyrs. Then, he says, when one had received the name of a certain Prophet as his own name (for this was practiced by them), they adopted new names after making the change, in place of the names of idols which had perhaps been given to them by their own parents. For they called themselves by the names of *Elijah, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Samuel, and Daniel*, so that one could hear them demonstrating the noble and true *Israel of God*—who was hidden to the Jews—not only by their deeds but by names properly and significantly explained, etc.

It is also well-known that now names are commonly changed by many at Confirmation <gloss>commonly called 'in der Firmung'</gloss>, as noted by *Contzen, cited question 5, 7*.

## ADDITION.

Captains who account for "blind names" <note>original: "blinde Nahmen." This refers to 'shadow' soldiers or fake names on a muster roll used to embezzle pay.</note> in their purses shall make fourfold restitution. *Dutch Military Law, article 70.* Prostitutes who wished to keep public brothels were accustomed to change their names. *ibid. article 69.* Propagating a family name from the maternal line is granted by the grace of the Prince. *Zahn, On Lies, book 2, chapter 63, number 1.* Concerning names composed to cause terror, see *Rupertus on Florus, book 3, chapter 10, § 20.*

Useless names should not be investigated or disputed. *Barbosa, book 12, chapter 14, axiom 1.* Beautiful names are to be sought after most greatly, so much so that if they were for sale, they ought to be bought at the highest price. *axiom 2.*

> Names are an omen; Idmon was prescient of the future
> And it is said Hippolytus was torn apart by horses.
<note>A play on words: "Hippolytus" in Greek suggests being "unleashed by horses." Idmon was a seer in Greek mythology.</note>

*Where there is conformity of the Name, there is a presumption of identity of the body or the thing. axiom 3.* It is useless to dispute over a *Name* when the certain quality of the thing is found to be established. *axiom 4.* A name to which a person does not fit, its legal disposition cannot fit either. *axiom 5.* *Names* are bestowed at will, by which one person can be easily distinguished from another. *axiom 6.* Those things which differ in their proper *Names* differ in the thing itself. *axiom 7.* The nature of collective names is such that they do not grant the whole to individuals (as happens in distributive names), but only grant according to a part. *axiom 8.* Those things which are fit for various uses receive a more specific name from that use to which they are applied by the will and designation of the head of the household: for when the use and designation cease, the name also ceases. *axiom 9.* Mere naming bestows no legal right. *axiom 10.*

# Letter N.

Often, even when things have changed, the old names are still observed. <note>original: "Sæpè rebus mutatis nomina tamen vetera observantur." Axiom 11.</note> What is not permitted to someone under their own name will not be permitted under another's name. <note>original: "Nomine suo quod alicui non licet, nec alieno licebit." Axiom 12.</note> A diversity of names does not change the substance of a thing. <note>original: "Nominum diversitas non mutat rei substantiam." Axiom 14.</note> On those who are called "Nominators," see Mr. D. Tabor in *Ariadne’s Thread*, table 4, book 27, title 7. Anyone is permitted to assume a name, provided there is no fraud. See Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 6, number 42. On the benefits of good names, see the same author, book 1, chapter 11, number 48 and following; and on whether it is legal to change a name, number 72; also Jakob Gretser, book 1, *On the Bishops of Eichstätt*, chapter 2, page 164. On the declaration of a name, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 86. Having one and the same name belonging to two people sometimes causes harm. Mr. Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 7. To Fabius was given a new surname, "The Delayer," which was the salvation of the Republic; he was called the "Shield of the Empire" by the people. <note>original: "Cunctator... Imperii scutum." Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus was a Roman general famous for his "Fabian strategy" of attrition against Hannibal.</note> Florus, book 2, chapter 6, section 27. Lucius Sicinius Dentatus, on account of his immense bravery, was called the "Roman Achilles." <note>original: "Achilles Romanus."</note> Agellius, book 2, chapter 11. J. C. Oelhaffius was called the "Inventory of Imperial Politics" by a certain man of great reputation. Joachim, the Elector of Brandenburg, was nicknamed the "German Nestor." <note>original: "Nestor Germanicus." Nestor was the wise, long-lived counselor of the Greeks at Troy.</note> Fabius was called the "Shield" and Metellus the "Sword" of the State; Vespasian, however, was called the "Delight of the Human Race" because he allowed no poor person to leave his presence unhappy. <note>original: "deliciæ generis humani."</note> Apion the Grammarian was called the "Cymbal of the World" by his emperor Tiberius Caesar; Budé was called the "Prodigy of France." <note>original: "mundi cymbalum... Galliæ portentum." Guillaume Budé was a famous French humanist.</note> The name "Philip" is altogether ominous for Great Lords. See Richter in *Economic Axioms*, axiom 4, example 2, page 18. Regarding the names Sextus and Caius and what occurred with them, as well as the city of Padua and the tomb of Saint Anthony, see Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain, *Historical Report*, part 6, page 166. Scipio Nasica, because he was the wisest of men, was called "The Little Heart." <note>original: "corculum."</note> See Alciatus’s *Emblems*, 149, letter B. Among the lineage of the Lords of Reuss, it has become the custom that all members of that family bear only one baptismal name, namely Henry; and so that a distinction between persons can be recognized, they are accustomed to add "Henry the Elder," "the Middle," "the Younger," or "the First," "Second," or "Third." <note>original: "Heinrich der Aeltere, Mittlere, Jüngere." The Reuss family famously named every male member Henry (Heinrich) in honor of Emperor Henry VI.</note> Sometimes they use something else, taken from their physical height or appearance. In France, whoever rules the County of Laval always bears the name "Guy de Laval." Among the noble lineage of the von Bünau family, it is well known that only three names are in use: Rudolph, Günther, and Henry. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, volume 1, additions to book 4, chapter 7, page 545. Three Henrys, Kings of France, died violent deaths. Likewise, five Kings of Scotland named James. See Lansius in *Oration against the Gauls*, folio 292; on the Henrys, Counts of Plauen, see Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 398.

What it means "to give the name of the Court." See Mr. D. Tabor, *On Successive Obligations*, page 262 and following. What it means "to make a name" and "to contract by names." <note>original: "Nomen facere & nominibus contrahere." A bride changes the name of her family and assumes her husband's. <note>original: "Nupta familiæ suæ nomen immutat, & mariti adsumit."</note> Cypreus establishes God as the author of this practice, as He who bestowed the name upon the woman from the man, so that from *Isch* <note>original: "Isch" (man in Hebrew).</note>, by the addition of one letter, she might be called *Ischa* <note>original: "Ischa" (woman in Hebrew).</note>, as if "man-ess" from "man." <note>original: "quasi à viro vira."</note> Although this seems not to be ascribed immediately to God himself, but rather to Adam, who, when he first beheld Eve, said: "This is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; therefore she shall be called *virissa* <note>original: "virissa" (a Latinization of the Hebrew wordplay for woman).</note>, because she was taken from man," Genesis 2, verse 23. ### 10. Namely. <note>original: "Nemlich. Nempe."</note>

This word is accepted as an explanatory particle: namely, for example, to wit, etc., which have a precise force. Law "when a certain person," section 1, in the Digest *on interest*; Law "if in a sale," joined with the gloss in the Digest *on common estates*; Law "time," where see Jason in the Digest *on matters judged*; and in Law "if to you," section "personal," in the Digest *on pacts*. Bartolus on Law 1, in the Digest *on the Aquilian Law*. Decius, Counsel 47, number 2, and Counsel 423, number 15. Cravetta, Counsel 227, number 7, and Counsel 273, number 9. This word also restricts, declares, and modifies preceding words. <note>original: "Hæc dictio est etiam præcedentium restrictiva, declarativa & modificativa."</note> Law "namely," in the Digest *on what grounds those of age...*; Law "if in a claim," in the Digest *on common estates*; the next-to-last section in the *Institutes on Attilian Guardians*; chapter "most recent," in the Decretals *on the meaning of words*.

However, the words "to wit" or "namely" do not stand restrictively, but only demonstratively, when the proper names of all those things which are included under the general names have been expressed. ### 15. Tying the Knot, or Taking Away Manhood. <note>original: "Nestel verknüpffen, Mannschafft nehmen. Ligare ligulam."</note>

Regarding the curse of "The Binding" <note>term: "ligatio" — a folk magic practice involving tying knots to cause impotence or bad luck</note> and its effect on marriage, Delrio has much to say in *Disquisitions on Magic*, page 417 and following; see also the *Treasury of Exorcisms*, page 630, etc. Bodin in his treatise *On Demonomania*. Such a cure no doctor or person of true and sincere religion would easily undertake, and Lotichius himself condemns it. He also reports how manifold magical binding is; these bindings are nothing but diabolical conjurations, loose talk, and devil-summoning <note>original: "lose verbos tene und Teuffelsbeschwerungen"</note> worthy of the heaviest punishments. A catalog of these bindings is recounted by Cornelius Agrippa (an author most skilled in this superstition, if anyone is) in book 1 of *Occult Philosophy*, chapter 40. "It remains," *he says*, "now to see a matter of great wonder, and that is the binding of men into love or hatred, into sickness and health, and the like." Likewise, the Binding of Thieves and robbers, so that they cannot steal in a certain place; the Binding of Merchants, so that they cannot buy or sell in a certain place; the Binding of an Army, so that it cannot cross a certain boundary; the Binding of Ships, so that they cannot leave port by any force of the winds, even with infinite sails stretched by the wind. Likewise, the Binding of a Mill, so that it cannot be turned by any force; the Binding of a Field, so that crops cannot be produced in it; the Binding of a certain Place, so that nothing can be built upon it; the Binding of Fire, so that it cannot be lit in a place, or so that some combustible thing, even when placed in a very strong fire...

### 17. New Year’s Gifts. <note>original: "Neue Jahr Schenckungen. Strenæ."</note>

To *Lord Martin Mager in the "Treatise on the Armed Advocate," chapter 5, number 51*, it seems probable that the custom of giving "strenae" <note>Ancient Roman New Year's gifts, often considered an omen for the coming year.</note> flowed to us from the custom of clients giving gifts (concerning which see the same author, *number 48 and following*), which was done on the Calends of January: as *Tranquillus* <note>Suetonius (Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus), Roman historian.</note> writes: The Roman Knights were accustomed to bring a "strena" every year to Augustus Caesar at the Capitol, even when he was absent, on the Calends of January. This is still observed everywhere among us today, though in a different manner. For the highest Italians give to the lowest; in England, however, as *Polydore Vergil* testifies in "On the Inventors of Things," *book 5, chapter 2*, the inferiors bring the gift to the superiors, and individual Princes to the King. In Germany, they bring gifts without distinction—the inferior to the superior as well as the superior to the inferior, and equals to equals—who nevertheless give something in return to the givers, so that liberality may be mutually compensated as a sign of goodwill. See *Dracon on the "Origin and Law of Patricians," book 1, chapter 6, number 6, my folio 56 and following, and Sagittarius, "Illustrious Questions," decade 4, question 9.* Monasteries commonly give gingerbread to the Patron’s counselors for a New Year.

Regarding New Year's Gifts and to whom they are owed, see the Oration of *Lord Albert Hunger, 16, part 2*, who in the same part, *Oration 20*, has some things to say about the Calends of January and how they were formerly celebrated by the pagans.

### 18. New World. *Mundus novus.*

Concerning the **New World**, and its conversion, see the *Revealer of Secrets on the Philosopher’s Stone, folio 63, 81, and following, and throughout.* See also my own collections on the New World. Likewise, the **Letters from Japan and China** published in the year [16]27 at Münster. *Peaceful Composition, folio 10, column 2*, where it discusses the Apostolic Preachers. *Tertullian to Pal. Aeon. regarding the Atlantic, etc.* *Keckerman in the preface to Geography, folio 524 and 545.* Historical-

<column-break/>

prophetic probabilities in the literal historical exposition, folio 30 and following. *Guyon, Various Lessons, volume 2, folio 867, etc.* *Bertius’s Tables on the Southern and Polar Lands.*

Concerning the **Islands of the New World**, which Pope Alexander VI <note>The Borgia Pope who issued the Bull "Inter Caetera" in 1493, dividing the New World between Spain and Portugal.</note> granted to the jurisdiction and dominion of the Catholic King, Ferdinand of Aragon, for the purpose of propagating the Christian faith, see *Book 7 of the Decretals, book 1, title 9, page 74 and following.*

It should be noted here that in the year **1492**, the care and provision of ships with the most ample and complete equipment was given to **Christopher Columbus** of Genoa, who was burning with a wondrous desire to travel through new regions. Truly, before 150 years ago, there was such ignorance of navigation even among the Western peoples—specifically because the maritime use of the **Astrolabe** had not yet been devised—that they by no means dared to depart from the coast and commit themselves to the deep ocean. Instead, cautiously hugging the shores, whenever they reached the high seas or dangerous shallows, they immediately retreated as if some barriers had been placed there by nature or a deity, and they considered it a kind of sin to stretch further.

That the entire earth is now habitable, and that **Antipodes** <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe.</note> exist, is passed down by *Martin, Illustrious Century 6, disputation themes 6 and 7; add Jonston, folio 70, etc.*

Whether the Castilians <note>The Spanish.</note>, while reserving sovereignty for the native Princes, would have been able to hold the New World? See *Antoine Pipre on Moral, Civil, and Military Intentions, chapter 203.*

## 19. New Reports. News.

Today many are seen to suffer from that vice which Julius Caesar also attributed to the Gauls. "It is a Gallic custom," he says, "to compel travelers to stop, even against their will, and to inquire what each of them has heard or learned about any matter; and the common people surround merchants in the towns, forcing them to declare from which regions they come and what things they learned there. Moved by these rumors or hearsay, they often enter into deliberations regarding the most important matters, which they must necessarily repent of immediately, since they are slaves to uncertain rumors, and most people give them fabricated answers according to their wishes." Thus says Caesar. <note>Original Latin: "Hæc Cæsar." This refers to Caesar's *Gallic Wars*, Book 4, Chapter 5.</note>

The Athenians were also of such a kind; concerning whom St. Luke writes in Acts 17, verse 21: "For all the Athenians, and the strangers and guests, spent their time in nothing else but either to tell or to hear some new thing." Indeed, to be ignorant of what has happened or is happening elsewhere is like being held in a <term>workhouse</term> <note>original: "ergastulo," a Roman private prison for slaves</note> or a perpetual prison; yet vanity must be avoided. Moreover, those Princes are not called "Political" <note>In this context, "political" refers to being state-wise or prudent in governance.</note> who do not have certain news <note>original German: "die nicht gewiſſe Zeitung haben"</note>, especially concerning things upon which much depends for them, and for their land and people. Private individuals and citizens, however, should not be too greedy for novelties, lest they be forced to hear these little verses:

> Anxiety for new things is the habit of fickle men:
> Concern for their own affairs is the habit of serious men.

Truly, one must act cautiously in publishing news. For many are accustomed to, and are able to, fish out the mind and the innermost recesses of the soul from such reports. However, the spreading of news is not always vanity, but sometimes <term>pseudo-political secrets</term> <note>original: "pſeudopolitica arcana," refers to deceptive statecraft or propaganda</note>; see Jacques Hurault, *On the Offices of State*, folio 510. Victories are spread, the opposing side is disparaged, and disasters are feigned to deceive the common people (because the world, as it is said, wants to be deceived), so that the public might favor this or that party, etc. Thus, after the Battle of Ivry <note>original: "Cladem Jurenſem," 1590, a decisive victory for Henry IV of France</note>, the Duke of Mayenne attributed and credited the victory to himself, which had actually been on the opposing side: saying such a lie <note>original: "mendacium"</note>, if one can maintain it for just a few days, is worth many thousands of florins. See the histories of that century, or Serre in the history of Henry the Great, King of France, during the siege of Paris.
And that false rumors are spread even through pamphlets during times of sedition, Peleus writes in his *French History*, volume 4, page 46. See also Diodorus Siculus, book 11, number 35.

## ADDITION.

"Out of Africa, always something new" <note>A famous ancient proverb, "Ex Africa semper aliquid novi," originally from Aristotle and Pliny</note>, because animals of different species gather at the water springs, which are found in few numbers in those parts, mingle with one another, and are accustomed to give birth to a third species. *Besold, Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

Thus, "tiger-dogs" are said to have been born from a young tiger and dogs; mules from a stallion and a she-ass; Indian hens <note>likely referring to turkeys, which were often called "Indian hens" or "Calicut hens" in early modern Europe</note> from a cock and a peahen. *Lord Harsdörffer.*

Nature always produces something new. *Barbosa, book 12, chapter 24, axiom 6.* That which comes from a declaration is not called "new," *axiom 5.* It is one thing to be made anew, and another for that which was already made to grow or be extended, *axiom 3.* Novelties are not to be introduced, *axiom 2.* Those things which emerge anew require new help, *axiom 1.* Immediately see Ummius in *On Procedure*, page 406 at the end, and pages 670 & 771. On the precautions to be taken in reviewing news, see *Zeiller, century 1, Letters, page 555.* Regarding the question "What news?", see Julius Bellus in *The Political Hermes*, book 2, page 138. "There is nothing new under the sun!" Ecclesiastes 1, verse 10. Most elegant on this matter is the preface to *Aulæorum Romanorum*. Charming novelty flatters the eyes, strikes the mind, stirs the affection, and plays with the intellect as if with chaste loves. See *Turkish Tapestry*, page 7. In Spain, they allow no new things to be brought in or out; therefore, he who has a new shirt must first dip it in water <note>original German: "daſſelbe zuvor in das Waſſer ſtecken muß." This may refer to avoiding the stiff appearance of newness to evade sumptuary laws or cultural taboos against vanity</note>. *Zeiller, Spanish Itinerary, page 66.* In the laws of the city, those words of the famous Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 2, are appropriate: "Wicked and lowly men, who are very busy in doing nothing, finally become a laughingstock." "You who always love new things, and soon abandon what you possess," *Petronius, page 159, line 22.* Those who want to know "what boils in every man's pot" <note>original German: "die wiſſen wollen / was in eines jeden Hafen ſiedet"</note>. Novelty turns all eyes. "Letters of novelty" are given in France and serve as a certain possessory remedy. *Lord Christoph Philipp Richter, page 6, Consultation 8, number 119 folio 135.* 
"Nothing is new under the sun." For every earlier thing has provided a standard for the later thing. *Tertullian, book 1, Against Marcion, chapter 9.* And those things which are now believed to be very ancient were once new. *Tacitus, Annals, book 11.* Observe the circle of things returning into themselves: you will see that in this world nothing is extinguished, but by turns they decline and rise again. A due change is owed to all things, and in all of them there is a certain circle, as it were, so that just as the seasons change, so too do customs. *Tacitus, Annals, book 2.*

## 20. Nothing, Nothing Excepted. Nothing. With None Excepted.

"Nothing" <note>original: "Nihil"</note> is a universal negative word, and he who swears that he will "obtain nothing" excludes himself from every petition. *Chapter "Statutum," section "Provisurus," under "Rescripts" in the 6th book of the Decretals. Romanus, Consultation 379, in the beginning; add Tuschus, letter D, conclusion 313.*
The clause "nothing excepted," <note>original German: "nichts ausgeſcheiden"</note> however, suffers no modification or restriction whatsoever. Since it is certain that the nature and property of that negative clause "with none excepted," just like any other negative disposition, is such that it is extended even unto infinity, nor does it admit any modification at all.

To do nothing and to do very little are considered equal. <note>Barbosa, book 12, chapter 10, axiom 1.</note> "Nothing" and "useless" are held as equivalents. <note>Axiom 2.</note> Nothing comes from nothing. <note>Axiom 3.</note> "Little" and "nothing" are equated. <note>Marius Antoninus, book 2, Various Rules 18, number 6.</note> The particles "not... but" are often placed for "not only... but also." <note>Pacius, Analysis of the Code, page 417, number 7.</note> To "act for nothing" <note>original Latin: "Nihil agitur"</note> is the same in law as being of no importance or weight. <note>Mr. Doctor Ludwig, commentary on the Institutes regarding usufruct, section 3.</note> "Nothing in any way" <note>original Latin: "Nil ullo modo"</note> is understood to apply even when a Dispensation exists. <note>Cevallos, Common Opinions against Common Opinions, question 808, number 59.</note> For this wording has such strength that it blocks every possible Dispensation. <note>Tiraqueau, on the law "if ever," under the Glossary "it shall return," number 93.</note> In the following numbers, he attributes the same power to the words "in no way" <note>original Latin: "nullatenus"</note> and "thoroughly" <note>original Latin: "penitus"</note>, treating them as absolute terms that accept no limitation or modification. <note>Raudensis, response 22, number 32, book 2; Barbosa on the dictionary of usufruct, under the word "nullatenus," 226, number 13, and the word "nullo modo," 228, number 4.</note> "Not certainly" <note>original Latin: "Non utique"</note> means "not always" or "not only." <note>Mr. Doctor Tabor, on arms in general, in the Preface, number 3.</note> "To exclude nothing" <note>original German: "Nichts ausbescheiden." ## 21. Niece / Spinners, Spindle-kin. Blood Relatives.

The Saxons call <term>Blood Relatives</term> <note>original Latin: "Cognatas"</note> the "closest nieces," or also the "closest spinners" and "spindle-kin" or "spool-kin." <note>original German: "die nächſte Niffteln, oder auch nächſte Geſpinne und Spiel- oder Spuelmagen." Glossary on the Municipal Law of Magdeburg, article 23, number 2; text in the Saxon Land Law, book 3, article 15, at the end.</note> And they are called "Spinners" or "Spindle-kin" because of their office; for spinning is innate to women, and this is their coat of arms, just as a sword belongs to men. <note>Municipal Law of Magdeburg, article 23, in the glossary.</note> And because of the "spindle-way," the law has given this name to women and to all related through the female side, and calls the "closest spinner" in Latin a <term>Cognata</term> <note>a relative on the mother's side</note>.

<column-break/>

Georg Rotschitz in the treatise on Dowries, <term>Gerada</term> <note>The "Gerada" was a specific portion of an inheritance, often household goods and clothes, that went only to female heirs in Germanic law.</note>, etc., article 14, number 4. Moreover, I believe the word *Nifftel* <note>Niece</note> is derived from the Latin *neptis*.

# ADDITION.

Regarding grandchildren and nieces. <note>Rudinger, century 2, observation 22.</note> "Spindle-kin" <note>original German: "Spielmagen"</note> are those who are related to us through the spindle <note>the female line</note>. <note>Schneidewin, on legitimate agnatic guardianship, number 9.</note> Regarding the "Niece-Gerada" <note>original German: "Nifftelgeradam"</note> which is given by custom in Leipzig and Chemnitz, and what pertains to it, see Berlichius, conclusion 28, number 48.

## 22. New Breaking / Noval Tithes.

Regarding <term>Noval Tithes</term> <note>Tithes collected from land that has been newly brought under cultivation.</note>. On Noval and Tithe rights, see the treatise by Johann Werndle on Tithe Law.

It must be noted here that it is not a "new breaking" if one plows up meadows, because tithes were already being given from them before. Likewise, fallow fields <note>original German: "Egarten"</note> which were cultivated in former times, or lake-beds that are sown at certain times, cannot be considered "new breakings."

The question is asked, however, whether it is a "new breaking" when one plants trees anew on a meadow or in a forest? This is denied, because such a thing only concerns the "small tithe."

Although the law may be disputed as to whom the <term>Noval Tithes</term> belong, it has been observed thus far in many Provinces: that the Noval Tithes—the "new breaking" or Noval-Tithes—do not belong to those who claim the right of tithe from ancient times, but rather belong to the higher Magistrate. This was disputed in the case of Hans Ruden of Hedigsheimb against those of Rosenburg, concerning a mandate for the seizure of Noval Tithes in the Middle March; and in the case of the Landgrave of Hesse and the Canons of St. Alban in Mainz, concerning the Noval Tithes in the village of Loheimb, situated in the Gerau region. <note>Mr. Rutger Ruland, Decisions on Controversial Law, question 19; see also my work On Majesty, folio 176.</note> There I discuss the "Forest Sheaf" <note>original German: "Forſtgarb"</note>, which the authorities are accustomed to impose on newly cleared land because of the depletion of their forest, and because they permit the "rooting out" <note>the clearing of stumps; see above under letter A, number 77</note>.

But truly, this cannot be maintained in Ecclesiastical Courts, nor does it have a basis in reason. For in the beginning, all tithes were "Noval" <note>newly established</note>; thus, there would be none that did not belong to the lords of the places. Regarding the grievance brought at Regensburg in the year 1594 concerning the collection of Noval Tithes, see in the Composition of Peace, question 62, page 336.

Mascardus teaches how the tithe of new lands is to be proven in his work *On Probations*.

## ADDITION.

The right to collect tithes <note>Latin: *Jus decimandi*</note> granted within a general territory also includes the tithes of newly cultivated lands. <note>Citing Klock, volume 1, counsel 41, number 10.</note> On the subject of newly cultivated lands <note>Latin: *Novalia*</note>, see Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter, part 6, chapter 31, number 9 and following; and Gottfried Antonii, *Disputations on Fiefs*, 12, thesis 7, letter D. The word *Novale* is ambiguous. In its broad sense, the legal expert Gaius defines it thus: "A *novale* is land cut off, which has rested for a year." <note>Citing the Digest, *de Verborum Significatione* (On the Meaning of Words).</note> Gaedd. explains this as land recently broken—that is, split, turned, and cultivated by the plow—which is accustomed to rest every other year to renew its strength. In this way, almost all fields can be called *novales*, since they commonly rest for a year. In this broad sense, the name *novalia* also applies to land that is commonly called *Bräckland*. <note>German: *Bräckland*, referring to fallow land or land being broken up for the first time in a cycle.</note> The Duke of Brunswick, in his published Land Ordinance, stated: "Whatever is planted in the fallow, when it is smoothed with the harrow after sowing, the tithe for it belongs to the regular tithe-lord." The second meaning is narrower, where *novale* refers to a field newly brought under cultivation, of which there is no memory of it ever having been cultivated before. See also Petrus Gregorius in his *System of Universal Law*, book 1, chapter 2, number 2. "A *Neureut* and *Neubruch* <note>German legal terms for newly cleared land and new breakings of soil.</note> is nothing else than ground and soil that has been broken up for the first time—such as when one clears [reutet], meaning digging out, burning out, and rooting out brush, twigs, trees, old stumps, stony roots, and the like, and then breaking it up and planting it." This field retains its designation as long as the memory of the clearing and the first cultivation exists.

**Question:** To whom do the tithes of these newly cultivated lands belong? We must distinguish between Canon Law <note>Church law</note> and Customary Laws. Under the Common Canon Law, if the field is situated within a certain parish, the tithes undoubtedly belong to the Parish Church. However, if the new land exists in no limited parish, the Episcopal or Cathedral Church (or the Bishop in whose diocese it lies) claims them by right. Under Customary Law, by virtue of the right of sovereignty and territorial authority, the tithes of new lands belong to the secular Princes and Estates of the Empire. Sometimes it is expressly stated that "the tithe-jurisdiction over new clearings, new fields, and wherever the boundary crosses, is not taken away nor given up." Some give a few *Batzen* or *Kreutzer* <note>small coins of the era</note> annually to the Lord of the Territory for the "district tithe" <note>German: *Zentzehenden*</note> through a legal settlement, a precedent of which I know from the year 1599. Others make a threefold division of new lands: 1. Either the land already subject to tithe takes a new form, such as a meadow being turned into a field; 2. Or land previously sterile is brought under cultivation; 3. Or a forest is converted into a field by uprooting the trees. In the first case, the person who

<column-break/>

collected the tithe from the land before the change took place continues to receive it. In the second case, it is accepted that the tithes are owed to the church in whose parish they arise; if they are not in a specific parish, they are left to the Diocesan Bishop. These are the lands commonly called "new clearing tithes." <note>German: *Neubruchzehend*.</note> In the third case, I believe the tithes should be applied to the diligence of the possessor, provided that the right of hunting is not hindered thereby; for if it is, they are owed to the Prince or the Magistrate of that place because of the loss of hunting profits. This last type is called a "root-clearing or stump-tithe." <note>German: *Neugereuth oder Stockzehend*.</note> H. D. Obrecht, in his *Political Reflections*, title 11, advises that "every Lord should inquire with watchful diligence throughout his entire land what woods, bushes, mountains, valleys, hedges, and other uncultivated places he has that could be cleared, broken up, and made into fruitful acres, fields, meadows, gardens, vineyards, and fishponds, or even established as villages, market towns, farmsteads, dairies, sheep-folds, and bee-farms." Regarding whether it is a *novale* or a *neubruch*, see the Cardinal in chapter 1, question 6, *On Tithes*, who concludes that it is not. This is also confirmed by Riminaldo the Elder, counsels 530 and 536, where it is further argued that "even if the meadows previously gave no tithe, they must nevertheless be subject to tithe after cultivation." See the legal opinion given by Mr. Dr. Christoph Heldens on November 12, 1612, concerning new lands, which I will discuss on another occasion. On new clearings, see Mr. Speidel’s *Collection of Legal Questions* under this word.

### 23. Clause: *Not in the form of an elegant legal petition, but a simple narrative of history.*

#### Narrative of history.

"Although this clause is very common in the formulas for legal petitions <note>Latin: *libellus*, the formal written statement of a plaintiff's case</note>, legal teachers nevertheless say" that such a clause has little or no effect in cases where a full legal investigation is required, and thus where a request of any sort is not permitted. <note>Citing Ferrarius on the form of a petition in real actions.</note> Indeed, there are some who believe that a petition is entirely invalidated and destroyed by this clause. <note>Citing Petrus Anchoranus and Thoming.</note>

***

### ADDITION.

Regarding the clause: *Not in the manner of a solemn petition, but of any request whatsoever.* See Ummius in *Legal Process*, page 262. A protestation that a filing is not in the form of a solemn petition, but by way of a simple complaint, ensures that the case can proceed summarily <note>Latin: *de plano*, meaning without formal complexity</note>. It seems, therefore, that this protestation is useless in ordinary cases. See the *Forum of Protestations* published by our own Mr. Felwinger, page 398, number 27.

## 24. Lower Courts, Chieftains, Lordship, Low Jurisdiction. <note>German: *Nidergericht, Häuptling, Herrlichkeit*; Latin: *Jurisdictio bassa*</note>

The lower courts <note>German: *Niedergericht*</note> commonly belong to the nobility, who in Swabia were formerly called bailiff-lords <note>original: *Vogtsherren*</note>, and in East Frisia chieftains <note>original: *Häuptling*</note>. Their legal right is called "Lordship" <note>original: *Herrlichkeit*, a term for a manorial territory with its own jurisdiction</note>: for example, "the Lordship of N." as they are called elsewhere.

But what belongs to the lower or hereditary courts, particularly according to Saxon Law? Beatus discusses this <note>referencing *Decisions*, volume 5, On Judicial Matters, part 5, volume 1, from the beginning and many following pages</note>, where he cites a response from the Leipzig Jurists <note>original: *Scabinorum*, members of a legal lay court</note>. He refers all civil matters to these hereditary rights: goods, debts, estates—whether landed, mobile, movable or immovable—even if they amount to more than 300 florins. Likewise, petty theft <note>original: *Dieube*</note> involving less than 3 shillings is to be punished, not only on the day of the crime but also on the following days. Other minor infractions and misconduct are included: for instance, if someone in a city or village carries a knife, crossbow, or other weapon improperly; or plays games not permitted by law; or if one insults another with secret, shameful words, accuses them of lying, hits, pushes, or strikes them until they are black and blue—provided that no danger of death, duel <note>original: *Fleischkampffer*</note>, or open wounds results, even if the insult is legally termed an "atrocious injury" <note>Latin: *atrox injuria*</note>. Furthermore, the hereditary judge may punish any party who behaves disobediently before the court or fails to comply with what they agreed to in court, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

Nobles endowed with Royal Rights <note>Latin: *Regalibus*</note> and jurisdiction over both high and low justice <note>Latin: *Jurisdictione mero mixtoque Imperio*</note>, who were anciently called Chieftains <note>original: *Häuptlinge*</note>, as noted by Mr. Tabor <note>in *On Suffrage*, page 226</note>.

### 24. Low Court, Chieftain, Lordship. <term>Low Jurisdiction</term> <note>original: "Jurisdictio bassa"</note>.

The Low Courts are commonly held by members of the nobility, who in Swabia were formerly called bailiff-lords <note>original: "Vogtsherren"</note>, and in East Frisia "Chieftains" <note>original: "Häuptling"</note>; their legal right is called "Lordship" <note>original: "Herrlichkeit"</note>, as in "The Lordship of N.," as they are called elsewhere.

As to what specifically belongs to the Low or Hereditary Courts according to Saxon law? Beatus discusses this in volume 5, *On Judicial Matters*, part 5, volume 1, from the beginning and through many following pages. There, based on a response from the Leipzig Jurors <note>The Scabini or Schöffen were lay judges/jurors who provided legal opinions</note>, he refers all civil matters to these hereditary rights: namely, rents, debts, and properties—whether landed, movable, or immovable—even if they amount to more than 300 florins. Likewise, they handle thieves who have stolen less than 3 shillings, who are to be punished not only on the same day but also on the second and following days. They also handle other minor breaches and misconducts: for example, if someone in a town or village carries a knife, crossbow, or other weapon improperly; or plays games not permitted by law; or if someone insults another with secret, shameful words, accuses them of lying, hits, shoves, or beats them "black and blue," provided that no danger of death, no "flesh-hacking" <note>original: "Fleischkampffer", likely referring to mutilation or deep wounding</note>, or open wounds result, even if such a breach or insult would be called a "severe injury" <note>original: "atrox injuria"</note> in the law. Furthermore, the hereditary judge has the power to punish a party who behaves disobediently before the court or who fails to comply with what they agreed to before the court, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

Nobles endowed with Regalian rights, and with jurisdiction of "High and Low Authority" <note>original: "mero mixtoque Imperio", referring to the power to inflict capital punishment and handle civil/administrative matters</note>, were in ancient times called Chieftains. See Mr. Dr. Tabor, *On Suffrage*, page 226.

### 25. Storage Fee. <note>original: "Niederlag-Geld"</note>

A storage fee is that which is collected from wines purchased in a certain location.

->ADDITION.<-

See <term>Land-Dues</term> <note>original: "Bodenschatz"</note>. Mundium, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 3, number 142. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 78, number 3. Wehner, in *Practical Observations*, under the word <term>Land-Dues</term> <note>original: "Bodenschatz"</note>.

Regarding the Low Countries, or Lower Germany, one should certainly consult Mr. Martin Beer in his *Handbook of Ancient and Modern Geography*, page 42 and following.

Whether a statute regarding the admission of someone into a College—which stipulates that they must have lived for more than three years in a famous German Academy—can be extended to the Belgian Academies? See Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter, part 1, counsel 42, in its entirety. Charles V wanted to reduce the Low Countries to the form of a province. Besold, *On Politics*, book 1, chapter 1, number 41.
