Orange <note>A principality in what is now southern France</note> is indeed rich in wine and grain, and also bears fruit and saffron; however, the soil is said to bear no oranges: *In Orange there are no oranges* <note>French: "En Aurenge il n’ya point d’orenges"</note>. ### 28. Nuns. <note>Latin: *Moniales*</note>

That "Nonnus" is the same as "Monk" <note>Latin: *Monachus*</note> is clear from the *Franciscan Chapters, book 5, chapters 2 and 3.* See also Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings, book 5, chapter 13,* and Hospinian, *On Monks, page 3.*

Nonna, meaning nuns, as Jerome writes *to Eustochium*: "And those who, having experienced the dominance of husbands, prefer the freedom of widowhood, are called chaste and Nuns <note>Latin: *Nonnæ*</note>."

And the word "Nonna" seems to descend from the Hebrew *Nin* <note>original: נין</note>, which signifies a youth and a person who is celibate. From this also comes the Spanish *Ninnio* <note>modern: *Niño*, meaning child</note>. This word is therefore attributed to Nuns because they not only live as celibates, but must follow the purity of infants.

The Egyptians also called men and virgins distinguished by piety and holiness of life *Nonnos* and *Nonnas*; from this, Gerard Falckenburg, in the *Dionysian Letters prefixed to Nonnus*, conjectures that the name of "Nonnus" was given by his fellow citizens (for he was an Egyptian from Panopolis) to that poet who also published a Greek paraphrase of the Holy Gospel according to John, on account of his most holy and innocent character. See Heinsius in *Aristarchus, page 38*, and the Lexicon of Matthias Martinius.

<column-break/>

Hence the Rule of St. Benedict, which is found in the most recent edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers, volume 6, part 1, page 433*, decrees thus:
> Let no brother dare to call another by his simple name; but (as is fitting) the Seniors shall name the Juniors their "brothers," and the Juniors shall call their Seniors "Nonnos," which signifies paternal reverence; however, the Abbot shall be called Lord and Father by all.

He who "knows" <note>a legal euphemism for sexual relations</note> a nun commits three—and indeed, as the Canons say, most serious—crimes: namely, incest, adultery, and sacrilege. See Hippolytus de Marsiliis, *Singularia 215*; Bernhard Diaz in *Criminal Practice, chapter 75, title on nuns, page 129*; and see especially Abel Strasburg, *Counsel 10, number 4, etc.*

All and individual Nuns, of whatever religion or order they may be, must remain under perpetual Enclosure <note>Latin: *Clausula*</note> in their monasteries. See the *unique chapter on the status of regulars, book 6 of the Decretals*, and the *Council of Trent, session 25, on regulars, chapter 5.*

Regarding Nuns, and that they are exempt from the imposition of tithes, subsidies, and other burdens; and that Nuns are bound, whether tacitly or expressly, by their religious profession, and that their receptions into the order are null and void if the obligation of Enclosure is violated, was established by Pius IV and V, as can be seen in *volume 7 of the Decretals, book 3, title 18, chapters 1 and 2.*

The same Pope Pius V decreed in *the cited chapter 3* that the requested faculty to leave the Enclosure is not denied to Nuns in cases of necessity such as fire, illness, leprosy, or epidemic.

Gregory XIII granted entrance into the monasteries to Prelates and others having care of the Nuns, but only in cases of urgent necessity and with a small retinue, in *the said book 7 of the Decretals, chapter 4.*

For whatever reason or cause, a Nun, of whatever status or condition she may be, cannot and should not exit the monastery except in cases expressly stated in the law. And no Roman Pope ever more diligently cared for the Enclosure of Nuns than the Supreme Pontiff Pius V himself, who even gave a refusal to a certain very noble virgin seeking exit due to illness and poor health, exhorting her that it is more glorious to die with Christ than to live among the allurements of the world. He granted dispensations for exit in only these three pressing cases: *fire, plague, and leprosy*. And so that Nuns might be set apart and separated from all sights and charms of worldly impurity, the faculty of going out from the monastery walls is forbidden to them, except in the said cases.

From this it also follows that Nuns cannot and should not be summoned in any way to the "noise of the forum" <note>the public turmoil of the law courts</note> to appear personally, *chapter 2 at the end, on judgments, in the 6th book*. Indeed, not even the Abbess herself, to whom the oversight of the entire monastery is entrusted, may leave the monastery walls, even for the purpose of visiting monasteries subject to her, according to the *gloss on the word 'alia' in Clementine 2 on regulars.*

The Enclosure of Nuns is a matter of Law, according to the *unique chapter on the status of regulars in the 6th book* and the *Council of Trent.*

### 28. Nuns. <term>Moniales</term> <note>the Latin term for a female member of a religious order living under a rule</note>

It is clear that "Nonnus" is the same as a Monk, as appears from the *Capitula Franciscis*, book 5, chapters 2 and 3; see also Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book 5, chapter 13; see Hospinian on Monks, folio 3.

Nuns, or *moniales*: Jerome writes to Eustochium: "And those who have experienced the mastery of husbands and prefer the freedom of widowhood are called chaste and Nuns."

And the word "Nonna" <note>Nun</note> seems to descend from the Hebrew *Nin*, which signifies a youth or a celibate. From this also comes the Spanish *Niño* <note>boy/child</note>. This word is therefore attributed to Nuns because they not only live as celibates, but also ought to follow the purity of infants.

The Egyptians also called men and virgins who were distinguished by piety and holiness of life "Nonnos" and "Nonnas." From this, Gerard Falckenburg, in the *Dionysian Epistles* prefixed to Nonnus, conjectures that the poet Nonnus (who also published a Greek paraphrase of the Holy Gospel according to John) was given the name Nonnus by his countrymen (for he was an Egyptian from Panopolis) because of his most holy and innocent character. See Heinsius in *Aristarchus*, folio 38, and the Lexicon of Matth. Martinius.

<column-break/>

Hence the Rule of St. Benedict, which is found in the most recent edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, volume 6, part 1, folio 433, decrees: "Let no brother dare to call another by his simple name; but (as is fitting) the seniors shall name the younger ones their brothers, and the juniors shall call their seniors 'Nonnos', which signifies paternal reverence; but the Abbot shall be called Lord and Father by all."

To have carnal knowledge of a nun involves three crimes, and indeed, as the Canons say, the most serious outrages: namely, incest, adultery, and sacrilege. Hippolytus de Marsiliis, *Singularia* 215; Bernhard Diaz in *Criminal Practice*, in the canonical chapter 75, title on nuns, folio 129. See generally Abel Strasburg, counsel 10, number 4, etc.

All and singular Nuns, of whatever religion or order they may be, must remain under perpetual Enclosure <term>Clausura</term> <note>the legal and religious requirement for cloistered nuns to remain within the walls of their convent</note> in their monasteries. See the single chapter on the state of regulars in the 6th book of Decretals, and the Council of Trent, session 25, on regulars, chapter 5.

Regarding Nuns, and that they are exempt from the imposition of tithes, subsidies, and other burdens; and that Nuns are bound either tacitly or expressly once they have professed their religion; and that their reception into the order is null and void if the obligation of Enclosure is violated—these were established by Pius IV and V, as can be seen in volume 7 of the Decretals, book 3, title 18, chapters 1 and 2.

The same Pontiff Pius V established in the cited place, chapter 3, that the requested permission to leave the Enclosure is not to be denied to Nuns in the necessity of fire, illness, leprosy, or epidemic.

Gregory XIII granted entrance to the Enclosure to Prelates and others having care of the monasteries of Nuns, but only in cases of urgent necessity and with a small retinue. See the said book 7 of the Decretals, chapter 4.

For whatever reason or cause, a Nun, of whatever state or condition she may be, cannot and must not leave the monastery, except in cases expressed in law. And no Roman Pontiff ever more diligently cared for the Enclosure of Nuns than the Supreme Pontiff Pius V himself, who even gave a refusal to a certain very noble Virgin seeking an exit on account of infirmity and ill health, exhorting her that it is more glorious to die with Christ than to live among the enticements of the world. In only these three pressing cases—fire, plague, and leprosy—did he grant dispensations for departure. And so that Nuns might be set apart and separated from all sights and wantonness of secular filth, the power of leaving is forbidden to them from the precincts of the monastery, except in the said cases.

From this it also follows that Nuns cannot or should not be summoned in any way to the noise of the courts to appear personally. See chapter 2 at the end, on judges, in the 6th book of Decretals. Indeed, not even the Abbess herself, to whom the leadership of the entire monastery is entrusted, may leave the precincts of the monastery, even for the purpose of visiting monasteries subject to her. See the gloss on the word "other" in Clementines 2, on regulars.

The Enclosure of Nuns is a matter of law: see the single chapter on the state of regulars in the 6th book, and the Council of Trent, session 24.

*Session 24, chapter 5 regarding Regulars and Constitutions* <note>original: "de Regul. & Constit." refers to the rules governing religious orders</note> of Pope Pius V concerns the Ordinaries <note>the local bishops</note>, ensuring that they see to it that these rules are observed according to the tenor of Boniface VIII as soon as they are able. But if nuns, even those who are exempt from local jurisdiction, should leave the enclosure without the Bishop's license, both they and their Superiors—by whose license they left—must be punished by the Ordinary with ecclesiastical censures and other penalties. See Paul Zypaeus in his *Analysis of Pontifical Law, book 3, title on Regulars, page 325.*

Monasteries that are "in the making," or while they are being built, do not yet have the Enclosure <note>the strict rule of remaining within the monastery walls</note>, nor the penalties for those entering. Queens and female Founders may enter out of their own devotion, but they may not enter the monasteries of Men. See the same Zypaeus in the *cited place, page 327.* Refer to the Council of Trent and the declarations there in *Session 25, chapter 5,* where there is more concerning the Enclosures of Nuns. And generally concerning Nuns, see the *Synodal Statutes, page 156, and Cornelius à Rinthein in The Roman-Catholic Jurist, chapter 54.*

## ADDITION.

Vestal virgins or nuns do not succeed in fiefs <note>they cannot inherit feudal land holdings</note>. Carpzov <note>Benedikt Carpzov, a prominent German jurist</note>, *part 2, decision 171, number 12.* A woman who, after the death of her husband, falsely claims to be a nun, is compelled as a penalty for her lie to return to the Monastery if she later marries in the secular world. Zahn, *On Lies, book 2, chapter 99, number 1.* Women of distinguished holiness were once surnamed *Nonni*. Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Lessons, book 5, chapter 12.* Soon, priestesses were called *Nonnae*. Saubert, *On Sacrifices, page 144.* For what a *Nonaria* <note>original: "Nonaria" historically referred to a prostitute who appeared at the ninth hour, but the text discusses the etymological confusion or relation to "Nonna"</note> is and why she is so called, see Rupert in his *Epistolary Mercury, page 662.* Among the *Venetians*, by a law of the Magistrates on August 31, 1569, even those who approach monasteries to speak with the nuns themselves are punished. Nuns are more fully, and less mutably, called *Sanctimoniales*. Rittershulius, in *The Novels <note>refers to the Novellae Constitutiones of Justinian</note>, page 109, number 9.* For one who defiles a nun, to see how manifold a crime he commits, one should look to the *Gloss of Canon Law in canon 14, 'on virgins,' cause 27, question 1.* This is also praised by Philippus Decius in *Counsel 306, number 3, and Counsel 579, number 5.* He says that such a person commits: 1. Incest. 2. Sacrilege. 3. Adultery. Lord C. Rittershulius in *The Novels, page 82, number 84.* On whether adultery is committed with a nun, see Jacob Ayrer in the *Historical Process, part 1, chapter 7, observation 5, number 17.*

### 29. Notary.

A Notary, or Scribe <note>original: "Tabellio"</note>, is a Public Person, exercising or managing the office of the scribeship, ordained for public utility and fortified by the authority of a superior. Heinricus Cnaustius, *On the Art of the Notariate, at the beginning.* Jacob Bornitius defines it otherwise in his *Treatise on Instruments, book 2, title 12.* And the name is derived from "noting." To *Note* is the same as to sign, or to diligently write and observe those things which are done and said by the parties. Hence they are named from the *notes* <note>shorthand or marks</note> which Notaries once used for speed in writing. *Digest, book 33, section 1, on the causes of majors.* Jacob Spiegel in his *Lexicon of Law under the word* Notaries. Budaeus reports that such shorthand-writers existed both in Rome and 

<column-break/>

still today in the Parliament of Paris, who with a certain marvelous skill catch almost all the words of the Advocates and Judges. *In his annotations to the Pandects <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, law 'to be absent' with the following law, on the causes of majors.* Understand these "notes" according to Bornitius, in the *cited place, under the word 'to note,'* as either the first letters of words, or Characters and Signs; see above under *Abbreviations.*

He is also called a *Tabellio*, namely from *Tabula* <note>a tablet or board</note>, because in former times it was customary to write on Tablets. *Codex, law 15, at the end, on the faith of Instruments.*

*Likewise they are called Librarians, who should weigh and consider everything well.* <note>original German: "die alles wohl wiegen und erwegen sollen"</note> Bornitius, *cited place, section 'otherwise'*; or from books <note>Latin: "liber"</note>, because they formerly used the inner bark of trees instead of paper. See the Lexicon of Martinus, *under the word book (liber), page 1506.*

They are also commonly called *Scriniarii <note>shrine-keepers or archivists</note>, so that they should keep everything secret in their hearts as if in a shrine.* <note>original German: "so alles in ihrem Hertzen, als in einem Schrein geheim behalten sollen"</note>

In former times, Notaries were also called *Chartulary Judges*; because they were certainly privileged by the Emperor so that whoever wished could litigate before them. *Thus, even to this day, power is given before them, protests and appeals are filed, and other such acts are performed which otherwise properly belong to the authorities and the holders of the courts.* <note>translated from the original German</note>

He is also called a *Public Servant* <note>original: "Servus publicus"</note>: not because a Notary is a slave by condition—for a slave cannot be a Notary, as slaves are considered as nothing; *indeed as dead, according to the law 'concerning servitude,' 209, in the Digest on the Rules of Law.* Rather, he is so called because he ought to be, and is bound to be, of service by virtue of his office to all who implore and require his duty, to the poor and the rich alike. Schneidewein, in *section 'when however an impubes,' number 7, in the Institutes on adoption.*

*Therefore, when one lays out silver and gold for them and thus retains them <note>original: "subarrihret," referring to an earnest-money payment</note>, they must allow themselves to be employed. Thus, the very same Notary who delivers a retort or protest for one person can immediately be required to deliver a counter-protest to the person he previously served. Although Lord Dr. Harprecht differentiates this in his treatise on retorts: for Notaries do not lease out their labor to a person like Advocates do, but rather they remain and ought to be entirely impartial.* <note>translated from the original German</note>

No one, however, can create Public Notaries except the Emperor or the King of the Romans, or even the Pope in the Lands of the Church, or those to whom the power of creating Notaries has been granted by a singular Privilege. Those to whom this power is granted are commonly called Counts Palatine (but without a County); see Bornitius, *On Instruments, book 2, title 14*; Cnaustius, *On the Notariate, pages 3, 4, and following*; and add my own work, *On Majesty, page 260.*

Regarding the form and manner of creating Notaries, see Jacob Bornitius, *On the Differences of Instruments, book 2, chapter 16, where in the section 'furthermore,' etc.* he says: *A Notary is also invested by means of a reed or pen: with the handing over of his proper tools, such as pen, paper, ink, and writing instruments.* <note>translated from the original German</note> Likewise by the tradition of a golden Ring and the placing of a simple Biretta <note>a doctoral or professional cap</note>,

They are also granted a unique Sign, commonly called a <term>Notary Signet</term> <note>original: "Notariat-Signet und Zeichen"</note>, which is attached to legal Instruments to guarantee their testimony. It is not permitted to seal documents with another’s seal; however, if the official signet happens to be missing, he may use his own signet ring in its place, with the following clause: **In the absence of my Notary signet, confirmed with my usual personal seal.** <note>original German: "In Mangel meines Notariat-Zeichens, mit meinem gewöhnlichen Pitschier bekräfftigt."</note>

Seven Notaries were established in the city [of Rome] by Pope Clement, across the seven regions, for the purpose of diligently recording the deeds of the Martyrs. These seven Notaries were overseen by seven Deacons, and these were called Regional Notaries <note>Latin: "Regionarii"</note> because they were divided among the seven Regions. Their office and regional division did not quickly disappear, as they were still present in the city during the time of Popes Adrian and Paschal.

Notaries either choose their own Sign, or it is given to them by their Creator <note>the authority who appoints them, such as the Emperor or Pope</note>. They also usually add some motto or proverb in place of a Symbol, as they say. This Notary Sign itself ought to be chosen from many with such judgment that it remains permanent and is retained; the Notary should not, perhaps out of regret, choose another to use later. For if he did, it could easily happen that he would be accused not only of fickleness but even of forgery. Indeed, the custom of some who use printed type for their Signs does not please me. It is better to use hand-drawn Signs. For this reason, they are called manual signs, **hand-marks, which are to be drawn and made by a free hand.** <note>original German: "Handzeichen, die aus freyer Hand gezogen und gemacht seyn sollen."</note> See Cnautius, *On the Art of the Notary.*

The writing of a Notary alone is not believed without witnesses. See the *Novels* <note>The "Novels" or *Novellae Constitutiones* were the final part of Emperor Justinian's body of civil law</note> constitution 6, collection 4, and constitution 49, chapter "but even if" <note>Latin: "sed etsi"</note> collection 6; and as others teach following the Gloss in the general law, *Code on book-keepers, book 10.* This was also established by the most recent Ordinance published by the Divine Maximilian I <note>Holy Roman Emperor</note> at Cologne in the year [15]12, in the **section "and according to the common law,"** <note>original German: "§. und nach dem von gemeinen Rechten."</note> where among other things required for the solemnity of Instruments by both Common Law and Custom, it is stated **that witnesses be brought in, whose names and surnames shall all be clearly described therein.** <note>original German: "daß die Zeugen darzu genommen, deren aller Namen und Zunamen klärlich darinn beschrieben werden sollen."</note> On whether a Notary provides more proof than a single witness, see Valasco, *Consultation 89.* Can he draft a Will outside his territory by consent of the parties? See Valasco, *Consultation 9.* Also, can a Notary be counted among the witnesses? See Bernhard **Herzog in the Instruction on Testaments, title 5.**

But more on Notaries can be found in Kitzel in his individual disputations; Chockier *on exemptions, volume 2, part 1*; and Speid in the *Sylloge, parts 1 and 2, under the word Notarius.*

**Question:** Whether, and in which cases, may a Notary name himself in a Will? It is beyond doubt that, as a rule, a Notary is prohibited from naming himself or a son remaining under his legal power, under penalty of forgery <note>original: "falsi." Under Roman law, the Lex Cornelia de Falsis punished the forgery of wills and documents</note>. *Law 'quis' 6. Digest on the Cornelian Law regarding forgery. Bald. counsel 96. n. 3. book 2. & counsel 92. num. 3. book 5. Farinac. p. 8. throughout.* This very rule is, however, limited unless the testator himself signs with his own hand, stating that the Notary wrote it by his command. *Farinac. d. p. 8. num. 201. & following.* Or unless the Notary named himself for the purpose of a debt owed as a fee. *Farinac. part 8. n. 218.* where he also adds other limitations. See also *Tuschus p. 5. practical conclusions letter N. conclusion 77. The praised Mr. Brinckmann, in the cited place, Position XI. question 18.*

Where does the word **Notary** come from? Their definition, requirements, and the jests cast against them. *Mr. Felwinger in 'The Judge' p. 477. following. On the Refutation of the Legality of Notaries. Nuremberg Statutes 8. l. 2.* Legality, upon which the credibility of an instrument depends, must be proven above all else. *Ant. Taffara* wrote on the errors of Notaries; *Honthemius* wrote on the Art of the Notary. To these add *Satler's Notary Book, Adam Volckmann, and Höpingk on the Law of Seals.* Regarding ungodly Notaries, see *Schneidew. on the Institutes p. 837. num. 10.* A Notary cannot draw up instruments through the mediation of an Interpreter <note>meaning the Notary must understand the parties directly to ensure accuracy</note>. *Bald. on law 'judices' 12. num. 5. Code on sentences & interlocutories. Mantic. on conjectures of last wills book 3. title 13 n. 2.* Is a Notary presumed to have been requested? ### 30. Notoriety. *Notorietas.*

Every Notorious fact, to be called "notorious," requires two companions: namely, appearance and existence. Notoriety is a certain addition to an Entity, and therefore, unless the substance is established, the notoriety—which is a quality—cannot be established. *Bald. in c. bona n. 22. on elections. Dec. in c. consuluit. n. 3. on appeals. Felin in c. super literis. num. 32. on rescripts.* For it is impossible to prove a quality without the substance: since accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, an 'accident' is a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing</note> cannot be understood outside of a subject. Therefore, the truth must be proven first, and afterwards, that it is notorious. *Mascard. on probations conclusion 1103 num. 21. Farinac. qu. 21. n. 108.* where he cites many, and in *n. 18 says* that many things are called notorious which nevertheless are not, and that notoriety is spoken of daily while what it actually is remains unknown. *Clar in pr. Crim. §. fin. quaest. 9.*

And it must be noted in practice: when a Judge proceeds upon a notorious crime, the Order of Judgment <note>the standard sequence of legal steps</note> ought to be preserved; that is, the party ought to be summoned so that he 

<column-break/>

may be able to defend himself and bring forth his excuses. This is because a thing cannot be called notorious when either the party itself being present denies it, or if he is absent and was not summoned. Following *Ancharan. Butr. Peregrin. Boss. Menoch. & others; Franc. Anton. Costa Counsel 1. num. 122. See also Vincent. Caroc. on remedies against Sentences exception 17. f. 24.*

And those Doctors who say that a summons is not required in a notorious case, but that one may proceed to a declaratory judgment lightning-fast <note>original: "fulminanter," meaning an immediate, thunderous legal action without the usual delays</note>, understand this to apply only when the crime, its qualities, and its circumstances are all notorious, and when it is notoriously established and certain that the Accused has no defense nor any just excuse. *Genovese Practice Ant. cap. 23. n 16. Felin. in c. sacro on sentences of excommunication. Riccius decision 241. p. 1.* For if the crime were indeed notorious, but its qualities and circumstances were not, since a defense might be available to the delinquent, the party must by all means be summoned, and the Judge must receive proofs regarding the notoriety according to the Order of Law. *Aemil. Ferret. counsel 31. n. 33. p. 1. Farinac. question 21. n. 99. & following. Costa d. loc. n. 123. following.* where he has much to say on the notorious and notoriety. In *n. 129. & following* he teaches how one should understand the saying that a confession made in court creates "Notoriety of Law." Likewise, notoriety may be induced and proven through Acts brought into the Court, and whatever is done in court may be called notorious to the Judge. Likewise, notoriety may be induced by many witnesses legitimately examined, as well as from Instruments, and finally from a sentence because of its authority, etc. It would be absurd, he says, to understand the said conclusions simply: for if we speak of a Confession made in Court, Acts, witnesses, or Instruments, these never create notoriety unless the opposing party has been given a deadline and the case has been concluded; for although the lack of a right may be established from the acts, it is not said to be established until the conclusion of the case, etc.

<header>Letter N.</header>

contains. Axiom 13. Many things are called "notorious" <note>In legal terms, *notorium* refers to a fact so obvious or well-known that it requires no formal proof in court.</note> which are not. Axiom 14. When a notorious fact is charged, it is said to be established "clearer than light." Axiom 15. Regarding Notorious facts, see the Case of Emperor Justice against Frederick of the Palatinate and his *Apologies*, where this matter is most accurately disputed by both sides. The law <note>original: "l. 6. §. nunciatores. ff. ad SC. Turpill." Referring to the Digest of Justinian.</note> takes "notorious" to mean evidence of a crime. Augustine, in Letter 160 to Aprigonius, calls it *Notaria*, as do Apuleius in book 7 of *The Golden Ass* and Trebellius in his life of Claudius, although Baronius observes in volume 1 that Augustine, in Letter 150 to Marcellinus, says *Notoria* rather than *Notaria*. Hermann Hugo, in *On the First Origin of Writing* (page 196), as well as Sichard and Pacius, report that there are those who would establish proof even for a thing that is certain, evident, and notorious. This is rightly rejected by them. For those things which are evident do not need proof. And those things which are notorious ought not to be proven, but at least must be proposed or alleged in court, according to Mynsinger and Mascardus. Even if there is some proof of the evident or notorious, it is certainly not proof of the fact itself (since it is established to all that such things are true), but rather proof that the fact is indeed "notorious" if that notoriety is denied. See Ummius in *On Process* (page 629 in my edition).

It is not enough for a fact to be notorious unless the specific qualities or circumstances of that fact are also notorious. Denaisius in *Disputation on the Right of Pure Command*. Notoriety carries with it a sense of public scandal. Marcus Antonius, book 3, resolution 11. On when a declaratory sentence is required for something to be considered notorious, see book 1, resolution 50.

A notorious fact, while it does not excuse one from the burden of alleging it in court, does relieve one of the burden of proving it. Schneidewin on the *Institutes*, page 716. Notoriety is obscured by any controversy, or by a probable cause for doubt. Marcus Antonius, book 1. A notorious injustice is considered equal to a notorious nullity.

### 31. **Self-Defense.** <term>Moderation of blameless defense</term> <note>original: "Moderamen inculpatæ tutelæ." This is the legal principle that one may use force in self-defense, provided it is proportional and only as much as is necessary to repel an attack.</note>
->The moderation of blameless defense.<-

The <term>moderation of blameless defense</term> is said to occur when a person could not defend themselves in any other way; this is properly called a "necessary defense," or in the common tongue, *a true self-defense* <note>original German: "ein rechte Nothwehr"</note>. This applies when the defense is of such a kind and degree as the necessity demands. Therefore, he who commits a homicide within the limits of "blameless defense" (with a true self-defense) is not to be punished. Indeed, such a homicide is excusable not only by the <term>Law of the Forum</term> <note>Human/Civil law</note> but also by the <term>Law of Heaven</term> <note>Divine/Moral law</note>, as taught by Peter Binsfeld, Vasquius, Graevaeus, and August Vischer in his treatise on unforeseen duels. For that which is done by permission of the law deserves no punishment. All laws and all legal systems permit one to repel force with force <note>original: "vim vi repellere." A fundamental maxim of Roman law.</note>.

<sig>Besold, Volume I.</sig>

<column-break/>

All laws permit this. Farinaccius in *Criminal Practice*, Gail, and Berlichius; add also Master Bullaeus in his *Academic Discourses*. He who acts by the permission of the law does not act against the law; hence he does not commit a crime and should not be punished. For where there is no crime, there should be no punishment.

However, if someone was indeed provoked but exceeded the <term>moderation of blameless defense</term>, they are to be punished not with the ordinary penalty (as a murderer), but with an <term>extraordinary penalty</term> <note>A lesser, discretionary punishment used when the full criteria for a capital crime were not met.</note>, specifically for the degree to which they exceeded the limit. This is because <term>malice</term> <note>original: "dolus"</note>—which must be present for an ordinary penalty to apply—is absent here. In a person who has been provoked, the law does not presume a malicious intent to kill, but rather the necessity of defense. As the saying goes: "Wounds are not given by measure," nor can a provoked person hold a scale in their hand to ensure they strike no harder than intended. Tiraquell, *On Temporary Penalties*. Therefore, some degree of forgiveness is due to one who, having been provoked, wished to avenge himself; the state of an angry mind is rightly taken into account. See my own *Disputation on Homicide* among the Tübingen disputations, and my *Commentary on Justice and Law*.

**35. Benefit, Clause: to my benefit and the benefit of mine. Utility, Clause: for my utility and that of my people.** <note>original: "Nußen. Utilitas."</note>
The effect of this clause is considered to be of small importance, and its utility consists in this: namely, that it should not appear that the loan was given to the debtor for gambling or some other extravagance. For such a loan is not recovered if the one giving the loan was a fellow-gambler, or if the one receiving the loan was a spendthrift. In which case, the debtor will not be helped by the Macedonian exception against the creditor. Speckhan, <term>century</term> 3, <term>question</term> 28, <term>class</term> 28.
So too, a loan given to a City, a Church, or a ward <note>original: "pupillo"</note> is not recovered otherwise than if it clearly appears that it was turned to their benefit, as in the cited law, number 23.
Furthermore, it is true that if someone contracts with a person likely to consume the loan soon, such a contract is so invalid by Law that it cannot even be confirmed or made valid by an oath: As Alciatus wished in the chapter *cum contingat*, <term>number</term> 206, under the title *on oaths*, through law *si quis* 8, of the <term>Digest</term> regarding buyers.
Therefore, this clause creates a presumption that the money was truly converted to the benefit of the debtor, until the contrary is proven. Unless, however, the person is such that they cannot receive a loan, such as sons under paternal power, etc.

### 36. New Wine. *Vinum novum.*

Walther treats the question of when new wine should be drunk in *On the Privileges of Doctors, page 88, at the end*, and touches upon the question on *page 7, Law 10, regarding the distribution of military rations, book 12, title 37*: We command through all provinces that the <term>ration</term> <note>original: "annonam." The state-controlled grain and food supply.</note> of new wine be given to all units and soldiers starting from the month of November, since the distribution of old wine seems too costly. Lucas de Penna, in his most laborious reading of the last three books of the Code, in *said book 10, page 149*, wasted many words on the derivation of the month of November and in untying the question of whether cheese is also included under the term "rations," since it is good for the use of soldiers; there, following the Archdeacon at *distinction 4*, he brings up the manifold uses of cheese. He ought rather to have shown what should properly be understood by "units" <note>original: "numeros." Referring to military cohorts or divisions.</note> in this law, regarding the meaning of which word our legal experts deal in *Law "What he says" 2, section "army" 1, on those who are noted with infamy; in Law "from that time" 42, of the Digest on military wills; in Law 1, section "if any of the soldiers" 2, of the Digest on the possession of goods from a military will.* He should have shown us which wine should properly be called "newly-made" or "new," and which should be called "old." For Law *If anyone [bequeaths] wine 9, final section, joined with laws 10, 11, and 12 of the Digest on legacies of grain, wine, or oil*, teaches that this point is not so clear in the law. There, if "old wine" is bequeathed, it is said first that this legacy must be estimated from the habit of the testator—how many years old the wine was that the testator used as "old." But if that does not appear, it is added secondly that "old" must be understood as that which is not "new" (a definition taken from the removal of the opposite, which are not infrequent in Law); that is, wine of the previous year is included in the term "old." For if they observed it otherwise, what end or what beginning would be taken for the end of the "old"? And in this sense, Johann de Platea in his *lecture on said law 10, page 133, column 3*, correctly writes: It is clear here that wine is called "old" once it passes a year, and "new" when it has not yet completed a year. But in last wills, "old wine" is understood to be even two or three years old. If it was not provided by the contracting parties that equally good wine should be returned, it is nevertheless not permitted for a debtor to return new wine for old—and thus an inferior thing of the same kind. *Law "When anything" 3, of the Digest on credited things, if a certain thing is sought.* Ludovicus de Ponte Romanus, as if this were said to everyone, writes thus in his *Singular 375*: You should know how to prove to me through the Law that new wine ought to begin to be drunk on the first day of the month of November, and the drinking of the old be ceased; say that it is the <term>text</term> in Law "We command," Code on the distribution of military rations. Bartolus, in his *commentary on said Law 10, page 50, column 3*, thinks this should be noted against a guardian who, after the first of November, made the household of a ward drink old wine; he is held to make good the loss from his own funds that the ward feels in his family estate, because he ought to have made them drink new wine, since the distribution of the old was wasteful. ### 37. Recently. Nuper.

### 38. Novation. Neuerung. Novatio.

Novation <note>The legal act of replacing an existing obligation with a new one, thereby extinguishing the old debt</note> is not understood to have occurred today unless it was expressly and by name agreed upon between the parties, stating: **hereby the old obligation shall be dead and settled.** Master Ludwig's *Notes on Wesenbeck* on *Novations*, number 6. Therefore, whether these words are inserted into the later obligation—**and the previous obligation shall remain uncancelled**—or if the intent to "novate" <note>create a new legal debt</note> is simply not expressed in the later document, the original obligation remains. In this difficult matter, Master Doctor Biccius reported a victory in legal practice against a jurist of great name. Novation is not to be presumed where it is not apparent. *The final law of the Code on Novations*. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, 6, Thesis 3, letter a. Decius, in *Counsel 400*, number 9, limits this when he says: in compatible contracts, such as a partnership or a loan, a novation is considered to have occurred even today, even if it is not expressly acted upon. This is supported by Baldus in his commentary on the *Code*, and in his *Counsels*, volume 1. Gabriel Romanus, book 3, *Conclusions on the title of Novation*, conclusion 1, number 160. Cagnolus, in his *Repetition of Singular Laws*, number 130, testifies that this limitation is approved by the common opinion of the Doctors of Law. Discussed at length by Barbosa, book 12, chapter 22, *Axiom 1*: Novation is a type of payment. *Axiom 2*: Novation is made by verbal stipulation alone. Master Doctor Ludwig.

### 39. New Testament. Novum Testamentum.

# Letter N.

Singer’s *Politics*, chapter 28. Bocer’s *On the Crime of Lese-Majesty*, chapter 2, number 90. Polydorus Ripa’s treatise *On Nighttime*, chapters 40 and 89. The ancients divided the night into specific parts, the first of which they called **lamp-lighting** <note>original Greek: "λύχνων ἁφὰς"</note> or "at the first torch," likewise "when the lights are lit." After this followed **advanced night**, **the time of silence** <note>original: "conticinium"</note>, **bed-time** <note>original: "concubia nox"</note>, **the dead of night** <note>original: "intempesta"</note>, **midnight**, **cock-crow**, etc., concerning which Censorinus's *On the Birthday* should be consulted.

It must be known generally that, in ancient times before the era of the Seleucids <note>A Hellenistic empire (312–63 BC) following Alexander the Great</note>, the division of hours we use today was unknown. Instead, the Jews divided the day roughly into darkness and light, evening and morning. They divided that entire interval, which the Greeks call the **nychthemeron** <note>original Greek: "νυχθήμερον"; a full 24-hour period of day and night</note>, into quarters which they called **watches** <note>original: "vigilias"</note>, just as the Romans and Greeks did.

The first quarter lasted from sunset to midnight, which in the Holy Scriptures is called **evening** <note>original Greek: "ὀψὲ"</note>. This was followed by the second quarter, called the **middle watch**, from midnight to the rising sun; it was so named because it was cast between two suns, namely between the setting of the previous light and the rising of the following light. Next was the **morning watch**, from sunrise to noon, which in the Gospel is called **early morning** <note>original Greek: "πρωΐα"</note>. The last and fourth watch was midday, from the sixth hour to the twelfth, and the setting of the sun. Our Lord mentions the **second and third watch** in Luke 12. In Mark, the first part is called **evening** <note>original Greek: "ὀψὲ"</note>, the second **midnight** <note>original Greek: "μέσον νύκτας"</note>, and the third **cock-crow** <note>original Greek: "ἀλεκτοροφωνία"</note>. Among the Arabs, Persians, and other Eastern nations, the custom remains even today to mark the day not by clocks, but by the natural intervals of morning, noon, and evening. Scaliger records these matters in *On the Emendation of Time*, book 1, in the chapter on hours and the remaining parts of the day, and in book 7 on Jewish reckoning.

Similarly, the Romans in their camps divided the night into four watches. Because it seemed impossible, as Vegetius says in *On Military Matters*, book 3, chapter 8, for individuals to remain awake on watch through the entire night, the watches were divided into four parts by the **water-clock** <term>clepsydra</term> <note>A device that measures time by the flow of water</note>, so that it was not necessary to stay awake for more than three nocturnal hours. From this come those formulas found in historians: "In the first, second, or third watch," etc. One should consult Lipsius, book 1 of *On Roman Military Matters*, dialogue 9; Rupert’s *Observations on Florus*, book 4, chapter 2, section 37: *Nocturnal attacks*. Also book 2, chapter 17, section 14: *Nocturnal battles*; book 3, chapter 5, number 23. Bernegger’s *Questions on Tacitus*, 199. You may add the naval battle of Gorgopa by moonlight in Xenophon, *Greek History*, book 5, page 545.

A **Nocturnal Despoiler** <note>original: "Nocturnus Populator"</note> is the name given to one who wastes fields, sets fire to crops, cuts vines, or brings damage to trees at night. See the *Gloss* on the law *C. qu. unic. lic. se sine Jud. vind.* Marta, *Newest Digest*, volume 2, title on despoilers, chapter 1, section 2. Such a person, just like a bandit, may be killed by anyone for the sake of the public good. Join this with Prospero Farinacci, book 4 of *Criminal Practice*, title 14, question 125, number 204 and following. Hilliger on Donellus, book 17, chapter 2, letter 9, where he says near the end: "This is, I believe, the one case in which killing is permitted for the defense of property,

<column-break/>

viewed not so much as a private offense or loss inflicted, but for the sake of public peace." Master Struve, *On Private Vengeance*, chapter 3, aphorism 6. According to the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BC</note>, a **night thief** may simply be killed. Master Struve, *On Private Vengeance*, chapter 4, aphorism 10, numbers 3, 4, 5, 6.

Regarding **Nocturnal Rites**, called "Nyctileia," Servius testifies in his commentary on the *Aeneid*, book 4, why Bacchus was called the "Nyctileian Father." As Ovid says in book 1 of *The Art of Love*:

> Pray to the Nyctileian Father, and the nocturnal rites,
> That they might command the wine not to harm your head.

And in *Metamorphoses*, book 4, story 1, he is called **Nyctileus** <note>A name for Bacchus/Dionysus meaning "He of the Night"</note>. See Neander in the *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 205 and following.

Things that happen at night are difficult to prove. Barbosa, book 12, chapter 25, axiom 4: "An act done at night carries as much weight as one done by day." (See more fully at axiom 3). "Night hinders the recognition of a person," axiom 2. "Crimes committed at night should be punished more severely," axiom 1. Formerly in the Roman Senate and forum, the Law of the Twelve Tables was observed: **"Let the setting of the sun be the final limit"** <note>original: "Sol occasus suprema tempestas esto"</note>; that is, let it be the final deadline for legal judgments when the sun sets. See Master Rupert on the title *De O. I.*, chapter 18, section 31. **Judgment should not be given at night.** Master Biccius in *Aureis*, page 759. Berlich, volume 1, conclusion 74, number 1. C. Rittershuf in *The Novellae*, page 527, number 61. Because of **staying out all night** <note>original: "abnoctationem"</note> outside the house without a probable and just cause, against her husband's will, a husband may divorce his wife; see the same work, page 228, number 5. Regarding **sleepwalkers**, see Master Speidel in *Notable Matters* under the word **Schlaffgänger** <note>German for "Sleepwalkers"</note>. Vischer, *On Duels*, page 587 and following. Langius, volume 2. Levinus Lemnius, book 2 of *On the Occult Miracles of Nature*, chapter 5. Johann Horst and Tandler. I conceive of no ornament in this vast machine of the world without variety and the distinct alternation of things. Not far from the market town of Tribur on the Rhine stands an apple tree which bears apples every year on Christmas night. In a good year, they grow as large as a bean, yet are shaped like a tiny apple, complete with blossoms, stem, and other parts, hard and stiff; in other years, however, they are only the size of a pea. Within a single hour, the tree achieves its bloom and fruit, a phenomenon observed with great diligence by the inhabitants according to the Old Calendar. At other times of the year, it bears wild crab apples, which are like any others of their kind. If legal instruments <note>original: "Instrumenta"; legal documents or contracts</note> were completed around midnight, which day should be assigned to them? See Felinus on chapter 1, number 9, regarding the reliability of instruments; also Lord Birckmann on Notaries, Position 40, question 71.

Regarding individual nights, that is, for individual 24-hour periods: see Berlichius, part 2, conclusion 34, number 53. Why a transaction may be made at night, though a legal sentence may not: Giphanus in *Legal Process*, pages 157 and 74. Regarding things that happen at night, people are rightly presumed to be ignorant; see Everhardus extensively at location 107, number 2. Regarding the proof of things done at night, see the same. If a crime is committed at night, it is presumed to be premeditated, for the law presumes against one acting under the cover of night. Rudinger, century 3, observation 81, number 3. On the **Twelve Nights** <note>original German: "Von zwölff Nächten"; likely referring to the Rauhnächte, the twelve days of Christmas associated with supernatural events</note>: Lord Johann Michael Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 822, section 15.

Night is opportune for ambushes and secret machinations; hence Menander says: <term>Night is the leader of many evils <note>original Greek: "την νυκτα πολλων ειναι αρχηγον κακων"</note></term>. Night is the author and guide of very many evils. The ancient Royal Law of Romulus stated: "Do not hold nightly vigils." The Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law (c. 450 BC)</note> cautioned that no one should stir up nocturnal gatherings in the city. The Gabinian Law decreed that whoever stirred up secret assemblies in the city should be punished by capital punishment according to the custom of the ancestors. See the declamation of Porcius Latro against Catiline. Furthermore, King Agesilaus of the Spartans suggested to his Lacedaemonians that it should be permitted to kill those who organized nocturnal gatherings during the time of the Theban incursion without a trial, as recorded by Aelian in book 4 of *Various Histories*, chapter 27. Likewise, following the same reasoning, Liagondas, the Legislator of the Thebans, abolished all nocturnal sacred rites because he feared they might serve as veils for secret gatherings.

The mother of dreams, the gentle, quiet, weary, pitch-black, Moor-colored queen of shadows, the gatekeeper of rest, the dispeller of cares. She is the princess of darkness, the heroine who leads the starry host on watch with silver-bright armor and, as a victorious princess, chases away the sunbeams. The bright luster of this goddess resembles the peacock's eye-tail, which spreads into a circle, guides so many heavenly lights, and discovers the blue tent above the great field of heaven. Night brings many thousands of suns and is the high fountain of moisture. Night is depicted as a stout female figure, crowned with poppy heads (because such seeds induce sleep), having on her

<column-break/>

back two large black wings; her clothing is black, full of bright stars. Before her lie two small children marked with broken or crooked feet, of which one is white and the other brownish; the former is said to signify Sleep, and the latter Death, as our late Lord G. P. Harsdörffer <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658), a celebrated German poet and scholar</note> testifies from the writings of Philostratus.

On the word **to spend the night** <note>original German: "benachten"; to be overtaken by night or to secure something for the night</note>, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 9, page 151, where he describes a gate made half of boards and topped with transparent railings, which is closed during the night hours.

The circumstance of night-time does not necessarily aggravate the crime of theft: Marius Antonius, book 3, resolution 20, chapter 4, although it does induce a presumption against one acting at night: the same author, book 3, resolution 37, number 5. Legal proceedings are prohibited from being held at night: Giphanus in *Legal Process*, my copy page 73, end.

### 41. Necessity. <note>original German: "Noth"; Latin: "Necessitas"</note>

In a state of necessity, no legal relief is given to one who has set resources aside, and therefore one who has brought great distress upon himself is not to be assisted. One ought not to be forced to restrict oneself to doing something, even if one is capable of doing it; for the law does not require that a person do everything they are physically able to do. Hartmann Hartmann, book 2 of *Miscellany*, chapter 1, observation 13.

If necessity does not demand it, the Country or the Law does not grant a remission of duty. Barbosa, book 12, chapter 5, axiom 1. When the cause of necessity ceases, that which was granted or introduced because of that necessity also ceases. Axiom 2. Necessity that one brings upon oneself voluntarily is not assisted by the law. Axiom 3. Regarding those who are obligated by necessity, legal interpretations ought to be more favorable than if they were obligated by their own free will. Axiom 4. Necessity does not permit one to sin. Axiom 5. In times of necessity, legal privileges are silent <note>Meaning they are temporarily suspended</note>. Axiom 6. Necessity and piety are held as legal equals. Axiom 7. Inevitable necessity does not allow the specific form of a law to be fulfilled by a mere equivalent action. Axiom 8. Necessity does not deserve a reward. Axiom 9. For the sake of avoiding necessity, many things are granted which would be prohibited if they were done purely by choice. Axiom 10. Not everything permitted to a judge’s power is subject to the necessity of the law. Axiom 11. Necessity is close to force; indeed, force is nothing other than necessity imposed on a contrary will, and vice versa, necessity is force to which we succumb unwillingly. Axiom 12. No necessity excuses that which could have been avoided. Axiom 13. In moral matters, the necessity of the end creates the right. Axiom 14. Things done because of necessity ought not to be used as legal precedents for general arguments. Axiom 15. Necessity has no law <note>The famous maxim "Necessitas non habet legem"</note>. Axiom 16. Jacob Ayrer, in the *Historical Process*, part 2, chapter 2, page 473. Necessity makes lawful what is otherwise not lawful by right. Axiom 17. By necessity, many things become permissible which are normally prohibited by law. Jacob Ayrer, part 1, chapter 8, observation 4, number 20. Things done out of necessity are not considered to be done in fraud. Axiom 18. In times of necessity, no one is expected to be generous. Axiom 19. When necessity is urgent, every legal immunity is removed. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 8.

Letter N.

Book 8, chapters 3, 11, and 45. Human necessity, which gives rise to the secondary law of nations <note>original: "juri Gentium secundario"; laws common to all civilized peoples</note>, is of two kinds. The first is simple and absolute, which is evident in the distinction of ownership, the acquisition of things, the use of commerce, and the obligation of contracts. The other kind is conditional, based on the hypothesis of human malice, which takes place in wars, captivities, and slavery. After Bach, Lord Doctor Biccius in his "Golden Preludes," thesis 34, letter q. **Necessity breaks iron** <note>original: "Necessitas frangit ferrum"; a legal proverb meaning that extreme need can override strict laws</note>. Rittershusius in the *Novellae*, page 467, number 8, and page 149, number 4. Necessity makes room for "payment in kind" <note>original: "dationi in solutum"; giving an item instead of money to settle a debt</note>, see the same. There are legal scholars today who can be compared to necessity, for they know no law. Walther on the *Privileges of Doctors*, page 490. The word "must" <note>original Latin: "oportet"</note> designates only a moral necessity. Hugo Grotius, book 2, *On the Law of War and Peace*, number 1 at the end; see Cujacius on law 84, section 1, regarding the Rules of Law. Juridical College of Strasbourg regarding things entrusted, thesis 27, number 3. Salmasius, title *On Usury*, chapter 5, page 110. Regarding **Friends in Need**, see the elegant little treatise by Schuppius.

**Need, Suffering, Fear, Hate.** These four words are transposed 24 times <note>referring to a linguistic or poetic exercise in permutation</note>. Lord G. P. Harsdörffer, of blessed memory.

It is not within a Lord's arbitrary will to burden his subjects with taxes; rather, **public necessity and utility** are required for this, as handed down by Ferrarius, *On Fiefs*, book 6, chapter 5; Franciscus Lucanus in his treatise *On the Privileges of the Treasury*, page 3, section 1. Obrecht in his *Political Deliberations on the Improvement of Land and People*, page 25. When the cause of necessity ceases, the extraordinary collection of taxes must also cease. Petrus Gregorius, *On the Republic*, book 3, chapter 9. Waremund ab Ehrenberg, *On Royal Subsidies*, chapter 8, number 11. In case of necessity, many things are permitted which are otherwise prohibited, as Zorer beautifully declares in part 1, question 1, number 170. Jean Bodin, *The Republic*, book 5, chapter 5, number 896. Add Nevizanus in *The Nuptial Forest*, book 5, under the title "How to Judge," number 48. Since necessity is a mighty weapon, subject to no law, but rather creates the law itself and cares for no privileges. Bullæus, Counsel 1, number 127. Regarding the word "must," when it does not imply absolute necessity; likewise the words "is bound" and "owes," see Everhardus, Location 93, number 17. Necessity excuses sales made for that reason. Zorer, part 2, question 4, number 317. Whether such things can be retracted and how, part 2, question 3, number 221 and following. How necessity may be recognized, see the same author, part 1, question 7, number 543. Johann Christoph Assum wrote *The Weapon of Necessity for the Poor*. On the different types of necessity: Knipschild, *On Family Entails of the Nobility*, chapter 11, number 461. Boërius, decision 44, number 27. Cacheranus, decision 167, number 5. A **Year of Need** <note>original: "Nothjahr"</note>, that is, a year of high prices and famine. Lord Johann Michael Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 571, section 27.

### 42. Noses. Nasus.

In Constantinople, a Bulgarian woman and her little daughter each wore a beautiful golden ring through their noses. Besold’s *Circuit*, Volume I.

<column-break/>

"As a golden [ring] in the nostrils [of a pig], so is a beautiful woman [without discretion]." <note>original Latin: "aureus in naribus ejus mulier pulchra"; a reference to Proverbs 11:22, though the text cites chapter 10</note> A beautiful woman is to her husband like a golden ring in the nose. Schweigger in his *Travel to Constantinople*, folio 43.

Emperor Rudolph was distinguished by an **aquiline nose** <note>a curved, eagle-like nose</note>, which they judged among the Kings of the Persians to be a mark of wisdom and a sort of "ivy of a good mind" suspended by nature. Caspar Dornavius on *Rudolph of Habsburg*, page 14. The Turks once sent five thousand noses from slain Christians, along with 40 banners and several prisoners, to Constantinople. Zeiller, century 5, *Letters*, page 94. The nostrils were cut off as a punishment for adulterers. C. Rittershusius in the *Novellae*, page 680, number 22. The reason why noses drip so much in winter, especially among children and old people, is because the brain is contracted by the cold, and children and the elderly have much moisture and waste within them. Zeiller, said century 5, page 394.

Regarding a girl with a fine nose, Catullus wrote: "Greetings, girl with a nose not of the smallest." <note>original: "Salve non minimo puella naso"</note> Regarding "turning the nose" <note>mocking or deceiving</note>, see Höppingk *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 14, number 28; discussed most extensively by Lord Harsdörffer in the *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, volume 113, pages 47 to 51.

Regarding the nose mentioned by Catullus, see Philippus Carolus in the *Manuscript Roman Library*. How should Catullus’s mention of a nose be understood? Is it about an excessive nose, which he uses to insult a certain girl? Nevertheless, he refers to these words of the Poet in poem 13:

> I will give you an ointment, which the Loves and Cupids
> gave to my girl:
> which, when you smell it, you will ask the Gods,
> Fabullus, to make you all nose.

### 43. Nassau. Nassovia.

Count Johann the Elder of Nassau fathered 25 children with his three wives: 14 with the first, 4 with the second, and 7 with the third and last. From these, he lived to see 57 grandchildren and 3 great-grandchildren, making 85 children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren in total. Lady Juliana of Nassau learned the Latin language quite well and was married in the year 1603 to Landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel. The wife of the Lord Count of Nassau-Saarbrücken, Lady Maria Elisabeth (daughter of the Lord Margrave of Baden-Durlach), spoke the Latin language very well, was well-instructed in philosophy, and wrote beautiful verses, as testified by Lord Harsdörffer in the second part of the *Ladies' Conversational Games*. Count Ludwig of Nassau, General of the Spanish Cavalry in the year 1604, contracted smallpox, from which he died at Arnhem, as Schadaeus testifies in Sleidan's *Commentaries*, book 29, part 3. That the Lords Counts of Nassau resided in Nuremberg, at the monastery grounds of the Barefoot Friars... <note>original: "Barfüssern"; referring to the Franciscan friars who wore sandals</note>

In the year 1645, on the very Kalends <note>the first day</note> of January, in St. Thomas Church in Strasbourg, the Princess Sibylla Magdalena—Marchioness of Baden and Hochberg and wife of John, Count of Nassau, Saarbrücken, and Saarwerden—was laid to rest and entombed. ### 44. Nuremberg. Norimberga.

The Republic of Nuremberg is called "Little Venice." Draco on *Patricians*, page 254. The Nuremberg Patricians are emulators of the Venetians. The same author, pages 206 and 267. A praise of the Nuremberg Republic, page 256. See my own work in the *Comparison of the Nuremberg Republic with the Venetian Republic*, published for the third time, in various places. 

Nuremberg, though situated on a completely sterile plain, is second to no other city in Germany in its abundance of goods, wealth, or size. The same is true for Bergamo in Italy. Besold in *Politics*, book 1, chapter 12, number 59, version 7. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 35, number 6. It is a **common workshop of the world** <note>original Greek: "κοινόv τι της γής εργαστήριοv"</note>. See the praised Lord Limnaeus, book 1, chapter 11, number 100, page 178. Nuremberg, by anagram: **Rule for the world** <note>original: "Orbi regna", an anagram of "Noriberga"</note>. See Vogel, century 1, song 6. Nuremberg has three waters—the Schwarzach, Pegnitz, and Regnitz—in its coat of arms, to which it added the half-eagle when they were incorporated into the Empire.

### 45. Nut. Nux Myristica.

Regarding nut oil, see the *Frankfurt Reformations*, part 2, title 7, § 12, regarding "eternal interest" <note>long-term financial rents paid in goods like oil</note>. The harvesting of hazelnuts is forbidden at certain times. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 2, number 49.

The trunk and tree of the nutmeg <note>original: "Muscatnüß"</note> look not unlike the peach tree, but it is not very tall. Before the nuts are quite ripe, they stand in bloom like an opened rose. When they ripen, they enclose the bloom and are then gathered. This happens in the month of harvest <note>September</note>. They expend no labor on it and sell them by the measure; one measure holds 26 pounds and is given for half a Batzen or a Carlin <note>small silver coins of the period</note>. Zeiller, century 5, *Epistles*, page 328.

<column-break/>

and following. It does not escape me that empty, wind-filled nuts without meat stay at the top of the liquid, while heavy ones, full of intact fruit, are carried to the bottom. Petronius, page 195. In the northern lands, hazelnuts grow in such quantity that several thousand barrels of them are transported from there to Germany. Zeiller, century 5, *Epistle*, page 1, 8. On the island of Hven, which was formerly inhabited by the descendants of the giant Hullnella, there was once a small woods of hazel bushes, none of whose nuts ever became worm-eaten. Zeiller, century 5, *Epistle*, page 51. Nuts were under the protection of Jupiter. The reasoning behind scattering nuts <note>at weddings</note>. Cypræus on *Betrothals*, page 106. Regarding nut-eaters on the island of Damma, see Johann Jacob Saar in *East Indies*, page 40.

### 46. Numbering. Numerare.

Regarding the principle of number, it is the same as regarding number itself. Barbosa, book 12, chapter 29, axiom 1. The plural number includes the singular. Axiom 2. A plural expression is satisfied by the number two. Axiom 3. Authority is preferred over number <note>meaning the quality or rank of witnesses/sources matters more than the quantity</note>. Axiom 4. The person of the elected does not increase the number, nor is he counted in the number of the electors. Axiom 5. Regarding those counted and those "supernumerary" <note>beyond the fixed number</note>. C. Rittershusius in the *Novellae*, page 551, number 10. The prolixity <note>wordiness</note> of numbers in legal instruments, page 295, number 7. Numerical notes or ciphers <note>digits as opposed to written words</note> do not hinder legacies today, unless they are obscure or confused. Page 296, number 8. What it means to be "referred into the numbers." See Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 8, number 140.

### 47. Nine in Number. Novenarius numerus.

The number nine is the highest and most perfect of all, which excludes and contains all others, yet cannot be increased by any number except by unity <note>one</note>. Scaliger, *Exercise* 365. Regarding the number nine, see Piccart's notes on Seneca’s *Medea*. The number nine was sacred to the Pythagoreans and Magi, to whom it is distributed because it arises from three threes. Three is a perfect number; "all good things should be three." Neander in *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 94. Three Graces, three Fates, a triple voice, three elements. Ibid. Furthermore, the number three is divine and sacred. Virgil in *The Sorceress Ciris*: "And nine times she binds the threads of three different colors." In the *Pharmacopoeia*: "Three times I surround you with these three-fold threads." In Statius Papinius, book 4 of the *Thebaid*, the mage at the beginning "pours out the generous liquors of Bacchus nine times into the hollowed earth." Pliny, book 28, chapter 4: some heal groin ailments by tying a thread pulled from a loom with nine and seven knots. Thus says Piccart. 

Regarding the years 7 and 9, what comes from them, and what are called the "Climacteric years" <note>perceived critical turning points in a person's life</note>; likewise regarding the year 56, which is called the "Heroic Climacteric," see Matthias Bernegger, question 114, from Tacitus. King Og of Bashan had an iron bed 9 cubits long. Deuteronomy 3:11. Meanwhile, following the advice of Horace, we have suppressed [a work]—not indeed for nine years, for we were not giving birth to an elephant, but for one and even a second...

...into another year. *Philipp Carolus in A Taste of Philology.*

Several people attribute perfection to the number nine. *Plutarch on Homer, page 56. Limnaeus in Public Law, book 3, chapter 1, number 33.* According to some opinions, the lark sings for three hours in the morning, three at noon, and three in the evening <note>A folkloric observation of 3+3+3 totaling nine</note>. The sixty-third year—since it is composed of the unlucky numbers seven and nine multiplied by one another [7x9=63] and creates a doubled evil—is a climacteric year <note>original: "climactericus"; a critical point in life thought to be dangerous or transformative, particularly the "Grand Climacteric" at age 63</note>. See extensively Christoph de Zobel in *Deschiz* and Bieland in *The Triumphal Chariot*, page 2, section 3. Market days for the Romans occurred every ninth day <note>original: "Nundinæ"; the Roman market cycle</note>. For since in the past most Romans led a rustic life and lived more often in the country than in the city, they came to the city every ninth day, as testified by Pliny, book 18, chapter 3, and Macrobius, book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 16. The *Trinundinum* <note>a period covering three market cycles</note> is three times nine, that is, it encompasses 27 days. *See C. Rittershusius on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 185 in my copy.*

### 48. Nature, the Law of Nature. *Natura, Lex Naturæ.*

A cleric ought not to learn physics <note>original: "Physicam"; here meaning natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</note>. *Sprenger in Fragments of Public Law, page 238.* *The Book of Nature* was printed by Johann Bämler at Augsburg in 1478. It is fitting to look precisely at and follow the nature of each thing. *Barbosa, book 12, chapter 3, axiom 1.* By natural law, all things are common. *Axiom 2.* The nature of a thing, not its accident <note>original: "accidens"; a non-essential or temporary quality in Aristotelian philosophy</note>, should be observed. *Axiom 3.* Nature yields to a miracle. *Axiom 5.* Nature and art do nothing in vain. *Axiom 11.* The nature of a thing should be attended to rather than its simple name. *Axiom 12.* What nature ordains remains eternal; and as Sophocles beautifully said in *Oedipus*, the laws given from heaven, of which God the Father alone is the author, are neither put to sleep by oblivion nor do they grow old. *Christoph Rupertus, dissertation 1 on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 6.* Everything that comes from nature is best. *Pindar, cited in Limnaeus, century 2, epistle 2.* Nature is content with little; see the verses, more elegant than elegance itself, by Christoph Rupertus on *Valerius Maximus*, book 4, chapter 3, in the *Political Dissertations*, and Lipsius, century 3, epistle 5: "I knew a happy man, not he who had what he wanted, but he who did not desire what was not granted by fate." See *Turkish Carpets*, page 35. Everything in excess is an enemy to nature. *G. C. Walther on the privileges of Doctors, page 182.*

Nature is painted in the form of an image with many breasts <note>A reference to the "Lady of Nature" or the "Artemis of Ephesus" archetype</note>, standing on a pedestal like a bust, with her outstretched arms bound to it with chains, signifying that nature is bound by fundamental causes. *Lord Harsdörffer.* On what is "nature naturing" and "nature natured" <note>original: "Natura naturans & natura naturata"; Scholastic terms for God as the creative force versus the created world</note>, see Eberhard, location 107, number 3 at the end. Nature does not make leaps <note>original: "Natura non facit saltum"; the principle that natural changes are gradual</note>. *Knipschild on Entailments, chapter 9, number 74.* Father Caspar Schott published *Curious Physics, or the Marvels of Nature*, comprised of twelve books, in quarto, at Würzburg in 1662. Martin Schockius wrote a *Diatribe on Natural Law*. To someone who was strenuously asserting that natural law is to be preferred to written law, Martin Luther

<column-break/>

replied: "It may be true, but therein lies the error: that everyone wants to imagine it resides precisely in his own head." *Zinckgref, German Apothegms, page 253.*

### 49. Naked. *Nudus.*

Regarding why the Africans go naked, *see Lord Harsdörffer in the German Secretary, part 3, title 27.* Why the Moors go naked, *in the same place, and part 10, title 33.* Not all Moors go naked. *Michael Hemmersam* in the *Description of West Indian Travels, page 39.* Once, those who were naked were blind to lust. *Limnaeus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, number 92.* In Mr. Führer’s *Travel Book* on leaf 108, a place is mentioned called Gerendel—in German, "a naked man"—for whoever wishes to go there must go naked so that he is not robbed by the thieves who live in the mountains <note>The logic being that robbers cannot take anything from someone who has nothing</note>. Naked people steal and hide things. *Michael Hemmersam* in the *Description of West Indian Travels*, which I published, *page 73.*

Regarding Silesian cities, the author of the *Silesian Grievances* writes on page 56: Many presented themselves naked or in their shirts—even though they were rich and wealthy merchants, distinguished doctors, and affluent citizens—leaving with their families, never again to ask after their possessions. But no. *The same is reported of Captain* Heinrich von Nebran, *in Abelin, part 2 of the European Theater, Year 1631, page 353.* On what it means to find "nakedness" in a wife, see *Albericus Gentilis, book 9 on Marriages, chapter 6; Bullæus in Counsel, page 358.* A naked man has this privilege: he cannot be stripped. <note>A legal paradox: one who has nothing is immune to further loss of property</note> *Law "itaque fallo" 12, in the preamble, Digest on Theft; single chapter on the restitution of stolen goods.* Regarding a non-resident, roaming criminal <term>Malefiz-Person<gloss>A person accused of a serious crime or "malefice"</gloss></term> who is alone, as they are girded with a belt, they must pay 7 1/2 pennies in passage money <term>Fürgang-Geld<gloss>A toll or fee paid for safe passage or to appear before a court</gloss></term> to present themselves. *Suttinger, observation 70, number 5, at the end.*

*Pliny complains about nature because he produced man—for whose sake all other creatures were made—weaker and more feeble than any other living thing. Indeed, he is cast into the world naked, without weapons and clothing, having no power of his own. Above all, nature clothes this one animal with the resources of others, while for the rest she has granted various coverings: shells, barks, hides, thorns, shaggy hair, bristles, fur, plumage, wings, scales, and fleeces. Even the trunks and trees she has protected from cold and heat with bark, sometimes a double layer. Only man is cast out naked on his birthday upon the naked ground, immediately to wailing and weeping; no other of so many animals is prone to tears, and these right at the very beginning of life.*

### 50. Note well.

Things that are noteworthy are usually specifically marked so they do not seem neglected. *Barbosa, book 12, chapter 17, single axiom.*

### 51. Nobody. <note>original: "Niemand. Nemo."</note>

No one gives what they do not have. <note>original: "Nemo dat, quod non habet."</note> *Barbosa, book 12, chapter 9, axiom 1.* No one can transfer more rights to another than they themselves possess. *axiom 2.* No one is seen to choose a path by which their own judgment would be subverted. *axiom 3.* No one is bound to do the impossible. <note>original: "Nemo tenetur ad impossibile"; a fundamental legal principle that one cannot be legally required to perform an impossible task.</note> *axiom 4.* **Nobody**, in whatever nobility, honor, dignity, or being they may be. *Limnäus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 35, number 27.* The word "to no one" <note>original: "nemini"</note> denotes an all-encompassing exclusion. *Marius Antoninus, book 1, final resolution, case 42.*

> Whom should I accuse, except that "No One" <note>original: "Utin"</note> of the Homeric Polyphemus? (None) *Lipsius, Single Century of Epistles, 17.* <note>A reference to the Odyssey, where Odysseus tells the Cyclops Polyphemus his name is "No One" (Outis/Utin) so that when he is attacked, the Cyclops cries out that "No One" is hurting him.</note>

### 52. Nightingale. <note>original: "Nachtigall. Luscinia."</note>

See *Clajus on the Resurrection, number 24.* The nightingale, in her perfect art of song, maintains the right beat; now she holds still, soon she sings several notes in one breath without change; now she bends her voice, now she sings a little softer, now with a trembling voice, now with a louder one; sometimes she makes short phrases, sometimes long ones.

->Hear, the artistic nightingale wakes,<-
->sips and laughs.<-

Regarding the Nightingale, see *Drexel in The Gold Mine, pages 159, 160, 161.* When the trees are in leaf and the herbs are springing up, for fifteen days and nights without ceasing, she pours out the clearest songs from her slender throat. Pliny asserts that a nightingale sang in the mouth of the infant Stesichorus <note>Stesichorus was a Greek lyric poet; such legends often suggested a child was destined for greatness in poetry or music</note>. One sold for six thousand sestertii—150 Thalers—which was white (otherwise a nearly unheard-of thing), to be given as a gift to Agrippina, the wife of Emperor Claudius. They have often been seen to sing when commanded, and to sing in turns. *Bembo in the History of Venice* writes concerning Columbus that he discovered six islands, which they call the Canaries, in which islands the nightingales sing in the month of November. *Spartanus said of the Nightingale:* You are a voice, and nothing more. <note>original: "Vox es, prætereaque nihil."</note>

When the nightingales that are kept in rooms strike up and begin to sing shortly after Christmas, summer will come soon; but if she sings slowly, then summer will be slow to arrive. *Johann Coler in Economics, book 15, chapter 42.* These sirens of the air, the fleeting little psaltery <note>a stringed instrument</note>, the noblest among those who swing the wing; she can constrain her voice to match the whispering brooks, the rider to the horse, singing songs of victory and mourning, etc. Soon, like the little water rustling through the rugged gravel, her master-voice is colorfully and swirlingly curled, so that the character of every tone is found within her tone.

->Around Orpheus’s grave there nest nightingales,<-
->with wonder-curled sounds.<-

->One hears the sweet nightingale,<-
->With her wonder-lovely sound,<-
->Counting the species of flowers.<-

<column-break/>

->The whitish-green leafy tree,<-
->Gives her love leaves and space,<-
->To choose the nest and roof.<-

*Mr. Dilherr in Contemplations of the World, Field, and Garden, page 362.*

### 53. Fixed by Nail. <note>original: "Nagelvest. Terræ affixa."</note>

If a house is sold with its movables and items attached to the walls, **whatever is riveted and nailed therein** <note>original: "nied- wied- und Nagelvest"; a legal term for fixtures that are permanently attached to a property</note>, for a single price. *Franzkius on Fines, chapter 16, number 375.* **With all that is riveted and nailed**, or **whatever is fixed to the earth, riveted, and nailed.** Included under this clause are those things which are attached, furnished, or built into the ground, partitions, and walls, which pass to the buyer as members of the house. *Argument from the law "scaphum" 44, etc.* However, those things which are not so fixed to the ground, even if they are kept in the house, are there for another use, and therefore are not acquired by the buyer. *Law "in vendendo" 60, etc.* Thus, images placed for pleasure do not pass with the sold house. *Goedd. on Law 241, number 2.* It is otherwise if they were attached to the house in such a way that they could not be removed without defacing it. *Vivius, opinion 202, number 4.* The same must be said if this clause is omitted in the instrument of sale, unless the parties have agreed otherwise, as *Carpzov* teaches in *Forensic Jurisprudence, part 2, constitution 33, definition 20,* etc., which the Nuremberg Reformation also follows.

Regarding what "rivet and nail" <note>original: "Nied und Nagel"</note> comprises, see also the laws concerning legacies and statues. Regarding what comes under the name of "appurtenances" <note>original: "Pertinentiarum"</note>, see *Socin, consultation 47.* *William Onciacus* teaches what constitutes the appurtenances of a house in question 44.

### 54. Once More. <note>original: "Nochmals. Rursus."</note>

The word **once more** <note>original: "nochmals"</note> joins a past time with a past and future time. *Schvvanmann in decision 10, number 51.*

The expression **once more**—in Latin *rursus, iterum, denuò, ulterius*—and what its effect is. *Klock, volume 3, consultation 182.*

Whether and how the words *rursus* (again), *iterum* (a second time), and *sæpius* (frequently) differ. *Boerius, decision 131, number 15.*

### 55. Unless. <note>original: "Nisi."</note>

What does the particle "unless" <note>original: "nisi"</note>, which is usually added in protocols to the calculation of deadlines, denote? *Schvvanmann, book 1, Proceedings of the Imperial Chamber, chapter 27, number 13.*

More on this particle in *Mr. Speidel, On the Nobility, page 224.* The word **unless** <note>original: "nisi"</note> has a restrictive force. *Marius Antoninus, book 1, final resolution, case 42.* The phrase **not unless** <note>original: "non nisi"</note> provides the form. *book 1, ref. 94.* If "if" <note>original: "si"</note> is used for "unless" <note>original: "nisi"</note>. *Forster, book of miscellaneous observations, last chapter.* The phrase **not otherwise** <note>original: "non aliter"</note> and the word **unless** <note>original: "nisi"</note> establish the legal form. *Nicolaus Losæus on the Law of Universities, part 3, chapter 5.*
