### 56. Negatives. <note>original: "Negativa."</note>

Concerning the proof of a negative. *Martinus de Fano and Franciscus Herculanus Perachinus in 8. Cologne 578; add Obrecht in the Disputation on the Proof of a Negative.*

A negative denies more than an affirmative confirms. *Marius Antoninus, Venetian Resolutions, book 1, resolution 20, number 7.* By whom a negative must be proved: *book 2, resolution 5, number 15 and following.* A negative is proved by those witnesses without whose presence the act could not have been carried out. *Klock, volume 1, consultation 10, numbers 710, 711.* A simple negative from a witness is valid when they testify about something that is likely known to the witness. *Klock, consultation 10, number 716.* A negative is proved by the production of a legal instrument and the reading of the records. *Klock, volume 1, consultation 29, numbers 95, 96.* For a negative to be proved by witnesses, it is necessary that the witnesses can remove the act from the senses <note>meaning they can testify that the event was not seen, heard, or perceived where it otherwise would have been</note>. *consultation 29, number 686.* A negative is effectively proved by those through whom an affirmative act ought to have been done: this is called a "determinate negative," and is restricted to the actions of certain persons. *Klock, consultation 29, numbers 878, 879.*

A double negative affirms. *Gæddaeus on the Meaning of Words, at law 237;* though not always. *ibid.* Whether one basing their case on a negative is bound to prove it. *Cævallos, question 145.* How a negative may be proved. *Lanfranco in Practice, title on witnesses, number 122.* Whether and which negatives must be proved. *Lanfranco, title on Proofs, at said law, number 4.*

A negation placed before or after a universal sign alters its nature and makes it equivalent to its opposite. *Everhard, Location 7, number 12; add Location 150, number 12.*

### 57. Neustadt. New City. <note>original: "Nova urbs."</note>

**Neustadt** is named from "new buildings." *Limnäus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 6, number 18.*

**New City** <note>original: "Nova Civitas"</note>, **Wiener Neustadt** in Austria, is so called because of continuous fires; because it is renewed almost every year and appears new and reborn from the new buildings, it has as its coat of arms the city walls with a new tower on a red field. *Cuspinianus in Austria, page 25.* **The Hungarian Neustadt** <note>Baia Mare</note>, **at the Transylvanian borders, is famous for its grand gold and silver mines and the mint.** More can be found in Zeiller’s *Description of the Kingdom of Hungary*, page 165 and following, page 265 and following. **Regarding the Polish Neustadt,** Zeiller writes **in the *Description of the Kingdom of Poland*,** page 77. **However, many places are named with the word Neustadt.** Just as Zeiller **in the *Description of Poland*,** page 221, also mentions Neuburg (or "the New Place" in Pomerelia), Neudenburg,

<column-break/>

two types of Neumarck, and Neutreich, all in Prussia. To say nothing of Neu-Sol <note>Banská Bystrica</note>, Novo Zolio, Neofolio, Neusiedel, the Neusiedler See, Neudorff, Neumarck in Transylvania, Neugrad, and Neudorff in Hungary, about which the sons of geographers will tell much.

### 58. Newly-baked Noblemen. <note>original: "Neugebackene Edelleut."</note> Recently created nobles.

Who the "new men" <note>original: "Novi homines"</note> are. *See Limnäus in Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, page 136.* A "new man" among the Romans in the Republic was the first from his family to have held a Curule Magistracy <note>a high-ranking public office</note>; and concerning these, Valerius Maximus *book 3, chapter 4* rightly writes: It often happens that those born in a humble place rise to the highest dignity, while the offspring of the most noble lineages, falling into some disgrace, turn the light received from their ancestors into darkness. Consider that speech of Marius in Sallust, an invective against the nobles: "Compare my 'newness' with their pride;" and a little later: "They despise my newness, I despise their laziness; my fortune is thrown in my face, theirs are their shames; if they rightly despise me, let them do the same to their own ancestors, for whom, as for me, nobility began from virtue." On recent nobility, see the excellent work of Draco *On Patricians, page 293, number 6.* Ulrich, Count of Cilli, when he wished to speak with John Hunyadi, the governor of the kingdom of Hungary, and Hunyadi did not refuse if they met at his camp, Ulrich said: "I, a Prince born of a Prince and from a high family, will not come to you, a new man, and one only ennobled in our own time." To which John replied: "I do not compare myself to your ancestors, but to you; though I do not yield even to them, for I, by fighting for the Christian religion, have gained a greater light for my posterity than those who brought it to you; and just as the Countship of Cilli is shamefully extinguished in you, so that of Bistric gloriously arises in me." **"Money-bags"** <note>original: "Pfeffersäck"</note> **and "paper noblemen"** <note>those who bought titles or received them on paper without military merit</note> who have recently been added to the Equestrian order should not be named. *Mundius on Counts Palatine, chapter 3, number 22.* They are called **newly-baked noblemen, peppered with nobility.** *ibid.* Curtius Rufus, whom some claimed was fathered by a gladiator, attained the Praetorship by the vote of the Emperor; at which time Tiberius veiled the disgrace of his birth with these words: "Curtius Rufus seems to me to be born of himself," as Tacitus reports in *book 11 of the Annals.* The same can happen to others who have fortune as their mother, even if born from the lowest commoners. *Limnäus, volume 1, additions to book 1, chapter 10, page 104.*

Now men are more concerned with coats of arms than with virtue. **A newly-baked nobleman had received such insignia for his new nobility: At the top of the shield was a sow, and at the bottom an eagle, and above it he wrote: "Thus it pleased the gods"** <note>original: "Sic placuit superis"</note> **(meaning, that he had been ennobled). When he had hung his shield in the tavern, another man came along and wrote underneath:** "To submit eagles to pigs." <note>original: "Aquilas submittere porcis."</note> Philip

### 59. Fools. <note>original: "Narren. Stulti."</note>

Johann Geiler wrote the *Ship of Fools*. <note>original: "Novem Stultiferam," likely referring to the Latin version of "Das Narrenschiff."</note> Fools ought not to be in a better condition than the wise. *Barbosa, book 17, chapter 53, axiom 1.* Folly is presumed rather than a gift. *axiom 2.* Erasmus of Rotterdam himself admits that he spent no more than seven days' work on his *Praise of Folly* <note>original: "Moriae suae"</note> and that without the help of any books. *Adages, chiliad 3, century 2, adage 40.* It is a part of wisdom to be slightly foolish. <note>original: "Sapientiæ pars est leviter desipere."</note> *Lipsius, century 2, Epistle 7.* One person falls in love with this subject, another with that.

Marcion, a Greek, wrote a **Treatise on Radishes**. *Rango on Hairpieces, pages 14 and 15.* Cato wrote of **Cabbage**, Phoenias of the **Nettle**, Themison of the **Plantain**, Hippocrates of **Barley-water or Gruel**, King Juba of **Euphorbia**, Erasistratus of the herb **Loosestrife** <note>original: "Weiderich"</note>, Democritus of the number 4 and the **Chameleon**, Pythagoras of the **Shallot**, Diocles of the **Turnip**, Asclepiades of **Chamomile**; Favorinus praised Thersites <note>a famously ugly and Greek soldier from the Iliad</note> and the **four-day fever**; Hugbald the Monk and Synesius praised **baldness**; <note>original: "die Glaß," likely "Glatze." Synesius famously wrote a "Praise of Baldness."</note> Pico della Mirandola praised **rudeness**; Matthias Czanakius praised the **crow or harm**; Pirckheimer and Fabricius Campanus praised **gout**: Johannes

A. Rupert praised the **night-owl**, and Bruno praised the **Devil**. Giovanni della Casa of Florence, Archbishop of Benevento, Dean of the Apostolic Chamber and chief Nuncio in the entire Venetian domain, wrote a poem in Italian rhythms in which he celebrated the praises of sodomy and pederasty, calling it a divine work and affirming that he took great delight in it and knew no other Venus <note>goddess of love</note>. The book was printed in Venice by Troiano Navo; a copy of it was in the Library of the University of Tübingen. *Master Bernegger in "The Demolition of the Loreto Idol," page 79.*

Who is to be called a fool: *Menochius, book 6, preface 45, number 8.* Neander, in the *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 256, says one must be foolish at least once a year: *For so Seneca says in "On Tranquility of the Mind" near the end: "For if we believe the Greek poet, sometimes it is even pleasant to be mad." Arrogance is characteristic of fools; wise people recognize that their wisdom is nothing. Fools know everything and cannot err. *Luther on Proverbs 30, number 2, in the notes.*

A distinguished Prince in Italy kept a private secretary who was tasked with creating a **Chronicle of Fools** for him, recording all the follies that occurred throughout his entire court. *Antenor in "Salomon."*

Human life suffers from this disease: that while a good portion of men are foolish, they all seem wise to themselves. *Draco on Patricians, page 267, number 35.* Fools boast that they alone are wise and that they are the "Suitors of Penelope" <note>an idiom for those who waste time seeking what they cannot have</note>; those who are ignorant of many things judge themselves the most learned of all. *Bulkeus, consultation 1, number 171.* The Quirinalia was a festival of fools. *Master J. M. Rittershuf on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 112.*

A fool is one who does not know his own name. *The Code on instituting heirs.* Regarding **hazing** <note>original: "Hänseln," referring to mocking initiation rituals</note>, see *Limnäus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 1, number 64.* In the Imperial Recess of Augsburg from the year 1500, in the section on **jester-fools** <note>original: "Schalcksnarren"</note>, we read that even fools were granted coats of arms by Princes and Nobles, though a limit was placed on this license in that same place. *Limnäus in Public Law, book...*

### 60. Neighbors. Vicini.

A neighbor can be forced to sell property for the enlargement of a nunnery's garden, just as anyone can be compelled to sell for the expansion of a Monastery. Sprengel, *On the Law of Buildings*, page 88.

For the sake of neighborly relations, many things are granted even against common law <note>original: "jus commune"; the general legal principles of the time</note> which otherwise would not be permitted. Barbosa, book 19, chapter 15, example 1. A neighbor is not presumed to be ignorant of his neighbors' actions, but rather to know them very easily. Example 2: Jacob Ayrer in the *Historical Process*, part 1, chapter 15, page 378, and chapter 1, observation 1, number 49. See also Ummius, *Dissertation on the Process* 16, thesis 11, number 80, page 690 in my copy at the end, and page 691 at the beginning. A fact is presumed to be known in a neighboring place if it is known in a remote one. Barbosa, in the same place, example 3. Vices are often easily "drunk in" from faulty neighbors. <note>meaning neighbors tend to influence each other's bad habits</note> C. Rittershufius in *The Novels*, page 201 at the beginning. A neighbor is presumed to know the deeds, life, and morals of his neighbor, page 609, number 7. *How one neighbor should provide peace and security to another*, <note>original: "Wie ein Nachbaur den andern befrieden soll"</note> see the *Statutes of Nuremberg*, title 26, law 14; and the *Customs of Orleans*, chapter 14, folio 74. It has been customary to leave a space two and a half feet wide between the buildings of neighbors for the ability to walk around them. Constantine decreed that the houses of private citizens should be removed from public gardens by 100 feet, and from other public buildings by a distance of 15 feet. Later, it was deemed sufficient for private buildings to be separated from public granaries by a 15-foot interval. Regarding the **easement of light or air**, <term>servitus luminis vel aëris: a legal right to prevent a neighbor from blocking one's light or ventilation</term> it was established that 10 feet should be left between private structures, and 15 between public ones. Brisson, *Selected Antiquities from Civil Law, book 1, chapter 2.*

If a plot of land is divided between two people, but without a wall, hedge, or fence, a neighbor cannot place dung <note>original: "fimum"</note> or any other thing there that could produce smoke, a foul odor, or damage to the other neighbor. Cavalcanti, book 5, on crimes or quasi-contracts, decision 8, number 63.

Whether it is permitted to place a dunghill <note>original: "sterquilinium"</note> against a common wall. Ferrari, in the *Form of Petitions for dividing an inheritance or individual property*, section "and regarding future gains," number 2.

A custom can be established whereby the owner of a wall is compelled to sell it to a neighbor. Gratian, chapter 957, number 47. If it appears from the beginning that a wall belongs to only one neighbor, and the other is granted the right to lean against the wall without payment, in case of doubt it is presumed that the grant was made as a right of **easement** <note>original: "jure servitutis"</note> and not as joint ownership. Cavalcanti, book 5, on crimes or quasi-contracts, decision 8, number 65.

A neighbor ought to do nothing for the purpose of spite or damage to his neighbor. Master Christoph Philipp Richter, part 1, counsel 55, numbers 2 and 6, folio 338 and following; Master Tabor, *On the Law of Beer*, chapter 3.

<column-break/>

Section 10, Gail, book 2, observation 69, numbers 10, 11, 12, 26, 29. Jason on law 5, in the Digest *on justice and law*, number 8, and on the law "quo minus," number 38, in the Digest *on rivers*. Cothmann, volume 2, counsel 93, number 56 and following. Mævius on the *Law of Lübeck*, book 3, title 12, article 8, number 16. When the word "neighbor" is used, it is understood to include a neighbor who is not the most immediate one. Page 4, chapter 2, number 1, folio 3, through the law "not only," in the Digest *on the notification of a new work*. See Tiraqueau, volume 3, on the *retrait lignager* <note>a legal right of a family member to buy back ancestral land sold to a stranger</note> section 1, "on the lignager," gloss 9, numbers 21 and 22.

Jacob, wishing to build a large structure in his house, agreed with his neighbor that he might demolish a certain ancient wall and, at his own expense, rebuild one in the same place fit for bearing the weight, to be held in common between them as an **undivided property**. <note>original: "pro indiviso"</note> Once the wall was raised to a height of 12 feet, the other neighbor prohibited it. Berous decided the case in question 26 in favor of Jacob.

Whether a neighbor wishing to build near a common wall is bound to observe the form of the final law in the Digest *on the regulation of boundaries*. Tesauro, decision 115, throughout. It is permitted to build on a common wall even against the will of a partner, so far as it pertains to decoration—such as if plastering or painting is done—but no account is taken of that if security has been given against **threatened damage**. <term>damno infecto: a legal guarantee against potential damage caused by a neighbor's building project</term> *Gratian, chapter 437, final number.* One cannot later place stone stairs on a wall belonging to another in which a neighbor has already set beams. Cavalcanti, book 5, on crimes, decision 8, number 22. On the distinction of whether a wall is common as an undivided or divided property, and the effect of this distinction, see Cavalcanti, part 2, at the beginning, *on contracts*, decision 9, number 10.

Mindanus, in his *Commentaries on Injunctions*, 23, number 49, writes that some people earnestly charge their officials to deal with neighbors in such a way that they themselves do not have to complain about the neighbors, but rather the neighbors should have to complain about the officials' bothersome behavior.

Neighbors are also dealt with under the word **Overhang**. <note>original: "Uberhang"; refers to branches or structures hanging over a property line</note> When a formal protest before neighbors may suffice: see the *Forum of Protests*, page 97, throughout. One argues correctly from the custom of neighbors. Zorer, part 2, question 9, number 710. That which is observed in neighboring Provinces is to be observed here. Question 9, number 709. The Lords of exempt places *are not called subjects, but neighbors, just as if they were seated in the vicinity outside the territory of any Duke.* <note>original: "werden nicht subditi, sondern vicini genannt..."</note> See *Mundium on Duties and Honors*, chapter 2, number 14, 15, 242, 262. Great benefit comes to our buildings if we happen to have a neighborhood that retains that old custom of duty, not stained by ill-will, not accustomed to lies, nor deceptive, nor deceitful, nor learned in the art of pretense, whether suburban or even urban. ### 61. After-Right. <term>Nachrecht: a residual legal obligation remaining after one has officially left a territory.</term>

Question: What does this little word mean, or what effect does it have in the discharge papers <note>original: "Abschieden"</note> of subjects, in which it is frequently inserted: "With reservation of the customary *Nachrecht*"? Among us, it is the custom that when a subject moves to a foreign lordship and requests a discharge from his previous master, the first master grants it because of the subject's good behavior, but with the reservation that if the lord needs him for the identification of property, for testimony, or in another way, he must still present himself within a year and a day.

### 1. Umpire. Arbiter. <term>Obmann: the third arbitrator chosen to break a tie between two others.</term>

Often an agreement is made <note>original Latin: "compromittitur"</note> such that the appointed arbitrators may take an *Obmann*. From this it is asked: whether the Third Man thus elected by the Arbitrators is a Consultant rather than an Arbitrator? *The Mirror* <note>original: "Specul."; likely the Speculum Iudiciale</note> in section "it follows," 7, number 18, *on arbitration*; likewise Bartolus in the law "if one," principally number 2, *Digest: on the same*, indeed affirm this. But it is answered that this teaching does not apply to "Arbitrators of Law," that is, to those who are elected by the necessity of a statute or an agreement, such as these are; furthermore, said teaching has no place regarding a third person assumed by the will of the litigants, for then Bartolus himself says in the cited law "item if one" that he is an Arbitrator. For he who is assumed by the power granted to the Arbitrators seems to be assumed by the will of the litigants: since he is seen to choose who has granted the power of choosing to another; see Modestin. Pistor, part 2, question 73. The same author in the preceding question 72 teaches that a compromise is valid in which power is given to the Arbitrators to choose a third man, commonly called an *Ob- oder Drittmann* (Umpire or Third Man). For although such a compromise might not seem valid by strict law, it is nevertheless valid by the benefit of the Praetor <note>a Roman judicial official</note> who can compel the Arbitrators to reach an agreement. For a better understanding of this question, the distinction of Jacob Schultes in his notes on the same Pistor is most useful: Either (1) the compromise is simply for two people, without attributing to them the power of choosing a third if they happen to disagree, and then it is undoubtedly a valid compromise...

### 2. Authority, High Authority, Superior Jurisdiction. *The Right of Superiority.*

It is properly the right of superiority <note>original: "jus superioritatis"</note>, see Wesenbeck, *Counsel 213, number 10.*

What is High <term>Fraisch</term> <note>a term for high criminal jurisdiction involving capital punishment</note>, Summoning, Capital, and Manual Authority? And what is attached to the same? See Bidenbach, *question 7.*

Where a Lord has granted a fief to a noble with all High and Low judicial Authority, and established it: whether the Lord has thereby divested himself of all authority, or whether he may nonetheless use it at his pleasure? See Bidenbach, *question 8.*

The Sublime Territorial Right <note>original: "Sublime Territorii jus"</note> is called High Superiority or Jurisdiction <note>original: "Bottmäßigkeit"</note>, namely when it is taken for territorial jurisdiction, by whose power a Ruler can deliberate on any matter, ordain Magistrates, and enact Laws, as Livy testifies it was in the time of the Romans, *book 1, decade 1*; Keller, *On the Juridical-Political Office, book 2, chapter 12, folio 402, toward the word "sublime".*

# Augmented Treasury of Practice

Therefore, it must be accurately judged whether **high authority** <note>original: "hohe Obrigkeit"</note> belongs to a Prince by virtue of his **territorial sovereignty** <note>original: "Lands-Obrigkeit"</note>—and thus encompasses full "high command" <term>merum Imperium; the power of life and death and the highest level of legal jurisdiction</term> and the power of decreeing and commanding—or whether it refers only to the "Right of the Sword" <note>original: "gladii Jus"</note>.

It must likewise be carefully examined whether Nobles are **free in their person** <note>original: "ihrer Person frey seyen"</note>, or whether their villages and subjects also constitute a **separate immediate territory** <note>original: "sonder territorium immediatum"</note>, etc.

How jurisdiction and its specific types are proven is discussed in the *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 88.* Likewise, how one jurisdiction ought to assist another can be seen in the *Marburg Counsels, volume 4, counsel 36.*

*How and in what form high and middle authority are to be distinguished and recognized* is demonstrated by many in the *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 19.* See also *Beatus in Decisions, tome 5, part 5, on judicial matters, volume 1, folio 91, and many following.*

->**ADDITION.**<-

Out of the reverence due to the Magistrate, citizens should never speak ill of him, even if it be true. Regarding the penalties for one who speaks against or disparages the Magistrate through lies, see *Zahn on Lies, book 2, chapter 65, number 4.*

**The authority in a Republic, as in the Civil Body, is in the place of the brain,** *Obrecht in Political Reflections, page 6.*

What is meant by **"by virtue of authority and office"** <note>original: "Von Obrigkeit und Amts wegen"</note>, see *Lord Biccius in Golden Works, page 792.* **For the sake of office** <note>original: "Amts halber"</note> or out of the necessity of office: *Law "cum quadam" 26, there: "we find it generally defined that after the office is laid down, all actions which a Tutor or Curator undergoes out of the necessity of office are transferred to the former ward or adult," Code on the administration of tutors.* *Law "mater" 2, there: "since there is a great difference between a voluntary accusation and the necessity of office."* **Official duty** <note>original: "Amtspflicht"</note> is discussed in *chapter "cui portio" 6, there: "impeded by the duty of necessity."* **By way of office** <note>original: "Amts wegen"</note>, *12th Question, 1, final law, there: "they ought to have received enough through the necessity of office," Code on the possession of legacies.* **What usually happens in the way of innovations and changes under a new authority when the old authority changes.** *Zorer, part 2, question 16, number 1056.* Superiority <note>sovereignty</note> is always deemed reserved to the grantor, in whatever way liberty may have been granted, even if it is said that all rights were granted to them. For a Prince imitates the Divine ordinance when, by granting small portions of his Majesty to subjects, he nevertheless reserves Superiority to himself, so that whatever is in his Republic depends on him alone and is referred to him alone. *Barbosa, book 17, chapter 72, axiom 7.* Superiority induces a presumption of Jurisdiction, not of ownership. Axiom 8. Superiority is deemed proven by proven acts of subjection. Axiom 9. **To high authority belong at all times capital crimes that carry penalties of limb and life,** <note>original: "Maleficia, so Leib und Lebensstraff auf ihnen tragen"</note> which are extensively enumerated by **Besold under the word Capital Court** <term>Halßgericht; literally "neck-court," referring to the court with the power of execution</term>. *Coler in Executive Process, part 2, chapter 1, number 116. Wehner in Observations under the word Zent <note>a regional district court</note>.*

<column-break/>

The Great Magistrates among the Romans did not hold office for long, so that by the memory of private life, to which they were to be returned, and by the fear of a trial for extortion, they might abstain from injuries. *Christoph Forstner in Notes on Tacitus, book 2 of the Annals, chapter 34, number 1, page 190, and several following.* What kind of Magistrate ought to be chosen is taught from Aristotle by *Lord Felwinger in The Judge, page 447.* **Where the authority is disputed, many a person must pay a penalty to both places, or else he cannot be safe;** <note>original: "Wo die Obrigkeit strittig, muß mancher an beyde Ort Straff geben, oder kan nicht sicher seyn"</note> such Lords ought rather to reach an agreement so that they do not produce contradictory sentences, although he is preferred before whom the lawsuit was first contested. *Adam Keller on the Juridical-Political Office, book 2, chapter 12, page 418.*

**3. Observance.** <note>original: "Observanz"</note> See below under the words Usurpation and Observance.

That interpretation of agreements ought to be adopted and retained which the outcome of the matter—that is, the observance and execution by the parties—demonstrates. Since from those things which are done and observed by the parties in the time that follows, it is known what their intention was in the beginning. Indeed, subsequent observance declares the very nature of the act. By which reasoning, privileges, laws, and statutes also daily admit of clarification through subsequent use and observation; see *Schultes, book 2, question 55, number 34 and following, and extensively Petrus Fontanella in the treatise on antenuptial pacts in the Index under the word "observantia".*

->**ADDITION.**<-

Subsequent observance ought to be attended to before all things. *Zorer, part 1, question 1, number 106.* Between custom and observance there is some subtle difference. *Barschamp in the Root of Clauses, chapter 14, number 17.* Observance creates law between the parties; among others, it does so only by the first act, because it consists in fact. *See my work on the Style of the Court, theses 86 and 87.* Observance is sometimes taken for law. *Law 24, on Municipalities. Finckelthaus, observation 70, number 11. Gail, book 1, observation 36.* **Thus, in our opinion, it remains fairly with tradition.** <note>original: "Also bleibt es unsers Erachtens auch billich bey dem Herkommen"</note> Ancient use and observance (which is handed down as being designated by German words) *Klock on Collections, chapter 20, number 91. Wehner in Practical Observations under the word* **Tradition** <term>Herkommen; established custom or precedent</term> *pages 287 and 692*, although others restrict "observance" to the style of the court; see *Carp—* <note>The text cuts off, likely referring to the legal scholar Carpzov.</note>

### 4. Or. [Latin: *Seu*]

The word "or" <note>original: "seu"</note> is a disjunctive conjunction <note>a word that presents a choice between two alternatives</note>, according to Law 2 of the Code *On Professors and Physicians*, which is placed between diverse things and stands as an expansion to a different matter. Hieronymus Gratus, *Counsel* 153, number 42, part 2.

So also, the nature and property of the word "or" <note>original: "vel"</note> is such that by its nature it is placed between diverse things and notes that a different case is being proposed. See the text in book 1 of the Digests *On Doubtful Matters*. Cephalus, *Counsel* 256, number 43, line 2. Castillio, *On Usufruct*, chapter 33, number 24. See Everhard in *Legal Topics*, under the topic of the nature of alternatives.

# ADDITION.

The word "or" <note>original: "seu"</note> is sometimes considered to be used for the sake of expansion. And this is indeed true whenever one of those things joined by that word is contained within the other, as in the proposition. Otherwise, the word "or" <note>original: "seu"</note> designates the same thing as "either," "whether," or "or" <note>original: "aut, sive, vel"</note>. Yet all of these regularly designate a disjunction, for instance in things left behind:
<meta>Besold Volume I.</meta>

<column-break/>

just as, conversely, in those things left to persons, they designate a conjunction <note>meaning both parties are included rather than just one</note>. Discussed at length by Busius in his *Commentary on the Pandects*, book 33, folio 212. The nature of the word "or" <note>original: "oder, sive, aut"</note> is such that not all things are verified together, but disjunctively; namely, so that when the first head is verified, the second ceases. Klock, volume 2, *Counsel* 64, number 10.

On alternatives, see both at length and accurately Zorer, part 2, question 8, number 641 and the three following. Barbosa, book 1, chapter 55, axioms 1 through 5. On alternating sessions, see Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, numbers 133, 142, and 148. On alternating sealing, see Limnäus, book 9, chapter 1, number 222. In alternatives, the choice belongs to the debtor; this holds true if a contrary meaning is hidden in the proposition, which is recognized by the critical particle "only," Law 35, *On the Nature of Things*. Otherwise, other causes also grant the choice to Dr. Tabor.

"Or" <note>original: "aut"</note>, a disjunctive particle in section 1 of the Institutes *On Useless Stipulations*, is sometimes seen to be used for a conjunctive one, as is occasionally the custom in book 53 *On the Meaning of Words*. For example, future fruits are rightly included in a stipulation, Law 73 *On Verbal Obligations*. Vinnius on the said section 1 *On Useless Stipulations*. Valerius Wilhelm Forster, *Book of Successive Observations*, last chapter. Lord Dr. Tabor, *On Arms*, chapter 1, number 8. In alternatives, when one is sufficient, see Limnäus, book 8, chapter 6, number 40. The disjunctive particle "or" <note>original: "vel; oder"</note> is indeed placed between diverse things, yet they have the same effect, per the text in book 1 *On Doubtful Matters*. Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, book 1, chapter 9, number 40. Reinking, *On the State of the Empire and Church*, book 1, class 5, chapter 10, number 28. Dr. Cob on book 2 *On Feudal Rights*. Forster, *Book of Successive Observations*, last chapter. Regarding the alternative "or" <note>original: "oder"</note>, one must diligently check whether it is also found in the old deeds of acquisition. If it is omitted in the old deeds, then the alternative does not apply, and one must, for example, provide the "Christmas-steward" <note>original: "Weihnachtmeyer"; a type of tenant or feudal official</note> himself and not the money. In the case of V. against R., many reach an agreement in tithe matters and take an alternative: one year money, the other year chickens or lambs in kind.

In E., the subjects must give one out of twenty lambs in kind, the other in money, at 28 pennies <note>original: "Pfenning"</note>. A certain bailiff took three pennies one year, and the next year the chicken itself as a tithe. The question is: Must the customary gift <term>Weisat or Weiset; a traditional payment or gift from a tenant to a lord</term> be taken at the old value? The response is: no, because as time changes, that which was determined according to the course of a specific time also varies. Therefore, the valuation <note>original: "aestimatio"</note> included in an alternative obligation is not to be understood simply, but rather as the customary gift is worth at any given time. Especially, however, the old surcharge can no longer apply when the owner <note>original: "Eigenherr"</note> would be harmed beyond half of the fair price <term>laesio ultra dimidium; a legal principle allowing a contract to be rescinded if the price is less than half the true value</term> according to the old valuation. Since valuation implies buying and selling, for that reason Law 2 of the Code *On the Rescinding of Sale* applies beyond all doubt: as Hartmann Pistoris relates in book 3, question 4, number 8. In all alternatives, even if the words seem to conflict, that interpretation must be avoided by...

...lest the other party be harmed. Fontanella. The disjunctive word **or** <note>original German: "oder"</note> is sometimes taken as a conjunctive <note>meaning "and"</note>. Klock, volume 3, counsel 121, number 28.

Alternation is presumed among equals. Zorer, part 2, question 8, number 640. A reduction to equity <term>Reductio ad æquitatem; the legal adjustment of a contract or obligation to ensure fairness when circumstances have changed fundamentally</term> is usually performed if the price of grain in a time of scarcity far exceeds the value current at the time the census <term>census; here referring to a fixed annual payment, ground rent, or tax</term> was established. See, I pray, *Treasury of Decisions* 154 at the end and the Addition. The same applies if the valuation of money has increased. *Treasury of Decisions* 126. What if the payment of a burden has been distributed in one specific way for a long time? *Treasury of Decisions* 238. A reduction of a contract to equity must be made if the matter, through the passage of time, becomes unfair or the cost grows infinitely. Besold, counsel 230, number 21 and counsel 249, number 11. Christoph Philipp Richter, decision 199, number 144. If a payment becomes unfair over the course of time, it should be reduced to equity by a judge. Besold, counsel 277, number 87. Such burdens should be remitted in a Christian manner by Lords who have been reduced almost to a pittance. Mundius, *On Offices*, chapter 7, number 437. If an inequality is discovered after the fact, it must be reduced to equality. Mundius, *On Offices*, chapter 7, number 36. Often times occur when it would be unfair for the generality of the laws to be strictly observed. Peckius, *On the Rules of Canon Law*, rule 7, number 2.

The copulative particle AND <note>original Latin: "ET"</note> is sometimes put for the disjunctive OR <note>original Latin: "AUT"</note>. This is not new in Law. [Citations to the Digest and Code]. Conrad Rittershusius on Law 23 of the Digest, page 238 in my copy.

Six species of Alternations are found in Law. Regarding what those are, see Schneidewin in *Institutes*, page 942, number 9 and following.

### 5. Public Instrument <note>original German/Latin: "Offen Instrument. Publicum Instrumentum."</note>.

A Public Instrument <term>Publicum Instrumentum; a formal document created by a public official that serves as authoritative legal proof</term> is one that is made publicly, or which consists of and is confirmed by public authority. [Citations to the Code].

A writing is understood to be made publicly if it is done by public persons—that is, by the Prince and Magistrates, or others to whom the power of making a public instrument has been committed. [Citations to the Digest and Code]. This also includes Notaries, who are considered public persons. [Citations]. For the Emperor either makes something publicly himself or grants others the power to perform it. Hence the instruments of Notaries are said to be publicly made. [Citations].

<column-break/>

Private instruments, on the other hand, are those made privately by private persons. [Citations to the Code].

A Public Instrument produces full and perfect proof. For it is "proven proof," and does not need further proving. Hence that which is proven through a Public Instrument is called "manifest" <note>legally evident or undeniable</note>. [Citations].

## ADDITION.

A later creditor protected by a public instrument is preferred over a creditor holding an earlier private writing. Zorer, part 1, question 12, number 1079. **Obligations or instruments drawn up before the authorities, in which a piece of property is pledged, take precedence over a private written agreement.** <note>original German: "Die vor der Obrigkeit aufgerichte Obligationes oder Instrumenta, darinnen ein Stück verunterpfändet, gehet einer Privat-Verschreibung vor."</note> Zorer, part 2, question 6, number 406; question 20, number 7052. **Whether the same holds true when the obligation and instrument are drawn up and completed by the debtor and three witnesses, or by a notary and witnesses.** <note>original German: "Ob dergleichen auch Statt habe, wann die Obligation und Instrument von dem Schuldner und 3. Gezeugen, oder von Notarien und Gezeugen aufgericht und gefertiget ist."</note> Zorer, part 2, question 16, numbers 407, 409 and following; also question 20, number 7053. Ancient private books are not to be trusted, and the antiquity of a writing alone does not create legal credibility. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 1, chapter 19, page 70. In ancient matters where lighter proofs suffice, ancient books may offer proof: ibid. Concerning public and private instruments, **what obligations completed with hand and seal bring with them and are capable of**, <note>original German: "was die mit Hand und Petschafft gefertigte Obligationes mitbringen und vermögen"</note> question 5, number 349 and following. There is always a presumption in favor of the truth of an official instrument. Barbosa, book 9, chapter 73, axiom 3. Public instruments receive no outside interpretation, but it is necessary that meaning be taken from the very words themselves, axiom 14. The term "instrument" in the matter of proofs is used in four ways: 1) Broadly, for any document informing the case and the judge. 2) Narrowly, for a writing proving something. 3) More narrowly, for a writing containing an agreement, distinguished from court records, accounts, and wills. 4) Most narrowly, for a public instrument, which is distinguished from private handwritings <term>chirographis; documents written and signed by private parties without official seals</term>. See more in Dr. Biccius. What a public instrument is and its various species, thesis 128; what a "forensic" <note>court-related</note> document is, and how it differs from an absolutely public instrument, thesis 128. The credibility and force of an absolutely public instrument is so established that it does not need witnesses, nor can it be weakened by them. But the force of a "forensic" instrument, though written as if publicly, is not truly public in the same sense, since it requires witnesses and can be called into doubt. This cannot be said of truly public ones. Instruments generally provide stronger proof than witnesses, *Acts of Lindau*, page 410.

Letter O.

A writing strengthened by a statute or custom provides proof everywhere. *Cravertus on Ancient Times, part 1, section 7, number 6.* A statute annulling a legal document is not considered to annul the contract described within that document. *Carlo de Crassis on Exceptions, in the prelude, number 153.* In the City of Venice, a private writing has the force of a public instrument. *Decianus, response 22, number 10, volume 3.* A statute speaking of "instruments" must be understood as referring to effective ones, not those that are void. *Johann Baptist de Castellis, section "it does not stand in the way," if it be said. Mynsinger, response 61, number 20.* A statute ordering a document to be executed is understood to apply only if the document is legally valid. *Vivius, opinion 832, number 69.* If a statute grants "ready execution" <note>A legal fast-track to enforcement without a full trial</note> to a document, it is understood to apply when the matter is liquid and clear <term>liquid; a legal term meaning the debt or obligation is for a certain, undisputed amount</term>. *Menochius, Remedy 3, number 190.* A statute may prohibit raising a defense of compensation against a document, as well as "peremptory" defenses <note>Defenses that completely bar a claim</note>, those limiting execution, or those that can be proven immediately. *Vivius, opinion 832; Carocius on Obligations, part 2, question 76.* See also other useful points in *Tenninus, caution 257.* Although by the disposition of a statute proof against a document may not be admitted, it is nonetheless permitted against the presumption resulting from that document. *Corsetus, on the word "Proof."* It is not enough for a document to be shown outside of court; see the *Forum of Protestations* published by our Mr. Felvinger, *page 152, number 10.*

### 6. Opening. *Right of Opening.* <note>Latin: *Jus aperturæ*</note>

Does the "Opening"—which Princes sometimes possess in the houses of the nobility—carry with it territorial sovereignty? *See Bidembach, question 22, and Hering on the Law of Burghers, number 733, etc.*

"Opening" is called an *openable fief* <note>Latin: *aperibile feudum*</note> in ancient documents. Also called "given-up fiefs" <note>German: *aufgebiye Lehen*</note>, the nature of which seems to be that they are hereditary. *Acts of Sayn against Trier, folio 26 and following,* where Hillenus, Bishop of Trier, granted the Castle of Sayn as a fief to the Counts of Sayn in the year 1152 under this condition: *That if it should happen that we have a war with anyone against whom they cannot provide us help, they must exit the Castle and grant us power over it without their disinheritance; so that when the war is finished, they may return to the Castle as their own fief.*

Opening is numbered among the Sovereign Rights <term>Regalia; the exclusive rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign ruler</term> and the law of the territory. This is because it is categorized under the "Superior Advocacy" <note>German: *Vogtejam*</note>, which exists by *right of princedom*, as testified by *Knich, on the Sublimity of Territorial Law, chapter 4, number 314, section 394 and following.* It relates to fortifications and the laws of war, which can only belong to a **Superior** <note>A high-ranking lord or sovereign</note>, according to *chapter 1, "Which things are Sovereign Rights," and Gaeddäus in the counsel on the restitution of the Barons of Vallendar, number 399.*

Its standard form is as follows: "Also shall the aforementioned N. and all his heirs hold the mentioned city and fortress open to us and ours, and be ready to let us and ours in and out for all our necessities,

<column-break/>

to remain and be contained therein, against everyone, no one excepted, yet without significant harm to them, in good faith."

Opening is sometimes derived *from Lordship or ownership*, as among co-heirs, and sometimes *from a pact* or agreement, as among allies.

It is also sometimes a great bond and almost implies a *subjunction* <term>subjunction; a state of being legally subordinate to another authority</term>, yet the territorial sovereignty of a Prince cannot be proven by it alone. Thus, the fortress and County of Ortenburg are subject directly to the Empire <note>meaning they were "Imperial Immediate," answering only to the Emperor</note>; nonetheless, the fortress of Ortenburg is bound to the Electoral House of Bavaria by the "Opening" and other ways. For this reason, it can be said not undeservedly that the "Opening" is an *unequal treaty* <note>Latin: *fœdus inæquale*</note>, where one party not only courteously observes the majesty of the other but also exists as their client. This matter is found in the *Acts of Ortenburg, folio 192 and following.*

In the Year of Christ 1391, Count George and Count Etzel of Ortenburg completely bound and united themselves with Duke Frederick in Bavaria, his brother, and his heirs, to have the "Opening" in their castles against everyone, no one excepted, as their rightful lord. The Counts signed this and promised it in place of an oath, where these words are also found:

> We shall also sit peacefully in our aforementioned Lords' land with ourselves, our people, and our castles; and if we wish to begin anything, whatever the matter might be, we shall do so according to the advice of our aforementioned Lords: therein we shall follow them and be obedient. We vow to them upon our honor to keep and fulfill this, simply and faithfully.

Another letter dated 1294, given by Count Etzel alone, contains the following: "Acknowledge for us, all our heirs and descendants, for the great grace and promotion that the Lords Dukes Stephan and Johann, guardians of Duke Henry, have done for us with the fortress Ortenburg, which they have handed over and returned to us, etc. Therefore we shall attend to and serve Duke Henry, etc., his heirs and descendants, of the Lordship in Bavaria, with our aforementioned fortress of Ortenburg, against everyone, no one excepted; and it shall also be an open house for all their necessities, as often and frequently as they have need, with our good will, without contradiction from anyone. We shall and will not bind or unite ourselves with our aforementioned fortresses and Lordships against anyone else, but will remain with the Lord Duke Henry, etc., his heirs and descendants in Lower Bavaria, his land, and his people."

*The Right of Opening <note>Latin: "Jus aperturae"</note>, commonly called* the Opening <note>German: "die Oeffnung"</note>, *is not in itself an indication of subjection or landed vassalage, but is customary in feudal cases, confederations, and similar unions without any prejudice. This was noted and confirmed at the Imperial Chamber Court, as witnessed by the author of the* Defense of Waldeck <note>original: "Waldeckischen Ehrenrettung"</note> *part 2, chapter 24, page 193, in a very famous* exemption *case, with the following words: "Even if," says the Reporter, "the Counts have bound themselves by their services and by making free access available to the Dukes, it does not follow from this that they and their county are immediately subject to the jurisdiction and rule of the Dukes."*

*For it does not follow: "He has the right of entry in my citadels, and I am obligated to him for performing services; therefore, my citadels and I are subject to him." Rather, it can be inferred from this that the said citadels are not subject to him; otherwise, this agreement would have been made in vain.* Meichsner, *volume 3, decision 6, number 54, with which the co-reporter agreed in number 72; and thus finally the sentence against exemption was delivered and published.*

*And it should be noted further that in that case, when a Lord sues for the deprivation of a fief because the Vassal denied the Opening, one must primarily look at whether the Vassal did so by right, through malice, or without probable cause.* Rosenthal, *On Fiefs* <note>original: "de feud."</note>, *chapter 8, conclusion 2, letter G; Cavalcanti, counsel 120, number 18; Cravetta, counsel 8, number 15 and following. To this also points the* Defense of Waldeck *cited in the chapter specifically concerning whether a felony was committed or not regarding a "denied Opening." An example is cited in the Landgraves of Hesse, who always notified the Counts of Waldeck of their own arrival and that of their people, and not only insured them against damage and expenses, but also allowed such costs to be deducted from the district tax <note>term: "Kreißsteuer" (an imperial tax collected by the regional administrative circles)</note>. This is also the opinion of the feudalists, who give the civil lords this moral advice:* that Lords ought to be civil, *and not "fall into the house of the Vassal with the door" <note>German idiom: "mit der Thür ins Haus fallen," meaning to act too abruptly or without warning</note>, etc.*

### 8. Without, -less, Un-, etc. <note>original: "Ohn, Los, Un, &c."</note> Without <note>Latin: "Absque"</note>.

*What the particle* In- *effects among the Latins whenever it is placed before a verb or noun—such as "unlearned" <note>Latin: "indoctus"</note>, "inconstant" <note>Latin: "inconstans"</note>, "inconstancy" <note>Latin: "inconstantia"</note>, "unarmed" <note>Latin: "inermis"</note> (one who is without learning, without constancy, and without arms)—the prefix* Un- *does the same among the Germans. ### 9. **Without Disturbance or Infringement.** <note>German: "Ohne Irrung und Eintrag"</note> Without hindrance. <note>Latin: "Absque impedimento"</note>

The nature of these words, **without disturbance or infringement**, is to encompass all cases and all persons. *Final Law, section 5, verse "num initium," of the Digest on ignorance of law and fact.* <note>Latin: "ff. de jur. & facti ignorant."</note> Menochius, *Counsel 1, 157, number 22, folio 2.* Tiraquellus, *in the repetition of the Law "if ever" in the preface, number 118, Code on the revocation of donations.* <note>Latin: "C. de revoc. donat."</note>

### 10. **Immediately Subject to the Empire.** <note>German: "Ohne Mittel dem Reich unterworffen"</note> Directly subject to the Imperial power. <note>Latin: "Immediatè Imperio subjectum"</note>

The words of the Chamber Court Ordinance <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, *part 2, title:* **that the matter of disputed possession between parties who are immediately subject to the Empire, etc.** cannot be understood in any other sense than that the assets themselves—in whose name the litigation is primarily conducted, or which are complained of as having been seized—must also be immediately under the Empire. The person seeking a legal remedy represents and refers to their status as a State of the Empire <note>An "Imperial State" (*Reichsstand*) was an entity with a seat and a vote in the Imperial Diet</note> beyond controversy, as seen in the **Ortenburg Acts against Bavaria** <note>A famous 16th-century legal battle over Imperial Immediacy between the Counts of Ortenburg and the Duchy of Bavaria</note>, *volume 2.* And since it is very well known in the Empire, as the Reporter <note>The legal official presenting the case to the court</note> *in the same place, number 4* testifies, and as all Treasury and Mandatory cases also teach: only those are truly held as States for the Empire who simultaneously possess assets held directly from the Empire, by reason of which they contribute taxes and are called to the Imperial Diets. Common understanding and observation cannot be twisted elsewhere, nor can the customary interpretation of the Empire be extended against common use and practice to those for whom the Ordinance or Constitution expresses nothing specifically, since it speaks expressly only of those who are "immediate" <note>Those holding their land and authority directly from the Emperor without any intermediate lord</note>. Therefore, since there are infinite cases and processes regarding pledges, seizures, and Treasury matters in which jurisdiction is found based on nothing other than the fact that the seized or pledged assets are subject to the Empire along with the persons, one must attend to and follow not what is found rarely, but what is observed frequently and commonly.

The Reporter therefore concludes in *the cited vote 2, number 6* and says: Wherefore, when the lawsuit in our case is not moved by reason of any thing which is subject to the Empire through an intermediary <note>Latin: "mediate"</note> along with its possessor, but rather is subject to another lord along with its owner, the *said Constitution* on seizures cannot be extended to such a case according to common, daily practice; and thus some of the States of the Empire agree that the Constitution on Seizures must be accepted in this way, etc.

And although further, in decreeing legal processes, consideration is rightly given to persons (since without them nothing can be decreed or decided), nevertheless this does not necessarily happen because of

<column-break/>

the persons primarily, but because of the things and assets which are possessed immediately from the Empire, and in whose name and for whose sake they are named as States of the Empire, as has been said. From this it is also easily apparent that the words of the cited title 21, **immediately subject to the Empire**, are to be understood precisely by reason of the assets, as is proved from Treasury cases, in which proceedings are not taken against those who do not possess the assets; the Laws also support this, so that after the person or their origin is set aside, the consideration of the place of residence <note>Latin: "domicilii"</note> is more closely attended to.

->ADDITION.<-

**Immediately** <note>German: "Ohne Mittel"</note> is a word used broadly. Schwannmann, *Decision 10, number 107, at the beginning:* the word **immediately** must be understood according to the subject matter. *In the same place, number 114, at the beginning:* The Constitutions on seizures as well as pledges admit a distinction of cases, specifically when the assets are immediately under the Empire. *In the same place, number 25:* Since distinctions between things are to be removed, the words **without mediation** would have been added superfluously. *Number 26.*

### 11. **Offering, To Offer.** <note>German: "Opffer, Opffern"</note> Sacrifice. <note>Latin: "Sacrificium"</note>

It was accepted from the Primitive Church that before the Holy Communion, songs should be recited by the Clergy, which duty of singing was called the *Offertory* <note>Latin: "Offertorium"</note>. During this, the people offered donations to the Priest performing the Liturgy in front of the Altar. Tertullian refers to this *in his Apology, chapter 39*, where he says: "Each person puts in a small gift on a monthly day, or when he wishes and is able. For no one is compelled, but confers it voluntarily." These offerings which are made publicly at the Altar are called *Offertories* <note>Latin: "Offertoria"</note> because of the feast or the Divine offering, as Isidore witnesses in *book 6 of his Etymologies, chapter 19.*

But regarding the law of Offerings, Sacrifices of First Fruits <note>Latin: "Primitiarum Sacrificiis"</note>, etc. *from title 30, book 3 of the Decretals*, see Hackelman, *Canonical Dispute 8, throughout.* Cardinal Baronius *in the year 741.* Lotichius *on Petronius Arbiter, book 2, chapter 15.* The Synodical Statutes of Constance, *folio 134.* Rinthelin, *chapter 60.*

It should be noted here that it was once a solemn custom to place things donated or handed over to the Church, or at least the legal instruments for them, upon the altar. *Alemannic Law, title 1*, where concerning a Deed of Donation <note>Latin: "Charta Donationis"</note> to the Church, it is placed upon the altars in the presence of the Priest who serves that same Church. *Bavarian Law, title 1:* and then he should place the letter itself upon the altar, and thus hand over the money. A formula for this matter is handed down in the *Chapters of Benedict the Levite, book 6, chapter 285:* and he holds the writing itself before or above the Altar, saying to the Priests and guardians of that place: "I offer to God and dedicate all the things which are held inserted in this chart." See Bignon *in his notes on the Formulas of Marculf, folio 430.*

->ADDITION.<-

The **offering penny** <note>German: "Opfferpfenning"</note> has ceased. Klock, *Counsel 51, number.*

### 12. Ear-Tribute <note>German: "Ohrbede"</note>, or Love-Money <note>German: "Liebgeld"</note>. Charitable Subsidy.

### 14. Organ. Musical Instruments. <note>Latin: "Organa"</note>

In the time of Louis <note>Louis the Pious</note>, hydraulic music (others call it water-music) commonly called **Organs** began in France, specifically in the Palace at Aachen. Besold, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

to be composed with marvelous art in imitation of the Greeks, through the industry of a certain George, a Venetian priest, and at the expense of King Louis, such as Michael had forged out of gold in Constantinople. See Beck on Aachen, folio 102, as well as Cardinal Baronius in the index of the *Annals*. Le Grand, folio 150 and following. They are called "Organs" as if they were "Instruments"; hence we still call a species of organ an "Instrument."

However, organs were seen late in Venice; beforehand, the *Rigabella*, *Torsella*, and *Ninfala* were in use, as attested by Heinrich von Pflaumern in his *Italian Mercury*, folio 48. Once their excellence became known, they began to be erected in all the somewhat larger churches, so that today there are no fewer than 143 organs in that city. The same author in the same place, folio 47, teaches what the *Rigabella*, *Torsella*, and *Ninfala* were.

### 15. Original, Main Deed, Main Bond. Originale, Autographum.

A primary instrument—that is, one of its own origin—is called an *Original* <note>original: "Originale"</note>, commonly known as the "Original," "Main Deed," or "Main Bond." See law *sancimus* 3 of the Code on various rescripts. It is also called an *Authentic* <note>original: "Authenticum"</note> document, specifically by reason of its creator <note>original: "ratione efficientis"</note>. See the said law 3 and law 2 of the Digest on the reliability of instruments. The word comes from the Greek *authentien* <note>original: ἀπὸ τῇ αὐθεντεῖν</note>, meaning "by the author," according to Paul in his *Sentences*, book 5, section 12. Indeed, "authenticity" <note>original: αυϑεντία</note> is the same as power or authority. Hence, an "authentic" document is one that possesses authority and power, or bears its author's name, so that it may be valid. Therefore, an Authentic is the primary writing of an instrument, flourishing with original and valid authority. See Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter I, conclusion 239.

A "Copy" <note>original: "Exemplum"</note> is the opposite of an Authentic Instrument, as it is transcribed from the first or authentic version. See law 2 of the Digest on the reliability of instruments. It does not have its own origin.

A Public Instrument differs from an authentic one as a species differs from its genus. See Parladorius, *Daily Matters*, book 2, section 11, expansion 2, number 10, page 375.

->ADDITIO.<-
<note>Addition</note>

By reason of its form, one instrument is an *Authentic* or Original (the Main Deed); another is a *Schedule* or Draft <note>original: "Scheda seu Imbreviatura"</note>; another is a Copy taken from the authentic (a certified extract <note>original: "ein vidimirter Auszug"</note>); and another is a note (a memorial). See *Strasbourg Collection of Law*, law 22, title 4, thesis 3, page 1. The Imperial Chamber Court <note>The supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> requires

<column-break/>

original documents and does not trust copies. See Mundius, *On the Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 332 and following. Copies do not constitute proof unless the Original is produced. Barbosa treats this most extensively in book 5, chapter 29, throughout the whole axiom. Authentics must be produced in court along with the copies. See Rittershusius in *The Novels*, page 626, number 8. On the distinction between an Authentic and a Copy, see the same, page 626, number 7. On what constitutes an Authentic, see the same, page 14, number 10. However, by another name, an Authentic is also called an "Exemplar" or "Exemplarium," as in Ulpian, law 10, section *in duob. Exemplariis* of the Digest regarding how a testament is opened. That law speaks of a "twin exemplar" of a testament—that is, when two identical originals of a testament exist <note>original German: "wann zwey gleichlautende Original eines Testaments vorhanden seynd"</note>.

The name "Original" also applies to the "Authentic," as Gratian teaches in Volume 5 of *Forensic Disputes*, chapter 889, numbers 2 and 3; and Rittershusius in *The Novels*, part 9, chapter 24, number 4. However, Mascardus (question 6, number 75, volume 1) and Gilhausen (in *The Judicial Tree*, chapter 6, part 3, number 31) believe this is done improperly. An obligation for theft is not contracted if someone merely copies (that is, makes a transcript <note>original Greek: ἀναγραφήν</note>) of Titius's accounts for himself and takes a copy from the original. See law *cum plures* 15 on things possessed by judicial authority, law 8 on the division of a family estate, and law 1 on how a testament is opened. For I prefer to take the word "copying" <note>original: "describendi"</note> in its proper sense, with Brissonius (under the word *describere*), rather than with the Gloss on this law, which interprets it as the clearly opposite acts of deleting and filling in—though the person may still be held liable for fraud. See Dr. Tabor in *Gleanings of Crimes*, page 128.

See C. Rittershusius on law 23 of the Digest regarding rules of law, page 200 at the beginning, where he discusses the authentic copy (a "Copey") and the summary (an "Extract"); only the authentic constitutes proof.

### 16. Military Service Fee. Hostenditiae.

Military Service Fees <note>original: "Hostenditiæ, Ostendienst"</note> are the payments or stipends rendered to the Lord of the Fief by a vassal who either cannot or will not go into military service with him, nor substitutes another suitable person for himself. They are rendered, I say, to compensate for and redeem the labor that was to be performed in military service. See Rittershusius in *Feudal Divisions*, chapter 2, book 2, number 32.

This name is derived from "enemy" <note>original: "hoste"</note>, as the feudal text in title 40 seems to imply in the phrase "those going against the enemy," and likewise, "they make an enemy." Rittershusius says in the same place: "I once thought the name *Hostenditiarum* seemed to be derived from the old verb *Hostire*, which means 'to equalize' or 'make even.' From this also comes *Hostimentum* in Plautus's *The Ass-Dealer*, which Festus correctly explains as a 'compensation for a benefit.'" I was led to this thought because I read in Gunther, book 8:

> "Let him compensate and redeem his own labor with a fee," etc.

But *Oost* is an Army, and *Dienst* is service. See my work *On the Nature of Peoples*, page 73. The Italians also use *hoste* for an army. See Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations* 7, thesis 6, letter E, where he says:

### 17. Austria. <note>original: *Oesterreich*</note>

Following the Emperor, the King of the Romans, and the Electors of the Empire, come the Archdukes of Austria, who outshine other Dukes just as Archbishops outshine Bishops. This is provided for among other things in the Privileges of the Archdukes of Austria: **That a Duke of Austria shall be regarded as a Count Palatine in the Diets <note>the *Comitia* or imperial assemblies</note>, and shall nonetheless have and keep the first place after the Electors in seating and walking on the right side of the Empire.** See Lord Jos. Nolden in his *Treatise on Nobles*, chapter 9, number 173 and following.

The Archdukes of Austria also hold the place of prefects, from whom, by special Privilege, there is no appeal, as witnessed by Zasius in his title *On the Office of the Consul*, under number 4. He deals with these Privileges at greater length and legally in Counsel 15, beginning *in causa vertente*, number 44, volume 2; as does Matthias Stephanus in *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, leaf 156. Add Lord Goldast, volume 1 of the *Constitutions*, also in the *Rationalibus*, and Volume VI of the *Symphorematum*, where many Privileges of the House of Austria are recorded. Also see below under the letter P, at the word *Pfandung* <note>Distraint or seizure of property</note>, where in the section beginning *und obwol* and following, it is discussed whether the privileges of the praiseworthy House of Austria are also to be understood to apply to the Burgraviate of Burgau, etc.

### 18. Forever, eternally, for eternal days. Perpetually. <note>original Latin/German: *Ewig, ewiglichen, zu ewigen Tagen. Perpetuo.*</note>

This word is universal, and when used by someone renouncing a right, it excludes them for all time in which a succession could reach them; conversely, for those not renouncing, it includes them always and infinitely in every case. *Final law, Code on legitimate trusts; Baldus on the law of will; Tiberius Decianus, response 50, number 18, volume 1; Menochius, counsel 297, number 64.* Unless it is understood as a total exclusion, the word would not seem to be used in its proper significance, nor would it achieve its effect, since it is the opposite of a temporary exclusion. Johann Goeddaeus *among the Marburg consultations, consultation 26, volume 1, number 99 and following.* However, in Civil Law, "perpetuity" is to be understood "provided things remain as they are" <note>original Latin: *rebus sic stantibus*</note>. See *Barbosa in his dictionary under the word "perpetually."*

The word *eternally* <note>original German: *ewiglich*</note> signifies infinity, *based on the law "simply," paragraph "finally" regarding fraud and fear; Code on various rescripts; Decianus consultation 516, number 15; Parisius consultation 20, number 13; Menochius consultation 95, number 4, and consultation 233, number 25.* This is indeed according to the property of speech, Socinus *the elder, consultation 84, number 5 and book 3; Menochius consultation 275, number 33 and following.* In a case of doubt, when something is said to be perpetual, it is understood to be without a pre-defined time, Bartolus *on the law "it suffices" regarding the recovery of undue payments; Alexander consultation 216, number 6, book 7.*

### 19. Eternal Course. Perpetual motion. <note>original Latin/German: *Ewiger Lauff. Motus perpetuus.*</note>

Everyone acknowledges that there is perpetual motion in Nature: especially if we consider (as is proper) the untiring power of generation, which also ensures that every corruption of one thing becomes the generation of another.

But whether it can be achieved by art—that something might move perpetually and specifically in a local sense—many have affirmed this, yet to my knowledge, no one has actually demonstrated it in reality.

However, Cornelius Drebbel <note>1572–1633, a famous Dutch inventor and "alchemist" at the court of King James I</note>, an English Chemist and Mechanic, is said to have found a different method and discovered a *Perpetual Mobile*. Regarding this matter, there exists his letter to James, King of Great Britain, published by Joachim Morsius.

In it he writes: "To make it certain that I have knowledge of the cause of the prime mover, I can construct a globe that rotates perpetually according to the course of the heavens once every twenty-four hours, or as many more times as I see fit, so that even in a thousand years it would not fail once. It shows us the Years, Months, Days, Hours, the course of the Sun, Moon, and all the Planets and Stars whose motion is known to men. Likewise, various kinds of instruments which, at a certain time or even continuously, produce a harmonious musical concert. In short, whatever can be done by weight, by rotating steel, by flowing water and fire, this knowledge provides forever; but the expenses alone make it less profitable if a great force is required. Furthermore, to better confirm that I understand the cause of the motion of things upward and downward, and what carries the earth and water in the midst of the air: I suspend the earth in the middle of the water like a globe in a closed glass, and the water in the middle of the air, and the air in the middle of the fire, so that one element surrounds the other like one circle around another. Or, conversely, I place the air in the middle of the water like a globe, and the water in the middle of the earth, embracing each other just as the air embraces this orb of the earth. And in this way, I make the high low, the low high, the light heavy, and the heavy light. Moreover, I push standing water upward to a height of ten, twenty, or more feet. And because I have discovered the cause of the wind, I build machines that blow vehemently. And with the knowledge of the ebb and flow <note>the tides</note>, I make an instrument that always flows and ebbs twice every 24 hours, showing the months, their days, the course of the Moon, and the hours of the tides forever."

But on this matter, one may consult Burggravius's *Biolychnium* in the letters, *folio 41*, and Staritzius in the *Treasury of Heroes, folio 13 and following.*

## 20. Common Opinions.

A common opinion <note>original: *opinio communis*—the consensus of legal scholars when the law itself is silent or ambiguous</note> obtains the force of Law. It is not permitted to judge against a common opinion. A judge who decides against it "makes the suit his own" <note>original: *litem suam facit*—a legal term meaning the judge becomes personally liable for the damages if his departure from standard legal consensus causes a wrongful loss</note>. However, it ought not to be held if it is not supported by firm reasons or any Law. In the Imperial Chamber <note>original: *Camera Imperialis*—the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, judgments have often been made against common opinions. Justus Oldekop, *On the Oath in the Other’s Soul, pages 73, 74.* On when a common opinion has its place, Justus Oldekop, *against Carpzov, page 245, number 15, page 163, number 31, page 163, number 30.* When a common opinion is discovered to be false by a specific case of Law or a concluding reason, it is not to be followed in judging. Klock, *volume 2, consultation 42, numbers 20, 21, 23.* On the Choice of Opinions, Matthæus Matthesilanus of Bologna.

To attack common opinions and pursue subtleties belongs to the Schools <note>academic or theoretical debate</note>; but for the court, it is to hold to common opinions. Corasius, *On Common Opinion.* Whether and when a common opinion must be adhered to. Knipschild, *On Testamentary Trusts, chapter 16, number 369.* The authorities of Doctors <note>legal scholars</note> who are destitute of reasons are not to be attended to. *Chapter 11, number 197.* A judge who judges against a common opinion judges no less by ignorance, and "makes the suit his own," than one who judges against the Law itself. Dr. Bitsch, *In Cases for a Friend, in the Prolegomena, number 10.* Although it has been taught by most that no account should be taken in judging and advising of a common opinion which is evidently false, which can be refuted by law or destroyed by a better, urgent, and vehement reason; others, however, want the authority of a common opinion to be so great that it prevails even over law and truth, and they say it must be followed in judging even if the contrary sentiment is truer. Whence Vivius, *Opinion 398, number 60,* says: it is in a way to "put one’s mouth against heaven" <note>a metaphorical expression for extreme arrogance or challenging an established, almost divine order</note> if anyone recedes from a common opinion in judging and advising, even if the case of law seems to be to the contrary. As Matthæac has skillfully said, *book 2, On the Path of Law, last chapter, number 30:* After the Empire of Justinian, more than a thousand years ago, this opinion of the Jurists <note>original: *Jurisprudentium*</note> began to claim royal authority and power for itself, and to exercise the strength of Princes or Lawgivers in all things. This opinion alone, while the Emperors were intent on and occupied with greater matters, dared to consult for the world, to give rights and laws, and to bear and prescribe legal responses to those consulting, just like the Oracles of the ancients. And Contius, *book 2, Subsequent Readings 18, at the beginning:* Pragmatic and courtroom men read every most stale interpreter of Law more diligently and frequently than the authorities and Laws of the Jurists or Emperors. How then will they allow themselves to be convinced? Whence, after Baronius, Nevizanus writes, *book 5, number 67, at the verse "case of law":* Even if the case of law is most present, yet it is a wonder to see a man of eminent science who answers a case of law without a revolution <note>re-reading</note> of books. Bitsch, *in the place cited, number 11,* at great length.

<column-break/>

That opinion is to be embraced by which, in doubt, sin is avoided. Barbosa, *book 13, chapter 25, axiom 2.* Among contrary opinions, that one is to be followed which reconciles the matter with a distinction. *Axiom 3.* That opinion is presumed truer which is received and approved by the majority of the Doctors <note>legal experts</note>. *Axiom 4.* One referring to many opinions usually seems to establish the last one. *Axiom 5.* Where we have a common opinion, we ought not to care for the singular sentiments of certain individuals. *Axiom 7.* A common opinion obtains the force of Custom. *Axiom 8.* A common opinion is stronger than a legal fiction. *Axiom 9.* When we have a case within the terms [of the law], we must stick to it, just as the Bolognese stick to their *Caroccio* <note>original: *temoni*—referring to the wagon-pole of the 'Caroccio', a symbolic battle-chariot of the Italian city-states; here it means staying true to a guiding standard</note>. Bullæus, *in Consultations, page 153 in my copy.*

### What a "truffa" judgment <note>original: *Sententia truffa*—likely referring to a deceitful, nonsensical, or "mockery" judgment</note> is, Zahn, *On Lies, book 3, chapter 4, number 8.*

Common opinion must be retained in advising and judging. *Cf. Altdorf, pages 216, 339.* Common opinion is to be adhered to in Practice. Marius Antoninus, *book 1, Resolution 9, number 14; and Resolution 102, number 22.* Common opinion is to be kept in Practice. *Book 1, resolution 23, number 10;* or rather the more common one. *Book 2, resolution 59, case 10.* The opinion of ancient Doctors is to be protected rather than that of the moderns. *Book 2, resolution 46, number 6.* Ancient Doctors are superior to moderns in weight, number, and measure. Bullæus, *consultation 3, number 84, page 453 in my copy.* An opinion, although it is common, if it is not proven nor aided by reason, ought not to be followed. Marius Antoninus, *book 2, resolution 48, number 9.* The opinion of a Doctor not alleging law, reason, or authority, is not to be attended to. *Book 2, resolution 59, case 2, at the end.* If a judge judges according to common opinion and interpretation, even if that opinion is against theoretical truth, nevertheless the sentence is valid and the judge is excused from sin. Lord Tabor, *On Transfer, page 184.* No account of common opinion is to be had if it is destitute of texts or firm reasons. Vivius, *Decision 440, number 15.* Jacob Menochius, *book 2, presumption 71, number 24, page 9; in the canon "Chorepiscopi" 5, after the middle: "and what lacks reason, it is necessary to extirpate." Distinction 86.* Paul Christinæus, *volume 1, Belgian Decisions 96, number 18.*

## 21. Obligation.

In the City of Kaufbeuren <note>original: *Kauffbaurn*</note> and its surroundings, as also in Überlingen <note>original: *Uberlingæ*</note> and many other Imperial Cities, there is a custom that if a legal instrument of mortgage <note>original: *hypothecæ*</note> or obligation is not drawn up before the Chief Secretary <note>original: *Archigrammateo*</note> and the scribe of the City, the Creditor has no right of proof from it; and that such a Statute or Custom is valid is held by Mynsinger, *Response 9, numbers 2, 20, 21, decade 1.* Through an obligation, one arrives at alienation <note>the transfer of property or rights to another</note>. Klock, *volume 1, consultation 35, number 218.* An obligation without cause <note>legal justification</note> is ineffective. *Consultation 11, number 121 and following.* A mortgage does not attach to an uncertain obligation, nor does the burden endure after it has come to a privileged person. Klock, *consultation 23, number 358.*

**Ob** is an augmentative preposition <note>meaning it intensifies the word it is attached to</note>. **Obligo** means to bind very strongly and firmly. Lord Biccius in *Aurea*, page 381. Barbosa, book 13, chapter 5, axiom 11. In a general obligation, those things do not come forward which, in a specific case, one likely would not have intended to bind. Axiom 10. Regarding an obligation "to do," whether the defendant is released by providing the "interest" <note>the monetary value of the performance</note>. Law 18, regarding payment. Such handwritten bonds and confessions that are void and empty should be reclaimed from creditors or formally demanded back to avoid various difficulties. And when the year is out, all prescribed things shall be off; they shall be "dry letters," dead and without defect. Lord Doctor Tabor in *Criminal Gatherings*, page 202. On individual and divisible obligations: Eguinarius Baro, a Frenchman.

Whether a Creditor returning a handwritten bond <note>original: *Chirographum*—a legal document signed by the debtor</note> to his debtor is seen as having easily agreed not to seek payment? Concerning gold and silver, and also other movable property, one may perform and make <term>declarations</term> <note>original: *fassiones*—formal legal acknowledgments or confessions of debt or property ownership common in Hungarian and Germanic law</note>. Augustinus Wagner in *Hungarian Land Law*, part 1, title 3: "of certain declarations which cannot be overturned." Part 1, title 61, there: "declarations and bonds of debt." Of those declarations and confessions which require a lawful statute and assignment or not. Part 1, title 63: "which declarations require Royal Consent or not."
