## 22. Waste. Desert.

**Oede** <note>Waste or wasteland</note> signified to our ancestors inheritance, patrimony, goods, or fields: from which hereditary goods that are more precious and refined are called **Kleinodia** <note>Jewels or heirlooms</note>. **Einöde** refers to a desert or some uncultivated place. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation 1*, thesis 2, letter a.

It has come to pass in these days, through lack of diligence and oversight, that people almost everywhere let go of **waste and unbuilt properties**—the uncultivated goods <note>original: *bona inculta*</note>—and take almost no notice of them, because they cannot be brought to profit immediately without effort and expense. More on this in Lord Obrecht’s *Political Thoughts on the Improvement of Land and People*, page 143 at the end and following, and page 93, number 6; page 94, number 8. Land lying waste and unbuilt is not to be burdened with taxes and assessments. Zorer, part 1, question 11, number 827.

### Often. Frequently.

In how many acts the word **often** <note>original: *sæpè*</note> is verified is a question not asked in vain. And although some require two acts—through the text in the final law joined with the rubric of the Code *If often in total restoration* and Law 29, section 4, regarding the Julian Law on adultery—and others require three or four, as Ayrer reports from Socinus and Jason in Law 1, the only one, in the Code on errors of calculation, numbers 143 and 144; nevertheless, since a rule should not be made from special examples, I think that in this matter of ours, it must be left to the **arbitration of the Judge**. For not all things are determined by the Law; some are at the Judge's discretion. Argument from Law 1, final section, in the *Digest* on the right of deliberation. Tusclus, letter A, conclusion 471, number 4.

### Although. Even if.

**Although** <note>original: *Obgleich* / *Etsi*</note>, even if; a word of what efficacy it may be. Berlich, 2, conclusion 40, number 36.

## 23. Order. Arrangement.

**Order** <note>original: *Ordnung* / *Ordo*</note> is the master of beings. Bartholomæus Socinus in Law 1, number 4, in the *Digest*. See by all means Limn., book 8, chapter 6, number 57.

**To order**, to set, to do, to give. Limn. in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 35.

The order of writing shows the **order of the will**. Barbosa, book 13, chapter 30, axiom 8. The order of writing is always observed in Dispositions. Axiom 7. The order of naming designates the order of affection and charity. Axiom 6. The order of words designates the order of the intellect. Axiom 5. A prerogative is argued from the order. Axiom 2. **Anticipation** <note>taking a right before it is due</note> is hateful in law. Zythander von Buder, *On the Rights of Brewing*, part 1, chapter 4, number 3 and following.

### 25. Burden. <note>original: "Onus"</note>

See above under the word **Grievance** <note>original: "Beschwerung"</note>. One should not be weighed down by vexations, weariness, or troubles. If these words appear in a **Privilege** <note>a private law or special grant</note>, the question is: how are they to be understood? Balduin on law 1 of the Code *concerning those things under the name of penalty*, number 27; and also there Barbat. Law *bona fides* 57, Digest *on the Rules of Law.* One should not undergo several burdens at the same time and for the same thing. Discussed widely by Barbosa, *book 13, chapter 22, axioms 7 and 8.* A burden attached to a thing causes the thing to pass along with it (axiom 11). Lord Dr. Tabor *on Suffrage, page 232, number 8; and in so far as page 235, numbers 9 and 10.* Burdens are to be enjoined by the votes of all. Rittershufius in the *Novels, page 342, number 23.* It is unjust for someone to be burdened by the act of another. Hugo Donellus *on Civil Law, page 1433, 50. B.*

Things that are said "in passing" <note>original: "Obiter"</note> or along the way are not taken into consideration. Law *naturalem* 5, Digest *on acquiring ownership*; law *si quis post hanc* 6, Code *on private buildings.* Barbosa, *book 13, chapter 2, axiom.*

### 27. Offering. <note>original: "Oblatio"</note>

On Offerings: Marianus Socinus the Elder; Troilus Malvetius of Bologna. An offering <note>of payment</note> together with the sealing and depositing of the money has the force of payment. Klock, *volume 2, counsel 39, number 188 and following.* An offering without depositing frees the buyer neither from the principal nor from the interest. *Counsel 39, number 372.*

An offering made in Court takes the place of payment and release. Law 1, Code *on those who can [be preferred] in pledge.* Barbosa, *book 13, chapter 4, axiom 1.* He who has made an offering is no longer in default <note>original: "in mora"</note>. Axiom 2. Things offered voluntarily can be accepted without sin. Axiom 4. On the part of the Creditor, a delay <note>default</note> occurs if the debtor has offered the money or even any other thing owed to the creditor at the proper place and time, and the creditor refused to accept it without just cause. Lord Dr. Biccius in *Aureis, page 620.* What the offering of a debt, and its sealing and depositing, may effect. Conr. Rittershufius in the *Novels, page 265, number 9.*

### 28. Easter. The Paschal Feast. <note>original: "Ostern. Festum Paschale."</note>

As soon as the first day of Easter has dawned, let no prison hold anyone enclosed, and let the bonds of all be dissolved. Law 3, Code *on Episcopal hearings.* The French either release captives for a few days during the days of Easter or free them entirely. Georgius von Daffel, a very great friend of mine, on Law 6, Code *on holidays, theses 43 and 44.* Olearius, *Persian Travel Description, concerning Muscovy.*

The Moon, which the ancient Germans worshiped, was called Hertha or the Earth our grandmother, also Venus, Estar or Ostar; hence the month of Ostar or April, as well as the word and festival of **Easter** come, which the English call *Easter*. Grotius calls the venerable festival of the Passover "the Festival" by excellence <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν"</note> in his *New Testament commentary on Matthew chapter 27.* Prolix on this matter are St. Fagundez, *Pr. III, book 1, chapter 5,* and the Doctors of Canon Law: Panormitanus, the Cardinal, *Clementine 1, on privileges, question 11, and others.* Diego Covarruvias, *book 1, title 2, chapter 17, number 1, on Tithes.* Rodolff Hospinian *on the origin of Christian Festivals.* Durandus, in various places. ### 30. Place. <note>original: "Ort. Locus."</note>

A "place" is not an entire estate, but a certain portion of an estate. <note>Law 60 of the Digest, "On the Signification of Words." The Digest is a massive 6th-century collection of Roman legal opinions.</note> For an estate <note>original: "fundus"</note> is something whole, and we usually understand a "place" to be without a farmhouse. An estate, however, is the substance and contains everything held by the soil. Javolenus in *Law Question 115, On the Signification of Words.* A place is accidental and clings to its subject; therefore, it is said that it is not size that separates a "place" from an "estate," but our own legal attachment to it. Barbosa, *book 10, chapter 27, axiom 1.* A "place" is a required formality <note>original: "solennitas"</note> of a legal instrument. *Axiom 2.* The "place of contract" <note>original: "Locus Contractus"</note> must always be sought out where it was celebrated, the reason being that it is always taken into account. *Axiom 3.* For a place to be exempt or not exempt from a territory are considered equal matters. *Axiom 4.* On what a "place" is: Lord Dr. Biccius, *On Possession, page 80.* A place is not merely that surface surrounding an external body, but that which is contained within that surface; and where it is continuous. With this, the description of the Dialecticians coincides: that a place is not only that in which we stand, but the entire scope—what is before and after, what is to the right and left, above and below—and not just the scope, but the entire interior space by which we are contained: upward, downward, and the middle of the place. Gödd. on *Law "Locus" 60, number 2, Digest "On the Signification of Words."* The place does not hinder piety. <note>A reminder that one can be holy regardless of their physical location.</note> Schuppius in *The Patient Job, page 56.*
<margin>See below under the word **Port**, regarding the Ottoman Porte <note>The central government of the Ottoman Empire.</note>.</margin>

### 31. Fruit, Fruit Tithes. <note>original: "Obst, Obstzehenden. Pomum."</note>

If a house is bequeathed, is the garden also owed, if it is contiguous? Mantica, *On Conjectures of the Last Will, book 9, title 2, number 36.* See the word **House**. A person is considered "present" even if they are in the gardens. *Law "Praesens" 5, Digest "On Procurators."* Rudinger, *Century 2, observation 59, number 2.* Barbosa, *Axioms, book 14, chapter 65, axiom 2.*

Small tithes <note>original: "Minores decimæ"</note> are provided from gardens, trees, the offspring of animals, and other fruits of the earth. Henricus Krolovv, *On Tithes, thesis 13.*

<column-break/>

and those cited there. Under the "Minute" or "Small Tithes," fruit is counted, along with whatever grows on trees. Besold in *Politics, letter Z.*

In O. A. <note>Likely *Ober-Amt*, a local administrative district.</note>, three Palatine subjects refused to give house or fruit tithes to Lord T. for a long time, instead relying on a claim of prescription <note>A legal right gained by long-term use or the passage of time.</note>, arguing that for so and so long, no fruit tithe or "smoke-hens" <note>original: "Rauchhanen" — a traditional tax of poultry paid by a household to a landlord.</note> had been collected. Lord T., however, appealed only to the letter of investiture <note>original: "Lehenbrief"</note>, covering things great and small, dead and living. He finally wrote to His Imperial Majesty, stating that if he were entitled to it, His Imperial Majesty should protect him in it without personal cost, and if he were not entitled, he would desist. He prevailed, except in the case of a single peasant who produced an ancient letter from a nobleman, showing the property had been sold to him free of tithes. However, since all lands in this place are subject to tithes, the dispute has been postponed.

The communities of S. and W. understand the point regarding fruit tithes to mean that where someone has three, four, or more trees standing in a field or vineyard, or has entire orchards, the tithe shall always be given from such trees. Furthermore, under such trees, as far as the shadow of each extends, both village communities shall not be obliged to give any [other] tithes. But where roughly one or two trees stand in a field or vineyard, only the tithe from under those trees shall be given, and nothing from the fruit above. From this, it is clear to see that regarding the very small house-gardens where there are perhaps three or four little trees, not a single letter is written nor anything mentioned. But "the inclusion of one is not the exclusion of another" <note>original: "unius inclusio, non est alterius exclusio"</note>, and the communities must prove their exception. Indeed, these communities have refused the tithe not only in the very small house-gardens but also in the large gardens, even where they have harvested two or three sets of sixty <note>original: "Schock"</note>, and where thirty to forty trees stand in many a garden.

In Borra and Ottensoß, the fruit tithe is said to be undisputed. In S., the fruit tithe is paid in money, whether the harvest succeeds or not. Regarding trees watered with wine: Drexel in *The Golden Mine, part 2, chapter 6, page 162.* "Boundary tree" <note>original: "Marckbaum"</note>, "Cutting tree" <note>original: "Schneidebaum"</note>, a "timbered tree" which has a covering—so it is called in the ancient laws of the Lombards. Lord Schottelius in *The German Main Language, folio 444.*

King Charles in France had the custom of always eating a peeled apple after a meal. He used this to test his sons to see which was the most obedient. Schuppius in *Lucidor, number 6.*

On the Gold Coast of Guinea, they hold trees to be their gods, their *Fretisso Dafianam* <note>A corruption of "fetish."</note>, which, as they believe, provides them with fish.

### 32. Dettingen. Oettingen.

Regarding these Counts, one must certainly consult Sprenger in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 443 and following; likewise, most recently, *The High-Countly Windischgrätz-Oettingen Lineage*, Volume 3, where it says: "The ancient High-Countly Oettingen lineage is one of the oldest in the Holy Roman Empire; the countly line is traced back in proper order through 27 generations to this time, from Grayo or Cayo, Count of Oettingen. He was held in such high regard and favor by Emperor Otto the First and Great that His Imperial Majesty gave him his sister, the widow of the Count of Eberstein, in marriage in the year 933."

The lineage of the Lords of Oettingen is very old, having already flourished during the reign of Emperor Otto I, from whom they received the addition to their coat of arms. Eberhardus is found in written documents in the year 1130; Guno and Ludovicus flourished around the year 1140. Ludovicus traveled to Syria with Emperor Frederick II. They have allied themselves through marriage with the House of Austria, the Palatinate, Württemberg, Baden, Anhalt, and other noble houses in Germany. They were also Landgraves in Alsace, and to this day, those of Fleckenstein hold their lordship in Alsace as a fief from the Counts of Oettingen. Nördlingen also recognized them as lords and patrons in former times. Many storks reside in Dettingen and have their nests in the castle. However, when both Ludovicus the father and son, Counts of Dettingen, had to go into exile <note>original: "ins Elend ziehen" – often implying religious or political exile.</note> due to their religion during the time of Emperor Charles V, the storks immediately flew away with them as if they were their companions. During the entire time the Counts were absent—nearly seven years—the storks were no longer seen in Oettingen until the Counts were

<column-break/>

restored by the Emperor to their land and people; then all the storks came flying back again. In Gravina, the Duke has forbidden anyone to harm a stork under penalty of corporal punishment; and it is notable that no one has ever heard of a stork being defeated or killed in a fight against snakes. Megiser, *In the Delights of Naples*, page 169. Conradus, Count of Oettingen, took the daughter of the Landgrave of Alsace, Heinrich, as his wife and became Landgrave in Alsace; among his descendants, the Landgraviate of lower Alsace was sold to Lord Johannes of Lichtenberg, Bishop of Strasbourg. More on this in Zeiller, *Continuation of Germany*, page 111.

See Bucelinus in *German Genealogies, Notitia*, page 112. They have sought that right of the County since time immemorial. Becker in *Public Law*, page 170. Add the *Oettingen Funeral Rites* performed for Lord Gottfried, Count of Oettingen, by M. Johann Georg Schwalbach, Imperial Poet. What churches and monasteries the Counts of Oettingen founded; what journeys they made to the holy places. Lord Bock, in *Oettingen Splendor*, in the notes on page 67: they allied themselves with the Arch-House of Austria through marriage, page 89.

### 33. Oldenburg. Oldenburgum.

The title or inscription of the Counts of Oldenburg. Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 9, number 23. The lordship of Jever was awarded to Count Johann of Oldenburg by judgment, and was afterwards confirmed in the revision of 1591. More in Zeiller, *Continuation of Germany*, page 455. The kings of Denmark and Holstein descend from the Counts of Oldenburg, page 220. Sprenger, in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 449. Otto I, through marriage, acquired the County of Alvensleben. Once, while thirsty during a hunt, he received a precious silver and gilded vessel—shaped like a hunter's horn—from a maiden who emerged from a cleft in the Osenberg that had opened up. Although the maiden requested he drink from it to maintain unity within his lineage, he did not wish to drink but instead poured the beverage backward over his horse. The horse's hair fell out as a result, and he hurried away from there to his companions. This drinking vessel, which is still kept in Oldenburg today, was presented visually in a copperplate engraving by Hermann Hammelmann, Licentiate of Holy Theology and Superintendent, in his *Oldenburg Chronicle*, part 1, chapter 10, page 20. Zeiller, *Continuation of Germany*, pages 191, 192. ### 34. Ortenburg. Ortenburgum.

The Counts of Ortenburg in Carinthia <note>Kärnten, a province in modern-day Austria.</note>, of the younger lineage that recently died out, and the family of Amadis in Italy <note>original: "Welschland," a term used historically by German speakers to refer to Romance-speaking areas, primarily Italy or France.</note>, received the power from the Emperors to create Counts Palatine <note>original: "Hofgraven," officials with specific judicial and administrative privileges granted by the Emperor.</note>. See Zeiller, letter 3, page 506. The Counts of Ortenburg, as well as the Counts of Thurn, were hereditary Imperial Counts Palatine. See Mundius, *On Counts Palatine*, chapter 1, number 25.

<column-break/>

Chapter 3, number 50. The privilege of Charles V, by which on March 21, 1554, at Nuremberg, he created Gabriel, Count of Ortenburg, and his successors as Counts Palatine, inserted this clause: that they are not compelled to seek confirmation of the privilege. See Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 10, number 45. The town of Spittal an der Drau belongs to a Count of Ortenburg, who has a palace there. However, these counts descend from Lord Gabriel Salamanca, a Spanish nobleman (though others are of a different opinion regarding this Salamanca, believing him to have been a native of Portugal), whom Emperor Ferdinand I elevated to the rank of Count and enfeoffed with the County of Ortenburg in Carinthia. For the old Counts of Ortenburg, who ruled the land of Carinthia for many years in former times, completely died out in Carinthia around the year of Christ 1420 or 1416; only one branch of them remains, to be found near Vilshofen in Bavaria. See Zeiller in *German Itinerary*, page 570. Regarding the Counts of Ortenburg, with the addition of the older line, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, volume 1, additions to book 4, chapter 4, page 410.

Count Frederick of Ortenburg was held in high regard by Duke Albrecht. Frederick of Stubenberg, while a prisoner, very urgently and most highly entreated this Count—as a kinsman—to offer only this: that he be released from prison on bail to go to those of Bavaria and Salzburg to announce the termination of the alliance and union. The Prince granted it, saying: he did not begrudge Stubenberg this honor. Gerhard von Roo, page 57. Under the Duke of Bavaria, by reason of particular goods, are the Counts of Ortenburg. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 4, number 94, at the end.

Regarding the lineage of the Counts of Ortenburg, see Gabriel Bucelinus, Monk of the Order of St. Benedict and Theologian of the Imperial Monastery of Weingarten, part 3 of *Genealogical Notices of Germany*, pages 197 and 108. Also Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 397.

### 35. Tender of Payment. <note>original: "Oblatio"</note>

Regarding the tender of a debt <note>original: "oblatione debiti"</note>, see Dr. Biccius in *Golden Matters* <note>original: "Aureis"</note>, section 5, thesis 28, at the end. *The Forum of Protests*, page 69. Barbosa, book 13, chapter 4, throughout the axioms. Regarding the tender of a work or labor, Dr. Biccius in *Golden Matters*, section 4, thesis 94. A simple tender <note>An offer to pay or perform without actual delivery, usually to fulfill a legal requirement.</note> operates so that a penalty may be avoided. See Dr. Felwinger, *Forum of Protests*, page 171, via the law *Celsus* at the end of the Digest *on arbitration* <note>original: "ff. de arbit."</note>; and there is a Gloss, and there Salycet on the law *acceptam* in the Code *on interest*. To avoid a penalty, the law allows for compensation by right <note>original: "ipso jure"</note> from another quantity owed. There is a notable Gloss on the law *si constat* in the Code *on Compensation*. Even a simple tender stops the running of interest. Whether a tender made only in words accomplishes anything: see the same source in the *Forum of Protests*, number 4.

### 36. Omens.

Swarms of bees are considered a bad omen <note>original: "malum omen"</note>. Master Rupert, observations on Florus, Book 2, Chapter 6, Section 14, 2. Great and heroic spirits have often been prophetic <note>original: "μαντικὰ" (mantika)</note>, and even while doing something else, they can foresee their own or others' fortunes. The same author, Book 4, Chapter 2, Section 79. Omens foretelling slaughter in war. Master Dilherr, Volume 1, *Academic Disputations*, page 647 and following. Omens are not to be despised by Christians, page 656. Sad omens in war should not undermine a good cause, nor make men timid, but rather make them cautious, page 757. Various memorable omens or signs that occurred during the marriage arrangements of Archduke Sigismund Francis and Lady Maria Hedwig Augusta, Countess Palatine of the Rhine, are described at length in the work on the *Broken Branch of the Princely Austrian Regents, Year 1665, pages 14 and 15.*

The famous Rupert cites as many writers on omens as possible in his notes on Valerius Maximus, Book 1, Chapter 5. Ridiculous omens <note>original: "Omina ridicula"</note>. The same author in his *Political Dissertation* on chapters 6, 7, and 8. Omens offered by divinity. In the same place, the feeding of chickens as an omen; see Valerius Maximus, Book 1, Chapter 8, Dissertation 2. Master Rupert on omens from clothing and color. Rupert on Florus, Book 1, Chapter 12, paragraph 7, 2. Also regarding birds sitting nearby, Book 1, Chapter 12, Section 20, 3.

### 37. Double Adultery. see Adultery.

Double adultery <note>original: "Oberhurerey" or "Adulterium duplex"</note>. This refers to a case where both parties involved in the act are married to others. Hartmann Pistoris, observation 32, numbers 53 and 54. Alemann in *Palestra Consult.* pages 5, 37, 38, 40, 42, 43.

### 38. Fallow Fields and Grazing.

When the fallow fields <note>original: "Oesch"</note> are empty, or in the empty fallows. *Acts of Lindau*, folio 309. The winter fallow, the summer fallow. The fallows should be left in peace. *Acts of Lindau*, folio 865.

### 39. Sovereign Head. Head of the Empire.

Head of the Empire <note>original: "Caput Imperii"</note>; the Emperors often attributed this title of honor and power to themselves in the Imperial Recesses <note>The "Recess" was the official summary of the decisions made at an Imperial Diet</note>. Imperial Recess of the Year 1530, section "the like." Also 1566, section "We also wish, as Roman Emperor and Head of the Roman Empire."

### 40. Omissions.

To omit is to act <note>original: "Omittere est facere"</note>. Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 586, and those cited there. That which is omitted is held to be omitted. Barbosa, Book 13, chapter 20, axiom 1, at length. An omission made through forgetfulness is not held as a deliberate omission, axiom 6. The word "especially" is sometimes understood even if not present. Mantica, *On the Conjectures of Last Wills*, Book 11, title 17, number 30. Something is deemed omitted if it was not expressly stated by those making the arrangement. *Acts of Lindau*, page 114 at the end, and page 556 after the beginning.

### 41. Olff. Help.

"Olff" or "Ulff," that is, Help <note>original: "Hülff" or "auxilium"</note>, hence the names Rudolf, Landolf, Ludolf, Gangolf, Arnolf, Adolph. Master Schottelius.

### 42. Without Prescription.

Often used as a word of flattery <note>original: "Ohne Maßgebung" - a phrase often used in petitions to mean "without wishing to dictate to your judgment"</note>. Londorp, Volume 1, *Public Acts*, Book 6, chapter 154.

### P.

Emperor Charles V is said to have asked in every city about the three "P's": how things stood with the *Prætore* (the Magistrate), the *Pastore* (the Pastor), and the *Præceptore* (the Teacher). The letter "P" and its opposite are frequently found placed in the *Pandects* of our law <note>The Pandects, or Digest, is a massive compilation of Roman law</note>. Brisson, *Single Book of Miscellanies*, my page 392.

### 1. Lease. Renting.

Although this word is sometimes used for a <term>long-term lease|emphyteusis</term> or a perpetual tenancy, and is taken for a fixed rent <note>hence "Pachtkorn" or rent-grain</note>, it also sometimes denotes a standard contract of hire or lease <note>original: "conductio"</note>. *Mirror of the Saxons* <note>original: "Sachsenspiegel"</note>, Book 3, article 21, number 4, in the Glossary. Master Ernest Cothmann, *Legal Responses* 97, number 12, volume 2. *Emphyteusis* <note>A type of long-term land lease where the tenant improves the land</note> is derived from the Greek *ἐμφυτεύω* (to plant/implant), from which the German also comes.

### ADDITION.

Regarding grain-rent and money-rent. Limn. in *Public Law*, Book 6, chapter 4, number 20.
On the phrase "to put out for lease" <note>original: "in Pacht thun"</note>, see Salmasius, *On Bank Interest*, page 516. Master Doctor Tabor, *On the Law of Partnership*, chapter 2, number 15, at the end. "Pacht" and "pachten" are also said of those who have received the use of a field for a certain portion of the crops. Master Hahn on the Digest, Book 19, title 2, number 7 at the end, and number 8. At the end, the lessee is called a "Pachtmann."
On the words "Pfachtener" (tenant), "Pfachtmüller" (lease-miller), and "Pfachtzins" (lease-rent), see Master Tabor, *On Reassignments*, page 101.

### 2. Pallium.

The Pallium is a mark of Archiepiscopal dignity; it is taken from the body, that is, the Altar of Blessed Peter, as a sign of Apostolic unity.
But regarding this Archiepiscopal Pallium, see Serarius, *Matters of Mainz*, Book 3, folio 486 and following; and Cucchu, Book 1, *Institutes of Canon Law*, title 10. Baronius in the *Index of Annals*. Longus in the *Chronological Breviary*, folio 270. Alzedo, *On Episcopal Dignity*, folio 152, etc.

### ADDITION.

Add Sprenger in *Fragments of Public Law*, page 232 and following. Limn. in *Public Law*, Volume 2, *Additions to Book 3*, chapter 3, page 151 and following. Zeiller in his *Itinerary of Italy*, page 143, tells of the Pallium (or *Casiola*) of an English King, which was so heavily laden with translucent pearls that one could hardly wear it for more than a quarter of an hour. See "Mantel" [Cloak] above. Regarding the E. M. I. ### **6. Paradise. Paradisus.**

Regarding the **Paradise** and **Hells** of the Cannibals (the eaters of men), and those of the Romans and Greeks, etc., see Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 2, book 1, chapter 26, page 184 and following, where he notes that all nations expect a reward for good actions and virtues after this life; add my own work in *Politics: On Religion and Rewards*.

->ADDITION.<-

God—whose power is greatest, whose goodness is best, and whose wisdom is wonderful—adorned this garden with his own hands with such beauty, delight, pleasantness, fertility, and security, that we have nothing written or painted from which we can sufficiently estimate it. The most delicate **gardens of Adonis**, or the most celebrated gardens of **Juno and Alcinous**, would be mere rubbish and not worth a straw if we were to compare them with it. Here was an incredible abundance of most fragrant flowers, imitating gold on one side and gems or silver on the other; the most ample supply of every kind of fruit. For the vast garden itself was brightened by gracious mercy, irrigated by four most healthful rivers, and refreshed by the pleasant tranquility of the eastern region, where they believe it was located. Master Johann Michael Dilherr, in *Philological Apparatus*, Dedicatory Letter.

Do you examine the Sacred Scriptures? You will see gardens born together with the birth of the world, which God himself assigned as a dwelling for the first man, and as it were, the seat of a blessed life. Lipsius, *On Constancy*. Regarding Paradise—where it was, and whether it is to be understood at least spiritually—see **Augustine**, *The City of God*, Book 13, part 2, chapter 21; and the commentary there by Ludovicus Vives.

### **7. Pasquinade. Infamous Libel.**

It is entirely clear from the **Imperial Constitutions** and the punishments imposed by them that the crime of **Pasquinades** and **Infamous Libels** <note>original: "Pasquillorum & Famosorum Libellorum"</note> is most grave. No upright or honest man will deny this, although malicious men may think it a light matter and indulge in it too much today, as Oldendorp heavily complains in his notes on the law *diffamari*. *Code on the Manumission of Freeborn Persons*, number 5. Wesenbec on the Title of the Code *On Seditious Persons*. Heig, Book 2, question 31, number 1.

It is called a **Pasquill** <note>A "Pasquinade" or "Pasquill" is a public lampoon or satire</note> because all kinds of slanderous writings used to be fixed at night to the shop of **Pasquillus**, a Roman tailor. After his death, a marble statue in gladiatorial dress was erected there. The reason Infamous Libels were posted in that place was that the tailor Pasquillus himself was accustomed to criticize the Pope and the Cardinals with wonderful liberty and impunity because of their excesses. See Zwinger in *The Theater of Human Life*, volume 21, book 3, page 3709, under the word "Pasquillus." But more certain facts on this matter are found in the *Topography of Rome*, recently published in Frankfurt, where the following is stated: As to what that marble statue was...

...regarding **Pasquino** <note>original: "Pasquinus"; the famous "talking statue" of Rome</note>, as it has long been commonly called, some have expressed doubts. Most, however, agree that it is a statue of a gladiator, or, if you prefer, of Mars or some other soldier. It remains in a physical posture as if wanting to strike, and beneath it lies another mutilated marble trunk or fragment of a second statue, which we take for certain was the enemy with whom he was fighting. Some report that this is a statue of one of the two chief guards of King Alexander of Macedon, who was also called by the name **Pasquino**, as suggested by a certain author who printed the ancient marbles and bronze statues of the city. How long this sign has stood there is not entirely clear, but it is easy to believe by conjecture that it dates from the time those buildings near which it stands were erected—namely, two hundred years ago or thereabouts. Indeed, the buildings were erected by Francesco Orsini <note>original: "Francisco de Ursinis"</note>, the Prefect of the City, as is read on the lintel of the doorway. Finally, two things occur to me to be said at present regarding a monument of this kind: First, that **Defamatory Libels** <note>original: "Famosi Libelli"; also known as Pasquinades</note>, as they are commonly called, which were once accustomed to be composed by imprudent and minimally pious men, used to be hung under this statue because it is in nearly the center of the city, so that they might be more easily read by passersby. The second, which is indeed wonderful, is that despite so many great passing years, this statue has persisted there to the prejudice of both public and private figures, and there has never been anyone who, out of zeal for piety and the Christian Religion, dared to remove it from there, whereby the opportunity for posting such libels or Pasquinades would be taken away. For they say that when a certain primary Prince <note>likely referring to a Pope, though unnamed</note> had decided that it should be thrown into the Tiber, he was immediately answered politely by one of his courtiers, who warned him not to command it be removed from there, *for it would happen that it would rail against Princes more severely under the water than above the ground.* And so, as is seen, it has persisted from that time until now.

Regarding the name of the Pasquinades and the origin of the name, one can also look to Lord Henricus von Pflaumern in his *Italian Mercury*, folio 262 and following, where he relates that he heard there were certain men among the highest ranks who were so little moved by that wantonness of the slanderous that they even studiously sought out and read the insults commonly presented against them by Pasquino. If indeed they heard the truth, they checked the tongues of the mockers through the amendment of their lives, rather than through investigation or punishment; and as is found in Demosthenes, they washed away the insults of the slanderers with good deeds.

Whether the capital punishment for a **Defamatory Libel** (established in the *Single Law of the Code on Defamatory Libels* and *article 110 of the Criminal Ordinance*) should also be imposed on those who have signed their own names and profess themselves to be the authors, see Nebelkra, *decision 16*. Likewise, whether he who objects to a true crime of someone through a **Defamatory Libel**

<column-break/>

should be punished with the penalty established for authors and publishers of Pasquinades, see the same author, *question 17*. Add Cothmann, *Academic Response 50, number 146*, where he treats many things regarding Defamatory Libels and their punishment, namely when it ought to take place or not. See also Menochius, *case 263, number 35, etc.*

But Lord Bocerus wrote a specific treatise on Defamatory Libels, and I also have certain things in my *Disputation on Injuries 1, thesis 31, etc., as well as Disputation 2, thesis 21.* That custom has withdrawn from the death penalty imposed on Defamatory Libels is noted by Lord Doctor Harpprecht at *paragraph 1, number 210, Institutes on Injuries.*

Whether poets are held liable by an action for injuries on account of Satirical Poems is explored by Lord Valerius Arithmaeus, a certain friend of mine while he lived, in his *Disputation on the Poetic Art*, where he writes thus: the Siren of Venusia <note>referring to the Roman poet Horace, who was from Venusia</note> urges the negative in the *Book on the Art of Poetry*:

> ->**To painters and to poets,**<-
> ->**There has always been an equal power of daring anything.**<-

*The same, Book 2, Satire 1:*

> ->**If anyone**<-
> ->**Has torn into one worthy of reproach, while being himself blameless,**<-
> ->**The legal tablets will be dismissed with a laugh, and you, sent away, will go free.**<-

*Juvenal, Satire 1:*

---

> ->**--- For who is so patient**<-
> ->**Of the unfair city, who so iron-willed, that he can restrain himself?**<-

To this authority, this reason is added: that all things which were written with the intention of correcting and amending should not be drawn into suspicion of injury, and therefore should not be punished. Lambert Daneau illustrates this proposition with examples in *Book 2 of Christian Ethics*. And poets have this goal set before them: that they may draw us back from the most impure opinions, from cruelty and all treachery and impure lust; that they may deter us from the most shameful things, raise us up from the filth of greed, call us back from rashness, and incite us to vigor against other outrages and vices, alluring us toward integrity of life, faith, religion, and equity. Natalis Comes, *Book 1 of Mythology, chapter 2*. And a general reproach is an injury to no specific person. However, when one writes against vices without a name, he who becomes angry is his own accuser. Pelargus in *Apologetic Antithesis, thesis 13*. Hence, when a certain Physician-Poet had written a Satire against an unlearned Physician, and a Jurist defended it publicly, saying: that those who creep into public offices through primary petitions are not legitimately called. There were those who thought themselves to be gnawed at, and therefore they acclaimed the sentence of the Juridical Faculty, by which it was nevertheless answered: that no action for injuries applies, since both the Poet and the Disputant kept themselves within the boundaries of generality. On the contrary side, there is this fact: that to no one is it granted, out of private affection...

For the rock of the rule remains unmoved: when the intent to injure is set aside, the action for injury must also be set aside. <note>original: "l. 3. l. 26 l. 44. ff. de injur." referencing the Digest on injuries.</note> Since intent constitutes the crime, just as consent constitutes a contract. <note>original: "l. 53. ff. de furt." referencing the Digest on theft.</note> For both Divine and Civil Law disapprove of private vengeance, and specifically of brawling. <note>original: "l. 13. §. æquissimum. ff. de usufruct."</note> Indeed, if Cicero is held to the light of truth when writing history <note>original: "l. 6. ff. de injur."</note>, why should one who publishes a Satirical Poem to the contempt and ignominy of another not be marked with the black pebble of a heinous injury? ### ADDITIO.
<note>Latin for "Addition"</note>

Defamatory libels <note>original German: "Schmähschrifften"</note>, where neither the author, nor the printer, nor the name of the place is included, and how they are to be punished according to the Imperial Recesses <note>original German: "Reichs-Abschied"</note> and the Imperial Criminal Court Ordinance <note>original German: "peinlichen Halsgerichts-Ordnung"</note>: see the City of Nuremberg’s Refutation of the Information regarding the state of the Imperial Postal Service in Nuremberg. A. 2. A defamatory libel <note>term: "Libellus famosus"; a written document intended to ruin a person's reputation.</note> is so called from the baseness of the slanderer who intends to tear apart anyone's good name with defamatory papers; for the honor of men is not situated in such a slippery place that it can be stained by someone’s petulant tongue. <note>original: "l. un. in fin. de fam. libell."</note> This is because honor is only taken away by law or by a judicial sentence for a crime. <note>original: "t. t. de his, qui not. infam."</note> Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist.</note> calls a book pertaining to the infamy of someone (specifically from the intention of the writer and the effect of the alleged crimes) what is called in German a "Schmähbrieff" <note>slanderous letter</note>, and commonly a "Pasquillus" <note>Pasquinade</note>, because defamatory epigrams <note>original Greek: "ἐπιγράμματα" (epigrammata)</note> were posted at Rome on the public statue of Pasquino the Tailor. <note>Citing Dauth on Testaments, Ludwell, Wehner, and Zeiller's Italian itinerary.</note> It is otherwise taken generally for any sort of reproach that makes a defendant of the one who devises it, writes it, or acts with malicious intent so that any of these things should happen; <note>original: "§. 1. J. de Injur."</note> or the one who sings it; <note>original: "l. 15. §. 27."</note> or the one who suppresses it. <note>original: "l. un. C. d. t."</note>

Properly speaking, a defamatory libel is made through writing <note>original: "per Scripturam"</note>, whether it be handwritten or printed. Imperial

<column-break/>

Recess at Augsburg, Year 1530. §. "and thereafter through the ordinary printing presses." But nevertheless, it can also be made analogously through a picture, likewise a sculpted or cast work. <note>original: "l. 5. §. 10. ff. de injur."</note> Imperial Recess, Year 1548, title "On Defamatory Libels" <note>original German: "von Schmäh-Schrifften"</note>: "painted, carved, cast, or made." Thus, the species of defamatory libels considered in general are: the defamatory libel proper, the defamatory picture, and the sculpted or cast work. <note>Citing Dr. Bleccius.</note> Guazzo mentions such a defamation in *Civil Controversies*, book 1, where a picture was fixed at night above the door of a certain nobleman’s house, which expressed to the life the image of the host himself wearing two horns upon his head. <note>An allusion to cuckoldry.</note> Pope Adrian VI wanted to throw a Pasquino into the Tiber, but he was advised against it, because the Pasquino on land only sang <note>meaning: "criticized"</note> during the day; however, if he became a frog in the water, one would have no rest from him day or night. <note>Citing Zeiller and Zahn.</note> In the year 1659, when Carnival was held in Rome, Pope Alexander VII had three "Pasquillants" <note>libellers</note> ride through the city backwards on donkeys, holding the tail in their hand, and they were hung all over with the pasquinades they had made against the Pope, his cousins, and the Cardinals.

Alciatus, in book 2, chapter 22, records a festive poem once fixed to the stone statue of Pasquino in Rome:

> At last, Great Pontiff, grant a hat <note>The red hat of a Cardinal.</note>
> To your Pasquino who asks for it.
> If I am without sense, a rude block of marble,
> We see that many Bishops are also created
> Who are even more stony than I am.

See Dauth on Testaments. Prohibiting Pasquino is in vain. <note>Citing Clapmar on the Secrets of Republics.</note>

### 8. Patriarchs. Patriarcha.

A Patriarch, according to Blessed Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century encyclopedist.</note> in book 7 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12, as reported in the Canon Law, is interpreted in the Greek language as the "highest of the Fathers": because he holds the first place after the Apostolic seat; and therefore, because he performs the highest honor, he is designated by such a name, such as those of Antioch, Alexandria, Jerusalem, etc. Patriarchs preside over an entire nation embracing several Provinces, and they have jurisdiction not only over Bishops, but also over Archbishops. See König in the *Political Theater*.

Furthermore, the dignity of the Patriarchate was discovered and established by Positive Law <note>Man-made law rather than divine or natural law.</note>, according to Joan. de Selva in his treatise on benefices. See Hugo on the four Prelates, and Erasmus à Chokier in the *Constitutions of the Lateran Council*.

...mainly Lancellottus in *The Temple of All Judges*, *book 2, chapter 3*, where he has much to say on the origin, concern, and sublimity of this Priesthood and Magistracy, as well as the Pallium and Mitre of the Patriarchs, etc.

That the Archbishop of Toledo is also called a Patriarch, and possesses all the privileges granted to the four true Patriarchs, is established by Mauritius Alzedo in *On the Dignity of Bishops, chapter 10, number 42*, since Pope Martin V <note>Pope Martin V (reigned 1417–1431) ended the Western Schism.</note>, in the year of our Lord 1422, the second year of his pontificate, granted him such a privilege in these words: *Moreover, to be able to use and enjoy freely and lawfully all and singular prerogatives, privileges, and insignia which could in any way belong to the said Patriarchs.*

The Greeks still have four Patriarchs today (as witnessed by Mr. Fürer in his *Egyptian Itinerary, folio 76*): The *Constantinopolitan*, who presides over the European Churches; the *Antiochian*, who cares for the monasteries and churches in Beirut, Tripoli, Aleppo, and other places in Asia; the *Alexandrian*, who presides over churches in Egypt and Arabia, and has his seat in Memphis or Cairo; and the *Jerusalemite*, who manages the care of monasteries dispersed through Syria and performs sacred rites every August 15th in the Monastery of Mount Lebanon.

### 9. Beadle. Beadle.

Beadle, herald, lictor, attendant. This word seems to some to be derived from *badizo* <note>original Greek: βαδίζω, meaning to walk or step</note>, to move or put to flight, because they say it is very common for these men [to be on the move].

<column-break/>

But there is no doubt that it descends from the French *Bedau* or *Pedeau*: for always where a diphthong is found, the letter *l* was once placed there, which is now omitted: as *aulne* from *ulna*, now *aune*, etc. Therefore, a Beadle <term>Pedellus</term> is like a runner, standing at the feet of the Rector <note>The head of a university or ecclesiastical body.</note>. *Ego on Academies, folio 27.*

#### ADDITION.

Fr. Junius thinks this should rather be called a *Beutell* in *On Academies, chapter 4, page 136*; see Middendorp, *book 1, chapter 21, page 184.* Lanf. in *Thesaurus of Academies 18, letter b*, and Limn. in *Public Law, book 8, chapter 10, numbers 16 and 17.*

### 10. Capital. Criminally.

When the question is about a criminal case, **concerning a capital matter that carries corporal punishment,** <note>original German: "von einer peinlichen Sache, so Leibsstraffe auff ihr hat." In early modern law, "peinlich" (painful) specifically referred to crimes punishable by physical pain or death.</note> it is not permitted to appeal; but where such a question is absent, even if one proceeds criminally—perhaps for a fine to be applied to the treasury—then an appeal will have to be admitted: for, so that the Constitution may apply, all its qualities must be verified. Johannes Andreae in *chapter 1 on homicide in the 6th book*. Claros in *Criminal Practice, question 85, section 'where it is debated'.* Therefore, one who is to petition for appellate processes over a fine, either to the party or the Treasury on account of a civil cause which is neither penal nor criminal—**that is, neither capital nor involving corporal punishment**—must observe (according to Peter Friedrich in *On Processes, book 1, chapter 9, number 21*) that he uses the words of the constitution, **that a capital proceeding was initiated against him,** and thus by believing the narrative, the processes might be denied. See Rutger Ruland on *Ferrara's Processes, folio 13*, where he teaches that while an appeal may not be made in criminal matters, he shows how the process of an inquiry can be challenged.

The word *criminally* <note>original Latin: "criminaliter"</note> has a broader meaning among the Latins than **capital** <note>original German: "peinlich"</note> does among the Germans: for this German word always implies corporal punishments and the like; the former Latin word does not likewise. See Friedrich in the cited location, number 22, and especially Mr. Matthias Stephan in his *Preface to the Criminal Constitution of Emperor Charles V* <note>The "Carolina," the first body of German criminal law, 1532.</note>, where he asks: **whether that word "peinlich"** pertains only to those punishments that are afflictive to the body, or whether it is also extended to other lighter ones; and Cothman, *Academic Responses 1, number 191 and following*; add my own work *On Appeals, chapter 7, number 4*, and in *Selected Questions, book 5, question 3; likewise Valentin Riemer on Jurisdiction, question 3.*

### 11. Judicial Questioning, Torture. *Criminal Questioning, Torture.*

A frequent and customary means exists for extorting the truth—especially in public and more atrocious crimes—from defendants who are usually inclined to flee or deny their crimes: this is *Torture*. Whether this practice conflicts with Theological and Political principles is something one might doubt, and not without reason. Surely the most wise Legislator, the Lord God, nowhere revealed such a means in Holy Scripture. For this reason, Wilhelm Zepperus in *Explanations of the Mosaic Forensic Laws, book 5, chapter 10*, as well as Antonius Praetorius in his treatise *On Witchcraft, folio 179 etc.*, and most recently Johann Grevius in his *Reformed Tribunal, book 1, chapter 4, folio 71 etc.*, condemn these violent interrogations. If they were so necessary that justice could not be administered, criminal judgments exercised, or the truth elicited without them, many might rightly wonder why that most sharp avenger of crimes and most prudent investigator of them did not command such a support and protection to be used—especially in that commonwealth where He dealt with a stubborn and stiff-necked people.

Nor was it only the Israelite people who were ignorant of those torments; even in the Kingdom of Aragon and other places still today, Gomez attests that torture cannot be imposed by a judge for crimes, in *Resolutions, volume 3, chapter 13, from the beginning.*

The English also do not approve of the same today, as noted by Grevius *in the cited chapter 4, folio 80 etc.*, and Thomas Smith, *The Commonwealth of England, book 1, chapter 27.*

The invention of torments seems to be Pagan and Tyrannical, devoid of all charity and compassion, which is owed in its own way even to the guilty and the accused. It is not that Christians are forbidden from using anything simply because it was used by Pagans; but this method of inquiry is more suspect to some for that very reason. Since tyrants primarily use it to protect their own dominance, Polydore Vergil assigns its invention to Nimrod—the first and primary of tyrants—in *On the Inventors of Things, book 2, chapter 3.* What if someone were to ascribe torture to a

<meta>catchword: Besold's Volume I.</meta>

<column-break/>

tyrant even more cruel? Namely, to Antiochus Epiphanes, who for this reason earned the nickname "Epimanes" <note>"The Madman," a play on his title Epiphanes, "The Illustrious."</note> in the Church. For Josephus writes of him in his *Book on the Rule of Reason* <note>Known today as 4 Maccabees.</note> that he ordered a certain pious Maccabee to be dragged into the midst and, by the sacrilegious hands of executioners, to be stretched out most atrociously. They tied his hands behind his back, whipped him most cruelly, tied weights to his feet, bound him to a wheel, and extended him in a circle so that, with his internal organs displaced and his veins distended, his pains and punishments increased immensely. But even before this, torture by the wheel was known in Athens. See Meursius, *Attic Antiquities, folio 169.*

The instruments and methods of twisting are horrifying and detestable even by name alone. I shall speak only of the <term>equuleus</term> <note>Literally "little horse"; the rack.</note>. Hieronymus Magius—in the book he wrote *On the Rack* while a prisoner in Constantinople after the disaster at Cyprus—thinks this was a wooden frame standing on four feet and lacking a bottom, which held drums and ropes on both sides. By these, the hands and feet of the guilty were pulled, not without great pain to the entire body. Others call the rack *fidiculae* from the word for "strings" <note>original Latin: "fides," like the strings of a lyre.</note>; for just as strings are stretched by tuning pegs and bridges, so were those being tortured stretched by the torment of the *fidiculae*. And they suffered other tortures besides; they were beaten with whips, burned with glowing plates, and their skin was torn with iron claws.

Other types of torments are recorded by Mr. Bocer, *On Torture, chapter 5, number 20 etc.*, and Grevius *in the cited chapter 4, folio 48*. Paris de Puteo even professes a sort of "art of twisting" in his *Treatise on the Syndicate, section on Torture, on the word 'repeated,' folio 961.* The Illyrians and Macedonians were also accustomed to elicit secrets by wine as much as by torments, according to Tubero, *On His Own Times, book 6, folio 145.*

And certainly, the modes of Torture are so varied, and the pain endured by those undergoing it is so exquisite, that the punishment is said to be heavier than the cutting off of both hands. *Novell 134, final chapter.* Hence Cassiodorus says in *Variae Epistolae, book 3, letter 46*: it is more pleasant to seek the hope of a swift death than to endure the cruelties of torment; for among the final gasps of agony, the prayer is to perish rather than to live. Because the detestable sensation of punishment excludes the desire for the sweetest safety. For this reason Seneca also says in *On Benefits*: it is a kind of mercy to kill quickly, because it brings with it the final end of torments; but the most bitter cruelty is that which drags out the punishment. And in *Letter 22 to Lucilius*: no one is so timid that he would rather hang forever than fall once. Thus, people are more easily found who offer themselves up to die voluntarily, as Lucas de Penna reports from Julius Celsus in *On the Dignity, book 12.*

The system of torments is also attacked for this reason: because many have confessed that they committed what

yet that it was perpetrated by others, the reality of the matter has taught all too seriously. Conversely, the toughness and obstinacy of some under torment is so great that even by the most exquisite tortures they could not be driven to a confession of those crimes of which they were either then known to be guilty, or which the truth—the daughter of time—later revealed. Very many examples of this kind are reported by Valerius Maximus (Book 8, chapter 4), Alexander ab Alexandro (Book 1, *Genialium Dierum*, final chapter), Fulgosius (Book 8, chapter on "The Questionings"), Richter (*Economic Axioms*, 217), and Grevius (Book 1, chapter 5, page 128, etc.; and Book 2, chapter 4, page 304, etc.). 

Among these, a truly remarkable case is mentioned by St. Jerome in his *Letter to Innocent* (Volume 1, page 234). A woman, accused by her husband of adultery with a young man, consistently denied the crime while being tortured. The young man, however, said she had committed adultery; unable to endure the torments, he confessed to having done what he had not actually done. Because of this, both were condemned to death by the Consul—in whom there was more vigor than justice—but the truth was revealed by a miracle. For the lying youth was struck by the sword and lost his head with a single blow. However, although the woman was struck seven times with the sword, with the blade aimed not only to slash but also to pierce the throat, the iron always bounced back from her flesh as if from a flint stone, except for the final blow, after which she was carried out as if dead to be buried. But at last, having been found alive and her wound treated, when she was finally acquitted by judgment, the truth was discovered.

To this may be added those things related by Servin in his *Pleadings* (Volume 2, page 402 and following), where he deals with a certain host accused of the crime of assassination and unjustly tortured.

How constant the Christians once were in the profession of their faith is testified to by Pliny the Younger himself in his *Letter 47*, where he says:
> those who are truly Christians, it is said, cannot be compelled to do anything [against their faith]:

and all the authors of Ecclesiastical History prove this to be most true. Regarding the wonderful constancy of the ancient Martyrs—who, though most cruelly mangled by torments, refused to confess what others liable for this alleged crime might have—one may look to Eusebius (*History*, Book 5, chapter 1). Yet there were nonetheless some who, either terrified or overcome by the bitterness of the punishments, suffered a moment of human weakness. Regarding both types, there is an illustrious passage by the Holy Martyr Cyprian in his *Sermon 5, On the Lapsed*.

And concerning the former group, he says:
> They possess the same sincerity of heart, the same integrity of tenacious faith. Leaning upon the unshaken roots of the heavenly precepts and strengthened by Gospel traditions, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, nor destined torments, nor losses of family property, nor physical punishments.

Days were set for the testing of their faith; but he who remembers that he has renounced the world—here Cyprian certainly refers to the formulas of Baptism, by which those being baptized renounce the world and its pomps—knows no day of the world,

<column-break/>

nor does he now count time, who hopes for eternity from God.

Concerning the latter type, the same most holy and grave writer says: He can complain about torments who has been overcome by torments, and he who has been conquered in pain can offer the excuse of pain. Such a person can be asked and say:
> I certainly wished to fight bravely, and mindful of my Sacrament <note>Cyprian here calls Baptism a "Sacrament," referring to the military-style oath of allegiance (sacramentum) sworn to God during the rite.</note> I took up the arms of devotion and faith; but as I fought in the struggle, various tortures and long-lasting punishments overcame me. My mind stood stable and my faith strong, and my soul struggled for a long time, immovable against the racking pains. But when the cruelty of the most harsh Judge worsened—as now lashes tore me when I was already exhausted, now clubs beat me, now the rack <term>equuleus</term> <note>A wooden frame used to stretch the body until the joints dislocated.</note> extended me, now the iron claw <term>ungula</term> <note>A tool used to rake the flesh from the ribs.</note> dug into me, now the flame scorched me—my flesh deserted me in the struggle, and weakness in turn failed me; it was not my soul, but my body that failed in the pain.

There are also those who, although guilty, remain silent even in torments. A certain Sembicus of Elis, along with some companions, cut down and sold quite a few bronze statues from the Olympic grounds. Then, daring even greater things, he plundered the Temple of Diana the Presider. But he was soon captured; while refusing to betray his companions, he was mangled by exquisite tortures for an entire year, during which he finally breathed his last. And from this, a proverb was commonly born: *He suffers worse than Sembicus.* Erasmus, in his *Adages*: *worse than Sambicus.*

And Botero reports (Book 1 of his *Sayings*, page 88b) concerning a certain man of Milan subjected to questioning <note>In legal contexts, "questioning" (quæstio) is a euphemism for torture.</note>, who said:
> *I deem it better to be tormented a thousand times in the arms than once in the throat.* <note>original: "Io stimo meglio l' eße tormentato mille volte nella braccia, che una volta nella gola." This is a play on words: he would rather endure the rack (which stretches the arms) than the gallows (the rope around the throat).</note>

I judge it better to be tortured a thousand times in the arms than once in the throat. Marsilius also tells this, cited by Delrio (Book 5, *Disquisitions on Magic*, section 9, page 106).

Furthermore, as witnessed by Paris de Puteo in his *Treatise on Syndicates* (under the word "torture," section "heavier torture"): Lawyers are accustomed to harden the hearts of their clients and say to those imprisoned who fear being tortured: it is better to hang once in torture than to stand forever on the gallows. And there is usually a "school" of these sayings in the prisons, as Andreas de Isernia says in the *Constitutions of the Kingdom*. They are accustomed to say to those about to be tortured: "What if you had broken arms? Would you not endure the doctor setting the bones with pain? What if you were distressed by the iliac passion <note>A historical term for severe abdominal pain or bowel obstruction.</note>, would you not bear it? What if you had the Gout, would you not endure the pain, or would you kill yourself?" etc.

There are also those from whose confessions nothing certain can be gathered, as is reported concerning Brother Juniper in the *Franciscan Antiquities* (which Philippus Bosquierus published, century 3, chapter 22). Having been captured by the tyrant of a certain castle (whose name was Nicholas), he was immediately placed on the rack and cruelly stretched, his whole body being pulled apart. When asked who he was, he replied that he was "the greatest sinner."

At last, someone running to the place of the Brothers of that same location asked the Guardian <note>The local superior of a Franciscan friary.</note> to come to a certain traitor who was about to be hanged; who seemed to care nothing for confession, nor the salvation of his soul, nor the death of his body, so that he might lead him to confession. There are also found those who, when they have committed some capital crime, either before they are subjected to the "Question" <note>The formal legal term for interrogation under torture.</note> or while they are being tortured, seem to achieve for themselves—by the use of certain writings or the pronunciation of words—the ability to remain silent and feel nothing at all. They have so firmly persuaded themselves of this that there have been those who, relying on this confidence, voluntarily offered themselves both to prison and to the "Question." Commonly they call this the "Witchcraft of Silence."

For the Devil, whose interest is that crimes are not punished but accumulated daily, confirms such people in evil; and he not only obstructs the organs of the voice so that they cannot speak, but also oppresses them with a heavy sleep, so that they neither hear the interrogation nor feel the torments. Meanwhile, however, those hanging use these words and verses as a form of <term>ἀπάτης</term> <note>original Greek: "apates," meaning deceit or illusion.</note>:

Besoldi Tom. I.

<column-break/>

—never tell the King. And the most illustrious jurist Paulus Grillandus testifies that he has several times discovered in fact that those applied to torture and hoisted up slept with their heads hanging down, as if they were lying in bed, without any lamentation or shouting at all; and at the pulls of the cord they were like a marble statue, and while they were being hoisted, at the beginning they said certain words in a low voice, and then they were silent, like those sleeping. Sometimes also through other witches, however remote, those applied to torments are bound by the witchcraft of silence: just as a certain witch, according to Sprenger in *Question 5* in Innsbruck, used to boast that whenever she had at least a thread from the garments of someone detained, she could effect so much that no matter how much they were tortured, even unto death, they could confess nothing.

That torments are a fragile and deceptive thing is clear from this: because pain governs them; and the nature of each person, both of mind and body, moderates them. And as Cicero says in *For P. Sulla*, the inquisitor rules, lust bends, hope corrupts, and fear weakens, so that in such a narrowing of circumstances, no place is left for the truth. Thus also the same Cicero, in the second book of *Rhetoric*, thinks that one ought not trust in pain; because one person is more resilient than another in pain, because one is more ingenious at inventing stories, and finally because one can often know, or suspect, what the Inquisitor wants to hear: which when he has said it, he understands that there will be an end to his pain. Likewise in the *Partitions*: often the "Questions" must be resisted, because many fleeing pain have very often lied in torments, and preferred to die by confessing a falsehood than by truly denying it through pain. Many also have neglected their own lives to free those who were dearer to them than they were to themselves. Others, however, either by the nature of their body, or by habituation to pain, or by fear of punishment or death, have endured the force of the torments.

Others have lied against those whom they hated. Relevant here is the response of Ulpian, who in *Law 1, section 23 of the Digest on the Question*, writes thus: Many, by patience or the hardness of the torments, so despise the torture that the truth can in no way be squeezed out of them; others are of such impatience that they would rather lie about anything than endure the torments. Thus it happens that they even confess in various ways, so that they implicate not only themselves but also others.

That singular light and ornament of the Church, not only of Africa but of the universal world, St. Augustine, professes not obscurely nor in one place only that he abhors the little cords, the rack, etc. In *Letter 159* and following, he praises Marcellinus the Tribune because he unearthed the horrendous deeds of the Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa.</note> not by extending them on the rack, nor with furrowing iron claws, nor with burning flames, but by the beating of rods.

The same St. Augustine says in *The City of God, Book 19*, that it is intolerable, to be lamented, and to be watered, if it were possible, with fountains of tears...

# Expanded Practical Treasury

*Left Column*

Chapter 6: because although the Judge tortures the accused for this reason—to avoid unknowingly killing an innocent person—the same tragedy occurs through the misery of ignorance: he kills a man who is both tortured and innocent. He tortured him specifically to avoid killing the innocent, yet by doing so, he killed him anyway. <note>This is a famous argument from St. Augustine’s *City of God*, Book 19, Chapter 6, regarding the "misery" of a judge who cannot know the heart of the accused.</note>

For if, following the wisdom of such men, the accused chooses to flee from this life rather than endure those torments any longer, he will say he committed what he did not commit. Once he is condemned and killed, the Judge still does not know whether he has executed a guilty or an innocent man—the very man he tortured to avoid killing an innocent person. Thus, he tortured an innocent man to find the truth, and while still ignorant of it, he killed him.

The commentator Ludovicus Vives, a man of great judgment, adds nearly identical points there. <note>Joannes Ludovicus Vives (1493–1540) was a Spanish humanist who criticized the judicial systems of his era.</note> He says: "If we torture men so that the guiltless do not die, so that we might pity them more than if they had simply been executed, it is because torments are often more grievous than death itself. Do we not daily see many who prefer to suffer death rather than torture? They confess to a fictional crime, certain of their execution, just to escape the rack. Truly, we have the souls of executioners if we can endure the groans and tears of a man expressed with such pain, when we do not even know if he is guilty."

Those Trochaic and Iambic single-verse poems <term>monostichs</term> are rightly cited here, used as proverbs:

->From true questioning or false questioning, you may extract the same result,<-
->Often fictional, often false, every questioning brings forth lies.<-
->He lies, who cannot endure the pain,<-
->He lies, who can endure the pain.<-
->A cruel interrogation elicits the false as easily as the truth.<-

The great Justus Lipsius, in his *Letters*, century 2, letter 41, so highly commends Michel de Montaigne—a Noble Frenchman and certainly a most wise man—that he numbers him among the Seven Sages of Greece, or even considers him wiser than those seven. This man, in Book 1 of his *Essays*, chapter 5, writes as follows: <note>original: "C' est une dangereuse invention, que celle des Gehennes, & semble que ce soit plustost un essais de patience, que de verité : & celuy, qui les peut souffrir, cache la verité, & celuy, qui les ne peut souffrir."</note> "The invention of the rack and interrogations is a dangerous one; it seems to be a test of patience rather than of truth. For both he who can endure and suffer the torments, and he who cannot, hide the truth." That is to say: the invention of the rack and questioning is dangerous, appearing to be more an exploration of physical endurance than of reality.

The Magistrate <term>Praetor</term> considers acts performed out of fear to be null and void, and certainly rescinds them. Yet there is hardly any torture more severe than that inflicted on the body through torments and questioning. Furthermore, both natural and civil reason dictate that no one is bound to betray themselves. <note>This refers to the legal maxim *nemo tenetur se ipsum prodere*, a foundation for the modern right against self-incrimination.</note> Hence, any statements containing an admission of a fault or crime by the respondent are held to be "un-answerable," and the common school of thought teaches that these can be denied even under oath. See Fulvius Pacianus, *On Proofs*, book 1, chapter 7. Hence, in the legal codes (Cause 15, Question 6, Canon 1), it is decreed that writings extorted in any way through fear, fraud, or force

<column-break/>

*Right Column*

should have no validity to the prejudice or harm of the writer. Furthermore, every confession made out of necessity does not deserve belief; it is a most wicked thing to judge anyone based on suspicion or an extorted confession.

However, if someone should argue that if torture were omitted, many crimes and outrages would remain hidden and never be brought to light, I wish to respond not with my own words, but with those of Chrysostom and Augustine. For John Chrysostom says in his 46th homily *To the People of Antioch*: "God does not demand an account from everyone here, lest you despair of the resurrection and cease to expect a judgment, as if everyone gave their account here. On the other hand, He does not permit everyone to go unpunished, lest you think all things lack divine providence. Truly, He both punishes and does not punish. Inasmuch as He punishes, He shows that He will demand an account from those punished here and those elsewhere. Inasmuch as He does not punish, He makes you believe there is some fearsome Tribunal after this present pilgrimage." And Augustine, in Book 3 of his work *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 2, says: "Let a man mercifully correct what he can. What he cannot, let him bear patiently, and with love let him groan and mourn, until God from above amends and corrects it, or until the harvest comes to root out the weeds and winnow the chaff." Although he wrote this concerning Church Discipline, it seems rightly applied to public punishments and the penalties of crimes.

Nevertheless, I do not think that Questioning and Torments should be commended on the grounds that long-standing gout was sometimes cured by them—of which violent experiment Fabricius reports two examples in his *Surgical Observations*, century 1, observation 79. <note>Wilhelm Fabry (Fabricius Hildanus) was a famous 17th-century surgeon; the "cure" mentioned here is likely a dark joke or a rare medical anomaly where extreme shock altered the patient's condition.</note> Yet, all legal experts confess with one voice that it is just, consistent with reason, and even useful to the State that torture sometimes be used. The customs and laws of almost all nations approve this, and daily experience likewise makes it manifest: namely, so that crimes do not remain unpunished. Since crimes are regularly committed in secret, they could hardly be dragged into the light or the truth known through any other investigation. Otherwise, an opportunity for offending would be opened up. See Gomez, volume 3, *Various Resolutions*, chapter 13; Farinaccius, question 4; Peter Erodius, book 9, *Adjudicated Matters*, title 10; Lord Bocer, *On Torture*, chapter 1, number 6; Hering, *On Sureties*, chapter 10, number 440, etc.; Parthenius Litigiosus, book 2, chapter 8; Philipp Steinhaufen, on the *Digest* regarding questioning. Martin Delrio also attests in his *Magical Investigations* (book 5, section 8) that this is the common opinion of theologians. Paris de Puteo specifically writes: "Torments are not to be considered inhumane and cruel, because without the fear of Torture the world could not stand in Peace; for the wicked hate to sin for fear of punishment." *Treatise on Syndicates*, section on Torture.

Indeed, if the truth were to be extorted by no pain or suffering at all, but witnesses and presumptions had to be used perpetually, one would necessarily complain—

### Letter P.

It is complained that either criminals must be dragged to punishment even when no private confession is forthcoming, or that out of a hundred villains, scarcely one would be punished. This is because properly qualified witnesses can very rarely be found, since adulteries and other most serious crimes are committed without witnesses, and all men are so composed that they will not confess a crime of their own accord if they know it must be atoned for by death.

Indeed, no one fails to see what the future of human life would be, and what the state of any Republic would become, if out of many villains only one or two were snatched away to their deserved punishment, while the rest—whose crimes could not be proven by sworn witnesses or their own confession—were dismissed with impunity. Clearly, this would offer not just a window, but wide-open doors for repeating crimes and for preying upon others according to one's wicked lust.

<margin>Book 1, Letter 116.</margin>
For this reason, Saint Isidore of Pelusium <note>A 5th-century monk and prolific letter writer from Egypt</note> says: "Since as a seeker of truth you have a wise tool in the manifold engine of torments, use it with fear during judgment; for the Divine Law established you as a terror to the wicked."

And Quintilian the Elder <note>A reference to the *Declamations* traditionally attributed to the Roman rhetorician Quintilian</note> says in *Declamation 307, near the end*: "It is difficult," he says, "for sick bodies to endure against pain; and it is easy for a sound mind to hold fast to the persuasion you have once put on. Therefore, an art was invented; those nightly thoughts, that memory of the past—that is the grave interrogation when wounds are inflicted, when the mind is persuaded that there is no end to the torments."

And Michael Montanus <note>Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592), the famous French essayist</note> acutely conjectures in *Essays, Book 2, Chapter 5*, that a conscience weighed down by crime is hardly equal to bearing the pains, whereas innocence is more strong. 
<note>original French: "Elle pense, ait, que le fondement de ceste invention, vient de la consideration de la conscience..."</note>
"He believes," it is said, "that the foundation of this invention comes from a consideration of the conscience. For to the guilty, it seems that conscience aids the torture to make him confess his fault, and it weakens him; on the other hand, it strengthens the innocent against the torture."

Charles Philippe Hattron elegantly writes in *On Piety and the Kingdom*, page 270: "The cause of those confessing on the rack is indeed pain, not a remorse of the soul; but a conscience of the crime committed is believed to follow the pain, and for these people, silence is bent at the same time. Those who are innocent are firmer; for though they feel the same sensation of torture, they have no reason to repent at the same time, but truth assists their constancy."

An innocent man, trusting in God the Avenger of innocence, can say with Galeatio Ubaldo of Perugia <note>A legal scholar from Perugia, Italy</note> in *Book 2, page 102*: "I do not flee from this; I demand this contest, in which I hope to stand firm through constant endurance of torments and remarkable tolerance, to break all the force of the torments, and to bear them as patiently as they inflict them: they will find me to be a rock against a battering ram. Virtue is at its sharpest when necessity finally strikes it out, and the wretched possess more 

<column-break/>

impetus and greater constancy. There is more constancy and greater consolation in that memory. When the limbs ache, constancy and innocence will come to the aid of that pain. I shall feel it, certainly, and I shall even grieve: for what virtue strips away the human senses? Nevertheless, just as a ship that travels the seas touches them with its lowest and most common part, while the rest stands out and is high up, so I shall run through these torments with that best part—that is, the soul—lifted up and, as it were,

-> Like Palinurus from the high stern. <-
<note>A reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*; Palinurus was the pilot of Aeneas’s ship. The phrase suggests maintaining one's direction and oversight even in a storm.</note>

These are my meditations, or internal imaginings, with which I fortify myself and my mind:

-> Though the body be sick, let the mind be strong; <-
-> and without arrogance, I prepare for every outcome. <-
-> Wherever the fates drag me, secure virtue will follow. <-

And although in the Old Testament tortures were unknown or not commonly used, we know that other nearly identical means were employed, and were usually applied in doubtful and hidden crimes whose authors were unknown, as seen in *Joshua 7:14, 1 Samuel 14:30, and Jonah 1:7.* <note>These biblical passages refer to the "casting of lots" to identify a guilty party when no witness exists.</note> So also back then, a miraculous investigation of adultery was practiced through the bitter potion, as in *Numbers 5:13, etc.* <note>The "Trial of the Bitter Water," where a suspected adulteress drank a mixture that would supposedly cause her physical harm only if she were guilty.</note>

Nearly similar to this was the Statue of Venus in the city of Constantinople, which stood from the time of Constantine the Great until the Emperor Justin, mentioned by Nicolaus Alemannus in his *notes on the Secret History of Procopius, page 83.* To this statue, he says, when young women suspected of vice approached, if they were indeed untainted, they departed safely. But the clothing of those who had been corrupted was immediately pulled back, exposing their private parts. The exact same thing happened to married women who had defiled themselves with secret adulteries, and they would immediately confess the matter.
<margin>See Gyllius, page 263.</margin>

Equally wonderful is what Estienne de Lusignan reports in his *Description of the Island of Cyprus, Chapter 14, page 64b.* Namely, that in Nicosia there were two stones between which the accused were forced to stand if they denied a deed of which they were accused; then the stones would spontaneously constrict the guilty person so that they would profess the truth.
<note>original French: "Il y avoit aussi une Eglise Grecque..."</note>
"There was also a Greek Church in the same City near the Carthusians called Arcomose, that is to say, Prince of the Oath, in which were two marble stones, where they put those who did not want to confess the truth: and then, if he who was led there was guilty, these two stones would tighten by themselves and without the help of man, little by little, until the sufferer had confessed the truth."

In that ancient Jewish Republic, there was greater simplicity and honesty, as men lived conformably as one nature, one nation, and one religion, and thus there was less confusion of affairs in it...

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the use of judicial torture.
