# Enlarged Practical Treasury

Hence, the institutions of that People <note>The ancient Israelites</note> are not so well-suited to the Republics of these times, in which there is tenfold greater malice and lust for every kind of crime, and where people of the most diverse nations—and thus of diverse temperaments and morals—cohabit not just in one Region or City, but in the same town, village, and hamlet. Consequently, the method for administering justice and detecting outrages in the great confusion that now exists in the world is much more difficult than it was in the Jewish Polity. Keckerman, *Practical Disputations, 32, question 4.*

And the English, who are otherwise said to lack instruments of torture, nevertheless applied them to Catholics who were suspected of the Crime of Majesty <note>High treason; original: "criminis laesae maiestatis"</note>, as is reported in the booklet titled *British Justice*, near the end.

And indeed, if we observe the rules of our legal experts and the institutions of wisely formed Republics, it is difficult to accuse torture of injustice or cruelty, 
<margin>Bartholomew Keckerman, aforementioned Practical Disputation 32, question 4.</margin> 
provided they maintain that a confession extorted by force is not to be believed at all, and that torture is not regularly to be applied unless it is first established as a *body of the crime* <note>original: "corpore delicti"</note>—for instance, that a man has been killed, or a theft or similar crime has been perpetrated. Menochius, *Arbitrary Cases, century 2, case 269, no. 4*; Faber’s Code, *book 9, title 21, definition 17.* If the Romans had observed this in the past, that slave mentioned by Valerius Maximus in *book 8, chapter 4* would not have spoken falsely because of torments. Accused of killing Alexander, the slave of T. Fannius, and tortured by his master on that account, he most consistently maintained that he had committed the deed. Thus, he was handed over to Fannius and executed; a short time later, that very Alexander, believed to be dead, returned home safe and sound.

If our own men of Tübingen <note>The university town in Germany</note> had once observed this, they would not have prostituted their reputation—if indeed the stories are true which Ludovicus Gilhausen in *Criminal Arbitrations, chapter 6* and Godelmann in *On Witches, book 3, chapter 10* relate as follows: when two young men practicing the mechanical arts were traveling abroad, one returned home shortly after, wearing the other's clothes by exchange. The parents and relatives of the absent one, immediately gathering from the change of clothing that their son had been killed by the one who returned, accused him of homicide before the local judge. The judge immediately threw the accused into prison without further investigation. And when the accused consistently denied the deed, he was subjected to torture, where, out of excessive torment, he confessed that he had killed his companion, taken his clothes, and spent his own money at an inn. For this, he was finally condemned and placed on the wheel <note>A brutal form of execution where limbs were broken</note>, where he piously exchanged life for death. After a few days had passed, the traveling companion returned safe and unharmed. In perpetual memory of this event, and as a sign of a most unjust condemnation, an image of a man placed on a wheel was 

<column-break/>

carved into stone there in the church, and the faculty of the Magistrate to hear criminal cases was then revoked; nor is he permitted to condemn anyone without a decree from the Faculty of Law.

However, although I myself heard similar stories recounted by my elders when I was still a boy, I am fully persuaded that the image of the man on the wheel appearing in the windows of our church is actually a Martyr—specifically the image of Saint George; for I remember seeing a completely identical image elsewhere. See Surius *in the Life of George*, also the <term>High School of the Sick</term> <note>original German: "hohe Schul der Krancken"; likely referring to a charitable or medical text</note>. Moreover, Baronius reports from ancient manuscripts in his *Martyrology for April 23* that George, who along with Saint Martin is a patron of the Church of Tübingen, suffered the punishment of the wheel; however, consult Zahn here, *On Lies, book 1, chapter 29, p. 98.*

Furthermore, a forced confession must be plausible and contain circumstances that are not inconsistent. Hence Tertullian, in his *Apology*, though he had said the Laws prescribe that those who confess should be condemned, soon adds that judges are not content with confession alone, but consequently demand the quality of the deed, the number, the place, the manner, the time, etc.

Moreover, for there to be a place for "the question" <note>Judicial torture</note>, some evidence <note>original: "indicia"</note> of the crime committed by the defendant must precede it. Menochius, *Arbitrations, book 1, question 84.* For it is necessary that Judges, even in those criminal matters involving public trials, do not begin the investigation of truth with torments, but first use likely and probable arguments. *Law 8, Code on Questions.* Nor should they admit witnesses unless they are above all exception. See Merlin, *Decision 62.*

And such evidence is likewise necessary that can be called credible or probable, which our people call "proximate." Menochius, *book 2, case 270, no. 13.* <term>Criminal Court Ordinance, article 20</term> <note>Referring to the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the 1532 legal code of the Holy Roman Empire</note>: **That without honest evidence, no one shall be questioned under pain.** Hence our best Doctors <note>Legal scholars</note> teach that if a defendant is tortured without sufficient preceding evidence, he cannot be condemned based on his confession alone, even if it is ratified a thousand times, and even judicially. Mynsinger, *century 5, observation 23*; Farinaccius, *Criminal Practice, book 1, title 5, question 37.*

Likewise, the manner of the torments depends not only on the quality and condition of the person (Menochius, *case 271*), but on the manner and weight of the evidence. <term>Criminal Court Ordinance, article 58.</term> Hence, the Interpreters establish certain degrees of torture, which Grillandus explains in his *Treatise on Questions* and Clarus in *question 64*. And frequently, prudent legal consultants decree not torments themselves, but the terror and fear of torments. Langlaeus, *Semestria, last chapter.*

Just as the ancient Romans were not ignorant of this. Livy records two excellent examples in *book 19, decade 4*, concerning Xychus; these are the words: Brought at first...

<summary>This page discusses the strict legal requirements for judicial torture, emphasizing that a crime must be proven to have occurred (corpus delicti) and sufficient evidence (indicia) must exist before torture can be used. It includes a cautionary tale from Tübingen about a false confession that led to a wrongful execution, though the author questions the local interpretation of the church's "man on the wheel" iconography.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion on the limits and proper administration of judicial torture, shifting from the general justification of the practice to specific historical examples of its psychological impact and the strict warnings by legal scholars against excessive cruelty and superstitious methods.</meta>

...Xychus <note>A figure from historical accounts of conspiracies</note>, for example, denied the charges so inconsistently that when even a small amount of fear was applied, it became clear the Judge was ready; he could not bear the sight of the torturer or the whips, and he exposed the entire sequence of the crime and his own role in it.

Another example is found in Book 27 <note>of Livy's History of Rome</note>, while he reports that one of the Numidians, who had been detected by a Campanian woman for bringing news to Hannibal, the enemy of the Romans, had constantly denied the act. However, when he understood that the instruments of torture were being summoned and prepared, he immediately confessed. There is also an excellent example in Tacitus, Book 15, regarding Natalis and Scaevinus <note>conspirators against the Emperor Nero</note>, written in these words: *Natalis and Scaevinus were summoned and questioned separately as to what the conversation had been and what the matter was; then suspicion arose because they had not given matching answers. They were put in chains, and they could not endure the sight and the threats of the torture instruments.*

**Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus** <note>A 16th-century French jurist</note> also warns in his *Syntagma, Book 48, Chapter 12*, that judges should not employ new types of torture, for such things belong to a tyrant like Phalaris <note>an ancient Greek tyrant famous for his "brazen bull" torture device</note>, not to a Christian. **Gomez** agrees in his *Various Resolutions*, where he adds: one must cry out against severe and cruel Judges who affect a vain and empty glory, and who, seeking greater offices in the Republic because of this, impose new types of torture on wretched defendants and exceed the limit prescribed by law. **Parthenius Litigiosus** <note>A pseudonym for the jurist Simon Ulrich Pistoris</note> argues the same in Book 1, Chapter 14, where he discusses the <term>Danish Mantle</term> <note>a heavy wooden barrel worn as punishment</note>, <term>Spanish Caps</term> <note>head-crushing devices</note>, the <term>English Virgin</term> <note>likely a variant of the Iron Maiden</note>, <term>Brunswick Boots</term> <note>leg-screws for crushing the shins</note>, etc.

Our laws also prescribe such moderation of torture so that the defendant likely remains safe and unharmed, and does not lose a life or a principal limb. *Law on the limit of questioning, Digest: on questioning.* <note>original: "l. quæstionis modum. ff. de quæst."</note>

And rightly does *Parthenius Litigiosus* lash out at "masked" and stupid Judges who tear apart wretched captives with tortures intolerable to human patience; indeed, with eyes fed on blood like a wild beast, which always thirsts for blood once tasted, they frequently order the tortures to be doubled.

Various remedies are provided in our Law by which help is usually given to those unjustly tortured against either the fraud or the error and ignorance of a Judge or Magistrate, concerning which see **Matthias Stephani** on the *Criminal Constitution of Charles V, article 20.*

And although accomplices in a crime can sometimes be questioned about their associates and participants—namely, if it concerns proving a crime that could not have been committed by a single man without the help of associates—see **Janus Langlaeus**, *Semestria, Book 9, Chapter 1.* Yet it seems harsh that, as happens among the Gauls <note>the French</note>, someone already condemned to death, both in the ordinary and extraordinary manner, should be tortured even as a "corpse" <note>someone legally dead</note> to betray his accomplices. See the *Codex Fabrianus, Book 9, Title 21.*

<column-break/>

In truth, credit should not be given to a confession expressed on the <term>rack</term> <note>original: "equuleus," a wooden frame for stretching the body</note> (or when the rack was in sight) so that a defendant can be condemned by it, unless he—again, after some interval of time, and questioned far away from the tortures—persists in the same confession. *Langlaeus, Semestria, Book 9, Chapter 2.*

However, **Antonius Faber** warns in his *Code* that not too long a time should be given to him, lest he devise reasons for overturning the truth which he had confessed.

First and foremost, those who, in the manner of Tyrants, even use torture as a punishment are to be detested, as **Tertullian** <note>an early Christian author</note> says in his *Apology, Chapter 2*; to whom it rightly seemed absurd in that same place that Christians were tortured not to confess, but to deny. Hence the same author wrote to **Scapula**, the Governor of Carthage: *What more,* he says, *is commanded of you than to condemn the guilty who confess, but to bring back to torture those who deny? You see, therefore, how you yourselves act against the commands, so that you compel those who have confessed to deny. Thus you admit that we are innocent, whom you do not wish to condemn immediately upon confession.* See **Cujacius**, *Observations 14, Chapter 34.*

And there also exist other complaints of the ancient Christians regarding the neglect of the order of law and of trials: **Justin** in his *Apology*, **Cyprian** against Demetrium, **Arnobius** in Book 8, and **Lactantius** in Book 5.

To these illicit types of torture, I also add superstitious methods, such as the <term>trial by cold water</term> <note>original: "probatio per frigidam aquam," the "swimming" of suspected witches</note>. This is an invention of the Devil and is not without an implicit pact with him; for while men wish to know hidden things through a method neither permitted by law nor having natural reason, the Devil runs to help and extends his assisting hands. **Zieritz** on the *Criminal Constitution of Charles V, Article 20.*

Likewise, if magical charms or similar things are found under the arm of the one being tortured, further torture can indeed be decreed; *Codex Fabrianus, Book 9, Title 21, Definition 3.*

But nevertheless, **Delrio** <note>a Jesuit scholar and demonologist</note> rightly denies in his *Disquisitions on Magic* that magical and superstitious ceremonies should be employed during torture.

Some (these are the words of **Grillandus**) have said that against the <term>spells of silence</term> <note>original: "maleficia taciturnitatis," a magical charm believed to make a prisoner unable to feel pain or speak</note>, certain remedies may be found which are composed of various prayers.

From these they say that all ligatures and spells of this kind are dissolved, so that the defendant may suffer the gravest tortures and torments in his body. Truly, it is not fitting that evil be driven out by an equal evil.

Similarly, a <term>Confessor</term> <note>a priest</note> ought not to be present at the torture, as **Delrio** records in his *Disquisitions on Magic, Book 6.*

It is also rightly done today that witnesses are not tortured as they once were; though this can still happen if a witness is inconsistent or wavering and denies having been present at a business where it is established that he was indeed present.

It emphasizes that a confession obtained through torture must be freely reaffirmed later to be legally valid.</summary>

# Enhanced Practical Treasury
**Page 816**

...admitted; furthermore, Paris de Puteo <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan jurist famous for his work on trials and duels</note> concedes this in the often-cited section on torture, in the paragraph regarding witnesses. This point is explained best of all by Lord Doctor Tabor in his work *On Confrontation*, part 2, page 56.

And finally, although a Judge, for the sake of investigating the truth and uncovering a crime, ought to be a "subtle investigator" <note>term: *subtilis indagator*; a judge who uses clever or psychological methods to find the truth</note>, even questioning regarding remote circumstances and pretending he wishes to do what he does not, following the logic of the chapter "offert" <note>a legal reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX</note> regarding presumptions—where Solomon says, "bring a sword," etc., pretending he wishes to divide the boy, etc. (this is commonly called the "subtle diligence of investigation"). Nevertheless, he should not use those arts which Paris de Puteo seems to approve of in his *Tractate on Syndicates* <note>a study of the legal accountability of officials</note>, in the section on torture, where he writes: a certain noblewoman was detained on the grounds that it was said she had plotted her husband's death, but nothing could be proved. The Regent <note>a high-ranking official or governor</note> had her called to him secretly in his chambers and said he wanted to take her as his own; he pretended to kiss her, and by reasoning with her and promising her release, he extorted a confession of the murder of her husband, for which she was subsequently beheaded. Others also extorted confessions from those under investigation during a dinner by promising release, pledging that he would cause them no harm, and speaking humanely with them. He adds that these kinds of persuasions are more effective at extorting confessions than the cord <note>a common torture device for stretching the limbs</note>. But see Langlaeus, Book 4, where he also treats this question of whether it is lawful to craftily trap a defendant's confession. Relevant here is also the discussion on "equivocation" <note>using ambiguous language to hide the truth</note>, about which Delrio writes in Book 5 of *Disquisitions on Magic*.

Caspar Antonius Thessaurus reports that when a defendant has cleared the evidence against them through torture, they can sometimes nonetheless be punished extraordinarily and condemned to pay the legal expenses.

Regarding the degrees of torture, see Göhauf in *Proceedings Against Witches*, page 156, and Hondedeus. Also regarding "territion" <note>term: *territio*; the act of showing the instruments of torture to a prisoner to induce fear without actually using them</note>, and what evidence is required for each degree; he teaches at the end that he who cannot be tortured also cannot be terrified. See also Bocer on torture, chapter 5.

That no one is to be tortured more than once a day for more than an hour, according to the constitution of Pope Paul IV, is reported by Göhauf in *Proceedings Against Witches*, page 125.

Regarding the repetition of torture, especially if the defendant is unwilling to ratify the confession, the same Göhauf treats this extensively. He demonstrates that a person is only to be tortured through three turns <note>three separate sessions or applications</note>.

Mynsinger observed that a person who has been tortured and confessed can always be seized again if new evidence emerges, and they do not have the defense of "a matter already judged" <note>term: *res judicata*; the legal principle that a case cannot be tried twice</note>. Tuschus concludes that famous thieves can be tortured regarding other crimes.

One who knows of a crime and does not reveal it can be tortured, according to the writings of Servin in his *Pleadings*, volume 3.

<column-break/>

However, there is no place for torture where banishment is given in place of a penalty. Wesenbec notes at the end of his 156th counsel that the torture should not be more grievous than the penalty itself.

Is a defendant saved who does not confess? See the Talmud in *Sanhedrin*, page 45.

Truly, regarding Torture, see Cavalcanius in *On the Royal Arm*, part 3; Matthaeus Stephanus on the *Office of the Judge*, book 9; and many others including Zanger, Grevius in his individual tractate, and Speidel in his *Collection of Questions* under the entry "Torture." Also Octavian Spatharius in *Criminal Practice*, Fornerus in *Daily Matters*, and Delrio on *Magicians*. For the "Fidiculae" <note>term: *fidiculae*; small cords or strings used to bind and twist the limbs during interrogation</note>, see Marcellus Donatus and the *Fabrian Code*.

The "Painful Question" <note>note: *Peinliche Frag*; a legal term for judicial torture</note>, the Rack <note>original: *Folter*</note>, so called from the turning of the windlass. Torture in France is equally common to all social ranks. Lord Walther on the *Privileges of Doctors*, chapter 17. The examination or torture is more severe than the cutting off of both hands. ## 12. Criminal Court Process. *Processus Criminalis*.

See Bocer in the consultation inserted in the treatise on torture, question 2.

There are certain Imperial Cities which, by privilege, do not observe the Ordinary Process in criminal matters. Thus, the City of Hall <note>Schwäbisch Hall</note> in a certain letter to the Legal Faculty of Tübingen, held the following words: "Therefore We, by virtue of Imperial pri-

<column-break/>

vileges and immemorial custom, are not obligated to initiate an ordinary process in criminal matters; rather, after hearing the accused persons regarding their crime, We have the power to judge behind closed doors without any formal process, etc." It is said that this is also the practice in Esslingen, Reutlingen, and elsewhere.

Regarding at whose expense criminal processes are to be undertaken, this was discussed above under the letter G, at the entry "Court Costs." Add Beatus, *Decisions*, volume 5, on Judicial Matters, page 5, volume 2, folio 859, etc.

## 13. Pestilence. *Pestis*.

Goclenius, in *On the Plague*, folio 2, provides several examples of horrendous plagues; he also mentions a Plague that kills only sheep, folio 62. He teaches how to recognize if the earth or air is corrupted on folio 148.

Quercetanus, in *On the Plague*, folio 43, mentions that Plagues occur after slaughters <note>i.e., after major battles or wars</note>; see the same author on prognostic signs in chapter 4, folio 79, and on causes in chapter 7, folio 98 and 125, and also chapter 6 throughout. He likewise provides political preservation measures on folio 195. On the plague, see Mercurialis, and Andreas Denzel in his special treatise. Likewise, Matthäus Untzner in his *Antidote for the Pestilence*. I myself also have much on this in my treatise *On Life and Death*. See also the 10th Disputation of Hartmann; Baronius in the *Indian Annals* under the word "Plague"; Paulus Zacchia in *Medico-Legal Questions*, book 3, title 3, throughout. Bisciola, *Leisure Hours*, book 14, chapter 9, where he has an observation against Plinius regarding the origin of the pestilence, its duration, and its efficacy.

Regarding a great plague formerly in Swabia, and how "sweetly" those infected with that disease died, see Felix Faber in *Swabia*, folio 152.

On the plague of Lyon, see the *French Mercury*, volume 15, folio 1 and following.

Whether it is permissible to flee in a time of plague? See the dissertation of Ludwig Bär.

Whether a Lord, King, etc., can eject those infected with an epidemic plague—or those suspected of it—from their homes without a hearing or defense, and command that their movable goods be burned (such as beds, skins, and similar items in which the plague is easily preserved)? See Peguera, decision 8.

Marquard Freher, in *Parerga*, book 2, chapter 2, reports that some cities use this right by privilege: that in drafting Wills, the witnesses are not required to gather in the presence of the Testator, nor to be present for the drafting, reading, and sealing of the Will. Instead, it is sufficient for their signatures and seals to be added anywhere—for instance, by sending the Will to their houses. This is evident from Law 1 of the Code *on testaments*. While this is indeed against the usual observation of the law, the Emperors nevertheless granted in Law 8 of the Code that this be done in a time of plague, out of "fear of contagion," as they call it. This fear usually deters witnesses from approaching those whom they hear are bedridden and contemplating a Will, immediately suspecting they suffer from the plague; thus, it is difficult during a raging pestilence to find witnesses and signers to attend the testators.

The Emperors, therefore, in times of plague, granted a remission to witnesses so that they would not be required to approach the testator—or rather to the testators, so they would not have to force and summon witnesses into their sight—with these words: *For it is permitted for witnesses to be joined and associated with those oppressed by such a disease* <note>original Latin: "Testes enim hujusmodi morbo oppressis... jungi atque sociari remissum est." This refers to a relaxation of Roman law which usually required witnesses to be in the immediate physical presence of the person making a will.</note> (this is the correct reading according to the cited Freher, in various places). See Lord Bullæus in *Academic Perils*, discourse 3, and disputation 3 on the Municipal Law of Württemberg, from the notes of my brother, thesis 32.

Whether women may be admitted as witnesses in such a testament, see Francisco de Sousa on Law 9 regarding the Rules of Law, part 2, number 23, and Peregrinus, decision 8.

Regarding the fact that in times of plague a tenant may leave without penalty, paying rent only up to the day they inhabited the house, Vincent Carocius teaches this (following others) in *On Leasing and Hiring*, part 3, leaf 308, number 41; unless the lease was originally made during the time of plague, because then the tenant ought to blame himself, according to Carocius in the same place, number 42. There, at number 47, for every purpose and effect and to remove all doubts, he gives the advice that a tenant should quickly issue a formal notice along with the offering of the keys.

## ADDITION.

The most prudent Senate of Venice <note>Venice was a pioneer in public health and quarantine measures, being the first to establish a "Lazzaretto" or quarantine station.</note> ensures that letters tied with linen threads are not brought into their cities during times of plague. Hornigk, *On the Law of Posts*, Theorem 21, page 288. The pestilential vapor is transplanted via linen, cloth, carpets, feathers, and thread. Ibid, page 287. One who is under arrest and swears not to leave the place of arrest, yet flees when the plague breaks out, is not a perjurer. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 3, chapter 8, number 24.

A salary is owed to a Doctor <note>term: Doctor; likely referring here to a Doctor of Laws or a Professor, though it could apply to medical doctors in this context</note> who is hindered by the plague, according to Lord Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, chapter 8, § 43. Everyone agrees that something has been relaxed regarding the formalities in a testament made during plague-time, but as to what exactly that consists of, the opinions of the Doctors of Law vary. The late Lord Ludwell discusses this most extensively in *On Last Wills*, latter part, chapter 3, shortly before the end. Under Civil Law <note>term: Civil Law; specifically the Roman Law tradition as used in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, in making a testament during plague, the observation of the required seven witnesses is not relaxed, but only their "joining and association" <note>This means the witnesses did not have to stand right next to the dying person, but could witness from a distance to avoid contagion.</note>; for they are said to be oppressed not by the disease itself or bedridden, but by the fear of that contagious disease. In the Imperial Chamber <note>term: Imperial Chamber; the *Reichskammergericht*, the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, however, it was upheld that a testator seized by the plague may make a will before only two witnesses. Lord Bick in *Golden Matters*, section 3, thesis 79, letter rr. The people of Marseille, whenever they labored under a plague, would have one of the poor offer himself to be fed for a whole year at public expense with the purest foods. Afterward, adorned with sacred branches and garments, he was led through the whole city with curses, so that the evils of the city might fall upon him, and thus he was cast out. Petronius in the *Fragments of Petronius Arbiter*, page 12.

Once, because of a single pillow-bed that had been thrown into a back corner of a house, and after the passage of 7

<column-break/>

years, was carelessly stirred and shaken again, a cruel plague was stirred up. Lord Leonhard Wurffb., *On the Number Seven*, page 341. GOD can well protect His own in the plague, just as He preserved Doctor Justus Jonas <note>A prominent Lutheran reformer and friend of Martin Luther</note>, who ate an onion that his father had removed from a pestilential ulcer; and in Holstein, a child who sucked the poisonous milk from its mother who had died of the plague. Meigerius in *The Core of History*, book 1, chapter 3. More on the Plague in Zeiler, century 1, *Letters*, pages 519, 520, and in his *Travels of Italy*.

In the town of Lauf, a theologian once observed during the plague that the sparrows fled from the infected houses and no longer stayed upon them. The Spaniards say the plague crawls with 3 Ls, namely *Luego* (quickly), *Lexos* (far), and *Largo tempore* (for a long time). *Historians of Turkish history relate that at Constantinople, a bronze horse was erected by Apollonius of Tyana <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and reputed magician</note>, a noble Magus, upon which an equestrian statue sat: as long as it was safe, the city was also safe and immune from the pestilential plague; but when Muhammad <note>Referring to Sultan Mehmed II, who conquered Constantinople in 1453</note> demolished it, the plague raged there most fiercely every year during the summer months.*

During cycles of mortality, fruit is harmful. Zeiler, century 4, question 31, page 155. Nothing cleanses the pestilential air sooner than vinegar. Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher, a Jesuit scholar who was one of the first to propose that plague was caused by microscopic organisms</note>, *Treatise on the Plague*, page 375.

How the plague was able to be propagated through specifically poisoned materials and scattered powder in the years 1542 and 1606 at Reichenstein, and in the year 1630 at Milan in Italy, is to be read with amazement. Zeiler in *German Travels*, page 520, chapter 24; in *Italian Travels* in the description of Milan; and the continuation of Abelin’s *Historical Chronicle*, folio 265, letter B, likewise testifies how the plague was spread by poison <note>There was a common early modern belief in "plague-spreaders" (pestisparsores or unteors) who intentionally spread the disease using ointments or powders.</note>. *Whether the plague should be considered a great or modest inconvenience, and whether a tenant may move out and seek a remission of rent because of an intervening plague.* J. T. Sprenger, *On the Physician*, page 76 and following. By law, it is permitted to burn a private house infected with the plague along with all the things that are in it. Latherus, *On the Census*, book 1, chapter 17, number 18. In the year 1554, there was such a terrible plague in Hungary, Transylvania, and neighboring lands that the people, out of pain, tore their own hands and arms with their teeth, fell into one another, and miserably killed themselves. Jobus Fincelius, *On Wonders*, part 1. Ofeas Schædæus reports in part 3, and the continuation of Sleidan, book 25, folio 1075: That in the year 1600 at Turin in Piedmont, six persons were executed who had poisoned the houses with the plague; and a barber confessed that he had killed more than 2,000 persons with it in the year 1599. ### 14. Signet, Seal-Stamp, Signet Ring. Seal.

"Petschafft" <note>The German term for a seal-stamp.</note> is the same as "Sigillum" (Seal), regarding which see below under the word *Sigillum*.

<margin>Besold, Volume 1.</margin>
In ancient writings, the term *Betschaden* is found; for so it appears in letters of arms (commonly called a "Grant of Arms") given to the Lebzelter family by Emperor Frederick in the year 1474: "...and my..." there: "they shall have and carry the aforementioned coat of arms and jewel, and use them in all and any honorable and upright matters and business, in jest and in earnest, as well as seals, signets <note>original: "Betschaden."</note>, and jewels." This word *Betschaden* was changed to *Petschaten* in the confirmation of Rudolph: "...and all of that..." there: "seals, signets, jewels, etc." It comes from the ancient word *Pittacium* <note>A label or slip of parchment.</note> used in Petronius, where it says:

<column-break/>

Labels <note>original Latin: "Pittacia."</note> were fixed to the necks of the wine-jars with this title: *Opimian Falernian, one hundred years old*; that is, indices or titles fixed to jars and casks, signifying the wine's origin and age. Bornitius *On Instruments*, book 1, chapter 20. Then the Glossary says $\pi\iota\tau\tau\acute{\alpha}\kappa\iota o\nu$ (pittakion) is a short note, a *Pittacium*. Martin in the *Philological Lexicon*. From this, a more likely and easier contraction is *Petschafft*, and its transfer to a signet ring or other seal. The word *Pistatium* is also found scattered through the ancient Constitutions in Goldast, which seems to be a scribal error <note>original Latin: "$\sigma\phi\acute{\alpha}\lambda\mu\alpha$ Scriptorum."</note>. For *Pittacium*, not *Pistatium*, corresponds to the Greek $\pi\iota\tau\tau\acute{\alpha}\kappa\iota o\nu$, unless one thinks the "S" was changed to "T" through usage. Thus says Bornitius in his treatise *On Instruments*.

Signet rings, called *Sigillarii* by Vopiscus and commonly known as *Pitschier-Ring*, are used to seal Testaments and other documents; the ancients also used them to seal up deposited money, household furniture, and all provisions.

Anyone was permitted to have such a ring, even if they had not obtained the "Right of Gold Rings" <note>original Latin: "jus aureorum Annulorum." In Roman law, the right to wear gold rings was a specific legal privilege originally reserved for the senatorial and equestrian ranks.</note>, the use of which was varied and, among the Ancients (as I just said), very great. For because of the multitude of servants, everything shut away was kept sealed by the masters, and thus they were protected from theft, as Pliny says.

Hence Seneca complains in *On Benefits*, book 3, chapter 15, that more trust is placed in rings than in the souls of men. See Arumæus, *Justinian Exercises*, leaf 117.

The characters or engravings on these rings, according to Marquard Freher in *Parerga*, book 1, chapter 20, were not formerly hereditary or familial as they are today, but were made at the whim of each person, and usually held some hidden meaning. For thus Pompey (as Plutarch reports in *Pompey*) had a lion holding a sword; and others, according to Dio, say that he (as well as Sulla) had three trophies engraved on his ring; Galba had a dog leaning its head out from the prow of a ship, according to the same Dio; Pliny the Younger had chariots. King Seleucus had a nautical anchor as his ring-seal, as Clement of Alexandria reports in *The Instructor*, book 3, because he himself had been born with a birthmark on his thigh similar to an anchor, according to Justin, book 15. Among the Egyptians, however, according to Aelian, all the bravest men wore an engraved scarab beetle, because that animal is without a female <note>The ancient Greeks and Romans mistakenly believed scarabs were a single-sex species that self-reproduced, making them symbols of self-creation and strength.</note>.

Regarding these rings, a Law of Solon is very notable, found in Laertius and mentioned by Freher in the cited place: "It is not permitted for a ring-maker to keep the seal or the pattern of a ring which he has sold or been commissioned to make." Perhaps for this reason: lest any opportunity for manufacturing a forgery be left behind.

And these signet rings do not fall under the name of "ornaments," because they were not prepared for the sake of adorning the body, but for serious uses, and are as a pledge of good faith. Law by argument 15.

To some, a seal-stamp <note>original: "Pettschaft."</note> seemed to be a "Bettschad," which is the same as a "Bettschäide"—a bed-frame or headboard in which the coats of arms of both spouses' families were traditionally painted. The Leipzig jurists state: **If you have dispatched your own messenger to your debtor, sent him a letter, and therein requested that he send the money back to you safely by that same messenger, which he then did, handing over the committed money to the messenger: even if the messenger has not yet arrived with the money, and it cannot be known whether he was murdered on the way and the money taken from him, or whether the messenger himself carried it off; nevertheless, the loss of such money may not be to the disadvantage of the debtor, but you shall justly bear the loss yourself according to the circumstances of the case.** B. R. W. Carpzov, part 4, constitution 41, definition 13, at the end.

Erasmus of Rotterdam is himself a witness to the personal and somewhat arrogant inscription on his own seal in his *Adages*, volume 3, century 5, adage 42; it was finished with this motto: **I yield to none.** <note>original Latin: "Cedo nulli." ## 15. Out-Citizen. <note>original: "Pfalburger" or "Pfalburgeri." This refers to people who claimed the rights of city citizenship while living outside the city walls on the lands of other lords.</note>

That citizen who retains his primary residence in a city to which he is registered, but is considered a "false citizen," is called by the old German name *Pfalburger*. What the meaning of this word is remains obscure. Some think an inhabitant who is not a full citizen is called a *Pfalburger*, meaning "one who sits between his stakes." <note>original: "der zwischen seinen Pfälen sitzt." Referring to the 'Pfahl' or stakes/palisades marking a city's outer boundary.</note> Freherus believes a "false citizen" is signified by it. In some places they are called *Pactburger* because they are citizens not absolutely, but under a certain pact—"under a certain pact or agreement"—

<column-break/>

whether by a certain and named annual payment or tax, or for a certain time, as Jakob Werner Killinger argues in his treatise on *Ganerbschaft* <note>A form of joint inheritance or shared property ownership in German law.</note>, discourse 3, number 88. Lord Draco does not think this is true in his *On the Law and Origin of Patricians*, chapter 3, folio 244, number 21. For the purpose of the prohibition against receiving *Pfalburgers* resists this; it does not hinder "pact-citizens." See Draco in the cited place and Arumæus on the Golden Bull, chapter 16, folio 267 and following. See my own work *On the Law of Citizens*, folio 48, and *On the Nature of Peoples*, folio 64.

### ADDITION.

An inhabitant is one who has a residence somewhere. The Greeks call this a <term>paroikon</term> <note>original: "πάροικον." Literally, one who dwells near or beside.</note>, "neighboring inhabitant"; the Germans call it a *Pfalburger*. Besold, Book 1 of his *Politics*, chapter 11, number 16, page 391. There was never any province in which there were more or more famous *Pfalburgers* than in Swabia <note>original: "Alemannia."</note>. Nor have they ceased to exist even now. The Counts of Sulz, on account of the Landgraviate of Klettgau and Rheinau, still today hold the right of citizenship by pact with the people of Zurich. Likewise, the Barons of Hohensax for the Baronies of Sax and Forsteck in the Rhine Valley and Bürglen in Thurgau. Others elsewhere. See more in Melchior Goldast von Haiminsfeld's *Rationali*, page 80: "Who the Pfalburgers are, and that such should not be accepted from other lordships without the consent of the previous lord." Zorer, part 2, question 2, number 99 and following. Why the reception of *Pfalburgers* was forbidden in the Golden Bull <note>The Golden Bull of 1356, which regulated the election of the Holy Roman Emperor and prohibited cities from protecting the subjects of other lords.</note> and other Constitutions, see Knipschild on *Imperial Cities*, book 2, chapter 29, number 75.

## 16. Palatinate, Palace. Palatium.

It is commonly taken to mean "Palace"; hence **Pfalzgrav**—Count of the Palace. From this also comes the **Palatine Court** <note>original: "Pfalenz-Gericht."</note>, which is a unique kind of jurisdiction, restricted almost entirely to feudal cases. See my work *On Counts*, number 8.

But let us trace a more ancient origin. Varro, in book 4 of *On the Latin Language*, says: "The Palace is of the Fourth Region." It is so named because the "Palantes" <note>Wanderers.</note> came there with Evander; or because the Palatines, who were also Aborigines from the Reatine territory, settled in that place which is called the Palatium. Martinius, in his *Philological Lexicon*, says that "Palace" is an appellative for an Imperial residence, a Basilica, or a Praetorium. **Palace** <note>original: "Pallast."</note>, for which 200 years ago the word *Phallenz* was used, means a royal house, a word which the Greeks also used for a long time. Meursius in his *Glossary* under the word <term>palation</term> <note>original: "παλάτιον."</note>. "Palatine" pertains to the Palace, and from this, all those having an office in the court were called Palatines. Lehmann, book 2, chapter 6, question 13.

And it should be noted that formerly, judgment was passed in the Palace for cases handled in the presence of the King, whereas in the countryside <note>original: "Pago."</note>, it was before the Count or the local judge. See Bignon in his notes to the *Formulas of Marculf*, folio 419.

And such Palaces existed in several Cities: and in them the Emperors or the Palatines <note>Officials of the palace court.</note> administered justice. Hence the word **Pfaltz** <note>Palatinate or Palace Court.</note> is sometimes used for a Judicial Court, as in Strasbourg. See Josias Nolden, *On the Status of the Nobility*, chapter 8, number 153, etc. Thus in Trier there is a building, now the Archbishop's house, which is called the **Palace** <note>German: "der Pallast."</note>; it was formerly under the Frankish Kings, and for a long time afterward, the seat of the Counts Palatine. See Freher on Ausonius’s *Mosella*, folio 123, and the same author on Peter von Andlau, folio 158 (noting that these Counts Palatine held the perpetual Prefecture or Advocacy of that city, from which that region of the City around the Palace is still called the **County** <note>German: "die Gravschaft."</note>). And Goslar was named a **Palace-City** <note>German: "Pfaltz-Stadt."</note> because the Imperial Courts used to be convened there. See Pomarius in the *Magdeburg Chronicle*; Henning Arnisaeus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, number 15, folio 322 in my edition. By the same logic, Palaces are considered buildings consecrated to the Emperor. In the single law of the Code [of Justinian] concerning Palaces in royal cities, it is listed (chapter 1, *What are Regalian Rights*, 2. Feuds. 56) there: "Palaces in the accustomed Cities." This is as if to say no one is permitted to inhabit Royal Palaces except the Prince himself, who holds the Regalian rights. See the law *nulli*, Code, *On the Office of the Rector of a Province*; see also Mr. Martin Mager’s treatise *On Armed Advocacy*, chapter 2, number 57.

Regarding the most ancient Seat of the Palatine Electors in Bacharach, see the *Gleanings of Palatine Antiquities on this side of the Rhine*, folio 25. There the author relates: <insert>that the ancient **Counts Palatine**, Electors, who from the time of Pepin and Charlemagne ruled the whole area called "Little France" from Brabant across the Meuse, Moselle, and Rhine, held their court and residences—long before they were at Heidelberg or anywhere else—at Bacharach, or what is the same thing, at the old castle of Staleck.</insert> And this, says the same author, I want specifically understood regarding the **Count Palatine**, who was always an Elector of the Empire either by succession or Imperial authority; to this belonged the **Count Palatine of Staleck**, or the **Palatinate on the Rhine**. Therefore, the common opinion from ancient times until now, observed by all writers, is that Bacharach is the oldest city of the Palatinate—meaning the Electoral Palatinate. Since the first institution by Otto III, the **Counts Palatine** who were Electors generally had their Electoral Chancery and residence there, until it moved to Heidelberg after nearly 200 years. The reason why the Elector preferred this place and Staleck Castle over others was that the Rhine is most pleasant and useful there, and the place where the Imperial Diets were held of old—where Emperors were deposed and appointed—was located closest to Bacharach; I mean the King's Seat <note>The *Königsstuhl* at Rhense.</note> near Rhense, now belonging to the Landgrave. There they blew the trumpet or trombone when necessary, so

<column-break/>

that the four Rhenish Electors could each hear it in his own land, etc. Thus far the author of the *Gleanings*.

Regarding the House of **Pfaltz**, see the *Acts of Count Palatine George Hausen*, passim.

### ADDITION.

The word **Pfaltz** signifies nothing other than the Court of the Emperor or a Prince; treated at length by Draco, *On Patricians*, pages 209–210; Becker in *Public Law*, page 168, **concerning the Palatinate**.

*Saxon Mirror*, book 3, article 62, in the Summary number 2, folio 431b, column 1. Zeiller wrote a *Topography of the Palatinate of the Rhine* in the year 1645.

### 17. Counts Palatine. <note>original: "Pfaltzgravon. Comites Palatini."</note>

These are now not only enrolled in the order of Princes, but are superior to many Dukes. Thus the Counts Palatine, commonly called **Pfaltzgravon**, were formerly the Judges or Prefects of the Palace, Hall, or Court of the Emperor: **Judges of the Imperial or Royal Court**. Borcholt, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, number 34. Now they can be called **Chamber or Court Judges** <note>German: "Cammer- oder Hofrichter."</note>. In ancient times they were also called Court Counts, as can be seen in Günther’s *Ligurinus*, book 6, verse 561:

> And Reinald at the same time, of whom one was the Court Count,
> The other in the Church, etc.

Likewise in book 7, verse 558, as well as book 8, verse 342. They are also called **Mayors of the Palace**, **Mayors of the House**, etc., regarding whom see Coccius on Dagobert, folio 92, where he discusses their institution and authority in the Kingdom of France; also Fauchet, *On Origins*, book 1, chapter 10; Sleidan, *On the Four Monarchies*, folio 319.

The Palatines and Mayors of the House formerly even acted with severity against Princes, as in the time of Charles and Pepin. And perhaps it is from this that the Palatine Elector had the right to judge the Emperor. From this also come the Palatine of Hungary and the Palatines of Poland, regarding whose authority see the writers on the *State of Poland*, folio 5.

In place of the Mayors of the House, in France there are *The Constables* <note>French: "Les Connestables."</note>; see Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 2, folio 60.

Today, those who are invested with a Principality or region that has been raised to a **Palatine-county** <note>German: "Pfaltz-grafschaft."</note> are called Counts Palatine. Reinking, book 1, *On Secular and Ecclesiastical Government*, chapter 13, number 18. Thus in Germany, the Counts Palatine of the Rhine shine with great preeminence and are decorated with the Electoral dignity, holding the first rank among the secular Electors. Marquard Freher in his treatise *On the Origin of the Palatines*; see König, part 1, in *Political Theater*, chapter 36, number 33 and following; Hubert Thomas of Liege in *Annals*, book 1; and my own work *On Counts*, number 8; also Caspar von Lerch, *On the Equestrian Order*, folio 25; and *The Grand Almoner of France*, folio 45.

The **Golden Bull** <note>The Golden Bull of 1356 was a decree that served as the constitutional law of the Holy Roman Empire for centuries.</note> in chapter 5 seems to indicate that the **Palatine** <note>The Count Palatine of the Rhine, one of the seven Prince-Electors.</note> is the **Judge and Overseer of the Empire**. This office was first conferred upon Count Rudolph of the Palatinate of the Rhine around the year 1250 AD by the common will and consent of the Princes. Georg Alt of Nuremberg writes as follows in his *Chronicle*:

<note>original: "Bey diesen Zeiten machten etlich deß Reichs..."</note> *During these times, several members of the Empire, and especially the spiritual Electors, formed an alliance and agreement against King Albert due to various doubts. They accused him of having killed his lord, Adolf, in a war, and therefore judged him unworthy of royal honor. For this reason, the other most prominent Princes of the German Nation appointed Duke Rudolph, Count Palatine of the Rhine, as a judge of the Roman Empire, so that from that time forward, he should perform that office through his courage: so that the Roman Kings might be moved to undertake nothing evil or worthy of reproach in the Empire, by which they might be judged unworthy of the Roman Royal Highness.*

But this office was personal, chosen based on the industriousness of the individual; it was not transferred to his descendants under the same conditions by which Rudolph obtained it.

And regarding this question—**whether the Count Palatine is the judge of the Roman Emperor?**—one may consult Schrader, *On Feuds*, part 10, section 7, number 70; Mr. Wilhelm Anton in his *Corollaries to the Treatise on the Five-Year Term*, folio 27; Lehman in his *Disputations on Title 5 of the Golden Bull*, folio 3 and following; and Freher on Peter von Andlau, folio 194, face 2. There, he explains that this singular and most exceptional privilege seems to descend from the ancient **Palatine Countship** <note>original: "Palatina Comitiva."</note>. Just as the **Prefect of the Palace** <note>A high-ranking administrative and judicial official in the Frankish court.</note> judged in the Royal Court and the Tribunal of the Franks with the widest jurisdiction over everyone, with absolutely no one exempt, so too the Prince himself—if he allowed himself to be sued by anyone (for no good Prince would place himself above all laws and justice)—was required to stand before this official. This very proof of the highest honor remained with the Palatine of the Rhine (excluding the Saxon Palatine) in this German Empire, as confirmed by Charles IV in the **Golden Bull**, chapter 5.

Regarding the **Saxon Palatines**, see Werdenhagen, *On the Hanseatic Republic*, part 3, folio 131.

Conrad, Count Palatine of the Rhine, died in the year 1195. The dignity, along with the entire territory, fell by the Emperor's favor to Henry the Saxon, who from that time always used the title "Duke of Saxony and Count Palatine of the Rhine" in his letters. I have seen countless letters written by him: I have seen a letter from Emperor Otto dated 1206, in which he greets him in the same manner. The author of the *Great Belgian Chronicle* acts no differently on page 221; nor does Mr. Meibomius in the *History of Henry the Lion*, folio 40.

Regarding the **Law and Privileges of the Imperial Counts Palatine**, who are Counts without a County, see Arumäus, volume 3, folio 39, and many

<column-break/>

following pages, as well as my own work *On Majesty*, folio 200; and the *Privilege of Joachim von Grünthal*, which was printed at Tübingen; and Sagittarius in his *Inaugural Dissertation on the Law and Privileges of the Count Palatine*.

He who falsely boasts of being a **Count of the Sacred Palace** and likewise exercises the rights belonging to the Palatines, ought to be punished with the death penalty, or the ultimate punishment. See Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 30, number 1; and Bonifacius, *On Theft*, page 321 at the end. The question is asked whether a Count Palatine can exercise the granted acts through a substitute, for example, in another city? This is denied. However, there are some to whom a special privilege has been granted to create **Vice-Counts**. They are also called **Imperial Counts Palatine** who are specifically gifted with this title by His Imperial Majesty and exercise such law as pertains even to the **Major Regalia** <note>The high-ranking rights and powers reserved for a sovereign, such as granting nobility or legitimizing heirs.</note>, such as granting the "benefit of age" <note>Allowing a minor to legally act as an adult.</note>, legitimizing children, creating Nobles and Doctors, etc. There exists on this subject G. Mr. Neudörffer, that most excellent physician of Nuremberg, had the broadest power to create Doctors of all faculties, even of Theology. Sometimes even lower-ranking persons obtained this Countship, such as: Johann Bauerschmied, a Pastor in Seuckendorff, and also Neudörffer, that famous mathematician. There also exist very extensive privileges of the Palatine Countship granted to Johann Baptist Baumio von Baumsdorff, a Jurist, and to his son Johann Georg, confirmed and fortified in the year 1631. Alexander Stockamer, a judge of our tribunal and at the same time a celebrated Count Palatine, in two acts even granted noble family coats of arms to those he legitimized. Most recently, there is a *Historico-Politico-Legal Dissertation on the Imperial Counts Palatine* by Johann Christian Viliz of Quedlinburg, printed at Halberstadt in 1664, who in paragraph 10 lists the acts they can perform if they have obtained the broadest privileges, such as creating: 1) Nobles. 2) Doctors. 3) Licentiates. 4) Masters. 5) Notaries. 6) Bachelors. 7) Poets. 8) Appointing guardians. 9) Interposing decrees for the sale of property. 10) Confirming wills. 11) Granting the benefit of age. 12) Strengthening the unions of offspring. 13) Confirming adoption. 14) Emancipating children. 15) Freeing servants. 16) Wiping away the mark of infamy. 17) Legitimizing children. 18) Granting coats of arms. 19) Sealing with red wax. 20) Creating official transcripts. 21) Granting exemptions. 22) Granting hereditary nobility. 23) Appointing Imperial Councillors. 24) Using legal prescription. 25) Enjoying singular protection. 26) Presenting transcripts. 27) They do not lose their privileges through non-use. Thus far Viliz.

### 18. Pledge-fief. Feudum pignoratitium.

A pledge-fief <note>original: "Pfandlehen"</note> is established in such a way that if the Lord confesses in the Investiture <note>The formal ceremony of granting a fief and the document recording it</note> that he has granted this fief to the Vassal for a certain sum of money, it remains free for him to redeem it once the money has been repaid. *Zasius in Epitom. feud. page 2. num. 23. & following; Schrader on Feuds page 2. chapter 4. num. 57. & following; Rosenthal on Feuds chapter 2. conclusion 77; Fichard vol. 2. counsel 7. num. 5; Friedrich Martin on the Law of Censuses chapter 1. num. 187.* See *Gottfried Antonius, Feudal Disputations 1. thesis 7. letter g. & folio 95. letter f. Vultejus on Feuds book 1. chapter 18.*

Sometimes such fiefs are given in perpetuity <note>original: "auf ein Ewiges"</note>, and then they are conceived roughly under this form: **"So that neither we nor our heirs, nor anyone else, shall ever redeem the named city, castle, etc., from him or his bodily heirs who are sons, nor shall we dispossess them or take the property from them. Yet with this condition: if these [Persons] of [Place] should pass away without legitimate bodily heirs who are sons, then the same city, castle, lordships, etc., all and each with their belongings, shall fall back to us, or if we are no longer here, to our other heirs, solely and entirely without any redemption, return, or payment, and without any disturbance or contradiction from their other heirs or anyone else on their behalf, as they have pledged themselves to us and our heirs in this regard. And we and our heirs wish to be their Gracious Lords for this reason, and to uphold, protect, and defend them against any claim, faithfully and without deceit. They shall also be obedient and ready for us, and thereafter for our bodily heirs who are sons (should we have any), and for no one else with the same cities, castles, and lordships, and keep them open for all our necessities, to let us and ours, whom we appoint for it, in and out, and to maintain us therein, against everyone, no one excepted, yet at our own cost and provisions and without significant harm to them; also all faithfully and without deceit."**

Regarding whether women succeed in a pledge-fief: Viewed strictly by the rigor of the law, Knichen (*on Pacts of Investiture part 1. chapter 3. num. 256*) and Rosenthal (*chapter 2. conclusion 77. num. 3*) think women should be excluded, although the custom of Germany states the opposite, as attested by Zasius (*part 12. num. 24*) and Gail (*2. observations 159. last number*). For pledge-fiefs are not "proper" or "rectal" fiefs <note>Fiefs following the standard rules of inheritance and service</note> but are "degenerate" fiefs <note>original: "feuda degenerantia"</note>, and therefore can only be established by express agreements. *Counsel of Strasbourg volume 2. counsel 58. question 1.*

Regarding whether and when a pledge-fief is pre-

<column-break/>

scribed <note>A legal term meaning the loss or acquisition of a right through the passage of time</note>, Rosenthal teaches in *on Feuds chapter 60. conclusion 80. num. 11.*

### 19. Pledge-money, Pledge-holding, By-way-of-pledge. Antichresis.

Although the words **Pledge-money** <note>original: "Pfandschilling"</note>, **Pledging** <note>original: "Verpfändung"</note>, and similar terms, when reduced to a legal understanding, denote a simple pledge, yet when they are used in a context where the interpretation of both law and common usage can be considered, the interpretation of common understanding should be accepted over the strict legal one. *Law: 'that stipulation' 38. § 'this also', 7. there Bartolus on the Digest 'On Verbal Obligations'; Romanus counsel 4. num. 6.* According to the custom of Germany, a purchase and sale with a pact of redemption <note>An agreement where the seller can buy back the property later</note> is commonly called **Pledge-money**. *Zasius counsel 12. num. 11; Wesenbeck counsel 2. num. 91; Counsels of the Academy of Ingolstadt volume 4. among the counsels of illustrious lawyers counsel 12; Arumæus in the cited place, num. 75.* See *Friedrich Martin on Censuses in the index at the word 'Antichresis', and the word 'pledge-fief', where there are certain notable points, especially folio 48. and following.*

And **Pledging** <note>original: "Pfandung"</note> is properly a sale with a pact of redemption in Germany. See *Georg Everhard 1. counsel 54. num. 45.* who in *number 48. and following* recounts the differences between a contract of sale and a pledge contract, and in *number 77* says that, notwithstanding any prescription, it can be redeemed, as also in *counsel 60. in the same volume* and also *see volume 4. counsel 10.*

The words **Pledging**, **Pledge-money**, and **Repurchase** <note>original: "Wiederkauff"</note> are also synonyms and terms signifying the same thing. Thus Zasius rightly says in the *cited counsel 12. num. 11* that in common speech, no difference is made between the term "sale" (where immovables are sold with a pact of redemption) and the term "pledge," but one is used for the other. *Arumæus cited decision num. 79.*

Whoever holds a castle through a pledge contract, commonly called a **Pledge-holding** <note>original: "Pfandschafft"</note>, makes the fruits <note>Profits, crops, or revenues produced by the property</note> his own, and they are not counted against the principal debt, according to the custom of Swabia and almost the general custom of all Alemannia <note>An old name for Southwestern Germany</note>, as Martin Uranius attests in *volume 2. counsel 56. num. 5.*

For just as custom can introduce a new species of contract, as Angelus elegantly argued in *§ 'the law therefore' in the 'Authentica' regarding not alienating*, so too can custom approve a contract. *Balduinus in the law 'through various' Code on Mandates.*

For even if someone performs an act that is commonly considered acceptable, even if in truth it might not be licit (as it tastes of usurious depravity <note>The sin or crime of charging excessive interest</note>), it is nonetheless not to be judged usurious. *Bartolus in the law 'who may be a fugitive' § 'at Labeo' Digest on the Aedilian Edict.*

See also *Matthias Coler counsel 27. and following*, where he has much to say about such a contract, especially *counsel 31*, regarding who ought to prove the belongings and li-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal complexities of pledged property (mortgages), specifically looking at the jurisdictional rights of the person holding the pledge and the process of legal seizure (pignoration) within the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

<header>Expanded Treasury of Practical Law</header>

and the limits of such pledged goods: and how they are to be separated from other mixed assets.

The question is asked: if goods are pledged for bad <note>original: "schlecht Geld" — likely referring to debased or devalued currency</note> money, must one accept the low purchase price? Cravetta, in *counsel 692*, affirms this, for the interest is derived from the utility of the property.

Natta, in *counsel 496*, advised on when a pledge-payment <note>original: "Pfandschilling"</note> may pass into a full purchase.

And it should be noted that an Estate of the Empire holding a town through a contract of antichresis <note>A legal arrangement where a creditor manages a property and keeps its profits in place of interest payments</note> as a pledge-holder <note>original: "Pfands-Inhaber"</note> cannot institute a change of religion. For subjects must conform themselves to the religion of that Estate of the Empire which holds immediate jurisdictional lordship over them; but one who possesses a town only by way of a mortgage, as a pledge-holder, obtains no Lordship of Jurisdiction, since he exercises jurisdiction not in his own name but in the name of another. Therefore, he himself cannot command the religion of the subjects, as they must conform themselves to their own proper Lord. See *Compositions of Peace, question 39.*

Nevertheless, it is deduced in the *Strasbourg Counsels, vol. 1, counsel 1, question 1*, that such pledge-lords are entitled to confiscations within the mortgaged goods.

In olden times, territories were often assigned to others through antichresis in such a way that one should not, nor would one, redeem this city, fortress, etc., all together or any part of them, from the lender, nor from his legitimate sons that he now has or may have in the future.

But if he or his legitimate sons pass away and none of them are left alive, then the heirs of his sons, or the sons or daughters, shall allow the redemption and be obedient when we desire it of them: yet in such a way that we redeem the aforementioned pledge into our own hands, and they shall not allow anyone else to redeem it, nor shall they redeem one part without the other; and when we wish to perform the redemption from the heirs of his legitimate sons, the redemption shall be made for the named sum of money, etc., and they shall make the payment at one of the cities, N. or N., whichever they wish. Furthermore, if the aforementioned N. or his heirs wished to pledge one or more of the aforementioned castles, they may well do so, provided it is without harm to our redemption by us, our brothers, and our heirs, in the manner prescribed above.

The expression "by way of pledge" <note>original: "Pfandsweis"</note> is a compound, and it sounds the same as if one were to say "after the example and likeness of a pledge," yet it does not signify a true pledge. See Battista Cesare in *Counsels of Illustrious Jurists, part 2, counsel 67, number 29, and the final counsel, number 44, part 3.*

Most accurately, Mr. Doctor Tabor [writes] concerning the double amount, *page 256 and following, recent edition.* When an Estate [of the Empire] possesses a city as a

pledge-holder through the price of antichresis, [the question of] whether he can change the religion [is discussed by] Limnaeus, *volume 2, Additions to book 1, chapter 9, page 132.* The words: pledge-payment, pledge-money, by way of mortgage, when added to a contract—[the question is] whether they make it a pledge-contract. Christoph Philipp Richter, *part 2, counsel 21, number 2, 6, and following, folio 119, and number 29, folio 124.*

### 20. Seizure. Pignoratio.

On these matters, see the *Chamber Precedents* under the word "Pfandungen" (Seizures). Likewise, Gail, *single book*, and many points in Schwanmann in *Chamber Observations*; Roding, *on Chamber Law*; Beatus, *decisions, volume 5, part 5, on judicial matters, volume 2, folio 236, etc.*

If an immediate person <note>Someone who reports directly to the Emperor without an intermediary lord</note>, by reason of his own person, seizes the property of another immediate person and encroaches upon his immediate territory, and wishes to acquire the right which he holds from Austria, there is a place for the constitution of seizure <note>original: "Pfandung"</note>; for this is not the case described by Roding, *folio 64.*

It is pleasing to refer here to the following legal response, in which the requirements of seizures and the privileges of the House of Austria are discussed.

---

->Illustrious, High-born Prince, my humble and entirely obedient service is and remains at Your Princely Grace’s disposal at all times.<-

Gracious Prince and Lord: Your Princely Grace, under the date of December 20th of the year just passed, graciously commanded me to draft a legal opinion regarding the act of violence, as well as the tearing down of Your Princely Grace's customs stations and coats of arms. I was to direct my thoughts to this: whether Your Princely Grace, in this case, could fittingly and without disadvantage seek and obtain a Mandate of Seizure without Clause <note>original: "Mandatum Pignorationis sine Clausula" — a specific legal order from the Imperial Chamber Court that allowed for immediate action without a preliminary hearing</note> at the Imperial Chamber Court? According to my incumbent duty, I would have gladly complied with this immediately, had I not been stricken at that very time with a severe illness, indeed to such an extent that it was entirely impossible for me to complete this or any other work.

But because the Almighty has somewhat improved my condition again: I have pursued such a task with all diligence, and for my part, have found the matter somewhat doubtful.

And although seizures by great nobles are carried out not only by themselves but also through others—whether from their family and officials or total strangers—it is the rule that what a person does through another, they are seen to have done themselves, just as an injury caused by a third party is judged to have been committed by the one who ordered it. <note>original: "l. sed etsi. §. si jussu. ff. si servus. ubi Bart. n. 4. ff. de injur." — Legal citations referring to the Digest of Justinian and the commentary of Bartolus de Saxoferrato.</note>

In such a case, it is only necessary that the third party acts not only by the command and mandate of the Prince or Lord, but also for the sake of and in consideration of the Lord’s own interests; this must be narrated and expressed in clear words in the legal petition. For if the third party takes something out of private greed or a desire for revenge for their own benefit, it is not the Lord, but the person who performed the seizure themselves, who must be summoned before their own competent judge because of such violence. <note>Gaill, *On Seizures*, observation 5, number 3.</note>

Furthermore, the ratification of the Lord will be considered proven not only from his confession and mandate, but also if he had the opportunity to return the seized property or release a captive, yet did not restore them. <note>Imperial Recess of the year 1594, Regensburg, paragraph "When also in matters of seizure." Schwanmann, *Observations of the Imperial Chamber Court*, 66.</note>

However, when I look through the report submitted back in subservience by Your Princely Grace's officials at Z., I can find nothing other than that the Burgrave, Master Builder, and other servants of the city of H., presumably because of a claimed <term>free Bürst</term> <note>Likely a local privilege regarding wood-gathering or a specific trade exemption</note>, and also because they presume to exempt themselves from the tolls belonging to Your Princely Grace at those places, have carried out this forbidden seizure.

And I can judge it even less likely that the Archducal House of Austria is directly seeking a right in this place, because I am well aware that although H. is attached to the aforementioned House regarding <term>superiority</term> <note>High jurisdictional authority or sovereignty</note>, it nevertheless possesses special laws and several <term>Regalia</term> <note>Royal rights or privileges held by a local power</note> that are otherwise not usually granted to provincial towns.

Since, if Austria were to claim such rights for itself, this seizure would, in my opinion, have been carried out by the officials of the upper County and Lordship of Hohenberg, who reside at Fridingen, and not solely by the ministers of the city of H.

From which it follows that no <term>Mandatum sine Clausula</term> <note>original: "Mandate without Clause" — an urgent court order requiring immediate compliance without the opportunity for a prior hearing</note> should be issued against H., nor likewise against Austria, especially at this time; instead, better inquiries must first be gathered as to whether and to what extent the aforementioned House of Austria is interested in this matter, and whether they seek a right for themselves or for their provincial town H., and also whether their Archducal Highness or their government at Inns-

**Wolff von Habsburg against Austria, May 15, 1571**, and in the case of **Württemberg against Austria** in Gylman, volume 3, folio 241 and following. This is consistent with what Tilmannus de Benignis reports: that legal proceedings against the House of Austria, insofar as they concern their hereditary lands, should not be judged according to the **Constitution on Seizures** <note>The *Pfändungsexekutionsordnung* or Constitution on Seizures was an Imperial law regulating how a creditor could seize property from a debtor. The Habsburgs claimed their hereditary lands were exempt from these specific Imperial court procedures.</note>. However, regarding **Swabia**, the Lordship of **Burgau**, and the Bailiwick of **Hagenau**, there is no such objection. *Aposp. Syn. in Const. Cam. prax. impetr. f. 40.*

On the other hand, it is well known that the House of Austria desires to extend its privileges indiscriminately to all cases in every way. Gylman, *Symphorem. vol. 1. part. 2. tit. 17. petition 2. fol. 321. col. 2.* The author of *Symphorem*, volume 3, in the decisions or precedents of the Imperial Chamber, section "Austria," reports: that **Emperor Charles V** at the Diet of Augsburg, following the mature advice of the Electors, Princes, and Estates, declared that appeals from the Provincial Court in Swabia should be made to the Duke of Austria, and that no appeal from there to the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> should be accepted, nor should any process be issued against the House of Austria in the Chamber. His Imperial Majesty also commanded the Chamber Court, under penalty of **30 marks of pure gold**, not to accept any appeal from the Swabian Provincial Court or other Austrian courts, nor to allow any process to proceed against the House of Austria, nor to presume any judgment over those privileges. Instead, they must let Austria enjoy its privileges, including an "annulling clause" <note>A legal clause that automatically voids any court action taken in violation of the stated privilege.</note>. Furthermore, His Majesty issued another declaration in the year [15]31, commanding the Chamber Court under penalty of **50 marks of pure gold** (with an annulling clause) to completely abstain from appeals and judgments in all processes against Austrian liberties and to obey previous orders.

For my part, I am concerned that **H.** <note>Likely a placeholder for a specific town or territory involved in the current case.</note> might perhaps be pulled into the Austrian hereditary lands, because several hundred years ago it passed from the **Count of Fürstenberg** to Austria. Moreover, the privilege of the late **Emperor Charles IV** from the year 1366 specifically counts whatever belongs to Austria in the **Black Forest** among the Austrian hereditary lands. Thus, one could argue that the aforementioned distinction of Austrian lands—and the idea that one could grant mandates based on the Constitution on Seizures regarding certain Austrian territories—is only to be understood as applying to the Bailiwicks of Swabia, Hagenau, and other such properties which the House of Austria does not own outright or as a fief from the Holy Roman Empire, but holds only as a **pledged security** <note>A *Pfandschilling* refers to territory held as collateral for a loan; the Empire often "mortgaged" lands to the Habsburgs for cash.</note>.

However, no one who knows the circumstances of these parts will doubt that **H.** and the surrounding area is not a pledged security from the Empire, but is an **Austrian owned and hereditary land**. 

<column-break/>

On the other hand, it can easily be inquired in **Speyer** <note>The city where the Imperial Chamber Court was located.</note> or other places whether it is currently the practice to grant all mandates against Austria.

The second requirement of the Constitution consists in this: **that the person whose property was seized was in possession (or quasi-possession) of the thing, and that the seizor undertook the seizure in contemplation of seeking a new legal right.**

In this requirement, as well as in the fourth (namely, that the cause must be **Civil, not criminal**), I find no error, according to my limited capacity.

Regarding the third requirement, however—namely, **whether a "third thing" (that is, an innocent thing) was taken or seized on account of another matter**—a doubt arises. This is because the **toll-posts** <note>original: *Zollstock*</note> might be viewed as the very thing in dispute. Consequently, their removal or destruction might be cited as a simple "disturbance of possession" rather than a "seizure" or distraint.

Indeed, it is required above all in the Constitution on Seizures that the thing or person taken be a **"third party,"** as they commonly call it: **innocent**. This means the item seized or taken must be seized on account of **another** thing or person. It must be something outside of the disputed matter or the disputed right, outside the use of the thing or right being litigated, and not a part of the disputed item. Or, it must be something that, without controversy and by the confession of the seizor himself, belongs to another (or at least is not denied to be so). It should have nothing in common with the contested right. For example: if, because someone's jurisdiction or possession was disturbed, their **subject** or their **goods** are taken and seized; or if there is a dispute over the right to gather wood or graze livestock, and because of that, perhaps the **wagon, horses, or the drivers** are seized and taken along with the disputed wood. *Imperial Recess of the year [15]94 at Regensburg, section "But where in seizures," where it is established that the Constitution on Seizures applies and mandates should be decreed only in those cases where a "third thing," and one not at all in controversy, is said to have been taken. Gaill, On Seizures, observation 3, number 10.*

Therefore, if the very thing or person that is the subject of the controversy is seized or taken, this Constitution will not apply. For example: if there is a dispute over the right to sell wine, and the **wine itself** is carried away; such an act is judged to be a simple disturbance rather than a seizure, and it pertains to the **ordinary judges** rather than to the Imperial Chamber. *Rhodingius, on Chamber Law, book 1, title 16, number 14 and following.*

However, because that **distinction between an "Innocent thing" and a "Disputed thing"** is difficult to differentiate, the Chamber Court does not observe it so strictly in...

## 21. Parish, Parish Churches. Parochia.

Regarding Ecclesiastical benefits <note>The income-producing office of a clergyman.</note>, see the individual treatises of Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse and François Douaren; also Nicolaus Gimonteus, and specifically regarding Parishes, the individual treatise of Filesac. But it is asked: what is a Parish Church, and from where does that name come? It is answered that those benefits to which a more diligent care of souls is attached are commonly called **Parish Churches** <note>Original: *Pfarrkirchen*</note>, the name being derived from the ancient temples of early peoples. For "Parish Priest" <note>Original: *Parochus*</note>, according to Cicero's letters to Atticus, is named <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ παρέχειν"</note> "from providing," because it signifies "to supply." For in ancient times, the duty of the *parochi* consisted in supplying and providing wood, salt, and similar things to legates or magistrates, and those who were sent out for the sake of public utility. Budé calls the inhabitants of the same temple "Parochi," and a "Parish" a place and a sacred neighborhood, in his *Pandects* at the last law "On Municipals." See also Ricci, *Episcopal Practice*, folio 787.

Which benefits are reserved? Book 8 of the *Decretals*, book 1, title 11.

Bishops, or those who stand in the place of the Ordinary <note>A church official with immediate jurisdiction, like a bishop.</note>, have the right and power to make two parishes out of one for significant reasons, even against the will of the Patrons <note>The laypeople or entities who had the right to appoint the priest.</note>, if a just cause persuades such a division. Azorius—
