### 22. Penny. Coin.
<note>Latin: *Pfenning. Nummus.*</note>

The word **Penny** [Pfenning] can generally be used for all sorts, as when one says thick pennies, broad, thin, large and small, gold and silver pennies. See Tileman Friesen, *Mirror of Coins* [Münzspiegel], book 2, chapter 3.

Moreover, they think the word *Pfenning* is derived either from the word *pecunia* [money], or from **Pfandung** [distraint/seizure], as if it were *Behandung* [handling], from *apprehendendo* [taking hold of], and said to be so named from its frequent use.

A French "thick-penny" [dicker-Pfenning] is worth six and a half *Batzen*, which makes 26 *Creutzer*; 11 *Albus* and 6 *Pfenning* in Bohemian currency; 8 *Groschen* and 8 *Pfenning* in Upper Rhine currency; and 8 *Groschen* in Meissen currency; and twelve-and-a-half *Schilling* in Lübeck and Magdeburg currency. Jacob Alemannus in *Palæstra Consultat.*, consultation 8, principal question 1, part 37.

A Lorraine or "Cardinal" thick-penny is worth five and a half *Batzen*, which makes 22 *Creutzer*; 9 *Albus* and 7 *Pfenning* in Bohemian currency; 7 *Groschen* and 4 *Pfenning* in Upper Rhine currency; and 10 *Schilling* in Lübeck and Magdeburg currency. Jacob Alemannus, in the same place, part 38.

Regarding the value, stability, issuance, and minting of the Penny, Alemannus has much in consultation 8, principal question 1, part 47. Likewise, Tileman Friesen in *Mirror of Coins*, book 2, chapter 10, section 13, and book 4, chapter 3, section 25, where things not unworthy of knowing may be seen.

Goldastus <note>Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a Swiss jurist and historian</note> in *Alemannic Matters*, volume 1, part 2, folio 395, testifies that the *Pantingum*, which we call *Pfenning*, is a purely German word. It is the sixteenth part of a Bernese unit; among those of Constance, Schaffhausen, and others, the twelfth; among the Palatines and Rhinelanders, the fourteenth. It is said to come from *behanden* [to handle], which the ancients contracted to *Pfanden*, like *Behandung*—as if you were to say "manual" or "handy"—on account of its convenience and its necessary and daily use.

Since some years ago even smaller coins were being formed by certain people in greater abundance than was proper, and those same smaller coins were being weakened in their alloy and weight, the Estates [of the Empire] were enjoined that no more small coins should be minted at all. **Imperial Recess** <note>An official decree of the Holy Roman Empire</note> of the year 1524, section "Furthermore, after the Batzen"; *M.O.* <note>Likely *Monetæ Ordinatio*, or Minting Ordinance</note> of the year 1559, section "where, however, against this"; **Imperial Recess** of the year 1500, section "therefore although" and the following sections; and finally that the coins be re-minted, according to Master Achatius Hülfen in his *Opinions on Minting*.

The crime of extortion <note>original: *Crimen Repetundarum*; the crime of a public official taking bribes or illegal fees</note> can be committed even with a single coin. Schneidewein on *The Division of Things*, the section on hens, number 1. The glosses <note>marginal legal commentaries</note> mean that any legal action may be granted even for a single coin; however, in the Imperial Chamber Court, when someone was sued for the theft of two coins, the action was rejected with great indignation. ### 23. Paymaster, Chief Paymaster. Treasurer, Supreme Treasurer.

Among the senior officers of the army is listed the Treasurer and Guardian of the Camp Treasury <note>original: *Quæstor & Custos ærarii Castrensis*</note>, the Chief Paymaster <note>original: *obriste Pfenningmeister*</note>, who collects the money necessary for war, guards it once collected, and pays it out. Reinhard König in *Political Theater*, part 3, chapter 10, under number 4. Today they are called Commissioners.

### ADDITION.

Supreme Treasurer, the Chief Paymaster. Liebenthal in *Political Collection*, Exercise 14, thesis 30.

### 24. Guardian, Ward-master, Caretaker, Foster-father, Protector, etc. Tutor.

Guardians <note>original: *Tutores*</note> are named from "protecting" <note>original: *tuendo*</note>, because they must protect and defend the Ward <note>original: *Pupillum*; a child under legal guardianship</note>. Section 2 of the Institutes, book 1, section 1 of the Digest on guardianship; book 1 of the Digest on minors. For a Guardian is considered to be in the place of the owner regarding the Ward's property when he is administering the guardianship, but not when he is plundering the Ward. The law *qui fundum* 7, section *si tutor* 3, in the Digest on the buyer. By the Italians he is called *Defensore del Pupillo*, by the French *Tuteur*, by the Germans, a *Pfleger, Vormund, Gerhaber, Pflegvatter, Pflegvogt, Treuhalter, Treuhänder, Momper*. This last term is very common along the Rhine, and seems to be taken from the French, as *Momper* is like *mon Pere*, that is, "my Father." Dr. Joachim Cluten in his *Justinian Distributions*, 14, book 1, thesis 4. But soon be-

<column-break/>

low I will reveal a derivation that is perhaps more fitting. However, because of the frequent and customary frauds of Guardians, Albericus de Rosate, Spiegel in his *Lexicon* under the words *tutela* and *Tutores*, and Antonio Piaggi in his *Treatise on Guardianship*, question 1, number 3, think they are called *Tutores* as if they were "Takers" <note>original: *Tollitores*; a Latin pun on *Tutor* (protector) and *Tollere* (to take away)</note>. Antiquity is certainly full of such examples. Paul Montanus on *Guardianship*, chapter 7, number 7 and following; nor are they lacking in our own century. Hence the Emperor Maximilian, regarding those who were of such a greedy nature, used to jokingly call them *Gernhaber* <note>meaning "Glad-havers" or "those who like to possess"</note>, adding the letter "N" to the local word. For the Austrians call Guardians *Gerhaber* <note>Caretakers</note>. So too others are called *Vormund* <note>Guardian</note>, but because of their abuse of the role, they are called by <term>antiphrasis</term> <note>a figure of speech where a word is used to mean its opposite</note> as if it were *vor dem Mund* <note>"in front of the mouth," implying they snatch everything before it reaches the ward</note>. Whence our Germans say: "The Guardians <note>original: *Vormunder*</note> often act so that not much is left for the Mouths-to-follow <note>original: *Nachmunden*; i.e., the wards</note>." See my work on *Succession and the Election of Government*, last chapter.

Therefore, our Law looks out for the protection of Wards by various means.

First, a Guardian is bound to create an inventory. And if this is not done, the "Oath in Litigation" <note>original: *Juramentum in litem*; a sworn statement by the plaintiff regarding the value of the disputed property</note> is granted to the Ward against him. Plotus on *Oaths in Litigation*, folio 50, under number 31. But Antonius Monterus, in Decision 11, judges that this cannot be brought against the Guardian’s heirs unless the legal contest was started while the Guardian was alive.

A Guardian cannot seek a salary, although sometimes a Judge may establish one for him on account of future labors. Monterus, Decision 29. *Mundiburdis* or *Mundiburdium* means protection, or *Momberdeye* <note>German: *Munt* is an ancient term for legal power/protection</note>. It was also called *Mamburgium* and *Mandiburgium*.

The Guardian himself was sometimes called *Mundiburdis*. Ripuarian Law, title 37, section 3: "If anyone presumes to lead away a free-born girl or woman who is under the protection of the King or the Church, and takes her from her protection <note>original: *de Mundiburde*</note> without the parents' will, let him be judged guilty of 60 shillings." From this, I think the word for curators is contracted to *Momper*.

*Mundium* means guardianship or protection <note>original: *Mund*</note>. Melchior Goldast, *Alemannic Laws*, title 52, section 2: "If however they are alive, they do not belong to him who fathered them, but the protection <note>original: *Mundio*</note> belongs to that first husband."

Amerbach notes that the word *Mundium* often occurs in the Laws of the Lombards, and mostly signifies guardianship: hence *Mundualdi* <note>Protectors/Guardians</note>. Likewise *Vormunden* and *Mundlin* are clearly Germanic words.

*Selpmundia* <note>Self-protection</note> means to be of one's own right, outside of guardianship. Lombard Law, title 83: "Let no free woman living under the jurisdiction of our kingdom and the laws of the Lombards be permitted to live in the judgment of her own power, that is, in *Selpmundio*, but she must always remain under the power of men, or certainly the King." From *Selb* <note>Self</note> and *Munding* <note>Protection</note>. But regarding the word *Mund*, see Bignon in his notes on the *Formulas of Marculf*, folios 504, 506, 528; Dr. Meibom on the *History of Henry the Lion*, folio 33; and my own treatise *On Covenants*, folio 54.

Regarding Guardianship and Curatorship, an entire treatise exists, inserted among my *Legal Works*.

# ADDITION.

Even if a ward <note>original: *pupillus*; a minor child under the care of a guardian</note> has several paternal relatives <note>original: *agnatos*; relatives related through the male line</note> of equal proximity, the guardianship <note>original: *tutela*</note> is granted to the elder, according to Klock, *Consultations* 6, number 37. It is permitted to recover possession of a guardianship from which one has been removed by one’s own authority, Klock, *Consultations* 6, number 83. A guardian and administrator cannot initiate a malicious lawsuit, Klock, chapter 11, number 169 and following. The obligation of guardians is indivisible, compare 6, number 45.

Curators <note>officials appointed to manage the affairs of those unable to do so themselves, such as older minors or the mentally ill</note> are called <term>Trustees</term> <note>original: *Treyhalter*</note>. See Vult. at § 1. of the Institutes *On Curatorship*. Or <term>Providers</term> <note>original: *Versorger*</note>. *Nuremberg Reformation*, chapter 39, law 11, § 5. The Calendar <note>managing public accounts or schedules</note>; 8. The Divine or Imperial house. See extensively Mr. Tabor, *On the Crime of Extortion*, thesis 27, throughout. Protection <note>original: <term>Mundium</term></note> is nothing other than guardianship, derived from *Edmundi* <note>a reference to an oath of protection</note> from *Edt*, that is, an oath, and *Mund*, that is, mouth. Mr. G. Richter in his *Letters*, page 497.

Regarding the Guardian's oath. Rittershusius, in the *New Constitutions*, page 602, number 5. Regarding the Guardian's Inventory, ibid. page 346, number 45. Regarding a Guardian not completing an Inventory, page 341, number 19. Guardians should know it is their duty, above all, to record all the ward's belongings in an inventory, unless they wish to be marked with infamy and removed as suspicious, and be held liable for the ward's interests, law 7, principle, *On the Administration of Guardians*; law 24 of the Code, same title; final law, § 1 of the Code, *On the Arbitration of Guardianship*. And according to the *Nuremberg Reformation*, they are furthermore held to a monetary penalty of 50 Rhenish florins to be applied to the treasury, title 39, law 8, final §. They must defend the person of the ward, administer the assets, and provide their authority immediately in the business, § 2 of the Institutes, law 9, § 5 of the Digest, *On the Authority of Guardians*, where Mr. Ludwell in the *Notes on Wesenbeck*, number 5, and *Disputations on the Institutes* 3, thesis 7, letter C, notes they must intervene and provide authority in all causes in which the ward's condition could become worse. Anyone can be a Guardian or Curator, even one who is a creditor or debtor to the ward, if the debt is small. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 95, number 1. Sprenger, *On Small Matters*, page 100. Where the assets of the ward are meager, an inventory is not necessary, page 101.

## 25. Guardianship Accounts. <note>original: *Pflegrechnungen* / *Rationes Tutorum*</note>

By a certain anciently received custom, every Guardian is required to write a book of Accounts, though at the Ward's expense, in which they are bound to describe clearly and item-by-item all things given and received, income, expenses, and whatever they administered: so that everything is entered into it specifically from day to day, both regarding what is received and what is ex-

<column-break/>

pended. This was indeed done so that the truth or falsity can be drawn from it, or so that the contrary can be proven against him, according to the law *apparitores* in the Code *On the Collection of Taxes*; law 1, section *offic.* of the Digest *On Guardianship and the Settling of Accounts*; law *si quis* of the Digest *On Conditions and Demonstrations*. Nicolaus Janua, *On Private Writing*, book 4, title *On the books of Guardians, Curators, etc.*, number 2. He also says in number 3: it must be observed that these things should by no means be stated in generalities: so much so, that if everything is not stated clearly, or is stated only in general terms—regarding those things not recorded, or recorded only generally without the time, cause, day, month, and year, and the naming of persons and places—the ward can take an "oath in court" <note>a legal oath where the plaintiff estimates the value of damages</note> against the guardian who prepared such a Book. Thus, by that very Oath, the items and their quantity, price, valuation, fruits, and income are proven to have been received against the Guardian or Curator (who is bound to the creation of such a Book of accounts). Finally, one can generally swear in court against such a person just as if they had created no book at all, though always subject to a prior valuation by a Judge. Cravetta, *On the Antiquity of Time*, § limitation 4, number 44. Petrus Montanus, *Treatise on Guardianship*, chapter 32, rule 8, number 1. Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrations*, book 2, century 3, case 208, number 19 and following. He gives this reason: for the confusion of accounts has the same effect as if they were never made, since it is impossible to discern what was done.

It has pleased me to insert here the following Legal Opinion <note>original: *Responsum Juris*</note> written by me long ago, dealing extensively with the publishing and rendering of accounts by Guardians or Curators. It also discusses many things required in the rendering of such accounts, commonly called <term>Guardianship Accounts</term> <note>original: *Pfleg- oder Vormunds-Rechnungen*</note>, so that the Guardians and Curators may obtain a full release from them. Likewise, it teaches when Wards' accounts, once rendered, must be submitted again, and that a mother serving as a guardian is not to have her dowry <note>original: *dos*</note> restored before the accounts are given or exhibited, but that it must be withheld in the meantime.

In the year 1614, after the Lord's timely passing, all three children—the young Lord and the young Ladies—were left as minors alongside the aforementioned Lady Mother, now a widow <note>original: *Wittibin*</note>.

The administration of the household, entrusted and handed over with a free and honest disposition on June 21, Anno 1614, can be found literally in Exhibit B. During this administration, she, as the <term>Female Curator</term> <note>original: *Curatrix*</note>, granted and attached more than 16,000 guilders <note>original: *fl.* or *Gülden*</note> worth of assets to the first young lady, Maria Jacobe, contrary to the <term>Family Pacts</term> <note>original: *pacta familiæ*; legal agreements governing the distribution of noble or wealthy family estates</note> and against the refusal of the other gentlemen serving as co-curators. Because the more prominent post of the noted 16,000 guilders was observed among such intolerable outlays by the gentlemen co-guardians and was found to be undeniably contradictory, it was steadily opposed and excluded from the accounts until the curator, Mr. Melchior N. Mr. Melchior consented to this obligation because he had already, at that time, expertly extracted a negligent consent from his 19-year-old brother-in-law, the <term>Sole Heir</term> <note>original: *unici hæredis*</note>. This did not stop with this most prominent and excessive <term>injury</term> <note>original: *læsion*; a legal term for a loss caused by an unfair contract</note>; rather, when the mother could easily sense that her son was eager for the government <note>his own rule or administration</note>, she consented to step down and leave it to the <term>Minor</term> <note>original: *Minorenni*</note>. Additionally, according to the statement in the enclosed Settlement Exhibit C dated May 24, Anno 1621, she persuasively talked him into an unprofitable arrangement. Her son was attributed and pushed to take over not only 31,000 guilders in capital, but also an annual loss of 500 guilders from 1614 to 1618, and then from 1618 to 1621 inclusive, an annual interest of 1,550 guilders (of which the four-year loss amounted to 2,000 guilders and the three-year interest to 4,650 guilders, totaling 6,650 guilders). Thus, he was forced to take over a total of 37,650 guilders as a properly paying pension, even though she, the widow, had sat quietly in full and profitable use of the estate for the entire seven-year period, administered everything <term>at her pleasure</term> <note>original: *pro libitu*</note>, and presumably—according to the nature of the female sex—would not have forgotten her own interests.

However, this heard-of irresponsible procedure did not rest there; rather, efforts were made so that in the future, strangers might also enjoy the minor's liberality by participating. Thus, in 1623, when Lord Johann Caspar was twenty-one years old, he was skillfully guided, according to Exhibit D, to subscribe to and confirm with his seal the <term>Marriage Pacts</term> <note>original: *Heyraths-Pacta*</note> made between the Lord Governor <note>original: *Landvogt*</note> Georg N. and his mother.

Because it is not to be doubted, but rather will be clearer than the midday sun, that Lord Johann Caspar was not only greatly but <term>most enormously injured</term> <note>original: *enormiter, sed enormissimè lædirt*</note> during his minority, the first point to decide is: whether his Grace is not entitled to humbly implore His Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, for a <term>total restoration to the original state</term>? <note>original: *generalem restitutionem in integrum*; a legal remedy where the Emperor or a court voids a contract to restore a person to their previous financial position</note>

However, whether this settlement can be revoked along with other <term>youthful errors</term> <note>original: *juvenilibus erroribus*</note> remains unresolved.

Since a <term>grant of majority</term> <note>original: *venia ætatis*; a legal waiver allowing a minor to act as a legal adult</note> was granted by the <term>Imperial Chamber Court</term> <note>original: *Camera Imperiali*; one of the two highest courts in the Holy Roman Empire</note> (and not by the Emperor himself) based on a mere petition from a then nineteen-year-old, without a prior examination by a judge; the question is whether the right to petition for restitution is cut off. If that grant stands, can Lord Johann Caspar still make a claim, especially regarding obligations made concerning <term>immovable property</term> <note>Land or buildings</note>, or in what way can His Grace be helped in the absence of the "benefit of restitution"?

In conclusion, the Legal Consultant is kindly and confidently requested by Lord Johann Caspar to read through the summary narrative of the history and the four Exhibits A, B, C, and D. If, as is doubtless, useful questions occur to his high intellect, the Consultant is asked not only to raise those questions but to determine and legally argue them both <term>politically and legally</term> <note>original: *tam politicè quam juridicè*</note>, just as if they had been personally sent by His Grace's own hand.

Noble, steadfast, highly honored, and especially trusted Lord and Friend, I have maturely considered the <term>statement of facts</term> <note>original: *facti ſpeciem*</note> sent to me. I did not want to neglect sharing my humble thoughts with my beloved Lord on each proposed question via a <term>discourse</term> <note>An informal legal discussion or essay</note>, based on the report I received. Following this discourse, a formal <term>legal opinion</term> <note>original: *Conſilium*</note> of greater authority could then be requested from a local University Faculty of Law.

# Letter P.

...should be drafted. However, if such concerns were to be used not only for private information but were intended to be presented to the opposing parties, the facts would have to be stated somewhat more mildly, and several rather <note>original: *fat odiosæ Phrasis*; distasteful or offensive phrases</note> harsh expressions would need to be omitted.

To arrive at the matter itself, it should perhaps first be considered as a preliminary point whether His Excellency the Count can, without damaging his reputation, make use of the intended <term>Restoration to Original Standing</term> <note>original: *Restitution in integrum*; a legal remedy that cancels a contract and restores the parties to the position they were in before the agreement was made</note> against his own prior dealings and consent. In my simple opinion, this must always be answered in the affirmative.

*Since such a remedy is not only provided for by law but is also extremely favorable. <note>original: *l. 1. in Princ. ff. de Minorib.*; referring to the first law in the Digest concerning minors</note> And although that precept—that agreements must be kept—is suggested by Natural Law, <note>original: *l. 1. in pr. ff. d. pact.*</note> it is nevertheless equally consistent with natural equity that help be extended to minors who have been harmed against equity.* <note>original: *d. l. 1. ff. de Minor.*</note>

Likewise, those who have persuaded a <term>minor</term> <note>original: *Minorennem*; someone under the legal age of majority, usually 25 in this context</note> to their own advantage, leading him to agree to something that causes significant harm to himself and his kin, have more to fear than a minor *who implores the help provided by law against the deceptions of others.*

This is especially true because in such cases, the minor's opponents are bound in conscience not to maintain their illegally obtained profit or to leave the minor in a state of loss. And such a <term>Benefit of Restitution</term> <note>original: *Beneficium restitutionis*</note>—*especially where the minor is at a loss and the adversary is at a profit*—is not at all against the minor's reputation, considering that even powerful potentates, *and indeed those of legal age,* have not hesitated to rescind their harmful contracts in this way. *As Emanuel van Meteren reports concerning the Catholic King Philip II in his History of the Netherlands, book 5, page 285, and Rudolph Botereus in the history of his times, book 3, page 302. And the common conclusion is that a Prince can be restored to his rights to avoid a great loss.* <note>original: *Odd. d. restitut. part. 1. quæst. 4. artic. 14. Caldas in verb. Minor. num. 62.*</note>

Furthermore, a second preliminary question might be whether His Excellency the Count may immediately apply to and bring a complaint before His Roman Imperial Majesty, the Imperial Chamber Court, or another such court? For in the marriage pacts of the late Lord G. von H., of blessed memory—from which the current primary disputes must be decided and resolved—special <term>arbitration procedures</term> <note>original: *Austräg*; a specific legal process in the Holy Roman Empire for settling disputes between members of the nobility outside of ordinary courts</note> were designated among other things, and arranged as follows: should any future misunderstandings arise regarding this marriage agreement in one or more articles, or otherwise, which were not

<margin>Befoldus, Volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

clearly provided for or specified, both parties have bindingly promised and vowed to one another to choose four sensible, honorable persons from the families of both sides and entrust the matter to them for an amicable decision. In the event, however, that those chosen for the amicable decision could not agree, they should, with the consent of both families, take an umpire to themselves. Whatever these five persons then decide regarding the occurred errors and misunderstandings, with a unanimous or majority vote, *according to what is fair and good* <note>original: *ex æquo & bono*</note>, shall remain final and be accepted without refusal; nor shall either party have the power to initiate any appeal, reduction, or opposition.

It is also noted in the law *that arbitration courts* <note>original: *Austregæ*</note> (through which disputes or disagreements arising between the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire are settled and resolved among themselves) *are either special or common, or conventional and legal. And indeed, conventional or special ones are the conventional judgments of certain immediate Estates or illustrious families,* <note>original: *sonderliche gewillkührte Austräg*</note> *part 2, Ordinance of the Chamber Court, title 2, in the beginning. If such are in place, they are to be preferred over other common judges and must be strictly observed, according to the said part 2, title 2, and the argument of the law in the Digest. Denais in Chamber Law, chapter 156, number 1. And to prevent exceptions being taken regarding incompetence or nullity, one must proceed entirely before them.* <note>original: *arg. d. tit. 2. in pr.*</note>

However, I believe, primarily for two reasons, that regardless of such voluntary arbitration, this matter can nonetheless be brought *before an ordinary competent judge.* <note>original: *coram Judice Ordinario Competente*</note>

Firstly (1.), because the dispute is now not only about the previously mentioned marriage pact, but also about the administration of the estate and many other matters (as appears from the following deduction). *So that on account of the continuity of the case, the Ordinary Judge may be approached, bypassing that arbitrary judgment:* considering that the same <term>Arbitrator</term> <note>original: *Arbitrarius Judex*</note> has no power to rule *on the entire lawsuit and all parts of the present litigation.*

*And it is also established that the accumulation or concurrence of causes and actions creates an indivisible continuity of the case.* <note>original: *c. dispendio. ubi gl. & Dd. de rescript. in 6. Maranta. disput. 7. num. 30.*</note>

Similarly, no reasonable judge could easily consider that these matters—considering they are so strongly linked to one another and, as it were, flow from one another—should be <term>debated</term> <note>original: *ventilirt*</note> *before different judges, and thus partly before an arbitrator and partly before an ordinary judge. For the connection or continuity of a case [overrides] arbitration...*

...requires three judges. Petrus Friderich, regarding the continuity of a cause, chapter 1, number 13.

And it can be even less argued that His Excellency must allow all these reminders to be decided by <term>arbitrators</term> <note>original: *Arbitratores*; private individuals chosen to resolve a dispute outside of formal court</note>: because the aforementioned marriage contract speaks only of one kind of case, namely concerning disputes arising on the occasion of that nuptial pact. But <note>original: *At Compromissa stricti sunt juris*</note> arbitration agreements are subject to strict law and cannot be extended from one case to another, according to the arguments handed down by Berlichius, conclusion 4, number 2, etc. And regularly, no one is bound to enter into arbitration. <note>original: *l. furti §. qui jussu. ff. de his, qui not. infam.*; referencing the Digest of Roman law</note> where the gloss and Bartolus Lanfrancus in the treatise on arbitration, part 7, question 47, discuss this.

So (2.) in this matter, <term>Restoration to Original Standing</term> <note>original: *Restitutio in integrum*; a legal remedy allowing a minor to undo a contract that was harmful to them</note> will be principally sought. But in truth, an arbitrator chosen by agreement cannot grant restoration; for it is not his role to rescind a contract that is valid by law, and a full effect of restoration cannot follow from his sentence. <note>original: *l. fin. C. ubi & apud quem.*</note>

Indeed, an arbitrator cannot be approached as the primary authority to examine the cause for restoration and then pronounce that restoration is granted. Oddus, on restorations, part 1, question 32, article 9, number 85.

To reach the questions themselves, one must undoubtedly conclude regarding the first one that His Excellency may obtain Restoration to Original Standing. Considering that everything required by law to obtain such a benefit is contained here: for His Excellency was not only a minor at the time of these harmful actions, but also today the <term>four-year period</term> <note>original: *quadriennium*; the window of time allowed to claim restoration</note> prescribed by law for seeking restoration—which only begins to run after the completion of the twenty-fifth year—has not yet expired. <note>original: *l. ult. C. de temp. in integr. rest.*; referring to the Code of Justinian</note> Considering His Excellency was born into this world only in August, the year 1602. Likewise, the fact of <term>injury</term> <note>original: *læsione*; legal harm or financial loss</note> is in no way to be doubted, as shall afterwards be more fully shown by the grace of God.

So it is hoped that the opposing side will not be able to argue that His Excellency expressly ratified or approved these actions after reaching majority. If that had been done, the restoration would cease. <note>original: *l. 1. § 2. C. si major fuit.*</note>

However, for my part, I cannot conceive that His Excellency could obtain a "general" restoration to original standing from His Imperial Majesty; rather, I hold in my humble opinion that as many restorations must be sought as there were different business dealings in which our most illustrious Lord Count was harmed. A separate examination of the facts is required for each act, for which the opponents must not only be summoned but must also be heard regarding the matter.

<column-break/>

For although this petition is made by imploring the office of the judge—so that he may restore or grant an action out of his mere duty—nevertheless, when a petition is made in that manner, restoration is usually only granted by a magistrate after the cause has been fully examined. Oddus, part 1, on restorations, question 34, article 5. Because restoration is not granted except for a just cause, therefore an examination of the cause is necessary to determine if it is just or unjust. <note>original: *Abb. in c. ex literis. de restit. in integr.*</note> And furthermore, Restoration to Original Standing is called a Decree. Simoncellus, regarding Decrees, in the preface, number 30. But a Decree is not issued except with an examination of the cause. <note>original: *l. nec quicquam. §. ubi Decretum. ff. de offic. Procons.*</note> Therefore, restoration seems to require the same process.

And a full examination of the cause is also necessary when restoration is sought incidentally, especially when the cause of restoration falls decisively upon the entire principal business; in such a case, the cause for restoration must be examined no less fully than if it had been sought as the primary claim. <note>original: *l. 1. §. causa cognita. ff. de minor.*</note> Furthermore, even if the cause for restoration were to be examined summarily, the summoning of the opposing party is nonetheless required. <note>original: *l. in causæ. §. si causa cognita. ff. de minorib.*; and other citations</note> Oddus in the same place teaches that all those claiming interest, or who could claim interest in the case of the requested restoration, must be summoned. He adds that if such persons were uncertain, then a citation should be made through a general public proclamation.

From this it appears that in this matter, the aforementioned general restoration is difficult to obtain; rather, it must be sought specifically for each point, and the opponents must be heard on the matter. For the adversary is heard if he wishes to prove that restoration should not be granted. <note>original: *l. 1. § 2. C. si advers. creditor.*</note>

### Question Second.

Because it is to be noted from what was just stated that a citation of the opposing party is necessary to obtain restoration, one must at the same time petition His Imperial Majesty for <term>permission to act</term> <note>original: *venia agendi*; special legal leave required to sue a parent or superior</note> against his Lady Mother. For persons to whom reverence is owed—as our parents especially are—cannot be called into court without the order of a magistrate or without the permission of the Praetor. <note>original: *l. 4. §. 2. ff. de in jus vocand.*</note>

Fachinaeus teaches that this custom still endures today. <note>original: *10. controv. cap. 87.*</note> Schäffer, part 1, question 25, number 8, etc. And the Lords of the Imperial Chamber also hold this view. Hartmann, book 2, observations on the title of fiefs, chapter 45.

And although a lawsuit should be brought against the stepfather <note>original: *Vitricum*</note>—who can otherwise be called to court without special permission <note>original: *Fachinæ l. 10. contr. 88. Bruckmann. cons. 42. num. 17. tom. 1.*</note>—the claim must primarily be made against His Excellency’s mother, and against the District Governor only in his capacity as her legal guardian and husband.

Likewise, the civility and **respect due to a mother** <note>original: *Reverentia Dn. Matri debita*</note> require that before anything is brought before His Majesty in this matter, a friendly attempt at resolution should first be undertaken, either in writing or through a delegation, **or even through the mediation** <note>original: *vel etiam per interpositionem*</note> of close relatives. **For it seems fitting that the disputes of relatives be determined within the home or domestic hearth and among kin, rather than making them public in the open forum.** <note>original: *Congruens enim videtur esse, lites conjunctorum intra domum seu domesticos lares & conjunctos determinari, quàm in foro publico eas palàm facere. l. congruentius 4. C. de patr. potest.*</note> **Furthermore, the modesty of a debtor should not be rashly or suddenly pushed into judgment. It must therefore be seen as soon as possible that the entire matter is settled with the least amount of trouble. It is uncivil to drag a person immediately into court when the matter might perhaps be resolved through a friendly discussion or settlement. Reason and humanity suggest that someone should first be asked to pay a debt before a formal legal action is launched against the possessor. For if they pay, the creditor is satisfied by the same effort, and the possessor is not disturbed.** <note>original: *Hilliger. ad Donell. lib. 17. cap. 1. sub lit. b.*</note>

**And all these things will hold most strongly regarding a mother.**

Now, if this friendly discussion should prove fruitless, it will be necessary to submit a most humble declaration to the Roman Imperial Majesty. Then, in my humble opinion, the most advisable course would be to explain the circumstances of these matters in detail and most obediently request that His Imperial Majesty, **out of the fullness of his power** <note>original: *ex plenitudine potestatis*; referring to the Emperor's supreme legal authority to bypass standard procedures</note>, and not by way of the <term>Austräg</term> <note>original: *Austräg*; a traditional arbitration process for disputes between German noble estates</note> (since an appeal from the latter can be made **to the Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original: *ad Cameram*. Gail. 1. observ. 121. in princ.</note>), most graciously appoint certain distinguished **Commissioners** <note>original: *Commissarios*</note> (to handle this efficiently). These commissioners should be ordered to first hear these closely related parties as necessary and then, if possible, reconcile them in kindness. However, if this unexpectedly fails, they should either decide the case **by a sentence** <note>original: *per sententiam*</note> according to legal equity, or leave it to His Imperial Majesty’s most gracious decision, while reporting the state of the matter most obediently and in full detail.

At the same time, one could most humbly request that such an Imperial Commission be issued **in the best form and most fully** <note>original: *in optima forma, & plenissimè*</note>, especially since the **Power of Restoring** <note>original: *Potestas restituendi*; the power to grant a "Restoration to Original Standing"</note> should be specifically included within it. **For a delegate of the Prince can restore standing, according to the express text in the final law of the Code, "where and before whom."** <note>original: *Delegatus enim à Principe restituere potest per text. express. in l. fin. C. ubi & apud quem. Odd.*</note>

### Third Question.

Regarding this question, it may indeed seem strange that His Excellency's mother should be required to hand over the accounts mentioned, thereby arming or instructing His Excellency as a plaintiff against herself as a defendant.

**For anyone who desires to be restored to their original standing must first and above all prove that they have been harmed, because otherwise restoration cannot be obtained.** <note>original: *l. nam & postea. §. si minor. ff. de jurejur. l. minorib. C. de restit. in integr. Corn. cons. 50. num. 3. lib. 3*</note> **The reason is that everyone must prove that which is the foundation of their intention.** <note>original: *l. in exceptionib. ff. de probat.*</note>

**But injury is one of the two principal foundations upon which the intention of the person seeking restoration is based.** <note>original: *l. quod si minor. §. 1. ff. de minorib.*</note> **And therefore a minor, or anyone else seeking restoration to original standing, must allege and prove the cause for why they seek it. Furthermore, it is usually set as a rule that just as the plaintiff is not bound to the defendant, so conversely the defendant is not bound to produce their documents for the plaintiff.** <note>original: *l. 1. 4. 6. 7. & l. fin. C. d. edend. l. nimis grave 6. C. de testib.* and other legal citations</note>

However, all of this which has been indicated here—and which is **ordinarily** <note>original: *regulariter*</note> true—has a notable exception. The **Defendant** <note>original: *Reus*</note> must also **produce his documents** <note>original: *Documenta ediren*</note> if they are either **common** <note>original: *communia*; records that belong to both parties, such as shared estate accounts</note> to both, or if the **Plaintiff** <note>original: *Actor*</note> can otherwise **claim** a legitimate **interest** <note>original: *Interesse prætendiren*</note> in them. **Indeed, if it is in the interest of the one seeking the production of a document or letters, in that case, he can seek the production of the document either through an Edict or a subsidiary action based on the facts.** <note>original: *l. is, apud quem. C. de edend. l. 3. §. sciendum & §. interdictum. in fin. ff. de exhib. Gail. 1. obs. 106. num. 2.*</note>

And this especially applies in the present case, where one demands from the opposing lady those accounts which she is either still obligated to provide, or—if she has already done so—should have left **copies** <note>original: *Copias*</note> of at the Count's residence. For His Excellency's mother was either a legally appointed guardian or at the very least acted **as such** <note>original: *pro tali*</note> and held the entire administration in her hands.

**And that a defendant is absolutely bound to produce his accounts for the plaintiff, if such accounts were written either by order of or for the benefit of the plaintiff, and thus it is in the interest of the plaintiff that those accounts be produced, is taught with many arguments by Fulvius Pacianus, book 1, on proofs, chapter 63, from the beginning.**

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis regarding the financial dispute between a nobleman and his mother/stepfather. The previous page advised a respectful, out-of-court approach; this page details the specific legal requirements for a guardian (tutor) to provide a full accounting of an estate.</meta>

### Augmented Practical Treasury ###

Likewise, any Administrator is obliged to render accounts, according to the law <note>original: *l. 1. §. officio, ubi Dd. ff. de tutel. & ration. distrah. l. adver- num. 43.* — these are citations to the Digest of Roman Law regarding the separation of accounts in guardianship</note>. This requirement even extends to a father who does not have the usufruct <note>the legal right to use and profit from property belonging to another</note> of the assets. This applies most strongly to a Tutor <note>a guardian for a child under the age of puberty</note> or a Curator <note>a guardian for a young adult</note>. Legal experts extend this equally to a father acting as a tutor, or even to the closest male relatives or brothers who have managed a guardianship.

And although Her Excellency the Lady Mother might argue that an accounting has already taken place, much more is required for the restoration of a correct and sufficient accounting. These requirements—beyond any doubt—are not found in the current accounts. It must now be investigated whether these rules were observed or taken into account, and to this end, such account books must be produced. For if Tutors wish to be freed from the burden of guardianship, they must render an account; otherwise, the burden is not removed from them but increased.

For an account to be rendered correctly, many things are required. These are the primary requirements:

**First**, that the Book of Accounts be produced and given to the Wards <note>minors under guardianship</note>, whether they are children or adults, whose affairs were managed. This book must also contain an inventory of all the goods that were in the wards' estate at the start of the administration; at the very least, an Inventory of those same goods must be produced along with the Accounts.

For a Tutor must make an Inventory at the beginning and produce it after the guardianship has ended; otherwise, he is presumed to have acted with fraud <note>original: *in dolo*</note>, and an oath may be taken against him in court regarding the value of the matter.

Tutors must not only show the Inventory and the Accounts to their former wards who are now adults, but the actual book of accounts or all the papers—including the records of expenditures and receipts <note>original: *datorum & acceptorum*</note>—must be handed over to them. A tutor must return the Account Books to the ward. Note: where someone is bound to render accounts, he is also bound to produce the Account Books. Furthermore, he is even bound to physically deliver them.

<column-break/>

As he is bound to render an account, he is bound not only to produce the books but also to hand them over.

Now, it is not observed on this side that such an account was ever delivered to Your Excellency, because no such book of accounts appears anywhere in the Archives; and the burden of proving that this was done lies with the person making the claim.

**Second**, the remaining balances and whatever else must be paid to the wards are to be returned and settled. Rendering an account involves two things: rendering an account of all expenditures and receipts, and paying the remaining balance.

**Third**, it is necessary to show that the debtors with whom contracts were made were solvent and suitable at the time of the agreement. Otherwise, the risk falls upon the person who extended the credit.

**Fourth**, the accounts must be shown and calculated legally, so that the Master of the estate is correctly informed about all matters. This should not be done vaguely or in general terms, but through each specific type of entry, declaring: what was owed, from where it came, from what action the debt arose, for what cause, by whom, and to whom it was given or received. Because truth can only appear in specific details, not otherwise.

**Fifth**, an account must be rendered even for things *not* done which nevertheless ought to have been done.

**Sixth**, it is necessary that all legal instruments and documents be returned to the wards.

**Seventh**, that an account be made of the rents and profits <note>original: *redituum & fructuum*</note>, according to what could commonly have been collected.

**Eight**, that the accounts be rendered fully and in good faith <note>original: *bona fide*</note>.

**Ninth**, that the income <note>original: *introitus*</note> of the accounts be shown before the expenses <note>original: *exitus*</note>.

**Tenth**, that they be rendered to the judgment of a "good man" <note>an impartial, fair-minded person</note>. Furthermore, whatever has been committed through fraud or even slight fault is charged to the Administrator in the accounts, so that he must pay for it and bear the cost.

<summary>This page outlines the ten legal requirements for a guardian to provide a valid financial accounting to their ward, emphasizing that the physical account books must be surrendered and every specific transaction justified.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the obligations of guardians. It shifts from the general duty of a guardian to the specific, rigorous standards required when presenting financial accounts to a ward. It emphasizes that a guardian must act with the highest level of care, comparable to a prudent head of a household.</meta>

...curator. Regarding the mandate. For he owes as much diligence in administering the ward's affairs as he does his own, or rather, as much as a good head of the household <note>original: *bonus paterfamilias*—the Roman legal standard of a careful and prudent person</note> usually employs in his own affairs; otherwise, he is held liable by an action of guardianship <note>original: *actione tutelæ*</note>. *Law 1, in the preface, on guardianships and the separation of accounts; and the law "by tutors" on the administration of Guardianship.*

Next, it is also necessary that the one who renders the accounts demonstrates that good faith <note>honesty and sincerity of intention</note> is evident in everything he has done: so that he has neither subtracted anything from what he received, nor recorded an expense for something he did not actually pay. *The law "he who under condition," on conditions and demonstrations.*

Therefore, the entries placed in the account must be proven with authenticated documents. For a Tutor is not believed regarding expenses if they are large; however, in small matters, they are not believed unless they confirm them by oath, according to the distinction made by Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential legal scholars of the Middle Ages</note> in *Law 1, section "by office," number 1, on guardianships and the separation of accounts; see also Cornelius, consultation 320, around number 13, volume 3.* Indeed, accounts are believed insofar as they are against the tutor, but not insofar as they are in his favor. *Bartolus in the same place; Ferrari in the form for rendering a tutor's accounts, at the end, number 17.*

For this reason, to the extent that the accounts are denied, the Tutor must prove his accounts. Socinus <note>Mariano Socini (1482–1556), a famous Italian jurist</note> in *consultation 159, number 2, volume 2,* states that this is the common legal conclusion. Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a student of Bartolus and a major legal authority</note> says the same in *consultation 418, at the first part, number 6, volume 3.*

There are several other things which, depending on the variety of the case, are necessary for rendering accounts correctly and with integrity; however, legal scholars usually reduce these to four requirements. Namely: **first**, that the account books be produced and handed over; **second**, that the calculation be performed; **third**, that the remaining balance be returned; and **fourth**, that any fault be cleared by the payment of what is owed. *Baldus in the law "with the testament," number 4, Code on testamentary manumission; Socinus, consultation 149, number 3, volume 1; Cornelius, consultation 30, number 13, volume 3.*

Therefore, unless Tutors render accounts according to all these requirements, not only can an action of guardianship for the separation of accounts be brought against them—*Law 1 and the whole title on guardianship and the separation of accounts*—but an oath can be taken against them in court based on the mere presumption of fraud <note>original: *dolum solum præsumptum*—the legal assumption that the guardian acted dishonestly if they cannot account for the assets</note>. *The Gloss on Law 1, section "by office" at the word "will be held," on guardianship and the separation of accounts, through Law 1 of the Code on the oath in court; Bartolus, consultation 150, with the aforementioned number 5,* where he says that in an action of guardianship, it is a special rule that an oath may be taken in court for this reason. *Socinus, consultation 213, numbers 3 and 4, volume 2.* For a tutor is presumed to be at fault if he did not properly complete the accounts; likewise, there is a presumption against one who did not complete an Inventory. *Socinus, consultation 190, number 2, volume 2,* because an inventory and an account are treated as equal. *Law 1, section on slaves,* where Bartolus notes this regarding the separation of accounts.

Furthermore, it is established law that minors and young adults are not forced to immediately accept and approve the accounts offered by Tutors. Instead, they must be allowed to inspect and examine them deliberately over a fair period of time, and to raise exceptions or objections against the examined accounts. This is the text in the specific terms of *the law "when a slave," on conditions and demonstrations,* where the following response is given: For if he should offer

<column-break/>

the remaining balance in a bag <note>original: *folle*</note>, that is, in a purse <note>original: *crumena*</note>, he will not be immediately free of his obligation. Rather, he must render accounts in the way a slave usually does: that is, first to offer the accounts to be read, then to be calculated, so that the computations can be explored to see if they are reported honestly or dishonestly, and whether receipts are correctly recorded or not. These words also imply that the heirs or Masters should be informed by the knowledge of the accounts, so they know what was written and for what reason. And a little later, the text says: he was certainly not accustomed to simply signing off for his slave showing the remaining accounts, but did so only after reading, examining, and objecting, etc. This is pursued more extensively by Socinus, *consultation 190, "I remember," number 3, volume 2, and consultation 149, number 5, volume 1,* where he says: the rendering of accounts cannot be completed immediately in a single moment, but has a successive process. *According to the notes of Antonio de Butrio on the chapter "on the part" concerning witnesses, and Angelus, consultation 286, beginning "since," number 1,* where he says every Administrator can be compelled to show the volumes of accounts so that he may pay the balance. The volumes are shown, he says, to be seen, examined, and audited <note>original: *dispungenda*—the process of marking or crossing off items in an account to verify them</note>, to see if things were handled honestly or dishonestly, and what and how they were administered, and what and how much came into each person's hands. Otherwise, the account would not be said to be rendered in good faith. Schurff decided that the same applies to tutors: namely, that they must hand over the accounts to the wards to be examined, audited, and scrutinized. *Schurff, consultation 9, number 6, century 2, through the law "when a slave" on conditions and demonstrations,* which he says was promulgated by divine inspiration to prevent the frauds, deceit, and deceptions of tutors and curators, since the property of wards is exposed to risk from their tutors in many ways. Jason confirms the same in *consultation 219, "this matter," volume 2,* where he says: a Tutor who does not show the Book of accounts to the wards is presumed to be in fraud, suggesting he administered the affairs basely. He follows Anchoranus, who decided the same in *consultation 316, number 3.* Jason adds: therefore the volumes must be exhibited by the tutors so that the accounts may be explored, read, and calculated by the wards, and so it may be examined whether the receipts and expenditures were reported honestly or dishonestly. For this, he alleges the good text in *the law "if she who is to be free," 6, final section, on those to be set free,* regarding the words "the volumes of accounts must be rendered for the purpose of inquiring into, examining, auditing, and scrutinizing the accounts." And Jason adds there: namely, that the entire matter of accounts in guardianships depends on what is good and fair, and must be terminated with the greatest equity. For just as the contract and the action of guardianship are matters of good faith <note>original: *bonæ fidei*</note>, *Section "on actions," Institutes on actions,* so too the "un-contracting" <note>original: *distractus*—the dissolving of the legal relationship or the final settlement</note> which happens through the rendering of Accounts must be of the same quality. *Legal scholars on the law "on guardianship," Code on restoration to original condition,* which text Schurff alleges for this purpose in *consultation 17, century 1.* But it is better proven that the settlement is of the same nature as the contract it dissolves. *The law "from purchase," on pacts; Law 4, on justice and law.* Therefore, he says, the Judges who must judge in such a case of guardianship accounts should not make themselves difficult or delayed in carefully re-examining the accounts...

<summary>This page outlines the strict legal requirements for a guardian (tutor) when settling the finances of a ward. It emphasizes that accounts must be transparent, proven with documents, and subject to a thorough, unhurried review by the ward to ensure "good faith" and "equity."</summary>

Treasury of Practical Law, Enlarged

...the administration of the guardianship and the reclaiming of accounting reports, so that such cases—through which the protection of minors from loss is ensured—may proceed legally, etc.

Regarding this same point, Ferrariensis <note>Johannes Petrus de Ferrariis (c. 1350–1416), a noted legal scholar from Pavia</note> in the form for a legal complaint regarding the rendering of accounts for a guardianship, at the end of number 6, says that either the Judge himself ought to review the accounts of the guardians and perform the calculation, for they should not be simply accepted. *Law 2, "Where the ward is educated."* Or, he should provide expert and suitable arbitrators to work out the calculation of such accounts; these experts will diligently examine the account books produced to see what one party owes the other—what the guardian owes the ward, or vice-versa. For wards are not forced to simply accept accounts just as they are offered. *said Law 2, "Where the ward."* Nor are they held to believe their guardians; on the contrary, they may raise objections against their accounts. *said Law "When a slave," on conditions and demonstrations.* And in the case of a dispute, the guardians themselves must prove that good faith <note>original: *fidem*—meaning the reliability and honesty of the records</note> is established in their accounts. *Law "He who under condition," on conditions and demonstrations.*

Indeed, even if—what is more—the minors or young adults had approved the accounts of the guardians and had issued a receipt <term>quittatio <gloss>a formal discharge from debt or obligation</gloss></term>, nevertheless, if they later discovered some error or that they had been deceived after exploring the matter more thoroughly, they could always seek to have the accounts reviewed and examined, and to oppose and object to them. This remains true even if the receipt and release had been sworn under oath, because such a release is made because the adults believe themselves to have been satisfied and that they have received their rightful shares from the guardians. Therefore, when the opposite is found, the error should not harm them in avoiding losses; or, if there is doubt based on probable reasons, the accounts must be examined anew. *Castrensis, counsel 377, to the first, number 2, part 2; extensively Ancharano, counsel 330, "Having seen"; Jason, counsel 219, numbers 1 and 2, volume 2; most extensively Socinus, counsel 159, number 11 and following, volume 2.* This is supported by *Law "To the Eunuch," section "Accounting,"* where the gloss and Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a titan of medieval Roman law</note> on the excuse of guardians provide another reason: that it is one thing to render an account, and another to confess that it has been rendered. *Law "By constant," with the gloss, Code, "Who is powerful in pledge."* Because an account not sufficiently rendered can always be requested to be rendered again: as is the common conclusion of Baldus, Salycetus, and others in *Law "One," Code, on mathematical errors; Jason in section "Certain things," number 83, Institutes on actions;* and Schurff follows and examines this most extensively in the same terms in *counsel 9, numbers 8 and 9, century 2.* Therefore, a release made by a minor does not harm him. *Parisius, counsel 99, number 21, volume 1;* nor does it take away the right to restitution, even if the release was repeated. *Parisius, counsel 89, number 66, volume 1.*

This matter is so clear, open, and reasonable that no further discussion seems necessary. For what kind of rendering of accounts would it be, or how could they be held as authentic and legal, or by what reasoning would the ward's property be protected, unless this power of inspecting accounts, examining them, and raising objections was freely permitted to the minors or young adults whose guardianship was managed? And this must be allowed with a competent amount of time, and with the assistance of experts and honest men. Thus, let us conclude that in law, an account is not considered rendered which

<column-break/>

is not fully rendered, such that its credibility is established from every side. *Law "He who under condition," on conditions and demonstrations, section "Law if it is so written," on manumission in a will.* And it must be done so that from every specified detail, the truth of everything can appear. *Socinus, counsel 190, "I remember," number 1, volume 2; Schurff, counsel 9, "Having seen," numbers 3 and 4, century 2.* For that which is not understood in every part cannot be seen as approved. *Law "If a mother," on an undutiful will; Dynus in chapter "What is ratified," number 4, on the rules of law in the 6th book; gloss and Philippus Francus in chapter "The contested," at the word "he shall have known," on appeals, book 6; the text in the Clementines, "The cause," where the gloss at the words "full and certain knowledge," on elections; law "In the whole" 76, on the Rules of Law; law "For which," section "Julianus," Digest, on having a matter ratified; Romanus, counsel 343, "From the proposal," near the end, with many citations gathered by Tiraquellus in "Laws of Marriage," gloss 6, number 180, and on the right of withdrawal, section 36, gloss 2, number 30.* And an account not sufficiently rendered must be rendered again. *Johannes Andreae following Archidiaconus and Geminianus in chapter 1, on sick Clergy, book 6; Imola and Cardinal Zabarella in the Clementines 2, section "Those," on religious houses.* Nay, even if an account had been rendered and approved, it could still be retracted and a full review and calculation requested for up to 30 years due to a mathematical error, or ignorance of some omission or commission. *Bartolus number 1, Baldus number 1, Castrensis number 2, Jason numbers 3 and 6, Faber number 4, in the Single Law, Code, on mathematical errors; the gloss, Bartolus, and others in the Law "Likeness," Code, on the right of the treasury; Jason in section "Certain things," number 83, Institutes on Actions; Philippus Francus in the single chapter, final section, number 2, on sick Clergy, book 2; extensively Socinus, counsel 159, number 12, book 2, and counsel 73, around number 3, volume 1; and the text is in Law "To Aurelius" 20, section "Caius," where Bartolus comments, and in Law "Lucius," on legacies of freedom.*

Furthermore, that a general release cannot stand on its own unless the accounts have been properly rendered is confirmed by many: *Paulus de Castro, counsel 309; Ancharano, counsel 330; Bartolus; Socinus, counsel 159 and counsel 190; and most extensively Rolandus a Valle, counsel 49, volume 1.* In these places, having brought forward many arguments for this opinion, they conclude that if a guardian was released just as if he had rendered the accounts, nevertheless, if it appears afterward that they were either not rendered at all or rendered insufficiently, a release of this kind does not prevent the calculation from being repeated.

Likewise, regarding the release from the rendering of accounts, it is worth noting that even if a guardian was released after the account was rendered, he is nevertheless bound to produce the account books even after the release; so is the text in the *final law, section "Among other things," Digest, on legacies of freedom,* as noted by Bartolus there, followed by Socinus, *counsel 159*, and Hartmann Pistor, *observation 158, at the end.*

<meta>This page continues a legal discussion concerning family law and financial obligations. # Letter P.

...interest does not have to be paid during widowhood: for it is a matter of settled Law <note>original Latin: *certi namque Juris est*</note> that once a marriage is dissolved, the dowry returns to the woman or her heirs. *Single Law, section "Without doubt," Code on the action for a wife's property.* Likewise, the gift made on account of marriage <term>donatio propter nuptias <gloss>a gift from the groom to the bride, often matching her dowry in value</gloss></term> returns to the husband or his heirs, unless a pact regarding the profit from the dowry or the marriage gift is proven to have been made, or if the local Statute or custom dictates otherwise. *Final chapter, on donations between husband and wife. Hartmann Pistor, Book 1, legal questions, question 14, number 34, and Johann Schneidewin in said section "There is also another," number 6, Institutes on donations. Ernest Cothmann, Response 50, numbers 13, 44, and 47. Sichard agrees in the law "If for the children," 18, at the beginning, Code on donations before marriage.*

However, in this place, there is a Statute or Custom <term>Consuetudo <gloss>unwritten law established by long-term usage</gloss></term> which dictates that the marriage gifts or counter-dowry <term>Widerlag <gloss>a specific German legal term for the husband's contribution to the marriage fund, intended to support the wife if she outlived him</gloss></term> remain with the surviving spouse, especially after the state of widowhood changes.

And although the marriage contracts <term>Heyraths-Pacten <gloss>formal pre-nuptial agreements</gloss></term> of the late Lord G. von H. (of blessed and noble memory) specify in the section regarding death that in the case of there being no children, if the aforementioned Lord (by God's grace) should pay the debt of human nature <note>a flowery euphemism for dying</note> before his lady wife, then the ten thousand guilder dowry, as well as the use of the ten thousand guilder counter-dowry, belongs to the lady for her use and benefit during her lifetime; but after her death, such use of the counter-dowry shall be completely terminated and dead, so that the same shall revert and fall to the heirs of Lord G.

Yet it is correct in itself that this agreement <note>original Latin: *convention*</note> speaks only of that specific case where no heirs exist.

On the other hand, in the ninth section—"If it were to happen," etc.—it is ordained for the case where children *do* exist <note>original Latin: *in casu existentium liberorum*</note> that in such an event the Common Law <term>Jus Commune <gloss>the Roman-based legal system used across the Holy Roman Empire</gloss></term> is to be observed. And even though the context might seem to imply that the Common Law is only to be observed regarding the succession among the children, it is nonetheless provided by Law that a case omitted in contracts must be treated as omitted <note>original Latin: *casus omissus in contractibus debeat haberi pro omisso*</note>. *Alexander, Counsel 46, number 4, and Counsel 194, number 2, book 2; and Counsel 29, number 3, book 6. Socinus the Elder, Counsel 47, at the beginning of book 1, and Counsel 64, book 3; and the law "If stipulated," section "Chrysogonus" on verbal obligations. For it does not pertain to us to add or subtract anything from the words of agreements.* *Curtius the Elder, Counsel 52, number 4. And in pacts, a different case is not included, even if it has a greater reasoning,* *law "If the wines," Digest on the risk and benefit of a sold thing; which Anchoranus brings forward as the best text for this purpose in Counsel 141, number 4; and he felt the same in Counsel 245, number 3, at the end, and number 4.*

This is especially true when something was omitted entirely and does not follow from something else expressed in words. *Ruinus, Counsel 74, number 11, book 1. Baldus in law 1, last column, Code on those who open tablets.*

<column-break/>

...with others cited by Gabriel, Counsel 156, number 18, book 1.

Likewise, a case omitted in the dispositions of a last will that contains specific reasoning is left to the disposition of the Common Law. *Law "Most convenient," on children and posthumous heirs, where Jason [Maynus], Fichard, Counsel 89, number 4. Coler, Counsel 33, number 104, and Counsel 47, number 54. Pruckmann, Counsel 17, number 64. And this holds place even if the same or a greater reasoning were present.* *Hondedei, Counsel 1, number 9, Counsel 6, number 23, volume 1.*

Thus, in the present case, one cannot infer from the case where no children exist to the case where children were born, because in these two cases a different reasoning <note>original Latin: *diversa ratio*</note> is found in many ways. For in the case where no children exist, it was well-provided and ordered that the counter-dowry and respective dowry should remain with the surviving spouse for their lifetime: because spouses usually do and should love one another more than collateral heirs <note>relatives like siblings or cousins who are not direct descendants</note>.

But it is a far different matter in the current case, where there are legitimate children, whom parents tend to love more than themselves; they also prefer that their goods pass immediately to the children rather than remaining with the survivor—especially if the survivor enters a second marriage <note>original Latin: *ad secunda vota convolanti*</note>—to the significant disadvantage of the children.

Beyond this, and because this interpretation is entirely consistent with the general written Imperial Laws, and one thereby adheres more closely to the disposition of the Law, one should rightfully stick to it. For the words of agreements ought to be understood according to the Common Law. *Law "I ask," section "between the lessor," Digest on letting and hiring.* For the Common Law informs agreements and interprets them. And general words are to be understood just as the Common Law disposes; and if an agreement is ambiguous, it is reduced to the understanding of the Common Law. For he who contracts is presumed to have a mind that agrees with the Law's disposition. So also the words of the contracting parties are understood to be confirmed with the Common Law. And a contract is understood to be celebrated according to the understanding of the Law. And similarly, a pact receives its interpretation from the Common Law. And thus, in silent and ambiguous agreements, 그 interpretation is to be more accepted which agrees with the Common Law. For contracts receive a fitting interpretation from the Common Law so that they may be brought into harmony with it. And nothing is more common in the Law than to interpret the ambiguous wills of contracting parties according to the disposition of the Laws, as Cardinal Franciscus Mantica strengthens all these points with laws and authorities in *On Silent and Ambiguous Agreements*, book 3, title 7, at the beginning, where he brings forward even more points in that sense.

<summary>This page analyzes a legal dispute over a widow's right to a "counter-dowry" (Widerlag) based on a marriage contract. It argues that if a contract is silent on what happens when there are surviving children, the Common Law must take precedence, which typically favors the inheritance rights of children over the lifetime use of the surviving parent.</summary>

### Further Added Practical Treasury

And to the contrary, it should not lead to error that in the previously cited section regarding cases of death, these words are found: (the ten thousand guilders of dowry <term>Heyrathgut <gloss>the property a bride brings to her marriage</gloss></term>, likewise the use of the ten thousand guilders of counter-dowry <term>Widerlegung <gloss>a sum pledged by the husband to match the dowry, intended for the wife's support if she survived him</gloss></term>, which you granted to the Lady to use and enjoy for her lifetime) and that from this supposedly indefinite phrasing <note>original Latin: *ex hac putativâ indefinita locutione*</note> it might be concluded that in every case <note>original Latin: *in omnem casum*</note> the aforementioned noble lady should have the use of this counter-dowry.

However, said words must be accepted according to the subject matter <note>original Latin: *secundùm ſubjectam materiam*</note> and precisely concerning the case that is being decided there, and must in no way be extended beyond that: according to the laws already cited above. For even universal words ought to be restricted to that in respect of which they were pronounced <note>original Latin: *Nam verba etiam univerſalia reſtringi debent ad id, cujus reſpectu ſunt pronunciata*</note>, according to the laws introduced by Cravetta in his response for the son-in-law, numbers 189, 356, and 465. And general words do not contain cases unlike those expressed. Mantica, *On Tacit and Ambiguous Agreements*, book 27, letter b, number 5.

Furthermore, in that section, nothing else is dealt with or ordered except for the case where no children exist <note>original Latin: *de caſu non exiſtentium liberorum*</note>: That then, that is, in the named case <note>original Latin: *in caſu nominato*</note> (Law "the last," Digest on testamentary guardians; Pacianus, counsel 63, number 61 and following; Arumæus, book 2, decision 2, number 33) the ten thousand guilders of dowry should follow and belong to the surviving spouse, likewise the use of the ten thousand guilders of counter-dowry; and lest anyone should doubt whether then the usufruct <term>Uſusfructus <gloss>the legal right to use and derive profit from property belonging to another</gloss></term> should remain only for the days of widowhood <note>original Latin: *ad dies Viduitatis*</note>, it is added: which the Lady is entitled to use for her lifetime. For in the past, a usufruct left by a husband to a woman was lost by contracting a second marriage <note>original Latin: *Nam & olim Uſusfructus à Marito mulieri relictus, amittebatur contrahendo nuptias ſecundas*</note>, single law, Code, "If a woman to whom her husband left a usufruct marries a second time."

And if, at the time such a marriage agreement was drawn up, it had been the opinion that in every case the use of the counter-dowry should remain with the widowed spouse for the days of her life, one would not have simply stated that the use of the ten thousand guilders of counter-dowry belongs to the lady for the days of her life, but would have added a universal note for all cases, "at all times," or something similar. Because otherwise, an indefinite phrasing is restricted to the matter and the case for which the provision was conceived.

For an indefinite pronouncement does not, by its own meaning, equal a universal one, except out of human kindness; nor is it equated to a universal one when the same reasoning (as in this our case, through the things said above) does not underlie it. Tuschus, letter I, conclusion 86, number 26 and following.

Likewise, this is not contradicted by what was settled and ordered in the section "as long as also for the sixth" of the often-cited marriage contract: that for the lady widow, during the time of her undisturbed state of widowhood—whether children were produced from this marriage

<column-break/>

or not—for her maintenance, in terms of a permanent residence, wood, wine, grain, fish, and lard, seven hundred guilders should be properly and orderly delivered annually to the place of her domestic residence, along with other interest <term>Verzinſung <gloss>periodic payments made on a capital sum</gloss></term>, in good, current, non-devalued heavy Imperial coinage, to be taken and given at that same place. For through such words, "along with other interest," one is not to understand the use of the ten thousand guilders, but rather those funds which came into the hands of the husband from the wife's brought-in assets and patrimony, and which otherwise by law or by agreement must be paid with interest until repayment. Indeed, the word "interest," by its own nature and the property of the word, cannot be applied to the use of the counter-dowry. Considering that such a counter-dowry, as it belongs to the husband and his heirs regarding its ownership <note>original Latin: *quoad proprietatem marito ejusque hæredibus*</note>, can never be paid as interest to the widow, either by law or by agreement. For it is one thing to receive interest from a capital sum, and another to have the use of a sum of money.

For words are to be understood properly, unless the nature of the contract is changed thereby contrary to Common Law, or one of the contracting parties suffers a maximum loss, or a contradiction or some other absurdity arises therefrom, according to the common laws.

And this interpretation is finally also powerfully strengthened because in the section "it then happens that," whenever the lady spouse passes away before her husband without leaving legitimate bodily heirs, it is expressly ordered that the brought-in dowry should be left in the hands of the husband as the surviving spouse <note>original Latin: *ſuperſtiti Marito*</note> for his lifetime. However, in that same place, there is not a single clause, conjecture, or the slightest word to be found by which one could in any way presume that this dowry should not pass to the bodily heirs of the deceased lady spouse even in the case where children exist <note>original Latin: *in caſu exiſtentium Liberorum*</note>. For when a marriage is dissolved, the dowry returns to the wife's heirs, unless otherwise expressly disposed <note>original Latin: *Namque ſoluto matrimonio, dos revertitur ad uxoris hæredes, niſi aliud expreſſè diſponatur*</note>. Law 1, Digest on the dissolution of marriage.

And pacts regarding profit, or the dowry not being restored immediately upon the dissolution of the marriage, are of a stricter interpretation, whereby the dowry upon the dissolution of marriage belongs only to the children. Castrensis in Law 2, at the beginning, number 7, Digest on the dissolution of marriage.

And likewise, so great is the relationship between the dowry and the gift on account of marriage <note>original Latin: *propter nuptias Donationem*</note> that they walk with equal pace, and what is disposed concerning one is also considered agreed upon in the other. Authentic "Equality," Code on agreed pacts, section "There is also another," Institutes on donations, and in both places the Doctors of Law, especially Schneidewin.

It further distinguishes between regular maintenance interest and the specific legal rights over dowries and marriage gifts.</summary>
