### Questions Five & Six.

**R**egarding these questions, I can find nothing else than that the Lady Widow, during her administration and widowhood, as well as afterwards, must be properly pensioned. Her dowry <term>Heyrathgut <gloss>the property a bride brings into a marriage</gloss></term> and other assets brought in from the time of the death of her Illustrious and Most Noble Husband <note>original: "à tempore mortis illustris & Generosissimi Dn. Mariti"</note> must be returned to her, insofar as it can be proven that they came into his hands and were not repaid to her, but remained with the noble estate and lordships. This, in my opinion, is correct in itself and consistent with common written laws; furthermore, nothing to the contrary is stipulated in the marriage contracts.

**T**hus, I also cannot see why the Lady Widow should be given anything for her widow’s support <term>Widum <gloss>property or income set aside for a widow's lifetime use</gloss></term> or widow's sustenance <note>original: "Victalitio viduitatis"</note> as long as she had the administration and full maintenance. For otherwise the same thing would be paid twice <note>original: "Nam aliàs idem bis solveretur"</note>. Nor can a woman have a double dower <note>original: "Nec mulier duplex doarium habere potest"</note>, according to the teachings of Paulus Christinaeus, volume 1, decision 73, because two profitable causes would here converge upon one and the same dower, which ought not to happen.

**T**herefore, it was not at all necessary to designate an extraordinary annual enjoyment of five hundred guilders for this Lady Widow. Consequently, whatever was negotiated in the settlement and agreement <note>labeled "B." and "C."</note> may easily be overturned, either because it is void in and of itself, or through the remedy of restoration to original condition <term>Restitutione in integrum <gloss>a legal mechanism to cancel a contract and return parties to their original state</gloss></term>.

**L**ikewise, the Lady Widow, in her capacity as a guardian <term>Vormunderin <gloss>female guardian</gloss></term>, cannot claim this interest-income as compensation for her conduct of the guardianship and administration. For it is an undisputed point of Law that a Guardian or Conservator <note>original: "Tutor vel Curator"</note> cannot seek a salary, according to the Law regarding Guardians, 33, final paragraph. Guardians and Conservators must provide free, complete, and faithful service and effort, abstaining from all profit <note>original: "Quoniam Tutor vel Curator gratuitam, integram & omni lucro abstinentem fidem & operam præstare debet"</note>. This holds true even if the guardian was called away and hindered from his own private business for the sake of the ward.

### Question Seven.

**R**egarding this doubt, it is presupposed that the aforementioned endowment <note>original: "Dotatio"</note> occurred contrary to the family agreements, and was otherwise immoderate. This is to be learned from the

<column-break/>

said Family Pacts, especially since it is to be estimated by the judgment of a reasonable man <note>original: "ex arbitratu boni viri"</note>.

**A**nd although it is said that even if a brother is a minor, the Guardians can still be compelled to establish a suitable dowry for the sister, that text is to be understood as referring to an "abundant" dowry, as Gothofred says.

**N**evertheless, this is to be understood such that, in the meantime, the Dowry <note>original: "Dos"</note> ought to be competent and fitting to the dignity of her birth, the resources of the father or grandfather providing the dowry, and the status of the husband whom it is appropriate for her to marry. Account must also be taken of the number of the father's children and the custom of other women married in that family and region.

**I**f, on the other hand, action is taken against a Minor or his Conservators, the minor can seek restoration to his original condition <note>original: "Restitutionem in integrum"</note>.

**E**ven if His Excellency, being of minor age <note>original: "in Minorenni ætate"</note>, approved this donation, the remedy of restoration may still serve against such an approval. This is because it involves an enormous loss <term>læsionem enormem <gloss>a legal concept where a contract is so unfair that the value given is less than half the value received</gloss></term> and a taking not approved by Law. It also necessarily results in an unquestionable alienation <note>the transfer of ownership</note> of immovable property or annual rents, which are equated to immovable property.

**F**rom all of which it follows that His Excellency can either prevent his Lady Mother's dealings in this manner and seek the damages from his sister, or else he can hold his Lady Mother accountable as his guardian.

**I**ndeed, if a minor has been harmed by the business of a Guardian or Conservator, then the choice is given to him: whether he wishes to pursue a Restoration <note>to cancel the deal</note> or a personal action against the Guardian and Conservator themselves to recover damages from them. No prejudice is created against him by this choice. This has a manifest equity, as it would be uncivil to complain that a Minor does not rescind that which the Conservator himself performed.

This applies even more so in the case of personal assets <term>paraphernalia <gloss>property owned by a married woman that is not part of her dowry</gloss></term>.

Regarding what the Lady Widow might bring forward in this place concerning the dowry and personal assets, and what she might prove was handed over to her late, noble husband: this should be settled upon her as a pension (for it has a different nature than the 700 guilders of dower money <term>Widumsgelds <gloss>property or funds set aside for a widow's use after her husband's death</gloss></term> mentioned above). Gratianus testifies to this as common practice in decision 179, number 2, adding that it was so decided. Petrus Molignatus, in his treatise on retention, question 41, and Caspar Baëz, concerning the tenth part of guardianship, chapter 4, number 44, hold the same.

Furthermore, a set-off <note>original: "compensatio"</note> could be opposed against the mother suing for the dowry, following the doctrine of Baldus, counsel 99, number 3, at the word "testament," book 2; Castrensis, counsel 270, in the second doubt, book 1; and Tuschus, letter C, counsel 499, number 14.

This is all the more applicable here because the accounting did not proceed in an orderly fashion and according to the requirements already deduced above, to the extent that it must be rendered again <note>original: "adeò quod iterum debeat reddi"</note>, according to Rolandus, counsel 6, number 61, book 1; Menochius, case 208, number 37 and following; and Montanus, on guardianship, chapter 38, number 133. And thus, Your Excellency's demand can be considered a clear debt <note>original: "pro debito liquido"</note>.

And although the aforementioned opinion—concerning the retention of the dowry available to the ward against the Mother who administered the guardianship—is called into doubt by some, it applies most strongly in the case of a woman marrying a second time, or if it can be proven immediately that the woman is a debtor from the guardianship. Caspar Antonius Thesaurus, in *Forensic Questions*, book 2, question 28, writes at the end: but when the debt is not clear, the dowry is paid upon providing security, or the woman is put into possession by right of pledge and mortgage, with a prohibition on obtaining ownership or selling the property, until the Account is rendered.

This goes so far that even if the minor seems to manage his property poorly, he cannot implore the aid of restitution to his original state <note>original: "in integrum restitutionis"</note>; see Law 1 of the title "On those who have obtained a grant of majority." ### ADDITION.

Today, by the Political Constitution in the Imperial Diet of Augsburg in the year 1548, enacted by Emperor Charles V, a rule contrary to the Civil Law has been established: That the guardian <term>Vormund <gloss>a legal protector for a minor</gloss></term> shall give a proper account annually at the request of the authorities, and shall provide answer and explanation for his administration. The same is established in Saxon Law, as noted by Schneidewin on the title "On Atilian Tutors," number 3. In the Nuremberg Reformation, title 39, Law 7, it is required that accounts be rendered at the legitimate time; among various doubts, we think this is more in

<column-break/>

accordance with that Political Ordinance than with Civil Law: namely, in the case where accounts must be rendered before the guardianship or curatorship is finished. Exactly at what time this should happen is not expressed here, but is left to the judge or to that most honorable Guardianship Council. Otherwise, a year is understood to be the term (Berlichius, Conclusion 40, number 7, part 2).

An account book ought to contain: 1. expenditures and receipts <note>original: "data & accepta"</note>. 2. It should contain them fully and in good faith. 3. The placement of the time and day must be present. 4. The account book should contain things that are plausible and not contradictory. Before the accounts have been calculated, subtracted, and examined, no fraud in administration can be alleged, nor can a penalty take place (Escobar, On Accounting, chapter 42, number 19; Dr. Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings*, page 618).

### 26. Duty, Duty of the Oath. (Munus. Jusjurandum.)

It is doubted what sense those commands have which are frequently enjoined upon subjects by magistrates who have promised obedience by an oath, specifically with these words: "under penalty of the oath taken" <term>bey Eidspflicht <gloss>a German legal phrase binding an action to one's sworn duty</gloss></term>. It is well established that the meaning of this clause is that the thing is commanded under the penalty of perjury; as if someone had said: "I command this to you under the oath you swore to me, so that if you do not do it, you are a perjurer" (Stetler, On Oaths, book 1, chapter 16, last number, folio 111). And thus the sense of this phrase is "under penalty of the oath taken," that is, under the penalty which ought to be imposed on one who has violated an oath. Hence, that genitive "of the oath taken" does not stand intransitively, as they say—that is, "under the penalty which *is* the oath taken"—as Covarruvias notes in his repetition on the chapter "Although," paragraph 7, part 1, at the end. In that place he writes: all commands of a Rector of any University, such as that students should attend some assembly, are not to be taken so strictly, even if they are made "under penalty of the oath taken." It is not as if the commander himself wished to bind those so called to the crime of perjury if they did not do what was commanded of them. For it is to be presumed, considering the pious intention of the one commanding, that in these common assemblies (which especially are not of great weight), he only wished to recall the oath to their memory, lest the subjects omit to obey his precepts out of contempt; but not so that perjury would be committed by them. This is especially to be observed, so that one is not everywhere rashly condemned as guilty of perjury, even if he failed to do what a Superior commanded. This is also provided for in the Statutes of the University of Tübingen.

### ADDITION.

### 27. Compulsory Portion. <term>Legitima <gloss>the portion of an estate that a testator cannot legally withhold from their natural heirs, such as children or parents</gloss></term>

Concerning the Compulsory Portion and matters relating to the same subject, see the individual treatises by Marc Antonio Cucchi, Antonio Rubio, Claude de Battandier, Claude Chiflet, and Marc Mantua. Speidel contains various and many questions regarding the compulsory portion in his *Collection, parts 1 and 2, under the word "Legitima."*

On the origin and cause of the Compulsory Portion, see Antonio Guibert Costan, *book 1, chapter 15.*

->ADDITION.<-

The statutes of our homeland call the Compulsory Portion **a necessary inheritance** <note>original: "ein Notherbschafft"</note>, *law 29, law 3, paragraph "when a father"* <note>original: "wañ ein Vatter"</note>. According to the Nuremberg Reformation, just as grandchildren alone succeed not by branch <term>in stirpes <gloss>where a family group shares one portion</gloss></term> but by head <term>in capita <gloss>where each individual receives an equal share</gloss></term> when there is no will, so too, by equal reasoning, do they succeed in the compulsory portion due to them. The compulsory portion is substituted in place of alimony. *Novella 18, chapter 3; Barbosa, book 10, chapter 8, axiom 6.* The compulsory portion is called **the due natural share** or **duty-part** <note>original: "das gebührende natürliche Antheil oder Pflichttheil"</note>. For a compulsory part—that is, the part which the Law, following the requirements of nature itself, has confirmed and defined in *Novella 18, chapter 1*—must necessarily be preserved from the assets, not only for children who are not ungrateful to their parents, but also for parents from their children, and sometimes for brothers when parents do not survive. *Novella 1, preface and section 2.* Indeed, this must be granted under the honorable title of an inheritance. *Novella 115, chapter 3.* See Locam at the *final section of the Institutes "on inofficious testaments"* <note>a legal claim that a will is "contrary to duty" because it unfairly excludes heirs</note>; *Bachov on Treutler, volume 1, dispute 13, thesis 12, letter A; Rittershusius, part 6, on the Novellae, chapter 3, number 36; Carpzov, part 3, Constitution 9, decision 2.* Furthermore, this portion must be cleared of every burden, so that no legal disposition introducing a delay or any weight—for example, a trust <term>fideicommissum <gloss>an obligation to pass property to another</gloss></term>, see *Gail, book 2, observation 119*, or a life interest <term>ususfructus <gloss>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</gloss></term>, *Novella 18, chapter 3*—can have a place in this part of the assets. *Code, law 32 "on inofficious testaments," law 36, section 1.* Rittershusius explains the reasoning in *the cited part 6, chapter 4, number 27; Treutler, volume 1, dispute 13, thesis 12, section 6; Gail, book 2, observation 119.* Espich, in his *Specimen of Testamentary Examination, part 1, article 5, numbers 7 and 9*, treats extensively the burdens which the Compulsory Portion rejects.

The Compulsory Portion is considered from the time of the testator's death, namely, whatever his resources were worth at that time. *Code, law "when it is asked" regarding inofficious testaments.* And its valuation is made after deducting debt and funeral expenses. *Law of Papinian, section "a fourth," and the following authentication in the same title.* Philippus Cornæus, *counsel 202, column 6, volume 2;* Philippus Decius, *counsel 89 at the end, and counsel 231*, where it is most copiously declared. The compulsory portion of children, whether for one or many, **in the land of Franconia, according to ancient custom, is two-thirds of all goods.** Wehner, *Franconian Customs, 105, in the preface.* A fief that is purely and absolutely hereditary tastes of the nature of an allodium <note>land owned independently, without feudal obligations</note>. Klock, *volume 2, counsel 33, numbers 41 and 42*; it is calculated among the goods of the deceased when dealing with assigning the compulsory portion or its supple-

<column-break/>

ment. *Ibid, numbers 54, 55, and 56.* Fiefs are not counted toward the compulsory portion. *Cited counsel 33, number 53.* **Male-line fiefs are not counted in the Compulsory Portion.** The doctors of law distinguish between a new fief and a paternal fief. Alexander, *Counsel 8, volume 3*, where Charles Molinæus is cited. Those things which a husband gains from the assets of a predeceased wife according to Statute are to be deducted as debt before the account of the compulsory portion is held. Hartmann Pistor, *observation 12, number 18;* Wels, *counsel 87, number 11.* Whether a Statute stating that a father is bound to pay the Compulsory Portion for the crime of his son is valid? Vivius, *opinion 771;* Giovanni Ludovico, *Perugian decisions, 11, numbers 25 and following.* The compulsory portion of sons is removed by the Statute of Worms, *observation 12, title 39, and observation 10;* Vivius, *opinion 813.* See Antoine Fabre, *Errors, 3, Decision 15;* Cavallos, *question 115;* Juan del Castillo, *part 3, chapter 5, number 35.* The Compulsory Portion of children can only be diminished by Custom or Statute, but cannot be entirely removed. Grævanus, *Conclusion 122, book 2;* see Hartmann Pistor, *observation 131;* Giovanni Ludovico, *Perugian decisions, 21, number 50 and following;* Schrader on *the Institutes, section "but natural things";* Gratianus, *volume 1, discussion chapter 178, and volume 2, chapter 300.* A Statute that swallows up the entire compulsory portion of sons is not valid. Diaz, *rule 143.* Whether the Compulsory Portion can be drawn from Royal fiefs? Klock, *counsel 7, number 496.*

### 28. Plough Service. <term>Operæ ruricales <gloss>rural labor services owed by a tenant to a lord</gloss></term>

Regarding rural labor services, **Plough service** <note>original: "Pflugdienst"</note> (which those are bound to provide who can nourish ploughing horses or oxen from their fields, and who are therefore called **Teamsters, Horsemen, Field-servants** <note>original: "Ausspanner, Pferdner, Ackerknecht"</note>, etc.), these generally pertain to bringing grain, wood, wine, and whatever else comes to the Lords into the Manorial houses; manuring the fields, sowing, ploughing, smoothing with a rake, and carrying hay and other crops into the Lord's barn; **carrying the sheaves to the hunts**; and providing wagons and carts for any transport of butchery items. Ritter on Homage, *chapter 7, number 149.* **Two half-peasants usually hitch up together and stand as one [full peasant].** But these things are judged by custom and ought to be tempered with the honey of Christian charity. Opposed to these services, as a distinct species, is **Hand or Hook service** <note>original: "Hand-oder Happendienst"</note>: which labor **the day-laborers, who have no horses,** are forced to perform.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the Services which are performed with horses and pack animals, and that those who provide them are called **Hitchers, Horse-keepers, or Yard-holders** <note>original: "Anspanner, Pferdner, Huffner"</note>; whether and to what extent they are bound to provide services or labor for constructing the buildings of the Lords. Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 6, chapter 4, number 15.* The word *Urvum* signifies the curvature of a plough, and *urvare* means to plough or to define with a plough. The ancients used appropriate oxen, a bull and a cow, in the Etruscan rite for founding cities. A plough was used not only in founding a city, but also in overturning one. Whence **Carthage is said to have suffered the plough.** *Law 21, Digest, "By what means a life interest is lost."*

### 29. Prebend. Annual income for life. <term>Pfründ <gloss>an income or pension, often purchased to provide for one's old age</gloss></term>

In many places it is common practice for the public treasury to receive a certain sum of money from a private individual and grant them either sustenance or a pension (sometimes higher than common interest rates) for the duration of their life, commonly called a **Prebend-purchase** <note>original: "Pfründkauff"</note>. Lather *on Census, book 3, chapter 23, final number.*

->ADDITION.<-

**Soldier-fiefs** <term>Feuda Soldatæ <gloss>stipends or annual payments granted to knights or nobles under feudal law, rather than land</gloss></term> are granted to nobles reduced to poverty as an annual provision under a feudal title. Draco *on Patricians, page 327.*

### 30. Pound. <term>Libra <gloss>a unit of weight or currency</gloss></term>

Lord Speidel in his *Notables*.

A **Shipping-pound** <term>Schickpfund <gloss>a large commercial unit of weight used in maritime trade</gloss></term> holds 280 pounds, or *Liefpfunds*. 1 *Liefpfund* <note>original: "Liefpfund," likely a Livonian pound</note> is 14 pounds.

### 31. Philosophy.

The Holy Apostle Paul in Colossians chapter 2, while attempting to make the faithful more cautious in matters of faith, used this warning: "See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit of men." It is as if philosophy does not sit well with the integrity and simplicity of the Christian faith. And it is a common saying that in the earlier centuries of the Church, philosophy had a bad reputation among Christians. Tertullian, in his book *On Prescription against Heretics*, is entirely devoted to attacking philosophy, from which he teaches that heresies are both equipped and originate; for this reason, he calls philosophers the "Patriarchs of Heretics" in his work against Hermogenes. Likewise Saint Irenaeus, *book 1, chapter 19*; Saint Chrysostom, *homily 7 on 1 Corinthians and homily 65 on John*; Gregory Nazianzen, *oration 1 against Julian*; Saint Cyprian, in the book *On the Benefit of Patience* from the beginning. See especially Baronius in the *Annals*.

But since the name of "Philosophy" extends very widely, so that it is certain to embrace within its scope all disciplines and arts called "liberal," none of the Holy Fathers said the Apostle wished to condemn all these sciences. Therefore, Filesacus teaches what Paul understood in *Selected Works, book 1, final chapter*, where he demonstrates with reasons which parts of philosophy are condemned and which are approved, and how they can be of use to Christian philosophy; likewise, that philosophy is necessary and useful to a Christian. See also Baronius in his *Annals for the year 411, number 13.*

->ADDITION.<-

Marcus Antoninus [Aurelius], nicknamed "the Philosopher" because of his studies in philosophy, although he was Emperor and an old man, was not ashamed to go to the school of Sextus the Philosopher with a book for the sake of listening. And when a certain Lucius reproached him for this, he replied: "It is a beautiful thing even for an old man to learn; and I shall not cease to visit Sextus as long as there is something to be learned from him."

The word "Most Philosophical" <note>original: "Philosophissimus"</note> is found in the final law of the Code *on repudiation*. Protagoras attributed to rhetoricians "running eloquence" <note>original: "εὐγλωττίας τρεχέσας," meaning a quick-tongued fluency</note>, that is, a charm running through the uncertain periods of the tongue like lattice-work; but to philosophers "subtle cares" <note>original: "μερίμnas λεπτάς"</note>, that is, refined concerns, thoughts, and meditations—which Aristophanes and Lucian nevertheless mocked. The Spirit of heavenly Wisdom is the Mistress; human Philosophy ought to be her handmaid and follower. Not only is human Wisdom a handmaid to the Divine, but even the arts, such as Grammar, Geometry, Music, etc., serve human Philosophy itself as a mistress. There are those who, enticed by the charms of the handmaids, think little of the mistress, Philosophy; some have agreed with this in poems, others in...

*Xenocrates* once said wisely to a certain learned man aspiring to Philosophy: "Go away, for you do not have the handles <note>original: "ansas"; a metaphor for the necessary mental prerequisites</note> of Philosophy." *Mr. G. *Antigonus*, King of the Macedonians, prudently exposed the simulated philosophy of *Zeno*. For when he had frequently heard him declare that grief and sickness of mind do not fall upon a Philosopher, as he is a despiser of riches, the King wished to test the constancy of this saying. He instigated someone to falsely announce to *Zeno* that his fields had been plundered by enemies, his wife and children carried off, and other mockeries of fortune had occurred. Observing the philosopher mournful with a dejected face at these things, he laughed at and despised the simulated philosopher.

### 32. **Platz.** Decree.

<term>Placitum <gloss>a decree, assembly, or judicial decision</gloss></term> among the French was once understood in various ways. In one way, for an assembly of the Peers of the Kingdom or Empire, both special and general: where indeed the common affairs of the Province or Cities were treated; derived surely from the German word **Platz**, *that is*, a place designated for an assembly. *Knichen, on territorial law, chapter 4, number 48; see Mager, on armed advocacy, chapter 3, number 274 and following.*

Secondly, *Placitum* was taken for a forum and judgment. Thirdly, it is sometimes used for the decree itself. Fourthly and finally, the word *Placitum* is read as being used sometimes for the litigation itself, or a controversy and judicial lawsuit. *See generally Mr. Mager in the cited place, number 279, and many following.*

### 33. **Poeten.** Poets.

Regarding Poets in general, *see the Adversaria of Caspar Barth in the Index; and specifically regarding the Germans, the Preface of Taubmann to Virgil’s Culex and in the Praise of the Ass, folio 402.* Regarding French Poetry, *The Researches of France*; regarding the Tuscan [Italian], *Torquato Tasso in his prose, part 4, from the beginning.*
<meta>catchword: Tuscan</meta>

<column-break/>

*Guazzo* provides a comparison of Tuscan and Latin poetry in *Civil Conversation, Dialogue 7.* Are Poets made by a "divine fury"? *Bifciola, in Leisure Hours, book 10, chapter 6.* Poets are rarely wealthy, for poverty is their hereditary evil; *see Giovanni Battista Lauro, Epistle folio 28; and Boccalini in Parnassus*, for which reason their seed bloomed beautifully for them, but brought no fruit; instead, the radishes **became fools.** <note>This is a play on a German proverb suggesting that their efforts resulted in nothing substantial or that they were mocked.</note> Regarding <term>Poets Laureate <gloss>poets officially crowned with laurel wreaths as a mark of high honor</gloss></term> who do not even know how to compose a verse, *Bebel in his Opuscula*. *Lotichius* has an apology for the Poet in his notes on *Petronius Arbiter’s Satyricon, book 2, chapter 8*, where he relates that the origin of Poesy is most ancient, invented by the Hebrews, cultivated by the Pagans, and always held sacred by both; and that Poets are born, not made, and therefore are not insane. He likewise teaches that the subject of Poesy is most noble, its types are five, and that Poetic Philosophy is most ancient. Also, that Poets alone are truly wise, and they exist as the correctors of morals and common life. They have also been for the most part the Teachers of Kings and Emperors, by whom they were even raised to the highest dignities. Indeed, Prophets, Emperors, Kings, Pontiffs, Cardinals, Princes, etc., have not refused the name of Poet. And other similar points. The same *Lotichius* also taxes pseudo-poets and poetasters; see him where he argues for and against, indicating the virtues and vices of Poets. Against obscene poets there exists a *Dissertation by Nigronius of the Society of Jesus.* The Emperor Philip made not just one of the poets, but all of them—not only the bad, but also the good, not only the mediocre, but also the most excellent—be stripped of every honor and, as if a chasm had suddenly opened, made them rush to the underworld rather than descend; on which account the voices of indignant and lamenting Poets are recorded, which may be seen in *Arumaeus, on the Assemblies of the Empire, chapter 6, number 69 and following*, in the question: do Poets enjoy immunity from the duty of receiving guests? <note>This refers to the "right of lodging," where subjects were forced to house officials or soldiers.</note> where he has also collected many arguments for and against Poets.

More on this in *Drexel, The Gold Mine, page 197.* Six hundred gold pieces were given to Jacopo Sannazaro for just a few verses. *Ibid, page 256.* Phrynicus, an Athenian poet, was fined a thousand drachmas for putting on a tragedy <note>original: "Tragœdiam exhibens"; this refers to his play "The Capture of Miletus," which so upset the Athenians that they fined him for reminding them of their misfortunes.</note>. *Klock, On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 119, no. 2.* For why poets are excluded from immunities, see *Mr. Tabor, On Relocation, page 205.* Mr. Daniel Schwenzter was promoted in the year 1629 as a Poet of three languages: Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syriac. Trajano Boccalini (cited by Christopher Forstner in his *Notes on book 2 of the Annals of Tacitus, page 205*) argues that kings should honor poets with nothing, or at most something very small; if they have food and clothes, they have enough. For abundance and idleness ruin their genius—just as fat hens do not lay, and hawks, if they are not hungry, cannot be brought to the hunt: they are to be fed, not fattened. *Mundius, On the Counts Palatine, chapter 3, no. 287.* One should use poetry like a confection, or a dessert and a pastime. > Expect verses for verses from me, O poets;
> My mind is set on returning songs, not buying them.

To which someone replied:

> If fortune had given you verses for your verses,
> You would not have so great a crown upon your head.

Both the Spartans and Alexander the Great spared the houses of Pindar. For when they were laying waste to the Boeotians and Thebans with fire and plunder, they stayed away from the houses of Pindar alone,

Martial wittily mocks a certain poet, Ligurinus, who was too much, reading his poems to one standing, sitting, running, or doing I-don't-know-what else:

Thus you might call a poet who chatters at the wrong time both foolish and dangerous. *Mr. G. Richter, Oration 11, page 6.* Poetry is forbidden to Bishops, according to *Sprenger in Fragments of Public Law, page 238.*

### 34. Poland. Polonia.

In Poland, the King does not shine with the authority of an absolute Prince, but regarding war, peace, treaties, and matters of State, he finally decides only after consulting the Nobles of the whole Kingdom. Therefore, if an Ambassador makes many of these nobles friends to his own Prince, it may be hoped that the Crown of this Kingdom—which is generally granted to foreigners, and not by hereditary right or right of succession—might more easily be taken by the Ambassador’s master or his friend (should there be an Interregnum or a new King to be elected). For the Polish nobles do not want a King established from among the inhabitants and their equals, who would be weaker in himself and might perhaps introduce a tyranny, fueled by the ambition of his relatives, that is all too well known to the neighbors.

The Chancellor stands above others in dignity after the King; he attends to the requests of Ambassadors, and is appointed alternately, now from the Knights, now from the learned. Whenever he is from the Knights, he is usually away from the Court on military expeditions. There are two Estates of the Kingdom: the Senators and the Knights, who meet together at the Diet <note>term: "Comitia" (The Sejm or Diet)</note>. The former are more dignified in rank, but not in authority; the Senatorial Order, being chosen by the King, easily approves whatever the King approves. The deputies of the Nobles, however, put forth a freer vote and suffrage; for them, the Gift and Liberty of the Fatherland is the supreme Law and Hope. *Marselaer, In his "The Ambassador," book 1, chapter 30, folio 132.* Regarding the State of the Kingdom of Poland, add myself and those authors whom I praise in the *Treatise on the Mixed State of the Republic, folio 226 and following.* Especially also the *Polish Statutes*. Likewise, the *Brief Description of the Estates of Poland*. Poland was once under the Empire; see *Arumaeus, On the Diets, chapter 4, number 68.* On whether women reign in Poland, see the notes to *Daniel Otto, Public Law, folio 8.* On the Polish nobility and its nature, see the *French Treatise on the election of the Duke of Anjou, at the end.*

### 35. Politicians.

I have discussed who a true politician is, and the many abuses of this word, in my *Prolegomena to Politics, folio 48 and following*. See also Piccart in his *Commentary on Aristotle’s Politics, folio 5, etc.*; Jacques Auguste de Thou in *History of Gaul, book 52*; Bulenger’s *History, folio 64*; likewise Caselius, and the Reverend Father Drexel <note>Jeremias Drexel, a popular Jesuit devotional writer</note> in *Phaethon, part 1, chapter 15*. On the "Polytropes" <note>shifty or versatile people</note>, see Laelius Bisciola, *Subsecutive Hours, book 3, chapter 16; who discusses the same in volume 2, book 15, chapter 3*. He deduces who the "Politicians" and "Civilians" are. On the confusion of Rhetoric with Politics, see Talentoni, *On Recondite Matters, book 2, chapter 22*.

One should also note what Caspar Ens says in the second part of his *Morosophia, folio 274*. Regarding prudence, he says it consists in the moderation or governance of cities and empires, as well as of individual families—that is, in the well-ordered disposition of both public and private affairs: so that those things which are useful are procured, and those which are harmful are avoided. People of this sort are commonly called Politicians, who are

<column-break/>

wise to a fault, while they think that those truly wise men—who are intent on the knowledge of God and the contemplation of divine matters—should be excluded from the administration of empires or Republics. As if, indeed, the same man could not be both prudent and wise! But they are as far wrong as the heaven is from the earth. For although I am not ignorant that empires (as the leader of politicians, Cosimo de' Medici, used to say) are not governed by "Our Fathers" <note>original: "Paternosteris"; referring to the Lord's Prayer or rosary beads, suggesting that piety alone isn't enough for statecraft</note> or by some superstitious wisdom, yet I believe that counsel can be sought more safely from no one than from one skilled in Divine wisdom. But great prudence is needed here, lest we fall in with those sorts of men who are led not by the knowledge of the True and the Good, but by their own opinions conceived against all reason. Indeed, it is a wonder how often Politicians—that is, men wise in the ways of the world—err in their counsels: they are most foolish where they think themselves most wise. Hence it happens that they commit many uncorrectable sins, and having set aside God and Religion, they go to ruin themselves and lead others to it as well.

***

Things have now reached such a point that he is considered a "Politician" who can hide both his own and others' vices, wink at matters of religion, and flatter others (especially superiors) in all things, having no other end in view than to acquire both riches and honors, and thus live quietly and delicately. But those who despise these things are regarded as fools. O miserable men! Those pious ones are burning torches; you are mere smoke. The godly and simple are despised by the world, but they are made great by God. The world only cherishes and adores what appears rich, powerful, and beautiful; but God considers the internal things. What is vile and despised to the world is approved by God and exalted above the clouds. Which of these worldly men does not count among the fools those who do not hesitate to endure and suffer anything for the sake of the truth? What did that Political Governor <note>Porcius Festus, the Roman procurator</note> say to the Blessed Apostle Paul? *You are out of your mind, Paul; your great learning is driving you mad.* To which Paul replied: *I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking words of truth and soberness.* Festus, because he did not understand the mysteries Paul was teaching, considered Paul a fool, just as the world considers everything that does not savor of the worldly to be foolishness. Truly, Divine wisdom, whose foundation is the regeneration of the Spirit and firm trust in God, is nothing other than sheer folly to the world. But he is truly Wise for whom the world is vile because of God, and he knows much who has found the way to the final escape. In my judgment, only these are wise; the others, however wise they may seem to themselves, are not only foolish but insane. *The sum of Christian Wisdom consists in contempt for oneself.* If anyone should know all sciences perfectly, he knows little if he remains ignorant of himself. Fixed on external things, he does not know himself; it is as if he is a stranger in his own home.

It contrasts spiritual wisdom with worldly statecraft and provides a critical bibliography of political theory, including the controversial works of Machiavelli.</meta>

Ppppp
<meta>Catchword: Poli-</meta>

Blessed is he who strives to be wise in the manner prescribed by God, scorning the wisdom of the flesh. One *drop of Divine wisdom is better than an ocean of worldly wisdom.* The world measures happiness by riches and honors, according to the saying: *They called the people blessed who possess these things.* But Christ our Savior places that same happiness in poverty—not of a temporal kind, to be sure, but a spiritual one—saying: *Blessed are the Poor in Spirit.*

I also wish to add the remarks of the Reverend Father Conzed <note>Likely referring to the Jesuit author Balthasar Cordier, who wrote on the history of the Kings of Abyssinia/Ethiopia</note> in the dedicatory preface to his history of the Abyssinian King. Most people believe that those who have mastered the controversial and sublime secrets of Philosophy, Jurisprudence, and Theology through their intellect are immediately fit to manage the Republic, give counsel, handle business, undertake embassies, win over minds, and perform the duties of war and peace. They are deceived, and they deceive others. In the subtleties of Philosophy, many things are taught that are necessary for theologians, lawyers, and physicians; though these things may be useful to a Politician from a distance, they are not sufficient. Experience has also taught that even the most profound theologians are often unequal to the task of governing Churches. For it is one thing to be occupied in the contemplation of Divine things with an intellect raised to the heavens; it is quite another to rule man—a morose, changeable, crafty, secretive, and stubborn animal. Nor is the skill of Law alone equal to such a great task; the ends of lawsuits and controversies are deep, but different are the ends of common humanity, public laws, treaties, and human society. Therefore, the queen of sciences, Politics, which commands the others, is contained within its own unique precepts and institutions. Long ago, Socrates and Xenophon condemned the madness of those who, without study, deep thought, or teachers, consider themselves "Politicians" by some natural stroke of luck.

Furthermore, there are two types of men who are considered "Politicians" by the common folk. The first are not truly Politicians, though they are believed to be so by the most foolish: these are the men who adapt themselves like a new Vertumnus <note>A Roman god of seasons and change, here implying a "chameleon-like" person</note> to places, times, and people through affected gestures, style of dress, the bowing of legs, refined words, and calculated flattery. The grave legal scholar calls them "meddlers" <note>original: "Ardeliones"</note> and "fawning parasites" <note>original: "Gnathones," referring to a stock character from Roman comedy</note>. By their very actions, they betray their boastfulness and levity of mind; they admire themselves and believe they have earned the favor of others and are wonderfully "Political." The judgment of the Prudent is different; they do not doubt that such men are struck by the staff of madness. That delight in ceremonies and overly affected refinement is loathed not only by Princes but even by private citizens; through such silliness, one loses the grace and favor one seeks and instead breeds contempt. And no wonder: even the theaters feel nausea when comic parasites repeat their ridiculous antics. I shall never cease to praise and encourage civility of manners; but I judge it the mark of an imprudent man to place "civil Prudence" in that mere craftsmanship of movement and speech.

Others enter into Politics more perniciously, usurping that name to the ruin of the Republic. They roam far and wide, leading the citizens of the Church and the Kingdom into deception; they claim that Civil Doctrine
<margin>Besold, Volume 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

is a most hidden art. They claim the Republic and the Prince are preserved by a most secret "energy," much like the mysteries of Ceres and Mithras; just as Troy was supposedly safe because of the statue of Minerva, Rome by its sacred shields, and Egypt by the body of Alexander. When we investigate those mysteries, we find that just as those ancient nations were led by illusions, these "Pseudo-politicians" turn toward the unspeakable: they teach deception instead of virtue, and even teach vices themselves. There was never an age so fortunate as to lack such men, but in the memory of our grandfathers, Nicolaus Machiavellus <note>Niccolò Machiavelli</note> brought fame to this abominable sect.

## ADDITION.

See above: Machiavelli. A defense of Machiavelli—arguing that he was not a bad Politician—is provided by Mr. Rupert in his commentary on Valerius Maximus, *book 1, chapter 2, discussion 1, sections 1 and 2*, following the work of Alberico Gentili. Johannes Frischmann is called a "most political man" <note>original Greek: "politikōtatos"</note> whose heart tastes of wisdom by Rupert in the *Epistolary Mercury, page 580*. A Politician is "political" by way of living together and social order, which consists in Command and Obedience—that is, in the distinction of offices or dignities. See G. C. Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors, page 125*. "Political Soldiers" disagree in their judgment on sacred matters: Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 87, number 24*. For a judgment on Robert Bellarmine’s three books on the *Duty of a Christian Prince*, as well as Justus Lipsius’s *Six Books of Politics* and his two books of *Admonitions*, and also Johannes à Chockier’s *Six Books of Political Aphorisms*, see Drexel’s *Gold Mine, page 363 of my copy*. Our own Christoph Besold published two books on Politics in quarto at Frankfurt in 1620; the first deals with the Nature and Constitution of the Republic, the second with the Governing of the Republic in all its parts. Obertus Giphanius, a most famous Philosopher and Jurist, published *Commentaries on Aristotle’s Politics* in octavo at Frankfurt in 1608. Philipp Scherbius, a Professor at Altdorf, published *Discourses on Aristotle’s Political Books regarding the Republic* in octavo at Frankfurt in 1610. Regarding the most lucid commentaries of Michael Piccart on Aristotle’s *Politics*, as well as Lipsius’s *Politics* with the very useful index by Freinsheim, see Rupert in the *Epistolary Mercury, page 267*, from whose mouth flows a voice sweeter than nectar itself. Does Politics belong to Jurists or Philosophers? See Giphanius in *Politics, page 4, at the end*; Conrad Rittershusius in the *Preface to the Institutes, folio 14*; Antonius Montecatinus in the preface to his *Commentary on Aristotle’s Politics*; and Mr. Dr. Cobius in his *Manuscript Principles of Law, page 7*. The knowledge of Politics and Ethics in relation to Jurisprudence is discussed *ibid., page 15*, as well as the difference between them. *Ibid., page 6*, Public Law pertains to Politics.

The Machiavellian *Reason of State* <note>original German: "Ratio Status"</note> is nothing new, but is a work that has endured since the beginning of the world, as Reinkingk demonstrates in his *Biblical Politics*.

How many books of Aristotle's *Politics* are missing? Giphanius in his *Politics*, pages 9 and 10. <note>Hubert Giphanius (1534–1604) was a legal scholar and philosopher.</note> Lipsius, in Book 4 of his *Politics*, chapter 13, seems to defend pseudo-politicians <note>original: "Pseudopoliticos videtur defendere"</note>. He asks: "Is it lawful for a little fraud to be lightly mixed in?" <note>original: "Fasne est... ut leviter admisceatur aliquid fraudum?"</note> I think so; whatever those certain followers of Zeno <note>The Stoics, known for their rigid moral purity</note> may deny me, who approve only of that one direct path to praise through virtue. He adds: "Wine does not cease to be wine if it is lightly tempered with water; nor does prudence cease to be prudence if there is a tiny drop of fraud in it." He defines this as "shrewd counsel deviating from virtue and the laws for the good of the King and the kingdom." But let those politicians see to it that, while they defend the earth, they do not lose heaven. On the elegance of use, Simonides says in Plutarch's book *On whether an Old Man should engage in Public Affairs*: "The city teaches the man," <note>original: "Civitas docet virum"</note> as if the Senate and the forum are his school. Plutarch also says in that place: "Just as a man will not be a good ship's pilot who has never been to sea himself or in a storm, no matter how many rules he knows about steering a ship, so also there is no Politics without practical use." See more in *Giphanius on Politics, pages 6 and 7.*

Jean Bodin published a praise of the political discipline in the preface to his books *On the Republic*. <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher whose work established the modern concept of sovereignty.</note> "The utilities of this science," he says, "are so many and so great that all the empires of all people and their assemblies seem to stand by the help of this one right of association; and of all disciplines, this alone seems worthy of Princes, worthy of famous men, and worthy of Kings." *Nicephorus Gregoras, History of Byzantium, Book 8, Chapter 19:* <note>A 14th-century Byzantine historian.</note> "The idle handling of disciplines provided by books, whether it be slight or abundant, is like an organic body lacking a soul, which must be added through the experience of the senses; or it may be compared to various kinds of food piled into the stomach which require heat for digestion." Indeed, that heat is nothing other than frequent use and the experience of various things. The Duke of Alba <note>Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, a prominent 16th-century Spanish general and statesman.</note> used to call the knowledge we learn from books "cistern water," but that which we acquire through experience, "living water and water from the spring itself." While it is possible to find great spirits and refined minds under any kind of clothing, Kings nevertheless do not usually accept those who have come out of great Schools to use their services, even if they are learned and sometimes wise. Action strengthens the brain; contemplation weakens it. Formerly, Jurisprudence <term>Jurisprudence: the theory or philosophy of law</term> was almost a political faculty, as witnessed by *Cicero in Book 3 of On the Orator.* For legal experts were consulted not only about rain-drippings <note>A technical legal term regarding property rights and drainage</note> and wills, but about every business of the Republic. Many today claim this same thing for themselves—perhaps not arrogantly, if they would get to know not only the law books (in which mostly private matters are dealt with) but also political and historical works. The Lord Chancellor Reinkingk <note>Dietrich Reinkingk (1590–1664), a German constitutional lawyer.</note> has written a *Biblical Politics* through axioms.

### 36. Pollet. Bolleta.

*Boleta* <note>original: "Boleta, literæ securi passus vel transitus"</note>: letters of safe-conduct or passage. *Boletarius*: he who writes the letters of passage, the Master of the *Boletas*.
To the Italians, a *Bolla* is a seal or "bull," and to seal is *bollar*, as mentioned above under the word *Bull*. From this is said *boleta*, a sealed letter.

<column-break/>

### 37. Portugaleser.

The old Emanuel Portugalesers <note>High-value Portuguese gold coins named after King Manuel I</note> with the double cross contain 23 carats and 11 grains of fine gold. Approximately six and three-quarter pieces go to the Mark <note>A unit of weight for precious metals</note>, and each piece is currently worth twenty-one—but not "hard"—Thalers, which is ten Ducats. *Alemannus in palæst. consult. 8. quæst. princ. 1. partit. 22.*
Some coinage has its name from a place <note>original: "à loco"</note>, such as the *Portugaleser* in Portugal, *Engelotten* <note>Angel coins</note> in England, *Joachimsthaler* <note>The origin of the word 'dollar'</note> from the Joachim Valley, and *Turonenses* or *Turnes* from the city of Tours in France. *Auer on the Law of Coinage, chapter 13, number 71.*

### 38. Post, Postmeister. Posta, Magister Postarum.

Posts <note>original: "Postæ"</note> are public horses stationed along public roads, and those who oversee them are called Masters of the Posts, or commonly *Postmeisters*. These men provide not only the greatest utility to those making a journey or sending letters anywhere, but they also bring in no small tax revenue to the Treasury <note>original: "Fisco"</note>. These are discussed at length in *Limn. Addit. vol. 2. at l. 3. c. 9. p. 53.* Beyond all these uses, they also contribute greatly to the security of the Republic. For nothing can be more to the advantage of a Principality than if the Prince has well investigated whatever is being done in any corner of it. *Joachim Cluten in Syllog. rer. quotid. concl. 22. lit. b. at the end.* For this reason, they are also numbered among the Regalia <term>Regalia: the rights and privileges belonging exclusively to a sovereign</term>.
Hence, when in the year 1579 a certain Duke of Germany had arranged general posts into Belgium and Italy, this very act was severely forbidden by the Emperor in defense of his Majesty's rights. *Arnold Clapmarius on the Secrets of Republics, book 1, chapter 21, near the end.* And the office of Postmaster was confirmed by the Emperor in the years 1596 and 1597, while the remaining private and city couriers—the *Mezgerpost* <note>The "butcher's post," an informal mail system run by butchers who traveled to buy livestock</note> and *Nebenposten* <note>Side-posts or unofficial mail routes</note>—were abolished by a general Imperial decree. *Cluten, in the place cited, letter C. See also Matth. Stephanus on Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 1, number 110 and following; Sixtinus on Regalia, book 2, chapter 13, number 42.* To this also belongs the prohibition of new newspapers, so as to hinder traitors and secret correspondences.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding rural posts, city posts, side-posts, and butchers' posts. *Hornigk, book 2, on the Law of Posts, chapter 29, theory 1, page 297 and following.* In which part of Europe and territory the duty and exercise of the public post flourishes better is discussed at length by *Limn. vol. 2, Additions to book 2, chapter 9, Public Law, page 54 and following.* Whether the Post Office can be revoked at the whim of the Emperor? *Klock. vol. 1. counsels.*

### 39. Postulated Bishop. *Episcopus postulatus.*

There sometimes exist, says Cucchus in *Institutes of Canon Law, book 1, title 9, from the beginning*, men whose excellent skills would be of great use to the Church—such as their learning in letters, their great experience in affairs, and the integrity of their lives and conduct. However, something is lacking in them that acts as a hindrance to their being placed in charge of churches. Therefore, lest the Church lack suitable men for this reason, it has been established that a College, for the sake of public utility, may petition the Prelates to grant them these men as their superiors. This procedure in our law is called **Postulation**. For the Prelates, when approached for this reason and moved by the distinguished character and learning of those who are petitioned for, will admit the *postulation* if it seems right to them. After this (to avoid delay and expense to the churches), the **Postulated** individual will not require another election or confirmation, but will obtain every Right, just as if he had been elected and confirmed. But see *Cucchus in the cited place throughout*, where he teaches to whom the Postulation should be made, what kind of person the Postulated should be, and other relevant matters.

Hence, in a Bishopric where the Catholic religion has been changed, bishops who are either married or have some other similar quality that makes them ineligible for election are usually called **Postulated Bishops** or **Administrators**.

->ADDITION.<-

What a Postulation is: Otto in *Public Law, page 626.* It differs from Election and Nomination. *ibid.* It is carried out by those to whom the Election belongs. *ibid.* The Bishops called "Postulated" are those of the Augsburg Confession <note>Lutheran bishops</note>, who in the Imperial Diets have their seat on an intermediate and transverse bench between the Ecclesiastical and Secular estates; the Chancellor sits beside them, performing the direction in the name of the Archbishop of Mainz. *Sprenger in his Delineation of the Estates of the Empire, pages 345 and 346.*

### 40. Precedence. *Præcedentia.*

Regarding precedence and the prerogative of seating, see my *Individual Discourses; Riccius in Episcopal Practice, folio 617, etc.* On the order of the Kings of the Christian world, *Meillet on Tacitus, book 1, chapter 1, folio 8.* On precedence between Cardinals and the Princes of France, *Bulenger, History, folio 17.* On the controversy between the Venetians and the Genoese, and how it is a cause of great disturbances, *Intercano, book 4, folio 115b*, who also discusses the great power of the Genoese on *folio 87*, which failed primarily because of the Venetian wars, etc. Whether a son may sometimes precede his father? *History of Navarre, folio 554.* In the year 1476. *French Mercury, volume 15, folio 618.*

There were two Counts of the Empire, brothers by blood, born of Catholic parents; one of them defected from the Catholic faith and took a professed Nun as a wife, and fathered a son by her. Upon his death, who ought to be the heir and successor, especially in immovable property <note>real estate</note>—the son or the brother? Since a marriage of this kind is void by law, the response is easy in favor of the brother, as is proven in the *Settlement of the Peace*, last edition, question 46.

Is it right that Priests read certain Epistles and Gospels on Sundays? Zeiller, century 4, question 70, page 364. Priest. Borch, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, number 11. To be sure, there are also celibate men who are "tossed in the heat" <note>original Greek: "άπολοι ἐν καύματι," a reference to those struggling with the fire of passion</note>. Especially among those who are bound by a vow of celibacy, such that they do not indeed enter into marriage, but having abjured a "wife," they keep a "mother of the family" <note>a sarcastic legal reference to clergy keeping housekeepers who functioned as common-law wives</note>, not a Venus. *They give horns, and take them at the same time* <note>a Latin proverb usually referring to being cuckolded or making a fool of someone</note>. Lord Doctor Dorfch in *Vindication of Interventions*, page 42. On the marital status of Priests in the early Church, see Lord Beern in *The Thorough Refutation of the E.*, page 670. Parishioners labor more effectively to have suitable Pastors than those who are outside the Parish, Klock, volume 1, consultation 51, number 49; they have a right of retention in vacant sacred goods, ibid, number 50.

## 45. Primary Petitions. Bread-Letters.

Speculator testifies in book 4, part 3, *On Prebends and Dignities*, § "it remains," number 7, that he saw the sealed Privilege for Primary Petitions <note>original: "Primariarum Precum," the Emperor's right to nominate candidates for church vacancies</note> in the Churches of Germany. By that very fact, however, the power of conferring is not given to the Emperor, but the faculty of making one person be received, says Johannes Andreae in the additions there, letter H. See Boër, decision 32, number 1. Bursat, counsel 126, number 39 and following. Gail, 2, observation 155, number 7.

Whether Primary Petitions have a place today in Reformed Bishoprics, see the Counsel of Schvvanmann annexed to the *Chamber Observations*.

The granting of Primary Petitions, with a nomination following, removes the faculty from the usual collator <note>the person normally responsible for filling the vacancy</note> and renders the prebend "affected" <note>legally reserved</note>, see Stephan Gratiani, volume 3, *Forensic Disputations*, chapter 478, where he relates still other things concerning Primary Petitions.

The indulgence of Primary Petitions, with the Scholia of Jean à Chokier, see in the *Canonical Trismegistus* by Wolfgang Sigismund à Vorburg, folio 504, and Buxtorff on the *Golden Bull*, thesis 65. Freher on P. de Andlo, folio 179. Me, *On the Majesty of the Church*, folio 121. And Augsburg also had the Right of Primary Petitions, which appears from the diploma related at the end of my treatise *On Magistrates and Censors*.

A statute was made in a Collegiate Church to suppress Canons; for example: *There are 12 Canons in a foundation; it is decreed that they wish to let the number die down to 7.* It is asked whether he who has obtained the Primary Petitions must wait until 5 die off and only then have the seventh place? This is denied, because a statute of this kind is of the strictest law, and S.

# Practical Treasury Augmented

His Imperial Majesty <note>original Latin: "Cæsar. Majest."</note> can in no way be prejudiced in this matter, especially because, for such Unions, Conjunctions, and suppressions of benefices <note>A "benefice" is a church office that provides an income</note> to be valid, a formal inquiry into the cause is required. This must be done not only through a public citation—that is, so that all interested parties are summoned—but also based on legitimate reasons founded in law, namely for the evident utility of the Church. Otherwise, so many suppressions of benefices would result in grave prejudice to the Holy Pope, the Emperor, and the Church.

Certainly, if every Petitioner <note>original Latin: "Præsista," one who presents a claim or petition</note> had to wait until either the time of suppression ended or the number of prebendaries was reduced to a restricted limit, any Church or College could protect itself with such a suppression in fraud of Imperial Law <note>original Latin: "fraudem Juris Cæsarei"</note>. They would surely and favorably allege such a suppression if it had been made with the consent of the Holy Pope and the Emperor himself.

<term>Primary Petitions</term> <note>original Latin: "Primariæ Preces"; the special right of the Holy Roman Emperor to nominate a candidate to the first vacancy in a cathedral or collegiate church following his coronation.</note>, however, are nothing other than the right of designating, nominating, or presenting a suitable person for the first benefice to become vacant, belonging to His Sacred Imperial Majesty by the indulgence of the Holy Pope, as noted by Azor and by Gail (book 2, observation 155, number 7). Thus, in a word, it is the <term>right of presentation</term> <note>original Latin: "jus præsentandi"</note>.

Therefore, there is a place for this Right when a benefice is truly vacant and the person presented or designated is not admitted to take possession of it. It is otherwise, however, when a benefice is merely prevented from becoming vacant, which happens through retention by the supreme Prince or by suppression. For when suppressed benefices—before they become vacant—are already annexed and incorporated into either the Building Fund <note>original Latin: "Fabricæ"</note> or the daily distributions, they do not become vacant upon the death of those who held them at the time of suppression. Instead, they are prevented from becoming vacant by this preceding suppression and annexation. The reason for this distinction is that a Patron does not have the right of presentation, in terms of its effect, until the benefice has called for it, as argued by Covarruvias in *Practical Questions* (volume 2, chapter 38, number 12).

And the Sacred Congregation of Cardinals declared (Session 24, chapter 15 and Session 23, chapter 18) that in such a case, Canonries and benefices, before they become vacant, can be united and suppressed, notwithstanding any nominations, reservations, or attachments.

Unions of reserved benefices are valid if they were made before the vacancy occurs; if they were found to be made after the vacancy, they would be null. Furthermore, Primary Petitions are only general or uncertain regarding the first benefice to become vacant, without any restriction or determination to this or 그 (that) one; otherwise, they would be entirely subject to nullity, as they would create a "hope of future succession" and induce a "desire for another's death" <note>This was a legal principle intended to prevent people from profiting or wishing for the death of current office holders</note>, as per Gail (observation 155, number 6).

<column-break/>

Therefore, the right is not abolished by the suppression of some benefices or Canonries, as long as some remain that could become vacant, and thus such Imperial Petitions can be fulfilled in them. For whenever something is predicated of one out of many indeterminately and without relation to this or that specific one, such a predicate always remains true as long as even one of those many remains.

The following words are to be found in the Holy Papal Bull, by virtue of which the <term>Primary Petitions</term> are granted to His Roman Imperial Majesty:
*“Provided, however, that as soon as a person is nominated and has been provided with some benefice, his nomination, as made regarding other nominators or collators, shall expire by the law itself.”*

But I wish to add here the following deduction, regarding the question proposed above.

Most Reverend <term>Elector</term> <note>original German: "Churfürst," one of the high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire who elected the Emperor.</note>, most gracious Lord, let my most humble service be offered to Your Electoral Grace, together with earnest congratulations on the high position and honor you have obtained through singular Divine Providence. I have no doubt that Almighty God will let all this serve for the preservation and propagation of His Holy Church and for the excellent benefit of the entire Roman Empire, as well as especially for Your Electoral Grace’s lands and subjects; indeed, I will never cease to plead for this outcome incessantly with my priestly prayer.

Furthermore, may it please Your Electoral Grace to be graciously informed from the acts found in the Electoral Chancery that the currently reigning Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, by virtue of the undisputed and well-known <term>Right of Primary Petitions</term> <note>original Latin: "Juris Primariarum Precum"</note>—which has been newly confirmed again by His Holiness the Pope—has, out of singular Imperial grace, not only most graciously named and proposed my humble self to the worthy Provost and Chapter of the <term>Collegiate Church of St. Ursicinus</term>, but also most graciously approached Your Electoral Grace’s predecessors of most blessed memory to execute such a most gracious nomination and presentation in the proper manner.

And although the aforementioned Lords Provost and Canons <note>original Latin/German: "Capitulares," members of the governing body of the church</note> have raised an objection, claiming they had decided for specific moving causes to somewhat suppress the old number of the Lords Canons, and namely to let it die down to seven; therefore, before anyone from that reduced number of seven departs or is missing, I cannot have any admittance in this place.

Yet such reasons and excuses are from Your Electoral [Grace]...

# Letter P

His Princely Grace's most blessed Predecessor <note>original German: "Herrn Antecessorin"</note> did not ignore this at all. Instead, by a third repeated command <note>original Latin: "tertiô repetitâ jussione"</note>—and despite the objections raised to the contrary—the Predecessor approved my most humble and submissive request. Furthermore, the well-honored Lords Provost and Chapter were reminded of their duty to comply <note>original German: "schuldiger Parition"</note> with the Imperial Decree.

Therefore, I did not expect at all that the Lords Provost and members of the Chapter would persist in their refusal and objections. Nor did I expect that the most highly mentioned Predecessor of Your Electoral Grace would have given any weight to the recent, self-asserted arguments of the said Provost and Chapter, or graciously sent them to me for further lengthy counter-proceedings. This is especially true considering that in their argument <note>original German: "Deduction"</note> nothing new was brought to the table; rather, the previously understood main exception and objection were simply extended and elaborated upon. That very exception had already been deemed irrelevant by your late Electoral Predecessor. 

Furthermore, it is not proper for me to enter into a dispute or cast doubt on such a far-reaching question. This is especially true because it concerns a high royal right <note>original German: "Regalstück"</note> of His Roman Imperial Majesty—specifically the Primary Petitions <note>original Latin: "Primariarum Precum"</note>. To dispute how this right is understood, how far it extends, or whether it can be restricted or withdrawn by the statutes and regulations of the foundations (which run contrary to ancient foundations and established custom), could significantly prejudice and infringe upon His Imperial Majesty’s rights at other foundations and throughout the entire Holy Roman Empire.

Therefore, I most humbly and earnestly request Your Electoral Grace to graciously remind the well-honored Lords Provost and Chapter once more. In the event of an unexpected refusal, I ask you to seriously insist that, in accordance with the Imperial Nomination and Presentation, I finally be received and accepted. This is particularly urgent because, of the ordinary number of Canons <note>original Latin: "Ordinario numero der Canonicorum"</note> established since ancient times, not just one but several are missing. Furthermore, the question of whether a number restricted by an asserted Statute should be more highly regarded than ancient custom and the original foundation is a dispute that requires a deeper investigation <note>original Latin: "altiorem indaginem" </note>. In the meantime, while that is being settled, I should be admitted and allowed into possession (or its equivalent), at least regarding the office of Canon. This follows the arguments of the decisions handed down by the Roman Rota <note>The Rota Romana is the highest appellate court of the Catholic Church; "decis. 3. de præbend. in antiqu." refers to a specific legal ruling on church stipends.</note>.

And it is relevant here that just as the Treasury <note>original Latin: "Fiscus"</note> does not litigate while deprived of its property, neither should the Emperor. Furthermore, it is favorable for there to be more Canons, both for the sake of the church's dignity <note>original Latin: "ornatus"</note> and, primarily, to better perform the Divine Offices. This is taught by Jacopo Puteo in the decisions of the Roman Rota (Book 3, Decision 6). Therefore, in cases of doubt, one should judge against the suppression of Canons and in favor of the full ordinary number.

<column-break/>

It is no hindrance that the Lord Provost and the Chapter wish to claim that, even if my request were correct and conformed to the sacred Canons and the Council of Trent <note>original Latin: "sacrisque Canonibus, & Concilio Tridentino conforme"</note>, they still could not admit me before I give them due satisfaction. They claim I insulted <note>original Latin: "injurirt"</note> them in my previous petitions. However, with God and my best conscience as my witness, I have never had the slightest intent to injure <note>original Latin: "animum injuriandi"</note> them. On the contrary, I have always been, and remain, determined to revere the Lords Provost and Chapter in a dutiful manner and to show them all obedience, honor, and favor. Whatever has occurred here was intended solely for the sake of observing my legal rights <note>original Latin: "juris mei observandi causâ"</note> and to carry out my misunderstood entitlements to the best of my ability.

In such a case, any "intent to injure" is considered to be entirely absent. For when someone claims to have a right, they are not considered to be doing anyone an injury <note>original Latin: "non censetur alicui facere injuriam"</note>. This is found in the Law *Nullus* in the Digest on the Rules of Law <note>original Latin: "l. nullus videtur ff. de R. Jur."</note>, as well as in the legal counsels of Göden (Counsel 30, number 14, and Counsel 31, number 10). And certainly, in this case, the legal doctors teach that a person can be defended based on probability (Law *si verò*, paragraph *r.*).

Even though, as frequently stated, it is not my place to argue the main dispute itself—especially on the exclusive point of whether His Roman Imperial Majesty's high right of Primary Petitions <note>original Latin: "Jus der Primariarum precum"</note> should be weakened by the suppression of Canons, or whether the original foundation and ancient custom should be observed—one must also consider the following: the aforementioned right belongs to His Imperial Majesty by a unique grant from the Supreme Pontiff (the Pope). However, it is also held in view of his defense and universal Right of Advocacy and Patronage <note>original Latin: "Juris Advocatiæ & Patronatus"</note>, which is well known to belong to the Imperial Majesty in all bishoprics and churches. Thus, in the Imperial Recess of the year 1544 <note>original German: "Reichs-Abschied," the official record of the decisions of the Imperial Diet</note>, in the section beginning "But as the Electors, Princes, etc.," His Roman Imperial Majesty is called an "Advocate and Protector of the Christian Church."

Furthermore, even in the Bull of Pope Paul V <note>original Latin: "Bulla Pontificis Pauli V."</note>, the grant of Primary Petitions to the current most serene Emperor is based on the fact that His Majesty has devoted himself as a faithful Advocate of the unblemished Church. This appears from the formula of the Bull found in the *Rudiments and Summaries of Canon Law* by Wolfgang Sigismund von Vorburg (page 697 and following). And it is not entirely by the favor of the Popes, but because...

# Thesaurus of Practical Knowledge, Expanded
### Letter P

According to the custom received from our ancestors, the Emperor holds the right of nominating and presenting a candidate for the first vacant benefice. This is not merely a request for someone to be accepted as a favor, but a legal right in itself. Examples of such Petitions given during the times of Emperors Charles IV and Rudolph I are shown and cited by Paurmeister in his work *On the Jurisdiction of the Roman Empire, book 1, chapter 4.*

Although today’s Emperors—out of the affection they hold for the Supreme Pontiffs <note>The Popes</note>—may say that this right is established by the ancient custom of the Empire and strengthened by Papal confirmation, these words are spoken for the sake of duty and courtesy. They do not diminish the rights of the Caesar <note>The Emperor</note> or the Empire. It is a well-settled principle of law that a confirmation—even when made by one who has the power to confirm—adds nothing new to an act that is already complete in itself. This is noted by Menochius in his *Legal Opinions 75, 191, and 378.*

Specifically, regarding the fact that confirmations from Popes and Emperors grant nothing new but merely reinforce and strengthen old rights, this is taught by Gail in *Observations, book 2, observation 1.* Furthermore, Hostiensis asserts in his *Summary on the Use of Confirmations* that a confirmation presupposes a right already acquired. Natta also teaches in *Opinion 36* that the nature of a confirmation is not to grant something new, but only to bolster things previously held and possessed.

Now, since these Primary Petitions <note>term: <term>Primary Petitions</term> (Primariæ Preces): A specific imperial privilege allowing the Emperor to appoint one person to a position in every cathedral or collegiate church upon his accession.</note> belong to His Roman Imperial Majesty by most ancient and inherent right (as such a long duration of time serves as both a privilege and a clearly expressed grant), and indeed belong to him as the Advocate and Patron of the Church; it follows that any "suppressions" <note>The closing or elimination of church positions</note> must occur with His Majesty's consent. If such statutes were enacted without His Imperial Majesty's knowledge, they cannot hinder the Primary Petitions. For in the *Council of Trent, Session 24, chapter 15,* it is expressly provided that such suppressions must be made with the consent of the Lay Patrons.

And although the Lord Provost and the members of the Chapter have argued at length here, claiming that the Primary Petitions do not take effect unless there is a "vacant place" <note>Latin: "Locus vacans"</note>—taking into account the number of suppressed canonries <note>A canonry is a specific office or "seat" within a cathedral chapter</note> contained in the statutes and ordinances of the Most Reverend Ordinary—

Nevertheless, in my humble opinion, all of this is addressed at the very source of the Primary Petitions of our Most Serene Emperor, which was confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff in the year 1620. In that document, specifically in the second paragraph beginning "Furthermore, according to the agreements of the Nation" as found in Wolf Sigismund von Vorburg’s *General Summary of Canon Law, number 703,* it is expressly stated and found: that the aforementioned Imperial Primary Petitions shall not be hindered by any unions, annexations, suppressions, or extinctions, whether

<column-break/>

perpetual or temporary. These are the very circumstances in which we currently find ourselves.

Since we have this case explicitly expressed in the Papal Confirmation itself, and in the very terms we are using, it seems we should cease all further dispute. Against this, no authorities of the legal Doctors or even the Council of Trent itself can prevail. This is because the Supreme Pontiff, for a certain cause, can grant a dispensation even against the decrees of Councils in cases that do not concern the articles of faith—especially when there is a pressing necessity or to favor the Most Serene Emperor, who has served the Church excellently and to whom, therefore, the most ample favors are owed.

For these reasons, the most blessed predecessor of Your Electoral Grace previously graciously approved my intention. Likewise, the renowned University of Freiburg concluded—in the letters of intercession given for me in the year 1620 to the Most Reverend Bishop of Basel—that such statutes of suppression are subject to the strictest legal interpretation. They cannot prejudice the Emperor in his right, which was given by the Popes in the broadest possible extension. Such statutes should only be practiced when the election of a new Canon remains with the Chapter and not a new Bishop; otherwise, it could happen that any church might use such statutes to defraud Imperial Law and protect themselves against Imperial petitions.

Furthermore, it should not be overlooked that the Lord Provost and the Chapter have never actually practiced this alleged statute of theirs, nor has it ever come into reality. Indeed, they have broken it themselves through a contrary act. Therefore, it seems somewhat strange that they now presume to put this whole statute into effect specifically against me, or rather, to the prejudice of His Sacred Imperial Majesty.

->I await a response on this, etc.<-

->Dated July 21, in the year 1625.<-

### 46. Primogeniture. *Primogenitura.*

On the primacy of the first-born, see the individual treatise by Francesco Zoannetti and the *Historico-Political-Legal Treatise on the Succession of Julich*. Fusarius in his treatise *On Substitutions and Entails*, question 385 and following, where he has many useful questions concerning primogeniture and the Prerogative of Lines <note>the order of succession within family branches</note>. Mynsinger, *Observation 23*, book 3. Mascardus, *On Proofs*, conclusion 1263, number 25 and following. On whether in the goods of a County or a Majorate <note>term: <term>Majoratus</term>—an inheritance restricted to the oldest son to keep the estate intact</note>, the first-born alone should succeed entirely, and without diminution or division of the dignity and the goods, see Peguera, *Decision 113*.

On whether by these words, placed in the institution of a Majorate: "that the elder son who shall be surviving at the time of the death of the last possessor ought to inherit the Majorate," the representation of a grandson is considered excluded if the first-born son died before his father; so that in the succession of the Majorate in said case, the surviving second-born son should be preferred? Peguera examines this in *Decision 114*.

On whether females—when there are no males of the same line and degree—succeed in the goods of a Majorate or in Royal dignities by the right of Primogeniture, to the exclusion of more remote males. And what if such goods of a Majorate or Royal dignities are feudal <note>held under a lord in exchange for service</note>? Peguera discusses this in *Decision 115*.

And regarding primogeniture, Molina also has much in his individual treatise, as does the other Molina in the treatise *On Justice and Law*. The most noble Goldast also treats it in his *Senior*; and I myself <note>the author, Besold</note> in the treatise *On Succession and Election*.
