# Thesaurus of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

Delamotta, in his commentary on Molina regarding **primogeniture** <note>the right of the firstborn child to inherit the entire estate</note>, addresses whether a daughter’s dowry should be paid out of the firstborn’s assets; for this, one should consult Mr. Christoph Philipp Richter, part 6, counsel 5. If the administration of assets was granted to the firstborn, but he subsequently dies, the son of that firstborn is seen as taking precedence over the second-born brother. The esteemed Mr. Richter (part 4, counsel 1) states this, though a different rule applies if the administration was specifically entrusted to the "elder" member of the family; in that case, the elder brother of the firstborn is preferred over the firstborn’s own son. The reason, provided in the same text, is that the elder is presumed to be wiser. The right of primogeniture is founded upon Natural, International, Civil, Canon, and Customary Law.

Who may be called the "Firstborn"? Cardinal Francesco Mantica (in *Conjectures on Last Wills*) discusses whether the term "firstborn" refers to the son of a deceased firstborn or his brother, and which of them should be preferred. A bequest is considered left to the "firstborn" if the testator ordered the inheritance to pass to the "eldest by birth" or even the "eldest of the house." He also examines whether the firstborn is the only one admitted when a testator substitutes the heir's son and commands him to carry the testator's name and coat of arms.

In the region of Campania, the firstborn claims the paternal house and the surrounding area defined by the "flight of the capon" <note>original: "volatu Caponis"</note>. This means that however far a capon <note>a castrated rooster</note> can fly in a single flight when released from the upper part of the house, that land is subject to the same legal rights as the house itself; the people of Campania call this *Levol du chappon*. The right of primogeniture is observed in France, Spain, England, Hungary, Apulia, and the Duchy of Bavaria. Under Mosaic Law, all firstborn sons—and only they—were dedicated to divine service. *In Spain, when twins are born, the one who comes out last is considered the elder; they use the example of two stones in a pit, where the stone dug out last is held to have been in the pit longer than the one dug out first.* <note>original: "In Spania, wann Zwilling gebohren werden..." translated from German</note>. Notable authors on Primogeniture include Jacobus à Saa (a Portuguese), Jean Lecirier (of Paris), and Martinus Garatus (of Lodi).

The right of primogeniture introduces inequality among children. Christoph Rittershusius discusses whether a child legitimized by a subsequent marriage has the right of primogeniture

<column-break/>

over a child born later within the marriage. The firstborn is preferred over his brothers even if he is deaf, mute, etc., though in such a case, the nearest male relative <note>term: "agnatus"; a relative through the male line</note> must be appointed as his guardian. The right of primogeniture was introduced for the best of reasons. This right was also observed among the French in the city of Nicosia. In the Holy Roman Empire, the right to succeed to the Secular Electorates <note>the high-ranking princes who elected the Emperor</note> devolves by law to the firstborn alone, excluding all others. Regarding the difference between **Primogeniture** and **Majoratus** <note>term: "Majoratus"; a form of inheritance where the oldest member of a family succeeds, regardless of whether they are the direct descendant of the last holder</note>, see Besold. If a firstborn renounces his right in favor of a second-born brother, does he recover that right if the brother dies? See Boerius, decision 204.

### 47. Prior.

Although "Priors" are placed into two different categories, some say the term "Priorate" refers only to certain administrative roles and dignities held by monks and other Regulars <note>clergy living under a religious rule/order</note>. However, custom in some areas dictates that the name "Prior" is used for Prelates and secular Rectors of rural churches—and even those with the "cure of souls" <note>parish responsibilities</note> where the actual care is managed separately by Vicars.

Furthermore, one type of Prior is **Conventual** (found in a Collegiate Church), while another is merely **Cloistered**. The former is usually a permanent position, whereas the latter is a temporary one appointed by a Superior or an Abbot, acting properly as an "Obedientiary" <note>one who holds an office at the will of a superior</note>. The Conventual Prior is elected by the Chapter of the Convent. For more on their offices and dignity, see Lancellotti.

->ADDITION.<-

Does the term "Brothers" include the Prior? A distinction is made by Villalobos.

### 48. Privileges.

In a petition <note>original: "Supplicatione"</note> to obtain a summons for a person who has committed "contempt of privilege," it is required that the petition state the act was committed with "malice aforethought" <note>original: "dolo malo"</note> and by deliberate purpose against the privileges. Furthermore, it must be shown that the legitimate privileges were formally served to the defendant.

Moreover, it is required that the privileges be justly and legitimately registered <note>original: "insinuata"</note> with the Chamber <note>the Imperial Chamber Court, or *Reichskammergericht*</note>. If they have not been registered, the original documents must be attached to the petition. Transcripts <note>original: "Transumptis"</note> are not trusted in this case when a prior registration has not occurred.

# Letter P.

And thus, three requirements pertain to obtaining legal proceedings against violators of Privileges: (1) **The notification of the Privilege made to the Chamber and the party**, (2) **The transmission of the original document**, and (3) **The definition of intent** <note>original: *dolus*; in a legal context, this refers to establishing that a violation was intentional or fraudulent</note>.

To grant Privileges is a **Prerogative of Sovereignty** <note>original: *Juris Majestatis*</note>, and it belongs to the supreme power of making laws. For a Privilege is nothing other than a private Law. *See my work On Sovereignty, folio 149.*

Regarding the Interpretation of Privileges, consult *Schrader, counsel 23.*

Furthermore, it is one thing to be exempt, and another to be privileged: see *Meichsner, volume 2, book 1, folio 846.* Also see my own work, *Treatise on the Mixed State, chapter 6*, regarding when Privileges create a "mixed state" <note>a complex legal status involving overlapping jurisdictions</note>. Truly, there is hardly a village that does not boast of its Privileges: and almost nothing is more frequent than to cloak rebellions under the pretext of Privileges. It is relevant here that Privileges are not presumed to exist but must be proven. *Gryphiander on Islands, chapter 31, near the end.* See also my *Delibata*, regarding the revocation of Privileges, *folio 30 and 43.* *Matthaeus de Afflictis, decision 128.*

### ADDITION.

Derogatory and cancellation clauses <note>provisions in a new law that nullify previous conflicting rules</note> only remove illicit privileges. *Acts of Lindau, folio 444 at the beginning, page 439 in the middle.* **Privileges concern the right of ownership.** <note>original: *petitorium*; a legal claim based on the right itself rather than mere possession</note>. *Klock, volume 1, counsel 10, number 120; and counsel 29, number 952.* A Privilege is lost through non-use when the power of the privilege is formally left to the judgment and will of the privileged party. *Klock, volume 1, counsel 15, number 113, 114.* Special Laws are called Privileges. A Privilege is a law passed for one or a few citizens, whether it looks to their benefit or their detriment. Although today "Privilege" is mostly understood as something favorable, in the past, the imposition of a penalty or an edict issued against someone was called by that name. *Arnisaeus on Sovereignty, book 2, chapter 3, number 16.* However, only the Emperor has the power to impose Privileges, although this also falls to other Princes of the Empire according to the measure of their jurisdiction. *More in Becker, on Public Law, pages 240 and 241.* On whether the Emperor can grant privileges without seeking anyone's consent, see *Reinkingk on the Government of the State and Church, book 1, class 3, chapter 12, number 41.* Add the *Disputation of Hieronymus Wissendorff, held under Mr. Hahn, on the judgments of Royal Rights, thesis 54.* Personal privileges belonging to Princes by reason of their dignity pass to heirs by right of blood. *Knipschild on Entails, chapter 6, number 20.* Regarding what some establish—that a Prince can revoke a Privilege granted for free to a subject without cause—this can be defended neither by texts nor by reasons, even though *Knipschild* made that opinion his own in *book 1, on the rights and privileges of Cities, chapter 18, number 8.* *Enenckel on Privileges, book 3, chapter 3* piles up authorities and reasons for this. But *Besold, volume 1,*

<column-break/>

correctly refutes this in *chapter 5.* Add the reasons in *the same book 3, chapter 2, number 23 and following.* It is different if a just cause exists; *see the same work, chapter 6.* A case omitted in a privilege is considered to be left to the decision of common law. *Klock, volume 1, counsel 7, number 871.* Privileges and rights consisting of things done by free will are not lost through non-use. *Klock, volume 1, counsel 29, numbers 592, 593, 594.* A privilege granted to several people at once is not considered granted to one against the other. *Counsel 37, number 126.* Privileges are not lost through non-use. *Klock, volume 2, counsel 18, number 84.* The allegation of a privilege pertains not to the possessory claim, but to the claim of the right itself. *Klock, volume 3, counsel 149, number 52.*

Although Privileges are perpetual and real <note>attached to a thing or status rather than a specific person</note>, according to the text in the law titled *Forma*, section *quanquam*, in the Digest on Taxes, it can nevertheless happen that someone may lose a freedom or Privilege either by not using it or by a contrary act or deed. *Gail, book 2, observation 60, throughout; and the law in the Digest on Fairs.* For one who acts against their privilege is seen to have renounced it, especially if an opportunity for use was given in the meantime. For if no occasion arose where one could have used the privilege, then no fault can be imputed for not using it. *Gail, observation 60, number 1. Christinaeus, volume 1, decision 191, number 4. Richter, decision 86, throughout.* Therefore, when one rationally disputes the use or possession of a particularly unusual freedom, and shows only some contrary possession or a contrary act, the person claiming the privilege must prove possession, regardless of his written **register of local laws** <note>original: *Pantheidungsbuch*; a record book of village customs and court rulings in German-speaking lands</note>. This is because possession is not proven by documents, even if they were made regarding the handover, for by these it is only understood that the power to seize possession was granted. *Wesembecius in his notes on the Digest, regarding the acquisition or loss of possession.* And that possession is not proven through appraisal books, land registries, and similar records is excellently deduced by *Nicolaus à Passeribus on private writings, book 5, question 3; see Moller, 4th semester, 37.* Thus it was recognized in the regional laws, in the case of the heirs of the late Mr. Lorentz Schütter against Mr. Christoph Wilhelm von Zelcking, by public sentence on December 17, 1604. There it was stated: "As far as keeping the 56 florins against money is concerned, let the Defendant prove that the village of **Spillern** is in continuous possession of the article mentioned in the records and drawn from their local law register regarding the delivery of **criminals** <note>original: *Malefitzpersonen*; specifically those accused of capital crimes</note>; that will be heard." More in *Suttinger, observation 70, number 5.* Regarding whether and when privileges to do something can be barred by the statute of limitations. *Melonius in the Treasury of Feudal, Civil, and Criminal Law, volume 42, number 27.* Concerning privileges or freedoms which Roman Emperors and Kings [grant] to the lower authorities of the Holy Empire, such as **Electors, Dukes, Princes, Margraves, Counts, Barons, Cities, and Communities**, to thereby prevent their subjects from frivolous appeals...

### 49. Provost. Præpositus.

The word "Provost" (so called from *præponendo*, "placing before") is a general term and is predicated of anyone who presides over a Church or others. *Cujas on the Code, book 2, title on the excuse of duties.* But usage has prevailed that only he is called such who carries a certain care of Priority over others. According to the chapter *quamvis* <note>a reference to Canon Law</note>, a Provost is what the Greeks call an *Oeconomus* <note>a steward or manager</note>, that is, one who administers Ecclesiastical revenues and presides over the people under the Bishop. *Dr. König in the Political Theater, part 1, chapter 37, number 12.* Their jurisdiction is ordinary over the Canons and Clerics of their Church, whom they can restrain if they are delinquent or rebellious. *Chapter "irrefragabili," 13, on the office of the ordinary. König, cited location, number 14; see also Lancellotti in the Temple of All Judges, book 2, chapter 10, folio 905 and following.*

### 50. Process. Processus.

Regarding Lawsuits <note>original: *Processus*; encompassing the whole legal proceeding</note>, and what should be observed politically concerning them, *Antonio Palazzo* teaches in chapter 24. There are many who argue that lawsuits should not be encouraged, and indeed should not be easily initiated. Hence *Henry of Pflaumern* in the *Italian Mercury, folio 337*, urges that the humanity of the Viceroy of Naples should be imitated. He writes there that when the Viceroy proceeds to the Chapel on feast days for the sake of Divine service, accompanied by a line of nobles, men and women of any humble fortune are present and offer petitions <note>original: *supplices Libellos*; humble little books or papers</note> to him as he passes through the Hall. He accepts them all himself, and after the Divine service is finished, he reads them through and returns an answer as swiftly and justly as possible. I am indignant when I sometimes see our own lawyers, or presiding officials established in a far from equal administration, either inexorably reject the prayers of the wretched, or listen morosely with closed ears, a wrinkled forehead, and a proud brow. You should give these people the Neapolitan Viceroys as an example, who are so accustomed to treating people with humanity.

->ADDITION.<-

Nicolaus Clenardus, a Brabantian, used to say: *The Jews waste their money on feasts, the Moors on weddings, the Christians on lawsuits.* *Dr. Schupp in Lucidor, letter E. 9.* A process was invented at least for the information of facts. *Klock volume 3, counsel 149, number 334; counsel 164, number 11; and counsel 187, number 265.* The Athenians, at the start of a dispute, would deposit a certain quantity of money—namely a tenth part of that which was being litigated—with which reckless litigants were fined; this was also observed among the Romans. *Johannes de Deo, book 5, on cautions or sophistry, chapter 6, number 5; and book 6, chapter 5, number 1.* On the summary investigation of a cause, see *Zahn on Lies, book 3, chapter 9, numbers 110, 111.* The word "Process" is commonly understood in various ways. Thus, for a "pomp" or ceremony in law 41 of the Digest, where to give for a husband’s "process" means nothing other than to give so that the husband may use it in a parade, such as in the public processions of Consuls and other Magistrates, mentioned in the *Novella 105, chapter 1*. Many explain that law in this way. Others, however, explain those gifts of a wife for a husband's "process" as the expenses for promoting the husband through career ranks. *Digest, book 45, title on business conducted.* So also the word "Process" is sometimes popularly understood as progress in studies <note>original: *progressu in literis*</note>. In forensic <note>courtroom</note> use, however, it denotes nothing other than the legitimate order of a trial, the method and way by which the judge and litigants proceed until the disputes reach their intended end. Or if you prefer it more briefly: The competent order and form of judgments, or the legitimate method of handling judgments in order. *Dr. Fibig, part 1, on Judicial Process, chapter 1.* Process, Error, Duty. Also: War, Discord, Process. *Limnaeus, Public Law, book 7, chapter 10.*

## 53. Professor. Professor.

Regarding the three virtues of a <term>Professor</term>: that he speak clearly, speak with probability <note>plausibility or logical weight</note>, and speak briefly; see *Mercer*, Opinions, book 1, chapter 3. There he also teaches that a qualified Student of Law <note>original: *Juris Auditor*</note> must attend to these three things: *To understand, to believe, and to remember.*

However, the interpretation of the Laws is not permitted to everyone indiscriminately, but only to the "prudent"—that is, those taught by use and experience. Hence, the Emperor rightly decreed that public interpretations of the law are not to be committed to anyone unless they have been duly called into the order <note>officially appointed to a faculty</note>, in the *single law of the Code regarding professors in the City of Constantinople*.

From this, those who profess <note>teach</note> the Laws without a Privilege <note>a royal or imperial license</note> are ordered to be fined 10 pounds of gold and, moreover, expelled from the City. It was only permitted to teach the Laws in Royal Cities gifted with the rights of Universities <note>original: *Academiarum*</note>. For a Professor, by interpreting the laws, performs the duty of the Prince <note>the sovereign</note>. *Single law of the Code regarding liberal studies; Rebuffus; Lindemann in the History of Law, thesis 101.*

Should Doctors who have taught publicly for twenty years in Privileged Universities be numbered among illustrious persons and be made Counts? See *Anton Bullae* in *The Three Precepts of Law*, page 98; *Mr. Harprecht*; and *Reinking on Secular Government*. This is also where the term "Predecessors" <note>original: *Antecessores*; a title given to law professors in the later Roman Empire</note> comes from, according to *Christian Coler*.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding by what means Professors may seek their salaries, see *Mr. Biccius*. Professors, even if they are younger <note>junior in tenure</note>, are preferred over other Doctors <note>those holding the degree but not a teaching chair</note>, according to *Becker in Public Law*. Those who have taught publicly for 20 years are numbered among the Illustrious, as stated in the same place. Professors who appoint unworthy people in Universities should be punished, see *Walther on the Privileges of Doctors*. Professors can prohibit and keep away blacksmiths, coopers <note>barrel makers</note>, and other craftsmen who practice their trade with a certain noise from buying or renting neighboring houses. *Coler on Executive Procedure; Dr. Tabor on the Law of Beer, chapter 4.*

Assessors of the Imperial

<column-break/>

Chamber <note>the high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> are chosen from the number of Professors. ## 54. Provost, Supreme Field Provost.
## Supreme Prefect of Capital Matters.

In war, this person is our Prefect and Judge of capital matters <note>crimes punishable by death</note>. He administers justice and delivers delinquents to be restrained by the lower prefects of justice. He looks after the security of the roads and ensures that soldiers do not plunder anything in transit. *Reinhard König in the Political Theater, part 3.*

The name is derived from the [Latin] *Praefectus* or the French *Prévôt*.

---
->ADDITION.<-
---

The Executor of capital matters is the Provost <note>original: *Profoß*</note>. There is the Cavalry Provost, the Supreme Field Provost, and the Artillery Provost (the investigator of the armory). 

No one shall dare to snatch a prisoner out of the hands of a Provost under penalty of corporal punishment, or they shall stand in the prisoner's place <note>take on the prisoner's sentence</note>. *Dutch Military Law, article 78*. The nearest soldiers shall detain a public offender until the arrival of the Provost. *Imperial Military Articles, page 149.*

### 59. Protocol. *Protocollum.*

A protocol is a sudden annotation of a matter handled, or a first arrangement and rapidly completed writing, which embraces only the summary of the matter. See *Joachim Mynsinger on the title regarding the credibility of Instruments, chapter 1, number 29.* It is derived as if from the Greek *proton kolon* <note>original Greek: πρωτον κωλον, meaning "first limb" or "first member"</note>, **the first scribbling** <note>original German: **die erste Klitterung**</note>. See *Meursius*; it is used in the preparation of a Notary’s instruments, *Novel 44, chapter 2*. It contains either the first sketch of an instrument or a contract, without legal formalities, commonly called **the draft, not yet cleaned up** <note>original German: **das Concept, so noch nicht mundirt**</note>. From this, that which is transcribed from the Protocol, or even extended into a solemn form with its customary legal clauses, is commonly called a **Transumpt** <note>a formal copy</note>. See *Baldus in the rubric of the Code on the credibility of instruments*; and thus it is reduced into a "clean copy" <note>Latin: *in mundum redigitur*</note>. Once this clean copy has been filled and finished, only then does it have legal force; that is, when the instruments received into the clean copy have been confirmed by the signatures of the parties or the Notary. *Law 17, Code on the credibility of Instruments; Bornitius, On Instruments, book 2, chapter 3.*

A Protocol provides no legal evidence in court, although a Notary can derive an authentic and valid instrument from it; see *Mynsinger on the credibility of Instruments, chapter 15, folio 63, number 6, etc.*, unless the Protocol contains everything that an original requires—namely, the signature of the Notary and the application of the Notarial Seal, the time, and the place. Furthermore, the instruction of the subject must have been read aloud and explained in the presence of the parties and witnesses, etc. See *Bornitius, in the cited place, book 3, chapter 4.*

That the Protocol should be attended to rather than the extracted instrument was decided by *Joseph Sesse, Aragon Decisions 72*. An extract from a suspect Protocol—whether void or false—provides no evidence, as it comes from a "corrupt root"; rather, the suspicion, nullity, or falsity of the Protocol infects the Instrument and renders it likewise suspect, void, or false. *Cornelius, Council 70, number 11, book 3; Anchoranus, Council 432; Rolandus, Council 26, number 11, book 3; Hondedeus, Council 66, number 101.*

->**ADDITION.**<-

A Protocol must be faithfully preserved by the Notary. *Ilico Ummius in Legal Process, page 707.* Whether a Protocol must be produced if an instrument is alleged to be false, *ibid.* A Protocol contributes nothing to the authority of an instrument on its own, *ibid. Besoldus, Volume I.*

<column-break/>

On the rough and the extended Protocol, *Mr. Brinckmann* teaches soundly and at length in his most accurate *Inaugural Disputation on Notaries, position 27 and following numbers.*
The ridiculous derivation of "Protocol" by Accursius. *Conrad Rittershusius in the New Constitutions, page 631, number 35.* Where the word Protocol is derived from and what it is, *page 625, number 4.* Whether and when a Protocol provides legal evidence, *Lanfrancus in the Practice of Instruments, number 25.*

### 61. Provincial. *Provincialis.*

Provincials, as they are assumed into a part of the Apostolic care, have quasi-Episcopal jurisdiction in both the ecclesiastical and civil forums by Common Law and by Privilege. They can exercise this everywhere, since they do not have a fixed territory, although it is much more becoming to exercise it within the Monasteries of their own Province. This jurisdiction, however, regards only governance: for it does not extend to the ceremonial duties of a Bishop, although in many matters they have greater power than Bishops—for example, regarding absolutions and dispensations. *Emanuel Rodriguez in the Compendium of Regular Questions, under the word Jurisdiction.*

->**ADDITION.**<-

Provinces given to others which could not be defended. *Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, book 7, chapter 2, § 5.* Those ancient Romans believed that a good wife of a Governor or President was like the Phoenix, which they say is seen only after a long cycle of centuries: therefore, it was agreed that women should not be dragged into the Provinces, as they would do nothing else but what is usually done by those who are powerless amidst a golden harvest. *Mr. Rupertus in Universal History.*

### 63. Pyramids.

Concerning the Pyramids, which are located in a very wide and sandy field in the region of Cairo, see Christoph Fürer's *Itinerary of Egypt, Arabia, etc., folio 26 and following.* Built like mountains from the ancient rivalry and wealth of Kings, they are today distinguished into "greater" and "lesser" types; the former remain intact, while the latter have all collapsed. The largest of all is of an immensely vast height, constructed with as much artistry as splendor. The same Fürer provides a description of it in the place mentioned.

->ADDITION.<-

See Pancirollus in *The Lost Things <note>original: "Deperditis"</note>, pages 181 and 187 and following.* See also Zeiller in *Italian Itinerary, page 93.* Note Pliny's judgment on Phemis, when he calls his Pyramid—which three hundred and sixty thousand men had constructed over 20 years—an idle and foolish display of royal money. According to Scaliger, Egypt built the Pyramids so that, even if they could not endure for all of time, they might at least surpass the longest possible ages. The Egyptians keep the bodies of their Kings beneath these Pyramids and "Columns of Fire," because they believe the spirit, like a flame, should ascend to heaven; thus, they are freed from decay for several hundred, even over a thousand years, as can be read with wonder in Lord Athanasius Kircher’s *Oedipus*. Johann Helffrich also treats the Pyramids extensively in his travel narrative from Venice to Jerusalem, Egypt, Mount Sinai, Cairo, and Alexandria, specifically in the account of what happened on December 13th. Martial writes: *Let barbaric Memphis be silent regarding the miracles of the Pyramids.* For the origin of the name of the Egyptian Pyramids, see Mr. Dilherr, *volume 1, Academic Disputations, page 91.*

### 64. Palilia.

Pales was the Goddess of Shepherds, whose festival was the Palilia <term>Palilia: an ancient Roman agricultural festival aimed at purifying herds and shepherds</term>, as Paul (the abridger of Festus) says: "or Palilia, because sacrifices were made to her for the offspring <note>original Latin: "partu", referring to the birth of livestock</note> of the cattle." These are the words of Paul. Furthermore, it is clear that the Palilia were also called "Parilia," owing to the familiar exchange between the letters L and R among the ancients. It is well known that on that feast of the Shepherds (which is April 20th), Rome was founded by Romulus and Remus; regarding this matter, see (among others) Varro in *book 2 of On Agriculture*, and Rupert on *Florus, book 1, chapter 20, section 2.* That day was also formerly called the Palilia when the Emperor Caligula took power in Rome (I am speaking of him as a Prince here, not yet as a monster), serving as a token of the city's founding. *Smoky Palilia, Persius Satire 1:*

> -- To praise the lush countryside, where there are baskets,
> And a hearth and pigs, and the Palilia smoky with hay.

The shepherds celebrated these feasts in the fields on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May <note>April 21st</note> to ward off wolves and drive away diseases from the cattle. The poets call them "smoky" because, when they were celebrated, the shepherds would leap across a fire

<column-break/>

built from hay and stubble, believing that they were purified by this act.

### 65. Psalter.

Psalmists are Singers. See *Boreh on Fiefs, chapter 5, number 16.* Mr. Rittershufius shares a recommendation of the Davidic Psalms from *St. Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa* in his *Notes on Amphilochius, verse 273.*

The Psalter <term>Psalter: a stringed instrument, but also referring to the Book of Psalms</term> sounds poorly with the Cithara, and the Cithara with the Psalter. See Mr. Harsdörffer in the third part of the *Poetical Funnel, page 381*; add my own notes under the words *Journey* and *Nightingale*. Regarding the *Psalter of Mary*, which was printed in Ingolstadt in the year 1572, see Mr. Martin Beeren’s treatise on the *Invocation of the Holy Angels, page 143.* See the same author in his *Thorough Refutation, page 723 and following.* Regarding the order of the Psalms, one should read P. Pungus *On Secret Numbers*, concerning the praise of the Psalter. Beuß, in the funeral sermon for the Electress Palatine, *folio 4*, calls the Psalter "Medicine for the Soul"; likewise: "the guardian of children, the ornament of youth, and the solace of old age." Basil calls it: "A common treasure." Luther calls it "The Little Bible." Urbanus Rhegius calls it "A paradise and beautiful garden." Valerius Herberger calls it "The Catechism of the Old Testament."

### 66. Paratitla.

As to whether the word <term>Paratitla: short summaries or supplementary notes on legal titles, often used in Roman law</term> exists among authors other than Justinian in *law 1, section 12; law 2, section 21; and law 3, section 21*. The *Paratitla* of the Greeks were translated by Leunclavius; Mr. Dr. Rebhan treats this small word at length in *Selected Justinian Questions, Decade 6, Question 5, page 23 at the end and page 24 at the beginning.* The *Paratitla* of Justinian were written by the Greeks, meaning supplements to each title from other titles and places, with all parts of the Justinian Law reduced into a single harmony. Antonius Augustinus seems to have had a copy of these *Paratitla*. See more in Jacob Gothofredus, *Library of Roman Law, page 54.*

### 67. Pilgrim.

"Pilgram" <note>the early German/Italian variant of Pilgrim</note> is not a German word, but rather an Italian one, which flowed from the Latin *peregrinus* <note>meaning a foreigner or traveler</note>. See Zesius in his *Lustinne, number 335.*

*Peregrini* are those who, having taken a vow, set out for the sake of Religion: Pilgrims and Wayfarers. See Otto in *Public Law, page 680.* See also Megiser in *Delights of Naples, page 208 at the beginning*, where he writes about Pilgrims who, out of great devotion, carry a stone around their necks.

### 68. "Private" used for a Bath.

A Bath, in the *Theodosian Code, law 12, regarding billeting*, seems to be called simply a "private" <note>original Latin: "privatum"</note>; the text says: "nor shall anyone demand a 'private' (Cujacius reads 'anyone' in his notes) from the Master of the house." However, how "private" is used absolutely...

### 69. Practitioners.
<term>Practici (Practitioners)</term> <note>original Latin: "Practici" or "Pragmatici"</note>

Pragmatic lawyers, distracted by infinite business, cannot direct the strength of their intellect toward the reconciliation of legal texts. Lord Doctor Tabor, in *On Confrontation* <note>original: "de Confrontatione"</note>, Dissertation 3, theorem 10, page 173. Regarding the confidence of these pragmatists, there is an elegant passage in Pliny’s 6th Book of *Epistles*, 29: "That saying, which is attributed to Pollio, I have accepted as if it were truly his: 'By acting fittingly, it happened that I acted often; by acting often, it happened that I acted less fittingly.' For by too much persistence, one acquires a facility rather than a faculty, and develops rashness rather than true confidence."

In defense of Practice: Whatever the most learned and hardworking predecessors instill in the minds of recent students from the vast and wide-reaching body of Roman Law would be crippled in the schools without the doctrine of the courtroom. Mornac, *Observations on Law 25 regarding things credited*, at the end. One must deviate very little from ancient Practice, for the true interpretation of law is drawn from Practice. Gail, Book 1, Observation 1, number 18. Besold, Book 5, Counsel 233, number 206. Many practitioners, through an excessive freedom in learning, achieve only this: they undermine their own credibility. Limnaeus, Book 9, Chapter 4, number 25. For who truly qualifies as a "Pragmatic," see Johann Garf, *Tract on Expenses and Improvements*, Chapter 17, number 17. **Beloved practitioners are to be preferred over young Doctors. Saxon Police and Clothing Ordinance, page 14.** Those who are worn down in the courtroom and by real litigation, even if unwillingly, learn much of the world's malice. C. Rittershufius in the *Novellae*, page 550.

Practitioners are not deterred by a style that is either rough or unpolished. For although they may greatly love the beauty of pleasant speech, and as boys or adolescents were seen as eloquent in Greek and Latin by their teachers, once the reality of life has led them toward a masculine and forensic Prudence, they easily come to despise that delicate style, following the example of the greatest legal experts. See more in Lord Tabor on *Alienation*, page 362. A practitioner without theory is an infant of the laws, just as a theorist without practice is an idle spectator of the laws. It is worth more to be a theorist than a pure practitioner. See Lord Walther at length in *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 173. Very many things are decided by certain Law, about which our "pretty" pragmatists anxiously doubt, stumble, and fall. After Cujacius, see my friend Georg Cassel, *On the Law of the Lenten Season*, thesis 79.

### 70. Parabolani.
<term>Parabolani (The Reckless Ones)</term> <note>In the late Roman Empire, these were a guild of clerics who cared for the sick and buried the dead, often known for their boldness or inflammatory behavior.</note>

See Lord C. Rittershufius in the *Novellae*, page 107, number 118. Pacius in the *Annals of the Code on Bishops and Clerics*, number 36. Lord Doctor Georg Richter, *Orations*, decade 2, oration 9, throughout. Georg Christoph Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 397, at the end. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book 3, Chapter 23. Also Lord Tabor in the *Exercises of Besold*, Volume I.

### 71. Plynteria.
<term>Plynteria</term> <note>An ancient Greek festival of "washing" (from plynos) dedicated to Athena.</note>

The renowned Rupertus explains what the Plynteria are in Book 1, chapter 1, distinction 2 on Valerius Maximus, section 11. They celebrated the Plynteria at Athens. During the days of this festival, the statue of Minerva <note>Athena</note> was washed, and they diligently observed—both publicly and privately—that no one should attempt any business once the festival had begun, let alone when it was finished; as is recorded in Xenophon. The same Rupertus notes this in his *Observations on Florus*, Book 1, chapter 2, section 3, page 76.

### 76. Treaty of Passau. <term>Transactio Passaviensis</term>.

The Treaty of Passau, 1552. This treaty was later solemnly approved and accepted by the Emperor and the Estates at the Diet of Augsburg in 1555. See Goldast, Volume 1, *Imperial Constitutions*, page 566.

Whether the Treaty of Passau is a <term>Pragmatic Sanction</term> <note>A sovereign's decree having the force of fundamental law.</note>? See Lord Feltvinger, *On the Faith to be Kept with Heretics*, thesis 15. The Treaty of Passau has the force of universal law. Musculus, *On the Succession of Conventions and Anomalies*, Class 1, Member 2, Conclusion 5, letter A.

Whether immediate Nobles <note>Nobles who held their land directly from the Emperor rather than through a middle lord.</note>, even after the Treaty of Passau and the Peace of Religion, can abolish either religion; see Lord Lendersheim, *On the Law of Free Nobles*, thesis 14, letter d. Besold, *Politics*, Book 2, Chapter 2, number 42. The Religious Peace was decreed at Passau on August 2, 1552, and was confirmed in the years 1554 and 1566, by whose benefit our most sweet Fatherland became more peaceful. To what extent does the Religious Peace concern the immediate Nobles? Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, Chapter 2, number 322 and following. The Religious Peace is a Pragmatic Sanction and a fundamental Law of the Empire, not truly a spiritual matter. The same author in his *Counsels*, number 97. Mr. Johann Michael Dilherr, in his *Course of Time and the World*, states that the Treaty of Passau was put into effect on July 31, 1552, and that Elector Maurice of Saxony pressed hard for it, page 639.

Whether witnesses are included under the naming of "parties." Cravetta, *Counsel* 402. Lord Christopher Rittershusius, *On the Novels*, page 533, number 86. The opposing party. Limnäus, *Public Law*, Book 6, Chapter 2, page 51. Regarding the pretext of parties. Lord Rupertus, *Observations on Florus*, Book 3, Chapter 21, § 22. A judge must not be partial—<gloss>biased</gloss>—or favor one party over the other. ### 83. Pepper. <term>Piper</term>.

### 84. Pearl Catching. <note>original: "Perlenfang. Margaritarum captio."</note>

See Antenor regarding Solomon, chapter 3. Saar in the East Indies shows the manner of catching pearls. How pearl fishing is dangerous, see Mr. Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 257, § 20. Pearls like a Muscatel pear, page 257, § 19; larger than chicken eggs, page 55, § 15. Michael Hemmersam encountered pearls like juniper berries, called "Cros," in the sea known as the "Cres-Sea" <note>likely referring to the Sargasso Sea or coral-rich waters described by early explorers</note>, which is completely overgrown with yellow shrubbery; these were caught and exported by many sailors because they are good for "the stone" <note>a historical term for kidney or bladder stones, treated with powdered pearls</note>. Regarding precious pearls, see Dr. Georg Tobias Oelhafen's *The Noble Pearl of Marriage and the Home*.

### 85. Pegen. <note>A slang term for non-students</note>

A word frequently used in universities by students for those who are not of their order <note>the "town" in "town and gown" relations</note>; however, where it originates from is perhaps not known even to everyone who uses it. In common opinion, it comes from pitch <note>Latin: *pice*</note>, in which a large part of the common folk are occupied, such as beer brewers, coopers, and others. But it is more likely that it comes from the word *Paganus* <note>Latin for villager or peasant</note>: as if to say *Pagen*. For just as in Roman Law "Pagans" are opposed to soldiers (see the legal lexicon of Rodolphus Pratejus, folio 376, under the word *Pagan*), so too are others who are not students—that is, those not sacrificing to the "robed Pallas" <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom; a metaphor for university studies</note>—viewed by students as "robed soldiers" <note>original: *Militibus togatis*</note>, who are accustomed to calling them this out of contempt.

In Salerno there are Procopian peaches as large as melons. Megiser in *Delights of Naples*, my copy page 83.

### 89. Proclamata. <note>Legal Proclamations or Summonses</note>

A general proclamation suffices when there is a multitude of persons, even if they are specific, Klock, volume 3, counsel 173, number 13. This is restricted in number 14.

The posting of a proclamation and dictates is an act of jurisdiction, Klock, volume 2, counsel 27, numbers 44 and 45. When a proclamation is decreed in the Chamber <note>the Imperial Chamber Court</note>, Rudinger, century 4, observation 40. Whether a proclamation should be decreed in a mandate without a clause against a defiant party <note>original: *contumacem*</note>, Schvvanmann, observation 124, numbers 1, 2, 3. How and when a proclamation should be made? Schvvanmann, *On the Chamber Process*, part 1, chapter 31, number 25. To make a proclamation, a florin must be paid to the beadles for each person, chapter 72, number 12. If a proclamation is against several people, should it be made for each individual, and should one or more florins be paid? chapter 72, number 13 and following. If one legitimizes themselves before the proclamation is made, are they nonetheless bound to refund the "florin of defiance"? chapter 72, number 17. Whether a proclamation can be requested at the first term and decreed within six court days? chapter 72, number 18. A proclamation must be either purely decreed or denied, chapter 72, number 2. For the purpose of requesting a proclamation and instituting a process for defiance, must a certain time be prefixed? chapter 72, number 22. Before a proclamation is made, if no procurator is present in the records, no one is considered to have confessed, chapter 72, number 37. Where, by whom, and how a proclamation is made? chapter 72, number 10.

### 90. Pitch-makers, Pitch. <note>original: "Pechler, Pech. Picarius, Pix."</note>

Princely Bavarian Land Ordinance, Book 4, folio 18. Pitch-makers <note>original: *Picari*</note> and scrapers. They present themselves to be scraped and pitched. Rango, *On Wigs* <note>original: "Capillamentis, vulgò Parucquen"</note>, page 223. Otherwise, *Picari* is a type of torture where bodies of men are burned by dripping boiling pitch onto them. > The prison, and the horrible casting down from the rock,
> Lashes, executioners, the dungeon, pitch, metal plates, torches.

Plautus, *The Captives*, Act 3, scene 4, verse 65:

> May another pitch torment you at the hands of the Executioner, and
> Shine upon your head.

An ancient inscription reads:

> These Eternal Marks. The Acts of Laberta.
> They are written of a poisonous, treacherous, and deceitful woman.
> Of a hard heart. A nail and a rope of broom-fiber,
> To bind her neck. And glowing pitch,
> To burn her evil breast.

See Pareus in *Plautine Selections*. In Juvenal's Satire 8, it is asked: what is the "painful tunic" <note>original: *tunica molesta*</note>? It was a tunic made of broom-fiber, usually smeared with pitch and bitumen; they would dress the wretched and those condemned to death in it, and burn them in it, as Lipsius teaches regarding Seneca, Epistle 14.

Regarding pitch-makers or pitch-burners, Limnäus, volume 1, additions to *Public Law*, book 5, chapter 7, page 748 at the end. Near Letto Manopello <note>in Italy</note> in the year 1577, a pitch-mine was discovered where pitch is dug out in great quantities; it has a form like "Jew’s glue" <note>asphalt or bitumen</note>, but is otherwise used like other pitch. Megiser in *Delights*.

### 91. Legal Precedence. <note>original: "Præventio"</note>

Concerning the mutual right of precedence <note>term: <term>Præventio</term> refers to the "right of prevention," a legal principle where the first court to issue a summons acquires the exclusive right to hear the case</note> between the Imperial Chamber Court and the Aulic Council. Johann Andreas Gerhard, Doctor, in his *Discourse on the Supreme Courts of the Roman Empire*, pages 22 and following. Precedence is a legal act by which a defendant, who is equally subject to several ordinary judges both collectively and individually in the same case, is summoned before one through a lawful citation. This allows the defendant to decline the judgment of another court to which he might later be called for the same matter, because he has already been "prevented" by the first judge, to whom he must be remanded for this case. See Rennemann, question 7; Carpzov, *On Judicial Process*, title 9, article 3; Gail, book 1, observation 29. August Strauch held an inaugural disputation on this matter at Wittenberg in the year 1639. Precedence ensures that the judge to whom an appeal is now made is considered incompetent, even if he would otherwise have been competent.

### 92. Banquets. <note>original: "Panckete. Convivium."</note>

On the harmful excess found in magnificent banquets <note>original: "Pancketen"</note>, featuring many kinds of foreign fashions in eating, food, drink, spices, and sugar-work. The luxury of banquets is the sign of a sick State <note>original: "conviviorum luxuria est agræ Civitatis Indicium"</note>, according to Georg Obrecht in his *Political Reflections on the Improvement of Land and People*, published in 1617, pages 82, 83, and 279. See also the entries for **Fireworks** and **Hosting**. In Athenaeus, a man "happy in his belly" <note>original Greek: "Ὀλβιογάστωρ"</note> is one who measures happiness by the pleasure of the stomach—a glutton. Mr. Rupert, in his *Epistolary Mercury*, page 656, notes that such men are led not to the altar of Taurus, but to a table full of foods and delicacies <note>original: "mattyis," a term for gourmet starters</note> that provoke thirst. There, once they have emptied a massive bowl in a single draft, they are immediately initiated as revelers in the ritual books. An ancient poet calls them "sailors of symposia and rowers of cups" <note>original Greek: "συμποσίων ναύτας καὶ κυλίκων ἐρέτας"</note>.

A description of sweet food from Plautus’s *Pseudolus*:
> -- I shall season it with such sweetness,
> That whoever tastes anything I have prepared,
> I will make them gnaw off their very own fingers.

They even called such food "Jupiter’s Brain" <note>original: "Jovis Cerebrum," a proverbial term for the ultimate luxury</note>. Ennius, as quoted by Apuleius in his *Apology*, says: "I passed by the parrot-fish, almost the very brain of Jupiter." Lipsius, joking about the Westphalians, used to say that their rotten cheese was "Jupiter’s brain" to them. Lansius commends good food by saying it is so savory that it finds hunger even in those who are full. Saint Jerome, writing to Oceanus, says: "Not so that he may prepare royal feasts, nor cook pheasants <note>original: "phasides aves"</note> with slow vapors that reach the bone without dissolving the surface of the meat by a skillful tempering."

-> Q. <-

The letter Q is mute and almost superfluous. Following Quintilian and Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 204.

### 1. Quartermaster, Chief Quartermaster. <note>original: "Quartiermeister, Oberster Quartiermeister. Metator, Supremus Metator."</note>

To the Chief Quartermaster or Measurer <note>original: "Mensor"</note> belongs the positioning of the camp, the designation of the rampart and the ditch, and the assignment of lodgings and tents in the camp. Reinhard König in *Political Theater*, part 3, chapter 10.

-> ADDITION. <-

Add Fronsberg, *On Military Matters*, book 3, page 52. The **Court Harbingers** <note>original: "Hof-Furierer"</note> are either the chief measurers—the **General Quartermasters**—or those delegated by them. Under these are the measurers of the entire regiment, commonly called **Regimental Quartermasters**, or simply **Quartermasters**. Attached to them are the assistant measurers <note>original: "prometatores"</note>, the **Harbingers** <note>original: "Furierer"</note>. Dr. Tabor, in *On Billets*, page 83, calls them "Masters of the Ball" <note>original: "Ballet herren"</note>. In the articles of the Danish Royal Majesty, § 110: "If anyone sets himself against the Quartermaster, or takes any quarters not assigned to him, he shall be punished for the first eight days with bread and water, or more severely according to the circumstances and military law." Dr. Tabor treats the distribution of quarters extensively on page 118. These measurers are also called "Marshals of Lodgings" or "Forriers" <note>from the French "forrier," related to doors</note>. They are also called "Chalk-markers" <note>original: "Cretatarii," because they marked assigned doors with chalk</note>.

### 3. Five-Year Stay, or Respite Letter. <note>original: "Quinquennell, Anstands = Brieff"</note>
->Letters of Indulgence.<- <note>original: "Literæ induciales"</note>

A Prince has the power to grant a debtor a delay, or "Letters of Indulgence," so that they do not have to pay their debt for a year in the interim, as noted in the *Code of Justinian regarding Imperial Petitions*; sometimes this is extended to five years <note>term: <term>Quinquennium</term> refers to a five-year period</note>. *Final law, Code on those who may hand over their goods. My Sovereignty, folio 158.*

However, he cannot grant a delay beyond five years, as held by *Castrensis* in the aforementioned code. This also seems to be suggested in the text of the *Imperial Constitution of the Year 1584*, in the section: **Concerning ruined merchants. §. That they.** Since a grant of this kind should not be made if it causes grave prejudice to the other party. *Law 2, Code on Imperial Petitions.*

There is, however, a difference in the legal procedure between these delays. In the first case, which lasts one year, it is sufficient for the debtor to swear that he obtained it because of urgent necessity and without fraud. No other proof is required, nor should the Creditors be heard if they wish to prove the opposite. In the five-year stay, however, it is necessary for him to prove that he is so pressed by necessity that he is unable to pay the debt itself. *Nicolaus Janua, Treatise on Private Writings, book 3, regarding annual and five-year delays, number 6.* The same author, in the following numbers, treats the question: Should the debtor provide a security <note>original: "cautio," a financial guarantee or bond</note> during that annual stay to ensure payment at the end of the delay?

On the question of whether interest continues to accrue during this delay, *see Moller, 4th Semestrium, chapter 7.*

These Indulgences are granted to debt-ridden debtors for the purpose of ensuring they are not miserably tormented by daily and harassing demands for payment, so that they may have time in the interim to think of a convenient way to settle the debt. Since such a "moratorium" <note>term: <term>moratoria præscriptio</term> is a legal stay or delay of payment</note> does not take away the Creditor's right, but only delays it, and a delay of a small amount of time does not result in great prejudice, the Creditors are not permitted to attempt anything against such a Privilege while that delay is pending. *Val. Franc. on Sureties, chapter 3, number 151.*

And although the debtor, within the granted five-year period,

<column-break/>

ought not to be imprisoned, arrested, or harassed in any way regarding his debts: nevertheless, he must provide suitable security so that the Creditors are made more secure. For a stay of payment issued by the ruler <note>original: "moratorium rescriptum"</note> ought not to be valid unless a suitable guarantee <note>original: "fidejussio," a third-party pledge to pay</note> for the debt's payment has been provided. *Universal law, Code on Imperial Petitions.* This is done for the reason that the debtor might otherwise prodigally consume the goods that are still found safe in the intervening time, or flee entirely, and thus defraud his creditors. *Trentacinq. on payments, resolution 1, number 6; Guid. Pap. decision 109, number 2; Wurmser, 1st practical observation, title 28, observation 12.*

And letters of this kind can be granted without sin and with the integrity of justice, especially when there is a convergence of great difficulty and an impossibility of making payment. *Ant. Tessaurus, Piedmontese Decisions, 186, number 3,* where he adds that the Senate has judged it so. Charles V also decreed in the Diet of Augsburg in the year 1584, **in the Police Ordinance, folio 23**, that these Indulgences are not to be granted by the Emperor or Prince unless two conditions are met. Namely: (1) That the debtor who is about to obtain the five-year stay clearly demonstrates, under the testimony of the Magistrate where he has his home, that he has suffered the loss of his means. (2) Next, that this happened by chance or accident, and not by his own fault. Hence, help should not easily be given to failed merchants and "Bankrupts" who have squandered their goods through their own vice and luxury, and have fraudulently plunged others into poverty. **The willful Bankrupts and failures, who did not fall into ruin through unforeseen accidents or damages, but rather fell into bankruptcy through willfulness, excessive pomp, and the like.** *Lord Hering on Sureties, chapter 5, number 103, etc.*

Does a delay granted to a principal debtor for payment, by means of such letters of indulgence, benefit his sureties <note>original: "fidejussoribus," people who guarantee another's debt</note> who were not named in the Petition? This is denied by the common tradition of the Doctors... because this exception, which regards the person of the debtor (to whom mercy is granted to avoid the "handing over of goods" <note>term: <term>cessio bonorum</term>, a legal process where a debtor avoids prison by surrendering all assets to creditors</note>), does not extend beyond his person. *Janua, in the cited treatise, folio 608, number 3.* Because exceptions that are tied to a specific person do not pass to sureties, nor do they regularly benefit them. *Law on exceptions, Digest; Law on if a surety, regarding judged matters; and Law 1, Code on sureties.*

Thus we see in a similar case that a benefit granted to the principal debtor does not profit his sureties. *Law on if a surety, where the glosses of Bartolus and Alexander appear; Brunus in his treatise on the handing over of goods, question 25...*

<summary>This page discusses the legalities of "Letters of Indulgence" (moratoriums), explaining that while a sovereign can grant debtors a five-year stay on payments due to misfortune, this relief requires proof of honesty and security, and does not extend to the debtor's guarantors.</summary>

1872
**The Treasury of Enhanced Practice**
<meta>catchword: join,</meta>

question 6, number 8. In the same work, book 4, at the beginning of the question: Such a **moratorium privilege** <note>original: "Privilegium moratorium"</note> is attached to the person; therefore, it does not concern the **guarantor** <note>original: "fidejussorem"</note>. Instead, the doctors of law maintain that the debt can be demanded from the guarantor immediately, according to the chapter *Privilegium* concerning the Rules of Law in the 6th book of the Decretals. See also Decius at law *omnibus causis* number 6, where Cagnolus also notes this at number 8; add Valentin Francus on guarantors, chapter 3, number 148 and many following. See also Nicolaus Janua at the aforementioned place, folio 609, number 6 and following, who also asks at folio 611: Whether a subordinate may grant a moratorium delay by the authority of the Prince, etc.

And if those who have obtained **letters of delay** <note>original: "literas dilatorias"</note> for payment from the Prince cannot be arrested for the debt during that time, this is argued from the law *quoties* in the Code on Imperial Petitions. This is noted specifically by Jean Papon in book 10 of the *French Rulings*, title 9, on **respite and five-year stays** <note>original: "des respites & quinquenels"</note>, saying: it was so judged in the Senate that this is true even if said letters have not yet been served, provided a summons has intervened; and this is out of reverence for the Prince. But he says this does not prevent the legal process from proceeding against the one seeking such letters, provided that payment itself is not being pressed. He also notes other similar matters under the preceding title on **letters of state** <note>original: "des lettres d'estat"</note>.

The reason for the above is the principle that while a delay is pending, nothing should be changed or attempted <note>original: "nihil innovandum, nec attentandum sit"</note>, according to the law *si pars* in the Code on Delays. This is true unless, while the term is pending, the debtor who received the delay intends to flee, according to the law *ait Prætor*, section *si debitorem* in the Digest on fraudulent creditors. Likewise, unless there is another legal point upon which the delay was not granted: for when a delay is given for one point, one may proceed on another, according to the law *generaliter*, section *his autem* in the Code on Credited Matters, provided it is separate and not connected; otherwise, it is different. See Vitalis de Cambanis in the treatise on Clauses, under the clause: **Nothing is to be changed while security is pending** <note>original: "Nihil novari securit. pendente"</note>, folio 144 and following.

**Five-year letters** <note>original: "Literæ Quinquennales"</note>, and all privileges or moratorium decrees for payments, have no place in debts arising from a **crime** <note>original: "ex causa delicti"</note>, according to Guillaume de Cuneo. See also Petrus Costalius, part 3, and the law *si de dol.* 184 in the Digest on dowry rights.

**Moratorium delays** (which are so called because they "delay"—that is, retard, impede, postpone, and suspend until the end of the truce—the demands and petitions of creditors) are not easily to be granted against the debts of **laborers and hirelings** <note>original: "opificum & mercenariorum"</note>, (**daily or manual wages / of simple craftsmen** <note>original: "Tag- oder Lied-Lohn / schlechter Handwercksleut"</note>), who are accustomed to feed and sustain themselves and their families by daily sweat and labor. For their debts are not only privileged by **Divine Law** (Leviticus 19:17, Deuteronomy 24:14–15, Matthew 10:10), but in almost all places they are preferred over other creditors as being more privileged. See Löpen, decision 28, number 13, book 1; see the *Saxon Consultations*, volume 3, part 3, question 105; and Rebuffi on the *Constitutions of the Kingdom of France*, book 2.

<column-break/>

Likewise, there will be no place for this grant in **sworn debts** <note>original: "debitis juratis"</note>: because a disposition of the Prince speaking in general terms is not extended to a case where an **Oath** <note>original: "Juramentum"</note> has intervened. Natta, consultation 233, number 1, book 1; Afflictis, decision 5, where he testifies it has always been so judged. Add Menochius on judicial arbitration, case 403, number 4; Coler in *Executive Process*, part 1, chapter 4, number 16; and others.

I wish this also to be understood in the case where a debtor has **expressly renounced** this benefit. It is well established that anyone can renounce a favor introduced for their own benefit. For a woman can renounce the benefit of the *Velleian Decree of the Senate* <note>A Roman law that protected women from being held liable for the debts of others</note>, and a minor can waive the right to **total restitution** <note>original: "restitutionem in integrum"</note> if they have been harmed. Hence it seemed absurd to our Emperor Justinian to return to that which someone thought should be renounced. Nor does the law allow that which was once renounced to be restored. And these things proceed as a rule, unless the Prince grants a dispensation at the petition of the burdened debtor and makes **express mention of the oath or renunciation** in the decree—namely, that notwithstanding the oath and renunciation, the tenor of the Letters of Moratorium must be observed. This is especially so since the relaxation of an oath also falls within the power of a secular Prince, which is particularly held among us: since the power is found granted to the Imperial Chamber by his Imperial Majesty and the States of the Empire in the **Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original: "der Cammer Gerichts Ordnung"</note>, part 2, title on the **Relaxation of Oaths**.

Furthermore, letters of this kind are not to be extended to **Ecclesiastical or pious places**. For the favor shown to the Church is great, and is to be preferred even to public convenience. Marta, *On Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction*, part 4, chapter 171, number 7.

Nor do they apply to **Fiscal debts** <note>term: <term>debita Fiscalia</term> refers to taxes or monies owed to the state treasury</note>. For no one ought to demand anything damaging to the Treasury or the law. It is necessary for the Republic that fiscal debts be collected as quickly as possible. This conclusion is accepted by common consensus, unless the Prince, moved by special clemency, wishes to waive the privilege of his treasury and wait for the debtor’s "fatter fortune" <note>A legal idiom meaning waiting until the debtor has more significant assets</note>.

Nor are they extended to **debts of a ward** <note>original: "debita pupillaria"</note>: because the Treasury, the Church, and the Ward <note>A minor under legal guardianship</note> are usually equated regarding granted privileges. This is so unless the ward can feed and sustain themselves from their own means in the meantime.

Nor do they apply to a debt arising from the sale of **foodstuffs and provisions** <note>original: "eduliorum & rerum comestibilium"</note>, in the "larder," as they say...

<summary>This page details the legal limitations of moratoriums (stays of debt payment), noting that they do not protect guarantors, do not apply to criminal fines, and cannot be used against "privileged" debts like those owed to laborers, the Church, the State Treasury, or orphans.</summary>

# 4. Receipt. <term>Apocha</term>.
<note>An Apocha is a formal written acknowledgment of payment.</note>

An **Apocha** is nothing other than a writing made by a **Creditor** and given to a **debtor**, by which he declares that payment has been made to him by that same debtor. This is commonly called a **Quittance** <note>original: "Quittantia"</note> or **Receipt** <note>original German: "Quittung"</note>, from the French word *quitter*, which is the same as to liberate, **to count someone free and clear** <note>original German: "einen los und ledig zehlen"</note>. Both derive from "quiet" <note>Latin: "quies"</note>: because it renders the debtor "quiet" or settled, **so that one may no longer sue him** <note>original German: "daß man ihn nicht ferner ansprechen darff."</note>. Hence it is also usually called a **quieting** <note>original: "quietatio"</note>, as if it makes the debtor quiet. For it is a declaration of paid money, as in the Digest on the recovery of undue payments. It was called a **clearing receipt** <note>original: "Apocha evacuatoria"</note>, by which the creditor declared the money paid to him for the purpose of clearing the obligation, once the security was admitted. But when the security was returned, a clearing receipt was not given, as if the return of the **signed bond** <note>original: "Chirographi"</note> were sufficient to prove payment, Law 11 on Pacts. And a quieting does not so much bring about the payment as it does the **proof** of it, Law 46 at the end of the Digest on payments.

It must be noted, however, that **general receipts** <note>receipts covering all debts rather than specific ones</note> are "captious" <note>deceptive or tricky</note>, as witnessed by Magonius in the Lucca Decisions, 9, number 35. Pierre Rebuffus also notes that the Prudent Men rightly struck down "captious" liberations. Nevertheless, Göden says in Counsel 61, number 13, that these same receipts are most effective in universal or general actions. See also Andreas Scheffer, part two, question 15, throughout.

The words of a Receipt, however general they may be, ought not to be extended to a case that contains inequity within itself. See Cravetta, Counsel 221.

### ADDITION.

If a creditor has made two receipts for a debtor, what kind of payment is presumed to have been made? See Rudinger, Century 4, observation 17, number 4. When a general receipt may be requested, number 5. When a receipt should be made, see Hieronymus of Cologne on the rendering of accounts, chapter 4, paragraph 25. Whether a double payment is presumed from doubled receipts? Chapter 5, paragraph 4, question 8. A receipt, even if general, is not extended to things unthought of or unknown, even if a clause is added by which one promises that he will seek nothing further, chapter 8, paragraph 8. A receipt is made in faith of a dissolved amount when the person making the receipt has been satisfied in all things, Barbosa, book 15, chapter 7, axiom 1. No one can be compelled to make general receipts, axiom 2.

<meta>This page continues the legal encyclopedia under the letter Q, moving from the topic of moratoriums (stays of payment) into the legal requirements and effects of receipts and settlements, followed by definitions of Hanseatic "Quarter Cities" and the nature of "Sabbath Questions" in legal practice.</meta>

874
**Treasury of Practical Law, Enlarged**

<column-break/>

Debtors who produce **receipts** <note>original: "Apochas"</note> should not be easily condemned to provisional payment, according to Faber’s Code. After 30 days, a creditor cannot prove that payment was not actually made if they have already issued a receipt, as noted in the Code on non-enumerated money. This is supported by Zanger, Carpzov, and others, though some argue the rule differs in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiæ"; referring to moral or canon law rather than civil court</note>. If there are conflicting documents—one proving a debt and another proving payment—legal authorities like Pacianus suggest the matter should be decided by an oath. In his 1649 legal dissertation at Strasbourg, Johann Melchior Sax discussed the legal maxim: **"Pay first, litigate later"** <note>original: "Solve & Repete"; German: "Geld vor, Recht nach"</note>. For very small debts, a formal written discharge is not strictly necessary, according to Sprenger.

Those who act **cautiously** <note>original: "cautè"</note> ensure that receipts include specific language stating that the plaintiff, from now and for all eternity, in no way or manner—whether in or out of court, before lower, middle, or higher courts—shall sue, take action against, or complain against the defendant. Instead, they must declare themselves satisfied and fully paid once and for all. Likewise, they renounce all **legal exceptions** <note>original: "Exceptionum"; formal defenses used to void a contract</note>, such as the claim of insufficient consideration, deceptive persuasion, haste, erroneous or missed calculations, or **injury beyond half the value** <term>laesio enormis|A legal doctrine allowing a contract to be rescinded if the price was less than half the actual value</term>. They also renounce claims that something else was agreed or intended but not recorded in writing, or any other excuse the human mind could devise. They must intend to give up these rights entirely in an eternal, constant, perpetual, and irrevocable settlement. If someone pays a debt in full but loses the receipt or forgets they have it, and is subsequently sued and forced to pay again, they may sue for the return of the second payment once the receipt is found, according to Berlichius.

Regarding the specific effects and requirements of a receipt, see Zörer. Can those who have reached 18 years of age issue a receipt to their guardians without a **curator** <note>a court-appointed legal assistant for minors</note>? No, according to the Welser Court Ordinances. Those under 25 years old generally do not have the power to issue receipts without a curator, per the Altdorf consultations. For an extensive discussion on when a **proxy** <note>original: "Procuratore"</note> has the power to issue receipts, see Boerius.

### 5. Quarter City. The Four Metropolises of the Hanseatic Cities.

In the context of the Hanseatic League, the "Quarter Cities" <note>German: "Quartierstädt"</note> refer to the four principal cities of that 

<column-break/>

alliance. See part 1 of the **Brunswick Affairs, page 523.** Dr. Tabor also discusses this, as does Limnaeus in *Public Law*. I also recommend my patron in Basel, Dr. Remigius Fesch, in his work on *Alliances*.

### 6. Sabbath Questions.

Not every question deserves an answer; a foolish question refutes itself, as Justus Oldekop writes against Carpzov. A heated response is not necessarily an insult, according to Klock. True proof results from the answers given in court. Regarding **Sabbath Questions** <term>Quæstiones Sabbathinæ|Difficult or "singular" legal problems, traditionally debated by scholars on Saturdays (the Sabbath)</term>, and why they are so named, see Viglius van Zuichem and Espich. Rebhan disagrees, believing they are named for the *time* they are discussed rather than the *subject matter*. A "Sabbath consultation" is one that is unique, dangerous, and difficult. Rofredus of Benevento wrote on these, and Bullaeus proposes and decides thirteen such questions. Useless questions are listed by Limnaeus. Every legal question concerns a doubtful case, per Barbosa. Some ridiculous questions regarding Doctors of Law are noted by Walther; these are neither useful nor necessary, yet examiners sometimes propose them to candidates during exams. Zeiller notes that when everyone gives a different answer, it is as if no one has answered at all. To fail to respond to objections is a sign of an arrogant or unskilled mind, according to Mantica. Jacob Ayrer, in his *Historical Process*, details when a witness is bound to answer or not. A good response is praised for being distinct, serious, sharp, and courteous—not obscure, hasty, peevish, or proud, as Gerard de Stökken writes extensively. 

When the envoys of the defeated leaders Antony, Otho, and Maxentius made unfair demands, the victors Augustus, Vitellius, and Constantine dismissed them without any response out of just indignation. As the ancient poet says:

> He does not respond poorly, for the first man asked poorly.

This is found in Quintilian’s *Oratorical Institutions*. Who would blame the Emperors Constantine and Henry I? When the Bulgarians and Hungarians demanded tribute from the Empire, the former sent back animal dung and the latter a mangy dog, accompanied by bitter replies. One famous man was so celebrated for the fearsomeness of his response that he need not be named; when he admitted several envoys from the enemy, they were so terrified by his "Martial" face, his glowing eyes, and his breath full of rage that not one of them could utter the speech they had practiced to perfection. Instead, first one, then another, then a third of this—

### R.

### 1. Radiren. Erasure.
Whether and to what extent it is presumed that a "scraped" <note>erased by scraping the parchment</note> and crossed-out writing is false, is taught by Antonio Bullae, *in the tenth decade of counsels, response 2.*

->ADDITION.<-

It matters whether the erasure or cancellation is in a substantial part of the legal Instrument or not. If it is not, we will deny that it is thereby either spoiled or made suspicious, unless perhaps the erasure is so large that it induces a presumption of fraud. It is different if it happens in an accidental part. Thus Besold, *Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

**Treasuries of Practice, Augmented**

<note>This text continues a legal discussion on the status of captives from the previous page.</note> ...possession. <note>original: "l. 43. §. fin. de legat. 1. l. 3. §. 3. de homine lib. exhib."</note> On legacies and on the production of a free man. Christian captives do not become slaves, even if they are captured in a most just war. They can, however, be detained until they pay a **Ransom** <note>original: "Lytrum" from the Greek λύτρον</note>. Once this is paid, they are free along with all their goods. This is true unless perhaps they are released earlier under a sworn caution or even a simple promise <note>original: "auf Cavaliers-Parole"; on a gentleman’s word of honor</note>. This is treated extensively by Johannes Philippi, Jurisconsult, in *The Practical Use of Justinian’s Institutes, Book 1, Title 5, Section 4, Eclogue 37, numbers 1 to 5.* Now, military parties enter into certain mutual agreements regarding the payment of ransom for captives and the total sum, which agreement they call **a Cartel** <note>original: "ein Cartell"</note>, number 12. In former times, military pay was settled from the ransoms of captives, as noted by Klock *on the Treasury, Book 2, chapter 88, number 8*, and as is clear from Aristotle and Sabellicus *Book 3, Ennead 4 and Book 9, Ennead 3*. Today, however, these ransoms go to whichever private individual reduced the enemy to captivity; it is almost an accepted custom that the captive pays, in place of a ransom, an amount equal to one month's wages. Such was the humanity of the Greeks that those captured in war could redeem their freedom for a pound of gold. *Aristotle, 5th Book of Ethics, chapter 7.*

I can retain a person redeemed from the enemy until the ransom is paid, just as a hospitaller <term>caupo: an innkeeper or host</term> can retain the goods of a guest staying with him who does not pay, according to the accepted custom in Germany. Struvius *on Private Revenge, chapter 6, Aphorism 9, number 9, p. 68.* Regarding when the Captor holds the ransom of a prisoner of war and when the King holds it, see Boerius *Decision 178, numbers 3 and 4.* See also Fürer’s transaction with bandits regarding a **ransom** <note>original: "λυτρῳ"</note> in *Fürer's Itinerary, page 83.* **The Heathen Toll** <note>German: "Der Heiden Zoll"</note> is applied when Turks or Moors are ransomed. If one is released for money at or under 200 Crowns, he pays eight Ducats to the King for the toll. If he buys himself off for more than 200 Crowns up to 500, he gives 10 Ducats for the toll; from 500 Crowns to 1000, he pays 15 Ducats in toll. Megiser in *Delights of Naples, p. 236.*

### 3. Rappen. A tiny coin, struck with the sign of a raven.

**Rapp**, a small coin succeeding the Pfennig, named after the **Ravens** <note>German: "Corvi"</note> which are the heraldic insignia of the people of Freiburg, who were the first to strike this money. Although later Basel and other Republics struck the same coins under their own insignia, the original name remained. Hanfman *on Monetary Matters, among the Basel Disputations, volume 2, thesis 5, under letter f.* Commonly, 10 of these are worth one **Batzen** <term>Batzen: a silver-copper coin used in the Swiss cantons and southern Germany.</term>

->ADDITIO.<-

Auer repeats these things word for word in *The Law of Money, chapter 13, number 71.* See also Wehner under this word. Meichsner, *volume 1, folio 99 and following*, mentions **a pound of Rappen** in Kaisersberg. See also Auer, *chapter 12, number 66.*

### 4. Räthe. Councilors.

Regarding the process to be instituted against a **Councilor** <note>Latin: "Consiliarius"</note>, and whether a Council can excuse itself if it reports an action based on a command, even if that command cannot be produced, see very extensively Reusner, *volume 3, counsel 15 and following, especially 19 and 20*, where he also treats the punishment of such a Councilor.

->ADDITIO.<-

If the parties use the clause "whatever the Counsel may be, we shall follow it," whether they simultaneously renounce all right of Appeal: Pax Scala, *Book 4, chapter 19.* To this end, see the political dissertations of Mr. Winger regarding Councilors, and especially the excellent Disputations of Mr. Dr. Rebhan and Lauterbach regarding Counsel.

On this matter, see Mr. Harsdorff in his *Great Theater of Pleasurable and Instructive History, Appendix number 291.* Regarding the employment of a Wise Man's Counsel in legal cases: Pax Scala of Padua, *part 3, p. 1, folio 331.* Martinus Garatus of Lodi wrote regarding the Councilors of Princes.

**Kings play with their Councilors like they do with oranges: when they have tossed them around in their hands for a long time, they no longer value them.** To this, someone said: "Yes, when they no longer give off a good scent and become rotten," because the first Councilor of a Prince was being accused of laziness.

Whether every Magistrate ought to be flanked by Councilors: Lichenthal in *Political College, disputation 11, question 1.* Whether a Councilor who is not asked is bound to warn his Prince: *question 4.* Whether a Councilor is bound to go into the Consistory if he knows that some counsel is to be discussed to which he cannot, in good conscience, assent: *question 6.* Whether a Councilor should be punished if a counsel results in a disastrous outcome: *question 7.* **It is an "Oak-plan"** <note>German: "Eichen-Anschlag"</note>. Dr. Luther mentions this proverb in the *3rd Jena Volume, on leaf 273 or 248*, in the exposition of the 3rd Chapter of the Prophet Habakkuk, and says: "They are one's own plans, as they say, it is an **Oak-plan** <note>German: "Eichen-Anschlag"</note>, by which one means to say it is an **Own-plan** <note>German: "eigen Anschlag"</note>; just as one says **Oak-leaves stink** <note>German: "Eichen Laub stinckt"</note>, by which one means to say **Own-praise stinks** <note>German: "eigen Lob stinckt"</note>." This is because all of one's own plans certainly fail. An "own plan" is that which God does not give, and which one's own reason undertakes and devises, of which all of Scripture says they are in vain, and the whole of Ecclesiastes <note>original: "Prediger Salomon"</note> rejects such "own plans." For man is vanity—that is, nothing. Therefore, it is said of those who have such plans and believe they have hit the mark well, in this mocking proverb: **"Oak-plans and counsels are good, and they last a long time."** Martin Mylius in *The Pleasure Garden of Delightful Wisdom, page 479.* Whether for an Emperor, slow Councilors are more to be desired than those of sharp and subtle wit: Otto in *Law...*
