### 5. **Removal from the Council seat, oversight, etc.**
->To remove from the Senate, etc.<-

There is a long-standing distinction both in the Body of Law and in the practice and observation of the Roman Republic throughout all times, between whether someone has been moved and ejected from the Senate because of some disgraceful act, or whether they were merely passed over and not chosen. This is much like the difference in a parent’s will among children between "disinheritance" and "omission" <note>In Roman law, being "passed over" (praeteritio) was a legal technicality distinct from being explicitly disinherited for a cause.</note>; just as in military discipline, a discharge for cause <note>original: "causaria missio"</note> is one thing, and a dishonorable discharge is another.

In Augsburg, the following decree is read annually: We, Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1519–1556</note>, acknowledge for Ourselves and Our successors in the Empire publicly with this letter, and make known to everyone, that in the recently passed year [15]48, on the 3rd day of the month of August, regarding the governance and administration of Our and the Empire’s city, we have given an Ordinance, etc. *A little further down:* Item, the 31 newly elected persons shall immediately choose three from the higher society on the first round, and the 4th from the commonalty on the 2.nd, the remaining three from the commonalty on the 3rd round, but shall not require them to attend until the following offices are filled. Subsequently, the same 31 newest members of the Small Council shall choose from among themselves 7 Secret ones, and from those same 7 Secret ones, they shall choose 2 Caretakers <note>original: "Pfleger," a high-ranking administrative or guardian office</note>; yet none of these shall be removed or changed from the rank to which he was once appointed or elected, without serious, lawful evidence of his incapacity, significant misconduct, or other substantial causes, and even then, not otherwise than by the judgment of the aforementioned Council. However, the right of free departure shall remain unburdened thereby, and shall be as open to them as to others, etc. And it should be noted that no one is to be excluded from the Council seat on account of kinship, unless it is a relationship that prevents marriage or causes one to be rejected as a witness.

### 6. **Reason of State, the Law of the State.**
*Sluter in "Observations on Hippolithus à Lapide’s Dissertation on the Reason of State."* See *Mr. Speidelius in "Notable Observations," and Conring in "Political Observations on Machiavelli’s Prince."*

->ADDITION.<-

On the Reason of State in the first century, *Dr. Stirn on the Constitutions of Princes, book 9, sections 2, 3, 4, etc.*; in the second century *book 9, section 16*; in the third century *book 9, section 19*; in the fourth century *book 10.*

<column-break/>

Section 3. In the fifth century *book 10, section 6*; in the sixth century *book 10, section 9*; in the seventh century *book 10, section 12*; in the eighth century *book 10, section 12*; in the ninth century *book 11, section 3*; in the tenth century *book 11, section 3*; in the eleventh century *book 11, section 6*; in the twelfth century *book 11, section 9*; in the thirteenth century *book 11, section 12*; in the fourteenth century *book 11, section 15*; in the fifteenth century *book 12, section 1, etc.*; in the sixteenth century *book 12, section 6, etc.*; in the seventeenth century *book 12, section 11, etc.*

The term **Reason of State** <term>original: "Ratio Status"; the justification for a nation's actions based on its own interests rather than morality or law</term> was indeed not used by Latin writers, but was passed from the Italians to the French and other nations with such a strong assertion of custom that—what not many decades ago was used timidly, rarely, and with a disclaimer—is today bandied about among the formal vocabulary of politicians in daily writing and speech. Regarding things born outside the boundaries of the schools and adapted to the spirit of the civil stage (which is accustomed to serving the times), it is permissible to speak with those who lack neither reason for their authority nor authority for their reason, even when antiquity is lacking. Some have preferred to call it **Extraordinary Prudence**; but by that kind of name, the genuine force and nature of the thing, which the Italians noted not inelegantly as "Reason of State," is by no means clearly expressed. For a judgment on the work of Botero, on the rules of Palazzo, Chiaramonti, and Settala, see the *Excellent Mr. Boecler in the Program proposed at Strasbourg, March 7, 1648*, where he concludes: "Reason of State remains the enigma of the age, a matter of subtlety; with Proteus, it is Thetis; with Paris, it is Helen; with Ulysses, it is Penelope." <note>Boecler uses mythological figures known for changing shape or causing conflict to describe how slippery the concept of "Reason of State" is.</note> Mostly, the curious and ambitious cast aside things that should remain silent. Yet you would not exclude grave and prudent men from this business: whether they reasoned that things which could not be changed by others should be turned into wisdom, or whether they judged that by that very display and preaching of obscure matters, the curious are more truly deluded than educated, and that the names of deeper prudence are made public, rather than its true importance. Let them see how greatly they sin against the precepts not only of Justice, but of Prudence itself, who today instill nothing else into Princes but "Reason of State," that is, their own interest and utility. Indeed, even Horace once felt this way in that verse: "Utility is almost the mother of the just and the equitable." <note>original: "Est ipsa utilitas justi propè mater & æqui"</note> To be sure, this was among the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus, often stereotyped in this period as pursuing only pleasure or self-interest</note>, from whose family Horace also came, as Cujas says *on the law "All Peoples," 9, Digest on Justice and Law.* And from that same herd are almost all those pagan Advisors, according to *Cujas in the stated law.* Whatever other intention Pierre Gassendi might assign to his Epicurus, see *Gassendi in "The System of Epicurean Philosophy," part 3, title 11, page 443* and *Dr. Tabor on "Confrontations," page 61.* By the standard of "Reason of State," Justice today is ruled and directed not legally, but economically and politically, through right or wrong; nor is damage to the Conscience cared for, provided there is profit in the money-chest. Whence the following verses:

> When Justice ceased,
> To dwell upon the earth,
> Reason of State succeeded,
> A sea of calamities.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of social and criminal order, transitioning from the conduct of officials and the nature of litigation to the specific criminal laws governing robbery and highway crimes.</meta>

> What she might be, King Jupiter <note>This "she" likely refers to "Litigation" or "the Lawsuit," personified as a goddess of misery.</note>
> does not know, but they know well,
> those who have established her
> as a patroness in so many miseries.

From this, without a doubt, comes the German proverb regarding one of two litigants who is wealthier or more powerful, which is very common today: **"He is much too heavy for him."** <note>original: "Er ist ihm viel zu schwer." This implies that a powerful opponent has more "weight" in court.</note> See what follows in Oldekop’s *On Oaths in Another's Soul, page 84 at the end and 85 at the beginning.*

### 7. **Robbery.**

See Bökel, *in Visionary Disquisitions, 9, question 6.*
Not only are the main perpetrators of a robbery punished, but also those who provided them with help in any way. <note>original: "l. 1. ff. de receptat. l. 1. C. de bis, qui latron. occultat." Citing the Roman Digest and Codex on the punishment of those who harbor bandits.</note>

However, in deciding the punishment, the quantity and value of the items taken by the highwayman do not come into consideration: since **Article 126 of the Criminal Constitution** <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the unified criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1532.</note> does not determine this, but speaks generally and without distinction.

Thus in France, highwaymen who extort even the smallest amount of money from a traveler on the royal road outside the cities by armed force are put to death; and Bodin notes in *The Republic, book 2, final chapter*, that the same practice is accepted by the customs of the Milanese, who use the death penalty even for a single gold coin.

Plunderers are not simply bandits; they are those who wickedly rob a person of their goods without killing them. <note>original: "l. capitalium. 28. §. grassatores. 10. ff. de pœn." This distinguishes between "prædones" (plunderers) and "latrones" (violent bandits).</note> See Damhouder *in Criminal Practice, chapter 102, number 1.*

It is, however, generally concluded by legal scholars that those who have previously behaved well and have been led to such an attack only a single time should not be immediately punished with their lives. According to the **Common Law** <note>The *Jus Commune*, the body of Roman-based law used across Europe.</note>, those who have committed this crime only once are not to be executed, but are either to be condemned to the mines or banished to islands; the text is explicit in the law regarding capital crimes, in the section on highwaymen <note>original: "l. capitalium. §. grassatores. ff. de pœn."</note>. There it states that highwaymen who do this for the sake of plunder are considered close to bandits; and if they set out to attack and rob with a blade (therefore violence is required, and the statute punishing the **highway robber** <note>original: "Straßenrauber"</note> extraordinarily does not extend to someone who **steals a horse on the road** <note>original: "der auf der Straßen Roß stielet"</note>), they are punished by death, especially if they have done this frequently and on journeys. Others are condemned to the mines or banished to islands. The commentary on the same law regarding capital crimes holds the same, noting that if it is a first offense, one deserves mercy from the gallows; see Bocer, *on Feuds, page 165.* This is also proven by the text in the **Code on Episcopal Hearings**, which states that crimes do not receive the remission of pardon unless they were committed only once. There is another commentary to the same effect which states that if someone has acted as a highwayman only once, he is held under the Julian Law on public violence and 

<column-break/>

ought not to be hung from the gallows; Ludovico à Peguera also provides his assent in *Decision 40, number 7 and following.*

In the same way, Matthias Stephani, in his writing on **Article 127 of the Criminal Constitution of Charles V**, writes that it is not customary for highwaymen to be punished with the ultimate penalty and death unless every single one of these factors is present: namely, that they attack with a blade, intended to rob, and have done this frequently and specifically on journeys. See Faber in the *Code, book 9, title 24, number 3.*

So too, Bernhard Zieritzius, in his notes on **Article 126 of the Carolinian Constitution**, testifies that because of a matter not so great, a sentence of deportation was dictated by the Juridical Faculty of **Wittenberg** in the year 1616, even though that robbery had been committed with armed force and on the royal highway.

And Lord Francis Pfeil decides in almost a similar case (*Counsel 153*) that for an attempted but not fully completed robbery, a punishment of temporary banishment or eternal exile from the land should take place, according to both the **Imperial** and the **Criminal Capital Ordinances** <note>The *Halsgerichts-Ordnung*, literally the "Neck-Court Ordinance," referring to crimes punishable by beheading or hanging.</note>.

Therefore, the limitations and moderations of punishments—which are commonly applied to highwaymen and plunderers based on the Common Law and the unanimous conclusion of the same—are in no way contrary to **Article 126 of the Criminal Capital Ordinance**, which, while it sets as a rule that malicious robbers shall be punished with death, nevertheless explicitly refers to and draws upon the common Imperial laws. Thus, it fully approves and contains within itself all the restrictions and interpretations of said common laws; for the thing referred to is seen to be contained in the reference along with all its qualities, according to the common rules of law.

Regarding the most cruel death of robbers among the Etruscans, see Talentoni, *On Recondite Matters, book 1, chapter 19*, and **Virgil**, *Aeneid, book 8*, where he describes the cruelty of Mezentius, who was one of the Princes of Etruria, and says:

> He even used to join dead bodies to the living,
> Matching hands to hands and faces to faces,
> A kind of torture; as they flowed with gore and decay
> In that miserable embrace, he killed them with a long, slow death.

### **ADDITION.**

# Lit. R.

<note>original: "num, Rupertus obs. ad Flori lib. 2. c. 9. §. 3." This refers to legal commentaries on the Roman historian Lucius Annaeus Florus.</note> Divided spoils not yet captured; the same, book 4, chapter 12, section 24. 2. A tenth of the spoils vowed to Apollo. Book 2, chapter 4, section: The objective is to delay the enemy, book 3, chapter 5, section 18. The distinction between a thief and a highwayman <note>original: "furem & graffatorem." A thief steals by stealth; a highwayman by violence.</note>. Regarding the punishment of highwaymen, see Rittershusius in *New Works*, page 701. Does an oath given to a plunderer or bandit create an obligation? Zahn, *On Lies*, book 3, chapter 8, number 70 and following; Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, book 2, chapter 13, section 13.

If a messenger on a journey is robbed, wounded, or captured by bandits, or loses his own property through shipwreck or another accident without his own fault, the question is asked: can he claim that loss back from the person who sent him? By law, this seems to be denied; treated at length by Lauterbach, *On the Messenger*, thesis 64, chapter 10. What constitutes robbery <note>original: "Rapina"</note>, see Didacus in *The Rule of Sin*, part 2, section 1, number 2. Regarding wartime plundering, see Besold, *On the Art and Law of War*, chapter 8, folio 126. Who may be called a plunderer, and whether he loses his expenses and improvements made on a thing seized by force, see Cravetta, *Counsel 87*. How one who has been robbed can prove his loss, see Mynsing, century 5, observation 71. Whether and to what extent a territorial lord is bound to reimburse the losses of those robbed in his lands, Mynsing, observation 70. "Plunderer" is understood in two ways in the Law, Rittershusius on law 23, *Digest on the Rules of Law*, page 248. Who are "little bandits" or "bandit-catchers," see the same. Bandits and plunderers are contrasted there.

### 8. Robber Castles. <term>Castra prædonum.</term> <note>Literally "Camps of Plunderers."</note>

In German history, two hundred years ago and more, there is very frequent mention of **robber castles** <term>Raubschlösser</term>, and how they were destroyed; see Freher on Andlo, folio 196, book 2, chapter 11.

And regarding the Buchovia region, which was once full of bandits, and the many bandit hideouts destroyed there, see Bruschius, *On the Monasteries of Fulda*, folio 62.

For since there was no "public peace," and private individuals were devastating everything everywhere by declaring private wars, eventually those soldiers (who then were almost exclusively Knights, or nobles and their ministers) degenerated into plunderers.

Frederick I, Elector Palatine, most severely restrained and extinguished this madness of the plunderers; among other things, this praise is read inscribed on his tomb: *The Thunderbolt of Plunderers.* This same plague later gave cause for the Swabian League; see Freher in the cited place, and also Brower, *Annals of Fulda*, book 1, final chapter, folio 98.

->ADDITION.<-

See Lord Speidel in *Notable Matters*.

### 9. Maintaining Smoke and Light. <term>Larem fovere.</term> <note>Literally "To cherish the hearth."</note>

To have a "Lar"—that is, a hearth or a domestic dwelling—is called in German **the maintenance of smoke and light** <term>die Rauch- und Lichthaltung</term>, or **to have one's own smoke** <term>Einen eignen Rauch haben</term>.

Thus, in certain places, it is not permitted that anyone who is not a citizen, or who does not have

<column-break/>

special permission, should set up his own household, but he must instead take his meals with a host; see my work *On the Law of Citizens*, folio 81.

->ADDITION.<-

See Lord Speidel in *Notable Matters*.

### 10. Smoke-Hens, Carnival-Hens. <term>Gallinæ præstariæ.</term> <note>Tribute chickens paid to a lord.</note>

In the March <note>The Margraviate of Brandenburg.</note>, as witnessed by Scheplitz in *Brandenburg Customs*, part 2, title 3, number 6. The **smoke-hen** <term>Das Rauchhun</term> is a sign of jurisdiction; and to whomever it is paid, the jurisdiction over that subject entirely belongs to him, according to Pruckmann, *Counsel 21*, number 83, book 1, where he says these are called "Jurisdictional Hens." Add Husanus in the treatise *On the Property of Men*, chapter 6, number 64; Ernst Cothmann, *Counsel 42*, number 33 and following, and *Counsel 47*, numbers 146 and 162. He also says at number 164: this is especially true if such a custom is proven and other supporting evidence concurs. And that these hens signify "High Jurisdiction" <note>original: "merum Imperium." The power of life and death/high criminal justice.</note> is testified by Husanus in the cited place. In number 64, he gives this reason (as I said under the word "Serf"): because those hens fly up high and rest there, they therefore signify the "height" of the Law; Tileman, *On Benign Practical Observations*, Pentecost 5, observation 1. See above all Hering, *On Mills*, question 33.

In some places, such as with the Counts of Sulz in Glöckau, it is the custom that every subject who has his own "smoke" and uses the common lands pays one hen annually, which is called a **smoke-hen** <term>Rauchhenne</term>, to his lord as a sign of subjection.

->ADDITION II.<-

See above under the word **Hens** <term>Hennen</term>.

### 11. Tipsy, Lively. <term>Ebrius alacris.</term> <note>Literally "A cheerful drunk."</note>

*Risch* is an old German word for "lively," "gallant," or "fresh" <note>original: "gaillard, sive frisch, προθύμως (prothymōs)." The Greek term means "with readiness or zeal."</note>. In the martyrology of the Apostles, regarding a certain luxurious monk:

> Yet at the table
> He was ever lively <note>original: "rische"</note>
> and in full strength, etc.

Those who are half-drunk are called *Rüschig* <note>Tipsy/merry</note>, certainly from this "liveliness," because wine gladdens the heart of man, as Goldast teaches in *Ancient Admonitions*, folio 376. And even today we say of someone: *he is "räuschig"*, which is used sometimes for "lively" and sometimes for "strange."

See Lord Speidel in *Notable Matters*; Anton Hanffmann, *Resolutions on Monetary Matters*, 5.

"Regals" or "Philippics," commonly called **Real**, **Spanish**, **King’s-thick-coins**, or **Philippsthaler**. <note>Large silver coins issued by Philip II of Spain, commonly used in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

### 13. Rebels. <term>Rebelles</term> <note>Those who take up arms against their sovereign or refuse to obey legal mandates</note>.

See Friedrich Mindanus, *On Process*, book 2, chapter 46; also on the seditious, see Rosbach, *Criminal Practice*; Decianum, *Criminal Treatise*, book 7, chapter 32, throughout; Mascardus, *Conclusion 1257*, throughout, regarding whether a declaratory sentence <note>A formal court ruling declaring someone's status as a rebel</note> is required. Gail, *Observations*, book 1, observation 15, number 6 and following; and *On Arrests*, chapter 10; and *On Public Peace*, book 2, chapter 3, number 16. Add Molanus, *Treatise on Keeping Faith with Heretics*; and above under **Riot** <note>original: "Aufruhr"</note>, as well as under the word **Confiscation**; also Rittershusius on the *Constitution of Henry VII* regarding who are considered rebels.

A **State of the Empire** <note>A territory or prince with a seat in the Imperial Diet</note> does not seem to be able to declare its own subjects as rebels. For no one can be a judge in their own cause, and both subjects and Lords have certain **Arbitrators** <note>original: "Austregas," referring to the *Austrägalinstanz*, a system of internal courts for resolving disputes between members of the Empire</note>; see my work *On Caring for the Republic*, folio 170.

->ADDITION.<-

Rebels are generally most defiant. Mr. Rupert, in his *Observations on Florus*, book 3, chapter 19, section 2: The Romans pursued **Rebels and Traitors** more fiercely than other enemies. In book 1, chapter 20, section 1: Rebels and those serving the enemy lose their privileges. Mundius, *On the Counts Palatine*, chapter 5, numbers 78, 79. Are the **children of a rebellion** punished? Harpprecht on the *Institutes*, "On Public Judgments," number 47 and following. As far as conquered nations or even rebellious cities are concerned, the Romans judged it a matter of rashness if they were permitted to possess arms. Tacitus, *Histories*, book 2, chapter 6. Thus Julius Valens publicly fined the people of Vienne in Gaul, who were rebelling, by stripping them of their arms. The same in *Histories*, book 1, chapter 6. And this was altogether a solemn custom: to surrender to the Emperor, to lay down arms, and to command the conquered. Livy, book 4, chapter 10. Mr. Tabor, *On Arms*, chapter 3, number 2. Gigas deals extensively with **Rebellion** in his work *On the Crime of Lese-Majesty* <note>Treason against the sovereign</note> throughout. Arms are to be taken away from rebels and the seditious. Mr. Rupert—my teacher, to be honored even after his death—on Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter 3, section 4.

What it means to **rebel**. Papafava, *Decision 589*, number 4 and following. Regarding Rebels, see Marc Antonio Peregrini, *Treatise on the Rights of the Treasury*, book 3, chapter 8, folio 240 and following. Who is properly called a Rebel. Aymon Cravetta, *Counsel 542*. What a Rebel **forfeits and loses** when the crime is committed. Peregrini, *On the Rights of the Treasury*, title 8. On the **children of Rebels**. Peregrini, same book, title 9, folio 244. Whether an **inferior Prince** can declare his own subjects as rebels. Besold, *Treatise on Political Principles*, folio 175, number 5. Whether a firm peace can be made with rebels. Besold, *On Legates*, folio 181, number 8. The **goods of rebels** granted to others must be returned after the Peace. Boër, *Decision 33*, number 7.

### 14. Vengeance; "I will avenge myself." <term>Vindicta</term>.

The words: "I will vindicate myself," or "I will take revenge on such a person," (**I will avenge myself**, or **I will not let it go unavenged** <note>original: "ich will mich rechen, oder ich will's ungerochen nicht lassen"</note>), are in case of doubt to be understood as **legal vengeance** <note>Seeking justice through a court of law rather than illegal violence</note>, according to the teachings of Treutler, *Counsel 86*, number 28, volume 2; Bullæus, in *Academic Discourse 3*, miscellany 8; and in *Decade of Counsels 5*, question 6. For words that can be interpreted for good or for evil should, in doubt, be understood in a favorable way, so that the presumption of a crime is excluded. Alexander, *Counsel 188*, book 7; *Counsel 233*, column 1, book 6; Modestinus Pistoris, volume 2, *Counsel 22*, number 51. Baldus, *Counsel 98*, book 3, where he says that even boasting or **threats** made generally about "expelling someone from their possession" do not induce "just fear" <note>A legal standard for duress</note>, but should be interpreted in a milder sense and understood as a **lawful eviction**. Unless there are certain circumstances that suggest otherwise.

->ADDITION.<-

Vengeance is not to be inflicted. For it is not to be "taken," but rather an injury is to be "repelled." Barbosa, book 19, chapter 23, axiom 2. The words: **I will be zealous for that, or avenge it** <note>original: "Ich will das eyvern, oder rächen"</note>; or **I will remember this against you** <note>original: "Ich will dirs gedencken"</note>. Carpzov, *Jurisprudence of the Forensic Constitution of Saxony*, part 4, chapter 15, definition 9. Mr. Georg Adam Struve, *On Private Vengeance*, chapter 1, aphorism 7, number 2. Arumæus on the *Golden Bull*, discourse 6, thesis 17. Vengeance intended to cause pain to another out of hatred is **illicit by Natural Law**. Struve, same treatise, chapter 1, aphorism 3, page 6. It arises from immoderate anger, which provides a reason but does not pay heed [to moderation], ibid. number 1. It is not to be taken in the manner of wild beasts, but as right reason demands. Ibid. aphorism 2, number 1, page 3. It must be understood as legal vengeance, not vengeance of fact <note>i.e., through the legal system rather than physical retaliation</note>. Bullæus, *Counsel 5*, number 29; and the same in *Leisure Hours*, Academic Distinction 3, miscellany 8. Treutler, volume 2, *Counsel 86*, number 28.

If the threats are ambiguous, such as: **I will avenge myself on you, I will be zealous for that**, or **I will remember that**, it is to be left to the **judge's discretion** to decide based on the quality of the persons, the words, and the circumstances. Liebenthal in *Political College*, exercise 14, question 11. Whether and to what extent threats prove "fear" <note>coercion</note>. Cravetta, *Counsel 461*.

### 15. Account Books, Debt Books, Accounts. <term>Libri rationum</term>.

An **Account Book** (**Calculation books, books of income and expenditure** <note>original: "Rechenbücher, Bücher Einnehmens und Ausgebens"</note>) is defined as: the business of giving and receiving, trusting, obligating, and paying on one's own behalf. *Law regarding bankers*, section *account*, Digest "On displaying [documents]." Beust on the *Law on admonishing*, numbers 10 and 12, "On Oaths."

Account Books are of various kinds. For some are made by someone by reason of their **office**, as used to be the case for money-changers, *Law on certain*, section *Money-changers*, Digest "On displaying"; and **tax collectors**, *Law on payments*, Code "On the credibility of instruments."

Some accounts are indeed prepared by someone by virtue of their administration, such as the Books of Tutors and Curators, **Guardianship Accounts** <note>original: "Pflegrechnungen"</note>, and those of other persons of this kind. See Law 1, section "on the office," *On the Distraction of Tutelage and Accounts*. See above under the word **Guardianship Account**.

There are also books written at the discretion and will of any individual as circumstances require, and these are those which one prepares for oneself privately. See Nicolaus Janua, *On Private Writings*, book "q", title "on the book of accounts," number 4. On whether and when an Account Book provides proof, see the same author throughout that section in the following numbers, and Bolognetus on the Code, title *On Producing Documents*.

There are variations: to make the account of receipts and expenses equal and to leave no remainder; **to render a poor account** <note>original: "schlechte Rechenschaft machen"</note>. See Law "Stichus," 6, regarding the banker, in the Digest, *On the Status of Freedmen*: there it says, "he shall have rendered accounts and made them equal," that is, he shall have fully satisfied and paid what he received while administering or managing the master's affairs. Here Scaevola <note>A famous Roman jurist often cited in the Digest</note> is speaking of a slave agent. See Oldendorp, Class 6, *On Actions*, title *On the Claim for Undue Payment*, folio 799.

An Account Book serves as proof against the one who wrote it. See Bartolus <note>One of the most influential medieval jurists</note> on Law "a bare account," Code, *On Donations*, column 2, verse "around the second"; and on Law "certain," section "bankers," in the Digest, same title; as well as on Law "of warning," *On Oaths*. This applies whether those accounts were written in one's own hand, or by the hand of servants or administrators, provided they remain in the possession of the master. See Giovanni Bolognetus on Law 1, number 17, Code, *On Producing Documents*. This is understood to apply if it is a complete Account Book containing regular business; it is otherwise if it were a mere **slip of paper for a memorandum** <note>original: "Schedula quaedam pro memoriali"</note>. See Bolognetus in the same place. Furthermore, it is necessary that the cause of the debt be assigned, because if none were present, the accounts would hardly provide credit. For such a book cannot induce an obligation without a cause. See Baldus on the rubric *On the Faith of Instruments*, column 13, verse "but I ask," and see Law "with what is not owed," final section, Digest, *On Proofs*.

See more in Munnoz de Escobar's *Treatise on Accounts*, and Ayrer's *On Calculation Errors*.

## 16. Law, regarding Equity and Legal Processes. <note>original Latin: "De jure & æquitate."</note>

The caution <note>a form of legal security or bail</note> of "waiting for the legal outcome" <note>original German: "deß Rechtens auszuwarten"</note> is not sufficient to release a person from arrest <note>the seizure of a person or their property to ensure they appear in court</note>, as Modestinus Pistor teaches (part 3, question 110, number 7). This is because such a caution only provides security for the pursuit of the lawsuit; since the arrested party could pursue the case through a legal representative <note>Procuratorem</note>, he does not seem to have provided security to "stand for judgment" in person <note>original Latin: "de judicio sisti"</note>. Furthermore, if he remained under arrest, the winning plaintiff could demand the defendant be handed over to him directly according to Saxon Law <note>Jus Saxonum</note>, an execution against the person that could not otherwise be carried out.

Those words, "Fairness and Legal Process" <note>original German: "Billich und Rechtswegen"</note>, in statutes are to be declared according to possibility and essence, just as in any other legal disposition where the person making the arrangement is deemed to have conformed to the common law. Cited by Johann Goeddaeus in the *Marburg Counsels*, counsel 27, under number 167; Cornelius, counsel 24, number 11, volume 2; and counsel 307, number 2, volume 4.

->ADDITION.<-

To proceed with a "fictional equity" and from one's own head is not only dangerous but also reckless and full of superficiality. Equity that is not written in law, but arises from an undigested impulse and a perceived affection of the mind against the tenor of the written law, must never be followed, according to Justus Oldekop in his treatise against Carpzov, page 218. Since the Prince is the "asylum of justice," he is not presumed to decree anything other than what the Laws intend (Bertazolli, counsel 365, number 27; Cothmann, counsel 12, numbers 1 and 4). Nor is he presumed to have wished to abolish, with one or two words, the Laws which were thought out through so many sleepless nights <note>original Latin: "vigiliis," referring to the intense study of jurists</note> (Tuschus, volume 2, letter C, conclusion 1037; Antonius, on *moratory rescripts*, conclusion 49, number 83). Equity without Law or without a written right—which is not actually written but captured deceitfully—is a most pestilential poison, and for a man lacking resources in matters of life and citizenship, it is a dire plague (Johann Garfias, *Treatise on Expenses and Improvements*, chapter 1, number 28 and following). Therefore, it is only with difficulty admitted as an extraordinary measure against the law. See the elegant discussion by Zalius under number 3 regarding the separation of goods. Lord Tabor, in *On Twice as Much*, part 2, article 7, page 122, states: "Equity is the health of the Law." Rittershusius in the *Novels*, page 124, adds: "Equity prevails over strict law." Ibid, page 523, number 48: "Equity is preferred to rigor." See also Barbosa, book 1, chapter 39, axiom 10; and Dr. Cob, question 7, on whether equity is correctly distinguished into "written" and "unwritten," and question 6: "To each his own right without harm" <note>original German: "Einem jeden an seinem Recht ohne Schaden"</note>. See Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 10, page 149. This protestation applies if the one granting a fief delivers possession a second time, so that the right of the first remains safe (Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations*, 5, thesis 2, letter B).

God preserve us from the "equity" of Parliament and from the "expediency" of the Great Council, says Franciscus Marcus (part 1, decision 13). Regarding "cunning law" <note>original Latin: "Jus versutum"</note>, which consists of the hunting for syllables, see Azon in his summary of the Code on the Julian Law regarding adultery, number 15.

<column-break/>

## 17. Clause: With all Law and Justice. <note>original Latin/German: "Cl. Mit allem Recht und Gerechtigkeit. Cl. cum omnibus juribus ac pertinentiis."</note>

By these words—namely "with all its rights or appurtenances"—it appears that even "high jurisdiction" <note>original Latin: "merum imperium," the power of the sword or capital punishment</note> is included. See Munoch, *On Presumptions*, 97, number 39, book 3; Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5; and Wesenbeck, counsel 195, numbers 107 and 119, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

When a field is sold "with its rights and appurtenances," the question is asked: what is deemed to have been sold under these names? This is often debated regarding the written instruments and documents pertaining to the land (Agricola, *On Appurtenances*, chapter 2, thesis 3, question 13). Whether a grant of a castle with its appurtenances made by a Prince also transfers high and mixed jurisdiction as a consequence? See Gail, book 2, observation 61, number 15; Molina on the *Customs of Paris*, section 1, glossary 5, number 48; Vasquius, *Controversies*, book 1, chapter 3, number 9. The praised Agricola (chapter 4, thesis 5, question 19) notes that from the grant or sale of a castle "with all rights and appurtenances which the grantor or seller has there," nothing is proven unless those specific rights appear limited by other proofs. This is because such a grant is resolved into a clause stating: "insofar as those appurtenances are established to exist." (See the Digest, *On Legacies*, law 75, section 1). See also Agricola, chapter 5, thesis 7, letter a.

Regarding the force of the clause: "I sell the ground with all rights, whatever the sold thing has above it" <note>referring to mineral or air rights</note>, see Cravetta, counsel 377.

## 18. Law-Burg. <note>original German/Latin: "Rechtburg. Rachimburgius."</note>
A Rachimburgius, or "Law-Burg," is a Judge or an Assessor to a Count.

The terms *Rathinburgius* and *Ratmiburgius* are also found. In the Salic Law <note>The ancient law code of the Salian Franks</note>, title 60: If any *Rathinburgii* residing in the *Malleberg* <note>the hill or place of judicial assembly</note> wish to speak the Law, when they have discussed a case between two parties, they must tell those who seek the case. If the *Rathinburgii* have not judged according to the Salic Law, they shall pay 15 shillings <note>original: "sol. XV," a solidus was a gold coin</note> to those against whom they gave the sentence. But if those *Rathinburgii* spoke the Law, and the one against whom they spoke contradicts them and wishes to maintain this—thinking they judged against the Law—and he cannot prove it, he shall pay 15 shillings to each of the seven *Rathinburgii*.

In the Ripuarian Law <note>Law of the Rhineland Franks</note>, title 34, section 3: If a summoned person <note>original: "mannitus"</note> delays coming, for every judicial assembly <note>mallo</note>, if the one who summoned him swears with three *Rachimburgii* in the *Araho* <note>a sacred or official place</note> that he was lawfully summoned, he shall be judged guilty of a 12-shilling fine, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding who the *Rachinburgii* were, see Lord Tabor, *On Arms*, chapter 1, number 20, where he discusses them using the Ripuarian Laws as those "speaking the Law"—that is, the assessors of the Counts who sit with them in the "castle of counsel" <note>original Latin: "burgo consilii"</note>. See also Vossius, book 2.

### 19. The Right Hand: walking to the right or left hand. <note>original Latin/German: "Dextra manus. Rechte Hand, zur rechten oder linken Hand gehen."</note>

See Master Speidelius in his *Notabilia*.

->ADDITION.<-

See above under the entry *Removing Hands and Feet*. The left hand is more idle than the right <note>original Latin: "Otiofior est finistra dextrâ"</note>. See Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 2, number 212. Among the Turks, the left is considered more honorable. See Philippus Carolus, *Various Readings*, chapter 2. Among the Greeks, the left was more honored; among the Romans <note>original Latin: "Latinos"</note>, the right was more honored. This is clearly shown by the Church Councils, especially the Council of Chalcedon <note>A major church council held in 451 AD</note>, in which the Roman Legates and the Archbishops of Constantinople and Antioch occupy the left side—surely because the more noble people occupy the nobler side. Limnaeus adds more on this in book 4, chapter 9, number 92, volume 2 of his additions. The right hand is adorned with the military ring. See Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 6, page 203. Honor sits at the right side of virtue; hence, if there are many people, the one in the middle will be the most dignified, although in this matter the customs of each region must be observed. See Gail, book 1, observation 21, at the end—especially since differences are found regarding this matter. See Ruland, *On Commissions*, book 7, chapter 2, number 12, part 1; Pacianus, *On Proofs*, chapter 26, number 39; Nolden, *On the Status of the Nobility*, chapter 10, number 81. Salmasius, in his notes to Vopiscus, page 440, wrongly criticizes Lipsius for writing that those who worship were accustomed first to stretch out their hand and then immediately bring it to their mouth; for the opposite was done. In different times and different acts, different customs have been pleasing. See Lipsius, *Electa*, book 2, chapter 6; Muretus, *Various Readings*, book 10, chapter 1; *The Prince's Clock*, book 1, chapter 38; Olearius in the *New Oriental Travelogue*, page 9, and elsewhere. When the punishment of hand amputation is imposed, in case of doubt, the left hand should be cut off rather than the right, or a withered and weak hand rather than a healthy and strong one. See C. Rittershusius, *On the New Laws*, page 700, number 4. Amputation of the hand is the penalty for a Notary who writes an illegal contract. See the same author, page 638, number 6. In the records of the dedication of the University of Duisburg, page 99, it is read that for Doctors of Philosophy, instead of a kiss and embrace, the Right Hand is extended, and thus they are received into the order of Doctors of Philosophy.

### 20. To Pronounce Law. <note>original Latin/German: "Jus dicere. Recht sprechen."</note>

It is not permitted to pass sentence in someone else's territory, nor even in a feudal estate <note>original Latin: "in feudali"</note>. See the last law in the Digest *On Jurisdiction*. Thus, in the investiture of Bishop Hillenius of Trier in the year 1152, it is cautioned: "Regarding the same castle called Seyna, and the court of Seyna itself, with all integrity and utility belonging to it—excepting the allodial land <note>land held in absolute ownership, not as a fief</note> which was a gate and a certain area called the Orchard—they may set a day for their officials to pursue their legal rights when necessary." See the *Acts of Seyn against Trier*. In the Eberstein settlement at Gernspach, something was retained from the fief so that one might be able to pronounce law there.

<column-break/>

### 21. Denial and Delay of Justice. <note>original Latin/German: "Protractio Justitiæ. Rechts-Verweigerung und Verziehung."</note>

It is established and certain law that a plaintiff <note>original Latin: "Actorem"</note> must first sue the defendant <note>original Latin: "reum"</note> in the first instance before a competent judge. Indeed, if it happens otherwise, the sued defendant is entitled to a "plea to decline the forum" <note>a legal objection stating the court does not have jurisdiction</note>. However, if justice is denied or delayed to the plaintiff by the immediate judge several times, he is permitted to sue the defendant in the Supreme Court and implore the office of the higher judge, and to bring an action against him for the justice denied or delayed. Our Emperor Justinian testifies with indignation that this is most just in the *Novellae* <note>New Laws</note>, 17, chapter 3. "Know," he says, "that if anyone comes and petitions us, and when asked by us if he approached you first, he says he did approach you and did not obtain what is just, and we find this to be true, we shall turn our indignation upon you." Indeed, this is the common path: when a lower judge does not provide justice, the case is devolved <note>transferred</note> to the higher judge. See chapter *Licet*, 10, at the beginning; chapter *Ex tenore*, 11, *On Competent Courts*. See Matthias Stephanus, *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, part 1, chapter 7, member 2, number 149; see Caspar Ziegler in *The Scripture-Fass*, conclusion 1, in the limitation, number 2 and following; and myself in *On Appeals*, chapter 7, number 12.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding when justice is said to be denied, and how jurisdiction is lost due to the denial of justice: see C. Rittershusius, *On the New Laws*, page 572 and following. The city of Nuremberg was expressly privileged by the Roman Emperors, especially by Emperor Henry, so that the citizens there—whether men or women, for whatever matters it may be—should not be summoned before any foreign court, but rather be sued before their own judge in Nuremberg; provided, however, that justice is not refused to the plaintiffs by that same judge.

See Gail, book 1, observation 28; Gilhausen in *The Tree of Civil Judgment*, chapter 4, branch 1, *On Mandates*, section 7. Delayed and denied justice differ regarding the reason for the decreeing process. See Gilhausen, at the cited location, number 3. How and when cases are transferred to the Imperial Chamber Court due to denied justice, and the requirements for them: see Schvvanman, observation 167; Mynsinger, century 5, observation 82; Gilhausen, location cited, number 2. How the citation for denied justice is to be decreed: see Gail, observation 28, number 2. The denial or delay of justice requires documentation. See Mynsinger, century 2, observation 74.

### 24. Royal Rights. <note>original Latin: "Regalia"</note>

**Royal Rights** are considered in two ways: one, as qualities inherent to a territory, belonging only to the Lord of that territory; the other, as separable rights that may even belong to a foreigner, Meichsner, decision 156.

Royal Rights are singular rights belonging to the **Supreme Prince**, even in those places where others hold jurisdiction by the benefit of that Prince. And thus "Regalia" are considered in the book *On the Uses of Fiefs*... see Hering *On Mills*, chapter 19. (And formerly, Royal Rights were those rights which belonged to the Imperial Treasury everywhere in the Empire, Günther in *Ligurinus*, book 8: "All things were left free to the Roman Realm.")

Nor is there then a difference between Royal Rights and **Rights of Majesty** <note>original Latin: "jura Majestatis" — the inherent powers of a sovereign</note>, although in the aforementioned chapter, it is not absolute power that is listed, but primarily the profits of the Royal or Imperial Treasury.

It also defines "Regalia" as the specific sovereign rights and financial privileges belonging to a Prince or the Emperor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal encyclopedia under the letter R, moving from the legal definition of "Signs" (Indicia) to a detailed discussion of "Regalia"—the sovereign rights and privileges belonging to a ruler.</meta>

Afterward, since many <term>Regalia</term> <note>original: "Regalia"; these are "Royal Rights" or sovereign privileges such as minting coins or collecting tolls</note> passed to various Princes and Cities under different legal titles, a distinction had to be made between general Royal Rights and <term>Reserved Rights</term> <note>original: "Reservata"</note>. Reserved Rights are those specific Royal Rights which the Emperor has kept for himself and do not typically belong to the Estates <note>the various territories and rulers within the Holy Roman Empire</note> along with their territory. However, even these may be shared through a special privilege or commission. In such cases, they are seen to belong to the recipient not by their own right—that is, by right of territory or magistracy—but almost in the name of a proxy; see my *Treatise on Majesty, folio 143 and following.*

Furthermore, Reserved Rights are of a twofold legal nature: some are reserved for the person of the Emperor, and some are reserved for the Emperor and the Estates together, as a single Body.

It should be noted that in the granting of a Castle, Duchy, or County by a supreme Prince, even with "all power" <note>original: "cum omni Imperio"</note> and including a clause stating "with every right, none reserved," the Royal Rights and other Reserved Rights of Royal Majesty do not pass or transfer as a sign of supreme power. Instead, only those rights pass which can properly belong to the person receiving the grant, or to any inferior lord and particular owner of a Castle. For a King has a twofold right in a Castle or granted property: one as the special and "useful" owner <note>the person who actually uses and manages the land</note> of the castle itself, which is what he is understood to transfer; the other as King, who holds the "direct domain" <note>ultimate legal ownership</note> and Royal Right universally in the whole Kingdom, and from this Royal Right, nothing is transferred. The reason is twofold: First, because such royal rights belong to the rights of the Crown, and are annexed to it and inseparable; they are not "in commerce" <note>legally tradable goods</note>, meaning they cannot be alienated <note>sold or given away</note>. *Lucas de Penna in book 2, "On the Law of the Republic"; Sesse, "Decisions of Aragon," 175, number 3.*

The second reason is that although they can be granted in some way, they do not pass under any general wording unless they are specifically granted. See *Sesse, in the same place, number 5.*

One should also know that in France and other places, Barons and Lords of Lands do not have the same Royal Rights and power as the Princes of Germany have in their lands, where they can do and exercise everything that the Emperor does in the lands of the Empire. For the Emperor, by granting Royal Rights to someone, is seen to grant them everything that belongs to a Prince and concerns the utility of that land.

And therefore, today it is said that the Empire is divided: since every Estate of the Empire is "Emperor in his own land." *Strasbourg Counsel, volume 4, counsel 62, number 14.*

Royal Rights, such as the <term>Blutbann</term> <note>the "Blood Ban," or the right of high justice to pass sentences of capital punishment</note> and <term>Gericht</term> <note>court or jurisdiction</note>, etc., are regularly presumed to be feudal and <term>Lehenbar</term> <note>grantable as a fief</note>. Those rights are considered to be of the same quality which savor of the nature of Jurisdiction or Power, and they cannot be exercised by a private person by their own authority or right of ownership; rather, they are considered to require the grant of some superior, and especially an Imperial grant. Such rights primarily include <term>Zoll</term> <note>customs or tolls</note>, <term>Forst</term> <note>forestry rights</note> and similar things, as can be seen below in a certain Counsel

<column-break/>

under the word <term>Wucher</term> <note>Usury</note>, question 1; see also the *Counsel above under the word "Lehen" (Fief).*

But since many authors have written much about Royal Rights, such as *Rosenthal, chapter 4, throughout*, I will not add more here.

### ADDITION.

Arnisaeus, Rumelin in his commentary on the *Golden Bull, part 3, dissertation 2, thesis 21*, and others say that not only Monarchical Republics, but also aristocratic, democratic, and mixed ones have their own royal rights. Royal Rights and Jurisdiction are opposing species. *Mundius, "On Duties," chapter 2, number 150.* Even Imperial Cities have them, *chapter 2, number 163 and following.* Royal Rights belong only to the supreme Prince, as discussed extensively by *Barbosa, book 16, chapter 20, axiom 1.* Royal rights are not considered granted simply because general Jurisdiction has been granted, *axiom 2.* If a rule is granted to someone, can he grant it to others? *Otto, "On Public Law," page 316.* What Royal Rights are understood by these words: "I grant you the Royal Rights in this city"? *Bocer, "On Royal Rights," page 447, number 5.* Nobles have Royal Rights, such as the right of minting Money. *Anton Hanffmann, "On Monetary Matters," conclusion 11*, says this applies to the "Immediate" nobles <note>nobles who answered directly to the Emperor without an intermediate lord</note>, of whom there are three classes: Franconians, Swabians, and Rhenish. Let no one be surprised, since everything that can be said of the Immediate Estates also applies to them. An example is the Nobles in Franconia from the family <term>von Schaumberg</term>, to whom this right was granted by the Emperor. The red or blood banner, <term>die Blutffahnen</term>, signifies Royal Rights. *Limnäus, "On Public Law," book 4, chapter 7, number 23.* Jacob von der Graef wrote *On Royal Rights*. Likewise Camman; Conrad von <term>Einsidel</term>, Halle in Saxony, 1619, in octavo. On Royal Rights, there exists the Inaugural Thesis of the brothers Conrad and Benedict Carpzov, held at Wittenberg in 1619 and published at Jena. There also exists a Treatise on Royal Rights titled *On the paragraph "Soluta,"* Power, published at Wittenberg by Friedrich Pruckmann in the year 1592. Thomas Löffelholz, *Disputation 9, volume 7, Basel Disputations.* Jacob Nimmer in *volume 1, Basel Disputations.* Michael Wendland, *Disputation 12, volume 5, Basel Disputations.* Most recently, Christoph Hain von Löwenthal in *Idea of Public Law, page 362.*

Feudal Royal Rights are called <term>die hohe Mannschafft</term> <note>High Vassalage</note>. Minor Royal Rights are listed by Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relation, part 4, page 73*, there: a piece of bread from every batch of baked bread, a measure of wine from every cask.

### 27. Ruler. Emperor.

A sentence passed against a certain Jew, named Jodocus von Resch, <insert>who described himself as a Ruler of the common Jewish people.</insert> This man was condemned in the <term>Imperial Chamber Court</term> <note>original: "Camera [Imperialis]"; the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> to pay a penalty of two marks of fine gold to the Imperial Treasury, along with costs. February 20, Anno 1540. For although he proved that other Jews had written in this manner, nevertheless, because this title is unusual and suggests a proud and seditious spirit, no one ought to recognize such a title. Had he called himself by such a name in the Hebrew language, it seems the matter would be judged differently. Furthermore, although Jews live under the <term>Common Law</term> <note>original: "Jure Communi"; in this context, the Roman law as adapted for the Holy Roman Empire</note> within the Roman Empire, and thus may change their names, they cannot usurp this specific title. This is because the word "Ruler" <note>original: "Regierer"</note> requires a public office, from which Jews are excluded by law. Even if certain laws allow them to hold honors among themselves, he nevertheless went too far, and acted with deceit <note>original: "in dolo"</note>, for which he cannot be excused. And although this word has various meanings if translated from Hebrew into German, words should be understood specifically rather than generally when they are in doubt. Therefore, he must be punished with an extraordinary penalty for the crime of using a false name. These notes are from the *Decisions or Precedents of the Imperial Chamber*, under the word "Jew."

->ADDITION.<-

The title "Ruler" implies a public office joined with Jurisdiction and Command. Reinkingk, *On the Roman Empire*, 2. 2. 3. 39. See also Webner and Kæstel, *On the Jews*, Thesis 36. Jews are incapable of holding magistracies and public offices.

On this word, one should entirely consult Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, chapter 2, note 279, and the authorities cited there; also Sprenger, in *Illustrious Fragments of Public Law*, page 214.

### 28. Registry. The Archive.

In the entire administration of Government, the Registry <note>original: "Registratura"</note> handles nothing else, 

<column-break/>

except that by recording the contents of <term>Instruments</term> <note>legal documents, deeds, or contracts</note> and other writings, these matters are committed to certain books for the perpetual instruction and memory of the business. The instruments and writings themselves are replaced, preserved, and protected from destruction within their own established orders and arrangements.

A Registry that is most exact, well-instructed, and well-ordered consists in:

->Accepting,<-
->Inspecting,<-
->Weighing,<-
->Discussing, and<-
->Transcribing Instruments, both official and private.<-

From their contents, both the primary and supporting points are to be extracted and established,

->Commending all contents to memory.<-

->Furthermore:<-

In partitioning and separating instruments and other writings.
In placing and ordering everything under their proper books, and creating books with headings.
In searching through the chests of records.
In locating records in their designated places.

Finally, in keeping everything in its order, and protecting them from destruction and confusion.

I have chosen to add the following from the *Summary Report on the Form of an Artful and Perfect Registry*, by Master Jacob von Ramungen, printed at Heidelberg by Johann Mayer, 1571.

## Concerning the several excellent benefits which arise and come from the establishment and maintenance of a completely perfect Registry.

It is time that we indicate and hear what conveniences and advantages, what fruits and utilities, arise for a Lord or a Magistrate from the establishment and maintenance of our Registry. For that is the <term>final cause</term> <note>the ultimate purpose or goal</note> of every work and treatise, which one asks for, looks toward, and labors for. Although many great, excellent, and numerous advantages and benefits arise from our Registry—as a whole and perfect system—which a Lord or Magistrate may and can have, such that they cannot all be easily recounted, I will nevertheless choose only the most excellent, foremost, and best of them at this time, and initially recount only the common advantages and benefits.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on administrative governance, specifically detailing the ten primary benefits of maintaining a well-organized Registry for a ruling authority. It transitions from the general status of a ruler to the practical mechanics of record-keeping.</meta>

1. First, a Lord or **authority** has the advantage and benefit from our **Registry** <note>original: "Registratur"; the office responsible for maintaining official records and archives</note> that all his letters and writings—those concerning his lordship and authority, his honors, laws, and justices, and all his and his ancestors' affairs and actions—are preserved and protected together. For our Registry is such a system of governance that it preserves, guards, and maintains the reputation and status of all letters and written documents committed to memory in a permanent state and undisturbed order. In this way, nothing can easily be altered, misplaced, lost, disrupted, neglected, defaced, or damaged.

2. *Secondly* <note>original: "Secundò"</note>, a Lord can know from the recording of his Registry and from the report of its administrator what letters he actually possesses and for what matters he truly has written evidence. For the Registry provides and gives a thorough indication of what documentary and written proof, deeds, records, and testimony exist for every **Right** <note>original: "Jus"</note> and every action and matter, by which they may be defended, documented, shielded, and upheld.

3. Thus, *Thirdly* <note>original: "pro Tertio"</note>, a Lord can quickly see, recognize, and deliberate from such documentary and written records whether and what **interest** <note>original: "interesse"; a legal stake or claim</note> and **Right** <note>original: "Jus"</note> he has in any given matter.

4. *Fourthly* <note>original: "pro Quarto"</note>, in every occurrence, a Lord can **deliberate** and consult with himself and the registrar regarding what he ought to do in each matter, what he is authorized to do therein, and how he is **legally founded** <note>original: "fundirt"</note> and grounded. Even if he did not immediately have a specific documentary proof or written record regarding the matter, he can nonetheless more quickly deliberate and prepare himself as to **what he must do** <note>original: "quid sibi faciendum"</note>.

5. *Fifthly*, a Lord finds instruction and counsel from his Registry and its **administrators**, such as the registrar, on how he should conduct and adapt himself in every matter and action. This ensures he does not receive or accept any damage or disadvantage on their account, nor **prejudice** <note>original: "præjudiciren"; to harm or weaken a legal claim beforehand</note> his **Rights** <note>original: "Juribus"</note>. Rather, he may instead gain advantage and benefit, either maintaining and upholding a **Right** <note>original: "Jus"</note> that he previously held in such a matter, or **acquiring one anew** <note>original: "de novo acquiriren"</note>. For our Registry provides guidance and identifies what should be handled, undertaken, done, or left undone in every matter, and what authority, power, might, and right one has regarding it. *Likewise* <note>original: "Item"</note>, it shows what proof, credible demonstration, and written assistance one can rely and depend upon for the prevention

<column-break/>

of future division, disputes, error, misunderstanding, and the resulting laborious and tedious litigation, as well as the useless and unnecessary **expenditure** <note>original: "Expensirung"</note>, costs, and damages that might follow and be incurred therefrom.

6. And so, *Sixthly* <note>original: "pro Sexto"</note>, every Lord will find in his Registry and from its registrars a good report of what damage or disadvantage might arise and spring from any occurring matter. *Likewise* <note>original: "Item"</note>, he will see what advantage and **benefits** <note>original: "Commoda"</note>, what utility and **Rights** <note>original: "Jura"</note>, may **result and accrue** <note>original: "proveniren und accresciren"</note> to him.

7. Then, *Seventhly* <note>original: "pro Septimo"</note>, the Registry will further teach and instruct how one should and can prevent and avert such impending damage or disadvantage, if not entirely then at least in part. Likewise, it shows how one may obtain and secure the advantage and benefit revealed therein through proper means, in good faith, with equity, and through well-founded, lawful, and significant **legal actions** <note>original: "Bethädungen"</note>.

8. Thus, *Eighthly* <note>original: "pro Octavo"</note>, a Lord will find in his Registry a good report of what **Sovereign Rights** <note>original: "Regalien"; rights belonging exclusively to a sovereign, such as minting coins or collecting certain taxes</note> and other things he might be lacking, and *likewise* what he should strive for and work to obtain. Otherwise, the points just listed above also instruct and teach him, as does the second type of our **Renewal** <note>original: "Renovatur"; a systematic updating of administrative and land records</note>, which we have **treated** <note>original: "tractirt"</note> and indicated in our prepared work on that subject.

9. *Ninthly*, we have indicated and explained in another place—and therefore it has been well heard, noted, and understood—how much a good, whole, and complete **Renewal** <note>original: "Renovation"</note> matters to every lordship or authority, what benefit they receive from issuing it, and what great disadvantage and damage they must expect from the lack of it. Because such a **Renewal** and **Restoration** is necessary for their government and their **economy** <note>original: "Oeconomi"; here referring to the management of the state's resources</note>, they cannot well do without it or dispense with it, especially if they are minded to promote and create welfare and the best for themselves and their poor people and subjects. Therefore we say once again, as we did in that same place, that without the first part of the Registry and its orderly and diligent **observation and practice**, no complete **Renewal** can be undertaken, established, or maintained. To **judge** <note>original: "adjudiciren"</note> this specifically, there is no time or leisure here on this occasion.

10. *Tenthly*, we have also said and heard in another place, and mention it here as well, that a whole and complete Registry should follow a **Renewal**, as is proper and indeed necessary. This is because the Registry **preserves the renewed records** <note>original: "Renovata conservirt"</note> and

14. *Fourteenth* <note>original: "Decimo quartò"</note>, our Registry is also good and useful in that it provides advice (provided one requests a report and seeks its counsel) so that nothing is undertaken or handled today that contradicts what was done in times past. For example <note>original: "Exempli gratia"</note>, it ensures that a Lord does not today grant a matter that was refused and rejected by his parents or ancestors for significant, moving, and legitimate reasons. Through this, one may prevent and avoid nullity, legal prejudice, or irreparable damage and disadvantage.

### 30. Regulars.

The approval of a **Monastic Rule** <note>original: "Regulæ Monasticæ"; the set of guidelines governing a monk's life</note> (which is, as it were, the Law and Standard of perfection) belongs to the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> alone. Indeed, under threat of excommunication, Innocent III took care that no one should institute a **religion** <note>original: "Religionem"; here meaning a formal religious order</note> without the express approval of the Pope.

However, a Bishop can approve a certain hon-

<column-break/>

est way of living with simple folk, which nevertheless is not considered a "Religion" for that reason.

**Canons Regular** <note>Priests living in a community under a rule, often attached to a cathedral</note> of Cathedral Churches belong to the same Order and Religion as the Canons Regular of Monasteries, since both have the same habit and reason for profession. For both the former and the latter wear a linen habit and promise the same monastic Rule. And although they are sometimes not included under the name of "Monks" in penal matters, they are nonetheless truly **Religious** <note>A technical term for members of religious orders</note>, even though their Rule is also simply called "of the Clergy." See the *Compendium of Regular Questions* by Emanuel Rodericus under the word "Reformation."

And by virtue of the Rule, any professed member is bound under pain of mortal sin to only six things: (1) To obedience to a commanding Superior. (2) To not having personal property. (3) To not contracting marriage. (4) To the observance of the precepts of the Rule. (5) To not acting out of contempt. (6) To striving toward perfection, which is the end of all Religion—that is, to never despising the habits of virtue. See Rodericus in the cited place under the word "Religion."

Regarding **Regulars and Religious** wandering outside the cloisters, and regarding the punishment of those who, taking a vow of religion at a legal age, fail in their professed way of life and transfer to other Orders, see the *Seventh Book of Decretals, book 3, title 7, chapter 1.*

Truly, that wandering lust in those bound by a monastic vow is hateful to the sacred **Canons** <note>Church laws</note>. The Popes also hate those Religious for whom no way of life is pleasing, and who busily try to experience everything among all people.

Pius V, Supreme Pontiff, established that Regulars cannot hear the confessions of laypeople without the approval and permission of the **Ordinaries** <note>Usually the local Bishop</note>, as can be seen in the said *Seventh Book of Decretals, chapter 3.*

Many things regarding Regulars and Religious are found in the *Synodal Statutes of Constance, page 147,* etc. On the method of correcting Regulars, see the *Practice* of Octavius Spatharius, and on the reformation of Regulars, see John Baptist Lenzana, Carmelite.

### ADDITION.

See Mr. Speidelius in *Notabilia*.

### 31. Imperial Recess.

Because of new cases emerging after the **Golden Bull** <note>original: "Aurea Bulla"; the 1356 decree that functioned as a constitution for the Holy Roman Empire</note>, the Constitutions of the Empire or **Imperial Recesses** <note>original: "Recessus Imperii"; the official resolutions passed at the end of an Imperial Diet</note>, commonly called *Reichs-Abschied*, were issued. These can be defined as common pledges of the Republic—that is, of the Emperor and the Estates—sanctioned by the Emperors and various Estates of the Empire in the Diets for the administration and governance of the Empire itself.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of administrative records and legal procedures of the Holy Roman Empire, specifically focusing on the structure of the Imperial Diet (Reichstag), the formation of Imperial laws (Recesses), and the financial contributions (taxes) levied for defense against the Ottoman Empire.</meta>

# Letter R.

In the Imperial Diet <note>original: "Comitiis"</note>, three councils are held: one of the Electors, a second of the Princes, Bishops, Counts, and Barons, and a third of the Imperial Cities. The votes of each Council regarding proposed grievances are deposited in the full and entire <term>Imperial Council</term> <note>original: "Reichs-Rath"</note> for deliberation. These are then communicated to each Council and referred back and forth from one Council to another. Whatever is unanimously concluded by all Councils, along with the points on which they disagree, is offered to the Emperor as a common <term>opinion</term> <note>original: "Bedenken"</note>. After the Emperor has communicated and carefully weighed the matter with his advisors, the <term>Imperial Secret Councilors</term> <note>original: "Kayserlichen geheimen Räthen"</note>—separately from the <term>Imperial Aulic Councilors</term> <note>original: "Reichs-Hofräthen"</note>—if he has no significant objections, he assents to the common opinion. He may also agree with one particular Council regarding disputed points, especially if the votes on both sides are equal. Other Councils, or sometimes specific dissenting Estates, may proceed by raising exceptions, replies, rejoinders, and surrejoinders with the Emperor, until a final conclusion is reached. Once all matters judged irrelevant or relevant have been presented, whichever opinion is accepted by the Emperor and the majority of the Estates is recorded in writing at the Chancellery of Mainz <note>original: "Curia Moguntina"</note>. This office serves as the <term>Arch-Chancellery of the Holy Empire in Germany</term>. The document is drafted in the name of the Emperor and the Estates, formally conceived, and published to the Estates. These drafted and composed <term>conclusions</term> <note>original: "Beschluß"</note> are communicated to each individual Estate, publicly described, and approved by them a second time. Finally, in the said Chancellery of Mainz, they are cleanly and authentically transcribed—commonly called "cleaning up" and "engrossing" <note>original: "mundiren u ingrossiren"</note>—and reduced into an authentic form. This is signed by all individual Estates and Ambassadors and confirmed with the seals of the Emperor, the Electors of Mainz and the Palatinate (on behalf of all Electors), an Ecclesiastical Prince and a secular one (in the name of the other Estates of that same order), and a Prelate, Count, and Imperial City (in place of the remaining Imperial Prelates, Counts, Barons, and Cities). Of the two authentic scripts thus completed, commonly called the "Originals," one is deposited in the <term>Imperial Court Chancellery</term> and the other in the <term>Imperial Chancellery</term> at Mainz. Finally, a copy is transmitted to the Imperial Chamber Court <note>the "Camera"</note> so that legal proceedings may be decided according to it. These documents are ultimately called the <term>Imperial Recess</term> <note>original: "Reichs-Abschied"; the final summary of all laws passed at a specific Diet</note>. See Caspar Leipold on concurrent jurisdiction in Arumæus, volume 1, discourse 13, question 19, page 312 and following. Regarding the subscription of Imperial Receivers, see *The Composition of Peace*, folio 405 and folio 416, where an example is given of how the Emperor approves the transaction of the Estates in the form of law, etc.

### ADDITION.

Regarding what the Imperial Recesses are, see Stirnius on the Constitutions of Princes, title II, paragraph 15 at the end, and title 12, paragraphs 1, 2, and following. <term>Imperial Recesses</term> <note>original: "Recessus Imperii"</note> are the decrees of the Diet, or the common <column-break/> promises and pacts entered into by the whole Republic—that is, by the Emperor together with the Estates. They have the force of perpetual law and are proposed, enacted, and promulgated at various Diets for the very administration of the Empire. A "Saving and Reservatory Clause" <note>original: "Clausula Salvatoria & Reservatoria"</note> is usually attached to Imperial Recesses; even if not expressly stated, it is tacitly understood, so that the decrees maintain their validity "saving the rights of third parties" <note>original: "salvo jure tertii"</note>. See Dr. Christoph Philipp Richter in his *Counsels*, part 6, chapter 1, number 56, folio 12. Do they obtain the force of law without distinction? See Becker in *F. P.*, pages 239–240. How and by whom are Imperial Recesses reduced into form? See Limnäus in *Imperial Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 193 and following; and where are they stored? Number 195.

## 35. Imperial Assessment, Imperial Levy.
->Imperial Collection.<-

Those things are called "Assessments of the Holy Empire" which are imposed against the most cruel enemy of the Christian name, the Turk. These are paid not only from movable and immovable goods, whether feudal or allodial—<term>Imperial Recess of Speyer, Year 1544, in the paragraph "and namely shall," where it says: "from all their movable and immovable property and goods, whether they be fiefs or their own";</term> but they are also sometimes commanded to be paid by "heads" or persons themselves—not only the Lords and their spouses and children, but even the ministers, <term>male and female servants</term> <note>original: "Knecht und Mägden"</note>. See the Imperial Recess of Augsburg, Year 1400, the paragraph "Namely that all," and the Recess of Cologne, Year 1512, the paragraph "and so that the poor." Furthermore, not only the Laity, but also the Clergy, Churches, and Monasteries are subjected to this duty, whether they hold fiefs from the Emperor or not, as are all other Estates without exception, no matter how privileged they may otherwise be. <term>Imperial Recess of Speyer, Year 1542, paragraph "and namely shall," paragraph "and to this Christian," and paragraph "all Electors shall also." Likewise from the Year 1544, the paragraph "and namely shall all."</term>

## 33. Imperial Aulic Council. <note>original: "Reichs-Hofrath. Judicium Aulicum Imperii."</note>

Regarding the Imperial Aulic Council—the Emperor's personal high court—and its concurrent jurisdiction with the Imperial Chamber Court, as well as the fact that it also judges in religious cases, see Thomas Michael *On Jurisdiction*, conclusion 28; Valentin Riemer *On Jurisdiction*, letter S; and *The Composition of Peace*, my edition page 354 and following, where the status of the Aulic Council is discussed. Regarding whether an appeal can be made from this Council to the Emperor himself, see the *Brandenburg Deduction against Würzburg* concerning the town of Kitzingen, where it is stated that it was not previously unknown to accept procedural and suspensive remedies even in the Aulic Court, etc.

In Emperor Matthias's <term>Aulic Council Ordinance</term> <note>Matthias (reigned 1612–1619) issued significant reforms to the court's operating procedures.</note>, under the title "On Matters Belonging to the Aulic Council," in the section "We Command," the following is decreed: "We hereby earnestly command Our Aulic Council President and Councilors, and We will that, in deciding on citations, rescripts, mandates, and other legal processes, they shall carefully observe the privileges not only of Our Imperial Majesty, but also of Our and the Empire's Electors, Princes, Counts, Lords, Estates, the exempt Knighthood, and other <term>immediate and mediate subjects</term> <note>Immediate subjects answered only to the Emperor; mediate subjects answered to a local prince or lord.</note>—especially regarding the right of first instance. They shall burden no one contrary to these rights, but in deciding legal processes, they shall conduct themselves according to the common laws, the <term>Imperial Recesses</term> <note>Official summaries of the laws passed at an Imperial Diet.</note>, and well-ordered statutes, without violating the privileges of the Estates, etc."

### ADDITION.

How great an authority the <term>Aulic Council</term> <note>original: "Judicium Aulicum, deß heiligen Reichs Hofrath"</note> holds today in deciding major cases is evident from its constitution, which was confirmed by Ferdinand I

<column-break/>

and reorganized into a new order by Emperor Matthias. For the *Ordinance of the New Aulic Council*, title 2, states: "Into Our Aulic Council shall be accepted, justified, judged, and necessary actions expedited for all and every matter concerning Our Empire, the Holy Roman Empire, its sovereignty, rights, lordships, and justice, pledges, redemptions, <term>regalia</term> <note>Royal rights or privileges, such as minting coins or collecting tolls.</note>, and high and low <term>fiefs</term>, as far as such matters pertain to justice." See more in Hahn, *On Royal Judgments*, ibid. 17.

On the Emperor’s Aulic Council, see extensively Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 4, throughout. See Otto in *Public Law*, page 346, regarding the old ordinance of the Aulic Council; ibid. page 131 and following regarding the filling of seats on the Council, its functions, outlines, and conduct. See also the *Aulic Council Ordinance* renewed in the year 1654: title 1, regarding matters belonging to the Aulic Council and the judging of processes; title 2, how to handle the submission of legal petitions, memorials, and writings; title 3, regarding the oath of the Aulic Councilors; ibid. letter G. 11. On the naming and origin of the Aulic Council, see Johann Andreas Gerhard in *Discussions on the Supreme Courts of the Roman Empire, the Aulic and the Cameral*, pages 5 and 6. The Imperial Aulic Council does not always follow the Emperor's court <note>original: "Aulam"</note>, but more often the Emperor's court is in one place and the Aulic Senate is in another, though not far distant from it. Ibid. page 6. Why it is called the "Council of the Empire" <note>original: "Consilium Imperii, Reichs-Hofrath"</note> is discussed in the same place; add Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 4, number 1. A debate on the jurisdiction of the Aulic Senate is found in Limnäus, said book 9, chapter 4, numbers 5 and following. The Aulic Council Ordinance renewed by Emperor Ferdinand III in 1654 can be found word-for-word in Limnäus, volume 2 of the *Additions*, book 9, chapter 4. At the end of said chapter 4, Limnäus adds these words: "This Ordinance was not accepted by all the Estates, because it was not properly communicated to them, nor were they heard regarding their objections <note>original: "monitis"</note>; therefore, it should be properly dictated and further discussed at the next upcoming Imperial Diet, as the records of the Diet indicate."

How cases are transferred by appeal <note>original: "Appellationem"</note> to the Emperor's Court or the Imperial Chamber Court is excellently treated by Dr. Johann Andreas Gerhard, Counselor to the Count Palatine of Anhalt, in *Discussions on the Supreme Courts in the Roman Empire, the Aulic and the Cameral, in which they either differ or agree*, First Discussion, chapter 5, throughout. There, in section 2, he teaches that for an appeal to these supreme courts to be valid, it is required that the appeal be made step-by-step <note>original: "gradatim"</note>, not by "skipping over" <note>original: "per saltum"</note>; that is, the intermediate judge, if there be one, must not be bypassed (see exceptions in Roding, book 1, title 20, section 6 and following). Furthermore, the total value of the lawsuit must be high enough to be appealable. In section 3, he further
