## 34. Imperial Fiefs. <note>original: "Feuda Imperii"</note>

Regarding what an Imperial Fief entails, see *Mündelheim Records for Bavaria, folio 69* in the Documents.

Is the Emperor <note>original: "Cæsar"</note> the Judge if there is a dispute over an entire fief, a part of it, or a specific matter? See Wilhelm Anton in his *Corollaries to the Treatise on the Five-Year Period*, folio 29 and following.

The Diocese <note>original: "Stifft"</note> of Trier has an Imperial Privilege stating that all Imperial Fiefs that become vacant <note>original: "eröffnet," meaning a fief without an heir</note> within said Diocese shall fall to it; evidence of this is in the *Case of Sayn vs. Trier.* See Sprenger in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 375, at the end. The Palatinate also has such a Privilege; see Engelhard *On Taxes*, conclusion 2.

## ADDITION.

All fiefs of the Empire are "liege" <note>original: "ligia"</note>, or annexed to the Emperor and the Empire by the strictest bond. See Cöppen, *Observations on Fiefs, chapter 2, number 36.* Nicolaus Myier, *On the Princes and Estates of the Empire, chapter 92.* Can a fief that has lapsed <note>original: "apertum"</note> back to the Empire be granted anew as a fief to anyone? See Bocer, *On Regalian Rights, chapter 2, number 61, near the end of page 84.* Is the investigation into Imperial Fiefs the sole responsibility of the Emperor? See Mr. Stirn in *Five Titles of Public Law, volume 1, section 3 and following.*

Regarding how often Imperial Fiefs are to be received and how agents and procurators should conduct themselves, see the *Revised Imperial Aulic Council Ordinance*, title 3. In feudal cases—that is, those involving Duchies and Counties that have royal dignity annexed to them and descend immediately from the Empire <note>meaning they have no intermediary lord between them and the Emperor</note>—which stem from the Empire as a fief, the Emperor alone is the Judge. See Becker in *Public Law*, page 101.

The Emperor, by virtue of the <term>Capitulation</term><note>The "Wahlkapitulation" or Electoral Capitulation was a contract signed by the Emperor-elect upon his selection by the Electors, limiting his powers and protecting the rights of the Estates.</note>, is bound to incorporate lapsed fiefs back into the Empire. See Klock, volume 1, consultation 7, number 610. This is restricted in numbers 689, 692, 693, 694, 695. For Charles V, among other articles, this was also prescribed: when fiefs of the Empire became vacant during the time of his reign and fell back to him, if they yielded something significant, he should not grant them to anyone else. Instead, he should keep, seize, and incorporate them for the maintenance of the Empire, himself, and his succeeding Kings and Emperors, until such time as the 

<column-break/>

Empire returned to its full essence and prosperity. More on this in Limnäus, *Public Law, book 4, chapter 8, number 129.* Regarding Principalities that stem from the Empire as fiefs, see the same author, book 5, chapter 2, page 63. In the year 1595, it was praised of Rudolph II that he upheld the Holy Roman Empire; without the prior knowledge and consent of the Electors, he refused to grant to Philip II (his mother's brother) the Imperial Fiefs bordering the County of Burgundy but belonging to the Lordship of Nassau. Instead, he postponed the matter from one general Imperial Diet to another. Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain, in *Historical Reports, part 5, page 129.* The same author on page 117 notes that it did no small harm to the diminished Roman Empire that the Roman Emperors did not maintain the lapsed fiefs for the Holy Roman Empire, but granted them away in other directions. See more in said part. Regarding how the Imperial Fiefs were weakened, see the same author, part 6, page 144. If matters arose concerning Principalities or Counties that are held as fiefs from the Empire, and a full and final judgment was to be pronounced for one party, His Imperial Majesty reserved that adjudication for himself. See the *Imperial Recess of the Year 1521*, under the heading "Governance of His Roman Royal Majesty," section "whether also." See also the *Chamber Ordinance, part 2, title 7, law of fiefs 18, 2, folio 18.* Vultejus, *On Fiefs, book 2, chapter 2, number 9.*

## 35. Imperial Governing Council. <note>original: "Reichs-Regiment-Rath. Regimentum Imperii."</note>

Emperor Maximilian, after he had instituted the Chamber Court, also instituted the Governing Council—the Imperial Governing Council <note>original: "den Reichs-Regiment-Rath"</note>—in the year 1500 at the Diet of Augsburg. It was given all-encompassing and general jurisdiction and power to deliberate, define, and decree upon any matters whatsoever regarding the entire Empire, the Estates, and those under immediate Imperial authority. See the *Recess of Worms, 1521*, section "and whereas." This council acts in concurrence with the Emperor and the Empire in all Imperial business. See the *Recess of Augsburg, 1500*, section "if anyone," at the words "if one of them is aggrieved, and he brings it to Your Majesty and the Governing Council," and the title "On the Power and Authority of the Governing Council," at the words: "the Roman Emperor, or he whom he appoints in his stead, and the Governing Council shall have full power and authority: so that it may even assist the Chamber Court concerning the execution of its sentences."

The Emperor also asserts this concurrent jurisdiction for himself in the Decree and Admonition to the Imperial Aulic Councilors, dated July 1, 1596: that they must conform and regulate their decrees and decisions according to the Recesses and Ordinances of the Empire and the Chamber.

Indeed, the jurisdiction of the Emperor is universal and whole, until a process is initiated by the litigants in the Chamber Court and served to the defendant, at which point the court has taken precedence.

Just as for many years past, cases from the entire Empire were accustomed to be received and decided indifferently <note>In this context, "indifferently" means without legal distinction or preference between the venues.</note> no less in the Emperor’s Court, in the Imperial Aulic Council <term>Reichs-Hofrath</term><note>The judicial body serving the Emperor directly, often competing for jurisdiction with the Imperial Chamber Court.</note>, and in the "pre-empted" Chamber <note>original: "Camerâ præventâ"; this refers to the legal principle of "prevention," where the first court to take up a case gains the right to decide it.</note>, as Caspar Leipold proves in Arumæus’s *On Concurrent Jurisdiction*, volume 1, discourse 13, question 4, on my page 237 and following; see especially page 240 and following, and page 258 and following; likewise page 313 to the end and following. See also the *Necessary Remonstrance of Donauwörth*, page 191 and following, regarding the Imperial Governing Council <term>Regiments-Reichs-Rath</term>; add König in *Theatrum Politicum*, part 1, chapter 27, number 7.

In the Governing Council <note>original: "Regiments-Rath"</note>, only those matters occurred that concerned the Public State of the Roman Empire: such as any and all matters of the Roman King and his Holy Empire, law, peace, and the execution and maintenance of both, as well as resistance against the infidels <note>original: "Unglaubigen"; referring here to the Ottoman Turks</note> and other attackers of the Christendom of the Empire, and what is dependent upon those things. Whatever might have been brought forward and handled at the annual Imperial Assemblies <note>The Diets or meetings of the Estates.</note> was likewise referred to this Government of the Holy Empire. See the *Governing Ordinance* <note>original: "Regiments-Ordnung"</note> of the year 1500 at Augsburg, under the rubric "concerning the twenty who are ordained to the Royal Majesty and the Government of the Holy Empire, and their power." And the Governing Council differs from the Imperial Chamber Court <note>original: "Kayserlichen Cammer-Gericht"</note>: for to the latter were referred all judicial processes and legal justifications that otherwise belonged to the Imperial Majesty, and the expedition of those cases was committed and entrusted to it alone. See the *Thorough Instruction on the question of whether the Imperial Aulic Council has concurrent jurisdiction with and alongside the Imperial Chamber Court at Speyer in any and all matters without distinction?* found in Londorpius’s *Public Acts*.

### 37. Estates of the Empire. <note>original: "Reichs-Stände" or "Status Imperii"</note>

Properly speaking, those are called Estates of the Empire <note>original: "Status Imperii"</note> who, together with the Emperor—as a Christian body and assembly—have the right of establishing laws for the Republic, or the right of sitting and delivering an opinion in the Diets <note>original: "Comitiis"</note> and other Assemblies of the Empire,

<column-break/>

as per the Imperial Recess <note>The official summary of decisions made at an Imperial Diet.</note> at Cologne, the year 1512. See Paurmeister, *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, chapter 8, number 8.

It is asked: Can this be said of the Nobles? Sixtinus, in *On Regalian Rights*, book 1, chapter 4, number 74, and Buxtorff in his commentary on the *Golden Bull* <note>original: "A. B." for Aurea Bulla</note>, conclusion 5, deny it. But see my *Discourse on the Free Equestrian Order*.

When something has already been decreed and concluded by the Emperors and the Estates of the Empire, only then is the matter treated with that Nobility regarding the decreed things. See the Imperial Recess at Augsburg from the year 1500, under the rubric "What should be dealt with regarding the Knighthood <note>original: "Ritterschafften"</note> of Franconia, Swabia, and the Rhineland." See also Mingius, *On Territorial Superiority*, thesis 46, in the Basel disputations, volume 5.

Although there is no doubt—as it clearly appears from the *Golden Bull* in the preface, Buxtorff in his dissertation on the *Golden Bull* conclusion 5, letter C (and the doctors of law cited by him), and through many rescripts of the Emperors and other ancient monuments—that formerly the Nobles immediately subject to the Empire <note>Those who held their land directly from the Emperor without an intermediate lord.</note>, just like Princes, Dukes, etc., were counted among the Estates of the Empire. See Caspar Ziegler in the section "Land-Tenants" <note>original: "Landsassii"</note>, in the limitation of conclusion 1, number 44.

Today, however, this is not observed. And so there is a great difference between what was and what is now (following the legal principle: *the thing which was...*). Nor does the fact of being immediately subject to the Empire <note>original: "immediatam Imperii subjectionem"</note> urge anything to the contrary in this part, as he says in number 46, because the Free Knighthood <note>original: "die freye Ritterschafften"</note> of Franconia, Swabia, and the Rhineland still obey the Empire immediately and are subject to no Elector or other authority. See the Imperial Recess at Regensburg from the year 1577, section "We will," and the Imperial Recess at Augsburg from the year 1500, title "How one [should deal with] the Knighthood of Franconia." For these are different things: being an Estate of the Empire, and being immediately subject to the Empire. See Master Joachim Cluten in his *Syllabus of Daily Matters*, conclusion 26, letter K.

In the Imperial Recess of Worms from the year 1495, the Knighthood is indeed mentioned; likewise Charles V writes in the year 1555 to those assembled for the Diet, and makes mention of the Counts, Barons, Lords, or those of the Nobility and Estates, etc. See *The Composition of Peace* in the appendix, page 29.

It is established, however, that the Nobles were not present in the form of the Knighthood <note>meaning as a collective Estate</note>; see the cited place, page 31 and following, where it also explains why they are not called to the Diets today. Therefore, the phrase "those of the Nobility" <note>original: "die vom Adel"</note> is understood as the Barons, who are called Noble, or the Noble Councilors. It is interpreted this way also in the *Golden Bull* and elsewhere.

As for what the cause is that those nobles ceased to be Estates, Ludwig Gremp and Hieronymus zum Lamm, in the *Consultation on the Status and Vote of the Honorable Imperial City*, etc., bring forward two reasons, which Ziegler relates in the cited place, number 48. (1) Since the Nobility in part [became] subjects <note>original: "Landsassen"</note> of the Electors and Princes...

It explains that while the "Free Knighthood" remains directly subject to the Emperor, they are no longer considered full "Estates of the Empire" with voting rights in the Diets.</summary>

Lit. R.

...settled, as in Saxony, Bavaria, and Hesse: And (2.) the rest, who are still immediately subject to the Holy Empire <note>This refers to "Imperial Immediacy," where a person or entity was subject only to the Emperor, not to a local prince.</note>, such as those in Swabia, Franconia, Alsace, and along the Rhine, who wish to be free of all burdens and entirely privileged against taxes; for them, it has henceforth not been necessary to be summoned to the Imperial Diets, or to appear at all, etc.

**Estates** <term>Status</term> are those who possess high and low justice <term>merum mixtumque Imperium</term> <note>original: "merum mixtumque Imperium"; this refers to the full spectrum of legal authority, from capital punishment to civil disputes.</note> in their territories and all-encompassing jurisdiction, and who are also called to the Diets, where they have a vote and a seat: and thus they represent the Emperor himself in their territories. And yet some think that the **Nobles** <term>Nobiles</term> are to be understood as being, as it were, **Estates** <term>Stände</term> in their own territories. Reithvvein in *Formulary*, folio 270.

But that the Bishop of Würzburg, in religious matters, does not wish the Nobles to be equated with the Estates, appears from the response dated Würzburg, July 11, 1618, where it is stated among other things:

> Just as his Princely Grace [the Bishop] has always had and still has before his eyes the clear letter of the recently mentioned Peace of Religion <note>The Peace of Augsburg (1555), which established the legal basis for Lutheranism and Catholicism to coexist.</note>, as well as its meaning as considered by the Electors and Estates of the Empire during its deliberation, drafting, and publication; he does not recall having burdened any of the nobility belonging to or settled in the diocese in the slightest: Thus his Princely Grace cannot fathom from where, or in what words, those of the **Knighthood** <term>Ritterschafft</term> are completely equated and made equal to the Estates of the Empire.

> They [the Bishop's court] also fully believed that the aforementioned members of the Knighthood, in the council they held on this matter, should have easily found—since they (though without grounds) wish to claim that his Princely Grace has no right to command his subjects settled in that diocese under both spiritual and territorial authority (as the criminal jurisdiction <term>Zentbarliche</term> has nothing to do with these cases of Reformation)—that it was even less fitting for them, as mostly his Princely Grace’s vassals <term>Lehenleute</term>. And just as he assures them that he does not intend to let anything contrary to the Imperial statutes be carried out by his people, so he wishes to remind the said Knighthood to drop their high thoughts of "parity" and equality with the Imperial Estates, and to conduct themselves within the terms of the words and meaning of the Peace of Religion, under which no one among them has yet been burdened.

But because a certain most noble man, most skilled in every kind of learning, recently suggested some things to me by which it seems it can be proven

<column-break/>

that the Nobles may rightly be equated with the Estates, it seemed fit to set them down here:

That some wish to think (as is indeed known to me) that after the Roman Empire came to the Germans, and especially after feudal laws <term>Jura feudalia</term> arose, all **Nobles** were subject to the **Counts** <term>Comitibus</term> or other higher Estates, both in respect to their persons and their property regarding jurisdiction—this I cannot believe, and I hold instead: First, that neither before Charlemagne <term>Carolus</term> under the Frankish Kings, nor after him under the Roman Emperors, neither before the origin of fiefs <term>Feudorum</term> nor after, were the **Free Imperial Nobility** <term>Freye Reichs vom Adel</term> ever, in any way, subject to the Counts (I mean the Nobles in Franconia, Swabia, and the Rhine tract), but rather that they had to be brought to trial before the Emperor himself or his emissaries <term>Missis</term>, and these matters were held to be "greater causes" <term>pro causis majoribus</term> (namely by reason of the persons involved): regarding which an express law of the Emperor Charlemagne exists in the second book of the *Laws of the Lombards*, title 45.

For if even the Count of the Sacred Palace can only judge the cases of the poor and the less powerful, with the rest being reserved for the Emperor himself: what is to be said of the other Counts of "lesser clans" <note>original: "minorum... gentium"; a classical Roman reference applied here to lower-ranking counts.</note>, so to speak? Is it credible that they, with their peasant assessors <term>Assessoribus</term>, had the power to judge the Nobles (for whom at that time there was no more powerful order in the Empire)?

I firmly believe, and all the most ancient historians testify, that the Germans in these three provinces were always, from the time of Japheth <note>According to early modern genealogical theories, Japheth (son of Noah) was the ancestor of the Europeans and Germans.</note> onwards, most free, and that they never served any slavery (I am not speaking here of the slaves of private individuals) until Clovis the Great: except for what occurred from the Romans from time to time and at intervals, and then only in the borderlands.

The Kings, if these Germans occasionally had any, were Kings in name only; in truth, however, they were certain military leaders <term>Duces</term>, some for life, but some temporary for a specific war, which being finished, they were once again in the place of private citizens and were so regarded: for the **democracy** <term>Democratia</term> of the Germans, especially in these places, was absolute and pure, as Cluverius <note>Philipp Clüver (1580–1622), a celebrated geographer and historian.</note> extensively demonstrates in *Ancient Germany*, book 1, chapter 38 and following.

The presumption is in favor of liberty, and the contrary will be difficult to prove. Finally, the more excellent and outstanding among them, and those who deserved better of the fatherland, began to be held as Nobles, who afterwards propagated their nobility to their descendants, subject to no one, for as already said, they had no Kings.

# Enlarged Treasury of Practice
## Page 896

...I understand) and I do not hold the same view regarding the Bavarians. For although their form of government in the era of Caesar and Tacitus was democratic, they later had their own Kings long before the time of Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolo Magno"</note>. They were subjects of these kings, and after several changes, they were eventually succeeded by the Dukes of Upper and Lower Saxony and Bavaria, as well as certain Bishops, through the grants of Charlemagne and others. Therefore, they are more rightly **territorial subjects** <term>Landsassen</term> <note>A "Landsasse" was a member of the landed nobility who was subject to a territorial prince rather than directly to the Emperor.</note> and subjects of their **territorial princes** <term>Landsfürsten</term>. (I know that some disagree and believe that even the Saxons and Bavarians were free and immediately subject to the King of the Franks and his successors, the Roman Emperors; but by what reasons and proofs they hold this, I do not know, though I am most eager to learn.) This is because they were already subjects under their own kings before they were conquered by Charlemagne, Henry the Fowler <note>original: "Heinrico Aucupe"; Henry I, King of East Francia (919–936).</note>, and others, and subjected to the Roman Empire. This is especially true because the victorious Roman Emperors never incorporated or united those provinces into the German Kingdom or the Roman Empire as a **Crown Domain** <term>Dominium Coronæ</term> <note>Land held directly by the monarch to fund the state.</note> to be kept in their own hands—as happened for many centuries with Swabia, Franconia, and the Rhineland, namely from the reign of Clovis the Great <note>original: "Clodovæi M."; Clovis I, King of the Franks.</note> until Otto the Great. Instead, they handed them over—partly to the conquered kings themselves, though under a different title, namely as Dukes, and partly to newly established Bishops, Margraves, and Landgraves—as hereditary holdings, albeit under certain conditions.

When a potentate takes a land by sheer force, without any accommodation of the inhabitants, he rarely tends to increase the privileges of those subjects, much less to reclaim them *from being slaves or subjects into total liberty* <note>original: "ex servis vel subditis in omnimodam libertatem"</note>. Rather, if it turns out well, they are left in their old status. This was even more the case here, because the Saxons and Bavarians rebelled against Charlemagne even *after their subjection* <note>original: "post subiectionem"</note> and his many victories, and thereafter forced him to tear these lands into tiny fragments <note>original: "in minutas particulas"</note> so that they could be better kept in their duty by their particular Lords (whom he also wished to compensate) during the Emperor’s absence.

This, I hold, is the true **reason for the difference** <term>causa differentiae</term> as to why in these three provinces there is no "territorial subjection," while in the others it has always existed. And it does not hinder this view that in Tyrol, Austria, Jülich, etc., **primary nobles** <term>Nobiles Primarii</term> are found who were "immediate" in former times or still pretend to be so. For besides the fact that a **pending lawsuit** <note>original: "lis pendens"</note> still exists regarding this, it could also very well be that when the Em-

<column-break/>

-perors distributed such lands hereditarily to Dukes, Bishops, and others, they reserved certain small portions and gave them to **Frankish Nobles** <note>original: "Nobilibus Franciscis"</note> from among their most prominent soldiers, reserving their liberty for them. Just as in the districts of Saxony, Bavaria, and Jülich, **Imperial Cities** <term>Reichsstädte</term> <note>Cities that were self-governing and subject only to the Emperor.</note> are to be found which are not subject to the territorial prince. Now, just as these became Imperial Cities (regardless of the fact that the territorial prince's territory otherwise encloses those places), in the same way, Primary Nobles—though there will be few of them—could have come to "immediacy" through a grant, a reservation, or indeed through **long-term prescription** <note>original: "præscriptionem longissimi temporis"; a legal principle where a right is gained through very long, uninterrupted usage.</note>. For who among all people could know every circumstance and give an exact account of everything that happened 1000 years ago, given such a scarcity of written records?

Clovis the Great did indeed subdue Swabia <note>original: "Allemaniam"</note>, Franconia, and the Rhine Tract, and reduced the greater part of the conquered Swabians into actual slavery, as the historians of that time clearly write; he made almost all of them into bonded people. This is the origin and frequency of **serfdom** <term>Leibeigenschafft</term> in these regions. But because he and his descendants could not be without nobility, he undoubtedly took his nobility born of Frankish blood—whom he brought with him and with whom he won and conquered these lands—and distributed a good portion of the conquered lands to them and to his other well-deserving Dukes and Soldiers as a **reward for their devoted service** <note>original: "in præmium navatæ operæ"</note>. He compensated them this way, and certainly not just the lowliest, but rather the heads, colonels, counselors, and the like, as has happened at almost all times and as one still experiences daily. 

And although I readily believe that some of the Swabian and sent-in Roman nobility accommodated and flattered the Franks in time, both before and after the victory (as always happens), and thereby obtained from Clovis and his successors the right to be left in their liberty and property alongside the Franks—which the old **Capitularies** <note>Royal decrees of the Frankish kings.</note> also imply, in which one is left free to declare **by which law he wishes to live** <note>original: "quo jure vivere velit"</note>—it is nonetheless not to be doubted that the Franks took the best and most numerous estates for themselves, partly through the generosity of the victorious Kings and partly through other titles. But who would believe, given how times were then, that free Franks—from whom the proverb was born—and especially the most prominent leaders, would have subjected themselves to a Count of some district who was their equal and nothing more than a nobleman, just like them, for the sake of one or two...

# Letter R.

For the sake of two or three poor villages, he would not have allowed himself to be placed under the feet of others and made into slaves—for the ancient houses testify that no one person was given too much, **as is done today**, but rather that they **established colonies** <note>original: "colonias deducirt"</note> and gave a portion to each—**since the name of liberty is sweet, and soldiers, especially leaders, are usually more insolent after a victory than at other times.** <note>original: "cùm dulce nomen ſit libertatis, & milites, inprimis Duces, poſt victoriam plerumque ſoleant eſſe inſolentiores, quàm aliàs."</note> Rather, it is to be believed that they remained under the **immediate jurisdiction** <note>Direct legal authority of the King/Emperor without a middleman.</note> of their own king (who had not long before been newly elected), rather than suddenly allowing themselves—**after such a victory**—to be made equal to peasants and **subjected to the Count of some district** <note>original: "Comiti alicujus pagi ſubjiciren"</note> whom they had so recently elected themselves, and to be **treated** <note>original: "tractiren"</note> like beasts, especially since they had had no lord at all for nearly 70 years.

All the **High Courts** <term>Zentgerichten</term> <note>Local criminal courts with jurisdiction over serious "capital" crimes.</note> were staffed by nothing but peasants, **whom a Count presided over** <note>original: "quibus præfuit Comes"</note>. For it cannot be proven that a nobleman was ever a high court judge or a high court juror, **as they call them** <note>original: "uti nominant"</note>. **Who, however, would believe** <note>original: "Quis autem credat"</note> that such prominent persons, indeed even those **closest to the King** <note>original: "proximi à Rege"</note> themselves, would have allowed themselves to be **judged** in **matters of property, persons, civil, and criminal law** <note>original: "in realibus, perſonalibus, civilibus & criminalibus"</note> by mere peasants? It is much more believable that if the nobility had been subject to such **jurisdiction of the Counts**, those same courts—**given the great abundance of nobles at that time**—would have been staffed with nothing but noblemen. This is what happened with the Knightly Courts along the Rhine at Oppenheim, Ingelheim, Alzey, Nierstein, Saulheim, Mommenheim, Schornsheim, and others; yet none of these were **Counties** <note>original: "Comitatus"</note>, but for the most part only single villages. **In short**, the nobleman at that time did not allow himself to be judged by any peasant, but only by his equals. **Hence that much-celebrated word 'Peers', which undoubtedly takes its origin in Germany as much as in Gaul and England.** <note>The concept of "Peers" (from the Latin *pares*, meaning equals) implies that a noble can only be judged by someone of equal rank.</note> **Therefore the Counts judged only minor causes, and among persons of lower status, as proven above. The disputes of nobles, however, were resolved either by royal envoys, or perhaps through an amicable settlement by other nobles (which was very common 100, 200, or 300 years ago), or by the Count of the Sacred Palace, who was closest to the King, or finally by the King himself.** <note>original: "Judicabant ergo Comites tantùm ſuper cauſis levioribus... Nobilium autem lites dirimebantur à miſſis Regiis..."</note> This is attested to **in the criminal matters of Charlemagne’s speech to the nobles or soldiers (if indeed it is authentic)** <note>original: "in Criminalib. Caroli M. Oratio ad nobiles ſive milites"</note> in **these words:**

> But you, take care that you do not stain such great honor—which is a privilege won by the just labor of wars—with drunkenness, scurrilous behavior, or any other vice; lest that which we grant to you for glory should redound to punishment. We reserve the right to take such punishment from you, should you perhaps excel in vice, for Ourselves and our successors, the Kings of the Romans, forever.

> Likewise: Go, my soldiers, you shall be called Heroes, Companions of Kings (not slaves of Counts), Judges of Crimes, etc.

All of this (namely, that the **Counts** had nothing to do with the nobility, but that everything concerning the nobility was **handled by royal envoys**) is confirmed **from Turonensis Book II, chapter 44** <note>Referring to the 'History of the Franks' by Gregory of Tours.</note>, **where King Louis states:**
> We will and command that our Envoys (that is, Special Commissioners, not Counts of the districts) inquire diligently where free men (that is, nobles) remain in each County; and further, that this diligence and account be examined through each hundred, so that they may truly know and record those who are able to go on military expeditions.

**Thus far Turonensis. Having presupposed this (namely, that Nobles were not subject to Counts under Charlemagne), it is now asked: on what day, at what hour, in what place, with what witnesses, and by which Emperor were the Nobles—to the prejudice of the whole Empire—alienated from the Empire through shocking prodigality, and that hereditarily and irrevocably?** <note>original: "Quo præſuppoſito... qua die, qua hora... à quo Imperatore Nobiles... fuerint ab Imperio per ſtupendam prodigalitatem alienati..."</note> And since the nobility was the only estate in the Empire at that time—there were no others, even to this day—and since **in the Kingdom of the Franks the King's domain was always inalienable**, one must ask whether the nobility also **consented** to such an **alienation** of all Imperial Estates? Or can an Emperor or King really give away all his Free Estates at once, or even **successively (though if not all, let it be shown which ones and which ones not) so prodigally**? **Especially since in these regions the reason has ceased to exist for which the alienation of parts of Saxony and Bavaria was made: namely, the prolonged absence of the King or Emperor, the proximity of enemies, and the custom of subjects rebelling.** One **asks whether such Estates cannot appeal for their liberty even after a thousand years?**

**And since the principal sign of subjection is homage: It is asked again:** To which Duke in Swabia or Franconia, to which Landgrave or Count Palatine, or other Count, did these three Knightly Circles (or any part of them) ever pay homage alongside the peasants? And since they no longer pay homage today, **in what year, on what day, and for what reason** did they cease to perform such homage?

All of this, in my opinion, does not overturn what is cited **from Feudal Law regarding high and low sub-vassals from Cujacius** <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a famous French legal scholar.</note>. 2. The **Lombards** were Saxons, not Franks, and these **peoples had most diverse, indeed plainly contrary customs**. Therefore, even today there are two **Vicars** of the Empire: one for Frankish law, the other for Saxon law. **What then has Saxon or Lombard law to do with the Franks**, especially since the...

# Expanded Practical Treasury

The Lombards, without a doubt, completely changed their customs <note>original: "consuetudines"</note> after establishing a new Empire in Italy for the convenience of that new Kingdom.

3. Thus, every High Court <term>Curia</term> has its own customs, and does not resort to these "exotic" or foreign laws except when its own are lacking <note>original: "in defectu propriarum"</note>.

4. And who has ever heard the names "Valvasors" or "Valvasinos" mentioned in these regions? To all German political thinkers and historians, both old and new, these terms are **Bohemian villages** <note>A German idiom meaning something completely strange or incomprehensible.</note>. Let someone show me any mention of them under the Ottos, the Henrys, or the Fredericks <note>The author refers to the Holy Roman Emperors of the Saxon, Salian, and Hohenstaufen dynasties.</note> in the writings of a German author.

5. If the legal scholar Cujacius is correct in saying that "Valvasinos are those who are invested by Valvasors" <note>original: "Valvasini sunt, qui a Valvassoribus investiuntur"</note>, and that this contains the true definition of a nobleman, then the following must necessarily follow: 1. That those who do not hold fiefs from Valvasors, but only from the Emperor, or who hold purely **allodial property** <term>Allodial</term> <note>Land owned outright and freely, without any feudal obligation to a superior lord.</note>, are not noble—an opinion that has long been exploded and is manifestly false. 2. It must follow that before the rise of Feudal Laws, and especially before Valvasors (such as hereditary Dukes and Counts), there were no nobles at all; this is also false. For even in the times of Julius Caesar and Tacitus, an infinite multitude of nobles existed in these lands. As the gentleman himself so magnificently proves and explains in his cited treatise, the Germans were divided into the Noble-born <note>original: "Adelingos"</note>, the Free-born <note>original: "Frilingos"</note>, and the Bound-servants <note>original: "Lassos"</note>, and those closest to them, the Freedmen. I believe the number of nobles was vast, much like in Poland today. Gregory of Tours writes in Book 2, Chapter 9, that after crossing the Rhine and traversing Thuringia, the Franks created **Long-haired Kings** <note>original: "Reges Crinitos"</note> (Pharamund and his descendants) over themselves from their first and more Noble Family. Therefore, already in the year 420, there were noble families among the Franks, and indeed many of them. But where were the names of Fiefs, Vassals, and Valvasinos hiding then? They did not yet exist in the nature of things, as I see it.

Indeed, it would follow thirdly that more than 500 of the most distinguished noble families in the three Imperial Circles would not be noble at all. For it can be proven—if one goes from one ancestral house to another—that only 200 or 150 years ago, all these families were **allodial** (freeholders), and only since then, for the sake of greater protection and other reasons after the time of Rudolf I, have they been converted into fiefs. It would follow fourthly that a Valvasor—that is, a Prince or Count—who received a fief from another Valvasor, or even from a Valvasino or nobleman (though I could point out such cases), would thereby lose his rank and become a Valvasino, or perhaps even a peasant. For the jurist Vultejus calls the Barons and other higher nobles "Greater Valvasors" <note>original: "Valvasores majores"</note>, and refers to the remaining

<column-break/>

nobles as "Lesser Valvasors" <note>original: "Valvasores Minores"</note>, while he considers "Valvasinos" to be entirely non-noble. In short, no one yet knows what Greater Valvasors, Lesser Valvasors, or Valvasinos actually were. Therefore, I cannot believe Cujacius (with whom Peter de Andlo agrees in Book 2, Chapter 12) that the origin or definition of primary or inferior nobility, especially in these lands, depends on fiefs <note>original: "à feudis dependire"</note>—a question also treated by Reinkingk—much less that our nobles are "Valvasinos," who originally were not even properly Vassals <note>original: "qui propriè non erant olim Vasalli"</note> according to the first title of the first book of Fiefs. In this way, a "Question of Status" could easily be raised against many a nobleman, including myself. For 150 years ago, the ancestral house of Gemmingen was still allodial; later it was held from Speyer, and finally from Württemberg. Therefore, Speyer and Württemberg must have only then made my ancestors into noblemen, and they were none before? Indeed, we would still not be noble, according to the text in Title 10, Book 2 of the Fiefs, which says: "The rest, however, who do not hold a benefit <note>A 'beneficium' or fief.</note> from ancient times (that is, before the written books of Fiefs), even if they have newly acquired it from Captains or Valvasors, are nonetheless commoners." In this way, all noblemen would likely be peasants. For I do not believe that a single nobleman in these lands held a fiefdom in the time of Frederick I and Obertus de Orto. By this logic, the Counts of Oettingen and other Counts who possess their counties by **allodial right** would not be Counts; and those who only turned their counties into fiefs 100 or 200 years ago would only then have become Counts. Indeed, many and almost all Princes would have the right to create Counts, because they invest certain people with counties—a claim no one has ever made. Or, if Valvasors could still make Valvasinos today by granting them a fief, then every Count could make a Free Imperial Knight, which is absurd. Therefore, let Cujacius be gone, and let us acknowledge that the Feudal Laws or Lombard Customs cannot always be adapted to our German heritage.

Some wish to deduce the origin of the nobility from the hereditary offices of the old cathedrals and foundations; but I have found it to be a settled fact that the hereditary offices were filled from the ranks of the most distinguished noblemen and families, but never the reverse—that non-nobles were pulled into hereditary offices from which nobility finally emerged. The nobility does not have its origin from priests; it is much older. Those hereditary officials, or **Ministerials** <term>Ministeriales</term> <note>A class of unfree knights who rose to high status through administrative or military service to a lord or the church.</note> as some call them, were not ennobled by their office, but were already noble before they became officials. Indeed, "nobler nobles," so to speak—that is, the oldest and most distinguished families—were promoted to such hereditary offices, just as even today...

those so ennobled, **examples are readily available.** And if the noblemen originate from hereditary offices, then where have all the families and noblemen gone who lived in infinite numbers **in the time of Julius Caesar and Pharamond?** <note>Pharamond is a legendary early king of the Franks.</note> Did they then leave no **descendants** <note>original: "posteros"</note> behind, so that the Bishops would have had to create so many new noblemen again? And who gave the Bishops the **power to ennoble?** <note>original: "potestatem nobilitandi"</note> The Bishop of Bamberg has all the secular Electors <note>The high-ranking princes who elected the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> as his ceremonial officers; did he therefore make them Electors, or do the Electors **originally** descend from a Bishop of Bamberg? 

I hold instead that the nobility in the three Imperial Circles <note>The administrative groupings of the Holy Roman Empire, likely referring here to the Franconian, Swabian, and Rhenish Circles.</note> exists in a **three-fold or rather four-fold distinction.** 

The first are, as it were, the **Original Inhabitants** <term>Aborigines</term> <note>Referring to those who have been in the land since "time immemorial."</note> originating from the first, most ancient Germans and Alemanni who inhabited these regions. For even among those most ancient Germans, there were distinctions of rank, and thus there were both nobles and commoners, as **Tacitus, Caesar, Athenaeus (following Posidonius), Adam of Bremen, and others demonstrate.** 

The second group comes from the **Romans**, who distributed estates <note>original: "prædia"</note> in Germany across the Rhine to their **soldiers**, **under the condition that they and their heirs would possess them for military service.** Among these were undoubtedly many **Centurions, Tribunes, and Roman Knights**, and even impoverished **Patricians (that is, the sons of Senators).** After they had been there for a hundred years or more, they remained there following the invasion of the Franks, enticed **by the sweetness of their native soil**, and (like some others **from the first class of Nobles, namely the Original Inhabitants**) they timely **accommodated themselves** to the **Frankish Victors.** Therefore, they were not reduced **into servitude** like the others who were **more stubborn.** 

The third group, which constitutes the **greatest part, is descended from the Frankish Victors, a tribe that was always most free.** 

The fourth are the **more recent Nobles**, ennobled by the **Emperors from the time of Charlemagne until now**, who are nonetheless not easily received into the **Register** <term>Matricul</term> <note>The official roll or membership list of the Free Imperial Knighthood.</note> of the Free Knighthood.

When one must then admit, **from the aforementioned points**, that before the beginning of **Fiefs, Valvasors, and Valvasinos** <note>Terms for various levels of feudal vassals.</note>—indeed, even before the first beginning of the hereditary offices of the Bishoprics and Principalities—there were noblemen who were neither **sub-vassals** <note>original: "Valvasini"</note> nor **officials** nor hereditary officers, but were **free** (**as almost all, if not all, were in these regions**), then one rightly asks: were these same Free Nobles, who were neither **vassals** nor **sub-vassals**, neither **officials** nor **servants** <term>Ministeriales</term> <note>A class of unfree nobles who rose to power through service to a lord.</note>, subject immediately to the Empire or to a Prince? If they were "Imperial-free" <note>Subject only to the Emperor, not a local prince.</note>, when did they begin to become "Landed Subjects" <term>Landsässen</term> <note>Nobles who were subject to a territorial prince rather than just the Emperor.</note>, and how and why? If one wishes to say they were his landed subjects, **the question arises:**

<margin>Besold, Volume I.</margin>

<column-break/>

who made them landed subjects, and when? If one wishes to say that the **subjection** of the nobility began and originated from the holding of fiefs, then such a view is contrary to the well-founded **opinion** of many distinguished **modern legal scholars**: that **vassalage does not imply subjection.** It is contrary to clear **experience**, as many a Territorial Prince and feudal lord have settled with one another; the good fiefs were all granted voluntarily, while the poor ones were given only out of grace. I refer to all feudal records. **But who would believe** that someone would purchase **servitude** and **slavery**, or even take it upon themselves for the sake of two or three guilders of income? I myself hold such minor fiefs of three or four guilders, and they are among the very oldest, dating back three hundred years. **And even assuming** that one or several people wanted to do such a thing, is it therefore to be **presumed** that all the nobility were such beasts that they despised their liberty and, moreover, defected from their **ordinary Magistrate** <note>The Emperor.</note> and **subjected** themselves to another? **And assuming again** that they were so forgetful, did the Roman Emperors consent to such a defection? And could he not, as their **true Master, recall and reclaim** such **fugitive slaves** <note>original: "Servos fugitivos"</note> **whenever they fled?**

To proceed to the other main question: I can also hardly believe that the current Free Imperial Knighthood were ever the immediate subjects of the old Swabian or Franconian Dukes, or the Counts Palatine of the Rhine, or that they gave and took justice from them **actively and passively.** Instead, **the presumption is in favor of Liberty**, and the **burden of proof** does not lie with me.

I also do not believe that **any Duke of Swabia ever absolutely ruled all of Swabia, nor any Duke of Franconia all of Franconia, nor any Count Palatine of the Rhine the entire stretch of the Rhine**, with all high territorial authority **and territorial right.** I do not believe they had a **closed territory**, as they say, but only **certain scattered pieces here and there**: the income, the serfs <term>Leibeigene</term>, **and consequently** the villages in which there were only serfs. **As I see it**, it will be difficult to prove otherwise. The remaining estates belonged to the Empire, especially the cities (of which there were few in the Empire then), as well as all other Princes, Foundations, Counts, and the Nobility who were subject to the Empire alone. These also possessed much land, property, and villages; not everything belonged solely to the **Dukes of Swabia, Franconia, etc.** Indeed, the smaller part of the land was theirs; they were **mixed lords of all Swabia**, of the whole Circle.

<summary>The author argues that the German nobility's freedom is ancient and inherent, originating from Germanic, Roman, and Frankish roots rather than being a gift of servitude from later territorial princes or bishops. He asserts that holding a fief does not equate to being a subject and that historical dukes never held absolute, undivided power over their entire regions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's legal argument regarding the historical independence of the German nobility. He is specifically addressing the "Imperial Circles" (administrative districts of the Holy Roman Empire) and debating whether the high-ranking Dukes of Swabia and Franconia truly held sovereign authority over the local knights and lesser nobles, or if those nobles remained directly subject only to the Emperor.</meta>

### Treasury of Practical Law, Augmented ###

Circles, but Dukes in Swabia, in Franconia, that is, in some part of Swabia, of Franconia, on the part of the Rhine. Regarding the ancient **Counts Palatine of the Rhine**, it is obvious that even four hundred years ago they did not possess a shoe's breadth of land above Bacharach, whereas now they possess nothing below Bacharach. That the Swabian Counts, noble squires, and cities were not subject to **Conrad, Duke of Swabia** (later Emperor) *as Duke* <note>original: "tanquam Duci"</note>, we have a clear text in the Preface to the Old Ordinance of Rottweil from the year 1147. But when Pope Innocent [says] there: "He also compelled all Princes, Counts, noble squires, and cities belonging to the Holy Empire."

It does not argue to the contrary that they were called **Dukes of Swabia, Franconia, etc.**; *for a firm argument cannot be drawn from a title* <note>original: "à denominatione enim non firmum ducitur Argumentum"</note>. In Spain, and especially England, many a man styles himself **Duke** or **Count** <note>original: "Dux, vel Comes"</note> of a land in which he possesses very little or nothing; rather, it all belongs to the King. This is also proven by the example of **Gabriel Bethlen** <note>A Prince of Transylvania and leader of anti-Habsburg forces</note>, who was long ago titled *Prince of Hungary* by His Imperial Majesty, yet he is not for that reason Lord over Hungary; in England, such things are common.

In the meantime, I do not deny that they were (as the times were then) rich and powerful; I also believe that the neighboring nobility held closely to them *because of their reputation for virtue* <note>original: "propter opinionem virtutis"</note>, as happens today with the nobility even where they are not territorial subjects. One has an example in **Frederick the Victorious of the Palatinate** 150 years ago; indeed, even 100 years ago, **Franz von Sickingen**, a nobleman, could bring together 2,000 horsemen in his own name and besiege great cities.

It may well be, because they were very closely related to the Emperors, and the Emperors were almost constantly occupied with wars outside of Germany, that they were appointed by them for a time as **Governors** *in the name of the Emperor* <note>original: "nomine Imperatoris"</note>, or as Vicars over an entire Circle, or even further.

And everything I have indicated so far is further proven by the discussion of the question of the **regional courts** <term>Landgerichten</term>: for if the Dukes of Swabia, Franconia, etc., had possessed a closed territory and princely territorial authority, it must necessarily follow that the regional courts in Swabia and Franconia belonged to them, and that *law and justice were administered in their names* <note>original: "ipsorum nomine daselbsten jus & justitia administriret worden"</note>.

But to my knowledge, no one has yet said such a thing; rather, 500 or more years ago, there were a great many regional courts called **Imperial Regional Courts**, where everything was conducted in the Imperial name: just as in the year 1282, **Schweickhart von Gemmingen** was the Imperial Regional Judge in Wimp-

<column-break/>

fen. It was only much later that several regional courts in Swabia and Franconia were handed over to certain Estates of the Empire. Which I understand in no other way than that they are hereditary regional judges *in the name of the Caesar* <note>original: "nomine Cæsaris"</note>, just as the Counts of Sulz are Hereditary Court Judges at Rottweil.

But even assuming that the **Dukes of Swabia & Franconia**, and likewise the **Counts Palatine of the Rhine**, had noblemen as territorial subjects <term>Landsassen</term> <note>Nobles who owe service to a local prince rather than directly to the Emperor</note>, there would have been few of them—perhaps around Waiblingen, Göppingen, Würzburg, Bacharach, and a part of the Moselle. What then were the others? Free men and territorial subjects—and of whom? For it is certain from what was said above that none of those Dukes ruled an entire Circle.

But even granted this—that the old Dukes in Swabia and Franconia were territorial Princes and *Territorial Lords* <note>original: "Domini Territoriales"</note> of the entire Circle, and thus the nobility were territorial subjects, and these lands later fell back to the Emperor or the Empire—it does not follow that the members of the nobility should be titled or be the Emperor's territorial subjects rather than free Imperial nobility. For if those Dukes were universal Territorial Lords, it must follow that the Counts, and even the cities, were subjected to them in the same way. Now, just as those lands returned to the Empire after those Ducal families became extinct and are now Estates as before, why not also the noblemen? *Since everything usually returns easily to its origin* <note>original: "cum unumquodque facilè redire soleat ad suum principium"</note>. Thus it also goes with **pledge-money** <note>original: "Pfandschillingen"</note> when it is redeemed; likewise in France with the **appanage lands** given to the King's sons or brothers.

I am not unaware that some (including **Goldastus** <note>Melchior Goldast, a prominent Swiss jurist and historian of the era</note> among others) hold that the nobility anciently had only *modest coercion* <note>original: "modicam coercionem"</note> but not at all the **right of the sword** <term>jus gladii</term> <note>The power to impose the death penalty; a mark of high sovereignty</note>, which I cannot well grasp in such a bare and general way. In some places it is still true today, as mostly in the Odenwald, yet not always; likewise in the two "Zenten" <note>Administrative/judicial districts</note> in the Reichgäu, but outside those districts not at all. Sometimes the nobles were vigilant for themselves; if one was not granted a whole county, he perhaps earned a village. Indeed, the ancient, so-called **Counties under Charlemagne** were not all granted *as a whole* <note>original: "in corpore"</note>—who would say such a thing?—but many were broken up *piece by piece* <note>original: "membratim"</note> and given to nobles, monasteries, and others. Where did the authority go or remain then? Thus, the boundaries of the old counties are quite lost; therefore, I see no reason why the nobility should not have had the **right of the sword** and **absolute authority** <term>merum Imperium</term> in their villages from the most ancient times: except for those—

<meta>catchword: lis</meta>

He asserts that the local nobility held their own high judicial rights (the "right of the sword") directly from the Empire, rather than being mere subjects of regional princes.</summary>

# Treasury of Practical Law #

### Page 901 ###

...in those places where the **Hundred Courts** <note>original: "Centenæ," administrative and legal districts in the Holy Roman Empire</note> exist by tradition, which were also mentioned above. I also do not believe that **Conrad, Duke of Swabia**, held **High Jurisdiction** <note>original: "Hohe Obrigkeit," the legal power over life and death</note> in Michelfeld or Dreschklingen, or that he himself or his ministers in his name ever had someone executed there. **Who, therefore, held high jurisdiction** <note>original: "merum Imperium"</note> **there and in the neighborhood? Who punished criminals?** If he did not, much less did **Conrad the Franconian**, or **Conrad** or **Henry**, the **Counts Palatine**. Certainly not the **Emperor**, for no traces of any such Imperial criminal jurisdiction being exercised exist there. However, in the **Stieber-Hundred** <note>original: "Stieber-Zent"</note>, located two miles away, which even today is a pledge from the Empire—formerly pledged to the noble lords of **Hirschhorn** and today to the **Electoral Palatinate**—it is different. But in the **Upper Kraichgau**, and from there into the land of **Württemberg**, and all the way up the **Danube**, and up the **Rhine** beyond **Strasbourg**, even **Basel**, no such "Hundred" is known. Whoever owns a village possesses it, for the most part, **with every kind of jurisdiction** <note>original: "cum omnimodâ jurisdictione"</note>, with few exceptions where perhaps voluntary or conditional concessions or pacts occurred. Now, if one wished to deny the **right of the sword** <note>original: "jus gladii," the right to execute criminals</note> to the nobility in such places, to whom would one grant it? For the **Neighboring Princes** have all acquired their lands through **particular titles** <note>original: "Titulis particularibus"</note>, mostly from noblemen, foundations, counts, etc., and thus have no more rights than the **original possessors** <note>original: "primi possessores"</note> had. Thus, he who gave them the **advocacy** <note>term: "Vogtey" — the office of a protector or administrator of a territory, often on behalf of a religious institution</note> could also give them High Jurisdiction; indeed, he wished to do so: because he and his successors never exercised such rights for many 100, even 1000 years, nor appointed a servant who should exercise them **in the Emperor’s name** <note>original: "Imperatoris nomine"</note> (for the local judges were only appointed for **civil legal matters** <note>original: "Civilia judicialia"</note>), but **knowingly and deliberately** <note>original: "Sciens & Prudens"</note> let the **Nobles** <note>original: "Nobiles"</note> exercise them. **Gaeddaeus** <note>Johannes Gaeddaeus (1553–1623), a famous German legal scholar</note> speaks very incoherently on this matter regarding the **Free Knighthood**, like a blind man speaking of color: the reason being, he was born and raised in **territorial subjection** <note>term: "Landsässerey" — the state of being a subject of a local prince rather than being directly under the Emperor</note> and went no further; he does not know what kind of creature the Free Knighthood is; **his absurd sayings do not deserve a refutation.** The **Counts of Katzenelnbogen** were powerful but never had any **landed subjects** among the nobility. **Landgrave George** (**grandfather of the current Prince** <note>original: "moderni Principis Avus"</note>) began to claim this in the year 1566, and **the lawsuit still hangs in the Chamber Court** <note>original: "lis adhuc pendet in Camera"</note>. **Ziegenhain** lies in the **Principality of Hesse**; those same Counts were themselves landed subjects. Regarding **Nieda**, I know of no basis; I consider it to have happened **by force and by fact** <note>original: "vi & de facto"</note>, as it also went with those in the **Ginfsecker Valley**, all within human memory. The good people allowed themselves to be worn out by many tribulations due to a lack of protection, and did not wait for a final legal determination, except for those in the **Upper County of Katzenel-**

<column-break/>

**nbogen**. Unfortunately, many feathers have been plucked from the **Imperial Eagle** by more powerful interests successively here and there—not only noble feathers, but perhaps even larger ones.

As for the cited example of the **Lordship of Hohenberg**, I do not know its condition. **Granting** <note>original: "Posito"</note> that they have not had high jurisdiction from the nobility since ancient times, but have since **acquired it by prescription** <note>legal term: gaining a right through long-continued use</note> or otherwise, or even do not have it yet (as many more such examples can be found): yet such a thing cannot **prejudice** <note>legally disadvantage</note> those who do possess it: **for from a singular instance, nothing can be concluded regarding the universal.** <note>original: "a singulari enim ad universale nihil concluditur"</note>

Fourthly, regarding the fact that there are also **Counts** to be found who have held jurisdiction over the nobility settled in their counties, and still claim it: I am of the opinion that several may indeed have occasionally delivered judgment **among the Nobles** <note>original: "inter Nobiles"</note>: **but on the contrary, the Nobles more often delivered judgment to the Counts.** But all this was **by the agreement of the parties** <note>original: "per prorogationem partium"</note>; it was a voluntary judgment agreed upon by both sides. Because at that time there was no **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>term: "Kayserl. Cammergericht" — the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire, established in 1495</note>, and the **Emperors** were mostly away from the Empire, the parties sought voluntary justice wherever they could. I have had very many of those files, especially among others the very notable case where one from **Remchingen** and a **Gösler** litigated in eight different places **over the same cause at different times** <note>original: "super eâdem causâ diversis temporibus"</note> without effect, until finally the Emperor appointed **Lord George of Gemmingen**, Doctor of Both Laws and Cathedral Provost at **Speyer**, as **Commissioner** <note>original: "Commissario"</note>, who settled the matter. Commonly, someone who had a claim or was burdened by another named and proposed three Princes, Counts, or even more (of whose letters I have seen quite many) and wrote to his opponent that he might seek, take, or give justice before one of them. If the opponent would not give or take justice before any of them, the other complained of it everywhere to good friends, gathered a following, and issued a **challenge** <note>term: "Fehde" — a formal declaration of a feud or private war</note> to the opponent. From this came the **Fist-Law** <note>term: "Faustrecht" — the "right of the strong," or private warfare, common before the 1495 Perpetual Public Peace</note> and, even today, the **Law of Arbitration** <note>original: "Recht der Austräge"</note>: **for that long and ancient custom was finally confirmed by Law.**

I would like to see the cited **Fürstenberg** and **Helfenstein** documents in their proper form; the answer would undoubtedly be found, especially from those who are interested parties. Almost identical arguments were used by the **Electoral Palatinate** against the nobility; among other things, they presented a letter in which the words **Nobles, Non-Nobles** <note>original: "Nobiles, Ignobiles"</note> were found, **but in vain.** For such arguments were esteemed as nothing by **His Imperial Majesty**. Those ancient writings are to be understood in such a way that no...

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law #

### Page 902 ###

...might follow an absurd interpretation. Thus, the **Helfenstein letter of enfeoffment** <note>original: "Lehenbrieff"</note> can very well be understood as referring to the **direct fiefs** <note>original: "directo feudorum"</note> dependent on that County, which the local **Nobles** <note>original: "Nobiles"</note> possessed.

Furthermore, in former times, there was also a **third class of men** <note>original: "tertium genus hominum"</note>, the **Free Citizens** <note>original: "Freyburger"</note> or **Patricians** <note>original: "Geschlechter"</note>, who also wished to be called **Nobles**, just as they are now; however, they are not **Free Imperial Nobility**, for there is a distinction. In earlier times, the Empire was in a poor state, and there was a **great simplicity among men** <note>original: "magna simplicitas hominum"</note>. In the **tradition books of Fulda** <note>original: "libro traditionum Fuldensium," records of land donations to the Abbey of Fulda</note>, a great number of legal instruments can be found in which streams, mills, people, and **serfs** <note>original: "Leibeigne"</note> are transferred, even though in many of the named places there was never a stream or anything of the kind, but often only a poor piece of meadow or something similar. I myself have seen many such bills of sale; there were poor **scribes** <note>original: "Concipisten"</note> back then who used **fixed formulas** <note>original: "certarum formularum"</note> whether they were appropriate to the situation or not. And such letters of enfeoffment, regarding the **free Nobility of the Empire**, never actually took effect; indeed, they were likely never presented or brought to the notice of the nobility until now. Similarly, the **Count of East Frisia** for many years allowed himself to be secretly enfeoffed with those lands before he dared to reveal it, waiting until he saw his advantage. He succeeded through **force of arms and various arts** <note>original: "per arma & varias artes"</note> for a time, but it does not go that way for everyone, and the East Frisians are still restless; the day is not over yet.

I was just about to conclude when it occurred to me that the **Golden Bull** <note>original: "Aureæ Bullæ," the 1356 decree serving as the Empire's constitution</note> and the description of the **Imperial Estates** <note>original: "Reichsstände"</note> at the **Imperial Diets** <note>original: "Reichstäge"</note> were mentioned above. I recall that from the records of the **Common Penny** <note>original: "gemeinen Pfennings," an Imperial tax</note> of the year 1495, it is clear that even then the **Swabian Knighthood of the Shield of St. George** <note>A powerful league of knights formed to protect their rights</note> in the **Hegau** region, and far and wide around there, as well as in the **Ortenau**, were summoned to the Imperial Diets. It may well be asked why the other **Circles** <note>administrative districts of the Empire</note> or quarters—which for the most part possess more **regalia** <note>sovereign rights</note>, high authorities, and freedoms—were not also summoned? I know of no other reason than that in ancient times, no **Imperial Estate** was summoned individually to the Diets; rather, the Diets were only called in general through a **public decree** <margin>Add to this entirely Limn. volume 1. Addition to book 6. chapter 3. page 54. 42. preamble.</margin>. But when the Estates began to appear only sporadically or negligently, **Frederick III**, I believe, was first prompted to summon the Estates **individually** <note>original: "in specie"</note>. Because of the **negligence and carelessness of the Imperial Secretaries and Councilors**, many Imperial Estates were overlooked for a long time at the beginning. Indeed, many Princes—such as those of **Holstein, Pomerania, and Mecklenburg**—were (as I have heard) neither summoned to the Imperial Diets nor appeared there for many years. From this arose the still-ongoing disputes over **seating order** <note>original: "Session-Stritt"</note>...

<column-break/>

...and from this also came the **great imperfection** of the old **Matricula** <note>original: "Matricul," the official register of Imperial Estates used for tax and military levies</note>. Who then should be surprised that some of the **Knighthood** were overlooked? Nevertheless, the Emperor did summon those most familiar to the **Imperial Court** and the **Imperial Councilors**, such as those in the **Ortenau** and the **Shield of St. George** in the Hegau (if I am not mistaken), as well as those belonging to **Friedberg Castle**. Since a large part of the nobility usually came to the Diets with the **Electors and Princes**, and these could handle the Knighthood's affairs where necessary, they paid little attention to such oversights—especially because they thought it was to their benefit, as they would otherwise have had to help bear the **Imperial burdens** <note>taxes and military costs</note>, which they never wanted to do. Thus, they preferred to stay away from the Diets. And that is exactly the reason why, under **Charles V**, the Knighthood did not want to be summoned to the Imperial Diets, fearing they would have to contribute to the maintenance of the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original: "Cammergericht"</note> and other expenses.

Otherwise, I believe that if the Knighthood were summoned to the **Diets** <note>original: "Comitia"</note>, they would have their **seat** <note>original: "Session"</note> in the **Council of Princes** immediately after the Counts and Lords, and following their example, would be divided into three benches; even if not three, they would have at least one **decisive vote** <note>original: "votum conclusivum"</note> like the Counts, not just a **consultative one** <note>original: "consentiendi"</note> like the Imperial Cities.

But whether the **immediate freedom** <note>meaning they report only to the Emperor</note> of these Nobles has been proven regarding their persons, or truly regarding their subjects as well, let that be for others to judge.

# 38. **Imperial City**, **Free Imperial City**. **Free Imperial Cities**. <note>original: "Civitates Liberæ Imperiales"</note>

Concerning the Free Cities of the Empire, see my own individual treatise. Likewise, see Johann Steinwich on the rights of Cities, and Johann Michael Heintz on the subjection and liberty of Imperial Cities among the Strasbourg disputations, as well as Lehmann’s *Chronicle of Speyer* <note>original: "Chronicon Spirense"</note> in various places. Also, Mr. Mager’s treatise on Advocacy <note>original: "de Advocatia," referring to the legal office of a protector or bailiff</note>, in the many places indicated by the Index.

The **Imperial Cities** <note>original: "Reichs-Städte"</note> are cities and fortresses of the Roman Imperial Majesty and the Holy Empire, and they constitute the Empire’s own patrimony. Because of their demonstrated loyalty and constancy, they received their exemptions and freedom, as well as various **royal rights** <note>original: "Regalia"</note> and lordships, from the Roman Emperors. This was noted by Ferdinand II in a mandate to the Imperial Cities on May 14, 1631.

Furthermore, the Free Cities of the Empire stand in the place of a Province, according to the *Defense of the Free Imperial City of Speyer* <note>original: "Apologia meri Imperii Civitat. Spirens."</note>, page 199, where many points regarding the law of Cities are found throughout.

That the Imperial Cities formerly had a judge and were also obligated and sworn to the Bishop, see the *Worms Council* <note>original: "Wurmbsische Rathung"</note>, Book 3, section 4. In that same place, the **City-Master** <note>original: "Stadt-Meister," a high municipal official</note> also swears an oath to the Bishop, as seen in Book 3 and elsewhere, where the rights of the Bishop in the City of Worms are discussed. It is also written in the *Donauwörth Report* <note>original: "Donawertischen Relation"</note>, page 22, that Bishops in Imperial Cities have jurisdiction over Catholic citizens.

Free Imperial Cities <note>original: "Liberæ Imperii Civitates"</note> can exercise the rights of **territorial lordship** <note>original: "Lands-Herrlichkeit"</note> and **territorial sovereignty** <note>original: "Land-Obrigkeit"</note> in their own cities and their dependencies in the same manner as Princes do by their territorial right. See Matthias Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 1, part 2, chapter 1, number 63; Klock on Contributions, conclusion 19; Caspar Ziegler in the section on Landholders, conclusion 1, number 203; and Scipio Gentilis on Jurisdiction, book 3, chapter 22.

For they themselves are also directly subject to the Emperor and the Empire and are Estates of the Empire. Matthias Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 2, part 1, chapter 4, number 35; Gail, observation 1, number 19; see also *The Composition of Peace* <note>original: "Pacis Composit.," referring to legal settlements regarding religious and civil peace</note>, question 37, number 59, and question 34, number 26 and following.

They are also recorded in the **Imperial Register** <note>original: "Matricula Imperii"</note> drawn up in the year 1521, which is certain evidence of their status of **immediacy** <note>the status of being subject only to the Emperor, without an intermediate lord</note>. This is evident from the Decree of the Diet of Regensburg in 1575, in the section "When also Frankfurt," and from the year 1548, in the section "Although also in the government," etc. Ziegler, in the cited place at number 205 and many following, elaborates with great effort on what and how many rights and benefits these Free Cities possess; see him by all means. It should be known that the citizens in Imperial Cities are called **Imperial Citizens** <note>original: "Reichs-Burger"</note> for this reason: because they, together with the Council, constitute an Estate of the Empire. From *The Composition of Peace*...

<column-break/>

...published at Dillingen. For the citizens of Imperial Cities are subjects directly to the Emperor, as stated in the said *Composition of Peace*, question 37, number 52.

The Imperial City of **Friedberg** <note>original: "Fridbergensis"</note>, above many others, is fortified and endowed with many rights, according to the author of the *Thorough Report on the Royal Rights of the Imperial City of Friedberg* <note>original: "gründlichen Berichts der Reichsstatt Friedberg Regalien"</note>, chapter 2, number 15, and chapter 1, number 203. It states there: that they are graced with the **Imperial Feud-right** <note>original: "Reichsvehd," the right to declare a legal private war</note>, the right to arrange their own wars, to provide the highways with **escort** <note>original: "Gleit," safe-conduct protection for travelers</note>, to collect customs, milling fees, road tolls, and bridge, market, and hoof taxes; to make ordinances and statutes, to issue punishments, to appoint administrations and offices, and to hold council and court, and to grant privileges and immunities.

Imperial Cities also possess, within their own kind, the same rights that a Prince has in his Principality. And that which is **Princely** <note>original: "Landsfürstlich"</note> supreme power in a Prince, or **Countly** <note>original: "Grävlich"</note> in a Count, is **City-like** <note>original: "Städtlich"</note> in the Cities. Meichsner, volume 2, book 1, decision 8, numbers 2 and 3; Ziegler in the cited place, number 218; Bidembach in *Noble Questions*, question 1, number 10; see also Riemer on Jurisdiction, X, 2.

Regarding the rank, seat, and vote of an Imperial City, see two separately published legal opinions <note>original: "Consilia"</note> on this matter: whether they are called to the Diets and whether they have a consultative or decisive vote. See the said opinions, as well as Arumäus on the Imperial Diets, chapter 4, number 126, and chapter 7, number 145. On the power to change religion in Imperial Cities, see *The Composition of Peace*, question 37 and following, and the *Donauwörth Report* and its *Refutation*.

Many cities that were subject to various lords, especially ecclesiastical ones, seized their liberty. Thus, concerning **Kempten** <note>original: "Campidono"</note>, Bruschius writes in his work on Monasteries, page 25: There was a very ancient fortress there on the neighboring Hillermontana hill, so named from the Iller River flowing past. This fortress, which at this time is even demolished and devastated, they are accustomed to call the **Burghald**. It was the ancestral seat of the Dukes of Swabia until the time of Charlemagne. The fortress, together with the town, was subject to the Abbots. And, in the year of Christ 910, the monastery, town, and castle were plundered and devastated on all sides by the Huns invading Germany. Around the year 1336, under Abbot Burchard—who fled from the monastery because of the irreconcilable discords of the monks—the Bishop of Constance was appointed as Commissary by the Roman Pontiff. He put a Governor in charge of the monastery, a priest and provost named Conrad Clangenberger, who resided for some time in the Hillermontana fortress. His concubine, Rosina Lattmerin, stole a chest full of letters and diplomas <note>original: "diplomatibus," official charters or grants of rights</note> and sold those letters to certain neighbors who eagerly sought them. Assisted by these letters and made more daring, the citizens of Kempten—and with such a provost sitting at the helm, who was an idle man, winking at everything for the people of Kempten and being too fair and favorable to them—now labored strenuously in establishing...

# Expanded Practical Treasury
<note>original: "Thesauri Practici Adaucti"</note>

...for the construction and completion of its City fortifications, Towers, and walls. When these were completed according to his wish, Kempten <note>original: "Campidonum"</note> began to raise its crests and to be called and named a City <note>original: "Civitas"</note>, which previously was not enclosed but always open to the Abbot and accessible to all men at all moments. Then it began to draw and snatch to itself many liberties and immunities of the Abbey, and also to obtain certain ones with the favor and consent of the Lords of the Convent. Under this very Provost <note>original: "Præposito," a high administrative official in a monastery</note>, the Abbot lost the Keys to the City Gates, which had always previously been in the Abbot's hand. In short, to put many things briefly: this Provost proved to be unfaithful, unfortunate, and a very harmful Administrator of this Monastery, which is said to have been due to a certain Bishop of Constance, Nicholas, and the discords among the brothers.

Henry of Mittelberg was elected in the year 1356 under Pope Clement VI. He resided for the most part in the Castle of Hillermont, today called Burghalten. He usually went about dressed in a white tunic, with a furry pouch always hanging at his side; thus he was accustomed to descend every day on horseback from the castle into the Monastery, and there hear the holy mass in the Temple of All Saints.

However, it happened once that while the Abbot was descending, and the guards of the Castle were not watching very faithfully, the Castle—contrary to the hope or expectation of the Abbot, who feared nothing violent—was occupied by the Citizens toward evening. It was plundered and overturned on the very day of St. Martin, when all the Senators and principal Citizens had been invited to carry out the wine-filled Christian feasts of Martinmas <note>original: "Martinalia"</note> with a solemn procession and a sumptuous banquet. The Abbot, returning to the Castle from the Temple, was caught by his ungrateful guests; he is said to have been immediately thrown down the steps by two Citizens, Bustarus and the elder Otecarus, but he escaped by flight to Schweighausen, where, having mounted a rustic horse and with some servants accompanying him, he reached Isny <note>original: "Isnam"</note> unharmed that same night. In this seditious destruction of the Castle, a chest full of letters and diplomas <note>original: "diplomaticus"</note> was lost, which the Citizens destroyed in a fire.

The next day, the people of Kempten elected their first Consul <note>original: "Consulem," referring to the office of Burgomaster or Mayor</note>, Henry Schultetus, who also afterwards held this day as solemn for a long time, dedicated to the creation of new Magistrates, kept as a Feast day until the time of Abbot John of Ryetheym. The cause of this rebellion and foul devastation was on the lips of the Citizens: that daughters of the Citizens had been dragged by force into the Castle and violated by the Abbot's servants and officials <note>original: "Ministerialibus"</note>. Abbot Henry, having reported the matter to Emperor Charles IV, brought it about that the Senate and People of Kempten <note>original: "S. P. Q. Campidonensis"</note> were forced both to pay a large fine and to freely return the Castle to the Abbot—either to be rebuilt or to be left deserted—which, however, a little later the same Abbot sold entirely to the aforementioned Republic <note>referring here to the city-state of Kempten</note>. He died in the year 1382.
