Mention is deservedly made of the consensus of the Electors: For already in the year 1216, in the Court or Assembly of Princes held at Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipoli"</note>, it was decreed that it was not permitted for the Emperor to alienate <note>transfer ownership of</note> any of the Imperial States: and then, by the consensus and judgment of all, a certain exchange made by Frederick II was rescinded. Hund, in *Metropolis Salisburgensi*, vol. 1, p. 200.

In turn, many Cities formerly obeyed Princes, which later came under the Empire, though with certain rights reserved to the old Princes who held power there. Even Bishops held certain jurisdictional rights almost everywhere in the Cities where they were Bishops: as can be seen regarding Regensburg <note>original: "Ratisbona"</note> in Hund, vol. 1, p. 220. Also p. 238 etc., and p. 267. Regarding mixed Cities which are States, see my work in the treatise *On the Law of Universities* <note>original: "de Jure Universitat."</note>, the *Brunswick Acts against Brunswick*, Counsel 5. Knichen in his overview, and Dauth p. 200. And generally on Cities, Scipio Gentili, book 3 *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 22. Bocer *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 8, number 81 and following. Waremund, book 2 *On Alliances*, p. 29 and following. And Bocer argues in his treatise *On the Crime of Majesty*, chapter 2, number 100, that the crime of treason <note>original: "crimen Majestatis"</note> can be committed against Imperial Cities. Regarding the privileges of Imperial Cities and their citizens, see *The Composition of Peace*, p. 368.

Imperial Cities (either by express privileges of the Emperors or by prescription exceeding human memory, which obtains the force and effect of a privilege granted with certain knowledge) possess jurisdiction which the Emperors used to exercise through <term>Imperial Prefects</term> <note>original: "Reichsvögt," officials appointed by the Emperor to act as judges or administrators</note> in

<column-break/>

their cities, both regarding legal cases and persons. They obtain the same power that Princes, Counts, and Barons have in their own Provinces: Paurmeister establishes this specifically in *On Jurisdiction*, book 2, last chapter, number 17, and Martin Mager in *On Advocacy*, chapter 6, number 189.

Regarding the office of the <term>City Amman</term> <note>original: "Stadt-Amman-Amt," a local judicial or administrative official</note> in the City of Lindau, the family named Butscher possessed this office several centuries ago by right of pledge. Haider, treatise *On Imperial Prefects*.

The office of Amman in the Imperial Cities belonged to the Emperor; it subsequently passed to Princes, Counts, and Lords. Thus, the Amman-office in Biberach, the tax, and the Amman-office in Buchau once belonged to the family of Helffenstein.

Imperial Cities in the time of Charles V almost displayed the form of a democracy; because this was prone to sedition, the aforementioned Emperor converted it into an aristocracy after the Schmalkaldic War <note>A religious war fought from 1546–1547</note>, though not everywhere; he abolished the Guilds <note>original: "hat die Zünfften abgethan"</note>.

## 39. Imperial Tax, Levy. Imperial Collection.
<note>original: "Reichssteuer, Anlag. Collecta Imperialis."</note>

Imperial Tax, Imperial Levy, Imperial Aid, is an <term>Imperial Collection</term> <note>original: "Collecta Imperialis"</note> which is imposed upon everyone subject to the Empire for the benefit of the whole Empire. Gail, book 2, observation 53. Such as the Turkish tax <note>original: "Türckensteuer, Türckenhülff"</note>, and the Roman Expedition <note>original: "Römerzug," a tax to fund the Emperor's journey to Rome for coronation</note>, which Feudal and Justinian laws call an "extraordinary contribution" <note>original: "extraordinariam Collationem"</note> to provide for the most successful expedition of the Imperial Power. *On what things are regalian*, book 2, feudal law, section 1. Code *On which duties or payments*. A collection is also imposed for the preservation of the Empire’s Governance <note>original: "zu Erhaltung deß Reichs Regiments"</note>. Only the Roman Emperor imposes this Imperial Collection, the Imperial Tax, and then only with the consent of the Imperial States. Hence, in the Recesses of the Empire <note>official resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note>, this clause is usually added: "and we have agreed with them, and they in turn with us."

In former times, the Roman Emperors, through appointed officials, collected the tax directly from all the intermediate subjects of the Imperial States themselves; however, it is now done through the Estates from their subjects, as touched upon in the matter of the Teutonic Master against Oettingen, in Meichsner, vol. 2, book 1, decision 6, number 64, p. 620. Ruland, *On Commissioners*, part 4, book 2, chapter 6, number 65.

## 40. Imperial Diet. <note>original: "Reichs Tag" / "Comitia Imperii"</note>

Concerning the Diets, see especially Mr. Arumæus in his most complete treatise on the *Imperial Diets*. Bertram, in the same Arumæus, volume 1, discourse 9. Mr. Goldast in *Bohemia*, folio 435.

**Imperial Diet**, called *Diæta*, and the most ancient term is *Diet* for a multitude or gathering of people. Goldast, in his *Ancient Admonitions*, folio 371. Nithart writes:

> Now it has turned around,
> Shameless, false people <note>original: "Diet"</note> have increased their court.
> Brother Werner:
> There you comforted the people <note>original: "Diet"</note> when with nails
> You were struck upon the Cross.
> Strickere, in the *Deeds of Charlemagne*:
> That he with his people <note>original: "Diete"</note>
> commanded a court there
> at his seat in Aachen.

From this comes **Diæta**, meaning a public assembly, the Diet, the Provincial Diet, the Circle Diet, the Imperial Diet; regarding which there is a witty saying by Emperor Charles V: *A Diet gives birth to a Diet, and the birth suffocates the mother.* <note>A joke suggesting that one meeting only leads to another, and the process of meeting prevents any actual results from being "born" or finalized.</note> *Diætæ* also refers to nations for the ancient translator of the Psalms: *Thiat* means nation, *Thiadon* means nations, *Thiede* means nations, *Thiadekunne* means generations, etc.

How matters used to proceed at the Imperial Diets, see the individual treatise joined to Christoph Lehmann's *Speyer Chronicle*, and a similar treatise annexed to the *Two Consultations* regarding the voice and session <note>voting rights and seating order</note> of an Imperial City.

Are other assemblies lawful? See Limnäus on the *Public Law* of Daniel Otto, folio 58. Can the States be personally summoned to the Diets? Valentin Riemer, *On Jurisdiction*, Book 1. Whether the nobility belong to the Imperial Diets, see above at the word "Imperial States" <note>original: "Reichs-Stände"</note>, etc., and Lerch, *On the German Knightly Order*, folio 91 and folio 138.

Regarding the summons <note>original: "Ausschreiben"</note> to the Imperial Diet, it should be known that besides the place and day,

<column-break/>

the cause for holding the Diet must also be expressed in them; specifically for this purpose, so that the person summoned may deliberate upon them maturely in advance and be able to instruct his legates <note>representatives</note> more fully and cautiously, if he is to send any. And otherwise, it is a general rule—and consistent with the nature of any citation—that besides the name of the summoner and the person summoned, the day and place, mention should also be made of the cause. Gail, book 1, observation 51. Although the Emperor may issue those letters to the States in the manner of a command rather than a request, nevertheless, because a large part of the law of the Diets also pertains to the States, it is fair and consistent with German liberty that they be addressed with words that are not overly imperious. Hence, there was a departure in later times from the ancient form of calling, which seemed to carry a certain harshness of command. And while the older Emperors used the words *order, bid, command* <note>original: "gebieten, heissen, befehlen"</note>, as in the reformation of Frederick III in the year 1442 and in the summons to the Diet at Augsburg in 1530 by Charles V; the more recent Emperors now temper their authority to summon to the Diets with a gentler address, not without the highest praise for their notable clemency. See Bertram in Arumæus, volume 1, *On the Diets*, discourse 9, thesis 20, where he adds: "For this reason, I would rather think that nothing of his Majesty is lost if the Emperor calls the States to the Diet so that he seems not so much to summon as to request; nor are the rights, privileges, or liberty of the States diminished if they are ordered to come for the sake of the Empire."

## 41. Imperial Bailiff, Imperial Bailiwick. <note>original: "Reichsvogt, Reichsvogtey" / "Præfectus Imperialis, Præfectura Imperialis"</note>

In olden times, generally, not only did monasteries have their own Advocates <note>Vögte</note> and Stewards <note>Castenvögte</note>; but the Imperial Cities also had their particular Imperial Prefects, Imperial Bailiffs, Imperial Sheriffs <note>original: "Reichs-Schultheiß"</note>, and Imperial Amman <note>administrative officials</note>. These individuals, in the name of his Imperial Majesty, administered and managed justice, or at least the High Jurisdiction <term>Blutbann <gloss>The power to try capital crimes involving the shedding of blood</gloss></term> of those places distinctly. Lit. R.
Besoldus, Volume I.
Yyyyy 2

...many) <note>This continues a list of examples from the previous page.</note> that a similar situation occurred particularly many hundreds of years ago regarding the conflict and the City of Lindau: Specifically, the aforementioned Abbey, following its initial foundation by Count Adelbert (whom some call of Buchhorn, some of Bregenz, and some of Rorbach) during the time of Emperor Louis the Second <note>original: "Kayser Ludwig des Andern"; likely referring to Louis the German or Louis the Younger, ca. 866 AD</note>, was placed under a Steward-Advocate <note>original: "Castenvogt"; a secular official appointed to manage and protect the temporal affairs of a religious institution</note>. Among other things, it was granted an exemption (according to its first privilege dated in the year 866) stating that regarding its court-churches, or places, or fields, or remaining possessions, no one should take up the knightly office except the Advocate or Steward of the monastery. This official was to hold court twice a year, though he could not bring more than twelve horses with him; he was to collect one-third of the court fees, while the Lady Abbess was to pocket the remaining two-thirds.

*Furthermore, regarding those matters which still pertain to this and are found in Pythæus, Erasmus à Chockier reports them in French in his "Treatise on Feudal Advocates," question 1, number 9, folio 4 and following.*

The rights which an Imperial Advocate <note>original: "Reichsvogt"</note> once held are clear from two privileges of Rudolf I given to the citizens of Lindau in *the year 1274 and following*, where among other things it is held: That no public judge, Duke or Count, or anyone of judicial power, may or should dare to constrain them concerning possessions of forensic law <note>i.e., matters subject to the public court</note> lying within their city, or in any other secular or civil causes whatsoever; nor should they be bound to answer complainants before anyone other than the Advocate or his substitute in the Palace of the Lady Abbess, and in her presence; nor may the Advocate, nor a Duke, Count, or anyone else, by reason of any judgment against any of the aforesaid citizens in cases which are to be handled before the Advocate or his substitute in the Palace of the Abbess, dare to strike them with a sentence of proscription <note>original: "proscriptionis sententia"; a sentence of outlawry or legal banishment</note>. Furthermore, if someone’s own servant, or someone living in the possession of liberty in the said town as a citizen, should close his final day <note>i.e., pass away</note> and his status is revealed, a third part of his movable goods shall go to the Lord, if natural heirs are seen to survive; if not, half of the movable goods shall be assigned to the Lord. Furthermore, if a man subject to the Advocate’s jurisdiction should have a domicile in the aforesaid town as a citizen, he shall not be bound to perform any personal service to the Advocate. However, when that man subject to the Advocate dies, whatever right belongs to the Church—to which he belonged—regarding the deceased or those things which were of his condition, shall be given without fraud. Additionally, whoever has possessed any estate pertaining to the market of the aforesaid town under any title for the space of a year and a day, peacefully and quietly without legal reclamation or interruption (the claimant being present in the Province), he shall possess that estate peacefully as before. Also, if anyone should depart this life from among his parents without a natural heir, his inheritance shall devolve to the father or mother. If,

<column-break/>

however, the parents do not exist, then the nearest heirs proceeding from the paternal or maternal line shall succeed the deceased.

And in the second privilege, the following things are read: We promise therefore to the said citizens by a special kind of gift, that we shall never alienate, pledge, or exchange the Advocacy belonging to us and the Empire, which is commonly called the Stewardship <note>original: "Cast. vogit." / "Castenvogtei"</note>. We will that this itself be observed by our successors, unshaken for all eternity. Likewise, we establish that no public judge, nor Duke, nor Count, nor anyone of judicial power, shall be able to summon them in any way concerning possessions of forensic law subject to their city, or in other secular causes whatsoever, except before the Advocate or his substitute judge, in the Palace of the Lady Abbess and in the presence of the Lady Abbess. Furthermore, a proscription by the Advocate, Duke, Count, or other judge by reason of any judgment ought not to enter or touch the city of any of these citizens. Also, their city ought to enjoy such right and liberty, namely, that whatever outsider of servile condition is received by the aforesaid citizens as a fellow-citizen—if the same stays in the city of the said citizens for the space of one year without hindrance or reclamation by his Lord (provided the Lord knows he is residing in the town)—he shall thereafter remain forever free and released from all service to his Lord. If, however, service is demanded by his Lord from the same received citizen, provided it is proved within the term of that first year that he belongs by right to servitude, the Lord is bound to be entirely content with a third part of whatever is given to the Advocate on his behalf in the name of service. Moreover, if someone’s own servant, convicted of servitude, dies in the city of the often-mentioned citizens, a third part of his movable goods shall go to the Lord, if carnal heirs are seen to exist; if not, then half of the movables is assigned to the Lord. Likewise, if any man subject to the Advocate is resident in their city, he is not bound to perform any service of his person to the Advocate; but if the same man subject to the Advocate has entered the way of all flesh <note>original: "viam carnis ingressus fuerit"; died</note>, whatever right the entire Church (to which he is seen to belong) appears to have in him or in those who are of the same condition, shall be given without fraud. Also, no Knight or Monk can or is bound to acquire any estate in the city of the aforesaid citizens by hereditary right: And if any estate is given to any monastery or other religious persons for the sake of God, they are bound to sell it within the term of one year; if they neglect to do this, from then on the property of that same estate passes freely and quietly to the nearest heirs of the giver. Also, whatever child, separated from his parents with his own things, shall emigrate from this light <note>i.e., die</note> without a carnal heir, that same inheritance shall clearly fall to the father or mother.

### 44. Religion and Religious Peace. *Religio, Pax Religiosa.*

On Religion and the Religious Peace <note>referring to the legal frameworks like the Peace of Augsburg (1555) or the Peace of Westphalia (1648)</note>, see especially the *Composition of Peace*. On whether the Religious Peace is a pact or a law, see *Composition of Peace* in the preface at letter gg, question 25, and said preface at letter oo. Where there is not one single religion, there is no peace, and even the conditions of peace are disputed and cause much unrest. *Composition of Peace*, question 62, toward the end. And where there is dissent in religion, there is surely the dissolution of the Empire. It is otherwise in Turkey; for those living there have no power but are like slaves, just as the Jews were in Babylonia, etc.

Whether it is permitted for any unmediated member of the nobility <term>ungemittelten vom Adel: nobility who held their lands directly from the Emperor rather than through a local prince</term> to adopt a foreign faith, whether he holds the high or only the lower judicial authority <term>vogteyliche niedergerichtliche Obrigkeit: administrative and lower court jurisdiction</term>? See Bidembach, *Questions on the Nobility*, 3.

Whether a distinction is to be made between landed subjects <term>Landſäſſen: those residing on a lord's estate</term> and the unmediated nobility regarding the exercise of religion: specifically, whether the landed subjects may only practice the exercise for their own person, or whether they might freely establish such worship in their churches, schools, and territories, just as the unmediated knighthood does? See Bidembach, question 4.

Whether an exempt member of the nobility is authorized to change his religion, whether he held one faith or the other before or after the established Religious Peace? See Bidembach, question 5.

If a Prince and a member of the nobility are not of the same faith: whether they can force the subjects in a common market town or village to follow each of their respective faiths? Or in the case of their resistance, whether they could expel them, and whether the subjects are obliged to leave? See Bidembach, question 6.

Religion is a general term and includes everything that is done against conscience. Whenever, therefore, a prohibition is made so that no one is disturbed in his religion, everything is considered prohibited by which the conscience is rendered less free.

Since ecclesiastical jurisdiction regarding religion, conscience, and ceremonies for persons of the Augsburg Confession <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church</note> is said to be suspended according to the section: "so that it be against the Augsburg Confessional religion, faith, and appointment of ministries." From this they conclude that it is certainly also suspended in matrimonial cases in respect to them; for where there is no diocese, there is no longer any spiritual jurisdiction. And under those words—"Religion, Faith, Church Custom" (although no specific mention is made of matrimonial cases)—the same are thought to be included, based on the identity of the reasoning and the final cause

<column-break/>

of the Religious Peace: which is the same in both instances. Because the reasoning of the law holds in one case just as in another, the law is not said to be "extended" to the case, but rather is said to "comprehend" that case, as a genus includes its species.

Furthermore, religion differs in one way or another regarding marriages among the followers of the Augsburg Confession compared to the Catholics, since the former by no means consider marriage to be a Sacrament, and they judge these cases by different laws.

Thus, the Estates of the Augsburg Confession have their own special Church Ordinances <note>original: *Kirchen Ordnung*</note>, to which are attached Marriage Ordinances <note>original: *Ehe Ordnung*</note>, where provisions are made concerning marriages, the consent of parents, degrees of kinship, etc.

Whether in an Imperial City <term>Reichs-Stadt: a city self-governed and answerable only to the Holy Roman Emperor</term> a law may be made that no one shall attain citizenship unless he professes the Augsburg Confession? I say no, if that entire city was not Lutheran from the beginning.

Likewise, when both religions are practiced in an Imperial City, whether public processions should be allowed for the Catholics, as well as going publicly and solemnly to the sick? This was disputed in the Donauwörth affair <note>original: "Donawertiſchen Sache"; a 1606 religious conflict that was a precursor to the Thirty Years' War</note>. And I think such processions cannot be hindered: since he who grants the antecedent is necessarily deemed to permit the consequence.

Whether in Free Cities it is permitted to reclaim monasteries even if they were occupied before the Transaction of Passau <note>1552 treaty that guaranteed religious freedoms</note>? The answer is yes. For 1) this is nowhere prohibited. And what is granted to the Estates does not pertain to the Imperial Cities, where the Emperor has more legal right, who is not grouped with the Estates; according to the style of that constitution, the Imperial Cities and the Estates are dealt with separately, and the Cities are set in opposition to the Estates. 2) It is sanctioned in the section "On Imperial Cities" that each shall leave the other in peace concerning religion. But the recovery of what is one's own is not thereby hindered. And it says "in his goods," meaning those for which he has ownership, not those of which he is a violent possessor. Likewise, the Estates and the citizens of both sides are compared there, but the Estates must restore what one has taken from the other before the Peace.

Catholics in the matter of the Religious Peace always have a well-founded intent, and what is not clearly proven to be granted by the opposing side is rightly said to be prohibited. See *Composition of Peace*, questions 31 and 35.

That peace can be given to heretics through pact and treaty, but not through law, is deduced in the often-cited *Composition of Peace* in the preface at letter vv.

On the difference of the Religious Peace regarding Imperial Estates and Territorial Estates, see *Composition of Peace*, question 27, number 44.

It should be noted that if the Estates of the Empire, according to the axiom of the adversaries, by virtue of the Religious Peace...

The Turks are the strictest observers of their own Law, and yet they tolerate those embracing entirely contrary confessions. The Turks are less scrupulous than the Greeks and many other nations. ### 45. Relics. <note>original: "Reliquien. Reliquiæ."</note>

On Relics, see Filefacus, *Select Works*, chapter 13, and Paul Zypaeus in his *Analysis of Papal Law*, book 3, title "on relics and the veneration of Saints," folio 369 and following. ### 46. Remission of Malefactors. <note>original: "Remissio Delinquentium"</note>

Concerning the remission of delinquents <note>In a legal context, "remission" refers to the transfer of a prisoner from the place of arrest to the place where the crime was committed</note>, see Hunnium in *Criminal Discourses*, folio 18, etc. See also my own work in the treatise *On the Competent Forum* <note>original: "de foro Competent."</note>; Rutger Ruland in his notes to Ferrari; Montani’s *Process*, folio 51, etc.; and Speidel in the *Sylloge*, letter R, under the entry "Remission of delinquents," part 1, paragraph 2.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the Remission or Transmission of Defendants for a crime to the place in which they perpetrated the crime, see extensively C. Rittersh. in *The Novels*, page 568, number 57. That such remissions are still frequently practiced today, see the *Precedent* in Georg Rittersh. *On the Right of Asylum*, page 151, number 1.

### 47. Remonstrants. <note>original: "Remonstrantes"</note>

Regarding the schisms in Holland <note>This refers to the Remonstrants, a Dutch theological movement that broke away from the Reformed Church over the issue of predestination</note>, see the *German Letters* of Sandæus.

### 48. Renewal. <note>original: "Renovatur. Renovatio."</note>

Regarding "Renewal" <term>Renovatur: the formal legal process of updating land registers, feudal titles, or administrative records to ensure rights were not lost to time</term>, Mr. Jacob von Ramingen <note>A 16th-century pioneer in the field of archival science and record-keeping</note> has issued a useful reminder, as he did for "Registration," and therein stated among other things: First, necessity requires one to consider and deliberate upon what exactly one wishes to have renewed.
**First:** A principality or an entire landscape, or a county, and thus a province, and thus an entire territory of some province; or otherwise a lordship and domain, or a single market town, or otherwise a single estate. 
**Second:** Seigniorial rights <note>original: "Herrlichkeiten"</note>, or only the returns and revenues <note>original: "Reditus sive proventus"</note>, or both together. 
**Third:** Or otherwise some specific Rights <note>original: "aliqua Jura"</note>.

If a province or an entire landscape is to be renewed, then it is especially to be considered and observed what kind of regalia <term>Regalien: high sovereign rights, such as coining money or mining, belonging to a ruler</term> and legal rights a province or such a landscape might and should have according to Common Law or Custom. And then, what kind of lordships, cities, castles, fortresses, fortified sites, villages, hamlets, and

<column-break/>

farmsteads are attached with full ownership <note>original: "dominio"</note>; likewise, what is then attached to such a province and landscape as property, and likewise, what therein is held as a fief.

If a lordship is otherwise to be renewed, it would again be necessary to consider and observe what kind of regalia—by right or custom—such a lordship should or may have, either by special grant <note>original: "ex speciali concessione"</note>. Likewise, what kind of intangible rights <note>original: "Jura incorporalia"</note> it holds, whether by Common Law, or again by certain custom, or by special grant, or by prescription of the longest time <note>a legal claim based on very long-term uninterrupted use</note>, or from some contract or pact, or other just title.

Thereafter, whether such a lordship is a free, allodial property <note>privately owned land free of feudal obligations</note>, or a fief, or a pledge-holding subject to repurchase, etc.

**Third:** What kind of goods <note>original: "Bona"</note> belong to such a lordship, are attached or annexed to it, what among them is owned outright, and then what is a fief. Likewise, what is attached not by ownership, and even less by the right of usufruct <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note>, but solely by reason of either high, mixed, or simple jurisdiction <note>original: "meri, aut mixti aut simplicis Jurisdictionis"</note>, or moderate coercion, or some other pre-eminence, and is thus subject to the lordship solely for the sake of the magistracy or other seigniorial authority. Likewise, where the estate is attached solely by ownership, or whether the beneficial ownership <note>original: "utile Dominium"</note> also belongs to it.

**Fourth:** What goods such a lordship has that others possess, use, and enjoy, but for which they are bound and obligated by law or justice to perform services or give payments. Likewise, what and which among these have been granted as a fief <note>original: "in feudum concessa"</note>, and what kind of fief, and of what nature. Likewise, what perpetual leasehold goods <term>Bona Emphyteutica: land held on a long-term lease where the tenant improves the land in exchange for a low rent</term> are among them, what yearly rents <note>original: "Canones"</note> and services have been and should be performed from them. And then, those things which are distributed to sharecroppers or tenant farmers <note>original: "Partiariis aut Colonis"</note>. Likewise, those things which are granted, leased, or rented for a certain time.

In every one of the aforementioned points, every lord who wishes to have any land or lordship renewed must prepare himself.

->ADDITION.<-

Renewal adds no new right, but confirms that which it finds. Barbosa, book 16, chapter 30, axiom 30. A silent renewal of a contract is deemed to be made according to the form and manner of the express contract. Axiom 2.

**Revenue Chamber** <note>original: "Rent-Kammer"</note> is the common name for that which must be established as a priority in every Republic. For Civil Policy, which encompasses the entire civilian administration of the State, requires above all else innumerable expenses to be bestowed upon persons and things. ### 50. Rent-annuities. <note>original: "Rentgülden"</note>

In the County of Mansfeld, a **Rent-annuity** is the name given to the amount by which the price of copper exceeds the expenses incurred in its production. Moller, *On the Saxon Constitutions*, part 3, constitution 25, number 7.

->ADDITION.<-

Rent-annuities cannot be pledged as collateral without the consent of a Judge. Berlich, conclusion 29, number 12. In the Statutory Law of Hamburg, I find it permitted, Part 2, title 1, article 4: <note>original German: "Der jenige, so Geld ausleihet..."</note> *Whoever lends money may stipulate, promise, and have written for himself up to 6 for every 100, and no more, in interest and rents.* Ericus von Könne, *On Brokers and Brokerage Fees*, thesis 58. Regarding rent-dues and incomes, see Lord Speidelius in the *Mirror of Notable Things*, page 1061. On the method of leasing <note>original: "Arrendæ"</note>, or hiring out for returns or pensions—called *auf Renten verleihen* in German, and *faire un arrendement* in French—it accords with the Spanish *arrendamiento*. See Lord Tabor, *On Contracts and Provincial Tenant Law*, thesis 18.

### 51. Representation. <note>original: "Repræsentatio"</note>

The **Right of Representation** <note>A legal rule where the children of a deceased heir "represent" their parent to claim an inheritance</note> did not exist under Salic Law <note>The ancient law code of the Salian Franks</note>. For that law, in title 62, admitted only the closest relatives and rejected all grandchildren. See Bignon in his notes to *Marculf’s Formulas*, folio 557.

->ADDITION.<-

Representation is not understood to be a gift. Barbosa, book 16, chapter 33, axiom 1. Repre-

<column-break/>

sentation is favorable and consistent with Divine Law, and is to be extended to all subject matter. Axiom 2. On the nature of the right of representation, see C. Rittershausen in *The Novels*, page 380, number 7; its origin, page 381, number 7. Representation is not extended beyond the sons of brothers, page 414, number 6. It is extended beyond great-grandchildren, page 394, number 16.

### 52. Reprisals. <note>original: "Repressalien"</note>

**Reprisals** are called *Fehden* <note>feuds</note> or *Pfändungen* <note>distraint/seizures</note> of goods and persons in German. This is when one person is captured or detained for the sake of another, or one person's property is seized for another's property. See the text in chapter 1, *On Injuries*, book 6. Bartolus, in this treatise, says: Reprisals are granted on account of an injustice done to someone in a City that is not subject to the one granting the reprisals. Lignagius, in the treatise *On Reprisals*, part 4, 2, preface to question 10. If a matter cannot be settled through the path of Law, it is otherwise; he teaches that reprisals can lawfully be granted against a Magistrate of a City for an injustice done to someone. But see Paride del Pozzo in the treatise *On Syndics*, title on the office of the Syndic, the section beginning *Quidam de Regno*, throughout. Therefore, reprisals share the same logic as war: for there, too, an innocent subject is punished and suffers loss on account of a guilty Prince. See my own work *On Majesty*, folio 170.

The term **Reprisals**—also called *pressalia* by Isernius and Afflictis in the *Neapolitan Constitutions*, title on punishing reprisals—is derived from the Italian *presa*, which signifies "a capture," according to Cujas. Or it comes from *reprimendo* <note>repressing</note>, because through them the injustice of others is repressed. Peter Frider, *On Process*, chapter 46, number 4, book 1.

Is it permitted for the vassals of one King, in order to avenge injuries inflicted upon them in foreign Kingdoms, to seize the persons and goods of said foreign Kingdoms for the guilt of others, using Reprisals on their own authority? If it is concluded that it is not, what penalty should the captors suffer? See Peguerra, decision 111.

<note>original German: "Pfänden, arrestiren, kümmern..."</note> No one should seize, arrest, trouble, or detain the person, property, or goods of anyone for the sake of foreign matters or debts, unless that person has made themselves liable for it. If it does happen, the person who does it or allows it to be done forfeits their claim and demand against the principal debtor, and must restore fourfold to the person seized, arrested, troubled, or detained that which was extorted from them. *The Novels*, "that pledges not be made for others," and the Code, "that a wife not be held for her husband." Pfeil, counsel 38, at the beginning.

Regarding Reprisals, see Augustin Seidenmelzer in Arumæus, volume 2, discourse 8.

Can Reprisals be defended by law? And who can grant them? Likewise, against whom can they be granted? And finally, what are the just causes...

### ADDITION.

Are the States of the Empire <note>The individual territories or princes within the Holy Roman Empire</note> bound to require the consent and authority of the Emperor or the Imperial Chamber <note>original: "Cameræ," the high court of the Empire</note> to use reprisals against foreigners when there is a danger in delay <note>original: "periculum in mora"</note> and an opportunity to use reprisals exists? Regarding reprisals, see Johannes Jacobus à Canibus of Padua, volume 12, folio 275, and Martinus Garatus of Lodi, volume 12, folio 275 of the same treatise.

Cujacius, in his commentary on the Code, states: "By our customs," Cujacius says in the aforementioned place, "we use this law not against our own countrymen, but against foreigners, and only with the permission of the Prince. For example, if Spanish sailors plunder the goods of a French merchant, that merchant may, by the same right, plunder the first Spaniard he encounters." Although reprisals are generally prohibited, they are sometimes granted. If they are granted and the one seeking reprisal lies, what is the penalty? See Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 70, throughout. (Gerhard Johannes Vossius derives the word *repræfalias* <note>a variant spelling</note> from the fact that it "represents" or restores to the victim that which was snatched away by the plunderer.) Reprisals are regularly considered unjust. Most recently, Mr. Struvius, in his elegant treatise *On Private Vengeance*, chapter 12, aphorism 1, number 2, page 187, notes they were accepted because of the many diverse jurisdictions. See also number 3, page 188. For how many requirements they rely upon and which ones, see chapter 12, aphorism 1, number 3; they are not granted against certain specific persons. Ibid., number 6, page 189.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the supposed reputation found in clothing: imaginary hair <note>original: "imagination Haar," likely referring to wigs</note>, a patient beard, a respectful hat <note>original: "Responsion Hut"</note>, an indifferent hat-band, an embassy feather <note>original: "Legation Feder"</note>, a varied collar, a matching camisole, a malcontent doublet <note>original: "malcontent Wammes"</note>, etc. See Speidel in the *Mirror of Notable Things*, page 713. Reputation is no insignificant jewel. Limnæus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 3, number 6. Regarding this matter, see the entry above under the word **Spain**. To this belongs the term *myriamphoron* <note>original Greek: μυριάμφορον</note> (which, according to Suidas the interpreter, is the word for "ten thousand amphorae"). See Limnæus in *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 11, number 98. Herodotus, in book 2 (or *Euterpe*), records the clever plan of Amasis, King of the Egyptians, for producing respect and honor among the citizens and common people. For this Amasis was one of the common people, yet was designated King by the Egyptians. When he saw that he was held in contempt because of the memory or recollection of his humble origins, and was not being honored as a King but as a private citizen, he placed a gold wash-basin <note>original: "pelvim"</note> in a prominent and convenient place in the city. The citizens immediately began to follow it with divine worship and veneration. Once Amasis noticed this, he called an assembly and explained that the basin was the very one in which they used to vomit, urinate, and wash their feet, yet now they treated it with divine honors and worship because it had been placed in a different position. In the same way, he explained that although he was of humble birth, because he was now their King, he must be honored differently. He achieved his goal through this artifice. See Giphanius in *Politics*, page 130. Regarding the "Lie of Reputation"—how this lie imposes itself upon us and what it is—see Zahn, *On Lies*, book 1, chapter 27, number 1.

Mauritius Bolanus, volume 5, folio 114. *On the Restoration of Dowry* by Gothofredus Beneventanus. Restoration to the original state <note>original: "Restitutio in integrum," a legal remedy where a court restores a person to their previous legal position as if a specific event or contract had never occurred</note> is not even granted against a 40-year prescription <note>A legal time limit after which a claim can no longer be made</note> based on a claim of ignorance, according to Klock, *Counsel* 48, numbers 136 and 137. And although many doctors of law hold the opposite view (number 138), more support the negative opinion regarding 100-year or immemorial prescriptions, as cited under numbers 139, 140, 142, and 143. Restoration to the original state on the grounds of ignorance can be sought up to one hundred years, see *Counsel* 51, 60; and it takes place against a forty-year prescription (number 62). The contrary is argued and proven in numbers 83, 84, and following. Restoration returns that which the injury took away, according to Zorer, *part 2, question 1, number 6*; Wurmser, *book 1, title 25, observation 4, number 7*; Gail, *1, observation 114, number 2*; and extensively by Barbosa, *book 16, chapter 51, axiom 1*. Once restoration to the original state has been denied, it is sought again in vain, unless it is sought based on a new cause or a different point (axiom 2). Restoration to the original state is reciprocal (axiom 3), unless the matters are distinct and have nothing in common with the matter in which someone was injured, according to law 28 of the Digest *on minors* <note>original: "ff. de min." refers to the Digest of Justinian, title 'De minoribus'</note>; see also Tobias Ulrich à Gulchen’s *On Restoration to the Original State*, thesis 11, letter B. Restoration ought to be handled before the main question of the case is argued, Barbosa, in the same place, axiom 7. **In what time the restoration should be sought and determined**, see Zorer, *part 2, question 1, number 23 and following, where there are limitations; likewise question 3, number 174*; **when such time begins to run**, *question 1, number 25 and following, where there are limitations*; and regarding those who are absent or ignorant, see also *question 3, number 175 and the following*. Restoration to the original state is not permitted unless a glimmer of a good legal right appears <note>original: "fumus boni juris," literally "the smoke of a good right," meaning a plausible case</note>, Lancellotti, *On Attempts*, part 2, chapter 14, number 1 and following, and provided that the negligence of the injured party is not proven. An appeal may be made from a sentence in which restoration is denied, and a minor <note>A person under the age of 25 in Roman law</note> can be restored for the purpose of appealing, Law 38 of the Digest *on minors*, Law 1 of the Code *if more often*, and Duarenus on the same. If an appeal is not permitted—as in the Imperial Chamber Court—a revision can be sought and obtained against a sentence issued by the court itself after restoration was denied; see the cited *Disputation* by à Gülchen, thesis 7, and the legal precedents cited there. Add Schwanmann, *book 1, chapter 75, number 27 and following*, and the same in *observation 182, number 2*. Regarding who should be read on the topic of Restoration to the Original State, see Drexelius in *The Gold Mine*, page 228, and Mr. Suttinger, *observation 102, throughout*.

### 57. Retaliation. Retorsio.

On the various meanings of the word "Retorsio" <note>Retaliation or "turning back" an injury upon the giver</note>, and that the retaliation of injuries is against all reason, see the specific treatise by Rennemann. ### The Facts of the Case.

The Highly Reverend, Noble, and Valiant Lord Wilhelm Michael, Knight of the most praiseworthy Teutonic Order <note>A Catholic military order founded in the 12th century</note>, of the Bailiwick of Franconia, etc., previously had a legal retaliation delivered via a notary and witnesses to the residence and home of Doctor S. The content of this was that the Lord Commander [the Knight] had been credibly informed that the aforementioned Dr. S. had recently, during a meal or drinking party, publicly vented and allegedly said: That the Lord Commander was not only a man without honor and—saving your grace <note>original: "salva venia," used here to apologize for the insult he is about to repeat</note>—a rogue, but also that he considered all those who eat and drink with the Lord Commander to be similar flighty people and rogues. These inflicted injuries the Lord Commander wished to push back into the lap of Dr. S. in the best form, as is right and proper, not with the intent of injuring <note>original: "non animo injuriandi"</note>, but of defending <note>original: "sed defendendi"</note> himself. He declared he considers Dr. S. to be nothing other than a rogue who has forgotten his honor, and views all those who have or will keep company with him in the same way, for as long and as much as until Dr. S. can sufficiently prove his claims against the Lord Commander according to the law; and whatever else may be further found in the mentioned retaliation, which is attached here under Letter A.

However, since the aforementioned Dr. S. himself was not at home, but only his brother-in-law was present during the formal delivery <note>original: "Insinuation"</note> of the document, the Most Serene Prince and Lord, Lord Johann Caspar—Administrator of the High Mastership in Prussia, Master of the Teutonic Order in German and Italian lands, Lord of Freudenthal and Eulenberg, Privy Councilor to His Roman Imperial Majesty, etc.—sent copies of the above-mentioned retaliation to the Honorable Council of the City of Heilbronn. In an accompanying letter, he reported that although a retaliation had reportedly been served to Dr. S., His Princely Grace nonetheless understands that Dr. S. is being left in his post and function as unbothered as before. Since a serious demonstration of consequences is necessary here, His Princely Grace desires to know whether the Honorable Council, on their own behalf and by virtue of their authority, would take serious and legal action against the said Dr. S. and hold him to provide sufficient satisfaction to the aforementioned Lord Commander and all other interested parties, or not; as can be more fully heard in His Princely Grace's letter, attached under Letter B.

Following this, and to prevent all further danger and inconvenience, it was indicated to Dr. S. by decree that...

### As for what otherwise concerns the
### facts of the matter itself, namely whether

the aforementioned *insulting words* <note>original: "verba injuriosa"</note> were uttered because several members of the Honorable Council had been guests of the Lord Commander just a day before, spoken by Doctor S., and perhaps cast out of anger due to a previous, adverse transaction and with underlying drunkenness—as shown by the enclosed *examination under letter C.*—and also attested before several Council members, although he, *Doctor S.*, claims not to remember it. As may be gathered from the enclosure *under letter D.*, which we have not neglected to send in this written form for the sake of further information, awaiting the requested well-meaning resolution.

<column-break/>

Accordingly, We, the Dean and senior Doctors of the Faculty of Law at the University of Tübingen, have been kindly requested to provide our advisory opinion on the presented facts of the case <note>term: "Facti Speciem" (the form of the fact); a legal summary of the circumstances of a case</note>. To provide helpful compliance, we have maturely deliberated on this in our assembled College and found, from the writings sent to us and cited in the facts of the case, that the matter is of no small importance, both in itself and because of its significant consequences, and because the Excellency of the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order takes a strong interest in it.

For although (1.) it is undoubtedly the law, and in itself fair, that if someone is shamefully attacked by another, those who have business with him are also portrayed as dishonest and are held to be equally and similarly insulted by the inflictor of the injury; nevertheless, such a thing can be harmful to the good conscience neither of the injured party <note>original: "Injuriato"</note> nor of others who support him in honorable matters or have conversation with him.

*For as Saint Cyprian writes truly and elegantly in his Letter to Cornelius: It is not he who hears, but he who commits the insult, who is wretched. And when the guilty do injury to the innocent, those who believe they are doing the injury are actually the ones suffering it. And that no one’s reputation is taken away by injuries or insults inflicted by any other person, nor can another person’s crime defame a third party, is taught throughout the treatise on reputation, especially in book 2, number 16, by Marquardus Freher. This is because no one can be infamous unless he is the one who sins (Law 7, in the beginning, of the Digest "on things done through fear"). Seneca also taught this throughout his book: that an injury does not affect a wise man. And the same is to be judged regarding libelous pamphlets and similar types of injury spread or published against someone, as the same Freher records in the cited place, number 8.*

Although also, secondly, that person to whom a retaliation is directed, *for the same reasons and rationales just mentioned*, is not to be held as dishonest, much less to be removed from his service and honorable status.

*For that such great force is by no means to be attributed to retaliation that it could brand the one who receives the retaliation with infamy has recently been sufficiently proven by Henningus Rennemannus in his "Treatise on the Right of Retaliation," folio 140 and following, as well as folio 172 and following. He teaches that the contrary opinion lacks law, precept, and example; since only because of one's own crime, and indeed one committed from a real and true offense, can someone's reputation be endangered, not because of a retaliated offense, which is not properly a crime, but merely something imaginary. Because, clearly, those who retaliate do not actually wish for the one to whom the retaliation is directed to be a thief,*

<meta>catchword: a thief,</meta>

917

...a thief, or a traitor himself, following that example; he is the sort of person who should, by their own judgment, be held as a thief, robber, or plunderer, etc., until a decision is reached. Furthermore, it has been sufficiently proven and taught at length by Lord Arumæus <note>Dominicus Arumæus (1579–1637), a significant German jurist</note> in Book 2, Decision 13, as well as by Marquard Freher <note>German jurist and statesman (1565–1614)</note> in *On Reputation* <note>original: "de existimat."</note> Book 3, Chapter 2, Number 2, that someone affected by an injury should not be immediately suspended from their office, nor should they be forbidden from exercising their duties.

Indeed, otherwise a very vast harvest would be provided to turbulent minds for throwing honest men from their seats and status of honor. This is because nothing is easier than to pin crimes even on the most honest men; yet nothing is more futile than to condemn someone based on the light breeze of opinion without proving the crime, as the text speaks in Chapter 6, Action 15, Question 7. Therefore, our laws have healthily cautioned that a Judge should not be deceived by lightly stirred-up rumors, and should not recklessly harass and judge countless innocent people who are merely marked by rumor, but should instead investigate the matter with a full inquiry. [Citing:] *Judices oportet* <note>original: "It behooves Judges"</note>, Code on Judges; *judicantem* <note>original: "one judging"</note>, 30th Question 5; *eorum qui* <note>original: "of those who"</note>, 11th Question 3.

From which it then appears that, just as it cannot be harmful to the well-established honor of the Lord Commander <note>original: "Herrn Commenthurn"; a regional administrator of the Teutonic Order</note>, or those who maintain fellowship with him, even if Doctor S. poured out the accused words and still persisted in them, because the highly-regarded Lord Commander seems to have, in a way, demanded and recovered his taken or damaged honor through the performed retaliation <note>term: "Retorsion" (legal retaliation); the principle of repaying an injury in kind to restore one's legal standing</note> from the alleged insulting master. [Citing:] *the traitor* <note>original: "traditor"</note>, by Lord Harprecht <note>Johannes Harprecht (1560–1639), a professor of law at Tübingen</note> on the title of the Institutes regarding injuries.

<margin>This action 12, number 92.</margin> Likewise, it cannot be harmful to the honor, office, and status of the honorably mentioned Doctor S., even though this sharp retaliation was suggested to him, or notified and made known to an Honorable and Highly Wise Council.

But regardless of all this, we for our part hold that the well-regarded Council acted very reasonably and rightly in suspending Doctor S. from his office for a time. This is especially because it has already been established through the sworn deposition of a witness—who is, in our opinion, irreproachable—that this injury occurred, which provoked the Lord Commander’s retaliation. Those words, of which Doctor S. was convicted by the witness's deposition, are in and of themselves quite grievous and cannot be justified. Furthermore, persons of even higher status might take an interest in and be concerned with this matter (if this case reaches a wider scope).

Considering that the words were directed by Doctor S. against "German Houses" <note>original: "Teutſche Häuſer"; referring to the estates and administrative centers of the Teutonic Order</note>, and that one should not make oneself so common with them, and that even those who have dealings with the Lord Commander are accused of enrichment—this might perhaps be interpreted in the sense that such treachery was being engineered or arranged against His Majesty and his obedient servants.

<column-break/>

Moreover, even if Doctor S., according to the status, condition, and circumstances of that time, wanted to warn one or another person against having too much fellowship with the Lord Commander, this should have been done with much more modest words and not with such notoriously honor-violating words as "loose people," "rogues," and "traitors" (which sufficiently demonstrate an intent to injure and treat with contempt <note>original: "quæ injuriandi contumeliaque afficiendi animum ſatis edocent"</note>).

For it is established that one may most rightly and equitably proceed to suspension not only for a notorious or legitimately proven crime, but also because of the infamy of a crime arising from it—either because it is doubted whether the infamous person committed the charged crime or not, or because the quality of the crime is ambiguous. [Citing:] Joan. Imola on the *Clementines*, note 11; Bonifacius de Vitalinis, note 20, on punishments.

And it is also established that the same suspension may be rightly carried out without a formal trial or legal proceeding, indeed without any prior formal warning, especially if it is only done for a specific or indefinite time. [Citing:] Gloss on *Presbyter if by the people* <note>original: "Presbyter ſi à plebe"</note>, 2nd Question 5; Bonifacius de Vitalinis, note 48.

And by suspension, an unbridled tongue is sometimes restrained so that it may learn to strive for modesty. Law 1, where the gloss and the Doctors comment on punishments. Law 1, paragraph "I think" <note>original: "puto"</note>, where Gothofredus, Accursius, Albericus, and others comment.

Likewise, we could not judge that the Lord Commander remitted this injury, or even could have remitted it. This is because, as already understood, the entire highly praiseworthy Teutonic Order <note>original: "Teutſche Orden"</note> is mocked <note>original: "ſugillirt"</note> herewith. Moreover, since the Lord Commander, by virtue of the vows he has taken, is to be held as a truly religious person <note>In this context, a "religious person" is a member of a holy military order bound by monastic-style vows</note>, it is judged that he was not empowered to forgive this injury without the consent of his Superior.

For it is established that those in Religious Orders do not have a "will" or "won't" <note>original: "velle aut nolle"; a legal concept meaning members of orders have no independent legal agency apart from their superior</note>. Baldus, counsel 1, at the end, note 7, book 3; Cardinal Zabarella, counsel 28. And a Prelate has greater power over a member of an Order than a husband over a wife. Oldradus, counsel 267, note 6; Cardinal Tuschus, book M, conclusion 326, at the beginning.

And although Doctor S. further claims to know nothing of those words of which he is now accused, but wishes to excuse himself with drunkenness, such a circumstance is not yet proven. Furthermore, the words themselves, mentioned by the witness cited above, give almost as much to recognize that they did not flow from such a drunken man whose wine had taken away all sense...

It further notes that the Lord Commander cannot unilaterally forgive the insult because he is bound by religious vows and the honor of the entire Order is at stake.</summary>

# Added Practical Treasures
### (Thesauri Practici Adaucti)

and his mind was so occupied that he could not have fallen into the intent of injuring.

Based on all this, we, for our part, are of the opinion that for the time being, the further examination of witnesses sought by the Lord Commander <note>original: *Herr Commenthur*; a high-ranking administrative official in a military religious order, such as the Teutonic Knights</note> should be suspended, as it is feared this might only serve to increase bitterness and long-windedness. Instead, Doctor S. should be directed to provide sufficient satisfaction <note>original: *Satisfaction*; a formal legal or social reparation for an insult to honor</note> for the injuries <note>original: *injurien*; in this context, verbal slanders or insults</note> inflicted upon the Lord Commander, based on the judgment of honorable men <note>original: *ex arbitratu bonorum virorum*</note>. He should declare himself in writing in such a way that both the Lord Commander and the entire Highly Praiseworthy Order may be satisfied. Specifically, he should state that if such words were spoken by him, he is sorry for it and duly asks for forgiveness. He should further declare that he did not intend to mean anything shameful toward the often-mentioned Lord Commander or anyone else, and that he knows or can say nothing dishonorable about the Lord Commander, but rather holds him to be an honorable cavalier and wishes to praise him as such at all times.

Truly, we ought only to forgive an injury to a neighbor who has wronged us if he asks fraternally, supplicates, and requests pardon (*Canon: "If it is not illicit," 29, Cause 23, Question 4*). In such a case, it is inhumane and against brotherly charity not to grant a place for forgiveness. See Hartmann’s *Practical Observations*, Book 2, Title 29, final observation, where he adds that one who has obtained such a request by prayer, so that no action for injury is taken against him, does not become "infamous" <note>original: *infamem*; a legal status of disgrace that carried the loss of certain civil rights</note>, nor is he seen to confess to any crime.

And to give satisfaction in cases of injury is to affirm by testimony that one regrets having said those things. See Freher, *On Reputation* <note>original: *de existimat.*</note>, Book 3, Chapter 9, Number 15, where he says the ancient formula for this kind of apology was: *I would wish it undone; I say you are unworthy of this injury, etc.* Muretus agrees in his *Commentaries on Catullus, on our page 40.*

It is also likely that an Honorable Council, or others, could obtain enough from His Princely Grace the Grand Master and the Lord Commander himself that they might be satisfied with a collective satisfaction or apology. Thus, the matter would be laid to rest for the sake of peace, and whatever occurred in this place would be abolished, canceled, and lifted by the authorities of both sides in such a way that it should not harm or disadvantage either party in their honor, status, reputation, or good name.

Should one or the other party, contrary to expectations, not comply with such an accommodation, it is our opinion that the Lord Commander’s request for further witness examination must be granted. However, each party should be allowed their defense, as well as the posing of proper articles and questions for a better understanding of all circumstances.

For although this matter has not yet reached a formal trial, nevertheless, because the question now is solely what

<column-break/>

an Honorable Council, by virtue of its authority, has to undertake or do, and whether the Lord Commander was entitled to initiate such a retaliation <term>retorsio; the legal principle of responding to an insult with an equivalent insult to neutralize the original offense</term>; for this, a summary process <note>original: *summarius processus*; a simplified, faster legal proceeding used for less complex or urgent matters</note> is sufficient.

For in summary cases, a formal Complaint <note>original: *Libellus*</note> is not required, nor is the Joinder of Issue <note>original: *Litis contestatio*; the formal start of a trial where both sides agree on the point of dispute</note>; and many exceptions regarding the reception of witnesses are usually permitted there (*based on the reasoning of Decius, counsel 54, in the third column of the case*), for all the solemnity of the law and the "noise of the court" <note>original: *strepitus judicii*; a technical term for the complex and loud formalities of a full trial</note> is removed. See Romanus, counsel 20, number 8, where there is an annotation on the word "remitted." Also Tuschus, letter S, conclusion 891. Marcellus Cala, *On the Method of Articulating*, glossary 3, our page 51, and elsewhere.

If the matter were then proven by the Lord Commander in his retaliation as alleged, and the testimony of his witnesses—who have already stood firm—were strengthened, and if the circumstances put forward by Doctor S. for his excuse were not brought to light, then the aforementioned retaliation would remain in full force (which we hope will not happen, nor are we of the opinion that it will reach such a length or the leading of further witnesses). In such a case, the matter would become even more burdensome, and the suspension—especially in this instance—might not easily be canceled.

Therefore, how one should behave in that event will be determined by further information and the Lord Commander's intentions.

->Done in our College, September 14, the Year 1629.<-

Regarding the proper mode of Retaliation <note>original: *Retorsionis*</note>, see Georg Adam Struve, *On Private Vengeance*, Chapter 10, aphorism 10, numbers 4 and 5, page 117. The legitimate formula for retaliation is if we call the slanderer an "honor-thief" or an "honor-violator." Whether we correctly use this formula—"you have long been a rogue"—against a slanderer is discussed in the same number 4. On "Retaliating a Crime," see the same treatise, Chapter 19, aphorism 6, number 5, page 87. Retaliation for injuries is granted against distinguished persons. Against a principal and an agent, ibid. number 4, page 114. Against a Client whose Advocate spoke an insult in his presence, ibid. number 5. But not against Parents, ibid. number 6. Nor against a Patron, number 7. Nor against the Lord of a Fief, number 8, ibid.

If someone provoked by injuries retaliates with the same, he does not commit an injury (*Law 25, section 1, Digest on Procurators; Law 14, section 6, Digest on the Goods of Freedmen*), provided that he does it immediately and with the intent of defending himself rather than seeking revenge. Lord Ludwig, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 311; see also the same in his *Notes on Wesenbeck*, number 8. A special treatise on the Law of Retaliation or "Retorsio" was written by

### 58. Reserved Right, Imperial Reserved Right.
### The Emperor’s Reserved Right.

Concerning the Emperor’s Reserved Rights <note>original: "Reservatum Imperatoris"</note>—*concerning the Imperial Highness* <note>original: "von der Kayserlichen Hochheit"</note>—and what things are referred to them, see Lord Hermann Stamm in the treatise *On Personal Servitude*, book 3, chapter 7, number 3, etc. Among other things, the following are commonly counted among the Imperial Reserved Rights: the restoration [legitimation] of those born out of wedlock; the "Grant of Age" <note>original: "Aetatis venia"; a legal decree allowing a minor to be treated as an adult for the purpose of managing their own affairs</note>, by which minors are enabled to administer their own affairs to the effect that they are considered adults in all matters; the granting of reprisals; the establishment of postal services and public couriers throughout the Empire; the creation of Kings, Princes, Counts, and Barons with royal dignity; the founding of Universities; the creation of Doctors and Notaries; the Right of Citizenship; the power of conscripting soldiers in the Empire; the remission of damages inflicted on subjects during a time of war for the sake of obtaining public peace; and the adjudication of the greater Duchies and Counties of the Empire, etc. See above under the word **Regalien** <note>Regalia; the various rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign</note>.

### 60. Rhine. The Rhine River.

The most famous river of Germany; it is not so named from "purity" <note>original: "à puritate"</note> as if it would detest and submerge illegitimate children <note>A reference to the ancient folk belief that the Rhine would drown illegitimate babies but float legitimate ones</note>, but from "running" <note>original: "von rinnen"</note> or from the Greek *rheo* [to flow]. Hence the ending of many places is "Rohn" or "Rhen"; such as *Beyren* by the *Rhon* at the springs or source. *Blaubehren*, a town in Württemberg, situated at the source of the Blau River (so called from its blue color), is as if [it were] "by the Blue Rhon." And the village located on the opposite ridge of the mountain is called *Jennen-beyren*, that is, "beyond or across the springs." For *Jenz-nen* or *Jenet*, "the other side" <note>original: "Jenseits"</note>, is "beyond" or "across." See Goldast, *Alemanic Matters*, volume 1, part 1, folio 179.

->ADDITION.<-

*Hrein*, pure, sincere; from this the river *Rhein*, with the aspiration transposed. Lord G. Richter in *Epistles*, page 513. Regarding the Count of the Rhine, see Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 3, number 17. The Rhine is the border of the Roman Empire. Lord Rupert on Florus, book 4, chapter 12, paragraph 39. The Elector Palatine <note>The Prince-Elector of the Palatinate</note> counts among his *Regalia* the right of gathering river gold in the Rhine, which he exercises from Marchemio all the way to the village of Gelsz; he likewise reserves for himself the gold mine, the old water [backwater], islands, and river-islands. [Also] the breaking of ice, duck-snaring, bird-trapping, beaver-catching, and the "Head-Stitch" <note>original: "Hauptstich"</note>, which is the Sturgeon; which the fishermen, once caught, are bound to send to Heidelberg for one florin as a recognition of his lordship. Johann Theodorus Sprenger, in *Public Jurisprudence*, page 417. Maurer, *On Water Law*.

### 61. Revision. Revision of the Acts.

**Revision** <term>Revision: An extraordinary legal appeal used in the Imperial Chamber Court (Reichskammergericht)</term> is an extraordinary remedy by which those harmed in the Imperial Chamber are helped, out of a certain kindness, through Commissioners of the Emperor and the Estates of the Empire deputized for that purpose. Bender, in the cited treatise, conclusion 1. See Valascus, *Consultation* 51; and Bulla, *Academic Discourse* 10.

Since Revision is a last resort <note>original: "extremum refugium"</note>, and no further remedy remains according to the section "In Case" <note>original German: "§. Im Fall"</note>, title 53, and the law "If anyone against" <note>original: "l. si quis adversus"</note> 5, Code of the Emperor, it follows that one must proceed in it with the greatest caution, and everything must be done with the most deliberate mind. Bender, in the cited place, conclusion 19, number 1 and following. Therefore, lest the Reviewers decree anything rashly, either against a party or against the Chamber, it is worthwhile and highly necessary that they read through and re-examine the Acts as diligently as possible, and also most exquisitely and perfectly examine and weigh the reasons for the sentence assigned by the Assessors <note>The judges or legal experts who assisted in the initial ruling</note>. This is according to the text of the said title 53, section "And thereupon" <note>original German: "§. Und darauf"</note> and section "And they shall" <note>original German: "§. Und sollen"</note>. If they find those reasons just and legitimate, they shall confirm the prior sentence; but if not, and if it

<column-break/>

appears that the sentence was delivered for unjust and frivolous causes, they may retract it. This is argued from the said section "And thereupon" and section "And they shall." For the Reviewers will confirm the sentence if it is established that it was well-judged; if badly, they will retract it; but if it was partly bad and partly good, they will reform it. But see Bender in the cited conclusion, number 3 and following.

In which cases Revision is to be denied, and whether a denied revision can be sought again, see the *Decisions of Alvarus Valascus*, volume 1, counsel 51.

The Judgment of the Imperial Chamber Court was forced to come to the aid of the "rashness of Revision" by a specific Decree <note>original: "Senatusconsulto"</note>. Regarding its validity and meaning, the following discourse treats:

->That such a Decree should have no power may be concluded from the following.<-

Where, first of all, this phrase, **any party** <note>original German: "einige Parthey"</note>, must be properly noted, as it corresponds to the word "whosoever," which is clearly universal. Law "When anything" <note>original: "l. cum quid"</note> Digest on *Credited Matters*. Thus, it must be extended infinitely. Johann Goddaeus, among the *Marburg Counsels*, counsel 18, number 175, volume 1. And that phrasing, on account of its generality, is accustomed to be drawn even to improper cases. The Doctors of Law on the law "Of one" <note>original: "l. unius"</note> paragraph "to be known," Digest on *Inquiries*. Thus, all litigants without distinction, who think they have been harmed by any Chamber sentence, can flee to this most wholesome remedy of Revision, granted and established by the authority of the supreme Prince and the Estates of the Empire, as if to a "sacred anchor" <note>A metaphor for a final hope or last resort</note>, with every obstacle absolutely removed and every hindrance cast far away.

Gleicher Gestalt in Fällen"</note>, all sorts of means were ordered and prescribed by which rashly undertaken Revisions might be countered; yet it was always added thereto that, in and of itself, nothing is taken away from the parties regarding their Revision or Appeal <note>original: "Syndicat"</note>, and such means are in no way to be cut off from them, etc.

# Lit. R.

### On the Revision of Judicial Sentences

Whether a party should be rejected by the Judge, or whether the judge himself has the authority to decide <note>original Latin: *cognoscere*</note> if a Revision should be granted. For it has been (1.) deliberately and collectively ordered that while a Revision is pending, the execution <note>the legal enforcement of a judgment</note> should not proceed, but should instead be stayed. Since, therefore, a Revision by its very law suspends the execution of a sentence and carries an effect that is not only devolutive <note>transferring the case to a higher court</note> but also simultaneously suspensive, it follows that the judge from whom the appeal is made <note>original: *Judicem à quo*</note> has his hands tied immediately after the petition for Revision is made. He cannot attempt anything further, whether by enforcing the judgment or by trying to decide if the appeal should even be allowed. For even the act of deciding whether a Revision ought to be admitted is a preparatory step toward execution. Where the final consequence is prohibited, the preceding steps are also considered forbidden, especially when they have a necessary dependence on one another. This is no different than how the removal of a general category or the destruction of a principal thing naturally results in the removal of the specific type and the destruction of the accessories. That every act leading toward a forbidden thing is also interdicted is commonly proven by our doctors through various legal precedents. <note>The author cites several legal authorities here, including the *Corpus Juris Civilis* and Matthew Stephani’s *Dialectica Juris*.</note>

It is relevant here that in cases where an appeal produces not just a devolutive but also a suspensive effect, it is not permitted to attempt anything by any means. <note>Citing Covarruvias and Rolandinus à Valle.</note>

Likewise, (2.) it can be learned from the records of the Speyer Deputation Meeting <note>a committee of the Imperial Diet</note> that while they considered ways to prevent the Highly Esteemed Imperial Chamber Court <note>the *Cammergericht*, the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> from being so frequently burdened by Revisions sought indiscriminately—which had previously harmed justice and its enforcement—they postponed a final decision until a general decree by His Imperial Majesty and the Estates could be made. However, they did conclude that any party seeking a Revision is required, if the opposing party requests it, to swear the Oath of Calumny <note>original: *Juramentum Calumniae*; an oath that the legal action is not brought in bad faith or for the purpose of harassment</note>. This must be done either in person or through a sufficiently authorized lawyer before the Chamber Judge, the President, and the Assessors. Once that oath has been taken, the requested Revision must be presumed valid; the lower judge should not regard it as a frivolous delay but is required to admit the requested Revisions without distinction.

Because (3.) in this same Deputation Decree, it is established that in cases of Mandates, specifically for the release of a prisoner <note>original: *de relaxando captivo*</note> and for decrees of alimony <note>original: *decretorum alimentorum*</note>, a Revision shall be 

Besoldi Vol. I.

<column-break/>

denied to no one. However, while the Revision is pending, the ordered compliance for the release of the prisoner must proceed upon the offer and provision of sufficient bail <note>original: *caution*</note>, and the prisoner shall be set free. Likewise, in matters of alimony decrees, the effect of the sentence shall not be suspended, but the execution shall proceed unhindered.

Since the execution is allowed to proceed—even while the Revision itself is preserved—only in cases of Mandates for releasing prisoners and alimony decrees (despite their significant legal favor and the lack of danger that can be recovered after a delay), it is logically concluded that in all other Mandate cases, which are worthy of less favor—and especially in cases where the opposing party claims a questionable profit or where they are neither imprisoned nor in need of a specific sum of money for their daily maintenance—there is even less reason to prevent the stay of execution under any pretext. For if something is admitted in a case where the reasoning is stronger and greater, that same thing cannot be considered prohibited where the reasoning is weaker. <note>A principle of legal logic: *a fortiori*.</note>

Because the executive effect of a sentence is not suspended uniquely and solely in the two aforementioned Mandate matters (prisoner release and alimony), it must be held as irrefutable that a Revision undertaken in all other Mandate cases removes <note>halts</note> the judgments, the compliance orders <note>original: *Paritori-Beſcheid*</note>, and their execution. It also effectively restrains and prevents the judges of the lower court from any further proceedings that would be detrimental to the announced Revision.

For it is well known that just as an exception in specific cases usually invalidates a Rule, so does it confirm the same Rule in cases not excepted. <note>Original Latin: *exceptio firmat regulam in casibus non exceptis*. Citing the Digest of Justinian.</note>

And the common rule applies here: that the exclusion of one thing is the inclusion of the other. <note>Original: *excluſione unius, alterius incluſio exiſtat*.</note>

And what is prohibited in one case or species is considered permitted in general; and conversely, what is granted in a specific case may be seen as prohibited in general. <note>Citing various laws.</note>

Contrary to this, a supposed Decree of the Senate <note>original: *Senatusconsultum*</note> alleged by the opposition—which claims that Revisions for acknowledged debts should not be allowed or accepted at this Highly Esteemed Imperial Chamber Court—should cause no hindrance.

For firstly, it might be strongly doubted whether this Honorable Imperial Chamber Court can, through any Senate Decree or other ordinance, take away the benefit of Revision <note>original: *beneficium Reviſionis*</note>, or at least restrict it in any part, considering the Imperial and public laws already cited above...
