<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the "Revision" process (the highest level of appeal) within the Holy Roman Empire. The previous page established that when a Revision is requested, the execution of the sentence is suspended, and the original judge's authority over the case is temporarily halted. This page argues that the right to appeal is a fundamental law that cannot be overridden by a single judge’s discretion or local court customs.</meta>

-># Treasury of Practical Law, Augmented<-

cases, and often repeated Laws, to every person who is aggrieved by some Cameral sentence <note>original: *sententiam Cameralem*, referring to a judgment from the Imperial Chamber Court, the *Reichskammergericht*</note>, this benefit <note>a legal right or privilege</note> is granted indefinitely, generally, and indifferently.

Now, however, no one can deny that no person can take away from the Estates <note>original: *Statibus*; the constituent territories and princes of the Empire</note> what is found to have been introduced by general law, by the common pledge of the Estates, and as a singular benefit.

And just as in the Roman Empire <note>referring here to the Holy Roman Empire</note> the power to make laws is considered to belong commonly to the Emperor and the Estates, as noted by Franz Burckhard in the treatise *On the Exemption*, book 3, chapter 14; Lehmann *in the Speyer Chronicle*, book 7, chapter 124; Paurmeister, book 2, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 2, number 50, etc., also number 63 and many following. So likewise, it is permitted to no one else to derogate from the Laws, or to not merely interpret them, but at the same time to establish what is effectively a new law through interpretation, except for him who has the power to make Laws. (Citing the Code of Justinian, title *On Laws*; and Martin Becanus in *Scholastic Theology*, title *on laws*, chapter 6, question 4; Donellus in *Commentaries* 13; Enenckel in the treatise *On Privileges*, book 2, chapter 2, number 14).

And so, the power to publish Decrees regarding the Visitation <note>the official audit and oversight of the court</note>, to decide doubts of the Chamber, and to do similar things is found to be ascribed jointly to the Emperor and the Estates in the Fundamental Laws of our Empire. (Citing Denaisius in *Chamber Law*, section *Common powers of the Emperor and Estates*).

And although in the law "It is not doubted" <note>original: *l. non ambigitur. 9. de ll.* from the Digest</note> it is said that the Senate can make law, this is by no means to be understood otherwise than if the authority of the Superiors <note>the sovereign power</note> intervenes, or if the Fundamental Laws of the State so allow. Indeed, in ancient times, the Senate could not do this without the knowledge of the Prince; rather, deliberations were first instituted with the Princes, and the speeches of the Princes themselves—which explained the circumstances of the whole matter—showed what would be just, useful, and honorable for the State, and they asked the Senate whether it pleased them to so decree. (Citing Bellonius, *Legal Calculations* 4, chapter 5, number 5). And thus Muretus notes on the said Law 9 that most Decrees of the Senate mentioned in our law were made in the times of the Emperors, but only following such a Speech by the Emperor. (Citing Brisson, *Selected Antiquities* 16).

Although a Style <note>original: *Stylus*, meaning a specific court's established procedural custom</note> may be introduced by a Judge, it ought only to regard the order of proceeding, and even then it only carries weight if it concerns a minor prejudice <note>a small legal disadvantage</note>. (Citing Cravetta, *On the Antiquity of Time*, part 4, number 36).

Nor does a Style regard the decision of the case, but rather the order of proceeding; and it deals only with those matters that are left to the judge's discretion. (Citing Alexander, consultation 63, book 2). And so, if such a custom were contrary to the law, it must either be confirmed by a superior or introduced by a judge who possesses the power to make Law,

<column-break/>

otherwise it is not valid. (Citing Grammaticus, consultation 1, and Joseph Ludovicus, *Decisions of Lucca* 36).

It appears, however, in every way that the aforementioned Decree of the Senate <note>original: *Senatusconsultum*</note> was not conceived regarding the process or judicial order, but rather concerns the merits of the principal case, and would also bring about a special, most intolerable prejudice <note>legal harm</note> and far-reaching consequence for the common Estates. This would be the case if one wished to extend and interpret it as the opposing side does: namely, that it should be placed in the power and discretion of the Judge—who has already once aggrieved a party, and whose further harm is therefore feared—to decide whether a Revision, granted to everyone by the public and inviolable law of the Empire, ought to be admitted or denied. Especially since a Judge who has delivered a sentence is thought to love, defend, and cherish it as the offspring of his own mind, and in turn is considered to take offense at all those remedies which tend toward the overturning of that same sentence.

In particular, both the Judge and the party themselves should be satisfied with what is found introduced in the Imperial Recesses <note>resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note> and Ordinances to avoid calumny <note>original: *ad evitandam calumniam*, meaning malicious or groundless litigation</note>, which is sometimes committed in a frivolously requested Revision. Namely, that the party seeking a Revision can be required to take the "Oath of Malice" <note>original: *Juramentum malitiæ*, a sworn statement that the legal action is not taken in bad faith</note>, and they must also expect to pay for other damages and inconveniences in the event that the previous judgment is confirmed.

The opposing party should no less rightly shrink from arguing so laboriously that the Revision undertaken by Lord N. of N.—who is supported by so many Councilors of the highest faith, sincerity, and experience—is being undertaken frivolously, calumniously, and against conscience.

But even assuming that the cited Decree of the Senate were valid in and of itself, it could in no way be applied to the present case, nor to this matter which is limited and qualified by its own unique and known circumstances. For such a thing must be taken and understood according to those known terms of Law and the traditions of our Interpreters, where it is asked whether and to what extent the judge from whom the appeal is made <note>original: *Judex à quo*</note> is bound or able to grant an appeal that the adversary claims is frivolous.

For a Supplication (or Revision) succeeds in the place of an appeal <note>original: *appellationis*</note> and walks with it at an equal pace. For beyond the differences written in law, the statutes regarding the case of an appeal also have a place in the case of a Supplication. This is asserted by Rebuffus in the treatise *On Supplications*, question 1, citing Angelus and Salicetus. And the final gloss on the single law in the Code *On the Sentences of the Praetorian Prefects* is attested by Ferrarius to be approved by everyone.

<summary>This page argues that the right to a "Revision" (a high-level appeal) is a fundamental imperial law established by the Emperor and the Estates, which cannot be blocked by an individual judge's procedural custom or personal discretion. It emphasizes that a judge who issued a sentence is naturally biased toward defending it and therefore should not have the power to deny the right to appeal that sentence.</summary>

### Thesaurus of Legal Literature R.
Aaaaaa 2

Ferrarius Montanus, in his work *On Petitions*, at the end of the chapter and in chapter 2 near the end, states that one can lawfully argue from the right of an appeal to the right of a petition <note>original: *Supplicationem*, a formal request for a higher authority to review a case</note>. This is the view of Capycius in his *Decisions*, since they proceed on equal footing, and the Petition succeeds in the place of an appeal and assumes its nature. This is also supported by Rolandus a Valle in *Counsel 94*, numbers 4, 11, and 12, where he cites still others.

Now, however, there is a solemn and unanimous tradition among our Doctors of Law <note>original: *Dd.*, abbreviation for *Doctores*</note> that all Judges are bound to accept an Appeal that is offered within the fixed and appointed days in every possible way (citing *Novella 126*, final chapter). They go so far as to dare to say that an appeal must be granted even to the Devil (Paris, *Counsel 28*, number 11). Likewise, one may sometimes physically resist a judge who does not allow a challenge (Lancellotti, *On Attempts*, part 2, chapter 12, and the final chapter, number 216).

Soarez, in his *Common Opinions*, letter A, number 121, promotes as a common rule that an appeal is never to be denied when someone can doubt the fairness of the case, whether in fact or in law.

And although it is also found to be accepted that in "notorious" <note>original: *notoriis*; in law, this refers to facts so obvious they require no proof</note> cases an appeal is prohibited, and therefore one should not give way to a deceptive or stalling challenge that proceeds from reckless boldness (citing the *Digest* on appeals).

Likewise, although they commonly say that an appeal is denied to those convicted and those who have confessed (citing the *Digest* and the *Code* on confessions; and the *Decisions* of Guido Papa, 339).

Nevertheless, they all declare with one voice that even someone who can bring forward a probable cause against their own confession can fly to the protection of an appeal. (Clarus, final section, question 94; Covarruvias, *Practical Questions* 23).

Furthermore, a confession is not held to be "clear and liquid" <note>original: *clara & liquida*, meaning undisputed and legally transparent</note> if it admits any dispute or doubt (Lancellotti, *On Attempts*, part 3). Or if the confession is at least revoked and alleged to be erroneous, as Sigismund Scaccia relates in his *On Appeals*, where he attests to the common opinion.

It is also the duty of the Judge, based on the principles of justice and necessity, to receive an appeal rather than to reject it based on a suspicion of injustice or recklessness; for many things are called "notorious" which are not actually so. Care must therefore be taken so that what is doubtful is not treated as notorious.

Based on this foundation, Scaccia further proves that in a case of doubt, a Judge ought to lean his judgment toward the admission of the appeal. Especially since nothing is so notorious that some excuse

Besold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

cannot be presumed to compete against it (Nevizanus, *Counsel 37*, who cites Curtius).

In the same way, the status of "notorious" does not produce its usual effects when something is alleged that might obscure or cloud it (Lancellotti, part 2, chapter 12). He adds that although it is said one cannot appeal from a notorious matter, one *can* appeal from the *declaration* of it being notorious. While such a challenge is standing, if an execution of the sentence is carried out, it suffers from the vice of an "attempted act" <note>original: *attentatorum*; illegal actions taken by a judge while an appeal is pending</note> no less than in any other appealable case. From this, a granted appeal regularly results in a "suspensive effect" <note>stopping the enforcement of the ruling</note>, which usually blocks such attempts (Jason, *Counsel 187*). Scaccia agrees with this.

Similarly, the executive path <note>immediate enforcement of a debt or judgment</note> does not take place when a solemn and "guaranteed instrument" <note>original: *Instrumentum guarentiatum*, a contract or deed that includes a clause allowing for immediate enforcement without a trial</note> is in some way obscured, as Blancus relates in his treatise *On Compromises*. He infers there that even regarding a guaranteed instrument, a compromise can be requested when it is obscured by some cause.

It should also be noted that a "Revision of a Revision" is not granted. Thus, someone who has once sought a Revision cannot seek it a second time; but the person against whom a Revision was sought can later seek one himself if he loses in the Revision Court. This is for the sake of equality, which must be strictly observed in legal judgments.

In East Friesland <note>a territory in Northwest Germany</note>, one can either appeal from the Count's High Court to the Imperial Chamber Court, or seek a Revision from the Count himself. This Revision, as a substitute for an appeal to the Chamber Court, shares its nature. And thus, in that place, things not proven can be proven, and things not deduced can be deduced, etc.

Is a Revision common to all co-parties? Mastrillus denies this. In the Revision case of Bavaria against Ortenburg, the votes of both the Chamber and the Revision were utilized; therefore, the Brandenburg envoy publicly protested against it during the publication of the judgment, as can be seen in the Ortenburg Acts, folio 347.

Regarding the timeframe in which a Revision must be sought, see Mr. Bicc in *Golden Rules*, section 5, Treasury 175. After the midpoint of that section, he discusses how the three-month period expressed in the ordinance should be understood, as cited in Treasury 175. Whether the jurisdiction for a Revision is "ordinary" <note>meaning a standard part of the legal process rather than an extraordinary favor</note> is discussed immediately by Ummius in *On Process*, page 163; and whether it can be extended on page 164.

A Revision is not admitted in the Imperial Aulic Council, though it is different in the Imperial Chamber Court <note>original: *Camera*, the *Reichskammergericht*, the other supreme court of the Empire</note>, according to Klock, volume 1, consultation 6, numbers 95 and 96. It "feeds the immortality of lawsuits" <note>original: *Immortalitatem litium nutrit*; a common legal complaint that appeals allow cases to drag on forever</note>, consultation 45, number 9. It must be requested in writing (number 5). It does not stop the execution of the sentence (number 1). Regarding how and when it should be registered (number 2): the Document of Revision <note>original: *Revisions-Schrifft*</note> must be submitted within two months from the time the resolution was obtained (observation 100, number 5) and must be drawn from the previous case files, otherwise it is punishable (number 8). The Revision Councilors <note>original: *Revisions-Räth*</note> should finish the commission within two months or report the cause of the delay in the meantime (number 7). 

Today, a Revision must be sought according to the Imperial Recess of the year 1654 <note>original: *R. J. de Anno 1654*, a major piece of constitutional legislation for the Empire</note>, in cases involving 125 [units of currency], within four months from the day the sentence was passed, under penalty of forfeiture. This is done before the Elector of Mainz <note>the Arch-Chancellor of the Empire</note>, or—if he has an interest in the case—before the Elector of Trier, through a petition. In this petition, it is stated that the supplicant feels greatly aggrieved by the sentence passed on such-and-such a day in the Chamber Court (of which a copy must be attached) and was therefore forced to seize the remedy of Revision prescribed in the ordinance. He asks that this be notified to His Imperial Majesty, the future Revision judges, and the Chamber Court. For the formula, see Schvvanmann, book 1, *Process of the Chamber Court*, chapter 75. <margin>62. **Reut.** A cleared grove.</margin>
In Latin, this is a "cut-down grove" (*nemus excisum*). Hence even today we say "to root out" <note>original: *ausreuten*</note> when a forest or a waste place is cleared and prepared for cultivation. Thus Bruschius, in *On Monasteries*, regarding Michelsfeld <note>original: *Michaëlis Campo*</note>, folio 86, says: "Reut," "Riet," and "Rode" are the names Germans usually give to those places which were formerly

<column-break/>

wooded, but later converted into fields. There is a great multitude of these in Germany, which was once entirely forested. Thus today we have place names like Bayreuth <note>original: *Barreut*</note>, Reutlingen, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

There are also other places, formerly forested and now more cultivated, which took their names from this: Hedenreut, Castnersreut. From this comes the phrase: "going to the clearings" <note>original: *Reuts gehenden*</note>, a newly cleared field, "Neureut," "Rodland." See Wehner under the term: "Noval-Tithe" <note>original: *Noval-Zehend*; a tithe on newly cultivated land</note>. Mr. Speidel under the term: "New Break" <note>original: *Neubruch*</note>. Werndle, book 4, chapter 1.

<margin>63. **Reukauff.** A fine for changing one's mind.</margin>
Is a penalty agreement added to a contract of buying and selling <note>original: *emptio venditio*</note> because of "repentance" <note>changing one's mind about the deal; commonly called *Reukauff*</note> valid? It is less doubtful that this agreement is valid regarding the seller, because otherwise, by the disposition of the law, a seller who does not keep the contract out of a certain insolence and recklessness and refuses to deliver the item is held liable for "interest" <note>damages</note>; especially if he no longer has the ability to deliver the item. Regarding the buyer, there is more doubt: for Hartmann Pistor, in *Observations 8*, number 5 and following, teaches in specific terms that the addition of such a penalty—in a case where the buyer would not stand by the contract or pay the price—is not valid, as it is made in "fraud of usury" <note>a legal trick to bypass laws against excessive interest</note>. He testifies that the Lay Judges of Leipzig <note>original: *Scabinis Lipsiensibus*</note> have ruled in this way.

However, the aforementioned theory—that the addition of a penalty in obligations to give is considered to be in "fraud of usury" and is invalid—only holds true in a contract of a loan, and not in other contracts. Since "buyer" and "seller" are correlative terms governed by the same judgment and discipline, etc., this penalty agreement also rightly holds valid regarding the buyer. Matthias Berlich deduces all this more extensively and proves it with very many texts and authorities in *Decision 43*.

->ADDITION.<-

See Schneidewin, section "on actions," page 863. A completed purchase is not rescinded because of "repentance," even if it occurs immediately (Code of Justinian, *On contracting a sale*, law 12; *On rescinding a sale*, law 3), even if double the price is offered (law 6). This is unless, as we read in law 2, "enormous loss" <note>original: *enormis læsio*; a legal concept where a contract can be voided if the price is less than half the true value</note> occurs alongside the repentance. This must certainly be distinguished from the case where "repentance" is allowed in a sale celebrated in writing, as the Emperor writes in the Institutes, *On Buying and Selling*, as long as something is missing from the formalities; there, the mere disagreement of the party is enough to produce the intended effect, and the "repenting" person is not forced to allege or prove any cause for his change of heart. Compare Donellus, *Commentary 14*, 22, page 304. When the contracting parties set a certain sum of money as a penalty in the contract (which penalty for backing out is called "New Money" <note>original: *Neugeld*</note>...

## 64. Judicial Office. *Officium Judicis*.

Wesenbeck teaches in *Counsel 7* that it is safer to implore the <term>Office of the Judge</term> <note>The discretionary power of a judge to act on their own authority to ensure equity</note> than to institute a formal legal action.

### ADDITION.

A judge proceeding based on facts alone is no different from a private citizen. Indeed, an unjust judge is viler and lower than any private person, and not even worthy of the name of judge. See Oldekop in two treatises against Carpzov, folio 272. No one can be both the Plaintiff and the Judge at the same time, as discussed extensively by Nicolaus Myler in his treatise on the *Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 20, page 222.

The Office of the Judge is twofold, according to Ilico Ummius in *On Process*, page 933. The office of the judge is very often exercised in place of a formal action, page 426, at the end. Those cases where that office is used in the likeness of an action are, for instance, when either no action is provided in Civil Law, but only some kind of pursuit <note>original: *persecutio*</note>, as in cases regarding salaries properly speaking, Law 1 and the entire title on extraordinary cognition, where truly the judge's office is most required. See Winther, part 2, *Assessors*, chapter 3, number 33 and following. Or, an action may indeed be available, but because the case requires speed and must be dispatched summarily, only the Office of the Judge is implored. Such are cases of <term>threatened damage</term> <note>original: *damni infecti*</note>, the <term>notification of a new work</term> <note>original: *operis novi nuntiationis*; a legal halt to construction</note>, and likewise cases of <term>spoliation</term> <note>theft or illegal seizure</note>, sequestration, and the taking of pledges. Regarding the clause: "By imploring the noble office of the judge," see Ilico Ummius in *On Process*, pages 177 and 264. Should the judge’s office be implored for the most trivial matters? Timpler, in book 4, chapter 6, question 5 of his *Politics*, confirms the affirmative with nine reasons, which may

<column-break/>

be seen there. Even by Law the matter is clear: namely, that a legal action can be brought against someone for even the smallest thing, as can be seen in the *Country Law* <note>original: *Landrecht*, likely the Saxon Hallore law or similar regional code</note> book 2, article 29, in the gloss at the end: *I tell you, for the sake of a penny one may sue another.* <note>original: "Ich sage dir, um einen Pfennig mag einer den andern beklagen."</note> I remember a similar minor lawsuit over a penny in Wöhred, in the matter of Mrs. R. against S. Haffner. Add here Mr. Felwinger’s *The Judge*, page 483. Concerning a case involving six <term>batzen</term> <note>a small silver coin</note>, and how the Consul settled that dispute, see the same in the cited place, page 394. Can a judge judge according to what is pleaded and proven against his own personal knowledge? Boecler discusses this accurately in *The Judge*, page 25. *The water-graves <note>officials in charge of ditches and water rights</note> of Oettingen must swear that they will pronounce no one's judgment wrongly, and will be intent that no wrong happens to the child in the mother's womb, the calf in the cow, the bird in the air, or the fish in the water.* <note>original: "Die Wassergraven zu Oettingen müssen schwören..." This is a traditional oath of comprehensive justice.</note> More on this in Limnaeus, volume 1, *Additions to Law 4*, chapter 4, page 402.

The "Ring of Necessity" among the Egyptians had a token. What it means "to run to the ring" <note>likely a reference to a tilting game or quintain</note>, book 6, chapter 4, page 102. We learn from Pliny that rings were usually taken off the dying; he says in book 33, chapter 1, near the end: *Out of a certain religious scruple, rings are drawn off from those heavy with sleep or from the dying.* An example is found in Tiberius: when he was failing, his ring was pulled off, which he soon requested back upon regaining consciousness, as Suetonius witnesses in his *Life*, chapter 73. ### 68. Knights, Orders of Knighthood, and Dubbing. Knight, Equestrian Order. <note>original: *Ritter, Ritter-Orden, zu Ritter-schlagen. Eques, Ordo Equestris*</note>

Concerning Knights, the Equestrian Order, and their origin, etc., see Fauchet's specific treatise *Knights* <note>original: *Chevaliers*</note>. The *Chronicle of Chronicles* by Gualterus, part 2, throughout. The anonymous *Historico-Political Discourse* printed at Rostock in quarto.

It is a mark of military virtue to honorably seek a soldier's death for the Fatherland, Cicero, Book 1 of *On Duties*. Since we are born not so much for our parents as for our Fatherland, and given the equality of terms, one ought to succor and obey the Fatherland rather than the parents. Decianus, Response 82, number 15 and following, volume 1. This, however, is especially the duty of a Knight, according to the *Gloss on Saxon Law*, book 1, article 20, at the beginning: **"A knight shall swear the oath that he will not fear death, in order to protect widows and orphans, and where it is proper to protect."** Conversely, many nobles have suffered the loss of their dignity because, through the disgrace of fear and flight, they surrendered fortified places to the enemy, as noted by Werner Gebhard, book 1 of *Princely Table Talk*, chapter 29.

Regularly, however, no one is born a knight,

<column-break/>

but is created, either by the King himself or by the Commander of the King’s army; and this is done either because of military virtue or wisdom. I discuss this in *On Majesty*, folio 185, and *On the Rights of Citizens*, folio 103. For with knees bent, he is struck lightly on the shoulder with a drawn sword, and the Prince addresses him with these words in French: *Be a Knight in the name of God.* <note>original: *Sois Chevalier au nom de Dieu*</note>. This form of creating a knight in England during the Saxon era was shown by Ingulf <note>An 11th-century chronicler and abbot</note>, who lived at that time, in these words: He who was to be consecrated to legitimate military service would, on the preceding evening, make a confession of his sins with contrition before a Bishop, Abbot, Monk, or Priest, and being absolved, would spend the night in the Church devoted to prayer. On the next day, about to hear the sacred rite, he would offer his sword upon the altar; and after the Gospel, the Priest would place the blessed sword upon the Knight’s neck with a blessing. Having partaken of the sacred Mysteries of Christ, he would then remain a legitimate Soldier. This did not entirely die out under the Normans. For John of Salisbury writes in the *Polycraticus* that a solemn custom grew up that on the very day someone is decorated with the military belt, he solemnly goes to Church, and with his sword placed and offered upon the altar, as if a celebrated profession had been made, he devotes himself to the service of the altar and promises the Lord the perpetual service of his sword—that is, of his office. For then, in addition to the sword, the belt and gilded spurs were added as ornaments, which is why they are called "Gilded Knights" <note>original: *Milites & Equites Aurati*</note> today. I do not doubt that this custom descended from the most ancient Germans; among whom, according to the author Tacitus, the first honor of youth was to be adorned by the Prince with a shield and a spear <note>original: *frameâ*</note>; for before this they seemed part of a household, but now part of the Republic.

And to this effect are the writings of Mr. Jos. Nolden, *On the Status of the Nobility*, chapter 6, number 66 and following, where he writes: The custom of creating knights has moved far from ancient times today. For formerly it was a reward for bravery. But today Kings and Princes make the rights of the equestrian order a matter of trade, and put them up for sale as if at an auction. Cornelius Agrippa, *On the Vanity of Sciences*, chapter 80; on nobility. Bodin, *On the Republic*, book 3, chapter 8. **They even provide letters and seals for it, Münster, book 3 of the *Cosmography*, chapter 22.**

So that in truth it can be said, along with Antonio de Guevara, book 3 of the *Dial of Princes*, chapter 31 near the end: the fathers gripped the sword by the hilt, but the sons receive it by the point. One must carefully note the difference observed in ancient times in Westphalia among the nobility, as appears from old legal documents in this manner: *We, Johann of N., Knight, and Heinrich the Squire, hereby acknowledge, etc.* <note>original: "Wir Johann von N. Ritter, und Heinrich der Knappe, bekennen hiemit, &c."</note>. For he who had legitimately obtained the dignity of a <term>Golden Knight</term> <note>Latin: *Eques Auratus*; a high-ranking knight often appointed by a monarch or the Emperor</note>, he was called *Knight* <note>original: "Ritter"</note>; but he who was a man-at-arms—whom we call *eligible for knighthood* <note>original: "Rittermåssig"</note>—was called a *Man-at-arms* <note>original: "Armiger"</note>, a *Shield-bearer* <note>original: "ein Wappener", "Escuyer", or "Edelknecht"</note>. Johannes de Trota, Golden Knight; Johann Morfaim and Henricus Bock, Men-at-arms.

It was very common for nobles and other primary soldiers, on the day before a battle or shortly before entering the fray, to be struck three times on the head with a drawn sword to make them more courageous; thus they were designated as Golden Knights. Even Bishops sometimes did this. See Wigulejus Hund in *The Metropolis of Salzburg*, volume 1, page 22.

Regarding the *Golden Knights*, I cannot pass over, says Oldendorp <note>Johann Oldendorp (c. 1487–1567), a German jurist</note> in his *Treatise on Exceptions*, that which a certain very learned interpreter of Tacitus relates. He says that when we considered these words, it recently came to mind that he whom we call a *Golden Knight* in Latin was formerly called *a Third* <note>original: "ein Dritter"</note> because of the two accompanying horsemen; just as Pausanias explains at length the ancient custom which the French observe to this day; but later he was called *Knight* <note>original: "Ritter"</note>, with the letter D removed.

He is called a *Golden Knight* because in Rome knights were once

<column-break/>

distinguished from the common people by golden rings, just as they now use golden spurs and harnesses. For in the Roman Republic there were three orders: namely the Senatorial, the Equestrian, and the Plebeian. The same is found in Oldendorp’s *Treatise on Actions*, class 5, on beneficial actions, my page 740, under "Knights."

Whether *Clerical Knights* <note>original: "Geistliche Ritter"</note> should succeed in feudal estates? See Gottfried Anton, disputation 6, thesis 9, title G.

There were also *Half-knights* <note>original: "Halbritter"</note>. See Crusius, part 3, book 6, chapter 18, page 164.

For the custom of imitating soldiers and the Rule of the Military Order, see the *Great Belgian Chronicle*, joined with Wippo, page 244.

Also in the *Life of Chevalier Bayard*, written in French, in the additions on page 450, many excellent things are found concerning the oath of knights. For the Knights of the Soldiers of the Holy Sepulchre, see the *Chronicle of the Franciscan Order of Stricter Observance*, page 743.

Concerning the sacred military orders throughout Spain, see Osorius, book 1, page 11 and following, and the French treatise in 16mo.

Reiner Reineccius has much regarding knights and their origin and progress in *On the Original Descent of the Nobility*, page 122 and following; and Bisciola discusses whether the Equestrian order among the Romans was plebeian or noble in his *Leisure Hours*, book 13, chapter 12, where he gathers many things worth knowing about knights.

Furthermore, it should be noted here that the sons of nobles were once admitted into the Equestrian dignity by the hanging of a shield, the placing of a helmet, and the girding of a sword; the servants joined to them were admitted to the right of bearing arms by a <term>slap</term> <note>Latin: *alapa*; a ceremonial blow, often the last one a knight would take without fighting back</note> and a sword. For it was not permitted for just anyone to carry weapons; so much so that Frederick I <note>Emperor Frederick Barbarossa</note> permitted merchants traveling for business to have swords, not to be girded with them, but to be tied to the saddle or thrown into the carriage; but he forbade them to peasants and all others. See *On Maintaining Peace*, book 2 of the *Feudal Laws*, title 27, section 5; and Otto of Freising, book 2, *On the Life of Frederick*, chapter 13.

Now, by custom, the right of bearing arms is granted equally to nobles and to servants—that which is commonly called *making oneself liable* <note>original: "verhafft machen"</note>. And for youths thus initiated, it was formerly shameful and disgraceful to stay at home and waste the strength of their better years in dishonest leisure.

Hence the old poet Gastus says: *What use is a young knight who does not seek knighthood?* <note>original: "Was soll ein junger Ritter, der nicht Ritterschafft begehrt"</note>. Nicolaus Myler in *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 16, page 144. For that reason, they set out abroad and visited all the Christian kingdoms to provide aid to Kings and Princes struggling against enemies, especially against the enemies of the Christian name, as Goldastus testifies in his *Ancient Admonitions*, page 402.

Nor did Princes easily admit men to their courts unless they were proven in life, character, and vigor, which matter finally earned the name of dignity, so that knights were addressed <term>par excellence</term> <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν"; preeminently</note> as *The Valiant* <note>original: "Strenui" or "Gestrenge"</note>. And today, to the misfortune of a failing Republic, that laudable rigor of Princes is so loosened and relaxed that even they themselves now hold the palm in another direction...

### 69. Knighthood, Free Imperial Knighthood, Immediate Nobility of the Empire. See above under the letter F.

Concerning the estates of the Free Imperial Knighthood, their tax contributions and levies—especially when such lands are alienated or pass into foreign hands in other ways—how these matters are handled, and other questions related to this, the following Legal Response (which was written by me some years ago in the name of the Legal Faculty of Tübingen) treats the subject, which I have chosen to insert here.

Whereas His Roman Imperial Majesty, also King of Hungary and Bohemia, our Most Gracious Lord, upon the humble petition of the Free Imperial Knighthood in Franconia, has most graciously addressed the Illustrious and High-born Prince and Lord, Lord N. N., Duke of O., regarding the refusal of tax contributions for many various estates. These lands were previously represented by noble owners within the said Knighthood, but have since been brought into the possession of the highly-praised Duchy of O. through purchase, exchange, or other means, or have fallen to it as a reversion or open fief and were subsequently fully incorporated. His Majesty has commanded that such tax contributions must be paid in the same manner as if the said estates were still possessed by the Knighthood, just as the well-spoken Knighthood has repeatedly and urgently petitioned His Princely Grace and his honored predecessors, citing various old and new privileges obtained from the reigning Roman Emperors.

->I.<-

Accordingly, the first question is whether His Princely Grace and the successors to the Duchy of O. are obligated to pay the customary tax contribution to the said Knighthood from those noble estates which were never previously subject to the Duchy, but belonged solely and uniquely to the Knighthood and were incorporated into it, and always contributed to it, but have now been purchased by the Duchy of O. or otherwise acquired through an "onerous title" <note>A legal term for a transfer involving payment or service, rather than a gift</note>, and remain in its possession?

->II.<-

Whether His Princely Grace is obligated to pay for those noble estates which the Knighthood held as a fief from his ancestors at all times, and which have now returned to the Dukes of O. either through purchase or through the death of the vassals...

Now, when we, the Dean and other Doctors of the Faculty of Law at the common high school <note>University</note> of Tübingen, were graciously requested to consider this matter according to its importance, with diligence and as a collective body, and to provide a detailed legal opinion on the questions raised above with arguments for and against, as well as to disclose what should or should not be done in this difficult matter without prejudice to your Princely Grace; therefore, in humble compliance, we have read in our assembled College the files delivered to us, especially the privileges claimed by the Knighthood and the memorials most obediently submitted to His Roman Imperial Majesty. Having maturely deliberated upon them, we find that as far as the first question is concerned, it might be considered—not without appearance of truth—that your Princely Grace is not at all bound to pay this demanded contribution: in con-

sideration that such estates were undoubtedly handed over to your Princely Grace or your ancestors not with such a burden, but as free, clear, and independent <term>allodial</term> <note>property owned outright without a feudal superior</note> land, and in the purchase contracts or other documents drawn up regarding this, no such burden was stipulated or mentioned. > For it is established that a seller, or another alienating an estate for a price, is held not only to a guarantee against eviction if the thing is taken away; but also if another burden is found to be attached to it, he is obligated by the common laws.

This is especially applicable here, as it is obvious that in the sale of free noble estates, their immunity and freedom are highly valued, and they are usually sold for a much higher price.

Secondly, such noble estates are usually allodial and free-owned, and the nobility is nowhere forbidden from selling them among themselves or even to higher estates. Indeed, it is obvious that within human memory, as well as one, two, or more hundred years ago, such free noble estates have always been transferred and sold in great numbers to spiritual and secular estates, princes, counts, lords, and cities, so that often separate territories were formed and grew out of such noble estates brought together piece by piece; as happened with the Lower Palatinate. For there, the dominion of the Elector Palatines grew out of various contracts and inheritances, which Marquard Freher <note>1565–1614, a prominent German jurist and historian</note> teaches in more than one place, and as Lehmann also hints in the *Speyer Chronicle*, folio 295, book 4, chapter 7.

At that time, among other things, they set down a settlement in the thirtieth article with the following formal words on how the <term>alienation</term> <note>the transfer of ownership to another</note> of knightly estates might be prevented, so that they do not fall into foreign hands: "Since from of old a great

Lit. R.

“The number of the nobility has decreased, and a significant portion of their estates has been withdrawn from them. For this reason, unless a regulation is established among us, we must expect our downfall to become increasingly likely as time goes on, and ultimately, through this path alone, our certain and irrecoverable collapse would follow. We have thus resolved and agreed that henceforth everyone—to whom his free Knightly and Noble estates are available for sale—shall strive, as much as may be done with justice and good opportunity, for the honor and welfare of the common Knighthood, to allow the same to come back into the hands of the nobility. Or, where it could not happen without significant disadvantage and harm to the owner, the estates shall nevertheless be given and sold to those who are not related to us <note>meaning those outside the noble order</note> in no other way than with the reservation of the common Knighthood’s rights, and upon the old traditional contribution <note>referring to the taxes or dues paid to the knightly treasury</note>. In particular, however, for this reason, no one shall enter into a sale with anyone who has restricted <note>original German: "abgestrickt," meaning to legally bind or limit</note> the free purchase of estates within his territory, unless equality is maintained toward us and such restrictions are abolished.”

From which it is to be seen that a member of the nobility is not *absolutely* <note>original: "absolute"</note> inhibited or forbidden from selling his free estates to another social class. Rather, they are only reminded to refrain from such alienation <note>the transfer of ownership</note> henceforth, as much as may be done with justice and good opportunity, *and indeed not out of necessity* <note>original: "& quidem non ex necessitate"</note>, but for the honor and welfare of the common Knighthood. *These words are not prescriptive or imperative, but only exhortatory* <note>original: "Quæ verba non præceptiva aut imperativa, sed adhortatoria tantum existunt"</note>.

Furthermore, in the indicated Noble Ordinance, it is commanded that from that time on, no knightly estate shall be sold otherwise than with the reservation of the old traditional contribution. Thus, one might hold that if such a contribution is not *expressly* <note>original: "expressè"</note> *reserved* <note>original: "reservirt"</note> in the sale or other *alienation*, then it also may not be demanded, but rather *accrues* <note>original: "accresciren"</note> to the remaining members of the free Noble Knighthood. This is especially true since the common Knighthood has itself to blame if they did not redeem such estates within the proper time, but instead allowed them to remain in foreign hands. For the Knighthood also occasionally cites specific *Privileges* <note>original: "Privilegia"</note> and *Pacts* <note>original: "Pacta"</note> established among themselves, by virtue of which they, *in the name of* <note>original: "nomine"</note> the whole Knighthood or its *individual members* <note>original: "particularium membrorum"</note>, claim the <term>Right of Proximity</term> <note>original: "Juris congrui," a legal right of first refusal for neighboring land owners</note> or <term>Retraction</term> <note>original: "retractus," the right to buy back land sold to an outsider</note> when free Noble estates are sold to others outside their circle. Therefore, they have only themselves to blame if they sleep through such a redemption, even if a disadvantage is brought upon the Knighthood generally or specifically through these purchases or other *alienations*.

Thirdly, all of this has all the more
<margin>Besold, Volume I. <note>Refers to Christoph Besold (1577–1638), a prominent German jurist.</note></margin>

<column-break/>

appearance of truth because the Knighthood in common—and much less their free Noble estates, which are directly subject to the Holy Roman Empire <note>term: Immediacy; these nobles answered only to the Emperor, not to local princes</note>—is punished with no certain tax assessment. Instead, they are entirely free, and *for that reason* <note>original: "eoque nomine"</note> are distinguished from other Imperial Estates upon whom a specific tax assessment is imposed.

*And from this it happens that the Nobles, especially in Swabia* <note>original: "in Sueviâ præsertim"</note>, *for many years now, have boasted that they are freer than the other greater Estates and endowed with greater Privileges, about which Nauclerus* <note>Johannes Nauclerus (1425–1510), first Rector of the University of Tübingen</note>, *the first Chancellor of the University of Tübingen, generation 43, page 231, writes thus: The nobility has ranks; for there are Princes, there are Counts and Barons, and there are Nobles of a lower rank. The Princes precede the others not only in dignity and clarity of lineage, but also in power; they have lands and the broadest Dominions. Counts and Barons and other Nobles are dispersed throughout all of Swabia, adorning the region from all sides like flowers in the fields. And what seems wonderful, while Princes, Counts, and Barons, as often as the necessity of the Empire demands, perform obedience to the Emperor as subjects; nevertheless, the Nobles of the lower rank say they are exempt, and serve no one except for pay, nor do they allow their subjects to serve; and yet they all recognize the Roman Emperor as their natural Prince.*

Even if a tax is requested from the Imperial Knighthood by the Imperial Majesty or the Holy Roman Empire, it still does not happen *imperatively*. *For it is established that the nobles are by no means called to a share of the Imperial burdens like the other Estates, but are requested by the Imperial Majesty* <note>original: "Constat enim quod nobiles haut in partem onerum Imperialium vocentur, ut cæteri Status, sed requirantur à Cæsarea Majest."</note> for a voluntary, "compassionate aid," without any specific tax assessment. *This is something that the Imperial Recesses emphasize everywhere* <note>original: "id quod passim Imperii Recessus inculcant"</note>, *and especially* the <term>Imperial Recess</term> <note>The official summary of decisions made at an Imperial Diet (meeting).</note> at Augsburg of the year 1500, under the title "what one should negotiate with the Knighthood in Franconia, Swabia, and the Rhineland (regarding aid against the Turks)," *where it is held thus:* "We, or he who shall sit in our place, and Our ordained Government, shall and will also seriously negotiate and speak with the Knighthood in Franconia, Swabia, and the Rhineland regarding the above-mentioned Christian undertaking and the protection of the Holy Empire. Since they, for the sake of their ancestors' service, have received their honor and dignity from the same Empire, as well as the greater part of their property, they should give their faithful aid, as well suits them as Christian-believing knights and servants of the Holy Empire."

*The same is found* <note>original: "Idemque reperitur"</note> in the Ordinance of the Government established at Augsburg, *in the same year* <note>original: "eodem Anno"</note>, title "on the tax of Knights and Servants," *as also* in the Imperial Recess at Speyer *of the year 1542, section* "Accordingly we have." *Likewise* in the Imperial Recess at Regensburg *year 1576, section* "Then further we will not omit."

*And there are indeed those who say that the Free Nobles were formerly numbered among the Estates of the Empire...*

<meta>This page continues the legal debate regarding whether estates transferred from the Imperial Knighthood to a territorial prince (specifically the Duke of O.) remain liable for the Knighthood's voluntary taxes. It builds on the previous page's discussion of the Knighthood's statutes and the nature of "immediate" noble status under the Holy Roman Emperor.</meta>

The fact that these same nobles ceased to be summoned to the Diets <note>original: "Diætas," the formal deliberative assemblies of the Holy Roman Empire</note> of the Imperial Estates was actually accepted in their favor, so that they would not be bound to bear their share of the expenses of the Imperial Chamber Court <note>original: "Cameræ Imperialis," the highest judicial body in the Empire</note> or undergo other burdens of the Estates. Thus, they now enjoy greater immunity and are not required to pay the collections decreed by the Estates. Concerning this matter, Heinrich Brüning in his *Discourse on Various Types of Universities, thesis 18, toward the end*, writes: "I would believe that the Nobility and certain Cities were not unwilling to allow themselves to be passed over by the summons, so that in this way they might obtain a mitigation of the burdens of the fixed assessments <note>original: "der gewissen Anschläg"</note>, and that those contributions which are collected for the Emperor's particular military expeditions might become more tolerable."

Even when the Imperial Knighthood <note>the *Reichsritterschaft*, a group of immediate nobles who answered only to the Emperor</note> sees fit to grant such a "charitable aid" <note>original: "mitleidige Hülff," a term for voluntary financial support given to the Emperor</note>, it is not strictly assessed; rather, each individual contributes according to his conscience and what he deems appropriate for the matter, with one person sending his contribution without knowing what another has sent.

Since, as has now been explained, the noble estates in Swabia are free in and of themselves, yet bound by a certain burden: it follows from this that when they are sold or given away as free and owned property, the new possessor—if he is not part of the Knighthood and has not consented to such voluntary assessments—cannot be burdened with them in any way. For on such estates, neither the Knighthood nor even the Imperial Majesty himself can claim any mortgage <term>hypothec|a legal claim or lien on property used as security for a debt</term>, as otherwise occurs by reason of collections and other similar burdens. As the law states: "Since those things which are given by request <note>original: "precariò"</note> cannot be demanded by any right. Nor does any action lie to force someone to give something by request."

All of this is strengthened, fourthly, because these contributions granted by the Knighthood are not to be considered "real burdens" <term>onera realia|obligations attached to the land itself regardless of who owns it</term>, but merely personal ones, or at least mixed; so that they do not seem to pass to any subsequent possessor in the manner of truly real burdens. For the Knighthood—that is, the noble knights and servants—grant such things primarily because of the personal privileges they hold as free, immediate nobility of the Empire <note>meaning they were "immediate" subjects of the Emperor, not subject to any intermediate prince</note>, who are not subject to any other Estate in terms of authority or in any other way. They grant this as a kind of compensation for such distinguished immunity. Later, however, this contribution is moderated, valued, and paid among themselves (as is customary in mixed burdens and according to their nature) "by the scales" <note>original: "secundùm æs & libram," an ancient legal phrase meaning precisely by weight and measure</note>, or according to the ratio and quantity of their inheritance, namely however much it amounts to in interest, yields, or even landed estates, wherever they may be situated.

In addition, it must be considered, fifthly, that such estates were not left to a

<column-break/>

stranger, but were transferred to an Estate of the Empire <note>a "Stand," such as a Duke or Prince</note>. Thus, in one way or another, they remain subject to His Roman Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire by reason of Majesty and supreme Majesterial jurisdiction. Through this, it is arranged that the quite heavy assessment with which the Duchy of O. is burdened toward the aforementioned Roman Empire (above other principalities) can be more conveniently paid and borne.

Indeed, such alienations of noble and free estates are understood to occur while preserving the supreme jurisdiction of the Emperor. Since they become part of the territory of some Estate of the Empire to which those estates are added, they remain—just as that entire territory does—under the faith of the Empire. Therefore, that alienation is in some way tolerable, nor is it joined with such great fraud against the public devotion, as authorities like Gylman, Bodin, and others teach in almost similar terms. For a thing suffers a partial reduction more easily than a total destruction.

And lastly, His Princely Grace is not only in the possession of liberty, or something like it, and thus holds the role of the defendant—and in doubt, one must rule for the defendant and the possessor—but some of these same estates were incorporated into the Duchy of O. many years ago, even well over 30 or 40 years, and have thus been released from such a burden through "lawful prescription" <term>præscriptionem|a legal principle where a right is gained or an obligation lost through the passage of time</term>.

Universal liberty and supreme jurisdiction cannot, indeed, be prescribed for eternity. *Bodin, on the Republic, book 1, chapter 9, etc.* However, because in the present case, as has already been said above, those noble estates are transferred while preserving the supreme jurisdiction of the Emperor, and can be considered as part of the territory or province to which they are added, it seems that such prescription can proceed.

On the other hand, however, no small number of significant foundations and reasons could be brought forward, by virtue of which it would seem more in accordance with the laws and Imperial constitutions that all noble estates—which have at all times belonged solely and uniquely to the Knighthood and been incorporated into it, and have always contributed to the same—should in no way be transferred as free and clear without the expressed consent of Your Imperial Majesty and the Knighthood. Nor should they be exempted from the immediate jurisdiction or subjection of the Empire from the body of the Knighthood without the intervening formalities that are otherwise required by the laws and Imperial statutes in the alienation of Imperial property and rights...

It further suggests that after 40 years of incorporation into the Duchy, any such tax obligations have legally expired through prescription.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding the financial obligations of noble estates. Specifically, it addresses whether estates formerly belonging to the Imperial Knighthood remain liable for Imperial taxes after being sold to a territorial prince or another higher-ranking Estate.</meta>

# Letter R.

...created, dismembered, or made subject to another Estate <note>original: "Stand," referring to the various ranks of the Holy Roman Empire's social and political hierarchy</note>; rather, all justice—by whatever name it may be called—and especially the <term>Contribution</term> <note>a term for taxes or military levies</note> due to His Imperial Majesty, the Holy Roman Empire, and the body or treasury of the common <term>Knighthood</term> <note>the *Reichsritterschaft*, or Imperial Knighthood, who held their land directly from the Emperor</note>, must remain entirely undiminished for His Imperial Majesty, the Empire, and the body of the Knighthood.

This is because, first, individual sellers—*transferring these estates to a prince or another Estate of the Empire by some other title* <note>original: "aliove titulo in principem vel Statum alium Imperii hæcce prædia transferentes"</note>—cannot transfer more rights than they themselves possessed. Furthermore, by their own selling—which is often done thoughtlessly or as a result of poor household management—they can in no way cause prejudice <note>legal harm or loss of rights</note> *to a third party, and especially not to a superior* <note>original: "tertio & præsertim superiori"</note>. Natural equity <note>original: "Billigkeit"</note> makes this point clear and undeniable without further elaboration.

To this end, we find it handed down in similar cases that if Nobles buy the lands of peasants, <note>original: "Baurengüter"</note> those lands nevertheless remain subject to their original services and burdens; these must be provided by the Noble buyer no less than by the peasant. Even the Church, when acting as a buyer (though it is otherwise highly privileged), is held to this obligation. <note>Citing Canon Law: "Can. si tributum. qu. 1." etc.</note> For *a thing passes along with its burden* <note>original: "Res enim cum onere suo transit"</note>, and a possessor does not change the legal status of a thing through *common laws* <note>original: "iura vulg."</note>.

And although some may say that in cases of doubt, immunity is also extended to property acquired afterward <note>Citing Tapia, Alexander, Rollandus a Valle, and others</note>, and specifically that a privilege of exemption given to any Church is extended to all adjacent lands or those included under it <note>Citing Bartolus and others</note>; from which they likewise conclude that if immunity is granted to a castle and it later grows into a city or village, the exemption accompanies the whole <note>Citing Balduus and others</note>. This is because *an accessory part shares the nature of the principal thing* and an addition takes on the nature of that to which it is found attached. Thus, some argue that these estates should enjoy the <term>immunity</term> of the Duchy of O., as they are now a part of it.

However, since in an "exorbitant" <note>legal jargon for something that deviates from common law, like a tax break</note> and less favorable matter, there should be no extension from the principal to the accessory <note>Citing Jason and Everhardus</note>, many have more justly judged that an exemption—being "odious" <note>legally restrictive</note> and a matter of strict law—must not be extended beyond its specific cause <note>Citing Bero</note>.

<column-break/>

Neither should it be applied to things acquired afterward <note>Citing Moditius, Natta, and others</note>. Hence, it is established that a Church enriched by the purchase of secular lands does not earn immunity for them <note>Citing Petra and Meichsner</note>. Likewise, a Noble purchasing commoner fields is held to the original burdens <note>Citing the Code of Justinian and various feudal disputes</note>. Indeed, we see that even the Divine House <note>the Church or Imperial treasury</note> has acknowledged the duties that the previous owner had paid <note>Citing Bossius</note>.

And so, the jurisdiction of one province is not extended to a newly added place <note>Citing Brunus and others</note>, nor is the new place ensnared by the statutes of that province. For it is just that things which are separate or separable should be valued according to different laws <note>Citing Cantiuncula and Laurentius</note>.

Secondly, all reasons of plain equity apply here which militate against <term>exemption</term> when a free estate is acquired by another Estate. This is discussed and complained about here and there in the <term>Imperial Recesses</term> <note>original: "Reichs-Abschieden," the official summaries of the decisions of the Imperial Diet</note>: namely, that the Holy Roman Empire is not only significantly weakened in its members by foreign potentates, but that some members also separate themselves from it. Many prelates, counties, lordships, and principalities are taken away, divided, and severed by all sorts of means, so that their tax assessment can no longer be maintained, etc. <note>Citing the <term>Imperial Recess</term> of the year 1570 and 1548</note>.

To encounter these inconveniences, the Emperors are now bound by the Seven Electors <note>original: "Septemviris"</note> in their <term>Capitulation</term> <note>the contract an Emperor signed upon election</note> not only to abstain from pawning Imperial lands but also to revoke those that have been alienated. They promise that they will not give away, sign over, pledge, provide for, or in any other way alienate anything, but will work their hardest to bring back what has escaped. <note>Citing the Imperial Capitulation and Choppin</note>.

For this reason, when a nearly identical question was raised concerning the Burgrave of Meissen <note>original: "Burggravio Misniæ"</note> at the Diet of Augsburg, the Estates ordered <note>original: "jusserunt Ordines"</note> that if he currently held or should in the future acquire other lordships and lands that were already included in the Holy Roman Empire’s registers and tax assessments, he must also bear and pay his due contribution for them.

Imperial Recess of the Year 1548, section: "with the envoys," etc.

Likewise, in the <term>Burgundian Transaction</term> <note>A 1548 treaty that reorganized the status of the Low Countries (the Burgundian Circle) within the Holy Roman Empire</note>, although the Low Countries were exempted from certain duties for various reasons, it is nonetheless written into the agreement: "Yet this treaty and grant shall be without prejudice to the Holy Empire in those lands previously associated with it, and nothing shall be taken away from the Empire thereby." This transaction is found in the Imperial Ordinances of <term>Goldastus</term> <note>Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a famous Swiss jurist and collector of imperial documents</note> for the year 1548.

Furthermore, it is only when a territory or estate <term>immediately subject</term> <note>answering directly to the Emperor without an intermediate lord</note> to the Empire is occupied by an Imperial State through a contract or transaction—and with the unanimous consent of the other States—that the Emperor cannot disturb that possession without cause. <note>Citing legal authorities: Friedrich von Mindan, book 2; Gilman, volume 1; Peregrinus on the laws of the treasury; Rauchbar; and others.</note>

Moreover, because the very structure of the Empire depends on it, it has been established by general law that the <term>Imperial Fiscal</term> <note>The Emperor's treasury or legal prosecutor's office</note> should investigate those who remove members from the Empire and "reap a harvest for themselves from the public ruin" <note>original: "fegetemque ex publico exitio sibi metunt"</note>: 
> We have agreed that a list of those Estates that have withdrawn or are currently withdrawing shall be sent to Our Imperial Treasury through the Mainz Chancellery; Our Imperial Prosecutor shall hereby have the command to proceed against those who have withdrawn, and also to cite those who are in the process of withdrawing to represent their interests. Imperial Recess of the Year 1548, section: "Several others, however."

Such legal processes are usually granted not only to the Imperial Prosecutor against those who seize Imperial Estates or their properties, but also at the request of the <term>Knighthood</term> <note>The *Reichsritterschaft*, or Imperial Knights</note> against the possessors of noble estates who seek to withdraw from the <term>Knight’s Tax</term> <note>original: "Rittersteuer," a tax paid by the knights to support their own corporation and the Empire</note>. Indeed, such a process was carried out at the request of the Franconian Knighthood in the year 1651, and Imperial decrees were obtained several times in the same name against the possessors of noble estates, as can be found in the records sent to us.

Thirdly, His Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire are significantly interested in this matter in many ways, especially regarding the <term>Contribution</term> <note>Military levies or taxes</note>. Therefore, such <term>alienations</term> <note>sales or transfers of land</note> cannot take place to the Empire’s detriment. At the very least, the taxes and other such burdens must remain attached to the land, regardless of any such transfers. This is not only obvious in itself, but also clearly observable because His Imperial Majesty’s <term>immediate jurisdiction</term> <note>direct legal authority</note> and the right of appeal are snatched away. Furthermore, the personal and real obligations—for

<column-break/>

which the Knighthood is bound to His Majesty as his "noble servants and bodyguards" (as they are accustomed to calling themselves), or for which they show themselves willing whenever required—would thereafter vanish and be greatly diminished.

For the Knighthood cannot serve His Imperial Majesty with their bodies if the estates are withdrawn from them and their descendants, <note>original: "tanquam alter succus & sanguis"</note> as if it were their very sap and blood. *Since the splendor of families consists also in wealth, and especially in their subjects* <note>Citing Jean Bodin’s "The Republic," book 3, and Stefano Guazzo</note>. The Knighthood in general cannot maintain any soldiers for the benefit of His Imperial Majesty (as happened within living memory during the Hungarian wars against the <term>arch-enemy of the Christian name</term> <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>, with entire regiments of horse and foot) if the estates are diminished and dispersed in such a manner. By such transfers, people seek to force an exemption from the common Imperial taxes and other burdens.

And because His Roman Imperial Majesty has recently—presumably in place of the personal service the nobility used to provide at their own expense—undertaken the <term>quartering of troops</term>, this right of His Majesty is also made difficult and hindered. Alternatively, those who still remain within the Knighthood are even more heavily burdened (not strictly out of necessity, but out of civic duty and because they are asked) to contribute and pay into the "Knight’s Chest" <note>The common treasury of the Imperial Knights</note> when a large number of noble estates are removed and withdrawn from this body.

Fifthly, it is of the highest importance to the common Knighthood that their "Body" <note>original: "Corpus," referring to their legal corporation</note> remains undivided. Therefore, the benefits flowing *from individual parts toward the common good of the entire Order* should not be blocked or cut off. No individual member—that is, one or another free Imperial Noble—can cause prejudice to this right by contracting or bargaining otherwise. This is especially true by virtue of the significant privilege granted by the late Emperor Maximilian II, dated at Augsburg on May 25, 1566. This decree established and ordered that henceforth all and every noble seat and estate belonging to the common Knighthood shall be considered or held as one single "Body." Should it happen in the future that some alienate their estates through sale or other means into the hands of persons of higher or lower rank, the taxes, assessments, and burdens that have stood upon them from of old shall remain upon them in the future as often as necessity...

### Rudolph II. Letter B.

required, shall be paid and settled there, regardless and without respect to whether and how such persons who acquire such estates might be privileged and exempt for those or any of their other properties.

And it is further added there: We also wish to have expressly revoked <note>original: "derogirt," a legal term for repealing or partically annulling a law</note>, by Our Imperial Majesty's power and knowledge through this letter, any and all privileges, freedoms, and exemptions that might be contrary to this Our statute, decree, order, grace, and liberty, and which might be understood or invoked in this case, etc.

Similar and even stronger privileges are further recounted in the records by Dr. Johann L., deputy of the <term>Imperial Knighthood</term> <note>A class of minor nobles who were "immediate" subjects of the Emperor, meaning they had no lord between them and the Crown</note> in Swabia. Particularly noteworthy is the late Emperor Rudolph II, of most laudable memory, whose Imperial Majesty in the year 1601 declared, extended, and explained the indicated liberty, decree, and order to this extent: that any and all Estates of the Holy Roman Empire, high and low, clerical and secular, must continue to pay the tax <note>original: "Steuer"</note> upon the summons of the Knighthood to their appointed stewards <note>original: "Truchenmeistern"</note> for any lands they already held or might yet acquire which, from that time, were represented in the <term>Contribution</term> <note>The collective tax quota paid by the knightly class to the Empire</note> of the Free Imperial Knighthood in Swabia. This must be done without any evasion or contradiction, regardless of the nature of the lands—whether they be fiefs or owned outright, clerical or secular, belonging to lords or nobles, or simply common or prominent estates—and whether they are purchased by other Estates, or otherwise acquired, or if the fiefs revert to a lord, or are forfeited, or alienated in any other way, in whatever manner and form it may be.

From which it follows that such transfers and sales—at least insofar as they are intended to grant full immunity and exemption from common knightly burdens—are by law unworthy and not binding. *Since whatever contradicts public law, and its status and utility, and is undertaken to the prejudice of others, or of the Empire and Emperor themselves, without the usual and solemn consent of all interested parties,* must be held as powerless and unworthy.

As the aforementioned Dr. Johann L. plausibly argues, the status and existence of the Knighthood could not continue if such lands were significantly diminished or withdrawn, along with the taxes and other common aid attached to them. Instead, it would necessarily lead to ruin and failure, all to the great damage

<column-break/>

and detriment of Your Imperial Majesty and the Holy Empire.

*It is well-established that an act or deed done against the precept and prohibition of the Law is undoubtedly void* <note>citing the Code of Justinian and the Digest regarding legal obligations</note>. *And although the Law does not proceed further by annulling the deed itself, nonetheless, he in whose favor that act was forbidden can challenge and rescind it* <note>A reference to Roman inheritance law regarding children who were passed over in a will</note>. *In such cases, even if a son has been passed over, the will is not void by law, though the Praetor grants this passed-over son the faculty of challenging the will, even if in the meantime the will does not cease to be valid by law* <note>original Latin note: "glossa communiter approbata," referring to the standard legal commentary used by medieval and early modern lawyers</note>.

Sixthly, although these privileges partly speak *even of past sales*, and suggest that even lands purchased before these privileges were obtained remain burdened with the old obligations—and that the Knighthood should be authorized to demand them—otherwise privileges, like *general laws*, are only to be applied *to future business*. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently shown from the above deduction that the content of these many cited privileges is not inconsistent with equity itself, common law, and the Imperial Constitution. Therefore, it follows further that the Roman Imperial Majesty, as well as the Honorable Imperial Knighthood, are free to vindicate their justice in this matter, and no *prescription* <note>A legal claim that a right has been lost or gained because a certain amount of time has passed</note> or statute of limitations shall be an obstacle to them.

*For although one might be able to claim a prescription so as not to pay the Emperor directly, or not be subject to him* <note>Citing various legal authorities including Meichsner and Oldradus</note>, the Emperor himself commands that the <term>Imperial Chamber Court</term> <note>The highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> should determine whether an Estate has been fairly withdrawn and has claimed a prescription against the Empire's taxes <note>Imperial Recess of the Year 1548</note>. *Furthermore, a general prescription does not suffice when it concerns a change of status, and thus involves maximum prejudice* <note>meaning a major loss of rights or legal standing</note>.

*And although in ancient times, all Fiscal actions were abolished after a period of 30 or 40 years,* and thus exemptions from payments against the Prince or the Treasury might seem to cease in those same years, *nonetheless, due to the present state of the Empire...*

But furthermore, some strive to persuade with a clearly new effort that a matter is not called "immemorial" if its beginning can be shown in any way, *Covarrū. in c. poſſeſſor. 2. part. relict. §. tertius n. 8. Therefore, in court, it is proved that a time lacks memory when it is sufficient to call witnesses venerable for their white hair, who testify that they have neither seen the beginning themselves, nor seen men who saw it, but have always heard the contrary from their ancestors. Burgund. tit. des juſtices §. 2. Capic. deciſ. 193. Maſtrill. deciſ. 114. n. 47. Seraphin. deciſ. 1102. num. 4. & deciſ. 1367. num. 1.*

From this, one can perceive what kind of immemorial time is necessary to prove this immunity, which we are now discussing. But truly, since immunity from <term>contributions</term> <note>original: "collectis"; generic term for taxes or assessments.</note> is quite odious <note>In legal terms, "odious" means a privilege that benefits one person while burdening others or the public good, and is thus interpreted strictly.</note> and therefore subject to strict law and contrary to public utility, it is not without reason accepted that anyone wishing to be immune from them by right of prescription is bound to the proof of the following requirements: *First*, that when summoned to provide the duties, he refused it under the pretext of some cause, and from that time forty years have passed, according to the law *si cum scimus. where Bartol. However, because in our estimation Your Princely Graces could not, regarding the estates mentioned in this question, invoke or claim any suitable title providing immunity from taxes, and it is obvious in itself: if anyone, whoever they may be, purchases an estate from a free nobleman—which was at all times taxable to the common **Knighthood**, and also in many ways obligated to the Roman Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire—he could not, by such a change of possessor, ascribe any immunity to himself. Especially since the Knighthood has brought many complaints against this and has obtained from the Imperial Majesty the serving privileges, decrees, and other assistance, we for our part strongly fear that one will successfully claim a lack of good faith <note>original: "adverſo defectum bonæ fidei"</note>, and thus a failure of a necessary requirement for strengthening a prescription, even an immemorial one.

And it is established that even through immemorial time, neither knowledge nor patience is presumed where the injustice of the title is apparent, as *Cephal. notes in conſil. 316. n. 30. vol. 3. CavalC. dec. 46. n. 222. & ſeq. part. 1.* This is especially true in a corporation or body <note>original: "univerſitate ſeu corpore"</note>, which is accustomed to change daily; and if ignorance is presumed in it, then observance achieves nothing, as *Menoch. notes after Alciat. in lib. 3. præſumpt. 103. num. 37.*

...by a faulty, invalid, or unjust title, which could not provide a basis for <term>prescription</term> <note>The legal process by which a right is acquired or a debt is cancelled through the passage of a long period of time.</note>, *Raudenf. decif. Pisan. 9. n. 17. Casp. Roderic. de annuis reditib. lib. 1. q. 14. num. 6. Covarruv. in c. possessor. p. 2. §. 8. num. 4. ad fin. de R. Jur. in 6.
