Following this, and according to the instructions now extensively detailed for both sides regarding the arguments that might be raised for or against the highly noble House of O., we, for our part, remain of the opinion that this first question should be answered with a distinction. Namely, those noble estates (which we learn from old records, and especially from the **Annals of Martin Crusius**, were bought up over time in great number by the old <term>Princely Counts</term> <note>original: "Gesfürsteten Graven"; counts who had been elevated to the rank of Prince of the Empire.</note> of O., and were later struck together with other Countships and lands during the elevation of the territory and brought into one body, distinguished by <term>Ducal dignity</term> <note>The rank and status of a Duke.</note>) are now to be regarded as a true <term>pertinence</term> <note>A legal dependency or subordinate part of a larger estate.</note> of such a Duchy, and should henceforth be unburdened by the **Knighthood** or anyone else. This is in consideration that these lands, towns, castles, villages, and estates have altogether entered into the <term>Imperial Assessment</term> <note>original: "Reichs-Anlag"; the tax quota a territory owed to the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, and if they were to be further burdened, in whole or in part, with other duties from the Knighthood or elsewhere, His Princely Grace, as the holder of such a Duchy, would find himself burdened with a double tax, contrary to all law and equity, and against the customs of the Holy Roman Empire.

Because also, as we believe, the Imperial Assessments of this Duchy of O. have been granted for several long years now, and presumably newly acquired lordships, towns, castles, and other estates were taken into consideration and observed—and the assessment has become all the more significant—the Imperial Majesty or the Holy Roman Empire will, by the same logic, not permit His Princely Grace to be further burdened by the Knighthood.

> For if separate territories flow together into the same name, the same rule, and the same sovereignty, so that they are plainly merged, then that which is extinguished is not considered, but passes into the laws of its principal, according to the text in *Novell. 8. cap. 2. §. l. 20. ff. Tyranno. de instrum. legat. Bart. ad l. 36. C. de appell. in fin. Choppin. 1. de doman. tit. 6. n. 11. Cravett. consil. 454. per tot. Meichfner. tom. 2. lib. 1. dec. 9. n. 14.* Just as this is confirmed by the example of the

<column-break/>

**Dauphiné** and the **County of Valentinois** <note>original: "Delphinatus & Comitatus Valentinienfis"; regions in France used here as a legal precedent for merging territories.</note> by *Guido Papæ. dec. 265.* and by the example of the **Duchy of Asti**, *Cacheranus dec. 22.*

Should such estates be found, however, which have not yet entered into the common Imperial Assessment which the noble Duchy of O. is obliged to pay, and are held as completely free both against the Holy Roman Empire and the Knighthood—and for that reason have contributed nothing, or instead of this, have withdrawn from the Knighthood or the Imperial Majesty so that no benefit has accrued to them, or in this view, the Princely O. Imperial Assessment was not increased: therefore it follows, in our estimation, that His Princely Grace still has to reach an agreement in this matter with the Imperial Majesty or the Knighthood.

Because His Princely Grace also graciously desires us to reveal our legal opinion on what might be done or left undone in this difficult work, without prejudice to him and his ward, as well as other Estates of the Empire: we are of the humble opinion (though without any presumption) that it would be better if His Princely Grace could negotiate with the Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire so that, in view of these newly obtained noble estates, the assessment is increased somewhat, and these estates, like other members of the Duchy of O., are completely incorporated into it and remain free from the claims of the Knighthood.

In consideration that even if His Princely Grace were to enter into a tolerable settlement with the Knighthood regarding the contribution (which could presumably be obtained without difficulty in those parts), the Roman Imperial Majesty might still, sooner or later, seek and demand other rights upon these estates, namely the <term>quartering</term> of troops, legal <term>appeals</term>, etc.

If a settlement is also reached with the Knighthood, it would be advisable that the Imperial Majesty, or where necessary, also the **Electors**, ratify, confirm, and validate the same. Especially they should grant one such thing: that beyond what is promised to the Knighthood by this new composition, those estates shall generally and regarding all rights remain with the Duchy of O. just like its other dependencies, and shall be unchallenged by anyone.

And this our decision, set down here, could not be hindered by the reasons for doubt mentioned at the beginning, which have already largely received their dismissal through the subjoined deciding reasons and through the distinction made.

For although, for one thing, His Princely Grace might not have been granted such estates specifically with an indication of the now-disputed burdens; such a thing is nevertheless understood for itself and **by the law itself** <note>original: "ipso jure"</note>; therefore...

# Practical Treasury Augmented

...no special expression is necessary: because in all sales, the justice and rights belonging to the higher authority—especially current and future assessments and taxes—are implicitly understood. Thus, if by virtue of such high authority, new or old burdens of jurisdiction and sovereignty are imposed or required in those places, these fall upon the buyer. Under the name of such a <term>title defense</term> <note>original: "factæ evictionis"; the legal obligation of a seller to defend the buyer's title or compensate them if the property is lost to a superior claim.</note>, the seller may not seek or demand anything, unless it was specifically and expressly negotiated by the sellers that all the goods should be free even against the authority, or in our case, against the Knighthood regarding all contributions.

<note>The following Latin passage argues that general guarantees of title are insufficient for specific legal burdens.</note>
Because whenever <term>eviction</term> <note>original: "evictio"</note> arises from the nature of the matter, a simple and general promise concerning eviction does not suffice; instead, a special and express one is required in such a case, as declared by Bartolus in *l. si filiæ*, at the end, where Baldus at number 8, Angelus at the end, Castrensis on the last word of *C. famil. ercisc.*, Becc. counsel 24, number 34, Cravett. counsel 211, number 6, book 2, Petra on *fideicommiss.* article 52, number 69, Menochius book 3, preface 112, number 12, who testifies to the common opinion, and the Roman Rota in the newest various decisions 152, number 4, part 2.

And although, secondly, it is not forbidden to alienate noble estates in their proper measure, such alienation cannot be tolerated to the prejudice of the common knightly system, nor primarily to the disadvantage of His Roman Imperial Majesty. Nor can a loss of their rights be brought upon His Imperial Majesty and the common Knighthood through such a sale.

Where a territory and a titled lordship have coalesced from various noble estates, this occurred many years ago and with the consent of His Imperial Majesty (as was mentioned above regarding the Duchy of O.). Such territories were subsequently brought into the Imperial tax assessments. However, it now remains with His Imperial Majesty to either allow this further or to prevent it: since he can be compelled to this by no law.

And although such alienations of knightly estates have occurred toward different Estates of the Empire, and neither the Knighthood in general nor one of its incorporated members undertook the <term>redemption</term> <note>original: "Auslösung"; the right of a family or group to buy back noble land to keep it within their rank.</note>, this should not be a hindrance, as there was often a lack of funds. One could also cite examples where the buyers would not allow the redemption to take place.

Even if, thirdly, the knightly estates are not burdened with a specific fixed assessment, and their contributions are called a sympathetic, voluntary aid; it cannot be concluded from this that when a noble estate

<column-break/>

is sold to an Estate of the Empire that is not a member of the Knighthood, that for that reason—should the occasion arise and the common Knighthood grant such an aid or undertake an assessment for the preservation of the common good—the aforementioned alienated noble estates are free and immune.

<note>The following Latin section explains that taxes (collectae) are often discretionary but still legally rooted in the land.</note>
For although noble estates are not specifically bound to a certain <term>collection</term> <note>original: "collectam"; a tax or assessment.</note> regarding time or quantity, they are nonetheless found to be indefinitely bound to His Imperial Majesty by reason of the right to demand some collection, to be determined at the discretion of the Equestrian Order <note>The Imperial Knighthood.</note>. And this right is rooted in the estates themselves, and passes along with them to any possessors whatsoever. It is in the nature of "collections"—which are an extraordinary duty and burden—that they have no fixed payment in terms of either time or quantity. And it is the conclusion of the interpreters of the Common Law that he who has the right of collecting ought not to command, but to entreat the collections; all violence should be absent, and persuasion should hold the primary place. Wintzler, *On Collections*, observation 5, from the beginning and number 7, and after others alleged by him, Philipp Honon, *Political Disputations* 5, thesis 90, page 290; Bocer, *On Collections*, chapter 4, number 8.

There are also many provinces of Germany which are not bound to such burdens except by the consent and pact of the Estates. When the Electors and Princes of the Empire wish to impose a tax, the custom almost everywhere is that they first request a <term>Landtag</term> <note>A provincial diet or assembly of estates.</note> for that purpose. That one must stand by the privileges and customs of such provinces, and that nothing should be changed from ancient morals, is proven by Maulius after Heigium, *On Homage*, chapter 9, number 119; and law 8 of the Code *On Laws* supports this. Hence, collections in certain places are called <term>Beden</term> <note>original: "Beden"; from the German "bitte" (request), referring to taxes that were technically requested by the sovereign and granted by the estates.</note>.

Now, if in a principality that is thus privileged in respect to extraordinary collections or provincial taxes, a free Imperial Nobleman or even a foreigner should buy something, but afterward, when the province grants a voluntary tax for the preservation of the common good, he wishes to withdraw those goods and declare them free, this will in no way be permitted to him (as indeed happens daily).

Therefore, conversely, it is not to be expected of His Imperial Majesty or the free Imperial Knighthood that they should allow the ancient, free noble estates—which have at all times "given and laid" <note>An idiom for paying taxes and fulfilling duties.</note> with the Knighthood—to be withdrawn from them without compensation or other recompense, especially regarding the voluntary aid or that distinguished right. This is because it would deprive His Imperial Majesty of the <term>immediate subjection</term> <note>original: "immediata subjectio"; being subject directly to the Emperor without an intermediate lord.</note> by virtue of which He receives this voluntary aid and other services from the noble...

### Second Question.

Regarding the second question concerning the mentioned noble estates, in our humble opinion, it must first be investigated as a matter of fact whether these estates are <term>of the territory</term> <note>original: "de territorio"; meaning belonging legally to the geographical jurisdiction of a specific lord.</note> and are to be considered a part of the Duchy of O. or not? For some are of the opinion that free noble estates—even if they stem as fiefs from another <term>Estate of the Empire</term> <note>A territory or person with a seat in the Imperial Diet.</note>—are not subject to the territorial sovereign's authority, but are instead attached directly to the Holy Roman Empire regarding appeals, contributions, and in all other ways. From this, it should be noted that such estates are not to be considered part of the territory of the land or lordship from which they stem as fiefs, but rather are merely voluntary <term>assigned fiefs</term> <note>original: "aufgetragene Feuda"; property originally owned outright (allodial) that is "assigned" to a lord to be received back as a fief in exchange for protection.</note> and are united with the territory of the <term>Feudal Lord</term> <note>original: "Domini Feudalis"</note> only for the purpose of protection.

<margin>Azevedo, book 6, on the Spanish Constitutions, title 2, rubric note 215. Angelus, counsel 247. Socinus the Younger, counsel 28, number 21.</margin>
<note>original: "Unionis enim diversi sunt modi..."</note> For there are various modes of union, and among others, a union is sometimes made with another larger territory solely for the sake of protection.

Therefore, it is provable that 200 or 150 years ago, all <term>ancestral houses</term> <note>The primary family seats of the nobility.</note> were <term>allodial</term> <note>Owned outright, free of any feudal obligations to a superior lord.</note>, and only since then, for the sake of greater protection and other causes after the time of Rudolf I, have they been "assigned" as fiefs.

And this is a true mark of a fief, which the <term>granting lord</term> <note>original: "Dominus infeudans"</note> lends from his own territory to a vassal or nobleman by way of a benefit and feudal gift, when he retains the right of <term>recourse</term> <note>The right of subjects to appeal a legal case to the sovereign.</note> for the subjects, the right of appeal, and other <term>Sovereign Rights</term> <note>original: "Regalia"</note>. Just as in other cases, even if a certain Prince—on account of outstanding deeds in war or peace performed for the benefit of the state, or for some other cause—has conferred cities, villages, or towns upon a Bishop or Noble as a royal benefit, together with every kind of jurisdiction, <term>high and low justice</term> <note>original: "mero mixtoque Imperio"; the authority to handle both capital crimes and civil disputes.</note> to be exercised in a very large territory; or if he has granted a Barony, Margraviate, County, or Duchy to anyone...

<column-break/>

...and under whatever title and prerogative; nevertheless, the obligation of loyalty and the <term>clientage</term> <note>The relationship of a dependent vassal to their protector.</note> owed to the King, as well as that jurisdiction which is supreme with the granting Prince, remain. By his right, appeals from inferior judges, or petitions and recourses, and other causes are brought to him as the supreme head and Father of the state. Other rights of superiority do not seem to be transferred or abdicated by him, even if he has used the most abundant and ample words in this matter regarding their meaning.

<note>Citations: Molinaeus on the Customs of Paris, title 1, §1, gloss 5, on the word "le fief" (the fief), number 49. Mynsinger, century 6, observation 99. Otto on Public Law, chapter 11. Surdus, counsel 275, volume 2.</note> Hence, whatever things were once part of the territory of a certain Prince, when he lends them as a fief to another, he nevertheless remains the territorial sovereign over them, and the vassals are <term>land-settled subjects</term> <note>original: "Landſäſſen"; residents who owe allegiance to the local territorial prince.</note> at least regarding those goods. <note>Citations: Compiler of the Symphorema, Imperial Chamber Petitions, volume 1, part 1, title 2, regarding reconvention, vote 1, number 176, folio 125, column 1. Peregrinus, counsel 1, number 15, volume 1.</note>

We, for our part, incline more toward the view that in case of doubt, a fief should not be considered an "assigned" fief, but rather it should be held that the Lege Lord gave it generously to the vassal from his own property. <note>original: "Est enim feudum beneficium tale..."</note> For a fief is such a benefit that is given to someone out of benevolence in such a way that the ownership of the benefited immovable thing remains with the giver, but the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of a property without owning it.</note> of that thing passes to the receiver, so that it belongs to him and his feudal heirs forever, to the end that he and his heirs may faithfully serve the Lord. (Book 2 of Fiefs, title 23).

Now, however, a presumption must be taken according to that which usually happens and is more consistent with the nature of the thing itself.

It is also established that formerly the <term>sub-vassals</term> <note>original: "Valvaſini"</note> were invested by the <term>vassals</term> <note>original: "Valvaſoribus"; intermediate lords.</note>, as in Book 2 of Fiefs, title 10, where Cujacius notes that the true origin and definition of Nobility is contained therein.

And although the Counts and other Lords in Swabia, Franconia, and along the Rhine might not have reserved the territorial sovereign authority in these fiefs of theirs, this would have resulted from negligence, and because in olden times one looked more toward military service than toward matters of jurisdiction.

<note>original: "Namque ut amore & dilectione..."</note> For so that the Prince might be safer in love and affection, he gave fiefs to brave men to be used and enjoyed (Cujacius, book 8, observation 14; Choppin, book 2 on the Domain, title 14, number 7; Carolus Tapia in the rubric on Princely Constitutions, chapter 4, number 21), so that he might bind them by that bond, they being prepared to shed or draw blood, to lose or perish indiscriminately for him (Book 2 of Fiefs, titles 7 and 28, and there Borgninus on the Cavalry, number 1, chapter 1).

<meta>This page continues the legal argument concerning whether noble fiefs (Lehen-Güter) located within a sovereign's territory should be subject to the territorial prince's taxes or the Imperial Knighthood's contributions. It specifically addresses how these estates might have historically transitioned between different jurisdictions.</meta>

of the nobility, which undoubtedly refers to such fief-holders, who were members of the <term>Territorial Estates</term> <note>original: "Landsstand"; the representative body of a territory's social orders.</note> in O. However, it is presumed that through various disturbances, they gradually took the opportunity to make themselves more and more free. This is mentioned in Crusius <note>Martinus Crusius (1526–1607), a famous historian of Swabia.</note> in Book 6, Chapter 5 of his Annals, regarding a war undertaken in the year 1395 by the late Count Eberhard of Württemberg (called "the Gentle") against his noblemen who had opposed him.

The fact that such estates came to be included in the <term>contributions</term> <note>Taxes paid by the Imperial Knighthood to the Empire.</note> of the Knighthood likely occurred because they were held by free and ancient nobles who thereafter paid taxes into the "Knight’s Chest" on their property, <term>wherever it was situated and of whatever condition</term> <note>original: "ubicunque sita, & cujuscunque conditionis"</note>. Just as we see that a citizen, in his place of residence, can be taxed even by reason of property situated outside that territory; and that a tax can be lawfully imposed on citizens even for goods located elsewhere, specifically outside the territory of the taxing authority. This is taught by Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century Italian jurist.</note> on the Code regarding women and their residence, as well as by Guido Papae, Decision 5, number 2, and Gail, Book 2, Observation 53, number 10. Thus, in the <term>Imperial Chamber Court</term> <note>The highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, it was judged in a certain case that citizens can be taxed by reason of property located outside the city’s territory, as noted by Münzinger, Century 5, Observation 22, and specifically in the case of the Master of the Teutonic Order against Donauwörth, cited by Rosenthal on fiefs, Chapter 5, Conclusion 80.

Therefore, in several Imperial Cities, the <term>Patricians</term> <note>The ruling elite families of a city.</note> have had to allow their fiefs and other estates to be burdened with taxes in their place of residence where they hold citizenship, even if those estates are located outside the jurisdiction of that Imperial City. Since taxes, as a <term>mixed burden</term> <note>original: "onus mixtum"; a legal term for a tax that falls on both the person and the property.</note>, can be levied upon one who is subject to the taxing authority's power in view of their entire patrimony.

Thus it is evident that several nobles in the County of Hohenberg and in estates located within its territorial sovereignty—specifically the Scheeren von Schwarzenburg regarding the estate and village of Oberhausen—have attempted to claim these as free noble estates. This is despite the fact that these were granted as fiefs by the late King Ferdinand with <term>lower jurisdiction</term> <note>The right to judge minor crimes and civil disputes.</note>, yet with the <term>sovereign rights</term> <note>original: "regalibus"; the "regalia" or royal prerogatives reserved for the monarch.</note> and all other rights belonging to the territorial prince's authority being reserved. Because they have been paying taxes to the Knighthood, they now seek to assert them as free noble property, which is currently causing burdensome legal disputes.

From this consideration, one can see how the Princely fiefs of O. might have come into the Knighthood's contribution. It follows that such estates, <term>once the right of the vassals is dissolved</term> <note>original: "resoluto jure Vasallorum"</note>, must necessarily return to the Princely liege lord free and unburdened by such external contributions. For it is not at all to be presumed—indeed, it is notorious and manifest—that these estates, when they were still part of O. and before they were granted to anyone as a fief, were never intended to be subject to noble contributions.

<column-break/>

Therefore, when such estates return to the state they were in <term>before the granting of the fief or the first investiture</term> <note>original: "ante infeudationem vel primam investituram"</note>, they must be restored to the liege lord with the same rights and immunities.

Namely, since a vassal can in no way impose a servitude, a <term>usufruct</term> <note>The right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property.</note>, or a similar burden upon a fief; or if he does so, such a burden must cease once the right of the giver is dissolved. For a vassal is bound to keep the substance of the feudal property <term>in good repair</term> <note>original: "sartam tectam"; literally "patched and roofed."</note>. And it is said in the Digest that a usufructuary can make the condition of the property better, but not worse. The same is affirmed regarding a vassal in the book of fiefs. For that reason, a usufructuary is not permitted to impose a servitude on the property held in usufruct. And if it should be done, that right is owed more from a promise than from a legal constitution, so that the common rule applies: <term>when the right of the giver is dissolved, the right of the receiver is also dissolved</term> <note>original: "resoluto jure dantis, resolvatur etiam jus acceptoris"</note>. This is affirmed as common opinion by Pinellus and Soarez. That a servitude imposed on a feudal property by a vassal is dissolved by the death of the vassal is commonly taught by Schrader, Surdus, and others. By this same reasoning, when a vassal disposes of the annual fruits of a fief for some specific work, that disposition vanishes upon the death of the vassal, according to Vultejus.

And it does not hinder this argument if the fiefs, as long as they were possessed by noble vassals, were not burdened by the territorial prince's authority, or if their holders were never anciently considered territorial subjects or members of the <term>Territorial Estates</term>. One should not conclude from this that such estates were never "of the territory" or a part of the territory of the lord granting the investiture. For in former times, and even according to feudal law, <term>a vassal was not made a subject</term> <note>original: "Vasallus haut subditus efficiebatur"</note>, and feudal estates passed to the vassal with the jurisdiction and obligation being reserved. Whence it is said that "vassal" and "subject" are entirely different categories, as noted by Gail, Wesenbeck, Decianus, and at length by Zacharias Vietor in his work on exemptions.

Hence, a superior, such as the Pope or the Emperor, can be the vassal of another but cannot be a subject, as noted by Hotman, Vultejus, Zasius, and Rosenthal.

And the lord of the fief has a jurisdiction confined within the boundaries of feudal litigation, and he does not dare to go beyond it, according to the decree *Pastoralis* regarding sentencing and matters already judged.

jurist Paurmeister <note>Tobias Paurmeister von Kochstedt (1553–1608), a prominent German legal scholar.</note>, Book 2, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 8, number 41. Excellent points by Marta in the said treatise, part 4, century 1, case 16, numbers 12 and 20; and by Guido Papæ, Decision 42.

Because, in conclusion, these fiefs have been an ancient <term>appurtenance</term> <note>original: "Pertinenz"; a legal accessory or dependency of a larger territory.</note> of the Duchy of O. or its associated counties and lordships, and by reason of ownership <note>original: "ratione proprietatis"</note> have never been separated from it nor belonged to the <term>Knighthood</term> <note>The Imperial Knighthood, which claimed direct subordination to the Emperor, bypassing territorial princes.</note>, it follows from this: that when the ownership with the right of use, or the right of the fief <note>original: "proprietates cum usufructu sive jure feudi"</note>, is lawfully consolidated again by whatever means, then, when the cause for this tax contribution ceases, the effect—the contribution itself—must necessarily cease as well <note>original: "cessante causa hujus contributionis, auch der effectus sive ipsa contributio nothwendig cessiren thue." A common legal maxim: when the reason for a law or tax ends, the law or tax itself ends.</note>.

### Question Three.

From what was explained in the previous question, it follows naturally that the Imperial <term>Privilege</term> <note>A special legal grant or exemption issued by the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> does not apply at all to the estates mentioned in the second question—which the Knighthood has at all times held as fiefs from the noble Duchy of O. Instead, in cases of doubt, it should much more likely be applied only to those fief-estates about which the following fourth question is written. Even if His Imperial Majesty, in granting these privileges, had included the estates from the second question, this could not stand according to the law. This is because once such estates have returned to O. and attained their old status as an ancient appurtenance of the same, they are included under its customary tax burden; furthermore, Your Princely Grace, as the <term>liege lord</term> <note>original: "Lehenherr"; the lord who grants a fief to a vassal.</note> of these estates, is in no way bound to the Knighthood.

And to this point it is relevant that a Prince cannot take away an acquired right from another against their will <note>original: "jus quæsitum Princeps alteri invito adimere nequeat"</note>, law 2, section *if anyone*, from the beginning, in the Digest *if anyone in a public place*. Peregrinus, *On Trusts*, article 59, number 119. Signorolus de Homodeis, counsel 10, number 4, and counsel 218, number 21. And privileges ought not to be extended to the injury of another <note>original: "Privilegia ad alienam injuriam non debeant porrigi"</note>; this is the text in law 40, in the Digest *on the administration and risk of guardians*. Antonius Faber <note>A celebrated 16th-century jurist from Savoy.</note> in the Code, title 2, definition 22, and title 11, definition 1. Seraphinus, Decision 351, number 7.

It is also provided for by law that those privileges which are obtained to the prejudice of a third party <note>original: "in Præjudicium tertii"</note>, and by concealing the rights of another lordship, are not valid. Felinus in chapter *not some*, number 12, on rescripts. Bartolus on the law *Gallus*, section *but if*, in the Digest *on children and posthumous heirs*. Parilus, counsel 1, number 71 and following, book 1. And thus a privilege that absorbs the right of another, or which is obtained by keeping the truth silent regarding possession or another right which a third party holds in good faith, is not valid; because it is presumed to have been issued due to excessive persistence and from being too busy, so that it had not been considered that the right

<column-break/>

of another would be harmed by it. Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> on the chapter *some time ago*, number 2, on Privileges; and on chapter 1, on rescripts.

And although further every privilege receives the widest interpretation against the one who grants it, it nevertheless should not nor can be interpreted in such a way that the right of a third party is harmed by it; indeed, the words of the privilege themselves ought to be restricted in their meaning so that the third party is harmed less. Panormitanus on the chapter *because around*, on Privileges. Alexander, counsel 215, volume 1.

Add to this that all the Emperor's rescripts, benefits, grants, etc., have this silent clause annexed: **saving the rights of the Empire and of everyone else** <note>original: "salvo jure Imperii & cujuscunque"</note>. Bodin, *On the Republic*, book 1, chapter 8, number 104. Marsilius, *Singularia* 483. Arnisæus, book 1, *On the Right of Majesty*, chapter 5, number 20. Gail, 2, observation 48, number 6. Wesenbeck, counsel 21, number 5. Gylman, volume 1, part 2, title 11, vote 7, numbers 14, 20, and 44. Seraphinus, Decision 827, number 1. Mantica, *On Tacit and Ambiguous Agreements*, title 19, number 23.

This point from Natta <note>Marcantonio Natta, an Italian jurist.</note> can also be adapted to our current question: that the Emperor cannot change the status or diminish the honor of old vassals <note>original: "Imperator non possit mutare statum, aut minuere honorem veterum vasallorum"</note>, counsel 686. Cacheranus, counsel 49, number 12. Baldus, counsel 329, number 4, volume 1. Elegantly stated by Capicius, Decision 162, number 4. Nor can he increase dignities to the injury of others, Antonius Faber, book 6 of the Code, title 27, definition 15. But that he always wishes the dignity and loftiness of illustrious persons to be unharmed in a general grant. Raudensis, *On Equivocation*, chapter 28, number 112. Knichen, in the *Encyclopedia*, chapter 10, number 156, following Natta, Schrader, and Pacianus. Add Cacheranus, counsel 49, in its entirety. Since, naturally, it is the office of the Supreme Prince to protect everyone's jurisdictions and legal status, not to disturb them. See the Imperial Capitulation <note>The *Wahlkapitulation*, a contract the Emperor-elect signed with the electors.</note>, section 2, where it says:

> to leave every Lord and Estate with their highnesses, dignities, rights, power, authority, etc.

Antonius Faber, book 3 of the Code, title 12, definition 5, number 2. And he should not suppress or harm his own members, Denais in *Assertion of Chamber Jurisdiction*, page 254. Cothman, counsel 28, number 108, volume 1. But rather he should preserve every State of the Empire in that condition in which it was from its beginning and origin, Vultejus, counsel 35, number 205, section *but the law*, number 3, Marpurgensis. And he should provide that the dignity of the Estates and families remains safe, law 1, section *if a slave*, in the Digest *on inspecting the womb*. Goras, 3, *Miscellanies*, chapter 3, number 1.

# Augmented Treasury of Practical Law

...returns to the Duchy of O. again, in all respects and with the distinction raised in the first question—namely, when such estates were not previously included in the Princely O. assessment. Thus, if His Princely Grace were also forced to contribute to the **Knighthood** <note>The Imperial Knighthood consisted of free nobles who were "immediate" to the Emperor, meaning they recognized no lord between themselves and the Emperor.</note> on their account, he would be doubly burdened. For through such a surrender of a fief and the subsequent investiture, neither the persons nor, much less, the estates could be withdrawn from the **immediate jurisdiction** <note>Direct legal authority under the Holy Roman Emperor, bypassing local territorial princes.</note> of the Holy Roman Empire, nor from the common Knighthood, insofar as they are bound to it. 

And as suggested in the preceding second and third questions, neither the Imperial Majesty nor the vassals of the Duchy of O. can prejudice <note>In a legal sense, to "prejudice" means to harm or diminish someone's existing legal rights or claims.</note> their feudal lord regarding fiefs which have always remained the property of the Duchy of O. while bringing contributions to the Knighthood. Conversely, it follows from the same principle of equity that the vassals who have surrendered their own property to the Princely House of O. to be held as a fief <note>A process called "oblation," where a landowner gives their free land to a powerful lord and receives it back as a fief for protection.</note> cannot thereby prejudice or harm the Imperial Majesty or the Knighthood. This is according to the writings of Sixtin in *On Royal Prerogatives*, chapter 8, sections 67 and 68, where he writes: 

<note>original: "Si Comes vel Baro ut securior esset..."</note> *If a Count or Baron, in order to be more secure or for some other reason, recognizes his County or Barony as a fief from some inferior Prince, his prior dignity is still retained in this case, as it was obtained from the supreme Prince [the Emperor] alone.* 

And a little later: 

*Just as the dignity of Royalties and the Royal Rights of the Counts and Barons of the Empire are not diminished by such aforementioned sub-fiefs, so too they do not lose the liberty by which they are immediately subject to the Empire, nor are they subjected to the jurisdiction of the feudal lord. For ordinary jurisdiction and feudal jurisdiction are entirely different. Even if they greatly desired it, they cannot, through such feudal recognition, exempt their person or property, which are immediately subject to the Empire.*

In the same sense, the compiler of the *Symphorematis*, volume 1, part 1, title 4, page 300, says: 

*Nobles are accustomed to recognize their **allodial lands** <term>Allodial lands</term> <note>Land owned outright by the holder, without any feudal obligations to a superior lord.</note> as fiefs from Princes, not because they wish to create a prejudice against themselves, but to provide for themselves with "abundant caution" <note>A legal term for taking extra precautions to ensure security.</note>.* 

See also Knichen, *On Territorial Law*, chapter 1, number 226; and Matthæus Stephani, book 2, *On Jurisdiction*, part 1, chapter 7, number 177: 

*An immediate Estate [of the Empire] can recognize its allodial lands as a fief from a Prince of the Empire; however, by this very act, no superiority or jurisdiction is granted over the person of the vassal, his property, or his subjects.*

This is supported by the teachings of Bruningius, *On the Law of Universities* <note>In this context, "University" refers to any legal corporate body or collective group, such as a city or a guild.</note>, conclusion 16; Paurmeister, book 2, chapter 8, number 48; and Azevedo, volume 4, *Constitutions of Spain*, title 3, number 2, where he says: 

*A vassal who submits himself to another person acts in vain and achieves nothing to the prejudice of his first lord.* 

For it is in the interest

<column-break/>

of the Emperor and all the Estates that the Estates of the Empire, and those immediately subject to it, be preserved in their entirety for others, according to chapter 1 of *The Prohibition of Alienating Fiefs* by Frederick. Therefore, if anyone has a superior—for example, the Emperor—that agreed-upon and spontaneous subjection will achieve nothing, even if an oath is involved. This is found in the text *we believe you* <note>original: "c. ea te credimus"; a reference to Canon Law regarding oaths.</note> concerning oaths. See also Knichen, number 177; Jacobinus de San Georgio, *On Homage*, at the beginning, number 21. For in an obligation, however general it may be, those things that are tacitly forbidden are not included. See law 1, section *he who mandated*, and law 42, in the Digest *on the office of the delegate*. Also Craverta, counsel 106, number 6, and counsel 170, number 2; Decisions of Milan 2, number 142, book 2; Caroccius, decision 117, number 2. Consent is only deemed given for those things that *can* be transferred, according to law *Lucius*, 21, penultimate section, in the Digest *on municipal matters*. See also Peregrinus, *On Trusts*, article 6, number 11, because due to an unsuitable means, a general statement only operates as far as it is able. Everhardus in *Topics*, location 5, number 1.

### Fifth and Final Question.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'B' at the start of the section, featuring floral and foliage patterns.</image-desc>
Regarding this question, we see no doubt—nor does any reasonable doubt appear—as to why Your Princely Grace should not be summoned and invited to these **Conventions** <note>Regional or knightly assemblies where taxes and local governance were decided.</note> through your special deputies, and be allowed to vote just like the others. For it is most just that he who feels the burdens should also perceive the benefits <note>original: "Cùm qui incommoda sentit, commoda etiam percipere eundem, æquissimum existat." A fundamental legal principle of fairness.</note>. 

Furthermore, when something must be done collectively or in the name of a **University** <note>Again, meaning a corporate or collective body.</note>, each individual who has an interest must be summoned by name and admitted to cast a vote. For natural reason dictates that common business should be conducted by common counsel, and natural reason has the force of law. Where the law is lacking, natural reason suffices. 

Likewise, decisions in legal cases can be inferred from natural principles, as noted in the text on *Genesis* <note>A reference to using the biblical book of Genesis as a source for "natural law" principles.</note> and the commentary by the Abbot on elections.

And **what touches all must be approved by all** <note>original: "quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus debet approbari"; a famous legal maxim (Quod Omnes Tangit) used throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance to argue for the necessity of consent in taxation and governance.</note>. The consensus of all to whom the matter pertains, or whose rights are at stake, is required.

Therefore, those who hold noble estates are sometimes summoned to such conventions even if they are not of noble descent. For it belongs to the very essence of colleges and corporate bodies that there should be at least a convention and common deliberation, as stated by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher.</note> in *The Republic*, book 3, chapter 7, number 331; Althusius <note>Johannes Althusius (1563–1638), a legal scholar and father of modern federalism.</note>, *Politics*, chapter 4, number 8 and following; and Schönborn, book 1, *Politics*, 11. A college or body cannot long endure if deliberations are instituted separately. So says Besold <note>Christoph Besold (1577–1638), a jurist and professor at Tübingen.</note>, *On the Law of Colleges*, last chapter, number 7.

Lit. R.

And when something is to be carried out in the name of a **Corporate Body** <term>Universitas: in Roman law, a collective legal entity, such as a guild, town, or order, that acts as a single "person" in the eyes of the law</term>, it is required that all members be summoned, according to the Code of Justinian and legal resolutions by Trentacinquius. And if anyone is not expressly summoned, they may act on the grounds of **contempt** <note>In this legal context, "contempt" refers to the injury or slight caused by being intentionally excluded from a process one has a right to join</note>, or may invalidate what has been done, according to the decrees on the election of Abbots.

Thus, it is also provided by law that in deciding matters and acts concerning the whole as a whole, or the Corporate Body as a Corporate Body, not just one or another part, but all parts of the Order or College must be summoned, according to the text specifically handed down in the laws concerning city councilors, which is commended by Paulus de Castro and others in the laws regarding collective names.

Furthermore, since such acts do not concern the owners of noble estates only as a collective, but involve the particular advantage or disadvantage of individuals, all those who have an interest must be summoned to their consultations, as per the text in the laws regarding rural estate services where Bartolus comments.

And because, as suggested above, all noble, **taxable estates** <term>talliabilia prædia: lands subject to a "tallage" or specific property tax</term> and Castles, and those who are obliged to contribute with the Knighthood, are combined into one **Body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note>; it follows that their owners, as members, have their own appropriate office and voice in consulting on public acts as a whole. According to legal theory, matters concerning everyone as a whole must be consulted upon and approved by everyone appointed with the voice of the Corporate Body. To this end, the common theory applies: that no one should be burdened or obligated without being heard and defended, a principle proven by **Natural Law and the Law of Nations** <note>The "Law of Nations" (Jus Gentium) refers to the core legal principles thought to be shared by all civilized peoples</note>.

And for this, there is no need for a specific title; this seems to apply most strongly in the matter of our case, in which we are dealing not with outsiders, but with fellow members of a college. Nearly all legal doctors agree on this, including Innocent, Johannes Andreae, and others.

Hence it is said that in the acts of a Corporate Body, in which matters are discussed concerning the Body itself and its individual members, a majority consensus is not sufficient, but all must expressly consent. So it is also handed down that in actions of this kind, if there were a thousand members, the actions of almost all would not harm a single dissenter. By this rule, Oldradus concludes that one person who has a share in a mill can resist all the others who wish to sell such a mill, etc.

Regarding this question, however, it might further be called into doubt whether His Princely Grace should have only one vote, or as many 

<column-break/>

noble estates as he holds in his hands? To be sure, one should be informed that even at the **Imperial and Circle Diets** <note>The Reichstag (Imperial Diet) was the general assembly of the Holy Roman Empire; the Circle Diets (Kreistage) were regional assemblies</note> this question has come up: whether a **plurality** <note>a majority</note> should be counted according to **arithmetic proportion** (that is, by the number of persons) or rather by taking into account **geometric proportion** (that is, according to the size of the tax assessment)? On which matter Wilhelm Antonius has recently written.

But because this question has not yet been decided, and so far as we know, it has not been the custom among the Knighthood for votes to be counted by estates (or that a nobleman, if he acquires more than one estate, should therefore have two votes): we leave it to the highly enlightened judgment of His Princely Grace and his Council. We suggest whether this controversy should be bypassed and set aside, or whether, in view of **notorious equity** <note>original: "notoriæ æquitatis" — fairness that is so obvious it requires no further proof</note>, since His Princely Grace has to represent a good number of former noble estates in the matter of contribution, he might be allowed to appoint a certain number of persons or be given power through a special agreement, etc.

### 70. Knighthood, Men-at-arms. The Equestrian Order.

Those terms are collective names, encompassing not only individual or particular Nobles, but also the Corporate Body of Nobles itself. Thus also those words, "those of the Knighthood or the Men-at-arms," encompass not only individual persons, but also the corporate body or collection of Nobles itself, as Schrader writes. This is sufficiently proven according to the same law: a legal writ obtained against the "men of a certain place" must be understood so that, by virtue of that writ, not only the individual men of that place, but also the corporate body of those men can be called to court. This is because they proceed equally, whether a provision mentions "the Nobility" or "those who are of the Nobility." As the doctors of law hand down, it is the same whether a provision mentions "Perugians or Florentines" or "those of Perugia or Florence." For a provision speaking indefinitely about "Citizens" is understood to refer not only to individual men, but to the City itself, or the Corporate Body.

# Added Practical Treasury

->[The term Indiction is used]<- simply in one way for a burden or duty imposed upon subjects by a Prince or Emperor. Or, as Alciatus defines it in the law *Among the public* <note>Latin: "inter publ." referring to a specific law in the Digest</note> regarding the *Signification of Words*, it is that which is proclaimed by the edict of a Prince to his subjects, usually not encompassing a specific quantity; and in this sense, it is not used here. At the beginning, these **Indictions** <term>Indiction: a 15-year cycle used for dating documents, originally tied to tax assessments in the Roman Empire</term> were made as public necessity or utility demanded. But later they began to be annual. In another way, however, it is taken for that space of time which consisted of three **lustra** <term>Lustrum: a five-year period</term>, that is, three five-year periods, which is the same as in the law *Likewise it is asked* in the section *Who, having completed* in the Digest regarding *Leasing*. By this cycle, these kinds of Indictions or duties were exacted. And the *Speculator* <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a famous jurist known by the title of his work, the "Speculum Iudiciale"</note> says in Section 2, Column 2, at the verse *After the years*, regarding the *Editing of Instruments*, that this was introduced in the time of the Romans. In the first lustrum or five-year period, iron was paid for manufacturing weapons for the soldiers. In the second, silver for the stipendiary soldiers. In the third, gold was assigned to the treasury for the preservation of the Republic, and according to some, for the setting up of statues. When these lustra were finished, the **Indiction** was finished, and it began anew. Bertazolli, *On the Clauses of Instruments, Glossary 4*. From that Indiction, it was thus introduced that Notaries place the year of the indiction itself in legal **Instruments** <note>In this context, an "Instrument" refers to any formal legal document or contract</note>, or the Indiction itself denoting the year, such as *In the fifth Indiction*, meaning the fifth year of the Indiction. This can always be found by dividing the years of the Lord by the number fifteen and adding three, because the third Indiction was occurring at the time of Christ’s Nativity; and thus the Indiction is obtained. This is easily recognized from these verses placed by the *Speculator* in the place mentioned above, when he says:

> If you divide the years of the Lord by fifteen,
> Adding these three, the certain Indiction is marked.

The *Gloss on the chapter "Among the beloved," regarding the validity of Instruments* adds another, namely:

> If nothing remains, it will be the fifteenth Indiction.

If the Indiction has been placed erroneously or corruptly by the Notary, what is the law? And is there a custom everywhere that it must be included? See Bertazolli in the cited place, Glossary 4, Clause 1, throughout.

For it is otherwise certain, unless custom has received it differently, that the omission of the Indiction vitiates (invalidates) the Instrument. This is supported by the *Authentica* <note>A collection of Justinian's Novels</note> and various chapters in the Decretals regarding the validity of Instruments. Natta in *Counsel 47*, and Ruinus in *Counsel 23*, say that the Instrument is invalidated even if the Notary left a space for the indiction to be added later, or when the Notary wrote "In the Indiction" and yet could not supply the number. Ruinus says the Instrument is void even if the Indiction could be figured out from the years already placed on the document, for the reason that the indiction is required for **substance** <note>In legal terms, a "substantial" requirement is one that is essential to the document's legal existence, not just a clerical detail</note>. Josephus Ludovicus says this is the common opinion in *Decision 13*, which

<column-break/>

Covarruvias follows as the more common view in *Various Resolutions, Book 2, Chapter 12*, where he treats this matter more fully. Natta says that a Prince, by his ordinary power, cannot fix the defect of a missing Indiction; unless, however, custom (see Bertazolli) would make those Instruments valid without the placement of the Indiction. Felinus says the same in his commentary on the chapter *Among the beloved*. Similarly, if there is a doubt regarding an error in the Years of the Lord and the Indiction, the error is to be presumed in the Indiction rather than in the Years of the Lord, according to Covarruvias, Decius, and Cagnolus.

***

However, the opinion regarding the invention of the Indiction devised by the "reformer of time" (Joseph Scaliger, *On the Emendation of Time, Book 5*) is not approved by Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a Cardinal and ecclesiastical historian</note> for the *Year of Christ 312*. Scaliger says that from the exhibition of the five-year gifts of Constantine's Empire until his twenty-year jubilee, a period of fifteen years was established, and thus the number of Indictions was invented. But since Scaliger relies on a false foundation—thinking that Constantine's five-year festival was celebrated in this year, when we have already seen he had begun the seventh year of his Empire when he defeated Maxentius—the entire structure built upon it must likewise collapse. And would that it were as easy for those men to establish true things as it is to destroy false ones. We shall add, however, what we have sometimes happened to conjecture.

***

Therefore, having first exploded those theories which are brought forward by certain more recent writers regarding the beginning of Indictions as far back as the times of Augustus without any testimony (for why—to keep silent about other reasons—does Censorinus, an excellent author who wrote long before these times and treats exactly all the ancient systems of counting years then in use, make no mention at all of Indictions?), we also agree that they were not invented for the purpose of marking the number of years before the year 312. This is partly because no mention of them is held among outsiders before the time of Constantine, and the first mention in Ecclesiastical monuments is found in the Council of Rome under Pope Julius (who succeeded Sylvester) and in Saint Ambrose's *Letter to the Bishops of the Province of Emilia*. It is also because it is made clear from the Greek records that the "Constantinian Indictions" began to be counted under the consuls of the said year.

***

But for what cause it came into use that a fifteen-year number of this kind was invented for counting years under the name of an Indiction remains a matter to be especially investigated. Truly, that something might be begun and finished in a period of fifteen years and recorded in the public tablets, no other reason could be found among the ancient memories of this time except for the **stipend**... <note>The text cuts off here, likely referring to military pay cycles</note>

## ADDITION.

I should think that the name of **Angerona** <term>Angerona: A Roman goddess often depicted with her finger to her lips, symbolizing the secret name of Rome that was forbidden to be spoken</term> would sooner be revealed than the secret name of Rome. Master Rupert, in *Letters of Mercury*, page 157. Angerona is not the goddess of every kind of silence, as is commonly thought, but of that silence by which religious law commanded the second name of Rome to be kept quiet and hidden; for this very reason Angerona was made a Goddess, depicted with her mouth bound and sealed. See the most beautiful and accurate discourse on this matter by the famous Salmasius in his notes on Solinus, chapter 1; Master Rupert, in the cited place, page 158 at the end. The Christians had their own **subterranean cities**, so to speak, in which they lay hidden during times of persecution. ### 74. **The Roman Imperial Office, The Roman Empire. The Emperor of the Romans.**

Regarding the Roman Empire, and whether it is even now rightly called "Roman," see Francesco Zoanetti’s *singular treatise*. Marta in his *Treatise on Jurisdiction, throughout*. The Strasbourg Disputations of Lehmann. Arumaeus *On the Diets, throughout*. Rumelin *On the Golden Bull, page 1, dissertation 1, question 5, and in the annotations there*. Speidel. Wurmser in *Exercises in Public Law, 1, conclusion 10*. Limnaeus *On Public Law, volume 1, book 1, chapter 4*, where it is affirmed against

<column-break/>

Bodin, who should have known from the prophecy of Daniel that out of the four Monarchies, the last—that of the Romans—would endure until the end of the world. <note>Jean Bodin was a French political philosopher; the author is refuting his skepticism about the Holy Roman Empire's legitimacy</note> If this Empire is not with the Germans, it will be nowhere; for there is no Prince in the whole world who writes that he presides over it, except for the Romano-German Emperor. Therefore, the Monarchy of the Romans still flourishes in the German Nation. (The Druids used to sing that the possession of human affairs was portended for this nation when the Capitol was destroyed by a fortuitous fire under Vespasian, as Tacitus says in *Histories, book 4*). Hence, in the Recesses of the Empire, in Privileges, and other public Acts, the phrase **The Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation** is very often found written.

People from Mantua, Parma, Britain, Dijon, Lithuania, Hungary, and Poland were counted as being within the Empire in the year 1471 at the Diet of Ratisbon under Frederick III. There it is also mentioned that Emperor Sigismund, who was elected in 1411, had four Vicars: namely of Austria, Milan, Savoy, and Burgundy, etc.

The same Guyon, in the *cited chapter, folio 263*, attributes the fact that the Roman Empire has lost so much primarily to the Emperors of the Otto dynasty. He says that since the arrival of the Emperors named Otto, elected by the Germans, they managed the domains of the Empire so poorly that almost nothing remained to this Empire except the name alone. Thus, many would have great doubt in calling the designated person "King of the Romans." Furthermore, the Emperor of the Romans possesses nothing in Rome, and very little elsewhere. Following this, a Frenchman made a joke about certain initial letters signifying the ancient titles of the Romans, which were **S.P.Q.R.** <note>Senatus Populusque Romanus: The Senate and People of Rome</note> He said they signified **"So little as nothing,"** <note>original: "Si peu que Rien"</note> whereas they actually signify "The Senate and the People of Rome," etc.

## 76. Rosicrucians.

Injustice, a lack of charity, wickedness, usury, and similar vices have taken deep root in the souls of the men of our century; this was revealed by the corruption of the coinage <note>This refers to the "Kipper und Wipper" period, a hyperinflationary crisis in the Holy Roman Empire during the start of the Thirty Years' War.</note> which had invaded Germany in the years immediately preceding, driving even those who seemed at least civilly honest to most unjust and plainly dishonest bargains and demands. But the vanity and monstrous opinions lurking in the innermost minds of men were openly shown by the figment of the <term>Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross</term> <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret society of mystics whose manifestos published in the early 1600s caused a massive sensation and controversy across Europe.</note>: whether this group is more horrific or ridiculous leaves those judging truly uncertain. And yet there were infinite numbers who did not notice the trickery (I would hardly dare call it a joke); countless people who nourished their vain hopes upon it; and not a few who voluntarily defended these inanities in writing, offering their faith and labor to these Utopian Brothers. All of which provides evident proof of how easy it is to propagate even monstrous heresies, and that Germany—indeed, Europe—is pregnant with many dogmas contrary to good laws and truly anti-Christian. See Gaffendus <note>Pierre Gassendi, a French scientist and philosopher.</note> against <term>Fludd</term> <note>Robert Fludd, a prominent English physician and mystical philosopher who defended the Rosicrucians.</note> throughout, and especially page 249 and following.

Certainly, our German troubles could not have grown so easily if Fanaticism had not existed, along with some sort of opinion regarding a new <term>Schlaurafico</term> <note>original: "Schlaurafico" - a reference to *Schlaraffenland*, the mythical land of Cockaigne or "Lazybones Land." Here used sarcastically to describe a utopian or delusional political order.</note> Empire, which some imagined for themselves, believing with applause that the Swedish King <note>Likely referring to Gustavus Adolphus, who was seen by many Protestants as a messianic figure.</note> would be its leader.

### 78. **Horse Trade.** <note>Latin: *Venditio equi*</note>

The seller of a horse may be sued under the "redhibitory action" <note>An action to rescind a sale due to hidden defects</note> for all internal and non-apparent defects of the horse. Specifically, this applies if the horse is a kicker <note>Latin: *calcitrosus*</note>. *Law: bovem 43. verse: unde quidam. regarding the edict of the aediles.* Likewise, if it is "moon-sick" <note>periodic blindness</note> or frenzied, commonly called **staggers** <note>German: *Kollerend*</note>. *Law 1. §. according to Vivianus. 9. at the end.* Likewise, if it is so fearful or **skittish** <note>German: *scheu*</note> that it disturbs itself and breaks away. *In the aforementioned law: bovem.* Likewise, if it cannot be "cross-hitched" <note>harnessed to work with another horse</note>. *Law: aediles 38. §. it was asked. 8. frequently in the same law.* According to Speckhan, to "cross-hitch" <note>Latin: *transjungere*</note> *is to change the positions of the yoke-mates, to change the place in a four-horse team, to make a horse a wheeler <note>the horse closest to the wagon</note> that was accustomed to leading, or to make it the right-hand horse when it used to be the left, or vice-versa.* Likewise, if it is "retrograde," meaning it stubbornly backs up or **jibs** <note>German: *stettig*</note>. *Specul. title: on rescinding a sale. §. now it must be said. number 2.*

And finally, if it has "over-bones" <note>bony growths or splints</note> or galls <note>soft swellings</note>. *Specul. as cited above; Speckhan, in the cited question.* Where he says that, according to Saxon law, a horse seller is held liable for only three defects: (1.) that it is not retrograde, **that it is not stubborn**, (2.) that it does not suffer from hidden or invisible blindness: **that it is not cataract-blind**, and (3.) that it is not mangy, **that it is not broken-winded** <note>German: *haarschlechtig*; usually refers to respiratory issues or heaves</note>. *Coler. on procedures, part 2. chapter 1. number 71. and following.*

But this varies according to local custom, **and in some places there are certain and only four specific defects, among which blindness is not even counted.**

## 81. Ruckbürge. A subsequent guarantor of indemnity. <note>original: "Fidejussor succedaneus indemnitatis"</note>

A subsequent or "surrogated" guarantor is so called when the first guarantor provides another guarantor for himself, whom we commonly call a **Ruckbürgen** <note>a "back-guarantor" or sub-surety</note>, following the logic of the law *si plures* §. *plane pen.* in the Digest *on the administration of tutelage* and the law *quicunque 3* in the Code *on private estates*. This arises perhaps because, not having sufficient trust in the first guarantor, we choose another subsequent one who not only supports the credit of the first, as it were, but to whom we may also have recourse if the first should happen to be reduced to poverty. See especially Hering on *Guarantors* chapter 4, number 48 and many following.

And although some, especially Schneidewin in his commentary on the Institutes *on guarantors*, and Gail in *Observations* 2, observation 27, number 13, make no distinction between a guarantor of indemnity (of whom we speak below under the word **Schadlosbürgen**) and a subsequent guarantor, but take them for one and the same; nevertheless, it is clearly evident that these two differ from each other. This is because not every guarantor of a guarantor (or subsequent guarantor) is a guarantor of indemnity: since the former can be bound for the full amount <note>original: "in solidum"</note> even from the beginning;

<column-break/>

whereas the latter is held only for as much as the creditor is unable to obtain from the debtor. See Speckhan, century 3, question 32, class 1. But see Forner and Goeddæus on the law *si ita stipulatus 150* in the Digest *on the significance of words*. Hering on *Guarantors* chapter 4, number 62. In the meantime, however, it is not denied that even for the first guarantor, another guarantor can intervene who promises not the full amount, but only the indemnity <note>the loss protection</note>. Speckhan, in the same place, folio 374, number 6, at the end.

### ADDITION.

See *Schadburg*. Bartolus on law 1, number 2, in the Code *on convening the debtors of the treasury*, book 10. Suarez in *Thesaurus of Received Opinions*, number 138.

## 82. Ruffen. Proclamation. <note>original: "Proclama"</note>

The **Ruffen** <note>literally "The Calling"</note> is recognized and requested in the regional courts and other places when a matter concerns absent persons or minors, to see if anyone wishes to take up their cause, etc.

### ADDITION.

See Mr. Speid. in *Notes* number 142, letter R. Whoever "calls" for money when one is about to march against the enemy shall die. *Dutch Military Law* page 96. Regarding "Calling," see the *Nuremberg Statutes* book 1, 2, which "Calling" has fallen into disuse. **Bittruffen** means a proclamation regarding contempt of court <note>original: "in contumaciam"</note>. Schwanmann, book 1, *Processes*, chapter 72, number 39; book 2, chapter 3, number 31. The "Calling" was recognized, and fearing that further proceedings might be taken against them for contempt, I am, in case I should involve myself, expectant of the "Calling-Guilder" <note>a fee associated with this legal summons</note>. *Acts of the Teutonic Knights*, folio 189. Virgil in the *Bucolics*, Eclogue 3:

> "And when I was crying out: where is he rushing off to now?"

**Hungericht** <note>possibly a "Howling Court" or "High Court"</note> was an old criminal court in Franconia, the execution of which was perhaps carried out upon the pronunciation of the little word **Huy**; it was used in at least two places, one of them at Zeylißheim, which is today possessed by Lord Johann Wolff von Wolffsthal, Captain of the Steigerwald Knightly Order.

## 83. Ruge, Ruggericht, Ruggrav.
### Censure, Law-Count. <note>original: "Censura, Ruggravius"</note>

To **Rügen** <note>to rebuke or report</note> meant as much among the old Germans as to act, to accuse, to condemn—in a single word, to judge, to reveal, to report, to bring forward and display; also, after hearing both sides and diligent investigation, to settle and judge. # Enlarged Treasury of Practical Knowledge

<column-break/>

**Fiscal matters and fines** <note>original: "Fiscalische Sachen und Büssen"</note>, accused and brought forward in the seasonal courts, so that they may be condemned to the penalties established by the Laws. Master Gryphiander in his treatise *On Saxon Municipal Laws* <note>original: "de Weichbildis Saxon."</note> chapter 71, number 7 and following.

Among the Saxons, the **Magistrate** <note>original: "Scultetus," often a village mayor or sheriff</note> is bound to report a crime involving corporal punishment to the hereditary judge of the territory—to whom the **Hereditary Court** <note>original: "Erbgericht"</note> belongs—where the crime was committed. See the *Saxon Hall Mirror* <note>original: "Landrecht," specifically the Sachsenspiegel</note> book 3, article 19. They call that denunciation, as we also do in the common tongue, **The Reporting** <note>original: "das Rügen"</note>. In certain places, certain people from the common folk are deputized to report any crimes, even the smallest ones; these are called **Masters of the Report** <note>original: "Rügemeister"</note>. When, however, someone is bound by their office to report a crime—as is the custom among many peoples—and allows themselves to be corrupted by money so that they do not report the crimes, they are said to commit **Simony** <note>In this legal context, Simony refers to the corrupt "selling" of legal silence or justice, a term usually reserved for the sale of church offices</note> in the chapter *Nemo*, in the section *on Simony*. See also Lucas de Penna. Regarding whether a delinquent official ought to report themselves, Menochius affirms this in *On Arbitrary Judicial Decisions*. And see the *Württemberg State Ordinance*, where the **Court of Censure** <note>original: "Ruggericht"</note> is treated at length. Add also my own work, the treatise *On Censure*.

But what should be said of a defendant of a crime who gives himself up? Should he be absolved of the crime? Rebuffus denies this, as does Bayard and Bartolus, where the latter adds a **History of a certain Servant** who, on the Sabbath day, reported that he—along with other accomplices—had killed a Jew together with his children. He did this relying on the hope that he would obtain the reward of five hundred gold coins <note>original: "aureorum"</note> that had been established for an informant; but he was deceived, and instead of a reward, he received the noose.

However, it seems to be established otherwise in **Civil Law** <note>referring to Roman Law</note>, especially since it is in the interest of the State that crimes do not remain hidden. Bodin, in *The Republic*, recounts a contrary example concerning **Augustus Caesar**, who made a public pledge to give ten hundred thousand sesterces <note>original: "decies sestertium"</note> to whoever would bring **Coracota**, the leader of the bandits in Spain, alive to him. Coracota, having learned of this, presented himself voluntarily to Augustus Caesar, asserting that he himself was the leader of the bandits, and therefore petitioned Caesar to pay him the promised reward. Caesar, lest he be said to have broken the public trust and security, ordered that money established for the informant to be paid to him, and dismissed Coracota unpunished.

Is any subject bound to report a crime committed in their own house? See Modestinus Pistor.

Whether one who knows a crime is about to be committed

<column-break/>

is bound to reveal it in the external court <note>the secular court</note> and the internal court <note>the court of conscience or the church</note>, see the questions of Flores Diez.

The so-called **Judicial Denunciation** is to be compared to the **Court of Censure** <note>original: "Ruggericht"</note>. See the *Practice* of Octavianus Spatharius, where the person reporting does not take upon themselves the burden of proof.

Regarding the office of the **Censor**, see Meillet in his *Discourses on Tacitus*. On the burden and obligation of reporting, see Bonacina. Is it permissible to pretend to be a heretic so that heretics may be caught, and should their testimony be believed? See Molina.

But concerning **informants** <note>original: "delatoribus"</note>, their rewards, and when they deserve to be excused for a failed report, see Menochius and extensively Albericus Gentilis.

<meta>This page continues the legal encyclopedia's discussion on judicial administration and penalties, following the previous page's focus on the reporting of crimes. Lit. R.

**Fines.** In Strasbourg, there is the Censors' Court, commonly known as the **Court of the Seven Censors** <note>original: "Siebenzüchten-Gericht"; this was a morals court in Strasbourg consisting of seven members who handled minor offenses and disputes</note>, where matters concerning private injuries, brawls, quarrels, and similar things are handled. See the works of Master Bernegger regarding the *State of the Republic of Strasbourg* written in 1627. Regarding the **Police or Disciplinary Court** <note>original: "Policey- oder Zucht-Gericht"</note> in that same place, and how it is staffed by all the administrative rooms, see Master Joachim Strollius's *On the Governance of the Republic of Strasbourg*. Regarding the **court of fines** <note>original: "περὶ ζημιώσεων" (peri zēmiōseōn)</note> and concerning penalties and punishments, specifically if a Magistrate has imposed a heavier penalty on a Citizen, see Master Felvinger’s *The Judge*, page 388 and following.

**Fines are the fruits of jurisdiction.** <note>original: "Mulctæ Jurisdictionis fructus sunt"</note> Carpzov, part 3, *Criminal Practice*, question 109, number 41; Wesenbeck, number 6, *On the manner of fines*. Master Rebhan, *On Fines*, thesis 30. A fine is hindered by **prescription** <note>the statute of limitations</note>, so that a fine can no longer be demanded. Bocer, *On Regalities*, chapter 3, number 4. I do not wish this to be understood as applying to a fine already imposed and declared, for that is not prescribed even by a long passage of time (chapter *cum sec.* under the Laws on Heretics in the 6th book of Decretals), but only to a fine that has been threatened but not yet actually imposed. For those that still require a declaration, the legal experts at law 1 of the Digest *If someone does not obey the judge* teach that they are prescribed and extinguished within a period of one year, so that they can no longer be declared, even if some command was perhaps given—for instance, under a penalty of 20 gold coins—which command was not obeyed. Rebuffus at law 131, section 1, *On the Meaning of Words*.

However, Wehner says that in most places this is poorly observed by officials. **They only demand the fine for this or that transgression from the subjects after 3 or 4 years.** Master Rebhan, in the same place, thesis 35. Certain neighboring Nobles did something similar recently; because they share the fines, **they only demanded an appearance for a past offense after 8 years, and set a general "Punishment Day" throughout the whole High Jurisdiction** <note>original: "Fraisch"; this refers to a territory's high criminal jurisdiction where blood justice could be administered</note>. To them it was responded: such appearances had not been traditional for ages, as they are among the people in Franconia, and furthermore the offender was not caught or seized in the act.

### 84. **Flogging with Rods.** <note>original: "Ruten-Aushauung"; Latin: "Virgis Castigatio"</note>

It is sometimes customary, according to the nature of the crime committed, for the defendant to be publicly punished with rods by the Executioner; **he is flogged with rods.** This punishment with rods is ascribed to **High Jurisdiction** <note>original: "mero Imperio"; literally "mere empire," the power of the sword or the right to inflict corporal and capital punishment</note>. *Jacobus de Sancto Georgio on Fiefs; Gylman, volume 2, part 3, title 10.*

And it undoubtedly descends from **scourging** <note>original: "flagellatio"</note>, that punishment for slaves, which differed from **flogging** <note>original: "fustigatio"</note> and punishment with rods. See Barnabé Brisson, *Selected Antiquities*, book 3, chapter 9; Marcello Donato in his clarifications on Livy, folio 45. Regarding the scourging of the Jews, see Dilherr, *Selections*, chapter 18, and Baronius, Year of Christ 34, number 83.

The punishment of flogging is great and **infamous** <note>legally, "infamy" meant a person lost their civil rights, honor, and ability to testify or join a guild</note> when it is imposed for a shameful cause, law *ictus fustium* of the Digest *On those who are marked with infamy*. From which it is clear that this punishment, being infamous

<column-break/>

and usually rendering the flogged person infamous, should not be imposed except upon **base persons, and not at all upon nobles.** *Canon law, 26, question 5; the Roman Singul. 667; Ludovicus, decision 1, number 23.*

That this punishment is severe is known from this: if someone has been condemned to flogging, or to be publicly shamed by the **Miter** <note>a paper hat worn by criminals as a sign of public humiliation</note>, a legal representative <note>Procurator</note> is not admitted for him unless he has been placed in prison—just as is the case for one condemned to the punishment of banishment. According to the more common opinion, a representative is admitted for the latter; see Menochius in his treatise *On Judicial Arbitrariness*, book 1, question 80, number 41. There he says that **this punishment, because it brings infamy, is equated to death.** See him, and on the severity of this punishment, see Josephus Ludovicus. Regarding banishment to the workhouses or the **Argonautic chains** <note>original: "vincula argonautica"; a poetic reference to the galleys or rowing benches</note>, see Damhouder in *Criminal Practice*, chapter 51. And as Lindenbrog testifies regarding the Code title *If anyone should speak ill of the Emperor*, in the past, lashes were given at the whim of the executioner.

That henceforth in the Duchy of Württemberg the **punishment of flogging is abolished**, and the delinquents are instead **to be kept at public construction and labor**; (which I myself long ago considered advisable in my treatise *On Punishments and the Treasury*) and see also P. Contzen in the *History of the Abyssinians*, folio 212. This can be understood from the following Princely Order. Add Oldekop's two treatises against Carpzov, folio 237.

### By the Grace of God, Johann Friederich, Duke of Württemberg, etc.

Our greetings first, Dear Faithful Subjects,
We are in every way intended to allow **the course of dear Justice in Our Duchy and Lands to run straight**, and indeed, in the face of increasing vices, to sharpen the punishments (as a greater earnestness against the delinquent and a loathsome example to others). However, We have several times considered whether, in those cases and crimes that do not carry the ultimate penalty of death, but where the **malefactors** <note>criminals</note> have hitherto been sentenced by judgment and law to the hand of the Executioner for **flogging with rods, the cutting off of ears, or the like**, other punishments might be found in place of such corporal penalties. Through these, Justice would still be satisfied, and the criminals would nonetheless do penance according to their guilt. 

This is in consideration that **once the Executioner has laid a hand upon a sinner and delinquent, there is no means left for him to nourish himself and his family honestly among the craftsmen**, since such a person is shunned and driven out in all places. He is thereby almost forced to return to thievery and—
