<meta>This page continues the discussion on judicial sentencing and punishment from the previous page, transitioning from the collection of fines to the philosophy of rehabilitation. It specifically outlines a decree from Stuttgart in 1627 regarding the use of forced labor as an alternative to "infamous" corporal punishment for certain classes of offenders.</meta>

...eventually he must even face the noose. 
On the other hand, when other punishments are used—those not carried out by the **executioner’s** <term>executioner (Nachrichter): in this period, any contact with the executioner brought "infamy," a legal status that stripped a person of their honor and prevented them from practicing most trades</term> hand—the criminals do not fall into temporary shame alongside the loss of all honor. Rather, if such a person is still tolerated among **honest folk** <note>original: "Biederleuten"; refers to citizens of good standing and integrity</note>, then there might still be hope that such a sinner might reform himself and once again take up an honest trade or craft to support himself and his family with honor.

For these reasons, and in view of certain particularly moving circumstances (as it has sometimes reached us that the wise judge himself would often gladly see and wish for such a punishment, whereby the sinner might duly atone for his wrongdoing, and yet—especially when there is still hope for reform in him, or if he has never before been inclined toward evil deeds—escape the hand of the executioner), he might also be spared from temporary shame and the irreparable loss of his honor (as happens with **public flogging** <note>original: "Ruhten-Ausstreichen"; literally "stroking out with rods"</note> and the **clipping of ears**).

Furthermore, because excessive crimes frequently occur (especially among **poachers** <note>original: "Wildbret-Schützen"</note> and others who take to idling and seek their sustenance through forbidden means), which until now have not been viewed as capital crimes under the **criminal codes** <note>original: "peinlichen Rechten"; referring to the "Constitutio Criminalis Carolina" or similar high-court laws</note> but were perhaps punished with long-term imprisonment as an example to others. However, in such cases—if the criminal was unable to pay for his own **provisions** <note>original: "Atzung"; the cost of food and board in prison</note>—We often incurred great and useless expenses. Additionally, during the time of such **imprisonment in the tower** <note>original: "Thurn-Straff"</note>, the wife and children at home suffered want. Meanwhile, the criminal himself (especially if he schemed with the city guards so that wine was let into the prisons) did not regard the tower as a punishment, but rather as a rest from the labor for which man was otherwise created. Thus, the criminals themselves were little reformed, others were not moved to follow their example or feel dread, and even less was the public helped by this. Beyond this, We have also found what great inconveniences have been brought upon Us, as well as the communities, the **poor-boxes** <note>original: "Armen-Kästen"; local charitable funds</note>, and private persons, by bold vagabonds and healthy beggars, masterless wandering servants, and similar folk. Therefore, We have cause to consider means by which these may be abolished, such servants brought to correction, kept to labor, and the land cleansed of such people. In consideration of all this, and so that misdeeds which do not carry the ultimate penalty of death may nonetheless be viewed with sharp earnestness, those

<column-break/>

who still offer a hope for reform should not be made entirely dishonorable, but after due atonement, may afterward be tolerated again among honest folk. Likewise, those who are only made soft and lazy by long-term imprisonment should be compelled to spend their time in industriousness, and the wandering, useless folk should be kept to labor. Thus, we are intent on establishing a means of earnest punishment for the correction of such punishable fellows (among whom we also mean to include **profligates** <note>original: "Prodigos"; those who waste their inheritance or wealth recklessly</note> and spendthrifts for whom all previous warnings were ineffective, as well as disobedient, naughty children for whom their parents' discipline does nothing and for whom no improvement is hoped). This method has been practiced with benefit until now in many well-ordered lands, cities, and lordships, and through it, many a wayward person has been brought back to usefulness: namely, that they be held **to public works** <note>original: "ad operas publicas"</note>. Therein, they shall work in **shackles** <note>original: "Springern"; a type of leg iron that allowed for movement but prevented escape</note> and iron bonds for as long as it takes to fully atone for their crime according to its nature, as well as for their food and whatever else was spent on their account.

Now, so that this may be put into effect in matters to be decided through ordinary criminal law, we leave it to you, the judges, in those cases and offenses where life is not forfeited, to consider in your judgment whether the delinquents—according to the nature of their crime, age, and previous conduct—should be condemned **to public works** <note>original: "ad operas publicas"</note> for a period of time after paying for their food (if they are able to reimburse it). In such cases, you (the Official) shall send the judgment to our Chancery before publication, and you shall also await a decision as to which building they should be assigned and how they should be escorted there.

Concerning those criminals such as poachers, **profligates**, and others mentioned above, who are not legally sued but against whom We may proceed **by virtue of office** <note>original: "ex officio"; a legal proceeding initiated by the court itself rather than a private accuser</note>: you, the Official, after a preliminary inquiry and their arrest, and after a sufficient hearing of their crime, shall report the matter with all relevant circumstances to our Chancery—including their age, physical strength, and the nature of their previous conduct, their title, and their assets—and await further orders. This is Our intended meaning. Given in Stuttgart, the 12th of September, in the year 1627.

Letter R.

Doctor Tabor on the Crime of Fraud <term>Stellionate (Stellionatus): a Roman law term for a variety of fraudulent acts, such as selling the same piece of property to two different people</term> page 34 & 44. And on the same page it is called: The Flogging-Broom <note>original: "Saupbesen"</note>. See Master Speidel in the Notable Remarks on the letter R, number 144, on beating at the pillory <note>original: "zu Steupen schlagen"</note>, Carpzov in the treatise on crimes, part 2, question 56, number 41; and in the same part 2, question 53, on remitting the punishment of the pillory <note>original: "den Staupenschlag einem erlassen"</note> to someone. Part 3, question 150, number 75. Regarding those who are to be restrained by rods, see Bocer on Jurisdiction, chapter 5, number 37 at the end. Under the Law of Justinian, a distinction is made between beating with a club <note>original: "fustigatio"</note>, flogging with a whip <note>original: "flagellatio"</note>, and the beating with chains, number 38, where by "chains" he understands rods.

Beating with a club, devised by Tarquin, is done either with whips or with rods, as discussed extensively by Schönborn in his *Politics*, page 299 and following. Freeborn men <note>original: "ingenui"</note> were not beaten with whips, according to Rupert, book 1, chapter 1, difference 2, section 10, regarding Valerius Maximus; also Philipp Carolus in his *Taste of Philosophy*, Dialogue 3.

Nobles are not to be beaten with whips or clubs; one shall not beat them at the pillory <note>original: "man soll sie nicht zur Staupen schlagen"</note>. Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 4, number 66.

### 85. Acquisitions and Gains. <note>original: "Nungen und gewonnen. Acquisita."</note>

Under this category, that which someone receives from a Father or from paternal goods during the marriage is not properly included—not indeed by title of inheritance, but by gift, yet in contemplation of a future inheritance. This is because such things possess the likeness of an inheritance and perform its role, or are of the same right, condition, and nature, according to the express text in the Law *if not by death* in the Digest on inofficious testaments. For things that were otherwise destined to come to a person through succession are not held to be "acquired property," as noted by Johannes Faber in the preface to the *Institutes*, number 7. From this, Boër infers in the *Customs of Bourges* in the title concerning marriage customs, section 2, column 2, that a gift made by a parent to one of the spouses (to whom the recipient was otherwise the heir of the donated thing) is not considered an acquisition <note>original: "conquæstus"</note>, and therefore the other spouse shall have no part in it. Johannes Saisfon teaches the same in the *Customs of Tours*, title 22, article 1, on the phrase "community of goods," as does Chassanée in the *Customs of Burgundy*, rubric 4, section 2, on the word "acquisitions," numbers 4 and 5. Nicolaus Valla in *Doubtful Matters*, treatise 13, number 2, says that what is donated during the marriage enters the community of property, with the exception of parents in the direct line, such as from a father or mother.

The rule is that neither in dowry agreements nor in any Statute where it is arranged that "goods acquired during the marriage are to be shared between the Spouses" are those things included which were acquired solely by the effort and industry of one or the other, rather than both. Johannes Lopez on the Gains of a Husband, chapter 5, number 8; Segura on the Gains of a Husband, number 158; Sanz Morquecho on the Division of Goods, book 2, chapter 11, number 15; Ancharano, Counsel 102, number 3; Nicolaus Everhard, Counsel 135; Gail, book 2, observation 78, last number; Wesenbeck on the Digest regarding the Rites of Marriage, number 6; Peck on the Testaments of Spouses, book 2, chapter 2, number 1.

The opinion of these authors is confirmed by the common nature of a partnership <note>original: "societatis"</note> that has been simply entered into, in which only those things are shared which come 

<margin>Besold, Volume I.</margin>

<column-break/>

from profit and trade <note>original: "ex lucro & quæstu"</note>, not those which arrive from elsewhere, according to the law *to be entered into* <note>original: "l. coiri"</note> 7 and following in the Digest on Partnerships. Hence, even those things which are acquired through a gift between living persons <note>original: "donationem inter vivos"</note> or by some other lucrative title, the legal doctors commonly deny belong to the marital acquisitions in the place cited above, as do Sanz Morquecho in the said book 2, chapter 15, number 18 and following; Garcia on Marital Acquisitions, number 101 and many following, especially number 114; Friedrich Solis on property acquired during marriage, question 9, numbers 9, 10, and 19 at the end.

But others disagree and say that things acquired by any means are shared, even gifts and inheritances. They argue that the words "to gain" <note>original: "gewinnen"</note>, "to acquire," or "to profit" are general terms and signify any increase of the estate, whether it comes from a lucrative cause or a burdensome one <term>Burdensome cause (onerosus): a legal transaction where something is given in exchange for something else, like a purchase, as opposed to a gift</term>. For "to acquire" is the same as "to profit," in the chapter *from the transmitted* concerning tithes. Indeed, who can be said to profit more than one who obtains a thing by a lucrative title? See Rosacorba in *Forensic Practice*, chapter 71.

Nor is this new in such Statutes and customs: since sometimes even things acquired through inheritance are shared, as noted by Nicolaus Everhard, Counsel 135. And Chassanée, in his commentary on the *Customs of Burgundy*, rubric 4, section 2, on the word "acquisitions," number 4, teaches that under the name of "acquisitions" come: gifts between the living, legacies left by reason of death, and an inheritance bequeathed by the testament of a stranger (to whom we were not the heirs-at-law). These are considered acquired unless found to be specially excepted. Papon, *Arrests*, book 15, title 2, article 16; Nicolaus Valla on *Doubtful Matters*, treatise 13, number 2. In that place, Valla responds to the aforementioned law *to be entered into* 7 by stating that it applies to a conventional partnership—one entered into for the sake of profit. It is otherwise in a partnership introduced by municipal law and custom—namely, a community of all goods, movable and immovable, which have been sought out. This does not conform to Common Law, as noted by Covarrubias, volume 1, part 2, chapter 7, section 1, number 6; Garcia on Expenses, chapter 13, number 14; and on Marital Questions, number 31; Wesenbeck on Marriage Rites, number 6; Gail, observation 79, number 9. It differs from a conventional partnership in many ways, as noted by Sanz Morquecho in the said chapter 15. Therefore, its nature must be sought from the Statute, the custom, and the agreements of the contracting parties rather than from Common Law, as Garcia says in the cited place, number 32; and Johannes Lopez, chapter 6, numbers 1, 18, and 19, where he teaches that gains from any cause whatsoever and however acquired are to be shared. Nevertheless, it is established by the constant tradition of the doctors who wrote on marital acquisition that things acquired by gift, legacy, or other lucrative cause from parents and other kinsmen during the marriage—by a spouse who could have succeeded them as an heir-at-law—are held as hereditary and therefore not shareable. As taught by Papon, *Arrests* 16, and book 7, title 3, article 19; and Nicolaus Valla, treatise 13, number 2.

But concerning the acquisitions of spouses, see the singular treatises of Suarez, Lopez, Segura, and dispute 3.

### 96. Turnips. [Ruben]. *Rapa*.

Regarding giant **turnips**, see Zeiller’s *Italian Itinerary*, page 194. In the city of **Terni**, the great turnips are praised, and Pighius reports in *Hercules Prodicius* on page 275 that he saw turnips there, one of which weighed more than 30 pounds. Schrader writes in book 3 of *Monuments of Italy*, folio 266, of turnips over 40 pounds. Leander Albertus writes, in his *Description of Italy*, page 93, that a single donkey can hardly carry seven of them. Because of the size of these very heavy turnips, a starving person could well satisfy himself on a single one. And one might well say here that people eat in the city of Terni solely because of this magnificent fertility—just as that writer from Milan wrote the proverb that one eats in Milan alone because of the great quantity of edible goods. In the *Cologne Travel-Booklet*, page 203, it is stated that when several noblemen at Terni were dining at midday and asked the innkeeper to show them a turnip, he took it for a joke and a mockery, and gave them to understand that he knew nothing of these things. Therefore, the said innkeeper either did not understand the Germans, or did not concern himself much with turnips. It is thus nothing new that people in a place want to know nothing of a thing, even if they are right next to it; just as I recounted above regarding **Basel**, that no one there could show me the **Hebrew letters** carved in stone, or wanted to know anything about them, though I was at the very end of the street where they were, and I had to advise and help myself by searching around diligently.

Regarding the "Significance of the letters of the Hebrew Alphabet, exhibiting the order of all Nature, according to the mind of the Cabalists" <note>original: "De literarum Alphabeti Hebraici significatu, totius Naturæ ordinem exhibente, ex Cabalistarum mente"</note>, see Father Caspar Schott in *Curious Techniques or Wonders of Art*, book 12, chapter 17. ### 97. Rain, Droplets. *Regen, Trüppfen. Pluvia.*

In the year 1036, near **Naples**, there is **Mount Vesuvius**; there, it rained reddish ash across the entire region, so that everything was covered as if with snow. Megiser in *Delights of Naples*, page 79. Why Jupiter was called "The Rainer" <note>original: "Pluvius"</note>, see Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, pages 22, 23. Regarding portentous rains, see Zeiller, century 4, question 27, page 135, concerning **purple-colored rain** in Brussels. Speidel in *Notables*, folio 887. "By the exception of an unusual case, such as immoderate snow or rain" <note>original: "Exceptione casus insoliti, qualis esse potest immoderata nix, pluvia"</note>, Alexander, *Counsel* 108, book 3; Gomez, volume 2, *Resolutions*, chapter 3, number 3. "A buyer of grain which was still in the blade [unharvested] is protected, even if he took upon himself the accidental risk by a special pact" <note>original: "Emptor frumentorum, quæ adhuc in herbis erant, se tuetur, quamvis speciali pacto casum fortuitum in se receperit"</note>. Baldus, *Counsel* 247, at the end, book 3; Menochius, *Counsel* 27, number 2, book 1; Rauchbar, in book 90, question 29, number 19; Menochius, book 2, *On Judicial Arbitrage* 99, century 1, case 80, number 9.

**Egypt** is rainless. Schweigger in his *Travel Description*, chapter 12, page 257. Regarding **droplets**, see the *Nuremberg Statutes*, title 26, book 3, throughout. "It is not permitted to make water fall upon the roof of a neighbor by diverting one's eaves-drip, unless one has an easement [right of way]" <note>original: "Aquam non licet facere cadere super tecto vicini aliando suum stillicidium, nisi habeat servitutem"</note>. Cavalcanti, book 4, *On Delicts*, section on contractual questions, decision 8, number 76. In all of Egypt there are no rains, or they are very rare, one or two at most in a year, in the month of April or November, and those of only a few hours. Sometimes no rains moisten **Cairo** for several years; they are more frequent in **Alexandria**, yet these too are rare and meager. Lord Fürer in his *Travels*, page 18. Rains are rare on the journey to **Jerusalem**, page 100. There are several kinds of waters: for some spring forth from their own head with a perpetual flow and are called **spring water** or even **living water**, of which kind is also **well water** (Law 1, § 1, *on springs*); and "eaves-drip" <note>original: "opportunitillii"</note>, which falling from the sky is called **rain water**, which also includes **snow-melt** (the entire title *on rain water*); some are carried by a certain force and, being flowing, are called **river water** or a stream (§ and indeed 1, § streams 2, *Digest on the division of things*); some waters are called **stagnant** or standing, likewise **marsh waters**, which are contained in ponds, marshes, and lakes (Law 1, § 1, *as in public rivers*); some, by reason of their properties and qualities, are called **hot** or **cold**, of which Ulpian makes mention (Law 1, § "The same Labeo," *on daily water*).

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on agricultural matters and natural phenomena under the letter R. Lit. R.

...some are temporary, while others are perennial. <note>original: "perennes"</note> Law 1, paragraph 1, regarding public rivers. Law 1, paragraph 1, speaks of **daily water**; some is called **summer water**, which is especially useful to use in the summer, although we sometimes use it in the winter as well (Law 1, paragraph "summer," through the whole title on daily and summer water). Some is **daytime water**, and some is **nighttime water**, which is drawn during the night (Law "if so" 7, on how servitudes are lost). Finally, another type is commonly called **daily water** by the founders of the law: that which can be drawn continuously (Title on daily water). However, not all such water can be drawn by right of servitude; only that which is perennial, such as water drawn from a spring or a river (Law 1, paragraph 5, on daily water). For a water pipe cannot be granted from a lake that is not permanent, or from a pond (Law "opening" 28, on Urban Estates). But this servitude can also be established in such a way that it is permitted to search for water and to lead it once found (Law "Labeo" 16, on Rural Estates). The drawing of water is done through another's land; for water can only be led through public places with the permission of the Prince (Law "if in public" 18, paragraph 41 and following, on rainwater). Regarding the method of leading water: there are various ways to lead water, about which one should see **Vitruvius**, book 8 on architecture, chapter 7, and **Frontinus** in his book on the aqueducts of the city of Rome. The most common methods are considered to be through lead pipes, or clay pipes, or through masonry channels, or even through stone-paved conduits; however, the latter may only be used when it has been specifically agreed upon (Law "if first" paragraph 1, on rainwater). The reason is that this method is associated with greater damage to the land serving the water. On the error of astrologers regarding rain, see Zahn's *On Lies*, book 1, chapter 18, number 4.

Thus the legal experts of Jena ruled in the month of May, 1630, upon the consultation of **Hans Georg von Hochberg of Uhlfeld**. He had 20 stacks of grain <note>A "Schock" was a unit of measurement, usually sixty items</note> grown on your peasant estate at Bartschefeld during the various harvest times, which he wished to bring into the barn because bad rainy weather was feared at that time. Therefore, you asked your horse-farmers <note>original: "Pferdbauren," tenants who owed labor service with their horses</note> to bring it in for wages, noting the reason so that it might not be spoiled or ruined by the rainy weather. To this, the aforementioned teamsters, your subjects, answered that they were not minded to do so unless the "fifth wagon" also went along <note>This likely refers to a specific local custom or labor demand regarding the number of wagons used or the share of the load</note>. Therefore, you asked them once more—since at that time it was impossible to use the fifth wagon—that they should bring in the grain with 4 wagons for wages, and show this goodwill to you as their court and hereditary lord <note>original: "Gerichts- und Erbherrn"</note>, especially since they worked for other people for wages and the grain would mostly spoil without such help due to the rain. However, they persisted in their refusal, whereby the aforementioned 20 stacks of grain were almost entirely ruined by the ensuing rainy weather. Since they willfully 

<column-break/>

inflicted this damage upon you, which they could well have prevented, it is fair that the aforementioned suffered damage be replaced and restored by them according to the circumstances of the case. See also Johannes Philippi in *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*, Selection 31, book 1, title 3, paragraph 2, number 6.

### 98. Roe-catching Right. [Jus venandi Capreolos].

Regarding the **right to hunt roe deer**. <note>original: "De Jure venandi capreolos"</note> See Knipschild, *On the Rights and Privileges of Imperial Cities*, book 2, chapter 7, numbers 27, 28, 29. Mr. Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings*, page 568 and following. **Roe deer** are commonly counted as "high game" <note>original: "hohen Wild," game reserved for the higher nobility, like red deer</note>, according to Finckelthaus, observation 41. In Franconia, see Weizenegger on hunting, chapter 4, paragraph 26. In Bavaria, see the *Bavarian Constitution*, the Escort Ordinance, chapter 2, paragraph "what however," where it says: roe deer shall not be understood to be among the "red and black game" <note>Red game usually meant stags; black game meant wild boar</note>, etc. The catching of roe deer is usually reckoned as "low hunting" <note>original: "niedern Jagt," hunting rights often available to lower nobility or specific landowners</note>.

### 99. Ruprecht.

That is, "bright in peace" <note>original: *clarus quiete*</note>. *Berecht* means "notorious" or "well-known." **Ruprecht** is one who desires peace, helps toward peace, advises peace, and is with peace. Mr. Speidel in *Notables*, page 887.

### 100. Reymund. Reimundus.

From "Mouth of the Dance" <note>original: *Deß Reyen-Mund*</note>, one who leads the dances by singing. My teacher Mr. Speidel says otherwise in his *Mirror of Notables*, page 890, as if it were "Pure-Mouth" <note>original: *Reinesmundes*</note>.

### 101. Riedesel.

Bucelinus presents the genealogy of the **Knights Riedesel of Eisenbach** in *Knowledge of Germany*, page 256.

### 102. Councilor. [Rathherr]. Senator.

Whether it is expedient to commit several functions to one **Councilor** <note>original: *Senator*</note>, see Knipschild, *On Imperial Cities*, at book 5, chapter 1, number 27. Senatorial power does not liberate one from paternal power <note>The legal authority of a father over his household</note>. The same author, book 6, chapter 1, number 6. The term **Magistrate** <note>original: *Magistratus*</note> is used, beyond its abstract meaning which denotes the office itself, in a very broad concrete sense, so that it is attributed to every public person holding a more honorable office or sustaining some care of matters pertaining to the City—specifically in opposition to private citizens. Festus says: "Magistrates are those who, through their commands <note>original: *Imperia*</note>, are more powerful than private citizens." Cicero, in *On the Laws*, mentions that formerly all those who held the power of judgment and the taking of auspices were called "Magistrates." In this sense, even **Senators** are included. Mr. Tabor in *Ariadne's Thread*, regarding the Senate. Gothofredus in his notes on the same; though they are otherwise excluded from the strict definition. Frantzke, in his commentary on the Digest, "On Senators," number 5. 2. Technologically <note>In the sense of technical terminology</note>, and then again either properly and adequately, or too strictly. Properly, and among philosophers and legal experts, it refers only to that public person who possesses some command <note>original: *Imperium*</note> or at least their own jurisdiction. Hence Aristotle, in *Politics* book 4, chapter 15, defines a Magistrate as one who has the power of deliberating, judging, and commanding, but especially the power of commanding.

### 103. Rakos. Hungarian Assemblies.

In Hungary, the meeting of the Assemblies is called "Rakos" <note>original: "Ragkus"; referring to the Rákos field where the Hungarian Diet often met</note>. See the New Acts of the year 1542, paragraph **"we have also."** Limnaeus in "Public Law," book 9, chapter 1, number 8. In Poland, it is called "Rokosz" <note>original: "Rokoff"</note>; Limnaeus treats this word at length in "Public Law," volume 2, additions to book 9, chapter 1, number 9, page 349 at the end and 350 at the beginning. **In Dalmatia is the old, famous city of Ragusa <note>Modern-day Dubrovnik</note>, which stands for itself, yet is under the protection of the Turkish Emperor, as he possesses much in Dalmatia.** Zeiller in his "Itinerary of Hungary," published in 1646, folio 3.

### 104. Wealth. Riches.

In matters of wealth and the ownership of property, a present state is not presumed to have existed in the past. Klock, volume 2, counsel 7, numbers 209, 211; compare counsel 8, numbers 81–84. The dignity and splendor of families are preserved and propagated through wealth. Klock, volume 2, counsel 53, number 73. Anyone is presumed to grow richer day by day; compare counsel 7, number 210. Everyone is presumed to have been enriched by their own industry and fortune, counsel 70, number 67; though this is limited in numbers 68, 69, and 70. One who is only seemingly rich, a vain boaster of resources, is called by the Greeks by the most elegant term <term>Phantasioplax</term> <note>original: Φαντασιοπλὰξ; one who creates a phantom or illusion of wealth</note>, who only appears to be wealthy; Law 3, final paragraph, Digest on "Commodatum" <note>Loan for use</note>. C. Rittershuf, on Law 23 of the Digest regarding the Rules of Law, page 216. On who must prove that someone has become wealthier, see Schultes, "Practical Questions," 31, book 1. On what must be articulated when we wish to prove that someone has been enriched from our own property, see Schultes, book 1, question 32. In the examination of witnesses, a witness is always usually asked, among other things, about their wealth: **"How rich he is."** <note>original: "Wie reich er sey."</note> Or how much he holds in goods. Schneidewin on the Institutes, book 1, title 6, page 30, number 11. Regarding the Stoic art of growing rich, one should see Seneca, epistle 17, section 119. Who is rich and who is poor cannot be determined so simply, but must be left to the judgment of the judge, and thus must be judged according to the quality of the persons and the things

<column-break/>

involved. For a nobleman can be called poor even if he has a thousand in assets, whereas on the other hand, a peasant is considered rich if he possesses a hundred. Just as a "poor person" is not only someone who lacks the necessities to sustain life, but also one who cannot live according to the condition of their social status; so a "rich person" is one who can live according to the quality of their status in such a way that something always remains left over from their income. Sprenger, "On the Modicum," page 4, section 5, where many authorities are cited. He who calls someone rich or poor is bound to prove this assertion. Neapolitan Decisions 377; Villalobos, page 309; Soarez, D. 99; Didacus, book 2, resolution chapter 6, number 2, section number 7. K. century 6, conclusion 27. Menochius discusses the signs from which one is presumed rich or poor in book 3, presumption 59, and book 6, presumption 25; and how "opulent" and "wealthy" differ. Boerius, decision 145, number 4. In the year 1627 at Tübingen, Georg Hieronymus Marstaller solemnly and at length disputed "On Wealth" under Besold to obtain doctoral honors; he did so without a parade of authorities, but from mere citations of the laws, covering the qualities and favors of wealth, its hatreds, and the preservation of riches—a truly difficult thing today and the "art of arts." Schuppius contributes to this in his "Dissertation on the Art of Growing Rich," as does the "College of Political Disputations" of Felwinger on the <term>Chrematistike</term> <note>original: ΧΡΗΜΑΤΙΣΤΙΚΗ; the art of wealth-acquisition</note>. (He divided this into "Natural" and "Artificial." Artificial he further divided into that which is "pre-eminent," such as Trade, and that which is "closest to the natural," which Aristotle called "primary exchange.") And most recently, the treatise of Master Suefer, Counselor of Brandenburg, titled: **The Shortage of Money in Germany, 1664.** Bayreuth. **In this book, the author shows the causes of the great shortage of money, why it arose, why it still lasts and spreads, with instructions on how a happy increase of wealth and fortune in our fatherland may be prayed for and hoped for.** Amphilochius compares unstable riches to a prostitute, who now flatters and smiles upon this lover, now that one, then again another and another, but keeps faith with none, deluding them all. More in Rittershuf’s notes on Amphilochius, page 40. Wealth is a cause of war. Master Rupert on Florus, book 3, chapter 9, section 3, and a cause of ruin likewise. Cicero in his "Letters to Atticus" says: *You will trust in your strongbox.* Seneca says: *You have the money of a brilliant inheritance, and you can also inflict a wound upon it.* Heinsius in his "Letters," page 423. In whose strongbox "Zeus the Golden" <note>original: ζεὺς ὁ χρυσὸς</note>, the husband of Danaë, has a well-consecrated seat. Plautus in "Aulularia," act 4, scene 8, line 1: *The griffins who inhabit the golden mountains I alone surpass in riches: for I care not to mention those other kings, those beggars of men: I am that King Philip.* Rupert in "Mercury's Letters," page 600.

> The Musician, the Astrologer, the Advocate, the Scribe, the Poet,
> Hold books and many offspring, but no brass coins.

Antigonus, King of the Macedonians, wished to persuade his son Demetrius to such a marriage—to take an old woman, but a rich one—alleging this verse from Euripides: <term>where there is profit, one must serve even against nature</term>. <note>original: ὅπε τὸ κέρδος, παρὰ φύσιν δουλευτέον</note>

Letter R.

...by means of a play on words in this manner: <note>original: "ὅπερ τὸ κέρδος, παραφύσιν γαμητέον" (hoper to kerdos, paraphysin gamēteon)</note> "as is the profit, so must one marry against nature." Scherbius in *Politics, my page 358.* When Pope Innocent IV was at his last gasp, he said to his friends who stood weeping around his deathbed, leaving them with these final words: <note>original: "quid lamentamini, nonne vos omnes divites relinquo? quid ultrà requiritis?"</note> "Why do you lament? Do I not leave you all wealthy? What more do you seek?" whereupon he gave up his spirit. Cluver, *History, p. 575.* Wealthy and beautiful wives are to be avoided. Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in *Syntagma of Universal Law, book 9, chapter 18, number 12.* Some consider it more prudent for a man to act by taking a wife without a dowry and abstaining from a wealthy one. For, as Francesco Petrarch says in *Remedies for Both Fortunes, book 1, dialogue 64*: "Dowry and beauty are the stimuli of conjugal pride; and where a great dowry enters, there the husband’s freedom exits—which, if it had been dear to him, would not have been sold for any price." This is borrowed from Plautus in *The Ass-Dealer*, when he says:

> I accepted the silver, and sold my command for a dowry.

Since large dowries require large dotal settlements <term>dotalitium: a provision or property set aside for a widow</term>, it easily happens that children are so burdened by the establishment of it that they can hardly preserve their paternal estate, and the proverb finds its place: "Rich wives, poor children." <note>original German: "reiche Weiber, arme Kinder"</note> Hartmann Pistor, *question 37, number 18.* To hide riches is often a part of prudence. Apuleius in his *Apology, book 1*, praises those opulent people who live without noise, with modest habits, and with their resources concealed, managing great wealth without ostentation. Regarding such people, Erasmus in *Adages, chiliad 3, century 10, proverb 52*, recites a verse of Homer:

> Let him possess in silence whatever gifts of the Gods are present.

And Horace in *Epistles, book 1, letter 17*:

> But if the crow could feed in silence, he would have
> More of a feast, and much less of brawling and envy.

Juvenal in *Satire 6*, writing against the "inferior and more wicked sex," says:

> Nothing is more intolerable than a wealthy woman.
> Meanwhile, she is foul to look at, and ridiculous;
> Her face is bloated with much bread-paste, or she smells 
> Of greasy Poppaean ointments, which stick to the lips of her wretched husband.
> She comes to her lover with her skin washed; but when does she
> Wish to seem beautiful at home? Ointments are prepared for lovers;
> For them is bought whatever the slender Indians send here.
> At last she reveals her face and removes the first layers of 'plaster.'
> She begins to be recognized, being pampered with that milk 
> For which she takes a troop of she-asses with her as companions.

Where note: the Bread-paste, the husband's lips being gummed up, the revealing of the face, and the removing of the first "plaster" <note>original: "tectoria," a term usually used for the smooth finish on a wall, here used mockingly for heavy makeup</note>.

On the use of soaked bread as a mask, one should consult Rango, Rector of the Berlin Gymnasium, in the treatise *On Wigs* <note>original: "de Capillamentis, vulgò parucquen"</note>, *my page 226.* No one is presumed to have been enriched by crime unless it is proven. *Final law, Code on Edicts.* Alciatus, *On Presumptions, rule 3, presumption 5.* Mascardus, *conclusion 10006, number 12.* And any industrious person is presumed to be able to become wealthy. Baldus, *on the law concerning the death of a guardian.* Lord Christoph Philipp Richter, *part 6, counsel 31, number 14, folio 273.* He who claims someone is either wealthy or poor is bound to prove this intention. *Neapolitan Decisions, 377.* From what things a man is presumed wealthy or poor is discussed by Menochius, *book 3, preface 59, and book 6, preface 25.* A man is not presumed wealthy who has many children, since he can hardly suffice for nourishing the children and providing dowries for the daughters, even if he has property. Mundius, *On Duties and Honors, chapter 6, number 654.* Riches should not be exposed to envy, nor should the lowliness of a patrimony be uncovered. Mundius, *On Duties, chapter 4, number 48.*

### 105. Rainbow. Iris.

The bow is otherwise a sign of war, as one of the ancient weapons; but it signifies the peace attained when it has no string. Lord Dilherr in *Reflections on the World's Fields and Gardens, chapter 15, pages 526, 527.* The opal-colored bow, drawn without a string, shows God's rich grace and the row of bright colors. The most beautiful painting of the clouds, the earth's highest crown and wreath, the splendor of nature, the embroidered and soon-faded ribbon of heaven, the herald's color of peace (between God and men). Lord Harsdörffer in *The Poet's Funnel, part 3, page 389.* On whether rainbows were seen before the Deluge, see Zeiller at length, *century 5, Letters, page 362*; also *century 4, question 30, page 154.* Doctor Herlicius wrote a *Historico-Physical Discourse* on the Lunar Iris or "Night-bow" on March 16, Anno 1609.

### 106. Ring-leaders. Author of sedition.

See Wolfgang Krüger's *Catalog of Various Emperors and Kings*, under the name of Thomas Müntzer <note>A leader of the German Peasants' War</note> in *Limnaeus, Public Law, book 2, chapter 9, number 146.* Petrus Pappus in *Dutch Military Law, page 67.* Petrus Gnodalius, *On the Peasant Tumult in Germany.*

### 107. Imperial Subjects. Subjects of the Empire.

On these words, Limnaeus should be consulted in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 3, page 105; book 1, chapter 12, numbers 26 and 28.* *Acts of Lindau, page 349, at the end.*

### 108. Rare Things. Rara.

Mantica, *On Conjectures of Final Wills, book 6, chapter 6, number 13*; see also my work *On the Style of the Court, in the Preface.* Rare things do not come into legal consideration. *Law 3, Digest on Laws.* "A rare bird on the earth, and very much like a black swan." That which is rare is dear, and every honor becomes cheapened by a multitude of competitors (as stated in Livy, *book 1, chapter 10*). To this point belongs that saying of Cornelius Nepos in *Miltiades*: That to the people—

### 109. Recess. <note>original: "Receß. Receſſus."</note>

"Recess" is a term called a "barbarous word" <term>receſſus: in the Holy Roman Empire, this refers to the "Reichsabschied" or the final formal decree issued at the conclusion of an imperial assembly or court session</term> by Goldast, in his *Reply for the Emperor, chapter 10, page 104.* An oral recess should not exceed three or four lines. If it cannot be contained in such a brief space, it should be presented in writing. Christoph Schwanmann in *Processes of the Chamber Court, book 1, chapter 42, numbers 2 and 3.* And thus it is maintained by custom. In the same place, see the *Deputation Recess of the year 1600, section "whether also indeed," folio 29, verso* where it is repeated again, though saving the judge's discretion. One must abstain from injurious and impertinent recesses, *cited chapter 42, number 6.* Recesses should be kept by the Proctors in both German and Latin, *cited chapter 42, number 9.* In oral recesses, it is not permitted to proceed beyond the "Duplicates" <term>duplicas: a second stage of legal pleading</term>, *cited chapter 42, number 14.* For the form of a recess for producing an "imploration of the noble office of the judge" <term>imploratio nobile officium: an appeal to the judge’s equitable power to correct a legal wrong</term> for revoking attempted actions, see Schwanmann in *Processes of the Chamber Court, book 2, chapter 11, numbers 8 and 9, my page 75.* For the form of a recess regarding a mandate of non-offense, the same author, *book 2, chapter 20, numbers 5 and 6, page 220.* For the forms of recesses in a case regarding the law *diffamari* <note>original: "l. diffamari," a law regarding the right to force a slanderer to prove their claims or remain silent</note>, the same, *book 22, chapter 22, number 16, page 265.* For the form of a recess for concluding general acts based on prior records, the same, *book 2, chapter 13, numbers 14 and 15, page 105.* For the form of a recess for producing the acts of a prior instance, *cited book 2, chapter 11, numbers 6 and 7, page 75.* It is not permitted to produce a "writing in place of an oral Recess" <note>original German/Latin: "Schrifft, an ſtatt mündlichen Receß"</note> where acting in writing is forbidden. Schwanmann, *Processes of the Chamber Court, book 1, chapter 53, number 8.* On the Oral Recess, one should consult Johann Andreas Gerhard in *Discourses on the Supreme Courts of the Roman Empire, the Aulic and Imperial, page 93 at the beginning, and page 96 at the end.*

### 110. Counterclaim. <note>original: "Reconventio"</note>

A counterclaim <term>reconventio: a defendant's claim against the plaintiff in the same legal action</term> does not proceed in executive matters <term>executivis: summary legal proceedings for the immediate enforcement of a debt or judgment</term>. Theophilus Gisebert on *Counterclaims, chapter 13, number 14.* Johann Peter Molignatus on *Counterclaims, question 41.* Christian Lenz on *Nominations and Cessions of Actions, chapter 34, number 33.* On the cases in which a counterclaim has no place, see Sprenger at length in *Public Jurisprudence, page 348,* and in *Fragments of Public Law, page 175.*

### 111. Regress. <note>original: "Regreß. Regreſſus."</note>

On the Reservation of Regresses <term>regreſſus: the right of a person to seek recovery or indemnity from a third party</term>, see William of Monferrat, the Catalan.

### 112. Retraction. <note>original: "Retractus."</note> See above under "Hereditary Redemption." <note>original German: "Erbloſung"</note>

Johann Baptista Costa on *Retraction.* Bonaventura Gauer in *Basel Disputations.* Stollius in the *Inaugural Disputation on the Law of Family Retraction* <term>retractus gentilitius: the right of family members to buy back ancestral property sold to outsiders</term>, held at Altdorf in 1662. *Supplement to Wehner, page 21.* The Right of Retraction is, as it were, a contract by which we solemnly revoke a certain alienated thing within a defined time. ## S.

The insignia of Poland have a white eagle on a red field, around whose neck the letter **S.** is entwined, because many of their Kings with the name Sigismund were believed to portend victories for the kingdom. Since, however, the Turks abhor images, the letter alone fulfills the role of the figure.

Marcus Messala Corvinus composed an entire book on the power of the letter **S.** See Lipsius, *On the Pronunciation of the Latin Language, chapter 2.*

### 1. Salic Law. <note>original: "Saalrecht. Lex Salica."</note>

Regarding the Salic Law, and from where its name comes, see Raudensis, *decision 41,* and Bisciola, *Leisure Hours, volume 2, book 10, chapter 2.*

The "Salic" Law is called the Law of the Hall <note>original: "Lex Aulae"</note>; or conceived from the Fiscal Land, or the Hall <note>original: "Aula"</note>; see my own work, *On Succession and Election, folio 131, etc.* Add *The Antiquities of Paris, my folio 200.* Also Anton le Pippre, *chapter 124, on Intentions*, who most recently defended the Salic Law—which excludes women from Royal succession—against the attack of Jacob Meyer, the Belgian historian. And he adds this, however: those Princes who betroth their daughters to the Kings of France ought to establish the same Law in their own Kingdoms.

**Saalleicht** <note>A term referring to witnesses or peers in a feudal court, related to the Germanic "Saalmann"</note>; this little word is found in several ancient documents. "He proved it with his *Saalleichten*, or *Saalmanleichten*," who were perhaps the Peers of the Court. This little word *Saalbrieff* is found twice in the same document. "Maurer places the property into the hands of his *Saalleut* with proper 'Saal' <note>referring to the formal transfer ceremony in the court hall</note> and by judgment <note>original: "Urthel"</note>."

### 2. Sabbath. <note>original: "Sabbathum"</note>

Regarding the Sabbath, see Ricquium on the *Jubilee, book 1, chapter 2*, and the entry for "Sunday" <note>original: "Sonntag"</note>.

## ADDITION.

The Moors <note>In this 17th-century context, referring to West Africans</note> keep their Sunday on our Tuesday, which they call *Diofetiffos* <note>A term from Michael Hemmersam’s travelogues regarding West African 'fetish' days</note>. They perform no work until evening, when they bring palm wine to their King, which he provides to the nobles or *Capesfiern* <note>Captains or local headmen</note> for their enjoyment. Michael Hemmersam. Regarding Sabbath questions, see the letter Q, number 6. Our ancestors worshiped the Sun, as Cluverius argues in *Ancient Germany, book 1*, and understood the one true God through it. Thus, the word "Sonntag" <note>Sunday</note> means as much as "special" or "particular," and the first day of the week was therefore named Sunday. The sun makes men black, bleaches linen, softens wax, hardens clay, clarifies oil, and darkens meat. <note>These were common Aristotelian observations on the physical effects of heat</note>. Aristotle provides the reasons in *Section 38, Problem 1, § 10*. Regarding the Sabbath River <note>A legendary river that was said to stop flowing on the Sabbath</note>, see Lord Leonhard Wurffbain on the *Number Seven, page 97*. Whether it is permitted on the Lord’s day to adopt, emancipate, free a slave, make wills, draft instruments for contracts, enter into agreements, write an inventory, or allow pacts and transactions; whether it is permitted for Doctors <note>meaning learned professors or legal scholars</note> to provide counsel for legal cases, or for students to study on those days? Ummius addresses this in *Process, my page 315*. On the last question, see also Doctor Tabor, *Disputations on Wesenbeck 6, question 4*. Whether doctoral promotions should be held on feast days? See Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors, page 95*. Doctors—not only of Theology but also of Law and Medicine—can study and provide counsel to those who seek it on feast days, provided they have first performed and attended divine service in a timely manner. G. C. Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors, page 314 and following*. Regarding the "idle Sabbath" and the "Sabbath journey" <note>the maximum distance permitted to walk on the Sabbath in Jewish law</note>, see Pancirolli in *The New Reports, page 715 and following*. Neander shows at length from where the word Sabbath is derived in his *History of the Bacchanalia, my page 187 and following*. Hospinian, *On the Origin of Feasts, page 8*.
*Besold, Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

Henricus Ernestius, Professor at the Knight’s School in Sorø, has written a treatise on the Sabbath. Whether athletic exercises are permitted on the Sabbath, see Lord Dilherr in *The Way to Salvation, pages 725 and 732*.

### 3. Matters. <note>original: "Sachen. Causæ."</note>

The word *Sach* <note>German: "Sache"</note> encompasses all types of civil and criminal, judicial and extra-judicial disputed matters, concerning which one person can be or become at odds or in conflict with another. For the word *causa* <note>Latin: "cause" or "case"</note> is general, pertaining as much to civil matters as to criminal ones, and as much to judicial proceedings as to those outside of court, both before the contestation of a lawsuit and after, according to the glosses and commentaries of the Doctors, especially Alciatus, verse 40, in the law *causas*, section *lites*, in the Code *On Transactions*. And it is so general that among the Rhetoricians, those three types of causes <note>Judicial, Deliberative, and Epideictic</note> encompass all controversies that can occur in the world. *Judicial Acts concerning the Homage of the City of Braunschweig, part 2, page 45, number 53.*

### 4. Saxon. <note>original: "Sachs. Saxo."</note>

Knives in our language are called *Sachs* <note>The "seax" or "sax", a single-edged knife or short sword</note>. Gregory of Tours, in *History, book 4, chapter 51*: "Then two youths with sturdy knives, which they commonly call *Scramsaxos*, infected with poison and bewitched by Queen Fredegund—while they pretended to handle another matter—struck him in both sides." Godfrey of Viterbo in the *Pantheon, part 17*:
> That short sword itself is called *Saxa* among them,
> From which the Saxon is noted to have derived his name.
Lipsius, *Centuria 3, Letters to the Belgians, Letter 44*. From a very old Latin-German Psalter: *Scharsachs*, a shaving razor. Lindenbrogius in the *Glossary of Old German Laws*: *Schersar*, a razor; in a Latin-German Glossary: *Sachs*.
Hence the common saying among the Saxons, *Sassen*, which means to shave the hair with a razor. Meibom on *Widukind, page 44*.
Others derive "Saxons" from "sitting" <note>original: "sitzen"</note>, thus *Holzesassen*, those who dwell in the woods. See Reineccius, *On the Origins of the Saxons*. Add Albinus, *Meissen Land-Chronicle*, in the appendix, page 392, where the etymology of this word, as well as the arrival of the Saxons and their settlements in Germany, are discussed at length. The same author in title 16 treats at length: How the Electorate and Duchy of Saxony passed from the Dukes of Saxony, Westphalia, and Engern to the Margraves of Meissen (Emperor Sigismund, after the family of Albert the Bear <note>original: "Urforum"</note> became extinct, gave the Electorate of Saxony—which had devolved back to the Empire—as a fief to Frederick I, Margrave of Meissen. From him the current Electors of Saxony are descended. Bocer, *On Regalia, chapter 2, number 61*), and how this Electorate passed from one lineage to another. In title 17, he adds and proves with examples that the House of Meissen and Saxony always behaved well toward the Roman Emperors.

Zeiller <note>Martin Zeiller (1589–1661), a prolific German geographer</note> published the *Topography of Upper Saxony* in the year 1650, and the *Topography of the Circle of Lower Saxony* in 1652. Reiner Reineccius, in his *Commentary on the Origins of the Saxons, pages 6 and 7*, indicates that these names—Sacae, Saxae, Saxones, Sassones—are the same, and refer to the same people. G. ## 5. Saxon Law. <note>original: "Sachsenrecht. Jus Saxonicum."</note>

On the subject of Saxon Law, Mr. Johann Gryphiander provides much that is pleasant and worth knowing throughout his treatise *On the Saxon Town-Law* <term>Weichbild: a system of municipal law common in medieval Germany</term>, especially in chapter 37 and many following. Regarding the origin, progress, and utility of Saxon Law, Matthäus Colerius prefixed a unique Oration to his treatise *On Executive Process*, which he delivered publicly at the University of Jena.

The Saxon Law <note>original: "Lex Saxonica"</note>, divided into eighteen chapters, can be found in the works of Johannes Herold and Friedrich Lindenbrog. Wippo, in his *Life of Emperor Conrad the Salic*, calls the Law of the Saxons "most cruel," undoubtedly because the death penalty was frequent and common within it. However, it appears to have been written for Saxons who had already converted to Christianity: for mention is made there of the principal festivals of the year, and the death penalty is imposed upon the sacrilegious and perjurers.

Regarding the compilers of the more recent Saxon Law, which circulates under the title of the *Mirror* <note>original: "Speculum", referring to the *Sachsenspiegel*, the most influential German law book of the Middle Ages</note>, Albert Krantz disputes this in *Saxonia, book 2, chapter 21*, rightly denying that Charlemagne was the author of the *Mirror*.

Adam of Bremen, in *book 2, chapter 19*, asserts that Harold, King of the Danes, famous for miracles, delivered laws to the Saxons. His words are these: "It is most certain that he established laws and rights for our people, as well as for those across the Elbe and the Frisian nation, which they still strive to observe by the authority of such a great man." <note>original: "Certissimum verò est, eum tam nostro populo..."</note>

In the time of Frederick Barbarossa, the *Law of Soest* <note>original: "Jus Susatense"</note> flourished in old Saxony, which Henry the Lion handed over to be used by the new city of Lübeck after it was brought under his power. An anonymous poet writes:

> *Now brothers and as if one nation*
> *Then under judges, whom the King himself would impose,*
> *And his legates, the Saxons were permitted to use*
> *Their ancestral laws and the honor of liberty.*
> *By this final treaty they were joined to the Franks,*
> *So that the race and people might harmoniously become one,*
> *And always obey one King equally.*

Adam of Bremen, in *book 1, chapter 7*: "All who were accustomed to resist having been routed and brought under his power, this condition was proposed by the King and accepted by them: that, casting aside the worship of demons and abandoning their ancestral ceremonies, they should receive the Sacraments of the Christian faith, and, united with the Franks, they should become one people with them." See Heigius, *Question 8*.

On whether and to what extent Saxon Law should be deferred to, see Scheffer, *final part, question 14*.

<column-break/>

Saxon Law flourished most greatly in Silesia in former times, and judgments were obtained from Magdeburg <note>Silesian towns often looked to the "superior court" of Magdeburg for legal rulings</note> until the year 1545, when that city fell under the Imperial Ban. On that occasion, Ferdinand I forbade this and directed the parties to Prague. See Schickfus in the *Silesian Chronicle, book 3, chapter 22*; see also Caspar Schifordegher, *book 1, treatise 30, question 7*, where he discusses at length whether the customs of Saxon Law are to be observed in Silesia.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding who compiled, glossed, and expanded the *Sachsenspiegel* <note>The "Saxon Mirror"</note>, as well as the *Saxon Town-Law*, see Schottel in *The German Main Language, folio 1201*. Whether lawsuits in the March of Brandenburg, the Duchy of Brunswick, Lüneburg, etc., should be decided according to Saxon Law or according to Civil Law <note>Roman Law</note>? See Liebenthal in *Political Collection, Dispute 9, question 10*. The Saxons were formerly governed by twelve Counts or Nobles. Krantz, *book 2 of Saxonia, chapter 22, page 4*. Andrzej Lipski, Chancellor of the Kingdom of Poland, wrote *Practical Observations collected from Civil and Saxon Law*.

Regarding the customs of the Saxon people, and their unwritten and written law, and the first author of that which now exists under the name of the *Mirror*: see Heigius, *Question 8*. For what the *Saxon Term* <note>original: "Sächsische Frist", a specific legal grace period</note> is, see Kittersb. on the *Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 202, at the beginning, and the authors cited there*.

## 6. Estate Registry. <note>original: "Saalbuch. Liber censualis."</note>

A book in which taxable property and rents are recorded is called in Barbaric Latin an *æstimum*; in German it is called a *Saalbuch*, from *Sala*, that is, a hall or basilica, because in it are described the estates that pay rent to the Royal Hall <note>The "Saal" or hall was the center of a lord's administration</note>. Johannes Aventinus, *Annals of the Bavarians, book 4*, at the beginning. Friedrich Martini, *On Rents, chapter 1, number 14*, and in the *Index under the word 'census', which has various meanings*; also under the word *Saalbuch*.

->ADDITION.<-

See Schmugk, *Forensic Skirmishes 6, thesis 117*. Wehner, *Practical Observations on this term*. Otto in *Public Law, page 589*. Limnäus in *Public Law, book 2, number 34*. Zeiller, *Century 4 of Letters, page 382*. Whether *Estate Registries* constitute proof against peasants. Furthermore, Ummius in *Process, pages 702 and 711*. Moller, *4th Semester, 37*.

## 7. Salt Pan. <note>original: "Saltzpfann. Salina."</note>

See Gonzalo de Miedes, *Treatise on Salt*: "You make the tables sacred by the placement of saltcellars and the images of the Gods." Saubert, *On Sacrifices, page 395*. Regarding sea salt, where no salt is found, see T. Sprenger in his *Exchange Practice, pages 20 and 21*. Stephan Gratiani reports several things about salt that are not unworthy of reading in *volume 1, forensic disputes, chapter 179*. See the *Halographia* of Johann Thölde and the *Dictionary of Alchemy* by Roland, *folio 410*.

Saltworks are located either in a public or a private place.

place. In that case, they are public and belong to the Sovereign, both in terms of ownership and the right to their profits. In this case, they belong to private individuals, provided that the tax due on them is paid to the treasury. And this follows the old Roman law. Thus, a tax on private salt supplies <note>original: "Salinariæ annonæ"</note> was first imposed by Lysimachus in Thrace; however, as Athenaeus relates a memorable story, the salt springs immediately dried up as if nature itself were recoiling from the tax, and only returned once the tax was removed. Under Ancus Marcius and Livius the Censor (who was thereafter called "the Salter" <note>original: "Salinator"</note> in Rome), in France under Philip the Tall, and in Germany, specific Judges were formerly appointed over the salt works, whom they called *Salt-counts* <note>original: "Saltzgraven"</note>. Later, when the greed for possessing everything grew, these were taken entirely from private individuals, assigned to the Royal Treasury, and numbered among the *Regalia* <term>Regalia: the exclusive rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign</term>. This is why salt mines were granted to the Electors by Charles IV through a special grace, and today they are only possessed by permission of the Sovereigns, who hold their authority from the Emperor.

The mineral of salt and the method of making it were discovered by Elizabeth—wife of Emperor Albert I, daughter of Meinhard, Count of Tyrol and Gorizia, and Duke of Carinthia, and the most illustrious sister of Conradin on her mother’s side. A woman of great and sharp intellect, she found them at Hall near Gmünden in Upper Austria; not ungrateful for the gift of God, she provided salt for all the monasteries in Austria.

Johannes, the brother of Albert, Duke of Brunswick, was the first to devote labor to the Lüneburg salt works and opened a new vein there in the Year of Christ 1269, which was far more abundant than the one that had previously flowed, and the work prospered in his hands. Many Abbots and Prelates of monasteries were accustomed to derive their livelihood from these salt works. Later, the people of Lüneburg violently usurped them, for which they were condemned by Pope Nicholas and Emperor Frederick III Augustus. In Italy, Jacobus Dondus, a physician and mathematician of Padua, was the first to teach how to coagulate salt from the waters of Aponus, so that from 1000 pounds of water, one pound of salt could be made, around the year of Christ 1370.

The most excellent salt works in Europe are in the County of Burgundy, in the city of Salins, where the whitest salt is boiled, and from which an immense and barely credible revenue arises, exceeding 300,000 pounds annually. The Saxon salt works at Halle are scarcely inferior to these and are not the least among those of Germany. These were granted by Emperor Otto to the Archbishopric of Magdeburg and were thus made subject to Episcopal Law. Later, they were granted in part as a fief to the citizens of Halle by the Archbishops (with the Magdeburg Chapter ratifying it), while part was designated for the "Archbishop’s Table" <term>Mensalia: lands or revenues set aside specifically for the sustenance of a bishop or prelate</term>. This was done under the law that the citizens pay a certain quota of those revenues to the Archbishops, commonly called *concerning the outflows* <note>original: "um die Ausläuffe"</note>; however, this payment is reduced or waived for the Bishop if the price of wood becomes too expensive; otherwise, they keep the remainder for themselves. Archbishop Ernest established this by decree in the year 1379, such that each of his successors

<column-break/>

is bound to swear in the Archbishop’s Capitulation <note>A formal agreement between a candidate for the office of Bishop and his electors</note> that they will not grant these "Table" salt works to any others but the citizens of Halle. Thus, the lordship of the salt works remains with the Archbishop, as they reject all alienation as "Table property" and cannot be subjected to the lordship of another; at the very least, their use is liberally granted to the subjects.

On whether and to what extent salt works are numbered among the *regalia*, see *Marburg Counsels*, volume 1, counsel 9, from the beginning, etc. Regarding salt works, add *Heigius, book 1, question 14; also Guidius on metals, title 8.*

### ADDITION.

Salt was used for sacrificing; hence it is called "divine salt" <note>original Greek: "sal θεῖος"</note> by Homer and "beloved of the gods" <note>original Greek: "θεοφιλὸς"</note> by Plato. Salt is a symbol of perpetual friendship; Lot’s wife was turned into a pillar of salt. Saubertus treats this at length in *On Sacrifices, page 631 and following*. On whether the statue remained and exists today, see Saubert, in the same treatise, page 633. *On Salt-counts*, see Sprenger in *Public Jurisprudence, pages 210 and 405*. On the salt tax, *Salt-money* <note>original German: "Soutsgeld"</note>, page 211.

The Egyptians formerly so loathed all salt that they would not even eat salted bread; indeed, since they especially loved purity of life, they thought all provocations of wickedness should be removed: for salt excites lust because of its heat and awakens and sharpens the feminine power. Pancirollus, *On Memorable Things, page 58*. Spilling salt on the table is an omen of depth <note>meaning a profound or bad omen</note>, page 59.

A salt source: *Hall or Salt-spring* <note>original German: "Hall oder Saltzbrunn"</note>. Limnäus in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 25*. Regarding salt works, see *Füver’s Journey, page 10; Master Tabor on Relocations, pages 251 and 253. Salt-pans: Salt-boiling* <note>original German: "Saltzpfannen: Saltzsieden"</note>. Limnäus in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 16, number 21*. On *how salt is prepared*, see *M. Zeiller, century 5, page 34; how to purify it and make it sweet, page 154. Salt-mine as it is burned <note>processed via heat</note>, page 212. Properties of salt, page 262, 398. Why it is used in the "Deposition" <note>A traditional hazing ritual for new university students</note>, four causes, page 363.* Sowing salt designates perpetual infertility: *Liebenthal in the Political College, Exercise 5, thesis 12*. To protect oneself against black salt: *C. Rittershufius in the Dedication to the Novels*. In Mr. Plater’s Cabinet of Curiosities, blue salt was shown to me. On the different colors of salt, *Zeiller, Spanish Journey, page 388*. In Lüneburg, a wild boar discovered the salt spring: *Zeiller, German Journey, page 368*. On fossil salt in Poland: *Klock, On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 11, numbers 12 and 13*. On Hungary and Italy, *book 2, chapter 9, number 8*. Regarding the praise, utility, purity, color, flavor, vigor, and duration of salt, see the same work, *book 2, chapter 9, numbers 1 and 2*. *On Salt-nobles* <note>original German: "Von Saltz-Junckern"</note>: *Sprenger in Public Jurisprudence, page 405; Draco on Patricians, pages 316 and 242.* A salt-cellar was kept in offerings: Saubertus, *On Sacrifices, page 395*. The salt-cellar in sacrifices: *Master Rupert, book 4, chapter 4, in the notes to Valerius Maximus.* Anyone who desires to avoid that tickling of Venus <note>lust</note> will restrain himself from the frequent use of salt. Pancirollus in *New Discoveries, page 441.*

Regarding Salt-mountains in Persia, see Olearius in his *Description of the Persian Journey* <note>original: "Persianischen Reißbeschreibung"</note>, pages 692 & 581. Rock salt <note>original: "Sal gemmae"</note> there is as clear as crystal. There are also salt mountains and salt mines in Russia, pages 355 & 372.

J. T. Sprenger writes most extensively on salt-works in *Fragments of Public Law* <note>original: "Fragm. Juris Publici"</note>, page 197 and following. That salt was used in both Pagan and Jewish sacrifices is evident from that passage of Livy: "that they might hold the salt-cellar and the sacrificial dish for the sake of the Gods."

On salt-works, see Bulenger’s treatise *On the Taxes of the Roman People*, chapter 16. On the types of salt-works, where the revenues of salt-works are granted to others upon receipt of some payment, see Menochius, counsel 98. Regarding Salt, see Mr. Harsdörffer in *The Poetical Funnel* <note>original: "Poetentrichter"</note>, part 3, page 399. The "Covenant of Salt" is found in Numbers 18. For victims were sprinkled with salt; of what kind that was, Sabellicus mentions in book 8, *Ennead* 2. Why is salt used in all sacrifices? See Zeiller, century 4, question 93.

### 8. Safeguard. <note>original: "Salvaguardia"</note>

Whoever violates the security of the Prince commits, by that very act, the crime of treason <term>crimen laesae Majestatis: the crime of injured majesty or high treason</term>, according to the law *Majestatis* in the Digest. Regarding safeguards specifically, this was concluded by Jean Papon in book 5 on arrests, title 7, concerning safe-conducts and the infringement thereof. See also Paolo di Castro, counsel 324, number 9, volume 1; Guido Papa, decision 418, number 1; and Cacheranus, decision 88, number 16; provided, however, that true malice <note>original: "dolus"</note> is present.

->ADDITION.<-

No harm shall be done to those under safeguard, upon pain of corporal punishment. See *Dutch Military Law*, page 79, and there Peter Pappus in the annotations. A safeguard is a great benefit. See Mundius *On the Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 340. Question: Whether the Vicars <term>Vicars: officials acting in place of the Emperor during an interregnum</term> can grant a safeguard to anyone while the Empire is vacant? See Becker in *Public Law*, page 91.

The penalty for a broken safeguard: Chasseneuz *On the Customs of Burgundy*, title on Justices, rubric 1, number 47, page 73; and Tessaurus, decision 132. Whether and when a safeguard can be granted by the Prince to the vassals of Barons: see Mastrillus, decision 263.

### 9. Jointly, Jointly and Severally. <note>original: "Samt, samt und sonderlich. Conjunctim, Sigillatim."</note>

The phrase "together with" <note>original: "unà cum"</note> joins subsequent items with those immediately preceding: and such is the nature of this word that it joins the extremes between which it is placed more strongly than if it were a simple

<column-break/>

conjunction <note>original: "copula"</note>, as Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century jurist</note> teaches regarding the law *Gallus*, section *quidem recté*, where Jason also comments, number 14, in the Digest *On children and posthumous heirs*. This is proven in the final law, where Jason comments in the Code *On the wardship of minors*. And it should be noted that in Mandates, one person can act while the others are absent or deceased.

Regarding the clause "jointly and severally" <note>original: "samt und sonderlich"</note>, see Modestinus Pistoris, part 3, question 118, number 4.

In suretyships, however, and other obligations where several people are bound for the whole <note>original: "in solidum"</note>, it is customary to add: "One for all, and all for one" <note>original: "Einer für all, und all für einen"</note>. This is joined with a renunciation of all legal benefits that might hinder the solidary obligation of two co-debtors.

->ADDITION.<-

What the phrase "together with" denotes: see Gottfried Antonius, *Feudal Disputation* 6, thesis 5, letter f. What "jointly and severally" <note>original: "Insolidum samt und sonders"</note>, "one for all, and all for one" means: see Johannes Philippi, Jurisconsult, in *The Practical Use of the Institutes*, book 3, title 21, section 4, Eclogue 62, number 9. With "undivided and unshared hand" <note>original: "mit ungeschiedener, und ungetheilter Hand"</note>, ibid. Add here Hartmann Pistoris, observation 112, number 25; see the title "One for all." *Marburg Counsels*, volume 1, counsels 24 and 71.

### 10. Joint-Fief. <note>original: "Samtlehen. Simultanea Investitura."</note>

The word *Samtlehen* <term>Samtlehen: a German feudal term for a fief held simultaneously by multiple relatives or members of a dynasty</term>, although it can be understood in two ways—either that the fief is common and belongs to the common lineage, or that it is common in the sense of being "simultaneous," meaning several people are invested with it at once—it is nevertheless closer to the common usage of speech among us Germans that this word be understood and explained as a fief common to the entire lineage <note>original: "agnationi"</note>, as Johann Fichard testifies in counsel 8, number 13, volume 1, citing Henning Göden under the rubric *On Fiefs*, number 16.

### 11. Savoy. <note>original: "Saphoy. Sabaudus."</note>

Concerning Savoy and the Savoyards, see Vanderburch, Guillaume Paradin, and *The Knight of Savoy*. That the Duke of Savoy regards the Emperor as his superior—besides the fact that he always and everywhere professes himself to be a Vicar of the Empire and a Vassal of the Emperor—is established even by this single argument: that he is accustomed to be called to the Diets <term>Comitia: the Imperial Diet or assembly of the Holy Roman Empire</term>. That this right belonged to him from of old and is still preserved for him intact and well-maintained <note>original: "fartum tectumque"</note> to this time is shown by the signatures of the Imperial Recesses <term>Recesses: the official resolutions or decrees of the Imperial Diet</term> from the years 1542, 1551, 1559, 1566, 1570, 1576, 1582, 1594, 1598, etc. Consequently, he is a State of the Empire and subject to the Emperor; see Arumaeus, *On the Diets*, chapter 4, number 118, etc.

## 14. Damages and Expenses. <note>original: "Schaden und Unkosten. Damna & impensæ."</note>

A pact in which a debtor promises in a formal instrument of obligation that if he does not pay the debt at the appointed time, he will then stand by an oath regarding the damages and interest <term>Interest: in this context, "id quod interest" or the legal compensation for loss</term>; or even by the simple and bare assertion of the Creditor himself—that all damages and expenses, as the creditor shall state them with simple words, with or without an oath, shall be reimbursed, and that his mere words shall be believed—is this valid, and to what extent? And what remedies are available to the debtor against a Creditor seeking unfair expenses and unjust damages, when the Creditor states the damage too highly and excessively? See Speckhan, who treats this at length, century 3, question 29, class 1. Beust on the law of oaths by agreement, page 235 and following. Schneidewein on the book of successions, number 10. Coler on executive process, part 1, chapter 19, number 118, with many following.

Under the term "damage" <note>original: "damni"</note>, German *Schaden*, "interest" <note>lost profit</note> does not seem to be included: since it is a far different thing to suffer a loss than to fail to make a profit. Hardevvig Daffel, counsel 29, book 1, number 18 and following. It must be known, however, that in the condemnation of "damages" <note>original: "der Schäden"</note>, only intrinsic damages are included, such as the expenses for Proctors, Advocates, Notaries, and similar persons involved in the judgment. For example: if because of my absence due to a lawsuit, I suffered a theft which would not have happened had I been present; or if, while traveling for the sake of the lawsuit, I suffer some damage or loss of my things on the journey—suppose I fell among thieves, or suffered shipwreck, or being seized by illness I incurred the expenses of sickness—these damages are not included in the condemnation, nor are they to be reimbursed to me. This is because they are not intrinsic damages of the lawsuit itself, but extrinsic or outside the suit; they come about through another accident, separate from the litigation, and thus are not even covered by the office of the Judge, according to the teachings of Mr. Matthias Stephanus, *Treatise on the Office of the Judge*, book 6, chapter 5, number 18. He says in the following number that it is otherwise if the damages are personal: such as if, because of attending the lawsuit, I could not practice my trade; for those are not extrinsic to the litigation; therefore the judge [may award] for that damage in the condemna-

### 15. Harmful, harmless. Saving the rights of a third party. <note>original: "Schädlich, unschädlich. Salvo Jure tertii."</note>

The clause "saving the rights of a third party" <term>Salvo jure tertii: a legal provision ensuring that an agreement between two parties does not negatively affect the existing rights of a person not involved in the agreement</term>, when inserted into feudal letters <term>Literis feudalibus: documents granting land or titles under the feudal system</term>, is of such efficacy and virtue that it reserves for anyone the right they might have in those feudal goods, and no prejudice or detriment can be brought against anyone through that enfeoffment <term>Infeudation: the granting of a fief or feudal property</term>. Schrader, consultation 48, number 30, volume 2. Matthew de Afflictis in chapter 1, number 30 and following, regarding those who hold as successors. Furthermore, even if the said clause is not expressly found in the letters of investiture <term>Investitura: the formal ceremony or document of handing over a fief</term>, nevertheless all feudal letters, by the power of the law, have this interpretation within themselves: that this clause is understood to be included, and that the Prince granting the fief or performing the investiture is not deemed to have wished to prejudice the rights of a third party. Schrader, in the place cited. Alexander, consultation 3, book 5. Decianus, consultation 185, number 11, and consultation 468, number 26.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

The promises of others or the acts of others do not bind a third party. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 187. It is beneficial to the Republic that the rights of a third party be heard. Immediately see Ummius in *On Procedure*, page 449. When prejudice is done to a third party by a delivered sentence, page 949. The right of a third party is of no use for making a legal defense <note>original: "excipiendum"</note>. Barbosa, book 18, chapter 13, axiom 1. A third party is not hindered from using their own right by the fact that others are litigating, axiom 2. On the clause: **Saving the rights of others.** <note>original: "Salvo jure aliorum"</note> Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputation* 7, thesis 10, letter E. On the clause: **Saving the rights of the parties, to each party harmless to their rights.** <note>original: "Salvo jure partium, jedem Theil an seinen Rechten unschädlich"</note> See *The Forum of Protestations*, page 327, number 56. What is called the property of a third party in cases of pledging. Schwanmann, observation 63, number 1 and following. All mandates and decrees of the Prince must be understood with justice and saving the rights of the third party. Everhardus in *Legal Commonplaces*, page 784. The right of a third party cannot be opposed. Marius Antoninus, book 1, resolution 88, number 14, and book 2, resolution 57, number 73, unless it is by the law itself exclusive of the rights of the acting party. Book 2, resolution 1, number 20. One alleging their own moral turpitude is not to be heard against a third party. *Altdorf Consultations*, page 149.

### 16. Indemnity guarantor. <note>original: "Schadlosbürge. Fidejussor indemnitatis."</note>

An indemnity guarantor <term>Fidejussor indemnitatis: a person who guarantees to pay a creditor only the remaining amount that could not be recovered from the primary debtor</term> is one who obligates himself to that which the creditor was unable to recover from the debtor; or who promises in support for however much less can be demanded from the principal debtor. Digest, Law 6, *on novation and delegation*; Law 19, section 3, *on the Velleian Senate-Consult*; Law 7, *on guarantors*; or who approaches for the remainder of an unpaid quantity, Law 45, section 11, *on the Law of the Treasury*. And he is commonly called a **Schadlosbürge** <note>German: "indemnity guarantor," literally a "harm-less-guarantor"</note> because his security <term>Cautio: a legal guarantee or bond</term> must turn away the damage. Argument from Digest, Law 71, final section, *on the meaning of words*.

This guarantor cannot be sued before the principal debtor has been exhausted <term>Excussus: the legal process of "exhausting" a debtor by seizing and selling their assets before turning to a guarantor</term>. And this is accepted by the nature of the obligation more than by the legal benefit of the guarantee: since it must first be established how much the creditor can obtain from the principal, so that the promise of indemnity may take place. So much so that this benefit cannot be rightly renounced even by means of an oath, according to the truer and more common opinion of the interpreters. This is both because an oath follows the nature of the act to which it is added, and also because an oath applied in any contract takes on all the conditions, implications, and limitations that the contract to which it is added possesses. See Gail, book 2, observation 27, numbers 13 and 23. Fachinaeus, book 3, controversy 15. Calvin in the *Lexicon*, under the word "indemnity guarantor." Speckhan, century 3, class 1, question 32, folio 373.
