#### ADDITION.

The indemnity guarantor <note>original: "Indemnitatis Fidejussor" or "Schadloßbürg"</note>, or subsidiary guarantor, is one who intervenes only to be held liable for whatever amount cannot be recovered from the principal debtor. See the Digest *law 63 on guarantors* and Gœddeus on the Digest *law 150 on the Significance of Words, number 2*. If such a person is sued by a creditor before the principal debtor, he can use the <term>Defense of Excussion: a legal right allowing a guarantor to refuse payment until the creditor has exhausted all legal remedies against the primary debtor's assets</term>. This was already established even before the new legal benefit was granted, as noted in the *Codex Justinianus, book 46, title 1, thesis 18, number 2*. As Köppen rightly observed in *Observation 31, number 9*, this right arises not so much from a specific legal privilege of guardianship, but from the very nature and condition of the promise itself, as per the Digest *law 116 on Verbal Obligations*. Amaya also notes in his commentary on the *Code regarding Decurions* that for a promise of indemnity to take effect, one must first wait to see if and what the creditor has obtained from the principal debtor. Only then, as a secondary resort, can the guarantor be pursued for the remainder—or as the legal expert says in the Digest *law 45, paragraph 11 on the rights of the treasury*, for the "residue of the unpaid quantity"—or even for the total failure of the primary obligation. See Carocius *on Excussion, part 2, question 14*, and the Marburg Jurists, *Counsel 24, number 217 and following*. In Freiburg im Breisgau, no subject is permitted to obligate themselves as a guarantor for more than 100 or 200 Gulden without the consent of the authorities. Obrecht in *Political Reflections, page 88*.

### 17. Sheep Farming. <note>original: "Schäferey" or "Pecuaria"</note>

The question arises whether anyone may dispose of their own soil as they wish in matters of grazing and sheep farming, even if it harms another and changes the prior form of the land—for instance, if another person holds <term>Forest Rights: the legal right to manage or use timber and resources within a specific wooded area</term> in that place—especially if the same practice is observed in neighboring areas? Furthermore, is a <term>Prescription: the acquisition of a right or title through the passage of time or long-standing custom</term> admissible against such an observation? See *Strasbourg Counsels, volume 1, counsel 8, question 4*.

### 18. Rogue. <note>original: "Schalck" or "Schalcus"</note>

*Schalck* is a word from the Middle Ages and is the same as servant or minister. Hence *Gottschalck* (Servant of God), *Marschalck* (Servant of Horses, i.e., Marshal), and *Schalck* in the kitchen. But because the fraud and cunning of servants were frequent everywhere, *Schalck* was used metaphorically for a "crafty person." From this, *Schalcum*, which some authors use, refers to damage given fraudulently, commonly called a "roguery" <note>original: "Schalckheit"</note>. *Sinschalck* or *Sinneschalck* refers to an ingenious or clever man.

#### ADDITION.

*Schalck* is an ancient word signifying a minister and servant. Draco *on Patricians, page 118*; Limn in *Public Law, book 3, chapter 1, number 76*; Caspar Barth (that most celebrated philologist, who read up to 2,800 authors, regarding whom see Thomas Reinesius, *Various Readings 1, 2*, and Master Rupert in the *Epistolary Mercury, pages 194 and 195*), *Animations on William the Breton’s Philippide, book 8*.

# Augmented Treasury of Practice

To "leap" <note>original: *schalten*</note>, that is, to come in, to occur, or to be placed in between; or rather, because it steps forward, or skips a day. This occurs because of the remaining 6 hours in each year, which every fourth year results in one more day than in other years: namely, the 24th of February, the "Sixth day before the Kalends of March" <note>original: *Sexto Calend. Martii*</note>. Therefore, it is called **Bissextile** or **Intercalary**, because these words (*Sexto Calend. Martii*) must be counted twice, according to the verses:

> The "Double-Sixth" is held on the sixth Kalends of March,
> On the latter day, the feast of Matthias is celebrated:
> Though "Matthias, Matthias" is said, the feast day
> does not change.

That is, the 24th day of February must be placed twice in the calendar during a leap year, so that the first 24th day of February is the "leap day" <note>original: *Schalt-Tag*</note>, and the second 24th day is the day of St. Matthias the Apostle.

Regarding the **Intercalation of the Jews**, see the Talmud in *Sanhedrin*.

Regarding **leap years**, and the fact that in Medicine and the visiting of mineral springs <note>original: *acidularum*</note> absolutely no account should be taken of them—since the matter is merely a human convention—the Lord Melchior Sebitzius treats this accurately in his *Treatise on Mineral Waters*, section 1, dissertation 10, number 16 and following, page 271, etc. And it should be noted that in a leap year, regarding tax assessments <note>original: *Losungen*</note>, as well as legal restorations, etc., those two days are held as one, according to Law 3, paragraph 3, *on minors*; see Gœddæus on Law 98, *on the Significance of Words*.

### ADDITION.

Regarding that Law 3, paragraph 3, *on Minors*, Großmann treats this most extensively in *On Civil Time*, theses 6, 7, and 8. See also Caranz, *Treatise on Natural and Legitimate Parts*, chapter 12, paragraph 5, number 16, where, however, he unnecessarily corrects the text of Law 98 of the Digest *on the Significance of Words* and reads "29" instead of "28"; but he is inconsistent with himself in number 15 compared with number 13. On the **false opinion of leap years**, see Mr. Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 44.

**To intercalate** <note>original: *Intercalare*</note> is the same as to interpose or to place between; from which poets also speak of "intercalary verses" <note>refrains</note>. An "intercalary day" is mentioned in Law 2 of the Digest *on various time prescriptions*; an "intercalary month" in Law 98, "when the bissextile is at the Kalends," paragraph 2 and the final paragraph of the Digest *on the Significance of Words*. Rittershusius treats this in depth in *On the Laws of the Twelve Tables*, page 19.

### 20. Donations and "Grease-Money" for Officials. <note>original: *Schanckung, Schmiralien der Amtleute. Donatio, Barrattaria.*</note>

In a **conditional donation** <note>original: *donatio sub modo*</note>, or one given for a future cause, a "warranty against eviction" <note>term: *Evictio* — a legal guarantee that the recipient will not be deprived of the gift by a third party with a better legal claim</note> must be provided, based on Law 1 of the Codex *on donations*. <column-break/>

*on Eviction*, number 499. This also applies to a **remuneratory donation** <note>term: *donatio remuneratoria* — a gift given as a reward for past services, which the law treats differently than a pure gift</note>, based on Law 34, paragraph 1, and Law 27 of the Digest *on donations*. Compare Hannedæl, *Imperial Exercises* 9, question 10.

Regarding **Barratry** <note>original: *Barattaria* — the corrupt act of a judge or official who refuses to perform his duty or do justice unless paid a bribe</note>, where a judge does not perform justice except for money, see the *Practical Supplement to Webner’s Observations*, page 10. "To forgive a debt is to give a gift," according to Hartmann Hartmann, book 2, chapter 44, observation 3, number 6. A remuneratory donation can be made by a tutor or curator in the name of a ward or minor, ibid. number 6. And **King Alphonso** of Aragon is also said to have graciously accepted a radish from a peasant. "Munificent" <note>original: *Munificus*</note> is he who bestows gifts; "Munifex" is he who performs a duty, according to Tabor, *On Transfers*, pages 75–76. ### 21. Executioner. <note>original: *Scharffrichter* (German) and *Carnifex* (Latin)</note>

Regarding the Executioner, and whether his office is considered infamous among all peoples, see Lipsius *in his commentary on Tacitus's Annals, book 2, folio 504,* Pontanus in *part 3 of the War, folio 754,* and myself *On Nobility, folio 106.*

Should those be punished "who kill or harm an executioner when he does not execute properly?" <note>original: *die einen Nachrichter umbringen oder beschädigen, wann er nicht recht richtet?*</note> See Aleman’s *Palestra, chapter 9,* the *Imperial Capital Punishment Ordinance* <note>original: *Peinliche Halßgerichts-Ordnung*—the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina</note>, and there Matthias Stephanus and Zieritz. Also see a recent history where, for a similar reason, an executioner and his wife were killed, recorded in the *French Mercury, volume 11, folio 531.*

The question is asked whether someone's punishment can be remitted so that they may perform the office of the executioner—"that he allows himself to be used for the execution as a sharp-judge or hangman?" <note>original: *daß er sich zur Execution für ein Scharffrichter oder Hencker gebrauchen lasse?*</note> And although Böckel, in his *Criminal Disquisitions 6, folio 103, section "quin usi,"* testifies that this practice is accepted in Germany, Italy, France, and Spain—meaning many people guilty of death were declared free of the punishment they had rightfully earned, solely because they performed that blood-stained office and violently removed other guilty parties from life to death with the sword or other punishment in place of the Executioner <note>original: *an statt deß Nachrichters*</note>. However, it is concluded that this should not be granted lightly, nor the punishment entirely remitted, lest there otherwise exist more executioners than criminals. See Jean Papon, *Notary Decisions, chapter 10, on remissions.* For why were the laws carried out? Why were punishments given? Why were investigators and judges of criminal matters appointed? Why should a crime be harmless and unpunished? A crime, by its nature, follows its author, against whom the just vengeance that comes from the laws burns; otherwise, under the guise of impunity and the grace of immunity, there would be an enticement to iniquity, whereas judgments are the medicine for depravity, etc.

### 22. Treasure. <note>original: *Schatz* (German) and *Thesaurus* (Latin)</note>

On the subject of treasures, see Caspar Bitsch’s singular treatise. Remarkable accounts are found in Camerarius, *Hours of Leisure, century 1, chapter 63 and following, also century 2, chapter 72 and following.* Also Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 2, folio 134.* Treasure, by the right of universal domain, belongs to the Prince; and according to Saxon Law, subjects have rights only to the surface of the land.

Regarding a treasure found in a house that was recently sold: to whom does it belong? See Wilhelm Anton in *Corollaries to the Treatise on Five-Year Terms, folio 22 in my edition.*

### ADDITION.

On a finder of treasure who lies about it, see Zahn, *On Lies, book 2, chapter 46, throughout.* On military treasurers, commonly called paymasters <note>original: *Zahlmeister*</note>, see Rudinger, *century 5, observation 73.* If a treasurer or administrator <note>original: *massarius*</note> of a city or other corporation is a debtor to that same Republic, he must demand payment from himself; otherwise, he is held liable and punished, according to Losæus, *On the Law of Corporations, part 3, chapter 6, number 14.*

Regarding treasurers who do not always have public money ready at hand, see Bonifacius, *On Theft, page 257, number 76.*

A treasure found by subjects or servants is acquired for their Master, as noted by Mr. Bitsch in *thesis 39, end.* Collenutius, in *book 3 of the History of Naples*, writes: A marble statue was found in Apulia with its head bound by a brass circle, inscribed with these words: *“On the first of May at sunrise, I shall have a golden head.”* <note>original: *Calendis Maji oriente Sole aureum caput habebo*</note> When a Saracen captive skilled in the magical arts explained this to King Robert (for he ordered the King to observe the point on the ground where the shadow of the statue's head fell at the stroke of the first of May), the King found a great treasure by digging in that spot, which proved useful to him in many military expeditions. The Saracen was granted his freedom and great rewards.

### 24. To Decide or Separate. <term>Scheiden</term>.

The word *scheiden* has several meanings. For it signifies to settle an action, to compose a dispute, to divide a matter to its core, or to discern boundaries, as is clear to anyone skilled in the German language. Johann Goeddaeus, among the *Marburg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 26, number 121. See "Abscheid" for a Recess <note>original: *Recessu* — a formal decree of an Imperial Diet</note>, "Ends-Besold"

<column-break/>

for a Sentence, "Schicht und Scheidung" for the division of goods: "Scheiden" for that which is to bring into harmony: likewise "Scheid" is said for a boundary. Goeddaeus, in the same place. Hence, where a word of multiple meanings occurs in a statute or any other disposition, it must be accepted according to the subject matter and that which is most fit for it. [See the law] *ejus causas* in the Digest *on conditions and demonstrations*. Surdus, consultation 179, number 52, and consultation 198, number 22, so that a correction of common law is avoided (Surdus, consultation 245, number 11) and less prejudice is caused (the same author, consultation 383, number 19 and following), or so that absurdity is removed, which is especially to be avoided in statutes. Goeddaeus, same place, number 122 and following.

### 26. Rogue. <term>Schelm</term>. <term>Nebulo</term>. (See above page 87).

Saubertus, in *On the Sacrifices of the Ancients*, page 239, [notes that] to have left one's shield behind was a primary disgrace. See Mr. Adam Keller *On Intestate Succession*, title 15, number 9. Or *Schelm* can also be said as if it were "Schlim" <note>likely meaning "bad" or "crooked"</note>.

Regarding the clause by which debtors promise that if they do not keep their debts or promises, they wish to be considered wicked, lying, and infamous—that they want to be dishonest, lying, and unfit people if they do not pay. See Hering, *On Suretyship*, chapter 9, number 146, etc.

## 27. Gifts. <term>Donare</term>. <note>Latin: *donare*, to give or grant.</note>

When the word "I give" is used in a will to appoint an heir, the appointment is considered valid. Jason <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a famous Italian jurist</note> notes this in his commentary on the law, because the law prefers that words be understood in an informal sense rather than letting a person's last will and testament fail. As the Roman jurist Papinianus states, in cases of wills, we should not always stick to the strict definition of words, since people often speak improperly or use the wrong terms. One should not ask what technical words were used, but rather where the intention of the person’s will was directed.

### ADDITION.

It is permitted for anyone to use charms or flattery to induce others to give them something. Barbosa <note>Agostinho Barbosa (1589–1649), a Portuguese bishop and expert in canon law</note> notes this; see also the section above on "Gifts" <note>original: *Schenkung*</note>.
Regarding "Confessional Pennies" <note>original: *Beichtpfennigen*; small fees or donations given at the time of confession</note>, see the *Opinions of the Theological Faculties of Leipzig and Wittenberg* and the works of Johann Gerhard.

## 28. Bailiffs. <term>Lictores</term>. <note>Latin: *lictores*, originally the attendants who carried the fasces before Roman magistrates; in the 17th century, this referred to low-level law enforcement officers or sergeants.</note>

Bailiffs are the opponents of violence once it has occurred; they are cast into every kind of servile duty and are often men of ruined reputation. The Spaniards call them *Merinos* and *Alquaziles*, the Italians *Sbirri*, and the French *les Sergeans*. In our language, we call them *Häscher* <note>Catchers</note>, *Menschenfänger* <note>Man-catchers</note>, and so on—those who immediately lay hands on a person. There is a legal question as to whether they may kill someone who resists arrest to avoid being captured.

### ADDITION.

Cicero testifies in his speech for Rabirius that a public assembly is defiled by the presence of a Bailiff or an Executioner. Other authors discuss what kind of persons should be appointed as bailiffs, and whether they should be counted as citizens or if they are "infamous" <note>original: *infames*; a legal status where a person loses certain rights and social standing due to their profession</note>. In ancient Rome, their homes were located outside the city walls. The name "Lictor" comes from the Latin word for binding. In Greek antiquity, they were called *rabdouchous* <note>original: ῥαβδούχους, meaning "rod-bearers"</note> and *Sergentarios*.

## 29. Ship and Gear. <term>Instrumenta ad fundum pertinentia</term>. <note>Latin: "Tools belonging to the land."</note>

When a piece of land is left to someone in a will, should the

<column-break/>

tools belonging to the land—commonly called "Ship and Gear" <note>original: *Schiff und Geschirr*; a German legal idiom referring to the moveable equipment, vessels, or tackle necessary to run a farm or workshop</note>—be considered part of the legacy? The answer is: when land is bequeathed, its equipment does not go with it unless it was specifically mentioned. This is especially true if the equipment was not originally part of the estate or was not purchased specifically as a fixture <note>original: *pertinentz*</note> of that property.

### ADDITION.

On whether the equipment goes with a legacy of land, see Agricola’s treatise on fixtures.

## 30. Navigation. <term>Navigatio</term>.

On seafaring and navigation, see the treatise by Guevara, attached to the third book of his *Epistles*.

### ADDITION.

On navigation, sea charts, and naval architecture, see the extensive work of Mr. Joseph Furtenbach in his *Mirror of Art* <note>original: *Kunstspiegel* (1663)</note>. Other authors discuss how a shipwreck is proved and the history of ships made of papyrus. The "Right of Anchorage" <note>original: *jus anchoragii*</note> is a fee paid for the stationing of ships. Giovanni Battista Riccioli, in his *Reformed Geography*, provides a brief chronicle of voyages to the New World (or regions nearly new) from the year 1270 onwards. There is also a dissertation by Mr. Böcler titled *The New Argo*, regarding "Heroic and Fatal Ships" of more recent times.

The word "Sailor" <note>original: *nauta*</note> is ambiguous. There are also "mid-sailors" <note>original: *mesonautæ*</note>, or "half-sailors." In Mr. Plater’s Cabinet of Curiosities in Basel, I was shown a piece of the ship of Francis Drake, the Englishman. See Böcler’s *New Argo*, page 17. Regarding how sailors on a ship should be consoled in times of great danger, see Rupert’s philological dissertations. Those who have once entered a ship and the sea are at the mercy of the winds and do not return to land whenever they wish. As Horace says in his Odes: "The fearful sailor puts no trust in painted ships."

When someone proclaimed him happy and all but blessed because of his possession of many well-equipped ships, that famous and wise Spartan (recorded in the notes of Plutarch) refuted him with this stinging remark: "I am not moved," he said, "by a happiness that hangs from a rope." <note>original: *felicitate à funiculo pedente*; referring to the ropes of a ship’s rigging, implying his wealth was physically precarious.</note> Perhaps that wise man would have said nothing different even if he had been led as a spectator to that stupendous mass which Ptolemy Philopator built. Even a "delicate" ship, no matter how much it is dedicated to eternity by the curious devotion of posterity, does not escape destruction, nor can it command or provide a victor immunity from shipwreck. Theophilus, Emperor of the East, acted wisely when he learned that a ship laden with merchandise had arrived belonging to his wife, the Empress Theodora, intending to make a profit from trade or business. ### 31. Shilling, double shilling.
->Shilling.<- <note>original: *Solidus*</note>

The word "Shilling," <note>original: *Schilling*</note> which we use daily, is a name for weight and quantity. In gold, a shilling is the 20th part of a gold piece; in silver, it is the third part of a half-ounce <note>original: *semunciæ sive Lathonis*</note>. This portion was called the *sextula* by the Romans. And every Shilling <note>original: *solidus*</note> consists of 12 half-pennies <note>original: *obulos*</note>. It is also used as a term for a specific coin in both gold and silver. In gold, the Shilling in the time of Justinian was equal to 2 Thalers, as Tilemannus Friesen notes in his *Mirror of Coinage*, book 4, chapter 4. In silver, it is regularly used for a specific coin divisible into 12 parts. Twenty of these coins made a pound. The silver shilling was calculated in various ways, but it always had its own certain alloy <note>original: *liga*</note>, and it was not something that existed only in the imagination.

Different origins of the name "Shilling" are handed down. Freherus thinks the Shilling is named as if it were a *Siliqua* <note>a small Roman weight and coin</note>. For he says the word was written that way in antiquity. To the Romans, a *Siliqua* was the fourth part of an ounce. Tilemannus derives it from *Schellern*, which is to say "to ring" <note>German: *klingen*</note>, because it gives off a clinking sound; or from *Schiden*, hence *Schidling*, like a "divided penny" <note>German: *Schide-Pfenning*</note>, because it is not a whole [solid] unit, yet it rings <note>German: *das klinget*</note>.

The Shilling <note>original: *Solidus*</note>, although it is understood as the "Gold Shilling" when mentioned in law, is nonetheless understood according to common custom as the "Small Shilling," that is, of small currency. See Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a primary authority on medieval law</note>. It is valued at twelve old coins of the Magdeburg standard, or sixteen new ones, which are current and used so that one can buy beer and bread with them. The *Gloss on Saxon Law*, book 2, article 45, states: in the Saxon lands, a "Shilling Penny" <note>German: *Schilling Pfenning*</note> is said to contain twelve old coins or sixteen new ones. See Johannes Schneidewein.

Sometimes the Shilling is also used to mean a "Groschen," which the common people call a "Peasant's Groschen" <note>German: *Baurgroschen*</note>, which is exchanged for eighteen Meissen coins. Köppen notes in his *Legal Decisions* that it is observed by custom that for a Shilling (which in German is called a *Baurgrosch*), it is not twelve Meissen coins that are used, but eighteen old ones...

Modestinus Pistor, Counsel 27, numbers 41, 51, and following, volume 2.

The double shillings, however, shall go at 153 pieces to the Mark, contain 14 *Loth* and 4 grains of fine silver, and the fine silver Mark shall be valued at 12 florins and 9 groschen. Alemannus, in the cited location.

### 32. Schilling Estates.

In the Principality of Lüneburg, there are certain estates called "Schilling-Hauer" <note>referring to a type of tenant holding</note>, which

<column-break/>

the peasant receives with the payment of one shilling; he can also be given notice to leave with one shilling, just as he himself can resign the farm with one shilling. However, it is not gladly permitted that a peasant whose ancestors lived on such a farm and helped bear the country's burdens should be dismissed and evicted from the Schilling-farm without cause. But if he should be negligent in paying rent or performing services, or otherwise conducts himself improperly, then the notice of dismissal may indeed be given. See Clamer, *Legal Promptuary*, title 11. They are much like the "Schuppflehen" <term>small feudal holdings or "shack-fiefs" usually held by laborers</term> in Swabia.

### 33. Shield and Helmet. Insignia.

See Mr. Speidel in *Notables*.

### ADDITION.

Insignia are depicted upon the shield itself, which is why the insignia of the nobility are called "Coat of Arms with open shield and helmet" <note>original: *Wappen mit offnen Schild und Helm*</note>. There exists a singular treatise by Bartolus on this matter, which they say the incomparable Doctor composed on the occasion of Emperor Charles IV granting him the right of the shield and the insignia of nobility. See Gabriel Paleotti on *Spurious Children*, chapter 15; Hopingk on *The Right of Insignia*, chapter 5, number 61. Counts Palatine cannot grant arms with an open visor <note>original: *aperta galea*</note>. Mund. on *Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 297.

It appears that the Dutch terms for painting or depicting (*Schilden*, *Mahlen*, or *Schildern*) come from these painted shields, just as the signs and shields of innkeepers are seen among us, featuring a picture from which the house takes its name. It is also common to say that an innkeeper has "calculated over the shield's edge" <note>original: *über Schildsrand gerechnet*</note>, meaning he has charged far too much in total. Regarding helm-covers, silk bands, helmet-straps, and shield-straps (*loris clypeorum*), one may read Goldast, *Alemannic Matters*, in the *Adversaria* to the history of Eckard the Younger, chapter 5, page 196, part 1, volume 1. Fabron. in the *Report on the Origin of Coats of Arms* regarding the Hessian armorial book of Wesselius and Spangenberg, book 6, regarding broken shields and helmets. Stumphius, book 6, *Chronicle*, chapter 25; book 7, chapter 37.

### 34. Shield-Fief. Feudum scutiferum.

Sometimes this is taken to mean a "Masculine Fief," as in the following clause: "As a proper male-fief, which we and our male heirs of the fief, now and in the future, shall and will receive, carry, and earn according to the law, custom, and habit of male-fiefs, and as an old ancestral and shield-fief <note>original: *Vätter-und Schildlehen*</note>."

But I believe it is also taken to mean a noble fief that one must serve as a "shield-companion" (*Schildgenoß*). There is also Title 4 of the Feudal Laws, section 74, regarding the fiefs of shield-bearers <note>original: *de Feudis Scutiferorum*</note>.

Hereditary succession leads to that well-known clause in female fiefs <note>original Latin: *feudis foemininis*, referring to fiefs that could be inherited by daughters</note> and those passing to any heirs whatsoever: *Yet that to us and our heirs, should it fall to us, there shall always be given a liegeman who is a peer of the coat of arms from the nobility <note>original German: "Wappensgenoß von Adel"</note>, who shall man the fief and do for us as much as a liegeman should do for his feudal lord by right and custom, etc.*

And it should be noted that "to have a shield and coat of arms" is taken to mean "to be Noble": for in ancient times, only the Noble Squires <term>Edelknecht: a term for a member of the lower nobility who had not yet been knighted</term> who held a shield and performed military service were called *Squires* or *Weapon-bearers* <note>original: "Escuyers" (French) and "Waffenträger" (German)</note>. This was not because they carried weapons for others, but because they themselves bore arms. Hence, heraldic "insignia" are called "arms."

->ADDITION.<-

"Shield-fiefs" and "Free-fiefs" are synonyms, according to Besold, *Part 5, Counsel 231, number 14.* This is nothing other than what is called a "Squire’s Fief" <note>original Latin: *Feudum Scutiferi*</note> in the *Books of Fiefs, book 4, title 74*, as the same author teaches in the cited passage, number 16. Indeed, among writers of German history, a "Squire" <note>original Latin: *Scutifer*</note> is he whom the Germans formerly called an *Edelknecht*—that is, a Nobleman not yet honored with the dignity of Knighthood. Likewise, a "Squire’s Fief" is a Noble Fief, which is contrasted with a "Burgher’s Fief" <note>original German: "einem gemeinen Burgerlehen"</note>, as well as with a fief granted by the delivery of a banner, called a "Banner-fief" <note>original German: "Fahnenlehen"</note>, which has an illustrious dignity attached to it. See more in Mr. Speidel's *Notable Mirror, page 1115.*

### 35. Sentries. Watches.

When a camp is measured out, watches <note>original Latin: *excubiae*</note> must be placed around it, which are either by day or by night; soldiers should undergo both in turns. The General, moreover, should ensure that the appointed guards are visited from time to time, and for that reason, he should receive military tokens <term>tesseras militares: small tablets or passwords used by the Romans to verify that a guard was at his post</term> from them during his rounds. Peter Gregory of Toulouse says that the Romans diligently observed this in *The Republic, book 6, chapter 9, section 9.* Add Schröder in Arumaeus, *volume 1, discourse 23, on the law of war, thesis 5, letter c.* However, if these guards are found to be lazy in their duty, they are subject to capital punishment, *according to the law regarding sentries in military affairs*, nor is there any excuse for negligence. Vegetius, *book 3, chapter 5.* Hence, some praise Epaminondas the Theban because, while walking the rounds of the watch during a time of great danger, he found a guard sleeping and ran him through with his sword, asserting: "I found a man dead [in his duty], and I left him dead." Franciscus Patricius, *book 9, title 3.* The Spanish do not punish the negligent with a milder penalty; they throw one found sleeping at his post from the walls or the rock upon which he was keeping watch. Schröder, in the place cited, alleging Ayala, *On the Law of War, book 3, chapter 17, number 3.*

Furthermore, Monluc notes somewhere in *his history* that there is no watch more secure, nor one that perceives the enemy more accurately from afar, than if the guards lie on the ground and apply an ear to the earth.

<column-break/>

As to whom the guarding of a City belongs—whether to the Lord or to the Community—see Peter Fontanella *in the treatise on prenuptial agreements, clause 4, glossary 10, part 2, where he discusses this at number 17 and following.* He teaches that the custody of the city keys, as well as the election of the Guards, pertains to the City Councilors <term>Decuriones: administrative officials or members of a municipal senate</term>, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

He who leaves the sentry post <note>original German: "Schildwacht"</note> before he is relieved shall die, unless it be that the enemy drives him back. In *Dutch Military Law, page 148 and page 89*, there is a discussion regarding a soldier who is found sleeping on his sentry or watch post. Sentries <note>original: "Sentinellen"</note> are so named from "perceiving" <note>Latin: "sentiendo"</note>; in Latin they are called "those who lie out in front" <note>Latin: "praecubitores" or "procubitores"</note> and the "first guards." In more recent Greek they are named *skaptrai* <note>original: <unclear>σκάπται</unclear></note>; by others, *prophylakes* <note>original: <unclear>προσφύλακες</unclear></note> or "outer guards" <note>original: <unclear>ἐξωφύλα</unclear></note>.

See Mr. Harsdörffer in his *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories, title 47, regarding strong soldiers, numbers 4 and 5.* If a castle to which watch-duties were owed is destroyed, see Boer, decision 212, number 14, on whether the duties are owed to the replacement.

### 36. Letter of Protection. Letters of Safeguard.

Those letters by which execution of a judgment is requested are called *Schirmbrieff* <note>literally "Shield-brief" or "Letter of Protection"</note>, when in the Court of Rottweil <note>an Imperial High Court</note>, etc., a summons by edict <note>German: "Beleitung"</note> is followed by an "introduction" or "seizure of property" <note>German: "Anleitung"</note> resulting from a first Decree. If no one appears, a right is obtained which has the force of a seizure under the second Decree, and concerning this, a *Schirmbrieff* is given to the local authorities where the property is located, who are then bound to execute it. *See above under the word* "Anleiten."

Consequently, those Magistrates are called "Protection-lords" <note>German: "Schirmherren"</note> who are implored by the judges of the Consistory of Rottweil and other Provincial Tribunals to carry out the execution after a sentence of Banning has been passed against someone, and after the seizure of property from the first and second Decrees (the former of which they call *Anleiten*, the latter *erlangt Recht*). For those executors are called "Lords of Shelter and Protection" <note>German: "Schuß- und Schirmherren"</note>, that is, "Lords of Entry." *Rottweil Court Ordinances, page 2, title 13.*

Furthermore, "Letters of Shelter and Protection" <note>German: "Schuh- und Schirmbrieff"</note> also refer to privileges of protection which the Emperor occasionally grants even to private persons. These are commonly called "Letters of Safeguard" <note>Latin: "literæ Salvaguardiæ"</note>, stating that they, their children, and their property shall be under the protection and shelter <note>German: "Schutz und Schirm"</note> of the Imperial Majesty and the Holy Roman Empire. Hence, anyone offending such a person who has security from the Emperor is said to commit the crime of Treason <note>Latin: "læsæ Majestatis"</note>; see Gigas *in the treatise on the Crime of Treason, folio 48.* These letters of safeguard, or *Schutz- und Schirmbrieff*, are also sometimes letters of insurance or safe-conduct.

### 37. Sleep, Sleepwalkers. *Somnus, Noctambulo.*

Concerning those who sleep and walk in their sleep, as well as the lethargic, the comatose, those in a deep stupor, and all kinds of drowsy persons, see by all means Paolo Zacchia in *Medico-Legal Questions, book 2, title 1, questions 12 and 13.*

->ADDITION.<-

Mr. Speidel, in the *Speculum*, and above under the word ***Night***.

Augustus Vischer, in *On the Duel, page 593 (in my copy)*, lists a great number of authors who should be consulted regarding walking about in one’s sleep. Among these, the foremost are Philippus Theophrastus <note>The famous physician Paracelsus</note> and Jacobus Horstius, who wrote a specific book on sleepwalkers. Sleepwalkers are people of an unequal "complexion" <term>Complexion: in medieval medicine, the balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</term>, having either too much cold or moisture, or both together in the brain. Thus, while they are in a very deep sleep, their senses and some movements are suspended; yet they possess a hotter and drier heart and liver. The heat of their seething blood and the agility of their "spirits" <note>The "vital spirits" believed to carry commands from the brain to the muscles</note> make the mind, brain, and other organs of movement very ready to move themselves spontaneously to perform various tasks from place to place. Augustus Vischer, in his treatise *On the Unforeseen Duel, page 587 and following*, lists what the causes of sleepwalking are. He also discusses why such people are stronger while sleeping, so that they climb and penetrate places which they could never have reached while awake; and why they approach precipitous places, otherwise extremely dangerous, without danger or falling. Vischer, in the said treatise, page 589. Is it true, as some write, that if a sleepwalker is called out to by his own name, he falls into immediate danger because of that very calling of his proper name? Levinus Lemnius thinks so in *On the Occult Miracles of Nature, book 2, chapter 5, folio 168*, but Vischer disagrees in the said treatise on page 

<column-break/>

590 (in my copy); and on page 591, he recounts examples that are amazing and worthy of reading.

Regarding what promotes sleep, see Zeiler, *century 4, question 87, page 442 and following.* **On the sleeping-sickness** <note>original German: *Von der Schlaffsucht*</note>, see Mr. Harsdörffer in *The Great Theatre of Joyous and Instructive Histories, volume 196, throughout.* **On the Seven Sleepers** <note>original German: *Siebenschläffern*; likely referring to the legend of the youths of Ephesus</note>, the same author, *volume 114, throughout.* On the midday nap, see Mr. G. Richter at length in his *Letters, pages 574 and 580.*

### 38. Silesia. *Silesia.*

There are those who derive the name of Silesia from the Slesa (also called the Elsa) river. Someone else thinks it is so named as if it were a **Closure** <note>original German: *Schluss*</note> from the Latin word *Clausa*, that is, a "lock" or in our own dialect a "sluice" <note>original German: *Schleuß*</note>, because it "closes" Germany off as a kind of fortification and bulwark against the incursions of the Sarmatians and Tatars. Dubravius, however, is the authority for the idea that it was first so named by the Slavic Bohemians. Seeing the Poles, Meisseners, Pomeranians, people of the March <note>Brandenburg</note>, and other miscellaneous crowds "creeping" into that area and gradually stealing in, they began to call them **Slesitas** from the word for "creeping" in their native tongue. Finally, he derives "Sudetes" <note>The mountain range</note> from the Slavic word *Slezack*, meaning a "stranger" or "newcomer," by a plausible conjecture. The names **Slesiazia** and **Slesizia** found in Slavic monuments seem to agree with this. Mr. Goldast, *On Bohemia, book 1, chapter 14, number 3.*

But concerning this illustrious Province, see Curaeus and Henelius in their particular histories. Schifordeggher also has certain things in his treatises toward the end.

The Kings in Bohemia style themselves **Supreme Dukes and Land-Princes in Upper and Lower Silesia**; the other principalities are described as incorporated into and subject to the Crown of Bohemia.

On whether Silesia uses **Saxon Law**? <note>original German: *Sachsen-Recht*</note> See above under the word ***Saxon Law*** and Treutler, *disputation 1, thesis 10.* In a confirmation by Rudolph II concerning a Silesian marriage contract, His Majesty refers back to the customary Saxon Law of the land.

On Silesian Fiefs, see Curaeus, *On Silesia, folio 303.*

->ADDITION.<-

Hendel wrote a *Silesiographia* <note>A description of Silesia</note>, according to Mr. Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire, chapter 25, page 271.* On the name of Silesia, see Limnaeus in *Public Law, book 3, chapter 8, numbers 77 and 78.* In the Silesian Knightly Court, or the **Silesian Knightly Law and Court of Honor** <note>original German: *Schlesischen Ritterrecht und Ehrengericht*</note> in Volckmann (which Silesia preserves for itself as a supreme royal right and the touchstone of true Nobility), before anyone is admitted—before he steps before the **Knights' Bench** <note>original German: *Ritterbanck*</note>—he is compelled to lay down his sword. Georg Wentzki, *On Silesian Knightly Law and the Court of Honor, page 97.*

# Letter S.

> Ass-eaters they once called the Silesians,
> The cause of the matter was a question long born.
> Near Reichenstein <note>A town in Lower Silesia known for gold mining; modern Złoty Stok</note> is a mountain rich in gold and mines:
> Here was a "Golden Ass" so named.
> Because only the Silesians held these mines,
> They carry the name as if they were eaters of the ass.

See Zeiller in *Travels through Germany*, page 505. The Princes of Silesia are divided into 14 Duchies, each of which was given its name from its capital city. Kniptschild, *On Entails*, chapter 1, numbers 18 and 124. They are not "immediate" <note>In the Holy Roman Empire, "immediate" status meant answering only to the Emperor, without an intermediate lord</note> but recognize the King of Bohemia as their superior lord. Ibid, number 124. There is a double nobility in Silesia: one which recognizes the superior administration—commonly called the **High Office** <note>original German: *das Oberambt*</note>—together with the King of Bohemia, which is commonly called **the Eleven Estates** <note>original German: *die eilff Stände*</note>, and which has no seat in the Provincial assemblies. The other nobility, however, which lives under the Princes, has the right to a seat in the said assemblies. Regarding the office in Silesia which they call the **High Captaincy** <note>original German: *die oberste Hauptmannschaft*</note>, see Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire*, page 264. Concerning Breslau <note>Modern Wrocław</note>, the same author on page 264 and following notes that it is the capital city of Silesia and formerly had its own special Dukes; upon their deaths, it returned to the Kings of Bohemia by right of direct lordship in the year 1337.

How Silesia came to the Empire. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Reports, part 3, page 24.*

How Silesia was drawn to the Polish Crown. *Part 6, page 132.*

The Austrian nobles of Mastmünster are bound, in times of hostility, to go to the town of Ensisheim <note>original: *Enshelm*</note> and to hold and open its keys. *Jal. on Fiefs, last part, number 13.* Schrad, *On Fiefs, part 1, chapter 2, number 49.* The keys of St. Peter are given, along with herbs and wheat. The Escurial Palace <note>The royal site in Spain</note> has 14,000 doors, and for these, 700 pounds <note>original: *7 Centner*</note> of keys. "Locks should not at all times open locks." Zeiller, *Epistles, continuation 4, page 6.* It is said there were two twins in Austria who possessed such a quality that if they merely touched doors with the side of their bodies or bumped against them, the locks would open. Langius in *Miscellany 1, Epistle 35.* Keys should remain with the Elder. Höpingk *On Seals, chapter 6, number 28.* On the delivery of keys, see extensively Cyprian *On Betrothals, chapter 5, question 14, number 2.* Rittersh. in *Novels, page 227.* Possession is not transferred by the bare delivery of keys and documents, unless the delivery is made with the intent <note>original: *animo*</note> of delivering and acquiring possession. Christoph Philipp Richter in *Counsels, part 4, chapter 16, number 61, folio 104.* Possession is acquired neither by intent alone, nor by physical act <note>original: *corpore*</note> alone, but by intent and physical act together, *law "possideri" 3, section Besold Volume I.*

<column-break/>

*1. Digest, on acquiring or losing possession.* However, when the intent is expressly established, then one must see whether a title preceded it; if not, by the delivery of keys or documents, possession is not transferred, but only custody. Joseph Mascard. *Volume 3, On Evidence, Conclusion 298, number 12.* No logical conclusion holds from the delivery of keys to the induction of possession. It does not follow that because she handed him the keys during her lifetime, and the letters belonging to the estate, that she therefore and by that very act immediately delivered possession to him. This is especially true since administrators of others' property, tenants, curators, and proxies are entrusted with keys and respectively with letters and seals to use them in administration and to defend themselves in litigation, yet they can by no means obtain or acquire possession through this. When a key is lost and a new one is made, something must be added. Höpingk *On the Right of Seals, chapter 14, number 179.* One who retains the general key remains in possession. Keys are said to be a part of the thing itself. Bullæus in *Counsels, page 326.* Divorce <note>original: *repudium*</note> was performed by the taking away of keys. Rittersh. in *Novels, page 227, number 1.* Concerning the keys to the gates and doors at Trier, Limn. in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 48, page 345, in the Addition.* When the key to stolen property is found on someone. *Supplement to Wehner, page 34.*

In Cologne, there was constant strife with the Bishop, wherefore once Emperor Rudolph I commanded that the city keys be carried two miles from the city, and a battle be fought over them with the Bishop’s people. Then the city, after great bloodshed, maintained its right, its keys, and its city government. Limn. in *Public Law, volume 1, Addition to book 7, chapter 10, page 217.* On carrying keys to meet someone, see Limn. *volume 1, Addition to book 5, chapter 4, page 728.* Imperial Cities offer the keys of their gates to the arriving Emperor. Knipschild *On Imperial Cities, book 2, chapter 1, numbers 49 & 67.*

In Aachen, the "Christofelsen" <note>Likely a reference to a specific patrician family or office-holding group</note> are those who for the most part occupy the Electoral Court and keep the keys. Limn. *volume 2, Addition to book 7, chapter 2, page 83.*

Concerning breaking and entering by means of a "laconic" or counterfeit key, using a picklock or a thief’s key <note>original German: *Dieterich oder Diebschlüssel*</note>, see Carpzov, *Criminal Questions, part 2, question 79, number 41.* Menoch. *5, Presumption 31, number 17.* Mr. Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings, page 481.* Concerning the keys to the Castle of Pressburg <note>Modern Bratislava</note>, which seven Hungarian lords have, each one individually, so that no one can enter without the others. Martin Zeiller in *Travels through Hungary, page 203.* If counterfeit keys or other instruments of that kind, suitable for opening locks, are found on someone, is it evidence of a committed theft? Bocer *On Inquiries and Torture, page 226, number 14.* One might not find the key to the law until both parties have become poor or even entirely ruined.

In Mr. Plater’s Cabinet of Curiosities, there is a model of an Italian lock; it is said that an Italian man, being jealous of his wife, locked his wife—*in that part where she was a woman* <note>original: *eâ parte, qua mulier erat*</note>—when he traveled away, and thereby demonstrated a singular invention. Regarding such a "lock of chastity," see Zeiller’s *Travels through Italy*, page 63 at the end and page 64 at the beginning. This account agrees entirely with the instrument shown to me in Basel; and that lock of chastity shown to me is said to have been made by a person from Nuremberg. When keys are handed over at the house, the heir immediately acquires ownership and possession. Bullæus, *Legal Counsel* 8, number 75. An innkeeper is by no means freed from the duty of providing custody just because he handed the key to a guest's chamber or bedroom, according to the opinion of the Gloss and Bartolus on the Law 7, number 1 of the Digest regarding sailors, innkeepers, and stable-keepers; and Baldus on the Title of the Code regarding deposits, and on Law 4 of the Code regarding hiring. To this must certainly be added what our Master Scheurelius advises in his *Inaugural Disputation on Inns*, section 142, citing Rebuffus’s *Treatise on Inns*, numbers 9 and 10: because this class of men usually possesses several keys for a single bedroom or chest, etc. If a depositor says a valise was opened by a counterfeit key <note>original: *clavem adulterinam*</note>, the depositor cannot merely swear an oath to prove this but must prove it through witnesses. Carocius, *On Deposits*, part 1, title on the oath in litigation, number 36. Regarding the Custody of the Keys to City Gates, see Nicolaus Boerius of Bordeaux, volume 16, folio 181.

Keys signify lordship and the full power to open and shut; for which reason they were also attributed to the two-faced Janus <note>The Roman god of beginnings, gates, and transitions</note>. Regarding the locksmith's trade, see Limnäus in *Public Law*, volume 1, Addition to book 4, chapter 8, page 636.

### 40. Castles. <note>original: *Schlösser. Castra.*</note>

Medieval writers take "Castle" <note>Latin: *Castrum*</note> to mean a town, such as the Castle of Valenciennes, the Castle of Ghent, the Castle of Leuven, and similar places. Aubertus Miræus, *Codex of Donations*, chapter 6, folio 29.

One who simply sells and grants a thing is seen to grant and sell it with its inherent connections. Digest, title on rural servitudes; on the sale of slaves; and the Code on servitudes and water. Therefore, when a Castle is sold, its Court and Jurisdiction <note>The legal right to hold court and exercise authority</note> are also seen to be sold with all its appurtenances. Digest, title on the action of purchase.

However, when a Castle is sold, mills that belong to the community are not included: because only the castle itself is considered sold along with the jurisdiction inherent to that Castle or Village. Romanus, *Counsel* 444. Crotus, *Counsel* 55, number 15. I would say otherwise if the Castle had been sold

<column-break/>

with all its rights and appurtenances, provided that the mills were not privately owned; based on the text with the Gloss in Law 10 of the Digest regarding precautions, where the possession and ownership of all the goods of one who is adopted pass to the adopter without any physical seizure.

But if a territory is sold, are the Castles and towns of that territory also considered to be relinquished and sold? I answer that a Castle is not considered sold: because a Castle and a territory differ greatly from one another, and one does not fall under the name of the other, as judged by Baldus, title on those who sell the Court, column 4, number 7; and Alexander on Law 3, number 27, and there Aretinus at the end, Digest on acquiring possession. These agree with the statements by Bartolus and others in the Code on the jurisdiction of all judges. Paris, *Counsel* 20, number 58, book 1. Gozadinus, *Counsel* 5, column 1. For if a Castle were to fall under the name of "Territory," it would be as if to say that the accessory item pulls the principal item along with it.

Thus, even in the simple granting and possession of some Castle, the right of Territory and superiority <note>The highest authority or sovereignty over a region</note> is not immediately granted, since a Castle can belong to one person, and yet the supreme power belongs to another. Charles Molinæus on the *Customs of Paris*, title 1, section 1, gloss 5, number 55; and Antonius Peregrinus in the *Treatise on the Rights of the Fisc*, book 1, title 2. For it does not follow: "He has the Castle; therefore he also has the territory or jurisdiction." Bidembach, *Questions on Nobility* 1, number 22 and following. Hieronymus de Monte, in the *Treatise on Boundary Regulation*, chapter 78, number 14. Knichen, *On Saxon Law*, under the word "Dukes," chapter 4, number 63.

Castles that are not attached to Cities, even if they do not have "pure power" <note>original: *merum Imperium*; the highest level of judicial authority, including the power of life and death</note>, nevertheless have that jurisdiction which the defenders of cities exercise, as Obrecht delivers after Bartolus in *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 6, number 66. Moreover, that Jurisdiction, from the Code on City Defenders and on magistrates, number 8, is joined with "mixed power" <note>original: *mixto Imperio*; jurisdiction over civil matters and lesser crimes</note>, through the New Constitutions 8, and the Digest on the office of the judge. Obrecht, said chapter 6, number 63; to which Rosenthal also tends in *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 6.

The jurisdiction of a Castle and a territory is in itself one incorporeal thing, and consequently indivisible. Oldradus, *Counsel* 121, number 16. Hence, jurisdiction in a territory depends indeed upon the jurisdiction in the Castle, as if from a head—just as water which is drawn from a reservoir <note>original: *Castello*; here meaning a water tower or cistern</note> depends upon that reservoir. Oldradus, *Counsel* 121, number 15. But on the other hand, it is in everyone's mouth that the accessory does not flow into the principal. Pacianus, *On Proofs*, book 1, chapter 27, number 23. From which it follows that a benefit granted to a village of some territory is not extended to the Castle of that territory and the territory itself.

Varro, book 4 of *On the Latin Language*. Among the Greeks, a citadel of this kind is called an *Akropolis*, that is, a high...

### 41. Insults. Cases of Slander. <note>original: *Schmachsachen. Causæ injuriarum.*</note>

If a defendant is acquitted, the plaintiff is not necessarily marked with infamy <note>term: *infamia*; a loss of legal standing or reputation</note>; the text is found in Law 3 of the Code regarding false accusations. Wurmser, decision 19, book 1. Bartolus, counsel 111, where he concludes that a "reservation of honor" can be made even if the defendant is acquitted. Meichsner, decision 4, folio 32, volume 1. Calvolus in *Practice* 51, conclusion 12, number 5.
A person who insults another is not excused by claiming they are merely repeating what they heard. Although such a defense exists, the disease of detraction is a plague; through this kind of whispering, **rumor acquires strength as it goes** <note>original: *fama vires acquirat eundo*; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note>, even if the intent to injure or defame was absent (and how much more so if it were present) in the one of whom it was spoken. Marquard Freher, *Treatise on Reputation*, book 2, chapter 9, number 16 and following; Law 15, section 2 of the Digest regarding injuries. Furthermore, even one who utters injurious words only conditionally is held liable for injury, as per the text in Law "Condition" 100 and Law 120 of the Digest regarding Verbal Obligations. Hence, Zasius records that he used this text to refute an opposing advocate, as noted by Mr. Bocer, class 3, disputation 4, of Besold’s first volume.

<column-break/>

thesis 28, letter d. Is a person infamous if they apologize for an injury or reach a settlement with the injured party? See Kirchov, volume 5, counsel 9. Regarding one who boasts of having "known a woman carnally" <note>original: *carnaliter cognovisse*; a euphemism for sexual relations</note>, see Mr. Bullæus in *Pentad of Counsels*, counsel 3.
Does a legal petition offered in the Imperial Chamber have the force of a "joinder of issue" <note>term: *litis contestatio*; the formal start of a trial after the initial pleadings</note> and make an action for injury perpetual? Rutger Ruland, *On the Process of Ferrari Montanus*, folio 84.
Regarding what some say—that the truth of an accusation excuses the injury—it is required that the crime was truly committed and not previously known or manifest; otherwise, it is not excused, as handed down by Andreas Gail, 2, observation 99, and Græven, conclusion 99, number 8 and following.
Concerning the words, **"he has taken what belongs to me,"** <note>original German: *er hat mir das Meinige genommen*</note> see Uranius, volume 3, folio 301, number 2.
In the Republic of Ulm, a person is held liable for injury if they say to any woman, **"you beautiful woman."** <note>original German: *du schöne Frau*</note> See Uranius, volume 3, folio 299, number 37.
Regarding injuries, see my own *Disputations* on this matter, which are found in volume 2 of the Tübingen disputations.

### 42. Graft. Judicial Bribery. <note>original: *Schmiraken. Barataria.*</note>

Since bribery and the reception of gifts are done by a judge clandestinely, for that reason, proofs are admitted that would otherwise not be admitted at all; according to the writings of Joseph de Sesfè, *Aragonese Decisions* 214. There, in number 2, he says that although even a thousand individual witnesses might not provide proof, three witnesses testifying to a specific or individual act are sufficient to prove a judge's bribery, because of the sophisticated frauds used by a judge committing such a crime.

->ADDITION.<-

*Baratare*, that is, to squander or alienate, from the Italian *baratare*, to exchange. Regarding bribery committed by a judge or his advisors, see Mr. Speidel in *Notables*, letter S, number 85. When something is given to a judge so that he might expedite a matter more quickly, he by no means incurs the charge of bribery: for this gift is not considered to be for the purpose of corrupting the judge. See Spórmacher, *On Wounded Justice*, part 2, title 3, chapter 4, page 587; Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrations*, question/case 342, 343.

### Formal Release of Debt. Imaginaria solutio.

A formal release <note>original: Acceptilatio; a verbal contract in Roman law where a creditor discharges a debtor without payment</note> is an imaginary payment. Schneidewein on the *Institutes*, page 562. Petrus Gregorius Tholofanus, book 21, *System of Universal Law*, chapter 19, throughout. An invalid formal release is still valid as a pact or agreement. Rittershusius in *The Novels*, page 154, number 5. On the presentation of formal releases, page 13, number 6. A formal release stops the accrual of interest. Ummius, *Disputations on Process* 21, thesis 8, number 45. A formal release cancels a legal action. Christian Lenz, *On the Transfer of Names and Actions*, chapter 32, member 5, number 9; when it may occur, see the same, number 8. The defense of formal release is "real" <note>attaches to the debt itself</note>, number 7. A transferee <note>someone who bought the debt</note> can be barred by this defense, number 10. Regarding defenses against a formal release, Nicolaus Vigelius is very extensive and diligent in *Method of Civil Law*, part 7, book 24, chapter 11, number 5. 
1. The defense holds unless someone other than the Creditor gave the release. 
2. Unless only one of two or more Creditors gave the release. 
3. Unless a ward <note>minor under guardianship</note> gave the release. 
4. Unless a servant <note>or slave</note> gave the release. 
5. Unless it was given to someone other than the debtor. 
6. Unless it was given to a servant. 
7. Unless it was given to a son under paternal power. 
8. Unless it was given to a ward. 
9. Unless it was given to only one of several debtors for the same thing. 
10. Unless a husband gave it to his wife. See these and the following, up to the 26th Defense, extensively in that location.

There is a twofold prerogative of **Written-Subjects** over **District-Subjects** <note>original: *Amtfassiis*</note>. ### 48. Weight and Fineness. <note>original: *Schrott und Korn*. The intrinsic goodness of money.</note>

The intrinsic goodness of currencies consists in two things: namely, in the alloy <note>original: *ligâ*; see Budelius, book 1, chapter 8</note> or the preciousness of the material, and in the weight. We Germans, speaking popularly, say: "In content and weight" <note>original: *Im Gehalt und Gewicht*</note>, or "in weight and fineness" <note>original: *im Schrott und Korn*</note>. For "alloy" <note>original: *Liga*</note> here is nothing else in German than "content and fineness" <note>original: *Gehalt und Korn*</note>. Indeed, just as a kernel is in the husk, so gold or quicksilver [silver] is in the copper. Valentinian calls this the "appearance" <note>original: *speciem*</note> in law 1 of the Code *on ancient metal money*. Weight <note>original: *Pondus*</note> is truly "weight or scrap" <note>original: *Gewicht oder Schrott*</note>, from "scrapping" or "cutting off" <note>original: *Schrotten oder Abschneiden*</note>. Hence we say payment ought to be made according to the intrinsic goodness that existed at the time of the contract, that is, in **weight and fineness** <note>original: *Schrott und Korn*</note>, as they were given or prescribed. Budelius, *On Money*, book 1, chapter 7, number 3. Gail, book 2, observation 73.

<column-break/>

on the paragraph "of good faith," number 33, *Institutes on Actions*. Gail, book 2, observation 73, number 7.

The extrinsic goodness of money, however, is what is contained in the estimation, value, currency, and use of the coin. We Germans call it the **Value of the Coin** <note>original: *den Werth der Münze*</note>. Schneidewin, on the said paragraph "of good faith," number 33. "How the coin is current and valid" <note>original: *Wie die Münze gäng und geb ist*</note>. Fichard, *Consultations* 46, volume 2. The Academy of Leipzig, *Consultations* 27, among the *Consultations of Modestinus Pistoris*, volume 2. Whether the quantity of money denotes the value of money, see Johann Robert, book 3, chapter 6, where more things pertaining to this are found.

Auer, *On the Law of Money*, thesis 34. When the **weight and fineness**, and thus the intrinsic goodness of the coin, is changed, thesis 102. Regarding hard Thalers, good in **weight and fineness**, thesis 108. And it is called "quality" <note>original: *qualitas*</note> in law 7 *on the usufruct of those things which are consumed by use*; law 2 of the Code *on weights*, book 10; law 2 of the Code *on ancient metal money*. In German: "Fineness of content" <note>original: *Korngehält*</note>, or "that which holds in the assay" <note>original: *der hält in der Prob*</note>, "weight" <note>original: *Schrott*</note>. In Saxon: "The White" <note>original: *das Witte*</note>.

Concerning the words **Weight and Fineness** <note>original: *Schrott und Korn*</note>, see Matthias Berlich, book 2, conclusion 35, numbers 5 and following; and at number 40, conclusion 39, when the bodies [coins] are borrowed piece by piece. Since the smaller coins were weakened in alloy and weight, it was enjoined upon the States that no more smaller coins at all should be minted, and finally that the minters <note>original: *monetarii*</note> should be held accountable, as witnessed by Mr. Achatius Hülsen in his *Reflections on Money* from the year 1606. ### 49. Debts. <note>original: *Schulden. Debita.*</note>

The word **Debt** <note>original: *Schulde*</note> is used most widely and encompasses absolutely all debts, whether they arise from a contract or from a legal wrong <note>original: *delicto*</note>. See the law "debtor" in the Digest *on the Significance of Words*; the second to last paragraph of the Institutes *on the penalty for reckless litigation*; the law "but whether" in the Digest *on seeking an inheritance*; the law "peculium," paragraph "if the slave himself" in the Digest *on the peculium*; the last law of the Code *on those who cannot manumit*; the law "he who in fraud," paragraph "from all" in the Digest *on who and by what causes*; the law "if a trust," paragraph "lest anyone" in the same; the law "according to Julian" at the end, in the Digest *on the causes for which one enters into possession*. Furthermore, even he who can be sued by an action for a thing <note>original: *actione in rem*; a claim for property</note> is said to be a debtor, at least in a broad sense, as Bartolus teaches on the law "dominion" in the Code *on that which is done with him*. Likewise, it is not a matter of doubt that by the naming of a debt, those debts are also included in respect of which a legal action has been instituted in Court, and which has proceeded not only to the joinder of issue <note>original: *litis contestationem*</note> but even further. *Legal Acts of the City of Braunschweig concerning the Oath of Allegiance*, part 2, folio 62, number 70.

Regarding when execution [of a judgment] occurs in the matter of debts, see Lord Doctor Biccius in *Aureis*, section 5, thesis 157. There is a common German saying: **Old debt does not rust.** <note>original: *Alte Schuld rostet nicht*; meaning that the obligation to pay does not disappear simply because time has passed.</note> This is cited and explained by Moller, book 2, *Semestria*, chapter 18, number 4, page 170. Whether money is most safely invested in the redemption of debts, **when one acquires a debt-certificate of 100 for 70, 60, or 50?** <note>original: *wann man Schuldbrieff 100. per 70. 60. 50. erhandelt?* This refers to buying debt at a discount, a form of speculation.</note> It seems so to many through the teaching of Gomez, *Resolutions*, book 2, resolution 2, number 6, because this is both permitted by law—law *Nomina eorum* 17, *Regarding Inheritances or Actions*—and it is useful, since all the rights and profit of the seller pass to the buyer, law *Emtori* 6, *Regarding the Sale of Inheritances or Actions*. But the buying of debts easily leads one into suspicion of **Sycophancy** <note>original: *Sycophantiæ*; here meaning malicious litigation or "buying into" a lawsuit</note>, and sometimes nothing beyond the sum actually paid for them can be extorted by the redeemer, see Wesenbeck’s *Paratitla* on the sale of inheritances or actions, through law 22 and the final law of the Code *Regarding Mandates*. See Cujacius, volume 6, observation 16; however, for those redeemers, see Hilliger on Donellus, commentary 13, 43, letter E. These excuses of debtors are heard daily in the streets and at banquets: **"Other people, princes, lords, and communities also owe me; when they pay me, I will also pay,"** or, **"I am supposed to pay everyone, but no one wants to pay me."** Hirschfeld in *Inaugural Disputation on Exceptions*, page 5, thesis 6. **One debt does not hinder another**, Zoier, part 1, question 9, number 620. **When a debt is bought for half or a smaller part at a low price, whether such a thing is allowed and not to be held as usury?** Zoier, part 2, question 15, number 1012 and following. **When someone in these times sells a bond for 400 Guilders which states 1000 Guilders, whether the buyer can claim a legal injury in the future?** <note>original: *læsionem prætendiren*; referring to "laesio enormis" or being cheated out of more than half the value.</note> See *Legal Considerations*, printed at Basel, 1643, question 2. In what manner payment is to be proven can be found in Mascardus, *On Evidence*, volume 3, conclusion 1318, or Menochio, *On Presumptions*, book 3, presumption 35, where they say that for demonstrating payment, conjectural or presumptive proof suffices; see Carpzov, part 2, constitution 29, decisions 11 and 12.

In honor of John of Beverly, Archbishop of York, the town of Beverly grew to a fair size because the right of **Asylum** <note>A place of sanctuary where the law could not seize a person.</note> was granted to the location, which was a free and safe refuge for debtors and those suspected of capital crimes, in which was placed a stone chair with this inscription:

->In every way.<-

An insolvent **Bankrupt** <note>term: *Decoctor* <gloss>Literally "one who has boiled away" his assets; a spendthrift or bankrupt.</gloss></note> who is unable to pay also incurs infamy under Saxon Law, according to Johann Philippi in *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*, book 1, title 6, § 1, selection 41, number 4. And he is punished by the wearing of a **Yellow Hat**, number 5, where: The Elector of Saxony, in the most recent *Resolutions of Provincial Grievances* published in the year 1661, under the title *On Matters of Justice*, § 78, decreed that such bankrupts be affected by the shameful wearing of a yellow-colored hat in these words: **"and where a bankrupt in the said two cities, or other places of our land, could not provide full payment to his creditors, but nevertheless moved them to a voluntary remission and release from imprisonment, in such a case he shall indeed be set at liberty; however, for a period of time, according to the discretion of the ordinary judge, to indicate the evil life he led in negligence and wastefulness, he shall be required to wear a yellow hat, and thereby provide an example to others of his kind to keep house better than he did."** Regarding the "cutting up" of debtors, see Gellius, book 20, chapter 1; Quintilian, book 8 of the *Institutes of Oratory*, chapter 6.

"There are some things," he says, "not laudable by nature, but granted by law, such as the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The ancient foundation of Roman law, c. 450 BCE.</note> which allowed the body of the debtor to be divided among the creditors; a law which public custom later rejected." Tertullian also mentions this in his *Apologeticus*, chapter 4. More can be found in Rittershusius on the *Laws of the XII Tables*, page 210. Also in the *Novels*, page 151, number 20. **Debts with or without a written bond**, Limn. in *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 5, number 61. Whether a debtor, knowing of a transfer, is released by the payment made to the original creditor instead of the new claimant, see Christian Lenz, *On Debts and Assigned Actions*, chapter 31, part 2, number 10 and following.

which also from the <term>Stewards</term> <note>original: *Gastaldiis*; officials in Lombard law who managed royal estates or local districts</note> or <term>Local Officials</term> <note>original: *Schuldasiis*; a Latinized form of the German *Schultheiß*</note>, or the Provosts of a place, according to their own law, etc. It is also called *Schuldaiis* in the **Lombard Law**, title 2: "If anyone has a case and tells his case to his *Schuldais*, and the *Schuldais* himself neglects to provide justice within four days, if both litigants are under one *Schuldais*, then the *Schuldais* himself shall pay 6 gold coins to the one who brought the claim, and 6 gold coins to his Judge."

### § 2. Debt-Tower. Prison for Debtors.

Although under **Civil Law**, a case against a debtor

<column-break/>

should not begin with an arrest <note>original: *captura*</note>, as per the law *ob æs.* 12, *Regarding Obligations and Actions*; rather, the order prescribed by the Divine Pius must be observed in law *à Divo Pio* 15, section *in venditione* 2, *Regarding Judged Matters*. Indeed, according to a constitution of Constantine, even for public debts, one cannot be handed over to prisons. For he says, "The prison is for punishments; it is a prison for criminal men," law 2, *Regarding Exactions*, book 10. Nevertheless, because there is now a great frequency of <term>Bankrupts</term> <note>original: *decoctorum* or *banccarotorum*; literally "those who have boiled away their assets" or "broken their benches"</note>, they are confined in public prisons, **they are placed in the Debt-Tower** <note>original: *auf die Schuld-Thürn gelegt*</note>. See Val. Forstter, *On Jurisdiction*, part 2, my folio 425. The **Saxon Constitution**, second part, title *Regarding the Debt-Tower* <note>original: *vom Schuld-Thurn*</note>, states there:

*If anyone residing in or staying within our lands—whoever they may be—should borrow so much, mismanage people's money, or otherwise become indebted so that all his belongings and goods (after legal assistance, seizure, and execution) are not sufficient or enough for payment; or if he enters into a guarantee beyond his means and cannot obtain a reprieve from his creditors, and if the mentioned creditors cannot be satisfied in any other way: then, at the request and petition of one or more creditors, he shall satisfy them, or otherwise settle and reach an agreement with their good knowledge and will. And no transfer of his goods or <term>Cession of Assets</term> <note>original: *Cession bonorum*; a legal surrender of property to avoid prison</note> which he might perform or undertake without the consent of his creditors shall release or free him from this.*

This is also commonly done in many cities, especially where trade flourishes.

And this prison is assigned to debtors for custody until they pay. It has little or nothing in common with those prisons mentioned above under the word **Prison** <note>original: *Gefängniß*</note>; for it is neither underground nor dark like the prison for criminal men, nor is it imposed as a punishment itself, nor does it aim at punishment or penance. Rather, it is imposed solely for the purpose that the defendant remains for a short time in places or lodgings designated as a prison until he satisfies the Creditor. The Doctors [of Law] call this a **"tedious prison"** <note>original: *carcerem tædialem*; a prison meant to wear down the debtor's resolve through boredom/confinement</note>; see Speckhan, century 1, question 19, at the end. It does not pertain to "High Jurisdiction" <note>original: *merum Imperium*; the power of life and death</note>.

For more matters looking toward this, see Lord Wilhelm Anton in his treatise *On Letters of Moratorium*, chapter 1, number 9, etc.; Beatus in *Decisions*, volume 15, *On Judicial Matters*, part 5, vol. 1, folio 803, etc.; and volume 2, *On Contracts*, part 1, folio 31, regarding whether one can obligate oneself to prison; Hermann Stamm, *On Personal Servitude*, book 1, title 4, chapter 4; and myself in *Select Points of Law*, where I deal with the *Cession of Assets*.

On this word, see Rudinger, century 4, observation 52; Berlich., 2, conclusion 28, throughout. Regarding this "evil dwelling," read by all means Schmuck, *Legal Skirmish* 3, thesis 100.

The *nervus* was also called a "dog" by the ancients, as well as a "pup" or "whelp": just as the Greeks called it *skolax* <note>original: σκόλαξ; literally "puppy," used as a metaphor for a biting restraint.</note>, as noted in the same place.

### 53. **Bond. Written Document.** <note>original: *Schuldverschreibung. Chirographum.*</note>

In <term>guarantees</term> <note>original: *cautionibus*</note> and **Bonds** or **Instruments**, that is, in <term>written debt obligations</term> <note>original: *Schuldverschreibungen*</note>, debtors not infrequently grant and leave to their creditors the power—if the faith of the payment is not kept, that is, *in the event of any non-compliance*—to seek a trial or use the help of a judge. However, this should not be done by leaping from one court to another at will; they renounce the Law "where the case began" <note>original: *Legi ubi cœptum*; a Roman law principle that a case should stay in the court where it started.</note>. Mindanus teaches that this clause is valid, citing his work *On Extraordinary Processes*, book 3, chapter 5. He calls this a "permissive change of judgment," meaning that a trial begun in one place can be pursued and finished in another, or before another judge. Likewise, the debtor can be summoned and arrested in all places at the creditor's whim, without any jurisdictional restriction.

The same holds true if several remedies are permitted to the creditor—for instance, if the power is granted to arrest the person, to seek <term>enforcement mandates</term> <note>original: *Mandata executorialia*</note>, or to seize a pledge on one's own authority. For even then, notwithstanding that the creditor might try one path, they can also move to another when the opportunity arises, until they reach a sufficient payment. This is because those remedies were granted to the creditor’s discretion not as alternatives, but cumulatively, so that they are not at all removed by the initial choice. See Guido Papæ, Council 114, and Coler, *On Executive Process*.

So too is a contract valid which states that, in the event payment is not made by the appointed day, all the debtor’s goods may be <term>sequestered</term> <note>placed in temporary legal custody</note> by the office of the judge, as taught by Mr. Knipschild in *On Contracts*, exercise 4, question 31.

->ADDITION.<-

**Bonds** must contain the true cause of the debt, and the quality and value of the items assigned, otherwise enforcement is not immediately granted, according to Suttinger. Also, such obligations are not ratified by the court beforehand. A **bond** is usually written before the debt is received, according to Dr. Biccius. It is binding if the cause expressed in it followed afterward. If the bonds are burned, debtors who are minors <note>original: *pupillares*</note> can be sued based on the inventory. A bond does not prove itself within two years; after two years,

<column-break/>

it does provide proof, though the defendant still has the right to the <term>exception of money not counted</term> <note>original: *exceptione non numeratæ pecuniæ*; a legal defense where the debtor claims they never actually received the cash they signed for.</note>, according to Dr. Biccius. Interest-bearing guarantees, if they remain with the creditors <note>i.e., if they have been paid off but not returned</note>, shall lose their force; *they will be dead and dry letters.* A <term>unsecured creditor</term> <note>original: *Chirographarius Creditor*</note> correctly pays on behalf of a debtor. Whether a creditor is bound to hand over the debt-claim to an unsecured creditor who offers payment is discussed in Lenz.

Regarding a lost bond, the recovery of the same, and its renewal, see Gail. The loss of a legal document is proven by the creditor’s oath alone, according to Jacob Bornitius. This fails, however, in an excessively difficult case, or if no conjectures or presumptions are present.

### 54. **Swabian Lease. Lease for a fixed time.** <note>original: *Schuppflehen. Locatio ad certum tempus.*</note>

Estates which peasants cultivate, yet in which they have no hereditary right or right of transition to their heirs, are called this in Swabia <note>original: *Suevia*</note>: *Because the heirs are "shoved" away from it* <note>original: *Weil die Erben davon geschupfft werden*; a play on the word *Schuppflehen* and the German *schupfen*, meaning to push or shove.</note>, and after the death of the holder, one of the children must buy the property anew, and even then only for the duration of his own life. They are also called *Fall-Güter* <note>Escheat-lands or falling-estates</note>: because they "fall back" to the lord. These fiefs seem not unlike the <term>precarium</term> <note>A land-holding held by prayer or request, revocable at the will of the owner.</note>. This custom seems to smack of the lordship which either the Romans introduced into Germany or the Franks into Alemannia; see my work *On Monarchy*, page 80.

->ADDITION.<-
See Wehner under this word.

### 55. **Protected Subjects, Lord of Protection and Shield.** <note>original: *Schutz- und Schirmsverwandte, Schutz- und Schirmsherr.*</note>

He is called a **Patron** to whose guardianship, clientele, patronage, and protection a Church, Prince, Count, City, or other Corporation—while still recognizing a Superior and having free administration of its own affairs—subjects, commits, and commends itself together with its subjects and fortunes for a certain fee, while preserving its original power, jurisdiction, liberty, and former Lord. He is commonly designated the **Lord of Protection and Shield** <note>original: *Schutz- und Schirmherr*</note>. From this, the clients do not become subjects, but are called **Protected Subjects** <note>original: *Schutz- und Schirmsverwandte*</note>.

On the other hand, it is also noted that "Protection and Shield," or the reception into the guardianship and patronage of the Empire and the Caesar <note>the Emperor</note>, does not prove <term>immediacy</term> <note>original: *immediatetatem*; the status of being subject only to the Emperor without an intermediate lord.</note>, nor does such reception prejudice a Lord who previously held rights, as is related in the Chronicles...
