### 53. Written Debt Obligation. <term>Chirographum</term> <note>A handwritten bond or document signed by the debtor</note>.

In securities and bonds or legal instruments—**in the written debt obligations**—debtors not infrequently grant and leave to the creditors the power, if the promise of payment is not kept (**in the case of any non-performance**), to seek a trial or use the judge’s aid. However, this should not result in jumping from one court to another at will. They renounce the law "where the case began" <note>original: *Legi ubi cœptum*; a legal principle stating a case should stay where it started</note>, a clause which Mindanus (in *Extraordinary Processes*, book 3, chapter 5) states is valid. He calls this a "permissive change of judgment," meaning a trial begun in one place can be pursued and finished in another, or before another judge, and the debtor can be summoned and arrested in all places at the creditor's whim, without any restriction of jurisdiction.

The same holds true if multiple remedies are permitted to the creditor—for example, if the power is given to arrest, to obtain executive mandates, or to seize a pledge on one's own authority. For even then, despite the fact that the creditor might try one path, he can move to another when the opportunity arises until he reaches a sufficient payment. This is because these remedies are granted to the creditor’s judgment not as alternatives, but as a combined set, so that choosing one does not at all remove the others (according to Guido Papa and others).

Likewise, Lord Knipschild teaches that an agreement is valid stating that, in the event payment is not made by the appointed day, all the debtor's goods may be seized by the office of the judge.

->ADDITION.<-

**Written debt obligations must contain the true cause, and the quality and value of the attached items, otherwise execution of the debt will not be granted immediately**, as noted by Suttinger. Furthermore, such obligations are not ratified by the court beforehand. A bond is usually written before the debt is actually received (Lord Biccius). It becomes binding if the "cause" <note>The underlying reason for the debt, such as a loan or sale</note> expressed in it actually followed. If the bonds are destroyed by fire, the debtors of wards <note>original: *pupillares*; children under guardianship</note> can be sued based on the Inventory. A bond does not prove itself within a two-year period; after two

<column-break/>

years it does provide proof, though the defendant is still allowed the <term>plea of money not paid</term> <note>original: *exceptione non numeratæ pecuniæ*; a defense where the debtor claims they signed the bond but never actually received the money</note>. Usurious securities, if they remain with the creditors after being voided, lose their power; **they shall be dead and dry letters.** A <term>Chirographic Creditor</term> <note>A creditor whose claim is based only on a simple written bond rather than a formal public record</note> correctly pays for a debtor. There is also discussion on whether a creditor is bound to yield to a chirographic creditor who offers to pay the debt.

Regarding a lost bond, its recovery, and its renewal, see Gail. The loss of a legal instrument is proven by the oath of the creditor alone (Bornitius). This fails, however, in excessively difficult cases, or if no conjectures or presumptions are present.

### 54. Shove-Lease. <term>Locatio ad certum tempus</term> <note>A lease for a fixed period</note>.

Estates which peasants cultivate, yet in which they have no hereditary right that can pass to their heirs, are called this in Swabia: **Because the heirs are "shoved" <note>German: *geschupfft*</note> away from it, and after the death of the holder, the property must be bought anew by one of the children, though only for his own lifetime.** They are also called *Fall-Güter* <note>Reversionary estates</note> because they "fall back" to the Lord. These leases seem not unlike the *Precarium* <note>A Roman legal form where land was held by prayer or request, revocable at the will of the owner</note>. This custom seems to reflect the dominion which either the Romans introduced into Germany or the Franks into Alemannia.

->ADDITION.<-

See Wehner under the letter S for this word.

### 55. Protected Dependents and Protector. <term>Clientes, Protector</term>.

A Patron is defined as one to whose guardianship, clientele, sponsorship, and protection a Church, Prince, Count, City, or other community—while still recognizing a Superior and having free administration of its own affairs—submits itself, its subjects, and its fortunes for a certain fee. This is done while preserving their original power, jurisdiction, liberty, and their previous Lord. Such a person is commonly called a **Lord of Protection and Shield** <note>German: *Schutz- und Schirmsherr*</note>. The clients, however, do not become subjects by this arrangement, but are called **Protected Dependents** <note>German: *Schutz- und Schirmsverwandte*</note>.

Conversely, it is taught in the Chronicles that receiving **Protection and Shield**, or being taken into the guardianship and sponsorship of the Emperor and Caesar, does not prove "immediacy" <note>original: *immedietatem*; direct status under the Emperor without an intermediate lord</note>, nor is the Lord who previously held rights prejudiced by such a reception.

### [Advocacy and Protection]

From the *Chronicle of Riddagshausen* <note>A Cistercian monastery in Lower Saxony.</note> by Henricus Meibomius, page 33 and following:

Some local lords <note>original: *Toparchæ*</note>, despite being bound to the defense of monasteries and their subjects, often suppress them. Instead of providing patronage, they attack, trample, plunder, burden, oppress, and whip them, abusing both the people and the property, as well as the privileges and rights of the monasteries. For this reason, they are hatefully called <term>Storm-lords</term> <note>original: *Sturmherrn*</note> by many, instead of <term>Protectors</term> <note>original: *Schirm-herrn*</note>; see Keller, *On Judicial and Political Office*, book 2, chapter 11. Add also the *Necessary Reminder of Donauworth*, part 1, page 10 and following: for indeed, the first step after "protection" is often invasion (Petrus Gregorius, *On the Republic*, book 11, chapter 11, number 6). This leads to a dispute over the respective rights of protection, subjection, and the estimation of jurisdiction (Petrus Frederus, *On Processes in the Chamber*, chapter 14, number 4). Histories everywhere bear witness to this, on which matter one may consult Maulius, *On Homage*, title 11, number 2; and Ziegler, *Common Conclusions*, section on Land-tenants, number 98.

Our Emperors today hold their function from the office of the Patriciate, in that they are the Advocates and Patrons of the Roman Church; they are **Advocates, Defenders, and Protectors of the Christian Church** <note>original: *Advocaten, Beschütz- und Beschirmer der Christlichen Kirchen*</note>. See Draconius, *On the Origin and Right of Patricians*, book 2, final chapter, number 15, page 176. The <term>Right of Advocacy</term> <note>original: *Jus Vogtrecht*</note> belonged to the Emperor as a recognition of his Superiority, which the Emperors used to grant to Princes, Estates, and others.

Furthermore, it is established that the right of Patronage or protection granted to a Patron over his Clients gives him no jurisdiction: hence it is commonly said, **"Protection and defense grant no sovereignty"** <note>original: *Schutz und Schirm gibt kein Obrigkeit*</note>. See Zafius, consultation 7; Gail, observation 54; Natta, consultation 636; and Sixtinus, *On Regalia*, chapter 14.

Consequently, he cannot prescribe the manner of their Religion, nor can he impose taxes <note>original: *collectas*</note> upon them. (Wintzler, *On Taxes*, chapter 21; Gail, observation 54).

Moreover, <term>Defenders</term> <note>original: *Schutz-herrn*</note> are one thing, and <term>Advocates</term> or <term>Chest-Bailiffs</term> <note>original: *Castenvogt*; an official who managed the financial 'chest' of a church or monastery</note> are another. The former are taken on for defense; the latter founded the monasteries, and since they are situated within their territory, they reserved many rights for themselves, and usually territorial Superiority. See Chokier, *On Advocacies*.

The dignity of defense by its nature accompanies Jurisdiction, because Jurisdiction was discovered and established for the sake of defending subjects. Therefore, the Ordinary of a place <note>The local bishop or official with regular jurisdiction.</note>, within his territory—by respect of his general Jurisdiction and by right of the Magistracy—is bound to keep not only his subjects but also foreigners safe, secure, and unharmed from violence and injury. (Petrus Frederus Mindanus, *On Processes*, chapter 14). For superiority is nothing other than protection and defense, by reason of Jurisdiction or the universal governance of a territory (Thomas Michael, *On Jurisdiction*, thesis 44). This right belongs to the Imperial Cities just as it does to other Estates (Dominicus Martinus Mager, *Treatise on Armed Advocacy*, chapter 3).

<column-break/>

number 87. And this ordinary protection, belonging to one by power of superiority, extends not only to temporal things and persons, but also to ecclesiastical ones (Mager, chapter 5 and chapter 9), even if those ecclesiastical goods and persons are otherwise exempt and not subject to superiors (Mager, chapter 8), because exempt places and exempt persons are compared to foreigners (Chokier, *On Ordinary Jurisdiction over the Exempt*, part 2).

For this reason, subjects cannot submit themselves to the protection of another: **Because by doing this, an infringement is made against the Lord of the Land** <note>original: *Dann hierdurch dem Landsherrn ein Eingriff beschicht*</note>.

Whether it is better to be a taxpayer or a Client is taught by Antonius Pippre in *Moral Intentions*, chapter 20. In a time of necessity, **to commit oneself under the protection and defense of a powerful one is laudable** <note>original: *sich unter eines Mächtigen Schutz und Schirm zu begeben, laudabile est*</note>, according to the teachings of Calderinus, discourse 14. But **whether one should submit to one nearby or one far away?** See the same Calderinus, discourse 24 and following. Also, whether a city can subject itself to another by reason of protection? See Chokier, *On Jurisdiction over the Exempt*, question 18.

Regarding the Advocacy of ecclesiastics, monasteries, etc., see also Hospinian, *On Temples*, book 5; Hotman in the *Feudal Lexicon* under the word *Advocatia*; Lehmann, *Chronicle of Speyer*, book 2, chapter 36. See also *Revived Documents of Monasteries in Württemberg*, and above under the word **Kastenvogt**. Monasteries used to take a Defender at their own pleasure; often even the Founders did not reserve the Right of Advocacy for themselves (*Acts of Palatine vs. Kaisersheim*, page 180).

For defense was undertaken for the benefit of the monks, and it could be repudiated again (Crusius, *Annals*, part 2, book 1, page 111).

However, all these things are to be judged based on long-standing custom and the letters of Foundation.

Thus, under the protection of the Austrian Archdukes, by reason of the County of Tyrol, are the Bishops of Aquileia, Brixen, and Trent. (Felix Fabri, *On Swabia*, book 1, chapter 5).

In the Bishoprics of Naumburg, Meissen, and Merseburg, the Electors of Saxony claim the Right of Advocacy for themselves (Hortleder, vol. 1, book 5).

On the Advocacy of the ancients, see the fine work of Caspar Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 47, chapter 4.

Thus Pliny the Younger was created Patron of Tifernum, even as a boy (Book 4, Epistle 1).

Thus also the Palatines often held the patronage of the people of Speyer (Lehmann, final book, chapter 75).

...one part belongs to the Weimar branch, while the other half belongs to the Coburg branch. <note>This refers to the Ernestine duchies of Saxony, which were frequently partitioned between different branches of the family.</note>

Regarding this Patronage, protection, Clientage, or <term>Advocacy</term> <note>original: *Advocatia*; also known as *Vogtei*, the office of a secular lord acting as protector for a church or territory</note>—as it is called in the barbarous tongue—and its first and most ancient origin, and how it has been received through the common use and custom of the entire Roman Empire and approved by the most recent Recesses of the Empire <note>The official resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note>, and indeed concerning its entire legal framework, see: *Bodin, book 1, chapter 7; Mager, in the treatise On Armed Advocacy, throughout; Petrus Gregorius, On the Republic, book 11, chapter 11, number 6; Gail, book 2, observation 54; Althusius, On the Republic, chapter 7, section "similar also"; Matthæus Wesenbeck, counsel 48; Rittershufius, On Feudal Parts, book 5, chapter 2, question 15; Vultejus, On Fiefs, book 1, chapter 8, number 17; Draconius, On the Right and Origin of Patricians, book 1, chapter 6; Ziegler, in the section on Land-tenants, section 1, various places; Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputation 1, page 33, letter r.* To add more after these authors would be nothing but "doing what has already been done," <note>original: *actum agere*; a Latin idiom meaning to waste effort on finished business</note> yet see also my own work, *On Treaties, page 56, etc.*

The following legal Response also pertains to this same matter:

Since here and there in Swabia there are several different free noble villages and estates where a Spiritual or Secular Estate of the Holy Roman Empire has held the **Right of Protection and Shelter** <note>original: *Schutz- und Schirms-Gerechtigkeit*</note> from of old—and in some places even takes the oath of homage from the subjects for that reason—but where, on the other hand, all jurisdiction belongs to the nobleman: the question is asked whether the nobleman may be molested or hindered in his **Exercise of Religion** by such a Protector, or whether any legal entry could be made against him if he wished to change his religion.

To this question, it is rightly answered by *Hermann Esaias Rosacorb, Forensic Practice, chapter 29, near the end*: that Protection and Shelter grants nothing toward the effect of changing Religion, just as neither the **Right of Patronage** <note>original: *Jus Patronatus*; the right to appoint clergy</note> nor **Investiture** <note>the formal act of granting a fief or office</note> achieves anything here; for otherwise, there would be a place for a greater Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction. And this must especially hold true when the issue is not about changing Religion, but preserving it. For that protection, or the right of Advocacy as they call it, does not regularly grant jurisdiction. See *Natta, counsel 636, number 95, volume 3; Gail, book 2, observation 54, number 2 and following; Schurff, counsel 7; German Academy Counsel, volume 4; Wesenbeck, counsel 5, part 1; Wehner, under the word* **Protected-dependents** <note>original: *Schirms-verwandte*</note>. This opinion is confirmed by *Law 7, On Captives and Postliminy, as well as the chapter "Ex Parte" in the Decretals on Privileges.* And the things I said in my *Treatise on Appeals, chapter 4, section 5, and also in the Dissertation on the Law of Treaties, chapter 5, number 12*, also contribute to this point.

Hence, it is a common tradition among interpreters of the Law that through submission to a Protector, no other right is transferred than the right of defending. *Zasius, counsel 7, numbers 6 and 14, volume 2; Caspar Ziegler, section on Land-tenants, conclusion 1.*

<column-break/>

number 82. Consequently, those placed under the protection of another are not called his subjects; for they are referred to as **Clients**, **Protected-Subjects** <note>original: *Schutz-Unterthanen*</note>, and **Protected-Associates** <note>original: *Schutzverwandte*</note>. Therefore, territorial jurisdiction is not proven by Advocacy, or by the right of Clientage or protection—whether it be simple protection or whether it includes the inspection of administration. *Thomas Michael, On Jurisdiction, conclusion 55.* Also, the right of Guardianship is different from Stewardship <note>original: *Vogteja*</note>. *Knichen, On Territorial Right, chapter 4, number 98, etc.* Likewise, territorial power—the **Sovereignty of the Land** <note>original: *die Lands-Obrigkeit*</note>—cannot be proven from this, even if they are called the **Supreme Protectors** <note>original: *die Oberst-Schirmherrn*</note>. *Ruland, On Commissions, book 2, part 4, chapter 13, number 12; Vietor, On Exemptions, conclusion 20*, where he notes from *Natta* that protection is rather an evident sign that Jurisdiction and superiority are *not* held. Indeed, if a penalty is sought through specific pacts of protection, it appears that such a right is not held by the law itself.

So too, the *Distinguished Martinus Magerus von Schönberg, in his most absolute treatise On Armed Advocacy, chapter 2, number 225*, teaches that beyond defense and things annexed to it, nothing more of the law belongs to modern Protectors; they have "narrow fringes" <note>original: *strictasque habere fimbrias*; a metaphor meaning their authority is strictly limited</note> and cannot be extended beyond the boundaries of defense. The same *Lord Magerus* attests that this same opinion—namely, that protection or Advocacy grants no command or Jurisdiction over Clients to the Patrons and Protectors—is approved and received by a great consensus of both ancient and modern interpreters. He proves this with many reasons and sufficiently answers the contrary arguments in *chapter 12, number 386, and many following*. He writes there in *number 434*: that notwithstanding other impediments or recurring reasons for compulsion, those who are under a certain protection are at all times freely able to preserve their ancient religion or assume a new one, provided it is approved in the Empire.

To which end, in the **Peace of Religion of the year 1555**, the paragraph "Also, no Estate shall [oppress] the other," etc., is usually cited, because it essentially means that the Right of Protection and Shelter shall have nothing to do with Religion.

Likewise, many Imperial Cities are under the "Hereditary Protection" of neighboring Princes, yet they undoubtedly remain **immediately subject** <note>meaning they answer only to the Emperor</note> to the Holy Roman Empire. Similarly, very many monasteries and houses of God are immediately subject to the Holy Roman Empire, yet they nevertheless have their Hereditary Protectors. All of this can be said even more so of those cases where that protection is established by a specific agreement <note>original: *ex pacto singulari*</note>. However, one must not lose sight of the fact that some rights of protection, by virtue of specific agreements and other circumstances, are "fuller" and consequently bring with them a degree of subjection and respective Jurisdiction.

It cites the 1555 Peace of Augsburg to affirm that the right of protection is separate from the right to determine religious practice.</summary>

Indeed, just as jurisdiction—and almost all rights that savor of some jurisdiction or <term>Sovereignty</term> <note>original: *Imperium*</note> and subjection—are judged more by use and custom (varying according to the diversity of persons and places) than by fixed rules of law; so too this axiom, by which we assert that <term>Advocacy</term> <note>original: *Advocatia*; also known as *Vogtei*, the office of a secular protector</note> does not regularly grant jurisdiction, is not universal. For there are Advocates of certain monasteries who, besides the management of the economy and the accounts of revenues, possess criminal and sometimes even civil jurisdiction.

Thus Rosenthalius notes (*chapter 4, On Fiefs, conclusion 14, number 4, letter d*) that by agreement or custom, jurisdiction can be added to Advocacy. This is almost always the case for Princes over the monasteries situated within their district; they hold the Advocacy, and together with it the exercise of <term>High Justice</term> <note>original: *des Blutbanns*; literally "the blood-ban," the power to impose capital punishment</note>, the inspection of economic administration, and other temporal matters. So much so, that without their consent, the immovable property of the monastery cannot be pledged or alienated. And this Right of Advocacy over monasteries is usually granted to Princes within their territories by the Emperor using this formula of words: <note>original: **Mit allen Prälaturen und Clöstern, deroselben weltlichen Obrigkeiten, Schutz-Rechten und Advocatien**</note> **"With all prelatures and monasteries, their secular authorities, rights of protection, and advocacies,"** as noted by Wehner in *Practical Observations, word: Vogtey.* In such a way then, for example, the Imperial letters of fief regarding the Margraviate of Baden and Hochberg, etc., among others also have this clause: <note>original: **Mit Landen, Leuten, Clöster und Clösters Vogteyen, Mann und Mannschaftten, Lehen und Lehenschaiften, Geist- und Weltlichen, Zwing und Bännen, etc.**</note> **"With lands, people, monasteries and monastery-advocacies, vassals and retinues, fiefs and fief-holdings, spiritual and secular, jurisdiction and bans, etc."**

From all of this which has been detailed up to this point, it appears with hopeful sufficiency that, although at times <term>Protection and Shield</term> <note>original: *Schutz und Schirm*</note> carries with it an authority and respective subjection, this does not happen regularly or from the very nature of protection. Rather, it is necessary in every way that other jurisdictional acts, depending on the supreme right of the territory, were brought and practiced along with it. Nothing further can be dealt with on this in a general thesis, but a more extensive report will be necessary in every case.

And what Mr. Mager writes contributes to this (*chapter 10, number 523 and following*): that Advocacy always has an annexed Jurisdiction which is rooted in the law of the territory, or if by long-standing use or <term>Prescription</term> <note>The legal acquisition of a right through long-continued use or possession</note> jurisdiction adheres to the Advocacy or is found annexed to it. However, whether these apply in this or that village must be judged from various circumstances.

So too Erasmus à Chokier in the *Treatise on Feudal Advocacy, question 28*, where he asks whether Advocates possess <term>high and low justice</term>? <note>original: *merum & mixtum Imperium*</note> At number 2, he teaches: all these things depend on the Diploma of Advocacy or the prescription of time, and he cites Wamesius, *Counsel 481, On the Right of Patronage, volume 2.* For prescription through use and custom is equivalent to an express <term>Investiture</term> <note>The formal act of granting a fief or office</note>, as seen in Besoldus, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

Andreas Knichen teaches this in *On the Sublime Rights of Territory, chapter 5, number 50.* Otherwise, Advocates are not usually entitled to high and low justice (under the title *On Fiefs, Guardianship and Stewardship*), unless jurisdiction has been entrusted to them as feudatories. For in that case, high and low justice is deemed to have been granted, as is recorded by the common consensus of the Doctors, according to Cardinal Mantica, *On Tacit and Ambiguous Agreements, part 2, book 23, title 18, number 17.* These are the words of Erasmus à Chokier.

But I must not leave this unmentioned: although <term>Protected Subjects</term> <note>original: *Schirmverwandte Unterthanen*</note> are bound by custom to provide the Oath—which they call the <term>Duty of Protection</term> <note>original: *Schirmspflicht*</note>—nevertheless, Superiority or Jurisdiction is by no means proven by it. For such an <term>homage</term> <note>original: *homagium*; a formal acknowledgement of loyalty</note> usually provided by clients for the sake of protection can be called neither an oath of security nor of fidelity, but has some kinship with the oath provided by a Prince's counselors and the like by reason of their close association, as Mr. Mager writes in *chapter 10, number 138, etc.*

And Chokier adds in the said place: through this oath, the Protector acquires no Superiority or Jurisdiction over the Clients; just as an Immediate Noble of the Empire, being a Counselor of some Prince, is not subject to that Prince (to whom he is a Counselor) regarding jurisdiction in real and personal actions not concerning his office. Instead, according to the contingencies of the case, he must be summoned either in the Imperial Chamber or before the <term>Arbitration Courts</term> <note>original: *Austragis*; specific courts in the Holy Roman Empire for resolving disputes between estates</note>. This is because an oath ought not to operate beyond the intention of the one swearing it (*Counsel of Marburg 15, number 360, volume 1*), but must be restricted to the consent of the swearer (*Schrader, On Fiefs, part 10, section 13, number 14*).

So also most recently Johannes Bruningus, in the *Dissertation on Homage, conclusions 9 and 10, chapter 1*, reports that Clients perform a "familiar homage" by reason of protection or defense, implying that no bond of subjection arises from it. This is because, as he asserts in the subsequent thesis 13, not every and any oath of fidelity that is performed attributes Jurisdiction to the one to whom it is sworn; see also Beatus, *Decisions, volume 5, on judicial matters, part 1, folio 729, etc.*

And Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus asserts in *The Republic, book 11, chapter 11, number 6*, that the cause of protection does not hold any right of ownership, just as mercenary auxiliary soldiers are not the masters of the Republic simply because they were called to its aid, help, and protection for a wage.

But all these things are said saving the judgment of the more Prudent, and those better versed in Public Law.

### 56. Swearing, Oath. Juramentum.

An Oath [*Schwur*] is so called because those swearing take a far most heavy burden upon themselves; <note>original: *sie nehmen ein schwer Ding auff sich*</note> **they take a heavy thing upon themselves,** as they are constituted before the most august and tremendous tribunal of Heaven and Earth—that is, of the Creator and his Creatures—as if in the presence of all things above and below. They rouse all of nature against themselves, pronouncing a plainly horrendous sentence: they wish to be deprived of nature's benefits necessary for this life, and of God’s favor and His most desired sight. They devote themselves to eternal tortures and unquenchable fire if they knowingly deceive: <note>original: *Sie stellen sich für gehägte Bänck, fällen selbst ein Urtheil, und schreyen Zetter über sich*</note> **They place themselves before the hedged benches of the court, pass judgment themselves, and cry out for vengeance upon themselves.** Jacob Ebertus, in his *History of Oaths*, folio 18, face 2.

### 57. Scoundrel. Nobilis.

A Nobleman [*Nobilis*] is called a *Schufft* by the Saxons. This appellation is today ignominious due to a "lowering" of its use <note>original: *usu ταπεινώσεως*; refers to the linguistic process where a title of honor becomes an insult</note>, although in itself it is honorable. For it seems to descend from the Hebrew *Shophet*, which signifies a Judge. Certainly, this word is found used with the same notion still among the Germans and Belgians: *Schöppen*, *Scheffen* <note>original: *Schöffen*; lay judges or aldermen</note>. Nor are the French *Eschevins* <note>magistrates</note> derived from anywhere else. Master Josias Nolden, *On the Status of Nobles*, chapter 1, number 29.

Add Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 6, chapter 1, number 17.

### 58. Protection-Bailiff and Stall-Money.
### Payment on account of protection, Market money.

Just as the secular authority of the Magistrate and the Lords has the power and right to provide for the common territory, to protect church properties, and generally to defend everyone throughout the entire lordship according to right and equity; so too is it proper for them—and no one else—to collect the <term>Protection and Bailiff Fees</term> <note>original: *Schutz- und Vogtgeld*</note> from church properties. They also have the right to have the <term>Stall-Money</term> <note>original: *Standgeld*; a fee for market stalls</note> collected at the annual and weekly markets. They are to maintain protection over the church festivals, to proclaim the peace, to punish criminals, and all emoluments arising from and attached to these matters belong to them alone.

### 59. Swabia, Swabian Land. Suevia.

The seats of the ancient Swabians [*Suevorum*] are in our age held by the Swedes, Poles, Prussians, Pomeranians, Lusatians, Bohemians, Moravians, Thuringians, Hessians (or Catti), and Franks. Basilius Faber in the *Treasury of Scholarly Erudition*. And although the Swabian Empire was so great, it was not however a absolute monarchy <note>original: *Dominicum aut παμβασιλικὸν*</note> but a confederation, in which almost innumerable nations were included, all of them German, just as the Swabians themselves are from the Mountain...

### 62. Impregnation. *Graviditas.*

Regarding simulated pregnancy, see Paolo Zacchia in *Medico-Legal Questions*, book 3, title 2, question 8. On superfetation <note>a second conception during an existing pregnancy</note> and molar pregnancy <note>a non-viable mass in the uterus</note> in pregnant women, see the same in the same place, book 1, title 3, throughout; and on death caused by childbirth, *ibid. title 4.*

And it should be noted here that a father is bound to provide a dowry in the name of his son for a virgin whom the son has seduced, and to support the offspring. However, he retains the right to deduct whatever he provided on the son's behalf from the son's legal inheritance, according to the teachings of Antonius Faber in the *Code*, title *lest the son by the father*, 9, book 4, definition 3. There, he asserts it was so judged in the Senate of Savoy. It is also of the greatest interest to a father that his son not be afflicted with such disgrace that what he cannot pay in money, he must pay in his body <note>i.e., through physical punishment or imprisonment</note>, law 1, last paragraph, *Digest on Punishments.*

Doctor Navarrus, on the rubric *thou shalt not commit adultery*, chapter 16, folio 115 and following, writes back in these words: He who deceives a virgin with persistent prayers and appeals, gifts, or false persuasions, without a promise of marrying her, is held liable in both courts <note>The "external" civil court and the "internal" court of conscience/confession</note>. In the external court, he must provide satisfaction; in the internal court, however, he is bound either to marry her, or to satisfy her so that she remains content, or to compensate her for all the damage that has come to her from it—namely, how much more she needs to obtain such a husband as she would have obtained while remaining a virgin, according to the judgment of an upright man, and something more besides, because of the shame she will suffer her whole life, and because of the insults she will receive from her husband on that account. Indeed, beyond the aforesaid, he is also obligated to appease her father and satisfy him for the injury inflicted. The same is taught in the *Decisions of the Roman Rota collected by Farinacius*, decision 770, numbers 2 and 3. Gutierrez, book 1, *Canonical Questions*, chapter 37, numbers 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12, joined with number 23, where he says he has obtained this in practice. And at number 28, he writes thus: that the seducer is bound not only to give the dowry which such a virgin would usually receive, but is additionally bound to provide what the corrupted woman needs more because of the defloration to find a husband equal to herself; nor are parents bound to suffer this injury by marrying their daughter to an unworthy man because of the defloration. For there is no doubt that through defloration a girl is made worse in terms of her reputation and honor, and therefore she needs a far greater dowry to find an equal husband; and the seducer, who gave cause for the damage, is bound to compensate for it. **And although the amount the dowry should be is left to the discretion of the Lord Judge, one must nonetheless look at the status of the parents, the qualities of the girl, and the wealth of the defendant, etc.** <note>original: *Und ob gleichwol...*</note> Thus teaching, Antonius Tessius, *Piedmontese Decisions*, 3, number 2. Navarrus in his *Manual*, chapter 16, number 16. But if the man by persistent [requests]...

### Page 990

...through persistent entreaties, appeals, gifts, or persuasion—even without a formal promise of marriage—a man has deceived a virgin, he is held to make satisfaction in both the secular and ecclesiastical courts <note>original: *in utroque foro*; literally "in both forums," referring to the civil court and the court of conscience/church court</note>. Thus, a distinction is made between a <term>seducer</term> <note>original: *stupratorem*</note> who misled and deceived a virgin, and a man to whom a virgin voluntarily consented after only a slight request. For if she was urged with great importunity or driven by gifts, she is considered "coerced" enough for this legal effect (following the argument of Law 1 in the Code *on the ravishing of virgins*). It is not only true but well known that the crime of <term>seduction</term> <note>original: *stuprum*; referring to illicit sexual intercourse with a virgin by consent or seduction rather than force</note> can, due to concurrent circumstances, be punished by death, or by flogging and banishment. See Farinacius in *Criminal Practice*, title on crimes of the flesh, under the word *stuprum*. Likewise, when the seducer is destitute <note>original: *inops*</note> and cannot provide a dowry to the seduced girl, he shall then be flogged and condemned to exile. See Petrus Gregorius in *The System of Law*, book 36, chapter 9, under the rubric "on the seduction of virgins," number 5; also Gutierrez, book 1, *Canonical Questions*, chapter 37; and my own dispute defended by Mr. Andreas Rizinger, thesis 26, page 61.

Certain legal scholars <note>original: *Dd.*, abbreviation for *Doctores*</note> seem to hold the opinion that a full dowry need not always be established by the seducer for the girl. Instead, they argue he must only provide that additional amount necessary to be given beyond a standard dowry—as a sort of supplement—on account of her lost virginity, which would not have been given to the daughter had she not been seduced. They argue the full dowry should only be paid by the seducer if the girl can no longer find a husband of the same social condition and quality as she could have if she were still a virgin; or if the girl or her parents (upon whom the burden of providing a dowry otherwise falls) do not have the means to dower her worthily due to poverty. For if she herself or her parents have the means, then the seducer would not be held to the full dowry, but only to that "surplus of damage" she suffers because of the seduction—specifically, the need to provide a larger dowry than would have been required otherwise. However, this opinion is entirely rejected by Farinacius in *Criminal Practice*, question 47, regarding the dowry, number 547. He writes these words: "But this limitation seems contrary to the mind of all the cited Doctors, and even against the Laws upon which they rely. These laws intend for the dowry to be established by the seducer for the seduced girl not as a backup when she or her parents cannot pay, but simply out of hatred for and as a punishment for the crime." He also says: "In my view, the aforementioned opinion is quite doubtful, as I have never seen a distinction made in practice regarding the poverty or riches of the girl and her parents. Rather, judges have decreed that the requested dowry must always be given and established by the seducer, including that extra amount necessary to be given to a husband because of her lost virginity." He cites Jason, Cacheranus, and Bermonus.

<column-break/>

...on public concubinage, number 17. See also Menochius on *Judicial Arbitrations*, book 2, case 288, who says that the contrary arguments provided by Diaz in *Canonical Criminal Practice* apply only in the "court of conscience" <note>the internal moral or spiritual realm</note>, but not in the "external or contentious court" <note>the public legal system</note>. Berlichius supports this in part 5 of his *Practical Conclusions*, where he says Farinacius rightly rejects the contrary opinion as erroneous. **Thus, one should not look at or consider whether and what kind of husband the deflowered woman might acquire in the future.** <note>original German: *So ist auch darauff nicht zu sehen, oder zu gehen, ob und was die Deflorirte künfftig für einen Mann erwerben möchte.*</note> Antonius Gomez argues for and against this, ultimately concluding that the seducer is bound to dower the seduced woman even if she marries a man of the same condition and quality as if she were still a virgin, or even if she received an adequate dowry from her father, her mother, or from her own marriage. I addressed this in the dispute on punishments defended by Rizinger, page 61. It follows that the seducer is bound to pay the dowry to the seduced woman immediately after the seduction is committed; it is not necessary to wait for the time of a wedding, since it could happen that the seduced woman never finds a husband. See Berlichius and Harprecht, volume 4, page 937. Cacheranus continues in the place cited above, saying that one should not only consider the dowry that would have been provided by the girl's father, but the seducer is bound to give more. This follows a decision by the Abbot, followed by the *Apostilla* to the *Summa Angelica*. Cacheranus concludes: "And so it was judged by the most excellent Senate that a seduced daughter must be dowered according to the qualities and means of the seducer, taking into account the quality of the virgin herself, so that the dowry is larger than if it had been established by the father for a virgin daughter." According to Divine and Canon Law (Deuteronomy 22), the seducer must give the girl's father 50 shekels—**fifty shekels of silver** <note>original German: *funffzig Seckel Silbers*</note>—also on account of the injury done to the father. On the contrary, however, Harprecht and Berlichius speak in terms far different from ours in a specific case: namely, where it is notorious (either by the girl's own confession or other proof) that the girl came to the young man's bed naked and consented to the seduction. In this case, the aforementioned scholars say that although the seducer can be compelled neither to marry nor to dower such a girl, the father of this girl can still sue the seducer for the estimation of the damage resulting to him—that is, the "surplus" he now lacks because he will need a greater sum of money to dower his seduced daughter. Otherwise, virginity and an honest life are presumed; and a virgin is always presumed to have been deceived and seduced until the contrary is clearly proven.

## ADDITION.

Regarding the *Care of Pregnant Women* <note>original: *De Cura Gravidarum*</note>, Mr. Dr. David Herlicius published a very useful book in octavo at Anklam during his <term>medical residency</term> <note>original: *Physicatu*; refers to his term as a district physician</note> in the year 1584. It was later enlarged and printed in quarto in the year 1602 during his residency at Stargard. Pregnant women among the later Romans used to sacrifice to the Goddess Egeria because they believed she could easily deliver the conception from the womb, according to the witness of *Festus*. She is the same as Lucina, <note>Greek: *εὐλείθυϊα*; Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth</note> Genitalis, and the so-called "Nixian Gods" <note>original: *Diis Nixiis*</note>, because they were believed to assist the struggles <note>original: *nisus*</note> of those in labor and to act as midwives for offspring striving toward the light. The Glosses identify Egeria as Nixia. Thomas Reinesius beautifully restored this passage against Barthius in *Various Readings, book 1, chapter 8; see also Rupertus, Observations on Florus, book 1, chapter 2, section 4, number 2.*

I congratulate you on a woman who is <term>ripening</term> <note>original: *capricatam*; a metaphorical term comparing the final stage of pregnancy to the ripening of figs</note>, that is, near to childbirth after her months are complete. *Caprification* is the process by which gnats flying out of wild fig trees and penetrating into figs bring about maturity. Hence, a "capricated" person is one who is premature or near to birth. *Pregnant women and those in childbed should not be molested. Articles of Emperor Maximilian II, article 8; Dutch Law of War, pages 62 and 63; Mr. Dr. Tabor on Metathesis, page 266. Striking pregnant women is dangerous. Dutch Law of War, page 64.*

Verulamius <note>Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam</note> teaches *in the Silva, page 596:* That if a pregnant woman eats rue or coriander seeds, she will bring spiritual and ingenious children into the world; but if she enjoys coarse food, onions, and beans, her children will show poor understanding. *Mr. Harsdorffer in the German Secretary, part 10, title 21.* Once, when a pregnant woman ate many hazelnuts with their shells, she brought a foolish son into the world.

Regarding the signs of pregnancy, see *Baptista Caesar in Illustrated Counsel 54, page 3.* The wild Moors, or Daboyers, have their wives with them, and if they are pregnant and the pains of birth overtake them, they often—when things go hard—tread the child out of the mother's body with their feet; they press 

<column-break/>

the top of the children's heads flat, so that they all look as if pieces of their skulls had been chopped off. Their ears, noses, and lips are slit wide. Michael Hemmersam, in his travel description, notes that a painting of St. John's camel-skin was the cause of a hairy birth. A painting of a bear was the cause of a hairy birth. In former times, people brought beautiful images and pleasant paintings before the eyes of pregnant matrons, according to the indication of Oppian in his book on hunting:

> The Spartans are often accustomed to practice this:
> While they see their wives swelling with a pregnant womb,
> They set out excellently painted tablets and splendid things, etc.
> While they survey the tablets and beautiful forms with their eyes,
> The astonished Spartan women give birth to those who are beautiful of face.

Antonio de Torquemada tells of a female person who, because of her crime, was banished to a desolate island. She became pregnant by an ape for the third time, and each time brought forth a son who was indeed similar to a human, but hairy over the whole body.

## 63. Switzerland. Helvetia.

The Suevi, Suebi, Swabians, Sueones, Swedes, and Swedish people, in fact and truth, fall under the same derivation and signify the same nation, although settled in different regions and places. *Reineccius in Commentary on Saxon Origins, page 7.* It is for this reason that the region where the Swedes dwell—who are now called the Swiss, a mountain and Alpine people of the Helvetians, and from whom that entire nation received its name—is called Suecia, Suicia, or *Switzerland*. They boast that they are Suevi, brought from the Kingdom of the Swedes into these Alps; see, among many others, *Mr. Goldast on Bohemia, book 1, chapter 5.*

## ADDITION.

Zeiller wrote the *Topography of Switzerland* in the year 1642. In the year 1654, an *Appendix to the Topography of Switzerland* in folio. *Hottinger* wrote a dissertation on the method of reading Swiss histories. Simler wrote *On the Republic of the Swiss*. Leonhard Wurffbain in *Reports, part 6, page 205 and following*, discusses the respect of the Swiss toward illustrious persons. See *Draco on Patricians, page 246*, whom you should certainly consult. The Swiss are defenders of the Catholic faith, *page 177.* The Swiss have no central treasury, which they do not need. *Klock on the Treasury, book 1, chapter 15, number 1.* There are, however, those to whom the care of public money is committed. *Number 8.* At Basel, there are Triumvirs who manage the supreme care of the more sacred Treasury. *Number 9.* No tax is given for the wine and grain that any citizen consumes at home. *Number 10.*

The Swiss people still possess an innocent simplicity in their unchanging clothing...

### 64. Sword-Kin. <note>original: *Schwertmage*; Latin: *Agnatus*</note>

The closest male relative on the father's side, who is called an *Agnatus* <note>a relative tracing descent through the male line</note> in Latin—as seen in the *Institutes* regarding the legal guardianship of agnates, in the section "moreover, they are agnates"—is called a **Sword-Kin** among the Saxons. Georg Rotfchitz, in his treatise *On Dowries and Legacies*, etc., article 14, number 3. For the word *Mage* <note>Kin/Relative</note> here signifies the concept and origin of blood-relatives: just as the stomach <note>German: *Magen*</note> otherwise contains food and digestion, and gives the liver an origin for the blood. The **Sword**, however, indicates the man, as he is the one who carries it. Yet the *Weichbild* <note>a collection of medieval municipal laws</note>, article 25 in the commentary, also calls a Sword-Kin one who is a guardian and champion for his underage relative and carries a sword. See Scherz, in the *Domestic School of Language*, folio 140.

The word *Magum*, however, is a very ancient word and signifies a house, a dwelling, or even a family. Serrarius, *History of Mainz*, book 1, chapter 4. From this comes *Neomagum*, as if saying "New-home" or "New-houses," and it corresponds with the Hebrew <term>Mabon</term> <note>a place of residence or habitation</note>, or *Magum*, of the same meaning. See above under the word *Heim* [Home] and Reiner Reineccius in his *Commentary on the Deeds of Charlemagne*, folio 14, where he says: "I agree with the conjecture of Rhenanus, who says that *Magum* signified 'house' to the ancient Gauls." This must be understood as the Germanic language of the Gauls—that is, a chamber—restricting the meaning to a part, which for the ancients expressed the whole building or even a fortification. Hence, among Roman writers, we find *Drusomagus*, *Rothomagus*, *Neomagum*, etc., as if you were to say: Drusus-chamber, Roth-chamber, New-chamber.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the difference between **Agnatic** <note>male-line</note> and **Cognatic** <note>female or blood-line</note> Law, see Rittershusius in the *New Constitutions*, page 477, number 1; add Schneidewin, page 104, number 8 and following, whom Pichardus unfortunately translates as "Oynotomus"; Lord Tabor in *Criminal Scraps*, page 252. Agnates are called **Sword-Kin** because they are fit for military service. Johann Oldendorp of Marburg,

<column-break/>

Consultation 5, number 64, volume 2. From this, a male-only fief <note>a landed estate</note> is also commonly designated as a **Sword-fief** <note>original: *Schwertlehen*</note>. Knipschild, *On Trusts*, page 20, number 66, and the authors cited there.

On the word **Sword-Kin**, see Schneidewin on the *Institutes*, page 41, at the end; Rudinger, *Century 4*, observation 53.

### 65. His / Its. <note>original: *Sein*; Latin: *Suus*</note>

The nature of the word **His** <note>original: *Sein/Sua*</note> is such that if it refers to a thing held in common with others, it designates a proportional share. It has the force of a distributive particle, signifying only that part which is the property of the speaker or the disposer in that matter—even if it were a third or a twentieth—as taught by Bartolus on the law concerning the "choice of a slave," section "Labeo." Also Jason, number 5, in the Digest on legacies, book 1. For, if it is said: "That which is mine, that which is **his**," and that thing is not entirely mine or entirely his, then this particle "mine," "yours," or "**his**" is considered to be placed distributively, as if it were describing a proportional part—namely, that which is mine, yours, or his, whether it be very small or large. See Johann Goeddaeus among the *Marburg Consultations*, volume 3, consultation 26, number 78, etc.

->ADDITION.<-

That thing is properly said to be "**one's own**" <note>original: *suum*</note> in which one has full disposition and ownership. Barbosa, law 17, chapter 77, axiom 1. No one is presumed to throw away **his own** in a case of doubt (axiom 5). No one is compelled to serve as a soldier at **his own** expense (axiom 6). The word "**His**" <note>original: *Suum*</note> is a possessive pronoun; it demonstrates the present time. Marius Antoninus, book 2, response 59, case 21. On the use of the pronoun "**His**," see Lord Rupert on the title *On the Origin of Law*, chapter 8, section 24, near the end.

"**His**," as a word, does not always imply ownership. Schneidewin on the *Institutes*, page 672, number 58 and following.

### 66. Clause: Saving his feudal justice, and harmless to anyone in his rights. <note>original: *Seiner Lehens Gerechtigkeit, und männiglichen an seinen Rechten unschädlich*; Latin: *Salvo jure feudi & tertii*</note>

By putting forward this clause, the party expressly protests and makes it a matter of record that they do not wish to cause prejudice <note>legal harm or disadvantage</note> in any way to their own right, nor to the rights of others or third parties. This is supported by the text in the Law "If to a debtor," section 1; the Law "Just as," section "It does not seem," in the Digest on the ways pledges or mortgages are ended; and the Law "Neither the grandfather" in the Code on the emancipation of children, etc. See Beuer in the *Saxon Opinions on Contracts*, folio 563, etc.

### 67. The Same. <note>original: *Selbige*; Latin: *Ea*</note>

The word "that" or "**the same**" <note>original: *eam* or *eum*</note> is repetitive of preceding matters, including all their qualities. Cephalus, consultation 140, number 17 and following.

## 68. Self-Judgment. <note>Latin: *Vindicta privata*; the act of taking the law into one's own hands.</note>

Is it ever permissible for a Vassal or a Lord, bypassing legal actions or other legitimate remedies, to resort to arms and pursue his rights through the benefit of plunder without punishment? Obertus seems to argue in the affirmative <note>original: *Affirmativàm tueri videtur*</note> in his writings on feudal law. Indeed, in the past, nothing was more frequent than to avenge and untangle injuries and private disputes through war and weapons; such a war was considered "just" as long as it had been formally declared. This was commonly called **Fist-Law** <note>German: *Das Faustrecht*; the medieval custom of the "right of the strong" to settle disputes by force</note>. However, the most beneficial Constitutions of our modern Empire shrink from this practice. To them, those judgments which our people call **Self-Judgment** <note>German: *Selbstgericht*</note> are utterly hated as the most destructive plagues of public peace. This is established in the Imperial Recesses <note>resolutions of the Imperial Diet</note> of the years 1495, 1500, 1522, 1555, 1557, 1559, 1566, 1570, and finally 1576, which contain the strongest defenses of the Public Peace.

### ADDITION.

See Speidel in his *Mirror of Fist, Rider, and Club Law*. Also Rittershausen, Besold, and Gothofredus Antonii regarding **Trial by Combat** <note>Latin: *Monomachia probatoria*; a duel used as legal evidence</note>. See also Paulus Voet on duels and Christopher Crusius on feudal readings. In the Privileges of Altdorf, Lord Johannes Derrer framed the theme this way: Is it permitted—especially in difficult and criminal cases where a judge is available—to settle disputes and controversies between illustrious and noble persons through a duel when other evidence is lacking? He rightly denies this in the same work.

## 69. Primary Debtor. <note>German: *Selbstschuldner*; Latin: *Principalis debitor*</note>

It is a certain and common tradition of the Doctors of Law that <term>guarantors</term> <note>Latin: *fidejussoribus*; those who promise to pay if the original debtor fails</note> are entitled to three legal benefits. The first is the *benefit of order* (also called the benefit of "discussion"). The second is the *benefit of division*, or the *Letter of the Divine Hadrian*. The third is the *benefit of assigned actions*.

Regarding the benefit of *order*, it should be known that under the Law of the Code, a creditor had the choice of suing either the primary debtor or the guarantor first. Today, however, according to the newest laws of the *Authentica* <note>a collection of Justinian's later laws</note>, the creditor is required to sue the primary debtor before suing the guarantor. If the creditor disrupts this order and sues the guarantor first,

<column-break/>

the guarantor can raise an "exception of order" or "discussion," demanding that the creditor first sue the primary debtor and exhaust his assets. As the saying goes: **he must first seek payment from the Primary Debtor before he sues the guarantor.** For a guarantor is not sued as long as the primary debtor is solvent.

The second benefit, that of *division*, applies when there are several guarantors. If only one of them is sued, he can request (under the rule established by the Emperor Hadrian) that the creditor be compelled to divide the claim and seek only a proportionate share from each individual guarantor.

The *benefit of assigned actions* occurs when a creditor transfers his legal rights against the other co-guarantors to the one guarantor who actually pays the debt. Since a guarantor normally has no direct legal claim against his fellow guarantors—as there is no contract between them—once he is sued for the whole amount and pays it, he can demand that the creditor "cede" or hand over his rights to sue the others.

Having established these points, the question arises: if a guarantor has also designated himself as a primary debtor (which often happens)—**signing himself as a guarantor and primary debtor**—making another’s debt his own, can he still protect himself with the "benefit of order"? Ignoring unnecessary arguments to the contrary, I respond that in such a case, **where the guarantor is simultaneously a primary debtor**, the benefit must be denied to the guarantor. This is because, in that instance, the person who was previously a guarantor has stripped off the role of guarantor and placed himself in the position of the Debtor. Otherwise, if the word **Primary Debtor** <note>German: *Selbstschuldner*</note> accomplished nothing, why would it be included? If there were no difference between a simple guarantor and one who designates himself this way, why use distinct names? It is undisputed that words must be interpreted so that they actually achieve something. We see this in legal principles: in human arrangements, no word should be considered added without the power to act. In contracts, not even the smallest word—not even a single syllable—should be devoid of its operative force. For if we do not observe this strictly, words in contracts would be subject to trickery and mockery, and they would be not just idle, but offensive. Legal parchments would be filled in vain.

## 71. Session. Seating Precedence.

Regarding the prerogative of **Seating** <note>term: *Sessio*; the formal right to a specific seat in an assembly, reflecting one's rank and precedence</note>, there is a common treatise which may be consulted. See also Johannes Bolognetus on the law regarding **Certain Petitions**.
Dominicus Arumäus discusses the **Seating of the Estates** <note>the various ranks of society</note> in the Imperial Diets in his treatise on the **Diets of the Empire**, chapter 7, number 18 and 50, and throughout the following. Regarding **Seating Disputes** at the Imperial Diets and how they are to be settled, see Geistkoffler’s *Three Discourses*, chapter 3.
The question of whether a **Doctor of Law** should precede a **Nobleman** is explored by Arumäus in discourse 32. There is also a unique consultation by the celebrated Mr. Thomas Lansius regarding the prerogative of the **Soldier** versus the **Scholar**.
It may be asked which title carries greater dignity: **Count** <note>Latin: *Comes*</note> or **Marquis** <note>Latin: *Marchio*</note>? As far as **Common Law** <note>Latin: *Jus commune*; the subsidized Roman law used across Europe</note> is concerned, there is no doubt that a Marquis is to be preferred to a Count. This is discussed at length by Boër in his treatise on the authority of the Great Council, part 2, question 1, number 6—unless the same person happens to be both a Count and a Marquis simultaneously, as he is then preferred to one who has been distinguished by only one of those titles, according to the teachings of Jason on the law of joined things, number 18, in the Digest on legacies.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, regarding the **Spaniards**, it seems certain that the title of **Count** is more excellent than that of **Marquis**. For almost everywhere in their Royal Laws, the Counts are placed before the Marquises. This can be found in many places, such as in law 11, title 1, part 2, and this order is rarely reversed; therefore, it should be followed, according to the law "whenever" in the Digest on **Usufruct**.
If you consult the annals of Spain, you will easily discover that the title of Count is the most ancient, while that of Marquis is, by contrast, very recent.
Indeed, in former times, Counts even ranked above **Dukes**, as shown by the Acts of the ancient Councils, which were accustomed to be signed thus: "Ella, Count and Duke," and "Fandilla, Count and Duke," as witnessed by Vasco in the *Chronicles of Spain*, volume 1, chapter 22. See also Parladorius, *Daily Matters*, book 2, chapter 13.
Regarding the **Precedence** between a **Spaniard** and a **Frenchman**, see Majolus in *Dog Days*, page 1151; and Valdesius wrote a unique treatise on this matter, where many general points on this subject are contained. This very dispute was the reason why the Spanish Ambassador sat separately at the **Council of Trent**, and not among the other envoys, as reported in the signatures of the Council of Trent. In the same place, at the end of the second session, it is held that: a seat in an improper place should not prejudice the rights of anyone.
In the year of Christ 1608, at the **Diet of Regensburg**, the counselors of the Elector of Saxony were given the following instruction:
> Whether the **Seating Dispute** should not be settled by an impartial drawing of lots, or perhaps suspended entirely.

### ADDITION.

See Limnäus in **Public Law**, book 6, chapter 2, at the end, where he says: lest any rivalry arise by reason of **Precedence** <note>Latin: *Præcedentia*</note>; see under the heading "Precedence." We read of seating prerogative contests everywhere, especially between the Kings of **France** and **Spain**, as witnessed by Natale Conti, book 11. Also at the coronation of **Charles V** between the people of **Genoa** and **Siena**, where it nearly came to arms, as witnessed by Paolo Giovio, book 37 of his *Histories*. See Borius in Arumäus, volume 1, discourse 14, thesis 16, regarding the **Right of Seating** in the Diets. Limnäus in **Public Law**, book 6, chapter 3, number 18.
> A Catholic and a Protestant were quarreling over precedence; then one said they should let the **Calendar** be the judge, in which the Papist days [Saints' days] come first.

See Mr. Harsdörffer in the appendix to his *Great Stage of Pleasant and Instructive Stories*, number 106.

### 74. To take one's own life. Suicide. <note>original: *Autochiria*; from the Greek for "self-handing"</note>

Concerning those who bring death upon themselves, see Böckel in *Investigations into Visions*, inquiry 6, number 20. Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 3, book 2, chapter 14 and following. Onciac, question 38. Verdier, *Various Readings*, my folio 164. Bullae: in *Precepts of Law*, precept 2, number 26, etc. See also my own *Disputation on Homicide* and my *Treatise on the Consideration of Life and Death*.

Whether someone is permitted to kill himself, and whether he who kills himself commits a sin? See Bonacina, *On Contracts and Restitution*, dispute 2, final question, section 1, point 5. Add Father Hieronymus Drexel’s *The Forerunner of Eternity*, chapter 2, section 8, folio 147, where he records several examples of death held in contempt and bravely inflicted upon oneself; and finally he adds: "Therefore, should such great strength in the face of death belong to the most vain of men, while Christians, relying on God as their Helper, tremble and lose heart? Death is not an evil, but the fear of death is an evil. I beseech you, let us examine the things themselves, not the shadows of things." If we believe Seneca, "Death is Nature’s best invention, and the remedy for all evils." Why then do we tremble at the end? Great and immortal eternal pleasure will receive us. We can be unconquered; we cannot be unshaken. We must pass across. Regarding the hidden power of disease or madness, which compels one toward the precipice of destruction, illustrated with examples, see by all means Laelius Bisciola, *Leisure Hours*, book 3, chapter 3.

<margin>From the works of Besoldus, volume 1.</margin> Of those who had killed themselves, Tarquinius Priscus <note>an early king of Rome</note> ordered their bodies to be nailed to a cross, according to Pliny, book 36, chapter 15. Under the Emperors, their heads were cut off at the sources and raised on a cross, according to Xiphilinus in *Severus regarding Niger*. In the same author and in Herodian regarding Albinus, and Plutarch regarding Cleomenes, it is said that Ptolemy ordered his body to be crucified and sewn into a leather sack <note>original: *culeum insutum*; referring to the *Poena Cullei*, a Roman punishment where a criminal was sewn into a sack with animals and drowned</note> up to the head. And it seems to have been the custom that all the most abandoned men, and those most hated in the manner of parricides <note>those who kill their parents</note>, were sewn into a sack either before or after their execution. See Pontanus in *Attic Wars*. Bellarmine, volume 3, chapter 286, folio 266. See also my work *On Life and Death*, folio 100, etc., and my *Disputation on Homicide*, thesis 4, etc. Likewise Bisciola, *Leisure Hours*, volume 2, book 14, chapter 1. Servin, *Pleadings*, volume 3, folio 529.

<column-break/>

Farinacius, however, in *On Investigations*, question 11, under number 80, hands down the opinion that according to the law, the truer and more common view is that the corpse of those who kill themselves out of a **weariness of life** <note>original: *taedio vitae*; a legal term for depression or existential exhaustion</note> ought not to be hanged or treated with cruelty, but should merely be deprived of a Church burial. Those who take their own lives in the Duchy of Würtemberg are to be buried according to the Würtemberg Provincial Ordinance near the end, where three cases are distinguished, folio 363.

But it is asked: when a woman who is pregnant drowns herself, whether the **offspring existing in the mother's womb** <note>original: *partus utero matris existens*</note> should be buried under the gallows along with the mother, to whom Christian burial is rightly denied? I say no, lest the innocent be punished; therefore, perhaps the offspring should be cut out <note>via a post-mortem caesarean section</note>.

When someone is found hanging by a noose or fallen from a height, is it presumed that they killed themselves? See the annotations to Julius Clarus, book 5, final section, number 200.

Is it permitted to kill oneself for the sake of preserving one's chastity? See Camerarius, *Historical Meditations*, century 1, chapter 78.

->ADDITION.<-

How many classes of suicide <note>original: *autochiriae*</note> there are; whether suicide is an ethical vice; whether a soft nature and a desire to preserve life is better than a sinful suicide <note>original: *αυτοχειρία*</note>; whether in any case suicide is permitted; whether it is permitted to kill oneself so that one is not forced to sin; or whether it is permitted to perish in order to flee slavery. See Mr. Dannhauer, in a special Disputation held in 1627 on this matter. Question: Can anyone harm himself with impunity, or lay violent hands upon himself? Aristotle simply denies this in *Ethics*, book 5, last chapter, because such a **self-killer** <note>original: *αυτόχειρ*</note> is unjust both toward himself and especially toward the Republic, which he robs of a useful member and citizen. This same view agrees with the Law of Nature (based on the argument in the Digest *On Justice and Law*, book 3), Divine Law (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Kings 2:6; 1 Corinthians 6:20), and Canon Law (the canon *If it is not permitted*, cause 23, question 5). But concerning Civil Law, there is a grave controversy. Ungepauer defends the affirmative in his *Exercises on Justinian's Institutes*, exercise 1, question 13, and in a special treatise *On Self-Killing* <note>original: *Propricidio*</note>, following the text in the Digest *On the Private Fund*, book 9, section 7. However, the law in the Digest *Under the Cornelian Law on Assassins*, book 4, final section, seems to strongly oppose this. See Mr. Cobius on section 3 of *The Law of Nature, Nations, and Citizens*, question 3. Balthazar Gomez de Amescua in the treatise *On Power over Oneself*, book 1, chapter 7. Wilhelm Schröter in *A Decade of Stoic Principles*, principle 2. Wolpman *On Death*, chapter 1, thesis 26, and several following.

Regarding **suicide** <note>original: *propricidio*; literally "killing of one's own self"</note>, consult Heigius, volume 2, question 36: *On the goods of those who have taken their own lives.* See also Robertus, *Judicial Review*, book 1, page 12. A slave is considered "bad" if he does something to remove himself from human affairs <note>i.e., attempts suicide</note>, for it is presumed that one who dared such a thing against himself might also dare something against another. See Law 23, section 3 of the Digest <note>original: *ff. de Ædil. Edict.*; a reference to Roman civil law</note>.

<margin>**Suicide** <note>original Greek: *Αυτοχειρία*; "work of one's own hand"</note> as a defender of chastity.</margin>
Master Rupertus, in his commentary on Florus, book 1, chapter 7, section 11, notes: *The matron expiated her honor with steel.* This refers to the history of **Lucretia** <note>a legendary Roman heroine whose suicide after being raped led to the overthrow of the monarchy</note> and Sextus Tarquinius, mentioned by Diodorus Siculus in the *Excerpta Peiresciana*, page 252. Examples of virgins and most honorable women who vindicated themselves from impurity or rape by a voluntary death were also collected among Christians by **Hugo Grotius** <note>a foundational figure in international law</note> in book 2 of *On the Law of War and Peace*, chapter 19, section 5, page 292 at the end. To this, add the example reported by Procopius in his *Secret History*, page 95.

<margin>**Suicide** is inexcusable.</margin>
Rupertus, in his commentary on Florus, book 4, chapter 2, section 70, disapproves of the practice among German women. In book 3, chapter 3, section 16, he lists its proponents, but in book 3, chapter 15, section 17, suicide among the Heathen nations is extensively criticized. See Master Rupertus on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 6, section 7. Add also book 3, chapter 2, section 7, and book 9, chapter 13, section 1. Note the strange case of a certain German in book 9, chapter 13, section 2. It is not just to take a life from another to achieve an end—namely, the preservation of my own affairs. For it is just that another’s life be preserved; therefore, one could equally conclude from the same principle that my own life should be sacrificed to maintain what is just. But it is not just to kill another in such a situation, even if mercy is granted to one who did such a thing out of love for preserving his own life. On this, see the notes of **Johannes à Felde**, Doctor of Laws, on Hugo Grotius’s *Law of War and Peace*, pages 439–440. Regarding those who have taken their own lives out of the vice of anger or excessive impatience, it is right that their corpses be treated with severity; since they have cast off all human feeling, nothing else remains but to use their bodies as an example to deter others. See the same à Felde in the cited tract, page 393. Life is counted among external goods, and it belongs to a man, but it is his own to guard, not to destroy—perhaps for this reason: that no one truly has the right to kill himself. Yet, our life can be "lost" or given up, but not through vice or excessive anger or despair; rather, we may undergo death for our country, for our friends, and for our brothers. To lay violent hands upon oneself is a vicious act, which is prohibited because of its inherent flaw. Ibid. page 382.

### 75. The Sick, Leper-Houses, and the "Separate-Sick." <note>original German: *Siechen, Siechenhäuſer, Sonder-ſiechen*</note> Lepers and Leprosaria.

It is evident that the appointment of overseers for a leper-house, the auditing of their accounts, and the visitation and inspection of the house etc., belong to the **Right of Sovereignty** <note>original: *jus Superioritatis*</note>. For administration is tied to visitation, and visitation is tied to the jurisdiction of the **Ordinary** <note>original: *Ordinarii*; the local authority or judge</note>, as noted by Nicolaus Everhardus the Younger, counsel 1, numbers 176 and following, volume 1. This Ordinary, regarding lay hospitals (and thus much

<column-break/>

more so for leper-houses), is the superior Lay Lord of the territory. See Aldericus Mascardus, *On the Interpretation of Statutes*, conclusion 1, number 164 and following.

Concerning our local **leprosy**, whether it is the same as that of the Jews, and why it is less frequent and savage today, I have said some things in my tract *On Life and Death*, folio 78 and following. Regarding leprosy, see also Mercurialis, *On Diseases of the Skin*, folio 179.

Lepers are called **Separate-sick** <note>original German: *Sonderſiechen*</note> because they are separated from other sick people.

### ADDITION.

**If a Magistrate** <note>original German: *Ammeiſter*; a chief municipal official</note> **becomes sick**, or if he who dies or becomes sick. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 3, page 68. Whether a marriage is dissolved on account of leprosy: C. Rittershusius in *The Novels*, page 240, number 4. If a healthy person nevertheless wishes to consummate a marriage with a leper, taking no account of the disease, should they be prohibited by the Magistrate? See Cypraeus, *On Betrothals*, page 548, number 2.

**A leper inherits neither fief nor inheritance** <note>original German: *Ein Ausſätziger erbet weder Lehen noch Erbe*</note>; but if he received the fief before the disease and becomes sick afterward, he retains it and passes it on as any other man. *Crusius* in *Feudal Lessons*, page 40. According to **Saxon Law**, no man or woman on their sickbed can give away any of their goods worth more than five shillings without the consent of their heirs. *Schneidewin* on the *Institutes*, page 252, at the end.

### 76. Seal. <note>original: *Sigillum*</note>

A seal or sign <note>commonly called a **Seal, Signet, or Stamp**; original German: *Sigill, Petſchafft oder Pitſchier*</note> is a **character** <note>original: *character*; a distinctive mark</note>, that is, a note and form which is impressed for the sake of proof and faith. See the chapter *Inter dilectos* in the section *on the credibility of instruments*. This may be done with a signet ring (Law 74, *On the Meaning of Words*) or with another sign and seal. For men sign in various ways, provided that the sign they use has a **distinctive form** <note>original Greek: *χαρακτῆρα*</note>, that is, a shape or an engraved image. See Law 22, section 4 of the Digest, *on who can make a will*, and Law 22, *on witnesses*.

When an instrument is not corroborated by the **Public Seal** of a magistrate designated for business, but has only a **private seal** attached, it is not considered a public instrument. While it may prove the truth of the judgment or act it mentions, it is merely a private writing. It proves and operates against the one who wrote it, but it does not establish faith or legal proof against a third party. See Innocentius and the Doctors in chapter 2, *on the credibility of instruments*; Socinus, counsel 108, column 3; and Cravetta, counsel 46, number 5. Menochius distinguishes in the same way between the public or customary seal of a magistrate used for business and a private seal, in *On Arbitrary Judicial Decisions*, book 2, case 113. This distinction is confirmed by Felinus in chapter 3, *on the credibility of instruments*, and Baldus, counsel 464, number 1, part 1. There are certain reasons for this distinction: namely, that private seals can be stolen more easily and used for fraud than the public seals of Princes, Nobles, and Cities, which are therefore guarded with great care. *Panormitanus.*
