# Title S.

...in the chapter *After the Cession*, number 15, on the topic of proofs. Wesenbeck, Counsel 11, number 36; and Counsel 27, number 12, regarding Law 2, section "He however," of the Code on the Abolition of the Status of Freedmen <note>original: *C. de Lat. lib. toll.*</note>.

There are two types of **seals** in the law. The first is the **authentic seal**, which creates legal trust <note>original: *fidem facit*</note>, such as the seals of Emperors, Princes, and similar Great Magnates; this is called a **public seal** by virtue of its public office. Indeed, judges—both those with ordinary jurisdiction and those specifically delegated—are permitted the use of a seal to guarantee the reliability of their records. This applies to summonses as well as other substantial legal actions. The form for this is established by Durandus <note>original: *Specul.*; referring to the *Speculum Iudiciale*, a famous medieval legal manual</note> in the title on citations, section "Now concerning citations," number 2. Where there is only one judge, a single seal is used; if there are many, multiple seals may be applied, though one is sufficient, as noted in the same place and by Thesauro, book 2, forensic questions, final question, number 10, etc.

The second type consists of **private seals**, which do not make a writing "authentic" <note>meaning they do not carry the inherent legal weight of an official state document</note>. This is because a private seal is not applied to confirm the legal status of the writing, but only as a testimony; it carries only the same weight as a signature. This is discussed at length by Socinus, Counsel 258, book 2, number 7, and Romanus, Counsel 303, at the end.

Indeed, it seems a seal has less weight for proving a case, especially against a third party, because a seal by itself says nothing and speaks nothing; it is a **mute and uncertain witness** <note>original: *testis mutus & incertus*</note>. See Baldus on the title *Concerning the Peace of Constance*, verse "Imperial," number 8; and Menochio, case 131, at the beginning.

We employ seals or signs in legal documents <note>term: <term>Instruments</term>—any formal legal document or deed</note> for the sake of greater security, and with them, we fortify and protect the contents. This is because truth is impressed more deeply upon the eyes than the ears <note>a reference to the visual nature of evidence in the Institutes of Justinian</note>. Therefore, many seals attached to letters create a greater and more powerful proof. Caspar Antonius Thesauro, book 2, forensic questions, final question, number 9.

The affixing of a seal is done to authenticate and confirm the reliability of the acts, according to the text and gloss on the chapter *It has arrived* regarding guarantors. The application of a seal renders a writing authentic and worthy of trust (Baldus on the law of good faith, Code on Oaths), and it implies the approval of the entire writing, even if written by another. This is discussed extensively by Gabriel, Common Conclusions, conclusion 1 on proofs, conclusion 4, throughout.

For a seal to be beyond doubt, it is necessary that it be impressed **whole and recognizable**. The Canonists <note>experts in Church law</note> state this in the chapter *Regarding these things* on the reliability of instruments. Hence, if a signature is made but does not appear to be sealed, it is not valid (Law 22, section 3 of the Digest on who can make a will). See also Menochio, case 113, and presumption 57, book 2; Covarruvias, Practical Questions 22; and Antonius Gabriel, conclusion 4, number 23, book 1.

From the application of a seal, the **consent** of the person to whom the seal belongs is proven, or at least presumed (Law 51 and Law 126, section "Chrysogonus" of the Digest on Verbal Obligations). Likewise, the application of a seal is a sign of ratification and confirmation. Baldus notes on the law of fraud regarding military wills that a delegation of authority can be proven solely by the seal of the one delegating. Innocentius agrees in the chapter *Since against* regarding proofs.

Furthermore, it provides perfect proof against the person who sealed it, as handed down by Cephalus, Counsel 141,

<column-break/>

number 11, volume 1. This holds as long as nothing was done through deceit or fraud (Law 2 of the Code on the property of others). See Menochio, book 2, presumption 57 and following, throughout.

That which is affixed against the owner's will or without their knowledge does not prejudice them (Law "Caius Sejus" on pledge actions; Schurff, Counsel 7, numbers 5 and 17, number 13, hundred 1; Schrader, book 2, Counsel 32). For it is often discovered that a seal was applied through deliberate fraud. If anyone **imitates another's seal**, they fall into the **crime of forgery** <note>original: *crimen falsi*</note> and are liable to undergo the penalty of death, or banishment and flogging, depending on the circumstances (Law "What if a forgery," Digest on Forgery). Everyone ought to use their own sign and not that of another.

For whoever makes or carves a counterfeit sign, or whoever uses illicit signs, is punished under the Cornelian Law on Forgery <note>original: *L. Cornelia de falsis*; a Roman law dating back to Sulla that established penalties for various types of fraud and forgery</note>.

However, witnesses who lack a signet ring or other seal may use the ring or seal of another without penalty for forgery (according to the section "They can," 5, of the Institutes on the ordering of wills). But the person who uses another's sign must state why they have employed it (Law "To the witnesses," section "If by himself," Digest on witnesses; Francesco Marc, 1st decision, 992).

For a seal applied without someone's knowledge and through fraud does not bind them. Mascardus, conclusion 1302, number 8; Menochio, presumption 57, numbers 8 and 9. It is different when one's own proper seal is impressed. Marc, decision 991; Bornit on Instruments, book 1, chapter 29 and following.

A seal placed alone without supporting evidence <note>original: *adminiculis*; literally "props" or "supports"</note> is like a **mute and uncertain witness**, as Baldus says. It is an inanimate thing that can easily be corrupted or stolen, and a false one secretly substituted in its place. Therefore, the signature and the sealing of the party and the witnesses are usually required together. Truly, **two bonds bind more strongly than one** (Law "Joined in the matter," Digest on legacies). Variety seen by the eyes, suggested to so many senses, and placed safely in the hands is more and more confirmed. Thus, in a solemn Will, the use of both the hand <note>the signature</note> and the sign <note>the seal</note> is necessarily required. If any of the witnesses has not written his name, but has nevertheless sealed it, it is as if he had not been present. But see Bornit on Instruments, book 1, chapter 21.

If the seal is removed, the legal document is annulled and spoiled for the same reason that a signature is deleted (according to the text in the Authentica *It is not observed*, Code on Wills). There, it states: If a testator [intended] a Will...

# Augmented Treasury of Practice
<page-num>998</page-num>

...if he has happened upon the deed or has removed the seals <note>original: *signa removerit*</note>. *Novel 119, chapter 9, section 1, 30. Code, ibid. or if he has broken the seal, Law 23.* Or if he has disturbed the signs <note>original: *signa turbaverit* - referring to the physical wax seals</note> *Law 22, section 3, Digest: Who can make a will.* Since a seal is also required for the formal validity <note>original: *solennitatem*</note> of a Will, and was used by the Testator as a formal requirement, it follows that by removing it, he is seen to have withdrawn from his previous intent. Therefore, that Will, being no longer formal, is not intended to be valid in the way it ought to be.

The use of seals was primarily introduced to avoid forgeries; for a seal cannot be forged as easily as handwriting, as Suetonius shows in his life of *Nero*, chapter 17. See also Caspar Antonius Thesauro, book 2, forensic questions, question 10, from the beginning.

When should credit be given to the seals of others? See Mynsinger on the reliability of instruments, chapter 7, number 3, and page 33.

On the recognition of seals, see *Judicial Precedents of the Imperial Chamber*, under the word "recognition of seals."

The right to seal letters belongs to the universal Lord of the territory, according to Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, counsel 47, volume 1, throughout the discourse.

By the harmonious assertion of the Doctors [of Law], it is held that if a public instrument is sealed, and the seal is broken or removed, the legal weight <note>original: *fides*</note> of the instrument nevertheless endures. Zasius, book 1, counsel 2, numbers 37 and following, along with those cited there.

You will find more on seals in Bornitius's treatise on instruments, page 81 etc. and page 88; Ludolph Schrader, counsel 32; Montero à Cueva, decision 12; Menochius, book 2, presumption 57, etc.; Borelli on the Edicts of Magistrates, book 2, chapter 13; Master Martin Mager, treatise on the Armed Advocacy, chapter 14, number 80 and following; Kirchner, The Chancellor, book 4, chapters 2 and 3.

On the efficacy, authority, and proof of seals, see extensively Matthias Coler, counsel 28, number 220, etc., and Rutger Ruland in the notes to the processes of Ferrariensis Montanus, page 124.

->ADDITION.<-

The breaking or removal of seals is presumed to have been done by the person with whom the instrument is found. *Law 17, chapter 27, axiom 4.* A thing is presumed to belong to the person whose seal is on it. If there is a dispute between two people over things belonging to them because both use the same seal, the items should be awarded to the possessor; but if they are not with them but held by a third party, they are divided between the contenders. Barbosa, Law 17, chapter 27, axiom 5. Who may be considered "entitled to a seal" <note>German: *Siegelmäßig* — referring to those of a social rank, such as nobility or high officials, legally permitted to use a heraldic signet</note>. Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 11, number 247. The country judge ought to be "entitled to a seal." Höpingk on the Law of Seals, chapter 4, number 72. "Seal and Letter" <note>German: *Siegel und Brieff* — a formal legal document or certificate</note> provide immediate proof. *Chapter 11, number 252 and following.* On the custody of seals, *chapter 6, throughout.*

The Treasury's wealth <note>original: *Res fisci est*</note> will have its coffers swell less if the profit from the seal decreases or vanishes. A sealed copy is prepared for "milking" <note>original: *emulgendun* — likely a cynical reference to the collection of fees for official copies</note>. Justus Oldekop on swearing in another's soul, page 55. Concerning the objection against "Seal and

<column-break/>

Letter" <note>German: *Brieff*</note>. Schneidewein on the Institutes, page 1003. A seal <note>German: *Siegel*</note>, from the Latin *sigillum*, was a mark of nobility. *Law: When Gold, 19, section: The Bed, 8.* Thus the seals and images of ancestors were gathered together. *Digest, on gold and silver, Law: The question, 12, section: Papinian, 23.* Add Caspar Antonius Thesauro, book 2, forensic questions 100, number 4; contrary to Budé, law 17, section "The Chapel" <note>original: *Capella*</note>, and also Theodor Höpingk, chapter 17, number 29. And on the law of insignia, Lorenzo Pignoria, book 1, section: Letter 1, page 7, argues that the seal-engraver should keep an impression of the coat of arms to prevent all fraud; for signet rings <note>German: *Pettschafften*</note> are sometimes forged. For this reason, the law provides that in the affairs of private persons, the seal alone proves nothing without a handwritten signature. See above under the word **Bath**.

### 77. Silver Purchase, Broken Silver.
->Purchase of silver.<-

Under Civil Law, it is established that metals should be sold to the treasury rather than to private individuals; hence the German Princes reserve for themselves the purchase of metals in their territories, commonly called the **Silver Purchase** <note>German: *Silberkauff*</note>. *Law 1, Code, on metals.* This is also observed regarding Salt in France, as cited by Farinacci, question 104, inspection 2, number 64; and below in Italy, Afflitto, chapter 1, on the things which are Royal <note>original: *quæ sunt Regalia* — sovereign rights</note>. Thus the right to grant permission to private individuals is reserved to the Prince, so that they may search for rocks, stones, and metals. Afflitto, in the cited chapter "Which things are Royal," under the word "Silver-works," number 8.

->ADDITION.<-

What "Silver Cakes" <note>German: *Silberkuchen* — refined silver ingots or masses</note> are. *Rudinger, century 1, observation 63; Thomingius, decision 30, number 12; Supplement to Wehner, page 61.* Our most August Emperor himself, as well as the most Serene Electors of Saxony and Brandenburg, and the most illustrious Dukes of Württemberg and Mecklenburg, have in recent years most strictly ordained—by renewed edicts in their territories—that no gold or silver, whether worked, obsolete, or even prohibited from exported coinage, should be sold or distributed anywhere other than in their own mints and administrative offices. Master Tobias Oelhafen on the Goddess of Money, page 239. Today, the German Princes in their territories that produce metals have reserved the purchase of metals for themselves, commonly called the **Silver Purchase**. *Köppen, decision 59, number 13; Heigius, book 1, question 13, number 60.* Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentoratum*</note> was chosen by the Romans as a public treasury for tributes, into which a vast amount of silver was brought. Hence "Silver-Valley" <note>original: *Silberthal*</note>, or "Silbertina" for Strasbourg. Limnäus in Public Law, book 7, chapter 3, number 2. Concerning "Silver-Tax" <note>German: *Silberzins*</note>, the same, book 6, chapter 4, number 20. Coins of Domitian and Justinian were found...

# 80. Slaves. *Sclavi*.

It was a task of the greatest difficulty to tame and subdue the Slavic people in Bohemia and neighboring places. For as the Slavs first entered Bohemia and its borders, they never ceased to cause hostile trouble for the Germans <note>original: *Teutonibus*</note>, to whom they were not very welcome guests at the beginning. For this reason, the Germans, bearing it most reluctantly that they were nourishing foreigners in their bosom like certain serpentine beasts, labored constantly to drive the Slavs back from the occupied seats; or, if that could not be done because of their great number, at least to put a bridle on them, lest they dare to progress or raid further. From this, great wars arose, with the Slavs fighting for possession and the Germans for their right. And fortune mostly favored the Germans, so that they led the conquered and captured Slavs into the most miserable servitude, and distributed them everywhere through Europe like beasts of burden, destined for public works. From this was born that common formula of speaking, which not only the Germans but most Europeans still use today: that they employ "Slavs" <note>original: *Sclavos*</note> for "servants" and "slaves" <note>original: *mancipiis*</note> in common speech. See Mr. Goldast, *On Bohemia*, book 2, chapter 1, and add Me. *On the Three Types of Domestic Society*, specimen folio 32.

->ADDITION.<-

On Slaves, see Limn. in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 8, number 77. Zeiller, *Italian Itinerary*, page 112. Properly, *Slavvni* denotes "noble," but now it refers to anyone...

# The Expanded Treasury of Practice

Germans, French, Italians, and Spaniards compete in their names for a Slave: *Schlaff*, *Esclave*, *Schiavon*, *Esclavo*. The name comes from the nation of the Slavs <note>original: "Sclavum... ex nomine gentis est"</note>, who were the last to be reduced to servitude by Christians; just as the ancients used to name their slaves after the conquered nations of the Getae, Dacians, Syrians, etc. See Besold, *On Politics*, book 1, chapter 10. **Those who have nothing to live on, or who cannot pay the penalty for their evil deeds, or parents who cannot feed their children, are made into slaves. According to Hemmersam in his *West-Indian Voyage Description*, page 54, they are sold to the sugar-masters. Page 55: They must be slaves forever. Page 56.** The *Catasta* <term>A wooden platform or stage used in slave markets</term> was a rigid and sturdy place where slaves for sale were displayed with feet marked with gypsum <note>White chalk or gypsum was used to mark newly imported slaves who had not yet been sold in the city</note>; they were also stripped naked so that buyers could inspect them to ensure no disease or defect was hidden. Tibullus writes:
> I speak of what is known; he himself holds the kingdom, whom the barbarian platform often forced to bear gypsum-marked feet.
And Persius, *Satire 6*:
> To have fed fat Cappadocians on the rigid platform.

# Letter S.

...of the preceding things. Klock volume 2, consultation 35, numbers 28 and 29. The word "If" creates a condition, unless an absurd interpretation would follow from it. Did. book 2, chapter 4, number 3, verse "nor will it hinder that the Royal." The word "If" generally and regularly denotes a condition, as does the particle "When" <note>original: "cum"</note>: examples are found in Law 48 *on the condition of debt*, Law 45, paragraph 3, *on verbal obligations*, Law 22 *regarding the day of a legacy*; add C.I.A. *on conditions and demonstrations*, thesis 7, number 3, and thesis 24, and the following, paragraph 28 (others say 31) in the *Digest on legacies*. And there, Wesenbeck notes that "if" is also taken for "although," or "even if," in Law 31, verse "and therefore" *on the Reception of Arbitrators*, Law 7, paragraph 10 *on the Macedonian Senate-Consult*, and Law 15, paragraph 2, there: "if however," *regarding force or stealth*; Law 12, final paragraph *on mandates*; Law 78, final paragraph *on the contract of sale*. "If" is sometimes used for "whether," following a Greek usage <note>original: "per Gracismum"</note>. Rittershusius, *Feudal Partitions*, 225, 337. On the difference between "If" and "When," see Forster, *Book of Successive Observations*, chapter 11. "If" can also mean "because." Val. Wilhelm Forster, *Book of Successive Observations*, final chapter.

### 84. Provided that. Dummodò.

That phrase *so fern* <gloss>as far as / provided that</gloss> designates a condition and is clear in itself, as testified by Borgnin. Cavalcanti in his *Treatise on the Usufruct of a Relict Widow*, section 2, numbers 42 and 44. He notes that these words—*provided that*, *on the condition that*, *in the case that*, etc.—not only introduce a condition but also denote that it ought to be and must be perpetually observed. Magonius, *Decisions of Lucca*, 89, numbers 10 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

The particle "Provided that" creates a condition. Tiraquell, *On Retractions*, book 1, section 8, glossary 8, single number. "Provided that a right has not been acquired by another." Marius Antonius, book 1, reference 10, number 2; book 1, reference 29, number 8; reference 104, number 24. Under the clause "if it is so." The same author, book 1, reference 58, numbers 2, 3, and following. Regarding the clause "If it shall be established to be so." Cravetta, consultation 592.

### 85. Pay, Mercenary, Soldier. Stipendium, Merces, Solidatus.

A *Solidatus* <term>A soldier, literally "one who is paid"</term>, according to Vegetius, is the name given to one to whom pay <note>original: "Stipendia"</note> has been promised by the Emperor. From this, the common term *Soldner* <gloss>mercenary/soldier</gloss> is undoubtedly derived, meaning one who receives pay, and *Sold* <gloss>pay</gloss> for the stipend itself. Indeed, the Roman people served as soldiers at their own expense for over two hundred years; finally, the Senators <note>original: "Patres," referring to the Patricians/Senators</note> decreed that the soldier should receive a stipend. As military affairs succeeded happily, in order to further inflame their spirits, they used to add grain and clothing to the money for the infantry, and for others, a horse. From this, they began to be called the "Enrolled" <note>original: "Matriculati"</note> and the "Paid" <note>original: "Solidati"</note>. Oldendorp, *On Actions*, class 5, *on beneficiary actions*, page 742.

For others, the origin of this word (*Soldat* <gloss>Soldier</gloss>) comes from the *Solidus* <term>A gold coin</term>, which Hincmarus testifies was worth 40 denarii in his book *On the Life and Acts of the Blessed Remigius*; or from *Sold*, which signifies stipend and wages. The Abbot of Ursperg writes concerning Emperor Philip: "Since he did not have the money to provide wages or pay <note>original: "solaria sive solda"</note> to the soldiers, he was the first to begin selling off the estates which his father

<meta>catchword: Befoldi Volume I.</meta>

<column-break/>

had acquired." For Carloman, in a religious Edict found in Aventinus, book 3, says: "Because of frequent wars, a portion of the Church's money—namely 12 Denarii, which we call a *Solidum* <gloss>shilling/solidus</gloss>—shall be contributed to me, so that rewards worthy of their labors may be paid to our soldiers."

The Feudal lawyers also derive this name from *solidi* <note>the coins</note>, book 2, title 10. A *Soldata* is a certain annual, voluntary payment, so named because it usually consists of a donation of shillings; sometimes, however, it consists of wine and grain.

The etymology of *Soldaten* <gloss>Soldiers</gloss> can also be derived from the Gallic *Soldurii* <term>Retainers or sworn companions who shared the fate of their leader</term>; see my work *On the Free Equestrian Order*, at the beginning.

->ADDITION.<-

See above under the word *Landsknecht* <gloss>Infantryman</gloss>. Dr. Dinner in *The Bat-Soldier*. Erycius Puteanus wrote regarding military pay. Today’s soldiers, under the name of "billeted guests," demand not only what they call "the services" <note>original: "les services"</note>—and under that name include wood, candles, salt, and a bed (*Holtz, Liecht, Saltz, Lagerstätt*)—but they also require sumptuous feasts and delicacies for the throat. Tabor, *On Billeting*, page 114. "The donkeys <note>The pack animals or perhaps a metaphor for the burden of supply</note> are not built for the citizens, but only for the soldiers." Dr. Tabor, in the same place, page 123. Those who are discharged and sent away from the service, while still pretending to the name of Soldiers, actually become "pups in the woods and ravenous wolves in the groves," as Baldus says in Law 1, at the end, *on those who can surrender their goods*. There are those who think, along with Leodegarius à Quercu in his *Poem on Peace*, that "stealing is the pouch of war," the dowry of battle: terrestrial planets, chicken-catchers. See more in Dr. Tabor's *Aphorisms*, page 30, regarding the *Heyducken* <term>Hajduks; irregular foot soldiers or brigands in the Balkans and Central Europe</term>, who do not hesitate to throw themselves into deadly danger for their patrons for a daily morsel of bread. Page 39: More eminent soldiers, some of whom they call Captains, others Colonels—regarding the origin of which word see Tabor in *Hoplophoria*, page 1377—or there are lower ranks. See the same, and Otto in *Public Law*, chapter 19, page 472. Those who are called "booted soldiers" <note>original: "Caligati milites"</note> are defined in *Novel 74, section "whoever however"*; also Law 6, section "but also the booted" *on military matters*, where "booted" is said simply <note>original: "ἁπλῶς"</note> for a soldier. Cinuzzi, *On Military Discipline*, book 51, number 57. Petrus Pappus in *Dutch Military Law*, page 88. Julius Ferretus wrote on military matters. Count James of Purlilia, *On Military Matters*. Claudius Coteræus, *On the Law of Soldiers*. Ayala, *On the Law and Duty of War*. Baron von Hoëneck, *On the Privileges of Soldiers*. Martinus of Lodi, *Treatise on the Soldier*. Johann Jacob von Wallhausen in his *Art of War*. Conrad Dieterich published a *Discourse on War-Robbery and Booty*.

Regarding the recruitment of soldiers, their levying, the denial of passage, the passage of troops through another’s territory, and the guarantee of compensating for all future damage, see Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 79.

In Strasbourg, there are the Lords of the Thirteen, secret counselors, who are commanded to recruit and discharge those involved in fortifications, armory matters, cavalry and infantry, mercenaries, trumpeters, along with their captains; they also handle secret matters communicated by various potentates or estates, etc. Stollius, in his *Description of the Republic of Strasbourg*. Master Bernegger puts it more briefly: The Lords <term>Tredecimviri</term> <gloss>The Thirteen Men</gloss> take care of the city's defenses, the armory, the stable (namely the purchase of horses), the recruitment, as well as the inspection of the soldiers and the salaried knights, and whatever pertains to military service. Regarding which soldiers are prohibited from being recruited, see Liebenthal in *Political Collection*, Exercise 14, thesis 22. On whether soldiers should be recruited and accepted without distinction, see Zeiller, century 4, question 21, page 93.

### 87. Solemnities. *Solennitas.*

A solemnity is whatever special requirement is needed beyond mere consent, and whatever is added to the formation of the law of nations <note>original: "juris Gentium"</note>, according to Baldus on the law *If a Letter* in the Code *on trusts*; it is an indivisible act. Baldus says the same in the law *brought forward* 2, number 7, in the Code *on sentences*: that a solemnity consists in performing a formal act according to the form of the law. A solemnity is something distinct, and differs from both substance and form, as noted by Innocent in the chapter *Because just as*, column 2, *on elections*. Baldus, in law 1, column 2, number 4, in the Code *on the most sacred Churches*, says that although we use these words interchangeably, they differ: for form is one thing, solemnity another, and substance another. Form is the pattern of the text in a Will, or the interrogation and response in a formal promise <term>stipulatio</term>. Examples of solemnity are the summoning of witnesses, the formal request, the writing, and similar requirements. Substance, however, is the disposition itself and the matter itself—that is, the essence of the thing. Law *the substance of obligations* in the Digest *on actions and obligations*. See Bertazolus in his *Treatise on the Clauses of Instruments*, Clause 4, glossary 20; and Everhard in *Legal Topics*, under the topic "from a defect of form."

<column-break/>

->ADDITIO.<-

Regarding Solemnities, and the extent to which they ought to intervene in every act, or are presumed to have intervened, there exists a singular treatise by Scipio Gentilis.

### 88. As often and as much. *Toties, quoties.*

By the words "As often as," <note>original: "Toties, Quoties"</note> it seems that a very free discretion is granted, without any restriction of time, to do that which has been granted in this manner. Law *As if* 7, paragraph 1, in the Digest *on producing documents*; and law 15, paragraph 1, and the gloss there on the word "again." Antonius Gabriel, *Common Conclusions*, book 7, title *on crimes*, conclusion 15, number 3 and following, where he says this clause is fit to imply infinity; Jacob Schultes, in book 2 of *Practical Questions*, question 55, number 1, calls this the more common opinion. See Marta in the *Treatise on Clauses*, part 1, clause 348.

->ADDITIO.<-

Boer discusses the clause "as often as" in decision 131, number 10, along with the thirteen following points.

### 89. Shall. *Oportet.*

The word "shall" <note>original: "oportet," meaning "it is necessary"</note> implies precise compulsion or necessity, as proved in law 1 at the beginning, there: "first it is necessary to know," in the Digest *on Justice and Law*. However, sometimes, by reason of the subject matter, it is used improperly to imply only propriety, and is explained as "it is fitting" <note>original: "decet"</note>; the text is in law 1 at the beginning, joined with the gloss, in the Digest *on Justice and Law*, and in the preface of the *Institutes* from the beginning. So also the word "is bound" <note>original: "tenetur"</note>, which regularly implies necessity (Clementine decree *I went out of Paradise*, paragraph *And because moreover* at the end), changes its nature because of the subject matter, as in the text in the chapter *Among other things* *on the sentence of excommunication*.

Similarly, the word "ought" <note>original: "debet"</note> is used improperly because of the subject matter, and is sometimes placed for "can" <note>original: "potest"</note>, and conversely the word "can" for "ought," in the text joined with the gloss in law 2 of the Code *where a property action exists*, and in the law *to observe*, paragraph *after this*, in the Digest *on the office of Proconsul*. And sometimes the word "ought," by reason of the subject matter, is placed for "it is fitting," even if a precise word precedes it entirely, according to chapter 1 *on the marriage of minors*. Schrader, *On Fiefs*, part 10, section 29, number 26; Nicolaus Everhard in the topic "from the subject matter," number 17; Stephanus Gratianus, volume 1, *Forensic Discussions*, chapter 146, number 19. On how the word "shall" <note>original: "sollen"</note> is understood in mandates, see Master Wilhelm Anton in the treatise *On Letters of Moratorium*, page 509. Likewise, the same author teaches in the said treatise, chapter 29, numbers 5 and 6, when those words "shall be void and incompatible" are to be understood.

->ADDITIO.<-

The word "to owe" or "must" <note>original: "debere"</note> is of such a nature and efficacy that it removes all exceptions, and therefore even the exception of prevention. Shall... <meta>Catchword: Shall</meta>

### 90. But [Sondern]. But [Sed].
The nature of this adversative word is that it is placed between diverse things and demonstrates an open diversity between them, both in law and in fact; according to the singular teaching of Socinus, in *law "fandum," number 7, Digest on exceptions.* Octavius Vulpellus in his *Treatise on Prepositions, Adverbs, and Conjunctions, on the word "sed," at the section "& ponitur." Hermann Vultejus among the Marpurg Consultations, consultation 35, number 79, volume 3.*

->ADDITIO.<-

*But [Sed], Boerius, decision 155, number 20. But [Sed]*, standing for *but also [sed &]*, Lord Doctor Biccius *in "aur." page 293 of my copy.* This is of the first edition. For a second edition, enlarged from the author's manuscripts, is promised at Strasbourg from Josias Städel in octavo.

### 91. Especially, chiefly [Sonderlich, fürnemlich]. Principally [Præcipuè].
The word **principally** [præcipuè, fürnemlich] is implicative, and thus includes the contrary case, even if not expressed. *Gloss on law 1, on the word "præcipuè," Digest on witnesses.* Just as concerning the word **most of all** [maximè], the word **especially** [sonderlich] was judged by the gloss on *law 31, on the word "æstimari," Digest on the Aquilian Law, paragraph "in l. quod si minor," paragraph "restitutio," on the word "in venditione," Digest on minors.* Jason *on law "qui se patris," number 34, Code on "unde lib." Everhard in "loc. à natùr. diction. implicet." Molina on the Customs of Paris, part 1, section 2, gloss 4, number 37.* And see what I said above, under the word **Also** [Auch]. Volckmar Hess in his *Treatise on Witnesses, century 4, conclusion 40, number 117.*
The word **particularly** [præsertim] is properly placed comparatively, and carries the same weight as the word **most of all** [maximè], *Calder. consultation 548. Gemin. consultation 16, number 4, at the section "non obstat,"* where it is noted that it does not induce a necessity of proving that which is said through the word **particularly** [præsertim] or **most of all** [maximè], *Tusch. practical conclusions, letter D, conclusion 338. Symph. Gylman. volume 1, part 2, folio 215, number 11.* But the word joined with the word **AND** [ET] is adversative to the preceding points in fact, but not in law, *Boer. decision 155, number 20.*

### 92. Otherwise others [Sonsten andere]. Otherwise [Aliàs].
These words are understood to refer to similar things. See *The Composition of Peace, folio 426.*

### 93. Sunday [Sonntag]. The Lord's Day [Dies Dominica].
In memory of the Lord's Resurrection and as an act of thanksgiving, the day itself on which it occurred was called the "Lord's Day," by none other than the Apostles themselves. For even John

<column-break/>

the Evangelist mentions the day being called such; likewise Ignatius, and others closest to the times of the Apostles; and they established that it should be celebrated, not only at the anniversary revolution of the months' cycle, but at the recurrence of the same first day of every week. *Baronius in the Annals for the Year of Christ 34, number 52.*

->ADDITIO.<-

See the term **Sabbath**.

### 94. As well as, etc. [So wol, als]. Both, and [Tam, quàm].
The words **both** [tam] and **and** [quàm] are distributive, and they attribute the action to each statement. *Law "si cui legatorum," Digest on "ut in poss. legat." Grat. 9, consultation 9, number 99, book 1. Menochius, consultation 400, number 1*, and by their nature they are resolved into singularity. *The final law, Code on "dot. promiss."* See examples in the *Acts of Lindau, folio 438.*
These words sometimes stand augmentatively—for instance, if a Privilege is granted to someone in all things and through all things, just as a certain person has, and it is subjoined, **both** [tam] as to jurisdiction, **as well as** [quàm] to other things, then the clause itself extends [the right]. Sometimes it restricts, as when a partnership is contracted for all things to be acquired, **both** [tam] from art **as well as** [quàm] from works; then the partnership itself is restricted to the things explained by the clause. *Marta, on Clauses, part 1, clause 372.*

Whether a penalty is owed <note>original: "Utrum debeatur pœna"</note> when someone, despite a set penalty of 10 or more Guilders, vows <term>verredt</term><note>A formal renunciation or vow to cease a behavior, often under a self-imposed or agreed-upon fine.</note> not to gamble, and then plays anyway regardless of such a promise? Thus, the defendant is obligated to open his conscience—namely, whether he promised and vowed to the plaintiff that he would never again play a game for as long as he lived, neither with cards, dice, nor bowls <note>original: "Boßkugeln"</note>, and that as often as he was found gambling, he would owe the plaintiff 100 Thalers. Since he did not uphold this and played cards at P., he was legally obligated to pay the plaintiff the agreed-upon penalty for every time he played, according to the law, etc.

On the ruinous nature <note>original: "De pernicie"</note> of gambling, see *Lord Wilhelm Anton in his treatise on Five-Year Postponements, folio 483; Maurit. ## 97. Hospital. [Spital]. Hospitale.

A hospital is called a venerable and pious place, just like a church, and therefore all privileges granted to churches are extended to hospitals and other pious places. *Schneidewin on prescriptions, species 4, under number 18.*

Hospitals established by the authority of a Bishop enjoy ecclesiastical immunity, *Archidiac. in chapter "definit." 17, question 4,* followed by *Baldus in law "si quis ad declinandum," section "in omnib." number 2, Code on Bishops and Clergy; Paul de Castro, consultation 458, volume 2; Alexander, consultation 9, column 1, volume 1; fully treated by Remigius, treatise on the immunity of the Church, extension 17, on the word "Hospitals."*

On whether and to what extent hospitals belong to the clergy, see *Costa, consultation 4; Tutsch. practical conclusions, on the word "Hospital"; Ludovic. decisions 2 and 8, where he discusses who has the right to visit <note>inspect</note> hospitals.*

On the hospitals and alms of the old Frankish Emperors, much is found in *Grand-*

### 98. Spoliation Cases. <note>original: "Spolisachen. Causæ spolii." Cases involving the wrongful deprivation of property or rights.</note>

For the practice in cases of spoliation, see Franciscus Pfeil, *Legal Opinions*, 27. Rosacorb. in *Forensic Practice*, chapter 35. And whoever enjoys the older possession is to be protected in it, the same Pfeil, opinion 172. On the recovery of disturbed possession, Pfeil, opinion 173. On the case of spoliation and the interdict <note>A legal remedy or injunction to restore possession.</note> for obtaining possession, Rosacorb. chapter 40.

The canon "regarding restoration" <note>original: "Can. redintegrandæ"</note> has its place in the goods of the Church, and therein an account is held of the fruits <note>Profits or produce of the land.</note>

<column-break/>

collected and to be collected, and of damages and interest, Meichsner, volume 4, decision 19. On the spoliation of the Clergy, see book 7 of the *Decretals*, book 3, title 3. Chokier, *On Feudal Advocates*, folio 120.

Whether and to what extent a possessor in bad faith may be expelled from possession by force of deed <note>original: "viâ facti"</note>? *Strasbourg Legal Opinions*, volume 1, opinion 28, question 8. Spoliation is presumed when an older possession is proven. Possession is presumed to be secret or violent if the adversary proves an older possession. Nicolaus Vigelius in *Method of Controversial Law*, book 2, chapter 11, page 374.

->ADDITION.<-

A spoiler <note>One who wrongfully takes possession.</note> is bound to restore not only the seized thing but also the fruits, and furthermore is held liable for damages and interest. Law "If regarding possession," 4. Code "From whence by force." Ferrar. in *The Forum*, in the case of despoiled possession, section "for reintegration," number 1. The despoiled person is to be restored before all else <note>original: "Spoliatus ante omnia est restituendus"</note>. This takes place not only in immovable things (real estate) but also in movable things. Jacob Ayrer in *Historical Process*, part 1, chapter 11, page 307.

Spoliation differs from distraint <note>original: "pignoratione" - the legal seizure of goods to satisfy a debt.</note>. Lord Rittersh. in *New Constitutions*, page 168, number 5. "Spoil" is defined in various ways by <term>Jurisconsults</term><note>Legal experts or lawyers.</note> and historians, ibid. One who ratifies a spoliation can be sued just as the spoiler himself. Barbosa, book 17, chapter 47, axiom 3. Spoliation or restoration cannot be claimed if something was done by the authority of the law. Marius Antoninus, book 1, refinement 81, number 10. Attempted spoliation is more odious than simple spoliation, book 1, resolution 100, number 2. The most recent spoliation must be cleared first, ibid, number 7, and final resolution, case 72. A judge "spoils" if he proceeds in a way that is legally null, ibid. A despoiled person is not to be restored if they lost possession through their own fault, such as if they renounced their right, ibid, numbers 8 and 9.

A despoiled person is not to be restored if their lack of right is notorious, and the right of the other is notorious, ibid, number 10, and book 1, resolution 59, case 24. If it is notoriously clear regarding the lack of right of the one seeking restoration, the despoiled is not to be restored before all else. Jacob Ayrer in *Historical Process*, part 1, chapter 11, page 307.

The despoiled person is to be restored before all else, nor is he bound to answer to the proposed action before then. Suttinger, *Observations*, 39, number 1; even if he be a robber, number 2. Even if the opponent offers proof of ownership or lordship on the spot <note>original: "in continenti"</note>, number 3. Even if the opponent objects with the rule: "he acts deceitfully who seeks that which he must soon restore," number 4.

### ADDITION.

Legal Fees **or Deposits** <note>original: "Sportulæ oder Einlag"</note>, *Limn. vol. 2. Addit. to book 7. chap. 2. page 84.* Regarding the fees that must be paid, *Ilico Ummius in Process page 886.* and those from whom they cannot be demanded, *page 887.* On the fees of Senators, *Rittersh. in New Constitutions page 130. number 5. page 131. number 6.* An ordinary judge does not regularly receive court fees, commonly called **Filing or Court Money** <note>original: "Leg- oder Gerichtgeld"</note>.

These fees are called <term>Sportulæ</term> <note>From the Latin 'sportula,' meaning a small basket.</note> based on an ancient Roman custom. In the past, powerful Romans used to offer their clients a meal or lunch in small baskets or little hampers when the clients came to their doorsteps to pay their respects (**to wait upon them**). This was a substitute for a formal dinner, that is, a legitimate banquet. Such small baskets or *sportulæ* are named from *sporta*, a vessel made of thin twigs in which those small gifts and distributions were placed. Later, the term *Sportulæ* was expanded to denote salaries, gift-money, daily allowances, and honorariums. Finally, they began to be called *Sportulæ* when given to the executors of lawsuits; the Greeks call them *diasēma* <note>original Greek: διάσημα</note>, *Lord Doctor Rebhan on the Expenses of Lawsuits, thesis 12. throughout.*

### **Claims and Demands.** <note>original German: "Sprüche und Forderung." Latin: "Obligationes & Actiones."</note>

The word **Claims** <note>original: "Sprüche"</note> in our vernacular refers to the obligations and legal actions that can be brought against someone, *Johann Goedd. among the Marburg Consultations, consult. 28. num. 174.* **When one has something to claim against another.**

Under the name of a lawsuit or business (**Claims and Demands**), even criminal cases are included, *law 'Judiciorum' in the Digest on accusations; law 'in criminalib.' in the Code on jurisdiction; Cujas, 9. observations 21. & 24. chapter 16.*

### 100. Staple Rights, or Free Warehouse. <note>original German: "Staffel- Stappel- Gerechtigkeit, oder freye Niederlag." Latin: "Jus Stapulæ."</note>

It is established that the use of commerce and navigation ought to be free; the consequence of which is that no one can be forced to display his merchandise in this or that place, *Mynf. consult. 19. num. 3.* where he says the Imperial Chamber Court judges as such; *Sixtinus on Royal Prerogatives, chap. 5. num. 29.* unless the one forcing the merchant has the <term>Right of Emporium</term> <note>Also known as Staple Right; the legal privilege of a city to require passing merchants to unload and offer their goods for sale for a set period.</note>, **the free warehouse or staple right**, that is, the right regarding the display of goods, derived from an Imperial Privilege or from long-standing prescription. For he who has the Right of Emporium, **the Staple Right**, can compel and force those passing through to stop there and sell their goods in that same place, *Mynfing. & Sixtin. in the cited places; Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, consult. 9. book 1.* which tends greatly to the growth of a City or Commonwealth. By such a Privilege of the Emperor regarding the display of certain goods (which should not be extended to other specific goods), the people of Cologne, Mainz, and Speyer—who among other things specifically by their Privilege claimed **the third and last**

<column-break/>

**Staple on the Rhine**, based their legal intent when seeking a Mandate against **the Electorate of the Palatinate, concerning the holding of Speyer ship-goods and fair-goods at Oppenheim.** *Symphorem. vol. I. part 2. title 18.* On the Danube, this right is held by Regensburg, Ingolstadt, and Passau. On the Weser, by Bremen; on the Elbe, by Magdeburg, Hamburg, etc. The rights of some of these Cities extend only to food items, and sometimes to other specific goods. *Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, cited consult. 9. num. 82.* And he concludes that whoever has the Right of Emporium, **the free warehouse**, means that those transporting goods cannot seek new routes to avoid displaying them; for it should not be permitted indirectly when something is found to be prohibited directly for some reason. In such cases, all those things are deemed prohibited through which the effect of the prohibited acts might follow, based on the arguments of *Parisius consult. 83. vol. 3; Cornelius consult. 221. num. 1. vol. 4; Alexander consult. 194. num. 14. vol. 2. & consult. 95. num. 5. vol. 2; Thomas Mauritius on the law of conducting, title 3. num. 23.* Likewise, in number 25, he treats how the Right of Emporium, **the free warehouse**, is established by prescription; see him there.

But regarding Staple Rights, see also Hermann Esaias Rosacorb, *chap. 85.* Pfeil, *consult. 190.* Me on Majesty, *folio 204.* Strasbourg Consultations, *vol. 2. consult. 62. questions 4. & 5.* and Marburg Consultations, *vol. 4. consult. 17. & 18.* also Werdenhagen on the Hanseatic Republics, *part 3. chap. 20. folio 539. and many following pages,* and Jacob Marchant *in the description of Flanders, book 1. f. 113.*

**The Right to grant a free warehouse** <note>original: "Das Jus, eine freye Niederlag zu ertheilen"</note> also belongs to those who have absolute power over their own people, even if they courteously respect the Majesty of another. Thus, Wroclaw <note>original: "Uratislavia"</note>, in the year 1511, obtained Staple Rights from King Ladislaus, *Jacob Schickfus in **the Silesian Chronicle**, book 1. chap. 38. f. 186.*

### ADDITION.

Addit. to book 2. chap. 9. num. 130. 131. 132.* In the Empire, no one except the Emperor can establish or grant Staple Rights, *Fritsch on Fairs, chap. 10. num. 25.* There are many Cities in Germany that possess Staple Rights either with or without the privilege of holding Fairs, *chap. 10. num. 33.* Leuber wrote a full inquiry into the Staple Rights of Saxony; Dauthius wrote on *The Staple of Magdeburg* against the Count of Barby.

One should certainly see here *Besold, consult. 3. decade 1.* "Staple" comes from the old Teutonic *Stapa* or *Stapel*, which was explained as "market" in Latin in an ancient Latin-Saxon Lexicon once seen at Heidelberg, as testified by *Salmasius on Attic Law, chap. 5.* *Fritsch on Fairs, chap. 10. num. 11.* The City of Leipzig by Right holds and exercises...

### 101. Stem. <note>original: "Stamm." Latin: "Stipes."</note>

A **Stem** <note>Latin: *stipes*, literally a log or tree trunk.</note> is the name given to a common parent from whom several people have descended, just as Isaac was the stem of Esau and Jacob. Only males can truly belong to the name and the stem; for females depart from the stem and the name when they are joined in marriage to one who belongs to a foreign stem and name, or at the very least, they do not retain the name of the stem, according to the writings of Georg Everhard, *volume 2, counsel 42, number 14.*
Regarding the term **Cippus** <note>Latin for a pedestal or boundary stone, often used in legal contexts for the "trunk" of a family tree.</note>, who may be included under it? See Gratian, *Forensic Disputes, volume 5, dispute 901,* and Fusarius, *On Substitutions, questions 348, 451, and following.*

### ADDITION.

The little word **Stem** <note>German: "Stamme."</note> only encompasses males, according to Knipschild, *On Trusts, chapter 1, number 64; chapter 8, number 129.* On **Ancestral Arbitration** <note>German: "Stamm-Austräg." A legal process for settling disputes between members of the same noble family.</note>, see Limnäus, *On Public Law, book 9, chapter 5, number 3.*

### 102. Ancestral Fiefs or Forefatherly Fiefs. <note>German: "Stamm-Lehen oder Altvätterliche Lehen." Latin: "Feudum antiquum."</note>

A fief is said to be "by agreement and foresight" when it is granted to someone for themselves and their children or descendants, or those connected to the family, without making specific mention of heirs. It is commonly called an **Ancestral or Forefatherly Fief**, as noted by Andreas de Isernia, *in chapter 1, number 3,* and Antonius Gabriel, *Common Opinions, book 6, title on the Significance of Words, conclusion 3, number 22.* See also Fichard, *volume 1, counsel 18, number 32,* and Mynsinger, *century 3, observation 67.* Vultejus defines a fief of agreement and foresight as one in which succession occurs by right of blood, according to the disposition of Feudal Law, *chapter 8, number 6.* This type of fief is called "familial" by some, based on the law regarding religious and funeral expenses. Baldus, *in the code regarding trusts.*

### ADDITION.

Regarding the fief by agreement and foresight, the Lord Doctor Ludovici writes most extensively in his *Feudal Synopsis, chapter 4.* See Knipschild, *On Trusts, chapter 1, number 14, and citations there,* and add Gottfried Anton, *Feudal Disputations 1, thesis 5, letter C at the end.* A masculine fief is called an **Ancestral or Sword-Fief** <note>German: "Stamm- oder Schwerdtlehen." A fief that can only be inherited by males (the "sword" side of the family).</note>, Knipschild, *On Trusts, chapter 8, number 130,* and Gail, *book 2, observation 49, number 1.*
Regarding **Ancestral Fiefs** <note>German: "Stammlehen."</note>, one should definitely consult Rosenthal, *On Fiefs, chapter 2, conclusion 10.*

### 103. Ancestral Estates. <note>German: "Stammgüter." Latin: "Bona avita."</note>

**Ancestral Estates** are those which the donor did not acquire or obtain himself, but

<column-break/>

those gained from his ancestors, such as a grandfather and the like, and which have their origin from them: according to the text of the *Saxon Constitution 12, part 2, at the beginning.* Therefore, by the term **Ancestral Estates**, it seems only those are understood which we have acquired from the paternal line, but not the maternal line. Indeed, the cited Constitution mentions the grandfather [avus], but not at all the grandmother [avia]; this agrees with *Constitution 31 of the same part 2, there:* **And to maintain the same within the lineage.** Speaking properly of the term "family," only agnates <note>Relatives on the father's side.</note> are included, not cognates <note>Relatives on the mother's side</note>, *from the law on the definition of family in the Digest.*
However, the opposite has been pronounced by the Jurists of both Leipzig and Wittenberg, as Moller testifies in *book 1, chapter 36,* so that estates are held as **Ancestral Estates** without distinction, whether they come to us from the paternal or maternal line. This is based on the aforementioned *Constitution 31 at the end,* which says that by the term **Ancestral Estates**, those must be understood **which do not come from the parents alone, but from the grand-parents.** With this latter word, there is no doubt that the grandmother is signified no less than the grandfather, according to Moller in the cited place at the end. Regarding the right of **Retraction** <note>The right of a family member to buy back ancestral land sold to a stranger.</note> in Ancestral Estates, see *Consultations on the Saxon Constitutions, book 1, question 19 and following.*

### ADDITION.

Under Saxon Law, ancestral estates [bona avita] imitate the nature and condition of fiefs. **Ancestral Estates** are compared with "old fief-properties" in the German language, Knipschild, *On Trusts, chapter 9, numbers 5 & 6.* How **Ancestral Houses** <note>German: "Stammhäuser."</note> differ from buildings left as a trust in the name of a family, see the same author, *chapter 1, number 17;* they can be alienated [sold], as noted there. Today, hardly any traces or ruins of these remain, ibid.
See also Wehner, Rudinger, *2nd observation 29, under the word "Stammgüter."* Sichard, *on the Code regarding the recovery of property, law 3, number 6.*

### 104. Military Law and Spear-Justice. <note>German: "Stand- und Spieß-Recht, Kriegs-Recht." Latin: "Judicium hastatum criminale, Jus militare."</note>

This is what military men call the criminal judgment of the spear. From the start of a war, all soldiers are compelled to swear an oath that they will justly punish transgressors of the military articles, indulge no personal feelings, but judge as Military Law prescribes, as their own conscience admonishes, and as God, the stern avenger of injustice, demands. From this, if someone happens to sin against one or another military article, on the appointed judicial day, the entire army is convoked, **and the criminal is presented, and finally, following the prior verdict and law, he is chased through the spears** <note>A form of military execution or punishment, similar to "running the gauntlet."</note>; **meanwhile, all ensigns <note>Standard-bearers.</note> who are present stick the points of their banners into the earth until the verdict is passed; then they raise them and let them fly toward the rising sun; if he is a...**

<meta>This page continues the discussion of military law and punishments before transitioning into the etymology and legal status of cities and municipal rights.</meta>

...had it been a shooting offense, he is tied to a pillar and shot by others who step toward the sun. *Schröder, On the Law of War, final thesis, in the Basel Disputations, volume 5.*

In a Criminal Military Court, a **Regimental Provost** <note>Latin: *Scultetus*; German: *Regiments-Schultheiß*. A high-ranking military official overseeing justice.</note> is required, who, having taken an oath, selects twelve Assessors for the most part, a Court Clerk, and a Bailiff <note>German: *Gerichtsschreiber und Webel*</note>, whose services he uses for writing and issuing summons. On the appointed day, the trial is conducted punctually at eight o'clock in the open air; everyone is warned by the beat of drums to observe their assigned watches in the meantime, or whatever else is collectively commanded. Others are not prohibited from attending the trial if they wish to watch. Furthermore, both the Plaintiff and the Defendant are allowed to name one of these twelve, if they wish, to act as their advocate. After deliberating in secret and sharing counsel, the Advocate comes forward and, having requested permission, institutes either an action or an exception, produces witnesses, and so on. And so that no one is deprived of a defense—which is a matter of Natural Law—nor condemned to death unheard, the same trial is repeated three times. When these things are finished, the defendant is either acquitted or condemned to the punishment of the sword, the gallows, or a tree, etc., from which he hangs for three days; however, he is never condemned to the common gibbet. And this is called an **Ordinary Military Court** <note>Latin: *Judicium Militare ordinarium*</note>. In the "Piked" Criminal Court <note>Latin: *hastato Criminali*</note>, which the Germans call the **Law of the Pike** <note>German: **Spieß-Recht**</note>, the procedure is perhaps the same. *See Schröder in the same place.* And I, at the end of my *Treatise on the Art and Law of War*, set forth the entire process of a Military Court.

To this pertains the Summary Court, commonly called the **Summary Justice** <note>German: **Stand-Recht**; literally "standing law," referring to a court-martial held on the spot.</note>, which takes place primarily in notorious cases; and just as the two prior types of trials take three days, this one is established and completed in only one. In this court, no delay is granted to an evildoer as in others; rather, where the **Articles of War** <note>German: **Articuls-Brieff**</note> have been broken, he shall be hanged from a tree without any mercy, and the cause of his death written on a note and pinned to his chest over the heart. If the case is not a capital offense, the process varies and is called a **Chamber Law** <note>German: **Cammer-Recht**</note>. Concerning all these matters, see more fully *Andreas Reuter in his Military Ordinances* and *Georg Obrecht in the Disputation on Military Discipline, theses 11 and 74.*

## 105. City, City Law, Market Law, City Walls. <note>Latin: *Civitas, Jus Civitatis, Moenia*.</note>

The word **City** <note>German: **Stadt**</note> is derived from the Roman *Stativa* <note>Latin: permanent quarters or stations</note>, as noted by *Johann Herold in his Commentary on the Roman Stations in Coastal Rhaetia, chapter 11*, and was adopted into the use of the German language. For the Romans usually wrote their words in abbreviated form and used to carve the syllable **STAT.** for *Stativa* or *Statio*. These things do not need many assertions for confirmation. For you will find few municipalities and few cities ending in *Stadt* that are not very ancient and made famous by Roman habitation. Thus, we use *Canstadt* for *Castris Stativis* <note>Latin: "Stationary Camps"</note>. In the same view, a "Camp" <note>Latin: *Castrum*</note> is sometimes taken for a Town, because towns were enclosed with a rampart and trenches in the manner of military camps. Fortresses, however, were called *Castella*. *Lipsius in Lovan., book 1, chapter 6.*

For various meanings of the word *Civitas* <note>City/Citizenship/State</note>, see *Ziegler in his Preface, section on Civitas; also Werdenhagen on Hanseatic Matters, part 2, page 583.*

Regarding the manner in which many cities in Germany were built by Henry the **Fowler** <note>Latin: *Aucupsi*; Henry I, King of East Francia</note>, so that eight peasants always had to support one citizen in the city, and likewise concerning the difference of **Burgesses** <note>Latin: *Burgenfium*</note>, see *Albinus, Chronicle of the Lands of Meissen, title 11, folio 156.*

Rome was once the Head of the World and the Empire; later Constantinople; finally Aachen. Aachen is the City of the Empire and the Royal Throne, see the *History of Aachen, page 15, and Petrus de Andlo with the notes of Freher there, page 157*, where he says that Aachen, as the principal seat of the Frankish Empire, seemed to be raised up as a "New Rome," not otherwise than Constantinople was of old, etc.

Municipal Law is defined as that which the people of one City or jurisdiction have concluded among themselves to hold. Just as those of Cologne around the Rhine have the Law of Charles confirmed, *Municipal Code <note>German: **Weichbild**</note>, article 1.* The German version has it thus: Market Law is this, which the market-people in olden times established among one another by their own statute <note>German: *Willkühr*; here meaning a law created by the will/decree of the community</note>. From ancient custom according to the Law of Charles, such as those of Cologne across the Rhine, those of Magdeburg, and other good cities. Where the gloss notes: it is called "City Law" because every city statuted it for itself by Divine guidance according to their own judgment, and such law is called a **Statutory Law** <note>German: **Willkür-Recht**</note>. Market Law is that which the market-people established among themselves. City Law is—

<meta>This page continues the legal and historical analysis of municipal rights, transitioning from military law on the previous page to the definitions, origins, and jurisdictional powers of cities within the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

S. T. <note>original: *Salvo Titulo*; a standard abbreviation in legal texts meaning "saving the title" or referring to the section heading.</note>

It is the case that the people of a city decided among themselves when they began to build together. From this, it is established that Market-Right, City-Right, Ordinance, and the Municipal District <note>original: *Weichbild*; a term referring to the jurisdiction and territorial limits of a city</note> are synonyms. Gryphiander, *On the Weichbild*, chapter 77, number 7 and following.

Formerly, Counts also granted City-Right (*Stadt-Recht*), as may be gathered from Crusius, *Additions to the Swabian Annals*, folio 37.

In the Roman Empire, according to its modern state, the power to confer the spirit and life—that is, the Right of Citizenship or City-Right (*Stadt-Recht*)—upon a place belongs to the Emperor alone, as a Greater Regalian Right <term>Regale Majus: a supreme right belonging exclusively to the sovereign</term>. (Similarly, Market-Right is mostly given as a fief.) This is argued in the *Code of Justinian* on Metropolises; Obrecht, *On Regalia*, thesis 8, conclusion 188 and following; Matth. Steph. *On Jurisdiction*, book 2; Clapmar, *On the Secrets of State*, book 1, chapter 20 at the end. And on this matter, an illustrious example is recorded regarding Emperor Maximilian I. In the year 1514, he prohibited Count Albrecht of Mansfeld, who presumed to grant a certain village the Right of City, with these words: "Since it is not fitting for you, nor anyone else, to establish City-Right or other things that belong to the high sovereignty without permission, we command, etc." See Bruning, *On Various Types of Universities*; Mr. Joachim Cluten, *Daily Matters*, conclusion 22, letter D; see Mr. Crusius, book 5, part 3, folio 264; and my own work, *On the Right of Majesty*, folio 205. This is so true that if someone establishes a city without at least the Emperor's tacit consent, it is not truly a city, nor can it use city rights. See the Privileges of New Cities, specifically the Privileges of the City of Monhaim.

It must be noted here that the Right of the City (*Stadt-Recht*) differs from the Right of Citizenship (*Bürgerrecht*), which is not among the Prince's reserved rights; rather, its granting usually belongs to the Senates and Magistrates of cities. In this matter, the Prince cannot prejudice the citizens. See my work, *On the Right of Universities*, folio 258.

City-Right does not imply absolute and mixed power <term>merum & mixtum imperium: the legal authority to exercise high and low justice, including the power of the sword</term>, but only Territory and a certain Jurisdiction. See the *Digest*, "On the Meaning of Words," and the notes there. And territory is said to exist on both land and water; see Georg Everhard, volume 1, counsel 12, number 6.

Furthermore, "Urbs" and "Civitas" differ. For "Urbs" <note>the physical city</note> denotes the buildings themselves standing within the walls; the word is derived from *urvo*, that is, that part of the plow seen to be curved, with which the walls themselves were marked out. "Civitas" <note>the community or state</note>, however, designates the gathering of men and these same citizens. Bartolus and others note this commonly in the law. Cicero also observed this difference between these names when he says in his speech for Sextius: "When the small gatherings of men, which they later called *Civitates*; then the joined dwellings, which we call *Urbes*." See my *Political Preliminaries*, folio 39.

Can a city establish a collection or tax? See Menochius, counsel 1201.

<column-break/>

That cities sometimes grow out of monasteries is witnessed by Crusius in his *Annals*, where he writes of the city of Donauwörth: that Donauwörth at the time of the Counts of Dillingen was no city, but only a few fisherman's huts on the Danube. There, Huipoldus II, Count of Dillingen, built and inhabited Castle Wert on the rock around the year 908. His successor Manigoldus, around the year 1040, brought the Holy Cross (from which the monastery takes its name) from the Greek Emperor and established a nunnery for his sister Irmentraut in the castle. This was later occupied by Benedictine monks, and subsequently made into a city by Emperor Henry VI around the year 1194. See the *Necessary Reminder of Donauwörth*, part 1, folio 20.

How a City differs from a Castle, Village, etc.? See Marcellus Donatus in his *Explanations*, folio 150.

Formerly in the Empire, in the time of Charlemagne, there were only twenty-one Metropolitan Cities. See Sleidan, *On the Four Monarchies*, folio 329.

Can Princely Cities <note>cities belonging to a local prince rather than directly to the Emperor</note> punish the ministers of Princes? See the Constitution of Emperor Adolph with the commentary of Freher, folio 3.

Should one jumping over the walls be punished with death? I have discussed this in the treatise *On the Law of Things* and in *Legal Deliberations*. In Cologne, anyone who climbs over the city wall or fortification is publicly executed. *Statutes of Cologne*, final part, title 1, folio 56.

...the suburbs are also included. Carpzov, *Illustrious Decisions*, 2, number 1. Those who are called "Suburbanites" <note>original: *Vorstädter*</note> and "Small-towners" <note>original: *Kleinstädter*</note>, *Decisions* 2, number 21. Suburbs are not strictly parts of the city, but rather appendages. Hence the French call suburbs *Faulxburgs* <note>modern: *Faubourgs*</note>, as if they were a "Fore-castle" <note>original: *Vorburg*</note>, or in German a "Fore-city" <note>original: *Vorstadt*</note>, because they are located before or in front of the city. Since they are not bounded by the city walls, but situated before the city, see the *Digest*, book 2, title 1. Knipschild, *On the Privileges of Imperial Cities*, book 1, chapter 1, number 81. Suburbs do not come under the specific name of "city," as noted by the jurist Johann Philippi in *Practical Use of the Imperial Institutes*, book 1, title 3, section 1, number 4; but they are included under the general term, number 5. Even parishioners living far away are considered citizens, number 6. Suburbs of a city placed under an ecclesiastical interdict <term>Interdict: a punishment where a community is excluded from church rites</term> are likewise interdicted, number 7. Suburbanites may be raised to the rank of the Consulate and the Senatorial order, number 8. What is done in the suburbs is said to be done in the city, number 9. Regarding what is said to be done within the "contained area," number 12. A testator leaving all his household provisions is said to have also left those he keeps in the suburbs, number 13. Inhabitants of the suburbs are not "rustics" <note>original: *Rustici*; i.e., peasants or country-folk</note>, number 14. See the Response of the Leipzig Jurists, number 15. On the Law of granting the faculty to found a city, see Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 2, chapter 9, number 128 and following. A "Haynstädt" <note>original: *Haynstädt*; likely a reference to a 'Heimstatt' or specific large city status</note> means a large city, Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 1, number 60.

City-law delays or privileges <note>original: *Stadtrechtliche Verzieg*</note>, *Marburg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 26, number 217. The words "the ownership of our city" <note>original: *unser Stadt dominium*</note> denotes the city's ownership, Symphoreme Gylman, volume 1, part 1, title 2, folio 741, number 39. Regarding cities that issue summons, Becker, *On Public Law*, page 179. On the right to grant citizenship, or "to give city-law" <note>original: *Stadtrecht zu geben*</note>, see the same, page 81.

### 106. City-Judge. Prætor urbanus.

Those are called city-judges who exercise all jurisdiction whatsoever in the City or Town over which they preside, Mynsing, *Responses* 3, numbers 11 and 14, decade 13. For we regularly judge a thing by the calling of its name: especially since names show the common usage of speaking, according to the law *Labeo* in the *Digest* on legacies.

### ADDITION.

The City-Judge is to be spared from the actual quartering of soldiers <note>original: *Einquartirung*; the mandatory housing of troops in private residences</note>, Mr. Doctor Tabor, *On Quartering*, page 264. Regarding who is understood as the City-Judge at Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentinæ*</note>, Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 3, number 22. Regarding the power of the *Subasci* <note>A Turkish administrative or military official</note> or City-Judge among the Turks, Johann Philippi, *In Practical Use of the Institutes*, book 4, title 18, section 11, *Eclogues* 95, number 7.

### 107. City-Tax. Imperial city collections.

It was an ancient custom, introduced by our earliest Kings, that certain and ordinary annual gifts should be presented to the Kings and Emperors who ruled Germany by the immediate Estates of the Empire <term>Immediacy: those holding land directly from the Emperor without an intermediate lord</term>, whether the greatest, the middle, or the lowest, and whether sacred or secular, in the public and general Diets <note>original: *Comitiis*; parliamentary assemblies</note>. Some of these were tributes from conquered peoples; others were "precarious" <note>original: *precaria*; voluntary or requested</note> gifts from free people, such as from Citizens, offered according to the spirit and character of each region. Some traces of this remain in the annual collections of the Imperial Cities, commonly called "City-Tax" <note>original: *Städt-Steuer*</note>, which are still paid to our Emperor today. On this occasion, the cities themselves introduced those annual payments which they demand individually from their citizens according to the manner and condition of their fortunes, and which they call "Taxes" <note>original: *Steuras*</note>; see Mr. Goldast, *On Bohemia*, book 2, chapter 11.

### 108. City-Bailiwick. Advocatia.

What do these words, placed in a deed of purchase and sale, import: "sells the City-Bailiwick <note>original: *Stadt-Vogtey*</note> of N. with the court, all justice, and appurtenances"? Virgil Pingizer answered this in his *Decade of Consultations*, consultation 1, throughout.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the Provincial City-Bailiwick, Engelbrecht, *On the Emperor*, thesis 91. Regarding the Advocates <note>original: *Advocatis*; legal representatives or bailiffs</note> of Worms, the Bishopric of Würzburg, and the Monasteries of Fulda, Kempten, and Weissenburg, see Knichen, *On Territorial Law*, chapter 4, number 33. Also regarding the Monastery of Corvey, Letzner in the *Corvey Chronicle*, chapter 14; add Paurmeister, book 2, chapter 10.

### 109. The Dying. Agonizantes.

Who are the "dying" <note>original: *Agonizantes*</note>, and when is someone said to be placed in the "article of death"? See Paolo Zacchia, *Medico-Legal Questions*, book 2, title 1, question 19, where in number 14 he says that those in the throes of death <note>original: *agonizantes*</note> do not differ from those placed in the "article of death" except according to a greater or lesser space of time by which they are distant from death. For we first say a sick person is placed in the "article of death," and soon after, as the person struggles and draws closer to death, we call them "dying," etc.

### ADDITION.

Whether a dying person <note>original: *moribundus*</note> in their final moments is presumed to be of sound mind, see Mantica, *On Conjectures of Last Wills*, book 2, title 6, number 3. *The last words of the dying Seneca: Translated into German by Gottfried Wilhelm Sacer: With an added speech by Justus Lipsius on Slander, printed at Bautzen by Johann Scheibe in duodecimo.* It is established from Ptolemaeus Hephaestion, cited in Photius's *Library*, page 187, that wise men have read books even when they were already about to die. For what the ancients taught concerning the immortality of the soul, see Wirdung on Tacitus's *Agricola*, chapter 46, and Rupert on Florus, book 4, chapter 2, section 71. The dying are equated with the dead...

[Testimonies] are prepared, or certainly do not seem to be the response of a sound and well-composed mind, as proven by Casivensis in *Counsel* 155, book 1, and Molin in *Counsels* 31 and 32, number 13 and following, and as Höpingk shows in *The Law of Seals*, page 450. He asked them to speak more clearly, saying that his departure from this life would be more pleasant if he were allowed to learn something even as he died.

### 110. Statutes. <note>original: Statuten. Statuta.</note>

I have commented on certain matters regarding Statutes <term>Statuta: local laws or ordinances enacted by a city or corporation, as opposed to universal Roman or Canon law</term> in my notes on the *Digest*, book 1, title 1, law 9, and in the third disputation on the Statutes of Württemberg. Some points are also found in the collection <note>original: Sylloge</note> of Johann Jacob Speidel under the word "Statute," parts 1 and 2, and extensively in Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter S.

## ADDITION.

Statutes are to be understood not according to the "husk" <note>original: "secundùm corticem"; meaning the literal or superficial wording</note> but according to their reason and intent. Zorer, part 1, question 5, number 356; Barbosa, book 17, chapter 49, axiom 14. Statutes do not bind those who are probably ignorant of them (axiom 16). Statutes derive their interpretation from the Common Law (axiom 1). Whether and when Statutes apply not only to future cases, but also to past or pending cases, or to acquired rights, see Zorer, part 1, question 5, number 395.

Whether and when Statutes extend outside a territory and bind foreigners: Menochius, *Counsel* 74. Whether a Statute speaking of a specific person is extended to a foreigner regarding property located within the territory of those making the statute: Cevallos, question 724; Menochius, *Counsel* 75.

### 111. Tax, Ordinance. <note>original: Steuer, Satzung. Collecta.</note>

Tax, Service, and Petition-tax <note>original: "Steuer, Dienst und Beth." Beth was a specific historical tax, often a "requested" contribution that became a fixed obligation</note>. See the Records of the Teutonic Knights <note>original: "Teutſchherrische Acta"</note> in the *Roll of Documents*, folios 21 and 22. The *Beth* is like a census or tribute; it is even paid by foreigners. Klock, volume 1, counsel 9, number 51.

A "Collection" <note>original: *Collecta*</note> is a public contribution for the convenience or necessity of the State, ordered by the Magistrate. In German, it is called *Steuer* (Tax), *Satzung* (Ordinance), *Hülffgeld* (Aid-money), *Anlag* (Assessment), or *Beth*. Indeed, what the legal authors call a "contribution" in the *Digest* (book 26, title 7, law 32) is today commonly called a "collection" by custom. Besold, volume 1.

<column-break/>

Heigius, question 17, number 29, part 1. It is called by another name, "Collation," in the *Digest* (book 7, title 1, law 27, section 3). It is also called an "Indiction" <term>Indictio: originally a Roman tax assessment cycle, later used for various taxes</term>, and also a "Tribute." In some places, a tax is called *Berna*, from which comes the German expression "to put on a bear" <note>original: "einen Bären anlegen"</note>. See Andreas Knichen, *On Saxon Law*, chapter 5, number 335. My colleague, Mr. Bocer, discusses this in his treatise *On Collections*, chapter 1, number 2. But Knichen is mistaken: "to put on a bear" actually means "to make debts," after which the debt collectors <note>original: "exactores"</note> begin to "growl" like bears.

A collection is either ordinary, such as a tribute—the annual civic *Beth* or taxes—or it is extraordinary, and is called an assessment <note>original: "Schatzung"</note>.

Whether those of the nobility are obliged to pay taxes on their estates located within principalities, just like others? See Bidembach, question 18.

Whether a Prince can tax noble estates, houses, gardens, vineyards, fields, and meadows located in his land at his pleasure, as he does with other civic properties? Or, on the other hand, if a subject of a Prince buys property from a nobleman, can the nobleman dissolve such a sale if the subject refuses to pay? See Bidembach, question 19.

Are nobles bound to contribute anything from lands they have acquired from peasants <note>original: "die Hüfen-Landes"; land measured in 'hides' or farm units</note>, which the nobility have brought under their own control and added to their fiefs in recent years? Modestinus Pistor teaches that they are indeed bound, writing these notable words in *Counsel* 9, number 49: "When such newly purchased peasant lands are not converted into knightly estates, nor are specific knightly services attached to them, the nobility are obliged to pay common taxes and assessments on them—just as they do on their other properties that they do not hold by service—especially those assessments levied for the maintenance of the Public Peace <note>original: "Landfriedens"</note>, which is no less important to the nobility than to the cities." Similarly, if nobles buy the property of peasants <note>original: "Baurens Güter"</note>, those lands nevertheless remain subject to their previous burdens and services, and must be provided by the noble purchaser no less than by a peasant. Even the Church as a purchaser (which is otherwise highly privileged) is bound to do this.

Because when they feel the benefit, it is also necessary that they feel the burden. Since the nobility are participants in the benefits of the community—all common rights and uses—it is fair that they do not reject the services most closely associated with them, such as neighbor-service and common service. Natta, *Counsel* 460; Menochius, *Counsel* 444.

Some ascribe the right to collect taxes to "Pure Power" <term>Mero Imperio: the highest form of sovereign authority, often including capital punishment</term>, but this did not prevail in the case of Speyer versus Speyer, or the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order versus Heilbronn. Others, perhaps more correctly since it concerns a pecuniary benefit, ascribe it to "Mixed Power" <term>Mixto Imperio: authority involving civil jurisdiction and lesser criminal matters</term>. The judges of the Imperial Chamber hold it to be a singular right...
