...by Royal right <note>original: "jure Regali"</note>, having nothing in common with common Jurisdictions, according to the unique chapter on what constitutes regalia <note>original: "quæ sint regal."</note>. This principle was deduced in the case of Wangen against the Bercken of Labis, though this could be subtly disputed at greater length by many. See Master Rutger Ruland, *Decisions on Controversial Law*, question 11.

Taxes <note>original: "Collectæ"</note> are rightly imposed and demanded by him who possesses the Royal rights and high jurisdiction, commonly known as **the territorial sovereignty** <note>original: "die Landts-Obrigkeit"</note>. See Andreas Knichen, *On Territorial Law and High Power*, chapter 3; and Matthaeus Stephanus, book 2, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 2. For example, taxes are imposed by the Emperor for the public utility of the entire Empire.

Even if the ownership of a farm is exempt because it belongs to the clergy or the nobility, the tenant <term>Emphyteuta: a person who holds a long-term or perpetual lease on land in exchange for an annual rent and improvements</term> or farmer <term>Colonus: a tenant farmer tied to the land</term> can still be taxed as a citizen, specifically by reason of his "useful domain" <note>original: "ratione utilis sui dominii" - referring to the right to use and profit from the land even if one does not own the title</note>. See Marta, *On Jurisdiction*, part 4; also the *Acts of Lindau*, folio 105.

A village or hamlet is subject to that City to which it pays taxes. Baldus teaches that Cities are in possession and ownership of the Villages and Forts from which they receive tax collections. Hence, the payment of a census <note>a type of land tax or quit-rent</note> argues for and proves the ordinary Jurisdiction of Sovereignty; it proves that a Village belongs to the territory of the one to whom the tax is presented, as Knichen argues at length. Likewise, the excise tax on inns <note>original: "gabella Cauponaria"</note>, which is paid in the name of beverages—commonly called **the beverage tax** <note>original: "Umgeld"</note>—is paid in recognition of sovereignty and is considered a token of subjection. This is true unless custom has introduced something else, such that the tax is found to belong only to a lower jurisdiction.

But concerning Taxes, see the disputation of Caspar Klock in volume 1, and also Thomas Winckler and Master Bocer. See also my own treatises *On the Law of Majesty* and *On the Treasury*.

Regarding Taxes outside of a territory, see my *Counsels*, and the *Counsels of Strasbourg*, volume 2, counsel 61.

On this whole matter, one should most recently consult Master Wesenbeck in his special treatise *On Contributions*. ## 112. **Stepmother.** <note>original: Stieffmutter. Noverca.</note>

See Master Speidel in his *Notables*. Burchard Berlich, an Electoral Saxon Councilor, wrote a treatise *On the Law of Stepmothers*.

### ADDITION.

Stepmother <note>original: "Noverca"</note> is, as it were, a "new chest" <note>original: "nova arca"</note> <note>This is a Latin etymological pun: a 'new chest' or 'new ark' perhaps implying a new repository for family goods or a new household structure</note>. How the assets of a child's first marriage are to be left in the hands of the biological father and the stepmother, and how the assets of both parents thereby acquire a mortgage <note>a legal claim to ensure the children's inheritance</note>. The laws presume against stepmothers and their "stepmotherly charms" <note>original: "novercalia delinimenta"</note>. A stepmother is presumed to be poorly disposed toward her stepchildren. See Barbosa at length. Whether a stepmother may be summoned to court without special permission. Stepmotherly instigations. Stepmothers are preferred over stepchildren regarding their own mother's dowry. A stepmother is preferred over stepchildren regarding paraphernalia <term>Paraphernalia: property or goods owned by a married woman that did not form part of her dowry</term>. A stepmother is not preferred over stepchildren if she herself must be endowed from certain goods and that obligation to provide a dowry precedes the obligation made for the current dowry. One who kills a stepmother is held to the penalty for parricide <term>Parricide: the legal crime of killing a close relative, which carried much harsher penalties than simple murder</term>. A stepmother who kills stepchildren is held to the penalty for parricide. Should a small child be fed and educated by a father who brings in a stepmother, or by the grandmother?

Master Harsdorffer, in the *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, volume 2...

### 113. Foundation. *Fundatio*.

In an ancient foundation charter <note>original: "Stifft-Brieff"</note> from the year 1115, the following words are to be found: "May it please that this testament be inserted, so that from that day on which this transfer was made, neither Luitfridus himself, nor any of his parents, nor any of the secular princes, nor any count, nor the Bishop of Speyer, nor anyone else should rashly invade or possess these same properties of the Servants of God dwelling in N. N. <note>A placeholder used in legal formulas for a specific name to be inserted later</note>, and this he has attested by God and all His saints and by the day of the terrible Judgment, and intimately requested that no one should either scatter or diminish the aforesaid things, nor exchange them, nor grant any of it as a fief <term>beneficiet: the act of turning property into a feudal land-holding or 'benefice'</term>, nor appoint any prelate over the same estate against their will. If anyone by chance—which God forbid, and indeed by the mercy of God and the patronage of St. Gregory and all the saints I do not think will happen—whether from relatives or strangers, and of whatever condition or power, should attempt by any cunning to bring any disruption against this Testament, which I have ordained for the love of Almighty God and the veneration of St. Gregory and all the saints: first, let him incur the wrath of Almighty God, and let God take away his memory from the land of the living, and blot out his name from the book of life, unless he repents; and let his portion be with those who said to the Lord, 'Lord, depart from us,' and with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed with an open mouth and the abyss absorbed alive; and let him incur eternal damnation, and being made a companion of Judas the traitor, let him be held bound in eternal torments." For another example, see the Testament of St. Remigius in the *Code of Donations* by Aubertus Miraeus, folio 11; add Scribanius, *Origins*, folio 62, and *Revived Documents of the Monasteries in Württemberg*. From these things it is clear how wrongly those act who profane ecclesiastical goods and consume them for other uses.

On which matter Petreius also has certain things in *On Monasteries*, folio 56, especially section 6, and I also advised in my treatise *On Ecclesiastical Majesty*.

Regarding the suppression of Canons in the foundations <note>original: "Stifftern"</note>, see the Council of Trent, Session 24,

<column-break/>

chapter 15. That one should not let old foundations perish, but rather preserve them, exists as a singular discourse, which Petreius also teaches in the cited place, folio 56.

->ADDITIO.<-

Regarding "Strand" <note>The shore or beach</note>, see Harsdörffer in the *Poetic Funnel*, part 1, page 94.

### 116. Punishment. Penalty.

Regarding various types of execution, Camerarius discusses them in *Historical Meditations*, century 1, chapter 87; and the law of retaliation <note>original: "pœna Talionis"</note> in the same, chapter 99; and in century 2, chapter 79, regarding the punishment of brute animals.

Regarding the necessity of punishment, John of Salisbury writes elegantly in *Epistle 33*: "He opens the way to the excesses of many who, by overlooking the errors of his subjects, provides them the audacity to do wrong." See my own treatise *On Punishments*, from the beginning.

<column-break/>

Punishments justly imposed by human laws are considered to be inflicted by God Himself. According to Cornelius Agrippa in *On Occult Philosophy*, book 3, chapter 41, the Masters of the Hebrews say that God remits punishment to no one. Hence the Assembly of Hezekiah <note>Referring to a Jewish tradition or midrash</note> handed down that after the destruction of the Sanctuary <note>The Temple in Jerusalem</note>, although no order of judicial execution remained, nevertheless four types of punishment by which men used to be condemned—no one guilty of death escaped without retaliation. For he who had deserved death by stoning was, by God’s dispensation, either thrown from a roof, trampled by wild beasts, or overwhelmed by a ruin or an accident. But he who had deserved fire ended his life either consumed by a blaze, by a venomous bite, the strike of a serpent, or by poison. He who was to perish by the sword was slaughtered either by the violence of the Empire, a popular riot, a faction, or the ambushes of robbers. He who was to be hanged by a noose was either suffocated in a whirlpool of water or extinguished by some other strangulating plague. By this reasoning of doctrine, even the great Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note> thought that the Gospel of Christ should be explained: *He who strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword.*

Furthermore, even the Pagan philosophers declared this order of retaliation to be *Adrasteia* <note>Adrasteia was a Greek goddess of inescapable destiny and retribution.</note>, namely, the inevitable power of Divine Laws, by which in future cycles each is repaid according to the reason and merits of a prior life. Thus, one who ruled unjustly in a former life might fall back into a state of slavery in another life; one who polluted his hands with blood might be forced to undergo retaliation; and one who lived a beastly life might be cast down, having been revolved into a brute body. <note>This refers to the concept of metempsychosis or reincarnation as a vehicle for justice.</note> Add Antonius de Balingen in *Solace for the Afflicted*, section 4, chapter 13, where he treats certain things from Medina concerning the fate and passion of those who are punished; and the same author in section 6, chapter 5, etc., discusses the utility of punishments. Among other things, he says: "The history of many centuries has demonstrated more than enough that almost no office is more excellent in the eyes of the wise than some public vengeance upon the wicked. For what else do the wicked cry out amidst their lashes, except that mortals should repent of a nefarious life and learn—lest they be subjected to the same punishments as themselves—to establish a life of virtue." If we hear their voice less clearly, we are surely worse than the Pagans themselves, whose ears that voice struck amidst the groans and the crack of lashes. Witness the Virgilian Phlegyas, of whom the Prince of Poets <note>Virgil</note> writes in book 6 of the *Aeneid*:

> —And most wretched Phlegyas warns everyone,
> And testifies with a great voice through the Shadows:
> 
> "Be warned; learn justice, and do not despise the Gods."

Punishment ought to be applied to the one to whom the injury is done. <note>The text here likely refers to the legal principle of restitution or that the penalty must be relevant to the specific harm caused.</note>

injury. Klock, volume 1, counsel 8, number 45. Punishment is owed for the revenge of an injury or contempt toward the one whose command was transgressed. Counsel 29, number 864.

Bocerus, in *On the Punishment of Thieves*, chapter 2, number 107 and following, reviews various provincial punishments, among which is "precipitation into the waters" <note>original: *præcipitatio in aquas*, a form of execution by drowning</note>, called *the Witpen* <note>original: *das Witpen*</note>. **Question:** By what proportion should punishments be inflicted? Those who have passed judgment on this matter—both philosophers and jurists—disagree. Horn, in *Ethics*, book 3, chapter 13, number 7 and following, page 490, laboriously defends the **Arithmetic** proportion and cites *Arnisæus* and others in support. Wesenbeck seems more successful in his refutation when he examines the distinction made between the law and the executor of the law. In his *Notes on Justice and Law*, number 11, and in his commentary on the *Cornelian Law on Forgery* at the end, and in the work itself on punishments (number 5), he refutes the idea that punishment should be established in the abstract without **respect of persons** <note>original: *προσōποληψία* (prosopolepsia), meaning partiality or favoritism based on social status</note>, but in the concrete, it should not be done without a selection of persons. Hornejus accepts the **Geometric** proportion more strictly, insofar as it pertains to what is owed to or enjoined upon someone as a citizen from the public treasury, such as rewards and burdens. For this reason, he removes the contract of society from distributive justice, although it happens by accident that partners take unequal portions just as they contribute unequally to the capital. On the other hand, Wesenbeck, in *On the Partnership*, number 6 (a position Bach critiques in the same place), and Crispus, take this term in an extended sense for the calculation of profit in an adequate proportion to the sum contributed. Similarly, Wesenbeck, in his *Notes on the Privileges of Creditors*, number 7, reduces the equality in the meeting of creditors (pro-rated to the amount of debt) to a Geometric rather than an Arithmetic proportion.

But it is clear that among creditors, it is not public property being divided. Golius (in *Ethics*, book 5, chapter 2) and Wesenbeck (in the cited location) defend the Geometric view. Dr. Ludwig, in his *Notes on Wesenbeck*, number 11, excellently argues that Wesenbeck’s opinion and that of the common jurists is not without foundation, though leaving room for anyone's judgment. But putting these aside, Dr. Cobius has treated this question solidly and quite broadly in *Principles of Law*, question 3; he thinks the imposition of punishments should be ascribed to **Arithmetic** proportion rather than Geometric, and asserts that this opinion is more congruent with Aristotelian principles. <note>In legal philosophy, Arithmetic justice treats everyone the same regardless of status, while Geometric justice adjusts the penalty or reward based on the individual's social standing or merit.</note>

To avoid punishment, the opinion that one believed they were engaged in a lawful act is sufficient, even if that belief were foolish and gross. Klock, volume 1, counsel 37, numbers 304 and 305. Why investigators and eradicators of crimes were called *the Knowing Ones* <note>original: *Wissende*, a term for the initiated members of the secret Vehmic courts of Westphalia</note>. Old glosses: punishment is *Wizi*; penal is *Wizlih*; to punish is *Wizen*; unpunished is *ungewizzinot*. See more in Freherus, *On the Secret Judgments in Westphalia*. He who exercises his own right does not deserve punishment, Klock volume 1, counsel 50, number 319. ### 117. Patrolling. To track, pursue, and hunt down those who infest the safety of the roads.

The lord of a territory who receives "safe-conduct money" <note>original: *das Gleit-Geld*</note> is bound to track, pursue, and hunt down those who infest the safety of the roads, seas, and rivers. This is what we call **Patrolling** <note>original: *das Straiffen*</note>. Sometimes, where there is a great filth <note>mass</note> of robbers, he must maintain entire troops that ride out against them, commonly called **patrolling bands** <note>original: *straiffende Rotten*</note>; sometimes he shall even set prices for their capture. Likewise, on the sea and in rivers, he should have scout and excursion ships—**outpost ships** <note>original: *Außlager-Schiff*</note>—to scout for the safety of the water, protecting it and purging the sea and rivers of evil men. Likewise, he must make an ordinance that whenever someone is attacked and harmed on the road, the bell shall be rung, and the officials and subjects, as soon as they are alerted and become aware of it, shall hurry after the perpetrator so that he may be brought to justice and the stolen goods restored to the victim. Likewise, he should come to an agreement with neighbors to come to each other's aid, which one authority is bound to do for another, as are the nearest settled subjects. Imperial Recess of the year 1548, section *Ferner*; and of the year 1559, section *Wofern aber*, etc.

### ADDITION.

Regarding Emperor Maximilian's decision in the year 1489, upon which the Swabian League was formed against **patrolling mercenaries** <note>original: *streiffende Landsknecht*</note>, one may read Pontus Heuterus of Delft, *History of the Netherlands*, book 7, folio 341. Treated at length by Schottel in *The German Main Language*, folio 452. The right of tracking, pursuing, and hunting down those who plunder fields and bandits on public roads: Most recently, G. C. Hansemann in his inaugural disputation held at Strasbourg in 1665, titled: *The Restored Peace-Officer* <note>original: *Irenarcha Restitutus*</note>. Richardus, counsel 63, number 8, volume 2. ## 118. Strenuous or Strict. <term>Strenuus</term>. <note>The German terms "Streng" or "Gestrenge" were formal titles of address for the lower nobility and high-ranking officials, meaning 'Strict' or 'Strenuous' in the sense of being vigorous in duty.</note>

Nobles are distinguished by certain preeminent titles above other commoners. For some are called "Generous," others "Most Noble and Strenuous" (**Noble, Strict, or Honorable** <note>original: *Edle, Streng, seu Gestrenge*</note>), following the Latin *Strenuum* and the Greek *sthenea* <note>original: $\sigma\theta\epsilon\nu\epsilon\alpha$</note>; the former signifies strength and readiness to conduct affairs, while the latter signifies something great, sharp, and manifest.

However, the title *Strenui*, or *Strict/Honorable*, should not be used for everyone indiscriminately. It is reserved especially for those who come from a greater and more distinguished lineage and family, or those who are otherwise appointed to offices that carry an annexed dignity. In Germany, these include the Lieutenants of Princes (**Governors** <note>original: *Statthalter*</note>), as well as Prefects of the Court (**Stewards** <note>original: *Hofmeister*</note>), Marshals, and Chancellors of Princes. <note>Matth. Stephani, treatise *On Nobility*, chapter 6, number 15.</note> Accordingly, the English use the word "Strong" to denote power.

### ADDITION.

The title **Gestreng** <note>Strict/Honorable</note> arose from the "strict proceedings" against enemies, that is, from "deeds strenuously performed" <note>original: *à rebus strenuè gestis*</note>. <note>Mr. Harsdörffer in the *German Secretary*, in the preface.</note>

## 119. Strict Law. <term>Jus summum</term>. <note>Literally "the highest law," often used in the sense of "the letter of the law" without regard for mercy.</note>

Is the "highest law" the "highest injury"? <note>This refers to the Roman legal maxim *Summum ius, summa iniuria*, suggesting that a law applied too strictly, without regard for circumstances, becomes an injustice.</note> See Jacob Martini, *Illustrious Disputations*, century 1, disputation 2, question 9.

### ADDITION.

The question is asked whether all sinful acts can be punished by men. First, internal acts are excepted, even if they come to the knowledge of others through a subsequent confession. The reason given is that it is not consistent with human nature for a right or obligation among men to arise from purely internal acts. However, in punishing criminal and sinful actions, the "intent" <note>original: *consilium*</note> is chiefly inspected. It is not always necessary for an external act to occur; hence it is not absurd for those who have undertaken some evil plan pertaining to the destruction of the entire Commonwealth, or of him who holds the **sovereign power** <note>original: $\tau\grave{o}\;\kappa\acute{v}\rho\iota\omicron\nu$ (to kyrion)</note>, to be punished, even if they have brought nothing to effect.

Secondly, those things which a man cannot escape due to weakness <note>original: *imbecillitatem*</note> are not to be punished. The reason is that these are close to things that are impossible to do; and since we cannot be driven to the impossible by coercive force, it follows that we deserve more pardon the more difficult the tasks enjoined by the Laws are to perform. See more in Johann à Felde, Doctor of Both Laws, in his *Annotations on Hugo Grotius’s On the Law of War and Peace*, page 403.

<column-break/>

Equity is preferred over rigor. <note>Discussed extensively by Barbosa, book 1, chapter 39, axiom 1; Mr. Dr. Cobius; Obrecht, *On the Principles of Law*, chapter 17, number 71 and following.</note> Regarding whether there is such a thing as "written equity," see Mr. Dr. Georg Adam Heher in the theme joined to the *Privileges of Altdorf*. Many people wrongly confuse the path of justice with the path of clemency. Specifically, they do not distinguish between **fairness** <note>original: $ἐπιείκειαν$ (epieikeian), the Greek concept of equity</note>, which interprets the Law, and **Relaxation**. The latter removes a Law for a probable cause or suspends its force; the former declares that a deed was, from the beginning, not included within the intent of the law. <note>Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, book 2, chapter 20.</note> The latter (Relaxation) refers to the rights of the Prince or Sovereign, while the former (Fairness) refers to jurisdictional rights. <note>Mevius, *On Lübeck Law*, book 4, title 15, article 1, number 20.</note>

Our Mr. Cregelius, in *On the Dispensation of Punishments*, thesis 63, teaches excellently in what sense "the highest law" is called "the highest injury." On whether we ought to follow equity more than strict law in judging, see Liebenthal in *Political College*, exercise 12, question 7. See also **Right and Equitable** <note>original: *Recht und billich*</note>.

### 121. The Mute and the Deaf. <term>Mutus & Surdus</term>.

Regarding the mute and the deaf, Paolo Zacchia has many things worth knowing in *Medico-Legal Questions*, book 2, title 1.

## ADDITION.

How a confession may be obtained from a mute person. Examples of the tongue being cut out due to the pain of torture. The method of receiving testimony from a mute person, and how a mute person should swear an oath and give a deposition, see Justus Oldekop, *Criminal Observations*, title 4, observation 42.

Although humans are by nature more inclined to speaking than to writing, nevertheless, through art and industry, the opposite can be taught. Francisco Vallesius writes that his friend Pedro Ponce <note>original: *Petrum Pontium*</note>, a monk of the Benedictine order, clearly demonstrated this. He taught those born deaf to speak by no other method than first teaching them to write, pointing with his finger at the actual objects signified by those characters; then, he provoked them to movements of the tongue that corresponded to those characters. Thus, just as those who can hear begin with speech, for those whose ears are blocked, it is more correct to begin with writing. Camerarius, *Leisure Hours*, century 2, page 28. The same author in century 1, page 171, records a person mute and deaf from birth who, along with a sister equally mute and deaf from the womb, skillfully reads, writes, calculates accounts, and performs other duties typical of those who hear and speak. He also shows how welcome mute "gesticulators" <note>likely referring to sign language users or mimes</note> otherwise are to Princes and Ottoman Sultans. Century 1, pages 358 and 414. The deaf and the mute cannot be judges. Master Felwinger discusses this beautifully in *On the Judge*, page 436 and following. Master C. Rittersbuf. in *Novell.* page 519, number 36.

### 122. Hour. <term>Hora</term>.

There are two kinds of hours: one is the season-

Besoldus Volume 1.

<column-break/>

al kind, which the Greeks call *kairikas* <note>original: $\kappa\alpha\iota\rho\iota\kappa\grave{\alpha}s$</note>, which increase or decrease based on the sun's progression or regression over our hemisphere. For in the time of the winter solstice <note>original: *Brumæ*</note>, the daylight hours are shortest and the night hours are longest. Conversely, at the summer solstice, the hours of the night are shortest, and those of the natural day are longest. Polletus in *History of the Roman Forum*, book 1, chapter 9, folio 80, number 6; see also Albericus Gentilis, *On the Designations of Various Times*, chapter 6.

The other kind is the equinoctial hours, which the Greeks call *isemerinas* <note>original: $\iota\sigma\eta\mu\epsilon\rho\iota\nu\grave{\alpha}s$</note>, which are now commonly used in our mechanical clocks <note>original: *automatis*</note> and other sundials <note>original: *Sciotericis*</note>, where we divide any civil day into twenty-four equal parts, without regard to the artificial or natural length of the day. Polletus, in the place cited above.

On the law of hours, see Polletus, folio 93; and Caspar Barthius has much on hours in general in the index of his *Adversaria*.

## ADDITION.

By reason of a single hour or even the smallest moment of time, one legal instrument is said to be prior to another, although the specific hour is not customarily written in instruments out of necessity. Sprenger, *On Trifles*, page 150. Zorer, part 2, question 20, number 7039. The Emperor Augustus added the moments of the hours to his letters. Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 8, number 14. "Hours" (*horæ*) are named after Horus, that is, the Sun. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 1, chapter 21. They are the parts into which the day is distinguished; for example, an hour in the Roman Republic is a twelfth part of the natural day. Regarding hours, one may note the "prescription of 20 hours," by which a husband or father who catches an adulterer in the act—whom he does not wish to or cannot (because it is not permitted) kill—may detain him for twenty continuous hours of day and night for the purpose of testifying to the matter (so that he may be shown to those who might later bear witness against him). Law 25, preface, and the Gloss there on the *Julian Law on Adultery*. Oldendorp, *On Squatters' Rights and Prescriptions*, title on adultery. However, an hour does not grant a creditor priority in a pledge; rather, if the same thing is pledged to two people on the same day, even at different hours, neither is preferred over the other, but the thing is pledged to each for the whole amount. Law 16, second to last paragraph, *On Pledges and Hypothecs*. A similar example is found regarding excuses from guardianship in Law 6, *On Excuses from Guardianship*, and Law 2, paragraph 1, *On the Significance of Words*. The "major part of the day" is said to be the first seven hours, not the final ones. Why so? The true reason why the first seven constitute the major part, and not the last seven, is rooted not in quantity but in the utility and convenience of conducting business. See Goedd. on the aforementioned Law 2 at the end. Cujas in the treatise *On the Prescription of Various Times*, chapter 2, where he cites Law 26 *On the Work of Freedmen* as relevant here. Or rather, it is because the Romans primarily devoted the morning hours to judicial business. But since it is said in the aforementioned Law 2, paragraph 1, "To any day," it is asked whether this includes the civil day, as Rebuffus asserts? This is more correctly denied. See Goedd. on said law, number 30. In Basel, the hours in the city and in the countryside do not strike at the same time. Therefore...

4 Hours for Prayer.

7 Hours for Sleep.

## 123. Sum. <term>Summa</term>.

The term "Sum" is to be understood as referring to a coin or to counted money, as handed down by Jakob Thoming, Decision 19, number 15, and the law *si servus plurium* at the end of the Digest on Legacies, book 1.

## 124. Summary Process. <term>Processus summarius</term>.

Regarding judgment and the summary process, see Matthäus Stephani, *On the Office of a Judge*, book 5, chapter 2; Calam, *On the Manner of Articulating*, gloss 3, folio 51, etc.

It should be known here that "summary knowledge" is usually understood in two ways in the law. In one way, it is in respect to the order of the proceedings—when, for instance, the case proceeds plainly, without the "noise" or formal "figure" of a full trial. In such cases, there is no need for a formal Bill of Complaint or a formal Contestation of the Lawsuit. The solemnities of holidays (established for the needs of men) are not observed, and delays, exceptions, and dilatory or frustrating appeals are not admitted. See Gail, book 1, observation 78, number 4. In the other way, summary knowledge is named separately in respect to proof alone—when, for instance, semi-full proofs, presumptions, and indicators are sufficient, especially if the matter concerns a minor grievance. See Stephani in the cited location, number 3, etc.

A Supreme Prince can proceed summarily, provided that the natural process of law is still observed. See especially Mola in *The Marketplace of Law*, question 2, title 2. Sometimes one may even begin from the ex-

<column-break/>

ecution <note>The enforcement of a penalty or seizure of property.</note>. See my own work, *On the Right of Majesty*, page 163. But this is not permitted except in "notorious" cases <note>cases where the facts are so obvious they require no proof</note>, and where, because of the power of the defendant, it is not possible to observe a standard process; otherwise, if someone is condemned abruptly by such a process, justice is prostituted. See my work *On Appeals*, chapter 2, number 18, folio 68 and following.

Furthermore, even when someone is condemned by a Supreme Prince and cannot appeal, the sentence must not be executed precipitately. Law *si vindicare* 20, Code on Punishments; Græven, conclusion 110. See my work *On Appeals*, chapter 2, number 12.

In the Supreme Courts, the "points of the law" and the rigor of the process are not considered so much as the driving force of Justice. Innocent, in the chapter *on causes*, regarding *res judicata*; Bertrand, counsel 6; Rosenthal, chapter 1, conclusion 32, number 70. My work *On Appeals*, chapter 2, number 22. But in the Imperial Chamber, the "salutary clauses" in petitions are not to be attended to by the judge. Ordinance part 1, title 22, and the word *wiewol* <note>German: "although"</note> in the additions.

### ADDITION.

As to which causes may receive a summary process, see Ilico Ummius, *On Process*, my page 582; Zorer, part 1, question 13, number 1171 and following.

Regarding the causes in which a summary judgment has a place, see *The Forum of Protestations*, page 399. For what is required when proceeding summarily, see Lanfranco in *Practice*, on delegated and summary causes, number 2.

In a summary cause, when proof by oath is sufficient, likewise when semi-full proof is sufficient, and when it is not: see Lanfranco in the cited location, number 9.

### 127. Synagogue.

Regarding the *Synagogues of the Jews*, see Becanus's *Analogies, chapter 6 and chapter 12, etc.*

#### ADDITION.

The *Jewish Churches*, which they call *Synagogues*, are in this case in a better legal position than Christian churches, for Synagogues enjoy "religious law," and thus soldiers cannot be quartered in them. <note>original: "milites in illa hospitare nequeunt." This refers to the legal immunity of sacred spaces from being used as barracks for troops.</note> *Law 4, Code: On the Jews.* However, in the building of a *Synagogue*, a certain form must be observed, so that a new *Jewish Synagogue* does not rise as a new structure without the permission of the Prince; however, there is liberty for propping up an old one. *Final law, last paragraph, of the same title.* But they are not permitted to exalt it, or make it larger or more precious than it was before. *Chapter 7, On the Jews.* Johann Theodor Sprenger, *On the Law of Building, page 88.* Johannes Buxtorf published *The Jewish Synagogue.* <note>Buxtorf was a famous 17th-century scholar of Hebrew and Jewish customs; this book was a standard text for Christians studying Judaism at the time.</note>

The *Synagogues of the Jews* are themselves made inviolable by the Decrees of the Popes and the Constitutions of the Emperors. Marquardus de Susannis, *part 1, chapter 3, number 18.*

The Magistrate will permit the repair of ruinous ones, and even the rebuilding of those that have completely collapsed, but he will forbid the erection of new ones. *Chapter "Judæi" 3, Chapter "consuluit" 7, on the Jews; Final Law, Code, same title.* Marquardus de Susannis, *part 1, chapter 3, number 6.* Whether a *Jewish Synagogue* can receive an inheritance? Pacius, *Analysis of the Code, page 610 in the middle, and page 78, number 18.*

Regarding the *Synagogues and Schools of the Jews*, their antiquity and propagation, their sacred objects, various kinds of studies, teachers as well as students: in the year 1664 in the Public Auditorium at Nuremberg, Master Johannes Held—Public Professor of the Hebrew Language and Rector of the Gymnasium—delivered an Inaugural Oration. On the differences between a *Synagogue and a Jewish School* in the *said Oration, page... in Besoldus, Volume I.*

### 128. Syndicate. <note>In this legal context, a "syndicate" or "syndic" refers to a person appointed to represent a corporation, university, or community in legal matters.</note>

Regarding the *Syndicate*, see the *Complete Treatise* of Paris de Puteo; Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions, letter S, word: Syndicate*; and Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 1, folio 696, etc.*

#### ADDITION.

Syndics, Procurators, and Actors <note>Legal agents or representatives.</note> can initiate and move actions that belong to the "university" itself. <note>original: "universitati." In 17th-century law, a *universitas* refers to any corporate body or legal collective, such as a town or a guild, not only an educational institution.</note> Losæus, *On the Law of Universities, part 1, chapter 3, number 208.* The Syndics of universities are said to have free and general administration. *number 109.* They can sell the property of the university without a specific mandate. *number 110.* They are equated to guardians. *number 111.* Whether and when Syndics and public administrators can settle a matter regarding the property of the university itself, and whether and when such a settlement holds. *number 112.*

A Syndic acts for an assessor. Ilico Ummius *On Process, page 41.* Regarding custom, Farinacius notes that Judges are no longer "syndicated" <note>This refers to a process where a judge was held personally liable or investigated for a bad ruling.</note> if they have judged poorly through lack of skill. This is also what Gail seems to want, *Book 1, observation 153, last number*, when he asserts that a Syndicate is not permitted except in cases of malice. Ilico Ummius *On Process, page 377 (my copy).* To be held in a Syndicate, that is, to "make the lawsuit one's own." <note>A legal phrase meaning a judge becomes liable for the damages in a case because of a faulty ruling.</note> Rittershusius *On the Novels, page 9, chapter 6, number 135.* What a Syndicate is, and whether it is used against the Imperial Chamber itself. Master Biccius, *in Golden Sections, section 5, thesis 176.*

Properly, he is called a Syndic who is appointed by a university or a college. Losæus, *On the Law of Universities, part 2, chapter 1, number 40.* He is appointed for business as well as for legal judgments. *Ibid, number 26.*

On the Law of the *Syndicate*, and from where it drew its origin, Paulus Christinæus, *volume 2, Belgian Decisions, decision 84.*

The custom of kissing the FEET of the Pope flowed either from the Romans—whose other citizens, Plutarch writes, kissed the feet of the Priests—or from Caligula Caesar, who, according to Seneca in *On Benefits* 2.12, reached out his left foot to be kissed by Pompeius Pannus as he was giving thanks. Neander in the *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 241, where there is more on the kissing of shoes. ### 133. Singichten. The Summer Solstice. <note>original: "Solstitium æstivum"</note>

#### ADDITION.

The term *Singichten*, that is, the summer solstice, is treated extensively by Doctor Dürr in his *Inaugural Disputation on Manorial Courts*, thesis 21, and by Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 3, page 75, number 16. ### 135. Remedy of Seisachtheia. <note>original: "Sifachtiæ remedium"</note>

#### ADDITION.

That is, the "Relief of the Burden" <note>original: "Relevatio oneris"</note>, Giphanius in *Treatise on Process*, chapter 27, page 211. To ensure that Roman debtors paid their creditors, the Laws of the Twelve Tables first permitted creditors to keep debtors assigned to them as if they were slaves and prisoners. This assignment and these chains—or the debtor's prison—lasted a very long time, even into the era of the Jurists, as witnessed by Aulus Gellius in book 20, chapter 1, at the end, where Africanus writes: "Many wicked debtors despise even the chains and assignment." However, to counter this severity, the Greeks, by the authority of Solon, introduced a remedy for debtors which they call <term>Seisachtheia</term> <note>original: "Sifachtiam," from the Greek σεισάχθεια, meaning a "shaking off of burdens"</note>, that is, the Relief of the Burden. Eventually, even the Romans used this—though sometimes used by wicked Tribunes of the Plebs or wicked Consuls—and it is called "New Tables" <note>original: "novæ tabulæ," referring to the cancellation of debts</note>. For more on how this was introduced by the Prince and wisest Legislator of Athens, see Master G. Richter’s *Letters*, page 373.

### 136. Shrubs. <note>original: "Stauden. Frutex."</note>

#### ADDITION.

Consider the Laurel, the juniper, the terebinth <note>turpentine tree</note>, and other species of which Pliny writes in book 14, chapter 16. Although these, with cultivation, can sometimes be raised into a proper tree, see Scaliger, *Exercise 139*. Master Tabor treats this extensively in *Gatherings on Crimes*, page 413. Reeds are a genus of shrub, page 414. They are related to trees, ibid. "I shall plant shrubs in the swirling waters" <note>original: "Idæo frutices in gurgite fistam"</note>, Petronius in the *Satyricon*, page 187.

<column-break/>

Laurel wood has the power to produce fire, as Martin Mylius explains extensively in *The Pleasure Garden of Delightful Wisdom*, folio 581 and following, especially when the trees in the forests are struck together by strong winds. If one rubs ivy and laurel wood against each other, it easily produces fire. If one takes two dry laurel leaves and places finely crushed sulfur between them, then rubs the leaves vigorously against each other, they ignite to such an extent that one may light a candle from them, ibid. This agrees with what was remarkably cited above under the title "Mulberry" from Michael Knaben’s *Grafting Book*.

Juniper <note>original: "Wacholder"</note>. The Swiss say *Reckholder*, which might almost be *Riechholder* <note>"smell-dear"</note>, as it produces a smoke that people "hold dear" to smell. It is also called *Kranwertstauden* <note>thrush-bush</note> because the fieldfares <note>original: "Kranwetzvögel," a type of thrush</note> follow it closely, enjoy eating it, and grow quite fat from it. In Saguntum <note>original: "Saszgunt"</note> in Spain, a pagan temple dedicated to the goddess Diana is said to have stood in ancient times, the beams of which were brought there from the island of Zante <note>original: "Zayntho"</note>. These beams were also of juniper wood, and as the story goes, this temple was built some 200 years before the destruction of the city of Troy. It still stood in that city when Hannibal captured it; Hannibal spared it because it was a consecrated temple. At that time, the juniper beams were still strong and undamaged. According to that calculation, they would have lasted over a thousand years. Martin Mylius, in the same place, page 533. This is a fine age for a durable wood.

Regarding the wonderful effect of the Elderberry <note>original: "Holderbeer"</note> in preserving a person for a long life, Mylius recounts at length in the cited work, folio 271: A Prince lost his way while hunting and came upon a small peasant hut, where an old peasant sat before the door weeping because his father had beaten him. When the Prince wanted to know why the father had beaten him, the old son said it was because he had carelessly let his grandfather fall. The Prince saw the three old fellows and asked about their diet, and learned that they used elderberry mash or elderberry juice annually at a certain time. More can be found there.

### 138. Parting-water. Gold-dissolving water. <note>original: "Scheidewasser. Chrysulca aqua." This refers to nitric acid (aqua fortis), used to separate gold from silver.</note>

Gold-dissolving water is that by which mixed metals are led away or separated, commonly called *Aqua fortis* or "Parting-water" <note>original: "Scheidwasser"</note>. Alciatus gathered from the words of Ulpian <note>a Roman jurist</note> that the ancients were ignorant of its power, as seen in the law *The same Pomponius writes*, section *But if it be led away*, in the Digest *On the Recovery of Property*.

Regarding gold-dissolving water, see Rittershusius in his commentary on the *Institutes*, section 26, *On the Division of Things*.

### 139. Stelcke. Stilicho.

->ADDITION.<-

Stilicho <note>The famous Roman general of Vandal origin.</note> is the name *Stelcke*, which still remains in use in Saxony and Dithmarschen, according to Cyprian, *On Betrothals*, page 198.

### 140. Very. Enough. <note>original: "Sehr. Satis."</note>

->ADDITION.<-

"Rich in an insane manner" <note>original: "Dives insanum in modum"</note>. To undertake an "insane great" business, that is, a very great one. "Insanely well," that is, very well. "Insanely much," that is, most vehemently. Add to this Rupertus on Florus, book 2, chapter 6, section 35.

### 141. Staff-bearer. Tournament Official. <note>original: "Stabler. Tornamentarius."</note>

->ADDITION.<-

In the 28th tournament, they were so called; regarding their office, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 5, number 118.

Master craftsmen of the trades, who from olden times have received their confirmation, as well as their staff and sacred relics <note>original: "Stab und Heiligen"; likely referring to the ceremonial symbols and patron saint icons of a guild</note>, shall receive and take up such confirmation, staff, and relics from our officials in our court, and shall act therein as has been the custom from olden times. *Covenants and Agreements between M. and E.*

### 142. Tavern. Public House. <note>original: "Schenckstatt. Taberna."</note>

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the "Right of the Pour" <note>original: "Schenckrecht"; the legal right to serve or sell alcohol</note>, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter

<column-break/>

5, number 79. In the village of Herpersdorf, the right to serve drinks was taken away from Martin Geuder; however, where a man provides for his wife—who has given birth and is a woman in childbed—any drink of wine or beer, approximately one bucketful brought into his dwelling, he shall have the power to do so. Also, to share from such drink with a sick person; this shall in every case be considered harmless and permitted. *Nuremberg against Bavaria, regarding the point of Restitution*, folio 81.

Nobles are accustomed to brew not only for the use of their own families, but for the use of their subjects, and to sell it through their own stewards and innkeepers—"Pourers and Hosts" <note>original: "Schencken und Wirthe"</note>—see Master Tabor, *On the Law of Beer*, chapter 3, section 3. It is mere tyranny and open injustice if nobles extort grain from their subjects for a small price and, in turn, force poorly brewed beer upon them; see Balduin, *Cases of Conscience*, book 4, chapter 6.

If a Prince grants to some nobleman or cleric the right of establishing a tavern, "to set up a public house" <note>original: "eine Schenckstatt aufzurichten"</note>, does he thereby prejudice the neighboring cities, such that they cannot oppose such a new work? Master Doctor Tabor, in the cited chapter 3, section 10.

Regarding public houses that were not previously public houses, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 35, number 29. For who tavern-keepers are and concerning their rights, see Virgilius Pingizer, question 58; Gratianus, *Forensic Discourses*, 898; Menochius, book 3, counsels 668 and 798. Can someone be prohibited from leasing his house to a guest? See Menochius in the cited places. The utility of the Republic demands, and necessity persuades, that there be places established by public authority in which nothing other than the business of hosting must be carried out, and public innkeepers who have hung out an open sign; Georg Ludwig von Linvenspur in his commentary on the *Princely Württemberg Provincial Ordinance*, title *On Hosts and Givers of Hospitality*, number 9.

### 143. Seed. <note>original: "Saamen. Semen."</note>

When different seeds are sown in one field, see Werndorf, *On Tithes*, book 2, chapter 1, page 55.

->ADDITION.<-

When a "seed" <note>meaning biological offspring</note> is called to succession, all descendants are considered called unto infinity, even natural and collateral ones; Knipschild, *On Trusts*, chapter 1, number 205. 

The seed cast into the earth, having seemed to languish and die, turns white as it decays; it grows green and is born, gradually increasing and maturing; with the morning dew it flourishes, and when water is poured more largely from above, it arms itself with ears of corn—with little spikes to keep away the birds—it rises upon a stalk and puts forth leaves, turning yellow as it advances. With a lowered brow, it withers until it dies. Afterwards, it is threshed, and the fruit having been separated from the chaff, men live by the grain and animals by the chaff, as is required for the use of men; Gramondus.

### 144. Soap. Smegma. <note>original: "Saiffen. Smegma." Smegma is a Greek-derived Latin term for a cleaning agent or detergent.</note>

->ADDITION.<-

In the city of Tripoli, soap is prepared in great abundance; Fürer in his *Travelogue*, page 101. In some places, it is customary that soap-boilers are permitted to buy tallow <note>original: "Inschlitt"; animal fat used for soap and candles</note> neither from the butchers nor within several miles. *Extract from the Nuremberg Book of Customs, printed 1621.* Soap-boilers shall not buy tallow from butchers, even within five miles of here, under penalty of 5 florins; however, the butchers here in the city, in Wöhrd and Gostenhof, as well as the meat-stall holders, shall be obliged to deliver all tallow to the tallow-house for the common city supply, and not sell it elsewhere, under penalty of 20 florins. *On February 26, 1662*, the Margrave of the highlands, Christian Ernst, had a mandate published concerning mining ordinances, in which he categorizes mining and stream-works <note>original: "Saiffenwerck"; in mining, this refers to washing ore from alluvial deposits, though the word shares a root with soap/washing</note> together. Likewise, the newly uncovered veins, rafts, and stream-works opened by prospecting, clearing, or tunneling; ibid. The tax on oil and soap in Naples brings in 104,000 Ducats annually; Megiser in *Delights of Naples*, page 234.

### 146. Silk. Sericum.

->ADDITION.<-

Pancirollus explains what a "glass toga" <note>original: "Toga vitrea"</note> is in *Lost Discoveries*, page 406 of my copy: "Silk garments were woven on the Island of Cos from the finest, thinnest, and most delicate thread, so that they were transparent like glass, and thus easily subjected the parts of the body to view. In ancient times, a pound of silk was purchased by the Romans for a pound of gold; Zorer, part 2, question 18, number 5064. Raw silk, a shapeless offspring, is processed in many ways; Obrecht in *Political Reflections*, page 16. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 68, number 4. Spain is noble for its silk and wool; number 5. The abuse of silk garments; book 2, 94, numbers 24, 25, and 26. In Milan, Venice, Florence, and Genoa, many thousands of people seek their living from silk; Obrecht in *Political Reflections*, page 125. Henry II, King of France, was the first to wear silk—specifically silk stockings—at the wedding festival of his sister, which today even the dregs of the people in France use; Limn. volume 1, *Additions to Public Law*, book 6, chapter 2, page 4.

Silk [Sericum] takes its name from the fact that two monks, during the reign of Emperor Justinian, brought it from India to Byzantium...

### 149. Scribe. <term>Scriba</term>.

->ADDITION.<-

In former times, Scribes held a far more honorable position than today. Master Dilherr in *Synopsis of Aristotelian Politics*, page 78. Hence the Recorders <note>original: "Memoriales"</note>, called in Greek *sacred-remembrancers* <note>original: "hieromnēmones"</note>, *superintendents* <note>original: "epistatai"</note>, and *recorders* <note>original: "mnēmones"</note>, are **the city Secretaries.** Regarding the lowliness of Scribes among the Romans, yet the dignity of others, the Illustrious Rupertus treats this in his work on the *Origin of Law*, chapter 8, sections 6 and 7, which you should certainly consult. We also read that certain blind persons have learned to write extremely well. They had a tablet made of porphyry stone, gold, or another metal, into which were carved all the letters necessary for writing from A, B, C, all the way to Z. Afterward, taking a steel stylus, sharp and skillfully made for the purpose so that it could be freely guided and drawn through all those carvings of the letters: those blind persons practiced their hand through those letters so many times until, by use and the guidance of the tablet, they had sufficiently grasped the form of the letters from first to last and committed them carefully to memory, so that they could paint letters even on something other than the tablet. Once this was done, after long practice, they could even join and connect the letters, express syllables, and write words, until finally they could set forth all the thoughts of their mind through writing no less than if they were endowed with sight.

The son of Kamzaris <note>original: "Filius Kamzaris"; likely a reference to the Talmudic figure Kamzar, famous for his calligraphic speed</note> held four pens in his hand at once, etc. If a word consisted of four letters, he expressed each one at a single stroke, a fact which Saubert however omitted in silence in *On Sacrifices* <note>original: "de Sacrific."</note> number 713.

Why it is that those who deal with pens are always proud. See Mr. Harsdörffer in his *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive History* in the last appendix, number 148. The nature of pens <note>original: "Federn," which also means "feathers"</note>, and of those who wield them, is that they always want to fly high, even when they must remain on the earth in their inability.

Ludovicus Morus <note>Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan</note> let the following harmful speech be heard: that with a small writing knife and a quill, as well as with all kinds of dangerous and cunning plots and written deeds, he trusted himself to accomplish far more than with open wars, because he had a free, open hand at any time to keep, cancel, overturn, or twist them entirely or in part according to his pleasure. More in Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain, *On Truces and Peace* <note>original: "de Induciis & Pace"</note> page 65.

In Molsheim there is an ingenious desk <note>original: "Pult"</note>, upon which one can lay 50 or perhaps even more books at once without losing one's place. It stands on a table, like a reel or windlass; there are many boards that can be rotated, and five or more books can lie next to each other on one board.

What Tacitus says in *Annals* 11. 14. concerning the Egyptians, as if they had first invented writing, cannot well be sustained; but that Cadmus brought the same from Phoenicia into Greece, likewise that in Italy the Etruscans received the said art from Demaratus the Corinthian, and the Aborigines from Evander the Arcadian, may be more readily believed. The office and dignity of a Secretary is so highly esteemed that it has been compared by Francesco Sansovino and others to the service of the angels, who are the closest to God's throne. Mr. Harsd.

Scaliger indeed denies that one could write on ivory, but he is refuted by Martial, book 14, epigram 5:
> Lest sad wax dim your weary eyes,
> Let black letters be painted upon snow-white ivory.

### 152. Silence. *Silentium*.

->ADDITION.<-

A tacit trust <note>original: "fideicommissum tacitum"</note> in law 103 on Legacies I is taken for a fraudulent one. Tacit faith is found in law 1 of *On those who are unworthy* or law 46 *On claiming inheritance*, and law 17, section 2, *On usufruct*. A tacit agreement <note>original: "pactio tacita"</note> in law 50, section 2, *On the goods of freedmen*, stands for a clandestine one; and a "tacit sum" in law 47 *On agreements* stands for a sum not secured by public or bank testimony. Tacit and express agreements are judged the same when the tacit is naturally included in the express. Barbosa, *Rich Source*, pages 696–697. Gail, book 1, observation 116, page 5. Peregrinus, *Paduan Decisions*, chapter 3, number 11. One cannot have a "tacit of a tacit" <note>An implication drawn from another implication</note>. Costa in *On Retroactivity*, Monography 12, on chapter 2, number 4. Nor should a tacit thing be deduced from another tacit thing. Surdus, *Legal Consultations* 329, number 14. The express has greater power than the tacit. Klock, volume 1, consultation 29, number 235. On the injunction of silence, whether for a certain time, a long time, or in perpetuity. 

He who remains silent is seen to consent in favorable, meritorious, and desirable matters, especially if a reason of blood or kinship concurs. A silent person does not consent in heavy or burdensome matters: in prejudicial matters, in the reduction of one's own legal rights, in personal obligations, or in deposits. Faber on *Silence*, thesis 23. "Laws fall silent" <note>original: "Leges silent"; from the famous phrase *inter arma enim silent leges*—laws fall silent in times of war</note>—Cicero in his *Speech for Milo* and Emperor Leo, *Novel* 91. Campana, *On the Pope*, chapter 11, on punishments and remedies. Islands: Isaiah chapter 41, verse 1. Night: Virgil, *Aeneid* 2. Likewise, we say the Moon "is silent" when it does not appear, and "Paternal Power" is silent when it rests, or when its exercise is checked by an oath. Laurentius Tenninus in *Treatise on Precautions* 186, number 153. To rashly blurt out a friend's secret is vanity and iniquity. Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 14, section 81; on the revelation of a Confessor, ibid section 97. "Honorable is the voice of one whose breath stinks to himself because many things have rotted in his mouth" <note>A metaphor for someone who keeps secrets so long they metaphorically decay rather than being revealed.</note> Philippus Carolus on Gellius, chapter 23. On silent greetings <note>original: "von stillschweigenden Grüssen"</note>. Zeiller in *Itinerary of France*, page 419. An example of supreme silence is shown by Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 139. Silentiaries <note>original: "silentiarii"</note> are what the Secretaries are called. Limnaeus, book 8, *Public Law*, chapter 8, number 5.

On imposing perpetual silence. Schneidewein on the *Institutes*, page 772, number 18. A slanderer upon whom perpetual silence is imposed is held to provide security against coming back; how execution is carried out in all negative acts of will. Olibanus in *Commentary on the Digest on Actions*, part 2, book 1, chapter 33, number 18. Contardus on the law *diffamari*, chapter 1, number 41. Things belonging to custom and habit are understood as expressed by the parties through a tacit understanding. Klock, volume 2, consultation 42, number 261.

Secret letter <note>original: "Schleichbrieff"</note>. Letters of manumission.

A secret letter is issued over that which is alienated by exchange. Johannes Thomas Freigius in *Legal Practice*, folio 6.

### 155. Subtleties. *Subtilitates*.

Just as if boys about to collect quicksilver <note>mercury</note> scatter it entirely, so interpreters, by distributing laws too subtly, dissipate them and lose them under their hands. Crusius on the *Evidence of Crimes*, part 1, chapter 78, numbers 10, 11, 12. Zahn on *Lies*, book 2, chapter 81, at the end. Forster in his *History of Law* in the life of Bartolus, chapter 27, writes: Bartolus, in obscure matters, followed the judgment of right reason rather than excessive subtlety.

Subtlety will excuse me. For if someone falls into error in those things which concern the "tips of the law" <note>the finest legal technicalities</note>, they are easily forgiven. Pope Innocent III in the chapter *per tuas literas* on Simony, supported by Cardinal Francesco Mantica in *Conjectures on Last Wills*, book 6, title 6, number 13, and those cited there. Subtlety is twofold: one is rational, which contributes to the interpretation of the Law, and which is necessary and not to be despised (Law 1, Code, *On professors*; Law *tanta* 2, section 15, Code, *On the Authority of the Digest*; Law 10, section *plurium* 5, Digest, *On Questions*). The other is captious, which tends toward deceiving the simple-minded; the authority of law breaks this kind of "prudence" (Law 5, *On Transactions*; Distinction 20), because it leads to ruin (Law *fancimus*, Code, *On the Trebellian Decree of the Senate*). Reinking, class 2, chapter 11, number 42. Thus subtlety is enjoined upon judges (Law 13, section 3, Code, *On Judgments*). Wretched and excessive subtleties (Law 13, Code, *On Usufruct*; Law 7, Code, *On Institutions and Substitutions*; Law 59, section 1 at the end, *On the Law of Dowries*; the last Law, Code, *On Laws*; Law 30, Code, *On the Law of Dowries*; *Novel* 136, chapter 4 at the end), by which young students are worn down even to weariness and nausea.

### 170. School. Scholastics. High Schools [Universities]. School.

As the magnetic mountains, says Lord Hippolytus de Collibus, although they are unknown to many, turn the edge of steel (if rubbed with a magnet) toward their own parts: so Academies and Schools, because of the erudition of those teaching, draw many people to themselves from any part of the world—even those separated by the vast distance of many lands. See his booklet *On the Increase of Cities*, chapter 11. Obrecht in his **Political Reflections on the Improvement of Land and People**, page 122. I spoke of the **Nuremberg Lecture Hall** in my **Comparison of the Nuremberg Republic with the Venetian**, which is the twelfth among the Orations of Rupert, page 551. A **School** is nothing other than a **lesser Church**, and a **Church** is nothing other than a **greater School**. Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 143. From where the Schools of Christians were born; likewise, page 29, regarding the **Children's Schools in Constantinople**. Schweigger in his *Travel Book*, chapter 31, page 111. In the year 1648, there were 318 students in the Gymnasium of Strasbourg; of these, 143 were promoted on April 3rd, and the names of those who carried off the prizes for virtue and industry were inserted into the program.

Theophrastus was the first to invent the name **Scholastic**. Among good authors, it is used in various ways, and one may observe nearly six distinct meanings:
1. It signifies those who are still in School.
2. All those who live among letters, even if they are outside of Schools.
3. It signifies an elegant man, and is opposed to the barbarian and unrefined.
4. The term "Scholastic" very often pertains to the praise of learning and eloquence.
5. The naming of a "Scholastic" also carries a meaning of contempt, especially among the common people, who are accustomed to calling an unskilled or foolish man a "Scholastic" or a "man of the school."
6. An Advocate [Lawyer] is called a Scholastic. Why Ad-

<column-break/>

vocates are called Scholastics is shown at length by Conrad Rittershusius in *Novels*, part 9, chapter 7, number 10. Sometimes the word **Scholar** implies the "Doctors" [Professors], Walther *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 17 and following. A Scholastic is an animal ridiculed by everyone. Likewise, the "Nation of Scholastics" are called "dripping with fatness" <note>original: "madens pinguetè"; likely a satirical reference to the dense, heavy style of medieval commentators</note>—those who wrote commentaries and Questions on the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard and the *Summa* of Thomas Aquinas. Gisbert Voetius *On the Game of Dice*, page 15. Regarding scholastic discipline, see Johann Valentin Andreæ in *Supplements for Christian and Literary Matters*, page 494. Regarding the inspectors of elementary schools, page 595. 

Scholastic men are unfit for politics. Theodotus of Chios, a mercenary Master of Rhetoric, had persuaded Pompey of the same with a "pedagogical dilemma," and by this very act showed enough how unfit for political counsel are "men of the school." Hither belongs the judgment of Thuanus in Book 39 regarding Pope Paul V, that he disturbed many things because he did not possess political virtues, having been educated in the shadows and among flocks of monks. For one lives one way in monasteries, and another way in courts; and again, it is one thing to command monks, another to rule. Add Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 10, final chapter. Nicephorus Gregoras in Book 8 of his *Byzantine History*, page 154, in his excuse to the Emperor, who had offered him the dignity of Universal Librarian. He is also wordy on this matter in his *Public Law* throughout, where he simultaneously treats this question: whether such a Right belongs only to the Pope, and whether no Academies can exist without his approval? The reasons of those affirming this are held in Book 8, chapter 1, number 40 and following; the reasons of those denying it are in number 43. What should be held regarding Academies formerly privileged by the Pope alone? See the same place. Add Otto in *Public Law*, chapter 24, page 704. Regarding those who hurry too quickly and prematurely to the Academies, one should see the **Academic Icarus** of our Dilherr <note>Likening over-eager students to Icarus, who flew too close to the sun before he was ready</note>.

### 172. Saltpeter. Nitrum. <term>Nitrum: historically used for both naturally occurring natron and manufactured saltpeter (potassium nitrate) used in gunpowder.</term>

In Poland and the March <note>the Margraviate of Brandenburg</note>, and other places in Germany, the craft of boiling alum, and especially saltpeter—*to boil saltpeter*—is practiced everywhere at public expense, where 20 or more saltpeter-boilers are maintained here and there. They are given a license by the Sovereign or the Magistrate to dig wherever nitrous earth is found, for the sake of the public good. It is mostly made from the urine of humans and other animals, and of sheep in stables, in cellars, on walls, and in old monasteries. When the water of the dug-up nitrous earth is poured out, it produces a lye, which is boiled down by fire into "stone salt" <note>sal petrae, hence "saltpeter"</note>; how it is truly purified and cast, the chemists know. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 34, number 19; see also book 2, chapter 35, number 5, and book 2, chapter 9, number 9. Joachim Schepliz in *Customs of Brandenburg*, part 4, title 5, § 12. There is no doubt that the Sovereign can impose laws on saltpeter mines, according to Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 34, number 15; Rauchbar, *Questions* 22, numbers 11 and 12.

### 177. Waste-book. Scartafaccia.

The *Scartafaccia* is a record which bankers keep for the memory of all things—exchanges and goods—which they have to negotiate in the Fair, both in their own name and in the name of their agents. On the left they note the names of the debtors, but on the right the creditors. Such a *Scartafaccia* can be changed and underlined, therefore it has no *probative force* <note>legal weight as evidence</note>, unless it is after an acceptance has occurred—as when the entry is crossed through with a line by both contracting parties—or after a balance sheet has been presented; in which case no more can be changed in the *Scartafaccia* than in the balance sheet. Sprenger in *The Practice of Exchange*, page 99.

### 178. Settled accounts. Saldatis computis.

See above under the word *Account Books*, likewise the clause *for the remainder and for the balance*. The words: *for the balance of the present list*, only have the effect that the creditor cannot pursue anything further regarding that credit. For this general clause (*for the remainder*) is restricted to the things specifically mentioned. *Treatise on law, if from many, 89*, where Naevius, number 1, *Digest on payments*. Surdus, decision 217, number 6.

### 179. Sham Contracts. Contractus simulati.

See above, page 180. To which should be joined the Inaugural Juridical Disputation held in the year 1664 at Strasbourg by Ernst Erlenkamp, *On Simulated Contracts*. Zahn also treats simulation throughout his *Treatise on Lies*, book 1, chapter 39; also book 3, chapter 8, number 52. A simulated contract is said to be a body without a spirit, a contract without a soul, showing something outwardly by color, containing nothing inwardly. <note>original: "Contractus simulatus dicitur corpus sine Spiritu..."</note> The aforementioned applies when there is a simulation of a contract regarding itself; it is otherwise when there is a simulation of one contract to hide another, and it was sworn that each and every thing was true. In that case, the simulated contract is validated by the oath, so that the one swearing cannot go against the contract without perjury. Besides Caepolla, praised above on page 180, one should primarily consult Moderus of Verona in his *Treatise on Simulated Contracts*, in the 7th presumption near the end. Augustinus Beroius, counsel 165, number 1, volume 1. Unless an absolution <note>from the oath</note> has been obtained. The same Beroius, cited *Counsel*, number 26.

# T.

What the letter T signifies in the decrees of the Senate. <note>original: "T. Litera in Senatusconsultis quid significet."</note> Petrus Gregorius in *Syntagma Juris*, book 47, chapter 34, number 7.

## 1. Gutters. Eaves-drip. <term>Stillicidium: the legal right or obligation concerning rainwater dripping from the eaves of a house onto a neighbor's property.</term>

Whoever supports the gutters is exempt from the cost of laying them. For the burden of supporting them—which the other party lacks and which is almost never without inconvenience—excuses one from the burden of expenses.

And regarding what can be found in the Statutes or elsewhere, that such expenses ought to be shared, this is to be understood from equity when such gutters are located between both houses and can do as much damage to one as to the other.

### ADDITION.

In Frankfurt, gutters are called "channels" <note>original: *Canäl*</note>. *Frankfurt Reformation, part 8, title 7, paragraph 8.*

## 2. Day. *Dies*.

The "Day" is understood in five different ways in law (contrary to Alciatus, who, in his commentary on the law regarding the meaning of words, posits only three).

1. It is *Natural*, consisting of 24 hours, beginning at midnight and ending at the following midnight, according to the Roman custom. <note>original: "more Romanorum"</note> Reference: Macrobius and Jason on the law of holidays.

2. *Artificial*, which only encompasses the light from morning to evening, or whenever the Sun is above the earth. In the chapter on homicide, it consisted of twelve hours. Whence our Savior said in John 11: "Are there not twelve hours in the day?" <note>original: "Nonne, inquit, duodecim sunt horæ diei."</note>

3. It is *Legal*, or emergent, which is calculated precisely from moment to moment. Law 3, paragraph on minors, in the Digest.

4. It is called *Conventional*, according to what the parties agree upon, because contracts derive their force from the agreement of the parties. In case of doubt, if not otherwise declared by the parties, it is 24 hours, and thus Natural.

5. And the last is the *Ecclesiastical* day, which begins at various times, as Jason pursues at length in the aforementioned place.

In Public Instruments, it is required that the day always be added, as per the authorities on contracts and public receipts, as well as in the favors granted by Sovereigns.

But in private instruments and letters, the date is not necessary, according to the laws on pledges and deposits. Baldus notes this in his commentary on the credibility of instruments. Likewise, in private instruments, the signature of the writer is not required; however, the opposite holds true for the instruments of Notaries.

Regarding witnesses, the specific day or the presiding Consul <note>In ancient Rome, years were identified by the names of the serving Consuls.</note> is not required to be clarified; it is enough for the witness to testify that they remember the act in question. It follows that if a witness, when asked about the day, responds that they do not remember, they may still provide proof.

Regarding the names of days, as well as their measurement and distribution, see Robertus, book 1, chapter 1; Albericus Gentilis on the definitions of various times; and Brissonius on the title regarding Spectacles.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

If someone promises to pay "within these days" <note>original: *istis diebus* or *dieser Tag*</note>, it is to be understood as within two days. Johann Philippi on the practical use of the Institutes, book 3. A writing without a day or Consul is useless and suspect. *Acts of Lindau*, page 97. Is it necessary for the day and Consul to be expressed in a private writing? Klock argues no, but the contrary is proven in other sections. Annual payments are commonly called *Tagzeiten* <note>literally "day-times" or "term-days" for payments</note>. One day, or two or three, have contributed much to the safety of the Republic. Mr. Rupertus on Florus. On the uncommon notion of the word "Day," see Casaubon on Suetonius' *Augustus*. Festive days are well-suited for ambushes. <note>original: "Festi dies apti insidiis."</note>

Regarding what "bound days" <note>original: *gebundene Tage*; likely legal deadlines or court-days</note> are, see Georg Rittershuf. "Night" is used for "Day" in the phrase: "beyond 14 nights" one shall pay a debt that is acknowledged or won in court.

The Athenians were accustomed to measuring the day from sunset to the next sunset; the Babylonians, by contrast, from sunrise to the next sunrise; the Umbrians from noon to noon. The Romans, however, being most devoted to military affairs, followed the example of the Egyptians (according to Plutarch). For a certain military reason, they measured the day from midnight—as if from the first military watch—to the following midnight. This was because in time of war, many things must necessarily be done at night so that at sunrise forces can be joined; it is better for those who are prepared to begin the task than for those who are acting to be just getting prepared. What is usually taught here regarding Roman religious days—"black" days, cut days, and split days <note>original: *religiosis, atris, intercisis, diffissis*</note>—can be sought from Macrobius and Gellius. The city of Braunschweig has the power to establish and set "Days" <note>likely market days or assembly days</note> in their city. "To come to days" <note>original: *Zu Tagen kommen*; meaning to reach a settlement or a specific court date</note>. *Thorstag* was the name for what we now call *Donnerstag* <note>Thursday, or "Thor's Day"</note>. *Druhtintische Tag* for the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>.

### 6. Baptismal Books. *Liber seu matricula curati.*

Since the book of the Priest or Pastor is an effective means of proof regarding many things, the question is asked: whether through his book, in which the names and surnames of those who were cleansed by him at the sacred font of baptism are described here and there, the age of a person can be correctly and validly proven? And I conclude that it is so, according to the tradition of Johann Mauritius, *Treatise on Restitution to the Original State, chapter 321.* He says all of France approves this, and records that no fraud results from this method of proof; for the Priests do this with the primary intention of knowing which parishioners they have, and so that their age may be incidentally clear. Since they will achieve no utility or financial advantage from it, they are presumed to have described the age truly. And for this opinion, it was judged so, as reported by Franciscus Vivius, *Decision 184, number 2, book 1;* Nicolaus Janua, *Treatise on Private Writings, book 5, page 926, number 16,* where he says: It should be observed, however, that in our times, this 

<margin>
*Besold, Volume 1.*
</margin>

<column-break/>

disputation seems vain and overly subtle—namely, whether the Curate's own book creates proof of someone’s age—since it was most clearly decreed and concluded by the Fathers in the **Council of Trent** <note>A major 16th-century ecumenical council of the Catholic Church</note>**, session 24, title on the reformation of Marriage, chapter 1, near the end, at the verse: "let the Pastor have a book."** Namely, that the Pastor must have a book in which he faithfully describes and notes all those things that belong to the care of those subject to him. From which it is gathered that, without any doubt, faith must also be placed in him regarding those things in the book. For otherwise, this precept would be useless if it accomplished nothing. See also *me, on the Treasury, page 224, etc.*

### 7. Assessment of Costs. *Taxatio expensarum.*

The condemnation of expenses <note>The court order for one party to pay costs</note> is one thing, and the assessment <term>Taxatio</term> <note>The formal calculation of the specific amount owed</note> of the same is another: for Assessment is not a new condemnation, but only a demonstration and declaration of that quantity which is understood to be included in the condemnation. *Law "to Maevius" 41, section 1, Digest on Legacies 2; law 4 at the end, Code on Actions of Purchase; law "if ever" 6, Digest on Legacies; law "with his own" at the end, Code "if someone for another or for himself."* Baldus in *law "termination" 4, Code on Fruits and Expenses of Litigation, number 6, at the verse "now I ask whether," and following.* Antonius Faber in his *Code, book 2, title on Proctors, definition 14, number 1, at the verse "Assessment, however, is not new," etc.* Berlichius, *Decision 122, number 2, at the end.*
