### 8. Will. Testament. <note>original: *Testamentum*</note>

The formalities of wills are governed by Civil Law, and therefore certain individuals can compose wills by a singular Imperial Privilege, observing only the requirements of proof and the formalities descending from the Law of Nations. I have seen such a privilege granted by Rudolph II <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1576–1612</note>, drafted with the following wording: **"In the same way, we exempt and provide for, out of our Imperial perfection and power, the named N. N., their legitimate bodily heirs, and the heirs of those heirs, that wherever they or their own may in the future, according to their opportunity, make a Will or Codicil <term>Codicil: a legal document that modifies or adds to an existing will</term> of their last wishes (which should nonetheless be written by their own hands, or at the very least signed and secured and confirmed with their seals), and leave them behind after their passing, that the same Will and this wish etc. (provided they are not otherwise against Law and Equity) shall have force and standing, and shall be powerful and binding equally before Spiritual and Secular Laws and Courts, just as if the same had been executed, finished, and concluded in the best and most elegant form and manner according to the use of the Law and the custom of each Land, in the presence and confirmation of witnesses and notaries: unhindered by anyone. Against this, no liberties, laws, ordinances, statutes, or land or city customs shall exist, nor shall they in any way derogate from or prejudice this our grant in the law, etc."**

And there is no doubt that the Emperor can grant such a privilege, and that a will so made—provided there is a perfect expression of will—is valid. For the Roman Prince <note>Referring here to the Emperor as the successor to Roman authority</note> can prescribe whatever form and formality of making a will he wishes, according to the text in the Code *on testaments*, law 19. Since the right of making a will comes from the Laws (Digest *on the meaning of words*, laws 120 and 130), the Prince is indeed above the laws and released from them (Digest *on laws*, law 31). This is to be understood, according to the true and common opinion of the Doctors of Law, regarding Civil Laws, and among other things, regarding the formalities of wills (Code *on testaments*, law 3; Dauth in his *treatise on testaments*, number 5; Johannes Corasius, *Miscellany of Civil Law*, book 2, chapter 25, number 5).

Hence, Antonius Faber in his *Code*, book 6, title 5, definition 22, records: that even to the prejudice of one who would otherwise have succeeded according to an earlier Will, he who obtained the faculty from the Prince to make a will without formalities is understood to have made a valid will. This is because no one can be said to have acquired a Right before the death of the testator, because ne-

<column-break/>

-ither does any heir, nor any inheritance, seem to exist for a living person (Digest *on the sale of inheritance*, law 1; Digest *on acting as an heir*, law 1), where he adds that it was so judged in the Senate of Savoy, through the text in law 9, where the gloss and Sichardus (number 16) discuss testaments.

**"That which is added in a note in the future shall be equally valid as if the same were inserted word for word into the Will"**—that this clause is not valid can be proven from the writings of Thomas Herbai, *Daily Matters*, chapter 8, where he teaches that a testator cannot ensure that legacies, which he might later give with a smaller number of witnesses present, are ratified.

But my brother fought for that clause in his notebooks <note>original: *adversariis*</note>: which I have now inserted at the end of the 155th thesis of the 3rd Disputation on the Municipal Law of Württemberg.

->ADDITION.<-

Ludovicus Lana, a jurist of Brescia, wrote a *Handbook on the Formulas of Wills*; Hermann Mejer wrote *On Testamentary Succession*; Magdalen wrote *On the Witnesses of Wills*. Executors are called "Mouth-men" <note>original: *MundsMänner*</note> in the *Inaugural Disputation on the Trenarchs* held at Strasbourg, 1665, page 21. Jacobus à Canibus wrote a treatise *On the Executions of Last Wills*; and Henricus Wilhelmus Erhard of Speyer disputed for his degree *On the Executors of Wills* at Strasbourg in 1665. Out of spouses who made a will together, one can revoke their disposition (Klock, volume 3, consultation 100, number 23). **In Utrecht, no one may make a will without a grant and permission from the noble Court**, as can be seen from the Will of Mr. Johann Carl von Rehlingen. Baldus notes (on law 5 of the Digest *on verbal obligations*) that under the power of disposing at will, succession by a person dying without a will <note>original: *ab intestato*</note> is also included; which is all the more to be said here, where it appears from the circumstances and the clause that those making the agreement also felt this in the case that they died without children (as in Curtius Junior, volume 1, consultation 4, number 5; Surdus, Decision 272, number 14; Mr. Tabor, *On Dowry Pacts*, page 87).

The Oelhaf family was granted a special privilege regarding the making of wills by Maximilian I at Innsbruck on January 18, 1507:

> That future Oelhafs of both sexes
> May enjoy for all time
> This new liberty: that they may record
> The final thoughts of their minds without the formalities
> Required by common law, to be valid in any place;
> Provided that two witnesses of blameless life and faith,
> Or at most three, are added in haste.

Tacitus writes concerning the customs of the ancient Germans: "They had heirs, each their own children, and there was no Will." <note>Tacitus was a Roman historian who contrasted the "simple" virtues of Germanic tribes with the perceived decadence of Rome.</note> This passage from Tacitus is taken from chapter 20, which begins: "The Germans in every house are naked and dirty." And a little later: "They live among the same livestock, on the same ground." Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman law</note> by no means condemns succession without a will, nor does he call it illegitimate; however, he grants that masters of property may also provide for friends and benefactors.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding testaments and wills, specifically focusing on the validity of wills presented to sovereigns, the interpretation of a testator's intent, and the legality of unusual or immoral conditions placed upon heirs.</meta>

The most august Emperor Ferdinand III, regarding Bohemian Law <note>original: *Juris Bohem.*</note>, Book 3, see also the Response of Burian, Reason for decision 1, declares that shackles are placed upon liberty if such freedom is entirely forbidden. They object: the license to make a will gives occasion for many lawsuits. This, however, happens only by accident. This is discussed at length by Lord Tabor in *Elements of Jurisprudence* <note>original: *Element. Jurispr.*</note> part 2, thesis 26; the same in the Program of September 12, 1653, proposed very broadly at Strasbourg. Regarding a testament offered to a Prince or a Count, the celebrated Tabor—greater than all praise—established an analytical-synthetic treatment on Law 19 of the Code concerning Testaments. If a courtier, counselor, or any other private person offers his last <term>Eulogy</term> <note>here meaning a final statement or will</note> to a Prince of the Empire through a formal petition, firm strength is granted to this disposition, just as if he had written his last will in the presence of seven witnesses solemnly called for this act. The presence of the Prince stands in place of witnesses. Yet, if it is doubted whether the testament was actually filed with the Prince or not, the Prince alone is scarcely to be believed; rather, I judge that at least two witnesses are required for proof. Nicolaus Myler discusses this throughout chapter 28 of *On the Princes and States of the Empire*. The incomparable Lord Ludwell wrote a most accurate and peculiar treatise on last wills, which he also brought to public light. On the "implicit testament"—a matter not known to everyone—Espich wrote excellently in part 2 of *Specimen of the Examination of Testaments*. What is required if a testator wishes his will to remain secret? See Johannes Fichard, volume 2, counsel 71, number 7 at the end, and volume 1, counsel 43. The mind of the Testator must be investigated by a Judge not from only one part of the Will, but through all its small details, just as a hunter is accustomed to search for hares through all the recesses of the forest with a diligent tracking—as Baldus advises in the Law on necessary servants. One is bound to search everything and always labor to possess the truth. A Testament can also be changed tacitly. Regarding a legacy left under the condition of the Roman Catholic Religion <note>original: *Religionis Pontificiæ*</note>, one should see Jacob Alemann in *On the Law of Money*, page 973. On a trust <term>fideicommisso</term> <note>a legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of another</note> left under the condition of changing one's religion, see Pfretshner on families, page 45. Modestinus, in Law 27 on conditions of institution, reports and decides a case of an uncivil and nearly inhuman last will, eluded and ignored by the "civil wit" of the heir. "A certain man," he says, "had written his heir into his will under such a condition: if he threw my remains (<term>leipsana</term> <note>original: λείψανα</note>, as Ulpian calls them in Greek, that is, ashes... or if <term>nekrokausia</term> <note>original: νεκροκαυσία; the practice of burning the dead</note> had already passed out of use by Ulpian’s age, as some record... let us understand the dead man or the bones of the dead man... the body or the remains of the limbs) into the sea."

<column-break/>

The written heir did not obey the condition, but instead buried the testator according to the custom of the ancestors. Those coming <term>ab intestato</term> <note>heirs who inherit when there is no valid will</note> thought the written heir should be expelled from the inheritance on the grounds that the condition was not fulfilled. It was asked: what is the Law? There was the same vow, but not the same target, end, and intention of the one vowing. We read in Ovid’s *Fasti* from verse 653: "And a great part..." and likewise "to send me into the Tiber..." Modestinus rightly responds to this case in general terms, saying that the heir is to be praised for not throwing the remains of the testator into the sea according to his wish, but instead delivering them to burial out of mindful respect for the human condition. Furthermore, the Jurist declares that it must be inquired whether such a testator was of sound mind—one who so utterly forgot his own human condition—so that consequently his will is clearly null; or, if he is proved to have been of sound mind in other matters, this specific wish is nevertheless ignored as being inept and fighting against good morals.

From the testaments of friends, how much did the Emperor Augustus receive? See Obrecht in *Political Secrets*, page 29, and in *Political Reflections*, page 119. In the Statute of Minden, it is said that no one can make a will unless he leaves a third part of his goods safe for his heirs-at-law. Bullaeus, in his *Counsel*, asks what a "wise man" can add if the testator wanted the will extended to the sense of a wise person, and whether he can supplement a legacy left to a son so that it may be valid by right of institution. Likewise, whether he can add a clause derogatory to a prior will. See Mantica on conjectures of last wills.

### ADDITION.

Lansius, in his *Consultation for Germany*, testifies that in Europe no war has been concluded without the involvement of German Princes. The nation of the Germans is most brave. See Hermann Conring, *On the Roman-German Empire*, chapters 1 and 2. Germany was once a wild place and lacking in resources, but now how greatly it is cultivated and abounds in arts, towns, and wealth! Lipsius, *On the Greatness of Rome*, book 1, chapter 3. Althamer, in his commentary on Tacitus, writes: "I have wished several times for Germany to have either a Cicero or a Livy who might celebrate our grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and the entire nation from its deepest roots, but in vain." The <term>Capitulation</term> <note>The formal agreement of rights and duties between the Emperor and the Electors</note> from Charles V down to Ferdinand III is uniform on this point: **namely, that the Royal and Imperial offices, at court and otherwise in the Empire, are to be filled and provided for by none other than native-born Germans.** Limnäus, volume 2, addition by J. P. to book 1, chapter 12, folio 358.

Cosmographers also refer the three northern kingdoms—Denmark, Sweden, and Norway—to Great Germany, as witnessed by Albert Krantz in the preface to book 1 of *Saxonia*, near the end. Gothofridus Antonii, *Feudal Disputations* 1, thesis 1, letter C.

A praise of the Germans is presented by Lipsius, century 1, epistle 28, and century 3, epistle 85. Also *Miscellaneous Epistles* 27. Bodin, in his *Method of History*, chapter 5, **writes that the Germans surpass all other nations in friendliness: the Asians in military discipline; the Romans in religion; the Hebrews in philosophy; the Greeks in geometry; the Egyptians in arithmetic; the Phoenicians in astrology; the Chaldeans; and all peoples in all manner of ingenious craftsmanship.** Regarding the praise of Germany, see Zeiller in the preface of his *German Itinerary*, which he wrote in folio in the year 1632, and its *Continuation*, which he published in 1640. Afterwards, he wrote a *Compendium of the New-Ancient German Itinerary*. See also Chalcocondylas *On Turkish Affairs*, book 2, page 306, line 10 and the following lines. **Question:** Can the Scepter of the Empire be conferred upon anyone other than a German? Otto, in *Public Law*, page 164, says no. **Question:** Is someone to be called a German who is born outside of Germany while his father is still living? Otto, page 167, affirms this.

Conrad Peutinger wrote discourses on Germany; also on the antiquity of Germany. Michael Maier, Count Palatine, wrote *On the True Discoveries of Germany*, published at Frankfurt, 1619. Heinrich Pantaleon wrote *On the Illustrious Men of Germany*. Melchior Adam of Silesia wrote *The Learned Century in Germany*. Leonhard Wurffbain in his *Historical Relation*,

<column-break/>

page 240. Conring, *On the Borders of the German Empire*:

> O Germany, discoverer of a gift <note>Likely referring to the invention of the printing press</note>,
> Than which antiquity gave nothing more useful:
> You who teach us to write books by pressing,
> Blessed in crops, renowned also for metals,
> And rich in cattle: fertile in the gem
> Which your ancestors call *glessum*,
> The Greeks *electrum*, the Latins *succinum* <note>These are all terms for amber</note>.
> Mighty in Princes, powerful in men:
> Who with grey-blue eyes and flaxen hair:
> Large of body, fierce in spirit
> Hedged with strength and prodigal of life
> Attack and provoke the enemy.
> Hail, O glorious Germany.

More can be found in Neander’s *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 115.

### 10. German Masters. The Master of the Order of Saint John.

See above under the word **Johanniter** <note>The Knights Hospitaller</note>, and Gualtherus’s *Chronicle of Chronicles*, part 2, folio 5 and folio 100. Antonius Faber, *On the Government of Religion*, book 1, folio 54, number 77 and following.

### 11. German Language. <gloss>The German Tongue.</gloss> See above under the word "Language."

A specimen of the older German language will be preserved for us by the most noble Goldast through his edition of the *Ancient Parenetica* <note>Advisory or moralizing poems</note>; he likewise explained various older German words in his notes. Freher did the same in his notes on the *Treaty of Louis of Germany and Charles, King of Gaul*; as well as in specimens of the Saxon and Alemannic dialects. Relevant here is the *Paraphrase of the Song of Songs* by Abbot Willeram, with notes by Paulus Merula, and the *Book of the Gospels* by Otfrid. Also Georg Heinisch in *German Language and Wisdom*. And the <term>Confession</term>, as it was once performed in the vernacular tongue before a priest by the Eastern Franks and Thuringians, which Christoph Brouwer has in *Antiquities of Fulda*, book 2, chapter 14. Regarding the excellence and antiquity of the German language, Gropius Becanus and Adrianus Schrieckius deal with this at length in several small works. But Abraham Vandermyle discusses it best. And Serrarius, in *Moguntiacarum*, book 1, chapter 11, proves that the ancient language of Mainz was a purely German dialect, namely Gallic. But there are nonetheless those who make the Gallic or Celtic language and the German language entirely distinct: which Camden also seems to do in his *Britannia*, folio 17 (in my copy), where he compares many Celtic words with British ones, which seem more foreign to German ones; see my work *On the Nature of Peoples*.

Regarding the antiquity of the Saxon language, Gryphiander also writes excellently in *On the Municipal Law* <note>original: *de Weichbild*</note>, chapter 38.

Heigius, book 1, question 8, teaches when the German language was first committed to letters; see also Verdier, *Diverse Readings*, folio 437 (in my copy), and Arumäus in his *Treatise on the Imperial Diets*, chapter 7, number 138, where he discusses **when the Latin language ceased, and when the German language began in its place.** And that this occurred around the year 1243.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Germanic heritage, shifting focus from political and legal history to the history of the German language and its onomastics (the study of names). It connects the previous discussion of German identity to the linguistic transition from "barbaric" ancient names to Latinized forms.</meta>

1037
Lit. T.

It was begun to write public and private documents in the Germanic language, yet using Latin letters: although already in the time of **Charlemagne** <note>original: *Caroli M.*</note> an attempt had been made to record that same language in writing by whatever means possible. And that the Germans then also began to initiate their own people into the sacred washing <note>A reference to Christian baptism</note> with the names of Saints and Latins, whereas they had previously used ancestral and barbaric names, is attested by **Christoph Hartmann** in the *Annals of the Hermitage of the Holy Mother of God Monastery* <note>The Benedictine Einsiedeln Abbey in Switzerland</note>, page 246.

That the Germanic language is not the first and oldest—contrary to the claims of **Goropius Becanus** <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus was a physician who famously and eccentrically argued that Antwerpian Brabantic was the language spoken in Paradise</note>—is proven by **Christian Becmann** in his *Introduction to the Latin Language*, chapter 5, page 22 and following, and in his *On Origins*, page 139, etc.

Regarding the Germanic and Gallic <note>French</note> languages, see also **Lord Lansius** in his *Consultation*, in the oration against France, page 309, etc., and **Antoine Pippre** in *Moral Intentions*, chapter 27.

It is well-established to anyone who more exquisitely understands the sound and sense of these languages that very many Germanic words are indebted to Latin; see especially **Robigius**, book 10, *On Critical Matters*, chapter 18. Conversely, since the Teutons "Romanize" in their words and especially in their sentences, it has happened that, in turn, certain of our words have been granted "Forensic Latinity" <note>Legal Latin terminology</note> by the jurists, as can be seen in the same Robigius, in the cited location, chapter 19.

However, how great the abundance of the Germanic language once was, and to what extent it has degenerated today, appears from the following list of proper names occurring here and there in histories, of which only a very small part is seen inserted here.

### ADDITION.

Even to this day in France, Italy, and Spain, many different whole or partial words are found which have their origin from the Germans; and for that reason, one or another nation could never understand each other outside of these same German words. If they ever wished to abolish those German words, they would have to invent entirely new ones to replace them in their language. Lord Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Relations* <note>original Latin: *Relat. Hist.*</note> part 8, page 238, at the end. Emperor Maximilian I offered great sums of money and rewards if anyone could bring to light a German public letter <note>original German: *offenen Brief*</note> that had been written in German 500 years prior. Beatus Rhenanus, book 2, chapter 5, notes that the Franks used the Germanic language. Regarding when the Germanic language began to be written, see Limnäus, volume 2, additions to book 1, chapter 6, number 61. **Emperor Rudolph** provided by edict that all mandates, edicts, privileges, dowry pacts, contracts, and other writings of that kind should be drawn up in the Teutonic <note>German</note> language. Lit. T. 1041

In Lorraine and Brabant, when they act in the Chamber, they are compelled to translate French acts into German or Latin. See Wehner in the *Dedicatory Epistle of his Observations.* The language of the Germans is most ancient. See Limnaeus, *Public Law of the Empire, Book 1, chapter 6, number 50 and following.* A Prince achieves immortal glory, whoever first chooses to establish a Professor of the German Language in his university; we read that Francesco de' Medici, Duke of Tuscany, did this, as he commissioned Diomedes Borghesi—having been authorized with the most ample salary—to publicly profess the Tuscan language in the Academy of Siena. The Magnificent Mr. Harsdörffer <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658), a Nuremberg poet and polymath dedicated to purifying the German language.</note> says more on this in *Specimen of Philology, pages 95, 96, 167, and 168*, where under the name of "cultivating the vernacular" he understands in *number 4* that a dictionary should be compiled in which all the roots, compounds, derivatives, phrases, and proverbs of our language are reduced to alphabetical order; and in *number 5* that all legal, feudal, medical, surgical, technical terms, and the modes of speaking of all mechanics should be collected into a finished work. In Feudal Law, German words are frequently found, regarding which see Hotoman, Lazius, Beatus Rhenanus, and others. Besold, in *chapter 23 on the Immunity of Language*, says the following: "The Feudal Law we use abounds even with mere Germanisms, and has many Germanic voices which are miserably twisted by interpreters ignorant of German antiquities, and by prejudice are generally snatched away from us and their true origin," just as the author here relates many things. Maltera <note>original Latin/German: *Malter*</note>, a measure of grain. Banerium <note>original Latin/German: *Panier*</note>, a military standard. Clusæ, for the passes of mountains. Galia <note>original Latin/German: *Galeer*</note>, a galley or three-banked ship. Stuba <note>original Latin/German: *Stube*</note>, a heated room. Morganaticum <note>original Latin/German: *Morgengab*</note>, a "morning gift" <note>A gift given by a husband to his wife the morning after their wedding.</note>. Harnascha <note>original Latin/German: *Harnisch*</note>, armor. Lobium <note>original Latin/German: *Laube*</note>, an arbor or lodge. Mantus <note>original Latin/German: *Mantel*</note>, a cloak; *immanitare*, to invest with a cloak. See more in Schottel’s *On the Main German Language, folio 128 and following.*

### 13. Thaler. *Thalerus.*

Some derive the "Thaler" from "Talent" or from Besold’s *Volume I*

<column-break/>

from "Metal": others (and more correctly, see Jacobus Alemannus in *Palæstra of Consultations, 8, principal question 1, part 32*) from the German word *Thal* <note>Valley</note>, because in the Joachim Valley (*im Joachimsthal*), they were either the first or the best struck compared to others, and from there—<unclear>from the valley</unclear>—they were named "Joachim Valleyers" <note>The word "Thaler" is the origin of the English word "Dollar."</note>.

And indeed, in the year 1518, the first Joachim-Thalers were minted, as noted by Matthesius in the *Chronicle of the Mining-Sermons* appended.

Formerly, the power to mint Thalers was not granted to every State of the Empire, but was specifically restricted. *Recess of the Imperial Diet at Augsburg, February 14, 1551, paragraph "further we decree," etc.* This prohibition, since it seemed impossible for Thalers to be exterminated or inhibited, was finally relaxed by Ferdinand’s *New Minting Ordinance at Augsburg, August 19, 1559, paragraph "after however," etc.*

Regarding the value and issuance of Thalers, it was ordered in the Recesses of the Empire as follows: *Recess of the Imperial Diet, in the same place, May 30, 1566, paragraph "therefore we have,"* with the two following, in the words: "We decree, that the whole Thaler, of which one piece is worth 69 Kreutzers, shall go 8 pieces to the Cologne Mark <note>A standard unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 233 grams.</note>, and shall hold 14 Loth <note>A weight unit; 16 Loth equal one Mark.</note> and 4 Grains: thus the fine Mark is produced for 10 Guilders and 12 Kreutzers." Budelius, *On the Matter of Money, book 1, chapter 18, number 7*, where he notes that eight Thalers weigh a Mark, and contain fourteen Loths and four Grains of pure silver; or what is the same, ten Denarii and sixteen Grains. See Alemannus, *in Palæstra of Consultations, consultation 8, principal question 1, and partition 32.*

The words "hard Thalers" <note>original German: *harte Thaler*</note>, placed in a bond or instrument of obligation, are to be understood as Imperial Joachim-Thalers; therefore, payment must be made in that coarser money—in "coarse coin" <note>original German: *grober Müntz*</note>—and not in small money or money debased with copper. This is because the proper, original, and fundamental meaning of the German word "Thaler" in the vernacular implies not small coins or groats, but coarser money. *Law 27, paragraph 1, Digest on gold and silver; Law 78, paragraph 4, on legacies 3.* For one thing is not paid for another to an unwilling creditor. *Law 2, paragraph "the giving of a loan," 1, Digest on credited things; Law 16 and following, Code on payments; Law 19, paragraph 3, Digest on letting and hiring.* But one must stand by the agreements and express pacts; otherwise, words placed thus, "with good Thalers," would be futile, which ought not to happen. For they are to be interpreted in such a way that they produce some effect. *Law "if ever," 109, at the beginning, Digest on legacies 1. Baldus on the rubric of the Code on contracting a sale, in the 9th question.* This holds place to such an extent that a person promising 20 Saxon or Imperial Thalers is not released by paying the value in other Joachims or Thalers (although I do not deny that if the specific things owed are no longer found, the value—

<meta>This page continues a legal and economic discussion regarding currency, specifically focusing on the regulations surrounding the "Thaler" and the rights of creditors and debtors when specific coinage is required for repayment.</meta>

[the obligation] is rightly discharged. (Law 14, Section 2, Digest on Legacies 3.) <note>Latin: l. 14. §. 2. ff. de leg. 3.</note> For an unfair condition ought not to be imposed on one person by another, according to the rule: "It ought not" (Law 74, Digest on the Rules of Law). <note>Latin: l. non debet 74. ff. de R. J. This refers to a fundamental principle in Roman law that one party should not be unfairly burdened by the actions of another.</note> This would happen, however, if a Creditor were forced to receive small change, for an inconvenience would occur, and a loss would result from it, since one is more easily deceived in counting and spending it, and it would consume much time. Small coinage <term>moneta minuta; petty cash or change</term> is also heavy in weight, dangerous to transport from place to place, and not of a certain value everywhere; indeed, smaller money is cast from bronze and copper, and its intrinsic goodness does not correspond to the goodness of larger money.

And although there might be some difficulty in this matter, it was plainly resolved by the Imperial Ordinance of Ferdinand I, published at Augsburg in the year 1559, in the section "the now-mentioned Imperial coins," <note>German: die ietzt gemeldte Reichsmuͤnzhen</note> in which it is clearly expressed that no one is compelled to accept small change for any payment of a notable sum beyond 25 florins; all other debts, even if not specifically expressed, must be paid in larger coinage. On this question, see Matthias in *Executive Process, part 1, chapter 10, number 7 and following*; Peter Friedrich Mindanus *On Mandates, book 2, chapter 63, number 7*; Virgilius Pingizer, *Saxon Questions 40, number 20 and following*; Alemannus in *Consultations of the Palæstra 8, at the beginning*.

And note that "Payment-Talers" <note>German: Zahl-Thaler</note> are contrasted with "Hard Talers." <note>German: den harten Thalern; high-quality silver coins.</note> Just as it is different with the French Franc and the "piece of Franc," so it has also gone in Germany with the Guilder.

### ADDITION.

An Imperial Taler <term>Reichsthaler; the standard large silver coin of the Holy Roman Empire</term> is worth:
* In Nuremberg: 1 1/2 florins, 90 kreuzer, or 22 1/2 batzen.
* In Brunswick: 36 Mariengroschen.
* In Leipzig and Meissen: 24 "good" groschen.
* In Hamburg and Lübeck: 3 marks or 24 shillings.
* In Lüneburg: 32 shillings.
* In Bremen: 72 grote.
* In Frankfurt: 72 florins. <note>original: 72 fl. This likely refers to a specific exchange rate or a typo for kreuzers in the source.</note>
* In Amsterdam: 2 1/2 florins or 50 stivers.
* In Danzig: 90 groschen.

How the distinction between Imperial Talers and "poor" Talers and Guilders was introduced: see Zorer, part 2, question 17, number 1096. Why, during the increased coinage activity, trade was mostly conducted in Talers and not Guilders as before: question 18, number 5009, section 4 and following. How payment should be made when a loan was made in specific types, such as Talers: question 17, number 2085. Whether the loaned Talers must be delivered in the same minting as received: question 17, number 2093. Regarding good, hard Imperial Talers, and how they should be current and valid at the time of payment: Auer *On Monetary Law*, thesis 103. Regarding hard Talers, "good in weight and purity": <note>German: gut in Schrot und Korn; a technical term meaning the coin meets the legal standards for total weight and silver content.</note> thesis 108. Regarding good, current, and valuable Imperial Talers, as they were received, good in weight and purity, unclipped, each of which weighs 2 <term>Loth; a unit of weight, approximately 14-15 grams each, totaling about 29-30 grams per coin</term> of silver: thesis 114. In non-prohibited Talers current in the Holy Empire: thesis 97. Certain Austrian Talers, which were minted in 1446,

<column-break/>

are considered to be the oldest.

**Taler-Despisers.** <note>German: Thaler-Verächter</note> Mr. Harsdörffer in *The Great Theater of Joyful and Instructive History*, volume 115, number 3. Whole Imperial Talers, halved, and half-quarter Talers. In previous years, the Taler was changed neither in alloy nor in weight, and before things were altered, its value was increased to 210 groschen. More in Leuber, *On Reduction, page 72*. What Talers are described as unchanged and undebased: Klock, *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 48*.

102. If the specific type of coin owed is no longer found, and cannot be paid by the debtor, it is asked whether the debtor is freed by paying the estimated value plus interest. The great-grandfather of the Most Illustrious Count N. N. of O. had borrowed twenty thousand Talers—of the kind called "Schlickian"—more than a century ago from the great-grandfather of the Most Illustrious Count N. N. of D. He had pledged to make the payment in that same species of money, in Schlick-Talers, <note>Schlickenthalern: coins minted by the noble Schlick family in Bohemia (the origin of the word "Taler").</note> meanwhile giving a certain Barony to the same creditor as <term>antichresis; a legal arrangement where the creditor holds a property and uses its income in place of interest payments</term>. The great-grandson, wishing to redeem the pawned Barony, offers the creditor's great-grandson and successor the payment of the said borrowed sum in Joachim-Talers <note>Joachimicis: another name for the high-quality silver coins from Joachimsthal.</note> indeed, but with a bonus of two thousand Talers, if it were of such interest to him. The creditor refuses to receive payment in this type of money, appealing to the written bond <note>chirographum</note> and its tenor, according to which the payment must be made in Schlick-Talers. The debtor replies that such Talers can no longer be found, at least not in such a large sum, and for that reason, he had also offered such a large bonus in place of interest. The creditor clings to the bond, saying that as his great-grandfather stipulated, and as the debtor’s great-grandfather promised, faith must be kept in all things. The matter was finally brought to the Emperor Charles V, who tried by all means to settle this case with an amicable composition, but in vain. Since he suspected that the Creditor was greedily eyeing the debtor's Barony, the Emperor issued a decree to the Most Illustrious Schlick family, ordering them to mint enough Talers under that original old seal to pay the debt, and to hand them over to the debtor (who was to provide the costs). Once this was done, by satisfying the creditor with those actual Schlick-Talers, he redeemed his ancestral Barony; and thus the most wise Emperor, by his sagacity, mocked the unfairness of the Creditor. Many more cases are in Mr. Rebhan, *On Selected Questions of Civil Law, question 1664, number 3*.

Lit. S.

How one should estimate and value goods in divisions <note>Referring to the legal division of an estate among heirs.</note>, see above under the word Appraisal. <note>original German: *Anschlag*</note>. When someone still holds the Usufruct <term>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another</term> upon them, the goods are appraised only to facilitate the division, not so that the valuation should be considered a sale price, unless this is expressly stated, especially regarding immovable property <note>real estate</note>. Regarding the valuation of movable property <note>original German: *Fahrniß*</note>, see my work in *Disputation 4 on the Municipal Law of Württemberg*. After the inventory is made, one must divide with the pen, or on paper, what belongs to each person according to the circumstances of the case. First, however, one must settle with those who have claims on arrears of goods or otherwise have something to seek by Right of Vindication <term>a legal action to recover property from someone who is not the owner</term>; one must also make as many divisions as there are different cases to consider in such a work. When everyone knows on paper and sees what belongs to them, they come to the assignment, which is to be made by the judge according to his free discretion in the best and most equitable way; and when the portions are set, as equally as can be, they are to be distributed by lot.

On the Division of goods, inheritances, rights, and feudal property. See Guido Papæ, decision 289, throughout. Berlichius, part 3, conclusion 21. Whether the choice in a division belongs to the minor, or how it is to be done. Berlichius, in the same place. Cævallos, question 340. Vivius, decision 437. Scheffer, part 1, question 4. Rauchbar, book 1, question 40. Whether in a division a thing should be awarded to him who holds the larger portion of that thing. Hartmann Pistoris, observation 147. Rosenthal on Feudal Law, chapter 9, member 1, conclusion 53. On feudal division. Matthias Wesenbeck, consultation 41 and consultation 267. Christinaeus, part 1, decision 388. On the division between brothers and feudal succession. Matthias Wesenbeck, Consultation 68, Consultation 115, and Consultation 187.

## 16. Dearness. <note>Latin: *Annonæ caritas*; refers to times of high prices, inflation, or food scarcity.</note>

Two hundred and more years ago, one gave 12 florins in annual interest for 100 florins of capital <note>an interest rate of 12%</note>; on the other hand, salaries—in money as well as in wine and grain—were very small: because of the simplicity and temperance of the ancients. For instance, a castle-dweller, or guardian of the fortress in time of war <note>Latin: *custodi Arcis tempore belli*</note>, was given annually, besides wood, 12 pounds of good Würzburg pennies, 12 *malter* <note>a unit of dry volume</note> of spelt, an Esslingen *eimer* <note>a bucket or cask</note> of wine, a pig, and salt-cakes. So also, seven watchmen and gatekeepers were each given individually, annually, 2 pounds of Würzburg pennies and 2 *malter* of spelt; and additionally, for food, each of these watchmen and gatekeepers received 9 *malter* of spelt, less 6 *viertheil* <note>quarters</note>. All according to the Geislingen measure. See my work *On Life and Death*, folio 15, where I discuss the causes of this cheapness, as well as in the miscellaneous corollaries added to my *Commentaries on several titles of the Pandects*, book 1, corollary 5.

Two hundred years ago, it is also found that to a noble person who wished to enter the clergy, his secular brothers gave 20 Hallish pounds annually, and provided him with a spiritual benefice <note>an ecclesiastical office providing an income</note> which might yield 40 pounds; see the Testament in the Montbéliard Council, volume 1 of the *Various Consultations* published by me.

And certainly, the quality or debasement of currencies has a great effect; thus, in the years 1622 and 1623, here in Tübingen, a measure of wine was sold for two florins.

In the year 1268, in Thuringia, a bushel of wheat cost 18 pennies, a bushel of rye 16 pennies, and an old hen 2 pennies. In the year 1280, a bushel of rye cost 22 pennies, and 8 herrings cost one penny. Johann Binhard in the *Thuringian Chronicle*. See above under the word Heller. Also, in former times, a Colonel’s commission was 100 pounds of *Heller* <note>small copper coins</note>. Lehmann in the *Speyer Chronicle*, folio 218 and folio 761; who also in book 7, chapter 84, folio 872, reports that an Imperial meal cost 37 florins. Add Mariana on *Weights and Measures*, chapter 24, and see below under the Consultation on the word Usury, etc., question 1, reason 9, where it is discussed at length how and in what manner lordships, villages, etc., were sold 200 and more years ago, and the reasons are added as well.

### ADDITION.

**Scarcity** <note>original German: *Theurung*, referring to periods of high inflation or famine</note> is prevented when the prices of foodstuffs are not increased and they are kept within the country, and when a certain tax or price control is established; likewise, when people are compelled to sell their goods. See Zorer, part 1, question 12, numbers 941 to 945. Regarding the causes of the high cost of grain, see the Oration of the Distinguished Mr. Virdung held at Altdorf in 1614, which is the eighth among his published orations; to which the ninth should be added, concerning the remedies for this evil. On **Scarcity**, see **Mr. Dilherr's "Course of Time and the World"** <note>original German: *Zeit- und Weltlauff*</note> page 571 at the end, page 772 at the beginning, and page 763. There was no bread in all the world, Genesis 47, verse 13 <note>The OCR lists chapter 27, but this is a citation for the famine in Egypt found in Genesis 47:13</note>; this should be understood as referring to a specific part of the world, not the entire globe, according to Limnaeus in *Public Law*, volume 1, Addition to book 2, chapter 8.

On the grain supply, see Köppen, 2, observation 138. Regarding grain officials, what they are liable for, and whether they are responsible for grain removed by theft, see Vincent Hondedeus, 2, counsel 30. Grain should be bought up by the Prince when it is abundant, so that when it fails, he may provide for his subjects; see Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 81, number 6.

Hoarders of grain <term>original Latin: *Flagellatores annonæ*, literally "floggers of the grain market," referring to those who drive up prices by withholding supply</term> can cause the greatest poverty, as noted in the same work, book 2, chapter 82, number 1. They should be punished so that the Treasury and the community are protected, numbers 2 and 3.

If the Turks come across anyone who burdens goods with an unjust price, they lead him to the Praetor <note>a magistrate or judge</note>, who hangs a sounding board with clanging cymbals from his neck. The officers then lead him through the city streets—not without great infamy—while the common people gather from everywhere at the sound of the clanging cymbals. They especially lead him through the streets where the sellers of those same goods reside. After he is led home, they inflict 70 lashes upon him and command him to pay one aspro <note>a small silver coin</note> for each lash, as reported by Balthasar Conrad Zahn in his *Ichnographia*, chapter 4, number 15. The author of the *Turkish Chronicles*, published by the Frankfurt bookseller Wilhelm Sterlin, also mentions this punishment for usurers in part 4, under the title **On the Authority of the Subasci or City Judge**, folio 133. See also Johann Philippi, Jurist, in *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*, book 4, title 18, section 11, Eclogue 95, number 7.

### 17. Cathedral Canons. <term>Latin: *Canonici*; German: *Thumherren*</term>

Formerly, as witnessed by Gretser in *The Saints of Eichstätt*, book 1, chapter 17, folio 233, not a few bishops—especially those who came from Ireland and Britain to Germany—professed the monastic life before their episcopate. Even after being made bishops, they did not renounce this profession, establishing congregations and colleges which were called and indeed were Monasteries, and their members were Monks. In the history of the bishops themselves, the temple which we now call the Primary or Cathedral church, along with its attached dwellings, is several times called a **Monastery** <note>Latin: *Monasterium*</note>. It is certain that the German name **Münster**, which is applied to cathedral churches in many places, descends from *Monasterium*, because those first

<column-break/>

Canons (who are now called **Cathedral Canons**) professed a regular life <note>a life following a "rule," similar to monks</note>, having been taught by their first masters, many of whom, as said, were monks. St. Boniface himself founded a monastery in his Metropolitan See at Mainz and had none but monks as canons, who continued in this way of life for a long time. Thus also in 1071 it is called the Monastery of St. Martin by Marianus Scotus, and in the year 1081 the Episcopal Monastery; see Serarius, *Mainz*, book 1, chapter 18, and book 5 regarding Archbishop John II. See also Otto of Freising, book 5 of the *Chronicles*, chapter 24, where one may gather that the first canons of Freising had professed the monastic life.

### ADDITION.

Sacred houses are called temples and "Lord's houses" <note>Latin: *dominica*</note>, from which flowed the German word **Thum** or **Thumherr**.

See C. Rittershusius in the *New Constitutions*, page 109, number 9. *Dom* is the same as *dominicum*, which is why the ancients wrote: **Princedom, Christendom, Judaism, Cathedral Canon, Cathedral Church** <note>original German: *Fürstendom, Christendom, Judendom, Domherr, Domkirch*</note>. The residing and governing **Cathedral Canons** are held in such high esteem in many episcopal churches that, even as individuals, they **take precedence** <note>original German: *vorgehen*</note> over Abbots, Counts, and Barons who are not exempt, or who are not States or Councilors of the Roman Empire, at the proper time and place. Zacharias Beichtling, Doctor of Laws, in *Resolution of Canonical Observations*, page 67.

### 18. Cathedral Church, Cathedral Foundation, High Foundation, see above under the words Church and Episcopal Church.

A **Cathedral Church** <note>German: *Thumkirch*</note> is a Metropolitan Basilica or Episcopal Church, whence the Canons are called **Cathedral Canons** <note>German: *Thumherren*</note>. Some derive the name from *Dominicum* <note>The Lord's</note>, but in my judgment it is more correctly derived from *Domus* <note>House</note>. For the older and principal churches were the Houses of the Martyrs and Apostles; in the past, a church was almost never built without relics or some whole body of a martyr. Thus, formerly every church was so called, but later only the principal ones. Also, formerly **Duoma** was used for a judgment, as witnessed by Freher in *Saxon Symbols*, C.

It is called a Cathedral Church in which the Bishop himself resides with a College or Chapter, commonly called a **Cathedral Foundation**, **Cathedral Church**, or **High Foundation** <note>German: *Thumstifft*, *Thumkirch*, *Hohestifft*</note>, to distinguish it from a Collegiate Church <note>German: *Collegiat-Kirch* or *Stifft*</note> and a Parish Church <note>German: *Pfarrkirch*</note>. And from this it likewise descends that bishops are frequently mentioned by historians not as having "governed," but as having "sat" in the Chair <note>Latin: *Cathedra*</note> for so many years. Indeed, the Chair is the true mark of public profession and doctrine in the Church, just as Christ Himself says in Matthew 23, verse 3, that the Scribes and Pharisees sit in the Chair of Moses—that is, they publicly hand down and teach the Law of Moses. See also C. Laur. Ohm, *On Episcopal Law*, thesis 17, under letter r.

21. **Title.** <term>original Latin: *Titulus*</term>

Regarding the simplicity and luxury of Titles, see Mr. Dracon in *The Origin and Law of Patricians*, book 3, in the appendix to chapter 2; where he writes from the beginning: To the Nobles, as well as to the Patricians, it was once written as: **the Honorable and the Best.** <note>original German: *denen Erbarn und Besten*</note> Today, even men of the lower benches <note>meaning those of lower social or professional standing</note> are not content with the title of Noble. Hence it is said: when Virtue decreases, the arrogance of Titles increases.

Regarding the historical progression of Titles, Münster writes thus in book 3, chapter 21: **As soon as the Free-men <note>original German: *Freyen*</note> kept their first and old title (the Noble), the Counts immediately wanted a higher title, and to be called the Well-born. <note>original German: *Wolgebohrnen*</note> The Princes, who were above the Counts in rank, also wanted a higher title, and to be called the High-born. <note>original German: *Hochgebohrnen*</note> Only the Free-men have kept their title, the Noble—though today they walk with titles equal to Counts—which title every noble-squire <note>original German: *Edelknecht*</note> still wants to have in our times, etc.** The same author writes in the same book, chapter 20: **In former times, the title of "the Noble" was given only to Princes and great Lords, as the Pope still has the custom of writing only to Dukes: "to the Noble Duke of Saxony and Bavaria." Other nobility below the Princes had other names in former times: namely, Ever-Free and Middle-Free. The Ever-Free <note>original German: *Semper-Freyen*</note> were the highest free-men. The Middle-Free <note>original German: *Mittel-Freyen*</note> were those of knightly rank,**

<column-break/>

**whom people called Vassals <note>original German: *Dienstmänner*</note> and Noble-squires. Below the Free-men were the Free Citizens (free-born and Patrician citizens) and Free Landowners. The sons of Princes were called Noble Lords, their wives Ladies, and their daughters Maidens, whom people now call *Fräulein*.** <note>The term *Fräulein* was originally a high title for the daughters of the upper nobility, only later becoming a general term for unmarried women.</note>

Emperor Manuel, a contemporary of Frederick Barbarossa, is spoken of with such bombast in Albert of Stade’s work for the year 1179: "Manuel, in Christ God a faithful Emperor, Born-in-the-Purple <note>original Latin: *Porphyrogenitus*</note>, divinely crowned, Ruler, Powerful, Exalted and ever August, and Magnificent Moderator of the Romans." This same old song is repeated by Krantz in *Saxonia*, book 6, chapter 37, and *Metropolis*, book 7, chapter 5. However, much more empty and ridiculous is another clamor from the same Manuel, reported by Camerarius in the *Nicephorian Chronology*, in this manner: "Manuel, faithful King in Christ, born in the purple, Emperor of the Romans, most excellent in piety, ever venerable, August: Isauricus, Cilicicus, Armeniacus, Dalmaticus, Ungricus, Bohemicus, Crabaticus, Lazicus, Ibericus, Bulgaricus, Servicus, Zecchicus, Chazaricus, Gothicus <note>These titles claim dominion over various regions including Croatia, Hungary, Bohemia, and many regions in the East and Balkans</note>: who is the governor from God, Heir to the Crown of Constantine the Great, and in his soul cherishing all his Laws." Other similar pompous Titles are found in Pontanus’s *Bellaria*, volume 3, from the beginning.

On the other hand, Mr. Meibom, in his notes on the *Bulla of Andronicus*, page 9, says: "The highest Princes, both Ecclesiastical and Political, did not turn away even from the lowest Titles." He adds examples. In a letter from Conrad of Dorfstad, a Noble Dynast or Saxon Baron, for the year 1357, these words appear: *with the connivance of the honorable man, Lord William, King of the Romans.* A letter from Magnus "the Torquatus," Duke of Brunswick, is closed in this way: **Hereby has also been present the Honorable Prince, Bishop Albert of Halberstadt. In the year 1370.** Werner and Otto, Noble Dynasts in Egeln, addressed Otto, Duke of Brunswick, thus: **Werner and Otto the Nobles of Hademersleben, and Lords at Egeln, to both the Respected Prince, our Lord Duke Otto of Brunswick, our ready and willing service, etc.** The letters were given in the Year of Christ 1341. The same Otto, or another of the same name, begins a certain Instrument of Donation this way: "By the grace of God, we Otto, Noble-Youth <term>original Latin: *Domicellus*, a title for a young nobleman not yet knighted</term> of Brunswick and Lüneburg." The year assigned is 1329.

So in the year 1401, **Duke Leopold of Austria is still called by a Knight in an old letter: the High-Well-born Prince and Lord.**

But how greatly does the modesty of that simple age differ from the insolent pride of our own wanton time?

The custom of adding the names and titles of Counties or families was almost non-existent; it was also rare before the time of Henry IV, after which it became common, according to William of Habsburg, book 3, chapter 7, page 70; see also the *Researches* of Pasquier.

The title of "Excellency," which was formerly granted only to the Emperor, began to be displeasing to those of lower rank when it was withheld from them, according to Limnaeus in *Public Law*, volume 2, Additions to book 4, chapter 6, page 246. Draco, in book 2 of *On the Law of the Patricians*, calls **Titles the miscarriages of ambition**.

->22. Publication of Title.<-

He who possesses someone else's property, or a right in someone else's property, is bound to "publish his title" <note>This means to legally produce the document or proof of ownership</note>, as handed down by Fulvius Pacianus in *On Probations*, book 1, chapter 61, numbers 26 and 32; Rosenthal in *On Fiefs*, chapter 8, conclusion 33, number 8; in the additions at number 12 regarding the penalty for one who denies it. But he who possesses property under a "buy-back agreement" <term>original Latin: "pacto de retrovendendo"</term> is not bound to publish his title. Likewise, ancient possession relieves one from the burden of proving the title, according to the *Marburg Legal Opinions*, 9, number 29, etc., volume 1.

->23. Deathbed.<-

See Polydore Ripa in the singular treatise *On Actions Performed at the Moment of Death*; add the Legal Opinion of Zuntus for the wife; see also **Dying**. <note>original German: "Sterbende"</note>

->24. Gravediggers. Corpse-Carriers.<-

"Vespae," "vespillones," and "funerarii" are called "Nekrophoroi" <term>Greek: Νεκροφόροι, literally "corpse-bearers"</term> by the Greeks, "Fossoyeurs" <note>French for "gravediggers"</note> or rather "those who carry bodies into the earth" by the French, and **Corpse-Carriers** <note>original German: "Todtenträger"</note> by the Germans. In well-ordered Republics, the Magistrates require these men to walk about in a peculiar kind of clothing, or with a sign or bands of variegated colors—red, white, etc.—

<column-break/>

so that healthy people may avoid them and not be infected by contagion. These are different from those who actually bury the dead: the **Gravediggers** <note>original German: "Todtengräber"</note>. In some places there are also **Soul-Wardens** <note>original German: "Seelwarter"</note>, who speak to the dying. Likewise, there are the **Beguines** or **Soul-Nuns** <note>original German: "Seel-Nonnen", religious women who cared for the sick and the dead</note>.

If these people kill those infected with the plague after committed robbery or theft, they are beheaded, according to the *Saxon Constitutions*, volume 2, part 4, question 69, number 1; and the *Constitutions of Augustus*, part 4. For it often happens that those whom the malignancy of the plague did not consume and whom the kindness of Jehovah wished to save, are killed by the malignancy of men, who violently rush upon the sick and hasten their lives to a premature and untimely death, or extinguish them with malignant and harmful medicines or other types of poisonous drugs. See Wilhelm Böckel in *Disquisitions on Visions*, 6, number 10.

->ADDITION.<-

In Law 31 of the Digest, "On Evictions," Budaeus reads the word as "Vespertilio" <term>bat</term>, others as "Vespillo," others "Vispillo," others "Bispillo." Properly speaking, among the Ancients, the **Vespillones** were those who used to carry out and bury people of meager fortune or those hated by the public during the evening time <term>original Latin: "vespertino tempore", from which the name is derived</term>. See Suetonius in *The Life of Emperor Domitian*, chapter 17; Eutropius, book 7. Our Dilherrus says: "I would say most simply, though relying on no one else's authority, that the very foulness of this office is enough reason why no one would easily allow these vile and abject men, contaminated by such filthy duties, to be thrust upon them in place of those accustomed to more honest service; and for that reason, a buyer should receive a guarantee from the seller." He adds that he could defend himself by the example of those slaves who were sent into the arena to fight with beasts, whom the Overseers <term>Aediles</term> expressly included in their edict, so that the buyer would make that known to the seller. It is well known that this class of "corpse-bearers" <term>Greek: νεκροφόρων</term> was considered shameful, as indicated in Law 7 of the *Trebellian Decree* and Law 72 "On Payments," where the Jurist says: "If he has given a corpse-bearer or otherwise shameful man as payment." Cujacius thinks otherwise; commenting on Law 50 "On Agreements," he explains *Vespillo*—following Fulgentius—as a stripper or looter of corpses, and refers to Law 3, section 7 "On the Violation of Tombs," which deals with punishing these "harpyies." See Turnebus, *Adversaria* 14, chapter 3. In the Dominican cemetery at Basel, among other things worth seeing, an elegant painting is displayed, commonly called the **Dance of the Dead** <term>original Latin: "chorea mortuorum"</term>. It represents in a long series the fragile fate of the entire human race struggling with death; by this Law, she summons persons of every sex, age, and condition, leading away the willing and dragging the unwilling under the shadows, **making scepters equal to hoes**. <note>A famous artistic theme emphasizing that death comes for both kings and peasants</note>

In Strasbourg, Roman monuments are found in several graves, for they show hollowed stones there in which something of ash and human bone is covered with a stone; yes, also ash...

## 25. Redeeming the Life-Debt. <term>Monetary penalty for a killer</term> <note>original: "Todten-Hals lösen" / "Poena homicidæ pecuniaria"</note>

Among certain Northern peoples, namely the Danes, Poles, Swedes, Frisians, Holsteins, etc., it has been accepted for many years that killers, without distinction, are punished only with a monetary fine; this they call <term>redeeming a life-debt</term> <note>original German: "einen Todten-Hals lösen"; This refers to the historical legal practice of 'Wergild', where a murderer could pay a set fee to the victim's family to avoid further retribution.</note>. See Bodin, *On the Republic*, book 6, chapter 6; Ludovicus Romanus, *Singularia* 709; Covarruvias, book 2, *Resolutions*, chapter 9, number 2; Heig, part 2, question 24, number 43; see also Mr. Wilhelm Anton in the *Corollaries to the Treatise on Five-Year Periods*, page 33.

However, Valentin Winther rightly disapproves of this custom in his *Parthenia Litigiosa*, book 1, chapter 13. Since God himself commands that the murderer should expect to suffer the same fate he inflicted, Stephen, King of Poland, and the modern King of Denmark have often judged against this custom.

### ADDITION.

Statutes that punish willful homicide only with money are of no worth nor are they valid. See this at length in Pappus's *Dutch Military Law*, page 25, and the sources cited there. Regarding the <term>redemption of a life-debt</term>, see Carpzov, *On the Royal Law*, chapter 9, section 11, number 33; Schwarz, *On the Right of Pardoning*, thesis 10, letter C, pages 64 and 65.

## 26. Mortal Wounds. <term>Lethal wound</term> <note>original: "Tödtliche Wunden" / "Vulnus lethale"</note>

Regarding mortal wounds, see the specific treatise *On the Inspection of Wounds* by Bernhard Suevus. It should be noted here that in former times, if the wounded person did not die, the law looked at the intent rather than the fact that death did not follow; unless the injured person was someone of great name, or another crime coincided with the act.

### ADDITION.

How one should recognize a mortal wound. See this at length in Pappus's *Dutch Military Law*, page 21. A wounded person who dies 40 days after receiving a wound is held to have died not from the wound, but from another occurrence. See the same, page 21. Regarding the five wounds of the Savior, see Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 9, chapter 9, number 202. A formal protestation about the inflicting of a wound does not free one from the penalty for a committed homicide. See *The Forum of Protestations*, page 245, number 47 and following. If a master orders someone to be wounded but expressly forbids the agent to kill, then if the agent kills nonetheless, the master is not held to the ordinary penalty, because he himself did not have the intent to kill. See Mr. Dr. Ludovicus, *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 386. By an earthquake, a broken portion of a mountain laid low the army of the Gauls who were attempting to plunder the Delphic temple, and the most crowded ranks were scattered, turning red from

<column-break/>

the wounds of the enemy. A storm followed, which consumed those who were exhausted from their wounds with hail and lightning. The leader Brennus <note>Brennus (died 279 BC) was a chieftain of the Gauls who invaded Greece.</note> himself, when he could no longer bear the pain of his wounds, ended his life with a dagger. See Georg Rittershusius, *On Asylums*, chapter 10, number 8. Regarding the many types of individual wounds, see Schneidewin, page 615.

Wounds in which parts of the body are lethal. See Boër, *Decisions* 323, number 3. The difference between an ulcer and a wound, number 2.

A master appears to be lethally wounded if he dies within a few days, say three or even eight days, after receiving the wound. See Boër, question 323. Otherwise, one is said to be lethally wounded who has received a large and deep wound, or who is tormented by continuous pain, such as when one is struck in the nerves, from which spasms and death itself easily arise. See Baldus, *Counsels* 328, book 2; Crusius in *Feudal Lectures*, chapter 8, page 58, letters B and C. In the case of two people inflicting a mortal wound, what penalty should be applied to the first person in a situation where it is not clear from which wound the deceased perished? See Hartmann Pistor, *Observations* 27; see also Millæus in *Criminal Practice*, folio 9, number 18.

## 27. Occurrence of Death. <term>The event of death</term> <note>original German: "Todsfall" / Latin: "Mortis eventus"</note>

The word <term>occurrence of death</term> is not simply the same as "after death," but signifies something more, namely, the actual event of death; as such, it suspends a whole promise upon the uncertain outcome of death, which is characteristic of a gift made in anticipation of death. See Hartmann Pistor, book 3, question 8, number 52.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the <term>death toll</term> <note>original: "Todtenzoll"; a tax or fee paid upon a person's death.</note>. See Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, chapter 3, number 196. What constitutes a "grievous" payment. See Klock, volume 1, counsel 29, number 862. The payment of a death tax is most hateful, and is presumed to be usurped through fear or tyranny. See the same, numbers 880 and 915.

*Mr. Klee, the pastor in Ruprechtsau near Strasbourg, wrote his own funeral sermon and had it printed.*

One who is established in the moment of death <note>original Latin: "in articulo mortis"</note> is similar to one already dead. A woman ought not to offer her dowry to her husband while he is established in the moment of death. See Zorer, part 2, question 7, number 602; Bartolus in the *Treatise on Witnesses, or on Proving Death*; Richter, decision 66, number 15, on the phrase "because in such occurrences of death." See Menochius, 6, presumption 49; Hartmann Pistor, observation 103. These words, "until death," or "until his will," when joined together, mean the same thing. See Boër, counsel 13, number 18; Sichard on the Code, title *On the services of freedmen*, law *If at the time*, number 25, where it is explained in a different meaning than here. Seneca, in the book *On Tranquility of Mind*, chapter 11, says: "The wise man counts himself among his own borrowed goods, and lives as if he were lent to himself, ready to return himself to those who reclaim him without sadness." And the same in the book *Of Consolation to Marcia*, chapter 11, says that man is "of a borrowed spirit" <note>original: "spiritus precarii"</note>.

## 28. Homicide. <term>Homicidium</term> <note>The act of one human killing another; the text distinguishes between intentional murder and accidental or negligent killing.</note>

For homicides, see Farinacius, Tiberius Decianus, Bocer, and many others; and on the severity of intentional homicide, Hering wrote a specific treatise.

He who provides the cause of death through playfulness (for instance, through a joke, **or when several of them are jesting with one another**) is punished not with the ordinary penalty <note>The "ordinary penalty" for murder was typically death.</note>, but only with temporary exile. *Digest*, book 48, title 8, law 4, section 1.

**Especially when the deceased person himself provoked the defendant, neither he nor his relatives can now demand anything because of this fault,** <note>original German: "Sonderlich, wann der Entleibte den Beklagten selbst angemuthet, kan weder er, noch die Seinige propter hanc culpam anjezo etwas fordern"</note> Moller on the Saxon Constitutions, part 4, constitution 10, number 10. See Speckhan, century 3, question 6, class 2, number 5, where he says from the Elector's Constitution 10 that if the one provoked does not kill but only mutilates or wounds the provoker, he owes nothing on this account; since the text there expressly says **that he shall be obliged to give some compensation.** <note>original German: "daß er einigen Abtrag zu geben schuldig seyn solle."</note> For both are at fault, and indeed the provoker is in greater fault; thus, one fault is rightly balanced against the other. Schrader, part 9, chapter 4, number 47 near the end. Berlich, final volume, conclusion 16, number 2; and see also *Digest*, book 11, title 5, law 2, section 1.

If aggression is proven, there is never a place for the ordinary penalty, according to the teachings of Thomas Metzger, criminal consultation 3. See my own work in the *Disputation on Homicide*, folio 28. And Schneidewein teaches that the aggressor has the intent to strike back, in his notes on the *Institutes*, book 1, title 2, number 15.

In case of doubt, however, he is presumed to be the aggressor who throws the other to the ground and holds him down, as Farinacius proves in question 125, number 446. Likewise, he is presumed to be the aggressor who is found with more companions than the other, Bertazolus, consultation 1, book 1, number 10; Farinacius, the same question 125, number 469; because it is not likely that one person would attack two or three, but rather the opposite. Menochius, *On Judicial Arbitrariness*, book 2, case 363, number 10. Mascardus, *On Evidence*, conclusion 72, number 4, and conclusion 1244, number 7. And he is also presumed to be the aggressor who went about armed, or was more heavily armed, and was carrying weapons more suited

<column-break/>

to killing, as the same Farinacius teaches in the same place, number 449 and following.

But on the subject of aggression and excess, one may also look at José Sesse, decision 104, and Kremberg in his treatise on *Necessary Defense*.

Homicide committed in a brawl <term>rixa</term> <note>A sudden, unplanned fight or scuffle.</note> more by chance than by will, diminishes the penalty. *Digest*, title "On Assassins" [ad L. Cornel. de Sicar.], law 1, section "The Divine." Even if someone kills another in the heat of a brawl without thinking, that homicide is said to be negligent, or rather to happen more by chance than by will. Peguera, decision 14; Hondedei, consultation 99, number 45; Farinacius, question 126, number 48. **If then a case [of accident] is to be presumed when a homicide occurred in a brawl: then this must hold all the more when two people are joking with weapons alone, and clearly no rancor, quarrel, or ill-will is involved.** <note>original German: "Wann nun ein Casus alsdann zu præsumiren, ubi in rixa homicidium factum fuit: also muß solches vielmehr statt haben, da ihrer zween allein, mit Wehren gegeneinander schertzen, und kündlich kein Rancor, Zanck oder Widerwillen enthalten ist."</note> For in other cases, homicide against the person of a friend is considered accidental, Jason on the law *lex*, number 22, *De Legibus I*. Likewise, the intent to kill is excluded by words spoken before and after the deed, as Bursatus says in consultation 271, number 12 and following, and Mandellus, consultation 46, number 9 near the end and following, where he proposes an example almost identical in detail regarding one who had asked his companions not to offend anyone or start a brawl. And similarly, the intent to kill is not to be presumed in one who, after the blow is struck, shows some probable signs that he regrets having killed him, according to Cepolla, consultation 31, number 5 and following. And Farinacius says he has very often seen such signs observed by judges, question 126, final number.

Likewise, innocence is proved by a single witness, and any half-full proof is held to be sufficient. Gabriel, title "On Witnesses," conclusion 1, number 37; Mascardus, conclusion 491, number 17, and conclusion 904, number 10.

And also Farinacius, *On Homicide*, question 126, title 14, number 30: in such a homicide where friends or soldiers joke with swords, or where one of two wrestlers dies wounded by his companion's knife, he calls it negligent if some fault preceded it (namely, if the play was either illegal or in an unusual place); but nevertheless, he teaches that no greater penalty can be imposed than temporary banishment, and he brings forward many others to this opinion. See also Menochius, book 2, case 400. And Farinacius, in the same place, number 33, speaks of the case where one kills another while fighting together jokingly with swords, even unsheathed ones, where he calls that homicide negligent and to be punished extraordinarily; however, he cites Marcilius, consultation 91, throughout, who laboriously teaches that no penalty has a place here.

And the penalty due to the **authorities** <note>original: "Obrigkeit"</note> is **to be moderated** according to the quality of the deed and the persons; namely, that it should be either a fine of fifty gold coins or temporary exile. Farinacius, the same question 126, title 14, number 44 and following.

On accidental homicide, see the consultations of Habenfenbec, volume 2, consultation 156, from which many things pertain...

### 29. Carrier. <term>Portitor</term> <note>In feudal and administrative law, a "carrier" or "representative" who acts or holds a fief on behalf of others.</note>

A carrier cannot be sued for the whole amount <note>original Latin: "in solidum"</note>, because he is only an administrator, so that he may bring in the debts as well as possible; and if he cannot, individuals must be sued separately.

### ADDITION.

One carrier in the name of everyone, *Gothofredus Antonius, Feudal Disputations, page 116, letter f, page 144. B. in one word: Carrier [Portitor], see Rittershusius, Feudal Part, page 124.*

### 30. Transfix. <term>Transfix</term> <note>A legal document or clause physically attached to an original deed, often by piercing it or using the same seal.</note>

Sometimes, another writing is usually appended and "transfixed" to an authentic instrument; its articles, which perhaps should have been inserted or excepted but were omitted, are added to the original itself, which from then on is called a "Transfix," which one is accustomed to hang onto contracts, but under the same seal, *Bornitius on instruments, book 1, final chapter.*

### ADDITION.

Wehner under the letter T, this word. Transfix or Signature regarding the Style of the Chamber, see *Höpingk on the Right of Seals, chapter 1, section 50 and sections 52. Satler in Formulas, folio 209 and following.*

### 31. Eaves-drip Rights. <note>original Latin: *Stillicidium*; German: *Trauffrecht*</note>

The urban servitude <note>A legal obligation or "easement" attached to a city property.</note> of eaves-drip is twofold: one is affirmative, namely the right of diverting the eaves-drip—specifically, that you may divert and have my eaves-drip received onto your ground or your buildings. The other is negative, namely the right of *not* diverting the eaves-drip. Therefore, the affirmative servitude of diverting the eaves-drip is said to exist when someone has the right to divert or channel rainwater from their roof onto the area or roof of a neighbor, <note>original German: "daß die Trauff, auf deß Nachbauern Dach oder Hof falle"</note> so that the eaves-drip falls onto the neighbor’s roof or courtyard. It should be known that no one can divert the eaves-drip from their roof and direct it onto the roof of a neighbor's house or area if such a servitude has not been established. For every house and area is presumed to be free of such burdens. This is expressly provided for in Saxon Law: <note>original German: "daß niemand mag seinen Trauff hangen in eines andern Manns Hof"</note> that no one may hang their eaves into another man’s yard.

The negative servitude of *not* diverting the eaves-drip occurs when the person whose eaves-drip falls onto my area—for instance, if I have a cistern to be filled for which my own house's eaves-drip is insufficient, or if I have a garden adjacent to my buildings which can be conveniently irrigated by my neighbor’s eaves-drip—acts to ensure the neighbor does not divert that drip elsewhere, but brings it nowhere else than into my buildings or garden. This is called the servitude of "not diverting the eaves-drip," in which the "dominant" estate <note>The property that benefits from the legal right.</note> is the one that receives the water; therefore, the repair of the gutters also pertains to that person (see Schneidewin on the section regarding estates, number 7 and following, in the *Institutes on Urban Estates*).

### ADDITION.

See Donellus, *Commentaries* 11, chapter 5; Bocer, class 4, dispute 7, thesis 51; Mynsinger on the *Institutes on Servitudes*, section 1; Duarenus in the commentary on the title of the *Digest* regarding Urban Estates, in the preface; Caepolla on *Servitudes*, chapter 29; Theophilus, Cujas, Wesenbeck; and Lord Doctor Ludwig's *Disputation on the Institutes*, page 88, letters c and d, and page 89, letter e. Under Saxon Law, it is also not permitted to divert eaves-drip into a neighbor’s area without the establishment of a servitude. *Landrecht*, book 2, article 49, at the beginning, states: "That no one may hang his eaves into another man’s yard," and likewise in the *Weichbild* <note>The municipal law code for Saxon cities.</note>, article 124.

### 32. Dreams. <note>original Latin: *Somnia*; German: *Träum*</note>

Regarding the opinions of the philosophers on divination through dreams, Jakob Martini treats this in *Illustrious Philosophical Questions*, century 9, dispute 7, question 3, and the following question. He discusses how Solomon's request made to God in dreams could have pleased God so much that he obtained a singular gift of wisdom from Him (3 Kings 3 <note>Modern Bibles refer to this as 1 Kings 3.</note>), even though dreamers do not have the free use of their reason. The same author teaches to what extent the omens of dreams are to be listened to in the same work, century 8, dispute 8, question 5. But Pererius deals extensively with dreams in book 2 of *On Magic*.

### ADDITION.

Aristotle writes in chapter 17 of *History of Animals* that people are found who never have

<column-break/>

any dreams. Lord Otto von [Min?] knew of no dreams for the entire duration of his life (Zeiller, *Letters*, page 604). Regarding what is to be held concerning dreams, see Zeiller, century 4, question 73, page 378 and following, regarding natural dreams. The same author, page 382 and following. Caspar Peucer wrote a treatise on divination from dreams. On how dreams are to be interpreted, see Junianus Majus, the Italian. The rituals of reporting dreams pertaining to the State. How much the Brazilians <note>Refers to the indigenous peoples of Brazil.</note> attribute to dreams (Claude Barthélemy Morisot, *Discussions*, book 1, chapter 8, on Valerius Maximus). 

A triple kind of dreams is offered: Natural, Divine, and Diabolical. Regarding these, the renowned Virdungus once wrote that natural dreams only offer some non-vain and non-deceptive appearance when the soul of man is not "drunk" with various cares, nor heavy with food and drink, nor fouled by the filth of lusts, but is pure, clear, and purified—as if withdrawn from the storm of the body into a certain sanctuary or rather a harbor, becoming entirely its own. He confirmed this opinion of his from Galen and Xenophon. 

Regarding divine and diabolical dreams, since he saw it was doubted whether the dreams that were seen by ancient heroes and Kings outside the Church—which predicted great and illustrious events—were all "struck from the same coin" (that is, none of them from a divine source, but all alike predicting the future by the breath of demons), he settled the whole controversy with this boundary: those dreams which commanded some crime, superstition, or something impious, he denied were sent by the "Father of Lights," <note>A biblical title for God (James 1:17).</note> but rather said they were belched forth from the dark and horrific jaws of hell. He collected many examples of dreams (Claude Morisot, discussion 1, on chapters 6, 7, and 8 of Valerius Maximus).

Regarding the dreams of those who are awake <note>likely referring to daydreams or visions</note>: Lord Harsdörffer, in the *Great Theater of Delightful and Instructive History*, title 114, numbers 11 and 12. Regarding a certain dream, title 95, throughout. "The dream is like the almond tree, which blossoms in the night" (Lord Harsdörffer, in the *Poetic Funnel*, part 3, page 453).

### 33. Beam Rights. <note>original German: *Tramrecht*; Latin: *Jus immittendi tigni*</note>

The right of inserting a beam <note>A joist or structural timber.</note> into the wall of a neighbor, commonly called *Tramrecht*, is an urban servitude (see Schneidewin on the section regarding estates, number 5 and following, in the *Institutes on Urban Estates*).

### ADDITION.

That it is permitted to insert a beam or joist into another’s wall (Law 20 of the *Digest* on Urban Estates). And he who owes this servitude is only bound to support the neighbor’s beam, but is not also bound to repair the wall (Law 8, section 2 of the *Digest* on claiming servitudes; according to Lord Doctor Ludwig).

It specifically examines the weight of a nobleman's or a prince's word of honor in legal contracts compared to a formal oath.</meta>
