<header>Letter T.</header>

**Honors and Faith**, are held as binding for debts, deeds, and completions. <note>Cited from Chassanaeus in *Catalogus Gloriae Mundi*, part 8, counsel 34; Decianus, response 82, number 32, volume 4.</note> And what Homer writes in the *Iliad*, book 18, speaking of Agamemnon, supports this:

> Soon, as the word is spoken, the thing itself is completed.
<note>original Latin: "Mox simul ac dictum verbum est, res ipsa per- acta est."</note>

And it is practiced daily that wherever a Prince, Count, or one of the Nobility promises something, or signs a document, **by his Princely, Countly, or Noble Honor, Loyalty, and Faith**, everything and anything incorporated into that writing must be held firmly, inviolably, and well. He is duty-bound by law to follow and live by it, just as if he had sworn it with a physical oath <note>A "physical oath" (German: *leiblicher Eid*) was a formal oath taken while touching a sacred object or raising the hand, carrying heavy spiritual and legal penalties for perjury.</note>, under the penalty of perjury. See on this question both sides in Sester, *On Oaths*, book 1, chapter 16; add Baptista Caesar in *Illustrious Counsels of the Doctors of Law*, counsel 34, number 14, and the following counsel, number 13, etc.

However, just as excessive familiarity among people and the abuse of things breeds contempt, <note>A reference to the legal maxim *familiaritas contemptum parit*.</note> so too it happens that Nobles, for whom it is common to swear by their "lineage faith" <note>original Latin: "fidem gentilitiam"</note>—those for whom such words are more often in their mouths than their dear daily bread, as Nolden speaks in *On the Nobility*, chapter 12, number 43—render themselves suspect. They are no different from those who offer themselves to give testimony without being asked. <note>Citing various Roman law digests on procurators and witnesses.</note>

If a Nobleman binds himself in a guarantee within a main contract <note>original German: "in einer Hauptverschreibung"</note> through words equivalent to an oath, such as **by Noble, Countly Honor, Loyalty, and Faith**, should mandates without a specific clause be decreed in the Imperial Chamber? <note>The *Reichskammergericht* or Imperial Chamber Court was the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> See Nolden in the cited place, number 43 and following.

Whether Nobles, Barons, Counts, etc., who have acted as guarantors <term>fidejussores</term> <note>A person who legally guarantees the debt of another.</note> for others and have renounced the benefit of cession <note>The "benefit of cession" allowed a guarantor to avoid payment until the primary debtor was sued; renouncing this meant they could be sued directly.</note> **by Noble, Lordly, and Countly Honor**, should be granted relief? See Nolden, chapter 12, number 50 and following.

Whether a Nobleman who violates a settlement promised "by faith" (**by Noble Faith**) falls under a legal penalty? <note>Citing Code of Justinian on transactions.</note> See Nolden, *On the Nobility*, chapter 12, number 62 and following.

Whether a daughter renouncing her inheritance rights <note>A common practice where noble daughters were given a dowry in exchange for giving up further claims to the family estate.</note> under a promise of her high birth and nobility can, despite that renunciation, still succeed to her father's goods? See Nolden, *On the Status of Nobles*, chapter 12, number 68 and following.

Likewise, whether a noblewoman intervening for her husband and renouncing her legal rights **by her Lady-like Honor and true words**, does so validly? See Scheffer, part 1, *Practical Questions*, question 36.

Concerning a promise or assertion **by one’s Priestly or Clerical Loyalty and Honor**. See Lehmann in *Moral Theology*, part 4, folio 163.

<meta>Besoldus Volume I.</meta>

<column-break/>

Since it is fitting for upright and honest men, especially Nobles, to keep their faith—whereby their promises are regarded as equal to a physical oath—this applies much more forcefully to Princes and other Magnates. See especially Hartmann Pistor, book 4, question 6, throughout. For King Alphonso was accustomed to say: *The word of Princes ought to be worth as much for the sake of faith as the oath of private men.* So too Charles V, when asked by Louis, Elector Palatine of the Rhine, why he kept his word to Luther, <note>Refers to the "safe conduct" granted to Martin Luther at the Diet of Worms in 1521, which Charles V honored despite pressure to treat him as a heretic.</note> replied: "Even if the faith of promised things were exiled from the whole world, it must still reside with the Emperor." <note>Citing Tholosan on the Republic and Reinking on secular government.</note> The words of Princes and Emperors ought to be held as an Oath. <note>Citing Krantz, book 6, *Saxonia*, chapter 46.</note> On this matter, Frederick I Barbarossa writes as follows in Günther’s *Ligurinus*, book 3:

> You ask for oaths? I think it base for a King to swear
> To a lesser man: Law and reverence are accustomed to dwell
> In the bare word of a King, greater than any oath.
> It is not fitting for slippery things to move upon the lips of a King;
> It does not befit a King to forge lies with a sacred mouth.
> Royal words are holy and full of their own weight;
> Once spoken, they allow no legal retreat.

And there is nothing that shines more brightly in a Prince and similar persons than a firm and unblemished faith. Baldus says it most greatly befits a Prince to say: *What I have written, I have written* <note>The words of Pontius Pilate regarding the inscription on the Cross.</note>, and *God has spoken once, and those things which have proceeded from my lips I shall not make void.* A Prince ought to be as immovable as the pole star in the sky and the cornerstone in the earth, and he ought to have one pen and one tongue. <note>Citing various legal authorities such as Socinus and Hippolytus de Marsiliis.</note>

Therefore, those guarantors are to be despised—as Master Bullæus says in that place, along with their terrible Advocates and Patrons—who, as soon as they are summoned regarding their obligations, do not imitate the example in Tobias chapter 5, verse 3, but instead break their faith and promises. They interpret their obligations craftily and maliciously; indeed, they dare to boast that no obligation should be so firm that they cannot call it into doubt. <note>Citing Hering on guarantors and Winther on litigation.</note>

Let many of the Germans be ashamed, therefore, of their fluid faith, because they have so drifted from the custom of their ancestors...

Tacitus was a Roman historian who often praised the "noble" simplicity and honesty of Germanic tribes to shame the corruption of Rome.</note> From this comes that common saying: **In the good, old German way.** <note>original: "Auf gut alt Teutsch."</note>

In ancient times, obligations were very brief; today they are very long, and are extended to the length of a whole ox’s hide: **Small handwriting, great faith: now great handwriting, small faith.** <note>original: "Kleine Handschrifft, grosser Glaub : itzo grosse Handschrifften, kleiner Glaub." ### 35. Faithfully and without Deceit. <note>original: "Treulich und ohne Gefehrd. Bona fide & absque dolo."</note>

This clause, **faithfully and without deceit**, is nothing other than a clause stating that "evil intent" <term>dolus malus (evil deceit or fraud in legal contracts)</term> is absent and shall be absent. <note>Citing various laws from the Digest of Justinian regarding stipulations and judgments.</note> See Hering, *On Suretyship*, chapter 17, number 17, etc.

Thus, if deceit is committed, this clause ensures that the promisor is held liable to the one taking precautions for the amount of their interest <note>original: "id, quod interest," referring to the actual financial loss or damages.</note> according to the laws on verbal obligations. Wesenbeck <note>A famous 16th-century jurist.</note> teaches somewhat more boldly that by the power of this clause, a certain metamorphosis of contracts is induced, so that from a contract of **strict law**, it becomes a contract of **good faith**. <note>In Roman law, a "Strict Law" contract (stricti juris) followed the literal letter of the agreement, while a "Good Faith" contract (bonae fidei) allowed a judge to consider what was fair and equitable.</note> In such a case, the performance of deceit and good faith seem to be made equal. But in this, he is refuted by Johann Goeddaeus. For according to Andreas Scheffer, it would have been necessary for this "metamorphosis"—which is certainly unknown to the whole of Jurisprudence—to have been introduced long ago. Yet a stipulation that "evil deceit is and shall be absent," when added to a loan or another contract of strict law, is nowhere read to alter the principal legal standing or to imbue a strict law contract with the condition of good faith. But see the whole of Scheffer’s question for the understanding of this clause; add also Lord Wilhelm Anton and Barschamp in their treatises on clauses.

## ADDITION.

**In good true faith.** <note>original: "In guten wahren Treuen."</note> Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7. Regarding the clause: **faithfully and without deceit**, and what it imports, see Berlichius and Alemannus regarding

<column-break/>

the *Law of Money*, page 688; Conrad Rittershusius on feudal law, and Webbe under that word.

### 36. Tribute. <note>original: "Tribut. Tributum."</note>

Concerning tributary provinces, I deal with this in my *Treatise on Subaltern Jurisdictions*, page 68.

So also Chios paid tribute to the Turk, paying 12,000 Ducats annually so that it could preserve its liberty, yet the inhabitants were not permitted to fortify the city. And truly, where there is no Beylerbey <note>A high-ranking Ottoman provincial governor.</note>, there tributary provinces exist, according to Soranzi. However, the condition of subjects is one thing, and that of Tribute-payers is another; Christians outside of the tributary provinces are treated more harshly among the Turks, whom they despoil of arms. Nor do they permit them to enter fortified cities. Tarduccius records the conditions that Murad <note>Ottoman Sultan Amurath/Murad.</note> imposed on defeated Princes.

And such tributary provinces, if they should rebel, can be sought again by war and reduced into slavery, in the same way the Jews were subverted by the Babylonians.

By pretext of this same law, the Venetians lost Cyprus, as Johann Sturm reports at the end of his work *On Administering War Against the Turks*. He writes: When Selim I, Emperor of the Turks, having oppressed the Sultans, occupied Egypt, he converted the Tribute—which the Kings of Cyprus were previously accustomed to pay to the Sultans in merchandise—into eight thousand Ducats. He granted the tranquil possession of Cyprus to the Venetians, as if they were **Vassals** bound by a pact of annual Tribute. Even so, the Venetians did not want those eight thousand to be called "Tribute," but merely a "gift of honor." <note>The Venetians tried to frame the payment as a diplomatic courtesy rather than an admission of being subjects to the Sultan.</note>

But this Selim, reclaiming Cyprus from the Venetians through a special demand, asserted that they had lost their right to the fief of the Kingdom of Cyprus (which they had possessed until then under the pact of annual tribute), and that it had fallen back to the Patron and Superior Lord. He claimed that, contrary to the faith owed to the Lord of the fief, the Venetians had opened Cyprus to the enemies of Selim, the Spanish pirates, and had permitted them to bring and sell plunder taken from Cilicia into Cyprus with the permission of the Venetian Magistrate. Therefore, although some previous Turkish Emperors had tolerated the Venetians on their island, Selim was reclaiming what was his. If they returned it spontaneously and willingly, peace would not be violated, and the safety of the Republic and its subjects would be well consulted. If they refused, Selim would nonetheless recover it by arms. The Venetians, although they were heavily afflicted and struck by several continuous years of high prices, scarcity of food, and even the horrific fire of their Naval Arsenal the previous year, nevertheless responded with a great and lofty spirit that Selim had no just cause...

### 38. Comfort, Comforter. Protection, Protector. <note>original: "Trost, Tröster. Trustis, Protector."</note>

Advocacy (which today is commonly and properly called "Protection and Shield," <note>original: "Schutz und Schirm, Schutz- und Schirms- Gerechtigkeit."</note>) was formerly called by the Germans *Trost* or *Trustis*, that is, faithful advocacy or guardianship. Lord Martin Mager in his most elegant treatise *On Armed Advocacy*, chapter 2, number 241. Consequently, it is fitting that the Protectors themselves be called "Comforters" <note>original: "Tröster." In this archaic legal context, "Trost" refers to the security or "comfort" provided by a legal protector.</note> from this word; they were also called *Pfleger* [Caretakers], as noted by Stumpff in the *Swiss Chronicle*, book 17, chapter 3, and *Schaffner* [Stewards] in book 5, chapter 3, and in ancient centuries they were called *Besorger* [Providers]. Mager, in the cited place, number 242. The Saxons also use *Trost* for a Governor. For what "Comforts" <note>original: "Tröstungen."</note> are, see Fritsch, *On Fairs*, chapter 7, number 80.

### 39. Threats, Word of Threat. Threats. <note>original: "Tröuen, Treuwort. Minæ."</note>

He who threatens, with a conceived mind of doing harm, to set fire to the house of another—**that he wants to set a red rooster upon his house** <note>original: "daß er ihme einen rothen Hanen auf sein Hauß setzen wolle." A common early modern German idiom for arson.</note>—must be burned alive. Farinaccius, part 3, question 110, number 157. Damhouder in *Criminal Practice*, chapter 103, number 11. For in the most atrocious crimes, the attempt is held as the effect, according to the law *if anyone* in the Code *On Bishops and Clerics*. Farinaccius, question 124, number 11. See Böckel in *Disquisitions on Visions*, 6, last number; and the *Penal Constitution of the High Court of Charles V*, article 176, and the Commentary there.

On the difference between a threat <note>German: "Trohen"</note> and a formal challenge or feud <note>German: "Absag oder Fehden"</note>, see Schneidewein, *On the Institutes*, page 1139.

### 40. Printing. Typography.

On the origin of Typography, see Bornitius, *On the Sufficiency of Things*, folio 164, etc.; Serrarius, *On Mainz*, book 1, chapter 37; Majolus, volume 1, final colloquy, folio 423; Herzog in the *Chronicle of Alsace*, book 2, chapter 64, folio 127; Meteranus in the *History of the Netherlands*, book 4, folio 218, under the year 1573; Middendorp, *On Academies*, book 1, chapter 22; Hermann Hugo, *On the Origin of Writing*, chapter 34; Felix Fabri, *On Swabian Matters*, folio 68, etc. See also my own work, *On the Art of War*, folio 60, in a special discourse. This discourse, like several of my others, was stolen by some "shadow-dweller" <note>original: "tenebrio" — used here to mean a plagiarist or someone operating in the shadows</note> who, having concealed my name, inserted it into his own discourses and published it at Frankfurt.

In the compendium or summary of the first volume of the *Annals* or *Histories on the Origin of the Kings and the Frankish People*, dedicated to Lord Lawrence, Bishop of Würzburg and Duke of Eastern Francia, the following words by Abbot Johannes Trithemius are found at the end of the book regarding this matter:

The present work of the 

<column-break/>

Chronicles was printed and completed in the year of our Lord 1515, on the eve of the Virgin Margaret, in the noble and famous city of Mainz—the first inventor of this art of printing—by Johann Schoeffer, grandson of the late honorable man Johannes Fust, citizen of Mainz, the primary author of the said art. It was he who finally began to devise and investigate the art of printing by his own genius in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1450, in the 12th Indiction, during the reign of the most illustrious Roman Emperor Frederick III. At that time, the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Theodoric Pincerna of Erpach, Prince-Elector, presided over the Holy See of Mainz. However, in the year 1452, he perfected and brought it (with divine grace favoring the work of printing) to completion, through the labor and many necessary inventions of Peter Schoeffer of Gernsheim, his assistant and adopted son. (To whom he also gave his daughter Christina Fust in marriage as a worthy reward for his many labors and inventions). Moreover, these two already named men, Fust and Peter Schoeffer, kept this art in secret (all their assistants and household members were bound by oath not to manifest it in any way). But finally, around the year of our Lord 1462, the art was spread through various provinces of the world by these same household members, and it received no small increase.

->ADDITION.<-

See **Printer** <note>German: "Buchdrucker"</note>. The carelessness of typographers has so mangled and truncated this author for us that the Thracian women hardly tore Orpheus, or the Bacchantes Pentheus, more miserably <note>A classical reference to the violent dismemberment of mythological figures, used here to complain about bad editing</note>, page 21. They sent Petronius out from their hands in such a state that he has more soot than Vulcan's beard. See the illustrious Rupert, *Example 2*, book 1, chapter 1. In Valerius Maximus, where Rupert discusses the burning of books, he notes it is neither a new nor an evil thing. Regarding the impious writings of Protagoras, which suffered the same punishment among the Athenians, read Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Laertius in *Protagoras*. ### 41. Drunkenness, Drinking Healths. <note>original: "Trunckenheit, zutrincken. Ebrietas, Propinare."</note>

Regarding drunkards and drunkenness, see *Georg Obrecht, On Necessary Defense, chapter 6, number 58* and many following. *Hering, On Guarantees, chapter 7, number 119 and following. Paolo Zacchia, in Medico-Legal Questions, book 2, title 1, question 11.* <note>Zacchia is often considered the father of modern forensic medicine.</note> Mundius in the *treatise on Defamation, chapter 3, number 102 and following. On the various ways of becoming intoxicated and the vices of drunkenness, Camerarius, Historical Meditations, century 1, chapter 93 and following. Guyon, Diverse Lessons, volume 1, folio 269 and following,* where he discusses intoxicating drink and the degrees of drunkenness; see also *Baptista Caesaris, Various Counsels, part 3, counsel 55.*

Regarding the restraint of the luxury of gluttony and drunkenness, see Master Hermann Lather, *On the Census, book 2, chapter 3, and Gumpelzheimer in the Gymnasim on Academic Exercises, partition 5, section 1, pages 290 and following.*

Whether Drunkenness excuses one in crimes: for instance, if homicide or some similar crime has been committed, should it then be punished by the ordinary penalty or some milder one because it was perpetrated by a drunk person? See *Daffel, counsel 13, book 1.* It is said that such a person should be restrained by a milder and extraordinary penalty, as is clear from the text <note>original: "in l. omne delictum. §. per vinum. ff. de remilit." - referring to the Digest of Roman Law regarding military crimes committed under the influence.</note>. Baldus makes this specific point regarding the chapter on "Excessive Drinking" <note>Latin: "cap. crapula"</note> in the laws on the life and honesty of the Clergy. For such a person is not judged to have offended or sinned out of purpose, study, or diligent effort, but rather by a certain impulse and weakness. For the ordinary penalty to apply, malicious intent <term>dolus</term> <note>The legal concept of "dolus" refers to the deliberate intention to commit a wrong.</note> must occur simultaneously, which is not presumed in such a drunkard. Hence, the Emperor <note>Referring to the Code of Justinian, "If anyone speaks ill of the Emperor."</note> established that a person who speaks ill of the Emperor while intoxicated should not be punished. The text regarding Lot also supports this, where Lot’s unexpected drunkenness excused him from the sin of incest.

However, they are not to be entirely excused, but should be punished according to the judge's discretion and the quality of the crime, especially when the fault preceded the event—namely, when they were engaged in an illicit activity.

Indeed, there are those who believe that drunk offenders should be afflicted with a double penalty: because the beginning of the wrongdoing lies within the drunkards themselves, as it was in their power to avoid the drunkenness which is the cause and fuel of the crime. Thus, as Aristotle testifies in *Politics, book 2, chapter 10*, Pittacus of Mitylene <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece (c. 640–568 BC).</note> passed a law providing that if drunk people struck someone, they should be condemned to a greater penalty than if they had done it while sober.

<column-break/>

Therefore, Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1519–1556).</note> established in his hereditary Provinces that drunkenness should not provide an excuse in killings, which are often committed by those full of wine. For that most prudent Prince judged that it is not without fault when a man daily engorges himself and provides the cause of his own drunkenness. The same is sanctioned in the **Württemberg Court Ordinance.**

But in this and similar cases, the tradition of Nicolaus Everhard the Younger should not be omitted, who distinguishes between <term>Drunkenness</term> <note>original: "Trunckenheit"</note> and <term>Habitual Drunkenness</term> <note>original: "Vertrunckenheit," defined as the habit of being full/drunk.</note>. Drunkenness arises from a specific occasion, while habitual drunkenness is born from a vicious habit.

In the first case, when someone is intoxicated not by purpose or industry, but deceived by the unknown strength of the wine, a homicide committed by him is not punished with the ordinary penalty. This is because he is compared to a madman or a dead man; consequently, malicious intent and the will to sin are absent. Without these, a crime is either not punished or, if it is struck, it is at least with a milder penalty—which is called the true and divine sentiment by Menochius.

In the second case, he who knowingly and prudently becomes intoxicated out of custom must sometimes be struck with the ordinary penalty. For as Menochius says in the cited place, affected or deceitful drunkenness is worthy of a heavy penalty:
> One who knows his own folly or bad habit, and yet drinks, is acting with intent and is to be severely punished.
But even then, that intent was not specifically destined for the resulting act.

On this Question, one may also look to *Johann Baptista Caesaris, part 3, counsel 55; Knipchild in Exercises on Contracts; and Martin, Illustrious Questions, century 4, dispute 6.*

To what extent it is permitted to use wine, and whether drunkenness should be granted to a wise and good man? See especially *Laelius Bisciola, Leisure Hours, volume 2, book 14, chapter 2,* where he reviews the observed customs of various nations on this matter and explains many passages from sacred and secular writers.

The most pernicious custom today of drinking for someone's health, commonly called <term>drinking healths</term> <note>original: "das Gesundheits Trincken"</note>, has become so prevalent that a person is considered ungrateful and injurious toward another if he refuses to stand up and, in one gulp, drain a large cup for that person's health and thereby intoxicate himself. But let these "health-drinkers" listen to Saint Ambrose in his book *On Elias and Fasting, chapter 17.*

## ADDITION.

The custom of drinking and becoming intoxicated among the Germans is to be regarded more as a public skill <note>original: "artificio publico"</note> than as an individual vice. For this reason, they have refused to abolish it as something good and laudable, remaining for a long time in the drinking chamber; they were praised for this by Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, the Roman historian who described the customs of Germanic tribes.</note> when he said: *The Germans deliberate [while drinking], etc. volume 2, Additions by Limnäus to Public Law, book 1, chapter 6, page 88.* On a glass belonging to King René of Sicily, a figure of the Savior and Mary Magdalene was painted, with the inscription added:

> **Whoever drinks this cup empty shall see God.**

And on the rim of the glass in large gold letters: **Whoever empties me in one draft shall see God and Mary Magdalene.** Limnäus, *volume 2, additions to Public Law, book 1, chapter 6, folio 84. In the year 1517,* **Lord Sigmund von Dietrichstein established the Knightly Order and Society of Saint Christopher for the purpose of abolishing and avoiding swearing and health-drinking,** <note>original: "Zutrinckens" – the practice of challenging others to drink.</note> which most of the Lords and Nobility of Styria, Carniola, and Carinthia joined; more can be read about them in Hieronymus Megiser’s *Carinthian Chronicle.* In parts of Switzerland, specifically in **Uri**, a person who commits a crime while drunk is not only punished with imprisonment but is also prohibited from drinking wine for a year; nor does he obtain permission to drink wine again unless it is granted to him by the entire Swiss community. Neander in his *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 174. Richter, in *Epistles, page 513.* **A crime committed in drunkenness shall not be excused, but shall be punished more severely,** <note>This reflects a legal debate: does being drunk make you less responsible, or more responsible for losing control?</note> Pappus in *Annotations on the Dutch Military Law, page 126 and following.* See Emperor Maximilian II’s article 56, in the *cited place, page 151.* Limnäus, *In Public Law, book 6, chapter 5, numbers 22 and 103. ### 43. Turkish Tax. <term>Collecta Turcica</term> <note>A special imperial tax levied to fund military defense against the Ottoman Empire.</note>

For the contribution to the military expedition against the Turks, proclaimed due to public necessity, everyone—both Clergy and Laity, no matter how highly privileged and with absolutely no one excepted—is bound to pay. See the Imperial Recess <note>original: "Reichs-Abschied"; the formal summary of decisions from an Imperial Diet</note> at Worms, August 17, 1495, under the heading "On the Common Penny" <note>original: "von dem gemeinen Pfenning"</note> at the end of the first section: *All and every person, whether they be spiritual or worldly, woman or man, of whatever dignity, station, order, or being they are, none excluded, etc.* See the Imperial Recess at Augsburg, July 2, 1500, under the heading *that the clergy shall always give one guilder from 40 guilders of income*, and the following heading: *Item, it is intended that all spiritual persons, men and women, whether they be exempt or not, shall give one guilder every year from 40 guilders of all their income, rents, interests, and profits.* See the Imperial Recess at Speyer, April 11, 1542, section *and namely, all shall*, verse *none excepted, also regardless of all contracts, indulgences, and traditions that might be contrary to this levy.*

Specifically, three Imperial Recesses (as cited by Jacobus Alemannus in *Consultations of the Gymnasium*, consultation 5, folio 249 and following) should be read on this matter for the weight and generality of their words: namely, those given at Speyer on June 10, 1548, in the section *but as we, together with the Princes, etc.*; at Regensburg, October 12, 1576, in the section *and after this respectable assistance, etc.*; and in the same place on August 19, 1594, in the section *now after the proposed, etc.*

Furthermore, that a tax can be imposed on the Clergy due to public necessity is recorded by Tessaurus, decision 234, number 10; Hartmann, book 3, observation chapter 2; *Miscellaneous Observations*, 7; Gail, 2, observation 32; Schurff, consultation 44, century 1; and Thomatus, *On Taxes*, section on exaction, numbers 2, 44, and 46. For the laws of necessity are most bitter, and they make lawful that which is otherwise unlawful.

### ADDITION.

The Turkish tax is classified among extraordinary burdens; see Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 7, numbers 63 and 64; add those that follow at number 66. Whether Turkish taxes are imposed on persons for their things, or on the things themselves, see Klock, volume

<column-break/>

I, consultation 27, numbers 21 and 39; whether they are ordinary or extraordinary burdens, ibid. numbers 131 and 136. It is a matter of grief that several States of the Empire have sought profit and personal gain from the imposition and collection of the Turkish contributions; see Klock, consultation 276 and 277, and the cited Petrus Matthæus, Royal Historiographer, book 6, *Historical Narrative* 4, number 4, page 170. From the universal levies of the Turkish tax <note>original: "der Türckensteuer"</note>, the Nobles are not exempt. For a granted immunity is not understood to cover those things required by necessity; see law 1, Code, *That no one is exempt from the purchase of grain*; Wintzler, *On Taxes*, decision 6, number 13; Author of the second part of the *Discourse on the Turkish War*, page 2.

### 44. Tournament, Tournament-Book. <term>Ludi Torneamentorum</term> <note>Games of jousting and knightly combat.</note>

The games of tournaments were most frequent among our ancestors; whence Sebastian Meichsner, in the Preface to the *Imperial and Royal Land and Fief Law of our German Ancestors, etc.*, laments:

> Since the knighthood avoids tournaments,
> And the priesthood rides in armor,
> And worldly monks rule spiritual parishes,
> Thus we must lose land and people.

Regarding the *Tournament-Book* <note>likely referring to Georg Rüxner's famous 1530 "ThurnierBuch," which listed tournament histories</note>, several wise politicians and historians of this time consider it suspect and untrustworthy, not indeed because of the jousts themselves, but in respect to the fabricated circumstances [surrounding them].

But regarding tournaments, see Mr. Vischer, *On Duels*; Dracon, *On Patricians*, folio 77; and Majolus, *On the Dog Days*, folio 775; Bisciolus, *Subsequent Hours*, volume 2, book 6, chapter 6, where he discusses whether tournaments are the "Game of Troy" <note>original: "Trojae ludus"; an ancient Roman equestrian display</note>, and the type of death noted for Theseus, etc.

Against tournaments, however, theologians of old said and wrote much; see Cantipratensis, folio 443, and the notes there.

And that such tournaments were hated by the Citizens where they were celebrated, because of the luxury and [illicit] romances, is shown by the jousts at Basel in the year 1217; these were conducted with a great crowd but ended in a mournful and bloody conclusion. See Guillimann, *Habsburg*, book 6, last chapter, folio 408.

Regarding which Patricians participated, see book 7, chapter 35, number 10; book 6, chapter 5, number 48; add Dracon, *On Patricians*, page 269, numbers 40, 41, 42. A nobleman may [appear] before...

*A tournament <note>original: "Hoplomachia," a Greek-derived term for heavy-armed combat</note>, which is commonly called by the corrupted word "torneamen," or more correctly "the Trojan troop" <note>original: "Trojanum agmen"</note>, and which the Italians in their native tongue call a "giostra" <note>joust</note> after the open field, is contrasted with that course where knights are carried across a racecourse <note>original: "Catadromo"</note>. ### 45. Tyrol. Tyrolis.

The incorporated counties and lordships of the same include Burgau, Kirchberg, Weissenhorn, Feldkirch, Bregenz, Bludenz, Sonnenberg, Montfort, Hohenegg, the Upper and Lower Bailiwicks in Swabia, Nellenburg, the Lordship of Hohenberg, Senfriedsberg, Ehingen, Schelklingen, and Berg, which belong to the High Jurisdiction of the Upper Austrian Government.

->ADDITION.<-

In the year of Christ 1370, Tyrol received the next rank after the Margraves from Charles IV as a Princely County. *See Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain in Historical Relations, part 4, page 64, and part 7, page 234.* How Gorizia and Tyrol were joined through marriage is specifically indicated in *Wiguleus Hund, in the 1st part of the Extinct Bavarian Lineages, folio 73*; also how the territory situated toward Trento, Brixen, Carinthia, and Friuli—the Lordship of Meran, <gloss>part of Ulten,</gloss> was brought to Tyrol. How Tyrol and Gorizia were again separated through a brotherly division. How Bolzano and Carinthia were brought to Tyrol. How Tyrol and Carinthia were again divided from each other. Finally, however, when Henry, Duke of Carinthia and Count of Tyrol, died without male heirs of his body around the year 1335, the Roman Emperor Louis the Bavarian again separated these territories. Specifically, he granted the Duchy of Carinthia to the aforementioned Elizabeth (Henry's sister) and the sons left behind by Emperor Albert I. But the County of Tyrol he distributed to Henry’s only surviving daughter (who in various histories is called "Maultaschin" <note>Margaret, Countess of Tyrol, nicknamed "Mouth-Pouch," traditionally due to a facial deformity or her outspoken nature</note> because of her unusual mouth). 

*Besold, Volume I.*

<column-break/>

This Margaret bequeathed the County of Tyrol to the House of Austria, and finally ended her life in Vienna in the year of Christ 1366. *These matters, here only briefly outlined, are recounted most extensively by Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain in the special Habsburg-Austrian Historical Relation, pages 26 and 27. The County of Tyrol belongs to the Archdukes; Margaret, called Maultascha, gave it with the consent of her estates to her cousins, the Archdukes Rudolph, Albert, and Leopold of Austria. This county remained under their lordship until Charles V assigned it to his brother Ferdinand I. Johann Theodor Sprenger in the Delineation of the Estates of the Empire, page 303.*

### 46. To close with door and hinge. <note>A legal phrase describing a fully enclosed and legally defined property or jurisdiction.</note>

->ADDITION.<-

*That is,* to have the <term>Right of Emphyteusis</term> <note>a long-term or permanent lease of land in exchange for a rent and improvement of the property</note> within the "four stakes" <note>the traditional boundary markers of a property</note>. *It is also said of livestock penned in stalls, "pecora inclusa" <gloss>enclosed cattle</gloss>. Schwannmann, observation 75, no. 3.* To bind the cattle in the stall with stakes. *The same, observation 105, nos. 1 and 2.* The tenant also enjoys peace within his rented "four stakes." *Schneid. page 615, no. 9.* To judge over the "four high stakes." *Adam Keller, on judicial-political office, book 2, chapter 12, page 403.* The land "with door and hinge," as the saying goes, is thus a <term>Territory</term> enclosed and shaped by certain *Limits and Boundaries* <note>original: "Limitibus & Terminis"</note>. *Nuremberg vs. Bavaria regarding the point of Restitution, folio 23.*

### 47. Tower Guard, Tower. <term>Philacista Turris</term> <note>A prison tower or a guard of the same.</note>

->ADDITION.<-

*In a difficult matter, the judge may deliver his sentence from atop the tower. Villalobos on towers and prisons. Mr. Dr. Tabor on Change of Place, page 108 at the end, and 265 at the end. A stay in a wretched prison is the burial of the living, the consumption of goods, the consolation of enemies, and the testing of friends.* In Lower Saxony, such as in the capital of Magdeburg, the guards are called the *Racmeister* <note>likely "Rat-masters" or "Rat-catchers," implying a lowly, grim occupation</note>, and they perform a less honorable duty; in Paris, however, the Governors of the prison are called "Most Noble and Most Respected."

*Regarding the jailers <note>original: "Commentarienses," officials in charge of the prison records and custody</note> and their punishment, see Helfrich Hunnius in the Criminal Discourse, chapter 131, folio 99 and following. The jailer: 1. Must guard the defendant, knowing that the risk of custody pertains to himself: for whatever punishment the defendant was to receive, the jailer suffers that same punishment if the defendant escapes; nor is he heard if he offers a lowly person, such as the prison doorkeeper, to the judge for the sake of freeing himself. Law 4, Code on the custody of defendants. 2. Every month he must report to the judge the number of those locked up, their crimes, their ranks, and their ages in a commentary [register]. Law 5, section 1. When any of the prisoners die, there is a presumption against the guard, so that, if he does not prove that he was without fault, it is presumed that*

...that the prisoner died by the guard's own deceit or fault. Justus Oldekop, in *Criminal Observations, title 3, observation 12, number 1*, notes that this was once treated quite carelessly by judges in a case where two guards (or bailiffs) reported on a woman who had died after being thrown into prison on a charge of witchcraft <note>original: "veneficii"</note>. They claimed the devil had broken her neck and that they had heard the sound of the snapping before the prison door. Indeed, if anyone dies today in such an "evil stay" <note>a euphemism for a dungeon</note>, it is very rarely said that they passed away due to torture, the filth and misery of the prison, or the guard's negligence; rather, it is said that they laid hands on themselves or were strangled by a demon—especially if they were captured for the crime of magic. ### 50. Cloth. <note>original: "Tuch" or "Pannus"</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding what is owed when woolen and linen cloths are bequeathed, see *Mantica on Conjectures of Last Wills, book 9, title 3, number 24.* Whether a bequest of a "cloth shop" <note>original: "apotheca pannaria"</note> refers to the location or the merchandise, see *Mantica, book 9, title 2, number 52.* Regarding cloth-dyers who lie using adulterated colors, *Zahn on Lies, book 2, chapter 97, number 4.* Those who sell faulty cloths—that is, those who knowingly offer for sale cloths that are over-stretched or deceitfully dyed—see the *Supplement to Wehner, page 17.* On cloth-makers and loden-weavers, see the *Bavarian Land Ordinance, folio 20.*

A small portion of cloth, which is commonly called <term>le chantillon</term> <note>a sample or swatch; modern French: "échantillon"</note>, is taken when it is given to a shearer for shearing, so that it remains with the Master as a mark to recognize the cloth itself. *Höpingk on the Law of Seals, final chapter, section 78.* For several 

<column-break/>

hundred years in a row, the Venetians had to provide a gold-woven piece of cloth to the Roman Empire, but Otto III waived this for the Lordship of Venice when he was so grandly entertained by Pietro Orseolo, the Doge at that time. *Zwinger in the Theater, folio 758. Cavil. A.D. 992. Mr. Leonhard Wurffbain, Historical Relations, pages 121 and 165.* There were "Gynæciarii" <note>female weavers or workers in imperial factories</note> who wove Imperial cloths and garments in a specific place called a "gynæcium." *Title 7, book 11 of the Code*, and there *Steinberg*. Under that title concerning cloth officials is joined the title concerning the cloths themselves and their dyeing, *title 8*, regarding "holoberi" garments—that is, all-silk and gold-threaded—and the dyeing of the sacred murex <note>the shellfish used to make royal purple dye</note>. King Edward III of England established the cloth-making industry in his Kingdom. *Klock on the Treasury, book 2, chapter 68, number 3.*

In *Law 6 of the Digest on the Property of the Condemned*, there is mention of "ragged goods" <note>original: "puncularia bona"</note>, named after *panniculis*—that is, the filthy and cheap rags in which defendants were usually dressed, and which they wore because they needed money for daily use; hence the term "ragged person" <note>original: "pannosus"</note>. *Wesenbeck on this title, numbers 4 and 5.* From this law, we understand in passing by what kind of legal species the soldiers claimed the garments of our crucified Savior for themselves. For undoubtedly these were given by Pilate, who then presided over the Province; see the words: "to the one who garments [them] bravely." *Anton. Matthæus on Crimes, page 832.* When the Duke of Alba was tyrannizing the Netherlands, a fustian weaver <note>a maker of heavy cotton-linen fabric</note> settled in Meiningen in the County of Henneberg and promised the Elector he would give one penny for every ell of fustian. This fustian weaver had several journeymen who entered into marriage and fathered children, whereby the whole little town was beautifully built up. *Antenor in Solomon, part 1, chapter 7.*

Tablecloths that do not burn. *Mr. Dilherr in Time and Worldly Course, page 231, section 25.* Those about to attend someone else's feast were compelled to bring their own napkin <note>original: "mappa"</note> to the table for themselves. Hence Martial says:

> Hermogenes never brought a napkin to dinner,
> But Hermogenes always brought one back from dinner. <note>A joke about Hermogenes stealing napkins from his hosts.</note>

Among the Imperial Jewels <note>original: "Clinodia Imperii"</note> is also numbered the tablecloth with which the table of the Last Supper of the Lord was spread. *Dubravius, History of Bohemia, book 22, page 208. Goldast in Imperial Ordinances, page 21.*

### 52. Grapes. <note>Latin: "Uvæ"</note>
### ->ADDITION.<-

Anacharsis <note>a 6th-century BCE Scythian philosopher</note> said: The vine bears three types of grapes: "the first for pleasure, the second for drunkenness, and the third for sorrow" <note>original Latin: "primam uvam voluptatis, secundam ebrietatis, tertiam mæroris"</note>. Concerning the "walking grape" and the "bee-grapes" <note>original: "Apianis uvis," likely referring to sweet Muscatel grapes that attract bees</note>, see Drexel in *The Gold Mine* <note>a reference work by the Jesuit writer Jeremias Drexel</note>, pages 113, 114, and 115. How grapes may be harvested in the middle of winter as fresh as if they were just off the vine, page 117. On the size of grapes and on "hanging grapes" <note>grapes preserved by hanging them from the ceiling</note>, pages 117 and 118. The Turks do not drink wine, yet they eat the grapes. In Innsbruck, there is a grape that grew with a "long beard" three and a half feet <note>original: "Schuh" or "feet," a unit of measurement</note> long. In the year 1541 in Germany, at Albersweiler not far from the city of Landau, two grapes were found during the autumn harvest that each had a long beard. These were first presented to the Elector Ludwig, Count Palatine, and then by His Electoral Grace to King Ferdinand and other princes of the Empire at Speyer as a miracle to behold. These bearded grapes were accurately depicted by the painter Heinrich Vogther, according to the reports of Lycosthenes and Wolff. In the year 1599 in Strasbourg, in the residence of the Count of Mansfeld's cathedral chapter, two grapes were to be seen which had been sent from the Eysel as a special wonder. One of them had a beard about half a Strasbourg ell <note>a unit of length, roughly 24 inches</note> long, while the other was much shorter. The hairs were not unlike red silk, somewhat dark yellow in color, leaning toward brown; they hung down neatly one after another, like a man's long beard. Martin Mylius describes this in *The Pleasure Garden of Delightful Wisdom*, page 132. Regarding Faustus’s vines, see Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 186 and following. Dr. Plater owns a spoon made of grapevine wood, a wood which is otherwise useless for anything.

*According to some, Adam ate a grape [rather than an apple], following the verse: "The fathers have eaten the sour grape."* <note>original Latin: "Adam uvam comedit... Patres comederunt uvam acerbam"</note> Boër, decision 51, number 3.

*It is sometimes permitted to eat grapes in another's vineyard, but it is not permitted to carry them away with impunity.* Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus in *The System of Universal Law*, book 37, chapter 7, number 6. On grapes that are very large, see Zeiller in *Travels in Italy*. Tamaraca <note>a region in colonial Brazil</note> carries three grapes in its coat of arms. On grapes, see Antenor in *Solomon*, chapter 9, where he discusses at length the "Musa of Serapion" <note>likely a reference to the banana</note> and the "Apples of Paradise."

### 53. Tobacco. <note>Latin: "Tabacum"</note>
### ->ADDITION.<-

Tobacco is forbidden in Russia. Olearius, in his *Description of the Persian Journey*, 

<column-break/>

book 3, chapter 6, pages 197 and 269; and in the *Persian War Camp*, page 645, where one must [lose] nose and lips [as punishment]. A Persian merchant, who was ignorant of this prohibition, arrived in the camp with nine bales of tobacco, thinking he would make good money from the soldiers. But when the King learned of it, he had the tobacco-seller thrown onto a woodpile along with his tobacco and made them go up in smoke together. Ibid. Tobacco was first brought from the Indies to England around the year 1585, where today specific "tobacco houses" are found everywhere, just like beer houses. Zeiller in *Travels in Great Britain*, page 63. There is a specific little treatise on tobacco titled: *The Dry Drunkenness*. From the simple pipes made for the use of tobacco, approximately fifty thousand guilders <note>original: "florenorum"</note> are brought into the Dutch Treasury annually; one can easily guess, therefore, how much they gain from the use of the tobacco itself. Caspar Barlæus plays elegantly with the subject of tobacco in his *Enigmas* <note>riddles</note> as follows:

> *I am not drunk, though I am "drunk" [inhaled], a drink of the people*
> ->*and yet I am not.*<-
> *I am chewed by those in the West, yet I was never food.*
> *When I am "drunk," thirst itself grows; I am a victim*
> ->*of the common crowd,*<-
> *I am twisted, cut, scorched, and burned there.*
> *Men pierce me, and having seen this gift of the gods,*
> *Every right hand is found ready for my destruction.*
> *Some cut me into pieces, some dry my moist*
> ->*bodies with fire,*<-
> *Some apply flames and torches.*
> *Those who flee leisure, lose their leisure in us,*
> *And with great diligence, they accomplish nothing.*
> *By which I am caught, I am destroyed; by which I am enclosed, I am*
> ->*driven from the mouth,*<-
> *And whoever loves my dishes soon blows them away:*
> *O matron, who opens your shining home to me,*
> *Receive the spit of such illustrious labor as your reward.*

Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 1, chapter 14, numbers 28 and 29. From tobacco, an ointment for all wounds and a juice for all internal illnesses can be made.

*The Spaniards cure those with dropsy <note>edema/swelling</note> with tobacco water.* G. Richter in *Epistles*, page 592. See Zeiller, *Miscellany of Epistles*, epistle 71, century 4, question 160, page 501. On whether tobacco should be counted among the means of nourishment, see the same, page 82. Tobacco pills make it so that one can easily endure hunger and thirst. Mr. Harsdörffer in *The Great Theater of Delightful and Instructive Stories*, volume 148, number 3. The Hessians have begun to plant tobacco, which is transported to Hamburg and as far as Pomerania. The Moors keep tobacco pipes in their mouths, which they call a *Kaschot*; some are so large that half a hand's worth of tobacco fits inside, and the tubes are an arm's length long. First a little tobacco, then a drink of wine.

# Enlarged Treasury of Practical Knowledge

### 54. Triumph. <note>Latin: "Triumphus"</note>

The right of triumph among the ancients. An "ovation" <note>a lesser form of a military triumph</note> is ranked before a full triumph. The most splendid triumph is seen to be when one does not actually hold a triumph <note>referring to a victory so decisive or moral that the ceremony is unnecessary</note>. See Christoph Rupert, dissertation 1 on Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 8. A complete description of a triumph is held in dissertation 2, at chapter 8. The festivals of triumph and joy against the Germans were established in vain: "The Germans were triumphed over more than they were conquered" <note>original Latin: "Germani triumphati magis fuere, quam victi"</note>. L. Wurffbain, in *Historical Reports*, part 1, page 6.

### 55. Granddaughter. <note>Archaic German: "Tiechter"; Latin: "Neptis"</note>

Grandson <note>Nepos</note>, Granddaughter <note>Neptis</note>, Great-grandson <note>Pronepos</note>, Great-granddaughter <note>Proneptis</note>, Great-great-grandson <note>Abnepos</note>, Great-great-granddaughter <note>Abneptis</note>. Found in the *Marriage Ordinance of Rothenburg ob der Tauber, 1656*. A granddaughter's husband is called a *Progener*, and a grandson's wife is called a *Pronurus*.

### 56. Tavernic Law. <note>Latin: "Thavernicale Jus"</note>

Tavernic Law. Tavernic Courts. Master of the Royal Taverners <note>The "Magister Tavernicorum" was one of the highest judicial offices in the Kingdom of Hungary, originally overseeing the royal treasury and the "Tavernic" towns</note>. Dr. Tabor in his *Comparison of Roman and Hungarian Law*, part 1, section 2. A. number 15.

->Master of the Treasury. <note>Germanized Hungarian: "Tharnack-Meister"</note><-

How and in what manner the legal proceedings of the Free Cities are sent to the Master of the Treasury. *Tripartite Work of Hungarian Customary Law*, part 3, title 10, page 142. This word is also found in part 3, title 11, page 142. The "Tavernic Bench" <note>a court of appeals for royal towns</note>, ibid. page 143. Masters of the Royal Taverners, ibid. page 141.

### 57. Tenure. <note>Latin: "Tenuta"</note>

The holding or safekeeping of possession, called *Tenuta* in Latin.
*Whether a tenure can be retained by the mind <note>intent</note>, even if it has not been physically grasped.* Fichardus, volume 2, counsel 140, number 14.

### 58. Trisoley. <note>A legal fee or tax term</note>

See above under the word Court-clerk <note>Gerichts-schreiber</note>, also under the word *Schas* <note>a tax or tribute</note>, and the passage there from Limnäus.

### 1. Vagrants. <note>Latin: "Vagabundi"</note>

Regarding these, see Wilhelm Anton in his *Treatise on Five-Year Periods*, chapter 68, number 78.

### ADDITION.

Those who block the roads, market-haunters, vagabonds, land-runners <note>German: "Landläuffer"</note>, mutinous servants, highwaymen <note>German: "Hanenreuter"</note>, who in troops 

<column-break/>

wander through regions, pillaging public and private roads and attacking the unsuspecting; concerning their punishments, see Law 28, § 10 *on punishments*, and the second section of the *Imperial Recess of Augsburg*, 1555, at the verse "and with the mentioned destruction" and following, page 430. *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber*, part 2, 15, at the end. On who may be called a vagabond, see Gail, book 1, observation 1, number 4, and observation 57, number 4. Gothofredus at Law 20, § 1 of the *Digest on the Work of Freedmen*.

### 2. Valuation. <note>The value of money</note>

By this word is denoted the extrinsic value <note>face value</note> of a coin. For it is not enough for a coin to have sufficient weight and a public stamp, unless it has also been publicly defined by a fair, constant, and certain estimation, according to Law 3 *on injury* and Law 30 *on that which is in a certain place*. Because a coin is like a Law, which rests upon public and constant authority, so that it can always and consistently be made equal to all salable things (whose estimation varies), and thus it can achieve its own purpose.

### ADDITION.

Auelus treats extensively on the estimation of money in *On Money*, chapter 12, number 55 and following. Also Willibald Pirckheimer on the estimation of ancient coins; Joseph Scaliger; Willebrord Snell on numismatics; Camerarius; and Agricola on the price of ancient coins. Covarruvias on the change of money, 1559 edition.

Whether a coin has an imposed value, and whether that is of the essence of the coin? See Leuber *On Monetary Reduction*, page 45. Concerning valuation, appraisal, and estimation, the same author, page 50.

### 3. Vassal. <note>Latin: "Vasallus"</note> See above under the word Feudatory. <note>German: "Lehenmann"</note>

In olden times, the faithful who provided service were called *Vassals*, as in the *Laws of the Alemanni*, title 36, there: "whatever person it may be, the Vassal of a Duke or Count." *Laws of the Bavarians*, chapter 11, title 15: "whether a Vassal of the King or of a Duke, let all come to the assembly." The Chapters of the Bishops of Reims and the Rouen Provinces in the Palace of Quierzy to King Louis in the year 1318 [mention] "in the company of the *Drudi* and the Vassals." *Drudi*, however, according to Falconius's *Antiquities*, book 9, chapter 15, are understood to be the faithful ones, taken from the Germanic word *Drutte* <note>related to "Traut" or "Treue," meaning loyal/beloved</note>.

### ADDITION.

In Saxon Feudal Law, vassals are simply called "Men" <note>German: "Manne"</note>, as if endowed with manliness and a vigorous and upright spirit. Petrus Heige, part 1, question 2, number 85. If a vassal acts as an advocate against his Lord, he loses the fief. Klock, volume 2, counsel 4, number 187; but see numbers 191, 192, and 193. One who causes a great loss of inheritance to the Lord is deprived of the fief, number 188. More on this word is provided...

### 4. **Fatherland. Homeland.** <note>German: *Vatterland*; Latin: *Patria*</note>
The term "homeland" is usually applied not only to the broad significance of an entire province, but also equally to the city where one has their residence <term>domicile</term>, as Bartolus declares in his commentary on Law 3 of the Code "On Natural Children." This is especially true where a City holds the primary leadership of a Province, as the same text says near the end. See the *Opinions of Illustrious Jurists*, by Battista Cesare, opinion 73, number 6, part 3. "One's homeland is where one fares well" <note>original Latin: *Patria est, ubi bene est*</note>; it is also said to be acquired through an oath of fealty <term>homage</term>. But if someone is the son of a city's legal representative <term>Syndic</term>, he shall not be subject to the burdens <note>taxes or civic duties</note> of the citizens.

->ADDITION.<-

A proverb has become common concerning the "Malean yoke" <note>referring to Cape Malea, a dangerous Greek promontory; the proverb suggests that those sailing past it should forget their hopes of returning home due to the danger</note>, by which those who round that promontory are commanded to forget their journey home, or their return to their Homeland; see Rupert’s commentary on Florus, book 2, chapter 9, section 4, and the citations therein. In any legal matter, the Homeland is considered to be an exception <note>meaning laws are often interpreted to favor the interests of one's own country</note>. Barbosa, book 14, chapter 10, axiom 1. To avoid or shun one's homeland is impious (axiom 4). A person is presumed to be of such character as their homeland is (axiom 5). Everyone is presumed to be endowed with the customs of their homeland. Thus Ummius in *On Legal Process*, page 633. The homeland is threefold: that of origin <note>birthplace</note>, of residence <note>domicile</note>, and the common homeland <note>the state or empire</note>. Rittershausen in *The Novellae*, page 560, number 15 and following. Everyone ought to care for the homeland. Munschius in *On Offices*, chapter 1, number 264; chapter 6, number 481. We are presumed to desire all the best things for the homeland (Ummius, page 633). We are more strictly bound to the Homeland than to our own Father; Klock, volume 1, opinion 37, numbers 388, 389, 390. A Prince should not easily withdraw from the ancestral rite, worship, language, and way of life. Stirn in *On the Constitutions of Princes*, volume 3, section 10.

The homeland is twofold <note>referring to one's local city versus the Roman Empire or State</note>. Hugo Donellus in *Commentaries on Civil Law*, 980, 40. b. Everyone owes duties to the homeland (566, 60. a). Mr. Speidel in his *Collection of Legal Questions*, under the word "Homeland"; see the famous speech of Camillus, the Roman Dictator, on behalf of the soil of the Homeland in Livy, book 5, chapter 51. The Homeland is preferred even over a Kingdom. Love of the homeland. "Location shapes character" <note>original Latin: *Situs format ingenia*</note>. A noble mind refuses to survive the destruction of the homeland. Death for the homeland is noble. Mr. Rupert in his observations on Florus, throughout the index.

### 5. **Paternal Authority. Paternal Power.** <note>German: *Vätterlicher Gewalt*; Latin: *Patria potestas*</note>

The statute of limitations <term>prescription</term> sleeps <note>is suspended</note> while Paternal Power lasts. Klock, volume 2, opinion 68, number 35. On paternal power, and its effect and force, see the absolute treatise by Paschalius; add Acacius Enenckel on the *Privileges of Parents and Children*; Scipio Gentilis in the treatise *On Maternal Goods*, chapters 1 and 2; and my own writings in several places in my legal treatises.

Does paternal authority still endure today in Saxony? See the *Consultations on the Saxon Constitutions*, book 1, question 28.

<column-break/>

Philippus Paschalius, a citizen of Cosenza, wrote on the power of Paternal Authority, whom Nicolaus Myler cites in *On the States of the Empire*, page 276. Paternal Power is the basis and foundation for acquiring the right to use <term>usufruct</term> of secondary property <term>adventitia</term> <note>property a child inherits from someone other than the father, such as a mother or outsider</note>. Klock, volume 2, opinion 65, numbers 1 and 2. To the mother—inasmuch as she does not have the children in her power—the right to use such property is by no means granted (ibid., number 3). The right of Paternal Power endures even over a son who is an old man (number 4), nor is it removed by geographical distance (number 6); see also opinion 77, numbers 5 and 6.

Paternal Power ought to consist in duty and affection <term>piety</term>, not in cruelty. Barbosa, book 14, chapter 10, axiom 6. The right of Paternal Power, once extinguished, cannot be revived (axiom 7). Paternal power makes an oath fall silent <note>axiom 8; meaning a father's authority might invalidate an unauthorized oath made by a child</note>. On the comparison of Paternal power with the power of a master over a slave, see Rittershausen in *Sacred Readings*, page 584. Whether achieving a Doctorate or entering Monasticism dissolves paternal power; see Mr. Dr. Ludvv. in *Disputations on the Institutes*, page 34. Some wrongly say that the children of Jews, if they receive baptism, are freed from paternal power. Vigelius, *Method of Civil Law*, book 1, chapter 13, rule 25; Zasius in *Individual Books of Questions*, 3.

Parents must not abuse Paternal Power. Christoph Philipp Richter, part 2, opinion 4, number 65 and following, folio 21. By the right of Paternal Power, the right to use property <term>usufruct</term> is granted in the secondary goods of children. Part 4, chapter 15, number 23, folio 91. A paternal grandfather and great-grandfather have all descendants in their power, unless they have left it through legal release <term>emancipation</term>. Part 6, opinion 33, number 4, folio 282. In how many ways, and by what means, Paternal Power is acquired: Hugo Donellus in *Commentaries on Civil Law*, 57, 60. a; 58, 10. a; what it contains, 64, 20. a. Paternal Power is acquired from a lawful marriage (57, 40. b). In what ways Paternal Power is dissolved (65, 10. b). One who is himself under Paternal Power cannot have another person under his own power (58, 20. a). Johannes Philippi, the Jurist, deals at length with Paternal Power in *The Practical Use of Justinian’s Institutes*, in the index, where he establishes that Military Service, a Doctorate, and the Clergy do not liberate one from Paternal Power. Councilors of any State of the Empire are exempt from Paternal Power, following the example of the Roman Patricians. However, this does not apply to armed soldiers, nor to those in the legal profession <term>togati</term>, nor a Monk, nor a Priest, nor a Doctor. Adult children are freed from Paternal Power through marriage, and also through separation from the father's household management <term>economy</term>. Children placed under Paternal Power acquire for the Father whatever they acquire from the Father's resources. Ibid. Mr. Speidel in *Collection of Legal Questions*, under the word "Paternal Power." On what path and in what manner paternal power ceases and is taken away, see the *Decree or Tripartite Work of Hungarian Land Law*, part 1, title 56.

...understood in two ways: first, materially and effectively, for all those who received their substance and result from the father—and in this way, only those descending from the father are included, because in the father's collateral relatives there is no substance or effect of the father. Second, subjectively, or comprehensively, for all those who are contained under the line and are subject to the line in which the father is contained. In this way, those joined to the father collaterally are said to be of the "father’s line," and even these collateral relatives are contained under that same line; see the legal advice of Cravetta, council 150, numbers 4 and 5.

### ADDITION.

Paternal goods should go to the paternal side, and maternal goods to the maternal side; or, as this rule is expressed in verse:

->Maternal goods go to the maternal side, paternal to the paternal side.<-
<note>original Latin: *Maternis cedant Materna, Paterna Paternis*</note>

This is what Guillaume Ranchin calls the "Right of Reversion" <term>jus Reversionis</term> in his treatise on intestate succession, section 14, number 8. Although this rule is customarily applied not only to the succession of ancestors <term>ascendants</term>, but also to descendants and collateral relatives, it is chiefly disputed regarding ancestors. In that case alone, it is called a "most doubtful question in Law" by Baldus Novellus in his treatise on dowries, part 12, question 14, number 55. It is described as a "very ambiguous passage" and a "question for a friend's practice" by Jason in his commentary on the Law *Post*, number 105; a "wonderful case" by Paolo di Castro; and a "grave question disputed for many years" by Mynsinger. Antonio Gomez calls it a "singular and subtle doubt" in his commentary on the Laws of Toro, number 7, and Grassus calls it an "arduous question" in his section on intestate succession. It is noted that there is a "common opinion against the common opinion" regarding this matter, not only by Cavallos in his *Mirror of Common Opinions*, but also by many other cited authors—some affirming the positive and others the negative view—as taught by Tiraqueau, Vazquez, Gabrielli, Vivius, Tessauro, Gomez, Grassus, Berlich, and Johann Melchior Bitsch in his *Cases for a Friend*, page 15 and following.

## 7. Parricide. <note>German: *Vattermord*; Latin: *Parricidium*</note>

Regarding Parricide <note>the killing of a parent or close relative</note>, see the *Criminal Discourse* of Helfrich Hunnius, page 235, etc.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the modern penalty for parricide, see Damhouder in his *Criminal Practice*, chapter 89, number 3. The word "parricide" is derived from "equal case" <note>original: *pari casu*</note> and began to be used for the killing of those who are most closely joined to the killer, and in many ways

<column-break/>

are most equal, such as Parents and Children. Spouses are also "equal in spirit" according to the law on donations between husband and wife. Among other relatives as well, a certain singular equality of kinship is perceived, which means that when they are slaughtered, a "parricide" is committed, though not in its most atrocious form <note>referring to different degrees of legal severity</note>. This is perhaps why this derivation was preferred over others by Bachov, volume 2. 

As for why a cat is used today instead of an ape <note>referring to the *poena cullei*, an ancient Roman punishment where a parricide was sewn into a sack with a dog, a rooster, a viper, and an ape</note>, and whether it is because apes are expensive in Germany and highly valued, see Petrus Papus in his *Dutch Military Law*, page 56. 

In Spain, not far from Ilerda, in a village called Cervera, in the month of August A.D. 1344, a strange child was born who had two heads and four feet. The parents, who were terrified by this, agreed that it should be buried alive. However, the local authorities had the parents punished with the "penalty of parricide" <term>pœna parricidii</term>, regardless of the fact that it was an unnatural birth. Regarding those who advise parricide, and whether they should be punished with the same penalty, see Pappus, page 57.

Mr. Speidel, in his *Collection* under the word "Parricide": The punishment for parricide among the ancients is discussed in *Dutch Military Law*, p. 56. It is no longer used today.

## 8. Improvements. <note>German: *Uberbesserung*; Latin: *Melioramenta*</note>

This is the term commonly used in Swabia for the "beneficial ownership" <term>utile Dominium</term> of a long-term tenant <term>emphyteuta</term>: because whatever he builds upon such leased estates beyond the fixed rent <term>Canonem</term> belongs to the tenant. This vocabulary truly suits the long-term lease <term>emphyteusi</term>, because uncultivated goods are given in such leases so that they may be improved.

### ADDITION.

See Mr. Speidel in his *Notable Observations*, letter V, number 15.

## 9. Overhang. <note>German: *Überhang*; Latin: *Rami ex arbore vicini*</note>

Regarding the overhang of trees and fruit—to whom do they belong? See Clessen’s dispute on the acquisition of ownership, thesis 12.

### ADDITION.

See Johann Philippi in his *Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian*, book 2. Mr. Speidel in his *Notable Observations*, letter B, number 34. According to Saxon Law, branches from a neighbor's tree hanging over onto my land are mine, so that I am allowed either to cut them off or to collect the fruit from them; see the *Municipal Law* <term>Weichbild</term>, article 125, and the *Land Law* <term>Landrecht</term>, book 2, article 52. The gloss there states: whatever fruit grows on the branches of a tree that hang over a neighbor's property and falls onto that ground shall belong to and remain with that neighbor. See the *Reformation of Frankfurt*, part 8, title 13, section 2. One is not allowed to cut back roots as freely as branches, as Mr. Tabor notes in his *Clusters of Legal Questions*.

## 10. Sending [a criminal] across the Rhine or the Danube. Banishment.
<note>original German: Uber den Rhein, oder die Thonau weisen. Relegatio.</note>

The question of whether the sentence of a Judge extends its power even outside the territory of the one pronouncing the law is a complex one. Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist</note> explains it this way in his commentary on the law *Cunctos Populos*, number 50: he says that either the penalty inflicted by the sentence regards the person themselves who committed the crime, or it regards their goods. In the first case, he distinguishes further: either the penalty regards a prohibition from a certain place—for example, if a person is banished <term>relegatur</term> so that they are forbidden from staying in a certain location—in this case, the sentence of banishment, or as Bartolus says in the German of his day, *Landsverweisung* <gloss>expulsion from the land</gloss>, has no power outside the Judge's territory. *Law 7, section 10, Digest on Banishment.*

And it is for this reason that a banishment—by which a criminal is condemned by the Magistrate of Tübingen to the Hungarian borders to serve against the Turks—is not valid under Common Law <term>Jus Commune</term> <note>The "Common Law" here refers to the Roman-based legal system used across continental Europe, not the English system.</note>. Bartolus, *ibid.* However, that law is modified: (1) by reason of consequence. For when one is barred from their place of residence, the place of their origin is also deemed prohibited. (2) If it is to avoid public harm or for the common good of the Republic that the condemned person is prohibited from approaching some external and distant place. (3) If a contrary custom has been introduced: such a custom flourishes everywhere in Germany, where, for example, a person must swear an oath [to stay away] across the Rhine or the Danube <note>original German: einer über den Rhein oder Thonau schwören muß</note>, even if the jurisdiction of the banishing Judge does not extend that far. Antonius Berneder, a great practitioner of German law, in his *German treatise* titled *A New Capital Court Ordinance, title 5, article 2.*

Or, which is the second case of the sub-distinction: the sentence regards the diminution of the person's status—that is, it contains the person's excommunication or legal infamy <term>infamia juris</term>. Such a penal sentence follows the condemned person outside the territory and has force everywhere. The reason is that such a penalty clings to the person and follows them wherever they go. *Law 9, Digest on Requests.* In the second main case, namely when the penalty regards the goods of the one who committed the crime, Bartolus distinguishes again: either the penalty of deprivation or confiscation of goods is established by Common Law for the crime, or by special law—such as Municipal Law, local prescription, or custom. In the first case, it is concluded that the sentence of deprivation or confiscation extends its power to goods located outside the territory of the judge, and that the judge of the place where the goods are located, rather than the judge in whose district the crime was committed, should seize the goods.

Besoldus, Volume I.

<column-break/>

From this it follows that if some nobleman, who holds very large fiefs from various Princes, should kill his wife with a dagger, and having been accused of parricide <note>In this context, "parricide" refers to the murder of a close relative, here a spouse.</note> by his wife's blood relatives, is condemned to perpetual imprisonment as a penalty; and if he is rendered infamous <term>infamis</term> by such a sentence, and thus lacks the legal standing to appear in a Lords' Court: then he can be deprived of his fiefs. This applies not only to the fiefs he holds from the Prince in whose territory the parricide was committed and the sentence passed, but also to the fiefs he holds from other Princes.

In the second case, namely when the penalty of deprivation of goods is imposed on the offender by a *special* law, it is concluded that the sentence of deprivation and confiscation does not extend to goods located elsewhere. Bartolus, *ibid.* Panormitanus, *ibid.* Gail, *book 2, observation 124.* Hence this question is elegantly asked: if someone possessing goods under different territories kills themselves, and the Lord of the place where the crime occurred claims the right of confiscation for himself based on local prescription (contrary to Common Law), does the sentence of deprivation extend to goods located elsewhere and exclude the children? Likewise, to which Treasury <term>Fiscus</term> do the goods located elsewhere go? The negative opinion should be embraced as more legal, yet in such a way that those goods located elsewhere go to the lord of the place where the property is situated. The reason is that in this case, the penalty of confiscation is imposed by special law; see my work *On Selected Matters, book 1, question 45, and in the treatise On Territory, folio 275.* Add Peguera, *decision 89.*

Mr. Speidel in his *Collection* under the word *Relegatio*. Besoldus in his *Politics, book 1, chapter 12, number 78, verse 7, most extensively.*

## 11. Buying in bulk, or by the lump. Sale by aversion.
<note>original German: Uberhaupt kauffen, ins Meß kauffen. Venditio per aversionem.</note>

To be sold "by aversion" <term>per aversionem</term> is to be sold by the "body" or as a specific item: which is contrasted with selling by quantity, weight, number, or measure. See Mr. Bocer in his *Classified Disputations on Buying, thesis 18, etc.* and Calvalcanus in *On Tutors and Curators, section 5, number 38, folio 162.*

A purchase or sale is said to be made "by aversion" because we contract the business as if "turning away" <note>This plays on the Latin *aversio* (turning away).</note>; that is, the matter is neither fully perfected nor well-examined, and the buyer takes all risk <term>periculum</term> upon himself, while the seller turns away <term>avertat</term> all potential loss onto the buyer. Costalius on *Law 62, section 2, on Contracting a Purchase.* This is also called selling "as a whole" and for a "clean price." *Law 35, section "In these", Digest on the same title; Law 36, Digest on the Aedilian Edict.* Thus, buying "in bulk" <gloss>überhaupt</gloss>...

It also defines "sale by aversion," a legal term for buying goods in bulk where the buyer assumes all risks of the uninspected lot.</summary>

Header: Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Expanded

Work is said to be *contracted and hired* <term>locatum & conductum; the Roman law category for service and labor contracts</term> when it is not hired by specific feet or measurements, but <note>original Greek: ἐν ὁμάδῃ</note> "as a whole" <gloss>in a lump sum</gloss> for a single price. This is at the risk of the contractor until it has been approved. *Law on work, 36. Law on that condition, 51. Digest on hiring and contracting. Speckhan, century 3, question 19, Class 1, number 3.* What if the buyer is delayed in measuring it? See *Costalius on Law 1 of the Digest regarding the risk and benefit of a sold item.*

In a "sale by aversion" <term>venditio per aversionem; a sale of goods in bulk rather than by weight or measure</term>, since the sale is made for a single price, and all risk, loss, profit, and disadvantage are turned away <gloss>averting the risk</gloss> from the seller and transferred to the buyer; it follows that the purchase and sale in this case are considered so complete that immediately after the price of the sold thing is established as a whole, and the transfer of risk from the seller to the buyer is made, all risk, loss, profit, and disadvantage regarding the sold item belong to the buyer. *Speckhan, in the same place, number 3, beginning.*

### 12. Venice. Venetia.

Regarding the Venetians, Fredericus de Marselaër writes thus in *On the Ambassador, book 1, folio 133*: Since the Ambassador believes it is not a little difficult to deal with the Republic of the Venetians, where business must be untangled with so many men who are driven by a supreme mutual distrust, fear of ruin, and a love of equality and self-preservation, they labor so that no one may excel above the rest. The Republic is exceptionally studious of Peace and thus worthy of long-lasting tranquility; it has always acted not so much to rule over anyone as to serve no one. And since the Venetians preserve and learn the most accurate and absolute reports of the governments of the entire world, instructions for an Ambassador come from nowhere else but this Republic, as if from a "Trojan Horse" or a "Gymnasium of Political Affairs." Here too, more attentively than anywhere else, it is noted whatever an Ambassador does or attempts. Inasmuch as the Venetian Ambassadors are most intent on knowing and penetrating the secrets of foreigners, so in turn it is feared here lest the same curiosity and care occupy and educate the foreigners residing there. Therefore, the inhabitants are not permitted to visit an Ambassador whenever they please, to frequent his house, or to meet or receive his servants. Yet one could hardly deny that here (where men also live and men rule),

<column-break/>

nothing is impassable or closed off to the industry, bribery, and faithful silence of an Ambassador.

And he adds later: Furthermore, in this Republic, the first office is that of the elected *Duke* <gloss>the Doge</gloss>; the next is that of the six *Procurators of Saint Mark.* These men hold permanent offices; the rest are defined by specific times. A *Commander* <note>original: Deductor</note> of the army is indeed taken, but only for a time, and he is a foreigner; lest perhaps, swelling with authority or military glory, he should invade the Empire. And although the Duke of the Venetians is first in rank, he nevertheless does not deliberate or decide anything separately without the *Council of Ten* (which is the highest among them); he does not even report a letter from a foreign Prince or Ambassador unless someone from the aforementioned Council of Ten is present by chance or by summons. Indeed, the vote of any Senator is counted no differently than that of the Duke himself; and therefore, for the sake of reason and the good of the Republic, the Senators freely oppose him. Finally, the Duke responds to foreign Ambassadors only in the name of the Republic, and says nothing other than what the Council of Ten has decreed. A man of great reputation in this Council is the Secretary, who must be cultivated by the Ambassador.

Add Contarenus *On the Republic of the Venetians*, and the treatise translated from Italian into our native tongue by Megiser and titled **Venetian Glory** <note>original German: Venediger Herrlichkeit</note>, also the treatise *Concerning the Notable Things of the City of Venice.*

Regarding Venetian affairs under Charlemagne, see *Cardinal Baronius, Annals for the Year of Christ 810, at the end.*

### ADDITION.

Today many agree that a golden ring was given to the Venetians by Alexander III for the "Wedding of the Sea," and our Piccartus joins these in *Historical-Political Observations, decade 16, chapter 5,* moved by the authority of *P. Justinian.* But *Josephus Laurentius, in Polymathy, book 2,* demonstrates from the archives of the Venetians that this "wedding" was celebrated long before the Roman Pontiff Alexander took refuge in the city of Venice. In this ceremony, the Sea is joined to the Republic as if in a most holy marriage, which the Republic addresses with these solemn words: *We wed thee, Sea, as a sign of true and perpetual lordship.* And although writers claim that Pope Alexander III gave rise to this ceremony in Venice, these same authors constantly affirm and confirm that it was instituted as a most certain sign and infallible pledge of the undisputed dominion which the Republic acquired and possessed by right of war long before.
