### 13. Burning, burning alive. <term>Comburere; death by fire</term>

Execution by burning alive is not without reason categorized among the supreme punishments by Callistratus in the *Law on Capital Crimes, 28, Digest on Punishments*. The severity of this punishment is also noted by Valerius Maximus in Book 6, Chapter 3. Tertullian, in *On Flight in Persecution* and his *Book on the Soul*, complains that burning people alive was common in his time. Formerly, this punishment was practiced only against men of servile condition, whose status is generally worse regarding the scale of punishments. For examples and cases of when slaves were subjected to such execution, see Rudolph Forner in *Daily Matters, Book 1, Chapter 7*.

Furthermore, as the malice of men increased daily, it became necessary to increase the punishments as well. Thus, this type of execution was eventually transferred even to free persons, at least for more atrocious crimes, such as sacrilege (*Law 6, Digest on the Julian Law regarding Embezzlement*), robbery, and so on.

It is also established that this punishment was frequent for military offenses, as we read throughout the texts that deserters, traitors, and those who report secret plans to the enemy 

<column-break/>

are to be burned alive (*Law on Damage, 8, section 38, Digest on Punishments*). The same applies to those who labor to ensure that Romans are plundered by barbarians (*Law 'if anyone,' 9, Code on Military Affairs*) and those who cut off their own fingers to avoid military service (*Law on Recruits, 5, Theodosian Code*).

Following this example, Christian Princes in later times decreed that heretics should also be punished as if they were deserters and abandoners of the legitimate military <note>The "military of Christ"</note>, so that the rising evil might be met with severity.

It is also established that this penalty was once instituted for counterfeiters of money, for those who damage the dikes of the Nile, for arsonists of houses and piles of grain, for magicians and soothsayers, and for those guilty of high treason <term>Læsæ Majestatis; a crime against the dignity of the sovereign</term>, as the same Forner proves in the aforementioned Chapter 7.

Otherwise, the bodies of those condemned to be burned could be requested so that the ashes and bones might be committed to burial, according to the *text of Law 1 at the end, Digest on the bodies of the punished*.

For the cases in which the punishment of burning takes place today, and why witches <note>original German: Sagæ</note> should not be burned alive, see *Speidel, in Legal-Political Notables, under the section 'Fire,' folio 304*.

->ADDITION.<-

Anyone who has brought harm to humans or animals through the magical arts is burned with fire today according to the *Criminal Court Ordinance of Charles V, Article 109*, and the *Princely Württemberg Territorial Law, section on Sorcery*. Add the citations by Harpprecht, section 5, on public judgments, number 257. Good Princes often ordered that the records of public debtors be burned (imitating Agis, the leader of the Athenians, regarding whom see *Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, 7; Peter Heig, Question 10, and following*); by this very act, they completely removed the anxiety of cares from the wretched debtors. *Master D. Tabor, on Double the Amount, Part 1, Article 4, number 6.* Regarding the penalty for one who burned a written document, see *Zahn, Treatise on Lies, Book 2, Chapter 81, number 6*.

### 14. Honorarium or Gift. <term>Munus; a gift, often implying a bribe in a legal context</term>

That the councillors and officials should take no gift <note>original German: Verehrung</note> is provided for in the Tübingen Contract. See the *Authors on Baratry* <term>Barateria; the crime of judges taking bribes</term>.

->ADDITION.<-

On whether a noble young lady may give her dowry and jewelry to her husband, see *Joh. Baptista Costa, Counsel 87; Nicolaus Myler on the Princes and States of the Empire, Chapter 27, page 286*. Gifts are given with the intent of corrupting a judge. *Walther on the Privileges of Doctors, page 387.* A judge who is a "gift-eater" <note>original Greek: δωροφάγος</note>, see the same, and *Rittershusius on the New Constitutions, page 536, number 101*. In France, it is permitted for judges to accept wine in small vessels, but not in large casks.

### 16. To change, to alienate. To Alienate <term>Alienare: To transfer the ownership of property to another</term>.

Under the name and prohibition of "alienation," only that alienation which is voluntary is included, not that which is necessary, according to Law "Divus Pius," at the end of the beginning; Law "in estimations," on the petition of inheritance; Law "alienations," on the Digest *On the Division of Family Property*. This is because the Laws command that help be more easily given to one who is placed under necessity against his will than to one who freely exercises a voluntary act. Law "if a guarantor," paragraph "if necessary," and the notes there by the Doctors on the Digest *Who are compelled to give security*. Jacob Thoming, decision 31, number 40.

It must be noted here overall what the Interpreters commonly pass down: that even when some prohibition of alienation exists, the benefit of receiving the fruits <term>fructuum: Profits or products of the land, like crops or rent</term> can nevertheless be granted. Hering, *On Guarantees*, citing many in favor of this opinion, chapter 7, number 195. Whence also Jason in Law "son of the family," paragraph

<column-break/>

"Divi," in the second lecture, column 11, in the 12th limitation, on the Digest *On Legacies 1*, writes: that one prohibited from alienating a thing may nonetheless lease the fruits for the entire duration of his life.

### ADDITION.

When alienation is prohibited, a long-term lease is also considered prohibited, Klock, volume 2, counsel 51, numbers 27 and 28. Regarding when an alienation or transfer is said to be made to a "more powerful person," and on the understanding of the title in the Code *That it be not permitted to more powerful persons*, Klock volume 2, counsel 39, number 41; counsel 51, number 21. Some have the right of alienating yet do not have the lordship or ownership, and conversely, many are prohibited from alienating who nevertheless have ownership, Hahn, observation 4 on Sutholt. What alienation is according to the opinion of Seneca, book 5 *On Benefits*, in the same place.

## 18. Encumbrance, Encumbered Goods, Part-Right.
->Goods subject to restitution.<-

The German word, *verfangen* (entangled), *Verfangenschafft* (encumbrance), by its own proper force, signifies debt and obligation: as it is also used in the Statutes of Ulm where *Verfangenschafft* is joined with the "legitimate portion," ***part 1. title 10. §. 2.*** there: *the children and parents are deprived of their Legitimate portion and due duty-share or other encumbrance*. The Legitimate portion is indeed a debt. ***law 36. §. 2. Code on inofficious Testaments.*** <note>A legal term for a will that fails to provide for close relatives, thus violating "duty."</note>

We call them *Encumbered Goods* when the immovable property is tied to the children of the first marriage, and the parents have nothing from them further than the *usufruct* <term>usumfructum: the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</term> or the wear-and-tear. Master Adam Keller ***on intestate succession, title 29. number 80.*** notes that in many places, even today as in the past, it was observed almost everywhere in that Province: that after a marriage was dissolved, either "Encumbrance" or "Part-right" was in use. Regarding encumbered goods, or those subject to restitution, certain points are handed down by Udalricus Zasius <note>A famous 16th-century German jurist</note> in his *commentaries on the Digest, title on the usufructuary, regarding how security is given, number 6.* And how the alienation or transfer of ownership can be fully prohibited by Statute is found in the text of the *Digest, book on the contract of sale, law "if in the purchase," section 1.*

Which estates the **parents** may neither **sell, pledge**, nor otherwise **alienate** <note>original: "alieniren"; meaning to transfer ownership to another</note>, and even if it should happen that they had actually **transferred**, **delivered**, and **handed over** the same to a **stranger** before their **death**, their **children** would still have the **might and power** to demand back such **estates** bound to them, without any **repayment** to the stranger, no differently than happens with alienated **fief-estates**, *according to the chapter "Titius," if the deceased's fief was contested; see Keller at the cited place, numbers 51 and following.*

**The Division-Right** <term>Theil-Recht: A customary law requiring a remarrying parent to set aside a portion of the estate for children from the first marriage.</term> is what we call it when **parents**, after a dissolved marriage, must **divide** with the **children** if they marry again: and they take only a **child's portion**. In both cases, the **children** have nothing more to demand, and are considered settled for their **paternal** and **maternal** inheritance. Thus, they inherit nothing more, even if the surviving **father** or **mother** leaves no other **children**, but only a **wife**.

### ADDITION.

The old **Law of Entailment** <term>Verfangenschafft-Recht: A legal restriction where property is "caught" or "entangled" for the benefit of heirs, preventing its sale by the parents.</term> still flourishes in many places in Germany. See *Herbajus, Daily Matters, folio 97; Arithm. peric. 1. dispute 6. thesis 10; Besold, Politics, book 1, chapter 10, number 19, verse 3.* The **Law of Entailment** is observed in many places; see what it is in *Knipschild on Trusts, chapter 15, number 22.* In Esslingen, it is observed for both a man and a woman entering into second vows [remarriage]. *Chapter 15, number 23.* **Can an entangled estate be granted to others through a last will to the detriment of those to whom it is already bound?** See *Espich in "Specimen of Testamentary Examination," part 1, article 6, numbers 2 and 3.* Adam Keller treats both **Division** and **Entailed Right** in *Judicial-Political Offices, book 2, chapters 10 and 22, page 551.*

## 19. Settling, Contracting. Settlement. <note>original: "Vergleichen, Vertragen. Transactio."</note> See above under the word "Uniting."

If, with the jurist Gaius in the *Digest, law "they contracted," on the Signification of Words*, we love the truth, we must admit that these words **to settle, to contract, to negotiate** <note>original: "vergleichen, vertragen, abhandlen"</note> among Germans in our native tongue—and in its more frequent or common meaning—generally denote the same thing as what the Latins call "to bargain" (*pacisci*), "to agree" (*convenire*), or to settle by any means whatever business in which the consensus of two or more people is required. And **Contract** or **Negotiation** <note>original: "Vertrag, Abhandlung"</note> is the same as what the Latins call a "pact" (*pactum*) or "agreement" (*conventio*). For we are commonly accustomed to speak or write thus: **They have fundamentally settled and agreed upon the purchase, and it has been thus negotiated that the buy-**

<column-break/>

er, etc. See especially Ernst Cothman, *volume 3, response 50, number 16 and many following.* Consult Altdorf, *counsel 99, folio 625.* Yet, they are most often taken for a **settlement** (*transactio*), which the word **Contract** <note>original: "Vertrag"</note> seems properly to denote.

### ADDITION.

A judge [Prætor] ought not to suffer parties to come to arms whom he can settle by his own jurisdiction. *Digest, law "if usufruct," 13, section "most equitable," 3; and law "illicit," 6, section "lest the powerful," 2, on the office of the governor.* **The amicable hearing and settlement** does not depend on the will and whim of the litigants, but is done by public authority. *Justus Oldekop on the Right of Justice, page 28.* Injury [unfairness] in a settlement is not considered according to the true value of the thing, but in view of the doubtful outcome of the lawsuit. *Klock, volume 2, counsel 57, numbers 9 and 10. Berlich disagrees in "Conclusions," 2, conclusion 42, number 12; see Eberhard Fabricius in "Gail Explained," book 2, observation 70, section 1.* One basing a claim on a settlement must prove fulfillment on their own part, so much so that a failure of fulfillment harms them even in the smallest detail. *Klock, volume 1, counsel 51, number 216.* **A thin settlement is often better than a fat judgment.** <note>A common legal proverb: "Ein magerer Vergleich ist offt besser als ein feister Abschied." It suggests that a small, guaranteed compromise is better than a long, expensive lawsuit with an uncertain but potentially larger payout.</note> Baldus, in *chapter 1, final section, on keeping the peace, in Feudal Customs*, says he does not believe it is true that parties can be forced to submit to a common friend [arbitrator], which is alleged by *Arum. book 2, Decision 11, number 72; see Gail on the Public Peace, book 2, observation 8, number 9; Hartmann, title 1, observation 4; Wurmser, title 3, observation 1.* **He who does not keep sworn contracts, let him lose what he has.** Melonius *in the Treasury of Feudal, Civil, and Criminal Law, title 16, number 22. When two contracts exist concerning one thing, the last shall be kept. The same, title 16, number 29.*

### 22. **Verlassen.** <note>German: To leave, bequeath, or abandon.</note> A Bequest <note>original: "Relictum"</note>.

The verb "I leave" <note>original: "relinquo"</note>, when used separately without regard to the inheritance and applied to a specific item, is never extended to the whole estate, nor to the formal appointment of an heir. This is proven in the Law *Cogi*, 16, section *And Generally*, 2, of the Digest on the Trebellian Decree of the Senate. Dynus considered this text the only one relevant to this point, and Bartolus says there that Dynus brought it as an argument that the word "leave," when applied to a single thing, is not extended to a direct or indirect appointment of an heir. That text proves even more according to Bartolus, in that the legal expert speaks generally: the same applies to any indirect word which, when applied to a specific thing or quality, is never extended to the appointment of an heir or the whole of the goods. Alexander in the Law *Humanitatis*, number 2, Code on the property of minors. Baldus, consultation 409, volume 5. Cornelius, 161, volume 1. The Canonists in the chapter *Raynutius* on Wills. And this is the common opinion, according to Vivius, book 1, *Common Opinions*, under the word "leave." Julius Clarus, question 38 on Wills. And through that text, a formal limitation is given to the Law 1, section *From the farm*, of the Digest on the appointment of heirs: where the text states that one who is appointed to a specific thing—when no one else is appointed to the whole—is treated as the universal heir. This holds true when the specific appointment was made using direct "civil" words; it is otherwise if made through "inflexed" or "oblique" words—for example, if he says, "I leave the farm to Titius." For he will not be the universal heir, even if no one else was appointed. Angelus in the section *From the farm*. Text in the Law *In these words* of the Digest on the appointment of heirs. Suarez on the Law *Since in the former*, Code on inofficious wills, section 6, "It is asked," number 2. And this conclusion is so true—that the word "leave" applied to a specific thing or quantity does not create an appointment of an heir—that even if such a word is applied to a son, the same must be said, chapter *Cunctis*, section *Furthermore*, as found in Besoldus, Volume I,

<column-break/>

where it is cautioned that it is not enough to "leave" something to a son, unless it is left by the right of appointment <note>original: "jure institutionis"; a formal legal requirement for a son to be named an heir rather than just a recipient of a gift</note>. Bartolus and Baldus on the Law *In these words* of the Digest on the appointment of heirs; in the final law of the Code on the division of a family estate; and in the *Newest Constitution* of the Code on inofficious wills, the Law *Since it is unworthy* on wills. Suarez, in the cited place, refutes those holding the contrary, and in number 3 of this conclusion, he adds this limitation: unless the testator, through those indirect or oblique words, by applying them even to specific things, had divided his entire patrimony among several people in his will. For then those words, even if oblique, carry the force of direct words, provided the will otherwise had the formal presence of witnesses; see especially Suarez at the cited number 3, who adds two more limitations to this in the following numbers.

If, however, the word "leave" were applied not to a specific thing, but to the whole estate [the university of goods] when no other universal heir has been named, then it is interpreted as an appointment of an heir. Baldus, consultation 136, volume 3. Romanus, consultation 189. Cornelius, consultation 162 at the beginning, volume 1. Alexander, consultation 50, volume 7. Jason in the *Newest Constitution*, number 33, Code on inofficious wills. Schurff, consultation 92, century 2. The singular Gloss in the *Authentica* on heirs and the Falcidian law, in the section *If indeed nothing remained for the parts*. Text in the Law *The Divine* on the military will. Fully treated by Salyicetus in the Law *Since it is unworthy*, Code on those who are unworthy. Hence, if I say, "I leave my goods to Titius," I am seen to have appointed him heir, which is a word that requires two things to concur. First, when another has not been universally appointed; it is otherwise if another was appointed, because then it is not interpreted as an appointment of an heir. But what will the word "leave" mean then? I say that if the Testator said, "I leave my goods to Titius," it is understood as a **trust-bequest** <term>fideicommissum: A request in a will asking an heir to give specific property to someone else.</term>, of which there is a case in the Law *Nam* at the end, Digest on the Trebellian Decree. Suarez, cited place, number 6. Or by way of a quota or part—for example, "I leave half, a third, or a fourth, or another share of my goods to Titius"—it is a **simple legacy** <term>legatum: A specific gift of property or money in a will, as opposed to inheriting the whole estate.</term>. Law *If a part of the goods*, Digest on legacies, 1. If, however, he had said, "I leave a third of my inheritance," then a trust-bequest is also induced by such words. Gloss on the Law *The woman*, final section, Digest on the Trebellian Decree. Salyicetus in the cited Law *Since it is unworthy*. Secondly, it is required that this word be added in a formal will in which seven witnesses are present. It is otherwise if it is added or uttered in a document in which an appointment of an heir cannot be made, such as in **Codicils** <note>Codicils were less formal than wills and, in Roman law, could not be used to name a primary heir, only to give smaller gifts or trusts.</note>; because then it is not interpreted as an appointment of an heir, but as a trust-bequest, according to Salyicetus in the cited Law *Since it is unworthy*, via the Law *Scævola*, Digest on the Trebellian Decree. Add Suarez, in the often-cited place.

Vivius, book 1, under the word "leave." Suarez, rule 45 and following. Menochius, book 4, *On Presumptions*.

## 23. To Bequeath or Provide. <note>German: *Vermachen, verschaffen*; Latin: *Legare*</note>

The word *Lego* <note>original: "I bequeath"</note>, although by its nature it produces a specific legal title (as seen throughout the entire title *on legacies* 1, 2, and 3), nevertheless, if a testator adds the word *Lego* to the whole of his goods—for example, "I bequeath all my goods to Titius," or "I bequeath part of my goods to Titius and another part to Sempronius"—the word *Lego*, insofar as it is applied to the whole of the estate, is interpreted as having the force of a formal **institution of an heir**. <term>Institution of an heir: The legal act of naming a primary successor to the entire estate, rather than just giving a specific gift (legacy).</term> This is according to the notable text in the chapter *Raynaldus*, on the words "furthermore he bequeathed," in the section on wills; see also Schurff, consultation 73, century 1; and Alciatus on the words of the law in the *Digest: On the Significance of Words*. Certainly, the word *Lego* was extended broadly in the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The ancient foundation of Roman law, c. 450 BCE.</note>, but was later narrowed by interpretation, as noted by Maier in *On Wills*, book 1, chapter 5, number 7. Conversely, if another heir has been instituted and the word *Lego* is attached to a specific thing or amount, it is not interpreted as an institution of an heir, but remains a **Legacy**, based on the apparent intent of the testator. This is the common conclusion in the law. See generally Bolognetus in the headings on the *Digest: On Legacies 1*.

## 24. Oath of Reduction. <note>German: *Verminderungs-Eid*; Latin: *Juramentum minorationis*</note>

The "Oath of Reduction" or "Diminution" is the name used in the Saxon courts <note>The *Forum Saxonicum*, referring to the regional legal system of Saxony.</note> for the oath by which a defendant, who has been sued for violence against property or injury to a person, moderates or reduces the damages estimated by the plaintiff. See Moller, book 3, *Semestria*, chapter 38. Once this oath is taken, the Judge must condemn the defendant to pay exactly the amount declared in that oath.

If, however, the defendant refuses to take this oath, then the judgment is made for the amount estimated and taxed by the plaintiff, neither more nor less. See Andreas Rauchbar, book 1, *Saxon Questions*, question 9, where he asks: Is a defendant bound by Saxon law to provide this oath if the plaintiff did not request it before the "Contestation of the Lawsuit" <note>The formal start of a trial</note> or the "Guaranda" <note>A term in old Germanic law related to providing security or legal defense</note>?

### ADDITION.

Add Hartmann Pistor, book 1, question 16; Coler, *On Executive Process*, part 1, chapter 9, number 59; Berlichius 5, conclusion 61, number 65 and following.

## 25. Traitor. <note>German: *Verräther*; Latin: *Proditor*</note>

Although traitors may at first seem pleasing to those whom they have helped, shortly thereafter they suffer worthy punishments, as proven by Camerarius in *Historical Meditations*, century 2, chapter 60; the same author in the following chapter deals extensively with the "reward" and "worthy wages" of traitors.

<column-break/>

### ADDITION.

Johann Christoph Neander, in his *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 252, treats at length the idea that rewards for those who report treachery and conspiracies (which the Greeks call *mīnytra* <note>original: "μήνυτρα"; rewards for information</note>, though wrongly called *mīnytra* for "divine rewards" by Apuleius) ought to be decreed in a Republic.

Traitors do not succeed in **entails**. <term>Entails (fideicommissa): Property arrangements where an estate is kept within a specific family line and cannot be sold.</term> Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 8, number 4. By treachery and **baratry**, the dignity of a Count's retinue is lost. Mundius, *On Offices and Honors*, page 185. "Baratry" <note>original: "barattaria"</note> is a barbaric word, *barattare*, which means to exchange, just like *barre*; hence it refers to the fact that justice is "exchanged" for money. Decianus, *Criminal Treatise*, book 8, chapter 1, number 9. Regarding Traitors, see Schönbner in *Politics*, book 7, chapter 16, throughout. On the punishment of Treachery, see the **Imperial Penal Code** <note>original: "peinliche Halsgerichts-Ordnung," likely the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina of 1532.</note>, article 94. Treachery must be reported to the Superior, article 27. On a lying informant, see Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 25, throughout.

## 26. To Pledge or Pawn. <note>German: *Versetzen, verpfänden*; Latin: *Oppignorare*</note>

No one can deny that the word *versetzen*, in the proper sense of the language, is the same as to pledge, or to hand over in place of a security, and is in no way suited to a sale. Baptista Caesar in *Illustrious Legal Consultations*, consultation 61, number 5, part 2. This should be noted in cases where it is asked whether a thing was sold under a "buy-back agreement" or whether it was only pledged.

See also Göden, consultation 109; Coler, consultation 29, number 69, volume 1; Berlichius, part 2, conclusion 2, number 7, where he states that the words *versetzet* [pledged], *verschrieben* [assigned in writing], and *abgelöst* [redeemed] do not signify a purchase, but a pledge; since words ought to be reduced to their legal meaning, and "redeeming" implies a contract of pledge. Add Wesenbec, consultation 2, number 19, where he deals with the investigation of whether a contract is a purchase or a pledge.

### ADDITION.

How one may pledge another's property. Zorer, part 2, question 6, number 400. The pledging of another's property is not valid, Carpzov, decision 127, numbers 4 and 9, unless the Owner consented to the mortgage (number 5), or the thing is obligated by his will (number 6). Whether a security under a mortgage of all goods is sufficient in cases of arrests [of property], see Schvvanmann in *Process of the Imperial Chamber Court*, book 1, chapter 13, number 18, page 88.

## 27. To Insure or Secure. <note>German: *Versichern*; Latin: *Cavere, Assecurare*</note>

The word *versichern* denotes a guarantee <note>original: "cautionem"</note> and security. Jacob Schultes, notes on Modestinus Pistor, part 2, question 77, number 4.

Letter V.
Uuu uuu 2

It must be known, however, that the term **Security** <note>Latin: *Cautio*</note>, when used simply in Praetorian Law, is understood to mean "sufficient security," which is provided through sureties or pledges. <note>original: *l. 7. §. stipulationum. ff. de Prætor. stipulat. l. 1. §. caveri. de collat. bonor.*</note> <term>Praetorian Law: A flexible body of Roman law developed by judges (Praetors) to supplement or correct the strict statutory law.</term> But the term **Security**, when used simply in civil law or by a Testator, is understood to mean a "bare promise," which is made through a **stipulation**, unless something else is stated or added—such as when someone promises to provide security "suitably" or "sufficiently." <note>See Schneidewin in the beginning of *Institutes on the security of tutors*, number 5 and following.</note> <term>Stipulation: A formal verbal agreement in Roman law where one party asks a question and the other responds with a matching promise.</term>

->ADDITION.<-

On the word **to assure** <note>Latin: *assecurare*</note>, see the authorities cited by Lord Tabor in *On the other such thing*, page 32. The word **To Insure/Assure** <note>German: *Versichern*</note> in common and extra-judicial use sounds more like the warmth of someone inviting another to enter a contract, rather than implying a formal legal security or bond. <note>See Lord Doctor Biccius in *Legal Responses on the risk of hired locations*, above under the word *Landsknecht*.</note> Regarding whether security for **producing a person** <note>Latin: *de Repræsentando*</note> must necessarily be provided in cases involving those whose property is pledged, see Schwannmann, observation 55. On whether security is needed for **appearing in person** when mandates are issued without a clause under Title 23, Part 2 of the Ordinance, see the same author, observation 115. Security for **appearing in court** and for **paying the judgment** is without effect in cases where the matter is already determined and judged. <note>Schwannmann, decision 10, number 18.</note> A person offering sufficient written security cannot always, and in all cases, obtain the requested release of property or person. <note>Schwannmann, Decision 2, number 1.</note>

### 28. Promise, Defense. Advocacy. <note>German: *Versprechung, Verspruch*; Latin: *Advocatia*</note>

**Advocacy**, or the Right of Defense, is more commonly called in the vernacular **Defense** or **Promise** <note>German: *Verspruch, Versprechniß*</note>; that is, a protection, derived from the verb *versprechen* (to promise/defend), just as these terms are used in the *Form of the Treaty between Unnamed Princes* which Waremb ab Ehrenberg presents in *On Treaties*, book 2, near the end of page 205; where in section 2 it is held:

> It should also be that someone, whoever they might be, attacked us Princes, our people, or those who stand in our **defense and protection** <note>original: *Versprechniß und Schirm*</note>, etc.

And from this, a Defender is called a **Lord of Defense** <note>German: *Verspruch-Herr*</note>, and the fee that is paid annually to a Protector is called **Defense-Money** <note>German: *Verspruch-Geld*</note>. See Lord Mager, *On Armed Advocacy*, chapter 2, number 253 and following.

### 29. Defense, Help, and Maintenance. Protection. <note>German: *Vertheidigung, Hülff und Handhabung*; Latin: *Protectio*</note>

The naming of Advocacy in our common language is also done through the words **Defense**, **Help**, and **Maintenance** <note>German: *Theidigung, Hülff, Handhabung*</note>, which are used everywhere as synonyms for defense, as can be seen in the **Treaty of Burgundy**, established at Augsburg in the year 1548, where in section 1 it begins:

> But nonetheless, such terms of Advocacy or protection are placed: "and on the other hand, to be included in the Holy Empire’s protection, shelter, defense,

<column-break/>

and **help**." <note>See Mager, *On Advocacy*, chapter 2, number 252.</note> <term>Treaty of Burgundy (1548): An agreement that settled the status of the Burgundian territories within the Holy Roman Empire, granting them protection in exchange for taxes.</term>

### 30. To Cause. <note>Latin: *Causam dare*; German: *Verursachen*</note>

See Lord Speidelius in *Notable Matters*.

->ADDITION.<-

Blame is fruitlessly directed at someone who provided the cause for the very thing in which they intend to say a fault was committed. <note>Barbosa, book 3, chapter 53, axiom 4.</note> Fault cannot be imputed to one who did not do what they were not bound to do. <note>Axiom 17.</note> It is the same thing for a cause not to exist as it is for it to be extinguished. <note>Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 8, number 285.</note> When the final cause <note>the ultimate purpose</note> ceases, the law itself fails. <note>Chapter 5, number 62.</note>

### 31. Related or Adherent. <note>German: *Verwandt*; Latin: *Adhærentes*</note>

The word **Related** <note>German: *verwandt*</note> is equivalent to the words **belonging to**, **adhering**, **accomplices**, and **followers**, the meaning of which is very broad. It includes not only subjects, but also vassals, household members, Counselors, and others who are in any way devoted to another, even if they are not subjects, as noted by Georg Everhard, following Baldus, Bartolus, and Salicetus. <note>Volume 1, consultation 28, number 1.</note>

> Thus, in the **Privileges of Exemption** against the **Imperial Court of Rottweil**, those are also included who are attached to the most noble House of Austria by no specific form of jurisdiction, since they alone hold the high sovereignty. <term>Imperial Court of Rottweil: One of the high courts of the Holy Roman Empire; "Privileges of Exemption" allowed certain territories or people to bypass its jurisdiction.</term>

And that the word **Relatives** <note>German: *Verwandten*</note> is to be understood as blood relations, but not those related by marriage, I have stated in *Select Legal Matters*, part 1, folio 124.

->ADDITION.<-

The term **Next of Kin** <note>Latin: *Propinqui*</note> includes both sexes. <note>Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 1, number 104.</note> When "next of kin" are called, it is not presumed that there was a consideration for preserving the male line of descent. <note>Ibid.</note> Proximity of blood is described by words, but not created by words. <note>Barbosa, book 14, chapter 97, axiom 1.</note> The affection of close friendship or of mastery often gets in the way of the truth. <note>Axiom 2.</note>

### 32. Renunciation of Noble Daughters, until a vacant inheritance occurs. <note>Latin: *Renunciatio filiarum Nobilium...*</note>

It is well-established by German customs, especially among the Nobility, that daughters—in favor of their brothers and to preserve the male lineage—renounce their right to succession and the parents' estate upon receiving a certain portion <note>a dowry</note>, usually by oath. Regarding this custom and its validity, see the *Strasbourg Consultations*, volume 1, consultation 63, and Menochius, consultation 412, and especially the individual treatises of Dauth, Kellenbentz, Giphanius, and Dalner.

However, since it often happens that those for whose sake the renunciation was made die without male heirs...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on legal renunciations, specifically focusing on the rights of daughters and the "vacant occurrence" (reversion) of inheritance when male lines fail. It follows the previous page's introduction to legal instruments and obligations.</meta>

# Treasury of Practical Knowledge, Augmented

It happens that commonly in an Instrument of Renunciation—the **Letter of Renunciation** <note>German: *Verzigsbrieff*</note>—such a clause is added: **"We renounce and relinquish all goods and inheritance that might descend from our parents, yet in such a manner and until a vacant occurrence <note>German: *ledigen Anfall*; this refers to a situation where a previously claimed inheritance becomes available again because the primary heirs have died out</note>, etc."** This clause ensures that for a daughter who renounces, there remains a place and a right of return to her portion of the paternal, maternal, and fraternal goods and succession. Specifically, since the daughter renounced for that case—namely, for as long as males survive—then naturally, when the condition ceases, its effect also ceases. Or, when the cause of the impediment and exclusion ceases, the exclusion and impediment themselves cease <note>Legal argument based on the Digest: "where the law ceases, the effect ceases"</note>. For a reservation preserves the right of the one making the reservation <note>original: *Reservatio enim conservat jus reservantis*</note>, but only for that one case; if males are present, then the condition expires. See the *Consilia* of Husanus.

And in the meantime, the daughter is not considered excluded, but only suspended from the succession; once the obstacle is removed—namely, upon the death of the brothers or all their legitimate male children to whom she could have succeeded before the renunciation—she succeeds to her portion. See Cravetta, *Consilia* 127 and following.

Lord Kellenbentz also gives this reason here in Question 18, number 6: namely, that renunciations of this kind are matters of "strict law" <term>Strict Law: *Stricti juris*; a legal interpretation that follows the exact letter of the agreement without expanding its scope</term>, and therefore they are not to be extended. See Socinus, Brunus on the *Statutes Excluding Women*, Riminaldus, Surdus, and Decius. Instead, they are to be understood exactly as they are limited: since a limited renunciation usually produces a limited effect. It should only benefit those in whose favor it was expressly placed.

**And the reservation regarding a "vacant occurrence" <note>German: *ledigen Anfall*</note> has this effect: that when the case occurs, it is held as if one had never renounced.** This is according to the writings of Georg Everhard, the *Marpurg Consilia*, and Fichard.

**Whether the grandson of a daughter can make use of this "vacant occurrence"?** Phanutis de Phanutis teaches this in his *Treatise on Dowries*.

Regarding a daughter renouncing in favor of her father: whether, if males fail, she may succeed against the Father’s Will? See Ludovicus, *Decision 85*.

**Whether a renunciation made simply, "until a vacant occurrence,"** stands if the brothers who existed at the time of the agreement die leaving no males, but only daughters: can these paternal nieces be an impediment to the renouncing daughter regarding the portion she yielded to her brothers? See Kellenbentz on Renunciations, Question 19.

He decides that the daughters of a deceased brother

<column-break/>

do not stand as an impediment to the renouncing sister. In every legal disposition, the reason for it must be investigated first; if that reason ceases, the disposition itself immediately falls apart. And if the phrasing or disposition is general, that generality comes from the intention of the parties; it must be restrained by the presumed or intended reason even if the words are precise. For the intended reason governs any disposition, no differently than a bridle governs horses or a rudder governs a ship.

If a renunciation is made by a sister with an added pact that, upon the death of Titius and Sempronius without children, she may return to her goods: does this hold upon the death of only one of them without children, so that while the other survives, she is excluded from the deceased's inheritance? See Tessaurus, *Decision 187*.

Likewise, regarding the return of succession if a woman has reserved it for herself in the event of failing males, **"until a vacant occurrence,"** how far and against which heirs does this extend? See the aforementioned Lord Kellenbentz, Question 20.

Regarding reintegration **from a vacant occurrence** <note>German: *vom ledigen Anfall*</note>, see the *Decisions of the Rota* in the Perusian case of the Nini family, published separately.

Can a daughter dispose of the reserved right of the **vacant occurrence** in favor of her husband if she dies before the males? Kellenbentz seems to affirm this in his *On Renunciations*, Question 22. But I think the contrary is more true, because it is like a trust <term>Fideicommissum: A legal request where property is held for another's benefit</term> initiated by a pact, and an uncertain condition prevents it from passing to heirs. See Noal and Cravetta.

That a daughter who renounced her paternal and fraternal goods under oath, and later wished to involve herself in the inheritance, was restrained by a penal mandate in the Imperial Chamber <term>Imperial Chamber: *Camera*; the supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire</term>, is clear from the precedent in the case of *Holdingshausen vs. Holdingshausen*, June 26, 1591. See Lord Rutger Ruland.

A renunciation of succession made by children to parents, even if valid because of an accompanying oath, does not stand in the way of the children if the renouncing person dies before the parent. In that case, the children (the grandchildren) can still succeed to their grandfather or grandmother and seek the inheritance. This is taught in several laws <note>Citing the Digest and Code of Justinian regarding the rights of children and the "death of the survivor"</note>. In these places, with almost no one disagreeing, they pass this down with one voice, so there is no doubt that this doctrine is approved by the common consensus of the Doctors of Law. See Hartmann Pistor, where he examines thoroughly if and how far this conclusion proceeds; also see Caspar, *Forensic Questions*.

<summary>This page discusses the legal mechanics of how daughters can reclaim inheritance rights through "vacant occurrence" clauses even after signing renunciations. It emphasizes that such exclusions only last as long as male heirs survive and details the rights of grandchildren in these complex succession cases.</summary>

# Book V.

Whether a daughter, who is excluded from paternal succession through renunciation or by entering a monastery, should be counted as a party in respect to the remaining children, see altogether Hartmann Pistor, in the aforementioned book 4, question 8.

However, it is commonly asked: are daughters forced to renounce by necessity? That the **renunciations** <note>original: *Verzig*; a legal surrender of rights</note> **of noble daughters** are not introduced by custom in such a way that the daughters must perform them necessarily and against their will, is a point no one sufficiently experienced in the law would undertake to maintain. For it is established that these renunciations consist solely in the will of the renouncers, and indeed a free and spontaneous one (Bolognetus on the law *naturali* § *nihil commune*, Part 2, number 141; Andreas Dalner on various legal renunciations, § 5, number 1). Even where there are equally strong and notable reasons to the contrary, they may not be forced into this.

Furthermore, in establishing a custom, the mere frequency of acts and simple usage does not simply prove the consent of the people; rather, it must also be shown that this was done with the intent of establishing a law and introducing a custom (Panormitanus in the final chapter, number 12, *de constitutionibus*; Cravetta, counsel 17, number 14; Decius, counsel 215, number 4).

And likewise, one who uses **Common Law** <note>original: *Jure communi*; refers here to the body of Roman and Canon law used across Europe</note>, even if they have conducted acts in that manner for a thousand years, still prescribes nothing; because the "intent to possess" <note>original: *animus possidendi*</note> is lacking in him (law *sine possessione* 25, on usucaption). Truly, the renunciations of daughters agree with Common Law and the decree *quamvis* regarding pacts in the sixth book of the Decretals; for they proceed not from necessity (as a custom would enjoin upon daughters) but at least from free will. Therefore, it cannot be argued that they have been interposed with the intent that they thought to establish a custom and a general necessity of renouncing. Since no custom is introduced from voluntary acts (Porcius, counsel 106, number 64; Decius, counsel 437, number 5). And this opinion—that daughters, to whom a dowry is established and paid at the time of their marriage, are in no way bound to renounce as if by accepted custom, nor is a renunciation considered tacitly interposed if omitted—is proved with many reasons by Lord Barthold Kellenbentz in his treatise on the renunciation of succession, question 7, throughout. And almost the same was decided in a similar case (especially if a possessory remedy was instituted) by the formerly distinguished Assessor of the Imperial Chamber, Johann Meichsner, volume 3, decision 14.

Likewise, that the renunciations of noble daughters are not forced in these places, but are left to the free choice of the daughters, is irreducibly recognized by the solemnity that always takes place therein. For it is well known and no one can deny that noble daughters who are renouncing are assigned an assistant <note>original: *Beystand*; a legal guardian or counsel for the ceremony</note>, and they are led away or

<column-break/>

aside three times, and are always earnestly asked by those present whether they wish to give up their inheritance of their own free and unconstrained will. Only when they have answered this sufficient reminder in the affirmative must they then swear a **physical oath** with raised fingers <note>original: *cörperlichen Eyd mit aufgesetzten Fingern*; a formal swearing gesture</note>. All of this would be unnecessary—indeed, ridiculous to hear—if the noble daughters were required to renounce.

And thus, that frequent use of renunciations confirms our opinion rather than the opposite; for if, through a pact of this kind, they had intended to transfer the universal law to all daughters of that family, both male and female, they would without doubt have ceased the interposition of renunciations entirely and been content with the establishment of the dowry alone. Since an oath (which this pact cannot lack) is a kind of **spiritual torture** and binds the soul (Wesenbeck, counsel 23, number 25). Therefore, since until now girls have wished to use solemn renunciations—which agree with the disposition of Common Law and descend from each person's free will—it must be said that they did not wish to derive or transmit any necessity of renouncing to their descendants.

Furthermore, renunciations are not uniform, and it is left to the discretion of the renouncing daughters, or their curators and assistants, how the renunciations regarding the **reserved vacant occurrence** <note>original: *vorbehaltenen ledigen Anfalls*; the right to the estate should the male line fail</note> are to be conditioned: whether it should be directed toward the paternal, or also maternal, fraternal, and even sisterly inheritance; and whether it can be taken away through the last possessor's testament, or when he leaves only daughters.

For some renunciations are **general**, others are **special**. It is called General when a daughter renounces paternal, maternal, fraternal, and finally all succession. It is Special when she renounces a specific succession, for example, only that of the Father, or even a **fief** <note>original: *feudo*; property held on condition of feudal service</note>: regarding which see Andreas Dalner on various legal renunciations, chapter 2, number 52.

Renunciations are divided into **judicial** and **extrajudicial**. A judicial renunciation is one made in court, with the judge sitting on the Tribunal, or entered into public records. In this case, even if no witnesses are used, the renunciation is nonetheless held as valid; for those things done in court exceed the solemnity of all contracts (law 19, Code on testaments). An extrajudicial renunciation is one made before a Notary and witnesses, or in the presence of the Father and kinsmen only (see Berlich, practical conclusions, part 2, conclusion 43, number 5). And such are commonly made in the **Court of Rottweil**, in the **Swabian Provincial Court**, and also in the **Court of Württemberg**, as the Ordinances of all these courts attest and permit to be done.

Among the requisites regarding the form of these renunciations, the first to present itself is...

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence. Signature: Uuu uuu 3. Catchword: certio- (likely for "certioratio" or "certainty").</meta>

<summary>This page argues that the renunciation of inheritance by noble daughters is a voluntary act of free will rather than a mandatory custom, proven by the elaborate court ceremonies where daughters are asked three times if they consent. It distinguishes between general renunciations of all family property and special renunciations of specific estates or fiefs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of inheritance renunciations, specifically detailing the four essential requirements—notification, a fair dowry, a voluntary oath, and the presence of witnesses—that make a daughter’s renunciation of her family estate legally valid.</meta>

# Expanded Treasury of Practical Law

**Certification.** It is well established that for a renunciation to be valid, it is necessary for the daughter to be **certified** <note>original: *certioratio*; a formal notification of legal rights</note> regarding her rights and the potential prejudice she faces. *Giphanius on renunciations, counsel 2.* Since no one is considered to have given up what they did not know belonged to them (*Chapter "Veniens" and Chapter "Quemadmodum" on oaths; Law "Legitimam," Digest on the petition of inheritance*), a renunciation performed without this notification is void by law. *Law 39, final paragraph, Code on the Velleian Decree of the Senate.* Omitting this notice implies a suspicion of trickery and fraud; for it is presumed that brothers might act in this way for the sake of deceiving their sister. *Law 35, Digest on pacts; Law "Qui cum," paragraph "Qui per," Digest on transactions.*

It is required (2.) that an **appropriate dowry** <note>original: *dos congrua*</note> be established for the daughter, according to the quality of the estate. *Chapter "Quamvis" on pacts, in the 6th book.* For the dowry takes the place of the **legal portion** <note>original: *legitima*; the minimum inheritance guaranteed by law</note> and is likened to it. *Barthol. Kellenbentz, question 2, numbers 32 and 42.* It is especially fitting for daughters to be dowered, since otherwise they might be held in hatred by their husbands (*Final law, Code on the Velleian Decree of the Senate*) or, due to poverty, might make a living from their bodies and break the bond of marriage. And so that this dowry might reach the measure of the legal portion, as *Treutler* wished (*part 2, dispute 7, thesis 2, letter b*).

Once sufficient notification has preceded, and a dowry has been established—taking into account the resources of the estate, the number of children, the status of the husband, and local custom—there follows (3.) the **Oath**, *the said chapter "Quamvis."* By this, daughters renounce all goods of the parents, brothers, etc., or even only the goods of the parents. *The oft-cited chapter "Quamvis"; Wesenbeck on the Digest regarding oaths.* This oath is not to be extorted by force, fear, or fraud, but must be offered from the free and spontaneous will of the one swearing, as is clear from the points cited above.

A doubt occurs here: whether in this case, for persons of high rank, a simple pledge of faith suffices—**"Princely Loyalty, or Noble Truth and Faith"**? <note>original: *Fürstliche Treu, oder Adeliche Treu und Glauben*</note> *See Jos. Nolden on the status of Nobles, chapter 12, number 68 and following.* Natta denies this (*at chapter "Quamvis," number 5*), as does Jal (*in the Authentic "Sacramenta puberum," Code on sales against minors*). Whenever an act in Law is not valid without an oath, then an oath is precisely required, and a pledge of faith does not suffice in place of it. *Natta in the cited place.* In this case, the oath is required as a substantial foundation; therefore, it must be performed precisely and "to the nail" <note>meaning: with perfect accuracy</note>, and it should not be fulfilled by an equivalent, namely through the interposition of faith. *Law 13, Code on testaments.*

It is required (4.) that there be the intervention and presence of parents and kinsmen to exclude trickery and any suspicion of fraud. This is achieved if it is done either judicially (*Law 19, Code on testaments*) or celebrated in the presence of the father—who is considered the best friend of his children (*Law 50, paragraph 2, Digest on the goods of freedmen; Final law, Code on the curatorship of the insane*)—and the kinsmen. For the presence of these people similarly excludes all suspicion of trickery and fraud. *Law "Transactionem" and the Doctors there on transactions; Wesenbeck, counsel 3, number 66.* Especially if

<column-break/>

kinsmen from both the maternal and paternal families are present together. *Mynsinger, response 59, number 19, decade 6.* Nor should they be able to hope for any advantage from it, directly or indirectly. *Law 1, "What we say," Digest on the authority and consent of tutors.*

On the question: Does a woman once excluded by a male remain excluded forever? (Regarding this, see the consultations of Mr. Wolf in the 2nd decade, and among the *Illustrious Consultations* published by my care, 14.) *Ludovicus Molina in his treatise on Spanish primogeniture, book 1, chapter 6, number 22*, along with the Doctors cited there, distinguishes whether the woman renounced simply or through **suspensive words** <note>legal terms that delay an effect rather than canceling it</note>. In the first case, he says she must be called excluded forever. In the second, however, she is admitted to the succession if the males, in whose favor that renunciation was made and by whom she was excluded, have died. For that reservation made in such a case through those kinds of suspensive words preserves the right intact for the one reserving it. *Heigius, question 26, number 16; Law "Si quis" 14, paragraph "Reliqui," Digest on religious matters and funeral expenses; Law 4, paragraph 1, Digest on the modes of pledges or mortgages.* And the word **"until"** <note>original: *donec*</note> stands suspensively, and induces only a temporary exclusion, not a perpetual impediment; by this means, the birth of the disposition is delayed, and consent is removed from the act. *Alex. Raudensis, Milanese Decisions, or Treatise on Univocal Analogy, book 1, chapter 27, number 15 and following.* And since it is limited, it also produces a limited effect. *Law "In agris" 16, Digest on acquiring the ownership of things.*

This is considered so true that not even the living brothers can alienate that portion which the sister reserved for herself in the event of the males failing, while that condition is pending; nor can they transmit it to their own daughters, either by testament or by intestacy. *Law "Final," paragraphs 2 and 3, Code on the commonality of legacies; Alb. Brunus, treatise on the statute of excluding women, article 10, questions 4 and 45; Cravetta, counsel 127.* See *Mynsinger, response 57, number 6; Marburg Consultations, counsel 21; Meichsner, book 3, decision 2.* (Regarding what the clause implies, **"that the son may deal with and rule over the renounced goods as he pleases, etc."** <note>original: *daß der Sohn mit den renuncierten Gütern handlen und walten möge, nach Gefallen, &c.*</note>, I have spoken in decade 1 of the *Consultations, folio 213 and 237.*)

For just as an heir bound to the restitution of hereditary things under some condition cannot transfer them to others in the meantime. *Law "Marcellus" 3, paragraph "Res quae," Digest on the Trebellian Decree of the Senate; Final law, Code on legacies; Paris, counsel 48, number 16, volume 3; Gail, book 2, observation 137, throughout.*

And a husband with **usufruct** <note>the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</note>, a **long-term tenant** <note>original: *emphyteuta*</note>, and a **vassal** are, for that reason, prohibited from all power of alienating, because once their own right is extinguished, they are bound to the restitution of the thing granted as a dowry, usufruct, long-term lease, or fief. *Law "Neque Mater" 14; Law "Ususfructus" 66, Digest on the right of dowries; Laws 2 and 3, Code on the right of long-term leases; Chapter "Imperialem," on the prohibition of alienating fiefs, by Frederick.*

<summary>This page details the legal requirements for a daughter's renunciation of inheritance, emphasizing the necessity of informed consent, a fair dowry, and a formal oath. It also discusses how conditional language can allow a woman to reclaim inheritance rights if the male line fails.</summary>
<keywords>renunciation, dowry, legal portion, oath, noble status, inheritance law, suspensive conditions, usufruct, alienation of property</keywords>

--- Page 1089 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the renunciation of inheritance rights by daughters, specifically focusing on the conditions under which such a renunciation remains valid or can be reversed if the male line of the family fails.</meta>

In this case, since the brothers are likewise bound to the restitution of the portion due to the daughters from the paternal succession, the alienation <note>the transfer of property to another</note> can by no means subsist while the condition is pending. And so it was decided in the Imperial Chamber <note>the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> in the case of Ambrosius Reichers against **Heinrich Sauerzapff** in the year 1570, as reported by Rutger Ruland in his *Chamber Decisions*, question 22. He adds that such an alienation does not proceed even in a most favorable case, namely in the institution of an heir; an opinion also approved by Hubert Giphanius in his treatise on renunciations, page 65.

However, Antonius Faber, in his *Pragmatic Errors*, dissent from this opinion. He establishes that a daughter who renounces—even under the words "until he gives," etc.—is excluded in perpetuity if a male has acquired the paternal inheritance even once. This is not necessarily by the force and intention of the pact, but rather by the acquisition of the inheritance once it has been entered and acknowledged, lest the inheritance seem to have come to another from a certain day or to a certain day, contrary to the laws of inheritance institution. See Mr. Wolff, in his *Eleven Consultations*, consultation 2, number 34 and following.

And although Husanus, in a counsel published by me and inserted into my *Counsels*, volume 1, wishes for a woman once excluded to always remain excluded in perpetuity: yet such an opinion is almost universally rejected <note>original German: "so wird doch solche Meynung fast ins gemein verworffen"</note>. To prevent future disputes in similar cases, for the security of the renouncing daughters, the renunciation should be drafted as a **fideicommissum** <note>a legal trust where property is held for another's benefit</note>, so that after the passing of the last male line, the daughters have free access to the paternal goods, etc., and the renunciation shall not bind them. It may be otherwise if the renunciation is made simply upon a vacant succession.

If a father and mother assign a dowry and other things for their daughter’s departure <note>original German: "Abfertigung"; a settlement or send-off</note> so that she may renounce, and she does so, then it is an irrevocable contract—"I give so that you may do"—and the father and brother are bound, nor can the parents ordain a contrary disposition.

Even when noble daughters and other persons of high status are admitted to equal inheritance, the landed noble estates are nonetheless valued for the sons, while the daughters are settled with money. Fachin testifies in his *Controversies*, book 3, that such an ancient custom also exists in Swabia.

Does a promise to renounce have the force to exclude the promisor from all inheritances, just as if it had actually been performed? See Nicolaus Everhardus the Younger, volume 1, counsel 6. To this may be added Boerius, Fichardus, Mynsinger, and Wesenbeck.

But regarding renunciations, see Giphanius, to whom several counsels on that matter are attached, as well as Barthol. Kellenbentz and Musculus.

<column-break/>

In the individual treatises: *Counsels of Marburg*, volume 1 and volume 4; the *Illustrious Counsels* published by me, numbers 13 and 14; Johannes Bolognetus on the law of stipulations; and on the final law of the Code regarding pacts. There also exists a disputation on this matter among those from Basel, volume 5, by Philipp Dobner, and the *Sylloge* of Johann Jacob Speidelius under the word "renunciation." See also the counsels of myself and my brother, of pious memory, decade 1, counsel 5. Add the *Counsels of Strasbourg*, volume 2, and the *Codex Fabrianus*.

### ADDITION.

Henricus Breulaeus was the first in Germany to "break the ice" <note>original: "glaciem fregit"; meaning he was the first to write extensively on this</note> with his treatise on the Customary Renunciations. Butrigarius enumerates fifty-three species of renunciation in his treatise on the renunciation of civil law. Georg Christoph Walther provides a formula for the renunciation of succession or inheritance in chapter 4, where a daughter retains her full and safe right of succession by virtue of an interposed reservation: "but if in future time, sooner or later, the case should happen that the male line should die out and perish, and thus the inheritance should come and fall back to the female line: then I and my heirs wish to be no longer renounced, and expressly reserve for ourselves the right of return to the left-behind goods in every way." <note>original German: "wann aber in künfftiger Zeit... uns den Regreß zu den hinterlassenen Gütern expresse und ausdrücklich in allweg vorbehalten haben."</note> And in this case, if the brothers, in whose favor the renunciation was made, should depart from life while the father is still surviving, it must be said that the daughter is admitted to the father’s succession notwithstanding the renunciation. See also Pfretfchner on renunciations. A woman renouncing under the condition "until or as long as males live" is admitted when the males fail. Knipschild on trusts, chapter 8.

### 33. Fortress. A Stronghold. (*Veste. Fortalitium.*)

By which word a stronghold or castle is designated. It is also said of a place fortified with ramparts or embankments, even if lacking a house or dwelling. Johann Goeddaus, among the *Marburg Counsels*.

### ADDITION.

Fortresses are nothing other than a number of bulwarks <note>original German: "Bollwerck"; bastions or defensive walls</note> laid out in such an order that one can protect the other. Bonajut. Lorin. in his fifth book. See also Schmuck’s disputation on fortresses, where it is stated: Fortresses are built to hold up the enemy and cause them to lose time; from which lost time many inconveniences arise, such as lack of munitions, death, evil plagues in the army, and especially the arrival of relief forces <note>original German: "Entsatzung"; the lifting of a siege by outside troops</note>,

### 34. On. *Super*.

The word *super* <note>original Latin: "super"; German: "auf"</note>, in phrases such as "on the estate of N." etc., "Lordship," etc., legally implies a pledge or a mortgage. [Citations: Coler, counsel 27; Bartolus on the law *fundus*; Albericus de Rosate on the law *cum ii sicuti* and the Doctors of Law there].

### 35. In that case. *Illo casu*.

Those words "in that case" <note>original German: "auf dem Fall"</note>, that is, "in that event" or "then" (for these words denote the same thing, according to Rolandus à Valle, counsel 38, volume 4), are of a limiting and restricted disposition. Rolandus à Valle, counsel 70, volume 3. And Decius notably says in counsel 336, at the end, that those words "in that case" limit a *fideicommissum* <note>a legal arrangement where property is held by one person for the benefit of another</note> such that the testator's instruction is not extended beyond that specific case. The same author in counsel 273 says that those words restrict the disposition precisely to the case expressed. For these terms, namely "then" or "in that case," have a restrictive force. Decianus, counsel 13, volume 2. Nor can they be verified except in the case expressed. Decius, counsel 63; Pacianus, counsel 63. And it is restricted to the case formally expressed. Rolandus à Valle, counsel 39, volume 4; Decius, counsel 339; Arumæus, book 2, decision 9.

->ADDITION.<-

"Then" <note>original German: "Alsdann"</note>, a particle by its nature restrictive and specific, excludes any other case. Altdorf Counsels, pages 450, 462, 457. Alemann, *On the Law of Money*, page 350. "Then and in that case." Marius Antoninus, 2. R. 59.

### 36. Having taken the advice of legal experts. *Adhibito Consilio JCtorum*.

If those unskilled in the law are appointed as Judges, they can and should employ Assessors <note>legal advisors who sit with a judge to provide expertise</note> learned in the laws, so that they may judge by their advice. In this way, the lack of knowledge is supplied by the Assessors. And thus we see daily that any judges, especially minor ones, seek the Counsels of Legal Colleges and Benches of Magistrates <note>original: "Scabinatuum," referring to the Schöppenstühle or lay courts common in Germany</note>, which opinions are like certain Precedents and are valid in individual cases where the law is in question. Judges are commanded to do this especially in criminal matters by the *Carolina* Constitution <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the unified criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire established by Charles V in 1532</note>, article 189.
Furthermore, we see in certain places, says Matthaeus Stephanus in his treatise *On the Office of a Judge*, book 1, chapter 5, that a practice occurs (which Johannes Ferrarius Montanus testifies is the most foolish of all and happens among the Westphalians, book 3) where, after the accusation and response—whatever they may be—have been made back and forth, the Judge seeks a verdict from the 

<column-break/>

bystanders, who neither had knowledge of the case nor were authorized with the function of judging. These people, departing for a short while (sometimes well-drunk), return and immediately pronounce whatever seemed good to them and "came into their mouth" <note>a Latin idiom for saying whatever occurs to one first without thinking</note>, and it stands as the verdict.
Truly Johannes Ferrarius writes that this is the most foolish thing of all; yet it is observed in certain cities of Pomerania, according to the same Stephanus, number 35, where he says: "And I have it from other trustworthy sources that it also happens in Hamburg in the lower court and elsewhere." It is rightly said that a verdict of this sort from the common crowd is of no importance. For it is the duty of a competent Judge to know the case and to judge upon it. Indeed, a Judge should bring forth a verdict not abruptly, but with deliberation. Ferrarius, in the place cited.

->ADDITION.<-

Whether the Legal Advices or Informations, at any time and in any part of the Trial, even after the conclusion of the case—likewise brief Reports, Recapitulations of the Acts and similar writings, as well as Testimonials or Intercessions of lower Judges on behalf of one of the litigants, and other things of that kind—should be shared with the opposing party? See Oldekop, *On Swearing an Oath on Another’s Soul*, page 89. Regarding the drafting of a verdict, whether and how the opinions of legal experts, faculties, and benches of magistrates should be obtained <note>original German: "Wegen Verfassung eines Urtheils, ob und wie der Rechtsgelehrten Juristen, Facultäten und Schöppenstühle Bedencken einzuholen"</note>. Zorer, part 2, question 20. See also under "Well-considered."

### 37. At least. *Saltem*.

The property of the word *saltem* <note>at least</note> is that it diminishes those things which are said. [Citations: Code of Justinian, Bartolus, Hart. Pistor].

->ADDITION.<-

It is enough that the words perform some minimum effect. Marius Antoninus, 1. Resol. 46. *Saltem*, see Barbosa on definitions, number 5; it is inclusive rather than restrictive, not meaning "only" but "at the minimum." [Citations: Digest 77; Vossius, *On the Vices of Speech*, book 1, chapter 35, page 159]. He criticizes Lipsius, though he does not cite him by name. Cicero: "Snatch this grief from me, or at least <note>original: "saltem"</note> diminish it." This little word is not in the decision itself, but in the reasoning of the decision, just as in the law 54, "on Bishops and Clergy," where the sense is that although the kidnapper deserves much heavier punishments, yet that the woman might have [the minimum] as a consolation. Professor Tabor.

### 38. Clock, Clock-place. *Uhr, Uhrstatt*.

*Uhrstatt* <note>a legal term for a guarantee or place of security</note> is used for a guarantee, and is as much as a deposit and full security <note>original German: "und ist so viel als ein Hintersatz und völlige Versicherung"</note>.

The term "Uhrling" is found in ancient monuments, but what it signifies is not entirely clear to me, says Speidelius in letter V, number 210. However, "Uhrling" means as much as one who affects or strives for more ancient things, or the affectation of a more powerful right—one who is eager to be better or more significant in ancient status and old rights. ### 39. Imperial Vicars. *Vicarii Imperii*.

Such a Vicariate <note>The office of a deputy who exercises Imperial power when the Emperor is absent or the throne is vacant</note> belongs to the Elector of Saxony as a Count Palatine; however, this Palatine-Countship is in Saxony and Westphalia, and not in Meissen. This is seen from a letter of enfeoffment by King Sigismund from the year 1414 (in which he granted as a fief to Lord Eric, Duke of Saxony, Engern, and Westphalia, the land of Saxony and the Palatine-Countship of Saxony and Westphalia).

Regarding what power the Imperial Vicars have, see Master Wilhelm Antonius in the treatise *On Letters of Moratorium*, in the Corollary, folio 26; whether they can grant five-year letters <note>original Latin: "Literas Quinquennales"; a type of legal grace period for debtors</note>, the same treatise on page 89 teaches. That Vicars cannot establish Universities <note>original Latin: "Academias"</note>, but that such a right belongs to the Emperor alone, as does the creation of Doctors, Licentiates, etc., is deduced in *The New Apocalypse of Lucius Verus*, "For the Innocence of the Emperor against Rebels," consideration 26, paragraph 3. There it says: The Palatine Vicar acts in all things as a provider, administrator, and regent <note>original German: "Provisor, Verwalter und Verweser"</note>. His power is in matters that either cannot suffer delay at all, or not without inconvenience; and yet those actions are not valid unless the Emperor later approves them. But truly, to establish Universities or to create new Princes are matters that not only allow for delay but require it. For this reason, the people of Strasbourg did not seek their University from the Vicar, but from the Emperor, etc.

But regarding these Vicars, see Master Gevvold, *On the Seven Electors*, chapter 11. There also exists a disputation on this matter among the Basileans, volume 5. Add Arumaeus, volume 3, discourse 1, and on the Golden Bull, discourse 3, thesis 24; likewise *On the Diets*, chapter 3, number 52 and following, and chapter 7, number 11, etc. See also my work *On Successions and Elections*, folio 215, etc., paragraph 4. For opposing treatises by Bavaria against the Palatinate, see above under the word "Bavaria."

### ADDITION.

If it so pleases you, see also Becker in *Public Law*, pages 88 and 147 following. Whether even the absence of the Emperor gives rise to a Vicariate is a very sharp conflict among the Doctors. Engelbrecht, *On the Romano-German Emperor*, thesis 67, at length. See the small book *On the Right of the Palatine Vicariate of the Rhine*, printed at Heidelberg in the year 1614; likewise the dissertation of Schütz *On the Imperial Vicars and Their Power*. On the Saxon Vicariate upon the death of the Emperor, see August Brunnius in *The Political Triad of Electors*, page 423. Vicars seal in the name of their principals. Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 5, number 54 and following. Jacobus Sbrozzi wrote *On the Power of Vicars*. Whether the Elector Palatine, when the Empire is vacant, is the vicar of the same in the regions of the Rhine, Swabia, and in Franconian Law (as the Golden Bull, chapter 5, once stated) is contested today between him and the Elector of Bavaria; see Limnaeus at length in *Public Law*, volume 2, additions to book 3, chapter 11, folio 215 and following.

<column-break/>

### 40. Vidimus. Copy, Example. See above under letter A, word "Copy".

The clause found in certain Privileges stating that one should believe even a bare "Vidimus" <note>literally "we have seen"; a certified copy of a document</note> prepared by a Notary is not to be understood so crudely, as otherwise an opportunity would be given for many forgeries; rather, it is to be noted that once a Privilege has been legitimately published, etc.

### ADDITION.

Johann Baptista von Baumssdorff and his son Johann Georg had the freedom to "vidimate" <note>authenticate by inspection</note> privileges, instruments, deeds, and writings, to which full faith was to be granted both inside and outside of court, in every way as if they had been authenticated by a Prince, Prelate, Count, Baron, City, Commune, Province, or other court. Mundius reports a similar privilege in *On the Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 328. The Count should first inspect the originals, read them, and compare them with the copies, number 330. The Imperial Chamber Court requires the originals, 332 and 333. A privilege stating that the "vidimus" is to be made entirely equal to the original, number 335.

### 41. Visitation. *Visitatio*.

Regarding the Visitations and Visitors of Dioceses, see the *Constitutions and Decrees of the Diocesan Synod of Constance*, part 4, title 8. There it is arranged that individual Dioceses should be visited once a year, or if it cannot be done due to the breadth of the Diocese, at least every two years. For such a duty of visiting, men who are grave, discreet, upright, skilled in the knowledge of the affairs to be handled, and beneficed men <note>clergy holding a church office with an endowment</note> of good name and example should be delegated. The Visitors are bound to the Bishop by a special oath to exercise the commissioned duty faithfully, with all rancor, hatred, love, and bias set aside, and they must burden no one with superfluous expenses, nor ask for or extort anything for the visitation, except those things which pertain to moderate living and the necessary expenses of the visitation.

## ADDITIO.
<note>Latin: "Addition" or "Supplement"</note>

On the annual visitations of Pastors in the Principalities, see C. Rittershusius in *New Works, page 95, number 63.* Regarding the Visitors themselves, see *page 127, number 118.* Those visiting parents, brothers, sons, or siblings in Universities do not enjoy their specific legal privileges. ### 42. Perhaps. *Forsan.*

The words "perhaps" <note>original Latin: "fortè" or "forsan"</note> in a factual context imply a doubt regarding the facts, not a doubt regarding the law. Jason in *On Transacting, law "if from false things," number 5.* Hence it is commonly said: *Perhaps* is solved by *perhaps*. Therefore, a witness testifying using the word "perhaps" proves nothing, because he appears to be testifying doubtfully. Antonio de Butrio, *Legal Counsel 45, section "it does not stand in the way."* Although these words by their nature imply doubt of fact when applied to an event, this is not always true; see the gloss on the chapter "Part," under the word "if perhaps," concerning the celebration of Mass. Albericus in his dictionary under the word "perhaps" notes that while they imply doubt, they can sometimes imply information or a softening of a statement, depending on the circumstances of the case, though they regularly imply doubt. However, legal experts deciding a case through a similar phrasing are not said to "doubt," but to resolve and decide absolutely, according to the teachings of Cardinal Tuschi, *Practical Conclusions, letter D, conclusion 281.*

## ADDITIO.

The word "perhaps" <note>original Latin: "fortè"</note> implies a motivating cause. Marius Antoninus, *Reflections, book 3, 40, number 48.* Cujas on *The Proxy, law 43 "The Mute."* Experts often respond under the "perhaps of doubt," namely for the sake of modesty, as in *Giving Security, law 8, section 2.* See Barbosa under this word, chapter 127, number 6 and following. Giovanni Pietro Surdi, *Decision 78, number 5.*
The word "perhaps" sometimes denotes truth, and sometimes doubt. Rolando à Valle on *The Making of Inventories, part 2, question 20, number 7.* Words uttered by a legal expert should be understood in a civil or technical sense; it is otherwise if uttered by a layperson <note>original Latin: "idiota," meaning one without professional training</note>, for then they must be taken simply, as they occur to a common person. Symphorus Gylmann, *volume 1, part 1, title 3, vote 3, folio 220.* The word "perhaps" is not always used in a doubting sense. Berlich, *part 2, decision 286, numbers 2, 3, 4.*

### 43. Vizthum. Vice-Lord.

The term "Vizthum" <note>original Latin: "Vicedominus"</note> is properly defined, according to the opinion of the *Speculator* <note>The nickname for the influential jurist William Durandus</note>—whom Lord Mager cites in *Armed Advocacy, chapter 2, number 260*—as the title for the administrators of Episcopal property and jurisdictions.

<column-break/>

The Bishopric of Bamberg, for instance, maintains such a continuous official in Carinthia, chosen from the Cathedral Chapter of that same church. However, see Mager, *at the cited location, number 257 and the two following.* He is, in a sense, the Lord, because he acts in the Lord's stead. In Italian, he is called *Visconte* or *Vice-Comes* <note>Viscount</note>.

Regarding the word "Vizthum," see Hund in the **Bavarian Genealogy**, *part 2, near the end.* This word has different meanings depending on the region. In ancient times in Bavaria, it was equivalent to a Vice-Dominus, or as one might say, a Vice-Roy in Naples, or today a Governor in Milan. For since the sons of Louis IV stayed mostly outside the lands (such as in the Netherlands and Brandenburg), and Louis himself was previously occupied with the Empire, they appointed such Statthalters <note>Governors or deputies</note> or Vice-Dominoes. As can be seen from the old appointments of the highly respected family of the Lords of Nothafft (of whom there were about twelve Vice-Dominoes at Straubing, Landshut, Amberg, and Ligenfeld; and today, Lord Heinrich Nothafft, Baron of Werenberg at Misenfeld, at Schernegg, Hag and Petmos, etc., is the Chamberlain to his Roman Imperial Majesty and a highly renowned Imperial Court Councilor), these officials had absolute power. They had the authority to appoint and remove all services in the land, and only lacked the power to start a war without the knowledge of the Sovereign. Today, however, such an office in Bavaria has been restricted and turned into a mere presidency or judicial office of the established government.

In Austria and other places, the office of Vizthum is of much lower status, and in those parts, it is as much as saying a "Malefizthum" office <note>a pun combining Vizthum with "Malefiz," or capital crimes</note>, that is, one which has to judge over the <term>Blood Ban</term> <note>original German: "Blutbann," the right to exercise high justice or capital punishment</note>. In the new Bavarian territorial laws, it almost seems to have this significance as well, as a special article is described there regarding "Vizthum-matters" and how they are to be handled. According to this view, the derivation would have to be taken not from *Vice* <note>deputy</note>, but from *Vitiis* <note>vices or crimes</note>.

## ADDITIO.

Regarding the Vizthum, see Draco on *Patricians, page 180, number 19.*

As if a vice-lord. See Wehner, *Observations, under the word "Lieutenant," page 350.* Zasius in *Epitome of Fiefs, part 12, number 9.*
