Page 1096
Header: Enlarged Practical Treasury

And so, a **Judgment** <note>original: "Urtheil"</note> is a "partitioning" <note>original: "Bertheil"</note>, that is to say, a distribution of justice.

Whether a Judge is bound to give the reason for a sentence passed? See Lord Wilhelm Anton in his *Corollaries to the Treatise on Letters of Moratorium*, page 22. Likewise, whether a decided matter <term>res judicata | a legal case already decided by a court and therefore not subject to further appeal</term> makes law? Ibid., page 35.

## ADDITION.

In place of the word **Judgment**, the word **Resolution** <note>original: "Abschied," a term often used for formal court decrees or the final decisions of an assembly</note> is often used. Strictly speaking, that which is issued in ordinary proceedings is called a Judgment, while that which arises from the legal process itself is called a Resolution. Suttinger, observation 78, number 1. There are also two types of Resolutions: the **Interlocutory** (provisional) and the **Definitive** (final) Resolution; see more in Suttinger, number 2. On what must be observed in every Resolution, see number 7. That one should not state the cause or reason within the Resolution, see number 4. Resolutions are issued immediately after publication according to the fee schedule, observation 100, number 3.

A sentence is a matter of **strict law** <term>stricti juris | interpreting the law exactly as written without equitable flexibility</term>. From a sentence, no more ought to be inferred than what is necessarily inferred from it, as Melonius explains at length in his *Index of Forensic Matters* under the word "Sentence." A sentence passed against a Principal debtor cannot be mandated for execution against the sureties [guarantors], as discussed at length by Melonius and those cited there. When the conformity of three sentences does not result in **Execution** <note>The formal enforcement of a court's ruling</note>, see Oldekop in *Criminal Observations*, volume 5, observation 30. There are as many Sentences as there are chapters [points] of a Sentence. Law "also" 29, § 1, where the Gloss on the word "other" in the Digest *On Minors* <note>original: "ff. de minor."</note> and Law "what however" 21, where the Doctors of the Digest *On Arbitrators* <note>original: "ff. de receptis, qui arbitrium"</note> discuss this. Cujacius, book 12, observation chapter 2, especially when the points admit separation. That a sentence can be called unjust or void in part—namely, in those chapters acting against themselves—see the chapter "Raynut," 16, *On Testaments*. See more in Schwantmann’s *Decisions*, page 141 and following. If several chapters are defined simultaneously by a Sentence, and an Appeal is interposed only against certain ones, that appeal does not extend beyond those common Chapters, as Christoph Besoldus confirms and follows from the decision of Boërius in the *Treatise on the Oath of Appeal*, chapter 5, number 5; he adds the calculated reason that my adversary’s Appeal cannot help me except insofar as the appeal was made, just as it cannot benefit the adversary himself beyond that point. A Sentence is regularly indivisible, so that it cannot be valid in part (Law 27, Digest *On Dividing an Inheritance*); this fails, however: 1. by reason of diverse things and persons, so that it is passed regarding the property or person of one, but not the property or person of another. Bartolus on the Code *If regarding a common cause*, number 7. 2. If a division of the sentence happens after the fact—for example, a Judge condemned me to ten, I appealed saying I was burdened by five, and I succeeded in this; thus the sentence will be valid for part and not for part. Bartolus on the Code *Against a decided matter*, number 7. 3. By reason of diverse chapters, since there are as many Sentences as there are facts and Chapters. Just as there are as many

<column-break/>

stipulations as there are sums or things to be known (Digest *On Verbal Obligations*). 4. Whenever several are condemned for one sum, although it is one Sentence, they do not therefore become multiple parties promising one sum; rather, if each is held for the whole, the Sentence is split among the persons according to Papinian, so that those who are condemned owe at least their individual shares. Ulpian in Law 10, section 8. It makes no difference whether someone appeals from a whole Sentence or from certain chapters of a Sentence; in which case, however, the other species of the lawsuit upon which no appeal was made are not rescinded, unless they were connected. Whether a Sentence will be good or bad, the appellant is heard regarding the Summons, provided he does so not simply, but with the clause "insofar as the Sentence is against him"—**as much as the judgment is against him, or as much as it burdens him** <note>original German: "soviel ihme das Urtheil zuwider, oder soviel es ihn beschweret"</note>. This clause limits the Appeal of the challenger, so that he does not seem to have appealed except on the condition that the Sentence is contrary to him. While these things are true in practice, I do not know if they can be tolerated regarding the truth of our law. If a Sentence contains several and diverse chapters, and the appellant flees to the benefit of Appeal not generally but only for the parts adverse to him, the opposing party cannot use the communion of that benefit; and the Judge of the appeal can partly confirm and partly reform such a Sentence passed in the first instance, even if this was neither alleged nor sought by the party. Gail, book 1, observation 110; Zinzerling, conclusion 19.

Interlocutory or final judgment, recognition, or decree. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 10. No judgment should be issued without a certain inquiry. How to conduct such an inquiry is taught by Tennin, caution 113. A judge should not judge according to his own discretion, but according to the prescribed law. *Dutch Military Law*, page 39. How a passed judgment grows into a **decided matter** <term>rem judicatam</term>, and in which cases this does not happen: Zorer, part 2, question 14.

A Judge is not bound to give the reason for his sentence. <note>original: "Judex non tenetur sententiæ suæ causam reddere." This was a significant debate in early modern law regarding judicial transparency versus finality.</note> Baldus on the Code *On sentences and interlocutory decrees*. Altdorf Counsel, response 55. Lord Dr. Ludwig, Notes on Wesenbeck *On the Decided Matter*. Jacobus Alemannus denies this in *The Gymnasium of Consultations*, page 660. Lord Dr. Biccius, however, strongly advises that the judge should not add the cause, so that new lawsuits arising from it may be cut off; a bare acquittal, or condemnation, or remission to the records is sufficient. In this matter, he considers that even certain Universities err. **He is a fool who expresses the reason in a sentence.** Panormitanus on the chapter "As if," *On Sentences*.

Sentencing and re-judgment: see Wesenbeck, book 1, counsel 29, number 62. The Germans call it a **Judgment of Devolution** <term>judicium devolutionis | a legal process where a case is transferred from a lower court to a higher one because the lower court failed to act</term> when they say **the matter has not yet matured at the court** <note>original: "die Sach sey an das Gericht nicht erwachsen"</note>. When someone has **three conforming sentences** <note>original: "tres conformes sententias" | three separate court rulings that agree on the outcome</note> in their favor, the remedy of Appeal ceases (see page 184), provided the winning party raises an exception against such an Appeal. It does not stand in the way that the **Imperial Chamber Court** <term>Camera Imperialis | the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</term> does not always attend to the conformity of three Sentences. For if this were understood simply, it would cause great **lengthiness** <note>original: "Weitläufftigkeit"</note>, and matters that are clear and rely on **hand and seal** <note>original: "auf Hand und Siegel beruhende Sachen" | documents that are formally signed and notarized</note> could be delayed. See Bullaeus in his *Counsels*, page 185 (in my copy).

A sentence passed against a dead person is valid if the Judge did not have that fact established from judicial allegations, even if he otherwise knew it as a private citizen. See Barbosa, book 16, chapter 44, axiom 1. A sentence passed against a previous sentence is not valid (Law 1, Code: *When an appeal is not necessary*). See Socinus, rule 438; Scaccia, *On Appeals*, question 11, number 194 and following, and question 8, number 102, inference 1. On whether and when a sentence is declared void due to the **non-transportation of the records** <note>original: "ob non transportationem actorum"</note>, see Farinacci, counsel 167, section 2, decision 40. Regarding a sentence passed upon the desertion of an appeal, see François Marc, decision 1. **Preliminary or Final Judgment** <note>original: "Vor- oder End-Urtheil"</note>: see Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 5, chapter 16, page 374.

Regarding the declaration of a sentence, see Peter Wesenbeck, counsel 38; François Marc, decisions 670 and 745. A sentence cannot be declared more than once. See *Symphoremata Gylmanni*, volume 4, part 1, vote 4, number 13; Scaccia, *On the Adjudicated Matter*, Glossary 14, question 17, number 52.

### 86. Challenging a Judgment. To Appeal.

**To challenge a judgment** <note>original: "Urtheil straffen," literally "to punish a judgment"</note> is the same as to appeal. See Henning Göden, counsel 29, number 10, volume 2; *Saxon Glossary*, article 74, where it says: "You should know, that which we call Challenging a Judgment is called an **Appeal** <note>original: "Beruffung"</note> in Imperial and Canon Law." See also Moller, *On the Saxon Constitutions*, part 1, constitution 19, number 1. For we say that a person appeals when they implore aid from a superior against the injury of another Magistrate (Law 1, near the end: *For what causes majors...*).

#### ADDITION.

Can a Senator's sentence be appealed today as it was in antiquity? See François Marc, decision 75. Can the judge from whom the case is appealed be a judge in the case

<column-break/>

of the appeal itself? See Christoph Besold, *Treatise on Appeals*, chapter 4, number 11 and following; Petrus Gregorius Tholosanus, *On Appeals*, book 4, chapter 17, page 452, throughout. ### 87. Usage and Tradition. Observance.

See above under the word **Observance** <note>original: "Observanz"</note>.

It is established that even a single act of interpretation suffices for usage and observance. See Bender, *On Revisions*, conclusion 20, number 65. And in such interpretive observance, a long span of time is not required; it is enough that it was observed that way at some point. See Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, counsel 47, number 20, volume 1. Thus, an observance that follows in the same terms declares what the preceding reserved right was (Everhard, in the same place, number 19), even if such an observance were not correct. See Cravetta, counsel 492, number 6. Usage and **usurping** <note>original: "usurpantia" | the long-term exercise of a right</note> also confirms an agreement; see at length *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 1, counsel 1, question 2.

#### ADDITION.

See my own work in the *Inaugural Disputation* solemnly held at Strasbourg, *On the Style of the Court*, theses 86 and 87, and my recent notes there. Regarding usage and observance, one should consult Lord Doctor Tabor, *On Suffrage*, page 243, at the end.

**The defendant shall answer him clearly, or one shall write him his enforcement** <note>original: "Der Beklagt soll ihm lauter antworten, oder man schrieb ihm sein Vollung"</note>. *Bauern-Gericht* 1459. ### Winged Courts. <note>original: "Vlögel-Gerichter."</note>

**Winged Courts** are tribunals outside the walls of the old city of Cologne, serving as if they were **wings attached to the rest** <note>original Latin: "quasi cæteris alæ appendentes"</note>. Limnaeus, volume 2, addition to book 7, chapter 10, page 186. These tribunals were formerly suburban, but now, though enclosed within new walls, they remain in their own power and district. (Ibid.)

### 93. Birds and Fowling. <note>original: "Vögel, Vogelfang. Avis, Aucupium."</note>

->ADDITION.<-

Duke Eberhard graciously granted to the people of Reutlingen that they may catch blackbirds and similar birds in their vineyards during autumn when the grapes are ripe. Limnaeus, volume 2, addition to book 7, chapter 42, folio 319. The otherwise barbarian Turks hold birds to be **free living creatures** <term>ζωα ελευθερα | a Greek phrase meaning animals that are naturally free and not subject to human ownership</term>, as holy, privileged, and exempt little animals that delight both God and men. Busbecq, in his 3rd Epistle, tells of a Venetian who, in Constantinople,

<column-break/>

having treated a large bird unmercifully, was dragged by the Turks before a criminal judge. Lord Dannhauer, in his *Evangelical Memorial*, folio 690. Concerning two little sparrows that come from a castle or a tree: Zeiller, century 2, question 46, page 241. ...look white in winter, according to Zeiller in his *Travels through Italy*, page 38. Regarding **lark-fowling** <note>original: "Lerchenstreichen," the practice of catching larks with nets</note>, this is forbidden to the peasantry, idlers, and other common folk; it is treated like other forms of **minor hunting** <note>original: "Nieder-Weidwerck," hunting rights pertaining to small game</note>, and no one is permitted to engage in such netting on another’s land and soil. More on this can be found in the *Leipzig Revenue Matters*, chapter 30, throughout. It is believed <note>original Latin: "Creditum est"</note> that the lark carries one claw on its feet that is twice or thrice as long as the others, so that when it has settled on the ground, it can quickly spring high into the air and escape danger, as noted by Libavius in his *Singularities*.

Elector Johann Sigmund of Brandenburg once shot a **white lark** with a rifle ball on the Leipzig field while it was flying and singing; this occurred in the presence of the famous poet Friedrich Taubmann, who composed a poem <note>original: "Carmen"</note> about it. Old Austria formerly bore five golden larks on a blue shield as its coat of arms, according to Adam Berg in the *New Mint Book*, folio 3. In the East Indies, there are beautiful **parrots**, red on the back with small yellow feathers; they are somewhat smaller than those from America but learn to speak much sooner. Our barber, writes Levinus Hulsius, had one that would crow whenever the rooster crowed, and when the cat meowed, it would cry out as well. It also called out, "Get to work, cook! Get to work!" He might have received a hundred thalers for it in Holland, whereas there one can easily obtain one for a glass flask worth two batzen <note>a small silver coin</note>. The **Right of Fowling** <note>original Latin: "Aucupandi Jus"</note> is counted among the Royal Prerogatives <note>original Latin: "Regalia"</note>, according to Klock, volume 1, consultation 29, number 185; it is inherent to the jurisdiction of a territory (ibid, number 745), and the exercise of this right serves as conclusive proof of the possession of said jurisdiction (Klock, ibid, number 187). Flying creatures <note>original Latin: "Volucres"</note> are whatever are able to fly, thus bees, wasps, flies, and butterflies are flying creatures, yet they are not **birds** <note>original Latin: "aves"</note>, as noted by Sebastian Medicis in *On Fowling*, part 1, number 31. If someone gives two hawks annually, those goods are not therefore presumed to be feudal, according to Gottfried Anton, *Feudal Disputations* 15, thesis 7, letter E. ### 89. Undivided Goods. *Bona indivisa.*

->ADDITION.<-

Unmixed, undivided, and undisturbed. *Limn. in Public Law book 7. chapter 10. page 201.* On undivided goods see *Master Speidel in Notables* under the word "undivided," regarding its legal force, *Klock volume 3. counsel 182. numbers 561 & 438.*

### 90. The First Cut <note>original: "Vorschnitt"</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

*At harvest time, the right of preference in reaping.* <note>original Latin: "Messis tempore jus prælationis in metendo." This refers to a feudal or local right where certain parties were entitled to begin the harvest before others.</note> *Master Dürr on Manorial Courts thesis 11. 28.*

### Wing Courts <note>original: "Vlögel Gerichter"</note>.

Wing Courts are tribunals located outside the walls of the old city of Cologne, hanging off the others like wings <note>original Latin: "quasi cæteris alæ appendentes"</note>. *Limn. volume 2. additions to book 7. chapter 10. page 186.* These tribunals were formerly suburban, but now, though enclosed within the new walls, they remain in their own strength and district. *ibid.*

### 91. Staple Goods <note>original: "Vendgüter"</note>. Merchandise subject to the staple.

->ADDITION.<-

Staple goods, as they have been called from ancient times, *Limn. in Public Law book 7. chapter 10. page 201. Most recently, Wehner’s Supplement page 69.* <note>Staple goods were items that, by law, had to be offered for sale at a specific market or "staple" town before they could be exported elsewhere.</note>

->ADDITION.<-

### 105. Out-dweller. Forensis.
An "Out-man" <note>original: "Außmann"</note> is a citizen who, although sitting outside the city, is nevertheless within the market jurisdiction or territory. ### III. Reason. Cause. <note>original: "Ursach. Causa."</note>

One must not focus on the act that was caused, but on the act that causes; the subsequent act is regulated and governed by the primary cause. See Franzkius on *laudemia* <note>term: "laudemium" — a fee paid by a tenant or vassal to a lord upon the transfer of property</note>, chapter 16, page 395. On the subject of "cause," Barbosa writes extensively, as seen above under the word "Fief" <note>original: "Lehen"</note>.

---

# W.

### 1. To Watch, To Keep Watch. <note>original: "Wachen, Wacht halten. Excubias agere."</note>

The question arises: can subjects be compelled to keep watch and perform sentry duty in the Lord’s castle without distinction? This question was debated in the case of Pappenheim against Elgaw. In that instance, the Lord alleged the rights of the Magistrate, claiming this right belonged to him by virtue of his authority. However, the Associate Judges <note>original: "Assessores"</note>, following the opinion of Jacob de Saint-George on homage <note>original: "de homag. col. ult."</note>, made a distinction: Subjects cannot be compelled to perform night or day guard duty in a castle unless there is an imminent danger of the Lord being betrayed, a time of war, or a necessary requirement for guarding—or unless they are bound to this by a specific contract or long-standing custom. Since in this case no necessity, danger, or custom was alleged, it was concluded that the subjects should not be burdened by it. See Master Rutger Ruland, *Decisions on Controversial Law*, question 23.

### ADDITION.

Whoever intends to go on watch must always appear fully armed. *Dutch Military Law*, page 115. He who leaves his sentry post before he is relieved shall die, page 148; unless the enemy should drive him back, ibid. Everyone is bound to perform watch duty in times of necessity, according to Mundius, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 1, number 205 and following, and numbers 267 and 303. Watch duty and the guarding of gates is not fitting for those outside the jurisdiction <note>original: "forenses"</note>, chapter 1, number 199; though there are exceptions, chapter 1, number 200.

### 2. Wax. <note>original: "Wachs. Cera."</note>

The use of green and black wax is permitted for general use. Red wax belongs only to those placed in high dignity and fortified by privilege: especially the Emperor, Kings, and Princes, as well as other Magistrates, Nobles, Doctors, and others. For just as the difference and preeminence of colors is observed in Coats of Arms, so it is also in the wax used for seals. See Bornitius, *On Instruments*, book 1, chapter 20.

The use or license of red wax—*to seal with red wax*—is usually granted to cities as a reward and privilege. See my work *On Legates*, page 19, as is evident from the grant of King Matthias in the year 1469, on the Eve of Saint Peter and Paul, made to the city of Bautzen <note>original: "Budissinensi"</note>. *Also, by our aforementioned Royal power and authority, we have granted the grace to our beloved and faithful subjects of the Crown of Bohemia in our Royal city of Bautzen, for their singular honor and adornment,*

<column-break/>

*and given that they and their descendants, henceforth and for all eternity, shall and may seal with red wax.*

Yellow wax, however, which is not in use among us but is rather considered common or cheap, is characteristic of the Kingdom of France. Gabriel Chappuys, *Dissertation on the Kingdom of France*, chapter 1. Bornitius, in the cited place, under the word "Although" <note>original: "Quanquam"</note>, according to the formula: *And sealed with a large seal of yellow wax* <note>original: "Et scellé de gros Seel du Cire laune"</note>. See *Antiquities and Researches of France*, page 164.

Nevertheless, the court of Rottweil <note>original: "Dicasterium Rovvilense"</note> makes use of it.

Regarding the wax upon which a seal is impressed: today it is either placed on paper or poured into a capsule and appended to the parchment. This is usually called the "Bulla" of the Emperor or Kings; in ancient times these were made of gold (Bornitius, cited place), perhaps because the seal itself was golden.

### ADDITION.

Great Princes and Republics are also prohibited from sealing their acts and letters with red wax [without privilege]. Mundius, *On Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 320. In the year 1656, the Lord Co-heirs <note>term: "Ganerben" — joint owners of a castle or estate under a family compact</note> and the Burgrave of Rotenberg Castle sealed with yellow wax set in green wax, but the City of Nuremberg sealed with yellow in red wax. See *Nuremberg against Bavaria regarding the point of Restitution*, page 82. See a similar passage on page 58.

On the various uses of wax, see Mr. Harsdörffer's *Conversations*, part 1, page 227. France and Rottweil seal with yellow wax; it takes its name from "growing" <note>note: a play on the German word "Wachs" (wax) and "wachsen" (to grow)</note>, ibid. Emperor Wenceslaus sealed the privilege he gave to the barbers <note>original: "Badern"</note> with white wax. We read that Emperor Frederick III created the Duke of Modena and Reggio, granting the faculty of sealing with white wax. The King of France attributed the same power to René, King of Sicily, in the year 1468. For the Kings of France have this peculiarity: they use white wax privately. The Kings of France use yellow wax for seals, and it was granted as a great favor to René of Naples and Sicily by Louis XI, King of the Franks/Gauls, that he might use the same. Kirchner, *On the Legate*, book 2, chapter 8, number 110. Wax of a green color is not to be considered so cheap, since Estienne Pasquier observed several letters of the King of France reinforced with wax of that color. And the University of Oxford also uses it, according to Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 1, chapter 11, number 33; who, at number 27 and following, writes much concerning white, green, and red wax. How the city of Lauingen obtained the freedom to seal with red wax from Emperor Otto I, see Zeiller in *German Itinerary*, page 154. Regarding the right of signing with red wax, see Mundius, *On Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 319 and following. Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 8, number 4. Most recently, Johann Christian Viliz, *On Imperial Counts Palatine*, in his annotations to section 10, on the phrase "to seal with red wax." Wax as a payment or pension from peasants, see Limnäus, in *Public Law*...

### 3. Guarding, Protection, Watchmen. <note>original: "Wachten, Hut, Schützen. Custodia."</note>

Custody proves that those borders belong to the one providing the guard. Law *in nomine* 2, section *in Sardinia*. Code, *On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect*. Menochius, counsel 147, number 17, with cited sources. It is an evident sign of the division of territories: Joseph Mascardus, *On Evidence*, volume 1, conclusion 402, number 2. Indeed, the act of placing guards or guarding to prevent damages denotes the lordship of jurisdiction: because the Lords of lands and castles are deputed as guardians at all times to prevent harm. Hieronymus de Monte, *Treatise on Borders*, chapter 52, number 6; and as referenced in Gylmann, *Judicial Matters*, book 2, decision 35, number 39, where he cites many others.

->ADDITION.<-

The guarding of castles is to be done at the expense of the lords. Mundius, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 4, number 64; except for the case in chapter 4, numbers 65 and 66. A "Fief of Guard" <note>original: "feudum Guardiæ"</note> is that which is given for labor and guarding to the person to whom the custody of a castle or town is committed. It is called *Guardia*, which among the Lombards signifies "custody," derived from the German *Guart*—from which comes *Warthe* <note>note: a lookout or watchtower</note>, meaning "custody," and *Guardianus*, meaning "guardian." Mr. Dr. Ludovici in *Synopsis of Fiefs*, chapter 4.

### 4. Watch-master. <note>original: "Wachtmeister. Excubiarum præfectus."</note>

He is commonly called the Prefect of the Watch. His duty (especially for a senior rank) is to organize and lead out the watches, and to keep the other prefects of lower ranks in strict discipline. He receives the military password <note>original: "Tesseram militarem"</note> from the Master of the Horse and distributes it secretly; if a tumult arises, he is to signal the army and indicate the place where the engagement must occur. Reinhard König in *Political Theater*, part 3, chapter 10, under number 4.

->ADDITION.<-

The ancient Greeks used to call those who have command over the watch *prophylakes* <note>note: Greek "προφύλακες"</note>, meaning "fore-guards" or "chiefs of the guards." Aeneas often calls them by this name in his *On the Defense of Fortified Positions* <note>original: "in Poliorcetico"</note>.

### 5. Weighing Tax. <note>original: "Waggeld. Vectigal pro ponderatione mercium."</note>

Weighing tax is a certain duty paid on account of the weighing of goods. For weights and measures are royal prerogatives <note>term: "regalia" — rights and powers belonging exclusively to a monarch</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the purchase of the scale at Nuremberg, see Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 4, chapter 4, number 84; on the weighing tax, the same author, book 7, chapter 17, numbers 14 and 17. Regarding just weights, see Rittershusius in *New Constitutions*, page 190. To whom the inspection of weights belongs was stated above under the words "Weight, Ell, and Measure" <note>original: "Gewicht, Eln und Maß"</note>.

### 6. Election, Choosing. <note>original: "Wahl, Wählen. Electio."</note>

The words "to choose" <note>original: "eligere"</note>, "to elect" <note>German: "Wählen"</note>, and "to will" <note>Middle High German: "Woliti"</note> are sometimes used <term>improperly</term> <note>original Greek: "καταχρησικῶς" (katachrēstikōs) — used in a non-literal or abusive sense</note> and loosely to mean to declare, approve, receive, and take into Lordship. This occurs when a legitimate heir succeeds and is inaugurated, and loyalty and subjection are promised and performed for him. See Melchior Goldast on Bohemia, book 6, chapter 20, number 9, where he adds: "What, I ask, shall we say of the Kings of Spain and France, regarding whom the word 'to choose' and 'election' is very frequently used, not only in Histories, but even in the laws and canons themselves?" There exists a formula for the inauguration of the King of the French, in which the Archbishop of Reims, in the name of the people alone, says that he "chooses the King." See Goldast in the cited location at the beginning.

->ADDITION.<-

In the election of the Knights of Saint Michael <note>a French order of chivalry founded by Louis XI</note>, ballots are placed in a silver basin. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 2. d. 54. Question: If the majority of the Electors, having ignored a legitimate citation, do not appear, or if they withdraw before the Election is finished, can the minority proceed with the Election? See Becker in *Public Law*, page 41 and following.

Regarding the free Election of the Emperor by the Germans, and how Charles V asserted that right for himself and his heirs, see Jacques Auguste de Thou, book 2 of his *Histories*, in the description of Germany near the end. If three out of seven Electors choose a colleague, they prevail over the remaining four who choose a stranger. *Saxon Mirror* <note>term: "Sachsenspiegel" — the most important law book of the German Middle Ages</note>, book 3, article 59, gloss at folio 426, b, column 2.

### 7. Election Day. <note>original: "Wahltag. Comitia Electoralia."</note>

The convocation of the Electors is a legal act by which the Elector of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinus"</note> summons the other Electors, under a specific form prescribed in the Golden Bull <note>original: "B. A." (Bulla Aurea)</note>, to carry out the Imperial election in the City of Frankfurt. Golden Bull, title 4, paragraph "furthermore as often as." See generally Arumaeus in his introduction on the Imperial Diets throughout, where he treats everything that might pertain to this exactly, and specifically in chapter 2, number 13, regarding when only the Electors began to be called; and in number 31, he teaches at length that an "Election Day" <note>original: "Wahl-Tag"</note> and a "Collegial Day" <note>original: "Collegial-Tag"</note> differ (as the King of Bohemia is accustomed to be present at the former, but not likewise at the latter).

->ADDITION.<-

On Election Days, see Limnaeus, book 2, Addition to law 2, chapter 15, page 88; and Becker in *Public Law*, page 37. A future Election must be announced not to the Nobles of the kingdom, but to the Elector himself, even if he is staying outside his Electoral territory. Whether that time can be limited by the Elector of Mainz; and whether all Electors must be summoned? Page 38.

### 8. Goods. <note>original: "Wahren. Merces."</note>

Under the term "merchandise" <note>original: "merces"</note>, movable things are indefinitely included (without making a distinction whether they are made of gold, silver, or any other material) which are accustomed to and can be brought into the commerce of buying and selling. Law 1 on the contract of sale; also the law on the "definition of merchandise," where Alciati and Brechaeus discuss the "Meaning of Words." This goes so far that in the matter of coining, even money (which it is well known is mostly melted from gold or silver) is accustomed to fall under the name of "merchandise." Bartolus on law 3, section C on nautical interest. But see Thomingius, volume 1, counsel 24, questions 6, numbers 2, 15, and 22, where he defends the contrary view.

->ADDITION.<-

Merchandise is numbered among movable things. Mundius on duties and honors, chapter 6, number 56. 8. The merchandise of merchants should not be subjected to burdens, chapter 6, number 45; and they are taxed according to their value, chapter 6, number 93. A mortgage on all goods, although it includes merchandise for sale, does not mean they cannot be freely sold or alienated. Marius Antoninus, book 2, Case 57, numbers 14 and 6.

### 9. Pasture, Right of Grazing. <note>original: "Waid, Waidgang. Jus pascendi."</note>

The "servitude of pasturing" is the name given to the right of grazing livestock on another's land; and for this to be a "real servitude" <note>a right attached to the land itself rather than a specific person</note>, it is required that one possess a neighboring estate to which this service is owed. Regularly, one is prohibited from grazing their animals in another's field unless they have an established or prescribed servitude; and even then, one must use the servitude exactly as agreed upon in the establishment or as it was prescribed. Therefore, if the prescription or agreement was for grazing sheep only on another's land, it is not permitted to graze oxen, swine, or horses there, nor can this servitude be used for a greater number of livestock than specified. See Schneidewin on the rubric and beginning of the title on rural estates, number 31 and following. Wehner under the word "Waidgang."

Where someone has the right of pasture by right of servitude, the owner of the land <note>original: "Dominus fundi"</note> may not change the face of the soil <note>i.e., plow it up or build on it to prevent grazing</note>. I discuss this in my *Deliberations*, book 8, question 4.

On the prescription of the right of grazing, see Pantchman, volume 1, second-to-last question. Most recently, Christoph Philipp Richter, part 1, counsel 35, number 12, folio 226, and number 22, folio 127.

->ADDITION.<-

Grazing fields are those in which livestock and herds are pastured; they are called "Waiden," and in some places "Zuschlag" or "Waide kämne." Pastures are either communal or private. There are two types of the common right of grazing: one is the servitude of "living pasture," which is spoken of during the time when acorns are on the trees and in the woods <note>term: "Mast" — the practice of grazing pigs on fallen acorns or nuts</note>; the other is "various pasture," which is said to exist during the time when there are no longer any fruits upon the earth. Private pastures are considered in two ways, either insofar as...

**10. Forest. Woodland.** <note>original: "Wald. Sylva."</note>

When a *woodland* is sold, it is not understood that the wood already cut there is sold; because in a sale made simply, by the nature of the sale, items already separated from the soil at the time of sale do not pass with it, according to the Law "On Selling," final paragraph of the Digest *On the Contract of Sale*. For this reason, if a field were sold, the grain already cut and lying there would not be included, but only that which is still hanging (growing), according to the final Law, penultimate paragraph of the Digest *On Acts Done to Defraud Creditors*. And when a <term>coppice-wood</term> <note>original: "sylva cædua," a forest managed by periodic cutting</note> is sold, it is not understood that the acorns which fell before the cutting of the forest are sold, but only those which were on the trees at the time of the cutting. Law "With Hand-Sown," paragraph "If a Coppice-wood," in the Digest *On the Contract of Sale*. It would be otherwise if "all the fruit of the forest" had been sold. Mozzius, *On Contracts*, title "On Buying and Selling," in my copy page 354, number 47. For by that word *all*, which is universal, comprehending everything and excluding nothing, all acorns would pass—both those present at the time of sale and at the time of cutting.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the borders of the forest <note>original German: "An den Vorsaumen deß Walds"</note>. *Acts of the Teutonic Knights*, page 184. What the woodland law <note>original German: "das Waldrecht"</note> is, see Knipschild, *On Imperial Cities*, book 2, chapter 7, number 107. He who has the right of gathering wood <note>original: "jus lignandi"</note> for burning in another's forest may not cut down healthy trees fit for building, but only dry brushwood and twigs. Number 108. What if he has the right to use wood for both the hearth and for building? Number 109. To whom the acorns belong <note>original German: "Eichel wem sie zugehören"</note> if someone has been granted the right to cut wood in a forest for five years. Melonius, in the *Treasury of Feudal, Civil, and Criminal Law*, title 9, number 57; see also above under **Wood**.

The right of gathering wood is proven by common reputation alone. In that place, Ummius in *On Procedure*, page 749. Freher, book 2 *On Reputation*, chapter 4, last number. It should not be doubted that the right of cutting wood can be granted as a <term>fief</term> <note>a grant of land or rights in exchange for service</note>. Gothofredus Antonius, *Feudal Disputations* 3, thesis 5, letter d. Regarding the sale of a coppice-wood, see Faustus, *Counsel* 435, for the treasury. Whether cut wood is included when a forest is sold, see Agricola, *On Pertinences*, thesis 3, question 15. For by the word "Forest" <note>original: "Sylva"</note>, a woodland or grove is signified. Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 7, chapter 23, number 2. The Distinguished Lord Scipio Gentilis, in the Digest *On Hunting*, thesis 43, wishes it to be understood that when a forest is granted as a fief, the right of hunting is also tacitly granted. Argument from Law 62 of the Digest *On Usufruct*. Lord Tabor, in *Criminal Gleanings*, page 970. Agricola, *On Pertinences*, chapter 2, thesis 3, question 1. Regarding the Imperial Forests and

<column-break/>

Woodlands <note>original German: "Von deß Reichswalden und Forsten"</note>, Goldast, *Imperial Transactions on the Majesty of the Empire*, part 2, page 34 and page 77. When, by reason of Princely Sovereignty and Lordship, or the enjoyment of the mast <note>original German: "Eckergenieß," the right to graze pigs on fallen acorns</note> of an oak forest, wild pears, apples, and other wild fruit are taken, should seizure mandates be decreed according to the constitution? Schwanmann, 78, number 11 and following. Regarding the words: "With all wood-rights and jurisdiction in wood and field" <note>original German: "Mit aller Holzlich und Gerechtigkeit in Holtz und Feld"</note>, see extensively Lord Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings*, page 59. Regarding wood, wasteland, and thickets <note>original German: "Mit dem Holtz, Wüstung, Gehölz"</note>, page 58. Forest fruit, acorns, beeches, wild fruit, and wild bees <note>original German: "Waldsfrucht, Eichel, Buchen, wild Obst wilde Immen"</note>. Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 6, chapter 3, pages 113 and 150. Regarding forest ordinances <note>original German: "Von der Waldordnung"</note>, Limnäus, book 7, chapter 35, number 30, pages 416–417. The entire forest around Nuremberg is divided into six districts <note>original German: "Hueth," or "guards"</note>, and each district is estimated at ten thousand *Morgen* <note>a traditional unit of land area, roughly what one person can plow in a morning</note>. Every peasant is obligated, for his boundary stones by which his lands are marked off from the Imperial soil, to drive a stake three feet long every year in the springtime. This marking is also inspected on horseback every seven years, and where the stones have been moved or are missing, they are replaced. The Council of Nuremberg received the freedom from Emperor Sigismund in the year 1433 to take in more forest-companions than before. Regarding felled trees, see Lord Tabor, *Gleanings* 10. What is contained under the name of "trees," Law 2, *ibid.*, thesis 9. What ivies are, *ibid.* What reeds are. The Egyptians used reeds instead of wood. A reed-bed is compared to a coppice-wood. A cut reed used to be weighed by the pound. *Ibid.*

**11. When, Since, Where otherwise, But when.** <note>original German: "Wann, Da, Wo anderst, Wann aber."</note> see above under the words **So, If, But If**.

The word *If* or *When* <note>original: "Si, Wann"</note> implies a condition rather than just a time, and it establishes a matter in an indivisible moment, so much so that it cannot be fulfilled except in its specific form. Bartolus on Law 1, *On Conditions and Demonstrations*. For example: "I bequeath one hundred to my wife, if she does not remarry and preserves her life as a widow." For if, having become a widow, she later remarries or lives dishonorably, she is deprived of the legacy and is compelled to return all fruits and profits received in past years. Law "If truly," and the following paragraph in the *Authentica* "On Marriages" and "To whom it was left" in the Code *On the Removal of the Indictment of Widowhood*. Paulus de Castro and others, in the final Law of said title. Cavalcanti, *On the Usufruct Left to a Woman*, number 117. For this condition requires perpetual, not merely temporary, widowhood. Cavalcanti, *ibid.*; see Tuschus, letter C, conclusion 598.

The word *Provided that* <note>original: "Dummodo"</note> has the same significance. Hence Aretinus says: a husband had left his wife as the mistress and usufructuary for her whole life, *provided that* she kept a chaste and widowed life. But if she moves on to a second marriage and leads a dishonorable life, because of the emphasis of the word *provided that*, she falls from (loses) the usufruct.

And whatever fruits the widow has gathered, she must restore them all. Cavalcanti, *On the Usufruct of a Wife, number 117.* Thus the word **provided that** <note>original: "dummodo"</note>, whether it implies a manner of acting or a condition, must be specifically fulfilled. Marta, *part 1, clause 34.*

The word **When** <note>original: "Quando"</note> implies a condition. Decius, *counsel 421, number 5.* Reusner, *book 3, counsel 27, number 82 and following.* It is the nature of a condition that it must be fulfilled before any benefit follows. *Law "Thais," section "Stichus," Digest on testamentary trusts of freedom; Law "He who to the heir," final section, Digest on conditions and demonstrations.* Ruinus, *counsel 181, number 2, book 2.* For a condition must be fulfilled in its specific form. Alexander, *counsel 130, number 1, book 2, and counsel 212, number 6, book 6.* M. For any act performed under a condition is considered as if it had never been done if that condition fails. Moller, *book 4, semestr. chapter 1, number 18.* See Jakob Schultes, *Practical Questions, book 1, question 51, number 26.*

The adversative phrase **but if** <note>original: "si verò"</note> implies that one of two opposing arrangements can be true, but not both. Therefore, if a father leaves his law books to a son who wishes to profess Law, **but if** he wishes to profess Medicine, he leaves him his medical books, the son cannot choose to profess both. Baldus, *counsel 412, book 1.* Because he cannot vary his choice. Alexander, *counsel 9, number 4, book 7.* See generally Tuschus, *letter D, conclusion 240.*

The word **Grant, or if** implies a condition. Klock, *volume 3, counsel 109, number 34.* **If** <note>original: "Si"</note> usually and regularly denotes a condition, just as the particle **when** <note>original: "cum"</note> does. Examples are found in *Law 48, On the condition of an undue debt; Law 45, section 3, On verbal obligations; Law 22, When the day of a legacy arrives.* Add C. J. **Provided that** <note>original German: "Wann nur"</note>, *Marpurg Counsel, case 28, number 121, volume 1.* **If** for **Whether**. *Whether they might mandate anything to their wives?* Florus.

### 12. Coats of Arms. Insignia.

Coats of arms are granted to Nobles with open helmets, **with an open helmet** <note>original German: "mit offnem Helm"</note>, so that it may appear from them that Nobles stand above others. Matthäus Stephani, *On Nobility, chapter 6, number 5.*

For although every family has its own insignia, which were invented to recognize families and lineages—*Law "Sanctified," section 1, On the division of things*—just as names were invented to recognize men—*Law "For recognizing."* Besold, *Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

recognizing. *Code on freeborn manumission.* See Nicolaus Noal, *On transmissions, chapter 33.* However, commoners—"sons of the earth"—cannot take these for themselves at their own pleasure and thus make their family distinguished. Rather, granting these belongs to the right of Majesty <note>the sovereign power</note>, and those who hold it from the sovereign. Hence the Spanish call a Noble a **Hidalgo**, as if "the son of someone" <note>original: "quasi filium alicujus"; a reference to the etymology *hijo de algo*</note>.

In particular, commoners cannot choose such coats of arms for themselves as the Nobility use today with open helmets, so that confusion may be avoided; otherwise, Nobles could not easily be discerned from commoners by arms and insignia. *Law 1, Code on those who are powerful.* To Doctors <note>holders of doctoral degrees</note>, however, even without a special grant from the Emperor, it is permitted to bear the insignia of Nobles with open helmets, **to bear a coat of arms with an open helmet and shield** <note>original German: "Wappen mit offnen Helm und Schild zu führen"</note>, provided they abstain from the specific insignia belonging to certain families. Chassanée, *In the Catalog of the Glory of the World, conclusion 20.* See my own work *On Nobility, page 156.* **Regarding open arms**, see my *Discourse on Nobility.* In Virgil’s *Aeneid, book 7*, mention is made of Helenor, son of Maeonius and Licymnia, **who had a shield, white, and no mark upon it, because he was not noble** <note>original German: "der ein Schild gehabt, weiß, und kein Zeichen daran, weil er nicht Edel gewest"</note>, *because in ancient times only Nobles had coats of arms, whence they were also called* **noble servants, shield-bearers, and coat-of-arms-bearers** <note>original: "Edelknecht, Schild- und Wappenträger, Escuyers"</note>.

**Regarding the helmets, ornaments, and shields, arms and colors of the Imperial Nobility and the Cities**, see Caspar von Lerch, *On the Equestrian Order, page 87*, where he teaches what difference existed between the Nobles and the Imperial Cities in this matter, and among other things has the following words: **The cities had their certain classes and separate army-shields, and to this hour they ornament their city arms and helmets; because they are not eligible for the tournament** <note>original German: "Thurnierfähig," meaning they lacked the high noble status required to compete in knightly tournaments</note>, **neither authorized nor by tradition. The free Knighthood, however, especially along the Rhine, have used both their ornamented helmets in common and in particular, as well as the image and memory of St. George (whom they chose as the spiritual and worldly patron of the Nobility from the symbol adopted at the time of the Christian faith), and also used him in their seals alongside the Imperial Eagle, together with the small shield in common, etc.**

Regarding the insignia of the Counts of Habsburg and the Archdukes of Austria, both old and new, Guillimanus discusses this in *Habsburgica, book 2, final chapter, at page 62 and following.* He records that there is an uncertain disagreement among writers as to who was the author of the more recent and now customary Austrian shield—purple, with a so-called silver band <note>the red-white-red fess of the Austrian flag</note>. Most of them, however, such as the continuator of the *History of the Holy War, book 2, chapters 3 and 7*, Heuter, *On the Origin of Austria, chapter 15, and others*, report that Leopold V, son of Henry, the first Duke of Austria of his line, brought it back from the siege of Ptolemais <note>modern-day Acre</note>. It is said that when he was soaked and covered with his own blood and that of the enemy, no white appeared on his tunic except for that which was covered by his sword-belt; he returned this as a symbol and monument of his virtue and fortitude to the memory...

...consecrated to perpetual use. Having occupied a certain tower, says the cited *Continuator of the Holy War* <note>original: "Continuator Belli Sacri," likely a chronicler of the Crusades</note>, when the Austrian [Duke Leopold V] raged quite fiercely against the resisting enemy, with many of his own men slain, he was forced to throw himself headlong into the sea. Being entirely covered in blood, only as far as his belt—which had blocked the blood from his white body—did he return to his men unstained. From this event, Frederick <note>Frederick, son of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa</note>, who after his father’s death was the Leader of the Christian military in the East and Emperor by the vote of the entire army, granted him new **coats of arms** <note>original: "insignia"</note> distinguished by the colors red and white. These events took place in the year of our Lord 1190. Others claim that Albert, son of King Rudolph I, won this glory of a new shield at the Battle of Orthogaric, when the white banner he was carrying was entirely splashed with blood and gore.

Whatever the certainty of that matter, it is well established that Albert presided over his father’s banner in that battle, and performed the task no less bravely and strenuously; he fought and, finally, celebrated these **coats of arms** <note>original: "Insignia"</note> before all others, leaving them to posterity along with Austria, of which he was the first of his family and nation to enter the Dukedom. Thus, he may rightly be seen, if not as their author and founder, certainly as their preserver and propagator. Guillimann, *final chapter, near the end.*

So also, a grant of **coats of arms and heraldry** <note>original: "Insigniorum & armorum"</note> made by someone for himself and his sons, or for himself and his family or paternal lineage, then those arms pass only to the sons or descendants of that family or lineage, following the form of the grant; however, they do not pass at all to maternal relatives or relatives by marriage. *Law "on the right of families," Code on religious matters and funeral expenses. Bartolus in his treatise on insignia, number 10.* Those descending from women are also not considered of the family or paternal lineage. *Law "pronunciation," at the end, Digest on the meaning of words.* Therefore, the arms do not pass even to their sons. Just as the Sovereign alone grants family **insignia**, commonly called **arms** or <term>Wappen</term> <note>German for coats of arms</note>, which contain signs of great deeds (regarding whose origin see Lipsius in his book *On the Roman Military*, Budæus in *book 2 on the origin of law*, and Chasseneuz in *The Glory of the World*, consideration 28, conclusion 10). So also it belongs to the same Sovereign to decide regarding their colors and arrangement. Chasseneuz in the cited place, consideration 59 and following; Stephani in the above-cited place, number 7, who has the following: Just as, he says, the families themselves are ranked in individual orders, so also the orders and dignities are distinguished among themselves by their **coats of arms**. Thus, formerly, there were certain and peculiar marks for Proconsuls and Legates. *Law 1, Digest on the office of Proconsul and Legate.* Today likewise there are certain marks of singular dignity used by Emperors, Kings, Dukes, Princes, Marquises, and Counts. There are also certain marks of dignity or office in general, such as those of Bishops, Rectors, Doctors, and the like, which anyone established in that dignity may use. *Cited place on the office of Proconsul; Law "sacred" on the division of things.*

To bear the **arms and insignia** of houses is an ho-

<column-break/>

-nor and a mark of nobility, as Baldus says in *Law "generally," section "but when," number 5, Code on institutions*; and Chasseneuz in *The Catalog of the Glory of the World, part 1, conclusion 12.*

Indeed, Nobles either have their **coats of arms** from a long series and ancestry of predecessors, or from a special grant of a Sovereign who, while conferring nobility, is also accustomed to add heraldry at the same time, although arms do not confer nobility by themselves. Thomas Horner in his response *on nobility, section "but if someone from the Emperor," etc.* It also seems that being noble is one thing, and having <term>open arms</term> <note>original: "offne Wappen," likely referring to legally recognized or public heraldry</note> is another. Thus, Latin Counts, although they can sometimes give <term>open arms</term>, cannot nonetheless grant nobility. Reinkingk, *on heraldic law, chapter 8, section 1, member 4, number 99.* See however Regner Sixtin, *book 1 on Regalia, chapter 5, number 104*; Reinkingk, *on Secular and Ecclesiastical Government, book 1, class 4, chapter 13, number 24.*

**Arms and insignia** are symbols of higher lordship and possession. See Knichen, *in the encyclopedia, chapter 14.*

It is admitted that Sovereigns formerly allowed great liberty in changing coats of arms. Master Meibomius in his notes to the *Golden Bull of Andronicus, page 33*, where he adds: I remember reading that Princes, Counts, and Lords throughout Belgium and neighboring places, when they had committed their names to the Holy War <note>The Crusades</note>, assumed uniform Lion symbols. Thus, the Duke of Guelders chose two lions, while the Hollander, Zeelander, Fleming, and those of Jülich, Berg, Jever, and many others chose one lion for themselves; which arms their descendants did not change at all. It also occasionally happened through custom that those who were conquered by others were forced to renounce their arms. Regarding this, I wish to include a passage from a manuscript rhyming Chronicle, in which the Poet speaks thus of Albert the Great, Duke of Brunswick, warring with Otto, the Noble Lord of Hamersleben:

> If the army of Born had won,
> His castle, and perhaps a third of his men,
> Thereupon, knights and squires,
> Would have divided their coats of arms.

(<term>Dividing arms</term> <note>original: "Wappen theilen"</note> is also to divide the spoils of war.)

> Those of his, as is the custom,
> When one triumphs over another,
> That he also takes his coat of arms.

Coats of arms were also sometimes changed as a form of punishment. Thus, as witnessed by Bernhard Hertzog in *The Alsatian Chronicle, book 5, page 76*, by King Albert of Austria, the coat of arms of Reinhard, Count of Hanau (who had served King Adolph of Nassau as a standard-bearer and remained with him when he was defeated) was changed: the yellow lion in a black field was stripped from him, and in its place he was ordered to carry red and yellow chevrons, as was also done to those of Königstein and Eppstein, etc.

For the reason why Otto Visconti of Milan honored his family arms with the image of a Viper, see Lælius Bisciola, *Subsequent Hours.*

Regarding heraldry, Welser also has the following noteworthy passage in *The Antiquities of Augsburg*, book 4, at the end: Although the Romans, and all antiquity before the Romans, were accustomed to using symbols—which we call Signs and Heraldry <note>original: "Signa & Insignia"</note>—since no army existed without Eagles, Dragons, or Banners (Vegetius <note>A 4th-century Roman military theorist</note> calls these "silent signs," distinguishing them from vocal and semi-vocal signals), and almost no Heroes in the Poets are found without images on their shields, nor signet gems without engravings, nor most cities without symbols; nevertheless, these are not to be held to the same single prescription as the **Heraldry** <note>original: "Insignia"</note> of our own age. Those who demand such a comparison are quite mistaken, and they ignorantly confuse things which we admit were drawn from the same source by the instinct of mother nature, but which we see were established by different rites according to the customs of the times. Indeed, the laws which today circumscribe Heraldry—whether by opinion or fixed law—however ancient they may be, do not predate Charlemagne, by whom I believe they were first sketched out; they were finally polished under Henry the Fowler <note>German King, r. 919–936</note> and his successors. These most brave Emperors wished for military virtue, to which they were devoted with their whole hearts, to be honored in this way. From this was born the form of the shield and the helmet, and also the name, for in every native language we call them **Arms** <note>original: "Arma"</note>. From the soldiers, they later flowed so extensively to the rest of the human race that they have pervaded all of Europe and even penetrated into Asia. We have even seen a small shield brought from the Chinese <note>original: "Sinis"</note>, on which, among other things, there was a shield painted in gold, conspicuous with a panther; upon the shield rested a helmet with an open visor latticed with bars, covered with ribbons or fillets hanging down on both sides; above the helmet rose a feathery crest, entirely according to the European custom. Or, if one finds it more credible, the Chinese by no means received these from the Europeans, but rather the same idea came to their minds spontaneously, just as it did to ours; for this can be argued with almost the same reasoning regarding engines of war <note>likely referring to gunpowder</note> and the art of printing.

### 15. Watchtowers. Lookouts.

To maritime jurisdiction belongs the erection of lookouts <term>Specula</term> <note>Latin for watchtower or high vantage point</note> to direct the course of ships from the deep into harbors;

> Lest the South wind drive them, snatched away, into hidden rocks,
> And he gives them to the shallows and girds the sands with a mound.

As the Poet says in the 1st book of the *Aeneid*. Such a tower exists at Pharos, an island in Egypt, a very high tower built of white stone upon a rock which is washed by the sea, according to Caesar in the 3rd book of the *Alexandrian War* at the end, or built by Ptolemy Philadelphus, according to Strabo, book 17.

It is called Pharos (**from the word to travel** <note>original German: "vom Pharen"</note>) because of its practical use, as Hegesippus says in book 4, chapter 27. **From the Greek *phainein*** <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ τοῦ φαίνειν</note>, as if it were **something visible** <note>original Greek: Φανερὸν</note>, that is, bright, because it directs the course of sailors with night fires. The Germans call it **Warte** [Watchtower]: hence **Warthaus**, a fortress, as if it were a house of protection; see Mr. Gryphiander’s *Treatise on Islands*, chapter 31, number 156 and following. Also Schottelius **in the German Mother Tongue, page 490.**

### ADDITION.

For those who are called "watchers" <term>Speculari</term>, see Mr. Dr. Tabor *On Arms*, chapter 1, number 14.

### 16. Water. Aqua.

Through the words, **"Water and Watercourses"** <note>original German: "Wasser und Wasserlauffen"</note>, according to the genuine meaning of the words and the style of many courts, public navigable rivers are by no means said to be granted, or things like them; rather, they are explained as ancient water channels, which are something different from public rivers, as Lucas de Penna specifically argued in his commentary on the *Law of the Use of Water*, column 2, after the beginning, in the *Code on Aqueducts*. Matthaeus de Afflictis in *chapter 1* regarding what things are royal [regalia], on the word *rivers*, number 7, says that in the form of Investitures three words are usually expressed: that is, "We grant the Castle with rivers, waters, and watercourses," but see especially Georg Everhard, *Counsel 47, number 33 and following, volume 1;* add Jacob Thoming, *Counsel 28, number 42 etc., volume 1.*

But regarding **Water and Water Law** <note>original German: "Wasser und Wasserrecht"</note>, see especially Noë Meurer’s *special German treatise*, where a certain Counsel by the most famous jurist Johann Goeddaeus is found appended from somewhere; and there may be added the most complete *Treatise on the Island* by Mr. Gryphiander.

### 17. Water-battles. Applying fortifications to riverbanks.

Whether it is permitted to build an embankment at a river (which we commonly call **Water-battles** <note>original German: "Wasserschlachten," referring to riprap or riverbank reinforcements to prevent erosion</note>) against floods or for the sake of fortifying one's own defense, even if it causes inconvenience to neighbors—**when one makes a bend or bulwark into the water against the adjacent properties?** I affirm this is allowed, according to *Law 2, section 9 of the Digest on rainwater, and Law 1, section 7 of the Digest on not doing anything in a public river.* **Rauchbar**, *book 2, question 27.* **Meurer, on Water Rights, page 3, question 12. See also the legal argument of Hamburg versus Lüneburg, printed in Hamburg in the year 1620 in quarto**, where this question is treated extensively and answered in the affirmative.

### 18. Water-Judgment, Water-Trial. Investigation by cold water.

In certain places, the practice of investigation by cold water <note>The "swimming test" for suspected witches</note> is accepted, though it is almost universally con-

<column-break/>

demned. This is because it is fallible, regarding which see **Servin**, *volume 1 on pleadings, folio 686.* **Hotoman**, *Feudal Disputations, folio 196.* **Zieritz**, *on article 20 of the Penal Constitution of the High Court <note>The Carolina</note>, and Goldast, Alemannic Matters, volume 1, chapter 14, folio 210.* Section: *Curious people with immodest eyes may watch as the naked women are submerged in the waters, etc.* Add **Rickius** and the **Histories** there, also **Melandrus** and **Göhausen**. As to why these poor women for the most part float upon the surface of the water (which experience confirms), physicists provide various reasons. **Goclenius** thinks it happens because of the air, and thus a light demonic inhalation, by which the body of the witch <term>Saga</term> <note>A female fortune-teller or witch</note>, which is heavy by its own nature, remains as if supported, restrained, and held back so that it is not submerged. And, just as a bladder thrown into the water cannot be sunk, no matter how great the weights placed upon it—even if the weight itself presses it down, the trapped air lifts and raises it back up—so the body of the witch, striving downward by its own nature, is as if balanced and carried by a breathable force which the demon secretly breathes into it, so that she can float on the surface of the water without danger of suffocation. **Arum.** *exercise 20, question 18.* Add **Heig.** *2, question 39, see throughout.* **Wilhelm Böckel**, *on visions, inquiry 6, number 32.* Add the Oration of **Mr. Friedrich Heinius** appended to my *Treatise on Punishments, folio 132.*

Similar in the past was the trial by glowing iron, regarding which see **Camerarius**, *Historical Meditations, 2, chapter 18.* **Notes of the Logothete**, *folio 10, etc.* And when in the past there was a dispute in Spain as to whether the Gothic or the Roman form of prayer was better, it seemed best to permit the controversy to be decided by the judgment of fire. Then, after a pyre was lit in the square, both the Roman and the Gothic books were thrown into the fire; concerning this matter, see **Mariana**, *History of Spanish Matters, book 9, chapter 18.*

### 20. Orphans' Court. Tutelary Judgment. <note>original German: "Waysen-Gericht"</note>

In the Duchy of Württemberg, this is the name given to a College of four or five members from the order of Senators or Judges. They look after the interests of wards <note>orphans or minors under legal protection</note> and almost always preside over the division of inheritances. For this reason, they are also called **Partition Judges** <note>original German: "Theil-Richter"</note>. This is certainly a laudable custom and seems worthy of imitation. Indeed, my brother—of pious memory <note>Latin: "p. m." or "piae memoriae"</note>—in his advice on how the nobility of the knightly and immediate order <note>nobles holding land directly from the Emperor</note> might be preserved (recorded in my *Treatise on Nobility, folio 128, number 12*), suggests among other things that such a court should be established by Imperial grant. He argues that experience teaches that many families live in poverty for the sole reason that the administration of their guardianships was handled too negligently.

### ADDITION.

Thus **Nuremberg** received its guardianship laws, organized into 35 chapters and called the **Guardianship Chambers** <note>original German: "der Wormundstuben"</note>, in the year 1506 from the Venetians under Doge **Leonardo Loredano**. See **Francesco Sansovino**, whom **Zeiller** praises in his *German Travels, page 104, at the end.* The person who suggested that the Nuremberg Republic should seek these guardianship laws from the Venetian Republic was **Conrad Imhoff**, who undertook the journey himself and obtained them. See **Pietro Giustiniani**, *History of Venice, book 11, folio 215*, and my own work, **Comparison of the Republic of Nuremberg with the Venetian**, *letter B. 3.*

### 21. Exchanging, Exchange-Money, Surcharge, Bill of Exchange. Exchange, Money-changing, Letters of Exchange. <note>original German: "Wechslen, Wechsel-Geld, Uff-Geld, Wechsel-Brief"; Latin: "Cambire, Collybus, Cambiales literæ"</note>

**To exchange** <note>Latin: "Cambire"</note> means to barter or to trade for profit. In the *Bavarian Laws, title 8*: "An exchange (this is what they call **Cambium**) shall have the same legal standing as a purchase."

**To exchange** <note>Latin: "Cambiare"</note> also means to barter or **to deal** <note>original German: "kämmen," likely related to "to comb" or "to broker"</note>, from which we get **Horse-dealer** <note>original German: "Roszkamm"</note> and the French word **Changer**. In the *Gallic Salic Law, title 50*: "however many there were who sold the thing, or exchanged it, or perhaps gave payment, etc."

From this come the **Campsores** <note>money-changers</note>, who make a profit from the exchange of money. There is also the ancient word **Campfor**. See *Martini’s Philological Lexicon, under the word "Cambium".*

Thus, today **Exchange** <note>Latin: "Cambium"</note> is the swapping of one type of coinage for another. **Leonardus Lessius**, *On Justice and Law, book 2, chapter...*

<column-break/>

3, doubt 1, number 1 and following. **Exchange** is sometimes called **Dry** <note>Latin: "Siccum"</note> and sometimes **Real**. It is called **Dry** when it is not a real exchange in fact, lacking a lawful subject and only using the name of "Exchange" as a cover. This "Dry Exchange" is committed in two ways: First, when someone gives money—say, in Florence—and receives a bill of exchange to be paid in Venice. A document is drawn up for this, commonly called a **Bill of Exchange** <note>original German: "Wechsel-Brief"</note>, which ought to be sent to the place where the money is to be paid. However, in reality, the debtor is only going to pay it in Florence, where the exchange was first made. The letters are written solely to simulate a contract between the giver and receiver of the exchange; because of this, it is called a "Dry" type of exchange. **Nicolaus Janua**, *On Private Writing, book 3, title on Exchange, number 8.* Second, it occurs when letters are sent to the trade fairs of a certain place where the debtor has neither money nor a business agent with whom he usually trades, nor any hope of having one. Instead, a proxy appointed by the money-changer receives the money there in his name, and sends it back to Florence to be paid with "Exchange and Re-exchange" <note>essentially charging interest on the transaction and then interest on that interest</note>. Under this simulation, usury—and interest upon interest—is paid, which is usually condemned by all laws. See the writings of **Pedro Augusto Morla** in his *Market of Law, part 1, title 9, on contracts of buying and selling, number 11 and following.* That such exchange is illicit is taught by **Janua**, *at the cited location, number 9 and following.*

**Real Exchange**, however, is that which truly has a subject and substance. In this, no element of a loan <note>Latin: "mutuum"</note> intervenes, and the goal—without any fiction—is that in fact and with effect, coins of different types (which are real commodities) are exchanged for one another. **Janua**, *as cited above, number 26*, where you will find many more things on this subject that are necessary to know.

Can a **shop manager** <note>Latin: "Institor," a person appointed to run a business or trade</note>, who is in charge of a shop or the handling of other mercantile business, accept letters of exchange without the owner or principal being consulted? See **Scheffer**, *Practical Questions, part 3, question 38, number 36.* He concludes that a manager or agent appointed to trade or manage mercantile affairs—even if they have a general mandate with free power of administration—cannot accept and issue letters of exchange without a *special* mandate. This is undoubtedly the truer and more widely accepted view. This was decided by the **Rota of Genoa** <note>a high commercial court</note> in *Decision 14, beginning "quemadmodum causa," number 88*, where it is stated that the power of exchange is never understood to be tacitly permitted to a manager, but there is a need for an express mandate for this. If such a mandate is lacking, the owner may raise a defense that he did not give the agent such power.

On **Exchange** and **letters of exchange**, **Renerus Budelius** has more in *On Coins and Monetary Affairs, book 1, chapter 25*, as does **Philippus Paschalis** in his *Treatise on the Power of the Father, part 1, chapter 8, number 65 and following.* See also the *Treatise on Trade in folio, the Basel Disputations volume 1, and the counsels of Costa, counsel 48.*

In the Seventh Book of the Decretals, Book 2, Title 12, Pope Pius V condemns all those **Exchanges** <note>original Latin: *Cambia*</note> known as "dry" <note>A "dry exchange" (*cambium siccum*) was a financial maneuver used to bypass usury laws. It simulated a currency exchange between different locations to hide what was essentially a high-interest loan.</note>, which are structured so that the contracting parties do not actually intend to conduct exchange at specific trade fairs or other locations. Instead, they pretend to do so. Those who receive the money provide letters of exchange, but these letters are never sent, or they are sent in such a way that after a certain time, they are returned void to where they originated. Or, even if no such letters are provided, the money is ultimately demanded back with interest at the same place where the contract was first made, and so forth.

Regarding the statutes and abuses of exchanges, see Antoninus, part 2, title 1, chapter 7, § 47; Laurentius de Radulphis on usury, chapter *consuluit*, part 2, question 26; Soto on justice and law, book 6, question 8, article 1; Navarro, chapter 17; and also Philippus Faber in his treatise on restitution, page 82, etc.

An **Exchange Fee** <term>original: *Collybus*; a Greek-derived term for a small commission on exchanging money</term> is what is given for the permutation of money (commonly called **Premium** or **Exchange-Money** <note>original German: *Auf-Geld, Wechsel-Geld*</note>). Or, as Jerome has it, it is the gift given for the Exchange. See Martinius in his Lexicon under the word *collybus*. From this come the **Money-Changers** <note>original Latin: *Collybistae*</note>, who sell small bronze coins for other money upon receiving an exchange fee. They are quite similar to bankers. Whether through art or long experience in handling and exchanging money, they are so skilled that they alone are considered to truly know the quality of gold, silver, or bronze. For this reason, people frequently go to them as expert appraisers of coins when they are uncertain about their value: for example, what a certain coin or shilling is worth, what kind of gold it contains, whether it is genuine or copper-plated <note>original: *subaeratus*; an ancient counterfeit technique where a base metal core was plated in silver or gold</note>, whether it is of equal weight, or if it has any flaws. But see Eberhard Speckhan, *Legal Questions*, century 1, question 68, where he discusses who are called "Bankers" in our Law and by other authors, and how varied their profession and duty are.

->ADDITION.<-

J. T. Sprenger wrote in 1662 a short **Exchange Practice** <note>original German: *Wechsel-Practick*</note> compiled from the most prominent writings on exchange, regarding how one may reclaim money if letters of exchange are lost. See Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 13, § 1. However, if the receiver lies for this purpose—claiming the letters of exchange are lost so that he may obliquely withdraw from the exchange contract—see the same work at number 2 regarding the penalty for the liar. When an **Exchange** is set for a period, such as 14 days sight, those 14 days do not begin until the letter of exchange has been presented, signed, and accepted. If someone keeps the exchange letter with them for 14 days or more without presenting it, that time does not count. **Double Usance** <note>original: *Usu doppio*; a standard commercial time frame for international payments</note> is a period of 4 weeks after the exchange letter is accepted, and one has an additional 3 or 4 grace or sight days beyond that. A **Letter of Exchange at Sight** <note>original: *Wechsel-Brief Auf Sicht*</note> means it is to be paid immediately.

Regarding Money-Changers, see Alemannus on *Monetary Law*, page 872. Regarding Bankers, page 871. On exchange interest and "agio" <note>the difference in value between different types of currencies</note>, see Dr. Tabor in Besoldus, Volume 1,

<column-break/>

regarding double the amount, page 318 and following. On who are called **Money-Changers** <note>original German: *Wechsler*</note>, see Wesenbeck’s Code on *Edenda*, number 4. On the **Privilege of Exchange**, see Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 7, chapter 16, number 33. Thomas de Vio, Hieronymus de Luca, and Fabianus Genuensis have written on Exchange, according to Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 229. There also exist treatises on Exchange by Johannes Medina, Raphael de Turri, Johannes à Salas, and the inaugural disputation of Hafner on commerce, from thesis 122 to 144. Exchange is a species of permutation <note>a legal category of contract involving the swap of one thing for another</note>. Discussed at length by Hahn in his *Digest Collection*, Dissertation 17, page 680. Exchange is primarily divided into "small" or "manual" <note>hand-to-hand exchange of coins</note> and "local" or "by letter" <note>transferring funds between different cities</note>; see Carpzov, book 2, response 92, and in his *Forensic Jurisprudence*, part 2, chapter 2, 26, decision 13, and chapter 30, decision 16. ### 22. Ways, Roads. <note>Latin: *Via*</note>

When there is a dispute regarding the repair of a ruined road and who is bound to perform it, a distinction is usually made between a public road and a private one. For if the road is private or a village path that was destroyed by a rush of water or by accident, then the owner is liable, or the neighbors contribute to the rebuilding or repairing of the village path. See law 1, § 4 of the Digest on private paths and tracks. It is otherwise in the repair of a public road, because then the neighbors are bound to the repair insofar as it is regulated and inspected by officials. See Franciscus Marcus, decision 594, number 6, part 1. This applies unless it is clear that the destruction happened through the act of some private individual, because that person should first be forced to restore it, in whatever way they caused the ruin and destruction. If, however, that person is insolvent <note>original: *non esset solvendo*</note>, then as a backup, the neighbors of the estates are held liable. See Cepolla on *Rural Estates*, chapter 3, number 38. Nevertheless, these neighbors shall recover this expense through recourse against the author of the destruction, even by taking possession of a neighboring estate if they have any, or through an action for "management of affairs" <note>original: *negotiorum gestorum*; a legal claim for expenses incurred when acting on behalf of another without their prior consent but for their benefit</note>, when such an action would be useful among neighbors, etc. See Costa in the treatise on *Subsidiary Remedies*, remedy 95.

Regarding the Curators of Roads (or by the composite name **Road-Curators** <note>original: *Viocuris*</note>), who and how many they were, and in what their office consisted, see Barnabas Brissonius, *Antiquities*, book 4, chapter 12; and Hornigk on the *Royal Right of Posts*, chapter 8, number 8.

->ADDITION.<-

Roads are the perpetual boundaries of jurisdiction. Barbosa, book 19, chapter 14, axiom 1. Public roads—**the common highways** <note>original German: *die gemeine Landstrassen*</note>—are numbered among the Royal Prerogatives <note>original: *Regalibus*; rights belonging to the sovereign</note>. See Bocer on *Regalia*, page 130. Regarding the **improvement of roads** and the tolls resulting therefrom, see Klock, volume 3, counsel 149, numbers 278 and 287. One who makes a road worse during an attempt at repair suffers force without legal remedy. See Struvius on *Private Vengeance*, chapter 6, aphorism 7, number 8, at the beginning of page 66. Strasbourg <note>original Latin: *Argentina*</note> was one of more than fifty forts that Drusus <note>Nero Claudius Drusus, a Roman general</note> built along the banks of the Rhine; hence the Germans perhaps called this place **at the Argen-Road** <note>original German: *an der Argen-Strassen*</note>. See Martin Beer in *Geography, Ancient and Modern*...
