### 23. Highway Ambush and Waylaying.
#### Treacherous hiding and occupation of the public road.

That treacherous hiding and occupation of a public road is called by us **a highway ambush** <note>original German: *eine Weglagerung*</note>, which is considered a most heinous crime. However, there is a distinction between **highway ambush** <note>original German: *Weglagerung*</note> and **waylaying** <note>original German: *Verwarten*</note>. The former—highway ambush—is committed by bandits and plunderers. The term **waylaying**, however, is done with the intent of taking revenge and usually happens at night, when companions, after a quarrel has broken out between them, go home, arm themselves, wait for their adversary to pass by in some location, and attack and wound him from ambush. In the first case, capital punishment takes place; in the latter, however, the delinquent is punished either by imprisonment or banishment, unless by chance grave wounds were inflicted, in which case the delinquent can be punished by the amputation of a hand, by beatings with clubs, or by execution <note>original Latin: *exclusione*; likely referring to exclusion from life/execution</note>. See Cothmann, *Academic Counsels 9, n. 27 and following.*

->ADDITION.<-

Robber-chasers <note>original Greek: *λῃσοδιῶκται*</note> are those who pursue and eliminate the small-time robbers who occupy roads and plunderers. In Lorraine, the official who is placed over them is called the *Prevost des Mareschaulx* (Provost of the Marshals), commonly and jokingly called **the red rod** <note>original German: *die rote ruer*</note>, Freher, *On Secret Courts, p. 39.* **All perpetrators, rapists, vandals, denouncers, land-extorters, outlaws, hedge-riders, highway robbers, peace-breakers, and rioters, as well as those who knowingly harbor, promote, follow, shelter, help, or are related to them**, it is certain that all of these fall under the penalty of the Imperial Ban. *Ordinance of the Land-Peace at Worms, from the Year 1521, titles 4 & 5.* Georg Christoph Hansemann in his *Inaugural Jurisprudential Disputation* held at Strasbourg in 1665, titled: *The Peacekeeper Restored*, page 23, at the beginning.

**On Snaphances** <note>original German: *Schnaphanen*; these were irregular soldiers or mounted highwaymen</note> see Dr. Tabor, a teacher who has served me well, in *Apoplismus page 226.* Those who occupy roads and other places and wait for passers-by for the sake of wounding or killing them are punished by the sword. Berlich, 4, conclusion 20, number 1 and following, even if they have not brought the act to completion, n. 4. Treacherous occupations for the sake of plundering or formal defiance <note>original Latin: *diffidationis*; a formal declaration of hostility</note> are considered a species of "breach of the public peace," n. 7. For the penalty of the sword, it is required that someone has occupied the road with malicious intent, n. 9 and 10.

<column-break/>

### 24. Blood Money. Weregild.

Weregild <note>original: *Wergeldus*</note> is a judicial settlement, the price paid for a crime committed, specifically the price of a killed man. And although a specific penalty of Weregild may not be owed to the kinsmen for a homicide; nevertheless, if those kinsmen do not wish to seek their own grief—felt from the slaughter of a father, brother, or other relative if a most atrocious injury was inflicted upon them—but have instead committed the right of avenging the death of the deceased to a Judge, they certainly perceive no profit from such a renunciation by virtue of the disposition of Saxon Law. Instead, the Judge or the Treasury gains all of it to cover the expenses incurred in conducting the criminal trial. Virgil Pingizer, *On Illustrious Questions, quest. 4 num. 7.* See also Beatus, *Decisions volume 5, part 5, on judicial matters, vol. 1, fol. 381*, regarding to whom **the Blood Money** <note>original German: *Das Wehrgeld*</note> belongs.

Regarding Weregild and its price or value, which must be properly examined, various opinions and calculations are reported, as witnessed by Jacob Aleman, *Exercises in Consultation 8, on the law of money, first question, part 1, 13*, whom you should consult.

->ADDITION.<-

**On Blood Money, Repayment-Money, Retribution-Money, Peace-Fine, Atonement-Money, Ninefold-Fine, Triple-Fine** <note>original German terms: *Wehrgeld, Wiedergeld, Wiedergeltung, Fredegild, Sühngeld, Neungeld, Dreigeld*</note>, see Schottelius at length *In the German Main Language, fol. 505.* A fine <note>original Latin: *Emenda*</note> has been introduced in place of Weregild. Carpzov, *part 1, decision 100, num. 12.*

Weregild must be paid to the kinsmen of the slain by one who exceeds the limits of blameless self-defense. Berlich, 4, conclusion 18, n. 34 and following. To whom it should be applied, n. 44, 45. What a full Weregild contains. Schneidewwin *on injuries § but also n. 7.* Weregild is not called "interest," but a "penalty." *said title § in sum n. 5.* Regarding Weregild and its payment, see Carpzov, *Criminal Practice p. 1, quest. 34, num. 12.* Wehner under the word **highest fine.** <note>original German: *höchste Gewette*</note>. Gellius, *Attic Nights book 11, chap. 1*, on the maximum and minimum fine. **A fine** <note>original German: *Buß*</note> is distinguished into **a severe or reasonable one**, into **great and light**, Carpzov, *Criminal Practice p. 3, quest. 130, n. 6.* It is distinguished simply into **a fine and a woman’s fine. Among the Saxons, a woman pays half as much as a man.** Zahn, *In the Municipal Outline, chap. 42, n. 2.*

### 25. To make fit for arms. The right of bearing arms.

It is a custom in Germany where Princes and Nobles, when their servants have reached full age, grant them the right of wearing a sword by striking them with a blow to the neck: **that they make them fit for arms, or make them servants** <note>original German: *daß sie dieselbe wehrhafft, oder zu Knechten machen*</note>, by which they place a finishing touch upon the trifles and follies of the first stage of life, and simultaneously declare him released from their parental or masterly power. Baldus in *law 1, § soldier, Digest on military wills.* For as Claudian says in *The Fourth Consulship of Honorius*:

## 26. Prohibiting Weapons and Public Drinking.
**Prohibitio portationis gladii & compotationum publicarum.**

This is a specific type of penalty sometimes imposed among us in cases of homicide: namely, for those who commit a serious excess in self-defense, or who accidentally kill someone during a brawl arising from drunkenness or public drinking. This penalty seems perfectly suited to the crime: specifically, that he who did not use his sword rightly should henceforth abstain from carrying it, and those who did not use wine properly should avoid public drinking sessions.

## 27. Warranty and Indemnification.
**Evictio.**

Eviction <note>The legal recovery of property by a judicial process, or the protection against it</note> is commonly called <term>Gewehr</term> <note>warranty</note>, <term>Wehrschafft</term> <note>guaranty</note>, or <term>Schadloshaltung</term> <note>indemnification</note>. This is not because these words, if you look at their proper meaning, are identical to "eviction," but because a thing is not understood to be "evicted"—at least in respect to time—if the legal authority, the <term>Gewehr</term> or <term>Wehrschafft</term>, is provided. This authority means that if the property is recovered from the buyer by law or judgment, the buyer has recourse against his "Author" (whom we call the <term>Wehrmann</term> <note>the warrantor</note>; and whom Besold, Volume 1,

<column-break/>

calls in French <term>Garant</term> <note>guarantor</note>, from the same source. Cujacius testifies in his *Commentary on the Feuds*, book 4, title 37, that this word comes from the ancient Germanic language); that is, the Seller; and the seller is held responsible to the buyer under the name of "authority."

In the instruments of purchase and sale where a warranty against eviction is promised, the following or similar words are usually inserted:
> We vow and promise for ourselves and our heirs, to the said N., his heirs and descendants, to complete, defend, and keep this purchase and sale free from claims, and therefore to do against everyone all that one should and must do for every secure warranty and completion, as often and as much as necessity requires, always at our own expense, without harm to the named N., his heirs and descendants, until they have been fully and completely satisfied in every instance for all the damages they might have incurred, and they are well-pleased with it. From this, neither we nor our heirs shall be freed, protected, or shielded by any spiritual or worldly law, neither currently held nor future privileges, freedoms, etc.

There is no contract in which a warranty against eviction is not granted, provided the transfer of property is not void. Tiraquell, *On the Nearest Relations*, section 1, gloss 1, number 12; Rub. *Counsels* 152. Some have judged this rule to be so true that they argue the seller is held liable even without an express promise of warranty, as seen in Surdus, *Decisions* 290, number 16; Cravetta, *Counsels* 211, number 6; Ruinus, *Counsels* 42, number 19, book 1; Tiraquell, *On Consanguineous Retraction*, at the end, number 46; see Caspar Antonius Thesaurus, *Forensic Questions*, book 2, question 23.

Regarding warranty in a sold fief, see Bullae, *Counsels* 7; and on warranty and notification, Meichsner, volume 4, decision 8. Whether an action for warranty is granted if only possession is recovered by law, see Wilhelm Anton in the *Corollary to the Treatise on Legal Delay*, folio 19, and Molinaeus, *Counsels* 49, where he suggests a legal precaution for how a second seller might direct the buyer back to the first seller.

### ADDITION.

Handover and Warranty <note>original: *Aufgifft und Wehrschafft*</note>—these words are read together for "Eviction" in the *Frankfurt Reformation*, part 2, title 3, sections 7, 9, 12, 14. *Supplement to Wehner*, pages 8, 72, and 73. On the indemnities of women, see Haymo Cravetta of Savitiano, volume 6, part 2, folio 281.

# 29. Currency. The Value of Money.
<term>Wehrung</term> <note>This German term refers to the monetary standard or valuation system used in a contract.</note>

The words "current currency or coin" <note>original: *gangbare Wehrung oder Müntz*</note> are to be referred to the money current at the time of the contract. Since, as a rule, the time of the contract must be looked at everywhere. See the law *si voluntatis* and the final law in the Code *on the rescinding of a sale* <note>Citations from the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*</note>; Laudensius *on money*, number 25.
Furthermore, we ought to interpret the words of any obligation according to the rules of Common Law. Br. on the law *heredes*, section *cum ita*, number 4, in the Digest *on the Trebellian Decree of the Senate*; Brunus *on money*, limitation 8, number 12, after the beginning; and through the law *cum quid*, 3, in the Digest *on the recovery of things*, at the end.
And that those words, "current currency," are to be understood regarding the estimation and value of money current at the time of the contract, appears from the manner of the said law *cum quid*; so that the understanding, according to that law, is tacitly present in the Law, that an equally good and indeed the same amount be returned, neither more nor less. Baldus on the law *illud, quod* 19, at the final verse "I ask," in the Code *on the Most Holy Churches*; Fabianus de Monte in the *treatise on buying and selling*, numbers 14 and 15; Berlich, book 2, conclusion 35, numbers 41 and 42; Henning Göde, consultation 78, numbers 5 and 6.
It is called <term>Wehrung</term>, however, because money ought to have a perpetual valuation. See the first law *on the contracting of a sale*.

->ADDITION.<-

Current and accepted valuation <note>original: *Geng und geb. Werdierung*</note>. "The Value" <note>original: *Der Werth*</note>; on how these words are to be understood, see Auer *on monetary law*, thesis 103, and those cited there.

### 31. Wives' Property. <note>original: *Weiber-Güter. Bona uxorum.*</note>

It is well established that a husband cannot be sued for the obligations of his wife unless he has made himself liable for her, according to the Code, *that the wife not be sued for the husband, nor the husband for the wife*. The punishment ought to be where the offense is, as the Emperor decreed in the law *sancimus* in the Code *on punishments*. Thus, just as the laws forbid wives from being disturbed due to the husband's fault, so too the rules of correlatives

<column-break/>

widely established in the laws prohibit husbands from being disturbed due to the wife's fault. In such cases, however, the husband's goods are considered to include not only what he had before the marriage, or what he later inherited for himself or otherwise obtained, but also what his housewife brought to the marriage as a dowry <note>original: *Ehesteuer*</note>, and what he attained or acquired from it or with it. Franz Pfeil, *Counsel* 38, number 3.

In Saxon Law <note>original: *Sächsischen Rechten*</note> it is provided that a man and woman shall have no divided property for their bodies <note>meaning they hold property in common</note>; likewise, that the husband has no other power over the wife's property than that of guardianship <note>original: *Vormundschafft*</note>, according to the *Landrecht*, book 1, article 31. This article, however, does not cover the case where a marriage contract has been drawn up with specific persons and conditions regarding how the property shall be managed by both sides; rather, it speaks only in the case where no special marriage settlement or agreement was made between the spouses regarding their property.

After the death of the wife, however, the husband keeps everything that is movable and portable, excluding the <term>Gerade</term> <note>The *Gerade* refers to a specific category of personal property—such as jewelry, clothing, and linens—that by custom was inherited only by female relatives.</note>. And yet, even if the woman had not specifically designated a marriage portion for her husband, the money she brought to him would be his just as much as hers, and after her death, it would remain his alone as an inheritance and property. The wife’s actions could not result in any disadvantage to his rights in such matters. Pfeil, *ibid.*, at the end.

### ADDITION.

By law, because of the marriage money or dowry <note>original: *Heyrathsgut*</note> they bring in, wives have not only a tacit mortgage on their husbands' property but also, by personal privilege, a "Right of Preference" <note>original: *Jus prælationis*</note> and retention, which is called "The Woman’s Right" in the Electoral Saxon Constitutions, specifically the *Order of Process or Courts*, title 43. Mr. Doctor Tabor, *On Guarantees*, chapter 8, section 12.

### 32. Suffragan Bishop. <note>original: *Weih-Bischoff. Pro-Episcopus, Suffraganeus.*</note>

### ADDITION.

When did the names for municipal jurisdiction <term>Weichbild</term> <note>A term referring to the legal district or jurisdiction of a city, often symbolized by a statue.</note> and the Roland statue <note>original: *Rulandi*</note> begin? Where several people have a communal hunt together, they shall have the lark-netting <note>original: *Lerchenstreichen*</note> in common; likewise the citizens in cities shall be entitled to the same on their municipal territory <note>original: *Weichbild*</note> and fields, where they are not fenced off. ### 35. Striking the Hunting Knife. <note>original: *Weidmesser schlagen. Flagro ligneo nates percutere.*</note>

If a Nobleman, to whom in the act of hunting the

<column-break/>

hunting knife is struck <note>A ritualized form of mild corporal punishment or hazing among hunters.</note>, either because in the exercises of engines or crossbows he missed the mark, or otherwise "got the sow" <note>original: *die Sau bekommen*; a German idiom for failing or making a mess of things</note> as we say, is struck by a jester with a certain wooden whip or paddle upon the buttocks, or is "pratched" <note>original: *gepritschet*; struck with a wooden slat</note> (which custom Simon Majolus proves in volume 2 of *Dog Days*, colloquy 6, folio 353, flowed down from the ancient Romans to the Germans), can he bring a legal action for injury? Joseph Nolden denies it in his treatise *On the Status of the Noble*, chapter 13, number 83 and following. Because an injury is not inflicted through joke and play, see the Digest, law 3, section 3, *on injuries*. Farinaccius, book 3 of *Criminal Practice*, question 105, number 125.

### 36. Weeping. <note>original: *Weinen. Flere, Lugere.*</note>

Talentonus teaches at length in *On Recondite Matters*, book 1, chapter 22, that those just born neither laugh nor weep, but only wail <note>original: *vagire*</note>, and that wailing is not weeping.

Whether it is a judgment of sorcery or witchcraft when one "cannot weep" <note>A common belief in witch trials was that the accused could not shed tears.</note>? I have spoken of this elsewhere in *Deliberations & Counsels*. Let Justus Oldekop be seen in *Criminal Observations*, title 4, observation 44. Nicolaus Brandr in *On the Lawful Method of Investigating Sorcerers and Witches*, part 1, thesis 24. Christoph Daurer in his *Tubingen Inaugural Dissertation, 1664, on the Denunciation of Witches*, page 63 and the two following pages.

->ADDITION.<-

In Jerusalem in the Temple there was a special gate or door at which the sorrowful entered, who were then comforted by the priest thus: "May the kind God, who dwells in this house, gladden and comfort you according to His gracious will." Mr. Harsdörffer in the *German Secretary*, part 3, title 26. On the "tears of trees," C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 1, chapter 2, page 4. To veil with tears: Job: "I wept over every weak person," and who is weaker than the deceased? Many heroes wept at the calamity of enemies, see Rupert on Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 1, section 5, and they held great honor for the living, ibid number 6. "Lacrimæ" <note>tears</note> without aspiration, and with a simple *i* or *u*. It is derived indeed from the Greek *dakryon* <note>original: *δάκρυον*</note> or rather *dakryma* <note>original: *δάκρυμα*</note>, whence *dacryma*, which occurs in Livy, but with the gender changed, just as happens in *glaucoma* and *schema*, which come from Greek neuters: but among the Latins they are also used in the feminine gender. Furthermore, the letters *d* and *l* were easily interchangeable <note>original: *εὐμετάβολοι*</note>. Hence *Dingua* [for *Lingua*], *Calamitas*, *Dacryma*. Victorinus observes *Prasilium* for *Præsidium*; Festus observes *Cassilam* for *cassida*, see Mr. Dilherr in *Philological Apparatus*, pages 111, 112, 113, 114.

## 37. Wine-Purchase, God’s-Penny, Drinking-Money, Holy Penny.
<note>original: *Weinkauff, Gottspfening, Nummi bibales, Denarius sanctus.*</note>

When earnest money <term>arrha</term> <note>A small payment made to seal a contract, often forfeit if the deal is broken.</note> is involved in a contract of buying and selling, there is room for repentance (backing out), according to the law *on contracts* at the end of the Code *on the faith of instruments*. It follows that he who revokes the contract is held to nothing more than either losing the earnest money he gave, or returning double what he received. Nor can one sue for damages in that situation, since the person revoking does not go against the contract, and thus does not harm the other: for it was the nature of the contract from the beginning that it could be revoked once earnest money was accepted. For he has only himself to blame who, when he could have bound and fortified the contract with the strongest bond—namely, consent based on good faith—instead used the more fragile bond of earnest money. Zasius, *Individual Responses*, book 2, chapter 24, number 2.

It does not stand to the contrary that the loss or doubling of earnest money is a penalty which 

<column-break/>

does not exclude damages: for earnest money is not given at the beginning, nor agreed upon as a penalty, but as evidence of a purchase, and so that it may be more clearly established that the price was agreed upon. But let us say that the loss of earnest money results in a penalty; nevertheless, it still provides the faculty of repenting, so that damages are excluded. Zasius, in the same place, numbers 4 and following, where he limits what was said about repentance when drinking-money <note>original: *bibales*</note> is given as witness to a contract, commonly called **Wine-Purchase** <note>original: *Weinkauff*</note>, as is the custom in Germany. For this type of drinking-money does not have the force of earnest money, but is given so that those who were present may remember the contract. In this case, repentance would not take place, since the contract relies on consent alone. It is similar when a penny of some Saint is given, commonly called a **God’s-Penny** <note>original: *Gottespfenning*</note>.

It is likewise limited if a specific penalty was expressed, or if the earnest money was given in place of the price, **as a down-payment or purchase-shilling**; for then not only does repentance have no place, but the contract—in which the matter is no longer untouched—cannot be dissolved even by the bare consent of both parties. The same applies in a marriage contract, though it is different in betrothals.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the refund of wine expenses, see Gail, book 2, observation 19, number 9. In the Municipal Statutes of Württemberg, the faculty of repenting is permitted within 14 days before the formal filing is made. Bocer, 3rd Dispute 22, title 50; however, the person repenting has this disadvantage: that he must pay the **Wine-Purchase** in full, and also respectively lose the **Earnest Money** <note>original: *Arrham*</note> or **Holding-Penny** <note>original: *Hafftpfenning*</note>, or restore it twofold. See the Princely Württemberg Land-Ordinance, part 2, title 13, *on the filing of contracts*, paragraph "but where," folio 281. Besold, in the same place, thesis 60, extends that law in thesis 62 to other contracts made regarding immovable goods.

## 38. White-Penny.
<note>original: *Weißpfenning*</note>

There are two kinds of "Whites"; some originated in Saxony and are called **Witten**, which those of Lübeck struck first, and later others as well. Tilemann Friese, *in the treatise on coinage, part 3, chapter 13, where he speaks of the value*. Others are in the Rhine region and are called **White-Pennies** <note>original: *Weißpfenning*</note>, according to which most currencies are to be valued, and even now—though not so frequently—they are appraised. Freher, *on re-coinage*.

### ADDITION.

See Auer, *on the Law of Coinage*, theses 11, 62, 67.

Otherwise, they call **Foreign** anything that is not German. Properly, however, **Foreign** <note>original: *Welsch*</note> comes from the Walloons, by which name almost all Gallo-Belgians are

### 37. Wine-Purchase Money, God’s Penny. <term>Nummi bibales</term>, <term>Denarius sanctus</term>.

When in a contract of sale and purchase <term>arrha</term> <note>Earnest money or a down payment used to bind a contract.</note> is involved, there is "room for repentance" <note>original: *locus pœnitentiæ*; the legal right to back out of a deal before it is finalized.</note> according to the law of contracts. It follows that he who revokes the contract is held to nothing more than either losing the earnest money he gave, or returning double the earnest money he received. In such a case, one cannot sue for damages, since the person revoking the contract does not technically "violate" it, and thus causes no legal injury to the other. For it was the nature of the contract from the start that it could be revoked once the earnest money was accepted. He should blame himself who, though he could have bound and fortified the contract with the strongest bond—namely, mutual consent based on good faith—chose instead to use the more fragile bond of earnest money. *Zasius, Single Responses, book 2, chapter 24, number 2.*

Nor does it stand to the contrary that the loss or doubling of earnest money is a penalty which does not

<column-break/>

exclude further damages. For earnest money is not initially given, nor agreed upon, as a penalty, but as evidence of the purchase, and to make it more evident that the price was agreed upon. But let us say that while the loss of earnest money results in a penalty, it nevertheless provides the faculty of "repenting" (backing out), so that further damages are excluded. *Zasius, in the same place, numbers 4 and following*, where he limits what was said about "repenting" to when <term>bibales</term> <note>Literally "drinking money," commonly called "wine money" or *Weinkauff*.</note> are given as testimony of the contract, as is the custom in Germany. This kind of "wine money" does not have the legal force of earnest money <note>original: *arrha*</note>, but is given so that those present may remember the contract. In this case, there is no "room for repentance," since the contract rests on consent alone. It is the same when a "penny of a certain Saint" is given, commonly called "God’s penny" <note>original: *Gottespfenning*; a small sum given to charity to seal a bargain.</note>.

This is likewise limited if a specific penalty was expressed, or if the earnest money was given in place of the price, as a "down payment" or "purchase-shilling" <note>original: *zum Ankauff oder Kauffschilling*</note>. In that case, not only is there no room for repentance, but the contract—in which the matter is no longer "whole"—cannot be dissolved even by the simple consent of both parties. The same applies in a marriage contract, though it is different in betrothals.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the refund of wine expenses, see *Gail, 2nd observation, 19, number 9.* In the municipal statutes of Württemberg, the faculty of repenting is permitted within 14 days before the formal filing is made. *Bocer, 3rd Dispute, 22, title 50.* However, the one who repents suffers this disadvantage: that he must pay the "wine money" in full, and also respectively lose the earnest money or "binding penny" <note>original: *Hafftpfennig*</note>, or pay it back double. *Princely Württemberg Land-Rights, part 2, title 13, on the filing of contracts, paragraph "but there," folio 281. Besold, ibid, thesis 60*, who extends that law in thesis 62 to other contracts made concerning immovable property.

### 38. White Penny. <term>Weißpfenning</term>.

There are two kinds of "whites." Some, born in Saxony, are called <term>Witten</term>, which the people of Lübeck minted first, and later others followed. *Telemann Frif. in the Treatise on Coinage, part 3, chapter 13*, where he discusses their value. Others are from the Rhine region and are called "White Pennies" <note>original: *Weißpfenning*</note>, according to which most currencies are to be valued; they are still used today, though not as frequently appraised. *Freher, on the re-minting of coins.*

->ADDITION.<-

See *Auer on the Law of Coinage, theses 11, 62, 67.*

### 39. Foreign, Italian. <term>Welsch</term>, <term>Italicum</term>.

Whatever excels in size, the Germans call "Italian." <note>original: *Italicum*</note> *Georg Fabricius, Annals of the City of Meissen, book 3, folio 223.* Thus a "Welsch Goose" <note>original: *Welsche Gans*</note> is a large Penelope-goose; "Welsch Nut" <note>original: *Welsche Nuß*; a walnut</note>, "Welsch Peas," "Welsch Chickens" <note>original: *Welsche Hüner*; turkeys</note>, etc. In this way, *Welsch* is taken to mean anything rare or foreign. Otherwise, they call *Welsch* "everything that is not German." Properly, however, *Welsch* comes from the "Walloons," by which name the Gallo-Belgians are usually called.

### 40. Weme. To Whomever.

The term "to whomever," or **weme**, is an unrestrained expression and excludes no one, as noted in the chapter *solicita*, 5, at the verse "whatever you bind" in the section on *Superiority and Obedience* <note>original Latin: *de majoritat. & obed.* from Canon Law</note>. This applies even in matters that are considered "odious" <note>Legally restrictive or burdensome.</note> or subject to limitation; the natural and broad meaning of this word must be maintained here as well. See Aretinus on the law *cum de legat.* in the *Digest on Testaments*, and Socinus, counsel 297.

->ADDITION.<-

The phrase **"Whoever that may be"** <note>original: *Wer der auch wäre*</note> does not even exempt those with special privileges. See Berlich, conclusion 62, number 19. Regarding the term "To anyone," see Vinnius on the *Institutes*, section 11, regarding the appointment of heirs.

### 41. Werchdegen. Overseer of workers.

The ancients used the term **Werchdegen** for those we now call a *Statthalter* <note>A governor, deputy, or lieutenant.</note>. The word seems to be composed of **Werck** (work), which is common, and the ancient word **Degen**, which used to mean "man" or "warrior." This is frequently found in old Alamanic histories: **the bold warrior, the valiant warrior, the strong warrior** <note>original: *der kühne Degen, der streitbare Degen, der starcke Degen*</note>, meaning the bold, valiant, or strong man or hero. Thus, a **Werckdegen** is a **Werckmeister** (master of works), a term we still use for a **Building Overseer, Construction Colonel, or Master Builder**. Consequently, the **Werchdegen** and **Work-Colonels** of the ancients seem to be nothing other than what we call a **Master Builder** today. See Killinger on *Joint Inheritance*, discourse 3, number 175 and following. These also seem to be the same people whom Caesar, in his *Gallic War*, calls **Vergobretos** <note>A high magistrate among the Gauls.</note>.

### 42. Werd. Island.

The ancient Germans called an island **a Werder**. See Schneidewein on the section *Island*, number 7, in the *Institutes on the Division of Things*. Also Noë Meurer in his *Treatise on Water Rights*. The meaning of this German word, as used in the deed of investiture for the Count of East Friesland, is discussed at length in the *Legal Counsels* of Johann Göddäus, regarding the washing up of the sea <note>original: *alluv. maris*</note>, number 344. I agree with Mr. Johann Gryphiander in his *Treatise on Islands*, chapter 1, number 14, and suspect that the term is general, covering islands as well as land added by river deposits or the shifting of riverbeds, and even the corners of land at the confluence of rivers. It is said to be derived from the word "to become" <note>original: *werden*</note>. Thus the Imperial town of Donauwörth is named as if it were a "Danube Peninsula." The Swedes call this a *Holm*, which is the origin of the name Stockholm and the endings of many other place names in that region. However, from **Werd** come the names **Werdun and Werden**. In these

<column-break/>

many cities and villages of Friesland end, such as Leeuwarden and Bolsward. See Ubbo Emmius in *The Republic of the Frisians*, though he interprets **Werd** as a mound or an elevated place suitable for both pasture and sowing. See Gryphiander in the cited place. Similarly, in Tübingen, a place is called **the Werd**, where there are public pastures by the Neckar and other nearby streams.

### 43. Westphälisch Gericht, oder Proceß. Westphalian Court or Process.

It is well known that many privileges of the Imperial States include the provision that they are **exempt from the Westphalian Courts.** <note>Also known as the Vehmic courts (Fehmgerichte), these were secret legal tribunals in Westphalia that exercised great power in the Middle Ages.</note> From this, it is clear that these courts once held great power and scope, as well as an intolerable severity. On this, see Freher’s specialized treatise and Mr. Gryphiander in his *Treatise on the Municipal Law*.

->ADDITION.<-

The Counts Palatine are privileged against the Westphalian Court. See Wehner under this entry and Mundius, *On the Counts Palatine*, chapter 3, number 339.

The **Reformation of the Westphalian Court** of the year 1495 is mentioned by Limnaeus, volume 2, *Additions to book 1*, chapter 12, page 279. See Mr. Speidel in his *Mirror of Notables*, pages 1359 and 1368. Also Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 10, page 140, and book 5, chapter 16, page 374. Regarding **Westphalian Judges**, see Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 3, chapter 6, page 57. Zeiller wrote a *Topography of the Westphalian Circle* in the year 1647.

### 44. Wette. Fine.

To the Saxons, this means "to fine"; hence **Gewette**, a fine. The Italians, turning this word into *guadia*, use it for a pledge or wager, just as the Saxon **Gewähr** (warranty) became *guaranda*. The etymology provided in the gloss on article 64, book 3, number 2, is not far off: "the little word **Wette** means as much as 'to cause woe'" <note>original: *wehe thun*</note>. See Gryphiander, *On the Municipal Law*, chapter 69, number 7 and following. To the ancient Alamanni, **Wizzi** stood for punishment; see Freher in *Alamanic Symbols*. The Saxons often change an 'S' into a 'T'.

### 45. Wetten. To Wager.

A wager <note>original: *Sponsio*</note> is so called because it is done or said "spontaneously" (of one's own accord); to pledge or promise is to speak, give, or promise of one's own accord. See Johann Göddäus on law 7, number 16, in the *Digest on the Meaning of Words*. Although this term for a wager is used <term>synonymously</term> <note>original Greek: *συνωνύμως*</note> by the Doctors of Law, we use it here for what we call in German a **Wettung** or **wetten** (to bet). It is correctly defined as a certain reciprocal promise by which the loser is obligated to pay money or something else; it was a playful promise and in ancient times was only undertaken as a game. See Caspar Antonius Thessaurus, *Forensic Questions*, book 2, question 19, at the beginning; on this matter see also Hering, *On Suretyship*, chapter 18, number 42, and the specialized inaugural dissertation from Strasbourg.

<meta>This page continues an alphabetical legal and linguistic encyclopedia. The previous page discussed the terms "Weme" (to whomever) and "Werchdegen" (overseer of workers). This page continues with the legal status of wagers (Sponsiones) and the etymology of town names ending in "-wick."</meta>

Molina, *On Justice and Law* <note>original: *de Just. & Jur.*</note>, treatise 2, disputation 508. Also, see my own work in *Selected Questions* <note>original: *delibatis*</note>, book 2, question 16.

Regarding **wagers** <term>Sponsiones: formal bets or promises made between parties</term>, Peter Binsfeld teaches whether and when they are permitted in his commentary on the chapter *naviganti* regarding usury, question 5, page 550. See also Stracha in his treatise *On Commerce*, where he discusses wagers; Philipp Fabri in the treatise *On Restitution*, page 112; Scheffer’s *Practical Questions*, book 1, question 34; and Pfeil, counsel 34. The latter also discusses penal stipulations in counsel 36—for instance, if someone plays at dice and agrees to pay one hundred, etc.

**Deposits for wagers** <note>original: *das Wetten*</note> occur when those disputing a matter place a sum in escrow <note>original: *sequestrum*</note> to be given to whichever side is proven right. Although this method of acquisition is not inherently illegal according to Dominicus Soto (book 4, *On Justice and Law*, question 8, article 2), the Magistrates of Amsterdam and others act rightly and prudently. They do not allow legal actions between merchants in these cases, as the practice would otherwise be abused in vain and reckless ways as an indirect method of profit. See Keckermann, *Course of Philosophy*, disputation 28, question 48, at the end.

If someone bets that another person will not come to a wedding, and that person is prevented from coming by chance or by **superior force** <note>original: *vis majori*</note>, the question is: **who has won?** <note>original: *wers gewonnen?*</note> It seems it should be said that the one who bet they *would* come looked more to the **will and inclination** to attend. On the opposing side, it is argued that the bet was based on the **deed itself** <note>original: *factum*</note>—what would actually happen, not what was intended. Similarly, if one bets that "if a ship arrives from Asia," one does not look at whether it was able or willing to come, but simply whether it arrived or not.

The primary effects of wagers are the legal actions arising from them:
(1) An **action based on a formal promise** <term>Actio ex stipulatu: a lawsuit to enforce a verbal contract</term> applies if the wager was made through a formal stipulation, provided the condition is met.
(2) An **action based on a simple agreement** <term>Actio ex pacto: an action based on an informal pact</term> if the wager was made by a "naked" agreement without formal ritual.

(3) An **action on the prescribed words** <term>Actio praescriptis verbis: a flexible legal remedy for contracts that don't fit standard categories</term>, which is granted not only against those who refuse to fulfill a condition they are capable of meeting, but also against one who refuses to hand over a pledge deposited with them to the winner.
(4) An **action for damages** restores the obligation if someone was drawn into a wager by deceit. Stracha, *On Wagers*, part 4, chapter 14.
(5) An **action regarding fraud** <note>original: *Actio de dolo*</note>, as when someone entices another into a wager through trickery; see the example provided by Stracha.

The following are grounds to invalidate these wagers: (1) **Deceit**; (2) **Verbal traps**, such as the joke: **"What will you bet? I know a town clerk who can neither write nor read"** <note>The trick being that the man's name is "Town-Clerk," or he holds the title but is illiterate.</note>. Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 85.

(3) **Force**; (4) **Fear**; (5) **Dishonorable cause**. See Caspar Antonius Thesaurus, *Forensic Questions*, book 2, question 19, and Besold, Volume 1.

<column-break/>

Number 6, where the return of what was paid is granted. (6) **Error**. Since one who is mistaken is not seen to truly consent; for nothing is so contrary to consent as error. Thus, consent and error cannot exist in the same person. (7) **A doubtful promise**. Zalius on law 108, number 11, *On Verbal Obligations*.

Regarding whether a wager made upon a judicial sentence being delivered in a certain way is legally valid, see Caspar Antonius Thesaurus, book 2, question 19.

On the law and manner of wagers, see also Thomas Hebraeus, *Daily Matters*, chapters 1 and 2.

### ADDITION.

See Mr. Speidel in his *Notable Observations*, letter W, number 100. Why wagers regarding the past should be more easily granted than those regarding the future: Zahn, *On Lies*, book 2, chapter 85, number 3. On a wager containing inequality, number 5. Wagers are accepted everywhere in the Roman Empire. Merchants' wagers are permitted, provided they are subject to the **moderation of a Judge**. Mr. Johann Philippi, Jurist, in the *Practical Use of Justinian's Institutes*, book 3, title 16, sections 10–12, says: **"The moderation of such betting is rightly left to the judicial office."**

On wagers, see Paul Christinaeus, *Belgian Decisions*, volume 2, decision 198 and following. According to **Saxon Law** <note>original: *Jure Sax.*</note>, **no judge shall rule over gambling or betting.** Schneidewein on the *Institutes*, page 499.

### 46. Wic. Vicus (Village/District).

**Wic**, according to Alfred the Anglo-Saxon, a very ancient writer whom William Camden praises in his *Britannia*, signified a **Fortress** <note>original: *Castellum*</note> to the ancient Saxons. Certain excerpts from Nicolaus Marschalk affirm the same, reading: **"Wic in the old Saxon language means a spot or small town in which the citizens and inhabitants of the place restrain themselves from violence,"** etc. For I do not dwell on Krantz, who in *Saxonia* (book 2, chapter 30) and *Metropolis* (book 2, chapter 3) affirms that to the Saxons, **Wic** is a **bay** <note>original: *Sinum*</note> of a flowing river, a pond, or the sea. Sethus Calvisius agrees in his *Chronological Work* (year 861), saying: **"Brunswick [Brunsvicum] takes its name from Bruno and from the bay [sinus] of the flowing river, which the Saxons in their language call a Wick; and part of the city is still today called 'the old Wick' [die alte Wick],"** etc.

Nor would I doubt that the Saxon **Wic** comes from the Latin **Vicus** (village/neighborhood). Just as from *Vella* (for so the ancients wrote for *Villa*, according to Frisius’s dictionary) arose the word **Wölle** (whence the Swabian *Weil* or *Weiler*), signifying a house or a modest cluster of houses, such as Rotwelle in the territory of Mansfeld, or Cowelle, mentioned in the records of the Monastery of Maria Vallensis. It is also pronounced with a fuller sound as **Wedel**, which is the name of a town in Holstein and a village near Riddagshausen. You may find compound names from this everywhere: Borchwedel and Steinwedel in the Lüneburg region; Saltwedel in the Old March of Brandenburg; and Langwedel in the diocese...

**47. Repurchase. Agreement to Sell Back.** <note>original: *Wiederkauff. Pactum de retrovendendo*</note>
->**Agreement to sell back.**<-

An agreement to sell back is commonly known as a **Wiederkauff** <term>Wiederkauff: a contract where the seller retains the right to buy the property back later</term>, occurring when a sale is conducted such that whenever the seller offers the price, the item is restored to them, according to Law 2 of the Code on agreements between buyer and seller. Nor is the buyer released by merely paying the interest on that law. For the buyer knows that the item can be taken away from him, and thus he is always in "bad faith" <note>original: *mala fide*</note> according to the rule of law. This is because the recovery of that item is a matter of pure faculty <note>a reserved right</note>. See Crassus, book 1, *Common Opinions*, chapter 3, question 7; Mynsinger, century 1, observation 16, and century 6, observation 70.

Wherever an agreement to sell back is attached to a contract of sale and a **smallness of price** <note>original: *modicitas pretii*</note> is involved—for instance, if the item was worth one hundred and is sold for fifty—then that contract is to be judged as **usurious** <term>fœneratitius: a disguised loan where the low price acts like interest</term>, even if the buyer is not usually a moneylender.

For we must judge an act to be done according to its nature, since the nature of a thing belongs to its essence. However, it is the nature of a sale that the price be conforming to the item sold. If an item is worth one hundred, it is commonly bought for one hundred; if not for one hundred, there is generally no massive excess or decrease in price according to common dealings. Lanfrancus de Orian, on the Clementines, regarding *Judgments*, number 34. If, however, the price is just, such a contract is lawful and is a true sale. Lanfrancus, in the same place.

Ludovico Molina deals with this contract at greater length in his treatise *On Justice and Law*, volume 2, dispute 373. Also Joannettus, *On Sales under Repurchase Agreements*, in his work on page 188 

<column-break/>

and following. Add Johann Jacob Speidel in *Sy-Quaest.* under the word *Pactum retrovendendi*, part 1, question 2.

---

->ADDITION.<-

Agreements to sell back in the purchase of goods from a **minor** (or bought in their name) are not valid, even if the rest of the contract stands. Klock, volume 2, counsel 42, number 13. This is further discussed in numbers 11 to 119. An agreement to sell back is considered part of the price and decreases the true value of the goods by a fourth part <note>original: *in quarta parte*</note>, counsel 42, number 26; though others leave this to be defined by the Judge’s discretion. The same, number 27. An agreement to sell back is a **burden** <note>original: *onus*</note>, because of which a property subject to repurchase must be valued at much less than it otherwise would be. Counsel 42, number 29. If added by a minor after an interval without a formal Decree, it is not valid. The same, number 36. It implies a **simulation** <note>a fake or hidden deal</note> if it is placed in a different document from the instrument of sale itself. Refuted in numbers 158 to 167. It differs from the actual act of repurchasing, number 76. If not placed in the sale document, it can be proven by witnesses, numbers 90, 91. Whether the right of repurchase <note>original: *Juri Reluendi*</note> can be lost through **prescription** <term>prescription: the loss of a legal right because it was not exercised within a certain time limit</term>. Klock, volume 2, counsel 61, number 108. Some say it expires after 30 years (counsel 42, numbers 81-83), while the contrary is asserted in number 227 and following, especially 233.

In the hands of the one buying under a repurchase agreement, the ownership of the thing bought is **revocable**. Baptista Aymus, book 2, *On the Law of Alluvion*, chapter 10, number 12. Martin Pegius, when he had written three books on the **Right of First Refusal** <term>Protimiseos: the right of a family member or neighbor to match a price and buy property before an outsider</term>, which he called "On Stepping-in and Standing-before" <note>original: *von Einstand und Vorstand*</note>, later specifically added a book on page 37 "On Reserved Repurchase Agreements" <note>original: *von vorbehaltenen Wiederkäuffen*</note>. The force and effect of this agreement is notable regarding the present time, because it makes the item of lesser value. Just as any other burden diminishes the price of an item, it is therefore not quite safe to follow the presumption of our Besold, who considers such an agreement usurious whenever a smallness of price occurs (e.g., if a thing worth 100 is sold for 50). Since the price of the thing is diminished by this very agreement, the setting of a lower price brings the transaction closer to **equality** rather than to a usurious excess. Regarding future time, the effect of the repurchase agreement is that **no prescription** can be opposed to it, not even one of a hundred years <note>meaning the right to buy it back never expires</note>. Mynsinger, observation 70, number last. This is the case even though Bachovius vainly disagrees. An agreement to sell back is lawful.

### 48. Counter-Gift. Gift in consideration of marriage.

What are dowers or endowments, in French *Dovaires*? *See Rebuff. on provisional sentences, glossary 3, folio 78.*

In our customs, this differs from the **Widum** <note>a widow's dower or endowment</note> and also from the **Morning-gift** <note>original: *Morgengab*; a gift given by a husband to his wife the morning after the wedding</note>. **Counter-gift** <note>original: *Widerlag*</note> is a gift given on account of marriage, which usually equals the dowry; and just as the dowry remains with the husband, so the **Counter-gift** remains with the wife for the days of her life, even if she should move on to another marriage. This is by custom, however, not by law, *see Sichard. on the title of the Code regarding gifts on account of marriage.* **Widum** is derived from "widow," *see below under* **Widum**. **Residence** <note>original: *Sitz*</note> is a life-long provision for a widow which the husband establishes for the wife, not the other way around. Regarding the Morning-gift, which is the price of virginity, *I have spoken above in its proper place.*

Regarding these gifts, one may look at *Bocer in the treatise on gifts, chapter 10*, where he teaches how they differ; likewise *Brunner on Collations, chapter 4, number 815*. And that in ancient times husbands endowed their wives, and not wives their husbands, *I have spoken above under the word* Marriage-portion <note>original: *Heyrathgut*</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

Excellent on this matter is *that legal response given at Altdorf on June 1, 1655*, where: Titius is obligated to pay interest to his son Sempronius for the marriage gift <note>original: *Donation propter Nuptias*</note> that was put in writing but not yet handed over. And although he maintained him with considerable expense in foreign lands, provided a wealthy marriage, and thereafter secured a high-paying service, such things—having been done out of fatherly affection—matter little to the case. Rather, he is nonetheless held by the law to give the marriage gift, because he married him to Caja and she promised a certain dowry, *law 19 of the Digest on the status of persons; authentic "dowry given" in the Code on gifts before marriage.* As stipulated by the law, *said Authentic and Novel 91, chapter 2, and there the Glossary and Johann Fab.* And even if the establishment of the marriage gift had stood solely at the father's discretion, he could no longer, after having put it in writing, escape the payment of interest after the delay; since those things which are voluntary at the start become a necessity afterward, *law 5 of the Code on Obligations and Actions, the final law of Besold, Volume 1.*

<column-break/>

*...below in the Code regarding the Velleian decree of the Senate, and in contracts of good faith* and similar dealings, interest should be owed from the time of the delay, *law 32, section 2 of the Digest on interest; law 34 of the same title; the final law of the Code on interest and fruits of the law. Add the Nuremberg Reformation, title 28, law 3.* This debt, which the father created by writing the marriage gift, fell upon the inheritance after his death, so that the son is entitled to demand the outstanding interest. This would be different only if the gift were immoderate, such that the other children were deprived of their legal portion; in which case not only could the father during his lifetime use the *benefit of competence* <note>a legal protection allowing a debtor to keep enough to live on</note>, so as not to be sued for more than he is able to provide, according to the arguments of *Johann Zanger on Exceptions, part 2, chapter 14*, but also after his death, the heirs and children could make use of it and at the same time enter a complaint regarding an undutiful gift, *law 1 and the whole title of the Code on undutiful gifts.* Otherwise, it is beyond all doubt that a mother, by paying out pensions, can neither prejudice her husband nor her children, nor obligate them in the slightest, *law 1 of the whole title of the Code: that a wife should not be held for the husband, nor a husband for the wife, and there the Glossary and the common teachers.* Regarding the Counter-gift, *see Zorer, part 2, question 7, numbers 570 and 573 following, 578, 584, 585.*

### 49. Redeeming, to release. To buy back. <note>original: *Wiederlösen, lösen. Reluere.*</note>

The verb *to redeem* <note>original: *luere*</note>, to release or buy back, applies only to pledges <note>collateral</note>, but not to buying and selling, as is clear *from the rubric of the Code on the redemption of pledges; see Ludolph Schrader, counsel 32, number 43, etc.*

### 50. Anabaptists. <note>original: *Wiedertäuffer. Anabaptistæ.*</note>

Regarding these, Lambert Hortensius writes thus in *On the Anabaptists, page 7:* In the beginning, it is well enough known to all that various errors began to creep into the Church just as the study of the humanities was being revived in our time. Most of these had their origin in obscure authors who were unrefined in good literature. But while some were more pestilential than others, no one failed to judge that one as the most ruinous to the world, by which the harmony of human society was disturbed: because nothing in life was held sacred, nothing held as one's own by right, there was no Magistrate, and one lived by no laws. Instead, in a reborn "Golden Age" (as is found in fables), mortals were supposedly forced to keep faith of their own accord. With these ideas as a foundation, the Anabaptists, those fanatic men, finally arose; relying on no judgment, devoid of reason and the law of nature, they began to pervert all things divine and human. For since they lived released from laws, they seem more to have followed the ritual of wild beasts and the life of brigands than the guidance of human nature. For they considered it pious to seize the property of others, to infest temples with sacrilege, to pollute everything with lust, to slaughter those not initiated into their same rites, to hold no courts or judgments, and to have wives in no fixed number according to their whim. See also Isacius Pontanus, *in the description of the city of Amsterdam.*

# Expanded Practical Treasury

...damensis <note>likely a reference to the legal scholar Joost de Damhouder</note> book 2, chapter 8, number 5 and following. This is also proven by the following examples.

*In the year 1525*, the Honorable Council of *St. Gallen* <note>a city in northeastern Switzerland</note> suffered much and heavy burden from the *Anabaptists* <term>original: *Wiedertäuffer*; a radical Reformation sect that rejected infant baptism</term>, which sect also established itself among them. Many were imprisoned; they held public conversations and *disputes* <note>original: *Disputationes*; formal theological debates common during the Reformation</note> with them. The Council was not inclined to punish anyone with death, as they had received reports from elsewhere that this achieved little and only served to make many of them stubborn. At last, however, their disobedient defiance grew so great that the Small and Large Councils of the city of *St. Gallen* agreed to have 200 honorable, sensible men from the common citizenry take a special oath for this case, and to be ready with weapons and armor at all hours, day and night. Whoever should not live according to the commands, will, decrees, and authority of the Honorable Council, but rather oppose it contrary to their sworn duty and seek to help themselves through their own force and caprice, etc., would be brought to obedience by hand and deed. No insolent violence would be given space or place, even if it reached the point of life and limb, etc. At this, the *Anabaptists* were so terrified that they let their storming and gathering subside after the Council's prohibition was issued, and the city came to peace. Then, after the city began to punish them with fines, they "let the milk down" <note>an idiom meaning they lost their fervor or gave up their resistance</note> and became as docile as little lambs.

*In the year of Christ 1526*, a wonderful and terrifying event occurred between two *Anabaptists* and biological brothers, *Thomas* and *Leonhard Schücker*, both of whom were residents under the jurisdiction of *St. Gallen* and were citizens, two notable, honest fellows in appearance and character. On the 7th day of *February*, along with their wives and siblings, at the onset of night, they had gathered in their father's house, located above the city behind the mountain called Buch and Mülleck. They joined together for a special friendly gathering and concluded half the night with joy. After midnight, however, they discussed and practiced the teachings of *Anabaptism*, even in the presence of their father and mother, adopting various gestures and ways; yet no one suspected that the dear brothers would commit anything gruesome against each other there. *Thomas* (either burdened with too much wine or otherwise displaced in his mind) towards the breaking of day on *February 8th* (which was "Mad Tuesday" <note>original: *unsinnig Dienstag*; a local name for Shrove Tuesday or Mardi Gras</note>, as they called it in *Thurgau*) grabbed his brother *Leonhard*—who was a tall, handsome, strong-as-a-tree man (though also afflicted with *Anabaptism*)—by the arm and commanded him to kneel down in the middle of the room,

<column-break/>

in the sight of his father, mother, and all his relatives. And when his father threatened him not to undertake anything improper, he answered: one should not worry, for nothing could happen there except what was the Father's will. Since *Leonhard* remained kneeling stiffly and desired with raised hands that the "will of the Father" be fulfilled, etc.; suddenly *Thomas* took a short, small side-sword <note>original: *Handdegen*; a light sword or dagger carried for personal defense</note> which he wore at his side, and struck off his brother *Leonhard's* head. Additionally, he nearly cut off his right thumb with the tip of the sword as he had his hands outstretched. At this, a great howling, screaming, and weeping arose, and everyone fled from the house, one from the other. *Thomas*, however, ran down the nearest way into the city, without a doublet or shoes, in nothing but his shirt and trousers, into the house of *Doctor Joachim Vadianus* <note>a famous Swiss humanist scholar and reformer who was then mayor</note> (who was Mayor at the time), and told him what great things had happened that morning and were fulfilled according to the Father's will, and how vinegar and gall had been drunk, etc. Yet he mentioned the deed itself not with a single word. At this, the Mayor rebuked him harshly with words for his deaf manner and disobedience, and had him clothed in shoes and a coat and led home again, for he saw well that he was not right in the head, yet he did not suspect any evil. But soon the cry of murder arrived, whereupon the Mayor sent a servant of the city up there, who found the misery that had occurred. Thus *Thomas Schücker* was imprisoned along with his wife. Initially, he claimed to have no knowledge of the deed, for he was not truly in his right mind. The following day, he confessed to the matter, and upon this, on the 10th day of the aforementioned month (on a Friday), he was executed by the sword as an act of mercy <note>meaning he was decapitated rather than facing a more agonizing execution</note>, to the great grief of everyone that this father had so miserably lost two such beautiful sons. For the family had been a pious, upright, and honest people, etc. Following this piteous deed, the enterprise of the *Anabaptists* in *St. Gallen* was entirely extinguished: for this terrifying fruit (by God’s judgment and permission) made people loathe such filth more than could perhaps have been achieved with the sword. Everything was stilled once the enemy of human salvation <note>the Devil</note> was seen so deeply here in his cabinet of arts, etc. *Stumpff* in the *Swiss Chronicle* <note>original: *Schweitzer-Chronick*; a famous history by Johannes Stumpf published in 1548</note> book 5, chapter 8, page 48 and following; the same in the last book, chapter 40, page 465, writes thus: *In the year 1525*, the sect of the *Anabaptists* arose, and thereafter for a long time miserably troubled the churches and caused great unrest in many places; therefore I must describe their restless life and fantasy at some length. The sect first arose in *St. Gallen* in *Thurgau*, and...

# Lit. W. 1125

and also in the **territory of Zurich**, and it crawled far and wide, an evil sect <note>The author writes from a perspective critical of the radical Reformation, common in legal and ecclesiastical texts of this period.</note> that sprang from several disobedient people who unexpectedly gained a large following for themselves. They despised all courts and authorities, as well as all common and civil laws, all orderly proceedings, and both temporal and spiritual powers. They held themselves alone to be holy and blameless, like the **Donatists** <note>A schismatic Christian group in North Africa during the 4th and 5th centuries that argued only the "pure" could belong to the church.</note> in the time of **St. Augustine** in Africa. They considered no church to be the Body of Christ except their own gathering; no faith to be the righteousness of Christ except their own faith. No one knew Christ but them. They alone were holy, without sin, and righteous. They said publicly that no sin could be harmful to them. Yet, in deed, they took upon themselves very crude and blasphemous sins; and most significantly, they repeated the baptism they had first received <note>original: *äferten*; meaning they invalidated their infant baptism by being baptized again as adults.</note>, letting themselves be baptized again in brooks and rivers; conversely, they denounced **infant baptism** as evil and damned. All temporal goods had to be held in common among them in deed and use; they regarded their neighbor’s belongings and property as their own, unmindful that God’s Commandment forbids desiring another’s property. They taught that no Christian should take interest, or repayment, or profit from loaned money or goods before God. Likewise, that no Christian may, before God and by the allowance of Holy Scripture, hold the **worldly sword** and authority—that is, the protection and shield of the pious and innocent and for the punishment and rejection of the guilty—nor carry the sword, especially regarding punishments of life and limb, and whatever concerns **criminal justice** <term>original: *Malefiß*; referring to capital crimes or high-court jurisdiction</term>. They said the use of the sword was tyrannical and heathen, full of revenge and unmercifulness. Likewise, that no one should swear, and therefore no one should take an **oath** in any case, if they wished otherwise to be a Christian. They relied strictly on the bare words of Christ: **"You shall not swear at all,"** etc. <note>A reference to Matthew 5:34.</note>, without considering the distinction between Apostolic and Spiritual, and also worldly authority and the administration of office; and that indeed God oftentimes swore by Himself, just as the Apostles many times called God as a witness, and that God Himself commands us, in cases of necessity where the love of God and neighbor requires it, to swear by His name alone, etc. Likewise, that a Christian should not and may not wage war, nor carry or use any defense, neither for his own good nor his neighbor's; and for this reason, they commanded that the **city gates** be lifted off their hinges and taken away. Likewise, they did not fear any kind of illness, nor did they want others to fear them; yet they despised and rejected all **medicine**, saying: if it were the Father’s will for one to die, no one would be able to help preserve this temporal life; if it were the Father’s will

<column-break/>

not, then no one would die. In short, they attributed everything to the **Will of God**, which in itself was not improper, but with it they tempted God to the highest degree by rejecting all His means and creatures. At times, they would sink down as if they were falling asleep, lying there for a while without speech; and when they stood up again, they began to sigh and roll their eyes, saying what great things they had seen and what secrets had appeared to them. Likewise, they cried here and there in the streets: "The Day of the Lord! The Day of the Lord! **Zion, Zion!**" Certain women and men slept together in bodily community and held marriage in low honor. When one slept with another’s wife, not much resentment followed. The daughters took poor care of themselves, taking "spiritual" men and brothers, and some said that flesh and blood could not defile the spirit, etc. Whoever warned or punished them, they were his deadly enemies. Entire books have been written about their teaching and adventures. Their cruel, rebellious, and injurious deeds moved all authorities to take notice and offer resistance. Many of them were executed and put to death here and there. However, beforehand in many places, such as **Zurich, Bern, St. Gallen, Zofingen, Grüningen**, and other ends, discussions were held with them, but little could be achieved with them. Many were imprisoned, but they refused to swear an **oath of truce** <term>original: *Urphed*; a formal promise not to seek revenge or return to a territory after being released from custody</term>, regarding the oath as a great sin and unbefitting a Christian. When they were killed, they went to their deaths laughing and singing; because of this, the remaining ones only became more stubborn. But when the authorities finally opposed them with persistent earnestness, and since many evil fruits daily sprang from this sect, the nuisance subsided of its own accord day by day. Many among them, the most prominent and seemingly the most spiritual, afterwards surrendered themselves to all the world's vices and decadence ahead of others. Many pious people, initially deceived by the appearance of their hypocrisy, returned from them to the Church of Christ. The city of **Münster in Westphalia** became full of these Anabaptists, and the Bishop was driven out. They chose for themselves a **tailor as king** <note>A reference to Jan van Leiden, who led the radical Münster Rebellion in 1534-35.</note>, and gave the whole Empire much to do, until the city was finally starved out, conquered, and the misery was settled with great bloodshed. *One may also see Bullinger against the Anabaptists, especially book 1, chapter 5, and book 2, chapter 1.* <note>original Latin: *Videri etiam potest Bullinger. contra Anabaptistas...* refers to Heinrich Bullinger, a major Swiss reformer.</note>

## ADDITION.

Regarding **Anabaptists** <note>original: *Wiedertauffern*; literally "re-baptizers," a radical Reformation group</note>, see the *Forum of Protestations*, published by Lord Felvinger, pages 360 and 364. See also Pingizer, question 18. Anabaptists are to be removed from our midst by fire, sword, and various punishments, according to Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 86, number 1.

### 51. Again, once more, a second time. *Iterum*.

Although the word *Iterum* <note>Latin: "again" or "a second time"</note>, by its proper definition, designates a doubling and is limited to the number two; nevertheless, in the matter of issuing legal instruments, it is interpreted according to the subject matter at hand—that is, "as often as is necessary." See the law *veluti*, section *hæc vox* in the Digest *on the production of documents* <note>original: *ff. de edend.*</note>; the gloss on the chapter *sua nobis*; and there Panormitanus on appeals; and Nicolaus Everhardus in *Legal Topics*, the topic "from the subject matter," number 10.

## ADDITION.

The word *rursus* <note>Latin: "backwards" or "again"</note> or *iterum* in the matter of criminal bail: when it is verified, see Oldekop in *Criminal Observations*, page 116 and following, where he explains the phrase "to present again" <note>original: *Wiederstellen, Wiedereinstellen*</note>. Crimes are increased by repetition. A repeated act is punished more severely, according to Jacob Ayrer in the *Historical Process*, book 1, chapter 5, observation 3, numbers 18 and 19. Antonius Corsetus has written a treatise on doubled words.

### 52. Retraction. *Recantatio*.

The legal action for a retraction <note>original: *auf einen Widerruff*</note> was introduced by custom and is unknown to Roman Civil Law. Although traces of it appear in more remote antiquity, as I have shown in my second dissertation on injuries among the Tübingen scholars, theses 17 and following; hence it is also perpetual, as per the same dissertation, thesis 33, for custom is held to be law.

That the action for a **Palinodia** <note>Greek term for a recantation or "singing back" of one's words</note> or a reclamation <note>original: *auf einen Widerruff*</note> is today a Civil action is defended by Marquard Freher, book 2, *On Reputation*, 9, number 4; Mynsinger, century 2, observation 98; Wurmser, *Practical Observations*, title 9, observation 8; and Andreas Gail, book 1, observation 65, number 5. Gail says it is accepted in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>The highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire</note> that the judgment is not criminal but civil when one sues for a retraction or Palinodia. Indeed, petitions regarding injuries are received there daily that conclude with a demand for reclamation. These could not be received or admitted if it were a criminal judgment, since by virtue of the Ordinance of the Chamber, part 2, title 28, section *Und sonderlich*, as well as by the custom of all Germany (though it is otherwise in Common Law, according to Clarus, section *fin.*, question 94, number 3, and Mynsinger, observation 96), no criminal case—except for a breach of the Peace—can or should be litigated there; see Mynsinger, *Responses*, 7, decade 1, number 15.

For this reason, it is accepted and approved that because this action is Civil, it can be accumulated with an action for damages for injuries—or joined in the same petition—and moved

<column-break/>

forward; see Wurmser, *Practical Observations*, title 47, *on Law*, observation 8 at the end.

In **Saxony**, after the new Constitution of Augustus, part 2, chapter 4, Moller (1st semester, 2) teaches that said action is criminal, because along with the retraction, a penalty of imprisonment or exile is joined, depending on the quality of the injury, according to the said Constitution 24, at the verse *Darüber auch und daneben*. However, Wesenbeck (in his commentary on the Digest *on injuries*, number 18) disapproves of this, arguing that said Constitution speaks of the Palinodia as something quasi-civil and separate from the criminal penalty. Thus, both are owed, which would be otherwise if both were criminal, because no one should be afflicted with two punishments; Berlich (5, conclusion 62, number 13) calls it a "mixed" action. But regarding **Retorsions** <note>The principle of "like for like" in legal retaliation</note>, see the individual treatises by Rennemann and Harpprecht on the title of the Institutes *on injuries*; also my own work in the dissertation on the Municipal Law of Württemberg, part 1, where I discuss injuries.

## ADDITION.

On whether the Action for Retraction for a Palinodia can be accumulated with an action for estimated damages for injury, see Lord Doctor Biccius, of blessed memory—from whom I, like a silkworm from mulberry leaves, received life, that is, the <term>to bene vivere</term> <note>original: *το bene vivere*; a mix of Greek and Latin meaning "the well-lived life" or "living well" in a moral and professional sense</note>—in the *Golden Sections*, section 4, thesis 165, letter ff, and the citations therein.

### 53. Church Endowment. *Dos ecclesiæ*.

A **Church Endowment** <note>original: *Widumgut*</note> is the dowry of the Church, a plot of church land <note>original: *mansus*</note> given in place of a dowry; these lands are afterwards granted to the peasants as hereditary estates.

### 54. As, just as, etc. *Sicut, Prout*.

Baldus, Paulus de Castro (in the second to last law of the Code *on institutions and substitutions*, etc.) teach that those words—*prout* [according as], *juxta* [according to], *secundùm* [following], *sicut* [just as], *quemadmodum* [in what manner], and similar terms—when placed in a settlement, investiture, privilege, sentence, contract, or similar disposition that refers back to something else, are to be understood not **conditionally**, but **causatively**. Hence Boër (decision 16) reports that in the Council of Bordeaux, over which he presided, a case was judged: when someone in a lower court had obtained restitution for contested goods so that he might possess them, use them, and enjoy them "just as his father had done," and the person condemned had requested proof of how the father of the plaintiff had possessed them before the sentence was executed, and having been refused, he appealed. It was judged: The words of the sentence are to be understood causally—*because* the father of the plaintiff had possessed them—not conditionally—*if* he had possessed them. Therefore, the appellee needed no proof, and the appellant was condemned to pay the expenses. But on this matter, see Moller, book 2, semester, chapter 32, throughout.

The word *Sicut* denotes an all-encompassing similarity, both in substance and in quality; see the law *sicut* in the Code *on actions and obligations*, final chapter, and there
