Lit. W. <note>Letter W</note>

Antonius de Butrio, in his notable 4th point on the restoration of stolen property, chapter *olim* <note>original Latin: "extra de restit. spoliat. c. olim"</note>. See also the title "On the Meaning of Words" in the Decretals <note>original: "extra d. V.S."</note>; Marianus Socinus Junior, consultation 76, number 44, book 1. Similarly, the word "so" <note>original: "ita"</note> signifies the manner and likeness, as noted by Hieronymus Gratus, consultation 86, book 1; Schrader, consultation 14, number 201. See also Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter D, conclusions 347 and 374. The word "as" <note>original German: "wie"</note> is equivalent to the word "according to" or "as if," and serves to repeat what came before, according to Klock, volume 2, consultation 29, number 11. The word "According to" <note>original: "Prout"</note> limits and modifies the legal arrangement, volume 2, consultation 10, number 47.

## 55. As mentioned above, or reported, in the manner just heard. *Ut supra.*

Through the words "as above" <note>original: *ut supra*</note>, everything previously narrated is considered repeated. Alexander, consultation 59, number 21, volume 3; Parisius, consultation 48, number 14, book 2; Decius, consultation 227, number 3. These words create a reference to everything stated above, as taught by Ruinus, consultation 183, volume 2; Socinus Junior, consultation 170, number 34, volume 2. See especially Laymann in the Honoldina case, number 379 and following.

Through the words "in the manner just heard" <note>original German: *jetzt gehörter massen*</note>, the legal arrangement seems to be restricted to what was previously expressed. Cravetta, consultation 98, number 8; Menochius, consultation 95, number 128. However, that relative word often refers not to the substance of the matter, but to its quality, as Bartolus testifies regarding the law *cunctos populos* in the Code on the Supreme Trinity <note>original: *C. de summ. Trin.*</note>. Therefore, it is added not restrictively, but for demonstration. See Bartolus on the law *omnes populi* in the Digest on Justice and Law <note>original: *ff. de J. & J.*</note>; Alciatus, consultation 6, number 5, book 6; as is usually the case in doubtful matters, according to Cravetta, consultation 301, number 5.

->ADDITION.<-

The words "as touched upon" <note>original German: *wie berührt*</note> have the force of a reference. Klock, volume 1, consultation 7, number 535. The word "Saving" <note>original: *Salvis*; meaning "excepting" or "reserving"</note> restricts what was said before. Klock, volume 2, consultation 10, number 49. On the word "above" <note>original: *suprà*</note>, see Tiraqueau, book 1, *On Retraction*, section 7, gloss 11, number 77. "Acknowledge as stands above" <note>original German: *Bekenn, wie obstehet*</note>. See broadly Höpingk on *The Law of Seals*, page 446. The word "as above" <note>original: *ut supra*</note> refers to preceding matters with their specific qualities, according to Marcus Antonius, *Legal Rules*, book 1, rule 4, number 6. The words "as was said" <note>original: *ut dictum fuit*</note> refer to the present part, book 1, rule 110, number 7. The word "aforesaid" <note>original: *prædictis*</note> refers only to what immediately precedes, book 2, rule 1, number 21.

## 56. Clause: As come down from of old.
->Clause: As is the custom.<-

This clause, when placed in <term>Investitures</term> <note>the formal ceremony of granting a fief or land-right</note>, does not always imply an "ancient fief" <note>original: *feudum antiquum*</note>. For an ancient fief can become a "new fief" in the person of a buyer or receiver if it is transferred by the Lord's will to a stranger—that is, someone not included in the original grant. Schrader on *Fiefs*, page 8, chapter 4, number 39; and Rosenthal, chapter 2, conclusion 22, number 1. This holds true even if the core content of the grant was not otherwise changed; it is enough that the line of succession has been altered. See the chapters on "who can testify" and "on brothers" in the *Libri Feudorum* <note>the Books of Fiefs</note>; Zasius, consultation 13, number 17, book 1; and the decisions of Thessaurus, decision 146, number

<column-break/>

10. Indeed, it is still made a "new fief" even if the Lord adds in the grant that he invests the person with this fief "just as the seller or transferor possessed it" or "held it from us as a fief." Rosenthal, conclusion 22, number 2.

->ADDITION.<-

The words "old tradition" or "brought down from of old" <note>original German: *alt Herkommen, oder von Alters hergebracht*</note> mean the same as saying it is an inveterate custom, so much so that "old tradition" has the force of a legal privilege or statute. Ancient practice is to be preferred over written law. Dr. Tabor, *On Voting*, pages 243, 244.

## 57. Hunting Preserve. *Bannus venatorius.*

On whether a "Forest" <note>German: *Vorst*</note> and a "Hunting Preserve" <note>German: *Wildbahn*</note> are the same thing, or what the difference is between the two, see Bidembach, question 15.

The right of hunting belonging to someone by reason of "greater game" <note>such as deer or boar</note> is called "high hunting" <note>original German: *die hohe Wildbahn*</note>; whereas "lower hunting" concerns smaller animals. Sixtinus on *Regalian Rights*, chapter 8, number 48. Thus, sometimes of two Princes or nobles, the right to hunt smaller game belongs to one, and the right to larger game to the other. Pruckmann, section on hunting, chapter 4, number 67, where it is held that whatever has been possessed by anyone is considered established by long-standing use. Cammann on *Majesty*, dispute 7, thesis 81; Parisius, consultation 14, number 25, book 1.

By territorial and regalian right—that is, by virtue of the Prince's sovereignty and high authority—the hunting rights of the District and Bailiff Lords <note>original German: *Cent- und Vogtherren*</note> apply. These include the right to call upon subjects and feudal tenants (even those not otherwise subject to the bailiff's criminal jurisdiction) for hunting duties <note>German: *Jagt-Folg*</note>, labor with horses or hands, and service in transporting hunting dogs, gear, and nets. It includes providing dog-lodgings, fodder for forest and hunting horses, the right to pass through estates, and providing provisions for hunters. It also includes the right to require that peasant and shepherd dogs be fitted with chains and heavy wooden clogs <note>original: *Prügeln oder Knütteln*; to prevent them from chasing game</note>, the right of seizing property for fines, forest fees, and similar consequences of the hunting preserve. In recognition of the "Forest Jurisdiction," these matters are handled by the Forest and Hunting Masters, as well as the courts for the forest, fields, game-watch, and timber. Officers and field guards may remain, punish, and summon offenders. If someone only holds criminal or bailiff jurisdiction <note>original: *Cent- und Vogtey*</note>, they cannot claim for themselves the forest rights or jurisdiction, nor other accessories of the hunting ban, such as publishing "Forest Ordinances," the enclosure and closing of woods, bird-trapping sites, or the rights of falconry and hawking. Leipold, in Arumæus, volume 1, discourse 13, question 11, folio 214.

->ADDITION.<-

The right of hunting belonging to Princes and Counts is called in German *Wildbahn* <note>hunting preserve</note>, or "hunting ban" in Latin, from which "Forest Right" <note>German: *Vorstrecht*</note> differs. These two

Hunting preserves and Forest Law <note>original: "Wildbahn & Forstrecht"</note> constitute one whole, which is called princely forest jurisdiction <note>original: "vorstliche Obrigkeit"</note>. And because a hunting preserve is held not only in the forests, but also in the fields, it is more correctly called a "wild animal ban" <note>original: "bannum ferinum"</note> than a "forest ban" <note>original: "bannum sylvestre"</note>, according to Bocer in *On Regalian Rights*, page 39. Hunting is classified as either "superior" or "inferior" <note>referring to 'high game' like deer and 'low game' like rabbits</note>; see Wehner under this word, and Lord Biccius in *Golden Matters*, page 185. Hunting preserves, tolls, and safe-conducts <note>original: "Wildbahn, Zoll, Gleit"</note> are indivisibly connected; they share the same legal judgment and determination, according to Klock, volume 1, consultation 29, numbers 72, 73, and 74. The contrary is asserted in numbers 356, 357, and 358.

## 58. Poachers. Takers of wild beasts. <note>original: "Wilderer. Ferarum captores."</note>

Arnisæus teaches in *On Majesty*, book 3, chapter 4, number 3, page 522, that one should not be overly harsh toward those who have hunted illegally. Indeed, whatever wrong these takers of wild beasts commit, they do not err except in that they disobey the orders of the Magistrate or enter the fields of others, which certainly is not a crime to be punished with such great severity. See especially Eberhard Speckhan, *Legal Questions*, century 1, question 98 throughout; Bossius in his *Criminal Treatise*, title on required defendants, number 1; and Heigius, book 1, question 15, number 79, where he recounts how Galeazzo Sforza <note>A Duke of Milan known for his cruelty</note> forced a peasant to eat a hare he had caught raw, including the skin, from which the man died, as recorded in Corio, volume 6 of the *History of Milan*. Henry II and Richard I, Kings of the English, used to punish those who took royal beasts by blinding them or emasculating them, as noted in Henlish’s lives of these kings. For Charles V, in the *Penal Constitution*, chapter 169, distinguishes between the taking of beasts from a fenced park, which he equates to theft (based on the law regarding the acquisition of possession), and the simple hunting of free wild animals, which he leaves to be punished according to the nature of the offense. Saxon Law <note>original: "Jus Saxonicum"</note> expressly forbids imposing a penalty of life or limb. The words are found in book 2 of the *Landrecht*, article 6: "When God created man, He gave him power over birds, fish, and all wild animals; therefore we have this testimony from God <note>original German: "daß niemand sein Leben an diesen dreyen verwircken kan"</note> that no one can forfeit his life because of these three." From this constitution, Thomingius and others conclude that it is never lawful for a judge to punish such offenses more heavily than by exile. Soto, in *On Justice and Law*, book 4, question 6, and Alfonso à Castro, book 1, chapter 6, call those "tyrants" who order anyone to be punished by death for killing a stag, valuing a beast more than a man. On this matter, John of Salisbury writes in the *Polycraticus*, book 1, chapter 4: "Some have broken out into such madness by the instinct of hunting vanity," he says, "that they become enemies of nature, unmindful of their own condition, and despisers of Divine Judgment, while to avenge wild beasts they subject the image of God <note>man</note> to exquisite tortures." If, however, the offenses are multiplied by deliberate choice, or if the intent to harm another is added to the hunting, there is no doubt that the penalty should be increased.

...law 28, section *solent*, on punishments. See also the *Strasbourg Consultations*, volume 2, where it discusses the punishment of poachers <note>original German: "der Wilderer"</note>.

Therefore, here as in theft, a "bad habit" <note>recidivism</note> is punished when there is no hope that the delinquent will change his mind, and he remains in stubborn contempt of the ordinary Magistrate.

## 59. Innkeeper. Host. <note>original: "Wirth. Caupo."</note> See above under the word Host/Guest-giver <note>original: "Gastgeb"</note>.

See Lord Speidel in *Legal Notables*. The right of keeping an inn in villages is chiefly included in the right of receiving guests and the right of selling food and drink <note>original: "esculenta & polenta"</note>, according to Zythander von Bude. Whether innkeepers are required to receive guests in every instance, see there, numbers 9 and 10.

### ADDITION.

See above under Guest <note>original: "Gast"</note>.

An innkeeper <note>original: "Wirth"</note> is called the "Father of the Family" <note>original: "Paterfamilias"</note> among the Franks, according to Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6. Regarding public innkeepers and hosts who hang out a public sign <note>original German: "die einen öffentlichen Schild aushencken"</note>, see Dr. Tabor, page 98. Those who have public signs of hospitality—who have hung out a shield—are seen as having entered into a contract with travelers by the display of the sign, promising that they will receive those who arrive and keep their things safe. This is limited if the house is already filled by a multitude of guests, or in the case of guests who suffer from a contagious disease.

In Saxony, a certain ordinance is made for innkeepers every half-year <note>original German: "Sachsen wird den Gastwirthen von halb zu halben Jahren ein gewisse Ordnung gemacht"</note>, governing how hosts should treat their guests, and what one should give and pay for a meal along with the drink (for as long as the tablecloth remains), as well as for a day and night’s fodder and stable-room for a horse. See the *Saxon Police Ordinance of 1612*, page 77. Regarding feasts <note>original: "Gastereyen"</note>, see page 69, where it is forbidden to serve more than 8 dishes to a nobleman, 6 to a Doctor, and 4 to other prominent people of the burgher class, or to hold too many banquets in a year. ### 60. Knowledge. From certain knowledge. <note>original: "Wissenschafft. Cl. aus rechter Wissenschafft. Scientia, Ex certa scientia."</note>

The word **Knowledge**, according to its proper and truest meaning, is nothing other, speaking in Latin, than *scientia*. This knowledge differs from mere belief, and stands quite apart from it. See Bartolus on law 1, number 7, regarding interrogatory actions. Since he alone is said to "know" or have "knowledge" who holds the truth as certainly perceived and understood. See chapter 1, the section "if a vassal [holds] a fief," and the notes there by Baldus on the phrase "certain knowledge" <note>original: "certa scientia"</note>. See also law 2, the section "likewise Labeo" on rainwater, and Jacob Thoming, decision 45.

Thus also the legal clause "from certain knowledge" <note>original: "ex certa scientia"</note> is of such efficacy that it excludes not only every presumption of error, but even the allegation and proof of error, ignorance, or fraud. See Bartolus, Baldus, and Jason on law "but even if requested," the final paragraph, in the Digest on if anyone provides security. See also Paris, consultation 96, number 70 and following, and Alexander, consultation 4, number 9. Likewise, this clause removes every presumption of simulation <note>a "simulated" act is one that is faked or performed for show without real intent</note>. See Schrader, consultation 46, number 24, volume 2, as well as removing the possibility of "subreption" and "obreption" <note>terms for obtaining a legal favor by concealing the truth or making a false statement</note> and any lack of intention. See Innocent on chapter 2, on the confirmation of the useful and useless, and Andreas in the final chapter on pending litigation.

->ADDITION.<-

Subreption and obreption are considered not to have occurred if the written words are found: **Knowing by Princely Power.** <note>original: "Aus Fürstl. Macht wissend."</note> See Christoph Philipp Richter, part 1, consultation 21, number 57, page 140. On the word **Knowingly** <note>original: "Wissentlich"</note> see Lord Doctor Biccius on *Dispensations*, thesis 498 and following. On what the clause "From certain knowledge" imports, see Klock, volume 3, consultation 143, numbers 63, 88-91, 93, 95, and 103; also consultation 155 and 182. See also Marius Antoninus, book 1, response 46. Regarding the **Court of the Knowing** <note>original: "von Gericht der Wissenden"</note>, see Schöttel in *The German Main Language*, page 504. It is not prohibited to dispute the will and knowledge of the Prince. See Gail, book 2, observation 56. This is because a Prince is sometimes poorly informed, and a Prince is never presumed to be pleased by anything except what is just and true. See Bullæus in *Consultations*, page 187.

### 61. Widow. <note>original: "Wittib. Vidua."</note>

Regarding the charity that one ought to exercise toward widows, see Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 1, last chapter.

That widows retain the family status and condition of their husband, and consequently his privileges, is taught by Guido Papa, question 389; Menochius, case 379; and Jacob Benius in *On the Privileges of Jurists*, privilege 98. For there remains in them an image of the husband, according to Baldus. Hence, a widow who was otherwise a commoner but married a patrician and thus became noble, retains the family status and condition of the husband. See Tiraquel, *On Nobility*, chapter 18, number 5. This is different for sons, however, who enjoy immunities only while the father is living, according to the writings of Benius.

<column-break/>

Why are the widows of the Kings of France called **White Queens**? <note>original: "Roynes Blanches"</note> The aforementioned Guyon investigates this in volume 2, book 3, chapter 38, page 719. *By conjecture,* he says, *it seems to me that this name came from two widowed Queens who were named Blanche: namely, Queen Blanche of Castile, wife of Louis VIII, and the other was Blanche of Evreux, widow of King Philip of Valois. But this name does not belong only to those who had it as a name; it is possible the people called them "White" because formerly, during their widowhood, they wore the white veil.* He adds there that Catherine de Medici, widow of Henry II, was called "Queen Mother" and not "White Queen," but the last widow up to the year 1609 was again called "White Queen." It is seen then, Guyon adds, that the people give names to many things through inadvertence and quite inappropriately.

In ancient times, widows did not remarry; see Meursius's *Supplement*, chapter 10.

->ADDITION.<-

**Widower** <note>original: "Witling"</note> was the term used among the ancients. See Schottel in *The German Main Language*, page 373. Regarding whether a condition inducing widowhood must be fulfilled by males in second marriages, see Mantica on *Conjectures of the Last Will*, book 11, title 19. The condition "if she shall be a widow" or "when she shall be a widow" is fulfilled even if she does not remain a widow, which is subject to limits. If a widow does not remarry, this condition is not to be considered dishonorable. See Carpzov, decision 156. If a widow remains in widowhood, whether a conditional disposition of property is valid is discussed in decision 156, number 2. It is to a widow's praise that she abstains from a second marriage. A widow possesses the right of retention of her husband's goods until she has received her dowry or has been satisfied regarding her statutory portion or other marital rights. See decision 69, number 14. A condition inducing widowhood is generally rejected, with certain limits.

Whether the name **Widows and Orphans** <note>original: "Wittib und Waisen"</note> also encompasses monasteries and convents, see Limnaeus, *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 5. A **Widow** is a protected person <note>original: "miserabilis persona" - a legal term for those deserving special judicial protection, such as the poor or bereaved</note>, even if she is of high status and great wealth. See Zorer, part 2, question 7.

A man must see to it during his life that his **Widow** has proper maintenance during her continued state of widowhood.

**Widows and Orphans** are called the **Loyalty Penny** <note>original: "Treuheller"</note> in the *Supplement to Wehner*, page 36.

## 62. Widow’s Seat. <note>original: "Wittumsiß"</note> House of Widowhood.

The residence <note>original: "habitatio"</note> which is usually established in marriage contracts by noble husbands for their wives, should they survive their husbands and live in widowhood; this we call a **Widow’s Seat** <note>original: "Wittumsiß"</note> (for the term **Dower** <note>original: "Wittumb"</note> descends from "widowhood"). This agrees with a gift made on account of marriage in that it enjoys the privilege of a "silent mortgage" <note>term: "tacita hypotheca" — a legal right to a debtor's property that exists automatically without a written contract</note>. This can be understood from the writings of Negusantius, member 4, number 47 and following; a silent mortgage is granted on the husband's property for maintenance both during the marriage and after it is dissolved. For when it concerns a favor, residence is also included under maintenance. See law 6, final paragraph, "On Legacies of Maintenance and Food." This was noted in the case of Agatha **Förderin** against **Schwenden**. Lord Rutger Ruland, *Decisions on Contested Law*, question 62. See my own dispute on the *Municipal Law of Württemberg*, 1, where I discuss the priority of creditors. And that a widow's **Dower** <note>original: "Wittumb"</note> is established as a life estate <note>original: "zum Leibgeding"</note> is taught by Modestinus Pistoris, counsel 22 and following, volume 1, and Cothmann, counsel 50, number 61.

By a dower or a personal usufruct <note>term: "usufruct" — the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it</note> through the **Life Estate** <note>original: "Leibgut"</note>, the dowry (or the property given as a dowry) is extinguished; the **Principal Estate** <note>original: "Haupt-Gut"</note> vanishes. See Cothmann, volume 4, response 48, number 54, and Bocer in the treatise *On Donations*, chapter 11.

If, therefore, a widow seeks her dower, the dowry can no longer be sought. This was introduced by Saxon custom contrary to Common Law. But whether this also takes place among Princely persons? I know it has been doubted. And I am more inclined to deny it. For they are not subject to the laws by which subjects are governed. Scheffer, part 1, question 39, where he discusses whether a noble widow succeeds by the tenor of the statute; and add Modestinus Pistoris, question 41. See also Al. Mascardus, conclusion 6. And it should be noted that a Dower is not owed to widows **who remain in the [same] household** <note>original: "welche in der Haushaltung bleiben"</note>. Furthermore, does a widow who sins against her own body <note>note: a euphemism for committing adultery or sexual misconduct</note> lose her dower? See Guyon, *Diverse Lessons*, volume 1, final chapter.

->ADDITION.<-

How an appanage <note>term: "Apanagium" — a provision of land or money for the younger children of a king or prince</note> differs from a dower <note>original: "Doario"</note>, see Springsfeld *On Appanages*, chapter 12, number 71 and following. **Widow’s Seat** <note>original: "Wittumsiß"</note> is more correctly spelled thus than how Besold writes it. Lord Doctor Tabor, *On Transpositions*, page 202. Regarding **Widow’s Money** <note>original: "Wittibgelden"</note>, see Lord Tabor, *On the Obligation of Succession in Office*, page 346. Are widows exempt from the **quartering of soldiers**? <note>original: "Einquartierungen"</note> See Tabor, *On Transpositions*, page 95. On the dower, see extensively Zorer, parts 1 and 2. Also regarding fiefs and

<column-break/>

## 63. Provided That. <note>original: "Wo anderst. Dummodo."</note>

The word "Provided that" <note>original: "Dummodo"</note> sometimes acts as "while," and sometimes introduces a condition; it is joined to an incomplete matter. Tiraquel, *On the Retraction of Relatives*, section 8, glossary 8, number 1. It designates a precise fulfillment, and that which it is attached to must necessarily be present. See Hieronymus Gratus, counsel 86, number 1, part 2.

->ADDITION.<-

On the clause: "Provided that the right of another is not sought," and whether it creates a "mixed executor." Marius Antoninus, *Legal Resolutions*, book 1, resolution 29, number 8. The word "provided that" does not always imply a condition, but an admonition. Marius Antoninus, book 1, resolution [?], number 2. And whether it implies a manner or a condition: book 2, resolution 31, number 2, 3, and 5.

## 64. Weeks. <note>original: "Wochen. Hebdomades."</note>

Weeks, which the Latins call *septimanas* and the Germans call **Wochen**, are understood as seven days according to common usage.

We do not begin our weeks on **Saturday** <note>original: "Sonnabend"</note>, like the Jews, nor on a Friday, like the Turks, but on **Sunday** <note>original: "Sonntag"</note>. Why this is done, Barthold Scheraeus in the *German Language School*, page 208, asserts the following: (1.) Because God began to create Heaven and Earth on a Sunday. Genesis 1, verse [?]. (2.) Because the Lord Christ, as some reckon, was born on the same day, and (3.) circumcised, also (4.) resurrected, and (5.) poured out the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles. Therefore (6.) Sunday is also called the Lord's Day <note>original: "κυριακὴ ἡμέρα"</note>. Revelation 1, verse 10. (7.) Because the Jewish Sabbath (our Saturday) was a sign or symbol and a reminder of Creation, sanctification, and the future Sabbath, Isaiah 66, verse 23, or of the good things to come, Hebrews 10, verse 1. Since all symbols and shadows must be abolished in the New Testament, the seventh Sabbath day no longer binds us, but we remain in our Christian freedom, concerning which see John 8, verse 36, and Galatians 5, verse 1, Colossians 2, verse 16 and following; and we keep Sunday instead of Saturday. See above under the entry "Sunday," and Bellarmine, book 3, *On the Worship of Saints*, chapter 11, and Meisner, *Philosophical-Theological Axioms*, page 232, number 46.

->ADDITION.<-

Beyond seven days, the beasts which are sent by Dukes to the Count (that is, the Prince) ought not to remain in individual cities. Only law, Code of Justinian, "On the Hunting of Wild Beasts." The Lord's Day, says Augustine, is not for Jews but for Christians...

### 65. Well-considered. With a deliberate mind. <note>original: "Wohlbedacht. Deliberato animo."</note>

The word **Well-considered** <note>German: "Wohlbedacht"</note> clearly discusses and excludes every allegation of error and ignorance, according to Paris *consultation 39, number 18, volume 3* and Pruckmann *consultation 49, number 64, volume 1.*

### ADDITION.

**Well-considered**, see *Upon advice had*. **Upon advice had or obtained**, Rittershuf *in the New Works, page 648.* Writing "from certain knowledge" <note>term: "ex certa scientia" — a legal phrase indicating the author is fully aware of the facts and acting intentionally, making the document harder to challenge</note> is considered to mean the writing was intended to be valid, as if the person had seen and read it, Höpingk *on the Law of Seals, chapter 15, number 156.* However, otherwise Magistrates and judges are not strictly bound to follow "informative advice," whether sought from the parties—see *Treatise 1, Distinction 1, theorem 7, letter d*—or sought by the judge himself, Berlich *1, conclusion 42, numbers 26, 27;* Schrader *part 10, section 14, number 93.* Nevertheless, when it is provided by Law in some place that a Judge must transmit the Acts to a College of Jurisprudence <note>A "Juristenfakultät" or faculty of law that provided expert binding opinions to courts</note>, and not draft or pronounce the sentence himself, then he must strictly follow that ordinance, Henning Renneman *on the Law of Transmission of Acts, chapter 11, number 6, page 155;* Dr. Tabor in *Criminal Gleanings, page 502.*

### 66. To Will. To Want. <note>original: "Wollen. Velle."</note>

The verb **I want** <note>original: "volo"</note> grants to each person the natural faculty of doing what pleases them, Oldrad *consultation 187, number 4.* Especially in last wills <note>testaments</note>, it implies a full disposition of property, through *Law "Pamphilo," paragraph "Propositum," of the Digest, "On legacies," book 3.*

And if this word is consistent with the institution of the will, the testator's wish shall be ratified, through *Law "Pamphilo," paragraph "Propositum," and there Bartolus, of the Digest, "On legacies," book 3.* The word "I want" is the source and root of all dispositions, Cornelius *consultation 309, number 9, volume 4.* Bartolus *on the law "On the choice of a slave," of the Digest, "On legacies," book 1,* and there Jason *number 44 and following* says that Bartolus's opinion is to be followed, Majer *on Testaments, book 1, chapter 5, number 12.* Certainly, where the intent of the Testator is clear, a dispute over the "tips of the words" <note>term: "apicibus verborum" — legal hair-splitting or pedantic insistence on literal wording over intent</note> is made in vain, *Law 3 of the Code "On children passed over"; Law "Father [gave] Severina"; Law "In conditions" of the Digest "On conditions and demonstrations"; and the final law of the Code "In what matters a pledge [is contracted]."*

<sig>Besold, Volume 1.</sig>

<column-break/>

However, it is otherwise in other cases, such as when I say: **"I want to sell you this or that for 20 or 30."** Through this word **"I want"**, the sale is not yet perfected or contracted, unless it were otherwise by the custom of speaking, *through the law "Labeo" of the Digest "On legacies of household goods."* The reason is that even if a contract of purchase and sale requires only consent, *through law 1, paragraph 2 of the Digest "On the exchange of things,"* and there Gothofredus says: it does not follow that by those words "I want to sell to you," a sale is introduced, just as it does not follow that "I want to give to you" therefore means "I give," based on the argument of *the penultimate chapter and there the gloss "On the rules of transferring to religion" in the 6th [book of Decretals], there:* it is one thing to profess a religion, another to vow to profess it; see Menochius *consultation 92.*

But what should be said of the word **"I want"** in a Marriage contract? For instance, if Titius says to Bertha, **"I want to contract Marriage with you,"** or **"I want to take you as a wife"**: **"I want to hold a wedding with you, or I want to take you for a wife,"** <note>German: "Ich will mit dir Hochzeit halten, oder ich will dich zum Weibe nehmen"</note> is a Marriage contracted through those words, or only an engagement <note>original: "sponsalia"</note>? To some, it seems that only an engagement is contracted through these words. Because the word **"I want"** <note>German: "ich will"</note>—in those things which depend solely on the will of the speaker—if it is joined to an infinitive designating the beginning of an act and its suspension, will be a contract of engagement, such as **"I want to contract, I want to take you as a wife."** And that this is the common opinion is witnessed by Matthaeus de Afflictis *in the Neapolitan Constitutions, book 3, title 19, column 2;* Boerius *consultation 40, number 54 and following;* Vivius *in "Common Conclusions," under the word "marriage," question 489.* See Mozzius *in the treatise "On Contracts," under "Marriage," on the substance and forms of marriage, number 24,* where in the *following* number he asks: whether through those words "I want to have you as a wife" or "I want to hold you as a wife," it can be said that a marriage is contracted? And he responds that it is so: For those words, **"I want to take you, I want to have you for a wife,"** are not of the future, but of the present time. And the usage of the German language does not carry this phrase, nor does it approve: **"I shall take you,"** see Cypraeus *on engagements, folio 27, paragraph SS and following.*

And furthermore, through the word "I want," when it is joined to a verb noting the execution of a completed act, and thus the exercise of marriage, a marriage is deemed contracted, as in the words said above. And this seems to be the common opinion of the Doctors *on the chapter "From the letters," where Hostiensis and Abbas on "Engagements"* [wrote]. And this is confessed among all: a marriage is deemed contracted when the word "I want" is joined to the thing itself: for example, **"I want to take you as a wife."** And that is felt by Baldus *on law 1, column 2 of the Code "On the highest Trinity"; the Doctors on the law "On the choice of a slave," final paragraph, of the Digest "On legacies," book 1; and on the law "Of the seller," of the Code "On the contract of purchase"; and by the common [opinion] of Angelus de Clavasio on the word "marriage," 2, paragraph 12;* Vivius *Common Opinions, word "Marriage," question 490.*

Concerning the words, **"I will never leave you,"** <note>German: "ich will dich nimmer verlassen"</note> see Cypraeus *on marriage, folio 65, number 13, etc.*

Likewise: **"Whenever I might want to take one [a wife], then..."** <note>German: "Wann ich wolte eine nehmen, so"</note>

## 67. Usury, Usurer. <note>original: "Wucher, Wucherer. Usuraria pravitas, Usurarius."</note>

A singular disputation on usury <note>term: "Usury" — historically, any interest charged on a loan, often considered a moral and legal evil</note> exists in my treatise *On Life and Death*.

Because of the hatred of usury, the Laws and Interpreters—in order to demonstrate the atrocity of the crime—rise up sharply against moneylenders as harsh, injurious, and wicked men.

The Romans also prohibited interest by many plebiscites <note>laws passed by the common people</note>, so that a heavier penalty was inflicted on a moneylender than on a thief, just as Marcus Cato wrote in the preface to his book *On Agriculture*. Certainly, Lucius Genutius, Tribune of the Plebs, brought a motion to the people that it should not be permitted to lend at interest: and Cato, loathing such types of profit, drove all moneylenders out of Sardinia, as Livy writes in books 7 and 32.

They are also called **The Butchers of the Poor** by Augustine in the chapter "What shall I say," cause 14, question 4, there: "Who is more cruel, he who steals something from another, or he who butchers the poor man with interest?"

<summary>This page discusses the legal definitions of "will" and "consent" in contracts and wills, emphasizing that intent must be expressed to have power, before beginning a section on the historical and moral condemnation of usury (excessive interest).</summary>
<keywords>will, volition, consent, contracts, testaments, Vollwort, beneplacitum, usury, interest, moneylenders, Roman law, butchers of the poor</keywords>

**Those of ill-repute**, according to the law *on wicked interest, 20. Code, from which causes of infamy; chapter "Infames," 2. final section, cause 3, question 7.* <note>The text labels usurers as "infamous," a specific legal status in Roman and Canon law that stripped a person of certain civil rights and the ability to testify in court.</note>

**Homicide.** When Cato the Censor was asked what it meant to practice usury, he indignantly replied: "What else is it but to kill a man?" *Menochius, 2. Arbitrary Judgments of Judges, case 398, number 2.*

**Plagues of Republics,** *Menochius, 2. Arbitrary Judgments, case 398, number 1.*

**Delinquents against God, Man, and good morals,** *Roland à Valle, consultation 57, number 7, volume 1.*

**Also on the crime of usury,** see *Decianus, book 4, Criminal Practice, 27; Covarruvias, 3. Various Matters, chapter 3; Sesse, decision 148.*

**On usury and interest** owed from grain, and on the purchase of rents in grain, barley, and wine—to what extent and how much such rents and revenues are permitted in the Roman Empire—see the *Political Constitutions* published at Frankfurt am Main in the year [15]77, title 19, section "Of the same" <note>original: "Desselben"</note>, and section "Upon this they set" <note>original: "Hierauf setzen"</note>.

That a lender may lawfully receive something beyond the principal <note>term: "Sors" — the principal or original amount of a loan</note> from his debtor, when it is offered freely as a gesture of gratitude and remuneration, with no prior request, obligation, or agreement intervening, is handed down by *Natta, consultation 498, number 28; Clarus, book 5, section on usury, in the preface; Marta in the New Digest, volume 3, title on usury, chapter 42; and Hieronymus Laurentius, from the decisions of the Rota of Avignon, 48,* writes that a certain defendant was released from a fiscal petition because it appeared he had not demanded the promised usury.

And it should be noted that the equity of the **Annuity Purchase** <note>term: "Gültkauff" — a common historical contract where a buyer paid a lump sum in exchange for a permanent annual rent or "interest," often used to bypass usury laws because the principal was not technically "repayable" on demand.</note> has this essential quality: that one may not demand the money back. And because a person is forced to do without their money, it is also fair that they have something annually. In the *Württemberg State Ordinance, title: On Usurious and other Prohibited Contracts,* a person is punished by a fine of one-fourth of the sum when prohibited pacts and conditions are attached to the loan; but where such things are done in an evil, usurious, and intentional manner, the entire principal sum is confiscated. How this Constitution is to be interpreted, see *Georg Everhard, consultation 18, volume 2, number 5,* where he deals with a similar Bavarian Statute. What has been accepted regarding this matter in the *Margraviate of Brandenburg* is handed down by *Scheplitz, part 2, title 1.*

**Nautical Usury** <note>term: "Usura nautica" — also known as "bottomry," a high-interest loan on a ship's cargo that only had to be repaid if the ship survived the voyage; essentially an early form of maritime insurance.</note> is still in use today, and the French call it *asseureur* [insurance]. There are unique Guilds of Merchants who take all occurring risks upon themselves and guarantee a safe and unharmed ship against water, fire, storms, friends, enemies, arrests by Kings, the negligence of sailors, etc. See *Pontanus's History of Amsterdam, book 4, chapter 4.*

**Mountains of Piety** <note>term: "Montes pietatis" — charitable, non-profit pawnshops run by the church or state to provide low-interest loans to the poor, distinguishing them from "wicked" usury.</note>—whether and to what extent they can be sustained or not? See *Book 7 of the Decretals, my page 408; and Paul Zypaeus in his Analysis of Pontifical Law, book 5, page 289, and book 5, pages 459 and following.*

Regarding **Grain- and Wine-Usurers** <note>original: "Korn- und Wein-Juden" — literally "Grain- and Wine-Jews," a historical pejorative term used for speculators of any background who hoarded resources to drive up prices.</note>, **City Wolves** <note>original: "Stadtwölffen"</note>, **Forestallers** <note>original: "Vorkäuffern" — those who buy goods before they reach the market to create a monopoly</note>, and the Turkish punishment of usurers, see *Johannes Philippi in The Practical Use of the Institutes of Justinian, book 4, title 18, section 11, Eclogue 95, number 2, section 7.* Who are usurers and what are usurious contracts? > You have no reason to complain that Franz von Borck paid Hans von Haussen interest upon interest on 600 Thalers, and that these should therefore be deducted again from the 3,000 Thalers, because the interest on the 600 Thalers is not "usury of usuries" <note>term: "Usura usurarum" — compound interest, which was often legally restricted</note>. For the 600 Thalers of overdue interest, once they were paid, were no longer to be considered interest, but became Hans von Haussen’s own money, from which he was well-entitled to make a new interest-bearing capital sum. You also cannot help yourselves with the fact that those same remaining 600 Thalers of interest were paid immediately <note>original: "in continenti"</note> out of the 3,000 Thalers that Hans von Haussen lent to Franz von Borck at interest, because it can be seen from the records that Franz von Borck had those 3,000 Thalers fully delivered into his custody, and he thus became the Master of the money given as a loan, and had the power to do with it as he pleased. Thus it stood with him whether he wanted to pay those 600 Thalers of interest from the advanced 3,000 Thalers or from his other money. Therefore, the mentioned 600 Thalers of interest paid cannot be shortened or deducted from the principal. Rather, you remain the heirs of Hans von Haussen...

### 68. Surgeon. <note>original: "Wundarzt. Chirurgus"</note>

The surgical craft was once entrusted to Physicians, but today it is assigned to Surgeons and Barbers. This role is also extremely necessary for the external care and healing of wounds, ulcers, scars, fistulas, and so on, through external means, especially in times of peace and war: hence the titles of Town-Surgeon and Field-Surgeon. From these men, singular skill and circumspection are required, so that in dangerous conditions they do not set their hand to the task without the advice and presence of Physicians. See Jacob Bornitz, *Treatise on the Sufficiency of Things*, treatise 2, chapter 20 throughout; add Jacob Faber’s *Treatise on Nourishment*, chapter 2, page 90.

On the examination of Surgeons, and Italian abuses, see Felix Würtz in his *Surgery* <note>original: "Wundarzney"</note>, chapter 9, page 47.

->ADDITION.<-

"Great Wound" <note>original: "Hrosswund"</note> in the *Law of the Alamanni*, title 65, § 25; *Law of the Bavarians*, title 1, chapter 6, § 2: "If the internal members have been wounded, which they call a *Hrosswund*." "Wund" means wound, but as for "Hross," it perhaps signified the viscera <note>the internal organs</note>, as noted by Schottelius in *The German Main Language*, page 688. Regarding what must be observed in the inspection of wounds, see Hornigk, *On the Law of Posts*, chapter 21, number 7. Nothing is more terrible than the very sight of wounds, according to Rupertus in his commentary on Florus, book 2, chapter 7, § 9. The women of our ancestors were stronger in this regard, of whom Tacitus wrote in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, chapter 7, § 4: "They carry their wounds to their mothers and wives, and these women do not fear to count or even suck the wounds." On frontal wounds, see Rupertus on Florus, book 1, chapter 18, § 17. To glory in wounds, book 4, chapter 12, § 7; to die by mutual wounds, book 1, chapter 10, § 8. On open wounds, on flesh or fresh wounds, on "fighter-wounds," on bone-cleaving wounds, and on lameness and scarring <note>original: "Lambden und Schandmal"</note>, see Johannes Philippi in *The Practical Use of Justinian’s Institutes*, book 4, title 4, § 9, Selection 34, numbers 1 to 6.

The question is asked: should Surgeons be promoted Doctors? Certainly, even today in Italy, Doctors of Surgery are promoted, and in France, Masters are promoted, as witnessed by Jacob Faber in *On Nourishment*, chapter 2, page 92. And this is indeed correct: for it is well known that the ancient Physicians also practiced surgery, as seen in the Institutes, section 6, and in the Digest, law 9 at the end, regarding the *Aquilian Law* <note>a Roman law on property damage and injury</note>, and law 4 of the Digest regarding the *Cornelian Law on Assassins*. For surgery is a significant part of medicine and its companion, as Gothofredus notes on the same law, letter G; and in the age of Hippocrates, the Physicians and Surgeons were the same people. The jurist Johann Cephalus writes in book 4, consultation 611, page 243, that in Piacenza, Surgeons took over the practice from the Doctors of the Medical College; in that consultation, he proves throughout that surgery is not a vile or sordid art, contrary to what André Tiraqueau (whom some called "the water-scooper") said in *On Nobility*, chapter 31.

<column-break/>

Later, however, Surgeons took a place of their own and handed down their art through a rational method, observing this in practice everywhere. But today, those who have merely learned how to shave a beard or hair, cut a vein, or apply a cupping glass, and mix incense, wax, and turpentine, dare to practice surgery without reason and without ever applying study—indeed, even those who never thought about surgery—to the greatest harm of men and the death of the sick.

If, therefore, the matter were up to my judgment, I would admit no Surgeon unless he correctly knew the theory and practice of his art: that is, <term>natural and non-natural things</term> <note>a traditional medical classification: "natural" things like organs, and "non-natural" things like air, diet, and exercise that affect health</note>, and those things that happen contrary to nature. Thus, I would altogether admit a Surgeon imbued with rational art to a degree, such as Wilhelm Fabricius Hildanus (the Swiss physician), Ambroise Paré (the Frenchman), Matthias Glandorp of Bremen, Francesco Peccerius, and others. The rest, without theory, are not worthy of the title of Surgeon, much less of literary honor. The reason why Surgeons ought to be literate is clear: for all the other parts of medicine—<term>dietetics, physiology, pathology, pharmacology</term> <note>original Greek: διαιτετικὴ, φυσιολογικὴ, παθολογικὴ, φαρμακετικὴ</note>, and whatever others there are—must be treated <term>theoretically</term> <note>original Greek: θεωρικῶς</note> and converted into "juice and blood" <note>meaning thoroughly mastered and internalized</note>. Why should Surgery not also be a significant part of Medicine? For Surgery—which is the other part of the method—is perfected not only by manual instruments but also by medicinal means for the cure of a wound; for example, not only is the application of a plaster required, but also a proper diet. Medicine’s <term>dietetics</term> <note>original Greek: διαιτετικὴ</note> certainly teaches this, which a mere unlearned surgeon does not know.

On the difference between ancient and modern Surgeons, see Mr. G. C. Walther, *On the Privileges of Doctors*, page 225. Criminal Ordinance, article 59: *If the accused has dangerous wounds on his body, the criminal interrogation shall be conducted against him in such a way that he is least injured in such wounds and damages.* Whoever maliciously causes another to bleed, whether with knives, daggers, stilettos, swords, "stars" <note>possibly a type of mace or spiked weapon</note>, or other weapons; compare Mr. Maevius, book 1 of the *Statutes of Lübeck*, title 2, article 1, number 47. Mr. Doctor Tabor, *On the Carrying of Weapons* <note>original: "Hoplophoria"</note>, page 149. Suetonius reports that Tiberius was able to wound a boy or youth with a "flick" or a finger-snap to the head <note>original: "Schneller oder Hirnschnallen"</note>.

### 69. Dignity. <note>original: "Würden. Dignitas"</note>

**Cl.** "With all dignity" <note>original: "Mit allen Würden"</note> regularly implies Authority and Jurisdiction. For jurisdiction is a dignity.

->ADDITION.<-

See above under **Honor**, and the word **Indignity**. "Dignity" <note>original: "Würde"</note> comes from "Worth" <note>original: "Werth"</note>, "worthy" <note>original: "würdig"</note>, so that those conferring a dignity might remember it is only to be granted to the worthy.

...strive, so that those receiving the requested dignity conduct themselves worthily. This is learnedly and extensively discussed by Dr. Paulus Hönn in his *Treatise on Dignities*, thesis 1, letter b.

## 70. Würzburg. <note>original: "Herbipolis"</note>

Otto of Freising recognizes the Eastern Franks in his *Chronicle, book 6, chapter 18*. The region of **Eastern Francia** <note>original: "Orientalis Francia"</note> is emphasized in the Frankish Annals for the year 824, by Thietmar in book 6, and by the author of the *History of the Sacred War* (published by Reiner Reineccius) in book 1, chapter 24. It is also mentioned by Otto of Freising in book 6, chapters 2, 6, 7, 8, and 16.

It is called **Ancient Francia** <note>original: "Antiqua Francia"</note> by the anonymous writer of the life of Charlemagne <note>original: "Caroli Magni"</note>, published by Heinrich Canisius (see book 1, chapter 25, and book 2, chapter 16).

You may find the same name in Aventinus, book 3. Emperor Henry IV calls it **Teutonic Francia** <note>original: "Teutonicam Franciam"</note> in the founding charter of the Gotha Monastery, dated in the year 1069. Lambert of Schafnaburg says the same. It encompassed Bavaria, Swabia, Saxony, Thuringia, and Frisia, according to the same Otto of Freising (book 6, chapter 11) and Godfrey of Viterbo. Rhenanus agrees in book 1 of *Germanic Matters*, saying: **Germanic Francia** began to encompass the entire German Kingdom, which today is called the Roman Empire. (Hence the Elector Palatine is the Vicar and defender of the **Franconian Law** <note>original: "deß Fränckischen Rechtens"</note>, while the Saxon is of the **Saxon Law** <note>original: "deß Sächsischen"</note>). However, the anonymous author of the Frankish Annals for the years 810 and 823 distinguishes Eastern Francia from Saxony, Bavaria, and Swabia <note>original: "Alemannia"</note>.

According to these sources, this is the region of Germany that we today call **Franconia** <note>original: "Franconiam"</note>—a modernized name, as Althamer noted in his commentary on Tacitus. Yet the name appears in Adam of Bremen (book 1, chapter 8), Sigfrid the Priest (book 1), and Gobelinus in his *World-Course* <note>original: "Cosmodromio"</note>, age 1, chapter 7 and age 6, chapter 18.

Regarding this, Krantz writes in *Saxony* (book 2, chapter 1): Germanic Francia is now wrongfully called **Franconia**, since the true Gauls <note>meaning the French</note> took the name for themselves. Nevertheless, some writers preserve the name and honor of that province, calling it Eastern Francia, etc. Trithemius says the same in book 1 of his *Abridgment of Annals*.

Rhenanus states in book 1 of *Germanic Matters* that this Eastern Francia was first called the district of **Maingau** <note>original: "Moingavv," referring to the region of the Main River</note>, and only later called Francia.

He also writes that it was called **Austrasia** <note>the "eastern land" of the early Frankish kingdoms</note>. Mr. Meibomius, in his notes on Widukind (page 52), names those who inhabit Gaul <note>modern France</note> as the **Western Franks**, as does Otto of Freising in his *Chronicle* (book 6, chapters 8 and 10).

Ausonius mentions **Western Francia** in his *Idyll 9*, as does an anonymous Panegyric addressed to the Emperor Constantine. Liutprand (book 1, chapter 6) and the continuer of Regino (at the year 939) call this **Roman Gaul**, because the people there spoke in the Roman <note>referring to the Romance or early French language</note> fashion.

<column-break/>

Hence they are still called **the old Romans** <note>original: "le vieux Romains"</note>. Regarding this, Aventinus writes in book 2: "Lyonese and Belgic Gaul were taken from the Roman Empire and transferred to Germany." Our people are accustomed to calling the former **the Frankish Empire** <note>original: "Franconreich"</note>, but they call the region of Germany from which the Franks originated **the Frank-land** <note>original: "Franconland"</note>, meaning the fatherland of the Franks—for they were born here, though they rule there.

Lupold of Bebenburg (chapter 3 of *On the Rights of the Kingdom and Empire*) and Aeneas Sylvius <note>the humanist scholar who became Pope Pius II</note> (*On the State of Europe under Emperor Frederick III*, chapter 31) believe those French Franks should be called **Frank-born** <note>original: "Francigenas"</note> rather than "Franks."

Paul the Deacon, in his *Miscellaneous History* (book 17), seems to call them **Lesser Gauls**, for while some identify Arbogast—the general and murderer of Emperor Valentinian II—as a Frank, Paul traces him to that Gallic people. Godfrey of Viterbo (part 17) asserts that Western Gaul between the Loire and Seine rivers was once called "Gaudina," but was renamed **Francia** or **Francigena** by Charles Martel, the grandfather of Charlemagne.

Rhenanus adds that "Roman Francia" was called **Neustria** or **Westria**, meaning the "Western Kingdom." Meibomius says the same.

Today, the **Bishop of Würzburg** holds Eastern Francia; he also styles himself the **Duke in Franconia** <note>original: "Hertzog in Francken"</note>. However, some make this title a matter of dispute (see my work *On the Free Knightly Nobility*, number 8). The Free Barons of Limpurg were once the Dukes of Franconia, **and even today their coat of arms bears witness to this**. On how **Franconia came to the Bishopric of Würzburg**, see Spangenberg in his *Life of Boniface* (page 103b).

Regarding the name **Würzburg**, some argue it should be **Würtburg**, as if it were the "castle of the father of the family" <note>original: "Patrisfamilias burgum"</note>. Reineccius notes in his *Annals of Charlemagne* (page 35) that among the Franks, a father of a family is commonly called a *Wirt*. Similarly, there are those who interpret **Wirtemberg** <note>the region of Württemberg</note> as the "mountain of the mother of the family" <note>original: "Matrisfamilias"</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

See Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 3, number 45, and volume 1 of his *Additions to book 6*.

Lanf. reports in *Consultations of Europe* (page 60) that the city was once famous for a **Temple of Diana**. On the **privilege of the Abbot of Würzburg**, see Knichen, *On the Law of Territory*, chapter 4, number 297, and Leonhard Wurffbain in *Historical Reports*, part 4, page 75. For more on **Würzburg**, see the aforementioned Wurffbain, part 5 (pages 92, 167, 125) and part 9 (page 257). Regarding the **Bishop of Würzburg** <note>original: "Episcopo Herbipolensi"</note>, see Sprenger in *Delineation of the States of the Empire* (page 315 onwards) and Nicolaus Myler, *On the Princes and States of the Empire*, chapter 12, number 5.

## 74. Signaling / Nodding. <note>Latin: *Nutus*; German: *Wincken*</note>

->ADDITION.<-

An oath is not performed by a nod, or by any other manner, by those who are able to speak, according to Zahn in *On Lies, book 3, chapter 3, number 47*. A nod is not a description of things, but an indication of consent, as Barbosa explains extensively in *book 12, chapter 30, axiom 7*. All those things that do not require specific words or formal solemnity are carried out by a nod. Thus, <term>trusts</term> <note>original: *fideicommissa*; a legal arrangement where property is left to one person to be handed over to another</note> may be left outside of a formal will by a nod. (See Rittershusius in *New Constitutions, page 293*; Knipschild *on trusts, chapter 6, numbers 27 and 242*). Legacies can be left by a nod, as Dr. Ludwell notes in his *Disputations on the Institutes, page 170, section d*. Likewise, the <term>assignment of a freedman</term> <note>original: *assignatio liberti*; designating which heir a former slave should serve</note> can be done by a nod; such an assignment is neither a legacy nor a trust (see *law 7 on the assignment of freedmen*). Similarly, delegations and all contracts are rightly entered into by a nod, as noted by Dr. Ludwell in his most accurate commentary on the title *Obligations and Actions*. An <term>admonition</term> <note>original: *admonatio*; a formal legal warning</note> can be carried out by a mere nod, without the injury of harsh words, according to Dr. Tabor in *On Admonition, page 201*. However, a nod is a deceptive sign; sometimes he who nods is actually in opposition, as Gothofredus notes on *law 52 at the end of Obligations and Actions*.

How something may be left by a nod is discussed by Hugo Donellus in *Commentaries on Civil Law, page 348, 30. a.* A trust can be left by a nod (page 578, 30. a.). Whether the consent of contracting parties is sufficiently signaled by a nod is discussed on page 745, 60. a. Among those who can speak, a nod is considered a certain indication of will (page 578, 30. a.). It is a sign of pride to offer no response, according to Cl. Rupert in his notes on *Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 5, § 1*, and Tacitus in *Annals, book 3, chapter 23*. What pride! This was Rupert's response to Florus, *book 1, chapter 7, § 7*. It is the custom of the Ethiopians to use nods instead of speech, as Pliny says in *book 6, chapter 30*; see Rupert in the aforementioned place. Nor was the innocence of Pallas <note>A powerful freedman under the Emperor Claudius</note> as pleasing as his pride was heavy: for when his freedmen were named as accomplices, he responded that he had never signaled anything at home except by nod or hand, or if more needed to be demonstrated, he used writing, so as not to associate his voice with them. Such was Domitian, who received Agricola—returning from great deeds in Britain—with a brief kiss and no conversation. How pleasing mute gesturers are to Princes and Ottoman Sultans is shown by Camerarius in *Historical Meditations, century 1, pages 358 and 414*. The art of speaking by nod is discussed in Italian by Giovanni Bonifacio, who teaches how a visible speech and a "mute eloquence" or "eloquent silence" can be formed by nods and signs (published in Venice, in quarto, 1616). Regarding a will made by a nod, which is valid in Canon Law but not in Civil Law, see the excellent work of Conrad Rittershusius in *Differences between Civil and Canon Law, book 4, chapter 3, at the beginning*; see also Berlich, *part 3, conclusion 6, numbers 21 and 24*.

## 75. Wagons, Weekly-Wagons. <note>Latin: *Currus*; German: *Wagen, Wochen-Wagen*</note>

->ADDITION.<-

A road must be so wide that passing wagons can yield to one another, unless one of them must reverse. The empty wagon shall yield 

<column-break/>

to the loaded wagon, and the lightly loaded one to the heavy one. (Zobel, *part 2, difference 45, number 1*). Regarding "Weekly-Wagons" <note>likely regularly scheduled freight or post wagons</note>, see Limnäus in *Public Law, book 7, chapter 9, page 153*. Regarding the so-called "wagon-pole duty" <note>original: *temonaria functio*; a tax or service related to providing wagons for the state</note>, see Dr. Tabor *on billeting, page 260*.
See also Military Stratagems, Kitchen-Wagons. The *arcera* (which the ancients called *arcela*) was a type of wagon, covered and protected on all sides like a large chest (*arca*), spread with garments, in which the very sick or the very elderly were usually carried lying down. See Varro, *book 4 on the Latin Language*. Of this kind are those vehicles and litters which our people call **sedan chairs** <note>original: *Sänfften*</note>, as well as **chamber-wagons** <note>original: *Kammerwägen*</note>. Wagon-service is discussed by Limnäus in *Public Law, book 6, chapter 4, number 15*. In Italy and Belgium, something is paid to the Magistrate for the license to use wagons, according to Klock in *On the Treasury, book 2, chapter 75*. Indeed, in Amsterdam, no one is permitted to ride in a carriage unless they are a nobleman, according to Sprenger in *Axioms of State, page 36*. No one can use a carriage in any city where the Sovereign Prince is staying as a guest, except for the Prince himself and Doctors <note>referring to those with doctoral degrees, who held high social rank</note>, as per Limnäus in *Public Law, book 8, chapter 8, number 118*.

## Counter-right. <note>Latin: *Reconventio*; German: *Widerrecht*</note>

->ADDITION.<-

A counter-claim is called a "mutual petition," in German: *Gegenklaag, Nachklag, Widerklag, Widerrecht*. Christian Lenz, *on the assignment of actions, chapter 34*. The phrase "to involve someone in a counter-claim" <note>German: *in das Widerrecht verfassen*</note> is found in *part 3, title 30 of the Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance*. See Dr. Struve, *on private vengeance, page 159*. Also, "to involve one in a counter-claim," Lenz, *chapter 34, number 11*; Dr. Biccius, *in the Golden [Theses], section 4, thesis 98*.

That vinegar can even be made from water is noted in the Gloss on law *on sales*, section 2, in the Digest *on entering a purchase*. It can be made with the scrapings of barrels, or if bread is dipped in vinegar and then placed in water, according to Neander in his *History of the Bacchanalia*, page 73 at the end. Wine is cooled with ice, as noted by Mundius in *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 3, number 205. It has happened that wine barrels were shattered and smashed by a thunderclap, yet the wine remained held together in one place for three days, even though the barrel was no longer there. Indeed, it has also happened that by a bolt of lightning, the wine within the barrels disappeared while the barrels themselves remained undamaged. Bock gives the reason for this in his *Notes on the Oettingen Brack*, folio 82: because the lightning, until it overcomes resistance, lingers within the liquid and exerts its force there, whereas it does not meet resistance from thin materials like the wood.

"Christ’s Tear" <note>Lachryma Christi</note> is an excellent wine that grows on Mount Vesuvius, according to Megiser in *Delights of Naples*, page 8, and Sprenger in *The Practice of Exchange*, page 15.

### On the Abomination of Brandy-Drinking

Guarinonius, book 4, chapter 33. On where one is permitted to distill brandy, see Sprenger, *On the Law of Building*, page 36. The excessive distilling of wine—which is prohibited in the State Ordinances and elsewhere in the years 1595 and 1603 through various mandates—as well as the large-scale production of starch <note>original: *Krafftmehl*; used in distilling and as a luxury good</note>, is hereby likewise forbidden. Every local authority is charged with faithfully upholding this, without respect to person, and collecting the forfeited fines. If there should be a reason to permit such things in prominent cities, it shall happen in no other way than by permission of the Council, and annually for only a certain number of bushels of wheat. Rittershusius on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, page 90, where there is an elegant passage about those who, if they committed a fault through drunkenness, are accustomed to lay the blame on the wine. It is not wine that should govern men, but men who should govern wine—at least those who are upright. But he who is wicked, if he drinks water or even lacks wine entirely, is still wicked by nature. Wenceslaus <note>likely referring to King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia, notorious for his drinking</note> was a scorner of gold and a lover of wine, *especially Fürstenberger wine*. Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 2, chapter 11, number 33, and the sources cited there.

Palm wine is completely white and has the taste of "new wine" <note>partially fermented grape juice</note> in Germany. It grows on high trees, like fir trees; when the Moors <note>original: *Mohren*; a historical term for Black Africans</note> want to get some, they tie a small jug around their waist with a rope or bast (as they call it)—the Moors call it a *Büth*. They do not climb the tree straight up, but rather around its curve; they then tie the small jug, bore a hole in the tree, and insert a small tube. Then the strength of the tree gradually drips this wine into the jug. However, it is never more pleasant to drink than on the first day, otherwise it turns sour. Michael Hemmersam, in the *Travel Description* published by me.

> The wine-sellers think not of GOD,
> They fake the wine, and add things in,
> Hanging sulfur inside, mixing it with water,
> Sparing no chalk, over-charging much,
> Yet one must suffer such things from them.
> Dr. Ambrosius Lobwasser.

Those who corrupt wines with lime and other forbidden mixtures—*those who prepare, smear, or falsify the wine with lime or similar harmful additions or "admixtures"*—see the Imperial Recess of 1577, title 26; see also the Imperial Recess of 1497, section 3. *Practical Supplement* in Wehner’s observations, under the word "Confiscation." If infants eat moderately cooked owl eggs before they have tasted wine, they are said to hate wine forever, and not only do they not drink it, but they even fear drunkards, as Philostratus and Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus testify in *History of the Gods*, chapter 8. Salmuth in the first volume of Panciroli, title "On Cellars," page 153, and Erasmus, volume 2, book 1, number 44, although there are those who

<column-break/>

deny that owl eggs can be found. Neæus in the *History of Bacchanalia*, page 146 (my copy).

On wine-sellers, see *Symphorema Gailliana*, volume 1, part 1, pages 150 and 151. *One man whom we were poking in the teeth for a long time yesterday—the other didn't understand and said he hadn't seen a toothpick; but he was informed when he heard that wine is the "tooth-poker" which cleans many and all teeth at once.* Mr. Harsdörffer, in the *Great Theater of Delightful and Instructive Stories*, in the last appendix, number 138. They place the wine in sold snow and ice, which is usually done in Hungary and similar hot places to cool the wines. Mundiunius, *On Duties and Honors*, chapter 3, number 205. Let a King about to drink wine remember that he drinks the "blood of the earth." Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 106, number 115. Antenor says in *Solomon*, chapter 10, that one should take a fresh Venetian glass and add a few drops of various spirits; thus one soon has lemon wine, then rosemary, then cherry, then raspberry wine. Taxes for wine: Boerius, page 246, number 1. On vinegary wine, Law 9, section 2 of the Digest, *On Contracted Purchase*.

The Moors, at their gatherings, have a pot of twelve measures full of palm wine, and they have a small vessel with it, with which they can scoop and drink, which they call a *Kolbos*; it holds about a pint. When they drink, they let some run past the mouth onto the earth, or they pour it on the ground with such quickness that it makes a sound like someone snapping their mouth.

### 77. Rolling Pieces. Allodial Properties.

->ADDITION.<-

On "rolling pieces" <term>walzende Stück; items of property or land that can be freely sold, moved, or transferred without the restrictions of feudal or inheritance law</term> and divisible goods, that is, such estates which someone possesses as allodial <term>allodialia; land owned outright, free of any superior lord's claims</term>. Dr. Georg Herpffer of Strasbourg, *Disputations*, question 19. Others more correctly call them "rolling goods" which are built up outside of inheritance law, which have no private lordship or common law. See Zobel, part 1, question 11, number 737. On whether such building-up is to be permitted, see part 1, question 12, at the end.

### 78. Weden, Widem. Places Devoted to the Church.

->ADDITION.<-

From *widem*, the word *bewidmet*, that is, endowed; and toward *widen*, from which places dedicated or devoted to Churches are called *Weden* <term>Weden or Widum; land or property legally attached to a parish church to provide for the priest’s livelihood</term>. Cypræus, *On Betrothals*, page 146.

Regarding a feudal castle <note>original Latin: *Castrum feudale*</note>, the Lord is bound to specifically prove the remaining dependencies (Klock, volume 3, counsel 87, number 69). Th. Polit. part 1; Speckle, part 1, *Architecture*, chapter 16). For what reason does a forest master <term>Forstmeister; a high-ranking official overseeing a royal or noble forest</term> grant a sod-flayer the right to the <term>Wasen; a German term for sod, turf, or the surface layer of a field</term>? A "sod wall" <note>original: *Cespititius murus*</note>: Walls were once made (as they are today in some parts of Germany) from clods and sods cut from the earth, especially in camps, as written by Vegetius (book 1, chapter 21). This is called a "molded wall" by Pliny and Isidore. It is a fortification of sods—that is, a rampart made of mud, sods, and driven stakes. House walls began to be made in this likeness. Hence the "sod wall" mentioned by Sidonius, Capitolinus, and Gildas the Wise. (Georg Erhard in *Symbols for Petronius*).

### 80. Meadows. Prata.

### ADDITION.

Regarding the theft of mown grass (Berlich). Mowing meadows. He who wishes to irrigate meadows so they become richer and more fertile cannot hinder one who has the right of grazing (Wurmser, *Observations*). See <term>Grass</term>, <term>Aftermath</term> <note>original: *Grommet*; the second harvest of hay in a season</note>, <term>Hay</term>, <term>Fallow</term>, <term>Tithe on newly broken land</term> <note>original: *Neubruchzehend*; a tax on land recently converted to agriculture</note>; add Neubrunner on *Fallows*.

<column-break/>

Regarding performing duties in respect to a meadow (Mundius). On the division of a meadow (Schneidewein). Hay is sold by weight in Speyer. The same is done in Nuremberg "at the great hay-scales" <note>original German: *bey der grossen Heuwag*</note>.

To have "hay-right" <term>Heurecht; a legal protection for a meadow to prevent grazing so hay can grow</term> refers to a meadow that is immune from cattle grazing for a certain time. Hence it is said: "This meadow goes into hay at St. George's Day," as if to say: it is being hayed or protected. That nobleman, for his pleasure by the water, had a bed made for himself out of sods; his head-cushions were sods, neatly shaped; there were sods between his feet and all around him. Above him, around the bed, were trees and the dwelling of birds. A thick-grassed meadow, whose fragrant herb-sods and colorful little flower-plots not only breathed the loveliest apothecary-air upon passersby, but were also visited and sucked by so many thousands of little bees, enriching them with honey before sending them back to their waxen kingdom. (More in Sigmund von Bircken, *The East-Land Laurel Grove*, page 81). Regarding meadows and meadow-rent (Speidel, *Mirror of Notables*). "What occurred on the 'Wailing Meadow' <note>original: *Wehewiesen*</note>, which is, as Cuspianus explains, a meadow named for catching or capturing" (Leonhard Wurffbain). Regarding meadow-tithes <note>original: *Wiesenzehend*</note> (Gudelinus). "A tithe from the meadows—namely, for one acre of meadow, pay one 'sow's stomach' <note>original: *Saummagen*; likely a specific local tribute or a vessel-measure</note> or four pennies in its place" (Limnaeus, *Public Law*). Subjects cannot divert water to irrigate meadows without the express permission of the Prince (Klock). A tenant farmer is forbidden from changing the nature of the property—such as turning fields into vineyards, meadows, or gardens, or vice versa—without the owner's prior knowledge and consent (Tabor, *On the Land-Tenure Contract*). Mountain meadows are mentioned by Werndle (book 4, *On Tithes*). "Whether the herding of goats on a small meadow-plot during times of war or plague is subject to prescription?" <note>legal expiration of a right or claim</note> (Carpzov, part 2). Regarding meadow-growth for a hereditary rent (Limnaeus). Cicero, in his *Paradoxes*: those shrewd appraisers of things value meadow areas highly because no one can damage that kind of possession.

Regarding the luxury of the meadows in Hungary (Klock, *On the Treasury*). Meadows (*Prata*) are so named because they are "ready" <note>original: *parata*</note> to receive fruit. As Columella elegantly writes in book 2: "The cultivation of the meadow is also necessary, to which the ancient Romans gave the first rank in agriculture; they also gave it its name from the fact that it is immediately..."

### ADDITION.

A common drainage area <term>impluvium; originally a Roman architectural feature, here referring to the space where eaves-drip falls</term> between two houses where the runoff from both falls (Frankfurt Reformation, part 8, title 7, § 9; Sprenger, *On Building Law*, page 91; Supplement to Wehner, page 73).

### 84. Willows. The Willow Tree. <note>original: *Weiden. Salix.*</note>

### ADDITION.

The willow tree is called *Salix* by the Latins, from the word *Salire*, which means "to jump into the height," or when said of plants, "to shoot up." Because this tree especially quickly and vigorously drives its branches upward; the Netherlanders give it its name for almost this very reason, and call it *Wilgen*, because it grows and increases **willingly and gladly** <note>original: *willig und gern*</note>, by itself without special care (Martin Mylius, Rector of the school at Görlitz, in the *Delightful Garden of Wisdom*, chapter 38, pages 524, 525). **Peasants and willows must be pruned often.** Matthesius writes in his *Mountain Postils* <note>original: *Berg-Postill*; a collection of sermons for miners connecting nature to faith</note> (page 69): When peasants wear gold and velvet, then the old proverb applies: **Willow-heads and a proud peasant must be trimmed once every three years.** (page 526). Willows are "shields," because in olden times, from such willow-

<column-break/>

-rods, shields were woven (page 431). The beaver loves the willow tree because of its bitterness, which is a special treat for him; he gnaws it with pleasure and also likes to build his home from it. Of this, Plautus <note>a Roman playwright</note> says: "You lie there gnawing at me, like a beaver at a willow stump" (page 531). In the Brunswick War Treaty of December 4, 1615, the appendages of mills, water, and willows are counted. And thereafter it stands: mills, mill-works, waters, ponds, fisheries, and willows.

Willows symbolize repentance (Master Harsdörffer, volume 4). On the willow grove and the fruit-losing willow (Boniface of Frankfurt, page 272; Doctor Tabor, *On Criminal Matters*, pages 414 and following). Willow switches <note>original: *Virgæ salignæ*</note>, **willow rods**. Willows for poles and for weaving. Regarding the willow grove and the cutting of a willow grove, see the word "Fisher." Regarding **planted willows** <note>original: *Saßweiden*</note> before they have taken root (Berlich, volume 5, conclusion 52, number 21). There are swamp-willows, brook-willows, sole-willows, hair-willows, glass-willows, and crab-willows <note>These are local German folk names for various species like the brittle willow or basket willow</note>.

### 85. Truth. <note>original: *Wahrheit. Veritas.*</note>

There is one GOD, and truth is of one nature with GOD (G. Richter, *In the Epistles*, page 262). Truth shines and glows more brightly when it is sought out (Boer, *Counsel 17, number 2*). Whether we ought to speak the truth always and everywhere is treated at length by Zahn in *On Lies* (book 1, chapter 49), where he reviews what theologians, ethicists, politicians, and jurists think about this question. What is truth? (Zahn, *On Lies*, book 1, chapter 1, number 1). Praises of truth (number 2). What does truth accomplish? (number 3). **He who plays the fiddle of truth gets the fiddle smashed over his ears** <note>A German proverb meaning those who speak harsh truths often face backlash</note>, which can only be understood regarding specific, private truths (Wendelin, *In Moral Philosophy*, book 1, chapter 36). The sweetness and utility of truth (number 7). Just as a lead coin, even if large, is of no value, while a silver coin, even if small, far exceeds it in price: so a single truthful man stands above a hundred liars. How shameful and foul it is that we will not tolerate a counterfeit coin in our purse, yet so easily tolerate a lying tongue in our own mouth (Drexel, *In Phaëthon*, chapter 37, number 3). The truth of an accusation excuses the accuser only when the crime objectified was such that it is beneficial to the Commonwealth to be known, even if the accusation comes from a spirit of injury and evil intention, or the sting of private anger (Zahn, *On Lies*, book 1, chapter 35, number 4). Certainly, truth is not to be rejected wherever it may be found, nor should we look at *who* says it, but *what* is said. Just as a wise man does not despise a precious stone even if it were found in the head of a dragon or a toad: so no one should reject the truth, since it depends not on the subject <note>the speaker</note>, but on the object <note>the fact</note>, even if it comes from the most wicked person...
