### 86. Wind, Calm. Ventus, Malacia.

Regarding **winds**, Michael Knab in *Hortipomolegio*, page 121. One does not live on wind <note>i.e., one cannot survive on empty talk or air</note>, Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 7, number 3. I struggle with the winds, a proverbial expression; Job, chapter 6: "You prepare speeches only for reproof, and you utter words to the wind," that is, empty, trivial things <note>Greek: *φλαῦρα* (phlaura)</note>, without weight or effect. Aulus Sabinus, *Elegy 2*, in the persona of Demophoon

<column-break/>

writing to Phyllis: "Now let the winds carry my words, which carried your sails," that is, let them vanish and gain nothing from you. The sailor must not lose a good **wind**; for if he were to do so, he would be obliged to make amends and pay the merchant for such damage, *Maritime Law of Wisby*, article 41.

Regarding the whirlwind—a most vehement, turning wind, twisting itself with a very great crash; regarding the force of the wind and the battles of the winds—see Rittershusius extensively on Law 23, Digest on the Rules of Law, page 42. **The traverser of fields and destroyer of flowers. The sharp judge of gardens, the tumult of wild winds scatters the cloudy sky; the rough enemy of the fields, the stern driver of clouds, the stormer of cliffs, the rider of waves.** More on this by Mr. Harsdörffer in *The Poetical Richter*, part 3, page 590. Also in his *Mathematical and Philosophical Hours of Refreshment*. South winds are the most harmful, and those cities which have a mountain to the south that blocks the wind are very healthy. The winds from the **rising of the sun** are the most beneficial to health. **Calm** <note>original: *Windstill*</note> is most magnificently described by Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Great Theater of Joyful and Instructive Histories*, volume 104, number 5. If large and fruit-bearing trees are uprooted by the wind, the possessor of an entailed estate makes them his own, Knipschild, *On Entails*, chapter 10, number 94. Regarding the Etesian <note>periodic Mediterranean</note> winds, Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 1, chapter 27, number 8. A neighbor cannot hinder the wind from my threshing floor by building, Boerius, decision 322, number 12. Whether it can be known from which parts of the world they blow, and how many winds there are in number? Keckermann in *Maritime Problems*, page 238 and following.

Winds are healthy because they bring serenity and dry and purify the air, such as the Eastern and Northern winds: namely the *Apeliotes* <note>Greek: ἀπηλιώτης</note>, or East Wind, and the *Aparktias* <note>Greek: ἀπαρκτίας</note>, or North Wind, along with their companions and associates, which they call "collateral" winds. The East Wind is so called because it breathes from under the sun <note>Latin: *Subsolanus*</note>: and indeed, from the equinoctial sunrise, it is hot and dry, and usually brings serenity; therefore it is judged most healthy. For the air in the East is also hot and dry; and this is because of the presence and longer stay of the sun, which excites heat there and consumes the moisture, both of the air and of the vapors contained in it. Its collateral wind to the right, toward the summer sunrise, is *Kaikias* <note>Greek: καικίας</note>, the Northeast wind or Hellespontus; to the left, toward the winter sunrise, is *Eurus*, or the Southeast wind. The North Wind, having obtained its name because it blows from the arctic pole, is cold and dry: it purges the air and drives away the malignant miasmas <note>Greek: μιάσματα</note> that are mixed in it, whence it is called the "broom of the sky" <note>Latin: *scopa coeli*</note>. The cause of its temperature is that the air in the North is cold and dry, partly because of the absence and distance of the sun, and partly because of the force of the cold drying and constricting the earth, so that vapors cannot be raised from it. The collateral winds emulate its temperament: toward the summer sunrise...

### 87. Cloudburst. <term>Cataracta</term> <note>literally "waterfall" or "floodgate"</note>.

### 88. Wolves. <term>Lupi</term>.

The response of the Giessen Faculty in the case of **werewolves** <note>original German: *Wehr-Wölffe*</note>, see Mr. Tabor on confrontation, disputation 3, thesis 14, page 77. "Wolves become foolish, and whatever they attack must die miserably in a state of madness." On a common, general wolf hunt, see Mr. Christopher Philipp Richter, part 3, counsel 3, numbers 2, 3, 4, 18, 19, and following. "Whether subjects can be required, used, and compelled by the high provincial authorities to pursue wolves and similar harmful animals," see the same source, number 24. In Italy, women who keep stables are accustomed to give [something] in cheese to whichever travelers they wish or are able, whereby they are immediately turned into beasts of burden and carry all necessary things; after the work is finished, they return to themselves. Yet there is no beastly mind in them, but a rational, human one is preserved <note>This refers to common early modern folktales of metamorphic magic and "traveler's tales" of witchcraft</note>. More in Christoph Daurer’s *Denunciation of Witches*, page 11. ### 89. Warranty. <term>Warantia</term>.

Warranty <note>original Latin: *Warantia*</note>, the legal recovery of a thing sought in judgment. To warrant <note>original: *Warantizare*</note> descends from the German *wahren*, that is, to preserve, to keep, to hold fast by letter and seal; or from *wehren* or *bewehren*, to defend. See Mr. Sax in his inaugural disputation on the legal maxim: *Pay and Then Seek Recovery*, thesis 14.

### 90. Delusion. <term>Opinio</term> <note>Opinion</note>.

Delusion <note>original German: *Wahn*</note>, or to imagine, to think. William Mafius wrote books on singular opinions. Opinion is twofold: just, namely if a thing cannot be known; and unjust, for one who makes an opinion for himself, see the *Saxon Mirror*, book 3, article 8, folio 333b, number 39. In certain cases, one must be sure; it is not permitted to merely "opine" in swearing, judging, or believing—that is, in religion. *Saxon Mirror*, ibid. "Most opinionated," for one of great authority, see Mr. Cobius’s *Principles of Law*, page 78.

### 91. Sausage-riders. <term>Cœnipetæ</term>.

Supper-seekers <note>original Latin: *Cœnipetæ*</note>, Sausage-riders <note>German: *Wurstreuter*</note>, or Plucking-boys <note>German: *Zupffenbuben*—terms for parasitic gatecrashers</note>, see Limnäus, *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 5, page 141 at the end. The licentious appetite of the supper-seekers daily gasps for the plates of others.

Since several members of the nobility have made a habit of discourteous riding-about to engagements, weddings, baptisms, funerals, and other honorable gatherings—and indeed in considerable numbers—practicing great wantonness, unheard-of defiance, arrogance, and an exceedingly Epicurean life, shamelessly bothering all honorable women; and since this is said to become more common every day in all places. When, therefore, much hardship is caused to many an honorable man in his own house during such honorable affairs, and more must be spent on such a "riding company" than on the invited guests, who, along with the host, are often not sufficiently safe from such company; and since this is no small harm, causing disparagement to those of the nobility living in the countryside and to the noble estate itself: We therefore cannot permit such riding-about at all, and we hereby completely forbid the same. Thus, from now on, no one who has not been invited in the proper way to such gatherings shall be found there or allow himself to be caught there; also, if one or more who are not invited should dare to present themselves, they shall by no means be received by the host or others. For if this is violated, not only...

### 89. Warranty. <note>Latin: *Warantia*</note>

### 90. Opinion. <note>Latin: *Opinio*</note>

Opinion, or to opine/to think; Guilielmus Masius wrote books on singular opinions. ### 101. Market Signals. <note>original German: *Wische*, literally a "wisp" of straw used as a marker</note>

### 107. Words. <note>original Latin/German: Vocabula / Wörter</note>

**Words.** Ulpian—whether considered as a Jurist or a Philosopher—was called <margin>"Is it found [in literature] or is it not?" <note>original Greek: κειται ἢ οὐ κειται</note></margin> due to his excessive diligence in investigating the nature of words (according to Athenaeus in *The Banquet of the Learned* <note>original title: Dipnosophista</note>). This was because, following the objection of Cynulcus in book 13, chapter 17 of Athenaeus, he knew nothing else but to inquire of others, <margin>"Is it found or if it is found?" <note>original Greek: κειται ἢ ει κειται</note></margin> "Has it been said or if it has been said?" Likewise, he was called a "word-hunter" <note>original Greek: ὀνομαθοθήρας</note> by the same author, Athenaeus, in book 14, chapter 16—that is, a catcher of words. <term>Doctor Tabor, *On Transpositions*, page 151.</term> Juvenal spoke of "Magnificent words" or "Herculean words" in Satire 2. Honeyed words, obscene words; see Rupert in *Messenger of Letters*, page 716. Regarding grandiloquence, see the same work, page 656. Monkeys drink blood. Deeds are more powerful than words. <term>Höpingk, *On the Law of Seals*, chapter 2, number 152, and citations therein; see also letter D, number 40.</term> New words must be coined. <term>Mr. Dilherr, volume 1, *Academic Disputations*, page 676, at the end.</term> One who is powerful in words is **the speaker or the word-keeper.** <note>original German: der Worthabende oder Worthaltende</note> <term>Limnaeus, volume 1, *Additions*, book 7, chapter 44.</term>

## 2. Tithes. <note>original: Zehend / Decimæ</note>

Regarding **Tithes**, whether from newly cleared lands, ecclesiastical benefices, or other kinds, and their law, use, privileges, etc., see Tyndarus, Petrus Rebuffus, Canisius, and Johann Werndle in individual treatises; add the *Synodal Statutes of the Bishop of Constance*, folio 134, etc.; Hackelman in *Disputations on Canon Law*, dispute 8; Stephanus, *Institutions of Canon Law*, book 2, chapter 6; *The Grand Almoner of France*, folio 244, etc.; *Basel Disputations*, volume 3, dispute on Tithes. On **Tithes in the Law of God**, see Joseph Scaliger in his *Opuscula*, page 61, and Wilhelm Schickard on *Royal Law*, folio 105, etc.

The word **Zehend** <note>Tithe, or "Tenth"</note>, or "lying within the tithe," is not to be understood as meaning "subject to a tenth," but rather as referring to a **territory and district**,

<column-break/>

as common usage—which we ought primarily to follow—demonstrates this. For one usually says, "as far as this or that village’s tithe goes," or "the estate is located in one or another tithe." This is used as if one were to say, "the territory and jurisdiction extend this far," or "this field is found situated in this or that territory." And so the word *Zehend* is used in two ways: (1) for a **district or territory**, and (2) for the **Tithes** <note>The tax itself</note>.

**Tithes** <note>original: Zehend / Decimæ</note> are manifold: the **Great Tithe** <note>original: groß Zehend</note> is paid from wheat, rye, spelt, oats, einkorn, barley, peas, lentils, beans, and all other fruits that grow on a stalk.

**Hay Tithe**: <note>original: Heuzehend</note> but regarding the "head" <note>original: Heubt. Likely referring to a chief tax or perhaps a misspelling of 'Heuboden' (hayloft) or 'Haupt' (main tax)</note>, to my knowledge, nothing is paid in any place.

**Minute or Small Tithe**: <note>original: Minut oder kleiner Zehend</note> under this is reckoned fruit and what grows on trees. Likewise: cabbage, turnips, flax, and similar produce. On the subject of the great and small tithes, see *Strasbourg Counsels*, volume 1, counsel 2, question 4, folio 55 and following.

**Blood Tithe or Living Tithe**, <note>original: Blut- oder lebendige Zehend / Carnaticus</note> the extraction of flesh, such as young pigs, piglets, and chickens. The Constitutions of Charlemagne state that in vineyards, fields, or meadows, and even in their buildings, they should be made to work, and they do not cease to exact **flesh-tithes** and wine from them against all justice. There, Vitus Amerbach says that by *Carnaticum* <note>Flesh tithe</note> is understood the tithe of meat, the **Meat Tithe** <note>original: Fleischzehenden</note>.

**Tithes on Wages and Merchant’s Profits**, concerning which see Rebuffus’s treatise on tithes. This species of tithe is not customary in Germany.

By the concession of the **Roman Popes**, the tithes of various places have passed into the hands of Princes and other laypeople in view of the benefits they have provided to the Church, as noted in the *Codex of Donations* by Aubertus Miraeus, chapter 34, in the notes. But indeed, that tithes—and even those from newly cleared lands—cannot come into the hands of lay magnates was decreed in the **Council of Vienne**; see Lazius on *Vienna*, book 2, chapter 5.

The **Tithe-holder** <note>original: Decimarius</note>, or he to whom the tithes from an estate belong by his own right, such as a **Parish Priest** <note>original: Parochus</note>; to whom they belong by investiture and who holds the privilege by law, so that he can prohibit crops from being exported from the field unless he has been notified, so that he may see that an accounting of those same crops is made. This is according to the traditions of Marcus Antonius in *Archiepiscopal Practice of the Neapolitan Court*, chapter 79, and Caspar Antonius Thessaurus, *Forensic Questions*, question 9, number 1. In the following number, he asks how long the crops should remain in the field after cutting before they are exported, so that no harm occurs from that delay.

To the owners of the crops: **Is it permitted to count from one field to another?** <note>original: "An liceat von einem Acker zum andern zählen?"</note> No; because through this, one might fraudulently divide the fields so that they would not have to pay any tithes. <note>Tithes were typically a 10% tax on agricultural produce. Owners sometimes tried to split land into smaller plots to fall under minimum taxable thresholds.</note>

Regarding the **legal expiration of tithes** <note>original: "De præscriptione decimarum"</note>, see Gilken on *Acquisition and Expiration*, page 102 and following, and page 712, part 3, chapter 8; and see my own work, decade 3, counsel 3; and in the *Counsels of Various Jurists*, counsel 19 and following. To see that tithes are also not given from certain crops by custom or expiration, see Piasecki in *Episcopal Practice*, part 2, chapter 4, number 67, page 335.

Chokier proves that tithes do not expire simply by a failure to pay them, in *Vindication against the Liberties of the Church*, part 2, chapter 2.

According to chapter *Sua* 25: "No one can be exempt from the payment of tithes, which are owed by Divine constitution." See also Gail, book 1, observation 38, number 1. Regarding **Pisistratus** <note>The 6th-century BCE ruler of Athens</note>, he says the following on page 47: He ex-

<column-break/>

acted a tithe of those fruits that came from the fields. However, one day while walking, when he saw an old man laboring in a stony place, he approached and asked what fruits he gathered from there. ### The Mandate of the Bishop of Bamberg

By the Grace of God, We, Johann Georg, Bishop of Bamberg, etc. <note>Johann Georg Fuchs von Dornheim, reigned 1623–1633</note>. Although our honorable and esteemed predecessors of blessed and mild memory issued open mandates and commands regarding how all danger in the assessment, collection, and delivery of tithes in our Bishopric, Principality, and territory should be avoided—both by us and by the subjects and dependents of our Bishopric who are obligated to give tithes, or those who

<column-break/>

wish to lease them <note>original: "bestehen," meaning to rent or contract the right to collect the tithes</note>—and how they should show themselves dutiful in this matter, and although it is proper that such necessary mandates should have been met with dutiful obedience; yet it has come to our attention through credible reports, and we find it ourselves to be only too true, that these mandates have been violated in more than one way. 

Rather, our subjects and inhabitants have presumed to show themselves frequently disobedient, improper, resistant, and fraudulent in the delivery of tithes—whether in the village or the field, whether "dead" (produce) or "living" (livestock), in wine, grain, hay, lard-seeds <note>seeds used for oil</note>, and other titheable fruits. Not only do they engage in all sorts of improper practices during the "striking" <note>marking/counting</note> and assessment of tithes, but they also form "mobs" or cliques in the villages to ensure that no one outbids another or allows a stranger to lease the tithes. Sometimes they even refuse to allow the tithe-lord himself to collect the tithes, binding themselves to one another under threat of their own private penalties.

Furthermore, in several places, they conceal the tithes during delivery, or they fence in and block off wide areas of fields near their houses to withhold the tithes of grain, meadow-grass, and fruit grown therein simply by means of the fencing—or they even haul it away without fencing. They presume to exempt one another and thus refuse what is due. In addition, they use dangerous methods such as **"evening-bucks"** <note>original: "Abendböcke," a slang term for moving crops secretly at twilight</note> and other nightly transport in many ways. Specifically, they presume to cut the grain without leaving the required "tithe-sheaf" lying in the field; and even where the tithe-sheaves are left lying, they are tied much smaller and thinner than the others. 

Likewise, in some places, the due tithe is withheld because the tithe-collectors or lessees are improperly demanded to pick up the cut sheaves themselves. Items: they graze the meadows down [before the tithe is taken], or they tithe the hay not by the proper portion, but by "bundles"—as much as one can tie or take from a stack with a fork—and they make the tithe-stacks smaller than the others. Thus, in various ways, they cause unjust, intolerable damage and reduction to the established tithe-rights of our Bishopric and its clergy and laity, contrary to law and equity. Moreover, they even attempt to interpret and explain the aforementioned mandates in some places to their own advantage, contrary to the express letter of the law. Since such disobedience and contrary interpretations are to us...

<meta>This page continues the legal exploration of tithes, transitioning from general academic disputes to specific regional legislation. It features a formal mandate issued by the Prince-Bishop of Bamberg in 1628, addressing widespread attempts by the peasantry and local communities to evade or manipulate tithe payments during the hardships of the Thirty Years' War.</meta>

...to permit or overlook such unjust, dangerous, and punishable intentions and behaviors in our Bishopric, Principality, Jurisdiction, and territory; thus, we are compelled to renew the aforementioned mandates of our ancestors and to clarify and explain the points that have been misunderstood, as we now do with the advice and consent of our worthy **Cathedral Chapter**.

We therefore earnestly command, under penalty of 40 Guilders <note>The Guilder (Gülden) was a standard gold or silver coin; 40 was a significant fine for a commoner</note>, and—depending on the investigation and findings of the case—heavier physical punishment for those who act against this our mandate. This shall be relentlessly pursued against every violator of this our command according to the circumstances. Whether through the aforementioned or other ways, however they may be or be named, no one shall cause any hindrance or delay to the **tithe-lords** or their **tithe-leasers** <note>original: "Zehendbeständner," those who contracted the right to collect tithes</note> regarding the rightful shares from village and field, dead or living (inspected or uninspected, nothing excepted, see above under **Newly Broken Land** <note>original: "Neubruch"</note>). Nor shall anyone use deceit to diminish the tithe. 

Particularly, everyone must refrain from the unjust and improper practice occurring in several places of taking "evening-goats" <note>original: "Abendböck"; likely a customary illegal perk or bribe demanded by harvesters</note>. Nor shall the reapers be permitted to carry home anything from the cut grain or bound sheaves in the evening. Furthermore, no one shall refuse or delay the tithe on account of demanding the improper "lifting up" of bound sheaves (as neither the tithe-lords nor the tithe-leasers are obligated to do this). Instead, every person shall obediently and willingly reach and give their due tithe—whether it be in some places the twentieth or thirtieth sheaf, or otherwise another known and undisputed tradition regarding all kinds of fruits. This applies, as stated above, to wine, grain, **refined seeds** <note>original: "Schmalsat," usually referring to oil-producing seeds like rapeseed or linseed</note>, (Werndle, in his work *On Tithes* <note>original: "de decimis"</note> page 54, calls it "excess-crop" <note>original: "Übersaat"</note>, cabbage, turnips, hemp, flax, onions, and the like), hay, or others, large or small, dead or living, in village and field, nothing excepted. This must be done without any deceit, without reducing the sheaves, haystacks, or whatever else they may be called, for the tithe-lords and their leasers, without any danger, diminution, or opposition. 

And if the appointed tithe-leasers or collectors are not present at every moment, the rightful tithe must nevertheless be left lying in the field. Furthermore, now and in the future, village societies and communities shall, in general and in particular, completely refrain from "bribing the tithes" <note>likely referring to tampering with the quality or count of the sheaves</note> or practicing deceit against the tithe-lords. Nor shall they divide themselves into "bands" <note>original: "Rottenweiß"</note> to decide who alone shall bid on the tithes. Rather, it shall be free for anyone, whoever they may be, regardless of where they reside or in which village the tithe is located, to bid for the tithe of each place and to

<column-break/>

bid for it, and to collect it according to their pleasure, as is proper, without hindrance from the village society or community in whose fields the tithe is located. All others must likewise comply, under avoidance of the aforementioned and other earnest punishments, which shall be undertaken against anyone according to their transgression, as stated above. 

We therefore command and bid all and each of our Head-Officials, Mayors, Caretakers, Treasurers, Bailiffs, and our other servants in every place to hold fast to this our mandate, to proceed relentlessly with punishment against violators, and to report the violation in every instance, so that further orders may be given regarding what the punishment shall be. Every person whom this matter touches should know how to conduct themselves accordingly. Given in our city of **Bamberg**, under our secret seal printed hereon, on Friday, the 30th of June, in the year 1628.

-> <image-desc>A circular printer's device or seal featuring the monogram "LS" in stylized, interlocking letters within a circular border.</image-desc> <-

Regarding the **tithes of animals** <note>original: "Decimæ animalium"</note> which, on account of wars, are born in a foreign place, to which place they are owed, see Boër, decision 13, number 54; Petrus Gregorius in *Syntagma Juris*, book 2, chapter 25, number 2. That **unusual tithes** are not to be demanded, and that the usage in the matter of tithes varies, and therefore custom is to be followed in them, see Paul Christin, volume 1, decision 236; Franciscus Marci, decision 17, part 1. Whether a **custom** that the tithe be paid in the barns is valid, see Cravetta, counsel 21. Concerning tithes, see Menochius, counsel 36; Camillus Borellus in *Summa Decisionum*, volume 1, treasury 19; Bulenger *On Tributes and Taxes* <note>original: "de tribut. & vectig."</note> folios 23 and 24. 

In the year 1473, it is stated in a letter regarding the tithe at **Arnhöchstatt**, that it shall fall due between the two "Days of Our Lady," namely the **Consecration of Herbs** <note>original: "Wurzweyhe," referring to the Feast of the Assumption, August 15</note> and the last "Day of Our Lady" <note>likely the Nativity of Mary, September 8</note>. **That which has been tithed once should not be tithed further** <note>original: "Decimatum semel amplius decimari non debet"</note>, Mundius *On Duties and Honors* <note>original: "de mun. & honor."</note> chapter 3, numbers 49 and 242. **If a field bears fruit twice or more in a year, tithes are to be paid that many times** <note>original: "Si ager bis vel pluries in anno ferat fructus, toties solvendæ sunt decimæ"</note>, Panormitanus in chapter *Ex parte* 21; Moneta chapter 4, number 12. 

According to **Saxon Law**, the land-heirs of a deceased vassal take that which he has earned; that is, if he lived to see the "interest day" <note>the due date for rent or taxes</note>, such as the **tithe of lambs** on Walpurgis <note>May 1</note>, the **tithe of all meat** on St. John's Day <note>June 24</note>, the **tithe of all corn** on St. Margaret's Day <note>July 20</note>, etc., and the man's sowing, provided the harrow has passed over it; Schneidewein on the *Institutes*, page 480 at the end. Among the **great tithes**, besides the items mentioned by Besold above, some also include rice and millet. To the **small tithes** also belong nuts. Likewise hemp, see Reusner, book 4, decision 2, number 10 and following.

### 3. **Hue and Cry.** <term>Judicium clamoris</term> <note>Latin: "The judgment of the cry." This refers to a formal public outcry required to initiate certain legal proceedings.</note>

Although under Common Law <note>original: "Jure communi"</note> the evidence of a committed crime does not strictly require the outcry of an accuser (*Chapter: evidence, regarding accusations*), under Saxon Law, however, accusations for <term>flagrant crimes</term> <note>original: "criminibus flagrantibus"; crimes where the perpetrator is caught in the act</note> must be initiated with a formal outcry, with **public shouting and the hue and cry** <note>original: "Gerüff und Zettergeschrey"</note>, as noted by Moller (*4. semestr. cap. 33. num. 12.*).

And according to the same Saxon Law, this judicial outcry in criminal matters marks the beginning of the trial. (*Saxon Territorial Law, Book 1, Art. 62.*: **the shout or hue and cry is the start of the lawsuit, and whoever raises the cry**—that is, who declares the crime to be flagrant and begins the trial with that solemn shout—**must pursue it according to the law**; see Treutler *vol. 1. disp. de Judiciis. 12. thes. 2. sub lit. a.*).

A crime is called "flagrant" whether someone is caught in the act or while fleeing from the crime. For one who flees before the Judge’s household or the accuser is punished just as if they were caught in the very act, according to the authorities cited by Moller (*lib. 4. semestr. cap. 33. num. 13.*). The same author says in the following section: even if the defendant is not caught in the act or in flight, our custom observes that once the corpse of the murdered person is brought to the place of judgment, an accusation is initiated with a Cry against the fugitive or hiding murderer. This is no longer done by the accuser themselves, as was once the custom among the Saxons (evident from the text of *Article 63 of the Saxon Territorial Law, Book 1*), but by a Herald. Because of his terrifying voice—as the punishment of the guilty usually follows immediately after—the common people call him the **Blood-Crier** <note>original: "Blutschreyer"</note>. This proceeds unless someone appearing in the name of the accused alleges reasons for his absence or why the trial should not be held with the Cry. In such cases, that customary shout is usually deferred, and it is pronounced **that the hue and cry shall for now be fairly stayed.** If, however, the crime brought to court is not obvious, or—as the Latin text in *Article 64, Book 2* says—**hand-having** <note>original: "Handhafft"; caught red-handed with the stolen goods or weapon in hand</note>, it must not be pursued with the Cry, unless the accuser wishes to be condemned for injury; **for where there is no red-handed deed, one must sue without the shout if one wishes to remain without harm.** But see Moller at the cited location, and Beatus in his *Decisions, vol. 5, part 5, vol. 1, page 557*, where he discusses when and to what extent the **Hue and Cry** should be permitted.

Albinus, in the *Meissen Chronicle*, derives this word from the Latin "to cite" <note>original: "citiren"</note>. **Because by this act, the perpetrators are cited, as it were, to give an account of themselves.** (*tit. 11. fol. 152.*)

### ADDITION.

Regarding this matter, one should consult Wehner in his *Practical Observations, Letter Z, under this word*. On when the **Hue and Cry** should be omitted, see Christoph Phi-

<column-break/>

lippus Richter (*part 5. cons. 1. num. ult. fol. 3.*): The whims of accusers are not to be indulged, as the well-known practice speaks against it, regarding **the staying of the hue and cry and the holding of highly necessary capital trials until something criminal has been proven.**

### 4. **Witnesses, Witness Oath.** <term>Testes, Juramentum testium.</term>

Regarding witnesses for a University, see Beatus (*decis. tom. 5. fol. 581.*). The principle that **one witness is no witness** <note>original: "unus testis nullus testis"; a fundamental rule of medieval law requiring at least two witnesses for proof</note> is found in Salmuth’s *Sanhedrin (fol. 100 & 201)*, where he teaches that striking terror into witnesses is the same as saying: **Remind them of the punishment for perjury.** That ecclesiastical persons cannot testify in a criminal case without the consent of the Pope was decided by Peguera (*decif. 52*). Regarding not producing enemies as witnesses, see Camerarius (*meditat. historic. centur. 1. cap. 19*). A witness summoned under a false name is not bound to appear, according to Pfeil (*consil. 169*). Whether witnesses examined before an arbitrator are valid in another trial? See Daffel (*consil. 9*). On the judge's discretion in granting credibility to witnesses, see Joseph Ludovicus (*decis. 3*).

Whether a **priest** <note>original: "Sacerdos"</note> should be required to take the **witness oath**? See Beatus (*vol. 2. fol. 274 to 867*). **When someone is left to their word of honor** <note>original: "bey seiner Treu gelassen"</note> by custom or consent of the parties, if they testify falsely, are they a perjurer? See Freher (*lib. 1. parerg. cap. 20*).

### ADDITION.

A witness testifying outside the specific points of the case <note>original: "extra Articulum"</note> proves nothing (Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleatus lib. 1. obs. 95*). The production of witnesses must be done at the expense of the one producing them (*obs. 99*). According to *Festus*: "Classical witnesses," who were also called "wealthy," were those of unimpeachable faith and fit sponsors of the truth, not those counted only by head or the poorest citizens; in short: **Witnesses whom no one could reproach.** In the Epistle to the Hebrews, a great multitude of witnesses is called a **cloud of witnesses** <note>original Greek: "νέφος μαρτύρων" (nephos martyron)</note>. A witness who offers themselves voluntarily is considered suspect, and their testimony deserves little credit (*Canon law, Case 5, Question 5*). See Mynsing (*cent. 4. obs 3*) and Dr. Tabor on *Confrontation (page 77)*. On whether and when **hearsay testimony** <note>original: "Testimonium de auditu"</note> is admitted, see Hartmann (*lib. 2. tit. 15. obs. 3*). An unsworn witness is not believed (Fabricius *obs. 101*). The oath can be waived for witnesses by the will of the parties (*sect. 2*). Witnesses must be provided with travel money <note>original: "viaticum"</note> and the expenses they would likely have incurred at home (Fabricius *obs. 99. sect. 2*). A witness should be provided with full expenses, and nothing should be deducted that they would have likely spent at home (*sect. 3*). On when the confrontation of witnesses is to be done and what must be observed therein, see Alfonso Vilagut in *Practical Canonical Criminal Law, book 4.*

### 5. Gypsies. <term>Zingari</term> <note>original: "Zigeuner. Zingari." This section reflects 17th-century European legal views and prejudices toward the Romani people.</note>

These people falsely claim they are from **Egypt**, and that they are exiles driven from their home by the gods to atone for the sins of their ancestors—who supposedly refused to receive the Virgin Mother of God and the child Jesus with hospitality—by a seven-year exile. They impudently feign that, otherwise, calamity and sterility would be close at hand. But experience shows the matter is quite different. For they are nothing other than a **handful of thieves** and a most wretched collection of idle and fraudulent men, gathered from various nations that are not so remote, but neighboring. Pitching tents outside cities, in fields, and at crossroads, they beg for their living through treachery, robbery, deception, and bartering, and by delighting people with **divination by palm-reading** <note>original: "chiromantica divinatione"</note>. See Martin Mager, *On Armed Advocacy*, chapter 8, number 77 and following.

<column-break/>

In a certain old Italian book, or **itinerary to Jerusalem** <gloss>itinerary</gloss>, Book 5, these types of **Gypsies** <gloss>Cingari</gloss> are said to be the descendants of Cain, wanderers and **exiles** <gloss>exiles</gloss> on account of his sin; which is absurd, since all such people perished in the universal flood. But if one desires to know more of these matters, let him see Polydore Vergil, *On Inventors*, folio near the end; Guyon, *Diverse Lessons* <gloss>lessons</gloss>, volume 2, folio 472; Istuanhu in his *Description of Hungary* <gloss>Hungary</gloss>, in the Index under the word "Cingari"; Reinhard König in *Political Introduction*, part 2, chapter 10, number 52 and two counsels; and Bernhard Zieritz on the *Criminal Constitutions*, on the phrase "uncertain dwellings"; and especially J. B. Gramaye, *Africa Illustrated*, book 6, chapter 1, folio 138; and myself, *On the Law of Citizens*, folio 80, and in the *Introduction*, book 1, folio 181. To these, join by all means the *Novellas* of **Miguel de Cervantes**, specifically *The Little Gypsy Girl* <note>original: "la Gitanilla"</note>. **Gypsies expelled from Milan and Parma?** See Surius, Year of Christ 1552, page 844.

### ADDITION.

If you desire notable facts about Gypsies, see the first discussion of Cl. Rupert on Valerius Maximus, book 2, 6; Camerarius, century 1, *Historical Meditations*, chapter 17, century 75; Schönborn, *Politics* 3, 16; Limnäus, *On Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 161 and the three following; and the same, century 1, *Epistles*, page 414 and following. In Turkey, the law of the nation allows women by public **privilege** <gloss>privilege</gloss> to prostitute themselves to Turks as well as Christians with impunity. Limnäus—my friend who is to be honored even after death—volume 1, *On Public Law*, book 9, chapter 1, number 165, and the laws cited there.

### 6. Interest, Annual Interest, Registration of Interest, Hereditary Interest, Lease. <term>Census</term> <note>original: "Zins, Jährliche Zins, Zinsschreibung, Erbzins, Pacht. Census." The term "Census" here refers to a type of annual payment or rent derived from property.</note>

How a **census** <note>annual payment/rent</note> is established, and how a **reserved census** <note>a rent held back by the seller of a property</note> differs from a **constituted census** <note>a rent created by a contract of sale for a sum of money</note>; likewise regarding rents from the title of purchase and its requirements, see Carolus à Knipberg, *On Hereditary Fiefs*, chapter 4, number 16 and following. Also, in case of doubt, whether a rent is presumed to be feudal, emphyteutic <note>a long-term lease of land</note>, or common; ibid. number 171, etc.

Whether **annual payments**, annual interest <gloss>and</gloss> and leases, are removed by **prescription** <term>prescription</term> <note>A legal "statute of limitations" where a right is lost if not exercised for a certain period.</note>? A distinction is made between future and past payments. **Only past payments**, and not future ones, are subject to prescription, according to Law 7, final section, on the prescription of 30 or 40 years; there it is manifest that the **prescription** <gloss>prescription</gloss> is computed from the beginning of each year (Law 28, *Digest*, "How use is lost"). Then, both in contracts and in last wills, for subsequent years in annual debts, the obligation is born on a certain day or under a condition (Law 16, section 1, *Digest*). Therefore, for the **following** <gloss>following</gloss> years before the day the obligation is due, prescription does not **run** <gloss>run</gloss>, according to the express text in chapter *olim fam* 20, extra, regarding censuses; and this is the common opinion, as was judged several times in the **Imperial Chamber Court**, as Mynsinger <gloss>Mynsinger</gloss> reports in century 3, observation 13.

<meta>This page continues the legal encyclopedia under the letter 'Z,' focusing on the definition and classification of financial instruments such as "census" (annuities or rent-charges) and "usura" (interest). It explores whether these financial rights should be treated as movable or immovable property under the law.</meta>

<page-num>1151</page-num>
<header>Book Z.</header>

Regarding the form for contracting a **census** <note>In this context, a *census* refers to a financial arrangement where one party provides capital in exchange for a yearly payment, similar to an annuity or a ground rent</note>, see the Decretals, Book 7, Volume 2, Title 13. There, Pope Pius V states that a *census* is a contract involving fruit-bearing immovable property for a sum of money; he specifies that the *census* cannot be increased or created based on the fruits themselves, and its price, once established, must remain fixed. Indeed, according to the decrees of Canon Law, a *census* is a type of pension paid out of Church revenues. It can also be defined as anything paid annually in a specific quantity or sum, according to Hostiensis. More commonly, however, a **Census** is called a certain contract by which a person holding full ownership of a thing transfers the useful and direct ownership <note>original: "dominium utile directum"; a legal distinction where one party manages/uses the property while another holds the formal title</note> to another for one hundred gold coins, under the agreement that five gold coins (or whatever amount local custom dictates) be paid to him annually and perpetually from that property.

The question often arises whether annual returns should be counted as movable or immovable property. Most scholars categorize perpetual annuities and rents—or those owed for a long period, such as thirty years or more, commonly known as **hereditary rents** <note>original German: "Erbzinse"</note> or **leases** <note>original German: "Pächte"</note>—as immovable property. This is the common opinion held by many, including Molina, who notes that nearly everyone agrees on this point. On the other hand, temporary returns owed for only a short time are categorized as movable property.

Another safer distinction is based on the object of the debt: they are counted as immovable if they are owed from immovable property, provided their due date has not yet arrived <note>original German: "die noch nicht fällig seyn worden"</note>. In that case, they are treated similarly to "pending fruits" <note>crops still in the field that are considered part of the land</note>.

If the returns are owed from movable property (such as cash), or if the due date has already passed <note>original German: "die fällig und betagt seyn"</note>, they are counted as movable property. This is because returns that have already begun to be owed, and for which a legal action can be brought to collect them, are regarded as movable assets. Various legal experts, such as Gail and Mynsinger, show the practical use of this question in matters such as the prohibition against selling the immovable property of minors, or in legal injunctions that do not apply to movable property.

The term **Rent-bearing** <note>original German: "Zinsbar"</note> is used in various ways. Sometimes it refers to a property subject to a census, meaning a **hereditary rent** <note>original German: "Canonem Erbzins"</note> or some other eternal burden lying upon an estate. However, it almost always implies that money was given not as a gift, but as a loan for profit. **Rent** <note>original German: "Zins"</note> or interest is given because of the principal sum and is said to be added to it,

<column-break/>

suggesting that a loan contract has been made.

I will not add more on this subject, as it has been treated with extreme precision by Frederick Martin in his treatise on *censibus*, by Felicianus de Solis in the same, and by Roderic on annual and monthly returns. One may also consult Peter Fontanella’s work on prenuptial agreements and Costa on subsidiary remedies.

->ADDITION.<-

Treated most extensively by Mr. Speidel. Christopher von Hagen published a treatise on the use of interest. One is not obligated to pay any **average** <note>original German: "Haverey"; in maritime law, this refers to the shared contribution to losses or expenses incurred for the safety of a ship</note> from **bottomry money** <note>original German: "Bodmerey-Geld"; a loan taken out by a ship's captain using the ship's hull as collateral</note>. See the Statutes of Hamburg, Part 2. The concept of **average** is likewise mentioned in other sections. Bottomry was discussed above on page 132. Interest is brought in every month, which is the origin of the term "Calendar" <note>the Roman *Kalendarium* was an account book for debts and interest due on the first of the month</note>. Hence, lenders were called "monthly exactors," and Basilius called the months **the fathers of interest** <note>original Greek: "μῆνες τόκων πατέres"</note>. On the **redemption of hereditary and eternal rents** <note>original German: "Von Ablösung der Erb- und ewigen Zins"</note>, see Mr. Tabor's recent edition. A creditor who accepts interest for the future tacitly agrees not to demand the principal in the meantime. A creditor to whom higher interest was promised, but who accepts lower interest for several years, is seen as having tacitly agreed to the lower rate; this also holds true for City Creditors. Anyone who remains silent for twenty years or more is generally barred from seeking past interest. Whether the States of the Empire can permit a 6% interest rate in their provinces, thereby deviating from the Imperial Constitutions, is discussed at length by Everhardus Fabricius.

Whatever has been paid in interest above 5% must be deducted. Dr. Johann Hermann Stamm notes a case from October 14, 1623, involving Peter Walters against the Rector and Fathers of the Society of Jesus in Trier. The judgment was reformed so that the appellant was only obliged to pay them the sum after deducting the excess annual interest they had already received. A similar ruling was seen in the case of Nagel against Brones Kamp in 1629. Regarding Law 40 (*l. lecta*), it was said long ago: "Read by many, understood by few." (Fulgosius remarked that this Law 40 is so obscurely written that the author seemed to wish not to be understood).

<note>This page discusses a famous legal problem from the Digest of Justinian (specifically Digest 45.1.122) involving two parties, Lucius Titius and Publius Maevius, and how jurists like Papinian and Paul interpreted their contract.</note>

on the law regarding inofficious wills <note>Latin: "ff. de inoff. testam." refers to a section of the Digest</note>) is neglected by many for that reason. Freigius, in his tables on this part, page 240, boasts that he settled the matter with such a verse:

-> It was called "read," but not "understood": but from <-
-> this time, Reader, it will be understood by you. <-

But he spoke in vain, because even in his own resolution, many things were said incorrectly. This is how it should be understood: We must look at the Problem of the Jurist and the Resolution of the Case. The Problem is proposed in the Case: both in its circumstances and in itself. In the **Circumstances of Place**, where this case was proposed: namely in the auditorium of Aemilius Papinian <note>One of the most celebrated Roman jurists, serving as Praetorian Prefect</note>, the Jurisconsult; that is, it was debated in the consistory and council of the Praetorian Prefect by Paul and Ulpian, his assessors. <note>original: "l. ult. §. in bis C. de temp. appell." — referencing the Code of Justinian</note>

**The Documents:** For the case was proposed from a "caution," that is, an instrument or written security of a contract, or a note of hand <note>original: "syngrapha" and "chirographum"</note> regarding money received as a loan. **In itself**, where we must first look at the stipulation of the principal. Lucius Titius (the debtor) wrote that he had received (as a loan) from Publius Maevius (the creditor) fifteen <note>original: "quindecim" — he notes that "thousand" is implied because the symbol for 1,000, known as a 'temo', was omitted in the printed edition</note> thousand denarii as a loan, counted out to him from the house (from the private chest or box of the Creditor, not, as is otherwise done in the market, from the banker's table). And these 15,000 are to be given as "proven and correct" (meaning he would restore them in proven currency) on the coming Kalends <note>The first day of the month</note>. Cujacius understands this as the "next" Kalends; though "defined" times can be understood for "undefined" ones, so that we do not assume too narrow a timeframe. Publius Maevius (the creditor) stipulated, and Lucius Titius (the debtor) pledged by promising in return.

**Interest:** Penal interest was inserted into the stipulation for greater security of restitution, as follows: if on the day written above, the sum (15,000 denarii) is not given—that is, returned, paid, or satisfaction made in that name—to Publius Maevius (the creditor) or to whomever that matter shall belong (the heir or the good-faith possessor, or more generally, **to the faithful bearer of the letter** <note>original German: "getreuen Brieffs-Inhabern"</note>), then in addition to the principal, for however much later I shall pay (for however much later I pay after the Kalends) in the name of a penalty, for every 30 days—that is, for each month—one denarius per every hundred denarii is to be given <note>original German: "monatlich von 100. Realen einen, das Jahr 12. pro cento"</note>, which is 12 percent per year. Again, Publius Maevius (the creditor) stipulated, and Lucius Titius (the debtor) pledged.

Next, regarding the **subject pact made at the same time** <note>original: "in continenti"; a legal term for an agreement made immediately alongside the main contract</note>: when the promisor (debtor) noticed right then and complained about the brevity of the formal deadline: the meaning of the stipulation was changed and bound. It was agreed between the contracting parties that he (the debtor) ought to pay back to Publius Maevius the Creditor from the above-written sum (15,000 denarii) monthly;

<column-break/>

three hundred denarii (**the Creditor is willing to be satisfied with partial payment, as long as the debtor delivers back to him only 300 denarii monthly**). Thus, only after 50 months—which is 4 years and 2 months—would he receive the entire principal from the whole sum and the whole principal for him (the Creditor Maevius) or his heir.

<margin>Against: it was agreed.</margin>

<margin>Section: It was asked.</margin>
**The Question** arises here—since there had been no mention of interest in the pact—regarding the obligation of interest, because the number of months suitable for payment had passed (**the debtor had let the deadlines pass**). Does the pact also tacitly include interest or not? And is interest owed on the *entire* principal from the time of the stipulation, or rather, according to the added pact, only for the amount of time in which there was a cessation or delay made in payment?

The **Resolution** of the proposed case is governed by the accepted opinion of Paul, who proposed it. This is based on the reasoning that pacts made at the same time as a stipulation are believed to be included within it. That is, they are contained in the stipulation itself, so that it is not necessary for the Praetor to act, nor for the defendant to raise an "exception of the pact" <note>A legal defense</note>, since that exception can and ought to be supplied by the judge's duty to adjudicate fairly. This is true even if it is not on the part of the plaintiff <note>referencing various laws on interest and agreements</note>, which teach that interest can be sought from a pact added at the same time to a "strict law" contract <note>original: "stricti juris"; contracts where the letter of the law was followed strictly without equitable flexibility</note>. **The Decision itself:** Therefore, it should be held as if the stipulation had been conceived from the beginning according to the form of the pact. Thus, interest is only owed from the time of the cessation (the delay). For it is as if he had stipulated from the beginning for the money to be paid through individual months, and added interest if it were paid later.

**The case is applied:** specifically, what is owed or not owed? After the first month of the first installment is finished, interest begins to run; that is, more than 30 denarii cannot be demanded by law, and thus no more than 3 denarii in the name of interest. When two months are finished, no more than 60 denarii and 6 in interest. When three months are finished, no more than 90 denarii and 9 in interest.

Interest is **not** owed on the whole principal of 15,000 denarii, since the principal itself, by virtue of the pact, could not be sought earlier or all at once.

<margin>Section: the pact, however.</margin>
The contrary opinion having been rejected, the **thesis** is proposed: for some said: 1. That the pact which was added to the stipulation (at the same time) pertained only to the reduction of the principal, not to the interest which, in the prior part of the contract, had been simply brought into the stipulation (regarding the whole principal, not the individual months for which there was a delay).

2. And that the same pact was only useful for an **Exception**; that is, it would benefit the debtor if he used it by raising a legal defense. For it would not benefit him if he omitted the exception or failed to raise it.

<header>Letter Z. 1153</header>

<margin>Counter-arguments.</margin> And therefore (he concluded) that if the money is not paid in the appointed installments, interest is owed from the day of the formal promise <note>original: "stipulatio"; the verbal contract of Roman law</note>, just as if it had been specifically expressed in those terms, <margin>as at the end of this law; that is, so that if a portion of the principal is not paid in the appointed installments, interest is provided retroactively:</margin> not only from the day that the delay <note>term: "mora"; a legal default or failure to perform an obligation on time</note> occurred in paying the installment, but from the day that Publius Maevius stipulated the whole principal was to be paid, namely the next Calends <note>The first day of the month</note>.

The paragraph beginning **"But when"**: This is refuted by two reasons, the first of which is derived from the effect of the agreement. For since the delay of the principal's payment and its distribution into installments was introduced by the agreement, such that the whole amount should not be demanded at once but only in parts, it follows that the interest is also delayed, suspended, and distinguished by intervals of time. Thus, interest is not owed from the day of the initial promise, but from the day of the cessation and default, starting from each defined month, in proportion to each installment.

The second reason restricts the Opponent by the confession of what was demanded. Even if (as the opponent Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> demanded, as Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a leading 16th-century legal humanist</note> argues against Book 1, Section "if anyone simply" on Verbal Obligations; though Reusner argues this refers to Papinian or someone else) he brings the agreement only as an "exception" <note>term: "exceptio"; a defendant's plea that makes the plaintiff's claim unenforceable</note> (for it would also operate by the law itself, as the following paragraphs show), nevertheless the obligation for interest will not be triggered by the law itself. That is, interest on the whole principal cannot be demanded, but only for the times of default. For it is not understood that something can be demanded which, if it had been demanded, could have been invalidated by an "exception of the agreement" being opposed. <note>original: "l. 127. de V. O." — referencing Digest 45.1.127</note>

The paragraph beginning **"But even if"**: This singular case must be excepted if something else was specifically expressed: namely, that if the installments were not paid on their day, interest would be owed retroactively from the day of the promise, so that interest on the whole amount would be triggered. <note>reference to Reusner, number 79</note> For when they stipulate for the (total) quantity which is collected in the middle period (the time falling between the default and the formal promise): and when the Creditor has prohibited the day of payment and stipulates for himself interest for the whole time: if a delay in paying occurs, it is as if a condition has been met, and interest is owed on the whole sum (from the time of the delay). And this is treated as a penal condition.

The reasoning for the exception is taken from the similar provision of "fruits" <note>term: "fructus"; the produce or profit generated by an asset, like crops from a field or rent from a house</note>. For just as a provision can be made concerning fruits—if a promised field is not delivered by the appointed day—so that the fruits of that field are calculated retroactively from the day of the contract and restored; <note>referencing Digest laws 64 and 126 on Verbal Obligations</note> so too it can be expressly agreed that because the principal was not paid on its day, interest is inflicted from the day of the Contract.

This Exception is not blocked by Law 17 in the Digest on interest. The response is that in that case, smaller interest rates were paid. Therefore, because they were not paid on a certain day, higher rates cannot be inflicted from the day of the Contract, but they can be from the day of Default. 1. Certainly 2. larger rates are added to the smaller ones.

### 9. Anger, *Ira*.

An act is presumed to have been done in the heat of anger by the very fact that it is proven that an occasion for anger was given. See Farinacius *On Punishments*, number 48, and Menochius *On Arbitrary Judicial Cases*, case 361, number 6, where he identifies a twofold deliberate intent.

### ADDITION.

An act is not presumed to have been done out of anger unless it is proven, according to Vasquius, chapter 18, number 32 and following. For how long an act is presumed to be done in anger is discussed in numbers 37 and 39. Anger is presumed to last for up to thirty days, according to Klock, volume 3, counsel 184, number 11. Whether an oath sworn in anger is binding is discussed by Zahn in *On Lies*, book 3, chapter 8, numbers 109 and 110. An oath sworn through anger is validated by perseverance <note>meaning if the person continues to uphold it once calm</note>, Zahn *On Lies*, book 3, chapter 4, number 43.

The more noble a person is, the slower they are to anger, according to Limnaeus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 1, number 2. More on anger can be found in Rudinger, century 5, observation 89. Master Tabor, in *On Admonition*, page 197, provides a festive comparison from Aristotle in book 7 of the *Ethics*, chapter 7; likewise in book 2 of the *Great Ethics*, chapter 6, and book 6 of the *Eudemian Ethics*, chapter 6, where he compares one seized by the emotion of anger to hasty servants and dogs <note>referring to Aristotle's idea that anger "hears" reason but hears it incorrectly, like a servant who runs off before hearing the whole order</note>; this is treated extensively on page 197 and following. Whatever is done in the heat of anger is considered void, as treated most fully by Barbosa, book 9, chapter 85, axiom 1. It is more difficult to restrain anger than to perform miracles, *ibid*. Often, a change of will turns anger into mercy, axiom 2.

2. We should not dare to soothe the first burst of anger with speech; it is deaf and mindless. We must give it space; remedies are effective during remissions. We should not try to touch swollen eyes, for we might incite the stiffening force of the movements, nor other vices while they are boiling. See Master Rupert in *Letters of Mercury*, page 182. Seneca, *On Anger*, book 3, chapter 14. The letter of Xerxes was most foolish and worthy of laughter, which he wrote—kindled by I know not what anger—to Mount Athos. See Hermann Hugo, *On the First Origin of Writing*, page 112. A limit must be set for anger, and one should be provoked only as reason dictates, according to Struvius in *On Private Vengeance*, chapter 1, aphorism 2, number 2, page 5. Immoderate anger gives birth to insanity. See C. J. A. *On Testaments*, number 6; Perez in *On the Code regarding Sentences*, number penultimate.

On the medicine for the soul from the wounds of Christ: the gall <note>original: "Gallen"; bile, often associated with bitterness and anger in humorism</note> is useful against anger. One should consult Master Dilherr, who has served the whole Church excellently, in *The Course of Time and the World*, page 737. Do not touch the smoking nose of a bear <note>a proverb meaning do not provoke someone who is already furious</note>, Pierius Valerianus, book 11. The remedy against anger is delay, Master Rupert, dissertation 1 on Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 1. "Learn, but let anger fall from your nose, and the wrinkled sneer," Persius, *Satire 5*. Regarding the punishment of those who swear out of heat or anger: those in the heat of living anger are not masters of themselves,

<column-break/>

Statutes of the City of Worms, the year 1495. It is difficult to temper grief and anger, Law 36, section 8, *On Adultery*; and crimes committed from these emotions are punished more mildly, book 2, *On Abolition*. Clarus, book 5, final section, question 60, number 19, states that this should be denied outside of cases of just and still-boiling grief. Article 137, the passage "He who committed a homicide out of anger." Number 35, Law 3, section 3, regarding the Silanian Senate-Consult; Law 7, final section, regarding the Julian Law on Extortion; Law 5, Code on Injuries. ### 10. House of Correction, *Zuchthaus*, *Spinnhouse*. *Ergasterium*.

The Dutch, in a singular manner, use a certain public prison to restrain the extravagant, the wicked, and vagrant men, as well as to compel able-bodied and idle beggars to labor, and to tame unbridled lust. There they practice crafts (about which Bornitius writes in his treatise *On the Revenues of the Treasury*, book 2, chapter 1, and I in *On the Treasury*, chapter 3, section 13). This building (commonly called the *Zuchthaus*) is constructed for this purpose like a large and spacious palace, and is divided into various chambers and workshops suitable for mechanical trades. The idle, the extravagant, disobedient sons, and malicious people of that sort are shut inside so that they may earn their food by labor and the work of their hands, and finally, having returned to a better fruit and life, they may be released as improved, gentler, and patient of labor. See Pontanus in his *History of Amsterdam*, book 2, chapter 19. Truly, out of fear of this public censure, very few able-bodied beggars, idle people, spendthrifts, and such "useless burdens of the earth" <note>original Latin: "inutilia pondera terrae"</note> are found in the streets. Bornitius, cited chapter 2. Master Wolff, *Political College*, disputation *On Laws and their Sanction*, etc., thesis 23, number 9.

Where he adds: Such a house exists not only in Amsterdam, but in almost all Dutch cities, and indeed even in German ones, such as Bremen, Lübeck, Hamburg, etc. There is also in Amsterdam a spinning house (commonly called *het Spinnhuyß*), in which girls and women of honest citizens are confined—those who are devoted to gain and idleness, or who are suspected or caught because they have made a profit from their bodies, or wished to do so. Pontanus, cited book, chapter 11.

### ADDITION.

In Amsterdam, at the beginning of the month of April in the year 1595, a Workhouse <term>Ergasterium; a Greek-derived term for a workshop or penal workhouse</term> was established in which petty thieves, wretched beggars, and all those shut up are kept; some even bound in shackles, yet in such a way that they can freely attend to work and exercise their hands. For some are compelled either to rasp Brazil-wood <note>used to make red dye</note> into the finest sawdust and crush it with a grater, or to weave cotton cloths <term>bombasios; a type of fabric usually made of silk and wool or cotton</term>, and to do or work at other things. Add Zorer, part 2, question 18, numbers 4 and 93. Master Speidel, in *Notable Matters*, under this word.

### 11. To. [Latin: *Ad*]

The word "to" [Latin: *ad*] implies proximity, not internal inclusion. Therefore, if someone proves they have possessed a ditch "up to" another bank, it does not include the bank itself. Cardinal Tuschus, *Practical Conclusions*, letter D, conclusion 293, at the beginning, states this is because it is a deceptive and doubtful proof, which is interpreted against the one offering the proof. See Alexander, *Counsel* 54, number 8, book 5.

This word also implies a condition. For instance, if I promise you a hundred "at the discretion of an honest man," the obligation is considered to be under a condition—namely, if the judge or an honest man has made a declaration—and before that declaration, nothing is owed. See the same Alexander, *Counsel* 72, book 5. Likewise, if I promise to give you ten "at my will," it is understood as "if I wish," and thus is conditional. Alexander, in the cited place, number 14; but see also Tuschus in the same place.

->ADDITION.<-

The preposition *Ad* [To/At] increases the significance of a word, as seen in the words: to move toward [*admovere*], to apply [*adhibere*], to seize [*adprehendere*], and to notice [*animadvertere*]. Thus Bartolus and his followers in the law *Quid Iberus* 13, *On Urban Servitudes*, established this rule: *Ad* is placed to mean "near" [Latin: *juxta*]. See the *Vocabulary of Both Laws*, part *Ad*, page 16, and the final gloss in the cited place 13, on the phrase "at the wall" [*ad parietem*], which means "too close." See Master Tabor on *Admenatione*, thesis 16. On how *Ad* is joined to words, see Master Dilherr in the *Philological Apparatus*, page 181.

### 12. To confirm in honor, to advise, etc. To Endow. [German: *Zu Ehren bestättigen, berathen, &c.* Latin: *Dotare*]

How the words "confirmed in honor, advised, etc." are to be understood in a person's legal disposition is taught by Pfeil, *Counsel* 9, where he writes: "If a maiden’s goods have been given to someone to be used for an annual pension until she is provided for in honor and dowered <note>The German phrase 'zu Ehren berathen und ausgesteuret' refers to the formal provision of a dowry and the social recognition of a woman's marriage</note>, and that same maiden, her friends, and her guardian have betrothed her to an honorable fellow in holy matrimony—either purely or *de praesenti* <note>meaning a binding legal marriage contract made in the present moment</note>—and the marriage is otherwise unchallenged, then the person to whom the goods were given under the aforementioned condition is bound to surrender and hand them over. He may not protect himself or delay in court by arguing that the wedding ceremony with the church procession and other bridal pomp has not yet taken place." When a legal disposition in a contract refers to the "time of the marriage," it is sufficient to fulfill or satisfy the condition of marriage that the marriage vows have actually proceeded—that is, that the girl is betrothed "by words of the present," as they say. There is no need for carnal union, a feast, or other celebrated ceremonies to occur, according to the teachings of Pfeil, which holds even more weight when it concerns the favor of the girl <note>The law often favored the interests of the bride to ensure her financial security</note>.

->ADDITION.<-

See Wehner, letter Z, under this word.

### 13. Property brought in. Paraphernalia. [German: *Zugebracht Gut*. Latin: *Paraphernalia*]

Paraphernalia <note>from the Greek 'para' (beside) and 'pherne' (dowry); this refers to property that a wife owns in her own right, separate from the dowry managed by her husband</note> cannot be alienated <note>The original text is 'al' followed by the note 'likely alienari'</note> by the husband, as Cothmann teaches at length in his *Response* 94, number 4 and following.

->ADDITION.<-

A husband, as a connected person, may appeal in a case concerning paraphernalia without a specific mandate from his wife. Eberhard Fabricius, book 1, observation 133, section 1. A wife does not have the privilege of priority for the value of her former paraphernalia. Eberhard Fabricius in *Gail Enucleated*, book 2, observation 92. Regarding paraphernalia property, see Matthias Wesenbeck, *Counsel* 63, and Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, book 1, *Counsel* 40. Whether the fruits <note>profits or yields</note> of paraphernalia fall to the husband's profit so that he cannot be forced to return them, see *Thesaurus of Decisions of Piedmont*, 187. Does a statute concerning "fruits" include the profits of dotal property? See Surdus, *Decision* 192. Paraphernalia property belongs to the wife, and the husband regularly has nothing to do with it. Zorer, part 2, question 7, numbers 506, 508, etc., where he lists the limitations. The husband's own property is tacitly pledged to cover the wife's paraphernalia property. Zorer, part 1, question 1, number 256 and number 308. But whether this tacit pledge is granted with a privilege of priority, and what if an express mortgage was added, see the same, numbers 309, 259, and following.

### 14. Inflow, Increase. Alluvion. [German: *Zufluß, Zuwachs*. Latin: *Alluvio*]

We call this "alluvion," concerning which see Coppola in the *Treatise on Rural Predial Servitudes*, chapter 35. Alluvion is defined as a latent or hidden increase—specifically when a public river gradually wears away one person's land and adds it to another's land so secretly that it cannot be detected by the human eye exactly how much or at what moment it was added. Therefore, if something is added to my field or land not secretly and gradually, but openly and clearly by a sudden force or the violence of a river, it does not become mine, but remains the property of the previous owner. See Schneidewin on the paragraph "furthermore" in the *Institutes on Acquiring Ownership of Things*. Master Gryphiander writes extensively on this in *On Islands*.

->ADDITION.<-

Master Bicc. in *Golden Truths*, page 191, section 3, thesis 23. Silting up [German: *Anschütt*], called *proschysis* <note>original Greek: πρόσχυσις - a pouring upon or inundation</note> and *proschosis* <note>original Greek: πρόσχωσις - an accumulation of earth or silting</note> by the Greeks. Whether a servitude <note>a legal right to use another's land</note> is increased when the land itself is increased by alluvion. Carpzov, book 1, title 5, response 45, number 9 and following; Agricola, *On Appurtenances*, chapter 7, thesis 3, question 4. The right of alluvion has no place in lakes and ponds; for although they may rise and fall, they nonetheless retain their own boundaries. Bocer, *Disputation* 5, class 4, thesis 7; compare with law 24, section 3, *On Water and Keeping Out Rain Water*. Master Gamb. writes extensively in *On Alluvions*, thesis 43. In public and larger lakes, the right of alluvion does take place: if rivers...

The term "accrual" <note>Latin: "accrescendi"</note> is derived from alluvion, which is why the right of accrual is compared with alluvion in law 33 at the end, Digest *On Usufruct*. It is used generally for any kind of addition. Thus Justinian says a third part of the world "accrued" to him in law 2, penultimate section, Code *On the Authority of the Digest*; and the legal experts in law 30, section 1, and law 56, *On the Acquisition of Ownership*, write that something "accrues" to our estate little by little. Hence Sallust, addressing Cicero, says: "Give an account of how much patrimony you have acquired, and what has accrued to you from lawsuits." More specifically, it refers to that addition where a portion of an inheritance, legacy, or trust that has failed falls to and is joined with a co-heir or co-legatee; see the Digest *On the Accrual of Usufruct* and the Code *On Removing Escheats*. This is treated most extensively by Lord Doctor Ludwig in *On Last Wills*, first part, chapter 5, throughout. In Jena, in the year 1639, a small book was published entitled: *Golden Treatises on the Right of Accrual by Four Most Noble Jurists* in duodecimo. On who acquires what is added to estates by alluvion, see Knipschild, *On Trusts*, chapter 12, number 97, where he teaches that what is added by alluvion to lands subject to a trust belongs to the beneficiary of the trust. Regarding alluvion, encircling by water <note>original: "circumluvione"</note>, and flooding, see Pacius in his *Analysis of the Code*, the entire title on Alluvions and Marshes. ### 15. *Appurtenances.* <note>original German: "Zugehörung"; Latin: "Pertinentiæ"</note>

Under the name of appurtenances are included those things which are designated by statute, custom, or law to be attached to something else. See Innocent on the chapter *Cum ad fedem*, number 2; Antonio de Butrio, number 23; Panormitanus, number 11, *On the Restitution of Spoils*; Socinus the Elder, *Counsel* 47, number 4, volume 1; Baldus, *Counsel* 420, number 6, volume 1; Decius, *Counsel* 516, number 23; and Hieronymus de Monte, *On Regulating Boundaries*, chapter 80, number 7.

Regarding what specifically comes under the name of appurtenances, see especially Rosacorba in *Forensic Practice*, chapter 104; Lord Hering in the treatise *On Mills*, question 35; Jacob Thomingius, *Counsel* 20, number 73 and following, volume 1; Aymon Cravetta, *Counsel* 345 and *Counsel* 480; the *Acts of Sayn against Trier*, folio 50; Friedrich Mindanus, *On Withdrawing Processes*, book 3, chapter 20; and Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 12, conclusion 15.

Those words, *with all appurtenances and rights* <note>original: "mit allen Zugehörungen und Gerechtigkeiten"</note>, are universal and exclude nothing, according to the laws in the Digest *On Credited Things* and *On Legacies*. That this generality of words can be extended to improper cases is taught by the Gloss on the Code *On Four-Year Prescription*. This is especially true in the arrangement of names, and thus of contracts, as noted by Jason on the Digest *On the Notification of New Work* and Baldus on the Code *Without Census or Relics*, and even to unusual cases as argued in the Digest *On Pacts* and the Code *On Transactions*.

Under the word "appurtenances," in grants of Castles and villages, the territory also comes, and consequently, even high and low justice <note>original: "merum, mixtumque Imperium"</note> and Jurisdiction, as asserted by Parisius, *Counsel* numbers 16 and 20, volume 1; Fichard, *German Counsels* 20, number 10; likewise a bombardment engine <note>original: "bombarda"</note>, etc. See Barbosa on the Digest *On the Dissolution of Marriage*.

When a castle is sold or granted with appurtenances, the word "appurtenances" is not understood to include the fields <note>private farmlands</note>, but only the Jurisdiction and similar rights which adhere to the Castle, according to Curtius Junior, *Counsel* 158, number 26, and Cravetta, *Counsel* 54, number 9, and *Counsel* 234, number 2.

Thus also he who is invested with a Castle and its territory indeed has Jurisdiction over all the estates situated within the enfeoffed territory, yet he does not have the ownership or dominion of the fields themselves, as noted by Curtius Junior, *Counsel* 41, number 9, and Roland à Valle, *Counsel* 46, number 29.

When a house is bequeathed, *and everything that is within it*, legal rights and actions <note>such as debts or lawsuits</note> are not included, as Lord Wilhelm Anton teaches in his *Corollaries to the Treatise on Letters of Moratorium*, folio 19.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding Appurtenances see Berlich, *Decisions* 2, 191.
*A Mass vestment together with all its appurtenances*, Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 6, chapter 2, page 61.

16. Clause: **To have, to hold, to sell, to pledge, to exchange, to hand over, to pawn, and to do and leave as one pleases.** <note>German: "Zu haben, zu halten..."</note> Clause: To have, to hold, to pledge, to exchange, to hypothecate, and to do as one likes, etc. <note>Latin: "Ad habendum..."</note>

This clause, inserted into letters of investiture <note>The formal documents granting a fief to a vassal</note>, is understood and explained differently by various authorities. For there are those who say that the Lord, through this clause, gives power to the Vassal so that he may freely hand over the fief to outsiders or whomever he wishes, even without the Lord being asked or informed.

But so that the force and energy of this clause may be better understood and interpreted, the opinions of the Doctors of Law regarding it must be cited.

First, there are those who maintain that this clause must be understood according to the nature of the contract to which such an agreement is attached. However, the nature of a fief is such that it cannot be alienated <note>Transferred to another owner</note> without the consent of the Lord.

But if this interpretation were admitted, there would be no force at all to this clause, and nothing more would seem to be granted to the Vassal. Therefore, that opinion is rightly rejected, as it is against the common Rule of Law, which dictates that words and such agreements placed in contracts should not be idle, but should always accomplish something.

Therefore, other Doctors interpret this clause thus, saying that the Vassal, by virtue of that clause, can not only alienate the fief without the consent of the Lord, but even transfer the direct ownership <term>Directum Dominium: The ultimate ownership held by the lord, as opposed to the 'useful' ownership (dominium utile) enjoyed by the tenant</term> to another, so that those goods are no longer fiefs, but are considered under the same law as other things which one holds by full right, and for which one recognizes no other superior. And so the Feudalists Belviso, Isernia, Alvarottus, and Laudensis seem to think.

But since through this interpretation feudal goods would completely lose their nature and property, and this would undoubtedly be against the will of the direct Lord; a middle way, more consistent and conforming to equity, is provided by some Doctors. They follow the example of the Emperor Justinian, who advised that in such a conflict of opinions, a middle path should be chosen. According to their opinion, that clause has the effect that the Vassal may, because of it, alienate his feudal goods even without asking the Lord, and dispose of the fief freely. Socinus the Elder, consultation 252, question 2, book 2.
