### 18. **Before or after**. **Before & after**. <note>original German: "Zuvor oder hernach"</note>

When witnesses testify using the words "before" or "after" (*zuvor oder hernach*)—for instance, that something happened before or after a wedding, or before or after a war—if their statements are contradictory (such as when some say a thing happened before and others say it happened after), they are to be reconciled in this way: those who said "before" should be understood as meaning "before the end," such as before the wedding or war was finished. Those who said "after" should be understood as meaning after the act had begun or the contract had been entered, while it was still ongoing and not yet completed. See Laurentius Tenninus in the *Treatise on Clauses*, Clause 267, number 1.

<column-break/>

The nature of the word "prior" or "first" is such that when it is expressed in law, it establishes an order; if this order is reversed, the act cannot be valid. Abbas in the chapter "By letters," paragraph "it is noted," *On Restitution of Spoils*, following the text in Law 2, paragraph "first," *On Vulgar and Pupillary Substitution*. Hering, *On Sureties*, chapter 10, number 469. See Lord Wilhelm Anton in the *Treatise on Five-Year Periods*, chapter 29, number 20.

### ADDITION.

On what the word "before" (*ante*) imports, see Marius Antoninus, book 1, reference 44, numbers 3, 12, and 14.

### 19. **Right of Consultation**. **Consultation**. <note>original German: "Zugrecht"</note>

If one city, by custom, is accustomed to seek consultation <term>Consultatio: A legal procedure where a lower court seeks the opinion of a higher or more established court on a difficult case</term> from another city, this is not strictly an "appeal" in the way a lower court appeals to a superior. Rather, it is a type of extension of jurisdiction, and it is a matter of will, not necessity. See Dauth, *On Testaments*, page 13. Lehmann, pages 317 and 652. Lord Adam Keller, *On Juridical-Political Office*, 2, chapter 27, page 588. For example: from Überlingen to Rotweil, from Stockach to Zell, from Ach to Mengen, from Menzgen to Freiburg in Breisgau. Also see my own work *On Appeals*, page 109, and likewise *Chamber Doubts*, letter A, page 37. Volume 1, *Symphorema*, chapter 7.

However, it is proper that if the place of consultation is bypassed and the case is brought directly to the Imperial Chamber Court, the parties should at least have first requested the consultation from those places that usually admit them, provided both parties appear before them together. But if the case records are not produced voluntarily, then the places of consultation themselves cannot grant "Compulsories" <note>Orders to compel the production of documents</note>, because an equal has no authority over an equal <note>original: "par in parem non habet imperium"</note>. Instead, one must go to the Imperial Chamber Court on the grounds of justice being denied or obstructed. Richvvin, page 280.

### ADDITION.

Wehner, letter Z, under this word.

### 20. **Step by Step / Stroke for Stroke**. **Successively**. <note>original German: "Zug um Zug"</note>

It sometimes happens that two people accuse each other of homicide, theft, robbery, banditry, or some similar social crime. To uncover the truth of the imputed crime, when other legal and sufficient evidence is lacking, they may mutually offer to undergo torture, "to suffer one pull after the other" <note>original German: "einen Zug um den andern zu leiden"</note>. A doubt is not without reason raised for the judges of the case: whether this agreement and spontaneous offering of theirs is legally valid, and thus whether it should be carried out? Although there are arguments provided by Eberhard Speckhan (century 3, question 17, number 2) that might move judges to accept this offer and execute the agreement, the contrary opinion is more true and is followed in practical use, judgment, and sentencing by judges...

### 21. Guilds, Corporations. Craft. See above under the word: Trade.

It is beyond doubt that merchants, tanners, and other craftsmen may have their own Colleges (commonly called *Zunfften* <note>German: Zünfte</note>, also in certain places called *Innung* or *Gilden* <note>German: Innungen, Gilden</note>), provided that this is granted to them by law, by custom, or by a special Privilege of the Prince: see my work, *On the Law of Colleges.* Otherwise, all such associations are disapproved. Even if there were one or two thousand people, they could not, by gathering together on their own without such permission, create an approved Guild or elect a Judge. Guilds are considered approved and lawful when their possession or status is proven by their letters of foundation and privileges granted by the Magistrate; or if they customarily appoint a Syndic <note>A legal representative or business manager</note>, meet in a certain place, conduct guild-related business, and possess a common chest—known as a *gemeine Laden*—and a Seal. However, all these signs are not required simultaneously or jointly; one or two may suffice, as demonstrated by Mr. Berlich in *Decision 150*, which you may consult.

For how crafts should be practiced, see Bornitius, *On Sufficient Matters, book 2, chapter 5.*

However, Guilds or "Tribes" <note>original: "Tribus"</note> are another matter when they are used to establish a democratic form of government. After the Smalkaldic War <note>A conflict (1546–1547) between the forces of Emperor Charles V and the Lutheran Schmalkaldic League</note>, Emperor Charles V abolished them in most cities so they would not be so easily incited to unrest. See my work *On Democracy, page 65.* Likewise, Charles V abolished the guilds in Augsburg, though they had not existed in that form before; see the *Augsburg Calendar Acts, A. 3. b.*

In the Duchy of Württemberg, the *Handwercker Zünfften* <note>Craft Guilds</note> are regarded in a twofold manner.

In the *Council of Worms* <note>original: "Wurmsischen Rathung"</note> at letter S. 2. b., the following guilds are recounted: **Upper Cutlers, Weavers, Shield-makers, Grocers, Tailors, Bakers, Coopers, Farmers, Smiths, Shoemakers, Tanners, Wine-lifters, Fishermen, Sack-carriers, Vinedressers, Carpenters, and Furriers**, etc. All of these collectively were required to attach their guild seals to the decision reached there, alongside the Bishop, the Chapter, the Burgomaster, and the Court.

On the antiquity of Colleges and Confraternities, see Guyon, *Diverse Lessons, volume 1, page 241.*

*Should someone be tolerated in the guilds if they have been insulted?* Laurentius Kirchov treats this question based on the facts in *volume 5 of Various Counsels, counsel 9.*

->ADDITION.<-

*Innungsbrieff* <note>A guild charter or letter of incorporation</note>, that is, Concessions and

<column-break/>

Confirmations from Princes, are considered to be granted privately and prohibitively with respect to others. Berlich, *part 1, decision 26, number 7.* This *Innungsbrieff* granted the Bridle-makers’ guild the peculiar right to manufacture the specific works that were under dispute. On the *Kauffmanns-Innung* <note>Merchant Guild</note>, see Oldekop, *On Oaths in Ancient Spirits, page 78.*

*Consules artium* <note>Guild masters</note>, or *Zunfftmeister*, cannot issue rulings except on causes pertaining to their own office. See Ummius in *Process, page 423.* On this entire subject, see Mr. Speidel in *Notables, under this word*; Rodinger, *century 5, observation 96.* Regarding *Zunfftbücher* <note>Guild books/registers</note>, see Besold, *Politics, book 1, chapter 12, number 28, last verse*; they are equated with public legal instruments, *ibid.*

On *Handwercks-Zunfften* <note>Craft Guilds</note>, see above under the word *Monopoly*, and the word *Schwertag* <note>A "Sword Day," often referring to a guild's assembly or a day of judicial combat/public display</note>, and add Limnäus in *Public Law, book 4, chapter 8, number 308*; and extensively Mr. Speidel in the *Mirror of Notables, page 1389 and following.* The phrase *ein beschlossen Amt* <note>a closed office</note> refers to a Guild consisting of specific persons or at least those who have been formally admitted. Mevius in *Lübeck Law, book 4, title 13, article 3, numbers 11, 12, 13.* On Guilds, Companies, Assemblies, and Banns, see the Author of the *Wehnerian Supplement, page 16.*

### 23. Compulsory Mills. Molendina bannaria.

On *Molendinis bannariis* <note>Ban-mills; mills where subjects were legally forced to grind their grain</note>, see entirely Mr. Johann Hering, *Treatise on Mills, question 11, throughout.*

Even if the subjects of a Lord have gone to the Lord’s mill for a very long time, they cannot be compelled to grind there in the future because of this, according to the teachings of Covarruvias in *the chapter "Possessor" on the Rules of Law in the Sext, part 2, re-reading section 4*; Franciscus Balduinus, *On Prescription, part 4, question 5*; and Borcholt, *in the single chapter, "Which things are Regalian."*

For going to a mill is a matter of "mere faculty" <note>original: "merae facultatis"; a legal term meaning a discretionary right or a freedom to act that does not create a binding obligation through mere repetition</note>; and those things which consist of mere faculty are not taken away by prescription <note>The acquisition of a right or obligation through long-term continuous use</note>. See the law *viam publicam* in the Digest *On Public Roads*. Coras, *Miscellany, book 6, chapter 21, number 2 and following.* Nor is a right ever acquired from those things which are done out of favor or gratuitously. See the argument in the law *qui jure familiaritatis* in the Digest *On Acquiring Possession.* To this pertains the rule that he who has received the nobles of a certain family as guests for a very long time is not obligated to continue doing so, nor are his heirs...

**24. *Shared lordship among two or three lords, collective lordship. Common jurisdiction in the same place.*** <note>original: "Zwey- oder dreyherrige Herrschaft, gesamte Herrschaft. Communis jurisdictio in eodem loco."</note>

It is nothing new for a single province to be burdened by the rule of several lords—one claiming the supreme Sovereignty, another simple Jurisdiction, another the **right of the sword** <note>original: "jus gladii"; the power to impose the death penalty</note>, and another claiming other rights. See Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 6, conclusion 85, number 10. It is not infrequent to find provinces shared by two, three, or four lords, where one holds the **territorial princely authority** <note>German: "die Landfürstliche Obrigkeit"</note>, another the **sovereignty of the land** <note>German: "die Lands-Hoheit"</note>, a third the **hunting rights** <note>German: "die Wildbahn"</note>, a fourth the **princely authority** <note>German: "die Fürstliche Obrigkeit"</note>, a fifth the **high district and capital court** <note>German: "die hohe Craiß und Cent"</note>, and a sixth the **advocacy and hereditary court** <note>German: "die Vogtey und Erb-Gericht"</note>. See Caspar Ziegler in *On Landed Estates*, conclusion 1, number 75 and following; Meichlner, volume 2, book 2, decision 4, numbers 26 and 27, and book 3, decision 33 and following; Sixtin, *On Regalities*, chapter 4, number 82. See especially Caspar Leipold, *On Concurrent Jurisdiction*, question 12; and my own works *On Monarchy*, leaf 12, and *On the Mixed State*, at the final leaf.

When two lords are equal in jurisdiction and sovereignty and possess a territory without it being physically divided <note>original: "pro indiviso"</note>, one cannot exercise jurisdiction by himself or through another without the other’s consent, even if the jurisdiction belongs to each of them in its entirety. This is because **an equal has no authority over an equal** <note>original: "par in parem non habet Imperium"</note>. See the Law *for a Magistrate* regarding the reception of arbiters, and the chapter *it became known* regarding elections. However, they must agree regarding the use and exercise of that jurisdiction. Therefore, if they refuse or are unwilling to do so, they are compelled to come to an agreement by the provision and mandate of a superior authority. See Peguera, decision 10, at the beginning.

The form of agreement regarding the use and exercise of this shared jurisdiction is noted by writers as being primarily of two types. The first is that the said lords use the jurisdiction by alternating turns, dividing the use of the jurisdiction by time periods. So says Angelo on the Law

Befold, Volume I.

<column-break/>

2, section *from these*, number 3, in the *Digest* regarding verbal obligations. But Peguera adds at number 4: "With all due respect to such highly learned men, this form of dividing the use of jurisdiction by time has never pleased me, because of the many inconveniences that could arise and follow from it."

The **first inconvenience** is that if one lord’s time expires, and the other cannot recover the case files for civil or criminal causes that were not dispatched or finished, justice will be delayed, and perhaps could not be dispatched within the time limits established by law.

The **second inconvenience** arises from **precipitated justice**, which the officials of one lord will shorten and accelerate during their own time so that the officials of the other lord perceive no benefit or profit from those cases.

The **third inconvenience** is that if one lord has sometimes proceeded well and legally, the other may proceed poorly or with favoritism. Perhaps out of envy or enmity, he might acquit someone who should be condemned, or condemn someone who should be acquitted; he might finish the "good" cases (profitable ones) but leave the small, brief, or ruinous cases for the next lord. See Law 1, section *it must be known*, in the *Digest* regarding the convening of magistrates.

The **second form** of reaching an agreement regarding the use and exercise of said jurisdiction is that all the lords who possess the territory as a whole and without division should constitute and elect one **common judge**: namely, one **Bailiff**, one **Assessor**, and one **Scribe**, and other ministers who, in the name of the lords, constitute only one Court in which justice is administered to the subjects. But see Peguera, in the cited decision 10, number 6 and following.

It is not absurd in secular matters for two heads to be established for one territorial body. See Pacian, *On Probations*, chapter 36, book 2, number 90 and following. And just as a castle or territory can be divided, so too the jurisdiction attached to it is divided in the same way. See the same Pacian, cited chapter 36, number 79.

The sharing of jurisdiction breeds the **neglect of justice**, according to Law 2, at the verse *natural*, in the Code on when and for whom a fourth part, book 10. Conversely, by the division of a castle and territory and its attached jurisdiction, the discords of the lords are removed. See Pacian, cited chapter 36, number 92. Indeed, if two or more lords disagree over the exercise of jurisdiction, their subjects—and especially their superior—can compel them to reach an agreement. See Gail, *On Pledges*, chapter 20, number 7; Pacian, cited place, number 58 and following, where he recounts several (specifically seven) ways by which these mutually disagreeing lords can most easily be brought back to concord.

Where jurisdiction is common, or many people in one place are involved in the exercise of jurisdiction, what can or should be done regarding **religion**? This is treated in the *Composition of Peace*, earlier edition, question 38, leaf 368, as well as question 65.

Furthermore, it is well known by what remedies a vassal who does not administer justice may be [recalled] to his duty...

...to perform service, according to both feudal law (on which see Rosenthal, chapter 12, conclusion 4, numbers 53 and 57; and chapter 18, conclusion 33, number 68 and following; and Schrader on fiefs, part 10, section 9, number 40) as well as Common Law (on which see Gail, book 1, observation 18; and Peter Friedrich Mindanus, book 2, chapter 53, number 19 and following), they can be compelled.

In villages where several members of the nobility reside and the jurisdiction is held in common, nevertheless, to avoid confusion and quarrels, all high and low jurisdiction—as well as everything attached to it—is left entirely to each possessor within their own castle and its immediate perimeter. ### 25. Compulsory Jurisdiction and Ban. Territory, District.
<note>The German "Zwing und Bann" refers to the right of a lord to command, forbid, and hold a monopoly on certain services within a specific area.</note>

A city can exist without a territory (Law 2 *Regarding the City* in the preface and in Law 239, section *The City*, and the Law *Assets of the City* with the following law in the *Digest* on the Significance of Words; Meichsner, *Chamber Decisions*, 3, number 17, volume 2, book 2). Nevertheless, every city, even outside its walls, usually has a community of fields and a territory—that is, its own boundary, agricultural district, municipal zone, and jurisdictional area <note>original: "Etter, Oesch, Weichbild, Zwing und Bann"</note>, as interpreted by Gylman, *Symphorema*, volume 1, part 2, title 2, regarding the counter-suit in the case of Erfurt against Mainz, number 156 and following; and Rosenthal on fiefs, chapter 5, conclusion 6, number 3—and it possesses this by regular rule. Law 8 of the *Digest* on the Significance of Words.

Thus, a territory is said to be among the appurtenances and accessories of a city (Innocent in the chapter *When at the seat*, number 7, regarding the restoration of seized property; Oldradus, counsel 176 at the end; Boërius, question 227, number 7). For the city is within the territory, and the territory is within the city (Adrian Gylman, *Judged Matters*, book 2, decision 35, number 19).

Furthermore, estates adjacent to a city, or situated and existing within its borders, are presumed to be under the jurisdiction of the city (Menochius, *On Presumptions*, 3, preface 100, number 1). And so, in this respect, under the name of "City," there also come the villages, suburbs, and districts (Gylman, book 2, decision 12, number 21).

->ADDITION.<-

Whether the words "with *Zwing, Bann*, and all appurtenances" contain every kind of jurisdiction is a grave and intricate question. Bailiwick jurisdiction, a low-court compulsion in civil matters, and the

<column-break/>

punishment of minor crimes—which, in view of "all-encompassing" jurisdiction, seem to be included in its scope—since when one says "all," one excludes nothing (Law 68 of the *Digest* on Legacies; Law 13 of the *Code* on Mandates). This phrasing, according to Natta (counsel 154, number 3), is of such strength that it even removes that which was disposed by law; indeed, it embraces those things which otherwise would not seem to be included, as Romanus testifies (counsel 271), who says that universal words included in a specific enumeration of "Regalia" <note>The sovereign rights or prerogatives of a ruler</note> include even those Regalia not specifically expressed (via Law the last, section 3 of the *Digest* on triticum and wine legacies; Law 32 of the *Digest* on the Trebellian Decree of the Senate; and Borcholten on Regalia, chapter 1, numbers 11 and 12). 

But notwithstanding these points, we say with Klock (counsel 24, *Contributions*, question 2, pages 39 and 50, column 2) that even if one has committed to "all jurisdiction," the "Pure and Mixed Power" <note>original: "merum & mixtum Imperium"; this refers to high justice (capital punishment) and low justice (civil/minor criminal matters)</note> is still not necessarily always contained therein. This is because that universality ("all") is not predicated on several things differing in kind, but on several things differing in number, as noted by Baldus... which Mynsinger reports in decision 13, response 3, number 87, part 1. See Hieronymus Agricola on *Penalties*, chapter 4, thesis 5, question 19; add Mr. Speidel in his *Notables* under the letter Z, number 62; and Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 49, number 2.

### 26. Discord. Controversy.
<note>original: "Zwietracht. Discordia."</note>

The word "Discord" is quite general, equivalent to the word "controversy," and encompassing absolutely every controversy moved in any way, whether inside or outside of court, regarding law or fact, without any distinction made as to whether the process in that controversy reached the joining of the issue <note>original: "litis contestationem"; the formal start of a trial</note> or even further, or whether it did not. (Law *Not Only*, section *If the status*, of the *Digest* on Procurators; Law *Lucius*, section *Three heirs*, and there the gloss on the word "moved"; and Bartolus on the *Digest* regarding the Trebellian Decree; Law 1 of the *Code* on Testaments; Law *If a controversy* of the *Code* on Evictions). See the Court Records of the City of Braunschweig regarding the Oath of Allegiance, part 2, number 71, page 62.

->ADDITION.<-

Is it expedient for a Kingdom or Republic that discords be nourished among the nobles of the realm or the senators? Piccart in his commentary on Aristotle’s *Politics*, pages 699 and 670; also in *Political Observations*, decade 7, chapter 4; Arnisaeus in *Politics*, book 2, chapter 4; Peter Gregory, book 24 on the Republic, chapter 9, section 3; Mr. Felwinger on *Factions*, dissertation 1, question 1.

"But should any clarification or discord arise." Limnäus in *Public Law*, book 8, chapter 1, page 146. See above under the words "Dispute" <note>original: "Mißle"</note> and "to trouble" <note>original: "behelligen"</note>.

### 29. Fence. 
<note>Latin: "Sepimentum."</note>

->ADDITION.<-
To protect one's possession, it is permissible to break and destroy a fence (Klock, volume 3, counsel 149, number 74, and those cited there). A Lord is permitted to secure fields or meadows with a fence, even if it hinders those who hold hunting rights there (Klock, volume 1, counsel 31, numbers 26, 27, 28). See **Garden Rights**. Sometimes a "Garden Right" <term>Garten-Recht: the legal right to enclose a piece of land</term> is granted by a community to a piece of field in exchange for a sum of money or a trade, allowing that piece to be fenced in. When a surface or something fixed to the soil—such as a fence or something similar—is destroyed, but nothing is taken from the ruins, it has been doubted whether the laws regarding seizing a pledge apply (Schwanmann, observation 90, number 1 and following). Regarding picket fences, which are transparent; also regarding wattle fences <term>Ederzaun: a fence made of woven branches or split wood</term> with boards or planks, see the *Frankfurt Reformation*, part 9, title 4, paragraphs 6 and 7. When bees fly over a fence, they belong to whoever catches them (Berlich, 5, conclusion 50, number 17). A plank fence as thick as a man, woven with thorns, is mentioned by Zeiller in his *Travels through Hungary*, page 360. How to proceed against those who damage the fences of uninhabited estates is discussed by Zorer, part 1, question 12, number 101 and following. A case of mixed or low jurisdiction <term>jurisdiction over minor offenses</term> involves small excesses, such as over-fencing without disturbing the boundary stones; see Dr. Oelhafen in his counsels. Regarding field fences, see above under the word **Village**, addition to paragraph 8. Because of two gaps in a meadow fence, there was a great dispute in L. in the year 1566 as to whether the community's cattle were driven in and out there at the proper times, and likewise whether hay and after-grass <term>Grummet: the second harvest of hay</term> were hauled out. In such cases, one must look to local custom. See the *Treaty of Pomerania* entered into with Wallenstein and Arnheim, article 23, stating that he shall not tear down any fences or buildings (Dr. Tabor, *On Quarters*, page 129, preamble). Regarding the inspection of defective fences, or "hedge-viewing" <term>Hagschau: a traditional community inspection of boundary fences</term>, see the *Acts of Lindau*, volume 10, folio 813. "To pacify" <note>German: "Befrieden"</note> or "to give peace" is the same as to fence in (folio 370, preamble).

<column-break/>

Rittershusius discusses the legal spacing of fences and stone walls in his work on the *Laws of the Twelve Tables*, class 3, part 2, chapter 10, throughout. The Teutonic Order is privileged to protect its villages with ditches, fences, planks, and oriels <note>original: "Dillen und Erckern"</note>, according to the *Acts of the Teutonic Knights*. No one in the community shall break open, tear apart, or carry away another’s fence or railings, whether in the village or the field; otherwise, for every pointed or blunt fence stake, or for every railing that he brings home or has torn out, he must pay a fine of 4 pounds to the community and, in addition, compensate his neighbor for the damage (*Megeld’s Community Ordinance*). P. von L. enclosed a sizeable piece of field from his communal farm at R. with fences for a garden and a pond, separating himself from the community’s shared herding rights, and used those fields on the heights for his own cattle’s pasture. However, when the community objected to this innovation, he reached a settlement and gave 22 guilders plus 6 guilders for the "earnest money" <term>Leihkauff: a fee paid to seal a contract</term> to the community as compensation. He also surrendered his right to use their remaining common pastures and meadows, agreeing not to frequent them henceforth. February 14, 1630.

In snails, a tooth is found hidden near the tail, which not even every cook easily notices; instead of being able to say anything about it, she might well laugh at the idea. The use of substitute teeth is not new, but is of the greatest antiquity. Horace (Book 1, Satire 8) writes:

Where Lambinus expressly notes that Canidia’s teeth were not her own, but belonged to another and were surgically installed. Chabotius concludes they were "adopted" rather than naturally attached, due to the ease with which they fell out. Martial also writes (Book 1, Epigram 73):

<note>Latin: "Armamentarium." German: "Zeughaus."</note>

There is a decree of Charlemagne regarding *Brunnae*, stating that no one should presume to sell them outside our kingdom.

35. **Gout.** <note>original: "Zipperle," a diminutive of Zipperlein, an old German term for gout</note>. Known in Latin as *Podagra*.

->ADDITIO.<-

See the recent writing of *Dr. Gailfusius* titled **Defiance to Gout** <note>original: "Trutz den Podagram"</note>. A mild case of gout does not provide an excuse from personal duties, but it is otherwise if the condition is severe. Regarding whether one suffering from gout has an excuse only during the time he is afflicted, or at all times, see *Johannes de Platea* at the title *those who excuse themselves by reason of illness, book 10 of the Code.* Posidonius, a name of no small account among the Stoics, while suffering from gout, exclaimed in the midst of the pain: *“Pain, you accomplish nothing; however troublesome you may be, I will never admit that you are an evil!”* On the innocence of stones <note>kidney/bladder stones</note> and gout, there exists an *Oration of the Honorable Mr. Johann Saubert from the year 1637.* The incomparable *Pirckheimer* wrote a Praise or Apology for Gout. Philander von Sittenwald, part 2, vision 5: *The best thing about gout is when the pain stops. If he should eat or walk, he has neither hand nor foot; but in the throes of misery, he has hands, feet, and toes, yes, an abundance of limbs. The Moors are not subject to the French disease <note>syphilis</note> nor to gout; see Mr. Harsdörffer in the German Secretary, book 33, title 34.*

As to whether someone can be removed from office because of the disease of Gout, see most recently *Mr. Dr. Christopher Philipp Richter, part 1, counsel 24, throughout. Martin Pansa*, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, wrote an *Anti-Gout Counsel* in the year 1613. Regarding the twin offspring of Bacchus <note>god of wine</note>, one of the better and one of the lesser sex: namely Priapus and Gout <note>Podagra</note>, the former of whom he fathered by Venus, or by the nymph Naja, but the latter truly from Venus. Gout is the daughter of both Bacchus and Venus, who loosen the limbs, and she herself loosens the limbs. *Tiraquellus, book 15 on marriage, number 44.* Neander in the *History of the Bacchanalia, page 76.*

Medicine knows not how to remove the knotted gout <note>original: "Tollere nodosam nescit Medicina podagram"</note>, *Law 'Martius' in the Digest on 'locati' <note>hiring/leasing</note>; and there see Bartolus, Baldus, and Salicetus* along with others via *Felinus at the chapter 'Presbyterum' at the end, and the Glossary there, and Johannes de Ana. They are called **Evening-eaters** <note>original: "Zabendszehrer"</note>, or "Supper allowances" <note>Latin: *Cœnatica*; see Book 3 of the Code, under the title 'Concerning the distribution of military provisions'</note>. The scholar Cujacius considers this a new and military term, used as if the soldiers demanded a certain sum of money for their dinner—an "evening-eater fee"—as noted by Dr. Tabor in *On Billeting*, page 125. The French call this *la passade* <note>a small gift or allowance given to a traveling soldier or beggar</note>. The cited author understands this to include vinegar, oil, fish sauce, brine, honey, and boiled wine.

**Supper** <note>original: "Nachtimbs"</note> used to mean a "meal." The "Princely Supper" is mentioned in Heberer's *On Egyptian Servitude*, book 1, chapter 3, page 18. The little word *Nachtimbs* was also commonly used in Strasbourg. However, in that region, *Imbs* <note>the root of the modern German word 'Imbiss' or snack</note> is understood as side dishes or stewed vegetables. Therefore, the princes must have lived quite poorly at times, since this "Princely Supper" is mentioned so modestly. A "respectable morning-snack" <note>original: "Morgen-Imbis"</note> is mentioned by Heberer in book 4, chapter 23, page 633. Heberer also describes how a Swedish pastor held his evening meal and treated his guests: he had a long table set, upon which the first course for supper was laid out—a respectable milk-bucket filled with salted butter, and next to it a large cheese, larger in circumference than a plow-wheel. The cheese was prepared with singular skill, and the following verses were printed upon it in clear letters, as if with a mold:

> Let it not be presented,
> Unless a festive day is celebrated.
> 
> <note>original Latin: "Non præsentetur, Nisi festa dies celebretur"</note>
> 
> That is:
> The cheese shall not be set out,
> Save when a great feast falls about.

The author provides more details in the same place. The "Midday snack" <note>original: "Mittags-Imbis"</note> is likewise mentioned by the author on page 639.

## 42. Driving to the Alps. <note>original: "Zu Alp fahren"</note> To send herds into mountain pastures.

### ADDITION.

The mountains are called **Alps**, which is a Celtic and German word. Josias Simler, in his beautiful commentary written about the Alps, says that "Alp" and "Alpen" are those mountains upon which one does not gather hay to keep for the winter; rather, one only puts oxen and other cattle there for grazing. Therefore, "driving to the Alp" means the same as driving the cattle into the mountains for pasture. On the height of the Alps, see Mr. Rupert's *Observations on Florus*, book 2, chapter 6. Zeiller treats this matter extensively in his *Itinerary of Italy*, page 26: where the Alps begin and end, their length and breadth, and their height (pages 26, 31). Also, who first crossed the Alps? (page 31).

## 45. Bridle-Money. <note>original: "Zaumgeld"</note> A gift for the horse's halter.

### ADDITION.

In Naples, a fortress was named *la Briglia*, which means "The Horse's Bridle," for the following reason: When Emperor Charles V returned from Africa to Naples, he saw many white horses without bridles depicted on the houses throughout the city. He asked what the horses signified, and when he understood that they represented the liberties of the Neapolitans, he ordered this castle to be built—under the pretext of it being a pleasure house—which overlooks the city of Naples. It serves like a bridle on a horse to subdue it, so that it does not resist its master. See Megiser in *Delights of Naples*, page 25. The nobility of Naples have a council <note>original: "Session"</note> called the *Capuana*; their coat of arms is a horse in a red field with a golden bridle. This coat of arms has its origin in the year 1253, from King Conrad. When the citizens of Naples refused to let him in, he eventually gained power over them after an eight-month siege. He ordered the walls, towers, and fortresses of the city—as well as many palaces—to be torn down, and drove many of the most prominent citizens into exile. When he later came to the Cathedral and found a beautiful bronze horse without a bridle standing before the church door (which had been placed there in ancient times as an ornament), King Conrad ordered a bridle to be placed upon it and these two verses to be engraved:

> Hitherto unbridled, it now obeys the reins of a master;
> The just King subdues this Neapolitan horse.
> 
> <note>original Latin: "Hactenus effrenis Domini nunc paret habenis, Rex domat hunc æquus Parthenopensis equum."</note>

Megiser, *Delights of Naples*, page 44.

When a horse is sold or given to someone by a Master, it is permitted for the Squire <note>original: *Scutifero*</note> to accept something as **Halter-money** or **Bridle-money**. Jason cites this text along with the Gloss in the Code, book 12, 'On the Marshals' <note>Latin: *de Stratoribus*</note>. See also Schneidewein, page 858. To pay for a fully equipped stallion with saddle and bridle: see Leonhard Wurffbain, *Historical Relations*, part 5, page 101.

# 46. Dwarf. Pygmy.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the place where dwarfs dwell according to the opinion of the Persians: Adam Olearius states in his *Description of a Journey to Persia*, book 5, chapter 27, page 620, that Alexander went to Khorasan and wandered as far as India, subjecting all the land to himself. At the request of the Indians, he also placed an iron palisade <note>original: "eisern Stacket"</note> between the mountains against the dwarfs, which must remain standing until Judgment Day. On the question of whether human stature is decreasing, see Besold’s *Politics*, page 835, at the end.

A fief <note>a land grant under the feudal system</note> is not terminated or lost because of "too many" (meaning a hermaphrodite <note>original: "intellige Hermaphroditum"</note>), dwarfs, cripples, etc. See the *Saxon Law*, article 4, book 1; Crusius on feudal succession, pages 39 and 18. Regarding "imperfect persons," see Schneidewein on fiefs, part 3, number 106. A story is told of Jacobus Castellio, a legal expert sent by the people of Bologna to the Pope. When he was introduced into the Pope's presence, he began his speech while standing. The Pope, seeing that the man was of such tiny stature, thought he was kneeling and commanded him to stand up, even though he had not bent his knee at all. This caused everyone to laugh quietly, and the man was so disturbed that he could not even whisper, let alone deliver the speech he had prepared. See Kirchner’s *On the Ambassador*, book 2, chapter 4, number 96. It is more advisable for such a little man <note>Latin: "homuncioni"</note> to sit rather than stand, according to the advice of Ovid <note>original: "Nasonis"</note>, which he suggests to short lovers: *If you are short, you should sit, lest while standing you appear to be sitting.* <note>Latin: "Si brevis es, sedeas, ne stans videare sedere."</note> Furthermore, no one who wishes to be seen as great among foreigners will send dwarfs or pygmies as ambassadors, unless they are being sent to the Homeric battles against the cranes. <note>A reference to the legendary war between pygmies and cranes mentioned in the Iliad.</note>

Trees that remain small but still bear fruit are called dwarfs. It is reported by Majolus, Antonio di Torquemada, and others that at the furthest end of India toward the east, near the source of the River Ganges, there live dwarfs who are at most 3 spans tall <note>a "span" is roughly 9 inches; thus about 27 inches</note>. The women give birth at 3 or 5 years of age and die at 7, 8, or 9 years. Others place them at the borders of Africa, others in Europe, and in Greenland. See Zeiller, *Second Century of Letters*, Epistle 80. Augustus expressed a dislike for dwarfs and those with deformed limbs, calling them "mockeries of nature" <note>original: "Gespötte der Natur"</note>. See Suetonius in his *Life of Augustus*, chapter 83, at the end. Similarly, Emperor Alexander Severus gave his dwarfs to the people, as they were unseemly for his court, as Lampridius testifies in chapter 34, folio 347. Piccart recounts more in his 27th decade, chapter 5, page 328 and following, and in chapter 7. Arngrimur Jónsson also gives examples of dwarfs in his *History of Iceland*, book 1, chapter 4, page 38. Zeiller, in his *Second Century of Letters*, Epistle 87, and in his *Third Century*, Epistle 90, records that at the wedding feast or nuptials of Duke Wilhelm of Bavaria and Princess Renata of

<column-break/>

Lorraine held in Munich in February of the year 1568, among other things, a great pie was served. Hidden inside it was a little dwarf belonging to Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, dressed in a very well-fitted cuirass <note>a piece of armor</note> and carrying his heraldic banner. This dwarf, who was also the aforementioned height of three spans, jumped out of the pie, walked around on the table, sang, and offered his hand to the princely persons with very proper and modest reverence. In this same pie, there were also up to 40 well-cooked dishes and warm foods, which Duke Albrecht of Bavaria’s master cook, named Peter Keyser, had specially made, as can be read in the description of this festival printed in Munich on royal paper, on page 66. More on dwarfs can be found in Zeiller’s *German Itinerary*, pages 350 and 354. Just as Plautus spoke of a "morsel of a boy," so a most beautiful writer who translated Aretino expressed "a morsel of a painter" in imitation: *How I wish*, he said, *to encounter that morsel of a little painter here?* <note>Latin: "Ut ego... frustum illud pictorculi hic offendere cupiam?"</note> Philippus Caroli, in his *Roman Library*, page 12, mentions dwarfs carried by ants. Mr. Harsdörffer, in his *Great Theater of Entertaining and Instructive Stories*, book 47, number 8, mentions a dwarf riding on a farmer as if on a horse.

There are two kinds of dwarfs and pygmies: some are found in almost all regions of the world, though they are rare, providing material for the delight of princes and the admiration of spectators. Others, however, are believed to fill entire provinces elsewhere and constitute nations or races of small people. Felix Plater, in his *Observations*, book 3, says that at the wedding of the Duke of Bavaria, there was a dwarf fully armed with a short spear and girded with a sword, hidden in a meat pie so he could not be seen. Placed on the table, he burst out from the broken pie and, jumping about with a drawn sword like a gladiator, moved everyone to laughter and wonder. In the castle of the Elector of Saxony in Dresden, a pygmy skeleton is shown, less than a cubit in height <note>about 18 inches</note>, with such solid bones and such perfect proportions that one might suspect they were the bones of an embryo; so testifies Bartholin in *On Pygmies*, chapter 6. In the March <note>Brandenburg</note> and Lusatia, a complete skeleton with a skull, two feet and three fingers long, was found, as Leonhard Thurneysser writes in Jonston. Regarding entire nations of pygmies, see Caspar Schott in his *Curious Physics*, pages 424, 425, 426 to 429.

### 50. Sorcery, specifically natural. Magia naturalis.

->ADDITION.<-

Regarding natural magic, Giambattista della Porta—whom Bodin, in his *French Refutation of the Opinions of Wier*, refers to as being among the evildoers because he describes a magical ointment—but Porta himself complained of this injustice in the latest edition. More on natural magic can be found in M. Zeiller, century 4, question 100, throughout. Fracastoro, *On Sympathy and Antipathy*. For natural magic, consult the late Mr. Harsdörffer in *The Great Theatre of Joyful and Instructive Histories*, volume 139, throughout. Concerning the charming <note>magical recovery</note> of lost

<column-break/>

things, see the same work, volume 192, number 3, and above under the word *Jew* <note>original: "Jud."</note>. Concerning treasure found through the art of magic, which can happen with divining rods and in other ways, see Mr. Harsdörffer, volume 161, number 11. Concerning "fetching the goat" <note>a folkloric term for a demonic summoning or a specific type of theft</note>, see Carpzov, *Forensic Jurisprudence of Roman-Saxon Law*, part 4, constitution 2, definition 9. On magical arts that produce wonders and crimes, see Pierre Grégoire, *Syntagma of Universal Law*, book 34, chapter 19, throughout. Johann Philippi, Legal Consultant, in *Practical Use of the Institutes*, book 4, title 18, § 5, Eclogue 87, number 10. The Lay Judges <note>original: "Scabini"</note> of Leipzig in the month of November, 1661, regarding a consultation from the Senate of the Imperial City of Mühlhausen: "When you sent us the confession <note>original: "Urgicht," a formal confession of a crime</note> of the prisoner Elisabeth Werner, along with other records of the investigation... the prisoner, under fairly sharp questioning <note>a euphemism for questioning under torture</note>, admitted and confessed that she allied herself with the Evil Foe <note>the Devil</note> and accepted baptism from him, as well as a silver coin as money, which he promised to give her weekly, although he did not keep the promise. Furthermore, she committed inhuman fornication with him three times. After she brought something into the world through such fornication that looked like a bumblebee, the Evil Foe made a black powder out of it and gave it to her. Afterwards, she used it to bewitch Georg Hofmann and later Nicol Kobloch, so that both had to die... If the prisoner voluntarily persists in such confessions before the convened capital court, or is otherwise convicted as is right: she should, because of such inhuman fornication, alliance, and committed sorcery, be punished with death by fire. With Rightful Verdict."

Sorcery was dealt with more extensively above, under the word *Witches* <note>original: "Hexen"</note>, where on page 389 I discussed the confessions of poisoners and hags, in which they identify their accomplices. That passage of mine was cited in 1664 in Tübingen by Christopher Daurer of Hamburg in his *Inaugural Dissertation on the Denunciation of Witches*, page 69, where he accumulated more authors, such as Reinkingk in *Response on Witches*, question 2, number 270; Johann Strauch in *Dissertation on Justinian’s Private Law* 29, thesis 9; Tanner, volume 3, disputation 4, *On Justice*, question 5, doubt 2; the author of *The Cautio Criminalis* <note>Friedrich Spee, who argued against the reliability of torture in witch trials</note> at length in doubt 44 and many following; Mayfart in the *Christian Reminder to Powerful Regents on how to eradicate the vice of Witchcraft*, chapters 12, 13, 14, 24, 32, 33, 44; and throughout Lerchheimer in *Christian Doubts concerning Sorcery*, article 17, pages 202 to 205. Goldast, in *Reflections on the Confiscation of Sorcerers' Goods*, page 111, letter i, also attributes this opinion to Melander in *Resolved Questions*, number 7, regarding the process against hags, folio 102; to the legal experts of Altdorf; to Rittershusius; to Petrus Wesenbeck; to Albrecht; and to Torreblanca—though he errs in citing Torreblanca, for he does not assert this in the cited places nor elsewhere.

## 56. Zones. Whether the three zones are uninhabitable.
### ADDITION.
Antiquity believed that there were three uninhabitable zones on the globe. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 1:

> Of which the middle one is not habitable due to heat; 
> Deep snow covers two: between each of these he placed 
> as many, and gave them a temperate climate, 
> with flame mixed with cold.

The stupendous voyages of our own century have revealed the contrary. Many things pertaining to this are found in Besold, *On Politics*, book 1, chapter 10, number 7, verse 3, at length. Whether the torrid zone is uninhabitable? Panciroli in *Newly Discovered Things*, pages 18, 20, 21. Klock, *On the Treasury*, book 1, chapter 27, number 1, where the error of Aristotle and Pliny is rebuked, numbers 2, 3, 4. Mayfart in *Compendium of Geography*, page 77 and following. Why the torrid zone is temperate in some places, in the same treatise, page 78. Four minor circles divide the entire surface of the earth into five zones, of which one is Torrid, two are Frigid, and as many are Temperate. The Torrid zone, situated in the middle of the others, is so named from the perpetual heat of the sun, to whose path it is subject, and it is cut in the middle by the equator. One of the Frigid zones is Northern, between the Pole and the Arctic Circle; the other is Southern, between the Pole and the Antarctic Circle. One of the Temperate zones is bounded by the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer, and is Northern; the other is Southern, and is terminated by the Antarctic Circle and the Tropic—

### 57. **Plums.** <note>original Latin: *Pruna damascena*</note>

->ADDITION.<-

The highest praise is given to the Hungarian plums or damsons, which are called *Damascena pruna* by writers because they were first brought to Germany from the mountain in Syria called Damascus. All other plums yield to these; they cool the body and carry the bile out of the system, and are good for hot fevers and illness. Michael Knab in the *Hortipomolegio* <note>A treatise on orchard management and fruit trees</note>, page 78.

### 59. **Toe.** <note>original Latin: *Lentus* — likely a misprint or linguistic note in the original, as *Lentus* usually means "tough" or "slow" in Latin, while the entry discusses the German homophones</note>

->ADDITION.<-

Tough <note>German: *Zähe*</note>, meaning viscous; Toe <note>German: *Zehe*</note>, a digit of the foot; Ten <note>German: *Zehen*</note>, the number. Mr. Harsdörffer. One who stands on his toes. Every finger, toe, or tooth has its specific fine, according to the <term>Weregild</term> <note>A historical legal value placed on a person or body part, paid as compensation</note> due for it, which is the tenth part. Carpzov, part 1, Decision 100, number 3, and those cited there.

King Henry II, Duke of Bavaria, having been wounded by the charge of a wild beast so that a boot helped his gait, was called the "Stilt-walker" <note>original Latin: *Grallator*</note>, and later "The Lame" with greater likelihood of truth. Mr. Rupert in *Universal History*, page 163 (in my copy).

An example of a woman who can write, sew, feed herself, and even dress and undress herself with her toes. Zeiller, century 3, Letter page 614; add also his *German Itinerary*, page 356. The Turkish Emperor's lackeys walk on the toes of their feet. Hornigk, *On the Law of Posts*, chapter 8, page 128. Mr. Speidel in the *Mirror of Notable Things*, page 750 (in my copy).

*Atta*, an ancient word of Sabine and Greek origin, signifies one who does not know how to stand still while walking, but always seems to hop; this necessarily happens to those who do not walk on the whole foot, but press down on the tips of the feet. Festus, from the correction of Casaubon: those are called *Attæ* who, due to a defect of the legs or feet, do not press down with the soles, and touch the ground more than they actually walk. Many things on this are found in Mr. Rupert on Pomponius, book 3, chapter 2, paragraph 36.

### 60. **Time.** <note>original Latin: *Tempus*</note>

->ADDITION.<-

Christoph Besold, Tübingen 1614, in quarto, wrote on the signs of the times. On the "balsamic time," see Mr. Dilherr in *The Course of Time and the World*, 526, 527. Regarding time expressed and articulated in a legal document, if someone does not approve it, see what the law says in Berlich, decision 97. How "immemorial time" <note>A time period extending beyond the reach of memory or record</note> is to be proven. Hondedei, book 1, counsel 79. "Time sets its tooth into all things, and tears everything away with it." Opitz. This is often used: "No counselor is better than time" <note>original Greek: *σύμβολος οὐδείς ἐστὶ βελτίων χρόνος*</note>—namely, after God. Regarding the smallness of time, see Spreger, *On the Modicum*, page 112. Regarding the clause "still at this time," and what it imports, see the law *quod Servius*, counsel of Zasius, book 5, paragraph 1. On the words "at which time," and what they mean, see Rudinger, century 5, observation 98. The lapse of time does not remove a punishment. Christoph Philipp Richter, part 5, counsel 6, 44, folio 22. On the little word "at all times" <note>German: *jederzeit*</note> and what it signifies, see part 1, counsel 40, number 3, folio 264. Octavius Vulpius, *On the Signification of Prepositions and Adverbs*, under the word "always" <note>Latin: *semper*</note>. "According to the time," that is, according to the condition of the time, see Mr. Rupert in *Epistolary Mercury*.

### 61. **Plaits.** <note>German: *Zöpff*</note>

This is a disease of the hair which is called the <term>Mährenflecht</term> <note>Commonly known as *Plica polonica*, a condition where hair becomes matted into a felt-like mass, often associated with superstition in early modern Europe</note>, the Polish Night-locks, Night-weaving, Jews' plaits, Elf-locks, or Wood-plaits; our people in Nuremberg call them "powder-set." The highly learned Hercules Saxoniae, in his time, wrote a special book on the Night-locks. Tacitus, in *On the Customs of the Germans*: "A husband expels an adulteress from the house in the presence of relatives, having cut off her hair and stripped her." To the adulteresses—who, after they shared that with others which belonged to their husbands alone—the hair (or plaits) was cut off and they were thrust out of the house. From this, false hair and wigs have their origin. M. C. T. Rango, Rector of the Berlin Gymnasium, treatise *On Wigs*, chapter 4, pages 48, 49. On "Maidens' plaits," see the same, chapter 8, member 7, number 17. On "Tours" or plaits, see the same, number 6. On solitary curls hanging at the temples, or attached to the ears, or knotted hair, in German *Zöpff*, which could also be called "horns." Ibid, number 11. The Nazarites let their hair grow: "All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall pass over his head until the days are fulfilled for which he separated himself to the Lord; he shall be holy, letting the locks of the hair of his head grow long" <note>A translation of the Latin citation of Numbers 6:5</note>. Absalom is commended for the beauty of his hair in 2 Samuel 14:26, 27: "There was no man so beautiful as Absalom in Israel." Gottschalcus Holem, an old author who wrote under the Papacy shortly before Luther, on the twelve sermons for the Sundays after Pentecost.

### 62. Timidity. Fear. <note>original German: *Zägheit*; Latin: *Metus*</note>
->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the fear of soldiers before a battle: see Christoph Rupert, Dissertation 1, chapters 6, 7, and 8; and Book 1 of Valerius Maximus. Experienced commanders, when they observe such fear in their soldiers before a fight, are not easily accustomed to drawing up the battle lines; Matthias Bernegger shows this through very fine examples in his *Questions on Tacitus's Germany*, page 9. "I turn as pale as a rhetorician about to speak at the altar of Lyon," <note>original Latin: *Adeò serè palleo, ceu Lugdunensem Rhetor dicturus ad aram*</note> says Juvenal. Lucan writes: "They fear the things they themselves have imagined." <note>original Latin: *Quæ finxère, timent*</note> And Petronius Arbiter followed him, saying: "Fear first created gods in the world."

### 63. Modest, Chaste. <note>original German: *Züchtich, Keusch*; Latin: *Castus*</note>
->ADDITION.<-

Regarding the praise of chastity: see Francesco Vivio, *Neapolitan Decisions*, 454. Nature willed that certain parts of the body be removed from sight for the sake of modesty. Hence, in Euripides, Iphigenia is praised, and in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book 13, Fable 6, Polyxena is praised because, even in the moment of death, they took care to cover those parts that should be hidden. For the poet says of her:

> Even then she took care to veil the parts to be covered,
> As she fell, and to preserve the honor of chaste modesty.

Examples of chaste persons who were advised to engage in sexual intercourse for the sake of their health, but who refused and would not consent: Zeiller, *Epistles*, Century 5, page 206, and page 694. Recent examples of chastity: the same author, Century 4, Question 32, page 148 and following. For the sake of defending one's chastity, it is permitted to kill a kidnapper of virgins, widows, or wives, and any violent rapist. For since virginity and chastity are among those things without which—as Seneca teaches in Book 1 of *On Benefits*, Chapter 11—we can indeed live, but in such a way that death would be preferable, and which, once lost, are entirely irreparable just like life itself: hence its defense even with the killing of another is rightly granted. William Ames, Book 5, *On Conscience*, Chapter 31, number 8. Moreover, if a woman allowed herself to be overcome, she would expose herself to the danger of consenting to the sin due to the difficulty of the will's resistance, if she does not do what she can to escape. Georg Adam Struve, *On Private Vengeance*, Chapter 5, throughout.

### 64. Tongue. <note>original German: *Zung*; Latin: *Lingua*</note>
->ADDITION.<-

If a dog receives a wound, it needs no medicine other than its tongue; for if it can reach the wound with its tongue and lick it, there is no need for a surgeon’s hand. Luis de Granada, *On the Symbol of the Faith*, Book 1, Chapter 15. One should certainly see, if it pleases, Mr. Harsdörffer in the *Poetic Funnel*, part 3, page 501. Erasmus published a singular treatise *On the Tongue*. A rooster, even if tongueless, can speak: Limnäus, Volume 2, *Additions to Book 5*, Chapter 2, number 9.

### 65. Confectionery, Sweets. <note>original German: *Zuckerwerck, Schleckwerck*; Latin: *Tragemata*</note>
->ADDITION.<-

Delicate pastries <note>original Latin: *Nebulæ deliciariæ*</note> were sent to a youth, but they were poisoned; however, he escaped death. Sodalis Parthenius, Book 2, Chapter 8, page 317. Jeremias Drexel in *The Gold Mine*, page 186. Paraíba <note>A province in Dutch Brazil</note> bears six sugar loaves in its coat of arms. How sugar is manufactured: Mr. Fürer in his *Travels*, page 43. In and around Recife <note>original German: *Resistzt*</note> there are over 120 sugar mills. Michael Hemmersam, in the *Description of West Indian Travels* which I edited, page 112. In every sugar mill there are two or three hundred people, mostly slaves and Moors, some of whom must perform only the rawest labor. Ibid., regarding fish that are caught with sugar canes, where two people have enough to eat from just one head. The same author, page 58: Much sugar grows in Guinea; they are long canes, and when they reach the length of a finger, they get knots and then continue to grow until they reach the height of a man. They do not ripen quickly, yet they are available in quantity and are eaten for pleasure by both Germans and Moors. When they go fishing, they take four or five canes with them when the sun shines harshly to quench their thirst, because they are very juicy. There are no sugar mills in the land of Guinea, so it is only eaten raw. Michael Hemmersam in the *Description of West Indian Travels*, page 46. The pressing of sugar from canes: Klock, *On the Treasury*, Book 1, Chapter 14, number 138. Sugar: how it grows and how it should be made. Also, how eight people work until the sugar is poured into the mold, with each task having its own specific name: Megiler in *Delights of Naples*, page 127 and following.

Anyone who speaks obscurely does so at his own peril. Final Gloss on the law "If a tree," 17, *Digest on Urban Servitudes*.

George Acacius Enenckel <note>An Austrian jurist and historian</note> writes in Book 2 of *On Privileges*, chapter 2, number 14: A witness can clarify his own obscure statements if the judge wishes, or he may be examined once more. Wurmser <note>Bernhard Wurmser, a prominent legal scholar</note> says in Book 1, observation 6, number 1, section 2: It harms a contracting party if they have entered into a contract obscurely <note>original Latin: *obscure contraxit*; meaning that the person who writes an unclear contract is responsible for the confusion</note>. Hartmann Hartmann <note>A 16th-century German jurist</note> writes in Book 2, observation 3, title 26: A legal foundation cannot be sought from that which is uncertain and obscure. As stated in the law *duo sunt* in the Digest regarding the testimony of guardians: An ambiguous or obscure statement by a witness receives its clarification from the common usage of speech, according to Jakob Ayrer in the *Historical Process*, part 1, chapter 8, observation 5, number 6. There is also that excellent warning from Gamaliel in the *Pirke Avot* <note>A collection of ethical teachings from the Talmudic era; original: *Pirke Aboth*</note> chapter 1, section 16: "Abstain from a doubtful thing." What you doubt, do not do—as Pliny says.

One who doubts does not differ from one who is ignorant. Barbosa <note>Agostinho Barbosa, a Portuguese canon lawyer</note> in Book 4, chapter 52, axiom 1.

In doubtful matters, the middle path is to be chosen. Francesco Vivio, *Neapolitan Decisions*, 492. A judge who pronounces that a case "is not clear" to him <note>original Latin: *non liquere*; a legal term where a judge avoids a verdict due to lack of clarity</note> shows himself to be unskilled and a poor practitioner, according to Cavalcanti, Book 5, decision 1, number 59. Nicolaus Valla wrote on doubtful matters in Paris, in the year 1577. In doubtful cases and those not clearly decided by law, it is permissible to imitate and follow the examples of others. Barbosa, Book 4, chapter 53, axiom 1. Something is called "doubtful" when it can be applied to two different meanings. Axiom 8. Doubtful words are to be interpreted against the person who bases their claim upon them. *Acts of Lindau*, folio 80. Matters expressed for the sake of removing doubt do not usually harm common law. Klock, volume 1, counsel 51, number 158. In cases of doubt, words are considered to have been uttered for demonstration, not for restriction. Klock, volume 2, counsel 26, number 42. Some people are accustomed to affecting ambiguity and obscurity in their answers with great effort, imitating the oracles of the ancient "Vejovis Apollo" <note>An epithet for Apollo associated with ill-fortune or the underworld</note>, who was called *logies*—that is, "the oblique one"—for the reason that he would deceive his consultants with oblique and ambiguous responses, sending them away much more uncertain than when they had arrived. Kirchner in *On Legations*, Book 2, chapter 6, page 34. A negation makes a matter doubtful. Schwannmann in Decision 10, number 61. Felinus Sandeus, chapter *si Clericus*, section 1, regarding competent courts.

### 67. Future. <note>original German: *Zukünfftig*; Latin: *Futurum*</note>

Any of us prefers to receive a small thing today and renounce a greater future and uncertain benefit. Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, an influential medieval jurist</note> on the law *quis pro eo*, section 6, number 17, regarding bail. Roma on the law *pactum dotale* 3, number 6, regarding collation, following those lines of Claudian <note>A Roman poet</note>:

> — — Everything in the future
> Is despised, and the presence of one's own fruit persuades us.

And there is that common proverb: Eggs for the present are better than chickens for tomorrow <note>original Latin: *Ad præsens ova cras pullis sunt meliora*; a variation of "a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush"</note>. Gloss on law 8, on the word *monco*, regarding transactions. Barbosa, Book 6, chapter 30, axiom 2. Future contingencies are uncertain among us, whence we say: there is no determined truth regarding future contingencies. Axiom 3. Future things are not considered and do not impede unless they are certain and infallible. Axiom 1. Words in the past tense denote a completed act and are not pulled into the present or future. Klock, volume 2, counsel 42, number 30; though see also numbers 143 to 155. Words of the present or past tense are sometimes pulled toward the future if they cannot be verified in the present. Klock, volume 1, counsel 149, number 182.

### 68. Tsar. <note>original: *Zaar*; Emperor of Russia</note>

Regarding where this word comes from and what it means, see Adam Olearius <note>A 17th-century scholar and traveler</note> in his *New Oriental Journey*, page 149. Limnäus, volume 2, additions to Book 2, chapter 2 of the *Public Law of Germany*, pages 3 and 4.

### 69. Rent Redemption. <note>original German: *Zinßlofung*; Latin: *Retractus censualis*</note>

The redemption of a rent-charge. Asphin on the *Law of Retraction*, conclusions 45 to 49.

### 70. Zereth.

"Down to the Zereth." Acts of the Teutonic Order <note>original German: *Teutschherrisch*; refers to the military-religious order of knights</note> in the Roll of Documents, folio 137. Perhaps it is understood there as "the Lazareth" <note>A hospital or infirmary, especially for contagious diseases</note>.

# A SUCCINCT TREATISE
## ON THE JUDICIAL PROCESS
### CHAPTER ONE,
### ON THE COMPETENT FORUM.

---

I. **C**oncerning the Judicial Process, with God’s kind help, I intend to speak briefly and according to modern and more frequent practice; I believe this can be done most conveniently if we follow the order that the nature of this matter and its progression naturally suggest.

<margin>
(a) In the past, the method of proceeding under Civil Law <note>original: *Jure Civili*; refers to the body of Roman law</note> was entirely different. For the modern process mostly follows Canon Law <note>original: *Jus Canonicum*; the law of the Church</note>, from which it was derived. It is one thing to "declare the law" <note>original: *Jus dicere*</note> and another to "judge" <note>original: *judicare*</note>. Regarding this, it should be noted that in the past, Summons <note>original: *Citationes*</note> were not in use; instead, the Plaintiff <note>original: *Actor*</note> called the Defendant <note>original: *Reum*</note> to law by his own authority, and could pull or push one who refused. The Defendant, however, freed himself from this harassment by promising "bail" <note>original: *vadimonium*</note>, that is, by pledging that he wished to appear in Court. And this was called "calling to law" <note>original: *in jus vocare*</note>. This took place before a Magistrate who had jurisdiction, before whom the Plaintiff narrated the facts; the Praetor <note>A Roman magistrate</note> or Governor gave the Plaintiff an action suitable to this narration; the Defendant, in turn, narrated his defenses. And this was "declaring the law." For Magistrates did not investigate the facts, but gave a Judge, who afterwards looked into whether the matter stood in fact as it was proposed by the Plaintiff and Defendant on either side. It was the custom, moreover, that those who had finished their study of Law should sit at the feet of the Magistrates—that is, in the lower seats—for the sake of learning practice and so they might be promoted to other offices; the Magistrates committed cases to these men to be investigated, and for that reason, they were called "Foot-judges" <note>original: *Pedanei Judices*; essentially low-ranking judges who sat at the 'feet' of higher officials</note>. And
</margin>

II. Now, therefore, since he who desires to bring a lawsuit into Court must first of all determine which Judge he ought to approach, and whether that Judge is competent, the beginning of our treatment will be the *Competence of the Forum* <note>original: *Competentia Fori*</note>. (a)

<column-break/>

<margin>
certainly these Foot-judges did not have full Jurisdiction, but only the power of investigation <note>original: *notionem*</note>. They did not decide on the law, but only on the facts; they likewise heard and examined witnesses, and finally judged whether the given action belonged to the Plaintiff or the defense to the Defendant. However, they did not summon the parties. And it is from this that in the past, lawsuits reached their end much more quickly, as gathered from the law *l. 3. ff. de his, quæ in testam. delentur* <note>A reference to the Digest of Justinian</note>. Indeed, many disputes were even carried out before the Emperors, who briefly judged them after hearing the parties on the spot and immediately, as can be seen in the aforementioned law.
</margin>

<margin>
(b) For in the past, trials were mostly conducted in open and public places for the sake of avoiding suspicion. This custom even persists today in the *Summary Court* <note>original German: *Standrecht*</note>, in the *Court of Rottweil* <note>original: *Rotwilensi*; a famous Imperial court in Germany</note>, and in the *Hundred Courts* <note>original: *Centgerichten*</note>, that is, criminal trials which are conducted under the open sky. Thus among the Jews, trials were conducted in the Gates; among the Romans in the Forum; but afterwards Courthouses <note>original: *Prætoria* or German *Rechtshäuser*</note> were built; see Speidel in *Notables* under the words *Court* and *Law-house*. And thus even today, the place of judgment is called a "Forum" out of respect for that ancient custom, although lawsuits are no longer practiced in the public market-square.
</margin>

III. The **Forum**, however, is the place of jurisdiction in which trials are exercised (Cujas <note>Jacques Cujas, a famous 16th-century legal humanist</note> in his commentary on the Code, *On the jurisdiction of all judges*), either because the litigants bring their controversies to that place, just as merchants bring the things they wish to sell, or because in the past, trials were mostly public, performed in the bare area of the forum and open to the sky (François Pollet, *History of the Roman Forum*, book 1, chapter 2). (b) And so the competent forum is that place of trial which is necessarily approached by the Litigants, or where at least the Defendant (if the plaintiff has the choice), whether willing or unwilling, is bound to answer, and which he cannot escape even if he most desires to.

<meta>catchword: IV. And</meta>

# Discussion

IV. And thus **Legal Competency** <note>original: *Competentia Juris*; the legal authority of a court to hear a specific case</note> stands as the basis and foundation of a Judgment: *(c)* and for this reason, it is said that a lack of Jurisdiction is the greatest possible defect. Such a proceeding does not even deserve to be called a "Judgment" if the Judge lacks the power to declare the law <note>original: *Jurisdicendi facultate*; the faculty of speaking the law</note>. Furthermore, a "nullity" <note>a legal void or invalidity</note> arising from an incompetent court is considered an incurable and irreparable vice. It is so serious that it is not even considered to be covered under a statute or other provision *(d)* that otherwise rejects or overlooks all technical nullities. Indeed, if the lack of jurisdiction is evident from the records, the Judge may attend to it voluntarily—even if not requested—and can rescind the sentence even if a party is absent or was not summoned.

*(c) For if a Judge is incompetent, everything done in his presence is void. And even though a Defendant may appear before an incompetent Judge and fail to object, what is done remains void, unless he expressly "extends jurisdiction"—that is, unless he waives his rights and his objection to the incompetency. But if he "joins the issue" <note>original: *litem contestetur*; the formal start of a trial where the parties agree on the point of dispute</note> knowing the Judge is incompetent, then that act of joining the issue is treated like a Contract; thus the Defendant is held to answer as if by a new Contract, whereas previously he was not bound.*

*(d) When it is said that a local statute rejects all "nullities," this must be understood to apply only to those nullities that arise from a lack of formalities—not natural formalities, but those invented only through the subtleties of Law. However, it is a matter of Natural Law <note>fundamental justice seen as inherent to humanity</note> that no one is bound to answer except to a Judge to whom they are subject. Thus, under the name of "nullities of positive law" (that is, Civil Law, which can also be called "accidental" nullities, whereas nullities of Natural Law can be called "substantial" ones), there might fall such things as a flaw in the form of the complaint, or the failure to name the specific legal action or the family name.*

V. Hence it is further said that a summons from an incompetent Judge may be ignored with impunity: *(e)* and if the Judge proceeds in "contumacy" <note>contempt of court for failing to appear</note>, the Sentence is void by the law itself <note>original: *ipso Jure*</note>, and there is no need to invalidate it through an appeal. However, a different answer is given in the law regarding a person summoned from another jurisdiction by a Provincial Governor <note>original: *Præsidem*</note>: in that case, the person ought to come, since it belongs to the Governor to judge whether he has jurisdiction or not. One summoned to law should not despise the authority of the one who presides over the <column-break/> jurisdiction. This is understood to mean that in such a case, the person is naturally subject to the jurisdiction of the one issuing the summons, but perhaps holds a "Privilege" <note>a special legal exemption or status</note> that exempts them from it. Even then, they must appear; otherwise, the privilege is denied.

*(e) A Judge can be incompetent for two reasons: namely, by the law itself <note>original: *ipso jure*</note> or by a Privilege. One who is summoned to a judge who is incompetent by the law itself does not have to come, nor is he bound to; he may ignore the summons without penalty. If, however, the Judge is competent by the law itself, but the person summoned holds a Privilege exempting them, that person ought to appear out of honor for the competent Judge and allege their Privilege. The reason for this difference is that where a Judge is competent by the basic law, he has a "founded intention" <note>a valid starting assumption of authority</note> which can only be struck down by a specific legal objection.*

VI. Furthermore, the Plaintiff follows the forum of the Defendant <note>original: *Actor sequitur forum Rei*; the general rule that you must sue someone in their own home court</note>. *(f)* But a defendant is assigned to a forum for various reasons, of which six are primary: (1) Domicile. (2) The location of the property in dispute. (3) The location of the crime or "delict." (4) The location where the Contract was made. (5) An agreement to meet <note>original: *Conventus*</note>. and (6) The quality or nature of the case.

*(f) An exception to this thesis is the Law regarding defamation, which will be discussed below in Chapter 2, Title 5.*

VII. First and foremost, everyone is assigned to a forum in the territory and place where they hold citizenship or Domicile: <term>where he is a citizen, or has performed the oath of hereditary fealty <note>original German: *da er verburgert, oder die Erbhuldigung geleistet*</note></term>. *(g)* This species of forum is the most extensive and grants the widest jurisdiction and power. For the Judge of the Domicile can hear any case: *(h)* both in the name of "personal actions" <note>lawsuits against a specific person for a debt or service</note> and also regarding property situated elsewhere. Likewise, in a "real action" <note>a lawsuit regarding physical property or land</note>, even one concerning possession, *(i)* one may sue an opponent either in the place of their Domicile or in the place where the property is located. To the point that almost no cases can be found...

<summary>This page defines the "Competent Forum," explaining that a judge must have jurisdiction for a ruling to be valid. It establishes that while a plaintiff usually must sue in a defendant's home court (domicile), there are specific exceptions based on contract, crime, or the location of property.</summary>
