<page-num>1175</page-num>
<header>on the Judicial Process.</header>

...cases are argued which cannot be aired before the Judge of Domicile <note>the judge in the place where the defendant lives</note>; and this concurs with all other reasons for establishing a legal forum <note>original: *fori fortiendi rationibus*</note>, as Frideric Hiltrop agrees in *The Judicial Process, part 1, title 2, On the Competent Forum, number 24.* There, at number 29, he notes: *if in a real action* <note>original: *reali actione*; a lawsuit concerning physical property like land</note>*, the case was litigated before the Judge of Domicile, then through letters of request* <note>original: *literas requisitoriales*; a formal request from one court to another</note>*, it is requested of the Judge passing the sentence that the Judge of the local area execute the sentence as a legal aid.* Indeed, a subject can even be punished in the place of his Domicile, even if he committed a crime outside his Lord's territory, *Law 1, section 2, Code: "where regarding crimes"; Joseph Ludovicus, Lucca Decision 16, number 18; Cöppen Decision 43; Thoming Decision 90.* (k) But nevertheless, all these things only take place if the forum of Domicile is not preempted by the forum of the place where the property is located, where the contract was made, or where the crime occurred. *Penultimate Law, Digest: "on Jurisdiction"; Law "if anyone" 7; Law "where begun" 30; Digest: "on Judgments"; Gail, book 1, observation 29, number 5; and there Gravaeus, consideration 2, number 8; Decian in "Criminal Practice," book 4, chapter 21; Farinaccius, question 7, number 59.* (l)

(g) In the place of Domicile, **where one is a citizen or lives domestically** <note>original: *da einer verbürgert, oder häuslich wohnet*</note>, anyone can be summoned indifferently in the name of all actions and controversies. And thus, first, a Citizen—for example, one of Ingolstadt who has a house in Augsburg—can be summoned in Ingolstadt by reason of that house, **in his right of citizenship** <note>original: *in seinem Burgerrecht*</note>. But it is objected in the *final Law of the Digest "on Jurisdiction"* that one who speaks the law outside his territory is not obeyed with impunity; but in this case, the Judge of Ingolstadt speaks the law outside his territory; Therefore, etc. I respond: in the proposed case, the Judge of Ingolstadt does not speak the law regarding a house existing in a foreign territory, but only to the person—that is, to his own Citizen—so that he may restore that Augsburg house to the other person who is claiming it.

(h) **Suppose** someone made a contract in Ulm who is a citizen of Munich, or promised to make a payment in a certain place: he can indeed be summoned in that place by reason of the contract, but also in the place of his domicile where he is a citizen, so that the plaintiff has the choice.

(i) For although in possessory interdicts <note>legal orders regarding who currently holds property</note> it seems to be dealt with only as a matter of fact, and thus the Judge of Domicile can do nothing with authority outside his own territory; nevertheless, in this case, it is discussed not as a mere matter of fact, but also in some way as a matter of law. For possession is indeed a matter of fact, but in possessory judgments, it is not considered unless it is lawful. Therefore, the inquiry itself—whether the alleged possession is true or not—is not of fact alone, but also brings some matter of law with it.

<column-break/>

(k) A citizen can be accused criminally in the place of his domicile, even for crimes committed elsewhere in a distant place: because the crime always clings to the person, even if they committed the offense elsewhere and contaminated another territory.
But what if the punishment is heavier in the place of the crime than in the place of domicile? For example, if a citizen of Ingolstadt commits adultery in Saxony, where adultery is a capital offense: the question is, how should the adulterer be punished in Ingolstadt, where adultery is not a capital offense for the first time? It is more likely that he ought to be punished according to the place of domicile where he was captured. For the Judge of Domicile cannot judge according to a foreign statute. But on the contrary, if a Saxon committed adultery in Ingolstadt and was to be punished in Saxony, he ought not to be beheaded: The reason is that, although the same logic applies to opposites, in criminal matters one usually inclines toward the more merciful side.

(l) It must be known that "preemption" <note>original: *praeventioni*; when one court takes priority over another</note> takes place only in those cases where someone has two possible Judges; and whoever is approached first and has seen to it that the summons is issued, the lawsuit must be finished before him. The Defendant has the legal objection of "preemption" and "pending litigation" <note>original: *litis pendentiae*</note> if he is summoned elsewhere.

## VIII.
Furthermore, *Domicile* <note>original: *Domicilium*</note> is a designation of Law, not of fact; *(m)* nor does the mere possession of a house, which is prepared in a foreign city, create a Domicile. *Law "freedman" 17, section "a house alone," Digest: "to the Municipality"; Law 4, Code: "on Inhabitants," book 10.* And so it can happen that a House is found without a Domicile, and a Domicile without a House. Nor is everyone who has a house in some place and inhabits it immediately thought to have established a domicile there: but in addition, they say it is necessary that he inhabit it in such a way that he has established his seat there with the intention of remaining permanently, not for the sake of a time: **That one has settled there domestically and permanently.** <note>original: *Daß einer allda häuslich und beständig gesessen seye.*</note> *Law "it makes no difference" 26, Digest: "on captives"; Law "of him who" 27, section 1, Digest: "on the Municipality"; Law 7, Code: "on Inhabitants," book 10; Donellus 17, chapter 12.* Hence inhabitants, whom they commonly call **Residents** <note>original: *Beysiß*; people who live in a city but aren't full citizens</note> or **Out-burghers** <note>original: *Pfalburger*; people living outside the walls but holding city rights</note>, are regularly held to answer in the place of their residence; see *Gail, book 2, observation 35.*

(m) One domicile is of law, another of fact. That of Law is what Citizens have, because they have the intention of remaining there permanently. For although those who are inhabitants—and indeed even the Citizens themselves—can withdraw and renounce the Law of the City, this nevertheless only happens through specific actions: for regularly they have the intention of staying. If, however, they withdraw, then by reason of actions already born in that place, from which...

<page-num>1176</page-num>
<header>Dispute</header>
<sig>X. Sor-</sig>

to which they withdraw, they are held to respond, provided they are found there. If, however, they are not found there, they must be summoned in the place of their new Domicile. *Domicile of fact* <note>original: *Facti domicilium est*</note> is that which, for example, Students and similar people have, who are essentially guests in a place; they have a domicile of fact because they are there in fact, but it is not a Domicile of Law. For it neither subjects them to the Law or the burdens of the City, nor do they come to the site of the Academy with any intention other than eventually leaving again.

IX. It must be noted here, however, that sometimes someone resides <gloss>(n)</gloss> in a place under such a condition that they only fall under that jurisdiction regarding business contracted there, or regarding crimes committed there. And so, for the most part, free Nobles living in Cities, as well as Syndics, Officials, and Councilors of Great Lords or Imperial Cities (who are bound to those Lords not by origin or Citizenship, but only by office) cannot be summoned in that place for all cases. For this reason, they usually take care to protect themselves in their letters of appointment, **in the letters of appointment** <note>original: *in den Bestallungs-Briefen*</note>. For foreigners <gloss>(o)</gloss> elected to Offices in a City do not become Citizens or subjects there, even though they enjoy the privileges of Citizens; and therefore, the local statutes are not observed regarding their inheritance. *Paris de Puteo in the treatise on Syndics, section: "city official," chapters 1 and 2; Menochius, counsel 86, numbers 8 and 27, and counsel 129, number 15; Scheffer, 1, question 39; Modestinus Pistoris, question 41; Cardinal Tuschus, letter L, conclusion 72, number 4.*

Conversely, in some places, one is not permitted to possess property in a Prince's territory except with the burden of personal subjection; **Which brings with it the oath of land-homage.** <gloss>(p)</gloss> Furthermore, a vagabond can be summoned anywhere. *Hiltrop, cited location 18, etc.* And finally, the rules regarding the Domicile of Origin found throughout our Law—*Law 1, Law 4, Code: "on municipalities and origin"; Law "Assumption" 6, in the beginning, Digest: "on Municipalities"*—are no longer considered regarding the effect of Jurisdiction if someone has renounced the Right of Citizenship. *Gail, book 2, observation 36; Afflictis, Naples Decision 384, and there his annotator Caesar de Ursillis; Reverend Father Paul Laymann in Canonical Conclusions on Jurisdiction, chapter 1, number 6. (q)*

<gloss>(n)</gloss> As a precaution, it should be noted that if anyone seeks a domicile of residence without the right of Citizenship, **when someone [wants to]**

<column-break/>

**live in another place and yet not be a citizen**, then he acts cautiously if he ensures that he only wishes to be summoned there by reason of future contracts and crimes, but not by reason of contracts already celebrated elsewhere, or property located elsewhere. He can protect himself through a protest and letters of reversal. But then the Prince or Magistrate will see whether he wishes to grant such a thing or not. And a Prince's Councilor can see whether or not it is expedient to grant such advice to the Prince. If, however, he later buys something, he can procure such an exception for himself anew (if only the Magistrate permits it) or include it in the first Caution.

<gloss>(o)</gloss> *Foreigners* <note>original: *Forenses*</note>, if they live in a place as Councilors or Officials, are not held as absolute subjects, except by reason of crimes and contracts by which they bound themselves during their Office. Nor is the statute of the place where they die observed in their inheritance, but rather the place of origin or where they hold Citizenship; although otherwise, a deceased person is regularly succeeded according to the statute of the place where they die. Furthermore, in other cases, an intestate person <note>someone who dies without a will</note> is succeeded according to the Statutes of the place where the immovable property is located; thus it can happen that if the deceased leaves immovable property in different places, he is succeeded by different laws. Moveable property, however, is divided according to the Statute of the place of death, if he was a Citizen there or a privileged Inhabitant, such as Councilors and Officials are considered. The opposite occurs with a Will: for if a Bavarian makes a Will in Venice by virtue of the Venetian statute before two witnesses, it is also valid regarding property located in Bavaria, even though more witnesses are required there. The reason for the difference is that otherwise, a person would die partly tested and partly intestate, which the logic of law does not allow. For he who made a Will is deemed to have accommodated himself to the statute of whatever place.

<gloss>(p)</gloss> For example: if some Swabian Noble has immovable property, **landed estates** <note>original: *Landgüter*</note>, in Bavaria, he can be summoned here in Bavaria even regarding contracts which he celebrated elsewhere (in Swabia, for instance, or anywhere else), provided he also performed homage in Bavaria; otherwise if he did not perform it. The reason is because the **landed residency** <note>original: *die Landsässerey*</note> makes someone a subject and Citizen, which **landed residency** is induced through homage, **through the oath of land-homage** <note>original: *durch die Landshuldigung*</note>. From that oath, however, the oath of Office, **the official duty** <note>original: *die Amtspflicht*</note>, and the oath of a Vassal, **common feudal duty** <note>original: *gemeine Lehenpflicht*</note>, differ greatly: for in the oath of subjection, one promises **to be subject, obedient, and expectant** <note>original: *unterthänig, gehorsam und gewärtig zu seyn*</note>; but in the oath of Vassal and Office, one only promises **to be faithful and gracious** <note>original: *treu und hold zu seyn*</note>. See Speidel in Notable Matters, word: *expectant* <note>original: *gewärtig*</note>, folio 417, etc.

<gloss>(q)</gloss> Today, if anyone renounces the right of Citizenship, he is freed from all jurisdiction of the place of origin **where he was born as a Citizen.** But in Roman Civil Law, it was otherwise.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal jurisdiction from page 1176. While the previous page focused on "Domicile" (where a person lives), this page explains "Forum Rei Sitae"—jurisdiction based on where a person's property is located.</meta>

<page-num>1177</page-num>
<header>On Judicial Process.</header>

X. Secondly, one obtains a legal venue <note>original: *forum*</note> by reason of the location of the property <margin>(r)</margin> <note>original: *ratione rei sitæ*</note>, even if one does not have a settled Domicile there. <note>Citing various legal authorities: *c. fin. ext. de foro compet. l. quod legatur. 8. ff. de Judiciis. l. 1. § 1. & t. t. C. ubi in rem actio. l. forma 4. §. is verò. 2. ff. de censibus.*</note> This applies as long as the property is immovable <note>meaning land or buildings</note>. For if the dispute concerns movable property <note>such as livestock or goods</note>, Cujacius notes in his commentaries that a lawsuit can only be brought in the place where the item is located or found if the defendant is also found there.

Indeed, this must be understood with a distinction: if, for example, a man from Ulm stays in Ingolstadt with a horse that I believe belongs to me, I cannot simply sue him here and claim the horse. Instead, he has the right to be called back to his home court, especially if he provides a guarantee <note>original: *cautionem*</note> that he will appear for trial. It is a different matter, however, if he is a fugitive or someone difficult to bring to court; in that case, we turn to the Law regarding Arrests <margin>(s)</margin> and ask whether that horse can be seized. It is one thing to determine if a court is competent to hear a case, and another to determine if permission is granted to bind someone by an arrest. See also Hiltrop and the Lord President. 

But, if movable goods are brought to a certain place with a permanent purpose <margin>(t)</margin> <note>original: *perpetuâ destinatione*</note>, then they can be sued for there just like immovable property. <note>Citing *arg. l. Senatus 16. §. fin. ff. qui satisdare cog.* and Schultes.</note>

<margin>(r)</margin> For example, by reason of a house which a Citizen of Ingolstadt owns in Augsburg. Such a citizen can first be sued in Ingolstadt, as has been said, which is in the place of his Domicile, **in his right of citizenship** <note>original: *in seinem Burgerrecht*</note>. In that case, the Ingolstadt judge is not exercising the Law outside his territory, but is commanding the Citizen as his subject to do this or that—for example, to restore the house to the Plaintiff. Nevertheless, that Citizen is also considered subject in some way to the Council of Augsburg regarding that house located in Augsburg, so that he can likewise be sued in Augsburg. It is at the choice of the Plaintiff whether to go to the Ingolstadt or the Augsburg Judge. The Augsburg Judge has jurisdiction over that house. Therefore, even if the owner is a Citizen elsewhere, he is bound to defend his property or relinquish it.

It is different with movable things. The reason is that, for example, the man from Ulm (to stay with the example in the thesis) is using the public road, which ought to be safe for every Citizen of the Empire. If the Plaintiff says it is inconvenient for him 

<column-break/>

to go to another Judge, the defendant can reply that it is equally inconvenient for him to be delayed here and wait for the end of a trial.

<margin>(s)</margin> Seizures <note>original: *Arresta*</note> are so called when someone is stopped and, as it were, fixed in a certain place. For "Arrest" among the French means "firm." From this, they call judgments that have become final "Arrests," as being firm. Generally, however, such arrests are prohibited and only permitted in certain cases, as Gail teaches. If a case arises where someone can be arrested, then that arrest is not released unless the arrested person provides a guarantee to appear for trial in the place of the arrest. But if the person who requested the arrest does not follow through—that is, **when the arrestor does not bring a suit regarding the arrest within a certain time** <note>original: *wann der Arrestant in gewisser Zeit auf den Arrest nicht klagt*</note>—it is released by law. For it is unjust to detain someone by arrest without proving the reasons for the arrest in court, and in such a case the arrestor is liable for expenses. A legal venue usually becomes competent specifically through this act of arrest.

<margin>(t)</margin> For example, if someone has a shop <note>original: *Boutiquam*</note> in a certain place, **when someone carries on a trade in a foreign place and has an overseer or factor there** <note>original: *wann einer in einem fremden Ort ein Handel treibt, und daselbst einen Institutorem oder Factor hat*</note>, then he can be sued in the name of that commerce and those goods in the place where he carries out that trade. The reason for the difference is that goods being transported, **which one carries through** <note>original: *die man durchführet*</note>, are not subject to the jurisdiction of the place they are passing through. On the contrary, for one who carries on trade, for example, in Venice, it is fair that he can be sued in the name of that trade, since he derives a benefit from the location.

XI. Likewise regarding an incorporeal thing <margin>(u)</margin> <note>a "thing" that cannot be touched, like a legal right</note>, such as a jurisdiction or an annual rent, etc.; when there is a dispute, the action can be brought in the place where that Right is claimed. For such Rights are counted as immovable property. This also applies to personal debts, **to simple or current debts** <margin>(w)</margin> <note>original: *auf schlechte, oder lauffende Schulden*</note>. For in their name, one may bring an action both against the debtor and against a third party who is in possession of such Rights, in the place where they can be collected. However, this is only to be understood if the dispute is brought regarding such Rights directly and principally.

<margin>(u)</margin> For jurisdictions and similar things are accessories to immovable property and are attached to it.

<margin>(W)</margin> Let the case be this: Titius, a Citizen of Munich, owes me 100 florins by virtue of...

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "re," likely continuing with "vigo-re" (by virtue of) on the next page.</meta>

It distinguishes between immovable property (land), which always grants jurisdiction, and movable property, which generally does not unless it is part of a permanent business or has been legally seized via "arrest."</summary>

regarding a simple hand-written bond <note>original: *Chirographi*; a document signed by a debtor acknowledging a debt</note>, I have so far understood there is an interest, and I am a citizen of Augsburg. And this holds true only if the case is primarily about this debt; for if this debt were involved only as an accessory matter, the ruling would be otherwise.

<margin>
(x) It should be noted here that by a claim for inheritance <note>original: *petitione hæreditatis*</note>, one can first seek the actual ownership of the inheritance, and this is called an <term>Ownership trial</term> <note>original: *Judicium petitorium*</note>. (2) Sometimes a possessory action is initiated, where the Plaintiff only asks to be put into possession, and this is much better: because it is not necessary to prove as much, and through this, the burden of proof is transferred to the other party. For the position of the Defendant is always more favorable, and the condition of the one in possession is better. And even if this is done, the right to a full ownership trial always remains preserved.
Nevertheless, the possession of an inheritance can be sought by a double remedy: namely, either by an injunction to obtain possession, which is like a lawsuit, or by the pure and noble office of the Judge, <term>by virtue of office and authority</term> <note>original: *von Amts und Obrigkeit wegen*</note>, out of pure equity. This latter remedy is more prompt and has fewer requirements. (3) It can also happen that several people claim to possess the inherited goods, and so such possession is called "litigious" <note>disputed</note>. Then the Judge who is approached does not ask about the right of one or the other's possession, but only investigates who truly possesses it; once this is known, the ordinary ownership and possessory trials remain available to everyone. However, when the Office of the Judge is implored, or...
</margin>

XII. Furthermore, a claim for inheritance (x) can be initiated not only in the Domicile of the Defendant <note>original: *Domicilio Rei*</note>, but also in those places where the inherited items are discovered, as per the *single law of the Code, where inheritance is treated* <note>original: *l. unic. C. ubi de hæreditat.*</note> and there Wesenbec <term>in his notes at the end of law 7 of the Code on the claim of inheritance</term>. But truly, if an entry into possession of the inherited items is requested, and the Office of the Judge is merely implored, but a formal Lawsuit is not intended: see Menochius *on acquiring possession, remedy 4, questions 52, 53, 54, and following*; Achill, *Personal treatise on obtaining possession, number 71 and following, folio 31, etc.* Likewise, if the case concerns litigious or temporary possession (which others call an interim or *Provisional medium*, see Gail *observation 5, book 1*), this can hardly be done otherwise than in the place where the thing is located, according to Vultejus *on the single law of the Code, where possession is treated, number 42.*

<column-break/>

concerning disputed possession <note>original: *litigiosa possessione*</note> is alone contested, then it must be sought not in the place of the defendant's domicile, but in the place where the property is located <note>original: *loco rei sitæ*</note>. The reason is because here it is considered a matter of mere execution, not a formal lawsuit. Moreover, execution belongs to the Judge of the place where the property is located; Therefore, etc. because otherwise the Judge would not be able to execute the sentence, <term>but would have to</term> <note>original: *sondern müßte bey*</note> <term>ask the favor</term> <note>original: *darum begrüssen*</note> of the Judge where the property is located.

<margin>
(y) The reason is that as long as someone stays in another's territory, he must accommodate himself to the laws of that place; if, therefore, he offends against the Laws, he obligates himself to punishment. These things are true, however, only if he is caught there; for if he is captured elsewhere, according to modern customs he is not sent back to the place of the crime, according to the saying: "Where I find you, there I shall judge you." For the Great Lords fear lest, by such an act of sending him back <note>original: *remissionis*</note>, one might acquire some right in another's territory; nevertheless, today such Transfers <note>original: *Remissiones*</note> are made out of friendship. In the past, however, Magistrates were only Officials: not the proprietary Lords of the jurisdiction itself, and thus they had no cause for difficulty in denying transfers. But when offenders are sent back by right of neighborliness, it does not happen except with intervening Letters of...
</margin>

XIII. Thirdly, *by reason of a crime* <note>original: *ratione criminis*</note>, one obtains a legal venue in the place where the offense was committed, and there the offender can be punished, even if he is a foreigner (y) and has a Domicile established elsewhere, *law 1 & the Authentic "in which Province" of the Code, where crimes are treated, Novel 69.* For the crime grants jurisdiction over the offender, even to a judge from elsewhere, *chapter "it is permitted by reason," in the Extravagantes & chapter "Roman" on the competent court in the 6th book of Decretals.* Gail *on pledges, observation 3, number 11.* And this holds place even if the offender shines with greater dignity (z) or holds a privilege so that he cannot be sued except under a certain Judge, according to Lord Magerus *on Armed Advocacy, chapter 10, number 505 and many following.* Likewise, such a person can be punished with a heavier penalty than what is prescribed in Common Law, if another penalty is established by municipal law in the place of the crime, according to Bartolus *on the law "all peoples," number 10, on the supreme Trinity.* And indeed, to such an extent does the offender obtain a venue in the place of the committed crime: that there he can be afflicted with a penalty not only of the body, but also of deprivation (aa) and confiscation of goods located outside the district of the Judge in whose territory the crime was committed, *based on the chapter "you have requested," in the Extravagantes on the competent court;* yet in such a way that regularly those goods go to the Treasury <note>original: *Fisco*</note> of each respective place, Farinacius *question 25, number 94*; the Lord President *volume 3, counsel 65, final question.*

<meta>This page continues a legal discussion on jurisdiction—the authority of a court to hear a case. It specifically addresses "prorogated" or "extended" jurisdiction, which occurs when parties agree to use a judge who would not normally have authority over them.</meta>

<page-num>1180</page-num>
<header>Disputation</header>
<columns>2</columns>

...delegate for a collection of cases. From this, we find it decided that the jurisdiction of Commissioners, even those obtained from the Emperor, can be extended by agreement <note>original: *prorogari*—this refers to "prorogation," a legal process where parties consent to a court's authority</note>, *Mynsinger, Century 2, Observation 52; Gail, Book 1, Observation 33, number 3; Observation 35.*

(gg) <margin>The reason is that a non-entity has no qualities; <note>original: *non Entis nullæ sunt qualitates*—a logical maxim meaning you cannot grant attributes to something that does not exist.</note> therefore, where no jurisdiction exists, it cannot be extended.</margin>

(hh) <margin>But it seems that the power of judging can be given to an arbitrator, since arbitrations are treated like formal judgments, *Law 1, Digest on the acceptance of arbitration.* The response is that an Arbitrator does not have Jurisdiction <note>the formal power of the state to declare the law</note>, but only "cognition"—that is, the power to hear the facts—but not the authority to pronounce the law or to execute an arbitral sentence. As for the saying that arbitrations are treated like formal judgments, this should only be understood regarding the procedure and the form of the trial, not regarding legal power. For arbitrations do not extend jurisdiction. Indeed, such an Arbitrator cannot execute a sentence; instead, we agree that if we must, we shall go to another Judge who possesses jurisdiction to carry it out.</margin>

(ii) <margin>The reason is that a Judge appointed for a specific case is considered a private citizen regarding all other cases.</margin>

### XVI.

Furthermore, **extended jurisdiction** has no place unless the case in question is of the same nature. (kk) Thus, a criminal Judge cannot, even by agreement, judge civil cases; likewise, the jurisdiction of an appeals judge, a feudal judge, etc., cannot be extended to other types of cases. *The Presiding Lord <note>likely the author's teacher or the head of the legal faculty</note> in Deliberations on the Digest, Book 5, Question 9.* Although in the past such an extension could occur, (ll) in both personal and property-related actions—even without the consent of the competent Judge whose court was bypassed, *Vultejus, Law 1 on Jurisdiction, numbers 119 and 166.* But today, where Jurisdiction is very "jealous" <note>original: *Zelotypa*—meaning rulers are very protective of their legal authority</note>, an extension should not happen against the will of a superior, (mm) *Graevius, Conclusion 40, number 11.* For it is in the interest of a Lord that his subject not be judged by another; because such an act could easily prejudice the rights of the superior. Thus, a Lord of a fief is permitted to "evoke" <note>remove a case to his own court</note> a cause if a Vassal <term>Vassal: a person who held land under a lord in exchange for service</term> wishes to extend jurisdiction against the Lord's will, *Gail, Book 1, Observation 4, number 45; Rosenthal, Chapter 12, Conclusion 1, number 43, etc.* (nn)

(kk) <margin>Regarding the fact that criminal jurisdiction cannot be extended, the reason seems to be</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>that no one is the master of his own life and limbs, and thus he cannot bargain or transfer rights concerning his life and limbs. Furthermore, since extended jurisdiction requires the same "species" of authority in the judge being agreed upon, the jurisdiction of an appeals judge cannot be extended to cases of "First Instance" <note>the first trial of a case</note>, nor can a feudal judge hear non-feudal cases, or vice versa. The reason for all this is that a Judge appointed for a specific kind of case is regarded as a private person without jurisdiction when it comes to cases of a different kind.</margin>

(ll) <margin>The reason is that in the past, all jurisdiction was exercised by Magistrates not in their own name, but in the name of the Emperor; at that time all Judges belonged to the Emperor, and thus one could not prejudice another.</margin>

(mm) <margin>For everyone wants to hold authority by their own right, and will not suffer their jurisdiction to be undermined.</margin>

(nn) <margin>Understand this to be in a feudal case.</margin>

### XVII.

Equally, if someone has a **Privilege of Court** <note>original: *Privilegium fori*—a right to be tried in a specific court, such as a church court</note>, granted not so much for his own sake as for the sake of the competent Judge; (oo) then the extension or waiver of that court cannot be done without that judge's permission. Thus, a Cleric <term>Cleric: a member of the clergy or church official</term> cannot extend the jurisdiction of another judge (even another ecclesiastical one) without the consent of his own Diocesan Bishop. Moreover, he is not permitted to extend jurisdiction to a secular court (pp) even with the consent of his Bishop, *Chapter "Significasti" 18, On competent courts.* Because private agreements cannot derogate from public law, *Chapter "If Diligent" 12, same title,* though Bocerus, following Cujas, wrongly thinks otherwise in his *Treatise on Jurisdiction, Chapter 7, number 10 and following.*

(oo) <margin>For otherwise, a third party or a superior would be prejudiced. In this way, a Cleric is not his own master regarding Clerical Privileges, but conducts himself as a member of a body—either of a Diocese or of the whole Clerical Order.</margin>

(pp) <margin>For example, the Bishop of Eichstätt <note>original: *Eystettensis*</note> can permit a Cleric subject to him to be summoned before the Bishop of Regensburg <note>original: *Ratisbonensi*</note>; since this only tends toward the prejudice of the Bishop of Eichstätt, not the whole Clerical Order. But if the Bishop wanted to permit a Cleric of his Diocese to be summoned before a secular Judge, that would tend toward the prejudice of the entire Clerical Order, not just one Diocese; and therefore it cannot be done.</margin>

### XVIII.

There is, furthermore, a certain species of extension...

It also notes that members of the clergy cannot waive their right to church courts for secular ones because that right belongs to the Church as a whole, not the individual.</summary>

of <term>prorogation</term> <note>the extension of a court's authority over a person who would not normally be under its power</note>, when someone specifically and by express renunciation promises that in all places, (qq) wherever they may be found, they can be summoned or even arrested: no privilege or exception standing in the way, as noted by Bartolus, Zasius, and the Doctors of Law in the Digest regarding jurisdiction. Thus, it is also common for a clause to be added to a legal document of obligation stating <note>original: "daß man einen vor allen, auch Geistlichen Gerichten, vornehmen könne"</note> "that one may be summoned before any court, including spiritual courts." In that case, in the <term>Episcopal Courts</term> <note>the courts of a Bishop</note>, even for civil matters, debtors can be summoned, and a sentence of <term>excommunication</term> <note>exclusion from the sacraments and church community, often used as a legal penalty to force payment</note> is usually pronounced against them, as seen in the chapter *Significasti* on competent jurisdiction. The Lord Presiding Officer also discusses this in his *Practical Treasury* under the entry "Spiritual Jurisdiction." However, in certain places, a local statute forbids it, stating <note>original: "daß kein Bürger den andern, weltlicher Sachen halber, für ein geistlich Gericht fordern solle"</note> "that no citizen should summon another before a spiritual court for the sake of worldly matters." Such a statute exists in Cologne. *Statutes of Cologne, Title M, folio 87 and Title P, folio 113 and following.*

<margin>
(qq) This clause should be noted as a precaution, and it can be inserted into all legal instruments of obligation, especially into <term>debt bonds</term> <note>original German: "Gült-verschreibungen"—documents recording a debt or annuity</note>, where it is usually permitted <note>original: "daß man einen alsbalden mit Mandatis Executorialibus beklagen, und zur Bezahlung anhalten könne"</note> "that one may immediately sue with executive mandates and compel payment."
</margin>

Against this, however, it seems to stand that jurisdiction of a different kind is being extended, and thus it would be void. But the response is that through such a pledge of faith and submission, the person's conscience is bound to the Ecclesiastical Judge, and thus the jurisdiction of the Ecclesiastical Judge is sufficiently established.

### XIX. Finally, by Reason of the Case, (rr)
one must approach the Ecclesiastical court in purely spiritual cases (namely those which concern the Christian faith and the holy Sacraments: such as heresy; chapter *excommunicamus*, section *adjicimus*, on heretics; matrimonial disputes, Council of Trent, session 24, on the Sacrament of marriage, canon 2; and similar matters). And to this also belong matters that depend on spiritual things: (ss) such as cases of divorce, <term>defloration</term> <note>legal cases involving the loss of virginity or seduction</note>, the registration of offspring, and <term>legitimation</term> <note>the legal process of determining if a child was born of a lawful marriage</note>; namely, when it is doubted whether someone was procreated from a legitimate marriage or not? (Chapters *porrò* and *de illa* on divorces; chapter *prudenter* on donations between husband and wife; chapter 1 on who are legitimate children). Likewise, cases of <term>usury</term> <note>the sin of charging excessive interest on loans</note> and similar ecclesiastical crimes,

<column-break/>

the investigation and punishment of which belong to the Bishops; whether they are committed by laypeople or by clergy (chapter 1 on the Office of the Ordinary Judge; chapter *novit* on judgments). The Ecclesiastical Judge is also competent in "mixed cases"—those which have something temporal attached to something spiritual: such as <term>benefices</term> <note>church offices that provide an income</note>, the right of patronage <note>the right to nominate a priest to a parish</note>; chapter *quanto* on judgments; <term>tithes</term> <note>the tenth part of agricultural produce paid to the church</note>, and all rights and revenues of the church and <term>pious places</term> <note>charitable institutions like hospitals or orphanages</note> (chapter *si duabus* on appeals; chapter *si Clericus* on competent jurisdiction). This also includes wills and legacies for pious causes (Council of Trent, session 22, chapter 8). Furthermore, all cases brought against the clergy belong there, whether they concern property, personal matters, civil disputes, or criminal charges. Also cases of injuries by which church persons are affected by laypeople, etc. And see all these matters in the *Synodal Constitutions of the Bishopric of Constance*, part 4, title 2.

<margin>
(rr) It was said above that in all cases a defendant can be sued in their place of residence; however, this is to be understood according to the type of jurisdiction that magistrate holds. Since, therefore, certain cases arise which do not belong to secular jurisdiction, it follows that by reason of those cases, another court must be approached. And every Catholic Christian essentially sustains a "double personhood": first, a secular one regarding civil business, and thus they have a civil magistrate; and secondly, an ecclesiastical one with respect to spiritual matters, and in this view, they have another judge, namely an ecclesiastical one, and are subject to spiritual jurisdiction. For example, if someone is suspected of heresy, that crime is ecclesiastical, and so the Ecclesiastical Judge investigates it—whether the person is a heretic and to what degree—but later, punishing the heretic with the death penalty belongs to the secular magistrate, specifically regarding the execution of the punishment, but not the investigation of the crime.
</margin>

<margin>
(ss) Those cases mentioned here belong to the Ecclesiastical Magistrate both because they are connected to spiritual matters and by reason of the crime—again, as far as initiating the investigation of it, but not regarding the passing of the secular penalty. For example, when the question is whether a certain contract is usurious or not, investigating this belongs to the Ecclesiastical Judge; but whether this or that person actually performed such a contract is a matter of fact for the secular judge.

...is only an explanation of the mind and will of the Lord of the fief among his Vassals, and thus that dispute is said to be purely feudal. For if a dispute occurs between two Vassals that is not to be decided based on feudal law or concerning a fief, then the ordinary Judge must be approached.

(xx) Why, however, a Cleric can be summoned as a Vassal before a secular court, but not as the possessor of a secular thing (as was said in the preceding thesis), the reason for the difference is that a Cleric summoned regarding a fief is not summoned as a subject, but purely as a Vassal in the name of the fief, setting aside his Clerical personhood. But if he is summoned in the name of a "thing" <note>Latin: *nomine rei*; referring to property ownership</note>, it suggests a certain subjection less honorable to the Clerical order. A Vassal, however, is only an "honorary subject." And finally, Canon Law (*Extr. de Feud. concedit*) allows Lords to give judgment to Cleric Vassals in the name of the fief.

(yy) If a purely feudal action or dispute exists, then if it concerns two Vassals who also hold other non-contested fiefs from the same Lord, that dispute must be conducted before the Lord. But if the litigants do not hold other fiefs from that Lord of the fief, then that dispute belongs either to the Ordinary Magistrate or to the <term>Peers of the Court</term> <note>Latin: *Pares Curiæ*; a jury or panel of equals who held land under the same lord</note>. Hardly any other reason can be given for this matter than that it is almost everywhere accepted by custom; however, it is similar to Barbarian custom.

**XXII.** When, however, there is a dispute between a Lord and a Vassal, such as when the case concerns the Lord—that is, the Lord's loss or gain is involved in that question (as if the Lord is held to a Vassal for <term>eviction</term> <note>the legal recovery of property from a person by a superior title</note>)—then the Peers of the Court (<term>the feudal people, or the men’s court</term> <note>original German: *die Lehen-Leut, oder das Mann-gericht*</note>) stand as Judges, *c. unic. de Investit. in marit. factâ, c. unic. An apud Judic. vel Curiam, etc.* Rosenthal, *d. t. cap. 12. concl. 3.* But if the Vassal, summoned before the Peers by the Lord, denies that he is a Vassal, (zz) or if the Lord, summoned by the Vassal, does not recognize him as such, the controversy will belong to the Ordinary Judge of the matter, Rosenthal, *cap. 12. concl. 4. num. 9.* And some Lords also have the practice (especially those who assert that their Vassals are simultaneously their subjects) that all feudal disputes may be aired in their Courts, or the Court of the Palace.

(zz) Namely, if the Plaintiff <note>Latin: *Actor*</note> says the thing is feudal, but the Defendant <note>Latin: *Reus*</note> denies it, then the matter is by that very fact not purely feudal, and consequently the dispute belongs to the ordinary Magistrate. Indeed, only that case is held to be purely feu-

<column-break/>

-dal when both the Defendant and the Plaintiff admit the thing is feudal; but if in the proposed example the Plaintiff, for example, says the disputed thing is not feudal and thus claims it as his own, while the Defendant pretends to possess it as a fief, this dispute, as one not purely feudal, must be handled before the Ordinary Magistrate, who, when he has determined the thing is feudal, will remit the dispute to the Lord of the fief.

# CHAPTER II.
## ON VARIOUS TYPES OF JUDICIAL TRIALS.
### THESIS I.

Trials are divided in various ways. And (1) some are **Public**, and some are called **Private**: which Division, however, in today's Practice, seems to have hardly any use. And now it is more expedient to know which Trial is called *civil*, and which *Criminal*? On which matter there is also a discordant Opinion, as the presiding Doctor discusses in the debate, *from book 5 of the Digest, question 4.* And it is most commonly gone into that opinion, that when in a Trial the action is principally for private benefit, (a) whether it descends from a **wrong** <note>Latin: *delicto*; a private injury or tort</note> or from a **contract** (provided the party asks for something to be awarded to himself), then the Trial is called *Civil*. But when it arises from a crime, and the action is principally because of a committed crime for a penalty to be applied to the **Treasury** <note>Latin: *Fisco*; the public purse</note>; that is, for the public benefit or vengeance, then it is always called a *Criminal* Trial: whether a corporal or only a pecuniary penalty is to be inflicted, Duaren. *l. disp. 35.* Menoch. *consil. 265.* Marcell. Cala on the manner of articles, *gloss 5 f. 45. etc.* Hiltrop. *part 1. t. 4. num. 1.* Truly, from any crime, one can act in two ways, civilly and criminally. (b) *Section "in summa," Institutes on injuries; final law, Digest on private crimes; the law "who in the name," 25; the law "today," second to last, section 1, Digest on the Cornelian law regarding forgeries.* Civilly for interest <note>financial compensation</note>, and thus for the pursuit of family property; criminally for punishment, Maranta *part 4. distinct. 1. num. 4. & 8.* In the former way, the pursuit is done through an **Action**, which is called "on the facts" <note>Latin: *in factum*</note>; in the latter through an **accusation**. And neither of these removes the other, *law on common property, Digest on partnerships, law 7 at the end, law 9 on the recovery of stolen goods, Peguer. decision 27.*

But truly, when it is asked whether an appeal can be made in a criminal case: (c) then, according to the opinion of several authors, a case is only considered as such <note>meaning "criminal" for the purpose of restricting appeals</note> if it **carries a corporal punishment** <note>original German: *welche ein Leibstraff auf sich trägt*</note>. And so where such a punishment is not at issue, even if the case concerns a **Fine to be applied to the Treasury**, (d) they say an appeal must nonetheless be granted, according to Peter Friedrich Mindanus in *On Extraordinary Processes*, book 1, chapter 9, sections 8 and 12; Matthias Stephanus in the preface of his commentary on the *Criminal Ordinance of Charles V*; and the Lord President in *On Appeals*, chapter 7, paragraph 4. However, this does not seem to be proven, based on the argument in the *Institutes on Public Judgments*, paragraph 11.

(a) Namely, a Civil action is one that tends toward the private advantage of the Plaintiff. But a Criminal accusation is one instituted either by the Treasury—**the authorities by virtue of their office** <note>original German: *die Obrigkeit von Amts wegen*</note>—or even by a private person, but not for their own advantage, but rather to procure public vengeance, whether that vengeance be a corporal penalty or a monetary fine to be applied to the treasury.

(b) A Criminal action does not prejudice a Civil one, nor does it consume it, or vice versa. The reason is that they aim at different ends.

(c) According to the custom of Germany, there is no appeal in Criminal matters, lest the execution of the sentence be delayed by the appeal; however, recourse to the Prince is granted. And so in the Imperial Chamber, when a Defendant proposes that the process instituted against him was null, or that he is burdened against natural equity, then those petitions are accepted. For this sometimes happens when Municipal Cities or Landed Vassals possessing **high jurisdiction** <note>original German: *den Blutbann*; literally "the blood-ban," referring to the power to pass sentences of death or mutilation</note> most unfairly burden those criminally accused. In such cases, recourse is given **to the regional princes** <note>original German: *zu den Landsfürsten*</note>.

(d) This is nonetheless called **Criminal** <note>German: *Peinlich*</note>; however, this term *Peinlich* is not derived from *Pein* <note>meaning physical torture or agony</note>, but from *poena* <note>Latin for "penalty"</note>, so that it is, as it were, "penal" or a "penal punishment," etc.

**II.** Furthermore, there is a common division of Judgments, by which some are called **Ordinary**, others **Extraordinary**. But this division, as it was considered of old, is no longer in use; see the Lord President in his *Deliberations from Book 5, Question 3*. Today, however, one Judgment is called **Ordinary**, and the other **Summary** (e), as noted by Maranta in *The Mirror*, part 4, distinction 9. We are accustomed to call a **Summary** judgment that in which the proceedings are simple <note>Latin: *de plano*; literally "on the level ground," meaning an informal proceeding without a raised tribunal</note>, without the noise and formal appearance of a Trial; with the veil lifted, as they say, (f) or with only the

<column-break/>

truth of the fact inspected. Conversely, a trial is considered **Ordinary** when the proceedings follow the solemn order of judging, according to the *Clementines*, chapter *Saepe*, where it discusses the meaning of words. But although a case may proceed summarily, those requirements of the Judgment which descend from **Natural Law** or the **Law of Nations** must nonetheless be observed. Thus, even in a Summary Judgment, there must be a Summons, based on the argument in the *Clementines*, chapter *Pastoralis* on matters judged. Likewise, necessary Proofs cannot be omitted, according to the chapter *Novit* in the *Extraordinaries on Judgments*. On the other hand, there is no need here for a formal legal complaint <note>Latin: *libello*</note>, but a petition of any sort suffices, provided it contains only a clear narrative of the fact; and even that act which immediately follows the filing of the petition has the force of the **joinder of issue** <note>Latin: *litis contestationis*; the formal beginning of a lawsuit where the parties agree on the point of dispute</note>. Furthermore, shorter delays are granted, and these are to be cut short as much as possible. The Oath of Calumny also ceases <note>an oath where parties swear they are not acting out of malice</note>; see extensively Marcellus Calatractus on the method of articulating, glossary 3, paragraph 1, at the end of "appearance of a Trial"; Cacheranus's *Piedmontese Decisions*; Hiltrop, part 1, title 4, number 43, etc. Indeed, certain cases admit a Summary Process by their very nature: (g) it has a place in cases of **future maintenance** <note>Latin: *alimentorum futurorum*; payments for food and basic support</note>, because it is expedient to settle these simply, and even on a holiday, according to the Law 2 of the *Digest on Holidays*. Cases involving **Mandates** <note>legal commands</note> also have a Summary Process (h), where the trial begins with a Command. So too one proceeds Summarily when dealing with the execution of a sentence, etc. Althusius recounts many more cases in his *Dicaeologica*, book 3, chapter 54, number 5, etc. Sometimes Commissions are also issued by Princes so that a case may be handled summarily; however, in cases of doubt, this is not presumed to have been done; see Schrader, counsel 37. (i) By the statutes of many places, as also in the **Electorate of Bavaria** <note>original German: *Chur-Bayrisch Landrecht*</note>, part 1, title 1, articles 3 and 4; title 10, articles 1 and 2; and title 11, article 10, it is at the choice of the Plaintiff to institute either a Summary or an Ordinary Process. Once this is finished, the sentence is indeed ordered for Execution; but the defeated party can later return to an Ordinary Process, according to Maranta in the cited distinction 9, numbers 9 and following, and Fachinaeus in *Controversies*, book 10, chapter 80 and several following. So also in certain Courts, once a **Supplicatory Process** (k) is finished, one may still proceed by an Ordinary one. <meta>This page continues the legal analysis of judicial procedures, moving from the distinction between criminal and civil actions to the specific mechanics of "summary" versus "ordinary" trials and the difference between possession and legal ownership.</meta>

# on Judicial Process

In a conflict, one pursues one’s right. However, this does not prejudice the **ordinary and fuller investigation** <note>In legal terms, an "ordinary" trial is the full-length, formal procedure, whereas a "summary" trial is expedited.</note> which must be established later at the request of the party.

(e) A **Summary Judgment** is one in which only the process of **Natural Law** is observed. This process consists of three things: (1) first, that the parties are summoned, because if a case proceeds against an absent person who has not been summoned or heard, it is seen as contrary to natural equity; (2) it requires that both parties be heard—that is, the **Plaintiff** <term>Actor: the party bringing the case</term> tells the facts, while the **Defendant** <term>Reus: the party being sued</term> defends himself. (3) By Natural Law, it is required that the Judge believe neither party at first, but having heard both and weighed the merits of each side's case well, he finally delivers a sentence without haste. By contrast, in an **Ordinary Judgment**, all the "solemnities" <note>Formalities or strict legal rituals</note> of the process must be observed, which are required not only by the Law of Nature, but also by **Positive Law**—that is, the Civil and Canon <note>Church</note> laws.

(f) This distinction is drawn from antiquity. For formerly (and indeed, it is still observed this way in some places today), among other formalities of the Ordinary Judgment was this: that the Judges sat **behind tapestries** <note>original: "post Tapetes"; this refers to a curtained-off area for formal judicial deliberation</note> and heard each person separately one after another. None of this occurs in a summary judgment, where, as with many other rituals, this formality is removed, and the case proceeds "on the level" <note>original: "de plano," meaning a less formal proceeding held on level ground rather than on a raised judicial bench</note> as quickly as possible.

(g) This applies to matters that require a swift resolution and cannot suffer delay, such as in cases of **alimony** <note>original: "alimentis," referring to basic maintenance and support</note> and similar needs.

(h) These are called **Mandates**, where one begins with a "precept" or order—that is, where the matter is such that it does not seem to require an investigation of the cause, but rather just an execution of the law. However, in cases of Mandates, after the summary process is finished and the execution ordered, the Ordinary Process still remains available. The sentence from a summary process does not become a "judged matter" <note>original: "rem judicatam," a final ruling that cannot be appealed</note> except regarding the immediate execution in the interim. For example: Caius gave Titius a loan of a thousand florins under a mortgage of all his goods, with this clause: <term>that in case of non-payment, the creditor shall have the power to seize all and every one of the debtor's goods, with or without legal action, to take them for himself, and to keep them in hand until full payment, to use and enjoy them, unhindered by anyone.</term> <note>original German: "daß im Fall nicht haltens der Gläubiger Macht haben soll..."</note> In this case, if the debtor Titius resists, the creditor Caius cannot simply enter the mortgaged land and take it by force; nevertheless, those and similar clauses (which are called **Executive Clauses**) have a specific effect. Since the debtor has essentially pronounced a sentence against himself by signing the clause, the creditor can ask the Ordinary Judge, with all the Defendant's excuses removed, to 

<column-break/>

order that he be placed in possession of the mortgaged goods. This holds true even if the debtor has excuses—for instance, claiming he never received the money—he still cannot delay the execution of the sentence delivered in the Mandate case. Instead, the only thing left for such a debtor is that, after the execution is carried out, he may then institute an **Ordinary Process**. The prior sentence must stand in its execution until a different judgment is made; in the meantime, the question is not whether the judgment was "good or bad," but only whether a sentence was delivered. Thus, a sentence is demanded for execution even if the opposing party claims the sentence is void or that they should be restored to their previous state, unless the nullity is immediately obvious or appears clearly from the records. If the matter requires a deeper investigation, the sentence is to be executed without distinction, and the party burdened by that sentence is sent to the Ordinary Process.

(i) The reason for this is that a **summary process is odious** <note>In legal Latin, "odiosus" means the law looks upon it with disfavor or interprets it strictly because it bypasses standard protections and formalities.</note>.

(k) The **Supplicatory Process** <note>A process based on a "supplication" or formal petition to a ruler or high court</note> is of two types. Sometimes a response is written to the petition of one party after the other side has also been heard and the cause investigated; then that "Rescript" <note>A written reply from a ruler or high official that has the force of law</note> is ordered for execution. But sometimes someone offers a petition to the Court and a response is written without the other party being heard. In that case, the response does not burden the opponent, but is struck down by a simple contradiction to the case—that is, <term>if he offers to go to law</term> <note>original German: "wann er sich deß Rechten erbietet"</note>, that sentence or response is set aside. 

It should also be known here that this kind of process, which is commonly called Supplicatory, is not properly a "process," but is only, as it is usually called, an **official decree** <note>original German: "ein Amtlicher Bescheid"</note>.

### III. Thirdly, judgments are further divided into Possessory and Petitory <gloss>(l)</gloss>. <gloss>See the entire title on cases of possession and property.</gloss>

Because possession has nothing in common with ownership <gloss>natural law; final law; on acquiring possession</gloss> <gloss>(m)</gloss>, a dispute over **possession** is separated from a case of **ownership**. The Prætor <note>A Roman judicial official, here used as a general term for a judge</note> in **Interdicts** <note>Provisional orders to stop an action or restore a situation</note> or Judgments on Possession, does not ask about Ownership <note>original: "Dominio"</note>, but only about Possession—specifically, whether it is to be acquired, retained, or recovered. <gloss>See the entire title of the Institutes on Interdicts.</gloss> Therefore, in these cases, one must not act, prove, or pronounce judgment regarding ownership, but only regarding possession. This is done so it can be understood which of the litigants (while ownership or the main business is being investigated in another Judgment) the possession more rightly belongs to in the meantime. <gloss>law 1. paragraph 1.</gloss>

# Disputation
### 1

1. Section 2. Concerning private paths and rights of way. From this, possessory actions are also called **Interdicts** <note>original: "Interdicta"; in Roman law, these were expedited legal orders used to protect a person's possession of property without waiting for a full trial on ownership.</note>. (n) Skilled practitioners—for the sake of a faster resolution and because the advantage of possession is great and can be proven more easily than ownership—always look to see whether a possessory remedy can be pursued. (o) Only if these fail do they initiate an action regarding the property itself, as seen in the law **"He who has destined," 24, Digest, on reclaiming property.** <note>original: "l. is qui destinavit. 24. ff. de rei vindicat."</note> But when someone wishes to initiate a Possessory Judgment, the petition <term>libellus: a formal written statement of a plaintiff's case</term> must conclude with a claim for possession; the narrative of the ownership claim does not usually hinder this conclusion. See Tennin, **Precaution 197.** (p) However, there are some cases where a possessory action is said to have a "mixed cause" involving ownership; (q) and therefore, in such cases, victory cannot be hoped for without a title or other supporting evidence that proves—or at least suggests—ownership. Examples include matters of **Jurisdiction, Church Benefices, and Feudal estates**, etc. See **law 1, law 2, section "but also those," where the Doctors of Law comment on the Digest regarding interdicts.** <note>original: "l. 1. l. 2. §. sed & illa. ubi Dd. ff. de interdict."</note> See also Cacheran, **Decision 25, number 10**; Caesar Contard **on the single law, Code, on momentary possession, limitation 2, section 8, number 21.** Furthermore, Possessory and Ownership actions are sometimes joined together: (r) And then, if the ownership claim is sufficiently proven, it absorbs the possessory claim, and the ruling is made on ownership alone. But if the Plaintiff is not supported in the ownership claim, the sentence must be delivered only regarding the possession, according to **law 3, Code, on interdicts.** See Rutger Ruland **on articles, book 4, chapter 4**; Hartman Pistor, **part 1, question 45.** Likewise, if an action was brought regarding ownership, it is permitted to suspend that and pursue the possessory claim. (s) See Castrensis, **book 1, conclusion 278, at the beginning**; Cardinal Tuschus, **letter T, conclusion 412**; Hondedei, **consultation 25.** Regularly, the judge in the ownership case should be the same one (t) before whom the possessory case was finished. See Gail, **observation 32, number 11**; Menochius **on arbitrary rulings, case 171.** Finally, it must be known here that one type of possessory judgment is **full**, while another is **momentary** (u) or "most summary," as per the **single law, Code, on momentary possession.** See Hiltrop, **part 1, title 4, number 81, etc.** And they call the "momentary" judgment a decree for contested possession or a provisional decree (Vultejus **on the single law, Code, where it treats possession**) specifically when it is unknown who is the possessor, and both litigants claim to possess it. In that case (even while preserving the full 

<column-break/>

investigation <note>original: "cognitione"</note> concerning the possession), a decree is issued through a speedy process to prevent the parties from resorting to arms <note>A common legal phrase meaning to prevent physical violence or self-help.</note>, or to prevent one possessor from being defrauded. See Grævus, **conclusion 5, number 3 and following, and conclusion 1**; Gail, **observation 7.** In this "most summary" possessory action, an appeal has no place. See Grævus, **conclusion 7**; the presiding Lord **on appeals, 7, number 9.**

***

(l) It is too well known to need explanation that **Possessory Judgments** are those where possession is the issue; **Petitory Judgments** are those concerning ownership <term>dominium: full legal ownership rights</term>.

(m) Since possession, as is commonly said, is a matter of **mere fact**, the question in a possessory trial is not what right someone has in the "Principal Cause" (the ownership), but only whether they possess it. Hence, it can happen that someone is the **Possessor** and not the **Owner**, or conversely, the **Owner** and not the **Possessor**. In this latter case, the Owner retains "Civil Possession" <note>Legal possession recognized by law even without physical contact.</note> while the one holding the item has "Natural Possession" <note>Physical control or holding of the object.</note>.

(n) The term "Interdict" is used as if it were an **"interim dictum"** <note>original: "interim dicto"; meaning "spoken in the meantime." This is a historical word-play to explain that an interdict is a temporary ruling.</note>, until ownership is investigated. And certainly, someone obtains this interdict so that they are permitted to possess the item in the meantime, until the investigation regarding ownership is finished.

(o) Therefore, if possible, the possessory claim should always be intended first because a **Summary Process** is admitted there; add to this that possession can be proven more easily than ownership. For possession is a matter of fact, and a fact is perceived by the senses, whereas none of these apply to Ownership or law, which is therefore always more obscure.

(p) Understand this: provided that the conclusion of the petition speaks only of the possessory claim. Since the action being brought must be judged from the conclusion of the petition. The reason for this is that the ownership claim only serves to "color" <note>To provide a plausible legal background or justification.</note> the possessory claim, but is not considered to be brought into the petition by necessity. Suppose, for example, **Cornelius de Castro** has been thrown out of his property by **Titius**. He can use the remedy for recovering possession to regain that natural possession he lost, provided he proves (1) that he was in possession before he was thrown out, and (2) that he was expelled by Titius. If Titius then argues in his defense that the Castle from which he ejected Cornelius belongs not to himself but to someone else, Cornelius—to strike down this defense—can reply that this is a "defense based on the right of a third party," which therefore has no validity. The reasoning behind this is that sometimes the Plaintiff, in bringing a possessory action, adds a narrative about ownership, saying, for example, that he not only possessed that field or Castle...

# On Judicial Process.

...for many years, but also to have received it from his ancestors, etc. This narrative pertains indeed to the petitory action <note>an action regarding the legal right of ownership</note>, but it seems brought forward only so far as to "color" the possessory action <note>to provide a plausible basis or 'color of title' to the claim of current possession</note>, so that it might better win over the Judge. For a Plaintiff <note>original: Actor</note> who has been cast out of an ancestral Castle is more favored than one who alleges no cause at all for his possession.

(q) The reason is that in cases of this kind, it is also necessary by law to show that the possessory action is "colored" by a legitimate title. Indeed, jurisdictional rights, Church benefices, Feudal rights, and similar things, since they cannot be possessed without a title, must certainly be shown for that reason; otherwise, the presumption stands against the Plaintiff. The matter becomes clear through examples: suppose, for instance, I possess a house and am cast out of it; I can undoubtedly initiate an interdict <term>interdictum: an expedited legal order in Roman law to protect or restore possession</term> for recovering possession. Nor in this case do I need any "coloring" <note>legal justification for ownership</note> for such a possessory action, for every private person can possess a house, and is not considered incapable of possessing one. But if the Plaintiff, having been cast out of the house, also wished to claim some Jurisdiction over that house (if by chance it had any), it would be said to me: "Since you are a private citizen, you are not capable of Jurisdiction; therefore, first show that you are capable of Jurisdiction," and thus the burden would fall on me to allege a title for the acquired Jurisdiction. Since no private person is presumed to have Jurisdiction, in that case, the presumption would stand against me.

In matters of Church Benefices, suppose such a case: someone possessing a benefice or Parish is cast out of it. Once cast out, he cannot initiate an interdict for recovering possession unless he also proves himself to be the Parish Priest of that place. Since no one is presumed to be the Parish Priest of any certain place unless he has an investiture <term>investitura: the formal legal act of putting someone in possession of an office or land</term> or a presentation <note>original: præfentationem; a formal nomination to a church office</note>, here too a legal presumption stands against such a person. But if he indeed has the Investiture, yet it is argued that it is illegitimate, or obtained by stealth or deceit <note>original: sub- & obreptitiam</note>, etc., such an objection does not hinder him, since it pertains to the true petitory action; in a "mixed" possessory action, not the whole petitory matter, but only a part of it, is involved. And thus an evident difference appears between a title of possession and the right of possession which implies ownership.

But also in Feudal matters, the thing appears no less clearly: for if anyone claims a feudal right in a certain thing, he must likewise show this, since no one is presumed to be a Vassal <note>original: Vasallus; a person granted land in exchange for service</note>, but rather one is only made such through investiture.

<margin>Besoldus, Volume I. <note>referring to Christoph Besold, a prominent 17th-century German jurist</note></margin>
(r) That is to say, when for instance someone is cast out, and being cast out, he asks in Judgment that he be declared the true owner of that thing from which he was cast out, or at least that the possession taken from him be restored. This happens when someone wants to be fully secure but fears he might not prevail in the petitory action <note>the full trial on ownership</note>. Therefore, as a matter of greater caution, he joins both together, saying, for example: "I am the owner," so that by proving this I also seek possession; "yet I wish that if the proofs for Ownership are not sufficient, at least possession be awarded to me." Just as is customary in Wills; for example: "if this my last will is not valid as a testament, let it at least be valid as a codicil," <note>a codicil was a less formal document used to modify a will or provide instructions</note> etc.

(s) For example, I initiate a Petitory action and wish to claim a certain thing; however, I see in the progress of the case that I cannot prevail in the petitory action. It is therefore permitted for me, having dropped the petitory action, to move to taking up a Possessory action. The petitory action is dropped to speed up the case, because one proceeds more summarily <note>faster and with less formality</note> in a possessory action.

(t) Regularly, he who has judged in a possessory action ought also to judge in the petitory action. The reason is that he who has judged in the possessory action can more easily grasp the merits of the Petitory action, since he is already somewhat informed.

(u) "Momentary Possession" is that in which someone says he is in possession, and then the Judge recognizes most summarily (and as if in a moment) who possesses the thing; however, in such a case, a full possessory action remains available, as does the Petitory action. And in this Judgment, it is only asked who possesses, nor is it inspected whether he possesses legitimately or not; and this is done so that the parties do not come to arms <note>to prevent physical violence by maintaining the status quo</note>. But if the Judge sees that both are in possession, then he commits the thing to some third party as a sequestration <term>sequestrum: the temporary surrender of property to a neutral third party during a dispute</term>.

### IV. And likewise the ordinary Judgment, arising from Delegation.

And indeed, an ordinary Judge is usually called that person (w) who has Jurisdiction by his own right, not by another’s: that is, when it belongs to someone by the right of the Magistrate, by the very fact that he holds such a Magistracy. See Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a famous medieval commentator on Roman law</note> on law "more," number 4, "on Jurisdiction." Hiltrop, part 1, title 6. Those are called delegated Judges (x) to whom Jurisdiction has been granted by the mandate of a superior, or even of an ordinary judge, for the purpose of hearing and executing certain cases. See the whole title "on the office of him to whom jurisdiction is mandated," law "it is customary" 16, Digest on Jurisdiction <note>original: ff. de Jurisdict.; "ff" is the standard abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest of Justinian</note>. Hiltrop, part 1, title 7, number 11, etc. And certainly nothing is more frequent today than that Commissioners <note>original: Commissarii</note> are most humbly requested from the Imperial Majesty, or even from more powerful Princes. And Commissioners can be requested in certain cases by virtue of the *Austräg* <note>original: der Austräg; a traditional German legal mechanism for resolving disputes between the estates of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, Gail, book 2, observation 121. (y) However, it is not advised to seek these, because an appeal is granted from them to the Imperial Chamber <note>the Reichskammergericht, the high court of the Empire</note>. # Disputation

...a commission is decreed from the fullness of power, <note>original: "ex plenitudine potestatis"</note> so that His Imperial Majesty, by Imperial authority, would most graciously grant and issue a commission to specifically named persons. <note>original German: "daß Ihre Kayserl. Majestät eine Commission auf benannte Personen, aus Kayserl. Vollmacht, allergnädigst ertheilen, und ausschreiben wolle."</note> In such cases, these **Commissioners** (z) are very rarely given the power to deliver a final sentence; rather, they are only commanded to hear the parties in their arguments against one another, to investigate the circumstances of the entire matter, and, if possible, to settle the case amicably. <note>original German: "in der Güte vergleichen"</note> Furthermore, if such a settlement does not take place, they must send all the records, <term>Acta: the official case files and documents</term> along with their legal opinion, <note>original German: "Bedencken"</note> to His Imperial Majesty for a lawful decision.

Such Commissioners, or **Delegated Judges**, are required to notify the parties of the terms of the Commission (aa) through copies alongside the summons, and they must show the original document when the parties appear, according to the teachings of Zasius in his 9th counsel, number 2. These Commissioners appointed by the Emperor can sub-delegate their authority, <note>Latin: "c. Pastoralis. de Judic. deleg. Hiltrop. part. 1. tit. 8. (bb)"</note> and thus if a Prince or other high-ranking nobles are given the role of Commissioners by the Imperial Majesty, they usually sub-delegate the work to their own **Councilors**. <note>original: "Consiliarios"</note>

Likewise, in all delegations, the terms of the Commission must be strictly observed; (cc) and the Commissioner or Delegated Judge is bound to follow them most strictly. For indeed, outside the scope of the commission, he is seen to lack jurisdiction and power. However, if a case is committed to two or more people, then all must judge together, unless the commission contains the clause **"jointly and severally,"** <note>original German: "samt und sonders"</note> as seen in the laws regarding the office of delegates. (dd) If the person who delegated the authority dies, the delegation expires at the same time, unless the summons was already issued while he was living. (ee) Hiltrop discusses extensively how a Commission might expire through the death of the delegate, the delegator, or even the parties involved.

**Papal Legates** are also not merely ambassadors, (ff) but they carry out the duties of the Pope within the Kingdom or Province committed to them; they are his Delegated Judges.

<column-break/>

For this reason, they are called **Legates from the side**, <term>Legati à latere: high-ranking papal envoys sent directly from the Pope's "side" or immediate circle</term> not only because they are sent by the Pope himself, but because they are second only to him. See Nicolaus Boerius and Andreas Barbatias in their treatises on the power of Legates from the side, and Father Laymann in treatise 4.

(vv) All **Jurisdiction** flows from the Majesty or the Supreme Judge, as is taught in political science; but here we say someone has jurisdiction by their "own right" who holds it as a consequence of their **Office**, and not through the grant or delegation of another. Thus, today, **Ordinary Magistrates** are those who administer jurisdiction by virtue of their office, or by the power of their post. <note>original German: "die von Amts wegen, oder in Krafft ihres Amts"</note>

(x) This does not only apply to those to whom a specific case is committed by an Ordinary or a superior, but also to someone to whom an entire category of cases is sometimes delegated—for example, several cases that are mostly of the same nature. An example would be if someone were tasked with a general inquiry into **sorcerers**, etc. Similarly, sometimes not the whole case, but only a specific "article" of the case is delegated: for instance, when someone is ordered to examine witnesses to inquire into the truth of the case, but not to actually decide the whole case or deliver a sentence.

**Vicars** differ from Delegated Judges in this: an appeal from a Vicar’s sentence is not made to the person who appointed the Vicar, but to the superior of both. For example, an appeal from the Vicar of a Bishop goes not to that Bishop, but to the Archbishop. However, an appeal from a Delegated Judge’s sentence goes directly to the Delegator. A Vicar, therefore, is someone to whom the one who appointed him has handed over all his rights; thus, in a way, one would be appealing from the same person to the same person if one appealed from a Vicar to his appointer.

(y) In Germany, they call those judges **Austregas** <note>original: "Austregas in Germania"</note> who judge in the first instance between the "Immediate" States of the Empire <note>States that answered only to the Emperor</note>; an appeal from their sentence goes to the Imperial Chamber Court. They are called **Arbitrators**, <note>original German: "Austräg"</note> because they are given by convention, by virtue of a contract, <note>original German: "Krafft eines Vertrags"</note> having been established by the States in former times. There are various modes or types of these Arbitrators by which the States of the Empire can sue one another. One such method mentioned in the Chamber Court ordinances is that the Plaintiff may request a Commissioner from the Imperial Majesty by virtue of the **Arbitration rights**. For example, if the Bishop of Salzburg wishes to sue the Elector of Bavaria, he must nominate three Princes to him and allow the choice of before whom he wishes to be sued by virtue of the *Austräg*. The Bavarian must then choose one, or if he wants none of them, he must indicate a reason for suspicion or another cause. But regarding...

# On the Judicial Process.
