<margin>See Austregis in the *Thesaurus of Practice* under the word *Austräg* <note>original: "Austrägalinstanz," a system of arbitration for disputes between the states of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. Likewise Speidel in *Notable Matters* under the same word.</margin>

(z) It should be noted here that there is a difference between **Austregal Commissioners** and one who is appointed from the fullness of Imperial Majesty: the latter judges in the person of the Emperor, while the former are, as it were, Delegates of the [Imperial] Chamber.

(aa) For such Judges must prove their legal standing; otherwise they are not believed, even regarding the validity of a Summons.

(bb) Understand this to apply when the power of sub-delegating <note>passing the authority to a lower official</note> has been expressly granted to such Delegates in their Commission; otherwise, it is not allowed. The reason is that in a delegation, the specific skill and industry of a particular person is seen to have been chosen. There are, therefore, two kinds of Delegates: namely, some who can delegate further, and others who cannot. Just as **Ordinary Judges** <term>Judices Ordinarii: judges who have jurisdiction by right of their office</term> also exist in two types: first, those who have jurisdiction as a result of their office, <gloss>namely because they have been appointed as judges.</gloss> Second, others who have jurisdiction as a result of their territory, <gloss>by virtue of their territorial authority,</gloss> such as Princes, immediate Counts, and similar Estates of the Empire.

(cc) The reason for this is that whatever a delegate does outside (and much more so if against) their Commission is void, and does not even require an appeal.

(dd) When this Clause is missing, then all are required to judge together: because the person granting the commission is thought to have had regard for the persons and skill of each and every individual. However, that Clause is used when it is not known whether one or another wishes to accept the commission, or whether they can or wish to always be present for its execution.

(ee) For a legal proceeding is kept alive through the summons.

(ff) Understand this with a distinction: For sometimes the Pope sends **Legates** in spiritual causes where he has jurisdiction, and the thesis refers to these. But sometimes he sends Legates in temporal causes where he does not have jurisdiction, and these are true **Ambassadors**.

### V. Next follows the Proceeding based on the law *diffamari*, [from the Code] *on free-born persons set free.*
<note>The "Law Diffamari" (L. diffamari) was a famous legal remedy often called "put up or shut up." If someone publicly claimed you owed them money or committed a crime but refused to take you to court, you could use this law to force them to either sue you immediately or be silenced forever.</note>
This is not a formal lawsuit <term>actio: a legal claim</term>, but a plea for the judge's official intervention <term>imploratio officii: calling upon the judge's duty</term>, and a kind of defense, as Mundius treats in his *Treatise on Defamations*, chapter 4, number 29 and following. This is applicable when someone defames another (gg) either regarding a crime, or [by claiming] that the person

<column-break/>

owes him something, or possesses something belonging to him: then the defamed person can approach his Judge and ask that he summon the adversary and set a specific deadline for him to bring his claim (hh), or else that **perpetual silence** be imposed upon him. Gail treats this at length in Book 1, observation 10, and also discusses the process of this remedy in observation 12. He teaches especially that perpetual silence should not be imposed immediately upon a person's failure to appear <term>contumacia: legal "contempt" or failure to obey a court order to appear</term> (ii), but a double summons is required; and only after that is perpetual silence imposed on the defamer by a sentence; and that sentence brings a full legal disadvantage to him (kk). But if the summoned and alleged defamer appears and denies the defamation, and the defamed person who requested the help does not prove it, then the defamer is usually acquitted. However, when the defamer appears and confesses, or is convicted of defamation, then a deadline is usually set for him within which he must pursue the case regarding the defamation before a Judge; or if he does not do so, he is held to remain silent forever. Blarer treats this most extensively in a separate treatise written on the said law *diffamari*.

(gg) In the proceeding of the law *diffamari*, there is a double judgment: namely, the judgment on the defamation itself, and then on the principal cause. In the judgment on defamation, the defamed person is the plaintiff; but once that judgment is finished, when the defamer wishes to proceed in the main case, the defamed person (who was previously the plaintiff) begins to be the defendant.

(hh) For although normally no one is forced to sue against their will, a defamer binds himself to the necessity of suing through his own act of defamation.

(ii) If silence is imposed on someone due to their failure to appear, it happens only if the Plaintiff has first proved the defamation; if he does not do this, the absent party must be dismissed even from the summons.

(kk) That is, it produces an objection of a finished lawsuit <term>exceptio litis finitae: a legal defense stating the matter has already been decided and cannot be reopened</term>.

(mm) Nevertheless, a legal action for "Judgment Rendered" arises from his decision, *as stated in the law 'diem,' section 'stare' under the same title.* Formal agreements to arbitrate (*Compromissa*), however, are of such a condition that if they are secured by a penalty clause; (nn) then the winning party can sue for the penalty against the one who refuses to stand by the arbitrator's decision or award <note>original: "laudo"</note>. But once the ten-day period has elapsed, it is tacitly accepted, or acquires such strength that no appeal is granted against it; rather, it has the force of a settlement, *as explained at length by Cletzel on appeals c. 4. n. 47. and the Presiding Lord on appeals c. 3. §. 3.* An **Arbitrator** (oo) differs from an **Arbiter** in that the former is a friendly compositor, **a kind negotiator,** <note>original German: "ein gütlicher Unterhändler"</note> designated by the common consent of the parties without a penalty clause. (oo) An **Arbiter** and an **Arbitrator** differ in several ways. (1) A Legal Arbiter is bound to observe the judicial process; an Arbitrator is not, as he can proceed summarily. (2) An Arbiter is bound to pronounce according to written Law and Statutes, like a Judge; an Arbitrator, however, can deliver a decision based on equity and goodness. (3) An Arbitrator (commonly called a **negotiator/mediator**) <note>original German: "Unterhändler/ Vergleichsmann"</note> is usually appointed for the purpose of bringing the parties back to harmony, **so that he may reconcile them kindly,** <note>original German: "daß ers gütlich vergleiche"</note> whereas an Arbiter must regularly deliver a judgment. (4) There is no appeal from an Arbiter's decision; one must stand by it even if it is unfair, unless occasionally, when it is extremely unfair, a remedy is not denied; but from an Arbitrator's decision, a "reduction" is permitted—that is, the injured party can ask that the Arbitrator’s decision be reduced to equity. This reduction can be sought within 30 years, to be established by the judgment of a good man, that is, by initiating a trial.

### CHAPTER III.
# ON THE JUDGE, HIS OFFICE, AND RECUSAL.

### I.
The **Judge** <note>original: "Judex"</note> is so named because he speaks the Law <note>original: "Jus"</note> to the People; and in our law he is called a **good man** <note>original: "vir bonus"</note>, (a) *law 'continuus' 137, section 'cum ita' of the Digest on Verbal Obligations; law 'vir bonus' 18 of the Digest on satisfying judgments; law 'sed si unius' 17, section 'ait praetor' 5, at the phrase 'by the discretion of the judge, as if of a good man,' of the Digest on injuries.* See Menochius *on judicial discretion, book 1, in the preface, numbers 6, 7, 8, 9, & 10.* For he ought to have a twofold "salt": the salt of Knowledge, lest he be tasteless; and the salt of Conscience, (b) lest he be a Devil, *chapter 1 on judgments in the 6th book of the Decretals; Balbus on law 2 of the Code on pronouncing sentences from a notebook.* Although it does not seem necessary for a Judge to be literate. (c) *law 'expertes' 6 of the Code on decurions, book 10; Zasius on law 'si quis absentis' 5, section 'si Judex' number 6 of the Digest on actions and obligations.* For he can either take on **Assessors** <term>Assessores: legal experts who sit alongside a judge to provide advice on the law</term>: *the entire title of the Code on assessors; Hiltrop, part 1, title 10;* or more skilled experts are usually consulted.

---

(a) For although everyone and anyone is said or presumed to be good until the contrary is proved; nevertheless, a Judge is called a Good Man "preeminently" <note>original Greek: κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν</note> or according to excellence. And indeed in our Law, whenever mention is made of a *Good Man*—for instance, that a matter should be valued or decided by the discretion of a Good Man—it is always understood to be the Judge. And that is also what was said in the *preceding thesis*: that from an unfair decision of an arbitrator, a "reduction to the judgment of a good man" is granted—understand this to mean the Judge.

<column-break/>

(b) When it is asked whether a Judge is bound to judge according to his conscience, or truly according to the records and allegations, etc., it has a twofold sense. (1) Indeed, Conscience can be taken as knowledge of the fact: for instance, the Judge, from his own physical senses, saw or heard this or that himself, and therefore knows someone to be guilty or innocent, but the Records and the evidence demonstrate the opposite—and it is asked, what must be done? And indeed, if the Judge saw, for example, someone commit a homicide, and that person is afterwards accused before the same Judge, but without proofs: the Judge does not seem to sin in that case if he nonetheless acquits him, and thus acts against his own knowledge. The reason is that he does not know this as a Judge, but as a private person. Some, however, say that in this case the Judge ought to resign his office and be examined as a witness; for although the word of one witness does not suffice for condemning, nevertheless if he is beyond all reproach <note>original: "omni exceptione major"</note>, that is enough for judicial torture. But if, conversely, the Judge knows someone to be innocent who is nonetheless convicted by witnesses beyond all reproach, the Judge in this case certainly cannot condemn such an innocent person: because he would sin against his own Conscience and would truly become a murderer in the "court of the soul" <note>original: "foro animae"</note>; he ought therefore rather to abstain from his office regarding this case, and notify a substitute of his knowledge, committing to the substitute's discretion what should be done afterward. (2) In the second way, this question can be understood regarding that case where a Judge in his conscience thinks a penalty is too harsh, etc. For example, if a Judge were of the opinion that the **Carolina** <term>Carolina: the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, the fundamental criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire (1532)</term> was an unfair sanction in its criminal ordinance which commands that a thief who has stolen more than five gold coins from another by breaking and entering should be hanged. And in that case, the Judge can judge according to that law with a safe Conscience, even against his own judgment. The reason is that the Conscience or Judgment of one or another person ought not to prejudice the law, but rather everyone ought to subject themselves to the Laws, and not argue about them; seeing as that is only permitted when the question is whether a Law should be passed, but not when the question is whether a law already passed should be put into execution.

(c) For this reason, illiterate Judges used to judge in the past, because such offices were mostly granted to veteran soldiers as a reward, who had their **Assessors** sitting with them on lower benches; from which Assessors the **Pedane Judges** <note>original: "Judices Pedanei" — minor judges who sat on low seats (benches) rather than high tribunals</note> (concerning whom we have already spoken in *chapter 1, thesis 1 above*) were later taken. Whence from time to time in judgments of this kind...

**II.** Furthermore, the office of the Judge is called either **mercenary** <note>In this legal context, "mercenary" refers to the judge’s "bound" duty to follow specific legal formulas, acting as a servant of the procedural law.</note> or **noble**: (d) The former does not stand by itself but serves the case, or the action and the prosecutions which take place before the Judge, and thus serves the entire process to be carried out. Matthias Stephan, *On the Office of the Judge, book 2, chapter 5.* Conversely, they call the Noble office of the Judge that which stands by itself and does not serve the specific action: and so the Judge exercises it by his own authority, that is, by the authority of the Law, even if no specific action is proposed, *Stephani, same book, chapter 4.* Hence Longovallius, *on the Law of Command [Imperium], 3. n. 2. regarding Jurisdiction,* says that the Noble office of the Judge primarily originates and descends from **equity** <note>Equity refers to the principle of fairness that looks beyond the strict letter of the law to achieve a just result.</note>; namely, when no specific legal action can apply, and thus that defect is supplied by the office of the Judge; and what the strict law does not command is to be dispatched according to what is fair and good, no other protection having been left in the laws. And so it is said that the office of the Judge is to be preferred to the action; Rutger Ruland, *part 2, book 2, chapter 4, number 12.* because, of course, those things are dispatched more quickly which are done by the noble office of the Judge, and thus through a summary process; and also that which is not granted by strict law is decreed out of equity; and where the Judge would not provide relief, the aggrieved party would be destitute of all help: or where an action indeed applies, but relief is provided more quickly by the Judge’s office, *Stephan, book 2, chapter 4.* And for that reason, that common and solemn clause of the Advocates is not out of place: <gloss>hereupon humbly invoking the Lord Judge’s Most Noble Office.</gloss> (e) <note>original German: "hierüber deß Herrn Richters Hochadelich Ambt unterdienstlich anruffend."</note> (Although Matthias Stephani thinks that the mercenary office of the Judge should rather be implored, *book 2, chapter 5, number 3.*) For by this they imply that the party must be succored, not only more quickly, but also through a summary process; and also in the event that the instituted action perhaps has no place, and other ordinary remedies are lacking.

<margin>(d) The mercenary office of the Judge is indeed as if it were servile. (For a mercenary is called something like a <gloss>servant</gloss> <note>original German: "ein Dienstmann"</note>) it seems to be so named because a Judge proceeding from it is bound to follow precisely the formula and requirements of the action. But the Noble office, as if opposed to the Mercenary, is that when a Judge can do something out of equity against the rigor and solemnities of the Law, <gloss>by virtue of his office</gloss> <note>original German: "von Amtswegen"</note>. Certainly when a Prince does something, he is seen to do it from a Noble office or judgment for the reason that he is not strictly bound by the Laws.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>(e) This clause is very beneficial and effective, for it contains within itself as if it were said: if I cannot be helped from the Mercenary office of the Judge, let me at least be helped from the Noble office and equity.</margin>

**III.** And furthermore, since it is a serious thing to litigate before a suspected judge, *Law "Apertissimi," 16. Code on Judges.* Hence, commonly, both the Ordinary and the Delegate are said today to be able to be recused as "suspected," (f) Gail, *Observations,* 1. obs. 33. in the beginning. Zanger, *On Exceptions,* part 2, chapter 4, number 7. And so it is observed in practice that if anyone wishes to recuse an ordinary Judge—especially a College of some Municipal Town—he then reveals this to the Prince and seeks a transfer to another Tribunal. However, if someone wishes to call an illustrious College "suspected"—<gloss>such as the Imperial Aulic Council, the Imperial Chamber Court, a Prince’s Chancery, or a High Court</gloss> <note>original German: "als der Kayserliche Reichs-Hofrath, das Kayserliche Cammergericht, eines Fürsten Cantzley, oder Hofgericht"</note>—he is rightly not heard: but it is nevertheless permitted to object against the person of one or another Assessor: and then that person usually abstains from the duty of judging, Graevius, 1. conclusion 33, number 6, etc.

<margin>(f) Formerly, an Ordinary Judge was usually only one person, and therefore could more easily be made "suspected" than today, where everywhere Ordinary Judges are mostly several and constitute an entire College. Formerly likewise, appointed arbitrators took cognizance of the causes of suspicion, and a Bishop was joined to the suspected Judge; today, if Delegates or Commissioners (as they call them) are in any way suspected, that is indicated through a petition to the Delegating authority, with the joined request that another be named; this can be done without offense, and sometimes another Commissioner can be sought for a slight cause. However, to recuse an entire College, especially the Council of some great Prince, is considered disrespectful [incivil]: nevertheless, a party is permitted to ask the President that one or another Assessor not be admitted to the deliberation of the case.</margin>

But the Municipal Colleges of Cities can still today be rendered "suspected" in their entirety, and then one must petition the Prince to substitute another College, <gloss>that the matter be transferred from one city to another.</gloss> <note>original German: "daß man die Sache von einer in die ander Stadt weise."</note>

## CHAPTER IV.

## ON THE PETITION FOR OBTAINING A CITATION, AND CONCERNING THE CITATION ITSELF, ITS SERVICE, THE MESSENGER’S REPORT, AND THE RETURN OF THE CITATION.

### I.

**I**n handling judicial controversies, a certain Order has always been observed: which is seen in the legitimate discussion of the disputed matter, as well as in its definition or decision. However, since a Judge does not usually grant his office unless requested—and thus, unless he is first compelled, he cannot call an adversary into Court—nor is the adversary bound to come unless called; therefore, a petition (a) or a "suppliant booklet" <note>original: *libellus supplex*; a formal written request to the court to begin an action.</note> must first be presented to the Judge. This contains the summary of the action to be intended, so that the Judge may cite the party to be convened, *Matthias Stephan, On the Office of the Judge, book 5, chapter 1, § 1; Maranta, part 6, title on the offering of the booklet, at the end.* For this reason, it must also be entered into the records that the citation was made at the instance of a party, *Bartolus on the law "si finita", section "Julian", number 3, on damage not yet done.*

### II.

**II.** If, however, the Judge should decree a citation despite insufficient grounds for establishing Jurisdiction, he is not to be sued for expenses; rather, the cited person who appears may, by alleging the defect of jurisdiction, ask that the plaintiff be condemned to pay the expenses, (b) and that he himself be dismissed from the citation, (c) *Petrus Friderus, On Extraordinary Process, chapter 21, number 7.* For greater caution, a Judge sometimes decrees a citation "at the risk of the party" <note>This means the plaintiff bears the responsibility if the court is later found to lack jurisdiction.</note>. *See Gail, book 1, observation 31, number 4, and observation 119, number 7.* Furthermore, there are certain persons who cannot be called into court without permission (d): such as Parents of either sex to the infinite degree, and others to whom reverence is due, *law 13, Digest on calling into court.* Likewise, a wife may not properly summon her husband, nor a Subject summon the Republic or a Magistrate, *Alciatus on law 1, Code on calling into court.* Is this seeking of permission still necessary today? Although it is debated, *Vultejus, Scholastic Disputations, chapter 1; The Lord President in the "delibat", Digest book 2, question 7*, it is nonetheless safer to request it simultaneously in the suppliant booklet for the citation.

(a) When I know before which Judge I must act, the next step is to ensure my adversary is cited: because nothing is to be decreed against one who is not cited, as they are unable to defend themselves; and a Judge, by his office, grants nothing to anyone unless implored. Therefore, first of all, one must ask through a suppliant booklet that the party be cited.

<column-break/>

(b) A Judge indeed ought not to cite one who is not subject to his Jurisdiction, or where the court is in some way not competent; but if this is done at the instance (that is, the request) of the Party, the Plaintiff (the Actor), not the Judge, refunds the expenses to the person improperly cited who appeared and was dismissed from the instance. This is because, as I said, this was done at the request of the Party, and the Judge believed the claims of the petitioner, <term>in which he said that the matter was appropriate to this place.</term> <note>original German: "in dem er gesagt, daß die Sach daher gehörig seye."</note>

(c) A fine distinction should be noted here between being *absolved definitively* and being *absolved from the Citation*, or what is the same thing, *from the Instance*. For one is absolved definitively when one is freed from the entire cause, <term>when, for example, it is recognized that he is not obligated to pay anything.</term> <note>original German: "wann v. g. erkannt wird, daß er nichts zu bezahlen schuldig."</note> But he is said to be released from the instance—that is, <term>from the judicial compulsion</term> <note>original German: "von dem Gerichtszwang."</note>—<term>when it is recognized that the Defendant is not obligated to answer.</term> <note>original German: "wann erkennt wird, daß der Beklagte zu antworten nicht schuldig sey."</note> For it may happen that a Defendant of this kind remains nonetheless obligated, and can be sued in another place or time. Suppose, for example, you owe someone 100 florins under a condition, to be paid after three months; now, if you are sued before the condition is met or the three months have passed, you can object and ask to be absolved from the Instance; you nonetheless remain obligated, and after the condition...

<margin>(d) Formerly, when someone wished to call a person to whom they owed reverence <note>This refers to "Right of Patronage" or family status, where a social inferior (like a child or former servant) needed special permission to sue a superior.</note> into court, obtaining "leave to sue" <note>original: "veniae impetratio"</note> was absolutely necessary. This was for the specific reason that a plaintiff was permitted by his own authority to call a Defendant into court, and even to drag or order him to be carried there if he refused. Today, where no one is summoned except by the authority of a Judge, obtaining such leave might perhaps seem not so necessary; nevertheless, for greater caution, that leave can also be requested at the same time in the formal petition <note>original: "supplex libellus"</note> which one submits for the Citation.</margin>

## III.

A Citation is necessary in every preliminary act; <margin>(e)</margin> and if it is omitted, it renders the act null and void, according to Laurentius Tennin, *Caution* 19 and following, and Hiltrop, part 2, title 1. Citations are either Simple or Edictal. <margin>(f)</margin> A Simple citation is further considered twofold: for it is made either for a specific point of the case, or for the entire case. Generally, it is better for someone to be cited for the entire case; this is standard practice in the Imperial Chamber <note>The *Reichskammergericht*, the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, as noted by Mynsinger, observation 33, and Gail, book 1, observation 51, number 10. Also, as a matter of legal counsel, Cavallus suggests in his *Common Opinions*, question 22, that from the beginning of the case, the citation should be general—covering the whole case, every single day, and every act of the case up to and including the final sentence. This is especially done if someone is in distant parts or if their absence is feared.

<margin>(e) Understand this to mean that the person to be cited might suffer some disadvantage or prejudice. He must be cited so that he may come and defend himself; for defense is a right of natural law. Thus, if the ability to defend oneself is taken away—except in a very few cases (such as when the matter is notorious, there is danger in delay, or the Sovereign or Republic might be endangered thereby, etc., regarding which political experts should be consulted in their proper places)—the procedure is against nature and therefore void.</margin>

<margin>(f) An Edictal citation is one made either through a publicly posted writing or sometimes through a public proclamation <note>original German: "durch öffentliche Ausruffung"</note>.</margin>

## IV.

There is, however, a difference between a Citation and a Denunciation. <margin>(g)</margin> Indeed, it is called a "denunciation" when someone is summoned not because they are a primary party with an interest (such as a defendant or a plaintiff after the petition is offered and the citation

<column-break/>

decreed), but because it is thought to be in their interest to know: Tennin, *Caution* 5. Or, for example, if a seller is called to assist a buyer, according to *the Code on Eviction*, law 29. This is done so that the seller cannot later be sued for "eviction" <note><term>Eviction</term>: In Roman law, this refers to a buyer losing possession of property because a third party proved they had a better legal title. If the seller wasn't notified to defend the title, the buyer might lose their right to be reimbursed.</note>: Mangilius, *On Eviction*, question 9, number 6. In such a case, there is no need for the "denounced" person to appear, nor does his absence delay the Process; it is usually done solely for the sake of notice.

<margin>(g) That "denunciation" is one made for notice only, not so that the person is compelled to come, but only so that they cannot later pretend ignorance. For example: Titius sold me a house; Caius sues me and says that house is mortgaged to him for one hundred florins. Here, I as the possessor defend my property, and I can later sue Titius the seller for "eviction" if the house is taken from me. However, lest the Seller complain after the house is lost—or if I am condemned to pay those hundred florins—that he was not heard, or that he had legal defenses which could have easily defeated the action, he is "denounced." This informs him to come and defend me. If he does not come after the denunciation (which is his choice), then once I am condemned, he can be sued immediately for the loss. Therefore, when he comes to defend me, he is then called an "Intervening Third Party" or an "Assistant."</margin>

## V.

A citation is carried out by a messenger <margin>(h)</margin> to whom the Judge has specifically entrusted the task. This is done either by the Messenger’s spoken words or, which is safer, by a letter written by the Judge. The Citation is made either to the person cited or to their home (to the wife, children, etc.). If the person being cited is absent, <margin>(i)</margin> it is safer for a copy of the citation to be left there, or even fixed to the door, as per Mynsinger, observation 37. It can be served even on a holiday, according to Maranta, part 6, number 120, and others.

<margin>(h) In the Imperial Chamber, and almost all other Courts, there are sworn Messengers who execute Citations. If such a Messenger is not present, because sometimes a citation is given to a party in writing, then it must be served by a Notary. In the Imperial Chamber, a registered <note>original: "immatriculatus"</note> Notary is specifically required, as is also the case in the Imperial Court <note>The *Aula Caesarea* or Aulic Council.</note>.</margin>

<margin>(i) Or if he refuses to accept the Citation; for these two situations are treated as equal.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of "Citations"—the formal legal summons used to bring a party into court. It addresses specific circumstances such as summonses issued on holidays, summonses for people outside a judge's territory, and the "Edictal Citation" used when a person's whereabouts are unknown.</meta>

# Concerning Judicial Process.

<margin>(k) A person can also be cited on a holiday; the reason is that such an act is not part of "contentious jurisdiction" <note>This refers to the active, disputed phase of a trial</note>, but is merely a preparation for the exercise of jurisdiction. However, no one can be cited to actually appear on a holiday. 
It should be noted here that if someone is cited in this manner—for example, to appear ten days after receiving the summons—then this clause should be added, or at least understood: that if that tenth day falls on a holiday, they should appear on the following court day. Otherwise, the citation would not be legally valid.</margin>

### VI.
Even when a person being cited is not personally subject to a Judge’s jurisdiction, if they happen to be staying within that Judge's territory, the messenger may still cite them. However, if the person to be cited is located in a foreign territory, the citation is made through "Letters of Request" <note>original: "litteras Requisitoriales"</note>, as noted by Gail (Book 1, observation 56). These are directed to the Judge of that location, for outside their own territory, no one can perform any act regarding "contentious jurisdiction" <margin>(m)</margin> (according to the law *fin. ff. de Jurisd.*). That local judge then serves the citation to the person. This rule is expanded even if the person being cited is otherwise a subject of the citing Judge, as discussed by Zafius, who also deals with the case of students who, at the time of their admission, promised under oath that they would appear whenever cited regarding contracts.

<margin>(l) Specifically, in legal aid, or as they call it, by "the law of the City."</margin>

<margin>(m) Such is a Citation here, since it is a kind of command which cannot be issued except within one’s own territory.</margin>

### VII.
Sometimes a Judge can even cite someone in person—namely, if he has the person right in front of him (as noted by Matthias Stephanus and Gail). Furthermore, a person who is already present should not be cited; however, someone called for a different case is not forced to respond immediately, since they ought to come prepared. They are only forced to receive the "libellus" <note>The formal written complaint or legal claim</note> <margin>(n)</margin> (as discussed by the Presiding Lord in his deliberations on the second book of the Pandects). There is also a "real citation," which is done by the physical arrest of the person (as in the chapter *si Clericos*). This is regularly used today in criminal cases, according to Hiltrop (part 2, title 1).

<margin>(n) And to request a deadline by which he must respond.</margin>

### VIII.
An "Edictal Citation" <margin>(o)</margin> is the name given to a summons 

<column-break/>

which is posted on the doors of a Church, or the Courthouse, or in another public place. This takes place when the person to be cited is not in a certain location and cannot easily be notified, whether they are in hiding or are absent in good faith (Gail, book 1, observation 56). This edictal citation is to be posted in one place, or in several at the Judge’s discretion, provided it is likely to come to the notice of the person called. This citation also takes place when the interested parties are unknown, as happens in public auctions or in <term>debt and bankruptcy cases</term> <note>original: "den Schuld- und Gant-Sachen"</note>. Likewise, if someone buys an estate or a Castle and fears it may be burdened with mortgages or other encumbrances, then such a citation can be issued by the Imperial Chamber or the local Judge (if the goods are not "immediate") <margin>(p)</margin>. Gail suggests this as a precaution <margin>(q)</margin> for buyers of Castles and estates, so they may be secure against "eviction" <note>In this legal sense, "eviction" refers to losing the property later because someone else proved they had a prior legal claim or mortgage on it.</note>.

<margin>(o) This takes place in two cases: (1) when we do not know where the person to be cited may be found; (2) when we do not know who exactly should be cited. In the first case, a citation is appropriate when the person is a fugitive or so absent that their location is unknown; every Edictal Citation must be "peremptory" <note>A final notice that carries a penalty if ignored.</note>.</margin>

<margin>(p) That is, subject directly to the Emperor: in that case, the citation can be proposed by any Judge to whom they are subject. However, when those goods are "immediate"—<term>meaning they are free noble estates and not subject to any local lords</term>—then the citation can be issued by the Imperial Chamber or the Emperor’s Court.</margin>

<margin>(q) This is certainly most useful and should be well-observed in purchases and similar transactions.</margin>

### IX.
In every citation, the following must be expressed: the name of the Judge, the name of the party being cited and the party citing, along with the cause of the action, a safe place for the judgment, and a suitable day or deadline for appearing (Gail, book 1, observation 48).

### X.
Furthermore, regarding the deadline, a citation is either "peremptory" <note>final and mandatory</note> or "simple" <margin>(r)</margin>.

# Disputation

A citation is called **Peremptory** <note>original: "Peremptoria"</note> when someone is summoned in such a way <margin>(r)</margin> that a specific day is assigned to them for a final appearance, and indeed peremptorily <note>meaning final and non-negotiable</note>, so that if they do not appear, the case shall proceed one way or another. A third citation is also considered peremptory, even if that specific warning clause is not explicitly stated (according to Wurmser, title 6, observation 2). It is safer, however, for the usual warnings to be added to the third summons. In certain cases, and likewise in all **Edictal citations** <note>publicly posted notices when a person's location is unknown</note>, one summons is issued for all; here, the person cited is given 30 or more days (at the Judge’s discretion), specifically 10 days for the first, 10 for the second, and 10 for the last and final Peremptory Court Day (Wurmser, same location, observations 1 and 6).

(r) A **Simple Citation** is where someone is simply summoned to appear. A **Peremptory Citation**, however, is that which summons someone with a warning: if they do not come, their power to raise objections in the future is "perished" <note>from the Latin *perempta*, meaning destroyed or taken away</note>, and likewise that the Judge intends to proceed in **Contumacy** <note>a legal term for willful disobedience or failure to appear in court</note>. A simple citation becomes peremptory if someone is cited three times, or even only once but with the warning that if they do not come, their power to propose objections in the future is lost. Furthermore, understand that a peremptory citation which is final from the very first instance must contain within itself three simple terms—that is, as many days as are usually prescribed for three simple summonses—just as the clause cited in the main text demonstrates.

**XI.** Furthermore, the following must be diligently entered into the **Records**: both the report of the **Messenger** <margin>(s)</margin> and what was done regarding the **Edictal citation**; or, if the person to be cited lives outside the territory, <margin>(t)</margin> what was done in the name of that citation (Laurentius Tennin, caution 229; Hiltrop, part 2, title 1; Graevius, conclusion 54). Indeed, the report of the messenger is to be believed <margin>(u)</margin> if he describes the circumstances: that he legitimately cited the person, or how the citation was executed, or how the formal notice (discussed above) was made (Gail, book 1, observation 54; Mynsinger, book 6, observation 10; Vantius, *On Nullity from Defect of Citation*, number 40 and following; Graevius, conclusion 1). However, a citation is not valid <margin>(vv)</margin> if the messenger to whom it was entrusted does not execute it himself (Mynsinger, book 1, observation 7). An **illegitimately executed citation** is also made valid <margin>(x)</margin> if the cited person actually appears,

<column-break/>

(Mynsinger, book 2, observation 18). Likewise, the citation and its execution must be presented as evidence; <margin>(y)</margin> especially if the person cited is absent and the case must proceed in contumacy. Finally, a citation induces **pre-emption** <margin>(z)</margin> <note>original: "praeventionem," determining which judge has priority in a case</note>, perpetuates the **jurisdiction** of a delegated Judge, <margin>(aa)</margin> interrupts **prescription** <margin>(bb)</margin> <note>the statute of limitations</note>, and induces **pending litigation** <note>original: "litispendentiam"</note> (Hiltrop, part 2, title on the end and effect of citation). <margin>(cc)</margin>

(s) Specifically: in what places the citation was made and what its content was. The messenger's report must contain the time the citation was delivered, and whether it was given to the party himself in his house, or to his wife, children, etc.

(t) For example, it must be related what was written to the Judge of that place, what he replied, etc.

(u) For although otherwise a single witness is not believed—as if "one witness is no witness"—in this case, the Messenger is believed because he is appointed to this office by public authority and acts as a public person in this or that matter.

(vv) The reason is that if a messenger delegates the execution of a citation to someone else, he exceeds the limits of his office in this regard.

(x) And this is because the purpose of a citation is for someone to appear; therefore, if they have already appeared, the citation has achieved its goal, and once the goal is reached, the methods are no longer questioned.

(y) A trial for contumacy <note>disobedience</note> cannot be initiated unless it has been shown and proved that the defiant party was legitimately cited. Proof of this kind is made when the citation is produced in proper form and it is shown to the Judge how it was executed.

(z) That is, if someone perhaps has two possible Judges, then once one is chosen, the other can no longer be approached. The reason is that jurisdiction is considered already established by the fact that such a Judge was the first to issue the citation—that is, he delivered it to the party.

(aa) See above, Chapter 2, thesis 4, regarding the words "at the very least a citation was issued."

(bb) Namely, when the time periods established for "prescribing" <note>claiming ownership through long-term possession</note> are running in favor of the possessor; if then the true Owner has the possessor cited, the prescription is interrupted, and the time no longer runs, but the prescription must begin anew, provided good faith and other requirements are present.

(cc) When a citation is issued...

### CHAPTER V.
### CONCERNING CONTUMACY, AS WELL AS THE FIRST AND SECOND DECREE:
->And how one may proceed definitively against a contumacious party.<-

->I.<-

If one party or the other does not come to the deadline fixed in the summons <note>original: "citatione"</note>, they are held as **contumacious** <note>from *contumacia*, meaning willful disobedience or failure to appear</note>: (a) and this is called *Contumacy of the non-appearing party*. In terms of failing to appear, someone is considered contumacious who—after three summonses have been put forward, or three public edicts issued, or one issued in place of three (which is commonly called **peremptory**) <note>original: "peremptorium"; a final, mandatory summons that "destroys" the right to further delay</note>—scorns to make their appearance, *Law 53, on the Matter of Judgment; Law "and after the edict"; Law "to the peremptory", in the Digests on Judgments.* It must be noted, however, that the party who is present must formally accuse the absence or disobedience of the absent party: *Marantus, part 6, title on contumacy, no. 1; Graevius, conclusion 55, consideration 1.* For the office of the Judge ceases if it is not requested <note>meaning a judge usually does not act on their own initiative regarding a party's absence unless the opposing party asks</note>, *Law 4, paragraph "this however", in the Digests on threatened damage; Zasius on the law "to be hastened", final paragraph, no. 23, in the Code on Judgments; Tennin, caution 32 and following.* If someone does not appear at the first or second simple summons, it is customary to pronounce: (b) that the plaintiff has appeared obediently, but the defendant has not come forward as is proper. Therefore, another more pressing court date is set for the parties: And if the defendant then provides no sufficient reason for his absence, he shall be liable to pay the costs incurred for this day to the Lord Judge as well as to the obedient party. And then, at the very next available court session, the point of contumacy must be resolved first of all: and either the prior absence is held as excused, or the contumacious person is condemned to pay the expenses. Various causes, however, excuse contumacy: such as probable ignorance of the summons, illness, a wedding, flooding <note>original: "excursiones aquarum"</note>, etc. *Tennin, caution 166.*

<column-break/>

(a) Contumacy is of two kinds: **one** for not appearing, the **other** for not acting; that is, when someone is indeed present, but nonetheless does not do what they ought—for example, if they do not contest the lawsuit, if they do not respond to the articles of the case, or if they do not conclude their side of the case. In such instances of contumacy, the suit is held as contested, or the case as concluded, or the articles as confessed, etc.

(b) This **Interlocutory decree** <note>a temporary or intermediate ruling made before the final judgment</note> is pronounced when someone does not come to a simple summons. But if someone does not appear for a peremptory summons, then it is pronounced through an Interlocutory decree in this manner: In the matter of [Name], upon the disobedient absence of the defendant, the plaintiff is admitted to the proper proceedings on the main issue <note>original German: "in Sachen N. N. ist auf ungehorsames Ausbleiben deß Beklagten, der Kläger zu gebührender Handlung in principali zugelassen"</note>.

II. But after a Peremptory Summons, if the **plaintiff** <note>original: "actor"</note> does not come, and specifically before the filing of the formal complaint <note>original: "libelli"</note>; then the defendant asks to be released from the summons and for his expenses to be reimbursed, *Law 73, paragraph 1, Digests on Judgments; Law 13, paragraph 2, Code on the same title; Gail, book 1, observation 59, no. 1.* Nevertheless, the plaintiff may later resume the lawsuit after paying the expenses and obtaining a new summons, *Chapter "the actor", on Deceit and Contumacy, in the Sixth Book of Decretals.* But if the complaint has already been presented to the Judge, it is at the defendant's discretion (c) either to seek dismissal from the summons, or to take the burden of proof upon themselves and proceed with the main case. And if the defendant is then acquitted, they are entirely safe, *Gail, observation 50, no. 4.* But if the plaintiff wins (whose role the Judge fills in their absence), then nonetheless, out of hatred for the contumacy, the party who was contumacious pays the expenses, even if they are the victor. If neither party appears, the deadline is bypassed and every effect of the summons ceases, *Graevius, conclusion 59.* If the defendant appears after the peremptory deadline but does not respond (for there is also a certain contumacy in not responding, *Law "on age", paragraph "he who was silent", Digests on interrogatory actions; chapter 2 on confessions, in the Sixth Book*), then if the lawsuit has been contested, the plaintiff can ask for the case to proceed and for a sentence to be passed against the contumacious defendant, (d) *Gail, book 1, observation 60.* Indeed, if the case is sufficiently clear to the Judge, he pronounces in favor of the plaintiff; if not, he acquits the defendant, but nonetheless imposes the payment of expenses upon them.

(c) For if the defendant himself wishes to be freed from the entire case, then let him take the burden of proof (namely of his own intent or exceptions) upon himself, and request the process on the main issue. But if he desires to be released not from the entire case, but only from the Summons,

# Disputation

The plea of **incompetence of the court** <note>original Latin: *incompetentiæ fori*</note>, or the **declinatory plea of the court**, is established (*Tennin. caution 66*). This must be raised before all others: so that no one appears to consent to the Judge through a silent extension of jurisdiction <note>original: *tacitam prorogationem*; this refers to accepting a court's authority simply by participating in the trial without objecting</note> (*Zanger. 2. on exceptions 1. num. 4; Hiltrop. part 2. tit. 12. num. 46*). There is also the **plea of prevention** <note>original: *Exceptio præventionis*</note>, or **pending litigation** <note>original: *litis pendentiæ*</note>; this applies if the same lawsuit has already begun elsewhere. Indeed, a summons alone creates "prevention," provided it has already been formally served <note>original: *insinuata*</note> (a) (*Gail. 1. observation 29; Decisions of Guido Papa 421; Zanger. ch. 3*). Thus, in the Emperor’s Court, one cannot take action if the lawsuit has already been "prevented" <note>meaning already taken up</note> in the Imperial Chamber Court. Of a similar nature is the **plea of a suspect judge** <note>original: *Exceptio judicis suspecti*</note>, a matter I have already discussed above. There is the **plea of an unsafe place** <note>original: *Exceptio loci non tuti*</note>, for example, if someone is summoned to a place infected by the plague, or exposed to the ambushes of soldiers, etc. (*Clem. Pastoralis. §. notorum, on the matter of Judgment, ch. 47. ext. on appeals*). There is likewise the plea of **too narrow a deadline** <note>original: *termini nimis angusti*</note>, and the **plea of court holidays** <note>original: *exceptio feriarum*</note>. There is also the **plea of incapacity** <note>original: *exceptio inhabilitatis*</note>: either of the Plaintiff, the defendant, or even of the Proxy, or of an insufficient mandate, an unfit legal petition <note>original: *inepti libelli*</note>, and so on. To this category is also typically referred the **plea of spoliation** <note>original: *exceptio spolii*</note>; for a defendant is not bound to respond to a brought action unless the property seized from them has been restored by the plaintiff (*ch. "cum dilectus." on the order of cognitions; Zanger. 2. on exceptions ch. 18*). <note>original German: *Es darff keiner mit verpfändter Hand zum Rechten kommen.*</note> <insert>No one should come before the law with hands that are bound [by the seizure of their property].</insert> There is the **plea of the payment term not yet arrived** <note>original: *Exceptio termini solutionis nondum purificati*</note> (*§. temporales. Institutes on exceptions*), and the **plea of discussion** <note>original: *Exceptio excussionis*</note>, which is available to a guarantor <note>allowing a guarantor to insist that the creditor first sue the primary debtor before coming after the guarantor</note> (*Novel 4. etc.*).

(a) For if it has not yet been formally served, even if decreed by the Judge, the lawsuit is not said to be pending.

### III. Peremptory Pleas

These are pleas which exclude the action entirely <note>Peremptory exceptions "perish" or destroy the plaintiff's claim forever, rather than just delaying it</note>: such as the **plea of money not received** <note>original: *non numeratæ pecuniæ*</note> (b) (*Zanger. 3. on exceptions 14. n. 3. etc.; Tennin. caution 30*); this, however, only lasts for two years (*Law 14. in the beginning. Code on money not received*). The **plea of the Macedonian Decree** <note>original: *Exceptio SC. Macedon.*; a Roman law decree (Senatus Consultum) that forbade lending money to sons still under their father's authority</note>, which is available to sons under parental power who have accepted a loan (*Law 7. §. 3. & Law 11. Digest on the Macedonian Decree*). Also the **plea of the Velleian Decree** <note>original: *exceptio SC. Vellejani*</note>, which acts in favor of women who intervene [as guarantors] for others (*the whole title on the Velleian Decree*). Other peremptory pleas include the **agreement not to sue** <note>original: *pacti de non petendo*</note>, **res judicata** <note>original: *rei judicatæ*; the matter has already been decided by a court</note>, **settlement** <note>original: *transactionis*</note>, and **prescription** <note>original: *præscriptionis*; the statute of limitations</note> (*Ummius disputation 8. n. 41*).

(b) This plea applies when someone takes action against me on the strength of my signed note <note>original: *chirographi*</note>; I then have

<column-break/>

within two years the **plea of money not received**, if I have not yet received it. That is, I can say that the money was not counted out to me, but that I gave the note in the hope of future payment. The nature of this exception is such that the Plaintiff is then bound to prove the counting out of the money; for I cannot be expected to prove a negative—that is, that the money was *not* counted out to me. For caution’s sake, it is observed that the creditor should make the debtor expressly renounce the **plea of money not received**, for example: <note>original German follows</note> <insert>...and acknowledge that I have actually and in cash received this money, and hereby promise never again to claim that it was not delivered into my hand, and thus knowingly renounce the plea of money not received.</insert>

### IV. Furthermore, Dilatory Pleas

These must be proposed before the joinder of issue <note>original: *ante litem contestatam*; the formal start of the trial</note> (c), and indeed all at once (d) (*Moller. semest. 1*), unless those pleas only emerge after the joinder of issue (e) (*Marant. on exceptions num. 1; Ummius d. disp. num. 56*). See other limitations in *Hiltrop. d. tit. 12. num. 62. etc. and num. 85. etc.* Peremptory pleas, as a rule, are raised only after the joinder of issue: and indeed up until the conclusion of the case (*ch. 11. ext. on the order of cognitions; Ummius d. loc. num. 57; Hartman. 2. tit. 9. obs. 10*). But there are some (f) among the peremptory pleas which are also proposed before the joinder of issue, and carry the force of dilatory pleas; these are therefore called **privileged pleas**. Such are the **plea of prescription**, of **res judicata**, of **settlement**, etc. (*Hiltrop. tit. 12. num. 94*). However, there are statutes in some places which, to shorten lawsuits, prohibit such pleas from being raised before the joinder of issue; instead, they command that the issue first be joined, and then all pleas be proposed simultaneously (*Coler. on execution process part 4. ch. 1. num. 157. etc.; Surd. cons. 225. num. 12*). A Judge can also legally assign a deadline within which all pleas must necessarily be proposed (*ch. Pastoralis. extra on exceptions; Ummius d. d. 8. num. 60*). It should also be known that a defendant may use multiple pleas, even contradictory ones (g): either simultaneously or successively (*ch. "nullus" 20. on the Rules of Law in 6.* where *Dynus* and *Apostil.* note that no one is prohibited; and *Zasius on exceptions law "nemo" 43*). A person raising a plea is also not considered to have confessed [to the main charge] (*law "non uti"*).

# On Judicial Process

...and also 9. And there see Zafius on the Pandects, title "On Exceptions," chapter "exceptionem" in the Rules of Law. See also Camillus Borellus, volume 2, decision title 3, number 164; Everhard in the same place from private to habitual; Tennin, caution 28. **However, a defendant [Reus] by making a plea becomes a plaintiff [Actor]** (b), and he is bound to prove his plea conclusively (*Law 1*, where Zafius notes number 12; and *Law 2*, "On Exceptions"; Cravetta, counsel 201, number 18; and counsel 249).

---

(c) **The reason for this is** that after the <term>joinder of issue<note>original: *litem contestatam*; the formal point in a Roman-law trial where the parties have stated their claims and the case is ready for the judge's decision.</note></term>, the parties are seen to have waived **Dilatory Exceptions** <note>These are procedural pleas intended to delay the trial or point out technical errors rather than defeat the claim itself.</note>. Thus, after the joinder of issue, a plea regarding the **Incompetence of the Court** can no longer be raised, because the parties are considered to have extended the jurisdiction by a "quasi-contract" once they have undertaken the judgment. Likewise, one cannot plead against the **Mandate** <note>the legal authority of the lawyer</note> or the person of the opposing party, unless that person is clearly unfit—for example, an infant, a madman, etc.—for even the Judge himself is not accustomed to admitting such a person in court. Likewise, one cannot object to the **Summons** or similar matters.

(d) **Understand this: if it is possible.** For it is sometimes permitted to propose dilatory exceptions alternatively. For example: first, one may plead against the **legitimacy of the party**, arguing the opponent does not have the legal standing to be in court; once this point is settled, one may plead against the **Judge**; that point being finished, one may plead against the **Complaint** [Libellus]. Therefore, only then must all dilatory exceptions be proposed at once if their nature allows it.

(e) For example: if, after the joinder of issue, the location becomes **unsafe**, a party becomes **infamous**, or the seat of court is moved, etc.; or if these facts only then come to light. For in that case, one is not considered to have waived rights that were probably unknown.

(f) **Because they are of such efficacy** that someone possessing them cannot be compelled to the joinder of issue. <note>original German: *ist gar nicht vonnöthen, daß sich einer ins Recht einlasse*</note> It is not at all necessary for one to enter into the legal proceedings—for example, if the legal action is already time-barred <note>original: *præscripta*; the statute of limitations has passed</note>, if the matter has already been decided by a court sentence, if a settlement has been reached, etc.

(g) Thus, for example, someone can say: "I did not receive the money which you seek as a loan, or if I did receive it, I have paid it back." These pleas are certainly contradictory and cannot stand together, and yet it is permitted to plead this way, especially if an **heir** says it. This is because an heir might probably be ignorant of the deceased person’s actions. An heir-defendant can therefore say: "I do not believe that my father received this money from you as a loan, or if he did receive it, he undoubtedly paid it back," etc. Hence, that question of the **Theologians** arises here: whether someone can in good faith deny the counting out of money which they know for certain was counted out to them, but which they have already paid back,

<column-break/>

yet cannot prove the payment? For if he confesses to receiving the money, he must prove the payment. Therefore (if he has paid), he can say he received nothing, implying that he no longer owes anything.

(b) **And this is done because** a Plea is only then raised if the Plaintiff has a well-founded claim. For a plea "kills" [perempts] the Action, and thus presupposes the existence of a right belonging to the Plaintiff. For example, when I say, "I have paid," I presuppose that I received the money, and therefore I am bound to return it again if I do not prove the payment. Likewise, if someone says, "I killed him, but in my own defense," then the accuser has a well-founded claim, and the defendant is now at the point of defense; because he is bound to prove this, he is treated like a plaintiff.

V. **And this is also observed** even in **Civil Law**: if the Judge sees that the defendant is not immediately proving such a plea (i), and is raising it for the sake of **quibbling** <note>original: *cavillationis causâ*; stalling or legal hair-splitting</note>, the Judge may officially order the joinder of issue to proceed. <note>original German: *daß eingewandter Einreden ungehindert, der Beklagt auf die eingebrachte Klag, litem zu contestiren schuldig: ihme doch seine zu haben verstandne exceptiones, nach verfangnem Rechten fürzubringen, ohnbenommen seyn solle.*</note> This means that notwithstanding the raised objections, the defendant is obliged to contest the suit against the filed complaint; however, his right to bring forward the exceptions he believes he has, according to the law, shall remain unimpaired. (Hartman, tome 9, observation 1, number 8; Wurmser, tome 8, observation 3, number 2; Zanger, part 8, chapter 23, number 11). Finally, there is still another **plea against the claim** (k), or of an "incompetent action," which differs from a plea properly so-called, as was said in the dissertation *On the Manner of Reporting*, number 29.

(i) **Understand this to be a Peremptory Plea** <note>a plea that dismisses the whole case</note> raised with the force of a Dilatory Plea, if it requires a deeper investigation, etc., and the Plaintiff has a well-founded claim.

(k) There are, you see, not only "True Pleas," which presuppose a well-founded action, but there are also certain "Improper Pleas." These improper ones are commonly called **Pleas against the Claim** [Intentionis] or of an "Incompetent Action." For example: Titius seeks 100 from me under the title of a loan. If I then say, "I never received a loan from you," that is a Plea against the Claim. For I am saying the Plaintiff does not have a well-founded claim, and that no right of action ever belonged to him. But a true "Plea against the Action" is when I say: "I did indeed receive it, but I paid it back." For I admit the Plaintiff's claim, but I say it has been neutralized by payment.

# CHAPTER VIII.
# ON PETITIONS.

### I.

A **Petition** <note>original: *Libellus*; in this legal context, it refers to the formal written claim or "bill of complaint" that initiates a lawsuit</note> is a piece of writing that encompasses the intention of the plaintiff <note>original: *agentis*; the party bringing the suit</note> and demonstrates the type and form of the future litigation. Indeed, in lighter matters and those which ought to be settled summarily, it is sufficient for the request to be made before the Judge in plain words and entered into the Acts or the judicial protocol; this is commonly called an **Oral Complaint** <note>original German: *Mündliche Klag*</note>, *as noted in the gloss on chapter 1 "On the offering of petitions" in the Clementines.* However, in ordinary judicial proceedings, the Petition must be offered in writing; otherwise, the process is considered null and void, *according to the same chapter 1 and Speculator in the title "On the offering of petitions," paragraph "now it must be said," number 141.* Sometimes a Petition is "summary," where the facts are simply narrated; other times it is "articulated," when the facts are organized into specific articles or propositions, which they call positions or **Positional Articles** <note>original German: *Positional-Articul*</note>. Furthermore, if a Petition is "inept" <note>legally flawed or nonsensical</note>, the Judge must reject it by virtue of his office; for a judgment rendered on such a petition is invalid, *Gail, observation 66 and following; Obrecht's treatise on petitions, chapter 18, section 4.*

### II.

Furthermore, every Petition must be clear (though sometimes an "alternative" petition is admitted, *Tennin, caution 148; Gail, observation 62*), and it must necessarily "conclude" against the adversary, *Speculator in the aforementioned place, paragraph 1.* It usually contains the name of the Judge and the parties, as well as a description of the facts—the "narration"—joined primarily with a fitting "petition" <note>the formal request for relief or remedy</note>. Although the scrupulous formulas of actions <note>rigidly prescribed wording required in ancient Roman law</note> have been abolished today (on which *Obrecht writes elegantly in the same treatise, chapter 7 and following*), and it is not even necessary to provide the specific name of the legal action; (a) nevertheless, the petition ought to conclude properly in the manner of a **syllogism** <note>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> or even an **enthymeme** <note>a syllogism where one premise is implied</note>. It must be directed toward some action or other legal remedy—one or many—and fulfill their requirements, *Obrecht, chapter 11 and following.* (For although in this matter a too-captious and scrupulous religious adherence was observed in the past, that was more tolerable than the confusion of actions, the recklessness of litigating, and the lack of order so frequent everywhere today, *Cujas in his commentary on the Code "On*

<column-break/>

*formulas and the obtaining of actions"*). Thus, the law stands in the place of the "major premise," the narration of the facts represents the "minor premise," and the petition represents the "conclusion." For example: "Since no one ought to wrong another, and this is prohibited by all law" [Major Premise]. "Titus, however, in this or that manner, has affected me with insult and injury" [Minor Premise]. "Therefore, I pray that it be decreed **that he has done me too much wrong and injustice, and for such promised disgrace he should be bound to reimburse N. florins, all with the payment of court costs, etc.**" <note>original German: *daß er mir zuviel und unrecht gethan, auch vor solche zugesagte Schmach N. fl. zu erstatten schuldig seyn solle, alles mit Abtrag der Gerichts-Kosten, &c.*</note> In a petition, the "cause of seeking" <note>the legal ground for the claim</note> or the "means of concluding" must be entirely expressed. In a **personal action**, the "proximate cause" is the existence of an obligation, while the "remote cause" is the contract; both must be fully expressed. (b) In a **real action** <note>an action regarding property/ownership</note>, the proximate cause is ownership; the remote cause is the act from which ownership was caused; and there, expressing the proximate cause is considered sufficient, *Gail, observation 61 at the beginning; Tennin, caution 4.* In a claim for an inheritance or general business matters, a general petition suffices; but to avoid the difficulty of "liquidation" <note>the process of determining exact values or specific items</note>, (c) the advocate acts more cautiously if he names the particular items at the same time, *Gail, observation 68.* How the type of action is to be investigated from the circumstances of the fact is taught by *Obrecht "On Petitions," chapter 10*, which should definitely be consulted. Likewise, in petitions, the conclusion—or "prayer"—is primarily to be inspected: (d) for through it, the facts narrated are restricted to those things which are expressly stated in the conclusion, *Gail, observation 61, number 15.* Multiple actions may be "cumulated" <note>joined together in one suit</note>, (e) provided they do not cancel each other out: *discussed most extensively by Obrecht, chapter 21 and following to the end of the book; Bocer, class 6, dispute 11, throughout.* But these should arise from a single act (for if actions springing from different facts are joined, then there are considered to be as many petitions as there are actions), such as an "action under the Aquilian Law" <note>a claim for property damage</note> and an "action for injuries." Or an action for estimated damages and an action for **recantation** <note>original German: *Widerruff*; a formal retraction of a slanderous statement</note>, (f) **where one sues for a retraction**, *Gail, observation 65.* But one may not join a criminal and civil action for injuries, since both tend toward "vindicating" the wrong, *Gail, observation 66; Tennin, caution 61 and following.* However, a criminal action and a civil action can be joined if the latter concerns the recovery of property; (g) for then they tend toward different ends: as is, for example, a "useful Aquilian action" for

# ON JUDICIAL PROCESS.

(a) Nevertheless, anyone wishing to bring a suit must thoroughly understand the nature and requirements of the **Legal Action** <term>original: *Actio*; the specific legal category or right under which a plaintiff sues</term> that must be named, and must act according to those requirements.

(b) The reason for the difference—why in a **Personal Action** <note>a suit against a specific person based on a contract or debt</note> it is not enough to cite the "proximate cause," whereas in a **Real Action** <note>a suit regarding ownership of a physical thing or property</note> it is considered sufficient—is this: many people are owners of a thing but may not know exactly how that thing came to their ancestors. Therefore, it is enough to say, "this thing is mine, because it was always held as the property of my ancestors." Thus, in a real action, it is sufficient to allege the proximate cause, namely ownership. However, in a personal action, it is logically flawed to simply say: "you owe me because you owe me." Instead, the "remote cause" must be expressed—specifically, from which contract the debt arises.

(c) An example of this point of "liquidation" <note>the process of making a claim specific and certain</note> is as follows: someone petitions to be declared the closest heir to Titius who died without a will. The opponent denies this and claims instead that *he* is the closest heir. The Judge rules in favor of the Plaintiff. After this winning sentence, the Plaintiff is finally compelled to prove what exactly pertained to that inheritance: which lands, which movable goods, what money, etc. This subsequent process is called the **Point of Validation** <term>original: *punctum legitimationis*; the stage where the specific items and value of a claim are proven after the general right has been established</term>, for the facts must be clearly established. To prevent the Plaintiff from being forced to undergo a double trial—one for the main case and another for the Point of Validation—it is a wise precaution for the Lawyer to state in the Petition both that the Plaintiff is the closest heir *and* that the inheritance included such lands, goods, etc. Often, those in possession of an inheritance hide the assets, and the Plaintiff is forced to prove what was in the estate. It is more efficient, therefore, if both matters are proposed and brought to a conclusion in a single, simultaneous process.

(d) For the **Request** <note>original: *petitio*; the specific part of the document where the plaintiff asks for a particular remedy</note> is like the **North Star** and **Cynosure** <note>terms for the pole star used by sailors for navigation</note> toward which everything narrated in the Petition must be directed and regulated. Therefore, even if the narrative is perhaps ambiguous and one cannot gather what kind of action the Plaintiff has intended, certainty is usually drawn from the request.

(e) Those actions can be "cumulated" <note>joined together in one lawsuit</note> which tend toward different goals. For example, an action under the **Aquilian Law** <term>original: *Lex Aquilia*; a Roman law providing compensation for property damage caused by negligence or malice</term> aims at repairing actual financial loss, while an **Action for Injuries** <term>original: *injuriarum*; a claim regarding personal insult or damage to reputation</term> aims at avenging an insult. In such a case, the Plaintiff has been harmed in two ways: in his property and in his honor; therefore, he must be assisted in both cases by a legal remedy.

(f) And indeed, these can be combined because the "estimatory" action is purely for vindication, while the demand for a recantation is, as it were, a restoration of honor.

<column-break/>

...reparation for the damage received, and a criminal action for injuries seeking public vengeance.

(g) That is, specifically, what is missing from my **Patrimony** <note>one's total estate or wealth</note>.

(h) For in this way I can also petition <note>original German: *daß mir der Dieb mein Geld hab, und gehenckt werde*</note> "that the thief return my money and be hanged."

III. However, when multiple actions arise from a single act that would normally cancel each other out (so that if one is chosen, the other is lost), but one contains more—being "fatter" than the other—or one is harder to prove, then by subjoining certain clauses to the petition, it can be arranged so that the Judge, in delivering the sentence, is bound to look to that remedy which is best and more profitable for the Plaintiff, and which better fits the evidence produced. *See Gail, book 1, observation 61, number 10, etc.* Thus, it is more useful to intend an action under the Aquilian Law than an action on a lease (i) when damage has been done to a leased item. *See Tennin, precautions, 153.* For this reason, those are called **Salutory Clauses** or **Savings Clauses**. However, in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original: *Camera*; the high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, when someone wishes to obtain a Mandate without a clause, they are not admitted; rather, one is forced to name the specific constitution by virtue of which he requests the mandate be decreed. *Gail, book 1, observation 61, number 12.*

12. In other proceedings, however, these Salutory Clauses are entirely useful and are commonly formulated thus: <note>original German: *Hierüber und was sonsten, nach Gestaltsame dieser Sachen, auch derselben sonderbaren Umstand, könnt, sollt, oder möcht gebetten werden, dieses alles will Kläger in der besten Form petirt, oder gebetten, auch um forderliche Ertheilung Rechtens, und der Gerechtigkeit, das Adeliche mildrichterliche Amt dienstliches Fleiß angeruffen haben.*</note> "Regarding this and whatever else might, should, or could be requested according to the nature and special circumstances of this matter, the Plaintiff requests all this in the best possible form, appealing with diligent industry to the Noble and Equitable Office of the Judge for a swift delivery of Law and Justice." This clause (1) ensures that in a doubtful case, the petition should and can be interpreted in favor of the plaintiff; it is held as if it were drafted in the best possible way it could have been. *Ayrer, in History of Process, chapter 4, objection 6, numbers 33 and following.* (2) By virtue of this clause, the plaintiff is considered to have deduced all his rights specifically, even if he did not mention them. *Chapter 2, on the office of the ordinary; Doctors of Law on the chapter "since the beloved," on the order of cognitions.* (3) This clause works so that the judge, in judging, considers only the truth of the matter as it stands from the records, and not only the pe...

# DISPUTATION

The judge must look toward the plaintiff's request. And so, by virtue of that specific clause, a judgment can sometimes be rendered even upon a flawed petition, provided that the narrative of facts was skillfully presented. *Mynsinger, Decisions 3, Response 25, number 6; and Decision 6, Response 59, number 15.* Furthermore, an **articulated petition** <term>original: *libellus articulatus*; a legal complaint broken down into short, numbered points of fact</term> (about which Obrecht writes extensively in *chapter 17*) seems particularly useful for this reason: if the facts are reduced into simple and succinct sentences (which they call "articles"), the goal of the case (which rhetoricians call the **status** <term>original: *statum*; the central point or essential issue of a legal dispute</term>) can be more easily recognized. *Obrecht, chapter 10, number 2.* Such a petition is usually formed in this way:

*That the plaintiff submits his positional articles by means of an oath, stating that he believes them to be true by virtue of the oaths to be provided, as far as his own actions were concerned; but as for what concerns the actions of others, he believes them to be true. And he prays that the defendant be required to contest the suit, and also immediately respond to each and every article of the complaint by means of the oath of responding, using the words "I believe it is true" or "It is not true."*

If then one or another article should not stand, the plaintiff offers to sufficiently prove it, as is right. A clause or "caution" is added: *That he does not wish to be constrained or bound to any unnecessary proof.* See Strauch's *On Legal Particles, page 145.* By the power of this clause, a person is not forced to prove more than what pertains to the "status" of the case. If that clause were omitted, it might seem that the plaintiff had bound himself to the proof of each and every single detail, which are often added to Petitions superfluously and in overabundance. *Obrecht, chapter 16, number 7, etc.; Schrader, On Fiefs, part 2, section 9, number 12.* However, a person "posing" <note>the act of asserting a factual point in an articulated petition</note> a fact seems to confess what he asserts by the very act of posing it; nevertheless, he can revoke a certain position immediately, or even after the fact if he can prove an error was made. *Tannin, Caution 195.*

<gloss>
(i) For the petition is more substantial in that case because under the **Aquilian Law** <note>original: *Legis Aquiliae*; a Roman law regarding compensation for damage to property or injury</note> even the slightest fault is considered; but in an action for hire, only ordinary negligence is considered. It is therefore easier for me to prove the "slightest fault" than "ordinary fault." However, because in this case it is still disputed whether an action under the Aquilian Law is available to a lessor, the plaintiff can omit the specific name of the action and simply seek the restoration of damages in the best possible way.
</gloss>

And then it is the Judge’s duty to discern what must be done in that case.

IV. In **actions in rem** <term>original: *actionibus in rem*; lawsuits regarding property rights or ownership of a physical thing</term>, a clause is usually placed: *with all appurtenances, as well as accrued profits* <note>original German: *mit aller Zugehör, auch ab-habner Nutzung*</note>; (k) that is, with its appurtenances and the fruits already collected or yet to be collected. *Obrecht, chapter 16, number 29, etc.* Furthermore, a frequent clause is: *Compensation of costs and all damage, whether already accrued or that might accrue in the future.* <note>original German: *Abtrag des Kostens, und allen Schadens, so jetzt aufgeloffen, oder künftig auflauffen möchte*</note>. This is entirely necessary in all actions. *Obrecht, chapter 16, number 29.* For such expenses are regularly owed to the victor; so much so that if the Judge takes no account of them in the sentencing, he may be held liable to reimburse the party himself. *Digest, book 15, on Judges.* This holds true, however, only if they were specifically requested by the opponent; otherwise, they are not owed, nor is the Judge obligated for the "Interest" <note>compensation for loss or delay</note> due to their omission. *Unmius, disputation 6, number 57.* For a Judge does not grant his official service unless it is implored.

Another clause is still commonly added: *Saving* (or reserving) the right of adding, diminishing, correcting, or changing, etc. (l) *with the reservation to diminish or increase the complaint, etc.* <note>original German: *mit Vorbehalt, die Klag zu mindern, zu mehren, etc.*</note>. Such an amendment, which does not change the substance of the item sought or the action proposed, can regularly be made up until the judgment. However, one is only allowed to change the petition itself up until the **contestation of the suit** <term>original: *litis contestatio*; the formal point where the issues of a trial are joined and the case truly begins</term>. *Gail, observations 1, number 5; Schvvanman, on the Process of the Imperial Chamber, book 1, chapter 41, number 10; see especially Obrecht, chapter 20.* But this must be understood such that the expenses incurred by the opposing party because of such a change must always be refunded. After the suit is contested, if the entire petition is changed regarding the action itself or the facts, and the party objects, a new citation and process are necessary—unless the aforementioned clause is present. Finally, as for the effect of the petition: it interrupts **prescription** <term>the legal "statute of limitations" where a right is lost over time</term> and makes the matter "litigious" <note>legally under dispute, which restricts what can be done with the property</note>. *Code, on annual exceptions; New Constitutions 112, chapter 1.*

<gloss>
(k) This only applies in the case of a **possessor in bad faith** <term>original: *malae fidei possessore*; someone who holds property knowing they have no right to it</term>. For a possessor in good faith, especially as far as practice is concerned, does not restore fruits [profits] already collected, except from the time the suit is contested. For by the contesting of the suit, everyone who is not the Owner is established as being in "bad faith."
</gloss>
