## CHAPTER IX.

### ON DELAYS AND COURT RECESSES.

I. Once the petition has been offered, the defendant seeks a delay, either for contesting the suit, or for doing what is proper (a) to be done. Because a delay is usually sought not only in this article or point of the case, but also elsewhere, I shall say something about Delays in general. A delay is granted both to the plaintiff and to the defendant. To the defendant, indeed, for deliberating whether he wishes to yield or to fight; but to both for producing writings from both sides, for producing witnesses, or bringing forth instruments, for concluding the case, etc. *Law 27, Law 32, final section, Law 33 on arbitration; Law 7 of the Digest on recesses and delays.*

<note>(a) For example, for proposing exceptions—understand those which ought to be proposed before the joinder of issue, according to what has already been said above.</note>

II. A delay is either legal (defined by Law, *Bocer class 6, disputation 6, thesis 3, etc.* or by the style of the Court) or committed to the discretion of the Judge, who determines for the defendant the space of time within which he ought to respond or do something else: and specifically according to the distance of the locations and the gravity of the business, *Lord Nicolaus Everhard the Younger, counsel 5, number 27, volume 1; Bocer, said disputation 15, thesis 12; Gail, book 1, observation 91, number 1; Maranta on delays, number 15, etc.* A delay is also either simple or peremptory, (b) *Speculator on delays, section 2; Wesenbeck in the title on recesses.* And so sometimes a certain space of time is given to someone for every term and delay: and thus a term is sometimes prefixed for contesting the
<sig>Besold, Volume I.</sig>

<column-break/>

suit, or for responding to the positions, <note>original German: *dass in Verbleibung dessen, lis ex officio für contestirt gehalten, und die responsiones pro confessatis angenommen seyn sollen*</note> so that in the event of failure to do so, the suit shall be considered contested by the court's authority, and the responses shall be accepted as confessed. Furthermore, it should be known that every evidentiary term, or term fixed for producing witnesses, is peremptory: (c) so that if the examination is not produced within that term, it cannot afterwards be presented to the Judge, *Mynsinger, observation 71; Tesauro, decision 22, number 4; Bocer, disputation 15, thesis 9, class 6.* Therefore, a second delay must be sought before the first term has elapsed, or a prolongation of the first term must be requested, *Lanfrancus at the chapter "quoniam contra," chapter 2, number 15.* Sometimes even a delay is not given except by the intervention of an oath: and thus a fourth delay (d) of proof, and even more its prolongation, is not granted unless the petitioner swears <note>original German: *dass er zuvor nicht aufkommen, oder mit den Probationen fertig können werden*</note> that he could not come forward sooner, or could not be ready with the proofs. *Mynsinger, observation 70 and 72; Rutger Ruland on commissions, part 1, book 2, chapter 7, number 15.*

<note>(b) When someone does not act within a peremptory delay, they are then said to be contumacious <term>original: *contumax*; stubborn or willfully disobedient to the court's timeline</term> in not acting; if they do not come at all, they are contumacious in not coming, and the process proceeds in contumacy, and the power of doing that which should have been done within the term is taken away from them; sometimes they are even punished at the Judge's discretion. Sometimes not only is the power of further action taken away, but the matters are also held as confessed. As, for example, if someone does not respond to the articles within the peremptory term, then the articles are held as Confessed; however, when the suit is accepted as contested, then it is held as negatively contested, nor is the defendant held as having confessed. The reason for the difference is that before the joinder of issue, the Judge cannot condemn anyone, but only grant the plaintiff possession from the first Decree: since he does not know whether the person will contest the suit or rather raise an exception. But responses are only given when the suit is contested, and there the Judge can condemn the contumacious defendant, <note>original German: *weiln er sich in das Recht eingelassen*</note> because he has submitted himself to the law: for by undergoing the joinder of issue, the Defendant as it were enters into a contract.</note>

<note>(c) Every term assigned to someone for proving is of such a condition that if it has passed, proof cannot be made later. The Defendant is therefore forced to seek another delay, and indeed before the first term has elapsed; and that term is always peremptory, even if it is not expressed, since this happens by law itself.</note>

(d) After a fourth delay, no further extension is granted, but a "restoration to the original state" <note>original: *restitutio in integrum*; a legal remedy where a person is returned to their previous legal position as if a deadline had not passed</note> can be requested. However, this can only happen if someone was hindered by another person through no fault of their own. In such a case, through this restoration, they receive as much time for the deadline as they had during the fourth delay. Since restoration is nothing other than a return to the former state, it is judged as if they had never yet received that fourth delay.

III. Court recesses <note>original: *feriae*</note> are also delays granted by law, whether for Divine worship, the gathering of crops, or other designated purposes. They may also be granted extraordinarily due to unexpected events, such as for successful achievements, in honor of the Prince, or for similar reasons. *Law 4, Code on holidays. Specul. title on holidays. §.1. num. 3. Gail book 1. observation 53. num 9.* In all of these, the "judicial noise" <note>original: *judicialis strepitus*; a phrase referring to the chaotic activity of active litigation</note> falls silent. *Wesemb. in title on holidays. num. 2. & 11.* Nor can anything relating to "contentious jurisdiction" (e) be processed at that time; indeed, if anything is done then, it is considered void by law. *Law 6. & final law. Code on holidays.* Furthermore, one is not permitted to waive holidays declared in honor of God or the Prince. But for others, such as the harvest or the vintage, which are accepted for the benefit of the parties, a party may waive their right. (f) *Marant. part 4. dist. 16. num. 59. Menoch. on arbitrariness. case 30. num. 6. & 11.* And if someone is summoned—for example, to appear 30 days after the citation is delivered—then if the deadline falls during a holiday, they may appear on the next following court day. Furthermore, if someone is given a delay of, say, 20 or 60 days, or two months, to respond, the holiday days are not subtracted; rather, the time of that delay is continuous. But if holidays consume a large portion of that time, an extension or a new delay is granted. *Maranta in the rubric on delays. num. 18. Lanfranc. cited chapter 1. num. 9. verse 'nevertheless'.* And a delay must not be too short, *Tennin. caution 44.* If such a short delay is given, it can be appealed. *Chapter 1. extra. on delays. chapter 'dilectus' on procurators. Bocer. disputation 15. thesis 37. & following.*

(e) Contentious jurisdiction <note>original: *contentiosa jurisdictio*</note> is exercised when a Magistrate speaks the law between two litigants who are contradicting each other. "Voluntary jurisdiction," however, is when the Judge does something not out of duty, but at the request of a party who has no adver-

<column-break/>

-sary in that act. This occurs, for example, if two people ask for a contract they have made to be confirmed when they are not in disagreement; or if someone adopts, emancipates, or files a will before a Magistrate, etc.

(f) But this must be with the consent of the Judge, who is not forced to agree to the parties' waivers.

# CHAPTER X.

## ON THE JOINDER OF ISSUE,
## AND RESPONSES TO
## Positional articles; as
## well as concerning
## defense briefs.

### I.

IF the Defendant wishes to proceed to the merits of the case and cannot prolong the suit with "delaying exceptions" <note>original: *dilatoriis exceptionibus*; procedural objections intended to stall the case rather than defeat it permanently</note>, the next step is to contest the suit (a). Certainly, the "joinder of issue" <term>original: *litis contestatio*; the formal moment when the parties' opposing claims are joined and the trial officially begins</term> is the beginning and, as it were, the foundation of the judgment; it is often called its cornerstone. *Mynf. 3. observation 74.* Some even say the suit is contested by the Plaintiff as well. Hence *Vultej. 2. on jurisdiction. chapter 3. number 2.* says: the joinder of issue is the constitution of the judgment, made by the affirmation of one litigant and the contradiction of the other. Thus *Bocer. class 6. disputation 20. thesis 1. 4. & 5.* defines the joinder of issue as the narration made before the Judge by both sides. The Germans call it <term>Kriegsbevestigung</term> <note>literally "the fastening of the war," meaning the formalization of the legal battle</note> or <term>Verfahrung deß Rechtens</term> <note>legal procedure</note>.

(a) Through the joinder of issue, the position of the Defendant becomes worse, and that of the Plaintiff becomes better. This is because, through the joinder of issue, the Defendant is bound to the trial process and can no longer raise delaying exceptions; he is established in "bad faith," prescription is interrupted, etc.

### II.

Since the learned doctors <note>original: *Dd.*; an abbreviation for *Doctores*, meaning legal scholars</note> teach that before the joinder of issue, there is no "suit," and the plaintiff does not yet "seek" but only "wishes to seek," *Gail 1. observation 74. num. 2. Bocer. cited disputation thesis 7. etc.* Therefore, if it is omitted by the consent of the Judge or the litigants, the ordinary judgment will be void by law, as it is deprived of its substantial part. *Chapter 1. extra. on the joinder of issue. ### III.
**Joinder of issue** <note>original: *Litis contestatio*</note> properly occurs when the defendant in the main case, before a competent judge, contradicts the plaintiff's intention by responding negatively. Hostiensis *in the summary on joinder of issue. num. 1.* And certainly, a response made through the defendant's confession—**when the defendant is confessing to the filed complaint** <note>original German: *wann der Beklagt einkommener Klag geständig ist*</note>—is by no means to be considered a joinder of issue: indeed, it then appears there is no dispute at all. For there are no duties for a judge regarding one who confesses, except in sentencing. Obrecht. *on joinder of issue 2. number. 6.* etc. Bocer. *disputation 20. thesis 14. etc.* Likewise, the joinder of issue is either explicitly or implicitly negative. It is explicit when the narrative points of the <term>libel</term> <note>the formal written complaint</note> are simply denied, with these or similar words: **and the defendant absolutely contradicts the filed complaint, also entirely denying the narrative incorporated therein; wherefore he then herewith contests the suit purely negatively, and desires to be absolved from the instituted complaint, with compensation for costs and damages.** <note>original German: *und thut Beklagter der einkommenen Klag allerdings widersprechen...*</note> It is held implicitly, however, when the defendant denies the narrative as it is told, and says that the requests should not be granted: **when the [defendant] does not confess to the complaint in the way it was submitted with its particular circumstances.** <note>original German: *wann der Kläger der Klag, immassen selbige mit ihren sonderbaren Umständen einkommen, nicht geständig ist.*</note> Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance p. 3. t. 3. §. and after. Gail. 1. *obs.* 73. num. 1. This latter method is usually used when the plaintiff cannot deny the narrative of the facts entirely, but nevertheless contradicts certain circumstances on which the request for condemnation relies. And the joinder of issue produces various effects, listed by Bocer, *said disputation 20. thesis 28. etc.* Hiltrop. *pt. 3 t. 1. §. on the effects of joinder.* Namely, it continues actions that would otherwise expire over time: (b) and thus, once the issue is joined, an <term>action for injuries</term> <note>original: *actio injuriarum*; a lawsuit seeking damages for insults or physical harm</note> is made perpetual; likewise, every <term>prescription</term> <note>statute of limitations</note> is interrupted by the same, (c) *Law 1. §. 1. at the end. Code on annual*

<column-break/>

*exceptions. Final law. Code on 30-year prescription.* Gail. 1. *obs.* 74. num. 22. Even penal actions arising from crimes, once the issue is joined, pass passively in full against the heirs if the offender later dies. (d) *§. 1. at the end. Institutes on perpetual and temporary actions. Single law. Code on the crimes of the deceased, to the extent of the heir, etc.* The jurisdiction of an incompetent judge is extended <note>original: *prorogatur*; meaning the judge gains the authority to hear the case because the parties have formally joined the issue before him</note>. *Law 7. Law 30. on Judgments.* <term>Dilatory exceptions</term> <note>legal objections intended to delay the proceedings rather than defeat the claim</note> can no longer be raised. *Chapter 20. on sentences and res judicata. etc.*

(b) Because the joinder of issue is a kind of **quasi-contract**, and it renews, as it were, the prior obligation.

(c) For it introduces "bad faith," with which a prescription cannot proceed.

(d) The reason is what was just said: namely, that through the joinder of issue, the deceased entered into a certain quasi-contract; and quasi-contracts pass to the heirs, Therefore, etc.

### IV.
But when an **articulated libel** <note>original: *Libello articulato*; a complaint broken down into specific, numbered points or "articles"</note> is offered, (e) then together with the joinder of issue, one must respond to each individual Position that deserves a response, distinctly and explicitly: and indeed categorically, using the words **believes to be true, or not true.** <note>original German: *glaubt wahr, oder nicht wahr seyn.*</note> Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance p. 3. t. 13. §. 1. Gail. 1. *obs.* 73. num. 8. This is done not only for the purpose that the Judge might better understand the intention of the parties, but also so that the opposing party may know what they must prove, and not be burdened with superfluous evidence. And if a position is partly true and partly false, then one must respond with a distinction; the whole cannot be denied, but it must be declared in which part it is true. Mynsing 2. *obs.* 55. Hiltrop. *part 3. title on responses. num. 17.* Therefore, the response **does not believe it to be true in the manner articulated** <note>original German: *glaubt articulirter massen nicht wahr.*</note> is not sufficient. However, one does not have to respond to an incriminating position: Græv. 1. *conclus.* 82. n. 12. etc. Myns. *cent. 6. obs.* 93. Marant. *part 6. title on Interrogatories. num. 7.* Wurms. *title 15. obs.* 2. because no one is bound to betray themselves, unless the crime is brought into judgment principally and by way of a civil action: such as a case of debauchery, injuries, etc. (f) Positions of Common Law are also held to be "unanswerable," (g) Mynsing. 5. *obs.* 88. yet if someone should posit that it is so established by law—

# On Judicial Process.

### IV.
...under a specific statute or accepted custom, then it must be answered: see Graevius, conclusion 82, number 22, since this is a matter of fact. There are also deceptive and <term>unanswerable positions</term> <note>original: *positiones captiosæ irresponsales*</note>, which are constructed in such a way that no matter how the respondent turns, they are trapped; see *Speculum*, title on positions, § 10, and Gail, observation 82, number 12. In cases of doubt, <term>Positions</term> <note>specific statements of fact presented to the court for the opponent to admit or deny</note>, even if they seem irrelevant (b), are to be admitted, according to Rutger Ruland, *On Articles*, book 1, chapter 15. This is usually done with a clause inserted into the <term>interlocutory decree</term> <note>a provisional ruling</note>: **Saving the right of the impertinent and non-admissible** <note>original: *Salvo jure impertinentium & non admittendorum*</note>. This protest is also typically placed before the responses made by a party, as noted by Hiltrop, part 3, title 6. Camillo Borelli, in his *Summary of Decisions*, explains which positions do not require a response. But if they are notoriously foolish and irrelevant, the Judge—either after an objection by the party or by virtue of his office—must reject them, as Ruland states in *On Articles*, chapter 3, near the end.

<margin>
(e) **Articles** <note>original: *Articuli*</note> are brief positions into which the facts of a case are broken down, on behalf of which the Plaintiff comes to judgment; such facts must be resolved into these brief points. For articles are considered defective if they contain a double or ambiguous fact to which the defendant cannot respond.

(f) An example is given here regarding an **action for injuries** <note>original: *actio injuriarum*; a lawsuit involving personal insult or physical harm</note>, where one is held to confess—that is, where the crime or its proof pertains to the requirements of the action. For when something is narrated in an action that is not a requirement of that action, the articles then become unanswerable and do not deserve a response.

(g) **Unanswerable articles** are those which no one is bound by law to answer; thus, even if a party says they wish to respond under oath, that oath does not extend to unanswerable articles. These can be denied with a clear conscience even if they are true. For example: if someone brings a lawsuit against me regarding a loan, and then in that same action—entirely outside the subject matter—claims I have committed a theft, I can deny it with a clear conscience even if it is true, since such an article is unanswerable.

(h) **Impertinent articles** are those that do not pertain to the merits of the case, nor establish any requirement of the attempted action. However, so that a party cannot complain, they are sometimes admitted...
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
...when they are **adminiculatory articles** <note>original: *articuli adminiculatorii*</note>—that is, those which do not directly secure a victory but are thought to provide some slight support or "prop" toward victory.

(i) This clause implies that the acceptance and admission of such Articles—**that they are accepted** <note>original German: *daß sie angenommen werden*</note>—must not harm the adversary or create any legal prejudice.
</margin>

### V.
Once the **joinder of issue** <note>original: *litis contestatio*</note> has been made and the responses to the positional articles have been given, the defendant usually deduces his defenses and rights, either summarily or through **defensional articles** and <term>elencos</term> <note>refutations or lists of counter-arguments</note>. This is done by raising a **peremptory exception** (k) <note>a defense that completely kills or "perishes" the plaintiff's claim, such as proof the debt was already paid</note>, either one or several. The penalty for not responding is that the articles are held as **confessed** <note>original: *pro confessatis*; taken as true because they were not denied</note>. Furthermore, just as the defendant is bound to respond to the positions, so the **Plaintiff** <note>original: *Actor*</note> is bound to respond to the defenses. If this is done, the Plaintiff may then allege something against the raised exceptions if he wishes. This is called a **Replication** <note>original: *Replicatio*</note>. It is nothing other than the plaintiff's attack on and exclusion of the defendant's exception. Sometimes the written filings multiply, if the defendant offers a **Duplication** <note>a rejoinder</note> and the plaintiff a **Triplication**, or the defendant a **Quadruplication**. However, in well-ordered courts, such multiplication of writings is not allowed, as per the **Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance** <note>original: *Cammerger. Ordn.*; the procedural rules for the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, part 3, title 29. Nor is this typically done by skilled Advocates; rather, the "deduction of the cause" is reserved until after the evidence (l) has been presented, where it can be done more conveniently.

<margin>
(k) Exceptions against Responses—for example, that a certain article was not answered at all, or not answered categorically, etc.—against which exceptions a Replication is not admitted in certain courts, so that lawsuits are not dragged out over non-essential points.

(l) The reason is that if writings are multiplied before the witnesses are heard, it is done without a foundation; for the healthy and entire foundation of an action consists in the **proofs** <note>original: *probationibus*</note>. Therefore, before the proofs are present, it is useless to dispute the matter.
</margin>

# CHAPTER XI.
## ON COUNTERCLAIMS.

I.
It sometimes happens that the person to whom a <term>Libel</term> <note>the formal written statement of a plaintiff's case</note> is presented does not immediately set forth his defenses; instead, he in turn brings an action against the person who summoned him. This is usually called a **Counterclaim** <note>original: *Reconventio*</note>, or a **mutual petition** (a), or a <term>Gegenklag</term> <note>German: "counter-suit"</note>, as seen in the legal titles on mutual petitions and the Code concerning the sentences and interlocutory decrees of all judges. On the subject of the <term>Gegenklag</term>, Wolfgang Hirshbach and Paulus Nicolai held a special academic dispute at **Wittenberg** in the year 1611. Such a counterclaim is so permitted by Civil Law that a Judge is entirely bound to admit it; furthermore, the original plaintiff—whom they then call the <term>Vorklager</term> <note>German: "first-plaintiff"</note> and <term>Nachbeklagten</term> <note>German: "subsequent-defendant"</note> (while the original defendant is called the <term>Vorbeklagten</term> <note>German: "first-defendant"</note> and <term>Nachklager</term> <note>German: "subsequent-plaintiff"</note>)—is required to respond to it immediately. For it is considered consistent with equity <note>fairness</note> that since someone chooses to follow the judgment of a specific judge when bringing a suit, he ought not to disdain having that same judge preside against him in the same matter, even if he would normally have a right to a different court. This is so much the case that even a mediated Estate of the Empire (notwithstanding the privilege of <term>Austregarum</term> <note>a special right of German princes to have disputes settled by peer-arbitrators rather than standard courts</note>) can be counterclaimed, according to Gisebert in his treatise *On Counterclaims*, chapter 8 and following. Furthermore, a legal representative (b) is compelled to defend both the plaintiff and the defendant in a case of counterclaim, as noted by Molignatus in his treatise *On Counterclaims*, question 16.

<margin>(a) A counterclaim has a place even in those cases where the person being counterclaimed is otherwise not bound to answer, and where the court's jurisdiction was not originally established. If, for example, a citizen of <term>Ingolstadt</term> is sued by a Baron or Count before his own <term>Ingolstadt</term> judge, that citizen can then counterclaim against the Count (the original Plaintiff, or <term>Vorklägern</term>) for another cause before that same judge. This holds even if the Count is perhaps directly subject to the Empire and in no way a subject of the Most Serene Elector of Bavaria. The reason given here is that it is considered consistent with equity, etc.</margin>

<margin>(b) Provided, of course, that the representative previously held a mandate <note>legal authority</note> to take part in the original case.</margin>

II. Nor does it matter whether the judge is an ordinary official or a <term>delegate</term> <note>a judge appointed for a specific case</note> (c); for a counterclaim can be instituted even before the latter: see Gail, book 1, observation 35 at the end, and Frederick, book 3, chapter 6.

<column-break/>

number 10 and following; Molignatus, question 24 and following. It also has a place in <term>summary cases</term> <note>expedited legal proceedings</note>, as noted in the *Clementines* under the heading "often," and the commentary there regarding the meaning of words; Molignatus, question 44. It is even said that a Clergyman can be counterclaimed before a secular judge (d), as noted by Gail, book 1, observation 37, number 6; Mynsinger, book 2, observation 67, number 7; and Gisebert, chapter 11. I cannot personally approve of this, except in those cases where a Clergyman is compelled to answer before a secular person: Molignatus, question 32. Such are cases concerning properties that came to the Clergy with such an obligation attached; otherwise, a Clergyman cannot prejudice his entire order by approaching a judge of the person who sued him. There are also certain types of cases that reject a counterclaim: namely, purely criminal cases (e), spiritual matters, excommunication, matters of immediate possession (f), appeals, and feudal matters (g). See Molignatus, questions 35, 66, and following; Dr. Harprecht's dispute on process, decade 5, thesis 7, number 11; Gisebert, chapters 16, 26, etc. Likewise, those cases committed to an Arbiter do not allow counterclaims, per Molignatus, question 22. Similarly, if the original suit is <term>prejudicial</term> to the counterclaim <note>meaning the first case's outcome must be decided before the second makes sense</note> (b), then the counterclaim has no place. See Peter Frederick in the cited location; Sichard on the Code, law 14; Molignatus, question 47; Gisebert, chapter 14.

<margin>(c) Although a commission <note>the appointment of a delegate judge</note> is a matter of the strictest law and therefore should not seem to be extended, it is nonetheless silently understood that the person delegating the authority has, in cases of doubt and when the contrary is not explicitly stated in the delegation, conformed to common law.</margin>

<margin>(d) This cannot be done for this reason: where jurisdiction cannot be extended, it cannot be established through a counterclaim. Likewise, where someone cannot expressly consent to a judge (which a Clergyman cannot do, lest he prejudice his superior or rather the entire Order), he can even less do so silently. By a counterclaim, however, one silently consents to the judge of his adversary.</margin>

<margin>(e) For the first suit is either civil or criminal. If the first is civil, there is no place for a criminal counterclaim, because the judge of the counterclaim does not have the power to judge in criminal matters, as the types of trials are different. If the first suit is criminal, the accuser still cannot be counterclaimed criminally, so that criminal processes are not entangled, suspended, or prolonged; it is in the interest of the State that crimes be punished quickly. For example: I accuse you of theft; if you then counterclaim me as a thief in the same trial, you achieve nothing, because the process would be suspended for too long.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the procedural requirements for counterclaims (Reconventio), specifically addressing "prejudicial" cases where one judgment affects another. It then transitions into Chapter XII, which covers the various types of financial securities, guarantees, and oaths required of litigants to ensure that a court's judgment can actually be enforced.</meta>

<header>Dispute</header>

<margin>(f)</margin> These, rightfully for the sake of a swift resolution, ought not to allow a counterclaim.
<margin>(g)</margin> For they are of a different kind.
<margin>(h)</margin> Prejudicial cases are those where the judgment in one case brings prejudice to the other, or decides both at once. For example: someone sold me horses that he has in Munich for 200 florins; in the meantime, I give him 100 florins until the horses are delivered. Now, if the horses are seized by soldiers in the meantime, and I sue for the horses or the money given, while he initiates a **Counterclaim** <note>original: *Reconventio*</note> and demands the other hundred florins first—here one action prejudices the other. If one is decided, the other is also finished by that very fact, because the dispute here is: "Which of the two does the loss of these horses fall upon?"

III. And a Counterclaim must be made either before, during, or immediately after the <term>joinder of issue</term> <note>original: *litis contestatio*; the formal moment a lawsuit begins and the points of dispute are fixed</note>. Afterward, it is no longer admitted (i). It is also customary in the joinder of issue and in the responses to the <term>positions</term> <note>the specific facts or articles presented for the defendant to answer</note> to almost always add this clause: **that if the first-plaintiff and subsequent-defendant does not answer the submitted counterclaim, then the first-defendant and subsequent-plaintiff wishes to have his joinder of issue and the answer given to the positions on the first suit revoked.** Furthermore, the original Suit and the Counterclaim ought to proceed at an equal pace (k) <note>original: *pari passu*</note>. This is to be understood as applying if the facts of both cases are established (l); otherwise, a sentence in a <term>liquid</term> <note>a "liquid" case is one where the debt or claim is clear, certain, and undisputed</note> case can be issued first, and it remains entirely within the parties' rights to pursue the undecided case, even if the first one is appealed.

<margin>(i)</margin> The reason is that they ought to be resolved together, which cannot happen if the counterclaim begins only when the original suit is nearly finished.
<margin>(k)</comment> Namely, regarding the legal process.
<margin>(l)</margin> It is otherwise if one action is denied and the other is granted.

# CHAPTER XII.
## ON PROVIDING SECURITY, AND LIKEWISE THE OATH AGAINST CALUMNY AND MALICE; AS WELL AS ON THINGS TO BE GIVEN AND ANSWERED.

### I.
Before the litigants undergo the "gamble of the court" in the principal matter—that is, be-

<column-break/>

fore or immediately after the <term>joinder of issue</term>—it is appropriate for the parties to ensure that their efforts are not in vain. Therefore, guarantees and pledges, or <term>sureties</term> <note>people who take legal responsibility for another's debt or appearance</note> and securities are required. These we call **Security** <note>original German: *Bestand*</note> and **Legal Suretyship** <note>original German: *Bürgschafft zum Rechten*</note> (a). Indeed, one is relieved of the burden of providing a guarantee if they own <term>immovable property</term> <note>real estate, such as land or buildings</note> in the place of the court. This also extends to annual income established upon immovable property. If someone has assets outside the judge's territory, those may be subjected to a <term>mortgage</term> <note>original: *hypotheca*</note> as a guarantee only if a real or personal guarantee cannot be obtained through sureties within the territory. But if no other guarantee can be had, then a **guarantee by oath** <note>original: *juratoria*</note> is considered sufficient (b). A judge usually issues an <term>interlocutory decree</term> <note>a temporary ruling made before the final decision</note> (c) stating that someone must provide security; and only then is an oath-based guarantee admitted if the party diligently searches to see if they can find a surety, and swears that after a careful search, they could not obtain one. However, those suspected of being a flight risk are not admitted to this; rather, they ought to be arrested. Since no one should be burdened with unnecessary guarantees, the complex system and necessity of providing security introduced by the Emperor Justinian has been abolished among almost all nations.

<margin>(a)</margin> Security is provided by the plaintiff so that he may refund expenses [if he loses]; the defendant, however, provides a guarantee **to appear in court** <note>original: *de judicio sisti*</note>. The defendant is not required to provide security **for paying the judgment itself** <note>original: *judicatum solvi*</note> because otherwise, anyone could be sued or harassed with useless demands for security. But if there is a fear of wasting assets or if the defendant is a fugitive, then there is no place for security; instead, an **arrest of sequestration** <note>legal seizure of property</note> is used. A **Procurator** <note>a legal representative or agent</note>, however, is not admitted unless he provides security for paying the judgment or the principal party does so in his name; otherwise, no one is forced to litigate with a Procurator, as execution of a judgment cannot be granted against him.

<header>Concerning Judicial Process</header>

<margin>(b)</margin> For unless this were granted, then a poor person, who cannot provide security through pledges or guarantors, would be deprived of law and justice.

<margin>(c)</margin> The process through a judge’s interim ruling <note>original: *interlocutio*</note> is observed in this manner: when, for example, someone says they cannot provide a guarantee <note>original: *cautio*</note>, they are not immediately admitted to a sworn guarantee <note>original: *juratoria cautio*; an oath taken when one lacks the funds or friends to provide a financial bond</note>. Instead, the judge issues an interim ruling <note>German original: *gibt ein Bescheid*</note> that the guarantee must be provided; but if the party has searched diligently and cannot find guarantors, and can assert this under oath, then that which is lawful must be done. In German, the formula is usually drafted in this way: *In the matter of N. N. versus N. N., regarding the point of the guarantee, the ruling is that the defendant is bound to provide a surety of [amount] N.; however, if he seeks a surety within 14 days and cannot obtain one, then upon further request, whatever is just shall be done.* If, now that the deadline has passed, the Defendant appears and says he diligently sought guarantors but could not find any, only then is he admitted to the oath. That oath extends to two things: first, that he could not find guarantors, and second, that he intends to always present himself for judgment <note>original: *judicio sistere*; a promise not to flee the court's jurisdiction</note>.

## II. And the plaintiff indeed provides security for the refunding of expenses <note>original: *Auth. generaliter. Cod. de Episc. & Cleric.*</note>, even if he possesses movable property <note>citing Panormitanus</note>. And thus he can, despite having provided the guarantee, withdraw from the suit if he refunds the expenses. The defendant provides security to appear in court; but not for paying the amount that is adjudged <note>original: *non verò de solvendo quod est judicatum*</note>. But the defendant's attorney <note>original: *procurator*</note> is compelled to provide security that the judgment will be paid <note>original: *judicatum solvi*</note>, unless the principal [the client] had bound all his goods in the mandate <note>the legal document appointing the attorney</note>, as is almost always done in the instruments of appointment for an attorney.

## III. The oath to avoid or not commit calumny (d) <note>bringing a lawsuit for the sole purpose of harassing the other party</note> is twofold: *general* and *special*. The former is called the oath of Calumny (specifically so-called), and the latter is called the oath of malice <note>original: *malitiæ juramentum*</note>. The *General* oath, or the one for the whole case, is that by which the litigants religiously and solemnly assert that they are not initiating or defending the suit with a spirit of false accusation, but relying on their belief in their own right and confidence; and that they will continue to pursue the case in the same way. The formula for this

<column-break/>

oath is found in the Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber <note>original: *Ordin. Camer. part. 1. tit. 95*</note>. And regularly in every lawsuit (e), the oath of Calumny must be sworn, even in summary cases <note>simplified legal proceedings</note>. And indeed, according to Civil Law, this oath cannot be omitted without the process becoming null and void. But today in practice (f), if it is not demanded by one party or the other, it is omitted while the process remains valid; and if not demanded, it is considered tacitly waived. However, they deny that it can be omitted without nullity if it *has* been demanded. Therefore, if a judge or a legal official sees that a case has reached a conclusion where the oath was demanded but not actually sworn, he ought to rescind the conclusion *ex officio* [by virtue of his office] and command the parties to perform it via an interim ruling (g).

<margin>(d)</margin> Regarding the Oath of Calumny, see Zepper in *Discursu Jurid.* title 6, p. 73, and the sources cited there. Both parties take this oath of calumny, but not the oath of malice. For the Oath of Calumny properly so-called pertains to all judicial acts performed by either the Plaintiff or the Defendant. The Oath of Malice is taken only by that party who is suspected of some specific malice.

<margin>(e)</margin> For one can also commit calumny in summary cases.

<margin>(f)</margin> This is because of the fear of perjury, since parties—often not concerned for the health of their souls—swear rashly. Thus, this oath is considered tacitly waived if not demanded.

<margin>(g)</margin> The formula for this interim ruling is as follows: *In the matter of N. N., the ruling is herewith that the decision made is rescinded ex officio, and both parties are bound to provide the requested Oath of Calumny, and thereafter to conclude the matter, and then further, whatever is just shall proceed and take place.*

## IV. If the Plaintiff refuses such an oath, the defendant is released with expenses. If the Defendant does so, he is considered to have confessed. But the stubbornness <note>original: *contumacia*</note> of an attorney (h) does not harm the master [the client]. It is usually provided at the beginning of the suit: that is, during or immediately after the <term>joinder of issue</term> <note>original: *litis contestatio*; the formal start of the trial</note>. But nevertheless, it can be provided up until the conclusion of the case without a defect in the

the claim of nullity: indeed, even after the conclusion of the cause, before the sentence is delivered, Maranta states in his *Mirror, title on the Oath of Calumny, number 3* that lawyers <note>original: *procuratores*</note> swear not only in the name of their principal, but also upon their own soul. (i) *Chamber Ordinance, part 1, title 95.* Wurmser, *title 5, observation 8.* Berlichius, *part 1, conclusion 21.* Ruland, *on commissions 2, chapter 14.* Gail, *book 1, observation 13.* But if someone does not wish to swear upon their own soul, (k) they may seek a citation to see themselves exonerated, as per the *Chamber Precedents, section on the Oath of Calumny, at the verse "if a procurator."* However, a lawyer is not admitted here without a special mandate. (l) *Penultimate and last chapters on the Oath of Calumny in the 6th book of the Decretals.* In the Chamber Court, a general mandate for all causes is sufficient to include the taking of the oath: but our Doctors of Law require that the cause upon which the oath is to be taken be specifically expressed. <margin>(b)</margin> But the principal <note>the client</note> is summoned to swear.

<margin>(i)</margin> Namely, that they believe they are supporting a good cause.

<margin>(k)</margin> Suppose, if he doubts the truth of the cause, or is otherwise scrupulous in conscience, then likewise the Principal is summoned.

<margin>(l)</margin> An oath binds the soul, and therefore, because of the grave danger to the soul, it is required that someone gives a mandate for swearing deliberately and specifically: Note that it should seem a wonder to no one that the Oath of Calumny is performed by both sides: For it is merely an oath of belief <note>original: *juramentum credulitatis*</note>; and thus it can well happen that one party believes this, and the other the opposite; one believes the cause is good, the other that it is bad, etc.

---

V. The **Oath of Malice** <note>original: *juramentum malitiæ*; an oath sworn regarding a specific point where a party is suspected of acting in bad faith</note> is enjoined at the request of a party, or even by the judge's office, whenever a presumption of some malicious proposal is found to be active: the formula is found in the *Chamber Ordinance, part 1, title 74, chapter 1, section "in omnibus" on the oath of calumny in the 6th book.* And this can be done even if a general oath of calumny has preceded it. (m) *Græve, 1, conclusion 87, consideration 1, numbers 3 and 7.* And he who refuses this oath does not lose the whole case, but is held as having confessed only in respect to that specific article upon which he should have sworn regarding malice. Gail, *1, observation 87.* And it can be demanded even before the contestation of the suit: if, for example, someone is 

<column-break/>

presumed to be acting in bad faith regarding a dilatory exception <note>a legal tactic used to delay proceedings</note>. *Said chapter 2, said section "omnibus."*

<margin>(m)</margin> The reason is this: because specific matters move a person more, and one examines the conscience more closely if they undertake a consideration regarding a specific act.

VI. Very close to the oath of calumny is the *oath* which is commonly called **"of giving and responding"**; (n) so that once that has been performed, this is not thought to be necessary, according to Schwannmann, *1, chapter 45.* But it is enjoined upon the parties only (o) so that by the power of the oath given against bad faith, they may repeat the articles and respond to them. *Disputations of Bocer, said disputation 18, thesis 23.* And it is performed only if it has been demanded. (p) *Græve, 1, conclusion 79, consideration 2.* And the formula for the oath of giving, as well as responding, exists in the *Chamber Ordinance, part 1, title 69 and following.* However, positional statements <note>original: *positionales*; specific points of fact proposed by one party for the other to admit or deny</note> are not always offered by means of an oath; and even then, one does not have to respond by means of an oath.

<margin>(n)</margin> The "Oath of Giving" is that which the Plaintiff performs, who has given an articulated petition to the judge, and by it he asserts that those articles are true, or he believes them to be. The "Oath of Responding" is that which the Defendant performs, and by it he asserts that he has denied the Plaintiff's articles in good faith.

<margin>(o)</margin> The reason is because he has already performed the general one. For there is only one article of the Oath of Calumny, concerning the speaking of the truth; therefore it is not necessary to double it.

<margin>(p)</margin> For if it was not demanded, it is considered tacitly waived, just as was also said above concerning the oath of calumny.

### CHAPTER XIII.

### CONCERNING PROOFS: AND SPECIFICALLY CONCERNING COMMISSIONS for the perpetual memory of a matter. Concerning interrogatory and preliminary articles: concerning Witnesses, Instruments, Confession, and ocular Inspection.

#### I.

**IN** proofs consists the preservation of the parties, and it is incumbent upon anyone to prove the foundation of their intention (a), *Law "qui accusare," Code on "edendo," Law "ei, qui dicit"* <note>standard legal citations regarding the burden of proof</note>.

-># On Judicial Process.<-

### I.
References: *Digest on proofs; Josephus Ludovicus, conclusion 14.*
The proof provided by the **Plaintiff** <note>original: *Actor*</note> must be certain and conclusive, not doubtful or uncertain; nor is it enough for it to conclude that something is "possible," but rather that it is "necessary," as stated by *Josephus Ludovicus in the cited place.* However, a **negative** fact does not need to be proven, <note>b</note> since it is impossible for that to be done; for I cannot prove that I did *not* receive a loan from Titius—unless the negative contains an **implicit affirmation**, as per *Hiltrop, part 3, title 8, section on whom the burden of proof lies.* This is also discussed extensively by *Pacianus in his singular treatise.* 

Furthermore, although the **Defendant** <note>original: *reus*</note> must be acquitted if the plaintiff fails to prove their case, nevertheless, whoever has a **presumption** <note>a legal assumption of truth</note> in their favor shifts the burden of proof to the opposing party: *Speculator, title on proofs, section "to prove," number 12.* For example, if I prove that Titius targeted me with insulting words, it is then presumed that this was done with an **intent to injure** <note>original: *injuriandi animo*</note>, and I am not required to prove that intent. Thus, there is great use for the subject of presumptions, for which *Alciatus* and *Menochius* should be consulted. Regarding how proof should be made in individual causes and actions, *Mascardus* teaches this, as do *Dornspeger in his treatise on proofs* and *Marcellus Cala on the method of articulating claims.*

<note>a</note> Namely, that which he affirms.

<note>b</note> Understand this "as such"; however, a negative can be proven with an implicit affirmative, specifically when the negative denies in such a way that it also simultaneously affirms something. For example: "I did not receive the loan money in the presence of Gaius." Here, I am not only denying the loan, but simultaneously affirming that Gaius was not present—which can easily be proven.

### II.
But because it often happens that, due to the danger of either a **plague** or the **age** <note>c</note> of the witnesses, the ordinary time for trial cannot be awaited, therefore either party—or just one of them—can petition that the witnesses be examined **for the perpetual memory of the matter** <note>original: *ad perpetuam rei memoriam*; a procedure to record testimony before the witness dies or disappears</note>. References: *Rutger Ruland in his treatise on Commissioners, part 2, book 1; Bocer, class 6, disputation 23, thesis 4 and following.* 

And even if witnesses examined in this way are still alive after the formal start of the lawsuit <note>original: *litis contestationem*</note>, they do not need to be examined again. However, there is a difference here between the **Plaintiff** and the **Defendant**. <note>d</note> For the Plaintiff is compelled to initiate the action within a year: *Mynsinger, 4, observation 71; Hartmann Pistor, 1, question 39.* The Defendant, however (since it is not in their power to be sued), can always make use of these recorded testimonies. And for this reason, weightier causes must be present for the Plaintiff than

<column-break/>

for the Defendant for such an examination to be permitted, <note>e</note> *Gail, 1, observation 91, number 4.*

<note>c</note> Or also because of illness, etc.

<note>d</note> For example, if the Plaintiff seeks to have witnesses examined for the perpetual memory of the matter because they are already 60 years old, etc., this is not easily permitted to them unless those witnesses are also of frail health. This is because the Plaintiff can act immediately and thus forestall the death of the witnesses by a swift lawsuit. For the Defendant, however, if the witnesses are already old (60 years or even 50) or otherwise in frail health, the examination for perpetual memory is easily permitted. The reason for the difference is simple: it is not in the power of the Defendant to use their proofs whenever they wish; rather, this depends on the will of the Plaintiff, who might wait twenty years to initiate the action, perhaps for the sole purpose of ensuring the Defendant loses the ability to prove their defense due to the loss of witnesses.

<note>e</note> But once it is permitted to the Plaintiff, such testimonies are valid for only one year, after which they expire.

### III.
Sometimes witnesses are heard **summarily** <note>original: *de plano*</note>, that is, not according to fixed and carefully written articles, **but upon an oral presentation** <note>original: *Sondern auf einen mündlichen Anzug*</note>. This is usually done in summary proceedings, and especially in minor causes: *Speculator, section "now it must be seen" regarding witnesses.* 

However, if the formal complaint <note>original: *libellus*</note> is not "articulated" <note>divided into specific numbered points</note>, then it is not prohibited to offer **probatorial and defensive articles**; these are called **points of presentation** <note>original: *Anzugs-Puncten*</note>. These, however, must be drawn from the summary complaint; otherwise, the Judge can reject them: *Ruland, on articles, books 4 and 5*, where he says that **irrelevant and impertinent articles** <note>g</note> are those which, even if proven, help the cause neither directly nor indirectly. Nevertheless, in cases of doubt, and specifically with the clause **"saving the right of the impertinent"** <note>original: *Salvo jure impertinentium*; meaning the court accepts the points for now but reserves the right to ignore them later if they prove irrelevant</note>, they are to be admitted, as I have already hinted above. 

If, however, the complaint was articulated, and the defensive articles were offered together with the contestation of the suit, then the witnesses are examined according to those articles. Ruland warns in *Book 1 on Articles* that articles must be formed by Advocates with mature deliberation, since the entire strength and victory of the case consists in them; this is because a witness testifying outside of the article is not considered to have provided proof: *Farinacius on testimonies, question 71, throughout.* Sometimes articles are

(f) It is good and advisable to propose the articles to the witnesses, especially regarding a fact where the law may change based on slight circumstances. It is possible that a witness, if not warned about certain circumstances, might not report them.

(g) The reason is that nothing should be proved that is not relevant, and nothing should be omitted that might lead to a victory in the case and which a party is burdened to prove.

**IV.** Furthermore, since a witness sometimes responds affirmatively to an article, but that article—owing to various circumstances—is so structured that it is limited by them, or sometimes even entirely weakened. Therefore, the person against whom those articles are directed, whether they be the defendant or the plaintiff, offers **Interrogatories**: <note>original: *Interrogatoria*; formal questions used to cross-examine a witness to test the truth or detail of their testimony</note> which are proposed in the manner of a question; for example, if Article A states that the plaintiff was beaten by the defendant, then in the interrogatories it is customary to ask: **Whether the Plaintiff did not give cause for this? (k) Sometimes also a witness is led by interrogatories (l) toward a contrary deposition, or even toward wavering, as Ruland teaches in *On Interrogatories*, book 1, chapters 2 and 4; he also teaches in chapter 1 that if interrogatories are not proposed to the witnesses, then the examination is imperfect, and the witnesses must be examined on them again, which Tennin also delivers in *Caution 271*. In *Caution 281*, he also advises that an interrogatory ought to be posed so that the witness is forced to provide the **reason for their knowledge**. <note>original: *causam suae scientiae*; the factual basis for how the witness knows what they claim to know</note> Of the interrogatories, some are general, (m) from which either...

<column-break/>

...the qualification of one or all witnesses is elicited from their own confession, where one is compelled to reveal the quality of another, as per Ruland, *On Interrogatories*, chapter 8. Therefore, they sometimes call "personal" questions **Special** or **Causal** (n) which concern the merits of the case; these refer to one or more specific articles, Ruland chapter 9. Furthermore, for fear of **subornation** <note>the bribery or coaching of witnesses</note> of the witnesses, interrogatories are not to be shared with the opposing party, Ruland chapter 11; Lan. Tennin. *Caution 270*. Also, useless or "captious" <note>deceptive or trap questions</note> interrogatories should be rejected, Ruland chapter 12. And those are also considered **preliminary**: <note>original: *praeliminaris*</note> when, for example, the Defendant asks that in place of preliminaries, (o) his own defensive articles be proposed to the witnesses, Ruland chapter 5.

(k) <gloss>At what time did such a thing happen? In what place? Did anyone else see it?</gloss> <note>original: "Zu was Zeit solches geschehen? welchen Ort? ob es jemand anders auch gesehen..."</note>

(l) And these indeed must be drafted carefully. First, they must be directed at the fact proposed in the article, not at some extraneous fact, for that would be ridiculous. Second, they must be so structured that they limit the article. Third, all the circumstances of the fact contained in the article must be proposed to the witness. Fourth, they must contain the reason for the witness's knowledge.

(m) <gloss>For example: How old is the witness? How wealthy? What is their status and origin? Are they related to the producer or the leader of the witnesses? Do they have any gain or loss from the case? Have they spoken about this matter with the producer? Or been instructed by him regarding it? To whom do they wish the victory? Do they know their fellow witnesses? Are they such people to whom a truth may be trusted? Do they know anything dishonest about any of them?</gloss> <note>original: "Wie alt Zeug seye? wie reich? was Stands und Herkommens..."</note>

(n) Namely, those which are directed solely to the lawsuit itself.

(o) Preliminary interrogatories occur when a party asks that, instead of the standard interrogatories, the defensive articles of his adversary be proposed immediately at the start to the witnesses, which ought not to be done. (1.) Because otherwise a party would have the witnesses examined at the expense of his adversary; (2.) because in this way the opportunity to interrogate would be snatched away from the opposing party.

# Concerning Judicial Procedure.

(p) otherwise it is considered void; but it is within a party's liberty not to appear and to entrust everything to the legality and discretion of the Commissioner, according to Ruland in *On Commissions*, book 5, chapter 3. The opposing party may also present an **Adjunct** <term>Assistant Commissioner</term>, (q) who shall examine the witnesses together with the Commissioner and record their statements. *Witnesses*, furthermore, are strictly required to swear an oath, (r) and the party must be present for this administration of the oath; the Commissioner is also accustomed to warn the witnesses about the gravity and penalties of perjury. That oath, moreover, is not to be administered on a holiday: although witnesses may be examined on a holiday once the sacred rites have been duly performed without the vice of nullity, according to the *Extra* <term>Decretals of Gregory IX</term>, chapter 1, "On Holidays." A witness who has not sworn can still be produced, according to Hartmann Pistor, question 4. And this oath can indeed be waived expressly, but not tacitly, as noted by Mynsinger and Farinaccius. Nor is it sufficient if witnesses of high status testify **by their noble honors** <note>original: "bey ihren Adelichen Ehren"</note> or, if they are officials, **by their official duties** <note>original: "bey ihren Amtspflichten"</note>, as argued by Rauchbar and Setser. Furthermore, witnesses are to be heard in the absence of the party; otherwise, they prove nothing, as per the *Marburg Consultations*. And it must be enjoined upon them that they do not reveal their statements (s) before the publication of the examination. Finally, the witnesses' own statements must be read back to them, according to Hiltrop. Moreover, witnesses residing in a territory other than the judge’s must be heard by their own magistrate; (t) who is usually requested for that purpose through **letters of request** <term>literae mutui compassus</term>, or **by a letter of compass** <note>original: "durch einen Compass-Brief"</note>, as noted by Rauchbar.

<note>(p) Namely, to see the witnesses swear the oath.</note>
<note>(q) An *Adjunct* is one whom the adversary joins to the Commissioner and presents at the time the witnesses are to be examined; but he must be without bias and must even swear **that he has not advised or advocated for the party.** <note>original: "daß er der Parthey nicht gerathen, oder advocirt."</note></note>
<note>(r) Because swearing is a judicial act; whereas examining witnesses is only a consequent judicial act: since the weight of the testimony consists in the oath.</note>
<note>(s) Specifically, so that other witnesses cannot afterwards be coached to agree.</note>
<note>(t) Indeed, examining witnesses is an act of jurisdiction, and thus belongs in a foreign territory, according to Besold.</note>

<column-break/>

cannot be exercised in another territory, following the law in the *Digest*, "On Jurisdiction." If, therefore, for example, a lawsuit is pending before a Judge in Augsburg, but the witnesses are in Bavaria, the Augsburg Judge cannot send a Commissioner into Bavaria to examine witnesses there. Instead, he must request through "letters of mutual assistance" (as they are called) that the local Judge examine the witnesses regarding the articles and interrogatories, and send their testimonies back to the Augsburg Judge.

### VI. Before the Commissioner, it is permitted to raise exceptions against witnesses; however, the Commissioner should not reject them: (u) for that judgment does not belong to him. It is advisable to request that witnesses whom one wishes to challenge in court be included in a separate **Roll** (w) for total rejection: so that if the exception is sufficient, their deposition is not reported. (x) However, this is not the place to treat the exceptions against witnesses or the reasons for which a witness either merits no faith at all or has his statements rendered less credible; for this, one may consult Farinaccius and Volcmarus. Once the examination is duly completed, the Commissioner offers it to the Judge; and the Judge must see whether this is done within the established deadline: **whether the examination, or Roll of witnesses, arrived at the right time?** (y) Then, at the request of the parties, it is either made public or exceptions are raised against the persons of the witnesses.

<note>(u) The reason is that only the examination of witnesses was entrusted to him, not their rejection; therefore, he cannot exceed the limits of his mandate.</note>
<note>(vv) A *Rotulus* <term>Roll</term> (from *rotando*, "turning") is a folded or rolled paper.</note>
<note>(x) Lest the Judge be moved, perhaps even subconsciously, by those useless and rejected testimonies: for we are sometimes moved even by useless things.</note>
<note>(y) Because every deadline is final and absolute.</note>

### VII. Once the witnesses' testimony has been published, a copy of the examination is provided: and once their statements are known, it is not permitted to examine others on the same articles: (z) even in a case of appeal. This is due to the fear of **subornation** <term>bribery or coaching</term>. This rule is limited, however, if the person producing those witnesses did not know of them before, (aa) and confirms this by oath.

(z) The reason is that after publication <note>In this context, "publication" refers to the official opening and sharing of witness statements with the opposing parties.</note> the adversary knows the interrogatories <term>the specific questions asked</term> which, as I have already said, ought to be hidden from them; therefore, after the testimonies have been announced—that is, after the statements were made known—it is no longer permitted to produce more witnesses, because they could be suborned <note>Coached or bribed to lie.</note> regarding how they should respond to the questions.

### VIII. Now I shall proceed to the remaining types of Proof: and one such type is the *Confession of the adversary*. Now, a judicial confession made by a party or another in their name must be accepted, (*bb*) otherwise it does not prejudice the case, *final law, Digest on interrogatory actions; law "Certain," paragraph "If anyone in the absence," Digest on confessions.* Therefore, if an adversary confesses anything, then have that immediately recorded in the proceedings, Tennin, *precaution 28, numbers 11 and final;* Hiltrop, *part 3, title 17.* If, however, someone confesses something in writing, they can revoke it before it is accepted, Hiltrop, *at the same title, paragraph on the revocation of confession.* From this comes the customary clause, usually placed in all writings:
->with the acceptance of what is useful [to the case], and general contradiction or denial of what is contrary.<- <note>original: "mit Annehmung des dienstlichen, und gemeiner contradiction, oder Verneinung deß widrigen."</note>
Tennin, *precaution 26.* Furthermore, a judicial confession has the same effect as a judgment: for execution follows from it; and it is usually called the "fullest proof": *single law and the Doctors' commentary there, Code on Confessions;* Graevæus, *book 1, conclusion 79, number 3;* and it establishes a notorious fact, *final chapter on the cohabitation of Clergy;* extensively in Tennin, *precaution 28, where he discusses the confession of a crime* in criminal matters. A confession made outside of court, however, (*cc*) and not accepted, is nothing but half-proof <term>semiplena probatio</term>. Mascardus, *On Proof, conclusion 349;* Hiltrop, *part 3, title 17, on extra-judicial confession.* Likewise, an extra-judicial confession in personal matters must be made with a cause <note>A specific reason for the debt or obligation.</note>. Thus, it is nothing if someone says: "I owe you 100 florins," but it must be stated whether it is from a loan or some other cause. Soarez, *Received Opinions, letter C, number 229;* Maranta, *part 6, title on Confessions;* Hartmann, *title 11, observation 1.* Moreover, a confession that releases one from an obligation is worth more than one that creates an obligation, (*dd*) as Tennin teaches in *precaution 29.*

(bb) A confession is twofold, namely judicial and extra-judicial. A judicial one is

<column-break/>

most firm, but it can be revoked before it is accepted by the adversary. Hence, for precaution, Advocates observe that when an adversary confesses something, they accept it immediately with these words: **"And because the opposing party admits themselves that the matter is so situated, let it be accepted and received in the best form as a judicial confession and circumstance."** <note>original: "Und weil Gegentheil selbst bekennet, daß die Sach also bewandt, als habe man solches bester Form, als ein Gerichtliche Confession und Bewandnuß acceptiren und annehmen."</note>

(cc) Or an extra-judicial confession, though not accepted, is valid as half-proof (provided it is also proven by witnesses); however, if it is made in the presence of the opposing party and accepted, then it is also valid with the force of full proof. But regarding the effect of half-proof, see the *following chapter.*

(dd) On account of the favor of liberation <note>A legal principle where the law looks more kindly upon proving someone is free of a debt than proving they owe one.</note>. For it is more favorable to say: "Titius paid what he owed me," than "I owe Titius a hundred from a loan," etc.

### IX. Visual inspection, **the view**, (ee) is also quite excellent proof, and it prevails over every kind of proof: every proof is overcome if the visual appearance testifies to the contrary. The Presiding Lord in *Practical Theses, under the word* **Visual Inspection.** <note>original: "Augenschein"</note> And regarding those things which are proven through visual inspection, Hiltrop details them in *part 3, title 20 and following.* For a visual inspection, the parties must be summoned: before Ruland, *On Commissions, part 2, book 3, chapter 2,* etc.; Anton Bullæus, *question 6, folio 269.* The same proof is never considered excluded and may be undertaken by the judge on his own initiative even after the conclusion of the case: Cancerius, *various [resolutions] 2, folio 265;* Tuscus, *letter P, conclusion 774;* nor can it be renounced, Bullæus, *consultation 5, question 49.* Here also are employed **Surveyors**, **Master Builders**, **Surgeons**, **Physicians**, and other craftsmen, according to the nature and quality of the case, Pacianus, *on proof, book 1, chapter 47.* And from this, unless they have sworn an oath from the beginning of their office—**that they are not sworn masters [of their guild]** <note>original: "daß sie nicht geschworne Meister seynd"</note>—they must swear anew, (*ff*) Mynsinger, *observation 6, 34.*

(ee) Some cases are so constituted that their proof depends on evidence—for example, if the question is about the size of a field, then that is investigated through visual inspection with the employment of land surveyors, etc. Likewise, if someone has been injured and the question is the assessment of damages, surgeons are employed and the damage is inspected. Likewise, if the question is whether the deceased died from a wound, physicians are employed and the wound is inspected; the body is also opened so that it may be known whether the wound was fatal, or whether the injured man died from the negligence of the surgeon? etc.

<summary>This page discusses the legal weight of confessions and visual inspections (Augenschein) in court proceedings. It emphasizes that a judicial confession is the strongest form of proof once accepted, and that visual inspection by the court and experts (like surveyors or doctors) overrides other forms of evidence.</summary>

X. Regarding *Instruments* <term>legal documents used as evidence</term>, various and unique inspections occur: namely, concerning instruments that are proper or improper (gg), perfect, imperfect, drafted as a protocol or a finalized copy, authentic, a transcript, common, ancient, "Quarentigiated" <note>original: *Quarentigiato*; a document containing a clause allowing for immediate execution without further trial</note> (bb), public, private, etc. Jacob Bornitius discusses these at length in *On Instruments, book 2.* Indeed, even a private writing (about which Nicolaus of Genoa, also known as de Passeribus, published a unique treatise) serves as proof against the one who wrote it, provided it is acknowledged or supported by a comparison of handwriting. *Merchant and Artisan Account Books* (ii) also serve as proof, but only in matters pertaining to trade or craftsmanship, according to Gail, book 2, *observation 20.* Proof provided through writing also has this unique quality: it can always be introduced as if newly discovered, even after the conclusion of the case, according to Hartmann Hartmanni in *Treatise on Conclusions, observation 2* and Hiltrop, *part 3, title 10, section on producing instruments.* However, one is not permitted to overturn things already judged <note>original: *judicata rescindere*; reversing a final court decision</note> under the pretext of newly discovered documents (kk), according to *The Law of Emperors, 35, Digest on res judicata*; though there are exceptions mentioned by Mynsinger, *century 4, observation 60* and others. Finally, whoever produces a document is presumed to admit its entire content (ll), despite any protestation that they only accept the parts that favor them, as noted by Mascardus, *conclusion 91, title 5,* and Cravetta.

---

(gg) A *Proper Instrument* is one prepared by a public Notary or a Magistrate. An *Improper* one is where a writing is found in an archive, or likewise ancient stones, descriptions, etc.

(bb) A *Quarentigiated instrument* is one that contains executive clauses: and this is a German word turned into Latin: **a fully-secured instrument, by which one is well assured.**

(ii) *Merchant books* lose their credibility if they are found to be false in even a single instance—for example, if some entries are later found not to be canceled <note>original: *non extinctae*; marking a debt as paid</note> even though they were paid. If this is found just once, and the payment of an un-canceled entry is proven, then that book loses credibility in all other matters. These books must also have a specific date to be valid.

---

(kk) One is not permitted to produce any instrument against a sentence to challenge it; yet sometimes "restitution to the original state" <term>restitutio in integrum; a legal remedy to cancel a decision and return to the start</term> is granted if someone failed to produce a document before the sentence not out of negligence, but out of justifiable ignorance.

(ll) If a document has several chapters or articles, one of which benefits the person producing it while another harms them, then if they offer that document to the Judge, they are considered to approve it in its entirety. They cannot say they only approve the article that favors them.

### CHAPTER XIV.

## ON PROBATIVE OATHS: DEFERRED, SUPPLEMENTARY, PURGATION, AND FOR LITIGATION.

---

I.

First, the *Conventional oath* occurs: Aristotle defines this in *Rhetoric to Alexander, Chapter 8* as a statement made with Divine veneration, but devoid of proof. And indeed, he says "devoid of proof" correctly and legally; for it is not proof, but rather a relief from the burden of proving, *Law 30, Digest on oaths,* and Mascardus. This oath is used when the Plaintiff cannot provide proof or wishes to end the lawsuit quickly; he then offers the Defendant the chance to swear that he does not owe anything, and the Plaintiff will yield. Or, if the Defendant says to the Plaintiff: "If you can swear to it, then I will pay you." Only those who have full administration of their own affairs, or a special mandate, can defer <term>formally offer</term> such an oath (a). This oath is regularly offered in every type of case (b), even if nothing has been proven by the party offering it; and although the person to whom it is offered might prefer to prove their case rather than swear, they may still be required to do so. Even after the deadline for proof has passed or witnesses have been published, this can occur. For it is always considered a matter of manifest disgrace to be unwilling to swear or to refer the oath back. It is offered to those who are summoned...

### II. The Suppletory Oath

(e) <margin>The Suppletory Oath is when a Plaintiff proves his claim "semi-fully" <term>semiplenè</term>; then the Oath is deferred to him so that he may supply the defect in his proof. For it would be unfair for the defendant to be acquitted if the Plaintiff has already half-proven the case, as the presumption is then in favor of the Plaintiff. But in that case, it would also be unfair for the defendant to be immediately condemned; therefore, a middle path was found.</margin> is what they call it when it is deferred to the plaintiff to supplement his proof. However, when it is deferred to the defendant due to a lack of proof—which is the burden of the Plaintiff—it is more frequently called a **Purgatory Oath**. The Judge defers the former to the Plaintiff even if the other party has not requested it (*final chapter, on oaths*; Gail, book 1, *observation 108, number 3*). (f) <margin>The judge can do this if he wishes when he thinks he has already proven enough; however, it is required for proof, as if to say: "I am indeed destitute of sufficient proofs, but I can supply this defect with my conscience and my Oath."</margin> (Fachinæus, book 1, chapter 76). And in court, it is usually deferred when the Plaintiff has "semi-fully" proven the merits of his case (Fachinæus, book 1, chapter 18). But if an appeal is made against that judgment, and in the meantime the Plaintiff (who offered himself for swearing) should die, then death is held as the oath (g) <margin>The reason is that otherwise, the case could easily be evaded through an appeal or a delay of the lawsuit until the opponent dies. And because it is enough if the one to whom the Oath was deferred offers himself to swear, for then he has done what he could.</margin> (Mynsinger, book 1, *observation 13*). And furthermore,

<column-break/>

someone is judged to have "semi-fully" proven their case if they have on their side a single witness who is "above all exception" <note>A witness of such high character and reliability that their testimony cannot be easily dismissed</note> (*chapter "from insinuation," regarding proxies*; *final chapter, on succession without a will*). Other examples include an Account Book, a private writing strengthened by a comparison of handwriting, or an out-of-court confession made when the other party was absent. This is discussed extensively by Beust (on *law "of advising"*), and Tennin (*caution 1*). Here, the Judge also considers the condition of the person and likewise the nature of the case; (h) <margin>That is, the gravity. Hence there is no place for the oath in Criminal matters, in matrimonial matters, or in cases involving great sums of money, etc.</margin> for the Plaintiff ought to be a legal person who knows the truth through physical sense (Jason, on the said *law "of advising"*). Likewise, in a difficult matter of great importance, the oath is either not deferred at all, or only when the case has been proven *more than* "semi-fully." Furthermore, the **Purgatory Oath** (i) <margin>The Purgatory Oath is that which is deferred to the Defendant who is burdened only by certain suspicions. Where indeed in criminal matters this oath can and usually is deferred. For if it is not semi-fully proven, the Suppletory Oath cannot be deferred to the Plaintiff.</margin> is usually enjoined upon the defendant when the Plaintiff has proven neither "fully" nor "semi-fully," but nevertheless the defendant is found so burdened by certain suspicions that he ought rightfully to clear himself through an oath (*final chapter, final paragraph, regarding oaths*; also the title on Canonical Purgation; Errell, *Summary of Decisions*, volume 1, title 53; Berlichius, book 1, *conclusion 37*; Heigius, book 1, *question 40*).

(k) The <term>Oath of Value in Litigation [Juramentum in litem]</term> is properly an "Oath of Sentiment," where a thing—which is not restored due to the opponent's malice, or perished because of his malice—is estimated not according to its true price, but according to personal attachment. For it would be unjust then if the owner of the thing received only the true market value, because he perhaps would have been unwilling to sell his property. It often happens that someone holds a thing more dearly than the true proportion of its price requires. Therefore, here, because of the opponent's malice, the sentiment is also estimated, which no one can better tax and define than the owner himself. A similar thing happens in cases of personal injury, if someone says, for example, that he would have preferred to lose 100 Ducats than to have endured this insult.
</note>
<note>
(l) The second species of the Oath of Value in Litigation is when the true price or the <term>legal interest [interesse]</term> <note>original: "interesse"; this refers to the financial loss or potential gain lost by the plaintiff</note> is estimated for a thing that no longer exists; and thus, since it cannot be appraised by other evaluators by sight, the estimation must be made by the owner according to the true price. However, understand these things in those cases where the opponent’s malice did not intervene.
</note>

### III. The Oath of Value in Litigation is twofold:
And first, indeed, it is offered when a disputed movable thing is estimated based on sentiment (k) Borcholt on Oaths, chapter 2. And it is offered then when the defendant does not restore that thing, or it was caused by his malice, or even by gross negligence, that it was not restored (*law 68, on the recovery of property*; Bocer, class 6, dispute 18, thesis 88). And because here the sentiment—not the true price or the interest—is being proved, the swearing can be for an indefinite amount. The Judge, however, either defines a maximum sum within which the oath may be taken; or, if the one swearing wishes to tax his sentiment beyond the limits of equity, the Judge may trim away what is superfluous at his own discretion.
Furthermore, sometimes the true price of the thing (l) or the interest is estimated: namely, when the Judge cannot otherwise estimate the thing which perished, or the interest. Bocer, in the same place, thesis 199, etc.
