# CHAPTER XV.
## ON THE ALLEGATIONS OF THE PARTIES, THE CONCLUSION OF THE CASE, AND THE FILING OF THE RECORDS.

### I.
Finally, once the evidence has been produced, one must then study the legal allegations and the

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

deductions of the facts: commonly called the **Statement of Proof and Deduction** <note>original German: "Probations- & Deductions-Schrifft"</note>, and on the part of the Defendant, the **Writing of Exception and Refutation, or the Eliminatory Statement** <note>original German: "Exception- und Refutations- oder Elisiv-Schrifft"</note>. Afterward, both parties offer a **Concluding Statement** <note>original German: "Conclusion-Schrifft"</note>. In these writings, not only the laws, but also the facts are strengthened by the proofs: objections are made against the statements and persons of the witnesses, and all things are brought forward which (a) can be devised for proving anyone's intent, or for the invalidation of the opponent's proofs.

<note>
(a) That is to say, the Plaintiff brings forth his proofs and his legal rights against such a writing; the Defendant brings his exceptions, which he also strengthens both by the statements of witnesses and by the Laws, and at the same time refutes the Plaintiff’s proofs. Whence it is also called a **Refutation-Statement, or Eliminatory-Statement**, because not only are the exceptions strengthened, but the Plaintiff’s intent is refuted and eliminated. Furthermore, in the **Concluding Statement**, the Plaintiff repeats his legal rights and refutes the defendant's arguments, which the defendant then also does afterward.
</note>

### II. However, experienced practitioners disagree on how one should proceed in drafting such allegations.
See the *Speculator* on allegations, the section "now it must be seen." And some judge it to be better to propose each individual article, both of the Plaintiff and the Defendant, one by one, and to subject to each article the proofs that serve to confirm it. But this method does not please Adam Keller (book 2, *On Juridical-Political Offices*, chapter 29). Those do more correctly, therefore, who direct those writings toward the requirements of the action being attempted: and they proceed in almost the same way that skilled Judges are accustomed to do in reporting and deciding cases; so that nothing is omitted which a Judge ought to or can attend to; and nothing is added which does not lead to the victory of the case. For if this is done, cases are more entangled than unrolled, and the Judge is annoyed, and sometimes even confused and led into trackless wastes. Bulle, *Academic Discourse* 8.

### III. After both parties have been sufficiently heard, the case is usually concluded: Practitioners call the conclusion of the case "the Legal Ruling (b) or Resolution"
<note>original German: "den Rechtsatz oder Beschluß"</note> when the litigants on both sides renounce all allegations and exceptions, both of fact and of Law, for the sake of the sentence being delivered, (c) Gail, book 1, observation 107, number 3. Sometimes...

Even by the Judge <term>ex officio</term> <note>by virtue of his office</note> the case is accepted as concluded when, for example, one or the other party prolongs the litigation with useless deductions. In the main case, however, the matter is said to be concluded; at the point of an <term>interlocutory</term> <note>a provisional or intermediate ruling made before the final decision</note> decree, we use the term <term>submission</term>, *Hiltrop. part 3. t. 29. n. 22.* This is also done by the parties sometimes in writing, and more frequently orally; and to that end, the parties who have offered their writings are summoned **for the Oral Conclusion.** <note>original German: "zum Mündlichen Beschluß"</note> The closing of the case occurs sometimes "purely," that is, without any condition; sometimes, for instance, if a party can still prove something but does not know whether this will lead to the victory of the case, then the conclusion is usually made "with the offering of any fact." (c) The conclusion is made either "purely" or "with the offering of any fact." For that which is made purely, with the renunciation of further proof, the formula is usually as follows: **In the matter of N. N., I as advocate in the name of the Plaintiff have repeated everything useful, generally and for all time contradicted the evil and contrary, and do not acknowledge it through silence; and then have committed this entire matter finally to the Lord Judge’s reasonable recognition, and further have renounced proof and deduction, and have prayed for a speedy judgment.** <note>This formula is a formal surrender of the right to present more evidence in favor of a final verdict.</note>

(d) But another conclusion is sometimes made "with the offering of any fact," <note>original Latin: "cum oblatione si quid facti"</note> and this occurs when the defendant offers himself to the proof of some fact if it were not sufficiently proven, or if it were not proven at all, yet the Judge thought that proof of that unproven fact was necessary. The formula of this renunciation is like the one above at the beginning, up to the words "committed"; then: **yet expressly making myself offering in the event it is necessary to bring forward something further, especially...** (those points can be set down here) **that I offer in the name of my principal to bring such forward, thus I wish it concluded not otherwise than with the offering if any fact remains.** <note>This "conditional" closing allows a lawyer to save face if the judge decides more evidence is needed on a specific point.</note>

When, however, the case is concluded, they thereby renounce further proofs and deductions.

(f) When a definitive sentence is set forth in a Civil Process, then if the case has not yet been concluded by the parties, that sentence is considered null, and thus is rescinded without appeal. <margin>(g) In order for such instruments to be admitted for the first time after the conclusion of the case, two things are required: (1) that they have been newly discovered; (2) that the party acts in good faith—that is, that they did not know of the instruments before, or did not maliciously hide them, nor were they negligent in searching for them, so that they do not now wish to produce literary documents merely to prolong the litigation. **In the matter of N. N., if N. can and will swear a bodily oath to God, that he found the instruments and written documents now produced by him only after the conclusion of the matter, and did not know of them before, and also did not hold them back until this time to prolong the matter; then such documents shall be accepted and taken into due consideration.** <note>original German: "In Sachen N. N. wann N. könne und wolle ein leiblichen Aid zu GOtt schwören, daß er die von ihme anjetzo producirte Instrumenta und Schrifftliche Urkunden, erst nach dem Beschluß der Sachen gefunden, und zuvor nicht gewußt, auch solche nicht erst bis auf diese Zeit zu Verlängerung der Sachen aufgehalten, daß alsdann solche angenommen, und in gebührende Obacht gezogen werden sollen."</note> And in this case of newly discovered instruments, the opposing party can seek copies, propose their exceptions against them, and whatever else seems appropriate.</margin>

<margin>(b) Here a caution and a certain singular observation is proposed: namely, that even after the conclusion of the case, for the information of the Judge, the **Consultations and responses of Legal Consultants** <note>original Latin: "Consilia & responsa JCC."</note> and of legal Colleges may be offered to the Judge, even without the opposing party’s knowledge (for often the case is concluded, and yet the publication of the sentence occurs a long time later). Nor is the Judge compelled to share such Consultations with the opposing party; indeed, it is better that the opposing party knows nothing about this at all. But these Consultations must be so arranged that nothing new is proposed regarding the facts, but rather mere legal reasons previously omitted or not brought forward are deduced and adapted to the facts already established in the process. The reason why they should not be shared with the opposing party is this: because even if the Judge is highly skilled in law or can otherwise ask those more skilled, and thus those new legal allegations seem almost superfluous; nevertheless, if such reasons were written by Besold, Volume I,</margin>

by prudent **Legal Consultants**, they can be of great benefit and thereafter move the Judge significantly by the authority of such great Jurists.

IV. Finally, the Judge sometimes does not wish to decide upon the records himself, (i) but seeks the **judgment of some College** <note>referring to a University faculty of law or a high judicial board</note>: and then the parties, before the records are transmitted to the experts, are usually summoned somewhere so that they may appear on a certain day and term to see the records registered and legitimately enrolled, *Schrader part. 10. sect. 14. num. 19. and following; Bullae discourse 9.*

<margin>(i) When a Judge pronounces a sentence not from his own opinion but as instructed by others, then the sentence contains this clause: **It is decided according to the deliberation taken and advice received.** <note>original German: "Ist auf genommenen Bedacht und gehabten Rath zu Recht erkennt."</note> Sometimes the parties also request that the Consultation of some legal College or other skilled Jurists be sought.</margin>

***

### CHAPTER XVI.

->**OF THE REPORT, EXPENSES, SENTENCE, AND THE ADJUDGED MATTER.**<-

I. **I**n the past, lawsuits had to be finished within a certain time limit: *Law "properandum" in the Code of Justinian regarding Judges.* But nowadays, in all places, the instance is perpetual, *Mynsinger century 1, observation 51, note 9; Bullae consultation 6, question 1.* But if the sentence is to be conceived and reported by the expert Assessors, a certain and methodical system is prescribed, which they commonly call the **method of reporting**: concerning which matter, a **singular dispute** has already been proposed.

II. Regarding **Expenses**, however, this is observed: that regularly the loser is condemned to pay the expenses of the winner, and sometimes also the fruits and interest; unless a probable cause excuses him: (a) *Hiltrop part 4, last chapter, note 45, etc.* Which ought to be expressed in the sentence: **and the costs are, for moving reasons, compensated against each other.** <note>original German: "und seynd die Unkosten, aus bewegenden Ursachen, gegen einander compensirt." Meaning both parties cover their own costs.</note> (b) In some places, the loser is condemned to half or another part of the expenses from the moment he realized he was no longer supported by a good legal right. (c) *Hiltrop, cited location, number 48.* And indeed

The expenses of **interlocutory decrees** <note>provisional rulings made during a case</note> (d) are usually reserved until the decision on the principal case. However, costs arising from **contumacy** <note>willful disobedience or failure to appear in court</note> or the delay of the lawsuit must be paid immediately, according to Mynsing (1. *obs.* 23. & 45.) and Gail (1. *obs.* 151. *num.* 15.). Furthermore, expenses are awarded indefinitely in this manner: **That the defendant shall be bound to reimburse the plaintiff for the court costs incurred, upon the plaintiff’s various proofs, after also hearing the defendant’s additions and objections, according to the Judge’s moderation.** <note>original German: "Daß der Beklagte dem Kläger, den aufgeloffenen Gerichts-Kosten, auf sein Klägers unterschiedliches Darthun, auch deß Beklagten Zu- und Einred, nach Richterlicher Mäßigung zu erstatten schuldig seyn solle."</note> And then, once the itemized list of expenses has been presented and the other party has been heard, the Judge is accustomed to **tax** <note>to officially assess or limit the amount of</note> them, cutting away those that are superfluous and unnecessary (Gail 1. *obs.* 151. *num.* 2. etc.). If the total exceeds the sum of 20 florins, the Judge receives the oath of the prevailing party—**namely, that he laid out that much, and not less** <note>original German: "daß er nemlich so viel, und nicht darunter ausgelegt"</note>—and finally, he pronounces judgment upon the taxed costs thus proven by oath: **That the compensation previously awarded to the plaintiff is moderated to N. florins, which the defendant is also bound to pay to the plaintiff.** <note>original German: "Daß der, dem Kläger hiervor zuerkandte Abtrag, auf N. fl. gemäßigt, die er beklagt, auch ihme Klägern zu entrichten schuldig seyn sollen."</note>

> (a) The rule indeed is that the defeated party ought regularly to be condemned to pay expenses; however, this is limited if the defeated party had **probable causes** for litigating. For example, if he has one witness on his side; if he is an heir (for an heir likely litigates regarding the actions of the deceased); or if he has a well-founded intent which is only later struck down by an **exception** <note>a specific legal defense that nullifies a claim</note>. For instance, if he brings an action for a loan of 100 florins, and it is then defeated by an exception of payment, etc. In such cases, the expenses are **compensated** <note>offset so that each party bears their own costs</note>. A similar thing happens whenever the opponent wins by an **Oath**. The reason for this is that when my opponent is forced to complete his proof by an oath, it appears by this very fact that his case was not so clear as to put me in **bad faith** <note>Latin: "mala fides"; acting with knowledge of being in the wrong</note>, or to say that I litigated rashly, since he had to win by an Oath in the first place. Thus, only he who litigates rashly and has no probable cause for his suit is condemned to pay expenses; it is otherwise for one who acted in **good faith** <note>Latin: "bona fide"</note>.

> (b) **Offset and canceled against each other, so that each should bear his own costs.** <note>original German: "Gegeneinander compensirt und aufgehebt, daß jeder sein Unkosten selbst tragen solle."</note>

> (c) Although someone is immediately placed in **bad faith** by the **contestation of the lawsuit** <note>the formal start of the trial</note>, this is only to be understood regarding the ability to claim by prescription or to gain profits, etc., and not regarding the right to litigate. Therefore, so that this thesis may be rightly understood, let us suppose such a case: someone does from the beginning not know (which easily happens) that his opponent

<column-break/>

cherishes a good cause; then, according to equity, he is released from the payment of expenses. But I say that once he has learned from the process of the case that he is already, as it were, convicted and can no longer hold his position, and yet he litigates further, from that time he is bound to pay expenses: he has been established in **bad faith**.

> (d) Although sometimes the expenses of interlocutory decrees are suspended until the definitive judgment, using this or a similar formula: **And let the costs incurred on account of this dispute be reserved and postponed until the resolution of the main case.** <note>original German: "Und sollen dieses Streits halber aufgeloffene Unkosten, bis zu Erörterung der Hauptsache reservirt und verschoben."</note> This is usually done in those cases where an interlocutory decree is brought regarding a point of **Exception** (for example, against witnesses, etc.); however, regarding a point of **contumacy**, they must be paid immediately because of the dislike for such behavior.

> (e) The reason is that before the expenses are itemized, it is not known what the party has spent, and the Judge would act precipitously if he taxed the expenses immediately.

### III. A Judgment is either Interlocutory
(which is, for instance, brought regarding an incidental point of the case) or **definitive**, which finishes the whole dispute. Sometimes a ruling is said to have the **force of a definitive judgment** (f), even though it is not truly such (Hiltrop. *part.* 4. *t.* 1. §. 1. *interlocut. sentent.*). The judgment must be conceived according to the form of the **libellus** <note>the plaintiff's written petition or complaint</note> (g) (*L. C. de edend. clem. sæpè. §. verum. de verb. sign.* Borell. *tom.* 2. *t.* 30. *n.* 37. & *n.* 43.). Otherwise, if the judge pronounces against or beyond the form of the petition, the judgment is considered flawed. However, the reason for the condemnation or acquittal is not usually expressed in the judgment itself (*c. sicut nobis 16. de* Panorm. *de sent. & re judic.* Hiltrop. *part.* 4. *t.* 1. *n.* 25. & seqq.).

> (f) Namely, that interlocutory decree has the force of a definitive judgment which, while it does not finish the whole lawsuit, nevertheless brings some **irreparable prejudice**—as, for example, if a witness is rejected.

> (g) For if it is not conforming to the petition, it is void. But what if the Defendant is acquitted? Here it is certainly not conforming to the Plaintiff’s petition. I respond: It is nonetheless conforming to the petition of the **defendant**. For the judgment must be conforming to the petition of that party in whose favor it is pronounced.

### IV. After a Judge has once delivered
a judgment, whether it be fair or unfair, he cannot rescind or change it further. (h) (*l.* 14. *l.* 42. *l.* 55. *l.* 62. *ff. de Judic. l.* 9. *C. sentent. rescindi non posse.*). He can, however, clarify and inter-

...can be interpreted, according to Gail, book 2, observation 1, number 6. But that declaration must remain within the limits of a declaration: (i) nor can the Judge partially repeal, correct, or extend it, (k) according to Tennin, caution 11; add Cravetta, counsel 88, throughout. If a judgment was delivered based on the opinion of experts—for instance, surgeons, physicians, or other skilled craftsmen—some argue that it does not pass into a "matter already judged" <term>res judicata: a case that has been definitively decided by a court and cannot be reopened by the same parties</term>, but that more skilled experts can always be consulted. Therefore, as a precaution, the Judge should observe that he himself also inquires diligently and examines the experts, and ensures this is recorded in the Acts. (l) Tennin, caution 188. For then the judgment appears to be delivered based on the Judge's own understanding. Finally, a "matter already judged" differs from a sentence <note>a judicial ruling</note> as an effect differs from its cause: and thus a sentence, while an appeal is pending, is not called a "matter already judged" (referencing the Title of the Code *on the matter judged*). It only earns this name if it brings a complete end to the controversy (Law 1, *on the matter judged*). It is then held as truth (Law 25, *on the status of men*; Law 207, *on the rules of law*). And it cannot be rescinded under the pretext of newly discovered documents, nor even due to a mathematical error, (m) (Law 19 and following, Code *on transactions*; Fachinaeus book 1, chapter 51, etc.). From this, the "action on the judgment" arises, (n) and the prior action is transformed into it, so to speak (Laws 2 and 3, Code *on interest on a matter judged*; Law 8, Code *on things credited*).

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## ON APPEALS, NULLITY, AND EXECUTION.

### I.

If a sentence seems unjust, one is permitted to appeal to the next superior authority: (a) and this may be done either orally on the spot, (b) or in writing within 10 days, calculated from the moment the sentence was delivered or from the moment of knowledge (if one does not have a legal representative present at the proceedings). (c) (Novel 'Today', Code *on appeals*; Gail book 1, observation 139, number 5; Mynsinger 3, observation 11.) In other places, it is required by statute that the appellant swear an oath of good faith <note>original: *malitiae juramentum*, an oath that the appeal is not made out of malice or for delay</note>, and that the case exceed a certain sum, etc. (Gail 1, observation 119 & 126; Mynsinger 1, observation 6.)

(b) Because the Judge has performed his duty once. A Judge can only retract a sentence that has passed into "a matter already judged" if an express legal cause exists—for example, if the sentence is void, or if a cause exists for which the losing party should be granted "restoration to the original state" <term>restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy that restores a person to their previous legal position as if an event had not occurred</term>. Indeed, only the sovereign, who is above the laws, can rescind a sentence already delivered based on pure equity. Even so, he ought not to do this except for a great cause or public utility, etc.

(i) To "declare" in this context is also called by another name, "to clarify" <note>original: *leuterare*, derived from the German legal term *läutern*</note>. However, the Saxon method of clarification is different, having the force of an appeal, such that the sentence can even be corrected by it.

(k) It is understood that these things cannot be done under the guise of a declaration or clarification.

(l) That is, using this or a similar formula: **"based on advice received and our own opinion."** <note>original German: *auf gehabten Rath, und unser selbst Gutachten*</note>

(m) Nevertheless, restoration to the original state is sometimes granted,

<column-break/>

especially to Minors; and also to Adults for causes expressly stated in the law.

(n) This happens for this reason: if, for example, I have an action for injuries against Titius, and a judgment has already been made on that action once, for the second time I no longer bring the action for injuries, but an "action on the judgment" <term>actio judicati: a lawsuit brought to enforce a judgment already rendered</term>; thus the prior action for injuries is transformed in my favor into an action on the judgment, which is much richer and swifter than the original action for injuries.

(a) If there are several higher judges in succession, then one must appeal to the next highest; thus, if a sentence is delivered by a **Municipal City** <note>original German: *von einer Fürstlichen Stadt*</note>, one should not appeal immediately to the Imperial Chamber, but first to the Prince or his Consistory, to **his high court** <note>original German: *an sein Hofgericht*</note>, and then from that Consistory an appeal finally proceeds to the Imperial Chamber. If anyone, therefore, were to appeal immediately to the highest possible authority—as in the proposed case to the Imperial Chamber—then that appeal is sent back by the higher court to the intermediate one; the appeal is not considered entirely invalid, but the appeal must also be made through the one who delivered the sentence.

(b) An appeal is made orally if someone simply says, "I appeal." For words are sufficient if they are uttered on the spot, while the Judge is still sitting on the bench. However, the losing party is free to seek time for deliberation; **he can take time to consider the judgment.** <note>original German: *er kan sich des Urtheils einen Bedacht nehmen*</note> And if the opposing party has not "given thanks"—**has not expressed acceptance of the judgment** <note>original German: *sich des Urtheils nicht bedanckt hat*</note>—he can then take up a common appeal. For often...

Indeed, it happens that a judgment may not entirely please either party. When an appeal is not made immediately <note>original: "incontinenti"</note> on the spot, it must then be appealed in writing after an interval within ten days; once these have elapsed, the judgment passes into a "matter already judged" <term>res judicata: a case that has been definitively decided and cannot be reopened</term>. That ten-day period runs from moment to moment; therefore, the Protocol <note>the official record of the court proceedings</note> must record the exact hour the sentence was delivered as well as the hour the appeal was made or filed.

(c) This applies if, for instance, the party is not defiant <term>contumax: a legal term for someone who willfully refuses to obey a court order or appear when summoned</term>. For if a person is defiant, they cannot appeal.

## II. Furthermore, the **Records**, and the **Dismissory Letters** (d) <note>original: "Acta, & Apostoli"</note>—if they were not requested at the same time the appeal was filed—must be diligently sought within 30 days of the judgment being delivered. If this is not done, the appeal is considered abandoned (*Canon Law on appeals, Book 6; Law on the meaning of words 106; Clementine Constitutions on appeals*). Once these are obtained, the person appealing must present themselves before the Superior Judge within the timeframe (e) designated by the Lower Judge or prescribed by statute (Gail, book 1, observation 140). They must then deliver the **Records** to him, or announce that an appeal has been filed and seek a stay of execution (f) <note>original: "inhibitionem"</note>, and if the **Records** have not been released, they must seek a compulsory order (g) <note>to force the lower court to hand over the files</note>. It is also permitted to appeal before a Notary (h) and witnesses (Hiltrop, part 4, title 3, number 8, etc.). But the legal instrument drawn up thereafter (in which the content of the judgment and the appeal schedule are usually inserted) must be filed with the Lower Judge, so that he does not attempt any new actions or changes to the case.

(d) The formality discussed in the previous thesis is called the "formality of filing an appeal"; the request for the Records and Dismissory Letters also pertains to this. Indeed, the Records must be requested because the Superior Judge cannot recognize the injustice of a sentence unless he sees the Records. The Dismissory Letters <note>original: "Apostoli"</note> are the formal letters by which the Judge of the first instance transfers the case to the superior. These letters are sometimes *Refutatory*, which is when the Judge of the first instance gives only some writing in place of the letters, in which he says and believes the appeal to be frivolous, or that it cannot be appealed, etc.; for then he denies the appeal and issues *Refutatory Dismissory Letters*. However, the appellant can go to the superior for a compulsory order. It is, however, advised that the Dismissory Letters and Records be requested immediately along with the appeal, using this or a similar formula: **“Since I find myself aggrieved in many ways by the pronounced judgment: I hereby appeal in the best legal form to the next higher [Name of Judge], and I summon myself, and at the same time have requested the**

<column-break/>

**Records and Reverential Dismissory Letters.”** They are called Reverential Letters because the case is sent from the lower to the higher court out of reverence for the superior. If, however, the Letters and Records were not requested immediately with the appeal, then it must be done within 30 days. If the petition for the Letters is omitted, the appeal is still received in the Imperial Chamber (Fabricius in *Gaedaeus Enucleatus, observation 139, section 4*).

(e) This deadline is called the "fatal formality for prosecuting an appeal," and if it is not prescribed by statute, the Lower Judge—the one who delivered the sentence—can define it.

(f) A stay <note>original: "inhibitio"</note> is an order from the Superior which commands the inferior not to execute the judgment while the appeal is pending. Therefore, if any actions are attempted—and these must be revoked before all else—if the judgment was sent for execution in whole or in part before the stay but while the appeal was already pending (for an appeal by its very nature suspends execution), or if anything else is done to hinder the filed appeal. These matters must be revoked before proceeding further in the main case.

(g) That is, if the Lower Judge previously gave him Refutatory letters.

(h) An appeal can also be made before a Notary if the Judge is absent, or if perhaps someone does not dare to appeal in the presence of the Judge; he then does this before a Notary so that the appeal may be served to the Judge through him.

## III. If one is appealing from a definitive sentence <note>a final ruling that ends the case</note>, it is sufficient if one says, "I appeal." But from an interlocutory sentence <note>a provisional ruling on a specific point during the trial</note>, the appeal must always be made in writing, and "with cause"—that is, with an expression of the grievances (*Canon Law on appeals, chapters 59 and 18, Book 6*). This is because, as a rule, it is not permitted to appeal from an interlocutory ruling; and therefore, one is not allowed to bring forward other grievances in the presentation of such an appeal than those expressed in the appeal document (i). But in an appeal from a definitive sentence, things not yet presented can be presented, and things not yet proven can be proven (k) (*Code of Justinian, Law 4, on the timing of appeals*; Hiltrop, title 3, number 18, etc.). And an appeal has this primary effect: it suspends the execution of the "matter already judged." Therefore, if either the Judge of the first instance or the appellee attempts anything, those attempts are revoked before all else. But it seems unnecessary to add more regarding appeals, since a few years ago I wrote a separate treatise on this matter...

the Lord President has written, who may be consulted.

(i) Even if this expression is not made, the case can still proceed.

(k) And thus witnesses may be examined anew if they were not heard previously, etc.

IV. Regarding a sentence which is void by the law itself <note>original: "ipso jure nulla"</note>, (l) it is not necessary to file an appeal: *Title of the Code: when an appeal is not necessary*, for example, if it was delivered contrary to the order of the Courts <note>original: "contra ordinem Judiciorum"</note>, *Law 4, Code on sentences and interlocutory decrees of all Judges*. Likewise, if a sentence is brought forth against the tenor of a matter already judged <term>res judicata: a case that has been definitively decided and cannot be reopened</term>, *Law 1, Code: when an appeal is not necessary*. And if any other such things occur, which Vantius <note>Sebastian Vantius (1519–1570), an Italian jurist known for his work on the nullity of legal acts</note> proposes throughout his treatise *On Nullities*, and which were also mentioned scattered above. Such nullity can be proposed either before the same Judge who delivered the sentence, or a superior may be approached and the nullity argued before him. *Vantius on nullity, chapter: before whom nullity ought to be opposed, number 8 and following*. This is done either as the main legal action or as an incidental matter. (m) Or even by way of an appeal, *Hiltrop, part 4, title 17*. One may propose a Nullity within 30 years, and its filing suspends the execution of the sentence, provided it can be proven immediately <note>original: "incontinenti"</note>. (n) *Surdus, Counsel 99, number 18, volume 1*. Sometimes "restoration to the original state" <term>restitutio in integrum: a legal remedy that restores parties to their condition before a contract or judgment</term> is also sought against a sentence that has passed into a final judgment, *Hiltrop, part 4, title 10*.

(l) He who appeals says the sentence is unfair, even though no defect appears in the judicial order. If, however, a sentence is called "null," this happens where something was omitted or erroneously committed regarding the Process. Therefore, a sentence can be fair and yet still be null.

(m) Nullity is proposed "incidentally" when someone says: "I declare the sentence to be completely null, or if it is not null, I nonetheless prove it to be unfair." Thus, it can be sought as an alternative.

(n) But if it cannot be proven immediately, then the sentence must be executed, and only after execution may the nullity be disputed.

V. A sentence which has not been suspended by an appeal or a claim of nullity (o) must be sent for Execution. For judgments without execution are deceptive <note>original: "elusoria"</note>;

<column-break/>

and a sentence without execution is like a **bell without a clapper** <note>original: "campana sine pistillo"</note>, as the Doctors of Law say. However, the party must be summoned to see the execution carried out, (p) *Wurmser, title on the execution of sentences, observation 6*. A legal representative <term>procurator: a person authorized to act for another in court</term> seeking to execute the sentence does not need a new mandate. (q) *Decianus, Counsel 11, number 1, volume 1*. But so that a sentence which has become a final judgment may be executed more quickly, it is not permitted to appeal from a sentence that orders execution, unless an exception is raised against the execution that requires deeper investigation, or if the executor exceeds the proper bounds in carrying it out, (r) *Law 5, Code: whose appeals are not received; Law 4, at the beginning, Digest: on appeals; Wurmser, title 43, observation 20; Gabriel, Common Conclusions, title on appeals, conclusion 4*.

(o) When a sentence has passed into a final judgment <note>original: "rem judicatam"</note>, there is no need to initiate a new "action on the judgment" <note>original: "actio judicati"</note>; instead, the "noble office of the Judge" <note>the inherent power of a judge to ensure justice is served</note> may be implored so that, as if by a Royal hand, the sentence is sent for execution, and indeed without a full trial. But if it is not immediately clear that a sentence was delivered, or if the adversary denies that judgment was passed, then an "action on the judgment" is rightly initiated.

(p) And this is done so that he may see to it that no excess is committed in the execution.

(q) The reason is that execution is a necessary consequence, and thus an inseparable accessory to the principal case; hence, he who has a mandate in the principal case is thought to have it in the accessory as well.

(r) Add this: if that execution contains a new grievance <note>original: "gravamen"</note> which was not mentioned in the sentence.

VI. There remains also a remedy against sentences from which one cannot appeal, namely **Revision** (s), about which a specific treatise, primarily adapted for Chamber Law <note>referring to the *Reichskammergericht* or Imperial Chamber Court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, was written by Ludwig Bender. Likewise, an unfair sentence never passes into a final judgment as far as the Judge is concerned, *Gail, book 1, observation 153*. For always, even if no appeal was made, or even if the right to appeal was renounced, the path of the **Syndicate** <term>syndicatus: a legal process where a judge is held personally liable for a wrong or erroneous judgment</term> remains open. Thus, action can be taken against a Judge, (t) even without malice <note>original: "sine dolo"</note>, if he judged poorly through fault or error, to recover the costs of the litigation, damages, and interests. *Bartolus on Law 2, number 2, Code: on the punishment of a Judge who judges poorly*.

<columns>2</columns>

(s) This is the remedy which is then granted against the unfairness of a Judge when it is no longer possible to appeal from him. And so, from the Government of Straubing in Bavaria, an appeal is made to the Court Council in Munich; although it may not be possible to appeal from the Court Council, a **Revision** is still granted, which must be requested from the Elector himself, and that goes to the Privy Council. This Revision has a ten-day limit for filing, and must generally be completed within a year, though this timeframe varies almost everywhere according to different local statutes. Secondly, in a Judgment of Revision, no new facts can be introduced: for it is called a *Revision* <note>original: "Revisio"</note> for the reason that only the prior records are seen again, as it were, to see whether they were judged well, and the sentence of the Revision is formulated from those same prior records.

(t) A Judge, just like a doctor, promises two things by the very act of accepting a case: (1) that he is competent, <gloss>that he understands the matter</gloss>, and (2) that he intends to be diligent. If he is simply not competent, he is at fault because he involves himself in an art which he has not learned, and therefore he is held liable for the damage given to a party by his own fault, specifically through an "action on the facts" <note>original: "actione in factum"</note>, which is also sometimes called an *Action for bad judgment* <note>original: "Actio male judicati"</note>, or elsewhere an *Action of Syndication* <term>Actio Syndicatus: a legal action brought against a judge for failing to follow the law or showing bias</term>.

### CHAPTER XVIII.
### and last.
## ON CRIMINAL PROCESS.

->I.<-

How someone may be assigned a court based on the nature of their crime, and likewise what matters are considered Criminal cases, has already been mentioned above in various places. However, as far as criminal process is concerned, it is today clearly different than it once was; (a) or even than what is found prescribed in our Justinian law <note>The body of Roman law compiled under Emperor Justinian I</note>: for it was one way in public crimes, and another in those called "extraordinary" which pertained to private offenses, according to Bachovius on Treutler, last volume, dispute 31, theorem 1, letter A; and Harprecht on paragraph 1, number 2 of the Institutes regarding public Judgments; and Barnabas Brisson, book 2 of Roman Antiquities, chapter 12 and following. But above all, in almost every place, the old criminal process has been changed because today, in most crimes, the process is conducted by way of **Inquisition** <note>A system where the judge or state actively investigates the crime rather than just moderating between two parties</note>, and only the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscus"</note>, or the Magistrate, sustains the role of the accuser: **Electoral Bavarian Criminal Ordinance, in the beginning.** although the

<column-break/>

injured party, if they wish, can initiate an accusation. The Penal Judicial Ordinance of Charles V <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* of 1532, the first uniform criminal law in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, articles 2 and 4, and the **Electoral Bavarian Criminal Ordinance, article 3.** However, a private person never demands public vengeance if the crime does not concern himself or his kin. Likewise, in the Kingdom of Naples, no one is admitted to accuse unless he pursues his own injury or that of his kin, as stated by Clarus, book 5, opinion paragraph 1, number 6; and Giurba, consultation 61, number 6. In Belgium and France, even this is not permitted to private individuals unless they wish to conduct the Judgment together with the Fiscal officer, (b) according to Christinaeus, volume 4, decision 294, number 4. In this matter, one must adhere entirely to the statute or custom, Julius Clarus, book 5, opinion paragraph 1, number 6. And indeed, Aristotle in book 2 of the *Politics*, chapter 5, deems that in a well-constituted Republic, public accusations ought to be as rare as possible: and therefore it is safer if the duty of accusing is entrusted universally to a public magistrate, Decianus, book 3 on criminal treatises, chapter 4, number 7. However, Johannes Robertus, book 9, opinion chapter 12 and following, deems that the Inquisition was unknown to Civil Law. Yet it is more accurate for us to say that among the Romans, the extraordinary mode of proceeding in criminal matters (c) was the inquisition, based on Law 7, singular 14 on accusations; Law "if anyone" 10, Code on Bishops and Clerics; Law 1, in the beginning, Code on the custody of defendants; Law 1, Code on the Curious; Law 11, Law 1, paragraph "quietude," Digest on the office of the prefect of the city; Law "fitting" 13 on the office of the governor; Law "Divine" 6, Digest on the custody of defendants. Fachin, book 1, chapter 34. Bachovius, said dispute 31, theorem 1, letter E. Voltzius, treatise on inquisition, number 55 and number 72, etc.

(a) Formerly, those Judgments were called "public" which were exercised by virtue of the public Laws, for instance, from the Cornelian Law, the Julian Law, the Pompeian Law, etc. They were also called public because anyone from the people—that is, a private citizen—was admitted to accuse. But "private" Criminal matters were those which were not punished by specific and public Laws, and were also called "Extraordinary," because they were outside the order and number of public Crimes. But this difference is today entirely removed.

Formerly, however, the criminal process was initiated by Accusers, and any private person could accuse a delinquent and seek public vengeance through his accusation. The Romans even marketed this as a matter of great praise. Nay, and through this kind of accusati-

persons were raised to great offices and dignities; and thus anyone, even if they did not have a specific personal interest in the matter, was able to accuse.

By our current customs, almost no one accuses unless their own particular interest is at stake—for example, if one's husband, wife, son, father, etc., has been killed—or in similar cases where someone is personally harmed by a public crime. Today, however, the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscus"</note> or the Treasury Prosecutor—commonly called the Chamber Prosecutor <note>original: "Cammer-Procurator"</note>, the Fiscal, etc.—usually accuses by public authority. This procedure is not called an "accusation," but an **Inquisitorial Process** <note>original: "Processus inquisitionis"</note>: because the Treasury only inquires into the crime and brings the investigation to the Judge so that he may punish the crime.

<note>(b) This is done to avoid collusion, so that a false and fraudulent accuser is not substituted, etc.</note>

<note>(c) It appears from laws and histories that among the Romans, crimes were always solemnly vindicated through appointed Accusers. Indeed, a man was even considered a good Citizen if he accused many people. But in the Provinces, crimes were punished only through the Magistrate and by way of inquisition.</note>

### II. Denunciation <note>original: "Denunciatio"</note>, however, (d) contrary to what some think, is not a special method of proceeding (as noted in Bachov. *disp. 31. lit. D.*), but is among the reasons and causes from which an inquisition is reached. Denunciation, or the reporting of a crime, exists as a precursor to the inquisition: for the Judge takes information and evidence based upon it, and once these are gathered, he forms the formal charge or the inquisition (Clarus *d. §. fin. quæst. 7. from the beginning*). For truly, a "naked" denunciation—even by an offended party—is not sufficient to establish an Inquisitorial Process; it is only sufficient for an "informative" process <note>the preliminary gathering of facts</note>. Thus Clarus writes (*d. loc. number 7*) that anyone may go to the Judge and denounce an injury inflicted on themselves or another; the Judges then proceed with ease, though only after the proper evidence has been gathered.

<note>(d) Denunciation is closely related to a Criminal Accusation; however, it is not a unique Process in itself. The person who denounces a crime does not bind themselves to the formalities of a trial in the same way an Accuser does. Nor is he considered to be "accusing," but merely notifying the Judge of a crime for the Judge's information, so that the Judge may later inquire and dispose of the matter as he finds it. Thus, denunciation is merely a type of preparation for a criminal Inquisitorial Process.</note>

### III. Whenever a Judge wishes to institute an Inqui-

<column-break/>

-sitorial Process, something must always precede it (e) which opens the path of inquiry. So much so, that if the magistrate or criminal Judge should rush into an inquisition with no prior information and no reasonable cause, then the Process is void (*Hieron. Magon. decis. 22*) and the judge may be held liable for damages (*based on the law "severiter" in the Code regarding the excuses of Tutors; Magon. d. loc. num. 13. etc.; Voltz. cons. 2. which is joined to his treatise on inquisition, number 101 and following*). And similarly, the States of the Empire as well as the provincial States—who hold the Right of High Justice <note>original: "welche den Blutbann haben," referring to the authority to pass sentences involving "blood" or capital punishment</note> and possess the criminal courts <note>original: "peinliche Gericht"</note> by virtue of their estates—and their officials are held liable for damages if they maliciously, or at least (f) through an "action on the facts" <note>original: "facti actione"</note>, institute an action against someone without legitimate cause, whether out of ignorance of the law or some other fault. They are also liable if they apply torture without observing the proper order of law, or otherwise do not proceed correctly (*based on the law "nec magistratibus" 32. in the Digest on injuries; Farinac. in criminal practice question 127. num. 35. etc.; Myns. 5. obs. 69; Bocer. on adultery cap. 3. number 151. etc.*). Such private denunciations are permitted so that crimes do not remain unpunished; especially a wounded or otherwise offended party can complain to the Magistrate, and on the occasion of such complaints or denunciations, an informative Process is usually instituted (g) (*Tusch. L. D. concl. 192 and following*). Even an enemy is admitted to inform the Judge (*Magon. decis. 22. number 10 and following*). In other places, the obligation to denounce even falls upon the subjects (*Modest. Pistor. part. 2. question 61*). For certainly, the one denouncing is not considered to take the burden of proof upon himself, but leaves the entire burden to the conscience and zeal of the Magistrate (*Octav. Spathar. in the practice of Rules fol. 107 and following; Hermannus Stam. on personal servitude, book 2. cap. 11. num. 21. See also Cravett. cons. 319. num 4; Bursat. cons. 954. num. 151. vol. 2.*). See the Imperial Recess at Augsburg, Year [15]51, in the Minting Ordinance <note>original: "Müntz-Ordnung"</note> at the end. And as a precaution, it should be noted here that the denouncer should only notify the judge of the evidence and suspicions he has, rather than reporting someone as a "guilty criminal" whom he cannot prove to be so; this is also suggested by the Electoral Bavarian Criminal Code <note>original: "die Chur-Bayrische Malefiz-Ordn."</note>, article 4.

-># Disputation<-

(e) To initiate an **Inquisitorial Process** against someone is a serious matter that can cause great harm to their reputation. Therefore, since a Magistrate must fulfill his duty without causing unjust harm to anyone, it follows that a Magistrate cannot start an investigation against a person unless there is prior evidence. This evidence must not only make the person a suspect but should be so convincing that they could be subjected to torture <note>In the legal system of this era, judicial torture was a regulated step used to extract a confession when evidence was strong but not yet complete.</note> or condemned, provided the accused does not offer other defenses to excuse themselves. This is for the following reason: it is ridiculous and useless to arrest someone who cannot be condemned or at least questioned under torture. Indeed, nothing is more common in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>The high court of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> than for lawsuits to be brought against reckless Magistrates who have either ordered someone to be tortured or thrown them into prison without a well-founded reason and sufficient evidence.

(f) That is to say, if this arrest was made through the fault or ignorance of the Judge and Magistrate, he is held liable for the interests and damages of the accused. If, however, it was done out of malice, an action for "personal injury" <note>original: "injuriarum actio"</note> may be brought against him.

(g) When a private individual reports a crime to a Magistrate—saying that this or that person has committed such an offense—the Magistrate to whom the report is made should not immediately leap to a **Criminal Process**. Instead, he must first inform himself. If the official or Magistrate wishes to start a criminal case, he must ensure it is sufficiently well-founded; and this must happen *before* the accused is arrested. However, if there is a fear that the accused might flee—that is, if the preliminary information-gathering cannot be done so secretly that it won't reach the ears of the offender—then the person accused of the crime can be arrested or even re-imprisoned, especially if they are a person of low social status.

### IV.

There are two types of inquisition <note>original: "inquisitio"</note>: (h) one to discover the crime, and another to punish it. The process to discover a crime is often carried out in several ways: (1) namely, by appointing denouncers and other officials to report wrongdoings, as noted by <term>Clarus <note>Giulio Claro (1525–1575), an influential Italian jurist.</note></term> in his final section, question 7. In ancient times, the <term>Irenarchs <note>original: "Irenarchæ"; from the Greek for "peace-rulers," these were officials responsible for maintaining public order.</note></term> served this role. (2) Through established <term>Censorial Courts <note>original: "Durch Rueg-Gericht"; local courts used to report moral failings or minor crimes.</note></term> and <term>Land Visitations <note>original: "Lands-Visitationes"; official tours of inspection to oversee regional administration.</note></term>. Sometimes (3) a general investigation is conducted via witnesses regarding people of "bad condition"—for instance, asking whether there are thieves or robbers in the city, or regarding crimes in general, such as whether adulteries or other offenses are being committed. Sometimes also (4) an investigation is "special" regarding the crime but "general" regarding the person; for example, when a murder is known to have happened, but the perpetrator is unknown.

<column-break/>

Sometimes (5) an investigation is "special" regarding the person but "general" regarding the crime; such as when it is asked whether a specific official has behaved badly in his office. This is discussed by <term>Farinaccius <note>Prospero Farinacci (1544–1618), a famous Roman jurist known for his works on criminal law.</note></term> in his *Criminal Practice*. These methods of investigating can be pursued out of a concern for public welfare, even if a rumor of the crime has not yet spread, (i) based on the Code concerning the custody of defendants. However, if it is discovered that someone is likely under suspicion of a crime, a "special" and "informative" inquiry can and should be made against them. But one must not leap immediately to arrest and the punitive phase of the investigation process unless sufficient evidence is present, as stated in the law and the <term>Imperial Criminal Law Ordinance <note>original: "Peinliche Richts-Ordn."; the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* of 1532, the standard criminal code for the Empire.</note></term>, articles 9 and 219. (I have already warned of this above in number 3). Because the process of investigation diminishes a person's reputation among good and serious men, a Judge must proceed with the utmost caution, as noted by <term>Cothmann <note>Ernest Cothmann (1557–1624), a German legal scholar.</note></term> and <term>Menochius <note>Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), an Italian jurist.</note></term>. If the matter is then supported by suitable witnesses or prepared with fit evidence, and the judge can thus proceed to a formal and ordinary investigation, then the accused (being present and held in chains) must be given the "bill of investigation" in place of an indictment. (k) He must also be provided with the evidence, the names of the witnesses, (l) other facts working against him, and the opportunity to defend himself.

---

(h) The investigation is primarily of two types: one for the sake of inquiring, the other for the sake of punishment. The first is a preparation for the second: for an inquiry is made to find the crime so that it may be known whether a punitive investigation should be started. This latter is nothing other than the public criminal process itself initiated against someone.

(i) This means investigations are initiated "ex officio" <note>By virtue of the magistrate's office/duty, rather than by a private complaint.</note>.

(k) Or sometimes he is even accused orally.

(l) In some places, such as in <term>Bavaria</term>, the names of witnesses are not shared with the person accused of a crime; however, in other places, this is done.

-># On Judicial Procedure<-

...it is customary, and perhaps fairer, because otherwise the **Defendant** can hardly raise objections against the witnesses and their characters.

### V. What legal evidence exists...
...regarding a special investigation to be instituted against someone for a crime is discussed by Menochius, Farinacius, and Fachinaeus. First and foremost, the Judge must be certain of the <term>body of the crime<note>original: "corpore delicti"; the physical evidence that a crime has actually been committed.</note></term> (m). That is, it must be proven that a person was, for example, actually killed, or a theft or similar crime was truly committed (see the <term>Imperial Criminal Code<note>original: "Peinliche Gerichts Ordnung" (the Carolina); the foundational criminal law code of the Holy Roman Empire, issued in 1532.</note></term>, article 6). For if the crime is unknown, or if it is not clearly established, an investigation aimed at punishment cannot be instituted; nor can the defendant be condemned, even if he confesses to the crime (n). This is supported by Bocer, Clarus, and Moller. However, this rule fails in the case of crimes where no physical traces remain after the act, such as adultery, poisoning, and the like—which are commonly called "transient acts." In those cases, the body of the crime can be proven through evidence and strong conjectures.

### VI. Although some argue...
...that a Judge can proceed to <term>arrest<note>original: "Capturam"</note></term> even with no preceding evidence, Article 11 of the **Constitutio Carolina** cautions that public defamation or just and legitimate evidence must precede imprisonment. It further states that a contrary custom is invalid, as it is irrational. This applies even if the case involves an <term>exceptional crime<note>original: "crimine excepto"; a category of particularly heinous crimes, like treason or witchcraft, where normal legal protections were often bypassed.</note></term> (o) or a crime where no physical traces are visible. This is especially true for persons of higher social standing. However, the evidence required to proceed with an arrest does not need to be as urgent or as strong as the evidence required to authorize **torture**; lighter evidence suffices. It is enough that some degree of information has been gathered. Furthermore, a defendant is sometimes released from the distress of prison by providing <term>security<note>original: "cautione"; similar to modern bail or a bond.</note></term> (p), or they may be committed to the custody of guards. It is left to the Judge's discretion whether the person under investigation should be released under <term>guarantors<note>original: "fidejussores"</note></term>. However, Bocer notes that these are not strictly "guarantors" in the traditional sense (q). Where such a security is allowed, it must be made under a specific penalty which the guarantors bind themselves to pay if the defendant does not appear. A formula for this bond in criminal matters is provided by Hering.

---

(m) Hence, it is customary that if someone confesses to many thefts, for example, he is not immediately believed; rather, inquiries are later made in those locations to see if such thefts or other crimes were actually committed at that time. Otherwise, no confessions should be accepted.

(n) This is a "precaution" for thieves and other defendants: under **torture**, they may confess to many horrendous crimes they never committed, while hiding the ones they actually did. If inquiries are then sent to those places and the response is that nothing similar was committed there, the defendant can claim he only confessed because he could not bear the pain. Furthermore, even if they confess the truth under torture and later deny it, they generally cannot be tortured more than once for the same crime. Indeed, someone is said to have replied when asked why he did this: *“it is better for me to be tortured three times than to be hanged just once.”* In all these and similar circumstances, a Judge must be cautious and consult experts if necessary.

<column-break/>

(o) This rule is set aside in the crime of <term>Treason<note>original: "læsæ Majestatis"; literally "injured majesty," crimes against the sovereign or the state.</note></term>, where there is a danger that the defendant might flee or maliciously plot something else.

(p) This security is primarily used for minor offenses where only a monetary fine is imposed.

(q) The reason is that the guarantors are not (nor can they be) bound to the same thing as the principal defendant. No one can pledge their own body or life for another, since no one is the master of these things. Therefore, such a guarantor promises to pay, for example, a certain number of florins if the principal defendant flees.

### VII.
Prison also ought to be a matter of custody, not punishment, (r) according to the law *aut damnum* in the section *solet* regarding punishments, and the first law of the Code regarding the custody of defendants. See also the <term>Imperial Criminal Code<note>original: "Peinliche Gerichts-Ordn."; the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina of 1532.</note></term> articles 11 and 218. For this reason, in the <term>Imperial Chamber Court<note>original: "Camera Imperialis"; the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire.</note></term>, if anyone complains about the harshness of their imprisonment, it is customary for conditions to be mitigated by mandates, and even commissioners are often sent to inspect the prison, as noted by Heringius on bail, chapter 18, number 141, and Ruland on commissions, book 4, chapter 1. Likewise, whenever there are several accomplices in the same crime, they are ordered to be kept separate, (s) as per the Imperial Criminal Code, article 11, where Matthaeus Stephani and Bernhard Zieritz comment. However, those who break out of prison, even if they are later found innocent of the original charge, must still be punished with a discretionary penalty, (t) according to the law *in eos* on the custody of defendants and the first law of the Digest on prison-breakers. See Farinacius, question 30, number 20, etc.; Ludovicus à Peguera, Decision 1; Tuschus under the letter C, conclusion 88; and Fachinaeus, book 9, chapters 64 and 66. Some argue (u) that such an act seems to be a confession of the crime, as Clarus records in his final section, question 21. Yet one is punished more mildly, and sometimes even excused, if they return of their own accord, according to Hondeda, second consultation 94, and Marius Giurba, criminal consultation 34. Nevertheless, a person who was unjustly seized—if, based on probable conjectures, they fear an unjust danger is imminent—may flee by any means possible, (vv) according to Covarruvias, first book of various resolutions, 2; Decianus in his criminal treatise, book 13, number 4; Farinacius, question 30, number 131, etc.; Kremberg in his treatise on defense, question 7; Torreblanca in his work on demonology, book 3, chapter 41; and Bocer in the cited place, thesis 61 and following.

<margin>(r) Hence also in France, as Bodin testifies, filthy and underground prisons are prohibited by Royal edict; and the Germans have always been blamed on that account for using foul prisons.</margin>

<margin>(s) Namely, so that they cannot collude together.</margin>

<margin>(t) For they show contempt for the authority of the Magistrate.</margin>

<margin>(u) But this is not observed in practice: for they say that by breaking prison, a man does not properly confess the crime, but by that very act he makes himself more liable to <term>torture<note>original: "torturam"; the judicial use of pain to extract a confession, which was a standard part of the legal process at this time.</note></term>.</margin>

<margin>(vv) Does this mean they may even kill the <term>Jailer<note>original: "Commentariensem"</note></term> or the guards? This question belongs to the theologians, etc.</margin>

### VIII.
Furthermore, the <term>bill of indictment<note>original: "Libellus inquisitionis"; the formal written accusation that initiated the trial process.</note></term> must contain the place and time of the

<column-break/>

crime, (x) according to the third law at the beginning of the title on accusations. This is true even though the trial is not invalidated if, provided the other party does not object, the time and place are later established during the course of the proceedings, (y) as Clarus notes in question 12, number 11. Likewise, the specific recording of the hour and day (z) is not usually required, according to the third law of the Digest on accusations, Mynsinger, second observation 40, and Bocer on adultery, chapter 3, number 99, etc. However, it seems fairer that, if the defendant requests it, the most precise time must necessarily be expressed—even before the <term>joinder of issue<note>original: "litis contestationem"; the formal start of a trial when the parties have defined their dispute.</note></term>—as argued by Köppen, book 2, observation 120. For indeed, the defendant's safety can often depend on it, if perhaps he wishes to prove that on that day or hour, he was not at the scene of the crime but elsewhere. See Hart. Pistor, observation 91, and Mezger, consultation 15, number 44. Similarly, a criminal indictment proceeds without a concluding prayer for a specific penalty: (aa) for the imposition of punishment arises from the laws, tempered by the discretion of the Magistrate, as Mezger notes in the cited consultation 15, number 45.

<margin>(x) The reason is that it is easier for one accused of a crime to defend himself if the time and place are added; namely, in the case where he is innocent, he can prove he was not in such a place at that time. Also, witnesses can be convicted of falsehood if, for example, one testifies to a different location than what was mentioned in the indictment.</margin>

<margin>(y) If, however, the time and place do not appear in the course of the trial, then the Judge may regard such evidence—not restricted to a specific place and time—as suspicious, even if the party does not object. This is because in criminal matters, the Judge must investigate everything thoroughly, even those things which the party does not raise as an objection.</margin>

<margin>(z) And this is for the reason that while the accuser might not know the hour and day so precisely, the Defendant might use that as a pretext to quibble and seek an opportunity to escape. On this matter, the express text cited here in the third law of the Digest is limited by the Doctors of Law: if the Defendant can provide sufficient reasons why it is necessary for his defense to know the exact hour and day, then the accuser can be compelled to provide it.</margin>

<margin>(aa) For even in antiquity, the punishment was not expressed in the sentence itself (which must nevertheless match the indictment); rather, if the crime was established, the ordinary punishment was already fixed by law. Thus, criminal sentences were conceived in this manner: *“Lictor, bind his hands and do as the law requires.”*</margin>

### IX.
Whether a <term>legal representative<note>original: "Procurator"; an attorney or proxy allowed to act on behalf of a client.</note></term> can intervene in criminal cases is a matter of various disputes among the Doctors of Law. See Gail, book 1, observation 51; Menochius on discretionary matters, questions 20 and 80; and Clarus, in the final section, question 32 and following.

# Concerning Judicial Process.
->And following, Virgil Pingitzer, Questions; Fachinaeus;<-
->Book 1, chapter 24 & following; Vultejus, Disputations, chapter 11.<-

And indeed, regarding the accuser, today by the custom of the court, a <term>Procurator<note>A legal representative or agent authorized to act on behalf of another in court.</note></term> is admitted. (bb) **Imperial Criminal Code** <margin>(bb) Formerly, a Procurator was not admitted even on the side of the Accuser; this was because the accuser was required to register himself and bind himself to a similar penalty if he was found to have made a false or malicious accusation. It was otherwise if he acted in good faith. However, that registration did not bind him to a similar penalty out of contract, but out of the crime of <term>calumny<note>Maliciously making a false accusation.</note></term>.</margin> Article 12, and there see Matthaeus Stephani. But this is not the case for the Defendant, (cc) <margin>(cc) No one can act as a Procurator for an absent Defendant when the penalty cannot be carried out against the absentee—for the sentence would be illusory. However, even an absent person can be punished with the penalty of <term>relegation<note>A milder form of banishment where one is sent away from a specific area but does not lose civil rights or property.</note></term>; therefore, a Procurator is compelled to pay any monetary fine.</margin> if the case is such that a penalty usually follows, up to and including <term>relegation</term>, (dd) <margin>(dd) Understand this inclusively, although there are some who wish it to be understood exclusively.</margin> according to the law *absentem* 5 in the Digest *on punishments*. However, to present the reasons for an absence, a <term>defensor<note>A defense counsel or advocate, distinct from a general procurator, specifically tasked here with excusing the defendant's non-appearance.</note></term> is also admitted. Those accused of a capital crime cannot be accused in their absence, and much less can they be condemned; (ee) <margin>(ee) The reason has already been given: because the sentence cannot be carried out.</margin> even if they are defiantly absent, according to law 5 *on punishments*. But only their goods are noted, (ff) <margin>(ff) This is done, however, with caution, so that nothing is sent to the fugitive; for this reason, <term>Curators<note>Legal guardians or overseers appointed to manage property.</note></term> are to be appointed to preserve the goods for the children and wife. But if anyone flees to an **Asylum**, then the notation of goods does not take place, and the use of the goods is granted to the one residing in the Asylum. The reason is that otherwise the privilege of the Asylum would be void. Thus, the Imperial City of **Reutlingen** with all its territory, the **Burgfried**, is an Asylum.</margin> and after a year they are confiscated; see Bachovius on Treutler, last volume, disputation 31, thesis 4; Cacheranus, decision 105, question 11. And today, they say those goods do not go to the Treasury, but are reserved for the benefit of the wife, children, and heirs. **Imperial Criminal Code**, article 206, where the Commentators speak. Clarus, final section, question 44, at the version *but today*, where he testifies that in some places this notation of goods has fallen out of use, and the penalty of the <term>Bannus<note>The Ban; a formal proclamation of outlawry or legal proscription.</note></term> has succeeded it; that is, the defendant is summoned three times at intervals of 14 days; after which, if he does not appear, (gg) <margin>(gg) In Saxony and certain other places, the execution of the penalty even against an absent person is done through an image [in effigy] if they have fled, and through a proclamation which they call <term>Zettergeschrey<note>original German: "Zettergeschrey"; a formal, loud public outcry or proclamation used to summon help or declare someone an outlaw.</note></term>.</margin> nor alleges excuses for his absence, he is held as convicted and is publicly proscribed, so that he may afterwards be killed with impunity; Wesenbeck *on accusations, number 13.* It is more equitable, however, that even a defiant person should receive a judgment in his favor in the principal case if his innocence is established, as per Zieritz on article 206 of the **Imperial Criminal Code.**

Besoldus Volume I.

<column-break/>

X. As for the proof of a crime, it ought to be fortified by suitable witnesses, or provided with the most open documents, or by indubitable evidence clearer than the midday sun, or supported by the defendant’s own confession; *canon 1, canon "we against no one," canon "the primates," cause 2, question 2; the final law of the Code on proofs.* Farinacius, *question 81, chapter 1 and following.* And two witnesses, above all exception, are sufficient. **Imperial Criminal Code**, article 66 and following. But it is also sufficient that the crime be proven, even if the defendant does not confess it, (hh) <margin>(hh) In this case, torture has no place, so that other proofs do not seem to be destroyed by a denial under torture.</margin> ibid. article 22, section 69. And witnesses must testify from their own knowledge, Farinacius *on witnesses, question 91*, and assign a reason for their statement. The Gloss and the Doctors on *the law "alone" of the Code on witnesses.* If sufficient proofs are lacking, but plausible evidence of the crime is present, an inquiry by **torture** is usually held, (ii) <margin>(ii) **Torture** only has a place if the crime is "semi-fully" proven—for instance, by one witness, or by another reason, such as by evidence sufficient enough to make the judge's conscience feel safe in believing the defendant is guilty and is only denying the fact maliciously. The quality of the Torture—that is, how severely and for how long someone is to be tortured—depends on the prudent discretion of the Judge, who forms his judgment in this part either according to the quality of the person (considering if they are old, young, a woman, etc.) or according to the gravity of the evidence; the heavier or more significant the evidence, the more severely the Defendant is usually tortured, all other things being equal. There are also degrees of torture. The first is <term>Territio<note>The "frightening" or "terror"; showing the defendant the instruments of torture or binding them without yet inflicting pain.</note></term>; for example, if someone is led to the place of Torture, or if the instruments of Torture are even applied to him, but without pain. The second degree is *elevation without weight*, and the third is *elevation with weight*, when...</margin> and this is sometimes repeated when new evidence arises; on which matter Zanger, Bocer, and others are entirely to be consulted. It should also be noted here that even after the conclusion of the case, witnesses can be received for the innocence of the defendant, *law 18, penultimate section, of the Digest on inquiries.* Gail, book 1, observation 120, number 11.

# Disputation on the Judicial Process.
->Catchword: [THEY] SAID<-

...one attaches a weight <note>This likely refers to the "strappado" or similar torture where weights were attached to the victim's body to increase the strain on the limbs.</note>. Torture is also usually repeated, but only if new evidence comes to light. It is also considered new evidence if the person who was tortured denies those things which they once confessed under torture, or if perhaps they were tortured too lightly the first time given the gravity of the evidence. However, torture is not permitted more than three times. The accused should not be tortured a second time too soon after the first; one must wait until the swelling from the previous torture has subsided, <note>original German: "bis der torquirte wieder zu seinen Kräfften komme"</note> until the tortured person regains their strength. 

An objection is raised here—that torture is entirely useless, based on this reasoning: A person being tortured can either endure the pain or they cannot. If they can, they will not confess even if they committed the crime; if they cannot endure it, they will confess even if they did nothing. At first glance, this argument seems effective enough that perhaps for this reason there is no place for torture in England. However, the response is that if the person being tortured is innocent, God essentially assists them, and they are bolstered by their own conscience. But if the accused is guilty, they are so driven by the "worm of conscience" <note>A common historical metaphor for the gnawing, persistent pain of a guilty conscience.</note> that it cannot help but appear that they are guilty, and they can scarcely avoid confessing because of their pressing conscience.

### XI. A Criminal Judgment is extinguished by the death of the accused:

See the whole title *if the accused or accuser is dead.* Except for the judgment of <term>high treason<note>original: "perduellionis"</note></term>, <margin>(kk)</margin> and extortion <note>original: "repetundarum," specifically referring to the recovery of funds extorted by officials.</note>: which can still be carried out even against deceased defendants with whom no legal action was taken, so that their goods may be claimed for the treasury. [Citations]. In other crimes, however, a monetary penalty only affects the heirs if the legal dispute was joined <note>The phase of a trial known as "lis contestata," where the issues are formally defined.</note> while the accused was alive. [Citations]. Likewise, a complaint for any crime is extinguished after 20 years. [Citations]. Except for the crimes of adultery and embezzlement, which expire in the course of 5 years. There are also certain crimes which, because of their atrocity, are considered perpetual <note>Meaning they have no statute of limitations.</note>, such as parricide and the substitution of a child <note>The act of fraudulently presenting a child as the legitimate offspring of someone else to secure an inheritance.</note>, <margin>(ll)</margin> [Citations].

---

<margin>(kk)</margin> That is, the crime of <term>Lese-majesty<note>High treason or an offense against the dignity of a sovereign.</note></term> in the highest degree, such as if someone is an open rebel, for example, or has attempted to betray the fatherland or plot against the life of the Prince.

<margin>(ll)</margin> For through this substitution, great prejudice is done to the legitimate children; thus, this legal action is rightly made perpetual in their favor.

<column-break/>

### XII. The ordinary penalty for anyone only takes place if [documented?]

and all other qualities <margin>(mm)</margin> concur which the penal law requires. [Citations]. Likewise, the punishment of a pregnant woman is delayed until she gives birth; and as long as she is pregnant, questioning by torture is usually conducted <note>Historically, some jurisdictions allowed the interrogation of pregnant women but forbid the death penalty until after delivery.</note> regarding her. [Citations]. If the accused, having been tortured, confesses nothing, they are usually released under caution (to present themselves later) rather than being acquitted: <margin>(nn)</margin> so that, naturally, if new evidence comes to light, they can be seized again. Some also believe that a sentence in criminal cases should not be handed over for execution immediately, and others even allow 30 days. <margin>(oo)</margin> [Citations]. And these things we have deemed sufficient to be proposed according to the nature of our undertaking.

---

<margin>(mm)</margin> Although in civil matters gross negligence is treated as <term>intent<note>original: "dolus"; the deliberate will to commit a crime.</note></term>, this is not the case in criminal matters; rather, true intent is necessary, according to the express text cited here. In those criminal cases alone which involve physical punishment <note>original: "pœnam corporis afflictivam"</note>, it should be understood as commonly said: that even a foolish or very slight excuse exempts one from intent, for it is otherwise in a crime involving a monetary penalty. Likewise, what is said—that in criminal matters the milder opinion should be followed—is also to be understood regarding physical punishments, and not monetary ones.

<margin>(nn)</margin> For if they were purely acquitted, they would have the defense of <term>res judicata<note>A matter already judged; preventing the same case from being tried twice.</note></term>. If, therefore, a sentence is not passed but the accused is only released under caution, then if new evidence arises, it can be combined with the old, and the interrupted case can be resumed.

<margin>(oo)</margin> This time period is not observed today. This is its origin: Emperor Theodosius used to have the habit of immediately condemning many who were often innocent, and in his rage, he ensured the punishment was carried out on those so condemned. When he once wished to enter the church in Milan, the excellent Bishop Ambrose closed the doors and would not let the Emperor in, treating him as a grievous sinner; after he had done penance, at the request of the most holy Father Ambrose, he ordered a constitution to be added to the Code, so that henceforth no criminal sentence passed would be handed over for execution before 30 days. This, however, as has already been said, is no longer observed today.
