# LEGAL DISSERTATION
## ON THE METHOD OF REPORTING,
### IN CIVIL CASES OF THE FIRST INSTANCE. <note>The "first instance" refers to the initial trial where a case is first heard, before any potential appeals.</note>

## PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'V' featuring floral and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Men of great Name and those most skilled in courtroom matters are often accustomed to claim, not without reason, that the tangled difficulty of legal practice, the uncertainty of lawsuits, and the length and accumulation of documents—and the expensive delays of trials resulting from these things—occur because the right and short investigation of the true legal core is often neglected or even ignored. <note>original Latin: (a) "veri Juridici investigatio recta atque compendiosa"</note> However, there seems to be no faster way to investigate this than if the competent legal action <note>original Latin: (b) "actio competens"</note> or other legal remedy is extracted from the presented facts, and all further things are referred back to that as if to a target or a pre-established goal. Anything alien to that goal should be either omitted or cut away; in this way, the **Method of Reporting**, or **Voting** <note>original Latin: "Votandi", referring to the formal casting of a legal opinion by a judge.</note> as they commonly call it—which skilled judges and deciders now use almost everywhere—may be accurately observed. Truly, it will be of no small benefit to those who will one day work in the courts if they have a more exact knowledge of this manner of reporting. Furthermore, *Rutgerus Rulandus* teaches in his work *On Articles*, book 2, chapter 1, that the investigation of the legal action (and thus the already mentioned method of reporting) concerns not only the lawyer and the judge, but also the Commissioner himself. He adds, among other things, that one who prepares interrogatories or articles <note>original Latin: (c) "interrogatoria, aut Articulos"</note> without this investigation turns this way and that as if in the dark, uncertain where to direct his steps. Conversely, once the type of legal action is known and its nature properly perceived, it is easy to find the exceptions, replies, and other such arguments of the cases, and to respond certainly and consistently regarding the law of the proposed case. Furthermore, that written proofs, or <term>Probation-Writings</term> <note>original German: "Probation-Schriff-ten"; these are formal documents submitted to the court to prove specific points of a case.</note>

<column-break/>

if they are directed not at the requirements of the attempted action but at the articles, are mere repetitions. They contribute as much to winning lawsuits as a "fifth wheel to a wagon," as the common saying goes; so warns *Antonius Bullæus* in his *Academic Discourse 8*, number 5, following *Master Adam Keller* in book 2 of *On Legal-Political Duties*, chapter 29. This method of reporting is also proposed by the compilers of the *Collection of Petitions*, volume 1, in the methodical treatise on the Process of the Imperial Chamber at the end; by *Rutgerus Rulandus* in his *Commentary on the Judicial Process of Johann Ferrarius*, page 155; by *Hermannus Esaias Rosacorb.* in *Forensic Practice*, chapter 2; by *Paulus Matthias Wehner* in *Observations on Practice* under the term <term>Judicial Affairs</term> <note>original German: "Justitien-Wesen"</note>, after article 40, chapter 1 and following; by *Henricus Bocerus*, class 6, disputation 7, thesis 29 and following; and by *Antonius Winter* in his *Assessor*, part 2, chapter 9. From all these sources, it seemed worthwhile to collect the following positions regarding that method of reporting (specifically in civil cases of the first instance), with controversial legal questions belonging here inserted throughout, and to propose them as a public exercise.

---

<note>original Latin: (a) The **Doctors** [of Law] say that the difficulties of the process do not consist in the business itself, but in the right method, which many do not possess. Moreover, a lawyer ought not to propose what a judge is not bound to attend to. Furthermore, a judge is hindered more than helped by excessive length, especially if things are not presented in order and if unnecessary matters are brought forward.</note>

<note>original Latin: (b) One must therefore first look into: 1. legal remedies, 2. their requirements, 3. the method of proving the same, 4. exceptions must be investigated, 5. replies, and 6. presumptions fighting for and against oneself. Regarding all these things...</note>

**Column 1**

can easily be seen from everything known from the beginning; what must be proven in the facts, and what might even be superfluous: for where someone has legal presumptions in their favor, there is no need for them to provide proof. For example, in an action under the **Aquilian Law** <note>original: "L. Aquiliæ". A Roman law providing compensation to owners of property injured by someone's fault.</note>, who did the striking? For what cause? Was it provoked by another? Was it done in a moment of danger? Was it out of hatred? Or for revenge? In a **managerial action** <note>original: "institoria... actione". A legal claim regarding business transactions conducted by an agent or manager.</note>, it should also be noted that the Manager is the agent. Hence, I can sue the Master if the Agent contracted debts with me, since he does so by the mandate and for the account of the Master. It is necessary, however, that these debts were contracted by the Manager by reason of the goods, or on their occasion, and not from squandering, etc.

(c) Therefore, the Articles <note>Specific points of law or fact presented in a case.</note> ought to be placed according to the nature of the legal remedies. Indeed, the interrogatories are to be gathered from the overturning of legal remedies. Moreover, it is better to proceed by interrogation to investigate the truth rather than by articles, namely in the examination of witnesses: the reason being that truth is more easily caught through interrogatories, <gloss>because of the unequal testimonies of the witnesses</gloss> <note>original German: "wegen der Zeugen ungleichen Aussagen"</note>, as can be seen in Daniel 13 <note>Refers to the Story of Susanna in the Apocrypha, where Daniel exposes false witnesses by questioning them separately.</note>, where he convicted the impious men falsely accusing Susanna by such a judgment and by their own responses.

(d) When the witness testimonies are made public, then the Plaintiff brings forward his proof, and the defendant his exception, and one of these is called the **Exception-brief** and the other the **Proof-brief** <note>original: "Exception- al- tera Probation-Schrifft"</note>.

# THESIS I.

FIRST, therefore, the Order of Nature requires that the **Case** or the **Species of Fact** (<gloss>the origin of the main dispute</gloss> <note>original German: "die Herkommenheit deß Haupt-Streits"</note>, as it is called by our people) be narrated at the threshold of the Report, as briefly and fully as possible; so that, namely, it may be known what is the hinge of the entire litigation (to which, indeed, respect must be paid in the rendering of the sentence). For from the fact, the quality of the intention becomes clear, both of the Plaintiff and the Defendant: namely, that from which the Law is said to arise, *law: "if from blows." 52. section: "on the slope." 2. regarding the Aquilian Law.* And therefore, it can hardly happen that a just and fair sentence is rendered unless the case is well understood: as the Emperors wrote back in a similar case *in the law "as responded" 15. Code regarding Transactions.* Moreover, the **species of fact** can be extracted from the formal complaint of the action intended, or from the Positional Articles, and the petition of the complaint, and the Defensive pleadings of the Defendant. Here, there is no reason for artistic orations, or an often long articulated complaint, and the responses given to individual articles, to delay the Judge (or the Reporter): nor even by the arts of Rhetoricians (with which they strive to move the mind of the Judge)

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

should they be moved; as Wehner says *in the cited place, chapter 8, at the beginning.* This artistry consists rather in reviewing the circumstances, which are considered to have such force and effect that by them the Law is either changed or distinguished, according to Rosacorb *said chapter 2.* For from a single variation of the case, for the most part, the position of the plaintiff or defendant is entirely changed, *as it is in law 65. Digest regarding the Rules of Law.* And the fact must be reviewed by anyone without any prejudice; just as it was proposed by the Parties on both sides. So that it can be noticed in which direction the Reporter inclines. And thus in the **Imperial Court** <note>original: "Curia Imperiali". Refers to the Imperial Chamber Court, the highest judicial body in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> (to avoid all sinister suspicion, and so that all circumstances may become better known to the rest of the Lord Assessors), in place of the Narration of the Fact, a series or extract of all the Acts is proposed: <gloss>(e)</gloss> as is clear from the Decisions of J. Meichsner. And this—which I wanted to mention in passing—all Reports must be made in the English <note>original: "Latino Idiomate". The text specifies Latin, but the translation is rendered here in English per instructions.</note> language.

(e) The fact can be reported in two ways, summarily and by extract.

## II. Once the species of fact is known, the next and second inspection will be whether the **Judicial Process** <note>original: "Processus Judiciarius"</note> (f) has been duly observed. For thus, if anything is committed or omitted against the usual order of the Courts, it is necessary that the nullity of the entire Process, and of the sentence itself (g), follows from there, as Vantius says *rubric 13. regarding Nullity from defect of Process, at the beginning.* Mynsing *response 2. number 3. and following.* However, the <term>point of legitimation</term> <note>The legal standing or capacity of a party to appear in court.</note> occurs first: which, because of the nullity arising from its defect, cannot be omitted even in a summary Judgment, according to Cravetta *consultation 100. at the beginning.* Vantius *rubric 11. regarding Nullity from defect of inability, at the beginning.* Maranta *in the mirror, part 4. distinction 16. n. 16. and following.* Berlich *part 1. conclusion 14. at the beginning.* Mascardus *conclusion 975.* And there it must be considered, <gloss>(h)</gloss> whether the principals themselves can stand in Court by themselves? Legal representatives or attorneys.</note> <gloss>(i)</gloss> or others acting and responding in their name, have legitimized their persons in the due manner (namely, through a **Mandate of Proxy** <note>original: "Mandatum Procuratorium"</note>, or by another reason), as Bocerus says, *class 6. disputation 7. thesis 30.*

<meta>This page continues the legal dissertation on procedural law, specifically focusing on the "Method of Reporting." Having previously discussed the gathering of facts and evidence, the author now moves into the formal requirements for a judgment to be valid, the distinction between "void" and "unjust" rulings, and the legal capacity of different individuals—such as minors, women, and legal representatives—to participate in a lawsuit.</meta>

# Concerning the Method of Reporting.

...material matters regarding the merits of the case. However, a judgment is only void if it was rendered against the principles of Law or Procedure. A distinction must be made here between an **unjust judgment** and a **void one**. A judgment is **void** if it is rendered against public law; however, it is **unjust** if it is rendered against the rights of a specific Party.

(g) Furthermore, it is one thing for the *judgment to be void*, and another for the *Process* to be so. First, therefore, one must ensure that the parties do not invalidate the Process, namely by not observing the formalities of the legal proceedings; then, the Judge shall also take care that he does not deliver a void judgment.

(h) Regarding the point of **legal standing** <note>original: "legitimationis"</note>, one must first see whether the parties present in Court have the legal personhood to stand in it. (z) If the Parties are not present, could they have appointed a **legal representative** <note>original: "Procuratorem"</note>? Or, if they act in another's name, can they do this without a mandate? Or, if they have a mandate, is it legitimate or properly drafted?

(i) One who acts for another does so either as a **legal representative**, where a mandate is required, or as a **connected person** (for example, a brother for a brother, a father for an emancipated son, or a husband for a wife, specifically regarding property over which he has rights). In such cases, **legal security** <note>original: "satisdatio"; a guarantee or bond</note> is required so that the opposing party is certain that, if they win, the judgment will be valid. However, that caution does not bind him to the payment of the judgment, but only to the ratification by the absent person. Or, someone acts for another while also acting for their own interest (as a husband by reason of a dowry, or a father by reason of property coming from outside sources <note>original: "adventitiorum"</note> of which he has the use), and in these cases, he is admitted without providing security.

### III.
**Minors** do not have the legal personhood to stand in Court without a **Guardian** <note>original: "Curatore"</note>, *according to the law regarding all cases, 11. Code: Who can give a tutor or curator.* A ward, therefore, with a **Tutor** <note>In Roman law, a Tutor managed the person/property of a child under puberty, while a Curator assisted those above puberty but under 25.</note> acting on their behalf, can be sued and can act; likewise, an adult [minor] must initiate a suit and receive a plea with the consent of a **Guardian**, *law 2. Code: On those who have legal personhood to stand in court.* (Provided that the formalities have been carried out by the Tutor (k), Mynsinger 2. observation 37; Laurentius Tenninus, *Caution 127*; and that this is established for the Judge by the presentation of the Tutorship or Guardianship papers, Gail 2. *observation 107*; Berlichius 1. *conclusion 16.*) If, however, they do not have a Tutor or Guardian, or if these refuse to perform their duty, the blood relatives and in-laws must be summoned so that the minors may be declared in **contempt of court** <note>original: "contumacia"</note>. (l) Matthaeus de Afflictis, *decision 262*; Mynsinger 2. *observation 35.* And as a precaution, Cardinal Tuschus suggests, *letter S. conclusion 148*, that for minors or wards, a party should always cause a **special guardian** to be given for that specific case, whether they are acting as plaintiff or defending the suit. See Gail 2. *observation 108.* Nevertheless, when an exception of minority

<column-break/>

was omitted, the Judgment accepted, and the sentence was delivered in favor of the minor (an older child), it shall be valid by the law itself, *through law "non eo minus" 14. Code: On Legal Representatives; law 1. there: "he shall have pronounced against you":* where the gloss on the *Code: On those who have legal personhood to stand in Court* and the *Institutes: On the authority of tutors* applies. Mynsinger 2. *observation 36.* In the case of **external property** <note>original: "adventitiis"</note>, where the son of the family does not have the right of use, then regardless of his age, the Father can litigate both as plaintiff and defendant: *based on the tradition from Gail 2. observation 72. number 24.* In the case of **earned property** <note>original: "profectitiis"; property derived from the father's estate or work done under his authority</note>, the son has no right of action at all. In other property matters, it is safer to obtain the consent of the Father, *final chapter, final section, on Judgments in the 6th book.* Martin Uranius *volume 1. consultation 22. from the beginning*; Hartmannus Hartmanni *title 5. on the Plaintiff, observation 7.* **Women**, although by Common Law they are not prohibited from appearing in Court, acting in their own cases, and defending themselves: *law 1. section "sexum", where Gothofredus comments on the Digest: on requesting.* Berlichius *part 1. conclusion 15. number 2*; Benckendorff *in his repetition of law 2. of the Digest on the Rules of Law, folio 210.* However, by the statutes of many places, even if they act for themselves, they must have a **guardian for the suit**, a <term>litigation guardian</term> <note>original German: "kriegerischen Vormund"</note>. Berlichius *in the cited place, number 3 and following, as well as part 2. conclusion 18.* But even without one, if they litigate and prevail, the judgment will be valid, Tiraquellus *in Laws of Marriage 16. gloss 8. number 75. folio 333.*

(k) It must be a **Tutor** who has taken the Oath of Security, created an Inventory, and completed the other required formalities: for only such a person acts rightly for the ward.

(l) Here it should be noted what the little word <term>summon</term> <note>original German: "ruffen"</note> designates. It is said to occur if all Legal Representatives are summoned by proclamation to defend an accused minor who lacks a blood-relative Tutor or Guardian; if they refuse to do this, a Legal Representative is given to the Defendant by the court's authority.

...one may oppose the judgment <note>The OCR "tentiam" completes the word "sententiam" from the previous page.</note>, according to Chapter *in nostra 4* at the end, *Regarding Prosecutors*. (m) <gloss>One can declare a judgment null if the mandate given was imperfect or entirely void. Therefore, an advocate must carefully watch whether everything in the proceedings has been correctly observed, especially whether the **mandate** <note>original: "Mandatum (der Gewalt)"</note> is lacking either entirely or at least in some specific point.</gloss>

(n) <gloss>If I am condemned in such a case by my adversary (who clearly had a representative appointed without a full mandate), the question is whether I can ratify the judgment to my own detriment; the answer is yes. The reason is the "favor of the party." Thus, in this way, one can also ratify a judgment brought against oneself by renouncing one's own favor; one is judged to have done this tacitly if one has appealed. If one remains entirely silent, one will not be deemed to have ratified it. For one who is silent is seen to consent only in favorable matters, not in those that are prejudicial.</gloss>

V. In places where, by virtue of statute or custom, a woman cannot be in court without the intervention of a **curator** <note>a legal guardian appointed for a specific legal task</note>, then she alone cannot rightly appoint a representative. Rauchbar, Book 1, question 2, number 50 and following. This is accepted regarding minors and others who are ineligible to litigate. *Law 11* and *Law 14*, Code *Regarding Representatives*. Wesenbeck, in the commentary on the Digests *Regarding Representatives*, number 4. However, according to **Common Law** <note>original: "Jure Communi"; the Roman legal tradition used as the standard across Europe</note>, although women are not prohibited from appointing a representative for their **separate property** <note>original: "bonis receptitiis"</note>, they cannot do so for **dowry property** <note>original: "bonis dotalibus"</note> or **paraphernal property** <note>original: "paraphernalibus"; property owned by a wife outside of her dowry</note> without the husband's consent (o). Johann Jacob Plebst, in the *New-Ancient Disputation on the Law of Württemberg*, part 2, thesis 63, at the end. And therefore, the husband is admitted to act in the name of the dowry and paraphernal property, even without providing legal security. Meichsner, volume 4, decision 36, number 1 and following. The Lord President in his *Reflections on Book 3*.

<column-break/>

*Digests, question 19.* Likewise, a **guardian** <note>original: "Tutor"</note> or curator cannot appoint a representative before the **joinder of issue** in a public cause, but they must appoint a **legal agent** <note>original: "Actorem"</note>, and therefore a decree of the Judge is required. Mynsing, 2, observation 38. Tennin, *Caution* 48. Furthermore, the mandate of a community is valid in every case if it is drafted thus: **"We, the Mayor, Council, and all Citizens of the City of N. etc."** <note>original: "Wir Burgermeister, Rath, und alle Burger der St. N. &c."</note> nor is it necessary that the names of individuals be expressed. Mynsing 3, observation 10. The Lord President in his *Reflections on Book 3, part 1, question 19*.

(o) <gloss>In dowry property, the husband is the master regarding the pursuit of legal actions, but not regarding the **alienation** <note>selling or giving away</note> of the property. **Paraphernalia** are those things left to the husband besides the administration [of the dowry].</gloss>

VI. To be a legitimate representative, one must fulfill the mandate of the principal. Law 1, in the beginning, Digest *Regarding Representatives*. However, certain clauses are usually added to mandates more out of custom than necessity. Thus a mandate stands even if no express mention was made of the **joinder of issue**, the conclusion of the case, or finally the hearing of the judgment. Mynsing, century 4, observation 99. But it is sufficient if, with certain necessary points expressed, it is added: **"That the attorney has power to handle, do, and undertake all other things according to the legal order, which the principal himself should, could, or might do if he were present at all times."** <note>original: "Daß der Anwald, alles andres, vermög Rechtlicher Ordnung, macht habe zu handlen, zu thun und fürzunehmen, was der Principal selbsten, so er jederzeit gegenwärtig wäre, thun solte, könte oder möchte."</note> Although some wish that by virtue of this or a similar clause, those things requiring a **special mandate** should also be deemed granted to the representative; nevertheless, such things must absolutely be inserted into the mandates. ...prepared in the Digest <note>original: "ff."; the Digest or Pandects of Roman Law</note> on Representatives, number 7. Master Harprecht on § *Procurator* 1. Institutes on those through whom we may act, number 240. However, those cases or acts which are not included in a **General Mandate**, but require **special mention**, are primarily: the Oath of Calumny <note>original: "Calumniæ"; a formal oath that the lawsuit is not being brought for malicious or fraudulent reasons</note>, and the taking, offering, or referring of any other oath; (p) likewise, a settlement <note>original: "transactio"</note>, and full legal restitution <note>original: "in integrum restitutio"; a remedy restoring a party to their original legal position</note>. (q) Similarly, such a mandate is required for an arbitration agreement <note>original: "compromissum"</note>, the receipt of payment, and many other things besides; Covarruvias, *Variar.* chapter 6; Mynsinger, observation 99; Master Harprecht, aforementioned § 1. number 241; Rosbach in *Civil Process*, title 20, number 14; Master President in *Deliberations*, book 3 of the Digest, question 15.

(p) <gloss>No matter how general a clause may be, it does not bind the soul. An oath, however, as a spiritual matter, concerns the soul; therefore, for the soul to be bound, it is necessary for a Special Mandate to be present.</gloss>

(q) <gloss>Because this is something outside the lawsuit and the legal process. That general clause refers only to the lawsuit and its prosecution. Restitution is also distinct from a judicial process, as is an arbitration agreement, the receipt of payment, etc.</gloss>

VII. If a Representative does not prove his Mandate, he is admitted under a **guarantee of ratification** <note>original: "cautio de rato"; a legal promise that the client will formally approve the representative's actions later</note>, Code on Representatives, Law 1. Master President, aforementioned place, question 13. This is especially true if he produces documents pertaining to the case, Harprecht, § 1. number 202, etc. Yet, in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original: "Camera Imperiali"; the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, even in this case, the mandate is not considered fully proven; rather, such an asserted Representative is only heard under the guarantee: **"Within a certain time, to bring in a full Power of Attorney"** <note>original: "Inner gewissen Zeit, ein vollkommenen Gewalt einzubrin-gen"</note>; *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court*, part 1, title 21, § "Furthermore we set and ordain." 

But one may act without a mandate if they are **Ascendants** or **Descendants** <note>parents, grandparents, children, or grandchildren</note>, and other related persons (up to the fourth degree), as well as in-laws, Law 3, § 3 of the Digest, and Law 35 in the preface of the Digest on Representatives. Tennin, caution 190. Master President, aforementioned place, question 18 at the beginning. Likewise, a **Husband** may act in the case of his wife; even where he otherwise cannot act by his own right, Gail, book 1, observation 133, at the beginning and number 5. All of these, however, are held to provide a guarantee of ratification, according to Law 39, § "if regarding dowry" 3, in the title on Representatives. These rules also apply provided that the will of the Master <note>the Principal/Client</note> does not openly conflict, Law *Pomponius* 40, final §, in the said title. Thus, a

<column-break/>

related person is not admitted if the Principal has already appointed a specific representative for himself, Magonius, *Decisions of Lucca* 6, number 11 and 15. Furthermore, a related person (r) is not admitted in cases requiring a **special mandate**, unless they claim their own personal interest, Law "a father for a son" 28, where Brugi on the Digest on Minors under 25 years. Nevertheless, all are able to swear the **Oath of Calumny**, Magonius, noted in decision 6, number 19. And finally, even a complete stranger is admitted for the purpose of **defense**: Law "of demanding" 12, Code on Representatives. Wesenbeck in the commentary on the Digest regarding Representatives, number 12. Provided, of course, he is prepared to give satisfaction <note>security or payment</note>, Law "he who is his own" 48, § "he who another" 2, and Law "it does not seem" 53, Digest on Representatives. (s)

(r) <gloss>A related person is only admitted without a Mandate if the party cannot have another Representative. The reason: because a human provision <note>choosing one's own attorney</note> removes the provision of the law. Thus, the Law provides that a father may act for a son so that the party is defended; if, therefore, the party is already defended by their own foresight, the Law's provision is no longer needed.</gloss>

(s) <gloss>An objection is raised: no one can bind another’s soul without a Mandate, but a related person has no Mandate; therefore, he cannot bind the soul of his principal. I respond: the related person is already in danger themselves because of the guarantee. (For the related person is held to provide security that the principal will accept and ratify whatever they have done; if the opposite happens and the principal does not accept it, the Representative themselves—that is, the related person—is liable). Furthermore, through the **joinder of issue** <note>original: "litis contestationem"</note>, he becomes the "Master of the lawsuit." Therefore, he can swear the oath of calumny, not upon the soul of the one for whom he acts, but upon his own—that he himself does not wish to be malicious. If this oath were not sufficient, the law which permits a relative to stand for another in court would be a mockery, because the oath of calumny must be provided in every case.</gloss>

Gail, book 1, observation 42, number 8, and observation 113, number 2 and following. Mynsinger, book 4, observation 93. ->Dissertation<-

...acts, and puts the scythe (as they say) to the root <note>original: "falcem ponit ad radicem"; a proverbial expression meaning to get to the heart of the matter or to take decisive action</note>, Vantius in rubric 2, from the beginning. It is a matter of Undisputed Law, however, that **the Plaintiff must follow the court of the Defendant** <note>original: "Actorem sequi forum rei"; a fundamental Roman law principle that a lawsuit should be brought in the defendant's home jurisdiction</note>, and the defendant is to be summoned before his own Judge, according to laws 2 and 4 of the Code *on Jurisdiction*, and the chapter "Since it is general" in the decretals *on the competent court*. Furthermore, a Defendant gains a court in the territory where he has his **domicile** <note>the place where a person has their permanent home or principal establishment</note>, according to law "absent heirs" 19, section 12 and the last section, and law 2 of the Code *on Jurisdiction*. Moreover, someone is summoned by reason of domicile indifferently; that is, in both personal and real actions <note>a "personal action" concerns a person's obligations or debts; a "real action" concerns property or physical objects</note>, even if the things in dispute are located under another jurisdiction. (u) Vultejus on law 1 of the Code *where a real action occurs*. The Master President in his *Deliberations* on book 5 of the Digest, question 7. And so, likewise in a real action concerning possession, it is permitted to sue one's adversary either in the place of his own domicile or in the place where the thing is located: Vultejus on the single law of the Code *where concerning possession*. However, not everyone who has a house in a certain place and inhabits it is immediately thought to have established a domicile there: based on the argument of law "it makes no difference" 36, Digest *on captives and return from captivity*. Donellus, book 17 of the *Commentaries*, chapter 12, and there Hilliger. Paurmeister, book 2 *on Jurisdiction*, chapter 9. Rather, it is where someone has established the **seat of their affairs and fortunes**; this is usually judged from external acts, Paurmeister, book 2 *on Jurisdiction*, chapter 9. And thus, they teach that the method for establishing a domicile in a certain region is if someone marries a wife in a certain place and lives there with her: Decius, counsel 28, beginning "And diligently," numbers 9 and 11. Another very common reason for establishing a court is the **performance of Homage**: (vv) and there one can always be summoned, <note>original: "da einer den Burger-Aid, Erbhuldigung, oder Landspflicht abgelegt, und erstattet"</note> <insert>where someone has taken and fulfilled the Citizen's Oath, Hereditary Homage, or Territorial Duty</insert>: for from that it follows <note>original: "daß solcher, regulariter, auch das selbsten Recht nehmen und geben müsse"</note> <insert>that such a person, as a rule, must also seek and grant justice in that same place</insert>: Thomas Maulius *on Homage*, chapter 1. The Master President *on the Right of Citizens*, dissertation 2, chapter 2, from the beginning. Hence also Counts, Barons, and Noble Land-holders <note>original: "Landsassii"; a term for nobles who held land and were subject to the territorial lord's jurisdiction</note> can be summoned even in personal matters before the Prince of the Territory: which was most fiercely disputed in the *Acts and Votes* of the case of **Ortenburg against Bavaria** <note>a significant 16th-century legal conflict regarding the imperial immediacy (independence) of the Counts of Ortenburg from the Duchy of Bavaria</note>.

---

(t) Regarding **Legitimation** (1), it must be seen whether the parties are legitimate, and then also whether a legitimate Judge exists; therefore, the point of competence belongs to the legitimacy of the Judge. However, this point cannot be acted upon unless the parties have first legitimized their own person; therefore, the le-

<column-break/>

gitimation of the persons must precede the legitimation of the Judge himself.

(u) Here it is objected: No one can speak the law outside his territory <note>original: "Jus dicere extra territorium nemo potest"; a rule limiting a judge's power to their own borders</note>, but if someone is summoned in their domicile to answer for things located outside the territory, the law is said to be spoken outside the territory; therefore, no one can be summoned in this way. But I respond by denying the minor premise: because in this case the law is not spoken regarding things located outside the territory, but regarding the **person** established in the domicile; and although as a consequence the citation also concerns the things, nevertheless the jurisdiction is founded only on the person. And here also, if the defendant himself is found outside the territory, or if there is a controversy regarding penalties, it is necessary for him to be summoned through **Letters of Requisition** (which occur when one Judge requests another to do what justice requires and to transfer the defendant there). It should be noted here that formerly, if a Judge then refused to administer justice, **reprisals** <note>original: "repressalias"; the legal right to seize property of a foreign jurisdiction's citizens if that jurisdiction denied justice</note> were even granted in the Empire; today, however, because it is not permitted to exercise these against subjects of the Empire, it is observed <note>original: "daß man Camera ratione denegatæ justitiæ klagt"</note> <insert>that one files a complaint in the Imperial Chamber Court by reason of denied justice</insert>.

(vv) Where someone performs homage, that is, <note>original: "da einer Landshuldigung thut, oder den Burger-Aid erstattet"</note> <insert>where one does Territorial Homage or fulfills the Citizen's Oath</insert>, there one is deemed to have a domicile, even if he does not live there; because domicile is a matter of Law, and so one can have a domicile and be summoned in several places, and indeed not only by reason of those goods where he is found, but of all goods. For example: someone has a domicile in Augsburg, Regensburg, and Ingolstadt; he could be summoned in Ingolstadt just as well by reason of goods located in Augsburg as if he were summoned in that very place. It should be noted, however, in this case, that there is a place for **prevention** <note>original: "præventioni"; the principle that the first court to take up a case gains exclusive jurisdiction</note>, as is the rule in all cases where someone has two Judges.

### IX.

Someone can be summoned into court (2) in the **place where the thing is located** <note>original: "loco rei sitæ"</note>, according to law 1 and the whole title of the Code *where a real action occurs*, and the final chapter of the decretals *on the competent court*; whether he possesses it in his own name or in the name of another (x), law 2 of the Code *where a real action*, and the section "to possess" in the Institutes *on Interdicts*; unless, by naming the Owner, he transfers the attempted Judgment to him, Ummius in his *Disputations on Process* 11, number 36 and following. And this seems to be settled if it concerns **immovable property** <note>such as land or buildings</note>. Regarding **movable property**, however, there is greater doubt. See the Master President in his *Deliberations* on book 5 of the Digest, question 7, folio 414. And certainly, if, for example, a man from Ulm stays in this city with a horse which I claim is mine, I cannot sue him here (y), but he has the **right of recalling the case home** <note>original: "jus domum revocandi"; the right to have a case moved to one's home court</note>, especially if he provides security for appearing in Judgment. It is otherwise if he is a fugitive or difficult to find...

[If a] debtor possesses goods, he can be summoned for that purpose, so that in a case of <term>contumacy</term> <note>original: "contumaciæ"; a legal term for a person's willful disobedience or failure to appear in court</note>, the creditor may be <term>put into possession</term> <note>original: "immittatur"; a legal procedure where a creditor is given control of a debtor's assets</note> of those goods. *Cited from chapter 1, section "contrahentes"; Covarruvias, Practical Questions 10, number 4; Tileman; Roener, Observations on Practical Law, chapter 31; Pauermeister, book 2 on Jurisdiction, chapter 4, number 100, etc.; Lord Fachinae, Counsel 39, book 1.*

(dd) <margin>Therefore, the place of payment is preferred over the place where the contract was made.</margin>

### XII. On Spiritual and Ecclesiastical Causes,
as well as cases against ecclesiastical persons, no one takes notice except an <term>Ecclesiastical Judge</term> <note>a church official, such as a bishop or his appointee, who presided over courts governing church matters and the clergy</note>; so much so, that a matter cannot even be submitted to a lay arbitrator (ee) *Corpus Juris Canonici in the chapter "contingit," on Arbitrators.* If, however, we are dealing with a purely <term>possessory matter</term> <note>a case concerning who currently holds or occupies property, rather than who owns the ultimate title</note>, Mynsinger notes that even in these cases, the secular judge is competent, *as does Gail, book 1, observation 18, number 4.* Sometimes, however, both the ecclesiastical and secular judge will be competent regarding the same matter; and such cases are thereafter called a <term>mixed forum</term> <note>original: "mixti fori"; a jurisdiction where church and state laws overlap</note>. (ff) In this way, the enforcement of an oath belongs to both, *based on the chapter "licet mulieres," 2. on Oaths; Gail, book 1, observation 25, number 4.* Which causes establish an Ecclesiastical Forum are listed in order in the Synodal Constitutions of the Bishop of Constance, *part 4, title 2.* Sometimes a clause is also added to the legal document of an obligation: <gloss>that one can be summoned before all courts, including spiritual ones.</gloss> <note>original German: "daß man einen vor allen, auch geistlichen Gerichten, vornehmen könne."</note> (gg) Indeed, in that case, in the Episcopal courts, debtors are accustomed to being convened even by reason of civil causes, and <term>excommunication</term> <note>the most severe church penalty, which at the time also carried significant social and legal consequences</note> is usually pronounced against them, *as noted by the Presiding Lord in the Treasury of Practice, under the word "Spiritual Jurisdiction."* Whether the <term>Privilege of the Clergy</term> <note>original: "Privilegium Clericorum"; the right of clergy to be tried only in church courts</note> which they have regarding the secular forum is from Divine Law or positive <note>man-made</note> law is a dispute so controversial that *Hieronymus Cavallos, question 550,* lists it among those where there are common opinions on both sides. *Christinaeus, volume 1, decision 203,* attempts to reconcile these with a certain distinction. But already in the Holy Council of Trent, *session 25, title on Regulars, in the decree on reform, chapter 20,* it was decided that the immunity of the Church and of ecclesiastical persons was established by God’s ordinance and by the sanctions of the Canons; to which end, what is held in *1 Corinthians 6 and Matthew 17, verse 24,* etc., seems to contribute, where the Reverend Father Lord A. Cont-

<column-break/>

-tzen [writes]. Indeed, matrimonial causes are said to belong to the secular judge according to Civil Law, *based on law 1, section "hujus" on Justice and Law.* Yet among the older Romans, and before the Emperors wickedly ascribed divine power to themselves, such questions pertained to the investigation of the <term>Pontiffs</term> <note>original: "Pontificum"; referring here to the high priests of the Roman state religion before the Christian era</note>: *Rodolph Forner, book 6, chapter 2.* Also from Canon Law, which the Council of Trent approved, *session 24 on the Sacrament of Matrimony, chapter 12,* practice usually follows this, *Covarruvias, on Espousals, part 2, chapter 8, number 1.* And that arrangement also seems to agree entirely with the Holy Scriptures, as *Cardinal Bellarmine, on Matrimony, chapter 32,* and *see the Presiding Lord's treatise on Nuptials, chapter 5, number 2,* where he compares *Luke chapter 12 and Matthew chapter 19, verse 4.*

(ee) <margin>In certain places, however, <term>real actions</term> <note>lawsuits concerning the ownership of land or physical property</note> concerning fields or other immovable goods are not permitted to be subject to secular judges, but the territorial lords draw them to their own court.</margin>

(ff) <margin>And although the secular judge can take notice in these matters, he is nevertheless bound to judge according to Canon Law, not Civil Law, as in causes of oaths, <term>prescriptions</term> <note>legal rights gained or lost over a period of time</note>, usury, hexes, etc. Hence, it should be noted in passing regarding an oath, that when someone gives a sworn obligation, <gloss>or a sworn oath of peace</gloss> <note>original German: "oder ein geschworne Urphed"; 'Urphede' was a specific legal oath where a person released from custody swore not to seek revenge</note> to someone, then a Count of the Empire or another high judge can relax the oath, but only for the purpose of taking action, not regarding the spiritual bond of the oath. For that belongs to the ecclesiastical forum. However, the violation of an oath is punished even in the secular forum, and insofar as it is punished civilly by reason of these secular penalties, the judge remits the oath.</margin>

(gg) <margin>An extension of church jurisdiction can indeed be made by a secular person; however, an ecclesiastical person cannot, on the contrary, extend the jurisdiction of the civil court. This is because a secular person is more a master of his own rights than a member of the clergy. For a secular person can renounce the law of his city entirely (such as a student at an University), which an ecclesiastical person cannot do—specifically regarding their Orders, if they hold those Orders—so that he cannot depart from the clergy. For then the subjection to the Bishop, or his <term>Ordinary</term> <note>the bishop or other official with regular jurisdiction over a specific territory or group of people</note>, inheres in him inseparably. In Cologne, in the statutes which are otherwise called the "Concordats," that extension of ecclesiastical jurisdiction is prohibited.</margin>

The <term>Reporter</term> <note>original: "Referens"; a court official or judge responsible for presenting a summary of a case to the full court</note> need not be anxious about the Summons. For through the act of appearing in court, a Summons—even if issued or executed with less formality—is strengthened: (ii) so that its invalidity can no longer be raised as an objection. Gail, *book 1, observation 58.* Mynsinger, *2, observation 18; and century 3, observation 90.* (kk) But if a sentence is to be pronounced against a <term>contumacious</term> <note>willfully disobedient or failing to appear</note> or absent party, then the summons must be investigated with great care. For the Summons (called in our language a <term>Citation</term>, a <term>Summons</term>, or a <term>Bidding</term> <note>original: "Citation, Ladung, Verheischung"</note>) must be counted among the essential elements of the legal process. If it is omitted, the act is rendered entirely void as it pertains to the absent party who was not summoned: Vantius, *rubric 12, on nullity from defect of Citation*, since it is a matter of Divine, natural, and civil law. Maranta, *in the Mirror, part 4, distinction 16, number 10.* Likewise, if it was performed incorrectly or illegitimately, it is considered equally invalid and produces no effect regarding contumacy. Mynsinger, *2, observation 18, at the beginning.* Lord Fachinae, *book 3, counsel 87, at the beginning.* And indeed, among several partners, it is not enough for one or two to be summoned; rather, all must be called, and the summons must be delivered to them: yet those summoned are bound to take up the lawsuit for their own portion. (ll) Berlichius, *book 1, conclusion 19, number 35 and following.*

As for the <term>service of notice</term> <note>original: "insinuationem"; the formal delivery of the summons</note>; it must be performed by a sworn messenger of the Judge, or by a notary and witnesses. Gail, *1, observation 54, number 6.* Mynsinger, *1, observation 77.* And if the person to whom the Summons is to be served cannot be met with, it is sufficient for the summons to be made at his house, or posted in that place where he is most accustomed to stay. Mynsinger, *2, observation 69.* Lord Fachinae, *3, counsel 49.* Thus, it is sufficient for the summons to be given to the wife in the husband's dwelling house. Mynsinger, *3, observation 37.* Furthermore, a <term>delegated judge</term> <note>a judge appointed to hear a specific case outside their usual jurisdiction</note> is bound to send a copy of his commission to the person being summoned. Mynsinger, *3, observation 1.* Regarding the execution of the summons, trust is given to the report of the messenger: and this report, like all other things pertaining to the Summons, must be entered into the **Acts** <note>the official written records of the court</note>. Mynsinger, *6, observation 10, number 7 and end.* Gail, *1, observation 54.* Tenninus, *caution 229.* Only then is it permissible to proceed to a finding of contumacy, when the defendant has been <term>peremptorily</term> (mm) <note>a final summons that leaves no room for further delay or excuses</note> summoned, *law "contumacia," 53, section 1, on matters already judged.* However, the laws do not necessarily require a triple Summons; a single deadline is sufficient, provided it contains as much

<column-break/>

time as a triple summons would; and provided the usual threat of penalty is added. *law "consentaneum," 8, Code: how and when a Judge; law "nonnunquam," 72, Digest on Judges.* Gail, *1, observation 53, number 22.* Sometimes, however, to prove the <term>malice</term> <note>bad faith or intentional evasion</note> of the absent defendant, it is customary to proceed even to a fourth summons out of a certain kindness. Mynsinger, *6, observation 9.* Wurmser, *title 2, observation 7.* **Edictal Summonses** (nn) <note>a public announcement, such as a notice on a church door or in a newspaper, used when personal service is impossible</note> take place only when someone cannot be summoned in another way: for instance, if the location is not safe, or if for some other reason (oo) the summons cannot reach the person summoned; or if he stays in remote places, or where he is located is unknown. Gail, *1, observation 57.* Antonius Winter, *in his Assessor, part 2, chapter 11, number 7.* Berlichius, *part 1, conclusion 11.* Virgilius de Boccatiis, *treatise on Summons.*

<gloss>(ii) One does not worry about the cause [the flaw in the summons], because the effect [the appearance in court] is achieved.</gloss>
<gloss>(kk) If, however, the Summons is not legitimate, then no one is considered contumacious.</gloss>

(1) By a verbal summons through a messenger. (2) Through subsidiary letters. (3) By a public edict posted on the doors of the Court, or in another public place. An edictalsummons is a "subsidiary remedy"; and therefore an ordinary summons must be attempted first.</gloss>

# Dissertation

### 1. at that point:

The written complaint <note>original: "libellum"</note> should be presented in every possible way. However, where a contrary custom exists—allowing, for example, a complaint to be proposed orally—that custom shall prevail. *Hartmann, title 8, observation 1, number 3; Berlich, part 1, conclusion 13.* An objection against an unfit complaint <note>original: "Exceptio inepti Libelli"</note> can be raised at any time. *Wurmser, title 8, observation 9.* From this, it follows that if a complaint suffers from any unfitness of form, the Judge ought to reject it even on his own initiative <note>original: "ex officio"</note>. *Jacob Schultes, practical observations, 6.* And certainly, the "Forms of Action" <note>specific legal formulas required in ancient Roman law</note> in the Code *on the removal of formulas and the obtaining of actions* have by no means been abolished; rather, they are only removed insofar as they acted as traps through the hunting of specific syllables. Although today it is not necessary to designate the specific name or category of an action by name—*Legal Doctors on the chapter "dilecti," title "on Judgments"*—it is nonetheless necessary for the complaint to contain the legal basis for the conclusion <note>original: "medium concludendi"</note>. *Gail, book 1, observation 61.* Furthermore, the facts and the petition joined to them must be so formed that they can be referred to a certain category of Action. *Based on law 1, in the preface and section 1 of the Digest "on the Edental."*

And, if it is not clear enough what Action someone has instituted, or if the legal basis for the conclusion cannot be certainly known from the narrative, then by virtue of the **salutary clause** <note>a "safety net" phrase used by lawyers to ensure the court considers the best possible legal interpretation</note> (which states: **in every better way, etc.** <note>original: "omni meliori modo &c."</note>), the party is deemed to have sought that which they ought to have sought, provided it matches the narrated facts. *Hart. Pistor, observation 71; Everhard Speckhan, century 1, chapter 67* (where he also mentions several other clauses usually inserted into complaints). This matter will be discussed below in *thesis 21.* Finally, although a complaint can be changed before the **joinder of issue** <note>the formal start of the trial; see note (pp)</note> (provided the increased expenses the opponent incurred on that account are reimbursed), it cannot be done after the issue is joined. Instead, one must proceed by a new judgment, unless someone wishes to make some slight correction or merely add a clarification. *See Berlich, part 1, conclusion 28; H. Pistor, book 4, question 22, at the beginning; Schultes, observation 48 and following; Obrecht, "on the Drafting of Complaints," chapter 20; the Lord Presiding Judge in the "deliberations from book 2 of the Digest," question 11.* Nor does the clause added to the end of a complaint—**reserving the right to change and add** <note>original German: "Enderung und Mehrung vorbehaltend"</note>—help toward the goal of allowing changes at any time, since that would be contrary to the order of the Law.

---

(pp) A complaint can indeed be changed even after the joinder of issue, as at any time, but only in such a way that a new joinder of issue is required. Because the Judgment is then different, 

<column-break/>

therefore a new joinder is also required. We, however, understand such a "change" here as one that occurs within the same process.

### XV. The **Joinder of Issue** <note>original: "Litis contestatio"</note>, (qq) 

called in German **the fastening of the conflict** <note>original: "die Kriegs-Befestigung," literally "the war-fortification"</note>, is considered among the foremost judicial acts. Because of this, the Doctors of Law are accustomed to calling it the cornerstone and the base and foundation of the whole trial. *Law 1 and the "offerantur" section of the Code "on the joinder of issue"; chapter 1 of the Extra, same title; Parladorius, "daily matters," chapter 14; Speckhan, class 2, question 15.* From this point, the trial is finally deemed to begin; before it, no trial is considered to exist yet. *Gail, book 1, observation 74, at the beginning.* And therefore, if it is omitted, the entire process collapses. *Maranta, in the "Mirror," part 1, member 10, number 1; Mynsinger, book 3, observation 74; Gail, book 1, observation 75.* If performed correctly, it produces many notable effects, which are listed in order by *Speckhan, class 4, question 16, as well as by Obrecht in the treatise "on the joinder of issue," chapter 10.* However, summary cases <note>shortened legal proceedings for simpler matters</note> do not require a joinder of issue—*Maranta, member 10; Mynsinger, book 1, observation 1, number 2*—unless something else has been introduced by custom. *Mynsinger, book 4, observation 62.* Issue is deemed to be joined when the defendant either simply denies the complaint or denies the facts as they are told. *Obrecht, treatise "on the joinder of issue," chapter 5 and following; Gail, book 1, observation 73, at the beginning; Schultes, "practical observations," 42.* This is not the case if he responds to specific positions individually. (rr) *Gail, observation 73, number 7 and following.* The lawsuit is also held as joined whenever the defendant fails to join the issue within the time limit set for that purpose. *Schultes, observation 47.* But it does not seem to be joined if the defendant denies the Plaintiff's intention but protests that he is not doing this with the intent of joining the issue. *Mynsinger, book 4, observation 49, and counsel 8, number 4.* The Judge accepts the issue as joined through an interlocutory decree <note>a decree given during the course of a case</note>, called in German **through a formal decision** <note>original: "durch einen Bescheid"</note>.

---

(qq) Some say the Plaintiff joins the issue affirmatively, but the Defendant joins it negatively. In this, it is sufficient to state the facts as the defendant believes they are; there is no need for him to say, "I do this with the intent of joining the issue."

(rr) That is, point by point, if indeed he cannot deny everything. It is one thing, therefore, to deny the complaint and the facts simply as they are told, and another thing to respond specifically to individual positions. For if someone responds to individual articles, it is done for one effect, and for another—

...and that response tends toward another end, namely toward relief from the burden of proof, not toward the joinder of issue <note>original: "litis contestationem"; the formal start of the trial's merits</note>.

XVI. The **Oath of Calumny** (ss) (**The Oath against Malice/Hazard**) vitiates the entire process if it is demanded from the start of the litigation and is not performed. *Vantius on nullity from a defect of process, number 19; Gail, book 1, observation 84.* And here, even "summary cases" <note>expedited legal proceedings</note> are not thought to be excepted. *Clement, "Saepe," section "citationem" on the significance of words; Setser on Oaths, book 3, chapter 4, number 4 and following; Scaccia on Judgments, book 2, chapter 1, question 18, number 141, etc.* However, although under Civil Law <note>Roman Law</note> the parties themselves cannot renounce this Oath (*Law 3, section 4 of the Code on the Oath regarding calumny; Ferdinand Vasquez, Illustrious Questions, volume 1, chapter 64, number 19, and volume 2, chapter 27, in the preface; Guillaume Forner, Select Works 2, chapter 4*), under Canon Law (which current practice follows), the process only contracts the defect of nullity if the oath was requested by a party and then omitted. *Chapter 1, section "propter" on the Oath of Calumny in the 6th book of the Decretals; Obrecht, Treatise on the Oath of Calumny, chapter 11, number 6; Gail, book 1, observation 84; Rauhbar, part 1, question 11, from the beginning.* Furthermore, in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>The high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> and other high courts, this demand must be made orally; it is not cared for if it is requested in writing or in a submitted document. **Decree of the Imperial Deputation for the year 1600, section "As also our [orders] and those of the Estates."** *Gail, book 1, observation 84, last number; Schvvanman on the process of the Imperial Chamber, book 1, chapter 45, number 21 and following; Obrecht, cited chapter 11, number 27; Rauhbar, cited question 11, number 1.* If, however, the **Referee** <note>original: "Referens"; the judge responsible for reporting on the case</note> discovers from the Protocol that the litigation was concluded on both sides after the Oath of Calumny was demanded but not performed, he ought to rescind the conclusion by virtue of his office. He must then enjoin the party, through an **interlocutory decree** <note>a provisional order made during a case</note>, to perform it (or even the **Oath of Giving and Responding**, *on which see number 18*). *Gail, cited observation 84.* Nevertheless, in the Imperial Chamber, a process of the first instance is not annulled, but a ruling is usually made on the principal cause, even if the Oath of Calumny, though duly demanded, had been omitted. *Gail, cited observation 84, number 3; Compiler of Imperial Chamber Precedents, section "Oath of Calumny," at the verse "when the parties."*

(ss) The <term>Oath of Calumny</term> <note>original: "Juramentum Calumniæ"</note> contains several chapters and concerns the whole case in general. For the "Oath of Malice" is imposed only if, in a single

<column-break/>

proposition, **or in a submission**, there is a suspicion that one or the other party is practicing calumny or proposing something maliciously. And this Oath of Malice can always be initiated during the cause: for in every part of a lawsuit, a party can commit malice.

XVII. When someone proffers an oath to another in Court, the first person must swear regarding Calumny (tt), if this is demanded. *Law "The Oath," 34, section "he who [proffers] the oath," of the Digest on Oaths; Rauhbar, 1, question 9.* This oath, however, is properly called the **Oath of Malice**, or the "special" (uu) oath of calumny. It is enjoined either at the request of a party or by the judge's office, whenever a presumption arises concerning some malicious proposition, or when a suspicion can be gathered from certain conjectures regarding the malice of the plaintiff or the defendant. *Chapter 2, section "in all things" on the Oath of Calumny in the 6th book; Gail, book 1, observation 87, number 3.* Whence the deferral of such an Oath can be made in any part of the lawsuit. *Cited chapter 2, cited section "in all things"; Berlich, 1, conclusion 31, number 2.* And there is a place for it even if the general Oath of Calumny has been performed. *Graeve, 1, conclusion 87, consideration 1, numbers 3 and 7; see Berlich, cited conclusion 31, number 3.* And he who refuses to perform this is held **as having confessed** <note>original: "pro confesso"</note> only in respect of that article upon which the oath of malice was requested. *Final chapter on confessions; Gail, book 1, observation 88; Rutger Ruland on Commissions, part 1, book 2, chapter 14, number 14.*

(tt) When someone refuses to perform the **Oath of Calumny**, he loses the entire case; however, when he refuses the **Oath of Malice**, he is only held as having confessed on that specific point.

(uu) And therefore it is safer, because special things are more pressing.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of legal procedures, moving from the initial complaint (the Libellus) to the formal commencement of the trial known as the joinder of issue (Litis contestatio).</meta>

1. **In that place**: the complaint <note>original: "libellum"</note> must be presented in every possible way. However, where a contrary custom exists—permitting, for instance, the complaint to be proposed orally—that custom shall prevail, according to Hartmann (*title 8, observation 1, number 3*) and Berlichius (*conclusion 13*). Furthermore, an objection regarding an "unsuitable complaint" <note>original: "inepti Libelli"; a complaint that is legally insufficient or poorly drafted</note> can be raised at any time, per Wurmser (*title 8, observation 9*). Consequently, if a complaint suffers from any formal unsuitability, the Judge ought to reject it on his own initiative <note>original: "ex officio"</note>, as noted by Jacob Schultes (*practical observations 6*). Certainly, the "Formulas of Actions" <note>standardized legal templates used in Roman law</note> were by no means abolished by the Code; rather, they were only removed insofar as they acted as traps for the unwary through hair-splitting <note>original: "aucupatione quasi syllabarum," literally "the hunting of syllables"</note>. Although today it is not strictly necessary to designate the specific name or category of the legal action, it is nonetheless essential that the complaint contains the "grounds for the conclusion" <note>original: "medium concludendi"; the legal reasoning connecting the facts to the requested relief</note> as Gail notes (*observation 61*). Both the facts and the subsequent petition must be shaped so that they can be referred to a specific type of action. If it is not clear enough which action someone has initiated, or if the grounds for the conclusion cannot be certain from the narrative, then by virtue of the **saving clause** <note>original: "clausulæ salutaris," often phrased as "in every better way, etc."</note>, the person is deemed to have sought what they *should* have sought—provided that this also fits the narrated facts. Hartmann Pistor (*observation 71*) and Everhard Speckhan (*Century 1, chapter 67*) mention this and several other clauses usually inserted into complaints. This subject will be treated further below in thesis 21. Finally, although a complaint can be changed before the **joinder of issue** <note>original: "litem contestatam"; the formal point where the parties agree on what is being litigated</note> (pp)—provided the expenses the opponent incurred because of the change are reimbursed—it cannot be changed after the issue is joined. Instead, a new trial would be required, unless one only wishes to make a slight correction or add a clarification. See Berlichius, Pistor, Schultes, and Obrecht. Even a clause added to the end of a complaint, stating **"reserving the right to change and increase,"** <note>original: "Enderung und Mehrung vorbehaltend"</note> does not allow for a change to be made at any time, as that would be contrary to the order of Law.

---

*(pp)* A complaint can indeed be changed after the joinder of issue, as at any other time, but only in such a way that a new joinder of issue is required. Because the judgment is then something different,

<column-break/>

therefore a new joinder is also required. However, we are not referring here to the kind of change that happens within the same proceeding.

XV. **Joinder of Issue** <note>original: "Litis contestatio"</note> (qq), called by the Germans **the fortification of the war** <note>original: "die Kriegs-Befestigung"; a metaphor for the parties' formal commitment to the legal "battle"</note>, is considered among the principal judicial acts. Hence, doctors of law are accustomed to calling it the "cornerstone" and the "base and foundation of the whole trial." From this point, the trial is finally considered to truly begin; before it, no "trial" is yet deemed to exist. If it is omitted, the entire process collapses. When performed correctly, it produces many notable effects, which Speckhan and Obrecht list in order. However, **summary cases** <note>expedited proceedings for simple matters</note> do not require a formal joinder of issue, nor do cases where a different custom has been introduced. The joinder is considered to have occurred when the defendant either simply denies the complaint or denies the facts as they are narrated. It is not joined merely by answering specific points <note>original: "positiones"</note> distinctly (rr). A lawsuit is also held as joined whenever a defendant fails to join issue within the time set for that purpose. However, it is not considered joined if the defendant denies the plaintiff's claim but protests that he does not do so with the *intent* of joining issue. The Judge accepts the issue as joined through an **interlocutory decree** <note>original: "interlocutoriam," a provisional order</note>, known in German as **a Bescheid.**

---

*(qq)* Some say that the plaintiff joins issue "affirmatively" and the defendant "negatively." In this act, it is sufficient to report the facts as the defendant believes they stand; it is not necessary to say, "I do this with the intent of joining issue."

*(rr)* That is, answering article by article <note>point by point</note> if he cannot deny everything. It is one thing to simply deny the complaint and its narrative, and another to respond distinctly to specific points. For if someone responds to individual articles, it is done for a different purpose and a different

It emphasizes that while modern law is less rigid about specific legal formulas, the joinder of issue remains the essential "cornerstone" that officially begins a trial.</summary>

# On the Manner of Reporting. 2247

...and this response aims toward another end, namely toward relieving the burden of proof, not toward the joinder of issue <note>original: "litis contestationem"; the formal moment the legal issues are finalized for trial</note>.

XVI. The Oath of Calumny (*ss*) (**the Oath against Malice**) <note>German: "der Aid für Gefährde"; an oath where a party swears they are acting in good faith and not to harass their opponent</note> completely invalidates the Process if, having been demanded from the start of the lawsuit, it is not sworn. Vantius *on the rubric of nullity from a defect of process, number 19.* Gail, *book 1, observation 84.* And here even summary cases <note>expedited legal proceedings</note> are not thought to be excepted. *The Clementines, "Sæpè" in the section on citations regarding the meaning of words.* Setser, *on Oaths, book 3, chapter 4, section n. 4 and following.* Scaccia, *on Judgments, book 2, chapter 1, question 18, number 141, etc.* Although under Civil Law <note>Roman law</note>, the parties themselves cannot waive this oath: *Law 3, section 4, Code on the Oath regarding Calumny.* Ferdinand Vasquez, *Illustrious Questions, volume 1, chapter 64, number 19, and volume 2, chapter 27 at the beginning.* Guillaume Forner, *2nd Select, chapter 4.* However, under Canon Law <note>Church law, which heavily influenced court practice</note> (which Practice also follows), the Process only contracts the defect of nullity if the oath, having been requested by a party, is omitted, *chapter 1, section "propter" on the Oath of Calumny in the 6th.* Obrecht, *Treatise on the Oath of Calumny, chapter 11, number 6.* Gail, *book 1, observation 84.* Rauchbar, *part 1, question 11, from the beginning.* And also in the Imperial Chamber <note>original: "Camerâ Imperiali"; the supreme court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> and other courts, this demand must be made aloud <note>original: "vivâ voce"</note>; it is not cared for if it is requested in writing or in a submitted document. *Decree of the Deputation, from the year 1600, section:* **"As also ours and the Estates'."** Gail, *book 1, observation 84, last number.* Schvvanman, *on the Process of the Chamber, book 1, chapter 45, number 21 and following.* Obrecht, *cited chapter 11, number 27.* Rauchbar, *cited question 11, number 1.* If, however, the Reporter <note>original: "Referens"; the judge responsible for summarizing the case for the full court</note> discovers from the Record that the case was concluded on both sides after the Oath of Calumny was demanded but not sworn, he must rescind the conclusion on his own initiative <note>original: "ex officio"</note> and enjoin the party through an interlocutory order <note>a temporary ruling made before the final judgment</note> to swear it (or even the Oath of Providing and Answering, discussed in section 18). Gail, *cited observation 84.* However, in the Imperial Chamber, the process of the first instance <note>the original trial level</note> is not annulled, but a pronouncement is usually made on the principal cause, even if the Oath of Calumny, though duly demanded, was omitted. Gail, *cited observation 84, number 3.* *Compiler of Imperial Prejudices, section on the Oath of Calumny, at the verse "when the parties."*

(*ss*) *The Oath of Calumny contains several chapters and concerns the whole case in general. For the Oath of Malice is imposed only if, in a specific*

<column-break/>

*proposition or in a submission* <note>German: "oder in ein Fürbringen"</note> *a suspicion arises that one or the other party is acting with calumny or proposing something maliciously. And this Oath of Malice can always be brought into a case; for in every part of a lawsuit, a party can commit malice.*

XVII. He who proffers an oath to another in court must first swear regarding Calumny (*tt*), if this is demanded, *Law on Oaths, 34, section "he who [proffers] an oath," Digest on Oaths.* Rauchbar, *1, question 9.* This oath, however, is properly called the Oath of Malice, or the special (*uu*) oath of calumny: and it is enjoined either at the request of a party or by the court’s own initiative <note>original: "ex officio"</note>, whenever a presumption exists regarding some malicious proposition, or a suspicion of malice in the plaintiff <note>original: "agentis"</note> or the defendant <note>original: "fugientis"</note> can be gathered from certain conjectures, *chapter 2, section "in all," on the Oath of Calumny in the 6th.* Gail, *book 1, observation 87, number 3.* Hence the offering of such an oath can be made in any part of the lawsuit, *said chapter 2, said section "in all."* Berlichius, *1, conclusion 31, number 2.* And there is a place for it even if the general Oath of Calumny has already been sworn, Grævæ, *1, conclusion 87, consideration 1, numbers 3 and 7; see* Berlichius, *said conclusion 31, number 3.* And whoever refuses to swear this is held as having confessed <note>original: "pro confesso"</note> only with respect to that specific article upon which the oath regarding malice was requested, *final chapter on Confessions.* Gail, *book 1, observation 88.* Rutger Ruland, *on Commissions, part 1, book 2, chapter 14, number 14.*

(*tt*) When someone refuses to swear the Oath of Calumny, he loses the entire case; but when he refuses the Oath of Malice, he is only held as having confessed in that specific article.

(*uu*) And therefore it is safer, because special things are more pressing.

XVIII. To the Oath of Calumny, the Oath of Positions is so closely related—commonly called by practitioners the "Oath of Providing and Answering"—that when the former is sworn, the latter is thought not to be necessary; but it is customary only to enjoin the parties to repeat the articles (*nn*) and answer them by virtue of the oath given on account of calumny. Schvvanman, *Process of the Imperial Chamber, book 1, chapter 45.* Magenhorst, *on the Ordinances of the Chamber, part 3, chapter 15, section "in this fourth term."* Scaccia, *book 2 on Judgments, chapter 1, number 38.* However, that oath of providing and answering is sworn only if it has been...

...duly demanded: and what is sought by both sides must be provided, Grævæus. conclusion 79. consideration 2. number 1. 3. 5. etc. But unless it is demanded **by word of mouth** <note>original: "vivâ voce"</note>, it can be omitted without the defect of nullity. And just as the one offering "positions" <note>statements of fact submitted for the opponent to admit or deny</note> is not necessarily bound to offer the **Oath** <note>original: "Juramentum"</note>, Ferrarius in the form of the Plaintiff’s position, on the word "places by Oath," number 3.

<margin>(vv vv) The Reason is because one article of the **oath of calumny** <note>an oath where a party swears they are acting in good faith and not out of malice</note> is that the person questioned intends to tell the truth.</margin>

XIX. And finally, the **conclusion of the case** <note>original: "conclusio causæ"</note> (*xx*) is also so necessary by custom that unless the case has been legitimately concluded, any sentence passed is null and invalid, Mynsing. 3. observation 17. And this must be done **by word of mouth**, even if it was done in writing. **Imperial Chamber Court Regulations** <note>German: "Cammergerichts-Ordnung"</note> part 3. title 22, and following. And it is permitted for the Judge, if sufficient delays <note>extensions of time</note> have been granted, to accept the case as concluded (*yy*) even against the will of the parties. Mynsing. cited observation at the end. Above all, let the **Reporter** <note>the official or judge responsible for summarizing the case for the court</note> consider here whether the conclusion was made **purely** <note>without reservations</note>, or with an offer "if anything factual" <note>original: "si quid facti"; a conditional closing</note>? For in this latter case, such a clause must be added to the definitive sentence: *First, the made **Eventual-Conclusion** <note>German: "Eventual-Beschluß"</note> (zz) is accepted as pure, and thereafter further, after all submissions, recognized as right, etc.* Conversely, whether it was concluded by the Parties purely, or with the aforementioned protestation; nevertheless the Reporter must consider whether the case needs a deeper declaration or information, Gail. 1. observation 107. number 9. For in this case, the sentence should not be rushed, but the Judge ought to rescind the conclusion made by the parties, and advise the litigants on what further must be done (*aaa*) Bocerus class 6. dispute 27. thesis 13. Truly, for a judge, a case is never "concluded"; rather he can always, by virtue of his office, question a party, not only for clarifications of past actions, but even to establish his intention anew, Gail. cited observation 107. number 6. and following. Cævallos, question 821. Also admitted after the conclusion are **Witnesses**, or **Instruments** <note>legal documents</note> newly discovered, chapter "pastoralis", on exceptions. Cævallos question 650. Mynsing. 2. observation 53. and 4. observation 60. Cravett. consultation 716. And finally, allegations and in-

<column-break/>

formations of Law—for example, the **Legal Opinions of Doctors** <note>original: "Consilia Doctorum"; expert opinions from law professors</note>—can be exhibited even after the conclusion, Gail. cited observation 107. number 13. Mynsing. 6. observation 56. final number.

<margin>(xx) "Conclusion of the case" is the **legal statement or conclusion** <note>German: "der Rechtssatz oder Schluß"</note>, and it is said to be concluded in a case when the parties say they wish to conclude—that is, they wish to prove or propose nothing further, but to leave the decision of the case to the Judge.</margin>

<margin>(yy) Then it is done with these words by an **Interlocutory order** <note>a provisional decree that does not end the whole case</note>, "that the matter is herewith accepted as concluded by office" <note>German: "daß die Sach hiemit ex officio für beschlossen angenommen seye"</note>.</margin>

<margin>(zz) One conclusion is final, another is "eventual." It is called **Eventual** when someone says, "I will conclude in the event that **my opponent does not want to bring in anything new.**" <note>German: "wann mein Gegentheil nichts neues mehr einbringen will"</note> A conclusion "**if anything factual**" <note>original: "si quid facti"</note> intends this: namely, that a party offers itself to prove that which was indeed proposed as fact by them, but not yet proven. A **pure conclusion** is the opposite of an eventual one and one with an offer "if anything factual"—that is, when someone concludes without any reservation or protest.</margin>

<margin>(aaa) A Judge must do everything he does through **interlocutory orders**, if they do not define and decide the case.</margin>

XX. Having set forth these matters concerning the formal or substantial order of the **Process** <note>legal proceeding</note> preceding the investigation of the case; we must proceed to the **Material** aspects, or the case itself. Therefore, in the third place, it comes to be reported: by what **action** <note>original: "actio"; the specific legal claim or category of lawsuit</note> was the matter conducted, and whether it was correctly and conclusively formed and attempted? For according to the specific type of action, the sentence must be formed and regulated by the Judge, (*bbb*) *Symphorema* volume 1. in the methodical treatise on the Process of the Imperial Chamber, title "manner of reporting," number 3. and there the terms of individual actions must be observed; lest they be indiscriminately and unskillfully confused, and the sentence be challenged for nullity, Gail. on Imperial Arrests, chapter 5. number 11. and following. Truly, a sentence cannot be passed where no action is applicable, *Law "si pupilli" 6. section 6. let us see 12. Digest on business conducted, Law "quis servandarum" 14. final section, on prescriptive words, gloss at section 1 on the word "according to" at the end, final Law on Obligations.* Whence a Judge, by virtue of his office, must reject a plaintiff acting without a suitable action, even if the opposing party does not object, *Gloss and Doctors on Law "ubi pactum" 40. Code on transactions. Barbosa in axioms of Law, axiom 9. number 5.* Here, however, the Reporter should not so much...
