# On the Manner of Reporting. 1249

The Reporter ought to be concerned with the **name of the Action**; asking what is being sought, from what cause, and by what right? He can cast all these things into the form of a **Syllogism** <note>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> to form a more certain judgment; for since every case, even if presented as a set of "positions" <note>factual statements</note>, is nothing other than an argument by which either the Plaintiff tries to prove that something should be given or done to him, or the Defendant tries to prove he should be acquitted. *Wehner, Practical Observations, letter r, on the word "Justice/Essence", chapter 4.* Regarding the examination of the **fact**, however (as Oldendorp advises in the formula for investigating actions, which is joined to his treatise on exceptions), one must weigh not just one or two small parts, but the whole: so that it may better appear whether the fact is simple or complex, and what the circumstances of time, things, and persons are. *Argument from law "good faith" 31. § 1. Digest on deposits.* For he says that in such an immense world of business, no one can rightly discern what law or what action belongs to whom, unless he first has the fact **precisely explained** <note>original: "ad amussim explicatum"</note>: (*ccc*) he therefore blames those who barely hear the whole matter from the litigants and are not accustomed to judging its quality, etc. He adds that one must see, above all, to what form of business it belongs: whether it is a **contract**, or a **quasi-contract** <note>an obligation that looks like a contract but is created by law rather than agreement</note>, or indeed a **wrongdoing** <note>original: "maleficium," a delict or tort</note>, or a **quasi-wrongdoing**: or whether it involves no contract or action at all, but is only a question of the ownership of things. Finally, whether the nature of the fact is so varied that the case cannot be reduced to a certain or named legal form, etc. And even here, the beginning and the **cause** of each contract must be looked at. *Law "if a proxy," 8. at the beginning & § 4. Law "the same" 10. § "if anyone" 4. Digest on mandates. Law "if only" 12. on the Macedonian Decree. Law 1. § "but if the thing" 12. & following section. Digest on deposits.*

(*bbb*) That is, the sentence must be made to conform to the **petition** <note>original: "libello," the written complaint</note>. And the defendant must be condemned according to what was sought, or acquitted of what was sought; however, this acquittal is to be extended even further than what was sought.

(*ccc*) Here it should be noted (1) in a fact that is complex and involves several contracts, one must look to the principal business and the goal of the parties' intention, not to what happens incidentally or by chance. (2) In a varied and complex business, one must first look not at what followed...

<column-break/>

...by accident, since even after the **joinder of issue** <note>original: "litem contestatam," the formal start of the trial</note>, the parties' disputes may tend toward another remedy or action than what was proposed in the petition and upon which the issue was joined; however, that is not considered, because the issue was not joined on that point. The lawsuit is founded upon the **petition** and the **joinder**; therefore, heterogeneous or foreign elements, lacking a suitable foundation, fall away on their own and can be ignored. For those things brought forward after the joinder of issue must all refer back to the petition and the joinder of issue, and the exceptions joined to it.

To understand the **remedies of the Law**, not only are authors on "Actions" helpful, but **subsidiary remedies** <note>backup legal options used when standard ones fail</note> are necessary, which can be used in the absence of standard actions and remedies; Joannes Baptista Costa wrote a unique treatise on these. Likewise, one must know the **office of the Judge**, on which Matthaeus Stephani wrote; then **Restitutions to the original state** <note>original: "Restitutiones in integrum," a legal remedy to cancel a contract or judgment to avoid unfairness</note>, on which Francesco Oddus, Caldas, and others wrote.

### XXI.

The type of action is gathered not only from the specific nature of the fact, but primarily from the **conclusion of the Petition** <note>original: "Libelli conclusione"</note>, or the request. *Gail 1. observation 61. num. 13. Schneidewin at § "of all" num. 117. etc. Institutes on actions. Bocer class 6. dispute 3. thesis 33.* Since the form of the Petition is said to consist in its conclusion; *Baldus on law 2. num. 2. on the word "besides," Code on proofs.* From this, the **Reporter** will be able to know the type and quality of the action being attempted. *Chapter "your letters." Decretals on delays. and the gloss there.* And although the Doctors of law commonly judge that two things should be considered in the petition regarding this investigation—namely, the **means of concluding** and the **conclusion itself** (for other mixed-in things are usually little cared for)—nevertheless, the conclusion is the most important part, declaring the action itself. After Jason, Zasius, and others, Rutger Ruland teaches this in his work *On Articles*, book 2, chapter 2, throughout: and among other things he adds that the conclusion alone amplifies, regulates, and restricts what was narrated. Furthermore, if the fact is such that several actions are applicable to it (just as several remedies can apply to a single fact, examples of which are proposed in Law "of common property" 45, Law "if from a cause" 47, and the three following, Digest *on partners*), then the person will be seen (in case of doubt) to have proposed that action which is **more useful** and can be gathered from what was narrated. *Law "if anyone with the intention" 66. Digest on Judgments.* Especially if a **saving clause** <note>original: "clausula salutaris," a phrase such as "or for whatever other better remedy" added to the end of a petition</note> has been added: <note>original German: "und dieses alles, auch was sonsten nach Gestalt dieser"</note> and all this, as well as whatever else according to the form of this...

# Dissertation 1250

...of these matters, could, should, or might be requested; all this the Plaintiff <note>original: "Kläger"</note> desires, sought in the best legal form, and has called upon the noble, merciful office of the judge for the speedy granting of justice. Ayrer, in *part 1, chapter 4, observation 6.* From this, if someone binds themselves to many claims in a petition <term>libellus; the formal written statement of a plaintiff's case</term>, and yet one is sufficient for the victory of the case, the Reporter or the Judge shall choose that one. Rutger Ruland, in *the said chapter 2, number 23; who also in chapters 3 and 4* illustrates with many examples how, when several actions present themselves, the more useful one is to be chosen. However, this clause <note>the "general clause" allowing for various legal interpretations</note> is not to be extended to contradictory things; therefore, if someone attempts one action and adds the said clause, they cannot succeed in a different, competent action that is contradictory to the one attempted. Alexander, *Counsel 121, number 11 and following, book 1.* Also, if from the conclusion of the petition a certain kind of action is gathered, but in other produced documents or writings it is noticed to have changed, the Reporter must nevertheless firmly stick to the first action. This is because a plaintiff, by choosing one path, cannot recur to another. *Law "what in the heir," 9, section 1, Digest on the taxation of actions.* Ruland, *said chapter 2, number 24 and following.* Antonio Gabriel, *Common Conclusions, book 2, title on Actions, conclusion 1 and following.*

## XXII.
Having unearthed the action, fourthly, it will be necessary to investigate and observe: what are the **substantial requirements** of the attempted action? These were most excellently collected by Oldendorp in his *Classes*, as well as by Schneidewin *on the title of the Institutes regarding Actions.* And the members of the Imperial Chamber Court <note>the "Camerales," high-ranking legal officials</note> follow in this part Joannes Petrus Ferrariensis, Petrus Jacobus Aurelianensis (who supplied what was missing in Ferrariensis), Odofredus, Roffredus, and Arnold von Haersolte. To this end, what Rutger Ruland has in his *Treatise on Articles* is especially useful. Furthermore, once the state of the case and its requirements are thus found, the next step will be to undertake an **examination of the proofs** from the Acts; and to inquire whether the state of the case has been sufficiently and adequately proven by the Plaintiff, and in what manner. Bocer, *said disputation 3, thesis 34.* Here it must certainly be noted that not all requirements of the attempted action must always be proved by the plaintiff; rather, one must see which ones, by **legal presumption** <term>juris praesumptio; a legal assumption that stands until disproven, which relieves a party of the burden of proof</term>, are considered proven until 

<column-break/>

the defendant has proved the contrary. *The same Menochius, on presumptions, book 1, question 33,* and Pacianus, *treatise on proofs, book 1, chapter 8,* where it would be easy to demonstrate this with examples.

## XXIII.
It is indeed quite difficult in judicial disputes to investigate **what must be proven**, and to whom the necessity of proving must be assigned; since this varies in almost every formula of action. But Mascardus (who wrote a very lengthy work on proofs) can assist the Reporter significantly, as can Marcellus Cala (who writes more successfully on the manner of articulating and proving), and also Oldendorp in his *treatise on the Proof of words and deeds*, in which he provides many rules relating to this. Above all, however, it must be known: that everyone is bound to prove the **foundation of their intention** <note>the core facts supporting their legal claim</note>; and indeed the Plaintiff must do so before the Defendant. Joseph Ludovicus, *conclusion 14.* However, this rule only applies to the one who affirms, not the one who denies. Pacianus, *on Proofs, book 1, chapter 6 and following.* Therefore, when it appears from the Acts that the Plaintiff's intention is not well-founded due to a lack of necessary proof, there is no need for the Reporter to laboriously examine the Defendant's defenses, unless he wishes to undertake this labor eventually and for greater caution. For it is an undisputed rule of law: that when proof is lacking, the one upon whom the **burden of proof** falls must lose the case; and the adversary shall prevail. Even if the Defendant has provided no evidence, if the Plaintiff fails to prove his case, the Defendant must be acquitted. *Law 4, Code on producing documents; law 2, same title on proofs; law 9, Code on exceptions; law 25, Digest on the Law of the Treasury.* Vivius, *decision 236.* Christinaeus, *volume 2, decision 88.* Agostino Barbosa in *Axioms of Law, under the word "Plaintiff."* For the right is measured not by the person of the Defendant, but by the person of the Plaintiff. *Law 1, section "he who [claims] the inheritance," Digest if a part of an inheritance is sought. (ddd)*

<insert>
(ddd) He who seeks an inheritance or a part of an inheritance is measured not by what the possessor has occupied, but by his own right: and even if he is the heir to the whole, he shall still claim the inheritance, even if you possess only one thing; or if he is heir to a part, he claims that part, even if you possess the whole inheritance.
</insert>

# On the Method of Reporting

<sig>Ttt tttt 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: marii</meta>

It is pleasing to add: That the best (1.) method of proof is if a **Confession** of the adversary can be obtained, <note>original: "l. unic. ubi Dd. C. de Confess." refers to a specific law in the Code of Justinian regarding confessions.</note> (eee) For if the defendant <term>reus; the party being sued or accused</term> confesses in Court, the entire dispute is removed; which as such can be nothing, unless it concerns a matter of controversy. And therefore we find it so established by law, that one who has confessed is considered as one judged, and is condemned by his own sentence, *Law 1, Law 3, Law 6 in the preamble, and elsewhere in the Digests, as well as the aforementioned single law of the Code on Confessions.* Thus, from that point on, the role of the **Judge** <note>the official who weighs evidence</note> ceases here, and the role of the **Magistrate** succeeds in compelling the defendant to satisfy the plaintiff, <note>original: "actori"</note> *as cited in the Digest on the same title and the Code on the execution of judged matters. Donellus, book 24, commentary 1, from the beginning; Trentacinquius, book 2, title on Confessions, Resolution 2; Mascardus, conclusion 344 and 348.* Furthermore, a judicial confession, once accepted by the opposing party, has ready execution <note>meaning it can be enforced immediately without further trial</note>, *Parladorius, Daily Matters, final chapter, part 1, section 4; Mynsinger, observation 51.* And a Confession also purges every defect of the process, *Mynsinger, observation 77; Antonio Merenda, Legal Controversies, chapter 10.* Such a Confession is elicited, moreover, chiefly by the interrogation of the party; which today is mostly done through **positional articles** <term>articles consisting of specific statements of fact that the opponent must admit or deny</term>: *Marantas, on Judicial Order, part 6, rubric on Positions, number 13.* To these, the opposing party is bound to respond by means of an oath (concerning which see above, *number 18*), and indeed categorically, (fff) using the words, **"believe it to be true, or believe it not to be true, without any preamble or addition,"** <note>original: "glaub wahr, oder glaub nicht wahr, ohn alle Vortwort und Anhang"</note> *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court, part 3, title 15, section "Secondly."* And although by common law, very many articles—being multiple, impertinent, (ggg) deceptive, or concerning Law—are not received; nevertheless, in the **Imperial Chamber** <note>the highest court of the Holy Roman Empire</note> all must be answered (with only the legal position excepted), *Gail, book 1, observation 82, number 11 and following.* This is done for the reason that a defendant might not always be able to raise an exception against the articles (even those most correctly written) and maliciously delay the lawsuit. However, a Judge, seeing that some Positions should not have been admitted, treats them as non-admitted and rejects even the depositions of **Witnesses** received upon them: especially if the party has protected themselves with the clause "saving the right of impertinence" <note>a legal reservation that allows a party to later argue that the evidence was irrelevant</note>. *Mynsinger, book 2, observation 56.* But indeed, an erroneous confession, even if sworn under oath, can be revoked (bbb); *Cevallos, question 652.* even if it has been reduced to writing and accepted by the ad-

*Besold, Volume I.*

<column-break/>

-versary. *Antonio Gabriel, title on Confessions, final conclusion.* But if the confession is made through a **Procurator** <term>a legal representative or agent</term>, it is permitted to retract it, even if the error is not demonstrated. *Francesco Vivius, decision 384.*

(eee) For where a confession is present, the role of the Judge or the ordinary process ceases, and the **executive process** <note>a faster, summary legal proceeding</note> succeeds. Thus, in many cases, an executive process is granted, such as in a "guaranteed instrument" <note>a legal document with a clause allowing immediate enforcement</note> fortified with executive clauses; likewise in cases of Mandates, concerning all of which one should consult *Petrus Friderus Mindanus on the Process to be extracted in the Chamber; likewise the Treasury of Executive Law by Rutger Ruland.* An executive process is also given in monitory mandates, even those fortified with the clause **"that he has the power to seize the pledge for himself, with or without legal proceedings."** <note>original: "daß er Macht habe das Pfand an sich zu ziehen, mit oder ohne Recht"</note> Finally, when something must be done which the Law commands, we can then use the executive process, or proceed by way of a Mandate.

(ff) To a multiple article—that is, one containing several facts or several circumstances—a distinct response must be given.

(ggg) *Impertinent matters are to be admitted in case of doubt, with the Clause: "Saving the right of impertinent matters."*

(bbb) *But error, because it is not presumed, must be proven.*

**XXV.** Next, **Proofs** are made through **Witnesses**. However, because very many exceptions are usually objected and opposed here—both to the Witnesses themselves, or to their production, reception, and examination, as well as to their testimonies, statements, or depositions; and this either to the effect of repelling them entirely, or at least of diminishing their credibility—a certain universal synopsis of these has been collected by *Speckhan, century 3, class 3, question 15; as also by Mr. Johann Jacob Speidel in his collection of legal questions, both in the first and second parts, under the word* **"Witnesses."** And because also all such exceptions, according to the modern use of the Courts, the parties reserve for themselves to be proposed and deduced by a solemn protestation only after the attestations have finally been published: *Speckhan, said class 3, question 17.* The **Reporter** <note>the Referens</note> must accurately weigh in judgment what and how much to believe of the Witnesses; and also which party's Witnesses ought to prevail? On this, see *Prospero Farinacci's treatise on Witnesses, as well as that of Rudolph Volcmar...*

# Dissertation

The *Practical Conclusions on Witnesses* by Marius will be of the greatest help to him. Witnesses who say contradictory things are to be brought into agreement whenever possible, <note>original: "c. cùm tu. 16. ex. de Testib." refers to a chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding witness reconciliation.</note> as noted by Cavallos. However, a single witness—as noted by Vivius—is not sufficient, nor are "singular" witnesses <note>witnesses who testify to different, isolated facts rather than the same event</note>. Those speaking from hearsay <note>original: "de auditu alieno," literally "from the hearing of another"</note> generally do not provide proof. Even less weight is given to those who have a personal interest or disadvantage in the case, unless they have renounced that interest. Furthermore, those marked by legal infamy <term>infamia; a status of dishonored legal standing due to crime or immoral profession</term> are excluded. Similarly, parents cannot be witnesses against their children, nor children against their parents—even if the opposing party consents. A husband is not a fit witness in his wife’s case, and vice versa.

Nevertheless, some less-than-ideal or "unfit" witnesses are admitted if the truth cannot be discovered in any other way (iii); provided that other witnesses could not have been present. In such cases, blood relatives, in-laws, and household members are accepted. Furthermore, unless witnesses are produced within the specific deadline set for evidence (kkk), they will no longer be heard. To provide proof, they must be examined after the opposing party has been summoned, unless a different custom is accepted. Indeed, if witnesses are examined while a party is absent due to unavoidable necessity, they prove nothing. They also provide no proof if they are examined together or in the presence of the parties. Moreover, witnesses are strictly compelled to take an oath unless the parties waive it; if they are not sworn, they prove nothing. Nor are they presumed to have sworn unless

<column-break/>

it appears in the legal Acts <note>the official court records</note>. Finally, although the "publication" of testimony <note>the formal process of opening and sharing written depositions with both legal teams</note> is not considered the essential substance of the trial process, its effect is that once published, the same or other witnesses cannot be produced again regarding the same or directly contradictory points (lll).

> (iii) As in accidental and sudden cases, etc., where other witnesses cannot be found or called upon so quickly.

> (kkk) Every deadline for providing proof is "peremptory" <note>final and absolute</note>, unless an extension is requested before the deadline passes.

> (lll) Because of the danger of bribery <note>original: "subornationis"</note> and because the questions to be asked are now known to the parties.

### XXVI.
Thirdly, **Public Instruments** (mmm) <note>official documents such as contracts or deeds</note> provide full "faith" <note>legal credibility</note>. They have such great power of proof that they do not require additional witnesses. Hence, such documents are called "proven proof" and are considered clear; they carry a presumption of truth, both in fact and by law.

> (nnn) Regarding the specific formalities by which public instruments are to be drafted, see the **Imperial Recess of Cologne** from the year 1512, concerning the duties of public Notaries; add also Parladorius, *Daily Matters*.

The authority of these kinds of public instruments—namely those drafted within the court records or by a public official, that is, a **Notary** (along with witnesses)—is such that as long as nothing is proven to the contrary, they are believed. For a document can be challenged by witnesses, whether they are the ones listed on the document itself or others; however, in such a case the judge must cautiously and diligently inspect the character of the Notary and the witnesses, and which of them proposes the most likely truth (ooo). Furthermore, letters are held to be public instruments...

# On the Method of Reporting.

...documents that are **sealed by princes, lords, the city, or even administrative officials.** <note>The author cites Nicolaus Everhardus the Younger and Rutger Ruland, prominent legal scholars of the 16th century.</note> Nor are sealed transcripts (ppp), also known as a **Vidimus** (qqq) <note>Latin: "We have seen"; a certified copy of a legal document.</note>, rejected: as noted by Gail and Mynsing. This is true provided they were created after those with an interest in the matter were summoned. The same weight is given to **Rolls, Land Registers: Interest, Tax, and Account Books**, as well as others that carry public testimony. Furthermore, **the debt-books of merchants and craftsmen** (rrr) provide proof in their own way: but only in matters pertaining to their specific trade or office. I will not add more here, as Jacob Bornitius has written on literary documents, and Nicolaus Janua (also known as de Passeribus) of Padua has published a copious treatise specifically on private writings; one may turn to them for further help. Finally, anyone who presents a document in court is seen to prejudice themselves if any part of it works against them: even if they protest that they are only producing it "for the useful parts," <note>original: "In passibus utilibus"</note>. Likewise, anyone who challenges a document can no longer use it to their own advantage.

<gloss>(mmm) Public instruments are those which are drawn up before a Notary and (by Civil Law) four, or (by the Law of Nations) two witnesses; these witnesses must also sign their names.</gloss>
<gloss>(nnn) A public instrument carries three presumptions: namely, that it was performed solemnly, that it is true, and that it was created by the consent of the parties. Nevertheless, proof is still admitted against an instrument through indirect means—for example, by showing that it is not public, but a forgery or a sham, etc.</gloss>
<gloss>(ooo) That is, whether one should believe the witnesses named in the document or outside witnesses.</gloss>
<gloss>(ppp) Because they are transcribed from the original.</gloss>

<gloss>called a *Vidimus* because they were seen by a public official and compared with the original.</gloss>

Furthermore, if such a book is torn, falsified, or deceptive, it is no longer valid.</gloss>

### XXVII.
There is also (4) a certain species of proof: Ocular Inspection, **the site visit** (sss): <note>original German: "der Augenschein," literally "the eye-shine" or physical view.</note> to which legal practitioners are so accustomed to defer that they say no proof is more certain or better. Although it cannot be denied that such proof is extremely necessary in certain cases, it is always the Judge's role to decide whether the case requires an ocular inspection or not. Therefore, a Commissioner appointed to examine witnesses cannot undertake an ocular inspection without a mandate from the Judge. The Judge, then, can decree it either at the request of both litigating parties, or one of them, or by his own office and initiative. It can be requested at any time; even after the conclusion of the case or after the deadline for evidence has passed. However, both parties must be summoned to this inspection: (ttt) since for any act that might be prejudicial, everyone who has an interest must be summoned.

<gloss>(sss) Sometimes witnesses are produced at the site of the dispute; **they are led to the "eye-view" (site visit), so that they may know better how to testify about the matter.**</gloss>
<gloss>(ttt) For the party themselves demonstrates what should be noted in their favor during the ocular inspection.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the weight of evidence in legal proceedings. Having established what constitutes full proof (like multiple witnesses or public documents), the author now addresses "half-proof" and how a judge resolves cases where the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive. It then transitions to the defendant's side of the case: the use of "exceptions" or legal defenses to block a claim.</meta>

### XXVIII.

Finally, proof is sometimes only **"half-full"** (*semiplena*); through which, specifically, the Judge gains some belief in what happened, but not so much that he is legally bound to follow it when pronouncing a sentence. In this case, the Judge may grant the party a **supplementary oath** <note>original: "suppletorium juramentum"; an oath used to "top up" incomplete evidence so a judge can reach a verdict.</note>. <note>References to Fachinaeus, Mynsinger, Hartmann, and Hiltrand follow.</note> Such proof is considered to be made by: a single witness who is beyond all reproach <note>original: "omni exceptione major"</note>; a private document supported by a comparison of handwriting; or a confession made while the other party was absent. <note>References to the Code of Justinian and legal scholars Mascardus and Gabriel follow.</note> However, if the proof is not perfectly "half-full," or if the nature of the case and the status of the person do not allow for a supplementary oath, then an **oath of purgation** <note>original: "purgationis jusjurandum"; a "clearing" oath where a defendant swears their innocence to overcome weak evidence against them.</note> is enjoined upon the defendant.

### XXIX.

If, however, the requirements of the initiated action have been proved by the plaintiff (and thus his claim/intention is founded), the Reporter <note>The "Referens" or official summarizing the case for the court.</note> must inquire in the fifth place whether these claims have been shattered by the defendant's defense and **exception**, or not? This is gathered from the **"shattering articles"** (*uuu*) or defensive points of the Defendant, with which he strives to weaken the Plaintiff’s weapons as if with a shield. It is so important to know this that even if the Plaintiff has provided proof, if the Defendant’s exceptions are fit and relevant, the Defendant must nevertheless be acquitted by their help. In this regard, it is commonly said that an **Exception** is the exclusion of an action that otherwise stands by right. <note>original: "Exceptionem esse, Actionis jure subsistentis, exclusionem"</note>. Along the same lines, the jurist Paulus responds in the law that it makes no difference whether someone has no action by the law itself, or whether that action is weakened by an exception. First and foremost,

<column-break/>

one must know here that an exception of **Intention** is one thing, and an exception of **Action** is another. <note>original: "aliud esse exceptionem Intentionis, aliud Actionis"</note>. On this matter, Oldendorpius <note>Johann Oldendorp (c. 1487–1567), a hugely influential German jurist.</note> notably writes in his handbook on exceptions. Regarding the material cause, commentators set out the division as follows: some exceptions concern the intention (the facts), while others concern the action (the law). They call it an exception of the **Action** or of **Law** when the plaintiff technically has a legal right to sue based on his filed complaint, but the fairness (*aequitas*) of the exception undermines it. On the other hand, they call it an exception of **Intention** when the plaintiff has absolutely no right of pursuit at all, moving the lawsuit only on the basis of facts; in that case, the exception—finding no legal action or right—excludes only the factual intention.

Furthermore, one must not be ignorant of what it means for an obligation intended by the plaintiff to be removed **by the law itself** (*ipso jure*), or for a defendant to be freed by the law itself. Likewise, what does it mean for an action to vanish or be shattered **by the help of an exception** (*ope exceptionis*)? When a defendant who has been sued owes nothing "by the law itself," the effect is that even if no exception is raised, the Judge, understanding by his office that the defendant is legally free, must reject the plaintiff and acquit the defendant. <note>Reference to the famous medieval jurist Bartolus follows.</note> However, an action is shattered "by the help of an exception" when the Defendant, if he did not raise his defense, would be condemned by the strict letter of the law—and he could not even sue to get his money back once paid—even though it is not fair for him to be condemned. <note>This distinction highlights the difference between a case being legally void from the start versus a case being valid but unfair due to specific circumstances like a private agreement not to sue.</note> Exceptions that demonstrate that the plaintiff’s action is finished "by the law itself" preclude the start of the lawsuit (*www*). Furthermore, exceptions of intention sometimes have a general effect, deferring or destroying the entire claim; others, however, only undermine a part—that is, they shatter one or two points or positions of the plaintiff while the others remain.

# On the Method of Reporting.

...has indicated (and to this also are directed those things which *Rutger Ruland in the treatise on Interrogatories* has collected). And from this, such articles of exception, presented by the summoned Defendant, are commonly called **Elisive** <note>original: "Elisivos"; from the Latin "elidere," meaning to shatter or strike out. These are defenses intended to completely "shatter" the plaintiff's legal claim.</note>. However, that exception which is called "of intent" (xxx) is usually handled conveniently in the fourth question: specifically, when it is debated whether the Plaintiff's intent <note>In this context, "intent" (intentio) refers to the formal legal claim or the basis of the lawsuit.</note> has been proven. Furthermore, as was stated above in *number 22*, the Plaintiff's bare assertions are not to be trusted, but must be proven; that rule must also be understood to apply to the defendant's exceptions. For although in many articles of law the *Defendant* is in a more favorable position (as noted in *law: "favorabiliores" 125* and there by *Decius in the Digest on the Rules of Law*), nevertheless regarding the act of proof, *Plaintiffs* and *Defendants* are equal. For just as the *Plaintiff* is bound to prove his intent, so also the *Defendant* is bound to prove the exception which he opposes (*law: "in exceptionibus" 19, in the preface, Digest on Probations; Ayrer in Process, part 1, chapter 6, observation 1*). Whence it is also said that the *Defendant* becomes a plaintiff by raising an exception (*law 1, Digest on exceptions*). And therefore, the proposed exception must be proven in its own form and specific type (*Cravetta, counsel 249*).

---

(uuu) <margin>*Defensive Articles* pertain properly to the exception of intent; *Elisive Articles* pertain to the exception of the action.</margin>

(vvvvv) <margin>That is, they are privileged, and we oppose them before the contestation of the suit <note>original: "ante litem contestatam"; the formal stage where the parties join issue.</note>.</margin>

(xxx) <margin>For it is the same thing to ask whether the action and its requirements are proven, or whether the "exception of intent" has force. For example: *Titius* asks me for a hundred florins given to me as a loan. I deny that I received them; this is an "exception of intent." This should be dealt with when asking if the requirements of the action are proven, and there is no need for a separate discussion or chapter in the report. But if I admit that I once received a hundred, but have paid them back, that is an "exception of the action," and it must be handled individually by the *Reporter*.</margin>

---

### XXX. Likewise, it may further happen that an unjust Exception is shattered by a **Replication** <note>original: "Replicationem"; the plaintiff's reply to the defendant's defense.</note> from the Plaintiff (*in the preface of the Institutes on Replications*). It is considered to be named from this: that it seems to "unfold" or open up the fairness of the action (which was touched upon and entangled by the *Defendant* making the exception) and to lay bare the injustice of the exception (*law 1, section 1, Digest on exceptions; Hotman in the preface of the Institutes on replications, statement 2*). Thus, just as the exception

<column-break/>

excludes the action; the *replication* excludes the defendant's exception (*cited location 1, section "illud" 2*). For example, when someone has made an agreement with his debtor not to seek money from him, but afterward they agree to the contrary—that is, that it is permitted for the creditor to seek it (*in the preface of the said title, Institutes on Replications*). Again, it sometimes happens that a *Replication*, which at first glance is just, may work an injustice; then there is need for another allegation for the sake of helping the *Defendant*, which is called a **Duplication**. So too a **Triplication** sometimes weakens a Duplication, and a **Quadruplication** weakens that, and so on (*section "rursus" 1, Institutes, said title*). But commonly, the *Produced Acts of the Parties* are called *Replies*, *Duplies*, *Triplies*, etc., even if they do not contain the shattering of Exceptions or Replications properly so-called, but only a refutation of the adversary persisting in law or in fact. Nevertheless, in the **Imperial Chamber Court** <note>original: "Camera Imperialis"; the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, as well as in other properly ordered courts, it has been wholesomely established that such writings should not be multiplied; nor should the progress of debates be extended beyond a "duplication" (inclusive) in delaying matters, or up to a "triplication" (also inclusive) in decisive exceptions (*Ordinance of the Chamber Court, part 3, title 20, section "Wo aber"; Schneidewin on the title of the Institutes on Replications, number 3*). This, however, is not to be understood as if the Judge could not admit allegations either below or above the predicted number, whether at the petition of the parties or by his own office, according to the quality of the case (*Ordinance of the Chamber Court, said part 3, title 38*). Regarding this examination of exceptions and replications, a judgment free from all bias is required in the *Reporter*; by which he may compare and weigh against each other the arguments, proofs, refutations, and legal allegations or disputes of the *plaintiff* and *Defendant*: so that finally it becomes clear which of them relies on better and firmer reasons and proofs? (*Symphorema of legal allegations, methodical treatise, number 5*).

### XXXI. After a full and diligent examination of all the aforesaid, finally the *Reporter* should say what is to be pronounced in the case, and how the form of the sentence should be drafted. And indeed, if a controversy exists in law, the *Judge* or *Reporter* ought to observe that he should not judge otherwise,

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the duties of the court reporter (Referens) and the judge, moving from the weighing of evidence to the final act of rendering a judgment. It emphasizes the balance between written law and judicial discretion.</meta>

...[the reporter] shall speak, as much by the statutes of the place and the customs, as—in their absence—by the Laws and Constitutions; and if these do not suggest a certain decision, by the accepted opinions of the learned Doctors <note>original: "Doctorum sententiis"; referring to the consensus of legal scholars which held legal weight in this period</note>. This is found in the *Institutes on the Office of the Judge, the Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance part 1, title 13, and title 58; Gail, book 1, observation 36, number 14; and Master Heinrich Nebelkra, Forensic Decisions, book 1, decision 1.* 

And it is relevant here what Saint Ambrose once warned the Judge, which is also cited in the *Canon Law (Causa 3, Question 7)*: "A good Judge," he says, "does nothing by his own whim or according to the purpose of his personal will; (yyy) but he pronounces according to the Laws and Rights, he obeys the Statutes of the Law, and does not indulge his own desires. He brings nothing from home that is already prepared or meditated upon; but as he hears, so he judges, and as the nature of the business reveals itself, so he decides. He complies with the laws, he does not oppose them; he examines the merits of the case, he does not change them." 

And although a Judge ought to follow equity <term>equity: (æquitas) a principle of fairness used to mitigate the harshness of strict legal rules</term> more than strict law in judging, and ought to provide relief where evident equity demands it (*Digest on the Rules of Law; Code on Judges; Master Harprecht on the Office of the Judge*), nevertheless, very few things are to be committed to the Judge’s own discretion (zzz), as Menochius reports from Plato and Aristotle. 

However, because written laws do not exist for every single thing, nor could the legislators foresee all possibilities (*Digest on Laws*), therefore those matters for which the law defines nothing certain must necessarily be left to the discretion of the Judge. If, therefore, there is ambiguity regarding a fact, the reporter will follow and report what seems more credible to him—especially since the question of fact is placed within the power of the one judging (*Digest on Municipal Law; Menochius, cited above*). 

Since, however, the interpretation of facts often deceives even the wisest (*Digest on Ignorance of Law and Fact*), he shall therefore form his judgment and confirm the movement of his mind from the testimonies and arguments which he finds to be closest and most suited to the matter at hand (*Digest on Witnesses*). Truly, a certain method or rule cannot be given for every doubt or reason for decision that occurs in individual cases; rather, all these things must be committed and left to the prudence and diligence of each Reporter. Let it suffice for us to have noted for now those things which are commonly to be observed within a report; but if anyone desires more, let him look especially to the complete treatise on this subject of ours by a certain man, distinguished in judgment and erudition, which we hope and urge will soon be made public law.

<column-break/>

(yyy) That is, when a judge brings something "from home"—suppose a certain prejudiced affection or an opinion—before he has sufficiently heard the parties.

(zzz) Because of the diversity of individual judgments <note>meaning that individual opinions vary too much to be reliable without the law.</note>.

### XXXII.
Finally, the Reporter must take care to bring forth a sentence that is certain and clear (*Institutes on Actions, section 32*) and conforming to the Lawsuit: that is, it must not be passed concerning anything other than that which was petitioned (aaaa) (*Vivius, decision 1; Tenninus, caution 246*). Furthermore, it should contain either a condemnation or an acquittal (*Digest on Exceptions*). However, one is not strictly bound to insert the exact words "acquittal" or "condemnation," but an equivalent term is sufficient (*Valdus on Nullity from Defect of Process*). 

Also, the party must be cited to hear the sentence, unless they have a procurator <note>a legal representative or attorney</note> present in the court records (*Gail, book 1, observation 109*). The sentence must be passed against the same person; namely, if the trial was conducted through the procurator himself (*Cavallos, question 458; Gail, book 1, observation 111*). While a sentence is valid if pronounced in the presence of the Procurator, even if the principal party has died, the Judge—if he knows that a party has died—is usually accustomed to decreeing a citation against the heirs to resume the case (*Gail, cited above; Mynsing, observation 85; Don Garfias Mastrellus, decision 136*).

(aaaa) Unless necessity persuades otherwise, or unless it is a summary case <note>a simplified, faster legal proceeding.</note>.

If these have not been petitioned, the Judge is by no means bound to award them by virtue of his office, although he may do so (*Laurentius Tenninus, caution 29*). Likewise, those expenses, once the litigation is finished and ended...

# On the Method of Reporting.

<margin>(bbbb) Expenses must be proven through vouchers <note>original German: "durch Zettel und Urkund"</note>, and once the expenses are so proven, only then does the Judge estimate and tax them—that is, he judges whether they were necessary, etc. *Besold, Volume 1.*</margin>

...no further [expenses] can be sought, according to Law 3, where the Doctors <note>Legal scholars or professors of law</note> comment on the *Code concerning fruits and expenses*. See, however, *Berlich, decision 127*. A person is condemned to pay expenses because they either delayed the proceedings (wherefore the Doctors are accustomed to calling these "Expenses for Delaying the Process," *Petrus de Ferrariis in the form of a Libel in a real action, on the word "and expenses," gloss 25, number 3*. These are regularly to be paid immediately; however, if the Judge had omitted the condemnation for them, he can supply it up until the definitive sentence. *Chapter 'si em litibus', 5. 'on fraud and contempt'; Mynsinger, 1st observation 23 & 45; Lanfranc in the Golden Practice, title 1 'on expenses,' number 16 and following.*) or because the adversary obtained victory in the case, according to Law *Properandum*, 13. §. "if however" 6. *Code on Judgments*. (Practitioners call these the "Expenses of Victory"). *Ferrariis & Lanfranc in the cited places.* The defeated party is held liable, and they must restore the litigation costs which the victor spent on the case before the joinder of issue <term>joinder of issue: (litis contestatio) the formal stage in a trial where the parties' positions are set and the contest officially begins</term>, *Afinius in Judicial Practice, § 32, chapter 2, expansion 53*. That general axiom is limited, however, when the defeated party is deemed to have had a "just cause" for litigating, *Vivius, 1st decision 47; Martin Uranius, volume 1, consultation 19; Gail, 1st observation 152, number 3*. Yet, a contemptuous party <term>contemptuous: (contumax) someone who willfully disobeyed or ignored the court's authority</term> is always condemned to pay expenses, even if they win. *Mynsinger, 4th observation 67.* Furthermore, the Judge ought to tax and moderate the expenses with a fair estimation: *Berlich, 1st conclusion 78.* (bbbb) and once so taxed, the victor is ordered by an interlocutory decree <term>interlocutory: an intermediate ruling made before the final decision of the case</term> to prove them by oath: "that he has spent and suffered no less and no more than this in court costs," <note>original German: "daß er darüber, und nicht darunter, an Gerichts-Kosten ausgegeben und erlitten hab"</note> *Gail, 1st observation 152, numbers 11 & 12, and book 2, observation 102, number 21*. Next, if the Reporter believes the defeated party ought to restore the expenses, he must also condemn them to pay future expenses to be made in the same case and resulting from the same litigation, *Afinius in Judicial Practice, § 32, chapter 2*. Conversely, when he thinks the costs of the litigation should be "compensated" <note>meaning each side pays their own costs</note>, it is necessary that he express the "just cause of compensation" in the sentence, for example, in this or another way: "The court costs are therefore compensated and balanced against each other for moving reasons," <note>original German: "Die Gerichts-Kosten deßhalben, aufgeloffen, aus bewegenden Ursachen gegen einander compensirend, und vergleichend"</note> *Gail, 1st observation 251, number 23*.

If, however, the requested expenses were neither adjudicated nor compensated, the Judge himself is held liable to pay them from his own pocket; because he is deemed to have "made the case his own." <term>made the case his own: (litem suam facere) a legal doctrine where a judge becomes personally liable for damages or costs due to a failure to follow proper procedure</term>

### ON THE METHOD OF REPORTING IN THE SECOND INSTANCE, OR the Judgment of Appeal.

I. IN cases of Appeals, or the "Second Instance," the facts and the status of the case are likewise to be deduced from the libel <term>libel: the formal written statement of the plaintiff's case</term> and the Acts of the first instance; and what was judged in the first instance must be touched upon. Then the Reporter ought to consider and weigh the point of Legitimation <term>legitimation: the legal standing or right of a party to bring the appeal</term>, and the rest of the process, as has already been said above regarding cases of simple complaint or the first instance. However, let him pass over incidental points—those annexed, connected, or dependent in the process—in silence, so that he does not "redo what is done" <note>original Latin: "ne actum agat," a phrase meaning to waste time repeating things already settled</note> and become tedious with loquaciousness; let him only mention that those points have already been decided long ago. He should take care, however, lest his own sentence now to be rendered be hindered by some prejudice of a previously issued interlocutory decree, or be noted for contradiction. *Symphoremata of Supplications, Part 1, in the treatise on the method of Chamber Process, at the end.*

II. Next, the care of the Reporter consists in the examination of both the Formal and the Material aspects of the case. Thus, he will first consider: Is the jurisdiction of the higher judge established? That is, was the appeal made properly? And have the "fatals" <term>fatals: (fatalia) strict legal deadlines which, if missed, result in the loss of a right or the dismissal of a case</term> for interposing the appeal been observed by the appealing party? *Bocer, in the often cited disputation 3, thesis 38.* Whether the appeal was made properly, and whether the jurisdiction of the immediately superior Appeals Judge is established, will be clear from the instrument of Appeal or the acts of the first instance. *Symphoremata, in the cited place.* Indeed, if a defect appears here, it is customary to pronounce: "That the matter has therefore not matured, and for that reason is not to be accepted, and also that [Person N.] is obligated to reimburse [Person T.] for the expenses incurred therein," etc. <note>original German: "Daß die Sach dahero nicht erwachsen, deßwegen nicht anzunehmen, auch der N. dem T. deßhalb aufgeloffenen Unkosten zu erstatten schuldig, etc."</note> The Judge is bound to pronounce upon the desertion <note>failure to prosecute</note> of an Appeal, even if nothing was objected regarding it by the Appellee. *Mynsinger, 3rd observation 22, at the beginning; Mr. President on Appeals, 10, number 1.* An appeal is deemed properly interposed if it was made within ten days; which begin to run from the moment the sentence was rendered, and in the moment of the same ho...

...are finished. <note>original Latin: "Novell. 23. cap. 1. auth. hodiè. C. de Appell." refers to Justinian’s New Constitutions and the Code regarding appeals.</note> This time period is counted as "useful" <term>useful time: (tempus utile) a legal term for a period where only days on which legal business can actually be conducted are counted</term> from the beginning (and thus, if no proxy is present at the proceedings, it runs only from the day of knowledge); however, as time progresses, it becomes continuous. <note>original: "c. concertationi. 8. ibi: postquam fervevit."</note> This is discussed extensively by John Melchior Cletzelius in his treatise on appeals, and by Scaccia. There is also a "fatal" deadline <term>fatal deadline: (fatale) a strict legal time limit that, once passed, extinguishes a right</term> of thirty days regarding the filing of an appeal: within this time, if the appellant has not requested the records and the *Apostoli* <term>Apostoli: brief letters or notices issued by a lower judge to a higher judge, acknowledging that an appeal has been filed</term>, or if they requested them but did not receive them within the assigned days, they are considered to have waived their appeal. This is noted by the Honorable Presiding Judge in his treatise on appeals, chapter 8, number 7. The deadline for introducing or starting the prosecution of an appeal is set either by a person <note>e.g., a judge's specific order</note> or by the Law. Thus, in the Imperial Chamber Court, six months are prescribed for the notification "or the filing of the appeal" <note>original German: "oder der Einbringung der Appellation"</note> according to the Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 30. Under Canon Law, the space for prosecuting an appeal is one year; and for a necessary and evident cause, it may be two years. Within this time, if the appellant does not prosecute the appeal, the sentence remains valid. However, the time limits for finishing an appeal are currently observed neither in the Chamber Court nor elsewhere.

<margin>(a) And in such a case, the parties are usually joined so that they may proceed anew in the main cause; sometimes the appellant is also left in silence regarding those matters.</margin>

III. Regarding the **Formalities** of Appeals, when nothing is lacking, the Reporter <term>Reporter: (Referens) a judge or official tasked with summarizing the facts and legal issues of a case for the full court</term> weighs the material evidence, looking into the nature and quality of the business brought into Judgment. Now, a case is brought into an Appeals Court either primarily as a "Complaint of Nullity" <term>Nullity: (Nullitas) a claim that a judgment is legally void due to a fundamental procedural error</term>, or the "Injustice" of the decision is added together with the Nullity. This is usually done when there is no complaint about the fairness of the outcome, but the appellant intends only to show that the sentence is void and ought to be rescinded. And when this cause of nullity is primarily intended, the main business itself is transferred to the same Judge, so that they may examine the merits brought in the first instance and

<column-break/>

either confirm or reform the sentence based on the same or new records and proofs. However, if some defect appears not only in the sentence but in the process of the First Instance <term>First Instance: the initial trial court where a case is first heard</term> (for instance, if everything is so confused that the legal petition is unfit, or the records are so mangled and imperfect that the Judge cannot inform his mind by them), then the prior sentence is not only reformed, but it is also usually pronounced: "that the judgment was null, and the appeal was superfluous," <note>original German: "daß nichtiglich geurtheilt, und überflüssig appellirt"</note> (a) "also where the parties do not intend to release each other from further claims and demands, that they are obliged to do so in a proper manner and in the appropriate places," <note>original German: "auch wo die Partheyen einander ferner Sprüch und Forderungen zu entlassen nicht gemeint, daß sie solches gebührender massen, und an gehörigen Orten... zu thun schuldig seyn."</note> or even before the very Judge to whom the appeal was made. Sebastian Vantius and Vincentius Carocius describe the causes for which both a sentence and the process itself can be argued as null. Finally, one may propose Nullity even if the Appeal has been abandoned.

IV. In the **combination of Nullity and Injustice** (namely, when the appellant intends "that by the judge of the previous instance in the spoken judgment, if not nullly, yet poorly judged") <note>original German: "daß vom Richter voriger Instanz mit gesprochenem Urtheil, wo nicht nichtiglich, jedoch übel geurtheilt"</note> by the usage of the Chamber, the Reporter’s vote is distributed into two parts: considering (1) the nullity of the first instance and (2) the injustice. However, the court should not easily reject a sentence because of nullity, but should pronounce on the merits of the case in the main appeal if they are clear.

V. Once nullity is excused and it is recognized that the jurisdiction of the appealed Judge is established, the merits of the main case must be judged, and it must be seen whether the prior Judge ruled well or poorly. Here it is the duty of the Reporter to diligently search out what has been newly alleged and proven by the parties in the second instance, beyond those things which were brought in the first instance. Likewise, whether the new causes are so relevant...

# On the Manner of Reporting.

VI. Furthermore, this examination cannot be carried out more conveniently than if the procedure here follows the requirements of the intended action (just as I described in cases of simple complaint). The grievances and proofs of the appealing party, and then the defenses and exceptions of the party being appealed, should be weighed on the faithful scales of Justice. From these elements, it will naturally become clear how the controversy between the parties—revived once more through the Appeal—ought to be defined. It should be noted, however, that the sentence of the original Judge is sometimes only "reformed" <term>reformed: a partial modification of a verdict rather than a total reversal</term>: specifically, when it is not overturned or upheld in every single point. Likewise, a sentence can be confirmed in part by the higher Judge and declared null in another part, according to Vivius, Decision 53.

VII. Finally, in the sentencing of an appeal, the matter of expenses must also be considered. Indeed, if the party being appealed loses, the expenses are to be balanced or shared. If, however, they win and the appellant is defeated, all just expenses must be awarded to the victor without distinction, as supported by Maranta, Gail, and Mynsing. Truly, one who obstructs or defers an appeal will not be able to excuse themselves from the payment and reimbursement of expenses, based on the laws concerning appeals and the treatise by Scaccia.

### ON THE REPORT TO BE MADE IN A
->criminal case.<-

I. Although it may not seem so simple in Civil Law to distinguish what constitutes a Public Judgment versus a private one, or what is "ordinary" versus "extraordinary," those distinctions have now largely fallen out of common use. Today, a case is considered to be handled "criminally" when someone seeks not their own personal advantage or private vengeance, but rather public retribution—namely, a punishment to be paid to the Public Treasury <term>Public Treasury: (Fiscus) the state’s financial department, which received fines from criminal cases</term> or a physical penalty to be inflicted upon the body. This is supported by Soarez, Rosbach, and the Honorable Presiding Judge. To this, Matthew Stephen adds in his commentary that there are now almost no "public accusations" <note>Public accusations refers to the ancient Roman system where any citizen could bring a charge; by this period, the state took over that role.</note>

<column-break/>

in the old sense. Instead, in most criminal cases, the procedure follows the method of Inquiry <term>Inquiry: (Inquisitio) a legal process where the judge or state actively investigates the crime rather than just acting as an umpire between two private parties</term>; and the Public Treasury alone, or its procurator, takes on the role of the accuser. This is established in the **Electoral Bavarian Criminal Ordinance** <note>original: "Churfürstl. Bayrische Malefiz-Ordn."</note> and by legal scholars like Clarus and Christinæus. This Inquiry is two-fold: one intended to "discover" the crime (which they call "informative") and another tending toward "punishing" the crime. Since this latter type heavily burdens the reputation of the person under investigation, it should only be initiated if the crime and its perpetrator are clearly established through formal reporting and sufficient information. Furthermore, as a rule, the "body of the crime" <term>body of the crime: (corpus delicti) the physical evidence that a crime has actually been committed, such as a corpse in a murder case</term> must be established beforehand.

<margin>
(a) (That is, it must be shown that a person was killed, a theft was committed, or a similar crime occurred.) For if this is unknown, or if it is not clearly established, the accused cannot be condemned, nor can an Inquiry tending toward punishment even be started—even if the alleged delinquent confesses to having committed the crime. <note>This highlights a key protection: a confession alone was not enough to convict someone if there was no proof a crime had actually happened.</note>
</margin>

<gloss>(a) This applies if the crime is "permanent" (leaving lasting evidence), not "transient." For example: theft and homicide are permanent, whereas adultery is considered transient.</gloss>

II. In this matter, the Reporter should proceed just as was described for the Civil process: specifically, he should narrate the Facts and observe whether the substantial elements of the criminal process—received either by law or custom—have been followed. He should also examine the intent of the Accuser and the defenses of the Accused, evaluate the evidence of both, and indicate whether or what kind of punishment may be appropriate, and so on.

III. But because in Criminal Proceedings quite a few unique rules have been introduced which are not admitted in Civil cases, I would like to briefly review some of them. For instance, the summons here is usually "real": that is, the accused is thrust into prison or bound by arrest. To justify such imprisonment, even "lighter" evidence or signs <note>original: "indicia leviora"</note>...

(b) There are three degrees of evidence: (1) some are sufficient for arrest, and these are "light" because of the danger of flight; (2) for torture, "heavy" evidence is required; (3) finally, for condemnation, the proofs must be, as they say, "clearer than the midday sun." <term>clearer than the midday sun: a legal standard requiring evidence to be beyond any reasonable doubt before a final sentence.</term>

IV. Regarding contempt through absence, <term>contempt: the legal term for failing to appear in court when summoned.</term> the law does not proceed against an absent person; rather, it is customary for their goods to be recorded. *Digest, book 48, title 19, law 5; Matthias Stephani and Bernhard Zieritz in their Notes on the Criminal Ordinance of Charles V, article 206.* However, by the custom of certain places, it has become established that the accused is summoned three times at intervals of 14 days: (c) after which, if they do not appear and do not offer excuses for their absence, they are held as convicted and are publicly outlawed, such that they can be killed with impunity. Elsewhere, the execution is even customarily carried out in effigy. *Wesembeck in his Summary on Accusations, number 13; Anton Bullaeus on the Criminal Ordinance, article 155; Rosbach in Criminal Process, title 1, chapter 6.* Attorneys (d) are also not admitted in criminal proceedings, neither on behalf of the defendant nor the accuser. *Master Fachinaeus, book 1, chapter 24; Böckel in Visions on Public Justice, inquiry 3, section 16; The Presiding Lord in the Selection from Book 3 of the Digest, question 20.* Nevertheless, a defender is admitted to propose the causes for the absence. *Rosbach in the cited treatise, title 1, chapter 2, number 21 and following, as well as chapter 3; Matthias Stephani on the Criminal Ordinance, article 88.*

(c) This is commonly called a "hue and cry" <note>original: "Zettergeschrey"</note>. If the accused then fails to appear, they are declared to be under "outlawry for murder" <note>original: "Mordacht"</note>.

(d) But a Magistrate having criminal jurisdiction can accuse through an attorney, whom they commonly call the *Fiscus* or *Fiscal* <note>original: "Fiscal," a state prosecutor</note>. A private accuser in criminal matters cannot appoint an attorney because they are required to register themselves and thus bind themselves to the "parity of the crime" <term>parity of the crime: the rule that if a private accuser fails to prove their case, they must suffer the punishment the accused would have faced.</term>. An attorney cannot be bound to this.

V. In a criminal indictment, the place and time must be expressed in all cases: (e) *Digest, book 48, title 2, law 3 at the beginning; Mynsinger, observation 2, number 40; Köppen, observation 2, number 120; Metzger, counsel 15, number 65; Hartm. Pistor, observation 59; Clarus, Criminal Practice, question 12, number 7 and following; Grivellus, Decisions of the Senate of Dôle, 43; Bocer on Adultery, chapter 3, number 98, etc.* But indeed, the mere narration of the fact is sufficient; neither a formal conclusion nor the designation of a specific penalty is necessary, (f) *Digest, title on the Turpillian Decree, law 1, section 1; Rosbach, title 1, chapter 7.*

<column-break/>

number 9, etc. And so the Reporter <term>Reporter: the official summarizing the case for the court.</term> must choose the type of address and the penalty to be applied, primarily based on the quality of the narrated facts.

(e) Especially if the defendant seeks this to prepare their defense and does not do so maliciously; in this way, contrary laws can be reconciled. (f) Because the penalty follows by operation of law itself.

VI. Regarding proofs, many unique rules are also observed in this process: they must be, above all, clearer than the midday sun; *Code, title on proofs, final law.* So much so, that a woman is regularly not admitted as a witness. *Canon Law, chapter "Forus" 10, section "Testes," extra. V. S. Clarus, 5th Sentence, final section, question 24.* And to obtain the confession of the accused, torture is also sometimes used. But only when the accused is burdened by heavy and close indicators—which are called "red-handed and sufficient indicators" <note>original: "Redlich, und genugsante Anzeigen"</note> in the *Criminal Ordinance, article 18, etc.*—*Digest, book 48, title 18, laws 1 and 8; Imperial Criminal Ordinance, article 20.* On these matters, one should consult Farinacius, Zangerus, Bodinus, and others who treat torture professionally. However, it seems worthwhile to advise here that new and cruel types of instruments of torture are not to be employed. Thus, the Court of Paris refused to use a certain monstrous type of torture, even on the person of the assassin of **Henry IV**, King of France, which some Italian or other was suggesting. *André Favyn in the History of Navarre, book 19, folio 1293.* Furthermore, the confessions of the accused are not held as certain unless they persist in them; that is, they must ratify them after some interval for the "confirmation of the law" <note>original: "Elogium Juris"</note>, as they call it. *Clarus, question 64, number 4; Rosbach, title 1, chapter 18, number 6, etc.* In a criminal case, moreover, it is never considered so closed that something new cannot be produced. *Metzger, Criminal Counsel 9, folio 136, at the verse "For not indeed."* And finally, officials who accuse out of the necessity of their office, even if the defendant is acquitted, are not condemned to pay expenses and damages, unless their malice is established. *Clarus, final section, question 7 at the end; Francesco Merlinus, decision 99, number 12, etc.; Farinacius, question 135 and following; Mynsinger, observation 5, number 69; Bocer on Adultery, chapter 3, number 151, etc.; Voltz in Counsel 2, which is joined to his treatise on Inquisitions, number 165, etc.* But regarding these matters, we shall at some point, with God’s favor and permission, establish a separate treatise.

(g) If the defendant denies a confession once made, that is a new indicator for repeating the torture, but that repetition only takes place twice.

# DISSERTATION
## ON REGALIA,
### THESIS I.

It seems worthwhile to conduct an inquiry into Regalia <note>original: "Regalibus"; refers to the rights and privileges belonging specifically to a sovereign.</note> somewhat more thoroughly than is usually done by political writers, and to gather the relevant points from the fields of law and modern practice. This effort is justified because, in the discussion of the State, almost no doctrine is found to be more fertile or useful than this one.

II. Since in every discipline, care should be taken for the matter itself rather than the words, the terminology of *Regalia* must be investigated first of all. Everyone agrees that they are so named after the King <note>original: "à Rege."</note>, as noted by Rosenthal, Sixtinus, and Bocer. This is because these rights are proper and reserved to the Emperor; and in Canon, Civil, and Feudal Law, the Emperor is frequently designated by the name of "King," as seen in the Code of Justinian and the Books of Feuds. In this same way, the Law passed regarding the Emperor's power and command was called the *Royal Law* <note>original: "Lex Regia."</note>. Strictly speaking, while the words "Regal" or "Regalia" are considered adjectives in other Latin contexts—just as Cicero speaks of "Regal

<column-break/>

power," a "Regal name," the "Regal adornment of the State," or "Regal purple"—he also says that to be wise and to prophesy *is* "Regal." Furthermore, one finds "Regal sense" and the "Regal summit" in the Code of Justinian. Similarly, according to Festus, certain animal entrails are called "Regalia" when they promise unexpected honor to the powerful, inheritances to private and humble citizens, or dominion to a son still under his father's authority. However, in this specific legal context, the word deviates from its usual form and takes on the nature of a noun <note>original: "substantivi inducit naturam."</note>, primarily through the authority of Feudal and Canon Law. Indeed, Civil Law <note>The "Jus Civile" or Roman Law of Justinian.</note> never recognizes the word "Regalia" as a noun.

III. Since these rights (commonly called Regalia) are found in every perfect State—whether it be a Monarchy, an Aristocracy, or a Democracy—and since they are as broad as the concept of Majesty itself (which belongs to every State), they are very aptly called "Rights of Majesty" by Cicero, and "Rights of Supreme Command" or the "Sum of All Things" by Livy. Baldus calls them the "Sacred of Sacreds"; others call them "Inseparable Sacred Rights" or "Sublime Rights." The Greeks call them <term>sovereign authority <note>original: "κυρίαν ἀρχὴν"</note></term> and <term>sovereign government <note>original: "κύριον πολíτευμα"</note></term>. The Germans generally seem to call them <term>Imperial Sovereignty <note>original: "Kayserl. Hoheit"</note></term> and <term>Reserved Rights <note>original: "Reservaten"</note></term>, as noted by Clapmar, Arnisæus, and Einsiedel. Furthermore, Sixtinus (following Schrader) writes that in Germany today these rights are designated by the word <term>Dominion <note>original: "Herrlichkeit"; literally "Lordliness" or "Glory," referring to the jurisdiction of a lord.</note></term>. Wehner agrees with this, adding that the term is beyond all doubt.

<summary>This page introduces a legal dissertation on "Regalia," defining them as the sovereign rights reserved to a supreme ruler (the Emperor) and explaining how the term evolved from a Latin adjective into a formal legal noun.</summary>
<keywords>Regalia, sovereignty, Imperial law, Lex Regia, Rights of Majesty, Herrlichkeit, jurisdiction, legal terminology</keywords>

--- Page 1270 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 1261 regarding the definition and classification of "Regalia" (sovereign rights). The text transitions from debating terminology to defining the essence of these rights as inherent to supreme power rather than as mere rewards for service.</meta>

Dissertation

...he adds, we are clearly unable to approve. For that term is also verified in Jurisdiction, and superiority, and other granted Royal rights; as is also clear from the already cited Wehner: and hence Cothman correctly advises that this term must be understood according to the subject matter and the circumstances of the persons. *Academic Counsel 39, no. 8.*

IV. Therefore, we define **Regalia**, or the **reserved rights of Majesty**, as follows: they are certain rights joined to the supreme Power <note>original: "summo Imperio"</note>, flowing immediately from it; by virtue of which one either acts, commands, permits, or even demands something that pertains to the necessity of the State <note>original: "Reipubl."</note> or its utility. Arnisæus relates other definitions, as does Einsiedel. Among them, however, that definition which Johannes Borcholt provides must be entirely rejected, where he calls them "Rights which are granted to the Roman Emperor as a reward for the immense labor which he sustains for the Empire." For if we wish to look more deeply into the cause of these Rights, we will find that they are attributed to Majesty not as rewards, but rather that they follow Majesty as a shadow follows a body. For they flow from the very nature of Majesty; which, since it is the supreme head of the State that governs all things, must also have those rights within its power, without which the Empire could not subsist. Arnisæus, to whom you may add Einsiedel. (a)

<note>original: (a) "Ac si in præmium immensi laboris..."</note>
(a) And if the Regalia were granted as a reward for immense labor, it would follow that they are all held "precariously" <note>A legal term meaning held at the will or pleasure of another.</note> and depend on someone else's judgment; yet they are the most proper attributes of Majesty. Likewise, Borcholt’s definition would be broader than the thing defined, because it would simultaneously include things which the Emperor possesses by right of allodium <note>original: "jure allodii"; land or property owned absolutely, without any superior lord.</note> from the Empire. This definition is also too narrow, since according to it, those rights which do not recognize this form <note>the form of a "reward"</note> would have to be barred and excluded from the number of Regalia: and in this way we would have very few Regalia. Furthermore, these Regalia assert the Prince's labor more than they compensate for it, such as the power of waging war, establishing laws, the right of administering justice, etc.

V. And since **Majesty**, in its proper meaning, denotes the supreme power of managing the State, and by this power it exercises those rights which are called **Regalia**,

<column-break/>

it is therefore clearly wrong to list "absolute power" (or power freed from the laws) as a specific type of Regalia under a special name. This is because that does not constitute a peculiar right, but rather all Regalia proceed from it, and are contained within Majesty as if in a fountain. And so, since it participates in all types of Regalia, it cannot constitute a single specific type. Arnisæus. *Einsiedel disagrees.*

VI. Some are accustomed to dividing Regalia, or the Rights of Majesty, into **Ecclesiastical** and **Political** (or secular). Clapmar, Arnisæus, Camman, and Einsiedel. However, it pleases us here to set aside for now the Right of Majesty regarding the Churches (if any such right belongs or can belong to it) and to treat purely Political Regalia. Sixtinus also teaches that the subject matter of these is purely secular. (b) The most accepted division of these is that some are called **major** and others **minor**. Borcholt, Rosenthal, Sixtinus, and Camman. Bocer, however, calls some the Regalia of **Majesty** and others the Regalia of the **Treasury** <note>original: "Fisci"; the public purse or state finances.</note>. But Conrad von Einsiedel believes that the essence of Majesty is placed in certain rights, while others pertain to Majesty indeed, but in a different way—namely, they do not concern its essence, but only its existence; and so that Majesty might better achieve its end, these provide easier means, serving either the state in general or its essential rights, and supplying the necessary funds. In this view, Camman considers that the *major Regalia* (or those of Majesty) adhere to the person and the "bones" of the Prince, and are therefore highly personal, attached to the Crown itself, and are more powerful and purely Royal: likewise, they exist "outside of commerce" <note>original: "extra commercium"; meaning they cannot be bought, sold, or traded like private property.</note>. He judges the rest to be only in the manner of Privileges; a view which also pleases Thomas Michael and Fachin. Nevertheless, if we weigh the matter more accurately, the rights of the treasury—the minor Regalia—if they are [dependent on] supreme power and eminence...
