->Concerning Sovereign Rights.<-

...to belong to preeminence; and especially the power of establishing them seems to flow from Universal Dominion, *from the lordship over the land* <note>original: "aus der Grund-Herrschaft"</note>, according to the **Lord Presider in his dissertation on the Rights of Majesty, chapter 1.** Thus, Sovereign Rights <term>Regalia: the specific powers and prerogatives belonging to a supreme ruler</term>, or the Laws of Empire, differ entirely from those privileges or rights which are given to a Prince either for preeminence, or solely in consideration of dignity, or even for the sake of external ornament: **Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, book 3, chapter 1, number 1; The Lord Presider in his dissertation *On Majesty in General*, chapter 7, number 4.** Such honors the Prince has also shared with the Empress <note>original: "Augustæ"</note>, as noted in the **Digest, law *Princeps*, paragraph 1, *on laws*.**

**VII.** Furthermore, we do not believe that the true number and nature of these Rights can be sought from the single chapter on what constitutes Sovereign Rights in the *Customs of Feuds* <note>The *Libri Feudorum*, a collection of feudal law</note>. For Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa, Holy Roman Emperor</note> promulgated that Chapter, and in it is determined not what the Laws of the Empire are in general, but what the cities of Italy owe to the Emperor beyond their sworn faith and obedience. **Camman, *disputation* 2, number 47 and following.** This is clearly seen from the ancient and most elegant poet Gunther, in *The Ligurian*, book 8, verse 567, where he sings:

> Afterward, the question was moved carefully
> Concerning the ancient Law of the Kingdom;
> Which a long period of disuse and the ancient error
> Of a neglected time had obscured.
> And first the Italians <note>original: "Ligures"</note>, being asked by the King about this,
> Named taxes, ports, the rights of minting money,
> Along with mills, tolls, rivers, and bridges;
> Also that which they call "Fodrum" <note>A tax for the maintenance of the Emperor and his retinue during travels</note> in the common tongue,
> And the head-tax <note>original: "Capitolicium"</note> at a fixed time, etc.

We consider even less that the "Right of the King" <note>original: "Jus Regis"</note> recounted by the Prophet Samuel in **1 Kings, chapter 8** <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 8</note> serves to enumerate Sovereign Rights. This is despite the claims of **Arnisæus in his treatise *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 1, number 4; Camman, *disputation* 2, thesis 10;** and also **Einsiedel, chapter 1, number 3, etc.** For it is the view of **St. Thomas [Aquinas] in *On the Government of Princes*, book 3, chapter 11, and book 2, chapter 9,** that tyrannical rights—or at least the customs of those who maintain a lordly monarchy—are described there.

<column-break/>

As seen in **Caspar Sanctius on chapter 8 of 1 Kings, number 19 and following; Martin Becanus in his *Analogy*, chapter 6, question 9;** and extensively in the **Lord Presider’s dissertation *On Majesty in General*, chapter 8.** Indeed, if the Laws of Empire to be used licitly in times of necessity were enumerated here, as some wish, those rights would also have belonged to the Judges or the Jewish Republic. For a democracy possesses the same rights as a monarchy, and thus the Prophet Samuel would not have held them up as a warning against kings. Finally, some authors mentioned by **Camman, *disputation* 2, thesis 83,** do not offer a fixed distinction of the Rights of Majesty, but only bring forward certain headings. They say the highest class of such Rights is to hold the supreme and absolute command <note>original: "Imperium"</note> over subjects; that is, the power of ordering and executing the order. From this fountain, they derive the rest like small streams. Other divisions of Sovereign Rights or Rights of Majesty by various authors are reviewed by the same **Camman, *disputation* 2, thesis 75; Arnisæus, book 2 *On Majesty*, chapter 1, number 3, etc.** However, it pleases us now to deal with the principal ones and distribute them into the following classes.

***

### CHAPTER I.

## CONCERNING THE POWER OF SUPREME AUTHORITY REGARDING LAWS.

**O**f all the Rights of Majesty, the highest—and therefore the one from which we rightly begin—is the power of establishing, repealing, and interpreting Law and Statutes. **Bocer, here in chapter 2, number 6, and *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 1, number 5; Sixtin, *On Sovereign Rights*, book 1, chapter 2, number 9.** This Right was so sacred to antiquity that they traced its first origin from the immortal Gods. **Camman, *disputation* 4, thesis 4 and following.** Truly, making laws is the unique property of the one who holds the first place in the State; since he gives the law and does not receive it, except from the most high God. This is to rule not only according to the laws, but also over the laws themselves, as **Plutarch says in *Flaminius*. Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 3, at the beginning.** In this view, **Bartolus on the law *Imperium*, number 7, in the Digest *on jurisdiction*,** refers the power of making laws to the supreme and greatest...

# Dissertation

...refers to the degree of Empire, to which others also agree. Although, following Bocer, **Einsiedel** *here in chapter 2, numbers 32 and following* disagrees, and likewise **Camman** *disputation 4, thesis 12* asserts that by this very fact, **Bartolus** and his followers manifest their own weakness in Political matters too clearly. However, just as the meaning of "Jurisdiction" is sometimes expanded to encompass all the power of a Prince—in which sense **Seneca** writes in *On Clemency*, book 1: *“Which cities fall, which arise; it is my jurisdiction”* <note>original Latin: "Quae ruunt urbes, quae oriantur; mea Jurisdictio est." Seneca uses "jurisdiction" here as a poetic synonym for total control over the fate of nations.</note>—even though the sense of this word does not conform to the analogies of our Law. In the same way, Bartolus says, not so foolishly, that all things reserved for the Prince in preeminence as a sign and use of Empire belong to the "greatest pure power" <term>merum imperium: the highest form of legal authority, including the power of life and death, usually reserved for the sovereign</term>. Thus, he takes that "greatest power" to mean either territorial jurisdiction or the Right of Majesty.

**II.** Furthermore, what has been said regarding the Prince's power concerning Laws must all be understood as referring to **universal laws**, which in Roman Law are called *Constitutions* <note>original: "Constitutiones"</note>, *Institute on Natural Law and the Law of Nations, section "but also what the Prince," etc., and the entire title of the Digest on the Constitutions of Princes.* Today, however, they are designated as **Imperial Recesses** <term>Imperial Recess: the formal collection of resolutions passed by the Imperial Diet (Reichstag) at its conclusion</term>, because they are usually established by the Emperor with the advice of the States of the Empire. They are called "Universal" not only because they bind everyone, but also because they can be established concerning all matters that pertain to the administration of the supreme Empire.

**Particular laws**, however, which we commonly call **Statutes**, can indeed be established by anyone who possesses full jurisdiction and subjects through the benefit of some superior; namely, a Duke in his Duchy, a Marquis in his Marquisate, or a Count in his County. **Bocer** *here, chapter 2, number 62;* **Einsiedel** *chapter 2, number 27.* But nevertheless, these are valid only insofar as they do not contradict general laws. *Digest, law 3, section "The Divine," on the violation of a tomb; Code, law 2, on the office of the praetorian prefect,* and similar citations. **Bocer**, *said chapter, number 63.* Or indeed, they must not derogate from the right held by a superior, nor extend themselves beyond the power and jurisdiction granted by Majesty. In this view, even Municipalities, Universities, and indeed even Colleges can establish statutes according to the measure of jurisdiction belonging to them.

<column-break/>

And so **Bocer** *chapter 4, number 64* establishes that the power of creating statutes is wrongly ascribed to the **Sovereign Rights** <term>Regalia</term> of Majesty; since they are only valid insofar as Majesty has allowed them by special approval or general concession. Although that power is sometimes referred to the Sovereign Rights granted by the Emperor to the States, or it ought to be referred to territorial superiority. However, as for what was handed down—that statutes ought not to be contrary to superior laws—this should by no means be understood as referring to the **Civil Law of Justinian** (to which, certainly, the States of the Empire can freely derogate through contrary statutes), but rather to the **Recesses** and other public Laws of the Roman Empire. **Einsiedel** *chapter 2, number 28 and following.* But truly, the universal laws themselves presuppose the Laws of Nature and of Nations, as well as the Ecclesiastical Canons; and only then can the Emperor add his own special laws pertaining to the public state.

**III.** Furthermore, just as the authority of Laws depends on the Emperor alone, so too does the power to remove their obscurity and to interpret them belong to him alone. *Chapter "among other things" 31, on the sentence of excommunication; Law 1 and the final law of the Code on Laws.* To be sure, **Legal Experts** <note>original: "Jure-Consulti"</note> can interpret laws: *Constitution "every" on the rationale and method of teaching law, to the Ancestors; the entire title of the Code on Professors in the city of Constantinople.* So too **Judges** can choose the fairer course in lower court sentences, *Code, Law 8, on Judgments,* and in a case not decided by law, they can proceed through interpretation to similar cases, *Digest, Law 11 and following, on laws.*

But that **Absolute Interpretation**, which belongs to Majesty, differs in many ways. **Einsiedel** *chapter 2, number 21 and following;* see **Camman** *disputation 4, thesis 105 and following.* Since the laws of the Republic ought to be of service, and since the Republic varies according to place, time, and person, the laws must sometimes be varied and changed; but this must not be done except by the one who has the power of making laws. **Camman**, *disputation 4, thesis 108 and following.*

**IV.** Just as Majesty alone establishes Universal laws, so too is it within the same power to bestow **privileges**, which our Doctors therefore ascribe to the Sovereign Rights. **Petrus Gregorius** *book 6 on the Republic, title "n";* **Bodin** *book 1, last chapter;* **Bocer** *here, chapter...*

<summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of legal authority in the Holy Roman Empire, distinguishing between "Universal Laws" (Imperial Recesses) created by the Emperor and "Statutes" created by local lords or institutions. It emphasizes that while local bodies can make their own rules, the ultimate power to create, change, and authoritatively interpret law rests solely with the Sovereign Majesty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of the Prince’s rights (Regalia), moving from the general nature of laws to specific exceptions: Privileges and Dispensations. It builds on the previous discussion regarding the sovereign’s "pure power" (merum imperium).</meta>

number 233. For a **privilege** is a private, or singular law <note>original: "privata lex." This is the etymological root of the word 'privilege.'</note>, as noted by Isidore in his *Etymologies*, book 15, chapter 18, and Donellus in his *Commentaries*, book 11, chapter 5. It is also called a **Singular Law** in law 16 of the Digest *on laws*. Today, it is mostly understood to refer to **favorable grants**, although in the past, even the imposition of a punishment or an edict issued against a specific individual was called by that name, according to Arnisæus in *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 3, number 16. Certainly, privileges should not be granted without an examination of the cause, nor should they be granted to the prejudice of a third party, as Mynsinger notes in his *Observations*, book 4, observation 70. In this regard, it is said that in cases of doubt, grants of this kind must be interpreted more strictly <term>strictius interpretandæ: a legal principle where special favors are read narrowly so they don't unfairly harm others</term> (laws 56 and 192, section 1, *on the Rules of Law*). Furthermore, if another person's right is taken away by such a grant, they have a legal defense based on **stealth or misrepresentation** <term>sub- & obreptio: "subreption" is hiding the truth, and "obreption" is telling a falsehood to gain a favor</term>. Thus, we find it handed down that a grant of Privileges is valid if it is done from the "fullness of power," which neither the ignorance of an absent party nor the contradiction of a present party can hinder (Rolandus à Valle, *Counsel* 4, number 47, volume 3; Natta, *Counsel* 636, number 153 and following).

**V.** Since Privileges are **private laws**, and the power to abolish laws resides in the judgment of the Sovereign <note>original: "Majestatis"</note>, it follows that they are, by their nature, **revocable**. This is true if they were granted by favor <term>precariò: at the will of the grantor, rather than as a permanent right</term>, and not by way of a contract or gift. For in privileges properly so-called, this clause is always silently inherent: ***provided things remain as they are, and stay in the same state*** <note>original Latin: "Rebus sic stantibus, permanentibusque in eodem statu." This is a fundamental legal doctrine that a promise is only binding as long as the circumstances don't fundamentally change.</note> (*on Decimes*, chapter *Suggestum*; *on spiritual kinship*, chapter 1; *on prescription*, second to last chapter; and the Lord Presiding Judge in his *Selections from the First Book of the Pandects*, question 13 and page 43). Hence, when a Prince dies, it is customary to petition for such privileges to be confirmed by the successor. Confirming them is considered a sign and token of superiority (Græveus, *Practical Conclusions*, book 2, conclusion at the beginning; Knichen, *on the law of territory*, chapter 3, number 208). Nevertheless, even immutable Privileges are usually confirmed for the sake of greater authority (Rosenthal, *on feuds*, chapter 6, conclusion 68, number 1; and Baron Enenckel, *on privileges*, book 3, chapter 20, numbers 5 and 11).

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER II.
## ON DISPENSATION.

### I.
The Right of **Dispensing** also rests upon the power of making, abolishing, and interpreting laws. Here, **"to dispense"** is taken to mean doing a favor for someone, though this is less correct Latin, as Zasius (following Budé) notes in his commentary *on law 1, number 2, regarding laws*. In this sense, a **dispensation** is defined as a **Regalian Right** by which a relaxation of the law is made in a particular case for certain persons, based on a just and sufficient cause. This happens while the law in general, its vigor, and its underlying reason remain intact. It applies to minor matters, or to those things which are not evil in themselves <term>malum in se</term>, but are evil only because they are prohibited <term>malum prohibitum</term>. In this way, it is distinguished from the granting of Privileges and the declaration or interpretation of laws (Covarruvias, *on the Decretals*, part 2, chapter 6, section 9, number 2, etc.). Moreover, the power of dispensing applies only to **positive laws** <note>original: "legibus solum positivis." These are laws created by humans/states, rather than natural or divine laws.</note>. Even in those cases, legal scholars require a just and legitimate cause; so much so that a person granting or seeking a dispensation without a reasonable cause is seen not only to sin, but those who have an interest in the matter can legally challenge the grant on the grounds of stealth or misrepresentation (following the argument in the Digest *on punishments*, law "of the banished"; Cammann, *disputation 4 on Majesty, thesis 65*).

### II.
Furthermore, there are various cases for dispensation. Among them, the first that occurs is the **legitimation of natural and illegitimate children** <note>original: "spuriorum"</note>, which is commonly numbered among the **Greater Regalian Rights** <note>original: "Regalibus majoribus." These are the highest prerogatives reserved exclusively for the Emperor or Sovereign.</note> (Novels 74, chapter 2, and Novels 89, chapter 9; Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 2, number 5; Sixtinus, chapter 2, number 30, book 1; Tuschus, letter L, conclusion 218). For this reason, it seems this power does not belong to Dukes, Marquesses, etc. (Bocerus, chapter 2, number 112), nor to the Imperial Chamber (Cammann, disputation 4, thesis 48; Sixtinus, *on Regalia*, book 1, chapter 4, number 107). However, if a father already has "natural" <note>In this context, children born of a long-term concubine but not a legal wife.</note> and legitimate children, the legitimation of others is not considered valid; nevertheless, even in this case, something different can be specifically provided for in the **Instrument of Legitimation** <note>the formal legal document</note> (Gail, *Observations*, book 2, observation 142, numbers 3, 7, and 9; Tapia, *on the Constitutions of Princes*, chapter 5, number 44, etc.). And legitimation is not revoked regarding the Right of Succession even if other legitimate sons are recognized by the father after the fact.

Bocer, chapter 2, number 70 and following. In this matter, the consent of **agnates** <term>agnatorum: relatives related through the male line</term> or **cognates** <term>cognatorum: relatives related through the female line</term> is not strictly necessary here, as Bocer teaches against the opinion of Forster in the cited place, number 87. However, this applies only to a certain extent: in such a case (namely, when that consent is lacking), the children who have been made "legitimate" by the Prince do not succeed to the inheritance of those relatives who did not consent. See Valentin Forster, *On Successions*, book 6, chapter 37, number 36. This is supported by law 9 at the beginning of the Code *on natural children* and *Novel 89*, chapter 4; although Bocer (cited chapter 2, number 93) and Einsiedel (*On Regalia*, chapter 2, number 95) disagree. Furthermore, it is correctly judged that those who are legitimized do not exclude **legitimate daughters**—who might otherwise be removed from succession by a local statute—unless the Emperor specifically intended this and some probable cause exists (see Gail, *Observations*, book 2, observation 140; Fachinæus, book 6, chapter 1). Even less does a legitimation prejudice the rights of male relatives in an **ancient fief** <term>feudo antiquo: an ancestral estate held under feudal law, usually restricted to blood heirs</term>. See Einsiedel at the cited place, number 103; Hartmann Pistor, part 6, book 2, question 40, number 6.

III. The Emperor can also legitimize the children of another's Empire, provided they are present within his own territory or Empire; in that case, the legitimation is valid even outside the territory. But regarding property located elsewhere, it is unlikely that such a legitimation would be accepted, because **"scepters are not to be confused"** <note>original: "sceptra non sunt confundenda"; meaning the jurisdictions of different sovereigns should not overlap</note> (Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 7, conclusion 19, number 10; Arnisæus, *On the Right of Majesty*, book 2, chapter 3, under number 17). Likewise, the Emperor would not be permitted to perform such an act if he were himself situated in a foreign territory. See Bocer, chapter 2, number 102; Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 2, number 8. Furthermore, regarding the power to legitimize, no distinction should be made between **natural children** <term>naturales: children born of a long-term concubine</term> and **spurious children** <term>spurios: children born of casual affairs or "wandering love"</term> <note>original: "vaga Venere"</note>. Einsiedel (chapter 2, number 75 and following) proves this well against Bocer. But as for those procreated from an illicit marriage—such as **incest** or **adultery**—their legitimation is not strictly a "legitimation" in the proper sense, but rather a type of **dispensation** or special pardon (*Novel 74*, last chapter; *Novel 89*, last chapter; Forster, *On Successions*, book 6, chapter 36, number 16). The Presiding Lord <note>referring to the author's teacher or the head of the academic dispute</note> disagrees in his *Reflections on the first book of the Digests*, question 13, folio 115, as does Fachinæus (book 3, controversy chapter 57). Additionally, the Emperor not infrequently grants the power of legitimizing to those who are called **Counts Palatine** <term>Palatii Comites: high-ranking officials or "Counts of the Palace" with delegated imperial powers</term>; however, their power does not extend to the children of Princes, Counts, and Barons (Sixtin, book 1, chapter 4,

<column-break/>

number 114). See Michael Nizolius, allegation 1, and most recently Johann Christian Vilitz regarding the *Imperial Counts Palatine*, in his *Annotations*, section 10, under the word "Legitimize."

IV. Following Legitimation is the **Restoration of Reputation** <term>Famæ restituendi: a legal act restoring the "good name" and civil rights of someone who had been declared "infamous" or dishonored by a court</term>. Thomas de Piperata wrote about reputation in volume 11, part 1, folio 8. This is also commonly associated with the **Greater Regalia** <term>Regalibus majoribus: the highest rights reserved strictly to the sovereign</term> (Digest, book 1, section 10, *on requesting*; and section 1, *on marriages*; law 4 at the end, *on punishments*; and the Code *on those who have received a sentence*). See Bocer, chapter 2, number 115; Sixtin, chapter 2, number 21, book 1; Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 3, number 15, and part 2, question 22. Thus, an inferior Prince who restores the reputation of someone who is actually the subject of another ruler achieves nothing; for such a restoration only has power within that Prince's own jurisdiction (Bocer, number 115; Peregrinus, *On the Rights of the Treasury*, book 1, title *on those who hold from the treasury*, number 54). This is supported by the **Imperial Recess of Augsburg** from the year 1526, section "Und wol." Nor can the Emperor, by restoring the reputation of the subjects of another State, thrust them upon their own lords against their will (Bocer, *On Jurisdiction*, chapter 8, number 80; Georg Everhard, counsel 9, numbers 18 and 29, book 2). The Presiding Lord notes this in his *Reflections on the second book of the Digests*, question 13, folio 62. Through this restoration, the prior **stain of infamy** is removed, as if no dishonest life had preceded it (Chodor, *Various Letters*, letter 64; Imperial Law in the Code *on marriages*; law 1 in the Code *on those who have received a sentence*). From that point forward, the person can give testimony and preside over public offices (Canon Law, chapter *testimonium* in the title *on witnesses*; and the chapter *si testes*, cause 2, question 3; Freher, *On Reputation*, book 3, chapter 2, number 11).

See Harmenopoulos, book 1, title 4, section "only the Prince"; Bocer, here in chapter 2, number 131; Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 3, number 1. Although the Emperor Leo, in *Novel 28*, suggests that this "pardon" or grant can be obtained from any local ordinary judge, Sixtin (chapter 2, number 21) still considers this grant to be among the **Reserved Rights** <note>original: "Reservatis"; rights held only by the Emperor</note>, so much so that not even the **Imperial Chamber Court** <term>camera Imperialis: the highest judicial body of the Holy Roman Empire</term> can claim this right for itself (Bocer, number 133; Thomas Michael, *On Jurisdiction*, thesis 32, at the end). ->### On Royal Prerogatives.<-

I understand this to apply to Princes and other Magnates, should any of them wish to obtain this permission. The States of the Empire, however, are also accustomed to granting it to their own subjects. *Würtemberg Territorial Law, part 4, title 27.* The Emperor also grants this power to certain Counts Palatine. According to Civil Law, a specific age and the suitability of the individual person are required here, *Law 2, Code: On those who seek the benefit of age.* <note>The "benefit of age" (venia aetatis) was a legal grant allowing a minor to be treated as a legal adult.</note> In such cases, these individuals are considered as adults in the administration of their goods, *Law 10, Code: On appeals; last law, Code: If one has become an adult.* Nor do they enjoy the "benefit of restitution" <term>beneficio restitutionis: the legal right of a minor to void a contract or legal action that was disadvantageous to them</term> if they have been harmed. *Cassiodorus, 7. Various Epistles, 4; Law 1, Code: On those who seek the benefit of age; Law 3, at the beginning, On minors.* However, they can neither alienate <note>sell or transfer</note> nor burden their immovable property with a mortgage, *Penultimate law, Code: On those who seek the benefit of age; last law, Code: If one has become an adult; Simoncellus, book 3, title 8, number 24.* This is unless the Prince has also specifically permitted the alienation. If, however, the minor wishes to be "restored" <note>reinstated to their previous legal protections</note> against the very obtaining of this permission, I believe they should be heard in their own way. *The Presiding Lord in the Deliberations, folio 79.*

V. It seems unworthy for a Prince to make a child <term>impuberem: a child below the age of legal puberty</term> capable of making a will, *argued from the last law, Code: On military testaments; law "more," final section, On acquiring inheritance.* For a defect of understanding <note>mental incapacity due to age</note> cannot be removed by any dispensation. *Bl. on law "Barbarius," Digest: On the office of the Praetor.* Nevertheless, in a child very close to puberty, such circumstances can concur that something else might be said. *Angelus on the said final law, Code: On military testaments; Jason on law "rescripts," 7, Code: On petitions to be offered to the Emperor.* Furthermore, here belongs the power of "absolving" <note>releasing someone from an oath</note>—to relax a prisoner's oath <note>original: "Urphed". This was a formal oath sworn by a released prisoner promising not to take revenge or legal action against the authority that imprisoned them.</note> given to the Lord who took the oath from him, so that he may use the law against that same Lord. *Bocer, cited chapter 2, On Regalia, number 135; Einsiedel, On Regalia, chapter 2, number 252; Presiding Lord in the Deliberations, folio 87 and following.* This relaxation is also usually granted in other cases, *final law at the beginning, Digest: To the municipalities; last law, Digest: On military matters; penultimate law, Code: On transactions; Novel 51, in the preface; Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court, part 2, article 24; Fachinæus, 3. Controversies, 13.* Thus Emperor Charles V used this power when he 

<column-break/>

absolved the Electors Maurice and Joachim from the oath given to the Prince of Hesse regarding his liberation, and pronounced them released from the bond of obligation. *Thuanus, book 6, near the end.* But in this case, properly speaking, someone is declared to be absolved rather than actually being "absolved" by the act itself. *Setser, On Oaths, book 2, chapter 6, number 3 and following.* And this absolution must be sought while the matter is still intact, and before perjury is committed. *Charles de Crassis, treatise On Exceptions, 12, number 30.* Likewise, it cannot be obtained unless the opposing party has first been heard. *Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber Court, at the cited place; Presiding Lord in the Deliberations.*

VI. Also belonging here is the right to grant "moratorium stays" (which in German they call *Anstand-Brief* <note>a letter of respite</note> or *Quinquennel* <note>a five-year stay of debt</note>, and in French *lettres de respit*), to the effect that debtors cannot be harassed by creditors within the granted time; hence the Saxons usually call these "Becoming Iron" <note>original: "Eisern werden". This refers to "Iron Letters" (literae ferreae), which were sovereign stays of execution that "stiffened" or froze a debtor's obligations.</note>. *Law 2, Code: On petitions to be offered to the Emperor; Wehner, under the word "Anstands-Brief"; Einsiedel chapter 2, number 291 and following.* These stays are not granted except for a grave cause—namely, when some merchant is the author of his own poverty not through luxury, or laziness, or any act of his own, but when through some misfortune his resources slip away such that he cannot keep a merchant's faith. *Reformation of the Police of Augsburg, Year 1548, title: On ruined merchants; and Frankfurt, Year 1577, title 23.* On this matter, the singular and absolute treatise by Wilhelm Antonius, recently published, may be consulted.

***

### CHAPTER III.
## ON ROYAL POWER CONCERNING JUDICIAL MATTERS.

I. The Emperor, or another possessing Majesty, is the Supreme Judge; therefore, he judges everyone and is judged by no one. This supreme jurisdiction belonging to him must rightly be asserted as part of the Royal Prerogatives and supreme eminence, as *Einsiedel* sufficiently proves against Bocer, *chapter 2, number 311 and following.* By virtue of this, therefore, he can judge in his own cause. *Law 3, On those who are deleted in a testament; 41, On appointing heirs; final section at the end, Institutes: On vulgar substitution.*

substitutes the following: The Lord Presiding Official, in his dissertation on the **Rights of Majesty** (Chapter 5, number 10), states: Even if the sovereign takes notice of other matters, he can proceed summarily and simply, without the formal structure of a trial, and with all the formalities of positive law set aside. <note>original: "summariè ac de plano, absque figura Judicii, sublatisque omnibus solemnitatibus Juris positivi." This refers to a "summary" proceeding where the usual complex steps of a lawsuit are bypassed for the sake of speed or sovereign authority.</note> See *Law "At whose hands," Digest: On manumissions*; Maranta in *Judicial Processes*, distinction 9, numbers 3 and 8; Rodolphinus on *The Dukes of Italy*, number 216.

Majesty also deals with the greatest causes, the investigation of which is forbidden to others. Thus, in the Roman Empire <note>referring here to the Holy Roman Empire</note>, the Emperor alone hears and pronounces judgment on the Major Fiefs of the Empire when they are disputed in a property trial <term>petitorio Judicio: a legal action focused on the ownership of property rather than just its possession</term>. See the *single chapter under the title "At whose hands or by whom feudal controversies are decided"*; *Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 7*; Gail, book 1, observation 29, number 3 and following. This also applies to the proscription of the Princes of the Empire. *Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, part 2, title 18*; Heig, part 1, question 9, numbers 42 and 52. Regnerus Sixtinus, book 1, chapter 4, number 8, where he ascribes the right of inflicting a general Ban <term>Jus generalis Banni: the power to declare someone an imperial outlaw</term> to the Royal Prerogatives <term>Regalia: the distinct rights and powers belonging to a sovereign</term>, following Gail, *On the Public Peace*, 6, number 9 and following, chapter 11, number 3; and book 2, chapter 1, number 27; and his treatise *On Imperial Arrests*, chapter 10, number 18. Similarly, some refer the investigation of the crime of Majesty <note>high treason</note> to this same category. Sixtinus, book 1, chapter 2, number 18; Franciscus Vivius, book 2, decision 208, number 2. Vivius extols this power so highly that he does not believe it passes even with a general grant of Royal Prerogatives. However, this opinion seems to lack a certain and stable reasoning. See *Law 7, paragraph 3, Digest*; *Law 4, Code: On the Julian Law of Majesty*; Bocer, *On Royal Prerogatives*, chapter 2, paragraph 248; and finally, *On the Crime of Majesty*, last chapter, number 2 and following.

II. To these I add supreme authority <note>original: "summum Imperium"</note> and jurisdiction without appeal: that is, that no one can appeal against a sentence of Majesty. *Law 1, at the beginning, Code: From whom it is not permitted to appeal*; Bocer, 2, number 242. Thus, those who have hitherto appealed from a "badly informed Caesar" to the same person "to be better informed" <note>A legal maneuver where a petitioner asks the ruler to reconsider a decision based on new information.</note> seem to have had no hope of victory, but rather a desire to elude their adversaries. Einsiedel treats this extensively in chapter 2, number 55 and many following. On the other hand, it is permitted to appeal to Majesty from all others. *Law 45, Digest: On conditions and demonstrations.* Indeed, this right so belongs to Majesty that it cannot be alienated <note>transferred or sold</note> from itself. Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, number 3 and following; Clapmarius,

<column-break/>

*On Secrets*, chapter 29; Bocer, chapter 2, number 243. In this way, jurisdictions return to that source from which they first flowed and halt their course through an appeal. Bodin, *On the Republic*, chapter 10. Although the Emperor cannot grant to others the Royal Prerogative itself of which we speak, he is not prohibited from granting a "privilege of non-appeal" <term>Privilegium de non appellando: a legal grant ensuring that a lower court's decision cannot be challenged in a higher court</term> to some inferior. *Law 1, paragraphs 2 and 4, Digest: From whom it is not permitted to appeal*; *Law 37, Code: On appeals.* In the same way, appeal from the Electors is forbidden by the *Golden Bull of Charles IV, title 8*. It is well known that privileges of "non-appeal" granted by Emperors are quite frequent. These are, however, sometimes limited or restricted to a certain sum of money. See the *Symphorema*, last volume, throughout. Other privileges are granted by the Emperor alone, and therefore the right of delegating a case with the clause, "with appeal removed" <note>original: "Appellatione remotâ"</note>, is numbered among the Royal Prerogatives of Majesty. *Law 1, paragraph "sometimes," Digest: From whom it is not permitted to appeal*; Matthæus de Afflictis, at the title *What are the Royal Prerogatives*, number 87; Sixtinus, book 1, chapter 2, number 15 and following. Even when appeal is removed, there remains nevertheless the remedy of Supplication <term>Supplicatio: a formal petition for mercy or review addressed directly to the sovereign</term>, which is also called a retraction or a "complaint of recourse." See the *Law "which supplication," Code: On offering petitions to the Emperor*; *Single Law, Code: On the sentences of the Praetorian Prefects*; *Last law, paragraph 5, Code: On the times of appeals*; *Novel 119, chapter 5*; Arnisæus, book 2, *On the Rights of Majesty*, chapter 4, number 7 and following. Akin to this within the territory of the Empire are the "Revisions" <note>referring to the review of cases in the Imperial Chamber Court</note>: *Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, part 5, title 53*; and in Saxony, the remedy of *clarification* and *higher clarification* <note>original: "der Läuterung, & der Ober-Läuterung," specific Saxon legal procedures for challenging a judgment</note>. See *Constitutions of Elector August, part 1, constitution 10*; Hahn on the *Law of Judicial Process*, thesis 58.

Others say that the force of Majesty consists in this: that it judges all people; and this is to be understood in both civil and criminal cases. Hence the right of establishing punishment, or of life and death, belongs to Majesty. (a) The Lord Presiding Official, *On the Rights of Majesty*, chapter 5, at the beginning; Clapmarius.

# On Royal Prerogatives

Book 1, chapter 17. In this view, High Jurisdiction <note>original: "Imperium merum"—historically the "power of the sword," or the legal authority to inflict capital punishment</note> is commonly asserted to be a Royal Prerogative. See Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 11; Vultejus, *On Fiefs*, book 1, chapter 5, number 7; Peregrinus, *On the Law of the Treasury*, book 1, at the beginning, number 10. Bocerus, however, in his treatise *On Royal Prerogatives*, chapter 1, number 25, disagreeing, speaks of High Jurisdiction granted to others; yet, insofar as it inheres in the territorial sovereignty <note>original: "der Lands-Fürstlichen Obrigkeit"</note>, it is far more complete than that which common magistrates possess. Therefore, it can be called "Regal" or "Justiciary," because it proceeds from the Emperor alone. Hence, a Prince can not only predetermine a specific penalty for each crime but also, beyond the established penalty, take vengeance more severely against some for the sake of setting an example. See *Code of Justinian: On Marriages*, law 29; *Code: On Punishments*, law 20. Sometimes he can even condemn a delinquent—one known most certainly to him—without a summons or other similar procedures, and begin with the execution. See Morla in *The Emporium*, title 2, question 2. For the "evidence of the deed does not require the outcry of an accusation," as the commentary says in *Clementine Constitutions: Pastoralis, on things judged*. <margin>(a)</margin> Yet those who permit Majesty to begin with execution do not exclude an investigation <note>original: "cognitionem"</note>, but only the manifest formal process, if such a process cannot be applied without danger. Aerodius, *On Judged Matters*, title 2, book 7, chapter 29. Indeed, it is rightly considered tyrannical that Tiberius had Asinius Gallus condemned in the Senate while he was absent, on the very day he was the Emperor's guest and was drinking sociably with him. See Dio Cassius, book 58.

<margin>(a) And indeed, this type of right belongs to Majesty by a double right: (1) by reason of origin, for all others hold their rights from the Emperor; (2) by reason of dignity and absolute power.</margin>

II. And so, granting pardon for a crime and restoring the condemned to life must be placed in the category of the Major Royal Prerogatives. *Digest: On things judged*, law 45, § 1; *Digest: On Investigations*, law 1, at the end; *Digest: On Punishments*, law 4, at the end, law 9, § 11, law 27, § "if however," and law 31. *Code: On Petitions to be offered to the Emperor*, law 7; law 10 and the entire title in the *Code: On those who have received a sentence*. Einsiedel, chapter 2, number 66, etc.; Camman, dispute 4, thesis 68 and following. This seems to have been the reason why Charles V, when granting sublime power—nearly royal in nature—to the Senate of Milan, reserved this right of remitting

<column-break/>

penalties to himself by a special exception. Bodin, *On the Republic*, book 1, chapter 8, number 81, and chapter 10, number 164. Consequently, magistrates properly so-called cannot remit the punishments of the criminals they have condemned, <margin>(b)</margin> nor should they be "more merciful than the laws" in their judging. *Novels*, 82, chapter 10; Camman, dispute 4, thesis 70 and 72. Camman adds that the remissions of punishments (which they call the "gracing" of the accused, or commonly <term>Pardon: "Begnadigung" in German</term>), whether total or partial, are wrongly referred to High Jurisdiction alone. However, even the one who rules should not pardon every kind of crime for any delinquent. See *Code: On Punishments*, law 14; *Code: On the Episcopal Audience*, law 3. Camerarius, in his *Centuries*, the last chapter. <margin>(c)</margin> Above all, those crimes are excepted here which offend Divine Majesty, or which have a fixed punishment established by Divine Law, such as a crime considered to be plainly voluntary homicide. Camman, dispute 4, thesis 78 and following; Einsiedel, in the same place, number 67, folio 165; Arnisaeus, *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 3, number 6.

<margin>(b) A lower magistrate can temper a punishment for a cause provided by the laws, just as Tiraquellus records a hundred such causes; but Majesty can remit a punishment even against the laws, either out of pure grace or for another cause not sufficient according to the written laws—for example, out of pure grace he remits punishments of positive law, or for an insufficient cause he can even remit the penalty for homicide.</margin>

<margin>(c) He who held "pure empire" (High Jurisdiction) as it existed among Roman Magistrates could not grant grace; therefore, the power of gracing/pardoning belongs to Majesty or to Territorial Jurisdiction.</margin>

III. And if a person who has been deported or outlawed <note>original: "Bannitus"</note> is restored, the effect of this restoration must be judged based on the various ways of restoring. As Bocerus rightly advises, chapter 2, number 116 and following. However, a restorative grace does not benefit a person regarding property that was alienated by the treasury <note>original: "fiscus"</note> before the restoration. *Code: On the four-year prescription*, law 2; *Digest: On Minors*, law 24, § Scaevola. Just as the fruits <note>profits or produce</note> which the Treasury turned to its own use from the confiscated property are not included in the restoration. *Novels*, 115, chapter 2, § 14; Camman, in the same place, thesis 91.

# 1270 CHAPTER V. Dissertation

## WHAT THE SOVEREIGN POWER CAN DO REGARDING REWARDS AND HONORS.

->I.<-

Just as there is a great necessity for punishments, so too is it a great benefit to the health of the State if virtue is not left without rewards. It is of no less interest to the State that examples of virtue and good service be encouraged by the invitation of rewards, than that the wicked be restrained by the fear of punishments, as Kirchner (disputation 19, thesis 1, letter a) rightly feels against Bodin (Book 5 of *The Republic*, chapter 4). Hence, among the "Greater Royal Prerogatives" <note>original: "Regalibus majoribus"</note> is also placed the power of conferring the title of Duke, <margin>(d)</margin> Marquis, Count, Baron, etc. (Title *On the Fief of a March*; and the title *Who is Called a Duke* in the *Usages of Fiefs*; Rosenthal, *On Fiefs*, chapter 5, conclusion 2; Sixtin, Book 1, *On Royal Prerogatives*, chapter 2, number 113 and following; Camman, disputation 4, thesis 23 and following). To the Archdukes of Austria, <margin>(e)</margin> however, this royal right is uniquely granted; so much so, that they can rightly create not only nobles, but also Counts and Barons (Sixtin, Book 1, *On Royal Prerogatives*, chapter 4, number 34 and 64 and following; also chapter 5, number 127; Cluten in his *Collection*, thesis 25, where he cites the Privilege from Münster’s *Cosmographia*). Beyond these, this power is found to belong to no others among the Princes of the Empire, but to the Emperor alone: from whose Majesty, as if from a perennial fountain, all dignities are said to flow forth like streams (Law *Sacrilegis* 5, *Code of Justinian: On Various Rescripts*; Gail, Book 1, observation 30, number 21). To this also pertains the creation of Counts Palatine, so called in an abusive sense <note>meaning a title used outside its original strict legal context</note>; Sixtin (Book 1, chapter 4, number 103) asserts there is a great number of them in Germany (chapter 4, numbers 103 and 115).

---

<margin>(d)</margin> We speak here of title and honor alone, when the Emperor confers a title on someone without territory—for instance, if he makes a Duke or Prince out of a Count or Baron; we have an example in the Duke of Friedland <note>Albrecht von Wallenstein</note>, the Prince of Hohenzollern, Eggenberg, Liechtenstein, etc., where their domains were joined and the title of Duke was given to them. Thus the Count of Württemberg, the Count of Savoy, and the Count of Guelders were made Dukes. If, however, a territory is conferred at the same time—<gloss>when someone is invested with a banner-fief</gloss>—that will be discussed in the following chapter.

<column-break/>

<margin>(e)</margin> The Archdukes of Austria are privileged above others; in their own territories, according to Zasius, they are almost Kings.

II. And such honors (distributed only by the Emperor or those who possess Majesty) are also rightly considered the Orders of Knighthood. <margin>(f)</margin> Various types are found in various regions (Camman 5, thesis 10; Nolden, *On the Status of Nobles*, chapter 6, number 23 and following). And especially pertinent here is the Right of Ennobling <note>original: "Jus nobilitandi"</note>: because the Emperor alone can ennoble men, and it is placed in his judgment whom he wishes to make noble (Sole Law, *Code: On those who have received notice from the Prince*; law 10; penultimate law in the preface, section 1, *On Decurions*). This is shown at length by Tiraquellus in his treatise *On Nobility*, chapter 6, as well as by Carlos Tapia on the *Rubrics of the Pandects: On the Constitution of the Prince*, chapter 4, number 112 and following; Arnisaeus, Book 2, *On Majesty*, chapter 3, number 10; Nolden, *On the Status of Nobles*, chapter 6. And the illustrious Pliny says in his *Panegyric* that it belongs to Caesar to preserve and create nobles: a power which is also attributed to the King of the Persians in the Book of Esther, chapter 6, where it is written: "This man shall be honored, whomever the King has willed to honor." Lest the dignity be tainted by unworthiness, some military or civil <note>original: "togata," referring to the toga of a magistrate or scholar</note> virtue must be looked for in conferring nobility (Einsiedel, chapter 2, number 136). Then, one so ennobled truly attains the rights of nobility (Einsiedel, same location, number 137). However, whether the Emperor can ennoble someone to the effect that they may be admitted to equestrian games and to the Chapters of Canons—<gloss>to the high cathedral chapters</gloss> <margin>(g)</margin>—presents a greater doubt, which we shall see in the discourse (add Camman, disputation 4, thesis 31 and 42; Einsiedel, same location, number 138).

---

<margin>(f)</margin> <gloss>The knightly orders, when someone is dubbed a knight.</gloss> Equestrian dignity, however, differs from nobility: the former is only temporary <note>held for life</note>, while the latter is transferable to heirs.

<margin>(g)</margin> It is probable that those who are expressly ennobled in such a way that they have this right may be admitted to those knightly games: because it is only a certain civil honor, regarding which the Emperor can dispense at his pleasure. But I would think that this does not fall within the Emperor's competence regarding a Chapter of Canons; the reason for the difference is that it would be against the intention of the founders, and thus against the law of contract, which the Emperor cannot violate, etc.

### III.
Furthermore, a father who has obtained Nobility also has a noble son, even if the son was already born at the time the rank was achieved <note>original: "l. 5. ff. de Senatorib." – referring to the Digest of Roman Law regarding the status of children born before a father attains senatorial rank</note>. Regarding a Doctor of Law, however, it is more accurate to say that they possess a true, though temporary <note>meaning personal rather than hereditary</note>, nobility, even against the objections of Einsiedel. This is supported by the Political Ordinances <note>original: "Ordinationis Politicæ"</note> from the 1530 and 1548 Reformations of Augsburg in the section "On Doctors." All the contrary arguments made by Einsiedel only prove that Doctors do not possess *hereditary* nobility, a point which we also concede.

### IV.
To this I also refer the *right of creating Doctors, Licentiates, and Masters*: this power is also commonly granted to Counts Palatine <note>High-ranking officials of the Imperial court with the power to grant titles and degrees</note>. Such Doctors created by the Emperor or the Counts Palatine are commonly called (b) "Bullati" <note>named for the "bulla" or seal on their diploma; these were honorary degrees granted by decree rather than university examination</note>. It is often asked whether they ought to enjoy the same privileges as those promoted in a University. Einsiedel affirms this, and Limnæus proves it with many examples. However, if a specific statute requires a "promoted" Doctor or Licentiate (such as for the dignity of an Assessor in the Imperial Chamber Court), those with honorary degrees are rarely admitted. This is because statutes must be interpreted exactly as the words sound. Furthermore, Limnæus refers to the Baccalaureate as a dignity belonging to the Royal Prerogatives. The Emperor also grants—and the Counts Palatine are authorized by him to grant—the Poetic Laurel. It is said that the first Poetic Laurel among the Germans was granted to Conrad Celtis <note>A famous German humanist scholar and poet</note> by the favor of Emperor Maximilian I. To these we also add the power of creating Scriveners or Nota-

<column-break/>

ries. Such notaries, if they obtain their authority not from the Emperor or a Count Palatine but only from a State of the Empire <note>a local prince or territory</note>, cannot draft wills that are valid outside of that specific territory.

<insert>
(b) For this reason, they are to be considered equals: because their dignity proceeds from the same source. This is because both the Universities and the Counts Palatine create Doctors by the authority of the supreme Emperor, not by their own right. However, those created by decree (Bullati) must still be examined; if this is not done, a great error is committed.

## CHAPTER VI.
# ON THE SOVEREIGN APPOINTMENT OF MAGISTRATES.

### I.

The power to create Magistrates (a) for the administration of Justice is also rightly counted among the Royal Prerogatives of Majesty. This is supported by texts in the feudal laws and the Roman Code regarding judges and bribery. For as Pomponius says, what does it matter that there is Law in the City unless there are people who can administer the laws? For whose benefit would that Royal Prerogative of making laws exist if there were no ones to healthily distribute the Rights derived from them to the subjects? The power granted to Magistrates has its root in the Sovereign Majesty, in whom it exists most highly and properly. Therefore, Majesty contains within itself the jurisdictions of all Magistrates. However, lower Princes can appoint magistrates according to the jurisdiction granted to them. (b) Nevertheless, Jean Bodin <note>A famous French political philosopher</note> does not correctly conclude from this that the creation of magistrates is not a Royal Prerogative. As Einsiedel well proves, even then, those magistrates are appointed only by the permission of the Emperor, and by his silent or express consent.

expressed. And although in that single chapter <note>referring to the *Libri Feudorum* or Books of Fiefs, a standard medieval legal text</note>, the Sovereign Rights <term>Regalia: the specific rights, honors, and powers reserved for a sovereign ruler</term> are not explicitly listed, except for the appointment of Magistrates for the administration of Justice: nevertheless, deputies, local defenders, and other similar officials are rightly added to these: as Arnisaeus correctly judges in *On Majesty*, book 2, chapter 4, under number 11.

<margin>(a) The Law is a silent magistrate, but the magistrate is a speaking and living law; the soul of both is Majesty, and thus they proceed from the same source.</margin>

<margin>(b) Just as lower Princes can grant Statutes within the scope of their jurisdiction, they can also create magistrates through a secondary grant of power.</margin>

II. And since the Princes of Germany (c) (although they are found to possess greater power than the ancient Roman Governors and other officials) are nonetheless perpetual Magistrates: according to Arnisaeus, book 2, *On Majesty*, chapter 4, number 15. From this also, the royal benefits, or "Royal Fiefs," which our people call Banner and Scepter Fiefs <note>original: "Fahn- und Scepter-Lehen"; these were the highest class of fiefs held directly from the Emperor, symbolized by a banner for secular lords and a scepter for ecclesiastical ones</note>, depend upon and are granted by the Emperor alone; according to *Title 34, book 2 of the Fiefs; the Golden Bull of Charles IV in the title "On the Rights of the Count Palatine"; the Worms Ordinance of the year 1521, in the section "and we reserve for ourselves"; Bocer, chapter 2, number 59 and following; Einsiedel, book 2, number 19 and following.* And thus Rudolph I, Count of Habsburg, when Austria in his time was left without a legitimate heir, granted it—as a vacancy of the Empire—to his son Albert. From this comes the origin of the Dukes of Austria. By the same reasoning, the right of establishing the supreme imperial courts is a Sovereign Right belonging here: such as the Aulic Council <note>original: "der Reichs-Hof-Rath"; the Emperor’s personal judicial council</note>, the Imperial Chamber Court, and the Rottweil Court. Daniel Otto in his *Discourse on Public Law*, chapter 19, number 9.

<margin>(c) When Princes are granted the fiefs of Duchies, Counties, Baronies, etc., which contain within them the dignity of Sovereign Rights, they are by that very act appointed as quasi-magistrates and Lieutenants of the Emperor in that territory. The high courts or imperial tribunals are also in the place of a Magistrate.</margin>

## CHAPTER VII.
## ON VARIOUS SOVEREIGN RIGHTS CONCERNING THE CONSTITUTION OF THE COMMONWEALTH.

### I.
**I** refer here to the care and Right of the Imperial Diets <note>original: "Reichstag-Ausschreiben"; the formal summons or calling of the imperial assembly</note>. For the power of summoning them seems to belong to Majesty alone; and nothing is more contrary to that Majesty than if subjects were allowed to hold assemblies without the Prince's nod, and to deliberate on the highest affairs of state. *Einsiedel chapter 2, number 300; Camman 6, thesis 8 and following; Arnisaeus, book 2, On Majesty, chapter 4, number 16 and following*, where he wrote: the convocation of the Diets belongs to Majesty precisely when it belongs to one person in such a way that it is a crime for the rest to meet for the sake of taking counsel without his summons; he illustrates this with examples. However, although in the [Holy] Roman Empire the consent of the Electors is also necessary in this matter <note>original: "Sixtin. book 1, chapter 4, number 29"</note>, as some words of the Imperial Recesses <note>The final resolutions or decrees of an Imperial Diet</note> also imply, Jean Bodin (in *On the Republic*, book 9, number 122) quite unfairly strips our Emperor of his Majesty on those grounds. This is because Julius Caesar once shared this right with the people, and later Tiberius—excluding the common people—truly shared it with the Senate. *Camman, in the cited place, thesis 84.* Hence, almost equal to this is the power of permitting Corporations <term>Collegia: legal bodies, guilds, or organized societies</term>, which is also referred to among the Greater Sovereign Rights. *The whole title in the Digest on Corporations and Bodies; Matthias Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 2, part 2, chapter 6, number 58; Joachim Stephani on Jurisdiction, book 1, chapter 8, number 38, and book 4, chapter 6, number 1.* And since these are regularly unlawful, they are granted only by the authority of the Prince. *Camman 2, thesis 37 and following.*

### II.
Another such sovereign right is the power of granting the Right of Citizenship <note>original: "Jus Civitatis"</note> by express or tacit will. *The single law, where Cujas comments, Code on the Metropolis of Beirut, book 11; Constitution on the Peace of Constance, the section "we will"; Bocer 2, number 231; Einsiedel 2, number 206 and following.* Indeed, a city established by the authority of an inferior person would seem worthy neither of the Privileges nor the name of a "City." *Chapter "you have signified," the section "furthermore," in the decretals on the significance of words.* And so today, regarding the constitution...

Likewise, the Right of admitting or receiving Jews is usually reduced to the Sovereign Rights <term>Regalia: the specific rights and privileges held only by a sovereign ruler</term>. This is found in the *Imperial Recess* <term>Reichs-Abschied: the formal resolutions passed by the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire</term> from the year 1548, in the title *concerning Jews and their usury*. See also the *Police Ordinance* of the year 1577, title 20; Sixtinus, book 1, chapter 5, n. 16; and Einsiedel 2, n. 283. For this reason, in the Golden Bull <term>Aur. Bull.: a decree issued by Emperor Charles IV in 1356 that served as a constitutional document for the Empire</term> of Charles IV, under the title *concerning Gold, Silver, and other Ores*, this sovereign right is granted to the King of Bohemia and the other Electors by special grace.

<margin>(a) An **Ambassador** <note>original: *Legatus*</note> is one sent by a superior to another superior, such as a King to a King. A **Commissioner** <note>original: *Commissarius*</note> is when a superior sends someone to an inferior subject. When an inferior sends to a superior, they are called **Emissaries** <term>Abgesandthe: a German term for deputies or messengers sent from a lower to a higher authority</term>. When someone sends an ambassador who does not have the authority to do so—such as rebels or those whose sovereignty is disputed—they send **Agents** <note>original: *Agentes*</note>, which is to say, messengers.</margin>

III. The *Right* of Embassy (a) also pertains to the constitution of the Commonwealth; therefore, subjects are not permitted to send or receive Ambassadors. (Clapmarius, book 1, chapter 18; Arnisaeus, book 2 on *Majesty*, chapter 5, number 16). Indeed, as Cicero says in *Against Vatinius*, Ambassadors are messengers of Peace and War, caretakers, interpreters, and authors of Military Counsel, etc. Therefore, they cannot be sent by anyone except those who have power over all these matters and who can give mandates concerning them. However, nothing prevents the choice of ambassadors from being made by a Senate or a Chancellor, provided they receive their mandates from the Sovereign Power. Consequently, those sent by rebels to report on their demands and desires are not called Ambassadors so much as they are called Messengers.

The Princes of Germany claim the Right of sending Ambassadors, which they pretend to have by Privilege; nevertheless, if this is true and such a Right belongs to them, it must be understood as being without prejudice to the Empire and the Emperor, nor does it extend to the enemies of the Empire.

Likewise, if Ambassadors are sent to them and they negotiate anything to the prejudice of the Emperor, then the Princes, by virtue of the oath of loyalty they have sworn, ought to denounce those matters to the Emperor.

IV. So too, the power to strike treaties <note>original: *fœdera*</note> with foreigners for the protection of the Commonwealth is usually

<column-break/>

counted among the Sovereign Rights—and indeed the "greater" ones—pertaining to the Constitution of the Commonwealth. (Novellae 105, in the beginning; Clapmarius 1, chapter 20; Sixtinus 2, chapter 1, number 29; Waremundus ab Erenberg 1 on *Treaties*, 1, numbers 40 and 42; chapter 2, number 28 and following; and book 2, chapter 1, number 34 and following). From this it follows that it is unlawful for lower Princes or those Cities which are in the position of private citizens to contract treaties. (Law 16, *Digest on the meaning of words*; Arnisaeus 1, *Politics*, 12, page 327; and chapter 8, page 434). And thus some also say that by Privilege and tacit concession, this Right has been granted to the Electors, the Princes of the Empire, and likewise to the Free Imperial Cities. (Waremundus 1, chapter 2, numbers 228 and 231). However, such treaties further require that they be founded upon the preservation of the public peace, and that not only the Empire but also the Emperor be specifically excepted from any hostile action. (Camman 5, thesis 85 and following).

<margin>(b) Because defense is the duty of the superior and the ordinary Lord; but he who seeks another defender either treats his own Lord with contempt or is defecting from him.</margin>

Furthermore, the consequence of this is that it is by no means permitted for a People or a City that recognizes a superior to subject themselves to the protection of another more powerful ruler without the superior's consent: (b) unless it has been otherwise accepted by the customs of the ancestors. (*Imperial Recess* of the year 1548, § 4; Thomas Michael, *Disputation on Jurisdiction*, thesis 138; The Presiding Lord in his *Treatise on Treaties*, chapter 3, number 13).

V. Not inaptly, one might also refer here to the *Power of granting Security, or Safe Conduct*, to murderers or other criminals, so that they may defend and prove their innocence. (c) (Law 4, *Digest on punishments*; Law 1, where the Doctors discuss the *Digest on the Julian Law of Majesty*; Knichen, *On the Saxon Law of not appealing*, under the word *Dukes*, chapter 5, number 96; Bodin, book 5, chapter 6, pages 603 and 605). However, for such security to be valid, the crimes committed must be expressly entered into the records. (Bodin, cited number 605). Nor does the security of arriving always include the security of departing. For such safe conduct is given for the purpose of stating one's case in Court, and as a protection against violence and the hardship of prison, but not against the execution of the Law. (Mynsinger, century 1, observation 82; Johann Molanus, *On keeping faith with heretics*, book 2, chapter...

### VI.
To these we add the **Right of fairs and markets**, referencing the *Digest* book 1 and the *Code* 'concerning fairs.' For the care and regulation of commerce and public trade, because of their extreme necessity and utility, belongs entirely to the Majesty <note>Here "Majesty" refers to the office of the sovereign ruler or the Emperor</note>, as argued by Camman in *Discourse 6, thesis 2 and following*. Today, the more famous fairs of the Empire or of a single Province are called *Nundinae*, or **Large Fairs** <note>original: *Messen*</note>; these are held at certain fixed times with a very large gathering of merchants in those places where the right to hold them has been granted by the benefit of the Prince or by long-standing custom—such as the Frankfurt Fairs in Germany. However, the *Mercatus* are smaller fairs of a single city or village, called **Annual Markets** <note>original: *Jahrmärckt*</note>. Cujas, in his *Commentary on the Code 'concerning Fairs.'* From both of these, however, the weekly market—the **Weekly Market** <note>original: *Wochenmarckt*</note>—differs; since cities and villages cannot do without these, they can be established by any local magistrate (Bocer, 2, number 239). Furthermore, the Emperor is not accustomed to granting the Privilege of Fairs unless the neighbors and adjacent cities are first heard, since it may affect their interests (Gail, book 2, observation 69, number 25; Gothofredus on the *Digest* book 1 'concerning Fairs'). Once this right is granted, public security for those who gather there for the sake of the market is understood to be granted at the same time. Therefore, under the pretext of a private or civil debt, they cannot be summoned, imprisoned, or arrested (see the cited law where Sichardus notes this). Also, the Prince may, for a valid reason, revoke this right and transfer it to another city (following the legal argument in the chapter *translato* from the *Decretals*), as occurred when the Frankfurt Fairs were at one time transferred to Mainz. Similar to this right is the Right of the Emporium, called the **Free Storage or Staple Right** <note>original: *freye Niederlag, oder Stappel Gerechtigkeit*</note>;

<column-break/>

which also only the Emperor bestows. Those who enjoy this right can compel and force merchants to stop there and offer their goods for sale (Mynsinger, century 5, observation 19, number 3; Nicolas Everhard the Younger, counsel 9, book 1; Maulius, *On the Right of Transport*, title 3, number 21 and following). In such cases, those transporting goods by carriage or ship may not seek out new routes to avoid such a "staple" or deposit (Everhard, number 82).

### VII.
The **Right of the Archive** <note>original: *Jus Archivi*</note> also seems to belong to such Sovereign Rights; specifically, that documents deposited within it are legally valid and provide proof, even if they otherwise lack certain formalities. See Ruland, *On Commissions*, part 1, book 5, chapter 4. Add Camman, *Discourse 6, thesis 78 and following*. This right seems to belong to all States of the Empire and extends even outside their own territory (Ruland, in the same place).

### VIII.
Furthermore, to the greater Sovereign Rights that serve to avert the inconveniences of social life and procure its comforts, we add the **Right of Language or Idiom**, by which a certain language is prescribed to everyone in a territory (d). Bodin, *On the Republic*, book 1, last chapter, number 172. It is even traded as a "secret of state" <note>original: *arcano*</note> that conquered provinces should be forced to use the language of the ruler (Clapmar, book 3, chapter 22). By this reasoning, the Romans made their language the vernacular in nearly all their provinces (The Presiding Lord <note>referring to the professor or head of the academic disputation</note>, *On the Growth of Empires*, last chapter, number 10), so much so that even the Greek language was once prohibited in Rome (The Most Eminent Cardinal Baronius, *Year of Christ 402, number 13*). So too, Rudolph I ordered that contracts should no longer be written in Latin, but only in German (Lehman, in the **Speyer Chronicle**, book 5, chapter 107).

<insert>
(d) Thus in Sacred matters we use the Latin language to preserve the majesty of the Roman Church.
</insert>

### IX.
To these Sovereign Rights we likewise add the **Right of establishing and confirming Public Routes**, which we call **Posts** <note>original: *Postas*</note>, according to the title in the *Code* 'concerning public transport', book 12.

## X.
To these same Sovereign Rights, we also add the **Right of Minting Money**: and indeed both the striking, stamping, and establishing of its value and power, as well as the method of rejecting and abolishing it, *title 56, "what are Sovereign Rights," book 2 of Feuds.* This right has, for many centuries now in all States, belonged to the Majesty and the head of government, *the penultimate and last laws of the Code "concerning false money," and law 1 of the Code "concerning the power of ancient coinage," book 11.* The Recess of the Imperial Diet of Nuremberg of the year 1570, § **Then also the Right of Coinage** <note>original: *Alsdann auch die Müntz-Gerechtigkeit*</note>. Clapmar, *book 1, chapter 16.* Bocer, *2, number 222 and following.* Einsiedel, *chapter 2, number 212.* Camman, *discourse 6, thesis 12 and following.* Discussed at length by Arnisæus, *on Majesty, book 2, chapter 7.* However, although that Right is also shared with the Princes and Estates of the Empire, and today is divided into almost as many parts as there are Principalities, Counties, and Cities; nevertheless, this occurs by a singular privilege of the Emperor, and thus the essence and form of such a Sovereign Right remains secure. Hence, anyone who dares to mint even honest money without the knowledge of the Emperor is judged to commit the crime of treason <term>crimen laesae maiestatis: an offense against the dignity and authority of the sovereign</term>. *laws 1 and 2 of the Code "concerning false money."* Bocer, *on the Crime of Treason, chapter 2, number 61 and following.* And for the same reason, one who adulterates the money of any State of the Empire is punished with the same penalty as if it had been done to the Emperor's own coinage. Bocer, *on the law of money, chapter 2, number 1.* Furthermore, to this Sovereign Right of currency must be connected the **system of weights, measures, bushels, and ells**; so that for these, a certain 

<column-break/>

standard or quantity may be prescribed for the more successful use of commerce, *law 9 of the Code "concerning collectors," book 10.* Camman, *discourse 6, thesis 42.* The Lord Presiding Officer, *on the Rights of Majesty, chapter 8, number 9.* As well as the power to establish a banking table, **to set up an exchange** <note>original: *einen Wechsel anzustellen*</note>. *the said title 56, "what are Sovereign Rights."* Papon, *book 5, title 1, decree 8.* Extensively in Bocer, *chapter 3, number 181 and following.* Although others wish for the name "Banking Tables" <note>original: *Argentariarum*</note> to be understood as metal mines. *Einsiedel on Sovereign Rights, chapter 3, number 30 and following.*

### CHAPTER VIII.

### ON THE SOVEREIGN RIGHT WHICH
### MAJESTY POSSESSES IN PUBLIC
### PLACES (a).

(a) **Common places** <note>original: *Loca communia*</note> belong to all nations by reason of their use, and by reason of ownership belong to no one. However, **public places** <note>original: *Loca publica*</note> belong to the people where those places exist, by reason of both ownership and use. Nevertheless, regarding jurisdiction, both belong to the Majesty, and these roles do not exclude each other; for a Prince holds jurisdiction over his subjects, not ownership. That jurisdiction pertains only to direction, ensuring that everyone uses these things properly, and that they do not plot anything against the Commonwealth through their use. Thus, he prohibits the use of navigation to enemies and others who would harm the Commonwealth. Likewise, in places where hunting is permitted, an order of hunting is given so that species do not perish; in this way, liberty is not hindered, but rather preserved.

**I.** Although the **sea**, and through this the **sea shores**, are counted among common things—*§ 1 of the Institutes "on the division of things"; law 14; law 30 at the end of the Digest "on acquiring ownership of things"*—nevertheless, regarding jurisdiction, they are considered to belong to the Ruling Prince—*law "shores" of the Digest "Lest anything in a public place..."* Noë Meurer, <term>On Water Law</term> <note>original: *vom Wasserrecht*; a famous 16th-century treatise on maritime and river law</note>, folio 85 and following. The Lord Presiding, *on the law of things, chapter 1, number 8.* Thus, the sea is argued to belong to the nearest [ruler] for one hundred miles, and even beyond if it does not approach another's province, as Alberico Gentili discusses in *Spanish Advocacy, book 1, chapter 8.* Likewise, an **island** born in the sea becomes the property of the one who occupies it (b), since it is believed to belong to no one; *§...*

<column-break/>

<warning>Left edge of second column is tightly bound/clipped, resulting in partial words at the start of many lines.</warning>

...the Island section of the *Institutes on the Division of Things; law 7, paragraph 1 of the Digest on acquiring ownership.* Nevertheless, the supreme power and jurisdiction over it belongs to him who holds the province on the nearest mainland—*argued from law 9, "Island," of the Digest on Judgments.* Cepolla, *on Rural Servitudes, chapter 26, number 14.* Gilander, *on the Island, chapter 11.* In this respect also, **ports** (both artificial and natural) are counted among Sovereign Rights, not only regarding taxes but also regarding jurisdiction and command—*title 56, book 2 of Feuds.* See Bocer, *chapter 3, number 2 and following.* Einsiedel, *chapter 3, number 54.* Arnisæus, *on Majesty, book 3, chapter 5, number 3.* Camman, *7, thesis 46.*

(b) But as private individuals, not as Princes; however, the Spaniard [King of Spain] holds the New Islands <note>Refers to the Americas/West Indies</note> by right of war.

**II.** At this point, **navigable rivers** and those from which they become navigable must also be added to the Sovereign Rights of Majesty—*said title 56, book 2 of Feuds.* These same rivers are under public care and protection, and again by reason of jurisdiction—*law 2 of the Digest "concerning rivers"; the whole title of the Code "on aqueducts," book 11.* Bocer, *chapter 2, number 163.* Sixtin, *book 2.* Arnisæus, *book 3, chapter 5, number 2.* Camman, *discourse 7, thesis 16 and following, as well as thesis 28 and following.* Einsiedel, *chapter 3, number 274 and following.* From this perspective also, regarding the more principal rivers, if they flow through the lands of nobles, the Princes are accustomed to exercise the right of territory there—*Johann Bidenbach in "Consilia of the Noble," question 13.* If a river separates two territorial Lords and serves as a boundary, then each has jurisdiction to the middle. By the same reasoning, **riverbank rights** <note>original: *ripatica*; the right to collect dues or manage the banks of a river</note> are numbered among Sovereign Rights in the often-cited *title 56, book 2 of Feuds*; and indeed not only in respect to taxes, but also by reason of other rights which the Emperor has on the banks of public rivers—*Peregrinus, book 1 on the Law of the Fisc, title 1, number 24.* See Bocer, *chapter 3, number 135 and following.* Einsiedel, *chapter 3, number 59 and following.* Camman, *discourse 11, thesis 4 and following.* Although otherwise the ownership of the banks belongs to those whose estates they border—*§ "of banks" 4 of the Institutes, and law 5 of the Digest on the Division of Things.* (c) Likewise, **mills** belong to Sovereign Rights—*Hering on Mills, question 9 and following.* This is because it is not permitted to build a mill in a public river without the license of the Prince—*law...*

**III.** Furthermore, among Sovereign Rights, **Palaces** are also counted: (d) as often stated in title 56. Bocer chapter 2. number 162. Arnisaeus book 3 *On Majesty* chapter 5 at the end. Einsiedel chapter 2. number 260. Sixtin book 2. chapter 17. Camman 7. thesis 16. and many following. Namely, these are buildings prepared for the use of the Emperor, and excluded from all use by private citizens and common habitation; law "to no judgment" 14. *Code* <note>original: C.</note> on the office of the Rector of the province; law "Whoever" 17. *Code* on public works; and the single law of the *Code* on Palaces and lordly houses, book 11. Likewise, the German Emperors chose certain cities for themselves as their accustomed habitations, and from such palaces they are called **Palatine Cities** <note>original: *Pfalz-Städt*</note>, among which are primarily placed **Aachen** <note>original: Aquisgranum</note>, **Goslar**, and also the **Nuremberg Castle**, as well as the **Tübingen Castle**, *Podmen*, etc. From these Palaces descends the name of the **Counts Palatine**: and in general, whoever serves in the sacred Palace is called **Palatines** throughout the entire title of the *Code* on the privileges of those who serve in the sacred Palace. Lord Johannes Jacobus Speidel in *Notable Matters* on the word **Counts Palatine** <note>original: *Pfaltzgrafen*</note> from the beginning.

<gloss>(d) In every great city, the Emperors had magnificent houses, and by reason of them, the right to stay there, which was followed by the rights of lodging for the courtiers—*lodging for the court staff* <note>original: die Einquartierung für den Hofstaat</note>.</gloss>

**IV.** Similarly, to these Sovereign Rights are added **public roads** (e) —*the common provincial or Imperial free military roads* <note>original: die gemeine Land- oder Kayserliche freye Heer-Strassen</note>, title 56. book 2. *On Feuds*. Heinrich Bocer *On Sovereign Rights* chapter 2. number 144. etc. Einsiedel chapter 2. number 262. and following. Camman 5. thesis 21. and following. Arnisaeus book 3. chapter 5. number 1. This is to be understood primarily by reason of the care and power over them. And thus, the knowledge and execution of a crime committed on a public road belongs to the Lord of the territory; not to him who has jurisdiction on one or the other side of the road. See Bocer in the stated place

<column-break/>

number 145. Einsiedel in the stated chapter 2. number 266. Sixtin book 2. chapter 2. number 16. Camman 5. thesis 36. and following. And so, among the Sovereign Rights is also numbered the **Right of Escort** <note>original: Jus conducendi</note>, *territorial authority to escort on free military roads* <note>original: Gleitliche Obrigkeit, auf freyer Heer-strassen zu gleiten</note>. Thomas Maulius in his treatise on the right of escort, title 1. where he says this right passes along with territorial jurisdiction. For the right of escort is an effect of the sovereign status of the public road. Therefore, the opinion of those who say that he who holds the Sovereign Right of the public road is obligated to compensate the traveler for damage is not absurd (for although it is not stated openly, it seems to be promised tacitly) which the traveler suffered there through the injury of a robber; *Imperial Recess at Augsburg, of the year 1559. §. So that then the authorities* <note>An "Imperial Recess" was the final resolution of an Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. See Bocer in the stated place number 154. and following. Camman 5. thesis 42. and following. Einsiedel in the stated place number 265. Arnisaeus in the stated place. Maulius in the stated place titles 3. 7. and 9. Especially in that case when a toll or tax was paid on that account; and Matthias Mynsinger asserts this is confirmed by the precedents of the Imperial Chamber, century 5. observation 70. Gail book 2. observation 64. and the **Saxon Law** agrees in these words: *If someone gives a safe conduct, he shall also protect him from harm* <note>original: Wann einer einem Gleit gibt, der soll ihn auch vor Schaden behüten</note>, *Saxon District Law* <note>original: Landr.</note> book 2. article 27.

<gloss>(e) By reason of care, protection, and jurisdiction.</gloss>
