### CHAPTER IX.

## CONCERNING SOVEREIGN RIGHTS THAT BRING SOME FISCAL BENEFIT.

**I.** The **Treasury** <note>original: Fiscus</note>, as far as our purpose is concerned, is the **Exchequer** <note>original: Ærarium</note> of the Prince, or of another holding Majesty, embracing all things that pertain to his pecuniary benefit: fortified by certain privileges, and instituted for the use and maintenance of Majesty. Einsiedel chapter 3. number 8. and following. And in this regard it is said that no one can have a Treasury unless he recognizes no superior: Nicolaus Betfius *On the compacts of illustrious families* page 429. and in respect of such

It also introduces the concept of the Fiscus, or public treasury, as a sovereign right intended for the support of the state.</summary>

# Dissertation

Our learned Doctors distinguish the **Treasury** <note>original: *fiscus*</note>, by its privileges, from other treasuries and common purses held by cities and others, which do not enjoy these privileges unless they have acquired them legitimately. See Einsiedel in the cited place, number 14.

(a) The Treasury consists partly of the **Domain**, or the goods of the Crown, which we call **the Chamber estate** <note>original: *das Kammergut*</note>; and partly of other revenues owed to the Majesty alone. For in the beginning, it seemed entirely appropriate for the Republic that a certain portion of public goods be assigned to its supreme moderator to suffice for daily expenses. Thus, when something must be spent for the utility of the Republic or the dignity of the ruler, he does not find it necessary to immediately resort to exactions <note>extraordinary taxes</note>. Arnisaeus, *On Majesty*, book 3, chapter 3, at the beginning. To these also belong the **tributes**, or burdens on fruits (*Digest* 7.2. at the end, and *Digest* 13 regarding expenses on dotal property). These are offered by reason of the possession of private soil (*Code* 2, and the final law "without census" and others; Arnisaeus, *On Majesty*, last book, last chapter, number 8; Mr. Speidel under the word **Tax** <note>original: *Steur*</note>, in *Notabil*).

<margin>(a) In Roman Law there was a difference between the **Treasury** <note>original: *Fiscus*</note> and the **Public Treasury** <note>original: *Ærarium*</note>. For the *Fiscus* belonged to the Prince, while the *Ærarium* belonged to the people. Just as today **the Provincial Estates** <note>original: *die Landschafft*</note> or the Provincial States have their own Chest and revenues: likewise **the Cities and Villages** <note>original: *die Städt, Dörffer*</note> have a Purse or Chest.</margin>

And it is called the Treasury <note>Fiscus</note> not merely because of the money, but because of the **privileged methods** by which it can be made wealthier.

The goods of the Prince are distinguished by some as follows: (1) certain goods belong to the Prince as a **private individual**. Thus our Emperor holds Austria as a private person by right of the Empire, as **his hereditary land** <note>original: *sein Erbland*</note>. (2) There are goods called the **Dowry of the Crown** <note>original: *Dos Coronæ*</note>; for a marriage is considered to have been entered into between the Kingdom (or Crown) and the Prince. These are called **Domainial Goods**, or **permanent Chamber goods** <note>original: *beständige Kammergüter*</note>. (3) Some are specifically called **Fiscal goods**, which are, as it were, the fruits of Jurisdiction and its execution. Belonging to the "Domain" properly so called are certain immovable goods whose fruits the Prince makes his own, as well as Tributes, or **the ordinary tax** <note>original: *die ordentliche Steur*</note>.

**II.** The Treasury is likewise increased—and this prevents us from having to reach for extraordinary remedies to enrich it—by the **proceeds from fines and penalties**; (b) which

<column-break/>

are therefore ascribed to the **Sovereign Rights** <note>original: *Regalibus*</note> (stated in Title 56, book 2 of the *Feuds*; Law 5 and the last law, § 4, of the *Code* "on the manner of fines"; law "Whoever" § "if ignorant" of the *Code* "on heretics"; **Imperial Chamber Court Ordinance, part 1, title 15, §** "Imperial Fiscal," and the following paragraph; Bocer number 8; Einsiedel chapter 3, number 68 and following; Kamman, discourse 9, thesis 27 and following). However, this Sovereign Right is found to belong to other lower authorities, and even to Nobles, either by a grant from the Emperor or certainly by immemorial prescription (Chapter "concerning certain things," § "furthermore," in the *Decretals* "on the meaning of words"; Bocer, ibid, number 17 and 18). In this view, it is said today that the proceeds of fines and penalties are the **fruits of Jurisdiction**. Knissenthal chapter 5, conclusion 63; Einsiedel, cited place, number 117; Kamman, cited place, thesis 56; Mr. Speidel under the phrase "Trespass and Fine" <note>original: *Frevel und Busser*</note>. Of the same law are the **goods of the condemned and the proscribed** (often cited Title 56; Bocer chapter 3, number 59 and 60; Einsiedel *On Sovereign Rights* chapter 3, number 177 and following; Camman, cited discourse 9, thesis 2 and many following). This must, however, be understood according to the tenor of the **New Constitutions** <note>the *Novels* of Justinian</note>; where property is not taken from all condemned persons (d) (Novel 134, last chapter; *Authentica* "goods of the condemned," *Code* "on the goods of the proscribed"; **Imperial Criminal Court Ordinance, Article 218** <note>original: *Peinliche Halsgerichts-artic. 218*</note>; Einsiedel, cited place, number 184; Kamman, cited place, number 8 and following; Arnisaeus *On Majesty*, last book, chapter 6, number 15 and following). But even today, the goods of a **traitor** <note>original: *perduellis*</note> go to the Treasury (Einsiedel 3, number 198 and 199; Sixtin 2 *On Sovereign Rights*, chapter 20; Kamman, discourse 10, thesis 66 and following; Arnisaeus book 3, chapter 6, number 2 and many following). As do those of **heretics**, and even more so of **sorcerers and witches** <note>original: *Sortilegorum, & Lamiarum*</note> (Chapter "declining," in the *Decretals* "on heretics"; chapter "since according to," in the same title in the *Sext*; Mr. Friederich Martini in the Appendix to the title "on annual revenues"). Likewise, if someone kills himself out of a bad conscience regarding a crime and fear of future punishment, and the crime is of such a nature that confiscation takes place, then his goods also belong to the Treasury (*Digest* 45.2 "on the law of the treasury"; *Code* 2 "who can make a will"; Peregrinus *On the Law of the Treasury*, book 4, title 4; Menochius *On Arbitrary Judgments*, case 284).

<margin>(b) Because the Prince cannot manage all business at the expense of his own Chamber, he is forced to resort to extraordinary means of collecting money. However, this is burdensome to the subjects, therefore the benefits [of fines...]</margin>

<summary>This page defines the Treasury (Fiscus) as a sovereign right, distinguishing between the ruler's private property, crown lands, and revenues derived from the legal system. It details how fines, confiscations from criminals (including traitors and witches), and the estates of certain suicides serve as primary sources of state income to avoid over-taxing the citizenry.</summary>

(c) General fines and the confiscation of territories belong to the Emperor; however, particular fines regarding a specific territory belong to lower lords. In the case of the Nobility, these are not considered Sovereign Rights, but are called **common offenses and fines** <note>original: *gemeine Frevel und Bussen*</note>.

(d) **A later law repeals an earlier one** <note>original: *Lex posterior derogat priori*</note>, but the Constitution of Frederick (title 50) is more recent than Justinian’s law. Therefore, it should repeal Justinian’s; however, this is answered by the limitation placed here. Otherwise, a special law repeals a general later law even if the special one is earlier in time, unless the general law specifically and by name repeals the earlier one. If this is not done, we remain with the rule that **the specific repeals the general** <note>original: *species deroget generi*</note>. This is especially true when the general law is still observed in certain specific cases. **III.** To these Sovereign Rights are also added the goods of those contracting incestuous marriages, as noted in the said title 56, *Which are sovereign rights*, book 2 of the Feuds; also in the law *if anyone 6* joined with the authority on incestuous marriages in the Code and the Novels (Chapter 2, section 1, § 2). Although the Constitution of Emperor Frederick in the said title 56 seems to speak generally, it nonetheless receives a restriction from Justinian law. Under that law, it is provided that the goods of those contracting incestuous marriages be left to their legitimate children up to the third degree of kinship. If there are no children, the goods go to their parents up to the second degree. If even these are not living, the goods are granted to a brother, sister, paternal uncle, or paternal aunt. Only if all these relatives are lacking are the goods finally brought into the treasury <note>original: *fiscus*</note>. See Cujas on this location, and Bocer (chapter 3, number 53 and following), and Arnisæus on Majesty. We do not, however, extend this penalty to incestuous betrothals <note>original: *sponsalia*</note> (e). See Schneidewin on the title of marriages. Nor do we extend it to incestuous carnal union without marriage. Teffaur and Sixtinus agree, though Einsiedel dissents. Truly, incestuous marriages celebrated publicly give rise to confiscation, even if physical union did not follow. This is because the Sacrament is publicly prostituted, and marriages exist even without physical union, according to the legal argument that **consent, not cohabitation, makes a marriage.**

<column-break/>

This is found in the rules of law, and Sixtinus (chapter 11, number 49), where again Einsiedel dissents. To this also belong the goods taken from those who are **unworthy** <note>original: *indignis*</note> to inherit. This is covered in the said title 56 and various sections of the Digest regarding the rights of the treasury and those who are disqualified as unworthy. See Bocer (chapter 3, number 38) and Camman.

In such a case, when a person who is unworthy loses an inheritance, it is presumed he did so through fraud. Thus, the Treasury excludes any substitute heir, contrary to the opinion of Bocer. However, these advantages also belong to those who hold territorial jurisdiction. See Camman and his 8th dispute.

(e) Penal laws are subject to a stricter interpretation, especially where the underlying reason is not the same. The reason for the difference in betrothals is that they can be rescinded, and in them, there is room for repentance. In carnal union, however, the scandal is not as public as in a marriage, nor is such a great injury done to the Sacrament.

**IV.** **Unclaimed goods** <note>original: *Bona vacantia*</note> also fall to the treasury by Sovereign Right, as frequently stated in title 56 and the Digest and Code regarding the rights of the treasury and vacant goods. However, in this matter, paternal and maternal relatives—even beyond the 10th degree—are preferred over the Treasury. See Bocer and Camman. And here likewise can be referred that quite unjust custom of the French, where the inheritances of foreigners fall to the treasury; they call this <term>le droict d' Aubaine</term> <note>The "Right of Aubaine" was a historical law in France where the state claimed the property of a deceased foreigner who was not naturalized.</note>, as if it refers to those born elsewhere. See Petrus Gregorius and Arnisæus. Likewise, items held as abandoned: namely, all things movable or immovable which are possessed by no one. Strabo mentions how the Roman Emperors in **Egypt** once searched through a certain Magistrate to see if there were any vacant goods, deserted possessions, or other things without a master, so that they might be incorporated into the Domain or the ownership of the Emperors. So too, half of a **Treasure** <note>original: *Thesauri*</note> found in a public or fiscal place belongs to the treasury if found by chance; but if one searched for it deliberately, the whole of it belongs to the treasury. See the end of the chapter *Which are sovereign rights*, and Bocer and Einsiedel.

But wherever it may be found, if it was detected by the Lord of the place through the use of magic arts, I would judge that it belongs entirely to the Treasury <note>original: *fiscum*; the state's central fund</note>. See Bocer in the cited location, number 180; Einsiedel at number 392 and 419, etc.; Camman, 8th thesis, 33, etc. Furthermore, it is even more the case today that a Treasure found in a Sacred or religious place is claimed for the Church. See Schneidewin on the section "Treasure," number 9, Institutes on the Division of Things; Peregrinus, book 4 on the Right of the Treasury, chapter 2, number 7; contrary to Bocer, chapter 3, number 179; Caspar Bitshius’s treatise on treasures, number 238, etc.

### V.
To the Sovereign Rights <note>original: *Regalibus*</note> are also joined the mines of gold and every other precious metal. Indeed, in some places this is by custom by reason of ownership—see the Constitution of Henry VI in Goldast, volume 3 of the Imperial Constitutions, page 362, which is also cited by Einsiedel, book 3, number 327; the Golden Bull <note>The 1356 decree defining the structure of the Holy Roman Empire</note> under the title **concerning gold, silver, and other ores** <note>original: *von Gold, Silber, und andern Erz*</note>; and the **Saxon District Court** <note>original: *Sächsisch Landgericht*; likely referring to the *Sachsenspiegel*</note>, book 1, article 35, where it says **all treasures** <note>original: *alle Schätze*</note>, and likewise mines, which are themselves subterranean treasures, **deeper than the plow goes, belong to the Royal power** <note>original: *tieffer dann der Pflug gehet, gehört zum Königlichen Gewalt*</note>. Regarding Civil Law, however, our Doctors say this is only to be understood regarding the metallic tax <note>original: *Canonem metallicum*; a fee paid to the sovereign for mining</note>. See laws 3 and the penultimate law of the Code on Miners, book 11; Bocer, book 3, number 164, etc.; Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 306 and following; Lord Speidel in his Notable Observations under the entries **Mine** <note>original: *Bergwerck*</note> and **Ore Pits** <note>original: *Erzgruben*</note>. And they extend this to all fossils and metals of any kind, such as alum, etc., as well as precious stones, gems, and marble, and their mines. See Arnisaeus, last book, chapter 5, number 4, page 555; Camman, disputation book 7, thesis 85 and following, and thesis 91 and following, as well as thesis 193. Hence we see mention made in title 56 of the income from salt works, **salt springs** <note>original: *Salzbrunnen*</note>. See Bocer, book 3, number 175 and following; Einsiedel, book 3, number 328 and following; Camman, disputation 7, thesis 102; as well as pitch works, or mines of pitch. See Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 335 and 337; Camman, 7, thesis 101.

### VI.
Although in ancient times the capture of wild beasts was permitted to everyone—see the section "Wild Beasts" in the Institutes on the Division of Things, and law 1 of the Digest on Acquiring Ownership of Things—since indeed wild beasts belonged to no one, and thus ceded to the one occupying them (see law 3 of the same title); today, however, wild beast hunting <note>original: *Venationes*</note>, (f) or rather the Law of the Forest—**Forest

<column-break/>

Jurisdiction** <note>original: *die Forstliche Obrigkeit*</note>—seems to be added to the number of Sovereign Rights. See Arnisaeus at length in book 3 on Majesty, chapter 4, throughout, especially at the end; Camman, disputation 7, thesis 65 and many following, as well as thesis 74, etc.; Heigius, part 1, question 9, number 44. There, he says nothing is truer or more manifest, unless one wishes to close their eyes in clear light. See, however, the Dissertation of Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 348 and following; as well as Bocer, chapter 1, number 30 and many following. And for this reason also in the investitures <note>legal ceremonies granting land or rights</note> by which Sovereign Rights are granted in Germany, there is usually a standard clause: **with the ground, game preserve, and hunts** <note>original: *mit Boden, Wildbann, Jagten*</note>, etc. This was perhaps done by the right of the victors, so that the Franks, the Alemanni, and other Northern peoples retained this right for themselves because they occupied other provinces. Nor is it new that in different places certain rights are held as Sovereign Rights which elsewhere are not recognized as such. Thus in Sicily, it was formerly not permitted to marry off a daughter without the King's license, which was also practiced elsewhere. See Arnisaeus, book 2 on Majesty, chapter 3, under number 10. But this is said historically and by example; it should not be understood as if it were approved. Truly, just like hunting, several authors also refer the right of fowling <note>bird hunting</note> to the Sovereign Rights. See Camman in the cited disputation 7, thesis 56. In this view, in title 56 of the second book of the Feuds, the income from fishing is joined to the Sovereign Rights. See Bocer, chapter 3, number 140 and following; Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 136 and following; Camman, 7, thesis 54 and following; Lord Speidel under the entries **Fish, Fishing** <note>original: *Fisch, Fischfang*</note>. All these things are to be judged according to the use and custom of each specific place.

---

(f) It is asked whether hunting is prohibited by right, so that a Prince can protect and maintain this prohibition with a clear conscience? I answer that it seems probable that the Princes who occupied a land by force reserved the right of hunting for themselves. Thus the Franks occupied all of Gaul and Alemannia and other German regions by force, and by the right of war reserved many rights for themselves—indeed, even the ownership of the estates. They left these to their subjects only by the law of colonies and enjoined upon the subjects various provisions of labor, such as **forced labor** <note>original: *Frohnen*; feudal corvée labor</note>, etc.
It is also asked whether hunting is a Sovereign Right? The objection is that even Nobles lacking Sovereign Rights have the right of hunting. I answer: it is not established that the simple right of hunting is a Sovereign Right, but rather the Law of the Forest, or forest jurisdiction—**forest jurisdiction** <note>original: *die forstliche Obrigkeit*</note>—which contains many things, such as the prohibition of hunting and protection.

# 1281
### On Sovereign Rights

-> de Regalibus <-

of the forests, the power of promulgating ordinances concerning the cutting of wood, the gathering of acorns, and regarding pastures—these are Sovereign Rights <note>original: *Regalia*</note>, and they are granted along with the territory.

An objection is raised: these rights are varied, therefore they are not Sovereign Rights, which are supposed to "cling to the bones" <note>An expression meaning rights that are inseparable from the person of the sovereign</note>. I respond: Nothing prevents certain Sovereign Rights from being different in different places, because even the nature of the greatest Sovereign Rights varies according to the different forms of Government.

VII. Furthermore, joining these Sovereign Rights are also the **Tolls** <note>original: *Vectigalia*</note>, which are commonly called *telonia* <note>original: *telonia*; Greek-derived term for customs houses or tax offices</note>. *See Title 56, "Which things are Sovereign Rights"; Code of Justinian, Law 6 on Tolls; Digest, Law 7, section "Publica" on the meaning of words; Digest, Law 10, beginning, on Tax Farmers and Tolls; the entire Title of the Code on Tolls, that new ones cannot be instituted. See also Bocer, chapter 2, number 187 and following; Einsiedel, chapter 2, number 228; Camman, dispute 11, thesis 47; Arnisæus on Majesty, chapter 7, number 4.* Therefore, it is not permitted for a Prince in his own Province, nor a Count, nor a Baron, nor the Senate of an Imperial City in its district, to institute new tolls or increase old ones without consulting the Emperor. *Mynsing, century 5, observation 27; Einsiedel, chapter 2, number 234.* And today, for the institution of new tolls, in addition to the Emperor’s authority, the consensus of the Prince-Electors is also required. **Imperial Recess of the year 1576, section "Furthermore we are also..."** <note>original: *Reichs-Abschied... Weiters seyn wir auch*; an Imperial Recess was the official summary of decisions made at an Imperial Diet</note>. *Einsiedel, cited location, number 231 and 236.* In the same way in the Kingdoms of France, England, Spain, Denmark, Poland, etc., this Sovereign Right has been restricted by the will of the High Nobility and the Estates of the Realm. *Dan. Otto, in his dissertation on public law, chapter 11, page 432; Camman, dispute 11, thesis 48.* This is to prevent a Prince from granting something due to improper pressure or petitions. Indeed, it is not even permitted to transfer tolls from one customary location to another if it prejudices the neighbors. *Petrus Fridericus, book 2 on Mandates, chapter 42; Bocer, chapter 2, number 195; Einsiedel 2, number 246.* And if some inferior official, without waiting for the Imperial promise, should institute a new toll by his own Law and Judgment, he is seen to incur the penalty for High Treason <note>original: *læsæ Majestatis*</note>, according to *Fridericus, Bocer, and Einsiedel at the cited location, number 238.*

VIII. Finally, the **Extraordinary Contribution** <note>original: *extraordinaria Collatio*</note>

<column-break/>

belongs here, which usually goes by the name of **Collections** <note>original: *Collectarum*</note>. This is done either for the most auspicious expedition of the Royal Person, or for another necessary and useful cause for the State. *Cited Title 56, book 2 of the Feuds.* This is commonly called an **Imperial Tax** <note>original: *Reichs-Steuer*</note> or **Imperial Levies** <note>original: *Reichs-Anlagen*</note>, and even the **Rome and Turk Expedition Tax** <note>original: *Römer- und Türcken-Zug*; taxes raised specifically for the Emperor's journey to Rome for coronation or for wars against the Ottoman Turks</note>. Different from these are the **Circle Taxes** <note>original: *Craiß-Steuer*</note>, which are commanded for the defense of several Imperial Circles or a single one. **Imperial Recess of the Year 1582, "besides and above such," and of the Year 1504, section "in the event."** There are also territorial or Provincial Collections, which the Estates of the Empire introduce for the particular necessity and utility of a territory, by virtue of the Sovereign Rights obtained from the Emperor; we call these **Land Taxes** <note>original: *Land-Steuer*</note>. *Camman, final dispute, thesis 65 and 76; Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 248; Arnisæus, final book, final chapter; Caspar Klock, treatise on Contributions, chapter 4; Bocer, chapter 3, number 210.*

IX. To this also belongs the **Fodder Contribution** <note>original: *Collatio Fodri*; Title 56, book 2 of the Feuds</note>, as well as **Billeting** <note>original: *Metata*</note> and **Hospitality Fees** <note>original: *Epidemetica*; Code of Justinian, book 12</note>. *Metata* are those things provided to arriving soldiers or others. *Epidemetica* are the prices by which one redeems oneself from the burden of taking in guests; Gothofredus calls this, in the common tongue, **Quartering** <note>original: *Einquartierung*</note> or **Quartering-Money** <note>original: *Quartier-Geld*</note>. Frederick also mentions this in the Constitution of the Peace of Constance, section "to us, however," in these words:
> To us, however, as we enter Lombardy, they shall provide the customary and Sovereign *Fodder* <note>original: *Fodrum*</note>, which they are accustomed and ought to provide.

And Emperor Conrad in his Constitution on Benefits, section "fodder," says: 
> We wish to have that *Fodder from the Castles* which our predecessors had; but that which they did not have, we in no way demand.

By that word (which descends from the German **Feed** <note>original: *Futter*</note>), is contained not only fodder for horses, but also grain and all things necessary for the sustenance of the Imperial army. *Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 350; Camman, final dispute, thesis 66.*

X. Not much different from the Sovereign Right just mentioned are the provisions of **Compulsory Transport** <note>original: *Angariarum*</note>,

See also Bocer, chapter 2, number 245; Einsiedel, chapter 3, number 220, etc.; and Camman, dispute 11, thesis 12 and following. 

The burden of compulsory transport <note>original: *angariarum*</note> corresponds with our German term **Compulsory Labor** <note>original: *Frohnen*</note>, which is to **perform common services**. From this also comes the term **Ember Days** <note>original: *Frohnfasten*; literally "Lord's Fasts," the four seasonal periods of fasting and prayer in the liturgical calendar</note>, which are sometimes called "Compulsory Services" <note>original: *Angariæ*</note>. Furthermore, the term **Frohn** <note>an archaic German word meaning "lordly" or "holy"</note> is the same as **Common** or **Public**; hence we have the terms **Corpus Christi** <note>original: *Frohn-Leichnam*; literally "The Lord's Body"</note>, **High Altar** <note>original: *Frohn-Altar*</note>, and **Holy Festival** <note>original: *Frohn-Fest*</note>. Supplementary transport services <note>original: *Parangariæ*</note>, however, are payments or services demanded in addition to the standard compulsory transport. 

Finally, whoever enjoys the Right to impose all such duties and burdens also has the power to grant immunity and vacation from them. See Law 1 and the entire Title of the *Digest* on censuses; and the entire Title of the *Code* on immunities that no one may grant, Book 10; and the single law (where the Glossary is found) in the *Code* regarding those who have received an exemption from the Prince. See also Carlos Tapia on the Title of the *Digest* concerning the Constitutions of the Prince, chapter 4, number 30; Vasquius on succession and creation, section 26, number 81; and Camman, dispute 4, thesis 96 and following. However, if such an exemption tends toward the prejudice or harm of others, it is by no means to be approved.

# CHAPTER X and last.
## ON SOVEREIGN RIGHTS CONCERNING WAR AND MILITARY PREPARATIONS.

### I.
To these Sovereign Rights (which are likewise proper to Majesty) belongs the power of declaring War (specifically offensive war, for defensive war is permitted by nature), of holding a draft, and of preparing an army. See Law 3, section "The Same" in the *Digest* on the Julian Law of Treason; Law 17 in the *Code* on military affairs, Book 12; the Canon Law "What is blamed," section "The order however," question 1; and the Canon "Julianus," question 3; and the Ordinances of the Imperial Chamber, part 2, title

<column-break/>

15, in these words: **By the Imperial Majesty, or our grant and permission.** Also the Recess of the Imperial Diet of Augsburg in the year 1555, the section **But where beyond this**, to be read with the following. See Bocer on the *Law of War*, book 1, chapter 5; Einsiedel, chapter 2, number 34 and following; Arnisæus, book 2 on *Majesty*, chapter 5, number 1 and following; and Camman, dispute 5, thesis 48 and following. 

Consequently, the Estates of the Empire <note>The Princes, Electors, and Cities that held a seat in the Imperial Diet</note> do not have the license to wage war by their own regular and proper authority. For it would provide a very ready occasion to weaken the authority of the Imperial Majesty and to entangle the Empire in civil wars if everyone were permitted to seek justice for themselves everywhere with an armed hand. *Einsiedel, in the place cited, number 40.* 

Just as the Right not to initiate an armed war is a Greater Sovereign Right; so also that consequence (which in German is called **The Following, Mustering, and Selection** <note>original: *Folg, Musterung, Auswahl*</note>; see Lord Speidel under the terms **Following and Journey**, etc., by which subjects are bound to follow the Prince if he initiates a war or if one is initiated against him) is considered to be of the same legal status. See Knichen on the *Saxon law of non-appeal*, under the word "Dukes of Saxony," chapter 5, number 310; and on the *Law of Territory*, chapter 3, number 352. 

In this view, in the Title *Which things are Sovereign Rights*, **Armories** <note>original: *Armandiæ*</note> are also joined to Sovereign Rights; and by that word is understood the right of having factories for war weapons and public arsenals, which is considered to belong to the Prince alone. See the entire Title of the *Code* regarding factory workers; *Novella 85* on arms; Einsiedel, chapter 2, number 257; Camman, 5, thesis 64 and following; Clapmar, book 2, chapter 6; and Arnisæus, book 2 on *Majesty*, chapter 5, numbers 2 and 7.

### II.
Related to these is the Right of fortifying a City and erecting fortresses. *Camman, 5, thesis 67; Arnisæus, book 2, chapter 5, number 8; Lord Speidel under the word **Fortress**.* And thus King Stephen of England, so that he might show himself more indulgent to his subjects and at the same time better fortify himself against Henry II, had granted his subjects the power of raising and fortifying Castles in each of their territories; however, he soon repented of his liberality when he found them to be made more stubborn because of it. *William of Malmesbury in the "New History."* 

Nevertheless, for those of lower rank or the Estates of the Empire, it seems to be permitted for them to hold a draft and to look out for the security of themselves and their subjects by fortifying certain places (to which it may be permitted to flee in a time of hostile incursion)...

## Concerning Sovereign Rights.

...is mentioned. Einsiedel, chapter 2, *numbers 42 and following.* It is held, however, that the **Right of Opening** <note>original: *Jus aperiendi*, or *die Öffnung*</note> always belongs to the Emperor. Likewise, the fruits of war—namely occupied places and whatever else victory provides—belong to the one under whose auspices the war was conducted; that is, to the Majesty. See the chapter on military law, at the end, and the gloss there on the phrase "the Prince’s portion," distinction 1; and the gloss on the chapter "let him say," on the word "all," question 5, case 23.

III. **Reprisals** <note>original: *Repressaliæ*; a legal recourse where a state allowed its citizens to seize the property of a foreign nation's citizens to compensate for a debt or injury</note> **rest upon the same logic as war.** This is because in war even the innocent are struck so that their Lord may be driven to do justice; the same occurs in reprisals, and thus they are considered a "small war." Therefore, the right to grant them belongs to the Majesty. Einsiedel 2, number 248. Camman 5, thesis 68. These consist of compensation for an injury or damage caused by a foreigner, whereby we detain the people or things of that same place if their Superior refuses to administer justice. Rudinger, Century 4, observation 32, number 1.

IV. **And finally, the right to end wars that have been started by making peace and to withdraw again from arms** is correctly established by the Doctors as a **Major Sovereign Right** <note>original: *Regale majus*; these are the essential rights of a ruler that cannot be separated from the crown</note>. Bodin, final chapter, book 1. P. Gregory 11, *On the Republic*, 13, number 3. Arnisæus, *On Majesty*, chapter 5, number 14. The Prince can also, in such a case, remit damages inflicted upon private citizens for the sake of the public good. Camman, cited location, thesis 73.

->*A Stimulus for the Gaping Page.*<-
<note>The following section is a "filler" (Suscitabulum), often used by early modern printers to fill empty space at the end of a section with academic praise or miscellaneous notes.</note>

During the disputation, Doctor J. A. was not **difficult** <note>original Greek: *dyskolos*</note> but **gentle and easy-going** <note>original Greek: *eukolos*</note>. Aristotle, *Topics*, book 8. This is certainly rare in great minds, who often cannot endure sharp debaters, especially if they oppose them with persistence. But this man of ours, with such mildness and tolerance, very patiently listened to all who often disputed in a most immodest and hateful manner. He responded most calmly and instructed them with such mildness and incredible courtesy that he drew everyone into admiration of him. And indeed, this art of disputing is very difficult when combined with the highest Erudition, which is necessarily required; this is a gift belonging to few. For it often happens in practice

<column-break/>

that a man fails, even if his reason does not. And because it is not within everyone's power to dispute, as the saying goes, few are truly skilled in the discipline of disputation. Augustine, *Sermon 38 on the Words of the Lord*. Nazianzen. Augustine, *Soliloquies*, book 2, chapter 14. But for this most practiced man, it was not difficult; it was easy, and this great gift of God seemed almost innate to him. He was able to untie **Gordian knots** <note>referring to solving incredibly complex problems</note> so effectively that nothing could seem so intricate or so involved that he could not easily unravel it and make it clear. In the *Life of J. A., page 340 and following.* It is recorded of Julius Caesar that he joined battle with the enemy fifty times. Authors report something similar about Emperor Henry, the fourth of that name, that he engaged with the enemy sixty-two times. Our leader here has engaged in battles not fewer in number, but far more, with various adversaries, and he emerged superior and victorious, relying on and using the **sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.** However, these Ecclesiastical contests are far more beautiful than those others, since they are for the most part bloodless. Let me be permitted to imitate Socrates; just as he said he performed the duty of a midwife <note>Socrates famously compared his method of questioning to midwifery, helping others "give birth" to the truth</note> and drew out the truth by questioning and doubting, so I will perhaps help you in your labor by moving and seeking, lest you give birth to some "abortion of novelty." Philippus Carolus, formerly a Professor at Altdorf and later the Imperial Librarian at Vienna, in his *Taste of Philology*. Keslerus once wrote a *Method of Disputation*. Let us abstain from unnecessary disputations concerning God and divine matters. For here too one must hold the **middle way** <note>original Greek: *mese*</note> between those who completely condemn disputations on religion, such as Bodin, and those who admit them indiscriminately. Most recently, Johann Ludwig Prasch in his *Notes on the Politics of Justus Lipsius, book 1, page 31.* On the utility of disputations, see Limnæus, *Public Law, book 8, chapter 6, numbers 71, 74, and volume 1, Additions to book 7, chapter 6, number 71*; and there Ærodius is cited, *On Judged Matters, book 10, title 19, chapter 2, page 965.* For a responsive letter in which a Teacher thanks a Student for the dedication of an Academic Exercise, see Mr. Rupert in his *Epistolary Mercury, page 200 and following.* He also provides excellent formulas for Dedications.

...prohibits, in the praised treatise on pages 391 to 395. We read concerning Thomas Erastus <note>a 16th-century Swiss physician and theologian</note>, the Physician and Philosopher, that he himself wonderfully extolled Academic Disputations for the sake of exercising both discovery and judgment, and for strengthening the nerves of the intellect. He even said that he had never been present at any Disputation from which he did not perceive a fruit that was not to be regretted. One who holds two lectures is bound to dispute twice, according to the Gloss on the canon "Sanctorum," distinction 2; this is brought up by Felinus regarding one practicing two arts, because such a person is held to the burdens of both in offerings and similar matters, as noted by Carpzovius, *Decisions*, part 2, decision 194, number 21. Should the disputations of witness testimonies <note>original: *attestationum*</note> be abolished? Carpzovius, decision 42, number 2. The judge can alter, restrict, or extend the deadline fixed for proposing the Disputations of witnesses according to the reason and state of the case, as well as the status of the litigants, *ibid.* number 5. Through disputing and opposing, the truth emerges more clearly, according to the final law, section "mixta," in the Digest *On Duties and Honors*. And opposites placed next to each other shine more brightly, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, whom Cornelius refers to in Counsel 5, volume 3. Jacob Thomingius, decision 27, number 5. And just as spices <note>original: *aromata*</note> smell more strongly and fragrant the more they are crushed, so the truth, the more it is ground and attacked, the more splendidly it moves forward into the light once the clouds have been driven away. Castro, Counsel 23, "aroma usually," in volume 1. Cravetta, counsels 135, 202, and 988. Thus Baldus said not inelegantly: "He opens a way with iron, who climbs through opposition." Baldus on the law "precibus," Code *On minors and other substitutions*. Klock, in *Counsels*, volume 2, counsel 16, numbers 1, 2, and 3. Regarding the manner of disputing in England, one should see Mr. G. Richter in his *Select Letters*, page 23, there: He carefully noted the manner of disputing at Cambridge <note>original: *Cantabrigiae*</note>, where first of all they

<column-break/>

pronounce the conclusion in formal words. "Therefore, you are mistaken." Only then do they begin to prove the propositions, which custom is also observed in other places in England. For the custom at Paris <note>original: *Lutetiae*</note>, see page 25, there: In the College of the Sorbonnists <note>The Sorbonne</note>, a learned monk disputed for the degree of Bachelor in Theology, a manner of disputing which he had previously known as described by Sleidanus in book 3 of his *History*. A rule between Richter and Johann Baptist Cromfilem is mentioned in Richter’s *Select Letters*, page 24. Concerning judicial quarrels: <note>The following section is translated from the original German legal phrasing regarding court settlements.</note> The judge of the first instance shall apply himself to settle the parties in doubtful matters—not only before the beginning of the legal state and Joinder of Issue <note>original: *Litis Contestation*; the formal start of a trial</note>, but also in any part of the judgment—through all suitable means and ways, including amicable reminders, in order to prevent all extensive and costly legal proceedings. However, before he proposes a settlement to the parties, he must inform himself well in the matter, and always carefully direct his aim in these amicable settlements so that a party conducting a publicly unjust case is not permitted to continue it, nor is the party who is in the right burdened by it, nor is justice delayed against the will of the other party. Recess of the Empire <note>original: *Recess. Imp.*</note>, Year 1654, section "secondly the judge of the first instance shall." In this, the Emperor and the States of the Empire undoubtedly looked back to the first law of the Digest *On Transactions* and the second law of the Code on the same, as well as the requirements of a transaction to be seen in Gailius, book 2, observation 70, number 12. More may be found in Justus Oldekop in the treatise *On the Oath in the Soul of Another*, page 22. Concerning those who multiply legal fees <note>original: *sportulas*</note> along with lawsuits, see page 5. More things were said regarding Disputations above, under the letter D. Now, with the help of the good God, I take my hand from the tablet <note>original: *manum de Tabula*; a traditional phrase meaning the work is finished</note>.

*Let the Poet sing with a grander quill*
*The sacred monuments of the divine laurel,*
*With which you aid the labors of our <term>Themis</term> <note>the Greek goddess of Justice and Law</note>*

*And various cares.*
*Live as the glory of both the Muses and Justice,*
*Live; publish many similar treatises polished*
*By your zeal, and may favorable*
*Apollo look kindly upon you!*

### ABBOT. ABBESS. ABBEY.

Mendicant orders <note>Religious orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans who relied on charity</note> do not have an Abbot, but rather a Prior or a Guardian. Page 5. Number 11.
Abbots are named among the Leaders or Nobles. In the same place.
Which Abbots shine with the highest dignity? In the same place.
— By what other titles they were distinguished by the Emperors. In the same place.
Concerning the Abbot of Kempten <note>original: "Campidonensi"</note>. page 6. a.
Abbots formerly held "both swords" <note>A medieval legal concept where a leader held both spiritual (religious) and material (secular/legal) power over their territory</note>. In the same place.
By whom and in what manner an Abbess is to be elected. In the same place.
— What kind of jurisdiction Abbots have over their Monks. In the same place.
An Abbess alone cannot act to the detriment of the Convent. In the same place.
Abbesses today hold jurisdiction. In the same place.
Whether an Abbess can grant benefices with the care of souls <note>A "benefice curata" is a church office that involves direct spiritual ministry to a parish</note>. In the same place.
Whether anyone can be the Abbot of two monasteries. In the same place.
Concerning exempt Abbots <note>Abbots whose monasteries were "exempt" from the local Bishop's authority, reporting directly to the Pope</note>. p. 276. a.
— Whether the investigation of criminal and matrimonial cases belongs to an exempt Abbot. In the same place.
Abbots who are presented by kings and appointed by the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> are in truth "Greater Prelates," since they have immediate Episcopal jurisdiction. p. 379. b.

### ABBREVIATIONS.

Abbreviations of words in legal instruments are to be avoided. p. 1. a.
— Those to be promoted to Bachelor status should be those who can read Abbreviations. In the same place. b.

### ALPHABET-LEARNER.

An alphabet-learner <note>original: "Abecedarius"; one learning the basics of reading or the fundamentals of a subject</note>. p. 74. n. 125.

### ABORTION.

# INDEX OF THINGS AND WORDS

-> A. <-

- Whether the duty on wine <note>original: "Datia vini"</note> is a royal prerogative. p. 1083. a.
- Whether the Excise Tax <note>original: "Accisa"</note> can be increased. in the same place.

### ACQUISITIONS <note>original: "Acquæstus" — Assets acquired during a marriage</note>

Property which someone receives from a father, or from paternal goods during a marriage, does not count toward acquired assets <note>Assets gained during the marriage to be shared between spouses</note>, if received not by title of inheritance, but by donation in contemplation of future inheritance. p. 953 n. 85.
- Things that would have otherwise come through succession are not considered acquired assets. in the same place.
- Property acquired through the work and industry of only one spouse, and not both, is not included among the communicable assets acquired during marriage according to a dowry pact or statute. in the same place.
- Whether things acquired through a donation between living persons <note>original: "inter vivos"</note> or by another lucrative title belong to marital acquisitions? in the same place. b.
- To acquire is the same as to gain. in the same place.
- Whether a wife has ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> or possession regarding acquired assets. p. 954. a.
- According to common law, all things acquired during a marriage belong to the husband who acquires them, not the wife. in the same place.
What comes under the name of "Conquest" and "Acquisition." <note>original: "Conquæstus & Acquæstus"</note> in the same place.
- Where more on this matter can be found. in the same place.

### RIGHT OF ACCRETION <note>original: "Accrescendi jus"</note>

The right of accretion <note>The legal right of a beneficiary to take the share of another beneficiary who cannot or will not take theirs</note> generally does not take place after an acquisition is made or a benefit is sought by another. p. 352. b.
- However, it does apply during the process of acquiring. in the same place.
Whether the right of accretion holds in an ancient fief. <note>original: "feudo antiquo"</note> in the same place.

### ACTS <note>original: "Acta" — Legal records and court documents</note>

What are judicial acts? <note>original: "Acta judicialia"</note> p. 349. n. 40.
By judicial acts are understood those things entered into public records. in the same place.
Judicial acts have perpetual and public authority. in the same place.
- Even if the judge who heard the case has died or been removed, the Acts establish a matter of public record from which the sentence is declared. in the same place. b.
If the acts of a lower court <note>original: "prioris instantiæ"</note> are unfit and incomplete, the entire process and the acts, with the evidence reserved, are usually quashed in the Chamber <note>Referring to the Imperial Chamber Court, the high court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. in the same place.
How acts are to be published. in the same place.
Acts are also generally judged to be such when something is done by the authority of a judge in any place, even outside of court. in the same place.
- Whether legal opinions <note>original: "Consilia"</note> are part of the Acts. p. 877. a.

### ACTION <note>original: "Actio" — A lawsuit or legal claim</note>

An action for injuries <note>original: "Actio injuriarum" — a lawsuit for defamation or physical insult</note> inflicted on the occasion of a pending lawsuit cannot be initiated until the lawsuit is finished. p. 626. a. see Injury.

### ACTUARY <note>original: "Actuarius" — A court clerk or registrar</note>

Concerning his office. p. 351. n. 43.
- When he may correct an error and supply what was omitted. in the same place.

### THE ACT <note>original: "Actum"</note>

"The act" denotes the completion of a legal instrument and its publication. p. 13. n. 17.

<column-break/>

### ACTS <note>original: "Actus" — Voluntary conduct or legal deeds</note>

One should not presume from our voluntary acts anything that is not necessarily concluded by them. p. 270. b. p. 618. b.
Whether an act already begun in one territory can be continued in another. p. 754. n. 4.
Prejudice is not inferred against the doer from a voluntary act. p. 310.

### ADAM

Adam. p. 74. n. 12.

### ADMIRAL

Concerning his duty. p. 36. n. 5.

### TO LEASE REVENUES <note>original: "Admodiare"</note>

Whether it is useful for officials to lease out <note>original: "admodiire"</note> the revenues and fines <note>original: "Gefälle und Frevel"</note>. p. 36. n. 5.
- The formula for leasing revenues. in the same place.

### ADOPTION

Concerning the adoption of the ancients. p. 45. n. 7.
Concerning adoption by the hair <note>original: "per capillum" — a ritual where the adopter cut the child's hair to symbolize a new family bond</note>. in the same place.
Concerning adoption by baptism <note>The spiritual kinship formed between godparents and godchildren</note>. in the same place.
- In our customs, adoption occurs through marriage. in the same place.

### ADOPTED

An adopted son is called an heir and a legitimate successor. p. 623.

### ADULTERY

Whether in this crime the male should be punished more severely than the female. p. 227. n. 1.
Concerning the punishment for adultery. in the same place.
- Whether, if one party confesses, the one denying adultery can be punished. in the same place.
- For a wife to lose her dowry on account of adultery, it is not necessary for the adultery to be proved directly; conjectures are sufficient. in the same place.
- The punishment of adultery belongs to "high justice" <note>original: "merum imperium" — the power of capital punishment and high criminal jurisdiction</note>. p. 228. b.
What an adulteress loses according to civil law. in the same place.
- If it is accepted by statute or custom that the use or administration of paraphernal goods <note>Property belonging to a wife over and above her dowry</note> belongs to the husband, whether he gains these on account of the wife's adultery. p. 229. b.
- A wife is seen to be able to inflict a more serious injury on her husband than if she commits adultery. p. 230. a.
- Whether an adulterer can be a witness. p. 232. a.
- Concerning the punishment of adultery in France <note>original: "Gallia"</note>. in the same place.

### ADVOCACY <note>original: "Advocatia" — Often refers to the office of a 'Vogt' or protector of a church or territory</note>

Concerning hereditary advocacy. p. 272. n. 5.
- To whom the right of advocacy belongs. p. 505. n. 4.

### ADVOCATE <note>original: "Advocatus" — A lawyer or legal representative</note>

An advocate can seek a salary in all cases, which otherwise is not owed unless specifically agreed upon. p. 17. n. 2.
Advocates have dignity without a degree. in the same place.
The body of advocates is a nursery <note>original: "feminarium," likely a typo for "seminarium"</note> of dignities. in the same place.
- Their office is a public duty.

### BUILDING <note>original: "Aedificatio"</note>

Repair and restoration are more favored by the law than new construction. p. 92. n. 19.

# HEREDITARY LEASE.
<term>Emphyteusis: A type of long-term or perpetual land lease where the tenant is required to improve the property and pay a regular rent.</term>

# F.

### FACT.

The act of a superior is held to be a **fortuitous event** <note>original: "casu fortuito"; an act of God or an unavoidable accident.</note>. *p. 68 b.*
In an act of a university or college which all members do: if it is required that it be done harmoniously, it is understood as being done with no one disagreeing. *p. 220 n. 16.*
It is more to act by deed than by words. *p. 346. a.*
Law is situated in the fact and the cause. *p. 560 b.*
The whole weight of the matter consists in the fact. *ibid.*

### FALCONS.

Concerning fowling by means of **falcons**. *p. 287 n. 7.*
- It is an invention of the German Princes. *ibid.*

### REPUTATION.

Reputation <note>original: "Fama"</note> is not sufficient evidence for torture. *p. 351. n. 44.*
Common voice and reputation exclude the plea of ignorance. *p. 352. a.*

<column-break/>

### BED <note>original: "LECTUS"</note>.

An objection <note>original: "Exceptio"; a formal legal defense</note> based on a settlement <note>original: "transactionis"</note> is not considered in a possessory trial <note>original: "judicio possessorio"; a legal proceeding focused on who currently holds property rather than who has the ultimate legal title</note>, but is instead rejected. p. 1068. n. 15.
More on settlements, p. 1072. n. 19.

### THE PEACE OF PASSAU.
Whether the Peace of Passau <note>original: "Transactio Passaviensis"; the 1552 treaty between the Holy Roman Emperor and Lutheran princes which laid the groundwork for the Peace of Augsburg</note> is a Pragmatic Sanction <note>original: "Sanctio Pragmatica"; a fundamental law or decree issued by a sovereign</note>. p. 868. n. 76.

Addressing as "thou" <note>original: "Tuisatio"; the act of using the informal "tu" (thou) instead of the formal "vos" (you). In a status-conscious society, this could be a legal matter involving insult or social standing</note>. p. 477. n. 11.

### APPRENTICE.
If anyone gives someone over to be instructed in any art with a contract to stay with them for several years, and that person flees, they are bound to serve the time again for the full duration, or at least for as many days as they were absent. p. 643.

### VAGABOND.

### VASSAL.
A vassal <note>original: "Vasallus"; a person who held land from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty</note>, if he assaults the lord or makes an attack on the lord's castle or house while the lord and his wife are present, is deprived of his fief <note>original: "feudo"</note>. p. 74 n. 1

If a vassal <note>original: "vafallus", a common spelling variant of "vasallus"</note> leaves behind multiple heirs and the fief <note>original: "feudum"; land held under the feudal system</note> remains undivided, then not all of them are required to receive investiture and swear the oath; instead, they choose someone from their number to receive the investiture in their common name. p. 641. n. 38.

Doubtful words are considered to be uttered demonstratively <note>by way of example</note>, not restrictively. p. 1172 a.
Words of the past tense denote a completed act. p. 1172. n. 67.
Words of the present or past tense are extended to the future when they cannot be verified in the present. ib.

### TRUTH.

The truth of one thing excludes the truth of the other. p. 461. b.
One should not care what others have said, but rather what can be said based on the truth. p. 675. b.
When the truth of an insult excuses the person who insulted <note>a legal defense where proving an accusation is true may mitigate a charge of slander</note>. p. 1140. n. 85.
A presumption has no effect where the truth appears to the contrary. p. 1141.

### UNDERTAKER.

An undertaker <note>original: "Vespillio"</note> who kills and robs those infected by the plague is punished as a thief. p. 1046. b.

<column-break/>

Regarding the undertakers of the ancients. ib.

### CLOTHING.

When a husband dies before his wife, the appraised clothes remain to the widow, even those worn out by the wife afterward. p. 545. n. 67.
Clothes obtained not for decoration but for covering the body. ib.
Whether an infant is clothed in the family inheritance <note>original: "almodio," referring to allodial or freehold property rights</note>. p. 546. a.
On the seizure <note>original: "executione"</note> of clothing. ib.
Spring or summer clothes which are owed to household servants or bequeathed annually, how they are to be provided. ib.
A master can demand back clothes from a servant who leaves before his time. ib.
Whether mourning clothes <note>original: "vestes lugubres"</note> are owed to widows from the husband's estate. ib.

### OLD TESTAMENT.

Old Testament. p. 33. n. 51.

### BANNER.

The German nations used the ceremony of the banner <note>original: "vexilli"</note> in every solemn matter. p. 86. n. 8.
Among the Germans and Lombards, banners were used in the execution of criminal judgments to signify the power of the court. ib.
Regarding Banner-Lords <note>original: "Panier-Herren," a rank of nobility entitled to lead their own troops under their own banner</note>. ib.
"To wave the small banner over someone" <note>original: "das Fähnlein über einen schvvingen," likely a ritual or legal gesture</note>. p. 280. a.

### WAY (ROAD).

Which ones are called public roads. p. 583. n. 19.
On the overseers of roads. ib.
They are counted among the royal rights <note>original: "regalia"</note>. p. 584. a.
Their defense belongs to the Prince. ib.
Although a Noble might be enfeoffed with a castle and its territory, and granted both high and low jurisdiction <note>original: "mixtum & merum imperium"</note>, a public road is not understood as granted. ib.
Whether a Duke and others, to whom high and low jurisdiction has been granted by the Emperor, have jurisdiction over public roads. ib.
If a killing occurs on a public road, whose jurisdiction will it be: the Lord's, or the one who holds the fief there with high and low jurisdiction. ib.
Roads are the permanent boundaries of jurisdiction. p. 584. b.
When there is a dispute over the repair of a ruined road, who is bound to it, and what the law says. p. 1113. n. 22.
On the overseers of roads. ib.
On the treacherous concealment and blockade of public roads. p. 1114. n. 23.

### VICARS OF THE EMPIRE.

What kind of power the Vicars of the Empire <note>high-ranking princes who administered the Holy Roman Empire during an interregnum</note> have. p. 1081. n. 39.
Whether the absence of the Emperor also gives place to a Vicariate. ib.
On the controversy between the Elector Palatine and the Elector of Bavaria regarding the Vicariate. ib.

### VICE-LORD.

Who is a Vice-Lord <note>original: "Vicedominus," a deputy or administrative official</note>? p. 1082. n. 43.

# Index of Subjects & Words.

### NEIGHBOR. <note>original: "VICINUS"</note>

Whether a neighbor can be compelled to sell for the expansion of a nuns' garden and the enlargement of a monastery. <margin>p. 783. n. 60.</margin>
Many things are granted for the sake of neighborhood, even against common law. <margin>ibid.</margin>
A neighbor is not presumed to be ignorant of the actions of his neighbors. <margin>ibid.</margin>
A neighbor can do nothing out of rivalry and to the harm of a neighbor. <margin>ibid.</margin>
When there is talk of a neighbor, it is understood to include a neighbor who is not the closest. <margin>p. 783. b.</margin>
One may rightly argue from the custom of neighbors. <margin>ibid.</margin>
That which is observed in neighboring provinces must be observed here. <margin>ibid.</margin>

### PROVISIONS. <note>original: "VICTUALIA"</note>

Whether peasants <note>original: "rustici"</note> can be compelled to sell provisions. <margin>p. 1100. n. 97.</margin>
Provisions are to be taxed <note>meaning price-controlled</note> every year. <margin>ibid.</margin>

### VILLAGE. <note>original: "VICUS"</note>

Village or Street. <margin>p. 1121. n. 46.</margin>

### WIDOW. <note>original: "VIDUA"</note>

A widow retains the family, status, and privileges of her husband. <margin>p. 1129. n. 61.</margin>
The condition "if she shall be a widow" is fulfilled even if she does not remain a widow. <margin>p. 1129. b.</margin>
Concerning a widow's competent right of retention regarding her husband's goods. <margin>ibid.</margin>
Concerning the house of widowhood. <margin>p. 1130. n. 62.</margin>

### ESTATE. <note>original: "VILLA"</note>

An estate <note>original: "Villa"</note> contains within itself jurisdiction over the district, the right of patronage, and similar things. <margin>p. 73. b.</margin>

### BOND. <note>original: "VINCULUM"</note>

Two bonds bind more tightly than one. <margin>p. 1091. n. 72.</margin>
Where bonds are equal, the first holds, and the second does not create an obligation. <margin>ibid.</margin>

### VENGEANCE. <note>original: "VINDICTA"</note>

How the words "I will avenge myself" <note>original: "ego me vindicabo"</note> are to be understood. <margin>p. 880. n. 14.</margin>
Vengeance is to be taken not in the manner of wild beasts, but as right reason requires. <margin>ibid.</margin>
Concerning private vengeance. <margin>p. 993. n. 68.</margin>

### WINE. <note>original: "VINUM"</note>

Concerning new wine. <margin>p. 773. n. 36.</margin>
In last wills and testaments, "old wine" is understood to be two or three years old. <margin>ibid.</margin>
If it was not cautioned by the contracting parties that equally good wine should be returned, it is nonetheless not permitted for a debtor to return new wine for old. <margin>ibid.</margin>
A statute speaking of wine also applies to grapes and unfermented wine <note>original: "musto"</note>. <margin>p. 774. a.</margin>
Unfermented wine is properly called new wine. <margin>ibid.</margin>
More on wine. <margin>p. 1136. n. 76.</margin>

### VIRGIN. VIRGINITY. <note>original: "VIRGO. VIRGINITAS."</note>

Concerning the signs of violated and lost virginity. <margin>p. 493. n. 39.</margin>

<column-break/>

Under the name of "virgins," maidservants are also included.
Whether a virgin known [carnally] by force is permitted to wear a bridal wreath <note>original: "sertum"</note>.
Whether virginity can be proved by an oath. <margin>P. 4</margin>

### VISITATION. <note>original: "VISITATIO"</note>

When domestic visitation <note>inspection</note> in another person's house may take place. <margin>p. 415.</margin>
Searching in another's house is permitted even for the sake of public utility. <margin>P. 4</margin>

Concerning the annual visitations of pastors. <margin>p. 10</margin>
One visiting parents, brothers, or children in Universities <note>original: "Academiis"</note> does not enjoy their privileges.
A visitor ought to proceed plainly and summarily <note>meaning without the formalities of a full trial</note>.

More on glass. <margin>p. 391. n.</margin>

### SHADOW. <note>original: "UMBRA"</note>

Shadow. <margin>p. 1021. n</margin>

Unicorn. <margin>P. 241.</margin>

### THE COMMUNITY. <note>original: "UNIVERSITAS"</note>

Concerning the law of the community <note>original: "universatis," referring here to a legal corporation or municipality</note>. <margin>p. 28.</margin>
The community does not die.
Whether and to what extent it can commit a crime, and lose the right of protection because of a crime. <margin>p. 344.</margin>
Whether any group of people can form a community.
The community has jurisdiction in matters committed to it.
Concerning the common area of the community.
What the community owes, individuals do not owe <note>original: "Universitas quod debet, singuli non debent" — a fundamental rule of corporate liability</note>. <margin>p. 3</margin>

In acts of the community in which the group acts as a single entity, whether the consensus of the majority suffices. <margin>p. 9</margin>

He who wills one thing, wills all things without which that one thing cannot proceed. <margin>p. 2</margin>

### WILL. <note>original: "VOLUNTAS"</note>

The act itself is not the question, nor is the outcome of the act examined, but the will and the causes for acting are what is considered. <margin>p. 675. a.</margin>

### TRUCE-OATH. <note>original: "URPHEDA" — referring to the Germanic legal custom of 'Urfehde', a solemn oath where a released prisoner swore not to take revenge for their' imprisonment.</note>

### USUFRUCTUARY. <note>original: "USUFRUCTUARIUS" — A person who has the legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another, provided the property is not damaged.</note>

Whether a usufructuary may claim the fruits <note>profits or produce</note> for himself before providing security <note>original: "cautionem"</note>. <margin>p. 772. b.</margin>
Whether he can be compelled by the office of a judge to provide such security. <margin>ibid.</margin>
What a usufructuary's security bond ought to contain. <margin>p. 773.</margin>
Where more may be found regarding usufructuary security. <margin>ibid.</margin>
A usufructuary does not gain the fruits unless he has actually gathered them. <margin>ibid.</margin>
A usufructuary must provide every care for the property, including modest repairs. <margin>ibid.</margin>

### USURY. <note>original: "USURA" — The practice of lending money at interest, often scrutinized in historical law.</note>

Concerning usury and interest owed on grain, and regarding exemptions of rents paid in grain, barley, or wine. <margin>p. 1133. a.</margin>
Concerning maritime usury <note>interest on sea-loans, often higher due to the risk of shipwreck</note>. <margin>ibid.</margin>
Whether usury can be sought beyond double the original amount. <margin>ibid. b.</margin>
More on the matter of usury on page 1151. a. and page 1152.

### USAGE. <note>original: "USUS"</note>

Things destined for pious uses cannot be changed. <margin>p. 341. n. 25.</margin>
That which has a certain interpretation through long-standing usage ought not to be changed, and is to be understood as it has been received by custom. <margin>p. 368. b.</margin>

### UTILITY. <note>original: "UTILITAS"</note>

Many things have been introduced against the standard rules of law for the sake of public utility. <margin>p. 154. b.</margin>

### GRAPE. <note>original: "UVA"</note>

Whether and when it is permitted to eat grapes in another person’s vineyard. <margin>p. 1061. n. 52.</margin>

### WOUND. <note>original: "VULNUS"</note>

Concerning the magnetic curing of wounds. <note>This refers to "sympathetic" medicine popular in the 17th century, where a salve was applied to the weapon that caused the wound rather than the wound itself.</note> <margin>p. 56. a.</margin>

Regarding one who orders a wounding but expressly forbids that the person be killed; if the agent kills them regardless, how the one who gave the order is to be punished. <margin>ibid.</margin>

days—namely three or eight days—the wounded person dies. <margin>ibid.</margin>

### WIFE. <note>original: "UXOR"</note>

When a husband’s goods are confiscated, the wife can deduct and reclaim her dowry and wedding gifts from the treasury <note>original: "fiscum"</note>. <margin>p. 184. a.</margin>

Whether he who keeps an adulterous wife is a fool. <margin>p. 201. b.</margin>
Which are the primary and secondary wives? <margin>p. 234. n. 8.</margin>
A wife can indeed obligate herself on behalf of others without her husband's consent, yet in such a way that nothing shall be prejudiced against the husband's portion which he has or expects from their common business. <margin>p. 544. n. 65.</margin>

Whether women’s ornaments given to a wife by her husband remain the wife’s upon his death. <margin>ibid.</margin>
It is a shameful thing for wives to be afflicted with beatings. <margin>p. 700. b.</margin>
Whether a wife loses the profits acquired during the marriage on account of unchastity committed during her widowhood. <margin>p. 954. a.</margin>
If a wife renounces the profits even after the marriage is dissolved, she is not held liable for losses. <margin>ibid.</margin>
Whether a wife is permitted to leave her husband on account of his chastisement. <margin>p. 1116. n. 30.</margin>
Let the words and deeds of husbands be like a mirror to their wives, by looking into which they may form and compose their own manners. <margin>ibid. b.</margin>
A husband regularly cannot be sued on behalf of his wife, unless he has made himself liable for her. <margin>p. 1117. n. 31.</margin>
